questions.answerText:
(a)
• Menarche (usually 10-16 years) marks sexual maturity; the cycle averages 28 days and recurs from puberty until menopause.
• Follicular phase: FSH stimulates the primordial follicles, which secrete oestrogen; about 200,000 primordial follicles are present at birth and one matures each month.
• Rising oestrogen signals the hypothalamus to stop FSH; LH is produced and the follicle ruptures about the 14th day (ovulation).
• Luteal phase: begins at ovulation and ends when flow starts; the corpus luteum forms and progesterone stays high; if the ovum is not fertilized within 48 hours hormone levels drop and the endometrium sheds; if fertilized, the corpus luteum keeps secreting progesterone and oestrogen until the placenta takes over.
(b)
• Proliferative phase: begins when menstruation stops; first 2-3 days are repair (regenerative); ripening follicles secrete oestrogen under FSH and the endometrium thickens, ending with a basal layer, a functioning layer and a cuboidal ciliated epithelial layer; lasts until ovulation.
• Secretory phase: follows ovulation under progesterone and oestrogen; the corpus luteum increases thickening, the lining becomes softer and more vascular, ready for a fertilized ovum (about 3.5 mm).
• Menstrual phase: after about 14 days of corpus luteum without fertilization, progesterone and oestrogen fall suddenly; the functioning layer is shed and expelled by uterine muscle contraction; it lasts about 3-5 days with total blood loss of 50-100 mls; fibrinolysis prevents clotting.
• Menstrual blood contains endometrial lining, capillary blood, mucus and dead ovum; the secretory phase is fairly constant in length while the proliferative and menstrual phases may vary.
(c)
• Discomforts: headache and bloating (largely from smooth muscle relaxation caused by progesterone), heaviness of lower abdomen and legs, breast tenderness, sleepiness, nervous tension, irritability, depression, cravings, digestive disturbances, increased vaginal discharge and micturition; some women have full premenstrual syndrome and slight pelvic pain at ovulation (Mittelschmerz).
• Advice: analgesics, reduced sodium in the diet, avoiding caffeine and stress, walking, emotional support and heat therapy; in severe cases refer to a physician.
(d)
• Proliferative phase: before ovulation, driven by oestrogen under FSH, endometrium repairs and thickens, length may vary.
• Secretory phase: after ovulation, driven by progesterone and oestrogen, endometrium becomes softer and more vascular, length is more or less constant.
questions.question:
Describe the menstrual cycle under the following headings:
(a) The ovarian cycle (follicular and luteal phases) and the hormones involved.
(b) The phases of the uterine cycle and the endometrial changes in each.
(c) Explain the clinical basis for the minor discomforts some women experience around menstruation and the nursing advice that relieves them.
(d) Distinguish between the proliferative phase and the secretory phase.

Describe breast self-examination (BSE) under the following headings:
(a) Definition and purpose.
(b) Timing.
(c) The steps of the procedure.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and the recommended practice.
(e) Explain the rationale behind the key steps and the abnormal findings that require medical attention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• BSE is a screening method in which the woman looks at and feels each breast for lumps, distortions or swelling, to detect breast cancer early when it is more likely to be treated successfully.
• It is essential especially combined with regular physical exams and mammography; about 20% of breast cancers are detected by physical examination rather than mammography.
(b)
Immediately after menstruation from day 5; for post-menopausal women on a fixed date every month; done once a month.
(c)
• Step 1: inspect both breasts in a mirror with shoulders straight and arms on hips (usual size, shape, colour, even shape).
• Steps 2 and 3: raise the arms and look for the same changes; look for fluid (watery, milky, yellow or blood) from one or both nipples.
• Step 4: lying down, use the opposite hand with finger pads flat and together in quarter-sized circles covering collarbone to abdomen and armpit to cleavage.
• Palpation pattern: start at the nipple in larger circles or use up-and-down rows; light pressure for skin, medium for middle tissue, firm for deep tissue down to the ribcage; Step 5: repeat standing in the shower.
(d)
• Nursing responsibilities: teach all women to routinely perform BSE monthly as part of overall screening; combine with clinical breast examination and mammography.
• Clinical examination every 3 years at age 20-39 and annually from 40; mammography every 1-2 years after 40 and annually after 50.
(e)
• Doing it monthly familiarizes the woman with how her breasts normally look and feel.
• Seek medical attention for dimpling, puckering or bulging of skin; change in nipple position or inversion; redness, soreness, rash or swelling.
• Covering the entire breast and all tissue depths ensures no lump is missed.

(a)
Periods stopped for 12 months; hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, low libido, depression, anxiety, mood swings, nausea, weight gain, brain fog, hair loss, lack of energy.
(b)
Menopause: a natural part of ageing, diagnosed once periods have stopped for 12 months; it ends the reproductive period and leads to infertility.
(c)
Caused by depletion of hormones (oestrogen, FSH, testosterone, progestogen); ovarian hormones are gradually withdrawn and ovulation ceases; the change is rapid, causing numerous symptoms.
(d)
• Health counselling to seek natural approaches; laboratory blood investigation if needed; hormone replacement therapy (oestrogen and progestogen); cognitive behavioural therapy; antidepressants or antihypertensives where indicated.
• Natural measures: healthy lifestyle, regular exercise, relaxing activities (tai chi, yoga, deep breathing), natural supplements, bioidentical hormones from plant sources.
(e)
• Health education: early onset may follow removal of uterus or ovaries, poor diet or excessive drinking; discuss that menopause leads to infertility.
• Evaluation: relief of symptoms.
questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman whose periods stopped 12 months ago complains of hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, low libido, mood swings and anxiety.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnosis/problem.
(c) Explain the physiological basis.
(d) List the priority nursing interventions.
(e) Outline health education and evaluation.

Describe infertility under the following headings:
(a) Definition and types (primary and secondary).
(b) Causes in females and in males.
(c) Diagnostic tests.
(d) Explain the clinical basis of why some couples are at higher risk (age, lifestyle and other risk factors).
(e) Distinguish between primary and secondary infertility.
questions.answerText:
(a)
WHO defines infertility as a disease of the reproductive system with failure to achieve clinical pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected intercourse; about 50 million couples are affected worldwide.
(b)
• Female causes: uterine abnormalities, endocrine dysfunction (pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, ovarian), pelvic inflammatory disease, cervical stenosis or poor mucus, fallopian tube blockage from STIs, Turner syndrome, fibroids, PCOS, severe anaemia, anxiety, malnutrition.
• Male causes: undescended testis, congenital abnormalities, testicular obstruction, mumps orchitis, prostatitis, absent or obstructed vas deferens, abnormal spermatogenesis or motility, sexual dysfunction (retrograde ejaculation, erectile dysfunction), smoking, alcohol, heat, marijuana.
(c)
Tests: history, physical examination, semen analysis (abstain 2-3 days, collect all ejaculate, analyse within 1 hour), post-coital test, ultrasound, endometrial biopsy, hysterosalpingography, hysteroscopy, laparoscopy; hormone and ovulation tests; cervical mucus test.
(d)
• Risk factors in both sexes: age, tobacco, marijuana, alcohol, being overweight or underweight, exercise issues; women's chances decrease with age and fertility issues are common over 35.
• In Nigeria, social and cultural pressure on motherhood leads affected couples to seek treatment, sometimes with abuse; the prevalence of infertility is highest in South East Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa.
• Clomiphene: an anti-estrogen that blocks oestrogen receptors at the hypothalamus and pituitary, increasing FSH to stimulate follicles (used to restore ovulation).
• Treatment depends on cause: medical, surgical (lysis of adhesions, septoplasty, tuboplasty, myomectomy), and assisted reproductive technologies (IUI, IVF, GIFT, ZIFT, ICSI, cryopreservation).
(e)
• Primary infertility: a couple has never achieved pregnancy despite 12 months of regular unprotected sex (or a woman unable to ever bear a child, including pregnancies ending in miscarriage or stillbirth without live birth).
• Secondary infertility: a couple has achieved pregnancy before but fails to achieve another after 12 months; it includes repeated miscarriage or stillbirth after a previous ability to carry to a live birth.
• Prevalence: secondary infertility 10.5% of women, primary 2%.
• Complications of treatment: multiple pregnancy (risk of premature labour) and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

questions.question:
A primigravida at term arrives in the labour ward. Findings: contractions every 10 minutes, strong and rhythmic, with a blood-stained mucoid discharge; vaginal examination shows the cervix dilating progressively; fetal heart rate is 120-160 beats per minute on hourly checks; the head is palpably high at the pelvic brim.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and the points that require escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Regular strong contractions with progressive cervical dilatation and show are true signs of labour; progressive dilatation is a definite sign.
• Show is blood-stained mucus from the operculum as the cervix dilates; blood comes from the detached chorion.
• Fetal heart rate of 120-160 beats per minute is the normal range.
• Latent phase lasts until 3-4 cm and may last 6-8 hours in a primigravida; the active phase runs from 3-4 cm to 10 cm at about 1 cm per hour.
(b)
• False labour (spurious labour): erratic irregular contractions without retraction, short, not increasing in intensity, relieved by walking, pain felt in the abdomen alone, common in primigravidae.
• Rupture of membranes can occur days before labour, so it is not a true sign; fluid can be tested with a Nitrazine swab (orange to navy blue if amniotic fluid).
(c)
• Rationale: hourly fetal heart recording in graph form; do not auscultate during a contraction because it can alter the rate.
• Escalate: a drop of 20 beats below or above the normal rate, thready pulse (may indicate pre-eclampsia), or a head that stays persistently high should be reported to the doctor.
• Bandl's ring (a retraction ring seen or felt per abdomen) is a sign of obstructed labour.

questions.question:
Describe the procedure for abdominal examination of the antenatal client under the following headings:
(a) Aims and preparation.
(b) Inspection.
(c) Palpation (fundal height, fundal, lateral and pelvic palpation) and auscultation.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice points to observe during the examination.
(e) Explain the rationale for each key step, including what deviations from the expected findings may indicate.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Aims: observe signs of pregnancy, assess fetal growth and health, detect deviations and locate fetal parts. Preparation: bladder emptied, supine with one pillow, arms by sides, screen drawn, relaxed hands.
(b)
Inspection: note size (should match gestation), shape (longitudinally ovoid), fetal movement, pigmentation, scars, striae, muscle quality and contour (dome-shaped normal; pendulous in multigravidae).
(c)
• Fundal height: estimate in finger breadths below the xiphisternum, or use McDonald's technique with a tape from the symphysis pubis (more accurate 20-31 weeks).
• Fundal palpation identifies the part in the fundus; lateral palpation locates the fetal back and limbs; pelvic palpation (Pawlik's grip when the head is not engaged) identifies the presentation, engagement and disproportion.
• Auscultation: Pinard's stethoscope over the fetal back while feeling the maternal pulse; fetal heart about 140 beats per minute.
(d)
• Hands must be clean and warm (cold hands induce abdominal muscle contraction); use the pads, not the tips, of the fingers, moving smoothly without sudden pressure; talk to the patient to aid relaxation.
• All information obtained must be considered together in making the diagnosis; if any information does not correspond, repeat and think again.
(e)
• Size: if dates are correct but the uterus is large, consider multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, a large fetus or a fetus plus fibroid.
• Shape: round suggests multiparity, transverse lie, obesity or polyhydramnios; depression at the umbilical level suggests occipito-posterior position.
• Fundal palpation: a breech in the fundus (95% of cases) denotes cephalic presentation; head in the fundus denotes breech presentation.
• Pelvic palpation is the most important manoeuvre because it diagnoses presentation, engagement and head-pelvis disproportion; engagement means the widest diameter has passed the pelvic brim.
• Fetal movement shows the fetus is alive; the back lies on the side opposite the movement; head fitting is assessed from 36 weeks because the pelvic capacity must be assessed.

questions.question:
Describe exclusive breastfeeding and the Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) under the following headings:
(a) Definition of exclusive breastfeeding and the types of breastfeeding.
(b) The aims of BFHI and the ten steps to successful breastfeeding.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities and the recommended practice.
(d) Explain the rationale for the steps and the consequences of deviation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• EBF: only breast milk is given for the first six months, no other liquids or solids, not even water, except ORS or drops/syrups of vitamins, minerals or medicines; continue breastfeeding with complementary foods up to 2 years or beyond.
• Other types: expressed breast milk feeding, partial (mixed) feeding, bottle-feeding, predominant, full, token breastfeeding and exclusive formula feeding.
(b)
• BFHI was launched in 1991 by WHO and UNICEF after the 1990 Innocenti declaration; aims to improve care of pregnant women, mothers and newborns and protect, promote and support breastfeeding.
• Steps 1-5: written policy communicated to all staff; train staff; inform pregnant women of benefits and management; help mothers initiate breastfeeding within one hour; show mothers how to breastfeed and maintain lactation even if separated.
• Steps 6-10: no food or drink other than breast milk unless medically indicated; rooming in 24 hours; breastfeeding on demand; no pacifiers or artificial nipples; foster support groups and refer mothers on discharge.
(c)
• Initiate breastfeeding within 30 minutes to one hour of birth with early skin-to-skin contact; feed on demand day and night; maintain eye contact and interaction.
• Working mothers can express milk into a clean covered cup: room temperature 7 hours, refrigerator 24 hours, deep freezer 7 days (another slide says not longer than six hours unless refrigerated).
• Advise mothers to eat a healthy diet rich in protein, carbohydrate, vitamins A and B, calcium and zinc and to take plenty of fluids; prepare the nipples from about 30 weeks.
(d)
• Babies should not be given water because of the misconception that breast milk alone cannot meet water needs; in Nigeria most mothers give water, and in 2015 Nigeria had the lowest EBF rate (17%) in Africa.
• The more the baby suckles, the more milk is produced; if a baby stops sucking the breast stops making milk.
• Pacifiers and artificial nipples, and non-milk feeds, deviate from policy; myths (figure sagging, milk going sour) militate against breastfeeding but are untrue.
• EBF reduces infant morbidity and mortality, reduces cot death and obesity risk, protects the mother against pregnancy and ovarian cancers, and spaces pregnancies.

questions.question:
Describe the placenta under the following headings:
(a) Development and structure at term.
(b) Functions (including hormones).
(c) Anatomical variations and diseases.
(d) Explain the clinical basis for the significance of selected variations (why some pose risk).
(e) Distinguish between the fetal and maternal surfaces of the placenta.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The placenta originates from the trophoblast, forming chorionic villi that are most profuse in the decidua basalis (chorion frondosum); villi float in a lake of maternal blood.
• At term: round, flat, about 20 cm in diameter and 2.5 cm thick at the centre, weighing about one sixth of the baby's weight.
(b)
• Functions: respiratory, nutritive (selects nutrients, stores glycogen), excretory, endocrine, storage (glycogen, vitamins A and D, iron), protective (but some bacteria, viruses and drugs cross).
• HCG maintains the corpus luteum (detected about 30 days, peaks at 60-80 days); progesterone relaxes smooth muscle (from about the 3rd month); oestrogen from the 6th week (urinary oestriol indicates fetal well-being); HPL aids breast growth and metabolism.
(c)
• Variations: succenturiate lobe, circumvallate, battledore and velamentous cord insertion, bipartite/tripartite, placenta accreta, placenta fenestrata, vasa praevia.
• Diseases: hydatidiform mole, calcareous degeneration, infarcts, oedematous placenta (hydrops fetalis), syphilitic placenta.
(d)
• Succenturiate lobe: if retained may lead to PPH; placenta accreta: separation becomes impossible.
• Velamentous insertion: vessels in membranes may separate during active management of the third stage.
• Vasa praevia: vessels across the os can tear when membranes rupture, causing severe fetal haemorrhage, suspected when bleeding coincides with membrane rupture.
• Infarcts occur in pre-eclampsia, essential hypertension and prolonged pregnancy; IgG gives immunity for the first 3 months.
(e)
• Fetal surface: smooth, whitish, shiny, covered by amnion and chorion with the cord at the centre and vessels radiating.
• Maternal surface: rough, bluish-red, 20 cotyledons separated by sulci, gritty lime deposits of no clinical significance.

questions.question:
Describe the signs of pregnancy under the following headings:
(a) Presumptive signs.
(b) Probable signs.
(c) Positive signs, including the methods used to confirm them.
(d) Explain why presumptive and probable signs cannot confirm pregnancy, naming the conditions that can mimic them.
(e) Distinguish between probable signs and positive signs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Presumptive signs suggest but do not positively indicate pregnancy: amenorrhoea (4 weeks), early morning sickness (4-14 weeks), bladder irritation (6-12 weeks), tiredness.
• Skin changes from melanocyte stimulating hormone: hyperpigmentation, chloasma, striae gravidarum and linea nigra.
• Breast changes from about the 4th week: tenderness, fullness, increased vascularity; nodular at 6-8 weeks; darker and wider areola by 12 weeks, prominent nipples, colostrum, Montgomery tubercles; quickening at 16-20 weeks.
(b)
• Probable signs are strong indicators but do not confirm: darker vulva; purplish soft vagina (Jacquemier's sign) and increased pulsation at the lateral fornices (Osiander's sign, about 8 weeks); soft, purplish cervix with increased secretion and operculum.
• Uterine signs: Braxton Hicks contractions, uterine souffle (8-10 weeks), Hegar's sign (6-12 weeks), enlarging uterus (8th week), abdominal enlargement (10th week), internal ballottement (16-28 weeks).
• Biological test for HCG is done for probable signs; it has been replaced by ultrasound.
(c)
• Positive signs are definitive and must be present to confirm pregnancy: fetal heartbeat, palpation of fetal movement and fetal parts, or ultrasonic evidence of a fetus (about 20 weeks).
• Methods: ultrasound scanning shows the gestational sac as early as 4 weeks; Sonicaid or Doptone at 12 weeks or earlier; plain abdominal X-ray from the 16th week.
(d)
• Presumptive signs can be mimicked by the contraceptive pill, hormonal imbalance, emotional stress, illness, gastrointestinal disorders, pyrexial illness, cerebral irritation, urinary tract infection, pelvic tumour and intestinal 'wind'.
• Probable signs can be mimicked by hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, pelvic congestion and tumours.
(e)
• Probable signs: strong indicators found on examination or tests (e.g. Hegar's sign, ballottement) that do not in themselves confirm pregnancy.
• Positive signs: definitive evidence of a fetus (heartbeat, fetal movement felt or seen, fetal parts palpated, ultrasound) that confirms the diagnosis.

questions.question:
Describe the essential drug concept and drug storage under the following headings:
(a) Definition and the essential drug list.
(b) Storage requirements and stock control.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice.
(d) Explain the rationale for each key step and the consequences of deviation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Essential drugs satisfy the health care needs of the majority of the population, available at all times in adequate amounts and appropriate dosage forms at a price the community can afford.
• They are selected for disease prevalence, public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety and cost-effectiveness.
• The list includes analgesics (paracetamol), multivitamins, lignocaine, anti-allergics (epinephrine, chlorpheniramine, promethazine), antidotes (atropine, charcoal), antimalarials (SP, ACT), antihelminthics, amoxycillin, cotrimoxazole, ferrous sulphate and folic acid, ORS.
(b)
• Storage keeps the quality and potency of drugs until dispensing; stores well ventilated, cool, dry and away from sunlight; vaccines stored at low temperatures.
• Humidity: repair roof leaks; secure doors and windows; do not store drugs directly on the floor.
• Arrangement: labelled, on shelves, cupboards, refrigerators, by classification (analgesics, antibiotics); stock cards record quantity received or issued, balance, date and signature.
(c)
• Maintain a good drug inventory and keep stock cards close to the medicines or in a secured filing system.
• Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is not recommended for children and pregnant women.
• The Drug Revolving Fund scheme: initial government capital with supplies replaced from sales to ensure continuous availability.
(d)
• Excessive heat can destroy drugs; humidity makes drugs absorb moisture and deteriorate fast.
• Vaccines lose potency if not kept cold.
• Poor stock control leads to stock-outs (essential drug system aims to ensure sustainable supply and eliminate waste).

questions.question:
Describe breastfeeding technique under the following headings:
(a) Preparation of the breasts and initiation of feeding.
(b) Correct attachment and positioning, and breastfeeding positions.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice when teaching mothers.
(d) Explain the rationale for correct attachment and the consequences of incorrect technique.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Start preparing the nipples from about the 30th week: wash, dry, rub with a little anhydrous lanolin, and draw out and roll each nipple gently; adopt a comfortable position.
• Initiate within 30 minutes of birth with skin-to-skin contact (baby laid naked on the mother's chest or abdomen in the first hour); feed on demand day and night.
(b)
• Attachment: baby's mouth covers the areola; held close and facing the breast; chin touching the breast, mouth wide open, lower lip curled outward, more areola visible above the upper lip, no pain to the mother.
• Detach by slipping a finger into the corner of the mouth to break suction; do not pull the baby off or force the mouth open.
• Positions: laid-back, cradle, cross-cradle (good for newborns and latching difficulties), rugby ball (caesarean, twins, premature), side-lying, upright/koala, dangle feeding, sling, double rugby ball, dancer hand (low muscle tone, preterm, Down's syndrome).
(c)
• Teach that there is no right or wrong way; comfort is most important; show the mother a few positions so she can feed while out and about.
• Support the mother with pillows or cushions to avoid back and shoulder strain; involve family members especially the father.
• Teach expressing milk into a clean cup when away; advise a balanced diet and adequate rest.
(d)
• If the baby bites on the nipple, he gets little milk, becomes furious and bites harder, causing sore nipples and areola.
• Gripping the areola leaves the nipple free and undamaged; incorrect positioning causes sore or cracked nipples and engorgement.
• Engorgement occurs when the baby is not correctly attached or cannot empty the breast.
• Correct positioning gives immediate relief of sore nipples (as stated in the difficulties section).

(a)
• Weight-for-age is the usual indicator; failure to gain weight is often the earliest sign of illness or malnutrition; growth charts compare the child's size with the normal range (z lines).
• MUAC is more useful as a screen for malnutrition (especially wasting) than as a measure of growth.
• Failure to gain weight in 3 successive months identifies a child at risk.
(b)
• Wasting (low weight-for-height, recent critical weight loss), stunting (low height-for-age, chronic) and underweight (low weight-for-age; may be stunted, wasted, or both).
• Marasmus (severe calorie and protein deficiency) versus kwashiorkor (severe protein deficiency with oedema).
(c)
• Rationale: growth monitoring detects early change; height and head circumference are particularly important when weight is not rising normally.
• Escalate: refer for management of malnutrition and infection; screening at any contact point; initial treatment with F-75 milk in severe cases (ICRC example).
questions.question:
A child's growth chart shows weight-for-age flattening over the last three monthly visits. MUAC is reduced, and the child is not gaining length as expected.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Tetanus is an infection caused by Clostridium tetani, a rod-shaped, gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium found in soil, dust and animal faeces; it releases tetanospasmin; also called lockjaw.
• Classified as generalized (about 80% of cases), neonatal, localized and cephalic tetanus.
(b)
• Spores enter through wounds (puncture wounds, burns, surgical wounds) or contaminated objects; the bacteria thrive in low oxygen such as deep puncture wounds or dead tissue; incubation is about 3 to 21 days; it is not passed from person to person.
• Under-immunization is an important cause; other risk factors: diabetes, chronic wounds, parenteral drug abuse, recent surgery, dental infections.
(c)
• Maternal tetanus occurs in pregnancy or within 6 weeks after it (unhygienic delivery or unsafe abortion); neonatal tetanus occurs within the first 28 days in babies of inadequately immunized mothers.
• Neonatal risk factors: umbilical stump infection, unsterile equipment and unclean hands, delivery away from facilities, soil or cow dung on the cord, circumcision, unvaccinated mother; early signs are weakness and failure to suck at 5-7 days.
• Complications: laryngospasm, fractures, pulmonary embolism, aspiration pneumonia, breathing difficulty, death (1 to 2 in 10 cases).
(d)
• Tetanospasmin travels by retrograde axonal transport to the spinal cord, cleaves synaptobrevin so GABA and glycine are not released, causing loss of inhibition, muscle spasms and autonomic hyperactivity.
• Effects: jaw stiffness, fixed grin, painful spasms triggered by noise or touch, opisthotonos, swallowing and breathing difficulty; once fixed to neurons the toxin cannot be neutralized; recovery needs new nerve terminals.
• Prevention: TTCV (6 doses: 3 primary from 6 weeks, minimum 4 weeks apart, plus 3 boosters); immunize women of reproductive age; clean delivery and cord care; wound care.
• Treatment (no cure): wound care, antitoxin (passive immunization), sedatives, antibiotics, airway and breathing support, feeding tube, quiet low-light environment.
• Mothers who recover still require vaccination because they have little or no natural immunity.
questions.question:
Describe tetanus in full:
(a) Definition, causative organism and classification.
(b) Aetiology/risk factors and pathophysiology.
(c) State how tetanus relates to pregnancy, childbirth and the newborn, and its common complications.
(d) Explain how the toxin spreads its effects through the nervous system and the resulting functional deficit, with preventive nursing measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Neonatal tetanus (tetanus neonatorum), tetanus within the first 28 days of life; prevented by TTCV given to women of reproductive age, during or outside pregnancy.
• Treatment uses antibiotics with immunoglobulins to neutralize circulating toxins and management of muscle spasms and respiratory failure.
(b)
• Before: identify causes (umbilical stump infection, unhygienic delivery, cow dung on the cord, unvaccinated mother, delivery away from facility).
• During: stop toxin production at the infection site along with wound care; give antibiotics and immunoglobulins; manage spasms.
• After/preventive: use topical antimicrobial solutions or creams for cord care instead of traditional substances; ensure clean delivery and cord care.
(c)
• Monitor muscular spasms and respiratory failure on a real-time basis; initial signs are weakness and failure to suck at 5-7 days.
• Danger signs: opisthotonos, trismus, irritability (continuous crying), grimacing and restlessness.
• Diagnosis is mainly clinical because cultures often fail to show the bacterium and antibodies are not reliable.
questions.question:
A six-day-old baby born at home to an unimmunized mother, whose cord stump was covered with cow dung, is brought in unable to suck, with locked jaw, backward arching of the neck and spine, and continuous crying.
(a) Name the condition and the immunization/drug relevant to its prevention and treatment.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after care.
(c) Describe the monitoring parameters and danger signs.

Describe the clinical investigations carried out for family planning clients under the following headings:
(a) The investigations done and the materials needed.
(b) The indications for urinalysis, Pap smear, VDRL, PCV/haemoglobin and pregnancy test.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before and after the investigations and the precautions to take.
(d) Explain the rationale for the investigations and for the examination rules.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Investigations: urinalysis (albumin, sugar, acetone); blood for Hb, PCV, malaria parasites and sickling; pregnancy test; Pap smear, VDRL, HIV screening, urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity.
• Materials include methylated spirit, litmus paper, urinometer, salicylsulphonic acid, acetic acid, Clinitest and Acetest tablets, sterile swab stick and urine container, transport medium, test tubes, blood sample bottles and rapid test kits.
(b)
• Urinalysis (colour, odour, amount, deposit, specific gravity): for urinary tract infection or cystitis and to evaluate its treatment.
• Pap smear: screening test collecting cervical cells to detect pre-cancerous changes in all new clients; VDRL: exposure to syphilis, genital ulcer or other STIs.
• PCV/Hb is not routine but done if the client is anaemic or bleeding; pregnancy test confirms or rules out pregnancy and differentiates intrauterine pregnancy from hydatidiform mole.
(c)
• Before: reassure the client, explain the procedure, ensure she is physically and emotionally ready.
• After: make the client comfortable, relieve anxiety about results with physical and emotional support, explain post-procedure actions to avoid complications.
• Precautions: handwash before and after, wear protective tools (mask, gloves), ensure sterility, avoid distractions, store and handle materials properly.
(d)
• Reasons for investigations: exclude pregnancy, detect abnormalities, treat appropriately and choose the proper family planning type.
• Clients needing tests are identified from medical and family history, age and lifestyle, contraindications (e.g. hormonal methods with a history of thromboembolic disorders), STI risk and baseline BP and weight.
• Examination rules: do not force the examination against the client's wishes; have a chaperone present to avoid sexual assault; provide privacy; avoid offensive words or facial gestures.

questions.question:
Describe the effects of pregnancy, labour and the puerperium on the urinary system:
(a) Frequency, retention and incontinence in pregnancy.
(b) The same in labour and the puerperium.
(c) State how these relate to complications such as delay in labour and postpartum haemorrhage.
(d) Explain why they may affect other systems and the preventive nursing measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Frequency: in the first 12 weeks the enlarging uterus in the pelvis limits bladder capacity; again in the last 4 weeks when the fetal head lies in the pelvis; physiological.
• Frequency with dysuria in mid-pregnancy suggests urinary infection; acute retention is rare (around 12 weeks if the uterus is retroverted); incontinence can occur in late pregnancy when the head is deeply engaged.
(b)
• Labour: pressure on the sacral plexus (more common in occipito-posterior position) causes increased desire to void or lack of sensation; the urethra stretches from 4 cm to about 15 cm, making micturition and catheterization difficult.
• Puerperium: increased urine secretion in the first 48 hours (physiological); retention from posture (bed rest, bed pan), lack of privacy, pain and lax muscle tone from over-distension.
• Incontinence: dribbling in second stage if the bladder is not emptied; trauma such as VVF; stress incontinence is more common in multigravida (lax pelvic floor).
(c)
• A full bladder delays the first and second stages of labour.
• It can cause bruising of the bladder and urethra and overstretching.
• It can lead to non-separation of the placenta and PPH.
• Abdomen should be palpated daily to rule out sub-involution and signs of infection.
(d)
• Close proximity of uterus, cervix and vagina to the bladder and urethra correlates their function during childbearing.
• Preventive: encourage the woman to pass urine every 2 hours in labour, empty the bladder at end of first stage, catheterize if needed, give privacy and early ambulation in the puerperium.

questions.question:
Describe the management of the puerperium under the following headings:
(a) Definition and the aims of care.
(b) Immediate care in the first 24 hours (the fourth stage).
(c) Subsequent care and the postnatal examination.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice.
(e) Explain the rationale for each key step and the consequences of omission.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Puerperium commences after expulsion of the placenta and lasts about 6-8 weeks; the process by which the generative organs return to the pre-gravid state is involution.
• Aims: promote physical well-being (correct anaemia, comfort, cleanliness, activity for involution); emotional well-being; prevent infection; promote breastfeeding; educate on baby care.
(b)
• The first hour is most critical (fourth stage), ideally in the labour ward; most PPH, shock or sudden collapse occurs then; pulse, BP, involution, lochia, perineum, bladder observed every 15 minutes.
• If BP is high, sedation is given orally or intravenously to prevent postpartum eclampsia; at the end of the hour she is cleaned up, offered a drink and encouraged to pass urine; uterus should be well contracted.
(c)
• Subsequent care: rest and sleep, ambulation 6-12 hours after delivery, protein diet, vitamins, fluids, iron and folic acid, bladder and bowel care, vulval toilet, postnatal exercises, breastfeeding, daily fundal height.
• Postnatal examination at 6 weeks: urine, vital signs, blood tests; general, abdominal, breast and perineal examination; doctor checks whether the cervix is closed; vaginal discharge and return of menses; baby's examination.
(d)
• Measure fundal height by the same person, at the same time, with the same instrument, after the woman empties her bladder; record vital signs, uterine tenderness, lochia colour, odour, amount and consistency, and wound healing.
• Prevent infection: reduce visitors, observe asepsis and antisepsis in vulval care; isolate or barrier nurse on suspicion of infection; emphasize the postnatal visit and family planning when educating the mother.
(e)
• Emptying the bladder regularly prevents PPH, subinvolution and urinary tract infection; catheterize if necessary.
• Early ambulation promotes well-being, good circulation and drainage of lochia; sufficient fluids, iron and folic acid prevent anaemia.
• Breasts must be emptied at each feed; nipples should be free of infection, cracks and engorgement.
• Postnatal examination ensures organs return to pre-gravid state, lactation is established, general health is good and family planning is addressed; common complications listed: vaginal discharge (infection), backache, headache, prolapse.

questions.question:
Describe counselling in family planning under the following headings:
(a) Definition and counselling skills.
(b) Principles of counselling and the GATHER steps for new clients.
(c) Explain the clinical basis (why) of informed choice and the danger of information overload.
(d) Distinguish between counselling new clients and counselling continuing clients.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Counselling is interpersonal communication in which the counsellor helps the client identify, clarify and resolve problems, make informed decisions and act on them; it is a provider-client interaction.
• Skills (verbal and non-verbal): active listening, encouraging cues, questioning, observation, paraphrasing, summarizing.
(b)
• Principles: treat each client well and keep confidentiality; interact and encourage questions; tailor information to need and stage of life; avoid information overload; provide the method the client wants; help the client understand and remember.
• GATHER: Greet respectfully and assure confidentiality; Ask about the client's experiences and intentions; Tell about choices (including no method); Help the client make an informed choice; Explain fully how to use the method; Return visits welcomed.
• Give condoms to everyone at risk for sexually transmitted infections (from the Explain step).
(c)
• Informed choice: a freely made, thought-out decision based on accurate, useful information.
• 'Informed' means clients have clear, accurate, specific information without information overload and understand their own needs; 'choice' means a range of methods and no pressure from providers.
• Too much information makes it hard to remember the really important information (information overload).
• Counselling is the 'heart' of family planning; with effective counselling clients continue a method, become satisfied and advocate its use by others.
(d)
• New clients: a six-step process of learning, weighing choices, deciding and carrying out the decision.
• Continuing clients: focus on experience and needs; tests and examinations are generally not needed unless a special situation calls for them; counselling is flexible.
• Continuing clients: resolve problems (new method or referral), answer questions, give more supplies and check the method is used correctly.

questions.question:
A woman in a hospital labour ward is to receive an oxytocin infusion to augment labour.
(a) Name the drug and its indications.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after.
(c) Describe the monitoring parameters and danger signs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Oxytocin: increases intracellular calcium in uterine smooth muscle causing contraction; indicated to induce or augment labour, control postpartum bleeding, manage incomplete or inevitable abortion.
• It also contracts myoepithelial cells around alveoli, causing milk ejection.
(b)
• Before: confirm absence of contraindications (cephalopelvic disproportion, malpresentation, cord prolapse, non-reassuring fetal status, active genital herpes, hypertonic uterus, unripe cervix, grand multiparity, uterine prolapse, risk of uterine rupture).
• Before: use only when the cervix is adequate and fetal maturity and position are favourable; give in a hospital where emergency and resuscitative measures are available.
• During: give by intravenous infusion, never by bolus injection.
(c)
• Monitor and record contractions, maternal heart rate, fetal heart rate and vaginal blood loss quarter-hourly.
• Danger signs: uterine hyperstimulation, fetal distress (bradycardia or tachycardia), hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, amniotic fluid embolism, water intoxication; notify the physician.

(a)
• Dramatic adaptation of body systems so the woman can cope with added work, nurture the fetus and prepare for labour and lactation; understanding helps the midwife identify deviations.
• Uterus: from 7.5 x 5 x 2.5 cm to 30 x 23 x 20 cm; weight from about 60 gm to 90 gm (as stated); becomes an abdominal organ; myometrial fibres hypertrophy under oestrogen.
• Uterine blood supply rises to 450-700 ml/min at term with uterine souffle; fundal levels: 12 weeks symphysis, 20 weeks umbilicus, 36 weeks xiphisternum, then lightening at 38 weeks.
(b)
• Cardiovascular: heart enlarges about 12%, blood volume up 50% (hydraemia, physiological anaemia); BP falls 10% early, rises slightly mid-trimester; supine position can reduce cardiac output by up to 25%.
• Respiratory: BMR increased, costal breathing, dyspnoea in up to 70%; digestive: oedematous gums, nausea in about 50%, indigestion, heartburn and constipation from progesterone.
• Skin: darkening in about 90% (chloasma, linea nigra, striae gravidarum); skeletal: altered gait and joint laxity; nervous: emotional instability; weight gain average maximum 11.5 kg.
(c)
• Hydraemia leads to physiological anaemia; supine hypotension causes fainting; progesterone causes heartburn and varicosities.
• Cervix: operculum guards against ascending infection; vagina: lactic acid from Doderlein bacilli raises secretion pH to 4.5-5.0, increasing vaginal secretion (leucorrhoea); breasts: Montgomery tubercles from 8 weeks.
• Minor disorders: not life-threatening but distress the woman and interfere with nutrition, sleep and chores.
(d)
• Hormonal changes (progesterone relaxing smooth muscle) affect gut, veins, ureters and bladder together.
• Preventive: teach posture, rest, diet, avoid lying supine, avoid prolonged standing, health education on minor disorders.
questions.question:
Describe the physiological changes of pregnancy in full:
(a) Definition and the changes in the uterus (size, position, blood supply).
(b) Changes in the cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, skin and other systems.
(c) State how these changes relate to common complications and the stage of pregnancy.
(d) Explain why they may spread effects to other systems and the preventive nursing measures.

Describe malaria in children aged birth to five years under the following headings:
(a) Definition, causative agent and mode of spread.
(b) Types of malaria parasite.
(c) Signs and symptoms, including signs of severe malaria.
(d) Explain the clinical basis for why children under five are more vulnerable and at higher risk of severe malaria.
(e) Distinguish between Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax malaria.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Malaria is a mosquito-borne disease caused by Plasmodium protozoa transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito; rarely by blood transfusion, organ transplant or from mother to baby during childbirth (transplacental).
• Pathophysiology: sporozoites enter the liver, multiply and mature, then merozoites invade and multiply in red blood cells, which rupture, causing cycles of fever, chills and sweating; the spleen may enlarge.
(b)
Five species infect humans: P. falciparum (deadliest, most prevalent in Africa), P. vivax, P. malariae (chronic infection, kidney damage, anaemia), P. ovale and P. knowlesi (mainly Southeast Asia).
(c)
• Symptoms appear 10 days to four weeks after infection: fever (most common), chills, headache, sweats, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, body aches, chest or abdominal pain; attacks last about 6-10 hours.
• Examination findings: high temperature, enlarged spleen, mild jaundice, enlarged liver, increased respiratory rate.
• Severe malaria signs: convulsions, impaired consciousness (cerebral malaria), respiratory distress, severe anaemia (pallor, lethargy), shock and organ failure.
(d)
• Children under 5 have lost maternal immunity and have not yet developed specific immunity; immune systems are still developing and they have limited prior exposure.
• P. falciparum can progress quickly with rapid parasite replication and a propensity to cause severe anaemia; young children cannot communicate symptoms and healthcare access may be limited.
• Children under five accounted for about 80% of malaria deaths in a WHO-cited statement; poverty, poor housing and antimalarial resistance add to risk.
(e)
• P. falciparum: deadliest; cerebral malaria, organ failure, anaemia, low blood sugar; most prevalent in Africa; main cause of malaria in children under five.
• P. vivax: most common outside Africa; fever, chills, headache, vomiting; relapses because dormant liver forms (hypnozoites) reactivate weeks to months later.
• Duffy-negative individuals are resistant to P. vivax (susceptibility depends on the Duffy antigen).

(a)
• The features suggest endometriosis: fragments of endometrial tissue deposited outside the uterine cavity respond to hormonal stimuli and bleed at menstruation.
• Features: secondary congestive dysmenorrhoea preceding and during menstruation, dyspareunia, pain on defecation, menstrual disturbance, infertility; asymptomatic in about 25%.
• It is benign, appears to improve or disappear in pregnancy and regresses at menopause.
(b)
Chronic salpingitis (abdominal pain, dysmenorrhoea, menorrhagia, dyspareunia); fibroids (menstrual disturbance); ovarian endometrioma/cysts; pelvic inflammatory conditions.
(c)
• Laparoscopic examination helps determine the extent; treatment depends on age, wishes about childbearing and preference.
• Hormone therapy (combined oestrogen and progesterone) produces decidual changes to achieve amenorrhoea.
• Refer for medical diagnosis and management.
questions.question:
A woman complains of pain before and during menstruation, pain during intercourse, pain on defecation and difficulty becoming pregnant. She says the pain eases during a previous pregnancy.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A fistula is an abnormal communication between structures that may occur within the genital tract.
• Types: vesico-vaginal, urethro-vaginal, recto-vaginal, uretero-vaginal and utero-vesical.
• Vesico-vaginal fistula: an artificial opening between the bladder or urethra and the vagina; very rare where good obstetric care is available.
(b)
• VVF causes: prolonged pressure of the vertex on the vagina during obstructed labour, obstetric operation, pelvic operation (e.g. radical hysterectomy), radiation burns after treatment for cervical cancer, untreated or recurrent cancer of the bladder or genital tract.
• Recto-vaginal fistula: an opening between rectum and vagina, most commonly when a sutured third-degree perineal tear does not heal properly.
(c)
• Recto-vaginal fistula is suspected when faeces are seen on the perineal pad, usually on the 3rd or 4th day postpartum.
• Obstructed labour with prolonged pressure of the vertex is a cause of VVF (stress incontinence is more common in multigravida).
(d)
• VVF features: incontinence of urine, several days of dysuria and haematuria, urinary infection, vaginal discharge, constantly wet vulva and perineum, excoriation of skin, ammonia smell, tenderness of the whole genital area.
• Treatment of VVF: Foley catheter left in situ 10 days or longer with sealed drainage; antibiotics; surgical repair if large, while small fistulae usually heal without operation.
• Recto-vaginal fistula: surgical repair of the rectum.
• Prevention: good obstetric care (from the statement that VVF is rare where it is available).
questions.question:
Describe genital fistulae in full:
(a) Definition and classification (types of fistulae).
(b) Aetiology of vesico-vaginal fistula and of recto-vaginal fistula.
(c) State how fistulae relate to obstetric care and to the puerperium.
(d) Explain why they affect the woman's urinary, skin and genital health and the resulting problems, with treatment and preventive nursing measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Weight (most common measure; recorded monthly in the first year), plotted on the growth chart (weight-for-age); also measure length, head circumference and mid-upper arm circumference.
• Failure to gain weight during 3 successive months places the child in the 'children at risk' list; also check for LBW, twin birth, spacing under 2 years, no exclusive breastfeeding, severe infections.
(b)
Faltering growth/risk of malnutrition: failure to gain weight or losing weight is often the earliest sign of illness or malnutrition.
(c)
• Growth is an increase in body size over time; no increase means the child is not growing; normal weight gain suggests the infant is healthy; growth charts are based on thousands of healthy children.
• If weight gain is normal, height and head circumference are usually normal, so they are measured particularly in children not gaining weight.
(d)
• Weigh correctly (scale zero, undressed, nearest 10 g for young children), plot on the chart, measure MUAC (screen for malnutrition) and length.
• Assess feeding: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, complementary foods from about 6 months; screen for infection; refer for treatment of malnutrition (e.g. F-75 milk in severe cases).
(e)
Teach caregivers nutrition, hygiene and immunization; evaluation: continued monitoring and weight gain on the chart.
questions.question:
An infant attends the child welfare clinic. Weight records show no weight gain over three successive monthly measurements.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings to gather.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnosis/problem.
(c) Explain the basis of monitoring growth.
(d) List the priority nursing interventions.
(e) Outline health education and evaluation.

Describe the drugs used for common pregnancy disorders under the following headings:
(a) Anti-emetics, antacids, haematinics and analgesics (indication, dosage, side effects).
(b) Antimalarial (SP) and antihypertensives.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice for each.
(d) Explain the rationale behind key points and the consequences of deviation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anti-emetics: for nausea and vomiting; Phenergan 25-50 mg daily, metoclopramide 10 mg tds; side effects: drowsiness, dry mouth, headache, dystonic reaction.
• Antacids: for hyperacidity, heartburn, peptic ulcers; aluminium hydroxide 10 mls tds, magnesium carbonate 250 mg qds, magnesium trisilicate 10-20 mls tds; side effects: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, flatulence.
• Haematinics: prevent and treat iron deficiency anaemia and neural tube defect; ferrous gluconate 30 mg tds, ferrous sulphate 200 mg tds, folic acid 5 mg daily; side effects: nausea, vomiting, dark stools, constipation.
• Paracetamol 1 g tds for mild pain such as low backache; side effect: nausea and vomiting.
(b)
• SP: 3 tablets (500 mg/25 mg) at scheduled antenatal visits in second and third trimester, at least one month apart; side effects: nausea, urticarial rash, allergy, headache, insomnia.
• Antihypertensives: methyldopa (no adverse effect evidence), beta blockers (propranolol, atenolol, labetalol), nifedipine, hydralazine in acute cases.
(c)
• Antacids: shake suspension; chew tablets thoroughly. Haematinics: give between meals (or with meals), teach diet to prevent constipation, do not give with antacids.
• SP: counsel on IPT benefit, screen for sulphonamide allergy, give in the presence of the health worker, document.
• Paracetamol: teach adequate rest.
(d)
• ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, captopril) are contraindicated: they can cause oligohydramnios, fetal anuria and stillbirth; diuretics reduce circulating volume.
• Beta blockers are contraindicated in asthma because of bronchoconstriction (caution needed).
• Preventive chemotherapy: malaria in pregnancy poses substantial risks to mother and fetus.

(a)
Heartburn, a minor disorder of the digestive system in pregnancy.
(b)
• It is a burning sensation due to reflux of gastric content into the oesophagus.
• Pathophysiology: progesterone relaxes the cardiac sphincter of the stomach, allowing reflux.
• Predisposing factor: the growing uterus puts pressure on the stomach, making it very troublesome between 30 and 40 weeks' gestation.
(c)
• Advise against rushing meals; take small meals at a time and rest after meals; take less fatty and greasy food.
• Advise avoiding bending over for too long; sleep with extra pillows; lie on the right side.
• Treatment depends on severity; in severe cases refer to the doctor, who will prescribe antacids (e.g. Magnesium Trisilicate mixture, Gelusil).
• Prevention: the measures above.
questions.question:
A woman at 34 weeks' gestation complains of a burning sensation in the upper abdomen that worsens after meals and when she bends over or lies flat.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors, the pathophysiology and the signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe the nursing management and prevention.

Describe growth monitoring of the child under the following headings:
(a) The measurements and how each is taken (weight, length/height, head circumference, MUAC).
(b) Plotting on a growth chart and frequency.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities and the recommended safe practice.
(d) Explain the rationale behind each key step and the consequences of deviation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Weight: lying scale for young children, wait until still, nearest 10 g, undressed; older children standing, nearest 100 g; check the scale reads zero and calibrate weekly.
• Height: barefoot, heels on floor, back against wall, stretch tall looking ahead with a sliding headboard; under 2 years lying length on a measuring board with the head held against the top board.
• Head circumference: measure the largest occipito-frontal circumference with a tape across the forehead and around the occiput, recorded to the nearest 1 mm.
• MUAC: midpoint between shoulder tip and elbow tip of the left arm hanging relaxed, to the nearest 1 mm, tape not too tight.
(b)
• Growth monitoring is regular measurement of size plotted on a growth chart to detect early changes; weight-for-age is most often used; gender-specific charts with growth (z) lines are used.
• Frequency: weight monthly (year 1), 2-monthly (year 2), 6-monthly to 5 years; head circumference at birth, 14 weeks, 12 months; MUAC 3-monthly; length/height 6-monthly.
(c)
• Record accurately, use correct technique and equipment, and plot on the chart at every visit.
• Pay attention to height and head circumference in children not gaining weight; MUAC is used as a screen for malnutrition.
(d)
• Remove wet nappies and clothing so the weight is accurate; zeroing and calibration prevent error.
• Head circumference is measured correctly because it is difficult to do accurately; little increase after 36 months.
• Failure to gain weight is often the earliest sign of illness or malnutrition, so missed monitoring delays detection.
• Growth lines move further apart with age, so the normal range widens.

(a)
• Correct attachment: mouth covers the areola, chin touching breast, mouth wide open, lower lip curled outward, more areola above the upper lip, no pain; the observed signs are the opposite, so attachment is incorrect.
• A baby biting on the nipple gets little milk and becomes furious; the mother develops sore nipples and areola.
(b)
Trauma from incorrect positioning of the baby's mouth at the breast versus infection with candidiasis (thrush); with thrush the nipples and areola are inflamed, pain persists throughout the feed and the baby may show signs of oral or anal thrush.
(c)
• Correct positioning gives immediate relief; express milk to feed the baby; rest the nipple to enable healing.
• Check the breast daily for early recognition; daily washing promotes healing; nystatin can be used (for thrush).
• Escalation: if inflammation, fever, redness and swelling develop (mastitis), continue breastfeeding and instruct on technique; abscess may need aspiration or drainage.
questions.question:
During a feed, the nurse observes a baby whose mouth does not cover the areola, whose chin is away from the breast, whose lower lip is turned in, and the mother reports pain. Nipples are inflamed and the pain persists throughout the feed.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Episiotomy: deliberate surgical incision of the perineum; lignocaine 0.5% 10 mls or 1% 5 mls infiltrated (takes 3-4 minutes, lasts about 1 hour); types: median, medio-lateral, J-shaped, lateral.
(b)
• Before: time correctly (when the presenting part is applied to the tissue); position dorsal or lithotomy; clean the perineum with antiseptic; infiltrate anaesthesia (needle 4-5 cm, withdraw to check no vessel punctured).
• During: cut one straight line during a contraction with sharp scissors; repair early to prevent sepsis, in 2 layers with absorbable catgut; pack the vagina; maintain sterility; test that anaesthesia is effective.
• Equipment: toothed forceps, needle holder, artery forceps, scissors, suture material, gauze swabs, wool mops, perineal pad, vaginal tampon, gown, mask, cap and gloves.
• After: analgesia for 48-72 hours; perineal toilet 4-hourly; empty bladder and bowel; keep wound dry; sitz bath 2-3 times daily; inspect for infection.
(c)
• Complications to monitor: haemorrhage, haematoma, infection, dyspareunia, temporary loss of libido.
• Danger sign: wound breakdown (resuture with non-absorbable suture after thorough cleaning).
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
• WHO recommends 6 doses for lifelong protection: 3 primary doses plus 3 boosters.
• The primary series begins as early as 6 weeks of age with a minimum interval of 4 weeks between doses; boosters in the second year of life (12-23 months), at 4-7 years and at 9-15 years.
• TTCV is included in routine immunization programmes and is administered during antenatal care contacts; it is given as DT, DTaP, Td or Tdap combinations.
(b)
• Clean birth practices: birth attendant's hands clean, handwashing or gloves during delivery, a clean delivery environment, safe disposal of birth waste, properly sterilized or decontaminated instruments.
• Cord care: use topical antimicrobial solutions or creams rather than traditional substances such as cow dung or soil on the stump.
(c)
• Nursing responsibilities: immunize women of reproductive age with TTCV during or outside pregnancy; practise clean delivery and cord care; educate on wound care.
• Safe practice: the vaccine can be administered safely during pregnancy and, handled safely, gives protective long-lasting immunity.
• Promote awareness of symptoms and access to primary health care; encourage delivery within health facilities.
(d)
• Immunizing the mother protects the newborn, because unvaccinated mothers and unclean birth practices cause neonatal tetanus (25,000 newborn deaths in 2018).
• The antibody response is slow to the first dose but improves rapidly with subsequent doses, which is why the full schedule matters.
• Deviation (unclean hands, unsterile instruments, traditional cord substances) leads to umbilical stump infection and neonatal tetanus; maternal tetanus follows unhygienic delivery or unsafe abortion.
• Nigeria is among the countries that had not reached elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus as of December 2020.
questions.question:
Describe the tetanus toxoid immunization of women and the safe delivery practices that prevent maternal and neonatal tetanus under the following headings:
(a) The recommended schedule of tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV).
(b) Safe delivery and cord care practices.

Describe adolescent sexual and reproductive health under the following headings:
(a) Definitions (adolescent, young people, early and older adolescence, adolescent SRH).
(b) Importance of adolescent SRH.
(c) Problems and health problems of adolescents.
(d) Explain why adolescents (especially girls) are more vulnerable and at higher risk.
(e) Distinguish between adolescents and young people.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Adolescence is the transitional phase of growth and development between childhood and adulthood; WHO defines an adolescent as aged 10-19; early adolescence 10-14, older adolescence 15-19.
• Adolescent SRH is the physical, mental and emotional well-being of adolescents in all matters relating to the reproductive system.
(b)
• Population: over 30 million Nigerians are aged 10-19; nearly one third of the population is 10-24; one in five people globally is an adolescent.
• Health: more than half of new HIV infections occur under 25; nearly two thirds of premature adult deaths are linked to behaviours that began in youth; empowerment of women must begin in adolescence.
(c)
• Problems: HIV vulnerability; unplanned pregnancy; early marriage (50% of girls married by 20); unsafe abortion; sexual abuse (harassment, coercion, rape, incest, trafficking); loss of schooling.
• Health problems: too early pregnancy, complications of pregnancy and childbirth, unsafe abortion, STIs (HIV/AIDS, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, herpes, syphilis, PID).
(d)
• Girls aged 15-24 are 3 times more likely to be HIV-positive than boys; teen mothers are twice as likely to die of pregnancy-related causes; adolescent girls are over 60% of women treated for unsafe abortion complications.
• Married girls are more at risk of HIV: more frequent sex and less ability to refuse or demand protection; the younger the girl at first intercourse, the more likely it is coerced.
• Perpetrators of abuse are often relatives, neighbours and acquaintances; barriers to services: clinic hours, transport, confidentiality, cost, provider attitudes.
• Determinants of SRH: education, information and agency; access to services and commodities; knowledge and confidence to resist sexual violence and coercion.
(e)
• Adolescents are aged 10-19.
• Young people are aged 10-24, a wider group that includes adolescents.

questions.question:
A baby is brought to the child welfare clinic. He was a twin, born with low birth weight, conceived less than two years after his sibling, and is not being exclusively breastfed.
(a) Identify the risk factors.
(b) State the complications for the child.
(c) Describe nursing and medical management options and justify the priority.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Children at risk include those with LBW, twin birth, spacing of less than 2 years, no exclusive breastfeeding, failure to gain weight in 3 successive months.
• Others: death of 2 or more siblings before 24 months, death of a parent, protein-energy malnutrition and severe acute infections (diarrhoea, measles, pertussis).
(b)
• Malnutrition makes the child susceptible to infection, slower recovery and increased mortality, and leads to growth retardation.
• Infections (diarrhoea, respiratory infections, measles, tuberculosis, pertussis, polio, neonatal tetanus, diphtheria); accidents and poisoning; behavioural disorders.
• LBW/preterm birth determines survival and healthy development.
(c)
• Promote exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, appropriate complementary feeding, regular growth monitoring, immunization, hygiene and safe water.
• Nutrition education for caregivers; treat infections early; family spacing counselling.
• Exclusive breastfeeding is emphasised for reducing morbidity by about 70%.

(a)
• The fetus obtains oxygen and nutrients from the placenta; lungs and gut are functionless and need little blood; fetal haemoglobin carries 20-30% more oxygen than adult haemoglobin.
• Temporary structures: ductus venosus (umbilical vein to inferior vena cava), foramen ovale (opening between atria), ductus arteriosus (pulmonary artery to aorta), hypogastric/umbilical arteries, umbilical vein.
(b)
• The umbilical vein carries pure oxygenated blood to the liver (the only vein with pure blood); the ductus venosus carries blood to the inferior vena cava where it mixes with impure blood.
• About 75% shunts through the foramen ovale to the left atrium; blood from the head, neck and arms returns via the superior vena cava to the right ventricle and pulmonary artery.
• Most of the pulmonary artery blood passes through the ductus arteriosus to the aorta; the rest goes to the placenta via the hypogastric and umbilical arteries.
(c)
• At birth the baby gasps, the lungs expand and blood flows to the lungs; the ductus arteriosus contracts and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
• Clamping the cord stops flow in the umbilical vein; the ductus venosus collapses to become the ligamentum venosus.
• Pressure falls in the right atrium and rises in the left atrium, closing the foramen ovale.
• The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres; the hypogastric arteries atrophy except the portions that remain as internal iliac and superior vesical arteries.
(d)
• All organs must be mature and normal to take over; the change is almost instantaneous.
• Immediate care of the baby: clear airway, establish respiration, Apgar score, double clamp and cut cord, provide warmth, label and weigh.

Describe fetal circulation in full:
(a) Definition and the temporary structures.
(b) The course of the circulation.
(c) State how fetal circulation relates to the newborn's transition at birth.
(d) Explain how failure of these changes may affect other systems, and the nursing measures in newborn care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fever (most common sign) that may come and go with well periods between; chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; attacks cycle of shaking chills, high fever, sweating, return to normal temperature.
• Examination findings: high temperature, enlarged spleen, mild jaundice, enlarged liver, increased respiratory rate; pallor and lethargy after three to four days of fever suggest anaemia.
• Check for severe signs: convulsions, impaired consciousness, respiratory distress.
(b)
Suspected malaria with risk of severe malaria/anaemia in a child under five.
(c)
• Plasmodium enters the bloodstream by infected female Anopheles bite, multiplies in the liver, then invades red cells; rupture of red cells releases parasites causing fever cycles; the spleen enlarges removing infected cells.
• Children under five have an immune system still developing and no acquired immunity, so infection can progress rapidly.
(d)
Seek prompt diagnosis and treatment; ACTs (e.g. artemether-lumefantrine) are used with dosage based on weight, prescribed by a health professional; convulsions need urgent attention.
(e)
Teach: sleep under treated nets, eliminate stagnant water, indoor residual spraying, long sleeves, repellents, seek early care and complete prescribed treatment.
questions.question:
A child under five years is brought to the health centre with fever that comes and goes, shaking chills, headache and vomiting. The mother reports the child has been ill for several days, and on examination the child is pale and lethargic with an enlarged spleen.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnosis/problem.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) List the priority nursing interventions.
(e) Outline the health education.

Describe endometriosis in full:
(a) Definition.
(b) Clinical features and aetiology.
(c) State how it relates to infertility and to the client's stage of life (pregnancy and menopause).
(d) Explain how it affects other systems and the treatment and nursing measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Endometriosis is a condition in which fragments of endometrial tissue or cells are deposited at sites other than the lining of the uterine cavity.
• These fragments respond to hormonal stimuli and bleed at menstruation.
(b)
• It may be asymptomatic in about 25% of cases.
• Features: pain from secondary congestive dysmenorrhoea preceding and during menstruation, dyspareunia, pain on defecation, menstrual disturbance, infertility.
(c)
• Infertility is among the clinical features.
• It is benign, appears to improve or disappear in pregnancy and definitely regresses at menopause.
• Treatment depends on the client's age, her wishes regarding childbearing and personal preference.
(d)
• Effects on bowel (pain on defecation) and pelvis (dyspareunia, dysmenorrhoea); Laparoscopic examination may help determine the extent of the condition.
• Hormone therapy: combined oestrogen and progesterone preparations to produce decidual changes in the endometrium, given to achieve amenorrhoea.

questions.question:
A couple has tried to conceive for 12 months with regular unprotected intercourse without success. The wife is 37 years old and smokes; the husband drinks alcohol. The wife had gonorrhoea in the past.
(a) Identify the risk factors for infertility.
(b) State the complications (including of treatment and psychosocial).
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Age (decline in women's fertility after 35); tobacco and alcohol use (affect sperm quality and fertility); STIs such as gonorrhoea can damage or block the fallopian tubes.
• Other listed risk factors: marijuana use, being overweight or underweight, exercise issues.
(b)
• Treatment complications: multiple pregnancy (premature labour and delivery risk) and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (swollen, painful ovaries), higher with IVF.
• Psychosocial: internal and external pressures and physical, social and verbal abuse of affected couples in Nigeria.
(c)
• Medical: ovulation-inducing agent clomiphene citrate; surgical: lysis of adhesions, tuboplasty, myomectomy, septoplasty; IVF if tubes are beyond repair.
• Assisted reproductive strategies: IUI (washed sperm placed in the uterus with a sterile catheter), IVF, GIFT, ZIFT, ICSI, cryopreservation.
• Lifestyle changes and improving frequency and timing of intercourse often improve chances; treatment involves one or both partners and is directed to the cause.

questions.question:
Describe the admission and management of a woman in labour under the following headings:
(a) Admission and history.
(b) General, abdominal and vaginal examination (indications and points to note).
(c) Subsequent observations and care.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice.
(e) Explain the rationale behind each key step and the consequences of deviation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Welcome the woman politely, reassure, explain procedures, treat relatives with courtesy; booked clients' cards are studied; unbooked clients are booked and previous labours asked about.
• Ask the time labour began, frequency and strength of contractions, show, membranes ruptured (time, colour, amount) and when she last ate.
(b)
• General: urine for albumin, sugar and acetone; membrane status; vaginal bleeding; psychosocial assessment. Abdominal: inspection, palpation, auscultation, contractions.
• Vaginal examination every 4-6 hours with strict asepsis; indications: diagnose labour, assess progress, confirm engagement or presentation, exclude cord prolapse, confirm second stage.
• Note vulva, perineum, liquor colour (green meconium, blood-stained antepartum haemorrhage, golden Rhesus iso-immunization), cervix, membranes, presentation, position, level of presenting part, moulding, pelvic adequacy.
• Contraindications to vaginal examination: heavy show, antepartum haemorrhage.
(c)
• Vital signs: BP 1-2 hourly, pulse and respiration hourly (15-30 minutes late), temperature 4-hourly; FHR hourly in graph form (normal 120-160), not auscultated during contractions.
• Bladder: pass urine every 2 hours; feeding: easily digestible food, glucose drinks or 5% dextrose; posture: lateral position to avoid vena cava compression; comfort and pain relief.
(d)
• Never leave the woman alone; record all observations; report abnormal findings; keep asepsis.
• When membranes rupture, put the woman on the bed and check the vulva for cord prolapse.
(e)
• Full bladder/bowel causes uterine inertia and delays engagement; thready pulse may indicate pre-eclampsia.
• A drop of 20 beats below or above the normal FHR should be reported; dry hot vagina signals gross dehydration.

(a)
• An episiotomy is a deliberate surgical incision into the perineum to enlarge the vaginal orifice and facilitate birth; it is planned surgery but often done as an emergency.
• Indications: minimize severe spontaneous trauma; delayed second stage with imminent tear, disproportion, rigid perineum, contracted outlet, abnormal positions; fetal distress; forceps, ventouse or breech delivery; preterm babies; previous complete perineal tear; primipara with a big baby.
(b)
Types: median, medio-lateral, J-shaped (Schuchardt) and lateral; the lateral type causes profuse bleeding, is difficult to repair and has been abandoned; bilateral medio-lateral is not recommended because of excessive bleeding.
(c)
• Timing: given when the presenting part is directly applied to the tissue; too early fails to release the head and causes profuse bleeding; too late leaves no time for infiltration or a tear may already have occurred; woman in dorsal or lithotomy position.
• Anaesthesia: lignocaine 0.5% 10 mls or 1% 5 mls; takes 3-4 minutes to act and lasts about 1 hour; cut with sharp straight blunt-ended scissors during a contraction.
• Repair: early suturing prevents sepsis and poor union; it is equivalent to a second-degree tear, so it is repaired in 2 layers (vaginal wound, then pelvic floor muscles and perineal body, then perineal skin); vagina packed and sterility maintained.
(d)
• Higher-risk clients are those with rigid perineum, contracted outlet, abnormal positions, a big baby in a primipara, preterm babies or a previous complete tear (as listed above).
• Advantages: prevents overstretching of pelvic floor muscles; reduces maternal exhaustion and PPH; reduces risk of cerebral damage to the infant from acidosis and hypoxia; heals faster than a ragged tear; prevents damage to urethra and third degree tear.
• Complications: haemorrhage, haematoma, infection, dyspareunia, temporary loss of libido; the scar may necessitate episiotomy in subsequent deliveries; it is an unnecessary injury if given without good cause.
(e)
• Median: midline incision from the centre of the fourchette about 2.5 cm posteriorly; less bleeding, easy to repair, heals better; may extend to the anus (third degree) or rectum (fourth degree) and gives less room for instrumental delivery.
• Medio-lateral: from the fourchette to the right or left at about a 45 degree angle between the tuberosity and the anus; cannot lead to a third degree tear (recommended for midwives) but is more difficult to repair.
• Care in the puerperium for either type: analgesia for 48-72 hours, perineal toilet 4-hourly, dry wound, sitz bath, inspect for infection, resuture if the wound breaks down.
questions.question:
Describe episiotomy under the following headings:
(a) Definition and indications.
(b) Types of incision with their advantages and disadvantages.
(c) Timing, anaesthesia and repair.
(d) Explain the clinical basis for which clients are at higher risk of needing an episiotomy, and the advantages and complications of the procedure.
(e) Distinguish between a median (midline) episiotomy and a medio-lateral episiotomy.

On postnatal day 7, a woman who delivered vaginally is assessed. Lochia is still bright red, moderate in amount, and her fundus is higher than expected. The clinic has a record of uterine weight at different times after delivery.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Expected progression: lochia rubra (red) 1-4 days; lochia serosa (pink/brownish) 5-9 days; lochia alba (creamy, greenish) 10-15 days.
• Expected uterine weight: 900 gm at end of labour, 450 gm at end of 1 week, 200 gm at 2 weeks, 60 gm at 6 weeks; involution reduces the uterus by about a finger breadth a day.
• Bright red lochia on day 7 is beyond the expected rubra stage of 1-4 days.
(b)
• A persistent red lochia is a warning sign of retained products of conception and likelihood of puerperal haemorrhage.
• Sub-involution: abdomen should be palpated daily to rule out sub-involution of the uterus and signs of infection.
(c)
• Rationale: a persistent red lochia must be reported without delay because of the risk of haemorrhage.
• Empty bladder regularly to prevent PPH and subinvolution; estimate fundal height daily using the same person, time and instrument.
• Record lochia colour, odour, amount and consistency; suspected infection: isolate or barrier nurse.

(a)
• Age 5 or younger with an immature immune system; risk is higher for premature babies; malnutrition raises pneumonia risk.
• Crowded places and air pollution or toxic fumes; viruses and bacteria in the child's nose or throat inhaled into the lungs.
(b)
• Bacteraemia and septic shock; lung abscess; respiratory failure (bluish skin, confusion, restlessness).
• Heart failure; pleural effusion, empyema and pleurisy with sharp chest pain.
(c)
• Seek medical help right away; treat with antibiotics, first-line amoxicillin dispersible tablets, often oral at a health centre; cotrimoxazole daily if HIV infected.
• Hospitalization is recommended only for severe cases; trained community health workers can diagnose and treat at community level.
• Nursing: promote exclusive breastfeeding and adequate nutrition, handwashing, reduce indoor air pollution, ensure immunization (Hib, pneumococcus, measles, pertussis).
questions.question:
A child under five, who was born prematurely and is malnourished, is brought in with fast, laboured breathing, rapid heartbeat, fever, vomiting and irritability. The family lives in a crowded home with smoky indoor air.
(a) Identify the risk factors.
(b) State the complications that may follow.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.

A woman presents with sudden lower abdominal pain, fever of 38-39 degrees C, tachycardia, malaise, nausea and purulent vaginal discharge. She had an abortion complicated by infection.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute salpingitis, inflammation of the uterine tube.
(b)
• Causes: post-abortal infection, gonorrhoea, peritoneal infection such as appendicitis or TB.
• Causative organisms: streptococcus, staphylococcus, E. coli.
• Features: sudden pain, pyrexia (38-39), malaise, tachycardia, nausea, purulent vaginal discharge.
(c)
