• Admit; bed rest until temperature subsides; monitor vital signs 4-hourly especially temperature and pulse; encourage adequate fluids; observe urinary output; balanced diet.
• Give prescribed antibiotics once vaginal and urethral swabs are taken (for gonococcal infection or to rule out syphilis) and prescribed analgesic.
• Unresolved acute stage causes chronic salpingitis (abdominal pain, dysmenorrhoea, menorrhagia, dyspareunia).

(a)
• Menopause is diagnosed once periods have stopped for 12 months; it is a natural part of ageing caused by depletion of oestrogen, FSH, testosterone and progestogen; it typically occurs between 40 and 60 years.
• Andropause is a gradual condition in men caused by a decrease in testosterone levels; not all men are affected.
(b)
• Menopause: hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, low libido, depression, anxiety, mood swings, nausea, weight gain, brain fog, hair loss, lack of energy.
• Andropause: erectile dysfunction, weight gain, hair loss, night sweats, reduced muscle mass, depression, anxiety, mood swings, hot flushes, low libido, brain fog, lack of energy.
(c)
• Medical: laboratory investigation of hormone levels; hormone replacement therapy (testosterone in men; oestrogen and progestogen in women); cognitive behavioural therapy; antidepressants or antihypertensives.
• Natural: healthy lifestyle, regular exercise, relaxing activities (tai chi, yoga, deep breathing), natural supplements, bioidentical hormones from plant sources; health counselling.
(d)
• Early onset can follow removal of the uterus or ovaries.
• Poor diet, excessive drinking and other behaviours leading to hormone deficiency can speed up the process.
(e)
• Menopause: hormones fall rapidly, causing sudden symptoms; all women experience it; it ends in infertility.
• Andropause: occurs gradually and may be so slight that symptoms are not apparent or appear late; most men do not have a large enough testosterone decrease to suffer from it.
• Andropause does not lead to infertility even though testosterone is lower.
• Diagnosis: menopause is clearer (12 months without periods); andropause relies more on blood tests for testosterone.
questions.question:
Describe menopause and andropause under the following headings:
(a) Definition and cause of each.
(b) Symptoms of each.
(c) Management (medical and natural).
(d) Explain why some people are at higher risk of early or severe symptoms.
(e) Distinguish between menopause and andropause.

A 35-year-old woman who wishes to have more children presents with menstrual disturbances, abdominal enlargement, frequency of micturition and constipation. Fibroids are suspected.
(a) Identify the risk factors/associated features.
(b) State the complications.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fibroids occur in about 10-20% of women over 30; the cause is obscure but hormonal; they may be interstitial, submucous or subserous.
• Pressure symptoms arise from size: dyspepsia, constipation, frequency, stress incontinence, retention of urine, haemorrhoids.
(b)
• Pain when fibroids undergo torsion, degeneration, extrusion through the cervix or malignant change.
• Interstitial fibroids may impair uterine contractions; fibroids may contribute to infertility.
(c)
• No treatment is needed if no symptoms; surgical: myomectomy ('shelling out' through the uterine wall) if she desires children and is under 40; hysterectomy if over 40 or family completed.
• Justification: myomectomy preserves the uterus for future childbearing, so it is the priority operation for this client.

(a)
• Oncology is the branch of medicine dealing with prevention, diagnosis and treatment of cancer; cancer is a malignant disease in which normal cells mutate and grow uncontrollably, invading surrounding tissues.
• A tumour (neoplasm) is an abnormal mass of tissue formed when cells grow and divide more than they should or do not die when they should.
(b)
• Benign: localized, well-defined borders, frequently encapsulated, do not invade or spread, often easily removed.
• Malignant: grow aggressively, irregular shape, cut through surrounding tissue causing bleeding, inflammation and necrosis, and can recur.
(c)
• Carcinogenesis is formation of cancer by genetic mutation in three stages: initiation (irreversible genetic alteration), promotion (reversible) and progression (irreversible, karyotypic instability).
• Carcinogens damage cellular DNA; examples: viruses (HIV, Kaposi sarcoma), drugs (heroin), hormones (oestrogen), chemicals.
(d)
• Risk factors: heredity, age over 50 and post-menopausal women, poverty, lack of access to screening, obesity, sun exposure, diet and additives, tobacco, alcohol, occupational stress, infections such as HPV and genital herpes.
• General signs: pain, fatigue, infection, organ dysfunction, bone marrow suppression and anaemia, anorexia and cachexia, cough, jaundice (liver), voice coarseness (larynx).
• Site-specific signs: difficulty urinating (prostate), constipation or change in stool (colorectal), haematuria (bladder/kidney), abnormal vaginal bleeding (cervix/endometrium).
• Biotechnology (gene mapping, in situ hybridization, microarray, cell culture) helps early diagnosis and choice of treatment.
(e)
• Benign: encapsulated, does not spread; malignant: invades and can metastasize.
• Benign tumours tend not to recur after removal; malignant tumours can recur.
questions.question:
Describe benign and malignant tumours under the following headings:
(a) Definitions of oncology, cancer and tumour.
(b) Features of benign and of malignant tumours.
(c) Carcinogenesis and carcinogens.
(d) Explain the clinical basis of risk factors and the general signs and symptoms of cancer.
(e) Distinguish between benign and malignant tumours.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Psychological method is the most important aspect: a clean, organized, calm and reassuring environment; a sympathetic, understanding midwife; giving information, allaying anxiety, involving the woman in planning and giving physical care.
• Support in labour: back massage during contractions, hygiene and comfortable positioning, bladder and bowel care, feeding.
(b)
• Analgesics relieve pain without unconsciousness (e.g. Panadol, aspirin, Fortral); narcotics allay anxiety, induce sleep and are strong analgesics (e.g. pethidine, morphine, Pethilorfan, Fortal, Tramal).
• Hypnotics induce sleep and are anticonvulsant (e.g. chloral hydrate, diazepam, paraldehyde); tranquillisers calm the patient (Phenergan); sedatives induce sleep (barbiturates).
• Lytic cocktail: a mixture of phenothiazine derivatives and pethidine given slowly intravenously to sedation, tranquility and analgesia; used in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, forceps and breech deliveries and caesarean section.
• Inhalational analgesia: used on healthy women in late first stage or second stage; Entonox (50% nitrous oxide and 50% oxygen) and Trilene (trichloroethylene).
(c)
• Types of anaesthesia: general; regional (epidural, spinal, pudendal block); local (e.g. lignocaine); spinal anaesthesia is injection into the subarachnoid space (CSF).
• Pudendal block: local anaesthetic near the pudendal nerves just below the ischial spines; paracervical block: 10 mls of 1% lignocaine into the lateral fornices; local infiltration: 10 mls of 0.5% lignocaine into the perineum for episiotomy.
(d)
• The midwife must know why a drug is given, its principles and main action; success and safety depend on the right drug or combination, adequate dosage, proper timing and checking the dose.
• Objective: maximum pain relief with maximum safety for the woman and fetus, by non-pharmacological approaches, drugs, or a combination.
(e)
• A woman already apprehensive about pain relaxes when admitted to a calm, reassuring environment, which is why the psychological method comes first.
• Paracervical block carries a risk of bradycardia, and fetal death may occur; drug actions overlap (a small narcotic dose acts as a sedative), so the reason for each drug must be known.
questions.question:
Describe the methods of pain relief in labour under the following headings:
(a) Psychological support.
(b) Drugs used (analgesics, narcotics, hypnotics, tranquillisers, sedatives, lytic cocktail and inhalational agents).
(c) Obstetric anaesthesia (general, regional and local).
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice required when giving drugs for pain relief.
(e) Explain the rationale for psychological support and the risks that follow from poor choice of technique.

A 55-year-old post-menopausal woman complains of profuse, offensive and occasionally blood-stained vaginal discharge, with inflamed vulva and vagina.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Senile (atrophic) vaginitis.
(b)
• Cause: withdrawal of oestrogen at the time of menopause.
• Menopause is the end of the reproductive period, with ovarian hormones gradually withdrawn and ovulation ceasing.
• Clinical features: vaginal discharge that may be profuse, offensive and occasionally blood-stained; vulva and vagina may be inflamed.
(c)
• Give prescribed oestrogen orally or by local application daily.
• Vaginal dryness is among menopause symptoms; HRT is a management option.
• Other causes of discharge (Trichomonas, Candida) should be excluded by examination of discharge; carcinoma considered (as in pruritus vulvae).

questions.question:
A woman complains of increasing abdominal girth, pressure symptoms, backache and dyspareunia. She suddenly develops severe abdominal pain.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ovarian cyst, with possible complication such as torsion.
(b)
• Classification: retention (distension) cysts, serous and mucous cystadenoma, papilliferous cysts, ovarian endometrioma, dermoid cysts.
• Clinical features: increasing girth, pressure symptoms, dyspnoea, varicose veins, oedema, backache, dyspareunia, pain, mental disorders.
• Complications: torsion, rupture of the cyst, bleeding, malignant changes, obstructed labour in pregnancy.
(c)
• Admit the patient; surgical intervention is sought.
• Ovarian biopsy may be taken through the laparoscope; if malignancy is suspected, total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
• With simple cysts, ovarian cystectomy may be possible, otherwise oophorectomy.

(a)
Cervical cancer (invasive stage), the second most common cancer in women.
(b)
• Predisposing: HPV infection transmitted sexually; early sexual intercourse, multiple partners, recurrent vaginal infections, smoking (as listed under avoidance of predisposing factors).
• Pathophysiology: HPV persistence leads to CIN at the squamo-columnar junction, progressing to carcinoma in situ, then invasion through the basement membrane over 5-15 years; spreads by direct invasion, later by metastasis.
• Signs: irregular bleeding, bleeding after intercourse, discharge (white, watery, brown, foul, blood-tinged), pain in intercourse, post-menopausal bleeding; advanced: pelvic or back pain, leg swelling, weight loss, VVF/RVF.
(c)
• Management: staging (FIGO) guides treatment; surgery, radiation, chemotherapy; pre-op diagnoses include chronic pain, anxiety, disturbed body image and deficient knowledge.
• Post-op: ineffective breathing pattern and airway clearance, acute pain, risk of infection, self-care deficit, impaired skin integrity, sexual dysfunction, impaired urinary elimination.
• Prevention: HPV vaccination, Pap smear screening, safer sex, treat vaginal infections, stop smoking, diet rich in fruits and vegetables, yearly pelvic examination for sexually active women.
questions.question:
A sexually active woman complains of bleeding after intercourse, foul-smelling blood-tinged vaginal discharge and pain during sexual intercourse.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management and prevention.

A breastfeeding mother presents with fever, and a red, swollen, painful area on one breast. She has had sore, cracked nipples.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mastitis, inflammation of the breast.
(b)
• It may be due to infection or milk (milk stasis), usually accompanied by fever, redness and swelling.
• Predisposing: sore or cracked nipples (trauma from incorrect positioning, or candida/thrush), engorgement, poor emptying; progression of inflamed area can lead to breast abscess.
• Breast abscess: a fluctuant swelling that develops in a previously inflamed area.
(c)
• Continue breastfeeding from the affected breast; instruct the mother on good breastfeeding technique.
• For abscess: simple needle aspiration or incision and drainage may be necessary; breastfeeding should recommence as soon as practicable to reduce further abscess.
• Prevention: correct positioning, check the breasts daily for early recognition, daily washing for breast hygiene, rest the nipple for healing, express milk; nystatin can be used for thrush.

(a)
Endometritis, inflammation of the endometrium.
(b)
• It is uncommon because the endometrium is constantly renewed in reproductive years and does not allow infection to become established.
• Causative organisms: Streptococcus faecalis, E. coli, Staphylococcus pyogenes, gonococcus, tuberculosis, chlamydia.
• Predisposing factors: criminal abortion, retained products of conception, uterine contraceptive device.
• Features: low back pain, pelvic pain, malaise, anorexia, pyrexia, tachypnoea, blood-stained purulent discharge.
(c)
• Admit; adequate bed rest; prescribed antibiotics and analgesics; gentle curettage if retained products.
• Histological examination to determine the cause.
questions.question:
A woman presents with low back and pelvic pain, malaise, anorexia, fever and blood-stained purulent vaginal discharge following an unsafe abortion.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A sexually transmitted infection (STI), infections spread from person to person through sexual contact.
(b)
• Examples: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, herpes, HPV, HIV, genital warts, pubic lice.
• Spread: vaginal, anal or oral intercourse; sharing of sex toys; mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy and birth.
• Predisposing: multiple sexual partners, unprotected sex, sharing sharp objects; Symptoms: unusual genital discharge, pain or burning on urination, abnormal bleeding or spotting, pain during intercourse, itching or irritation, fever, rashes or sores on the genitals.
(c)
• Control: get medical help as soon as signs appear, treatment on suspicion, contact tracing, post-exposure prophylaxis, ensure diagnosed persons take medication, no douching, no sex during menstruation.
• Prevention: comprehensive sexual education, condoms, abstinence, monogamy or avoiding multiple partners, vaccination, regular STI tests, open communication, dental dams for oral sex, avoid sharing sharp objects, antenatal check-ups.
questions.question:
An adolescent girl attends the clinic complaining of unusual genital discharge, burning sensation when passing urine, itching in the genital area and sores on the genitals after unprotected sex with a new partner.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management and prevention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Measles, a highly contagious viral infection that primarily affects children.
(b)
• Predisposing factors: lack or incomplete vaccination (two doses), weakened immune system, malnutrition, crowded living conditions, travel to endemic areas; under-fives have developing immune systems.
• Cause: single-stranded enveloped RNA virus (genus Morbillivirus, family Paramyxoviridae); humans are the only natural hosts; spread by respiratory droplets and airborne transmission, contaminated surfaces and close contact.
• Incubation 7-14 days; contagious 1-2 days before symptoms and from 3-5 days before the rash to 4 days after its onset; early symptoms last 4-7 days; fever often above 40 degrees C.
• Rash begins 7-18 days after exposure on the face and upper neck, spreads over about 3 days to hands and feet, and lasts 5-6 days.
• Complications: encephalitis, severe diarrhoea with dehydration, ear infections (1 in 10 children 0-5 years), pneumonia.
(c)
Early recognition to isolate and treat; contact tracing and public health measures; Prevention: MMR vaccine, first dose at 12-15 months and second at 4-6 years; high vaccination coverage, avoiding contact with infected people, good hygiene (handwashing, covering coughs), caregiver education.
questions.question:
A young child has a running nose, cough, red and watery eyes, fever and small white spots inside the cheeks. A few days later a rash begins on the face and upper neck and spreads downward. The child has not been vaccinated and lives in a crowded household.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe the nursing management and prevention.

Describe the safe motherhood initiative under the following headings:
(a) Definition and objectives.
(b) Pillars and components (antenatal care, postnatal care, clean and safe delivery, skilled birth attendance, family planning).
(c) Explain the clinical basis for why safe motherhood begins before conception and the role of nutrition.
(d) Distinguish between antenatal care and postnatal care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Safe motherhood is a UN initiative launched in 1987 to ensure women go through pregnancy and childbirth safely and give birth to healthy children.
• Objectives: improve quality and access to family planning and maternal health services; promote integrated cost-effective RH interventions through primary health care; promote efficient monitoring; reproductive health education for couples; operational research.
(b)
• Pillars: family planning, antenatal care, obstetric and newborn care, post-abortion care, STI/HIV/AIDS control.
• Components: antenatal care, postnatal care, clean and safe delivery, skilled birth attendance (the cornerstone of clean and safe delivery), family planning and reproductive care.
• Family planning methods: barrier, hormonal, IUDs, natural and permanent; with education and counselling on benefits, side effects and effective use.
• Agencies: WHO, UNFPA, UNICEF, USAID, World Bank, FIGO, MHTF; initiatives: SMI, EWEC, MCHIP, EMC, SMGL.
(c)
• Safe motherhood begins before conception with proper nutrition and a healthy lifestyle; planned pregnancy, appropriate prenatal care and early treatment of complications are essential.
• Adequate nutrition before, during and after pregnancy is essential for the health of mother and fetus.
• Clean and safe delivery minimizes the risk of infection for mother and baby, especially where access to advanced care is limited.
• Leading causes of maternal death: maternal sepsis, obstetric haemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, severe hypertension in pregnancy.
(d)
• Antenatal care is care received from health professionals during pregnancy to make sure mother and baby are as well as possible.
• Postnatal care is the support and medical attention to mothers and newborns in the weeks and months after childbirth: monitoring health, breastfeeding guidance, emotional support.

questions.question:
Describe the amniotic fluid under the following headings:
(a) Nature, source and volume.
(b) Composition.
(c) Functions.
(d) Explain the clinical significance of abnormal volumes of amniotic fluid.
(e) Distinguish between the chorion and the amnion.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Amniotic fluid is straw-coloured and alkaline; it is secreted from the amniotic membranes, exudates from the decidua and placental vessels, and fetal urine.
• Normal volume is 400-1,500 mls; it increases about 30 mls per week, is most abundant in mid-trimester and falls to about 1 litre near term (38 weeks), partly as the fetus swallows it.
(b)
Specific gravity 1,010; 99% water; pH 7.0-7.5; the 1% solid matter is lanugo, hair, epithelial cells, vernix caseosa, protein, glucose, sodium, potassium and calcium.
(c)
• Functions: protective medium against injury and shock absorber; equalizes pressure of uterine contractions over fetus and cord; permits free fetal movement.
• Functions: maintains fetal temperature; flushes the birth canal before and at delivery; provides nutritive material; helps impede entry of bacteria into the uterus.
• Functions: aids effacement and dilatation where there is poor application of the presenting part.
(d)
• Less than 300 mls is low volume (oligohydramnios).
• More than 1,500 mls is high volume (polyhydramnios).
• Polyhydramnios and multiple pregnancy are listed as possible reasons why the uterus may be larger than the gestational age, and as examples of overdistension that may trigger contractions.
(e)
• Chorion: thick, rough, opaque and fragile; lines the decidua vera; ruptures easily and can be retained at delivery of the placenta.
• Amnion: smooth, translucent and tough, much stronger than the chorion; forms the sac holding fetus, fluid and cord; derived from the inner cell mass; hardly retained and can be stripped up to the cord insertion.

questions.question:
After delivery of the placenta, the nurse notes a hole in the membranes with blood vessels running into it, and the mother continues to bleed.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A hole in the membranes with blood vessels running to it indicates a succenturiate (accessory) lobe of the placenta, possibly retained.
• A retained accessory lobe may lead to postpartum haemorrhage.
(b)
• Placenta fenestrata: abnormal hole in the middle of the placenta, may be wrongly taken for a missing lobe.
• Other variations: circumvallate placenta (opaque ring, no significance), battledore or velamentous cord insertion, bipartite/tripartite placenta, placenta accreta (embedded beyond normal level, separation impossible).
(c)
• Examine the placenta and membranes for completeness and measure all blood loss; check the uterus is well contracted; keep the woman under observation for at least one hour.
• Contraction and retraction act as living ligatures; ergometrine 0.5 mg or syntometrine 1 ml given after the placenta and membranes are out.
• Escalate: suspected retained tissue requires doctor review (for puerperal haemorrhage); To differentiate causes of bleeding (tears, atony), swab the vulva and examine perineum and vaginal wall for lacerations.

questions.question:
A woman presents with a very painful, tender, red, swollen and hot area near the vaginal opening. A Bartholin's abscess is diagnosed and marsupialization is planned.
(a) Name the procedure and drugs used.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before and after.
(c) Describe the monitoring parameters and danger signs.
(d) Describe the follow-up care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Marsupialization: the cyst or abscess is incised and thoroughly drained, the incision usually made on the inner labial surface and the walls of the cavity sutured; antibiotics and analgesics are given; swabs taken for culture and sensitivity.
• It is the best treatment because many abscesses recur.
(b)
• Before: adequate rest, reassure, relieve pain, explain the procedure to reduce anxiety; vulval shave is omitted because of pain and swelling; give a warm bath for cleansing and soothing.
• After: relieve severe pain with prescribed analgesic, observe the vulval area, vulval toilet 4-hourly, adequate rest.
(c)
Observe the vulva; danger signs: recurrence of abscess, infection with streptococci, staphylococci or gonococci.
(d)
Discharge after about 48 hours with instructions to maintain vulval hygiene, frequent baths at least twice daily, and complete the prescribed antibiotics at home.

(a)
• Poor diet and food insecurity; poverty, unemployment and high cost of nutrient-rich foods; limited education and nutrition knowledge.
• Frequent infections such as malaria, measles and recurrent diarrhoea; limited access to healthcare; cultural practices and food taboos; rural residence (rural rates of underweight, wasting and stunting were higher than urban).
• Marasmus is characterized by severe calorie and protein deficiency leading to extreme weight loss, muscle wasting and weakness.
(b)
• Wasting is life-threatening if untreated; weakened immunity, increased infections and lower response to vaccines; stunting and impaired cognitive development.
• Impaired cardiac and renal function, GI changes, delayed wound healing, and apathy or depression.
(c)
• Screen at any contact point; assess and monitor growth; give nutrition education to parents and caregivers; promote breastfeeding and appropriate complementary feeding.
• Treatment of severe malnutrition in Nigeria by ICRC uses F-75 milk during initial treatment; hygiene, safe water and immunization reduce infection-related malnutrition.
• Priority: nutritional treatment and prevention of infection.
questions.question:
A child under five years from a low-income rural family is brought to the clinic. The child is extremely thin with muscle wasting and weakness, and the mother reports recurrent attacks of diarrhoea.
(a) Identify the risk factors for this child's condition.
(b) State the complications that may follow (child and later life).
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.

Describe the introduction of complementary (solid) foods to an infant under the following headings:
(a) Definition and timing.
(b) The recommended steps of introduction.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practices to advise caregivers.
(d) Explain the rationale behind each key step and the consequences of deviation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Introduction to solid foods (complementary feeding) is the process of introducing foods other than breast milk or formula to meet the infant's growing nutritional needs.
• Timing: the AAP recommendation is about 6 months, when infants have the motor skills to eat from a spoon (e.g. sitting with support, holding the head up).
(b)
• Readiness signs: good head control, interest in what others eat, sitting with support and loss of the tongue-thrust reflex.
• Steps: start with single-ingredient runny purees (iron-fortified cereals, fruits, vegetables); introduce one new food every 3-5 days; move gradually to mashed and finely chopped foods; offer a variety of foods.
• Breast milk or formula remains the primary source of nutrition in the first year; solid foods complement milk and do not replace it; milk remains the primary drink until age one, then cow's milk can be introduced.
(c)
• Nursing roles: nutritional assessment and dietary histories, health education on balanced diets, growth monitoring, promoting exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months with appropriate complementary feeding.
• Advise gentle, responsive feeding: watch hunger and fullness cues; avoid force-feeding or pressuring the child.
• Advise consulting the paediatrician before starting solids; use locally available, culturally accepted and affordable foods; begin with small mashed portions.
• Hygiene: handwashing before preparing or feeding, safe food handling and clean water.
(d)
• Introducing one food every 3-5 days lets potential allergies or adverse reactions be identified systematically.
• Gradual textures help develop chewing skills and adaptation to different consistencies; a wide variety gives a well-rounded diet.
• Consequences of deviation: inadequate or poor-quality complementary foods contribute to malnutrition; pressure to eat can be detrimental to intake; contamination causes infections that impair appetite and absorption.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman in the second trimester is due for intermittent preventive treatment of malaria with sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP).
(a) Name the drug, dose and purpose.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after.
(c) Describe monitoring parameters and danger signs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, 3 tablets (500 mg sulphadoxine and 25 mg pyrimethamine each) at scheduled antenatal visits in the second and third trimester.
• Purpose: preventive chemotherapy to prevent malaria infection and its consequences in pregnant women; malaria in pregnancy poses risks to mother and fetus.
(b)
• Before: counsel on the benefit of IPT; screen for history of allergic reaction to sulphonamide.
• During: the drug should be taken in the presence of the midwife/health worker.
• After: document administration in the client record; at least one month interval between the 2 doses.
(c)
• Side effects: nausea, vomiting, urticarial rash, allergy to sulphonamide, headache, insomnia.
• Danger signs/rash needing review: urticarial rash or allergy.

questions.question:
A new family planning client attends the clinic. The nurse plans a Pap smear, urinalysis and pregnancy test before method selection.
(a) Name the procedures and state their purpose.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after.
(c) Describe the monitoring parameters.
(d) Describe referral and follow-up care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pap smear: screening test collecting cervical cells examined under a microscope to detect pre-cancerous changes, indicated for all new clients; urinalysis: albumin, sugar, acetone; pregnancy test: confirms or excludes pregnancy.
• Purpose overall: exclude pregnancy, detect abnormalities, treat appropriately and choose the proper family planning method.
(b)
• Before: reassure, explain the procedure and make sure the client is physically and emotionally ready; provide privacy and a chaperone; do not force the examination.
• During: handwashing, protective gloves and mask, sterile equipment, avoid distractions, avoid offensive words or facial gestures.
• After: make the client comfortable, relieve anxiety about results, explain post-procedure actions to avoid complications, store and handle materials properly.
(c)
Monitoring: results of the tests; in urine observe colour, odour, amount, deposit and specific gravity.
(d)
Referral: client needing further management may be referred; continuing-client counselling can refer elsewhere if needed.

(a)
Vesico-vaginal fistula (VVF), an artificial opening between the bladder or urethra and the vagina.
(b)
• Causes: prolonged pressure of the vertex on the vagina during obstructed labour, obstetric or pelvic operation, radiation burns after cervical cancer treatment, untreated cancer.
• Pathophysiology: abnormal communication between structures in the genital tract; Signs: incontinence of urine, several days of dysuria and haematuria, urinary infection, vaginal discharge, wet vulva and perineum, excoriation, ammonia smell, tenderness of the genital area.
(c)
• Foley catheter in situ for 10 days or longer with sealed drainage; prescribed antibiotics; surgical repair if large, small fistulae usually heal without operation.
• Prevention: very rare where good obstetric care is available; child marriage and motherhood are associated with high risk of VVF.
questions.question:
A woman had obstructed labour days ago. She now has continuous leakage of urine from the vagina, constantly wet vulva and perineum, excoriated skin and an ammonia smell.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State predisposing factors, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms.
(c) Describe nursing management and prevention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• First hour (fourth stage) is the most critical: most PPH, shock or sudden collapse occurs then; observe pulse, BP, involution, lochia, perineum, bladder and voiding every 15 minutes.
• Check that the uterus is well contracted, swab the vulva, examine the perineum and vaginal wall for lacerations, measure all blood loss, and examine the placenta and membranes for completeness.
(b)
Risk of/actual postpartum haemorrhage (uterus not well contracted), with need for continuous vigilance.
(c)
Contraction and retraction of uterine fibres act as living ligatures that compress blood vessels; oxytocin acts on uterine muscle to prevent haemorrhage; a full bladder can cause non-separation of placenta and PPH.
(d)
• Give ergometrine 0.5 mg or syntometrine 1 ml (i.m) after the placenta and membranes are out; check the uterus is well contracted; suture lacerations if necessary.
• Make the woman comfortable (change linen, sterile pad), check and record vital signs, keep her in the labour room for at least one hour, offer a drink and encourage her to pass urine.
• If BP is high, give sedation orally or intravenously to prevent postpartum eclampsia.
(e)
• Educate on care of the baby, the need for postnatal visit and family planning; promote breastfeeding.
• Evaluation: uterus well contracted, blood loss measured and controlled, vital signs stable.
questions.question:
A multipara has just delivered a healthy term baby and the placenta and membranes are complete. She is now in the first hour after delivery, looks pale and drowsy, and her uterus feels soft.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings to obtain.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnosis/problem.
(c) Explain the physiological basis.
(d) Give the priority nursing interventions.
(e) Outline the health education and evaluation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Aims: promote physical and mental health through health education; build a trusting relationship; monitor progress of pregnancy for maternal health and normal fetal development; reduce maternal and perinatal mortality; recognize deviations and manage or refer promptly.
• Further aims: ensure a live, mature, healthy baby; support the mother's choice of infant feeding and prepare for lactation; offer advice on parenthood; provide holistic care for her individual needs.
(b)
• Booking: women start visits as soon as pregnancy is suspected or menses are missed for two months, to confirm pregnancy and plan care; baseline B/P, blood values, urinalysis and fetal development are recorded.
• History areas: social, family (e.g. diabetes, sickle cell disease, hypertension, twins), medical (cardiac disease, diabetes, rubella, kidney disease), surgical (e.g. caesarean section, D&C), obstetric (menstrual, previous pregnancies, labour, puerperium, baby's history) and present pregnancy (LMP for EDD, morning sickness, bleeding, smoking, alcohol, parity).
(c)
• Investigations: Hb at booking, 28-32 weeks and after 36 weeks (more often if abnormal); PCV, FBC, Rhesus factor and blood group; VDRL/Wassermann and HIV; urine tested for glucose, albumin and acetone.
• Other tests: Rhesus antibody titre at booking, 28, 32, 36 weeks and before labour if Rhesus positive; vaginal examination at booking or at least once; X-ray or ultrasound to ascertain maturity; pelvic assessment by the doctor on primigravidae at 36-38 weeks.
• Subsequent visits: every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly; routine procedures repeat except full history; BP, urinalysis, weight and health counselling at each visit.
(d)
• History taking: be patient (especially with primigravidae), gain cooperation, provide privacy, be friendly and kind, ask direct questions, do not help her answer, use simple non-technical language.
• General examination: check BP, weight, height and urinalysis; ensure she empties her bladder, screen for privacy, explain the procedure; examine head to toe, breasts and lower limbs; report abnormal findings to the doctor.
• After examination: record findings in the antenatal notes, give routine drugs (haematinics and antimalarials), refer abnormal findings and give the next appointment with a thorough explanation.
(e)
• History taking is not just record keeping: it assesses her health, shows what to guard against in management and method of delivery, and helps decide whether hospital confinement is needed; previous caesarean scars may not stretch well in labour.
• Early booking confirms pregnancy and establishes baseline data that serve as a standard for later comparison; repeated Hb and antibody titres monitor anaemia and Rhesus status.
questions.question:
Describe the process of antenatal care under the following headings:
(a) The aims of antenatal care.
(b) Booking and the areas covered in history taking.
(c) Routine investigations and the schedule of subsequent visits.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities during booking, history taking and the general examination.
(e) Explain the rationale for history taking, for starting antenatal visits early and for the investigations done.

A primigravida is in established labour. Her bladder has not been emptied since admission and she says she has the urge to pass urine but cannot. She is lying on her back in bed.
(a) Identify the risk factors that predispose a woman in labour to bladder problems.
(b) State the maternal complications of a full bladder in labour.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• In labour the urethra stretches from 4 cm to about 15 cm or more, almost occluding the lumen, making micturition and even catheterization difficult.
• Pressure on the sacral plexus of nerves (more common with occipito-posterior position) can cause an increased desire to pass urine without being able to, or conversely a lack of sensation in the bladder, leading to retention.
(b)
• A full bladder delays the first and second stages of labour.
• Bruising of the bladder and urethra may occur, in addition to overstretching.
• A full bladder can lead to non-separation of the placenta and postpartum haemorrhage.
• If not emptied at the end of the first stage, there is dribbling of urine with each expulsive contraction in the second stage.
(c)
• Nursing: encourage the woman to pass urine every two hours and test all specimens; a full bladder and bowel can cause uterine inertia and delay engagement of the head.
• Nursing: keep the bladder emptied by catheterization at the end of the first stage or start of the second stage if it is full; use the lateral position to reduce vena cava compression. the priority is emptying the bladder because it prevents delay in engagement and postpartum haemorrhage in the third stage.

(a)
• Measles vaccine is typically given in combination with mumps and rubella (MMR) in two doses: the first around 12-15 months and the second around 4-6 years.
• Community-wide vaccination is the most effective way to prevent measles.
(b)
• Before: educate caregivers about measles prevention, signs and symptoms and the importance of vaccination; address misconceptions.
• During/after: maintain high vaccination coverage; practise hygiene.
(c)
• Measles danger signs: rash, fever, running nose, cough, red watery eyes, white spots inside the cheeks.
• Complications to watch for in disease: encephalitis, severe diarrhoea and dehydration, ear infections, pneumonia.
(d)
Follow-up: second dose at 4-6 years; isolate suspected cases and contact tracing; Vaccination builds herd immunity and protects those who cannot be vaccinated.
questions.question:
A 12-month-old child is brought for measles vaccination.
(a) Name the immunization and schedule.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after.
(c) Describe monitoring parameters and danger signs.
(d) Describe the follow-up care.

A nurse is to weigh an infant at a child welfare clinic as part of growth monitoring.
(a) Name the procedure and its purpose.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after.
(c) Describe monitoring parameters and danger signs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Weighing: weight is the most common way of assessing body size; it is easy and accurate; used for growth monitoring and plotted on a growth chart.
(b)
• Before: check that the scale reads zero (scales calibrated weekly); weigh the child undressed or in a vest only; remove the nappy, and always remove a wet nappy.
• During: young children lie on the scale; wait until the child lies still and record to the nearest 10 g; older children stand and are recorded to the nearest 100 g (0.1 kg), with all clothes removed except underpants.
• After: plot the weight on the growth chart (gender-specific charts) and compare with earlier measurements.
(c)
• Frequency: monthly in the first year, every 2 months in the second year, then every 6 months to age 5; also measured at each clinic visit.
• Danger signs: no increase in weight, or weight loss, which is often the earliest sign of illness or malnutrition.
• Also measure length/height, head circumference (birth, 14 weeks, 12 months) and MUAC (every 3 months) where needed.

(a)
Salpingitis is inflammation of the uterine tube, acute or chronic.
(b)
• Acute causes: post-abortal infection, gonorrhoea, peritoneal infection such as appendicitis or TB.
• Organisms: streptococcus, staphylococcus, E. coli.
• Acute features: sudden pain, pyrexia (38-39), malaise, tachycardia, nausea, purulent vaginal discharge.
• Chronic causes: unresolved acute stage; tuberculosis (very rare now).
• Chronic features: abdominal pain, dysmenorrhoea, menorrhagia, dyspareunia, vaginal discharge, backache, lethargy, loss of appetite.
(c)
• Chronic salpingitis leads to chronic pelvic infection; management includes bed rest, analgesics and surgical intervention.
• Fallopian tube blockage from STIs is a cause of female infertility.
(d)
• Acute: admit, bed rest until temperature subsides, vital signs 4-hourly (especially temperature and pulse), encourage fluids, observe urinary output, balanced diet.
• Give antibiotics once vaginal and urethral swabs are taken (gonococcal infection, syphilis) and analgesics.
• Prevention: treat STIs and post-abortal infection early (as listed in STI prevention).
questions.question:
Describe salpingitis in full:
(a) Definition and types (acute and chronic).
(b) Aetiology, causative organisms and clinical features.
(c) State how it relates to common complications such as chronic pelvic infection.
(d) Explain how it may affect the reproductive and other systems, and the nursing measures.

A woman 10 days after an unhygienic home delivery presents with jaw pain and difficulty opening her mouth; loud noises trigger sudden painful muscle spasms.
(a) Identify the risk factors that led to this condition.
(b) State the maternal complications.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Maternal tetanus follows unhygienic delivery practices or unsafe abortion or miscarriage practices, including septic procedures and wounds during pregnancy.
• Lack of protection by tetanus toxoid; maternal tetanus occurs during pregnancy or within 6 weeks of its end; incubation 3-21 days, most within 14 days.
(b)
• Muscle spasms in the back, abdomen and extremities; blood pressure fluctuations or rapid heart rate; seizures from difficulty swallowing; headache.
• Complications of tetanus: laryngospasm, fractures, pulmonary embolism, aspiration pneumonia, breathing difficulty, and death (1 to 2 in 10 cases).
(c)
• No cure: wound care, antitoxin therapy (passive immunization), sedatives to control spasms, antibiotics, airway clearance and breathing assistance, feeding tube, low sound and light.
• Prevention priority: TT-containing vaccine for women of childbearing age is the most cost-effective way to eliminate maternal tetanus; clean hands, gloves, a clean environment, sterilized instruments.
• Mothers who recover require vaccination because they have little or no natural immunity.

questions.question:
Describe the management of the third stage of labour under the following headings:
(a) Physiology and methods of placental separation.
(b) Signs of separation and methods of delivery of the placenta.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities and the safe practice.
(d) Explain the rationale behind each key step and the consequences of deviation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The third stage is separation and expulsion of placenta and membranes and control of bleeding; contraction and retraction reduce the placental site so the placenta buckles off the uterine wall.
• Schultze method (80%): separation starts at the centre with a retroplacental clot; fetal surface appears first. Matthews Duncan (20%): separation starts at the edge; maternal surface appears first with trickling of blood.
(b)
• Signs: cord lengthens, uterus becomes harder and mobile, small gush of blood, fundus rises.
• Methods: controlled cord traction (with Syntometrine 2 mls, 5 units oxytocin or 0.5 mg ergometrine), fundal pressure, maternal effort, Brandt-Andrews manoeuvre.
• Contraindications to controlled cord traction: preterm baby, macerated fetus.
(c)
• Place the left hand on the uterus to check that it is contracted (hard like a cricket ball) without meddling; observe for separation and bleeding.
• Fundal pressure only when the placenta has separated and the uterus is well contracted; the woman breathes through her mouth to relax abdominal muscles.
• After delivery: ergometrine 0.5 mg or syntometrine 1 ml i.m.; swab vulva, examine perineum and vaginal wall, suture if necessary; examine placenta and membranes for completeness; measure blood loss.
• Keep the woman in the labour room for at least one hour (fourth stage) of close observation.
(d)
• Controlled cord traction reduces the risk of PPH and shortens the third stage; success depends on knowing the oxytocic action and proper timing.
• Contraction and retraction act as living ligatures compressing vessels; clotting is of little value until later.
• A full bladder can lead to non-separation of the placenta and PPH.

questions.question:
A breastfeeding mother reports that her milk supply is insufficient. She has been anxious, sleeps poorly, takes a poor diet, and lacks privacy and support from her husband.
(a) Identify the risk factors.
(b) State the complications for mother and baby.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Causes of insufficient milk or failure of lactation: maternal illness, fetal death, emotional crises, fear, anxiety, very poor diet, pain, lack of privacy, lack of breast stimulation, pregnancy (increased oestrogen), an unsympathetic and uncooperative husband.
• Poor general health of the mother and poor nutritional status may also prevent breastfeeding.
(b)
• The supply of milk may be inadequate for the baby; the nutritional wellbeing of the mother may be endangered by lactation.
• If a baby stops sucking or never starts, the breast stops making milk.
(c)
• Nursing: correct positioning and attachment; put the baby to the breast on demand; let the baby empty one breast before the other; adequate diet with sufficient protein; sufficient rest and sleep; psychological support.
• Medical: metoclopramide may be prescribed to increase release of prolactin.
• Justification: if the mother is in good psychological status, correct positioning and attachment can eliminate the problem.
• Breastfeeding mothers should eat protein, carbohydrate, vitamins A and B, calcium, zinc and fluids.

(a)
• Growth is the increase in body size over time; the best method is to measure size and repeat later; five measurements: weight, height/length, head circumference, MUAC (and growth charts for monitoring).
• Weight monthly in the first year, every 2 months in the second year, every 6 months to 5 years; head circumference at birth, 14 weeks, 12 months; MUAC every 3 months; length/height every 6 months.
(b)
• Development is the way a child grows, changes and develops skills; five stages: newborn (0-3 months), infant (3-12 months), toddler (1-3 years), preschool (3-4 years), school age (4-5 years).
• Domains: communication and speech, physical (gross and fine motor), social and emotional, cognitive; all interlink at every stage.
(c)
• Factors: hereditary, nutrition, parents' behaviour, parenting, social and cultural practices, environment; also prenatal environment, sex, socio-economic status, ordinal position, intelligence, hormonal balance and emotion.
• Positive factors: good nutrition, stimulation and interaction, secure attachment, adequate sleep.
(d)
• The brain is most receptive in the first five years; early experiences influence neurological connections, behaviour, social skills, relationships and school readiness into adulthood.
• Head circumference assesses brain growth under 36 months; microcephaly suggests a small brain, a large head suggests hydrocephaly.
• Unmet developmental needs can cause future mental health problems (low self-esteem, poor attention, insecurity) and failure to acquire language and social skills.
• Lower socio-economic groups and poor nutrition are less favourable to development.
(e)
• Growth: increase in size (quantitative, measured by weight, height).
• Development: acquisition of skills and abilities in a predictable sequence across domains, with variation between children.
questions.question:
Describe growth and development of the child under the following headings:
(a) Definition and measurement of growth.
(b) Child development, stages and domains.
(c) Factors affecting growth and development.
(d) Explain the clinical basis of why early childhood is critical and why some children are at higher risk of delay.
(e) Distinguish between growth and development.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Nausea with or without vomiting, mainly retching rather than actual vomiting, most marked on waking but possible at any time of day; occurs at 4-16 weeks in about 50% of pregnant women.
• Assess for other conditions with similar symptoms (appendicitis), for persistent or severe symptoms, for starvation and dehydration, and for emotional problems.
(b)
Nausea and vomiting (morning sickness), a minor disorder of pregnancy in the digestive system; minor disorders are not a threat to life but distress the woman and can interfere with nutrition, sleep and household chores.
(c)
Associated with high levels of oestrogen and progesterone; hypoglycaemia may contribute; other suggested links are gastric overloading, slowed peristalsis, enlarged uterus and emotional factors; the exact cause is not known.
(d)
• Give understanding and encouragement that the problem should resolve between 12 and 16 weeks; involve the husband in her care; solve emotional problems.
• Close monitoring to ensure it does not become severe; rule out similar conditions such as appendicitis; avoid starvation and dehydration.
(e)
• Teach: dry biscuits or toast and carbohydrate snacks at bedtime and before rising with a cup of tea are better tolerated than full meals; avoid fatty, irritating food; eat easily digestible food; get up slowly.
• Teach: spices such as cola or chewing stick can refresh the mouth; avoid self-medication because it can be hazardous to the fetus. the expected outcome stated is resolution by 12-16 weeks and prevention of severe symptoms.
questions.question:
A primigravida at about 8 weeks' gestation attends the antenatal clinic complaining of nausea and retching, worst on waking in the morning. She fears she may be unable to cope and is tempted to buy drugs on her own.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings you would gather.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnosis/problem.
(c) Explain the physiological basis of the problem.
(d) List the priority nursing interventions.
(e) Outline the health education.

Describe cervical cancer under the following headings:
(a) Definition and types.
(b) Signs and symptoms (early and advanced).
(c) Diagnostic procedures.
(d) Explain the clinical basis for its development from HPV infection and why the disease is often detected late.
(e) Distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary prevention of cervical cancer.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cervical cancer is cancer occurring in the cervix; globally it is the second most common cancer in women after breast cancer; sub-Saharan Africa has the highest mortality burden.
• Types: squamous cell carcinoma (up to 90%), adenocarcinoma (mucus-producing cells) and mixed carcinoma.
(b)
• Symptoms appear only when cells grow through the top layer of cervical tissue: irregular bleeding, bleeding after intercourse, douching or pelvic examination, heavier longer periods, increased (foul, blood-tinged) discharge, pain during intercourse, post-menopausal bleeding.
• Advanced disease: back or pelvic pain, difficulty urinating or defecating, leg swelling, fatigue, weight loss, urine or faeces leaking from the vagina, bone fractures.
(c)
History, physical and speculum examination, rectal examination, Pap smear, colposcopy with biopsy, abdominal ultrasound, cystoscopy, chest X-ray, thermography and pelvic MRI.
(d)
• Progression from HPV infection takes 5-15 years through four stages: HPV transmission, acute infection, viral persistence with precancerous lesion, and invasion through the basement membrane.
• HPV is transmitted by sexual contact and usually causes no symptoms, so it is easily transferred unknowingly; change begins at the squamo-columnar junction (CIN from mild to severe dysplasia to carcinoma in situ).
• Early stages may be asymptomatic, and untreated cancer becomes invasive and metastasizes to distant organs.
(e)
• Primary prevention: avoid predisposing factors (delay sex, avoid multiple partners, treat vaginal infections, stop smoking), healthy diet, and HPV vaccination.
• Secondary prevention: screening and treatment of precancerous lesions in asymptomatic women (Pap smear, VIA/VIAM, HPV DNA, colposcopy).
• Tertiary prevention: treatment of cervical cancer (surgery and/or radiotherapy, chemotherapy in late stages) and palliative care.
• The four components of control: primary prevention, early detection, diagnosis and treatment, palliative care.

(a)
• HPV vaccine (Gardasil quadrivalent/Gardasil 9 or Cervarix bivalent); intramuscular; 3 doses after six months periods of starting the vaccine; females 9-26 years and males 9-15 years.
• Vaccination against HPV is the best preventive measure against cervical cancer.
(b)
• Before: raise awareness about the vaccine; health education to the girl and caregiver; confirm eligibility (a woman who had her uterus and cervix removed should not have the vaccine).
• During: give the vaccine intramuscularly as recommended; practise handwashing and sterility (from the general precautions given for clinical procedures).
• After: educate that vaccination does not replace screening; screening with Pap test is still advised from age 21.
(c)
Follow-up: complete the 3-dose schedule; later Pap smear screening according to age-based recommendations.
questions.question:
A 12-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother for HPV vaccination to protect against cervical cancer.
(a) Name the immunization, its route, schedule and eligible group.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after.
(c) Describe the follow-up care.

A 42-year-old woman in her seventh pregnancy, known to have anaemia and malaria, books for antenatal care in a developing country.
(a) Identify the risk factors for maternal death.
(b) State the maternal complications.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Extremes of age (younger than 18 or older than 40); too many and too frequent pregnancies; being in a developing country; conditions worsened by pregnancy (anaemia, malaria, CCF, glomerulonephritis).
• A grande multipara is prone to complications (history of present pregnancy).
(b)
• Direct: excessive blood loss, infection, high blood pressure, unsafe abortion, obstructed labour.
• Indirect: deaths from worsening of existing conditions such as anaemia, malaria, diabetes, sickle cell disease, CCF and glomerulonephritis.
(c)
• Antenatal screening to select high-risk women for hospital delivery with meticulous supervision; routine haematinics and antimalarials; Hb checks at booking, 28-32 and after 36 weeks.
• Wider strategies: improved antenatal, intra-partum and postnatal care, emergency obstetric services, family planning, health education.
• Justification: the aim of screening is to detect conditions putting mother and fetus at high risk, which reduces perinatal mortality.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman at 28 weeks' gestation complains of backache and cramps in her legs at night. She wears high-heeled shoes and sits for long periods.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnosis/problem.
(c) Explain the physiological basis.
(d) List the priority nursing interventions.
(e) Outline health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Backache (about 75% of women experience it at some stage), posture used to balance the gravid uterus, and cramps in the legs; sciatic-like pain may occur.
(b)
Minor disorders of pregnancy in the musculoskeletal system: backache and cramp; they are not life-threatening but distress the woman and should not be treated lightly.
(c)
• Pregnancy hormones soften the ligaments, and posture adopted to balance the weight of the gravid uterus contributes to backache.
• Cramp: actual cause not known; attributed to ischaemia or changes in pH or electrolytes (calcium, chloride, vitamin B), though there is no significant evidence; may be due to temporary circulatory changes in the legs.
(d)
• Health educate on posture; sleep on a flat surface or with a board under the bed; physiotherapy (tailor sitting position); lie on one side away from the discomfort with pillows supporting the limb.
• Cramp: calcium gluconate, milk, cheese, vitamin B; gentle leg exercises at bedtime or in a warm bath.
(e)
Teach good low-heeled shoes (low heels with a broad base), adequate rest and avoidance of long standing.

questions.question:
A woman at 28 weeks' gestation has a fundal height much larger than expected for her dates.
(a) Identify the possible explanations/risk factors.
(b) State the complications that may follow.
(c) Describe nursing and medical management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• If dates are correct but the uterus is large, possibilities are multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, a large fetus, or a fetus plus uterine fibroid.
• First review the date of the last normal menses and note the size of the patient.
(b)
• Polyhydramnios is more than 1,500 mls of amniotic fluid; overdistension (multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios) can stimulate the uterus to contract early.
• Round abdominal shape may reflect multiparity, transverse lie, obesity or polyhydramnios.
(c)
• Nursing: inspect size and shape, palpate (fundal height, lie, presentation), auscultate fetal heart; the history identifies LMP and EDD.
• Medical: ultrasound scan to ascertain maturity and number of fetuses; report to the doctor.
• Justification: all findings must be considered together; if information does not correspond, repeat and think again.

questions.question:
Describe pneumonia in children under five years in full:
(a) Definition and classification.
(b) Causes, risk factors and transmission.
(c) State how pneumonia relates to its common complications and to the stage of the child's care.
(d) Explain how pneumonia may spread its effects to other systems, and outline the preventive nursing measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pneumonia is a respiratory infection causing inflammation of the air sacs in the lungs, which may fill with fluid or pus, making breathing difficult; it ranges from mild to severe.
• Two main types: bacterial (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus) and viral (e.g. influenza, RSV, adenovirus, coronaviruses).
(b)
• RSV is the most common cause in young children; it is the leading cause of death in under-fives worldwide.
• Risk factors: age 5 or younger with a developing immune system (higher in premature babies); malnutrition, sickle cell disease, lung and heart disease; crowded places; air pollution or toxic fumes.
• Transmission: inhaled viruses and bacteria from the nose or throat; airborne droplets from a cough or sneeze; through blood especially during and shortly after birth.
(c)
• Signs in children: fast or laboured breathing, rapid heartbeat, fever, decreased appetite, vomiting, irritability, lethargy, possible bluish lips or nails.
• Treatment: first-line amoxicillin dispersible tablets; cotrimoxazole daily for HIV-infected children; community health workers can treat with oral antibiotics; hospitalization only for severe cases.
(d)
• Bacteraemia and septic shock (low blood pressure); lung abscess; respiratory failure (lungs fill with fluid, cannot transfer oxygen, bluish skin, confusion).
• Heart failure (20% of hospitalized patients also had heart problems); pleural effusion, empyema and pleurisy (sharp chest pain on breathing).
• Prevention: immunization against Hib, pneumococcus, measles and pertussis is the most effective way; exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and adequate nutrition.
• Prevention: reduce indoor air pollution, good hygiene in crowded homes, handwashing, HIV prevention and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.
• WHO/UNICEF GAPPD: protect, prevent and treat; seek medical help right away if a child has symptoms.

questions.question:
Describe Bartholin's cyst and abscess in full:
(a) Definition and aetiology.
(b) Clinical features of each.
(c) State how it relates to infection and recurrence.
(d) Explain the treatment, surgical procedure and nursing care (pre-operative, post-operative and on discharge).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cyst formation or abscess are two common conditions of the Bartholin's gland.
• A cyst occurs when the gland becomes blocked, usually after infection of the gland (Bartholinitis) with fibrosis within the gland or duct.
(b)
• Cyst: usually painless; may become acutely infected with streptococci, staphylococci or gonococci.
• Abscess: extremely painful, tender to touch, red, swollen and hot.
(c)
• Many abscesses recur; therefore the best treatment is marsupialization.
• Infecting organisms: streptococci, staphylococci, gonococci; swabs are taken for culture and sensitivity.
(d)
• Treatment: rest, analgesics, prescribed antibiotics, surgical excision of abscess for drainage; marsupialization: incision, thorough drainage, incision on the inner labial surface, walls sutured.
• Pre-operative nursing: rest, reassurance, pain relief, explanation, vulval shave omitted because of pain and swelling, warm bath.
• Post-operative: relieve severe pain, observe the vulva, vulval toilet 4-hourly, rest.
• Discharge: usually after 48 hours with instructions on vulval hygiene; frequent baths at least twice daily; complete antibiotics.

(a)
• Cervical erosion is not an ulcer but a red velvety area at the external os from outgrowth of columnar epithelium of the endocervix replacing squamous epithelium; it often follows chronic cervicitis.
• Features: most are symptomless; mucoid discharge, postcoital bleeding, low backache, dyspareunia.
• Aetiology: parturition, contraceptive pill, persistence of a condition normal in infancy.
• Treatment: cervical smear in all cases; diathermic cauterization or cryosurgery (carbon dioxide under pressure freezes tissue); conization under general anaesthesia.
(b)
• Cervicitis: infection of the cervical epithelium and stroma, usually following erosion; features and treatment as for erosion.
• Cervical polyps: nodular growths arising from the endocervix associated with chronic cervicitis; irregular bleeding especially after coitus.
(c)
• Women who have given birth or who take the contraceptive pill are more susceptible to erosion; chronic cervicitis predisposes.
• A cervical smear must be done in all cases to exclude cervical carcinoma.
• Polyps require histological examination to exclude malignancy, and dilatation and curettage to exclude endometrial carcinoma.
(d)
• Erosion: flat red velvety area at the os; usually symptomless or mucoid discharge; treated with cautery, cryosurgery or conization.
• Polyp: nodular growth on a stalk from the endocervix; bleeding after coitus; treated by twisting the polyp on its stalk until avulsed.
• After conization, advise the client that vaginal bleeding may occur when the tissue sloughs.
questions.question:
Describe the common conditions of the cervix under the following headings:
(a) Cervical erosion (definition, features, aetiology and treatment).
(b) Cervicitis and cervical polyps.
(c) Explain the clinical basis for why some women develop these conditions and why a cervical smear is required.
(d) Distinguish between cervical erosion and cervical polyp.

A woman with cervical cancer has a pelvic imaging report showing that the cancer has grown into the walls of the pelvis and is blocking one or both ureters causing hydronephrosis. There is no spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant sites. She also complains of urine leaking through the vagina.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• By the FIGO staging, cancer grown into the pelvic walls and/or blocking ureters with hydronephrosis and no lymph node or distant spread is Stage IIIB.
• Leakage of urine from the vagina (VVF) is listed among advanced cervical cancer features; stage IV would involve bladder or rectum or distant organs.
(b)
• Stage IIIA: spread to the lower vagina without pelvic wall involvement; Stage IIIC: spread to pelvic (IIIC1) or para-aortic (IIIC2) nodes; Stage IVA: spread to the bladder or rectum or growing out of the pelvis.
• Stage IIB: beyond the cervix into the parametria but not the pelvic walls.
(c)
• Staging is one of the most important factors in deciding treatment and success; clinical stage is based on physical exam, biopsies, imaging, cystoscopy and proctoscopy.
• Treatment options: surgery (e.g. radical hysterectomy, pelvic exenteration with colostomy and urinary diversion for locally invasive cancer), radiation and chemotherapy.
• Nursing: pre-operative diagnoses (chronic pain, anxiety, activity intolerance, disturbed body image, deficient knowledge); palliative care for advanced disease.

(a)
• Involution is the return of the generative organs to the pre-gravid state; the uterus shrinks by autolysis and ischaemia (self-digestion by proteolytic enzymes), assisted by contraction and retraction under oxytocin.
• Involution reduces the uterus by about a finger breadth a day; after-pains occur during breastfeeding.
(b)
• Uterine weight: 900 g at end of labour, 450 g at 1 week, 200 g at 2 weeks, 60 g at 6 weeks; cervix soft and flabby, then 2 cm, 1 cm, a slit; placental site healed by 8 weeks.
• Lochia rubra (red) 1-4 days; serosa (pink/brownish) 5-9 days; alba (creamy, greenish) 10-15 days; alkaline, heavy but not offensive odour.
(c)
• Persistent red lochia is a warning of retained products of conception and puerperial haemorrhage and should be reported without delay.
• Full bladder, lax muscle tone and infection cause sub-involution.
• Fundal height estimated daily by the same person, with the same instrument, after emptying the bladder.
(d)
• Kidneys: increased urine in first 48 hours; circulation: cardiac output rises for 48 hours and returns to normal in 4 weeks; blood: changes in clotting factors; skin: striae become silvery.
• Breasts: lactation begins 48-72 hours; GI: constipation from relaxed abdominal wall; musculoskeletal: abdominal wall flabby, responds to exercise.
• Ovulation: delayed in exclusive breastfeeders; menstruation may commence after about 4 weeks.
• Preventive nursing: early ambulation, bladder and bowel care, perineal care, breastfeeding, postnatal exercises, aseptic care.
• Shortness of breath after childbirth requires assessment to rule out PPH or other pathology.
questions.question:
Describe involution and lochia in the puerperium:
(a) Definition and the mechanism of involution of the uterus.
(b) Progressive changes in the uterus and the types of lochia.
(c) State how these relate to complications such as sub-involution and puerperal haemorrhage.
(d) Explain how puerperal changes affect other systems and the preventive nursing measures.

Describe breast milk under the following headings:
(a) Composition (water, fat, protein, carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals).
(b) Anti-infective and other protective factors.
(c) Explain the clinical basis of why exclusively breastfed babies are at lower risk of infection and allergy.
(d) Distinguish between colostrum and mature (hind) milk.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Approximate composition: water about 90%, fat 3-5%, protein 0.8-0.9%, carbohydrate (lactose) 6.9-7.2%, minerals 0.2%.
• Fats give more than 50% of calorie needs and supply DHA for brain, skin and retina; lactose gives about 40% of energy, aids calcium absorption and promotes lactobacillus; protein is easily digestible and includes lactoferrin.
• Vitamins: A, D, E (may prevent anaemia in preterm infants) and K (clotting factors; breastfed babies should receive vitamin K soon after birth); B-complex and C; minerals: iron, zinc, calcium, sodium, magnesium, selenium and copper.
(b)
• Immunoglobulins (IgA, IgG, IgM, IgE, IgD) protect the intestinal mucosa against bacteria and viruses; lysozyme destroys bacterial cell walls; lactoferrin binds iron so E. coli cannot obtain it.
• Bifidus factor promotes healthy intestinal flora (lactobacillus) and is anti-inflammatory; epidermal and insulin-like growth factors mature the digestive tract.
(c)
• Breastfed babies have lower risk of diarrhoea, gastroenteritis, respiratory, ear infections, asthma and eczema; EBF reduces morbidity by about 70%.
• Lower exposure to foreign protein creates tolerance rather than allergy; an infant's intestine cannot digest cow's milk protein before 6-9 months, which can act as an allergen.
• Breast milk changes stool pH and intestinal flora, protecting against bacterial diarrhoea; powdered milk carries a risk of bacterial contamination where hygiene is poor.
(d)
• Colostrum: first milk after birth, yellow, thicker; more lactalbumin and lactoprotein rich in antibodies giving passive immunity; very high IgA and markedly higher vitamin A than mature milk.
• Colostrum has lower carbohydrate content than mature milk; it acts as a laxative, helping to pass meconium and preventing jaundice.
• Mature (hind) milk: secreted later, differs from colostrum (higher carbohydrate).
• Lactation begins 48-72 hours after birth but is fully established about 10 days after birth (from the NURS notes).

(a)
Irregular lump, pain or tenderness, flattening or indentation, skin changes (peau d'orange), nipple discharge (may be bloody), axillary lymphadenopathy, sore or retracted nipple.
(b)
• Pre-op: deficient knowledge about cancer of the breast and treatment, anxiety about prognosis, fear of treatments, body image change or death, risk for ineffective coping, grieving, decisional conflict, chronic pain.
• Post-op: ineffective breathing pattern and airway clearance (anaesthesia), acute pain, risk for infection, self-care deficit (arm immobility), impaired skin integrity, body image disturbance.
(c)
Tumours arise from ductal or lobular epithelial cells; infiltration causes dimpling, skin thickening, nipple retraction, discharge and peau d'orange; spread is to axillary and internal mammary nodes and distant sites.
(d)
• Pre-op: admit, check vital signs, discontinue breastfeeding if lactating, give analgesic, skin preparation including armpit, obtain consent, psychological support, exercises.
• Post-op: head turned to one side for airway; vital signs quarter-hourly, half-hourly, then hourly until stable; observe wound for bleeding; NPO until bowel sounds return; IV fluids; intake-output chart; dressing; early ambulation; hygiene.
(e)
Health education: monthly BSE, clinical examination and mammography schedules; prevention of risk factors (smoking, alcohol, obesity, high-fat diet, breastfeeding for at least 1 year).
questions.question:
A woman presents with an irregular, hard lump in her breast, a reddish pitted skin like orange peel, a bloody nipple discharge and swollen lymph nodes in the armpit. Mastectomy is planned.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnoses/problems.
(c) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(d) List the priority nursing interventions (pre- and post-operative).
(e) Outline health education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Child health is a state of complete physical, mental, intellectual, social and emotional well-being, not merely absence of disease; modern concept emphasises care of the whole child.
• Factors: maternal health (nutrition, age, parity, ANC, spacing), socio-economic situation, family health, environment (sanitation, safe water), social support.
(b)
• Problems: low birth weight/preterm birth, malnutrition, infectious and parasitic infections (diarrhoea, respiratory infections, measles, TB, pertussis, polio, neonatal tetanus, diphtheria), accidents and poisoning, behavioural disorders.
• In 2020, 5.0 million children under 5 died (13,800 daily); infectious diseases including pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria remain leading causes along with preterm birth and intrapartum complications.
(c)
• Children at risk: LBW, twin birth, spacing under 2 years, no exclusive breastfeeding, failure to gain weight for 3 months, death of siblings or parents, PEM and severe infections.
• Neonatal mortality rate: deaths under 28 days per 1,000 live births; causes: LBW, asphyxia, birth injury, difficult labour, congenital anomalies, haemolytic disease, cord and placenta conditions, diarrhoea, ARI, neonatal tetanus.
• Neonatal deaths can be reduced by providing essential antenatal care; perinatal causes include poor antenatal and intranatal care, asphyxia and LBW.
(d)
• Malnutrition makes the child susceptible to infection, slows recovery, increases mortality and causes growth retardation (PEM, vitamin A, anaemia, iodine deficiency).
• Global under-five mortality fell 61% from 93 to 37 per 1,000 live births (1990-2020).
• Preventive: immunization, exclusive breastfeeding, nutrition education, clean water and hygiene, accident prevention, parenting support.
• Behavioural disorders result from inadequate parenting, lack of socio-economic support and broken homes.
questions.question:
Describe child health problems in full:
(a) Definition of child health and the factors affecting it.
(b) The major child health problems.
(c) State how these relate to children at risk and to vital statistics (neonatal and infant mortality).
(d) Explain how malnutrition and infection spread effects to other systems and the preventive nursing measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Two approved HPV vaccines: Gardasil (quadrivalent, Gardasil 9) and Cervarix (bivalent); recommended for females 9-26 years (ACIP/CDC).
• Dosage: 3 doses after six months periods of starting the vaccine; intramuscular; female 9-26 years and male 9-15 years; a woman whose uterus and cervix were removed should not have the vaccine.
(b)
• Screening techniques: Pap smear and cytology, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and with magnification (VIAM), HPV DNA identification, colposcopy and colposcopic biopsies.
• WHO: regular screening from 25 years; three-year interval for ages 25-45 and five years above 50; if only once, best age 35-45; not required above 65 if the last two smears were negative.
• By age: under 21 no screening; 21-29 cytology every 3 years; 30-65 HPV and cytology cotesting every 5 years (preferred) or cytology alone every 3 years; over 65 none if adequate prior negative screening and no high risk.
(c)
• The nurse is patient advocate, care provider, researcher, teacher, coordinator, collaborator and counsellor, ensuring early screening.
• Create awareness of HPV screening and immunisation services; community health education; continuing education for health workers.
• Media awareness; integrate screening, treatment of precancerous lesions and immunization; train health workers to serve adolescents; vaccinate young adolescents.
• Programmes must be affordable, effective and equitable, with monitoring and evaluation.
(d)
• Vaccination against HPV is the best preventive measure against cervical cancer.
• The Pap test is one of the most reliable screening tests and detects abnormal cells and precancerous changes so that they can be treated early; it is key for unvaccinated women.
• Women with a history of serious cervical pre-cancer should continue testing for at least 20 years after diagnosis, even beyond age 65.
questions.question:
Describe cervical cancer screening and HPV vaccination under the following headings:
(a) The HPV vaccines, dosage, route and eligible groups.
(b) Screening techniques and the recommended schedules by age.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities in prevention programmes.
