questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fainting in early pregnancy may be due to vasodilation under progesterone before compensatory increase in blood volume; in late pregnancy due to posture (supine hypotension), improved by turning to the side.
• Other causes: fatigue, stuffy room, anaemia, cardiac impairment.
(b)
• Varicosities: progesterone relaxes smooth muscle of the veins, causing sluggish circulation and ineffective valves; superficial veins of legs, vulva and anus may be engorged; vulval varicosities are very painful.
• Oedema: pressure of the growing uterus on the pelvic brim interferes with venous return; a degree is normal and may worsen during the day or in hot weather.
(c)
• Midwife should identify women at risk of varicosities (family history); pitting oedema reaching the ankle should be reported to the obstetrician.
• Oedema: ask whether rings feel tighter and ankles are swollen; test for pitting.
• Face puffiness may be due to anaemia, malnutrition, chronic nephritis or pre-eclampsia (from the examination section).
(d)
• Fainting prevention: avoid prolonged standing, sit or lie down when faint, avoid crowded stuffy rooms and lying on the back, take a good diet, treat medical conditions.
• Varicosities: avoid prolonged standing, calf exercises, rest legs raised, elastic stockings or crepe bandage, panty-girdle; in puerperium warm sitz bath with magnesium sulphate and cold compress.
• Pelvic congestion compounds varicosities.
• Hormonal and circulatory changes interact: progesterone affects veins and gut.
questions.question:
Describe the circulatory minor disorders of pregnancy in full:
(a) Fainting.
(b) Varicosities and oedema of the legs.
(c) State how they relate to the stage of pregnancy and to complications.
(d) Explain why they occur, how they may affect other systems, and the preventive nursing measures.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• STIs are infections spread from person to person through sexual contact; examples: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, herpes, HPV, HIV, genital warts, pubic lice.
• Spread through vaginal, anal or oral sex, sharing of sex toys, and mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy and birth.
(b)
Symptoms: unusual genital discharge, burning on urination, abnormal bleeding or spotting, pain during intercourse, itching or irritation, fever, rashes or sores on the genitals.
(c)
• Prevention: comprehensive sexual education, condoms, open communication, vaccination, abstinence, regular tests, treatment on suspicion, self-education on STIs.
• Prevention: avoid multiple partners, prefer monogamy, dental dams in oral sex, do not share sharp objects, know signs and symptoms, good personal hygiene, attend antenatal classes and check-ups.
• Control: post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), ensure diagnosed contacts take medication, contact tracing, no sex during menstruation, no douching.
• Control: no use of latex condoms with topical microbicides, get medical help at once, no anal sex.
(d)
• Nursing responsibilities: provide comprehensive sexual education, promote condom use and open communication, encourage regular testing and early treatment, and trace contacts.
• Offer family-planning counselling with condoms to everyone at risk of STIs (from the FP counselling steps).
(e)
• Condoms and barrier methods prevent unplanned pregnancy and STIs by providing individuals with information and tools to protect themselves.
• Early medical help and contact tracing limit spread; attending antenatal check-ups addresses mother-to-child transmission.
questions.question:
Describe the prevention and control of sexually transmitted infections among adolescents and young adults under the following headings:
(a) Definition, examples and modes of spread.
(b) Symptoms.
(c) Preventive strategies and control measures.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and the recommended safe practices.
(e) Explain the rationale behind each key measure and the consequences of deviation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Breasts hard, painful, may be flushed, heavy, tense and warm; occurs on the third and fourth day postpartum; assess how the baby attaches and feeds.
• Engorgement is temporary, lasting less than 24 hours.
(b)
Breast engorgement.
(c)
• Increased blood volume in the breast with oedema, especially when the baby is not correctly attached or cannot empty the breast.
• It indicates milk production is in full swing but the passage of milk into ducts and out of the nipple is not yet properly organized; lactation begins 48-72 hours after birth.
(d)
• Enable the baby to feed on the breast and empty it; feed the baby immediately when engorgement is noticed; gentle use of a pump in some cases.
• Empty the breasts at each feed (to prevent engorgement, ducts must be kept patent).
(e)
• Teach correct attachment and positioning (baby's mouth covers the areola, chin touching breast) and feeding on demand day and night.
• Evaluation: resolution within 24 hours as stated.
questions.question:
A mother on the fourth day after delivery complains that her breasts are hard, painful, heavy and warm. Her baby has been feeding poorly.
(a) State the nursing assessment findings.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Adolescent (10-19 years) pregnancy is at great risk; teenage mothers are typically physically, emotionally or economically unprepared and lose life options.
• Barriers to services: inconvenient clinic hours, transport, confidentiality, cost and attitude of health care providers.
(b)
Unplanned/unwanted early pregnancy with risk to mother and baby, and risk of unsafe abortion, STIs/HIV and sexual coercion.
(c)
• Teen mothers are twice as likely as older women to die of pregnancy-related causes and their children are more likely to die in infancy; adolescent girls make up over 60% of women treated for complications of unsafe abortion.
• Young girls aged 15-24 are 3 times more likely to be HIV-positive than boys; the younger a girl at first intercourse, the more likely it was coerced.
(d)
Provide adolescent-friendly confidential services; antenatal booking, HIV/STI testing and counselling; screen for sexual abuse and coercion.
(e)
Teach prevention: knowledge and confidence to resist sexual violence, family planning, STI prevention, importance of antenatal care.
questions.question:
A 16-year-old girl presents at the clinic with an unplanned pregnancy. She says she was afraid to come earlier because of the attitude of staff and the cost.
(a) State the nursing assessment concerns.
(b) Identify the nursing diagnosis/problem.
(c) Explain the basis (why adolescents are at risk).
(d) List the priority nursing interventions.

Describe lactation in full:
(a) Anatomy of the breast (structure, blood and nerve supply).
(b) Physiology of lactation (hormones, stages).
(c) State how lactation relates to the puerperium and common breastfeeding complications.
(d) Explain how lactation affects the mother and baby (systems, ovulation) and the preventive nursing measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The breasts (mammary glands) lie between the 2nd and 6th ribs on the pectoralis major, hemispherical in nulliparae and pendulous in multiparae; about 20 lobes with alveoli, lactiferous tubules, ducts, ampulla and 10-20 ducts to the nipple.
• Areola with Montgomery's tubercles/areolar glands; blood supply from mammary and axillary vessels; lymph to axillary glands; nerve supply poor because function is hormone controlled; nipple highly sensitive.
(b)
• Prolactin (anterior pituitary) produces milk; high oestrogen suppresses it in pregnancy and after about the 3rd day of delivery prolactin acts on alveolar cells.
• Suckling stimulates nipple receptors, hypothalamus and posterior pituitary to release oxytocin, which contracts myoepithelial cells to eject milk (let-down); stress inhibits let-down.
• Three stages: production, flow and maintenance of milk; more suckling means more milk; prolactin higher at night.
(c)
• Lactation begins 48-72 hours after birth and is fully established about 10 days after; colostrum is rich in antibodies and a laxative to meconium.
• Complications: engorgement (third/fourth day), sore or cracked nipples, mastitis, breast abscess, inadequate milk supply.
• Oxytocin during breastfeeding contracts the uterus, helping stop bleeding and causing after-pains.
(d)
• Exclusive breastfeeding with suckling on demand delays ovulation and menstruation; conception can still occur whether or not she breastfeeds.
• Preventive: correct attachment, emptying the breast at each feed, nipple preparation from about 30 weeks, healthy diet and fluids, rest, family support.
• Poor general health or maternal illness may prevent lactation and endanger the mother's nutrition.

questions.question:
A woman in labour has a fully dilated cervix, expulsive contractions every 1-2 minutes lasting about 60 seconds, a gaping vulva, a pouting anus and a visible presenting part. Her bladder is full.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Findings are signs of the second stage: OS fully dilated, expulsive contractions, trickling of blood or rupture of membranes, tenseness between coccyx and anus, vulva gapes, anus pouts, urge to push, presenting part visible, perineum bulges.
• Second stage runs from full dilatation to expulsion of the fetus; contractions become more frequent (1-2 mins) and longer (60 sec or more); accessory muscles come into play.
(b)
• Late first stage (active phase up to 10 cm) versus second stage: confirm full dilatation by vaginal examination.
• Full bladder may delay engagement and cause PPH; membranes should be ruptured artificially if still intact.
(c)
• Never leave the woman alone; confirm full dilatation by vaginal examination; catheterize the bladder if full.
• Continue observations more frequently; prepare the delivery trolley with strict asepsis; objectives: prevent infection, ensure the child is born alive without injury, prevent perineal injury.
• Escalate: delay in second stage or fetal heart abnormality (drop of 20 beats from normal 120-160) reported to the doctor.

questions.question:
A woman finds a single breast lump. On examination the lump is irregular, less mobile on palpation, is in the upper outer quadrant, with skin dimpling and nipple retraction; the tumour measures 3 cm and axillary nodes are movable on the same side, with no distant spread.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Malignant tumours have a shape that is difficult to define and are less mobile on palpation; infiltration causes dimpling and nipple retraction.
• Most breast cancers occur in the upper outer quadrant.
• TNM: T2 = greater than 2 cm but not more than 5 cm; N1 = metastasis to movable ipsilateral nodes; M0 = no distant metastasis (stage grouping IIA/IIB).
(b)
• Benign tumours: well-defined edges, encapsulated, freely movable.
• Ultrasonography identifies whether a lump is a cyst or a solid structure; fine-needle aspiration biopsy tests tissue or fluid for further diagnosis.
(c)
• Rationale: confirm by mammography, ultrasound, biopsy; treatment is chosen by stage, lymph node status, tumour size and histology.
• Escalation: refer to the doctor for diagnosis and treatment (chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, radiation, lumpectomy or mastectomy).
• Provide psychological support and education on screening.

(a)
• Fibroids are benign uterine tumours composed of smooth muscle and strands of fibrous tissue; the most common of all tumours.
• Types: interstitial (intramural, within the myometrium, may impair contractions), submucous (bulge into the cavity, may become pedunculated fibroid polypi) and subserous (under the peritoneal covering, may form a pedicle and become parasitic).
(b)
Incidence about 10-20% of women over 30; the cause is obscure but a hormonal connection is thought, as most fibroids atrophy after menopause.
(c)
• Fibroids may be symptomless; clinical features include menstrual disturbances and abdominal enlargement.
• Pain is rare unless they undergo torsion, degeneration, extrusion through the cervix or malignant change.
• Treatment may not be necessary without symptoms; if the woman wants children and is under 40, myomectomy is the operation of choice; over 40 or family complete, hysterectomy.
(d)
• Pressure symptoms: dyspepsia, constipation, frequency of micturition, stress incontinence, retention of urine, haemorrhoids.
• Myomectomy is an abdominal 'shelling out' of fibroids through incisions in the uterine wall, preserving the uterus for childbearing; hysterectomy removes the uterine body and cervix through the abdomen.
• Fibroids are also found among causes of female infertility (5-10% of infertile women) and of a uterus larger than expected for dates (fetus plus fibroid).
• For general surgical care see the pre-/post-operative care listed for gynaecological cancer surgery (airway, pain, infection, skin integrity).
questions.question:
Describe uterine fibroids in full:
(a) Definition and classification (types).
(b) Aetiology and incidence.
(c) State how fibroids relate to common complications and to the client's childbearing stage.
(d) Explain how fibroids may spread their effects to other organ systems and the resulting functional problems, with the nursing measures that apply.

A primigravida at 38 weeks says her abdomen has 'dropped' and she feels pressure in her pelvis, with frequent urination and backache. Abdominal palpation shows the fundal height is lower than at 36 weeks.
(a) Interpret the findings.
(b) State the conditions to be differentiated.
(c) Give the rationale for nursing actions and escalation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• At 36 weeks the fundus is at its highest level, touching the xiphisternum; at 38 weeks the lower uterine segment forms and the fundal height drops (lightening).
• Lightening occurs 2-3 weeks before term from softening pelvic bones and relaxation of the pelvic floor; the uterus descends into the true pelvis.
• It can lead to engagement of the head in a primigravida with firm abdominal muscles if there is no disproportion; urinary frequency results from pressure of the fetal head on the bladder.
(b)
• False labour (spurious): irregular painful contractions without retraction, relieved by walking.
• True labour: regular, rhythmic contractions, progressive cervical dilatation, show.
(c)
• Assess engagement by pelvic palpation and head-fitting from 36 weeks; check fetal heart (about 140/min) and contractions.
• Escalate: head that does not engage or suspected head-pelvis disproportion should be reported to the doctor.

questions.question:
Describe maternal mortality under the following headings:
(a) Definition and types (direct and indirect).
(b) Risk factors.
(c) Factors influencing maternal mortality in Nigeria.
(d) Explain the clinical basis for why some women are at higher risk and the consequences of maternal death.
(e) Distinguish between direct and indirect maternal mortality.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Maternal mortality is the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of duration or site, from any cause related to or made worse by the pregnancy or its management.
• Direct: deaths from obstetric complications of pregnancy, labour, puerperium, interventions or their after-effects; most common: excessive blood loss, infection, high blood pressure, unsafe abortion, obstructed labour.
• Indirect: deaths from worsening of existing conditions by pregnancy or delivery, e.g. anaemia, malaria, diabetes, sickle cell disease, CCF, glomerulonephritis.
(b)
Risk factors: extremes of age (under 18, over 40); too many and too frequent pregnancies; living in a developing country; conditions that can be worsened by pregnancy.
(c)
• Socio-cultural: patriarchal values, harmful traditional practices (gender-based violence, FGM), food taboos, child marriage and motherhood (VVF), religions not permitting blood transfusion.
• Political and economic: lack of political will, corruption, poverty; lack of access (transport, poor roads, siting of facilities); unskilled care, poor staff welfare; poor documentation and vital registration.
(d)
• Nigeria accounts for over 34% of global maternal deaths; the northeast has a death rate three times the national average.
• Conditions that worsen in pregnancy (anaemia, malaria, CCF) raise risk; global MMR fell from 385 to 216 per 100,000 live births between 1990 and 2015.
• Consequences for family: orphans with 66% higher risk of dying, loss of caretaker and economic contributor.
• Consequences for community/nation: less educated youths, increased crime, reduced productivity.
(e)
• Direct causes arise from the pregnancy process itself (e.g. haemorrhage, eclampsia-type hypertension, obstructed labour).
• Indirect causes arise from pre-existing disease aggravated by pregnancy; SDG target: global MMR below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030.

questions.question: A pregnant woman living with HIV has an undetectable viral load on antiretroviral therapy near term. Regarding delivery mode, the nurse should advise that:
options: Breastfeeding is automatically permitted without any precautions
Caesarean section is mandatory for every HIV-positive woman
Vaginal delivery is generally safe with an undetectable viral load
Formula feeding is required regardless of viral suppression
Antiretroviral therapy should be stopped before labour begins
questions.explanation: When maternal viral load is suppressed to undetectable levels near term, the risk of intrapartum transmission is very low, and vaginal delivery is generally considered safe rather than mandating routine caesarean section. Elective caesarean is instead reserved for women with detectable or unknown viral loads close to delivery. Antiretroviral therapy is continued throughout pregnancy, labour, and postpartum to maintain suppression.

questions.question: IMCI classifies ear problems in children. A child with ear pain, pus discharge for less than 14 days is classified as:
options: Chronic ear infection - requiring antibiotic and ENT referral
Acute ear infection - treated with appropriate antibiotics
No ear infection - ear pain treated with paracetamol only
Mastoiditis - requires urgent referral for IV antibiotics
Serous otitis media - managed with watchful waiting approach
questions.explanation: In IMCI, a child with ear pain or pus discharge for less than 14 days is classified as 'Acute Ear Infection' and is treated with appropriate oral antibiotics (amoxicillin in Nigeria) for 5 days plus a paracetamol for pain. Discharge for 14 days or more is classified as 'Chronic Ear Infection.' Swelling or tenderness behind the ear (mastoid) indicates mastoiditis - a severe classification requiring urgent referral. No ear pain or discharge is classified as 'No Ear Infection.'

questions.question: Superimposed pre-eclampsia develops in a woman with chronic hypertension. Which finding distinguishes superimposed pre-eclampsia from worsening chronic hypertension alone?
options: Headache and oedema in the third trimester
Detection of a small-for-gestational-age fetus on ultrasound
Development of new-onset proteinuria after 20 weeks
Requirement of increased antihypertensive medication doses
Higher blood pressure readings than in early pregnancy
questions.explanation: In a woman with chronic hypertension, superimposed pre-eclampsia is diagnosed when new-onset proteinuria (=300 mg/24 hours or PCR =30 mg/mmol) develops after 20 weeks, or when there is sudden worsening of hypertension (previously controlled) with new end-organ features (thrombocytopaenia, renal or hepatic dysfunction, pulmonary oedema). Worsening BP alone may just represent progression of chronic hypertension. New-onset proteinuria is the key distinguishing feature.

questions.question: After examination of the placenta and membranes, which finding is considered ABNORMAL and requires immediate action?
options: Fetal surface appearing smooth with vessels running to the edge
Cotyledons fitting together without gaps forming a complete circle
Membranes hanging freely from the cord as a complete sac
Placenta weighing 500 g and appearing uniformly red
Vessels radiating beyond the edge of the placenta
questions.explanation: Vessels radiating beyond the edge of the placenta suggest a succenturiate lobe with vessels in the membranes. This indicates a retained accessory lobe which can cause PPH and infection. Immediate investigation and manual removal may be necessary.

questions.question: A clinic offers a wide range of contraceptive methods and ensures no client is denied service based on marital status, age, or number of children. Which family planning principle does this best represent?
questions.explanation: The principle of choice in family planning services requires offering a full range of methods without discriminatory restrictions based on factors such as marital status, age, or parity. This ensures equitable access aligned with each client's autonomous preference. Restricting method availability based on such factors would violate this core principle.

Excessive dilute urine output with rising serum sodium after intracranial surgery suggests diabetes insipidus, caused by insufficient antidiuretic hormone secretion or action. Syndrome of inappropriate ADH would instead cause fluid retention and low serum sodium, the opposite pattern. Acute kidney injury and adrenal insufficiency, as well as hyperaldosteronism, do not typically present with this specific combination of dilute polyuria and hypernatraemia.
questions.question: A patient recovering from intracranial surgery develops excessive dilute urine output along with rising serum sodium. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
Hypertrichosis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Hypertrichosis is characterized by excessive hairiness resulting from an abundance of hair follicles. This can be localized or generalized and may be congenital or acquired. The condition differs from hirsutism, which is hormone-dependent excessive hair growth in specific distribution patterns.

options: Only entire lobes can be surgically removed
Individual bronchopulmonary segments can be surgically resected
Each segment has its own pleural covering preventing pneumothorax
Segments are too small to be identified radiologically
Segments share venous drainage making individual resection impossible
questions.question: The bronchopulmonary segments are the smallest independently functional lung units with their own bronchus, artery, and vein. Which surgical implication arises from this segmental anatomy?
questions.explanation: Because each bronchopulmonary segment has its own segmental bronchus and artery (note: veins run in intersegmental septa between segments), individual segments can be surgically resected (segmentectomy) while preserving adjacent healthy lung tissue. This is advantageous in patients with limited pulmonary reserve who cannot tolerate lobectomy. Understanding segmental anatomy is also critical for interpreting chest CT, bronchoscopy findings, and postural drainage positions.

Ischemic optic neuropathy in hypertensive retinopathy results from inadequate blood supply to the optic nerve head due to vascular compromise caused by the hypertensive arteriosclerotic changes in the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the optic nerve. This ischemia causes infarction of the optic nerve head, presenting as sudden painless visual loss with an altitudinal visual field defect. It is a serious complication that can cause permanent visual loss if not managed through urgent blood pressure control.
options: Chronic papilledema causing optic nerve head avascular necrosis
Toxic effects of elevated blood pressure on the optic nerve axons
Inadequate blood supply to the optic nerve head from vascular compromise
Inflammatory infiltration of the optic nerve sheath from choroiditis
Elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure from malignant hypertension

questions.explanation: For local anaesthesia before episiotomy, two fingers are inserted into the vagina along the intended line of incision. The needle follows the same line and is withdrawn to confirm it is not in a blood vessel before injecting on both sides. Lidocaine at 0.5% or 1% takes 3–4 minutes to act.
questions.question: Lidocaine for episiotomy is CORRECTLY administered using which technique?
options: Infiltrated into the cervix at 0.5% concentration before active pushing
Applied as topical gel on perineum 30 minutes before incision
Two fingers inserted into vagina guiding needle along incision line; withdraw before injecting
Administered intravenously in a 10 mg dose immediately before incision
Injected directly into the levator ani muscle using a spinal needle

questions.explanation: The Individualized Numeric Rating Scale incorporates behaviours specific to an individual nonverbal child, as identified by caregivers who know the child well, capturing that child's unique way of expressing pain more accurately than a fully standardized, generic tool. This personalized approach recognises that pain behaviours can vary significantly between children with complex communication needs. Involving caregivers as partners in developing and applying this tool improves the reliability of pain assessment in this population.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a nonverbal child with cerebral palsy uses the Individualized Numeric Rating Scale (INRS), which incorporates caregiver-reported behaviours specific to that child. What is the PRIMARY advantage of this individualized tool?
options: It eliminates the need for any caregiver involvement
It applies a completely standardized approach identical for every child
It captures the child's unique, personal indicators of pain more accurately
It removes the need for any ongoing reassessment over time
It is used exclusively for verbal, communicative children

questions.explanation: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis because it rapidly reverses bronchospasm, reduces vascular permeability, and restores blood pressure through combined alpha and beta adrenergic effects. Delayed administration significantly increases the risk of fatal outcomes. Antihistamines and corticosteroids may be given as adjuncts but do not replace the urgency of epinephrine.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient experiencing anaphylaxis should anticipate that the first-line emergency medication to be administered is:
A client with osteoporosis is counseled on dietary management. Which calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is described as ideal, with red meats and cola drinks to be avoided?
questions.explanation: A calcium-to-phosphorus ratio of 1:1 is described as ideal for osteoporosis management, with red meats, cola drinks, and processed foods that are low in calcium and high in phosphorus to be avoided. Ratios such as 1:3, 3:1, 2:5, and 5:2 do not match the ideal ratio specified in this dietary guidance for bone health in older adults.

Graft-versus-host disease occurs when transplanted donor immune cells recognise the recipient's tissues as foreign, commonly affecting the skin, gut, and liver. Skin rash and diarrhoea in the post-transplant period are classic early manifestations requiring prompt immunosuppressive treatment. Early recognition improves outcomes significantly.
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient who received a stem cell transplant and develops a widespread skin rash with diarrhoea two weeks later. The nurse should suspect:

questions.explanation: If a chest tube becomes disconnected, submerging the open end of the tube in sterile water creates an emergency water seal, preventing air from entering the pleural space while a new system is obtained. This prevents development of a pneumothorax or worsening of an existing one. The tube should not be clamped for an extended period, as this can cause tension pneumothorax.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with a pneumothorax notes the chest tube drainage system is accidentally disconnected from the tubing. The immediate priority action is to:
options: Clamp the chest tube indefinitely until repair
Remove the chest tube completely right away
Submerge the tube end in sterile water temporarily
Leave the system open to air until help arrives

questions.explanation: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the ventricles beating independently at a slower intrinsic rate, defines third-degree or complete heart block. This is a serious conduction abnormality often requiring pacing. It differs from first-degree block, which shows a consistent, simply prolonged PR interval.
questions.question: A patient's ECG shows P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently with no relationship between them, and a slow ventricular rate. This is most consistent with:
options: Atrial flutter with variable conduction ratio
Premature ventricular contractions in a bigeminy pattern
Potential benefits of the proposed procedure
Potential risks of the proposed treatment
The procedure to be performed in detail
The fees charged by each member of the care team
Adequate time to consider the pros and cons
questions.question: Informed consent requires that the patient is given information about all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires that information about the procedure, potential risks, benefits, and complications be provided to allow the patient to make a well-informed decision. While costs may be relevant, specific fees charged by individual team members are not a standard component of informed consent as defined in the nursing ethics literature. The core elements are information about the procedure itself and its risks and benefits.

options: After five years of attempting conception unsuccessfully
When the client expresses emotional distress about pregnancy
Only when uterine anomalies are found on ultrasound
After two or more consecutive unexplained miscarriages
After one pregnancy loss with no identifiable cause
questions.question: When is a referral for specialised testing most appropriate for a client presenting with recurrent pregnancy loss in a family planning setting?
questions.explanation: Recurrent pregnancy loss is defined as two or more consecutive miscarriages. This warrants specialised investigation including genetic karyotyping of both partners, antiphospholipid antibody testing, assessment of uterine anatomy via hysteroscopy or HSG, and hormonal evaluation. The threshold of two losses recognises the significant emotional burden and increased risk of underlying pathology requiring specialist intervention.

questions.question: For immediate control of postpartum haemorrhage due to atony in a low-resource birth setting, misoprostol is most commonly given by which route as a first-line measure?
questions.explanation: Sublingual misoprostol is favoured as a rapid, low-cost, first-line uterotonic in settings without ready access to injectable oxytocics, as it dissolves quickly and needs no needles or refrigeration. It stimulates uterine contraction to control atonic bleeding. Its ease of administration makes it especially valuable in community and low-resource births.

options: Direct mechanical damage to platelets from uterine bleeding
Release of thromboplastin triggering disseminated intravascular coagulation
Excessive uterotonic use causing consumptive coagulopathy
Amniotic fluid embolism causing widespread clot formation
questions.question: A woman with placental abruption develops widespread bleeding from venepuncture sites and abnormal clotting studies. Which mechanism explains this complication?
questions.explanation: Placental abruption releases large amounts of tissue thromboplastin into the maternal circulation, activating the clotting cascade excessively and consuming clotting factors and platelets, which precipitates disseminated intravascular coagulation. This presents as widespread bleeding, low fibrinogen, and deranged clotting studies. Prompt delivery and correction of coagulopathy with blood products are essential to manage this life-threatening complication.

Requiring an independent second-nurse verification for high-alert medications such as insulin is a recognised patient safety safeguard designed to catch calculation or dosing errors before administration, reducing the risk of serious harm from medications with a narrow margin of safety, rather than serving as an administrative formality or liability transfer.
questions.question: A nurse is required by hospital policy to obtain a second nurse's countersignature before administering a high-alert medication such as insulin. This safeguard is PRIMARILY intended to
options: shift full legal liability to the second nurse
reduce the risk of dosing or calculation errors
reduce the total time needed for administration
eliminate the need for any further documentation
Application of an occlusive dressing to the chest wall
Chest tube insertion for drainage and lung reexpansion
Positioning the patient in a supine flat position
Restriction of all intravenous fluid administration
questions.question: A patient with a hemothorax has blood accumulating in the pleural space. The nurse anticipates the priority intervention will be:
questions.explanation: A hemothorax requires chest tube insertion to drain accumulated blood, relieve compression on the lung, and allow monitoring of ongoing blood loss. This intervention also helps prevent complications such as fibrothorax if blood is left to organize in the pleural space. Large or rapidly accumulating hemothorax may require surgical intervention.

questions.question: The tendon of biceps femoris at its fibular head insertion is split into two parts by which ligament?
questions.explanation: The tendon of biceps femoris at its insertion on the lateral side of the head of fibula is split into two parts by the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee joint. The common fibular nerve closely follows the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula. Injury to biceps femoris or the fibular head can therefore damage the common fibular nerve.

questions.question: Two nurses disagree about whether to disclose a terminal diagnosis to a patient: one argues based on the rule that patients have a right to the truth, the other argues based on the emotional harm disclosure might cause. This disagreement BEST illustrates a tension between

The cell division process by which a single-celled fertilized egg ultimately develops into a mature organism and by which certain tissues (skin, blood) are continuously renewed is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: The cell-division cycle is both the mechanism for embryonic development from a single fertilized egg and the continuous renewal of cells in self-renewing tissues like skin and blood. Disruption of this cycle underlies both developmental defects and malignancies. Terminal differentiation, by contrast, is the process by which cells stop dividing and specialize.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with dumping syndrome after gastric bypass surgery should advise avoiding:
questions.explanation: Concentrated sugars create a hyperosmolar load that draws fluid rapidly into the small intestine after gastric bypass, triggering the cramping, flushing, and hypotension characteristic of dumping syndrome. Patients are advised to favour protein and fibre-containing foods eaten slowly in small amounts. This dietary pattern reduces symptom frequency and severity.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with chronic uncontrolled stress explains that prolonged elevation of stress hormones increases risk for which cardiovascular complication?
questions.explanation: Chronically elevated cortisol and catecholamines contribute to sustained vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and elevated blood pressure, raising long-term cardiovascular risk. This physiological burden explains the well-documented link between chronic stress and conditions such as hypertension and coronary artery disease. Stress management is therefore an important component of cardiovascular risk reduction.

questions.question: A client with Paget disease, a condition where new bone replaces old bone at a faster than normal rate, is informed of an increased risk for which malignancy?
questions.explanation: People with Paget disease, in which new bone replaces old bone faster than normal, have an increased risk of developing osteosarcoma. Rheumatoid arthritis, gout, osteomyelitis, and carpal tunnel syndrome are unrelated conditions with different underlying causes. This link is important for monitoring older clients with longstanding Paget disease.

During cord stump care, the nurse should advise giving sponge baths instead of tub baths until the umbilical stump has fallen off. Submersion in water can increase moisture around the stump, delaying natural drying and increasing infection risk. The diaper should be folded below the stump to keep it from rubbing and to allow air circulation, which promotes drying and natural separation.
questions.question: Regarding bathing practices during cord stump care, the nurse should advise:
options: Immerse the infant in a tub bath from day 2 onwards
Give sponge baths instead of tub baths until stump falls off
Clean the stump with alcohol swabs at every nappy change
Submerge the cord during bath to keep it soft and pliable
Apply petroleum jelly around the base to prevent drying

questions.question: For a patient with a newly diagnosed thyroid cancer, the nursing diagnosis of 'Anxiety related to new cancer diagnosis' is best addressed by which nursing intervention?
questions.explanation: Anxiety related to a new cancer diagnosis is primarily addressed through providing accurate, clear, and compassionate information about the disease, treatment options, and prognosis. Thyroid cancer, particularly papillary type, has an excellent prognosis with appropriate treatment. Honest information reduces uncertainty (a major driver of anxiety), empowers the patient to participate in treatment decisions, and builds therapeutic trust. Additional interventions include active listening, involving the patient in care planning, and facilitating referral to support groups or counseling if needed.
options: Prescribing anxiolytic medications to reduce the patient's anxiety
Transferring the patient to a psychiatric ward for counseling
Providing clear information about treatment options and prognosis
Asking family members to keep the diagnosis secret temporarily
Discouraging the patient from seeking information online
It focuses exclusively on religious preferences of the patient
It is delivered in the dominant language of the healthcare setting
It avoids discussion of cultural practices that may conflict with surgery
It is tailored to the patient's cultural values and uses interpreters
It is uniform across all patients to prevent perceived discrimination
questions.explanation: Culturally sensitive information sharing tailors teaching to patients' cultural beliefs, values, and practices, and employs interpreters or translated materials as needed. This approach ensures the information is received and understood within the patient's cultural framework, improving comprehension and adherence.
questions.question: Information sharing in preoperative teaching should be described as 'culturally sensitive' when:

options: Both conditions involve identical rates of hormone decline
Andropause always occurs before menopause in couples
Menopause causes no hormonal change, only andropause does
Menopause involves rapid hormone decline while andropause is gradual
Andropause involves a more rapid decline than menopause
questions.question: A 48-year-old woman experiences a relatively abrupt cessation of menstruation with pronounced hot flushes, while her 50-year-old husband reports a much more gradual decline in testosterone over several years. Which statement best reflects this difference?
questions.explanation: Menopause is characterised by a relatively rapid decline in oestrogen and progesterone as ovarian function ceases, whereas andropause involves a more gradual, variable decline in testosterone over years. This difference explains the more abrupt symptom onset in women compared to men. Understanding this contrast helps guide appropriate counselling and management for each condition.

questions.question: What lies in the rectouterine pouch in females?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the peritoneal space between the posterior wall of the uterus/upper vagina and the anterior wall of the rectum. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in females and commonly contains loops of small intestine (ileum). It can be accessed via the posterior vaginal fornix for drainage of pelvic abscesses or fluid aspiration (culdocentesis).

options: Emotional support prevents systemic progression of HIV infection
Emotional support replaces antiviral treatment in mild ocular disease
Psychological wellness has been proven to cure CMV retinitis permanently
Ocular complications are disfiguring and psychologically distressing for patients
Emotional support reduces CD4+ cell count decline in HIV patients
questions.explanation: Ocular complications of HIV, including CMV retinitis causing visual impairment, Kaposi Sarcoma affecting appearance, and the constant fear of blindness, are deeply distressing and psychologically challenging for patients. Nurses provide emotional support, address concerns, and connect patients with counseling and support groups to help them cope with these burdens. Psychological wellbeing is integral to treatment adherence, which is the foundation of successful HIV and ocular disease management.
questions.question: Emotional support for HIV patients with ocular complications is MOST important because:
People in close contact with a patient diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis should receive antimicrobial chemoprophylaxis. Which medication is listed as an option for this purpose?
questions.explanation: Close contacts of patients with meningococcal meningitis should be treated with antimicrobial chemoprophylaxis using rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone. Acyclovir is an antiviral used for herpes-related infections, metronidazole is used for anaerobic infections such as brain abscess and tetanus, levodopa treats Parkinson's disease, and tetracycline is not the option listed for meningococcal prophylaxis.

questions.question: A woman with endometriosis and pelvic pain is prescribed gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists. What is the expected effect on menstruation?
questions.explanation: GnRH agonists (leuprorelin, goserelin, buserelin) initially cause a "flare" of LH and FSH (days 1-2), followed by pituitary downregulation (receptor desensitisation), leading to markedly reduced LH and FSH, hypo-oestrogenism, and amenorrhoea. This "medical menopause" (pseudomenopause) causes regression of endometriotic implants. It is used for 6 months maximum to avoid bone loss. Add-back therapy (low-dose HRT) is given to reduce hypo-oestrogenic side effects (hot flushes, bone loss).
options: Shorter cycles from reduced luteal phase activity
Heavier periods due to endometrial proliferation
Normal cycles with reduced prostaglandin production

questions.question: A client is admitted with Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State after a recent chest infection. Which factor MOST commonly precipitates this presentation?
questions.explanation: Infections are among the most common triggers of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State because they increase counter-regulatory hormones and insulin resistance, worsening hyperglycaemia. Excessive insulin dosing would cause hypoglycaemia rather than this state, and beta-cell regeneration does not occur acutely. Overhydration and rapid weight loss are not recognised precipitating factors.

options: Retained products of conception after weeks
Subinvolution of the uterus over time
Uterine atony following delivery of the placenta
questions.explanation: Uterine atony, in which the myometrium fails to contract adequately after delivery, accounts for the majority of primary postpartum haemorrhage cases because effective contraction is essential to compress the spiral arteries at the placental bed. Retained products, subinvolution, and endometritis are more typically associated with secondary rather than primary haemorrhage. Active management of the third stage of labour is the key preventive strategy against atony.
questions.question: The most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage is:
A woman requests the most effective form of emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse. The midwife advises that the most effective option available is:
questions.explanation: The copper intrauterine device is the most effective form of emergency contraception when inserted within the recommended time frame after unprotected intercourse, working primarily by preventing fertilisation and implantation. It also provides ongoing contraception if left in place. Emergency contraceptive pills are effective but generally less so than the copper device.

questions.question: A patient with early glaucoma is prescribed a beta-blocker eye drop. The nurse must FIRST assess for which contraindication?
questions.explanation: Before a beta-blocker eye drop is prescribed or administered, the nurse must first assess for a history of asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or other obstructive airways disease. Beta-blocker eye drops (such as timolol) are absorbed systemically through the nasolacrimal drainage system and can precipitate severe bronchospasm in patients with reactive airway disease. This contraindication is absolute for non-selective beta-blockers, and alternative glaucoma medications (such as prostaglandin analogues or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) should be used in these patients.
options: History of allergic conjunctivitis from previous antibiotic drops
Previous allergic reaction to fluorescein dye during eye examination
History of asthma or obstructive airways disease before prescribing
History of uveitis or ocular inflammatory disease in either eye
Family history of angle-closure glaucoma in first-degree relatives

questions.explanation: Once a patient is stable and no longer needs intensive monitoring or organ support, continued ICU occupancy is not appropriate use of a limited resource. Timely step-down planning frees the bed for patients with genuine critical care needs. Discharge directly home would be unsafe without an intermediate level of observation.
questions.question: A patient admitted to ICU following cardiac surgery develops stable vital signs and no longer requires invasive monitoring. The most appropriate next nursing action is to:
options: Increase monitoring frequency beyond current requirements
Discharge the patient home directly from the ICU
Initiate step-down planning and transfer to a lower level
Request additional invasive lines before transfer occurs
Maintain ICU admission indefinitely for extra safety

questions.explanation: Spinal cord injury at the C4 level is associated with a high risk of respiratory failure because the phrenic nerve, which innervates the diaphragm, arises from cervical segments C3 through C5, so injury at this level can severely impair the primary muscle of respiration. Isolated bowel control loss, mild sensory loss in the fingertips only, complete preservation of motor function, and isolated taste loss do not capture the immediate life-threatening respiratory risk at this level.
questions.question: A patient with a spinal cord injury at the C4 level is at greatest immediate risk for which life-threatening complication due to the level of injury?
options: Mild sensory loss in the fingertips only
Complete preservation of all motor function
Respiratory failure due to diaphragm involvement

questions.explanation: Forceps delivery requires full cervical dilatation, a precisely known fetal position, and an engaged head at an appropriate station to ensure safe application and reduce risk of maternal and fetal trauma. Attempting forceps delivery with incomplete dilatation or an unknown position significantly increases the risk of serious complications. Ruptured membranes are also generally required before instrumental delivery.
questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman undergoing forceps-assisted delivery understands that a KEY prerequisite before application is:
options: Full cervical dilatation and a known fetal position
An unknown or undetermined fetal position
Disturbed thought process related to neuronal destruction
questions.explanation: Labeling drawers and using written reminders, pictures, or color-coding assists a patient's memory regarding what to do and the location of articles, addressing the nursing diagnosis of disturbed thought process related to neuronal destruction in the brain. This intervention does not directly target infection risk, skin integrity, airway clearance, or acute pain.
questions.question: A nursing intervention for a patient with dementia includes labeling drawers and using written reminder notes. This intervention primarily addresses which nursing diagnosis?

options: Walk barefoot inside the house to toughen the foot skin
Soak feet in hot water daily to improve circulation
Inspect feet daily and report any sores, blisters, or color changes
Trim toenails as short as possible to prevent ingrown nails
Apply moisturizing cream between the toes to prevent dryness
questions.question: The nursing care plan for a patient with diabetes mellitus includes teaching foot care. Which instruction is most important for preventing diabetic foot complications?
questions.explanation: Daily foot inspection is the most critical component of diabetic foot care because diabetic neuropathy reduces sensation, meaning patients cannot feel injuries. Blisters, sores, abrasions, or color changes that would normally be painful go unnoticed without deliberate daily inspection. Early identification of lesions allows prompt treatment before they progress to infected ulcers or gangrene requiring amputation. Patients should be taught to inspect all surfaces of the feet, including between toes, using a mirror if necessary, and to report any abnormality immediately.

Rising lactate reflects a shift to anaerobic metabolism when tissue oxygen delivery is inadequate to meet metabolic demand, a hallmark of ongoing shock and hypoperfusion. This is a clinically significant marker used to guide the adequacy of resuscitation, not a benign or irrelevant finding. Trending lactate over time helps assess response to treatment.
options: Improved oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues
Normal metabolic response requiring no further concern
Effective resolution of the underlying shock state
A laboratory artifact unrelated to perfusion status
Anaerobic metabolism from inadequate tissue oxygenation
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient in shock is asked to explain the significance of a rising serum lactate level. The nurse should explain that this reflects:

questions.explanation: Only the parietal pleura has somatic sensory innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerves, making it sensitive to pain. The visceral pleura has no somatic sensory nerve supply and receives only autonomic vasomotor innervation. This explains why pleural pain is sharp and well-localized to the chest wall.
questions.question: Which pleura has somatic sensory innervation?

questions.explanation: In cardiogenic shock, the heart's pumping ability is already impaired, so aggressive fluid administration can overwhelm the failing heart and worsen pulmonary congestion and oedema. Careful, cautious fluid management alongside inotropic support is typically preferred over the fluid boluses used in hypovolaemic shock. Recognising this difference prevents inappropriate treatment that could harm the patient.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient in cardiogenic shock should be cautious with aggressive fluid administration primarily because it may:
options: Have no effect on the patient's respiratory status
Worsen pulmonary congestion due to poor cardiac function
Replace the need for inotropic medication entirely
Immediately correct the underlying pump failure
Reduce the risk of pulmonary oedema significantly

questions.explanation: Treponema pallidum can cross the placenta after approximately 18 weeks of gestation and infect the fetus. Untreated maternal syphilis can lead to congenital syphilis in the newborn, manifesting as hepatosplenomegaly, joint swelling, palmar rash, anaemia, jaundice, and snuffles. Early treatment with penicillin G in the antenatal period is highly effective in preventing vertical transmission and congenital syphilis.
questions.question: A pregnant woman tests positive for syphilis on routine antenatal screening. The most important reason to treat her immediately is to prevent:
options: Vertical transmission to the fetus causing congenital syphilis
Maternal pelvic inflammatory disease worsening in pregnancy
Development of cervical cancer due to Treponema pallidum
Maternal HIV co-infection from untreated syphilis
Maternal death from cardiovascular syphilitic complications

questions.question: Which hemophilia type affects both sexes?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia C, caused by factor XI deficiency, shows autosomal inheritance affecting both males and females. It's generally milder than hemophilias A and B because factor IX (which factor XI activates) can also be activated by factor VII from the extrinsic pathway.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with asthma notes that oral fluids should avoid cold drinks specifically because:
questions.explanation: In asthma nursing management, oral fluids should avoid cold or iced fluids because cold temperatures can trigger or worsen bronchospasm in susceptible individuals. Cold air or cold water is a recognized trigger for exercise-induced and cold-air-induced asthma. Warm fluids are preferred as they help liquefy secretions without provoking bronchospasm.
options: Cold fluids stimulate the vagus nerve causing cardiac arrhythmias
Cold temperatures impair absorption of oral bronchodilator medications
Cold fluids may stimulate bronchospasm in asthmatic patients
Cold drinks suppress the cough reflex needed to clear secretions
Hypothermia from cold fluids reduces diaphragm contractility

questions.question: A postnatal woman reports constipation in the days following delivery. The midwife explains that this is primarily caused by:
questions.explanation: Constipation in the puerperium commonly results from reduced intestinal tone related to relaxed abdominal muscles, along with reluctance to strain due to perineal pain or fear of disrupting sutures. Encouraging adequate fluid intake, dietary fibre, and gentle mobilisation supports normal bowel function. Addressing pain relief adequately can also reduce fear-related straining avoidance that worsens constipation.
options: reduced bowel tone and perineal discomfort

questions.explanation: The Nigerian Constitution guarantees the right to a fair hearing, which generally includes a public trial within a reasonable time, although the court retains discretion to exclude the public in specific limited circumstances such as protecting public morality, safety, or the welfare of minors. Public proceedings remain the constitutional norm.
options: held entirely in secret at all times
conducted in an open, public hearing
conducted only before the Supreme Court
closed to the press under all circumstances
questions.question: A criminal trial involving a nurse accused of an offence against a patient is, according to the Nigerian Constitution, generally required to be
After a lumbar puncture, a patient is instructed to remain lying flat for several hours primarily to prevent which complication?
questions.explanation: Withdrawal of CSF during a lumbar puncture decreases CSF pressure, so the patient is kept horizontal for several hours to prevent a painful spinal headache caused by continued leakage and reduced cushioning of the brain. Infection, aspiration, hypertensive crisis, and cerebral edema are not the primary reasons for this positioning.

Progression from persistent HPV infection to invasive cervical cancer typically takes many years, often a decade or more, through intermediate precancerous stages. This extended timeline is what makes regular Pap screening effective for early detection and intervention. Most HPV infections clear spontaneously without ever progressing to cancer.
options: It occurs within days of HPV infection
It typically takes many years, often a decade or more
It occurs within a few weeks of HPV infection
It occurs within one menstrual cycle
It occurs only after menopause regardless of HPV timing
questions.question: A woman is diagnosed with cervical cancer and asks how long the progression from HPV infection to invasive cancer typically takes. What is the most accurate response?

questions.explanation: The tracheoesophageal septum is formed by fusion of two longitudinal tracheoesophageal ridges. This septum separates the respiratory diverticulum (ventrally) from the foregut/esophagus (dorsally). Abnormal formation of this septum, often due to abnormal growth of the ridges, results in tracheoesophageal fistulas with or without esophageal atresia.
questions.question: The tracheoesophageal septum is formed by fusion of:

questions.explanation: Tracheostomy is preferred for patients requiring long-term ventilation because prolonged endotracheal intubation causes vocal cord trauma, subglottic stenosis, and significant patient discomfort. A tracheostomy is more comfortable, enables oral feeding, facilitates weaning, and allows better secretion management. It is typically considered after 7–14 days of mechanical ventilation when the need for ongoing support is anticipated.
questions.question: Following a prolonged need for mechanical ventilation, a patient is scheduled for tracheostomy. The patient's significant other asks why this is necessary. The best nurse's response is:
options: 'It makes it easier for nurses to suction the airways quickly'
'It prevents the patient from speaking and reduces anxiety'
'Doctors prefer tracheostomies because they are easier to manage than endotracheal tubes'
'It permanently closes the airway from below and protects against aspiration'
'It is a long-term, safer alternative to an endotracheal tube when ventilation is needed for extended periods'

questions.question: A woman who has recently delivered and is not breastfeeding may expect return of ovulation within approximately how many weeks postpartum?
questions.explanation: In women who are not breastfeeding, ovulation typically returns within 4-6 weeks postpartum, with the first ovulation often occurring before the first menstrual period. This means women can become pregnant again very quickly after delivery if no contraception is used. Postpartum contraceptive counselling should begin during the antenatal period, and appropriate methods should be initiated before or at discharge to prevent closely-spaced pregnancies, which are associated with adverse maternal and infant outcomes.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy discloses a single same-sex sexual experience to a school nurse and worries this defines his identity permanently. What is the most appropriate professional understanding of this disclosure?
questions.explanation: A single same-sex experience during adolescence does not necessarily predict or define an individual's eventual sexual orientation, as adolescent sexuality can be exploratory. Providers should respond with non-judgemental support rather than premature labelling. This understanding helps prevent unnecessary distress or stigmatisation of normal developmental exploration.
options: It definitively confirms a lifelong homosexual orientation
It should be reported to law enforcement immediately
It indicates a paraphilic disorder requiring treatment
It should be dismissed as clinically irrelevant
It does not necessarily determine lifelong orientation
discharge the woman home to rest
delay reassessment for four more hours
questions.explanation: Crossing the action line on the partograph indicates significantly delayed labour progress and requires urgent clinical review to identify the cause and consider intervention, such as oxytocin augmentation or caesarean delivery. This graphical tool is designed to prompt timely action before prolonged labour causes maternal or fetal harm. Delaying response beyond this point increases risk of complications.
questions.question: A woman's cervical dilatation on the partograph crosses the action line during labour. The appropriate response to this finding is to:

options: A mitochondrial mutation causing muscle weakness
A chromosomal trisomy causing short-trunk stature
An X-linked mutation causing generalised short stature
An autosomal recessive mutation causing microcephaly
An FGFR3 gene mutation causing short-limb dwarfism
questions.question: Achondroplasia results from which genetic mechanism and typically presents with which combination of features?
questions.explanation: Achondroplasia is caused by a mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene, most often occurring sporadically, which disrupts normal cartilage growth at the growth plates and results in disproportionately short limbs relative to a near-normal trunk length, along with a large head and characteristic facial features. Intelligence in achondroplasia is typically normal, distinguishing it from other syndromes with cognitive impairment. Genetic counselling addresses the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern for future pregnancies.

The epiphyseal growth plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth through endochondral ossification. Premature closure, whether from trauma, infection, or corticosteroids, arrests longitudinal growth of that bone. If bilateral, this leads to short stature proportional to the extent and timing of premature closure. Conversely, delayed closure as in growth hormone excess before puberty leads to gigantism.
questions.question: Which condition would most directly result from premature closure of the epiphyseal growth plate?
options: Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency
Osteoporosis from reduced bone mineral density
Osteosarcoma arising from osteoblast precursor cells
Arrested longitudinal growth causing short stature before full height
Osteomalacia from impaired bone matrix mineralization

questions.explanation: Because peripheral parenteral nutrition is infused through a smaller peripheral vein rather than a central line, the vein is more prone to irritation and phlebitis from the osmolality of the solution. Regular site rotation and monitoring reduce this risk. Complications typical of central catheters are less relevant to this peripheral route.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient receiving peripheral parenteral nutrition should monitor closely for which site-related complication?
options: Cardiac tamponade from a central line
Air embolism from a central catheter

questions.question: What separates the breast from deep fascia?
questions.explanation: The breast is separated from the deep fascia covering the underlying muscles by a layer of loose areolar tissue called the retromammary space. This space allows the breast some mobility over the pectoralis major muscle. The space is important surgically as it provides a plane for mastectomy.

questions.question: Carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2a) is a second-line uterotonic for PPH refractory to oxytocin. What is a key contraindication to its use?
questions.explanation: Carboprost (Hemabate) 250 mcg IM is a prostaglandin F2a analogue used for PPH refractory to oxytocin and ergometrine. Its key contraindication is bronchospasm and active asthma, because prostaglandin F2a causes bronchial smooth muscle contraction (bronchoconstriction), which can trigger a life-threatening asthma attack. It is also used with caution in hypertension and cardiac disease. The dose can be repeated every 15 minutes (maximum 8 doses).

When the occiput points directly to the maternal side with the sagittal suture in the transverse diameter, this is described as an occipito-lateral position, in this case right occipito-lateral since the occiput points to the maternal right. This differs from occipito-anterior or occipito-posterior positions, where the occiput points towards the front or back of the pelvis respectively. This position often rotates further as labour progresses.
questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman notes the fetal presenting part is the vertex, with the sagittal suture in the transverse diameter of the pelvis and the occiput pointing directly to the maternal right side. This position is:
A nurse caring for a patient after intravenous cannulation should avoid selecting the antecubital fossa for long-term therapy primarily because this site:
questions.explanation: The antecubital fossa is located at a joint, making it prone to movement-related dislodgement and increased risk of infiltration or phlebitis with prolonged use, so it is generally reserved for short-term or emergency access rather than long-term therapy. Selecting a site on the forearm away from joints better supports stability for extended intravenous treatment. Understanding site selection principles reduces complications during prolonged therapy.
options: Restricts joint movement and risks dislodgement
Is the safest site for repeated blood draws
Provides the most stable long-term access
Is preferred for all long-term infusions
Has the lowest risk of infiltration overall

questions.question: The daily volume of pancreatic secretion approximates:
questions.explanation: The pancreas secretes approximately 1-3 liters (typically 1.5L) of fluid daily, containing both aqueous bicarbonate and enzymatic components essential for digestion. This represents a significant portion of total gastrointestinal secretions. The exocrine pancreas has enormous reserve capacity, with clinically significant maldigestion occurring only after 90% functional loss.

The external intercostal muscle is deficient anteriorly at the costochondral junction and is replaced by the external (anterior) intercostal membrane. This fibrous membrane continues the plane of the muscle to the sternum. The internal intercostal muscle conversely is deficient posteriorly at the angle of the rib.
questions.question: At which location is the external intercostal muscle deficient?

A patient with aspiration pneumonia received the following statement in the nursing plan: 'Imbalanced nutrition less than body requirements related to frequent cough and dyspnoea.' The best corresponding nursing intervention is:
questions.explanation: For imbalanced nutrition in respiratory patients, the nurse should encourage high-calorie, high-protein foods during periods when respiratory symptoms are less severe. Frequent small meals are tolerated better than large ones. Good nutrition supports immune function and wound healing. Oral intake is preferred over parenteral when feasible, as enteral nutrition maintains gut integrity.
options: Administering total parenteral nutrition (TPN) as first-line therapy
Restricting all oral intake until chest X-ray shows resolution
Providing only clear liquids to reduce risk of aspiration
Encouraging high-calorie foods during symptom-free intervals
Calculating the patient's caloric needs using the Harris-Benedict equation

questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (which itself arises from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the vermiform appendix. It runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to reach the tip of the appendix. This end-artery arrangement (with minimal collateral supply) means that thrombosis or inflammation affecting the appendicular artery can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery's location in the mesoappendix requires careful ligation during appendectomy. Variations in the arterial supply are uncommon, but occasionally the appendicular artery may arise directly from a posterior cecal artery.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the appendix?
A client with rheumatoid arthritis develops firm, non-tender lumps over the extensor surface of the forearm. Which extra-articular manifestation does this represent?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid nodules are firm, non-tender subcutaneous lumps that develop over extensor surfaces as an extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, reflecting underlying vasculitic inflammation. Tophi occur in gout, while Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes are osteoarthritis findings, and osteophytes are bony spurs rather than soft tissue nodules. Recognising this manifestation highlights the systemic nature of rheumatoid arthritis.

options: Epidural anaesthesia is mandatory for all women in the second stage
Regional analgesia must be discontinued at the onset of second stage
The woman's pain relief preferences from the birth plan guide management
Pharmacological pain relief is contraindicated during active pushing
IV opioids are routinely administered at the onset of the second stage
questions.question: Pain relief during the second stage is primarily managed in which way?
questions.explanation: Pain relief during the second stage is guided by the woman's preferences (as documented in her birth plan), maternal and fetal condition, and available options. The midwife continues to support the woman's comfort and hygiene, including sponging the face and neck. Bladder care and positioning are also important.

options: Automatically contraindicated all forms of hormonal contraception permanently
Can influence pregnancy outcomes and guides family planning decisions and prenatal care
Requires mandatory partner testing before any contraceptive method is initiated
Necessitates referral to a hematologist before family planning services are provided
Makes surgical sterilization the only acceptable contraceptive option available
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is a hereditary condition that can influence pregnancy outcomes, making it important to document in family planning history. Awareness of sickle cell status guides family planning decisions, informs about pregnancy risks (such as pain crises, increased infections, and anemia during pregnancy), and shapes prenatal care planning. Some contraceptive methods may be preferred over others in women with sickle cell disease based on their thrombotic and hormonal implications.
questions.question: A history of sickle cell anemia in a family planning client is important because it:
A midwife notes that a child has missed several scheduled immunisations due to prolonged illness. The MOST appropriate approach to catching up is to:
options: Restart the entire immunisation series from the beginning
Wait until the child reaches school age to resume
Give all missed vaccines simultaneously regardless of spacing intervals
Resume the schedule from where it was interrupted without restarting the entire series
questions.explanation: When immunisations have been missed or delayed, the general principle is to resume the schedule from where it was interrupted, giving missed doses as soon as possible, without restarting the entire series, as previously administered doses still provide some immunity and count towards the full course. Waiting until school age would leave the child vulnerable for an extended period. Appropriate minimum intervals between doses of the same vaccine must still be respected even when catching up.

Reflecting on mortality and reprioritising time after the death of a close friend is a common, normal psychosocial adjustment in older adulthood, related to increased awareness of the finite nature of life. This differs from a pathological grief reaction, clinical depression, or cognitive decline, which would present with additional distinguishing features. Distinguishing normal adjustment from pathology guides appropriate, non-alarmist support.
questions.question: A client expresses fear and sadness after a close friend's death, followed by a period of reflecting on her own mortality and reprioritising how she spends her time. This response is most consistent with:
options: An abnormal response requiring urgent psychiatric referral
A sign of cognitive decline requiring dementia screening
A pathological grief reaction requiring psychiatric admission
Clinical depression requiring immediate antidepressant therapy
A normal psychosocial adjustment involving mortality awareness

questions.explanation: Recognising the limits of one's own competence is a fundamental professional and ethical obligation; a nurse who lacks the necessary training or assessed competency for an advanced procedure should decline and seek appropriate training, supervision, or referral to a qualified provider, rather than risking patient harm by attempting an unfamiliar task.
questions.question: A nurse is asked to perform an advanced invasive procedure for which she has received no formal training or competency assessment. The MOST appropriate response is to
options: attempt the procedure carefully to help the team
perform it only if a senior colleague is nearby
proceed since refusing might seem uncooperative
delegate the procedure informally to a student nurse
decline and request appropriate training or referral

questions.explanation: An extreme leukocytosis (>100,000/mm³) with predominantly blast cells constitutes a haematological emergency known as hyperleukocytosis. The large, rigid blast cells increase blood viscosity and can form plugs in small vessels — a condition called leukostasis — most dangerously in the pulmonary (dyspnoea, hypoxia, pulmonary infiltrates) and cerebral circulations (confusion, headache, stroke). Urgent cytoreduction (hydroxyurea, leukapheresis, or emergent chemotherapy) is required. Nurses must monitor respiratory status, neurological function, and urine output closely.
questions.question: A patient's blood report shows WBC of 120,000/mm³ with 85% blasts. The nurse anticipates the patient is at risk for:
options: Leukostasis with pulmonary and neurological complications

questions.question: How does aspirin prevent clotting?
questions.explanation: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase, preventing thromboxane A2 synthesis in platelets. This reduces platelet aggregation and platelet plug formation, providing antiplatelet effects that last the platelet's lifetime (10 days), making aspirin useful for preventing thrombotic events.

Research consistently shows that infants may need to be offered a new food 10-15 or more times before accepting it. Initial refusal does not mean permanent rejection - it is a normal exploratory response to new tastes. Caregivers should be encouraged to persist with patient, repeated exposure without pressure or force, and to continue offering the food in small amounts at future meals. This approach gradually develops food acceptance and supports dietary diversity.
questions.question: When an infant refuses a newly introduced food, the nurse's guidance to the caregiver should include:
options: Remove the food permanently from the infant's dietary plan
Replace it with a similar food item of the same food group
Offer it again on multiple occasions as repeated exposure helps
Mix it with a sweet food to mask the unfamiliar taste
Add salt or sugar to make it more palatable for the infant

questions.question: A patient develops a petechial, purpuric rash during an episode of bacterial meningitis. Which organism should the nurse most strongly suspect?
questions.explanation: A petechial or purpuric rash in bacterial meningitis is classically associated with Neisseria meningitidis due to its propensity to cause meningococcaemia and vascular damage. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are common meningitis pathogens but are not typically linked with this characteristic rash. Listeria and E. coli are less common causes and do not classically present this way.

Focusing on comfort, dignity, and symptom control in accordance with a patient's own wishes near the end of life reflects the core goals of palliative care, which is ethically and legally distinct from euthanasia or assisted suicide, since its intent is to relieve suffering and support quality of life rather than to hasten or cause death.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient nearing the end of life focuses on comfort, dignity, and symptom control rather than curative treatment, in line with the patient's wishes. This approach BEST reflects
options: active euthanasia in a passive form
assisted suicide facilitated by the nurse
abandonment of the patient's care needs
a breach of the nurse's duty of beneficence

questions.explanation: Continuous renal replacement therapy requires specialised equipment, close haemodynamic monitoring, and rapid response to complications only available in intensive care. The potential reversibility of the injury supports aggressive, intensive management. Ward or outpatient settings lack the capacity for continuous filtration and monitoring.
questions.question: A patient with a potentially reversible acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy is best managed in which care setting?
options: Intensive care unit with continuous therapy capability
Home-based care with community nursing support
General medical ward with intermittent dialysis access
Step-down unit without continuous filtration equipment
Outpatient renal clinic with scheduled dialysis sessions

questions.question: Altered level of consciousness terminology describes a patient who responds only minimally with vigorous stimulation and may only moan as a verbal response. This level is termed:
questions.explanation: Stuporous describes a patient who responds only minimally with vigorous stimulation and may only moan as a verbal response, representing a deeper level of unresponsiveness than lethargy or obtundation. Confused patients are disoriented but more responsive, lethargic patients are drowsy but respond to gentle stimulation, and alert patients attend fully to the environment.

questions.question: A patient on mechanical ventilation has a PaCO2 of 65 mmHg with a normal pH of 7.38. This finding most likely reflects:
options: Normal ventilator settings with no adaptation needed
Acute respiratory failure requiring emergency intervention
Acute metabolic alkalosis unrelated to ventilation
Chronic hypercapnia with full metabolic compensation
A laboratory error requiring immediate repeat sampling
questions.explanation: A high PaCO2 with a normal pH suggests the kidneys have compensated over time by retaining bicarbonate, consistent with chronic hypercapnia often seen in patients with underlying chronic lung disease. This differs from an acute, uncompensated respiratory failure pattern. Recognising chronic compensation avoids unnecessary aggressive intervention.

options: A few scattered petechiae on the leg
Small bruise at a previous injection site
questions.explanation: Sudden severe headache with altered mental status in a severely thrombocytopenic patient may indicate intracranial haemorrhage, a life-threatening emergency. While minor bruising and petechiae are expected findings requiring monitoring, neurological change demands immediate escalation. Rapid intervention can prevent permanent neurological damage.
