What happens when the sample spot is placed below the solvent level in paper chromatography?
questions.explanation: If the sample spot is submerged in the solvent, it will simply dissolve into the bulk solvent rather than being carried up the paper by capillary action. This defeats the purpose of chromatography as no separation occurs. The sample must be above the solvent level for proper development.

questions.question: Why must pesticide residue levels be monitored in crude drugs?
options: To ensure consumer safety from toxic chemical exposure
questions.explanation: Pesticide residues (DDT, BHC, organophosphates) can persist on plant materials from agricultural application and may cause serious health effects including neurotoxicity, carcinogenicity, and endocrine disruption. Pharmacopoeial limits ensure residue levels are below harmful thresholds. Testing protects consumers from chronic low-dose exposure to these toxic chemicals.

questions.question: What is the drug to menstruum ratio typically used in simple maceration?
questions.explanation: The standard ratio is 1 part drug to 10 parts menstruum (1:10) for simple maceration. This provides sufficient solvent to extract the active constituents completely while producing a reasonably concentrated final product. The ratio may be adjusted for particularly active or inert drugs.

questions.question: In gradient elution LPLC, what happens to the mobile phase composition?
questions.explanation: Gradient elution involves progressively increasing the polarity (or strength) of the mobile phase during the chromatographic run, typically by increasing the proportion of a more polar solvent. This allows separation of both weakly and strongly retained compounds in one run. Weakly retained compounds separate first with weak mobile phase, then stronger mobile phase elutes retained compounds.

questions.question: When is steam distillation complete?
questions.explanation: Distillation is complete when no more oil is being collected, indicated by the volume of oil in the graduated receiver remaining constant over time. Continued distillation after this point wastes time and energy. The endpoint must be determined by careful observation of oil accumulation.
options: When the volume of oil becomes constant
When the plant material is dry
When the distillate is completely clear

questions.explanation: Glass wool is placed at the column outlet to retain the solid stationary phase while allowing liquid mobile phase to pass through freely. It acts as a physical barrier without significantly affecting flow rate or separation. This prevents column packing material from being washed out during elution.
questions.question: Which material is placed at the bottom of a chromatography column to prevent stationary phase escape?

questions.explanation: Diacytic (Caryophyllaceous or cross-celled) stomata have two subsidiary cells with their common wall perpendicular to the long axis of the guard cells, forming a cross pattern. This type is characteristic of Mentha species and Caryophyllaceae family. The cross-wise arrangement is diagnostic.
questions.question: In Diacytic stomata, how are the subsidiary cells oriented?
What do low extractive values indicate?
questions.explanation: Extractive values below the specified range suggest the drug has been previously extracted (exhausted), has deteriorated during storage, contains excessive inert matter, or has been adulterated with inferior material. Low values indicate insufficient active constituents. Each drug has minimum extractive value standards in pharmacopoeias.
options: Exhausted drug or adulteration with inert material

questions.question: In Vacuum Liquid Chromatography (VLC), where is the vacuum applied?
questions.explanation: Vacuum is applied at the outlet (bottom) of the column to pull mobile phase through the packed bed, increasing flow rate compared to gravity alone. This is safer than applying positive pressure at the top and provides faster separations than gravity flow. VLC is useful for initial fractionation of crude extracts.

Infusion is best for soft plant materials like leaves, flowers, and herbs where water can easily penetrate the tissues and active constituents are readily soluble. These materials have less dense tissue structure. Hard materials like bark and wood require the more vigorous extraction of decoction.
questions.question: What type of plant material is most suitable for infusion?
For essential oils more dense than water, what modification is needed?
questions.explanation: Most essential oils are less dense than water and float, but some heavy oils sink. For these, a solvent like xylene (less dense than water) is added to the graduated receiver to dissolve the oil and make it float above the water for easy measurement. The volume of oil = (volume of xylene + oil) - (volume of xylene alone).
options: Addition of xylene to make oil float

questions.question: Which morphological feature is NOT typically evaluated macroscopically?
questions.explanation: Cell wall thickness is a microscopic feature requiring magnification to observe. Macroscopic evaluation examines features visible to the unaided eye or with simple hand lens: overall shape, dimensions, surface features, color patterns, and fracture characteristics. Microscopic examination is a separate evaluation technique.

questions.question: Which drawing instrument should be used to mark the origin line in paper chromatography?
questions.explanation: A pencil must be used because ink from pens would dissolve in the solvent and interfere with the separation, creating additional spots on the chromatogram. Pencil marks are insoluble in most solvents and provide a permanent reference line. This ensures the origin line remains visible throughout the procedure.

options: Paper uses adsorption while TLC uses partition
Paper uses partition while TLC uses adsorption
questions.explanation: Paper chromatography primarily operates by partition of solutes between the water-bound stationary phase and the mobile solvent phase, while TLC uses adsorption onto solid adsorbents like silica or alumina. This fundamental difference affects selectivity and applications. The cellulose in paper acts as a support for the liquid stationary phase.
questions.question: What distinguishes paper chromatography from thin layer chromatography in terms of principle?

questions.explanation: Clavenger's apparatus is a specialized graduated receiver that collects the distilled oil and automatically separates and returns the aqueous portion to the distillation flask. The volume of collected oil can be read directly from the graduated portion. This allows continuous distillation and direct volumetric measurement.
questions.question: What apparatus is commonly used for measuring volatile oil volume during steam distillation?

questions.explanation: Sticky materials like gums, resins, fresh opium, or orange peel would clog the Soxhlet apparatus by blocking the siphon or causing the thimble to stick to the chamber walls. Only free-flowing powdered materials are suitable. Sticky materials require other extraction techniques.
questions.question: Which plant material type cannot be effectively extracted by Soxhlet method?

questions.explanation: Typically, three-quarters (3/4) of the final volume is collected as percolate before testing the drug for exhaustion. If the drug is exhausted, the marc is pressed and the expressed liquid is mixed with the collected percolate, then menstruum is added to reach final volume. This ensures complete extraction.
questions.question: In percolation, what fraction of the final volume is typically collected before exhaustion testing?
At what temperature is the extract dried for extractive value determination?
questions.explanation: The extract is evaporated to dryness in a tared dish and then dried in an oven at 100-105degC to constant weight. This temperature is sufficient to remove residual solvent and water without decomposing most organic constituents. The dried residue weight represents the extractive value and is expressed as percentage of the air-dried drug.

Iodine solution reacts with starch (specifically amylose) to form a characteristic blue-black complex. This is a highly specific and sensitive test for starch. Glycogen gives a reddish-brown color with iodine. The intensity of the color indicates the amount of starch present.
questions.question: What color does iodine solution produce when it contacts starch?
Why is frequent agitation important during maceration?
questions.explanation: Shaking or agitation replaces the saturated menstruum immediately surrounding the drug particles with fresh unsaturated solvent from the bulk, maintaining concentration gradients that drive diffusion. Without agitation, extraction would be slow and incomplete. The first 6 hours typically require the most frequent agitation.
options: To replace saturated solvent with fresh menstruum

questions.question: What type of material are Sephadex series gels made from?
questions.explanation: Sephadex gels are made from dextran polysaccharides that have been cross-linked to form a three-dimensional network with defined pore sizes. Different degrees of cross-linking (designated by numbers like G-25, G-50) provide different pore sizes for separating different molecular weight ranges. They are hydrophilic and biocompatible.

questions.question: What is the fundamental requirement for a compound to be analyzed by gas chromatography?
questions.explanation: Compounds must be volatile enough to vaporize in the injection port and remain stable under GC operating temperatures without decomposition. Non-volatile or thermally unstable compounds cannot be directly analyzed by GC. The sample must exist in the gas phase during separation.

questions.question: In the elution order on polar adsorbents, which functional group typically elutes last?
questions.explanation: Acids and bases have the strongest interactions with polar adsorbents due to their ionizable groups and hydrogen bonding capability, causing them to be most strongly retained. They require the most polar solvents to elute and therefore come off the column last. Saturated hydrocarbons, being nonpolar, elute first.

questions.question: Which support medium has largely replaced paper in modern electrophoresis?
questions.explanation: Agarose and polyacrylamide gels have become the standard support media for electrophoresis because they provide better resolution, more uniform pore sizes, and cleaner backgrounds than paper. Different gel concentrations can be used to optimize separation for different molecular size ranges. These gels also allow more sophisticated techniques like gradient gels.

options: To recover menstruum retained in plant tissue
questions.question: Why is the marc pressed after maceration of organized drugs?
questions.explanation: Organized plant materials (leaves, roots, barks) retain significant amounts of menstruum within their cellular structure even after draining. Pressing recovers this liquid which contains dissolved actives. The pressed liquid is combined with the initial macerate to maximize yield. This is less important for unorganized drugs like resins.

questions.question: What type of electrophoresis uses liquid buffer without supporting medium?
questions.explanation: Moving boundary (free solution) electrophoresis is performed in liquid buffer without any supporting gel or paper, though it has largely been replaced by zone electrophoresis methods. Without a support medium, separated components tend to mix by diffusion. This makes analysis and recovery more difficult.

Atropa belladonna has 62.5 to 174 stomata per square millimeter on the lower leaf surface, which is considerably more than the 6.0 to 37.5 on the upper surface. This large difference reflects the hypostomatous nature (more stomata below) of these leaves. The ranges help identify authentic belladonna material.
questions.question: What is the typical stomatal number range on the lower surface of Atropa belladonna?

questions.explanation: The mass spectrometer (MS) detector provides mass spectral fragmentation patterns that reveal detailed structural information about each separated compound. GC-MS combines the separation power of GC with the identification capability of MS. Other detectors only indicate the presence and quantity of compounds.
questions.question: Which GC detector provides the most structural information about separated compounds?

options: Characteristic breaking pattern when drug is snapped
questions.question: What does the term "fracture" refer to in macroscopic evaluation?
questions.explanation: Fracture describes the appearance of the broken surface when a drug (bark, root, wood) is snapped or broken. It may be short (clean break), fibrous (stringy), splintery, granular, smooth, or irregular. Different plant parts and tissues show characteristic fracture patterns that aid identification.

questions.question: How do trichomes help reduce water loss?
questions.explanation: Dense trichome coverage creates a still-air boundary layer over the leaf surface that reduces air movement, thereby decreasing the vapor pressure gradient and slowing water loss through transpiration. The trichomes also may reflect light, reducing leaf temperature and transpiration rate. This is particularly important for plants in dry environments.

The hydroxyl groups in cellulose paper can adsorb sample molecules through hydrogen bonding and other interactions, reducing their mobility and causing tailing. This reduces resolution and complicates quantitation. Cellulose acetate, where many hydroxyls are converted to acetate groups, shows less adsorption.
questions.question: What is the primary disadvantage of paper electrophoresis?
options: Adsorption of samples to paper reducing mobility

questions.question: What is the fundamental principle underlying electrophoretic separation?
options: Migration of charged particles in electric field
questions.explanation: Electrophoresis separates charged molecules based on their differential migration rates when an electric field is applied across a supporting medium. Positively charged molecules migrate toward the cathode while negatively charged molecules move toward the anode. Migration rate depends on charge, size, and shape.

questions.question: Why is stomatal index more reliable than absolute stomatal number for identification?
questions.explanation: The stomatal index (ratio of stomata to total epidermal cells) is relatively constant for a species regardless of environmental conditions during growth, while absolute numbers can vary with light, water, and nutrient availability. The index is therefore a more reliable diagnostic character. It provides standardization across different growing conditions.
options: Less affected by environmental factors and leaf age

questions.question: What characteristic feature of Cinchona bark is important for identification?
questions.explanation: The fracture characteristics of Cinchona bark (short, fibrous fracture with granular appearance) are diagnostic features used in macroscopic identification. The way a bark breaks reveals its internal structure and fiber arrangement. This is examined by breaking a small piece and observing the broken surface with a hand lens.

questions.question: Which component in a TLC system would cause fluorescence during UV light exposure at 254 nm?
questions.explanation: Silica gel G254 contains a fluorescent indicator that absorbs UV light at 254 nm and emits visible light, making the entire plate glow. Compounds that absorb UV appear as dark spots against the fluorescent background. This allows visualization of UV-absorbing compounds without chemical treatment.

options: To retain heat and prevent volatile loss
questions.explanation: Covering the vessel during preparation helps retain heat for more efficient extraction and prevents loss of volatile constituents like essential oils through evaporation. This is especially important for aromatic drugs. The cover also minimizes volume loss from evaporation.
questions.question: Why are infusion and decoction vessels often covered during preparation?

options: Using constant mobile phase composition throughout
Changing mobile phase composition during analysis
questions.explanation: Isocratic elution maintains constant mobile phase composition throughout the chromatographic run, suitable for separating components with similar retention characteristics. This provides the simplest operation and best baseline stability. Gradient elution, by contrast, varies the mobile phase composition over time.
questions.question: In HPLC, what does isocratic elution mean?

options: Sugars, tannins, mucilage, and plant acids
questions.explanation: Water-soluble extractive measures water-soluble constituents including sugars, plant acids, tannins, mucilages, glycosides, and water-soluble salts. This test is particularly relevant for drugs where these polar constituents are the active or important components. Hydrophobic compounds like fixed oils and resins are not extracted by water.
questions.question: What type of compounds are extracted by water-soluble extractive determination?

options: As percentage w/w of the drug
questions.explanation: Extractive values are expressed as percentage weight/weight (% w/w) of the air-dried drug: % extractive = (weight of dried residue / weight of drug taken) x 100. They may also be calculated on a moisture-free basis to account for variable moisture content. This standardized expression allows comparison between different samples and drugs.
questions.question: How are extractive values expressed?
What is the primary function of stomata in plant tissues?
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores that regulate gas exchange (CO2 intake for photosynthesis, O2 release, water vapor loss through transpiration) between the plant's internal tissues and the atmosphere. Guard cells surrounding the pore control opening and closing in response to environmental conditions. This regulation is crucial for plant survival.

Locating agents are chemical reagents that react with separated compounds to produce colored products, making invisible spots visible. Examples include ninhydrin for amino acids or iodine vapor for various organic compounds. These reagents enable visualization and identification of separated components that lack natural color.
questions.question: What type of detector reagent would make colorless components visible on a paper chromatogram?

options: Removal of heat generated by electric current
questions.explanation: Heat generation from the passage of electric current through the buffer is a major problem because it can cause convection currents, evaporation, and changes in buffer properties that disrupt separation. Efficient cooling systems are essential. Temperature variations also affect migration rates and resolution.
questions.question: What is the major technical challenge in all forms of electrophoresis?
What distinguishes HPLC from conventional column chromatography?
questions.explanation: HPLC uses high pressure pumps to force mobile phase through columns packed with very small particles, achieving faster and more efficient separations than gravity-flow column chromatography. The high pressure overcomes the resistance to flow created by the fine particles. This results in superior resolution and shorter analysis times.
options: Application of high pressure up to 400 atmospheres

questions.explanation: An Rf value greater than 0.9 indicates the compound has traveled nearly the entire length of the plate, showing very weak interaction with the stationary phase. This suggests the mobile phase is too strong or the compound is too nonpolar for the chosen system. Better separation requires using a less polar mobile phase.
questions.question: In TLC analysis, what does an Rf value greater than 0.9 typically indicate?

questions.explanation: Sample spots should be kept small (less than 1-2 mm diameter) to ensure good resolution and prevent overlapping of separated components. Large spots lead to diffuse bands that reduce separation efficiency. Concentrated samples applied in small volumes produce the best results.
questions.question: What is the recommended diameter range for sample spots applied to TLC plates?

questions.explanation: Ruthenium red specifically stains acidic polysaccharides, particularly mucilages and pectins, producing a pink to red color. This helps identify mucilage cells, canals, and cell walls rich in pectin. The stain is valuable for drugs containing mucilaginous constituents and for distinguishing cell wall components.
questions.question: What does ruthenium red stain in plant tissues?

questions.explanation: Acid-insoluble ash primarily consists of silica (silicon dioxide) from sand, soil, and contaminating earth that doesn't dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid. High acid-insoluble ash indicates adulteration with sand or earthy matter. Properly cleaned drugs should have very low acid-insoluble ash (typically less than 2%).
questions.question: What is indicated by high acid-insoluble ash content?
In temperature programming for GC, why is the temperature gradually increased?
options: To separate compounds with wide boiling point ranges
questions.explanation: Temperature programming allows separation of mixtures containing both volatile and less volatile components in a single run. Low boiling compounds separate at lower temperatures while the temperature is ramped up to elute higher boiling materials. Isothermal methods would be impractical for such mixtures.

TLC operates on the principle of adsorption where compounds in the sample compete for active sites on the solid stationary phase (typically silica or alumina). Separation occurs based on differential adsorption strengths of components. The mobile phase acts to elute compounds based on their relative affinities for the adsorbent surface.
questions.question: What type of chromatography is TLC classified as based on its separation principle?

questions.explanation: The "like dissolves like" principle states that polar (hydrophilic) solutes dissolve better in polar solvents while nonpolar (lipophilic) solutes prefer nonpolar solvents. This is because similar intermolecular forces exist between solute and solvent molecules. This principle guides solvent selection for extraction and chromatography.
questions.question: What is the "like dissolves like" principle in partition?
options: All compounds dissolve equally in all solvents
Ionic compounds dissolve only in water
Large molecules prefer large solvent molecules
Polar solutes prefer polar solvents; nonpolar prefer nonpolar

questions.explanation: Very hot water extracts more efficiently but may also extract undesirable substances like excessive tannins, cause precipitation of compounds upon cooling, volatilize essential oils, or destroy heat-labile active constituents. It may also coagulate proteins within cells, actually hindering extraction. Moderate temperatures often give better quality extracts.
options: Extraction of unwanted materials and possible degradation
questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of using very hot water for infusion?
In double maceration, what happens to the drug after the first maceration?
options: It is macerated again with fresh menstruum
questions.explanation: In double maceration, the marc from the first extraction is macerated a second time with fresh menstruum to extract residual actives. The two extracts are combined. This provides more complete extraction than single maceration. Triple maceration uses three sequential extractions for even more thorough extraction.

questions.question: Which extraction method would be most appropriate for Cinchona bark?
questions.explanation: Cinchona bark is hard and woody, requiring the vigorous extraction provided by decoction to efficiently extract the alkaloid constituents (quinine, etc.). Simple infusion would not adequately extract actives from this dense material. The boiling process is necessary to break down the tough bark structure.

Since water evaporates during boiling, the final volume must be adjusted by adding water (usually passed through the strained marc) to reach the specified volume. This ensures consistent concentration of the final product. Adjustment is critical for standardization and dosing accuracy.
options: Water is added to compensate for evaporation
questions.question: What is done after decoction to adjust the final volume?
What is the typical upper molecular weight limit for compounds analyzable by GC?
questions.explanation: Compounds larger than approximately 1000 Da typically lack sufficient volatility to vaporize and pass through the GC column without decomposition. Large molecules require excessively high temperatures that may cause thermal degradation. Derivatization can sometimes extend the molecular weight range.

options: Loss of electrons to the solution
questions.explanation: In acidic conditions, excess H+ ions protonate basic groups (like amino groups) on ampholytes, giving them a net positive charge. These protonated molecules then migrate toward the cathode. At alkaline pH, acidic groups lose protons and the molecule becomes negatively charged.
questions.question: Why does an ampholyte become positively charged in acidic conditions?
In GC analysis, what does "bleeding" of the stationary phase refer to?
options: Elution of stationary phase at high temperature
Loss of carrier gas through leaks
questions.explanation: Column bleeding occurs when the liquid stationary phase itself volatilizes and elutes from the column at excessively high temperatures, appearing as a rising baseline on the chromatogram. This contamination affects detector response and sensitivity. Operating within the specified temperature range minimizes bleeding.

Soxhlet extraction continuously distills and recycles the solvent, so fresh distilled solvent repeatedly contacts the sample while extracted material accumulates in the flask. This is much more efficient than maceration where the surrounding solvent becomes saturated. The same small volume of solvent extracts exhaustively.
questions.question: What is the main advantage of Soxhlet extraction over simple maceration?
options: Continuous use of fresh solvent through recycling

questions.question: Where is the crude drug placed in a Soxhlet apparatus?
questions.explanation: The powdered drug is packed in a porous paper or cellulose thimble placed in the extraction chamber. The thimble allows solvent to percolate through while retaining the solid drug material. This prevents the drug from blocking the siphon and allows efficient extraction without drug particles escaping.
options: In a thimble within the extraction chamber

questions.explanation: Guard cells are specialized, kidney-shaped cells that form the borders of the stomatal pore. They contain chloroplasts and can change shape to open or close the pore by altering their turgor pressure. The guard cells regulate the size of the stomatal opening in response to light, CO2 concentration, and water status.
questions.question: What are the specialized cells that border the stomatal pore called?

questions.explanation: Elution is achieved either by increasing ionic strength (salt concentration) which competes with sample binding, or by changing pH to alter the charge state of the sample or resin. Gradient elution progressively increases salt concentration for optimal separation. This disrupts the electrostatic interactions holding molecules to the resin.
questions.question: How are bound molecules eluted from an ion exchange column?
options: By increasing salt concentration or changing pH

questions.question: What does total ash represent in crude drug evaluation?
questions.explanation: Total ash is the inorganic residue remaining after complete incineration of the organic plant material at 450-525degC until carbon-free. It represents both physiological ash (minerals from plant tissues) and non-physiological ash (extraneous matter like sand, soil, dust). Total ash is expressed as percentage of the air-dried drug.

questions.question: In partition chromatography, equilibration of the solute occurs between which phases?
questions.explanation: Partition chromatography involves equilibration of the solute between two immiscible liquid phases - one stationary and one mobile. This is distinct from adsorption chromatography where equilibration is between a liquid mobile phase and a solid stationary phase. The liquid nature of both phases in partition chromatography is its defining characteristic.

Steam distillation specifically isolates volatile constituents like essential oils that have appreciable vapor pressure at 100degC. The steam carries volatile compounds out of the plant material and they condense together. Non-volatile constituents remain in the residue. This is the primary method for essential oil production.
questions.question: What type of plant constituents are isolated by steam distillation?

questions.explanation: Bitterness value quantifies the bitter taste intensity, which often correlates with the concentration of therapeutically active bitter principles (sesquiterpene lactones, alkaloids, iridoids). Bitter drugs are used as digestive stimulants because bitterness triggers gastric secretions. The bitterness value is determined by comparing to a standard quinine solution.
options: It correlates with therapeutic activity of bitter principles
questions.question: Why is bitterness value important for some herbal drugs?
What is a major limitation of CCC compared to HPLC?
questions.explanation: CCC generally requires longer analysis times (hours) compared to HPLC (minutes) due to lower separation efficiency and the need to use lower flow rates to maintain stationary phase retention. However, CCC offers advantages in sample recovery and prevention of denaturation. The choice depends on the specific application requirements.

Traditional column chromatography requires large volumes of organic solvents for elution, making it expensive and environmentally problematic. HPLC uses high pressure to achieve separation with much smaller solvent volumes. The large solvent requirement is a significant limitation for preparative separations.
questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of column chromatography compared to modern HPLC?
Why is paper chromatography considered less accurate than HPLC?
questions.explanation: Variations in paper quality, environmental conditions (humidity, temperature), and manual application techniques cause inconsistent results and poor reproducibility. HPLC uses standardized columns and automated injection, providing much better precision. Paper chromatography results can vary significantly between runs and operators.

questions.question: What partition coefficient range is optimal for countercurrent chromatography?
questions.explanation: K values between 0.5 and 2.0 provide optimal separation in CCC with reasonable retention times. Lower values mean the compound prefers the mobile phase too much (poor resolution), while higher values cause excessive retention and peak broadening. This range balances resolution and practical analysis time.

options: As soon as water contacts the drug
questions.explanation: The infusion time is measured from the moment the menstruum (hot or cold water) is added to the plant material, as this is when extraction begins. The duration varies depending on the drug and desired concentration. Typical infusion times range from 15 minutes to several hours.
questions.question: In infusion preparation, when does timing begin?

questions.explanation: Paper electrophoresis typically requires 12-18 hours for adequate separation of components due to the slow migration rates in the paper matrix under an electric field. This extended time is necessary for components to achieve sufficient separation distances. Faster methods like gel electrophoresis have largely replaced paper electrophoresis.
questions.question: What is the typical duration for a paper chromatography electrophoresis run?
At what temperature is plant material typically incinerated for ash determination?
questions.explanation: Incineration is performed at 450-525degC (typically 450degC), which is hot enough to completely combust organic matter to carbon dioxide and water while retaining inorganic constituents as oxides, carbonates, phosphates, and silicates. Higher temperatures might volatilize some mineral components; lower temperatures might leave carbon residue.

questions.question: What type of molecules can be separated by CM-cellulose?
questions.explanation: CM (carboxymethyl)-cellulose is a weak cation exchanger with negatively charged carboxyl groups that bind positively charged molecules. It is commonly used for protein purification when the protein has a net positive charge at the working pH. The weak exchange character allows elution under mild conditions.

questions.question: What is the consequence of applying too concentrated a sample in TLC?
questions.explanation: Overloading the TLC plate with concentrated sample causes streaking because the large amount of material cannot form discrete spots and instead spreads along the direction of development. This reduces resolution and makes interpretation difficult. Optimal sample concentration is crucial for obtaining well-defined, circular spots.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the preliminary moistening step in percolation?
options: To allow drug swelling before packing
questions.explanation: Preliminary moistening (imbibition) allows dried plant material to swell as the menstruum penetrates, preventing the drug from swelling after packing which would cause the column to become too tightly packed and impede flow. It also removes air from between particles that would create channels. This step takes about 4 hours.

options: Volume of oil / volume of water x 100
Weight of oil / volume of water x 100
Weight of plant / volume of oil x 100
Volume of oil / weight of plant material x 100
Volume of oil / volume of xylene x 100
questions.question: How is the percentage oil yield calculated?
questions.explanation: Oil yield percentage is calculated as: (Volume of oil in mL / Weight of plant material in grams) x 100%. This standardized expression allows comparison between different plants and extraction conditions. It is typically expressed as mL oil per 100g of plant material or as a percentage v/w.

Physiological ash is the mineral matter naturally present within the plant tissues, including carbonates, phosphates, silicates, and salts of sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium derived from soil nutrients absorbed during growth. This is distinguished from non-physiological ash which comes from external contamination.
questions.question: What does physiological ash represent?

options: Higher sensitivity than all other methods
Ability to record full UV spectra of eluting peaks
questions.explanation: The diode array detector simultaneously measures absorbance at multiple wavelengths, providing full UV spectra of each eluting peak. This spectral information aids in peak identification and purity assessment. It can also detect co-eluting compounds with different UV spectra.
questions.question: What is the main advantage of using a DAD (diode array detector) in HPLC?
What is the primary difference between infusion and decoction?
questions.explanation: Infusion uses boiling or cold water poured over the drug without continued heating, while decoction involves actively boiling the drug material in water. Decoction is used for hard, woody materials requiring vigorous extraction. Infusion is gentler and suitable for soft plant parts with easily extracted, heat-sensitive constituents.

questions.question: Which molecules always migrate toward the anode regardless of pH?
questions.explanation: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) always carry negative charges due to the phosphate groups in their sugar-phosphate backbone, making them migrate toward the positive anode at any pH. Proteins, by contrast, can be positive, negative, or neutral depending on pH relative to their isoelectric point.

questions.question: In which type of stomata are subsidiary cells arranged parallel to the guard cells?
questions.explanation: Paracytic (Rubiaceous) stomata have one or more subsidiary cells arranged parallel to the long axis of the guard cells and the stomatal pore. This type is found in Senna species and members of the Rubiaceae family. The parallel arrangement is easily recognized in surface views of the epidermis.

questions.question: Which detector is most commonly used in HPLC for compounds with aromatic rings?
questions.explanation: UV-visible detectors are most common because many pharmaceutical compounds contain chromophores (especially aromatic rings) that absorb UV light strongly, typically at 254 or 280 nm. This detection is sensitive, selective, and compatible with gradient elution. The detector response is proportional to compound concentration.

questions.question: What is the typical water content in the receiving flask after steam distillation?
questions.explanation: The condensed steam forms a large aqueous layer that separates from the essential oil layer based on density differences. This water is usually returned to the distillation flask (especially in Clevenger apparatus) to conserve heat and water. The small amount of oil is easily seen floating on or sinking below the water layer.

questions.question: What is the purpose of adding phloroglucinol to a plant tissue section?
questions.explanation: Phloroglucinol in hydrochloric acid is a specific stain for lignified tissues, producing a bright pink or red color. This helps identify lignified cell walls in xylem vessels, fibers, and sclereids. The reaction is immediate and distinctive, making it valuable for distinguishing woody tissues from non-lignified parenchyma.

questions.question: Why is optical rotation measured for some crude drugs?
questions.explanation: Many natural compounds (alkaloids, terpenes, sugars) are optically active (chiral) and rotate plane-polarized light. The direction (+ or -) and magnitude (degrees) of rotation are specific for each compound at given concentration, temperature, and wavelength. Optical rotation helps identify compounds and detect adulteration. Changes in rotation indicate decomposition or contamination.
options: To identify and assess purity of optically active compounds

questions.explanation: Silica (or platinum) crucibles withstand the high incineration temperatures (450-525degC) without melting, cracking, or contributing mineral contaminants to the ash. Porcelain crucibles may contribute alumina and other minerals. Silica crucibles are chemically inert and thermally stable, ensuring accurate ash determination.
options: Resistance to high temperatures without contaminating sample
questions.question: Why is a silica crucible used for ash determination?
Which carrier gas is commonly used with thermal conductivity detectors due to high thermal conductivity?
questions.explanation: Helium has very high thermal conductivity compared to most organic compounds, creating a large detector response when samples elute. Hydrogen also has high thermal conductivity but presents safety hazards. The large difference in thermal conductivity between carrier gas and analytes provides sensitive detection.

Anomocytic (Ranunculaceous or irregular-celled) stomata lack distinctive subsidiary cells - the surrounding cells are indistinguishable from ordinary epidermal cells. This type is found in Digitalis and many other plants. The guard cells appear to be surrounded by randomly arranged epidermal cells.
questions.question: What characterizes anomocytic stomata?
options: Subsidiary cells indistinguishable from other epidermal cells
Subsidiary cells perpendicular to guard cells
Four subsidiary cells in a ring

questions.explanation: Tris-HCl, pyridine, acetate, citrate, and phosphate buffers are commonly used because they maintain stable pH and provide ionic strength for elution. The buffer's pH and ionic strength are critical parameters that can be varied to control separation. Organic solvents cannot provide the ionic environment needed.
questions.question: Which buffer is commonly used in ion exchange chromatography?

questions.explanation: High-performance countercurrent chromatography (HPCCC) uses higher rotation speeds to generate approximately 240g centrifugal force, compared to about 80g for centrifugal partition chromatography. This higher force allows better stationary phase retention and the use of higher mobile phase flow rates for faster separations.
questions.question: Which CCC type generates approximately 240g of centrifugal force?
What is the partition coefficient (K) in countercurrent chromatography?
questions.explanation: The partition coefficient K is defined as the ratio of the concentration of a solute in the stationary phase divided by its concentration in the mobile phase at equilibrium. Optimal K values for CCC are between 0.5 and 2. Values outside this range result in poor resolution or excessive retention times.
options: Ratio of stationary phase to mobile phase volumes
Flow rate of mobile phase through column
Centrifugal force applied to the system
Ratio of solute concentration in stationary to mobile phase

questions.explanation: Although Soxhlet extraction is slow, it is economical because the same small volume of solvent is continuously recycled and reused. This minimizes solvent costs compared to methods requiring large fresh solvent volumes. The technique also requires minimal operator attention once started, reducing labor costs.
questions.question: Why is Soxhlet extraction considered economical despite long extraction times?
What is the typical particle size range for HPLC column packing materials?
questions.explanation: HPLC columns typically use particles of 5 or 10 micrometers diameter, which provide high efficiency (40,000-60,000 plates/meter) but require high pressure to achieve adequate flow rates. Smaller particles (3 micrometers) are used in UHPLC. Larger particles would give poorer resolution.

options: To minimize diffusion and fix separated zones
To serve as the electrode material
questions.explanation: The supporting medium (paper, gel, cellulose acetate) physically stabilizes the separated zones, preventing mixing by convection and diffusion after current is turned off. This allows recovery of separated components and permanent record keeping. The immobilization is a key advantage over free solution electrophoresis.
questions.question: In zone electrophoresis, what is the role of the supporting medium?

questions.explanation: Saturating the jar atmosphere with solvent vapors prevents differential evaporation during development, which would otherwise cause irregular solvent front movement and poor separation. This equilibration step is essential for reproducible and consistent chromatographic results. Without proper saturation, edge effects and distorted spots may occur.
questions.question: In thin layer chromatography, what is the primary purpose of applying a paper impregnated with mobile phase to the walls of the chromatography jar?
options: To prevent solvent evaporation from the TLC plate
To saturate the jar atmosphere with solvent vapors
To ensure uniform coating of the adsorbent layer
To increase the resolution of separated components
To reduce the time required for chromatogram development
They remain in the distillation flask
questions.explanation: Non-volatile constituents (resins, tannins, proteins, fixed oils, pigments) do not have sufficient vapor pressure to volatilize and remain as a residue in the distillation flask. Only steam-volatile compounds pass into the distillate. This selectivity makes steam distillation an excellent purification method for essential oils.
questions.question: In steam distillation, what happens to non-volatile plant constituents?

options: To assess contamination with non-drug plant parts
questions.explanation: Foreign organic matter includes parts of the plant not intended as the drug (e.g., stems in leaf drugs, leaves in flower drugs) or other plant species. Excessive foreign matter indicates careless collection, improper processing, or deliberate adulteration. Pharmacopoeias specify maximum limits (typically 2-5%) for foreign matter. This ensures drug quality and potency.
questions.question: Why is determining foreign organic matter important?

options: To serve as a mounting and clearing medium
questions.question: What is the function of glycerin in microscopic preparations?
questions.explanation: Glycerin serves as a mounting medium for temporary preparations, has a high refractive index that reduces light scattering and provides some clearing action, and prevents specimens from drying out during observation. Dilute glycerin can also stain aleurone grains. It preserves preparations for extended periods.

questions.question: Why is sodium hypochlorite used in microscopic preparation?
questions.explanation: Sodium hypochlorite acts as a powerful bleaching agent, removing dark pigments, tannins, and chlorophyll that obscure cellular details. It is particularly useful for heavily pigmented barks and leaves. After bleaching, the tissue must be thoroughly washed to remove residual hypochlorite before applying other stains.

The carrier gas acts as the mobile phase, carrying vaporized sample components through the column where separation occurs based on differential partitioning into the stationary phase. It must be inert to avoid reacting with samples or stationary phase. Common carrier gases include helium, nitrogen, and hydrogen.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the carrier gas in gas chromatography?
options: To serve as the mobile phase transporting samples

questions.question: What is the primary function of plant trichomes?
options: Protection from environmental stressors and herbivores
questions.explanation: Trichomes protect plants from various stresses: UV radiation damage, temperature extremes, water loss (by reducing transpiration), and herbivore attack (mechanical barrier and deterrent chemicals). Some trichomes secrete toxic or sticky substances. They may also reflect light and create a boundary layer that reduces air movement over the leaf surface.

Proteins are detected at 214-220 nm (peptide bond absorption) or 280 nm (aromatic amino acid absorption from tryptophan and tyrosine). The 280 nm wavelength is more specific for proteins and less sensitive to buffer interference. Continuous UV monitoring allows real-time detection as proteins elute.
questions.question: What wavelength is commonly used for UV detection of proteins in gel filtration?

questions.explanation: Chloral hydrate solution clears plant tissues by dissolving cell contents and rendering cells transparent, making structural details more visible. It swells and clarifies tissues without destroying cell walls. This allows better observation of cell arrangement and tissue architecture. The clearing process is reversible and does not damage specimens.
questions.question: Which reagent is used as a clearing agent in microscopic examination?
What is the primary disadvantage of TLC compared to HPLC?
questions.explanation: While TLC is excellent for qualitative analysis and screening, it provides less accurate quantitative results compared to HPLC due to variations in spot intensity, manual application, and environmental factors. HPLC offers better precision, reproducibility, and automated quantitation capabilities. TLC is primarily used for qualitative or semi-quantitative purposes.

questions.question: What is the driving force for mobile phase movement in classic LPLC?
questions.explanation: Traditional LPLC relies on gravity to move the mobile phase through the packed column at atmospheric pressure. This results in slow flow rates but requires no pumping equipment. The technique is simple and inexpensive but time-consuming compared to pressurized methods like HPLC.

Simple maceration typically requires 3-7 days of contact between the drug and menstruum with occasional agitation. This allows time for the solvent to penetrate the plant cells, dissolve active constituents, and for equilibrium to be established between the drug and surrounding liquid. Shorter times may give incomplete extraction.
questions.question: What is the typical duration for simple maceration?

options: To serve as the main separation column
To regulate mobile phase flow rate
To protect the analytical column from contamination
questions.explanation: The guard column is a short column packed with similar material as the analytical column, placed before it to trap particulates and irreversibly bound compounds that would otherwise contaminate and shorten the life of the expensive analytical column. It is periodically replaced while the analytical column is preserved.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the guard column in HPLC systems?

questions.explanation: Vein termination number is the average number of vein endings (veinlets that terminate within the mesophyll without connecting to other veins) per square millimeter of leaf, measured midway between midrib and margin. It indicates the density of the finest veinlet branching. Higher numbers indicate more extensive vascularization.
questions.question: What is vein termination number?
options: Total veins ending at leaf margin
Average number of vein endings per square millimeter
Different affinities for stationary and mobile phases
questions.explanation: Components separate based on their relative affinities for the stationary aqueous phase versus the mobile organic phase, determined by polarity and solubility differences. Compounds more soluble in the mobile phase travel faster, while those preferring the stationary phase move slower. This differential partitioning is the basis of separation.
questions.question: In paper chromatography, what causes components to move at different rates?

options: Number of stomata per epidermis cell
Average number of palisade cells beneath each epidermal cell
Ratio of palisade to spongy mesophyll
Number of veins per leaf area
questions.question: What is the palisade ratio?
questions.explanation: The palisade ratio is the average number of palisade cells (columnar photosynthetic cells) located beneath each epidermal cell in a leaf's upper surface. It is determined by counting palisade cells under a defined number of epidermal cells. This ratio is relatively constant for a species and helps in identification of powdered leaf drugs.

questions.question: What type of stomata has three subsidiary cells, one distinctly smaller?
questions.explanation: Anisocytic (Cruciferous or unequal-celled) stomata are surrounded by three subsidiary cells of unequal size, with one being distinctly smaller than the others. This arrangement is found in Datura and Cruciferae family members. The unequal sizes make this type easily recognizable.

Ion exchange separation is based on reversible electrostatic interactions between charged sample molecules and oppositely charged groups on the stationary phase. Molecules with greater charge density bind more strongly. Elution is achieved by increasing ionic strength to compete with sample binding or by changing pH.
questions.question: What is the primary principle of separation in ion exchange chromatography?
options: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged groups
When drug is added to water
questions.question: In decoction, when does timing begin?
questions.explanation: For decoction, time measurement begins when the water starts to boil, not when heating begins or when drug is added. The decoction time is typically 15 minutes of active boiling. This standardization ensures reproducible extraction since the boiling point is a defined temperature.

The partition coefficient is the ratio of the concentration of a solute in the stationary phase divided by its concentration in the mobile phase at equilibrium. It quantifies how a compound distributes between two immiscible solvents. This value is fundamental to liquid-liquid extraction and countercurrent chromatography.
options: Ratio of solute concentrations in two immiscible phases
questions.question: What does the partition coefficient (K) represent?

options: Characterizing and assessing purity of oils and liquids
questions.question: What is the refractive index useful for?
questions.explanation: Refractive index (RI) measures how much light bends when passing through a substance, which correlates with chemical composition and purity. Each oil or liquid has a characteristic RI range. Adulteration with other oils or deterioration changes the RI. This provides a rapid quality control test for volatile oils, fixed oils, and liquid preparations.

questions.question: What distinguishes glandular from non-glandular trichomes?
questions.explanation: Glandular trichomes have a specialized secretory head (usually multicellular) that produces and secretes substances like essential oils, resins, or mucilage, while non-glandular (covering) trichomes lack secretory structures and provide primarily physical protection. The presence of the glandular head is the defining characteristic.
options: Presence or absence of secretory head

questions.explanation: Organoleptic evaluation uses the human senses to assess macroscopic features: visual appearance (color, shape, size), odor (aromatic qualities), taste (bitter, sweet, astringent), and texture (smooth, rough, hard). This provides quick preliminary identification without instruments. It is the simplest and most rapid evaluation method.
questions.question: What is evaluated during organoleptic examination of crude drugs?
options: Sensory properties like color, odor, taste, and texture

questions.explanation: Sun-exposed leaves typically develop more palisade layers and higher palisade ratios than shade leaves because they need greater photosynthetic capacity to utilize high light intensity. Shade leaves have lower ratios with more spongy mesophyll for efficient light capture in low light. This plasticity occurs within species.
questions.question: How does the palisade ratio differ between sun and shade leaves?
options: Shade leaves always have higher ratios
Sun leaves typically have higher ratios

questions.question: Which factor does NOT significantly influence electrophoretic mobility?
questions.explanation: The color or visible light absorption characteristics of a molecule have no effect on its electrophoretic behavior, which is determined by charge, size, shape, and the applied electric field. Color is purely a spectroscopic property. Separation occurs based on physical and electrical properties, not optical ones.

In GLC, the stationary phase is a high-boiling liquid film coated onto the surface of an inert solid support material or the column wall. Sample components partition between this liquid phase and the gas phase. The liquid must be non-volatile at operating temperatures.
questions.question: In gas-liquid chromatography, what serves as the stationary phase?

options: They allow identification when macroscopic features are lost
questions.question: Why are quantitative microscopic values useful for powdered drugs?
questions.explanation: When drugs are powdered, macroscopic identification features are destroyed, but microscopic quantitative characters (palisade ratio, stomatal indices, vein islet numbers) remain determinable from fragments. These numerical values allow identification and detection of admixtures in powdered materials. They provide objective, measurable standards.

Infusions and decoctions are aqueous preparations without preservatives that provide excellent growth media for bacteria and fungi. They spoil rapidly and should be freshly prepared and used within 12-24 hours. Refrigeration may extend this slightly but fresh preparation is always preferable.
questions.question: Why should fresh infusions be consumed within 12-24 hours?
What type of solvent is required for Soxhlet extraction?
questions.explanation: Soxhlet extraction requires volatile solvents that can be vaporized, condensed, and recycled. Common solvents include hexane, petroleum ether, chloroform, methanol, and ethanol. Water or high-boiling solvents cannot be used because the technique depends on solvent evaporation and condensation cycles.

Sulphated ash involves treating the sample with sulfuric acid before ashing, which converts all mineral elements to their sulfate forms. This provides a more consistent and reproducible residue weight than regular ash methods. It is used particularly for materials where precise inorganic content measurement is critical.
options: To convert all minerals to sulfate form for gravimetric analysis
questions.question: What is the purpose of sulphated ash determination?

options: They accumulate as solvent evaporates and recycles
They return to the extraction chamber
questions.question: What happens to extracted compounds in the Soxhlet flask during cycling?
questions.explanation: As the volatile solvent evaporates from the flask and recycles to the extraction chamber, the non-volatile extracted compounds remain in the flask and concentrate. This allows accumulation of extracted material while using minimal solvent. The final concentrated extract is obtained after extraction is complete.

options: To characterize different classes of constituents present
questions.question: What is the purpose of determining multiple extractive values with different solvents?
questions.explanation: Different solvents extract different compound classes: water extracts polar constituents (sugars, tannins, glycosides), alcohol extracts moderately polar compounds (alkaloids, resins, phenolics), and ether extracts nonpolar substances (fixed oils, volatile oils, some resins). Multiple extractive values provide a chemical profile of the drug.

options: It aids in identification and indicates handling history
questions.explanation: Surface texture (smooth, rough, wrinkled, warty, hairy) is characteristic for specific drugs and helps distinguish authentic materials from adulterants. Surface condition also indicates proper drying and storage - excessive wrinkling or discoloration may indicate deterioration. Texture affects commercial grading and quality assessment.
questions.question: Why is the surface texture of crude drugs important?

questions.explanation: Gel filtration separates purely by size, not by charge or chemical properties. Resolution depends on physical factors like column dimensions, particle size, pore size distribution, flow rate, and sample volume. The technique is ideal when charge-based methods fail or when maintaining native protein conditions is essential.
questions.question: Which factor does NOT affect resolution in gel filtration?

options: Average number of stomata per square millimeter
questions.explanation: Stomatal number is the average count of stomata present in one square millimeter of epidermis. It is determined by counting stomata in several measured microscopic fields and calculating the average. This value varies between upper and lower leaf surfaces and between species, making it useful for identification.
questions.question: What does stomatal number represent?
Which LPLC modification uses particle size of 40-60 micrometers?
questions.explanation: Flash chromatography uses 40-60 um particles, which are smaller than those in classical column chromatography but larger than HPLC particles. This particle size provides improved resolution compared to traditional columns while still allowing reasonable flow rates under modest pressure. The technique provides a good compromise between speed and resolution.

questions.question: What type of compounds is CCC particularly well-suited to separate?
questions.explanation: CCC is especially useful for separating polar natural products, glycosides, and other compounds that might irreversibly adsorb to solid stationary phases in conventional chromatography. The liquid stationary phase provides gentler separation conditions. Many pharmaceutical natural products have been purified using CCC.

Sweet taste typically indicates the presence of glycosides (like those in licorice) or free sugars. Many cardiac glycosides have intensely sweet taste. Some sweet-tasting plants are used as natural sweeteners. However, sweetness does not always mean safety - some very toxic compounds taste sweet.
questions.question: What does a sweet taste in crude drug typically indicate?

questions.explanation: Actinocytic stomata have subsidiary cells arranged in a radiating or star-like pattern around the guard cells, with four or more cells extending outward like spokes. This type is less common but distinctive when present. The radiating arrangement is best seen in surface view preparations.
questions.question: Which stomatal type has subsidiary cells arranged in a radiating pattern?

questions.explanation: Successive extraction uses solvents in order of increasing polarity: petroleum ether -> benzene -> chloroform -> acetone -> ethanol -> methanol -> water. This systematically extracts compounds of increasing polarity, allowing their separation based on solubility. Each extract contains compounds of similar polarity.
questions.question: In successive solvent extraction using Soxhlet, what is the order of solvent polarity?
What type of analysis is typically performed on LPLC fractions?
questions.explanation: Collected LPLC fractions are typically analyzed by TLC to determine which fractions contain the same compounds so they can be pooled. UV or other spectroscopic methods may also be used. TLC is quick, requires little material, and effectively shows fraction composition. Similar fractions are combined for further processing.

As condensed solvent accumulates in the extraction chamber surrounding the thimble, the liquid level rises until it reaches the top of the siphon tube. The siphon then rapidly empties the chamber, returning the solvent containing dissolved actives to the boiling flask. This cycle repeats automatically.
options: By siphoning when level reaches maximum
questions.question: How does solvent return to the boiling flask in Soxhlet extraction?
In reversed-phase HPLC, what type of stationary phase is employed?
questions.explanation: Reversed-phase uses nonpolar stationary phases such as C18 or C8 bonded to silica, which is opposite (reversed) from normal phase chromatography. Polar mobile phases are used with these hydrophobic columns. This is the most common HPLC mode for pharmaceutical applications.

questions.question: What is the typical palisade ratio range for Atropa belladonna?
questions.explanation: Atropa belladonna has a palisade ratio of 6.0 to 10.0, meaning there are typically 6-10 palisade cells beneath each epidermal cell. This is relatively high compared to some other medicinal plants. The palisade ratio helps distinguish belladonna from potential adulterants with different ratios.

The color or appearance of the column glassware has no effect on the chemical interactions and physical processes that govern chromatographic separation. Separation depends on the properties of the stationary phase, mobile phase, and operational parameters. Glassware color is purely cosmetic.
questions.question: Which factor does NOT directly affect separation efficiency in column chromatography?

questions.explanation: Transfer of solute from one liquid phase to another is driven by concentration gradients. The solute moves from the phase where it is more concentrated to the phase where it is less concentrated until equilibrium (defined by the partition coefficient) is reached. Agitation accelerates equilibration by maximizing interfacial contact.
questions.question: In liquid-liquid extraction, what promotes solute transfer between phases?

questions.explanation: Cation exchangers have negatively charged groups (like sulfonate or carboxylate) that bind positively charged molecules such as proteins below their isoelectric point. The strength of binding depends on the protein's net positive charge. Bound proteins are eluted by increasing salt concentration or raising pH.
questions.question: Which type of ion exchanger would bind positively charged proteins?
What does the stationary phase retention (Sf) represent in CCC?
questions.explanation: Stationary phase retention (Sf) is the percentage of the column volume occupied by the stationary phase after equilibration with flowing mobile phase. Higher Sf values generally give better resolution but longer analysis times. Typical Sf values range from 50-80% depending on the system.
options: Volume of stationary phase remaining in column

questions.question: What is measured by the vein islet number?
questions.explanation: Vein islet number is the average number of vein islets (smallest areas of photosynthetic tissue completely surrounded by veinlets) per square millimeter of leaf surface, measured between the midrib and leaf margin. It indicates the density of minor vein branching. This is a stable character useful for drug standardization.
options: Total number of veins in leaf
Average number of vein islets per square millimeter

questions.explanation: Anion exchangers have positively charged functional groups (like quaternary ammonium) that attract and bind negatively charged molecules (anions). The oppositely charged ionic groups interact electrostatically. To elute bound anions, the ionic strength of the mobile phase is increased or pH is changed.
questions.question: What type of ion exchanger is used to separate negatively charged molecules?

questions.explanation: Paper chromatography requires only minute quantities of sample (microliters), making it ideal when sample availability is limited. This economy in sample usage is particularly valuable for expensive or scarce materials. The technique can provide useful qualitative information from very small amounts of material.
questions.question: Which advantage does paper chromatography offer for routine laboratory analysis?

questions.explanation: In most plants, stomata are more numerous on the lower (abaxial) leaf surface than the upper (adaxial) surface. Some plants have stomata only on the lower surface. This distribution minimizes water loss from direct sun exposure. Stomatal numbers and indices differ characteristically between surfaces for each species.
questions.question: How does stomatal number differ between upper and lower leaf surfaces?
options: Usually more numerous on lower surface
More numerous on upper surface always

questions.question: In column chromatography, what does the term "eluent" specifically refer to?
questions.explanation: The eluent is the solvent or mobile phase that flows through the column, carrying sample components with it. It provides the force for moving compounds through the stationary phase. The choice of eluent polarity is critical for achieving good separation.

Droplet countercurrent chromatography (DCCC) relies solely on gravity for the mobile phase to flow through the stationary phase in vertically held columns. This is the oldest form of CCC but has been largely replaced by centrifugal methods. DCCC is slow but requires no centrifuge equipment.
questions.question: Which CCC technique uses gravity alone for phase separation?

options: The temperature range where the substance transitions from solid to liquid
questions.explanation: Melting point is the temperature range where a substance changes from solid to liquid state. For fats and waxes, melting points are characteristic ranges (e.g., beeswax: 62-65degC, cocoa butter: 30-33degC) rather than sharp points because they contain mixtures of compounds. Melting point helps identify substances and detect adulteration.
questions.question: At what temperature are melting points typically determined for fats and waxes?
What is DEAE-cellulose classified as?
questions.explanation: DEAE (diethylaminoethyl)-cellulose is a weak anion exchanger containing tertiary amine groups that become positively charged at low pH, binding anions. It is "weak" because the charge depends on pH. This is useful for separating proteins and nucleic acids under mild conditions.

questions.question: In maceration with adjustment, what proportion of menstruum is initially used?
questions.explanation: In maceration with adjustment (used for unorganized drugs), 4/5 of the menstruum is used initially for maceration, then the final 1/5 is used to rinse the filter and adjust the final volume. The marc is not pressed since unorganized drugs (resins, balsams) don't retain significant menstruum. This ensures accurate final concentration.

Total ash significantly above the standard range for that drug suggests adulteration with inorganic materials, contamination with soil or sand, improper cleaning before drying, or admixture with inferior plant parts containing high mineral content. Ash determination is a simple quality control test. Each drug has specified ash limits in pharmacopoeias.
questions.question: What does excessive total ash content suggest about a crude drug?
options: Adulteration with inorganic matter or earthy contamination

questions.explanation: Alcohol-soluble extractive is most suitable for drugs containing alkaloids, resins, tannins, and other moderately polar organic constituents because these dissolve well in alcoholic solvents (usually 90% ethanol). Alkaloids and resins are generally alcohol-soluble but not water-soluble. This makes alcohol extractive value a good indicator of these constituents.
questions.question: Which extractive value test would be most appropriate for drugs containing alkaloids and resins?
Which advantage does CCC offer over conventional chromatography?
questions.explanation: The absence of a solid stationary phase eliminates irreversible adsorption, allowing complete sample recovery. This is particularly valuable for expensive or scarce compounds. The liquid stationary phase can also be easily recovered and reused after analysis.
options: Better resolution for all compound types

questions.explanation: Vein islet number is measured in the area midway between the midrib and the leaf margin because this region shows the most characteristic venation pattern for the species. The midrib area and leaf margins show atypical vein arrangements. Standardizing the measurement location ensures reproducible results.
questions.question: Where on the leaf is vein islet number typically measured?
What is the typical column dimension for analytical gel filtration?
questions.explanation: Analytical gel filtration columns typically have diameters of 7.5-8 mm and lengths of 25-60 cm to provide adequate resolution while using reasonable amounts of buffer and sample. Preparative columns are wider (22-25 mm diameter) to handle larger sample volumes. Longer columns generally give better resolution.

If the column packing dries out, it shrinks and cracks, creating channels through which the mobile phase preferentially flows, bypassing most of the stationary phase. This channeling destroys separation efficiency as sample components are not properly exposed to the adsorbent. The column must remain saturated with solvent throughout the procedure.
options: It creates channels and disrupts uniform flow
questions.question: In column chromatography, why should the stationary phase never be allowed to dry out during operation?

options: Likely presence of alkaloids or bitter principles
questions.question: In macroscopic evaluation, what is indicated by an intensely bitter taste?
questions.explanation: Intense bitterness usually indicates alkaloids (quinine, strychnine), sesquiterpene lactones, or other bitter principles. Many therapeutically active compounds are bitter. Traditional medicine often correlates bitterness with medicinal potency. However, chemical analysis is needed to identify specific bitter constituents.

options: Requirement for low-salt buffer loading conditions
questions.question: What is the major disadvantage of ion exchange chromatography?
questions.explanation: Ion exchange requires samples to be loaded in low ionic strength buffers so charged molecules can bind to the resin through electrostatic interactions. High salt concentrations shield charges and prevent binding. This necessitates desalting or dialysis of many biological samples before loading, adding preparation time.

questions.question: What does the swelling index measure?
questions.explanation: Swelling index measures the volume in milliliters occupied by 1 gram of plant material after swelling in an aqueous liquid for a specified time. It indicates the amount of mucilage or hydrocolloid present. Materials with high mucilage content (psyllium, isabgol, flaxseed) show high swelling indices. This is important for materials used as bulking agents or demulcents.
options: Volume increase when drug is mixed with water

questions.explanation: Hard barks, roots, and woods have dense, lignified tissue that water cannot easily penetrate. Boiling helps break down cell walls and improves extraction of constituents from this tough plant material. The high temperature and agitation of boiling are necessary to achieve adequate extraction from these recalcitrant materials.
options: Dense tissue structure requires vigorous extraction
They have low active constituent content
They dissolve better in cold water
questions.question: Why is decoction necessary for hard, woody drugs?

questions.explanation: In adsorption chromatography, components are separated based on their different affinities for adsorption onto the solid stationary phase surface. Compounds with weaker adsorption move through the column faster with the mobile phase. The strength of adsorption depends on the chemical nature of both the analyte and adsorbent.
questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of separation in adsorption column chromatography?

questions.explanation: Ninhydrin reacts specifically with amino acids to form a purple-colored complex (Ruhemann's purple) through reaction with the primary amine group. This makes it highly selective for detecting amino acids and peptides on chromatograms. The reaction is sensitive and produces characteristic coloration even at low concentrations.
questions.question: Which detection method is specifically used for identifying amino acid compounds in TLC?
In LPLC, what is the recommended ratio of stationary phase to crude sample?
questions.explanation: A large excess of stationary phase (100-500 g per gram of crude extract) is used in LPLC to ensure adequate separation capacity for complex mixtures. This high ratio provides sufficient theoretical plates and loading capacity. The exact amount depends on the complexity of the mixture and desired resolution.

questions.question: In the partition coefficient formula Kd = Cs/Cm, what does Cs represent?
questions.explanation: Cs represents the concentration of the solute in the stationary phase (often the more polar or aqueous phase). Cm is the concentration in the mobile phase. The ratio of these concentrations at equilibrium defines the partition coefficient, which indicates the compound's preference for one phase over the other.

Stoppered or sealed containers prevent evaporation of the menstruum, which would concentrate the extract unpredictably and waste solvent. This is especially important for alcoholic menstruums. If significant evaporation occurs, the extraction efficiency and final concentration would be affected.
options: To reduce loss of volatile menstruum by evaporation
questions.question: Why are stoppered containers used for maceration?

questions.explanation: In ascending mode, the less dense mobile phase is pumped from the bottom and rises through the denser stationary phase held in the column, forming droplets as it ascends. This mode is used when the mobile phase has lower density than the stationary phase. The opposite is descending mode.
options: Mobile phase is denser than stationary phase
Mobile phase is less dense and flows upward
Sample is loaded at the column top
questions.question: In CCC, what does the term "ascending mode" mean?

questions.explanation: The aromatic odor of umbelliferous fruits (anise, fennel, caraway, etc.) comes from essential oils containing compounds like anethole, carvone, and limonene. These volatile constituents evaporate at room temperature, producing characteristic fragrances. Odor quality and intensity indicate oil content and drug quality.
questions.question: Why does umbelliferous fruit have a characteristic aromatic odor?
Which material forms the basis for strong cationic exchange resins?
questions.explanation: Strong cation exchangers contain sulfonic acid (-SO3H) groups attached to the polymer matrix, which are fully ionized over a wide pH range. These strongly acidic groups effectively bind cations. Weak cation exchangers use carboxyl groups which are only ionized at higher pH values.

Paper chromatography has limited resolving power and cannot effectively separate very complex mixtures that contain many similar components. Modern techniques like HPLC provide much better resolution for complex samples. The method works well for simpler mixtures but lacks the separation efficiency needed for complicated analyses.
questions.question: What is a major limitation of paper chromatography compared to modern techniques?
Why must ash determinations be calculated on a dry weight basis?
options: To account for variable moisture content
questions.explanation: Crude drugs contain variable amounts of moisture (typically 8-12% for air-dried materials) depending on storage conditions and humidity. Calculating ash on a dry weight basis eliminates this variable moisture component, allowing meaningful comparison between samples. The calculation adjusts for the water content: % ash (dry basis) = [ash weight x 100] / [sample weight x (100 - moisture %)]

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Subclasses: nitrogen mustards, oxazaphosphorines, ethylene imines and methylmelamines, nitrosoureas, triazenes and hydrazines, alkylsulfonates and platinum coordination complexes.
• Examples: mechlorethamine, melphalan, chlorambucil, bendamustine, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, thiotepa, altretamine, temozolomide, dacarbazine, carmustine, lomustine, busulfan, treosulfan, cisplatin, carboplatin.
(b)
• Alkylating agents are electrophilic substances that react covalently with DNA and proteins by transferring alkyl groups, a nucleophilic substitution (SN1 or SN2).
• They require an electronegative group (e.g. chloride) and an electron acceptor such as nitrogen so that ions able to alkylate DNA and proteins form; they are not analogues of any endogenous molecule and bind no specific receptor.
• The main site is N7 of guanine; other sites include O6, N1, N3 of guanine, and sites on cytosine, adenine and thymine.
• They are non-cell-cycle specific, though cells are more susceptible in G1 and S, and the effect is mainly seen at replication when zones of DNA are unpaired.
(c)
• Bifunctional agents bind two bases or protein and DNA, and are more potent than monofunctional agents because crosslinks cause greater damage that is harder to repair.
• Limitations: they act on rapidly proliferating normal cells, causing myelosuppression, nausea, vomiting, mucositis, alopecia, neurotoxicity, and are mutagenic and carcinogenic.
• They are contraindicated in pregnancy because of mutagenic potential.
(d)
