• Nitrogen mustards: the bis(2-chloroethyl) group is essential and forms an aziridine cation; they derived from sulfur mustards with sulfur replaced by nitrogen for lower toxicity.
• Nitrosoureas (carmustine, lomustine): the nitrosourea group with 2-chloroethyl as the essential group; spontaneous degradation releases diazo-hydroxide and then the aziridine cation.
• Carmustine is bifunctional and lomustine monofunctional (cyclohexyl raises half-life); resistance through DNA repair (e.g. MGMT) applies to the class.
questions.question:
Describe the alkylating agents under the following headings:
(a) classification into subclasses and the main drugs
(b) general structural requirement and mechanism of action at DNA, including the reaction type and main sites
(c) the chemical basis for the greater potency of bifunctional agents and their limitations
(d) distinguish nitrogen mustards from nitrosoureas.

An electrophilic anticancer agent transfers an alkyl group to DNA bases through two possible reaction mechanisms; some agents bind one DNA base while others bridge two bases on the same or different strands.
(a) Identify the class.
(b) Outline the named reaction and its two mechanisms.
(c) Name the nucleophilic groups and DNA sites attacked.
(d) Identify the site at risk and the functionality difference (mono/bifunctional) and its impact.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Alkylating agents, electrophilic substances reacting covalently with DNA and proteins by transferring alkyl groups.
(b)
The reaction is nucleophilic substitution: SN1 in two steps (carbocation attacked by nucleophile) or SN2 in a single step.
(c)
• Susceptible groups: sulfhydryl, hydroxyl, phosphate, amine, imidazole and carboxyl.
• Predominantly N7 of guanine; also O6, N1, N3 of guanine; N3, N4, O2 of cytosine; N1, N3, N6, N7 of adenine; N1, N3, O2, O4 of thymine.
(d)
• Monofunctional agents bind a protein or one base; bifunctional agents bind two bases of the same or different strands, or a protein and DNA.
• Bifunctional agents are more potent as crosslinks inflict greater damage and are harder to repair.
• They are non-cell-cycle specific (more susceptible cells in G1 and S phases).

questions.question:
A thymine nucleoside analogue (deoxythymidine analogue) is given orally for HIV; about 85% is cleared by glucuronidation, half-life about 1 hour, and the patient develops severe anaemia.
(a) Identify the compound.
(b) Describe its physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties as stated (pKa, solubility, partition coefficient, stability).
(c) Describe its activation and metabolic pathway.
(d) State the clinical consequences, including interactions and uses.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Zidovudine (AZT), a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor.
(b)
Oral bioavailability about 65%; distributes to all body tissues including CNS (CSF/plasma ratio about 0.5); half-life about 1 hour.
(c)
• It is phosphorylated by cellular thymidine kinase to the nucleotide analogue, which inhibits RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase) and blocks DNA synthesis; viral polymerases are more sensitive than mammalian ones.
• Biotransformation about 85% by glucuronidation; renal excretion about 15%.
(d)
• Adverse effects: severe anaemia and leukopenia from bone marrow suppression (30% need transfusions), myopathy (10% long term), encephalopathy, seizures, hepatic steatosis, lactic acidosis.
• Toxicity is increased by drugs inhibiting glucuronidation (e.g. fluconazole, cimetidine) or extensively glucuronosylconjugated (e.g. benzodiazepines).
• Active against HIV-1, HIV-2, HTLV-1; resistant mutants emerge after more than 6 months; initial drug of choice when CD4 count is below 500/mm3, with transient benefit.

questions.question:
A man with type 2 diabetes who has no contraindication is started on a biguanide. His eGFR is later found to be below 30.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) Explain its mechanism.
(c) State therapeutic use, key adverse effects and renal limits.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Metformin (Glucophage), a biguanide; the only available medication in this class.
(b)
It lowers blood glucose primarily by decreasing hepatic glucose production and makes muscle tissue more sensitive to insulin.
(c)
• Historically first-line for type 2 diabetes; effective, safe, inexpensive, reduces microvascular complications, cardiovascular events and death.
• Weight neutral, does not cause hypoglycemia, and reduces cardiovascular mortality compared with sulfonylureas.
• Principal side effects: bloating, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, mitigated by gradual titration or extended-release form (twice-daily IR or once-daily ER).
• Cleared by kidney filtration; safe with eGFR of 30 or above; lactic acidosis is rare but occurs when eGFR is below 30; also B12 deficiency and worsening neuropathy.
• Current guidance: GLP-1 RAs or SGLT2 inhibitors preferred as initial therapy with ASCVD, heart failure or CKD.

(a)
Abacavir hypersensitivity (fever, rash, malaise, chills, headache); HLA-B*5701 screening is recommended before starting it.
(b)
• A positive HLA-B*5701 status is recorded as abacavir allergy; if testing is unavailable, abacavir may be started with counselling and monitoring for HSR.
• Prior to ART assess CD4 count, HIV RNA, drug resistance testing, co-receptor tropism, baseline FBC, SEU and creatinine.
• Plasma viral load is the most important indicator of response; undetectable should be reached within 16-24 weeks; a 0.5 log10 change is meaningful.
(c)
• Tenofovir (TDF) and lamivudine (3TC): renal toxicity; stavudine: neuropathy and lipodystrophy; zidovudine: anaemia and marrow suppression.
• Efavirenz: CNS effects; nevirapine: rash/SJS and hepatotoxicity.
(d)
Initial regimens: two NRTIs plus an NNRTI, or two NRTIs plus a PI (with or without ritonavir).
questions.question:
A woman is about to start abacavir. Her team assesses baseline CD4 count, HIV RNA, resistance testing, co-receptor tropism and HLA-B*5701. Later a different patient on another drug develops renal toxicity and a third shows neuropathy and lipodystrophy.
(a) Identify the structural/pharmacogenetic liability linked to abacavir.
(b) Explain the evaluation and monitoring pathway.
(c) Differentiate the related antiretrovirals by their characteristic adverse effects.
(d) Reason to therapeutic choice.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Methotrexate is a folate antagonist (folic acid analogue) used as an antimetabolite.
• Folates consist of a pteridine ring, PABA and glutamate; folic acid is essential for purine nucleotide and thymidylate synthesis.
(b)
• Folate is converted to polyglutamates, then reduced to tetrahydrofolate in two steps (folate to FH2, FH2 to FH4) by dihydrofolate reductase.
• FH4 serves as a methyl group (1-carbon) donor to deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to form deoxythymidine monophosphate (DTMP).
• Methotrexate has higher affinity for dihydrofolate reductase than FH2.
• It is taken up actively through the folate transport system and metabolized intracellularly to polyglutamates retained for weeks or months.
(c)
• Peak concentration 1-5 h after dose, high for about 6 h; 50% plasma protein bound; low lipid solubility, so no CNS entry.
• Routes: oral, IV, IM and intrathecal.
• Side effects: bone marrow depression, GIT epithelium damage, nephrotoxicity at high doses.
(d)
• Depletion of FH4 and DTMP leads to "thymine-less death" and inhibition of DNA synthesis.
• Rapidly dividing normal cells are also affected, explaining the toxicity.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of methotrexate:
(a) its class and the folate structure it mimics
(b) the enzyme and pathway it inhibits and the structural basis of its high affinity and retention
(c) the pharmacokinetic and toxicity features
(d) what happens when the pathway is blocked and the basis of its selectivity or loss of selectivity.

Describe the chemistry of raltegravir and integrase inhibition:
(a) its class and structural description
(b) the enzyme target and the step of the viral life cycle blocked
(c) the clinical basis of its use and limitation (resistance, latency, other agents of the class).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Raltegravir is an integrase inhibitor (INI), the first licensed for clinical use; it is described as a pyrimidinone analogue and also as a dihydropyrimidine derivative.
• Other integrase inhibitors listed: elvitegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir and dolutegravir.
(b)
• It binds integrase, a viral enzyme essential to replication of both HIV-1 and HIV-2.
• It prevents integration of HIV DNA into the host chromosome.
• Integrase has been pursued for many years as a potential target for new anti-HIV compounds.
(c)
• It is licensed for treatment-experienced adults infected with HIV-1 strains resistant to multiple other agents.
• Integrase inhibitors prevent integration but have no effect on viral DNA already integrated into host DNA.
• Because integrated HIV DNA can remain quiescent (latent), HIV cannot be cured despite good clinical control by combination therapy.
• RT inhibitors and protease inhibitors also have no direct effect on integrated viral DNA.

questions.question:
Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide contain a ring that makes them inactive when administered. Analogues were later developed to reduce toxicity, including glufosfamide, mafosfamide and C7, C9-dimethyl-ifosfamide.
(a) Identify the class and the lead drugs.
(b) Outline the activation route (named steps and enzymes).
(c) Identify the site at risk and the toxic metabolites.
(d) State the variants (prodrug or steric) developed and their rationale.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Oxazaphosphorines (alkylating agents): the prodrugs cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide.
(b)
• Inactive on administration because of the oxazaphosphorine ring; they need CYP activation.
• Hydroxylation allows the ring to open and releases the bis(2-chloroethyl) group, which generates the active cation.
• Main enzymes: CYP2A6, CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, CYP2C9 and CYP2C18; polymorphisms alter metabolism, action and toxicity.
(c)
• Active metabolites: 4-hydroxy-cyclophosphamide/4-hydroxy-ifosfamide, aldophosphamide and the mustard; acrolein is a toxic metabolite.
• Toxicities: neurotoxicity and nephrotoxicity; ifosfamide nephrotoxicity may lead to renal failure.
(d)
• Glufosfamide and mafosfamide do not require activation by CYP.
• C7, C9-dimethyl-ifosfamide uses steric hindrance to prevent formation of toxic metabolites.
• Rationale: reduce toxicity. Half-lives: cyclophosphamide 420 min, ifosfamide 90 min.

(a)
Cimetidine, an H2-receptor antagonist blocking H2 receptors of gastric parietal cells and inhibiting gastric secretion.
(b)
• Weak base, highly water-soluble.
• Plasma protein binding 20%; Vd about 1 L/kg; half-life about 2 h; total clearance 500-600 ml/min, mainly renal; oral bioavailability about 60%.
(c)
• 50-80% of an IV dose is recovered unchanged in urine; metabolites make up 25-40% of elimination: cimetidine sulphoxide (10-15%) and hydroxymethyl cimetidine (4%).
• Biliary excretion is about 2% of the dose.
(d)
• Cimetidine is one of the most potent and comprehensive inhibitors of drug metabolism used clinically, so it raises zidovudine toxicity.
• In advanced renal failure clearance falls from about 500 to under 200 ml/min and half-life rises to 4-5 h; 400 mg daily is recommended with minimal renal function.
• CNS effects (mental confusion) occur in elderly and in severe renal or hepatic impairment; effective concentrations are 0.5-1.0 ug/ml.
questions.question:
A drug described as the first histamine H2-receptor antagonist in wide clinical use is a weak base and highly water soluble. Its clearance is mainly renal and it is dosed lower in advanced renal failure.
(a) Identify the compound.
(b) State its physicochemical and kinetic properties as given (pKa, solubility, binding).
(c) Describe its metabolic pathway and metabolites.
(d) State clinical consequences including interactions and special populations.

Discuss substrate-mimic (active-site) antivirals and the evolution of resistance:
(a) the principle and examples (HIV protease inhibitors as gag cleavage site mimics, neuraminidase inhibitors as sialic acid analogues)
(b) relate primary, secondary and tertiary mutations to the structure and function of the target enzyme
(c) explain why this class tends to evolve resistance slowly and the trade-offs or limitations that result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Compounds that act as substrate mimics bind the catalytic site of a viral enzyme; examples include PIs (gag cleavage site mimics) and zanamivir/oseltamivir (sialic acid analogues).
• Substrate-mimic inhibitors contrast with the M2 channel blockers (amantadine, rimantadine), where a single mutation gives high-level resistance.
(b)
• Primary mutations appear first and are the few specific mutations that interfere with drug binding without reducing catalytic activity too much; the initial resistance may be modest.
• Secondary mutations enhance the level of resistance but often reduce catalytic activity and viral fitness.
• Tertiary (compensating) mutations may have no direct effect on drug-protein binding but increase enzyme efficiency to offset primary and secondary changes.
• For HIV protease, both protease and its cleavage sites can co-mutate to give cross-resistance to PIs.
(c)
• Most potential mutations give a nonfunctional enzyme and a nonviable or less fit virus, so resistance evolves more slowly than for M2 inhibitors.
• Single-mutation resistance to M2 inhibitors keeps the virus fully fit and quickly transmissible.
• Trade-off: compensating mutations restore fitness, so resistance can eventually become established.
• Fitness embraces viability, replication rate, immune evasion and transmission.
• Primary mutations are usually confirmed by site-directed mutagenesis into a wild-type background.

questions.question:
Describe the diuretics used in hypertension:
(a) classification and examples
(b) general structure and mechanism of action at the nephron
(c) the chemical basis of their adverse effects and limitations
(d) distinguish thiazide, loop and potassium-sparing diuretics.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide), loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide), potassium-sparing diuretics (triamterene, amiloride).
(b)
• Diuretics decrease blood volume and cardiac output, and decrease peripheral resistance during chronic therapy; they are drugs of choice in elderly hypertensives.
• All loop and thiazide diuretics except ethacrynic acid possess a sulfonamide group, relevant for sulfonamide allergy.
• Thiazides inhibit sodium and chloride reabsorption mostly in the distal tubules; they increase potassium and bicarbonate excretion and decrease calcium excretion; they do not affect normal blood pressure.
(c)
• Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperlipidaemia, hyperuricaemia (contraindicated in gout), hyperglycaemia (not safe in diabetes); not safe in renal and hepatic insufficiency.
• Long-term thiazide use may result in hyponatraemia.
• Potassium-sparing diuretics are weak diuretics and antihypertensives when used alone.
(d)
• Loop diuretics act on the ascending limb of the loop of Henle, are highly protein bound and reach urine by proximal tubular secretion.
• Loop diuretics are used for volume retention, decreased GFR or heart failure, and are less effective than thiazides for BP when dosed once daily.
• Potassium-sparing agents interfere with sodium reabsorption at distal tubules (collecting duct) and decrease potassium secretion.
• Hydrochlorothiazide can be used where hyperkalaemia is a risk, including with ACE inhibitors.

questions.question:
A patient started on a protease inhibitor regimen shows low oral bioavailability. A low dose of ritonavir is added, and the clinician warns about drugs that inhibit the hepatic mixed function oxidase system.
(a) Identify the class and the structural liability that causes the low bioavailability.
(b) Explain the metabolic pathway and interaction mechanism.
(c) Differentiate boosted partners and related classes.
(d) Reason to therapy and administration.
questions.answerText:
(a)
HIV protease inhibitors (e.g. ritonavir, lopinavir, atazanavir, darunavir); oral bioavailability only 4-10% due to extensive first-pass effect.
(b)
• Extensive biotransformation by the mixed function oxidase system in the intestinal wall and liver.
• Drugs that inhibit the hepatic mixed function oxidase system may increase PI plasma concentrations.
(c)
• Ritonavir at low dose raises levels of lopinavir (Kaletra, ritonavir listed as PK enhancer).
• Cobicistat does the same with atazanavir, darunavir and elvitegravir.
• PIs show some cross-resistance among themselves, but not with other antiviral drugs; the protease and its cleavage sites can co-mutate, giving cross-resistance to PIs.
(d)
• PIs are dosed PO, distributed in all tissues except CNS, active in both acutely and chronically infected cells, and specific for HIV protease without affecting human endopeptidases.
• Used in advanced HIV in combination with deoxynucleoside drugs; initial regimens are two NRTIs plus an NNRTI or a PI (with or without ritonavir boosting).

(a)
The modification yields 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), which blocks thymidylate formation and so inhibits DNA synthesis.
(b)
• Normal thymidine biosynthesis involves methylation of the 5-position of uracil's pyrimidine ring; fluorine replacing hydrogen there cannot be methylated.
• A stable covalent ternary complex forms between 5-FU, thymidylate synthase and a tetrahydrofolate cofactor.
(c)
• 5-FU is converted to the fraudulent nucleotide FdUMP, a dUMP analogue that is a competitive inhibitor of the thymidylate synthetase active site but cannot be converted to DTMP.
• Similar drugs working through similar mechanisms: gemcitabine and arabinosylcytosine (araC).
(d)
• Thymidine is not a normal component of RNA, so targeting the enzyme should selectively inhibit DNA formation.
• Used in carcinomas of breast, colon, pancreas and rectum; given IV or topically for skin cancer.
• It readily crosses the brain barrier and is rapidly metabolized in the liver (caution in hepatic impairment); about 20% excreted unchanged in kidneys.
• Adverse effects: bone marrow depression, ulceration of oral and GI mucosa, GIT hemorrhage, stomatitis, leukopenia, diarrhoea; consciousness disturbance at high doses.
questions.question:
Researchers replace the hydrogen at the 5-position of uracil with fluorine to block the conversion of uridine to thymidine.
(a) Predict the effect on thymidylate synthesis and DNA synthesis.
(b) Justify the prediction through the structure-activity logic of this antimetabolite.
(c) Name the active "fraudulent" nucleotide and the similar drugs.
(d) State the rationale for targeting this enzyme and the clinical use and adverse effects.

Describe the conjugation (phase II) reactions of drug metabolism:
(a) classification of the conjugation types
(b) the chemical basis of glucuronidation (reactants, enzyme, functional groups)
(c) the basis of the consequences for excretion (water solubility, bile, enterohepatic cycling) and special cases (intestinal conjugation, acetylator status)
(d) distinguish conjugation from functionalization.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Types: glucuronic acid conjugation, sulphate conjugation, conjugation with glycine, glutamine and other amino acids, glutathione or mercapturic acid conjugation, acetylation and methylation.
(b)
• Glucuronide formation is the most common conjugation; it involves reaction between uridine diphosphate glucuronic acid (UDPG) and drugs containing hydroxyl, carboxyl or amine groups.
• The reaction is mediated by glucuronyl transferase.
• Glucuronides are water-soluble acids easily excreted in urine and bile.
(c)
• Biliary secretion and intestinal reabsorption give enterohepatic circulation; a conjugate entering the intestine may be deconjugated by enzymes and the parent reabsorbed.
• Examples of drugs enterohepatically circulated: morphine and penicillins.
• Morphine is rapidly conjugated with glucuronic acid in intestinal mucosa cells during absorption.
• Phenobarbital induces glucuronyltransferase, enhancing conjugation of bilirubin; zidovudine is about 85% glucuronidated.
• Isoniazid-related phenytoin toxicity occurs mainly in slow acetylators.
(d)
• Conjugation (phase II) follows phase I, which introduces or exposes functional groups that can be conjugated.
• Phase I generally causes loss of activity; conjugates are excreted more easily.

(a)
Thionamides: carbimazole (first drug of choice) and propylthiouracil (PTU).
(b)
• Carbimazole inhibits thyroid peroxidase-catalysed iodination of tyrosine residues and the coupling of iodotyrosyl residues, reducing T4 synthesis; it also blocks T4-to-T3 conversion.
• Effect is delayed by up to 4 weeks; treatment usually 6-24 months with T4 checked every 4 weeks.
(c)
• Carbimazole initial 20-60 mg daily (maintenance 5-15 mg); it crosses the placenta and may cause neonatal hypothyroidism.
• PTU 300-600 mg daily, maintenance 50-150 mg; it is the drug of choice in pregnancy and lactation because of lower concentration in breast milk.
(d)
• Agranulocytosis (fever, systemic upset, mouth ulceration, sore throat) occurs in 0.1-0.5% suddenly, usually within the first 3 months, equally with both drugs; stop the drug immediately.
• After agranulocytosis one drug must not be substituted for the other.
• Rash: treat with antihistamines without stopping; sensitivity reactions need withdrawal, and cross-sensitivity is rare so the other drug can be tried.
questions.question:
Two thionamides are available for hyperthyroidism. One patient is pregnant, another develops fever, mouth ulceration and sore throat within three months of starting treatment.
(a) Identify the structural/chemical class and the two drugs.
(b) Explain their mechanism.
(c) Differentiate carbimazole and propylthiouracil in clinical choice.
(d) Reason from the adverse effect to monitoring and substitution.

To overcome DNA-repair resistance to alkylating agents, an inhibitor of O6-alkylguanine-DNA alkyltransferase was modified by adding a meta-aminomethyl group.
(a) Identify the lead compound and the enzyme it inhibits.
(b) Outline the named reaction/repair pathway involved.
(c) State the reagents/synthesis if given and the effect of the modification.
(d) Identify the repair pathway site at risk and other pathways.
(e) State the variant produced and the rationale.
questions.answerText:
(a)
O6-benzylguanine, an inhibitor of O6-alkylguanine-DNA alkyltransferase (MGMT).
(b)
MGMT directly removes the alkyl group from O6 positions and the chloroethyl group between DNA chains.
(c)
Adding a meta-aminomethyl group improved solubility and increased the capacity to inactivate the enzyme about 20 times.
(d)
• Other pathways: ABH2 and ABH3 remove methyl from N1, N7, N3 positions (of double-stranded DNA and single-stranded RNA).
• Base excision repair repairs other N-alkylation sites; nucleotide excision repair assists; mismatch repair corrects incorrectly paired nucleotides; homologous recombination and non-homologous end-joining resynthesize damaged DNA.
(e)
• Variant: the meta-aminomethyl derivative; rationale: more soluble and 20-fold better enzyme inactivation, countering a resistance mechanism.
• If repair fails the cell can undergo apoptosis via p53; malignant cells with altered p53 do not.

questions.question:
A humanized antibody produced by recombinant DNA technology binds HER2 on the surface of breast cancer cells and marks them for destruction by natural killer cells.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) Differentiate it from rituximab and bevacizumab and from interferons and aldesleukin.
(c) Explain the three general strategies of antibody therapy.
(d) State adverse effects and reason to its use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody produced by recombinant DNA technology; HER2 occurs in 25-30% of breast malignancies.
(b)
• Rituximab and bevacizumab are other monoclonal antibodies listed.
• Aldesleukin (interleukin-2) is a biological response modifier promoting T cell development, used in some renal tumours; interferons (alpha, beta, gamma) can stimulate NK cells.
(c)
• Strategy 1: antibodies bind tumor antigens, marking cancer cells as foreign for immune destruction.
• Strategy 2: block binding of cytokines or other proteins needed for uncontrolled growth, binding cytokine receptors on tumor cells.
• Strategy 3: antibodies conjugated to a lethal substance such as radioactive isotopes.
(d)
• Trastuzumab unwanted effects: hypotension, chills, fever, hypersensitivity reactions.
• Aldesleukin: flu-like symptoms, loss of appetite, rash, cardiac arrhythmias, GI disturbance, depression; interferon alpha-2(a) used for hairy cell leukemia with chills, leukopenia, fatigue, alopecia.

questions.question:
Discuss active metabolites as a drug design and development principle:
(a) the principle and the marketed examples (oxyphenbutazone, nortriptyline, oxazepam, mesoridazine, prednisolone, hydrocortisone)
(b) relate each to its parent and the metabolic reaction
(c) explain why active metabolites matter clinically and what trade-offs or limitations result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Metabolites were traditionally considered inactive, but many drugs are biotransformed to pharmacologically active metabolites contributing to therapeutic and toxic effects.
• Manufacturers have synthesised the active metabolites and marketed them as separate drugs.
(b)
• Oxyphenbutazone is the p-hydroxylated metabolite of the anti-inflammatory phenylbutazone.
• Nortriptyline is the N-demethylated metabolite of the tricyclic antidepressant amitriptyline.
• Oxazepam is the N-demethylated and 3-hydroxylated metabolite of diazepam; mesoridazine is the sulfoxide metabolite of the antipsychotic thioridazine.
• Prednisone and cortisone are reduced to active prednisolone and hydrocortisone.
(c)
• Contribution depends on relative activity and quantitative importance (plasma concentration).
• Accumulation after repeated dosing (desmethyldiazepam in geriatric patients) or in renal failure is a determinant.
• Other active metabolites: cyclophosphamide gives 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide; carbamazepine gives the 10,11-epoxide; temozolomide gives MTIC.
• Toxic metabolites such as acrolein show that metabolites can also cause harm.
• Prodrugs (inactive drugs activated by metabolism) are the related principle.

(a)
• Doxorubicin is an anthracycline cytotoxic antineoplastic antibiotic obtained from Streptomyces peucetius var. caesius.
• It has tetracycline-type ring structures with an unusual sugar, daunosamine, attached by a glycosidic linkage.
(b)
• First: intercalation between adjacent nucleotides forms a tight DNA-drug interaction and inhibits both DNA and RNA synthesis.
• Second: inhibition of topoisomerase II; the enzyme nicks both strands and reseals them after replication, and doxorubicin stabilizes the cleaved DNA-topoisomerase II complex, preventing recombination of the double strand.
• Third: it produces semiquinone free radicals, which reduce molecular oxygen to superoxide ions and H2O2 that mediate single strand scission of DNA.
(c)
• Tissues with ample superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase are protected.
• Cardiac tissue lacks superoxide dismutase and catalase, which may explain the cardiotoxicity.
• Clinically: cumulative dose-related cardiac damage causing dysrhythmias and heart failure.
(d)
• Given by IV infusion, rapidly taken up by tissues, does not cross the blood barrier, metabolized in the liver; bile is the major excretion route.
• Uses: acute lymphocytic and granulocytic leukemia, lymphoma, sarcoma, solid organ cancers; ADRs: bone marrow depression, stomatitis, alopecia, cardiac toxicity.
• Related drugs: epirubicin, idarubicin, valrubicin, daunomycin.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of doxorubicin:
(a) its chemical name/class, source and structure
(b) the three mechanisms of action and the structural basis of each
(c) the structural/biochemical basis for its cardiotoxicity and why some tissues are protected
(d) its pharmacokinetics, uses and related drugs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Monoclonal antibodies are proteins produced in the laboratory from a single clone of a B cell; trastuzumab, rituximab and bevacizumab are examples.
• Trastuzumab is produced by recombinant DNA technology and binds HER2 on the cell surface, found in 25-30% of breast malignancies.
(b)
• Strategy 1: antibodies bind tumour antigens on cancer cells, so the immune system sees them as foreign and destroys them; trastuzumab also targets HER2 cells for destruction by natural killer cells.
• Strategy 2: antibodies block the binding of cytokines or other proteins needed for uncontrolled growth, binding cytokine receptors on the tumour cell surface.
• Strategy 3: antibodies are conjugated to a lethal substance such as radioactive isotopes, to destroy tumour cells specifically.
(c)
• The antibodies differentiate cancer cells from healthy cells through tumour antigens; conventional agents affect all rapidly dividing cells.
• Trade-offs: trastuzumab causes hypotension, chills, fever and hypersensitivity reactions.
• Targeted delivery has a higher affinity for tumour cells but vehicles vary in stability, selectivity and target choice.
• Reduced systemic toxicity allows use in sicker patients.
questions.question:
Discuss monoclonal antibodies as a targeted strategy in cancer therapy:
(a) the principle and examples (trastuzumab, rituximab, bevacizumab)
(b) relate each of the three general strategies to how antibodies act
(c) explain why the strategy improves selectivity and what trade-offs or limitations result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antimetabolites bear resemblance to a cellular precursor molecule yet cannot support proper use or formation of the normal product; they mimic structures of normal metabolites.
• Three main groups: folate antagonists, pyrimidine analogues, purine analogues.
(b)
• Their similarity lets them interact at receptor/enzyme sites but not elicit the same action; they inhibit enzymes competitively or are incorporated into macromolecules forming inappropriate structures.
• Most act via nucleic acid biosynthesis; purines, pyrimidines, folates and related compounds are the useful drugs.
• Often the administered drug is a prodrug activated in vivo, e.g. conversion to nucleoside and then nucleotide.
• They are generally cell-cycle specific, killing cells in S phase.
(c)
• Because they affect rapidly dividing normal tissue, toxicities include bone marrow depression, damage to GIT epithelium, alopecia, sterility and teratogenicity.
• Methotrexate has low lipid solubility and does not cross the blood-brain barrier; high doses cause nephrotoxicity.
(d)
• Methotrexate (antifolate): higher affinity than FH2 for dihydrofolate reductase; FH4 depletion causes loss of DTMP (thymine-less death); polyglutamate derivatives retained for weeks or months.
• 5-FU (pyrimidine analogue): converted to FdUMP, a fraudulent nucleotide covalently bound to thymidylate synthetase; it cannot be converted to DTMP.
• Methotrexate is 50% protein bound and given orally, IV, IM or intrathecally; 5-FU is given IV or topically, crosses the brain barrier and about 20% is excreted unchanged.
• Both inhibit DNA synthesis through the DTMP pathway; 6-MP/6-thioguanine and fludarabine/pentostatin represent the purine group.
questions.question:
Describe the antimetabolite anticancer agents:
(a) their classification and the general principle by which they resemble natural molecules
(b) the chemical basis of their activity and cell-cycle specificity
(c) the chemical basis of their toxicity and limitation
(d) distinguish methotrexate from 5-fluorouracil.

A drug that interferes with blood vessel formation and with rapidly dividing cells is used in cancer. It can cause numbness and tingling in the feet and severe birth defects (phocomelia). A derivative is thought to have fewer adverse effects but causes neutropenia.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) State the rationale linking its action to tumor growth.
(c) Explain the mechanism.
(d) Differentiate the derivative and state adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Thalidomide, an antiangiogenic drug (angiogenesis inhibitor); lenalidomide is the derivative.
(b)
Angiogenesis is the normal process of forming new blood vessels; tumors need a blood supply to grow and spread, and cancer cells secrete chemicals promoting angiogenesis.
(c)
Thalidomide interferes with the growth of rapidly dividing cells and with the formation of blood vessels.
(d)
• Thalidomide: peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, pain, burning) and severe birth defects or fetal death in pregnancy (phocomelia).
• Lenalidomide is thought to cause fewer adverse effects but, unlike thalidomide, can cause bone marrow depression and neutropenia.

questions.question:
A drug that is an iminostilbene derivative is started at one quarter to one third of the target dose and increased every 2-3 weeks. The patient also takes oxcarbazepine-like aromatic anticonvulsants and develops a rash.
(a) Identify the drug and lead class.
(b) Name the metabolic activation and its active metabolite.
(c) Identify the site/pathway at risk (autoinduction, hypersensitivity) and the related variants.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Carbamazepine (CBZ), an iminostilbene derivative used in chronic epilepsy prophylaxis, trigeminal neuralgia and bipolar disorder.
(b)
• Extensively metabolized in the liver (over 99%), primarily by CYP3A4, to carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide, which is pharmacologically active (50% protein bound).
• Mechanism: inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels appears to be involved; it decreases transmission in the thalamic nucleus ventralis anterior.
(c)
• CBZ is a potent inducer of hepatic metabolism and induces its own metabolism (auto-induction); clearance rises over 6-12 weeks, hence gradual titration.
• It causes AED hypersensitivity syndrome with cross-reactivity to other aromatic anticonvulsants (oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital).
• Therapeutic range 4-12 ug/mL; toxicity includes blood dyscrasias (aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis); stop if WBC below 2500/mm3 or ANC below 1000/mm3.
• Protein binding 75-80%, bioavailability 75-85%; oral only (tablets, capsules, suspension).

(a)
Bleomycin, a cytotoxic antibiotic (given by injection).
(b)
It occurs naturally as a metal-chelating glycopeptide.
(c)
• It binds Fe(II) inside cells; the Fe(II)-bleomycin complex reduces O2; superoxide or OH radicals are generated.
• The radicals degrade DNA, leading to fragmentation and release of free bases; it is most effective in G2 phase.
(d)
• Rapidly distributed, cleared by renal excretion unchanged.
• Adverse effects: little myelosuppression, hyperpyrexia, pulmonary toxicity.
• By contrast doxorubicin (cardiac damage, marrow depression) and dactinomycin act by intercalation.
questions.question:
A glycopeptide isolated from Streptomyces verticillius, a naturally occurring metal-chelating compound, fragments DNA after binding a metal ion. It causes little marrow suppression but fever and lung toxicity.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) State the structural liability/feature involved in its chemistry.
(c) Explain its mechanism step by step.
(d) Differentiate it from other anticancer antibiotics and reason to its use.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Phase I (functionalization): oxidation (aromatic, olefin, benzylic/allylic, aliphatic, N-, O-, S- dealkylation, deamination, N-oxide, alcohols and aldehydes), reduction (aldehydes, ketones, nitro, azo) and hydrolysis (esters, amides, epoxide hydrase).
• Phase II (conjugation): glucuronic acid, sulphate, glycine/glutamine and other amino acids, glutathione (mercapturic acid), acetylation and methylation.
(b)
• Phase I reactions introduce or expose a functional group (e.g. OH, NO2) that can be conjugated, and generally result in loss of pharmacological activity.
• Glucuronide formation is the most common conjugation; glucuronides are water-soluble acids easily excreted in urine and bile.
• Biotransformation is carried out by enzymes mainly in the liver endoplasmic reticulum; most oxidative processes occur in liver microsomes with oxygen, NADPH and cytochrome P-450.
(c)
• Prodrugs are activated by metabolism, an exception to loss of activity.
• Prednisone and cortisone are reduced to active prednisolone and hydrocortisone; reduction is not a common pathway; hydrolysis of esters and amides is common.
• Many drugs form active metabolites that contribute to therapeutic and toxic effects.
(d)
• Phase I makes functional groups; phase II conjugates them with polar endogenous molecules.
• Metabolites can arise from parallel or consecutive pathways.
• The liver is the major site; the GIT is the most important extrahepatic site (morphine is conjugated by intestinal mucosa).
questions.question:
Describe the phase I and phase II pathways of drug biotransformation:
(a) classification of reaction types
(b) the general chemical effect and consequence for activity of each phase
(c) the basis of exceptions (prodrugs, active metabolites)
(d) distinguish phase I from phase II reactions.

An elderly hypertensive patient is given a diuretic that inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption mostly in the distal tubules. She has a sulfonamide allergy history and also has gout.
(a) Identify the drug class and a representative drug.
(b) State the structural feature relevant to her allergy.
(c) Explain its mechanism of action.
(d) State its therapeutic use and the key adverse effects, including why gout matters.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Thiazide diuretics, e.g. hydrochlorothiazide; thiazides are drugs of choice in elderly hypertensives.
(b)
All available loop and thiazide diuretics, except ethacrynic acid, possess a sulfonamide group, which matters in patients allergic to sulfonamides.
(c)
• Diuretics act by decreasing blood volume and cardiac output, and decrease peripheral resistance during chronic therapy; thiazides inhibit Na and Cl reabsorption mostly in the distal tubules.
• They increase potassium and bicarbonate excretion, decrease calcium excretion and do not affect normal blood pressure.
(d)
• Used as monotherapy or with other antihypertensives; hydrochlorothiazide can be used where hyperkalemia must be avoided, including patients taking ACE inhibitors.
• Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperlipidaemia, hyperuricaemia (hence contraindicated in gout), hyperglycaemia (hence not safe in diabetes).
• Not safe in renal and hepatic insufficiency; long-term use may cause hyponatremia.

questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of cyclophosphamide:
(a) its chemical class and why it is inactive as given
(b) the activation pathway, enzymes and metabolites
(c) the structural basis of its cytotoxic action and its toxicity (including how the toxic effect can be reduced)
(d) the basis for variability in its action and the analogues designed to avoid the toxicity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cyclophosphamide is an oxazaphosphorine alkylating agent, widely used as a DNA crosslinking cytotoxic chemotherapeutic, given orally and intravenously.
• It is inactive in parent form because of the oxazaphosphorine ring; it is a prodrug.
(b)
• The liver CYP microsomal system hydroxylates it to 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide and aldophosphamide, delivered to dividing normal and tumour cells.
• Hydroxylation disrupts the ring and releases the bis(2-chloroethyl) group that gives the active cation.
• Aldophosphamide forms acrolein and phosphoramide mustard; the main enzymes are CYP2A6, CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, CYP2C9 and CYP2C18.
(c)
• Phosphoramide mustard is the cytotoxic moiety; it crosslinks DNA strands, inhibiting replication.
• Acrolein is responsible for hemorrhagic cystitis; effect reduced by increased fluid intake and bladder irrigation with N-acetylcysteine, a sulphydryl donor forming a non-toxic compound.
• Other effects: pronounced effect on lymphocytes (immunosuppressant), nausea, vomiting, bleeding, alopecia, skin pigmentation, neurotoxicity and nephrotoxicity.
(d)
• Genetic polymorphisms of the CYP enzymes cause differences in metabolism, directly affecting action and toxicity.
• Half-life 420 min; uses include breast and ovarian cancer, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, CLL, sarcoma, neuroblastoma, Wilms' tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma.
• Ifosfamide analogues: glufosfamide and mafosfamide need no CYP activation; C7, C9-dimethyl-ifosfamide uses steric hindrance to prevent toxic metabolite formation.

questions.question:
Describe the cytochrome P-450 monooxygenase system:
(a) its chemical reaction, cofactors and name origin
(b) its location and structural/lipophilic features
(c) the basis for its non-specificity, inducibility and use in in-vitro studies
(d) the basis for variation among individuals and its role in activation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Oxidation of xenobiotics (R-H) to oxidized metabolites (R-OH) requires molecular oxygen and the reducing agent NADPH.
• One oxygen atom of O2 enters the substrate to form R-OH while the other is incorporated into water.
• The system is known as mixed function oxidases or monooxygenases; the key enzyme is cytochrome P-450.
• The name arises because the reduced (Fe2+) form binds carbon monoxide giving an absorption maximum at 450 nm.
(b)
• It is located in the endoplasmic reticulum, particularly abundant in the liver; when tissue is homogenized the reticulum forms microsomes.
• Being membrane-bound in a lipoidal environment, it explains why lipophilic xenobiotics are good substrates.
(c)
• It metabolizes almost unlimited diverse substrates due to substrate non-specificity and multiple enzyme forms.
• Some forms are selectively inducible by phenobarbital, benzo(a)pyrene and 3-methylcholanthrene (e.g. cytochrome P-448).
• Microsomal preparations with cofactors (NADPH, Mg2+) are used for in-vitro metabolism studies.
(d)
• Isoforms involved in drug activation include CYP2A6, CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, CYP2C9, CYP2C18; polymorphisms cause differences in metabolism.
• Oxidative biotransformation is the most common and important phase I reaction.

(a)
Options: thionamides (carbimazole, propylthiouracil), radioactive iodine (I131), iodine salts (saturated potassium iodide, Lugol's solution), beta-blockers, glucocorticoids and surgery (partial or total thyroidectomy).
(b)
• Thionamides inhibit thyroid peroxidase-catalysed iodination and coupling, reducing T4 synthesis.
• I131 is given orally as iodide solution or capsules, taken up in high concentration by the thyroid, emits beta radiation and permanently damages the gland.
• Iodine salts inhibit the synthesis and release of T3 and T4 with rapid onset, so they treat thyroid storm.
• Beta-blockers inhibit conversion of T4 to T3 and relieve palpitations, anxiety, sweating, tremor and diarrhoea; propranolol 20-80 mg three times daily.
• Glucocorticoids (prednisolone) decrease inflammation around the eyes in Graves' ophthalmopathy before radioiodine.
(c)
• I131 side effects: infertility and radiation toxicity (neoplasia, haematopoietic suppression, salivary and lacrimal toxicity); avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; lifelong thyroid hormone replacement.
• Iodine salts: rash, fever, metallic taste, GI irritation, bleeding disorders, anaphylaxis; fetal goitre with hypothyroidism; not commonly used.
• Beta-blockers are short term, do not control the underlying condition and should be avoided in asthma.
(d)
• Thionamides work gradually (delay up to 4 weeks) and can cause agranulocytosis; I131 is definitive treatment in Graves' disease and toxic multinodular goitre.
• Choice factors: large goitre (surgery), severe heart failure, pregnancy, previous iodine exposure, compliance and age.
questions.question:
Describe the treatment options for hyperthyroidism:
(a) classification of the agents (thionamides, radioactive iodine, iodine salts, beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, surgery)
(b) the general nature and mechanism of each
(c) the basis of their limitations and toxicity
(d) distinguish radioactive iodine from the thionamides.

A patient with Graves' disease and a large goitre is considered for definitive treatment with an oral radioactive agent, and another needs rapid control of thyroid storm.
(a) Identify the two agents.
(b) State the key forms, reagents and conditions given.
(c) Identify the tissue at risk and toxicities.
(d) State alternatives and cautions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Radioactive iodine (I131) and iodine salts (saturated potassium iodide solution/Lugol's solution).
(b)
• I131 is given orally as iodide solution or capsules; Lugol's solution is 10% potassium iodide plus 5% iodide.
• I131 is taken up in high concentration by the thyroid gland, emits beta radiation and permanently damages it, so lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is usually needed.
(c)
• I131 side effects: infertility and radiation toxicity (neoplasia, hematopoietic suppression, salivary and lacrimal toxicity); it crosses the placenta and is secreted in breast milk.
• Iodine salts inhibit synthesis and release of T3 and T4 with rapid onset; side effects: skin rash, fever, metallic taste, GI irritation, bleeding disorders, anaphylaxis; fetal goiter and hypothyroidism in pregnancy.
(d)
Both are avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding; surgery is preferred for large goitre causing obstruction; beta-blockers and glucocorticoids are adjuncts.

(a)
• Cimetidine is the first H2-receptor antagonist with wide clinical use; it is a weak base and highly water soluble, measured in biological fluids by HPLC methods.
• It blocks H2 receptors of gastric parietal cells; used for benign gastric and duodenal ulcer, erosive GERD, heartburn, Zollinger-Ellison, peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding prevention.
• Concentrations of 0.5-1.0 ug/ml suppress acid secretion; dosage forms: tablets 200, 400, 800 mg, syrup, ampoules.
(b)
• Oral bioavailability about 60% in healthy subjects (about 70% in peptic ulcer patients); two plasma peaks are often seen, and food delays absorption to give one peak.
• Metabolites account for 25-40% of elimination: cimetidine sulphoxide (10-15%) and hydroxymethyl cimetidine (4%); 50-80% of an IV dose is excreted unchanged in urine; biliary excretion about 2%.
• Vd about 1 L/kg; half-life about 2 h; clearance 500-600 ml/min; protein binding 20%; CSF/plasma ratio 0.1-0.2; it crosses the placenta and enters breast milk.
(c)
• Renal failure: clearance falls to under 200 ml/min, half-life 4-5 h; 400 mg daily with minimal renal function; under 20% is removed by haemodialysis.
• Severe cirrhosis lowers non-renal clearance; renal failure plus chronic liver disease can prolong half-life up to 10 times.
• Elderly: lower Vd, lower clearance, longer half-life; CNS effects such as confusion in elderly and in severe renal or hepatic impairment (higher CSF concentrations).
• Children: clearance is increased due to increased renal elimination.
(d)
Cimetidine is one of the most potent and comprehensive inhibitors of drug metabolism used clinically.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry and pharmacokinetics of cimetidine:
(a) its class, acid-base and solubility properties, and clinical indications
(b) the structural basis of its metabolism and its metabolites
(c) the basis of its altered kinetics and toxicity in special populations
(d) why it affects other drugs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Excretion is elimination of all drugs and/or metabolites; the kidney is the most important organ, with others being bile, sweat, saliva, gastric juice, lungs and breast milk.
(b)
• Renal excretion involves glomerular filtration, active tubular excretion and passive reabsorption.
• The kidneys receive about 25% of cardiac output (1.2-1.5 L/min), of which 10% is filtered; only free (unbound) drug and solutes are filtered.
• Lipid-soluble drugs are well reabsorbed; urine pH in the distal tubule determines reabsorption by non-ionic diffusion and pH partition theory, important for weak acids and bases.
• Excretion can be controlled with acidifying or alkalinizing salts (sodium bicarbonate, ammonium chloride); urinary pH varies with diet, exercise, drugs and time of day.
(c)
• Drugs secreted into bile pass to the intestine and may be reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation), e.g. morphine and penicillins; conjugates may be deconjugated and the parent drug reabsorbed.
• Alveolar excretion handles volatile liquids and gases; salivary excretion depends on lipid solubility, pKa and protein binding (rifampicin, phenytoin gingival hyperplasia).
• Most drugs in maternal blood are detectable in milk; an infant's immature renal and hepatic function can cause accumulation.
(d)
• Filtration: free drug passes the glomerulus; tubular secretion: active transport of organic cations and anions into the lumen.
• Passive reabsorption: lipid-soluble drugs return to blood, controlled by urine pH.
• Water is reabsorbed from the distal convoluted tubule under the control of antidiuretic hormone.
questions.question:
Describe the excretion of drugs and metabolites:
(a) classification of the routes
(b) the physicochemical basis of renal handling (filtration, secretion, reabsorption, pH partition)
(c) the basis of biliary and other excretion and the clinical consequences
(d) distinguish glomerular filtration, tubular secretion and passive reabsorption.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Didanosine is a purine deoxynucleoside; zalcitabine and stavudine are pyrimidine deoxynucleosides.
• They belong to the NRTI class.
(b)
• They are phosphorylated by cellular kinases to the corresponding nucleotide analogues.
• The analogues inhibit RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase), blocking DNA synthesis.
• Viral DNA polymerases are more sensitive to this inhibition than mammalian polymerases.
(c)
• Oral bioavailability is variable (didanosine about 40%, zalcitabine over 80%); renal excretion 40-75%; half-lives 1-3 h; distribution to all tissues including CNS.
• Adverse effects: painful peripheral neuropathy (up to 30%), pancreatitis (can be fatal), headache, insomnia, agitation, seizures (didanosine), arthralgia, fever, rash.
• Zalcitabine causes stomatitis and esophageal ulceration; all can cause hepatic steatosis and lactic acidosis; stavudine also causes lipodystrophy.
(d)
• Active against HIV-1 and HIV-2 including most zidovudine-resistant strains.
• Resistant mutants have been recovered from treated patients.
• Used in advanced HIV when patients are intolerant of or deteriorating on zidovudine.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of the deoxynucleoside antiretrovirals didanosine, zalcitabine and stavudine:
(a) their chemical classes
(b) the basis of their activation and activity
(c) the basis of their toxicity and pharmacokinetics
(d) the basis of resistance and loss of activity compared with zidovudine.

Two pyrimidine/purine deoxynucleosides, one a purine and two pyrimidine, are used in advanced HIV when zidovudine is not tolerated. A patient develops painful peripheral neuropathy.
(a) Identify the three drugs and class.
(b) State their structural classification.
(c) Explain their activation and mechanism.
(d) State pharmacokinetics, adverse effects and use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Didanosine, zalcitabine and stavudine, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (deoxynucleosides).
(b)
Didanosine is a purine deoxynucleoside; zalcitabine and stavudine are pyrimidine deoxynucleosides.
(c)
• They are phosphorylated by cellular kinases to nucleotide analogues, which inhibit RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase) and block DNA synthesis; viral polymerases are more sensitive than mammalian ones.
• Active against HIV-1 and HIV-2 including most zidovudine-resistant strains; resistant mutants have been recovered.
(d)
• Oral bioavailability variable (didanosine about 40%, zalcitabine over 80%); renal excretion 40-75%; half-lives 1-3 h; distributed in all tissues including CNS.
• Adverse effects: painful peripheral neuropathy (up to 30%), pancreatitis (can be fatal), headache, insomnia, agitation, seizures (didanosine), stomatitis, esophageal ulceration (zalcitabine), hepatic steatosis, lactic acidosis.
• Use: advanced HIV in patients intolerant of or deteriorating on zidovudine.

questions.question:
A patient has an HIV strain that is resistant to multiple other drugs. A 36-amino-acid peptide given subcutaneously, and a drug that binds a host co-receptor, are considered.
(a) Identify the class and the two drugs.
(b) Describe the structural/molecular target features.
(c) Describe the stage of the replication cycle affected.
(d) State adverse effects and resistance behaviour.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Entry inhibitors: enfuvirtide (T-20, fusion inhibitor) and maraviroc (coreceptor inhibitor).
(b)
Enfuvirtide is a 36-amino-acid peptide (polypeptide) that binds gp41 of the viral envelope; maraviroc is a CCR5 ligand mimic that binds specifically and selectively to CCR5.
(c)
• HIV entry is complex and each step is a target: viral gp160 envelope complex binds the host receptor CD4.
• Maraviroc blocks the receptor on the host cell membrane (co-receptor tropism is assessed before ART).
(d)
• Enfuvirtide is given subcutaneously with other antiretrovirals; side effects: local injection-site reaction, hypersensitivity, eosinophilia.
• Resistance can occur with enfuvirtide but there is no cross-resistance.
• Additional entry-related classes listed: fostemsavir (gp120 attachment inhibitor) and ibalizumab (post-attachment, IV).

(a)
• Vinca alkaloids inhibit polymerization of tubulin into microtubules, preventing spindle formation and arresting metaphase.
• Taxanes promote polymerization and stabilization of microtubules, forming stable non-functioning microtubules.
(b)
• Taxanes bind reversibly to tubulin; stabilised microtubules interfere with mitosis and cause cell death.
• Vinca alkaloids are cell cycle specific and phase specific.
(c)
Paclitaxel (Taxol) and docetaxel (Taxotere).
(d)
Taxanes are diterpenes with a taxadiene core, originally identified from Taxus (yew) plants.
questions.question:
A different tubulin-binding agent, a diterpene originally identified from yew (Taxus), is compared with a vinca alkaloid. Both interfere with mitosis but their effect on microtubules differs.
(a) Predict the opposite effects of the two classes on microtubule polymerization.
(b) Justify through the molecular mechanism.
(c) Name the improved/related analogues of the diterpene class.
(d) State the rationale linking structure and mitotic arrest.

Two alkylsulfonates are considered for conditioning before transplant. One is poorly soluble in water and was first given orally, the other is well soluble with oral and intravenous presentations. The patient is also taking phenytoin or itraconazole.
(a) Identify the two drugs and the structural group that makes them alkylating.
(b) Explain how their structures lead to the solubility difference and activation.
(c) Differentiate the two in route, metabolite, toxicity and indication.
(d) Explain the interaction with phenytoin and itraconazole and reason to therapeutic choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Busulfan and treosulfan; both carry sulfonates that are good leaving groups.
(b)
• In busulfan, removal of one sulfonate generates a cation that alkylates DNA.
• Treosulfan has two hydroxyl groups, making it more hydrophilic and water soluble with oral availability; in a pH-dependent reaction it converts to mono- and diepoxides that alkylate.
(c)
• Busulfan is poorly soluble in water so was oral (an intravenous form was released in 2000); treosulfan has both oral and intravenous presentations.
• Busulfan metabolite: glutathione conjugate; treosulfan: active mono- and diepoxide.
• Half-lives 120-180 min (busulfan) and 100-120 min (treosulfan).
• Toxicity: busulfan hepatic (veno-occlusive disease), treosulfan myelosuppression; indications: CML and myeloablative regimens (busulfan), ovarian cancer (treosulfan).
(d)
• Phenytoin is an inducer and itraconazole an inhibitor of cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize busulfan.
• Phenytoin reduces busulfan effects; itraconazole increases its effects with a higher risk of toxicity.
• Alternative drugs are sought, e.g. clonazepam instead of phenytoin.

(a)
• Most alkylating agents bind the major groove of DNA; minor-groove binders are being sought because they are more specific, less toxic and act by a different mechanism.
• Minor-groove binders may also bind proteins, linked to inhibition of gene transcription in cancer cells; examples include illudins (irofulven), tallimustine, brostallicin and tetrahydroquinolines.
(b)
• They have higher affinity for adenine and thymine bases and bigger structures with fused aromatic rings, which are related to cytotoxic action.
• Mel-flufen, a melphalan analogue, has better activity, is independent of p53 action and reduces angiogenesis.
• Bivalent analogues of melphalan and bendamustine were created (esterified with maleimide and linked by diamines).
• Quinoline conjugates (quinoline-N-phenyl-hydrazinecarboxamide mustard, with urea as a binder) and pyrrolo[1,2-b]isoquinoline derivatives are also being developed.
• Analogues of ifosfamide (glufosfamide, mafosfamide, C7, C9-dimethyl-ifosfamide) were made to reduce toxicity.
(c)
• Aim: lower toxicity, higher cytotoxic activity, greater specificity for the site of action and improved adherence, quality of life and survival.
• Existing limitation: alkylating agents cause mainly haematologic, renal and neurologic toxicity and are non-specific for cell type and site.
• Normal and tumour cells both have DNA-repair systems, a resistance mechanism in tumours.
• Many of the new agents are still under study.
questions.question:
Discuss the design of new alkylating analogues and minor-groove binders:
(a) the principle and examples of newer analogues (mel-flufen, bivalent bendamustine and melphalan derivatives, quinoline mustards, minor-groove binders)
(b) relate the structural parts to the property sought
(c) explain why these strategies improve specificity or reduce toxicity and the limitations that remain.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Altretamine has a higher half-life than thiotepa (240-600 min vs 70-120 min) due to the greater complexity of its molecule.
(b)
• In thiotepa the aziridine groups, stabilized by a thiophosphoryl base, are essential for cytotoxic activity.
• The active aziridine cation is generated by protonation of the ring nitrogen.
(c)
Thiotepa gives the active metabolite triethylene phosphoramide (TEPA); altretamine gives penta- and tetra-methylmelamine.
(d)
• Thiotepa is IV; myelosuppression; used in bladder, breast and ovarian cancer.
• Altretamine is PO; neurotoxicity; used in ovarian cancer; both are in the bifunctional group (ethylene imines and methylmelamines).
questions.question:
Thiotepa contains three ethyleneimine (aziridine) groups on a thiophosphoryl base. Altretamine is a methylmelamine whose alkylation mechanism remains unknown.
(a) Predict the effect of the structural complexity on half-life.
(b) Justify through the structure-activity relationship.
(c) Name the active metabolite.
(d) State rationale, toxicities and uses.

Describe targeted delivery and structural strategies used to improve chemotherapy:
(a) the principle and examples (tumour-targeted vehicles, melphalan locally infused, 1,4-dihydropyridine carrier for brain delivery, antibody conjugates)
(b) relate the parts of each to the properties they change
(c) explain why the strategy improves selectivity or reduces toxicity and the trade-off or limitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Specially targeted delivery vehicles aim to raise effective chemotherapy levels in tumour cells while reducing levels in other cells, increasing tumour kill and/or reducing toxicity.
• They have a higher affinity for tumour cells by interacting with tumour-specific or tumour-associated antigens.
• Melphalan given locally on retinoblastoma shows better action due to good penetration, lower systemic toxicity and lower risk of inducing secondary leukemia.
• Brain delivery systems use redox carriers: a hydrophilic prodrug linked to a lipophilic 1,4-dihydropyridine carrier.
(b)
• The lipophilic carrier allows penetration of the blood-brain barrier; oxidation in the brain forms a polar pyridinium salt that releases the active drug.
• Antibodies conjugated to radioactive isotopes or toxic substances can destroy tumour cells with the radioactivity or toxin.
• Monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab bind HER2 and mark cells for destruction by natural killer cells.
(c)
• Reduced systemic toxicity means the drugs can be used in sicker patients and can carry new agents too toxic for traditional systemic delivery.
• Delivery vehicles vary in stability, selectivity and choice of target.
• Conventional drugs lack specificity (affecting rapidly dividing normal cells), which is the limitation being addressed.
• Trade-offs: local delivery acts only at the site (systemic action needed for some tumours); antibody therapy has hypotension, chills, fever, hypersensitivity.

(a)
• Etoposide is an epipodophyllotoxin, a plant-derived topoisomerase inhibitor.
• It is a semi-synthetic derivative of podophyllotoxin obtained from Podophyllum peltatum (May apple, mandrake root).
(b)
• It inhibits the enzyme topoisomerase II, which unwinds and religates DNA during replication, leading to DNA strand breakage and DNA damage.
• It blocks the cell in the late S-G2 phase of the cell cycle.
• It can also affect mitochondrial function and nucleoside transport.
(c)
• It is given orally or intravenously and is well distributed.
• It does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
• It is metabolized in the liver and excreted mainly in urine.
• Adverse effects: myelosuppression, hair loss, nausea, vomiting.
(d)
Doxorubicin also stabilizes the topoisomerase II complex, and topoisomerase inhibitors are classed as plant-derived (etoposide) in the mechanism-based classification.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of etoposide:
(a) its chemical class, natural source and structural relationship to the parent compound
(b) the structural/biochemical basis of its action on DNA and cell cycle
(c) the basis of its pharmacokinetic limitations and toxicity
(d) the basis of loss of activity or resistance and related agents.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Physiological oestrogens antagonize androgens, so they are used in androgen-dependent prostatic cancer; the agonist is occasionally used through suppression of testosterone production.
(b)
Tumors derived from hormone-responding tissues may be hormone-dependent and inhibited by antagonists or hormones with opposing actions.
(c)
• Diethylstilbestrol and ethinyloestradiol are used palliatively; ethinyloestradiol has fewer side effects.
• Tamoxifen competes with endogenous oestrogens for the receptor and inhibits transcription of oestrogen-responsive genes (breast cancer).
(d)
• Flutamide and cyproterone are androgen antagonists for prostate tumors; GnRH analogues are also used.
• Progestins (megestrol, medroxyprogesterone) are used in endometrial and renal tumors; glucocorticoids (prednisolone, dexamethasone) inhibit lymphocyte proliferation in leukaemias and lymphomas.
• Oestrogens can recruit resting mammary cancer cells into the proliferating pool to be killed by cytotoxic drugs.
questions.question:
A man with androgen-dependent prostate cancer receives an oestrogen; a woman with breast cancer receives a drug that competes with oestrogens at the receptor. In the oestrogen class, one agent has fewer side effects.
(a) Predict the effect of oestrogen therapy on androgen action and testosterone.
(b) Justify through hormone antagonism.
(c) Name the drugs and the better-tolerated analogue.
(d) State the rationale and other hormonal agents used.

Describe the factors affecting drug metabolism:
(a) classification (age, species, sex, enzyme induction and inhibition, smoking, diet, disease)
(b) the basis of each effect
(c) the basis of the clinical consequences
(d) distinguish induction from inhibition.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Factors: age, species and strain, sex, enzyme induction, enzyme inhibition, smoking, diet, nutritional state and liver disease.
(b)
• Age: newborns have undeveloped oxidative and conjugative enzymes; metabolic ability approaches adult levels in about one to two months.
• Species: amphetamine is metabolized by oxidative deamination in man, rabbit and guinea pig but mainly aromatic hydroxylation in the rat; phenytoin also shows marked species differences.
• Sex: adult male rats metabolize many compounds faster than females (under the control of sex hormones); few reports in man (nicotine and aspirin).
• Diet: protein:carbohydrate ratio, indoles in brassica vegetables and charcoal-broiled beef induce; vitamins, minerals, starvation and malnutrition also influence metabolism.
(c)
• A decreased rate of metabolism increases the intensity and duration of drug action and may cause accumulation and toxicity.
• Smoking increases theophylline metabolism.
• Relative amounts of metabolites depend on enzyme concentration and activity.
(d)
• Induction raises enzyme synthesis (phenobarbital, PAHs); inhibition occurs through substrate competition or enzyme inactivation (cimetidine).
• Induction shortens drug action; inhibition prolongs it.
• Physiological factors and pathological states of the liver alter metabolism.

(a)
• Cancer cells divide without control, invade tissues and metastasize; features include uncontrolled proliferation, dedifferentiation, invasiveness and metastasis.
• Anticancer agents are classified by site of action or chemical class: alkylating agents, antimetabolites, anticancer antibiotics, plant products, hormonal drugs, protein kinase inhibitors and miscellaneous agents (e.g. monoclonal antibodies, hydroxyurea).
• By mechanism: alkylating agents, antimetabolites, plant-derived mitotic inhibitors, plant-derived topoisomerase inhibitors, hormones and miscellaneous agents.
(b)
• Rapidly dividing cells are more sensitive; non-proliferating cells in G0 usually survive.
• Normal and tumour cells go through the same cycle, differing only in the number of cells in each stage.
(c)
• Because they affect rapidly dividing normal tissues, they cause myelotoxicity, growth depression in children, sterility, teratogenicity, alopecia, GIT damage, nausea and vomiting.
• Alkylating agents are also mutagenic and carcinogenic.
(d)
• Alkylating agents are cell-cycle nonspecific; antimetabolites kill cells in S phase; vinca alkaloids are phase specific (M); etoposide blocks late S-G2; bleomycin is most effective in G2.
• Goals: cure (cancer disappears and does not return); control (stop growth and spread, extend life with best quality of life); palliation (relieve symptoms when control is unlikely).
• Cancers are categorised as carcinoma, sarcoma, leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma and CNS cancers.
• Surgery and radiation are the other modalities.
questions.question:
Describe the chemotherapy of cancer in general:
(a) the biological/chemical characteristics of cancer cells and the classification of anticancer agents
(b) the basis of selective toxicity and cell-cycle specificity
(c) the basis of the characteristic toxicities and limitation
(d) distinguish cell cycle specific from non-specific agents and the three goals of chemotherapy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• DNA viruses: double-strand (adenoviruses, herpesviruses/HSV, CMV, VZV, papillomaviruses, poxviruses), single-strand (parvoviruses), partial double-strand replicating via RNA (HBV).
• RNA viruses: double-strand segmented (rotavirus), single-strand positive (HCV, dengue, rhinovirus, rubella), negative segmented (influenza), negative nonsegmented (rabies, measles, RSV); retroviruses replicate via DNA (HIV).
(b)
• RNA viruses have relatively high mutation rates compared with DNA viruses by two orders of magnitude or more (about 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁵ mis-incorporations per base), thought to reflect lack of proofreading and mismatch repair.
• DNA viruses have lower rates but perhaps 100-fold higher than host DNA; HBV overlapping reading frames mean many mutations are non-viable.
• HIV and HCV exist as quasi-species or a swarm around a consensus sequence.
(c)
• All viruses have one main resistance mechanism: selection of random mutations (random changes followed by survival of the fittest).
• The proportion of wild-type virus falls under antiviral pressure while the resistant variant becomes dominant.
• Segmented genomes (influenza has eight segments) add reassortment as a further mechanism.
(d)
• In DNA viruses pre-existing polymorphisms may include resistant mutants; in rapidly mutating RNA viruses (HIV, HCV) there may be no practical distinction between pre-existing and de novo resistance.
• Primary mutations reduce drug binding; secondary mutations raise resistance; tertiary mutations compensate for lost fitness.
• Resistance is confirmed by introducing the mutation by site-directed mutagenesis into a wild-type background.
questions.question:
Describe the basis of viral mutation and quasi-species formation:
(a) classification of viruses by genome type with examples
(b) the chemical/biological basis of high mutation rates in RNA versus DNA viruses
(c) the basis of the limitation this puts on antiviral therapy
(d) distinguish pre-existing from de novo resistance and primary from compensating mutations.

A patient on an antiretroviral is complaining of hallucinations, abnormal dreams and dizziness, while another patient on a related drug develops skin rash with Stevens-Johnson syndrome and hepatotoxicity. Both drugs attach directly to reverse transcriptase.
(a) Identify the drug class and the two drugs.
(b) State the features of the class relevant to activity.
(c) Explain the mechanism at the molecular target.
(d) State therapeutic use and key adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs): efavirenz (CNS effects) and nevirapine (rash, SJS/TEN, hepatotoxicity).
• NNRTIs presently available: efavirenz, nevirapine, delavirdine, etravirine (doravirine and rilpivirine are also listed).
(b)
Unlike NRTIs which must be phosphorylated, NNRTIs are active in the form administered.
(c)
NNRTIs attack the same enzyme as NRTIs but, rather than integrating into the transcribed DNA, they attach to reverse transcriptase and prevent it converting RNA to DNA.
(d)
• Efavirenz: CNS effect (hallucination, dizziness, insomnia, abnormal dreams, confusion), teratogenicity, depression up to suicide attempt.
• Nevirapine: skin rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrosis, hepatotoxicity; first-line paediatric regimen includes nevirapine, zidovudine, lamivudine.
• Used in initial ART as two NRTIs plus one NNRTI.

(a)
• A prodrug is converted in the body to the active drug; valaciclovir (VACV) is the prodrug of acyclovir (ACV).
• Famciclovir (FCV) is the prodrug of penciclovir (PCV); valganciclovir (VGCV) is the prodrug of ganciclovir (GCV); adefovir dipivoxil (ADV) is the prodrug of the nucleotide analogue adefovir.
(b)
• Acyclovir and penciclovir are activated by viral thymidine kinase and then inhibit viral polymerase.
• Ganciclovir is activated by the kinase encoded by UL97 in CMV and inhibits the polymerase.
• Targets: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV for valaciclovir and famciclovir; CMV for valganciclovir; HBV for adefovir dipivoxil (polymerase inhibitor).
• Foscarnet (pyrophosphate analogue) and lamivudine/entecavir (nucleoside analogues) act on polymerase without being prodrugs.
(c)
• Activation by viral kinase gives selectivity: acyclovir was the first antiviral drug that was both potent and selective.
• Limitation: herpesviruses enter latency, and no therapy removes latent infection; antivirals reduce replication during an acute episode only.
• Antiviral resistance arises by selection of random viral mutations.
• Tenofovir (nucleotide) needs only two phosphorylation steps and its phosphonate is not cleaved by esterases.
questions.question:
Discuss the prodrug strategy in antiviral drugs:
(a) the principle and the examples (valaciclovir, famciclovir, valganciclovir, adefovir dipivoxil)
(b) relate each prodrug to its active form and activating enzyme
(c) explain why the strategy matters for selectivity and the limitations that remain.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hydroxyurea is a miscellaneous antineoplastic agent that is an analogue of urea.
(b)
• It inhibits the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase.
• Inhibition depletes deoxynucleoside triphosphate pools, which further inhibits DNA synthesis.
(c)
• It is an S-phase specific agent.
• Adverse effects: minimal myelosuppression, hypersensitivity, hyperglycemia, hypoalbuminemia.
(d)
• Uses: melanoma and chronic myelogenous leukemia.
• As an S-phase agent it, like antimetabolites, acts on replicating cells.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of hydroxyurea:
(a) its chemical class and relationship to a simple compound
(b) the enzyme target and the biochemical consequence
(c) the basis of its cell-cycle specificity and toxicity
(d) its uses and the basis of loss of activity or resistance.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Enzyme induction is an increase in the activity of hepatic microsomal enzymes (e.g. the cytochrome P-450 system) caused by an increase in newly synthesized enzyme.
• Inducers include phenobarbital, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (benzo(a)pyrene, 3-methylcholanthrene), pesticides and environmental xenobiotics.
• Auto-induction is when a drug induces the enzymes involved in its own metabolism, as with carbamazepine.
(b)
• Phenobarbital increases warfarin metabolism and markedly decreases its anticoagulant effect.
• Cigarette smoke polycyclic hydrocarbons induce P-450, so theophylline is metabolized faster in smokers.
• Inducers enhance metabolism of cortisol, testosterone, vitamin D and bilirubin; vitamin D3 breakdown causes osteomalacia with phenobarbital and phenytoin.
• Dietary indoles (brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower) and charcoal-broiled beef also induce.
(c)
• Induction increases the rate of metabolism and decreases duration of action.
• Dosage readjustment is needed when an inducer is started or stopped (warfarin with phenobarbital).
• Carbamazepine clearance rises over 6-12 weeks, so patients start on 1/4-1/3 of the maintenance dose and increase every 2-3 weeks.
• Trade-off: induced metabolism can reduce efficacy of the other drugs; inducers also raise adverse effects at early titration periods of carbamazepine.
questions.question:
Discuss enzyme induction as a principle of drug metabolism:
(a) the mechanism and the examples (phenobarbital, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cigarette smoke, carbamazepine auto-induction)
(b) relate the examples to their effects on other drugs and endogenous compounds
(c) explain why induction changes drug response and what trade-offs or limitations result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bifunctional active drugs: nitrogen mustards, nitrosoureas, platinum complexes, ethylene imines, methylmelamines and alkylsulfonates; prodrugs: oxazaphosphorines, triazenes and hydrazines.
• Examples marked as prodrugs: cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, temozolomide, dacarbazine, treosulfan.
(b)
• Oxazaphosphorines: CYP hydroxylation opens the ring and releases the bis(2-chloroethyl) group giving the active cation.
• Dacarbazine is activated via CYP (N-demethylation) and temozolomide by spontaneous hydrolysis at physiological pH, both to MTIC, which forms the methyl diazonium cation.
• Treosulfan converts pH-dependently to mono- and diepoxides; carmustine and lomustine degrade spontaneously to diazo-hydroxide.
(c)
• Activation is by CYP enzymes, except temozolomide (non-enzymatic); polymorphisms of CYP2A6, 2B6, 3A4, 3A5, 2C9, 2C18 alter metabolism and toxicity.
• Drugs have shorter half-lives than prodrugs requiring prior activation (e.g. cyclophosphamide 420 min vs melphalan 45-90 min).
• Distribution is wide but limited in testicular cancer and CNS (blood-brain barrier); lipophilic temozolomide crosses it for gliomas.
• Liver and kidney failure hinder treatment: liver enzymes activate and metabolize, kidneys excrete, so dose adjustment or switching is needed.
• Interactions: inducers (phenytoin) and inhibitors (itraconazole) of CYP change exposure to busulfan.
• Prodrugs designed to avoid CYP activation (glufosfamide, mafosfamide) aim to lower toxicity.
• Trade-off: toxic metabolites such as acrolein and variable activation among patients.
questions.question:
Discuss prodrug activation as a design feature of alkylating agents:
(a) which agents are prodrugs and which are active drugs
(b) the activation chemistry for the oxazaphosphorines, triazenes and nitrosoureas and the active species
(c) explain why the strategy matters for half-life, distribution and toxicity and the trade-offs or limitations that result (polymorphisms, interactions, organ function).

questions.answerText:
(a)
Temozolomide, an alkylating prodrug of the triazene/hydrazine class.
(b)
The triazene is inserted in a cyclic structure combined with the imidazole ring, giving a relatively small, highly lipophilic molecule.
(c)
• Unlike other prodrugs of the group (activated by cytochrome P450), temozolomide undergoes nonenzymatic activation by spontaneous hydrolysis at physiological pH.
• This gives the active metabolite MTIC, 5-(3-methyltriazen-1-yl)-imidazole-4-carboxamide, which forms the methyl diazonium cation that binds DNA.
• The imidazole ring confers a more rapid and located onset of action.
(d)
• Because it is lipophilic it crosses the blood-brain barrier, making it a good alternative to treat gliomas.
• It is given PO and IV; half-life 60-120 min; indicated for glioma and malignant melanoma.
• Toxicity: nausea and vomiting, and myelosuppression.
• Dacarbazine (IV) is activated via CYP by N-demethylation to the same MTIC.
questions.question:
A highly lipophilic, relatively small oral and intravenous drug containing a triazene group fused with an imidazole ring is used for glioma and malignant melanoma. It is not activated by enzymes.
(a) Identify the compound and its class.
(b) Describe its physicochemical properties relevant to distribution (pKa, solubility, partition coefficient and stability where stated).
(c) Describe its activation pathway and the active metabolite.
(d) State the clinical consequence of its properties and its main toxicities.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine, vindesine, vinorelbine) come from Vinca rosea, the Madagascar periwinkle.
• Taxanes are diterpenes originally identified from Taxus (yew), with a taxadiene core; examples are paclitaxel (Taxol) and docetaxel (Taxotere).
(b)
• Vinca alkaloids bind tubulin and inhibit its polymerization into microtubules, preventing spindle formation in mitosing cells and causing metaphase arrest.
• Taxanes reversibly bind tubulin and promote polymerization and stabilization of microtubules, forming stable non-functioning microtubules.
• Both interfere with mitosis, causing cell death; vinca alkaloids are cell-cycle and phase specific.
(c)
• Vinca alkaloids also inhibit leucocyte phagocytosis and axonal transport in neurons, linking to neuropathy.
• Shared side effects: phlebitis/cellulitis, nausea, vomiting, alopecia.
• Vincristine has mild myelosuppression and causes peripheral neuropathy; vinblastine is myelosuppressive.
• Vinca alkaloids are injected, metabolized in the liver and excreted in bile and faeces.
(d)
• Vinca: depolymerisation/prevention of assembly; taxanes: stabilisation of polymerised microtubules.
• Vinca alkaloids are plant alkaloids; taxanes are diterpenes.
questions.question:
Describe the plant-derived mitotic inhibitors:
(a) classification (vinca alkaloids, taxanes) with sources and examples
(b) structural features and the chemical basis of action at tubulin
