(c) basis of toxicity and limitation
(d) distinguish vinca alkaloids from taxanes.

Carmustine and lomustine are two nitrosoureas used for brain tumors. One has two 2-chloroethyl groups, the other has one 2-chloroethyl group and a cyclohexyl substituent.
(a) Identify the structural liability shared by both and the active species formed.
(b) Explain the degradation pathway.
(c) Differentiate the two drugs (functionality, half-life, route).
(d) Reason from the chemistry to their therapeutic use and toxicity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Both have the nitrosourea group and 2-chloroethyl as the essential group for activity.
(b)
• Spontaneous degradation of the molecule releases diazo-hydroxide, which decomposes releasing the aziridine cation responsible for the cytotoxic activity (DNA alkylation).
• Carmustine also carbamoylates protein, in addition to alkylating DNA.
(c)
• Carmustine is bifunctional (two 2-chloroethyl groups); lomustine is monofunctional with a cyclohexyl second substituent.
• The cyclohexyl does not contribute to cytotoxic activity but increases its half-life.
• Carmustine IV, half-life 15-90 min; lomustine PO, half-life 90 min; both give active diazohydroxide.
(d)
• Bifunctional agents are more potent because crosslinks inflict greater damage and are harder to repair.
• Both are indicated in brain tumors and melanoma; toxicity is myelosuppression.

(a)
• Atazanavir, darunavir, fosamprenavir, lopinavir, nelfinavir, tipranavir, saquinavir, ritonavir and indinavir are described as structural analogues of HIV protease; they are gag cleavage site mimics.
• Saquinavir mesylate, fosamprenavir, lopinavir/ritonavir, indinavir and darunavir are listed with trade names.
(b)
• HIV protease is an aspartic endopeptidase that cleaves viral polypeptide products to form structural proteins of the virion core and essential enzymes (reverse transcriptase, integrase).
• Inhibiting it blocks viral maturation, so the drugs act in acutely and chronically infected cells.
• They are highly specific inhibitors of HIV protease and do not affect human endopeptidases; they prevent post-translational cleavage giving immature noninfectious particles.
(c)
• Oral bioavailability is only 4-10% (extensive first-pass); extensive metabolism by the mixed function oxidase system in intestinal wall and liver; distributed to all tissues except CNS.
• Resistance emerges; some cross-resistance occurs among PIs but not with other antiviral drugs; protease and cleavage sites can co-mutate.
• Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, pancreatitis (rare), raised aminotransferases, rashes, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (very rare), anaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia.
• Inhibitors of the mixed function oxidase system may raise PI levels.
(d)
• PIs act at the later stage (immature budding particles), NRTIs at reverse transcription after phosphorylation.
• PIs are active against most strains resistant to nucleoside analogues.
• Used for advanced HIV in combination with deoxynucleoside antiretrovirals.
questions.question:
Describe the HIV protease inhibitors:
(a) classification and examples
(b) general structure and mechanism of action
(c) the chemical basis of their limitations (bioavailability, resistance, tissue distribution, toxicity)
(d) distinguish them from the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Dactinomycin (Actinomycin D), a cytotoxic (anticancer) antibiotic; the first antibiotic shown to have anticancer activity.
• Obtained from cultures of S. parvulus, S. chrysamallus and S. antibioticus; these compounds are chromopeptides.
(b)
The planar phenoxazone ring is the structural feature important for cytotoxicity, facilitating intercalation between DNA base pairs.
(c)
• It intercalates in the minor groove of DNA between adjacent G-C base pairs, interfering with RNA polymerase movement along the gene and so preventing transcription.
• It may also cause strand breaks and stabilise the DNA topoisomerase II complex.
(d)
• Uses: rhabdomyosarcoma, Wilms' tumor; life-saving for women with chromosarcoma found resistant to methotrexate.
• Used with vincristine and cyclophosphamide in solid tumors in children.
• ADRs: bone marrow depression, alopecia, erythema.
questions.question:
An antitumour antibiotic isolated from Streptomyces parvulus, a chromopeptide with a planar phenoxazone ring, is used in rhabdomyosarcoma and Wilms' tumor.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) State the structural feature responsible for its activity.
(c) Explain its mechanism at the molecular target.
(d) State therapeutic uses and the key adverse effects.

Describe the chemistry of carbamazepine:
(a) its chemical class, uses and mechanism
(b) the structural basis of its metabolism, active metabolite and protein binding
(c) the basis of its toxicity, interactions and altered kinetics in disease states
(d) the basis of loss of effect or dosing strategy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Carbamazepine is an iminostilbene derivative used for chronic epilepsy prophylaxis, trigeminal neuralgia and bipolar disorder.
• Anti-seizure activity relates to decreased transmission in the nucleus ventralis anterior of the thalamus; inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels appears involved; it depresses post-tetanic potentiation and may prevent cAMP increases.
• It is oral only: chewable and regular tablets, sustained-release tablets and capsules, suspension.
(b)
• Over 99% is hepatically metabolized, mainly by CYP3A4, to carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide, which is pharmacologically active and 50% protein bound.
• Parent drug protein binding 75-80% (albumin and alpha1-acid glycoprotein); free fraction 20-25%, as low as 10-15% when AGP is raised in trauma, heart failure and MI.
• Bioavailability 75-85%; Vd 0.8-2.0 L/kg.
(c)
• Therapeutic range 4-12 ug/mL; above 8 ug/mL nausea, dizziness, drowsiness, blurred vision, diplopia and ataxia may occur.
• Toxicity: osteoporosis, aplastic anaemia, agranulocytosis (stop if WBC below 2500/mm3 or ANC below 1000/mm3); AED hypersensitivity syndrome with cross-reactivity to oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbital.
• Liver cirrhosis or hepatitis reduces clearance (less CYP3A4) and may increase the unbound fraction; elderly have lower clearance (start 100 mg/d); third trimester clearance may fall; breast milk about 60% of serum.
(d)
• It is a potent enzyme inducer and induces its own metabolism (auto-induction), so initial doses are 1/4-1/3 of maintenance and increased every 2-3 weeks over 6-12 weeks.
• Wide inter- and intra-individual variability requires individualised dosing.

questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of zidovudine:
(a) its chemical class and parent nucleoside
(b) the structural basis of its activation and selectivity
(c) its metabolism and the structural basis of its toxicity and interactions
(d) the basis of resistance and loss of effect.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Zidovudine is a thymine nucleoside analogue (deoxythymidine), classed as an NRTI.
(b)
• It is phosphorylated by cellular thymidine kinase to the corresponding nucleotide analogue.
• The analogue inhibits RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase), blocking DNA synthesis.
• Viral DNA polymerases are more sensitive to this inhibition than mammalian polymerases.
(c)
• Biotransformation about 85% by glucuronidation; renal excretion about 15%; half-life about 1 hour; oral bioavailability about 65%; CSF/plasma ratio about 0.5.
• Toxicity: severe anaemia and leukopenia from bone marrow suppression, myopathy, encephalopathy, seizures, hepatic steatosis, lactic acidosis.
• Toxicity increases with drugs that inhibit glucuronidation (fluconazole, cimetidine) or are extensively glucuronosylconjugated (benzodiazepines).
(d)
• Highly resistant mutants have been recovered from AIDS patients treated for more than 6 months.
• Didanosine, zalcitabine and stavudine remain active against most zidovudine-resistant strains.
• Spectrum: HIV-1, HIV-2, HTLV-1 and other retroviruses; initial drug of choice with CD4 below 500/mm3 but effect transient.
• Used in combinations (Combivir with lamivudine, Trizivir with lamivudine and abacavir).

(a)
ACE inhibitors: ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril; ARBs: losartan, valsartan.
(b)
• ACE inhibitors act primarily through suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system by preventing conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
• They also block the major pathway of bradykinin degradation by inhibiting ACE.
• ARBs competitively block binding of angiotensin II to AT1 receptors, reducing vasoconstriction, sodium retention and aldosterone release.
(c)
• Accumulation of bradykinin is proposed as the mechanism of cough and angioedema with ACE inhibitors.
• ACE inhibitors can injure or kill a developing fetus; stop them in pregnant patients as soon as possible.
• Side effects: dry cough, hypotension, angioedema.
(d)
• ACE inhibitors remain the initial treatment of choice; ARBs are for patients unable to tolerate ACE inhibitors.
• ACE inhibitors are the treatment of choice in hypertension with CKD and proteinuria and reduce mortality in heart failure, after MI and in diabetes with proteinuria.
• Compelling indications: ACEI/ARB for diabetes and for heart failure; with CKD, ACEI or ARB plus thiazide, or CCB.
questions.question:
Describe the drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system:
(a) classification into ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers with examples
(b) mechanism of action at the molecular target
(c) the chemical/biochemical basis for their adverse effects and limitations
(d) distinguish ACE inhibitors from ARBs.

Discuss biological response modifiers and angiogenesis inhibition as approaches to cancer therapy:
(a) the principle and examples (aldesleukin, interferons, thalidomide, lenalidomide)
(b) relate the actions of each to the biology
(c) explain what each strategy improves and what adverse effects or limitations result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Biological response modifiers stimulate immune cells; cytokines are proteins released by immune cells on activation.
• Aldesleukin is interleukin-2 (IL-2); interferons alpha, beta and gamma; thalidomide and lenalidomide are angiogenesis inhibitors.
(b)
• Aldesleukin promotes development of T cells; it is used in some renal tumours.
• Alpha-2(a) interferon is produced in large quantities by recombinant DNA techniques and is used for hairy cell leukaemia; the exact mechanism is unknown but they can stimulate natural killer cells.
• Angiogenesis forms new blood vessels; tumours that reach a certain size need a blood supply and cancer cells secrete chemicals promoting angiogenesis.
• Thalidomide interferes with the growth of rapidly dividing cells and with blood vessel formation.
(c)
• Aldesleukin side effects: flu-like symptoms, loss of appetite, skin problems, cardiac arrhythmias, GI disturbance, depression and poor concentration.
• Interferons: well absorbed after IM injection; chills, dose-related leukopenia, fatigue, alopecia.
• Thalidomide: peripheral neuropathy and severe birth defects or fetal death (phocomelia).
• Lenalidomide is thought to have fewer adverse effects than thalidomide but can cause bone marrow depression and neutropenia.
• Anti-angiogenic agents are still being investigated as potential cancer therapies.

(a)
• Microsomal enzyme induction by phenobarbital increases warfarin metabolism and markedly decreases its anticoagulant effect.
• Phenylbutazone stereo-selectively inhibits metabolism of the more potent S(-) enantiomer of warfarin, causing excessive hypoprothrombinemia and hemorrhage.
(b)
• Induction is an increase in newly synthesized enzyme, raising the rate of metabolism and shortening drug action; inhibition mechanisms include substrate competition, inactivation of enzymes and hepatotoxicity.
• Phenytoin metabolism is inhibited by chloramphenicol, disulfiram and isoniazid; toxicity with isoniazid occurs primarily in slow acetylators.
(c)
• Inducers: phenobarbital, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; inhibitors: cimetidine (potent), MAO inhibitors for specific enzymes.
• Inhibition is less common than induction.
(d)
• When phenobarbital is started or stopped the warfarin dose must be readjusted.
• Reduced metabolism generally increases the intensity and duration of drug action.
questions.question:
A patient on warfarin begins phenobarbital and later another patient on warfarin takes phenylbutazone and bleeds. A third patient on phenytoin taking isoniazid, a slow acetylator, becomes toxic.
(a) Identify the metabolic liability in each interaction.
(b) Explain the induction and inhibition pathways.
(c) Differentiate the related drugs and their effects.
(d) Reason to dose adjustment and management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Methotrexate, a folate antagonist (antimetabolite, folic acid analogue).
(b)
• Folates consist of a pteridine ring, PABA and glutamate; in cells folate is converted to polyglutamates and reduced to tetrahydrofolate (FH4).
• Antifolates are designed to interact at cofactor sites of enzymes in the biosynthesis of nucleic acid bases.
(c)
• Dihydrofolate reductase converts folate to FH2 and FH2 to FH4; methotrexate has higher affinity for the enzyme than FH2.
• FH4 depletion depletes deoxythymidine monophosphate (DTMP), causing thymine-less death and inhibition of DNA synthesis; main action is interference with thymidylate synthesis.
• It is taken up actively by the folate transport system and metabolized to polyglutamate derivatives retained for weeks or months.
(d)
• Given orally, IV, IM or intrathecally; peak 1-5 h; concentration high about 6 h; 50% plasma-protein bound.
• Low lipid solubility, so it does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
• Side effects: bone marrow depression, damage to GIT epithelium, nephrotoxicity at high doses.
• It acts mainly in S phase (antimetabolite).
questions.question:
A child with leukemia is given an orally administered folic acid analogue that binds dihydrofolate reductase more tightly than its natural substrate, causing "thymine-less death". It does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
(a) Identify the drug and its class.
(b) State the structural background (what folates consist of) that explains its action.
(c) Explain its mechanism at the molecular target.
(d) State its pharmacokinetic features, therapeutic route options and key adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Potassium-sparing diuretics decrease potassium secretion, whereas thiazides increase potassium and bicarbonate excretion.
(b)
They interfere with sodium reabsorption at the distal tubules, primarily in the collecting duct region of the nephron.
(c)
Triamterene and amiloride.
(d)
• Rationale: counteract potassium loss; they have a weak diuretic and antihypertensive effect when used alone.
• Unlike potassium-sparing combination products, hydrochlorothiazide may be used where hyperkalemia cannot be risked, including patients taking ACE inhibitors.
• Thiazide side effects include hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.
questions.question:
Triamterene or amiloride is added to a thiazide-treated patient. When used alone they give a weak diuretic and antihypertensive effect.
(a) Predict the effect on potassium relative to a thiazide.
(b) Justify through the site of action.
(c) Name the drugs.
(d) State the rationale and when hydrochlorothiazide is preferred.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Against herpes viruses: valaciclovir, famciclovir, foscarnet, valganciclovir; against RNA viruses: zanamivir, oseltamivir, ribavirin; against HBV: lamivudine, adefovir dipivoxil, entecavir; against HIV: NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, raltegravir, enfuvirtide, maraviroc.
(b)
• Herpes drugs: prodrugs of acyclovir, penciclovir, ganciclovir activated by viral kinases; foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analogue polymerase inhibitor.
• Zanamivir and oseltamivir are sialic acid analogues inhibiting neuraminidase (influenza A and B).
• Ribavirin is a nucleoside analogue with possibly no direct viral target (HCV, RSV).
• HBV agents are nucleoside or nucleotide analogue polymerase inhibitors.
• HIV: raltegravir a dihydropyrimidine derivative blocking integration; enfuvirtide a polypeptide on gp41; maraviroc a CCR5 ligand mimic; PIs gag cleavage site mimics.
(c)
• Latency: herpesviruses persist for life; HIV DNA integrates and stays quiescent so HIV cannot be cleared.
• Viruses with over 100 serotypes (rhinovirus, papillomavirus) limit single agents; pleconaril covered about 70% of rhinovirus serotypes.
• High mutation rates select resistant variants.
(d)
• M2 channel blockers (amantadine, rimantadine) lose activity through a single mutation with a fully fit virus (91% of H3N2 isolates in 2005-2006 resistant).
• Neuraminidase inhibitors are substrate mimics; resistance is typically slower and needs primary then secondary and compensating mutations.
questions.question:
Describe the antiviral agents used in major viral infections:
(a) classification by target virus (herpes, influenza, hepatitis B, HIV)
(b) general structural nature and mechanism of each group
(c) the chemical/viral basis of their limitations
(d) distinguish neuraminidase inhibitors from M2 channel blockers.

A patient with heart failure and reduced glomerular filtration rate has volume retention. A diuretic acting on the ascending limb of the loop of Henle is selected; it is highly protein bound.
(a) Identify the class and representative drugs.
(b) State the structural feature relevant to allergy.
(c) Explain how it reaches its site and how it acts.
(d) State use, limits and adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Loop diuretics: furosemide and torsemide.
(b)
All loop and thiazide diuretics except ethacrynic acid possess a sulfonamide group, clinically relevant in sulfonamide allergy.
(c)
• They act on the ascending limb of the loop of Henle, inhibiting reabsorption of sodium and chloride.
• Being highly protein-bound, they enter the urine mainly by tubular secretion in the proximal tubule rather than glomerular filtration.
(d)
• Commonly used to control volume retention, more commonly prescribed with decreased GFR or heart failure.
• They do not lower blood pressure as effectively as thiazides as monotherapy, especially dosed once daily.
• Side effects of diuretics: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperlipidaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia; not safe in renal and hepatic insufficiency.

questions.question:
Discuss strategies to overcome DNA-repair resistance to alkylating agents:
(a) the repair pathways involved and their targets
(b) relate each to the example of the repair-enzyme inhibitor and its modification
(c) explain why the strategy improves activity and the trade-offs or limitations (normal tissue repair, p53 status).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• DNA repair is a defence in normal tissues but a resistance mechanism to chemotherapy in tumour cells.
• MGMT (O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase) directly removes the alkyl group from O6 positions and the chloroethyl group between DNA chains.
• ABH2 and ABH3 directly remove methyl from N1, N7 and N3 positions of double-stranded DNA and single-stranded RNA respectively.
• Base excision repair repairs other N-alkylation sites; nucleotide excision repair assists; mismatch repair corrects incorrectly paired nucleotides.
• Homologous recombination and non-homologous end-joining enable resynthesis of damaged DNA.
(b)
• O6-benzylguanine inhibits O6-alkylguanine-DNA alkyltransferase; a meta-aminomethyl group improved its solubility and increased enzyme inactivation about 20 times.
• The trend: drugs with release systems or specific carriers to the action site, less toxic analogues and strategies to bypass DNA repair systems.
(c)
• Inactivating the repair enzyme prevents removal of the alkyl lesion and so restores cytotoxic damage.
• If repair fails, the cell can undergo apoptosis via p53; malignant cells with altered p53 do not respond to control or undergo apoptosis.
• Damage severity depends on the injury and the difficulty of repair; crosslinks of bifunctional agents are harder to repair.
• Genetic polymorphism and organ function also affect toxicity.

questions.question:
Describe the chemistry and pharmacology of metformin:
(a) its class and the basis of its classification
(b) the mechanism of action and metabolic effects
(c) the basis of its toxicity and limitation, especially renal
(d) its position relative to other glucose-lowering classes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Metformin (Glucophage) is a biguanide and the only available drug in this class.
(b)
• It lowers blood glucose primarily by decreasing hepatic glucose production.
• It also makes muscle tissue more sensitive to insulin so blood glucose can be used for energy.
• It is weight neutral, does not cause hypoglycemia and reduces cardiovascular mortality compared with sulfonylureas.
(c)
• Principal side effects: GIT intolerance (bloating, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea), mitigated by gradual titration or extended-release form.
• It is cleared by kidney filtration; it may be used with eGFR of 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or above, since lactic acidosis, though rare, occurs when eGFR is below 30.
• It is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency and worsening neuropathy symptoms.
(d)
• Historically first-line for type 2 diabetes; effective, safe, inexpensive, reduces microvascular complications, cardiovascular events and death.
• It is more effective than DPP-4 inhibitors in lowering A1C and weight in monotherapy.
• Current guidance: first-line therapy depends on comorbidities and generally includes metformin plus lifestyle modification; GLP-1 RAs or SGLT2 inhibitors are initial therapy with ASCVD, heart failure or CKD.
• Immediate-release (twice daily) and extended-release (once daily) forms exist.

questions.question:
Describe the chemistry and pharmacology of the HIV entry inhibitors:
(a) their classes, structures and targets (enfuvirtide, maraviroc, and the other listed entry-related agents)
(b) the step of the viral entry process each blocks
(c) the basis of their adverse effects and resistance behaviour
(d) why they are reserved for particular patients.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Enfuvirtide (T-20) is a 36-amino-acid polypeptide fusion inhibitor that binds gp41 of the viral envelope.
• Maraviroc is a coreceptor inhibitor, a CCR5 ligand mimic that binds specifically and selectively to CCR5.
• Fostemsavir is a gp120 attachment inhibitor; ibalizumab-uiyk is a post-attachment monoclonal antibody given intravenously.
(b)
• HIV entry is complex and each step is a potential target; viral attachment involves binding of envelope glycoprotein complex gp160 to cellular receptor CD4.
• Maraviroc blocks the receptor on the host cell membrane; ibalizumab blocks HIV-infected cells from spreading virus to uninfected cells.
(c)
• Enfuvirtide: local injection site reaction, hypersensitivity reaction, eosinophilia.
• Resistance to enfuvirtide can occur, but without cross-resistance.
• Co-receptor tropism is assessed before ART initiation (relevant to maraviroc).
(d)
• Enfuvirtide is given subcutaneously in combination with other antiretrovirals.
• Ibalizumab is specifically for adults with HIV who have tried multiple medications and whose virus is resistant to other therapies.
• Two entry inhibitors have been formally approved: enfuvirtide and maraviroc.

questions.question:
An analogue of urea is used for melanoma and chronic myelogenous leukemia and causes minimal myelosuppression but hypersensitivity, hyperglycemia and hypoalbuminemia.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) State the reaction/enzyme inhibited and synthetic route if given.
(c) Identify the phase specificity and the site of action at risk.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hydroxyurea, a miscellaneous antineoplastic agent that is an analogue of urea.
(b)
It inhibits the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase, depleting deoxynucleoside triphosphate pools and thereby inhibiting DNA synthesis.
(c)
• It is an S-phase specific agent.
• Uses: melanoma and chronic myelogenous leukemia.
• ADR: minimal myelosuppression, hypersensitivity, hyperglycemia, hypoalbuminemia.

questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of 5-fluorouracil:
(a) its chemical class and structural relationship to uracil
(b) the structural basis of its activation and enzyme inhibition
(c) the basis of its toxicity and pharmacokinetic liabilities
(d) related drugs and why selectivity for DNA arises.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is a pyrimidine analogue, an analogue of uracil.
• It is a dUMP analogue working through the DTMP synthesis pathway; it was designed to block conversion of uridine to thymidine.
(b)
• Normal thymidine synthesis methylates the 5-position of uracil's pyrimidine ring; fluorine replaces hydrogen at this position.
• It is converted to the fraudulent nucleotide FdUMP, a competitive inhibitor of the thymidylate synthetase active site that cannot be converted to DTMP.
• It binds thymidylate synthetase covalently, forming a stable ternary complex with a tetrahydrofolate cofactor; DNA synthesis is inhibited.
(c)
• Given IV or topically for skin cancer; rapidly distributed, crosses the brain barrier and is rapidly metabolized in the liver (caution in hepatic impairment).
• Only about 20% is excreted unchanged in the kidneys.
• Side effects: bone marrow depression, severe ulceration of oral and GI mucosa, GIT haemorrhage, stomatitis, esophagopharyngitis, leukopenia, diarrhoea; consciousness disturbance at high dose.
(d)
• Gemcitabine and arabinosylcytosine (araC) work through similar mechanisms; cytarabine and gemcitabine are pyrimidine analogues.
• Thymidine is not a normal component of RNA, so the enzyme inhibition selectively blocks DNA formation.
• Used in carcinomas of breast, colon, pancreas and rectum.

questions.question:
Discuss enzyme inhibition as a principle of drug metabolism:
(a) the mechanisms and examples (cimetidine, MAO inhibitors, phenylbutazone-warfarin, chloramphenicol/disulfiram/isoniazid-phenytoin)
(b) relate the examples to their clinical outcome
(c) explain why inhibition changes drug response and what trade-offs or limitations result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Microsomal enzyme inhibition is not as common as induction.
• Mechanisms: substrate competition, interference with protein synthesis, inactivation of drug-metabolizing enzymes, and hepatotoxicity impairing enzyme activity.
• Certain drugs, e.g. monoamine oxidase inhibitors, are used clinically to inhibit specific enzyme systems.
• The antiulcer drug cimetidine is one of the most potent and comprehensive inhibitors used in clinical medicine.
(b)
• Phenylbutazone stereo-selectively inhibits metabolism of the more potent S(-) enantiomer of warfarin, causing excessive hypoprothrombinaemia and haemorrhage.
• Phenytoin metabolism is inhibited by chloramphenicol, disulfiram and isoniazid; isoniazid-related phenytoin toxicity occurs mainly in slow acetylators.
• Cimetidine raises zidovudine toxicity (it inhibits glucuronidation); drugs that inhibit the hepatic mixed function oxidase system raise PI levels.
(c)
• Reduced metabolism increases the intensity and duration of drug action.
• Decreased metabolic elimination may also lead to accumulation and toxicity.
• Clinical use: ritonavir at low dose boosts lopinavir levels; cobicistat boosts atazanavir, darunavir, elvitegravir.
• Trade-off: itraconazole raises busulfan toxicity; dose adjustments or alternative drugs are needed.

questions.question:
A patient receives an alkaloid from Vinca rosea (Madagascar periwinkle) by injection. It arrests cells in metaphase and she later develops numbness and tingling of the hands.
(a) Identify the class and the representative drugs.
(b) State the structural/botanical source features and phase specificity.
(c) Explain its mechanism at the molecular target.
(d) State pharmacokinetic features, shared and unique adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Vinca alkaloids: vincristine, vinblastine, vindesine (vinorelbine is also listed).
(b)
Obtained from Vinca rosea; they are cell cycle specific and phase specific, with effects manifest during mitosis.
(c)
• They bind tubulin and inhibit its polymerization into microtubules, preventing spindle formation in mitosing cells and causing arrest at metaphase.
• They also inhibit leucocyte phagocytosis and axonal transport in neurons.
(d)
• Given by injection, rapid cytotoxic effects; metabolized in the liver and excreted in bile and faeces.
• Shared effects: phlebitis or cellulitis, nausea, vomiting, alopecia.
• Vincristine: mild myelosuppression and peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling); vinblastine: myelosuppressant.

questions.question:
Discuss isosteric design in purine and pyrimidine antimetabolites:
(a) the design principle and the examples (6-mercaptopurine, azathioprine, allopurinol, 5-fluorouracil)
(b) how each part of the structure relates to its activation and action
(c) why the strategy gives selectivity or protection from degradation, and the trade-offs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Purine antimetabolite design began with an isosteric thiol/sulfhydryl group replacing the 6-hydroxyl group of hypoxanthine and guanine, giving 6-mercaptopurine (thiol analogue of hypoxanthine) and 6-thioguanine.
• 5-Fluorouracil was designed to block conversion of uridine to thymidine; thymidine biosynthesis normally methylates the 5-position of uracil.
(b)
• 6-MP is bioactivated by HGPRT to the ribonucleotide 6-thioinosinate (6-MPMP), a potent inhibitor of conversion of 5-phosphoribosylpyrophosphate to 5-phosphoribosylamine.
• Replacement of hydrogen at the 5-position of uracil with fluorine yields a stable covalent ternary complex of 5-FU, thymidylate synthase and a tetrahydrofolate cofactor.
• 5-FU is converted to the fraudulent nucleotide FdUMP; gemcitabine and araC work through similar mechanisms.
• Azathioprine, a heterocyclic derivative of 6-MP, was designed to protect the drug from catabolic degradation.
• Allopurinol is an adjuvant that prevents uric acid formation.
(c)
• Selectivity: thymidine is not a normal component of RNA, so targeting thymidylate synthase should selectively inhibit DNA formation.
• Trade-offs: azathioprine's antitumour activity does not surpass 6-MP and it is used as an immunosuppressant.
• Allopurinol is linked to kidney toxicity from purines released from destroyed cancer cells.
• Antimetabolites remain toxic to rapidly dividing normal cells (marrow, GIT); 5-FU causes GIT haemorrhage, stomatitis, leukopenia, diarrhoea.
• Fludarabine (triphosphate inhibits DNA polymerase, myelosuppressive) and pentostatin (inhibits adenosine deaminase) are further purine examples.

questions.question:
A patient with breast cancer is placed on an alkylating agent that is inactive as administered (oral or intravenous) and is activated by the liver CYTp450 microsomal system. After treatment she develops bleeding from the bladder.
(a) Identify the drug and its chemical class.
(b) State the structural features and activated metabolites responsible for its activity.
(c) Explain its mechanism of action at the molecular target.
(d) State its therapeutic uses and the key adverse effect linked to its structure, including how this effect can be reduced.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent of the oxazaphosphorine class.
• It is a prodrug: inactive in parent form and given orally or intravenously.
(b)
• Liver CYTp450 converts it to 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide and aldophosphamide.
• Hydroxylation disrupts the oxazaphosphorine ring and releases the bis(2-chloroethyl) group, which generates the active cation.
• Aldophosphamide is converted to acrolein and phosphoramide mustard; phosphoramide mustard is the cytotoxic moiety.
(c)
• Alkylating agents are electrophiles that react covalently with DNA by nucleophilic substitution; the main site is N7 of guanine.
• It cross-links guanine nucleobases on DNA strands, so the strands cannot uncoil and separate and replication is inhibited; the effect is cell-cycle nonspecific.
(d)
• Uses: breast cancer, ovarian cancer, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, CLL, soft tissue sarcoma, neuroblastoma, Wilms' tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma.
• Hemorrhagic cystitis is caused by the acrolein moiety.
• It is reduced by increasing fluid intake and by bladder irrigation with sulphydryl donors (N-acetylcysteine), which form a non-toxic compound with acrolein.
• Other effects: nausea and vomiting, bleeding, alopecia, skin pigmentation; it also affects lymphocytes and can be used as an immunosuppressant.

(a)
Doxorubicin, an anthracycline antineoplastic antibiotic.
(b)
• Structure: tetracycline ring structures with the unusual sugar daunosamine attached by glycosidic linkage.
• Mechanism 1: binds DNA tightly by intercalating between adjacent nucleotides, inhibiting DNA and RNA synthesis.
• Mechanism 2: inhibits topoisomerase II, stabilizing the cleaved DNA-topoisomerase complex and preventing recombination of the strands.
• Mechanism 3: produces semiquinone free radicals that reduce O2 to superoxide ions and H2O2, mediating single-strand scission of DNA.
(c)
• Tissues with ample superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase are protected; cardiac tissue lacks superoxide dismutase and catalase, a possible reason for cardiotoxicity.
• Clinically, cumulative dose-related cardiac damage leads to dysrhythmias and heart failure.
(d)
• Related structures: epirubicin, idarubicin, valrubicin (also daunomycin/idarubicin listed).
• Uses: acute lymphocytic and granulocytic leukemia, lymphoma, sarcoma, solid organ cancers; ADRs: bone marrow depression, stomatitis, alopecia, cardiac toxicity.
• Given IV, rapidly taken up by tissues, does not cross the blood barrier, metabolized in liver, excreted mainly in bile.
questions.question:
A cytotoxic antibiotic from Streptomyces peucetius var. caesius has a tetracycline-type ring structure joined by a glycosidic linkage to an unusual sugar. It causes bone marrow depression and cumulative cardiac damage.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) State its structural features and mechanisms of action, with the reagents/synthetic route if given.
(c) Identify the site/tissue at risk and why.
(d) State related variants and uses.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, e.g. ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril.
(b)
• They suppress the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system by preventing conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
• They also block the major pathway of bradykinin degradation by inhibiting ACE; accumulation of bradykinin is proposed to cause cough and angioedema.
(c)
• Treatment of choice in hypertension with chronic kidney disease and proteinuria; they reduce morbidity and mortality in heart failure, after recent MI, and in proteinuric renal disease and diabetes.
• Side effects: dry cough, hypotension, angioedema.
• They can injure or even kill a developing fetus; in pregnancy discontinue as soon as possible.
• Patients unable to tolerate ACE inhibitors are given ARBs.
questions.question:
A hypertensive diabetic patient with proteinuric kidney disease is started on a drug whose generic names end with -pril (ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril) and develops a dry cough.
(a) Identify the class.
(b) Explain the mechanism and the link to the adverse effect.
(c) State the clinical consequences and contraindication.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Selective beta-blockers (atenolol, metoprolol, propranolol, bisoprolol) block beta-1 receptors on the heart, decreasing rate and force of contraction and cardiac output.
• Beta-blockers with alpha activity: labetalol and carvedilol; with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA): acebutolol and pindolol.
(b)
• Alpha-1 antagonism gives peripheral vasodilation; labetalol (alpha-1 and beta) lowers peripheral resistance without substantial decrease in resting heart rate, cardiac output or stroke volume.
• Carvedilol antagonizes both alpha-1 and beta receptors and lowers standing BP more than supine BP.
• Acebutolol is cardioselective with mild ISA in therapeutic range; pindolol is used alone or with a thiazide-type diuretic.
(c)
• Beta-blockers are drugs of choice with coexistent coronary heart disease.
• Limitations: lethargy, impotence, bradycardia; not safe with asthma, COPD and diabetes; adverse effect on the lipid profile.
• Abrupt discontinuation can exacerbate angina and cause MI, so doses must be reduced gradually over at least a few weeks.
• Alpha-blocking beta-blockers carry the risk of orthostatic hypotension (carvedilol).
• Pindolol's antihypertensive response occurs within the first week, maximal after about 2 weeks or longer.
questions.question:
Discuss the structural design of beta-blockers for hypertension:
(a) the principle and examples (selective beta-1 blockers, beta-blockers with alpha-1 activity, beta-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity)
(b) relate the receptor activities to the examples (atenolol, metoprolol, propranolol, bisoprolol, labetalol, carvedilol, acebutolol, pindolol)
(c) explain why each design improves a property and the trade-offs or limitations that result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• DPP-4 inhibitors improve A1C without hypoglycemia, do not cause weight gain and are usually well tolerated.
• GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists give large benefits in lowering glucose and weight, and some prevent heart disease.
(b)
• DPP-4 inhibitors prevent breakdown of GLP-1 and GIP so the hormones stay active longer and lower glucose only when elevated.
• The agonists have similar effects to GLP-1/GIP but are resistant to breakdown by DPP-4.
(c)
• DPP-4 inhibitors: alogliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, sitagliptin.
• GLP-1 RAs: dulaglutide, exenatide (and extended-release), liraglutide, lixisenatide, injectable semaglutide, oral semaglutide (Rybelsus); dual agonist: tirzepatide.
(d)
• Rationale: native hormones are degraded rapidly so direct injection does not work well.
• Dosing varies from twice daily to once weekly; the most common side effect is nausea; metformin is more effective than DPP-4 inhibitors for A1C and weight in monotherapy.
questions.question:
Natural GLP-1 and GIP are broken down very quickly, so they work poorly when injected. Two drug strategies exploit them: stopping the enzyme that breaks them down, or using analogues resistant to it.
(a) Predict the effect of each strategy on glucose, hypoglycemia and weight.
(b) Justify through the mechanism.
(c) Name the drugs for each strategy.
(d) State the rationale and adverse effects.

A semi-synthetic derivative of a compound from the May apple (mandrake root) given orally or intravenously causes DNA strand breakage and blocks cells in late S-G2 phase.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) State its origin and structural relationship to the parent compound.
(c) Explain the mechanism at the molecular target.
(d) State pharmacokinetics, adverse effects and tissue limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Etoposide, an epipodophyllotoxin (plant-derived topoisomerase inhibitor).
(b)
It is a semi-synthetic derivative of podophyllotoxin obtained from Podophyllum peltatum (May apple, mandrake root).
(c)
• It inhibits topoisomerase II, leading to DNA strand breakage and DNA damage; it blocks the cell at late S-G2.
• It can also affect mitochondrial function and nucleoside transport.
(d)
• Given orally or intravenously, well distributed, does not cross the blood-brain barrier, metabolized in the liver and excreted mainly in urine.
• Adverse effects: myelosuppression, hair loss, nausea, vomiting.

(a)
Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), e.g. losartan and valsartan.
(b)
• ARBs competitively block binding of angiotensin II to AT1 receptors.
• This reduces angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction, sodium retention and aldosterone release.
(c)
• ACE inhibitors remain the initial treatment of choice; ARBs are used when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated (cough/angioedema are attributed to bradykinin accumulation with ACE inhibition).
• Compelling indications listed: ACEI/ARB for hypertension with diabetes and with heart failure; ACEI or ARB plus thiazide with CKD or previous stroke.
questions.question:
A patient who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor is given losartan or valsartan.
(a) Identify the drug class.
(b) State the receptor mechanism and effects.
(c) Identify the structural/mechanistic basis for tolerability differences and any prodrug or isosteric variant.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Both are alkylating prodrugs of the triazene/hydrazine class, with the triazene group; in temozolomide the triazene is inserted in a cyclic structure.
• The imidazole ring in both confers a more rapid and located onset of action; in temozolomide it combines with the triazene to form a relatively small lipophilic molecule able to cross the blood-brain barrier.
(b)
• Dacarbazine is activated via CYP (N-demethylation); temozolomide by nonenzymatic spontaneous hydrolysis at physiological pH.
• Both generate the active metabolite MTIC, 5-(3-methyltriazen-1-yl)-imidazole-4-carboxamide, which forms the methyl diazonium cation that binds DNA.
• Temozolomide: PO and IV; half-life 60-120 min; glioma and malignant melanoma.
(c)
• Dacarbazine: IV; half-lives 20 min and 300 min; melanoma, lymphoma, sarcomas.
• Toxicity: nausea, vomiting and myelosuppression.
• Dacarbazine regimens: 2-4.5 mg/kg daily for 10 days every 28 days, or 250 mg/m2 daily for 5 days every 3 weeks.
• In Hodgkin lymphoma combination: 150 mg/m2 for 5 days every 4 weeks, or 375 mg/m2 single dose every 15 days.
(d)
• DNA repair by MGMT removes alkyl groups from O6 positions, a resistance mechanism of the class.
• Polymorphisms of the activating CYP enzymes alter drug action and toxicity.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry of dacarbazine and temozolomide:
(a) their chemical class and structural features
(b) the activation chemistry to the active species and the structural basis of their action on DNA
(c) the basis of their toxicity, kinetics and dosing
(d) the basis of resistance and loss of activity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Imatinib, a protein kinase inhibitor (Bcr-abl tyrosine kinase).
(b)
Metabolism is mainly by CYP3A4; metabolites are excreted in faeces through bile.
(c)
• Successful in chronic-phase CML (remission above 90%), metastatic c-kit (+) GIST and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.
• Resistance develops mainly from point mutation in Bcr-abl tyrosine kinase.
• Adverse effects: abdominal pain, vomiting, fluid retention, periorbital oedema, pleural effusion, myalgia and CHF.
questions.question:
A protein kinase inhibitor produces remission in more than 90% of patients with chronic-phase CML and in metastatic c-kit positive GIST. It is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 and a patient develops periorbital oedema.
(a) Identify the compound.
(b) Describe metabolism and excretion.
(c) State clinical consequences, resistance and adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Strategy: use the natural hormones GLP-1 and GIP, which help maintain glucose levels but are broken down very quickly, so they work poorly when injected.
• DPP-4 inhibitors: alogliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, sitagliptin.
• GLP-1 RAs: dulaglutide, exenatide, exenatide extended-release, liraglutide, lixisenatide, injectable and oral semaglutide; dual GLP-1/GIP agonist: tirzepatide.
(b)
• DPP-4 inhibitors prevent the breakdown of GLP-1 and GIP, so they remain active longer.
• GLP-1 and dual agonists have effects similar to the natural hormones but are resistant to breakdown by DPP-4.
(c)
• DPP-4 inhibitors lower A1C without hypoglycemia, as they lower glucose only when elevated, and do not cause weight gain.
• GLP-1 and dual agonists give large benefits in lowering glucose and body weight; some prevent heart disease.
• Most are injected (twice daily to once weekly), except oral semaglutide.
• The most common side effect is nausea.
• Cost and insurance coverage limit use as first-line treatment.
• Metformin is more effective than DPP-4 inhibitors in A1C and weight lowering.
questions.question:
Discuss the incretin-based strategy for type 2 diabetes:
(a) the principle and examples (DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, dual GLP-1/GIP agonist)
(b) relate the role of GLP-1 and GIP and the DPP-4 enzyme to each class
(c) explain why the strategy improves glycaemic control and what trade-offs or limitations result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Amantadine and rimantadine are M2 channel blockers; zanamivir and oseltamivir are sialic acid analogues that inhibit neuraminidase (influenza A and B).
(b)
• A single mutation gives high-level resistance to M2 inhibitors and the virus remains fully fit; in 2005-2006, 109/120 (91%) of H3N2 isolates in the US were resistant.
• Substrate mimics bind the catalytic site, so most mutations give a nonfunctional enzyme; few specific mutations interfere with binding without reducing activity too much.
(c)
Primary mutations appear first; secondary mutations raise resistance; tertiary (compensating) mutations restore enzyme efficiency and fitness.
(d)
• Influenza has eight RNA segments; co-infection allows reassortment, so a resistant strain can combine with a highly infectious sensitive strain.
• Only a few oseltamivir-resistant cases were reported in the first year of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic.
questions.question:
Amantadine/rimantadine and zanamivir/oseltamivir were used against influenza. A single mutation caused high-level resistance to one pair and the resistant virus spread to contacts, while resistance to the other pair evolved more slowly.
(a) Identify the lead drugs and their classes.
(b) Describe the targets and how resistance arises in each case.
(c) Name the key mutation types involved.
(d) Identify the viral genome feature that adds a resistance mechanism and any prodrug or stereochemical variants.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Atenolol/metoprolol-type blockers block beta-1 receptors on the heart, lowering rate and force of contraction and cardiac output.
• Alpha-1 activity adds peripheral vasodilation; labetalol lowers BP without a substantial fall in resting heart rate, cardiac output or stroke volume.
(b)
• Labetalol acts at alpha-1 and beta receptors giving vasodilation and decreased total peripheral resistance; carvedilol antagonizes both alpha-1 and beta receptors.
• Carvedilol lowers standing BP more than supine BP, so orthostatic hypotension may occur.
(c)
Alpha activity: labetalol, carvedilol; ISA: acebutolol (cardioselective with mild ISA) and pindolol.
(d)
• Pindolol is used alone or with a thiazide-type diuretic; response within the first week, maximal up to 2 weeks or longer.
• Beta-blockers are drugs of choice with coronary heart disease but are not safe in asthma, COPD and diabetes and affect the lipid profile.
• Abrupt discontinuation may exacerbate angina and cause MI; doses should be reduced over at least a few weeks.
questions.question:
A hypertensive patient with coronary heart disease is on atenolol and develops bradycardia and lethargy. The prescriber considers beta-blockers with added alpha-1 antagonism (labetalol, carvedilol) or with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (acebutolol, pindolol).
(a) Predict the effect of each modification on heart rate, cardiac output and vascular resistance.
(b) Justify through the receptor pharmacology given.
(c) Name the improved analogues for each modification.
(d) State the rationale and cautions.

Several marketed drugs are themselves metabolites of other drugs: oxyphenbutazone, nortriptyline, oxazepam, mesoridazine. A geriatric patient on diazepam shows accumulation of an active metabolite.
(a) Identify the parent drug and metabolite for each pair.
(b) Explain the metabolic reactions involved.
(c) Differentiate related drugs by reaction type.
(d) Reason to the clinical significance of active metabolites.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Oxyphenbutazone is the p-hydroxylated metabolite of phenylbutazone; nortriptyline the N-demethylated metabolite of amitriptyline.
• Oxazepam is the N-demethylated and 3-hydroxylated metabolite of diazepam; mesoridazine is the sulfoxide metabolite of thioridazine.
(b)
Reactions: aromatic hydroxylation, N-demethylation, 3-hydroxylation and sulfoxidation (Phase I oxidative reactions by cytochrome P-450 in the endoplasmic reticulum).
(c)
Desmethyldiazepam is a metabolite that accumulates after repeated administration in geriatric patients and in renal failure.
(d)
• Many drugs give active metabolites that contribute to therapeutic and toxic effects; importance depends on relative activity and plasma concentration.
• Prednisone and cortisone are reduced to the active metabolites prednisolone and hydrocortisone.

questions.question:
Describe the hormonal agents used in cancer treatment:
(a) classification and examples (glucocorticoids, oestrogens, progestins, antagonists)
(b) the chemical/biological basis of their action
(c) the basis of their limitations or toxicity
(d) distinguish tamoxifen from flutamide, and diethylstilbestrol from ethinyloestradiol.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hormonal drugs include glucocorticoids, oestrogens, selective oestrogen receptor modulators, selective oestrogen receptor down-regulators, aromatase inhibitors, antiandrogens and progestins.
• Examples: prednisolone, dexamethasone, diethylstilbestrol, ethinyloestradiol, megestrol, medroxyprogesterone, tamoxifen, flutamide, cyproterone; GnRH analogues are used for prostate tumours.
(b)
• Growth of some tumours is influenced by the hormonal environment, especially for hormone-dependent organs; growth can be inhibited by hormone antagonists or hormones with opposing actions.
• Glucocorticoids inhibit lymphocyte proliferation (leukaemias, lymphomas), lower raised intracranial pressure and mitigate some side effects of anticancer drugs.
• Physiological oestrogens antagonize androgens, so they are used in androgen-dependent prostate cancer; oestrogens can also recruit resting mammary cancer cells into the proliferating pool.
• Progestins give temporary remission in endometrial and renal tumours.
(c)
• Hormonal agents are palliative in prostate cancer (diethylstilbestrol, ethinyloestradiol); ethinyloestradiol has fewer side effects.
• Hormone antagonism works only for hormone-dependent tumours.
(d)
• Tamoxifen competes with endogenous oestrogens for the receptor and inhibits transcription of oestrogen-responsive genes, important in breast cancer.
• Flutamide and cyproterone are androgen antagonists used in prostate tumours (conditions of increased androgen levels).
• Diethylstilbestrol and ethinyloestradiol are both palliative oestrogens for androgen-dependent prostatic tumours.

(a)
• Pharmacologic enhancers or drug boosters: ritonavir (RTV) at low dose increases blood levels of lopinavir (LPV).
• Cobicistat (Tybost) does the same in combination with atazanavir, darunavir and elvitegravir.
• Lopinavir/ritonavir (Kaletra) combines a gag cleavage site mimic with a PK enhancer.
(b)
• Protease inhibitors have oral bioavailability of only 4-10% because of extensive first-pass effect.
• They undergo extensive biotransformation by the mixed function oxidase system in the intestinal wall and liver.
• Drugs that inhibit the hepatic mixed function oxidase system may increase PI plasma concentrations.
(c)
• Boosting raises plasma levels of the partner protease inhibitor and is part of initial regimens (two NRTIs plus a PI, with or without ritonavir boosting).
• Trade-offs: lopinavir/ritonavir causes diarrhoea, increased cholesterol, headache, increased liver enzymes, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, abnormal stools.
• Because of the inhibition of oxidase enzymes, interactions with other drugs metabolized by this system are expected.
• PIs distribute to all tissues except the CNS.
• Some cross-resistance occurs among PIs.
questions.question:
Discuss pharmacokinetic boosting of antiretroviral drugs:
(a) the principle and examples (ritonavir with lopinavir; cobicistat with atazanavir, darunavir, elvitegravir)
(b) relate the metabolism of protease inhibitors to the strategy
(c) explain why the strategy improves exposure and what trade-offs or limitations result.

Discuss the principle of suppressing viral replication to limit antiviral resistance:
(a) the principle and the supporting examples (HIV and HCV replication rates, missed doses, drug holidays)
(b) relate the mutation arithmetic and viral load monitoring to the principle
(c) explain why the strategy limits resistant mutants and what trade-offs or limitations result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• HIV and HCV produce huge numbers of virions each day (about 10⁹ and 10¹² per day) in untreated patients.
• Resistance rate depends on mutation rate, number of virions formed per day and the proportion of progeny that are fit.
• Missed doses and drug holidays give the virus a better chance to mutate and become resistant.
(b)
• For HIV (about 9,000 nucleotides, mutation rate about 10⁻⁴ and about 10⁹ replications daily), about 9 x 10⁸ mutants arise daily; every point mutation occurs about 10⁵ times daily and every double mutant about 10 times daily.
• Plasma viral load is the most important indicator of response; 'undetectable' should be reached within 16-24 weeks; a 0.5 log10 change is meaningful.
• Resistance testing is done before ART; initial regimens use two NRTIs plus an NNRTI or a PI.
(c)
• A large (e.g. 8 log10) reduction in replication gives a corresponding reduction in formation and selection of resistant mutants.
• It is crucial to keep viral replication as low as possible throughout a single day and a long course of therapy.
• Resistant variants are selected so quickly that a treated person can pass resistant virus to contacts.
• Limitation: RT inhibitors, PIs and integrase inhibitors do not affect integrated viral DNA, so latent HIV cannot be cleared.
• Missed doses and drug holidays undermine suppression of replication.

(a)
6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP), a purine analogue (6-thioguanine is the thiol analogue of guanine).
(b)
Design started with an isosteric thiol/sulfhydryl group replacing the 6-hydroxyl group of hypoxanthine and guanine.
(c)
• It requires bioactivation to its ribonucleotide, 6-thioinosinate (6-MPMP), by the enzyme HGPRT.
• The nucleotide is a potent inhibitor of an early purine biosynthesis step, converting 5-phosphoribosylpyrophosphate to 5-phosphoribosylamine; the drugs are "fraudulent nucleotides".
• Azathioprine, a heterocyclic derivative of 6-MP, was designed to protect the drug from catabolic degradation; its antitumor activity does not exceed 6-MP.
(d)
• Parent drug and metabolites are excreted in the kidneys; well distributed.
• Side effects: bone marrow suppression and reversible toxic effects on liver.
• Azathioprine is used as an immunosuppressant; allopurinol is an adjuvant preventing uric acid formation (kidney toxicity from released purines).
questions.question:
A drug is described as a thiol analogue of hypoxanthine in which a sulfhydryl group replaces the 6-hydroxyl group. It is given orally and its heterocyclic derivative is used as an immunosuppressant.
(a) Identify the compound.
(b) Describe its structural design (physicochemical values such as pKa and solubility are asked for).
(c) Describe its activation pathway and active metabolite.
(d) State the clinical consequences, including uses of related agents and toxicity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The analogue (carboplatin) has the greatest half-life: 120 min versus cisplatin 25-50 min and 1440 min (biphasic).
• Toxicity: cisplatin causes ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; carboplatin causes myelosuppression.
(b)
• The larger substituent in carboplatin makes it take longer to be metabolized.
• Substituents stabilize the metal and are displaced by water, generating a cation that alkylates DNA.
(c)
Carboplatin.
(d)
• Rationale: the larger substituent slows metabolism and lengthens half-life.
• Mechanism: complexes enter cells by transporters, react with water to form positively charged reactive species (favored by low intracellular chloride) and bind N7 of guanine with inter- or intra-strand crosslinks.
• These inhibit transcription and DNA synthesis through strand breaks and coding errors, causing mutations and apoptosis.
• Uses: cisplatin in ovarian, testicular, head and neck and bladder cancer; carboplatin in ovarian and lung cancer; cisplatin raises toxicity with antibiotics and lowers plasma levels with anticonvulsants.
questions.question:
Cisplatin is replaced by a platinum analogue with a larger substituent in its structure, and the patient's dose-limiting toxicity changes from kidney/ear damage to marrow suppression.
(a) Predict the effect on half-life and toxicity.
(b) Justify through the structure-activity relationship of platinum coordination complexes.
(c) Name the improved analogue.
(d) State the rationale and the mechanism of action and uses.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Binding to an amino acid and a substituted phenyl group allowed oral availability of melphalan and chlorambucil.
• The aromatic ring keeps the molecule more stable and enables better distribution of the drug throughout the body before the cation forms.
• The benzimidazole ring of bendamustine gives stability and a local, faster action.
(b)
• Nitrogen mustards arose from sulfur mustards by replacing sulfur with nitrogen because of lower toxicity.
• The bis(2-chloroethyl) group is essential for activity: it forms the aziridine cation (heterocycle with 2 methylene groups attached to a positively charged nitrogen) that alkylates DNA.
(c)
Melphalan (phenylalanine), chlorambucil (aminophenyl butyric acid) and bendamustine (benzimidazole ring).
(d)
• Rationale: mechlorethamine is unstable, so analogues were created with higher stability and oral availability.
• Half-lives: melphalan 45-90 min, chlorambucil 90 min, bendamustine 30-40 min (shorter, consistent with faster local action).
• Routes: melphalan PO and IV, chlorambucil PO, bendamustine IV, mechlorethamine IV.
• Uses: melphalan in multiple myeloma and leukemia; chlorambucil in chronic lymphoid leukemia; bendamustine in chronic lymphoid leukemia and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma; mechlorethamine in lymphoma and Hodgkin's disease.
questions.question:
Mechlorethamine, the first nitrogen mustard, is an unstable molecule given only intravenously. Chemists modify it by attaching an amino acid (phenylalanine), an aminophenyl butyric acid, or a benzimidazole ring.
(a) Predict the effect of these modifications on stability, route of administration and distribution.
(b) Justify the prediction using the structure-activity relationship of the nitrogen mustards.
(c) Name the improved analogues produced.
(d) State the rationale for each modification and compare their half-lives.

Describe the chemistry of imatinib:
(a) its chemical class and target
(b) the structural/biochemical basis of its action
(c) the basis of its metabolism and adverse effects
(d) the basis of resistance and loss of activity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Imatinib is a protein kinase inhibitor, listed in the chemical classification of anticancer agents.
(b)
• It targets the Bcr-abl tyrosine kinase.
• It is successful in the chronic phase of CML (remission above 90%), metastatic c-kit (+) GIST and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.
(c)
• Metabolism is mainly by CYP3A4.
• Its metabolites are excreted in faeces through bile.
• Adverse effects: abdominal pain, vomiting, fluid retention, periorbital oedema, pleural effusion, myalgia and CHF.
(d)
• Resistance develops mainly from point mutation in Bcr-abl tyrosine kinase.
• Remission above 90% is reported in the chronic phase of CML before resistance emerges.

(a)
• Antitumour antibiotics produce their effects mainly by direct action on DNA; anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunomycin, epirubicin, idarubicin, valrubicin), actinomycins (dactinomycin) and bleomycins.
• Anthracyclines are obtained from Streptomyces; doxorubicin from S. peucetius var. caesius; dactinomycin from S. parvulus and others; bleomycin from S. verticillius.
(b)
• Doxorubicin: tetracycline-type ring structures with the sugar daunosamine by glycosidic linkage; intercalates DNA, inhibits topoisomerase II and generates semiquinone free radicals.
• Dactinomycin: chromopeptide with a planar phenoxazone ring that facilitates intercalation; binds minor groove between adjacent G-C pairs and blocks RNA polymerase movement.
• Bleomycin: metal-chelating glycopeptide that binds Fe(II), reduces O2 to superoxide/OH radicals which degrade DNA; most effective in G2.
(c)
• Doxorubicin: cumulative dose-related cardiac damage (dysrhythmias, heart failure), alopecia, bone marrow depression; cardiac tissue lacks superoxide dismutase and catalase.
• Dactinomycin: bone marrow depression, alopecia, erythema.
• Bleomycin: little myelosuppression but hyperpyrexia and pulmonary toxicity.
(d)
• Doxorubicin acts in three ways (intercalation, topoisomerase II, radicals); dactinomycin acts mainly on transcription via minor groove intercalation.
• Doxorubicin is given IV, does not cross the blood barrier, excreted mainly in bile; dactinomycin is used in rhabdomyosarcoma and Wilms' tumor.
• Doxorubicin is used in leukemias, lymphoma, sarcoma and solid tumors.
• Dactinomycin is combined with vincristine and cyclophosphamide in solid tumors in children.
questions.question:
Describe the anticancer antibiotics that act directly on DNA:
(a) classification and sources (anthracyclines, actinomycins, bleomycins)
(b) structural features and mechanism of each
(c) the chemical basis of their toxicity or limitation
(d) distinguish doxorubicin from dactinomycin.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Carbimazole and propylthiouracil are thionamide antithyroid drugs; carbimazole is the first drug of choice.
• Carbimazole inhibits thyroid peroxidase-catalysed iodination of tyrosine residues and the coupling of iodotyrosyl residues, reducing synthesis of T4 from iodine; it also blocks conversion of T4 to T3.
(b)
• Onset is delayed up to 4 weeks; carbimazole initial dose 20-60 mg daily, maintenance 5-15 mg; treatment 6-24 months; PTU 300-600 mg daily, maintenance 50-150 mg.
• Side effects: rashes, bone marrow suppression (agranulocytosis), vasculitis, hypothyroidism, lupus-like syndrome, hypoprothrombinaemia, hepatotoxicity; these are reversible.
• Carbimazole crosses the placenta and may cause neonatal hypothyroidism.
(c)
• PTU is the drug of choice in pregnancy and lactation because of lower concentration in breast milk.
• Agranulocytosis occurs in 0.1-0.5% of patients, suddenly, usually in the first 3 months, equally with both drugs; the drug must be stopped and the other not substituted.
• Rash and pruritus can be treated with antihistamines; sensitivity reactions need withdrawal, and cross-sensitivity is rare so the other drug may then be tried.
(d)
• Alternatives: radioactive iodine (I131), iodine salts/Lugol's, beta-blockers, glucocorticoids and surgery.
• Beta-blockers block conversion of T4 to T3 and relieve palpitations, tremor and anxiety while thionamides take effect.
• Monitoring: thyroid function tests every 4 weeks initially, white cell count when infection is suspected, liver function tests.
questions.question:
Describe the chemistry and pharmacology of carbimazole and propylthiouracil:
(a) their class and chemical action on thyroid hormone synthesis
(b) the basis of their effects and adverse effects
(c) the basis for choosing one over the other, and the loss of effect or toxicity that follows (agranulocytosis, cross-sensitivity)
(d) their relationship with other antithyroid measures.

A nucleotide analogue (not a nucleoside) is used for HIV and is noted to cause renal toxicity.
(a) Identify the drug and its class.
(b) Outline the activation steps and the structural group that distinguishes it from nucleoside analogues.
(c) Identify the structural feature at risk of cleavage and the variant listed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tenofovir, the nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NtRTI); the only NtRTI formally approved as at 2010.
(b)
• As a nucleotide analogue it needs only two phosphorylation steps to become active.
• It contains a phosphonate group that cannot be cleaved by esterases.
(c)
• Once incorporated at the 3'-terminal end it is more difficult to cleave off than regular nucleotide counterparts.
• The tenofovir form with renal toxicity is TDF.
• Combination with emtricitabine and efavirenz is listed (Atripla: two NRTIs and one NNRTI).

(a)
Amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker.
(b)
• Drugs of choice in elderly hypertensives and in those with co-existing asthma.
• They have a neutral effect on glucose and lipid levels.
• Side effects: flushing, headache, pedal edema.
• Compelling indication: hypertension with previous history of CAD (CCB, ACEI, ARB, BB); with stroke, ACEI/ARB plus thiazide or CCB.
questions.question:
A drug that blocks entry of calcium through calcium channels, causing vasodilation and reducing peripheral resistance, is chosen for an elderly asthmatic hypertensive patient because of its neutral effect on glucose and lipids.
(a) Identify the drug and class.
(b) State clinical consequences and adverse effects.

A smoker taking theophylline clears the drug faster than a non-smoker. Another patient on long-term phenobarbital and phenytoin develops osteomalacia.
(a) Identify the metabolic liability and the inducing agents.
(b) Explain the induction pathway.
(c) Differentiate the effects on endogenous compounds and other drugs.
(d) Reason to clinical and dietary consequences.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cigarette smoke contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzo(a)pyrene, potent inducers of microsomal cytochrome P-450 enzymes; theophylline is metabolized more rapidly in smokers.
(b)
Enzyme induction is an increase in the amount of newly synthesized enzyme, increasing the rate of drug metabolism and decreasing duration of action.
(c)
• Inducers also enhance metabolism of cortisol, testosterone, vitamin D and bilirubin; enhanced vitamin D3 metabolism by phenobarbital and phenytoin is responsible for osteomalacia.
• Phenobarbital induces glucuronyltransferase, enhancing bilirubin conjugation with glucuronic acid.
(d)
• Dietary indoles (brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower) and polycyclic hydrocarbons in charcoal-broiled beef also induce enzymes.
• Phenobarbital-induced warfarin metabolism needs dose readjustment on starting or stopping.

questions.question:
Describe the classes of antiretroviral agents:
(a) classification into the six categories with drug examples
(b) the general structural nature and mechanism of each class
(c) the basis of limitations and adverse effects
(d) distinguish NRTIs from NNRTIs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Six categories: NRTIs (zidovudine, didanosine, zalcitabine, lamivudine, abacavir, stavudine, emtricitabine), NtRTI (tenofovir), NNRTIs (efavirenz, nevirapine, delavirdine, etravirine), PIs, fusion/coreceptor inhibitors (enfuvirtide, maraviroc) and integrase inhibitors (raltegravir).
• PIs: ritonavir, indinavir, saquinavir, nelfinavir, amprenavir, lopinavir, fosamprenavir, atazanavir, tipranavir, darunavir.
• Newer entries listed include doravirine, rilpivirine, elvitegravir, bictegravir, dolutegravir, cabotegravir, fostemsavir (gp120 attachment inhibitor) and ibalizumab.
(b)
• NRTIs are nucleoside analogues phosphorylated by cellular kinases that inhibit RNA-dependent DNA polymerase and block DNA synthesis.
• NtRTIs are nucleotide analogues needing two phosphorylation steps, with a phosphonate group not cleaved by esterases.
• PIs prevent post-translational cleavage of polyprotein, giving immature noninfectious particles; entry inhibitors target gp41 or CCR5.
• Raltegravir is a pyrimidinone analogue that binds integrase.
(c)
• Adverse effects: efavirenz (CNS effects), nevirapine (rash, SJS, hepatotoxicity), zidovudine (anaemia), abacavir (hypersensitivity), tenofovir and lamivudine (renal toxicity), stavudine (neuropathy, lipodystrophy).
• Limitations: resistance emerges, no therapy clears integrated HIV DNA; RT inhibitors and PIs have no direct effect on integrated DNA.
(d)
• NRTIs must be phosphorylated and are integrated into the transcribed DNA; NNRTIs are active as administered.
• NNRTIs attach to reverse transcriptase and prevent conversion of RNA to DNA rather than integrating into the DNA.
• Both attack the same target enzyme.

questions.question:
A prodrug of acyclovir, a prodrug of penciclovir and a prodrug of ganciclovir are used for herpes infections.
(a) Predict the type of modification and its effect on the active species.
(b) Justify through the activation pathway described.
(c) Name the prodrug derivatives.
(d) State the rationale and the limitation of therapy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Valaciclovir (VACV) is the prodrug of acyclovir; famciclovir (FCV) of penciclovir; valganciclovir (VGCV) of ganciclovir.
(b)
• Acyclovir/penciclovir prodrugs are activated by viral thymidine kinase and then inhibit the viral polymerase.
• Ganciclovir is activated by the kinase encoded by UL97 and inhibits the polymerase (CMV).
(c)
Valaciclovir, famciclovir, valganciclovir; foscarnet is instead a pyrophosphate analogue polymerase inhibitor.
(d)
• Targets: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV (valaciclovir, famciclovir) and CMV (valganciclovir).
• Limitation: antivirals reduce replication during an acute episode but no therapy removes latent herpesvirus infection, so reactivation remains possible.
• Acyclovir was the first antiviral drug to be both potent and selective.

(a)
Reduction: prednisone and cortisone are reduced to the active metabolites prednisolone and hydrocortisone.
(b)
• Reduction is not a common pathway of drug metabolism; reductive reactions include reduction of aldehydes and ketones, nitro and azo compounds (azo dyes reduced to amines in liver and intestinal flora).
• Phase 1 reactions generally lose pharmacological activity; prodrugs are the exception.
(c)
• Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone and dexamethasone inhibit lymphocyte proliferation in leukaemias and lymphomas.
• They lower raised intracranial pressure and mitigate some side effects of anticancer drugs (supportive therapy).
questions.question:
A patient is given prednisone (a ketone) and the metabolite that results from reduction at the carbonyl is the pharmacologically active species. Glucocorticoids are also used in leukaemias and lymphomas.
(a) Identify the metabolic reaction and the active metabolites.
(b) Describe the type of reaction and how common it is.
(c) State therapeutic consequences.
