questions.explanation: A FLACC score of 9-10 indicates severe, uncontrolled pain requiring urgent analgesic intervention. The combination of constant facial grimacing (score 2), legs drawn up (score 2), rigid or arching activity (score 2), steady crying or screaming (score 2), and inability to be consoled (score 2) represents the maximum pain expression on each domain. Immediate assessment of pain etiology and administration of appropriate pharmacological analgesia is indicated, alongside non-pharmacological comfort measures and close monitoring of vital signs.

questions.question: Untreated maternal gonococcal infection at the time of vaginal delivery most classically causes which neonatal complication?
options: Severe purulent conjunctivitis within days of birth
questions.explanation: Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis, or ophthalmia neonatorum, develops within the first few days of life following passage through an infected birth canal and can rapidly progress to corneal ulceration and blindness if untreated. This is why routine ocular prophylaxis is given to all newborns shortly after birth. Prompt maternal screening and treatment during pregnancy reduces this risk substantially.

Copper ions released from the device provoke a sterile inflammatory reaction within the endometrial cavity that is toxic to sperm and ova, preventing fertilisation. Unlike hormonal methods, the copper IUD does not suppress ovulation. This local inflammatory effect is the accepted primary mechanism of copper-based intrauterine contraception.
options: It suppresses ovulation via hormonal feedback
It thins the endometrium to prevent bleeding
It blocks the internal cervical os physically
It creates a spermicidal inflammatory reaction
It alters vaginal pH to immobilise sperm
questions.question: Which of the following best explains the primary contraceptive mechanism of the copper-bearing intrauterine device?

options: Engagement, as the head enters the pelvic brim
External rotation, before the shoulders are delivered
Compaction, as the head moulds through the pelvis
Crowning, as the head distends the vulva
Restitution, as the head realigns with the shoulders
questions.question: During labour, a midwife notes the fetal head has undergone flexion, descent, and internal rotation, and is about to deliver by extension. Which cardinal movement follows extension?
questions.explanation: After the head is delivered by extension, restitution occurs first as the head rotates slightly to realign with the shoulders that remain in the oblique or transverse diameter of the pelvis. This is followed by external rotation as the shoulders themselves rotate into the anteroposterior diameter for delivery. Recognising this sequence helps the midwife anticipate and assist shoulder delivery.

options: Sleep exclusively lying face down at all times
Sleep only on the side of the more affected eye
Sleep flat with the head at the same level as the body
Avoid any use of pillows under the head
Sleep with the head of the bed elevated
questions.question: The nurse instructs a patient with Thyroid Eye Disease regarding sleeping position. Which advice is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Elevating the head of the bed helps reduce orbital venous congestion overnight, which can lessen morning eyelid swelling and proptosis in patients with Thyroid Eye Disease. Sleeping flat, face down, without pillow support, or favouring the affected side would not provide this benefit and could worsen periorbital swelling. This simple positional advice is a practical, low-risk nursing recommendation for symptomatic relief.

Liquefactive necrosis occurs when hydrolytic enzymes digest the dead tissue into a viscous liquid mass, a pattern characteristic of the brain due to its high lipid content and lack of supportive stroma. It is also typical of tissue destroyed by bacterial infection, where neutrophil enzymes drive digestion. This differs from coagulative necrosis, in which the tissue architecture is preserved rather than dissolved.
questions.question: A patient with a middle cerebral artery infarct undergoes brain imaging showing a cystic cavity where necrotic tissue was digested and liquefied. This pattern of tissue death is:
What is the most appropriate nursing action when a patient with Graves' disease has impaired eyelid closure due to exophthalmos?
options: Irrigating the eyes with normal saline every 2 hours
Using dark glasses during the day and taping eyelids during sleep
Applying lubricating eye ointment twice daily as needed
Requesting an ophthalmology consult and patching one eye
Elevating the feet of the bed to reduce orbital congestion
questions.explanation: When a patient with Graves' disease cannot completely close their eyelids due to exophthalmos, the exposed cornea is at risk for dryness, abrasion, and infection. The nursing interventions of encouraging use of dark glasses when awake (to protect from light and debris) and taping the eyelids shut during sleep (to prevent corneal desiccation and exposure keratopathy) protect the exposed cornea. The head of bed elevation reduces tissue edema that could worsen the bulging eyes.

Reintroducing nutrition after prolonged starvation causes a sudden insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, producing dangerous serum deficiencies. This electrolyte shift can precipitate cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and death if unrecognised. Nutrition must therefore be reintroduced slowly with close electrolyte monitoring.
options: Serum bilirubin and liver enzymes only
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a severely malnourished patient who is about to begin nutritional support. The nurse should monitor closely for refeeding syndrome by checking serum:

A client undergoing prolonged orthopedic rehabilitation reports feeling lonely and withdrawn due to reduced mobility and changes in daily activities. This is best identified as which psychosocial issue?
questions.explanation: Social isolation may arise due to reduced mobility or changes in daily activities during orthopedic rehabilitation, contributing to feelings of loneliness and potentially hindering overall wellbeing. Dependency on medications, sleep disturbance, loss of productivity, and grief are distinct psychosocial issues with different presentations. Recognizing social isolation allows nurses to encourage social support and connection during recovery.

options: Rinse and reuse sharps after simple wiping
Place them directly into a designated puncture-resistant sharps container
Wrap them in cloth before placing in any bin
Leave them on the instrument tray until the next case
Dispose of them in the regular general waste bin
questions.explanation: Sharps must be placed directly into a designated, puncture-resistant sharps container immediately after use to prevent needlestick injury and environmental contamination. General waste disposal or reuse after wiping poses a significant safety hazard. Correct sharps disposal is a core component of both infection control and occupational safety protocols.
questions.question: The recommended method for disposing of sharps in the postoperative OR cleaning process is to:

questions.explanation: Providing emotional support and reassurance reduces anxiety and psychological distress, which promotes the patient's cooperation with treatment, adherence to medication, and participation in recovery activities. Emotional support is a core nursing intervention that complements pharmacological treatment and enhances overall patient outcomes. While important, it does not replace medical treatment or directly alter intraocular pressure or visual acuity measurements.
options: Emotional support directly reduces intraocular pressure
Patient reassurance prevents the need for surgical management
Psychological comfort reduces anxiety and promotes cooperation with treatment
Emotional support replaces the need for pharmacological intervention
Emotional support improves the patient's visual acuity scores
questions.question: The nurse provides 'emotional support and reassurance' to a patient with an ocular condition PRIMARILY because:
A midwife explains that oxytocin, responsible for milk ejection during breastfeeding, is released from which specific glandular structure?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is synthesised in the hypothalamus but stored and released into the circulation from the posterior pituitary gland in response to suckling stimulation. Once released, it acts on myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli to cause milk ejection. This differs from prolactin, which is released from the anterior pituitary and controls milk synthesis rather than ejection.
options: the hypothalamus directly without pituitary involvement

questions.question: During a family planning consultation, a client with obesity asks about oral contraceptive pills. The nurse should advise her that:
questions.explanation: Obesity reduces the efficacy of some contraceptive methods and combined oral contraceptives (COCs) carry an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in obese women due to the prothrombotic effects of oestrogen combined with the metabolic changes of obesity. Clinicians must weigh the risks and benefits and consider alternative methods such as progestin-only methods or long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) in obese clients.
options: Only injectables are safe and effective in obese women
All oral contraceptive pills are safe for obese women
COCs may be less effective and carry higher VTE risk
Obesity is an absolute contraindication for all hormonal pills
Obesity has no effect on contraceptive pill efficacy

questions.explanation: Facial nerve palsy in the newborn commonly results from pressure on the facial nerve during delivery, often related to forceps application, and is recognised by asymmetric facial movement that becomes most apparent during crying, with the affected side failing to wrinkle or move while the unaffected side functions normally. Brachial plexus injuries instead affect limb movement rather than facial expression. Most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks as nerve compression subsides.
options: Klumpke's palsy affecting the lower limb
Erb's palsy affecting the upper limb
Facial nerve palsy from birth trauma
questions.question: A neonate presents with facial asymmetry noted only when crying, with the affected side failing to move while the unaffected side wrinkles normally. This is most consistent with:

questions.explanation: In DVT management, the affected leg should be elevated to reduce oedema and promote venous return. Elevation reduces hydrostatic pressure in the venous system, alleviating pain and swelling. Support stockings and compression wraps also help reduce discomfort and lower the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome. Calf massage is absolutely contraindicated in confirmed DVT as it may dislodge the thrombus and precipitate pulmonary embolism — a life-threatening complication.
questions.question: In managing a puerperal woman who develops deep vein thrombosis, which nursing position for the affected limb is most appropriate?
options: Applying a tight bandage to compress the affected vein aggressively
Massaging the affected calf to dislodge the clot and improve circulation
Maintaining the leg in a horizontal position at heart level at all times
Elevating the affected leg to reduce oedema and promote venous return
Keeping the affected leg in a dependent position to promote venous drainage

questions.explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in cirrhotic patients with ascites is typically monomicrobial, most commonly caused by Gram-negative enteric bacteria (E. coli 40%, Klebsiella 7%) followed by Gram-positive cocci (Streptococcus species, Enterococcus). Polymicrobial infection suggests secondary peritonitis (perforation). Diagnosis requires paracentesis showing ≥250 neutrophils/mm³ in ascitic fluid with positive culture. Empiric treatment with third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime) plus albumin reduces mortality and prevents hepatorenal syndrome. Secondary prophylaxis (norfloxacin or TMP-SMX) prevents recurrence. Primary prophylaxis indicated for patients with low ascitic protein or history of variceal bleeding.
questions.question: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is most commonly caused by:

options: Focal cerebral deficit of rapid onset
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization describes a stroke-type event as a focal cerebral deficit of rapid onset; whether it later proves to be a completed infarct or a resolving transient ischaemic attack is determined afterward. It is not classified as a chronic degenerative process, a peripheral injury or a psychogenic event based on this presentation alone.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden left-sided weakness that resolves completely within 45 minutes, with no infarct visible on later imaging. According to the WHO framework, how should this event first be classified while symptoms are present?

questions.explanation: Fever with severe neutropenia constitutes a medical emergency because the patient lacks adequate defence against infection. Immediate isolation precautions and prompt antibiotic initiation reduce the risk of fulminant sepsis. Delay in this situation can be fatal within hours.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with acute myeloid leukaemia notes a temperature of 38.6°C and an absolute neutrophil count of 250/mm³. The priority nursing action is to:
options: Wait for a repeat temperature before acting
Encourage fresh flowers to lift the patient's mood
Document the finding for the next ward round
Apply a tepid sponge and observe for one hour
Initiate neutropenic precautions and notify the doctor

questions.question: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) is most appropriate as an infertility treatment for which couple?
questions.explanation: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) is most appropriate for couples with mild male factor infertility (reduced motility or mild oligospermia), unexplained infertility, or cervical hostility. Processed sperm are deposited directly into the uterine cavity at the time of ovulation, bypassing cervical barriers and increasing the concentration of motile sperm available for fertilisation. IUI is contraindicated if the fallopian tubes are blocked, as sperm cannot reach the oocyte for fertilisation.
options: A couple requiring preimplantation genetic testing for inherited disease
A couple where the woman has severe endometriosis with ovarian involvement
A couple where the male partner has azoospermia confirmed on semen analysis
A couple with mild male factor infertility or unexplained infertility
A couple where the woman has complete bilateral fallopian tube obstruction

questions.question: Which midluteal progesterone level at day 21 of a 28-day cycle confirms ovulation?
questions.explanation: A midluteal (day 21 of a 28-day cycle) serum progesterone level greater than 30 nmol/L (approximately 9.54 ng/mL) confirms ovulation in clinical practice. Levels between 16 and 30 nmol/L are borderline. A level below 16 nmol/L suggests an anovulatory cycle. The timing of the test should be adjusted for cycle length - best done 7 days before the next expected period.
options: Greater than 16 nmol/L confirms luteal activity
Greater than 50 nmol/L indicates twin pregnancy

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient who just completed a bone marrow biopsy should prioritise which post-procedure action?
questions.explanation: Firm, sustained pressure after bone marrow biopsy reduces the risk of local haematoma, especially in patients with underlying bleeding tendencies. The site should be observed regularly for bleeding or swelling before resuming normal activity. Patients are usually advised to avoid lying directly on the site initially.
options: Apply ice only if the patient requests it
Allow the patient to lie on the biopsy site
Apply firm pressure and monitor the site for bleeding
Remove the dressing after five minutes

questions.explanation: Healthy sexual communication includes thinking twice before beginning sexual relations with a new partner and first discussing past partners, history of STIs, and drug use. This proactive conversation is a key component of responsible sex, enabling both parties to make informed decisions about their sexual health risks. Open communication is identified as fundamental to safe sex practices.
options: Performing a self-administered STI test at home before sexual contact
Completing a mandatory health screening at a registered medical facility
Obtaining written consent from both parties prior to sexual activity
Following a government-mandated sexual health disclosure protocol
Practicing healthy sexual communication before initiating a relationship
questions.question: According to the content, which approach to safe sex includes discussing past partners, history of STIs, and drug use before beginning a sexual relationship?
Kupffer cells are resident macrophages of the liver. Their location within hepatic sinusoids allows them to perform which primary function?
questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are fixed macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids. Their strategic position allows them to phagocytose particulate matter, old red blood cells, bacteria, and endotoxins arriving via the portal circulation from the intestine. They are the largest pool of fixed macrophages in the body, playing a critical role in immune surveillance and iron recycling from hemoglobin breakdown.

questions.question: A client with a suspected shoulder dislocation reports numbness and tingling in the affected arm. This clinical finding most strongly suggests involvement of which structure during the injury?
questions.explanation: Numbness and tingling indicate that nerves around the joint have been compressed or injured as part of the neurovascular complications of dislocation. Cartilage, capsule, and tendon involvement typically produce pain, swelling, or instability rather than sensory disturbances. The synovial membrane lining the joint does not transmit sensory nerve signals in this manner.

options: comply immediately to relieve the patient's distress
report the patient to hospital security for the request
avoid the topic entirely to prevent further discussion
increase sedation to prevent the patient from repeating it
explore the underlying reasons behind the request
questions.explanation: When a patient requests euthanasia, the nurse's first response should be to explore the underlying reasons, such as uncontrolled symptoms, fear, depression, or feeling like a burden, since addressing these unmet needs through palliative and psychological support can often reduce or resolve the desire for euthanasia, which remains illegal in Nigeria in any case.
questions.question: A dying patient repeatedly asks a nurse to help end their life, expressing feelings of being a burden to their family. The nurse's MOST appropriate FIRST response is to

questions.explanation: Nine flexor tendons accompany the median nerve through the carpal tunnel: four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, plus the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These tendons are enclosed in synovial sheaths within the tunnel.
questions.question: What structure accompanies the median nerve through the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: After tonsillectomy, refusal to swallow saliva, guarding behaviour, and an elevated heart rate together suggest inadequately controlled pain requiring further assessment and intervention, since swallowing can be particularly painful after this procedure. Calm behaviour, normal swallowing, and relaxed vital signs are reassuring findings suggesting adequate pain control. Recognising this combination of findings helps the nurse intervene promptly to prevent complications such as dehydration from reduced oral intake.
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a child immediately following a tonsillectomy. Which combination of assessment findings should prompt closer monitoring for inadequately controlled postoperative pain?
options: Refusal to swallow saliva, guarding behaviour, and elevated heart rate
Calm behaviour with normal, unlabored swallowing
Age-appropriate play activity with a relaxed facial expression
Normal vital signs with the child sleeping peacefully
Spontaneous conversation with no signs of distress

questions.explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a dangerous condition, and hospital-acquired diabetic ketoacidosis is the third most common cause of DKA after infection and non-compliance. This highlights the importance of capillary blood ketone monitoring during the perioperative period in diabetic patients. Anaesthetic nurses should have ready access to blood ketone monitoring equipment.
questions.question: Diabetic ketoacidosis in the perioperative period is considered which level of complication?
options: A manageable side effect of neuromuscular blocking drugs
A dangerous condition; hospital-acquired DKA is the third most common cause
An expected effect of inhalational anaesthetic agents
A predictable complication of regional anaesthesia

questions.question: Clomiphene citrate is used in infertility management primarily to achieve which effect?
questions.explanation: Clomiphene citrate is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator that blocks negative feedback at the hypothalamus, triggering increased gonadotropin release and stimulating ovulation in women with anovulatory infertility such as polycystic ovary syndrome. It does not directly address tubal blockage or male infertility. Ovulation is confirmed through mid-cycle monitoring during treatment cycles.
options: Increase sperm production in the male partner
Improve tubal patency after previous infection
Induce ovulation in women with anovulatory cycles
Reduce circulating androgen levels in the ovary
Thicken the endometrial lining before implantation

questions.question: Which laboratory result specifically reflects acute metabolic decompensation when reviewing a patient admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: Ketones in the urine (ketonuria) are a key indicator of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), reflecting the metabolic shift to fat catabolism when insulin is severely deficient. Urinalysis for ketones also screens for poor glycaemic control or missed insulin doses during annual review. Ketonuria warrants urgent clinical reassessment and may require hospital admission for management of acute diabetic decompensation.
options: Presence of ketones in the urine

questions.question: A patient recovering from a TIA asks how it differs from a completed stroke. What is the nurse's most accurate explanation?
options: Symptoms fully resolve without lasting infarct
No risk of future stroke exists
questions.explanation: A TIA is distinguished from a completed stroke because the neurological symptoms are transient and resolve completely without evidence of permanent brain infarction. It does not imply greater severity or guaranteed permanent paralysis, and it is not always surgically managed. Importantly, a TIA still carries a significant risk of a future completed stroke.

options: carry oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus
supply blood directly to the fetal liver only
carry blood exclusively from the fetal kidneys
carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta
questions.explanation: The two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated, nutrient-depleted blood from the fetus back to the placenta for reoxygenation and waste exchange, while the single umbilical vein carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus. This directional flow is opposite to the naming convention used for adult vessels, which can cause confusion for students. Understanding this flow is essential for interpreting fetal circulation and cord blood gas analysis.
questions.question: A midwife explains that the umbilical arteries differ functionally from the umbilical vein. The umbilical arteries specifically:

questions.explanation: As the blood in a cephalhaematoma is absorbed, haemolysis of the extravasated red blood cells releases haem, which is converted to bilirubin. This can cause hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice) in the affected neonate, potentially requiring phototherapy. The primary nursing intervention is to monitor serum bilirubin levels closely during the period of cephalhaematoma resolution and initiate phototherapy if bilirubin rises to treatment threshold levels. Surgical drainage is not indicated for cephalhaematoma management.
questions.question: The primary nursing intervention for preventing neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia related to a cephalhaematoma is:
options: Restricting fluids to prevent bilirubin excretion into the kidneys
Administering intravenous immunoglobulin to suppress haemolysis
Phototherapy prophylactically immediately after birth for all affected neonates
Monitoring serum bilirubin levels as the cephalhaematoma reabsorbs
Surgically draining the cephalhaematoma to prevent haemolysis

questions.explanation: The quadratus lumborum muscle forms the central posterior relation of each kidney. The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially, and the transversus abdominis muscle (its aponeurosis) lies posterolaterally. The diaphragm is posterior to the upper pole, and the subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run posterior to the kidneys.
questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately posterior to both kidneys?

options: During admission via group sessions with other patients
Through written materials sent to their homes by mail
After recovery when they are fully alert and comfortable
Before the surgery rather than during postoperative recovery
On the day of surgery in the preoperative holding area
questions.question: According to studies, most patients prefer to receive preoperative teaching:
questions.explanation: Studies show that many patients want to learn more about their surgery before the procedure rather than during the postoperative recovery period. Preoperative teaching is most effective when delivered in advance, as patients can process the information, ask questions, and prepare mentally and physically.

questions.question: A histology student observes a tissue section where cells show large basophilic cytoplasm with eccentric nuclei having a clock-face chromatin pattern. These cells are most likely which of the following?
questions.explanation: The combination of eccentric nucleus with clock-face chromatin arrangement and strongly basophilic cytoplasm (due to abundant rough ER for antibody synthesis) is pathognomonic for plasma cells. These cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes specialized for immunoglobulin production. The well-developed Golgi body adjacent to the nucleus creates the paranuclear pale zone called the 'Hof.'

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient under chronic stress explains that tight, tense muscles sustained over time most commonly result in:
questions.explanation: Chronic stress causes sustained muscle tension, particularly in the neck, shoulders, and back, which can lead to persistent tension headaches and musculoskeletal discomfort over time. Recognising this connection allows nurses to recommend relaxation techniques and physical measures such as stretching to relieve tension. Addressing the underlying stress often improves these physical symptoms.

questions.question: Major hemorrhage as an intraoperative complication refers to bleeding that is:
options: Expected blood loss within the planned surgical parameters
Post-surgical drainage from the wound into a closed drain
Oozing from a small capillary in the wound margins
Significant and potentially life-threatening during surgery
Minor venous bleeding controlled by electrocautery
questions.explanation: Major intraoperative hemorrhage is defined as significant, potentially life-threatening bleeding occurring during surgery, arising from vascular injury, surgical errors, or underlying coagulopathy. It is distinct from expected, manageable blood loss and requires aggressive resuscitation, surgical control, and blood product replacement.

questions.question: A patient undergoing ENT surgery requires specific additional PACU observations related to:
options: Cardiac rhythm changes unrelated to the airway
Airway patency and risk of postoperative bleeding into the airway
questions.explanation: ENT surgery carries specific risk of airway compromise from swelling or bleeding near the surgical site, requiring vigilant airway-focused observation in PACU beyond standard monitoring. Limb, urinary, or abdominal observations are not the priority focus for this surgical population. Recognising procedure-specific risks tailors PACU monitoring appropriately.

Discharge, dysuria, and itching following unprotected intercourse are classic features consistent with a sexually transmitted infection and warrant prompt screening and treatment. Non-infectious causes such as atrophic vaginitis are less likely given the recent exposure history. Partner notification and treatment should accompany the woman's care.
questions.question: A woman presents with foul-smelling vaginal discharge, dysuria, and vulval itching two weeks after unprotected intercourse with a new partner. Which broad diagnosis should be prioritised?

A nurse caring for an older client prescribed a medication that opens the airways via a puffer, or metered-dose inhaler, for COPD notes the client has difficulty coordinating the device. The most appropriate nursing intervention is to:
options: Assume the client will improve technique without any support
Switch to an oral formulation without further inhaler teaching
Recommend and teach use of a spacer device
Increase the medication dose to compensate for poor technique
Discontinue the inhaler since coordination cannot improve
questions.explanation: A spacer device attached to a metered-dose inhaler reduces the need for precise hand-breath coordination, improving medication delivery to the lungs for clients who struggle with standard inhaler technique, a common issue in older adults with reduced dexterity or coordination. Discontinuing the medication or simply increasing the dose does not address the underlying technique problem. Teaching proper spacer use is a practical, evidence-based nursing intervention.

questions.question: Written preoperative instructions are MOST valuable because they:
questions.explanation: Written instructions offer patients a lasting reference they can revisit after leaving the clinical setting, reinforcing verbally delivered information. They do not eliminate the need for verbal discussion or guarantee understanding on their own. Combining written and verbal teaching improves retention more effectively than either method alone.
options: Replace the requirement for informed consent documentation
Eliminate any need for verbal explanation entirely
Guarantee complete patient understanding without discussion
Provide a reference the patient can review after the visit
Are only useful for patients who cannot read at all

questions.question: In managing a primigravida at 36 weeks with mild preeclampsia (BP 145/95, no severe features), the most appropriate initial management at primary care level before referral includes:
questions.explanation: In a primigravida with mild preeclampsia at 36 weeks, primary care management before referral includes initiating antihypertensive therapy if blood pressure exceeds safe thresholds, monitoring fetal wellbeing, documenting all findings, and arranging urgent referral to a higher-level facility capable of managing preeclampsia and its complications (eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption). IV magnesium sulphate is given when there is imminent risk of eclampsia (severe headache, visual changes, clonus).
options: Reassurance and daily blood pressure monitoring at home alone
Starting antihypertensive therapy, foetal monitoring, and urgent referral
Immediate delivery by caesarean section at the primary care facility
Intravenous magnesium sulphate infusion and transfer without antihypertensives
Prescription of diuretics to reduce oedema and monitoring for 2 weeks

questions.question: A patient cannot constrict the pupil or accommodate the lens after a head injury. Which cranial nerve is most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve carries parasympathetic fibres controlling pupillary constriction and lens accommodation, so its injury produces a fixed, dilated pupil and accommodation failure. The trochlear and abducens nerves control eye movement only, not pupil size. The optic nerve carries vision and the trigeminal nerve carries facial sensation.

Hirsutism (male-pattern hair growth) in females typically results from androgen excess due to PCOS, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumors, or idiopathic causes. Evaluation includes testosterone, DHEAS, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels. Treatment includes androgen suppression, anti-androgens, and cosmetic hair removal.
questions.question: Hirsutism in females typically results from:

questions.explanation: The synaptic cleft measures approximately 20-40 nanometers wide, allowing rapid neurotransmitter diffusion (within microseconds) while maintaining electrical isolation between neurons. This narrow gap contains extracellular matrix proteins that organize synaptic structure and regulate neurotransmitter concentrations. The cleft width is optimized for efficient chemical transmission while preventing electrical coupling.
questions.question: The synaptic cleft, the gap between presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes, measures approximately which width?

questions.explanation: A fracture is defined as a break in the continuity of bone structure, distinguishing it from a dislocation which involves displacement of a joint, and a sprain or strain which involve ligament or muscle-tendon injury respectively. Subluxation refers to a partial joint displacement rather than bone discontinuity. Correct terminology guides appropriate imaging and management decisions.
questions.question: A client is diagnosed with a break in the continuity of bone tissue after a fall. Which term does the nurse use to document this injury?
Which structure lies immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery in the carotid sheath?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the internal carotid artery within the carotid sheath. The vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the artery and vein. The sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the sheath. This anatomical arrangement is important for central venous catheterization and carotid endarterectomy.

questions.question: A postoperative patient is at risk for atelectasis. The nurse's priority intervention to prevent this complication is to:
options: Restrict fluid intake to reduce secretions
Maintain the patient in a flat supine position
Limit ambulation until the fourth postoperative day
Encourage frequent deep breathing and repositioning
Administer sedatives to reduce respiratory effort
questions.explanation: Frequent deep breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, and repositioning help reinflate alveoli and mobilize secretions, directly addressing the primary causes of postoperative atelectasis. Early ambulation further promotes lung expansion and secretion clearance. These simple, low-risk interventions are foundational to postoperative respiratory care.

questions.question: A patient undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia develops muscle cramps, tingling around the mouth, and a positive Chvostek sign shortly after treatment begins. The nurse should suspect:
questions.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome releases intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids as malignant cells die rapidly, with phosphate binding calcium to cause hypocalcaemia. Perioral tingling, cramps, and a positive Chvostek sign are classic hypocalcaemic signs. Early recognition allows prompt correction and renal protection to prevent arrhythmia.
options: Normal side effect requiring no action
Simple dehydration from poor oral intake
Anxiety related to the new diagnosis

questions.explanation: Wound contraction is mediated by myofibroblasts within the granulation tissue that generate centripetal tension, pulling the wound edges together and reducing the overall defect size. It is especially important in healing by secondary intention, where extensive tissue loss would otherwise leave a large area to be covered by epithelium alone. Excessive contraction, however, can result in disfiguring contractures, particularly after burns overlying joints.
questions.question: A patient with a large open abdominal wound healing by secondary intention shows progressive reduction in wound size due to myofibroblast activity at the wound margins. This process is:

questions.explanation: The kidneys maintain acid-base balance by reabsorbing virtually all filtered bicarbonate (primarily in the proximal tubule via carbonic anhydrase), secreting hydrogen ions, and generating new bicarbonate through titratable acid excretion and ammonia production. About 4500 mEq of HCO3⁻ is filtered daily, and 99.9% must be reabsorbed to prevent fatal acidosis. Renal compensation for acid-base disturbances takes hours to days.
questions.question: The kidney regulates body pH by reabsorbing filtered:

questions.explanation: Effective fluid resuscitation in hypovolaemic shock should produce improving blood pressure, decreasing heart rate toward normal, and increasing urine output, reflecting restored perfusion. Persistent abnormal vital signs or unchanged perfusion indicators suggest inadequate resuscitation or an ongoing source of loss. Monitoring these trends guides the adequacy and rate of further fluid administration.
options: Continued cool, clammy skin with no change noted
Falling blood pressure despite ongoing fluid therapy
Persistently rising heart rate despite fluid administration
Improving blood pressure, heart rate, and urine output
No change in mental status following resuscitation
questions.question: A nurse administering intravenous fluids to a patient in hypovolaemic shock should monitor most closely for which sign of adequate response to resuscitation?
A gynaecologist explains to a patient that her fallopian tube has a funnel-shaped end near the ovary designed to capture the released egg. Which part of the tube is being described?
questions.explanation: The infundibulum is the funnel-shaped, fringed opening of the fallopian tube located near the ovary, designed to capture the released ovum at ovulation. This differs from the ampulla, which is the wider segment where fertilisation typically occurs. Understanding tubal anatomy helps explain mechanisms of both normal conception and ectopic pregnancy.

options: Skipping teaching until the barrier resolves itself
Speaking more slowly in the nurse's own language only
Providing written material only in the nurse's language
Relying on a young family member to interpret
questions.explanation: A qualified professional interpreter ensures accurate, unbiased communication of medical information across a language barrier, avoiding errors and the emotional burden that informal interpretation by family members can create. Simply speaking slower in an unfamiliar language does not overcome the barrier. Ensuring the patient receives comprehensible teaching remains essential regardless of language differences.
questions.question: Language barriers in preoperative teaching are BEST addressed by:

options: At transition points such as admission, transfer, and discharge
During the middle of a patient's inpatient stay on the ward
Only at the point of discharge from the hospital to home
During the surgical preparation phase immediately before operation
When the patient develops an unexpected drug adverse reaction
questions.explanation: Medication reconciliation—the formal process of comparing a patient's medication list with what is prescribed during care transitions—is most critical at transition points: admission (comparing home medications with admission orders), internal transfer (between units or levels of care), and discharge (reconciling inpatient and outpatient medications). These transitions are the highest-risk points for medication discrepancies that can cause preventable patient harm.
questions.question: Medication reconciliation as a patient safety practice is MOST critical at which point in the patient's hospital journey?

options: Diabetes insipidus from cortisol's effects on ADH secretion
Mineralocorticoid excess causing polyuria from potassium loss
Cortisol's suppression of antidiuretic hormone from pituitary
Nephrotic syndrome from cortisol-induced renal glomerular damage
questions.explanation: Monitoring urine output in Cushing's syndrome is related to cortisol-induced hyperglycemia. Excess cortisol stimulates gluconeogenesis, raises blood glucose, and when glucose exceeds the renal threshold, causes glycosuria and osmotic diuresis — leading to increased urine output. This can mimic or exacerbate diabetes mellitus. Nurses must monitor blood and urine glucose along with urine output to detect and manage this complication. Cushing's syndrome is a classic cause of secondary diabetes mellitus.
questions.question: The nursing intervention of monitoring urine output in a patient with Cushing's syndrome is related to which complication?
A patient receiving high-dose intraoperative opioids develops significant bradycardia. Which anticholinergic agent is typically given FIRST to treat this?
questions.explanation: Atropine is the standard first-line treatment for opioid-related or vagally-mediated intraoperative bradycardia, as it blocks muscarinic receptors at the sinoatrial node to increase heart rate rapidly. Neostigmine and sugammadex reverse neuromuscular blockade rather than treating bradycardia, while naloxone and flumazenil reverse opioids and benzodiazepines respectively but do not directly treat bradycardia.

options: Only if the client requests it
Only for investigations involving blood draws
questions.explanation: The nurse's role before clinical investigations includes preparing the client physically and psychologically, explaining the procedure, and obtaining informed consent, ensuring the client is ready and agreeable before any investigation begins. This preparatory role is distinct from actions taken during or after the procedure. Thorough pre-procedure preparation improves client cooperation and reduces anxiety.
questions.question: A nurse prepares a client both physically and psychologically, explains the procedure, and obtains informed consent before a planned clinical investigation. At which stage of the investigation process does this nursing action primarily occur?
A central venous pressure reading is significantly higher than expected in a patient receiving fluid resuscitation. This finding most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: An unexpectedly high central venous pressure during fluid resuscitation suggests the heart cannot effectively handle the additional volume, indicating fluid overload or impaired cardiac function. This should prompt reassessment of fluid therapy rather than continued aggressive administration. Recognising this pattern helps prevent pulmonary oedema.
options: Inadequate intravascular volume requiring more fluids
Normal physiological response to any fluid therapy
Arterial line malfunction unrelated to venous pressure
Improved cardiac output from effective resuscitation
Fluid overload or reduced cardiac function
Passive health maintenance through routine medical checkups
Active decision-making in areas of nutrition, fitness, and stress management
Disease prevention by strictly following physician prescriptions
Wellness maintenance by avoiding all risk-taking behaviors
questions.question: A patient who maintains an optimal diet, exercises regularly, and manages stress effectively is demonstrating which key aspect of wellness?
questions.explanation: Basic aspects of wellness include self-responsibility, dynamic growth, and daily decision-making in areas of nutrition, stress management, physical fitness, preventive health care, and emotional health. A patient who actively maintains optimal diet, exercise, and stress management is embodying wellness by making conscious daily choices that promote holistic health. This is distinct from reactive disease management.

questions.question: A nurse teaches a client about a urinary incontinence management technique that involves urinating, waiting a few moments, then trying again to ensure the bladder is fully empty. What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: Double voiding involves urinating, waiting a few moments, then trying again to ensure the bladder is fully empty, helping reduce residual urine and associated complications. Timed voiding establishes a regular schedule for urination, while bladder training gradually increases time between bathroom trips to strengthen bladder muscles. Biofeedback therapy helps individuals become aware of and control bladder function, and pelvic floor exercises strengthen the muscles controlling urine flow, none of which describe this specific double-attempt voiding technique.

Osgood-Schlatter disease is traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity, where the patellar ligament inserts during the growth phase. It affects adolescents (boys aged 12-15, girls aged 8-13) who are active in jumping and running sports. Repeated quadriceps contractions pull on the incompletely ossified tibial tuberosity. Treatment is activity modification and physiotherapy.
questions.question: Osgood-Schlatter disease involves traction apophysitis at which site in adolescents?

questions.explanation: Normal amniotic fluid at membrane rupture is typically clear or slightly straw-coloured, reflecting the absence of meconium staining, infection, or significant blood contamination. Green or brown discolouration suggests meconium passage, which may indicate fetal distress or post-maturity, while foul-smelling fluid suggests infection. Recognising normal versus abnormal colour guides the urgency of further fetal assessment during labour.
options: Thick green fluid with a strong odour
Cloudy yellow fluid with visible debris
questions.question: A midwife caring for a neonate notes normal amniotic fluid was released at membrane rupture. Which characteristic colour would be expected in this normal finding?
What is the most common site for peritoneal metastases in females?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in females and is therefore the most common site for peritoneal metastases, free fluid (ascites), and pelvic abscesses to collect. It can be assessed by pelvic examination (palpable through the posterior vaginal fornix) and accessed by culdocentesis for diagnostic aspiration.

options: Support psychological and physical recovery of survivors
Delay all care until the recovery phase fully ends
Focus exclusively on rebuilding damaged infrastructure
Replace the need for ongoing medical treatment
Avoid any further contact with affected populations
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient during recovery from a disaster event should incorporate health promotion activities primarily to:
questions.explanation: Health promotion during disaster recovery addresses both the physical and psychological needs of survivors, supporting long-term resilience and preventing secondary health complications such as untreated chronic disease or unaddressed trauma. Nurses often serve as community advocates during this phase, connecting survivors with ongoing resources. This holistic focus extends beyond the immediate emergency response.

Azoospermia, the complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate, is broadly classified into obstructive causes, where sperm production is normal but blocked from reaching the ejaculate, and non-obstructive causes, where sperm production itself is impaired due to testicular failure. Distinguishing between these categories, often using hormone levels and imaging, guides further management including surgical sperm retrieval or assisted reproduction. Accurate classification is essential for appropriate counselling.
options: Obstructive and non-obstructive causes of absent sperm
Primary and secondary causes of low sperm count
Congenital and acquired causes of low sperm motility
Hormonal and structural causes of abnormal morphology
Infective and autoimmune causes of reduced fertility
questions.question: A woman is diagnosed with azoospermia during infertility investigation. Her partner asks the nurse to explain the two broad categories of this condition. What are they?

questions.explanation: Mitomycin C (MMC) or 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) are antimetabolites applied to the subconjunctival space during trabeculectomy to inhibit fibroblast proliferation and reduce postoperative scarring of the filtering bleb. Bleb scarring is the primary cause of trabeculectomy failure, as fibrosis closes the surgical drainage pathway and causes IOP to rise again. These agents significantly improve the long-term success rate of trabeculectomy, particularly in high-risk patients such as those who have had previous eye surgery or inflammation.
options: Corticosteroid suspension to prevent inflammatory bleb failure
Topical adrenaline to reduce intraoperative hemorrhage risk
Mitomycin C or 5-fluorouracil to inhibit fibroblast proliferation
Topical antibiotics to sterilize the surgical field before incision
Topical pilocarpine to maintain miosis and anterior chamber depth
questions.question: A glaucoma patient undergoing trabeculectomy is MOST likely to receive which topical application during surgery to reduce bleb scarring?

A patient with a chronic diabetic foot ulcer has impaired wound healing linked to poor new blood vessel formation in the wound bed. Which growth factor is PRIMARILY responsible for stimulating new capillary formation in wound healing?
questions.explanation: Vascular endothelial growth factor is the primary stimulus for angiogenesis during wound healing, promoting endothelial cell proliferation and the formation of new capillary networks essential for delivering oxygen and nutrients to the healing tissue. Impaired angiogenesis, as seen in diabetes due to microvascular disease, is a major contributor to chronic non-healing ulcers. Adequate vascular endothelial growth factor signalling is therefore critical for successful granulation tissue formation.

questions.question: A midwife caring for a labouring woman with a known allergy documents this prominently and confirms it before administering any analgesia. This practice reflects which principle of safe intrapartum care?
questions.explanation: Verifying known allergies and other safety information before administering any medication is a fundamental patient safety practice that prevents adverse drug reactions and supports safe, individualised intrapartum care. This is part of broader principles of accurate documentation and communication within the multidisciplinary team. It does not replace but complements informed consent, which must still be obtained before any intervention.
options: Avoidance of documentation to save time
Verification of patient safety information before drug administration
Delegation of care to unqualified staff

questions.explanation: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini), when present, opens at the minor duodenal papilla, located approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. It represents the proximal part of the dorsal pancreatic bud duct. The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) opens at the major duodenal papilla along with the common bile duct.
questions.question: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) opens at:

questions.explanation: Atrial septal defect classically produces a fixed and widely split second heart sound because the left-to-right shunt equalises right and left atrial filling, making the splitting of the pulmonic and aortic components relatively unaffected by respiration. A continuous machinery murmur and radiofemoral delay are instead characteristic of patent ductus arteriosus and coarctation respectively. This auscultatory finding is a key clinical clue prompting echocardiographic confirmation.
questions.question: Atrial septal defect is characteristically identified on cardiac auscultation by:
options: A loud single first heart sound only
A fixed, widely split second heart sound
A continuous machinery-like murmur throughout systole and diastole
Radiofemoral delay detected on palpation of pulses
Absence of any audible murmur whatsoever

questions.question: The McGurk effect demonstrates which principle of sensory processing?
questions.explanation: The McGurk effect occurs when visual speech information (lip movements) conflicts with auditory input, producing a fused percept different from either alone. This illusion demonstrates mandatory audio-visual integration in speech perception, with vision influencing what we "hear." The effect highlights how the brain combines sensory modalities to construct coherent perceptual experiences.

questions.question: The round ligament of the uterus passes through which opening?
questions.explanation: The round ligament of the uterus passes through the deep inguinal ring (homologous to the spermatic cord in males), traverses the inguinal canal, exits through the superficial inguinal ring, and terminates in the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus. It represents the distal gubernaculum (the proximal part becoming the ovarian ligament). The round ligament contains smooth muscle, vessels, and nerves, and helps maintain the anteverted position of the uterus. Rarely, indirect inguinal hernias can occur in females alongside the round ligament (canal of Nuck).

questions.question: When a patient is on an endotracheal tube, suctioning should be performed when:
questions.explanation: Suctioning is indicated when patients with endotracheal tubes are unable to cough effectively to clear their own secretions. It is not performed routinely on a fixed schedule but rather based on clinical assessment findings such as audible secretions, decreased breath sounds, or increased airway pressures. Unnecessary suctioning is distressing, can cause hypoxia, and may damage airway mucosa.
options: Every hour regardless of the patient's secretion status
The SpO2 reading is above 98% on pulse oximetry monitoring
The patient is unable to cough effectively to clear secretions
The physician requests suctioning on morning ward rounds only
Auscultation reveals normal breath sounds bilaterally throughout

questions.question: In managing a client with a history of ectopic pregnancy who now desires contraception, which method is most strongly recommended?
questions.explanation: For women with a history of ectopic pregnancy, long-acting progestin-containing methods such as the subdermal implant or levonorgestrel-releasing IUS are strongly preferred because they suppress ovulation and prevent any fertilised oocyte from implanting in the fallopian tube. The copper IUD, while highly effective for contraception, does not suppress ovulation and carries a slightly higher proportional risk of ectopic implantation if contraceptive failure occurs.
options: Progesterone-only injectable administered every three months
A copper IUD as first-line despite the history of ectopic pregnancy
Natural family planning methods based on basal body temperature
Combined oral contraceptive pill for high contraceptive efficacy
A long-acting progestin implant or hormonal IUS to prevent ovulation

questions.question: A midwife caring for a newborn identifies excessive drooling, choking, and cyanosis during the first feeding attempt. This presentation raises suspicion of:
questions.explanation: Excessive drooling, choking, and cyanosis during feeding attempts in a newborn are concerning signs suggestive of a structural anomaly such as tracheo-oesophageal fistula or oesophageal atresia, which prevents normal passage of milk to the stomach and requires urgent investigation and surgical referral. These findings should never be dismissed as normal newborn feeding behaviour. Prompt recognition prevents complications such as aspiration pneumonia and allows for timely surgical correction.
options: Mild reflux requiring no further evaluation
Expected finding in all newborns during first feeds
Recurrent laryngeal nerve damage from surgical trauma
Hypocalcemia from parathyroid gland injury during surgery
Thyroid storm from residual thyroid tissue postoperatively
Hemorrhage causing tracheal compression at the incision site
Adverse reaction to the general anesthesia agents used
questions.question: A nurse caring for a post-thyroidectomy patient notes stridor, laryngeal spasm, and tingling around the mouth. The nurse should immediately suspect:
questions.explanation: Stridor, laryngospasm, and perioral tingling (Chvostek's or Trousseau's sign positive) in a post-thyroidectomy patient are emergency signs of hypocalcemia resulting from inadvertent removal or devascularization of the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery. Hypoparathyroidism causes dangerously low serum calcium, producing tetany, laryngospasm, and potentially fatal respiratory obstruction. Emergency treatment includes IV calcium gluconate. All post-thyroidectomy patients should be monitored for symptoms of hypocalcemia, and calcium gluconate must be available at the bedside.

options: Lateral lingual swellings and tuberculum impar
questions.explanation: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is formed by fusion of the two lateral lingual swellings and the tuberculum impar (first median swelling). The posterior one-third is formed by the cranial part of the hypobranchial eminence (second median swelling called the cupola).
questions.question: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is formed by fusion of which structures?

questions.explanation: A nurse who witnesses clear patient harm, such as an intentional tort committed by a colleague, and fails to intervene or report has failed a professional duty through omission, since nurses bear an independent obligation to protect patients from harm regardless of who is causing it, and silence in such circumstances can itself constitute negligence.
questions.question: A nurse who witnesses a colleague committing an intentional tort against a patient, such as battery, but does nothing to intervene or report it, may be found to have
options: no responsibility, since she did not commit the act
committed the tort herself by proximity alone
violated only administrative policy, not the law
failed a professional duty through omission

questions.explanation: Autonomic neuropathy results from damage to nerves controlling involuntary functions such as blood pressure regulation, bladder emptying and bowel motility, explaining this combination of symptoms. Peripheral sensory neuropathy would instead present with numbness or pain, while focal and mononeuritis patterns affect single or scattered nerves rather than systemic autonomic control. Diabetic amyotrophy primarily causes proximal leg weakness, not autonomic symptoms.
questions.question: A client with diabetes reports postural dizziness, bladder dysfunction, and erratic bowel habits. Which type of nerve damage explains this combination?

questions.explanation: Semen analysis (spermogram) is the essential first-line investigation for male partner infertility assessment. It evaluates semen volume, sperm concentration, total sperm count, motility (progressive and total), and morphology (using Kruger strict criteria). WHO 2021 reference values: volume =1.4 mL, concentration =16 million/mL, total motility =42%, progressive motility =30%, normal morphology =4%. Azoospermia (no sperm), oligospermia (<16 million/mL), or asthenospermia (reduced motility) guides further investigations.
options: Semen analysis (spermogram) assessing volume, count, motility, and morphology
Serum testosterone level to assess androgen production
Testicular biopsy to assess spermatogenesis histologically
Serum FSH to assess pituitary function
Scrotal ultrasound to detect varicocele or hydrocele
questions.question: A couple has been trying to conceive for 14 months without success. Which initial investigation for the male partner is most important?

questions.explanation: Adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving treatment for anaphylaxis because its combined alpha and beta-adrenergic effects reverse vasodilation, bronchospasm, and capillary leak that cause hypotension and airway compromise. Hydrocortisone and antihistamines have a role in anaphylaxis management but act more slowly and are adjunctive rather than first-line treatments. Oral medications are inappropriate in this acute emergency.
questions.question: A patient develops anaphylaxis intraoperatively with hypotension, bronchospasm, and widespread urticaria. The FIRST-line drug treatment is

A midwife teaches a student that the uterus should be palpable at or below the umbilicus immediately after delivery of the placenta if well contracted. A fundus palpated ABOVE the umbilicus and displaced to one side should raise suspicion of:
questions.explanation: A full bladder can displace and prevent full contraction of the uterus, causing the fundus to be palpated higher than expected and deviated to one side, which increases the risk of atony and haemorrhage. Prompt bladder emptying, by encouraging voiding or catheterisation if necessary, often allows the uterus to contract more effectively. This finding should never be considered normal or reassuring without addressing the underlying cause.
options: A full bladder preventing proper uterine contraction
Successful active management of the third stage

questions.explanation: Atropine, an anticholinergic agent, reduces salivary and bronchial secretions and can prevent vagally-mediated bradycardia during certain procedures such as those involving airway manipulation, by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. It has no direct analgesic, sedative, or antiemetic properties, and is not used to reverse neuromuscular blockade in the way glycopyrrolate is combined with neostigmine.
questions.question: Atropine is administered prior to certain anaesthetic procedures PRIMARILY to
options: reduce excessive salivary and bronchial secretions

questions.question: A Client Registration Form in family planning primarily serves which purpose?
options: Capturing basic demographic information and contact details
Documenting informed consent for the chosen contraceptive method
Recording the results of laboratory investigations at the first visit
Scheduling follow-up appointments for contraceptive monitoring
Gathering information about adverse events experienced with previous methods
questions.explanation: The Client Registration Form in family planning primarily captures basic demographic information and contact details such as name, age, address, contact information, marital status, occupation, and educational background. This form initiates the client record and establishes the administrative foundation for all subsequent documentation. Its logistics require an easily accessible and organized filing system for quick retrieval during subsequent visits.

options: Immediately after induction of general anesthesia
One hour after skin closure at the end of surgery
30 minutes before the surgical incision was made
Upon presentation of fever and wound redness on day five
At the time of postoperative ward discharge instructions
questions.question: In Rachel's case scenario, the cefazolin was administered:
questions.explanation: In Rachel's case, cefazolin was administered 30 minutes before the incision to ensure peak tissue concentrations were achieved at the time of skin incision—the period of greatest infection risk. Administering prophylactic antibiotics within the correct preoperative window is critical for effective SSI prevention.

questions.question: The extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the cytotrophoblast is termed which type?
questions.explanation: Extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the cytotrophoblast (and amnion) is called somatopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm. Extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the primitive yolk sac is called splanchnopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm. These terms are analogous to the intraembryonic mesoderm layers.

options: Discharge the patient home with oral antibiotics
Delay intervention until a specialist consult arrives
Initiate the sepsis bundle including cultures and antibiotics
Administer antipyretics alone and reassess in six hours
Wait for definitive culture results before any treatment
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected sepsis notes fever, tachycardia, and confusion. The priority nursing action is to:
questions.explanation: Early recognition and initiation of the sepsis bundle, including obtaining blood cultures and prompt administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics, significantly improves survival in suspected sepsis. Delaying treatment to await culture confirmation risks rapid deterioration to septic shock. Time-critical intervention is central to sepsis management protocols.

questions.question: A man complains of a dull ache and visible dilated veins in the scrotum, worse on standing. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
questions.explanation: A varicocele is dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus in the scrotum, often described as feeling like a 'bag of worms' and worsening with standing. It can impair fertility by raising scrotal temperature and impeding blood flow. It is a recognised, correctable cause of male infertility.

Before administering any laxative to an elderly patient, the nurse should assess for pre-existing dehydration or loose stools that would contraindicate laxative use. Elderly patients are particularly vulnerable to fluid and electrolyte imbalances from laxatives. The choice of laxative must also consider the patient's renal and hepatic function, concomitant medications, and the specific type of constipation mechanism involved.
questions.question: An important nursing consideration before administering a laxative to an elderly constipated patient is:
options: Monitoring for respiratory depression from stimulant laxative effects
Checking renal function before administering any osmotic agent
Ensuring the patient is seated upright to prevent laxative aspiration
Assessing for signs of dehydration if the patient already has loose stools
Obtaining ECG monitoring continuously during stimulant laxative administration

questions.question: Which muscle produces both shoulder adduction and medial rotation?
questions.explanation: produces shoulder adduction, extension, and medial rotation. It is a powerful muscle forming part of the posterior axillary fold. The muscle is commonly used in reconstructive surgery and is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.

Caseous necrosis produces a friable, cheese-like white appearance and is characteristically found within granulomas caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Microscopically the necrotic focus appears as amorphous granular debris without the preserved cellular outlines seen in coagulative necrosis. This distinctive combination of gross and microscopic features helps distinguish tuberculous granulomas from other granulomatous diseases.
questions.question: A patient with pulmonary tuberculosis has a lung biopsy showing structureless, cheese-like debris surrounded by a granulomatous rim. This necrosis is:

questions.explanation: Signs of muscle atrophy include reduced muscle mass, asymmetry between limbs, weakness, numbness or tingling, and trouble walking or balancing, along with possible difficulty swallowing or speaking and facial weakness. Sudden weight gain, increased bilateral muscle bulk, improved coordination, and decreased need for rest are not consistent with the wasting process described. These additional signs help the nurse recognize the broader systemic impact of muscle atrophy.
questions.question: A client with muscle atrophy reports that one arm appears smaller than the other, with associated weakness. Which additional finding would the nurse also expect as a sign of muscle atrophy?
The most important nursing intervention to prevent DVT in a post-operative patient is:
options: Applying heat packs to lower limbs
Keeping the patient strictly supine for 72 hours
Restricting all oral fluid intake post-operatively
Early ambulation and use of compression stockings
questions.explanation: Early ambulation (getting the patient up and walking as soon as clinically safe post-surgery) and application of graduated compression stockings (or pneumatic compression devices) are the most important non-pharmacological nursing interventions for DVT prevention. These measures reduce venous stasis — the primary component of Virchow's triad amenable to nursing intervention. Pharmacological prophylaxis (low molecular weight heparin) is prescribed by physicians based on risk stratification. Nurses must also ensure adequate hydration to reduce blood viscosity.

options: To ignore the observation since it involves a colleague
To report the observation through appropriate channels to protect patient safety
To handle the matter privately without any documentation
To assume the colleague already knows the correct procedure
To wait until a serious incident occurs before taking action
questions.explanation: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria's code of professional conduct requires nurses to prioritise patient safety and to report unsafe practices observed in colleagues through appropriate professional channels, since failing to act could place patients at ongoing risk. This responsibility exists regardless of personal relationships with colleagues and should not wait for an adverse event to occur before action is taken. Understanding this professional obligation supports a culture of safety and accountability in practice.
questions.question: A nurse observes a colleague administering medication without following correct identification procedures for a patient with a known allergy. According to the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria's code of professional conduct, what is the nurse's primary responsibility?
A child with untreated otitis media develops fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status. What complication should the nurse suspect?
questions.explanation: Infection can spread contiguously from the middle ear to the meninges, so otitis media complicated by fever, neck stiffness and altered mentation raises strong suspicion for secondary meningitis. A simple febrile seizure would not typically present with neck stiffness and altered mentation together. Gastroenteritis, cardiac arrhythmia and appendicitis do not explain this specific combination of findings.

options: Sudden changes in vision or new floaters suggesting retinal involvement
Mild periorbital puffiness without proptosis or visual change
Mild bilateral conjunctival hyperemia without discharge
Transient photophobia resolving spontaneously within hours
Mild bilateral ptosis without restriction of eye movement
questions.question: A nurse monitoring an HIV-positive patient for ocular complications should MOST urgently report which finding?
questions.explanation: Sudden changes in vision or the appearance of new floaters in an HIV-positive patient suggest serious retinal involvement such as CMV retinitis, toxoplasma retinochoroiditis, or retinal detachment, which are ophthalmic emergencies requiring urgent ophthalmological evaluation. Early detection and treatment of retinal opportunistic infections are critical to preventing irreversible vision loss. The nurse plays a vital role in monitoring for these symptoms and escalating care promptly to prevent blindness.

options: vagal manoeuvres alone without other treatment
questions.question: A patient in theatre suddenly develops a wide-complex tachycardia with a palpable pulse and is haemodynamically unstable with a falling blood pressure. The MOST appropriate immediate management is
questions.explanation: An unstable patient with a wide-complex tachycardia and a pulse requires urgent synchronised cardioversion, which times the shock to the R wave to avoid inducing ventricular fibrillation, unlike unsynchronised defibrillation which is reserved for pulseless arrest rhythms. Adenosine and vagal manoeuvres are used for stable narrow-complex tachycardias rather than unstable wide-complex rhythms.

Birth injury specifically refers to trauma sustained by the child during the process of labour and delivery. It results from the forces of labour and delivery or from physiological and environmental factors. Contributory factors include macrosomia, breech presentation, forceful extraction, and inexperienced personnel. Birth injury is distinct from congenital malformations, which arise from embryological development.
options: Trauma to the child sustained during the process of birth
Neonatal sepsis acquired during passage through the birth canal
Congenital anomaly resulting from maternal infection in pregnancy
Asphyxia occurring from cord compression before delivery
Any structural defect present from early embryonic development
questions.question: Birth injury is most accurately defined as:

questions.explanation: Maternal tetanus toxoid immunisation during pregnancy induces protective antibodies that cross the placenta, protecting the newborn against neonatal tetanus, a life-threatening infection that can occur through the umbilical stump if cord care is unhygienic, particularly in settings with low immunisation coverage. This vaccine has no direct effect on preventing rubella, hepatitis B, group B streptococcal disease, or syphilis, which require separate specific preventive measures. This is a key component of safe motherhood and newborn protection programmes.
options: Neonatal tetanus following unhygienic cord care
Neonatal hepatitis B infection at birth
Congenital syphilis at the time of delivery
questions.question: Routine antenatal tetanus toxoid immunisation is primarily aimed at preventing which condition in the newborn?

options: Primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony
Mastitis presenting with breast hardness and erythema
Deep vein thrombosis presenting with calf tenderness
Urinary tract infection with suprapubic tenderness
questions.question: Which postpartum complication is characterised by fever (=38°C), offensive lochia, uterine tenderness, and subinvolution on examination after day 1?
questions.explanation: Puerperal sepsis (postpartum endometritis) is defined as fever =38°C occurring after the first 24 hours and within 10 days of delivery. Classic features include: fever and rigors; offensive, profuse lochia; uterine tenderness on palpation; subinvolution of the uterus (fundus higher than expected for the day postpartum); and leucocytosis. Causative organisms include Group A and B Streptococcus, E. coli, and anaerobes. Treatment is IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole).

options: Hysterosalpingography to assess the female partner's tubal status
Serum testosterone level as the primary endocrine investigation
Y-chromosome microdeletion testing and scrotal ultrasound
Antisperm antibody testing in the female partner's blood
Prolactin level measurement to assess pituitary function
questions.question: Which investigation is most specifically indicated in assessing male infertility when the semen analysis reveals azoospermia?
questions.explanation: Azoospermia (complete absence of sperm) requires targeted investigation including Y-chromosome microdeletion testing to detect Azoospermia Factor (AZF) deletions on the Y chromosome, which account for 10 to 15% of non-obstructive azoospermia cases. Scrotal ultrasound assesses testicular size, echogenicity, presence of obstruction (epididymal dilation), and varicocele. Together, these investigations differentiate obstructive (correctable surgically) from non-obstructive (requires testicular sperm extraction for IVF-ICSI) azoospermia.

questions.question: A client reports that her older parent, who lives alone, has stopped bathing, is refusing to eat adequate meals, and is living in a home full of accumulated clutter and waste. The nurse recognizes this as which condition?
questions.explanation: The described pattern of refusing personal hygiene, inadequate nutrition, and unsanitary living conditions in an older adult living alone constitutes self-neglect, where the individual fails to meet their own essential needs without an external perpetrator being responsible. Caregiver neglect requires a responsible caregiver failing to provide care, emotional and physical abuse require perpetrator acts, and involuntary isolation syndrome is not an established classification in elder abuse literature.

The hepatic portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. The portal vein measures approximately 8 cm in length and has no valves.
questions.question: The hepatic portal vein is formed posterior to which structure?

A programme coordinator reviews compiled client records across multiple facilities to determine how many new clients adopted family planning methods over the past year. Which advantage of record keeping does this activity best illustrate?
options: It allows monitoring of programme progress locally
It eliminates the need for future client registration
It is solely useful for individual client billing
It has no bearing on programme-level planning
It is required only for international donor audits
questions.explanation: Record keeping allows healthcare planners to monitor family planning programme progress within a community by aggregating individual client data over time. This population-level insight supports resource allocation and programme evaluation, distinct from its role in individual client care. Effective aggregate monitoring depends on consistent, accurate record keeping at the facility level.

Clear, honest, and appropriately paced information helps patients form realistic expectations, which reduces uncertainty-driven anxiety more effectively than withholding information or focusing solely on negative outcomes. Early, rather than last-minute, teaching allows time for questions and processing. Addressing expected sensations, including pain, transparently builds trust and preparedness.
options: Delaying any teaching until immediately before surgery
Withholding all information to avoid causing distress
Avoiding discussion of postoperative pain entirely
Providing clear, honest information about what to expect
Focusing exclusively on worst-case surgical outcomes
questions.question: The goal of reducing anxiety and fear through preoperative teaching is BEST achieved by:
Penile erection is mediated by:
questions.explanation: Penile erection results from parasympathetic stimulation causing arterial dilation and compression of penile veins, leading to elongation and hardening of the penis. This vascular engorgement is mediated by nitric oxide and cyclic GMP. Sympathetic activation causes detumescence.
