questions.explanation: During shoulder joint abduction, the shoulder girdle undergoes upward rotation of the scapula. This scapular movement is essential for achieving full arm abduction beyond 90 degrees. The trapezius and serratus anterior muscles produce this upward rotation of the scapula.

The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) has three branches: ascending (to the hip joint and gluteal region), transverse (encircling the femur laterally), and descending (contributing superolaterally to the genicular anastomosis around the knee). The descending branch travels between vastus intermedius and vastus lateralis muscles and provides one of the anastomotic connections at the knee.
questions.question: The lateral femoral circumflex artery has three named branches. Which of these descends distally to contribute to the genicular anastomosis?

questions.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic fibers that are bronchoconstrictor and secretomotor to bronchial glands. These fibers are also important for the cough reflex. The sympathetic trunk provides fibers that are bronchodilators and inhibit secretion from bronchial glands.
questions.question: Which nerve provides bronchoconstrictors to the lung?

questions.explanation: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, descending in the parametrium (base of the broad ligament) to reach the uterus at the level of the internal cervical os. It crosses superior to (over) the ureter approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"), an important surgical relationship. The artery ascends along the lateral margin of the uterus in a tortuous course, giving off branches to the uterus and anastomosing superiorly with the ovarian artery. During pregnancy, it enlarges significantly to supply the gravid uterus and placenta.
questions.question: The uterine artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta into right and left common iliac arteries at the L4 vertebral level corresponds to a point on the anterior abdominal wall slightly below and to the left of the umbilicus (which lies at L3/L4 disc level). This surface marking is clinically useful for palpating the aorta and detecting abdominal aortic aneurysms. The bifurcation point can be located by drawing imaginary lines from the umbilicus toward the midinguinal points (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis) on each side. The median sacral artery arises from the posterior aspect of the aorta just before its bifurcation.
questions.question: The aortic bifurcation occurs at which surface landmark?

options: Provide redundant blood supply with extensive anastomoses
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between the two palmar arches?
questions.explanation: The superficial and deep palmar arches provide redundant blood supply to the hand through extensive anastomoses. This collateral circulation protects hand perfusion even with single artery occlusion. The arches interconnect via perforating branches and palmar metacarpal communications.

questions.question: The anterior cerebral arteries are connected by which vessel?
questions.explanation: The two anterior cerebral arteries are joined by the anterior communicating artery, completing the anterior portion of the Circle of Willis. This connection allows collateral flow between right and left anterior circulations. Aneurysms commonly occur at this junction.

The superior mesenteric artery is the principal vessel supplying midgut derivatives, extending from just distal to the major duodenal papilla to the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon. It originates from the abdominal aorta at the L1 level, immediately below the celiac trunk. Its branches include the inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic arteries, providing blood to the duodenum (distal to ampulla), jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and right two-thirds of transverse colon.
questions.question: The superior mesenteric artery supplies which embryological division of the gut?

questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure forms the lateral boundary, connecting the pterygopalatine fossa with the infratemporal fossa. The anterior wall is formed by the posterior surface of the maxilla. The medial wall consists of the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone.
questions.question: Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa?
What is the primary extensor of the thumb interphalangeal joint?
questions.explanation: extends the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and assists with extension at the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints. Its tendon forms the medial border of the anatomical snuffbox. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

The white pulp, consisting of periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) and lymphoid follicles, is the site of immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens and antibody production. T cells in the PALS respond to blood-borne antigens, while B cells in follicles produce antibodies. The marginal zone between red and white pulp contains specialized macrophages and B cells for antigen capture.
questions.question: What occurs in splenic white pulp?

questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament (zonules of Zinn) connects the lens equator to the ciliary processes. These zonular fibers transmit tension from the ciliary muscle to the lens capsule, controlling lens shape for accommodation. When ciliary muscle contracts, zonular tension decreases, allowing the elastic lens to become more spherical for near vision.
questions.question: Which ligament suspends the lens of the eye?
Which muscle tenses the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is the only muscle that tenses (lengthens) the vocal cords by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid. It is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

The foramen lacerum is closed in life by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal vessels and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above it in the foramen's upper part but does not traverse it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large opening.
questions.question: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by which structure?
What is the normal capacity of an adult stomach?
questions.explanation: The adult stomach has a mean capacity of approximately 1.5 to 2 litres when distended, though it can accommodate more. The stomach is a highly distensible organ with significant variation in capacity between individuals. At birth, the capacity is only about 30 ml, increasing to 1000 ml at puberty.

questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching lowest fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, along with contributions from the transversalis fascia. These arching fibers cross from lateral to medial, forming the superior boundary of the canal. The internal oblique muscle also contributes to the anterior wall laterally, where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament. The conjoint tendon (formed by the fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) reinforces the posterior wall medially but does not form the roof.

Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces in each kidney. Two or three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.
questions.question: Which structure indents each renal papilla?

questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth. The duct crosses the masseter superficially before piercing the buccinator. A small accessory parotid gland may be present along the duct on the masseter (socia parotidis).
questions.question: The parotid gland duct opens opposite which tooth?
Which muscle is the primary flexor of the hip joint, described as the great flexor, with its traction epiphysis being the lesser trochanter?
questions.explanation: The iliopsoas is the primary flexor of the hip joint, formed by the fusion of iliacus and psoas major. Their combined tendon inserts into the lesser trochanter, which is its traction epiphysis. The iliopsoas is active in walking, running, and sitting up. Weakness of iliopsoas is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated position.

The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen after traversing the facial canal. It then enters the parotid gland and divides into five terminal branches. Damage at this location causes complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including loss of taste to anterior two-thirds of tongue.
questions.question: The stylomastoid foramen transmits which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The inferior orbital fissure connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the orbit. The fissure is bounded by the greater wing of sphenoid, maxilla, and palatine bone. The maxillary nerve continues through this fissure as the infraorbital nerve. The infraorbital and zygomatic nerves and vessels pass through this communication.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the orbit through which opening?

questions.explanation: Lateral (external) rotation of the humerus is produced by infraspinatus, teres minor, and posterior fibers of the deltoid. The infraspinatus and teres minor are two of the four rotator cuff muscles. This movement rotates the arm away from the midline, making the thumb point laterally.
questions.question: What muscles produce lateral rotation of the humerus?

questions.explanation: The areola is a dark pink-brownish circular area of skin (22-60 mm in diameter) that surrounds the nipple. Its color varies with parity and race, darkening during the second month of pregnancy. The areola contains Montgomery's glands (areola glands) which enlarge during pregnancy and lactation.
questions.question: What structure surrounds the nipple?

questions.explanation: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle (over the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae), passing from lateral to medial as it descends toward the pelvic brim. It is crossed anteriorly by the testicular/ovarian vessels and lies posterior to the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. The ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the external iliac artery) at the pelvic brim, providing a consistent landmark. The relationship to psoas major is maintained until the ureter reaches the pelvic inlet, where it enters the pelvis.
questions.question: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of which muscle?

questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle forms the floor (bed) of the tonsillar fossa, separated from the tonsil by the tonsillar capsule. The palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus form the anterior and posterior pillars respectively. Loose areolar tissue separates the capsule from the superior constrictor, facilitating surgical dissection.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the tonsillar fossa?

questions.explanation: The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm. Its roof is formed distally by flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis. The floor consists of pronator quadratus distally and interosseous membrane proximally.
questions.question: Which space lies proximal to the carpal tunnel in the forearm?
Which muscle fibers are directed downward and forward?
questions.explanation: The external intercostal muscle is the most superficial intercostal muscle with fibers directed downward and forward. It extends from the rib tubercle posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly. The muscle is deficient anteriorly where it is replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane.

questions.question: Which vein forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The portal vein, positioned posteriorly within the hepatoduodenal ligament (posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery), forms part of the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The entire hepatoduodenal ligament (containing the portal triad) constitutes the anterior boundary. The portal vein is the most posterior structure within this ligament, closest to the foramen. Injury to the portal vein during surgical manipulation near the epiploic foramen can cause massive hemorrhage into the lesser sac. The foramen can be occluded by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament between thumb and fingers (Pringle maneuver).

produces wrist abduction (radial deviation) along with flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis muscles. It also abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm compartment.
questions.question: Which muscle assists with both wrist abduction and thumb abduction?

questions.explanation: Rotter's nodes (interpectoral nodes) lie between the pectoralis major and minor muscles. They are part of the axillary lymphatic drainage pathway. During modified radical mastectomy, these nodes may be removed along with the pectoral fascia. Their involvement affects staging and prognosis.
questions.question: What are Rotter's nodes?
Which structure separates the maxillary sinus from the orbit?
questions.explanation: The thin orbital plate of the maxilla forms the roof of the maxillary sinus and the floor of the orbit. The infraorbital nerve and vessels run in a groove on this surface. Fractures can cause orbital contents to herniate into the sinus (blow-out fracture). Dental roots may project into the sinus floor.

questions.question: The kidney hilum is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The renal hilum is positioned at the level of the transpyloric plane, which corresponds to the first lumbar vertebra (L1), though the kidneys themselves extend from approximately T12 to L3. At the hilum, structures are arranged from anterior to posterior as vein, artery, and pelvis (VAP), though the renal vein is most anterior and superior. The left kidney typically sits slightly higher than the right due to the presence of the liver on the right side.

questions.question: Despite being the great extensor of the hip joint, gluteus maximus has little action during which of the following?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus has little action during ordinary gentle walking on level ground. It acts mainly in rising from sitting, straightening up, walking upstairs, and running. This is a critical clinical distinction in assessing gluteal function and designing rehabilitation after injury.

questions.question: The left gastric vein drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left gastric vein typically drains directly into the portal vein near its origin behind the neck of the pancreas, though it may occasionally drain into the splenic vein. The left gastric vein receives esophageal tributaries from the abdominal esophagus, creating an important portosystemic anastomosis with esophageal veins draining to the azygos system. In portal hypertension, these anastomotic channels dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing life-threatening hemorrhage. The coronary vein is an alternative name for the left gastric vein, following the course of the left gastric artery along the lesser curvature.

questions.question: The common bile duct passes posterior to which part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The common bile duct descends posterior to the first (superior) part of the duodenum (retroduodenal portion), then continues behind or embedded in the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (infraduodenal portion). It finally passes through the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum (intraduodenal portion), joining the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla. This posterior relationship means that duodenal ulcers in the first part can erode into the bile duct or gastroduodenal artery. The duct's pancreatic portion may be compressed by pancreatic head tumors.

The junction of the middle and outer third of the clavicle is the weakest point. Most clavicular fractures occur at this location from indirect forces transmitted through the limb during falls. The medial fragment is typically displaced superiorly by sternocleidomastoid while the lateral fragment is displaced inferiorly by arm weight.
questions.question: What is the weakest part of the clavicle?
What type of synovial joint is the elbow classified as?
questions.explanation: The elbow joint is classified as a synovial hinge (ginglymus) joint, allowing uniaxial movement. Articulation occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus with the trochlear notch of the ulna and radial head respectively. This configuration permits flexion and extension movements.

questions.question: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) enters the thigh just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. Compression of this nerve causes which specific condition?
questions.explanation: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2, L3) causes meralgia paraesthetica, characterized by burning, tingling, or numbness on the anterolateral aspect of the thigh. It is a purely sensory nerve with no motor component. Common causes include obesity, pregnancy, tight belts, and direct compression. Treatment is conservative with weight loss and activity modification.
options: Meralgia paraesthetica (burning pain on lateral thigh)
Knee pain from saphenous nerve compression

questions.explanation: has no bony attachment distally; it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. This muscle is absent in approximately 15% of people without functional deficit. It can be used as a tendon graft source in reconstructive surgery.
questions.question: Which forearm muscle has no bony attachment distally?

options: Medial condyle of the tibia proximally
Inferior lateral supracondylar line and oblique popliteal ligament
questions.explanation: Plantaris originates from the inferior end of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur and the oblique popliteal ligament. It inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon together with gastrocnemius and soleus. Its long slender tendon can be mistaken for a nerve during surgery and is used in tendon repair surgery due to its length.
questions.question: Plantaris, a vestigial muscle, inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon. From which specific femoral site does it originate?

questions.explanation: Only the upper third of the rectum is covered by peritoneum on its anterior surface, the middle third has peritoneum on its front only, and the lower third is completely devoid of peritoneal covering. Posteriorly, the rectum is retroperitoneal throughout its length. This peritoneal relationship creates the rectovesical pouch in males and rectouterine pouch in females.
questions.question: What percentage of the rectum is covered by peritoneum anteriorly?
Which artery supplies the majority of the nasal septum?
questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine artery (from maxillary artery) provides the dominant blood supply to the nasal septum via posterior septal branches. The anterior ethmoidal artery and superior labial artery contribute anteriorly. Kiesselbach's plexus in the anteroinferior septum is the most common site of epistaxis.

states that nerves supplying muscles that move a joint also supply the joint itself. This explains why the wrist joint receives innervation from median, radial, and ulnar nerves. The principle helps predict joint innervation patterns throughout the body.
questions.question: What principle explains joint innervation from muscles crossing it?
Which sinus lies within the falx cerebri?
questions.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the attached superior border of the falx cerebri. It begins at the foramen cecum and runs posteriorly to the confluence of sinuses. The sinus receives superior cerebral veins and communicates with scalp veins via emissary veins. Arachnoid granulations project into it for CSF absorption.

Vastus lateralis is the largest component of the quadriceps femoris, lying on the lateral side of the thigh. It originates from the greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera. All four quadriceps components converge into the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament inserting into the tibial tuberosity.
questions.question: Which component of the quadriceps femoris is the largest and lies on the lateral side of the thigh?
What is the functional unit of liver according to the lobular concept?
questions.explanation: The classical hepatic lobule is a hexagonal structural unit with a central vein at its center and portal triads at the periphery (corners). Hepatocytes are arranged in plates radiating from the central vein with sinusoids between them. Blood flows from portal triads through sinusoids to the central vein. This is the histological/structural concept, though the hepatic acinus is a better functional unit.

questions.question: Which vessels pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to the fundus?
questions.explanation: The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass through the gastrosplenic ligament (omentum) to supply the fundus. These vessels represent 5-7 small branches that provide blood to the superior portion of the greater curvature. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the greater curvature to the spleen.

questions.question: Which nerve roots form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The upper trunk is formed by union of C5 and C6 nerve roots. Injury to the upper trunk causes Erb's paralysis with characteristic policeman's tip hand deformity. The upper trunk gives rise to the suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius.

The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots within the substance of the psoas major muscle. The lower part of L4 joins with L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk, which contributes to the sacral plexus. The lumbar plexus gives rise to several important nerves including the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, and obturator nerves, as well as branches to the psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles.
questions.question: Which spinal nerve roots contribute to the lumbar plexus?
Which hepatic structure contains the portal triad?
questions.explanation: The portal tract (portal triad) is located at the corners of hepatic lobules and contains branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, surrounded by connective tissue. Some also include lymphatic vessels. The portal triad delivers blood and removes bile from the hepatic lobule. The hepatic artery provides oxygen; the portal vein provides nutrients and metabolites from the GI tract.

questions.question: Which lymphatic trunk drains the right side of the thorax?
questions.explanation: The right bronchomediastinal trunk drains lymph from the right side of the thorax. It joins with right jugular and right subclavian trunks to form the right lymphatic duct. Alternatively, these three trunks may drain independently into the right venous angle. The left bronchomediastinal trunk usually drains into the thoracic duct.

questions.question: The appendicular artery is typically a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery arises from the ileocolic artery (the terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery) and runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to supply the vermiform appendix. The ileocolic artery divides into superior and inferior branches near the ileocecal junction, with the inferior branch giving rise to anterior cecal, posterior cecal, appendicular, and ileal branches. The appendicular artery's position in the mesoappendix makes it vulnerable during appendectomy, and its thrombosis can lead to appendicitis.

The body of the stomach extends from the cardiac orifice to the level of the incisura angularis, a constant notch on the lesser curvature. This angular notch serves as a reliable anatomical landmark separating the body from the pyloric portion. The incisura angularis becomes more prominent when the stomach is distended.
questions.question: What defines the lower limit of the body of the stomach?
What controls the external urethral sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter is composed of skeletal muscle and is under voluntary somatic control via the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). This sphincter can be consciously contracted to prevent or interrupt micturition. In males, it surrounds the membranous urethra; in females, it surrounds the middle third of the urethra at the urogenital diaphragm.

questions.question: What structure occupies the free edge of the falciform ligament?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) occupies the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament. It is the obliterated remnant of the umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. The ligamentum teres extends from the umbilicus to the left branch of the portal vein at the porta hepatis.

The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and pubic symphysis and inserts superiorly onto the xiphoid process and the costal cartilages of ribs 5-7. The muscle is intersected by three or four tendinous intersections that are firmly adherent to the anterior rectus sheath, creating the characteristic "six-pack" appearance in individuals with low body fat. These intersections represent remnants of the segmental myotomes from which the muscle develops and typically occur at the level of the xiphoid process, umbilicus, and midway between these landmarks.
questions.question: The rectus abdominis muscle inserts onto which structures?

questions.explanation: The hindfoot consists of the talus and the calcaneus. The calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest and strongest bone, absorbing shock and leveraging movement. The talus (ankle bone) articulates with the tibia and fibula superiorly and with the calcaneus inferiorly and navicular anteriorly, allowing ankle movement and weight transfer to the foot.
questions.question: The hindfoot consists of which two bones?

questions.explanation: The umbilicus typically corresponds to the level of the intervertebral disc between L3 and L4 vertebrae, though its position varies with body habitus, age, pregnancy, and previous surgery. The transumbilical plane passing through the umbilicus divides the abdomen into upper and lower halves and is used clinically to define abdominal quadrants. The skin at the umbilicus receives sensory innervation from the T10 dermatome ("belly button at T10"), making this a useful landmark for assessing spinal cord levels. In neonates, the umbilicus lies relatively higher (near L2).
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the umbilicus?

questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris. This high opening impairs natural drainage when standing upright. The sinus is the largest paranasal sinus and is present in rudimentary form at birth.
questions.question: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into which structure?

questions.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch, formed by the coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament, prevents superior displacement of the humeral head. This structure overlies the shoulder joint superiorly. The joint capsule is weak superiorly, making the arch essential for preventing upward dislocation.
questions.question: What prevents superior displacement of the humeral head at the shoulder?

questions.explanation: The heart and pericardium are the main contents of the middle mediastinum, which also contains the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, parts of the phrenic nerves, and the main bronchi. The middle mediastinum is the central compartment of the inferior mediastinum.
questions.question: What position does the heart occupy mediastinally?

questions.explanation: The superior orbital fissure transmits oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), and abducens (VI) nerves. It also transmits the superior ophthalmic vein. The fissure is bounded by the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid. The optic nerve passes through the separate optic canal.
questions.question: The superior orbital fissure transmits which cranial nerves?
How many leaves does the central tendon of the diaphragm have?
questions.explanation: The central tendon is trifoliate (three-leafed), resembling a clover leaf with right, left, and middle (anterior) leaflets. The right leaflet is the largest. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right and middle leaflets. The heart in its pericardium rests on the superior surface of the central tendon.

questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The iliacus muscle is part of the posterior abdominal wall, not the anterior wall, originating from the iliac fossa and inserting with psoas major onto the lesser trochanter of the femur as the iliopsoas tendon. The anterior abdominal wall muscles include three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) and two vertical muscles (rectus abdominis and pyramidalis). The iliacus is innervated by the femoral nerve and functions primarily as a hip flexor, while the anterior abdominal wall muscles are involved in trunk movement and increasing intra-abdominal pressure.

questions.question: What provides sensory innervation to the lateral forearm?
questions.explanation: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is the sensory continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve after it supplies the anterior arm muscles. It provides sensation to the lateral aspect of the forearm from elbow to wrist. This nerve emerges lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.

The levator anguli oris is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It elevates the angle of the mouth during smiling. The muscle arises from the canine fossa of the maxilla and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It lies deep to levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor muscles.
questions.question: The levator anguli oris muscle is innervated by which nerve branch?
Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, superior pole of the left kidney, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum fused to the transverse mesocolon. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum (anterior two layers); superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; inferiorly by the transverse colon and mesocolon; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac appear on imaging as fluid between stomach and pancreas.

questions.question: Which muscle elevates the first rib?
questions.explanation: The scalene muscles fix and elevate the first rib during inspiration. With the first rib fixed, the external and internal intercostal muscles elevate the other ribs upward toward it. The scalene muscles are accessory muscles of respiration and are particularly active during forced inspiration.

The mesoappendix is a triangular fold of peritoneum extending from the terminal ileum and its mesentery to the entire length of the appendix (base to tip), connecting it to the posterior abdominal wall. The appendicular artery (from ileocolic artery) runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix to supply the appendix. During appendectomy, the mesoappendix must be divided and the appendicular artery ligated. The mesoappendix contains fat, lymph nodes, and vessels. Occasionally, the mesoappendix may be short, leaving the distal appendix without mesenteric coverage.
questions.question: The mesoappendix is attached to which part of the appendix?
Which artery supplies the thyroid gland inferiorly?
questions.explanation: The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk (a branch of the subclavian artery) and ascends to supply the lower poles of the thyroid gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerve has an intimate relationship with this artery, passing either anterior or posterior to it. The superior thyroid artery supplies the upper poles.

In males, the spermatic cord passes through the deep inguinal ring (an opening in the transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels). In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through. The ilioinguinal nerve passes through the superficial inguinal ring but not the deep ring - it enters the canal by piercing the internal oblique muscle.
questions.question: What passes through the deep inguinal ring?
Which space lies between the pretracheal and investing layers of deep cervical fascia?
questions.explanation: The suprasternal space (of Burns) lies between the investing and pretracheal layers of deep cervical fascia above the manubrium. It contains the jugular venous arch, lymph nodes, and fat. The space extends laterally behind the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Infections can collect here forming a suprasternal abscess.

questions.question: The pharyngeal plexus is formed primarily by which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal plexus on the middle constrictor muscle is formed primarily by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve with contributions from glossopharyngeal (sensory only) and sympathetic fibers. Motor fibers originate from the nucleus ambiguus and travel via the cranial accessory to the vagus. The plexus supplies all pharyngeal and most palatal muscles.

Opponens digiti minimi draws the fifth metacarpal forward and rotates it laterally, deepening the palm and opposing the little finger toward the thumb. It is one of the three hypothenar muscles and is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
questions.question: What is the action of opponens digiti minimi?

questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) is a fibromuscular band arising from the right crus of the diaphragm near the esophageal hiatus that inserts onto the duodenojejunal flexure and sometimes the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supports the duodenojejunal junction and marks the transition from retroperitoneal (fixed) duodenum to intraperitoneal (mobile) jejunum. This landmark is important radiologically (widening suggests a mass in the pancreatic head) and surgically (identifies the site where the small bowel becomes mobile during laparotomy and marks the upper limit of superior mesenteric artery distribution).
questions.question: The ligament of Treitz suspends which structure?

questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum prevents bowstringing of flexor tendons during wrist flexion, maintaining mechanical efficiency. It maintains the carpal arch and serves as origin for thenar and hypothenar muscles. However, it creates the confined carpal tunnel space predisposing to median nerve compression.
options: Prevents flexor tendon bowstringing, maintains carpal arch
questions.question: What is the functional importance of the flexor retinaculum?

questions.explanation: The hyoglossus muscle is a key surgical landmark separating the lingual artery into three parts: above, on, and below the muscle. The hypoglossal nerve and lingual vein lie superficially on the muscle. Deep lingual and sublingual arteries arise from the lingual artery in relation to this muscle.
questions.question: The hyoglossus muscle separates which two important arteries?

questions.explanation: The caval opening (vena caval foramen) in the diaphragm is located at the T8 vertebral level in the central tendon. It transmits the inferior vena cava and terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve. The IVC is adherent to the margins of the opening, so when the diaphragm contracts during inspiration, it widens the opening and dilates the IVC, facilitating venous return.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the caval opening lie?

questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) enters the transverse mesocolon and divides into right and left branches that supply the transverse colon. The right branch anastomoses with the right colic artery (from SMA), while the left branch anastomoses with the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric artery), forming the marginal artery of Drummond at the splenic flexure. This anastomotic connection between SMA and IMA territories provides important collateral circulation. Variation in the middle colic artery is common; occasionally it may be absent or arise as two separate vessels.
questions.question: The middle colic artery divides into which branches?
The anterior belly of the digastric forms part of which triangle?
questions.explanation: The anterior bellies of the right and left digastric muscles form the lateral boundaries of the submental triangle. The hyoid bone forms the base (inferior boundary), and the mylohyoid muscle forms the floor. The triangle contains submental lymph nodes and is located in the midline below the chin.

questions.question: Into which lymph nodes does the bladder apex drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the superior surface and apex of the bladder drains to external iliac lymph nodes. The fundus drains to internal iliac nodes, while the neck drains to sacral and common iliac nodes. This drainage pattern is clinically important in bladder cancer staging and determining the extent of lymph node dissection required.

The primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at the 2nd month of intrauterine life. The ischium's primary centre appears during the 4th month, and the pubis during the 5th month. At birth, the hip bone is ossified except for the iliac crest, the Y-shaped cartilage, and a strip along the inferior margin.
questions.question: A primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at which gestational period?

questions.explanation: The iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) is one of the strongest ligaments in the body, triangular and Y-shaped. Its apex attaches to the anterior inferior iliac spine and its base to the intertrochanteric line. It reinforces the joint anteriorly, prevents overextension while standing, and reduces the muscle energy needed to maintain upright posture.
questions.question: Which Y-shaped hip ligament, described as one of the strongest in the body, has its apex attached to the anterior inferior iliac spine?

questions.explanation: Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are extensions of cortical tissue that project between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus. They contain interlobar arteries and veins. The cortical tissue in the columns and over the bases of pyramids contains the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules. Enlarged renal columns can mimic renal masses on imaging.
questions.question: Which structure extends between adjacent renal pyramids?

questions.explanation: The incisive foramen (canal) in the anterior hard palate transmits the nasopalatine nerves, which provide sensation to the anterior palate. The foramen also transmits terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. The nasopalatine nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve via the pterygopalatine ganglion.
questions.question: The incisive foramen transmits which nerve?
Which muscle originates from the inguinal ligament?
questions.explanation: The internal oblique muscle originates from the lateral two-thirds of the inguinal ligament (along with the iliac crest and thoracolumbar fascia), with its fibers running superomedially. The lowermost fibers arch over the spermatic cord, contributing to the anterior wall of the inguinal canal laterally and the roof of the canal throughout its length. The external oblique muscle does not originate from the inguinal ligament; rather, its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament itself. The transversus abdominis also takes origin from the inguinal ligament laterally, contributing to the roof of the canal.

questions.question: The lacrimal sac lies in which structure?
questions.explanation: The lacrimal sac occupies the lacrimal fossa, a depression formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of the maxilla. The sac receives tears from the canaliculi superiorly and drains into the nasolacrimal duct inferiorly. Dacryocystitis (infection of the lacrimal sac) causes swelling medial to the inner canthus.

The bundle of His (AV bundle) penetrates the fibrous skeleton and descends along the posterior edge of the membranous interventricular septum before dividing into right and left bundle branches. The right bundle branch continues down the right side of the septum, while the left bundle branch crosses to the left side and divides into anterior and posterior fascicles.
questions.question: Which structure gives rise to the right and left bundle branches?

options: Anterior and posterior interosseous nerves only
questions.question: What nerve innervates the wrist joint?
questions.explanation: The wrist joint is innervated by branches from three nerves following Hilton's law: median nerve (anterior interosseous branch), radial nerve (posterior interosseous branch), and ulnar nerve (deep and dorsal branches). This follows the principle that nerves supplying muscles moving a joint also supply the joint.

The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, bypassing the inguinal and iliac nodes. This drainage pattern follows the testicular vessels and reflects the embryological origin of the testes high on the posterior abdominal wall. In testicular cancer, metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes, not inguinal nodes (unless scrotal skin is involved). The scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This explains why orchiectomy for testicular cancer requires high ligation of the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring to include regional lymphatics.
questions.question: The testicular lymphatics drain to which nodes?

questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus is located in the muscular part of the right crus at T10. The oesophagus passes through it along with the anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal vessels, and lymphatics. Some fibers of the right crus form a sphincter around the oesophagus, contributing to prevention of gastro-oesophageal reflux. The left crus is smaller and does not have a hiatus.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the right crus of the diaphragm?
Which muscle attachment defines the lateral arcuate ligament?
questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament (lateral lumbocostal arch) is a thickening of the fascia covering quadratus lumborum, extending from the tip of the L1 transverse process to the 12th rib. The diaphragm's lateral part arises from this ligament. The medial arcuate ligament crosses over psoas major (from L1 body to L1 transverse process tip), allowing passage of the sympathetic trunk, while the median arcuate ligament connects the diaphragmatic crura across the midline anterior to the aorta at T12. These arcuate ligaments can be sites of neurovascular compression or serve as anatomical landmarks in retroperitoneal surgery.

questions.question: Which structure lies immediately medial to the medial pterygoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle of the pharynx lies medial to the medial pterygoid muscle, separated by a thin fascial layer. The medial pterygoid forms part of the lateral wall of the infratemporal fossa. This relationship is important when accessing the pharyngeal space surgically.

The first posterior intercostal space on the right side drains into the right brachiocephalic vein. The remaining intercostal spaces on the right drain into the azygos vein. On the left, the upper three spaces typically drain into the left brachiocephalic vein through the left superior intercostal vein.
questions.question: Which vein drains the first posterior intercostal space?

questions.explanation: The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for the flexor hallucis longus tendon on its inferior surface. It also receives the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon and serves as the attachment for the spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) and the deltoid ligament medially.
questions.question: The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for which tendon?

questions.explanation: The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery pass through the triangular interval. This space is bounded by teres major superiorly, long head of triceps medially, and lateral head of triceps laterally. The structures then enter the spiral groove of the humerus.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the triangular interval?
Erector spinae and gluteus maximus work together during which functional activity?
options: Hip abduction while in single-leg stance
Dorsiflexing the ankle during the swing phase of walking
Rising from a forward-flexed position (simultaneous hip and trunk extension)
Rotating the trunk in a sitting position
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus and erector spinae work together in rising from a forward-flexed position, simultaneously extending the hip and the trunk respectively. Gluteus maximus is the great extensor of the hip, particularly powerful in these loaded extension tasks. Weakness of either muscle group causes difficulty in rising from bending and is assessed in clinical examination of low back and hip pathology.

questions.question: What happens to diaphragm during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, causing its domes and central tendon to descend and flatten. This increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. As the diaphragm descends, abdominal viscera are pushed downward and the intrathoracic volume increases, reducing intrathoracic pressure.

Centroacinar cells are pale-staining cells unique to the pancreas that represent the intra-acinar portion of the intercalated duct. They secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid in response to secretin, which neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum. This bicarbonate secretion, combined with enzymes from acinar cells, produces complete pancreatic juice. Centroacinar cells distinguish pancreatic from salivary acini.
questions.question: What characterizes centroacinar cells?

questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas lies in the concavity formed by the C-shaped duodenum and indents the medial aspect of the second (descending) part. The pancreatic head is intimately related to the duodenum, particularly the second part where the bile and pancreatic ducts enter. This close relationship means that pancreatic head disease often affects the duodenum and vice versa.
questions.question: Which structure indents the second part of the duodenum medially?
What sphincter is at the gastroesophageal junction?
questions.explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a physiological sphincter at the gastroesophageal junction. Unlike the anatomical upper esophageal sphincter, the LES has no distinct anatomical structure but represents a zone of increased smooth muscle tone. The right crus fibers looping around the esophagus contribute to sphincter function.

questions.question: The patella, embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon, serves as a pulley with what biomechanical benefit?
options: Increases the weight of the quadriceps
Increases mechanical advantage in knee extension
questions.explanation: The patella is a true sesamoid bone serving as a pulley that improves the angle of pull of the quadriceps tendon, resulting in greater mechanical advantage in knee extension. Patellectomy significantly reduces knee extension strength. The patella slides within the trochlear groove during knee movements and is protected by thick hyaline cartilage on its posterior surface.

questions.question: The third part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by which vessels?
questions.explanation: The third (horizontal) part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein as they descend toward the root of the mesentery. This relationship can lead to superior mesenteric artery syndrome, where the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta (with the spine) posteriorly, causing partial or complete duodenal obstruction. Risk factors include rapid weight loss, scoliosis, surgical correction of scoliosis, and conditions causing loss of the mesenteric fat pad that normally cushions the angle between the SMA and aorta.

at the wrist joint (ulnar deviation) is produced by the combined action of extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris. These muscles work synergistically despite being in different compartments. The wrist joint permits movement along two axes as an ellipsoid synovial joint.
questions.question: Which movement at the wrist joint is produced by extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris?

questions.explanation: Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie in the posterior mediastinum alongside the esophagus and descending thoracic aorta. They receive lymph from the esophagus, posterior diaphragm, pericardium, and posterior intercostal spaces. Efferents drain primarily to the thoracic duct.
questions.question: Where do posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie?
The transverse cervical nerve provides sensation to which area?
questions.explanation: The transverse cervical nerve (C2-C3) emerges from the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and provides sensation to the anterior and lateral neck. It is a branch of the cervical plexus. The nerve crosses the sternocleidomastoid horizontally. Cervical plexus block affects this nerve causing anterior neck anesthesia.

The phrenicocolic ligament, extending from the splenic (left colic) flexure to the diaphragm at the level of ribs 10-11, supports the inferior pole of the spleen, preventing downward displacement. It creates a shelf-like structure that effectively suspends the spleen. The ligament also serves as a barrier between the left paracolic gutter inferiorly and the area around the spleen superiorly, potentially limiting the spread of peritoneal fluid, infection, or tumors between these compartments. During colonoscopy or surgery on the splenic flexure, division of this ligament may be necessary for adequate mobilization of the colon.
questions.question: The phrenicocolic ligament supports which structure?
Where is Morgagni's foramen located?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Morgagni is located anteriorly between the xiphoid and costal origins of the diaphragm. Hernias through this opening (Morgagni hernias) are less common than Bochdalek hernias but can allow omental fat or intestine to herniate into the anterior mediastinum. They are usually asymptomatic.

questions.question: Which ligament supports the uterus?
questions.explanation: The uterus is supported by multiple structures: the cardinal ligaments (most important, prevent prolapse), uterosacral ligaments (from cervix/upper vagina to sacrum, maintain position), pubocervical ligaments (from cervix to pubis), round ligaments (maintain anteverted position), broad ligaments (minimal support, mainly peritoneal folds), and the muscular pelvic floor (levator ani, particularly pubococcygeus). The perineal body also provides indirect support. Damage to these supports (especially during childbirth) can lead to uterine prolapse, cystocele, rectocele, or enterocele. The broad ligament, despite its name, provides minimal structural support.

Cardiac sympathetic innervation comes from the cervical (superior, middle, inferior/stellate) and upper thoracic (T1-T4) sympathetic ganglia. These send cardiac branches to the cardiac plexus. Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate (positive chronotropy), increases contractility (positive inotropy), increases AV conduction velocity (positive dromotropy), and causes coronary vasodilation. Stellate ganglion block can treat certain arrhythmias.
questions.question: Which sympathetic ganglia contribute to cardiac innervation?
What provides the blood supply to the radial nerve in the arm?
questions.explanation: The profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery accompanies the radial nerve through the spiral groove, providing its blood supply in the arm. Both structures wind around the posterior humerus together. Injury to the artery often accompanies radial nerve damage in humeral fractures.

questions.question: The small saphenous vein arises on the lateral side of the foot and ascends posterior to which malleolus before entering the popliteal vein?
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein arises from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch and ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus. It then passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, ascends between the heads of gastrocnemius, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.

questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the central part of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm, including both the pleural and peritoneal surfaces, in addition to its motor supply to the entire diaphragm. Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (such as in subphrenic abscess, perforated peptic ulcer, or ruptured spleen) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve, as both derive from the C3-C5 dermatomes. The peripheral parts of the diaphragm receive sensory innervation from the lower six intercostal nerves and subcostal nerve.

The second part of the axillary artery lies directly behind (posterior to) the pectoralis minor muscle. This anatomical relationship is used to divide the artery into three parts. The second part gives off two branches: the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries.
questions.question: Which portion of the axillary artery lies behind pectoralis minor?

questions.explanation: The vaginal artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (though it may arise from the uterine artery) and descends to supply the vagina. It gives off numerous branches to the anterior and posterior vaginal walls, anastomosing with branches from the uterine artery superiorly and internal pudendal artery inferiorly. This rich anastomotic network provides extensive collateral circulation to the vagina. The vagina also receives blood supply from the middle rectal and internal pudendal arteries. The upper vagina drains via uterine veins, while the lower vagina drains via internal pudendal veins.
questions.question: The vaginal artery typically arises from which vessel?
The lymphatics of the lower limb follow the saphenous vein and drain to which lymph node group?
questions.explanation: The superficial lymphatics of the lower limb accompany the great saphenous vein and drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. The deep lymphatics accompany the deep vessels and drain to the deep inguinal and then external iliac nodes. The popliteal nodes drain the posterior leg and lateral foot (accompanying the small saphenous vein). Lymphedema of the lower limb can follow radical inguinal lymph node dissection.

Complete section of a phrenic nerve results in complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the corresponding half of the diaphragm. The paralyzed hemidiaphragm shows paradoxical movement: moving upward during inspiration and downward during expiration. Unilateral paralysis is often asymptomatic; bilateral causes severe respiratory compromise.
questions.question: What happens with complete phrenic nerve section?

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space accompanied by the posterior circumflex humeral vessels. The space is bounded by teres minor superiorly, teres major inferiorly, long head of triceps medially, and surgical neck of humerus laterally. Injury can occur with shoulder trauma or humeral neck fractures.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the quadrangular space?
Which muscle retracts the mandible?
questions.explanation: The posterior (horizontal) fibers of the temporalis muscle retract (pull back) the protruded mandible. The masseter and medial pterygoid elevate, while the lateral pterygoid protrudes. Bilateral contraction of temporalis elevates the mandible; unilateral posterior fibers retract ipsilaterally.

Branches of the facial and lingual arteries supply the submandibular gland, with the facial artery providing the primary vascular supply. The facial artery passes deep to the gland before crossing the mandible. Venous drainage follows corresponding veins to the internal jugular system.
questions.question: Which vessel specifically supplies the bed of the submandibular gland?

questions.explanation: The superior and inferior lateral genicular arteries encircle the fibular collateral ligament at the lateral aspect of the knee, contributing to the lateral genicular anastomosis. The superior lateral genicular artery passes above the lateral condyle of the femur, while the inferior lateral genicular artery passes below the lateral tibial condyle. Together they provide important collateral circulation around the knee.
questions.question: The superior lateral genicular artery and the inferior lateral genicular artery both branch from the popliteal artery. Between them, what structure do they encircle at the lateral aspect of the knee?
Where does the greater splanchnic nerve arise?
questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the 5th-9th (or sometimes 5th-10th) thoracic sympathetic ganglia. It descends on the vertebral bodies, pierces the crus of the diaphragm, and synapses in the celiac ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation to foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, pancreas, spleen, etc.).

questions.question: The head of the femur is directed medially, upward, and forward, forming what fraction of a sphere?
questions.explanation: The head of the femur forms two-thirds of a sphere and is directed medially, upward, and forward. It articulates with the acetabulum to form the hip joint. The fovea capitis on the head transmits blood from the obturator artery through the ligament of the head of femur.

The deep palmar arch (formed primarily by radial artery) supplies blood to deep hand structures and gives off palmar metacarpal arteries. These metacarpal arteries provide important contributions to digital blood supply. The arch lies approximately 1cm proximal to the superficial arch.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the deep palmar arch?
options: Deep hand structures and palmar metacarpal arteries

questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies only the gluteus maximus. It exits the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. Injury results in loss of powerful hip extension, making it impossible to rise from sitting, climb stairs, or run effectively. Since gluteus maximus has little role in gentle walking, the patient may ambulate with minimal apparent deficit on flat ground.
questions.question: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies which single muscle?
Which nerve root is predominantly tested by the biceps reflex?
questions.explanation: The biceps reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root, though C5 also contributes. The reflex is elicited by tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa. Absence or diminution of this reflex suggests C6 nerve root or musculocutaneous nerve pathology.

The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, which connected the pulmonary artery to the aorta in fetal circulation, bypassing the non-functional fetal lungs. It closes functionally at birth and becomes a fibrous cord extending from the left pulmonary artery to the aortic arch.
questions.question: What is the ligamentum arteriosum?

questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter, composed of skeletal muscle and innervated by the inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve), is under voluntary control and can be consciously contracted to prevent or defer defecation. The internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, autonomic control) maintains resting anal tone. The puborectalis muscle contributes to the anorectal angle and fecal continence.
questions.question: Which structure controls voluntary defecation?

questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that synapse in terminal ganglia within or very near the walls of the pelvic organs they supply (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs). This is characteristic of parasympathetic innervation, where the preganglionic fibers are long and synapse close to or within the target organ, while postganglionic fibers are very short. The fibers travel via the inferior hypogastric plexus to reach their destinations but do not synapse there. The pelvic splanchnics also provide parasympathetic innervation to the distal hindgut from the splenic flexure to the upper anal canal.
questions.question: The pelvic splanchnic nerves synapse in which location?
Which artery supplies blood to the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: The cystic artery, most commonly arising from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle (75% of cases), provides the primary blood supply to the gallbladder. It typically divides into superficial (supplying the peritoneal surface) and deep (supplying the hepatic surface) branches. Anatomical variations are common, with the cystic artery occasionally arising from the left hepatic, common hepatic, gastroduodenal, or superior mesenteric arteries. Careful identification during cholecystectomy is essential to avoid injury to aberrant vessels or the right hepatic artery. The gallbladder may also receive small arterial branches from the liver bed.

questions.question: The inferior vena cava is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), to the right of the midline and anterior to the right common iliac artery. From this point, it ascends on the right side of the aorta, anterior to the vertebral column, receiving tributaries in an asymmetric pattern. The IVC passes through the diaphragm (caval opening in central tendon) at T8 level to enter the thorax and immediately empties into the right atrium. The formation level (L5) is slightly lower than the aortic bifurcation (L4).

The long head of triceps crosses both the shoulder and elbow joints, performing extension at the shoulder. At the elbow, all three heads of triceps work together to produce extension. The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.
questions.question: What is the action of the long head of triceps at the shoulder?

questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve, the deep terminal branch of the radial nerve, supplies extensor digitorum and all other extensor muscles in the posterior forearm compartment. The nerve passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle to reach the posterior compartment.
questions.question: What nerve supplies the extensor digitorum muscle?

questions.explanation: The inferior oblique muscle is the only extraocular muscle that protracts (brings forward) the eyeball along with extorsion, elevation, and abduction. It arises from the maxilla at the anteromedial orbital floor and inserts on the posterolateral inferior eyeball. The muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). It has no relationship with the common tendinous ring.
questions.question: Which muscle protracts the eyeball?

questions.explanation: The posterior portion of the hard palate is formed by the horizontal plates of the palatine bones. The anterior portion is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities and provides a rigid surface for the tongue during mastication.
questions.question: Which bone forms the hard palate posteriorly?

questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. It has a side of danger (medial side, closer to the ischial tuberosity) and a side of safety (lateral side). The quadratus femoris forms a protective muscular layer over the nerve as it passes posterior to the hip joint.
questions.question: The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) curves downward at which position between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter?
Which artery is the main blood supply to the face?
questions.explanation: The facial artery is the main arterial supply to the face, arising from the external carotid artery. It winds around the mandible anterior to the masseter and ascends toward the medial canthus. Branches include superior and inferior labial, lateral nasal, and angular arteries.

options: Fascia lata of the thigh only
Camper's fascia of the anterior abdominal wall
Transversalis fascia anteriorly and iliac fascia posteriorly
questions.question: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of which fascia, enclosing the femoral vessels and the femoral canal?
questions.explanation: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of the transversalis fascia anteriorly and the iliac fascia posteriorly, enclosing the femoral artery, femoral vein, and the femoral canal (containing lymphatics). The femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal into the femoral sheath inferior to the inguinal ligament.

The internal thoracic vein accompanies the artery of the same name, draining blood from the anterior chest wall, upper abdomen, and breast. It ascends to drain into the brachiocephalic vein on each side. The vein receives tributaries corresponding to the arterial branches.
questions.question: Which vein accompanies the internal thoracic artery?
Which nerve provides motor supply to diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. Each phrenic nerve supplies its corresponding half of the diaphragm up to the margin of the esophageal opening. Injury to the phrenic nerve results in paralysis of that hemidiaphragm with consequent elevation.

questions.question: Which flexure of the colon is located at a higher position?
questions.explanation: The splenic (left colic) flexure is positioned higher than the hepatic (right colic) flexure and also forms a more acute angle. The splenic flexure is attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament. This higher position of the left flexure is clinically significant in colonoscopy and surgical procedures.

questions.question: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by which division of the sciatic nerve?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2). The exception is the short head of biceps femoris, which is supplied by the common fibular division. The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body.

questions.question: The vermiform appendix typically arises from which part of the cecum?
questions.explanation: The vermiform appendix arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. The three taeniae coli of the cecum converge at the base of the appendix, serving as a reliable landmark for locating it during surgery. While the base of the appendix has a relatively constant position, its tip can be found in various locations: retrocecal (65%), pelvic (31%), subcecal (2.3%), preileal (1%), or postileal (0.4%). The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, runs through the mesoappendix to supply the appendix.

questions.question: What happens to old platelets in the spleen?
questions.explanation: Old platelets, like old erythrocytes, are recognized and destroyed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The spleen also serves as a reservoir for approximately one-third of the body's platelet pool. After splenectomy, platelet counts typically rise (thrombocytosis) due to loss of platelet sequestration and destruction. Splenic platelets can be rapidly mobilized in stress or hemorrhage.

The hepatic (right colic) flexure is related posteriorly to the lower part of the right kidney and anteriorly to the liver and gallbladder. This relationship means that right renal pathology may manifest as right upper quadrant pain mimicking hepatobiliary disease. The hepatic flexure is more mobile than the splenic flexure, attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the hepatocolic ligament (part of the greater omentum). The flexure receives blood supply from the right colic artery (from SMA) and right branch of the middle colic artery, with anastomoses forming the marginal artery.
questions.question: The hepatic flexure is related posteriorly to which structure?

questions.explanation: The tendon of popliteus passes deep to the fibular collateral ligament, separating it from the lateral meniscus. This is why the lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus. The popliteus tendon also creates a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule allowing its passage. The biceps femoris tendon is split by the fibular collateral ligament at the fibular head.
questions.question: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament is separated from the lateral meniscus by the tendon of which muscle?

questions.explanation: The supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (branches of the frontal nerve from V1) provide sensation to the upper eyelid and forehead. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper lid. Infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial canthus and side of nose. These are all branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensation to the upper eyelid?

questions.explanation: The anterior belly of the digastric is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects the embryologic origin from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively.
questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric muscle is innervated by which nerve?

options: Wrist position does not affect grip strength
Strongest grip in full wrist flexion
Grip strongest with wrist in slight extension
Strongest grip in full wrist extension
Strongest grip in neutral wrist position
questions.explanation: Maximum grip strength occurs with the wrist in 20-30° extension. This position optimally lengthens finger flexors for maximum tension development while stabilizing the wrist. Full flexion or extension reduces grip strength due to passive insufficiency or active insufficiency of finger flexors.
questions.question: How does wrist position affect grip strength?
How many bronchopulmonary segments exist in right lung?
questions.explanation: The right lung contains ten bronchopulmonary segments: three in the upper lobe (apical, posterior, anterior), two in the middle lobe (lateral, medial), and five in the lower lobe (superior/apical, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal). Each segment is functionally independent.

questions.question: What nerve supplies serratus anterior?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies serratus anterior, giving branches to each muscle digitation. The nerve descends on the superficial surface of the muscle and is vulnerable to injury during axillary surgery. Damage causes scapular winging.

options: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi
Plantar interossei, dorsal interossei, flexor hallucis brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
questions.question: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, and flexor digiti minimi brevis. Flexor hallucis brevis and adductor hallucis are supplied by branches of the medial and lateral plantar nerves respectively. The adductor hallucis assists in maintaining the transverse arch of the foot by drawing the metatarsals medially.

The right renal artery passes posterior to both the right renal vein and the inferior vena cava as it courses from the aorta (at L1-L2 level, just below the superior mesenteric artery) to the right kidney hilum. The right renal artery is longer than the left due to the aorta's left-sided position. Both renal arteries also pass posterior to the corresponding psoas major muscle and ureter. The arteries typically divide into anterior and posterior divisions before entering the hilum, supplying corresponding segments of the kidney. The right artery may give off the inferior suprarenal artery.
questions.question: The right renal artery passes posterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: The flexor compartment of the hand receives structures passing through the carpal tunnel, including flexor tendons and the median nerve. The tunnel's confined space makes it susceptible to compression syndromes. Any lesion diminishing compartment size can result in median nerve compression.
questions.question: Which compartment contains structures passing through the carpal tunnel?
Where does the suspensory muscle of the duodenum attach?
questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) extends from the right crus of the diaphragm behind the pancreas to attach to the duodenojejunal flexure. It contains both smooth muscle and fibrous tissue. Contraction of this muscle widens the angle of the duodenojejunal flexure and may assist in opening the duodenum for passage of contents into the jejunum.

Sudeck's point is the watershed area at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anal verge) where the last sigmoid artery (from inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of IMA). This represents a relatively weak point in the colonic blood supply, vulnerable to ischemia during periods of low blood flow, hypotension, or ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery during surgery. Another watershed area is Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure. Both areas may develop ischemic colitis, manifesting as abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and colonoscopic evidence of mucosal ischemia.
questions.question: Which artery anastomoses at Sudeck's point?
What are the nerve roots of the long thoracic nerve?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve arises from nerve roots C5, C6, and C7. It supplies the serratus anterior muscle with branches to each digitation. Injury to this nerve causes scapular winging, which becomes apparent when pushing against resistance.

The lower trunk is formed by union of C8 and T1 nerve roots. Injury to the lower trunk causes Klumpke's paralysis with claw hand deformity. The lower trunk continues as the medial cord after giving off no branches in the neck.
questions.question: Which nerve roots form the lower trunk?
What is the internal urethral sphincter composed of?
questions.explanation: The internal urethral sphincter is composed of smooth muscle (a thickening of the detrusor muscle at the bladder neck) and is under involuntary autonomic control. It is controlled by sympathetic innervation (hypogastric nerves), which causes contraction to maintain continence and prevent retrograde ejaculation in males. It relaxes during micturition under parasympathetic control.

questions.question: The anterior fontanelle is located at the junction of which sutures?
questions.explanation: The anterior fontanelle (bregma) is located at the junction of the coronal, sagittal, and frontal (metopic) sutures where the frontal and parietal bones meet. It is diamond-shaped and typically closes by 18-24 months. The fontanelle allows skull molding during birth and accommodates brain growth. Bulging indicates increased intracranial pressure.

The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein, measuring approximately 8 cm in length. The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein ascends to the porta hepatis within the free edge of the lesser omentum, positioned posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery, where it divides into right and left branches.
questions.question: The portal vein is formed by the union of which two vessels?

questions.explanation: The patellar ligament passes from the apex and adjoining margins of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It is a strong thick fibrous band representing the distal continuation of the quadriceps tendon. It blends with the medial and lateral patellar retinacula (aponeurotic expansions of vastus medialis and lateralis) providing additional stability.
questions.question: The patellar ligament, described as the distal part of the quadriceps tendon, ultimately attaches to which bony prominence?

questions.explanation: The anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending - LAD) descends in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, anterior left ventricular wall, and anterior right ventricle. It is the most commonly affected vessel in myocardial infarction. Septal branches perforate the septum; diagonal branches supply the lateral left ventricle.
questions.question: Which branch of the left coronary artery supplies the interventricular septum?

questions.explanation: The base of the axilla is formed by skin, subcutaneous tissue, and axillary fascia spanning from the fourth rib. This base is concave and forms the floor of the axillary space. The axillary fascia is continuous with the pectoral fascia anteriorly and latissimus dorsi fascia posteriorly.
questions.question: At which rib level is the axilla base formed?
What is the exocrine secretory unit of the pancreas called?
questions.explanation: The pancreatic acinus is the functional exocrine secretory unit, consisting of pyramid-shaped serous (enzyme-secreting) acinar cells arranged around a small lumen. The acinus is drained by an intercalated duct lined by centroacinar cells. Multiple acini drain into larger ducts, which eventually form the main pancreatic duct. The pancreas structurally resembles the parotid gland.

The regional lymph node is defined as the lymph node where lymph from an organ or body part drains to firstly.
