This is distinct from the sentinel lymph node, which is the first node to receive drainage from a tumor. Understanding this distinction is important for staging cancer and planning surgical interventions.
questions.question: Which lymph node receives drainage first from an organ?
Which sinus receives blood from the superior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus drains posteriorly into the confluence of sinuses (torcular herophili) at the internal occipital protuberance. From here, blood typically flows into the right transverse sinus more than the left. The confluence also receives the straight sinus and occipital sinus.

The renal medulla is composed of approximately 10-12 renal pyramids in each kidney. Each pyramid has its base directed toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting medially into a minor calyx. The renal columns (columns of Bertin) extend between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus.
questions.question: How many renal pyramids typically comprise each kidney?

questions.explanation: The levator labii superioris elevates the upper lip. It arises from the maxilla above the infraorbital foramen and inserts into the upper lip. The muscle is innervated by the zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve. Zygomaticus major and minor also contribute to upper lip elevation but primarily act on the angle of mouth.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the upper lip?
Which structure separates the right and left paracolic gutters?
questions.explanation: The mesentery of the small intestine, with its oblique root extending from the duodenojejunal flexure (L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (S1, right of midline), divides the infracolic compartment into right and left infracolic spaces. These spaces communicate laterally with the right and left paracolic gutters respectively. The paracolic gutters are depressions lateral to the ascending and descending colon where peritoneal fluid can track between the pelvis and upper abdomen. The right paracolic gutter communicates with the hepatorenal recess, providing a pathway for infection spread.

The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the boundary between the oral cavity and oropharynx. The arch contains the palatoglossus muscle and extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the oral cavity and oropharynx, bounded by these arches.
questions.question: Which structure separates the oral cavity from the oropharynx?
The vertebral artery gives off which spinal branch?
questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries give off anterior spinal arteries before joining to form the basilar artery. The two anterior spinal arteries unite to form a single vessel descending in the anterior median fissure. The vertebral arteries also give off posterior spinal arteries. These vessels supply the cervical spinal cord before receiving reinforcement from segmental arteries.

The taeniae coli represent three longitudinal bands where the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the colon is thickened and concentrated, running from cecum to rectosigmoid junction. The three bands are: taenia libera (free, anteriorly on ascending and descending colon), taenia mesocolica (at mesenteric attachment), and taenia omentalis (at omental attachment). Between the taeniae, the longitudinal muscle is thin, allowing the circular muscle to create sacculations (haustra). The taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, providing a surgical landmark. At the rectosigmoid junction (about 15 cm from anus), the taeniae spread to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer in the rectum.
questions.question: The taeniae coli are thickenings of which muscle layer?

questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve contains preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the T5-T9 levels of the spinal cord, which synapse in the celiac ganglion. This nerve pierces the diaphragm separately or with the sympathetic trunk and provides sympathetic innervation to the foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and small intestine to mid-duodenum) via the celiac plexus. The lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11) supplies the midgut, while the least splanchnic nerve (T12) and lumbar splanchnic nerves supply the hindgut and pelvic organs via the superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses.
questions.question: The greater splanchnic nerve carries preganglionic fibers from which spinal levels?
The medial longitudinal arch has the greatest height and is formed by which bones?
options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, and 1st-3rd metatarsals
Talus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and two cuneiforms
Calcaneus, talus, and first metatarsal only
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiform bones, and the 1st-3rd metatarsals. Its summit is the superior articular facet of the talus, making the talus the keystone of this arch. It is larger, higher, more mobile, and more resilient than the lateral longitudinal arch, dynamically changing most during movement.

The inferior boundary is where the medial pterygoid muscle attaches to the mandible near its angle. The fossa has no distinct floor but is limited inferiorly by this muscular attachment. Superiorly, it is bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid.
questions.question: Which structure forms the inferior boundary of the infratemporal fossa?

questions.explanation: produces both extension and adduction (ulnar deviation) at the wrist joint. It works with flexor carpi ulnaris to produce pure adduction by balancing extension and flexion forces. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm compartment.
questions.question: Which muscle extends and adducts the wrist?
Why does the phrenic nerve have a long course?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve has a long course from the neck (C3-5) to the diaphragm because of embryological migration of the diaphragm. The septum transversum initially forms in the cervical region and migrates caudally during development, carrying its nerve supply (from cervical segments) with it to its final thoracic position.

questions.question: The tibial nerve gives off which named cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa that contributes to forming the sural nerve?
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve gives off the medial sural cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa. This joins the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve to form the sural nerve, supplying the lateral side of the leg and ankle. The tibial nerve is the most superficial of the major neurovascular bundle in the fossa.

questions.question: The gallbladder fundus projects beyond which liver border?
questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where it may contact the anterior abdominal wall. This location corresponds approximately to the point where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis crosses the right costal margin (at the transpyloric plane). The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum on all surfaces. When the gallbladder is distended or inflamed (acute cholecystitis), the fundus becomes palpable at this location, and deep palpation causes inspiratory arrest (Murphy's sign).

questions.question: The ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres) transmits arteries from which named vessels to the femoral head?
options: Superior gluteal artery from the internal iliac
Inferior gluteal artery from the internal iliac alone
Acetabular branches of medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres transmits arteries from acetabular branches of the medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries to the head of femur. It is triangular and flat, with its apex at the fovea capitis and base at the acetabular notch. In adults, this provides only a minor blood supply compared to the retinacular vessels.

questions.question: The quadriceps tendon continues as which structure, with the patella embedded within it, attaching to the tibial tuberosity?
questions.explanation: The tendons of the four quadriceps components unite to form the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament (also called patellar tendon) with the patella embedded within as a sesamoid bone. This inserts into the tibial tuberosity. The patellar retinacula are aponeurotic expansions that provide additional lateral stability.

The middle lobe of the right lung is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. The horizontal fissure runs along the fourth rib anteriorly. The oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from both the superior and middle lobes on the right side.
questions.question: Which fissure separates the right lung's middle lobe?
What is the functional relationship between finger flexor sublimis and profundus?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes PIP joints independently of DIP joints. Flexor digitorum profundus flexes DIP joints and contributes to PIP and MCP flexion, providing power grip force. This two-layer arrangement enables independent or combined finger joint flexion for varied hand positions.
options: Both tendons have identical flexor function
FDS flexes PIP joints, FDP flexes DIP joints

questions.question: The olfactory nerves pass through which structure?
questions.explanation: Olfactory nerve axons from the nasal epithelium pass through multiple foramina in the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. These first-order sensory neurons synapse in the olfactory bulb above the cribriform plate. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.

questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the carotid triangle?
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded by the sternocleidomastoid (posterolaterally), superior belly of omohyoid (inferiorly), and posterior belly of digastric (superiorly). The triangle contains the carotid bifurcation, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve, and several other structures. It is a subdivision of the anterior triangle of the neck.

The geniculate ganglion is the sensory ganglion of the facial nerve located at the genu (bend) of the facial canal. It contains cell bodies of neurons carrying taste from the anterior tongue via chorda tympani. Herpes zoster infection here causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy and vesicles.
questions.question: The geniculate ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The deep perineal space (deep perineal pouch) is bounded superiorly by the inferior fascia of the pelvic diaphragm and inferiorly by the perineal membrane. In males, it contains the membranous urethra, external urethral sphincter, bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands), deep transverse perineal muscle, internal pudendal vessels, and dorsal nerve of penis. In females, it contains the urethra, external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscle, internal pudendal vessels, and dorsal nerve of clitoris (no bulbourethral glands). The space is traversed by the urethra (and vagina in females).
questions.question: Which structure passes through the deep perineal space?
Which structure forms the floor of the maxillary sinus?
questions.explanation: The alveolar process of the maxilla forms the floor of the maxillary sinus. Roots of the upper premolar and molar teeth may project into the sinus, separated only by thin bone or mucosa. Dental infections can spread to the sinus, and tooth extraction can create an oroantral fistula. The floor is typically 1-2 cm below the nasal floor.

The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) supplies the anterior superior nasal septum. The sphenopalatine artery supplies the posterior septum while the superior labial artery supplies anteroinferiorly. These vessels anastomose in Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), the most common site of anterior epistaxis.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the nasal septum anteriorly?

questions.explanation: The popliteus muscle weakly flexes the knee and unlocks it from full extension by rotating the femur 5 degrees on a fixed tibia (or medially rotating the tibia on an unplanted limb). It originates from the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus, inserting on the posterior tibia. It is innervated by the tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1).
questions.question: The popliteus muscle 'unlocks' the knee from full extension by rotating the femur by how many degrees on the fixed tibia?

questions.explanation: The anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six spaces arise from the internal thoracic artery, which is a branch of the subclavian artery. These arteries anastomose with the posterior intercostal arteries. The internal thoracic artery descends behind the costal cartilages approximately half an inch from the lateral border of the sternum.
questions.question: Where do the upper six anterior intercostal arteries arise?

questions.explanation: The valleculae (spaces between the tongue base and epiglottis) receive sensory innervation from the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus). The glossopharyngeal nerve also contributes sensation to this region. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in the valleculae. These spaces are bounded by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds.
questions.question: The vallecular receives sensory innervation from which nerve?

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor innervation to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).
questions.question: Which nerve provides general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue?
At which level does the aortic arch begin?
questions.explanation: The aortic arch begins at the level of T4 as a continuation of the ascending aorta. It arches backwards and to the left, passing over the left main bronchus. The arch ends at the level of T4/5 by continuing as the descending thoracic aorta. The aortic arch lies entirely within the superior mediastinum.

Each foot has 26 bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges (the great toe has 2 phalanges; the other four toes each have 3 phalanges). Understanding foot bone anatomy is fundamental to podiatry, orthopaedics, and diagnosis of stress fractures, Lisfranc injuries, and other foot pathologies.
questions.question: Podiatry is the medical specialty dealing with the study and care of the feet. The foot has how many bones in total (tarsals + metatarsals + phalanges)?

questions.explanation: The right vagus nerve descends to the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior esophageal plexus, and continues into the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve. The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior esophageal plexus, and continues as the anterior gastric nerve.
questions.question: Where does the right vagus form plexus?

questions.explanation: The hepatic artery proper, ascending in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) as part of the portal triad, divides near the porta hepatis into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver. The right hepatic artery gives off the cystic artery to the gallbladder. Significant anatomical variation exists in hepatic arterial anatomy (occurring in up to 45% of individuals), including replaced or accessory right hepatic arteries from the superior mesenteric artery and replaced or accessory left hepatic arteries from the left gastric artery.
questions.question: The hepatic artery proper typically divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) emerges through the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle at approximately the L3/L4 level, unlike other branches of the lumbar plexus which emerge from its lateral border. After piercing psoas, it descends on the muscle's anterior surface, dividing into genital and femoral branches. The genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring to supply the cremaster muscle and scrotal/labial skin, while the femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery to supply skin over the femoral triangle.
questions.question: The genitofemoral nerve pierces which muscle?

questions.explanation: The kidneys typically extend from the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12) to the third lumbar vertebra (L3) on the posterior abdominal wall. The right kidney is slightly lower than the left due to the presence of the liver. Both kidneys move inferiorly with respiration, descending as much as 2.5 cm during diaphragmatic contraction.
questions.question: At which vertebral levels do the kidneys typically lie?

options: Distributes extensor force, coordinates intrinsic-extrinsic action
questions.explanation: The extensor expansion (extensor hood) distributes extensor digitorum force and coordinates intrinsic hand muscle action with extrinsic extensors. Intrinsic muscles insert into the expansion, enabling their unique MCP flexion with IP extension action. This complex structure allows coordinated finger movements essential for precision grip.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of extensor expansion?
What is the primary arterial supply to the scalp anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries (from the ophthalmic artery of internal carotid system) supply the anterior scalp. The superficial temporal artery supplies the lateral scalp. Posterior scalp receives blood from occipital and posterior auricular arteries from the external carotid system.

The external intercostal muscle is deficient anteriorly at the costochondral junction and is replaced by the external (anterior) intercostal membrane. This fibrous membrane continues the plane of the muscle to the sternum. The internal intercostal muscle conversely is deficient posteriorly at the angle of the rib.
questions.question: At which location is the external intercostal muscle deficient?

questions.explanation: A small area of the posterior surface of the stomach near the cardia (where the two layers of lesser omentum separate to enclose the stomach) is "bare" and in direct contact with the left crus of the diaphragm, lacking peritoneal covering. This represents the only part of the stomach not completely invested by peritoneum. The rest of the stomach is completely covered by visceral peritoneum: anteriorly and posteriorly by peritoneum continuous with the greater and lesser omenta, and along its curvatures where the gastrosplenic, gastrohepatic, and gastrocolic ligaments attach. The bare area can be a site where gastric perforation communicates directly with the retroperitoneum.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach is LEAST covered by peritoneum?
Which position elevates the diaphragm highest?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is highest in the supine position and after a large meal due to upward pressure from abdominal viscera. When lying on one side, the dependent (lower) diaphragm is considerably higher than the uppermost one. Position affects diaphragm function and is clinically relevant.

The hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and left subcostal vein. It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum, crosses at T8-9, and drains into the azygos vein. It receives lower left posterior intercostal veins.
questions.question: What forms the hemiazygos vein?

questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery passes through an opening (hiatus) in the interosseous membrane between the tibia and fibula to reach the anterior compartment. It runs down the entire length of the leg into the foot, where it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the ankle. It also gives the anterior tibial recurrent artery contributing to the genicular anastomosis.
questions.question: The anterior tibial artery passes through which structure to reach the anterior compartment of the leg?
options: Over the superior border of the interosseous membrane
Anterior to the interosseous membrane superficially
Through the fibular notch of the tibia
Through an opening in the interosseous membrane

questions.question: Which structure causes the first constriction of the oesophagus at 15 cm from the upper incisor teeth?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper oesophageal sphincter and creates the first physiological constriction at 15 cm from the upper incisors. This sphincter prevents air from entering the oesophagus during respiration and regulates food entry. It is a clinically significant site for foreign body impaction and stricture formation.

options: Roof: inferior fibula; walls: tibia bilaterally; floor: calcaneus
Roof: inferior tibia; walls: medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) malleoli; floor: trochlea tali
Roof: superior surface of talus; walls: tibia; floor: calcaneus
Roof: superior tibia; walls: talus on both sides; floor: navicular
Roof: fibula; walls: medial and lateral malleoli; floor: navicular
questions.question: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by three bony components. Which correctly describes the roof, walls, and floor?
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (mortise) is formed by: the roof (inferior surface of the tibia), the lateral wall (lateral malleolus from the fibula), the medial wall (medial malleolus from the tibia), and the floor (superior surface of the talus, the trochlea tali). This mortise-and-tenon configuration provides inherent bony stability, especially during dorsiflexion.

questions.question: What replaces thymic tissue in adults?
questions.explanation: In adults, the involuting thymus is progressively replaced by adipose (fatty) tissue. This normal age-related change is called thymic involution. Despite fatty replacement, some functional thymic tissue usually persists even in elderly individuals. On CT scans, the adult thymus appears as fatty tissue in the anterior mediastinum.

questions.question: What attaches the diaphragm to the xiphoid process?
questions.explanation: The sternal part of the diaphragm consists of two small muscular slips (or sometimes just fibrous tissue) that attach to the posterior surface of the xiphoid process. These are the smallest attachments of the diaphragm and may be absent, leaving a gap (the sternocostal triangle or foramen of Morgagni) through which superior epigastric vessels and lymphatics pass.

questions.question: The spleen is located in which abdominal region?
questions.explanation: The spleen is situated in the left hypochondriac region, lying obliquely along the long axis of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left upper quadrant. It is protected by the rib cage and cannot normally be palpated unless enlarged. The spleen is related anteriorly to the stomach (via the gastrosplenic ligament), posteriorly to the left kidney (via the splenorenal ligament), superiorly to the diaphragm, and inferiorly to the left colic flexure (supported by the phrenicocolic ligament). The splenic notch on its superior border is a characteristic feature visible on imaging.

The olecranon fits into the olecranon fossa during extension while the coronoid fits into the coronoid fossa during flexion. This reciprocal architecture allows full range elbow motion (0-150°) while providing bony stability. The radial fossa accommodates the radial head during flexion.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the olecranon-coronoid architecture?

questions.explanation: The right and left bundle branches divide into Purkinje fibers, which form a subendocardial network that rapidly conducts the impulse throughout the ventricular myocardium. Purkinje fibers are larger than regular cardiac myocytes with fewer myofibrils, specialized for rapid conduction rather than contraction. They ensure coordinated ventricular contraction from apex to base.
questions.question: Into which fibers do the bundle branches terminate?

questions.explanation: The pancreas produces protease inhibitors (particularly pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor, PSTI) that prevent premature activation of trypsinogen within the pancreas. Enzymes are also stored as inactive zymogens in secretory granules. Premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsinogen (which then activates other proteases) causes acute pancreatitis with autodigestion of pancreatic tissue.
questions.question: What prevents premature activation of pancreatic enzymes?

questions.explanation: commonly results from repetitive overhead throwing activities. This is particularly seen in baseball pitchers, tennis players, and swimmers. Repetitive impingement of the rotator cuff tendons under the acromion causes inflammation, degeneration, and potential tears.
questions.question: Which condition involves repetitive overhead throwing?

questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli), a dilated lymphatic sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, is located anterior to the bodies of L1 and L2 vertebrae, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm and the abdominal aorta, and to the right of the aorta. It receives the right and left lumbar lymphatic trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvic, and abdominal walls), the intestinal trunk (from pre-aortic nodes draining abdominal viscera), and sometimes the lower intercostal trunks. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to enter the posterior mediastinum, ultimately draining into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli is located at which vertebral level?
The suspensory ligament of the ovary contains which vessels?
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian artery (from abdominal aorta at L2) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully clamped and ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (connecting ovary to uterus) contains no significant vessels. The uterine artery reaches the uterus via the parametrium (base of broad ligament).

questions.question: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) arises from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and attaches to which femoral condyle?
options: Anterior surface of medial femoral condyle
questions.explanation: The ACL arises from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia (just posterior to the medial meniscus attachment) and attaches to the lateral condyle of the femur. It is the weaker of the two cruciate ligaments with relatively poor blood supply. It becomes taut in full extension and prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia.

The bronchial arteries supply the bronchial tree from the main bronchi to the respiratory bronchioles. Two left bronchial arteries arise from the descending thoracic aorta, and one right bronchial artery arises from the third right posterior intercostal artery. These vessels provide oxygenated blood to airway structures.
questions.question: Which arteries supply the bronchial tree?

questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch is the peritoneal reflection between the bladder and rectum in males. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males when upright and can contain loops of small intestine (ileum). Fluid collections or abscesses may accumulate here. In females, the analogous space is the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), which is deeper.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the rectovesical pouch in males?
The lamina papyracea forms the medial wall of which structure?
questions.explanation: The lamina papyracea (orbital plate) of the ethmoid bone forms the thin medial wall of the orbit. It separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells. The name papyracea (paper-like) reflects its extreme thinness. Ethmoidal infections can erode through this wall causing orbital cellulitis or abscess.

The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the anterior surface of the epiglottis to the upper border of the hyoid bone. The thyroepiglottic ligament attaches the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage. The epiglottis is also connected to the tongue by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds. These ligaments maintain epiglottic position during swallowing.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the epiglottis to the hyoid bone?
The foramen ovale transmits which additional structure besides V3?
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus. The accessory meningeal artery supplies the trigeminal ganglion and dura. Foramen ovale is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone.

questions.question: Which two muscles in the anterior thigh compartment cross BOTH the hip and knee joints?
questions.explanation: Both rectus femoris and sartorius cross both the hip and knee joints. Rectus femoris originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and inserts via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. Sartorius originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and inserts into the superior medial surface of the tibia. The three vasti only cross the knee joint.

The two sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis (medial and lateral heads). They protect the tendons from compression during weight-bearing and increase the mechanical advantage of flexor hallucis brevis. Sesamoiditis (inflammation of sesamoid bones) causes plantar pain under the first metatarsal head and is common in dancers and runners.
questions.question: Sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded in the tendons of which muscle?

questions.explanation: The tensor veli palatini opens the Eustachian tube during swallowing and yawning, equalizing middle ear pressure. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3), unlike other palatal muscles supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. The muscle also tenses the soft palate.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the tensor veli palatini muscle?
The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at which approximate age?
questions.explanation: The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at approximately 7-8 years of age. The secondary ossification centres of the hip bone (for the iliac crest, Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and ischial tuberosity) all fuse completely by 20-25 years of age.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies latissimus dorsi?
questions.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve (C7, C8) from the posterior cord supplies latissimus dorsi muscle. The nerve descends along the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal artery. Preservation of this nerve is important during axillary surgery to maintain shoulder function.

Piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior share innervation from L5, S1. They also share the same insertion into the upper border of the greater trochanter and the same action as lateral rotators of the hip joint. This common heritage is useful clinically in understanding hip pathology.
questions.question: Piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior share a common innervation. What is their shared nerve root?
What contains the pleural fluid normally?
questions.explanation: The pleural cavity normally contains a small amount of serous (pleural) fluid that acts as a lubricant between the visceral and parietal pleural surfaces. This fluid is continuously produced and absorbed, maintaining a thin film that facilitates smooth lung movement during respiration.

questions.question: The nasal bones articulate superiorly with which bone?
questions.explanation: The paired nasal bones articulate superiorly with the frontal bone at the frontonasal suture. Laterally, they attach to the frontal processes of the maxillae, and inferiorly to the upper lateral nasal cartilages. Fractures of the nasal bones are the most common facial fractures. The bones provide support for the nasal bridge.

questions.question: Which portion of the anal canal is derived from endoderm?
questions.explanation: The anal canal above the pectinate line is derived from endoderm (hindgut), while the portion below originates from ectoderm (proctodeum). This embryological distinction explains the different characteristics of the two regions: superior to the pectinate line, the mucosa is columnar, venous drainage is to the portal system via superior rectal veins, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes, and innervation is autonomic (insensitive to pain). Below the line, the epithelium is stratified squamous, venous drainage is systemic (middle and inferior rectal veins), lymph drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and sensory innervation is via the inferior rectal nerve (painful).

The diaphragmatic pleura is the portion of parietal pleura that covers the superior surface of the diaphragm. It reflects onto the thoracic wall to become continuous with the costal pleura. The diaphragmatic pleura receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally.
questions.question: Which pleura covers the diaphragm's superior surface?
The short head of biceps femoris differs from the other hamstrings in which critical way?
options: It originates from the rim of the acetabulum
It is supplied exclusively by the obturator nerve
Does not cross the hip joint; supplied by the common fibular nerve
It inserts into the medial tibial condyle distally
It is classified as a medial compartment muscle
questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris does not cross the hip joint (originating from the linea aspera, not the ischial tuberosity) and therefore cannot extend the hip. It is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve, unlike all other hamstrings which are supplied by the tibial division. It only flexes the knee and laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed.

The prostate gland lies immediately inferior to the bladder neck in males, surrounding the prostatic urethra. The base of the prostate is continuous with the bladder neck. Prostatic enlargement (benign prostatic hyperplasia or cancer) commonly causes urinary symptoms by compressing the prostatic urethra and elevating the bladder base.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the male bladder neck?
The ureter is crossed anteriorly at the pelvic brim by which vessel?
questions.explanation: The ureter is crossed anteriorly by the testicular vessels (in males) or ovarian vessels (in females) near the pelvic brim, as these vessels descend from their aortic origins at L2 level toward the deep inguinal ring (males) or ovary (females). The ureter then crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or proximal external iliac artery) before entering the pelvis. In females, the ureter is subsequently crossed by the uterine artery approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"), an important surgical relationship during hysterectomy. The superior vesical artery travels with the ureter in the pelvis but does not cross it.

questions.question: What connects the azygos and hemiazygos systems?
questions.explanation: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins cross from left to right behind the esophagus and aorta at the levels of T8-9 and T7 respectively to drain into the azygos vein. These cross-communications provide collateral venous drainage pathways between the left and right sides of the thorax.

questions.question: What lies posterior to the male urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: In males, the seminal vesicles and ampullae of the vas deferens lie posterior to the bladder base, and the rectum lies posterior to these structures, separated by the rectovesical fascia (Denonvilliers' fascia). The rectovesical pouch of peritoneum separates the upper part of the bladder from the rectum. In females, the vagina lies directly posterior to the bladder.

The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), provides the blood supply to the vermiform appendix. It runs through the free edge of the mesoappendix, making it vulnerable during surgical mobilization of the appendix. This is typically an end artery with minimal collateral supply, so thrombosis can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery may give off a recurrent branch that ascends toward the ileocecal junction. Variations include occasional origin from a posterior cecal artery or rarely from the superior mesenteric artery directly.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the vermiform appendix?

questions.explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle. This is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The nerve descends with the superior thyroid artery. Damage affects vocal cord tension and causes voice fatigue and difficulty with pitch variation.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm (both pleural and peritoneal surfaces). Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (from subphrenic abscess, ruptured spleen, perforated peptic ulcer, ectopic pregnancy, liver inflammation, or cholecystitis) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip (C3-C5 dermatomes) via the phrenic nerve. This is called Kehr's sign when associated with splenic rupture. The peripheral diaphragm receives sensory innervation from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, referring pain to the chest wall and upper abdomen.
questions.question: Which nerve may cause referred pain to the shoulder?

questions.explanation: In both lung roots, the arrangement from superior to inferior is: pulmonary artery (uppermost), bronchus (middle), pulmonary veins (lowermost). From anterior to posterior: pulmonary veins (most anterior), pulmonary artery, bronchus (most posterior). Hilar lymph nodes are scattered throughout.
questions.question: Which structure is most anterior in right lung root?

questions.explanation: The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion receiving preganglionic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus via the oculomotor nerve. Postganglionic fibers travel in short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. Sensory fibers from V1 and sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing. The ganglion lies posterolaterally in the orbit.
questions.question: The ciliary ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?
At what sound pressure level does the stapedius reflex typically activate?
questions.explanation: The stapedius muscle reflex activates bilaterally at sound levels above 80 dB SPL to protect the cochlea. This acoustic reflex increases ossicular chain stiffness and attenuates low-frequency sounds. Testing this reflex provides valuable information about facial nerve and auditory pathway integrity.

questions.question: Which structure opens into the descending duodenum at the major duodenal papilla?
questions.explanation: The hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) opens at the major duodenal papilla in the descending (second) part of the duodenum. This ampulla is formed by the union of the main pancreatic duct and common bile duct in most individuals. The sphincter of Oddi surrounds the ampulla controlling the flow of bile and pancreatic secretions.

The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, suspends the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian artery (from aorta) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament must be clamped and divided during oophorectomy. The ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus medially, while the broad ligament provides only indirect support via the mesovarium. The round ligament extends from uterus to labium majus via the inguinal canal.
questions.question: The ovary is suspended by which ligament from the pelvic wall?

questions.explanation: The quadrate lobe, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe (located between the gallbladder fossa and falciform ligament), functionally belongs to the left lobe as it receives its blood supply from the left hepatic artery and drains bile via the left hepatic duct. The functional division of the liver (Couinaud's classification) is based on vascular supply and biliary drainage rather than external anatomical features. The main portal fissure (containing the middle hepatic vein) separates functional right and left lobes, running from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC, placing the quadrate and caudate lobes functionally on the left.
questions.question: The quadrate lobe of the liver receives blood from which branch?

questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves inferiorly toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Via this arch, it contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones.
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the dorsum of the foot. It anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form which arch?
Which part of the duodenum contains the major duodenal papilla?
questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater) is located on the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum, approximately 8-10 cm distal to the pylorus. At this site, the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi. The minor duodenal papilla, located 2 cm proximal to the major papilla, receives the accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini) when present. This anatomical arrangement is crucial for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

The azygos vein receives: right superior intercostal vein, lower eight right posterior intercostal veins, right bronchial vein, middle esophageal veins, and the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins from the left side. It drains much of the thoracic wall and mediastinal structures.
questions.question: Which veins drain into the azygos vein?

questions.explanation: Pancreatic juice contains DNAase and RNAase (nucleases) that digest deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid respectively into nucleotides. These nucleotides are further broken down by intestinal enzymes into nucleosides and bases for absorption. The pancreas secretes all major classes of digestive enzymes: proteases, lipases, amylase, and nucleases, making it essential for complete digestion.
questions.question: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests nucleic acids?
Which structure lies posterior to the head of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava lies posterior to the head of the pancreas (separated by the right renal vein and sometimes the third part of the duodenum), along with the right renal artery and vein, aorta, and origin of the superior mesenteric artery. The superior mesenteric vein ascends posterior to the neck of the pancreas (not the head), where it joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. The common bile duct runs in a groove on (or through) the posterior surface of the pancreatic head before joining the main pancreatic duct.

questions.question: Which muscle closes the vestibule of the larynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The aryepiglotticus muscle closes the laryngeal vestibule during swallowing by pulling the arytenoid cartilages toward the epiglottis. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function. The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral margins of the laryngeal inlet.

The supraspinatus muscle initiates the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction. The middle fibers of the deltoid then take over from 15-90 degrees. Beyond 90 degrees, scapular rotation by trapezius and serratus anterior is essential for achieving full overhead abduction.
questions.question: Which muscles initiate the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction?
Which duct drains the right side of the thorax?
questions.explanation: The right lymphatic duct receives lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, right upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart, and right surface of the liver. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. This duct drains into the right venous angle.

Below the arcuate line (linea semicircularis), located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis, the posterior rectus sheath is absent. At this level, all three aponeurotic layers (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) pass anteriorly to the rectus abdominis muscle, leaving only the transversalis fascia and peritoneum posteriorly. This anatomical arrangement creates a relative weakness that may be involved in direct inguinal hernias. The inferior epigastric vessels pierce the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line to enter the rectus sheath.
questions.question: The rectus sheath is absent posteriorly below which line?
The fibrous capsule anteriorly is replaced by which three structures from proximal to distal?
options: Patellar ligament, ACL, and synovial membrane
Fibular collateral ligament, patella, and patellar ligament
Patellar retinacula, PCL, and iliotibial tract
Tibial collateral ligament, patella, and patellar tendon
Quadriceps tendon, patella, and patellar ligament
questions.explanation: Anteriorly, the fibrous layer of the knee joint capsule is replaced by the quadriceps tendon (above the patella), the patella itself, and the patellar ligament (below the patella). These three structures provide strong anterior protection. The patellar retinacula blend with the capsule laterally providing additional support.

The left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein drains into the left renal vein, while the right gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein also receives the left suprarenal vein and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein. This arrangement makes the left testicular vein more prone to varicocele formation.
questions.question: Which vein drains into the left renal vein?
Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the lumbar triangle of Marcille?
questions.explanation: The lumbosacral triangle (Marcille's triangle) has the medial border of psoas major forming its lateral boundary, with the body of L5 vertebra medially and the ala of sacrum as its base. The floor consists of the transverse process of L5 and the iliolumbar ligament. This triangle is clinically significant as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at its lateral angle, making it an important landmark during pelvic surgery.

The azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus at T4 to drain into the posterior aspect of the superior vena cava. This creates a communication between the SVC and IVC systems, providing collateral circulation if either is obstructed. The azygos arch is visible on chest X-rays.
questions.question: Where does the azygos vein terminate?

questions.explanation: The tensor veli palatini muscle opens the auditory (Eustachian) tube during swallowing by pulling on the membranous lateral wall. The levator veli palatini also contributes. Salpingopharyngeus assists in opening the tube. This mechanism equalizes middle ear pressure with atmospheric pressure.
questions.question: Which muscle opens the auditory tube during swallowing?

questions.explanation: The stapedius muscle is innervated by the stapedial branch of the facial nerve. It dampens excessive ossicular chain movement in response to loud sounds above 80 dB. Facial nerve paralysis results in hyperacusis (sound sensitivity) due to stapedius muscle dysfunction.
questions.question: The stapedius muscle is innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people and from the left circumflex artery in 40%. The SA node is located in the superior part of the crista terminalis near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It is the primary pacemaker of the heart, initiating approximately 60-100 beats per minute.
questions.question: Which artery typically supplies the SA node?
Which part of the stomach has the highest concentration of parietal cells?
questions.explanation: The fundus and upper body of the stomach contain the highest concentration of parietal cells in the gastric glands. The cardiac region contains mainly mucous-secreting cells. The pyloric region contains mainly mucous cells and G cells (which secrete gastrin). This distribution reflects the functional specialization of different gastric regions.

questions.question: Which cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The lateral cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery (behind pectoralis minor). The medial cord lies medially and the posterior cord lies posteriorly to the second part. Below pectoralis minor, the cords give rise to their terminal branches.

The porta hepatis transmits the portal vein, proper hepatic artery (and its right and left branches), right and left hepatic ducts, nerves (sympathetic and parasympathetic), and lymphatic vessels. These structures, except the hepatic ducts, enter the liver while the ducts exit. The portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct) is enclosed by the hepatoduodenal ligament at the free edge of the lesser omentum.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the porta hepatis?

questions.explanation: In healthy adults, the apex beat (point of maximal impulse) is located in the 5th left intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line. This represents the most inferior and lateral point where the cardiac impulse can be felt. In children, the apex beat is one interspace higher (4th space). Displacement suggests cardiac enlargement or chest deformity.
questions.question: Which intercostal space corresponds to the apex beat?
Which layer directly surrounds the kidney outside the fibrous capsule?
questions.explanation: Perirenal (perinephric) fat is a layer of adipose tissue that lies outside the fibrous capsule and inside the renal fascia (Gerota's fascia). It cushions and protects the kidney. The renal fascia encloses both the kidney and suprarenal gland, while pararenal fat lies external to the renal fascia and forms part of the retroperitoneal fat.

The pharynx extends from the base of the skull to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6, where it becomes continuous with the esophagus. This landmark corresponds to the level where the cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter. The transition zone is clinically significant for foreign body impaction and surgical access considerations.
questions.question: At what vertebral level does the pharynx transition to the esophagus?
The cricoarytenoid joint allows which specific movement of the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The cricoarytenoid joint permits rotation and sliding movements of the arytenoid cartilages, which directly control vocal cord abduction and adduction. Tension changes occur primarily through cricothyroid joint movement, not cricoarytenoid articulation. The L-shaped base of the arytenoid pivots at the cricoarytenoid joint to open or close the rima glottidis.

A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts. The inferior mediastinum is further subdivided into anterior, middle, and posterior mediastina. This anatomical division is useful for localizing pathology on imaging.
questions.question: Which plane divides the mediastinum horizontally?

questions.explanation: The apex of the heart is formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and is the most inferior and lateral cardiac point. It lies deep to the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line in adults (4th space in children). The apex beat (point of maximal impulse) can normally be palpated at this location during systole.
questions.question: What is the most inferior part of the heart?
How many tendons insert into the greater trochanter of the femur?
questions.explanation: Seven tendons insert into the greater trochanter: gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, piriformis, obturator internus, obturator externus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior. The concentration of these insertions makes the greater trochanter a key landmark in hip anatomy. Avulsion fractures at this site carry significant functional implications.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes lie along the sternum?
questions.explanation: The parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum. They receive lymph from the anterior chest wall, medial breast, diaphragm, and upper abdominal wall. Efferents drain to the bronchomediastinal trunks and brachiocephalic veins.

The pleuroperitoneal membranes close the fetal communication between the pleural and peritoneal cavities. Failure of these membranes to close completely results in congenital diaphragmatic hernias, most commonly through the foramen of Bochdalek (posterolaterally). This is more common on the left side.
questions.question: What closes the pleuroperitoneal canal?

questions.explanation: The optic nerve is covered by all three meningeal layers (dura, arachnoid, and pia) from the sclera to the optic canal. At the canal, the dura becomes continuous with the periosteum of the orbit. Increased intracranial pressure can cause papilledema due to continuity of the subarachnoid space around the optic nerve.
questions.question: The optic nerve is surrounded by which meningeal layers?

questions.explanation: Each renal artery typically divides into five segmental arteries: apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior, and posterior. These are functional end arteries with no significant anastomoses, meaning occlusion of one causes infarction of that segment. This segmental anatomy allows partial nephrectomy without affecting remaining segments. Four segmental arteries arise from the anterior division; one (posterior) from the posterior division.
questions.question: How many segmental arteries typically supply each kidney?

questions.explanation: The central tendon of the diaphragm is shaped like three leaves (trifoliate). It has no bony attachments but is partially fused with the inferior surface of the fibrous pericardium. All the muscular fibers of the diaphragm insert into this central tendon.
questions.question: What shape is the central tendon?
The gastrocolic ligament connects the stomach to which structure?
questions.explanation: The gastrocolic ligament, part of the greater omentum, connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon. It contains the right and left gastroepiploic vessels along the greater curvature and represents the anterior two layers of the greater omentum before they descend and fold back. Division of the gastrocolic ligament provides surgical access to the lesser sac (omental bursa) and is a key step in gastric surgery, transverse colectomy, and pancreatic surgery. The avascular plane (relatively avascular window) between the gastroepiploic vessels and transverse colon can be developed to enter the lesser sac with minimal bleeding.

The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis, normally obliterates during the first year of life except for its distal portion, which remains as the tunica vaginalis (a closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis). The parietal layer of tunica vaginalis lines the inner surface of the scrotum (internal spermatic fascia), while the visceral layer covers the testis and epididymis. Failure of processus vaginalis obliteration leads to patent processus (communicating hydrocele) or congenital indirect inguinal hernia. The gubernaculum guides testicular descent.
questions.question: The processus vaginalis gives rise to which structure?
The long plantar ligament, an important supporter of the lateral longitudinal arch, passes from the calcaneus to which structures?
questions.explanation: The long plantar ligament (longest ligament in the foot) passes from the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the ridges on the plantar surface of the cuboid and the bases of the 3rd-5th metatarsals. It is a primary support for the lateral longitudinal arch. In combination with the short plantar (plantar calcaneocuboid) ligament, it forms the floor of the fibularis longus tendon groove on the cuboid.
options: Sustentaculum tali of calcaneus and talus
All five metatarsal bases and the navicular
Base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform
Plantar surface of cuboid and bases of 3rd–5th metatarsals

questions.explanation: Secretin, produced by S cells in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to acid, stimulates pancreatic ductal cells (including centroacinar cells) to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid. This neutralizes gastric acid and creates the optimal pH (7-8) for pancreatic enzyme function. Secretin also inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastric emptying, providing negative feedback control.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?

questions.explanation: The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula and then divides into the deep and superficial fibular nerves. At this point it is subcutaneous and highly vulnerable to injury from fractures, tight plasters, or prolonged cross-legged sitting. Injury causes foot drop due to paralysis of the anterior and lateral leg compartment muscles.
questions.question: The common fibular nerve winds around which specific part of the fibula to divide into its terminal branches?

questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensory innervation to the anal canal below the pectinate line, making this region sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature. The inferior rectal nerve also provides motor innervation to the external anal sphincter. Above the pectinate line, the anal canal receives autonomic innervation (from inferior hypogastric plexus), making it insensitive to pain but responsive to stretch. This difference explains why internal hemorrhoids (above pectinate line) are painless while external hemorrhoids (below the line) are painful.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation below the pectinate line?

questions.explanation: is a small triangular muscle that assists the triceps brachii in elbow extension. It lies on the lateral aspect of the elbow, blending with the triceps. Both muscles are supplied by the radial nerve and work together to extend the elbow.
questions.question: Which muscle assists triceps in elbow extension?
The ACL is slack during knee flexion and taut during full extension. It prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia and which other movement?
questions.explanation: The ACL prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia (or anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur) and hyperextension of the knee joint. When the knee is flexed at a right angle, the tibia cannot be pulled anteriorly because it is held by the intact ACL. ACL rupture is detected by a positive anterior drawer test.

The areola glands of Montgomery are intermediate in structure between lactiferous and sweat glands. They are greatly enlarged in pregnancy and lactation as subcutaneous tubercles. Their oily secretion acts as a protective lubricant during lactation, preventing nipple cracking.
questions.question: What are Montgomery's glands?

questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. It has orbital, palpebral, and lacrimal parts. The muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII). The palpebral portion produces gentle closure (blinking), while the orbital portion produces tight closure (squinting). Facial nerve palsy causes inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos).
questions.question: Which muscle closes the eyelid?

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland drains to prelaryngeal, pretracheal, and paratracheal lymph nodes, which then drain to deep cervical nodes. Lymphatic drainage follows the arterial supply. Understanding lymphatic pathways is crucial for thyroid cancer staging and surgical planning. Superior gland drainage differs from inferior drainage patterns.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the thyroid gland?
Which papillae on the tongue do NOT contain taste buds?
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae but do not contain taste buds; they provide the rough texture of the tongue. Fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae all contain taste buds. The circumvallate papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis.

The vas deferens crosses superior to the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, then curves medially, crossing over (anterior to) the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder. At the inguinal region, the vas deferens "hooks" around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery, crossing it from lateral to medial as it exits the deep inguinal ring. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. The vas is easily palpable in the spermatic cord and feels like a firm cord or thick string.
questions.question: The vas deferens crosses which vessel during its pelvic course?
The splenic artery typically runs along which organ's superior border?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery, the largest branch of the celiac trunk, takes a characteristically tortuous course to the left along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas, giving off numerous small pancreatic branches en route. It runs posterior to the stomach within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-6 terminal branches that enter the splenic hilum. Before reaching the spleen, the artery gives off the left gastroepiploic artery and short gastric arteries, which pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the greater curvature and fundus of the stomach respectively.

questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately medial to the kidney?
questions.explanation: The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially to each kidney, forming part of its posterior relation. A psoas abscess can cause confusion with renal pathology due to this proximity. The quadratus lumborum lies directly posterior to the mid-portion of the kidney, while the transversus abdominis and its aponeurosis lie posterolaterally.

questions.question: Which vein arches over the right bronchus?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus at the level of T4 before draining into the superior vena cava. This creates a characteristic arch visible on chest radiographs. The azygos arch relationship to the bronchus is an important anatomical landmark.

The azygos vein lies posterior and to the right of the esophagus in the posterior mediastinum. The descending aorta lies posterior and to the left of the esophagus. The thoracic duct lies posterior to the esophagus. The vagus nerves form plexuses around the esophagus.
questions.question: Which vein lies posterior to the esophagus?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all interossei muscles (both dorsal and palmar). The deep branch of the ulnar nerve enters the palm and curves around the hook of the hamate to supply these intrinsic hand muscles. Ulnar nerve palsy causes weakness of finger abduction and adduction.
questions.question: What nerve supplies the dorsal interossei muscles?
Which hip joint ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane and attaches medially to the ischium just posteroinferior to the acetabulum?
questions.explanation: The ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane. It attaches medially to the ischium posteroinferior to the acetabulum and laterally to the greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament. Like all three extracapsular hip ligaments, it becomes taut during extension, stabilizing the joint in the standing position.

questions.question: How does esophageal venous drainage occur in thorax?
questions.explanation: The middle third of the esophagus (thoracic portion) drains into the azygos venous system. The upper third drains into brachiocephalic veins, and the lower third into the portal system (via left gastric vein). These represent important sites of portosystemic anastomosis where esophageal varices can develop in portal hypertension.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explanation: The posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle. The anterior border of trapezius forms the posterior boundary, and the middle third of the clavicle forms the base. The apex is where the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius meet at the superior nuchal line.

The bare area of the liver is the triangular region on the posterior surface that is in direct contact with the diaphragm, devoid of peritoneal covering. This area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary ligament (superior and inferior layers) and is continuous with the groove for the inferior vena cava. The bare area represents the part of the liver that remained adherent to the diaphragm during embryological development. Small diaphragmatic veins in this region drain directly from the liver into the IVC without forming hepatic veins, and the right phrenic artery contributes to the vascular supply of this area.
questions.question: The bare area of the liver is related to which organ?

questions.explanation: The floor (inferior boundary) of the lesser sac is formed by the transverse colon and its mesocolon, along with the fusion of the anterior and posterior layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac (omental bursa) is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; posteriorly by the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and posterior abdominal wall; superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac are typically detected as fluid between the stomach and pancreas on imaging.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the lesser sac?
Which of the following is NOT among the structures passing through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits five structures: the pudendal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, internal pudendal artery and vein, and the tendon of obturator internus. The sciatic nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen. The lesser sciatic foramen enables re-entry into the perineum from the gluteal region.

questions.question: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve longer?
questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer than the right because of the embryological descent of the heart and great vessels. As the heart descends from the neck into the thorax, it carries the aortic arch (and the nerve looping under it) downward. The right subclavian artery descends less, so the right nerve is shorter.

There are 15-20 lactiferous ducts that open by the same number of openings on the summit of the nipple. Each duct drains one lobe of the mammary gland. Deep to the areola, each duct has a dilated portion called the lactiferous sinus where milk can be stored.
questions.question: How many lactiferous duct openings are on nipple?

questions.explanation: The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint in the body, primarily classified as a hinge-type synovial joint. It has two articulations: the tibiofemoral joint (femur with tibia, bearing most body weight) and the patellofemoral joint (femur with patella). Despite being hinge-like, the knee also allows rotation during the screw-home mechanism.
questions.question: Despite its complexity with two articulations, the knee joint is primarily classified as which type of synovial joint?
The superior deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from which structure?
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil drains to the superior deep cervical nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric node at the angle of the jaw. The soft palate and posterior tongue also drain to these nodes. The jugulodigastric node is also called the tonsillar node due to enlargement during tonsillitis.

Fibularis longus crosses the sole of the foot diagonally in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, inserting into the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This diagonal course provides critical support to the transverse arch by pulling the first metatarsal medially and maintaining the dome of the transverse arch. It is the most important muscular support for this arch.
questions.question: Which muscle crosses the sole diagonally in a groove on the cuboid, and in so doing provides the most important muscular support for the transverse arch?

questions.explanation: The coracoacromial ligament runs between the coracoid process and acromion of the scapula. Unlike other shoulder ligaments, it does not cross a joint or permit movement. It forms part of the coraco-acromial arch that prevents superior displacement of the humeral head.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the coracoid process to the acromion of the scapula?

questions.explanation: In the thorax, the esophagus is supplied by esophageal branches arising directly from the anterior aspect of the descending thoracic aorta. Additional supply comes from the inferior thyroid artery superiorly and left gastric artery inferiorly. Bronchial arteries also contribute small branches. Venous drainage follows a similar pattern.
questions.question: Which vessels supply the esophagus in thorax?
Which structure forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum is a thick connective tissue structure forming the roof of the carpal tunnel. It bridges between the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally. This converts the carpal arch into a tunnel through which flexor tendons and median nerve pass.

questions.question: The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of which sacral segment?
questions.explanation: The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of S2. This is a clinically important landmark for epidural and spinal anesthesia, as well as for assessing pelvic symmetry in musculoskeletal examination. The highest point of the iliac crest corresponds to the level of L4, used for lumbar puncture guidance.

questions.question: The mental foramen typically lies below which tooth?
questions.explanation: The mental foramen is typically located on the lateral surface of the mandible below the second premolar tooth or between the first and second premolars. It transmits the mental nerve and vessels (terminal branches of the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle). The foramen position varies with age and tooth loss. It is a landmark for inferior alveolar nerve block.

questions.question: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, defined as the midpoint between which two bony landmarks?
options: Pubic tubercle and anterior superior iliac spine
Medial malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine
Inguinal ligament and the femoral condyle
Anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
Pubic crest and posterior superior iliac spine
questions.explanation: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. At this point the femoral artery lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve. This is distinct from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, which overlies the femoral canal.

questions.question: Where do anterior intercostal lymphatics drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the anterior part of intercostal spaces drain into anterior intercostal nodes that lie along the internal thoracic artery. From these nodes, lymph passes to the parasternal nodes. Posterior intercostal lymphatics drain into posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.

questions.question: Which vein forms the continuation of the sigmoid sinus?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid arteries. At the base of the neck, it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. The vein receives the facial, lingual, pharyngeal, and thyroid veins.

The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments stabilize the sacrum, prevent its rotation under body weight, and form both sciatic foramina together with bones. They do not transmit the obturator nerve, which exits through the obturator foramen to supply the medial compartment of the thigh via its anterior and posterior divisions.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments?
options: Stabilize the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint
Prevent rotation of sacrum by vertebral column weight
Form the greater sciatic foramen with bones
Transmit the obturator nerve to the medial thigh
Form the lesser sciatic foramen with bones

questions.question: Which structure separates the tympanic cavity into superior and inferior compartments?
questions.explanation: The tympanic cavity is a single air-filled space without compartmentalization, though the articular disc divides the temporomandibular joint into compartments. The cavity extends into mastoid air cells posteriorly via the aditus ad antrum. The Eustachian tube provides communication with the nasopharynx.

questions.question: Full knee flexion may kink which artery, explaining the functional importance of the genicular anastomosis as collateral circulation?
questions.explanation: Full knee flexion may kink the popliteal artery, explaining why the genicular anastomosis is functionally important: it provides collateral circulation to maintain blood supply to the leg even when the popliteal artery is kinked. This anastomosis is formed by branches of the popliteal, femoral, lateral femoral circumflex, and anterior tibial arteries.

options: Bases of all five proximal phalanges
Bases of all five metatarsal bones
Heads of all metatarsals and bases of proximal phalanges
Only the first metatarsophalangeal joint exclusively
All tarsal bones as a group
questions.question: The plantar aponeurosis is the most important passive structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity to which structures?
questions.explanation: The plantar aponeurosis (plantar fascia) stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity (medial tubercle) to the heads of all metatarsals and the bases of the proximal phalanges. During toe extension (dorsiflexion) in push-off phase of gait, this aponeurosis is tensioned, raising the arch in a windlass mechanism. Plantar fasciitis involves inflammation at the calcaneal attachment.

questions.question: The fovea capitis of the femoral head transmits blood from which artery to the femoral head?
questions.explanation: The fovea capitis transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur). This vascular route is clinically important, as fractures of the femoral neck can disrupt primary blood supply and lead to avascular necrosis.

questions.question: The ureter crosses which muscle as it descends?
questions.explanation: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle in the abdomen, passing over the tips of the lumbar vertebral transverse processes. It is crossed anteriorly by the testicular/ovarian vessels and runs posterior to the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. At the pelvic brim, the ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or external iliac artery) to enter the pelvis, where it runs along the lateral pelvic wall before turning medially to reach the bladder. In females, it passes beneath the uterine artery ("water under the bridge").

questions.question: The gastrosplenic ligament contains which vessels?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament, a peritoneal fold connecting the greater curvature of the stomach (fundus region) to the hilum of the spleen, contains the short gastric arteries and veins (vasa brevia). These 4-6 small vessels branch from the splenic artery and vein near the splenic hilum to supply the gastric fundus. The left gastroepiploic vessels run in the greater omentum along the greater curvature, while the splenic vessels themselves course through the splenorenal ligament connecting the spleen to the left kidney, along with the tail of the pancreas.

questions.question: Which nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve is formed from cervical nerve roots C3, C4, and C5 ("C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"). It provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. The long course from neck to diaphragm reflects the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region.

The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, extending from the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis. It contains the portal triad (portal vein posteriorly, common bile duct anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery proper anteriorly and to the left) and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The hepatoduodenal ligament can be compressed manually (Pringle maneuver) to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding inflow to the liver. The gastrohepatic ligament forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum.
questions.question: Which ligament forms the free edge of the lesser omentum?

questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle. Compression at this site causes posterior interosseous syndrome with weakness of finger and thumb extensors but preserved wrist extension. The superficial branch of the radial nerve does not pass through supinator.
questions.question: What nerve passes through the supinator muscle?
The anterior ethmoidal foramen transmits which structures?
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal foramen in the medial orbital wall transmits the anterior ethmoidal nerve (from nasociliary) and vessels (from ophthalmic artery).
