These structures supply the anterior ethmoidal air cells, frontal sinus, and upper nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the ethmoid and frontal bones at the frontoethmoidal suture.

The optic canal in the lesser wing of the sphenoid transmits the optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery. The central retinal vein drains alongside within the optic nerve sheath. The canal opens into the posterior orbit and connects the middle cranial fossa with the orbital cavity.
questions.question: The optic canal transmits which two structures?

options: Lymphatics and loose connective tissue; femoral hernia
Femoral artery and nerve; femoral hernia
questions.explanation: The femoral canal, the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally contains lymphatics and loose connective tissue. It is the site of femoral hernias, which are more common in women (due to their wider pelvis and femoral ring). Femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (unlike inguinal hernias above and medial to it). They are at high risk of strangulation due to the rigid femoral ring.
questions.question: The femoral canal, the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, contains which structures and is the site of which type of hernia?

questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the skull through the foramen spinosum. It supplies the dura mater and inner table of the skull. Rupture of this artery causes epidural hematoma, typically from temporal bone fractures.
questions.question: Which branch of the external carotid artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum?
What does the lesser splanchnic nerve supply?
questions.explanation: The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from T10-11 ganglia, pierces the diaphragm, and synapses in the aorticorenal ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation primarily to the kidneys and suprarenal glands. Some fibers may also reach midgut derivatives. The nerve carries both efferent sympathetic and visceral afferent fibers.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of Wharton's duct?
questions.explanation: Wharton's duct (submandibular duct) is approximately 5 cm long and opens at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum. The duct runs forward on the hyoglossus muscle between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves. Stone formation is more common in this duct than in Stensen's duct due to its upward course and mucoid secretions.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the upper third of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the upper two-thirds of the anal canal above the pectinate line. The middle rectal arteries (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal arteries (from internal pudendal) supply the lower third. This mixed blood supply creates a watershed area prone to ischemia.

questions.question: The prostate is divided into how many lobes?
questions.explanation: The prostate gland is classically described as having five lobes: anterior (fibromuscular, no glandular tissue), posterior (palpable on digital rectal exam, common site of carcinoma), median (between ejaculatory ducts, may enlarge to cause bladder outlet obstruction), and right and left lateral lobes (largest, common site of benign prostatic hyperplasia). Modern zonal anatomy describes peripheral zone (70%, site of most cancers), central zone (25%, around ejaculatory ducts), transitional zone (5%, surrounds urethra, site of BPH), and anterior fibromuscular stroma. The median lobe may project into the bladder when enlarged, causing urinary symptoms.

questions.question: Which structure lies within Calot's triangle?
questions.explanation: Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) is bounded by the cystic duct inferiorly, common hepatic duct medially, and inferior surface of the liver (or right lobe) superiorly. Within this triangle lies the cystic artery (typically arising from the right hepatic artery) and Lund's lymph node (Calot's node), which may be enlarged in cholecystitis or cholangitis. The triangle serves as a crucial surgical landmark during laparoscopic cholecystectomy for identifying and safely isolating the cystic duct and artery (the "critical view of safety") before ligation and division. Anatomical variations in this region are common and must be carefully identified.

questions.question: Which structure forms the falciform ligament's free edge?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) is the obliterated umbilical vein that runs in the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. It joins the left branch of the portal vein at the inferior end of the fissure for the ligamentum teres. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, forming caput medusae.

The central tendon is a strong aponeurosis of dense fibrous tissue forming the central portion of the diaphragm. It is trifoliate (three-leafed) in shape, resembling a clover leaf. The heart rests on its superior surface within the pericardium. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right leaflet with the middle leaflet.
questions.question: What comprises the central tendon of the diaphragm?
Which layer of the gut wall contains Meissner's plexus?
questions.explanation: Meissner's (submucosal) plexus is located in the submucosa between the inner circular and the mucosa layers. It primarily regulates secretion and blood flow in the gut wall. The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers and primarily controls motility. Together these form the enteric nervous system.

questions.question: Where does the left inferior phrenic vein drain?
questions.explanation: The left inferior phrenic vein is usually doubled: one part drains into the inferior vena cava, while the other drains into the left suprarenal vein. The right inferior phrenic vein drains directly into the IVC. The superior phrenic vein (right side) also drains into the IVC.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the transverse mesocolon?
questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) and middle colic veins (to superior mesenteric vein) pass through the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon. The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the descending duodenum, serving as an important surgical landmark dividing the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The superior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, while the inferior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the peritoneum, not within the mesocolon itself.

The apex of the axilla forms the cervicoaxillary canal, providing passage between the neck and axilla. It is bounded by the first rib medially, the clavicle anteriorly, and the superior border of the scapula posteriorly. Arteries, veins, lymphatics, and nerves traverse this opening to reach or leave the upper limb.
options: First rib, clavicle, and superior scapular border
questions.question: Which structures form the boundaries of the cervicoaxillary canal (apex of axilla)?

questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine draining from the collecting ducts. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces per kidney. Two to three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.
questions.question: What structure indents the apex of each renal pyramid?

questions.explanation: The average weight of a healthy adult spleen is approximately 150 grams (about 7 ounces), though this can vary considerably. A useful mnemonic for splenic dimensions is the "odd numbers rule": 1 inch thick, 3 inches wide, 5 inches long, 7 ounces in weight, and related to ribs 9-11. The spleen can enlarge significantly in disease states (splenomegaly).
questions.question: What is the average weight of a normal adult spleen?

questions.explanation: In the female pelvis, the uterine artery crosses superior (above) to the ureter near the lateral fornix of the vagina - remembered by the phrase "water under the bridge." This relationship is clinically crucial during hysterectomy to avoid inadvertent ureteric injury during ligation of the uterine artery. The ureter runs along the lateral wall of the pelvis to reach the bladder.
questions.question: Which vessel crosses anterior to the ureter in the female pelvis?

questions.explanation: The splenic artery gives off the short gastric arteries (vasa brevia, 4-6 vessels) near the splenic hilum, which pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the fundus of the stomach. The splenic artery also gives off the left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, which runs along the greater curvature in the gastrocolic ligament. The left gastric artery arises from the celiac trunk (not splenic artery), while the right gastric and gastroduodenal arteries arise from the hepatic artery proper and common hepatic artery respectively. The short gastric vessels create collateral circulation to the stomach and must be ligated during splenectomy.
questions.question: The splenic artery gives off which gastric vessels?

questions.explanation: The fibrous pericardium is the tough, inelastic outer layer of the pericardial sac composed of dense fibrous connective tissue. It prevents overdistention of the heart, protects against infection from surrounding structures, and anchors the heart in the mediastinum. It is continuous superiorly with the adventitia of the great vessels and inferiorly with the central tendon of the diaphragm.
questions.question: Which structure forms the fibrous outer layer of the pericardium?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins as the cisterna chyli anterior to L1 vertebra, formed by lumbar and intestinal trunks. It ascends through the aortic hiatus into the thorax. At the root of the neck, it arches forward to enter the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).
questions.question: The thoracic duct begins at which vertebral level?
The posterior fontanelle is located at which suture junction?
questions.explanation: The posterior fontanelle (lambda) is located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures where the occipital and parietal bones meet. It is triangular and smaller than the anterior fontanelle. The posterior fontanelle typically closes by 2-3 months of age. Delayed closure may indicate hydrocephalus or skeletal dysplasia.

questions.question: Where is Bochdalek's foramen located?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Bochdalek (pleuroperitoneal canal) is located posterolaterally in the diaphragm. Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close this opening results in a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. These hernias are more common on the left side and can allow abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax.

The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the sartorius, and medially by the adductor longus. Its floor is formed by the iliopsoas laterally and the pectineus medially. Its roof is the fascia lata and cribriform fascia. It contains the femoral nerve, artery, vein, and deep inguinal lymph nodes arranged laterally to medially (NAVEL from lateral).
options: Inguinal ligament, sartorius, and adductor longus
Inguinal ligament, adductor magnus, and iliopsoas
Iliac crest, sartorius, and adductor longus
Inguinal ligament, rectus femoris, and adductor magnus
questions.question: The femoral triangle is bounded by which three structures?
The anal columns (of Morgagni) are found in which part of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The anal columns of Morgagni are 6-10 permanent longitudinal mucosal folds in the upper 15 mm of the anal canal, above the pectinate line, containing terminal radicles of the superior rectal veins (portal system). The lower ends of adjacent columns are connected by anal valves (semilunar mucosal folds), forming the pectinate (dentate) line. Superior to each valve is a small recess called an anal sinus, into which anal glands open. The columns have a plum-red color in living subjects due to the underlying internal rectal venous plexus, and internal hemorrhoids develop from these vascular columns.

questions.question: The three fascial compartments of the thigh are separated by septa passing from the fascia lata to which bony structure?
questions.explanation: Three fascial septa pass from the inner aspect of the fascia lata to the linea aspera of the femur, dividing the thigh into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments. Each compartment has distinct nerves, muscles, and vessels. Understanding compartment anatomy is critical in managing thigh compartment syndrome following trauma.

questions.question: Which structure forms the most concave impression on the splenic visceral surface?
questions.explanation: The gastric impression is the largest and most concave of the impressions on the splenic visceral surface, reflecting contact with the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach. It lies between the superior and intermediate borders. Other impressions include renal (from left kidney), colic (from splenic flexure), and pancreatic (from pancreatic tail).

questions.question: Which structure lies in both superior and middle mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves pass through both the superior and middle mediastinum as they descend from the neck to the diaphragm. Similarly, the superior vena cava lies in both regions. The thymus extends from superior to anterior mediastinum. Structures can span multiple mediastinal compartments.

questions.question: Where does the female urethra open externally?
questions.explanation: The female external urethral orifice opens into the vestibule, the space between the labia minora, approximately 2.5 cm posterior to the clitoris and immediately anterior to the vaginal opening. The orifice is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter and may be difficult to visualize in some women. Paraurethral (Skene's) glands open on either side of the orifice.

questions.question: Where does the middle cardiac vein run?
questions.explanation: The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus at its termination. It drains the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum, corresponding to the territory of the posterior interventricular artery. It is the second largest cardiac vein.

questions.question: The obturator internus exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen. Where does its tendon turn to insert?
options: Directly into the lesser trochanter of the proximal femur
Into the ischial tuberosity rather than into the trochanter
Into the rim of the acetabulum directly without turning
Turns 90° around the ischium then inserts into the greater trochanter's upper border
Into the trochanteric fossa on the medial femur
questions.explanation: The obturator internus tendon exits through the lesser sciatic foramen, turns nearly 90 degrees around the smooth lesser sciatic notch (using the ischium as a pulley), and then inserts into the upper border of the greater trochanter of the femur. The gemelli muscles (superior and inferior) arise from the edges of the lesser sciatic notch and merge with the obturator internus tendon, acting as its 'cheeks.'

questions.question: Which part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The third (horizontal or inferior) part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the right psoas major muscle, the right ureter, and the right testicular/ovarian vessels at approximately the L3 vertebral level. This portion of the duodenum runs transversely from right to left and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein, with the root of the mesentery of the small intestine crossing it obliquely. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can occur when the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly.

At the lower esophagus, esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal system, draining to portal vein) anastomose with esophageal veins draining the middle third of the esophagus into the azygos system (systemic circulation to SVC). In portal hypertension, these anastomoses dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing massive hematemesis. This is one of four main portosystemic anastomoses (others: rectum, umbilicus, retroperitoneal). The left gastric vein ascends along the lesser curvature to drain directly into the portal vein, receiving esophageal tributaries that create the anastomosis.
questions.question: Which vein forms a portosystemic anastomosis at the esophagus?

questions.explanation: The posterior intercostal veins lie deepest in the costal grooves and contain valves that direct blood flow posteriorly. The neurovascular bundle arrangement from superior to inferior is vein-artery-nerve (VAN). The veins are the largest and most superior structures in this arrangement.
questions.question: Which structure lies deepest in the costal groove?

questions.explanation: The cardiac impression on the left lung is larger than that on the right lung because the heart is positioned more to the left side. The left ventricle forms most of the heart's left border and creates a large concave impression on the left lung's mediastinal surface.
questions.question: Which impression is largest on the left lung?

questions.explanation: The lateral thoracic artery, a branch of the axillary artery, provides lateral mammary branches that supply the lateral portion of the breast. Additional supply comes from pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery and branches from posterior intercostal arteries in the 3rd and 4th intercostal spaces.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the lateral breast?
The two basic functions of the human foot are supporting body weight and providing leverage for locomotion. These are achieved through which structural arrangement?
questions.explanation: The human foot achieves its two basic functions through a segmented skeleton arranged in arches (longitudinal and transverse), supported by muscles and ligaments. This arrangement enables efficient locomotion, sparing of foot structures, and shock absorption. The arches allow the foot to adapt to uneven surfaces and serve as resilient springs to absorb shocks as in jumping.
options: Segmented bony arches supported by muscles and ligaments
Rigid flat bone platform without arching
Phalanges arranged in a single arch only

questions.question: Which muscles work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction?
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction (ulnar deviation). By contracting simultaneously, they balance flexion and extension forces while producing adduction. This demonstrates how muscles from different compartments can cooperate for specific movements.

White rami communicantes carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers from spinal nerves T1-L2 to the sympathetic trunk. They are white because the preganglionic fibers are myelinated. These fibers originate from intermediolateral cell columns in the thoracolumbar spinal cord. White rami exist only at T1-L2 levels.
questions.question: What are white rami communicantes?

questions.explanation: The sacrotuberous ligament and sacrospinous ligament, in conjunction with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. They primarily stabilize the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint under the weight of the vertebral column. These ligaments are critical surgical landmarks in posterior pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Which two ligaments, combined with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?

questions.explanation: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium that can stretch and accommodate changes in bladder volume without tearing. When the bladder is empty, the epithelium appears thick with 5-6 cell layers; when distended, it thins to 2-3 layers. This epithelium is impermeable to salts and water.
questions.question: What epithelium lines the urinary bladder?
Which artery typically does NOT arise directly from the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The common hepatic artery arises from the celiac trunk (along with left gastric and splenic arteries), not directly from the abdominal aorta. The aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (inferior phrenic, suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, inferior mesenteric artery), paired parietal branches (subcostal, four lumbar arteries), and the unpaired median sacral artery before bifurcating into common iliac arteries. Anatomical variations exist, with occasionally the common hepatic or left gastric arising separately from the aorta (replaced vessels).

questions.question: Which muscles elevate the scapula?
options: Upper and middle trapezius, levator scapulae
questions.explanation: Elevation of the scapula is caused by contraction of upper and middle fibers of trapezius and levator scapulae muscles. This movement is associated with elevation of the lateral end and depression of the medial end of the clavicle. Shoulder shrugging demonstrates this action.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct turn laterally?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum and veers to the left at the level of the T5 vertebra. At the root of the neck, it arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle. This anatomical course is crucial for understanding lymphatic drainage patterns in the thorax.

The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing. All infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) serve this function. They are innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) except thyrohyoid which receives C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.question: Which muscle depresses the hyoid bone after swallowing?
Which structure prevents food from entering the nasopharynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The soft palate elevates and tenses during swallowing to close off the nasopharynx, preventing nasal regurgitation. Levator veli palatini elevates while tensor veli palatini tenses the palate. The uvula contacts the posterior pharyngeal wall (Passavant's ridge) to complete the seal.

options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. It exits the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis. Injury to this nerve (during posterior hip surgery or gluteal injections) causes Trendelenburg sign due to loss of hip abduction and medial rotation. It carries no cutaneous branches.
questions.question: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies which muscles?

questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis is situated at the level of the lesser trochanter and is formed by the inferior gluteal artery, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
questions.question: The cruciate anastomosis, at the level of the lesser trochanter, provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and which major vessel?
The lesser trochanter, the traction epiphysis of which muscle, projects from the posterior surface of the femur and points in which direction?
questions.explanation: The lesser trochanter is the traction epiphysis of the iliopsoas muscle, the great flexor of the hip joint. It projects from the posterior surface of the femur and is conical, pointing medially. It marks the lowermost fibers of the gluteus maximus insertion.

The transpyloric plane, passing midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis (or midway between xiphoid and umbilicus), corresponds to the level of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and the lower border of vertebra T12. This important surgical landmark crosses numerous structures: pylorus of stomach (when supine), neck of pancreas, origin of the SMA and portal vein, duodenojejunal flexure, hila of both kidneys, fundus of gallbladder, root of transverse mesocolon, origin of IMA (at L3), and tips of ninth costal cartilages. The plane is used to define upper and lower abdominal regions in the nine-region scheme.
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the transpyloric plane?
The parotid duct pierces which muscle before opening into the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct pierces the buccinator muscle to open into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar tooth. The duct is approximately 5 cm long and crosses the masseter muscle superficially. Trauma to the cheek can damage the duct causing salivary fistula.

The superficial branch of radial nerve becomes subcutaneous on the lateral wrist as it passes over the anatomical snuffbox. This superficial position makes it vulnerable to trauma (handcuff neuropathy, tight watches, wrist lacerations). Injury causes numbness over dorsal thumb and radial hand without motor deficit.
options: Located in a deep protected position
Superficial over lateral wrist makes it vulnerable to trauma
questions.question: How does the superficial branch of radial nerve course affect its vulnerability?
From which artery does the proper hepatic artery arise?
questions.explanation: The proper hepatic artery arises from the common hepatic artery, which is a branch of the celiac trunk. The common hepatic artery divides into the proper hepatic artery and the gastroduodenal artery. The proper hepatic artery then divides into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver.

questions.question: The anterior arch of C1 articulates with which structure?
questions.explanation: The anterior arch of the atlas (C1) has a facet on its posterior surface that articulates with the dens (odontoid process) of the axis (C2). The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against this facet. This atlantoaxial joint allows rotation of the head. Fracture or ligamentous injury can cause atlantoaxial instability.

questions.question: What lies in the anterior mediastinum primarily?
questions.explanation: The anterior mediastinum (between the sternum and pericardium) contains primarily the thymus gland (or its remnant in adults), fatty tissue, and lymph nodes. In children, the thymus is prominent; in adults, it is largely replaced by fat. This space can be involved in thymomas or lymphomas.

G cells are enteroendocrine cells located primarily in the pyloric antrum (also in duodenum) that secrete gastrin in response to gastric distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion by parietal cells and has trophic effects on gastric mucosa. Gastrinomas (tumors secreting gastrin) cause Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with severe peptic ulcer disease.
questions.question: Which cell type produces gastrin hormone?
The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly adheres to which extracapsular ligament, making it more vulnerable to sporting injury?
questions.explanation: The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly attached to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament at its midpoint. This attachment makes it less mobile and more vulnerable to injury than the lateral meniscus. The tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus are often torn together in contact sports as part of the classic 'unhappy triad.'

questions.question: The inferior alveolar artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It descends with the inferior alveolar nerve to enter the mandibular foramen, supplying the mandibular teeth and bone. The mylohyoid branch supplies the mylohyoid muscle. The mental artery emerges through the mental foramen.

The inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening (foramen venae cavae) in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level, the highest of the three major diaphragmatic openings. This opening also transmits branches of the right phrenic nerve. The esophageal hiatus (T10 level) transmits the esophagus and vagal trunks, while the aortic hiatus (T12 level) transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. The IVC opening dilates during inspiration as the diaphragm contracts and descends, facilitating venous return to the heart.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pierce the diaphragm?
What are gray rami communicantes?
questions.explanation: Gray rami communicantes carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers from sympathetic ganglia back to all spinal nerves for distribution to blood vessels, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles throughout the body. They are "gray" because postganglionic fibers are unmyelinated. Gray rami exist at all spinal levels unlike white rami.

The right coronary artery arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus of the ascending aorta. It runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving off branches to the right atrium, SA node (in 60% of people), right ventricle, and posterior interventricular septum. In right-dominant circulation (70% of people), it gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.
questions.question: From which aortic sinus does the right coronary artery arise?

questions.explanation: The submental lymph nodes lie between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and drain the chin, central lower lip, floor of mouth, and tip of tongue. Efferents pass to submandibular and jugulo-omohyoid nodes. These nodes are examined when staging oral cavity cancers.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the chin?
Which artery forms the main contribution to the superficial palmar arch?
questions.explanation: The superficial palmar arch is formed primarily by the ulnar artery with contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. The arch curves across the palm at the level of the distal border of the fully extended thumb. It gives rise to three common palmar digital arteries.

The greater curvature is supplied by the right and left gastroepiploic (gastroomental) arteries, which anastomose along the greater curvature. The left gastroepiploic arises from the splenic artery and supplies the upper greater curvature; the right gastroepiploic arises from the gastroduodenal artery and supplies the lower greater curvature. The short gastric arteries supply the fundus portion of the greater curvature.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the greater curvature of the stomach?
What percentage of lymph drains to axillary nodes?
questions.explanation: Approximately 75% of lymph from the breast drains into the axillary nodes, primarily the pectoral (anterior) group. About 20% drains to the internal mammary (parasternal) chain. The lower quadrants may drain to inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes. This drainage pattern is crucial in cancer staging.

questions.question: How many functional segments does the liver have?
questions.explanation: The liver is divided into eight functionally independent segments (Couinaud segments I-VIII) based on the distribution of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts. Each segment has its own vascular inflow, outflow, and biliary drainage, allowing surgical resection of individual segments without damaging others. This segmental anatomy is crucial for hepatic surgery and understanding disease distribution.

On either side of the superior thoracic aperture, the opening is closed by the dense suprapleural membrane (also called Sibson's fascia). In the midline, structures pass between the neck and thorax. This membrane is a tent-shaped extension of endothoracic fascia that covers the apex of each lung.
questions.question: What closes the superior thoracic aperture laterally?

questions.explanation: The medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) arises from the profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery). It wraps around the posterior side of the femur, supplying the neck and head via retinacular vessels. In femoral neck fractures, this artery is commonly damaged, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head. It also contributes to the trochanteric and cruciate anastomoses.
questions.question: The medial femoral circumflex artery wraps around the posterior aspect of the femur and is the main blood supply to the femoral head. From which artery does it arise?

questions.explanation: The first part (superior part) of the duodenum, specifically its first 2 cm (duodenal cap or bulb), is the only portion that is intraperitoneal and mobile, being connected to the liver by the hepatoduodenal ligament. The remainder of the first part and all of the second, third, and fourth parts are secondarily retroperitoneal and fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. This mobility makes the duodenal bulb vulnerable to anterior displacement by posterior masses (e.g., pancreatic head tumors). The mobile first part is also the most common site of peptic ulceration.
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is most mobile?
Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along which vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along the femoral vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes. Afferent vessels reach the popliteal nodes from the knee joint and lymphatics accompanying leg arteries. Superficial popliteal nodes receive lymph from the region accompanying the small saphenous vein.

questions.question: At how many points is the ureter typically constricted?
questions.explanation: The ureter has three normal physiological constrictions: (1) at the pelviureteric junction where the renal pelvis joins the ureter, (2) where it crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and (3) at the vesicoureteric junction where it pierces the bladder wall. These are the most common sites for ureteric stone impaction.

The iliohypogastric nerve arises from the L1 nerve root (sometimes with minor contribution from T12), emerging from the lateral border of psoas major. It runs obliquely across the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum, then pierces the transversus abdominis muscle to run between it and internal oblique, providing motor innervation to these muscles. The nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch (supplying skin over the hip) and an anterior cutaneous branch (supplying skin above the pubis), crossing above and parallel to the inguinal canal. Injury during appendectomy or hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain and sensory loss.
questions.question: Which nerve root contributes to the iliohypogastric nerve?

questions.explanation: Adductor longus is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. It originates from the anterior surface of the body of the pubis, inferior to the pubic crest and lateral to the pubic symphysis, and inserts into the middle third of the medial lip of the linea aspera. Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle.
questions.question: Which muscle of the medial compartment is the most anteriorly placed, large, and fan-shaped, forming the medial boundary of the femoral triangle?
The prostate gland is related posteriorly to which structure?
questions.explanation: The prostate gland is related posteriorly to the anterior wall of the rectum (ampulla), separated from it by the rectovesical fascia (fascia of Denonvilliers). This relationship allows the prostate to be palpated during digital rectal examination (DRE), where the posterior surface of the gland can be assessed for size, consistency, symmetry, and nodules. The prostate is related anteriorly to the pubic symphysis (retropubic space of Retzius), superiorly to the bladder base, and inferiorly to the urogenital diaphragm. The prostatic urethra passes through the gland from base to apex.

questions.question: Which muscle protrudes the mandible when contracted bilaterally?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle protrudes the mandible when both sides contract simultaneously, assisted by the medial pterygoid. Unilateral contraction causes lateral deviation to the opposite side. The muscle has superior and inferior heads inserting on the articular disc and pterygoid fovea respectively.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies somatic sensation below the pectinate line?
questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensation below the pectinate line, making this area sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature. Above the pectinate line, the anal canal is supplied by autonomic (visceral) nerves and is insensitive to these stimuli but sensitive to stretch. This explains why internal hemorrhoids are painless while external hemorrhoids are painful.

Griffiths' point is the watershed area at the splenic flexure where the left branch of the middle colic artery (from superior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric artery). This represents the junction between the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories and is vulnerable to ischemia due to relatively poor collateral circulation. Another watershed area exists at Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid junction) where the last sigmoid artery meets the superior rectal artery. Both areas are susceptible to ischemic colitis during low-flow states.
questions.question: Which vessel anastomoses at Griffiths' point?
What provides the total left lung segment count?
questions.explanation: The left lung typically contains 8-10 bronchopulmonary segments depending on anatomical variation. The upper lobe has 4-5 segments (apicoposterior/or separate apical and posterior, anterior, superior lingular, inferior lingular) and the lower lobe has 4-5 segments (superior, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal, ? medial basal).

questions.question: Which cranial fossa contains the temporal lobes?
questions.explanation: The middle cranial fossa accommodates the temporal lobes of the brain laterally and the pituitary gland centrally. The floor is formed by the greater wings and body of the sphenoid and the petrous and squamous parts of the temporal bones. The fossa is wider than the anterior fossa. Multiple foramina pierce its floor.

The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by union of internal cerebral veins and basal veins, draining into the straight sinus. The straight sinus then joins the superior sagittal sinus at the confluence of sinuses. Deep cerebral structures drain via this venous pathway.
questions.question: The great cerebral vein of Galen drains into which sinus?

questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis through the inguinal canal, normally obliterates during the first year of life, leaving only the distal portion as the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Failure of complete obliteration leads to various clinical conditions: patent processus vaginalis allows peritoneal fluid to flow into the scrotum (communicating hydrocele) or permits herniation of abdominal contents (congenital indirect inguinal hernia). Partial obliteration with persistence of intermediate portions creates encysted hydroceles of the cord. Complete patency occurs in about 20% of adults.
questions.question: The processus vaginalis normally obliterates when?
What produces circumduction at the shoulder joint?
questions.explanation: Circumduction at the shoulder joint is a sequential combination of flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction movements. This creates a conical movement pattern of the limb. Multiple muscles act in coordinated sequence to produce this composite movement.

The white pulp of the spleen consists of lymphoid tissue surrounding central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS) and lymphoid nodules. It is the site of immune surveillance and antibody production in response to blood-borne antigens. The white pulp contains predominantly T lymphocytes in the PALS and B lymphocytes in the lymphoid follicles.
questions.question: What is the primary immunological function of splenic white pulp?
The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of which two deep leg veins?
options: Medial genicular and small saphenous veins
questions.explanation: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins. It traverses the popliteal fossa in the same fibrous sheath as the popliteal artery and terminates at the adductor hiatus to become the femoral vein. The small saphenous vein also drains into the popliteal vein.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: Superficial and deep parotid lymph nodes lie within or on the parotid gland substance. They drain the scalp, auricle, external acoustic meatus, and parotid gland itself. Efferents pass to the superficial and deep cervical nodes. The presence of lymph nodes within the gland complicates parotid tumor surgery and influences surgical planning.

questions.question: The tail of the pancreas extends into which ligament?
questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends laterally and slightly superiorly, reaching to within 1 cm of the splenic hilum in approximately 75% of individuals, lying within the splenorenal ligament along with the splenic artery and vein. This relationship is surgically significant during splenectomy, as the pancreatic tail must be identified and preserved to prevent iatrogenic pancreatitis or pancreatic fistula. The body of the pancreas lies anterior to the splenic vein (which runs along its posterior surface) and behind the posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa), separated from it by the gastrosplenic ligament.

questions.question: An atavistic epiphysis represents a vestigial bone once separate in ancestral species. Which of the following is a classic example in the lower limb?
questions.explanation: The calcaneal apophysis (posterior calcaneal epiphysis) is a classic example of an atavistic epiphysis. Traction epiphyses arise at tendinous insertions, while pressure epiphyses form articular surfaces. Traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis in adolescents is known as Sever's disease.

The left border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed almost entirely by the left ventricle, with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. This border extends from the 2nd left costal cartilage to the apex beat in the 5th intercostal space.
questions.question: Which vessel forms the left heart border?
How many intercostal spaces are present on each side?
questions.explanation: Since there are 12 ribs on each side, there are 11 intercostal spaces between them. Each intercostal space contains intercostal muscles, neurovascular bundles, and lymphatics. Understanding the anatomy of these spaces is crucial for procedures like thoracentesis and chest tube insertion.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the body of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The body and tail of the pancreas receive arterial supply from the splenic artery through numerous small pancreatic branches (dorsal pancreatic, greater pancreatic, caudal pancreatic arteries) as the splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreas. The head of the pancreas is supplied by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries forming anterior and posterior arcades. The pancreas has a rich blood supply with extensive anastomoses, though the pancreatic neck region may be relatively less vascular. The intimate relationship between the splenic artery and pancreas means that pancreatic pathology can affect the artery.

questions.question: Which bone forms the hard palate anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The palatine processes of the right and left maxillae form the anterior three-quarters of the hard palate. The horizontal plates of the palatine bones form the posterior quarter. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities. The incisive foramen transmits the nasopalatine nerve anteriorly.

The bones of both lower limbs total 60: 2 femurs, 2 patellae, 2 tibiae, 2 fibulae, 14 tarsals, 10 metatarsals, and 28 phalanges. This understanding is fundamental in trauma assessment and radiological interpretation. Each single lower limb contains 30 bones.
questions.question: How many bones are present in both lower limbs combined, considering femurs, patellae, tibiae, fibulae, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges?
Which structure does the sympathetic trunk NOT innervate?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunk does not innervate voluntary (skeletal) muscles, which are innervated by somatic motor neurons. The sympathetic system innervates cardiac muscle, smooth muscle in blood vessels and organs, sweat glands, and various viscera. Sympathetic fibers reach the body wall via gray rami communicantes.

Reticulocytes (immature red blood cells still containing RNA) normally comprise 0.5-1.5% of circulating red blood cells, representing the daily replacement of senescent erythrocytes. The reticulocyte count increases in hemolysis or bleeding (compensatory bone marrow response) and decreases in bone marrow failure or nutritional deficiencies. The spleen removes excessive RNA from reticulocytes (pitting function).
questions.question: What is the normal percentage of reticulocytes in peripheral blood?

questions.explanation: Flexion at the wrist is produced mainly by flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi radialis muscles. The flexor digitorum superficialis provides assistance to this movement. All wrist movements are performed by forearm muscles crossing the wrist joint.
questions.question: What produces flexion at the wrist joint?
options: Flexor carpi ulnaris and radialis, flexor digitorum superficialis

questions.question: The external anal sphincter is composed of which muscle type?
questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter is composed of striated (skeletal) voluntary muscle under somatic control via the inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve, S2-S4) and perineal branch of S4. It surrounds the entire length of the anal canal external to the internal sphincter and is divided into subcutaneous, superficial, and deep parts. The external sphincter provides voluntary control of defecation and maintains continence, particularly during sudden increases in intra-abdominal pressure. In contrast, the internal anal sphincter (derived from thickened rectal circular smooth muscle) is under involuntary autonomic control and maintains baseline anal tone.

The superior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe (caudate process) of the liver covered with peritoneum. The inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad, and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum along with the right crus of the diaphragm. The foramen provides communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs and typically admits two fingers, serving as a surgical landmark and potential route for accessing the lesser sac.
questions.question: Which structure forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen?

options: Bone shape alone maintains the arches
Muscle tone alone determines arch height
Bone shape, muscle tone, and ligament strength
Tendon length, joint capsule, and synovial fluid
questions.explanation: The arches of the foot are maintained by three factors: the shape of the bones, the strength of the ligaments, and the tone of the muscles. All three work together to maintain normal arch height. In pes planus (flat foot), ligamentous laxity and muscle weakness combine with bony changes to flatten the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.question: The arches of the foot are described as being maintained by three factors. Which combination is correct?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve divides into anterior and posterior divisions. The anterior division supplies adductor longus, brevis, gracilis, and pectineus (sometimes), and provides a cutaneous branch to the medial thigh. The posterior division supplies obturator externus and the adductor part of adductor magnus, and gives an articular branch to the knee joint.
questions.question: The obturator nerve divides into which two divisions upon exiting the obturator foramen?

questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas lies within the C-shaped curve formed by the duodenum, specifically nestled in the concavity of the second, third, and fourth parts of the duodenum. The head is the broadest part of the pancreas. A portion of the head, the uncinate process, extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
questions.question: Which part of the pancreas lies within the concavity of the duodenum?
Which vertebral level corresponds to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery?
questions.explanation: The common iliac arteries, terminal branches of the abdominal aorta, bifurcate into external and internal iliac arteries at approximately the L5/S1 level (lumbosacral junction), anterior to the sacroiliac joint at the pelvic brim. This bifurcation point corresponds to a point just medial to the midinguinal point on the anterior abdominal wall. The ureter crosses anterior to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the external iliac artery just distal to it), a relationship that is surgically significant. The right common iliac artery is crossed anteriorly by the superior rectal vessels, while the left is related to the sigmoid mesocolon.

The cremaster muscle receives motor innervation from the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2), which enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring and travels within the spermatic cord. The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis in response to stroking the inner thigh) tests this nerve and the L1-L2 cord segments. The ilioinguinal nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the scrotum and adjacent thigh but does not innervate the cremaster muscle. The cremasteric artery (from inferior epigastric) provides vascular supply to the cremaster muscle and travels alongside the nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve innervates the cremaster muscle?
The root of the mesentery extends from which two points?
questions.explanation: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure (at approximately L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (at approximately S1, right of midline), a distance of about 15 cm. Along this short root, approximately 6-7 meters of small intestine (jejunum and ileum) is attached. The root crosses the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum, abdominal aorta, IVC, right ureter, right psoas major muscle, and right testicular/ovarian vessels. This oblique orientation allows the small intestine maximum mobility while maintaining vascular supply and creating the characteristic radiating pattern of jejunal and ileal vessels.
options: Second part of duodenum to sigmoid colon
Duodenojejunal flexure to right sacroiliac joint

questions.explanation: The facial artery crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of the masseter muscle, where its pulse can be palpated. After crossing, it ascends toward the medial canthus as the angular artery. The artery winds around the mandible from the neck to reach the face. Facial vein crosses more anteriorly.
questions.question: The facial artery crosses which border of the mandible?

questions.explanation: Semitendinosus joins sartorius and gracilis at the pes anserinus on the superior medial surface of the tibia. As its name implies, semitendinosus has a long rounded distal tendon. All three pes anserinus muscles cross both the hip and knee joints from three different compartments, making this insertion a multi-compartment landmark.
questions.question: Semitendinosus inserts into the medial surface of the superior part of the tibia, joining which two muscles to form the pes anserinus?
Which lymph nodes drain the lower anal canal (below pectinate line)?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from the anal canal below the pectinate line follows the drainage of the external body wall, passing to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. This reflects the embryological origin of this region from ectoderm (proctodeum) and its somatic innervation. In contrast, the anal canal above the pectinate line (derived from endoderm) drains to internal iliac nodes along the superior rectal vessels, with some drainage via middle rectal vessels also to internal iliac nodes. This dual drainage pattern is clinically important in carcinoma of the anal canal, affecting surgical planning and lymph node dissection.

The obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4), formed within the psoas major from the lumbar plexus, emerges from the medial border of the muscle at the pelvic brim. It descends along the lateral wall of the pelvis, passing above the obturator vessels to reach the obturator foramen, through which it exits the pelvis to enter the medial compartment of the thigh. This medial emergence distinguishes it from other lumbar plexus branches (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves) which emerge from the lateral border, except for the genitofemoral nerve which pierces the anterior surface of psoas.
questions.question: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of psoas major?

questions.explanation: The primary function of the large intestine is absorption of water and electrolytes from the remaining indigestible food matter, converting liquid chyme into semi-solid feces. Approximately 1-2 liters of water are absorbed daily. The colon also absorbs short-chain fatty acids produced by bacterial fermentation and synthesizes vitamin K through bacterial action.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the large intestine?
The spleen develops in relation to which mesentery?
questions.explanation: The spleen develops within the dorsal mesogastrium (greater omentum) during embryonic development, explaining its position in the left upper quadrant and its peritoneal attachments. The gastrosplenic ligament (part of the dorsal mesogastrium) connects it to the greater curvature of the stomach, while the splenorenal ligament attaches it to the left kidney. Although the spleen is not a gastrointestinal organ, it receives its blood supply from the celiac trunk (via splenic artery) due to this developmental relationship. The tail of the pancreas also develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, extending into the splenorenal ligament.

questions.question: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from which vertebral bodies?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the anterolateral surfaces of the bodies and intervertebral discs of L1, L2, and L3 vertebrae (sometimes extending to L4), while the left crus arises from only L1 and L2 (sometimes L3). Both crura contribute to forming the esophageal hiatus, with muscle fibers from the right crus (and sometimes left) looping around the esophagus to create a muscular sphincter mechanism. The crura also form boundaries of the aortic hiatus, with the median arcuate ligament connecting them anterior to the aorta at T12 level.

The lesser omentum extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver and consists of the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments. The hepatogastric portion specifically connects the lesser curvature to the liver. This double layer of peritoneum carries the left and right gastric vessels along the lesser curvature.
questions.question: Which ligament extends from the lesser curvature to the liver?
What structure lies in all mediastinal regions?
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes are present in all regions of the mediastinum: paratracheal and brachiocephalic nodes in the superior mediastinum; parasternal nodes anteriorly; tracheobronchial and hilar nodes in the middle mediastinum; and paraesophageal and paravertebral nodes posteriorly. Lymphadenopathy is a common cause of mediastinal widening.

Both right and left renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is approximately three times longer than the right and crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC. The left renal vein receives the left suprarenal vein, left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein, and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein.
questions.question: Which vein receives the left renal vein?

questions.explanation: The palatopharyngeus muscle forms the posterior pillar (palatopharyngeal arch) of the fauces. The palatoglossus forms the anterior pillar. The tonsillar fossa lies between these two pillars. Both muscles descend from the soft palate but have different innervation patterns.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the posterior pillar of the fauces?
How long is the ureter in adults?
questions.explanation: Each ureter is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. The ureter descends on the psoas major muscle, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enters the bladder at the lateral angles of the trigone. It is a muscular tube that propels urine by peristaltic contractions.

The middle cardiac vein ascends in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus near its termination in the right atrium. It drains blood from the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum. It is the second largest cardiac vein after the great cardiac vein.
questions.question: Which vein accompanies the posterior interventricular artery?

questions.explanation: Only the first 2 cm of the first (superior) part of the duodenum, known as the duodenal cap or ampulla, is intraperitoneal. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, lying posterior to the peritoneum. This intraperitoneal portion is the most common site for duodenal ulceration (duodenal cap ulcers).
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is intraperitoneal?
The transversalis fascia forms which covering of the spermatic cord?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost fascial covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep inguinal ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis). These three concentric layers are acquired as the processus vaginalis descends through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent. The tunica vaginalis is the closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis, derived from the processus vaginalis.

questions.question: The facial vein commonly anastomoses with which intracranial structure?
questions.explanation: The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus. These connections lack valves, allowing bidirectional flow. Infections in the danger triangle of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis.

questions.question: Which component of the quadriceps femoris lies deepest, between the vastus medialis and lateralis?
questions.explanation: Vastus intermedius lies deep to the rectus femoris, between the vastus medialis and lateralis. It originates from the anterior and lateral surfaces of the shaft of the femur and inserts via the common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. It is innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) and extends the leg at the knee.

The porta hepatis (gateway to the liver) on the inferior surface of the liver contains the right and left branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery proper, and hepatic ducts, along with lymphatic vessels and hepatic nerve plexuses. The structures are arranged with bile ducts anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery anteriorly and to the left, and portal vein posteriorly. The hepatic veins and IVC are not at the porta but rather on the posterior surface of the liver. The porta hepatis forms the floor of the fissure for the ligamentum venosum and is continuous with the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.question: The porta hepatis contains which structures?

questions.explanation: Cloquet's node (node of Rosenmuller) is the most superior of the deep inguinal lymph nodes, located in the femoral canal (femoral ring) and receives lymph from the superficial and deep inguinal nodes. It drains to the external iliac nodes. The femoral canal is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath (lateral to the lacunar ligament, medial to the femoral vein) and represents a potential weakness where femoral hernias occur. Virchow's node is in the left supraclavicular fossa, Sister Mary Joseph node at the umbilicus, and Calot's node in Calot's triangle.
questions.question: Which lymph node is found in the femoral canal?

questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial or lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The internal oblique muscle contributes to the anterior wall in the lateral third of the canal (where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament) and forms part of the roof with the transversus abdominis muscle through their arching fibers. The external oblique aponeurosis forms the entire length of the anterior wall, the transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by conjoint tendon) forms the posterior wall, and the inguinal ligament forms the floor.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: The median nerve's formation from lateral and medial cords ensures it receives contributions from all nerve roots (C5-T1) except sometimes C5. This broad root distribution explains why isolated cord injuries may only partially affect median nerve function. The distinctive M-shaped formation in the axilla is clinically recognizable.
questions.question: What is the significance of the median nerve's dual cord origin?
options: Has no clinical or anatomical significance
Supply from both lateral and medial cords

questions.explanation: The kidneys extend from approximately T12 to L3 vertebral levels, with the hilum positioned at the L1 level (transpyloric plane). The right kidney typically sits slightly lower than the left (by about half a vertebra) due to the presence of the liver superiorly. The upper poles are closer to the midline and are related to the diaphragm and ribs (left kidney: ribs 11-12; right kidney: rib 12), while the lower poles are further from the midline. The kidneys lie obliquely, with the upper poles more posterior and closer together than the lower poles.
questions.question: The kidney is located at which vertebral levels?

questions.explanation: The superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath behind the rectus abdominis muscle. This provides an important collateral pathway between the subclavian artery (via internal thoracic and superior epigastric) and the external iliac artery (via inferior epigastric), bypassing the abdominal aorta.
questions.question: What connects superior and inferior epigastric arteries?

questions.explanation: The Achilles tendon does not have a true synovial tendon sheath like finger flexor tendons. Instead, it is surrounded by a paratenon (peritenon), a loose connective tissue sheath that allows tendon gliding and contains blood vessels. Two bursae are adjacent: the retrocalcaneal bursa (between tendon and calcaneus) and the superficial calcaneal bursa (between tendon and skin). Inflammation of the paratenon causes peritendinitis (Achilles peritendinitis).
options: A fascial tunnel from the posterior compartment
questions.question: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. It does NOT have a true tendon sheath but instead has which covering?

questions.explanation: is absent in approximately 15% of people without any functional deficit. When present, it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. The tendon is commonly harvested for use in tendon grafts and reconstructive procedures.
questions.question: Which muscle can be absent without functional deficit?

questions.explanation: The floor of the popliteal fossa from superior to inferior consists of: the popliteal surface of the femur, the capsule of the knee joint, the oblique popliteal ligament, and the popliteal fascia covering the popliteus muscle. The popliteal artery runs in close proximity to this floor, making it vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations.
questions.question: The floor of the popliteal fossa from superior to inferior consists of which structures?
options: Femoral popliteal surface, knee capsule, oblique popliteal ligament, popliteal fascia
Skin and superficial fascia of the posterior knee
Popliteus muscle, posterior joint capsule, and tibial cortex
Tibial nerve, popliteal artery, and popliteal vein
Femoral condyles and both medial and lateral menisci

questions.explanation: The right renal artery is longer than the left and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava to reach the right kidney. The left renal artery has a shorter, more direct course from the aorta to the left kidney. Both arteries arise at approximately L1-L2 level, just inferior to the superior mesenteric artery origin.
questions.question: Which renal artery typically passes posterior to the inferior vena cava?
Which muscle connects ribs to vertebrae posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The levator costarum muscles are twelve small muscles connecting the transverse processes of C7 and T1-T11 vertebrae to the ribs below. They elevate the ribs and are innervated by lateral branches of the dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves. They assist in respiration and lateral flexion.

questions.question: The fibular (peroneal) artery is a branch of which vessel, making it an indirect branch of the popliteal artery?
questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery arises from the tibioperoneal trunk, which is one of the two terminal divisions of the popliteal artery (the other being the anterior tibial artery). The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and the fibular artery. The fibular artery descends alongside the fibula in the posterior compartment.

The deltoid's three portions have distinct actions: anterior fibers flex and medially rotate, middle fibers abduct (15-90°), posterior fibers extend and laterally rotate. This multipennate architecture allows the same muscle to produce different movements depending on which fibers are active.
questions.question: How do the three deltoid portions contribute differently to shoulder function?
options: Anterior flexes, middle abducts, posterior extends

questions.question: Into which vein does the splenic vein primarily drain?
questions.explanation: The splenic vein joins with the superior mesenteric vein posterior to the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. The splenic vein runs from left to right along the posterior surface of the pancreas. It receives the short gastric veins, left gastroepiploic vein, pancreatic veins, and inferior mesenteric vein.

questions.question: The dorsal venous arch of the foot drains medially into the great saphenous vein and laterally into which vein?
questions.explanation: The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones. It drains medially into the great saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the great toe) and laterally into the small saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the little toe). This arch is the origin point of both major superficial veins of the lower limb.

questions.question: The external acoustic meatus is what total length?
questions.explanation: The external acoustic meatus measures approximately 2.9 cm in length from the concha to the tympanic membrane. The lateral one-third is cartilaginous containing cerumen glands, while the medial two-thirds is bony. Understanding this anatomy is essential for safe otoscopic examination and foreign body removal.

questions.question: Which cells line the splenic sinusoids?
questions.explanation: Splenic sinusoids are lined by discontinuous endothelium composed of elongated endothelial cells (stave cells) oriented parallel to blood flow with gaps (slits) of 2-3 ?m between them. This discontinuous arrangement allows flexible cells to pass through but retains rigid or damaged cells. The basement membrane is also discontinuous. This structure is unique to the spleen and facilitates its filtering function.

The tarsal tunnel contains the following structures passing from anterior to posterior (using the mnemonic Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry): Tibialis posterior tendon, flexor Digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial Artery and Veins, tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus tendon. Compression within this tunnel causes tarsal tunnel syndrome with plantar foot pain and paraesthesia.
questions.question: The tarsal tunnel is formed by the flexor retinaculum and bones of the medial ankle. Which structures pass through it from anterior to posterior?
options: Tibialis anterior tendon, deep fibular nerve, dorsalis pedis artery
Tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve, FHL
Fibularis longus, fibularis brevis, sural nerve, small saphenous vein
Extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, anterior tibial artery

questions.explanation: The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle layer forming the bladder wall and consists of three poorly defined layers: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. During bladder filling, the detrusor relaxes; during micturition, it contracts to expel urine. The detrusor is innervated by parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnic nerves S2-4) for contraction.
questions.question: What muscle forms the bladder wall?
Over which muscle does the lateral arcuate ligament arch?
questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch that extends from the tip of the transverse process of L1 to the 12th rib, arching over the quadratus lumborum muscle. It provides attachment for some of the muscular fibers of the diaphragm. The subcostal nerve (T12) and vessels pass deep to this ligament.

questions.question: The internal urethral sphincter receives which type of innervation?
questions.explanation: The internal urethral sphincter, a thickening of smooth muscle at the bladder neck, is under involuntary autonomic control (both sympathetic and parasympathetic), in contrast to the external urethral sphincter which is skeletal muscle under voluntary somatic control via the pudendal nerve. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric nerves) causes contraction of the internal sphincter and relaxation of the detrusor, promoting urine storage. Parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation, promoting micturition. The internal sphincter prevents semen from entering the bladder during ejaculation and contributes to urinary continence.

questions.question: Where in the small intestine is iron primarily absorbed?
questions.explanation: Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum as ferrous iron (Fe2+). Gastric acid helps convert ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous iron for absorption. Vitamin C enhances absorption while phytates and tannins inhibit it. Heme iron from meat is absorbed more efficiently than non-heme iron from plant sources.

questions.question: Which hormone is produced by the pancreatic alpha cells?
questions.explanation: Glucagon is produced by alpha cells in the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) and increases blood glucose by promoting hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. It opposes insulin action. Glucagon secretion is stimulated by low blood glucose, amino acids, and sympathetic stimulation. Alpha cells constitute about 20% of islet cells and are located peripherally in the islets.

questions.question: Which structure separates the supracolic from the infracolic compartment?
questions.explanation: The transverse mesocolon, a broad fold of peritoneum connecting the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall, divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The supracolic compartment contains the stomach, liver, spleen, and lesser sac, while the infracolic compartment is further divided into right and left infracolic spaces by the mesentery of the small intestine. These spaces communicate laterally via the paracolic gutters. The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses the descending (second) part of the duodenum and head of pancreas, serving as an important surgical landmark.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the orbit?
questions.explanation: The medial wall of the orbit is formed by bone (primarily the orbital plate of ethmoid), not muscle. The medial rectus muscle lies within the orbit adjacent to this bony wall. The thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells.

questions.question: The adductor tubercle is an important bony landmark on the medial aspect of the distal femur. Which tendon inserts here?
questions.explanation: The adductor tubercle on the medial aspect of the distal femur receives the insertion of the hamstring part of adductor magnus. This is the part of adductor magnus supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The adductor tubercle is palpable on physical examination and serves as an important landmark in knee surgery (origin of the tibial collateral ligament is just above it).

questions.question: Which forearm muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve?
questions.explanation: is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Anterior interosseous syndrome results in inability to flex the thumb interphalangeal joint and index finger distal interphalangeal joint.

questions.question: Which vein passes through the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein (formed by union of maxillary and superficial temporal veins) passes through the parotid gland substance. It divides into anterior and posterior divisions within the gland. The anterior division joins the facial vein; the posterior joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular. The facial nerve and external carotid artery also traverse the gland.

options: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
questions.question: The fibular (peroneal) artery, arising from the tibioperoneal trunk, descends laterally alongside the fibula in which compartment?
questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery descends in the deep posterior compartment of the leg, alongside the fibula. It supplies the lateral and posterior compartment muscles and gives off perforating branches that pierce the interosseous membrane to supply the lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis). It terminates by anastomosing with the lateral malleolar and calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery.

The cecum is the widest part of the large intestine (approximately 7.5 cm in diameter), and the diameter gradually decreases toward the sigmoid colon. This variation in diameter is clinically significant in colonic obstruction: according to Laplace's law, the cecum is most likely to perforate in cases of distal large bowel obstruction due to its larger diameter and thinner wall.
questions.question: Which segment of colon has the largest diameter?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct terminates by draining into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Before termination, it receives the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal lymph trunks. The duct has no valve at its termination.
questions.question: Where does the thoracic duct terminate?
Which muscle attaches to the pectineal line?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (formed by fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) inserts onto the pubic crest and pectineal line (pecten pubis), reinforcing the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medially. The pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line and is used in some hernia repairs (Cooper's ligament repair). The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and symphysis, not the pectineal line. The lacunar ligament (medial extension of the inguinal ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line.

questions.question: How many cusps form the pulmonary valve?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve has three semilunar (half-moon shaped) cusps: anterior, right, and left. Behind each cusp is a pulmonary sinus. The valve opens during right ventricular systole to allow blood into the pulmonary trunk and closes during diastole to prevent backflow. Unlike AV valves, semilunar valves have no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.

questions.question: Where is Griffiths' point located?
questions.explanation: Griffiths' point is the watershed area at the splenic flexure where the superior mesenteric artery territory (via the middle colic artery) meets the inferior mesenteric artery territory (via the left colic artery). This area has the poorest collateral circulation and is most vulnerable to ischemia in low-flow states. It is a common site for ischemic colitis.

In forced expiration, the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, internal/external obliques, transversus abdominis) contract forcibly. This pushes the abdominal viscera upward against the relaxed diaphragm, forcing it higher into the thorax. Quadratus lumborum also contracts to pull down the 12th rib.
questions.question: Which muscles aid forced expiration?

questions.explanation: The middle suprarenal artery (from the abdominal aorta) is unique in that it supplies the medulla directly without first passing through the cortex, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly to chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic neurons). The superior suprarenal artery (from inferior phrenic) and inferior suprarenal artery (from renal) supply primarily the cortex. This direct arterial supply to the medulla allows rapid hormone release (epinephrine and norepinephrine) in response to stress. The suprarenal glands have rich arterial supply from three sources but limited venous drainage (one vein each side).
