questions.question: The femoral ring is bounded medially by which structure?

questions.explanation: The six small lateral rotators of the hip joint are: quadratus femoris, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, obturator externus, and piriformis. Gluteus medius is primarily an abductor and medial rotator of the hip, not a lateral rotator. Gluteus medius is sometimes referred to as the 'rotator cuff of the hip' for its stabilizing role.
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is NOT among the six small lateral rotators of the hip joint?
What percentage of the pancreas is exocrine tissue?
questions.explanation: Approximately 99% of the pancreatic tissue is exocrine, consisting of acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes. Only about 1% consists of endocrine tissue in the form of pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans). The exocrine pancreas produces 1.5-2 liters of pancreatic juice daily containing enzymes for protein, carbohydrate, and fat digestion.

questions.question: What determines the safe position for hand immobilization?
options: Position maintaining ligament length and preventing contracture
questions.explanation: The "safe position" (MCP joints flexed 70-90°, IP joints extended, wrist slightly extended) maintains collateral ligaments at maximum length and prevents contracture. This position is also called the "intrinsic plus" position. Prolonged immobilization in other positions can result in permanent stiffness.

The arytenoid cartilages sit on the upper border of the cricoid cartilage lamina at the cricoarytenoid joints. These synovial joints allow rotation and gliding movements that abduct and adduct the vocal cords. The arytenoids are pyramidal with a vocal process (anteriorly) and muscular process (laterally).
questions.question: The arytenoid cartilages articulate with which laryngeal structure?

questions.explanation: The fovea centralis is a depression in the center of the macula lutea, representing the area of most acute vision. It contains only cones (no rods) and has minimal overlying retinal layers to reduce light scatter. The fovea is located temporal to the optic disc. Macular degeneration causes central vision loss.
questions.question: The fovea centralis is located in which structure?

questions.explanation: The lower third of the oesophagus receives its arterial supply from branches of the left gastric artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk. This creates an important portosystemic anastomosis with veins draining to both portal and systemic circulations. The upper third is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery and the middle third by oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta.
questions.question: Which artery primarily supplies the lower third of the oesophagus?
The spleen is related medially to which structure?
questions.explanation: The spleen's medial (visceral) surface has multiple impressions from adjacent organs: gastric impression anteriorly (related to stomach via gastrosplenic ligament), renal impression posteroinferiorly (related to left kidney via splenorenal ligament), colic impression inferiorly (near left colic flexure), and pancreatic impression at the hilum (tail of pancreas in splenorenal ligament). The spleen sits in the left hypochondriac region, protected by ribs 9-11. Its lateral surface is smooth and convex, molded against the diaphragm and posterolateral abdominal wall. The characteristic splenic notch marks its superior border.

The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle adducts (closes) the vocal cords by internally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. Other adductors include the interarytenoid and thyroarytenoid muscles. All adductors are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Bilateral adductor paralysis causes airway obstruction.
questions.question: Which muscle adducts the vocal cords?
Which structure separates the frontal lobe from the orbit?
questions.explanation: The thin orbital plate (roof) of the frontal bone separates the frontal lobe of the brain from the orbital contents. Fractures can cause CSF leakage into the orbit. The anterior cranial fossa lies above this plate. The frontal sinus may pneumatize into this region of the frontal bone.

The middle ear receives blood from multiple tympanic arteries: superior tympanic (middle meningeal), inferior tympanic (ascending pharyngeal), anterior tympanic (maxillary), and posterior tympanic (stylomastoid branch of posterior auricular). This rich vascular supply reflects the metabolic needs of the middle ear mucosa and ossicles.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies blood to the middle ear?
Which rotator cuff muscle is most commonly torn?
questions.explanation: is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle due to its position under the acromion. Repetitive overhead activities and age-related degeneration increase tear risk. The painful arc (pain during mid-abduction) is characteristic of supraspinatus tendonitis or tears.

questions.question: Which structure separates the frontal and temporal lobes?
questions.explanation: The lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) separates the frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe. The middle cerebral artery runs in this fissure. The insula lies deep within the lateral sulcus. Strokes affecting the middle cerebral artery often involve structures around this fissure causing characteristic neurological deficits.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the first dorsal interosseous muscle?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all interosseous muscles including the first dorsal interosseous. This muscle is easily visible and palpable on the dorsum of the hand between the thumb and index finger. Testing its strength (finger abduction) helps assess ulnar nerve function.

The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost of the three fascial coverings of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia as the cord structures pass through the deep inguinal ring. This fascia is continuous with the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial ring). These three layers enclose the contents of the spermatic cord and represent contributions from each layer of the anterior abdominal wall.
questions.question: The internal spermatic fascia is derived from which structure?

questions.explanation: Downward rotation of the scapula is performed by levator scapulae, pectoralis minor, and the rhomboids. This movement is opposite to the upward rotation needed for full arm abduction. Downward rotation returns the scapula to its resting position from the upward rotated position.
questions.question: Which muscles perform downward rotation of the scapula?

questions.explanation: The profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery) arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. It is the largest branch of the femoral artery and the main blood supply to the thigh muscles via perforating branches, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries.
questions.question: The profunda femoris artery arises from the femoral artery at what distance below the inguinal ligament?

questions.explanation: The taeniae coli are three longitudinal muscle bands that are characteristic external features of the large intestine (colon) but absent from the rectum and anal canal. These bands are shorter than the colon itself, causing sacculations (haustra) to form. The small intestine has a complete, continuous longitudinal muscle layer without taeniae.
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the large intestine from the small intestine externally?

questions.explanation: Psoas minor originates from the sides of T12 and L1 vertebrae and their intervening disc. It inserts into the pectineal line and iliopubic eminence. When present, it acts conjointly with psoas major and iliacus in flexing the thigh at the hip. Its long slender tendon is occasionally used as a landmark in pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Psoas minor, a variable muscle absent in approximately 40% of individuals, originates from which vertebral levels?

questions.explanation: Seven nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen: the sciatic nerve, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal nerve, inferior gluteal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerve. Together with six vessels and piriformis, these seven nerves constitute the 14 total structures passing through this foramen.
questions.question: How many nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
The knee joint stability depends primarily on muscles. Which muscle group is described as the MOST important in stabilizing the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is the most important muscle group for stabilizing the knee joint. The inferior fibers of vastus medialis and lateralis are particularly important stabilizers. Quadriceps weakness leads to instability especially on stairs and inclines. Rehabilitation after any knee injury or surgery focuses heavily on quadriceps strengthening exercises.

During inspiration, ribs 7-10 move laterally in a "bucket handle" movement, increasing the lateral (transverse) dimensions of the thoracic cavity. The upper ribs (2-7) move in a "pump handle" fashion, increasing anteroposterior diameter by pushing the sternum forward. These movements are coordinated during breathing.
questions.question: Which ribs produce bucket-handle movement?

questions.explanation: abducts the little finger away from the ring finger. It is one of three hypothenar muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve. The muscle forms the medial border of the palm in the hypothenar eminence.
questions.question: Which hypothenar muscle abducts the little finger?

questions.explanation: The superior epigastric artery is the other terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery. It descends behind the rectus abdominis muscle supplying it and the anterior abdominal wall. It anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac), providing collateral circulation between subclavian and external iliac arteries.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior body wall superiorly?

questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve, after synapsing in the celiac ganglion, provides sympathetic innervation to foregut-derived organs including the stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, small intestine, and proximal colon (to the splenic flexure). It also carries visceral afferent fibers for pain sensation from these organs.
questions.question: Which organs receive greater splanchnic innervation?

options: Base and styloid process of the 5th metatarsal only
Medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
Navicular tuberosity and the adjacent medial cuneiform bone
Bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsal bones
Calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon posteriorly
questions.question: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot. It inserts into which specific structures?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior inserts into the medial and inferior surfaces of the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal. It originates from the lateral condyle and superior half of the lateral surface of the tibia and interosseous membrane. It is the most powerful dorsiflexor and inverts the foot, active throughout the swing phase of gait.

questions.question: Which muscle causes nipple erection?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle cells disposed in a predominantly circular direction and radiating from the nipple base cause nipple erection. Their contraction, induced by cold, tactile, or emotional stimuli, causes erection of the nipple and wrinkling of the surrounding areola. This is an involuntary response.

questions.question: The cricothyroid joint allows which movement?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid joint between the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage allows anteroposterior tilting (rotation). This movement elongates or shortens the vocal cords, changing their tension. Cricothyroid muscle contraction tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, tensing the cords. The joint is a synovial joint with a capsule and ligaments.

questions.question: Which vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove?
questions.explanation: The great cardiac vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove alongside the anterior interventricular artery, then curves left in the coronary groove to become the coronary sinus. It drains the areas supplied by the left coronary artery (anterior left ventricle, anterior interventricular septum, and parts of right ventricle). It is the largest tributary of the coronary sinus.

questions.question: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) lies between which structures?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas, cul-de-sac) is the peritoneal reflection between the uterus anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly, representing the most inferior extent of the peritoneal cavity in females (approximately 5.5 cm from the anus and 7.5 cm from the vaginal orifice). It is bounded laterally by the uterosacral ligaments and can be accessed through the posterior vaginal fornix for drainage of pelvic abscesses (culdocentesis) or laparoscopic procedures. Fluid, blood, or pus in the peritoneal cavity gravitates to this pouch in supine or standing positions, making it clinically significant.

The ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver), representing the obliterated left umbilical vein, runs from the umbilicus to the liver within the free inferior border of the falciform ligament. Upon reaching the liver, it continues in a fissure on the visceral surface between the left and quadrate lobes before joining the left branch of the portal vein. The ligamentum teres may remain patent in portal hypertension, allowing portosystemic anastomosis through paraumbilical veins, potentially leading to caput medusae. At the umbilicus, it connects to the median umbilical ligament (obliterated urachus).
questions.question: The ligamentum teres hepatis is found in which structure?
What muscle initiates finger extension at interphalangeal joints?
questions.explanation: extend the interphalangeal joints while simultaneously flexing the metacarpophalangeal joints. This coordinated action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. Extensor digitorum extends the metacarpophalangeal joints but cannot independently extend interphalangeal joints without intrinsic muscle assistance.

options: Pronator teres for fine control only
Pronator teres for power/speed, pronator quadratus for sustained/slow pronation
questions.explanation: Pronator teres is active during rapid or forceful pronation, while pronator quadratus is the primary muscle for slow, sustained pronation. The quadratus maintains pronated position during precision tasks. This demonstrates functional specialization among synergistic muscles.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and pronator quadratus?
Which structure marks McBurney's point on the abdominal surface?
questions.explanation: McBurney's point, located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, marks the base of the appendix where it attaches to the cecum. While the position of the appendix tip is highly variable, the base is consistently located at the confluence of the three taeniae coli on the posteromedialaaspect of the cecum.

Trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges that project from the inner surface of the ventricles. They prevent the walls from adhering to each other during contraction, increase ventricular surface area, and may contribute to ventricular contraction. Some are attached at both ends (ridges), some at one end (bridges like the moderator band), and some are free (papillary muscles).
questions.question: What is the function of trabeculae carneae?

questions.explanation: The lower border of the soft palate marks the boundary between the nasopharynx above and the oropharynx below. The soft palate can elevate to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing. The pharyngeal isthmus connects these two regions and can be voluntarily controlled.
questions.question: Which structure marks the junction between the nasopharynx and oropharynx?

questions.explanation: The otic ganglion provides postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. Preganglionic fibers arrive via the lesser petrosal nerve from the glossopharyngeal nerve. The ganglion lies in the infratemporal fossa medial to the mandibular nerve below the foramen ovale.
questions.question: The otic ganglion provides parasympathetic innervation to which gland?

questions.explanation: The radial nerve accompanies the profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery through the spiral groove of the humerus. The nerve winds around the posterior shaft of the humerus between the medial and lateral heads of triceps. This close relationship makes the nerve vulnerable to injury in humeral shaft fractures.
questions.question: Which nerve accompanies the deep brachial artery through the spiral groove?
Where does the cervical pleura lymph drain anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The cervical pleura drains into the internal thoracic chain anteriorly and into the intercostal chain posteriorly. The parietal pleura's lymphatic drainage follows its vascular supply pattern. Coastal and mediastinal pleura also drain to the internal thoracic chain anteriorly.

questions.question: The posterior third of the tongue receives general and special sensory from which nerve?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor supply to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus.

Anterior to the lung apex lies the brachiocephalic vein (left side has left brachiocephalic vein crossing; right side has right brachiocephalic vein). The subclavian artery arches over the apex (groove on apex). Posteriorly lies the neck of the first rib and sympathetic trunk. Medially is the trachea and esophagus.
questions.question: What structure lies anterior to lung apex?

questions.explanation: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery consist of three or four arteries that perforate the adductor magnus muscle, contributing to the supply of the medial and posterior thigh muscles. The lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies the lateral thigh, while the medial femoral circumflex artery supplies the femoral head and neck.
questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to supply the posterior and medial thigh?

questions.explanation: The caval opening for the inferior vena cava is located at the level of T8 in the central tendon. It also transmits terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve and a few lymphatic vessels. This is the highest and most anterior of the three main diaphragmatic openings.
questions.question: At which vertebral level is the caval opening?
The foramen of Bochdalek is located in which part of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Bochdalek is a congenital posterolateral defect in the diaphragm (more common on the left side) that results from incomplete fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membrane during embryological development. This allows herniation of abdominal contents (stomach, spleen, intestines) into the thorax, potentially causing respiratory distress in neonates due to pulmonary hypoplasia. The foramen of Morgagni is an anteromedial defect between sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm. Both differ from the normal anatomical openings (caval opening in central tendon at T8, esophageal hiatus in muscular portion at T10, and aortic hiatus between crura at T12).

produces both flexion and supination of the forearm. It is most powerful as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90 degrees. The muscle has two heads proximally but a common tendon distally inserting on the radial tuberosity.
questions.question: Which muscle produces both flexion and supination of the forearm?
The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as which artery?
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as the femoral artery, lying lateral to the femoral vein. The femoral artery enters the femoral triangle at this level and gives off the profunda femoris approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to the thigh muscles.

questions.question: Which bone of the foot articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, the navicular anteriorly, the tibia superiorly, and both malleoli laterally?
questions.explanation: The talus articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, navicular anteriorly, tibia superiorly, lateral malleolus laterally, and medial malleolus medially. This unique articulation pattern makes the talus the keystone of the hindfoot. The talus receives no direct muscle attachments and is entirely dependent on its articular surfaces and ligamentous connections.

The lateral arcuate ligament (lateral lumbocostal arch) is a thickened band of fascia covering the quadratus lumborum muscle, extending from the tip of the L1 transverse process to the 12th rib. The diaphragm's lateral muscular fibers arise from this ligament. The medial arcuate ligament crosses over psoas major (from L1 body to L1 transverse process), while the median arcuate ligament connects the right and left crura across the aortic hiatus. These ligaments can compress neurovascular structures and serve as important surgical landmarks in retroperitoneal approaches.
questions.question: The lateral arcuate ligament extends from L1 transverse process to which structure?
The hepatic portal vein is formed posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. The portal vein measures approximately 8 cm in length and has no valves.

options: Exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region
Exit from perineum to gluteal region
Passage between gluteal and adductor compartments
Entrance from gluteal to femoral triangle
questions.explanation: The greater sciatic foramen (GSF) provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. In contrast, the lesser sciatic foramen (LSF) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region, enabling structures that exited the pelvis via the GSF to re-enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.
questions.question: The greater sciatic foramen's primary function is best described as which of the following?

questions.explanation: Anconeus is a small muscle that assists triceps brachii in elbow extension. It is located on the posterior aspect of the elbow, blending with the lateral head of triceps. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve.
questions.question: What is the function of anconeus muscle?
From how many lumbar vertebrae does right crus arise?
questions.explanation: The right crus arises from the front of the bodies of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs. The left crus is smaller and arises only from L1 and L2. Some muscle fibers from the right crus form a sling around the esophageal opening.

The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx or conjoined tendon) is formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles as they insert onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. This structure reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in its medial third, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Weakness or absence of the conjoint tendon in Hesselbach's triangle (bounded by lateral border of rectus, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric artery) predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The external oblique does not contribute to the conjoint tendon; instead, its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the canal and the superficial ring.
questions.question: Which muscle's fibers contribute to the conjoint tendon?
Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the submandibular triangle?
questions.explanation: The submandibular triangle is bounded superiorly by the body of the mandible, anteroinferiorly by the anterior belly of digastric, and posteroinferiorly by the posterior belly of digastric. The floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles. The triangle contains the submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, and submandibular lymph nodes.

The interatrial septum is the thin wall separating the right and left atria. It contains the fossa ovalis, a thumbprint-sized oval depression representing the site of the foramen ovale in the fetus. The limbus fossae ovalis is the prominent margin of the fossa. In approximately 25% of people, the foramen ovale remains probe-patent without functional significance.
questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left atria internally?
Which artery supplies the distal third of the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The left colic artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the distal one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, and left colic (splenic) flexure through its ascending branch. The ascending branch anastomoses with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery of Drummond. This anastomosis at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) represents the watershed between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories and is vulnerable to ischemia. The splenic flexure may be relatively poorly supplied by collaterals, making it susceptible to ischemic colitis in low-flow states.

Scapular protraction (abduction) is produced by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor muscles. During protraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves forward along with the scapula. This movement is used in punching, pushing, and reaching forward actions.
questions.question: Which muscles are responsible for scapular protraction?
What provides the primary blood supply to the rotator cuff?
options: Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral plus suprascapular
questions.explanation: The rotator cuff receives blood supply from three main sources: anterior circumflex humeral artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery, and suprascapular artery. A critical zone exists in the supraspinatus tendon with relatively poor vascularity, predisposing this area to degeneration and tears.

The external spermatic fascia, the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the external oblique muscle's aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. Moving inward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the innermost fascial layer is the internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring). The dartos muscle is in the scrotal wall, not directly covering the cord. These concentric layers are acquired sequentially as structures descend through abdominal wall layers.
questions.question: The spermatic cord receives its external covering from which muscle?

options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, and first metatarsal
Calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and all metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, and all five metatarsals
questions.explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals. Its summit is the subtalar articulation. It is smaller, more rigid, more stable than the medial arch, and makes more contact with the ground. It bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play and has limited mobility, built to transmit weight.
questions.question: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by which bones and is described as more rigid and making more contact with the ground?

questions.explanation: The cardiac notch is a deep indentation on the anterior border of the left lung created by the apex of the heart. This notch is located at the level of the fourth costal cartilage. Below the cardiac notch, the lung forms a tongue-like projection called the lingula.
questions.question: Where is the cardiac notch located?
What is the primary function of the thoracic cage?
questions.explanation: The thoracic cage primarily functions to protect the lungs, heart, and great vessels from external trauma. Additionally, it provides attachment points for muscles of the thorax, upper limb, abdomen, and back. The cage also plays a vital role in the mechanics of respiration through its elastic properties.

questions.question: The superficial inguinal ring transmits which structure in females?
questions.explanation: In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through the inguinal canal and exits via the superficial inguinal ring to terminate in the subcutaneous tissue and labium majus. The ilioinguinal nerve also passes through the superficial ring in both sexes (after traversing the canal). The round ligament is homologous to the gubernaculum testis in males (proximal gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament in females). Indirect inguinal hernias are much less common in females but can occur alongside the round ligament in the canal of Nuck (persistent processus vaginalis in females).

questions.question: What is the only electrical connection between atria and ventricles?
questions.explanation: The bundle of His (AV bundle) is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and ventricles, as the fibrous skeleton of the heart electrically insulates these chambers. It arises from the AV node, penetrates the fibrous skeleton, and divides into right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum. Accessory pathways (e.g., WPW syndrome) can create additional abnormal connections.

questions.question: Which cartilage forms the Adam's apple (laryngeal prominence)?
questions.explanation: The thyroid cartilage is shield-shaped with two laminae meeting in the midline to form the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). This prominence is more acute and prominent in males. The thyroid cartilage protects the vocal cords and provides anterior attachment for the vocal ligaments.

The right middle lobe contains two bronchopulmonary segments: lateral and medial. This is the smallest lobe of the right lung. The middle lobe is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. Middle lobe syndrome can occur from lymph node compression.
questions.question: How many segments are in right middle lobe?

questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain lymph from the lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, and lower anterior abdominal wall (below the umbilicus). Their efferents drain to the deep inguinal lymph nodes, which then drain to the external iliac nodes, common iliac nodes, and ultimately the para-aortic nodes. This drainage pattern explains why infections of the foot can present with inguinal lymphadenopathy.
questions.question: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain which areas of the body, and their efferents drain to which deep node group?
options: Lower limb only; draining to external iliac nodes
Lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, lower anterior abdominal wall; deep inguinal nodes
Only the genitalia; draining to internal obturator nodes
Only the lower limb below the knee; popliteal nodes
Only the gluteal region; internal iliac nodes

questions.explanation: The portal vein forms at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level posterior to the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein then ascends obliquely to the right in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and receives the left and right gastric veins.
questions.question: The portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?
From which vessel do inferior phrenic arteries arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior phrenic arteries are the first branches of the abdominal aorta and supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm. The right inferior phrenic artery gives off the suprarenal artery. These arteries are important in collateral circulation and can be a source of bleeding in trauma.

The descending thoracic aorta gives off nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces (3rd-11th). The upper two spaces are supplied by the superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk. The subcostal arteries (below the 12th rib) are also given off by the thoracic aorta.
questions.question: How many posterior intercostal arteries does aorta give?

questions.explanation: The right suprarenal gland is related anteriorly to the bare area of the liver and the inferior vena cava, posteriorly to the diaphragm, medially to the right celiac ganglion and IVC, and inferiorly to the upper pole of the right kidney. The left suprarenal gland has different anterior relations (stomach, pancreas, splenic artery, and lesser sac). Both glands are retroperitoneal and highly vascular, receiving arterial supply from three sources (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery) but having asymmetric venous drainage (right to IVC, left to left renal vein).
questions.question: The right suprarenal gland is related anteriorly to which structure?

questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels (arteries and veins, 4-6 pairs) passing from the splenic vessels near the hilum to the gastric fundus, and the left gastroepiploic vessels running to the greater curvature. The splenic artery, splenic vein, and tail of the pancreas run in the splenorenal ligament, not the gastrosplenic ligament. These two ligaments together connect the spleen to the stomach and posterior abdominal wall. Division of the gastrosplenic ligament is necessary during splenectomy, requiring ligation of the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels to devascularize the spleen.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the gastrosplenic ligament?
Which nerve supplies the fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves (C3-C5) provide somatic sensory innervation to the fibrous pericardium and parietal layer of serous pericardium. Pain from pericardial irritation is therefore sharp and well-localized, often referred to the shoulder (C4 dermatome). The visceral pericardium receives autonomic innervation and is insensitive to pain.

The jugulo-omohyoid lymph node (principal node of the tongue) is located where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. It receives drainage from the tip and anterior tongue (along with submental nodes). The node is part of the inferior deep cervical chain. Enlargement suggests anterior oral cavity or tongue pathology.
questions.question: The jugulo-omohyoid node drains which structure primarily?
What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and biceps?
options: They're antagonists: pronator teres pronates, biceps supinates
questions.explanation: Pronator teres and biceps brachii are antagonistic for forearm rotation: pronator teres produces pronation while biceps produces supination. However, both can contribute to elbow flexion when pronation/supination resistance is present. This demonstrates how muscles can be synergistic for one motion while antagonistic for another.

The cuneiform cartilages (cartilages of Wrisberg) are small rod-shaped elastic cartilages lying in the aryepiglottic folds anterior to the corniculate cartilages. They produce small elevations on the mucosal surface visible during laryngoscopy. The cartilages strengthen the aryepiglottic folds. Some individuals may lack these cartilages.
questions.question: Which cartilage lies in the aryepiglottic fold?

questions.explanation: The interureteric ridge (interureteric fold) is a smooth muscular ridge connecting the two ureteric orifices and forms the posterior boundary (base) of the trigone. The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the internal bladder base with the two ureteric orifices forming the superolateral angles and the internal urethral orifice forming the inferior angle.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the bladder trigone?

questions.explanation: The posterior mediastinum is bounded anteriorly by the pericardium (which forms the heart in the middle mediastinum). Posteriorly, it is bounded by the thoracic vertebrae from T5 to T12. The posterior mediastinum contains the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, and sympathetic trunks.
questions.question: What forms the anterior boundary of posterior mediastinum?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at the level of L1 as a continuation of the cisterna chyli, which is formed by the union of left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. The duct eventually terminates by draining into the left venous angle after receiving additional lymphatic tributaries.
questions.question: Which structure represents the continuation of cisterna chyli?
Why does diaphragmatic pain refer to shoulder?
questions.explanation: Pain from irritation of the central diaphragm (supplied by phrenic nerve C3-5) refers to the shoulder because the supraclavicular nerves (C3-4) supply the skin over the shoulder. This is an example of referred pain where stimuli from different areas share the same spinal cord segments.

questions.question: The obturator nerve supplies the medial compartment of the thigh. It exits the pelvis through which specific structure?
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve exits the pelvis by passing through the obturator foramen, along with the obturator vessels. It then divides into anterior and posterior divisions in the obturator canal. The anterior division runs anterior to obturator externus and adductor brevis, while the posterior division runs posterior to adductor brevis. It supplies the medial compartment of the thigh.

options: Articulates with the lateral femoral condyle
Provides attachment for knee joint structures only
questions.question: The fibula does NOT form part of the knee joint. Its role in relation to the knee is best described as what?
questions.explanation: The fibula does not form part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella. Its role is only to provide attachment for knee joint structures: the fibular collateral ligament (from the lateral epicondyle of the femur to the fibular head) and the biceps femoris tendon. The fibula mainly serves as a muscle attachment site and forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise.

The psoas major muscle is innervated by the ventral rami of lumbar nerves L1 through L4, which emerge from the lumbar plexus formed within the substance of the muscle itself. This segmental innervation pattern corresponds to the muscle's extensive vertebral origins from the bodies, transverse processes, and intervertebral discs of T12 through L5. The muscle serves as the chief flexor of the thigh at the hip joint and also assists in lateral flexion of the lumbar vertebral column when acting unilaterally.
questions.question: The psoas major muscle receives innervation from which nerve roots?

questions.explanation: The quadrangular space is bounded superiorly by teres minor, inferiorly by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps, and laterally by the surgical neck of humerus. Through this space pass the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels. Injury to these structures can occur with shoulder trauma.
questions.question: Which muscles form the boundaries of the quadrangular space in the axilla?
options: Teres major, teres minor, long head of triceps, surgical neck of humerus
Subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi, humerus
Teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, lateral head of triceps
Deltoid, teres minor, long head of triceps, humerus

questions.question: The left colic flexure is supported by which ligament?
questions.explanation: The phrenicocolic ligament extends from the splenic (left colic) flexure of the colon to the diaphragm at the level of the 10th and 11th ribs, helping to support and maintain the position of the splenic flexure. This ligament forms a shelf that supports the inferior pole of the spleen, preventing its downward displacement. The ligament also serves as a barrier between the left paracolic gutter and the area around the spleen, potentially limiting the spread of infection or fluid collections between these compartments during pathological processes.

The corrugator cutis ani muscle, formed by fusion of fibers from the longitudinal muscle layer of the rectum and the levator ani, inserts into the skin of the anal canal at the white line (intersphincteric line, or white line of Hilton). This line represents the lower border of the internal anal sphincter and the intermuscular groove between the internal and external anal sphincters. Some longitudinal muscle fibers also blend with the puborectalis anteriorly and extend to form the rectourethralis muscle (muscle of Roux) in males, extending toward the urethra.
questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the white line of Hilton?

questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of the fascia covering the anterior surface of psoas major muscle. It extends from the side of the body of L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process of L1. The lateral arcuate ligament overlies quadratus lumborum muscle.
questions.question: What does the medial arcuate ligament overlie?
What produces medial rotation of the humerus at the shoulder?
options: Subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major
questions.explanation: Medial (internal) rotation of the humerus is produced by subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, and anterior fibers of deltoid. This movement rotates the arm toward the midline so the thumb points medially. These muscles are predominantly anterior or on the subscapular surface.

questions.question: Which artery accompanies the hypoglossal nerve?
questions.explanation: The lingual artery arises from the external carotid at the level of the hyoid bone and is closely related to the hypoglossal nerve. The nerve crosses superficial to the artery as it loops forward. The artery divides into dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The hyoglossus muscle separates superficial from deep structures.

questions.question: Which cardiac chamber forms most of the anterior surface?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart. The right atrium contributes to the right portion of this surface, and a small part of the left ventricle forms the left border. This anterior position makes the right ventricle most vulnerable to anterior chest trauma. The left ventricle forms most of the diaphragmatic surface and left border.

The male urethra is approximately 20 cm (8 inches) long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) portions. It serves both urinary and reproductive functions, carrying urine and semen. The female urethra is much shorter at approximately 4 cm, serving only urinary function.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of the male urethra?
Which ligament connects the spleen to the greater curvature?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic (gastrolienal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach. It is part of the greater omentum and contains the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels. This ligament provides vascular connections between the spleen and stomach.

The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac trunk and has a characteristic tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas. It runs from right to left within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-7 branches at the splenic hilum. The artery gives off numerous pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, and the left gastroepiploic artery.
questions.question: Which is the largest branch of the celiac trunk?
The anterior tibial artery runs through the anterior compartment and enters the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery. It gives off which branch that contributes to the genicular anastomosis?
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery gives off the anterior tibial recurrent artery, which ascends to the front of the knee to contribute inferolaterally to the genicular anastomosis. This vessel pierces the anterior tibialis muscle and anastomoses with the inferior lateral genicular artery. Knowledge of this anastomosis is important for understanding collateral circulation when the popliteal artery is occluded.

questions.question: What connects breast skin to deep fascia?
questions.explanation: The ligaments of Cooper are fibrous strands that connect the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major, passing through the breast tissue. They provide structural support to the breast. Infiltration of these ligaments by breast cancer causes their shortening, producing the characteristic peau d'orange appearance.

questions.question: Where are Peyer's patches most concentrated?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are most numerous and largest in the terminal ileum, with 20-30 patches typically present in the last 60 cm of ileum. They are permanent aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the lamina propria and submucosa, located on the antimesenteric border. M cells in the epithelium overlying Peyer's patches sample antigens for immune surveillance. They can become inflamed in conditions like typhoid fever.

Gastrin is produced by G cells in the pyloric antrum and stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid and stimulates chief cells to secrete pepsinogen. Its release is stimulated by stomach distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin secretion is inhibited by low pH (negative feedback) and by somatostatin from D cells.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates gastric acid secretion?

questions.explanation: The medial basal segment is often absent or rudimentary on the left side, or it may be fused with the anterior basal segment. This anatomical variation contributes to the left lung having fewer total segments (8-10) compared to the right lung (10 segments). This variation is clinically significant.
questions.question: Which basal segment is often absent on left?
How many muscles constitute the gluteal region, including the six lateral rotators?
questions.explanation: The gluteal region contains nine muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae, piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, and quadratus femoris. These perform extension, abduction, lateral rotation, and stabilization of the hip joint.

questions.question: How do extrinsic thumb muscles complement thenar muscles?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic thumb muscles (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus and brevis, flexor pollicis longus) provide power and basic positioning. Thenar muscles provide fine motor control and opposition. This combination enables the thumb's unique versatility in human hand function.
options: Extrinsic muscles for precision grip only
Extrinsic for power grip, thenar for precision control

questions.question: Which lymphatic duct drains into the left venous angle?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct drains into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins). It collects lymph from the entire body except the right upper quadrant. The duct begins at the cisterna chyli (L1-L2), ascends through the thorax, and arches over the left subclavian artery to reach the venous angle.

questions.question: How do extrinsic and intrinsic factors contribute to shoulder stability?
questions.explanation: Shoulder stability requires both extrinsic factors (rotator cuff muscles, long head of biceps, negative intra-articular pressure, scapular position) and intrinsic factors (glenoid labrum, glenohumeral ligaments, joint capsule). Loss of either extrinsic or intrinsic factors increases dislocation risk.
options: Both extrinsic and intrinsic stabilizers are essential

questions.question: Which structure is most posterior in superior mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The esophagus is the most posterior structure in the superior mediastinum. From superficial to deep, the contents include: thymus gland, great veins (brachiocephalic veins and SVC), great arteries (aortic arch and branches), nerves (vagus and phrenic), trachea, esophagus, and thoracic duct.

The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot at the ankle. It passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and contributes to the toes via the deep plantar arch.
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery as it crosses the ankle to enter the foot?
Which trunk branches from the aortic arch first?
questions.explanation: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It ascends to the right and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch.

The laryngeal ventricle (sinus of Morgagni) is a space between the true vocal fold below and the false vocal fold (vestibular fold) above. It extends laterally into the saccule, which contains mucous glands that lubricate the vocal cords. The lateral wall is formed by the thyroid cartilage.
questions.question: Which space lies between the vocal and vestibular folds?

questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur, and empties into the femoral vein after traversing the saphenous opening. It has 10-12 valves.
questions.question: The great saphenous vein, the longest vein in the body, is formed at the foot by the union of which structures?
options: Medial marginal vein and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and posterior tibial vein
Small saphenous vein and dorsal venous arch
Anterior tibial vein and dorsal venous arch

questions.explanation: The arcuate line (linea semicircularis) marks the inferior border of the posterior rectus sheath, located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis, roughly at the level of the anterior superior iliac spine. Below this line, all three aponeurotic layers (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) pass anteriorly to the rectus abdominis muscle, leaving only transversalis fascia posteriorly. This anatomical feature creates a potential weakness that may be involved in direct inguinal hernias.
questions.question: The arcuate line of the rectus sheath is typically found at which level?
options: Level of anterior superior iliac spine

questions.question: The right suprarenal vein drains directly into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The right suprarenal vein is short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava on its posterior aspect, while the left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins). This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors the pattern of testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands receive blood from three arteries (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery respectively) but drain via only one or two veins, creating a rich arterial supply with limited venous drainage.

questions.question: All muscles of the medial (adductor) compartment are supplied by the obturator nerve EXCEPT which part of which muscle?
questions.explanation: All muscles of the medial compartment are supplied by the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) except the hamstring part of adductor magnus, which is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. Part of pectineus may also receive obturator supply. The dual nerve supply of adductor magnus reflects its dual embryological origin.

The frontal sinus drains through the frontonasal duct into the middle meatus via the infundibulum and hiatus semilunaris. Obstruction of this drainage pathway can lead to frontal sinusitis. The hiatus semilunaris is a curved groove in the lateral nasal wall.
questions.question: The frontal sinus drains into which nasal structure?

questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor affects the sternoclavicular, scapulothoracic, and glenohumeral joints through its action on scapular position. It produces depression, downward rotation, and protraction of the scapula. These scapular movements influence the position and function of the clavicle and shoulder joint.
questions.question: Which three joints does pectoralis minor movement affect?
Where does the right bronchial vein drain?
questions.explanation: The right bronchial vein drains into the azygos vein, while the left bronchial vein drains into the accessory hemiazygos vein. These veins return deoxygenated blood from the bronchial tree. The pulmonary veins, in contrast, carry oxygenated blood from the alveoli to the left atrium.

The 3rd right posterior intercostal artery typically gives off the right bronchial artery (though the origin is variable). The two left bronchial arteries usually arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta. Bronchial arteries provide the nutrient blood supply to the bronchial tree and lung tissue.
questions.question: What is significant about the 3rd right posterior intercostal?
The sternocleidomastoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Additional proprioceptive fibers from C2-C3 may contribute. Unilateral contraction of sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head ipsilaterally. Bilateral contraction flexes the neck.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between median and ulnar nerves in the hand?
options: Median for power, ulnar for precision muscles
Median for thenar precision, ulnar for hypothenar power and intrinsics
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies thenar muscles enabling precise thumb opposition for precision grip. The ulnar nerve supplies hypothenar muscles, all interossei, and medial lumbricals, providing intrinsic muscle coordination and power grip contribution. Together they enable both precision and power hand functions.

The sigmoid colon drains to sigmoid nodes along the sigmoid arteries, then to inferior mesenteric nodes around the inferior mesenteric artery origin. These eventually drain to para-aortic (lateral aortic) nodes. In colorectal cancer, lymph node involvement follows this drainage pattern and is crucial for staging. The lymphatic spread of left-sided colon cancers differs from right-sided cancers.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the sigmoid colon?

questions.explanation: The iliolumbar ligament extends from the transverse processes of L5 vertebra (and sometimes L4) to the iliac crest and iliac fossa. This strong ligament helps stabilize the lumbosacral junction and limits rotation at L5-S1. It forms an important surgical landmark in posterior approaches to the lumbar spine and pelvis. The ligament has superior and inferior bands; the superior band attaches to the transverse process and iliac crest, while the inferior band extends from the transverse process to the upper part of the sacral ala.
questions.question: The iliolumbar ligament connects which two structures?
options: L5 transverse process to iliac crest

questions.explanation: The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in rudimentary form at birth. The frontal and sphenoid sinuses become evident around age seven. This developmental pattern explains why frontal sinusitis is rare in young children. All sinuses reach full development by late adolescence.
questions.question: Which paranasal sinus is present in rudimentary form at birth?
Through which opening does the sympathetic trunk enter the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunks enter the abdomen from the thorax by passing deep to (posterior to) the medial arcuate ligaments. They descend on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, giving off lumbar splanchnic nerves. The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura to enter the abdomen.

The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer of the rectum, extending from the anorectal junction to approximately the level of the white line of Hilton, covering the upper three-quarters of the anal canal. It is under autonomic (involuntary) control, receiving sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric plexuses) that promotes contraction and parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) that causes relaxation. This sphincter maintains resting anal tone and unconscious fecal continence, while the external anal sphincter (striated voluntary muscle supplied by inferior rectal nerve) provides voluntary control.
questions.question: The internal anal sphincter is formed from which layer?

questions.explanation: The costocervical trunk is a branch of the second part of the subclavian artery (posterior to scalenus anterior). It divides into the superior intercostal artery (supplying the first two intercostal spaces) and the deep cervical artery (supplying deep neck muscles). This trunk is important in collateral circulation.
questions.question: What is the costocervical trunk?
What drains the area above the pectinate line in the anal canal?
questions.explanation: Above the pectinate line, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes (following the superior rectal vessels). Below the pectinate line, drainage is primarily to superficial inguinal nodes. This difference is clinically important in anal cancer spread: tumors above the line metastasize to pelvic nodes, while those below spread to inguinal nodes.

The caudate lobe, although anatomically part of the right lobe, is functionally part of the left lobe based on blood supply and biliary drainage. It receives blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and drains bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. Similarly, the quadrate lobe receives blood from the left hepatic artery and drains into the left hepatic duct.
questions.question: Which lobe of the liver is functionally part of the left lobe?
The testicular artery arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The testicular arteries (and ovarian arteries in females) arise from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level, just inferior to the renal arteries. This high origin reflects the embryological development of the gonads on the posterior abdominal wall before testicular descent or ovarian migration. The long testicular arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major, ureter, and external iliac vessels, enter the deep inguinal ring, and travel through the inguinal canal as part of the spermatic cord to reach the testes in the scrotum.

The middle rectal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (or occasionally from the internal pudendal artery) and passes medially in the lateral rectal ligament (lateral ligament of the rectum) to supply the lower part of the rectum. It anastomoses with branches of the superior rectal artery (from inferior mesenteric) above and inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal) below, creating collateral circulation. This vessel represents the junction between portal (superior rectal) and systemic (middle and inferior rectal) venous systems, a site of potential portosystemic anastomosis in portal hypertension.
questions.question: The middle rectal artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinuses drain into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. These sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid bone and vary greatly in size. Close relationship to the optic nerve and carotid artery makes sphenoid surgery particularly challenging.
questions.question: The sphenoid sinus drains into which location?

questions.explanation: The median sacral artery arises from the posterior aspect of the abdominal aorta just before its bifurcation at the L4 level (or sometimes from the aortic bifurcation itself). This small, unpaired vessel descends in the midline anterior to the sacrum and coccyx, supplying the posterior pelvic wall and anastomosing with the lateral sacral arteries (from internal iliac). It represents a caudal continuation of the dorsal aorta and may give small lumbar arteries. The median sacral artery is occasionally injured during presacral surgery or during anterior approaches to the spine.
questions.question: The median sacral artery arises from which vessel?

options: A single extensor tendon controls finger extension
Extrinsic extensors and intrinsics interact via extensor expansion
questions.question: How does the extensor mechanism coordinate finger extension?
questions.explanation: The extensor mechanism involves complex interaction between extensor digitorum (extrinsic) and intrinsic muscles through the extensor expansion. Intrinsic muscles (lumbricals, interossei) insert into lateral bands of the expansion, enabling MCP flexion with IP extension. This coordination is essential for normal finger function.

questions.question: The lesser occipital nerve is derived from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin of the lateral scalp posterior to the auricle. It ascends along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The greater occipital nerve (C2) provides sensation to the posterior scalp. Both nerves can be involved in occipital neuralgia.

(four muscles) produce finger abduction, moving fingers away from the middle finger axis. Palmar interossei (three muscles) produce finger adduction toward the middle finger. All interossei are supplied by the ulnar nerve and contribute to metacarpophalangeal joint flexion.
questions.question: Which interossei muscles produce finger abduction?

questions.explanation: An emissary vein passes through the foramen ovale connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus. Other emissary veins include those passing through the foramen spinosum (middle meningeal vein), mastoid foramen (sigmoid sinus), and parietal foramina (superior sagittal sinus). These valveless connections allow bidirectional flow and infection spread.
questions.question: Which foramen transmits the emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus?

questions.explanation: The transverse colon receives its arterial supply from branches of the superior mesenteric artery, specifically the middle colic artery and right colic artery branches. The junction between the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries occurs near the left third of the transverse colon. This represents the embryological boundary between midgut and hindgut derivatives.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the transverse colon?

questions.explanation: The upper pole of the left kidney is related to the spleen laterally. Other anterior relations of the left kidney include the stomach superiorly, the pancreatic body and tail centrally, the left colic flexure laterally and inferiorly, and coils of jejunum medially and inferiorly. The left suprarenal gland sits on the upper pole medially.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the upper pole of the left kidney?

questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, located immediately superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. Its margins, called the medial and lateral crura, are connected superiorly by intercrural fibers and give attachment to the external spermatic fascia. The superficial ring represents the external opening of the inguinal canal and transmits the spermatic cord in males or round ligament in females, along with the ilioinguinal nerve. The ring is larger in males than females, contributing to the higher incidence of inguinal hernias in males.
questions.question: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in which structure?
Which structure passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen is bounded by the lesser sciatic notch of the ischium, the sacrospinous ligament superiorly, and the sacrotuberous ligament inferiorly. The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hook around the ischial spine, and re-enter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the pudendal canal in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. The tendon of obturator internus also exits through this foramen. The sciatic nerve exits only through the greater sciatic foramen without re-entering the pelvis.

The greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone form most of the posterior orbital wall. The orbital surface of the greater wing forms the lateral posterior wall, while the lesser wing contributes superiorly. The optic canal is located at the orbital apex in the lesser wing. The superior orbital fissure lies between the wings.
questions.question: Which bone forms the posterior wall of the orbit?
Which structure contains the portal triad?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament, forming the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, contains the portal triad: the portal vein (posteriorly), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right). This ligament extends from the porta hepatis to the superior border of the first part of the duodenum. The portal triad arrangement is crucial for the Pringle maneuver, where the hepatoduodenal ligament is compressed to control bleeding during hepatic surgery.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the loose connective tissue layer of the scalp?
questions.explanation: The loose connective tissue layer contains emissary veins that connect the superficial scalp veins with intracranial venous sinuses. This layer is often called the danger area because infections can spread intracranially. The loose texture allows fluid and blood to spread widely in scalp injuries.

questions.question: Which bone contains the sella turcica?
questions.explanation: The sella turcica (Turkish saddle) is a depression in the body of the sphenoid bone housing the pituitary gland. It is bounded anteriorly by the tuberculum sellae and posteriorly by the dorsum sellae. The cavernous sinuses lie laterally. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses this region through the sphenoid sinus.

questions.question: What is the marginal artery of the heart?
questions.explanation: The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery that descends along the acute margin (right border) of the heart to supply the right ventricle. The left marginal artery (branch of the circumflex or left coronary artery) supplies the left border of the heart. These marginal branches are important anatomical landmarks in cardiac catheterization and surgery.

questions.question: What percentage of the small intestine length does the jejunum constitute?
questions.explanation: The jejunum constitutes approximately 40% of the total length of the small intestine beyond the duodenum. This represents about 2.5 meters of the 5-6 meter total small bowel length. The jejunum is characterized by being thicker-walled, more vascular, and having more prominent plicae circulares than the ileum.

The sinoatrial nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people, and from the left circumflex artery in about 40%. It courses posteriorly around the superior vena cava-atrial junction to supply the SA node. Occlusion can cause sinus node dysfunction, though collateral circulation often provides some protection.
questions.question: Which coronary artery typically gives rise to the SA nodal artery?
Which layer of the appendix contains abundant lymphoid tissue?
questions.explanation: The appendix has abundant lymphoid follicles in both the lamina propria and submucosa, unlike other parts of the intestine where lymphoid tissue is confined to the lamina propria. These follicles often extend into the submucosa, sometimes obliterating the clear boundary between layers. The appendix functions as a component of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT).

The internal carotid artery enters the skull through the carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone. It ascends through the carotid canal, passes above the foramen lacerum, traverses the cavernous sinus, and emerges to give off the ophthalmic artery. The sympathetic carotid plexus surrounds the artery in the canal.
questions.question: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through which opening?

questions.explanation: The floor of the inguinal canal is formed by the inguinal ligament (the rolled-under inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis) throughout most of its length, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament. The inguinal ligament extends from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. The roof is formed by the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, while the anterior wall is formed by the external oblique aponeurosis and the posterior wall by the transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: Retraction (adduction) of the scapula is produced by combined action of middle fibers of trapezius and the rhomboid muscles. During retraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves backward along with the scapula. This movement is important for pulling actions.
questions.question: What is the primary muscle for scapular retraction?
Which lymph nodes drain the ovary?
questions.explanation: The ovaries drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, following the ovarian vessels along which the lymphatics ascend. This drainage pattern reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys. In contrast, the uterine fundus drains to para-aortic nodes via lymphatics following the ovarian vessels, while the uterine body drains to external iliac nodes, and the cervix drains to external iliac, internal iliac, and sacral nodes. The upper vagina drains to internal iliac nodes, while the lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein within the superficial cervical fascia containing platysma. They receive drainage from the scalp and auricle. Efferents pass to the deep cervical chain.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the superficial cervical fascia?
The quadratus lumborum muscle is innervated by which nerves?
questions.explanation: The quadratus lumborum receives innervation from the subcostal nerve (T12) and the upper lumbar nerves (L1-L3 or L4), reflecting its position as the most lateral muscle of the posterior abdominal wall. This muscle originates from the iliolumbar ligament and adjacent iliac crest, inserting onto the medial half of the inferior border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae. It functions to fix the 12th rib during inspiration, extend the lumbar vertebral column bilaterally, and produce lateral flexion when acting unilaterally.

The basilar artery terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. It is formed by union of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. The artery gives off pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine branches during its course.
questions.question: The basilar artery terminates at which vertebral level?
How many separate joints are formed collectively by the 19 bones of the hand?
questions.explanation: The 19 bones of the hand (metacarpals and phalanges) collectively form 14 separate joints. These include the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints connecting fingers to palm and interphalangeal (IP) joints between finger segments. All are synovial joints with articular cartilage covering the bone surfaces.

questions.question: What impression is on the left lung medially?
questions.explanation: The left lung has several impressions on its mediastinal surface including: cardiac impression (the largest), aortic arch groove, descending aorta groove, subclavian artery groove, esophageal and tracheal grooves, and brachiocephalic vein groove. The aortic impressions are particularly prominent.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (which itself arises from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the vermiform appendix. It runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to reach the tip of the appendix. This end-artery arrangement (with minimal collateral supply) means that thrombosis or inflammation affecting the appendicular artery can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery's location in the mesoappendix requires careful ligation during appendectomy. Variations in the arterial supply are uncommon, but occasionally the appendicular artery may arise directly from a posterior cecal artery.

The occipital sinus lies in the attached border of the falx cerebelli and drains into the confluence of sinuses. It is the smallest of the cranial venous sinuses. The sinus communicates with the vertebral venous plexuses through the foramen magnum. It runs in the midline on the internal occipital crest.
questions.question: The occipital sinus drains into which structure?
The lingual tonsil is located on which surface of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior third (dorsal surface) of the tongue behind the sulcus terminalis. It forms part of Waldeyer's ring with the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils. The lingual tonsil is covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. Hypertrophy can cause airway obstruction or dysphagia.

questions.question: The cisterna chyli receives lymph from which trunks?
questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli) receives the intestinal trunk (draining abdominal viscera via pre-aortic nodes), right and left lumbar trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvis, and posterior abdominal wall), and sometimes the lower intercostal lymphatic trunks. It represents a dilated sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, located at L1-L2 level, anterior to the vertebral column, posterior and to the right of the aorta, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to traverse the posterior mediastinum and drain into the junction of left subclavian and internal jugular veins.

fibers produce both shoulder flexion and assist with abduction. The anterior fibers also contribute to medial rotation. The deltoid muscle as a whole is multipennate, with different fiber groups producing different movements.
questions.question: Which muscle abducts and flexes the shoulder?
How many vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: Six vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen: superior gluteal artery and vein, inferior gluteal artery and vein, and internal pudendal artery and vein. Together with seven nerves and the piriformis muscle, they constitute the 14 structures passing through this critical anatomical gateway from the pelvis to the gluteal region.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the parotid gland with sensory fibers?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) provides sensory innervation to the skin over the parotid gland and lower auricle. The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (not sensory to the gland). The facial nerve traverses the gland but doesn't innervate it. Parotid surgery risks great auricular nerve injury causing numbness.

The superior surface of the diaphragm is supplied by pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic arteries (branches of the internal thoracic artery) and the superior phrenic arteries (from the thoracic aorta). The pericardiacophrenic artery accompanies the phrenic nerve. The musculophrenic artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery.
questions.question: Which vessels supply the superior diaphragmatic surface?

questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal canal is formed by the lacrimal bone and maxilla, housing the nasolacrimal duct. The duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior meatus. The valve of Hasner at the inferior opening prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction requires dacryocystorhinostomy surgery.
questions.question: The nasolacrimal duct is formed by which two bones?

questions.explanation: The sternal part of the diaphragm arises from two small slips from the deep surface of the xiphoid process. The costal part arises from the inner aspects of the lower six ribs and costal cartilages. The vertebral part arises from the crura and arcuate ligaments.
questions.question: Which part of diaphragm arises from xiphoid process?
Where in the spleen are blood-borne bacteria primarily filtered?
questions.explanation: Blood-borne bacteria and particulate matter are primarily filtered and phagocytosed by macrophages in the red pulp cords and sinusoids. Blood flowing through the spleen is exposed to numerous macrophages that can recognize and remove opsonized bacteria and foreign particles. This filtering function is lost after splenectomy, increasing infection susceptibility.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the glenoid labrum?
