questions.explanation: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ridge surrounding the glenoid cavity that deepens the cavity, reducing dislocation risk. It increases the articular surface area and provides attachment for some glenohumeral ligaments. This structure contributes significantly to glenohumeral joint stability despite the joint's high mobility.

questions.question: What are the cusps of the mitral valve?
questions.explanation: The mitral (bicuspid) valve has two cusps: anterior (aortic) and posterior (mural). The anterior cusp is larger and more mobile, positioned between the mitral orifice and aortic orifice, while the posterior cusp is shorter and attached to more of the annular circumference. Mitral valve prolapse and stenosis are common pathological conditions affecting this valve.

The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hook around the ischial spine (covered by sacrospinous ligament), and re-enter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. This unique course makes the pudendal nerve vulnerable to compression at the ischial spine (pudendal neuralgia). The nerve to obturator internus follows a similar course. No other major structures pass through both foramina; the sciatic nerve and other gluteal region structures exit only through the greater sciatic foramen.
questions.question: Which structure passes through both greater and lesser sciatic foramina?

questions.explanation: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limb. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. The duct enters the right venous angle (junction of right internal jugular and subclavian veins).
questions.question: Which lymphatic structure drains lymph from the right upper quadrant of the body?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve's course around the medial epicondyle means elbow flexion stretches the nerve. Prolonged flexion (sleeping with bent elbow) can cause compression symptoms. This positional sensitivity explains why cubital tunnel syndrome symptoms may worsen at night and why sleeping with extended elbows helps.
options: Elbow flexion stretches nerve around medial epicondyle
questions.question: How does the ulnar nerve's course make hand position affect its function?
Which structure passes through esophageal hiatus?
questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits the esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, esophageal branches of left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The hiatus is formed by muscle fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm. Some right crus fibers form a sling around the esophagus.

questions.question: The mylohyoid line of the mandible provides attachment for which muscle?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle arises from the mylohyoid line on the internal surface of the mandible. The muscle forms the floor of the mouth, separating oral cavity from neck. Below the mylohyoid line, the submandibular gland rests in the submandibular fossa. The mylohyoid nerve (V3) innervates the muscle.

questions.question: Which artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm?
questions.explanation: The brachial artery is the main arterial supply to the arm and represents the continuation of the axillary artery. It begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into radial and ulnar arteries.

questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, medial to the deep inguinal ring. It ascends obliquely along the medial margin of the deep ring, passing medial to it (an important landmark distinguishing direct from indirect inguinal hernias), and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Within the sheath, it ascends posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery, providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian (via internal thoracic) and external iliac arterial systems.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the bare area of the liver?
questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver, the part of the posterior surface devoid of peritoneal covering and in direct contact with the diaphragm, receives blood supply from the right phrenic artery (and sometimes left phrenic artery). This triangular area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary and right triangular ligaments. The bare area lies between the two layers of the coronary ligament and is continuous with the inferior vena cava, which is embedded in a groove on the posterior surface. Small diaphragmatic veins from the bare area drain directly into the IVC.

questions.question: Which muscle is the ONLY component of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint and can therefore flex the thigh?
questions.explanation: Rectus femoris is the only quadriceps component that crosses the hip joint, originating from the anterior inferior iliac spine. Therefore, it can both extend the leg at the knee and flex the thigh at the hip. The three vasti originate from the femur itself and only cross the knee joint.

questions.question: Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the stylopharyngeus muscle?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) is the only cranial nerve that provides motor innervation to a pharyngeal muscle - the stylopharyngeus. All other pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). Stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing.

questions.question: What forms the superficial cardiac plexus?
questions.explanation: The cardiac plexus is formed by sympathetic fibers from the cervical and upper thoracic sympathetic ganglia and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerves. The superficial cardiac plexus lies beneath the aortic arch, while the deep plexus lies between the arch and tracheal bifurcation. These plexuses distribute fibers to the conducting system, coronary vessels, and myocardium.

The gastrohepatic ligament (pars flaccida) forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum, extending from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of the duodenum to the liver (extending to the fissure for ligamentum venosum and porta hepatis). It contains the right and left gastric vessels along the lesser curvature, and in some individuals, an aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery arising from the left gastric artery. The lesser omentum is continuous with the hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa), which forms its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver?

questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel (formed by the flexor retinaculum and medial ankle bones), accompanying the tibial nerve. It then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries, supplying the plantar foot and contributing to the toes via the deep plantar arch. Its pulse is palpated inferoposterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.question: The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through which structure, then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries?

questions.explanation: The superior, middle, and inferior pharyngeal constrictors form the muscular lateral and posterior walls of the pharynx. The superior constrictor extends from the pterygoid hamulus and pterygomandibular raphe to the median raphe. Gaps between the constrictors allow passage of nerves and vessels.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the pharynx?
The basilar artery is formed by the union of which vessels?
questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. It ascends in the pontine groove and terminates by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Branches include pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine arteries.

The anterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects embryologic derivation from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively. The digastric helps open the mouth and elevate the hyoid.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the anterior belly of the digastric?

questions.explanation: Small cricothyroid arterial branches from the superior thyroid arteries anastomose across the median cricothyroid ligament. This anastomosis crosses the ligament horizontally and must be considered during emergency cricothyroidotomy. The vessels typically run superiorly along the cricothyroid membrane.
questions.question: Which artery forms an anastomosis across the median cricothyroid ligament?
Which bone contains the cribriform plate?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is part of the ethmoid bone and forms the roof of the nasal cavity. It contains multiple foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium to the olfactory bulb. The crista galli projects upward from the cribriform plate for attachment of the falx cerebri.

The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) arises from the lateral cord and primarily supplies pectoralis major muscle. The lateral cord also gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve. It lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery.
questions.question: Which nerve branch arises from the lateral cord?
The transverse arch is formed proximally by which bones?
options: Bases of all five metatarsals only
Three cuneiforms and navicular bones only
Navicular and talus bones only proximally
Calcaneus and cuboid of the lateral column only
Three cuneiforms and cuboid proximally; five metatarsal bases distally
questions.explanation: The transverse arch is formed proximally by the three cuneiforms and the cuboid, and distally by the bases of the five metatarsals. When both feet are approximated, the medial borders form a complete transverse arch, with each foot representing a half dome. The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, contributing the bony factor to the transverse arch.

The quadratus lumborum muscle forms the central posterior relation of each kidney. The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially, and the transversus abdominis muscle (its aponeurosis) lies posterolaterally. The diaphragm is posterior to the upper pole, and the subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run posterior to the kidneys.
questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately posterior to both kidneys?

questions.explanation: The anterior two-thirds (oral part) of the tongue develops from the first pharyngeal arch (two lateral lingual swellings and median tuberculum impar). The posterior third (pharyngeal part) develops from the third arch (copula). The second arch contribution is overgrown. This embryologic division explains the different nerve supplies.
questions.question: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: The posterior vagal trunk, formed mainly from the right vagus nerve, sends a large branch to the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses. This distribution extends vagal innervation to the intestines as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas. The remaining branches supply the posterior surface of the stomach.
questions.question: Where does the posterior vagal trunk primarily distribute after entering the abdomen?
The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to which muscle group?
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) provides motor innervation to the infrahyoid strap muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. The thyrohyoid receives C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve. These muscles depress the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing.

Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of this triangle consists of transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon), representing a potential weak area in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery, in contrast to indirect hernias which emerge lateral to the artery through the deep inguinal ring.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?

questions.explanation: The foramen spinosum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, posterolateral to the foramen ovale. It transmits the middle meningeal artery and meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve. The foramen is located at the spine of the sphenoid. Accessory meningeal arteries may also pass through this foramen.
questions.question: Which bone contains the foramen spinosum?

questions.explanation: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus muscle by dividing into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk. The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. The popliteal artery gives five genicular branches contributing to the genicular anastomosis.
options: Anterior tibial artery and tibioperoneal trunk
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries
Peroneal artery and posterior tibial artery directly
questions.question: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of popliteus by dividing into which two initial divisions?

questions.explanation: The tendon of biceps femoris at its insertion on the lateral side of the head of fibula is split into two parts by the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee joint. The common fibular nerve closely follows the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula. Injury to biceps femoris or the fibular head can therefore damage the common fibular nerve.
questions.question: The tendon of biceps femoris at its fibular head insertion is split into two parts by which ligament?
Which structure bounds the superior thoracic aperture posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The superior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the first thoracic vertebra (T1). Anteriorly, it is bounded by the superior border of the manubrium sterni. Laterally, the medial borders of the first ribs and their costal cartilages complete the boundaries of this important opening.

questions.question: The quadriceps femoris is how many times stronger than its antagonist muscle group, the hamstrings?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is three times stronger than its antagonist, the hamstrings. It forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh and is the great extensor of the leg. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur and is considered the largest and one of the most powerful muscle groups in the body.

options: Anterior divisions supply flexors, posterior divisions supply extensors
questions.explanation: Brachial plexus organization reflects compartmental function: anterior divisions supply flexor (anterior) compartment muscles while posterior divisions supply extensor (posterior) compartment muscles. This organizational pattern continues from the plexus through the peripheral nerves, reflecting embryological development.
questions.question: How does the brachial plexus organization reflect compartment innervation?
The first metatarsal is described as the shortest and thickest metatarsal and bears the most weight. Which two bones are found at its head?
questions.explanation: The head of the first metatarsal contains two sesamoid bones, which increase the mechanical advantage of the flexor hallucis brevis and protect its tendons from compression. The first metatarsal is the most important in propulsion during walking and is also the most important attachment site for several tendons, making it clinically significant in hallux valgus and gout.

The right border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed by the right atrium. The left border is formed primarily by the left ventricle with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. The superior border is formed by the great vessels (aorta and pulmonary artery).
questions.question: What forms the right heart border radiographically?

questions.explanation: The median nerve is the only nerve passing through the carpal tunnel. It enters the hand between the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and lies anterior to the flexor digitorum profundus tendons. Compression of this nerve within the tunnel causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?
The stylomastoid artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The stylomastoid artery arises from the posterior auricular artery and enters the stylomastoid foramen to supply the facial nerve in its bony canal, the mastoid air cells, and the stapedius muscle. It anastomoses with the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery. The artery follows the facial nerve through the temporal bone.

options: Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
Tibial nerve, common fibular nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Common fibular nerve, popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal vein, popliteal artery, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
questions.question: In the popliteal fossa, the popliteal artery lies deepest and the tibial nerve most superficially. In what order, from lateral to medial, are the structures arranged superiorly within the fossa?
questions.explanation: At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve divides into the common fibular nerve (laterally, following the medial border of biceps femoris) and the tibial nerve (medially). From lateral to medial: common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, then popliteal artery (deepest). This arrangement changes inferiorly as the popliteal vein crosses to lie posterior to the artery.

questions.question: The tympanic plexus is formed primarily by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The tympanic plexus on the promontory of the middle ear is formed primarily by the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's nerve). Contributions also come from the caroticotympanic nerves (sympathetic). The plexus provides sensation to the middle ear mucosa. The lesser petrosal nerve arises from this plexus.

The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (C8, T1) from the medial cord provides sensation to the medial aspect of the arm. The intercostobrachial nerve (T2) also contributes to sensation in the axilla and medial arm. Both can be affected in axillary surgery or trauma.
questions.question: What nerve provides sensation to the medial arm?

questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery typically divides into frontal (anterior) and parietal (posterior) branches after entering the skull through the foramen spinosum. The frontal branch crosses the pterion area. The parietal branch supplies the posterior parietal region. Epidural hematomas most commonly involve the frontal branch in the pterion region.
questions.question: The middle meningeal artery commonly divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: On the left side, the pleural reflection passes inferomedially to the level of the fourth costal cartilage, where it deviates to the left margin of the sternum. This creates a shallow notch corresponding to the cardiac notch of the left lung. This differs from the right side where the pleura descends vertically in the median plane.
questions.question: At which costal cartilage does left pleural reflection deviate?
Into which vein does the right inferior phrenic vein drain?
questions.explanation: The right inferior phrenic vein usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left inferior phrenic vein is usually double, with one branch draining into the IVC and the other frequently joining the left suprarenal vein, which then drains into the left renal vein. These veins drain blood from the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

The porta hepatis (gateway of the liver) is a transverse fissure through which the portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic ducts pass. The portal vein and hepatic artery enter the liver while the hepatic ducts (right and left) exit. Lymphatic vessels and nerves also traverse the porta hepatis, which is bounded by the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.question: Which vessels enter the liver at the porta hepatis?
Which lymphatic structure drains most abdominal viscera?
questions.explanation: The pre-aortic (preaortic) lymph nodes, located around the origins of the three major unpaired visceral branches of the aorta (celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries), drain all abdominal viscera along the gastrointestinal tract from esophagus to upper anal canal, plus the liver, pancreas, and spleen. These nodes are grouped as celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric nodes. Efferent vessels from these nodes form the intestinal lymphatic trunk, which drains into the cisterna chyli. The cisterna chyli then gives rise to the thoracic duct.

Plantar interossei adduct (PAD - Plantar ADduct) and dorsal interossei abduct (DAB - Dorsal ABduct) in reference to the second digit (2nd ray), which is the anatomical axis of the foot. This is the same concept as the hand interossei, but referenced to different rays (middle finger for hand, second toe for foot). All interossei also flex the metatarsophalangeal joints.
questions.question: The fourth layer of foot muscles contains plantar interossei (3 muscles) and dorsal interossei (4 muscles). Plantar interossei adduct and dorsal interossei abduct in reference to which axis?

options: Through passive ligament and capsule action
Rotator cuff compresses humeral head into glenoid cavity
questions.question: How do the rotator cuff muscles stabilize the glenohumeral joint?
questions.explanation: Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability through their resting tone, actively compressing the humeral head into the glenoid cavity. The muscles form a tendinous cuff blending with the joint capsule, providing circumferential reinforcement. This active stabilization is essential given the joint's inherent bony instability.

questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the palatoglossus muscle?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve via cranial accessory), not the hypoglossal nerve like other tongue muscles. This exception makes it technically a palatal muscle rather than a tongue muscle. The pharyngeal plexus supplies all soft palate muscles except tensor veli palatini.

questions.question: The cruciate anastomosis is at the level of the lesser trochanter. Which four arteries specifically constitute this anastomosis?
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis at the level of the lesser trochanter is constituted by four arteries: inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA), and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral circulation between the internal iliac and femoral artery systems.
options: IGA, obturator artery, MFCA, and LFCA branches
SGA, IGA, MFCA, and LFCA arterial branches
IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris
SGA, IGA, obturator, and 1st perforating branch
MFCA, LFCA, popliteal, and descending genicular

questions.explanation: Lund's node (Calot's node) is located within Calot's triangle, bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver. This lymph node frequently becomes enlarged in cases of cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed during cholecystectomy. Calot's triangle is an important surgical landmark for identifying the cystic artery, which typically lies within this triangle. Careful dissection of this area is crucial during laparoscopic cholecystectomy to avoid injury to the hepatic ducts or right hepatic artery.
questions.question: Which lymph node is characteristically found in Calot's triangle?
Which region does the majority of the ileum occupy?
questions.explanation: The ileum predominantly occupies the right lower quadrant of the infracolic compartment, with the terminal ileum usually located in the pelvis. The ileum constitutes approximately 60% of the jejunoileal length. It characteristically ends at the ileocaecal junction on the medial aspect of the caecum.

is the only rotator cuff muscle that performs medial (internal) rotation of the humerus. It lies on the anterior surface of the scapula, filling the subscapular fossa. The other rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) are located posteriorly.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle performs medial rotation of the humerus?
How do the anterior and posterior interosseous nerves complement each other?
options: Anterior for deep flexors, posterior for extensors
Anterior for extensors, posterior for flexors
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies deep flexor muscles (flexor pollicis longus, radial half of flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus) while the posterior interosseous nerve supplies all posterior forearm extensors. This complementary distribution ensures complete innervation of forearm muscles from the radial and median nerves.

questions.question: The great auricular nerve is derived from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin over the parotid gland, lower ear, and angle of the mandible. It emerges at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and ascends on that muscle. The nerve is at risk during parotid surgery and facelift procedures.

The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering splenius capitis, levator scapulae, and scalene muscles (anterior, middle, posterior). The subclavian artery and brachial plexus emerge between the scalene muscles. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle superficially on this floor. Cervical lymph nodes lie within the triangle.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the posterior triangle?

questions.explanation: Extension at the wrist joint is produced mainly by extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris. The extensor digitorum provides assistance to this movement. All these extensors are located in the posterior compartment of the forearm.
options: Extensor carpi radialis longus, brevis, and ulnaris
questions.question: Which muscles produce wrist extension with assistance from extensor digitorum?
The testicular vein on the left typically drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle. This anatomical difference explains the higher incidence (90%) of left-sided varicoceles, as the perpendicular drainage into the renal vein, along with the longer venous column and potential compression by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon), creates higher venous pressure on the left. The left testicular vein lacks valves or has incompetent valves, facilitating retrograde flow and varicosity formation.

questions.question: The femoral nerve emerges from which muscle's lateral border?
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4), the largest branch of the lumbar plexus, emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle near the inguinal ligament and descends in the groove between psoas and iliacus. It enters the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle. Other branches emerging from psoas major's lateral border include the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves. The obturator nerve, in contrast, emerges from the medial border of psoas, while the genitofemoral nerve pierces through its anterior surface.

questions.question: Which bone articulates with all other cranial bones?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid bone articulates with all other cranial bones (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, ethmoid, zygomatic, palatine, vomer) and is called the keystone of the cranial base. It has a central body, greater and lesser wings, and pterygoid processes. The sella turcica houses the pituitary gland.

The splenic white pulp consists primarily of T and B lymphocytes organized around central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS containing T cells) and in lymphoid follicles (containing B cells). The white pulp is responsible for immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens and antibody production. It represents about 15-25% of splenic tissue and increases in infections.
questions.question: Which immune cells are found in splenic white pulp?
The left gastric artery arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left gastric artery is the smallest of the three branches of the celiac trunk (along with splenic and common hepatic arteries), arising at the T12/L1 level. It ascends to the cardioesophageal junction, giving off esophageal branches to the abdominal esophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature of the stomach in the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the right gastric artery. It supplies both surfaces of the stomach along the lesser curvature. An aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery, running in the gastrohepatic ligament.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the bladder?
questions.explanation: The superior vesical arteries (usually multiple branches) arise from the patent part of the umbilical artery and supply the superior surface and upper lateral surfaces of the bladder. The umbilical artery is obliterated distally (becoming the medial umbilical ligament) but remains patent proximally. The inferior vesical artery (in males) or vaginal artery (in females) supplies the bladder base.

The superior mesenteric artery and vein pass between the two peritoneal layers of the mesentery along with lymph nodes, lymphatic vessels, nerves, and fat. These vessels provide the primary blood supply and drainage for the jejunum and ileum. The superior mesenteric artery gives off 15-18 branches that form the arterial arcades.
questions.question: Which structures pass between the two layers of the mesentery?
The lesser petrosal nerve carries which type of fibers?
questions.explanation: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve to the otic ganglion. These fibers originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus. After synapsing in the otic ganglion, postganglionic fibers travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to provide secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland.

questions.question: Which branches arise from the first part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The first part of the axillary artery (from lateral border of first rib to upper border of pectoralis minor) gives off only one branch. This is the superior (highest) thoracic artery. The second part gives two branches while the third part gives three branches.

questions.question: Where do hilar lymphatics ultimately drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the lung drain into hilar (bronchopulmonary) nodes, and efferent lymphatics ultimately drain into the brachiocephalic vein. The lymph passes through pulmonary nodes, bronchopulmonary nodes, and tracheobronchial nodes before reaching the venous system. This pathway is important in cancer metastasis.

Extensor hallucis longus originates from the middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula and the adjacent interosseous membrane. It inserts into the dorsal aspect of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe and is innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). It extends the great toe, dorsiflexes the ankle, and can assist with foot inversion.
options: Superior half of lateral surface of tibia
Middle anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
Inferior third of anterior fibula only
questions.question: Extensor hallucis longus, innervated by the deep fibular nerve, originates from which structure?
Which nerve supplies pronator quadratus?
questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus. The pronator quadratus is the deepest muscle in the anterior forearm.

The descending colon is derived from the embryological hindgut, along with the distal third of the transverse colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Hindgut structures are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery and receive parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves. The midgut-hindgut junction occurs at approximately the left third of the transverse colon.
questions.question: Which embryological origin corresponds to the descending colon?
What drains blood from the breast?
questions.explanation: Blood from the breast drains into both the axillary veins (via lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial tributaries) and the internal thoracic veins (via perforating veins). During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become prominent and engorged. Venous drainage pathways are important routes for cancer metastasis.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the hepatoduodenal ligament (free right edge of lesser omentum) containing the portal triad as its anterior boundary. The superior boundary is formed by the caudate lobe of liver covered with peritoneum, the inferior boundary by the first part of the duodenum (superior or horizontal part), and the posterior boundary by the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum and the right crus of the diaphragm. This opening, typically admitting two fingers, provides the only communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs.

questions.question: Which part of the stomach is most anterior?
questions.explanation: The body of the stomach is the most anterior part, lying against the anterior abdominal wall in the epigastric region when the stomach is empty. The fundus extends superiorly and posteriorly beneath the left dome of the diaphragm, while the pyloric antrum angles to the right and posteriorly. The stomach's position varies with body position, respiratory phase, and degree of filling. When distended, the stomach extends inferiorly and the greater curvature becomes more anterior. The anterior surface is related to the diaphragm, anterior abdominal wall, left lobe of liver, and anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question: The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII), specifically by a branch from the nerve after it exits the stylomastoid foramen. The muscle elevates and retracts the hyoid bone during swallowing. It shares innervation and embryologic origin (second pharyngeal arch) with the posterior belly of digastric.

questions.question: The popliteal artery begins where the femoral artery passes through which structure in the lower thigh?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus. It then descends through the popliteal fossa and terminates at the inferior border of popliteus. The femoral artery travels through the adductor canal in the anterior thigh before reaching the hiatus.

The transverse colon is intraperitoneal, suspended by the transverse mesocolon from the posterior abdominal wall. The ascending and descending colon are secondarily retroperitoneal (covered by peritoneum anteriorly only), as is most of the duodenum (except the first 2 cm) and the pancreas (except the tail which extends into the splenorenal ligament). Secondarily retroperitoneal structures were initially suspended by mesentery during development but became fused to the posterior body wall. Primarily retroperitoneal organs (kidneys, suprarenal glands, ureters, aorta, IVC) were never suspended by mesentery.
questions.question: Which structure is NOT retroperitoneal?

questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is pierced by the parotid (Stensen's) duct before the duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar. The muscle forms the muscular component of the cheek and is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
questions.question: The buccinator muscle is pierced by which structure?

questions.explanation: The cupola (or apex) is the rounded superior portion of the lung that extends into the root of the neck, reaching 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle. It is covered by cervical pleura and the suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia). The subclavian artery arches over the lung apex.
questions.question: What is the lung at the apex called?
Which muscles form the posterior wall of the axilla?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the axilla is formed by subscapularis on the anterior surface of the scapula superiorly, and teres major and latissimus dorsi inferiorly. The posterior axillary fold extends farther inferiorly than the anterior wall and can be grasped between fingers.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist flexors and extensors in grip?
options: Wrist extensors stabilize wrist enabling grip strength
questions.explanation: During grip, wrist extensors isometrically contract to stabilize the wrist in slight extension. This prevents wrist flexion as finger flexors contract, optimizing finger flexor length-tension relationship for maximum grip force. This synergistic stabilization demonstrates functional muscle interaction.

questions.question: How many segments are in right lower lobe?
questions.explanation: The right lower lobe contains five bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The superior segment is also called the apical segment of the lower lobe and is the most dependent segment when lying supine.

The visceral pleura receives its arterial supply from branches of both the bronchial and pulmonary arterial systems. Venous drainage is to the pulmonary veins. Unlike the parietal pleura, the visceral pleura has no somatic sensory innervation and receives only autonomic vasomotor nerve supply.
questions.question: Which vessels supply blood to the visceral pleura?
Which nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter, composed of voluntary striated muscle, receives motor innervation from the inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) and perineal branch of S4. This allows voluntary control of defecation and anal continence. The pudendal nerve provides somatic innervation, making the external sphincter unlike the internal sphincter (smooth muscle under involuntary autonomic control). Damage to the pudendal nerve (during childbirth, surgery, or chronic straining) can lead to fecal incontinence. The pudendal nerve also provides sensory innervation to the anal canal below the pectinate line.

The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) typically joins the common bile duct within the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens at the major duodenal papilla. The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when patent, opens separately at the minor duodenal papilla approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. Anatomical variations exist, including separate openings of the pancreatic and bile ducts (pancreas divisum). The junction is surgically significant during ERCP and pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure).
questions.question: The main pancreatic duct typically joins the bile duct at which location?
The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows which movements of the foot?
options: Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion at the ankle
Circumduction only, without inversion or eversion
Inversion and eversion (with associated adduction and abduction)
Pronation and supination of the ankle
questions.explanation: The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows inversion and eversion of the foot, with associated adduction and abduction. These movements occur at the subtalar joint and midtarsal joints together. True dorsiflexion and plantarflexion occur at the ankle (talocrural) joint. The summit of the lateral longitudinal arch is at the subtalar articulation.

The cochlear aqueduct (perilymphatic duct) connects the scala tympani with the subarachnoid space, allowing communication between perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid. The aqueduct opens at the base of the petrous temporal bone. The vestibular aqueduct separately connects the endolymphatic system with the posterior cranial fossa. Patency varies among individuals.
questions.question: The cochlear aqueduct connects the scala tympani with which space?

questions.explanation: At the renal hilum, the renal vein lies most anteriorly, the renal artery lies in the middle, and the renal pelvis (with the ureter) lies most posteriorly. This arrangement can be remembered as "VAP" (Vein, Artery, Pelvis) from anterior to posterior. The hilum is located on the medial border of each kidney.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the hilum of the kidney most anteriorly?

questions.explanation: The interventricular septum has a small upper membranous part (approximately 1 cm) and a large lower muscular part. The membranous septum lies just beneath the aortic valve (specifically between the right and non-coronary cusps). Ventricular septal defects most commonly occur in the membranous portion near the tricuspid valve.
questions.question: Which part of the interventricular septum is membranous?

questions.explanation: A stable scapular base is essential for efficient glenohumeral motion. Scapular stabilizers (serratus anterior, rhomboids, trapezius) provide a fixed base from which glenohumeral muscles can act. Scapular winging demonstrates how loss of stability compromises shoulder function despite intact glenohumeral muscles.
options: Stable scapula essential for efficient glenohumeral motion
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between scapular stability and glenohumeral mobility?

questions.explanation: The left triangular ligament is formed by the approximation of the anterior and posterior layers of the left coronary ligament near the left end of the bare area, attaching the left lobe of the liver to the diaphragm. It is typically longer and narrower than the right triangular ligament. Division of this ligament is necessary to mobilize the left lateral segment of the liver during surgery. The ligament represents the reflection of peritoneum from the diaphragm onto the superior surface of the liver and demarcates the left lateral limit of the bare area of the liver.
questions.question: The left triangular ligament of the liver attaches to which lobe?
Which rib typically crosses the upper pole of the left kidney?
questions.explanation: The left kidney extends higher than the right, with its upper pole reaching the 11th rib, while the right kidney's upper pole typically reaches the 12th rib. Both kidneys lie on the diaphragm superiorly, which separates them from the pleura and lungs. The left kidney's higher position reflects the asymmetry caused by the liver on the right.

questions.question: Which neurovascular structure is the DEEPEST within the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint. This proximity makes the popliteal artery particularly vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures. The arrangement from deep to superficial is: artery, vein, then tibial nerve.

questions.question: The lateral ligaments of the ankle include which three named ligaments?
options: Anterior tibiotalar, posterior tibiotalar, and calcaneofibular
Anterior talofibular, tibiocalcaneal, and posterior talofibular
Anterior talofibular, posterior talofibular, and calcaneofibular
questions.explanation: The lateral ligaments of the ankle are: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL), and the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). The ATFL is the weakest and most commonly injured in ankle sprains. The CFL is the intermediate in strength, and the PTFL is the strongest. Together they stabilize the lateral side of the ankle joint.

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal vessels. Below the cords, sensation is provided by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. This sensory innervation triggers the cough reflex.
questions.question: Which structure provides the main sensory innervation to the larynx above the vocal cords?

questions.explanation: The median nerve provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. This sensory distribution is preserved in anterior interosseous syndrome (pure motor branch) but affected in carpal tunnel syndrome and more proximal median nerve injuries.
questions.question: What provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb?
The midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint is formed by which two articulations working together?
questions.explanation: The midtarsal joint (Chopart's joint) consists of two articulations working in concert: the talonavicular joint medially and the calcaneocuboid joint laterally. Movements at this joint complement subtalar movements to produce overall foot inversion and eversion. Chopart's amputation is performed through this joint for distal foot pathology, preserving the hindfoot for a functional stump.

The vertebral arteries enter the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum after ascending through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. They unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. The vertebral arteries give off the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries before joining.
questions.question: The vertebral arteries enter the skull through which opening?

questions.explanation: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV), the only extraocular muscle not supplied by the oculomotor nerve except lateral rectus (abducens). The superior oblique passes through the trochlea (pulley) on the medial orbital roof. It intorts, depresses, and abducts the eye.
questions.question: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by which cranial nerve?
Where does the spongy urethra begin?
questions.explanation: The spongy (penile) urethra begins where the membranous urethra exits the urogenital diaphragm and extends through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans penis. It is approximately 15 cm long and has two dilated portions: the intrabulbar fossa in the bulb and the navicular fossa in the glans.

The septum transversum is the mesodermal mass that forms the central tendon of the diaphragm. Initially located in front of the embryonic head, it migrates caudally during head folding. During this migration, cervical myotomes and nerves contribute muscle and nerve supply, explaining the phrenic nerve's long course from C3-5.
questions.question: What forms the central tendon embryologically?

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) descends through the anterior ethmoidal foramen to supply the anterior superior nasal septum and lateral nasal wall. It anastomoses with branches of the sphenopalatine artery posteriorly. The artery also supplies the anterior ethmoidal cells and contributes to the blood supply of the frontal sinus.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior nasal septum superiorly?
Which muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally?
questions.explanation: The risorius muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally, producing a grin or grimace. It arises from the parotid fascia and inserts into the angle of the mouth. The muscle is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It works with zygomaticus major in smiling. Some individuals lack this muscle.

Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal circulation (enterohepatic recirculation). About 95% of bile salts are recycled this way, conserving the bile salt pool. Ileal disease or resection disrupts this circulation, leading to bile salt malabsorption, steatorrhea, and potential bile salt diarrhea.
questions.question: Which segment absorbs bile salts for enterohepatic recirculation?

questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve (L3, L4). It runs with the great saphenous vein along the medial leg, from the knee to the medial malleolus and then to the medial side of the foot. It provides cutaneous sensation to the medial leg, ankle, and foot. It is at risk during stripping of the great saphenous vein for varicose vein surgery or coronary bypass grafting.
questions.question: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of which nerve and runs with which vein throughout most of the leg?
options: Common fibular nerve; great saphenous vein

questions.question: At what location does the brachial artery typically bifurcate into radial and ulnar arteries?
questions.explanation: The brachial artery bifurcates in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. This division occurs under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis into the radial artery (superficial) and ulnar artery (deeper). The cubital fossa provides a triangular space for this important vascular division.

The thymus consists of two elongated lobes and is a large organ in the fetus, occupying the thoracic cavity behind the sternum. It secretes lymphopoietin and plays a crucial role in T-lymphocyte maturation. After puberty, the thymus undergoes involution and is gradually replaced by adipose tissue.
questions.question: How many lobes does the thymus consist of?

questions.explanation: The pulmonary plexuses (anterior and posterior to the roots of the lungs) contain both parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve and sympathetic fibers from the sympathetic trunk. These plexuses provide the autonomic innervation to the lungs and bronchial tree. The visceral pleura receives only vasomotor supply from these nerves.
questions.question: Which plexus provides autonomic supply to lungs?

questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and vein cross anteriorly over the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship can cause superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, where the duodenum is compressed between the SMA and the aorta, leading to intestinal obstruction. The third part of the duodenum passes from right to left across the vertebral column at L3.
questions.question: Which vessels cross anterior to the third part of the duodenum?

questions.explanation: The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus, extending from the uterine pole of the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus just below the uterine tube attachment. It represents the proximal remnant of the gubernaculum (the distal remnant becoming the round ligament of the uterus). The ligament lies within the broad ligament (between its layers) and contains no significant vessels. The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) connects the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian vessels; it is not directly attached to the uterus.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the ovary to the uterus?
Which structure forms the medial umbilical fold?
questions.explanation: The medial umbilical fold is created by the peritoneum covering the medial umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated umbilical artery. There are paired medial umbilical folds (one on each side), in contrast to the single median umbilical fold in the midline formed by the urachus remnant (median umbilical ligament). Between the median and medial folds lies the supravesical fossa, while the medial inguinal fossa (site of direct inguinal hernias) lies between the medial and lateral umbilical folds, the latter being raised by the inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.question: The pterygomaxillary fissure connects which two regions?
questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure is a vertical opening between the lateral pterygoid plate (posteriorly) and the maxilla (anteriorly), connecting the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae. The maxillary artery and mandibular nerve branches pass through this fissure. It forms the lateral boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa.
options: Middle cranial fossa and pterygopalatine fossa

questions.question: Which nerves supply peripheral diaphragm sensory fibers?
questions.explanation: The peripheral part of the diaphragm (including the crura) receives sensory fibers from the lower six or seven intercostal and subcostal nerves. The central part receives sensory fibers from the phrenic nerves (C3-5). This dual innervation explains the referral patterns of pain from diaphragmatic irritation.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded laterally by the sartorius muscle, medially by the adductor longus muscle, and superiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor is formed by iliopsoas (laterally) and pectineus (medially), covered by fascia. The roof is formed by fascia lata. The triangle contains (from lateral to medial): femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space/lymphatics (NAVEL mnemonic). The femoral artery, vein, and canal lie within the femoral sheath (prolongation of transversalis and iliacus fascia), while the femoral nerve lies lateral to the sheath. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for femoral vessel access.

questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for fine adjustments of vocal cord tension?
questions.explanation: The vocalis muscle, lying parallel and inferior to the vocal cord, controls fine adjustments of cord tension. The cricothyroid provides gross tension changes by tilting the thyroid cartilage. The vocalis can selectively tense different portions of the vocal cord for pitch modulation.

The abdominal aorta terminates at the lower border of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4) by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries, slightly to the left of midline. This bifurcation point corresponds roughly to the level of the umbilicus and represents the transition from the abdominal aorta to the pelvic arterial system. The median sacral artery also arises from the posterior aspect of the aorta just before its bifurcation.
questions.question: At what level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate into common iliac arteries?
The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies which teeth?
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of maxillary nerve) supplies the upper molar teeth except the mesiobuccal root of the first molar (supplied by middle superior alveolar). The nerve descends on the maxillary tuberosity and enters the posterior superior alveolar foramina. It also supplies the maxillary sinus mucosa and buccal gingiva.

The inguinal ligament represents the rolled-under, thickened inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis, extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) laterally to the pubic tubercle medially. It serves as a retinaculum bridging the subinguinal space through which pass the iliopsoas muscle, femoral vessels and nerve, and lymphatics entering/leaving the thigh. The inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary (floor) of the inguinal canal and the base of Hesselbach's triangle. The lacunar ligament represents its medial extension, reflecting posteriorly to attach to the pectineal line.
questions.question: The inguinal ligament extends between which two points?
What percentage of the vocal cord structure consists of the arytenoid cartilage?
questions.explanation: The arytenoid cartilage comprises 40% of the vocal cord, while the remaining 60% is membranous (cricovocal ligament covered by mucosa). This anatomical proportion is important for understanding vocal cord pathology and surgical planning. The cartilaginous portion provides the posterior attachment point for the vocal ligament.

questions.question: Which movement at the hip joint has the greatest range, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees?
questions.explanation: Flexion-extension at the hip joint has the greatest range of movement, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees. Abduction-adduction has a range of 60-80 degrees, while internal-external rotation is 60-90 degrees. These ranges vary with the position of other joints and the state of surrounding soft tissues.

The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis when the inner thigh is stroked) is mediated by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2). The sensory stimulus from the femoral branch travels to L1-L2, and the motor response via the genital branch causes contraction of the cremaster muscle. Absence of this reflex may indicate testicular torsion.
questions.question: What is the cremasteric reflex mediated by?
Where does the right upper lobar bronchus branch?
questions.explanation: The right upper lobar bronchus (also called eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is in contrast to the left lung where the main bronchus divides within the hilum into two lobar (secondary) bronchi. This anatomical arrangement is clinically significant.

questions.question: Which opening connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear?
questions.explanation: The Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube opens into the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, connecting it with the middle ear cavity. The tubal elevation and tubal tonsil surround the opening. Tensor veli palatini and salpingopharyngeus muscles open the tube during swallowing to equalize middle ear pressure.

The sigmoid colon receives its blood supply from 2-4 sigmoid arteries (sigmoidal arteries), branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. These arteries descend in the sigmoid mesocolon, anastomosing with each other and with branches from the left colic artery superiorly and the superior rectal artery inferiorly, contributing to the marginal artery along the mesenteric border. Sudeck's point, at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from anal verge), represents a watershed area where the last sigmoid artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery and is vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the sigmoid colon?
The seminal vesicles are located posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles are located posterior to the fundus (base) of the urinary bladder, lateral to the ampulla of the vas deferens, anterior to the rectum (separated by rectovesical fascia), and superior to the prostate gland. They are elongated, lobulated structures that produce approximately 70% of seminal fluid volume, which is alkaline and contains fructose (energy for sperm), prostaglandins, and clotting factors. The duct of each seminal vesicle joins the ampulla of the corresponding vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra.

The lacrimal gland receives parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Preganglionic fibers travel via the greater petrosal nerve and nerve of the pterygoid canal. Postganglionic fibers reach the gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves. The pathway originates from the superior salivatory nucleus.
questions.question: The lacrimal gland is innervated by which parasympathetic pathway?
Which nerve supplies the costal pleura?
questions.explanation: The costal pleura receives sensory innervation from the intercostal nerves, which correspond to the dermatomes of the overlying thoracic wall. The blood supply to costal pleura is also from intercostal vessels. This arrangement means that irritation of costal pleura causes sharp, well-localized pain.

questions.question: The tensor fasciae latae muscle inserts into which named structure that runs to the lateral condyle of the tibia?
questions.explanation: The tensor fasciae latae inserts into the iliotibial tract (iliotibial band), a thickened lateral band of fascia lata running from the iliac crest to the lateral condyle of the tibia. It assists in flexion, abduction, and medial rotation of the hip, and helps stabilize the extended knee. Tightness of this structure is associated with iliotibial band syndrome.

questions.question: What is the length of the female urethra?
questions.explanation: The female urethra is approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches) long and extends from the internal urethral orifice of the bladder to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule. It is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall and passes through the urogenital diaphragm. The shorter length makes females more susceptible to urinary tract infections.

The pleural cavities are lined by mesothelium, a specialized layer of simple squamous epithelial cells. This smooth lining produces pleural fluid that lubricates the surfaces. The visceral pleura covers the lung surface while the parietal pleura lines the thoracic cavity walls.
questions.question: Which type of tissue lines the pleural cavities?

questions.explanation: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the inferior salivatory nucleus via the glossopharyngeal nerve and tympanic plexus. Fibers synapse in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers reach the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. This pathway controls parotid secretion. Damage causes reduced salivary flow.
questions.question: The lesser petrosal nerve carries fibers from which nucleus?

questions.explanation: The right gastric artery usually arises from the hepatic artery proper near the porta hepatis, though it may occasionally branch from the gastroduodenal or left hepatic artery. It descends to the pylorus, then ascends along the lesser curvature of the stomach within the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the left gastric artery (the smallest but most consistent branch of the celiac trunk). This anastomotic network along the lesser curvature provides collateral circulation and must be carefully ligated during gastric resections to avoid ischemia or bleeding.
questions.question: The right gastric artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The adult liver weighs approximately 1500 grams, constituting about 2.5% of total body weight in healthy adults. The liver is the largest internal organ and the largest gland in the human body. In newborns, the liver is proportionally larger, contributing to the characteristic protuberant abdomen of infants.
questions.question: What is the approximate weight of an adult liver?

questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli is located to the right of the abdominal aorta at the L1-L2 vertebral level, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. This dilated lymphatic sac receives the right and left lumbar lymphatic trunks, intestinal trunk, and sometimes lower intercostal trunks before giving rise to the thoracic duct. The cisterna lies anterior to the vertebral bodies and posterior to the aorta, in the retroperitoneal space. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus (crossing from right to left in the thorax) to drain into the venous system.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli lies to which side of the aorta?

questions.explanation: is not part of the rotator cuff; it acts as a medial rotator and adductor of the humerus. The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. These muscles fuse with the joint capsule and stabilize the glenohumeral joint.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?

questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the stomach lies anterior to the body of the pancreas, separated by the lesser sac (omental bursa). The anterior surface of the pancreatic body is covered by the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the lesser sac. This relationship is clinically important as pancreatic disease can cause epigastric pain.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the body of the pancreas?
The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the middle cranial fossa through which opening?
questions.explanation: The foramen rotundum provides direct communication between the pterygopalatine fossa and the middle cranial fossa, transmitting the maxillary nerve. The pterygoid canal connects with the foramen lacerum region, not the middle cranial fossa proper. This anatomical relationship is crucial for understanding trigeminal nerve pathways and regional anesthesia.

The cecum receives its blood supply from the ileocolic artery (terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery), which divides into superior and inferior branches. The inferior branch gives rise to anterior and posterior cecal arteries that supply the corresponding surfaces of the cecum. The ileocolic artery also gives off the appendicular artery (to appendix) and ileal branches. The superior branch of the ileocolic artery anastomoses with the right colic artery along the ascending colon. The cecum's venous drainage follows the arterial pattern, with ileocolic vein draining to the superior mesenteric vein.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies the cecum?

questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules characteristic of the ileum, especially prominent in the terminal ileum. These are permanent features of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) that play a crucial role in intestinal immunity. Peyer's patches are absent in the jejunum and located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
questions.question: Which lymphoid structures are characteristic of the terminal ileum?

questions.explanation: The pulmonary ligament is a loose fold of pleura that hangs down below the root of the lung. It is formed by the continuity of visceral and parietal pleura inferior to the hilum. It forms a sleeve allowing for expansion of the pulmonary veins during increased venous return.
questions.question: Where is the pulmonary ligament located?

questions.explanation: Above the pectinate (dentate) line, the anal canal is lined by simple columnar epithelium (rectal-type mucosa) forming the columns of Morgagni. Below the pectinate line, it transitions to stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium (in the intermediate zone) and then stratified squamous keratinized epithelium (in the cutaneous zone). The pectinate line marks the junction of endoderm and ectoderm.
questions.question: Which epithelium lines the anal canal above the pectinate line?

questions.explanation: The palatoglossus muscle forms the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of the fauces). It descends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. Unlike other tongue muscles, it is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory), not the hypoglossal nerve. The muscle elevates the posterior tongue during swallowing.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the anterior pillar of the fauces?
Which cells in the gastric mucosa produce pepsinogen?
questions.explanation: Chief (peptic or zymogenic) cells in the gastric glands of the fundus and body secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin. Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin by gastric acid (HCl) and autocatalytically by pepsin itself. Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach, working optimally at pH 1.5-2. Chief cells are basophilic due to abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum for protein synthesis.

questions.question: Which muscles, posteriorly related to the hip joint, separate it from the sciatic nerve?
options: Obturator internus, gemelli, and quadratus femoris
questions.explanation: Posteriorly, the obturator internus, the gemelli, and the quadratus femoris separate the hip joint from the sciatic nerve. Superiorly, piriformis and gluteus minimus are related. Anteriorly, iliopsoas, pectineus, and rectus femoris are anterior relations. Inferiorly, the tendon of obturator externus is found. These relations are vital during posterior hip surgery.

questions.question: Which chamber forms most of the left border of the heart?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle forms most of the left (pulmonary) border of the heart, with a small contribution from the left auricle (atrial appendage) superiorly. The left border extends from the second left intercostal space to the apex in the fifth intercostal space. This border is related to the left lung and pleura, separated by the pericardium.

questions.question: What is the fossa ovalis a remnant of?
questions.explanation: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale, which allowed blood to bypass the fetal lungs by shunting from the right to left atrium in utero. Functional closure occurs at birth with the first breath, though anatomical fusion may take months to years. A patent foramen ovale persists in about 25% of adults without usually causing problems.

questions.question: Where is the thoracic duct located initially?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at L1 and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, initially posterior to the esophagus. At T5, it moves to the left side of the esophagus and continues upward into the superior mediastinum where it arches forward to drain into the left venous angle.

Semimembranosus originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. Its reflected attachment forms the oblique popliteal ligament. Semimembranosus is named for its membranous (flat, broad) proximal tendon, in contrast to semitendinosus which has a long round distal tendon.
questions.question: Which hamstring muscle originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia?
What is the transversus thoracis muscle?
questions.explanation: The transversus thoracis (sternocostalis) is the anterior portion of the innermost intercostal layer. It is fan-shaped, spreading upward from the posterior aspect of the lower sternum to insert onto the inner surfaces of the 2nd-6th costal cartilages. It depresses the ribs during expiration.

questions.question: What is the function of the lumbricals in the hand?
questions.explanation: Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints of the fingers. This unique action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve while the medial two receive ulnar innervation.
options: Flex metacarpophalangeal joints, extend interphalangeal joints

questions.question: The appendix base is located at which anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: The base of the vermiform appendix has a constant anatomical location at the posteromedial wall of the cecum where the three taeniae coli converge, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. This convergence provides a reliable surgical landmark for locating the appendix during appendectomy, even when the appendix tip occupies a variable position (retrocecal, pelvic, subcecal, pre-ileal, or post-ileal). McBurney's point (one-third the distance from ASIS to umbilicus) represents the surface marking of the appendix base and is the site of maximal tenderness in appendicitis, but is not the actual anatomical landmark for finding the appendix during surgery.

questions.question: The two lateral compartment muscles, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve, primarily perform which actions?
questions.explanation: The lateral compartment contains fibularis longus and fibularis brevis, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2). Their primary actions are eversion of the foot and weak plantarflexion of the ankle. Fibularis longus also supports the transverse arch by crossing the sole. Lateral compartment injury impairs the ability to evert the foot.
options: Inversion and adduction of the foot

questions.question: What is the primary action of brachioradialis?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is primarily a flexor of the forearm, most effective when the forearm is in mid-pronation position. It also assists with both pronation from supinated position and supination from pronated position, returning the forearm to neutral. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve despite being an anterior compartment muscle.

questions.question: Which intercostal nerves supply the breast?
questions.explanation: The anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves supply the breast. These nerves convey sensory fibers to the skin, sympathetic fibers to blood vessels, and fibers to smooth muscle in the overlying skin and nipple. Pain from breast pathology follows these dermatomes.

questions.question: Which ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a double-layered peritoneal fold that connects the anterior and superior surfaces of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, extending from the umbilicus to the diaphragm. Its free inferior border contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (obliterated umbilical vein) and separates the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver. This ligament develops from the ventral mesentery and serves as an important surgical landmark during laparoscopic procedures.

questions.question: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though variations exist (occasionally draining into the superior mesenteric vein or the confluence of splenic and superior mesenteric veins). The IMV ascends from the pelvis, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries, and runs to the left of the inferior mesenteric artery. It passes anterior to the left psoas, left ureter, and left gonadal vessels before reaching the splenic vein. From there, blood flows via the splenic vein to join the superior mesenteric vein, forming the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck.

questions.question: Which ligament holds the long head of biceps tendon in the intertubercular groove?
questions.explanation: The transverse humeral ligament extends between the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus. It holds the tendon of the long head of biceps brachii within the intertubercular (bicipital) groove. The synovial membrane of the shoulder joint forms a tubular sheath around this tendon.

The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5 - "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provides the entire motor innervation to the diaphragm, including both muscular portions and central tendon. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Although the lower six intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12) provide sensory innervation to the peripheral parts of the diaphragm, they contribute no motor supply. Damage to one phrenic nerve causes paralysis of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, which appears elevated on chest radiograph. Bilateral phrenic nerve injury severely compromises respiratory function, particularly in supine position.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the diaphragm?

questions.explanation: The round ligament of the uterus passes through the deep inguinal ring (homologous to the spermatic cord in males), traverses the inguinal canal, exits through the superficial inguinal ring, and terminates in the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus. It represents the distal gubernaculum (the proximal part becoming the ovarian ligament). The round ligament contains smooth muscle, vessels, and nerves, and helps maintain the anteverted position of the uterus. Rarely, indirect inguinal hernias can occur in females alongside the round ligament (canal of Nuck).
questions.question: The round ligament of the uterus passes through which opening?

questions.explanation: The bronchopulmonary segment is the smallest part of the lung that can be surgically removed without affecting adjacent regions. Each segment has its own tertiary bronchus, arterial supply, and venous drainage. Segmentectomy preserves more lung tissue than lobectomy while treating localized disease.
questions.question: What is the smallest independently resectable lung unit?
How many papillary muscles are in the right ventricle?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle typically has three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal) corresponding to the three cusps of the tricuspid valve. Each papillary muscle gives chordae tendineae to two adjacent cusps. The left ventricle has only two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior), which are larger and stronger, each providing chordae to two cusps of the mitral valve.

options: Does not supply any flexor muscles
Supplies brachioradialis flexor despite being an extensor nerve
questions.explanation: The radial nerve primarily supplies extensor muscles but also innervates brachioradialis (elbow flexor) and extensor carpi radialis longus (proximal to lateral epicondyle). This reflects developmental muscle group origins. Brachioradialis, despite being anatomically anterior (flexor compartment), is functionally and embryologically an extensor group muscle.
questions.question: How does the radial nerve supply both flexors and extensors?

questions.explanation: The "critical zone" in the supraspinatus tendon has relatively poor vascularity, located approximately 1cm from its humeral insertion. This hypovascular area is more susceptible to degenerative changes and tears. The zone's poor blood supply impairs healing after injury.
questions.question: What is the significance of the critical zone in the supraspinatus tendon?

questions.explanation: The retrocaecal position is the most common location of the appendix, occurring in approximately 65-75% of individuals. In this position, the appendix lies behind the caecum, which may explain atypical presentations of appendicitis. Other positions include pelvic (most common after retrocaecal), subcaecal, preileal, and postileal positions.
