questions.question: What is the most common position of the appendix?

questions.explanation: The transverse head of adductor hallucis originates from the plantar ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints. Together with the oblique head (from bases of metatarsals 2-4), it inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit. The transverse head contributes to maintaining the transverse arch by drawing the metatarsal heads together.
options: Bases of metatarsals 2-4; medial longitudinal arch
Plantar ligaments of MTP joints; transverse arch
questions.question: The adductor hallucis has two heads. The transverse head originates from which structure and contributes to maintaining which arch?

questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinus lies within the body of the sphenoid with the clivus and pons posterior to it. The pituitary fossa is superior, and the cavernous sinuses with internal carotid arteries are lateral. The optic chiasm lies superiorly. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses the fossa through the sphenoid sinus.
questions.question: The sphenoid sinus relates posteriorly to which structure?

questions.explanation: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation decreases heart rate (negative chronotropy), decreases conduction velocity through the AV node, and slightly decreases contractility. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors (M2) in the SA node, AV node, and atrial muscle. The right vagus preferentially affects the SA node; the left vagus affects the AV node.
questions.question: Which effect does vagal stimulation have on the heart?

questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal artery (from superior thyroid artery) accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane. Together they supply the supraglottic larynx. The artery anastomoses with the contralateral vessel and with the cricothyroid artery. Damage during surgery can cause hematoma or bleeding.
questions.question: The superior laryngeal artery accompanies which nerve?

questions.explanation: Two-thirds of the breast's base lies on the pectoralis major muscle. The inferolateral one-third lies on the serratus anterior and external oblique muscles. The deep fascia of these muscles forms the posterior boundary of the retromammary space behind the breast.
questions.question: Which muscle lies deep to the breast medially?

questions.explanation: In life, the foramen lacerum is closed by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal arterial branches and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above the foramen within the carotid canal, not through it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large irregular opening.
questions.question: The foramen lacerum transmits which structure in life?

questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament is formed by the union of the medial borders of the two crura and crosses over the anterior surface of the aorta. This ligament forms the posterior boundary of the aortic opening. Occasionally, it can compress the celiac artery, causing the median arcuate ligament syndrome.
questions.question: Which ligament crosses anterior to the aorta?

questions.explanation: Beta cells comprise about 70% of pancreatic islet cells and are located centrally within the islets. They produce and secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose, amino acids, and incretin hormones (GLP-1, GIP). Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, making it the primary hormone for lowering blood glucose. Beta cell destruction or dysfunction causes diabetes mellitus.
questions.question: Which cells produce insulin in the pancreas?
The angle of inclination (neck-shaft angle) of the femur is approximately how many degrees in adults?
questions.explanation: The angle of inclination of the femoral neck to the shaft is approximately 135 degrees in adults. A decrease below 120 degrees defines coxa vara, while an increase above 140 degrees defines coxa valga. This angle is greater in children and decreases with skeletal maturity. It is critical for hip biomechanics and prosthetic design in hip arthroplasty.

questions.question: What is the thoracic duct's capacity?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct carries approximately 1-2 liters of lymph per day (though this can increase significantly after meals due to chyle from intestinal lacteals). It is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body. Injury to the thoracic duct (from trauma or surgery) can result in significant chyle leakage into the pleural cavity (chylothorax).

questions.question: How many lobes does the right lung contain?
questions.explanation: The right lung is divided into three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior) by two fissures: the oblique and horizontal fissures. The left lung has only two lobes (superior and inferior) separated by the oblique fissure. The presence of a middle lobe makes the right lung larger than the left.

The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on the medial surface of the mandibular angle and ramus, forming a sling with the masseter on the lateral surface. It arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and pterygoid fossa. The muscle elevates and protrudes the mandible. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3).
questions.question: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on which structure?

questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis is situated around the pituitary infundibulum and optic chiasma at the base of the brain. It provides collateral circulation when major arteries become occluded. The circle includes anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.question: The Circle of Willis is located around which anatomical structures?
options: Internal acoustic meatus and jugular foramen
Superior orbital fissure and optic canal

questions.question: Where does the axillary tail extend?
questions.explanation: The axillary tail (of Spence) is a process that extends from the upper lateral part of the breast into the axilla. It passes through an opening in the deep fascia and may reach as far as the third rib. Cancer in the axillary tail presents as an axillary mass.

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by I cells in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to fats and proteins. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion from acinar cells and contraction of the gallbladder. Secretin, released in response to acid in the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion from duct cells. Both hormones work synergistically to produce adequate pancreatic juice.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?

questions.explanation: The left colic artery (first branch of the inferior mesenteric artery) divides into ascending and descending branches near the descending colon. The ascending branch runs superiorly to supply the left (distal) third of the transverse colon and splenic flexure, anastomosing with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery. The descending branch runs inferiorly along the descending colon, anastomosing with branches of the sigmoid arteries. This anastomotic pattern creates collateral circulation between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories, though the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) remains a watershed area vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: The left colic artery typically divides into which branches?
Which vein forms the left border of the hepatocystic triangle (Calot's)?
questions.explanation: Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) has three boundaries: the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially (not a vein, despite the question's misdirection), and the inferior surface of the liver superiorly. Within this triangle lie the cystic artery and Calot's lymph node. The correct answer addresses that the common hepatic duct (not a vein) forms the medial boundary. Understanding this triangle's anatomy is crucial for safe cholecystectomy, as the cystic artery must be identified within it before ligation. Anatomical variations in this region are common.

The esophagus has four anatomical constrictions where it is narrowed. The first is at its origin (C6 level, 15 cm from incisors) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. These constrictions are clinically important as sites where foreign bodies lodge and where esophageal pathology commonly occurs.
questions.question: Which constriction is at the esophageal origin?
Which joint in the shoulder girdle provides the only bony link to the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The sternoclavicular joint connects the medial end of the clavicle to the manubrium of the sternum. This synovial joint is the sole bony articulation linking the shoulder girdle to the axial skeleton. Posteriorly lie important structures including the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

questions.question: What muscle action is tested by resisted elbow extension?
questions.explanation: Resisted elbow extension primarily tests triceps brachii strength, particularly the medial head which is most active in this action. Anconeus provides minor assistance. Weakness suggests radial nerve injury or C7 nerve root pathology.

The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, averaging 45 cm in length. It accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height. The femur articulates with the acetabulum superiorly and the patella and tibia inferiorly.
questions.question: Which bone accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm in length?

questions.explanation: Depression of the diaphragm significantly alters the vertical (superoinferior) dimensions of the thorax. When the muscle fibers of the diaphragm contract, the domes and central tendon descend. Elevation occurs when the diaphragm relaxes. The diaphragm is the most important muscle of respiration.
questions.question: What increases vertical thoracic dimension?
Which nerve forms the anterior vagal trunk supplying the stomach?
questions.explanation: The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the left vagus nerve as it descends on the anterior surface of the oesophagus. This trunk enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and supplies the anterior gastric surface. It also gives off a large hepatic branch and a pyloric branch.

Lymph from the superior (thoracic) surface of the diaphragm drains into parasternal, posterior mediastinal, and phrenic lymph nodes. Lymph from the inferior (abdominal) surface drains into anterior and posterior diaphragmatic lymph nodes, phrenic nodes, and superior lumbar nodes. Lymphatic vessels from the bare area of the liver communicate through the diaphragm with posterior mediastinal nodes.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive diaphragmatic lymph from the superior surface?

questions.explanation: The hip joint is a multiaxial ball and socket type of synovial joint, the largest and second largest weight-bearing joint in the human body. It allows movements in all three planes: flexion/extension in the sagittal plane, abduction/adduction in the frontal plane, and medial/lateral rotation in the transverse plane.
questions.question: The hip joint is specifically classified as which type of synovial joint?
The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous inferiorly with which named structure of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous with the fascia lata of the thigh. The superficial fascia, thick in women and impregnated with large quantities of fat, accounts for the prominence of the buttock. This fascial continuity has clinical implications for spread of infections between gluteal and thigh compartments.

Gastrocnemius is unique in that it plantarflexes the ankle only effectively when the knee is extended, because it crosses the knee joint. When the knee is flexed, gastrocnemius becomes relatively ineffective, and soleus becomes the primary plantarflexor. Gastrocnemius also flexes the leg at the knee and is innervated by the tibial nerve (S1, S2).
questions.question: Gastrocnemius can only plantarflex the ankle effectively under which condition?
options: When the knee is fully extended

questions.question: The popliteus muscle originates from the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and also from the lateral meniscus. It is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within which structure?
questions.explanation: The popliteus is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within the joint capsule of the knee. It passes through a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule (the popliteal hiatus) between the fibular collateral ligament and the lateral meniscus. Popliteal tendinopathy causes posterolateral knee pain during downhill walking when the PCL and popliteus are most active.

The puborectalis muscle (part of levator ani) forms a sling around the anorectal junction, creating an approximately 90-degree anorectal angle that contributes to fecal continence. During defecation, the puborectalis relaxes, straightening the anorectal angle to allow passage of feces. Paradoxical contraction of this muscle during defecation causes obstructed defecation syndrome.
questions.question: What forms the anorectal angle?

questions.explanation: The thoracic sympathetic trunk lies anterolateral to the vertebral bodies, just lateral to the anterior longitudinal ligament. It descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum and posterior mediastinum. Each trunk has 11-12 segmental ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion often fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion.
questions.question: Where does the thoracic sympathetic trunk lie?

questions.explanation: Each adult kidney is approximately 10 cm long, 5 cm wide, and 2.5 cm thick, resembling a large bean in shape. The left kidney is typically slightly longer and narrower than the right. Kidney size is clinically important, as small kidneys may indicate chronic disease while enlarged kidneys suggest acute processes or masses.
questions.question: What are the approximate dimensions of an adult kidney?

questions.explanation: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to decreased arterial oxygen (hypoxemia), increased carbon dioxide (hypercapnia), and decreased pH (acidosis). It is located at the carotid bifurcation and is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) monitors blood pressure changes.
questions.question: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to changes in which substance?

questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve has nerve root values C5, C6, and C7. It arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. The nerve supplies three muscles (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) before continuing as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
questions.question: What nerve root value is the musculocutaneous nerve?

questions.explanation: The splanchnic nerves are branches of the thoracic sympathetic trunk that carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the abdominal viscera. The greater splanchnic nerve arises from T5-9 ganglia, the lesser from T10-11, and the least (when present) from T12. They pierce the diaphragm to reach abdominal ganglia.
questions.question: What are the splanchnic nerves?
Which vein drains the fundus of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The short gastric veins drain the fundus of the stomach and flow into the splenic vein. There are typically 4-5 short gastric veins that pass through the gastrosplenic ligament. In portal hypertension, these veins can become dilated and form part of the portosystemic collateral circulation, potentially leading to gastric varices and bleeding.

The urethral crest (crista urethralis) is a longitudinal midline ridge on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra. Its most prominent part is the seminal colliculus (verumontanum), which contains the prostatic utricle and the openings of the ejaculatory ducts. The prostatic ducts open in grooves (prostatic sinuses) on either side of the crest.
questions.question: What is the urethral crest in the prostatic urethra?
What is the arterial arcade along the colon's mesenteric border called?
questions.explanation: The marginal artery (of Drummond) is a continuous arterial arcade running along the mesenteric border of the colon, formed by anastomoses between branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries. It provides collateral circulation and ensures blood supply if one major artery is occluded. Weak points exist, particularly at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck's point).

questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the entire diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves (C3-C5, with C4 being most important - "C3,4,5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provide all motor innervation to the diaphragm and most of its sensory innervation. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral half of the diaphragm. Peripheral parts receive additional sensory innervation from intercostal and subcostal nerves, but these provide no motor supply.

questions.question: Where are intersegmental veins located?
questions.explanation: Intersegmental veins (tributaries of pulmonary veins) run in the connective tissue septa between adjacent bronchopulmonary segments. These veins act as anatomical guides during surgical segmentectomy, helping surgeons identify and separate individual segments without excessive bleeding.

The inferior angle of the scapula is positioned at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra (T7) and overlies the seventh rib. This serves as a convenient landmark for counting ribs along the lateral chest wall during thoracotomy procedures. The angle moves laterally and forwards around the chest wall during scapular movement.
questions.question: At what vertebral level does the inferior angle of the scapula typically lie?
Which artery supplies the majority of blood to the greater curvature of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, a branch of the splenic artery, is the dominant vessel supplying the greater curvature of the stomach, anastomosing with the smaller right gastroepiploic artery from the gastroduodenal trunk. These vessels run along the greater curvature within the gastrocolic ligament, giving branches to both anterior and posterior surfaces of the stomach. The short gastric arteries contribute to the fundus but represent a minor component of the greater curvature blood supply.

questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery enters the rectus sheath by piercing which structure?
questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac artery) ascends medial to the deep inguinal ring and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Once within the sheath, it ascends on the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery (from the internal thoracic artery). The inferior epigastric artery gives off the cremasteric artery and sometimes a pubic branch. Its position medial to the deep inguinal ring makes it an important landmark distinguishing direct (medial to vessel) from indirect (lateral to vessel) inguinal hernias.

questions.question: What maintains negative intrapleural pressure?
questions.explanation: The elastic recoil of the lungs pulling inward, opposed by the chest wall's tendency to spring outward, creates and maintains the negative (sub-atmospheric) pressure in the pleural cavity. This negative pressure is essential for keeping the lungs expanded and prevents their collapse.

questions.question: Which structure separates the thenar and midpalmar spaces of the hand?
questions.explanation: The medial palmar septum joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone. This septum separates the thenar space (thumb side) from the midpalmar space (ulnar side). Each space contains specific flexor tendons and lumbrical muscles.

The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve by two branches in the submandibular region. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arrive via the chorda tympani, synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through without synapsing.
questions.question: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from which nerve?
The splenic vein lies posterior to which organ?
questions.explanation: The splenic vein runs along the posterior surface of the pancreas (in a groove or embedded within the pancreatic substance) from the splenic hilum to the posterior aspect of the neck of pancreas, where it joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. It receives numerous small pancreatic veins, the inferior mesenteric vein (typically), and the left gastric and left gastroepiploic veins. Its intimate relationship with the pancreas means that acute pancreatitis can cause splenic vein thrombosis, potentially leading to left-sided portal hypertension (sinistral portal hypertension) with isolated gastric varices and splenomegaly.

The detrusor muscle is composed of smooth muscle arranged in three poorly defined layers (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal). It is under involuntary control via autonomic innervation. Parasympathetic stimulation (via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction for micturition; sympathetic stimulation (via hypogastric nerves) causes relaxation for urine storage.
questions.question: What type of muscle forms the detrusor muscle?

questions.explanation: The right upper lobar bronchus (eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the right lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is unique to the right side. All other lobar bronchi arise within the hilum. The left main bronchus divides entirely within the hilum.
questions.question: Which bronchus is given off outside the hilum?
The 'windlass mechanism' of the foot refers to tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis during toe dorsiflexion. What effect does this have on the foot arches?
options: Flattens the medial longitudinal arch of the foot
Has no significant effect on any foot arch
Progressively flattens the transverse arch of the midfoot
Raises the medial longitudinal arch, converting foot to a rigid push-off lever
Only affects the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot
questions.explanation: The windlass mechanism (described by Hicks, 1954) involves tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis as the toes dorsiflexed during push-off. This raises the medial longitudinal arch, shortens the foot, and converts it into a rigid lever for efficient propulsion. This mechanism is impaired in flatfoot (pes planus) and hallux rigidus, reducing push-off efficiency.

The falciform ligament (and lesser omentum) develops from the ventral mesentery, while the greater omentum, splenorenal ligament, gastrosplenic ligament, and transverse mesocolon all derive from the dorsal mesentery. The ventral mesentery, present only in the region of the foregut, gives rise to the falciform ligament (connecting liver to anterior abdominal wall), the lesser omentum (connecting liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum), and the coronary and triangular ligaments (connecting liver to diaphragm). The liver and gallbladder develop within the ventral mesentery, explaining their peritoneal relationships.
questions.question: Which structure is derived from the ventral mesentery?

questions.explanation: There are typically 11-12 thoracic sympathetic ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion commonly fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion to form the stellate ganglion. Each ganglion connects to its corresponding spinal nerve via gray and white rami communicantes. The ganglia are interconnected by interganglionic segments.
questions.question: How many thoracic sympathetic ganglia exist typically?
Which peritoneal ligament contains the ovarian vessels?
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian vessels (artery and vein) and nerves passing from the lateral pelvic wall to the ovary. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus and contains no significant vessels. The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, with the ovarian vessels running in its superior lateral extension.

questions.question: The aditus ad antrum connects which two structures?
questions.explanation: The aditus ad antrum is an opening in the posterior wall of the epitympanic recess that connects the middle ear cavity with the mastoid antrum. Middle ear infections can spread to the mastoid air cells through this passage causing mastoiditis. The roof of the aditus is the tegmen tympani.

questions.question: What produces thumb extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint?
questions.explanation: extends the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. Its tendon forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox along with abductor pollicis longus. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

The connective tissue septa between adjacent bronchopulmonary segments act as natural barriers preventing the spread of infection between segments. However, aggressive infections like tuberculosis and carcinoma can break through these barriers. This anatomical feature is clinically important in limiting disease spread.
questions.question: What prevents infection spread between segments?

options: Cephalic vein, lateral pectoral nerve, thoracoacromial artery
questions.question: Which structures pierce the costocoracoid membrane of the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.explanation: The costocoracoid membrane portion of clavipectoral fascia between pectoralis minor and subclavius is pierced by three structures. These are the lateral pectoral nerve, the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery, and the cephalic vein joining the axillary vein. This membrane is continuous with the suspensory ligament of the axilla inferiorly.

questions.question: What is the function of the marginal zone in the spleen?
questions.explanation: The marginal zone, located between the white pulp and red pulp, contains specialized marginal zone B lymphocytes and macrophages that capture blood-borne antigens and particulate matter. It is the first site of contact between blood-borne antigens and the immune system. Marginal zone B cells can rapidly differentiate into antibody-producing cells without requiring T cell help.

Multiple factors maintain gastroesophageal junction competence preventing reflux: intrinsic LES tone, extrinsic compression by right crus sling fibers, acute angle of gastric entry (angle of His), positive intraabdominal pressure on the abdominal esophageal segment, and mucosal rosette at the cardia. Disruption causes GERD.
questions.question: What maintains gastroesophageal junction competence?

options: Dorsal cutaneous branch of ulnar nerve
questions.explanation: The superficial branch of the radial nerve supplies sensation to the dorsal aspect of the lateral three and one-half digits and the dorsal hand. The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve supplies the medial side. The posterior interosseous nerve has no cutaneous distribution.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies sensation to the dorsum of the hand?

questions.explanation: The danger triangle connects via the angular and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus without intervening valves. Facial infections in this region can lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis through retrograde venous spread. The triangle is bounded by the corners of the mouth and the bridge of the nose.
questions.question: The danger triangle of the face drains venously to which structure?

questions.explanation: The posterior meniscofemoral ligament is a strong tendinous slip joining the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle. The coronary ligaments attach both menisci to the tibial condyles. The transverse ligament joins the anterior edges of both menisci, allowing them to move together during knee movements.
questions.question: Which structure joins the posterior part of the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle?

questions.explanation: The reflected attachment of semimembranosus forms the oblique popliteal ligament, which strengthens the fibrous capsule of the knee posteriorly. Semimembranosus inserts primarily into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. The arcuate popliteal ligament is a separate structure arising from the posterior fibular head.
questions.question: The reflected attachment of the semimembranosus tendon forms which structure posteriorly in the knee?
The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery at which landmark?
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery as it passes beneath the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis, different from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament). The femoral artery enters the femoral triangle, lying lateral to the femoral vein in the femoral sheath. Just before passing beneath the inguinal ligament, the external iliac artery gives off the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries. The femoral artery later becomes the popliteal artery after passing through the adductor hiatus.

questions.question: What creates the aortic knuckle on X-ray?
questions.explanation: The aortic knuckle (or aortic knob) is the prominent shadow on a chest X-ray created by the aortic arch as it curves backward and to the left at the level of T4/5. This is a normal finding and an important landmark. Widening may indicate aortic aneurysm or dissection.

The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). Müller's muscle (superior tarsal muscle), a smooth muscle also elevating the lid, is innervated by sympathetics. Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis (drooping eyelid) along with eye movement deficits. Horner's syndrome causes mild ptosis from sympathetic loss.
questions.question: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by which nerve?
What produces scapular depression?
questions.explanation: Depression of the scapula is produced by lower fibers of trapezius and pectoralis minor muscles. This movement lowers the shoulder and is opposite to elevation. It occurs when lowering the arm from an elevated position or during downward reaching.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of left vagus) loops around the aortic arch and ligamentum arteriosum before ascending in the groove between trachea and esophagus to reach the larynx. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the right subclavian artery. This asymmetry reflects embryological development.
questions.question: Which nerve loops around the ligamentum arteriosum?

questions.explanation: The inferior mediastinum has three subdivisions: anterior (in front of the heart), middle (contains the heart), and posterior (behind the heart). The superior mediastinum lies above the horizontal plane through T4. This classification helps in understanding the location of mediastinal structures and pathology.
questions.question: How many subdivisions does inferior mediastinum have?
The pectinate line in the anal canal marks the junction between which embryological structures?
questions.explanation: The pectinate line represents the mucocutaneous junction where endoderm-derived hindgut epithelium meets ectoderm-derived proctodeal epithelium at the level of the anal valves. Above this line, the anal canal has columnar epithelium, venous drainage to portal circulation, lymphatic drainage to internal iliac nodes, and autonomic innervation. Below the line, it has stratified squamous epithelium, systemic venous drainage, lymphatic drainage to superficial inguinal nodes, and somatic (pudendal) innervation.

The subcutaneous olecranon bursa is located in the subcutaneous connective tissue directly over the olecranon process. This bursa can become inflamed from repeated trauma, causing olecranon bursitis known as "student's elbow" or "miner's elbow." The other two bursae are the intratendinous and subtendinous types.
questions.question: Which olecranon bursa lies in subcutaneous connective tissue?
Which part of the male urethra is widest?
questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra, measuring approximately 3-4 cm in length. It descends through the prostate gland from the bladder neck and contains the urethral crest on its posterior wall, with the prostatic utricle and openings of the ejaculatory ducts. The membranous urethra is the narrowest part.

questions.question: The gastroduodenal artery typically arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The gastroduodenal artery arises from the common hepatic artery (distal to the origin of the gastric and splenic arteries but proximal to the bifurcation into hepatic artery proper and gastroduodenal artery). It descends posterior to the first part of the duodenum, where it divides into two terminal branches: the right gastroepiploic artery (running along the greater curvature) and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (supplying the pancreatic head and duodenum). The gastroduodenal artery is intimately related to the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb and can erode into this vessel, causing life-threatening hemorrhage.

Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa throughout the gastrointestinal tract. It controls gut motility, including peristalsis and segmentation. Damage to this plexus (as in Chagas disease or Hirschsprung disease) causes severe motility disorders. It contains both excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons.
questions.question: Where is Auerbach's plexus located in the gut wall?
Which space contains the olfactory bulbs?
questions.explanation: The olfactory bulbs lie on the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the anterior cranial fossa. Olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium pass through the cribriform foramina to synapse in the bulbs. The olfactory tracts extend posteriorly from the bulbs. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.

questions.question: Where does the right bundle branch travel?
questions.explanation: The right bundle branch descends in the interventricular septum and crosses to the right ventricular free wall via the moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) to reach the anterior papillary muscle. From there, it divides into Purkinje fibers that spread throughout the right ventricle. This pathway ensures coordinated right ventricular contraction and explains why the moderator band is functionally important.

questions.question: What percentage of hepatic blood supply comes from the portal vein?
questions.explanation: The portal vein provides approximately 70% of the blood supply to the liver, while the hepatic artery contributes the remaining 30%. Despite carrying deoxygenated blood, the portal vein is crucial as it delivers nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract. The dual blood supply makes the liver relatively resistant to ischemic injury.

The upper medial quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3. The upper lateral quadrant receives L1 and T12. The lower medial quadrant receives S1, 2, 3, and the lower lateral quadrant receives L2, L3. This dermatomal pattern helps localize spinal pathology.
options: L1 and T12 vertebral levels only
questions.question: The cutaneous innervation of the upper medial quadrant of the buttock is derived from which spinal segments?
What nerve supplies the first and second lumbricals?
questions.explanation: The lateral two lumbricals (to index and middle fingers) are supplied by the median nerve. The medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers) are supplied by the ulnar nerve. This dual innervation pattern is unique among hand muscles.

questions.question: The medial ligament of the ankle joint is called the deltoid ligament. Which statement correctly describes its four components?
options: It is a single band with one attachment to the calcaneus
It has tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts
It consists only of the tibionavicular and posterior tibiotalar parts
It is a triangular ligament with apex on the fibula
It attaches from the fibula to the navicular, calcaneus, and talus
questions.explanation: The deltoid ligament is the medial ligament of the ankle, a strong triangular ligament with its apex on the medial malleolus. It has four parts: tibionavicular (to navicular), tibiocalcaneal (to sustentaculum tali of calcaneus), and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts (to the talus). It is significantly stronger than the lateral ligaments and rarely ruptures in isolation.

The perforating branches (three or four) of the profunda femoris artery perforate the adductor magnus to supply the muscles of the medial and posterior thigh. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical approaches to the posterior thigh, where inadvertent cutting of perforating vessels can cause significant hemorrhage. They are the main blood supply to the hamstring muscles.
questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to reach the posterior compartment of the thigh?
What is the standard length of the duodenum in adults?
questions.explanation: The duodenum is approximately 25 cm (10 inches) in length and represents the first and shortest part of the small intestine. Despite being the shortest segment, it is the widest portion of the small intestine. The duodenum is predominantly retroperitoneal except for the first 2 cm (the duodenal cap or ampulla).

The fundus is the dilated, dome-shaped portion of the stomach that lies superior to the level of the cardiac orifice and cardiac notch. It is usually filled with gas and is in contact with the left dome of the diaphragm. The fundus can be distinguished radiographically as the gas bubble seen in upright chest X-rays.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach lies superior to the cardiac notch?
What is the function of palmar interossei?
questions.explanation: Palmar interossei (PAD - Palmar ADduct) produce finger adduction, moving fingers toward the middle finger axis. There are three palmar interossei muscles compared to four dorsal interossei. All interossei also flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.

questions.question: The hepatic portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence, though variations exist. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and lacks valves.

questions.question: The 'screw-home mechanism' of the knee refers to which specific movement that occurs at full extension?
options: Medial rotation of the femur on the tibia in the last few degrees of extension
Both A and B describe the same event
Lateral rotation of the tibia on the femur in the last few degrees of extension
Locking of the patellofemoral joint only
Posterior translation of the tibia at full extension
questions.explanation: The 'screw-home mechanism' is the conjunct rotation that occurs in the final degrees of knee extension, when the tibia rotates laterally on the femur (in an open-chain position) or the femur rotates medially on the tibia (in a closed-chain position). Both descriptions describe the same biomechanical event. Popliteus 'unlocks' this mechanism to initiate knee flexion.

questions.question: What landmark indicates tracheal bifurcation level?
questions.explanation: The sternal angle (of Louis) at the level of T4/5 marks the tracheal bifurcation, the beginning and end of the aortic arch, the upper margin of the heart, and the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum. This is one of the most important surface landmarks in thoracic anatomy.

questions.question: Where does the internal thoracic artery arise?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It descends vertically behind the upper six costal cartilages, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum. It gives off anterior intercostal arteries, perforating branches, and terminates as superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular floor of the oral cavity, separating it from the neck. It arises from the mylohyoid line of the mandible and inserts into the median raphe and hyoid bone. The muscle is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve from the mandibular division. It elevates the floor of the mouth during swallowing.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the oral cavity?

questions.explanation: The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment, then pierces the deep fascia in the lower third of the leg to become cutaneous. It supplies most of the dorsum of the foot and toes (except the first web space, supplied by the deep fibular nerve, and the lateral border, supplied by the sural nerve).
options: At the level of the fibular head proximally
In the lower third of the leg by piercing the deep fascia
At the level of the ankle joint and mortise
In the popliteal fossa at the posterior aspect of the knee
At the level of the medial malleolus medially
questions.question: The superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies the lateral compartment of the leg. Where does it emerge as a cutaneous nerve?
What is the functional significance of the interosseous membrane?
questions.explanation: The interosseous membrane between radius and ulna serves multiple functions: separates anterior and posterior compartments, provides muscle attachment surface, transmits forces from radius to ulna, and contains apertures for interosseous vessels. It maintains the spatial relationship between the two forearm bones.

The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial and lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The canal runs obliquely (downward, forward, and medially) from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring, approximately 4 cm in length. The anterior wall is formed by external oblique aponeurosis (entire length) and internal oblique laterally; posterior wall by transversalis fascia (entire length) and conjoint tendon medially; roof by arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus; floor by inguinal ligament. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for hernia repair.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the inguinal canal?
Where does the left testicular vein drain?
questions.explanation: The left testicular (gonadal) vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava obliquely. This difference in drainage, along with the longer left testicular vein, explains why varicoceles are much more common on the left side (85-90% of cases).

questions.question: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) is a fibromuscular band arising from the right crus of the diaphragm near the esophageal hiatus (some sources describe both crura contributing), passing posterior to the pancreas to insert onto the duodenojejunal flexure and sometimes the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supports the duodenojejunal junction at the posterior abdominal wall and marks the transition from fixed (retroperitoneal) duodenum to mobile (intraperitoneal) jejunum. This landmark is important surgically and radiologically, as widening of the angle suggests a mass in the pancreatic head.

questions.question: The cricoid cartilage is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The cricoid cartilage is located at the C6 vertebral level. The lower border marks the transition from pharynx to esophagus and from larynx to trachea. This level also corresponds to where the carotid tubercle of C6 can be palpated and the carotid artery compressed. The middle cervical sympathetic ganglion lies at this level.

The straight sinus receives the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the inferior sagittal sinus. It runs in the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. The sinus drains into the confluence of sinuses (typically preferentially into the left transverse sinus). Deep cerebral structures drain via this pathway.
questions.question: Which sinus receives the great cerebral vein?
Which structure marks the transition from foregut to midgut?
questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla represents the embryological junction between foregut and midgut derivatives, marking the transition from celiac to superior mesenteric arterial supply. The duodenum proximal to this point receives blood from the celiac trunk (via gastroduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries), while the portion distal to it is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (via inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries). This vascular watershed reflects the embryological division of the primitive gut tube and has important implications for the blood supply and venous/lymphatic drainage patterns.

questions.question: The external spermatic fascia is derived from which layer?
questions.explanation: The external spermatic fascia is the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, derived from the external oblique aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. The three concentric fascial coverings of the cord (from outside to inside) are: external spermatic fascia (from external oblique), cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia). Each layer is acquired as the processus vaginalis and accompanying structures descend through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent.

Cardiac ischemic pain typically radiates to the left shoulder, left arm (especially the medial aspect and little finger), neck, and jaw, following the distribution of T1-T4 dermatomes that share spinal segments with cardiac afferents. This occurs because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal cord neurons. Some patients also experience epigastric discomfort or right-sided radiation.
questions.question: Where does referred cardiac pain typically radiate?
What passes through the aortic hiatus?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus at T12 transmits the descending thoracic aorta (which continues as the abdominal aorta), the thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. This is the lowest and most posterior of the three main openings. It lies between the crura rather than through them.

questions.question: Which structure forms the upper border of the pyloric sphincter on the transpyloric plane?
questions.explanation: The pyloric orifice lies on the transpyloric plane at the level of the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is an important surface anatomy landmark located approximately 1.25 cm to the right of the median plane. The pyloric sphincter can be identified by a slight surface constriction and the prepyloric vein of Mayo.

questions.question: Which nerve is the largest branch of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve (C5-T1) is the largest branch of the brachial plexus and the most frequently injured. It arises from the posterior cord and supplies all extensor muscles of the upper limb. The nerve is particularly vulnerable in the spiral groove of the humerus.

The tonsillar branch of the facial artery provides the main blood supply, entering at the lower pole. Additional supply comes from ascending palatine (facial), ascending pharyngeal, dorsal lingual, and lesser palatine arteries. The paratonsillar vein descends from the soft palate across the capsule and is regularly divided during tonsillectomy.
questions.question: The palatine tonsil receives its blood supply primarily from which artery?
The superior thyroid artery gives off which laryngeal branch?
questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery gives off the superior laryngeal artery, which accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane. The artery supplies the laryngeal structures above the vocal cords. The cricothyroid branch runs with the external laryngeal nerve to supply the cricothyroid muscle and anastomoses across the midline.

questions.question: Which muscle is the most powerful flexor of the elbow?
questions.explanation: is the most powerful and primary flexor of the elbow joint in all forearm positions. It has a larger cross-sectional area than biceps and inserts directly on the ulna. The muscle lies deep to biceps brachii in the anterior arm compartment.

questions.question: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus to continue as which artery?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus, to become the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa. The femoral vein similarly traverses the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal vein. The adductor canal lies superior to the adductor hiatus.

questions.question: Which structure passes posterior to the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava, covered by parietal peritoneum, forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), along with the right crus of the diaphragm. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant because the IVC can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver when the hepatoduodenal ligament (anterior boundary containing the portal triad) is manually compressed or clamped to control hepatic bleeding. The proximity of the IVC also means that the foramen provides a potential route for hemorrhage into the lesser sac following IVC injury.

The hip bone has five secondary ossification centres: two for the iliac crest, two for the Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and one for the ischial tuberosity. All five fuse by 20-25 years of age. The three primary centres (ilium, ischium, pubis) appear in the 2nd, 4th, and 5th months of intrauterine life, respectively.
questions.question: How many secondary ossification centres does the hip bone have in total?

questions.explanation: Goblet cells that secrete mucus are abundant in the large intestinal mucosa and increase in number toward the rectum. The mucus lubricates the passage of increasingly solid feces and protects the mucosa. Large intestinal crypts (of Lieberk?hn) lack villi and contain mainly goblet cells and absorptive colonocytes. Paneth cells are found only in the small intestine.
questions.question: Which cells are characteristic of the large intestinal mucosa?

questions.explanation: lumbrical canals are present in the hand as potential spaces surrounding the tendon of each lumbrical muscle. These canals lie between the index, middle, ring, and little fingers. Proximally they are continuous with one of the palmar spaces and can serve as routes for infection spread.
questions.question: How many lumbrical canals are present in the hand?

questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa is formed by the obturator internus muscle covered by obturator fascia, which contains the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) housing the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. The medial wall is formed by the levator ani and external anal sphincter. The fossa is bounded posteriorly by the gluteus maximus and sacrotuberous ligament, anteriorly by the posterior border of the urogenital diaphragm, and inferiorly by skin. The fossa contains fat and is a potential space for abscess formation.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa?
Which structure lies in the hypoglossal triangle?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) lies in the hypoglossal triangle (muscular triangle), a subdivision of the anterior triangle bounded by the midline, superior belly of omohyoid, and sternocleidomastoid. The triangle also contains the infrahyoid muscles and thyroid gland. The nerve passes from the carotid triangle into the muscular triangle.

questions.question: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandible through which opening?
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (a branch of V3) enters the mandibular foramen on the medial surface of the mandibular ramus. It travels in the mandibular canal supplying the lower teeth and emerges at the mental foramen as the mental nerve. The mylohyoid nerve branches before entering the foramen to supply mylohyoid and anterior digastric.

The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering the pharynx) and the prevertebral fascia. This potential space extends from the skull base to the mediastinum. Infections here can spread to the posterior mediastinum causing mediastinitis.
questions.question: The retropharyngeal space lies between which two fascial layers?
Which muscle forms the anatomical snuffbox floor?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid and trapezium bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. The boundaries are formed by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally, and extensor pollicis longus medially. The radial artery crosses the floor.

The superior intercostal artery (from costocervical trunk of subclavian artery) gives off the first and second posterior intercostal arteries. These are the only posterior intercostal arteries not arising from the thoracic aorta. This arrangement provides collateral circulation if the thoracic aorta is obstructed.
questions.question: What supplies the first two intercostal spaces?
Which ribs typically protect the spleen?
questions.explanation: The spleen lies deep to the left 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left hypochondrium. This relationship provides protection but also means that fractures of these ribs can lead to splenic rupture. The long axis of the spleen follows the line of the 10th rib. The spleen's position varies with respiration and body posture.

questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the nasal cavity through which opening?
questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine foramen in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa connects it with the nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the sphenoid bone and orbital process of the palatine bone. The sphenopalatine artery and nasopalatine nerve pass through it to supply the nasal cavity and septum.

questions.question: The sartorius muscle, the longest muscle in the body, performs which complete combination of actions?
questions.explanation: Sartorius (the tailor's muscle) acts on two joints. At the hip: it flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh. At the knee: it flexes the leg and medially rotates when the knee is flexed. The combined action of both sartorii brings the lower limb into the cross-legged sitting position typical of traditional tailors.
options: Extends hip and flexes the knee only
Adducts the hip and extends the knee
Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates hip; flexes and medially rotates knee
Flexes hip and laterally rotates the knee joint only
Abducts the hip and extends the knee only

questions.explanation: The puboprostatic ligaments extend from the posterior aspect of the pubic bones to the prostate and bladder neck in males, anchoring these structures. In females, the equivalent structures are the pubovesical ligaments. The lateral ligaments of the bladder (containing superior vesical vessels) also contribute to bladder support and fixation.
questions.question: Which ligaments anchor the bladder neck in males?
What drains the medial breast lymphatically?
questions.explanation: The medial part of the breast drains into the internal thoracic (parasternal) lymph nodes, forming a chain along the internal thoracic vessels. Some lymphatics from the medial part also pass across the sternum to anastomose with the opposite side, which explains contralateral breast involvement in cancer.

The head of the pancreas receives dual blood supply from pancreaticoduodenal arcades formed by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, representing the junction between celiac (foregut) and superior mesenteric (midgut) arterial territories. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal) divides into anterior and posterior branches that descend on their respective surfaces of the pancreatic head, anastomosing with corresponding anterior and posterior branches of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA). This rich anastomotic network provides collateral circulation between celiac and SMA systems.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the head of the pancreas?
Which cartilage forms the only complete ring in the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: The cricoid cartilage is signet-ring shaped and forms the only complete cartilaginous ring throughout the entire respiratory tract. This structural feature provides crucial stability and serves as an important landmark for emergency airway access. The cricoid is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway.

The transpyloric plane is an important anatomical landmark that passes through the first lumbar vertebra (L1), situated midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis. This plane transects numerous vital structures including the pylorus, neck of pancreas, origins of superior mesenteric artery and portal vein, duodenojejunal junction, and the hila of both kidneys. It serves as a crucial reference point for clinical examination and surgical procedures in the upper abdomen.
questions.question: The transpyloric plane intersects which vertebral level?
How many arterial arcades typically supply the ileum?
questions.explanation: The ileum is supplied by 3 to 6 tiers of arterial arcades formed by branches of the superior mesenteric artery. These multiple arcades provide collateral circulation and ensure adequate blood supply to the bowel. In contrast, the jejunum typically has only 1 to 2 arterial arcades with longer vasa recta.

options: They become lax to allow free extension
questions.question: During extension of the hip joint, the three extracapsular ligaments behave in which manner due to their spiral orientation?
questions.explanation: The fibers of all three extracapsular hip ligaments are oriented in a spiral fashion around the hip joint, causing them to become taut when the joint is extended. This stabilizes the joint in standing and reduces the amount of muscle energy required to maintain upright posture, demonstrating an important energy-conserving mechanism in bipedal locomotion.

questions.question: What nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve (C5, C6) supplies both supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. The nerve passes through the suprascapular notch (under the superior transverse scapular ligament) to reach the supraspinous fossa, then through the spinoglenoid notch to the infraspinous fossa.

options: Five: calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid, one cuneiform
Seven: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiforms
Six: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and two cuneiforms
Eight: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and four cuneiforms
Seven: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals
questions.question: The foot contains how many tarsal bones, and what are they?
questions.explanation: The foot contains seven tarsal bones: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiform bones (medial, intermediate, and lateral). The 26 bones of the foot include 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges. Understanding tarsal anatomy is fundamental to interpreting foot radiographs and managing tarsal fractures.

In the mnemonic 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?' each letter corresponds to a branch of the femoral artery: Deep external pudendal, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular, Profunda femoris, Superficial circumflex iliac. The profunda femoris is the largest and most important branch, giving rise to the perforating branches and circumflex arteries.
questions.question: The femoral artery branches are recalled using the mnemonic 'Does she scream during poking sessions?' Which branch corresponds to 'D'?

questions.explanation: Delta cells (D cells) comprise about 5-10% of islet cells and produce somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion, acting as a paracrine regulator. They are located peripherally in the islets. Somatostatin also inhibits growth hormone release from the pituitary (hence the name) and has widespread inhibitory effects on the GI tract.
questions.question: Which cells in pancreatic islets produce somatostatin?
Which pleura has somatic sensory innervation?
questions.explanation: Only the parietal pleura has somatic sensory innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerves, making it sensitive to pain. The visceral pleura has no somatic sensory nerve supply and receives only autonomic vasomotor innervation. This explains why pleural pain is sharp and well-localized to the chest wall.

questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the chorda tympani (from facial nerve) synapse in the submandibular ganglion suspended from the lingual nerve. Postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion also reach the gland via the facial artery plexus.

questions.question: Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the great saphenous vein receives tributaries from which three named veins?
options: Superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins
Popliteal, small saphenous, and accessory saphenous veins
Profunda femoris, femoral, and accessory saphenous veins
Dorsal venous arch, popliteal, and profunda femoris veins
Deep circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and internal pudendal veins
questions.explanation: Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the great saphenous vein receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac vein, superficial epigastric vein, and external pudendal veins. These tributaries are important surgical landmarks during saphenofemoral junction ligation for varicose vein surgery.

questions.question: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to which bony knee landmark, approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella). This is a key landmark for identifying the vein during varicose vein surgery and for cannulation. At the ankle, it ascends anterior to the medial malleolus.

The external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae, voluntary striated muscle) surrounds the membranous urethra as it passes through the deep perineal space (urogenital diaphragm). This sphincter provides voluntary control of micturition and is innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). The prostatic urethra is surrounded by the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle under autonomic control) at the bladder neck. The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm) and least distensible part, making it vulnerable to injury during instrumentation and the most common site of urethral rupture in pelvic fractures.
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external sphincter?
The hepatic veins drain directly into which structure?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (right, middle, and left, plus small inferior veins) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, representing the final pathway for blood that has perfused the hepatic sinusoids. The hepatic veins have no valves and run intersegmentally (between liver segments), in contrast to portal vein and hepatic artery branches which run within segments. The caudate lobe has separate small veins draining directly into the IVC, allowing it to maintain function in Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis). The close relationship between hepatic veins and IVC is critical in liver transplantation surgery.

questions.question: Five bones uniquely possess epiphyseal plates at BOTH ends. Which set correctly identifies all five?
questions.explanation: Most long bones have only one epiphyseal plate at one end; however, five bones are unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius. This feature is important in understanding growth patterns and fracture management in these bones.

The central artery of the retina is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It is an end artery running in the center of the optic nerve to supply the inner layers of the retina. Occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision. The artery enters the optic nerve about 12 mm behind the eyeball.
questions.question: The central artery of the retina is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: All four rotator cuff muscles (subscapularis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor) fuse with the lateral part of the joint capsule. Their tendons blend with the capsule to form the rotator cuff. The resting tone of these muscles helps stabilize the joint by pulling the humeral head into the glenoid cavity.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle does NOT fuse with the glenohumeral joint capsule?
Where is the AV node situated?
questions.explanation: The AV node is located in the lower part of the interatrial septum, within the triangle of Koch (bounded by the tricuspid annulus, coronary sinus orifice, and tendon of Todaro). It receives the impulse from the SA node and, after a physiological delay allowing atrial contraction, transmits it to the ventricles via the bundle of His. Its blood supply is typically from the right coronary artery.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the right crus of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the bodies and intervertebral discs of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3), while the left crus arises from only the upper two lumbar vertebrae (L1-L2). The crura are tendinous structures that ascend to insert into the central tendon. The right crus is longer and stronger, and some of its fibers form a muscular sling around the oesophageal hiatus.

The middle constrictor arises from the greater and lesser horns of the hyoid bone and the stylohyoid ligament. It overlaps the superior constrictor above and is overlapped by the inferior constrictor below. The muscle inserts into the median pharyngeal raphe. All constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.question: The middle constrictor muscle of the pharynx arises from which structure?
Which spinal segments provide afferent innervation from the kidney?
questions.explanation: Afferent (sensory) nerve fibers from the kidneys travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at T10-T12 and L1 segments. This explains the referred pain pattern of renal colic, which radiates from the loin to the groin along the distribution of these dermatomes. Ureteric pain follows a similar pattern as the ureter shares this innervation.

questions.question: The ethmoidal bulla is located in which meatus?
questions.explanation: The ethmoidal bulla is a rounded prominence in the lateral wall of the middle meatus formed by the underlying middle ethmoidal air cells. The hiatus semilunaris lies below it. The bulla is a key landmark during endoscopic sinus surgery. Above the bulla lies the suprabullar recess. The uncinate process lies anterior and inferior.

The left renal vein passes anteriorly to the aorta and posteriorly to the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) before draining into the inferior vena cava. This anatomical relationship can lead to compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA, a condition called nutcracker syndrome (or left renal vein entrapment syndrome), which may cause hematuria, left flank pain, and varicocele. The left renal vein is longer than the right (7-10 cm vs 2-4 cm) and receives the left testicular/ovarian vein, left suprarenal vein, and inferior phrenic vein before entering the IVC.
questions.question: The left renal vein passes between which two structures?

questions.explanation: The vagus nerves (CN X, both right and left) provide all parasympathetic innervation to the heart via the cardiac plexus. The right vagus preferentially supplies the SA node (negative chronotropy - decreases heart rate), while the left vagus preferentially supplies the AV node (negative dromotropy - slows AV conduction). Vagal stimulation also decreases atrial contractility.
questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart?
Where does the subclavian lymph trunk drain?
questions.explanation: The subclavian lymph trunk is formed by the union of efferent lymph vessels from the apical group of axillary nodes. It usually opens into the subclavian vein. On the left side, it may open into the thoracic duct. This represents the final pathway for breast lymph drainage.

questions.question: What is the effect of diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction causes the muscle to descend (central tendon is relatively fixed by the pericardium and IVC), increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrathoracic pressure (creating negative pressure that draws air in). Simultaneously, abdominal volume decreases and intra-abdominal pressure increases, displacing abdominal viscera downward and forward. The diaphragm is responsible for about 75% of the work of quiet breathing.

The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) and the root of the mesentery cross anteriorly to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant as compression by these vessels can cause superior mesenteric artery syndrome. The third part of the duodenum crosses the vertebral column from right to left at the L3 level.
questions.question: Which vessel crosses anterior to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum?

questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3). It carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. The nerve provides sensation to the temporal region, auricle, and temporomandibular joint. Misdirected regeneration causes Frey's syndrome.
questions.question: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of which division?
The lacteal vessels in intestinal villi drain into which nodes first?
questions.explanation: Lacteal vessels (lymphatic capillaries) in intestinal villi coalesce to form larger lymphatic vessels that drain to lymph nodes along the mesenteric border of the intestine (juxta-intestinal nodes), then to nodes along the vascular arcades in the mesentery (intermediate nodes), followed by nodes at the root of the mesentery along the superior mesenteric artery (superior mesenteric nodes), and finally to pre-aortic nodes (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric groups) before reaching the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This stepwise progression through multiple nodal stations allows for filtering and immune surveillance of intestinal lymph.

questions.question: The fabella is a sesamoid bone occasionally found in which muscle's tendon near the knee?
questions.explanation: The fabella is an accessory sesamoid bone occasionally found in the tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius, at the posterolateral aspect of the knee. It is present in approximately 10-30% of individuals. It can cause posterolateral knee pain (fabella syndrome) when it compresses the common fibular nerve or irritates the popliteus tendon. It is typically visible on lateral knee radiographs.

questions.question: The tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane form part of the ankle joint supports. These structures maintain which relationship between the tibia and fibula at the ankle?
options: They allow free rotation between tibia and fibula
They maintain tibiofibular mortise integrity for stable talus articulation
They create the lateral wall of the ankle
They only protect the interosseous vessels
They provide primary stability against valgus stress
questions.explanation: The tibiofibular ligament (syndesmosis) and interosseous membrane maintain the integrity of the tibiofibular mortise, ensuring that the distal tibia and fibula remain properly spaced for stable articulation with the trochlea tali. Disruption of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain or Maisonneuve fracture) significantly destabilizes the ankle joint and requires surgical fixation.

The right kidney's anterior surface is related superiorly to the right lobe of the liver (hepatorenal recess), the second part of the duodenum medially, and the right colic flexure and ascending colon inferiorly. Small intestine loops may also contact its anterior surface. The liver creates the largest impression on the right kidney's anterior surface.
questions.question: Which organ lies anterior to the right kidney?

questions.explanation: The infraorbital foramen on the anterior surface of the maxilla transmits the infraorbital nerve (continuation of maxillary nerve V2) and vessels. The nerve emerges about 1 cm below the infraorbital margin. It provides sensation to the lower eyelid, lateral nose, and upper lip. The foramen is a landmark for regional anesthesia.
questions.question: The infraorbital foramen transmits which nerve?

questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including motor and sensory cortices for face and upper limb. It also supplies Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant hemisphere. MCA occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia more marked in upper extremity and face.
questions.question: The middle cerebral artery supplies which cortical area?
What is the primary action of serratus anterior?
questions.explanation: Serratus anterior is the most powerful protractor of the scapula, pulling it forward around the chest wall. Paralysis of this muscle causes scapular winging, where the medial border of the scapula protrudes from the back. The muscle is supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).

questions.question: What causes hiccup?
questions.explanation: Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm accompanied by approximation of vocal folds and closure of the glottis. It commonly results from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings. It may also occur in pleurisy, peritonitis, or pericarditis affecting the diaphragm.

questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior wall of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver and diaphragm; and inferiorly by the transverse mesocolon. It communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow).

The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the cubital fossa roof and protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture. It distributes biceps force to the ulna and forearm fascia. Historically recognized as the grace of God tendon for protecting vital structures during bloodletting.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the bicipital aponeurosis?
options: Provides muscle attachment to bicipital fascia
Reinforces cubital fossa, protects neurovascular structures

questions.question: Which glands open into the bulbar urethra?
questions.explanation: The bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands) are paired pea-sized glands located in the urogenital diaphragm that drain via long ducts into the bulbar portion of the spongy urethra. They secrete a clear, mucoid pre-ejaculatory fluid that lubricates the urethra and neutralizes acidic urine residue. These glands are homologous to Bartholin's glands in females.

The median arcuate ligament is a fibrous arch that unites the right and left crura anteriorly across the aortic hiatus at the T12 level. It forms the superior boundary of the aortic hiatus through which the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes azygos vein pass. Occasionally, this ligament can compress the celiac trunk causing median arcuate ligament syndrome.
questions.question: What connects the two crura anteriorly?

questions.explanation: Fibularis tertius inserts into the dorsum of the base of the 5th metatarsal. It originates from the inferior third of the anterior surface of the fibula. Although in the anterior compartment, its eversion action makes it functionally similar to the lateral compartment muscles. It is sometimes absent as a normal variant. It is innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
questions.question: Fibularis tertius dorsiflexes the ankle and aids eversion. It inserts into which specific structure?

questions.explanation: After descending in the lateral compartment and passing behind the lateral malleolus, fibularis longus turns medially in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, crossing the sole diagonally to insert into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This unique oblique course allows it to support the transverse arch of the foot.
questions.question: Fibularis longus crosses the sole diagonally after turning medially in a groove on which bone, ultimately inserting into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform?
The superior hypogastric plexus is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The superior hypogastric plexus lies anterior to the lower part of the abdominal aorta and its bifurcation, extending from approximately L4 to the upper part of the sacrum, anterior to the L5 vertebra and sacral promontory. It represents the continuation of the aortic (intermesenteric) plexus and receives lumbar splanchnic nerves carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers.
