The plexus divides inferiorly into right and left hypogastric nerves, which descend into the pelvis to join the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses. The superior hypogastric plexus can be blocked or surgically divided to treat intractable pelvic pain.

The musculophrenic artery is one of the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery (the other being superior epigastric). It runs along the costal margin supplying the lower intercostal spaces (7th-9th via anterior intercostal arteries), the diaphragm, and the abdominal muscles.
questions.question: What is the musculophrenic artery?

questions.explanation: Fourteen structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen: one muscle (piriformis), seven nerves (sciatic, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerves), and six vessels (superior and inferior gluteal arteries and veins, and internal pudendal artery and vein).
questions.question: How many total structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen?

questions.explanation: Nine flexor tendons accompany the median nerve through the carpal tunnel: four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, plus the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These tendons are enclosed in synovial sheaths within the tunnel.
questions.question: What structure accompanies the median nerve through the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: The zygomatic bones form the prominence of the cheeks and lie on the inferolateral sides of the orbits. They articulate with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones. The bone has a broad connection with the maxilla medially and forms part of the zygomatic arch laterally. Fractures cause flattening of the malar eminence.
questions.question: Which bone forms the prominence of the cheek?
Which sinus opens into the inferior meatus?
questions.explanation: The inferior meatus receives the opening of the nasolacrimal duct beneath the inferior turbinate. No paranasal sinuses drain into the inferior meatus. The maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle meatus. The posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus. The sphenoid drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

Quiet expiration is a passive process resulting from elastic recoil of the lungs and relaxation of intercostal muscles and diaphragm. The ribs are depressed and the diaphragm elevated to its normal position. Lung recoil reduces size, increasing pressure inside the lungs to allow air flow outward.
questions.question: What characterizes quiet expiration?
The cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter for which structure?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus muscle, the lower part of the inferior constrictor, acts as the upper esophageal sphincter. It remains tonically contracted except during swallowing. Between cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus lies the dehiscence of Killian where pharyngeal diverticula (Zenker's) occur.

The inferior phrenic arteries are usually the first branches of the abdominal aorta, arising immediately after it passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, though they may arise from the celiac trunk. They supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm and give off superior suprarenal arteries. Each artery has a medial and lateral branch.
questions.question: From which vessel do the inferior phrenic arteries usually arise?

questions.explanation: The cystic duct (3-4 cm long, containing spiral valves of Heister) joins the common hepatic duct (formed by union of right and left hepatic ducts at porta hepatis) to form the common bile duct. The CBD (approximately 8 cm long) descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, passes behind the first part of duodenum, through the head of pancreas, and joins the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) in the wall of the second part of duodenum. Variations in this anatomy are common and surgically important.
questions.question: The cystic duct typically joins the common hepatic duct to form which structure?

questions.explanation: The promontory on the medial wall of the tympanic cavity is formed by the basal turn of the cochlea. The facial nerve canal runs above it. The oval and round windows are also located on the medial wall. The tympanic plexus lies on the promontory providing sensation to the middle ear mucosa.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial wall of the tympanic cavity?

questions.explanation: The arch of the azygos vein arches over the right lung root from behind. The right lung root lies within the groove created by the azygos arch. On the left side, the aortic arch passes over the left lung root, and the left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch.
questions.question: What structure arches over right lung root?
Which vessels run with the phrenic nerve?
questions.explanation: The pericardiacophrenic vessels (branches of internal thoracic artery and vein) accompany the phrenic nerve on each side as it descends through the thorax to the diaphragm. These vessels supply the pericardium, pleura, and diaphragm. The phrenic nerve lies between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura.

questions.question: Which nerve passes through the mandibular notch?
questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve (from anterior division of V3) passes through the mandibular notch with the masseteric artery to supply the masseter muscle. It also provides articular branches to the temporomandibular joint. The nerve crosses lateral to the temporomandibular joint and deep to the tendon of temporalis muscle.

Wrist position affects finger flexor and extensor muscle lengths through tenodesis effect. Wrist extension tightens finger flexors enhancing grip while passively flexing fingers. Wrist flexion tightens extensors causing passive finger extension. This relationship is exploited in tenodesis grip for spinal cord injury patients.
options: Wrist position affects finger flexor/extensor length affecting grip
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist position and finger function?

questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. The dorsalis pedis artery (continuation of the anterior tibial artery) runs between the extensor hallucis longus tendon medially and the extensor digitorum longus tendon laterally. Absence of this pulse, along with the posterior tibial pulse, indicates peripheral arterial disease.
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot. It is found just lateral to the tendon of which muscle?
The superior mesenteric vein lies to which side of the superior mesenteric artery?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vein lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery as they ascend from the root of the mesentery toward the pancreas. Both vessels cross anterior to the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum and the uncinate process of the pancreas. Posterior to the neck of the pancreas, the SMV joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. This relationship is important surgically, as the SMV must be identified and preserved during pancreatic and duodenal procedures. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can compress both the duodenum and potentially the SMV.

The ulnar artery is the larger terminal branch of the brachial artery, beginning below the elbow joint. It provides the main arterial supply to the medial forearm and forms the superficial palmar arch predominantly. The radial artery is smaller but more clinically accessible.
questions.question: Which artery is the largest terminal branch of the brachial artery?
What creates negative intrathoracic pressure?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, expansion of the thoracic cavity (through rib elevation and diaphragm descent) increases intrathoracic volume and creates negative pressure within the chest. This negative pressure draws air into the lungs. The pleural cavity pressure becomes more negative, preventing lung collapse.

Trypsinogen is the inactive precursor (zymogen) of trypsin, a protease that digests proteins. It is activated by enterokinase in the duodenum to form trypsin, which then activates other pancreatic proteases (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) in a cascade. Pancreatic juice contains multiple proteases, each cleaving peptide bonds at specific amino acid sequences. Premature activation within the pancreas causes acute pancreatitis.
questions.question: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests proteins?

questions.explanation: The aortic arch passes over and in front of the left lung root. The left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch. This anatomical relationship is visible on chest X-rays and CT scans and is important for understanding mediastinal anatomy.
questions.question: What arches over the left lung root?

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland is bound to the larynx and trachea by the pretracheal fascia. This attachment causes the thyroid to move with the larynx during swallowing. The isthmus overlies the second to fourth tracheal rings while the lobes extend from the thyroid cartilage downward.
questions.question: The thyroid gland is attached to which laryngeal structure?
What is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region?
questions.explanation: The greater tubercle of the humerus is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region. It projects laterally below and in front of the acromial angle. This prominence can be palpated and felt to move during rotation of the humerus.

questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for intorsion of the eye?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique is the primary intortor of the eye, also producing depression and abduction. The muscle passes through the trochlea before inserting on the posterolateral superior eyeball. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV). Superior oblique palsy causes vertical diplopia, worse on downward gaze and head tilt to the affected side.

questions.question: Which muscle produces pronation of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Pronation of the forearm is produced by pronator teres and pronator quadratus muscles. Pronator teres is more powerful and acts during rapid or forceful pronation. Pronator quadratus maintains pronation during slow movements and is the primary pronator during unresisted pronation.

questions.question: The anterior cranial fossa contains which lobe of the brain?
questions.explanation: The anterior cranial fossa accommodates the frontal lobes of the brain. The floor is formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, cribriform plate of ethmoid, and lesser wings of sphenoid. The crista galli provides attachment for the falx cerebri. Fractures can cause CSF rhinorrhea through the cribriform plate.

questions.question: Which segment of the duodenum is most mobile?
questions.explanation: The first 2 cm of the first (superior) part of the duodenum (the duodenal cap or bulb) is the most mobile as it is intraperitoneal with a mesentery. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal and relatively fixed. This mobility, combined with exposure to acid, makes the duodenal cap the most common site for duodenal ulcers (95% of duodenal ulcers occur here).

questions.question: The second layer of foot muscles contains the quadratus plantae and lumbricals. The quadratus plantae assists which extrinsic muscle in flexing the lateral four digits?
questions.explanation: The quadratus plantae assists flexor digitorum longus in flexing the lateral four digits. This assistance is needed because the tendons of flexor digitorum longus approach the digits from a medially oblique direction; quadratus plantae corrects this pull to a more longitudinal direction. It originates from the medial and lateral plantar surfaces of the calcaneus and is innervated by the lateral plantar nerve.

questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx), formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses, forms the medial part of the posterior wall and medial boundary of the inguinal canal. Weakness here predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The lateral part of the posterior wall is formed by the transversalis fascia.

questions.question: The ankle joint allows primarily which movements?
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (talocrural joint) primarily allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, with a small degree of rotation. Inversion and eversion occur primarily at the subtalar joint (talocalcaneal articulation) and midtarsal joints. The talocrural joint has a range of approximately 20 degrees dorsiflexion and 50 degrees plantarflexion in a healthy adult.

Biceps femoris has two heads: the long head from the ischial tuberosity (in common with semitendinosus) and the short head from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur. The short head does not cross the hip joint and is supplied by the common fibular division (not tibial division) of the sciatic nerve.
questions.question: Which hamstring muscle has a short head originating from the linea aspera and NOT from the ischial tuberosity?
Which muscle is NOT supplied by the pharyngeal plexus?
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle is supplied solely by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), not the pharyngeal plexus. All other pharyngeal muscles receive innervation from the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing. It is the only structure supplied by the motor component of IX.

Approximately 70% of people have right-dominant circulation, where the right coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery supplying the posterior third of the interventricular septum and diaphragmatic surface. About 10% have left-dominant (circumflex gives posterior interventricular), and 20% have co-dominant (contributions from both) circulation patterns.
questions.question: What percentage of people have right-dominant coronary circulation?

questions.explanation: Extrinsic hand muscles (arising in forearm) provide power for grip and basic finger movements. Intrinsic hand muscles (arising in hand) provide precision movements, finger positioning, and the unique lumbrical action (MCP flexion with IP extension). This combination enables both powerful and precise hand function.
options: Extrinsic for power grip, intrinsic for precision
questions.question: How do intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles work together?
Which muscle's contraction causes the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle, part of the levator ani complex, forms a U-shaped sling that loops around the anorectal junction, creating the anorectal angle of approximately 90 degrees by pulling the rectum anteriorly toward the pubic symphysis. This angle is a critical component of the fecal continence mechanism, as relaxation of puborectalis during defecation straightens the anorectal angle to facilitate evacuation. Damage to the puborectalis (such as during childbirth or surgery) or its nerve supply (pudendal nerve and direct branches from S3-S4) can lead to fecal incontinence. The muscle is in tonic contraction at rest.

questions.question: What nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres?
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres muscle. Compression at this site causes pronator teres syndrome, an entrapment neuropathy. This produces pain in the proximal forearm and sensory symptoms in the median nerve distribution.

questions.question: Which muscle is NOT innervated by the lumbar plexus?
questions.explanation: Piriformis is innervated by branches directly from the ventral rami of S1 and S2 (sacral plexus), not the lumbar plexus. The lumbar plexus (L1-L4) innervates psoas major (L1-L4), quadratus lumborum (T12, L1-L4 via subcostal and lumbar nerves), iliacus (femoral nerve, L2-L4), and obturator externus (obturator nerve, L2-L4). Piriformis is a muscle of the gluteal region and posterior pelvic wall, exiting the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. It serves as a landmark dividing structures exiting above it (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) from those below it (all others).

questions.question: Which artery passes through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae?
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery ascends through the transverse foramina (foramina transversaria) of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. It enters the foramen of C6 and ascends to C1, then passes posteriorly around the lateral mass of atlas before entering the foramen magnum. The vertebral vein accompanies the artery through these foramina.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The medial border of the brachioradialis muscle forms the lateral (radial) boundary of the cubital fossa. This muscle is a prominent flexor of the forearm that also assists with both pronation and supination from mid-position. It originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.

questions.question: The pubofemoral ligament of the hip joint limits which two movements?
questions.explanation: The pubofemoral ligament supports the hip joint inferomedially and limits extension and abduction. It is triangular, attaching superiorly to the iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merging with the capsule and lower band of the iliofemoral ligament. Strain of this ligament produces groin pain worsened by extension and abduction.

The red pulp comprises approximately 76-79% of normal splenic tissue and consists of blood-filled sinusoids and splenic cords (cords of Billroth). The red pulp is responsible for filtering blood, removing old or damaged erythrocytes, and recycling iron. It appears red due to the large number of red blood cells in the sinusoids.
questions.question: Which component comprises the majority of splenic tissue?
What increases the anteroposterior thoracic dimension?
questions.explanation: The anteroposterior dimension is increased by the "pump handle" movement of the true ribs (2-7), which pushes the sternum upward and forward. This occurs during inspiration. The bucket handle movement of ribs 7-10 increases the lateral dimension, while diaphragm descent increases the vertical dimension.

The internal iliac artery, formed by the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the L5/S1 level (pelvic brim), descends into the pelvis and typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at the level of the first sacral vertebra (S1), near the greater sciatic foramen. The posterior division gives off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries (all parietal branches), while the anterior division supplies both parietal structures (obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal) and viscera (umbilical, inferior vesical, middle rectal, uterine/vaginal in females, prostatic in males).
questions.question: The internal iliac artery typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at which vertebral level?
The cribriform plate is part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is the horizontal portion of the ethmoid bone forming the roof of the nasal cavity and floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It contains numerous foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers. The crista galli projects superiorly from the midline. Fractures cause CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia from shearing of olfactory nerve fibers.

questions.question: Which cartilage caps the apex of the arytenoid?
questions.explanation: The corniculate cartilages (cartilages of Santorini) are small conical nodules of elastic cartilage that sit on the apex of each arytenoid cartilage. They are located in the posterior part of the aryepiglottic folds. The cuneiform cartilages lie more anteriorly in the aryepiglottic folds. Both are visible on laryngoscopy as small elevations.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the tail of the pancreas lie?
questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends to the left and lies at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra (T12). The tail reaches the splenic hilum and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas, lying within the splenorenal ligament. Anteriorly, the tail is related to the splenic flexure of the colon.

questions.question: The carotid sinus is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) at the carotid bifurcation is innervated by the carotid sinus nerve (nerve of Hering), a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid body (chemoreceptor) is also innervated primarily by IX. These receptors monitor blood pressure and blood gas levels respectively. Carotid massage can slow heart rate via this pathway.

questions.question: The median cricothyroid ligament connects which two cartilages?
questions.explanation: The median (central) cricothyroid ligament connects the anterior aspects of the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. It is subcutaneous in the midline between the cricothyroid muscles. This ligament is crossed by the cricothyroid arterial anastomosis and is the site for emergency cricothyroidotomy.

questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the nasopharynx?
questions.explanation: The roof of the nasopharynx is formed by the body of the sphenoid bone and the basilar part of the occipital bone. The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) lies in the mucosa of this roof and posterior wall. The clivus (posterior cranial base) forms the anatomical background to this region.

The right renal vein (shorter than the left, approximately 2-4 cm) drains into the inferior vena cava at approximately the L1-L2 level, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta. The left renal vein (longer, 7-10 cm) crosses anterior to the aorta at the same level to reach the IVC. The right renal vein receives only the right gonadal and right suprarenal veins (sometimes), while the left renal vein receives the left gonadal, left suprarenal, and left inferior phrenic veins before reaching the IVC.
questions.question: The inferior vena cava receives which vein at the L1 level?

questions.explanation: The hilum of the spleen faces anteromedially toward the stomach, receiving the splenic artery (which divides into 5-6 branches before entering) and giving exit to the splenic vein. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the hilum to the greater curvature of the stomach and contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. The splenorenal ligament connects the hilum to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and tail of the pancreas. The splenic hilum typically shows a distinct notch (splenic notch) on its superior border, a characteristic feature visible on cross-sectional imaging.
questions.question: The hilum of the spleen faces which direction?
Which muscle flexes the elbow when the forearm is pronated?
questions.explanation: is the primary elbow flexor regardless of forearm position because it inserts on the ulna. Biceps brachii is less effective when the forearm is pronated because its supinating action is opposed. Brachialis is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.

The subcostal plane is a horizontal transverse plane passing through the inferior margins of the 10th costal cartilages (lowest point of the costal margin) on each side, corresponding to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Together with the transtubercular plane (L5 level) and the two vertical midclavicular planes, it defines the nine regions of the abdomen. The subcostal plane marks important anatomical landmarks including the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery, the level of the pylorus in some individuals, and the approximate position of the inferior border of the liver.
questions.question: The subcostal plane passes through which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe located below the cardiac notch. It is analogous to the middle lobe of the right lung. The lingula consists of superior and inferior lingular segments, which are distinct bronchopulmonary segments.
questions.question: What structure forms the lingula?

questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) lies lateral to the femoral artery as it exits beneath the inguinal ligament, outside the femoral sheath (which contains only the femoral artery, vein, and canal). The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty/Lymphatics) describes the lateral to medial arrangement. The femoral nerve rapidly divides into branches in the femoral triangle.
questions.question: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) exits the pelvis beneath the inguinal ligament. It lies in which position relative to the femoral artery?
The marginal artery of Drummond connects which two arterial systems?
questions.explanation: The marginal artery of Drummond (marginal artery of the colon) is a continuous arterial arcade running along the mesenteric border of the colon, connecting the superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arterial territories. It is formed by anastomoses between the ileocolic, right colic, middle colic, left colic, and sigmoid arteries. This vessel provides crucial collateral circulation to the colon and is particularly important at the splenic flexure, where the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial distributions meet. The weakest point in this anastomotic chain occurs at Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid junction).

The posterior auricular artery arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery above the level of the digastric and stylohyoid muscles. It supplies the auricle, scalp behind the ear, and gives off the stylomastoid artery (which supplies the facial nerve and middle ear structures). The artery ascends between the parotid gland and mastoid process.
questions.question: The posterior auricular artery is a branch of which vessel?
Which vessel is superior in the lung root?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery is the most superior structure in the root of both lungs. The main bronchus lies posterior to the vessels. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins are the most inferior structures in the root. This anatomical arrangement is constant and important during surgery.

options: Ischium; loose connective tissue and fat
questions.question: The non-articular portion of the acetabulum (acetabular fossa) is formed mainly by which bone and contains what?
questions.explanation: The acetabular fossa is the non-articular part of the acetabulum, formed mainly by the ischium. It contains loose connective tissue and a pad of fat. The articular surface is the horseshoe-shaped lunate surface covered by hyaline cartilage. The fossa is deficient inferiorly at the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.

The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from the S2, S3, and S4 spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers synapse in ganglia within the bladder wall and stimulate contraction of the detrusor muscle (for micturition) while relaxing the internal urethral sphincter. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via lumbar splanchnic nerves and superior hypogastric plexus) has the opposite effect, promoting urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter. Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter comes from the pudendal nerve (S2-S4), allowing voluntary control.
questions.question: The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from which spinal segments?

questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) provide parasympathetic innervation to hindgut derivatives (distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal). The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic supply to foregut and midgut derivatives (up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon). Sympathetic supply is via lumbar splanchnic nerves and the inferior mesenteric plexus.
questions.question: Which parasympathetic nerve supplies the hindgut derivatives?
How many segments are in left lower lobe?
questions.explanation: The left lower lobe typically contains four (sometimes five) bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The medial basal segment is often absent or fused with the anterior basal segment on the left side, unlike the right lower lobe which consistently has five segments.

The superior rectal artery represents the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery after it gives off the left colic and sigmoid branches, descending into the pelvis within the sigmoid mesocolon. It crosses the left common iliac vessels at the level of S3 and divides into right and left branches that descend on either side of the rectum, penetrating its wall and anastomosing with branches of the middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal) arteries at the level of the internal anal sphincter.
questions.question: The superior rectal artery is the terminal continuation of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder typically reaches the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis muscle crosses the right costal margin (approximately at the transpyloric plane). This surface marking corresponds to the point where the gallbladder may contact the anterior abdominal wall, making it palpable when distended or inflamed. Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest with deep palpation at this point due to pain) indicates acute cholecystitis. The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum.
questions.question: The gallbladder fundus typically lies at which anatomical landmark?
options: Right costal margin at 9th costal cartilage

questions.question: What is the function of splenic red pulp?
questions.explanation: The splenic red pulp filters blood and removes old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes through selective retention and phagocytosis by macrophages in the splenic cords. It also stores platelets (about one-third of the body's platelet pool) and serves as a reservoir for iron recycled from hemoglobin. The red pulp comprises about 75% of splenic tissue.

questions.question: The spinal accessory nerve supplies which two muscles?
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. The nerve emerges from the jugular foramen and descends across the posterior triangle. Injury during lymph node biopsy causes weakness in shoulder shrugging and difficulty turning the head against resistance.

In adults, the Eustachian tube lies at 45° to the horizontal plane, whereas in infants it is only 10°. This more vertical orientation in children predisposes them to middle ear infections. The tube is approximately 31-38 mm long with the posterior third being osseous.
questions.question: The Eustachian tube in adults lies at what angle to the horizontal plane?
The oval window is closed by which structure?
questions.explanation: The oval window (fenestra vestibuli) in the medial wall of the middle ear is closed by the footplate of the stapes, held in place by the annular ligament. The stapes transmits vibrations from the ossicular chain to the perilymph of the inner ear. Otosclerosis causes abnormal bone growth fixing the stapes, resulting in conductive hearing loss.

questions.question: Which chamber primarily forms the base of the heart?
questions.explanation: The base of the heart is formed primarily by the left atrium and a small portion of the right atrium. It is the posterior surface facing the vertebral column and esophagus. The four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the base. The term "base" refers to the posterior aspect, opposite to the apex, not to the inferior surface.

questions.question: Which structure receives blood from both celiac and superior mesenteric arteries?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon has a dual blood supply: the right two-thirds from the middle colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery (midgut supply) and the left third from the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut supply). The junction between these territories forms the marginal artery (of Drummond) and represents the watershed area most vulnerable to ischemia.

Lymphatic drainage from the appendix passes through lymph nodes in the mesoappendix to the ileocolic lymph nodes along the ileocolic artery, which subsequently drain to superior mesenteric lymph nodes along the superior mesenteric artery. From there, lymph flows to the pre-aortic nodes and eventually to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This drainage pattern follows the arterial supply (appendicular artery from ileocolic artery from SMA). Enlarged ileocolic nodes may be palpable in appendicitis and can contribute to diagnostic imaging findings in acute abdominal conditions.
questions.question: The appendicular lymph nodes drain into which nodal group?

questions.explanation: Subscapularis is supplied by the upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6) and lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6). Both nerves arise from the posterior cord. The lower subscapular nerve also supplies teres major muscle.
questions.question: What nerve supplies subscapularis muscle?
Which artery supplies the AV node in most people?
questions.explanation: The AV nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 80-90% of people (right dominant circulation) and from the left circumflex artery in the remainder (left dominant circulation). It typically arises near the origin of the posterior interventricular artery. AV node ischemia from right coronary occlusion can cause heart block.

Lumbricals originate from flexor digitorum profundus tendons (unique among hand muscles). This means lumbrical contraction (causing MCP flexion and IP extension) also reduces profundus tension. This coupling enables the delicate coordination needed for precision movements like writing.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of lumbrical muscle origin?
options: This attachment has no special anatomical significance
FDP origin couples DIP flexion with IP extension

questions.explanation: The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve supplies all muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) via its motor root. It also supplies mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor veli palatini, and tensor tympani. These muscles derive from the first pharyngeal arch mesoderm.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication?
Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the bladder trigone?
questions.explanation: The two ureteric orifices form the superolateral angles (corners) of the triangular trigone. The internal urethral orifice forms the inferior angle. The interureteric ridge connects the two ureteric orifices forming the base of the triangle. The trigone remains smooth even when the bladder is empty, unlike the rest of the bladder mucosa which is rugose when empty.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located along the external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein in the superficial cervical fascia. They receive drainage from the scalp and superficial neck structures. Efferent vessels drain to the deep cervical nodes. These nodes are distinct from the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein.

questions.question: Which structure forms the primary passive support of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and provides primary passive support. The stylomandibular ligament is merely a thickening of the parotid capsule and contributes minimally to joint support. Other ligaments provide secondary stabilization or perform different mechanical functions in the temporomandibular complex.

The superior cerebellar artery arises from the basilar artery just before its terminal bifurcation. It supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum, cerebellar nuclei, and superior cerebellar peduncle. The artery courses around the pons below the oculomotor nerve. Occlusion causes ipsilateral cerebellar signs and contralateral pain/temperature loss.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum?
Which structure lies in the free edge of the gastrosplenic ligament?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels (4-6 small arteries and veins) that pass from the splenic vessels near the hilum to supply the gastric fundus, and the left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) vessels that run along the greater curvature. The splenic artery and vein themselves course through the splenorenal ligament (along with the pancreatic tail), not the gastrosplenic ligament. During splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament is divided, requiring careful ligation of these vessels. The gastrosplenic ligament represents part of the dorsal mesogastrium and connects the greater curvature to the splenic hilum.

questions.question: Which muscle pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis?
questions.explanation: The aryepiglotticus muscle, running in the aryepiglottic fold, pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis, closing the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It acts like a purse-string sphincter. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function.

questions.question: The proper hepatic artery lies in which position within the portal triad?
questions.explanation: Within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum), the structures of the portal triad are arranged from anterior to posterior and right to left as: bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and portal vein (posteriorly). This arrangement is sometimes remembered as "DAV" reading from right to left anteriorly (Duct, Artery, Vein). The hepatic artery typically lies anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the bile duct, though anatomical variations are common. Lymph nodes and autonomic nerve plexuses also travel through the hepatoduodenal ligament.

questions.question: What structure lies between the subscapularis tendon and the scapula?
questions.explanation: The subscapular bursa is located between the subscapularis tendon and the scapula, reducing wear and tear during shoulder movement. Unlike the subacromial bursa, the subscapular bursa communicates with the shoulder joint cavity through a gap between the superior and middle glenohumeral ligaments. This communication allows potential spread of infection or inflammatory processes.

questions.question: Which surface of the lung faces the mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The mediastinal surface faces the mediastinum and contains the hilum where structures enter and leave the lung. This surface is in contact with the heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, and other mediastinal structures. The hilum is located on this surface opposite the bodies of T5, T6, and T7 vertebrae.

questions.question: Into which vein does the lower third of the oesophagus drain venously?
questions.explanation: The veins from the lower third of the oesophagus drain into the left gastric vein, which is part of the portal circulation. This drainage pattern creates a clinically significant portosystemic anastomosis at the gastro-oesophageal junction. In portal hypertension, these veins become dilated forming oesophageal varices that can cause life-threatening haematemesis.

The left renal artery passes posterior to the left renal vein as it courses from the aorta (at L1-L2 level, just below the superior mesenteric artery) to the left kidney hilum. The right renal artery, longer than the left, passes posterior to the IVC and right renal vein. Both renal arteries also pass posterior to the corresponding psoas major muscle and ureter. The left renal vein is longer than the right and receives the left gonadal vein, left suprarenal vein, and left inferior phrenic vein before draining into the IVC. This relationship is important in renal transplantation surgery.
questions.question: The left renal artery passes posterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: The base of the breast extends vertically from the 2nd to 6th rib. Transversely, it extends from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line. The axillary tail of Spence extends from the upper outer quadrant into the axilla. These landmarks are important for clinical breast examination.
questions.question: Which rib level marks the base of breast vertically?
Which vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, representing the final pathway for blood that has passed through the hepatic sinusoids. Unlike other veins, hepatic veins have no valves. The portal vein and its tributaries (splenic, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric veins) carry nutrient-rich but deoxygenated blood to the liver, where it mixes with oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery in the sinusoids before draining via hepatic veins. The hepatic veins and their relationship to IVC are crucial landmarks in liver surgery and transplantation.

questions.question: How many posterior intercostal arteries arise from thoracic aorta?
questions.explanation: Nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta, supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces. The upper two spaces receive their posterior intercostal arteries from the superior intercostal artery. Each posterior intercostal artery gives branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura, and the breast.

Bronchial and pulmonary arteries anastomose at the precapillary level, creating connections between the systemic and pulmonary circulations. This anastomosis allows some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The bronchial circulation comprises only about 1-2% of cardiac output.
questions.question: At which level do bronchial arteries anastomose?
Which vertebral level corresponds to the oesophageal opening in the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus in the diaphragm is located at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra (T10). The oesophagus passes through the muscular part of the right crus of the diaphragm at this level. This hiatus also transmits the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.

questions.question: What connects the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The scapular anastomoses provide collateral circulation connecting the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery. This involves suprascapular artery, dorsal scapular artery, and circumflex scapular artery. The anastomoses allow blood flow to the limb even with proximal vessel obstruction.

The maxillary vein is formed from the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa. It joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein within the parotid gland. The pterygoid plexus communicates with cavernous sinus and facial veins without valves.
questions.question: Which vein drains the pterygoid venous plexus?

questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve divides at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa (or sometimes higher in the thigh or even within the pelvis) into the tibial nerve (medial and larger) and the common fibular nerve (lateral and smaller). The tibial nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole, while the common fibular nerve innervates the anterior and lateral leg compartments.
questions.question: The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body. At the level of the popliteal fossa, it divides into which two terminal branches?
options: Sural nerve and posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh
Tibial nerve and common fibular nerve

questions.question: Which nerve descends on the right side of SVC?
questions.explanation: The right phrenic nerve passes through the superior and middle mediastinum descending on the right side of the superior vena cava (SVC) and heart. The left phrenic nerve similarly descends on the left side of the heart. Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm, providing motor and sensory innervation.

The pyramidalis muscle, a small triangular muscle anterior to the lower rectus abdominis (base on pubis, apex on linea alba), is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12). This muscle is variably present (absent in about 20% of individuals) and functions to tense the linea alba. The subcostal nerve also contributes to innervation of the abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin. The pyramidalis lies within the rectus sheath and represents a derivative of the rectus abdominis. Its clinical significance is minimal.
questions.question: Which nerve innervates the pyramidalis muscle?

questions.explanation: The sphincter of Oddi (sphincter ampullae) surrounds the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), controlling the release of bile and pancreatic juice into the second part of the duodenum. The sphincter choledochus surrounds the terminal bile duct just before its junction with the pancreatic duct, while the sphincter pancreaticus surrounds the terminal pancreatic duct. The sphincter of Oddi coordinates the flow from both ducts, relaxing in response to cholecystokinin during digestion and contracting between meals to allow bile storage in the gallbladder.
questions.question: The hepatopancreatic ampulla is surrounded by which sphincter?
Which structure separates the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac, separating it from the greater sac anteriorly along with the posterior wall of the stomach. This double-layered peritoneal fold extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of duodenum to the liver. The lesser omentum consists of the hepatogastric ligament (its membranous portion) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad), with the latter forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.

The obturator membrane is a fibrous sheet that almost completely closes the obturator foramen, the largest foramen in the body formed by the ischium and pubis. The membrane leaves a small gap superiorly, the obturator canal, through which the obturator nerve and vessels pass from the pelvis to the medial compartment of the thigh. Both obturator internus (internal surface) and obturator externus (external surface) muscles attach to the obturator membrane, with the former functioning as a lateral rotator of the hip and the latter as both a lateral rotator and adductor.
questions.question: The obturator foramen is closed by which structure?

questions.explanation: The occipital artery, a branch of the external carotid, supplies the posterior scalp. It ascends on the back of the neck, pierces the trapezius attachment, and runs in the dense connective tissue layer of the scalp. The artery accompanies the greater occipital nerve. Scalp lacerations in this region can cause significant bleeding.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies the scalp in the occipital region?
The greater trochanter is classified as which type of epiphysis, and which muscle exerts traction upon it, drawing it upward, medially, and backward?
questions.explanation: The greater trochanter is a traction epiphysis; gluteus medius pulls it upward, medially, and backward. Traction epiphyses arise at tendon insertions rather than at articular ends, unlike pressure epiphyses. The quadrate tubercle marks where the epiphyseal line crosses the intertrochanteric crest.

questions.question: Which cells are predominantly destroyed in the splenic red pulp?
questions.explanation: The splenic red pulp is the primary site for destruction of old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes (red blood cells). After their normal lifespan of approximately 120 days, erythrocytes become less flexible and are selectively engulfed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The iron from hemoglobin is recycled, while other components are degraded.

questions.question: Which vessel marks the medial boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the bile duct within the hepatoduodenal ligament as its anterior boundary, not medial. The superior boundary is the caudate lobe of the liver, the inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct), and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered by parietal peritoneum. This opening typically admits two fingers and provides communication between the greater and lesser sacs.

The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, with their broader surfaces dorsally and narrower surfaces plantarly, providing the bony factor to the transverse arch. The ligaments (deep transverse metatarsal ligament and interosseous ligaments), the muscle fibularis longus, the transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior all contribute to maintaining this arch.
options: The cuboid and calcaneus being wedge-shaped
The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being wedge-shaped
The plantar surfaces of all tarsals being flat
questions.question: Which factor provides the bony contribution to the transverse arch, with the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being specifically wedge-shaped?
Which duct drains the majority of the pancreatic tissue?
questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung begins in the tail and runs through the entire length of the gland, receiving numerous tributaries along its course. It drains the majority of pancreatic tissue and usually joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This ampulla opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

questions.question: The median arcuate ligament crosses anterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament connects the right and left crura of the diaphragm, passing anterior to the aorta at the T12 level, above the origin of the celiac trunk. In some individuals (1-2%), this ligament may be positioned lower, crossing anterior to the celiac trunk and potentially compressing it, a condition known as median arcuate ligament syndrome (celiac artery compression syndrome or Dunbar syndrome). This can cause postprandial pain, weight loss, and an epigastric bruit, though the clinical significance remains debated as many individuals with radiographic compression remain asymptomatic.

The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion because the trochlea tali (superior articular surface of the talus) is wider anteriorly. During dorsiflexion, this wider part engages the mortise more tightly, increasing bony congruence and stability. In plantarflexion, the narrower posterior talus is in the mortise, creating relative instability and increased susceptibility to inversion sprains.
questions.question: The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion than plantarflexion. Why is this so?
options: The wider anterior trochlea tali fits more snugly in the mortise during dorsiflexion
The deltoid ligament is placed under increased tension in dorsiflexion
The calcaneus supports the talus more during dorsiflexion
The Achilles tendon tightens and mechanically limits further dorsiflexion
The lateral ligaments are tighter in dorsiflexion only

questions.question: Which ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. It extends from the umbilicus to the liver, dividing the liver into anatomical right and left lobes on the diaphragmatic surface. The free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres (round ligament).

questions.question: Which bone contains the hypoglossal canal?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal canal is located in the occipital bone above the anterolateral margin of the foramen magnum. It transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII) from the posterior cranial fossa to the neck. The canal is about 1 cm long. Skull base fractures involving this canal can cause tongue paralysis.

The triceps reflex predominantly tests the C7 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon. Absence or diminution suggests C7 nerve root or radial nerve pathology.
questions.question: What nerve root is predominantly tested by the triceps reflex?
How many structures contribute to diaphragm development?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm develops from four embryological structures: (1) septum transversum (forming central tendon), (2) dorsal esophageal mesentery, (3) peripheral rim from body wall, and (4) pleuroperitoneal membranes (closing the pleuroperitoneal canals). Incomplete fusion of these components leads to congenital diaphragmatic hernias.

The pancreas extends obliquely across the posterior abdominal wall from the C-shaped curve of the duodenum (head) to the splenic hilum (tail) at approximately L1-L2 vertebral levels, though the tail may extend slightly higher. The head lies at L1-L2, the neck crosses L1, and the body and tail run along L1-L2 as they extend to the left. The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal (except the tail, which extends into the splenorenal ligament), lying anterior to the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vessels, aorta, IVC, left kidney, and left suprarenal gland.
questions.question: The pancreas lies at which vertebral levels?

questions.explanation: Only one small artery enters the scaphoid bone at the end closest to the thumb (distal end). This unique blood supply pattern makes the scaphoid vulnerable to avascular necrosis following fracture. The proximal fragment may lose blood supply if fracture tears the artery.
questions.question: What is the primary blood supply to the scaphoid bone?
options: Dual arterial supply proximally and distally
Direct branches from radial artery proximally

questions.question: What connects the papillary muscles to the valve cusps?
questions.explanation: Chordae tendineae (heart strings) are thin, strong tendinous cords that connect the papillary muscles to the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps. They prevent the valve cusps from prolapsing into the atrium during ventricular contraction. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes acute valvular regurgitation, often requiring surgical repair.

The glenohumeral joint capsule is weakest inferiorly, making this the most common site for dislocation. The capsule is thin and lax to allow wide range of movement, particularly abduction. Superior movement of the humeral head is prevented by the coraco-acromial arch rather than capsular strength.
questions.question: What is the anatomical position of the glenohumeral joint capsule's weakest area?

questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus contains (from superior to inferior): oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), ophthalmic division (V1), and maxillary division (V2). The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (VI) pass through the sinus cavity itself. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can affect all these structures causing ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the cavernous sinus lateral wall?

questions.explanation: The posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into the superior meatus. The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses. The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct. The sphenoethmoidal recess receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus.
questions.question: Which sinus drains into the superior meatus?

questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as a continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the internal and common carotid arteries. The vein joins with the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
questions.question: The internal jugular vein begins at which anatomical location?

questions.explanation: The deep group of the posterior compartment contains four muscles: popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and tibialis posterior. The superficial group contains three muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris. All muscles of the posterior compartment are supplied by the tibial nerve. It is the largest of the three leg compartments.
questions.question: The deep group of the posterior leg compartment contains how many muscles?

questions.explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins and deep facial veins. This valveless connection allows spread of infection from the infratemporal fossa to the cranial cavity. The plexus receives maxillary, middle meningeal, and deep temporal veins.
questions.question: The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with which important venous structure?
How many taeniae coli are present on the colon?
questions.explanation: There are three taeniae coli on the large intestine: the free taenia, mesocolic taenia, and omental taenia. These bands converge at the root of the appendix and disappear at the rectosigmoid junction. The taeniae are approximately 1 cm wide and their contraction creates the characteristic sacculated appearance of the colon.

questions.question: Which recess is deeper during expiration?
questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is shallow during inspiration when the lung expands into it, and becomes deeper during expiration when the lung retracts. This recess is clinically important as it is the site where pleural fluid accumulates in effusions and is the target for thoracentesis.

options: Collateral circulation bypassing proximal subclavian obstruction
questions.explanation: Scapular anastomoses provide crucial collateral circulation connecting first part of subclavian artery with third part of axillary artery. This enables continued limb perfusion even with proximal arterial obstruction. The anastomoses involve suprascapular, dorsal scapular, and circumflex scapular arteries.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the scapular anastomoses?
Which structure is palpable in the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox and is palpable in this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture. The radial artery pulse can also be felt crossing the snuffbox floor.

The lateral pterygoid assists in opening the jaw against resistance (along with gravity, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric). The suprahyoid muscles provide the main force when opening against resistance. Lateral pterygoid protrudes and depresses the mandible. All other muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close the jaw.
questions.question: Which muscle opens the jaw against resistance?

questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion hangs from the maxillary nerve (V2) by two pterygopalatine (sensory) branches in the pterygopalatine fossa. Parasympathetic fibers arrive via the nerve of the pterygoid canal (greater petrosal + deep petrosal). Postganglionic fibers supply the lacrimal gland and nasal/palatine mucosa. Sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended from which nerve?

questions.explanation: The piriform fossa (recess) is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels lie in the mucosa of the piriform fossa. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in this recess. The fossa is part of the laryngopharynx.
questions.question: The piriform fossa is bounded medially by which structure?

options: Sustentaculum tali of calcaneus to the navicular
questions.question: The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) supports the head of the talus and the medial longitudinal arch. Between which two bones does it pass?
questions.explanation: The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) passes from the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the plantar surface of the navicular, directly supporting the head of the talus. Its superior surface has a fibrocartilaginous facet that contributes to the articular surface for the talar head. Spring ligament rupture leads to talar head descent and collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.

questions.question: The anterior ethmoid artery is a branch of which parent vessel?
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid system. It supplies the anterior and middle ethmoidal air cells and frontal sinus. The artery enters the nasal cavity through the anterior ethmoidal foramen and supplies the anterior nasal septum.

The pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) is a fascial tunnel in the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa, formed by the splitting of the obturator fascia covering the obturator internus muscle. It contains the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels as they pass from the lesser sciatic foramen toward the perineum. The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) provides motor innervation to perineal muscles and sensory innervation to the external genitalia and perineum. Pudendal nerve block can be performed by injecting anesthetic near the ischial spine where the nerve re-enters the pelvis.
questions.question: Which structure is located in the pudendal canal?
What is the approximate length of the mesentery root attachment?
questions.explanation: The root (origin) of the mesentery is approximately 15 cm long, extending obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction. Despite this short root attachment, the mesentery fans out to accommodate the 5-6 meters of small bowel. The root crosses the third part of the duodenum, aorta, IVC, right psoas muscle, and right gonadal vessels.

questions.question: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles. Which of the following does NOT belong to this compartment?
questions.explanation: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius. Fibularis longus belongs to the lateral compartment, along with fibularis brevis. All anterior compartment muscles are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Paralysis of these muscles causes foot drop.

questions.question: The lingual artery typically arises from which parent vessel?
questions.explanation: The lingual artery is a branch of the external carotid artery arising at the level of the hyoid bone. It supplies the tongue through dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The artery passes deep to the hyoglossus muscle, which serves as a key surgical landmark.

questions.question: At what age does the appendix typically reach its adult position?
questions.explanation: The appendix reaches its definitive adult position by puberty. In infants and young children, the appendix has a relatively higher position, which explains why appendicitis in children may present with higher abdominal pain. The growth of the cecum pulls the appendix to a lower position. The base of the appendix remains constant at the confluence of the three taeniae coli.

questions.question: Which bone contains the foramen rotundum?
questions.explanation: The foramen rotundum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, transmitting the maxillary nerve (V2). It connects the middle cranial fossa with the pterygopalatine fossa. The foramen is round in shape, distinguishing it from the oval foramen ovale.

The internal spermatic fascia is derived from the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring. The cremasteric muscle and fascia are derived from the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. The external spermatic fascia is derived from the external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial inguinal ring. These layers represent the layers of the abdominal wall through which the testis descended.
questions.question: Which layer of the spermatic cord is derived from transversalis fascia?

questions.explanation: is the primary adductor of the thumb, bringing it toward the palm. It is supplied by the ulnar nerve, unlike the other thenar muscles. The muscle has two heads (oblique and transverse) that converge on the base of the proximal phalanx.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary adductor of the thumb?

questions.explanation: The Achilles (calcaneal) tendon inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus via the calcaneal tuberosity. The gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles all contribute to the calcaneal tendon. The calcaneal tendon is the strongest tendon in the body but is frequently ruptured in sudden powerful plantarflexion, such as in a jump landing. Bursae lie posterior and anterior to the tendon.
questions.question: The calcaneus is the largest and strongest bone of the foot and its primary function is to absorb shock and leverage movement. Where is the Achilles tendon inserted on the calcaneus?
What is the normal carrying angle of the fully extended forearm?
questions.explanation: The long axis of the fully extended ulna makes an angle of approximately 170 degrees with the long axis of the humerus. This carrying angle represents the way the forearm angles away from the body when carrying objects. The obliquity is more pronounced in females than males.

The testicular arteries arise directly from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta, just inferior to the renal arteries at approximately the L2 vertebral level, reflecting the embryological origin of the testes in the posterior abdominal wall. These long, slender arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major muscle, ureter, and external iliac vessels before entering the deep inguinal ring as part of the spermatic cord. The right testicular artery crosses anterior to the inferior vena cava, while the left crosses anterior to the left renal vein, then both pass through the inguinal canal to supply the testes.
questions.question: The testicular artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: From lateral to medial, the femoral triangle contains: Nerve (femoral nerve), Artery (femoral artery), Vein (femoral vein), and Empty space/Lymphatics. The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics) helps recall this order. The femoral sheath surrounds the femoral artery and vein (and the femoral canal), but not the femoral nerve.
questions.question: The contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial are arranged as which of the following?
The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses which part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the second (descending) part of the duodenum as it extends from right to left across the posterior abdominal wall. This attachment divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic (containing stomach, liver, spleen) and infracolic (containing small intestine and colon) compartments. The root also crosses anterior to the head of the pancreas and the superior mesenteric vessels. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical mobilization of the transverse colon and in understanding the spread of peritoneal infections.

questions.question: What epithelium lines the true vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The true vocal cords are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium, which is firmly adherent to the underlying vocal ligament without submucosa. This accounts for the pearly white avascular appearance on laryngoscopy. The rest of the larynx is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

questions.question: At what level does the deep palmar arch lie in the hand?
questions.explanation: The deep palmar arch is formed by the radial artery and deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery. It lies approximately one centimeter proximal to the superficial palmar arch at the level of the proximal border of the extended thumb. It gives off palmar metacarpal arteries and perforating branches.
options: One centimeter distal to wrist joint
One centimeter proximal to superficial arch

questions.question: Which vessel marks the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of the triangle is formed by the transversalis fascia, which may be reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. This triangle represents an area of potential weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, and direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Understanding this triangle is crucial for distinguishing direct (through the triangle) from indirect (lateral to inferior epigastric) inguinal hernias.

questions.question: What level are nodes behind pectoralis minor?
questions.explanation: Level II nodes (middle nodes) lie behind the pectoralis minor muscle. Level I (low nodes) are lateral to pectoralis minor. Level III (upper/apical nodes) are medial to pectoralis minor. This classification is used in staging breast cancer and planning surgical lymph node dissection.

questions.question: Which valve cusp is attached to the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: The septal cusp of the tricuspid valve is attached to the interventricular septum, while the anterior and posterior cusps are attached to the anterior and posterior ventricular walls respectively. The septal cusp receives chordae tendineae from the septal and posterior papillary muscles. Ventricular septal defects near the membranous septum can affect this cusp's support.

questions.question: Which muscle produces wrist flexion and abduction?
questions.explanation: produces both wrist flexion and wrist abduction (radial deviation). It is a prominent muscle in the anterior forearm, easily palpable lateral to palmaris longus. The muscle is supplied by the median nerve.

questions.question: The sole of the foot muscles are arranged in four layers. The first layer contains three muscles. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The first layer of foot muscles contains three muscles: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, and abductor digiti minimi. All three originate from the medial tubercle of the tuberosity of the calcaneus and the plantar aponeurosis. Abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis are innervated by the medial plantar nerve, while abductor digiti minimi is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.
options: Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
Abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis
Plantar interossei, dorsal interossei, flexor hallucis brevis
Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi
Anterior surface of the ankle between malleoli
Dorsum of foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus
Midway between lateral malleolus and calcaneus
questions.question: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated at which surface anatomical location?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery curves to enter the tarsal tunnel and then the sole of the foot. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. The four main pulse points of the lower limb are femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.

questions.question: Which structure prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction?
questions.explanation: Although no anatomical sphincter exists, a physiological lower esophageal sphincter (LES) mechanism prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction. This involves: (1) increased smooth muscle tone in the distal esophagus, (2) acute angle of entry (angle of His), (3) compression by the right crus of the diaphragm, (4) positive intra-abdominal pressure on the abdominal esophagus. LES dysfunction causes gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

questions.question: The trochanteric anastomosis, providing the main blood supply to the head of femur, is formed by which four arteries?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric anastomosis is formed by four arteries: superior gluteal (SGA), inferior gluteal (IGA), medial femoral circumflex (MFCA), and lateral femoral circumflex (LFCA) arteries. Disruption of this anastomosis in femoral neck fractures leads to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.question: Where does the azygos vein originate?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein is formed by the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and right subcostal vein at the level of L1-L2. It enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12. It represents the embryonic right posterior cardinal vein.

Iliopsoas is the most powerful hip flexor in the fully extended hip position. Its large cross-sectional area and optimal moment arm at the hip make it the most forceful. Rectus femoris is a significant hip flexor at lower hip flexion angles. Sartorius contributes but is much weaker due to its smaller size. Iliopsoas weakness is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated or supine position.
questions.question: The rectus femoris, sartorius, and iliopsoas all flex the hip. Of these, which is the most powerful hip flexor in the fully extended hip position?
The superior mesenteric vein receives blood from all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vein receives tributaries corresponding to branches of the superior mesenteric artery (jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic veins) plus the right gastroepiploic vein and inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins. The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein (behind the pancreas) rather than the superior mesenteric vein, though variations exist. The SMV ascends to the right of the SMA, passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum and uncinate process of pancreas, and joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.

The lesser sac (omental bursa) communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow, foramen of Winslow), bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament, posteriorly by the IVC and right crus of diaphragm, superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum. This communication allows peritoneal fluid to flow between the two sacs and permits spread of infection or hemorrhage. The foramen typically admits two fingers and can be used surgically to access the lesser sac. Foramina of Morgagni and Bochdalek are diaphragmatic defects, not communications between peritoneal sacs.
questions.question: The lesser sac communicates with the greater sac through which opening?

questions.explanation: The chorda tympani carries special sensory (taste) fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to submandibular and sublingual glands. It branches from the facial nerve in the mastoid, crosses the middle ear, and joins the lingual nerve. Damage causes loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior tongue.
options: Special sensory (taste) from anterior two-thirds tongue
questions.question: The chorda tympani nerve carries which type of fibers?

In the lower limb, the term 'sclerotome' refers to the area of bone and deep structures supplied by a single spinal nerve root. Hip pain from L3 sclerotome involvement can mimic pain from which structure?
questions.explanation: The L3 sclerotome includes the hip joint, which receives innervation partly from the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Pain from L3 root pathology can be referred to the hip joint, and hip joint disease can refer pain along L3 dermatomal distribution to the anterior thigh and knee. This bidirectional referral is explained by Hilton's law and the concept of sclerotome overlap between spinal levels.
options: Hip joint itself (L3 innervates the hip)

questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle elevates the pharynx and hyoid bone during swallowing, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) depress the hyoid. Longitudinal pharyngeal muscles collectively raise the pharynx to engulf the food bolus.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the hyoid bone and pharynx during swallowing?

courses.title: NMCN Exam: Practice Paper 1
courses.objectives:
Question paper 1 - 50
Question paper 51 - 100
Question paper 101 - 150
Question paper 151 - 200
Question paper 201 - 250

questions.question: A woman diagnosed with gestational hypertension continues to have elevated blood pressure readings at 14 weeks after delivery. This persistence beyond the expected postpartum resolution should now be reclassified as:
questions.explanation: Gestational hypertension that fails to resolve within 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as chronic hypertension, indicating that the underlying blood pressure elevation likely predated or will persist beyond the pregnancy. Ongoing follow-up and long-term antihypertensive management are then required. This reclassification also has implications for future pregnancy risk counselling.

Spermatogenesis, the production of sperm, takes place within the seminiferous tubules of the testes, which are lined with germ cells that develop into mature sperm. The sperm then travel to the epididymis for maturation and storage. Distinguishing production from maturation sites is important for understanding male fertility physiology.
questions.question: A male client is told that sperm are produced within coiled structures inside the testes before travelling elsewhere to mature. In which specific part of the testes does sperm production occur?

questions.explanation: Slander is a false statement that is spoken rather than written. When a nurse verbally communicates false information about a patient—to an employer or any third party—this constitutes slander, a quasi-intentional tort. Libel requires the false statement to be made in writing. The distinction between slander (spoken) and libel (written) is fundamental in defamation law.
options: Negligence, because a care standard was violated
Libel, because the statement was made over a recorded line
Slander, because the false information was spoken
Battery, because actual harm was caused to the patient
