• Hard end feel is a bone-to-bone end feel, as in full extension of the elbow joint

(b)
• Springy end feel is often experienced in meniscal lesions, as in the knee joint
• Empty end feel occurs in fracture and dislocation cases
• Capsular pattern end feel occurs in cases of restricted physiological ROM due to periarticular or intra-articular adhesions

(c)
Capsular patterns are said to exist when the capsuloligamentous complex of a joint is restricted, resulting in a characteristic loss of motion specific to that joint; the classic capsular pattern presentation is believed to exist in joints with osteoarthritis.

(d)
End feel is the resistance felt in moving a joint through its physiological range from physiological to accessory movement; because a capsular or pathological end feel indicates that periarticular or intra-articular adhesions or capsular restriction are limiting motion at that joint, the joint's restricted accessory movement will limit the physiological range needed for normal function of that limb segment, so identifying the abnormal end feel at the joint helps to explain a functional deficit felt distally in that limb during activity.

(a)
Brian R. Mulligan qualified as a physiotherapist in 1954 and gained his diploma in Manipulative Therapy in 1974; he proposed that injuries or sprains might result in a minor "positional fault" to a joint, causing restrictions in physiological movement, and his techniques were developed to overcome joint "tracking" problems or positional faults.

(b)
NAGs - Natural Apophyseal Glides; SNAGs - Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glides; MWMs - Mobilization with Movements.

(c)
These techniques are applicable when no contraindication for manual therapy exists, a full orthopaedic scanning examination has indicated local musculoskeletal pathology, a specific biomechanical analysis reveals localized loss of movement and/or pain associated with function, and no pain is produced during or immediately after the technique.

(d)
A passive accessory joint mobilization is applied following Kaltenborn's principles and must itself be pain free; while sustaining the accessory glide, the patient performs the comparable sign, which should be significantly improved; the therapist looks for a PILL response - Pain free, Instant result, Long Lasting - and if there is no PILL response the technique should not be advocated; the CROCKS principle also applies - Contra-indications, Repetitions (only three on day one), Over-pressure, Communications, Knowledge, Sustain the mobilization throughout the movement.

(e)
The techniques re-align the joint surfaces in the least provocative way to restore normal tracking during movement, since alteration in the shape of articular surfaces, cartilage thickness, ligament/capsule fibre orientation, or the direction of pull of muscles and tendons would otherwise alter joint position or tracking and provoke pain, stiffness or weakness; because the glide is sustained while the patient performs the symptomatic (comparable) movement, full range pain-free movement results if the correct treatment plane and grade have been found.

(f)
• NAGs are used for the cervical and upper thoracic spine, consisting of oscillatory mobilizations (not sustained), applied mid-range to end-range, and are the treatment of choice in highly irritable conditions
• SNAGs can be applied to all spinal joints, the rib cage and the sacroiliac joint, using a sustained glide while the patient performs the symptomatic movement, and are most successful when symptoms are provoked by movement and are not multilevel, but are not the choice in highly irritable conditions
questions.question:
(a) Define the Mulligan Concept.
(b) State the types of techniques in the Mulligan Concept.
(c) State the indications/conditions for application.
(d) Describe the method/procedure (including PILL and CROCKS).
(e) Explain the clinical basis for why the Mulligan Concept techniques are effective when symptoms are movement-provoked.
(f) Distinguish between NAGs and SNAGs.

A patient with low back pain has a restricted segmental movement felt at the L3-4 interspinous space on side-lying assessment.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Name the technique used to treat it.
(c) Describe the landmarks/procedure of the technique.
(d) What structure is at risk, and what precautions/contraindications apply?
(e) What is a modification/gentler variant of this technique?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Segmental restriction of the lumbar spine at L3-4.

(b)
Side-lying rotational lumbar thrust manipulation.

(c)
The patient lies on their side with hips and knees flexed; the therapist passively flexes the patient's legs until movement is felt at the L3-4 interspinous space, then grasps the patient's bottom shoulder and introduces rotation and lateral flexion until movement is felt at the same interspinous space; while maintaining this position, the patient is rolled towards the therapist, and the therapist provides a high velocity, low amplitude thrust manipulation of the pelvis in an anterior direction.

(d)
The lumbar interspinous segment/facet joints are at risk; general contraindications to manipulation include severe osteoporosis, tumor or malignancy, bleeding in a joint, a loose body in the joint, total joint replacements, joints near a growth plate, until a full diagnosis is reached, metallic implants, and acute inflammation.

(e)
A gentler variant is Posterior-to-Anterior (PA) mobilization, in which a postero-anterior force is applied via the pisiform/ulnar surface of the hand on the spinous process using oscillatory rocking movements rather than a high-velocity thrust.

(a)
Strain/Counterstrain is a technique used to decrease muscle tension and normalize muscle function; it is a passive technique that places the body in a position of comfort, thereby relieving pain.

(b)
Tender points are located - tense, tender, oedematous spots less than 1cm in diameter, which may run a few centimetres long in the muscle, may fall within a line, or have multiple points for one specific joint; the tender points are monitored as the patient is placed in a position of comfort (shortening the muscle); when the correct position is found, the tender point is no longer tense.

(c)
The position is held for 90 seconds, after which the point should be clear, and the patient is then returned to the neutral position.

(d)
The physiological rationale is based on the stretch reflex: the muscle is relaxed instead of stretched, and muscle spindle input is reduced, allowing for a decrease in tension and pain.

(e)
Because the physiological rationale is based on the stretch reflex, shortening the muscle to a position of comfort reduces muscle spindle input and allows the muscle to relax rather than provoking a stretch reflex, which is why relaxing the muscle at the tender point (rather than stretching it) is effective at decreasing tension and pain.

(f)
• Positional Release Therapy is based on the strain/counterstrain technique and follows the same procedure
• The difference is that PRT is an osteopathic mobilization technique that uses a facilitating force (compression) to enhance the effect of positioning, and contact and pressure are maintained throughout, whereas maintaining contact itself has a therapeutic effect
questions.question:
(a) Define Strain/Counterstrain technique.
(b) Describe the method/procedure, including how tender points are located and monitored.
(c) State the dosage/duration of the technique.
(d) State the physiological rationale.
(e) Explain the clinical basis for why a position-of-comfort approach relieves pain more effectively than direct stretching in this technique.
(f) Distinguish Strain/Counterstrain from Positional Release Therapy (PRT).

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: hypermobility in associated joints; total joint replacements.

(b)
If the associated hypermobile joint is not properly stabilized, the mobilization force can be transmitted to it, risking further instability at that joint.

(c)
I would properly stabilize the associated hypermobile joint so that the mobilization force applied to the joint being treated is not transmitted to it, using gentle progressive techniques appropriate to tissue tolerance.
questions.question:
A patient with a total joint replacement has an associated joint that is hypermobile.
(a) What are the risk factors for this patient during mobilization treatment of a neighbouring joint?
(b) What complications could occur if this is not managed appropriately?
(c) What management option would you choose, and justify it.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The tibial nerve, tested/mobilized by Tibial Nerve Mobilization: the foot is dorsiflexed and everted, dorsiflexion and eversion are maintained while applying overpressure to knee extension, then the leg is passively raised into hip flexion until tension is felt; hip adduction and internal rotation can be added for further sensitization.

(b)
The Peroneal Nerve Mobilization technique uses plantar flexion and inversion of the foot instead, with overpressure to knee extension and passive hip flexion; both are forms of Neural Mobilization (flossing/gliding) used to treat low back and radicular pain (LBRP).

(c)
Differential conditions include spondylosis, spondylolisthesis, muscle spasm, and disc herniation; mechanical low back or leg pain accounts for most cases, including lumbar strain, degenerative disc/facet processes, herniated disc, spinal stenosis, osteoporotic compression fracture, spondylolisthesis, traumatic fracture, and congenital disease, as well as referred pain.

(d)
Nerves cannot stretch like muscles but must still move as the body moves; nerve mobilization moves the nerve from a slack position to a position of tension repeatedly without over-tensioning it, which enhances nerve mobility, increases fluid dispersion, and helps prevent adverse effects of intraneural fluid accumulation/edema that would otherwise cause radicular symptoms distal to the site of compression.
questions.question:
A patient with low back and radicular leg pain has dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot maintained while overpressure is applied to knee extension, reproducing tension along the back of the leg.
(a) Identify the structure being tested/mobilized.
(b) What other related structures/techniques address this region?

A patient complains of neck pain with pain radiating into the arm, reproduced when the head is tilted toward the symptomatic side and pressure is applied to the head.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the pathophysiology?
(c) What is the management?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cervical radiculopathy, identified using the Spurling's test (Maximal Cervical Compression Test/Foraminal Compression Test), which is positive when pressure applied to the head, tilted toward the symptomatic side, radiates pain into the arm.

(b)
The test is used for musculoskeletal assessment of the cervical spine when looking for cervical nerve root compression; differential conditions producing similar pain include muscle spasm, spondylosis, retrolysthesis, spondylolisthesis, disc herniation, prolapsed disc, discogenic pain, and zygapophyseal (facet) pain syndrome.

(c)
Management includes Vertical Oscillatory Pressure (VOP), Transverse Oscillatory Pressure (TOP), ultrasound, exercises, cryotherapy, kneading massage, cervical traction, and use of topical NSAID.

(a)
Nwugarian Techniques involve the concept of thorough assessment, examination, reaching a physical diagnosis, and appropriate mobilization technique, following the SOAP format, dealing with spinal manual therapy only; specific tests peculiar to the Nwugarian method are Skin Rolling and Digital Pressure.

(b)
Indirect, Direct, Specific, and Non-specific manipulation.
• Indirect: the operator uses the limbs as natural levers to influence the spinal column, e.g
• Lumbar Rotatory and Lumbar Oscillatory Techniques
• Direct: involves direct manual pressure on the vertebrae, sometimes called pressure techniques, e.g
• Vertical Oscillatory Pressure and Transverse Oscillatory Pressure
• Specific: manipulative techniques intended to influence only one joint at a time
• Non-specific: the manipulative force falls on more than one joint at a time

(c)
VOP: the patient lies prone with the head resting on the back of the hands; the operator stands at the head end, places the thumbs on the spinous process, and applies rhythmic pressure followed by relaxation, with the origin of pressure from the operator's trunk; VOP is indicated for pain of bilateral distribution. TOP: the patient lies prone with the forehead on the back of the fingers; the operator stands to the side and directs pressure horizontally through the thumbs against the side of the transverse/spinous process in a pressure-relax sequence; TOP is useful when the pain has a unilateral distribution.

(d)
The operator's shoulders and elbows are held in flexion and extension respectively so the arms act as rigid pillars transmitting trunk movement to the thumbs; application of pressure by contraction of the intrinsic muscles of the hands should be avoided.

(e)
In the indirect technique, when a patient is lying on the side with the operator applying pressure on the pelvis and shoulder in opposite directions, the resulting force can cause torsion of the lumbar spine, as used in the Lumbar Rotatory Technique.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principles of Nwugarian manual therapy technique.
(b) State the types of Nwugarian technique.
(c) Describe the method of application of Vertical Oscillatory Pressure (VOP) and Transverse Oscillatory Pressure (TOP).
(d) State the safe site/precaution for applying these techniques.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Massage is typically the repetitive rubbing, stripping or kneading of myofascial tissues to principally improve interstitial fluid dynamics; it is the use of rhythmically applied pressure to the skin and soft tissues of the body.

(b)
The earliest available medical records indicate massage played an important role in the treatment of sick and injured people; the general knowledge of massage was known and practised by the Egyptians, Romans, Japanese, Persians, and Chinese; in Sweden in the early nineteenth century, Peter H. Ling, the acknowledged founder of curative gymnastics, used massage as a branch of gymnastics and incorporated French massage techniques into his system, appearing to be the founder of modern-day massage technique.

(c)
Massage is used to reduce tension, anxiety, and stress, and to promote overall circulation, relaxation, and flexibility.

(d)
A natural reaction when a part of the body hurts is to rub the injured area with the hand, which is why massage, along with manipulation, mobilization and muscle energy techniques, forms one of the major/notable groups of manual therapy techniques, alongside joint mobilization, traction and Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation as among the most frequently used techniques by physiotherapists in rehabilitation.

(e)
• Massage is the repetitive rubbing, stripping or kneading of myofascial tissues using rhythmically applied pressure to the skin and soft tissues, principally to improve interstitial fluid dynamics, reduce tension, and promote circulation and relaxation
• Mobilization is instead a slower, more controlled series of passive movements which does not go beyond the normal range of motion, comprising a continuum of skilled passive movements to the joint complex applied at varying speeds and amplitudes, intended to improve articular and soft-tissue (myofascial) bio-mechanical elasticity
questions.question:
(a) Define massage.
(b) Describe the historical evolution of massage as a treatment modality.
(c) State the physiological effects of massage.

A patient has neck pain that is reproduced by a specific movement, is not multilevel, and is not highly irritable.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Name the technique/procedure that would be used.
(c) Describe the landmarks/method of application.
(d) What structure is at risk, and what are the contraindications/precautions?
(e) What is a modification/variant of the technique?
questions.answerText:
(a)
A facet joint movement-related restriction/pain provoked by a specific movement.

(b)
SNAGs - Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glides (Mulligan Concept).

(c)
The therapist applies the appropriate accessory zygapophyseal glide while the patient performs the symptomatic movement; this must result in full range pain-free movement; SNAGs can be applied to all the spinal joints, the rib cage, and the sacroiliac joint, and are usually performed in weight-bearing positions.

(d)
The zygapophyseal (facet) joint is the structure being glided; SNAGs are not the choice in conditions that are highly irritable, and the technique must produce a PILL response (Pain free, Instant result, Long Lasting) - if there is no PILL response the technique should not be advocated; the CROCKS principle applies (Contra-indications, Repetitions - only three on day one, Over-pressure, Communication, Knowledge, Sustain).

(e)
SNAGs can be adapted for use in non-weight-bearing positions; NAGs (Natural Apophyseal Glides, oscillatory rather than sustained) are used instead in highly irritable conditions or for the cervical and upper thoracic spine.

(a)
Joint mobilization refers to manual therapy techniques used to modulate pain and treat joint dysfunctions that limit range of motion by specifically addressing the altered mechanics of the joint; it replicates normal joint mechanics while minimizing abnormal compressive stresses on the articular cartilage.

(b)
• Grade I: small-amplitude rhythmic oscillations at the beginning of the range
• Grade II: large-amplitude rhythmic oscillations within the range, not reaching the limit
• Grade III: large-amplitude oscillations up to the limit of available motion, stressed into tissue resistance
• Grade IV: small-amplitude oscillations at the limit of available motion, stressed into tissue resistance
• Grade V: a small-amplitude, high-velocity thrust to snap adhesions at the limit of available motion, requiring advanced training

(c)
The oscillation may be performed using physiologic (osteokinematic) motion or joint-play (arthrokinematic) techniques; Grade I and II are primarily used for joints limited by pain; Grade III and IV are primarily used as stretching maneuvers.

(d)
• Precautions include hypermobility in associated joints (which must be properly stabilized), total replacements, newly formed or weakened connective tissue, systemic connective tissue diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, and elderly individuals with weakened connective tissue and diminished circulation
• The only true contraindications to stretching techniques are hypermobility, joint effusion, and inflammation
• Special precautions are also needed for malignancy, bone disease detectable on x-ray, unhealed fracture, and excessive pain

(e)
With immobilization, there is fibrofatty proliferation leading to intra-articular adhesions, as well as biochemical changes in tendon, ligament, and joint capsule tissue, which causes joint contractures and ligamentous weakening; atrophy of the articular cartilage begins soon after immobilization is imposed, because joint motion normally moves synovial fluid that brings nutrients to the avascular articular cartilage and maintains extensibility and tensile strength of the articular and periarticular tissues.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principles of joint mobilization.
(b) State the types/grades of oscillation technique dosages.
(c) State the method of application of joint mobilization.
(d) State the safe application/precautions for joint mobilization.
(e) Explain the biomechanical basis of joint dysfunction/restriction that develops after injury or immobilization.

A patient has muscle weakness and imbalance following injury and needs strengthening.
(a) What is the provisional problem?
(b) What is the muscle/soft-tissue basis for the chosen technique?
(c) What is the initial management?
(d) What is the progressive plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Muscle weakness with imbalance in muscle tone.

(b)
Isotonic Contraction: the patient contracts the muscle while the practitioner provides resistance, allowing the muscle to shorten (concentric contraction) or lengthen (eccentric contraction).

(c)
Isotonic Contraction technique helps in strengthening weak muscles and improving muscle tone and balance.

(d)
Progression to Isokinetic Contraction, in which the patient contracts the muscle at a constant speed with varying resistance provided by the practitioner; this technique is often used in rehabilitation to improve muscle strength and endurance.

(a)
Muscle resistant to stretch/lengthening.

(b)
Golgi Tendon Organ Inhibition is based on the Golgi tendon organs, which are sensory receptors located at the junctions of muscles and tendons.

(c)
The practitioner applies pressure to the Golgi tendon organs; this pressure causes the muscle to relax, allowing for a more effective stretch.

(d)
Progressive plan: once relaxation is achieved, this can be followed by Isotonic Contraction (patient contracts the muscle while the practitioner provides resistance, allowing shortening or lengthening) to strengthen weak muscles and improve muscle tone and balance, or Isokinetic Contraction to improve muscle strength and endurance in rehabilitation.
questions.question:
A patient's muscle resists lengthening despite attempted stretching, and the therapist wants to use a technique that acts directly at the musculotendinous junction.
(a) What is the provisional problem?
(b) What is the muscle/soft-tissue basis for the chosen technique?
(c) What is the initial management?
(d) What is the progressive plan?

A patient presents with a hypertonic muscle in spasm that is difficult to lengthen on examination.
(a) What is the most likely provisional problem being treated?
(b) What is the muscle/soft-tissue basis for this problem?
(c) What is the initial physiotherapy management?
(d) What is the definitive/progressive muscular therapy plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Muscle spasm with hypertonicity of the affected muscle.

(b)
The muscle is held in a shortened, hypertonic state; Muscle Energy Technique (MET) uses the muscle's own energy through gentle isometric contraction to relax it via autogenic or reciprocal inhibition and lengthen it.

(c)
Initial management is Muscle Energy Technique (MET), an active technique in which the patient voluntarily uses the muscle from a precisely controlled position against a distinctly executed counterforce, unlike static stretching where the therapist does all the work.

(d)
Progressive plan - Post-Isometric Relaxation (PIR): the muscle is placed in a stretched position just before discomfort; the patient contracts the muscle gently against resistance for about 5 to 10 seconds; the patient then relaxes and the practitioner stretches the muscle further; this is repeated several times to achieve greater relaxation and lengthening, and can be combined with respiratory kinesis (inhalation for contraction, exhalation for relaxation) to increase efficacy.

questions.question:
A patient has knee pain, and a valgus stress test reproduces the pain on the medial side.
(a) Identify the structure implicated.
(b) What other structures can be examined at the knee and by which tests?
(c) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The Vagus (valgus) test is positive, implicating the medial collateral ligament.

(b)
• Varus test implicates the lateral collateral ligament
• Drawer's test (posterior and anterior) implicates the cruciate ligaments
• Appley's compression test implicates the lateral and medial menisci
• Thomas test implicates tensor fascia lata
• Tight iliotibial tract test checks for a tight IT band
• Patella grinding test elicits pain when the patella is grinded on the patellofemoral joint
• Patella apprehension test is used in case of patella dysplasia
• Mcmurrey test implicates the medial menisci
• Ely's test is for rectus femoris tightness

(c)
Each stress or provocation test loads a specific structure (ligament, meniscus, or muscle) so that the site and type of stress applied (valgus, varus, compression, grinding, or passive stretch) determines which structure is implicated when pain or laxity is reproduced.

questions.question: A pharmacist counsels a patient prescribed carbimazole. Which statement about carbimazole is correct?
questions.explanation:
Carbimazole is a prodrug rapidly converted to the active metabolite methimazole, which circulates throughout the body.
Thioureylenes inhibit thyroperoxidase-catalysed oxidation and so block iodination of tyrosyl residues, and the thiocarbamide group is essential for activity.
Only propylthiouracil additionally inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.

It is active unchanged and also blocks peripheral conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine
It is converted rapidly to propylthiouracil, which inhibits thyroperoxidase-mediated iodination

It is excreted unchanged in bile and does not inhibit thyroperoxidase directly

questions.question: In diabetic ketoacidosis, insulin lack causes elevated blood ketones. Which sequence best explains ketone formation?
questions.explanation:
Without insulin, glucose cannot be used by cells, so fat is mobilised and hormone-sensitive lipase is no longer inhibited.
The liver breaks fatty acids down into ketones, and their accumulation causes acidaemia with Kussmaul breathing.
Potassium leaves cells in exchange for hydrogen ions and is lost in urine.
options: Unrestrained lipolysis floods the liver with fatty acids that are oxidised to ketones
Unrestrained glycogenesis floods the liver with glucose that is converted into ketones
Excess glucagon antagonism floods muscle with amino acids that are converted into ketones
Unrestrained lipogenesis floods the liver with fatty acids that are stored as triglycerides
Excess insulin signalling floods adipose tissue with glucose that is oxidised to ketones

Nicotinic acid carries a carboxyl group and is titrated directly with sodium hydroxide using phenolphthalein.
Nicotinamide is too weakly basic for aqueous titration, so non-aqueous titration with perchloric acid and crystal violet is employed.
Neither compound is assayed by redox methods, which suit ascorbic acid and tocopherol.

Both are strongly basic but differ in aqueous solubility only
The acid is hydrolysed directly while the amide resists hydrolysis
The acid is oxidised directly while the amide is weakly reducing
The acid is neutralised directly while the amide is weakly basic

questions.explanation:
DPP-4 normally degrades incretin hormones that are secreted from the gut in response to food.

Sitagliptin is taken once daily, needs dose reduction in renal impairment and may cause nausea, abdominal pain and diarrhoea.

Inhibition of GLP-1 raises DPP-4 that increases insulin and decreases glucagon
Inhibition of alpha-glucosidase raises incretins that increase insulin and decrease glucagon
Inhibition of DPP-4 raises glucagon that increases insulin and decreases incretins
Inhibition of DPP-4 raises incretins that increase insulin and decrease glucagon

SHBG is increased by oestrogen, thyroid hormone and cirrhosis, and decreased by androgens, growth hormone and obesity.
Only about two percent of testosterone is free and able to enter cells.

questions.question: About sixty-five percent of circulating testosterone is bound to SHBG. In which clinical situation would SHBG and therefore total testosterone be expected to rise?

questions.explanation:
Glucocorticoids inhibit phospholipase A2, limiting release of arachidonic acid and thus prostaglandin and leukotriene formation.
They also reduce circulating T lymphocytes and other leucocytes and inhibit leucocyte migration into affected tissue.
These actions explain their use in inflammatory, allergic and autoimmune disorders.
options: Activation of phospholipase A2 increases arachidonic acid availability for mediator synthesis
Inhibition of phospholipase A2 reduces arachidonic acid availability for mediator synthesis
Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase alone reduces prostaglandin synthesis without affecting leucocytes
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase reduces mediator degradation within the inflamed tissue
Activation of lipoxygenase increases leukotriene synthesis and stimulates leucocyte migration
questions.question: Glucocorticoids suppress inflammation at several levels. Which statement identifies a key biochemical target?

Reversible aromatase inhibition throughout the body, with bone density loss
Reversible oestrogen receptor activation in bone, with bone density gain
Reversible aromatase inhibition throughout the body, with endometrial thickening

Adverse effects include hot flushes, fatigue, joint and muscle pain, bone density loss, hypercholesterolaemia and vaginal dryness.
It is contraindicated in premenopausal women and pregnancy.
questions.question: A postmenopausal woman with advanced breast cancer is switched to letrozole. Which mechanism and most notable class adverse effect apply?

Tamoxifen, antagonist in breast and endometrium with partial agonism in bone
Raloxifene, antagonist in breast and endometrium with partial agonism in bone
Clomiphene, antagonist in breast and endometrium with partial agonism in bone
Letrozole, partial agonist in breast and endometrium with antagonism in bone

questions.explanation:
Raloxifene is a SERM that antagonises oestrogen in breast and endometrium and acts as a partial agonist in bone and the cardiovascular system.
This profile retains bone benefit without the endometrial stimulation seen with tamoxifen.
Fulvestrant is a pure antagonist and letrozole is an enzyme inhibitor.

questions.question: A pharmacology student must pick the best statement on genetic polymorphism and prodrugs. Which is correct?

questions.explanation:

Unlike tamoxifen and toremifene, which are non-steroidal triphenylethylene SERMs, it has no agonist activity.
Tamoxifen at high dose is hepatocarcinogenic, whereas toremifene is not.
options: It is a steroidal pure oestrogen receptor antagonist without partial agonist activity
It is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor with partial agonist activity in bone
It is a steroidal partial oestrogen receptor agonist with tissue selective activity
It is a steroidal progesterone receptor antagonist without oestrogen receptor effects

questions.question: A hospital pharmacist reviews phase I and phase II enzyme polymorphisms. Which pairing of enzyme and substrate is correct?
questions.explanation:
Thiopurine S-methyltransferase inactivates azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine, while N-acetyltransferase 2 acetylates isoniazid, hydralazine and procainamide.

UGT1A1 metabolises isoniazid and hydralazine; TPMT metabolises irinotecan and ethanol
TPMT metabolises isoniazid and hydralazine; NAT2 metabolises azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine

questions.question: After TSH stimulation, follicular cells endocytose colloid. Which events release active hormones into the bloodstream while conserving iodine?
questions.explanation:
Endocytosed thyroglobulin enters lysosomes, where proteases digest it and free T3, T4, MIT and DIT.

options: Extracellular proteolysis releases T3 and T4; surplus MIT and DIT are excreted in bile
Lysosomal proteolysis releases MIT and DIT; surplus T3 and T4 are deiodinated and recycled
Lysosomal proteolysis releases thyroglobulin intact; surplus iodide is excreted in urine

Blocking ovarian aromatase removes feedback and increases FSH and LH pulses

questions.question: Newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is characterised by which pathophysiology and treatment need?
questions.explanation:
Type 1 diabetes follows autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, so patients secrete no insulin.

Autoimmune destruction of alpha cells requiring exogenous glucagon
Autoimmune destruction of delta cells requiring exogenous somatostatin

questions.explanation:

options: Hepatic failure from its partial agonist hepatic action
Hypothyroidism from its antagonist pituitary action
Osteoporosis from its antagonist skeletal action
Endometrial carcinoma from its partial agonist uterine action
Vaginal atrophy from its antagonist uterine action

questions.question: A thyroid storm patient needs rapid reduction of active hormone. Why is propylthiouracil preferred over methimazole in this setting?
questions.explanation:

It additionally blocks iodide uptake through the sodium-iodide symporter
It additionally binds thyroxine-binding globulin to displace circulating hormone

questions.question: A chemist explains why norethisterone is orally active whereas progesterone is not. Which structural change is responsible?
questions.explanation:

Removing the C19 methyl increases progestational activity five- to ten-fold, making it about seventy-five times as active as progesterone.

A 6-alpha methyl group together with removal of the 17-beta side chain
A 11-beta hydroxyl group together with addition of a C21 chlorine group

questions.explanation:

questions.question: A woman has been taking prednisolone for two years and stops abruptly. She develops weakness, dizziness on standing, nausea and hypotension. Which condition has occurred?

questions.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes presents with a blood glucose above 800 mg/dL, severe dehydration and confusion but no ketosis. Why is ketosis absent?

questions.question: A boy on recombinant GH develops headache, vomiting and papilloedema. Which adverse effect should be suspected and how should it be managed?
questions.explanation:

Hypoglycaemia requiring continuation of growth hormone therapy with dietary advice

questions.question: A researcher tabulates insulin effects by tissue. Which pairing of tissue and action is correct for the fed state?
questions.explanation:
Insulin is an anabolic hormone of the fed state that increases glucose, amino acid and potassium uptake in muscle and fat.

A woman taking a combined pill starts carbamazepine for epilepsy. Which advice is correct?
questions.explanation:
Enzyme inducers such as carbamazepine, rifampicin and phenytoin increase metabolism of contraceptive steroids, reducing effectiveness.
Alternative contraceptive methods should be considered with anticonvulsants or rifampicin.
Combined pills may also alter levels of lamotrigine, theophylline and ciclosporin.
options: Continue the pill alone because enzyme induction has no effect on hormones
Stop the pill entirely because enzyme inhibition raises contraceptive toxicity
Use an additional or alternative method because enzyme induction lowers contraceptive efficacy
Continue the pill alone because enzyme induction raises contraceptive efficacy
Double the pill dose because enzyme inhibition lowers contraceptive efficacy

questions.explanation:
Propranolol is not an antithyroid agent but reduces tachycardia, tremor, agitation and dysrhythmias that arise from adrenergic overactivity.
It is contraindicated in thyrotoxic patients with asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because non-selective beta blockade can precipitate bronchospasm.
Such patients need an alternative symptomatic strategy.
options: Propranolol is acceptable because it cures the autoimmune mechanism of disease
Propranolol is safe because it lowers thyroid hormone synthesis in the gland
Propranolol is contraindicated because it inhibits peripheral conversion to triiodothyronine
Propranolol is preferred because beta blockade will relieve bronchospasm in thyrotoxicosis
Propranolol is contraindicated because beta blockade may precipitate bronchospasm
questions.question: A young woman taking propranolol for thyrotoxicosis has a history of asthma. What should the pharmacist advise?

options: About 52 percent of whites and about 3.5 percent of Nigerians are poor metabolisers
About 5 to 10 percent of whites and about 35 percent of Nigerians are poor metabolisers
About 5 to 10 percent of whites and about 3.5 percent of Nigerians are poor metabolisers
About 25 to 30 percent of whites and about 3.5 percent of Nigerians are poor metabolisers
About 1 to 2 percent of whites and about 14 percent of Nigerians are poor metabolisers
questions.explanation:
CYP2D6 poor metabolisers account for about five to ten percent of whites and one to two percent of Southeast Asians, who often carry the reduced-activity *10 variant.
Nigerian data indicate about 3.5 percent poor metabolisers.
Frequencies differ by enzyme, so ethnic data must be matched to the specific gene.
questions.question: Poor metaboliser prevalence for CYP2D6 differs between populations. Which statement is correct?
Leuprolide produces pituitary stimulation when injected in pulses but suppresses gonadotropins when given continuously. Which mechanism explains the continuous-dose effect?
options: Direct cytotoxic destruction of gonadotroph cells
Downregulation and desensitisation of pituitary GnRH receptors
Competitive blockade of pituitary GnRH receptors immediately
Enhanced hepatic clearance of the peptide analogue
Feedback inhibition by rising ovarian inhibin concentrations
questions.explanation:
GnRH is physiologically secreted in pulses, and pulsatile agonist dosing mimics this to raise FSH and LH.
Continuous exposure downregulates GnRH receptors, reducing FSH and LH secretion and producing a hypogonadal state.
This permits use in endometriosis, advanced prostate cancer, central precocious puberty and controlled ovarian stimulation.

Prenatal growth is largely independent of GH, so affected neonates are normal in size at birth.
Postnatally GH deficiency produces short stature with mild adiposity, and hypoglycaemia occurs because of heightened insulin sensitivity.
Early recombinant GH allows these children to reach mid-parental height.
questions.question: A newborn with congenital GH deficiency has normal birth length and weight but later develops short stature with hypoglycaemic episodes. Why was size normal at birth?
options: Postnatal catch-up growth masks the deficiency until infancy ends
Placental IGF-1 fully compensates for growth hormone deficiency permanently
Prenatal growth does not depend on pituitary growth hormone secretion
Prenatal growth depends mainly on maternal growth hormone crossing placenta
Prenatal growth depends mainly on fetal thyroid hormone secretion alone

questions.explanation:
The oestrogen component inhibits FSH release, stabilises the endometrium and potentiates progestin action.
The progestin component inhibits the LH surge, thickens cervical mucus and alters the endometrium to prevent implantation.
Together they prevent ovulation and create an environment hostile to sperm and implantation.
options: Oestrogen mainly blocks the LH surge and thins cervical mucus; progestin mainly suppresses FSH
Oestrogen mainly stimulates FSH and thickens cervical mucus; progestin mainly blocks the LH surge
Oestrogen mainly suppresses LH and stabilises the endometrium; progestin mainly blocks the FSH surge
Oestrogen mainly suppresses FSH and thickens cervical mucus; progestin mainly stimulates the LH surge
Oestrogen mainly suppresses FSH and stabilises the endometrium; progestin mainly blocks the LH surge
questions.question: A woman using Microgynon (ethinyl oestradiol with levonorgestrel) is told that the two components have complementary effects. Which statement is correct?
A 35-year-old man with a macroprolactinoma presents with loss of libido, erectile dysfunction and visual field defects. How does excess prolactin cause the sexual dysfunction?
questions.explanation:
Hyperprolactinaemia suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, causing hypogonadism with low libido, erectile dysfunction and infertility in men, and amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and infertility in women.
Large tumours compress the optic chiasm, explaining visual changes.
Dopamine agonists are indicated to inhibit prolactin secretion and shrink the tumour.
options: Compression of the posterior pituitary producing diabetes insipidus
Excess conversion of testosterone to oestradiol producing hyperoestrogenism
Suppression of gonadotropin secretion producing secondary hypogonadism and infertility
Autoimmune destruction of testicular tissue producing primary hypogonadism
Direct stimulation of Leydig cell testosterone synthesis producing hypergonadism

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy with delayed puberty receives a high-dose androgen course and initially grows rapidly, but his final height is shorter than expected. Why?
questions.explanation:
Androgens stimulate skeletal growth and accelerate epiphyseal closure, so overly vigorous treatment gives early rapid growth but loss of final height.
Control is difficult because the effects on epiphyseal centres may continue for months after stopping therapy.
Careful dosing allows most boys to reach expected adult height.
options: Delayed epiphyseal closure shortens the total growth period
Increased aromatisation to oestradiol delays epiphyseal closure
Accelerated epiphyseal closure shortens the total growth period
Increased IGF-1 secretion delays epiphyseal closure
Suppressed growth hormone secretion shortens the total growth period
ACTH injections together with potassium supplements in all patients
A glucocorticoid together with fludrocortisone as a mineralocorticoid
Fludrocortisone alone because glucocorticoid secretion is preserved
A glucocorticoid alone because mineralocorticoid secretion is preserved
Dexamethasone together with an androgen as a mineralocorticoid
questions.question: A patient with Addison disease has high ACTH, skin hyperpigmentation, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. Which replacement regimen is appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Addison disease is primary adrenocortical insufficiency in which the cortex is destroyed, decreasing synthesis of all classes of adrenocortical hormones.
Replacement therefore needs a glucocorticoid and fludrocortisone, which has marked mineralocorticoid activity and is the most frequently used mineralocorticoid.
Raised ACTH explains the hyperpigmentation.

Corticosteroids fall into mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, glucocorticoids such as cortisol, cortisone and corticosterone, and adrenal androgens such as dehydroepiandrosterone.
Mineralocorticoids act mainly on sodium and potassium in extracellular fluid.
Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose and also influence protein and fat metabolism.
questions.question: An intern lists the three functional classes of adrenocortical steroids. Which line lists a representative of each class correctly?
A 40-year-old man reports enlarging hands, coarse facial features and prognathism, and MRI shows a pituitary adenoma. Which drug class reduces GH production when surgery fails?
options: Dopamine antagonists such as haloperidol acting on dopamine receptors
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide acting on somatostatin receptors
GnRH agonists such as leuprolide acting on pituitary receptors
Thyroid hormones such as levothyroxine acting on nuclear receptors
Recombinant GH such as somatropin acting on GH receptors
questions.explanation:
GH excess in adults produces acromegaly, with cardiovascular disease, airway obstruction and gastrointestinal malignancy shortening life expectancy.
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide and lanreotide reduce GH release, and pegvisomant or dopamine agonists are alternatives.
Dopamine antagonists, GnRH agonists, GH and thyroid hormone would not suppress somatotroph tumours.

questions.question: A fertility clinic considers letrozole for ovulation induction in polycystic ovary syndrome. Which rationale is correct?
options: Lower oestrogen reduces feedback, decreasing LH release to stimulate follicle growth
Higher oestrogen increases feedback, increasing LH release to stimulate follicle growth
Lower oestrogen reduces feedback, increasing FSH release to stimulate follicle growth
Higher oestrogen increases feedback, decreasing FSH release to stimulate follicle growth
Lower progesterone reduces feedback, increasing prolactin release to stimulate follicle growth
questions.explanation:
Inhibiting aromatase lowers oestrogen levels, releasing hypothalamic and pituitary negative feedback so that FSH rises and recruits follicles.
Letrozole and clomiphene are both effective in stimulating ovulation, and clomiphene has long been first choice for PCOS infertility.
Tamoxifen or oestrogen therapy may counteract letrozole.

questions.question: A patient on stable warfarin starts cimetidine and later has an INR of 6. Which mechanism applies?
options: Induction of CYP450 metabolism of warfarin decreases its plasma concentration
Inhibition of CYP450 metabolism of warfarin increases its plasma concentration
Inhibition of CYP450 metabolism of warfarin decreases its plasma concentration
Induction of CYP450 metabolism of warfarin increases its plasma concentration
Inhibition of renal tubular secretion of warfarin decreases its elimination
questions.explanation:
Cimetidine is a classical CYP450 inhibitor, so it reduces warfarin clearance and increases plasma concentration and adverse effects such as bleeding.
Inducers would instead lower warfarin levels and effect.
CYP2C9 is the main enzyme for warfarin, and genetic variants add further risk.

questions.question: A tuberculosis patient receiving isoniazid develops paraesthesia and a generalised seizure. Which vitamin supplementation is most appropriate and what is its biochemical rationale?
questions.explanation:
Isoniazid forms hydrazones with pyridoxal and impairs pyridoxal phosphate formation, producing functional pyridoxine deficiency.
Pyridoxal phosphate is the coenzyme for decarboxylation, transamination and racemisation, and its deficiency causes convulsive seizures.
Supplementing pyridoxine therefore corrects neuropathy and seizure risk.
options: Folic acid, restoring tetrahydrofolate for methylation and one-carbon transfer
Thiamine, restoring thiamine pyrophosphate for decarboxylation and transketolation
Niacin, restoring NAD for dehydrogenation and hydride transfer
Cyanocobalamin, restoring methylcobalamin for isomerisation and methyl transfer
Pyridoxine, restoring pyridoxal phosphate for decarboxylation and transamination
Antidiuretic hormone, reducing aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting ducts
Atrial natriuretic peptide, reducing sodium excretion in collecting ducts
Aldosterone, reducing sodium reabsorption in distal tubules
Oxytocin, reducing myoepithelial contraction in mammary alveoli
Calcitonin, reducing calcium excretion in proximal tubules
questions.question: Bilateral destruction of the supraoptic nuclei after head trauma produces polyuria with very dilute urine. Which hormone deficiency explains this?
questions.explanation:
The supraoptic nuclei synthesise ADH, which is transported to the posterior pituitary and released into the blood.
Without ADH, V2 receptor signalling falls, aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted into the collecting duct, and dilute urine is passed in large volumes.
Oxytocin comes mainly from the paraventricular nuclei and does not control water excretion.

options: Impaired activation of fluorouracil decreases exposure and therapeutic efficacy
Impaired absorption of fluorouracil decreases exposure and severe toxicity
Enhanced catabolism of fluorouracil decreases exposure and therapeutic efficacy
Enhanced activation of fluorouracil increases exposure and therapeutic efficacy
Impaired catabolism of fluorouracil increases exposure and severe toxicity
questions.question: Why might dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency be dangerous when a patient receives fluorouracil?
questions.explanation:
DPD is the main catabolic enzyme for fluorouracil, and about one percent of the population has deficient activity.
Reduced breakdown increases drug effect and toxicity, such as severe mucositis and myelosuppression.
Identifying carriers allows dose reduction or alternative therapy.

questions.question: A man with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism wants fertility rather than only masculinisation. Which gonadotropin pairing correctly matches testicular targets?
questions.explanation:
In men LH is the principal stimulus for testosterone synthesis in Leydig cells, while FSH is the main regulator of spermatogenesis.
Testosterone alone relieves hypogonadal symptoms but does not restore sperm production, which needs FSH activity.
Gonadotropin therapy is therefore used when normal spermatogenesis is desired.
options: LH stimulates Leydig inhibin synthesis; FSH supports Sertoli testosterone production
FSH stimulates Leydig testosterone synthesis; LH supports Sertoli spermatogenesis
LH stimulates Sertoli testosterone synthesis; FSH supports Leydig spermatogenesis
FSH stimulates Leydig oestradiol synthesis; LH supports Sertoli spermatogenesis
LH stimulates Leydig testosterone synthesis; FSH supports Sertoli spermatogenesis

questions.question: In the coupling reaction within thyroglobulin, which pairing of iodotyrosines gives each principal thyroid hormone?
questions.explanation:
Two diiodotyrosine molecules couple to form tetraiodothyronine (T4), whereas one monoiodotyrosine and one diiodotyrosine give triiodothyronine (T3).
Both reactions are catalysed by thyroperoxidase within thyroglobulin.
This explains why T4, with four iodines, is the more abundant secreted product.
options: DIT with DIT gives triiodothyronine; MIT with DIT gives thyroxine
DIT with DIT gives thyroxine; MIT with DIT gives triiodothyronine
MIT with MIT gives triiodothyronine; DIT with MIT gives thyroxine
MIT with DIT gives reverse thyroxine; DIT with DIT gives monoiodothyronine
MIT with MIT gives thyroxine; DIT with DIT gives triiodothyronine

questions.explanation:
Calcitonin is a 32-amino acid peptide from the parafollicular C cells and acts as a physiological antagonist of PTH.
It blocks osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and decreases the calcium the kidney reabsorbs, thereby lowering serum calcium.
Its main stimulus is a rise in plasma calcium.
options: Stimulation of osteoblast apoptosis and increased intestinal calcium absorption
Inhibition of osteoclast activity and reduced renal calcium reabsorption
Inhibition of osteoblast activity and increased renal phosphate reabsorption
Stimulation of osteoclast activity and increased renal calcium reabsorption
Stimulation of calcitriol synthesis and increased intestinal calcium absorption
questions.question: Calcitonin is released when plasma calcium rises. Which pair of actions explains its calcium-lowering effect?

questions.explanation:
Acarbose competitively and reversibly inhibits brush border alpha-glucosidases, slowing carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption.
This decreases postprandial hyperglycaemia and does not cause hypoglycaemia when used alone.
Undigested carbohydrate reaches the colon, causing flatulence, diarrhoea and abdominal pain.
options: Repaglinide, a reversible inhibitor of intestinal brush border alpha-glucosidases
Acarbose, a reversible inhibitor of intestinal brush border alpha-glucosidases
Sitagliptin, a reversible inhibitor of intestinal brush border alpha-glucosidases
Acarbose, an irreversible inhibitor of pancreatic alpha-amylase secretion
Pioglitazone, an irreversible inhibitor of hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase
questions.question: After a high-carbohydrate meal, a diabetic patient's postprandial glucose spike is blunted by a tablet taken just before eating. Which drug and mechanism fit?

options: Pituitary tumour that secretes excess TSH and increases thyroxine secretion
Autoantibodies that destroy thyroglobulin and decrease thyroxine secretion
Autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor and increase thyroxine secretion
Autoantibodies that block the TSH receptor and decrease thyroxine secretion
Benign adenoma that autonomously secretes thyroxine without TSH stimulation
questions.explanation:
Graves disease, or diffuse toxic goitre, is the commonest form of hyperthyroidism and is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder.
Autoantibodies to the TSH receptor act as stimulants, driving thyroxine secretion, and TSH receptor-like proteins in orbital tissue are thought to cause exophthalmos.
Toxic nodular goitre arises from an adenoma and usually lacks exophthalmos.
questions.question: A woman has tachycardia, tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss and protruding eyeballs. Which mechanism underlies her hyperthyroidism?

questions.explanation:
CYP2D6 handles more than sixty drugs, including metoprolol, timolol, thioridazine, nortriptyline and clomipramine.
In poor metabolisers, decreased elimination of the parent drug leads to higher concentrations, increased cardiotoxicity and adverse events.
Dose reduction or alternative drugs are needed.
questions.question: A patient with a CYP2D6 poor metaboliser genotype is prescribed metoprolol and thioridazine. Which clinical outcome is most expected?
options: Decreased response from rapid conversion to inactive metabolites
Increased response from enhanced activation of the prodrugs
Increased adverse effects from reduced parent drug clearance
Unchanged exposure because alternative pathways fully compensate
Decreased adverse effects from enhanced renal excretion
Blockade of D2 receptors removes tonic somatostatin inhibition of lactotrophs
Blockade of D2 receptors removes tonic dopaminergic inhibition of lactotrophs
Stimulation of D2 receptors enhances thyrotropin releasing hormone drive to lactotrophs
Blockade of D1 receptors removes tonic dopaminergic inhibition of somatotrophs
Inhibition of tuberoinfundibular neurons enhances GHRH drive to lactotrophs
questions.explanation:
Prolactin secretion is under predominantly inhibitory control, with dopamine from tuberoinfundibular neurons acting on D2 receptors of lactotrophs.
Antipsychotics and some gastrointestinal motility drugs block these receptors, releasing prolactin secretion and producing hyperprolactinaemia.
The resulting hypogonadism explains amenorrhoea, infertility and galactorrhoea.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman started on haloperidol develops galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Which mechanism most directly explains the raised prolactin?

questions.explanation:
Common effects of exogenous progestins include headache, mood swings, breast tenderness, irregular menstrual cycles, weight gain and gastrointestinal upset.
Less common adverse effects include increased clotting, liver and heart problems and severe allergic reactions.
Mood effects relate to progesterone's influence on GABA neurotransmission.
options: Hypoglycaemia and hot flushes with hirsutism
questions.question: A woman using a progestin-only injectable for contraception asks about possible adverse effects. Which pair is most characteristic?

questions.explanation:
Meglitinides stimulate insulin release by blocking ATP-sensitive potassium channels, with peak effect in about an hour and duration of about four hours.
They are taken just before each meal and are specifically useful in patients allergic to sulfur or sulfonylureas.
Adverse effects are hypoglycaemia and weight gain.
questions.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes who is allergic to sulfonamide-containing drugs needs a rapid insulin secretagogue taken before meals. Which agent fits?
options: Glipizide, a sulfonylurea with slow onset and long action
Pioglitazone, a thiazolidinedione with slow onset and long action
Metformin, a biguanide with rapid onset and short action
Repaglinide, a meglitinide with rapid onset and short action
Acarbose, an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor with rapid onset and short action

questions.explanation:
Stilbestrol given to pregnant women increased the incidence of carcinoma of the cervix in their female offspring.
This is an example of transplacental carcinogenesis and a major reason oestrogens are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Other effects of oestrogens include irregular bleeding, gallstones and acceleration of breast cancer.
options: Clear cell carcinoma of the cervix
questions.question: Diethylstilbestrol exposure in utero is linked to a specific cancer in female offspring. Which one?
Danazol, a weak androgen, is chosen for a woman with endometriosis. Which pharmacological property supports its use?
questions.explanation:
Danazol is a weak androgen used in the treatment of endometriosis, where lowering oestrogen-driven endometrial activity is desirable.
It acts partly by suppressing gonadotropin secretion.
Its use in women is limited by androgenic adverse effects.
options: Blockade of aromatase enzyme that reduces peripheral oestrogen output
Activation of oestrogen receptors that increases endometrial growth
Stimulation of gonadotropin secretion that increases ovarian steroid output
Antagonism of oxytocin receptors that reduces uterine contractility
Suppression of gonadotropin secretion that reduces ovarian steroid output
The lactone carbonyl at carbon one, with pKa near four
The enolic hydroxyl at carbon two, with pKa near twelve
The enolic hydroxyl at carbon three, with pKa near four
The primary hydroxyl at carbon six, with pKa near fourteen
The secondary hydroxyl at carbon five, with pKa near twelve
questions.explanation:
Ascorbic acid is the enolic form of a 3-oxo-L-gulofuranolactone, and its enediol system makes the C3 hydroxyl strongly acidic with a pKa near 4.1.
The C2 hydroxyl is far weaker, with a pKa near 11.6, so the vitamin forms a monobasic salt such as sodium ascorbate.
This acidity explains carbon dioxide release with sodium bicarbonate.
questions.question: Ascorbic acid effervesces with sodium bicarbonate despite lacking a carboxyl group. Which structural feature is chiefly responsible for its acidity?

questions.explanation:
Sertoli cells secrete inhibins that, with testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, provide feedback inhibition of pituitary FSH secretion.
Activin has the opposite effect and stimulates FSH release.
LH stimulates testosterone production by Leydig cells, and high androgen levels suppress gonadotropins.
options: Activin and testosterone suppressing FSH and LH release
Testosterone and prolactin stimulating FSH and LH release
Activin and oestradiol stimulating FSH and LH release
Inhibin B and testosterone suppressing FSH and LH release
Inhibin B and activin stimulating FSH and LH release
questions.question: Which hormonal pair lowers testosterone production in men by negative feedback on the pituitary?
A 78-year-old diabetic patient with mild renal impairment needs a sulfonylurea. Which choice minimises the risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia?
questions.explanation:
Elderly patients and those with hepatic or renal disease are more prone to sulfonylurea hyperinsulinaemia and hypoglycaemia.
Tolbutamide is short acting with inactive metabolites and carries less hypoglycaemia risk.
Chlorpropamide lasts 20 to 60 hours, and acetohexamide forms active metabolites, so both increase the danger.
options: Glimepiride, a long-acting agent with active metabolites
Glibenclamide, a long-acting agent with active metabolites
Tolbutamide, a short-acting agent with inactive metabolites
Acetohexamide, an intermediate-acting agent with active metabolites
Chlorpropamide, a long-acting agent with inactive metabolites

questions.question: A pharmacist reviews injectable insulin preparations. Which pairing of insulin and duration category is correct?
questions.explanation:
Insulin crystal size and complexing with zinc or protamine determine absorption rate, so amorphous zinc insulin is quick while large crystals persist longer.
Isophane and lente are intermediate acting, whereas protamine zinc and extended zinc insulin (ultralente) are long acting.
Different absorption rates between preparations guide the choice of insulin regimen.
options: Protamine zinc insulin is rapid and short acting; lente is long acting
Isophane suspension is rapid and short acting; semilente is intermediate acting
Globin zinc insulin is long acting; ultralente is rapid and short acting
Semilente (amorphous zinc insulin) is rapid and short acting; ultralente is long acting
Semilente (amorphous zinc insulin) is long acting; ultralente is rapid and short acting
Beta-ionone, produced by acid hydrolysis of retinol
Retinal, produced by controlled oxidation of retinol
Dehydroretinol, produced by selective hydrogenation of retinal
Retinoic acid, produced by reduction of retinal
Retinyl palmitate, produced by esterification of retinol
questions.question: A child with night blindness responds to vitamin A therapy. Which vitamin A form directly participates in the visual pigment cycle that regulates dark adaptation?
questions.explanation:
Retinal (retinene) is formed from retinol by oxidation and combines with opsin to form the pigment that regulates eye adaptation.
Retinoic acid supports epithelial differentiation but cannot be reduced back to retinal, so it does not restore vision.
Retinyl esters are storage forms that must first be hydrolysed and then oxidised.

options: Intravenous glucose is rapidly metabolised by erythrocytes before reaching pancreatic islets
Gastrin, secretin and gastric inhibitory peptide augment beta-cell insulin release
Intravenous glucose is bound to plasma proteins and cannot enter beta cells
Intestinal glucose directly depolarises beta cells through portal vein diffusion
Oral glucose lowers somatostatin release and removes all inhibition of insulin
questions.question: A fixed glucose load raises plasma insulin more after drinking than after intravenous infusion. Which explanation accounts for this difference?
questions.explanation:
Glucose in the digestive tract releases gut hormones including gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin and gastric inhibitory peptide, and stimulates vagal activity.
These signals augment insulin secretion beyond the effect of circulating glucose alone.
Oral glucose is therefore a more effective stimulus than intravenous glucose.

Metformin is not metabolised or protein bound and is excreted unchanged in urine, so renal disease allows accumulation.
Renal, hepatic, cardiopulmonary disease and alcoholism predispose to lactic acidosis, which is why they are contraindications.
Pregnancy and conditions predisposing to hypoxia are also contraindications.
options: Lactic acidosis from accumulation of unmetabolised drug excreted by the kidney
Hypoglycaemia from accumulation of active metabolites excreted by the kidney
Hepatotoxicity from accumulation of unmetabolised drug excreted by the bile
