Ketoacidosis from accumulation of hepatic metabolites excreted by the bile
questions.question: A patient with renal failure and alcohol dependence is prescribed metformin. Which risk is most concerning?

questions.explanation:
Oestrogens raise the HDL to LDL ratio and stimulate hepatic synthesis of sex hormone-binding, thyroxine-binding and corticosteroid-binding globulins.
They also preserve bone mass, promote positive calcium balance and cause salt and water retention.
Increased binding globulins alter total hormone concentrations in tests.
questions.question: A 58-year-old woman begins oestrogen therapy for menopause. Which metabolic effects are expected?
options: Raised HDL, lowered LDL and increased SHBG, TBG and CBG
Raised HDL, raised LDL and decreased SHBG, TBG and CBG
Lowered HDL, lowered LDL and increased SHBG, TBG and CBG
Lowered HDL, raised LDL and decreased SHBG, TBG and CBG
Raised HDL, lowered LDL and decreased SHBG, TBG and CBG

questions.question: A surgical patient given succinylcholine remains apnoeic for several hours. Which genetic basis is most likely?
options: Variant thiopurine methyltransferase that methylates succinylcholine slowly
Variant pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) that hydrolyses succinylcholine slowly
Variant NAT2 that acetylates succinylcholine slowly
Variant CYP2D6 that hydroxylates succinylcholine slowly
Variant UGT1A1 that conjugates succinylcholine slowly
questions.explanation:
Succinylcholine is normally hydrolysed rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase).
Deficient or atypical enzyme variants prolong paralysis and increase the drug effect.
The variant is a phase I-type hydrolytic polymorphism and has been described in Europeans.

questions.question: A 38-year-old smoker with migraine with aura requests a combined oral contraceptive. Which advice is most appropriate?
options: Prescribe it, because migraine with aura and smoking over 35 lower thrombotic risk
Prescribe it, because migraine with aura and smoking over 35 raise fertility
Avoid it, because migraine with aura and smoking over 35 lower hormonal efficacy
Avoid it, because migraine with aura and smoking over 35 raise thrombotic risk
Avoid it, because migraine with aura and smoking over 35 raise infection risk
questions.explanation:
Contraindications to combined pills include thromboembolic disorders, cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, migraine with aura, breast cancer, severe liver disease and smoking in women over 35.
Oestrogen raises clotting tendency, so these factors compound stroke and thrombosis risk.
A progestin-only or non-hormonal method is safer.

questions.question: Which statement about progesterone production in the menstrual cycle and pregnancy is correct?
options: The adrenal cortex under LH makes it in the luteal phase; the ovary takes over in pregnancy
The corpus luteum under LH makes it in the luteal phase; the placenta takes over in pregnancy
The corpus luteum under FSH makes it in the follicular phase; the placenta takes over in menses
The granulosa cells under LH make it in the follicular phase; the placenta takes over at ovulation
The corpus luteum under TSH makes it in the luteal phase; the placenta takes over in menses
questions.explanation:
After ovulation the ruptured follicle forms the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone under LH stimulation.
During pregnancy the placenta becomes the main source, with significant production from about the eighth to tenth week.
The adrenal cortex produces only small amounts in both sexes.

Ganirelix and cetrorelix are synthetic peptides that competitively block GnRH receptors, lowering FSH and LH without an initial stimulation phase.
This prevents premature LH surges during ovarian hyperstimulation, and degarelix is approved for advanced prostate cancer.
All peptide GnRH analogues are contraindicated in pregnancy and can cause hypersensitivity reactions.
options: Goserelin, a competitive blocker of pituitary GnRH receptors
Clomiphene, a competitive blocker of hypothalamic dopamine receptors
Ganirelix, a competitive blocker of pituitary GnRH receptors
Leuprolide, a partial activator of pituitary GnRH receptors
Octreotide, a competitive blocker of pituitary somatostatin receptors
questions.question: During controlled ovarian hyperstimulation, an antagonist is added to prevent a premature LH surge. Which drug and mechanism is correct?

questions.explanation:
Steroidogenesis begins with CYP11A1 converting cholesterol to pregnenolone, then 3-beta HSD forms progesterone and CYP17A1 yields androgens.
Aromatase (CYP19A1) is the final enzyme, converting testosterone to oestradiol and androstenedione to oestrone.
17-Beta HSD interconverts oestrone and oestradiol.
options: 3-Beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converting testosterone to oestradiol and androstenedione to oestrone
Side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1) converting testosterone to oestradiol and androstenedione to oestrone
Aromatase (CYP19A1) converting testosterone to oestradiol and androstenedione to oestrone
17,20-Lyase (CYP17A1) converting testosterone to oestradiol and androstenedione to oestrone
Aromatase (CYP19A1) converting progesterone to oestradiol and pregnenolone to oestrone
questions.question: A student traces oestrogen biosynthesis from cholesterol. Which enzyme step finally converts androgens into oestrogens?

options: Coenzyme A and pantetheine, carrying acyl units during acylation
Pyridoxal phosphate and pyridoxamine, carrying amino groups in transamination
NAD and NADP, carrying hydride in biosynthetic pathways
FMN and FAD, carrying electrons in oxidative phosphorylation
Tetrahydrofolate and cobalamin, carrying one-carbon units in methylation
questions.explanation:
Riboflavin deficiency causes stomatitis, dermatitis, sore throat and alopecia.
Its phosphorylated forms, flavin mononucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide, serve as respiratory coenzymes cycling between flavoquinone and flavohydroquinone.
The other pairs belong to niacin, pantothenic acid, pyridoxine and folate or cobalamin.
questions.question: A patient with angular stomatitis, glossitis and seborrhoeic dermatitis improves with a vitamin whose phosphorylated derivatives serve respiratory enzymes. Which coenzyme forms are involved?

options: Interference with cytotoxic T lymphocyte sensitisation and antibody-forming cell generation
Blockade of calcineurin and interleukin-2 transcription within T cells
Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase and purine synthesis in lymphocytes
Enhancement of cytotoxic T lymphocyte sensitisation and antibody-forming cell generation
Increased antigen expression by grafted tissue and faster revascularisation
questions.explanation:
Glucocorticoids lower antigen expression of grafted tissue, delay revascularisation and interfere with sensitisation of cytotoxic T cells and with generation of primary antibody-forming cells.
These actions underlie their use in transplant rejection.
Calcineurin inhibition and antimetabolite effects belong to other immunosuppressants.
questions.question: A transplant patient receives high-dose methylprednisolone for acute rejection. Which mechanism contributes to this benefit?

questions.explanation:
Factors that inhibit insulin secretion include hypoxia, hypothermia and stimulation of alpha-2 adrenergic receptors on beta cells.
Stress-induced epinephrine acts on these alpha receptors, preserving blood glucose for energy supply.
Glucose, amino acids, keto acids and glucagon are stimulants of insulin release instead.
questions.question: A hypothermic patient with severe hypoxia is hyperglycaemic despite intact beta-cell mass. Which statement about insulin secretion explains this?
options: Hypoxia, hypothermia and amino acid infusion inhibit insulin secretion
Hypoxia, hypothermia and beta-2 adrenergic stimulation inhibit insulin secretion
Hypoxia and hypothermia stimulate insulin secretion through alpha-2 receptors
Hypoxia, hypothermia and vagal stimulation inhibit insulin secretion markedly
Hypoxia, hypothermia and alpha-2 adrenergic stimulation inhibit insulin secretion

questions.explanation:
Reduced clearance in poor metabolisers lengthens pharmacological effect and raises plasma levels, so adverse reactions and toxicity are more likely.
Prodrugs may not be activated, metabolism may shift to alternative deleterious pathways and drug-drug interactions are exacerbated.
Lower starting doses are often needed.
questions.question: Which list best summarises potential consequences of poor metaboliser status for a drug cleared mainly by the deficient enzyme?
options: Prolonged effect, adverse reactions, toxicity and exaggerated drug interactions
Prolonged effect, reduced reactions, toxicity and diminished drug interactions
Shortened effect, reduced reactions, subtherapeutic levels and diminished drug interactions
Prolonged effect, reduced reactions, subtherapeutic levels and exaggerated drug interactions
Shortened effect, adverse reactions, toxicity and diminished drug interactions
Peripheral neuropathy and hepatotoxicity from prolonged exposure to isoniazid
Therapeutic failure and relapse from subtherapeutic exposure to isoniazid
Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity from cumulative exposure to isoniazid
Haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia from oxidative exposure to isoniazid
Photosensitivity and phototoxicity from prolonged exposure to isoniazid
questions.explanation:
NAT2 acetylates isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide, dapsone and caffeine, and slow acetylators clear them poorly.
Prolonged exposure increases effect and toxicity, and pyridoxine is used to prevent neuropathy.
Rapid acetylators have the opposite risk of lower exposure.
questions.question: A tuberculosis patient who is a slow acetylator at NAT2 receives standard-dose isoniazid. Which risk is increased?
A 62-year-old patient taking metformin for twelve years has macrocytic anaemia and paraesthesia. Which adverse effect is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Long-term metformin therapy can interfere with vitamin B12 absorption, causing megaloblastic anaemia and neuropathy.
Other adverse effects include gastrointestinal disturbance, a metallic taste and, rarely, lactic acidosis.
Periodic B12 monitoring is therefore advisable.
options: Impaired vitamin K recycling from long-term metformin use
Impaired thiamine phosphorylation from long-term metformin use
Impaired iron absorption from long-term metformin use
Impaired folate synthesis from long-term metformin use
Impaired vitamin B12 absorption from long-term metformin use

questions.explanation:
Repeated injections into one site can cause lipohypertrophy, which alters absorption and blunts predictable control.
Rotation of injection sites prevents it, and other insulin adverse effects include hypoglycaemia, hypersensitivity and visual disturbances.
Mecasermin and insulin share the risk of hypoglycaemia and lipohypertrophy.
options: Lipoatrophy at the injection site causing complete insulin resistance
Anaphylaxis at the injection site causing delayed insulin absorption
Hypoglycaemia at the injection site causing uniform insulin absorption
Visual disturbance at the injection site causing enhanced insulin absorption
Lipohypertrophy at the injection site causing variable insulin absorption
questions.question: A patient who injects insulin repeatedly in the same abdominal site notices a soft swelling and erratic glucose control. Which adverse effect does this suggest?

questions.explanation:
Metformin does not require functioning beta cells and does not stimulate insulin secretion.
It inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis, increases peripheral glucose uptake, impairs intestinal glucose absorption and lowers plasma glucagon.
Because insulin is not stimulated it lacks hypoglycaemia and weight-gain risk and suits obese patients with insulin resistance.
options: Increased glucagon secretion and increased peripheral glucose utilisation without stimulating insulin release
Increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and decreased peripheral glucose utilisation while stimulating insulin release
Reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis and increased peripheral glucose utilisation without stimulating insulin release
Reduced intestinal glucose absorption and increased renal glucose excretion without stimulating insulin release
Reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis and increased peripheral glucose utilisation by stimulating insulin release
questions.question: A researcher asks how metformin lowers glucose without causing hyperinsulinaemia. Which combination of actions is correct?

options: A mutant aquaporin channel that fails to respond to antidiuretic hormone
A mutant G protein that fails to couple PTH receptor activation to cAMP generation
A mutant calcium sensing receptor that over-senses calcium on chief cells
A mutant vitamin D receptor that fails to bind calcitriol in the intestine
A mutant thyroglobulin that fails to release hormones from the colloid
questions.explanation:
In pseudohypoparathyroidism the target tissue responds poorly to PTH, so calcium falls and phosphate rises even though PTH is high.
The defect is a mutant G protein that couples PTH receptor activation to cAMP production in target cells.
This contrasts with idiopathic or surgical hypoparathyroidism, in which PTH itself is absent.
questions.question: Pseudohypoparathyroidism produces hypocalcaemia despite high circulating PTH. What is the underlying defect?
A biochemist explains why cholecalciferol is classified as a secosteroid rather than a conventional sterol. Which structural feature is responsible for this classification?
questions.explanation:
Vitamin D arises when ultraviolet light breaks the C9-C10 bond of the sterol B ring in 7-dehydrocholesterol or ergosterol.
The resulting 9,10-seco structure keeps rings A, C and D with an open triene system including double bonds at C5 and C7.
This opened-ring triene explains its UV absorption and its instability toward light and oxygen.
options: Methyl migration forming a quaternary centre at carbon ten
Aromatisation of ring A with loss of the carbon-three hydroxyl
Photochemical opening of ring B between carbons nine and ten
Hydrogenation of the side chain double bond at carbon twenty-two
Cleavage of ring C between carbons eleven and twelve

questions.explanation:
Both insulin chains arise from proinsulin, a prohormone, whose connecting peptide is removed to give mature insulin.
C-peptide is released in equimolar amounts, so its level reflects endogenous beta-cell secretion.
Amylin is co-secreted by beta cells but is a separate gene product.
options: C-peptide, the connecting peptide excised from proinsulin
Glucagon, the counter-regulatory peptide excised from proinsulin
Somatostatin, the inhibitory peptide excised from proinsulin
Amylin, the cosecreted peptide excised from proinsulin
Pancreatic polypeptide, the F-cell peptide excised from proinsulin
questions.question: Proinsulin is cleaved before secretion of insulin. Which product is released together with mature insulin and is useful as a marker of endogenous secretion?
During an insulin tolerance test for suspected growth hormone deficiency, hypoglycaemia is induced. Which physiological response should be seen in a healthy subject?
questions.explanation:
Hypoglycaemia, deep sleep, exercise, stress and arginine after a protein meal all stimulate GHRH and GH release.
Somatostatin and IGF-1 are the negative regulators that suppress GH secretion.
Failure of GH to rise after hypoglycaemia supports a diagnosis of growth hormone deficiency.
options: Increased TRH drive raising growth hormone secretion from thyrotrophs
Increased dopamine tone lowering growth hormone secretion from lactotrophs
Increased somatostatin tone lowering growth hormone secretion from somatotrophs
Increased IGF-1 feedback lowering growth hormone secretion from somatotrophs
Increased GHRH drive raising growth hormone secretion from somatotrophs

questions.question: Pegvisomant binds the GH receptor with higher affinity at the first site than at the second. How does this produce antagonism?
questions.explanation:
Pegvisomant, a PEGylated mutant GH (B2036), binds one site with increased affinity while the second site has reduced affinity.
This differential binding still allows dimerisation but blocks the conformational change required for signal transduction.
Pegylation also slows clearance and improves overall clinical effectiveness.
options: Receptor affinity for IGF-1 is lowered while GH binding is preserved
Receptor dimerisation proceeds but the conformational change for signalling is blocked
Receptor dimerisation proceeds and signalling is amplified by prolonged JAK2 activation
Receptor dimerisation is prevented and the receptor is internalised permanently
Receptor expression is downregulated at the gene level by STAT inhibition

questions.explanation:
Iodide uptake is an energy-dependent process against a concentration gradient, mediated by the Na+/I- symporter and pendrin.
Mutations in these transporters cause some thyroid disorders because iodide cannot be concentrated for hormone synthesis.
Later steps such as organification, coupling and release occur only after iodide has entered the follicular cell.
options: Deiodination of thyroxine within peripheral target tissues
Coupling of iodotyrosines within the thyroglobulin backbone
Active concentration of plasma iodide within follicular cells
Proteolysis of thyroglobulin within follicular cell lysosomes
Oxidation of iodide by thyroperoxidase within the colloid
questions.question: A patient with a mutation in the sodium-iodide symporter develops goitre. Which first step of thyroid hormone synthesis is directly impaired?

options: Competes with iodide for uptake but carries a risk of aplastic anaemia
Competes with iodide for oxidation but carries a risk of agranulocytosis
Blocks hormone release into blood but carries a risk of hypocalcaemia
Blocks thyroperoxidase irreversibly but carries a risk of hepatotoxicity
Inhibits peripheral deiodination but carries a risk of cardiac arrhythmia
questions.explanation:
Perchlorate, thiocyanate and pertechnetate compete with iodide for uptake through the symporter into follicular cells.
Their use is uncommon because of the potential for aplastic anaemia.
They act at the first step of synthesis, before organification.
questions.question: Perchlorate was once used in thyrotoxicosis but is now rarely used. Which property explains both its action and the reason for its decline?

options: Alkaline, above pH eight, with protection from air and light
Mildly acidic, near pH six, with protection from air
Weakly alkaline, near pH ten, with protection from light
Neutral, near pH seven, with protection from air and light
Acidic, below pH five, with protection from air and light
questions.question: A pharmacist is compounding a thiamine hydrochloride oral solution for infants with beriberi. Which pH condition will best preserve potency during storage?
questions.explanation:
Thiamine is stable in acid but unstable above pH five, where the thiazole ring opens and potency is lost.
Oxidising agents, reducing agents and aldehydes (forming inactive Schiff bases) also degrade it.
Storage in glass protected from light further preserves the product.

options: Activity peaks at three to four carbons, with loss of activity if the urea moiety is modified
Activity peaks at ten to twelve carbons, with retention of activity if the urea moiety is modified
Activity falls steadily as chain length rises, with loss of activity if the aryl group is added
Activity peaks at one to two carbons, with retention of activity if the aryl group is removed
Activity peaks at six to eight carbons, with increased activity if the urea moiety is cyclised
questions.question: A medicinal chemist designing sulfonylureas lengthens the N-alkyl group of the urea. Which statement describes the structure-activity relationship?
questions.explanation:
In first-generation sulfonylureas, maximum activity occurs when the alkyl group has three to four carbons.
The urea moiety is essential and modification causes loss of activity, and an aryl moiety is also important.
Chlorpropamide, with a chloro substituent and propyl chain, has increased potency and a longer action.

questions.question: Following a thyroidectomy in which the parathyroids were damaged, a patient has perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm and a prolonged QT interval. Which biochemical profile is expected?
options: Normal calcium with high phosphate and normal calcitriol
Low calcium with high phosphate and low calcitriol
Low calcium with low phosphate and high calcitriol
High calcium with high phosphate and low calcitriol
High calcium with low phosphate and high calcitriol
questions.explanation:
Absence of PTH reduces bone resorption, renal calcium retention and renal phosphate excretion, so serum calcium falls and phosphate rises.
Without PTH stimulation of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is usually low.
Symptoms include tetany, paraesthesias and cataract, and treatment is usually with vitamin D supplementation.

questions.question: An analyst oxidises thiamine with alkaline potassium ferricyanide and extracts the product into isobutanol for measurement under UV excitation. What is the measured species and signal?
options: Dehydroascorbic acid, which absorbs visible light near 520 nm
Indophenol, which absorbs visible light near 620 nm
Thiochrome, which emits blue fluorescence near 450 nm
Lumichrome, which emits yellow fluorescence near 520 nm
Cycloguanil, which absorbs ultraviolet light near 240 nm
questions.explanation:
Alkaline ferricyanide oxidises the thiamine system into thiochrome, a tricyclic compound.
Thiochrome fluoresces blue, with excitation near 360 nm and emission near 450 nm, enabling sensitive fluorometry.
The other species listed derive from riboflavin, proguanil or ascorbic acid and are irrelevant here.

The Carr-Price reaction forms a transient blue carbonium-ion complex between antimony trichloride and the conjugated polyene of retinol.
The medium must be anhydrous because water destroys the reagent and prevents colour formation.
The other reagents listed target niacin, thiamine or ascorbic acid and not vitamin A.
questions.question: During identity testing, an analyst adds a dry chloroform solution of an unknown oily yellow vitamin to a Lewis acid reagent and immediately obtains an intense blue colour that fades. Which reagent produced this result?
options: Antimony trichloride dissolved in dry chloroform
Ferric chloride dissolved in aqueous ethanol
Alkaline ferricyanide followed by isobutanol extraction
Cyanogen bromide followed by aromatic amine
Receptor dimerisation, JAK2 phosphorylation, STAT activation and IGF-1 gene transcription
Receptor monomer, IP3 generation, calcium release and calmodulin activation
Receptor dimerisation, PI3K activation, mTOR inhibition and protein degradation
Receptor internalisation, nuclear translocation, hormone response element binding and transcription
Receptor dimerisation, adenylyl cyclase activation, PKA phosphorylation and CREB transcription
questions.explanation:
GH receptors are cytokine-type receptors that dimerise on binding a single hormone molecule and recruit JAK2 tyrosine kinase.
JAK2 phosphorylates itself and the receptor, activating STAT proteins and MAP kinase to regulate gene expression such as IGF-1.
The anabolic and growth effects are largely mediated indirectly through IGF-1.
questions.question: A researcher traces how growth hormone binding produces gene expression. Which sequence best describes intracellular signalling after a single GH molecule engages its receptor?
Which clinical scenario illustrates a pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction by enzyme induction?
options: Ketoconazole lowering plasma levels of a CYP450 substrate drug
Erythromycin lowering plasma levels of a CYP450 substrate drug
Rifampicin lowering plasma levels of a CYP450 substrate drug
Cimetidine lowering plasma levels of a CYP450 substrate drug
Quinidine lowering plasma levels of a CYP450 substrate drug
questions.explanation:
Inducers such as barbiturates, rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine and cigarette smoke increase CYP450 enzyme activity and decrease plasma levels and effects of co-administered substrates.
Ketoconazole, cimetidine, erythromycin, clarithromycin and quinidine are inhibitors that raise substrate levels instead.
Direction of the interaction therefore depends on whether the perpetrator induces or inhibits.

options: Tocopherol, which supports hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
Retinol, which supports hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
Cholecalciferol, which supports hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
Ascorbic acid, which supports hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
Phytonadione, which supports hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
questions.question: A patient on warfarin develops epistaxis and an elevated prothrombin time after an antibiotic course. Which agent most directly restores synthesis of the depleted clotting factors?
questions.explanation:
Warfarin and other coumarins inhibit vitamin K-dependent synthesis of clotting factors in the liver, causing hypothrombinaemia.
Phytonadione (vitamin K1) restores production of these factors and is used when anticoagulant-induced bleeding occurs.
Other fat-soluble vitamins and ascorbic acid do not supply this cofactor activity.

questions.question: A woman at 30 weeks has regular preterm contractions and needs a tocolytic acting through the same receptor family that oxytocin uses. Which agent suits her?
questions.explanation:
Atosiban competitively blocks oxytocin receptors, decreasing uterine contractions in preterm labour.
It is given by IV infusion, and the rate of infant death noted in trials is a concern.
Oxytocin would worsen contractions, and GnRH or vasopressin agents have no tocolytic role.
options: Cetrorelix, a GnRH receptor antagonist given subcutaneously
Atosiban, an oxytocin receptor antagonist given intravenously
Goserelin, a GnRH receptor agonist given subcutaneously
Conivaptan, a vasopressin receptor antagonist given intravenously
Oxytocin, an oxytocin receptor agonist given intravenously

questions.question: A patient takes a pill containing desogestrel and ethinyl oestradiol. How are the progestins grouped by generation?
questions.explanation:
Third-generation progestins such as desogestrel, norgestimate and gestodene were developed to lessen androgenic side effects.
First-generation agents are norethindrone-type, second-generation include levonorgestrel and norgestrel, and fourth-generation include drospirenone, dienogest and nomegestrol acetate.
Drospirenone is related to spironolactone and has anti-androgenic properties.
options: Third generation, developed to reduce progestogenic effects while retaining androgenic activity
First generation, developed to reduce androgenic effects while retaining oestrogenic activity
Second generation, developed to increase androgenic effects while retaining progestogenic activity
Fourth generation, developed to increase oestrogenic effects while retaining anti-androgenic activity
Third generation, developed to reduce androgenic effects while retaining progestogenic activity

questions.explanation:
Sulfonylureas block ATP-sensitive potassium channels on pancreatic beta cells, depolarising the membrane and opening voltage-dependent calcium channels.
The rise in intracellular calcium triggers exocytosis of insulin.
They therefore need functioning beta cells and are ineffective in type 1 diabetes.
options: Opening of ATP-sensitive potassium channels leading to hyperpolarisation and calcium efflux
Closure of voltage-gated calcium channels leading to depolarisation and potassium influx
Inhibition of DPP-4 enzyme leading to incretin accumulation and calcium influx
Activation of PPAR-gamma receptors leading to transcription and glucose transporter synthesis
Closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels leading to depolarisation and calcium influx
questions.question: Sulfonylureas lower blood glucose only in patients with some functioning beta cells. Which molecular event explains their insulin-releasing effect?

options: Reduced oxidation of the parent prodrug, decreasing activation
Reduced glucuronidation of the active metabolite, increasing toxicity
Reduced methylation of the parent prodrug, decreasing activation
Enhanced glucuronidation of the active metabolite, decreasing toxicity
Enhanced acetylation of the active metabolite, increasing clearance
questions.explanation:
UGT1A1 is a phase II enzyme that conjugates the active metabolite of irinotecan, and the *28 allele reduces enzyme expression.
Impaired glucuronidation raises exposure to the toxic metabolite, increasing the risk of severe neutropenia and diarrhoea.
Dose reduction may be needed in affected patients.
questions.question: Patients with variant UGT1A1*28 receive irinotecan. Which outcome is anticipated?

options: Dihydrotestosterone, because bone effects of testosterone depend on 5-alpha reduction
Raloxifene, because bone effects of oestrogen depend on receptor antagonism
Oestradiol, because bone effects of testosterone depend on conversion to oestrogen
Growth hormone, because bone effects of testosterone depend on IGF-1 release
Testosterone, because bone effects of oestrogen depend on conversion to androgen
questions.question: A man with aromatase deficiency has tall stature, unfused epiphyses and osteoporosis. Which treatment would correct the bone abnormalities?
questions.explanation:
Epiphyseal fusion and bone density in men depend on testosterone being converted to oestradiol by aromatase (CYP19).
Oestradiol corrects the bone abnormalities in aromatase deficiency but not in patients with an oestrogen receptor defect.
Some effects of testosterone, such as libido, also appear to require this conversion.

options: Strong binding to thyroxine-binding globulin limits its metabolic clearance
Poor glomerular filtration prevents its metabolic clearance
Extensive storage in adipose tissue prevents its metabolic clearance
Rapid enterohepatic recirculation prevents its metabolic clearance
Complete resistance to deiodination prevents its metabolic clearance
questions.explanation:
Both hormones are carried mainly on thyroxine-binding globulin, and T4 binds it more tightly than T3.
Only free hormone is available for action, metabolism and clearance, so strong binding prolongs T4 persistence.
T3 is cleared about twenty times faster, which is why single daily dosing suits levothyroxine.
questions.question: T4 has a plasma half-life of about a week whereas T3 lasts one to two days. Which factor best explains the long half-life of T4?

questions.explanation:
Retinol is destabilised by oxygen, trace metals, light and acid-driven isomerisation, so a single measure leaves other pathways active.
Antioxidants such as tocopherol or hydroquinone, chelators and opaque or amber containers each block a separate route.
Esterified forms and a pH near 6 further improve stability, making the combined approach the most protective.
questions.question: A pharmacy intends to market retinol palmitate drops. The batch shows potency loss, darkening and isomer formation after storage in clear glass beside a window. Which strategy best counters the combined degradation routes?
options: Acidic pH adjustment with clear glass and oxygen headspace
Light-protective amber packaging alone without any additives present
Metal chelator alone with transparent plastic packaging retained
Antioxidant, metal chelator and light-protective amber packaging together
Antioxidant incorporation alone with clear glass packaging retained

questions.question: An analyst notes that a yellow fluorescent riboflavin solution loses colour and fluorescence after sodium hydrosulphite is added. Which product explains this observation?
questions.explanation:
Reducing agents such as sodium hydrosulphite convert riboflavin to leucoflavin, which has lost the conjugated chromophore and is non-fluorescent.
Lumiflavin and lumichrome result instead from irreversible photolysis in alkaline or neutral media and both remain fluorescent.
Flavoquinone is simply the oxidised form of the vitamin, and thiochrome is derived from thiamine.
options: Lumichrome, a fluorescent neutral photolysis product of riboflavin
Leucoflavin, a non-fluorescent reduced form of riboflavin
Flavoquinone, the fluorescent oxidised coenzyme form of riboflavin
Thiochrome, a blue fluorescent oxidation product of thiamine
Lumiflavin, a fluorescent alkaline photolysis product of riboflavin
CYP2C19 poor metaboliser phenotype with deficient conversion of codeine to morphine
NAT2 slow acetylator phenotype with deficient acetylation of codeine to morphine
CYP2C9 ultra-rapid metaboliser phenotype with excessive hydroxylation of codeine
CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser phenotype with excessive conversion of codeine to morphine
CYP2D6 poor metaboliser phenotype with deficient conversion of codeine to morphine
questions.question: A 62-year-old man given codeine 25 mg three times daily for cough lapses into coma on day four. Plasma morphine is 80 mcg/L (normal 1 to 4). Which genotype explains this?
questions.explanation:
The very high plasma morphine and its glucuronides after a small codeine dose indicate rapid O-demethylation by CYP2D6.
Genotyping confirms ultra-rapid metabolism, and morphine toxicity then produces respiratory depression and coma.
A poor metaboliser would have shown minimal morphine formation.

options: Reduced amoxicillin metabolism lowers antibiotic levels in variant carriers
Increased omeprazole metabolism raises acid-suppressing drug levels in variant carriers
Reduced omeprazole metabolism lowers acid-suppressing drug levels in variant carriers
Reduced omeprazole metabolism raises acid-suppressing drug levels in variant carriers
Increased amoxicillin metabolism raises antibiotic levels in variant carriers
questions.question: In H. pylori eradication using omeprazole 20 mg and amoxicillin, cure rate was 29 percent in CYP2C19 *1/*1, 60 percent in *1/*2 and 100 percent in *2/*2. What explains this trend?
questions.explanation:
Omeprazole is cleared by CYP2C19, so *2 alleles reduce clearance and give higher concentrations and greater acid suppression.
Greater acid suppression raises gastric pH, improves amoxicillin stability and efficacy, and increases cure rate.
Wild-type extensive metabolisers clear omeprazole quickly and have lower cure rates.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes the proguanil phenotyping probe for CYP2C19?
questions.explanation:
CYP2C19 converts the prophylactic antimalarial proguanil into the active metabolite cycloguanil.
The metabolic ratio is urinary recovery of proguanil divided by that of cycloguanil, and values above 10 classify poor metabolisers while below 10 indicate extensive metabolisers.
Proguanil may therefore serve as a phenotyping probe for CYP2C19.
options: Proguanil is converted to cycloguanil, and a urinary metabolic ratio above 10 indicates poor metabolisers
Proguanil is converted to chlorophenyl biguanide, and a ratio above 10 indicates extensive metabolisers
Proguanil is converted to cycloguanil, and a urinary metabolic ratio below 10 indicates poor metabolisers
Proguanil is converted to cycloguanil, and a plasma half-life above 10 hours indicates poor metabolisers
Cycloguanil is converted to proguanil, and a urinary metabolic ratio above 10 indicates poor metabolisers
Excessive effect of isoniazid at standard doses
Excessive warfarin and phenytoin effect at standard doses
Reduced activation of clopidogrel at standard doses
Reduced activation of codeine at standard doses
Excessive effect of succinylcholine at standard doses
questions.question: Which clinical drug problem is most closely linked to CYP2C9 variant alleles such as *2 and *3?
questions.explanation:
CYP2C9 metabolises phenytoin, warfarin and NSAIDs, so variant alleles lower clearance and increase drug effect.
Patients with *2/*3 genotype needed a mean phenytoin dose of 150 mg daily versus about 314 mg for *1/*1.
Warfarin dosing similarly needs reduction in carriers.

options: A hormone-free interval allows withdrawal bleeding while maintaining the daily habit
A hormone-rich interval allows withdrawal bleeding while maintaining the daily habit
A hormone-free interval allows fertilisation to occur while maintaining the daily habit
A hormone-free interval allows ovulation to occur while maintaining the daily habit
A hormone-free interval allows implantation to occur while maintaining the daily habit
questions.question: A woman asks about the structure of a 28-day pill pack with 21 active tablets. What is the purpose of the 7 inactive days?
questions.explanation:
The usual regimen is 21 days of active pills followed by seven inactive days, which may be placebo or iron tablets in a 28-day pack.
The fall in hormone levels during the break produces withdrawal bleeding.
Pills are taken at the same time daily, and a vomited pill should be replaced promptly.

options: Three methyl groups at positions five, six and seven
Two methyl groups at positions seven and eight
Two methyl groups at positions five and eight
Three methyl groups at positions five, seven and eight
A single methyl group at position eight only
questions.explanation:
Alpha-tocopherol is 5,7,8-trimethyltocol, whereas the beta, gamma and delta forms carry two, two and one ring methyl groups respectively.
A fully methylated ring gives the most effective antioxidant behaviour and the greatest vitamin E activity.
Alpha-tocopherol therefore shows the highest biological potency among the tocopherols.
questions.question: Four tocopherols differ only in the number of methyl groups on the aromatic ring of the chroman nucleus. Which pattern accounts for the highest biological activity of alpha-tocopherol?
A baby born to a mother who lived in an iodine-deficient region has a hoarse cry, large tongue, umbilical hernia and developmental delay. What is the diagnosis and its mechanism?
options: Graves disease from maternal autoantibodies stimulating the neonatal thyroid gland
Cretinism from congenital thyroid hormone deficiency impairing nervous system development
Pendred syndrome from isolated cochlear defects impairing auditory development
Acromegaly from excess neonatal growth hormone stimulating soft tissue growth
Thyroid storm from excess neonatal thyroxine stimulating hypermetabolism
questions.explanation:
Thyroid hormone is essential for growth and nervous system development during infancy.
Congenital deficiency causes cretinism, with gross growth retardation and mental deficiency, which is preventable by early detection and replacement.
Congenital hypothyroidism is the most prevalent endocrine disorder of the newborn.

Oestradiol (E2) is the most potent natural oestrogen, followed by oestrone (E1) and then oestriol (E3).
Synthetic examples include ethinyl oestradiol and diethylstilbestrol, and conjugated preparations such as Premarin are also used.
Oestradiol and oestrone are interconverted by 17-beta HSD.
questions.question: Natural oestrogens differ in potency. Which ranking from most to least potent is correct?
A clinician wants a diagnostic test for the pituitary reserve of somatotrophs. Which synthetic hypothalamic analogue is used for this assessment?
questions.explanation:
Sermorelin is an analogue of GHRH that stimulates somatotrophs, so the GH response indicates pituitary reserve.
Protirelin is synthetic TRH used to diagnose thyroid disorders, and gonadorelin is used to assess LH responsiveness.
Octreotide inhibits GH and so cannot test for secretory capacity.
options: Gonadorelin, a GnRH analogue for growth hormone secretion testing
Protirelin, a TRH analogue for growth hormone secretion testing
Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue for growth hormone secretion testing
Protirelin, a TRH analogue for diagnosis of thyroid disorders
Sermorelin, a GHRH analogue for growth hormone secretion testing

questions.question: Thyroperoxidase catalyses oxidation of iodide by hydrogen peroxide and incorporation of iodine into tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin. Which products result first?
questions.explanation:
Organification attaches iodine to tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin, giving 3-monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and 3,5-diiodotyrosine (DIT).
Coupling of these residues, also catalysed by thyroperoxidase, then forms the iodothyronines.
Thyroxine-binding globulin is a plasma carrier and is not generated inside the follicle.
options: Monoiodotyrosine and diiodotyrosine residues within thyroglobulin
Reverse triiodothyronine and thyroxine within plasma proteins
Monoiodothyronine and diiodothyronine within follicular colloid
Thyroxine-binding globulin and prealbumin within plasma
Triiodothyronine and thyroxine residues within thyroglobulin

questions.question: Mifepristone is classed as an antiprogestin. What is its mechanism and a main use?
options: Competitive progesterone receptor antagonism, used for termination of early pregnancy
Competitive oestrogen receptor antagonism, used for ovulation induction in infertility
Competitive progesterone receptor agonism, used for maintenance of pregnancy
Irreversible 5-alpha reductase inhibition, used for treatment of prostatism
Irreversible aromatase inhibition, used for treatment of breast carcinoma
questions.explanation:
Antiprogestins competitively block progesterone receptors; mifepristone and onapristone are norethisterone derivatives.
Uses include contraception, labour induction, endometriosis and breast cancer, and metabolism involves CYP3A4.
Its antagonism removes progesterone support of the uterus, favouring contractions.

questions.question: Native somatostatin is clinically impractical because it is cleared within minutes. Which property of octreotide solves this problem?
questions.explanation:
Somatostatin has a plasma half-life of only one to three minutes, limiting therapeutic benefit.
Octreotide is about forty-five times more potent at inhibiting GH, has a half-life near eighty minutes, and exists as long-acting monthly intramuscular suspensions.
It is not orally bioavailable, so it is given by subcutaneous or intramuscular injection.
options: Greater potency and half-life near eighty minutes enabling depot formulations
Equal potency and half-life near three minutes enabling nasal formulations
Greater potency and half-life near eight days enabling annual formulations
Greater lipophilicity and half-life near eight hours enabling oral formulations
Lower potency and half-life near eight minutes enabling infusion formulations

questions.question: A patient with acromegaly on pegvisomant has rising serum GH but resolving symptoms. Which biochemical marker should guide dose titration?
questions.explanation:
Pegvisomant is a pegylated mutant GH that blocks the GH receptor without lowering GH secretion, so GH concentrations may rise and tumour growth should be watched.
Because the drug acts at the receptor, IGF-1 output reflects true receptor blockade and is used for monitoring.
GH measurements are therefore misleading during therapy.
options: Serum TSH, because receptor blockade makes IGF-1 levels unreliable
Serum GH, because receptor blockade makes IGF-1 levels unreliable
Serum glucagon, because receptor blockade makes insulin levels unreliable
Serum prolactin, because receptor blockade makes GH levels unreliable
Serum IGF-1, because receptor blockade makes GH levels unreliable

questions.question: A hypoglycaemic patient taking acarbose plus insulin is treated with oral table sugar and does not improve, while glucose tablets work. Why?
questions.explanation:
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors prevent breakdown of oligosaccharides and disaccharides into monosaccharides in the small intestine.
Pure glucose needs no digestion, so glucose rather than sucrose should be used to treat hypoglycaemia in these patients.
Acarbose is poorly absorbed and is metabolised by intestinal bacteria.
options: Acarbose increases glucagon release and opposes the effect of oral sugar
Acarbose increases insulin release and opposes the effect of oral sugar
Acarbose blocks absorption of monosaccharides such as glucose through intestinal transporters
Acarbose blocks hydrolysis of disaccharides such as sucrose into absorbable monosaccharides
Acarbose destroys sucrose in the stomach before it can reach the small intestine

questions.question: A woman starts clomiphene 50 mg daily from cycle day five. Which monitoring approach and dose adjustment are standard?
questions.explanation:
The usual regimen is 50 mg orally for five days beginning on day five of the cycle, increasing to a maximum of 150 mg daily if ovulation does not occur.
Ovulation is assessed with predictor kits, basal temperature charts or ultrasound, and oestradiol and progesterone confirm response.
Conception generally occurs within four to six cycles, and ovarian enlargement and multiple pregnancy are risks.

Monitor ovulation and continue indefinitely without any dose change if ovulation fails
Monitor blood glucose and raise the dose up to 500 mg daily if ovulation fails

Normal external male genitalia but absent internal male genitalia
Absent internal and external male genitalia with female duct development
Female internal genitalia with male external genitalia development
Normal internal male genitalia but under-masculinised external genitalia
questions.question: A boy has a mutation that eliminates the enzyme converting testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. Which developmental outcome is most expected?
questions.explanation:
Testosterone from fetal testes stimulates nearby Wolffian ducts to form the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles.
Dihydrotestosterone is required locally for development of male external genitalia, so absent conversion leaves them under-masculinised.

questions.question: Nandrolone, oxandrolone and stanozolol are used in debilitating illness. Which therapeutic evidence statement is accurate?
questions.explanation:
Androgens and anabolic steroids have been used to reverse protein loss after trauma, surgery or immobilisation, but supporting evidence is poor unless hypogonadism is present.
Bisphosphonates have largely replaced androgens for osteoporosis, and recombinant erythropoietin has replaced them for refractory anaemias.
Their use now is therefore narrow.

Biotin, mannitol, glycine and sodium chloride are neither strongly reducing nor catalytic toward the cobalt centre.
questions.question: A hospital pharmacist prepares an injectable multivitamin mixture containing cyanocobalamin. Which co-formulated agent most threatens its stability through reducing or catalytic interactions?

questions.explanation:
Oxytocin activates uterine oxytocin receptors, producing contractions that induce labour and reduce postpartum bleeding.

Atosiban does the opposite, relaxing the uterus in preterm labour.
questions.question: A multiparous woman bleeds after delivery from uterine atony. Which drug acts on oxytocin receptors to contract the uterus, and what toxicity must be anticipated?
options: Oxytocin, with risk of water retention and uterine rupture
Conivaptan, with risk of infusion-site reaction and uterine rupture

Desmopressin, with risk of fetal distress and hypertension

Perchloric acid, titrating the basic group with crystal violet

Sodium hydroxide, neutralising the acid with phenolphthalein indicator

The indophenol dye is coloured in its oxidised state and is reduced by ascorbic acid to a colourless compound, giving a sharp visual end point even in natural extracts.
Iodimetric and iodometric methods are used in the BP and USP for purer materials.
Alkaline ferricyanide, cyanogen bromide, sodium hydroxide and perchloric acid serve assays of thiamine, niacin and amines.

questions.explanation:
Low to moderate oestrogen inhibits GnRH, FSH and LH, but the pre-ovulatory oestradiol surge produces positive feedback and an LH peak that induces ovulation.
After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes oestrogen and progesterone that restore negative feedback.
If no pregnancy occurs, their fall leads to menstruation.

Negative feedback by a sustained oestradiol peak on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
Positive feedback by a sustained oestradiol peak on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis

High glucose and insulin raise it; amino acids and stress lower it

questions.explanation:
Alpha cells respond to a high protein, low carbohydrate meal and to epinephrine acting on beta-adrenergic receptors by releasing glucagon.
Rising blood glucose and insulin inhibit glucagon release.
This pattern helps protect against hypoglycaemia during fasting or stress.
questions.question: Which factors raise glucagon secretion and which lower it?

Glucuronidation at carbon three, giving polar conjugates that hydrolyse slowly

Esterification at the 17-beta hydroxyl, giving lipophilic esters that hydrolyse slowly

Esterification of the 17-beta hydroxyl with propionate, enanthate or cypionate creates oil-soluble esters that release testosterone slowly after injection.
17-Alpha alkylation instead gives orally active drugs such as methyltestosterone.
Propionate is potent but short acting, so longer esters suit chronic therapy.
questions.question: A formulator wants a testosterone preparation with a prolonged intramuscular depot effect. Which modification achieves this?

questions.explanation:
Neutropenia and agranulocytosis are the most dangerous adverse effects of thioureylenes, although rare with incidence of roughly 0.1 to 1.2 percent.
Sore throat and fever are warning signs, and the effect is reversible once the drug is stopped.
Rashes, headache, nausea, jaundice and joint pain are more common but less dangerous.
questions.question: A patient on carbimazole develops fever and a severe sore throat three weeks into treatment. What is the immediate concern and action?
options: Aplastic anaemia; switch to perchlorate and obtain a reticulocyte count
Agranulocytosis; stop the drug and obtain a full blood count urgently
Hypothyroidism; increase the drug and obtain thyroid function tests
Hepatic failure; continue the drug and obtain liver enzymes next week
Allergic rash; continue the drug and add an antihistamine at night

questions.question: A patient with an aldosterone-secreting adenoma has muscle weakness, hypertension and metabolic alkalosis. How does aldosterone produce this pattern?
options: Sodium excretion with potassium loss and hydrogen ion retention in renal tubules
Sodium reabsorption with potassium and hydrogen ion loss in renal tubules
Sodium excretion with potassium and hydrogen ion retention in renal tubules
Sodium reabsorption with calcium loss and phosphate retention in renal tubules
Sodium reabsorption with potassium retention and bicarbonate loss in renal tubules
questions.explanation:
Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen secretion in the renal tubule.
Excess leads to potassium depletion, causing muscle weakness, and loss of hydrogen ions, causing metabolic alkalosis.
Lack of aldosterone produces the opposite picture of sodium loss, potassium retention, low volume and arrhythmia.

options: Roughly four percent of the activity of retinol
Essentially no activity until converted into retinoic acid
Roughly twice the biological activity of all-trans retinol
Roughly equal to the activity of all-trans retinol
Roughly forty percent of the activity of retinol
questions.explanation:
3,4-Dehydroretinol is vitamin A2, found in freshwater fish, and carries an extra double bond in the ring.
This modification lowers biological potency to about forty percent of that of retinol (vitamin A1).
Potency is therefore reduced but not abolished, so it is neither equivalent to retinol nor inactive.
questions.question: A freshwater fish liver oil rich in 3,4-dehydroretinol is compared with a marine liver oil rich in retinol for biological potency. What relative activity should be expected for the dehydro compound?

They thin cervical mucus, speed tubal motility and cause endometrial hyperplasia
They thin cervical mucus, slow tubal motility and cause endometrial hyperplasia
They thicken cervical mucus, slow tubal motility and cause endometrial atrophy
They thicken cervical mucus, speed tubal motility and cause endometrial hyperplasia
questions.question: How do progestins contribute to contraception beyond suppressing ovulation?
questions.explanation:
Progestins mainly suppress GnRH, FSH and LH to prevent ovulation, with norethindrone as a partial exception.
Secondary mechanisms include thickened cervical mucus that impedes sperm, impaired tubal motility and atrophic endometrium.
They convert the endometrium from proliferative to secretory.

questions.question: A fasting person has falling blood glucose. Which hormonal change maintains glycaemia by acting through a Gs-coupled receptor on hepatocytes?
options: Rising glucagon increases cAMP and PKA activity to drive glycogenolysis
Rising insulin increases cAMP and PKA activity to drive glycogen synthesis
Rising amylin decreases cAMP and PKA activity to drive glycogenolysis
Rising somatostatin increases cAMP and PKA activity to drive gluconeogenesis
Rising glucagon decreases cAMP and PKA activity to drive glycolysis
questions.explanation:
Glucagon is a 29-amino acid peptide that binds a Gs-coupled receptor, raising cAMP and protein kinase A activity.
It activates glycogen phosphorylase, inactivates glycogen synthase, increases phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase and activates lipases.
These effects raise hepatic glucose output and maintain glucose during fasting.

questions.question: Radioactive iodine-131 is selective for the thyroid even though its gamma emissions pass through tissue. What accounts for the selective destruction?
options: Accumulation via the symporter and short-range beta particles that destroy follicular cells
Accumulation via thyroglobulin binding and long-range beta particles that destroy colloid
Accumulation via TSH receptors and short-range gamma rays that destroy pituitary cells
Accumulation via pendrin and short-range alpha particles that destroy parathyroid cells
Accumulation via the symporter and long-range gamma rays that destroy follicular cells
questions.explanation:
The symporter cannot distinguish 131I from stable iodide, so the isotope is concentrated in the gland and incorporated into thyroglobulin.
Gamma rays pass through without damage, whereas beta particles travel a very short distance and exert a powerful cytotoxic action selective for follicular cells.
The effect is delayed by one to two months and hypothyroidism eventually requires replacement.

questions.question: A patient has low thyroxine and low TSH. After intravenous TRH, TSH rises briskly. At which level is the lesion most likely located?
options: Thyroid hormone receptor, causing peripheral resistance
questions.explanation:
Low thyroid hormone with low TSH indicates failure above the thyroid, because primary disease would give a high TSH.
A brisk TSH response to exogenous TRH shows that pituitary thyrotrophs are intact, placing the defect in the hypothalamus.
Secondary disease would show little or no TSH response to TRH.

Poor metabolisers form little morphine and so show decreased response, whereas ultra-rapid metabolisers form excessive morphine.

questions.question: A patient with confirmed CYP2D6 poor metaboliser status is prescribed codeine for post-operative pain and gains little relief. Why?

Without iodine, thyroid hormone synthesis falls and negative feedback on the pituitary weakens, so TSH secretion rises continuously.
TSH promotes growth and vascularisation of the gland, producing a goitre, which may be grossly enlarged.
The enlarged gland often maintains near-normal hormone output unless the iodine deficiency is severe.

Low hormone output reduces feedback, so lowered TRH drives hypertrophy and vascularity
High hormone output increases feedback, so lowered TSH drives atrophy and fibrosis
High hormone output increases feedback, so raised TSH drives hypertrophy and vascularity
Low hormone output reduces feedback, so raised ACTH drives hypertrophy and vascularity

questions.explanation:
Mecasermin mimics IGF-1 and bypasses a defective GH receptor, so it treats growth failure due to GH receptor mutations, IGF-1 gene defects or neutralising anti-GH antibodies.

Somatropin, recombinant human GH given in higher doses

questions.explanation:
Extensive metabolisers carry normal enzyme content, poor metabolisers have deficient content and ultra-rapid metabolisers have excessive content.
Intermediate metabolisers fall between extensive and poor groups.

questions.explanation:
Free tocopherol is readily oxidised, especially in alkaline conditions, because of its free phenolic hydroxyl at the six position.

questions.question: To distinguish Cushing syndrome from normal physiology, a low-dose dexamethasone test is performed. What result confirms Cushing syndrome?

No suppression of ACTH and cortisol after dexamethasone
Exaggerated rise of ACTH and cortisol after dexamethasone
Complete suppression of aldosterone and renin after dexamethasone

questions.question: Vasopressin raises blood pressure at high concentration but conserves water at low concentration. Which receptor-signalling pairing correctly describes these two effects?

V2 raises cAMP for water permeability; V1 uses IP3 for vasoconstriction

V1 raises cAMP for water permeability; V2 uses IP3 for vasoconstriction

questions.question: A woman treated with testosterone for breast cancer develops hirsutism, deep voice and clitoral enlargement. Which statement correctly explains this?

Androgens in women reproduce postmenopausal oestrogenic changes through oestrogen receptor activation

questions.question: A diabetic patient with New York Heart Association class III heart failure is considered for pioglitazone. What should the pharmacist advise?
