options: Agonist in breast tissue but antagonist in bone, uterus and liver
Partial agonist in breast tissue but antagonist in bone, uterus and liver
Antagonist in breast tissue but partial agonist in bone, uterus and liver
Agonist in breast tissue and agonist in bone, uterus and liver
Antagonist in breast tissue and antagonist in bone, uterus and liver

questions.question: Compared with first-generation agents, second-generation sulfonylureas offer which set of advantages?
questions.explanation:
Glipizide, glibenclamide and glimepiride are more potent than first-generation drugs, partly through bulky lipophilic aryl and alkyl groups.
They also have fewer adverse effects, fewer drug interactions and longer duration, allowing less frequent administration.
Glipizide is given in divided doses before meals whereas glibenclamide and glimepiride suit single daily doses.
options: Lower potency, fewer drug interactions and less frequent dosing
Greater potency, more drug interactions and more frequent dosing
Lower potency, more drug interactions and less frequent dosing
Greater potency, fewer drug interactions and more frequent dosing
Greater potency, fewer drug interactions and less frequent dosing

questions.question: A pregnant woman takes a long-acting sulfonylurea near term. Which neonatal complication is most likely, and why?
questions.explanation:
Sulfonylureas cross the placenta and stimulate fetal beta cells, which can cause neonatal hypoglycaemia at birth.
For this reason pregnancy and lactation are contraindications along with hepatic impairment, renal insufficiency and type 1 diabetes.
Insulin is the preferred agent in pregnancy.
options: Hypocalcaemia, because the drug crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal parathyroids
Hypoglycaemia, because the drug crosses the placenta and blocks fetal glucagon release
Hyperglycaemia, because the drug is excreted in milk and inhibits neonatal insulin
Hyperglycaemia, because the drug crosses the placenta and suppresses fetal beta cells
Hypoglycaemia, because the drug crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal beta cells

questions.explanation:
TPMT inactivates thiopurines, so deficient activity increases exposure to active cytotoxic metabolites and enhances drug effect and toxicity.
The poor-metaboliser phenotype affects about one in a hundred whites and far fewer Asians.
Genotyping or phenotyping before therapy permits dose reduction.
options: Deficient thiopurine S-methyltransferase activity causes accumulation of cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides
Excessive thiopurine S-methyltransferase activity causes accumulation of cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides
Deficient CYP2D6 activity causes accumulation of cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides
Deficient N-acetyltransferase activity causes accumulation of cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides
Excessive UGT1A1 activity causes accumulation of cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides
questions.question: A child with leukaemia starts standard-dose mercaptopurine and develops severe bone marrow suppression. Which pharmacogenetic explanation is most likely?

questions.explanation:
Megestrol acetate is used to manage cachexia and anorexia because it promotes appetite and weight gain.
It is also used in endometrial cancer, allowing young patients to maintain reproductive function.
Progestins in general may cause weight gain, headache, mood swings and breast tenderness.
questions.question: A cancer patient with cachexia and anorexia is given megestrol acetate. Which effect is intended?
options: Decreased appetite and weight loss through its anti-androgenic action
Increased gastric emptying and weight gain through its prokinetic action
Increased appetite and weight gain through its progestational action
Increased appetite and weight loss through its antioestrogenic action
Decreased appetite and weight gain through its mineralocorticoid action

questions.question: A patient with euvolaemic hyponatraemia from inappropriate ADH secretion needs a drug that promotes free water excretion. Which agent fits?
options: Desmopressin, an agonist preferentially acting at V2 receptors
Octreotide, an agonist at somatostatin receptors in pancreas
Conivaptan, an antagonist at V1 and V2 receptors
Oxytocin, an agonist at uterine and mammary receptors
Vasopressin, an agonist at V1 and V2 receptors
questions.explanation:
In SIADH excess V2 stimulation causes water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia.
Conivaptan blocks V1 and V2 receptors, reducing aquaporin-2 insertion and increasing free water excretion.
Vasopressin and desmopressin would worsen water retention, and infusion-site reaction is a notable toxicity of conivaptan.

options: It was more frequent in SCD patients than in non-SCD controls
It was equally frequent in SCD patients and in non-SCD controls
It was less frequent in SCD patients than in non-SCD controls
It was absent in both SCD patients and non-SCD controls
It was present only in SCD patients carrying the HbSS genotype
questions.explanation:
The CYP2C19 poor metaboliser genotype is less frequent in SCD patients (about 0.9 percent) than in controls (about 4.7 percent).
Genotype and phenotype were completely concordant.
The implication is a risk of proguanil prophylaxis failure in poor metabolisers, and the mechanism of apparent protection in SCD is unknown.
questions.question: Nigerian sickle cell disease (SCD) patients and non-SCD controls were genotyped for CYP2C19. What pattern of poor metaboliser status is observed?
A retired athlete who misused anabolic steroids presents with jaundice, hypertension, azoospermia, reduced HDL and aggression. Which statement is accurate about these drugs?
options: Anabolic steroids lack androgenic activity because dissociation is complete in humans and animals
Anabolic steroids increase gonadotropin secretion and thereby enlarge the testes
Anabolic steroids raise HDL and protect the liver because they are never 17-alkylated
Anabolic steroids retain significant androgenic activity because dissociation is weaker in humans
Anabolic steroids are cleared by renal excretion alone and never cause hepatic injury
questions.explanation:
Animal studies suggested the anabolic effects could be separated from androgenic effects, but in humans the dissociation is much less marked.
Supraphysiologic doses suppress gonadotropins, causing azoospermia and testicular atrophy, and alkylated agents cause hepatic dysfunction and lower HDL.
Behavioural effects include dependence, aggression and psychotic symptoms.

questions.question: A chemist notes that fludrocortisone has much stronger sodium-retaining than glucocorticoid action. Which structural features give it mineralocorticoid dominance?
options: A 6-alpha-methyl substituent on the progesterone skeleton
A 17-alpha-ethynyl substituent on the cortisol skeleton
A 17-beta-ester substituent on the testosterone skeleton
A 19-nor modification of the cortisol skeleton
A 9-alpha-fluoro substituent on the cortisol skeleton
questions.explanation:
Fludrocortisone is 9-fluorocortisol, and fluorination at C9 greatly enhances mineralocorticoid activity relative to cortisol.
It is the most frequently used mineralocorticoid for replacement therapy in Addison disease.
The other modifications listed belong to oestrogens, progestins and androgens.

options: One unsubstituted beta-ionone ring allows cleavage into a single retinal molecule
Terminal epsilon rings allow symmetrical cleavage into two retinal molecules
Absent ring structures allow direct hydrolysis into two retinol molecules
Two unsubstituted beta-ionone rings allow central cleavage into two retinal molecules
Two hydroxylated rings allow oxidative cleavage into two retinoic acids
questions.explanation:
Retinol corresponds to roughly half of the beta-carotene skeleton, so symmetric cleavage can theoretically yield two retinal units.
Carotenoids with only one beta ring, such as alpha-carotene or cryptoxanthin, give one retinal and are less potent.
In the gut this conversion occurs in vivo, whereas controlled oxidation achieves it in vitro.
questions.question: Among dietary carotenoids, beta-carotene is regarded as the most efficient provitamin A on a molar basis. Which structural reason best explains this?

questions.explanation:
Hypothalamic and anterior pituitary hormones are peptides or small proteins that gastric acid and proteases degrade.
Parenteral, subcutaneous and intranasal routes bypass this breakdown and deliver active drug to the circulation.
Oral dosing would therefore give negligible bioavailability.
questions.question: Desmopressin and leuprolide are given by nasal or injection routes rather than as ordinary tablets. What is the main pharmaceutical reason?
options: Rapid renal excretion prevents any absorption from the gastrointestinal tract
Strong acidity causes irreversible binding to dietary mineral salts
Large lipophilicity prevents dissolution within gastrointestinal fluids altogether
Peptide structure leads to extensive proteolysis in the gastrointestinal tract
Peptide structure leads to extensive first-pass sulphation in the intestinal wall

questions.explanation:
After thyroidectomy there is no thyroid tissue, so the whole requirement must come from the tablet.
In Hashimoto thyroiditis the thyroid retains some activity and contributes endogenous hormone.
Overdose of levothyroxine risks atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis and symptoms of hyperthyroidism.
questions.question: A woman who had a total thyroidectomy needs a levothyroxine dose higher than her friend with Hashimoto thyroiditis. Why?
options: Surgery increases hepatic deiodination and lowers T3 production permanently
Hashimoto disease increases TSH receptor stimulation and raises free hormone
Surgery increases thyroxine-binding globulin and lowers free hormone permanently
No residual gland activity remains to supply endogenous hormone
Residual gland activity increases endogenous hormone and deiodination

questions.question: Two days after an hCG trigger for controlled ovarian stimulation, a woman develops abdominal distension, ascites, haemoconcentration and dyspnoea. Which complication is most likely?
options: Ectopic pregnancy with tubal rupture and haemoperitoneum
Premature ovarian failure with hypoestrogenic vasomotor instability
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with intravascular fluid depletion
Polycystic ovary syndrome with insulin resistant hyperandrogenism
Hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea and secondary amenorrhoea
questions.explanation:
OHSS is a recognised complication of gonadotropin ovulation induction, with ovarian enlargement, intravascular depletion, ascites, liver dysfunction, pulmonary oedema and electrolyte imbalance.
Thromboembolic events may follow, and multiple pregnancy is another major risk.
Patients therefore need close monitoring and the lowest effective stimulation.

questions.question: A drug company compares ER-alpha and ER-beta distribution. Which pairing is accurate?
questions.explanation:
Both are nuclear hormone receptors, but ER-alpha mainly regulates growth and differentiation of breast and endometrial cells and is implicated in breast cancer.
ER-beta is found in ovary, prostate, brain and bone, where it modulates bone health, neuroprotection and immune responses.
Oestrogens act through genomic and non-genomic mechanisms.
options: ER-alpha predominates in uterus and breast; ER-beta occurs in pituitary only
ER-alpha predominates in prostate and brain; ER-beta occurs in uterus only
ER-alpha predominates in bone and brain; ER-beta occurs in uterus and breast
ER-alpha predominates in uterus and breast; ER-beta occurs in bone, brain and prostate
ER-alpha predominates in liver and kidney; ER-beta occurs in uterus and breast

questions.question: A researcher compares the adrenal cortex and medulla. Which statement correctly assigns products and control?
questions.explanation:
The cortex makes up about eighty percent of the gland and synthesises corticosteroids from cholesterol under anterior pituitary ACTH regulation.
The medulla, about twenty percent, releases epinephrine and norepinephrine in response to sympathetic stimulation.
ACTH mainly regulates cortisol and plays only a minor role in mineralocorticoid secretion.
options: The cortex secretes steroids under ACTH control; the medulla secretes catecholamines under sympathetic control
The cortex secretes catecholamines under ACTH control; the medulla secretes steroids under sympathetic control
The cortex secretes peptides under CRH control; the medulla secretes steroids under TSH control
The cortex secretes steroids under TSH control; the medulla secretes catecholamines under ACTH control
The cortex secretes catecholamines under sympathetic control; the medulla secretes steroids under ACTH control

questions.explanation:
Levothyroxine absorption is enhanced by an acidic gastric environment, so proton pump inhibitors and antacids lower it.
Caffeine also reduces absorption, which is why dosing 30 to 60 minutes before meals is advised.
Reduced absorption lowers circulating T4 and consequently TSH rises, signalling inadequate replacement.
questions.question: A patient on stable levothyroxine starts taking an antacid and an iron supplement together with the morning dose, and TSH rises. What is the likely explanation?
options: Reduced absorption because acid is needed for uptake and cations bind the drug
Increased hepatic metabolism because antacids induce deiodinase activity throughout the liver
Increased absorption because levothyroxine absorption needs alkaline conditions and is released by cations
Reduced receptor binding because iron blocks nuclear thyroid hormone receptors in tissues
Reduced renal clearance because iron saturates thyroxine-binding globulin in plasma

questions.explanation:
Desmopressin is a V2-preferring agonist, so it reduces water excretion with far less vasoconstriction than vasopressin.
This makes it useful in diabetes insipidus and as a bed-wetting remedy for children.
It is given orally, intranasally or by IV or SC injection, and toxicity is mostly gastrointestinal disturbance and headache.
options: Dual V1 and V2 antagonism with minimal renal impact
Selective V1 agonism with minimal V2-mediated antidiuresis
Selective oxytocin receptor agonism with minimal uterine stimulation
Selective V2 agonism with minimal V1-mediated vasoconstriction
Selective V2 antagonism with minimal V1-mediated vasoconstriction
questions.question: A 7-year-old with persistent nocturnal enuresis is prescribed an intranasal vasopressin analogue to avoid pressor effects. Which property of desmopressin justifies the choice?

options: Ligand-independent receptor activity; adrenal androgen synthesis inhibitors such as abiraterone
Ligand-dependent receptor activity; aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole
Ligand-dependent receptor loss; oestrogen receptor modulators such as tamoxifen
Ligand-independent receptor loss; 5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride
Ligand-independent receptor activity; GnRH agonists such as leuprolide
questions.question: A 64-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer initially responds to androgen deprivation, then relapses with persistent androgen receptor signalling. Which mechanism and treatment are described?
questions.explanation:
Androgen receptor mutations or altered coregulators can make signalling ligand independent, so tumours become resistant to androgen deprivation.
Some such tumours respond to further depletion of androgens by inhibitors of adrenal androgen synthesis, such as abiraterone.
The receptor remains expressed and active in androgen-independent prostate cancer.

options: Humans reduce folate with dihydrofolate reductase, which sulphonamides inhibit selectively
Humans build folate from PABA, which sulphonamides mimic competitively
Micro-organisms build folate from PABA, which sulphonamides mimic competitively
Micro-organisms build folate from glutamate, which sulphonamides mimic competitively
Micro-organisms build folate from pteridine, which sulphonamides destroy irreversibly
questions.question: Sulphonamides kill bacteria that must synthesise folate but spare patients who rely on dietary folate. Which statement best accounts for this selective toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Folic acid contains pteridine, p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) and glutamic acid moieties, and bacteria assemble it from PABA.
Sulphonamides are structural analogues of PABA and compete for the bacterial enzyme, whereas humans cannot synthesise folate and obtain it from diet.
Human dihydrofolate reductase reduces folate to active tetrahydrofolate and is not the sulphonamide target.

options: Intracranial hypertension with slipped epiphysis and peripheral oedema
Gynaecomastia with scoliosis and carpal tunnel syndrome
Hypoglycaemia with lipohypertrophy and injection site reactions
Biliary sludge with gallstones and cardiac conduction disturbance
Hypogonadism with hot flushes and reduced libido
questions.explanation:
Octreotide frequently causes gastrointestinal upset, steatorrhoea, biliary sludge and gallstones after about six months, as well as sinus bradycardia and conduction disturbances.
The other clusters of effects belong to recombinant GH, mecasermin or GnRH agonist therapy.
Patients on long-term octreotide therefore need gallbladder and cardiac monitoring.
questions.question: After eight months of octreotide therapy for acromegaly, a patient has right upper quadrant colic and sinus bradycardia. Which adverse effects are most consistent?
An exam question asks which structural change in the progesterone A ring would lose progestational activity. Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation:
Progestational activity requires the 4-ene-3-one moiety, and moving the double bond to C5 abolishes it.
Replacing the 3-keto group with hydroxyl can retain activity, and 17-alpha hydroxylation or 6-alpha methylation enhances activity.
Only one oxygen function is required.
options: Introducing a 17-alpha hydroxyl group on the side chain
Replacing the 3-keto group with a 3-hydroxyl group
Introducing a methyl group at the carbon six alpha position
Shifting the double bond from carbon four to carbon five
Retaining a single oxygen function at carbon three or 17
Pituitary adenoma causing secondary hypothyroidism with low TSH
Toxic nodular goitre causing primary hyperthyroidism without exophthalmos
Graves disease causing primary hyperthyroidism with exophthalmos
Hashimoto thyroiditis causing primary hypothyroidism with myxoedema
Simple non-toxic goitre causing euthyroidism with normal antibodies
questions.question: A woman has fatigue, cold intolerance, bradycardia, hoarse voice, goitre and thickened skin. Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are strongly positive. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation:
Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune reaction against thyroglobulin or other thyroid components and is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate.
Myxoedema reflects subcutaneous deposition of glycosaminoglycans, and features include low metabolic rate, lethargy and bradycardia.
Fertility is reduced and miscarriage is more frequent.

questions.question: A man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is prescribed finasteride. Which enzymatic step is targeted?
questions.explanation:
In prostatic cells testosterone is converted by 5-alpha reductase II to dihydrotestosterone, the dominant androgen in these tissues.
This conversion mediates benign prostatic hyperplasia, so inhibiting the enzyme shrinks prostate tissue.
Dihydrotestosterone also drives development of the male external genitalia in the fetus.
options: 17-Beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, which converts androstenedione to testosterone
Aromatase, which converts testosterone to oestradiol
11-Beta hydroxylase, which converts deoxycortisol to cortisol
5-Alpha reductase type II, which converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
17-Alpha hydroxylase, which converts progesterone to hydroxyprogesterone

questions.explanation:
Oestrogen maintains bone mass by restraining osteoclast maturation and activity and by increasing expression of bone matrix proteins.
It also induces renal hydroxylase, generating active vitamin D3, and promotes positive calcium balance.
When oestrogen falls at menopause, resorption outpaces formation.
questions.question: A postmenopausal woman asks why her osteoporosis risk rose after menopause. Which oestrogen action is relevant?
options: Oestrogen increases osteoclast maturation and activity by modifying osteoblast-derived cytokines
Oestrogen reduces osteoclast maturation and activity by modifying osteoblast-derived cytokines
Oestrogen increases parathyroid hormone release and promotes renal calcium excretion
Oestrogen reduces osteoblast maturation and activity by modifying osteoclast-derived cytokines
Oestrogen reduces vitamin D activation by inhibiting renal hydroxylase enzyme activity
CRH from the hypothalamus stimulates TSH, which stimulates cortisol secretion
CRH from the hypothalamus stimulates ACTH, which stimulates cortisol secretion
CRH from the hypothalamus stimulates prolactin, which stimulates cortisol secretion
GnRH from the hypothalamus stimulates ACTH, which stimulates aldosterone secretion
TRH from the hypothalamus stimulates ACTH, which stimulates cortisol secretion
questions.question: Which statement correctly pairs a hormone with the hypothalamic factor and anterior pituitary hormone that regulate the adrenal cortex?
questions.explanation:
Corticotroph cells are stimulated by CRH and secrete ACTH, which acts on the adrenal cortex to regulate cortisol and adrenal androgens.
Physical or mental stress increases ACTH and therefore glucocorticoid secretion.
No inhibitory hypothalamic factor is known for corticotrophs.

options: Quinagolide, a selective non-ergot D2 receptor agonist
Haloperidol, a selective non-ergot D2 receptor antagonist
Bromocriptine, a short-acting ergot D2 receptor agonist
Pergolide, a mixed ergot D1 and D2 agonist
Cabergoline, a long-acting ergot D2 receptor agonist
questions.question: A patient with hyperprolactinaemia cannot tolerate ergot-derived dopamine agonists because of vasospasm. Which alternative belongs to the non-ergot group?
questions.explanation:
Dopamine agonists are first-line for hyperprolactinaemia and are classified into ergot derivatives (bromocriptine, pergolide, cabergoline) and non-ergot derivatives (quinagolide).
They lower circulating prolactin, shrink prolactin-secreting tumours and restore ovulation.
Haloperidol is a dopamine antagonist and would raise prolactin.

options: Decreased lipolysis from adipose tissue inhibition and increased peripheral glucose utilisation
Decreased gluconeogenesis from muscle protein anabolism and increased peripheral glucose utilisation
Increased insulin secretion from beta cell stimulation and reduced hepatic glucose output
Increased glycogen synthesis from muscle glucose uptake and reduced hepatic glucose output
Increased gluconeogenesis from muscle protein catabolism and reduced peripheral glucose utilisation
questions.question: Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose and are described as having anti-insulin action. Which combination of effects best accounts for hyperglycaemia?
questions.explanation:
Glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis and raise muscle protein catabolism, supplying amino acid substrates for new glucose.
They also oppose insulin action peripherally and mobilise and redistribute fat.
Chronic excess therefore produces diabetes, myopathy, central obesity and osteoporosis.

Dopamine continuously restrains lactotrophs, so interrupting delivery of hypothalamic dopamine to the pituitary raises prolactin.
This is unique among anterior pituitary hormones, whose secretion is mainly stimulated by releasing hormones.
It is also why dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine lower prolactin.
questions.question: Unlike most anterior pituitary hormones, prolactin rises when the hypothalamic connection to the pituitary is interrupted by a stalk lesion. Which regulatory principle explains this?
options: Hypothalamic control of prolactin is predominantly inhibitory rather than stimulatory
Hypothalamic control of prolactin is exclusively mediated by growth hormone
Hypothalamic control of prolactin is predominantly stimulatory rather than inhibitory
Prolactin secretion depends mainly on negative feedback from IGF-1
Prolactin secretion depends mainly on thyroid hormone inhibition of lactotrophs

questions.explanation:
High doses of iodide inhibit secretion of thyroid hormones, and symptoms subside within one to two days.
Over ten to fourteen days the gland becomes smaller, firmer and less vascular, which is useful before surgery.
The effect peaks in ten to fifteen days and then wanes, so it is used short term.
options: Enhanced iodination of thyroglobulin with increased gland vascularity
Permanent destruction of follicular cells with delayed hypothyroidism
Blocked peripheral deiodination with reduced circulating triiodothyronine
Competitive inhibition of iodide uptake with enlarged gland firmness
Temporary inhibition of hormone release and reduced gland vascularity
questions.question: A hyperthyroid patient is given a high dose of oral iodine solution before thyroidectomy. Which effect results?
Why is diazepam half-life about 20 hours in CYP2C19 *1/*1 individuals but about 84 hours in *2/*2 individuals?
options: The *2 allele encodes a defective receptor, so distribution is greatly reduced
The *1 allele encodes a defective enzyme, so clearance is greatly reduced
The *2 allele encodes a defective enzyme, so clearance is greatly reduced
The *2 allele encodes an overactive enzyme, so clearance is greatly increased
The *2 allele encodes a defective transporter, so absorption is greatly reduced
questions.explanation:
CYP2C19 metabolises diazepam, and homozygous *2/*2 carriers are poor metabolisers with a much longer half-life.
Asians have a high frequency of mutant CYP2C19 alleles, explaining slower diazepam metabolism than in Caucasians.
Extended sedation is the clinical risk.

questions.question: A pregnant woman with Graves disease needs treatment. Which choice is most appropriate and why?
options: Perchlorate, because radioiodine would damage the fetal thyroid
Potassium iodide alone, because radioiodine would damage the fetal liver
A thioureylene drug, because radioiodine would damage the fetal thyroid
Radioiodine, because thioureylenes would damage the fetal thyroid
Levothyroxine, because thioureylenes would damage the fetal thyroid
questions.explanation:
Thioureylene antithyroid drugs are drugs of choice in children, pregnant women and adults with milder Graves disease.
Radioiodine is best avoided in pregnancy and in children because of potential damage to the fetus.
Propylthiouracil crosses the placenta and enters milk less than methimazole because it is more strongly protein bound.

questions.question: Parathyroid hormone is produced from a precursor with a stepwise cleavage. Which fragment carries full biological activity?
options: The pre-sequence fragment spanning residues minus twenty-five to minus one
The pro-sequence fragment spanning residues minus six to minus one
The mid-region fragment spanning residues thirty-five to fifty
The amino-terminal fragment spanning residues one to thirty-four
The carboxy-terminal fragment spanning residues fifty to eighty-four
questions.explanation:
PTH is cleaved from preproparathyroid hormone (115 residues) to proparathyroid hormone (90) and then to the mature 84-amino acid hormone.
Biological activity resides in the amino-terminal region, so synthetic PTH 1-34 is fully active.
Loss of the first two terminal amino acids eliminates most biological effect.

questions.question: A formulation scientist examines the androgen SAR. Which feature is required for androgenic activity?
options: A 17-alpha side chain with a methyl group at carbon 19 retained
A 17-beta hydroxyl group with trans fusion of rings A and B
A 17-alpha hydroxyl group with cis fusion of rings A and B
A 3-hydroxyl group in beta orientation with a saturated ring B
An aromatic A ring with a 17-keto group and loss of carbon 18
questions.explanation:
Androgens need a 17-beta oxygen function for receptor binding, and oxidation of the hydroxyl to a carbonyl decreases activity.
Rings A and B must be trans, and unsaturated compounds show maximum activity.
17-Alpha methylation, by contrast, gives oral stability.

questions.question: A Nigerian pharmacist interprets a CYP2C19 genotype table. Which genotype corresponds to the poor metaboliser phenotype?
questions.explanation:
Homozygous inheritance of the defective *2 allele leaves no functional CYP2C19, giving the poor metaboliser phenotype.
*1/*1 individuals are extensive metabolisers and *1/*2 heterozygotes are generally extensive or intermediate.
Nigerian *2/*2 subjects also show high metabolic ratios, confirming the genotype-phenotype link.

questions.question: Antithyroid drugs normalise thyroid hormone levels in Graves disease, yet a patient's eye protrusion persists. What explains this?
questions.explanation:
Antithyroid drugs control hormone production but do not alter the autoimmune mechanisms or improve the exophthalmos of Graves disease.
Severe exophthalmia may need glucocorticoids or surgical decompression, while guanethidine eye drops relieve eyelid retraction.
Control of thyroid function therefore does not guarantee eye improvement.
options: Antithyroid drugs worsen the underlying autoimmune orbital process directly
Antithyroid drugs lower TSH so far that orbital tissue becomes hyperstimulated
Antithyroid drugs increase iodide uptake so orbital tissue becomes overloaded
Antithyroid drugs do not alter the underlying autoimmune orbital process
Antithyroid drugs cannot cross into orbital tissue because of protein binding

questions.question: Natural progesterone is poorly effective orally, so clinicians use synthetic progestins. Which explanation is best?
questions.explanation:
Progesterone is metabolised rapidly to 5-beta-pregnane-3-alpha,20-diol and conjugated as glucuronides and sulphates.
Structural modification such as 17-alpha ethinyl or 6-methyl groups lowers first-pass metabolism and enhances oral activity.
Natural progesterone is therefore given in oil intramuscularly or in other non-oral forms.
options: Rapid renal excretion without metabolism limits systemic availability of the natural hormone
Slow hepatic metabolism and conjugation limit systemic availability of the natural hormone
Rapid hepatic metabolism and conjugation limit systemic availability of the natural hormone
Poor intestinal absorption without metabolism limits systemic availability of the natural hormone
Rapid plasma esterase hydrolysis limits systemic availability of the natural hormone

questions.question: Medicinal chemists modify the phytonadione nucleus while retaining the side chain. Which modification would most likely diminish antihaemorrhagic activity?
questions.explanation:
Antihaemorrhagic activity requires an unsubstituted aromatic or hydroaromatic ring A, and extra methyl groups reduce potency.
Potency rises with side-chain length up to about twenty to thirty carbons, and unsaturation at C2 enhances function.
The positive isomers are far more active than the negative ones, so only ring A methylation is detrimental here.
options: Using the dextrorotatory stereoisomer of the isoprenoid side chain
Substituting methyl groups onto the unsubstituted aromatic ring A
Maintaining unsaturation at carbon two of the quinone ring
Using an isoprenoid side chain of twenty to thirty carbons
Retaining the unsubstituted ring A within the naphthoquinone nucleus

questions.question: A 60-year-old poor metaboliser at CYP2D6 receives nortriptyline at the usual dose of 150 mg daily and develops arrhythmia and confusion. What would be a more suitable starting dose?
questions.explanation:
CYP2D6 poor metabolisers clear tricyclic antidepressants slowly, so exposure is much higher at a given dose.
Mutant CYP2D6 individuals need approximately 10 to 20 mg daily compared with about 150 mg daily for normal enzyme function.
Toxicity also rises with other substrates such as metoprolol, venlafaxine and thioridazine.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with a prolactinoma starts bromocriptine. Why is therapy initiated at 1.25 mg at bedtime and titrated slowly?
questions.explanation:
Bromocriptine is an ergot D2 agonist whose common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, lightheadedness, orthostatic hypotension and fatigue.
Starting at 1.25 mg, increasing every few days and giving the dose at bedtime reduces these effects.
Less often it causes nasal congestion, digital vasospasm and CNS effects such as hallucinations or nightmares.
options: To prevent hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis and weight gain from insulin stimulation
To avoid agranulocytosis, sore throat and rashes from thioamide hypersensitivity
To maximise first-pass bioavailability, because only seven percent reaches circulation
To minimise orthostatic hypotension, nausea and lightheadedness from dopaminergic stimulation
To minimise hepatotoxicity, jaundice and cholestasis from ergot metabolite accumulation

questions.explanation:
A 17-alpha alkyl group blocks rapid oxidation of the 17-hydroxyl and so confers oral stability.
Most oral androgens and anabolic agents are 17-alkyl steroids, and hepatic dysfunction, cholestatic jaundice, peliosis hepatis and tumours may occur.
The jaundice is reversible on stopping the drug.
questions.question: Methyltestosterone is active by mouth whereas testosterone is not. Which structural change explains this and what is its major risk?
options: 17-Alpha methylation promotes hepatic oxidation but carries a risk of nephrotoxicity
17-Alpha methylation hinders hepatic oxidation but carries a risk of cholestatic jaundice
19-Nor modification promotes hepatic oxidation but carries a risk of cholestatic jaundice
11-Beta hydroxylation hinders hepatic oxidation but carries a risk of hypocalcaemia
17-Beta esterification hinders hepatic oxidation but carries a risk of cholestatic jaundice

questions.explanation: Diabetes complications result from multiple mechanisms: hyperglycemia directly damages vessels; aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol (accumulating in nerve, lens, kidney); advanced glycation end-products modify proteins; and oxidative stress injures tissues. Strict glycemic control prevents or delays complications by addressing the root cause.
questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency causes type 1 diabetes complications?

questions.explanation: Hexosaminidase A deficiency prevents GM2 ganglioside degradation, causing accumulation in neurons and progressive neurodegeneration. This autosomal recessive disorder causes developmental regression, blindness, seizures, and early death. Carrier screening reduces disease incidence in high-risk populations.
questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease?
What enzyme deficiency causes lactose intolerance?
questions.explanation: Lactase (lactase-phlorizin hydrolase) cleaves lactose into glucose and galactose in intestinal brush borders. Primary lactase deficiency develops in most humans after weaning, causing lactose intolerance symptoms. Undigested lactose draws water into the intestine osmotically and undergoes bacterial fermentation producing gas.

questions.question: Which technique cleaves DNA at specific recognition sequences?
questions.explanation: Restriction endonucleases recognize specific palindromic sequences (4-8 base pairs), cleaving DNA to generate defined fragments. These bacterial enzymes defend against bacteriophages while methylation protects host DNA. Restriction enzymes are fundamental tools for molecular cloning and DNA analysis.

Epinephrine activates β-adrenergic receptors on adipocytes, stimulating cAMP production and hormone-sensitive lipase activation. This mobilizes fatty acids from triacylglycerol stores for oxidation in other tissues. Epinephrine's lipolytic action supports energy provision during stress or exercise.
questions.question: Which hormone promotes lipolysis in adipose tissue during fasting?

questions.explanation: Marasmus results from severe total energy and protein deficiency, causing extreme wasting of muscle and fat stores. Unlike kwashiorkor, there's no edema because adaptation maintains albumin synthesis. Children appear "skin and bones." Metabolism adapts to starvation with decreased basal metabolic rate and growth arrest. Treatment requires gradual refeeding to avoid refeeding syndrome.
questions.question: Marasmus is characterized by:
Vitamin A is transported in blood primarily bound to:
questions.explanation: Retinol-binding protein (RBP) specifically transports retinol from liver stores to peripheral tissues. Each RBP molecule binds one retinol molecule and associates with transthyretin for stability. RBP levels reflect vitamin A status; severe protein malnutrition reduces RBP synthesis, impairing vitamin A mobilization even when hepatic stores are adequate.

Inosine monophosphate (IMP) is the first complete purine nucleotide formed after ten reactions. IMP is then the branch point for AMP and GMP synthesis through separate two-step pathways. This convergent synthesis to a common intermediate followed by divergent pathways is metabolically efficient and allows coordinated regulation of adenine and guanine nucleotide production.
questions.question: The first unique purine nucleotide formed in de novo synthesis is:

questions.explanation: Insulin is the major anabolic hormone, promoting glucose uptake (muscle, adipose), glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis while inhibiting gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, and ketogenesis. Insulin signals nutrient abundance, directing metabolism toward storage. These effects are mediated by receptor tyrosine kinase activation and downstream signaling cascades affecting enzyme activity and gene expression.
questions.question: Insulin promotes which metabolic processes?
What drives secondary active transport across membranes?
questions.explanation: Secondary active transporters harness energy stored in electrochemical gradients (typically sodium or proton) established by primary active transport. Favorable ion movement down its gradient drives unfavorable solute movement against its gradient through coupled conformational changes. This indirect energy coupling achieves concentration accumulation.

questions.question: What causes lactose intolerance in most adults worldwide?
questions.explanation: Most humans experience lactase decline after weaning (lactase non-persistence), causing lactose intolerance symptoms when consuming dairy. Lactase persistence from regulatory mutations allows continued expression, common in populations with pastoral histories. Lactose intolerance is normal; persistence is the derived trait.

questions.question: Metabolic syndrome is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome includes central obesity, insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides, low HDL), and hypertension. It dramatically increases cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes risk. Pathophysiology involves insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and altered adipokine secretion. Treatment focuses on weight loss, exercise, and cardiovascular risk factor management. The syndrome reflects modern lifestyle (excess calories, sedentary behavior).

questions.question: What percentage of total body calcium is in the skeleton?
questions.explanation: Approximately 99% of body calcium is in bone and teeth as hydroxyapatite crystals, serving structural functions. The remaining 1% in blood and soft tissues regulates critical functions including muscle contraction, nerve transmission, blood clotting, and enzyme activities. Despite small extracellular calcium mass, its concentration is tightly regulated because even minor deviations impair cellular function.

Peroxisomal β-oxidation is most active in liver and kidney, particularly for very long-chain fatty acids (>20 carbons) that are poor substrates for mitochondrial enzymes. The first oxidation step in peroxisomes transfers electrons directly to oxygen, producing hydrogen peroxide rather than FADH2. This sacrifices energy conservation for the ability to oxidize difficult substrates.
questions.question: Where does peroxisomal β-oxidation primarily occur in mammals?

questions.explanation: Isoleucine is both glucogenic and ketogenic, producing one molecule of acetyl-CoA and one molecule of propionyl-CoA. The propionyl-CoA can be converted to succinyl-CoA and enter the TCA cycle for gluconeogenesis. This makes isoleucine unique among branched-chain amino acids in contributing to both pathways.
questions.question: Isoleucine degradation produces which combination of metabolites?
What coenzyme is required for all transamination reactions?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), derived from vitamin B6, serves as cofactor for aminotransferases by forming Schiff base intermediates. The aldehyde group of PLP reacts with amino acid amino groups, facilitating amino group transfer. PLP deficiency impairs amino acid metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) coats proteins uniformly with negative charge, enabling separation by size. The anionic detergent denatures proteins and masks intrinsic charges, so migration depends solely on molecular weight. This technique is fundamental for protein characterization and purity assessment.
questions.question: Which technique separates proteins based on molecular weight?

questions.explanation: Complete glucose oxidation through glycolysis, citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation produces approximately 30-32 ATP molecules. The exact yield depends on shuttle systems transporting cytoplasmic NADH into mitochondria and proton leak across membranes. This represents the maximum energy capture from glucose catabolism.
questions.question: How many ATP equivalents does complete glucose oxidation theoretically yield?

questions.explanation: The characteristic fruity or sweet odor of breath in ketoacidosis results from exhaled acetone. Acetone is volatile and readily crosses from blood to alveolar air. While diagnostically useful, acetone represents wasted carbon that cannot be metabolized for energy. Its presence indicates severe ketone body overproduction.
questions.question: What causes the "fruity breath" odor in diabetic ketoacidosis?

questions.explanation: Plasma cells are differentiated B lymphocytes specialized for high-rate antibody secretion. Each plasma cell produces a single antibody specificity determined during B cell development. Long-lived plasma cells in bone marrow maintain protective antibody levels after immunization or infection.
questions.question: Which cells produce antibodies?

questions.explanation: PTH raises blood calcium primarily by stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption, releasing calcium and phosphate. PTH also increases renal calcium reabsorption while promoting phosphate excretion, and stimulates 1α-hydroxylase to activate vitamin D, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption. These coordinated actions rapidly normalize blood calcium when levels fall below normal range.
questions.question: Parathyroid hormone increases blood calcium by:

questions.explanation: Thymidylate synthase methylates dUMP to dTMP using N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate as methyl donor and reducing agent. This reaction uniquely produces dihydrofolate requiring reduction for continued function. DNA requires thymine rather than uracil, making this enzyme essential for DNA replication.
questions.question: Which base is methylated to form thymine?
Which molecule donates the second nitrogen atom incorporated into urea?
questions.explanation: The second nitrogen in urea comes from aspartate, which condenses with citrulline to form argininosuccinate in the cytoplasm. This nitrogen originates from various amino acids through transamination reactions that channel nitrogen to aspartate. The argininosuccinate synthetase reaction requires ATP and represents a key regulatory point in the cycle.

2-deoxyribose lacks an oxygen atom at the 2' position of the ribose ring, distinguishing DNA from RNA structurally. This modification increases DNA stability and resistance to hydrolysis compared to RNA. The absence of the 2'-OH group prevents certain degradation reactions that affect RNA molecules.
questions.question: What is the correct name for the pentose sugar found in DNA?

questions.explanation: Leucine degradation produces HMG-CoA, which can be cleaved to acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA or reduced to mevalonate. HMG-CoA is a branch point metabolite in cholesterol biosynthesis and ketone body formation. This connection links amino acid catabolism to lipid metabolism.
questions.question: Which intermediate is formed from leucine that can be reduced to mevalonate?

questions.explanation: Hydrophobic van der Waals interactions between stacked aromatic bases contribute significantly to helix stability. These π-π stacking forces, along with base pair hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic effects, and ionic interactions, cooperatively maintain double-stranded structure. Base stacking provides more stability than hydrogen bonding alone.
questions.question: What stabilizes the DNA double helix besides base pairing?
Which tissues can utilize ketone bodies for energy?
questions.explanation: All extrahepatic tissues with mitochondria can oxidize ketone bodies, including brain, heart, skeletal muscle, and kidney. The brain normally uses glucose but adapts to use ketone bodies during prolonged fasting, significantly reducing glucose requirements. Red blood cells lack mitochondria and cannot use ketone bodies.

questions.question: What is the template strand used during transcription also called?
questions.explanation: The antisense (template) strand runs 3' to 5' and serves as the template for RNA synthesis. This strand is complementary and antiparallel to the RNA transcript produced during transcription. The opposite strand is called the sense or coding strand because its sequence matches the RNA transcript (except T→U).

questions.question: Thyroid hormone affects calcium metabolism by:
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone stimulates bone turnover with resorption exceeding formation, potentially causing hypercalcemia and negative calcium balance. Hyperthyroidism increases bone remodeling rate, reducing bone density and elevating fracture risk. This is one reason why excess thyroid hormone replacement or hyperthyroidism requires monitoring and treatment. The skeletal effects are mediated through thyroid hormone receptors on bone cells.

questions.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) catalyzes the committed and rate-limiting step of the urea cycle in mitochondria. This enzyme requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator, linking urea cycle activity to amino acid availability. CPS I deficiency causes severe hyperammonemia because ammonia cannot be efficiently converted to carbamoyl phosphate.

Growth factor independence results from mutations in growth factor receptors, signal transducers, or downstream targets. Cancer cells produce autocrine growth factors or constitutively activate signaling pathways, proliferating without external stimulation. This autonomy is a defining cancer characteristic.
questions.question: Which property allows cancer cells to proliferate indefinitely without external growth signals?

questions.explanation: DKA treatment requires insulin to suppress ketogenesis and promote glucose utilization, along with fluid and electrolyte replacement to correct dehydration and acidosis. Insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, stopping fatty acid release, while promoting peripheral ketone body oxidation. Gradual correction prevents cerebral edema and other complications.
questions.question: Treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis requires:

questions.explanation: Oncogenes derive from proto-oncogenes that normally regulate cell growth but cause cancer when mutated or overexpressed. Examples include growth factors (sis), receptors (erb-B), signal transducers (ras), and transcription factors (myc). Single oncogene activation can contribute to transformation but usually requires additional mutations.
questions.question: What class of genes promotes cell division when mutated or overexpressed?
Phenylketonuria results from deficiency of:
questions.explanation: PKU is caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine and its metabolites (phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, phenylacetate) accumulate, causing intellectual disability if untreated. Tyrosine becomes essential. Treatment requires lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction. Newborn screening and early treatment prevent neurological damage. Pregnant PKU women must maintain strict control to prevent fetal damage.

Growth factor receptors (receptor tyrosine kinases) possess cytoplasmic domains with tyrosine kinase activity activated by ligand binding. Autophosphorylation creates docking sites for signaling proteins, initiating cascades controlling cell growth, differentiation, and survival. Examples include insulin, EGF, and PDGF receptors.
questions.question: What type of receptor has intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity?
What causes the neurological symptoms in vitamin B12 deficiency?
questions.explanation: B12 deficiency causes neurological damage through multiple mechanisms: the "folate trap" depletes tetrahydrofolate derivatives needed for nucleotide synthesis; methylmalonic acid accumulates from methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency; and impaired methionine synthesis affects myelin lipid methylation. Subacute combined degeneration affects spinal cord posterior and lateral columns.

Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate oxidase deficiency in tyrosine degradation. Homogentisic acid accumulates and polymerizes, causing dark urine on standing (ochronosis), cartilage/connective tissue pigmentation, and arthritis in later life. It's relatively benign compared to other amino acid disorders. There's no effective treatment; management focuses on arthritis symptoms. The condition provided early evidence for "one gene-one enzyme" concept.
questions.question: Alkaptonuria is caused by deficiency of:

questions.explanation: Most amino acids undergo transamination reactions that funnel their amino groups into glutamate, which serves as a collection center for nitrogen. This convergent pathway simplifies nitrogen metabolism by consolidating amino groups from various sources. Glutamate then undergoes oxidative deamination to release ammonia for urea synthesis or transfer nitrogen to other biosynthetic pathways.
questions.question: What percentage of amino acids in protein metabolism are transaminated to glutamate?
Glucagon secretion is stimulated by:
questions.explanation: Glucagon is secreted by pancreatic α-cells in response to hypoglycemia, promoting hepatic glucose output through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Amino acids also stimulate glucagon secretion, especially after protein meals, preventing hypoglycemia while promoting gluconeogenesis. Insulin and somatostatin inhibit glucagon release. The glucagon/insulin ratio regulates metabolic fuel selection.

questions.question: Iron absorption is decreased by:
questions.explanation: Phytates (inositol hexaphosphate) in grains and legumes, along with tannins (tea), calcium, and oxalates, inhibit non-heme iron absorption by forming insoluble complexes. Phytate reduction through fermentation, sprouting, or soaking improves bioavailability. Combining iron-rich plant foods with vitamin C-rich foods enhances absorption. Iron-fortified foods often use compounds with good bioavailability despite phytate presence.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes deoxyadenosine accumulation, toxic to developing lymphocytes and causing immunodeficiency. This was the first disease treated with gene therapy, demonstrating clinical gene correction feasibility. Enzyme replacement therapy and bone marrow transplantation are alternative treatments.
questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?

questions.explanation: Transfer RNA molecules serve as adaptors, linking specific amino acids to corresponding codons through anticodon-codon pairing. Each tRNA is charged with its cognate amino acid by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, ensuring translation fidelity. The cloverleaf secondary structure and L-shaped tertiary structure are characteristic of all tRNAs.
questions.question: Which molecule carries amino acids to the ribosome during translation?
Vitamin C functions primarily as a:
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid is a potent water-soluble reducing agent and antioxidant, donating electrons in numerous reactions. Besides collagen synthesis, it's involved in carnitine and neurotransmitter biosynthesis, drug metabolism, and regenerating oxidized vitamin E. As an antioxidant, ascorbate neutralizes reactive oxygen species, protecting cells from oxidative damage. Its reducing power is central to all its biological functions.

questions.question: Desaturation of fatty acids in mammals requires:
questions.explanation: Fatty acid desaturases are mixed-function oxidases that introduce double bonds using molecular oxygen as a cosubstrate. One oxygen atom is incorporated into water, while electrons from the fatty acid create the double bond. The desaturase system includes cytochrome b5 reductase, cytochrome b5, and the desaturase enzyme itself.

questions.question: The coenzyme form of thiamine is:
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the active coenzyme form, serving as a cofactor for oxidative decarboxylation reactions. TPP-dependent enzymes include pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. The thiazole ring of TPP stabilizes carbanion intermediates through resonance, essential for breaking carbon-carbon bonds adjacent to carbonyl groups.

The urea cycle incorporates two nitrogen atoms (from ammonia and aspartate) and one carbon (from CO2) into urea for renal excretion. This hepatic pathway prevents ammonia toxicity, particularly critical for central nervous system protection. Genetic defects in cycle enzymes cause hyperammonemia and severe neurological consequences.
questions.question: What cycle converts ammonia to urea in liver?
Which enzyme is responsible for oxidative deamination of glutamate?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible oxidative deamination of glutamate to α-ketoglutarate, liberating ammonia for urea synthesis. This enzyme is unique in its ability to use either NAD+ or NADP+ as coenzyme. The reaction proceeds through an α-iminoglutarate intermediate and links amino acid metabolism directly to the TCA cycle.

questions.question: In which direction does DNA synthesis always proceed?
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase catalyzes synthesis exclusively in the 5' to 3' direction by adding nucleotides to the 3'-OH group. This directionality is determined by the enzyme's active site configuration and the chemistry of phosphodiester bond formation. The constraint necessitates different synthesis mechanisms for leading and lagging strands.

questions.question: What causes hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A results from Factor VIII deficiency, impairing intrinsic coagulation pathway and causing prolonged bleeding. This X-linked recessive disorder affects males predominantly, with severity correlating to residual factor activity. Recombinant Factor VIII replacement prevents bleeding complications.

Glucagon and epinephrine activate adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP levels and activating protein kinase A. PKA phosphorylates and inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase while activating hormone-sensitive lipase. This coordinated response promotes fatty acid mobilization and oxidation during fasting or stress.
questions.question: Glucagon and epinephrine affect fatty acid metabolism by:
The primary function of vitamin E is:
questions.explanation: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) functions primarily as a lipid-soluble antioxidant, protecting polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes from oxidative damage. It donates hydrogen to lipid peroxy radicals, breaking the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation. Vitamin E deficiency, though rare, causes neurological problems due to oxidative damage to nerve tissue.

questions.question: Scurvy is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency causing impaired collagen synthesis. Clinical features include bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, poor wound healing, bone pain, and eventually tooth loss and death. Collagen is abundant in blood vessels, skin, and connective tissue; defective collagen causes fragility and bleeding. Scurvy was historically common among sailors until citrus fruits were recognized as preventive.

questions.question: What is the fate of ammonia produced from amino acid catabolism in humans?
questions.explanation: Ammonia enters the urea cycle in liver mitochondria, producing urea for renal excretion as the primary nitrogen waste. This conversion prevents ammonia toxicity, particularly detrimental to the central nervous system. The urea cycle coordinates with amino acid catabolism and the citric acid cycle.

questions.question: How many kilocalories per gram do lipids yield upon complete oxidation?
questions.explanation: Lipids provide 9 kilocalories per gram, more than double the energy from carbohydrates or proteins. This high energy density results from the highly reduced state of carbon atoms in fatty acids. The hydrophobic nature also allows anhydrous storage, further increasing energy efficiency compared to hydrated carbohydrate stores.

The P (peptidyl) site holds tRNA attached to the growing polypeptide chain during translation elongation. After peptide bond formation, this tRNA moves to the E site before being released. The ribosome coordinates movement between sites to ensure accurate and efficient protein synthesis.
questions.question: Which site on the ribosome holds the tRNA carrying the growing peptide chain?

questions.explanation: α1-antitrypsin deficiency causes lung disease from unopposed elastase and liver disease from misfolded protein accumulation in hepatocytes. The PiZZ variant produces misfolded protein that polymerizes in endoplasmic reticulum, causing hepatocyte injury. Liver transplantation cures both manifestations by providing normal protein.
questions.question: Which condition results from α1-antitrypsin misfolding and retention?

questions.explanation: Oxidative stress from infections, certain drugs (antimalarials, sulfonamides), or fava beans precipitates hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals. Without adequate NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione, RBCs cannot neutralize hydrogen peroxide and other oxidants. This causes oxidative damage to membrane lipids and proteins, leading to hemolysis.
questions.question: Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency is triggered by:

questions.explanation: High protein intake, particularly from animal sources, increases urinary calcium excretion by increasing acid load (from sulfur amino acids), which promotes bone calcium mobilization to buffer pH. Sodium intake also correlates with calcium excretion (40 mg calcium lost per 2300 mg sodium). These dietary factors affect calcium balance and long-term bone health.
questions.question: Urinary calcium excretion increases with:
The first step in ketone body synthesis is:
questions.explanation: Two acetyl-CoA molecules condense to form acetoacetyl-CoA, catalyzed by thiolase (also called ACAT). This reversible reaction is pulled forward by subsequent steps. Acetoacetyl-CoA is the precursor for both ketone body synthesis and cholesterol synthesis, making it a metabolic branch point.

questions.question: What describes the orientation of the two DNA strands relative to each other?
questions.explanation: Antiparallel orientation means one strand runs 5' to 3' while the complementary strand runs 3' to 5'. This arrangement results from Watson-Crick base pairing geometry and affects replication and transcription mechanisms. The antiparallel nature necessitates different synthesis strategies for each strand during replication.

Proteoglycans concentrate in extracellular matrices and on cell surfaces, where their glycosaminoglycan chains create hydrated spaces. These molecules resist compressive forces in cartilage, lubricate joints, and regulate cell behavior through growth factor binding. The negative charges repel each other, maintaining extended conformations.
questions.question: Where are proteoglycans predominantly located?
β-carotene is a provitamin for:
questions.explanation: β-carotene and other provitamin A carotenoids can be cleaved by intestinal enzymes to yield retinol (vitamin A). One β-carotene molecule can theoretically produce two retinol molecules, though actual conversion efficiency is lower. Carotenoids also function as antioxidants. Unlike preformed vitamin A, excessive carotene intake causes benign carotenemia (yellow skin) but not hypervitaminosis A.

Zellweger syndrome is characterized by absent or nonfunctional peroxisomes in all tissues, preventing oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids. These fatty acids accumulate in brain, liver, and kidney, causing severe developmental and neurological problems. The syndrome is usually fatal in the first year of life.
questions.question: Zellweger syndrome results from absence of functional:

questions.explanation: Cobalamin (vitamin B₁₂) has a corrin ring structure with a central cobalt atom, making it the only vitamin containing a metal ion. The cobalt exists in different oxidation states in various B₁₂ forms. Only microorganisms can synthesize cobalamin; animals obtain it through dietary sources. Humans depend entirely on animal products or supplements for B₁₂.
questions.question: Vitamin B₁₂ contains which trace element?

questions.explanation: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) leak from damaged hepatocytes into blood circulation. Elevated transaminase levels in serum indicate hepatocellular injury from various causes including viral hepatitis, toxins, or ischemia. The ALT/AST ratio helps distinguish different liver pathologies.
questions.question: Which diagnostic enzymes indicate liver damage when elevated in serum?

questions.explanation: Triose phosphate isomerase rapidly interconverts dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). This allows both trioses from the aldolase reaction to proceed through the same pathway. The enzyme is extremely efficient, with catalytic perfection near the diffusion limit, ensuring minimal accumulation of DHAP.
questions.question: Triose phosphate isomerase catalyzes interconversion between:

questions.explanation: N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate provides both the methyl group and reducing equivalents for thymidylate synthase. This reaction is unique in transferring a one-carbon unit at the methylene oxidation level and reducing it to methyl. Tetrahydrofolate oxidation to dihydrofolate requires reduction by dihydrofolate reductase for continued function.
questions.question: What coenzyme donates methyl groups for thymidylate synthesis from dUMP?
Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthesis by blocking:
questions.explanation: Oligomycin binds to the F₀ component of ATP synthase, blocking the proton channel and preventing ATP synthesis. This causes the proton gradient to build up, which eventually stops electron transport as well due to back-pressure. Oligomycin demonstrates the tight coupling between electron transport and ATP synthesis.

questions.question: Which metabolites can serve as gluconeogenic precursors?
questions.explanation: Lactate (from muscle glycolysis), glucogenic amino acids (from protein), and glycerol (from triglyceride breakdown) are major gluconeogenic substrates. These can be converted to oxaloacetate or other TCA cycle intermediates that lead to glucose formation. Acetyl-CoA from fatty acids cannot produce net glucose because the carbons are lost as CO₂ in the TCA cycle.

Glutathione peroxidase reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides, oxidizing glutathione to GSSG. Selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidases contain selenocysteine residues essential for activity. Selenium deficiency impairs antioxidant defense, increasing oxidative damage susceptibility.
questions.question: What enzyme reduces lipid hydroperoxides using glutathione?

questions.explanation: Glucosamine replaces the hydroxyl at carbon 2 with an amino group, often N-acetylated in biological molecules. This amino sugar appears in glycosaminoglycans, chitin, and glycoproteins. Glucosamine supplements are marketed for joint health, though efficacy remains controversial.
questions.question: Which modified monosaccharide contains an amino group at carbon 2?
Orotic aciduria results from deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Hereditary orotic aciduria is caused by UMP synthase deficiency, which catalyzes the final two steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis (orotate + PRPP→orotidine-5'-monophosphate→UMP). Orotic acid accumulates and is excreted in massive amounts. Patients develop megaloblastic anemia, growth retardation, and immune deficiencies. Treatment with oral uridine bypasses the enzymatic defect.

questions.question: How frequently do branch points occur in glycogen compared to amylopectin?
questions.explanation: Glycogen branches every 8-12 glucose residues, more frequently than amylopectin's 20-30 residue intervals. This highly branched structure allows rapid glucose mobilization essential for animals' metabolic demands. The compact spherical shape of glycogen granules efficiently stores large amounts of glucose with minimal osmotic effect.

Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome) involves absent or dysfunctional peroxisomes, impairing very long-chain fatty acid oxidation, plasmalogen synthesis, and other peroxisomal functions. Severe developmental abnormalities, neurological dysfunction, and liver disease result. Very long-chain fatty acids accumulate. The condition is usually fatal in infancy. Diagnosis involves measuring very long-chain fatty acids and identifying peroxisomal protein import defects.
questions.question: Zellweger syndrome affects which metabolic process?
What condition results from inadequate insulin secretion or action?
questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus encompasses metabolic disorders characterized by hyperglycemia from insufficient insulin secretion (type 1) or action (type 2). Chronic hyperglycemia causes micro- and macrovascular complications affecting eyes, kidneys, nerves, and cardiovascular system. Management requires blood glucose control through medication, diet, and exercise.

questions.question: Glycogen is primarily stored in which tissues?
questions.explanation: Liver stores about 100-120g of glycogen (10% of liver weight) for maintaining blood glucose, while muscle stores 400-500g (1-2% of muscle mass) for its own energy needs. Hepatic glycogen lasts 12-18 hours of fasting. Muscle glycogen lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot directly contribute to blood glucose maintenance.

questions.question: How many ATP equivalents are consumed per molecule of urea synthesized?
questions.explanation: Urea synthesis consumes four high-energy phosphate bonds: two ATP for carbamoyl phosphate synthesis, one ATP for argininosuccinate synthesis, and one additional ATP equivalent from fumarate regeneration. This high energy cost reflects the importance of ammonia detoxification for survival. The energy expenditure is justified because accumulated ammonia is far more toxic than the metabolic cost of its removal.

questions.question: Intrinsic factor is required for absorption of:
questions.explanation: Intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells, binds vitamin B₁₂ in the stomach, and the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum via specific receptors. Without intrinsic factor (from autoimmune gastritis, gastrectomy, or genetic defects), B₁₂ absorption is severely impaired, causing pernicious anemia. Absence of intrinsic factor necessitates parenteral B₁₂ administration.

questions.question: In starvation, ketone bodies serve primarily to:
questions.explanation: During prolonged fasting, ketone bodies produced from adipose tissue fatty acids become the brain's primary fuel, sparing glucose. This dramatically reduces the need for gluconeogenesis from amino acids, thereby preserving muscle protein. Without this adaptation, protein wasting would be severe and unsustainable during extended food deprivation.

Ribose-5-phosphate is the precursor for nucleotide biosynthesis, providing the ribose moiety for purines, pyrimidines, and nucleotide coenzymes. Rapidly dividing cells (bone marrow, intestinal mucosa, tumors) have high pentose phosphate pathway activity to meet nucleotide demands for DNA and RNA synthesis. This makes the pathway a target for cancer chemotherapy.
questions.question: Ribose-5-phosphate is primarily used for synthesis of:

questions.explanation: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) results from muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, preventing muscle glycogen breakdown. Patients experience exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, and myoglobinuria after intense exercise. Blood lactate doesn't rise normally during exercise because muscle cannot break down glycogen to fuel glycolysis. The condition demonstrates muscle's dependence on glycogen for intense activity.
questions.question: McArdle disease is caused by deficiency of:

questions.explanation: Complete UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) deficiency prevents bilirubin conjugation, causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus risk. Phototherapy provides temporary relief; liver transplantation is definitive treatment. Type II (Arias syndrome) involves partial deficiency responsive to phenobarbital.
questions.question: What causes Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I?
What is the active coenzyme form of riboflavin?
questions.explanation: Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) are riboflavin-derived coenzymes for oxidation-reduction reactions. These flavoproteins participate in electron transport chain complexes and numerous metabolic pathways. Riboflavin deficiency causes ariboflavinosis with symptoms including angular cheilitis and glossitis.

Lipogenesis converts excess acetyl-CoA from carbohydrate or protein metabolism into fatty acids for storage as triacylglycerols. This process occurs primarily in liver and adipose tissue when energy intake exceeds expenditure. Insulin stimulates lipogenic enzymes while fasting and catecholamines inhibit synthesis.
questions.question: Which process converts excess acetyl-CoA to fatty acids?
Which condition results from α1-antitrypsin deficiency?
questions.explanation: α1-antitrypsin deficiency allows unopposed neutrophil elastase activity, degrading lung elastin and causing early-onset emphysema. The misfolded protein also accumulates in liver, potentially causing cirrhosis. Smoking dramatically accelerates lung disease progression in deficient individuals.

Lac repressor binds the operator sequence, blocking RNA polymerase access to lac operon genes. Lactose (or allolactose) binding causes repressor conformational change, releasing DNA and permitting transcription. This classic example demonstrates negative regulation of gene expression.
questions.question: Which protein represses lac operon transcription in E. coli?
The rate-limiting enzyme of pyrimidine synthesis is:
questions.explanation: Aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase) catalyzes the committed step, condensing carbamoyl phosphate with aspartate. ATCase is feedback-inhibited by CTP and activated by ATP, coordinating pyrimidine synthesis with energy status and nucleotide needs. In bacteria, ATCase is a separate enzyme; in mammals, it's part of the multifunctional CAD protein (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, aspartate transcarbamoylase, dihydroorotase).

The classical complement pathway initiates when C1q binds antibody-antigen complexes (IgM or IgG). This triggers a protease cascade generating C3 convertase, leading to opsonization, inflammation, and membrane attack complex formation. Complement amplifies antibody-mediated immunity and directly lyses pathogens.
questions.question: What complement activation pathway is antibody-dependent?

questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor results from protein-energy malnutrition with disproportionate protein deficiency relative to calorie intake (often after weaning onto starchy diet). Characteristic features include edema, fatty liver, skin changes, hair discoloration, and impaired immunity. Differs from marasmus (total calorie-protein deficiency with wasting but no edema). Treatment requires careful protein repletion with micronutrient supplementation.
questions.question: Kwashiorkor is primarily caused by:

questions.explanation: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is converted to 5-fluorodeoxyuridylate (FdUMP), which forms a stable ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and methylenetetrahydrofolate, irreversibly inhibiting the enzyme. This "suicide inhibitor" prevents dTMP synthesis, blocking DNA replication. 5-FU is widely used in cancer chemotherapy, particularly for colorectal cancer. It's more toxic to rapidly dividing cells.
questions.question: 5-Fluorouracil acts as an antimetabolite by:
The enzyme that adds glucose residues to glycogen is:
questions.explanation: Glycogen synthase catalyzes the formation of α-1,4-glycosidic bonds, adding glucose units from UDP-glucose to the growing glycogen chain. This is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogen synthesis. The enzyme exists in active (dephosphorylated) and inactive (phosphorylated) forms, with insulin promoting dephosphorylation and activation.

questions.question: Which process must tumors undergo to obtain nutrients beyond diffusion limits?
questions.explanation: Angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation) supplies tumors with nutrients and oxygen while removing waste. The "angiogenic switch" occurs when pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF) overcome inhibitors, enabling tumor expansion beyond 2-3 mm diameter. Anti-angiogenic therapies starve tumors by blocking vessel formation.

questions.question: Newborns are given vitamin K to prevent:
questions.explanation: Newborns have low vitamin K stores because placental transfer is limited and intestinal bacteria (which synthesize vitamin K) haven't colonized the gut. Without prophylactic vitamin K administration, some infants develop hemorrhagic disease with serious bleeding risk. A single intramuscular injection at birth prevents this potentially fatal condition.

questions.question: What transporter system moves fatty acids into mitochondria?
questions.explanation: The carnitine shuttle transfers long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs across inner mitochondrial membranes where β-oxidation occurs. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I) catalyzes outer membrane transfer while CPT II regenerates acyl-CoA in matrix. Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT I, coordinating synthesis and oxidation.

Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) is unique among TCA cycle enzymes as it's embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It's a component of both the TCA cycle and the electron transport chain. The enzyme contains FAD as a prosthetic group and transfers electrons from succinate directly to ubiquinone in the respiratory chain.
questions.question: Which TCA cycle enzyme is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane?
Fructosamine and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) reflect:
questions.explanation: Fructosamine and HbA1c result from non-enzymatic glycation of proteins (albumin and hemoglobin respectively) and reflect average blood glucose over protein lifespan: 2-3 weeks (fructosamine) or 2-3 months (HbA1c). HbA1c is the gold standard for assessing diabetes control. Values >6.5% diagnose diabetes; target is typically <7% for diabetics. These tests aren't affected by acute glucose fluctuations.

Red blood cells lack mitochondria and depend entirely on glucose for ATP production via glycolysis, converting glucose to lactate. RBCs cannot use fatty acids, ketone bodies, or amino acids. Brain also requires glucose but can adapt to ketone bodies during fasting. The obligatory glucose requirement of RBCs (and brain) drives gluconeogenesis during fasting to maintain minimum blood glucose levels.
questions.question: Which tissue has an absolute requirement for glucose?
The respiratory quotient (RQ) for pure carbohydrate oxidation is:
questions.explanation: The respiratory quotient (CO₂ produced/O₂ consumed) is 1.0 for carbohydrate oxidation (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O). For fat oxidation, RQ is ~0.7 (less CO₂ per O₂ because fat is more reduced). Protein oxidation gives RQ ~0.8. Mixed diet typically gives RQ of 0.8-0.85. RQ measurement estimates substrate utilization and can identify metabolic abnormalities.

questions.question: How many acetyl-CoA molecules are produced from complete β-oxidation of palmitic acid?
questions.explanation: Palmitic acid (16 carbons) undergoes seven cycles of β-oxidation, producing eight molecules of acetyl-CoA. Each cycle removes two carbons as acetyl-CoA until only a four-carbon acyl-CoA remains, which is cleaved in the final cycle. The eight acetyl-CoA molecules can enter the TCA cycle for complete oxidation.

The Na+/K+ ATPase actively transports three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per ATP hydrolyzed. This electrogenic pump maintains electrochemical gradients essential for excitability, osmotic balance, and secondary active transport. Inhibition by cardiac glycosides like digoxin increases cardiac contractility.
questions.question: Which transport system maintains sodium and potassium gradients across plasma membranes?
Spermatozoa obtain energy primarily from:
questions.explanation: Sperm can use both glycolysis (in the principal piece) and oxidative phosphorylation (mitochondria in the midpiece) for ATP production. Fructose (from seminal vesicles) is the major fuel source, though sperm can also use lactate and pyruvate. The tail movement requires substantial ATP. Metabolic flexibility allows function under varying oxygen and nutrient availability.

Glucose-6-phosphatase is embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, catalyzing the final step of gluconeogenesis by hydrolyzing glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose. Only liver and kidney possess this enzyme, explaining why only these tissues can release glucose into blood. The enzyme is essential for maintaining blood glucose during fasting.
questions.question: Glucose-6-phosphatase is located in which cellular compartment?

questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the committed and rate-limiting step, oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone. The enzyme is inhibited by NADPH (product inhibition), regulating pathway flux according to NADPH needs. G6PD deficiency is the most common human enzyme deficiency, affecting over 400 million people worldwide.
questions.question: The rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway is:

questions.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the first irreversible oxidation and decarboxylation step, making it the rate-limiting enzyme.
