questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- The large intestine (colon) is the site of fibre action, including softening of stools and absorption of water; bacterial digestion of fibre produces water, gas and fatty acids, and any undigested carbohydrate reaching the colon may be broken down by intestinal bacteria.
- Water, sodium and the end products of bacterial digestion are absorbed in the large intestine (in contrast to the small intestine, where most nutrient absorption of glucose, amino acids and lipids occurs).
- Colonic bacteria are also a good source of menaquinones (vitamin K), supplementing dietary phylloquinone from plant foods.
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- Prolonged antibiotic therapy destroys the gastrointestinal bacteria that manufacture menaquinones, reducing this source of vitamin K.
3. Basis of distant organ/system effects
- Because a meaningful fraction of the body's vitamin K supply comes from colonic bacterial menaquinone synthesis, disruption of colonic bacterial flora (e.g. by antibiotics) combined with low dietary vitamin K intake impairs synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (prothrombin and others) made in the liver, producing a bleeding disorder in the vascular system - a functional deficit that appears far from the colon itself, in the coagulation system, illustrating how the colon's microbial function is integrated into whole-body haemostasis.
questions.question:
1. Describe the overall biochemical role of the large intestine (colon), including its main pathway of bacterial fermentation and its absorptive function.
2. State how disturbances of colonic function relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why impaired colonic/bacterial function produces effects in distant organs and systems (bleeding, bone).

questions.answerText:
1. Structure, synthesis and function
- Collagen, the major connective tissue protein in vertebrates, is formed from tropocollagen subunits; its triple helix is highly extended and strong, consisting of three separate polypeptide chains arranged as a left-handed helix (in contrast to the right-handed alpha-helix), with 3.3 residues per turn.
- Each chain forms hydrogen bonds with the other two, giving the molecule its characteristic strength; nearly one residue in three is glycine, proline content is unusually high, and modified amino acids such as 4-hydroxyproline and 5-hydroxylysine are present, with proline and hydroxyproline together making up about 30% of the amino acids.
- Function: as a fibrous, extended, water-insoluble structural protein, collagen provides tensile strength to connective tissue; covalent cross-links in collagen, catalysed by lysyl amino-oxidase, further alter and strengthen its mechanical properties.
2. Biochemical basis of the vitamin requirement
- 4-hydroxyproline, required in collagen, is produced when proline residues on the amino side of glycine residues in nascent collagen chains are hydroxylated by prolyl hydroxylase, a dioxygenase that uses molecular O2 (one oxygen atom attaches to proline C-4, the other converts alpha-ketoglutarate to succinate) and requires a tightly bound Fe2+ ion to activate O2; ascorbate (vitamin C) is required to reduce the ferric ion formed when the enzyme is inactivated during this reaction, regenerating active enzyme (itself being oxidised to dehydroascorbic acid).
3. Biochemical basis of connective tissue abnormality when hydroxylation fails
- Hydroxyproline stabilises the collagen triple helix by forming interstrand hydrogen bonds; collagen synthesised without adequate ascorbate is insufficiently hydroxylated and therefore less thermally and structurally stable than normal collagen.
- The resulting abnormal fibres are the biochemical basis of the skin lesions and blood-vessel fragility seen in scurvy, and (more broadly) of impaired wound and fracture healing, illustrating why an apparently minor deficiency in post-translational modification of a single amino acid can compromise the mechanical integrity of an entire structural protein.
questions.question:
1. Describe the structure, synthesis and function of collagen.
2. State the biochemical basis for the vitamin (cofactor) requirement in collagen synthesis.
3. Explain the biochemical basis of the connective tissue abnormalities seen when collagen hydroxylation is impaired (as in scurvy).

1. Describe the overall metabolic role of the brain, including its main fuel-utilisation pathways and how these are integrated with peripheral organs.
2. State how disturbances of brain fuel supply relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why defects that are primarily in peripheral organs (liver, pancreas) produce functional deficits in the brain.
questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- The brain's energy requirements depend on an uninterrupted flow of glucose; along with red blood cells, it relies exclusively on glucose as its energy source under normal feeding conditions, and it is not an insulin-sensitive tissue for glucose uptake (unlike muscle and adipose tissue), so its glucose uptake is not dependent on insulin signalling.
- Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) is present in certain cells of the brain (as well as liver, pancreas and intestine) and, because it requires a much higher glucose concentration for optimal activity and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, allows these tissues to sense and respond to changes in blood glucose concentration.
- During prolonged fasting/starvation, when the liver's ketone body output rises because acetyl-CoA generated from fatty acid oxidation exceeds the capacity of the depleted TCA cycle (its intermediates diverted into gluconeogenesis), the brain switches to using ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) as an alternative fuel when glucose is not readily available.
- Brain tissue also uses products of alpha-oxidation of fatty acids (an exception to standard beta-oxidation) to synthesise alpha-hydroxy fatty acids such as cerebronic acid, cerebrosides and sulphatides, and odd-carbon long-chain fatty acids that are structural components of brain sphingolipids (e.g. myelin).
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- Any failure to maintain blood glucose (hepatic glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis failure, as in von Gierke's disease) threatens the brain first, since it cannot use most other fuels under normal short-term conditions.
- Refsum's disease (lack of alpha-hydroxylase/phytanic acid oxidase) causes accumulation of phytanic acid and presents with severe neurological symptoms - polyneuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, nerve deafness and cerebellar ataxia - reflecting disruption of the alpha-oxidation pathway that brain lipid structures depend on.
- Zellweger syndrome (absence of peroxisomes) prevents oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, which then accumulate particularly in brain, liver and kidney.
3. Basis of peripheral-to-brain effects
- Because the brain has no significant fuel reserve of its own and depends on glucose supplied by the liver (via glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis) and, in starvation, on ketone bodies supplied by the liver, a defect that is anatomically located in the liver (e.g. glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency) or in the endocrine pancreas (insulin deficiency, which drives excessive hepatic ketogenesis) produces its clinical impact in the brain - hypoglycaemic dysfunction or, in uncontrolled diabetes, ketoacidosis affecting cerebral function - even though the primary biochemical lesion lies outside the brain itself.

1. Urea cycle
- Site: urea is the excretory end product of protein metabolism; the cycle involves mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthase I (and cytosolic reactions), and takes place in the liver (alanine nitrogen is incorporated into urea in the liver).
- Substrates: NH3 (from oxidative deamination of glutamate), CO2, 2 ATP (for carbamyl phosphate), aspartate (amino group supplied by transamination from glutamate via oxaloacetate), ornithine.
- Key enzymes and cofactors: carbamoyl phosphate synthase I; the reactions are carbamyl phosphate + ornithine -> citrulline; citrulline + aspartate (ATP -> AMP) -> argininosuccinate; argininosuccinate -> arginine + fumarate; arginine -> urea + ornithine. Fumarate returns to the citric acid cycle (malate -> oxaloacetate -> transamination to aspartate).
- Energetics: 2 ATP for carbamyl phosphate and ATP -> AMP for argininosuccinate.
- Products: urea (NH2-CO-NH2) excreted, regenerated ornithine, fumarate.
2. Clinical basis
- Amino groups are funnelled to glutamate, which alone is deaminated to a significant extent to release NH3 for urea synthesis.
- Muscle cannot synthesise urea, so exercising muscle converts pyruvate to alanine by transamination and sends it to the liver (glucose-alanine cycle), where alanine is reconverted to pyruvate and its nitrogen goes into urea or is transferred to other alpha-keto acids.
3. Carbamoyl phosphate synthase I versus II
- CPS I: mitochondrial, part of urea synthesis.
- CPS II: cytosolic, initial enzyme of pyrimidine biosynthesis; compartmentation therefore gives two independent pools of carbamoyl phosphate.

2. Explain the clinical basis of why ammonia and nitrogen handling depends on the liver, and why muscle relies on the glucose-alanine cycle.

questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- At rest and during moderate activity, skeletal muscle relies on both glycolysis and, with adequate oxygen, aerobic oxidation of pyruvate via the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation for ATP.
- During rapid, strenuous contraction, when the demand for energy is high and O2 supply is depleted, muscle relies on anaerobic glycolysis; lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+ so that glycolysis (with its low ATP yield) can continue.
- Muscle stores glycogen (in the cytoplasm of muscle cells, alongside liver) for its own use during exercise; muscle glycogen phosphorylase, unlike the liver isoform, is not activated by glucagon (muscle lacks glucagon receptors) and muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so muscle glycogen is used locally rather than to maintain blood glucose.
- Integration with other tissues: lactate produced by exercising muscle is transferred through the blood to the liver, where it is reconverted to pyruvate and then to glucose by gluconeogenesis (the Cori cycle); amino nitrogen from muscle protein breakdown is transferred to the liver as alanine (via alanine transaminase converting pyruvate + amino nitrogen to alanine), since muscle itself cannot synthesise urea - the glucose-alanine cycle.
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- Malignant hyperthermia, an inherited disorder triggered by certain anaesthetics, causes massive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, muscle rigidity, a dramatic rise in body temperature, and acidosis from excessive lactic acid production; wasteful cycling between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis is a probable contributing factor.
- Excessive anaerobic glycolysis during vigorous exercise causes lactic acid build-up, producing muscle cramps until oxygen returns and lactate is reconverted to pyruvate and oxidised.
3. Basis of a distant-organ effect (muscle to liver, and on to the whole body)
- Because muscle cannot perform gluconeogenesis or ureagenesis itself, the lactate and alanine it releases during exercise or fasting must be processed by the liver (Cori cycle and glucose-alanine cycle); a failure of hepatic gluconeogenesis to keep pace with muscle-derived lactate/alanine output (or a primary hepatic gluconeogenic defect) prevents the resupply of glucose to the blood, so that a demand generated in muscle produces its functional consequence (glucose deprivation, worsened lactic acidosis) via the liver, ultimately threatening glucose-dependent tissues such as the brain and red blood cells that neither muscle nor liver problems directly involve but that depend on the muscle-liver cycle being intact.
questions.question:
1. Describe the overall metabolic role of skeletal muscle, including its main carbohydrate and energy pathways and how they are integrated with other tissues.
2. State how disturbances of these muscle pathways relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why a metabolic defect or extreme demand in skeletal muscle produces effects in a distant organ (the liver) and causes a functional deficit there.

1. Describe the metabolism of xenobiotics (drugs and other foreign compounds) under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes and cofactors (Phase 1 and Phase 2)
- Regulation
- Products/purpose
2. Explain the clinical basis of drug interactions caused by cytochrome P450 induction, and how phase 1 reactions can convert some xenobiotics into toxic or carcinogenic species.
3. Distinguish between phase 1 and phase 2 reactions in xenobiotic metabolism.
questions.answerText:
1. Xenobiotic metabolism
- Site: mainly the liver (with lesser contributions from other tissues); the enzymes are largely located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (microsomes) and, for some phase 2 reactions, the cytosol and mitochondria.
- Substrates: xenobiotics - compounds foreign to the body, chiefly drugs, chemical carcinogens and environmental pollutants (e.g. polychlorinated biphenyls, insecticides, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons); more than 200,000 manufactured environmental chemicals exist, and at least 30 enzymes participate in their metabolism.
- Key enzymes and cofactors: Phase 1 - hydroxylation is the chief reaction, catalysed by monooxygenases (cytochrome P450s), hemoproteins with at least 14 families and roughly 35-60 distinct isoforms in human tissue; the general reaction is RH + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> R-OH + H2O + NADP+; P450s also catalyse deamination, dehalogenation, desulfuration, epoxidation, peroxygenation and reduction, and hydrolysis (by esterases) also occurs in phase 1. Phase 2 - conjugation reactions attach polar groups: glucuronidation (using UDP-glucuronic acid; also the pathway for bilirubin), sulfation (using a sulfate donor), conjugation with glutathione (catalysed by glutathione S-transferases, which also serve as an intracellular reductant), conjugation with certain amino acids, and methylation.
- Regulation: many cytochrome P450 isoforms are inducible - for example phenobarbital and other drugs cause hypertrophy of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and a three- to fourfold rise in cytochrome P450 within 4-5 days, mostly via increased transcription of P450 mRNA (though some induction involves mRNA stabilisation or effects on translation); metabolites of some xenobiotics can also inhibit or stimulate xenobiotic-metabolising enzymes. Certain P450s exist as polymorphic (genetic) isoforms with altered activity (e.g. CYP2D6, CYP2A6), explaining individual variation in drug response.
- Products/purpose: the overall purpose of both phases is to increase the water solubility (polarity) of xenobiotics so that they can be excreted (mainly in urine or bile); very hydrophobic xenobiotics would otherwise persist in adipose tissue almost indefinitely. Phase 1 can convert inactive "prodrugs" or "procarcinogens" to active/toxic forms, or convert active compounds to less active forms before conjugation; phase 2 conjugation usually produces inactive, excretable metabolites, though in rare cases conjugation can increase biologic activity, so "detoxification" is not always an accurate term for these reactions.
2. Clinical basis
- A drug interaction occurs when the effect of one drug is altered by prior, concurrent or later administration of another; the example given is a patient taking the anticoagulant warfarin (metabolised by CYP2C9) who is then started on phenobarbital, an inducer of that P450 - induction increases warfarin metabolism and can alter its anticoagulant effect, illustrating the clinical importance of enzyme induction.
- Phase 1 monooxygenases can convert some procarcinogens (such as certain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) into reactive epoxides and other reactive species that covalently bind DNA, RNA or protein (cytotoxicity), or bind protein and act as a hapten altering its antigenicity; such compounds are termed "indirect carcinogens" because activation occurs intracellularly, in contrast to "direct carcinogens" (e.g. certain alkylating agents) that react with DNA without needing metabolic activation. Epoxide hydrolase can protect against this by converting reactive epoxides to much less reactive dihydrodiols.
- Genetic polymorphisms in P450s (e.g. CYP2D6 affecting debrisoquin and sparteine metabolism, CYP2A6 affecting nicotine metabolism) cause some individuals to metabolise drugs poorly, so the drug can accumulate and produce toxicity, which is a biochemical basis for variable drug responses and adverse reactions between patients.
3. Distinguishing phase 1 and phase 2
- Phase 1 reactions chemically modify the xenobiotic, chiefly by hydroxylation (cytochrome P450/monooxygenases, using O2 and NADPH), and may activate, inactivate or only slightly alter the compound.
- Phase 2 reactions conjugate the phase 1 product (or, in some cases, the parent compound directly) with a polar moiety - glucuronic acid, sulfate, glutathione, an amino acid, or a methyl group - which usually markedly increases water solubility and promotes excretion, and phase 2 reactions are catalysed by a distinct set of conjugating enzymes rather than the P450 monooxygenases of phase 1.

questions.question:
1. Describe the overall biochemical role of cardiac (heart) muscle in fuel utilisation, including its main energy substrates and how they are integrated with the liver and adipose tissue.
2. State how disturbances of cardiac fuel metabolism relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why a defect that is primarily nutritional (e.g. thiamine deficiency) produces functional deficit in the heart as a distant organ.
questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- Heart (cardiac) muscle is described as a tissue that mainly uses fatty acids for energy but can also use ketone bodies when these are available, unlike the brain which relies on glucose (and, secondarily, ketone bodies) but not directly on fatty acids.
- In cardiac cells, the cellular energy sensor AMPK stimulates glycolysis by activating PFK-2, allowing the heart to increase glucose utilisation under conditions of metabolic stress, alongside its preferred use of fatty acids delivered from adipose tissue lipolysis and hepatic lipoprotein/ketone body output.
- Integration: cardiac muscle therefore depends on adipose tissue (as a source of circulating free fatty acids) and on the liver (as the source of ketone bodies during fasting/starvation and as the organ regulating overall fuel availability) rather than being self-sufficient in fuel supply.
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- Thiamine deficiency (beriberi), under chronic conditions, affects the cardiovascular system, producing hypertrophy and altered heart rate; this reflects the heart's dependence on thiamine pyrophosphate-requiring oxidative decarboxylation reactions (pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) for ATP production, since the heart cannot easily substitute these steps.
3. Basis of a nutritional-to-cardiac distant-organ effect
- Because cardiac muscle has a continuous, high oxidative energy demand and depends on thiamine-dependent enzymes to convert its fuel substrates (pyruvate from glycolysis, and TCA-cycle intermediates) into usable ATP, a defect that originates outside the heart - dietary thiamine deficiency - is expressed as cardiac dysfunction (hypertrophy, altered heart rate) rather than causing an obvious lesion at the site of the original deficiency, illustrating how the heart's specific metabolic dependency (rather than any structural abnormality of its own) determines where a nutritional defect becomes clinically apparent.

1. Glycogen metabolism
- Site: glycogen is the storage form of glucose in liver and muscle (granules in the cytoplasm coated with the synthetic and degradative enzymes).
- Substrates: glycogenesis - glucose-6-phosphate (after a meal, when blood glucose is high) via glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-glucose; glycogenolysis - glycogen and inorganic phosphate.
- Key enzymes and cofactors: glycogenesis - phosphoglucomutase (via glucose-1,6-bisphosphate), UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (UTP; driven by pyrophosphatase hydrolysis of PPi), glycogenin (primer protein carrying a tetrasaccharide of four alpha(1,4)-linked glucose on a tyrosine), glycogen synthase (adds glucose to non-reducing ends by alpha(1,4) bonds) and branching enzyme (amylo-alpha(1,4->1,6)-glucosyl transferase, makes alpha(1,6) branches). Glycogenolysis - glycogen phosphorylase (Pi cleaves alpha(1,4) bonds to glucose-1-phosphate and stops four residues from a branch point, leaving a limit dextrin) and debranching enzyme (amylo-alpha(1,6)-glucosidase; transfers three of the four residues to a nearby non-reducing end and hydrolyses the branch point).
- Regulation: three hormones - insulin, glucagon and epinephrine. Glucagon (low blood sugar) and epinephrine (stress) act through cAMP and protein kinase A: phosphorylase kinase is activated (which activates phosphorylase) and glycogen synthase is inactivated by phosphorylation (also by GSK3 and casein kinase). Insulin lowers cAMP and activates phosphoprotein phosphatase (PP1), inhibiting glycogenolysis and stimulating glycogenesis. Allosteric: in muscle, calcium (released in contraction) and AMP promote phosphorylase b -> a; ATP and glucose-6-phosphate inhibit phosphorylase and glucose-6-phosphate stimulates glycogen synthase; in hepatocytes glucose inhibits phosphorylase.
- Energetics: glycogen synthesis is endergonic and uses activated UDP-glucose (UTP) with irreversible PPi hydrolysis (DeltaG = -33.5 kJ/mol); glycogenolysis by phosphorolysis yields glucose-1-phosphate without ATP.
- Products: glycogenesis - glycogen (highly branched); glycogenolysis - glucose-1-phosphate (then glucose-6-phosphate) and free glucose from debranching; liver glycogen maintains blood glucose between meals.
2. Clinical basis
- Glycogen storage diseases are inherited defects of one or more enzymes of glycogen metabolism.
- Debranching enzyme deficiency: branch points cannot be removed, so glycogen is only partly degraded; abnormal glycogen accumulates in the liver (hepatomegaly) and less glucose is released, giving low blood glucose (hypoglycaemia).
- Von Gierke's disease: lack of glucose-6-phosphatase activity; symptoms are fasting hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis; there is also purine overproduction and hyperuricaemia.
3. Distinctions
- Glycogen synthase builds alpha(1,4) chains from UDP-glucose (needs branching enzyme for alpha(1,6) branches), is inactivated by phosphorylation and stimulated by glucose-6-phosphate; glycogen phosphorylase degrades chains using Pi, is activated by phosphorylation (via phosphorylase kinase), by calcium and AMP (muscle) and inhibited by ATP, glucose-6-phosphate and glucose.
- Liver versus muscle glycogen: between meals blood glucose is maintained by hydrolysis of liver glycogen; in muscle, phosphorylase is additionally activated by calcium released during contraction and by AMP, and glucose-6-phosphatase is found only in liver and kidney (so muscle cannot release free glucose).
questions.question:
1. Describe glycogen metabolism (glycogenesis and glycogenolysis) under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes and cofactors
- Regulation
- Energetics
- Products
2. Explain the clinical basis of glycogen storage diseases, including why debranching enzyme deficiency causes hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia and why von Gierke's disease causes fasting hypoglycaemia.
3. Distinguish between glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase, and between liver and muscle glycogen.

questions.answerText:
1. Structure, synthesis, transport and function
- Structure: glucagon is a peptide/protein hormone (made of amino acid residues, in the same class as insulin).
- Synthesis: secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, released when blood glucose levels are low.
- Transport: like insulin, glucagon is a "general" hormone transported by the circulation to its target tissue, chiefly the liver (hepatocytes bearing glucagon receptors).
- Function: glucagon raises blood glucose - it promotes glycogenolysis and stimulates the liver to release glucose into the blood; biochemically, glucagon binds hepatocyte receptors and raises intracellular cAMP, which (via protein kinase A) activates the phosphatase function of PFK-2 (lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and so inhibiting glycolysis), inactivates liver pyruvate kinase, and triggers a phosphorylation cascade that activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase, favouring glycogen breakdown over synthesis; glucagon also induces synthesis of the gluconeogenic enzymes PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase, favouring gluconeogenesis.
2. Relevant marker of glucagon action
- The insulin/glucagon ratio is the marker used to indicate which pathway (glycolysis/glycogenesis versus gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis) predominates: a high ratio (after a carbohydrate meal) favours glycolysis and glycogen synthesis, while a low ratio (fasting or a high-fat, low-carbohydrate meal) favours gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.
3. Biochemical basis of unopposed/excess glucagon action
- When glucagon action is unopposed (as in insulin deficiency), fructose-2,6-bisphosphate remains low, so PFK-1 is not activated and glycolysis is suppressed while fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is not inhibited, favouring gluconeogenesis; pyruvate kinase remains inactivated, sparing PEP for gluconeogenesis.
- Persistently high glucagon (via cAMP/PKA) keeps glycogen phosphorylase active and glycogen synthase inactive, driving continuous glycogenolysis and depleting hepatic glycogen while glucose output to the blood remains high, contributing to the hyperglycaemia of uncontrolled diabetes.
- Because gluconeogenesis is favoured, glucogenic substrates (lactate, glycerol, amino acids) are increasingly drawn on, and with insulin lacking to restrain lipolysis and ketogenesis, the combination of high glucagon and low insulin promotes ketoacidosis, as covered under ketone body metabolism.
questions.question:
1. Describe the structure, synthesis, transport and function of glucagon.
2. State the relevant laboratory or physiological marker used to assess glucagon's action.
3. Explain the biochemical basis of the metabolic derangements that follow excess or unopposed glucagon action (as in insulin deficiency).

1. Describe glycolysis under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes and cofactors
- Regulation
- Energetics
- Products
2. Explain the clinical basis of why the brain, red blood cells and exercising skeletal muscle are vulnerable when glycolysis or its oxygen-dependent continuation is impaired, including why lactic acid accumulates.
3. Distinguish between hexokinase (isoenzymes I-III) and glucokinase (hexokinase IV).
questions.answerText:
1. Glycolysis
- Site: cytoplasm; occurs at least in part in almost every living cell (Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway); it is an anaerobic process and is highly conserved in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
- Substrates: glucose (or glycogen, via glucose-6-phosphate), NAD+, ADP and Pi. Fructose, galactose and mannose enter as glycolytic intermediates: in liver fructokinase gives fructose-1-phosphate, split by fructose-1-phosphate aldolase into DHAP and glyceraldehyde (then glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate via triose phosphate isomerase and glyceraldehyde kinase), which bypasses hexokinase and PFK-1 so fructose entry is essentially unregulated; in muscle and adipose hexokinase gives fructose-6-phosphate; galactose goes via galactose-1-phosphate/UDP-galactose/UDP-glucose to glucose-6-phosphate; mannose goes via mannose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate.
- Key enzymes and cofactors: hexokinase (Mg2+-ATP), phosphoglucoisomerase, phosphofructokinase-1, aldolase (reverse aldol cleavage), triose phosphate isomerase, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (NAD+, adds Pi), phosphoglycerate kinase, phosphoglycerate mutase, enolase and pyruvate kinase. Stage 1: glucose is phosphorylated twice and cleaved into two glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate; stage 2: glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is converted to pyruvate. Mg2+ stabilises the phosphate groups of ATP.
- Regulation: controlled by the kinetics of the hexokinase isoenzymes and allosteric control of the three irreversible enzymes (hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase). Hexokinase I-III are inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. PFK-1 (most carefully regulated) is inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (made by PFK-2). Pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (feed-forward) and AMP and inhibited by ATP and acetyl-CoA. Insulin (high blood glucose) dephosphorylates PFK-2 so it acts as a kinase, raising fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and glycolytic flux; glucagon (low blood glucose, cAMP, protein kinase A) phosphorylates PFK-2 so it acts as a phosphatase, lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and also inactivates liver pyruvate kinase. Insulin (via SREBP1c) increases synthesis of glucokinase and pyruvate kinase. AMPK is a metabolic master switch.
- Energetics: 2 ATP are used in stage 1 and 4 ATP are made in stage 2, giving a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose; only about 5% of the available energy is captured. Overall: glucose + 2 NAD+ + 2 ADP + 2 Pi -> 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 H+. Complete aerobic oxidation of glucose is estimated at 30-38 ATP (recent estimate 29.85); cytosolic NADH must enter mitochondria by shuttles.
- Products: 2 pyruvate, 2 net ATP, 2 NADH. Aerobically pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA (pyruvate dehydrogenase, giving NADH and CO2) and enters the citric acid cycle; anaerobically it becomes lactate in animal cells (regenerating NAD+) or ethanol + CO2 in yeast, plants and bacteria.
2. Clinical basis
- The brain, red blood cells and exercising skeletal muscle depend on an uninterrupted flow of glucose; brain and red blood cells rely exclusively on glucose as their energy source.
- Red blood cells and other cells that lack mitochondria (or have low oxygen) release lactate, i.e. they depend on glycolysis with lactate formation.
- Without oxygen the electron transport chain stops, NADH builds up and NAD+ runs out; glycolysis stops unless pyruvate is converted to lactate to regenerate NAD+. Anaerobic glycolysis gives only 2 ATP per glucose. Lactic acid builds up in muscle and causes cramps; when oxygen returns lactate is converted back to pyruvate and oxidised.
- Malignant hyperthermia (an inherited disorder triggered by certain anaesthetics): massive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, muscle rigidity, a dramatic rise in body temperature (as high as 112 F) and acidosis from excessive lactic acid; wasteful cycling between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis is a probable contributing factor.
- Because glycolysis has a "turbo design", defects in its regulation can cause substrate-accelerated death (uncontrolled flux traps phosphate in glycolytic intermediates so ATP falls too low), as shown with mutant yeast.
3. Hexokinase I-III versus glucokinase
- Hexokinase I, II, III: found in varying amounts in many tissues and bound to a porin in the outer mitochondrial membrane (ATP readily available); high affinity for glucose (half-saturated below 0.1 mM, versus blood glucose of about 4-5 mM); inhibited by their product glucose-6-phosphate. Result: brain and muscle obtain glucose even when blood glucose is low, and cells do not phosphorylate more glucose than they need.
- Glucokinase (hexokinase IV): found in liver and in certain cells of pancreas, intestine and brain; needs a much higher glucose concentration (about 10 mM); not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate; in liver it diverts glucose to glycogen storage and to maintenance of blood glucose (after a carbohydrate meal the liver removes large amounts of glucose only after other tissues are satisfied).
- Glucokinase does not usually work at maximum velocity, so it is highly sensitive to small changes in blood glucose and acts as a glucose sensor (it initiates insulin release from pancreatic beta-cells). Its activity is regulated by GK regulator protein (binds GK, and moves into the nucleus, when fructose-6-phosphate is high; releases it when glucose rises, by exchange with fructose-1-phosphate) and its synthesis is increased by insulin.

1. Structure, sources, coenzyme forms and function
- Niacin is also referred to as nicotinic acid or nicotinamide; it is mainly found in fish, beef, chicken, turkey and pork, and to a lesser extent in coffee, tea, green vegetables and milk.
- It functions mainly as the coenzymes NAD and NADP, which act as hydrogen donors or electron acceptors in a wide range of redox reactions; it also functions in non-redox roles as a donor of adenosine diphosphate ribose (ADP-ribose).
2. Therapeutic use and monitoring
- Large doses of nicotinic acid are used in the treatment of hypercholesterolaemia, to lower total serum cholesterol and LDL and to increase HDL; the effect is monitored via the lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL) that this therapy is intended to improve.
3. Biochemical basis of deficiency and toxicity
- Classical deficiency of niacin results in pellagra, characterised by dermatitis, dementia, diarrhoea and death ("the four Ds"), with additional neurological and gastrointestinal manifestations; this reflects the essential role of NAD/NADP-dependent redox reactions in energy metabolism and tissue maintenance throughout the body, especially rapidly turning over tissues such as skin, gut and brain.
- Toxic levels of niacin may cause vasodilatory effects, gastrointestinal problems, liver injury, hyperuricaemia, gout, and elevation of plasma glucose concentration, showing that excess of this water-soluble vitamin, though usually excreted, can still produce dose-related adverse effects, particularly at the pharmacological doses used to treat hypercholesterolaemia.
questions.question:
1. Describe the structure, sources, coenzyme forms and function of niacin (vitamin B3).
2. State the therapeutic use of niacin and how its effect is monitored.
3. Explain the biochemical basis of the clinical features of niacin deficiency (pellagra) and of niacin toxicity.

1. Describe the overall biochemical role of the thyroid gland, including its hormone-synthesising follicle cells and its calcium-regulating parafollicular cells, and how these are integrated with other organs.
2. State how disturbances of thyroid function relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why thyroid dysfunction produces effects in distant organs and systems (nervous tissue, bone, cardiovascular system).
questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- The thyroid gland's follicles are its functional units; follicle cells secrete thyroxine, formed by combining tyrosine and iodine into tetraiodothyronine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which circulate bound to thyroid-binding globulin (TBG); thyroid activity is tested via the protein-bound iodine (PBI) test.
- Thyroxine has calorigenic effects (increases catabolism, producing extra body heat - 1 mg of thyroxine increases heat production by about 1000 calories), works with growth hormone to promote growth and development of tissues and organs (nervous tissue is particularly sensitive), and has direct metabolic effects: diuretic action, stimulation of protein and carbohydrate catabolism/cellular uptake, increased nervous system activity, increased heart rate, and (in excess) muscular weakness.
- Separately, the parafollicular cells of the thyroid secrete thyrocalcitonin (TCT/calcitonin), which decreases excretion of calcium and phosphate ions and increases osteoblast activity (calcium and phosphate deposition in bone) - directly linking thyroid gland function to bone mineral metabolism, complementing (and generally opposing) parathyroid hormone.
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- Hyperthyroidism (e.g. Graves' disease) shows elevated PBI, nervousness and irritability, and exophthalmos (oedema behind the eyes).
- Hypothyroidism occurring during fetal/early development causes cretinism (reduced metabolism, reduced growth, mental retardation); occurring in adult life it causes myxedema (reduced metabolism, reduced mental and physical activity, increased blood pressure, and accumulation of subcutaneous fluids).
3. Basis of distant organ/system effects
- Because thyroid hormone acts on nearly every tissue's metabolic rate and specifically affects nervous tissue development, thyroid hormone deficiency in early life produces its most serious functional deficit in the brain/nervous system (mental retardation) rather than in the thyroid gland itself; in adults, thyroid dysfunction is expressed through cardiovascular changes (altered heart rate, blood pressure) and connective/subcutaneous tissue (myxedematous fluid accumulation); and through calcitonin, thyroid gland activity is also linked to bone mineral deposition, so thyroid disease can have downstream skeletal consequences distant from the gland itself.

questions.question:
1. Describe the overall biochemical role of the kidney, including its main pathways in mineral, water and glucose handling and how they are integrated.
2. State how disturbances of these renal pathways relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why a renal transport defect produces effects in a distant organ or system and causes functional deficit there.
questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- Water handling: the kidney reabsorbs water from the glomerular filtrate using aquaporins (water-channel proteins, seven isoforms), recovering water at specific sites along the nephron; AQP2 is a key isoform in this process.
- Calcium handling: the major path of calcium reabsorption occurs in the proximal convoluted tubule and the ascending limb of Henle's loop (with the remainder reabsorbed more distally); calcium and sodium share a common active-transport pathway in the proximal tubule, whereas distal tubular calcium reabsorption is independent of sodium. Renal tubular reabsorption of calcium is increased by parathyroid hormone (PTH); overall calcium homeostasis balances bone resorption, intestinal absorption and renal tubular reabsorption against skeletal formation, renal excretion and intestinal excretion.
- Phosphate handling: dietary phosphate not absorbed is excreted; renal excretion of phosphate is much greater than that of calcium because dietary phosphate is absorbed to a greater extent; with normal renal function, urinary phosphate is about two-thirds of dietary phosphate, and its tubular reabsorption is regulated to control circulating phosphate levels.
- Glucose handling: the kidney, along with the liver, is a site where the final step common to gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis (release of free glucose by glucose-6-phosphatase) occurs, linking renal metabolism to whole-body glucose homeostasis.
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- Low levels of the aquaporin AQP2 in the kidney impair water reabsorption and produce nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, with dilute polyuria despite normal or high antidiuretic hormone.
- Because the kidney (like the liver) requires glucose-6-phosphatase to release free glucose from gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke's disease) affects renal as well as hepatic glucose release.
3. Basis of a distant-organ/system effect
- Because the kidney's calcium reabsorption works together with PTH-driven bone resorption and calcitriol-driven intestinal absorption to set whole-body blood calcium, a defect in renal calcium handling disturbs calcium available to distant tissues that depend on tightly regulated blood calcium for function - such as neuromuscular tissue, where hypocalcaemia produces tetany (muscle spasms and convulsions), illustrating how a renal transport defect can produce a functional deficit in a system (neuromuscular) anatomically remote from the kidney itself.

1. Gluconeogenesis
- Site: primarily the liver; under certain conditions (metabolic acidosis, starvation) the kidney can make small amounts of new glucose. Glucose-6-phosphatase is found only in liver and kidney. Pyruvate carboxylase is found within mitochondria.
- Substrates: noncarbohydrate precursors - lactate (from red blood cells and other cells lacking mitochondria, and from exercising muscle via the Cori cycle), pyruvate, glycerol (from fat metabolism in adipose tissue; converted by glycerol kinase to glycerol-3-phosphate, then oxidised to DHAP when cytoplasmic NAD+ is high), and glucogenic amino acids/alpha-keto acids, of which alanine is perhaps the most important (glucose-alanine cycle).
- Key enzymes and cofactors: the sequence is largely the reverse of glycolysis except for three bypass reactions of the irreversible glycolytic steps: (i) pyruvate carboxylase (biotin, ATP, CO2) converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate and PEP carboxykinase (GTP) converts oxaloacetate to PEP; (ii) fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase converts fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate (irreversible, DeltaG = -16.7 kJ/mol); (iii) glucose-6-phosphatase converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose, which is released into the blood.
- Regulation: driven by substrate availability (high lactate, glycerol and amino acids - high-fat diet, starvation, prolonged fasting), allosteric effectors and hormones. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is activated by citrate and inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; acetyl-CoA (high in starvation) activates pyruvate carboxylase; pyruvate kinase inhibition (glucagon, cAMP-dependent phosphorylation) retains PEP. Glucagon lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (releasing inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase) and induces PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase; cortisol stimulates synthesis of gluconeogenic enzymes; insulin depresses their synthesis (via SREBP1c). The insulin/glucagon ratio decides the direction of flux (high after a carbohydrate meal - glycolysis; low in fasting or a high-fat, low-carbohydrate meal - gluconeogenesis). High AMP favours glycolysis; low AMP favours gluconeogenesis.
- Energetics: energy-consuming; instead of generating ATP it needs hydrolysis of six high-energy phosphate bonds (2 pyruvate + 4 ATP + 2 GTP + 2 NADH + 6 H2O -> glucose + 4 ADP + 2 GDP + 2 NAD+ + 6 Pi).
- Products: new glucose released into the blood (with maintenance of blood glucose between meals once liver glycogen is depleted by prolonged fasting or vigorous exercise).
2. Clinical basis
- Brain and red blood cells rely exclusively on glucose, so failure to maintain blood glucose threatens them first; between meals blood glucose is maintained by liver glycogen breakdown, and when this is depleted gluconeogenesis supplies glucose.
- In von Gierke's disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency) glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose, which is the final step of both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in liver and kidney; free glucose cannot be released to the blood, giving fasting hypoglycaemia.
- Lactic acidosis is a prominent symptom of the disease (it is also associated with it in purine metabolism); lactate is a gluconeogenic precursor that cannot be converted to free glucose when glucose-6-phosphatase is missing.
- Associated purine overproduction and hyperuricaemia: enhanced generation of ribose 5-phosphate (PRPP precursor); the lactic acidosis elevates the renal threshold for urate, raising total body urates.
3. Cori cycle versus glucose-alanine cycle
- Cori cycle: lactate is produced anaerobically in skeletal muscle during strenuous exercise (and by red blood cells), travels in blood to the liver, is reconverted to pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase and then to glucose by gluconeogenesis.
- Glucose-alanine cycle: exercising muscle converts pyruvate to alanine by transamination with glutamate (alanine transaminase); alanine goes to the liver, is reconverted to pyruvate (and alpha-ketoglutarate to restore amino acid balance) and then to glucose. Besides recycling alpha-keto acids it transports amino nitrogen to the liver, where it enters urea (muscle cannot synthesise urea).
- Difference: the Cori cycle carries carbon skeletons as lactate; the glucose-alanine cycle carries carbon plus amino nitrogen as alanine.
questions.question:
1. Describe gluconeogenesis under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes and cofactors
- Regulation
- Energetics
- Products
2. Explain the biochemical basis of fasting hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis in von Gierke's disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency), and why the brain and red blood cells are most at risk when gluconeogenesis fails.
3. Distinguish between the Cori cycle and the glucose-alanine cycle.

1. Describe the alternative fatty acid oxidation pathways (alpha-oxidation, omega-oxidation and peroxisomal oxidation) under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes and cofactors
- Regulation or induction
- Energetics
- Products
2. Explain the clinical basis of Refsum's disease and Zellweger syndrome, including why tissues such as brain, liver and kidney are affected.
3. Distinguish between alpha-oxidation, beta-oxidation and omega-oxidation.
questions.answerText:
1. Alternative fatty acid oxidation
- Site: alpha-oxidation - removes carbons one at a time from the carboxyl end; omega-oxidation - endoplasmic reticulum of liver and kidney in vertebrates; peroxisomal beta-oxidation - peroxisomes (plants: major site).
- Substrates: alpha-oxidation - fatty acids with a methyl group on the beta-carbon that blocks beta-oxidation, notably phytanic acid (from dietary phytol/chlorophyll; milk is a good source); omega-oxidation - the omega (terminal) carbon of fatty acids; peroxisomal - very-long-chain fatty acids (C26-C36).
- Key enzymes and cofactors: phytanic acid alpha-hydroxylase (phytanic acid oxidase, "phytate alpha-oxidase") gives CO2 and pristanic acid (an odd-chain acid) which is then completely oxidised by beta-oxidation; peroxisomal flavoprotein acyl-CoA oxidase passes electrons directly to O2 forming H2O2, cleaved by catalase.
- Regulation or induction: peroxisomal oxidation is induced by a high-fat diet and hypolipidaemic drugs (e.g. clofibrate); omega-oxidation is normally minor but becomes more important when beta-oxidation is defective (mutation or carnitine deficiency).
- Energetics: no ATP is produced in alpha-oxidation; in peroxisomes the energy of the first oxidative step is dissipated as heat.
- Products: alpha-oxidation yields CO2 and odd-chain pristanic acid and is used to synthesise alpha-hydroxy fatty acids such as cerebronic acid of brain, cerebrosides and sulphatides, and odd-carbon long-chain fatty acids of brain sphingolipids.
2. Clinical basis
- Refsum's disease: lack of alpha-hydroxylase (phytanic acid oxidase), so alpha-oxidation does not occur and phytanic acid accumulates in tissues; presents with severe neurological symptoms, polyneuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, nerve deafness and cerebellar ataxia; symptoms regress with restricted dietary phytanic acid (avoid milk).
- Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome): absence of peroxisomes in almost all tissues, so very-long-chain fatty acids (C26-C36) cannot be oxidised and accumulate in tissues, particularly brain, liver and kidney.
3. Distinctions
- Alpha-oxidation removes one carbon at a time from the carboxyl end, is used when a methyl group on the beta-carbon blocks beta-oxidation (branched fatty acids such as phytanic acid), and makes no ATP.
- Beta-oxidation removes two-carbon units (acetyl-CoA) starting at the carboxyl end, mainly mitochondrial, ATP-yielding.
- Omega-oxidation acts on the terminal (omega) carbon in the endoplasmic reticulum, a minor pathway.

1. Structure, synthesis, transport and function
- Structure: PTH is classed among the peptide/protein hormones.
- Synthesis: secreted by the parathyroid glands - 4 or 5 small round bodies on the posterior surface of the lateral lobes of the thyroid gland.
- Transport: as a general circulating hormone, PTH is carried by the blood to its target tissues (intestine, kidney and bone).
- Function: PTH controls blood calcium homeostasis - it increases calcium and magnesium absorption from the intestines, kidneys and bone (raising blood calcium), increases renal tubular reabsorption of calcium, increases the rate of dissolution of both the organic and inorganic phases of bone, and increases phosphate excretion (lowering blood phosphate levels).
2. Relevant laboratory investigation
- Serum/plasma calcium concentration is the key laboratory correlate of PTH activity (normal total plasma calcium 2.25-2.75 mM, average 2.5 mM); PTH excess or deficiency is inferred from resulting hypercalcaemia or hypocalcaemia, and a hyperfunctioning parathyroid adenoma is identified as a cause of hypercalcaemia.
3. Biochemical basis of parathyroid disorders
- Hypoparathyroidism (PTH hyposecretion) causes hypocalcaemia, which results in tetany - muscle spasms and convulsions - reflecting calcium's role in neuromuscular excitability and transmission of nerve impulses.
- Hyperparathyroidism (PTH hypersecretion, e.g. from a primary hyperparathyroid adenoma) causes hypercalcaemia and drives excessive bone dissolution, producing a fibrous bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica, also called Von Recklinghausen's disease of bone), consistent with PTH's action of increasing the rate of dissolution of bone's organic and inorganic phases.
- Calcitriol (activated vitamin D) acts alongside PTH by stimulating intestinal absorption of calcium; in vitamin D deficiency, new bone formation slows and bone remodelling is impaired, compounding calcium-homeostasis disorders.
questions.question:
1. Describe the structure, synthesis, transport and function of parathyroid hormone (PTH).
2. State the relevant laboratory investigation for disorders of PTH secretion and how it is interpreted.
3. Explain the biochemical basis of the clinical features of hypoparathyroidism and hyperparathyroidism.

1. Describe the structure, sources, coenzyme forms and function of vitamin B12 (cobalamin), together with folate.
2. State the relevant laboratory findings used to identify vitamin B12/folate deficiency.
3. Explain the biochemical basis of the megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia and neurological features seen in vitamin B12 deficiency, and why it differs from folate deficiency.
questions.answerText:
1. Structure, sources, coenzyme forms and function
- Cobalamin (vitamin B12): the only dietary sources for humans are animal products (meat, meat products, poultry, fish, shellfish, egg yolk; lesser amounts in milk and milk products), because animals derive their vitamin B12 from microorganisms, the only source of naturally occurring vitamin B12. It functions as the coenzyme methylcobalamin in the conversion of homocysteine to methionine, and as adenosylcobalamin in the conversion of L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA (a Krebs cycle intermediate).
- Folate (folic acid): found especially in green vegetables, mushrooms, legumes, citrus fruits and liver (raw foods contain more than cooked, due to cooking losses); folate and cobalamin derivatives act as freely diffusing one-carbon carriers, functioning as coenzymes in mitochondria and cytosol to accept one-carbon groups generated from amino acid metabolism; folate is involved in metabolism of histidine, serine, glycine and methionine, and in purine and pyrimidine/nucleotide synthesis. Folate and vitamin B12 are both required for cell multiplication/assembling amino acids into protein, and folate helps B12 enter cells.
2. Relevant laboratory findings
- Folate deficiency is characterised initially by low plasma folate, followed by diminished RBC folate concentration, megaloblastic bone marrow cells, increased mean cell volume (MCV), and hypersegmentation of neutrophils, along with decreased blood cell count.
- Vitamin B12 deficiency shows an analogous sequence - initially low serum B12 concentration, then low cell concentration, and finally decreased DNA synthesis with elevated serum homocysteine and methylmalonic acid concentrations, culminating in anaemia.
3. Biochemical basis of the anaemia and neurological features
- Both vitamins are needed for DNA synthesis (via one-carbon transfer reactions), so deficiency of either impairs nuclear maturation in rapidly dividing bone marrow precursors while cytoplasmic (haemoglobin) maturation continues relatively normally, producing large, immature red cells released into the circulation - megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia - with associated fatigue, headache, irritability and shortness of breath.
- Because methylcobalamin is specifically needed to convert homocysteine to methionine, and adenosylcobalamin is needed to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, B12 deficiency additionally raises both serum homocysteine and methylmalonic acid (folate deficiency raises homocysteine but not methylmalonic acid, since folate is not required for the methylmalonyl-CoA reaction).
- Vitamin B12 deficiency is additionally associated with skin pallor, fatigue, insomnia, tingling and numbness in the extremities, loss of concentration, memory loss, disorientation, abnormal gait, and possibly dementia - neurological features not produced by folate deficiency alone, reflecting cobalamin's additional role that folate cannot substitute for.

1. Pyrimidine and deoxyribonucleotide synthesis
- Site: cytosolic carbamoyl phosphate synthase II starts the pathway; five of the first six enzyme activities reside on multifunctional polypeptides.
- Substrates: carbamoyl phosphate, aspartate, PRPP (added to the preformed base orotic acid), ATP/GTP, N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate (for thymidylate).
- Key enzymes and cofactors: carbamoyl phosphate synthase II; aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase); orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (orotate + PRPP -> orotidine monophosphate, OMP); OMP decarboxylase (-> UMP); UMP phosphorylated twice to UTP; CTP synthase (UTP -> CTP). Ribonucleotide reductase reduces the 2'-position of NDPs (hydride replaces 2'-OH) to make deoxyribonucleotides; thymidylate synthase converts dUMP to dTMP using N5,N10-methylene-THF (the only step needing a folate derivative; THF is oxidised to dihydrofolate); dihydrofolate reductase regenerates THF. Salvage: uridine/cytidine/thymidine/deoxycytidine kinases and thymidine kinase (activity rises with the cell cycle).
- Regulation: mainly at the first step, aspartate transcarbamoylase (inhibited by CTP, activated by ATP); OMP decarboxylase competitively inhibited by UMP (and CMP); CTP synthase inhibited by CTP and activated by GTP.
- Products: UMP, UTP, CTP, and dTMP/dTTP; deoxyribonucleotides serve only as DNA precursors.
2. Clinical basis
- Dividing cells must generate TMP and dihydrofolate and are therefore especially sensitive to DHFR inhibitors such as the anticancer drug methotrexate (also aminopterin, trimethoprim - all folic acid analogues). Methotrexate inhibits DHFR, depleting reduced folates, indirectly inhibiting thymidylate synthase, and reducing purine and pyrimidine synthesis and ultimately DNA synthesis.
- 5-Fluorouracil and 5-fluorodeoxyuridine are converted to FdUMP, a suicide substrate that irreversibly inhibits thymidylate synthase.
- Antimetabolites are toxic to normal cells, especially bone marrow and gastrointestinal tract (adverse effects: bone marrow suppression, GI effects, alopecia, hepatotoxicity); they are used for leukaemias, solid tumours, and (methotrexate, azathioprine) autoimmune disease.
3. Purine versus pyrimidine synthesis
- Pyrimidine ring is assembled as a free base and PRPP is added afterwards (orotic acid -> OMP -> UMP); purine ring is built up on PRPP.
- No branch in pyrimidine synthesis (UMP -> UTP -> CTP); purine pathway branches from IMP to AMP and GMP.
- Regulation: pyrimidines at ATCase (first step) versus purines at PRPP synthetase and amidotransferase.

1. Describe the overall biochemical role of the pancreas, including its endocrine and exocrine pathways and how they are integrated.
2. State how disturbances of pancreatic function relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why a pancreatic (endocrine) defect produces effects in distant organs and causes functional deficit there.
questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- Endocrine function: the islets of Langerhans contain beta cells, which secrete insulin in response to rising blood glucose (glucokinase acting as the glucose sensor) and promote glucose uptake, glycogenesis, protein synthesis and lipogenesis; and alpha cells, which secrete glucagon in response to falling blood glucose and promote glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. The insulin/glucagon ratio set by these two cell types is the principal hormonal switch between the fed (anabolic, glycolytic) and fasted (catabolic, gluconeogenic) states throughout the body.
- Exocrine function: the pancreas secretes digestive enzymes into the small intestine, including pancreatic alpha-amylase (carbohydrate digestion, yielding maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins), pancreatic lipase (with its cofactor colipase, hydrolysing triacylglycerols to 2-monoacylglycerols and free fatty acids), and the proteolytic zymogens trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase (activated in the intestine, trypsinogen by enteropeptidase and the others by trypsin).
- Integration: the exocrine pancreas supplies the enzymes needed to digest a meal into absorbable glucose, fatty acids/monoacylglycerols and amino acids, while the endocrine pancreas (via insulin) directs the tissues (liver, muscle, adipose) to take up and store these absorbed nutrients, linking digestion directly to fuel storage and later fuel release.
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- Hyposecretion of insulin (from beta cell failure) causes diabetes mellitus, with the cardinal signs of polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia, reflecting hyperglycaemia and the inability of insulin-sensitive tissues to take up glucose.
- Because insulin normally restrains lipolysis and ketogenesis, insulin deficiency allows unrestrained fat mobilisation and hepatic ketone body overproduction, leading to ketoacidosis in severe or untreated diabetes.
3. Basis of distant-organ effects
- Because insulin and glucagon are general hormones transported by the circulation, a defect confined to the pancreatic islets (loss of beta cell insulin secretion) removes glucose-uptake signalling from muscle and adipose tissue and removes restraint on hepatic glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis; the resulting hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis produce functional deficits in organs anatomically distant from the pancreas - for example cerebral dysfunction from ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemia - illustrating how a single-organ endocrine defect is expressed system-wide through the hormone's action on its distal target tissues.

questions.question:
1. Describe DNA replication under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes
- Basic rules/regulation
- Stages
2. Explain the biochemical basis of why replication is semi-discontinuous (leading versus lagging strand) and why Okazaki fragments and RNA primers are required.
3. Distinguish between the roles of DNA polymerase I and DNA polymerase III in replication.
questions.answerText:
1. DNA replication
- Site: the nucleus (chromosomal DNA); replication begins at defined origins - a single origin site in prokaryotes (e.g. oriC in E. coli) but multiple origins/replicators in eukaryotes (e.g. ARS, autonomously replicating sequences, in yeast).
- Substrates: the 5'-triphosphates of deoxyadenosine, deoxycytidine, deoxyguanosine and thymidine (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP), Mg2+, the parental DNA strands as templates, and a short RNA primer synthesized at the start of each new strand.
- Key enzymes: DNA helicase (energy-dependent unwinding of the duplex) and DNA gyrase/topoisomerases (relieve supercoiling), helix-destabilising protein (prevents rewinding), RNA primase/RNA polymerase (synthesises the RNA primer), DNA polymerase III (main chain-elongating polymerase in the elongation stage), RNase H (removes RNA primers) and DNA polymerase I (fills the resulting gaps with DNA and has proof-reading activity), and DNA ligase (joins the DNA fragments by forming a phosphodiester bond between a 3'-OH and a 5'-phosphate).
- Basic rules/regulation: replication is semi-conservative (each daughter duplex retains one parental strand as template), starts at the origin, proceeds always in the 5' to 3' direction, can be uni- or bidirectional, and is semi-discontinuous; origins are recognised by DNA replication initiator proteins, which effectively regulate when and where replication begins.
- Stages: (1) pre-priming - unwinding of the helix at the origin by helicase/gyrase; (2) priming - synthesis of a short RNA primer complementary to the 3' end of the template by primase; (3) elongation - DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides to the 3' end of the primer; (4) termination - RNA primers are removed by RNase H and replaced with DNA by DNA polymerase I (with proof-reading), and DNA ligase seals the remaining nicks between fragments.
2. Biochemical basis of semi-discontinuous synthesis
- DNA synthesis occurs only in the 5' to 3' direction because new nucleotides are added to a free 3'-OH group; since the two parental strands are antiparallel, only one strand (the leading strand, with its template running 3' to 5' relative to synthesis) can be copied continuously in the same direction as the replication fork opens.
- The other strand (the lagging strand) has its template oriented so that continuous synthesis in the 5' to 3' direction would run opposite to the direction the fork is opening; it is therefore copied discontinuously as a series of short (about 1000 base) fragments called Okazaki fragments, each requiring its own RNA primer to give DNA polymerase a 3'-OH to extend from, since DNA polymerases cannot start a new chain unaided.
- Because DNA polymerase cannot initiate synthesis de novo, an RNA primer (made by primase) is required at the start of the leading strand and at the start of every Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand; these primers are later excised (RNase H/DNA polymerase I) and replaced with DNA, and ligase joins the fragments into a continuous strand.
3. DNA polymerase I versus DNA polymerase III
- DNA polymerase III is the principal enzyme of the elongation stage, adding the bulk of new nucleotides to the growing DNA strand at the 3' end of the primer.
- DNA polymerase I acts mainly in the termination stage: it removes the RNA primers (in conjunction with RNase H) and fills the gaps left behind with DNA, and it carries out proof-reading activity that removes misincorporated bases, so replication fidelity is maintained.

1. Structure, sources and coenzyme function
- Vitamin B6 exists as several vitamers: pyridoxine (alcohol form), pyridoxal (aldehyde form) and pyridoxamine (amine form); pyridoxine is the most stable form, and its phosphorylated form is found in plants, while pyridoxal phosphate and pyridoxamine phosphate are found in animal products. It is mainly found in meat, whole grain products, vegetables, fruits and nuts, though substantial amounts are lost through food processing.
- Vitamin B6 functions as the coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) in amino acid metabolism, and also in the action of steroid hormones and in gene expression; PLP is used as a prosthetic group by glycogen phosphorylase and by most enzymes that alter the alpha-carbon of amino acids.
2. Biochemical basis of the requirement in amino acid metabolism
- PLP-dependent enzymes are involved as coenzymes in transamination, decarboxylation, cleavage, racemisation, transulfhydration and desulfhydration reactions of amino acids; all transaminases (aminotransferases), for instance, require PLP derived from vitamin B6 to catalyse the transfer of an amino group between an amino acid and a keto acid.
3. Biochemical basis of at-risk groups and deficiency
- Groups particularly at risk of vitamin B6 deficiency include the elderly (due to poor dietary intake), alcoholics (because excessive alcohol impairs the conversion of pyridoxine and pyridoxamine to PLP), renal patients on dialysis (abnormal loss of vitamin B6), and patients on drugs such as corticosteroids and anticonvulsants.
- Because PLP is required for so many amino acid-metabolising and neurotransmitter-related reactions, signs of deficiency include sleepiness, fatigue and neurological problems, reflecting impaired PLP-dependent enzyme activity in tissues (including the nervous system) with high demand for amino acid interconversion.
questions.question:
1. Describe the structure, sources and coenzyme function of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine and related vitamers).
2. State the biochemical basis for vitamin B6's requirement in amino acid metabolism.
3. Explain the biochemical basis of why certain groups are at particular risk of vitamin B6 deficiency, and the resulting clinical features.

questions.answerText:
1. Structure, synthesis, transport and function
- Structure: lipoproteins are the water-soluble form in which lipids (triacylglycerols, cholesterol) are carried in blood - spherical particles with a polar surface and a non-polar inner core.
- Synthesis: triacylglycerols are combined with membrane- and water-soluble proteins in intestinal cells to form chylomicrons; the liver synthesises VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein, carrying triglycerides and cholesterol).
- Transport: chylomicrons carry triacylglycerols from intestinal cells into the bloodstream via the lymphatic system; in the bloodstream, triacylglycerols are hydrolysed to glycerol and fatty acids, which are absorbed by cells and either processed for energy (via acetyl-CoA) or stored in adipose tissue. VLDL, LDL (low-density lipoprotein, "bad cholesterol") and HDL (high-density lipoprotein, "good cholesterol") each transport triglycerides and/or cholesterol between the liver, intestine, fat storage and peripheral tissues.
- Function: lipoproteins transport lipids through the bloodstream to tissues where they are stored, used for energy, or used to make hormones (steroid hormones are derived from cholesterol carried in this way).
2. Relevant laboratory investigation
- The lipid profile is used to assess lipoprotein status: recommended levels are HDL greater than 40 mg/dL, LDL less than 100 mg/dL, and total serum cholesterol less than 200 mg/dL; values outside these ranges (particularly high LDL/total cholesterol or low HDL) indicate an adverse lipoprotein profile.
3. Biochemical basis of atherosclerosis
- Cholesterol is insoluble in blood, and when present in excess (particularly as LDL cholesterol) it clogs arteries by forming plaque, since insoluble cholesterol accumulates within the vessel wall; saturated fats stimulate cholesterol synthesis in the liver, which can lead to cholesterol plaques building up inside arteries, restricting blood flow and providing the biochemical basis for atherosclerosis, while HDL ("good cholesterol") is associated with protection, consistent with the recommended direction of change in the lipid profile (raise HDL, lower LDL/total cholesterol).
questions.question:
1. Describe the structure, synthesis, transport and function of plasma lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL, HDL).
2. State the relevant laboratory investigation (lipid profile) used to assess lipoprotein status and how it is interpreted.
3. Explain the biochemical basis of atherosclerosis arising from disturbed lipoprotein/cholesterol handling.

questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
- Carbohydrate digestion: salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth (halted in the stomach by acid); the small intestine carries out most carbohydrate digestion via pancreatic alpha-amylase, which yields mainly maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins; brush-border disaccharidases (maltase, sucrase-isomaltase, lactase, trehalase) then hydrolyse these to monosaccharides, which are absorbed (glucose is about 99% absorbed).
- Fat digestion: dietary triacylglycerols and phospholipids must be emulsified into micelles before absorption; lingual and gastric lipases begin hydrolysis, but pancreatic lipase (with its cofactor colipase) in the small intestine is the major enzyme, acting on the 1 and 3 positions to yield 2-monoacylglycerols and free fatty acids; bile salts from the liver enable emulsification; fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and other lipids (including cholesterol) are absorbed dissolved in these micelles, so absorption of fat-soluble vitamins is impaired on a very low-fat diet.
- Protein digestion: endopeptidases (pepsin in the stomach; trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase from the pancreas) cleave internal peptide bonds; exopeptidases (carboxypeptidases from pancreatic juice, aminopeptidases from intestinal mucosal cells) remove terminal amino acids; brush-border dipeptidases complete digestion of dipeptides; all these proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens, activated by removal of a masking peptide (pepsinogen by gastric acid/autocatalysis; trypsinogen by enteropeptidase; trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase).
- Absorption: occurs mainly at the intestinal villi, where lymph and blood vessels transport absorbed glucose, amino acids and lipid products (as chylomicrons, via the lymphatics) into the circulatory system for distribution to body cells; the large intestine mainly absorbs water and completes fermentation of any undigested carbohydrate by bacteria.
2. Disturbances and common pathologies
- On a very low-fat diet, absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) is impaired, since they depend on micelle formation together with dietary fat.
- Because digestive proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens requiring sequential activation (enteropeptidase activating trypsinogen, trypsin activating the rest), failure of this activation cascade would impair protein digestion broadly.
3. Basis of distant organ/system effects
- Because the products of intestinal digestion (glucose, amino acids, chylomicron lipids) are the substrates that liver, muscle and adipose tissue depend on for fuel storage and synthesis, and because fat-soluble vitamin absorption depends on normal fat digestion/emulsification, a defect confined to the intestine (e.g. impaired fat digestion/absorption) produces its functional deficit in distant organs and systems that depend on those vitamins and nutrients - for example vitamin K malabsorption impairing hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and causing a bleeding disorder, or vitamin A/D malabsorption producing visual or bone disease - even though the primary lesion is in the gut.
questions.question:
1. Describe the overall biochemical role of the small intestine, including its digestive and absorptive pathways for carbohydrate, fat and protein, and how they are integrated.
2. State how disturbances of intestinal digestion/absorption relate to common pathologies.
3. Explain why a defect in intestinal digestion produces effects in distant organs and systems.

1. Describe de novo purine nucleotide biosynthesis and its salvage under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes and cofactors
- Regulation
- Energetics
- Products
2. Explain the clinical basis of gout and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (and other disorders of purine catabolism), and why brain, erythrocytes and leukocytes depend on salvage.
3. Distinguish between the de novo and salvage pathways of purine synthesis.
questions.answerText:
1. Purine nucleotide biosynthesis
- Site: liver is the major site; the enzymes of eukaryotes are multifunctional polypeptides that channel intermediates.
- Substrates: ribose-5-phosphate (-> PRPP), glycine (C4, C5, N7), aspartate (N1), glutamine (N3, N9), tetrahydrofolate derivatives (C2 and C8) and CO2 (C6); ATP.
- Key enzymes and cofactors: PRPP synthetase (ATP, Mg2+) -> PRPP; PRPP glutamyl (amido)transferase (glutamine displaces PPi, giving 5-phosphoribosylamine); then glycinamide synthetase, transformylases (folate), formylglycinamidine synthetase, aminoimidazole synthetase, carboxylase (biotin-independent), synthetase (aspartate), lyase (releases fumarate), second transformylase and cyclohydrolase, giving IMP; then separate branches to AMP (adenylosuccinate synthase, requires GTP) and GMP (IMP dehydrogenase, XMP, requires ATP); ATP-dependent kinases (adenylate kinase, guanylate kinase) then form di- and triphosphates.
- Regulation: PRPP concentration is the major determinant of rate; PRPP synthetase is feedback-inhibited by AMP, ADP, GMP and GDP; PRPP amidotransferase is inhibited by ATP/ADP/AMP at one site and GTP/GDP/GMP at another; AMP and GMP feedback-inhibit adenylosuccinate synthase and IMP dehydrogenase; cross-regulation (excess ATP speeds GMP synthesis, excess GTP speeds AMP synthesis); AMP and GMP inhibit HGPRT.
- Energetics: six high-energy bonds are used to form IMP from ribose-5-phosphate.
- Products: IMP, then AMP and GMP (and ADP, GDP, GTP; ADP -> ATP mainly by oxidative phosphorylation).
2. Clinical basis
- Gout: metabolic disorder of purine catabolism; genetic defects of PRPP synthetase (higher Vmax, higher affinity for ribose-5-phosphate or resistance to feedback inhibition) cause purine overproduction; serum urate exceeds its solubility so sodium urate crystallises in soft tissues and joints causing gouty arthritis (uric acid and urate salts are insoluble); most cases reflect abnormal renal handling of uric acid. Three enzyme defects lead to gout: PRPP synthetase (activity up), HGPRT (deficiency), glucose-6-phosphatase (deficiency). Allopurinol (an analogue of hypoxanthine) inhibits xanthine oxidase.
- Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: defect in hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (X-linked); intracellular PRPP rises, causing purine overproduction, hyperuricaemia, uric acid stones, severe nervous system malfunction and self-mutilation; death usually before age 20.
- Von Gierke's disease: hyperuricaemia from excess ribose-5-phosphate and lactic acidosis raising the renal threshold for urate.
- Xanthine oxidase deficiency: hypouricaemia with raised hypoxanthine and xanthine (xanthinuria, xanthine stones). ADA deficiency causes SCID (about 30% of SCID; B and T lymphocytes fail to proliferate); PNP deficiency causes immunodeficiency.
- Brain has a low level of PRPP amidotransferase and depends partly on exogenous purines; erythrocytes and polymorphonuclear leukocytes cannot synthesise 5-phosphoribosylamine so use exogenous purines; the liver supplies purines for salvage.
3. De novo versus salvage
- De novo: from amphibolic precursors, requires six high-energy bonds and PRPP amidotransferase.
- Salvage: phosphoribosylation of free purines (adenine -> AMP; hypoxanthine and guanine -> IMP/GMP by phosphoribosyltransferases) by PRPP, or phosphoryl transfer from ATP to nucleosides (adenosine kinase, deoxycytidine kinase); requires far less energy. There is no dietary requirement for nucleotides because of salvage.

1. Electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation
- Site: inner mitochondrial membrane in eukaryotes (plasma membrane in prokaryotes; thylakoid membrane in chloroplasts).
- Substrates: NADH and FADH2 (succinate), oxygen (terminal electron acceptor), ADP and Pi.
- Key enzymes, complexes and cofactors: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase / NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase; more than 43 polypeptides, FMN and at least 6 Fe-S centres; passes electrons to coenzyme Q and pumps 4 H+); Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, FAD, Fe-S; feeds Q but pumps no protons; also called ETF:ubiquinone oxidoreductase for fatty acid oxidation); Complex III (cytochrome bc1, Q cycle, passes electrons to cytochrome c; 6 protons in total translocated per the Q cycle); Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase; hemes a and a3, copper CuA and CuB; four-electron reduction of O2 to 2 H2O). Carriers: NAD-linked dehydrogenases, flavoproteins (FAD, FMN), lipid-soluble coenzyme Q (ubiquinone -> ubiquinol), water-soluble cytochromes (heme) and iron-sulfur proteins. ATP synthase (F1F0-ATPase, sometimes called Complex V): F0 is the proton channel with a rotating c-ring, F1 (alpha3beta3 gamma delta epsilon) catalyses ATP synthesis; the three beta subunits pass through three conformations.
- Regulation or coupling: chemiosmotic (Mitchell) hypothesis - electron transfer pumps protons out of the matrix, creating a proton-motive force (matrix more negative and more alkaline); ATP synthase couples proton re-entry to ATP synthesis. ATP-ADP translocase exports ATP (each ATP exported costs one H+; making and exporting 1 ATP costs about 4 H+). Cytosolic NADH cannot cross the membrane and uses shuttles.
- Energetics: released free energy is stored as the proton gradient; older figures NADH = 3 ATP and FADH2 = 2 ATP; newer table figures NADH = 2.5 ATP and FADH2 = 1.5 ATP. Total 30-38 ATP per glucose (recent estimate 29.85).
- Products: ATP, NAD+, FAD, and water (from O2).
2. Clinical and toxicological basis
- Inhibitors: rotenone blocks Complex I; antimycin A blocks Complex III; cyanide and carbon monoxide block Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase); oligomycin and atractyloside block oxidative phosphorylation at ATP synthase and the ATP/ADP translocase respectively. Blocking the chain stops proton pumping and ATP synthesis; NADH and FADH2 cannot be reoxidised.
- Uncouplers (e.g. FCCP, 2,4-dinitrophenol) disrupt coupling of electron transport and ATP synthase; at high doses they are lethal.
- Thermogenin (uncoupling protein) in brown adipose tissue provides an alternative proton flow back into the matrix, producing heat instead of ATP (useful thermogenesis).
- Electron leakage: a small percentage of electrons leak directly to oxygen forming superoxide, mainly at Complex I (and at Complex III when electron transfer is reduced by a high membrane potential or antimycin A), contributing to oxidative stress implicated in a number of diseases and aging.
- Inhibition of ATP synthesis also dissipates the Na+/H+ gradient and stops secondary active transport.
3. Glycerophosphate shuttle versus malate-aspartate shuttle
- Glycerophosphate shuttle: couples cytosolic NADH oxidation to mitochondrial FAD reduction; electrons are stored in glycerol-3-phosphate, which transfers them to FAD (so they enter at the coenzyme Q level and yield fewer ATP).
- Malate-aspartate shuttle: uses malate to carry electrons across the inner membrane, regenerating mitochondrial NADH.
- Both are needed because cytosolic NADH from glycolysis does not cross the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.question:
1. Describe the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation under the following headings:
- Site
- Substrates
- Key enzymes, complexes and cofactors
- Regulation or coupling
- Energetics
- Products
2. Explain the clinical and toxicological basis of the effects of inhibitors (rotenone, antimycin A, cyanide, carbon monoxide, oligomycin, atractyloside), uncouplers (2,4-dinitrophenol) and thermogenin on energy metabolism, including why electron leakage causes disease.
3. Distinguish between the glycerophosphate shuttle and the malate-aspartate shuttle.

questions.answerText:
1. Overall metabolism and integration
