questions.answerText:
A(i)
A morbillivirus of the Paramyxoviridae: enveloped, helical nucleocapsid, nonsegmented ssRNA, 120-200 nm, lacks neuraminidase; survives at 4 °C, for months at −20 °C and years at −70 °C; heat labile.
A(ii)
Highly contagious by respiratory droplets and aerosols; humans are the only reservoir; a frequent cause of death worldwide, with under 100 cases a year in the U.S.; SSPE occurs in about 1 per million infections.
A(iii)
• Incubation 7-13 days; high fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and photophobia; Koplik's spots appear after 2 days (buccal mucosa, 1-2 days), and a maculopapular rash 12-24 hours later lasts 2-5 days.
• Complications: bronchitis, bronchiolitis, croup, bronchopneumonia, otitis media, encephalitis (may be fatal) and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
• The patient is most infectious at the early catarrhal stage with respiratory symptoms.
B(i)
• Culture in human, monkey, bovine and dog kidney cell lines and continuous lines such as Hep-2; haemagglutination with monkey red cells; measles IgM by ELISA; PCR.
• In culture the F spikes cause cell fusion, forming syncytia (multinucleate giant cells).
C(i)
• Measles IgM offers a rapid means of diagnosis of primary infection; a significant rise in IgG between acute and convalescent sera also shows recent infection.
• A CPE is presumptive and identity is confirmed by neutralisation, haemadsorption-inhibition, immunofluorescence or molecular tests.
C(ii)
• IgM assays suffer from rheumatoid factor interference, re-infection and persistence of IgM; in re-infection IgM may be low or absent; culture can take up to 4 weeks.
• There is no specific antiviral; treatment is supportive (antipyretics, rest, fluids, humidification, vitamin A); isolation from the 7th day after exposure to 5 days after the rash; prevention by MMR vaccine.

Describe the complement fixation test (CFT):
A(i) the principle and the two systems;
A(ii) the specimen and reagents.
B(i) Set out the procedure.
C(i) Explain the interpretation of positive and negative results and of titres.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• CFT has two separate systems: the indicator system (sheep RBCs, complement and a specific haemolytic antibody called haemolysin or amboceptor) and the test system (antigen suspected of causing disease and the patient's serum).
• Both systems require complement: antigen-antibody binding needs complement, and haemolysin lysis of sheep RBCs needs complement.
A(ii)
Reagents: sheep RBCs, complement, haemolysin, antigen and patient's serum; paired acute and convalescent sera are used for titres; CFT detects total antibody, mainly IgG.
B(i)
Antigen, antibody and complement are added together and one of two outcomes must follow; sensitised RBCs are then added.
C(i)
• Positive: all complement is fixed by the antigen-antibody reaction, sensitised RBCs are not lysed (no haemolysis), showing specific antibody in the serum.
• Negative: no antigen-antibody reaction, complement stays free and binds the haemolysin-RBC complex, lysing the RBCs. A significant rise is four-fold or greater (e.g. 1/4 to 1/16 is significant; 1/8 is not).
C(ii)
• CFT and HAI detect only total antibody and are not so sensitive as EIA and RIA, which offer better sensitivity, specificity and reproducibility.
• Diagnosis is usually retrospective because convalescent serum is taken after recovery, and defining a significant rise depends on the assay; cross-reactivity between related viruses gives false positives.
• Immunocompromised patients may show reduced antibody, and blood products may transfer antibody.

questions.question:
Describe the prevention and treatment of influenza as a control measure:
A(i) the control measures available;
A(ii) the antiviral drugs and supportive treatment.
B(i) Explain the mechanism of amantadine, rimantadine and the neuraminidase inhibitors.
B(ii) Explain the other agents and the role of antibody.
C(i) Explain the limitations and the basis of resistance and vaccine failure.
C(ii) Explain the trade-offs and the burden.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Vaccine: inactivated (killed) virus given in the arm and also as a nasal spray, with an annual trivalent vaccine recommended; good hygiene, avoiding sick people and covering coughs and sneezes.
A(ii)
Amantadine and rimantadine act on influenza A; zanamivir (Relenza) and oseltamivir (Tamiflu) act on influenza A and B; supportive care is rest, fluids, antihistamines and acetaminophen.
B(i)
• Amantadine and rimantadine block the ion channel of the M2 protein, reducing its effect on virus release and pH regulation, and so inhibit uncoating.
• Neuraminidase inhibitors target the NA enzyme, which hydrolyses mucus and assists budding and release of virus.
B(ii)
• Nitazoxanide blocks maturation of influenza haemagglutinin after translation and upregulates innate antiviral mechanisms, but trials gave results unavailable or not encouraging.
• Antibody at mucosal portals of entry is protective against influenza and reinfection.
C(i)
• Influenza virus has developed a high rate of resistance to amantadine and rimantadine.
• Antigenic drift and shift decrease the effectiveness of the host immune response, so the vaccine must be updated annually; the genetic changes occur every 2 to 3 years.
C(ii)
• Amantadine has high oral bioavailability but plasma levels are higher in the elderly (reduced renal clearance); rimantadine is 75% metabolised in the liver; both need dose reduction in the elderly.
• Influenza is among the top 10 causes of death in the U.S., most in the elderly and small children; weakened defences predispose to secondary bacterial pneumonia, and complications include myositis and Reye syndrome.
• Influenza B undergoes only minor antigenic change and C is stable.
• Antigenic change by shift of influenza A is responsible for most epidemics.

A(i)
Passive protection supplies pre-formed antibody, which neutralises virus, agglutinates particles, activates phagocytes and complement; active vaccination instead induces long-lived memory.
A(ii)
Examples: horse anti-rabies serum and human rabies immunoglobulin; TBE specific immune globulin; CMV hyperimmune gamma globulin; immunoglobulins for parvovirus B19; the RSV monoclonal antibody synagis, which blocks attachment; mumps immune globulin; immune serum globulin for HEV; convalescent sera for arenavirus and Ebola infection.
B(i)
• Rabies post-exposure care: immediate wound cleansing with soap and water, tincture of iodine, alcohol 40-70%, suturing, antibiotics, and observation of the animal for 10 days.
• Passive immunisation: horse anti-rabies serum 40 IU/kg at day 0, or human rabies immunoglobulin 20 IU/kg around the wound and intramuscularly, with vaccine (HDCV) and essential booster doses.
• Pre-exposure prophylaxis with cell-cultured vaccine (HDCV; also nervous tissue and duck embryo vaccines) is for animal handlers, wildlife officers and veterinarians.
B(ii)
• After infected tick attack, specific antiviral immune globulin is given for post-exposure prophylaxis and is efficient within 2-3 days; it may also be worthwhile early in disease.
• HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is triple therapy for 4 weeks after needle-stick or at-risk sexual exposure, with immediate bleeding and washing of skin pricks; hospital pharmacies may hold stocks.
• Immunoglobulins block persistent parvovirus B19 infection; for RSV, ribavirin with hyperimmune globulin is more effective in severely ill infants.
C(i)
• HEV immune serum globulin does not prevent infection and may only ameliorate hepatitis; TBE immune globulin is efficient only within 2-3 days; convalescent plasma is described only for Argentine and Bolivian haemorrhagic fever and Ebola.
• Calcium elenolate in humans was effective only if treatment began immediately after infection.
C(ii)
• Doses are weight-based, and booster doses are essential.
• Timing decides success: ribavirin is effective in the first week; maternal and newborn therapy lowered HIV vertical infection from about 25% to under 3% only if breast-feeding is avoided.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Family Retroviridae, genus Lentivirus; HIV-1 (groups M, O, N; group M subtypes A to K) and HIV-2. Spherical enveloped virion of 80-120 nm; gp120 binds CD4 and gp41 anchors the spike.
• Diploid genome of two copies of positive-sense ssRNA (about 10 kb) with LTRs; genes gag, pro, pol, env plus regulatory tat, rev, vif, vpr/vpx, nef, vpu; pol codes reverse transcriptase, RNase H and integrase.
A(ii)
Sexual (semen, cervical secretions; ulcerative STIs increase risk); vertical (in utero, perinatal, breast milk, which raises risk by up to 28%); bloodborne (transfusion, organ donation, intravenous drug use, tattoo and piercing, needle-stick and healthcare-associated).
A(iii)
• Acute influenza- or mononucleosis-like syndrome (incubation a few days to 6 weeks, high viraemia, seroconversion), asymptomatic chronic stage of 5-15 years, symptomatic disease, then AIDS (CD4 below 200 cells/microlitre) with wasting, opportunistic infections, malignancies and neurological disease.
• WHO estimates 30-40 million infected and 2-3 million deaths per year, two thirds in Africa; prevalence from below 1% in Western communities to 40% in some African countries; clade B in the West, clades A, C and E in Africa and Asia; HIV-2 mainly West Africa.
B(i)
• HIV antibody tests are the screening test; positive results are confirmed by a battery of tests and a repeat sample. HIV antigen appears 3-7 days before antibody and shortens the window period.
• HIV RNA PCR (EDTA blood, plasma separated within 6 hours) diagnoses acute infection and monitors disease at three-monthly intervals; proviral DNA PCR detects integrated viral DNA in cells.
B(ii)
Maternal antibody may be present in neonates, so RNA or proviral DNA PCR is done at birth, 6 weeks and 12 weeks, followed by an antibody test at 18 months to show clearance of maternal antibody.
C(i)
• HIV is a chronic infection in 100% of cases and persists with antibody, so antibody positivity indicates infection. A positive PCR, or antibody persisting beyond 18 months, indicates vertical transmission.
• Treatment aims at complete suppression of viral replication (negative PCR); a positive RNA PCR on treatment may indicate non-compliance or drug resistance and a change of drug regimen.
C(ii)
• No test is 100% specific, so confirmation is required; the window period precedes antibody; neonatal antibody may be maternal.
• Immunocompromised patients may give reduced or absent humoral response, blood or blood products can transfer antibody (false positive), and PCR is prone to contamination (false positive).
questions.question:

A(ii) transmission;
A(iii) clinical syndromes and epidemiology.
B(i) Outline the laboratory diagnosis (antibody, antigen, RNA PCR, proviral DNA PCR, specimen requirements).
B(ii) Describe the diagnosis of infection in neonates.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Family Retroviridae has two subfamilies and eleven genera: Orthoretrovirinae (Alpha-, Beta-, Delta-, Epsilon-, Gammaretrovirus, Lentivirus) and Spumaretrovirinae (five spumavirus genera); viruses are also grouped into seven groups (e.g. ALSV, HTLV-BLV, lentivirus, spumavirus) and are endogenous or exogenous.
A(ii)
Spherical enveloped virions of 80-120 nm; a lipid envelope with surface glycoprotein projections and an inner core holding the genome and replicative enzymes; hexagonal capsid proteins. HIV has gp120 knobs and gp41, a p17 matrix and a cone-shaped p24 core with two RNA molecules, RT, integrase and protease.
A(iii)
Diploid genome of two copies of 7-13 kb positive-sense ssRNA, 5′ capped and 3′ polyadenylated, with LTRs at both ends; all encode gag, pro, pol and env; HIV also has tat, rev, vif, vpr/vpx, nef and vpu.
A(iv)
• Attachment to a specific receptor; penetration by fusion with the plasma membrane (some use the endosomal pathway); reverse transcription of RNA into dsDNA by RT; integration by integrase to form the provirus.
• Transcription from the provirus by cellular RNA polymerase II; translation into 2-3 polyproteins processed by viral protease; assembly and budding from the plasma membrane.
B(i)
• HIV binds CD4 on T-helper cells and also infects B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells and brain cells; T-cell-tropic viruses use co-receptor CXCR4 and macrophage-tropic viruses CCR5, and defective CCR5 alleles give some resistance.
• Replication is mainly in peripheral lymphoid organs, spleen, lymph nodes and gut lymphoid tissue; provirus persists in memory T cells, macrophages and microglia; massive daily CD4 destruction, with many uninfected bystander CD4 cells dying, leads to opportunistic infection.
B(ii)
Retroviruses infect invertebrates and vertebrates, causing neurological disease, neoplasms and immunodeficiency in humans, animals and birds; HIV is closely related to SIV of monkeys and entered humans from monkeys.
C(i)
• HIV-1 has groups M, O and N (M with subtypes A-K) and is worldwide; HIV-2 is confined to West Africa and countries linked to it; the clinical picture is similar but HIV-2 disease may be milder.
• HIV-2 was isolated from persons at special risk of sexually transmitted disease, is not associated with such severe illness and may even protect against later HIV-1 infection.
C(ii)
• HTLV-1 was the first human retrovirus discovered; it is spread by drug abuse, sex, transfusion in infected CD4 cells and from mother to infant via breast milk; about 5% develop adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma or HTLV-associated myelopathy after 10-40 years, and its tax gene transactivates the LTR and cellular oncogenes.
• HTLV-II was isolated from a patient with "hairy cell" leukaemia and is common in drug users without known disease; antibodies to the respective env proteins distinguish HIV from the T-cell leukaemia viruses, and HIV has no onc gene.

questions.question:
Describe viral genetic variation and mutation:
A(i) how variation arises in viruses;
A(ii) the difference between antigenic drift and antigenic shift.
B(i) Relate the process to influenza viruses.
B(ii) Relate the process to HCV, HIV and other viruses.
C(i) Explain the consequences for laboratory diagnosis.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for vaccines, treatment and control.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Fast-propagating RNA viruses have error-prone replication with a high mutation rate, generating many mutant variants (quasispecies or "mutant cloud") from the primary virus during individual infection.
• Pressure from the host immune system and antiviral drugs selects resistant mutants, giving new lines resistant to therapy and promoting progression of disease.
A(ii)
Antigenic drift is constant mutation that gradually changes amino acid composition; antigenic shift is substitution of a gene or RNA strand with one from an influenza virus of a different animal host.
B(i)
Influenza A: HA and NA undergo major and minor shift and cause most epidemics; B: minor shift only; C: antigenically stable; the changes occur every 2 to 3 years; the genome has 8 RNA segments and HA has 15 and NA 9 subtypes.
B(ii)
• HCV: 7 genotypes with over 100 subtypes, quasispecies, many isolates resistant to interferon and immune pressure changing the viral antigenic structure.
• HIV: genetic variability, rapid mutation, groups M, O, N and clades A-K, and rapid resistance to single drugs.
• HBV has 8 genotypes, and HBeAg may be absent despite high viral load because of mutation; dengue has four serotypes without cross-protection; TBE virus has 3 genetic subtypes of differing severity; HPV has over 100 types.
C(i)
• HCV genotyping by sequencing is a diagnostic test; HBeAg negativity does not exclude high viral load; a rise in HIV viral load on treatment suggests resistance.
• Antibody test sensitivity and specificity depend on the antigen used (four generations of HCV antibody assays added epitopes); cross-reactivity between related viruses (Japanese encephalitis and dengue) gives false positives.
C(ii)
• Influenza needs an annual trivalent vaccine; HIV vaccine is blocked by variability; infection with one dengue serotype does not protect against others, and sequential infection raises the risk of dengue haemorrhagic fever and shock syndrome.
• Influenza virus has developed high resistance to amantadine and rimantadine; HIV is treated with combination therapy (HAART) and a rise in viral load signals resistance needing a change of drugs.
• HCV genotype decides treatment duration (24 weeks for genotypes 2 and 3, 48 weeks for genotype 1); drugs are chosen to maximise compliance to avoid resistance, and the 80/80/80 adherence rule applies.

A(i)
• Zoonoses are infectious diseases of animals that can naturally be transmitted to humans; reverse zoonosis (anthroponosis) is when humans infect animals.
• Transmission is vertical (mother to offspring) or horizontal: direct contact, indirect contact (fomites), common vehicle (faecal contamination of food and water) and arthropod-borne.
A(ii)
Types: insect-borne, tick-borne, rodent-borne and vertebrate-borne.
B(i)
• Herpes B (monkey, bite); cowpox, monkeypox, pseudocowpox and orf (rodents, cats, cattle, squirrel, monkey, sheep, goat; contact through abrasions); rabies (various mammals; bite, scratch, respiratory); Ebola and Marburg (?monkeys; contact, iatrogenic); influenza A (birds, pigs; respiratory).
• Arenaviruses: LCM virus (Mus musculus), Junin and Machupo (Calomys), Lassa (Mastomys natalensis) via rodent urine; bunyaviruses: Rift Valley fever (mosquito; sheep, cattle), Crimean-Congo fever (tick) and hantaviruses (rodents).
B(ii)
• Human encroachment into natural habitats (Plasmodium knowlesi from macaques is an example), and consumption and trade of wild animals: SARS from civet cats that acquired it from horseshoe bats, Ebola linked to bushmeat, monkeypox in the Congo with falling smallpox immunity.
• Farmland expansion: Sumatran forest fires drove fruit bats to cause Nipah pneumonia and encephalitis in Malaysia and Singapore through contaminated fruit fed to pigs; bovine spongiform encephalitis emerged in the UK in 1986 after a change in animal feed processing.
• Survival in nature depends on a large animal population, a virus stable in the transmission phase, antigenic drift, mechanical arthropod vectors and persistence in rodents; climate change and globalisation also drive microbial threats.
C(i)
• BSL-4 is needed for laboratory diagnosis of all arenaviruses; neutralisation testing has an advantage over HI for screening arbovirus immunity (in Nigeria 63% had flavivirus HI antibodies).
• Dengue diagnosis in West Africa is complicated by co-circulating viruses causing similar fever (chikungunya, o'nyong-nyong, Zika); dengue was first detected in Ibadan in 1964 and 23.4% recent infection was reported in Ibadan.
C(ii)
• Ribavirin is used for most haemorrhagic fevers; yellow fever 17D vaccine and Rift Valley fever vaccines are available; control uses mosquito control, animal screening, tick control with acaricides and repellent clothing, and strict isolation with barrier nursing.
• Mapping of hotspots predicts relative risk of zoonotic emerging infectious disease events, with red showing the highest risk.
questions.question:
Describe zoonoses and emerging viral infections:
A(i) the definition of zoonosis and reverse zoonosis, and the ways viruses are transmitted;
A(ii) the types of zoonosis.
B(i) Relate these to the viral examples, their reservoirs and modes of transmission.
B(ii) Explain the drivers of emergence, with examples.
C(i) Explain the consequences for diagnosis.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for prevention and control.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Not all infected patients need treatment; indicators are clinical status (AIDS-defining illness), high viral load and/or low CD4 count; no cure exists and drugs are needed for life.
• Because the virus rapidly develops resistance to single drugs, they are used in combination as triple therapy (HAART), containing at least one nucleoside analogue and one protease inhibitor.
A(ii)
Zidovudine (AZT) with didanosine, 3TC (lamivudine), non-nucleoside inhibitors, protease inhibitors and fusion inhibitors; raltegravir (integrase inhibitor) and tenofovir (nucleotide RT inhibitor) are also listed among antivirals.
B(i)
• Lamivudine is converted to its triphosphate which inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase; the reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease coded by the pol gene are all targets of antivirals.
• AZT given to the mother during pregnancy reduces transmission of virus very significantly.
B(ii)
• Response is monitored by regular HIV RNA (viral load) testing; viral load falls rapidly within 4-6 weeks, the aim is an undetectable level, with a rise in CD4 count improving the immune system.
• Triple therapy for 4 weeks is post-exposure prophylaxis after needle-stick or at-risk sexual exposure; treating pregnant mothers from 14 weeks and at labour, and the newborn for 6 weeks, cut vertical infection from about 25% to under 3% if breast-feeding is avoided.
C(i)
• Resistance arises from viral mutations and is heralded by a rise in viral load, calling for a change of drugs; a positive RNA PCR on treatment may indicate non-compliance or resistance.
• Combination chemotherapy reduces the chance of drug-resistant virus emerging; drugs are chosen to maximise compliance.
C(ii)
• Therapy is lifelong; treatment of opportunistic infections and malignancies is equally important; all antivirals can have side effects.
• HIV integrates into memory T cells, and macrophages and microglia may act as reservoirs of provirus; despite this, treatment has changed outcome so that most patients live a normal life.
• Opportunistic infection therapy: aciclovir or penciclovir for HSV, foscarnet or ganciclovir for CMV, amphotericin and pentamidine for fungal and Pneumocystis infection, and streptomycin and isoniazid for mycobacteria.
questions.question:
Describe antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection as a control measure:
A(i) the principles and indications for treatment;
A(ii) the classes of drug.
B(i) Explain the mechanism of the drugs and the viral targets.
B(ii) Explain how treatment is monitored and the use of drugs for prophylaxis.
C(i) Explain the basis of drug resistance and its detection.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and trade-offs of treatment.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A flavivirus of the Flaviviridae (enveloped, positive ssRNA); named in 1947 after the Zika forest in Uganda, isolated from a rhesus monkey; recovered from a mosquito in 1948; first human cases in Uganda and Tanzania in 1952.
A(ii)
• Spread by bites of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, which bite by day and night and lay eggs near standing water, indoors and outdoors; the same mosquitoes transmit dengue, chikungunya and yellow fever.
• Also from mother to baby in pregnancy or around birth, through breast milk, blood transfusion and unprotected sex; virus stays active in semen longer than in blood and urine.
A(iii)
• Most people have no symptoms; when present they start 3-14 days after infection and are mild (rash, fever, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, malaise, headache), lasting 2-7 days.
• Complications: microcephaly and congenital Zika syndrome (limb contractures, high muscle tone, eye abnormalities, hearing loss), fetal loss, stillbirth, preterm birth, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, neuropathy and myelitis.
B(i)
Infection is suspected from symptoms in persons living in or visiting transmission areas or areas with Aedes vectors, and can only be confirmed by laboratory tests of blood or other body fluids.
B(ii)
Blood or other body fluids are tested.
C(i)
• The result must be differentiated from cross-reactive related flaviviruses such as dengue virus, to which the patient may have been exposed or previously vaccinated.
• Symptoms are common to other arboviral and non-arboviral diseases, so laboratory confirmation is required; congenital malformations occur after both symptomatic and asymptomatic infection.
C(ii)
• Cross-reactivity gives false positives, and dengue and chikungunya co-circulate with Zika; NSAIDs are avoided until dengue is ruled out because of bleeding risk.
• There is no specific treatment (rest, fluids, antipyretics, analgesics) and no vaccine; prevention is protection from mosquito bites (clothing, screens, repellents, nets) and eliminating breeding sites.
questions.question:
Describe Zika virus under the following headings:
A(i) properties and history;
A(ii) transmission;
A(iii) clinical disease and complications.
B(i) Outline the laboratory diagnosis.
B(ii) State the specimens and tests.
C(i) Explain how the results are interpreted.

Describe the control of viral haemorrhagic fevers:
A(i) the causative agents and the shared features that determine control;
A(ii) the general measures for avoiding hosts and vectors.
B(i) Explain the treatment and vaccines available.
B(ii) Explain the infection-control precautions in health care.
C(i) Explain the limitations of the measures.
C(ii) Explain the trade-offs created by nosocomial spread and mortality.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The agents are RNA viruses of four families: Filoviridae (Ebola, Marburg), Arenaviridae (Lassa, Junin, Machupo, Guanarito, Sabia), Bunyaviridae (Crimean-Congo fever, Rift Valley fever, hantaviruses) and Flaviviridae (yellow fever, dengue, Kyasanur Forest, Omsk).
• Shared features: lipid envelope; survival depends on an animal reservoir; higher occurrence in the tropics; spread by contact with reservoirs (rodents, arthropods), their excretions, secretions and blood, and person-to-person nosocomial infection.
A(ii)
• Avoid contact with hosts: control rodent populations, keep rodents out of dwellings, clean up nests and droppings safely; against insects use repellents, proper clothing, bed nets and window screens.
• If a human case occurs, decrease person-to-person transmission, isolate infected individuals and report to health authorities.
B(i)
• Treatment is supportive; ribavirin (for Arenaviridae and Bunyaviridae only) and convalescent-phase plasma (Argentine and Bolivian haemorrhagic fever, Ebola) are used.
• A vaccine is available for yellow fever; experimental vaccines are under study for Argentine haemorrhagic fever, Rift Valley fever, hantavirus and dengue; a live arenavirus vaccine against Junin virus has been introduced and Lassa vaccines are in development.
B(ii)
• Airborne and contact precautions for health care, environmental and laboratory workers; a negative-pressure room with 6-12 air changes per hour, exhausted outdoors or through a HEPA filter.
• Personal protective equipment: double gloves, impermeable gowns, leg and shoe coverings, face shields and eye protection, N-95 mask or PAPR; WHO and CDC produced a manual for the African health care setting.
C(i)
• Ribavirin is not FDA-approved and is effective in only some individuals; only yellow fever has a vaccine in use; the clinical features are nonspecific (incubation 2-21 days) so early recognition is hard.
• Surveillance criteria for suspected cases: temperature of 38.3 °C or above for less than 3 weeks, severe illness without predisposing factors, and two or more haemorrhagic features with no alternative diagnosis.
C(ii)
• Mortality: Ebola and Marburg 25-100% (pregnancy universally fatal), South American haemorrhagic fevers 15-30%, Lassa 2-15%, Crimean-Congo fever 15-30%.
• Explosive nosocomial outbreaks occurred with Lassa and Machupo; filovirus spread follows reuse of needles and syringes and exposure to infectious tissues, excretions and hospital waste; BSL-4 is needed for arenavirus culture.

A(i)
HAV: Picornaviridae, genus Hepatovirus; HBV: Hepadnaviridae, Orthohepadnavirus; HCV: Flaviviridae, Hepacivirus; HDV: unclassified (Deltavirus); HEV: Caliciviridae (genus unnamed); HGV is a Flaviviridae virus sharing 95% amino acid identity with GBV-C, a hepatitis C-like virus.
A(ii)
HAV 27 nm icosahedral non-enveloped; HBV 42 nm spherical with HBsAg envelope; HCV 60 nm spherical enveloped; HDV 35 nm spherical with HBsAg envelope; HEV 30-32 nm icosahedral non-enveloped.
A(iii)
HAV ssRNA 7.5 kb; HBV partially dsDNA 3.2 kb with four open reading frames (S, C, P, X); HCV ssRNA 9.4 kb; HDV ssRNA 1.7 kb; HEV ssRNA 7.6 kb.
A(iv)
• HBV attaches to and enters the liver cell; the core releases DNA and polymerase into the nucleus, where mRNA is made for HBs, HBc, polymerase and HBe proteins; one mRNA is reverse transcribed to make DNA for progeny cores; excess surface protein forms spheres and chains, and some DNA integrates, causing carrier state.
• HCV attaches through E1 and E2 to hepatocyte receptors, enters by endocytosis, translates its (+)RNA into a polyprotein and replicates through a negative-strand intermediate with NS5B polymerase, leaving by budding.
B(i)
• HAV replicates slowly in the liver without apparent cytopathic effect; HBV does not itself kill hepatocytes, damage arising when CTL kill infected cells, the strength of the CTL response deciding the course.
• HCV reaches the liver by tropism and causes inflammation, scar tissue, fibrosis and cirrhosis with risk of cancer; it shows low to moderate cytopathic effect and persistent infection with immune evasion; CTL kill HCV-infected hepatocytes via Fas ligand, TNF-α or perforin.
B(ii)
HEV can infect primates, swine, sheep and rats, and swine may be a reservoir in North America; Orthohepadnavirus infects mammals (humans, gibbons, chimps, woodchucks, ground squirrels) while Avihepadnavirus infects ducks, geese and herons.
C(i)
• Both are faecal-oral. HAV: heat- and acid-stable, incubation 15-50 days, vaccine available, fulminant disease rare, never chronic. HEV: heat-stable, incubation about 6 weeks (15-60 days), no vaccine (trials in progress), never chronic.
• HEV causes severe disease in pregnancy (up to 20-30% mortality, especially in the third trimester), is endemic in Asia, Middle East and North Africa through contaminated water, mainly in young adults, and is diagnosed by IgG anti-HEV seroconversion; HAV by IgM anti-HAV.
C(ii)
• Co-infection (acute simultaneous HBV and HDV) often gives fulminant infection and survivors rarely develop chronic infection (under 5%); superinfection occurs in an HBsAg carrier at any time, usually with rapidly progressive subacute or chronic hepatitis (chronic in 80%).
• HDV needs the HBsAg envelope; diagnosis is IgM anti-HDV for acute infection and IgG anti-HDV with HBsAg for chronic infection; transmission is parenteral (percutaneous common, sexual rare), incubation 21-45 days.

A(i)
HSV is neurotropic and travels retrogradely along sensory neurons to ganglia; VZV persists in spinal ganglia; rabies follows a bite; TBEV spreads by blood and lymph to the CNS.
A(ii)
Mechanisms: direct neuronal degeneration (TBEV), persistence of defective virus (SSPE), reactivation in immunosuppression (JC virus PML), infection of microglia and neurons (HIV), inflammation and demyelination (HTLV-1) and post-infectious syndromes (Guillain-Barré syndrome in Zika).
B(i)
• TBE: degeneration of neurons in spinal cord and brain with meningeal damage, flaccid paralysis of neck, shoulders and upper limbs; lethality 20-40% for the Far Eastern subtype and under 1-2% for the European subtype.
• Rabies: hydrophobia, seizures, hallucinations, coma and respiratory paralysis.
• SSPE: defective measles virus persists in the brain as a slow virus, with personality, behaviour and memory change, myoclonic jerks, blindness and spasticity, coma and death over months or years; about 1 case per million infections.
B(ii)
• JC virus causes PML; HIV causes AIDS dementia (memory loss, poor concentration, behavioural change), aseptic meningitis and encephalopathy; HTLV-1 causes tropical spastic paraparesis with demyelination; Zika causes microcephaly, Guillain-Barré syndrome and myelitis.
• Others: West Nile encephalitis, mumps involving the CNS, LCM virus meningoencephalitis, Lassa encephalitis with hearing loss, and HSV and CMV central nervous system infection in AIDS.
• Viruses have been linked circumstantially to multiple sclerosis, though no specific virus is tied to it.
C(i)
• CSF, serum, blood or autopsy material is used for TBE (ELISA, RT-PCR, neutralisation, mouse intracerebral inoculation); brain tissue for Negri bodies and dFAT in rabies; arenavirus work needs BSL-4.
• Multiplex PCR for EBV DNA and Toxoplasma gondii is used for brain mass lesions in AIDS; for HIV and rabies antibody presence can be diagnostic.
C(ii)
• Prevention: rabies post-exposure care and mass dog vaccination, inactivated TBE vaccine, MMR (measles), tick and mosquito control, reduced immunosuppression for polyomavirus, and antiretroviral therapy for HIV.
• TBE has no specific antiviral treatment (supportive neurological care, early immune globulin); acyclovir is used for HSV.
questions.question:
Describe viral infections of the nervous system as a general process:
A(i) the routes by which viruses reach the nervous system;
A(ii) the mechanisms of nervous system injury.
B(i) Relate the process to TBEV, rabies virus and measles virus (SSPE).
B(ii) Relate the process to JC virus, HIV, HTLV-1, Zika virus and other viruses.
C(i) Explain the consequences for diagnosis.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for prevention and treatment.

Describe the principles and practice of serological diagnosis of viral infection:
A(i) the antibody responses on which it is based;
A(ii) the classical and newer techniques.
B(i) Set out how specimens are collected and tests applied for paired sera and IgM.
B(ii) State the controls and quality assurance measures.
C(i) Explain how primary infection and re-infection are diagnosed and interpreted.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Serology is the mainstay of viral diagnosis; in a primary response IgM appears first, followed by a much higher IgG titre; in reinfection IgM stays the same or rises slightly but IgG rises rapidly and far earlier.
A(ii)
Classical: CFT, haemagglutination inhibition, immunofluorescence and neutralisation; newer: RIA, EIA, particle agglutination and Western blot. EIA and RIA can detect IgM or IgG specifically, while CFT and HAI detect total antibody (mainly IgG); EIA and RIA are the most sensitive.
B(i)
• A serum sample is taken as soon as viral aetiology is suspected (acute phase) and a second 10-14 days later (convalescent phase).
• IgM is detected by EIA, RIA and IF; seroconversion is a change from antibody negative to positive (e.g. HIV after a needle-stick injury, rubella after contact).
B(ii)
The sensitivity and specificity of any new method must be evaluated individually against the previous test.
C(i)
• Primary infection: a significant rise in IgG or total antibody (four-fold or greater by CFT and HAI; 1/4 to 1/16 significant, 1/8 not), presence of IgM, or seroconversion; a single titre cannot distinguish previous from current infection.
• Re-infection or reactivation shows a sharp, large rise in antibody with IgM low or absent; this matters in first-trimester rubella, where primary infection carries high risk of fetal damage but re-infection does not.
C(ii)
• Usefulness depends on the virus: for rubella and hepatitis A symptoms coincide with antibody; for respiratory and diarrhoeal viruses disease precedes antibody (diagnosis retrospective); for HIV and rabies, antibody alone is definitive.
• Problems: long time for paired sera, retrospective diagnosis; mild local infections such as genital HSV may give no detectable response; immunocompromised patients give reduced or absent response.
• False positives: cross-reactivity between related viruses (Japanese encephalitis and dengue), infectious mononucleosis and SLE reacting non-specifically, and blood products transferring antibody.
• IgM assays suffer interference by rheumatoid factor, re-infection and persistence of IgM for years; a significant rise is difficult to define and depends on the assay.

questions.question:
Describe antiviral drugs and their mechanisms of action:
A(i) the principles and strategies of antiviral drug development, and why selective toxicity is difficult;
A(ii) the classes of drugs that target the virus directly.
B(i) Explain the mechanism of action of acyclovir and its derivatives.
B(ii) Explain the mechanism of action of foscarnet, ribavirin, lamivudine, amantadine/rimantadine and interferon-α.
C(i) Explain the limitations of antiviral therapy, including side effects and resistance.
C(ii) Explain the trade-offs between the drugs (bioavailability, route, half-life).
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Antiviral drugs treat viral infections; unlike most antibiotics they do not destroy their target pathogens but inhibit their development. Viruses use host cell machinery, so it is difficult to find targets that do not damage host cells.
• Strategies target either the viruses themselves or host cell factors.
A(ii)
Inhibitors of virus attachment, virus entry, uncoating, polymerases, proteases, nucleoside and nucleotide reverse transcriptase, integrase and neuraminidase.
B(i)
• Acyclovir (a 2′-deoxyguanosine analogue) is monophosphorylated by thymidine kinase of HSV- or VZV-infected cells (phosphotransferase for CMV); cellular enzymes make the di- and triphosphate, which competes with dGTP as substrate for viral DNA polymerase and terminates the chain irreversibly.
• Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits HSV-1 DNA polymerase about 30 times more than human α-polymerase and forms little in uninfected cells, so cellular toxicity is low.
• Valacyclovir is the L-valyl ester of acyclovir, converted to acyclovir, with 3-5 times the bioavailability. Ganciclovir (extra hydroxymethyl group) is phosphorylated by CMV phosphotransferase, and its triphosphate half-life is 12 h versus 1-2 h for acyclovir. Penciclovir is a DNA chain terminator; famciclovir is its oral prodrug.
B(ii)
• Foscarnet (inorganic pyrophosphate) binds DNA polymerase at the pyrophosphate site and blocks release of pyrophosphate from the nucleoside triphosphate; ribavirin triphosphate inhibits viral RNA polymerase (not eukaryotic RNA polymerases I and II) and is active against many RNA viruses.
• Lamivudine (cytidine analogue; triphosphate) inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and HIV reverse transcriptase; amantadine and rimantadine block the M2 ion channel of influenza virus, reducing virus release and pH regulation.
• Interferon-α induces cellular enzymes that inhibit viral protein synthesis; it is given intramuscularly or subcutaneously and is effective in HHV-8, papillomavirus, hepatitis B and C diseases.
C(i)
• Only a few antivirals are approved because of side effects or resistance; viral variation complicates drug and vaccine development; no effective drug exists for many infections; all antivirals can have effects, some unexplained (e.g. thrombotic microangiopathy with valaciclovir in immunodeficiency).
• Early antivirals (idoxuridine, cytarabine, fialuridine) disappointed; influenza virus has developed a high rate of resistance to amantadine and rimantadine; drug failure in human trials is a general problem.
C(ii)
Acyclovir has reduced oral bioavailability and a short half-life; oral ganciclovir bioavailability is only 8-9%; foscarnet is given intravenously and cleared by glomerular filtration; interferon is not available orally; elderly patients need dose reduction of amantadine and rimantadine.

questions.question:
Describe direct microscopic identification of viruses:
A(i) the principle (light, ultraviolet and electron microscopy) and what inclusion bodies are;
A(ii) the specimens used.
B(i) Set out the staining and examination procedures.
C(i) Explain the interpretation of the characteristic inclusion bodies.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Light microscopy reveals characteristic inclusion bodies or multinucleated giant cells; ultraviolet microscopy shows fluorescent antibody staining; electron microscopy detects virus particles by size and morphology, revealing shape and structure.
• Inclusion bodies are virus-induced masses in the nucleus or cytoplasm, leftover protein from replication, marking sites of replication and made of collections of replicating virus particles.
A(ii)
Smears or films on slides, tissue sections and biopsy material; faeces for electron microscopy in viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus, adenovirus, astrovirus, calicivirus, Norwalk-like viruses); vesicles and skin lesions (herpesviruses, papillomaviruses).
B(i)
• Smears are stained with Giemsa, Wright-modified Giemsa, haematoxylin and eosin, eosin methylene blue, Lindner's, Castaneda's, Pollef's methylene blue or Macchiavello's stain and observed for inclusion bodies.
• Electron microscopy uses a magnification of about 50,000; immune electron microscopy uses virus-specific antibody to agglutinate particles or capture them onto the grid, increasing sensitivity and specificity.
C(i)
• Intranuclear: Councilman bodies (yellow fever, HBV, HCV; apoptotic hepatocytes), Cowdry type A (HSV, yellow fever), Cowdry type B (adenovirus, poliovirus), owl's eye (CMV).
• Intracytoplasmic: Negri bodies (rabies, in nerve cells of Ammon's horn of the hippocampus) and Guarnieri bodies (smallpox); nuclear inclusions arise with viruses replicating in the nucleus and cytoplasmic ones with cytoplasmic replicators.
• Electron microscopy can analyse any sample and identify any virus, and is the gold standard for viruses not showing up on routine tests or with conflicting results.
C(ii)
• Histology is not sensitive or specific and is only an adjunct; changes may be characteristic or non-specific.
• Electron microscopy is expensive, needs at least 10⁵ to 10⁶ particles per ml, needs specialised preparation and a skilled observer, cannot separate smallpox from other poxviruses and is less used now.

A(i)
• Two divisions: humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity binds free virus and blocks infection, while T-cell immunity recognises and destroys infected cells; CD4 and CD8 T cells recognise viral peptides bound to MHC class II and class I respectively.
• Initiation depends on early innate activation of antigen-presenting cells; APC and lymphocytes are drawn into lymphoid tissue by chemokines and cytokines and retained for a few days; induction occurs in lymph nodes draining the infection site, or the spleen if virus enters the blood.
A(ii)
• Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells recognise viral peptide on MHC class I through the T-cell receptor and release granule contents: perforin (pores), granzymes (apoptosis through the pores) and granulysin (lysis of the membrane).
• They also release IFN-γ and TNF-α, which transfer a signal to infected and neighbouring cells to enhance killing.
B(i)
CD4 T cells help induce antiviral antibodies and CD8 responses, act as effector cells, generate stable memory, may be cytotoxic less effectively, and Th1 cells release IFN-γ, TNF-α and IL-2 to orchestrate inflammation.
B(ii)
• B-cell activation occurs in follicles of spleen or lymph nodes; some become short-lived plasma cells, others with helper CD4 T cells become high-affinity long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells; long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow keep serum antibody.
• Cellular immunity plays the major role in clearing virus, whereas antibody protects against reinfection, especially at mucosal portals (influenza, HIV).
C(i)
• A prolonged tissue-damaging immune reaction is immunopathology, usually with persistent viruses that are only modestly cytodestructive themselves; a brief effect is regarded as immunoprotective.
• Mechanisms: increased secondary T-cell response (HBV); ADCC or complement-mediated lysis; virus-antibody complexes binding Fc receptors and increasing infected cells (dengue haemorrhagic fever, HIV); immune complex deposition (rash of rubella and measles).
• In HBV, liver damage arises when CTL kill infected hepatocytes; HCV-infected hepatocytes are killed by CTL via Fas ligand, TNF-α or perforin.
C(ii)
• Chronic damage may make the response autoreactive: circumstantial evidence links viruses to multiple sclerosis, insulin-dependent diabetes and possibly SLE, but this is unproved for any human autoimmune disease; infection may tip genetically susceptible individuals, with T cells orchestrating.
• Viruses escape CTL by downregulating MHC, inhibiting antigen presentation, killing APC or T cells (HIV) and antigenic hypervariability (influenza, HIV).
questions.question:
Describe adaptive immunity to viral infection:
A(i) its divisions and how it is initiated;
A(ii) the mechanism of cytotoxic T cells.
B(i) Explain the roles of CD4 helper T cells.
B(ii) Explain B-cell activation, antibody production and memory, and the relative roles of cellular and humoral immunity.
C(i) Explain how the immune response itself causes tissue injury (immunopathology).
C(ii) Explain the limitations: autoimmunity and immune evasion.

Describe hepatitis C virus (HCV) under the following headings:
A(i) properties (family, genus, virion, genome, genotypes, stability);
A(ii) transmission and epidemiology;
A(iii) clinical disease.
B(i) Outline the laboratory diagnosis (antibody, confirmatory, nucleic acid and genotyping tests).
B(ii) State the timing of the antibody response.
C(i) Explain how combinations of test results are interpreted.
C(ii) State the limitations and causes of misleading results.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Family Flaviviridae, genus Hepacivirus; enveloped spherical virion of about 60 nm with core protein and glycoproteins E1 and E2; positive ssRNA of 9.4 kb; ether- and acid-sensitive; 7 genotypes with over 100 subtypes (1a and 1b about 60% of cases); grows in culture only in hepatocyte cultures.
A(ii)
• Transmission is mainly parenteral: injection drug users with non-sterile syringes, frequent transfusions, needle-stick, tattooing; sexual and vertical transmission are rare (about 5% of infants of infected mothers, 15-20% if the mother is also HIV-positive); needle-stick risk is about 5% from an HCV-positive source.
• About 170-180 million people (3%) are infected worldwide, with the highest seroprevalence in Egypt (about 22%); HCV accounts for 90-95% of post-transfusion hepatitis; risk groups include recipients of clotting factors before 1987 (75-90%) and injection drug users (70-85%).
A(iii)
• Acute: incubation averages 7 weeks (2-26); most new infections are subclinical and jaundice occurs in less than 25%; symptoms include fever, fatigue, poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark urine, grey faeces, joint pain and jaundice.
• Chronic infection leads to cirrhosis within 20 years and hepatocellular carcinoma in a further 10; ALT fluctuates; extrahepatic features include rashes, arthritis, arthralgia, pruritus, myalgia, paraesthesia, sicca syndrome and progression of diabetes mellitus.
B(i)
• Antibody detection by EIA (four generations using core, NS3, NS4 and NS5 epitopes) shows past or present infection and is inexpensive, sensitive and specific; rapid antibody tests are available and RIBA confirms anti-HCV.
• Qualitative HCV RNA PCR confirms the diagnosis, helps early diagnosis of acute hepatitis C, shows active infection and is the gold standard for documenting response to treatment; quantitative RNA tests and genotyping (sequencing) are also used.
B(ii)
HCV-specific antibodies are generally detectable 7 to 31 weeks after infection, and individuals vary in specificity and timing of seroconversion.
C(i)
• Negative screening needs no action; positive screening alone gives "not known" infection and needs RIBA or HCV RNA; positive anti-HCV with positive RNA means current infection and requires evaluation for chronic infection and liver disease.
• Positive anti-HCV with negative RNA means past infection (or not known) and repeat RNA is advised; an indeterminate RIBA calls for HCV RNA testing or repeat anti-HCV.
C(ii)
• The antibody test cannot distinguish acute, chronic or resolved infection, has poor positive predictive value in low-prevalence populations and low sensitivity in immunosuppressed patients.
• ALT may be normal or elevated at different times and necro-inflammatory activity is not necessarily linked to ALT; PCR is prone to contamination (false positives).

A(i)
• In the fluorescent antibody assay a known antibody is tagged with a fluorescent dye; if the virus and the fluorescein-tagged antibody are homologous, the typical apple-green colour of fluorescein is seen in the cell under ultraviolet microscopy.
• Direct examination by antigen detection (immunofluorescence, ELISA) gives results within hours and is useful where management depends on a rapid result, e.g. RSV infection in neonates.
A(ii)
• Immunofluorescence of nasopharyngeal aspirates for RSV, influenza A and adenoviruses; HSV in skin scrapings; IMF on nasal washings for parainfluenza viruses.
• Rabies by immunofluorescence on skin biopsy, corneal impression or saliva, and by dFAT on brain tissue.
B(i)
• dFAT: brain tissue is collected and fluorescently labelled antibodies that bind rabies virus antigens are used to detect the virus, read by UV microscopy.
• For identification of virus grown in culture, the known tagged antibody is applied to the infected cells and viewed under UV.
C(i)
• Apple-green fluorescence in the cell means the virus and antibody are homologous; absence of the typical colour means they are not; dFAT is the gold standard for rabies on fresh brain tissue.
• IF is also used to detect IgM and to find specific antibody in EBV (indirect immunofluorescence), and TBEV in culture and ticks.
C(ii)
• The technique is often tedious and time-consuming, the result difficult to read and interpret, and sensitivity and specificity poor.
• Specimen quality is of utmost importance, and dFAT is highly accurate only on fresh brain tissue; IgM assays by IF can suffer rheumatoid factor interference and cross-reactivity.
questions.question:
Describe antigen detection by immunofluorescence:
A(i) the principle;
A(ii) the specimens and examples.
B(i) Set out the procedure.
C(i) Explain the interpretation of results.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Over 100 viruses infect many animal species; the family is grouped by tissue tropism, pathogenicity and behaviour: α (HSV 1 and 2, VZV), β (CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7) and γ (EBV, HHV-8) herpesviruses.
A(ii)
Size 100-200 nm, icosahedral symmetry, enveloped; the envelope contains 11 glycoproteins (B, C, D, E, G, H, I, J, K, L, M). The membrane is fragile: sensitive to drying, acids, detergents and organic solvents.
A(iii)
Double-stranded linear DNA that codes for most of the enzymes required for replication.
A(iv)
• The virion binds a cell surface receptor through its glycoprotein spike (HSV-1 and 2 have several receptors and use one); binding triggers fusion of the envelope with the host membrane, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm and then to the nucleus.
• In the nucleus viral genes are transcribed, proteins synthesised, the genome replicated and progeny assembled.
B(i)
α-herpesviruses: fast replicating, variable host range, typically destroy the host cell, latency in sensory ganglia. β-herpesviruses: slowly replicating, infected cells enlarge, latency in secretory glands, lymphoreticular cells and kidneys. γ-herpesviruses: replicate poorly, highly restricted host range, latency in lymphoid tissues (T-cell or B-cell specific).
B(ii)
• HSV: enters through skin or mucous membrane, multiplies locally, is taken up by sensory neurons and transported retrogradely to ganglia where latency is established. VZV: enters via the respiratory tract, multiplies, spreads haematogenously to skin and mucous membranes forming blisters, and persists in spinal ganglia.
• CMV: enters via the respiratory or upper gastrointestinal tract, multiplies, spreads haematogenously and persists in salivary gland cells, renal tubules and leukocytes. EBV: enters via the respiratory tract, proliferates and persists in B cells.
• Immunity: EBV leaves persistent antibodies and immunity to reinfection.
C(i)
• HSV-1: oral infection (gingivostomatitis) or keratitis; infects mouth, eye and CNS (above the waist) and some genital herpes; reactivates in the trigeminal ganglia.
• HSV-2: infects the genital and anal region, mostly mucous membranes of the genital tract (glans penis, cervix, vagina); reactivates in the sacral ganglia.
C(ii)
Varicella (chickenpox) follows primary infection in a non-immune individual (children); zoster (shingles) is reactivation of latent virus when immunity has fallen, in adults and immunocompromised patients; complications occur if primary infection occurs in an adult.

A(i)
• Infection may be productive (permissive cells, progeny released), abortive (non-permissive, no virions) or restrictive (transiently permissive, a few viruses made, genome persists, transformation possible).
• Steps: attachment (ionic, temperature-independent, by viral attachment protein to specific receptors), penetration, uncoating and eclipse, genome replication and protein expression, assembly and maturation, and release by lysis or budding; cells lacking the receptor are not susceptible.
A(ii)
Seven groups since all viruses must make positive-strand mRNA: I dsDNA, II ssDNA, III dsRNA, IV (+)ssRNA, V (−)ssRNA, VI ssRNA-RT (retroviruses) and VII dsDNA-RT (hepadnaviruses).
B(i)
• Adenovirus replicates in the nucleus with cellular proteins (early proteins push the cell into S-phase); poxviruses replicate in the cytoplasm with their own enzymes; parvoviruses replicate in the nucleus through a (−) strand and wait for the host cell to enter S-phase.
• Hepadnaviruses reverse-transcribe inside the particle on maturation; on infection the gapped genome is repaired, then transcribed.
B(ii)
• Reoviruses (dsRNA) have segmented genomes, each transcribed separately into monocistronic mRNA; picornaviruses (+)ssRNA act as mRNA with a polyprotein cleaved to mature proteins (naked RNA is infectious); togaviruses need two rounds of translation.
• (−)ssRNA viruses carry a virion RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (orthomyxoviruses segmented, rhabdoviruses non-segmented) producing monocistronic mRNAs; retroviruses have a diploid (+)RNA genome used as template for reverse transcription, not as mRNA.
• All DNA viruses except poxviruses replicate in the nucleus; all RNA viruses except orthomyxoviruses and retroviruses replicate in the cytoplasm; protein synthesis is always cytoplasmic.
C(i)
• Replication strategy defines the Baltimore groups; families end in -viridae and genera in -virus, and classification matters from family level downward.
• Antiviral targets follow the steps: polymerases, proteases, integrases, neuraminidases, attachment/entry/uncoating inhibitors (amantadine blocks the M2 channel) and reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
C(ii)
• Maturation occurs at the site of nucleic acid replication; naked virions may accumulate as inclusion bodies (DNA icosahedral viruses maturing in the nucleus are released on autolysis); enveloped viruses acquire the envelope by budding; poxviruses are released by lysis.
• Inclusion bodies show replication sites: intranuclear (Cowdry A in HSV, Cowdry B in adenovirus and polio, owl's eye in CMV) and intracytoplasmic (Negri bodies, Guarnieri bodies); once nucleic acid is uncoated infectious virus cannot be recovered (eclipse).
questions.question:
Describe virus replication as a general process:
A(i) the possible outcomes of infection of a cell and the basic steps of replication;
A(ii) the Baltimore classification groups.
B(i) Relate the process to the DNA virus examples.
B(ii) Relate the process to the RNA and reverse-transcribing virus examples and to the site of replication.
C(i) Explain the consequences for classification and for antiviral targets.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for assembly, release and laboratory detection.

Describe the haemagglutination (HA) and haemagglutination inhibition (HI) tests:
A(i) the principle and the viruses that can be tested;
A(ii) the conditions and red blood cells required.
B(i) Set out the procedure of the HI test.
C(i) Explain the interpretation of results and the diagnostic uses.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
HA is a simple test for detecting viruses with haemagglutinin on their surface; the HA interacts with red blood cells (rbcs) to cause agglutination. Paramyxovirus, orthomyxovirus, togavirus, adenovirus and reovirus can aggregate/agglutinate rbcs in suspension.
A(ii)
Specific conditions of temperature, pH and type of rbcs are required; Newcastle disease virus requires chicken rbcs and influenza virus requires human erythrocytes (measles haemagglutination uses monkey red cells).
B(i)
• Make serial doubling dilutions of the serum as in HA.
• Add an equal volume of virus at 4 HA units (4 HAU).
• Incubate for 1 hour at room temperature.
• Add 0.5% erythrocytes and incubate for 1 hour at room temperature.
C(i)
• Haemagglutination of rbcs is inhibited if the known antiserum is complementary to the suspected virus; if virus and antibody are not homologous the virus attaches to the rbcs and visible haemagglutination occurs.
• HI has been used for the diagnosis of influenza, rubella, Coxsackie A and B and ECHO virus in humans.
• HI detects total antibody (mainly IgG); a significant rise is normally a four-fold or greater increase in titre between acute and convalescent sera.
C(ii)
• CFT and HAI are not so sensitive as EIA/RIA; sensitivity and specificity depend greatly on the antigen used.
• Diagnosis is usually retrospective because the patient has probably recovered by the time convalescent serum is taken.
• Antigenic cross-reactivity between related viruses (e.g. Japanese encephalitis and dengue) may give false positives; in one study some HI-negative sera still contained dengue neutralising antibody (30%), so HI can under-detect immunity.

questions.question:
Describe vertical (mother-to-child) transmission of viruses:
A(i) the definition and routes;
A(ii) the viruses involved.
B(i) Relate the process to HIV, HBV and HCV.
B(ii) Relate the process to CMV, HSV, Zika virus, parvovirus B19, HEV and HPV.
C(i) Explain the consequences for diagnosis.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for prevention and control.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Vertical transmission is from mother to offspring: in utero across the placenta, perinatally (exposure to contaminated maternal secretions at delivery, premature or prolonged rupture of membranes) or postnatally through breast milk.
A(ii)
Viruses involved include CMV, HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV, Zika virus, parvovirus B19, HEV, HPV and HTLV-1.
B(i)
• HIV is the most important route in sub-Saharan and Central Africa; breast feeding raises risk by up to 28%; 13-40% of babies of untreated HIV-positive mothers are infected and 20% of infected infants develop AIDS in the first year.
• HBV spreads soon after childbirth (transplacental rare) and 80-90% of infected neonates become chronic carriers; HCV maternal-infant transmission is about 5% (15-20% if the mother is HIV-positive) and higher if the mother is HCV RNA positive.
B(ii)
• CMV is the most common agent of intrauterine infection and prenatal damage, also acquired perinatally from genital secretions or breast milk; HSV is acquired at birth from an infected mother (congenital rare); Zika is passed in pregnancy or around birth and virus is found in breast milk.
• Parvovirus B19 crosses the placenta, depletes red cells and may cause fetal death or hydrops fetalis (oedema, severe anaemia, cardiac failure); HEV maternal-infant transmission is often fatal, with up to 20% mortality in pregnant women; children under 5 acquire HPV respiratory papillomatosis in the birth canal.
• Zika in pregnancy causes microcephaly and congenital Zika syndrome (limb contractures, high muscle tone, eye abnormalities, hearing loss), fetal loss, stillbirth and preterm birth, after both symptomatic and asymptomatic infection.
C(i)
• Maternal antibody confuses neonatal diagnosis: HIV RNA or proviral DNA PCR is done at birth, 6 and 12 weeks with an antibody test at 18 months; a positive PCR or antibody persisting beyond 18 months means vertical transmission.
• In first-trimester rubella, primary infection carries high risk of fetal damage and re-infection does not, so primary infection must be separated from re-infection by IgM and a sharp rise in titre.
C(ii)
• Therapy of pregnant mothers from 14 weeks and at labour, with 6 weeks for the newborn, cut HIV vertical infection from about 25% to under 3% if breast-feeding is avoided.
• AZT given to the mother also reduced transmission of virus very significantly.
• Pregnant women in Zika areas should seek care and avoid mosquito bites (no vaccine); the HBV recombinant vaccine and parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin are options; no vaccine exists for HCV, HDV or parvovirus B19.

questions.question:
Describe the family Paramyxoviridae under the following headings:
A(i) classification (genera and members);
A(ii) morphology and structure;
A(iii) genome.
B(i) Explain the pathogenesis and tissue tropism of measles, mumps, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and parainfluenza viruses.
B(ii) Explain the role of cell fusion in the damage these viruses cause.
C(i) Distinguish RSV (Pneumovirus) from the paramyxoviruses.
C(ii) Distinguish measles virus from mumps virus.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three genera: Morbillivirus (canine distemper, rinderpest, measles), Pneumovirus (RSV, Nipah virus, Hendra virus) and the parainfluenza viruses (paramyxovirus types 1 to 4, mumps).
A(ii)
Enveloped, helical nucleocapsid, 150-250 nm in diameter with surface projections; the envelope has HN and specialised F spikes that initiate cell-to-cell fusion.
A(iii)
Single-stranded, nonsegmented RNA.
B(i)
• Measles: highly contagious by respiratory droplets; infects respiratory epithelium and replicates there, then spreads to the lymphatic system with viraemia and disseminates to conjunctiva, respiratory tract, urinary tract, small blood vessels, lymphatics and CNS.
• Mumps: enters and multiplies in the respiratory tract, then viraemia and localisation and multiplication in target organs: parotid glands, CNS, pancreas and testis; humans are the natural host.
• RSV: affects epithelial cells of the upper and lower respiratory tract, replicating and infecting adjacent cells, without viraemia. Parainfluenza types 1, 2 and 3 are second only to RSV as a cause of severe respiratory disease in infants; type 4 causes mild disease.
B(ii)
Fusion with neighbouring cells forms syncytia (multinucleate giant cells); the RSV fusion protein causes multinucleated giant cells, and mumps spikes include cell-fusing and haemolytic activities; in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis a defective measles virus persists in the brain, spreads by cell fusion and destroys cells (personality, behaviour and memory change, myoclonic jerks, blindness, spasticity).
C(i)
• Unlike paramyxoviruses, RSV has no haemagglutinin activity, no neuraminidase and no haemolytic activity; its nucleocapsid diameter is smaller; it has its own genus; it has two serotypes (subgroups A and B) and natural hosts of humans and chimpanzees.
• RSV: bronchiolitis (fever, cough, tachypnoea, cyanosis, wheezing) in children 1 to 3 years, otitis media and croup; a cold-like illness in children over 10 and adults; no vaccine yet.
C(ii)
• Measles: morbillivirus, 120-200 nm, lacks neuraminidase, incubation 7-13 days, 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik's spots then maculopapular rash, complications including encephalitis and SSPE; humans only reservoir; prevented by MMR.
• Mumps: one serotype, spikes with haemagglutinin and neuraminidase activity, incubation 16-21 days, parotid swelling, orchitis in post-pubertal males may lead to sterility; neutralising antibody is directed against haemagglutinin; live attenuated MMR vaccine and immune globulin.

questions.question:
Describe virus-induced cell damage as a general process:
A(i) how infected cells respond and are directly damaged;
A(ii) cytopathic effects and inclusion bodies.
B(i) Relate the process to intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in specific viruses.
B(ii) Relate the process to cell fusion, transformation and haemadsorption.
C(i) Explain the consequences for laboratory diagnosis.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for pathogenesis and outcome.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Cells show no apparent change, cell death or transformation; direct damage follows diversion of the cell's energy, shutoff of macromolecular synthesis, competition of viral mRNA for ribosomes and of viral promoters for transcription factors, and inhibition of interferon defences.
• Indirect damage follows integration of the viral genome, induced mutations, inflammation and the host immune response.
A(ii)
• CPE in culture is an alteration in cell shape and size or fusion to multinucleated giant cells (syncytia), usually a dying cell; it is specific for HSV and CMV but not for enteroviruses.
• The adenovirus penton base has toxin-like activity causing CPE.
• Inclusion bodies are virus-induced masses in the nucleus or cytoplasm marking sites of replication.
B(i)
• Intranuclear: Councilman bodies (apoptotic hepatocytes in yellow fever, HBV, HCV), Cowdry type A (HSV, yellow fever), Cowdry type B (adenovirus, poliovirus) and owl's eye (CMV).
• Intracytoplasmic: Negri bodies (rabies) and Guarnieri bodies (smallpox); excess HBsAg gives a "ground glass" appearance in HBV infection.
B(ii)
• Syncytia form with RSV, measles and other paramyxoviruses through F spikes; HIV forms syncytia in the laboratory but none are reported in AIDS patients, where many dying CD4 cells are uninfected bystanders.
• HPV causes hyper-proliferation, transformation and immortalisation; infected cells of influenza, parainfluenza and mumps viruses acquire the ability to stick red cells (haemadsorption).
C(i)
• Smears and biopsy are stained (Giemsa, Tzanck) to find inclusions, and CPE is observed in culture; histology is not sensitive or specific.
• Where CPE is absent, haemadsorption, interference and decreased acid production can reveal growth, and identity is confirmed by neutralisation.
C(ii)
HAV causes no apparent cytopathology and readily persists; HBV does not itself kill hepatocytes, damage being by CTL; the interplay of viral damage and immune response decides acute versus chronic outcome.

questions.question:
Describe molecular (nucleic acid) methods for detecting viruses:
A(i) the principle and the methods;
A(ii) the specimens and probes.
B(i) Set out how detection and quantification are done.
C(i) Explain the interpretation, including viral load and multiplex testing.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Classical methods (dot-blot, Southern blot) use specific DNA or RNA probes for hybridisation, with specificity depending on hybridisation conditions, and can quantify DNA or RNA.
• Newer methods depend on amplification of the target or the signal: PCR, ligase chain reaction (LCR), nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (NASBA) and branched DNA (bDNA, hybridisation with signal amplification, less sensitive than PCR).
A(ii)
Viral nucleic acids in patient samples are detected with complementary DNA or RNA (cDNA or cRNA) probes; where little nucleic acid is present PCR multiplies it; RNA must first be reverse transcribed.
B(i)
• Hybridisation: probe binds the target under set conditions; PCR: repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension, with the product detected by hybridisation, electrophoresis or sequencing.
• Quantitative methods (real-time PCR, Cobas Amplicor closed automated systems) give viral load assays for HIV, HCV and HBV.
C(i)
• Viral load monitors the course of disease and prognosis; the goal in HIV is a negative PCR on treatment; qualitative HCV RNA PCR confirms active infection.
• Multiplex PCR detects more than one virus, or a virus and another class of pathogen, e.g. EBV DNA and Toxoplasma gondii in brain lesions in AIDS.
C(ii)
• Classical blot sensitivity is often no better than conventional methods and bDNA is less sensitive than PCR; PCR can detect 1 DNA molecule.
• Contamination gives false positives for PCR, LCR and NASBA, reduced by closed systems; a positive result may not mean disease (latent CMV in healthy people).
• PCR is costly but falling in cost, and in-house PCR is easier to set up than other amplification assays.

A(i)
• Skin, mucosal surfaces and the hostile gut are barriers, but viruses enter through breaks in skin/mucosa, oral cavity, respiratory tract, urethra and insect bites.
• Innate defences act before adaptive immunity: to block initial infection, protect cells, or eliminate infected cells.
A(ii)
• Initiated by pathogen recognition receptors of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) family, on the cell surface or endosomal membrane of dendritic cells, macrophages, lymphocytes and parenchymal cells; TLR3 and TLR7/8 recognise viral RNA and TLR9 recognises dsDNA, promoting type I (α/β) IFN, IFN-stimulated genes and inflammatory cytokines.
• TLR expression is largely inducible, but TLR7/8/9 are constitutively high for rapid IFN production.
B(i)
• α/β IFNs bind the type I IFN receptor, causing transcription of more than 100 IFN-stimulated genes: the "antiviral state" inhibits cell protein synthesis and prevents viral replication in infected cells.
• IFNs also warn neighbouring cells, which increase MHC class I so that T cells can identify and eliminate infection; type I IFNs also activate NK cells and induce IL-12.
B(ii)
• NK cells kill cells with reduced MHC class I on the surface (e.g. CMV, HIV, herpesvirus, influenza virus, Ebola virus), releasing toxic substances like cytotoxic T cells, producing proinflammatory cytokines and interacting with dendritic cells.
• Cytotoxic granules hold perforin (makes pores), granzymes (induce apoptosis) and granulysin (lyses the target membrane).
C(i)
• Viruses stop MHC reaching the surface or downregulate MHC; kill or infect APC or destroy T cells (HIV); delay CTL-induced apoptosis (adenovirus, HIV, EBV); inhibit antigen processing and presentation (HSV, EBV, HIV, HPV, CMV).
• Others produce inhibitors of cytokines or chemokines (EBV, CMV), use antigenic hypervariability (influenza, HIV), block interferon synthesis (arenavirus NP and Z proteins), or resist interferon (many HCV isolates).
C(ii)
• Mortality follows when viruses jump species (Ebola, HIV), undergo major antigenic change (influenza) or when host immunity is compromised; the impact of a single mechanism varies with how each virus enters, replicates and spreads.
• Resolution of infection relies more on T-cell function than antibody, because viruses replicate within cells and spread cell to cell.
questions.question:
Describe the innate immune response to viral infection:
A(i) its role and timing, and the barriers viruses meet at entry;
A(ii) how innate defences are initiated.
B(i) Explain the mechanism of action of interferons.
B(ii) Explain the role of natural killer (NK) cells, with examples of viruses.
C(i) State the strategies by which viruses evade innate and cytotoxic defences, with examples.
C(ii) Explain the limitations of immune defence and its consequences for the host.

Describe the polymerase chain reaction (PCR):
A(i) the principle and rationale;
A(ii) the components and the template and enzyme requirements.
B(i) Set out the procedure and the detection of the product.
C(i) Explain the interpretation of results, including quantitative PCR.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• PCR is a rapid enzymatic method of making millions of copies of a discrete DNA sequence, based on annealing and extension of two synthetic oligonucleotide primers (amplimers) flanking the target, in repeated temperature-dependent cycles; it was developed in 1985 (Mullis, Nobel Prize 1993).
• Microbes are often present in specimens below the detection level of many systems; PCR can detect down to 1 DNA molecule and identifies slow-growing or non-culturable pathogens.
A(ii)
• Components: four dNTPs (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP), template DNA, two amplimers (30-40 nucleotide single-stranded oligomers, the most critical element), DNA polymerase, Tris buffer with KCl and MgCl2, and a thermal cycler.
• The template may be any DNA, needs little DNA and need not be highly purified (whole blood may be used); RNA is amplified only after reverse transcription; heat-stable Taq polymerase (Thermus aquaticus) replaced the Klenow fragment, which had to be replenished each cycle.
B(i)
• Denature the template at 95 °C with the two primers and four dNTPs; cool to 37-60 °C so primers anneal; raise to 72 °C where Taq polymerase extends the primers.
• The cycle is repeated 25 to 30 times, each product serving as template for the next round, in a single tube in a thermal cycler.
• The product is detected by hybridisation, electrophoresis, DNA sequencing, endonuclease digestion followed by electrophoresis, or digestion followed by hybridisation with nucleotide probes.
C(i)
A positive PCR is often hard to interpret because it does not necessarily indicate disease, e.g. latent CMV genomes amplified from healthy people's blood; quantitative (real-time) PCR measures viral load of HIV, HCV and HBV to monitor disease and prognosis.
C(ii)
• Contamination is the chief problem, since a minute amount gives a false positive; closed automated systems (real-time PCR, Cobas Amplicor) ameliorate this.
• PCR is simple and rapid but very expensive and needs vectors and probes built by complex, time-consuming steps; multiplex PCR can detect more than one pathogen.

questions.question:
Describe arthropod-borne transmission of viruses and its control:
A(i) the definition of arboviruses and vectors;
A(ii) the transmission cycles.
B(i) Relate the process to TBEV, West Nile virus, dengue, Zika and the haemorrhagic fever viruses.
B(ii) Explain how weather and season influence transmission.
C(i) Explain the consequences for diagnosis.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for prevention and control.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Arboviruses are viruses spread to people by the bite of infected arthropods such as mosquitoes and ticks; about 30 flaviviruses are arthropod-borne, mainly by ticks and mosquitoes.
A(ii)
Dengue and yellow fever use Aedes aegypti in a sylvatic and an urban cycle; the virus replicates in the mosquito during an extrinsic incubation period and only females transmit; tick vectors of TBEV pass virus transovarially.
B(i)
• TBEV: Ixodes persulcatus (Siberian, Far Eastern subtypes) and Ixodes ricinus (European subtype), about 15% of vectors infected, about 130 animal species as sources, rare spread by unpasteurised goat or cow milk, incubation 1-2 weeks.
• West Nile virus: Culex mosquitoes, birds as reservoir without symptoms, humans and horses as dead-end hosts; dengue and Zika: Aedes aegypti and albopictus, Zika also from mother to child, by sex and by transfusion.
• Rift Valley fever: Aedes mosquito; Crimean-Congo and Kyasanur Forest fevers: Ixodid ticks; Omsk fever: muskrat urine, faeces or blood; hantaviruses: rodents (the exception to arthropod spread).
B(ii)
TBE shows spring-summer seasonality; temperature change and dryness favour mosquito breeding and the rainy season changes bird, mosquito and human behaviour, so West Nile virus incidence is high at initial precipitation and dry air; the role of wind and pressure is unresolved.
C(i)
• TBE: blood, serum, CSF or autopsy material by ELISA, RT-PCR, neutralisation, culture in cell lines or mouse intracerebral inoculation, with ticks examined by IF and ELISA; West Nile by serology and RT-PCR; Zika needs laboratory confirmation and differentiation from dengue.
• Cross-reactivity between flaviviruses complicates serology, and neutralisation is better than HI for screening arbovirus immunity.
C(ii)
• Vector control: eliminate female Aedes, remove breeding sites (cover water containers, remove standing water, clean up trash and tyres), use larvicides and insecticides and community initiatives.
• Educate people to carry out vector control programmes in their homes.
• Personal protection: light, covering clothing, window screens, repellents, nets for daytime sleepers; tick control with acaricides and repellent-impregnated clothing.
• Yellow fever 17D vaccine, inactivated TBE vaccine for risk groups and mass vaccination in hyperendemic areas; no Zika vaccine.

A(i)
Family Arenaviridae, genus Mammarenavirus: Lassa, Junin, Machupo, Guanarito, Lujo (haemorrhagic fevers) and lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM) virus; the name comes from Latin arena (sand), after sand-like granular inclusions of captured cellular ribosomes seen by electron microscopy.
A(ii)
Polymorphic enveloped particles of 50-300 nm; they survive 15-30 minutes to several hours outside the host; they are sensitive to UV and sunlight, are destroyed by heating at 60 °C for 30-60 minutes and are inactivated by disinfectants.
A(iii)
Two segments (small S and large L) of linear ambisense (−) ssRNA: L codes the L protein (RNA polymerase) and matrix Z protein; S codes nucleoprotein NP and glycoprotein GP, cleaved into GP1 (receptor) and GP2 (fusion).
A(iv)
• GP1 binds membrane molecules (e.g. the transferrin receptor) and induces endocytosis; endosome acidification activates GP2, which stimulates uncoating and release of genomic RNA into the cytoplasm.
• Replication is in the cytoplasm; capsid assembly occurs at the inner cytoplasmic membrane, mediated by Z protein; virions may capture ribosomes and leave by budding.
B(i)
• Lassa virus enters through mucosal or skin lesions, propagates in regional lymph nodes and spreads by blood to viraemia whose level matches severity; main targets are monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells.
• NP and Z protein inhibit interferon synthesis and activation of macrophages and dendritic cells, blocking antigen presentation and cutting cytokine secretion; with immune insufficiency virus spreads to parenchymal organs and endothelial cells, with microcirculation disorders.
B(ii)
The Natal multimammate rat (Mastomys natalensis) continuously excretes Lassa virus in faeces and urine; LCM virus is in Mus musculus, Junin and Machupo in Calomys and Guanarito in Sigmodon; spread is by contact, food and dust aerosol; the infectious dose is 1-10 particles.
C(i)
• Lassa is the Old World virus (West Africa: Nigeria, Liberia, Guinea) causing most endemic cases; Junin, Machupo, Guanarito and Sabia are New World viruses of South America; Lujo was found in Africa (2008); Lassa was isolated in Nigeria in 1969.
• Lassa affects up to 300,000 people a year with 5,000-10,000 deaths; South American haemorrhagic fevers have 15-30% fatality; Lassa spreads human-to-human through body fluids, the others not usually, with explosive nosocomial outbreaks with Lassa and Machupo.
C(ii)
• LCM virus (first isolated in 1933) causes fever or meningoencephalitis and has a teratogenic effect; Lassa gives fever, ulcerative pharyngitis, cough, vomiting, then generalised haemorrhage with hepatitis, myocarditis, pneumonia, encephalitis, renal failure and hearing loss, shedding virus for 1-3 months.
• Diagnosis uses serology (ELISA) and PCR, with culture only at BSL-4; ribavirin in the first week reduces lethality and convalescent sera help; a live vaccine exists only for Junin virus.

A(i)
Family Flaviviridae has around 70 pathogens in three genera (Flavivirus, Pestivirus, Hepacivirus; pegivirus is also listed), about 30 being arthropod-borne. Flavivirus includes yellow fever, dengue, Japanese encephalitis, West Nile and Zika (mosquito) and TBE, Kyasanur Forest disease and Omsk haemorrhagic fever (tick); Pestivirus is veterinary; Hepacivirus is HCV.
A(ii)
