Enveloped spherical virions of 40-60 nm; TBEV has nucleocapsid C protein with envelope proteins M and E, and E glycoprotein spikes have receptor function and haemagglutinating activity; HCV is about 60 nm with E1 and E2; all are easily inactivated by disinfectants and heat.
A(iii)
Positive-sense, non-segmented ssRNA of about 9.6 to 12.3 kbp encoding non-structural proteins with enzymatic activity (helicase, protease, RNA polymerase).
A(iv)
• Entry is by receptor-mediated endocytosis; endosome acidification fuses the envelope with the endosomal membrane and the nucleocapsid reaches the cytoplasm, where the (+)RNA is translated into a polyprotein cleaved by viral and cellular proteases.
• Viral RNA polymerase copies the genome through a negative-strand intermediate; replication is in the cytoplasm, maturation in the endoplasmic reticulum, and progeny leave by budding (also described as release after cell lysis).
B(i)
• TBEV infects leukocytes, endotheliocytes, hepatocytes and neurons: after a tick bite it replicates at the bite site, spreads by blood and lymph to spleen and liver and finally the CNS, degenerating neurons (motor neurons of brainstem and cervical cord are most affected).
• Dengue: virus enters through mosquito saliva, localises to lymph nodes and liver, replicates, and circulates in blood; West Nile virus gives high-titre viraemia with necrosis, haemorrhage and inflammation in heart, brain, liver, kidney, intestine and nervous system.
• HCV attaches via E1 and E2 to hepatocyte receptors (HDL receptor, SR-BI, CD81, claudin-1, occludin).
B(ii)
Flaviviruses infect Vero, BHK-21 and chicken embryo fibroblasts and are lethal to newborn mice; TBEV has about 130 animal species as sources and Ixodes ticks as vectors; West Nile virus is carried by Culex with birds as reservoir and humans and horses as dead-end hosts; dengue and Zika are carried by Aedes.
C(i)
Flavivirus: arthropod-borne zoonotic arboviruses causing acute disease; Hepacivirus: a single species (HCV), transmitted parenterally, causing persistent infection with cirrhosis and carcinoma, and growing in culture only in hepatocyte cultures.
C(ii)
• Dengue: four serotypes, Aedes aegypti and albopictus, fever, headache, joint and muscle pain, haemorrhage, and DHF/DSS after sequential infection. Zika: most infections symptomatic mildly or not at all (rash, fever, conjunctivitis), with congenital Zika syndrome (microcephaly), Guillain-Barré syndrome, and sexual and mother-to-child spread.
• Zika must be confirmed by laboratory tests and differentiated from cross-reactive flaviviruses such as dengue; NSAIDs are avoided until dengue is ruled out because of bleeding risk; no vaccine or specific treatment exists for Zika.

questions.question:
Describe dengue virus under the following headings:
A(i) properties and serotypes;
A(ii) transmission and the vector cycle;
A(iii) clinical features and epidemiology.
B(i) Outline the laboratory detection and what has been used to measure infection.
C(i) Explain how the results are interpreted.
C(ii) State the limitations, causes of false results, and control.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Genus Flavivirus of the Flaviviridae (enveloped, positive ssRNA, spherical 40-60 nm); four serotypes are known and infection with one does not protect against the others because of different serological reactivity.
A(ii)
• Transmitted by the bite of female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus (about 5 mm, biting in early morning or late afternoon); males do not transmit; African monkeys are the suggested natural reservoir.
• A mosquito biting a viraemic person takes virus into its gut, where it replicates during the extrinsic incubation period, then transmits it for life to susceptible persons; in humans virus enters via saliva, localises to lymph nodes and liver and later circulates in blood (intrinsic incubation).
A(iii)
• Fever, headache, joint and muscle pain, vomiting and sometimes haemorrhage, with depression afterwards; sequential infection with different serotypes raises risk of dengue haemorrhagic fever and shock syndrome (weak rapid pulse, low blood pressure, altered mental status); incubation of DHF 2-5 days.
• Nearly 100 million are infected annually; it is endemic with yearly peaks and case fatality of 1-10% in Asia, Africa, Australia and the Americas; in Nigeria 45% were immune to dengue 2 and 23.4% recent infection was reported in Ibadan.
B(i)
• Haemagglutination-inhibition (HI) tests found HI antibodies against dengue 1, yellow fever, West Nile and Wesselsbron in 63% of Nigerians tested; neutralisation tests found dengue neutralising antibody in 48% of monkeys and 25% of galagos.
• Dengue was first detected by a molecular technique in 1964 in Ibadan.
C(i)
• A high HI prevalence shows past exposure to flaviviruses; in parallel tests 6 of 20 HI-negative sera (30%) had dengue neutralising antibody, so neutralisation is better than HI for screening arbovirus immunity.
• A single antibody result cannot separate previous from current infection; a rise in titre between acute and convalescent sera is needed.
C(ii)
• Cross-reactivity between related flaviviruses (e.g. Japanese encephalitis and dengue) can cause false positives; clinical diagnosis in West Africa is complicated by chikungunya, o'nyong-nyong and Zika.
• Control is by eliminating the female Aedes population and educating people on home vector control; ribavirin showed clinical suitability against dengue.

A(i)
Named from first isolation in human adenoids in 1953; genera Mastadenovirus (human), Aviadenovirus (fowl), Atadenovirus (ovine), Ichtadenovirus (sturgeon), Siadenovirus (frog); human types HAdV 1-57 in 7 species (A-G).
A(ii)
70-90 nm, icosahedral, non-enveloped; 292 capsomeres (240 hexons, 12 pentons); each penton has a base and a fiber with a knob that binds the host cell and acts as haemagglutinin; the penton base has toxin-like activity causing CPE.
A(iii)
Linear dsDNA of 26-45 kbp with inverted terminal repeats of about 100 bp, each strand covalently attached at the 5′ end to a virus-encoded protein.
A(iv)
• The fiber binds the Coxsackie and adenovirus receptor, the penton base binds integrin and the virus enters in a clathrin-coated endosome, uncoats and travels by microtubules to the nucleus.
• About 20 early proteins push the cell into S-phase; DNA replicates in the nucleus primed by the terminal protein; a large late transcript spliced into 18 mRNAs gives structural proteins; capsids assemble in the nucleus and the virus is released.
B(i)
• Adenoviruses infect epithelial cells of respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, bladder and eyes, multiplying in conjunctiva, pharynx or small intestine and spreading to regional lymph nodes, usually no further.
• They cause lytic infection, latent infection in lymphoid organs (tonsil, Peyer's patches) and oncogenic transformation (groups A and B, not seen in humans).
B(ii)
Parvoviruses replicate only in actively dividing cells; they cannot induce S-phase and wait in the nucleus for it, making fetal cells an excellent environment; B19 infects upper respiratory tract cells with intense viraemia for a week and persistent infection gives chronic anaemia.
C(i)
• Both are non-enveloped icosahedral DNA viruses. Adenovirus: 70-90 nm, dsDNA of 26-45 kbp, induces S-phase. Parvovirus: 18-26 nm, the smallest human viruses, linear ssDNA of either polarity, 60 copies of capsid protein, and cannot induce S-phase.
• Subfamily Parvovirinae (human) has Dependovirus (needs adenovirus or herpesvirus), Erythrovirus (B19) and Bocavirus; Densovirinae infect arthropods.
C(ii)
• Adenovirus infections are mostly mild and self-limiting in children (pharyngitis, pneumonia, keratoconjunctivitis, gastroenteritis); no specific treatment (ganciclovir, vidarabine, ribavirin, cidofovir; acetaminophen); diagnosis by EM, ELISA, DFA, PCR and culture.
• B19 causes erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek), arthropathy in adults, aplastic crisis and hydrops fetalis; no vaccine or antiviral, immunoglobulins block persistent infection; diagnosis by EM, IgM ELISA, PCR and dot blot hybridisation.

A(i)
• Cells respond to infection by no change, death or transformation; indirect damage can follow integration of the viral genome, induction of mutations in the host genome, inflammation and immune response. In restrictive infection few viruses are made, the genome persists and cells may undergo transformation.
• Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to copy RNA into DNA that integrates and serves for replication or as an oncogene; the first retrovirus found was the Rous sarcoma virus, causing tumours in chickens; HIV has no onc gene.
A(ii)
Cancers are associated with EBV, HTLV-1, HPV, HBV, HCV and HHV-8.
B(i)
• HPV infects squamous epithelia; low-risk types include 6 and 11, high-risk types 16, 18, 31 and 45; HPV DNA integrates into the cellular genome, causing hyper-proliferation, transformation and immortalisation; clearance occurs within 6 to 18 months in immunocompetent persons.
• Progression: koilocytosis, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia I-III, invasive cervical cancer; HPV 16 gives squamous cell cancer and HPV 18 adenocarcinoma of the cervix; cancers also of skin, larynx, penis, vulva, vagina and anus.
B(ii)
• EBV: Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, B-cell lymphoma; HHV-8: Kaposi's sarcoma and exudative lymphoma.
• HBV: higher HCC rate in chronic carriers, especially HBeAg positive; HCV: cirrhosis within 20 years and HCC in a further 10; HTLV-1: T-cell leukaemia.
• Adenovirus groups A and B can transform cells by integrating viral DNA, although oncogenicity has not been seen in humans; mouse polyomavirus and SV40 induce tumours when injected into infant rodents.
C(i)
• HPV: colposcopy, acetic acid test, Pap smear, ELISA or western blot, PCR; HPV cannot be cultured.
• HBV and HCV viral load assays monitor chronic infection; multiplex PCR detecting EBV DNA is used for brain lesions in AIDS.
C(ii)
• Vaccines: Gardasil (types 6, 11, 90% of genital warts), Cervarix (bivalent), Gardasil 9 (prevents 90% of cervical, vulvar, vaginal and anal cancers); avoid unprotected sex and screen young women.
• HPV has no specific treatment (removal of lesions); no effective antiviral exists for EBV; interferon-α is effective in HHV-8, papillomavirus, HBV and HCV disease.
questions.question:
Describe oncogenesis by viruses:
A(i) how viruses transform cells and cause cancer;
A(ii) the viruses and cancers involved.
B(i) Relate the process to human papillomavirus.
B(ii) Relate the process to EBV, HHV-8, HBV, HCV, HTLV-1, adenoviruses and polyomaviruses.
C(i) Explain the consequences for diagnosis and screening.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for prevention, control and treatment.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Chronic hepatitis B is treated with interferon, pegylated interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogues; hepatitis C with ribavirin plus interferon, and Harvoni (ledipasvir 90 mg/sofosbuvir 400 mg).
A(ii)
• HBV: nucleosides (lamivudine, telbivudine, emtricitabine, entecavir) and nucleotides (adefovir, tenofovir); entecavir 0.5 mg/day for at least 6 months; adefovir dipivoxil once daily; immune modulators include interferon, thymosin and therapeutic vaccines.
• HCV: 24 weeks with ribavirin 800 mg daily for genotypes 2 and 3, 48 weeks with 1000-1200 mg for genotype 1, genotypes 4, 5 and 6 like 2 and 3; Harvoni once daily for 8-24 weeks.
B(i)
• Lamivudine triphosphate inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and HIV reverse transcriptase; adefovir is a reverse transcriptase inhibitor, since HBV replicates through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase.
• Interferon-α induces cellular enzymes that inhibit viral protein synthesis; ribavirin triphosphate inhibits viral RNA polymerase and is active against many RNA viruses.
B(ii)
• Sustained virological response is the absence of HCV viraemia 6 months after treatment; sustained biochemical response is normal ALT for 6 months after therapy.
• Quantitative HCV RNA PCR is the gold standard for response; HBV DNA viral load shows efficacy of therapy.
C(i)
• Ribavirin alone cannot eradicate HCV and must be used with interferon; many HCV isolates are interferon-resistant because viral proteins block interferon-inducible antiviral proteins.
• Immune and drug pressure select resistant quasispecies, creating lines resistant to therapy that promote disease progression.
C(ii)
• Adherence is a key predictor of success: the 80/80/80 rule requires 80% of interferon and 80% of ribavirin for 80% of the time; interferon is not given orally (intramuscular or subcutaneous).
• Diet matters: about 0.8 g protein per kg body weight daily, less sodium because of fluid retention and ascites, and attention to liver fat.
• Potential HCV drugs were in phase I-III trials; HBV prevention is by vaccination, with no HCV vaccine.
questions.question:
Describe the treatment of chronic viral hepatitis as a control measure:
A(i) the drugs available for hepatitis B and C;
A(ii) the classes and regimens.
B(i) Explain the mechanisms of action.
B(ii) Explain the monitoring of response.
C(i) Explain the limitations and the basis of resistance.
C(ii) Explain the trade-offs, adherence and supportive measures.

Describe virus isolation and identification in cell culture:
A(i) the principle and the types of cell culture;
A(ii) the preparation and inoculation of the specimen.
B(i) Set out how growing virus is detected.
B(ii) Set out how the virus is identified, and the culture conditions.
C(i) Explain the interpretation of results.
C(ii) Explain the sources of error, limitations and biosafety precautions.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Isolation in cell culture is the original virus detection assay: the specimen is inoculated onto living cells in which the virus propagates, because viruses replicate only in living cells and not on cell-free media like bacteria; eggs and animals are difficult to handle.
• Primary cells (e.g. monkey kidney) are normal cells from freshly killed adult animals, passaged once or twice, support the widest range of viruses but are costly; semi-continuous cells (human embryonic kidney, skin fibroblasts) pass up to 50 times; continuous cells (HeLa, Vero, Hep2, LLC-MK2, BGM) are immortalised, easiest to handle but support a limited range.
A(ii)
Living cell cultures are established in plastic wells or Petri dishes; samples are homogenised in cell culture growth media, centrifuged or filtered to remove debris and bacteria, treated with antibiotics and then inoculated onto the cells.
B(i)
• Presumptive detection is by cytopathic effect (CPE): changes in cell shape and size and fusion to multinucleated giant cells (syncytia), usually a dying cell; CPE may be specific (HSV, CMV) or non-specific (enteroviruses).
• Without CPE: haemadsorption (red cells attach to infected cells; for viruses with haemagglutinin such as mumps, parainfluenza, influenza), interference (rubella detected by blocking CPE of echovirus or Coxsackie virus) and decreased acid production (phenol red stays red instead of yellow; certain enteroviruses).
B(ii)
• Definitive identification uses a specific known antibody: complement fixation, haemagglutination inhibition, neutralisation, fluorescent antibody (apple-green fluorescein under UV), radioimmunoassay, ELISA, immunoelectron microscopy, or molecular tests.
• Growth medium needs pH 7.2-7.4 and temperature 36.5-37.5 °C.
C(i)
CPE is only presumptive; a virus without CPE can still be detected by the other methods, and identity is confirmed by neutralisation, haemadsorption-inhibition, immunofluorescence or molecular tests.
C(ii)
• The main problem is the long period (up to 4 weeks) to a result; sensitivity is often poor and depends on the specimen condition and the condition of the cell sheet.
• Cultures are very susceptible to bacterial contamination and toxic substances in the specimen; primary cultures can contain adventitious agents such as mycoplasma, bacteria and SV40.
• Many viruses will not grow in cell culture at all, e.g. hepatitis B and C, diarrhoeal viruses, parvovirus; HPV cannot be cultured.
• All cell culture work is done under a laminar flow hood with negative pressure; culture of arenaviruses is done only in BSL-4 reference laboratories.

A(i)
An α-herpesvirus of 100-200 nm, icosahedral and enveloped (11 glycoproteins), with linear dsDNA; it replicates fast, destroys the host cell and establishes latency in sensory ganglia; the membrane is fragile.
A(ii)
Transmission is by direct contact with lesion fluid or saliva, sexual contact (genital herpes), perinatally (infected from the mother during birth) and, rarely, congenitally.
A(iii)
• HSV-1 causes gingivostomatitis and keratitis, infecting mouth, eye and CNS and some genital herpes; HSV-2 infects the genital and anal region, mostly genital mucous membranes (glans penis, cervix, vagina).
• The virus enters through skin or mucosa, multiplies locally, is taken up by sensory neurons and goes retrogradely to ganglia where latency is established; HSV-1 reactivates in trigeminal and HSV-2 in sacral ganglia.
B(i)
• Microscopy: Tzanck smear with Giemsa stain, and electron microscopy; virus culture; serology by ELISA, neutralisation, CFT and immunofluorescence; molecular diagnosis by PCR and DNA probe.
• Antigen detection by immunofluorescence on skin scrapings gives a result within hours; Cowdry type A intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions are seen in infected cells.
B(ii)
• Specimens are saliva, vesicle fluid, conjunctival fluid, corneal scrapings, skin swab and CSF.
• HSV produces a specific cytopathic effect in cell culture.
C(i)
• A specific CPE is presumptive and is confirmed by neutralisation, immunofluorescence or molecular tests; positive PCR or antigen shows virus, antibody serology shows exposure.
• Treatment: acyclovir orally or parenterally; ganciclovir, vidarabine and famciclovir orally; idoxuridine topically for eye and skin infection.
C(ii)
• Mild local infections such as genital HSV may not produce a detectable humoral response (false-negative serology); antigen detection is tedious, difficult to read and of poor sensitivity and specificity, and depends on specimen quality.
• Culture can take up to 4 weeks and is prone to bacterial contamination; PCR is prone to contamination (false positives); immunocompromised patients may give reduced antibody.
questions.question:
Describe herpes simplex virus (HSV) under the following headings:
A(i) properties;
A(ii) transmission;
A(iii) clinical disease and pathogenesis.
B(i) Outline the laboratory diagnosis.
B(ii) State the specimens and culture findings.
C(i) Explain how the results are interpreted and how infection is treated.
C(ii) State the limitations and causes of false results.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A β-herpesvirus: slowly replicating, infected cells enlarge, latency in secretory glands, lymphoreticular cells and kidneys; herpesvirus particles are 100-200 nm, icosahedral, enveloped with a fragile membrane and linear dsDNA.
A(ii)
Spread by close contact and blood transfusion; acquired prenatally, perinatally (maternal genital secretions, breast feeding) or postnatally (saliva by kissing, semen in sexual intercourse or artificial insemination, transfusion, organ transplant).
A(iii)
• Usually symptomless; the most common agent of intrauterine infection and prenatal damage causing congenital abnormalities; it may cause an EBV-like mononucleosis syndrome, and in graft recipients and AIDS patients widely disseminated infection (interstitial pneumonia, chorioretinitis, hepatitis, arthritis, gastrointestinal infection, encephalitis).
• It enters via the respiratory or upper gastrointestinal tract, multiplies and spreads haematogenously, persisting in salivary gland cells, renal tubules and leukocytes; it is associated with atherosclerosis and restenosis after heart surgery.
B(i)
• Cell culture is easy and grows with a typical cytopathic effect in 5-25 days on human diploid cells.
• Antigen detection and microscopy are insensitive; PCR is fast, reliable and more sensitive than cultivation; cytomegalic (owl's eye) inclusion bodies are seen in infected cells.
B(ii)
• Urine, saliva, vaginal secretion, breast milk (difficult) and leukocytes (difficult) can be used for cultivation.
• Culture sensitivity depends on the condition of the specimen and of the cell sheet, and cultures are susceptible to bacterial contamination and toxic substances.
C(i)
• A typical CPE in human diploid cells indicates CMV growth; PCR detects genomes but a positive PCR does not necessarily indicate disease.
• Rapid direct methods matter in severe CMV infections of immunocompromised patients, where clinical management depends on rapid results.
C(ii)
• Latent CMV genomes may be amplified from the blood of healthy individuals, making a positive PCR difficult to interpret; culture takes up to 25 days; antigen detection and microscopy lack sensitivity.
• Treatment is hyperimmune gamma globulin or antiviral therapy (ganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir).
questions.question:
Describe cytomegalovirus (CMV) under the following headings:
A(i) properties;
A(ii) transmission;
A(iii) clinical disease and pathogenesis.
B(i) Outline the laboratory diagnosis.
B(ii) State the specimens and culture conditions.
C(i) Explain how the results are interpreted.
C(ii) State the limitations, the causes of false or misleading results, and the treatment.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Acute infection: recovery with no residual effects, recovery with residual effects (e.g. acute viral encephalitis with neurological sequelae), death, or progression to chronic infection.
• Chronic infection: silent subclinical infection for life (CMV, EBV); long silent period before disease (HIV); reactivation to acute disease (herpes, shingles); chronic disease with relapses (HBV, HCV); cancers (EBV, HTLV-1, HPV, HBV, HCV, HHV-8).
A(ii)
• True latency: the virus remains completely latent after primary infection (HSV, VZV); the genome may be integrated into the cellular genome or exist as an episome.
• Persistence: the virus replicates continuously in the body at a very low level (HIV, HBV, CMV, EBV).
B(i)
• HSV is neurotropic: taken up by sensory neurons, retrograde transport to ganglia where latency is established; the immune system clears epithelial infection but HSV hides in ganglia; reactivation begins in neurons (HSV-1 trigeminal ganglia, HSV-2 sacral ganglia).
• VZV persists in the spinal ganglia of the intercostal nerves; when immunity weakens it spreads anterogradely into the sensory area of the nerve, forming shingles.
B(ii)
• CMV persists in salivary gland cells, renal tubules and leukocytes; EBV in B cells; HHV-6 and HHV-7 persist for life; adenovirus becomes latent in lymphoid organs (tonsil, Peyer's patches); BK and JC polyomaviruses persist in the kidney and reactivate in immunosuppression.
• HBV partial circular DNA becomes cccDNA and some DNA integrates into the host genome causing carrier state; HIV integrates as provirus in memory T cells and may reside quietly for years.
C(i)
• PCR is so sensitive that latent CMV genomes may be amplified from the blood of healthy people, so a positive PCR does not necessarily indicate disease; a single antibody titre does not distinguish previous from current infection.
• For HIV and rabies, which cause disease months or years after seroconversion, the presence of antibody is enough for a definitive diagnosis.
C(ii)
• Reactivation occurs when immunity falls (zoster; CMV disseminated infection in graft recipients and AIDS patients; polyomavirus in transplant, treated by reducing immunosuppressive doses).
• HIV needs lifelong antiretroviral drugs; chronic HBV/HCV carriers risk cirrhosis and carcinoma; for EBV no effective antiviral therapy is available.
questions.question:
Describe latency and persistence in viral infection:
A(i) the possible outcomes of acute and chronic infection;
A(ii) the difference between true latency and persistence, with examples.
B(i) Relate the process to herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus.
B(ii) Relate the process to the other viruses that persist or become latent.
C(i) Explain the consequences for laboratory diagnosis.
C(ii) Explain the consequences for prevention, control and treatment.

Describe rabies virus under the following headings:
A(i) properties (family, genus, morphology, genome, street and fixed virus);
A(ii) transmission and epidemiology;
A(iii) clinical disease.
B(i) Outline the laboratory diagnosis, including ante-mortem methods.
B(ii) Describe the direct examination of tissue.
C(i) Explain how the findings are interpreted.
C(ii) State the limitations and sources of false results.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Family Rhabdoviridae, genus Lyssavirus; bullet-shaped enveloped virus with helical symmetry and linear negative-sense ssRNA. "Rabies" is from Latin meaning to do violence and "Lyssa" is Greek for frenzy.
• Street virus is the virulent wild virus from a naturally infected animal (e.g. a dog) acquired through the bite or scratch of a rabid animal; fixed virus has virulence and incubation stabilised by serial passages (e.g. in rabbits).
A(ii)
• Transmitted most often by bite or scratch from infected animals, by aerosols where virus levels are high, and iatrogenically through corneal transplant; the dog is the most important reservoir, also bats, skunks, raccoons, cats, ferrets, cattle and foxes.
• About 1 case a year in the U.S., about 25,000 human cases a year in India from dog bite and more than 30,000 deaths a year in Asia; rabies is one of the most lethal infectious diseases and the only important pathogen in the family.
A(iii)
Incubation is usually 14 to 90 days or more depending on the bite site; pain and itching at the wound, fever, headache, stomach ache; then CNS involvement with hydrophobia, seizures and hallucinations, coma, respiratory paralysis and death.
B(i)
• Ante-mortem diagnosis in humans: immunofluorescence assays on skin biopsy, corneal impression or saliva; virus isolation from saliva and other secretions.
• Biopsy of brain (Ammon's horn, cerebral cortex) is examined for cytoplasmic inclusions called Negri bodies.
B(ii)
• Direct fluorescent antibody test (dFAT) is the gold standard: brain tissue is collected and fluorescently labelled antibodies that bind rabies virus antigens are used to detect virus.
• By light microscopy Negri bodies appear as eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in certain nerve cells containing virus, in the Ammon's horn of the hippocampus.
C(i)
Negri bodies are distinctive inclusions caused by rabies virus and serve as a diagnostic tool; a positive dFAT on brain tissue shows rabies antigen.
C(ii)
Histology is not sensitive or specific and serves only as an adjunct; the dFAT is highly accurate when performed on fresh brain tissue.

questions.question:
Describe the preparation and use of cell cultures for virology:
A(i) the definitions and types of culture and the purposes of cultivation;
A(ii) the growth medium and culture conditions.
B(i) Set out the preparation of a primary cell line (chick embryo fibroblast).
B(ii) State the quality control measures.
C(i) Explain the types of cell and their use for virus work.
C(ii) Explain the sources of error, limitations and biosafety precautions.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Tissue culture is the growth in vitro of cells, tissues or organs for more than 24 h; cell culture is growth of cells no longer organised into tissues; a cell line arises from a primary culture at the first successful subculture; primary cells come directly from tissue of humans, animals or birds, with limited passages but rapid division.
• Cultivation is used to isolate and identify viruses in specimens, to study structure, replication cycles, genetics and effects on host cells, and to prepare virus for vaccines; living cells can be tissue culture, embryonated hen's egg, animals or organs.
A(ii)
• The medium mimics the human system: pure deionised water at pH 7.2-7.4, buffering salts, the 20 amino acids, micronutrients (calcium, magnesium, trace elements), vitamins, growth factors (serum, chick embryo extract), additives (antibiotics, antifungals) and indicators.
• Conditions are pH 7.2-7.4 and temperature 36.5-37.5 °C.
B(i)
• A 10-day-old embryonated egg is cut open at the air sac, the embryo is moved with sterile forceps and scissors to a sterile Petri dish, the head is removed and the body placed in another dish, then in a conical flask and washed in PBS (pH 7.2-7.4, 37 °C).
• The tissue is chopped, washed and the PBS poured out; trypsin (25%) is added with a Teflon magnetic bar on a magnetic stirrer; after trypsinisation the turbid solution is poured off, washed 2-3 times with PBS and filtered through gauze.
• Growth medium is added to stop the enzyme and the cells are counted using trypan blue; cultures are grown in culture flasks with growth medium and viewed with an inverted microscope.
B(ii)
All cell culture work is done under a laminar flow hood with negative pressure, and antibiotics and antifungals are added to the medium.
C(i)
Primary cells support the widest range of viruses; semi-continuous cells (human embryonic kidney, skin fibroblasts) pass up to 50 times; continuous cells (HeLa, Vero, Hep2, LLC-MK2, BGM) are immortalised and passage indefinitely.
C(ii)
• Primary cultures can contain adventitious agents such as mycoplasma, bacteria and SV40, and cultures are very susceptible to bacterial contamination and toxic substances in specimens.
• Primary cells are expensive with an unreliable supply and pass only once or twice; continuous cells support a limited range; many viruses will not grow (hepatitis B and C, parvovirus, HPV).
• Culture of arenaviruses needs BSL-4 laboratories.

A(i)
Family Picornaviridae, genus Hepatovirus; 27 nm icosahedral, non-enveloped; ssRNA of 7.5 kb; heat- and acid-stable; fulminant disease rare, chronic disease never, not oncogenic.
A(ii)
• Faecal-oral spread through contaminated food or water: food handlers, raw shellfish, travel to endemic areas, close personal, household or sexual contact, day-care centres; blood-borne spread is rare (injecting drug users).
• Prevalence is high; in Shanghai in 1988 about 300,000 people were infected after eating shellfish from a polluted river.
A(iii)
• HAV replicates slowly in the liver without apparent cytopathic effects; in the absence of cytolysis it can readily establish persistent infection; jaundice results from liver damage, and antibody and cell-mediated responses develop.
• Incubation averages 30 days (15-50); jaundice in under 10% of children below 6, 40-50% at 6-14 years and 70-80% above 14; complications are fulminant, cholestatic or relapsing hepatitis; no chronic sequelae.
B(i)
• Serology: IgM anti-HAV and total anti-HAV; detection of IgM or rising IgG titres indicates active disease.
• Immunoelectron microscopy of faecal extracts shows 27-29 nm full and empty virus particles; ALT is followed with the serology.
B(ii)
Serum is used for antibody and faeces for virus particles.
C(i)
• For hepatitis A the onset of symptoms coincides with antibody, so IgM or a rising IgG titre indicates active disease; the course is charted with ALT, faecal HAV, IgM anti-HAV and total anti-HAV from 0 to 24 months after exposure.
• In a primary response IgM appears first followed by a much higher IgG titre; seroconversion is a change from antibody negative to positive.
C(ii)
• IgM assays suffer interference by rheumatoid factor, re-infection and unexplained persistence of IgM years after infection; patients with infectious mononucleosis may react non-specifically.
• Patients given blood or blood products may be falsely positive from passive antibody; immunocompromised patients may give reduced or absent antibody; vaccines HAVRIX (94%) and VAQTA (100%) show efficacy in studies.
questions.question:
Describe hepatitis A virus (HAV) under the following headings:
A(i) properties;
A(ii) transmission and epidemiology;
A(iii) pathogenesis and clinical disease.
B(i) Outline the laboratory diagnosis.
B(ii) State the specimens used.
C(i) Explain how the results are interpreted.
C(ii) State the limitations and causes of false results.

Describe the family Papovaviridae under the following headings:
A(i) classification;
A(ii) morphology and structure;
A(iii) genome.
B(i) Explain the pathogenesis and tissue tropism of the papillomaviruses.
B(ii) Explain the pathogenesis and tissue tropism of the polyomaviruses.
C(i) Distinguish the papillomaviruses from the polyomaviruses.
C(ii) Distinguish JC virus from BK virus.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The name comes from papilloma, polyoma and simian vacuolating virus SV40; two genera, Papillomavirus and Polyomavirus, cause lytic infections and benign or malignant tumours. HPV has over 100 types: low risk (6, 11, 42, 43, 44), intermediate (33, 35, 39, 52, 58), high risk (16, 18, 31, 45).
A(ii)
Small, non-enveloped, icosahedral viruses of 40-55 nm.
A(iii)
Double-stranded DNA; papillomaviruses are small circular dsDNA viruses.
B(i)
• HPV is host species-specific, infects squamous epithelia and mucous membranes (including cervical mucosa) with a predilection for skin and certain mucosae, and cannot be grown in cell culture.
• It causes cutaneous warts (types 2, 4, 7), genital warts (6, 11), recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (6, 11), oral papillomatosis and cancer; infection may become persistent and latent, with hyperproliferation, and is cleared within 6-18 months in immunocompetent persons.
B(ii)
• BK and JC viruses establish persistent infection in the kidney after a primary viraemia and reactivate in immunocompromised patients, causing secondary viraemia.
• Mouse polyomavirus is harmless in mice but induces tumours in infant rodents; SV40 gives subclinical infection in monkeys but tumours in baby rodents.
C(i)
• Papillomaviruses infect epithelia, cause warts and cancer and cannot be cultured; polyomaviruses persist in the kidney and reactivate in immunosuppression (polyoma means many tumours) and are diagnosed by culture, electron microscopy, nucleic acid, antigen detection and histopathology.
• HPV has vaccines and no specific treatment (salicylic acid, imiquimod, podofilox, trichloroacetic acid, cryotherapy, surgery); polyomaviruses have no specific effective antiviral (cidofovir and others tried), supportive care and reduced immunosuppression, and no control measures.
C(ii)
• JC virus was first isolated from the brain of a patient with Hodgkin's disease who had progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a rare, fatal subacute CNS infection; it persists in kidneys and is shed in urine more in pregnancy and immunosuppression.
• BK virus causes subclinical infection in children before age 10, sometimes upper respiratory symptoms, persists in kidneys and reactivates in the last trimester of pregnancy and after transplant immunosuppression; it was isolated from the urine of a renal transplant recipient.

questions.question:
Describe the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA):
A(i) the principle and components;
A(ii) the types of ELISA.
B(i) Set out the procedure of the indirect and sandwich ELISA.
C(i) Explain the interpretation of results and the applications.
C(ii) Explain the limitations and sources of error.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
ELISA replaced radioimmunoassays; a solid phase (polystyrene or polyvinyl 96-well plate) adsorbs antigen or antibody, an enzyme-linked antihuman immunoglobulin conjugate (horseradish peroxidase or alkaline phosphatase) binds the complex and the enzyme substrate gives colour.
A(ii)
Types: direct, indirect, sandwich and competitive. Direct ELISA: plate coated with antigen, casein covers uncoated plastic, enzyme-conjugated immunoglobulin binds the antigen, wash, add substrate.
B(i)
• Indirect: coat the plate with antigen; add a non-reacting protein (e.g. casein) to cover remaining plastic; add patient serum; wash to remove unbound antibody.
• Add antihuman immunoglobulin-enzyme conjugate; wash; add substrate and incubate at room temperature in the dark for 15 to 30 minutes; add stop solution; measure the colour.
• Sandwich: adsorb antibody onto the plate, add patient's serum to test for specific antigen, wash, add the immunoglobulin-enzyme conjugate, wash, add substrate and incubate in the dark and observe colour change.
C(i)
• Colour development indicates specific antibody (positive); no colour means negative; the higher the antibody concentration, the stronger the colour; a spectrophotometer measures absorbance quantitatively.
• Applications: infectious agents (e.g. HIV, HBV, HCV), antigen detection (HIV p24 antigen, HBV surface antigen), hormonal assays, clinical research, drug investigations and tumour tests.
C(ii)
• EIAs offer better sensitivity, specificity and reproducibility than CFT and HAI, but both depend greatly on the antigen used; IgM assays suffer interference by rheumatoid factor, re-infection and unexplained persistence of IgM.
• Cross-reactivity between related viruses gives false positives; immunocompromised patients may have reduced response; blood products may transfer antibody; HCV antibody ELISA cannot distinguish acute, chronic or resolved infection.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Disorders caused by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites passed directly or indirectly from person to person; a leading cause of death worldwide, particularly in low-income countries and in young children.
(b)
Person to person (touching, kissing, coughing or sneezing, exchange of body fluids; carriers may be symptomless), animal to person (bites, scratches, animal waste) and mother to unborn child (placenta, breast milk, birth).
(c)
Germs lingering on inanimate objects (tabletop, door knob, faucet handle), insect vectors (mosquitoes, fleas, lice, ticks) and contaminated food and water.
(d)
Route of transmission (an airborne agent can infect more people than one spread by direct contact) and survival time in the environment (a few seconds, e.g. HIV, versus hours or days, e.g. SARS-CoV-2).
(e)
Infected pets or animals biting or scratching; a pregnant woman passing microorganisms to her baby; germs spread by cough, sneeze or sexual contact.
(f)
Mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite or West Nile virus; deer ticks may carry the bacterium that causes Lyme disease.
(g)
Escherichia coli present in or on foods such as undercooked hamburger or unpasteurized fruit juice, which can spread microorganisms to many people from a single source.
(h)
Bacteria (strep throat, urinary tract infections, anthrax, tuberculosis, salmonella), viruses (common cold, HIV/AIDS, COVID-19, influenza, Ebola, hepatitis), fungi (ringworm, athlete's foot) and parasites (malaria); H. pylori is linked to stomach cancer and peptic ulcers.
(i)
Regular hand washing, vaccination kept up to date, staying home when ill, safe food preparation, cooking to the proper temperature and refrigerating leftovers, safe sex, not sharing personal items and travelling wisely.
(j)
They interrupt direct and indirect transmission; vaccination can drastically reduce the chances of contracting many diseases.
(k)
New diseases emerge, old diseases increase or re-emerge, bioterrorism, increasing antimicrobial resistance, breakdowns in public health systems, and greatly increased human mobility allowing epidemics and pandemics.
(l)
Immunosuppressive drugs or steroids, HIV/AIDS, certain cancers, malnutrition, implanted devices and extremes of age raise risk; some infections stay silent and reappear (chickenpox may become shingles).
questions.question:
A. Describe how infectious diseases are transmitted and prevented under the following headings.
(a) Definition and significance.
(b) Direct contact routes.
(c) Indirect contact routes.
(d) Factors that determine how quickly an agent spreads.
B. Relate these to the common examples.
(e) Examples of the direct routes.
(f) Examples of vector-borne transmission.
(g) Examples of food contamination.
(h) Examples of causes and consequences.
C. Explain how prevention improves safety and what limits it.
(i) Preventive measures.
(j) Why these measures protect patients.
(k) Limitations and challenges.
(l) Risk factors and trade-offs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Gram-negative bacteria mainly; the contaminants are pyrogens, and the most pyrogenic substances are endotoxins, which are heat-stable lipopolysaccharide-protein complexes found mainly in the cell walls of Gram-negative bacteria.
(b)
Microbial endotoxins or metabolites of microorganisms found on water used as vehicle or solvent, contaminated sources, and containers and glassware that are used.
(c)
Pyrogens are toxic, thermostable, water-soluble lipopolysaccharides produced from the metabolism of microorganisms; purified water allowed to stand may gain a high content of vegetative microorganisms.
(d)
When present in sufficient amount in parenteral products injected into humans, pyrogens cause febrile reactions (raised body temperature, chills, pains in the neck and head, general malaise); parenteral products, especially large-volume injections, must be free from pyrogenic contamination.
(e)
Depyrogenize instruments: heat glassware at 180°C for 4 hours, or 250°C for 45 minutes, or 650°C for 1 minute; or heat with strong alkali or oxidizing solution.
(f)
Anionic exchange resins and reverse osmosis remove pyrogens from water; Water for Injection is pyrogen-free, sterilized immediately after collection and used for parenteral preparations; the finished product is checked by pyrogen testing (in vivo rabbit test or in vitro LAL test).
questions.question:
A large-volume parenteral solution given to several patients is followed by raised body temperature, chills, pains in the neck and head and general malaise. Investigation points to the water used as vehicle and to the containers and glassware as the sources of contamination.
(a) Identify the likely group of organisms and the contaminant responsible.
(b) State the sources and routes by which this contamination reaches parenteral products.
(c) State the properties of the contaminant and the product or water conditions that support its build-up.
(d) State the consequence for patient safety.
(e) Outline the control measures for glassware and instruments.
(f) Outline the control measures for the water and the finished product.

An aminophylline injection is tested by the LAL test and no gel clot forms in a reaction held at 37°C for 1 hour.
(a) Identify the appropriate test.
(b) State the principle, reagents and procedure.
(c) State the controls and precautions.
(d) Interpret the result.
(e) State the limitations that affect reliability.
(f) State the corrective action or further testing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The Limulus Amoebocyte Lysate (LAL) test, an in vitro pyrogen test for bacterial endotoxin.
(b)
LAL is an aqueous extract of blood cells from the horseshoe crab Limulus polyphemus; endotoxin activates the proenzyme of LAL in the presence of divalent cations (calcium, magnesium, manganese), and the activated enzyme reacts with a low-molecular-weight clottable protein to form a gel clot when incubated at 37°C for 1 hour.
(c)
Positive and negative controls using the USP reference standard for endotoxins; all materials and apparatus depyrogenated at 250°C for at least 1 hour; reaction temperature 36-38°C; pH 5-7; reaction time not exceeding 1 hour.
(d)
A gel that keeps its integrity after slow inversion is positive for endotoxin; no clot is negative, but materials that denature protein or inhibit enzyme action, such as aminophylline injection and ephedrine HCl injection, may inhibit the lysate-endotoxin interaction, so this negative result may be invalid.
(e)
Limited to endotoxin from Gram-negative bacteria; sensitivity varies with endotoxin source; cannot measure fever-producing potential; concentration-dependent rather than dose-dependent; gel is hard to interpret and broken by slight agitation; variability from reagents, method, product and laboratory procedures.
(f)
The in vivo rabbit pyrogen test is the other recognised pyrogen test, and the LAL test is used where the rabbit test is practically impossible.

(a)
WFI is highly purified water used for parenteral preparations, free from microorganisms and pyrogens (bacterial endotoxins), produced to USP, EP or BP standards.
(b)
Filtration (removes large particulates), softening/demineralization (reduces hardness and ionic content) and reverse osmosis (eliminates dissolved salts, organic matter and microbes).
(c)
Electrodeionization (ion exchange with electrical current), ultrafiltration (removes pyrogens and endotoxins), then final distillation.
(d)
Conductivity ≤ 1.3 μS/cm at 25°C; TOC ≤ 0.5 mg/L; endotoxin ≤ 0.25 EU/mL; stored in 316L stainless steel, circulated at ≥ 70°C.
(e)
Solvent in injectables and IV solutions, cleaning of sterile equipment, containers and facilities, dilution for sterile formulations, and analytical and quality-control testing.
(f)
Contamination (microbial and endotoxin), energy-intensive distillation, and the need for rigorous validation and pharmacopeial compliance.
(g)
Stainless steel with circulation to avoid stagnation, circulation at 70°C or above, and regular cleaning and sterilization of tanks and piping.
(h)
Purified water allowed to stand may gain a high content of vegetative microorganisms.
(i)
RO eliminates salts, organics and microbes while ultrafiltration removes pyrogens and endotoxins.
(j)
Continuous conductivity and TOC monitoring for ionic and organic impurities, plus regular microbial and endotoxin testing.
(k)
Validated cleaning and maintenance for production and storage systems and compliance with pharmacopoeial standards.
(l)
Pyrogen contamination causes fever and chills in patients.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Detection of a specific antibody response, which is suggestive but not definitive; S. typhi shares O and H antigens.
(b)
Definitive diagnosis rests on isolation of S. typhi from blood, bone marrow or a specific anatomical lesion; blood culture is the mainstay of diagnosis.
(c)
Specimen types are blood, bone marrow or lesion.
(d)
The Widal test has moderate sensitivity and specificity, and is supported by clinical symptoms characteristic of typhoid.
(e)
S. typhi shares O and H antigens with other Salmonella serotypes and has cross-reacting epitopes with other Enterobacteriaceae.
(f)
False-positive results may occur in malaria, typhus, bacteraemia caused by other organisms and cirrhosis.
(g)
In endemic areas there is often a low background level of antibodies, and the cut-off varies between areas and times.
(h)
It can be negative in up to 30% of culture-proven cases.
(i)
Shared antigens and cross-reacting epitopes, other conditions, and background antibodies in endemic areas.
(j)
It varies between areas and between times in a given area.
(k)
Confirm by isolation of S. typhi from blood, bone marrow or lesion, and interpret serology with the clinical picture.

A. Describe the principles of rational antimicrobial therapy and combination therapy under the following headings.
(a) Purpose of combination therapy.
(b) Spectrum and route principle.
(c) Specimen and empiric principles.
(d) Host and drug factors.
B. Relate these to the common clinical examples.

(f) Endocarditis example.
(g) Diabetic foot and septicaemia examples.
(h) Gonorrhoea and tuberculosis examples.
C. Explain how the approach improves safety and what limits it.
(i) How rational selection improves safety.
(j) Consequences of avoiding the systematic approach.
(k) Compatibility and interaction trade-offs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Combination antibiotic therapy may be indicated for polymicrobial infections, to produce synergistic killing or to prevent emergence of resistance.
(b)
Antibiotics with the narrowest effective spectrum are preferred; route is evaluated daily and conversion from IV to oral therapy attempted as infection improves.
(c)
Culture and sensitivity specimens should be obtained before starting antibiotics; empiric therapy is based on likely pathogens for the infection site, patient history (hospitalisation, work exposure, travel, pets) and local susceptibility.
(d)
Host: allergy, age, pregnancy, genetic or metabolic abnormalities, renal and hepatic function, infection site, concomitant drugs and underlying disease; drug: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and tissue penetration (e.g. effective CSF concentration for meningitis).
(e)
A β-lactam plus an aminoglycoside produces synergistic killing; an aminoglycoside is commonly used in empirical regimens for febrile neutropenia and sepsis when P. aeruginosa is possible.
(f)
Low-dose gentamicin (3 mg/kg/day) with a penicillin or vancomycin for certain Gram-positive organisms; for enterococcal endocarditis penicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin for 4-6 weeks.
(g)
Ciprofloxacin with clindamycin or metronidazole to cover anaerobes; parenteral ciprofloxacin with a third-generation cephalosporin or an aminoglycoside in Gram-negative septicaemia.
(h)
Gonorrhoea therapy includes chlamydia coverage (azithromycin or doxycycline) because chlamydia coexists in up to 45% of cases; multidrug-resistant tuberculosis needs several drugs, sometimes six to seven.
(i)
Narrow-spectrum, culture-directed therapy with monitoring of temperature, WBC count and adverse events, dose adjustment for creatinine clearance and hepatic function, and review of concomitant drugs avoids toxicity and interactions.
(j)
Blind broad-spectrum therapy leads to more expensive and potentially more toxic agents, widespread resistance and difficult-to-treat superinfections.
(k)
Aminoglycosides must not be mixed with any drug in the same syringe, and injectable tetracycline is inactivated by penicillin; patients with type 1 penicillin hypersensitivity should not receive cephalosporins.
(l)
If there is no response in 2-3 days, re-check the diagnosis, therapeutic drug concentrations, immunocompromised status, isolated infection (abscess, foreign body) and resistance.

questions.question:
Two-fold dilutions of an antibiotic are prepared in a liquid medium, inoculated with an overnight broth culture of a test pathogen and incubated at 37°C. Some tubes show no detectable growth, and the microbiologist wants both the MIC and the bactericidal activity.
(a) Identify the appropriate test.
(b) State the principle, media and procedure.
(c) State how the MIC result is interpreted and what affects it.
(d) State the further test for bactericidal activity.
(e) State alternative or related methods and their limits.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Assay of antibiotics by dilution: serial dilution in broth (graded or two-fold dilutions in a liquid medium); end response is presence or absence of growth.
(b)
Diluted antibiotic in liquid medium is inoculated with an appropriate size of overnight broth culture and incubated at 37°C for 1-2 days (bacteria) or room temperature for 2-7 days (fungi); the minimum concentration preventing detectable growth is the MIC.
(c)
The MIC is read after incubation; it varies considerably with inoculum size, the medium used, incubation conditions and the nature of the test organism, so all must be considered.
(d)
Plate a loopful from tubes showing no growth onto sterile set agar, incubate, and observe for growth; the minimum concentration preventing growth is the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC).
(e)
Serial dilution in solid media (double-fold nutrient agar mixed with antibiotic solution; useful for several organisms on one plate, but each plate is one concentration); turbidimetric assay in microtitre plates; diffusion methods give a graded response (zone of inhibition).

(a)
Caused by Salmonella typhi, a Gram-negative bacterium; a similar often less severe disease is caused by Salmonella paratyphi A (ratio about 10 to 1).
(b)
Food and beverages contaminated by a chronic stool carrier (less commonly urine), sewage-contaminated water, contaminated shellfish or faultily canned meat.
(c)
Prolonged fever, sustained bacteraemia without endothelial or endocardial involvement and bacterial invasion and multiplication within mononuclear phagocytic cells of liver, spleen, lymph nodes and Peyer patches.
(d)
Prolonged fever, constipation in adults or diarrhoea in children, headache, malaise, anorexia, bronchitic cough and rose spots (up to 25%); complications in up to 10% include intestinal haemorrhage and perforation.
(e)
Supportive care; fluoroquinolones optimal in adults; safe water and food handling; vaccines (Vi capsular polysaccharide, Ty21a, acetone-inactivated parenteral).
(f)
A pH of 1.5 or less kills most bacilli, so antacids, H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors, gastrectomy or achlorhydria lower the dose needed; immune deficiencies increase risk.
(g)
Excellent tissue penetration, kill S. typhi in its intracellular stationary stage in monocytes/macrophages, higher gallbladder levels, fever clearance in 3-5 days and very low post-treatment carriage; inexpensive and well tolerated.
(h)
Nalidixic-acid-resistant S. typhi (NARST) is a marker of reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones, although nalidixic acid itself is never used for typhoid.
(i)
S. typhi causes the classic severe disease; S. paratyphi A causes a very similar but often less severe disease at about one-tenth the frequency.
(j)
Uncomplicated: fever, bowel disturbance, headache, rose spots; complicated: occult blood in stool 10-20%, melena up to 3%, perforation with right lower quadrant pain, and typhoid meningitis.
(k)
Fully sensitive: fluoroquinolone; multidrug resistant: fluoroquinolone or cefixime; quinolone resistant: azithromycin or ceftriaxone.
(l)
A chronic carrier is asymptomatic with positive stool or rectal cultures a year after recovery (15% of patients); eradicated with ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily for 28 days (or amoxicillin plus probenecid or TMP-SMZ for six weeks); carriers are excluded from food handling.

questions.answerText:

Careful history and physical examination, fever above 37°C as hallmark, raised WBC counts, and pain and inflammation signs in superficial, bone or joint infection; predisposing factors.

Collection of infected material, Gram or acid-fast stains, serologies and culture and sensitivity.

questions.answerText:

Chemical method: heating with a bactericide; mechanical method: aseptic filtration through a 0.22-μm filter. Every ophthalmic product must be sterile in its final container to prevent microbial contamination of the eye.
(b)
Heating with a bactericide results in the denaturing of bacterial protein.
(c)
Aseptic filtration through a 0.22-μm filter is the other common method of sterilising ophthalmic products.
(d)
Heating with a bactericide at 98-100°C for about 30 minutes; filtration through a 0.22-μm filter.

questions.question:
An ophthalmic plant is reviewing its filling operation, deciding between conventional aseptic filling and blow-fill-seal, and its control of raw materials and containers.
(a) Identify the microbiological risk.
(b) Explain how contamination arises.
(c) Name the monitoring and control measures.
(d) Differentiate the related approaches.
(e) Reason to the quality or regulatory decision.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Contact of airborne contamination with critical sites (the open product during filling, before application of closures, injection ports and vial septa), and microbial content of raw materials, preservative, intermediate products and active ingredients.
(b)
Through airborne contamination during filling and through contaminated raw materials, intermediates, actives and preservative; contamination of unpreserved or opened containers during use is also a route.
(c)
Controlled environment with HEPA filtration; microbial limit tests on raw materials before use; pre-sterilised plastic containers (gamma irradiation or ethylene oxide); sterility and pyrogen (endotoxin) tests on the finished product; endotoxin limitation for products injected into the eye; visual assessment for microbial growth.
(d)
Conventional aseptic filling versus blow-fill-seal (containers formed from plastic granules on-line, filled and sealed in one operation, theoretically lower contamination risk); final-container sterilisation by heating with a bactericide at 98-100°C for about 30 minutes versus aseptic filtration through 0.22 μm.
(e)
Blow-fill-seal is the better route to aseptic filling of ophthalmic medications; every ophthalmic product must be sterile in its final container and pass sterility and pyrogen tests.

questions.question:
A patient with a painless, clean-based genital ulcer has a reactive VDRL test at a titre of 1:2.
(a) Identify the appropriate tests.
(b) State the principle, reagents and procedure.
(c) Interpret the result.
(d) State the controls and limitations.
(e) State the corrective action and further testing.
(f) State the follow-up and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Screening with the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test or rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test, and confirmation with the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test; specimens: blood test or sample from the sore.
(b)
VDRL and RPR measure serum reagin titres, reported as serological dilutions (1:2, 1:4, 1:8); FTA-ABS measures specific IgG antibody against T. pallidum.
(c)
A reactive VDRL means a possibility of syphilitic infection at that time; a nonreactive result means no infection at that time; the titre reflects disease activity, with the highest titres in secondary and early latent disease.
(d)
False-positive results yield lower titres (1:1 to 1:4) and occur in 1-2% of the general population, from advanced age, bacterial infections (e.g. endocarditis, malaria, mycoplasma, tuberculosis), chronic liver disease, injecting drug use, Lyme disease, malignancies, pregnancy and viral infections (e.g. varicella, measles, HIV, mononucleosis).
(e)
Confirm a positive screen with FTA-ABS; lumbar puncture in late latent disease, unknown duration, HIV, neurological or ophthalmic signs, or treatment failure; HIV testing for all syphilis patients.
(f)
Titres at 6 and 12 months (sometimes every 3 months), expected to fall fourfold 6 months after treatment; FTA-ABS usually stays positive for life (24% seroreverted by 3 years in one study); partners notified and treated; penicillin is first-line therapy and the only acceptable treatment for neurosyphilis or pregnancy.

(b)
Failure of strict aseptic conditions during removal of cells (filtration, ultrafiltration or centrifugation); pockets of air or rough surfaces not penetrated by steam in the vessel and pipework act as reservoirs for foreign growth.
(c)
Nutrient-rich medium: carbon sources (glucose, sucrose, molasses), corn steep liquor (virtually a complete growth medium with carbon compounds, lactic acid, sugars, inorganic ions and growth factors), nitrogen, minerals, aeration and controlled temperature.
(d)
Serious or total loss of product; the finished product must satisfy requirements for potency, purity, freedom from pyrogens and sterility.
(e)
Strict aseptic conditions during cell removal; sterilization of equipment; medium sterilized with steam at or above 120°C; steam reaching all parts of vessel and pipework; aseptic transfer, sampling and additions; sampling to check no contamination by unwanted organisms; sterile air.
(f)
Pyrogens removed with charcoal; sterilization usually by filtration (dry heat for pure metal salts of penicillin G); vials of freeze-dried powder and/or suspension for parenteral use; random samples tested for potency, purity, pyrogens and sterility.

A. Describe the microbial sources and production of antibiotics under the following headings.
(a) Definition and producers.
(b) Soil microbes.
(c) Marine microbes.
(d) Production routes.
B. Relate these to the common examples.
(e) Actinomycete examples.
(f) Fungal examples.
(g) Marine examples.
(h) Semisynthetic examples.
C. Explain how semisynthetic and fermentation approaches improve the product and what limitations or trade-offs result.
(i) Why are semisynthetic derivatives needed?
(j) Why is fermentation used at scale?
(k) Steps of large-scale production.
(l) Limitations or trade-offs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Antibiotics are chemicals produced by microorganisms that kill or inhibit competing microorganisms; more than half come from actinomycetes, 10-15% from non-filamentous bacteria and about 20% from filamentous fungi.
(b)
Bacteria (e.g. Bacillus polymyxa producing polymyxin and colistin), actinomycetes (Streptomyces), fungi and algae; soil holds over 10⁹ microorganisms per gram.
(c)
Bacteria (Streptomyces producing cyclic peptides), fungi (mainly Ascomycota) and algae; about a million organisms per mL of seawater, a rich source of new metabolites.
(d)
Natural products, semi-synthesis from natural products (nucleus kept, structure altered), or chemical synthesis based on natural structures; large-scale fermentation or semisynthesis based on structure-activity relationships.
(e)
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin, streptomycin, neomycin), macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin), tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline), chloramphenicol, anthracyclines.
(f)
Penicillium chrysogenum (penicillins), Cephalosporium acremonium (cephalosporins), Penicillium griseofulvum (griseofulvin), fusidic acid and cyclosporin; statins (lovastatin, mevastatin).
(g)
Cephalosporin C from a marine Cephalosporium (Acremonium), gliotoxin from marine Aspergillus, trichoderins against mycobacteria and chlorellin from Chlorella algae.
(h)
Ampicillin, cloxacillin and amikacin.
(i)
Penicillin G has a relatively narrow spectrum, so other penicillins are produced by chemical modification of natural penicillins for desirable properties.
(j)
Large quantities can be produced by large-scale cultivation at reasonable cost, a feasible and sustainable method.
(k)
Discovery through small-scale culture optimisation, production by fermentation, semi-synthesis or synthesis, downstream processing and lead development (SAR, mode of action studies).
(l)
Yield depends on strain, medium and conditions, and sterile operation is required to avoid contamination.

C. Distinguish related infections and agents.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A Gram-negative diplococcus; infects columnar or cuboidal epithelium, attaches via pili and penetrates within 1-2 days; neutrophilic response creates purulent discharge; symptoms usually within 10 days.
(b)
A spirochete causing syphilis: primary (single painless clean-based ulcer, 10-90 days), secondary (rash including palms and soles, 2-8 weeks), latent (serology only; early under 1 year, late over 1 year) and tertiary (neurologic, cardiovascular; 10-40% of untreated).

An intracellular pathogen needing cell culture; usually asymptomatic (90% of women with endocervical infection); sequelae are PID, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.
(d)
A double-stranded DNA virus; HSV-2 causes most genital herpes and HSV-1 usually oral lesions; establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia; painful vesicles; shedding when asymptomatic.

Gonorrhoea: single-dose cefixime, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin plus chlamydia coverage; syphilis: penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM (first line); chlamydia: azithromycin 1 g single dose or doxycycline; HSV: acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir.

Women tend not to have symptoms and so have more serious complications; transmission is more easy from male to female (50% per contact for gonorrhoea).
(g)

(h)
They enhance compliance profoundly, reduce further transmission and reduce resistance.
(i)

(j)
HSV-1 generally causes oral lesions and HSV-2 generally genital lesions, though not exclusively.
(k)

(l)
Gonorrhoea: culture of the endocervix; chlamydia: cell culture; herpes: viral isolation by tissue culture; syphilis: serology (VDRL/RPR with FTA-ABS confirmation).

questions.question:
A sterile injection is examined by the in vivo pyrogen test using healthy adult rabbits. The sum of the three individual maximum temperature rises exceeds 1.4°C.
(a) Identify the test being performed.
(b) State the principle, procedure and media or reagents.
(c) State the apparatus precautions, animal criteria and controls.
(d) State the criteria for withdrawing rabbits and how the result is read.
(e) Interpret this result.
(f) State the corrective action or further testing.
(g) State the limitations of this test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The in vivo pyrogen test (rabbit test), which measures the rise in body temperature induced in rabbits by intravenous injection of a sterile solution of the substance being examined.
(b)
Rabbits are conditioned, starved the day before (water only), kept in retaining boxes, a baseline rectal temperature is taken (series over 30 minutes, averaged), the warmed test solution (38.5°C) is injected intravenously (inoculated into the ear lobe after disinfecting the ear lobe with methylated spirit), and rectal temperature (probe 5 cm) is read six times at 30-minute intervals for 3 hours. Dose not exceeding 10 mL/kg injected within 4 minutes. Media/reagents: isotonic saline is used for the preliminary test.
(c)
Syringes, needles and glassware must be depyrogenized; aseptic technique; sterile diluents and washing solutions; a control pyrogen test on representative portions of diluents and washing solutions; rabbits at least 1.5 kg, healthy, not recently used or previously failed; a preliminary test three days earlier with a-pyrogenic saline (rabbits with a difference above 0.6°C are excluded); thermometer accuracy 0.1°C.
(d)
Withdraw rabbits with a difference above 0.2°C between successive pre-inoculation readings, mean pre-inoculation temperature above 39.8°C or below 38°C. Any temperature decrease counts as zero rise.
(e)
Pyrogen-free requires no individual rise of 0.6°C or more above control and a sum of the three maxima not exceeding 1.4°C; since the sum exceeds 1.4°C, the product does not comply at this stage.
(f)
Continue the test using five other rabbits; the product is accepted as pyrogen-free if not more than three of the eight rabbits show individual rises of 0.6°C or more and the sum of the eight maximum rises does not exceed 4.3°C.
(g)
It is laborious, slow and time-consuming, its use may be limited for small volumes of parenterals, no two rabbits respond identically, and results are subject to error because slight excitement raises body temperature; merit: materials are readily available and no special training is required.

questions.question:
A. Describe microbial pathogens under the following headings.
(a) Definition and agents of disease.
(b) Classification.
(c) Pathogenic properties.
(d) Invasiveness factors.
(e) Examples of toxin-mediated disease.
B. Explain the basis of their pathogenic significance.
(f) Why intracellular versus extracellular parasitism matters.
(g) Why capsules are significant.
(h) Why opportunists cause disease.
C. Distinguish endotoxins from exotoxins.
(i) Compare source.
(j) Compare heat stability.
(k) Compare toxoid formation and nature.
(l) Compare examples and genetic basis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A pathogen is any microorganism that can cause disease; pathogenesis is the process leading to disease; agents fall into five groups: viruses, bacteria, fungi, some protozoa and helminths.
(b)
Primary (obligate) versus secondary or opportunist pathogens; intracellular (cytoplasmic such as viruses, Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Listeria; vesicular such as mycobacteria) versus extracellular pathogens (replicating in interstitial spaces, blood, lymph and epithelial surfaces).
(c)
Adhesion (fimbriae of ETEC and H. influenzae type b; glucans of Streptococcus mutans), host receptor sites, toxigenicity and invasiveness.
(d)
Intracellular or extracellular parasitism, antiphagocytic capsule, adaptation to the microenvironment and extracellular enzymes (hyaluronidase, collagenase, coagulase, lecithinase, staphylokinase, streptokinase).
(e)
Cholera (toxin co-regulated pili and cholera toxin raising cAMP, causing chloride secretion and rice-water stools), botulism (neurotoxin inhibiting acetylcholine release) and tetanus (tetanospasmin inhibiting glycine release causing spastic paralysis).
(f)
Intracellular parasitism within phagocytic cells (M. tuberculosis, Brucella abortus, Salmonella typhi) is characteristic of chronic diseases, whereas extracellular parasitism is characteristic of acute disease such as pneumococcal pneumonia.
(g)
Capsules promote adhesion, act against phagocytosis and shield against toxic metal ions and bacteriophages; they are characteristic of extracellular pathogens.
(h)
They rely on the activities of obligate pathogens or on trauma; opportunists are part of the body's own microflora, e.g. Bacteroides in the intestine causing peritonitis after trauma.
(i)
Endotoxins are produced generally by Gram-negative bacteria and exotoxins by Gram-positive bacteria.
(j)
Endotoxin is heat stable; exotoxin is heat labile.
(k)
Exotoxin forms a toxoid; toxins in general are soluble protein substances transported by blood and lymph with systemic effects remote from the lesion.
(l)
Exotoxins include cholera and diphtheria toxins (phage encoded), anthrax toxin (plasmid encoded), botulinum neurotoxin and tetanospasmin; endotoxins are the heat-stable lipopolysaccharide-protein complexes of Gram-negative cell walls, which act as pyrogens; the fungal aflatoxin is formed by Aspergillus flavus.

questions.question:
A. Describe the principle of antimicrobial resistance under the following headings.
(a) Conditions under which resistance emerges.
(b) How resistance genes spread.
(c) Role of mutation.
(d) Role of antimicrobial use.
B. Relate it to the common examples of resistance mechanisms.
(e) Tetracyclines.
(f) Chloramphenicol and macrolides.
(g) Fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides.
(h) Clinical examples.
C. Explain how responses protect patients and what limits them.
(i) Why antibiotic stewardship and combination therapy help.
(j) Surveillance and infection control.
(k) Why resistance is hard to reverse.
(l) Costs and trade-offs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Resistance emerges only when two components come together in a host or environment: the antimicrobial drug that inhibits susceptible organisms and selects resistant ones, and the genetic resistance determinant; selected genes and hosts then spread under continued selection.
(b)
Resistance is mobile: genes transfer among bacteria by bacteriophages, plasmids, naked DNA or transposons (some transposons contain integrons); genes are generally directed at a single family of antibiotic but several can accumulate in one organism.
(c)
In the absence of plasmids and transposons, step-wise progression from low-level to high-level resistance occurs through sequential chromosomal mutations, as in the initial penicillin and tetracycline resistance of N. gonorrhoeae.
(d)
Millions of kilograms are used each year in people, animals and agriculture, killing susceptible strains and selecting resistant ones; use of a single antibiotic for more than 10 days selects bacteria resistant to it and to several others.
(e)
Decreased permeability, increased efflux, ribosomal protection and enzymatic inactivation.
(f)
Chloramphenicol: decreased permeability, 50S mutations, and acetyltransferase (Cat gene); macrolides: guanine methylation on rRNA, efflux and plasmid-associated erythromycin esterase.
(g)
Fluoroquinolones: chromosomal mutation of gyrase or topoisomerase IV, reduced permeability and efflux (plasmid resistance less likely); aminoglycosides: enzyme inactivation, failure to penetrate and low ribosomal affinity.
(h)
Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (40-60% of nosocomial strains in the US and UK, with some vancomycin resistance), β-lactamases and metallo-β-lactamases inactivating carbapenems, triple-resistant N. gonorrhoeae, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and fluoroquinolone resistance in E. coli.
(i)
Cultures and sensitivity testing before starting antibiotics, narrow-spectrum agents and combination therapy (to prevent emergence of resistance) reduce selection pressure.
(j)
Tracking resistance and isolating hospital patients with resistant bacteria such as MRSA or vancomycin-resistant enterococci; a small rise in MIC while still 'susceptible' should alert clinicians to incipient resistance.
(k)
Resistant bacteria are slow to be lost even without the selecting antibiotic because of minimal survival cost, and resistance genes are linked with other resistance genes on the same plasmids, so multidrug plasmids are maintained.
(l)
Resistant infections double hospital stay and mortality and probably morbidity; MRSA mortality was 21% versus 8% for sensitive strains with 22% higher cost; infections can become untreatable when all available drugs fail.

questions.question:
A multidose ophthalmic solution is being formulated. Benzalkonium chloride, parabens or chlorhexidine acetate are candidate preservatives, used singly or in combination, and the product must stay sterile after the container is opened for repeated application to the eye.
(a) Identify the class of agent and the purpose of adding it to this product.
(b) State the mechanism of action and spectrum.
(c) State the properties required of an ideal preservative.
(d) State the other factors that affect preservative choice and activity.
(e) State the physico-chemical formulation factors that interact with the preservative system.
(f) Reason from this to selection or limitation in formulation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Antimicrobial preservatives (examples listed: benzalkonium chloride, parabens, potassium sorbate, chlorhexidine acetate, chlorocresol, polyhexamine gluconate); they maintain sterility once the multidose container has been opened for repeated application.
(b)
Preservatives are designed to prevent the growth or to destroy microorganisms accidentally introduced into the product when the container is opened during use.
(c)
It should act rapidly on the contaminating organism to stem proliferation of any chance contaminant, and be non-irritating when applied topically.
(d)
Preservative stability, chemical compatibility with other formulation components, compatibility with packaging materials, and concentration; it must be effective throughout the entire shelf-life, and combinations may give higher efficacy.
(e)
Isotonicity (equal to 0.9% sodium chloride; eye tolerates 0.5-1.8%), buffering capacity and pH equal to tear fluid (7.4), antimicrobial agents and/or antioxidants, viscosity-increasing agents and appropriate packaging; the buffer must not cause precipitation or deterioration of the active ingredient.
(f)
Preservative selection is a critical activity in product design; preservatives bind or are adsorbed onto membrane filter materials; the preservative itself must be tested for microbial limits before use; patients sensitive to preservatives need preservative-free products, often in single-dose formats.

(a)
A broad-spectrum antibiotic active against Gram-negative and Gram-positive organisms and serious anaerobic infection; bacteriostatic at low doses and bactericidal at high doses.
(b)
It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting peptidyl transferase activity (binding A2451 and A2452 of 23S rRNA) and interfering with substrate binding.
(c)
Highly active: Salmonella typhi, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, penicillin-resistant Bacteroides fragilis; sensitive: spirochetes, Rickettsia, Mycoplasma, Klebsiella, Chlamydia; not active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Enterobacter.
(d)
Dose determines static versus cidal action; paracetamol increases bioavailability; chloramphenicol is a potent enzyme inhibitor that inhibits metabolism of morphine and warfarin.
(e)
Decreased cell permeability; ribosomal protection by mutations on the 50S subunit; R-plasmid and chromosomal chloramphenicol acetyltransferase (Cat gene) that inactivates the drug by acetylation.
(f)
Bone marrow depression and aplasia; idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia (dose-unrelated); gray baby syndrome because neonates cannot conjugate the drug; reversible dose-related depression above 3-4 g/day for over 1-2 weeks; contraindicated in renal impairment, hepatic insufficiency, pregnancy, neonates and blood-forming diseases.
(g)
Uses: topical for conjunctivitis and external ear infections, earlier drug of choice in typhoid fever, second-line in tetracycline-resistant cholera, first choice for staphylococcal brain abscess; it penetrates CSF, but toxicity and contraindications (neonates, warfarin and morphine interactions) limit its selection.
questions.question:
A prescriber is considering chloramphenicol for a patient who is also taking paracetamol and warfarin, and for a neonate.
(a) Identify the class of agent.
(b) State the mechanism of action.
(c) State the spectrum.
(d) State the factors affecting activity and interactions.
(e) State the resistance mechanisms.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A synthetic quinolone antimicrobial with fluorine substitution, i.e. a fluoroquinolone (the prototype); fluorination at position 6 and a piperazine at position 7 gave high potency, expanded spectrum, slow development of resistance and better tissue penetration.
(b)
Dual action: inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II; binds the A subunit, preventing nicking and resealing, mainly in Gram-negative bacteria) and of topoisomerase IV (main target in Gram-positive bacteria); bactericidal through DNA digestion by exonucleases; low host toxicity because mammalian topoisomerase II has very low affinity for fluoroquinolones.
(c)
Highly susceptible: E. coli, Klebsiella, Salmonella typhi, Shigella, Neisseria, Haemophilus, Vibrio cholerae and others (MIC usually below 0.1 μg/mL); moderate: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Legionella, Staph. aureus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis; low or variable: Strep. pyogenes, Strep. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia; resistant: Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridia, anaerobic cocci.
(d)
It is less active at acidic pH; antacids, sucralfate and iron salts reduce absorption and food delays absorption; it raises plasma theophylline, caffeine and warfarin by inhibiting metabolism (CNS toxicity with theophylline); NSAIDs may enhance CNS toxicity.
(e)
Chromosomal mutation giving DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV with reduced affinity, or reduced permeability and increased efflux; plasmid-mediated resistance is less likely and resistance is slow, though increasing in Salmonella, Pseudomonas, staphylococci, gonococci and pneumococci.
(f)
Because of its wide-spectrum bactericidal activity, oral efficacy and good tolerability it is used for empirical therapy, but it should not be used for minor cases or where Gram-positive organisms and/or anaerobes are primarily causative; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and children except in pressing situations; tendon damage risk is higher above 60 years and with corticosteroids.
