questions.answerText:
(a)
Non-sterile products can introduce pathogens, leading to sepsis, organ infections or death; sterile products prevent infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients.
(b)
Aseptic techniques (procedures to prevent microbial contamination during preparation), controlled environments (cleanrooms with ISO classifications), sterilization methods (autoclaving, filtration or radiation) and quality assurance.
(c)
Testing for sterility, endotoxins and particulate matter; parenteral quality control: sterility testing, pyrogen testing, particulate matter testing and stability testing.
(d)
Single-dose: one sterile dose for immediate use after opening. Multi-dose: contain preservatives to prevent contamination and allow multiple uses (e.g. multi-dose insulin vials). Preservative-free: for patients sensitive to preservatives, often single-dose formats.
(e)
Products must comply with guidelines from the FDA (cGMPs), USP Chapters <797> and <800> for compounding, the EMA, and standards of USP, EP and WHO; parenteral products must meet strict pharmacopeial standards for sterility, pyrogens, particulates and stability.
questions.question:
A facility plans to manufacture sterile multi-dose insulin vials and preservative-free single-dose products for patients sensitive to preservatives.

(c) Name the monitoring and quality controls.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Sterile preparations administered by injection, infusion or implantation directly into the body, bypassing the GI tract, using syringes, needles or catheters.
(b)
Solutions, suspensions, emulsions, powders for injection, depot or long-acting formulations, biologics and parenteral nutrition.
(c)
Must be sterile, pyrogen-free and particulate-free; tested by sterility, pyrogen, particulate matter and stability testing.
(d)
Intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intradermal, intra-articular, intrathecal, epidural, intraperitoneal, intra-arterial and intraosseous.
(e)
Normal saline and dextrose solutions, corticosteroid depot suspensions, lipid emulsions for TPN, lyophilized ceftriaxone, hormonal implants, COVID-19 vaccines.
(f)
IV: antibiotics, chemotherapy, hydration fluids (rapid onset, 100% bioavailability); IM: influenza vaccine, hormonal injections; SC: insulin, heparin, monoclonal antibodies (self-administration).
(g)
Intradermal tuberculin test; intra-articular corticosteroids; intrathecal chemotherapy and pain management; epidural local anaesthetics and opioids; intraperitoneal dialysis fluids.
(h)
IV: infection or embolism; intra-articular: joint infection; intraperitoneal: peritonitis; intrathecal: high risk of complications.
(i)
Bypass the GI tract and first-pass metabolism, permit drugs with poor oral bioavailability, rapid effect in emergencies and use in unconscious patients.
(j)
Strict aseptic conditions needed, pain or discomfort at the injection site, higher cost than oral forms, and risks of infection, embolism or allergic reactions.
(k)
Sterility, pyrogen, particulate and stability testing assure absence of microbial contamination, fever-inducing substances and particles and retained efficacy; sterile products prevent sepsis, particularly in immunocompromised patients.
(l)
The choice depends on the drug's properties, therapeutic objectives and patient factors, balancing, for example, IM depot prolonged action against pain and limited volume, and SC convenience against small volumes.

A. Describe the laboratory diagnosis of gonorrhoea and chlamydial infection under the following headings.
(a) Culture of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
(b) Gram stain.
(c) DNA probes.
(d) Ligase chain reaction (LCR) and PCR.
(e) Chlamydia trachomatis methods.
B. State the factors affecting reliability of the methods.
(f) Effect of specimen collection.
(g) Effect of anatomical site and symptoms.
(h) Effect of the patient population.
C. Explain the basis of false or unreliable results and how this is detected or prevented.
(i) Why LCR cannot be used as a test of cure.
(j) Why culture and Gram stain miss infections.
(k) Detection of treatment failure and reinfection.
(l) Prevention of missed diagnoses.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Culture of the endocervical region is the gold standard used in all medico-legal settings; specimen acquisition is key, using a swab with a wire shaft and synthetic fibre tip.
(b)
Highly specific, less costly and quick; diagnostic if Gram-negative diplococci are seen within polymorphonuclear leukocytes.
(c)
High sensitivity and specificity; test concurrently for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis from a single specimen; more widely used than cultures at similar cost.
(d)
Use DNA or RNA amplification on urine or self-collected vaginal swabs; LCR sensitivity 95% and specificity 98-100%; more expensive than culture but easier for screening.
(e)
Cell culture (gold standard, specificity 100%, sensitivity 70-85%, needed because the organism is intracellular); direct fluorescent antibody and ELISA (easier, quicker, sensitivity 50-90%); DNA probe and nucleic acid amplification.
(f)
Chlamydia sampling uses a cotton-tipped swab left in the endocervix at least 30 seconds to collect columnar epithelial cells; endocervical collection for probes must be precise; wooden shafts or cotton tips may be toxic to N. gonorrhoeae.
(g)
Culture sensitivity: endocervix 40-60%, pharynx 59%, rectum 40-60%, symptomatic urethra 95-100%, asymptomatic urethra 50-70%; Gram stain similar (40-60% in endocervix).
(h)
LCR performance in asymptomatic, low-prevalence settings is unknown.
(i)
It will identify nonviable gonococcal nucleic acid.
(j)
Low sensitivity in the endocervix and in asymptomatic men (40-60% and 50-70%), and chlamydial cell culture sensitivity is only 70-85%.
(k)
Tests of cure are not needed for uncomplicated gonorrhoea; if a patient fails to improve, culture is required for susceptibility testing; infections identified after completing treatment are reinfection rather than failure; chlamydial follow-up testing at least 3 weeks after therapy.
(l)
Test for both gonorrhoea and chlamydia (coexisting chlamydia in up to 45% of gonorrhoea cases), screen all sexually active adolescents, and use specific tests such as amplification assays that allow easier screening.

questions.question:
A multidose ophthalmic solution is opened repeatedly for application to the affected eye. The microbial content of the raw materials, including the preservative, was not tested before they were used in production.
(a) Identify the likely organism or group.
(b) State the source and route of contamination.
(c) State the consequence for product quality and patient safety.
(d) State the control measures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The contaminants are microorganisms accidentally introduced into the product.
(b)
Opening of the container during use; microbial content of raw materials (including the preservative), intermediate products and active ingredients are potential sources; airborne contamination at critical sites (open product during filling, before closures, injection ports, vial septa).
(c)
Every ophthalmic product must be sterile in its final container to prevent microbial contamination of the eye; evidence of microbial growth is one sign of instability found on visual assessment.
(d)
Preservatives that act rapidly and remain effective through shelf-life; microbial limit testing of raw materials before use; aseptic filling in a controlled HEPA environment or blow-fill-seal; pre-sterilised plastic containers (gamma irradiation or ethylene oxide); final sterility and pyrogen (endotoxin) tests.

questions.question:
A benzylpenicillin fermenter, its medium, its sampling lines and the final product must all be rendered sterile.
(a) Select the appropriate methods.
(b) Explain the principle and mode of action.
(c) State the operating parameters.
(d) State the monitoring and validation.
(e) State the limitations.
(f) State the products unsuited to a method.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Steam sterilization of the medium and the vessel and associated pipework; sterile air supply; sterilization of the final product usually by filtration (dry heat for pure metal salts of penicillin G); some nutrients sterilized separately by batch or continuous sterilization and added aseptically.
(b)
Asepsis is ensured by engineering design and by steam that must reach all parts of the vessel and pipework; stainless steel withstands acid and alkaline media and allows easy cleaning and sterilization.
(c)
Medium sterilized with steam at or above 120°C, either in the fermenter or in ancillary plant; sterile medium cooled by chilled water in internal pipes or external limpet coils; the production process is aseptic.
(d)
Routine sampling to check that there is no contamination by unwanted organisms; instrumentation displaying temperature, pH, airflow, dissolved oxygen and exhaust gas analysis; finished product tested for potency, purity, pyrogens and sterility.
(e)
Pockets of air or rough surfaces not penetrated by steam act as reservoirs for foreign growth; production of benzylpenicillin is over-sensitive to temperature (heat tolerance less than 1%), so the product itself is sterilised by filtration, with dry heat only for pure metal salts.
(f)
Penicillin G salts other than pure metal salts are unsuited to dry heat, so filtration is used.

questions.question:
A. Describe the tetracyclines under the following headings.
(a) Classification by duration of action, with members.
(b) Structure, source and general properties.
(c) Mechanism of action in Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
(d) Antimicrobial spectrum.
(e) Mechanisms of resistance.
B. Explain the basis of their activity and limitations.
(f) Why are tetracyclines selectively toxic to microorganisms?
(g) Why is absorption impaired by dairy products, antacids and iron preparations?
(h) Why are they contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation and young children?
C. Distinguish long-acting tetracyclines (doxycycline and minocycline) from tetracycline itself.
(i) Compare half-life.
(j) Compare the effect of dairy products, antacids and iron on absorption.
(k) Compare metabolism, excretion and renal dose adjustment.
(l) Compare adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Group 1 shorter acting (t1/2 6-10 h): tetracycline, chlortetracycline, oxytetracycline; Group 2 intermediate (12-13 h): demeclocycline, methacycline; Group 3 long acting (18-20 h): doxycycline, minocycline.
(b)
Four-ring (four-cyclic) structure; broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotics obtained from soil actinomycetes; affect rapidly multiplying organisms; slightly bitter and weakly water soluble.
(c)
Gram-positive: enter the cytoplasm by an energy-dependent active transport system, bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and block attachment of tRNA and mRNA, so peptide chain growth fails; Gram-negative: enter the outer membrane by passive diffusion through pore channels.
(d)
Highly active against Rickettsia and Chlamydia (psittaci, trachomatis, pneumoniae); spirochetes (Borrelia burgdorferi, B. recurrentis); atypicals (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Ureaplasma urealyticum); Gram-negative bacilli (Vibrio cholerae, Brucella abortus, Helicobacter pylori, Yersinia pestis, Actinomyces israelii, Francisella tularensis); also intestinal amoebiasis and Trichomonas vaginalis.
(e)
Decreased cell permeability; increased energy-dependent drug efflux; ribosomal protection with decreased affinity of ribosomal binding sites; enzymatic inactivation of the drug.
(f)
The carriers involved in active transport of tetracyclines are absent in mammalian ribosomal (60S/40S) units, so they cannot damage the host but are selectively toxic to microorganisms.
(g)
These impair tetracycline absorption either by chelation or by altering gastric pH (except for doxycycline and minocycline); also, injectable tetracycline must not be mixed with penicillin because inactivation occurs.
(h)
They cross the placental barrier, are excreted in milk and are readily deposited in teeth, bones and tumours, causing impaired bone development and discoloration of teeth; contraindicated also in renal impairment, hepatic insufficiency and children under 10 years; intrathecal injection is to be avoided.
(i)
Tetracycline is shorter acting (t1/2 6-10 h) whereas doxycycline and minocycline are long acting (t1/2 18-20 h).
(j)
These impair absorption of tetracycline but not of doxycycline and minocycline.
(k)
Tetracyclines are metabolized in the liver to conjugated glucuronides, concentrated in bile (enterohepatic circulation) and excreted in urine by glomerular filtration, except doxycycline and minocycline; in renal impairment long-acting tetracyclines need dose adjustment except doxycycline.
(l)
Class effects include epigastric distress, diarrhoea, impaired bone development, tooth discoloration, photosensitization, superinfection and thrombophlebitis (IV); minocycline photosensitivity and vestibular toxicity are listed among chronic-use effects.

questions.question:
A. Describe the laboratory diagnosis of genital herpes (HSV infection) under the following headings.
(a) Clinical diagnosis.
(b) Viral isolation by tissue culture.
(c) Antigen detection and Tzanck tests.
(d) Serologic studies.
(e) PCR testing.
B. State the factors affecting the reliability of the diagnosis.
(f) Effect of the virus's properties.
(g) Effect of viral shedding.
(h) Effect of the stage of illness.
C. Explain the basis of missed or unreliable results and how this is detected or prevented.
(i) Why serology can fail.
(j) Why culture can miss infection.
(k) Why PCR is not universally used.
(l) Prevention of missed co-infections.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Recognition of multiple, shallow and tender ulcerations or vesicles on or around the genitalia.
(b)
The gold standard; can take up to 5 days; sensitivity is only 70-80%.
(c)
Both have lower sensitivity.
(d)
Not helpful during the primary illness because of the delay in antibody production.
(e)
Sensitive (96%) and specific (99%) but costly and of limited availability.
(f)
HSV is a double-stranded DNA virus that targets epithelial cells and is transported via neural tissue to sensory ganglia, where lifelong latent infection is established.
(g)
Shedding takes place during asymptomatic periods, so transmission can occur without visible lesions, and most infected individuals are unaware of their disease.
(h)
Initial episodes are more severe than recurrences; vesicles rupture and ulcerate, crusting by 14-21 days after first appearance; systemic symptoms may occur during the initial infection.
(i)
Antibody production is delayed, so serology is not helpful in the primary illness.
(j)
Sensitivity is only 70-80% and results take up to 5 days.
(k)
High cost and limited availability despite 96% sensitivity and 99% specificity.
(l)
A patient with genital ulcers should also be tested for syphilis and HIV.

(a)
Plastic containers are generally sterilized by gamma irradiation or ethylene oxide (ETO); most commercial liquid ophthalmic products are packed in pre-sterilised plastic containers.
(b)
Finished products are checked by sterility and pyrogen (endotoxin) tests.
(c)
A controlled environment using HEPA filtration to minimise contact of airborne contamination with critical sites (the open product during filling, prior to application of closures, injection ports and vial septa).
(d)
Containers are formed from plastic granules on-line, then filled with the drug solution and sealed in one operation.
(e)
Blow-fill-seal has a theoretically lower risk of microbial contamination than conventional aseptic filling and is considered better for aseptic filling of ophthalmic medications.
questions.question:
Eye drops are to be packed in plastic containers fitted with nozzles for dropwise use. Management is comparing conventional aseptic filling with blow-fill-seal technology.
(a) Select the method for sterilising the plastic containers.
(b) State the operating parameters and monitoring.
(c) State the conditions required for aseptic filling.

A. Describe the commercial production of benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) by fermentation under the following headings.
(a) Principle and type of process.
(b) Procedure: inoculum, cycle and harvest.
(c) Process parameters.
(d) Media and reagents.
(e) Application: extraction and further processing.
B. State the factors affecting its efficiency.
(f) General factors affecting production yield.
(g) Effect of oxygen supply and growth control.
(h) Effect of temperature and PAA level.
C. Explain the basis of failure or loss of yield and how it is detected or prevented.
(i) Cause of total or serious loss from contamination.
(j) Why extraction must be rapid and at acid pH.
(k) Why foam must be controlled.
(l) Detection and prevention of failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
An aseptic fed-batch fermentation in stainless steel tank reactors (30 to 100 thousand gallons); penicillin is a secondary metabolite produced in the stationary phase; production strain Penicillium chrysogenum superseded P. notatum (isolated by Fleming in 1926).
(b)
Spores (desiccated, lyophilised or under liquid nitrogen) grown into pure inoculum at log phase; 2 to 3 seed growth phases then a production phase of 120-200 hours; mini-harvest removes 20-40% of contents replaced with fresh sterile medium; penicillin excreted into medium and recovered at the end.
(c)
pH 6.4-6.8 during active production; medium sterilized by steam at or above 120°C; temperature controlled by chilled water in internal pipes or limpet coils; carbon use about 65% maintenance, 25% growth, 10% penicillin; key substrate limited to restrict net growth.
(d)
Batched medium with corn steep liquor as nitrogen source supplemented with chalk, magnesium, sulphate, phosphate, potassium and trace metals; fed sucrose or glucose (or molasses), ammonia gas and phenylacetic acid (PAA), which supplies the side chain and suppresses unwanted penicillins; antifoam silicone.
(e)
Cells removed by filtration, ultrafiltration or centrifugation; solvent extraction at pH 2-2.5 into amyl acetate, butyl acetate or methyl isobutyl ketone, then back into aqueous buffer at pH 7.5, crystallised, blended and dried; salt formation, charcoal pyrogen removal, sterilization (filtration), packing as sterile freeze-dried powder or oral dosage forms.
(f)
The producing strain, medium composition (carbohydrate, nitrogen, cations), fermentation conditions (pH, temperature, agitation, aeration) and mode of fermentation (batch, fed-batch or continuous).
(g)
Penicillin G production is aerobic; if the culture becomes too dense for the aeration, or oxygen falls below a critical level, biosynthesis falls even though growth continues, so a key nutrient is limited to restrict growth to the vessel's capacity.
(h)
Benzylpenicillin production is over-sensitive to temperature (heat tolerance less than 1%) and heat generated must be removed; PAA is expensive and high levels are toxic, so its feed is controlled.
(i)
Contamination with β-lactamase-producing microorganisms during cell removal can cause serious or total loss of product.
(j)
Benzylpenicillin is very unstable at the low pH (2-2.5) used for solvent extraction, so extraction must be carried out rapidly; whole broth extraction is best at acidic pH with 2-5% improvement.
(k)
Uncontrolled foaming from stirring and aeration loses culture/product in exhaust gases; systems detect foaming, apply backpressure and aseptically add defoaming agents (silicone).
(l)
Aseptic transfer and sampling systems with steam reaching all parts (no air pockets or rough surfaces); sampling to monitor growth, nutrients, penicillin concentration and absence of contaminants; instrumentation for temperature, pH, airflow, dissolved oxygen, exhaust gas; final tests for potency, purity, pyrogens and sterility.

questions.question:
A. Describe the antibiotic assay by agar diffusion under the following headings.
(a) Principle and objectives.
(b) Agar-well (cup-plate) procedure.
(c) Disc-diffusion procedure.
(d) Media and incubation parameters.
(e) Application.
B. State the factors affecting its reliability.
(f) Effect of the antibiotic's properties on diffusion.
(g) Effect of test conditions on MIC.
(h) Effect of the type of response.
C. Explain the basis of invalid or misleading results and how they are detected or prevented.
(i) Why zone sizes can mislead.
(j) How cross-streak results are read.
(k) How errors are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Antibiotic assay measures bioactivity in killing or inhibiting microorganisms, related to dose; objectives are guiding therapy, quality assurance, surveillance of potency or resistance, and research; in diffusion methods graded concentrations are tested and a graded response (zone of inhibition) is measured.
(b)
Agar melted and cooled to 45-50°C, seeded with the test organism and poured into a sterile Petri dish; surface dried at 37°C for 20-30 min; wells of 6-8 mm cut with a sterile cork borer; dilutions of the antibiotic placed in the wells.
(c)
A solid medium is evenly inoculated with the test organism and filter-paper discs impregnated with antibiotics are placed on the surface; a circular zone of inhibition forms around the disc if the organism is sensitive.
(d)
Agar medium such as Mueller-Hinton agar (used in the cross-streak method with 18-24 hour broth cultures); incubation 24-48 h for bacteria and 2-5 days for fungi.
(e)
Disc diffusion is the most commonly used sensitivity test in diagnostic laboratories; the well method can assess bacteriostatic/fungistatic activity and MIC; the cross-streak method assesses activity of an antibiotic-producing strain against a pathogen.
(f)
Antibiotics diffuse through the medium at a rate that depends on molecular size, chemical nature, rate of solubility and the type of growth medium.
(g)
MIC varies considerably with inoculum size, the medium used, incubation conditions and the nature of the test organism.
(h)
Zones of inhibition give only a rough indication of the relative activity of the antibiotic; dilution methods give an end response (presence or absence of growth) at one uniform concentration.
(i)
Zone diameter depends on diffusion rate rather than potency alone, so it only indicates relative activity.
(j)
Growth across the marginal line indicates non-susceptibility (resistance) of the pathogen to the producing strain, whereas growth away from the line indicates sensitivity.
(k)
Use of sterile equipment, defined 18-24 hour culture, correct seeding temperature (45-50°C), drying of agar and consideration of inoculum size, medium and incubation conditions.

questions.question:
A. Describe the macrolide antibiotics under the following headings.
(a) Members and chemical features.
(b) Mechanism of action.
(c) Spectrum.
(d) Mechanisms of resistance.
(e) Adverse effects.
B. Explain the basis of their activity, limitations and interactions.
(f) Why are Gram-negative bacteria resistant?
(g) Why is there cross-resistance, and how does telithromycin differ?
(h) Why do erythromycin interactions occur?
C. Distinguish erythromycin, clarithromycin and azithromycin.
(i) Compare absorption.
(j) Compare distribution and half-life.
(k) Compare elimination.
(l) Compare therapeutic uses.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Erythromycin, azithromycin, roxithromycin, spiramycin, clarithromycin and telithromycin (a ketolide); characterised by a lactone ring to which one or more deoxy sugars are attached.
(b)
They reversibly bind the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting translocation and preventing transfer of peptidyl tRNA from the A-site to the P-site, so polypeptide elongation stops; typically bacteriostatic, bactericidal at high concentrations in susceptible organisms.
(c)
Similar to penicillins and effective against penicillin-resistant strains: streptococci, Bacillus anthracis, Listeria, Clostridium tetani, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Legionella, Bordetella pertussis, Haemophilus, Campylobacter jejuni, Helicobacter pylori, Mycobacterium avium complex and M. leprae, Treponema pallidum, Mycoplasma, Ureaplasma and Chlamydia.
(d)
Methylation of a guanine residue on ribosomal RNA giving lower affinity, an active efflux system, and plasmid-associated erythromycin esterase.
(e)
Anorexia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea (gut motility stimulation); acute cholestatic hepatitis, especially with the estolate; ototoxicity; allergic reactions; QT prolongation; pseudomembranous colitis.
(f)
Lack of cell wall permeability to macrolides is the reason Gram-negative bacteria are resistant.
(g)
Clarithromycin and azithromycin show cross-resistance with erythromycin, but telithromycin can be effective against macrolide-resistant organisms.
(h)
Erythromycin metabolites inhibit P450 enzymes and raise serum levels of theophylline, oral anticoagulants, cyclosporines and methylprednisolone, and it increases the bioavailability of oral digoxin.
(i)
Erythromycin has variable absorption decreased by food (enteric-coated esters are more acid stable); clarithromycin is acid stable and well absorbed regardless of food; azithromycin is acid stable but food decreases absorption of capsules.
(j)
All have extensive tissue distribution without BBB or CSF penetration; clarithromycin and azithromycin penetrate extensively; erythromycin accumulates in prostatic fluid and macrophages; azithromycin accumulates in neutrophils, macrophages and fibroblasts and has the longest half-life (above 40 hours).
(k)
All are hepatically eliminated; clarithromycin is the only one partly eliminated by the kidney (18% of parent drug and all metabolites); none is removed by haemodialysis; erythromycin and azithromycin are excreted in bile as active drugs.
(l)
Erythromycin: respiratory, soft tissue, chlamydial, gonococcal and ophthalmic infections, acne, PID; clarithromycin: respiratory and skin infections, MAC, H. pylori eradication; azithromycin: extended spectrum, single-dose treatment of sinusitis, chancroid, non-gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis, MAC in advanced HIV.

(a)
Introduced in 1995 by Gibson and Roberfroid as a non-digestible food ingredient selectively stimulating growth or activity of colon bacteria; updated in 2004; in 2007 FAO/WHO described them as a nonviable food component conferring health benefit through modulation of the microbiota.
(b)
Resistant to stomach acid, not hydrolyzed by mammalian enzymes, not absorbed in the GI tract, fermentable by intestinal microbiota and selectively stimulate beneficial bacteria.
(c)
Fructans (inulin, fructo-oligosaccharides), galacto-oligosaccharides, resistant starch and glucose-derived oligosaccharides, pectic oligosaccharides and non-carbohydrate cocoa flavanols.
(d)
Soybeans, inulin sources, raw oats, unrefined wheat and barley, yacon, and oligosaccharides in breast milk (the original prebiotic).
(e)
Modulation of the gut microbiota, immune effects (SCFA, increased mucosal immunoglobulin), anti-pathogenic activity and improved mineral absorption (calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc).
(f)
They mainly ferment carbohydrates, are non-pathogenic and non-toxigenic, provide colonisation resistance and are often immunomodulatory.
(g)
They contain structures similar to those on the microvillus membrane that bind bacterial receptors and prevent attachment to the colonic epithelium; human milk prebiotics are anti-adhesive and can neutralise toxins.
(h)
It limits ammonia production and absorption and acidifies the colon (SCFA), protonating ammonia to ammonium; in constipation it has an osmotic effect, traps fluid and is rapidly fermented to SCFA and hydrogen, inducing peristalsis.
(i)
Fructans are linear fructose chains with 1-2 linkages and terminal glucose; GOS are lactose-extension products (tri- to pentasaccharides) that strongly stimulate bifidobacteria and lactobacilli.
(j)
Resistant starch is a branched glucan escaping upper gut digestion, producing butyrate; pectic oligosaccharides derive from pectin (galacturonic acid or rhamnose) with structures varying by source.
(k)
Carbohydrates fit the criteria best; cocoa-derived flavanols are non-carbohydrates recommended as prebiotics because they stimulate lactic acid bacteria.
(l)
Mineral absorption and bone health, blood glucose control, hypolipidaemic effects, IBD, prevention of colorectal cancer and skin and cardiovascular benefits.

A. Describe prebiotics under the following headings.
(a) Definition and history.
(b) Classification criteria.

B. Explain the basis of their effects.
(f) Why are bifidobacteria and lactobacilli beneficial?
(g) Why do GOS block pathogen attachment?
(h) Why is lactulose effective in hepatic encephalopathy and constipation?
C. Distinguish related types of prebiotic.
(i) Compare fructans and GOS.

(a)
Microbial and bacterial endotoxin (pyrogen) contamination of the water; WFI must be free from microorganisms and pyrogens, and strict monitoring is essential to prevent contamination.
(b)
Stagnation and failure to clean and sterilise tanks and piping allow contamination; storage must prevent contamination through proper circulation to avoid stagnation, and purified water allowed to stand may gain a high content of vegetative microorganisms.
(c)
Stainless steel (316L or higher) or equivalent; circulation at 70°C or above to prevent microbial growth; regular cleaning and sterilization of tanks and piping.
(d)
Conductivity ≤ 1.3 μS/cm at 25°C; total organic carbon ≤ 0.5 mg/L; bacterial endotoxins ≤ 0.25 EU/mL; microbial content non-detectable in sterile WFI; conductivity and TOC monitoring to detect ionic and organic impurities; regular microbial and endotoxin testing; validated cleaning and maintenance.
(e)
Bulk WFI: produced in large quantities by distillation or reverse osmosis followed by ultrafiltration, raw material for sterile products. Sterile WFI: sterilized, single-dose ampoules or vials, no added antimicrobial, for dissolving or diluting drugs. Bacteriostatic WFI: sterile WFI with an antimicrobial (e.g. benzyl alcohol), multi-dose vials, not suitable for neonates.
(f)
WFI is produced and regulated to pharmacopoeial standards (USP, EP/Ph. Eur., BP) and production systems require rigorous validation and compliance; water not meeting these specifications cannot be used for parenteral preparation.
questions.question:
A Water for Injection storage and distribution loop for parenteral manufacture is found stagnant and not regularly cleaned and sterilised.
(a) Identify the microbiological risk.
(b) Explain how contamination arises.
(c) State the storage and distribution controls.
(d) State the monitoring and quality specifications.
(e) Differentiate the related types of WFI.
(f) Reason to the quality or regulatory decision.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Aminoglycosides: natural products of soil actinomycetes or semisynthetic derivatives (e.g. amikacin, netilmicin); highly water-soluble, bactericidal inhibitors of protein synthesis.
(b)
They diffuse through porin channels; transport across the cytoplasmic membrane depends on a transmembrane electrical gradient coupled to electron transport; they bind the 30S subunit (streptomycin) or additional 50S sites and the 30S-50S interface, causing misreading and premature termination; killing is concentration-dependent with a postantibiotic effect.
(c)
Primarily aerobic Gram-negative bacilli; little activity against anaerobic microorganisms, facultative bacteria or under anaerobic conditions; limited against Gram-positive bacteria, so not single agents there; streptomycin and amikacin act on mycobacteria.
(d)
Concentration-dependent killing; not absorbed orally (all except neomycin are parenteral); poor CSF penetration; more than 90% excreted unchanged in urine so accumulation occurs in renal dysfunction; do not mix with any drug in the same syringe or infusion bottle.
(e)
Inactivation by microbial enzymes, failure to penetrate the cell, and low affinity for the bacterial ribosome.
(f)
Ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, neuromuscular paralysis and allergic reactions; elderly are susceptible; therapeutic drug monitoring is imperative; avoid other nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, amphotericin B, vancomycin, cyclosporine, cisplatin), caution with ototoxic drugs (vancomycin, minocycline, furosemide) and avoid in pregnancy.
(g)
An aminoglycoside is recommended in empirical regimens for febrile neutropenia and sepsis when P. aeruginosa is a potential pathogen, and with a β-lactam for synergistic killing; they are ineffective for anaerobic pneumonia; renal impairment, age and co-prescribed nephrotoxic drugs limit use in this patient.
questions.question:
Gentamicin is proposed for an elderly patient with impaired kidney function who has a possible Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection and is also taking other nephrotoxic drugs.

(b) State the mechanism of action.

(d) State the factors affecting activity and handling.

A pharmacy has potable water from the public mains, freshly boiled and cooled purified water, and water from a local storage tank. It must prepare a non-sterile mixture, a parenteral solution and a surgical irrigation.
(a) Identify the microbiological risk.
(b) Explain how contamination arises.
(c) Name the control measures.
(d) Differentiate the four types of water.
(e) Differentiate the forms of WFI for the parenteral and irrigation needs.
(f) Reason to the quality decision.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Water from a local storage tank or open source may be heavily contaminated with microorganisms, and purified water that is allowed to stand may gain a high content of vegetative microorganisms.
(b)
From local storage tanks or open sources such as wells, from standing of purified water, and from defects in plumbing; potable water must be supplied under continuous positive pressure in a system free of defects.
(c)
Use mains-supplied potable water or freshly boiled and cooled purified water; for WFI, pyrogen-free distillation or reverse osmosis, sterilization immediately after collection, circulation at 70°C or above and conductivity, TOC, microbial and endotoxin monitoring.
(d)
Potable: freshly drawn from the public mains, suitable for internal and external preparations. Purified: from potable water by distillation or reverse osmosis, freshly boiled and cooled before use. Water for preparation: potable or freshly boiled and cooled purified water, for non-sterile products such as mixtures. Water for Injection: pyrogen-free distilled or reverse-osmosis water, sterilized immediately after collection.
(e)
Bulk WFI (manufacturing raw material), sterile WFI (single-dose containers, no additive, for dissolving or diluting drugs) and bacteriostatic WFI (multi-dose, with an antimicrobial such as benzyl alcohol, not suitable for neonates).
(f)
Use water for preparation (mains potable or freshly boiled and cooled purified water) for the non-sterile mixture; use WFI for the parenteral solution and for surgical irrigation; do not use local tank or open-source water for any pharmaceutical preparation.

questions.question:
A. Describe local drug delivery to the ear under the following headings.
(a) Types of otic preparations.
(b) Advantages of local delivery.
(c) Delivery systems.
(d) Formulation of topical otic products.
B. Relate it to the common examples of otic preparations.
(e) Anti-infective examples.
(f) Formulation examples.
(g) Hazard examples.
(h) Biofilm example.
C. Explain how local delivery improves safety and what limits it.
(i) Why local delivery is safer.
(j) Why it improves efficacy.
(k) Limitations.
(l) Administration trade-off.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cerumenolytics, otic anaesthetics, otic anti-infectives, otic steroids and otic steroids with anti-infectives.
(b)
Bypass of the blood-perilymph barrier, higher local drug concentration and reduced side effects.
(c)
Four types are in use: topical, transtympanic, intratympanic and cochlear delivery; topical delivery is direct administration into the ear canal.
(d)
Drops, foams, gels, creams and ointments with drug dissolved or dispersed in water, glycerol, diluted alcohol or propylene glycol; solvent chosen on solubility because the dose volume is low; viscosity matters; traditionally acidic (pH 3-4) which inhibits bacterial growth; excipients include pH modifier, antimicrobial preservative, suspending agent, thickener, tonicity agent and ointment base.
(e)
Ofloxacin (a quinolone) for outer and middle ear infections; ciprofloxacin with dexamethasone for acute otitis externa and media; antibiotics prescribed include amoxicillin, amoxicillin/clavulanate and Cortisporin.
(f)
Ciprofloxacin foam is more efficacious than the solution for acute otitis externa because foam improves retention; acetic acid drops lower the pH of the ear canal; antibacterial or antifungal drops control growth.
(g)
Neomycin, polymyxin and chloramphenicol are intensely ototoxic if they reach the inner ear; an ophthalmic drop (Vasocidin) used off-label is intensely inflammatory to middle ear mucosa; earwax softeners with triethanolamine polypeptide oleate condensate (10%) can cause severe inflammation and damage to the eardrum and inner ear.
(h)
Elimination of biofilm bacteria requires 10-1000 times higher antibiotic concentrations than planktonic bacteria, which topical delivery can achieve.
(i)
Compared with systemic administration it limits systemic toxicity and the risk of emerging antibiotic resistance in otitis media, and gives rapid delivery with good patient compliance and the ability to combine drugs.
(j)
It gives a local concentration much higher than systemic administration can achieve and bypasses the blood-perilymph barrier.
(k)
Inner ear toxicity (cochlear and vestibular) from ototoxic agents; irritant or inflammatory excipients or off-label products; low dose volume demands high concentration and solvent solubility; viscosity or foam needed for retention.
(l)
The patient lies with the infected ear upward for 5 minutes, pumping drops in with slight pressure on the front of the ear, and residual drops are wiped away after 5 minutes.

questions.question:
A. Describe probiotics under the following headings.
(a) Definition.
(b) Common types.
(c) Requirements for a probiotic.
(d) Mechanisms of action.
(e) Health applications.
B. Explain the basis of their activity against pathogens.
(f) Why do organic acids inhibit pathogens?
(g) Why are bacteriocins of limited spectrum?
(h) Why does competitive exclusion work?
C. Distinguish probiotics from prebiotics.
(i) Compare definitions.
(j) Compare examples.
(k) Compare mode of action.
(l) Compare use together.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Live microorganisms which, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host (FDA/WHO); the term derives from a Greek word meaning 'for life'; Fuller defined them as non-pathogenic microorganisms that exert a positive influence on host health or physiology when ingested.
(b)
Lactobacillus species (L. acidophilus, L. casei, L. rhamnosus, L. reuteri and others), Bifidobacterium species (B. longum, B. breve, B. bifidum, B. infantis and others), other lactic acid bacteria (Enterococcus faecium, Streptococcus thermophilus, Lactococcus lactis) and non-lactic acid organisms (E. coli Nissle, Saccharomyces boulardii).
(c)
Positive effects on the GIT; acid and bile resistance; firm adhesion; high survival and rapid multiplication; exclusion of pathogen adherence; safe, non-invasive, non-carcinogenic and non-pathogenic; production of acids, peroxide and bacteriocins; durability through manufacturing, packing and distribution so they arrive alive.
(d)
Enhancement of the epithelial barrier, increased adhesion to mucosa with inhibition of pathogen adhesion, production of antimicrobial substances, competitive exclusion of pathogens, and modulation of the immune system (including interference with quorum sensing).
(e)
Oral health, diarrhoea (including antibiotic-associated and rotavirus), lactose intolerance, irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, cholesterol lowering, urogenital and vaginal health, food and skin allergy, anticancer effects and vitamin production.
(f)
Acetic and lactic acids are the main antimicrobial compounds and strongly inhibit Gram-negative bacteria; the undissociated acid enters the bacterial cell and dissociates inside, so death results from lowering of intracellular pH or accumulation of the ionized form.
(g)
Bacteriocins from Gram-positive lactic acid bacteria (lactacin B, plantaricin, nisin) have a narrow activity spectrum and act only against closely related bacteria, killing through pore formation and/or inhibition of cell wall synthesis.
(h)
Probiotics compete for adhesion space, nutrients and energy sources, and their organic and volatile fatty acids lower gut pH below that required by pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella; lactobacilli also induce mucin secretion that blocks adherence.
(i)
Probiotics are live microorganisms; prebiotics are non-viable food components (non-digestible, selectively fermented) that confer a health benefit by modulating the microbiota.
(j)
Probiotics: Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Saccharomyces boulardii; prebiotics: fructans (inulin, fructo-oligosaccharides), galacto-oligosaccharides, resistant starch, pectic oligosaccharides and cocoa flavanols.
(k)
Probiotics supply organisms that adhere, exclude pathogens and make antimicrobial substances; prebiotics selectively stimulate growth and/or activity of beneficial colon bacteria such as bifidobacteria and lactobacilli.
(l)
Prebiotics resist stomach acid and mammalian enzymes and are fermented in the colon, while probiotics must survive acid and bile; they can be combined, e.g. galacto-oligosaccharides with or without Bifidobacterium breve, and SCFA production by probiotics with prebiotics contributes to cholesterol lowering.

Of the monozygotic group, the majority (approximately 20 of 30) will be monochorionic, and 10 will be dichorionic. This distribution has important implications for the level of surveillance and the specific risks applicable to each pair.
questions.question: In 100 twin pairs, approximately how many will be monozygotic?

questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein is produced primarily by the fetal liver and yolk sac, leaking in small amounts across the fetal skin and through fetal urine and gastrointestinal secretions into amniotic fluid, then crossing into maternal serum. Open fetal lesions such as neural tube defects dramatically increase this leak, explaining the markedly elevated AFP in these conditions that forms the basis of AFP-based prenatal screening.
questions.question: Alpha-fetoprotein is produced by which fetal structure and leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal serum?
HbCC disease compared to HbSS disease during pregnancy is characterised by:
options: Milder clinical course with better prognosis
More severe anaemia and more frequent crises
Higher risk of bone marrow embolism
questions.explanation: HbCC disease generally has a milder clinical course than HbSS, with less severe haemolytic anaemia and fewer crises, because HbC does not sickle under physiological conditions. However, pregnancy still represents a significant risk period, with potential for anaemia and thrombotic events. HbCC patients tend to have a better overall prognosis than HbSS.

Severe anaemia occurs in over 70% of pregnant women with HbSS disease, reflecting both chronic haemolysis and the dilutional anaemia of pregnancy. An additional 20% have moderate anaemia. The combination of haemolytic and dilutional anaemia is particularly challenging, requiring careful monitoring of PCV and targeted transfusion or haematinic supplementation.
questions.question: Severe anaemia occurs in over what proportion of women with HbSS disease during pregnancy?

questions.explanation: Recto-vaginal fistula results from prolonged second-stage compression of the posterior vaginal wall between the fetal presenting part and the maternal sacrum, causing ischaemic necrosis. This contrasts with vesico-vaginal fistula, which results from anterior compression against the pubis. Both are consequences of the same fundamental mechanism of obstructed labour in a contracted pelvis common in teenage pregnancy.
questions.question: Recto-vaginal fistula formation as a complication of teenage pregnancy results specifically from compression of the posterior vaginal wall against which structure?
In Rh-negative women, at what gestational age is the first dose of anti-D prophylaxis routinely administered to prevent rhesus isoimmunisation?
questions.explanation: Routine antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis is given at 28 weeks gestation (with a second dose at 34 weeks in some protocols) to Rh-negative women who are not already sensitised. Anti-D prevents maternal sensitisation that could occur from spontaneous fetomaternal haemorrhage in late pregnancy, protecting future pregnancies from haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

options: It is faster than any surgical approach
It preserves fertility by avoiding uterine devascularisation
It is effective in coagulopathic patients
It can be performed by a midwife
questions.question: Uterine artery embolisation for PPH is characterised by which major advantage over surgical ligation?
questions.explanation: Uterine artery embolisation (UAE) is a minimally invasive radiological procedure that selectively embolises the uterine arteries, controlling PPH while preserving uterine blood supply through collateral circulation, thereby maintaining the potential for future fertility. This is its key advantage over surgical ligation or hysterectomy. It requires interventional radiology facilities and haemodynamic stability.

questions.question: Gender-based violence (GBV) screening should be routinely offered during antenatal care because:
options: Pregnancy heightens GBV vulnerability with obstetric consequences
All pregnant women are victims of GBV
GBV has no effect on fetal outcomes
Screening is required by Nigerian law
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is a period of heightened vulnerability to GBV (domestic violence, sexual violence), with direct obstetric consequences including abruptio placentae (from abdominal trauma), preterm labour, LBW, perinatal death, and maternal mental health disorders. Routine ANC GBV screening enables early intervention, safety planning, and referral to support services, improving both maternal and fetal outcomes.

questions.question: The most common type of breech presentation seen at term accounts for approximately 65% of cases. It is described as:
questions.explanation: Frank or extended breech accounts for approximately 65% of term breech presentations, characterised by hips flexed and knees extended bilaterally so the legs lie alongside the trunk. It is more stable than complete or footling breech because the presenting diameter is larger and fills the cervix better. Despite being the commonest type, all forms still carry increased morbidity compared with vertex presentation.

questions.question: A woman undergoing vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery has the cup applied over the posterior fontanelle area, termed the flexion point. What is the primary purpose of this correct placement?
questions.explanation: Correct placement of the vacuum cup over the flexion point promotes flexion of the fetal head during traction, presenting the smallest possible diameters through the birth canal and improving the chance of successful, safer delivery. Incorrect placement can lead to deflexion, increased trauma and higher failure rates. Accurate assessment of fetal position is therefore essential before application.
options: To promote head flexion and reduce the diameters presented
To avoid the need for maternal pushing
To bypass the need for correct fetal position assessment
Avoid interventions that reduce preload or afterload excessively
Encourage upright posture with vigorous mobilisation
Give aggressive diuresis to relieve congestion
Prioritise rapid delivery regardless of stabilisation
questions.explanation: In severe aortic stenosis, the fixed outflow obstruction means that excessive reduction in preload or afterload, such as from aggressive diuresis or vasodilators, can precipitate a dangerous fall in cardiac output and further syncope, so these should be avoided or used very cautiously. Vigorous mobilisation is not the priority in this haemodynamically unstable state. Delivery should follow careful maternal stabilisation rather than being pursued immediately without addressing the underlying haemodynamic risk.
questions.question: A pregnant woman with severe aortic stenosis is admitted with syncope at 30 weeks. Which INITIAL principle of management is MOST important?

questions.explanation: Umbilical artery Doppler velocimetry directly assesses resistance to blood flow in the fetoplacental circulation, making it the most targeted tool for monitoring uteroplacental insufficiency in pre-eclampsia. Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates severe compromise and warrants urgent delivery. Doppler changes often precede other signs of fetal compromise.
questions.question: Which fetal surveillance modality is MOST useful in monitoring uteroplacental blood flow in pre-eclampsia?
The MOST preventable cause of maternal mortality globally is:
questions.explanation: Postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony is the single most preventable cause of maternal mortality globally. Active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL) — including prophylactic oxytocin, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage — can prevent the majority of PPH deaths. It is the simplest, most cost-effective intervention in obstetric care.

questions.question: In Nigeria, in practice, what minimum PCV (packed cell volume) threshold has traditionally been used as the cut-off for investigating anaemia, based on local research by Lawson and Aimakhu?
questions.explanation: In Nigerian obstetric practice, a PCV of 30% (corresponding to a haemoglobin of approximately 10 g/dl) has traditionally been used as the practical cut-off for investigation, based on work by Lawson and Aimakhu & Olayemi showing that serious harm to the fetus does not occur until Hb falls below 10 g/dl. This is less restrictive than the WHO cut-off of 33% PCV and reflects the local epidemiological reality.

Intrapartum ultrasound is particularly valuable for locating the placental edge when brisk bleeding occurs in early labour, to exclude placenta praevia before vaginal examination. It is also used to confirm fetal viability, determine presenting part, assess amniotic fluid, and investigate sudden abdominal pain. It does not replace CTG.
questions.question: Intrapartum ultrasonography is MOST appropriately used to:
options: Replace CTG monitoring in all low-risk labours
Assess fetal size when head is engaged in active labour
Diagnose ruptured uterus by identifying free fluid
Determine amniotic fluid index before each vaginal examination Correct

questions.question: A pregnant woman is prescribed an antibiotic for a respiratory tract infection. Which commonly used antibiotic is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy due to its effect on fetal bone and teeth?
questions.explanation: Tetracycline is absolutely contraindicated throughout pregnancy because it deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent staining of the primary teeth and potential inhibition of bone growth. This effect occurs because tetracyclines chelate calcium and are incorporated into calcifying tissues. Safer alternative antibiotic classes, such as penicillins, are preferred for treating bacterial infections in pregnant women whenever clinically appropriate.

questions.question: Low birth weight is implicated in adult development of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: LBW/IUGR is associated with adult development of cardiovascular disease (hypertension, coronary heart disease), Type 2 diabetes, chronic renal disease, and obstructive lung disease — these are part of the Barker hypothesis of developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD). Thyroid disease is not a recognised long-term sequela of LBW in the major teaching materials.

options: Rupturing the membranes to release liquor
Mechanically dilating the cervix beyond 3 cm
Releasing prostaglandins from the decidua and membranes
Stimulating oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary
questions.explanation: Membrane sweeping involves digital separation of the chorioamniotic membranes from the lower uterine segment, triggering release of prostaglandins from decidual cells and fetal membranes. This promotes cervical ripening and may initiate labour, reducing post-term pregnancies. It is recommended from 40 weeks to reduce formal induction rates.
questions.question: Membrane sweeping (stretch and sweep) primarily induces labour by:

options: Soft irregular breech mass in the fundus
Firm rounded head ballotable in the fundus
Fetal heart heard below the umbilicus
questions.question: During Leopold's manoeuvre in breech presentation, which finding is characteristic?
questions.explanation: In breech presentation, the firm, rounded, ballotable fetal head is palpated in the uterine fundus while the irregular, soft breech is felt in the lower pole. The fetal heart is typically auscultated above the umbilicus because the back is uppermost. These findings on abdominal palpation direct the clinician to confirm with ultrasound.

questions.question: By how much does cardiac output increase during normal pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Cardiac output increases by 30–50% during normal pregnancy, peaking at 12–24 weeks. This results from increased stroke volume (due to decreased vascular resistance) early in pregnancy and increased heart rate later. From 5 L/min pre-pregnancy, it rises to approximately 7 L/min by the 20th week, facilitating nutrient delivery to the fetus.

questions.question: A woman with a compound presentation, where a fetal hand lies alongside the presenting head, is in early labour with reassuring fetal heart trace. What is the most appropriate initial management approach?
questions.explanation: Compound presentation with a reassuring fetal heart trace can often be managed expectantly with close monitoring, as the prolapsed limb may withdraw spontaneously as the head descends further into the pelvis during labour. Caesarean section is reserved for cases with fetal compromise, failure to progress, or other complicating factors rather than being automatically required. Attempting manual repositioning without appropriate anaesthesia or indication is generally unnecessary and carries risk of cord prolapse.

options: Umbilical cord compression reducing venous return
Fetal head compression activating vagal reflex
Fetal anaemia reducing oxygen-carrying capacity Correct
questions.explanation: Early decelerations are caused by fetal head compression as it descends through the birth canal, triggering a vagal reflex that slows the heart rate. They begin with contraction onset and return to baseline as the contraction ends (short lag time), with a characteristic V-shape. They are rarely sinister and often indicate progress in labour.
questions.question: Early decelerations on CTG are caused by:
Motherless children who survive their mother's death are how many times MORE likely to die within two years compared to children with two living parents?
questions.explanation: Children who survive their mother's death are up to 10 times more likely to die within two years than children with two living parents. Motherless children receive less healthcare, nutrition, and education. This stark statistic underscores that maternal mortality is not merely a women's health issue but a child survival and social justice issue with multi-generational consequences.

questions.question: An elevated amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level in the second trimester is MOST specifically associated with which fetal condition?
questions.explanation: Elevated amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein is most specifically associated with open neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida). AFP leaks from the open lesion into the amniotic fluid, raising levels. The finding of elevated AFP on amniocentesis, combined with acetylcholinesterase presence, is highly diagnostic of an open NTD. This is one of the principal indications for amniocentesis in prenatal diagnosis.

questions.question: Grand multiparity is defined as having had how many or more previous deliveries, and carries specific obstetric risks?
questions.explanation: Grand multiparity is defined as having had 5 or more previous deliveries. It is associated with specific obstetric risks including placenta praevia, placental abruption, malpresentation, uterine atony leading to postpartum haemorrhage, and uterine rupture particularly in the presence of a previous scar. Grand multiparae require careful monitoring and active management of the third stage of labour.

questions.question: Which of the 'Five Delays' has been added as a fourth category, encompassing barriers related to health systems accountability?
questions.explanation: The fourth delay (added to the original Three Delays Model) is delay due to poor quality of care at the health facility — including untrained staff, lack of essential medicines, blood, equipment, and adherence to protocols. Even when a woman reaches a facility, substandard care can result in preventable death. Improving quality of care is as important as improving access.

A fixed, isosthenuric specific gravity around 1.010 to 1.012 reflects the kidney's inability to concentrate or dilute urine, indicating intrinsic renal failure with tubular dysfunction. Pre-renal azotaemia, by contrast, typically shows a high specific gravity as the kidneys appropriately concentrate urine in response to reduced perfusion. Simple dehydration with intact renal function and diabetes insipidus would produce different urinary concentration patterns, and this is not a normal pregnancy finding.
options: Intrinsic renal failure with loss of concentrating ability
Pre-renal azotaemia with intact concentrating ability
Diabetes insipidus unrelated to renal failure
Simple dehydration with normal renal function
questions.question: A woman with acute renal failure has a specific gravity fixed at 1.010 to 1.012 on repeated urine samples. What does this finding MOST specifically suggest?

questions.explanation: Internal podalic version followed by breech extraction is a recognised technique for delivering a second twin in transverse lie, performed by an experienced obstetrician under appropriate conditions, converting the lie to allow vaginal delivery. Awaiting spontaneous correction risks cord prolapse or prolonged interval between twin deliveries with fetal compromise. Caesarean section for the second twin remains an option if these techniques are unsuccessful or contraindicated.
questions.question: A woman with twin pregnancy in labour has delivered twin one vaginally. On assessment, twin two is found to be in transverse lie. What is the most appropriate management option to consider?
options: Internal podalic version with breech extraction
Immediate abandonment of vaginal delivery attempt with no intervention
Fundal pressure to correct the lie

questions.explanation: Entonox is a 50:50 mixture of nitrous oxide and oxygen. It provides both effective analgesia and a high inspired oxygen concentration, making it safe for the fetus. Its rapid onset and elimination, due to low blood solubility of nitrous oxide, make it non-cumulative and ideal for self-administration by the labouring woman.
questions.question: Entonox used for inhalational analgesia in labour consists of:

questions.explanation: For every maternal death, 30 to 50 women suffer serious injury, infection, or disease (maternal morbidity). Almost 8 million survivors suffer serious morbidity annually. Pregnancy-related complications are among the leading causes of death and disability for women aged 15–49 in developing countries, making the true burden of maternal ill-health far greater than mortality figures alone suggest.
questions.question: For every woman who dies from pregnancy-related causes, how many survivors suffer serious morbidity?

options: A social consequence of teenage motherhood
A direct obstetric complication of teenage pregnancy
A genetic predisposition of neonates born to teenagers
A pharmacological effect of drugs used in teenage labour
A consequence of prematurity in teenage pregnancy
questions.explanation: Inadequate postnatal care for the baby in teenage motherhood is a social consequence of limited experience, knowledge, and support available to teenage mothers. Unlike neonatal hypoglycaemia or respiratory distress resulting directly from pregnancy complications, inadequate neonatal care reflects the teenage mother's own needs for education and support, requiring a multidisciplinary postnatal support network.
questions.question: Inadequate care for the baby leading to increased neonatal morbidity in teenage motherhood is MOST accurately classified as:

questions.explanation: Ketonuria in the presence of normal or low blood glucose in a woman restricting carbohydrate intake most likely reflects starvation ketosis from inadequate caloric or carbohydrate intake, warranting dietary review rather than assuming diabetic ketoacidosis, which is typically associated with hyperglycaemia. This should prompt dietary reassessment rather than being dismissed as normal, since prolonged starvation ketosis can have adverse effects on the pregnancy. Fetal renal dysfunction and urinary tract infection are not the typical explanations for this specific maternal ketonuria pattern.
options: A normal and expected finding requiring no dietary review
Diabetic ketoacidosis requiring emergency insulin infusion
Urinary tract infection as the most likely explanation
Starvation ketosis from inadequate carbohydrate or caloric intake
Fetal renal dysfunction causing maternal ketonuria
questions.question: A woman with gestational diabetes is found to have ketonuria despite normal blood glucose readings on a low-carbohydrate diet. What does this finding MOST likely reflect?

questions.explanation: The ICPD Programme of Action (Cairo, 1994) was a landmark international agreement that shifted population policy from demographic targets to reproductive rights and individual empowerment. It established reproductive rights as fundamental human rights, including the right to decide freely the number and spacing of children. This framework underpins current global maternal and reproductive health policies.
questions.question: Which organisation's Programme of Action (Cairo, 1994) first placed reproductive rights and women's empowerment at the centre of population and development policy?

questions.explanation: Couvade syndrome refers to sympathetic pregnancy symptoms (nausea, vomiting, weight gain, back pain) experienced by expectant fathers, thought to have psychosomatic or hormonal origins. It reflects the psychological impact of pregnancy on fathers/partners and highlights the need to involve partners in antenatal care and preparation. Recognition helps address family dynamics affecting pregnancy outcomes.
questions.question: Which psychological change in pregnancy is described as 'couvade syndrome' seen in expectant fathers?
options: Post-traumatic stress disorder from previous pregnancy loss
Phobia of hospitals during partner's pregnancy
Obsessive monitoring of fetal movements by the father
Sympathetic pregnancy symptoms experienced by the father

questions.explanation: Clear, informed, and voluntary consent for permanent sterilisation should be obtained well in advance of the day of surgery, allowing adequate time for reflection and discussion of alternatives, given the permanent nature of the procedure and the importance of avoiding decisions made under the stress or influence of active labour. Obtaining consent only verbally just before anaesthesia does not allow this reflection. Sterilisation clearly does require the woman's own specific informed consent, which cannot be provided by a partner on her behalf or simply assumed from her attendance at hospital.
questions.question: A woman requests sterilisation at the time of her third caesarean section. Which aspect of the consent process is MOST important to have addressed BEFORE the day of surgery?
options: Her partner's consent alone is sufficient regardless of her wishes
Consent obtained verbally just before anaesthesia is given
Consent is not required for this procedure
Clear, informed, and voluntary consent obtained well in advance of labour
Consent can be assumed from her attendance at hospital

questions.question: External cephalic version (ECV) is optimally performed at which gestational age?
questions.explanation: ECV is ideally performed at 36–37 weeks gestation, when the risk of spontaneous reversion to breech is lower and the fetus is mature enough for emergency delivery if complications arise. Performing it too early risks spontaneous reversion, while too late limits the fluid space needed for manoeuvring. Facilities for emergency caesarean section must be immediately available.

questions.question: At community level, which intervention has been MOST effective in reducing maternal mortality by ensuring safe delivery?
options: Universal induction of labour at 39 weeks
Skilled birth attendance at every delivery
questions.explanation: Skilled birth attendance at every delivery is the single most effective community-level intervention for reducing maternal mortality. A trained SBA can manage normal labour, recognise deviations, manage common complications such as haemorrhage and eclampsia, and initiate timely referral for complex cases. Ensuring SBA access for all deliveries addresses the critical safety gap for the majority of births.

Isoimmunisation (alloimmunisation) is the process whereby antibodies are produced against antigens from another individual of the same species. In obstetrics, an Rh-negative mother sensitised by Rh-positive fetal red cells produces anti-D IgG that crosses the placenta to destroy fetal red cells in subsequent pregnancies. This distinguishes it from autoimmunisation (antibodies against self).
questions.question: Isoimmunisation is defined as the production of immune antibodies in one individual against antigens of another individual of the SAME:

questions.explanation: The ALARA principle in prescribing during pregnancy guides clinicians to use the lowest effective dose of a necessary medication for the shortest duration required to achieve the therapeutic goal, minimising fetal drug exposure while still adequately treating the maternal condition. It does not mean avoiding necessary treatment altogether, since untreated maternal disease can itself pose significant risks to both mother and fetus. This principle balances the need for effective maternal treatment against the goal of minimising unnecessary fetal exposure.
questions.question: A clinician prescribing a necessary medication to a pregnant woman applies the principle of 'ALARA' (As Low As Reasonably Achievable). This principle PRIMARILY guides which prescribing decision?
A woman with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 32 weeks develops fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia during expectant management. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Discontinue expectant management and expedite delivery with antibiotics
questions.explanation: Development of fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia during expectant management of preterm prelabour rupture of membranes suggests chorioamnionitis, requiring discontinuation of expectant management with prompt antibiotics and expedited delivery, as continuing the pregnancy risks worsening maternal and fetal infection. Increasing tocolysis in this context would be inappropriate as it prolongs exposure to infection. Timely recognition and action are critical to prevent progression to severe sepsis.

questions.question: In which group of pregnant women is plasma volume expansion LARGEST and why?
options: Primigravidae, due to first-time physiological adaptation
Teenagers due to their higher cardiac output
Grand multiparae with large or multiple fetuses
questions.explanation: The largest plasma volume expansion occurs in older multiparae, in pregnancies with large fetuses, and in multiple pregnancies. The greater fetoplacental mass in these situations demands a correspondingly greater increase in circulating blood volume to meet oxygen and nutrient delivery requirements. Conversely, the smallest expansion occurs in pregnancies complicated by placental insufficiency or fetal growth restriction.

questions.question: A face presentation delivering in a mento-posterior position should be managed by:
questions.explanation: Persistent mento-posterior (chin-posterior) face presentation cannot deliver vaginally because the neck is fully extended and cannot extend further to negotiate the outlet. The presenting diameter in this position is too large for delivery. Caesarean section is therefore the mandated management for persistent mento-posterior face presentation.

Periventricular/intraventricular haemorrhage is a major complication of extremely preterm/ELBW infants, linked to the fragility of immature cerebral vasculature (germinal matrix). LBW infants, particularly ELBW (<1000g), have high rates of this complication. Long-term sequelae include cerebral palsy, mental retardation, and visual/learning difficulties.
questions.question: Periventricular haemorrhage, which is a major complication of prematurity/LBW, is linked to which risk factor?
A Rh-negative woman has an antenatal antibody screen showing anti-c antibodies rather than anti-D. What is the MOST appropriate approach to this pregnancy?
options: Manage similarly to Rhesus D disease with titre and Doppler surveillance
No fetal surveillance is required since it is not anti-D
Anti-D immunoglobulin should be given to treat this antibody
This antibody cannot cause haemolytic disease of the fetus
Only postnatal testing of the baby is required, with no antenatal action
questions.explanation: Anti-c and other non-D red cell antibodies can also cause significant haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, so affected pregnancies require similar antenatal surveillance with serial titres and middle cerebral artery Doppler assessment as for anti-D disease. Assuming no risk simply because the antibody is not anti-D would be a dangerous oversight. Anti-D immunoglobulin is specific prophylaxis against the D antigen and has no role in treating a different antibody that is already present.

questions.question: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) in pregnancy may be required for which specific clinical indication?
questions.explanation: TPN in pregnancy may be required for severe hyperemesis gravidarum that is completely unresponsive to antiemetic therapy, enteral nutrition, and hospitalisation. When oral and enteral routes are unavailable due to refractory vomiting, TPN provides essential calories, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals to prevent maternal malnutrition, Wernicke's encephalopathy, and fetal growth restriction. It is a last-resort intervention requiring intensive monitoring.
options: Severe hyperemesis unresponsive to other treatments
Mild nausea and vomiting of pregnancy
Iron deficiency anaemia unresponsive to oral iron

questions.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome results from ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary gland following massive postpartum haemorrhage and hypovolaemic shock. The enlarged pituitary gland of pregnancy is particularly vulnerable to hypoperfusion. This results in panhypopituitarism manifesting as failure of lactation, amenorrhoea, and adrenal insufficiency.
questions.question: Sheehan's syndrome can result from massive haemorrhage in a grandmultipara. This condition involves infarction of which structure?

questions.explanation: In occipito-posterior position, both the occiput and sinciput are felt at the same level above the symphysis pubis because the head is deflexed and the presenting diameter is larger. This contrasts with OP position where the head appears relatively large from side to side on abdominal palpation. In OA position, the sinciput is higher because the head is well flexed.
options: Both occiput and sinciput felt at the same level above the symphysis
Hard rounded mass in the fundus
Fetal heart heard clearly below the umbilicus
questions.question: Which of the following findings on abdominal palpation in occipito-posterior position helps distinguish it from occipito-anterior?

questions.explanation: Modified White Classification Class F denotes diabetic renal disease (nephropathy). Class H denotes coronary artery disease, Class R denotes proliferative retinopathy, and Class T denotes renal transplant. These advanced classes carry much higher maternal and perinatal risks. Pre-gestational diabetes types are classified as A (diet-controlled), B, C, D, and the advanced classes F, H, R, T.
questions.question: The Modified White Classification Class F of diabetes in pregnancy denotes:

questions.explanation: Ibadan has the highest recorded twinning rate in Nigeria at 52 per 1000 births (Nylander, 1971), contributing to Nigeria's overall high rate of 54 per 1000. The high rate in Ibadan reflects the Yoruba ethnic predominance and the genetic predisposition to dizygotic twinning in this population. This is one of the highest rates reported anywhere in the world.
questions.question: The highest twinning rate recorded from any single Nigerian centre is from:
A woman on regular antenatal care develops BP 145/95 mmHg at 38 weeks with no proteinuria and no symptoms. Which is the MOST appropriate initial approach?
options: Perform emergency caesarean section without delay
Increase surveillance frequency and monitor for progression
Start triple oral antihypertensive therapy at once
Discharge with no further blood pressure checks
Admit immediately for intravenous magnesium sulphate
questions.explanation: Mild new hypertension at term without proteinuria or severe features is initially managed with increased surveillance to detect progression to pre-eclampsia, rather than immediate aggressive intervention. Magnesium sulphate and emergency delivery are reserved for severe disease. Complete discharge without follow-up would risk missing rapid deterioration.

HbS results from substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta-globin chain, caused by a single point mutation (GAG→GTG). This single amino acid change alters haemoglobin's physical properties under low oxygen tension, causing polymerisation and sickling. HbC results from lysine substitution at the same position.
questions.question: Haemoglobin S (HbS) results from which specific amino acid substitution on the beta-globin chain?

options: Produce anti-D immunoglobulin for later use
questions.question: Intensive antenatal plasmapheresis in Rhesus isoimmunisation is used to:
questions.explanation: Intensive antenatal plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) removes anti-D IgG from the maternal circulation, reducing the titre and amount of antibody available for placental transfer. It may be used in severely sensitised women early in pregnancy before intrauterine transfusion is technically feasible (before 20 weeks). It is used in conjunction with, not as a replacement for, intrauterine transfusion when haemolysis is severe.

Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis in Rh-negative women without prior sensitisation is typically administered at around 28 weeks of gestation, when the risk of silent fetomaternal haemorrhage sensitising the mother begins to rise. A further dose is given after delivery if the baby is confirmed Rh-positive, and additional doses follow any sensitising event such as bleeding or invasive procedures. This timing aims to prevent maternal anti-D antibody formation that could cause haemolytic disease in a subsequent pregnancy.
questions.question: A Rh-negative woman with no evidence of prior sensitisation is being counselled about routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis. The first dose is routinely administered at approximately:
A woman in her 8th pregnancy presents at term with a transverse lie confirmed on examination. Which factor related to her parity MOST plausibly explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: Grand multiparity leads to laxity of the abdominal and uterine musculature from repeated distension, reducing the fixation that normally maintains a longitudinal fetal lie and predisposing to malpresentations such as transverse lie. This mechanism is distinct from placental or fluid-related causes of malpresentation. Increased uterine tone and cervical stenosis are not recognised features of grand multiparity.

questions.question: Mismanagement of the third stage of labour, specifically premature attempts to separate the placenta, causes PPH by which mechanism?
options: Disrupting partial placental separation causing bleeding from the incomplete placental bed
questions.explanation: Premature attempts to separate the placenta before complete separation disrupt the partial implantation site, causing haemorrhage from an incompletely retracted placental bed. The uterus cannot fully contract while part of the placenta remains attached. Passive management with premature cord traction is the most common form of third-stage mismanagement causing PPH.

questions.question: Low birth weight (LBW) is defined as a birth weight of less than:
questions.explanation: Low birth weight is defined as a birth weight less than 2500g, measured within one hour of birth irrespective of gestational age. VLBW is <1500g and ELBW is <1000g. LBW is strongly associated with perinatal morbidity and mortality and accounts for 50% of all neonatal deaths globally.

options: Internal rotational manoeuvres such as Rubin or Woods screw manoeuvre
Repeat McRoberts manoeuvre indefinitely without trying alternatives
Excessive downward traction on the head
Immediate abandonment with no further attempts
questions.explanation: When McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure fail to resolve shoulder dystocia, internal rotational manoeuvres such as the Rubin or Woods screw manoeuvre, which aim to rotate the fetal shoulders into a more favourable oblique diameter, are appropriate next steps. Excessive traction remains inappropriate throughout management due to risk of brachial plexus injury. A structured, stepwise approach following an established shoulder dystocia protocol optimises outcomes.
questions.question: A woman with shoulder dystocia does not respond to McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure. What is an appropriate next-line manoeuvre to consider?

options: Discontinue monitoring once the baby is delivered
Withhold magnesium sulphate since delivery occurred
Continue antihypertensive therapy and monitor for eclampsia
Discharge home since proteinuria has resolved
questions.explanation: Pre-eclampsia can worsen or first present in the postpartum period, and eclampsia may occur up to and beyond 48 hours after delivery, so antihypertensive therapy and seizure vigilance must continue. Resolution of proteinuria does not indicate resolution of the underlying disease process. Discharging or stopping therapy prematurely risks postpartum eclampsia or stroke.
questions.question: A woman with pre-eclampsia is 6 hours postpartum with BP 170/115 mmHg and no proteinuria on dipstick now. What is the MOST appropriate management?

questions.explanation: Women who develop severe pre-eclampsia before 27 weeks have approximately a 50% recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies, significantly higher than the 18% overall recurrence risk. This high recurrence necessitates pre-conceptional counselling, early antenatal booking, and heightened surveillance in future pregnancies. Aspirin prophylaxis is usually recommended.
