questions.question: Corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) are administered to mothers between 24-34 weeks gestation in threatened preterm labour to achieve which primary fetal benefit?
Anaemia in pregnancy is defined by WHO as a haemoglobin concentration below 11 g/dl. According to Lawson (1967), serious fetal harm specifically occurs below which Hb value in the Nigerian setting?
questions.explanation: Lawson (1967) and subsequent work by Aimakhu and Olayemi (2003) demonstrated that serious harm to the fetus does not occur until haemoglobin falls below 10 g/dl (PCV 30%) in the Nigerian obstetric population. This finding justified the use of 10 g/dl as the practical investigation threshold in resource-limited Nigerian settings rather than the WHO standard of 11 g/dl, given that strict application of the WHO threshold would classify the majority of Nigerian antenatal attendees as anaemic.

questions.question: A pregnant woman is advised to take her iron tablet with a source of vitamin C. This recommendation is based on vitamin C's ability to improve iron absorption through which specific mechanism?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) enhances non-haem iron absorption by reducing ferric (Fe3+) iron to the more readily absorbed ferrous (Fe2+) form and by forming a soluble chelate that remains available for absorption in the alkaline environment of the upper small intestine. This is why taking iron supplements with a vitamin C source, such as citrus fruit or juice, is commonly recommended to improve absorption efficiency. This mechanism is separate from vitamin C's other physiological roles, such as collagen synthesis and antioxidant activity.

Active pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) cannot be detected on plain X-ray as it involves soft tissue inflammation without calcification. Plain X-ray can detect calcified masses (fibroids, bladder stones), missing IUCDs, and teeth or bone fragments in dermoid cysts. MRI or ultrasound is better for soft tissue pelvic pathology.
questions.question: Plain abdominal X-ray can detect all of the following gynaecological findings EXCEPT:
Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia as a major cause of maternal mortality causes death primarily through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Eclampsia and severe pre-eclampsia cause maternal death through cerebral haemorrhage (from uncontrolled hypertension), HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets), acute renal failure, pulmonary oedema, and multiorgan failure. Magnesium sulphate prevents eclamptic seizures, and antihypertensive therapy prevents stroke. These are the key interventions reducing eclampsia mortality.

options: Routine maternal antibody titres only, without Doppler
Fetal kick counts alone without further scanning
Repeat cordocentesis performed weekly regardless of findings
No further surveillance is required after one transfusion
Serial middle cerebral artery Doppler assessment
questions.explanation: After an initial intrauterine transfusion, serial middle cerebral artery Doppler assessment is used non-invasively to monitor for recurrent fetal anaemia and to time any further transfusion appropriately. Assuming no further surveillance is needed risks missing recurrent severe anaemia. Maternal antibody titres become less useful for timing further intervention once transfusion has occurred, and repeated invasive cordocentesis without a non-invasive trigger exposes the fetus to unnecessary procedural risk.
questions.question: A woman with Rhesus disease undergoes successful intrauterine transfusion at 28 weeks. Which subsequent surveillance is MOST appropriate to time any further transfusion?
A woman at 22 weeks with SLE has a relapse confirmed during pregnancy. Which statement about lupus relapse in pregnancy is MOST accurate and relevant to renal monitoring?
options: Relapse risk is completely unrelated to pregnancy status
Renal surveillance is unnecessary once a relapse is confirmed
Relapse only occurs in the postpartum period, never antenatally
Relapse risk is increased during pregnancy, warranting close renal surveillance
Pregnancy reliably protects against lupus relapse
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of lupus relapse, including renal flares, making close ongoing renal surveillance essential once a relapse is confirmed to detect and manage worsening nephritis promptly. Pregnancy does not reliably protect against relapse, and relapses can certainly occur antenatally, not only postpartum. Reduced surveillance once a relapse is already confirmed would be inappropriate, since ongoing monitoring guides treatment adjustment.

questions.question: A patient presents after the 36th week for her first antenatal visit, having concealed her pregnancy. This scenario MOST directly reflects which biosocial risk factor in obstetrics?
questions.explanation: Late or no antenatal attendance due to concealment is a hallmark consequence of the social embarrassment associated with teenage pregnancy. By concealing the pregnancy to avoid stigma, the teenager misses the entire benefit of early antenatal booking, risk screening, and preventive interventions. This concealment directly contributes to higher rates of complications including undetected anaemia, pre-eclampsia, and unsafe abortion.

The continued occurrence of Rh isoimmunisation in the era of anti-D prophylaxis is primarily due to failure to administer anti-D when clinically indicated, or failure to give adequate doses when a large feto-maternal haemorrhage is detected. Human error in screening, documentation, and administration constitutes the major preventable cause of ongoing Rh sensitisation.
options: Failure of the immune system to respond to anti-D
Emergence of anti-D resistant Rh-positive strains
Failure to administer adequate anti-D when indicated
Reduced efficacy of modern anti-D preparations
questions.question: The continued occurrence of Rhesus isoimmunisation despite available prophylaxis is PRIMARILY attributed to:

A woman is uncertain of her LMP and presents at what she believes is 20 weeks gestation. An ultrasound dating scan shows a discrepancy of 3 weeks from her assumed gestational age. Which action is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: When there is a discrepancy of more than 2 weeks between menstrual dates and ultrasound biometry, the pregnancy should be redated using the earliest reliable ultrasound scan, which is more accurate than uncertain menstrual recall. This ensures appropriate timing of screening tests, surveillance, and any decisions about post-term management. Ignoring the scan or assuming post-term status without redating risks inappropriate intervention or missed surveillance.

Perinatal mortality is highest in teenage mothers and grand multiparae from low socioeconomic backgrounds because these groups accumulate the maximum number of biological risk factors (immature pelvis, uterine atony) and social risk factors (poor nutrition, inadequate antenatal care, delayed recognition of complications) simultaneously. The synergy of biological vulnerability and social disadvantage creates exponentially higher risk.
questions.question: In which maternal group is perinatal mortality specifically HIGHEST due to accumulation of both biological and social risk factors?
options: Teenage mothers and poor grand multiparae
Women who deliver in tertiary hospitals
Continuous insulin infusion is mandatory even without insulin use antenatally
Induction before 37 weeks is mandatory regardless of growth
No glucose monitoring is required during labour in this scenario
She can generally be managed similarly to a low-risk pregnancy with glucose monitoring
She must have an elective caesarean section regardless of other factors
questions.explanation: With good control on diet alone and normal fetal growth, a woman with gestational diabetes can generally be managed similarly to a low-risk pregnancy during labour, with glucose monitoring continued to detect any unexpected hyperglycaemia. Mandatory caesarean section or insulin infusion are not required simply because of the gestational diabetes diagnosis when control and growth are reassuring. Induction well before 37 weeks is not routinely necessary in this favourable scenario, and omitting glucose monitoring altogether would still be inappropriate given the underlying diagnosis.
questions.question: A woman with gestational diabetes has an ultrasound at 36 weeks showing normal fetal growth and good glycaemic control on diet alone. Which statement about her intrapartum care is MOST accurate?

questions.explanation: Hyperextension (starring) of the fetal head on ultrasound is a key criterion requiring caesarean delivery in breech presentation because vaginal delivery of a hyperextended aftercoming head risks catastrophic cervical spinal cord injury. The normal criterion for vaginal delivery requires a flexed fetal head. A hyperextended head presenting in the breech cannot safely negotiate the birth canal.
options: Hyperextended or starred fetal head on ultrasound
questions.question: Which of the following criteria MOST reliably indicates the fetal head is deflexed in a breech presentation, necessitating caesarean section?

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors are directly fetotoxic, causing renal tubular dysgenesis, anuria, and consequent severe oligohydramnios when used in the second and third trimesters. This is a specific drug effect rather than a nonspecific consequence of hypertension itself. Rubella, amniotic bands, and post-term pregnancy do not produce this particular pattern of renal dysgenesis.
options: Post-term pregnancy causing reduced amniotic fluid
Amniotic band syndrome affecting the fetal kidneys
Placental insufficiency from untreated hypertension alone
Fetal renal tubular dysgenesis from ACE inhibitor exposure
Congenital rubella infection acquired in the first trimester
questions.question: A woman with chronic hypertension conceives while taking an ACE inhibitor. Ultrasound at 22 weeks shows severe oligohydramnios and renal hypoplasia. Which mechanism BEST explains this finding?
DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) in obstetrics involves simultaneous activation of both clotting cascades, leading to:
questions.explanation: DIC involves systemic activation of both the intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation cascades, leading to consumption of clotting factors and platelets faster than they can be replaced, resulting in pathological bleeding. Paradoxically, microvascular thrombosis also occurs as part of the same process. Laboratory findings include prolonged PT and PTTK, reduced fibrinogen and platelets, raised FDPs, and fragmented red blood cells on blood film.
options: Consumption of clotting factors and platelets with pathological bleeding and thrombosis
Selective increase in Factor VIII only
Increase in all clotting factors uniformly
Equal contraction intensity in upper and lower segments
Dominance of fundal contraction with lower segment relaxation
Simultaneous contraction of all myometrial layers
Alternating contraction of the right and left uterine horns
Greater relaxation of fundus compared to lower segment Correct
questions.explanation: Uterine polarity describes the gradient of contraction intensity during normal labour, where the fundus contracts most strongly and the lower segment passively relaxes and dilates. This fundal dominance ensures that uterine force is directed downward toward the cervix and facilitates fetal descent. Absence of polarity leads to inefficient labour.
questions.question: The term "uterine polarity" in normal labour refers to;
Malaria as a cause of maternal death in Nigeria is primarily classified as:
questions.explanation: Malaria is classified as an indirect obstetric death — a disease that existed before or developed during pregnancy, not directly caused by pregnancy, but aggravated by the physiological changes of pregnancy (reduced immunity, increased susceptibility). In Nigeria, malaria in pregnancy contributes to maternal anaemia, severe malaria complications, and maternal death, particularly in primigravidae.

questions.question: Compensatory changes that maintain adequate tissue oxygenation in a severely anaemic pregnant woman include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The compensatory changes that maintain tissue oxygenation in severe anaemia include increased plasma volume, increased cardiac output, increased blood flow velocity, and DECREASED peripheral resistance. An INCREASE in peripheral resistance is NOT a compensatory mechanism; rather, it is associated with hypertensive states. When anaemia is severe enough that these compensatory mechanisms are exhausted (typically at Hb < 5 g/dl), high-output cardiac failure develops.

questions.question: A woman in labour receives intramuscular pethidine for analgesia shortly before an unexpectedly rapid second stage and delivery. What neonatal complication should the team anticipate?
questions.explanation: Opioid analgesics such as pethidine cross the placenta and can cause neonatal respiratory depression if delivery occurs within a few hours of administration, so the resuscitation team should be prepared with naloxone available if needed. This risk is time-dependent, being greatest when delivery occurs close to peak maternal drug levels. Careful timing of opioid administration in relation to expected delivery helps reduce this risk.

options: Continue routine antenatal care with regular monitoring
Immediate exchange transfusion regardless of symptoms
Emergency delivery to correct chronic anaemia
questions.question: A woman with sickle cell disease at 30 weeks has a PCV of 24% with reticulocytosis and is asymptomatic otherwise. Which management is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: A moderately low PCV with an appropriate reticulocyte response in an asymptomatic woman reflects her chronic haemolytic baseline and is managed with continued routine antenatal surveillance rather than aggressive intervention. Exchange transfusion, emergency delivery, corticosteroids, and urgent splenectomy are not indicated in the absence of acute complications. Overtreatment of a stable chronic anaemia can itself introduce unnecessary risk.

options: Immediate hysterectomy as the only option
Application of fundal pressure from above without addressing the uterus
questions.explanation: If manual replacement of an inverted uterus fails despite adequate tocolysis to relax the uterus, surgical correction under anaesthesia, potentially involving laparotomy, becomes the appropriate next step to achieve repositioning. Continued unsuccessful attempts without escalation risk ongoing haemorrhage and delay definitive treatment. Hysterectomy is reserved as a last resort rather than an immediate next step after failed manual replacement.
questions.question: A woman with confirmed uterine inversion following vaginal delivery requires urgent management. If manual replacement fails despite tocolysis, what is the most appropriate next step?
Approximately how many newborn infants die during the first month of life annually worldwide?
questions.explanation: Approximately 4.3 million newborn infants die during the first month of life annually, and a further 4 million are stillborn. A million or more children are left motherless each year. Motherless children are up to 10 times more likely to die within two years than children with two living parents, highlighting the profound inter-generational impact of maternal death.

options: Reduced risk of any scalp trauma
questions.question: A woman undergoing vacuum-assisted delivery has the procedure abandoned after failure to achieve descent, and caesarean section is performed instead. What specific neonatal complication should the team be vigilant for given the sequential attempts?
questions.explanation: Subgaleal haemorrhage is a serious, potentially life-threatening complication associated with vacuum extraction, particularly with failed or prolonged attempts, involving bleeding into the potential space beneath the scalp aponeurosis, and affected neonates require close monitoring for signs of hypovolaemia and anaemia. This risk underscores the importance of appropriate technique and timely abandonment of unsuccessful attempts. Early recognition and supportive management improve neonatal outcomes.

questions.question: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) can be performed as early as which gestational age, making it advantageous over amniocentesis for early diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chorionic villus sampling can be performed as early as 10-13 weeks gestation, compared to amniocentesis which is typically performed at 15-18 weeks. This earlier timing is a significant advantage as it allows earlier diagnosis of chromosomal and genetic disorders, giving couples more time to make informed decisions. However, CVS carries a slightly higher procedure-related miscarriage risk than amniocentesis.

questions.question: Which antihypertensive is PREFERRED for acute severe hypertension (BP >160/110) in pregnancy when IV access is established?
questions.explanation: Intravenous hydralazine or IV labetalol are first-line agents for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy when IV access is available, allowing rapid and controllable BP reduction. Sublingual nifedipine is avoided as it can cause precipitous hypotension and fetal distress. Oral medications act too slowly for hypertensive emergencies requiring immediate intervention.

The WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as a haemoglobin concentration below 11 g/dl or a packed cell volume (PCV) below 33%. This threshold accounts for the physiological haemodilution of pregnancy, which reduces haemoglobin below non-pregnant normal values. Values below 11 g/dl cannot be explained by physiological changes alone and require investigation for underlying pathology.
questions.question: According to the WHO definition, anaemia in pregnancy is defined as a haemoglobin concentration below which value?

options: Immediate delivery regardless of maternal or fetal stability
Immediate caesarean section regardless of presentation
Antenatal corticosteroids and consideration of tocolysis to allow steroid effect
questions.question: A woman in preterm labour at 29 weeks with intact membranes is being managed. Which intervention is most appropriate to reduce neonatal morbidity given the gestational age?
questions.explanation: In preterm labour at 29 weeks with intact membranes, administration of antenatal corticosteroids to promote fetal lung maturity, alongside consideration of tocolysis to delay delivery long enough for the steroid course to take effect, are appropriate interventions to reduce neonatal morbidity. Immediate delivery without these measures, in the absence of other urgent indications, would forgo this important opportunity to improve neonatal outcomes. Magnesium sulphate for fetal neuroprotection may also be considered at this gestation.

questions.question: Hypertension persisting more than how many weeks postpartum establishes a DIAGNOSIS of chronic hypertension?
questions.explanation: If hypertension persists for more than 12 weeks after delivery, it is classified as chronic hypertension rather than gestational hypertension. Gestational hypertension resolves by 12 weeks postpartum. Women with persisting hypertension require further evaluation for secondary causes and long-term cardiovascular risk management.

options: A platelet count trending downward over two days
A stable platelet count with no clinical bleeding
A rapidly falling platelet count over the past hour
Active bleeding from the gums or venepuncture sites
Associated coagulopathy with prolonged clotting times
questions.explanation: A platelet count above 70,000 to 80,000/uL that is stable and unaccompanied by clinical bleeding or coagulopathy is generally considered acceptable for spinal anaesthesia. A rapidly falling count, coagulopathy, or active bleeding all raise concern for an evolving consumptive process and favour general anaesthesia instead. Trend and clinical context matter more than the isolated number.
questions.question: A woman with pre-eclampsia has platelets of 95,000/uL and is scheduled for caesarean section. Regional anaesthesia is being considered. Which factor is MOST reassuring for proceeding with spinal anaesthesia?

questions.explanation: Mendelson's syndrome (aspiration pneumonitis) results from aspiration of acidic gastric contents, typically during general anaesthesia in obstetrics. Plain chest X-ray may show aspiration pneumonitis pattern, particularly in the right lower lobe. This is a recognised obstetric emergency for which plain chest X-ray is indicated.
questions.question: Which plain radiological finding in the chest of a pregnant woman would suggest Mendelson's syndrome?

options: Mild anaemia at 20 weeks with good oral tolerance
Routine prophylaxis for all pregnant women
Anaemia detected for the first time at 36 weeks
Quick and certain correction of total iron deficit
questions.question: Parenteral iron is MOST specifically indicated in the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy under which clinical circumstance?
questions.explanation: Parenteral iron is most specifically indicated when quick and certain correction of the total iron deficit is required, such as when oral iron is not tolerated, absorption is compromised, or when time constraints limit the duration of oral therapy (e.g., presenting late in pregnancy). The advantage of intramuscular or intravenous iron is the certainty of its delivery, bypassing gastrointestinal absorption variability.

questions.question: Of the five biophysical profile (BPP) components, which ONE is assessed using cardiotocography (CTG) rather than ultrasound?
questions.explanation: Of the five BPP components, only the non-stress test (fetal heart rate reactivity) is assessed by cardiotocography, while fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, fetal tone, and amniotic fluid volume are assessed by real-time ultrasound. Each parameter scores 0 or 2, with a maximum total score of 10. A score of 8-10 is normal; 4 or less in a term pregnancy generally warrants delivery.

options: Absent end-diastolic Doppler flow with oligohydramnios
questions.question: In delivery management of IUGR, which finding is a critical indication to deliver regardless of gestational age?
questions.explanation: A combination of absent end-diastolic velocities on umbilical artery Doppler with oligohydramnios is an absolute indication for delivery in IUGR regardless of gestational age. This combination indicates critical placental insufficiency with imminent fetal compromise. Another indication for delivery is absence of fetal growth on two USS evaluations 2–3 weeks apart. Cardiac output returns to normal pre-pregnancy levels approximately 2 weeks after delivery. The most critical period remains the immediate postpartum (first 12–24 hours) due to autotransfusion. Cardiac patients should be kept in hospital for at least 2 weeks postpartum and discharged only after confirming haemodynamic stability and absence of pulmonary oedema.
questions.question: Cardiac output returns to pre-pregnancy levels approximately how long after delivery?

questions.explanation: Locked twins is a complication unique to multiple pregnancy and cannot occur in singleton deliveries. It requires simultaneous descent of two fetuses in incompatible positions. While cord prolapse, uterine atony, abruption, and prolonged labour all occur in singletons (and are more frequent in twins), locked twins is exclusively a multiple pregnancy complication.
questions.question: Which of the following intrapartum complications is unique to multiple pregnancy and does not occur in singletons?

questions.explanation: During transvaginal ultrasound, the probe is introduced 3–6 cm into the vagina. This proximity to the pelvic organs allows higher frequency probes (5–8 MHz) to be used, giving better resolution of pelvic structures. The technique does not require a full bladder but is invasive and a chaperone is required.
questions.question: For transvaginal ultrasound, the probe is introduced to what depth into the vagina during scanning?
options: At the level of the cervical os only

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin, secreted in increased amounts during pregnancy, stimulates bone marrow hyperplasia and increases red cell mass by 14-25%. While plasma volume expands more dramatically (by 50%), the expansion of red cell mass is a genuine adaptive increase in oxygen-carrying capacity. The relative predominance of plasma expansion over red cell mass increase produces the physiological anaemia of pregnancy.
questions.question: The bone marrow in pregnancy becomes hyperplastic due to increased secretion of which hormone, resulting in an increase in red cell mass?

questions.explanation: Kielland's forceps are specifically designed for rotational delivery and are indicated for deep transverse arrest and persistent occipito-posterior position. They have a sliding lock that allows rotation of the fetal head from posterior or transverse to anterior. Their use requires significant skill and is associated with higher complication rates if improperly applied.
questions.question: Kielland's rotational forceps are specifically indicated in the management of which malposition?

questions.explanation: A weight of 45 kg or less is a recognised risk factor at the booking visit. Standard risk assessment criteria identify maternal weight below 45 kg (underweight) and above 100 kg (obesity) as high-risk parameters. Both extremes are associated with adverse maternal and fetal outcomes, including growth restriction and complications during labour.
questions.question: During a booking visit, which maternal weight parameter would IMMEDIATELY flag a patient as high-risk by standard risk assessment criteria?
The position of twins at the time of delivery with the leading twin in breech and the second twin cephalic can lead to which specific life-threatening complication?
questions.explanation: When the leading twin is breech and the second twin is cephalic, the chins of the two twins can interlock during delivery, causing locked twins. As the body of the first breech twin descends, the head of the second cephalic twin engages simultaneously, preventing delivery of either. This is a rare but potentially fatal complication requiring skilled immediate obstetric intervention.
options: Cord prolapse of the first twin
Direct parasitic invasion of kidney tubules
Mechanical obstruction of renal arteries by parasite clusters
Intravascular haemolysis releasing free haemoglobin causing tubular necrosis
questions.explanation: Severe falciparum malaria causes massive intravascular haemolysis, releasing free haemoglobin into the plasma. Haemoglobin is filtered at the glomerulus, precipitating in tubular lumina (particularly in acidic, concentrated urine) and causing direct tubulotoxicity and mechanical obstruction—classic blackwater fever with haemoglobinuria and ARF. This is an example of haemoglobin as an endogenous nephrotoxin.
questions.question: Falciparum malaria causes haemoglobinuria (blackwater fever) leading to ARF through which DIRECT mechanism?
If the second twin has not delivered within 30 minutes of the first twin, the management is:
questions.explanation: If the second twin has not been delivered within 30 minutes of the first, caesarean section is indicated because prolonged delay increases the risk of placental abruption, cord prolapse, fetal distress, and uterine atony. This time limit ensures active management of the second stage for the second twin. Other interventions are attempted before resorting to caesarean section, but it remains the final option.

Because pyelonephritis in pregnancy has a high recurrence rate, prophylactic low-dose antibiotics are often continued for the remainder of the pregnancy after successful treatment of the acute episode. Stopping antibiotics completely leaves a significant risk of recurrent infection. Monthly full-dose intravenous courses are unnecessary and impractical, and dietary modification alone does not prevent bacterial recurrence.
questions.question: A woman at 26 weeks with pyelonephritis is treated with intravenous antibiotics and improves. Regarding continued antibiotic prophylaxis for the remainder of pregnancy, which is MOST appropriate?
options: Antibiotics should only be resumed at the onset of labour
No further antibiotics are needed after the acute course
A repeat full-dose intravenous course is required monthly
Antibiotics are stopped and replaced by dietary modification
Prophylactic low-dose antibiotics for the remainder of pregnancy

questions.explanation: HELLP syndrome comprises Haemolysis (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia), Elevated Liver enzymes (AST/ALT), and Low Platelet count. It is a severe variant of pre-eclampsia with significant maternal and fetal morbidity. Prompt delivery is usually required once HELLP is diagnosed, regardless of gestational age.
questions.question: HELLP syndrome is characterised by which combination of laboratory findings?

questions.explanation: Liver histopathology in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy shows centrilobular bile stasis (bile plugs in hepatocyte canaliculi) without significant hepatocellular necrosis or inflammation, distinguishing it from hepatitis. Macrovesicular fat deposition is characteristic of acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Viral hepatitis shows hepatocyte necrosis with inflammatory infiltrate.
questions.question: Liver histopathology in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy characteristically reveals:

questions.explanation: The definitive treatment for HELLP syndrome is delivery of the fetus and placenta once the maternal condition has been appropriately stabilised, as the underlying pathology resolves with removal of the placental trigger. Prolonged expectant management risks progression to severe maternal complications such as liver rupture or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Timing of delivery balances gestational age considerations against severity of maternal disease.
options: Long-term antihypertensive therapy alone without delivery
Delivery of the fetus and placenta once maternal condition allows
Continued expectant management indefinitely regardless of severity
Plasma exchange as first-line before considering delivery

questions.question: A woman is undergoing an assisted vaginal breech delivery and the obstetrician avoids touching the fetal trunk until the umbilicus has delivered. What is the rationale behind this specific practice?
questions.explanation: Avoiding handling of the fetal trunk until the umbilicus has delivered spontaneously, often summarised as 'hands off the breech,' helps avoid stimulating premature respiratory effort or reflexes before the head is delivered, while also reducing unnecessary manipulation that could increase trauma risk. This principle guides the initial passive phase of assisted breech delivery before active assistance is required for arms and head. Deviating from this practice without indication increases risk of complications during breech birth.

options: It reduces amniotic fluid volume dangerously
It is ineffective for weight management in pregnancy
Fetal growth restriction, ketonuria, and nutrient deficiency
questions.explanation: Severe caloric restriction below 1500 kcal/day is contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes fetal growth restriction, ketonuria (potentially teratogenic), and nutrient deficiency at a critical period for fetal development. Unlike non-pregnant hypertension or obesity management, significant caloric deficit is inappropriate during pregnancy. The fetus's developmental needs take priority, and moderate healthy dietary adjustments are the appropriate approach.
questions.question: Severe caloric restriction during pregnancy is specifically contraindicated even in obese women PRIMARILY because:

questions.explanation: In antepartum haemorrhage, a Kleihauer test should be performed to estimate the volume of feto-maternal haemorrhage so that an adequate, individualised dose of anti-D can be calculated rather than assuming a fixed dose is sufficient. Placental origin of bleeding does not exclude fetal red cells entering the maternal circulation. Waiting for bleeding to completely resolve would unnecessarily delay time-sensitive prophylaxis.
options: Perform a Kleihauer test to guide the anti-D dose required
Assume the standard dose is always sufficient without testing
Give a fixed low dose regardless of haemorrhage volume
Delay anti-D until the bleeding has completely stopped
Withhold anti-D since bleeding is of placental origin
questions.question: A Rh-negative woman has an antepartum haemorrhage at 34 weeks from a suspected placental cause. What is the MOST appropriate approach to anti-D dosing in this situation?

questions.explanation: Caesarean hysterectomy is indicated when uterine rupture results in gross structural damage beyond repair, or when severe sepsis involves the uterus making preservation unsafe. Carcinoma of the cervix discovered at the time of caesarean section is another specific indication. It is a life-saving procedure in these extreme circumstances.
questions.question: Caesarean hysterectomy is indicated in which obstetric scenario?
options: Uterine rupture with gross damage or severe infection

questions.explanation: Eclamptic seizures are managed by protecting the airway and ensuring maternal safety, followed by administration of magnesium sulphate as the first-line anticonvulsant to control and prevent further seizures. Delivery is important but should follow initial maternal stabilisation rather than preceding seizure control. Diazepam is generally reserved for cases where magnesium sulphate is ineffective or contraindicated.
options: Await spontaneous seizure resolution without intervention
Immediate high-dose diazepam as first-line for all cases
Immediate caesarean section before seizure control
Protect airway, ensure safety, and administer magnesium sulphate
questions.question: A woman in active labour develops sudden tonic-clonic seizure activity with no prior history of epilepsy, in the setting of known pre-eclampsia. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

questions.explanation: A titre crossing into a level historically associated with significant risk of severe fetal disease should prompt prompt escalation to specialist fetal medicine assessment, including consideration of Doppler surveillance or invasive testing. Continuing routine visits, waiting for the next scheduled test, or discharging to lower-intensity care would all delay necessary specialist input. While titres can fluctuate, a rise of this magnitude cannot be safely dismissed as routine.
questions.question: A Rhesus-sensitised woman is being monitored and her antibody titre rises abruptly from 1:16 to a critical level associated with severe disease in a prior classification system. What is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Wait for the next scheduled titre before acting further
Discharge to midwifery-led care given her overall wellbeing
Escalate to specialist fetal medicine assessment promptly
Reassure the patient that titres commonly fluctuate harmlessly
Continue routine community antenatal visits unchanged

questions.explanation: The immediate priority following an eclamptic fit is airway protection, positioning in the left lateral position, and administration of magnesium sulphate to prevent recurrent seizures. Diazepam is reserved for fits that fail to respond to magnesium and causes greater sedation. Delivery and imaging are important but follow maternal stabilisation, not precede it.
questions.question: A 24-year-old primigravida develops eclamptic convulsions at home before hospital arrival. On arrival she is drowsy but breathing. What is the MOST appropriate PRIORITY action?
options: Secure the airway and give intravenous diazepam alone
Perform an immediate caesarean section before stabilisation
Obtain a CT brain scan before any drug treatment
Give oral antihypertensive tablets before airway care
Secure the airway and give magnesium sulphate

questions.question: The standard modern technique of caesarean section uses which uterine incision?
questions.explanation: The standard modern caesarean section (lower segment caesarean section, LSCS) uses a transverse incision in the lower uterine segment. This site is preferred because the lower segment is thinner, less vascular, and covered by peritoneum that can be reflected, providing better haemostasis and a more secure, less vascular scar that rarely ruptures in subsequent pregnancies.
options: J-shaped incision extending from lower to upper segment

questions.explanation: In occipito-posterior position, the presenting diameter is the suboccipito-frontal diameter measuring 10–11.5 cm. This is larger than the suboccipito-bregmatic diameter (9–9.5 cm) presented in the ideal occipito-anterior position. The larger diameter explains the prolonged labour and increased difficulty of delivery in persistent OP position.

questions.explanation: Placenta accreta carries a very high risk of massive obstetric haemorrhage, so planned delivery at a specialist centre with access to interventional radiology, cross-matched blood products, and a multidisciplinary surgical team is essential for safe management. Vaginal delivery, midwifery-led unit birth, or home birth are entirely inappropriate given the extreme haemorrhage risk. Failing to prepare blood products in advance would leave the team unable to respond promptly to catastrophic bleeding.
questions.question: A woman at 34 weeks with placenta accreta identified on antenatal imaging is being counselled about delivery planning. Which multidisciplinary consideration is MOST important?
options: Planned delivery at a specialist centre with blood support
Home birth is an appropriate option in this diagnosis
No blood product preparation is required in advance
Vaginal delivery at a local midwifery-led unit
Delivery can be managed without any special preparation

questions.question: A woman attending for preconception counselling asks about the ideal interval to wait after stopping long-acting reversible contraception before trying to conceive. Which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.explanation: With most long-acting reversible contraceptive methods, fertility generally returns promptly after discontinuation, and women can attempt to conceive as soon as they wish without needing to wait for an arbitrary fixed period or a specific number of normal menstrual cycles. Stating that a fixed twelve-month wait is required, or that fertility never returns, would be inaccurate and could cause unnecessary anxiety or delay in family planning. The specific method used is, in fact, relevant to this counselling, since return of fertility can vary slightly between different long-acting options.
options: She must wait for three normal periods first
She must wait twelve months regardless of method
Fertility never returns after using long-acting methods
The method type has no bearing on this
Fertility generally returns quickly; conception can begin anytime

questions.question: A woman undergoing induction of labour with oxytocin infusion develops uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate abnormality. What is the most appropriate immediate action besides stopping the oxytocin?
options: Consider tocolysis to relax the uterus
questions.explanation: Alongside stopping the oxytocin infusion, tocolysis with an agent such as terbutaline may be used to relax the hyperstimulated uterus and improve placental perfusion while assessing fetal condition. This combined approach addresses both the cause and the physiological consequence of hyperstimulation. Continued monitoring determines whether further intervention, including expedited delivery, becomes necessary.

questions.question: A multigravida with known chronic hypertension presents at booking with BP 145/92 mmHg. Urinalysis shows 2+ proteinuria. The NEXT important investigation is:
questions.explanation: A 2+ proteinuria on dipstick in a hypertensive woman at booking must be quantified with a 24-hour urine collection to differentiate pre-existing renal disease from early superimposed pre-eclampsia. Quantitative proteinuria >300 mg/24 hours in a woman with chronic hypertension before 20 weeks suggests chronic renal disease rather than pre-eclampsia, which develops after 20 weeks.

options: Give large empirical bolus, no calculation
Correct entire deficit as rapidly as possible
Avoid bicarbonate correction regardless of severity
Base correction on urine pH alone
Calculated bicarbonate deficit with gradual correction
questions.question: A woman with acute renal failure in pregnancy requires correction of metabolic acidosis. Which approach is MOST appropriate when calculating bicarbonate replacement?
questions.explanation: Correction of metabolic acidosis in acute renal failure uses a calculated bicarbonate deficit based on body weight, administered cautiously and gradually to avoid complications such as overshoot alkalosis or precipitating hypocalcaemia-related symptoms. An uncalculated large bolus or overly rapid full correction risks these complications. Completely avoiding correction in significant acidosis would leave dangerous acid-base derangement untreated, and urine pH is not an appropriate substitute for blood gas-guided calculation.

questions.question: Which type of abnormal lie is associated with multiple pregnancy, particularly involving the second twin?
questions.explanation: Transverse lie is specifically associated with multiple pregnancy, particularly involving the second twin after the first has been delivered. Once the first twin is delivered, the now-empty uterus and the remaining twin's ability to move freely can result in adoption of a transverse lie. Internal podalic version and breech extraction are the management options for this scenario. Multiple Pregnancy and Delivery (Questions 109–144)

In a woman with confirmed transverse lie at term without labour, external cephalic version may be attempted to correct the lie, with elective caesarean section planned if version is unsuccessful or contraindicated, since vaginal delivery is not safely possible in a persistent transverse lie. Awaiting spontaneous labour without a plan risks the serious complications of cord prolapse or obstructed labour if labour begins with the fetus still transverse. Proactive planning avoids emergency presentation of this high-risk situation.
questions.question: A woman with confirmed transverse lie at term with intact membranes and no immediate labour is being managed. What is the most appropriate general approach?
options: Attempt version or plan elective caesarean

questions.question: A woman is 10 days post-caesarean section and presents with continuous, painless watery vaginal discharge. What complication should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Continuous painless watery vaginal discharge following caesarean section, particularly after unrecognised bladder injury, raises suspicion of vesicovaginal fistula, an abnormal connection between the bladder and vagina allowing continuous urine leakage. Confirmatory investigations and specialist surgical repair are typically required. Early recognition and appropriate referral improve the chances of successful surgical correction.

questions.question: A bicornuate uterus is listed as a maternal cause of recurrent breech presentation. Which mechanism explains this association?
questions.explanation: A bicornuate or septate uterus has an abnormal cavity shape that structurally constrains the fetus in a breech position, preventing spontaneous cephalic version. The uterine septum or division creates a small horn that the fetal head fits into, leaving the breech in the lower segment. This explains why uterine anomalies are associated with recurrent breech presentations.

options: Her blood group and Rhesus status
The date of her last menstrual period
The degree of pulmonary hypertension and functional status
Her preferred mode of infant feeding
questions.question: A woman with an atrial septal defect and mild pulmonary hypertension plans pregnancy. Which factor MOST influences her overall risk classification?
questions.explanation: The severity of pulmonary hypertension together with maternal functional status are key determinants of cardiovascular risk in pregnancy for women with congenital heart disease such as atrial septal defect, guiding risk stratification and counselling. Blood group and Rhesus status are relevant to other aspects of antenatal care but do not determine cardiac risk. Last menstrual period, feeding preference, and educational background are not clinical determinants of cardiac risk in this context.

questions.question: CT pelvimetry uses approximately how much less radiation compared to conventional X-ray pelvimetry?
questions.explanation: CT pelvimetry uses approximately 4 times less radiation than conventional X-ray pelvimetry while providing more detailed pelvic measurements. It also detects small masses more easily and can assess pelvic shape accurately. Its disadvantages include higher cost and limited availability.

IUCDs are not the best choice for sickle cell disease patients because of their increased susceptibility to pelvic infections (due to functional asplenia and immune compromise) and the abnormal uterine bleeding that may worsen chronic anaemia. Norplant (levonorgestrel implant) is preferred for its membrane-stabilising effect on red blood cells in addition to effective contraception.
questions.question: Which of the following is a CONTRAINDICATION to the use of an IUCD in women with sickle cell disease?
The 'lifetime risk of maternal death' measure takes into account both probability of becoming pregnant AND probability of dying. It can be calculated as:
questions.explanation: Lifetime risk of maternal death is calculated as: MMR rate × 35 years (reproductive years), OR Total fertility rate × MMR ratio. It captures the cumulative mortality risk across a woman's reproductive life. In Nigeria with high fertility (TFR ~5–6) and high MMR, the lifetime risk of maternal death is among the highest globally, approximately 1 in 13 in some regions.
options: MMR × number of deliveries per year

questions.question: A grand multipara who breastfed her previous child for 2 years before conceiving again presents at booking with a low haemoglobin. This history MOST directly illustrates which mechanism of her anaemia?
questions.explanation: Prolonged lactation without an adequate interpregnancy interval depletes maternal iron stores that were not replenished before the next conception, compounding the iron demands of the new pregnancy and predisposing to iron deficiency anaemia. This mechanism is specifically linked to grand multiparity with short birth intervals and prolonged breastfeeding. Haemolysis, malaria, and B12 malabsorption are separate causes not directly implicated by this history.

questions.question: Normal haemostasis at the placental site after delivery depends on which primary mechanism?
options: Uterine muscle contraction occluding blood vessels and intravascular thrombosis
questions.explanation: Normal haemostasis at the placental site depends on two complementary mechanisms: physical contraction of the interlacing uterine muscle fibres (the 'living ligature') which mechanically occludes the spiral arteries supplying the placental bed, and concurrent intravascular thrombosis. Failure of either mechanism results in torrential haemorrhage. This is why oxytocics and manual methods to improve uterine contraction are the first-line treatment for PPH.

Antenatal corticosteroids, such as betamethasone or dexamethasone, given to mothers anticipated to deliver preterm between 24 and 34 weeks, accelerate fetal lung maturity by stimulating surfactant production in type II pneumocytes, significantly reducing the risk and severity of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. This effect is maximal when delivery occurs within 24 hours to 7 days after completing the course. Corticosteroids do not have a primary tocolytic, antihypertensive, or antiarrhythmic action in this context.
questions.question: A woman in preterm labour at 30 weeks is given a course of antenatal corticosteroids. This treatment is administered PRIMARILY to achieve which effect?

questions.explanation: The active phase of labour begins at 3-4 cm cervical dilatation with regular painful contractions. Cervical dilation of 3 cm with regular contractions 4 minutes apart represents transition into the active phase. The latent phase ends when dilatation exceeds 3-4 cm.
questions.question: A primigravida at 40 weeks presents with painful contractions every 4 minutes lasting 45 seconds with 3 cm cervical dilatation. Which phase of labour is she in?
Which monitoring interval is recommended for dichorionic twin pregnancies from 28 weeks onwards?
questions.explanation: Dichorionic twin pregnancies require weekly antenatal visits from 28 weeks to closely monitor for growth discordance, preterm labour, and maternal complications. Monochorionic twins require even more intensive fortnightly ultrasound scanning from earlier gestational ages. This intensive monitoring aims to identify complications early enough to intervene.

questions.question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Antibodies in this condition cause anaemia by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: In autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, autoantibodies bind to red cell surface antigens, marking the antibody-coated cells for premature destruction by the reticuloendothelial system, primarily in the spleen, or occasionally through direct complement-mediated intravascular lysis. This antibody-mediated mechanism differs fundamentally from anaemia due to impaired production, mechanical fragmentation, or nutritional deficiency. Diagnosis is confirmed by a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.

Clostridium welchii (perfringens) is the most common organism associated with septic abortion complicated by acute renal failure. It releases a potent haemolysin (phospholipase C) causing massive intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobinuria, and tubular necrosis. This combination of haemorrhage, sepsis, and direct nephrotoxicity from haemoglobin is particularly lethal.
questions.question: The MOST common organism responsible for septic abortion leading to acute renal failure is:

A 15-year-old primigravida who concealed her pregnancy presents in obstructed labour after prolonged impaction of the fetal head in the pelvis. Which delayed complication is she MOST at risk of developing days later?
questions.explanation: Prolonged obstructed labour causes pressure necrosis of the anterior vaginal wall and bladder base against the maternal pelvis, leading to vesico-vaginal fistula formation typically noted days after delivery as continuous urinary leakage. This is a classic delayed complication of neglected obstructed labour, particularly in young women with cephalopelvic disproportion. Uterine rupture and cord prolapse are acute intrapartum events rather than delayed sequelae.

questions.question: A woman with mitral valve prolapse and mild regurgitation is pregnant and asymptomatic. Which statement about her pregnancy risk is MOST accurate?
questions.explanation: Mild mitral valve prolapse with trivial or mild regurgitation is generally well tolerated in pregnancy and can be managed with routine antenatal monitoring rather than being treated as high risk. It does not carry the same risk profile as severe mitral stenosis, which causes significant fixed obstruction. Pregnancy is not absolutely contraindicated, and caesarean section is not mandated purely on the basis of this generally low-risk valvular finding, though some baseline cardiology input remains reasonable.
options: This lesion carries the same risk as severe mitral stenosis
Caesarean section is mandatory regardless of obstetric factors
Pregnancy is absolutely contraindicated with this diagnosis
No antenatal cardiac input is ever required for this lesion
This lesion is generally well tolerated in pregnancy with routine monitoring

questions.question: Which of the following is the MOST important complication unique to multiple gestation in the third stage of labour?
questions.explanation: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony is significantly more common after multiple gestation due to uterine over-distension. An overdistended uterus fails to contract effectively after delivery, impairing the physiological haemostatic mechanisms at the placental site. Active management of the third stage and uterotonic agents are essential.
options: Placental abruption of the second placenta
Cord prolapse during placental delivery Correct
Postpartum haemorrhage due to uterine atony

questions.question: The diuretic with the MAXIMUM dose of 500 mg used in the FIRST 48 hours of oliguria in ARF is:
questions.explanation: Furosemide may be used in the first 48 hours of oliguria in ARF at doses up to 500 mg, alongside mannitol (maximum 12.5 g), in an attempt to convert oliguric to non-oliguric ARF. However, these diuretics are not indicated if there is no response to volume challenge, as they may worsen tubular injury in established ATN. Dialysis should not be delayed awaiting diuretic response.

Failed induction of labour describes the situation where an adequate trial of induction, including cervical ripening, amniotomy and oxytocin to maximal appropriate dose, does not result in effective labour or sufficient cervical change, typically requiring reassessment and often leading to caesarean section. This differs from obstructed labour, which involves mechanical obstruction to descent of an engaged presenting part. Recognising failed induction promptly avoids prolonged, potentially harmful attempts at vaginal delivery.
questions.question: A woman undergoing induction of labour fails to achieve adequate cervical change or effective labour despite maximal oxytocin dose and amniotomy over an appropriate trial period. What is this outcome termed?
Which of the following correctly identifies the sacral hiatus used for caudal block?
questions.explanation: The sacral hiatus lies caudal to the 4th sacral tubercle between the two sacral cornua and represents the inferior opening of the sacral canal. It is the entry point for caudal anaesthesia. Obesity can make the sacral cornua difficult to palpate, which is the main contraindication to this technique.
options: Lies cranial to the 2nd sacral tubercle
Lies caudal to the 4th sacral tubercle between the two sacral cornua
Found at the iliac crest level
Placenta praevia, uterine atony, and PPH
Preterm labour and fetal growth restriction
questions.explanation: As a grand multipara, placenta praevia (due to multiple placental implantation sites), uterine atony (due to the over-stretched, poorly contracting myometrium), and postpartum haemorrhage (consequent on atony or abnormal placentation) are the specific risks. These directly result from the repeated stretching and scarring of the uterus and endometrium through multiple pregnancies requiring active third-stage management.
questions.question: A multigravida with her 6th pregnancy faces which COMBINATION of obstetric risks MOST specifically associated with grand multiparity?

options: To perform routine ultrasound scans at each visit
To prescribe iron and folate supplementation
To diagnose gestational diabetes in all women
To schedule the date of delivery
To ensure well-being of both mother and child
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the PRIMARY aim of antenatal care as a clinical service?
questions.explanation: The primary aim of antenatal care is to ensure the well-being of both mother and child throughout the pregnancy. This broad aim encompasses screening, prevention, early management of complications, and preparation for childbirth. All specific activities performed during antenatal care, from supplementation to ultrasound, are tools in service of this overarching goal.

Cord blood from an HbAA or HbAS sibling provides haemopoietic stem cells that can be transplanted to the affected child and reconstitute the entire haemopoietic system with normal haemoglobin-producing cells. The HLA match chance between siblings is 25%. The main risks are graft-versus-host disease and graft failure. Banking cord blood from subsequent unaffected siblings is possible.
options: Normal red cells that replace all sickled cells permanently
Haemopoietic stem cells capable of producing normal haemoglobin
Growth factors to enhance HbF production
questions.question: Cord blood transplantation from an HbAA or HbAS sibling can cure sickle cell disease by providing:

options: Reduce uterine blood flow, preserve fertility
questions.explanation: Uterine artery ligation aims to reduce blood flow to the uterus, thereby helping control postpartum haemorrhage, while preserving the uterus and future fertility potential, making it a valuable intermediate step before considering hysterectomy. It does not replace the need for uterotonic drugs, which continue to have an important role. This technique requires surgical expertise and is typically performed when conservative measures have failed.
questions.question: A woman undergoing surgical management of postpartum haemorrhage has uterine artery ligation performed as an intermediate step. What is the primary goal of this procedure?

questions.explanation: Intraoperative uterine atony causing bleeding from the incision edges is initially managed with uterine massage combined with prompt uterotonic administration to promote contraction and control bleeding before considering more invasive measures. Proceeding to hysterectomy without first attempting these standard measures would be premature in most cases. Escalation to compression sutures or other techniques follows if initial measures fail to control bleeding.
options: Immediate hysterectomy without trying conservative measures first
Close the uterus rapidly without addressing bleeding
Pack the abdomen and delay closure indefinitely
Uterine massage combined with uterotonic administration
Ignore the bleeding as it will resolve spontaneously
questions.question: A woman is undergoing caesarean section and immediately after delivery of the baby develops profuse bleeding from the uterine incision edges due to atony. What is the most appropriate immediate intraoperative management?

options: Activating collagenase and decreasing collagen concentration
Increasing collagen cross-links in cervical stroma
Reducing water content of cervical ground substance
Stimulating cervical smooth muscle to contract
Inhibiting hyaluronic acid synthesis in the cervix Correct
questions.explanation: PGE2 softens the cervix by stimulating collagenase activity, which degrades collagen fibers and reduces collagen concentration in the cervical stroma. Simultaneously, hyaluronic acid increases the water content of ground substance, causing cervical softening and effacement. This process is called cervical ripening.
questions.question: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) promotes cervical ripening by which mechanism?
The contraceptive method PREFERRED in women with significant cardiac disease is:
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptives and condoms are preferred for contraception in cardiac patients. IUCDs are associated with vasovagal reactions during insertion (which can precipitate arrhythmia) and risk of bacterial endocarditis. For completed family size, interval sterilisation (rather than at CS) is safer. Adequate birth spacing reduces the stress of repeated pregnancies on the heart. SUBTOPIC 4: DIABETES MELLITUS IN PREGNANCY
options: No contraception as it is irrelevant

questions.question: The 'uterorenal reflex' associated with severe concealed abruption can lead to which serious maternal complication?
questions.explanation: The uterorenal reflex in severe concealed abruption causes spasm of renal arterioles. If sufficiently widespread and prolonged, this leads to bilateral cortical necrosis, resulting in anuria and acute renal failure. This is a distinct mechanism from the ATN caused by hypovolaemia. Urinary output must be monitored closely (target >30 ml/hour).

The Bishop score evaluates five cervical and fetal parameters: dilatation, effacement (or length), consistency, position, and fetal station. Liquor volume is NOT a component of the Bishop score. A score of =8 indicates a favourable cervix likely to respond well to induction of labour.
questions.question: The Bishop score assesses cervical favourability for induction by assigning points to all of the following EXCEPT:
A non-reactive non-stress test (NST) in a 36-week pregnancy mandates which IMMEDIATE further investigation?
options: Biophysical profile or contraction stress test
questions.explanation: A non-reactive NST mandates immediate further evaluation with a biophysical profile or contraction stress test. The BPP provides additional information about fetal well-being through multiple parameters, and a reassuring score prevents unnecessary intervention. Immediate caesarean section without further evaluation would cause overtreatment of many fetuses who simply have a quiet sleep cycle, which also produces a non-reactive NST.

questions.question: A paracervical block provides rapid pain relief in labour but its major fetal complication is:
questions.explanation: Paracervical block causes profound fetal bradycardia due to rapid absorption of the local anaesthetic (bupivacaine 0.25%) into the uterine arteries and venous plexus close to the injection site. The local anaesthetic causes direct fetal cardiac depression and uterine artery vasoconstriction. This complication limits the use of paracervical block in modern obstetric practice.

Chronic intrauterine hypoxia in growth-restricted fetuses stimulates increased fetal erythropoietin production, leading to polycythaemia as a compensatory response to improve oxygen-carrying capacity. Maternal iron overload, excess glucose transfer, and maternal vitamin B12 excess do not directly cause this compensatory fetal response, and a primary bone marrow malignancy is an entirely different and much rarer explanation unrelated to the described clinical context of growth restriction.
questions.question: A preterm infant born at 28 weeks with growth restriction is noted to have polycythaemia at birth. Which intrauterine process MOST likely explains this finding?
options: A primary fetal bone marrow malignancy
Maternal vitamin B12 excess in pregnancy
Maternal iron overload transferred to the fetus
Excess maternal glucose crossing the placenta
Chronic fetal hypoxia stimulating increased erythropoietin production

questions.explanation: HbA1c in the first trimester provides the most useful assessment of long-term glycaemic control, reflecting average blood glucose over the preceding 2–3 months. A first-trimester HbA1c of 8% is highly suggestive of pre-existing type 2 diabetes. HbA1c >10% indicates significant risk of congenital malformation and is used monthly to monitor pregnancy management.
questions.question: Which investigation in the first trimester of a diabetic pregnancy provides the MOST useful assessment of long-term glycaemic control?

questions.explanation: Adequate iron supplementation during one pregnancy helps preserve maternal iron stores that would otherwise be further depleted by pregnancy, blood loss at delivery, and lactation, providing a reserve that benefits any subsequent pregnancy, particularly if the interpregnancy interval is short. This is especially relevant in settings where short birth intervals and prolonged breastfeeding are common, both of which further deplete iron stores. It is not primarily aimed at preventing infection, osteoporosis, or pre-eclampsia.
questions.question: A woman who received adequate iron supplementation throughout her current pregnancy asks why this benefit matters beyond the current pregnancy. The PRIMARY additional benefit of preserved iron stores at delivery is to:
Which of the following is a SOCIO-CULTURAL factor contributing to unsafe motherhood in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Son preference leading to repeated pregnancies until a son is born is a socio-cultural factor contributing to grand multiparity, a significant obstetric risk factor for haemorrhage, uterine rupture, and other life-threatening conditions. Other socio-cultural factors include low female education, gender inequity, early marriage, and belief systems preferring traditional birth attendants over skilled providers.
options: Son preference leading to high-parity pregnancies
Absence of magnesium sulphate at primary health centres
Lack of caesarean section capacity at secondary hospitals

questions.question: Outlet forceps delivery in face presentation mento-anterior position requires which condition of the presenting part?
questions.explanation: Outlet forceps delivery in face mento-anterior position requires the chin (mentum) to be pointing anteriorly with the head crowning on the perineum, exactly analogous to an occiput-anterior position for standard forceps. The mento-anterior orientation allows the head to flex under the pubic arch during delivery. Mento-posterior at the outlet mandates caesarean section.
options: Chin pointing anteriorly with head on the perineum
Brow at the level of the ischial spines

questions.question: Intrapartum care encompasses care during which specific period of the maternity care continuum?
questions.explanation: Intrapartum care refers specifically to the care provided to the woman during labour and delivery. It is the third component of the maternity care continuum, following pre-conceptional and antenatal care. Quality intrapartum care, including skilled birth attendance, is central to preventing the majority of maternal and perinatal deaths that occur around the time of delivery.

options: Persistently normal urine output throughout the illness
Isolated proteinuria with normal renal imaging
Anuria alternating with polyuria and hydronephrosis on ultrasound
Chronic hypertension with stable renal function
Gradual onset oliguria with normal renal ultrasound
questions.explanation: Alternating anuria and polyuria together with hydronephrosis demonstrated on ultrasound is a classic pattern suggesting obstructive uropathy as the cause of acute renal failure, reflecting intermittent complete and partial obstruction. Gradual oliguria with a normal ultrasound, isolated proteinuria, persistently normal output, or stable chronic hypertension do not fit this specific obstructive pattern. Prompt recognition allows for relief of obstruction, which can rapidly improve renal function.
questions.question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with obstructive uropathy as a cause of her acute renal failure. Which clinical scenario would MOST strongly suggest this diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Human placental lactogen (HPL) is the most important diabetogenic hormone in pregnancy, causing progressive insulin resistance particularly marked in the third trimester. Other antagonistic hormones include oestrogen, progesterone, cortisol, growth hormone, and prolactin. The increasing insulin resistance of pregnancy demands compensatory pancreatic insulin secretion.
questions.question: Which placental hormone is the most important diabetogenic hormone responsible for insulin resistance in pregnancy?
A woman at 34 weeks presents with painless bright red vaginal bleeding and a soft, non-tender uterus. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Painless bright red bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus is classically associated with placenta praevia, where the abnormally sited placenta bleeds without associated uterine irritability. Placental abruption typically presents with pain and a tender, sometimes woody-hard uterus. Uterine rupture is usually associated with severe pain and maternal shock, while vasa praevia bleeding is typically of fetal origin and associated with fetal compromise rather than isolated painless maternal bleeding alone.

A fetal scalp pH of 7.18 falls into a borderline range, generally prompting either a repeat sample within a short interval or consideration of expedited delivery depending on the overall clinical picture and trend of results, rather than being clearly normal or immediately requiring delivery on its own. Scalp pH sampling supplements CTG interpretation to guide decision-making in cases of concerning fetal heart rate patterns. Trends over serial samples are often more informative than a single isolated value.
options: Borderline, repeat sample or expedite delivery
questions.question: A woman undergoing labour has a fetal scalp pH sample taken due to a pathological cardiotocograph, returning a result of 7.18. How should this result be interpreted and acted upon?

questions.explanation: Perinatal loss causes profound grief that may include PTSD, major depression, anxiety, and complicated grief. In subsequent pregnancies, women have heightened anxiety, intrusive thoughts, and reduced enjoyment of pregnancy. Bereavement support, psychological counselling, and sensitive multidisciplinary care are essential. Offering parents the opportunity to see and hold the baby (if they wish) aids healthy grieving.
options: Absence of grief due to lack of attachment
Grief, PTSD, and depression risk in next pregnancy
Increased fertility due to hormonal changes
questions.question: The psychosocial impact of a perinatal loss (stillbirth or neonatal death) on a mother most commonly manifests as:

questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid) is most specifically associated with fetal conditions that impair swallowing or absorption of amniotic fluid, such as oesophageal atresia, duodenal atresia, or fetal neuromuscular disorders that reduce swallowing. Conversely, oligohydramnios results from reduced fetal urination (renal anomalies, IUGR). Recognising this distinction guides targeted investigation when abnormal fluid volumes are detected.
questions.question: Polyhydramnios detected on a late second-trimester ultrasound scan is MOST specifically associated with which fetal condition?

questions.explanation: Reduced fetal movements in a growth-restricted fetus, even with previously normal Doppler findings, warrant prompt cardiotocography and further biophysical assessment to reassess current fetal wellbeing, since fetal status can change over time. Reassurance without assessment could miss evolving compromise, while immediate delivery without any assessment would be premature. Repeating only the growth scan after a delay, or simply advising rest without formal assessment, would not adequately address this potentially significant symptom in a high-risk pregnancy.
questions.question: A woman with a growth-restricted fetus at 33 weeks has normal umbilical artery Doppler but reduced fetal movements reported by the mother. What is the MOST appropriate INITIAL step?
options: Perform cardiotocography and further biophysical assessment promptly
Advise delivery immediately without any assessment
Advise increased maternal rest as the sole action
Repeat only the growth scan in two weeks

questions.question: A woman with sickle cell disease presents in early labour and her partner's haemoglobin genotype is unknown. Which action is MOST appropriate regarding neonatal care planning?
questions.explanation: When paternal genotype is unknown, neonatal haemoglobin electrophoresis after birth is the appropriate way to determine the infant's status rather than assuming an outcome. Assuming the baby is definitely affected or unaffected without testing could lead to inappropriate reassurance or unnecessary anxiety. Early testing, not delay until school age, allows timely initiation of prophylactic measures if the child is affected.
options: Decline any neonatal testing since the mother is affected
Assume the baby is definitely unaffected without testing
Arrange neonatal haemoglobin electrophoresis after birth
Assume the baby will definitely have sickle cell disease
Delay testing until the child reaches school age

questions.question: Female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) during pregnancy is associated with which obstetric complication at delivery?
questions.explanation: FGM/C (particularly infibulation — Type III) is associated with obstructed labour, prolonged second stage, severe perineal lacerations, PPH, and perineal infections at delivery. WHO defines FGM as a human rights violation and a public health issue. Defibulation before or during labour is required for women with Type III FGM. Nigeria has a significant burden of FGM, particularly in some ethnic groups.

Macrosomia with increasing birth order combined with lax abdominal walls that allow malpresentation creates unsuspected fetopelvic disproportion leading to obstructed labour. The high parity creates a false sense of security, and the danger is compounded by malpresentation. Obstructed labour may then result in uterine rupture and maternal or fetal death.
questions.question: Which intrapartum complication arises SPECIFICALLY because of the combination of macrosomia and a lax uterus in a grandmultipara?

questions.explanation: Standard antenatal protocol shifts from monthly to fortnightly (every 2-weekly) visits from 28 weeks even in previously complicated pregnancies, unless additional risk mandates more frequent surveillance. Weekly visits are then reserved from 36 weeks onward. This schedule reflects the rising likelihood of late-pregnancy complications such as pre-eclampsia requiring closer monitoring.
questions.question: A woman with a history of pre-eclampsia in her last pregnancy books at 14 weeks in her current pregnancy. From 28 weeks, her antenatal visit frequency should change from monthly to:

A skilled birth attendant working at a primary health centre encounters a case of severe pre-eclampsia with a diastolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg. A loading dose of magnesium sulphate has been given. Her NEXT most appropriate action is to:
questions.explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia is beyond the scope of primary-level management once magnesium sulphate has been loaded; the priority is urgent referral to a facility capable of definitive care, including possible delivery and further seizure prophylaxis. Continued management, discharge, or delayed referral at this level risks eclampsia, stroke, or maternal death. Repeating the loading dose is unnecessary and risks magnesium toxicity.

questions.question: A woman presents in the third trimester with severe anaemia (Hb 4.5 g/dl) and early signs of cardiac decompensation. Which immediate management step takes PRIORITY over correction of the underlying cause of anaemia?
questions.explanation: In severe anaemia with impending or established cardiac failure, cautious blood transfusion, given slowly and covered with a diuretic to prevent fluid overload, takes priority over treating the underlying cause, since the immediate threat to life is cardiac decompensation from severe oxygen-carrying capacity deficit. Oral iron, folate, antimalarial, or antihelminthic therapy addresses the underlying cause but acts too slowly to correct an acute life-threatening situation. Packed red cells are preferred over whole blood to minimise the volume load in this scenario.

questions.question: A pregnancy with suspected severe fetal anaemia due to Rh isoimmunisation requires direct assessment and possible in-utero transfusion. The procedure MOST specifically indicated is:
questions.explanation: Cordocentesis, or fetal blood sampling from the umbilical cord under ultrasound guidance, allows direct assessment of fetal haemoglobin and haematocrit in suspected severe fetal anaemia from Rh isoimmunisation, and permits simultaneous intrauterine blood transfusion if needed. Amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling obtain amniotic fluid or placental tissue rather than fetal blood and cannot directly measure fetal haemoglobin. Non-invasive surveillance methods cannot provide this direct haematological information.

Bilateral renal cortical necrosis is believed to result from the coagulation changes characteristic of pregnancy (DIC tendency), causing fibrin thrombi in the glomerular capillaries with widespread necrosis of glomeruli. Renal arteriography shows a non-homogeneous or absent cortical nephrogram. Complete recovery of renal function is unusual after BRCN, distinguishing it from ATN.
questions.question: Bilateral renal cortical necrosis (BRCN) in obstetrics is thought to result from:
Vitamin C supplementation during pregnancy improves iron absorption by which specific mechanism?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) enhances non-haem iron absorption by reducing ferric iron (Fe3+) to the more absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) form in the intestinal lumen. It also forms a soluble iron-ascorbate complex that remains absorbable in the alkaline environment of the duodenum. Consuming iron-rich foods or iron supplements together with vitamin C-rich foods or supplements therefore significantly improves iron absorption efficiency.
options: Enhancing bone marrow response to iron
Immediate delivery by the most expeditious route
Change in maternal position and review in 1 hour
questions.explanation: A fetal scalp blood pH of 7.20 or below is defined as pathological acidosis and mandates immediate delivery by the most expeditious route available, typically emergency caesarean section or assisted vaginal delivery. A pH of 7.21-7.25 is borderline, warranting repeat sampling in 30 minutes. The 7.20 threshold represents significant metabolic acidosis indicating failure of compensatory mechanisms and imminent risk of severe hypoxic injury.
questions.question: A fetal scalp blood pH of 7.20 during labour mandates which immediate clinical action?

A woman undergoing caesarean section for placenta praevia is found to have placenta accreta with the previous caesarean scar site involved. What is the most likely definitive management if bleeding cannot be controlled by conservative measures?
questions.explanation: When placenta accreta causes uncontrollable haemorrhage that fails to respond to conservative measures such as uterotonics, balloon tamponade or compression sutures, peripartum hysterectomy becomes the definitive life-saving management. This is a recognised risk in women with placenta praevia overlying a previous caesarean scar. Multidisciplinary planning with senior obstetric, anaesthetic and blood bank involvement improves outcomes in anticipated cases.

Normal adult haemoglobin A (HbA) consists of two alpha (α) and two beta (β) globin chains (α2β2). HbA2 consists of α2δ2, and HbF (fetal) consists of α2γ2. Each globin chain is associated with a haem group containing iron, which binds oxygen. Disorders of these chains constitute the haemoglobinopathies.
options: Two alpha and two beta chains
Two alpha and two gamma chains
Two alpha and two delta chains
Two beta and two gamma chains
questions.question: Normal adult haemoglobin A consists of which globin chain combination?
A pregnant woman has a PCV of 31% at 28 weeks. According to local Nigerian obstetric practice, what is the MOST appropriate immediate management decision?
questions.explanation: A PCV of 31% at 28 weeks falls below the local Nigerian threshold of 30% PCV / Hb 10 g/dl that requires investigation. While this is not a crisis level, it represents mild anaemia that warrants investigation for the underlying cause (most commonly iron deficiency) and commencement of appropriate supplementation.
