questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Colles' fracture - a complete fracture of the radius bone of the forearm close to the wrist, resulting in upward (posterior) displacement of the radius and obvious deformity, classically termed a 'dinner fork' deformity.

(b)
Predisposing factors: a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH injury) is the most common cause; the usual victim is a middle-aged or elderly woman; the fracture is particularly common in patients with osteoporosis and most frequently seen in elderly women falling on the outstretched palm in a ground-level fall; the frequency in women increases sixfold between ages 35-39 and 60-64; in older male patients a Colles' fracture should prompt investigation for osteoporosis, as hip fracture risk is also elevated.

(c)
Pathogenesis and morphology: the extent of injury depends on the position of the wrist at impact and the amount of force from the trauma; bending and compressive forces from pressure on the volar aspect of the wrist result in dorsal displacement of the distal fragment and comminution; when the traumatic force hits an outstretched hand, force is transmitted dorsally through the wrist, fracturing the distal radius and displacing it dorsally, producing the classic 'dinner fork' deformity with associated pain, oedema, and limitation of range of motion. In older patients (fifty years and above), this is most frequently caused by low-energy trauma combined with osteoporosis, especially in postmenopausal women.

(d)
Clinical features: history of a fall on an outstretched hand, dorsal wrist pain, swelling of the wrist, increased angulation of the distal radius, inability to grasp objects; signs and symptoms include pain, numbness, tenderness, bruising and deformity of the wrist.
questions.question:
An elderly woman falls onto her outstretched hand and presents with dorsal wrist pain, swelling, and an obvious 'dinner fork' deformity of the wrist with painful limitation of movement.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the predisposing factors.
(c) Discuss the pathogenesis and morphology.
(d) Discuss the clinical features.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis and risk factors: medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) - tendinopathy of the medial common flexor tendon due to overload or overuse. It is highly prevalent in persons in the fourth through sixth decades of life, the peak working years, and equally affects men and women; the primary etiology is repetitive stress or overuse of the flexor-pronator musculature, associated with activities involving repetitive forearm pronation and wrist flexion; it has been related to golf, tennis, bowling, racquetball, football, archery and weightlifting, and to occupations such as carpentry, plumbing and meat cutting requiring repetitive forearm, wrist and hand motions; 75% of patients are symptomatic in their dominant arm.

(b)
Pathogenesis: the pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor digitorum superficialis (median nerve innervated) and flexor carpi ulnaris (ulnar nerve innervated) share a common origin at the medial epicondyle, forming the common flexor tendon; chronic repetitive concentric and eccentric contractile loading of the flexor-pronator group results in degenerative changes in the musculotendinous region of the medial epicondyle; a single traumatic event such as a direct blow or sudden extreme eccentric contraction may also cause it.

(c)
Complications: tenderness over the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis with local swelling and warmth; the range of motion may initially be full but can become limited over time, leading to a flexion contracture; it must be differentiated from ulnar neuritis (identified by a positive Tinel's sign) and ulnar collateral ligament instability (identified by the valgus stress test or milking test), which may coexist.

(d)
Investigations/management: radiographs are generally normal, although 20-25% of patients can have soft-tissue calcification near the epicondyle; electromyography is indicated for neurologic alterations, and MRI or dynamic ultrasonography may be useful in throwing athletes to evaluate the ulnar collateral ligament. Management is conservative in three phases: Phase 1 uses 'PRICEMM' (Prevention/Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Modalities and Medication) with NSAIDs and possible corticosteroid injection; Phase 2 introduces guided rehabilitation with range of motion, stretching and progressive isometric then resistive exercises; Phase 3 addresses correction of technique and equipment before return to sport. Justification: conservative (non-surgical) management is justified as the mainstay of treatment, since surgery is seldom necessary and is only recommended after failure of a disciplined 3- to 6-month non-operative programme with exclusion of other pathologic causes of pain.
questions.question:
A patient in the fourth to sixth decade of life, whose occupation involves repetitive forearm pronation and wrist flexion, reports pain of insidious onset along the medial elbow, worsened by resistance to forearm pronation and wrist flexion, with tenderness over the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis.
(a) Name the likely condition and discuss the risk factors associated with it.
(b) Discuss the pathogenesis.
(c) Discuss the possible complications.
(d) Discuss the investigation and management options available, and justify one.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Marasmus - a form of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM).

(b)
Laboratory/clinical findings: weight falls to 60% of normal, growth retardation and loss of muscle, emaciated extremities, anaemia, and manifestations of multiple vitamin deficiencies.

(c)
Mechanism of tissue changes: the overall deficiency of both protein and total calories leads to loss of muscle mass and emaciation of the extremities, together with immune deficiency, particularly affecting T cell-mediated immunity.

(d)
Outcome: the child is left with impaired T cell-mediated immunity, predisposing to infection.

(e)
Long-term complications: PEM of this type is also seen in the developed world, often developing in chronically ill, older, bed-ridden patients, with signs including depletion of subcutaneous fat in the arms, chest wall, shoulders or metacarpal regions, wasting of the quadriceps and deltoid muscles, and ankle or sacral oedema (cachexia); PEM is also a common complication in patients with AIDS or advanced cancers, where mediators secreted by tumours and during chronic inflammatory reactions contribute to its development.
questions.question:
An infant's weight has fallen to about 60% of normal, with growth retardation, loss of muscle, and emaciated extremities. There is anaemia and manifestations of multiple vitamin deficiencies.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Describe the laboratory/clinical findings.
(c) Discuss the mechanism of the tissue changes seen.
(d) Discuss the outcome.
(e) Discuss the long-term complications.

Minutes after exposure to an allergen with systemic distribution, a previously sensitized patient develops widespread vasodilation and airway swelling.
(a) Name the likely condition and discuss the risk factors associated with it.
(b) Discuss the pathogenesis.
(c) Discuss the possible complications.
(d) Discuss the investigation and management principle, and justify it.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis and risk factors: systemic (Type I) anaphylaxis/anaphylactic shock. Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity requires prior sensitization (previous exposure to the allergen); atopy is the tendency to display Type I symptoms to certain environmental antigens even without prior sensitization, and is a risk factor for this reaction.

(b)
Pathogenesis: anaphylaxis is IgE-mediated, involving mast cells and basophils; symptoms occur within seconds of exposure to the allergen; when the allergen has systemic distribution, the reaction is systemic (anaphylactic shock), producing widespread vasodilation and airway swelling, in contrast to a local reaction, which produces histamine-induced vasodilation and increased permeability limited to sites such as the eyes, nose and airways (watery eyes, runny nose, itching, redness, or allergy-induced asthma).

(c)
Complications: widespread vasodilation and airway swelling are life-threatening because they compromise the airway and circulation.

(d)
Investigation/management principle: because the reaction is IgE-mediated with mast cell/basophil release of histamine causing vasodilation and increased permeability, management is directed at reversing these effects and protecting the airway. Justification: recognition of the systemic nature of the allergen exposure and the immediacy of the IgE-mediated reaction (occurring within seconds) justifies urgent intervention to address the widespread vasodilation and airway swelling before they progress.

(a)
Diagnosis: Vitamin D deficiency, manifesting in this child as rickets (occurring in children whose epiphyses have not already closed); in adults, the same deficiency causes osteomalacia.

(b)
Etiology and pathogenesis: the major function of vitamin D is maintenance of adequate plasma levels of calcium and phosphorus to support metabolic functions, bone mineralization, and neuromuscular transmission; deficiency of vitamin D therefore impairs bone mineralization and neuromuscular transmission.

(c)
Morphology: in children, vitamin D deficiency produces rickets, affecting bones whose epiphyses have not yet closed; in adults, it produces osteomalacia.

(d)
Complications: hypocalcaemic tetany can occur as a complication of vitamin D deficiency, reflecting the impaired neuromuscular transmission from inadequate plasma calcium; vitamin D toxicity (the opposite disorder) causes, in children, metastatic calcification of soft tissues such as the kidney, and in adults, bone pain and hypercalcaemia.
questions.question:
A child whose epiphyses have not yet closed presents with bone deformity, in the context of inadequate plasma levels of calcium and phosphorus needed for bone mineralization and neuromuscular transmission.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the etiology and pathogenesis of this condition.
(c) Describe the morphological changes that occur.
(d) Discuss the complications.

(a) Describe the process of acute inflammation under the following headings:
   (i) definition and cardinal signs
   (ii) etiology
   (iii) stages
(b) Discuss the chemical mediators/mechanisms involved.
(c) Discuss the outcomes of acute inflammation.
(d) Discuss the clinical significance of acute inflammation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: inflammation is a normal, non-specific defense mechanism of the body intended to localize and remove an injurious agent, producing the cardinal signs of warmth (calor), redness (rubor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor) and possible loss of function (functio laesa)
• Etiology - exogenous causes: physical agents (mechanical - fractures, foreign bodies; thermal - burns, freezing; chemical - toxic gases, acids, bases) and biological agents (bacteria, viruses, parasites)
• Etiology - endogenous causes: circulation disorders (thrombosis, infarction, haemorrhage), enzyme activation (e.g. acute pancreatitis), and deposit of metabolic products (uric acid, urea)
• Stages - neurologic response: sympathetic nervous system causes constriction of blood vessels; vascular response (triple response) follows: a thin red line from vasodilation of capillaries (3-50 sec), a flush from vasodilation of arterioles (30-60 sec), and a wheal from increased vascular permeability and oedema (1-5 min)
• Stages - Stage I: local cytokine production incites the inflammatory response, promotes wound repair, and recruits the reticular endothelial system. Stage II: small quantities of cytokines released into circulation improve the local response, stimulating growth factors and recruiting macrophages and platelets; this acute phase response is usually controlled by decreasing pro-inflammatory mediators and releasing endogenous antagonists, aiming for homeostasis
• Stages - Stage III: if homeostasis is not restored, a significant systemic reaction occurs; cytokine release becomes destructive rather than protective, activating humoral cascades and the reticular endothelial system, with loss of circulatory integrity leading to organ dysfunction

(b)
• Mediators/mechanisms: bradykinin is released from injured cells and activates pain receptors; the sensation of pain stimulates mast cells (basophils) to release histamine; bradykinin and histamine cause capillary dilation, increasing blood flow and capillary permeability; a break in the skin allows bacterial entry, resulting in migration of neutrophils and monocytes; neutrophils phagocytise bacteria and macrophages leave the bloodstream to phagocytise microbes
• Acute phase response: begins within hours to days, with increased plasma acute-phase proteins (fibrinogen, C-reactive protein), increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fever, increased leukocyte numbers, skeletal muscle catabolism and negative nitrogen balance, generated after release of IL-1, IL-6 and TNF, which affect the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre to produce fever and induce lethargy via effects on the CNS

(c)
• Outcomes - Resolution: restoration to normal with limited injury, via neutralization of chemical substances, normalization of vascular permeability, apoptosis of inflammatory cells, and lymphatic drainage
• Outcomes - Healing by scar: tissue destruction, fibrinous inflammation, and purulent inflammation with abscess formation (pus, pyogenic membrane, resorption over weeks to months)
• Outcomes - Progression to chronic inflammation, when resolution mechanisms fail (short half-life of mediators, TGF-beta release, downregulation of leukotrienes, upregulation of IL-1 receptor antagonist, apoptosis of pro-inflammatory cells, and anti-inflammatory lipoxin production) do not terminate the response

(d)
Clinical significance: potential complications include infection (microorganisms penetrate oedematous tissue more easily), deep ulcers/erosion that may perforate, skeletal muscle spasm as a protective response to pain, and local complications such as obstruction, loss of sensation, and decreased cell function depending on the site affected.

questions.question:
A patient with a long history of heavy ethanol intake is found to have fatty change in the liver progressing to alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis, with portal hypertension.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the etiology and pathogenesis of this condition.
(c) Describe the morphological changes that occur in the liver.
(d) Discuss the complications and clinical course.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: chronic alcoholism, with alcoholic liver disease (ALD).

(b)
Etiology and pathogenesis: addiction to ethanol produces dependence and withdrawal symptoms, and is more common in males, with some genetic predisposition. Acute alcohol abuse causes drowsiness at blood levels of approximately 200 mg/dL, with stupor and coma at higher levels; alcohol oxidation by alcohol dehydrogenase depletes NAD, leading to accumulation of fat in the liver and metabolic acidosis.

(c)
Morphology: the main effects of chronic alcoholism are alcoholic liver disease, including fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, and cirrhosis, which leads to portal hypertension and increases the risk for development of hepatocellular carcinoma.

(d)
Complications and clinical course: chronic alcoholism can also cause bleeding from gastritis and gastric ulcers, peripheral neuropathy associated with thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome), alcoholic cardiomyopathy, and acute and chronic pancreatitis; it is a major risk factor for cancers of the oral cavity, larynx and oesophagus, a risk greatly increased by concurrent smoking or use of smokeless tobacco; use of ethanol during pregnancy can cause fetal alcohol syndrome, marked by microcephaly, growth retardation and facial abnormalities in the newborn, with reduction in mental function as the child grows older.

questions.question:
(a) Describe malignant neoplasia under the following headings:
   (i) definition
   (ii) nomenclature
   (iii) local behaviour
(b) Explain how a malignant neoplasm spreads/disseminates to a distant site.
(c) Explain the resulting functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: neoplasia is new, uncontrolled growth of cells that is not under physiologic control; malignant neoplasms are commonly called cancer, and the term 'cancer' implies malignancy
• Nomenclature: malignant neoplasm names generally end in '-carcinoma' (derived from epithelial cells) or '-sarcoma' (derived from mesenchymal cells such as fat or muscle); other categories include lymphoma (from lymphocytes), melanoma (from melanocytes), and malignant germ cell tumour
• Local behaviour: malignant neoplasms invade surrounding tissue; tumours arise from accumulated genetic and epigenetic alterations within single cells, causing the cell to divide and expand uncontrollably; not all malignant neoplasms form a tumorous mass - leukaemia and most forms of carcinoma in situ do not
• Secondary neoplasm: a secondary neoplasm is a cancerous tumour that is either a metastatic offshoot of a primary tumour, or an apparently unrelated tumour that increases in frequency following certain cancer treatments such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy
• Unknown primary: rarely, a metastatic neoplasm is found with no known site of the primary cancer, classed as a cancer of unknown primary origin

(b)
• Spread - basement membrane invasion: if a neoplasm is malignant, its cells must gain the ability to invade the basement membrane and surrounding tissue
• Spread - vascular entry: the malignant cells must then enter the bloodstream
• Spread - distant growth: the cells spread to and grow within distant organs, i.e. metastasize
• Consequence of dissemination: in most cases malignant neoplasms can metastasize to distant organs, invading and destroying the surrounding tissue at both the primary and secondary sites
• Prognosis of dissemination: malignant neoplasms, if untreated or unresponsive to treatment, will generally prove fatal, in contrast to benign neoplasms, which stay localized in one place

(c)
• Functional deficit - local: invasion and destruction of the surrounding tissue at the primary site impairs the normal structure and function of the organ of origin
• Functional deficit - distant: growth of metastatic deposits within distant organs likewise invades and destroys tissue at those secondary sites, so that the functional deficit of malignant disease is compounded across multiple organs rather than being confined to the organ in which the tumour first arose

questions.question:
(a) Define hypersensitivity.
(b) Classify the types of hypersensitivity reaction.
(c) Discuss the etiology and pathogenesis of each type.
(d) Describe the manifestations/morphology of each type.
(e) Distinguish between Type I and Type IV hypersensitivity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: hypersensitivities (allergies) occur when the immune system responds to a harmless substance as if it were a threat; an allergen is the antigen of an allergic response.

(b)
Classification: Type I (immediate hypersensitivity), Type II (cytotoxic reactions), Type III (immune complex hypersensitivity), and Type IV (delayed, cell-mediated hypersensitivity).

(c)
• Type I - etiology/pathogenesis: IgE-mediated, involving mast cells and basophils; symptoms occur within seconds of exposure to an allergen and require prior sensitization
• Type II - etiology/pathogenesis: subacute hypersensitivity, IgG and IgM mediated; cytotoxic reactions occur when antibodies bind to cellular antigens, promoting complement fixation, inflammation and phagocytosis
• Type III - etiology/pathogenesis: subacute hypersensitivity, IgG and IgM mediated; a widely distributed antigen reacts with antibody to form immune complexes that cannot be cleared
• Type IV - etiology/pathogenesis: delayed hypersensitivity, cell-mediated, taking one to three days to react; involves cytotoxic T cells, TH1 cells, and macrophages; agents act as haptens and elicit a response after binding to tissue

(d)
• Type I - manifestations: locally, histamine-induced vasodilation and increased permeability cause watery eyes, runny nose, itching and redness, and respiratory allergy-induced asthma; systemically, anaphylaxis/anaphylactic shock is associated with allergens of systemic distribution, causing widespread vasodilation and airway swelling; atopy is the tendency to display Type I symptoms without prior sensitization
• Type II - manifestations: classic example is a transfusion reaction
• Type III - manifestations: persistent inflammation and tissue damage, exemplified by farmer's lung, and associated with autoimmune disorders
• Type IV - manifestations: allergic contact dermatitis (e.g. poison ivy, heavy metals, TB tine tests)

(e)
• Distinguishing feature (mechanism): Type I is mediated by IgE bound to mast cells/basophils and produces an immediate reaction within seconds requiring prior sensitization; Type IV is cell-mediated (via cytotoxic T cells, TH1 cells and macrophages) and is delayed, taking one to three days to react
• Distinguishing feature (manifestation): Type I produces local reactions (watery eyes, runny nose, itching, asthma) or systemic anaphylactic shock with widespread vasodilation and airway swelling; Type IV produces allergic contact dermatitis where haptens bind to tissue before eliciting the delayed response

(a)
Diagnosis and risk factors: allergic contact dermatitis, a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction. Recognised triggers/exposures include poison ivy, heavy metals, and TB tine tests.

(b)
Pathogenesis: Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed, cell-mediated reaction that takes one to three days to react; it involves cytotoxic T cells, TH1 cells and macrophages; the triggering agents (such as poison ivy or heavy metals) act as haptens and elicit the response only after binding to tissue.

(c)
Complications: because the reaction is cell-mediated and delayed rather than antibody-mediated and immediate, it produces a more prolonged local tissue reaction (dermatitis) at the site of hapten binding compared with the immediate reactions of Type I hypersensitivity.

(d)
Investigation/management principle: recognition of the one-to-three day delay and the hapten-tissue binding mechanism (rather than an immediate IgE mechanism) justifies identifying and avoiding the specific contactant (e.g. poison ivy or heavy metal) as the basis of management, since the reaction is triggered only once the hapten has bound to the patient's own tissue.
questions.question:
One to three days after contact with poison ivy, a patient develops a delayed, cell-mediated skin reaction at the site of contact.
(a) Name the likely condition and discuss the risk factors/exposures associated with it.
(b) Discuss the pathogenesis.
(c) Discuss the possible complications.
(d) Discuss the investigation and management principle, and justify it.

(a) Define nutritional/vitamin deficiency disease.
(b) Classify the vitamin deficiencies (Vitamin A, Vitamin D, Vitamin C).
(c) Discuss the etiology, pathogenesis (functions lost) and morphological/clinical features of each.
(d) Distinguish between the effect of Vitamin D deficiency in children and in adults.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Nutritional diseases include dietary insufficiency, protein-energy malnutrition, and vitamin deficiencies.

(b)
The vitamins discussed are Vitamin A, Vitamin D and Vitamin C.

(c)
• Vitamin A - function/etiology: the major functions of vitamin A are maintenance of normal vision, regulation of cell growth and differentiation, and regulation of lipid metabolism; deficiency therefore impairs these functions
• Vitamin A - toxicity features (contrast to deficiency): acute toxicity produces headache, dizziness, vomiting, stupor and blurred vision; chronic toxicity produces weight loss, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, bone and joint pain, and teratogenic effects
• Vitamin D - function: the major function of vitamin D is maintenance of adequate plasma levels of calcium and phosphorus to support metabolic functions, bone mineralization, and neuromuscular transmission
• Vitamin D - deficiency (pathogenesis/morphology): deficiency causes rickets in children whose epiphyses have not already closed, osteomalacia in adults, and hypocalcaemic tetany
• Vitamin D - toxicity (contrast): in children, toxicity causes metastatic calcification of soft tissues such as the kidney; in adults, it causes bone pain and hypercalcaemia
• Vitamin C - function: ascorbic acid functions in a variety of biosynthetic pathways by accelerating hydroxylation and amidation reactions, such as activation of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases from inactive precursors, providing for hydroxylation of procollagen; it also has antioxidant properties
• Vitamin C - deficiency (morphology/clinical): deficiency results in the development of scurvy
• Common theme: each of these vitamins has both a deficiency syndrome and, in the case of Vitamins A and D, a distinct toxicity syndrome from excess intake, reflecting their role in normal cellular and metabolic regulation
• Clinical relevance: because Vitamin D governs calcium and phosphorus homeostasis needed for bone mineralization, its deficiency manifests as a bone-mineralization disorder, whereas Vitamin C deficiency, acting through collagen hydroxylation, manifests as scurvy, a disorder of connective tissue

(d)
• Distinguishing feature (children vs adults) - children: Vitamin D deficiency in children, whose epiphyses have not already closed, produces rickets
• Distinguishing feature (children vs adults) - adults: Vitamin D deficiency in adults, whose epiphyses have closed, produces osteomalacia instead; both groups may also develop hypocalcaemic tetany as a shared complication of the underlying calcium deficiency

questions.question:
(a) Describe AIDS/HIV infection under the following headings:
   (i) etiology
   (ii) pathogenesis
   (iii) clinical features
(b) Explain how this condition disseminates/leads to disease throughout the body.
(c) Explain the resulting functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Etiology: AIDS is caused by HIV, an acquired viral infection
• Pathogenesis: HIV destroys important white blood cells, specifically killing TH (helper T) cells, and weakens the immune system
• Classification context: AIDS/HIV is classified among the acquired immune deficiencies, in which a disease weakens the immune system, as distinct from a primary immune deficiency present at birth
• Clinical features: people with HIV/AIDS become seriously ill with infections that most people can fight off; these are called 'opportunistic infections' because they take advantage of the weakened immune system
• Distinction from other immunodeficiency: unlike severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), which is present at birth due to missing white blood cells, AIDS is acquired during life through HIV infection

(b)
• Dissemination - mechanism: because HIV specifically depletes TH cells, which are central coordinators of the adaptive immune response, its effect is not confined to one organ; the resulting immune weakness is systemic
• Dissemination - consequence: with a weakened immune system, organisms that would normally be cleared are able to establish infection in multiple organ systems as opportunistic infections, since the immune surveillance that would normally contain them throughout the body is lost
• Related context: cancer can also be viewed as a failure of immune surveillance, and immunodeficiency of this kind (whether from AIDS, drugs, or radiation therapy affecting the marrow) increases susceptibility to malignancy as well as infection
• Systemic nature: the deficiency in AIDS is therefore not localized to a single tissue but reflects a body-wide loss of protective immune function, which is why affected individuals are described as becoming 'seriously ill with infections that most people can fight off.'
• Overall summary: HIV disseminates its effect throughout the body indirectly, not by physically spreading an inflammatory lesion, but by destroying the TH cells on which immune protection of every organ system depends, so that opportunistic infections can then arise anywhere in the body

(c)
• Functional deficit - immune failure: the loss of TH cell numbers and function means the body can no longer mount effective humoral or cell-mediated responses against invading organisms
• Functional deficit - clinical consequence: this produces recurrent, severe, and often unusual (opportunistic) infections that a person with a normal immune system would ordinarily resist

(a)
• Types of healing by intention - First intention: occurs with minimal tissue loss; there is no granulation tissue formation
• Types of healing by intention - Second intention: occurs with significant tissue loss; granulation tissue forms, healing is slow, and scar tissue results
• Regeneration by tissue type: regeneration depends on tissue type; labile cells are capable of lifelong regeneration

(b)
• Mechanisms/therapies - RICE therapy for injuries: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation
• Mechanisms/therapies - Cold: causes local vasoconstriction and reduces local oedema
• Mechanisms/therapies - Heat and moderate activity: improve circulation, removing excess fluid, pain-causing mediators and waste metabolites, and bringing oxygen and materials for healing
• Mechanisms/therapies - Elevation improves fluid flow away from the damaged area; compression reduces accumulation of fluid but should be supportive, not restrictive, and should not cut off circulation
• Mechanisms/therapies - Physical therapy maintains joint mobility and reduces pain; splints prevent contractures that may fix joints in abnormal positions

(c)
• Outcomes: resolution (restoration to normal, with limited injury); healing by scar, involving tissue destruction, fibrinous inflammation, and purulent inflammation with abscess formation (pus, pyogenic membrane, resorption over weeks to months); or progression into chronic inflammation
• Outcome mechanisms (resolution): the inflammatory response must be actively terminated when no longer needed, via mechanisms such as the short half-life of inflammatory mediators, release of TGF-beta from macrophages, downregulation of pro-inflammatory molecules such as leukotrienes, upregulation of anti-inflammatory molecules such as the IL-1 receptor antagonist, and apoptosis of pro-inflammatory cells
• Failure of resolution: failure to terminate the inflammatory response actively results in chronic inflammation and cellular destruction; chronic inflammation shows less swelling and exudate, more lymphocytes, macrophages and fibroblasts, continued tissue destruction, and more fibrous scar tissue than acute inflammation

(d)
Clinical significance: whether healing occurs by first or second intention determines whether granulation tissue and scarring result; the amount of tissue loss therefore predicts the speed of healing and the extent of resultant scarring, which is why RICE therapy and physiotherapy modalities (rest, ice, compression, elevation, and controlled mobilisation) are used to limit oedema and support optimal repair.
questions.question:
(a) Describe tissue healing and repair under the following headings:
   (i) types of healing by intention
   (ii) regeneration by tissue type
(b) Discuss the mechanisms/therapies that support healing.
(c) Discuss the outcomes of healing.
(d) Discuss the clinical significance of the type of healing that occurs.

(a) Describe the process of adaptive/acquired immunity under the following headings:
   (i) active immunity
   (ii) passive immunity
(b) Discuss the mechanisms involved in each.
(c) Discuss the outcomes (protection/memory) of each.
(d) Discuss the clinical significance of the distinction.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Active immunity: acquired through exposure to a pathogen, which triggers production of antibodies by the immune system; it can be naturally acquired (exposure to a live pathogen, leading to a primary immune response and immunological memory) or artificially acquired (induced by a vaccine, a substance containing antigen that stimulates a primary response without causing disease symptoms)
• Passive immunity: the transfer of immunity, in the form of ready-made antibodies, from one individual to another; it can be natural (maternal antibodies transferred to the fetus through the placenta, or IgA transferred via breast milk/colostrum) or artificial (transfer of human or animal antibodies specific for a pathogen or toxin to non-immune individuals)

(b)
• Mechanisms - active immunity: when B cells and T cells are activated by a pathogen, memory B cells and T cells develop and a primary immune response results; these memory cells 'remember' the specific pathogen and can mount a strong secondary response if it is detected again
• Mechanisms - passive immunity (natural): maternal antibodies (IgG, the only isotype that crosses the placenta) are passed to the fetus via an FcRn receptor on placental cells, around the third month of gestation; IgA in breast milk is transferred to the infant's gut, protecting against bacterial infection until the newborn can synthesize its own antibodies
• Mechanisms - passive immunity (artificial): antibodies can be administered as human or animal blood plasma, pooled human immunoglobulin (IVIG or IG), or monoclonal antibodies; transfer of activated T cells ('adoptive transfer') is also possible but is rarely used in humans because it requires histocompatible donors and carries a risk of graft-versus-host disease in unmatched donors
• Vaccine types (mechanism of artificial active immunity): inactivated vaccines (micro-organisms killed with chemicals/heat, e.g. flu, cholera, plague, hepatitis A); live attenuated vaccines (cultivated to disable disease-inducing ability, e.g. yellow fever, measles, rubella, mumps); toxoids (inactivated toxic compounds, e.g. tetanus, diphtheria); and subunit/recombinant/polysaccharide/conjugate vaccines composed of fragments of the pathogen (e.g. hepatitis B subunit vaccine)

(c)
• Outcomes - active immunity: due to the formation of immunological memory, reinfection at later time points leads to a rapid increase in antibody production and effector T cell activity, so later infections can be mild or even unapparent; this immunity is both active and adaptive
• Outcomes - passive immunity: provides immediate protection, but the body does not develop memory, so the patient is at risk of being infected by the same pathogen later; immunity from passive immunization lasts only a short period

(d)
• Clinical use - passive immunity: used when there is a high risk of infection and insufficient time for the body to develop its own immune response, or to reduce symptoms of ongoing or immunosuppressive disease; artificial passive transfer is used prophylactically for immunodeficiency diseases such as hypogammaglobulinemia, and to treat certain acute infections and poisoning
• Risks of passive immunity: there is a potential risk of hypersensitivity reactions and serum sickness, especially from gamma globulin of non-human origin
• Historical/practical note: artificially induced passive immunity has been used for over a century to treat infectious disease and, before antibiotics, was often the only specific treatment for certain infections; most vaccines (for active immunity) are given by hypodermic or intramuscular injection, though some (e.g. live attenuated polio, some typhoid and cholera vaccines) are given orally to produce bowel-based immunity
• Clinical significance of the distinction: passive immunity is chosen when immediate, short-term protection is needed and there is no time to await an active response, whereas active immunity (natural infection or vaccination) is used to build durable, memory-based protection, which is the basis of vaccination programmes

questions.question:
Shortly after starting a blood transfusion, a patient develops a reaction in which antibodies bind to cellular antigens on the transfused cells, promoting complement fixation, inflammation and phagocytosis.
(a) State the diagnosis (type of hypersensitivity).
(b) Describe the laboratory/immunological findings.
(c) Discuss the mechanism of cell injury.
(d) Discuss the outcome.
(e) Discuss the long-term complications/prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: a transfusion reaction, an example of Type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity.

(b)
Laboratory/immunological findings: Type II hypersensitivity is a subacute hypersensitivity reaction that is IgG and IgM mediated.

(c)
Mechanism of cell injury: antibodies bind to cellular antigens (here, on the transfused cells), promoting complement fixation, inflammation, and phagocytosis of the affected cells.

(d)
Outcome: the transfused cells are targeted for destruction through complement fixation and phagocytosis as a direct consequence of the antibody-antigen binding on the cell surface.

(e)
Long-term complications/prevention: as with other hypersensitivity reactions, this immunologic dysfunction reflects the immune system's antibody response against antigens it identifies as foreign; recognition of transfusion reaction as a Type II, antibody-mediated cytotoxic process is the basis for careful cross-matching prior to transfusion to prevent the antigen-antibody interaction that triggers it.

(a)
Definition: when the immune system doesn't work the way it should, it is called an immune system disorder.

(b)
Classification: primary immune deficiency (being born with a weak immune system), acquired immune deficiency (a disease that weakens the immune system), hyperactive immune system (as with an allergic reaction), and autoimmune disease (an immune system that turns against the self).

(c)
• Etiology - primary: severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is an immune deficiency present at birth; a related cause is DiGeorge syndrome, in which improper development of the thymus gland diminishes T cell production; in severe combined immunodeficiency, lack of an enzyme means toxic waste builds up inside immune system cells, killing them and devastating the immune system
• Etiology - acquired: the immune system can be weakened by certain medicines, such as chemotherapy or drugs used to prevent organ transplant rejection; infections such as flu, mononucleosis and measles can weaken the immune system temporarily; smoking, alcohol and poor nutrition can also weaken it; HIV, which causes AIDS, is an acquired viral infection
• Related mechanisms of dysfunction: immunologic dysfunction can also arise from failure of lymphocyte programming, new self antigens, gene mutation, structural change (haptens, infection), and foreign antigens that closely resemble self antigens, causing cross-reactivity
• Congenital vs acquired dysfunction (general): immunodeficiency may be congenital/genetic (varied inborn errors) or acquired, the latter including drug- and radiation-induced causes, and cancer, which can itself be viewed as a failure of immune surveillance

(d)
• Pathogenesis - primary (SCID): children with SCID are missing important white blood cells, placing them in constant danger of infection from bacteria, viruses and fungi; this disorder is sometimes called 'bubble boy disease.'
• Pathogenesis - acquired (AIDS): HIV destroys important white blood cells and weakens the immune system

(e)
• Clinical features - primary: if a person is born with a severely defective immune system, death from infection by a virus, bacterium, fungus or parasite will occur without intervention
• Clinical features - acquired: people with HIV/AIDS become seriously ill with infections that most people can fight off; these are called opportunistic infections because they take advantage of weak immune systems

(f)
• Distinguishing feature - onset: primary immune deficiency (e.g. SCID) is present at birth, being born with a weak immune system, whereas acquired immune deficiency (e.g. AIDS) develops later in life from a disease that weakens a previously functioning immune system
• Distinguishing feature - mechanism: SCID results from a missing enzyme causing toxic waste build-up that kills immune cells, leaving children missing important white blood cells from birth, whereas AIDS results from HIV actively destroying (killing) TH cells during the person's lifetime
questions.question:
(a) Define immune deficiency.
(b) Classify the types of immune system disorder.
(c) Discuss the etiology of primary and acquired immune deficiency.
(d) Discuss the pathogenesis.
(e) Describe the clinical morphology/features.
(f) Distinguish between primary immune deficiency (e.g. SCID) and acquired immune deficiency (e.g. AIDS).

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: oedema is an abnormal accumulation of fluid beneath the skin or in one or more cavities of the body
• Types: generalized oedema, and organ-specific oedema such as cerebral oedema, pulmonary oedema, periorbital oedema, macular oedema, cutaneous oedema (e.g. contact dermatitis), myxoedema, and lymphoedema
• Fluid movement background: two major factors regulate movement of water and electrolytes between fluid compartments - hydrostatic pressure and osmotic pressure; fluid leaves the plasma at the arteriolar end of capillaries because outward hydrostatic pressure predominates, and returns to plasma at the venular end because inward colloid osmotic pressure predominates; hydrostatic pressure within interstitial spaces forces fluid into lymph capillaries
• Factors contributing to formation: increased hydrostatic pressure; reduced oncotic pressure within blood vessels; increased blood vessel wall permeability, as in inflammation; obstruction of fluid clearance via the lymphatics; and changes in the water-retaining properties of the tissues themselves (raised hydrostatic pressure often reflects retention of water and sodium by the kidney)

(b)
• Etiology (common/less serious causes): immobility (e.g. sitting or standing for long periods), burns, menstruation, pregnancy, the contraceptive pill, and salty foods
• Etiology (serious causes): kidney disease, heart failure, chronic lung disease, thyroid disease, liver disease such as cirrhosis, diabetes, arthritis, and malnutrition
• Mechanistic link to inflammation: increased blood vessel wall permeability during inflammation is one of the direct mechanisms of oedema formation described above
• Mechanistic link to malnutrition: malnutrition can cause oedema; this is consistent with the mechanism whereby reduced oncotic pressure within the blood vessels (from low plasma protein) allows fluid to accumulate in the tissues, as also seen in the hypoalbuminaemia and generalized/dependent oedema of kwashiorkor

(c)
• Clinical outcomes/symptoms: swelling of the skin, puffiness of the ankles, face or eyes, skin that stays hollow for a few seconds after being pressed (pitting oedema), aching body parts, and stiff joints
• Further clinical outcomes/symptoms: weight gain or loss, fuller hand and neck veins, and raised blood pressure and pulse rate

(d)
• Clinical significance: because oedema can result from a wide range of causes, from simple immobility to serious systemic disease (kidney, heart, liver, thyroid, or nutritional disorders), its presence and pattern (generalized versus organ-specific) should prompt evaluation of the underlying hydrostatic, oncotic, permeability, lymphatic or renal mechanism responsible
• Practical note: because increased blood vessel wall permeability during inflammation is itself a recognised cause of oedema, and because oedematous tissue allows microorganisms to penetrate more easily, oedema is not merely a cosmetic finding but can facilitate further complications such as infection
questions.question:
(a) Describe the process of oedema formation under the following headings:
   (i) definition and types
   (ii) factors contributing to formation
(b) Discuss the etiological mechanisms involved.
(c) Discuss the clinical outcomes/symptoms.
(d) Discuss the clinical significance of oedema.

(a) Compare and contrast acute and chronic inflammation under the following headings:
   (i) onset/duration
   (ii) vascular changes/exudation
   (iii) predominant cells
   (iv) tissue outcome
(b) Explain the clinical basis of the difference between the two.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Onset/duration - Acute: a short-term response
• Onset/duration - Chronic: persistent; may develop in the course of recurrent or progressive acute inflammation, or from low-grade irritants that fail to elicit an acute response
• Vascular changes/exudation - Acute: involves hemodynamic changes and exudate formation, with flush, flare and wheal, vascular damage, and more exudation
• Vascular changes/exudation - Chronic: shows fewer local vascular signs, with little or no/less exudation, but neo-vascularization occurs
• Predominant cells - Acute: presence of granular leukocytes, specifically neutrophils as the acute inflammatory cells
• Predominant cells - Chronic: presence of nongranular leukocytes, specifically lymphocytes and macrophages, together with fibroblasts
• Tissue outcome - Acute: little or no fibrosis
• Tissue outcome - Chronic: prominent fibrosis and more extensive scarring, with continued tissue destruction
• Chronic inflammation subtype - Nonspecific chronic inflammation: diffuse accumulation of macrophages and lymphocytes at the injury site, with macrophages arising from recruitment, local proliferation, and prolonged survival
• Chronic inflammation subtype - Granulomatous chronic inflammation: a distinctive, cell-mediated (delayed) immune reaction with aggregates of activated macrophages forming epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells (Langhans type or foreign body type); there is no elimination of the agent, only walling off, as with intracellular agents such as tuberculosis
• Following acute episode: chronic inflammation following an acute episode shows less swelling and exudate than the acute phase, with more lymphocytes, macrophages and fibroblasts present, continued tissue destruction, and more fibrous scar tissue

(b)
Clinical basis of the difference: acute inflammation is dominated by vascular changes and neutrophilic exudation aimed at rapid removal of the injurious agent with little fibrosis, so it typically resolves; chronic inflammation reflects either a failure to resolve the acute process or a persistent low-grade stimulus, so lymphocytes, macrophages and fibroblasts dominate, tissue destruction continues, and healing occurs by extensive fibrosis/scarring rather than restitution.

questions.question:
A worker sustains a shock from a low-voltage household current. Imaging and clinical assessment reveal a small blister on the thumb at the contact point, along with disruption of normal cardiac electrical impulses.
(a) Identify the pathological process affecting this patient.
(b) Describe the tissues/organs affected and the changes seen.
(c) State the differential considerations for this type of injury.
(d) Give the clinicopathological correlation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Identification: electrical injury, which may be fatal, and can arise from low voltage currents (as in the home and workplace) or high voltage currents carried in power lines or by lightning.

(b)
Tissues/organs affected and changes seen: there are two types of injury - burns (such as the small blister seen at the point of contact, e.g. on the thumb) and ventricular fibrillation with cardiac and respiratory centre failure, resulting from disruption of normal electrical impulses; 120 or 220 volts is high enough to cause serious injury, including ventricular fibrillation; alternating current induces tetanic muscle spasm, including of the chest wall muscles, producing death from asphyxia.

(c)
Differential considerations: low-voltage injury typically produces a small, localized blister at the contact point, in contrast to high-voltage injury; lightning injury (a high-voltage injury) produces large current flows and is more likely to cause paralysis of medullary centres and extensive burns, with a fern pattern, singed hair and fused coins sometimes seen on victims.

(d)
Clinicopathological correlation: the two mechanisms of death from electrical injury are burns and disruption of normal electrical impulses causing ventricular fibrillation or cardiac and respiratory centre failure; alternating current-induced tetanic spasm of the chest wall muscles can also cause death from asphyxia.

questions.question:
A patient presents with persistently raised blood pressure. The condition has developed in the setting of multiple gene mutations interacting with environmental factors such as race, age, lack of sleep, alcohol consumption and salt intake.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the etiology and pathogenesis of this condition.
(c) Describe the morphological changes that occur as a complication of this condition.
(d) Discuss the complications and clinical course.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: hypertension.

(b)
Etiology and pathogenesis: hypertension is an example of a multifactorial disorder, resulting from multiple gene mutations that interact with environmental factors, including race, age, lack of sleep, alcohol consumption, and salt intake.

(c)
Morphology: pathologic hypertrophy occurs in the left ventricle as a typical complication of hypertension; hypertrophy is an increase in the size of the cell and organ, and pure hypertrophy occurs only in the heart and striated muscles because these organs consist of cells that cannot divide; this represents an adaptation of heart muscle to an increased workload.

(d)
Complications and clinical course: the cellular adaptation of left ventricular hypertrophy develops as the heart muscle adapts to the increased workload imposed by the raised blood pressure; alcohol use is also noted as increasing the risk of ischemic heart disease and, when combined with smoking or oral contraceptive use, further increases the likelihood of myocardial infarction and stroke, conditions that are themselves linked to the same vascular (atherosclerotic) process as hypertension.

(a)
• Balance of deficit - Marasmus: an overall deficiency of both protein and total calories
• Balance of deficit - Kwashiorkor: protein deprivation is relatively more severe than the deficit in total calories
• Weight/muscle findings - Marasmus: weight falls to 60% of normal, with growth retardation and loss of muscle; the extremities are emaciated
• Weight/muscle findings - Kwashiorkor: this is not the dominant feature; instead, protein deficiency drives the other findings below
• Oedema/albumin status - Marasmus: not a defining feature of marasmus
• Oedema/albumin status - Kwashiorkor: hypoalbuminaemia with generalized or dependent oedema is characteristic
• Liver findings - Marasmus: not specifically described
• Liver findings - Kwashiorkor: fatty liver results from reduced synthesis of lipoproteins
• Additional findings - Marasmus: anaemia and manifestations of multiple vitamin deficiencies
• Additional findings - Kwashiorkor: skin lesions and hair changes
• Immune effect (shared): both marasmus and kwashiorkor produce immune deficiency, particularly affecting T-cell mediated immunity in marasmus, and defects in immunity with secondary infections in kwashiorkor

(b)
Clinical basis of the difference: in marasmus the deficiency of both calories and protein is global, so the body draws down its own muscle and fat stores, producing generalized wasting and emaciation without oedema; in kwashiorkor the calorie intake is relatively preserved while protein intake is severely deficient, so hypoalbuminaemia lowers plasma oncotic pressure to cause oedema, and reduced hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causes fatty liver, findings that are not features of marasmus.
questions.question:
(a) Compare and contrast Marasmus and Kwashiorkor (forms of protein-energy malnutrition) under the following headings:
   (i) balance of protein vs calorie deficit
   (ii) weight/muscle findings
   (iii) oedema/albumin status
   (iv) liver findings
   (v) immune effect
(b) Explain the clinical basis of the difference between the two.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: granulomatous chronic inflammation is a distinctive type of chronic inflammation, representing a cell-mediated (delayed) immune reaction
• Morphology: it consists of aggregates of activated macrophages that form epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells (of Langhans type or foreign body type); granuloma formation involves the massing of macrophages surrounded by lymphocytes
• Associated hypersensitivity mechanism: some granulomas are associated with deposition of antigenic material and represent a type IV hypersensitivity reaction
• Etiological classes: (1) bacteria - tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis (third stage); (2) parasites and fungi; (3) inorganic metals or dust - silicosis, berylliosis; (4) foreign body - suture (Schloffer tumour), breast prosthesis; (5) unknown cause - sarcoidosis

(b)
• Tuberculosis as intracellular agent: tuberculosis is specifically cited as an example of an intracellular agent causing granulomatous inflammation
• Mechanism of walling off: in granulomatous inflammation there is no elimination of the agent; instead, the massed macrophages, epithelioid cells and giant cells wall off the organism
• Significance of walling off: because the agent is not eliminated but only contained, the organism can persist within the granuloma rather than being cleared from the body, distinguishing this response from the acute inflammatory response, which aims to eliminate the injurious agent
• Contrast with acute response: this differs from acute inflammation, whose purpose is to localize and remove the injurious agent; granulomatous inflammation instead isolates an agent that acute mechanisms have failed to clear
• General chronic inflammation context: chronic inflammation of this kind results in continued tissue destruction and the deposition of more fibrous scar tissue compared with acute inflammation

(c)
• Functional deficit - local: the affected tissue develops a mass of chronic inflammatory cells (granuloma) with continued tissue destruction and fibrosis, altering the normal architecture of the involved organ
• Functional deficit - systemic: extensive granuloma formation and associated fibrous scarring, as with prominent fibrosis in chronic inflammation generally, can impair the normal function of the affected organ
questions.question:
(a) Describe granulomatous chronic inflammation under the following headings:
   (i) definition
   (ii) etiological classes
   (iii) morphology
(b) Explain why an intracellular agent such as tuberculosis is walled off rather than eliminated, and the significance for the host.
(c) Explain the resulting functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: atypical endometrial hyperplasia, which may represent an early neoplastic process.

(b)
Predisposing factors: endometrial hyperplasia is hyperproliferation of the endometrium, usually in response to unopposed oestrogen stimulation, in the setting of polycystic ovary syndrome or exogenous administration of hormones; pure hyperplasia typically occurs because of hormonal stimulation, e.g. prolonged oestrogen exposure causing the endometrium of the uterus to become thick.

(c)
Pathogenesis and morphology: hyperplasia is an increase in the number of normal cells in a tissue or organ and can represent a precancerous condition; this differs from neoplasia (the process underlying cancer and benign tumours), in which genetically abnormal cells manage to proliferate in a non-physiological manner unresponsive to normal stimuli; the effects of pathologic hyperplasia can provide a suitable foundation from which neoplastic cells may develop.

(d)
Clinical significance/features: atypical endometrial hyperplasia can lead to endometrial adenocarcinoma; the development of endometrial adenocarcinoma from endometrial hyperplasia is a typical example of how the effects of pathologic hyperplasia can lead to neoplasia, and females who exhibit hyperplasia of the endometrium are indeed more likely to develop cancer of these cells.
questions.question:
A woman with polycystic ovary syndrome and a history of unopposed oestrogen stimulation is found to have hyperproliferation of the endometrium, with atypical features on biopsy.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the predisposing factors.
(c) Discuss the pathogenesis and morphology.
(d) Discuss the clinical significance/features.

A patient involved in a motor vehicle accident presents with a wound characterized by damage to blood vessels and extravasation of blood into the subcutaneous tissue from impact with the vehicle's interior, together with a separate wound showing a tear of tissue with intact bridging blood vessels and jagged, irregular edges.
(a) Identify the pathological processes/types of wound present.
(b) Describe the tissues/organs affected and the changes seen.
(c) State the differential considerations (other wound types to exclude).
(d) Give the clinicopathological correlation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Identification: a contusion (from blunt trauma, with damage to vessels and extravasation of blood into tissue) together with a laceration (a tear or disruptive stretching of tissue with intact bridging blood vessels and jagged, irregular edges), sustained as injuries by physical agents in a motor vehicle accident.

(b)
Tissues/organs affected and changes seen: the contusion shows haemorrhage in the subcutaneous fat; the laceration shows torn tissue with intact bridging vessels and irregular margins. Motor vehicle accidents commonly cause trauma to the head (windshield impact), chest (steering column impact) and knees (dashboard impact), from impact with the interior of the vehicle or objects entering it, being thrown from the vehicle, being trapped in a burning vehicle, or asphyxial injury.

(c)
Differential considerations: these blunt-force injuries (contusion, laceration) are differentiated from sharp injuries such as incised wounds (long, shallow, sharp injuries without tissue bridges, with severely damaged bridging vessels), stab wounds (penetrating deeply), chop wounds (sharp and blunt features), and puncture wounds (from a long, narrow instrument, including gunshot wounds).

(d)
Clinicopathological correlation: injury depends on the shape of the object causing the injury, the amount of energy discharged at impact, and the tissues or organs bearing the impact; patterns of injury are modified by the use or lack of use of restraints (including airbag injuries), and the severity of external injury does not always correlate with the severity of internal injury, an important clinical caution in trauma assessment.

(a)
• Definition/course - Benign: the terms benign and malignant correlate to the course of the neoplasm; benign neoplasms stay localized in one place
• Definition/course - Malignant: malignant neoplasms invade surrounding tissue and, in most cases, can metastasize to distant organs; the term 'cancer' implies malignancy
• Local behaviour - Benign: benign tumours are circumscribed and localized and do not transform into cancer; examples include uterine fibroids, osteophytes and melanocytic nevi (skin moles)
• Local behaviour - Malignant: if the neoplasm is malignant, the cells must gain the ability to invade the basement membrane and surrounding tissue
• Spread - Benign: benign neoplasms may grow large but do not spread into, or invade, nearby tissues or other parts of the body
• Spread - Malignant: malignant cells enter the bloodstream and spread to and grow within distant organs; malignant neoplasms invade and destroy the surrounding tissue, may form metastases, and if untreated or unresponsive to treatment will generally prove fatal
• Intermediate category: a neoplasm can also be potentially-malignant, such as carcinoma in situ, which is localised and does not invade or destroy but, in time, may transform into a cancer
• Nomenclature - Benign: the name of a benign neoplasm often ends with '-oma', e.g. adenoma (benign neoplasm of glandular epithelium), fibroadenoma (benign neoplasm of the breast), leiomyoma (benign neoplasm of smooth muscle)
• Nomenclature - Malignant: the name of a malignant neoplasm often ends with '-carcinoma' or '-sarcoma', e.g. adenocarcinoma (malignant neoplasm of glandular tissue) and rhabdomyosarcoma; carcinoma is a malignant neoplasm derived from epithelial cells and sarcoma a malignant neoplasm derived from mesenchymal cells (e.g. fat, muscle)
• Exceptions in nomenclature: some tumours whose names end in '-oma' are in fact malignant, e.g. hepatoma (malignant neoplasm of liver), melanoma (malignant neoplasm of melanocytes), mesothelioma (malignant neoplasm of mesothelial cells) and seminoma (malignant germ cell neoplasm of testis)
• Secondary neoplasm: a secondary neoplasm is a cancerous tumour that is a metastatic offshoot of a primary tumour, or a tumour that increases in frequency following certain cancer treatments such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy

(b)
Clinical basis of difference: because benign tumours remain localized and do not invade or metastasize, they are generally curable by local removal, whereas malignant tumours invade the basement membrane, enter the bloodstream and spread to distant organs, so that even with treatment of the primary site, distant metastatic disease can remain and, if untreated or unresponsive, will generally prove fatal.
questions.question:
(a) Compare and contrast benign and malignant neoplasms under the following headings:
   (i) definition/course
   (ii) local behaviour (invasion)
   (iii) spread
   (iv) nomenclature
   (v) examples
(b) Explain the clinical basis of the difference between the two.

(a) Describe thermal burn injury under the following headings:
   (i) classification by depth
   (ii) effect of surface area involved
(b) Explain how a burn wound infection disseminates to affect distant organs.
(c) Explain the resulting functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Classification by depth: partial-thickness burns spare the dermal appendages and are pink, blistered and painful; full-thickness burns produce total destruction of the epidermis and dermis, including the dermal appendages, and are white or charred, dry, and anaesthetic due to destruction of nerve endings
• Effect of surface area: a burn exceeding 50% of total body surface, whether superficial or deep, is grave and potentially fatal; with more than 20% of body surface involved, there is a rapid shift of body fluids into the interstitial compartments, both at the burn site and systemically, with protein loss causing oedema, which can result in hypovolemic shock

(b)
• Local complication predisposing to spread: escharotomy incisions are performed to prevent compartment syndrome resulting from the fluid shifts caused by the burn
• Route of dissemination - infection: burns predispose to infection, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa being the most common opportunistic infection at the burn wound
• Route of dissemination - inhalation: persons trapped in burning buildings may also sustain inhalation injury, with soot noted in the nostrils and injury to the trachea, airway and lungs, providing a further route by which the injury affects organs beyond the skin
• Systemic spread mechanism: infection originating at the burn wound (or the inhalation injury to the airway) can disseminate systemically, consistent with the general pattern in which local infection is complicated by systemic spread to distant organs
• Distant organ affected - lungs: pneumonia is cited as one of the most common complications of thermal burns
• Distant organ affected - kidneys: septic shock accompanied by renal failure is cited as one of the most common complications of thermal burns
• Systemic complication - shock: the combination of fluid shifts (from loss of skin barrier and capillary leak) and septic shock together threaten circulatory integrity in the burned patient
• Summary of dissemination: thermal burn injury therefore disseminates to distant organs through two linked routes - infection of the burn wound (or inhaled toxic substances/soot reaching the airway and lungs) progressing to septic shock, and the systemic fluid/protein shift progressing to hypovolemic shock

(c)
• Functional deficit - respiratory: pneumonia and inhalation injury to the trachea, airway and lungs impair respiratory function
• Functional deficit - renal/circulatory: septic shock with renal failure impairs kidney function, while the combined hypovolemic and septic shock states impair overall circulatory integrity, producing the organ dysfunction that makes extensive burns potentially fatal

(a)
Diagnosis: farmer's lung, an example of Type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity.

(b)
Immunological findings: Type III hypersensitivity is a subacute hypersensitivity reaction that is IgG and IgM mediated, occurring when a widely distributed antigen reacts with antibody.

(c)
Mechanism of tissue injury: the resulting antigen-antibody complexes cannot be cleared, leading to persistent inflammation and tissue damage.

(d)
Outcome: the persistence of the immune complexes, rather than a single acute exposure, is what produces the ongoing tissue damage characteristic of this condition.

(e)
Long-term complications: Type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity of this kind is also associated with autoimmune disorders, reflecting the broader immunologic dysfunction that arises when antigen-antibody complexes are not effectively cleared from the tissues.
