questions.question: Emotional and psychological stress from ethical dilemmas in nursing leads to:
questions.explanation: Emotional and psychological stress from ethical dilemmas leads to anxiety, burnout, and moral distress among nurses, particularly in high-stakes ICU environments. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated these challenges. Unaddressed moral distress contributes to job dissatisfaction, decreased care quality, and increased turnover intentions among nurses. Institutional support is essential.

Fluid management in ARF involves maintaining fluid balance and avoiding fluid overload while ensuring adequate perfusion. Fluid administration is guided by urine output, hemodynamic status, and clinical signs of fluid overload or dehydration. Over-restriction can worsen prerenal components, while over-administration causes fluid overload. Individualized, closely monitored fluid management is essential.
questions.question: A key nursing intervention in ARF is fluid management, which involves:
options: Administering maximum IV fluids to prevent hypovolemia in all ARF stages
Maintaining fluid balance and avoiding overload based on urine output and clinical status
Restricting all fluid intake to less than 500 ml per day in all ARF patients
Restricting all intravenous fluids to prevent worsening of the renal failure
Using only oral fluid replacement regardless of the severity of ARF presented

questions.question: Which ethical approach helps nurses when a patient’s autonomy conflicts with beneficence?
questions.explanation: When autonomy conflicts with beneficence, the most ethical approach is to use ethical principles together with transparent communication and collaborative decision-making rather than mechanically prioritizing one principle over another. Each situation requires careful weighing of the patient's competence, the nature of the decision, potential consequences, and available support structures.
options: Defer to the family's judgment as it is more objective than either principle alone
Always prioritize autonomy over beneficence to avoid paternalistic practice
Apply non-maleficence exclusively to override both autonomy and beneficence
Always prioritize beneficence over autonomy to protect the patient's life
Use ethical principles together with communication and collaboration to find balance

questions.question: A conscious, competent patient with a reversible condition refuses a life-saving blood transfusion on religious grounds. The ethical principle most directly relevant to this situation is:
options: Non-maleficence, the duty to avoid causing harm
Justice, the fair distribution of healthcare resources
Autonomy, the right to make informed personal decisions
Beneficence, the duty to act in the patient's interest
Fidelity, the duty to maintain professional promises
questions.explanation: Respecting a competent patient's informed refusal of treatment, even a life-saving one, upholds the ethical principle of autonomy, which protects the individual's right to make decisions about their own body. While this may conflict with beneficence, autonomy takes priority when the patient has decision-making capacity and has been fully informed. Nurses support this right while ensuring the patient understands the consequences of their choice.

Compromised patient care is identified as arising from ethical dilemmas such as staffing shortages that impede nurses' ability to provide optimal care, potentially leading to delays in treatment and adverse patient outcomes. Moral distress-driven nurse burnout and turnover directly reduce staffing ratios, compromising the quality and safety of critical care provided.
options: Poor communication between nursing staff and the attending physician team
Inadequate pharmacological supplies and blood products in the clinical setting
Nurses with insufficient formal education in critical care clinical management
Staffing shortages and delayed treatment resulting from ethical dilemma-driven distress
Outdated hospital equipment and inadequate ICU infrastructure in Nigerian hospitals

questions.explanation: Ethical dilemmas can strain professional relationships within healthcare teams, leading to conflicts and breakdown in communication. This deterioration in teamwork can compromise patient safety and the overall effectiveness of healthcare delivery. Addressing ethical conflicts through structured approaches and ethics committees helps to restore team cohesion and improve patient outcomes.
questions.question: The impact of ethical dilemmas on professional relationships in nursing includes:
options: Reducing staff turnover by giving nurses a sense of purpose and moral clarity
Increasing patient satisfaction through open discussion of ethical challenges
Straining professional relationships within teams and compromising communication

questions.question: Which of the following best describes Priority 3 patients in the ICU model?
questions.explanation: Priority 3 patients are unstable and critically ill but have a reduced likelihood of recovery due to underlying disease or acute illness. They may receive intensive treatment with limits such as no intubation or CPR. This distinguishes them from Priority 1 (no limits) and Priority 4 (generally not appropriate).
options: Critically ill patients with reduced recovery likelihood due to underlying disease
Post-operative stable patients requiring only hemodynamic monitoring
Patients who are generally not appropriate for any ICU admission

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Triage data: vital signs and history, neurologic assessment findings and diagnostic data; circumstances, precipitating events, location and time of injury; whether the patient was unconscious after injury; how the patient reached hospital.
• Also ask the patient or companion about prior health status, medical/surgical history, medications (hormones, insulin, digitalis, anticoagulants), allergies, bleeding tendencies, time of last meal and date of last tetanus immunisation.
• Primary survey findings: airway patency, breathing/ventilation and chest injuries, circulation (haemorrhage, shock) and neurologic disability using the Glasgow Coma Scale.

(b)
• An emergent patient: life threatening, highest priority and seen immediately; conditions such as airway obstruction, shock, tension pneumothorax or a sucking chest wound fall in the immediate (red) category.
• Formal nursing diagnoses are formulated once the patient has been assessed, stabilised and tested.

(c)
• Primary survey (ABCD): establish a patent airway with the cervical spine protected; provide adequate ventilation using resuscitation measures when necessary; assess chest injuries first.
• Evaluate and restore cardiac output by controlling haemorrhage, preventing and treating shock and maintaining effective circulation; determine neurologic disability with the Glasgow Coma Scale.
• Secondary survey: complete health history and head-to-toe assessment, diagnostic and laboratory tests, ECG electrodes, arterial lines or urinary catheters, splinting of suspected fractures, cleaning and dressing of wounds.

(d)
• Rationale: the primary survey focuses on stabilising life-threatening conditions and emergency care must be rendered without delay; emergent patients need stabilisation, critical treatment and prompt transfer to the appropriate setting.
• Evaluation: the patient has been assessed, stabilised and tested; medical and nursing diagnoses are formulated, initial important treatment is started and plans for disposition (ICU, operating room or general care unit) are made.

questions.explanation: Visitors' and relations' apparel are listed as a reservoir for nosocomial microbes in the ICU. Wearing unwashed street clothes into the ICU can introduce pathogens from the community into the intensive care environment. Bringing personal items in controlled packaging, asking questions, and requesting privacy are not primary infection risks.

questions.explanation: Implementing and evaluating decisions is the final step in the ethical dilemma resolution process. The steps are: (1) identify the ethical issue, (2) gather facts and involve stakeholders, (3) consider ethical principles and legal guidelines, (4) collaborate with interdisciplinary teams, and (5) implement and evaluate decisions. Evaluation ensures accountability and informs future ethical decision-making.
options: The triage process used to prioritize patients during emergency admissions
The SBAR communication framework used in clinical handover situations

questions.question: Evaluating the impact of a decision after implementing it is the FINAL step in:

options: Nosocomial infections are a recent phenomenon first recognized in the 21st century
Hospital-acquired infections have existed for a long time but efforts to curtail them remain limited
Hospital-acquired infections have been completely eradicated in developed countries
All nosocomial infections are preventable with existing hand hygiene protocols alone

questions.explanation:
Hospital-acquired nosocomial infections have existed for a long time, yet limited efforts have been made globally to curtail them adequately. Even developed countries like the US and France report large numbers of cases. Nosocomial infections are not eradicated, not recent, and not preventable by hand hygiene alone — they require a multifaceted control strategy.*

questions.question: The most common ethical dilemma in critical care nursing involves conflict between:
questions.explanation: The most common ethical dilemma in critical care nursing is the conflict between patient autonomy (the right to refuse treatment) and beneficence (the duty to act in the patient's best interest). This arises when patients refuse life-saving treatments or when families demand aggressive care against medical advice, requiring careful ethical navigation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Emergency nursing care is the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of perceived, actual or potential, sudden or urgent, physical or psychosocial problems that are primarily episodic or acute.

(b)
• A separate specialty whose common goal is to restore physiological or psychological stability to the severely ill patient; it uses the nursing process and needs knowledge and skill beyond the nurse generalist.
• Its core knowledge applies to medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and psychiatry; emergencies occur in the community, on a nursing unit or in the ED, so nurses in any area must assess, prioritise and intervene quickly.

(c)
Emergency nursing encompasses independent, dependent and interdependent interventions.

(d)
• Disaster: a serious disruption of the functioning of a community or society causing widespread human, material, economic or environmental losses that exceed its ability to cope with its own resources.
• Disaster epidemiology is the use of epidemiology (study of distribution and determinants of health events in populations) to assess short- and long-term adverse health effects of disasters and predict consequences of future ones.
• Roles/uses: identify priority health problems, causes and risk factors; rapid needs assessment; demographic studies; surveillance; outbreak investigation; programme monitoring and evaluation; surveys.

(e)
• Emergency nurses are often responsible for life-and-death decisions, placing them at high legal risk, so priorities must be set quickly on sound knowledge and judgment.
• They must make triage decisions to expedite care and are at high risk of injury or illness from exposure to infections such as hepatitis, AIDS or other communicable diseases.

(f)
• Independent interventions are unique to nursing: management of the environment, teaching, counselling and initiating referrals.
• Dependent interventions are prescribed by appropriate health care personnel.
• Interdependent interventions (for comparison) are determined by multidisciplinary collaboration.

Describe emergency nursing under the following headings:
(a) definition
(b) scope, goal and knowledge base
(c) types of nursing interventions

The electrolytes that are typically elevated in ARF and require management include:
options: Potassium and other electrolytes that are usually high and require correction
Bicarbonate and calcium, which rise due to metabolic alkalosis in ARF patients
Phosphate and magnesium, which are lowered by impaired renal tubular secretion
Sodium and chloride, which accumulate due to impaired renal chloride excretion
Zinc and copper, which accumulate in renal tubular cells during ARF progression
questions.explanation: In ARF, electrolytes are typically high (particularly potassium, phosphate, and magnesium) due to impaired renal excretion. Hyperkalemia is a life-threatening complication of ARF that can cause fatal arrhythmias. Nursing interventions include electrolyte monitoring and correction of imbalances, with particular vigilance for hyperkalemia requiring urgent treatment.

questions.question: Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis in the ICU is important because it is:
options: Reserved exclusively for patients on mechanical ventilation in the ICU
Used primarily to assess kidney function and electrolyte balance in ICU patients
Less reliable than end-tidal CO2 monitoring for assessing ventilation adequacy
The only method for continuous real-time monitoring of oxygenation status
The single most important test for evaluating respiratory and metabolic disorders
questions.explanation: ABG analysis is described as the single most important test for evaluation of respiratory and metabolic disorders. It provides comprehensive information on pH, PaCO2, PaO2, bicarbonate, and base excess. It is not continuous (unlike EtCO2 monitoring), not limited to ventilated patients, and provides metabolic as well as respiratory information.

questions.question: Which of the following represents an ethical conflict between cultural beliefs and medical care?
options: A patient declining to share their medication history with the care team
A patient requesting a specific brand of medication based on personal preference
A patient refusing dietary changes recommended for post-ICU recovery
A patient refusing a blood transfusion based on deeply held religious doctrine
A patient asking for a second opinion before consenting to a surgical procedure
questions.explanation: A patient refusing a blood transfusion based on religious doctrines represents a conflict between cultural/religious beliefs and evidence-based medical treatment. This is a documented example of how cultural and religious values can shape patient views on medical interventions. Nurses must respect these beliefs while advocating for the patient's well-being through ethical and culturally competent communication.

options: Correct the underlying cause of the arrest
Replace the need for ongoing chest compressions
Sedate the patient during the resuscitation effort
Increase coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure
Directly restart electrical activity of the heart
questions.question: During ACLS, epinephrine is administered to a patient in cardiac arrest primarily to:
questions.explanation: Epinephrine works mainly through vasoconstriction, which increases coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure during chest compressions, improving the chance of return of spontaneous circulation. It does not directly restart cardiac electrical activity or treat the underlying cause. It is given alongside, not instead of, high-quality compressions.

questions.question: The primary mode of transmission of MRSA in healthcare settings is:
questions.explanation: MRSA is transmitted primarily by close contact with infected or colonized persons. This is why contact precautions, including gloves and gowns, are essential when caring for MRSA patients. While MRSA can also spread through environmental contamination, close physical contact is the primary documented mode of transmission in healthcare settings.
options: Airborne transmission via respiratory droplets from colonized patients
Vector-borne transmission by insects in the hospital environment
Close contact with infected or colonized persons in the clinical setting
Waterborne transmission through contaminated drinking water sources
Bloodborne transmission exclusively through needle-stick injury incidents

questions.question: An ethical dilemma arising from scarcity of ICU beds is best addressed through:
options: Exclusive focus on age, prioritizing younger patients for all available ICU beds
Restricting ICU admission to patients with private health insurance coverage
A first-come, first-served policy to ensure fairness without clinical assessment
Allowing families to negotiate directly with administration for ICU bed access
Evidence-based, transparent, and ethically defensible triage criteria and processes
questions.explanation: Ethical dilemmas from ICU bed scarcity are best addressed through evidence-based, transparent, and ethically defensible triage criteria. Principles of justice, utility, equity, and proportionality guide decisions about who receives available resources. Age alone, first-come-first-served, family negotiation, or insurance status as the primary criteria violate principles of fair and ethical resource allocation.

IV infusion sets, catheters, and urinary bags must be set up and changed using aseptic technique. This minimizes the risk of introducing pathogens into sterile body compartments. Aseptic technique is required for all invasive procedures, not only surgical ones, and not just for immunocompromised patients.
questions.question: The ICU nurse setting up IV infusion sets must use which technique?
options: Aseptic technique when setting up and changing all IV lines and equipment
No specific technique if the fluid and infusion set are newly unpackaged
Clean technique to balance infection risk with practical nursing realities
Standard precautions only, reserving aseptic technique for surgical procedures
Barrier technique only when the patient is immunosuppressed or infected

questions.explanation: When a competent patient refuses a life-saving blood transfusion, often based on religious beliefs, the primary ethical principle is autonomy — respecting the patient's right to make informed decisions about their own body and healthcare. While beneficence and non-maleficence create tension, respecting a competent patient's refusal is ethically and legally required in most jurisdictions.
options: Justice, ensuring all patients receive equal access to available blood products
Non-maleficence, preventing harm by overriding the patient's expressed preference
Beneficence, as the nurse must act in the patient's best interest above all else
Autonomy, respecting the patient's right to refuse treatment based on beliefs
Fidelity, maintaining the nurse's promise to provide the best possible care
questions.question: The ethical principle most relevant when a patient refuses a life-saving blood transfusion is:
Key elements of informed consent include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Unanimous agreement among all family members before any treatment proceeds
Comprehension by the patient of the information provided by the healthcare team
Competence verifying the individual's capacity to make a healthcare decision
Voluntariness ensuring the decision is made without coercion or undue influence
Disclosure of all relevant information including risks, benefits, and alternatives
questions.explanation: The key elements of informed consent are disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, and competence. Unanimous agreement among all family members is not a required element of informed consent. When a patient has decision-making capacity, their own consent is sufficient. Family consensus becomes relevant only when the patient lacks capacity.

questions.question: A nurse caring for an ICU patient notes that the endotracheal tube cuff pressure has not been checked in over twelve hours. This omission is significant because inadequate cuff pressure increases the risk of:
options: Improved secretion clearance from the lower airway
Enhanced patient comfort with no associated risk
Better ventilator synchrony with no infection risk
Reduced risk of any airway related complications
questions.explanation: Inadequate endotracheal cuff pressure allows secretions to leak around the cuff into the lower airway, a process called microaspiration, which is a recognised contributor to ventilator-associated pneumonia. Regular cuff pressure monitoring is part of standard ventilator care bundles. This is a patient safety issue, not simply a comfort consideration.

questions.question: Intrarenal ARF is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Intrarenal ARF involves direct damage to the kidney tissue itself from causes such as sepsis, nephrotoxic medications (e.g., aminoglycosides, contrast agents), ischemia, and glomerulonephritis. It is more severe and potentially less reversible than prerenal ARF. Treatment targets the specific cause of kidney damage and may require dialysis for severe cases.
options: Autoimmune glomerulonephritis causing antibody-mediated renal parenchymal damage
Obstruction of urine flow distal to the kidney by stones or tumor compression
Compression of the renal veins causing venous congestion and renal edema
Reduced cardiac output causing insufficient renal perfusion and ischemic injury
Direct damage to kidney tissue itself from sepsis, medications, or other causes
Justice, as resources used in resuscitation should be reserved for younger patients
Autonomy, respecting the patient's right to make decisions about their own care
Beneficence, as healthcare providers always know better than patients what is best
Non-maleficence, as withholding CPR prevents further suffering from failed resuscitation
Fidelity, as nurses must fulfill the patient's previously expressed verbal preferences
questions.question: The ethical basis for allowing a patient to refuse resuscitation through a DNR order is:
questions.explanation: The ethical basis for DNR orders is primarily autonomy — the patient's right to make informed decisions about their own care, including the decision not to receive CPR. This right must be respected even when family members disagree. DNR decisions should ideally be made through advance directives and documented clearly to guide the care team in critical situations.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Vital signs indicate life: pulse/heart rate, respiration, blood pressure, temperature, pupillary constriction to light and level of consciousness; end-tidal CO2, blood gases, electrolytes and pain are also monitored.
• Aim: there are limits compatible with life, so regular monitoring identifies deviations so corrective measures are instituted promptly.

(b)
Non-invasive: pulse/heart rate, blood pressure, pupillary reaction, temperature, respiration. Invasive: arterial blood pressure, central venous pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, cardiac output, left atrial pressure.

(c)
• Pulse 60-90/min (13 years and above); blood pressure 94-140/62-88 mmHg (over 13 years); temperature 36.2-37.2 degrees C; end-tidal CO2 35-45; oxygen saturation 90-100%; hourly urine output 0.5-1 ml/kg/hr.
• ABG: pH 7.33-7.45, PCO2 35-45 mmHg, PO2 75-100 mmHg, HCO3 22-28, BE +/-2; Glasgow Coma Scale 3-15; sodium 135-145 and potassium 3.5-4.5 meq/l, checked 4-hourly or more often.

(d)
• Invasive blood pressure monitoring is continuous and the most reliable; a high core with low peripheral temperature may indicate low cardiac output or infection.
• Equal reactive pupils mean the upper brainstem and third cranial nerve are intact, while unilateral dilatation and non-reactivity with depressed consciousness suggests impaired brainstem function.
• Intubated patients need more vigilance for CO2 retention, secretions in the tube and tube dislodgement; abnormal electrolyte readings are promptly corrected.
• Baseline ABG 5-10 minutes after ICU admission; repeat 30 minutes after ventilator changes, 45 minutes to 1 hour after extubation and 30 minutes after suctioning.

(e)
• Related cautions: pupil dilatation is not a reliable sign of arrest, and the 5Ps of compartment syndrome are not reliable in patients with decreased consciousness.
• Prevention: combine several parameters and invasive/continuous monitoring rather than relying on a single sign.
questions.question:
Describe monitoring of vital signs in the intensive care unit:
(a) what vital signs are and the aims of monitoring
(b) modes of monitoring
(c) parameters monitored with their normal values.
(d) Explain how the findings guide nursing decisions.

Beneficence as an ethical principle in critical care nursing requires nurses to:
questions.explanation: Beneficence requires acting in the best interests of the patient by providing care that promotes well-being and improves outcomes. It is distinct from following patient preferences blindly (autonomy) or administering all possible treatments regardless of benefit. Beneficence involves clinical judgment about what truly benefits the patient, balancing risks and benefits.
options: Act in the best interests of the patient by providing care that promotes well-being
Avoid all interventions that carry any risk of harm to the patient
Follow the patient's preferences even when these clearly worsen their outcome
Prioritize institutional interests above the individual patient's clinical needs
Administer all available treatments to maximize the chance of patient survival

questions.explanation: The four stages of ARF in sequential order are: Stage 1 - Initiation phase (onset of injury); Stage 2 - Oliguric phase (urine output less than 400 ml in 24 hours); Stage 3 - Diuretic or polyuric phase (urine output 3-6 liters per day); Stage 4 - Recovery phase (slow recovery that may require up to one year for complete resolution).
questions.question: The four stages of ARF in sequential order are:
options: Recovery, initiation, polyuric, and oliguric phases from mild to most severe
Diuretic, oliguric, initiation, and recovery phases in reverse clinical order
Oliguric, diuretic, initiation, and recovery phases based on urine output changes
Initiation, oliguric, diuretic (polyuric), and recovery phases in the correct order
Initiation, recovery, oliguric, and diuretic phases in progressive order

questions.explanation: Ethical dilemmas such as those arising from staffing shortages resulting from moral distress and staff turnover can impede nurses' ability to provide optimal care, potentially leading to delays in treatment and adverse patient outcomes. Moral distress-driven staff turnover creates understaffing, directly compromising patient safety and the quality of care delivered.
options: Nursing staff disagree about the most appropriate clinical intervention
The patient's family requests a second opinion on the clinical management
Documentation errors arise from the complexity of caring for ICU patients
Nurses receive insufficient training in advanced clinical monitoring techniques
Staffing shortages from moral distress impede optimal and timely patient care
questions.question: Compromised patient care as a consequence of ethical dilemmas occurs when:
A patient with metastatic cancer complicated by cardiac tamponade would be classified as which ICU priority?
options: Priority 4, because the underlying cancer is not reversible
Priority 4 Category A, as they are too well to benefit from ICU
Priority 1, because of cardiac tamponade requiring immediate intervention
Priority 3, because recovery likelihood is reduced by the malignancy
Priority 2, because the patient needs monitoring with possible intervention
questions.explanation: Patients with metastatic malignancy complicated by a reversible acute complication like cardiac tamponade are Priority 3 – critically ill but with reduced recovery probability because of the underlying disease. They may receive some intensive therapy with defined limits. Priority 4 applies when there is no anticipated benefit at all.

questions.question: A family insists their stable, conscious relative be admitted to ICU 'just to be safe' after a minor fall with no injury. The nurse should explain that ICU admission is reserved for patients who:
options: Have completed a minor procedure earlier that day
Have potentially reversible conditions needing intensive support
Are simply of advanced age with no acute illness
Have any request from concerned family members present
Prefer a private room away from the general ward
questions.explanation: ICU beds are a limited resource allocated to patients with physiological instability who need intensive observation or organ support, not for reassurance alone. A stable, uninjured patient does not meet these clinical criteria. Explaining this respects both resource stewardship and honest communication with the family.

options: 80% fraction of inspired oxygen in patients with chronic lung disease
40% fraction of inspired oxygen to maintain saturation above 90%
70% fraction of inspired oxygen with normal respiratory parameters
50% fraction of inspired oxygen with stable arterial blood gases
60% fraction of inspired oxygen as a discharge threshold criterion
questions.explanation: ICU discharge criteria specify that oxygen requirements should not exceed 60% inspired oxygen concentration. This ensures the patient can be safely managed in a step-down or ward environment. Higher oxygen requirements suggest ongoing respiratory compromise incompatible with discharge from critical care.
questions.question: At discharge from ICU, acceptable oxygen requirements should not exceed:

questions.explanation: A fast, regular, narrow-complex rhythm without clear P waves is characteristic of supraventricular tachycardia, arising from tissue above the ventricles. Sinus tachycardia typically shows identifiable P waves before each QRS. The narrow complex distinguishes it from ventricular tachycardia, which is wide-complex.
questions.question: A nurse reviews an ECG showing a regular rhythm at 160 beats per minute with narrow QRS complexes and no visible P waves. This is most consistent with:
options: Ventricular tachycardia with wide QRS complexes
Atrial fibrillation with an irregularly irregular rhythm
Sinus tachycardia with normal P wave morphology
Third-degree heart block with dissociated rhythms
Supraventricular tachycardia originating above the ventricles

questions.explanation: Allocating scarce resources such as ventilators among multiple patients centres on the ethical principle of justice, which concerns fair and equitable distribution of limited healthcare resources. This differs from autonomy, which concerns individual decision-making, or confidentiality, which concerns information privacy. Triage protocols developed with ethical input help guide these difficult allocation decisions.
questions.question: A nurse caring for multiple critically ill patients during a resource shortage must decide how to allocate limited ventilators. This scenario primarily raises the ethical principle of:
options: Fidelity, keeping promises made to individual patients
Veracity, ensuring complete honesty with each patient
Confidentiality, protecting each patient's private information
Autonomy, respecting each patient's personal preferences
Justice, ensuring fair and equitable resource distribution

questions.explanation: The word triage comes from the French word 'trier' meaning 'to sort.' In the emergency department, triage is used to sort patients into groups based on the severity of their health problems and the immediacy with which problems must be treated. This sorting process ensures that the most critically ill patients receive attention first, optimizing emergency resource utilization.
options: 'To treat' reflecting the primary purpose of triage as initial treatment
'To assess' reflecting the assessment-first approach in emergency nursing
'To sort' reflecting the process of sorting patients by severity of health problems
'To save' reflecting the goal of preserving life in emergency situations
'To prioritize' reflecting the ranking of patients by their clinical importance
questions.question: Triage in emergency nursing is derived from the French word meaning:

options: Cardiac dysrhythmias are adequately controlled at the time of discharge
Neurological stability with adequate seizure control is achieved
Patient requires continued renal replacement therapy indefinitely
Stable haemodynamic parameters without vasopressor support
Intravenous inotropic and vasodilator support is no longer necessary
questions.explanation: ICU discharge criteria include stable hemodynamics, controlled arrhythmias, cessation of IV inotropes, stable respiratory status, and neurological stability. A requirement for ongoing renal replacement therapy does not preclude discharge if other parameters are met, but it is not listed as a criterion supporting discharge. The need for chronic dialysis may allow discharge if critically ill acute problems are resolved.
questions.question: Cardiac discharge criteria from the ICU include all of the following EXCEPT:
The practice of keeping patients in the ICU when care is futile should be:
questions.explanation: Keeping patients in the ICU when care is futile should be discouraged, as it wastes scarce and costly resources that could benefit other patients. The decision to continue or withdraw therapy should be ethically grounded and based on clinical prognosis. Family wishes alone or financial considerations should not override clinical and ethical judgment.
options: Determined entirely by the family's wishes regardless of prognosis
Permitted indefinitely if no alternative level of care is available
Actively discouraged as it wastes scarce and costly ICU resources
Encouraged to prevent family distress and provide false reassurance
Based solely on the financial resources available to the patient
Completing all administrative requirements for effective hospital management
Advocating for nursing as a profession during governmental health policy discussions
Arguing against patient decisions that conflict with medical recommendations
Supporting and promoting the patient's rights, needs, and best interests
Requesting additional nursing staff to ensure adequate bedside care provision
questions.explanation: Advocacy in nursing means actively supporting and promoting the patient's rights, needs, and best interests. It includes ensuring patients are provided with clear, comprehensive information, facilitating communication between patients and the healthcare team, and speaking up when patient rights are at risk. Advocacy is a core nursing responsibility particularly in critical care.
questions.question: Advocacy in nursing ethics means:

options: Unilaterally decide to reduce the treatment provided
Raise the concern with the team for review
Discuss the concern only with the patient's family alone
Say nothing since decisions rest solely with physicians
Document the concern without further team communication
questions.explanation: When a nurse identifies a potential ethical concern about ongoing treatment, the appropriate action is to raise it with the multidisciplinary team to prompt a formal review of the care plan, ensuring the concern is addressed collaboratively. Acting unilaterally or staying silent both fail to appropriately advocate for the patient. Team-based ethical review supports balanced, informed decision-making.
questions.question: A nurse is concerned that a patient's ongoing critical care treatment is causing significant suffering with little chance of benefit. The most appropriate initial action is to:

A critical care nurse is required to continue aggressive treatment for a terminally ill patient at the family's request, although she believes palliative care would be more appropriate; she feels frustrated and guilty.
(a) Identify the problem indicated.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the underlying mechanism.
(c) Outline the management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Moral distress: nurses are unable to act according to their ethical beliefs because of institutional constraints or policies.
• Features: frustration, guilt and professional dissatisfaction; also anxiety, burnout, uncertainty and self-doubt.

(b)
• Predisposing factors: being compelled to give treatments believed futile or not in the patient's best interest (e.g. at the family's request), institutional constraints, resource limitations, increased patient mortality and rapid ethically charged decisions.
• Mechanism: the nurse knows the ethically appropriate action but is constrained from taking it, leading to psychological disequilibrium and emotional suffering.

(c)
• Create a supportive work environment where nurses can discuss ethical concerns and seek guidance; provide policies for ethical consultation and resources for coping.
• Ethics committees offer case consultation, conflict resolution and support for providers, reducing moral distress and giving clarity; preventive ethics includes support systems for staff moral distress.
• Institutions should provide regular ethics training, peer support, clear protocols and open dialogue; nurses should stay informed on guidelines, advocate for patient-centred care and collaborate with teams.
• Interdisciplinary collaboration through ethics rounds and ethics consultation services supports shared responsibility for ethical decisions.

questions.explanation: Ethics is grounded in philosophical reasoning about what is right and wrong, while law consists of rules created and enforced by governments with tangible sanctions such as fines or imprisonment. Not all laws align with ethical norms, and not all ethical obligations are legally enforced. Ethics and law are related but distinct frameworks.
options: Ethics is grounded in philosophical reasoning while law has enforceable sanctions
Ethics applies only to nurses while law governs physicians and hospital administrators
Law is based on cultural values while ethics is determined by religious bodies
Law is internal and personal while ethics is externally enforced by governments
Ethics and law are identical concepts applied differently in various contexts
questions.question: The difference between ethics and law in healthcare is best described as:

questions.explanation: A terminal patient refusing CPR while family demands full resuscitation illustrates the conflict between patient autonomy (the patient's documented refusal) and beneficence (the family's belief that resuscitation acts in the patient's best interest). This is a classic critical care ethical dilemma requiring sensitive communication, ethical consultation, and advocacy for the patient's documented wishes.
questions.question: Which of the following illustrates a conflict between patient autonomy and beneficence?
options: A nurse who disagrees with a colleague about the patient's fluid management
A terminal patient refusing CPR while the family demands full resuscitation
A physician failing to document a patient's clinical assessment findings
A patient in a coma for whom no advance directive or surrogate is available
A nurse administering medications accurately without patient knowledge

questions.explanation: Priority 1 patients are critically ill and unstable, requiring intensive treatment and monitoring that cannot be provided outside the ICU, including ventilator support and vasoactive drug infusions. No therapeutic limits are placed on their care. The other options describe patients who do not meet the full Priority 1 threshold.
questions.question: Priority 1 patients in the ICU Prioritization Model are characterized by:
options: Patients with terminal illness receiving comfort and palliative care
Post-operative patients with no requirement for hemodynamic support
Patients with chronic illness who occasionally need acute observation
Stable patients requiring standard nursing care without monitoring
Critically ill unstable patients needing intensive treatment and monitoring

questions.explanation: A falling Glasgow Coma Scale indicates evolving neurological compromise even when other vital signs are normal, and is an urgent indication for critical care referral. Waiting for imaging or relying solely on stable vitals risks missing a deteriorating brain injury. Early ICU involvement allows for airway protection and close monitoring.
questions.question: A nurse assessing a patient for ICU admission notes normal vital signs but a rapidly falling Glasgow Coma Scale after a head injury. This finding most strongly indicates the need for:
options: Urgent ICU referral for neurological deterioration
Discharge with outpatient neurology follow-up arranged
Delay of referral until imaging results are reviewed
Reassurance since vital signs remain within normal limits
Routine neuro-observations continued on the general ward

questions.question: Palliative care in critical care nursing is characterized by:
options: Symptom-focused management prioritizing comfort and quality of life
Restricting all medications to analgesics only in the terminal phase
Aggressive curative treatment with secondary consideration of comfort
Treatment aimed exclusively at extending the patient's life by any means
Withdrawing all interventions including nursing care in the final hours
questions.explanation: Palliative care involves symptom-focused management that prioritizes the patient's comfort and quality of life. It can coexist with active treatment and is not limited to the terminal phase. Engaging palliative care teams is recommended in cases of futile treatment to provide compassionate care that aligns with the patient's goals and values.

MRSA (Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is associated with healthcare-related bloodstream and catheter-related infections. It is transmitted by close contact with infected persons and is resistant to methicillin, amoxicillin, and penicillin. It is a gram-positive coccus, not a gram-negative rod, and requires specific antibiotics such as vancomycin.
options: It is eliminated by standard cleaning with soap and water in the ICU
It is effectively treated with standard doses of amoxicillin or penicillin
It is transmitted by airborne droplet nuclei and requires respiratory isolation
It is caused by gram-negative rods and spreads through contaminated water
It is associated with catheter-related infections and resistant to methicillin
questions.question: MRSA in the ICU is best characterized by which of the following statements?

questions.explanation: A progressively lengthening PR interval culminating in a dropped QRS complex, followed by resumption of the pattern, is the classic description of Mobitz type I, or Wenckebach, second-degree block. Mobitz type II shows a constant PR interval before sudden dropped beats. Recognising this pattern helps guide monitoring intensity and treatment decisions.
options: First-degree atrioventricular block with fixed delay
Normal sinus rhythm with occasional variation
Second-degree atrioventricular block, Mobitz type I
Second-degree atrioventricular block, Mobitz type II
questions.question: A nurse observes a progressively lengthening PR interval on successive beats until a QRS complex is dropped, then the cycle repeats. This pattern describes:

questions.explanation: Inhalation injury can cause progressive airway oedema over hours, potentially leading to complete airway obstruction even if initial symptoms appear mild, making early recognition and airway monitoring critical. Waiting for obvious distress before intervening can result in a difficult emergency airway. This risk is distinct from chronic lung changes that develop over a longer time course.
options: Chronic lung fibrosis developing within hours
Pneumothorax as the primary expected finding
Progressive airway oedema leading to obstruction
Immediate resolution of any airway swelling
No airway risk if the burn appears superficial
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with an inhalation burn injury should prioritise assessment for which early airway complication?

options: Providing identical care to all family members admitted to the same hospital unit
Allowing the family to make all medical decisions for all hospitalized patients
Making the family responsible for all nursing tasks to reduce hospital workload
Integrating the patient's family into the care process with respect and collaboration
Restricting all care decisions to family members rather than the patient
questions.question: Family-centered care as an ethical concept in nursing means:
questions.explanation: Family-centered care is an ethical approach that integrates the patient's family into the care process through collaboration, open communication, and respect for family values and cultural beliefs. It recognizes the family's vital role in the patient's well-being. This is particularly important in pediatric nursing and critical care where family support significantly affects outcomes.

questions.question: Dialysis therapy in ARF is indicated when:
questions.explanation: Dialysis therapy in ARF is indicated in severe cases where waste products and excess fluid cannot be adequately managed pharmacologically. Indications include severe hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, uremic complications, and fluid overload refractory to diuretics. Dialysis temporarily replaces kidney function until renal recovery occurs or, in irreversible cases, as long-term renal replacement therapy.
options: The patient's serum creatinine rises above 1.5 mg/dl from baseline values
The patient's urine output returns to normal with conservative management alone
The patient develops mild proteinuria and microscopic hematuria on urinalysis
Severe cases require waste removal and fluid correction beyond pharmacological management
The patient has completed the oliguric phase and entered the diuretic phase

questions.question: A nurse notes the cardiac monitor shows ventricular fibrillation with no pulse. The most appropriate immediate action is to:
questions.explanation: Ventricular fibrillation with no pulse is a shockable rhythm requiring immediate unsynchronised defibrillation combined with ongoing high-quality chest compressions until the defibrillator is ready. Synchronised cardioversion is used for certain unstable rhythms with a pulse, not for pulseless VF. Delay in defibrillation significantly reduces survival chances.
options: Prepare for immediate defibrillation while compressions continue
Administer synchronised cardioversion at a low energy
Give oral medication to control the rhythm first
Perform a precordial thump as the sole treatment
Wait several minutes to see if it resolves alone

questions.explanation: Long QT syndrome, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, Brugada syndrome, and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia are arrhythmic syndromes not due to structural heart disease that are associated with sudden cardiac death. They account for 5-10% of sudden cardiac deaths. These are electrical disorders, not structural or ischemic.
questions.question: Long QT syndrome and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome are examples of:
options: Complications of coronary artery disease in patients with hypertension
Post-operative arrhythmias in patients after open cardiac surgical procedures
Structural heart disease causing cardiomegaly and pump failure
Non-cardiac causes of sudden cardiac arrest such as metabolic disorders
Arrhythmic syndromes not due to structural heart disease, causing SCD

questions.explanation: Dullness to percussion with diminished breath sounds over the lower lung fields is characteristic of fluid accumulation in the pleural space compressing the lung, distinguishing it from the hyperresonance typically seen with pneumothorax. Recognising this pattern helps guide diagnostic thoracentesis and management. Consolidation from pneumonia typically produces dullness but with different associated findings such as crackles and bronchial breath sounds.
options: Fluid accumulation compressing the underlying lung tissue
Normal age-related change in lung sounds
Air trapped within the pleural space instead
questions.question: A nurse notes that a patient with a large pleural effusion has diminished breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the lower lung fields. The most likely explanation is:

questions.explanation: The normal PaO2 range is 75-100 mmHg. This value reflects adequate arterial oxygen tension in a normally breathing adult. Values below 75 mmHg indicate hypoxemia requiring intervention. The other ranges stated are either below normal (reflecting hypoxemia) or above normal and not specified in the document.
options: 90-120 mmHg indicating optimal oxygenation in mechanically ventilated patients
60-80 mmHg reflecting acceptable mild hypoxemia in critically ill patients
80-110 mmHg reflecting the standard for patients receiving supplemental oxygen
75-100 mmHg as the specified normal arterial oxygen pressure range
70-90 mmHg as the ICU standard for adequate arterial oxygenation
questions.question: The normal PaO2 range for ICU patients in arterial blood gas analysis is:
When a patient lacks decision-making capacity in the ICU, informed consent is addressed by:
options: Proceeding with all interventions without any form of consent documentation
Obtaining consent from the nursing team as the patient's primary caregivers
Relying on advance directives or consulting legally designated surrogate decision-makers
Waiting until the patient regains capacity before providing any treatment
Allowing the hospital administration to provide consent for all necessary treatments
questions.explanation: When a patient lacks decision-making capacity, advance directives guide treatment decisions, or legally designated surrogate decision-makers (next of kin or proxies) are consulted. In true emergencies without available directives or surrogates, emergency treatment principles permit life-saving interventions guided by beneficence. Ignoring consent or defaulting to administration is unethical.

questions.question: Non-cardiac causes of cardiac arrest account for approximately what proportion of cases?
options: 5-10% of all cardiac arrest cases with mostly arrhythmic causes
15-25% of cardiac arrest cases from causes outside the heart itself
50% of cases in young patients without prior known cardiac disease
30-40% of all cases from non-cardiac systemic disorders globally
10-15% of cases from structural cardiac disease not related to CAD
questions.explanation: Non-cardiac causes account for approximately 15-25% of cardiac arrest cases. The most common non-cardiac causes are trauma, gastrointestinal bleeding, aortic rupture, intracranial hemorrhage, overdose, drowning, and pulmonary embolism. Cardiac causes (coronary artery disease, structural heart disease, arrhythmias) account for the remaining 75-85%.

questions.question: A patient's PaO2 is 55 mmHg on room air, well below the ICU target range. This finding indicates the patient requires:
options: Only reassurance without objective clinical reassessment
Immediate discontinuation of all oxygen therapy
Fluid restriction as the primary corrective measure
No intervention since the value is within limits
Supplemental oxygen and further respiratory assessment
questions.explanation: A PaO2 of 55 mmHg is significantly below the expected normal range and reflects hypoxaemia requiring supplemental oxygen and further evaluation for the underlying cause. Delaying oxygen therapy risks worsening tissue hypoxia. Ongoing respiratory assessment guides the level of support needed.

questions.question: A nurse notes an ICU patient meets criteria for quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, including altered mentation, low blood pressure, and increased respiratory rate. This finding should prompt the nurse to:
options: Attribute all findings solely to sedation medication
Document the findings with no further action needed
Assume these are normal ICU baseline findings
Escalate for urgent evaluation of possible sepsis
Wait until the next scheduled round to reassess
questions.explanation: A positive quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score indicates a higher risk of poor outcomes from sepsis and should prompt urgent clinical evaluation rather than routine documentation or delayed reassessment. This screening tool helps identify patients needing more intensive monitoring and rapid intervention. Timely escalation can prevent progression to septic shock.

Contact precautions require the use of gown and gloves for direct contact with the patient or their environment to prevent transmission of organisms spread by direct or indirect contact. A fitted respirator is used for airborne precautions, not contact precautions. Correctly matching precaution type to transmission route is essential for effective infection control.
questions.question: A nurse is applying contact precautions for a patient with a multidrug-resistant organism. This primarily requires the nurse to:
options: Apply precautions only during invasive procedures performed
Use standard precautions only with no additional measures
Avoid entering the room under any circumstances
Wear a fitted respirator mask for every interaction
Use gown and gloves for all direct patient contact
Determine legal liability for adverse patient outcomes in the clinical setting
Override family and patient decisions when they conflict with hospital protocols
Replace the role of the multidisciplinary team in all ethical case management
Assess professional competence of nurses involved in ethical conflict situations
Provide a neutral platform for discussing ethical dilemmas and ensuring ethical decisions
questions.question: Hospital ethics committees in critical care primarily serve to:
questions.explanation: Hospital ethics committees provide a neutral platform for discussing ethical dilemmas, ensuring that decisions are ethically sound and legally defensible. They are particularly valuable in contentious cases such as disagreements about withdrawal of care. Ethics committees complement, rather than replace, the multidisciplinary team's ethical decision-making role.

The impact on reputation refers specifically to the nurse's professional credibility, which may be questioned if ethical issues are not handled appropriately. This affects trust from patients and colleagues and can have long-term career implications. Proper ethical education, consultation, and transparent decision-making protect both professional reputation and patient trust.
questions.question: Impact on professional reputation as a consequence of mishandled ethical dilemmas refers to:
options: A nurse's professional credibility may be questioned if ethical issues are mishandled
The patient's social standing is affected by disclosure of their diagnosis publicly
Patients lose trust in the healthcare system after experiencing ethical conflicts
The hospital's reputation suffers when ethical conflicts become publicly known
Physicians lose their medical license when involved in ethical violations

questions.explanation: Obstructive shock arises specifically from a mechanical blockage to blood flow, such as tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, or massive pulmonary embolism, distinguishing it from the other categories. Cardiogenic shock is due to pump failure, hypovolaemic shock to volume loss, and distributive shock to vasodilation, each with a distinct mechanism. Correctly matching mechanism to category supports accurate clinical reasoning and targeted treatment.
options: Neurogenic shock caused by mechanical vessel obstruction
Obstructive shock caused by mechanical blood flow blockage
Cardiogenic shock caused by excessive fluid loss
Distributive shock caused by primary pump failure
Hypovolaemic shock caused by widespread vasodilation
questions.question: A nurse is educating junior staff about the four main categories of shock. Which pairing correctly matches the shock type with its primary mechanism?

options: Justice regarding fair resource distribution decisions
Confidentiality and the patient's right to control information
Fidelity regarding institutional policy compliance only
Beneficence regarding direct clinical treatment decisions
questions.explanation: Sharing a competent patient's health information with family without consent breaches confidentiality, which protects the patient's right to control who accesses their personal health information. This is distinct from principles concerning resource allocation or direct physical harm. Respecting confidentiality, even with well-meaning intentions, is a core ethical and legal obligation in nursing practice.
questions.question: A nurse discovers that a critically ill patient's family has been given information about the patient's condition without the patient's prior consent, despite the patient being conscious and competent. This raises a concern primarily related to:
A chaplain’s unique contribution to resolving ethical dilemmas in critical care is:
questions.explanation: A chaplain's unique contribution to ethical dilemma resolution is providing insights into the patient's religious beliefs, spiritual values, and existential concerns. This is particularly valuable when cultural or religious factors influence the patient's or family's decisions about treatment. The chaplain addresses spiritual dimensions that other team members may not be equipped to assess.
options: Providing clinical expertise in pain management and palliative symptom control
Providing insights into the patient's religious beliefs and spiritual values
Reviewing the patient's insurance coverage and financial eligibility for treatment
Offering legal guidance on advance directive documentation and validity
Conducting formal psychiatric assessment of the patient's decision-making capacity
Confirms that the patient has a fever but is adequately peripherally perfused
Represents a benign finding in post-operative patients after major surgery
Indicates normal physiological response to stress in a recovering ICU patient
May indicate low cardiac output and is also an indicator of active infection
Suggests adequate peripheral perfusion with normal cardiac output
questions.explanation: A high core temperature with low peripheral temperature may indicate low cardiac output, reflecting peripheral vasoconstriction as a compensatory mechanism. It is also an indicator of infection. This pattern reflects poor peripheral perfusion despite a high central temperature and warrants urgent assessment of cardiac function and infection status.
questions.question: Temperature monitoring in the ICU is important because high core with low peripheral temperature:

questions.explanation:
Pupillary reaction monitoring is particularly important in patients with neurological problems because it assesses brainstem and third cranial nerve integrity. Unilateral dilation with non-reactivity and altered consciousness indicates brainstem dysfunction. While important in all ICU patients, it is most clinically significant for neurological monitoring.*

# SUBTOPIC 4: CARDIAC ARREST AND CPR IN CRITICAL CARE NURSING
questions.question: Pupillary reaction in the ICU is particularly important in patients with:
options: Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilatory support and monitoring
Septic shock requiring vasopressor support and fluid resuscitation management
Metabolic disturbances such as diabetic ketoacidosis requiring insulin infusion
Neurological problems requiring assessment of brainstem and cranial nerve status
Renal failure requiring continuous renal replacement therapy in the ICU

questions.question: The normal heart rate for infants aged 1-3 years in the ICU is:
questions.explanation: The normal heart rate for children aged 1-3 years is 90-140 beats per minute. The documented age-specific ranges are: 0-12 months: 120-160; 1-3 years: 90-140; 3-5 years: 80-110; 5-12 years: 75-100; 13+ years: 60-90 bpm. Applying pediatric-specific normal ranges avoids misclassifying a normal pediatric heart rate as tachycardia.
options: Between 120 and 160 beats per minute as in neonates at 0-12 months
Between 75 and 100 beats per minute as in children aged 5-12 years
Between 90 and 140 beats per minute as specified for this age group
Between 60 and 90 beats per minute as in adults and older teenagers
Between 80 and 110 beats per minute as in children aged 3-5 years

questions.question: A nurse administering intravenous fluids to a patient in hypovolaemic shock should monitor most closely for which sign of adequate response to resuscitation?
questions.explanation: Effective fluid resuscitation in hypovolaemic shock should produce improving blood pressure, decreasing heart rate toward normal, and increasing urine output, reflecting restored perfusion. Persistent abnormal vital signs or unchanged perfusion indicators suggest inadequate resuscitation or an ongoing source of loss. Monitoring these trends guides the adequacy and rate of further fluid administration.
options: Continued cool, clammy skin with no change noted
Falling blood pressure despite ongoing fluid therapy
Persistently rising heart rate despite fluid administration
Improving blood pressure, heart rate, and urine output
No change in mental status following resuscitation

questions.explanation: Navigating complex ethical situations without clear guidelines creates legal and ethical uncertainty, increasing the risk of legal repercussions and professional liability for nurses. This uncertainty is particularly challenging in areas such as informed consent, DNR orders, and withdrawal of treatment. Clear institutional guidelines and access to ethics consultation reduce this uncertainty.
questions.question: Legal and ethical uncertainty in managing ethical dilemmas in nursing leads to:
options: Greater use of advance directives by patients to prevent future uncertainty
Enhanced collaboration between the legal and nursing teams in patient care
Automatic referral of all cases to the court system for judicial resolution
Increased risk of legal repercussions and greater professional liability for nurses
Improved clinical outcomes as nurses are more careful in their practice

questions.question:
Describe end-of-life decisions in critical care:
(a) end-of-life care, withholding and withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment
(b) advance directives, DNR orders and palliative care.
(c) Explain how these guide nursing decisions.
(d) Explain why they may cause conflict or harm, and how this is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• End-of-life care is comprehensive support in the final stages of terminal illness that focuses on comfort, dignity and quality of life rather than cure.
• Decisions involve initiating, withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatments such as mechanical ventilation, dialysis and vasopressors; withdrawal is discontinuing treatment that no longer benefits the patient, guided by autonomy, beneficence and non-maleficence.

(b)
An advance directive is a legal document stating care preferences if the person cannot communicate; a DNR order reflects a patient's wish not to be resuscitated; palliative care in critical care manages symptoms and improves quality of life for patients and families through an interdisciplinary approach addressing physical, emotional and spiritual needs.

(c)
• Nurses honour documented wishes (autonomy), advocate for the patient's best interest and facilitate discussions between patient, family and medical team.
• Priority 3 patients may have limits on therapy such as no intubation or CPR; if deterioration is irreversible, withdrawal of therapy is carried out in the ICU and keeping patients when care is futile is discouraged.
• Administering high doses of painkillers for relief in a terminally ill patient follows the principle of double effect: the intent is pain relief, not death.

(d)
• Withdrawal of life support can be perceived as euthanasia, and families may see withholding care as giving up, insisting on aggressive treatment despite the patient's directive.
• Nurses experience moral distress when made to give treatment they think futile.
• Prevention: a family meeting with the interdisciplinary team (physician, nurse, social worker, chaplain) to explain prognosis and treatment limits, address emotional concerns and build consensus.
• Transparent, empathetic communication, advance directives, ethics committees and the four-quadrant approach (medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life, contextual features) also help.
• In the case described, the family agreed to transition to palliative care and the patient was extubated and given comfort care.
• Emotional resilience training and peer support for nurses are also recommended.

questions.question: A patient's arterial blood gas shows pH 7.32, PaCO2 32 mmHg, and bicarbonate 15 mEq/L. This pattern most likely represents:
options: Normal acid-base status with incidental findings
Metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation
Primary respiratory alkalosis with no compensation
Respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation
questions.explanation: A low pH with a low bicarbonate reflects a primary metabolic acidosis, while the reduced PaCO2 shows the respiratory system is compensating by blowing off carbon dioxide. Since the pH remains abnormal, compensation is only partial. Identifying the primary disturbance guides treatment of the underlying metabolic cause.

questions.question: Patients admitted to the ICU should ideally be referred BEFORE:
options: The family has had an opportunity to discuss the treatment plan
The senior nursing officer approves the level of nursing care required
Laboratory results confirm the severity of the presenting illness
The admitting consultant has reviewed existing hospital guidelines
Their condition reaches a point from which recovery is impossible
questions.explanation: ICU referral should occur before the patient's condition reaches a point from which recovery is impossible. Early referral maximizes the chance of recovery, reduces organ dysfunction, and shortens ICU and hospital stays. Waiting for laboratory confirmation or family discussions before referral may critically delay life-saving intervention.

options: Normal expected output for a critically ill adult
A catheter malfunction that requires no further action
Early acute kidney injury or inadequate renal perfusion
Improved renal function following recent treatment
Excessive fluid administration requiring diuretic therapy
questions.explanation: Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hr sustained over several hours is a recognised early indicator of acute kidney injury or inadequate renal perfusion in critically ill adults. This finding should trigger prompt assessment of haemodynamic status and possible causes. Early recognition allows timely intervention to prevent worsening renal function.
questions.question: During hourly urine output monitoring, an ICU nurse records less than 0.5 mL/kg/hr for three consecutive hours in an adult patient. This finding should prompt the nurse to suspect:

questions.explanation: A pregnant woman electing for a home birth according to her own informed preferences is an example of autonomy — the right to make decisions about one's own body and healthcare. Birth plans, choice of delivery method, and maternity decisions are classic examples of autonomy in healthcare. The choice should be informed and voluntary, made by the patient herself.
questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates the principle of autonomy in a maternity care setting?
options: A pregnant woman elects for a home birth according to her informed personal preferences
The midwife decides the birth plan based on clinical assessment of the mother
Family members choose the birthing method for the patient based on cultural norms
The hospital policy mandates all births take place in the delivery room only
The obstetrician determines the mode of delivery for all obstetric patients

questions.explanation: Rapid defibrillation is indicated when a shockable rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) is detected. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) are non-shockable rhythms managed with CPR and adrenaline. Sinus tachycardia and complete heart block are not indications for defibrillation in the same context.
options: A shockable rhythm such as ventricular fibrillation is detected
The patient has asystole (flat line) on the cardiac monitor display
The patient has complete heart block with haemodynamic instability
The patient is in pulseless electrical activity with organized rhythm
The patient is in sinus tachycardia with compromised blood pressure
questions.question: In the context of cardiac arrest management, defibrillation is indicated when:
A nurse suctioning a ventilated patient's endotracheal tube should limit each suction pass to approximately how long to avoid hypoxia?
options: As long as needed until secretions are gone
No more than about ten to fifteen seconds
Approximately one full minute per suction pass
There is no time limit for suction passes
Only a few seconds regardless of secretions
questions.explanation: Suction passes should be limited to approximately ten to fifteen seconds because prolonged suctioning removes oxygen from the airway and can cause significant hypoxia and dysrhythmias. Pre-oxygenating the patient before suctioning further reduces this risk. This time limit balances secretion clearance with patient safety.

questions.question:
Describe moral distress in critical care nursing under the following headings:
(a) causes
(b) mechanism
(c) clinical features
(d) complications/impact.
(e) State how it is recognised and monitored.
(f) Outline its management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Institutional constraints or policies that stop nurses acting on their ethical beliefs, such as being compelled to provide treatments they believe are futile or not in the patient's best interest (e.g. continuing aggressive treatment at the family's request).
• Contributing factors: resource limitations, increased patient mortality, rapid ethically charged decisions and staffing shortages.

(b)
The nurse knows the ethically appropriate action but is constrained from taking it, leading to psychological disequilibrium and emotional suffering.

(c)
Frustration, guilt and professional dissatisfaction; anxiety, burnout, uncertainty and self-doubt.

(d)
• Job dissatisfaction, decreased quality of patient care, increased turnover intentions, strained team relationships and communication breakdown that compromise patient safety.
• Also legal and ethical uncertainty with risk of liability, personal distress affecting mental health, delays in treatment and damage to professional reputation.

(e)
The ethics committee monitors unit practices and identifies recurring ethical challenges (preventive ethics).

(f)
• Create a supportive work environment where nurses discuss ethical concerns and seek guidance; policies for ethical consultations and resources for coping.
• Ethics committees provide case consultation, conflict resolution and support, reduce moral distress and clarify complex situations.
• Institutions should offer regular ethics training, peer support, clear protocols and open dialogue; train emotional resilience.
• Promote interdisciplinary collaboration (ethics rounds, team-building workshops, ethics consultation services) and simulation-based learning and mentorship.
• Nurses should advocate for patient-centred care, improve communication skills and reflect on their practice.

questions.question: A nurse notes absent P waves, a narrow QRS complex, and a regular rate of 50 beats per minute originating from the atrioventricular node. This rhythm is best described as:
options: Sinus rhythm originating from the SA node
Complete heart block with dissociated activity
Ventricular rhythm with wide QRS complexes
Junctional rhythm arising from the AV node
Atrial flutter with sawtooth wave pattern
questions.explanation: A junctional rhythm arises from the atrioventricular node when the sinoatrial node fails to initiate the rhythm, typically producing a narrow QRS complex without normal P waves, at a rate around 40 to 60 beats per minute. This differs from ventricular rhythms, which are wide-complex, and from sinus rhythms, which show a normal P wave before each QRS. Identifying the origin of the rhythm helps determine the underlying cause and appropriate management.

questions.question: Pain management in crush injury is considered crucial because:
questions.explanation: Pain management in crush injury is crucial for patient comfort and cooperation with treatment. Effective pain control allows the patient to participate more actively in their care, reduces physiological stress responses, and improves overall outcomes. While pain is also a sign of compartment syndrome, appropriate analgesic management does not mask the clinical signs when assessment is systematic.
options: Pain management replaces the need for fluid resuscitation in acute management
Pain is an unreliable indicator of compartment syndrome and must be masked
Analgesics prevent compartment syndrome by reducing intracompartmental pressure
It is crucial for patient comfort and cooperation with treatment and recovery
Untreated pain accelerates rhabdomyolysis and worsens acute kidney injury

questions.question: In a 1-year-old to 3-year-old child in the ICU, the normal systolic blood pressure is:
options: Between 50-70 mmHg systolic as in the neonatal period after delivery
Between 84-120 mmHg systolic as in children between 5 and 12 years
Between 94-140 mmHg systolic as in teenagers 13 years and above
Between 80-112 mmHg systolic according to age-specific ICU norms
Between 74-100 mmHg systolic as in 4-day to 1-year-old infants
questions.explanation: The normal systolic blood pressure for a child aged 1-3 years is 80-112 mmHg. The age-specific ranges are: 0-12 hours: 50-70; 0-4 days: 69-90; 4 days-1 year: 74-100; 1-3 years: 80-112; 3-5 years: 82-110; 5-12 years: 84-120; >13 years: 94-140 mmHg systolic. Applying the wrong age range can lead to misinterpretation.

Hypotension, tachycardia, and cool, clammy skin following significant blood loss are classic signs of hypovolaemic shock, where reduced circulating volume impairs tissue perfusion. The body compensates with vasoconstriction, producing the characteristic cool periphery, unlike the warm periphery often seen in early distributive shock. Rapid volume replacement is the priority intervention.
options: Obstructive shock from mechanical circulatory blockage
Hypovolaemic shock from blood volume loss
Distributive shock from vasodilation and sepsis
Neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury
Cardiogenic shock from primary pump failure
questions.question: A nurse assessing a trauma patient notes hypotension, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and a history of significant blood loss. This presentation is most consistent with:
Systemic clinical manifestations of crush injury include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Myocardial hypertrophy and progressive cardiac failure are chronic cardiac conditions, not systemic manifestations of acute crush injury. Systemic manifestations of crush injury include tachycardia, hypotension, fever, oliguria, and altered mental status — all reflecting the acute systemic inflammatory response, volume depletion, and organ dysfunction resulting from crush syndrome.
options: Oliguria from myoglobin-induced acute tubular injury and renal failure
Myocardial hypertrophy and progressive cardiac failure from systemic pressure
Fever and altered mental status as systemic inflammatory response signs
Tachycardia and hypotension from volume depletion and systemic inflammation
Fever, tachycardia, and hemodynamic instability from SIRS activation

questions.question: Respiratory monitoring in the ICU is particularly important for intubated patients because:
questions.explanation: Respiratory monitoring in ICU patients who are intubated requires vigilance for CO2 retention, secretion accumulation in the endotracheal tube, tube dislodgement, and other tube-related problems. Intubated patients cannot independently protect their airways or adjust their ventilation, making continuous respiratory monitoring critical for their safety.
options: Non-intubated patients never develop respiratory problems in the ICU
The capnograph provides the only accurate measure of respiratory function
Intubated patients require vigilance for CO2 retention, secretions, and tube problems
Respiratory monitoring replaces blood gas analysis in all ventilated patients
Respiratory rate monitoring alone is sufficient for ventilated ICU patients

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Risk factors: age (arrest becomes more common with age), male sex (affected more often), cigarette smoking (current and former smokers), high blood pressure, high cholesterol, lack of physical exercise, obesity, diabetes, family history; a prior episode of sudden cardiac arrest increases the risk of future episodes.
• Heredity, gender and age cannot be changed; tobacco use, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes and overweight/obesity can be changed.

(b)
• Recurrent sudden cardiac arrest/death: the heart abruptly beats in an abnormal or irregular rhythm, with no organised electrical activity, no consistent ventricular contraction and inadequate cardiac output.
• Loss of cerebral perfusion causes rapid loss of consciousness and cessation of breathing; survival with treatment is about 8% and many survivors have significant disability.

(c)
• Monitor vital signs (pulse, blood pressure) and heart sounds; monitor ECG and chest x-ray changes closely; monitor laboratory status (BUN, creatinine), electrolytes and nutrition; assess neurological status and response to treatment.
• Preventive measures: promote healthy diet, exercise and smoking cessation; blood pressure control and cholesterol lowering; administer medications as prescribed; oxygen by nasal prongs or face mask as indicated; IV solutions as prescribed.
• Encourage rest, semirecumbent in bed or chair, and assist with physical care; give emotional support to patient and family; educate on the cause of arrest, risk factors and prevention.
• Priority intervention: an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) - a battery-powered device that monitors the heart's electrical activity and delivers a shock when an arrhythmia or asystole is detected.
• Justification: ICDs are used as secondary prevention in people who survived sudden cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia, which is this patient's history.
questions.question:
An older male patient in the ICU is a cigarette smoker with high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity and diabetes, takes little physical exercise, has a family history of heart disease, and has survived a previous episode of sudden cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation.
(a) Identify his risk factors for sudden cardiac arrest.
(b) State the potential complications.
(c) State the monitoring parameters and the preventive nursing measures, and justify the priority intervention.

options: Improve the accuracy of rhythm interpretation only
Have no measurable effect on resuscitation outcomes
Allow the rescuer to rest without any consequence
Are required for at least thirty seconds between cycles
Reduce coronary perfusion pressure built up during compressions
questions.explanation: Even brief interruptions in chest compressions cause coronary perfusion pressure to fall rapidly, and it takes time to rebuild once compressions resume, reducing overall effectiveness. Team-based resuscitation aims to minimise hands-off time for tasks such as rhythm checks or shocks. This principle underlies coordinated, efficient resuscitation team roles.
