questions.explanation: Accountability in nursing is the responsibility and obligation to deliver high-quality, evidence-based care and to be answerable for one's actions, decisions, and performance while ensuring patient safety and adherence to professional standards. Nurses are accountable to patients, the profession, and the law, regardless of who gave the instructions.
options: Accountable only for tasks delegated by the attending physician in writing
Protected from legal liability by the hospital for all clinical decisions made
Required to report only to senior colleagues without direct patient accountability
Responsible and answerable for their actions, decisions, and patient safety
Exempt from professional accountability when following physician instructions

questions.explanation: End-of-life care focuses on ensuring comfort, dignity, and quality of life for individuals in the final stages of terminal illness rather than curative treatment. Key components include pain and symptom management, emotional and psychological support, spiritual care, and assistance for patients and families during the dying process. It is patient-centered and values-driven.
questions.question: End-of-life care in critical care nursing focuses primarily on:
options: Isolating dying patients to minimize their distress from other patients nearby
Administering maximal pharmacological therapy to reverse terminal conditions
Continuing aggressive life-sustaining treatment regardless of patient prognosis
Transferring all terminal patients to palliative wards immediately upon diagnosis
Ensuring comfort, dignity, and quality of life rather than curative treatment

questions.question: A nurse is educating staff on hand hygiene as the single most effective measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections in the ICU. This is because hand hygiene primarily:
options: Interrupts transmission of pathogens between patients and staff
Replaces the need for personal protective equipment entirely
Eliminates the need for any other infection control measures
Is only relevant before invasive procedures are performed
Has no proven impact on healthcare-associated infection rates
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene interrupts the transmission of pathogens between patients, staff, and equipment, making it the single most effective and evidence-based infection control measure in critical care. It complements, rather than replaces, other measures such as personal protective equipment and isolation precautions. Consistent practice at all points of contact, not only before procedures, is essential.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Needed because about one in four ICU patients acquires nosocomial organisms if the stay exceeds 3 days; measures cover three areas - personnel, environment and equipment.

(b)
Any staff member with a respiratory infection must be exempted from patient care for the period; no one is exempted from infection control rules.

(c)
Hand washing policies, a dress code and an orientation/education programme; a unit with distinct common and clean/sterile areas, clean entry, changing rooms before patient areas, about 210 cm between beds, good ventilation without open windows, an isolation room with hand washing facilities.

(d)
• Wash hands before each patient contact with alcohol-based rub; remove rings and cracked or chipped nail polish; scrub attire not worn outside and changed daily; visitors in gown and cap with minimal visitation.
• Equipment: sterilise properly, keep sterile items covered until use, wash, disinfect and sterilise reusables; change Cheatle forceps and jars daily.
• IV lines and sets every three days; urethral catheters and Ryle's tubes every 5-7 days; suction and oxygen tubing on alternate days; ventilator tubing and transducer dome every fifth day; suction bowls daily; oral toileting three times daily; laminar flow for injections where available.
• Keep aseptic technique in procedures, daily cleaning and dusting, periodic general washing down and prompt removal of waste; use personal protective equipment, disposable items and surveillance.

(e)
• Nosocomial infections such as MRSA blood stream/catheter-related infection and C. difficile diarrhoea; microorganism invasion can destroy well performed surgery or truncate recovery.
• Prevention: surveillance with accurate documentation and reporting, standard infection control principles (environmental hygiene, hand washing, PPE, safe sharps disposal), aseptic dressing and venepuncture; management of established infection: stop antibiotics for C. difficile.

(f)
• Hands and clothes of staff, tracheal tubes, urinary bags and catheters, linens and visitors' apparel are reservoirs, so hand hygiene, barrier measures and minimal visitation reduce spread.
• Reusable equipment and invasive lines are changed on schedule to prevent microbial build-up.
• Everyone participates in controlling infection in the ICU.
questions.question:
Describe infection control measures in the ICU under the following headings:
(a) indications
(b) contraindications (personnel restrictions)
(c) preparation (policies, environment, equipment)
(d) steps/routine measures and nursing responsibilities.
(e) State the complications of failure and how they are prevented or managed.
(f) Explain the rationale for key steps.

questions.explanation: A completely disorganised waveform without identifiable complexes in a pulseless patient represents ventricular fibrillation, a shockable rhythm requiring immediate defibrillation alongside chest compressions. This differs from asystole, which shows a flat line, and from pulseless electrical activity, which shows organised complexes without a pulse. Rapid rhythm recognition determines the correct emergency response.
questions.question: A patient's monitor shows a chaotic, disorganised waveform with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes, or T waves, and the patient is pulseless. This rhythm is:
options: Artifact from patient movement requiring lead replacement
Pulseless electrical activity requiring compressions only
Ventricular tachycardia with a palpable pulse present
Asystole requiring epinephrine as the primary treatment

questions.explanation: Shortages of critical care beds lead to reduced access, enforced transfers, and terminated procedures, but do NOT automatically result in improved prioritization. Scarcity creates pressure and adverse outcomes, not systematic quality improvement. Bed shortages are a clinical and ethical challenge, not an opportunity for better selection.
options: Far-reaching implications for clinical management of patients
Termination of urgent and elective surgical procedures
Reduced access to critical care services for patients
Enforced transfer of critically ill patients to other facilities
Improved prioritization leading to better patient selection
questions.question: Shortages of critical care beds may result in all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Electrolyte imbalances are listed among other causes of cardiac arrest along with respiratory failure and trauma. Specifically, abnormal potassium, sodium, calcium, and magnesium levels can cause arrhythmias that degenerate into cardiac arrest. The ICU objective parameters for these electrolytes identify the critical thresholds requiring intervention.
questions.question: Electrolyte imbalances can cause cardiac arrest primarily by:
options: Reducing blood volume and causing hypovolemic shock in unstable patients
Triggering arrhythmias and other non-cardiac causes of cardiac arrest
Damaging the coronary arteries and causing ischemic myocardial injury
Causing pericardial inflammation leading to constrictive pericarditis over time
Thickening the cardiac wall and reducing chamber compliance and filling

questions.question: Postrenal ARF in the ICU is caused by:
options: Sepsis-induced microvascular changes altering renal tubular cell physiology
Reduced cardiac output limiting blood delivery to the renal vasculature
Nephrotoxic drug-induced tubular necrosis causing renal parenchymal loss
Obstruction in the urinary tract such as kidney stones or blood clots
Autoimmune injury to renal glomeruli from immune complex deposition
questions.explanation: Postrenal ARF is caused by obstruction in the urinary tract, such as kidney stones, blood clots, benign prostatic hypertrophy, or tumors, that prevents urine flow from the kidneys. Treatment typically requires removing the obstruction to restore urine flow. Postrenal ARF is often reversible once the obstruction is relieved, if permanent kidney damage has not occurred.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with septic shock notes that despite adequate fluid resuscitation, blood pressure remains low. The next expected intervention is:
options: Initiation of vasopressor therapy to restore vascular tone
Immediate discontinuation of all haemodynamic support
Withholding antibiotics until blood pressure normalises
Positioning the patient flat with no further treatment
Further fluid boluses regardless of ongoing response
questions.explanation: When septic shock remains refractory to adequate fluid resuscitation, vasopressor therapy is initiated to restore vascular tone and maintain adequate perfusion pressure. Continuing unlimited fluid boluses without response risks fluid overload and pulmonary complications. Timely escalation to vasopressors, alongside source control and antibiotics, is central to septic shock management.

Hypertensive emergencies are listed under the Diagnosis Model's cardiac indications for ICU admission due to the need for intensive hemodynamic control. Stable angina, mild heart failure managed on oral therapy, and controlled arrhythmias do not meet ICU admission thresholds. Peripheral vascular surgery with stable hemodynamics is a Priority 4 example.
options: Controlled atrial fibrillation with normal ventricular response rate
Post-operative routine monitoring after peripheral vascular surgery
Stable angina with no hemodynamic compromise or dysrhythmia
Mild congestive heart failure managed with oral diuretics only
Hypertensive emergency requiring intensive hemodynamic management
questions.question: According to the Diagnosis Model, which cardiac condition is an indication for ICU admission?

questions.explanation: A falling mixed venous oxygen saturation with stable arterial saturation suggests tissues are extracting more oxygen because delivery is not meeting demand, often due to low cardiac output or increased metabolic need. This is an important early indicator of inadequate perfusion. It should prompt reassessment of haemodynamic status.
options: Increasing tissue oxygen extraction from reduced delivery
Excessive oxygen delivery relative to tissue need
Improved cardiac output meeting tissue demand
A benign trend unrelated to perfusion status
questions.question: An ICU nurse notes a patient's arterial oxygen saturation remains stable, but mixed venous oxygen saturation is trending downward. This trend most likely reflects:
The 5 Ps of compartment syndrome clinical hallmarks are:
options: Pressure, pitting edema, pallor, paresthesias, and permeability changes
Pain out of proportion, pallor, paresthesias, paralysis, and pulselessness
Pressure, pain, pulselessness, purple discoloration, and perspiration
Pain, pyrexia, pallor, paraesthesias, and progressive compartment swelling
Pyrexia, pallor, pain, pitting edema, and progressive motor weakness
questions.explanation: The 5 Ps of compartment syndrome are pain out of proportion, pallor, paresthesias, paralysis, and pulselessness. These represent progressive ischemic tissue injury from elevated intracompartmental pressure. However, these signs are not reliable in patients with decreased level of consciousness or who are unconscious, as noted by Guo et al. (2019), requiring compartment pressure monitoring.

questions.question: Life-sustaining treatment in critical care nursing refers to:
questions.explanation: Life-sustaining treatments are interventions such as mechanical ventilation, dialysis, vasopressors, and artificial nutrition that maintain vital functions and prevent death. Decisions about initiating, withholding, or withdrawing such treatments represent some of the most ethically complex situations in critical care. They are guided by patient preferences, advance directives, and ethical principles.
options: Supportive nursing care including turning, feeding, and hygiene maintenance
Any treatment aimed at curing the patient's underlying medical condition
Interventions such as mechanical ventilation or dialysis that maintain vital functions
Only cardiopulmonary resuscitation performed in the event of cardiac arrest
All medications administered in the ICU regardless of their clinical purpose

questions.question: Under Objective Parameters, a pulse rate that warrants ICU admission consideration is:
options: Irregular rhythm with no hemodynamic instability or symptoms
Between 80 and 100 beats per minute in a pediatric patient
Less than 40 or greater than 150 beats per minute on assessment
Greater than 100 beats per minute after moderate exercise
Less than 60 beats per minute in a trained athlete at rest
questions.explanation: The Objective Parameters Model specifies a pulse of less than 40 or greater than 150 beats per minute as a criterion for ICU admission consideration. These extremes represent potentially life-threatening hemodynamic compromise. A pulse of 60, 100 post-exercise, or 80-100 in a child does not independently trigger this threshold.

options: A normal expected post-operative laboratory finding
A laboratory error requiring simple repeat testing
Improvement in the patient's overall clinical status
A post-operative infectious or septic complication
Resolution of the underlying surgical condition
questions.explanation: Fever, tachycardia, and a significantly elevated white blood cell count following surgery raise concern for an evolving infectious or septic complication, such as a surgical site infection or intra-abdominal collection, requiring further evaluation. These findings should not be dismissed as routine post-operative changes. Prompt assessment allows early identification and treatment of a developing complication.
questions.question: A nurse notes that a patient's white blood cell count is significantly elevated alongside fever and tachycardia following abdominal surgery. This combination should prompt evaluation for:

questions.explanation: Alkalinization of urine in rhabdomyolysis aims to prevent myoglobin from precipitating in the renal tubules, which causes tubular obstruction and direct toxicity. Alkaline urine (pH > 6.5) keeps myoglobin in a more soluble form, reducing tubular damage and the risk of acute kidney failure. Sodium bicarbonate is commonly used to achieve urine alkalinization alongside aggressive hydration.
options: Increasing urine potassium excretion to prevent life-threatening hyperkalemia
Improving antibiotic penetration into the renal parenchyma to treat infection
Preventing myoglobin precipitation in the renal tubules and reducing tubular damage
Reducing the pH of blood to reverse metabolic acidosis in ARF patients
Reducing pain from ureteric spasm caused by myoglobin crystallization in urine
questions.question: Alkalinization of urine in rhabdomyolysis is aimed at:

questions.explanation: Advance directives serve nurses by guiding treatment decisions when a patient cannot express their current preferences due to incapacity. They reflect the patient's previously documented values and wishes and are legally binding in most jurisdictions. Advance directives help nurses and the healthcare team honor patient autonomy even when the patient cannot actively participate in decision-making.
questions.question: In the context of ethical dilemmas, advance directives serve nurses by:
options: Guiding treatment decisions when the patient cannot express current preferences
Allowing nurses to determine all aspects of patient care without physician input
Providing legal protection for nurses against liability from clinical decisions
Ensuring family members are excluded from all decisions about critically ill patients
Replacing the need for surrogate decision-makers in all incapacitated patients
Enable accurate documentation and reporting to assess infection prevalence
Provide definitive diagnosis of all cases of nosocomial bacteremia early
Administer empirical antibiotics before culture results are available
Replace routine infection prevention practices with monitoring only
Identify and isolate all infected patients immediately upon ICU entry
questions.explanation: Surveillance in ICU infection control involves accurate documentation and reporting of cases, enabling assessment of infection prevalence through systematic data collection such as temperature recording. It is the first component of infection control and guides preventive strategies. Surveillance alone does not replace treatment, isolation, or prevention practices.
questions.question: The primary role of surveillance in ICU infection control is to:

options: Prevents families from making decisions about withdrawal of therapy
Allows nursing staff to practice advanced procedures more frequently
Reduces organ dysfunction, length of stay, and costs of intensive care
Ensures all patients receive the maximum possible treatment at all times
Guarantees full recovery regardless of the nature of the illness
questions.question: Early referral to the ICU is beneficial because it:
questions.explanation: Early ICU referral improves recovery chances, reduces the extent and number of organ dysfunctions, decreases ICU and hospital length of stay, and reduces costs. It should occur before the condition becomes irreversible. Early referral is a systems improvement strategy, not a guarantee of full recovery or unlimited treatment.

questions.question: Vital signs in the ICU are defined as indicators of:
options: Hemodynamic stability in all patients admitted to the intensive care unit
Life; their presence is indicative of the presence of life in an organism
The response to treatment and the progress of intensive therapy interventions
The level of consciousness and adequacy of cerebral perfusion in ICU patients
The severity of illness and the degree of organ dysfunction in a patient
questions.explanation: Vital signs are defined as indications of life — their presence is indicative of life in an organism. They include pulse/heart rate, chest movement (respiration), blood pressure, temperature, pupillary constriction to light, and level of consciousness. The term 'vital' specifically refers to the signs of life, not just disease severity or treatment response.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Critical care is a service for patients with potentially recoverable conditions who can benefit from more detailed observation and invasive treatment than wards can safely provide; admission is appropriate if the condition is potentially reversible, the patient can reasonably be expected to survive, and the outcome is in reasonable doubt.
• Guiding steps: review co-morbidities and response to treatment, formulate a prognosis, discuss risks and burdens with patient and carers, and agree treatment ceilings in advance. Admission may be precluded by the patient's condition, co-morbidities, or a capacitated patient's refusal.

(b)
• Priority 1: unstable, needing intensive treatment and monitoring (ventilator support, vasoactive infusions), no therapy limits. Priority 2: intensive monitoring, may need immediate intervention. Priority 3: unstable with reduced likelihood of recovery, limits may be set.
• Priority 4: generally not appropriate - category A too well to benefit (e.g. stable diabetic ketoacidosis), category B too sick to benefit (e.g. irreversible brain damage, brain-dead non-donors); admission only individually at the ICU Director's discretion.

(c)
• Diagnosis model lists conditions by system (cardiac, pulmonary, neurologic, drug overdose, gastrointestinal, endocrine, renal, haematology, obstetric, multi-system, surgical); objective parameters include pulse under 40 or over 150, MAP under 60, respiratory rate over 35, PaO2 under 50, pH under 7.1 or over 7.7.
• Other factors: diagnosis and prognosis, severity of illness and coexisting disease, age, availability of treatment, response to treatment, recent cardiopulmonary arrest, anticipated quality of life and the patient's wishes.

(d)
Discharge when haemodynamics are stable, respiratory status is stable (extubated, stable ABGs, patent airway), oxygen requirement is not more than 60%, inotropes/vasopressors/vasodilators are no longer needed, dysrhythmias are controlled, and neurologic status is stable with seizures controlled.

(e)
• Critical care is a limited, scarce and costly resource that must target those most likely to benefit; shortages can reduce access, force transfers and terminate urgent and elective procedures.
• Decisions should be objective, ethical and transparent, and early referral improves recovery, reduces organ dysfunction and may reduce length of stay and costs.

(f)
• Admission criteria identify who should enter ICU (reversible condition, benefit from intensive treatment).
• Discharge criteria apply once physiology has stabilised and ICU care is no longer necessary, and are based on admission criteria, the admitting criteria of the next lower level of care and the availability of resources.
• Where deterioration is irreversible and active interventions no longer beneficial, therapy is withdrawn in the ICU; if a bed is needed the patient goes to the ward.
questions.question:
Describe the criteria for admission to and discharge from intensive care under the following headings:
(a) definition of critical care and guiding principles for admission
(b) the prioritisation (priority) model
(c) the diagnosis and objective parameter models and other factors considered
(d) discharge criteria.
(e) Explain why admission criteria are needed.
(f) Distinguish between admission criteria and discharge criteria.

questions.explanation: In the ICU, vital sign monitoring extends beyond the basics to include end-tidal CO2, arterial blood gases, electrolytes, and pain, which is now recognized as a vital sign. These reflect the complex physiological monitoring required for critically ill patients. Serum creatinine, urine output, chest X-ray, and wound assessment are important but not classified as vital signs.
options: Urine output and fluid balance sheet recorded every 24 hours
Wound assessment scores and pressure ulcer staging in immobile patients
Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels monitored daily
End-tidal CO2, blood gases, electrolytes, and pain assessment
Chest X-ray findings reviewed during morning ward round assessments
questions.question: Which of the following is included as a vital sign monitored in the ICU?

questions.explanation: Laboratory assessment for ARF includes blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and electrolytes as the primary markers of renal function and metabolic consequences. A comprehensive metabolic profile helps assess the extent of renal impairment and complications. Imaging such as ultrasound or CT scan may also be used to identify structural causes of ARF.
questions.question: Assessment for ARF in the ICU requires monitoring of which specific laboratory values?
options: Liver enzymes, coagulation profile, full blood count, and thyroid function
Blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, electrolytes, and complete metabolic profile
Blood cultures, inflammatory markers, and viral serology for infectious causes
Cardiac troponins, BNP, D-dimer, and arterial blood gas analysis only
Lipid profile, fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, and urine microalbumin levels

questions.explanation: A surrogate decision-maker is typically next of kin or a legally appointed proxy who represents the patient's interests when the patient cannot consent due to incapacity. Surrogate decisions should ideally reflect the patient's known values and preferences. Ethical conflicts arise when surrogate decisions contradict medical recommendations or the patient's perceived preferences.
options: A hospital administrator authorized to consent for institutional procedures
A next of kin or legally appointed proxy representing an incapacitated patient
A pharmacist designated to authorize medication changes in the ICU context
A nurse designated to make all decisions when the physician is unavailable
A social worker assigned to manage family conflicts in the ICU setting
questions.question: A surrogate decision-maker in critical care nursing is best described as:
A nurse observes ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads of a patient's ECG accompanied by chest pain. This finding is most concerning for:
questions.explanation: New ST-segment elevation with chest pain strongly suggests acute myocardial infarction from coronary artery occlusion and requires urgent evaluation for reperfusion therapy. While other conditions can cause ST changes, the combination with chest pain in this context is treated as a time-critical emergency until proven otherwise. Rapid recognition minimises delay to treatment.
options: Acute anterior myocardial infarction requiring urgent action
Old, resolved myocardial infarction needing no action
Normal early repolarisation requiring no intervention
Digoxin effect requiring routine monitoring only
Benign pericarditis unrelated to coronary occlusion

questions.question:
Describe sudden cardiac arrest under the following headings:
(a) causes
(b) pathophysiology
(c) clinical features
(d) complications and outcome.
(e) State the diagnostic and monitoring measures.
(f) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cardiac: coronary artery disease (leading cause), myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, hypertensive heart disease/left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and arrhythmic syndromes (long QT, Wolff-Parkinson-White, Brugada).
• Non-cardiac (15-25%): trauma, bleeding (GI bleeding, aortic rupture, intracranial haemorrhage), overdose, drowning, pulmonary embolism, poisoning; also electrolyte imbalance, respiratory failure, cocaine/amphetamine use.

(b)
The heart abruptly beats abnormally or irregularly; without organised electrical activity the ventricles do not contract consistently, so the heart cannot generate adequate cardiac output.

(c)
About 50% have no warning; otherwise non-specific chest pain, fatigue, blackouts, dizziness, shortness of breath, weakness, vomiting. At arrest: no palpable pulse, rapid loss of consciousness and breathing (loss of cerebral perfusion), blue-tinged skin, dilated pupils, convulsions.

(d)
Survival with treatment is about 8% and many survivors have significant disability; brain cells are irreversibly damaged after 3-5 minutes without perfusion.

(e)
• Recognition: unresponsive, absent/abnormal breathing, no carotid pulse (check no more than 10 seconds); ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia have identical signs and are differentiated only by ECG.
• After return of circulation: intensive monitoring of vital signs, neurological status and response to treatment, ECG and chest x-ray, BUN, creatinine and electrolytes, and identification of the underlying cause.

(f)
• Immediate: call for help, CPR at once, defibrillate shockable rhythms, advanced life support (airway, medications such as epinephrine every five minutes); targeted temperature management (24 hours, 32-36 degrees C) if circulation returns without consciousness.
• Nursing diagnoses: Decreased cardiac output/risk for decreased cardiac output, Ineffective breathing pattern, Activity intolerance/risk for activity intolerance.
• Administer prescribed medications, oxygen and IV solutions; monitor closely; encourage rest, semirecumbent position; assist with physical care.
• Give emotional support to patient and family; communicate clearly and work as a team with physicians and other specialists.
• Educate patient and family on cause, risk factors and prevention (healthy diet, exercise, smoking cessation, blood pressure and cholesterol control; ICD for survivors of VF/VT arrest) and plan discharge.

questions.explanation: Excessive tidal volumes relative to predicted body weight can overdistend alveoli, contributing to ventilator-induced lung injury, particularly in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome. Lung-protective ventilation strategies use lower tidal volumes to reduce this risk. This is a recognised complication rather than a benign setting choice.
options: Lower airway pressures throughout the respiratory cycle
Enhanced patient comfort and reduced sedation need
Reduced risk of barotrauma during ventilation
Improved oxygenation with no associated risk
questions.question: A nurse assessing ventilator settings notes the patient is on a high tidal volume for their predicted body weight. This practice increases the risk of:

questions.explanation: Discharge from the ICU is indicated when the patient's physiologic status has stabilized and ICU-level monitoring and care are no longer necessary. If conditions are irreversible with no further active intervention benefit, withdrawal of therapy in the ICU with transfer is also appropriate. Family requests or bed space pressures alone are not valid criteria.
options: The patient's family requests transfer to a higher comfort care facility
The ICU physician decides to free up bed space for new admissions
Laboratory values normalize despite ongoing hemodynamic instability
The patient develops an irreversible condition and requests discharge home
The patient's physiologic status has stabilized and ICU monitoring is no longer needed
questions.question: ICU discharge is indicated when:

options: Cleaning agents that damage sinks reduce their effectiveness as hand washing stations
Nurses spend too much time at sinks, reducing time available for patient care
Water from sink taps is unsafe for patient use due to calcium deposit buildup
They harbor microorganisms that can be transmitted to patients and staff
Drain blockages cause flooding that may damage vital ICU monitoring equipment
questions.explanation: Sinks and sink traps are listed as reservoirs for nosocomial microbes in the ICU. Organisms like Pseudomonas aeruginosa can colonize sink traps and aerosolize during water flow, potentially contaminating the immediate environment and infecting patients. This is one reason environmental hygiene encompasses sink cleaning and disinfection.
questions.question: Sinks and sink traps in the ICU are considered infection hazards because:

questions.explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis is transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei, requiring airborne precautions including a negative pressure room and use of a fitted N95 or equivalent respirator by staff. Standard, contact, or droplet precautions alone are insufficient to prevent transmission of this pathogen. Correct precaution selection is essential to protect staff and other patients.
options: Droplet precautions using a standard surgical mask
No isolation required once treatment has started
Standard precautions only with no additional measures
Contact precautions using gown and gloves alone
Airborne precautions using a negative pressure room and respirator
questions.question: A nurse educating a colleague about isolation precautions for a patient with confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis should emphasise the need for:

options: Maintaining adequate hydration and monitoring for signs of fluid deficit
Prompt treatment of infections and other underlying conditions causing ARF
Administering prophylactic dialysis to all high-risk ICU patients on admission
Monitoring medications with potential nephrotoxic effects on renal function
Early identification and management of known risk factors for renal failure
questions.explanation: Prophylactic dialysis for all high-risk ICU patients is NOT a prevention strategy for ARF. Prevention includes maintaining adequate hydration, monitoring nephrotoxic medications, promptly treating infections, and identifying and managing risk factors early. Dialysis is a treatment for established ARF when conservative measures are insufficient, not a preventive tool for all high-risk patients.
questions.question: Prevention of ARF in high-risk ICU patients includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Provide support and clear information to aid their decision
Avoid the conversation to prevent causing distress
Make the treatment decision on the family's behalf
Pressure the family toward a specific decision quickly
Withhold information about prognosis to reduce anxiety
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a family struggling to decide whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment from a loved one with an irreversible condition. The nurse's most appropriate ethical role is to:
questions.explanation: The nurse's ethical role in such situations is to provide clear, honest information and emotional support, enabling the family to reach an informed decision consistent with the patient's values, rather than making the decision for them. Avoiding the conversation or withholding information undermines informed decision-making. Supporting shared decision-making respects both patient autonomy, when previously expressed, and family involvement.

Diuretics in ARF management assist fluid and waste excretion where there is residual renal function. They are prescribed as part of the management alongside other interventions. Diuretics are more useful in early or prerenal ARF where some tubular function remains, and less effective in established intrarenal ARF with severely impaired tubular function. They do not replace dialysis in severe cases.
options: Restore normal glomerular filtration rate in all stages of ARF management
Prevent progression from the oliguric phase to the polyuric phase of ARF
Assist fluid and waste excretion where there is residual renal function available
Prevent hyperkalemia by promoting renal potassium secretion in the tubules
Replace dialysis as a less invasive alternative for all patients with severe ARF
questions.question: Diuretics in ARF management are administered to:
A nurse caring for a ventilated patient notices increasing peak inspiratory pressures with unchanged plateau pressures over several hours. This pattern most likely suggests:
questions.explanation: A rise in peak pressure with stable plateau pressure points to increased resistance within the airways, such as secretions, bronchospasm, or a kinked tube, rather than a change in lung or chest wall compliance. If both pressures rose together, a compliance problem such as oedema would be more likely. This distinction helps target the correct intervention.
options: Improved airway patency requiring no further evaluation
Decreased lung compliance from evolving pulmonary oedema
Reduced airway resistance from effective bronchodilation
A ventilator malfunction unrelated to the patient
Increased airway resistance such as secretions or bronchospasm

questions.explanation: Non-maleficence most directly justifies withholding an intervention that offers no clinical benefit, as continuing futile treatment causes unnecessary suffering without therapeutic gain. While beneficence also supports this decision, non-maleficence is specifically about preventing harm — and continuing futile interventions constitutes harm through unnecessary suffering, indignity, and resource misuse.
questions.question: The ethical principle that most directly justifies withholding an intervention that offers no benefit is:
options: Justice, ensuring the intervention is available for patients who would benefit
Beneficence, as withholding treatment represents the greatest benefit to the patient
Autonomy, as the patient has not explicitly requested the intervention be given
Non-maleficence, avoiding harm by preventing procedures that offer no clinical benefit
Fidelity, maintaining the nurse's commitment to evidence-based practice standards
Withhold further treatment until family arrives
Reduce oxygen delivery to prevent any toxicity risk
Immediately transfer the patient home for recovery
Optimise oxygenation, blood pressure, and identify the cause
Discontinue all monitoring since the crisis has resolved
questions.explanation: Post-cardiac arrest care focuses on optimising oxygenation and haemodynamics, targeted temperature management where indicated, and identifying the cause of arrest to prevent recurrence. Discontinuing monitoring at this critical, unstable phase would be unsafe. This post-resuscitation phase is a recognised, ongoing part of the arrest management continuum.
questions.question: Immediately after return of spontaneous circulation following cardiac arrest, the nursing priority is to:

options: Normal ventilator settings with no adaptation needed
Acute respiratory failure requiring emergency intervention
Acute metabolic alkalosis unrelated to ventilation
Chronic hypercapnia with full metabolic compensation
A laboratory error requiring immediate repeat sampling
questions.explanation: A high PaCO2 with a normal pH suggests the kidneys have compensated over time by retaining bicarbonate, consistent with chronic hypercapnia often seen in patients with underlying chronic lung disease. This differs from an acute, uncompensated respiratory failure pattern. Recognising chronic compensation avoids unnecessary aggressive intervention.
questions.question: A patient on mechanical ventilation has a PaCO2 of 65 mmHg with a normal pH of 7.38. This finding most likely reflects:
A critically ill patient's advance directive states no mechanical ventilation should be used, yet the family requests it during an acute crisis. The nurse's primary ethical obligation is to:
options: Provide ventilation temporarily to satisfy the family
Ignore the advance directive since the patient cannot speak
Delay any decision until the ethics committee decides
Follow the family's request over the advance directive
Uphold the patient's documented wishes in the advance directive
questions.explanation: A valid advance directive represents the patient's own previously expressed autonomous wishes and should generally take precedence over family requests that conflict with it, since it reflects informed patient decision-making. The nurse's ethical duty is to advocate for and uphold these documented wishes. Involving the ethics committee or palliative care team can help support the family through this difficult situation while respecting the patient's autonomy.

options: Long-term disability from nerve damage, muscle loss, or limb amputation
Post-traumatic stress disorder from the traumatic nature of the injury event
Acute kidney failure as an immediate complication of rhabdomyolysis development
Full neurological recovery with no residual functional deficit after treatment
Infection of the wound or fasciotomy site leading to septic complications
questions.explanation: Full neurological recovery with no residual functional deficit is an IDEAL outcome, not a documented long-term complication. Complications of crush injury include acute kidney failure, compartment syndrome, infection, amputation, long-term disability, and PTSD. Recovery varies, and many patients experience residual deficits depending on the severity and extent of the injury.
questions.question: Long-term complications of crush injury include all of the following EXCEPT:
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) used in ICU infection control must be:
options: Fluid repellent to prevent penetration of infectious secretions or blood
Reused after routine cleaning between patients to conserve resources
Made from any comfortable fabric to encourage compliance among staff
Selected based on the patient's diagnosis only and not the risk level
Used only during aerosol-generating procedures and invasive interventions
questions.explanation: All PPE used in ICU infection control should be fluid repellent to prevent penetration of blood, body fluids, and infectious secretions. PPE use is guided by the nature of the task and level of exposure risk, not only by the specific diagnosis. Reusing PPE between patients increases cross-contamination risk and is not appropriate practice.

questions.question: Risk factors for sudden cardiac death include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Regular moderate exercise and a low-calorie balanced diet intake
High blood pressure and high cholesterol with sedentary lifestyle
Cigarette smoking and a previous episode of sudden cardiac arrest
Obesity, diabetes mellitus, and positive family history of cardiac death
Age and lack of physical exercise with associated metabolic disorders
questions.explanation: Regular moderate exercise and a balanced low-calorie diet are protective factors, NOT risk factors for sudden cardiac death. Risk factors include age, cigarette smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, lack of physical exercise, obesity, diabetes, family history, and a prior episode of sudden cardiac arrest. Modifiable risk factors provide opportunities for prevention.

Cardiac arrest becomes more common with age because aging progressively increases the risk of coronary artery disease, structural cardiac changes, arrhythmias, and co-morbidities. The accumulation of risk factors over time and the degenerative changes in the cardiovascular system with age explain the exponential increase in cardiac arrest incidence from age 15 onward.
questions.question: The phrase ‘cardiac arrest becomes more common with age’ is best explained by:
options: Elderly patients are less compliant with medications and lifestyle modifications
Young patients have stronger immune systems preventing cardiac arrest causes
Age reduces the effectiveness of resuscitation making survival less likely
Elderly patients have more advanced care plans limiting resuscitation efforts
Aging increases risk of coronary disease, structural changes, and arrhythmias

questions.question: A nurse notes wide, bizarre QRS complexes at a rate of 180 beats per minute with no discernible P waves in a haemodynamically unstable patient. The priority intervention is:
questions.explanation: Wide-complex tachycardia in an unstable patient, such as ventricular tachycardia, requires urgent electrical treatment, typically synchronised cardioversion if a pulse is present, rather than delayed oral therapy. Vagal manoeuvres are appropriate for stable narrow-complex tachycardias, not unstable wide-complex rhythms. Prompt recognition and treatment prevent progression to cardiac arrest.
options: Immediate synchronised cardioversion or defibrillation as indicated
Vagal manoeuvres attempted before any other treatment
Watchful waiting with repeat ECG in thirty minutes
Reassurance since the patient remains conscious currently
Oral antiarrhythmic medication given over several hours

questions.explanation: Fasciotomy is the surgical decompression indicated when compartment syndrome develops and cannot be managed conservatively. It involves cutting the fascia to relieve intracompartmental pressure and restore perfusion to ischemic tissues. Early fasciotomy prevents progression to tissue necrosis, nerve damage, and limb loss. Prompt identification of compartment syndrome and timely surgical referral is a nursing priority.
questions.question: Fasciotomy is a surgical intervention indicated in crush injury when:
options: The patient develops acute kidney failure requiring renal replacement therapy
Rhabdomyolysis causes serum CK levels to rise above 1,000 units per liter
Compartment syndrome is present and cannot be managed conservatively
Deep vein thrombosis develops as a complication of prolonged immobility post-injury
Myoglobinuria persists despite aggressive IV hydration and alkalinization therapy

questions.explanation: A dampened arterial waveform with falsely low readings is commonly caused by air bubbles, kinking, or a clot at the catheter tip, which should be checked and corrected first. Acting on inaccurate pressure readings by adjusting vasopressors could cause harm. Troubleshooting the line restores accurate haemodynamic monitoring.
options: Check the line for air bubbles, kinks, or clot
Immediately increase the vasopressor infusion rate
Remove the arterial line without further assessment
Recalibrate only the bedside monitor software settings
Document the reading and continue routine care
questions.question: An ICU nurse notices the arterial line waveform has become dampened and the readings appear falsely low. The most appropriate first action is to:
Acute renal failure (ARF) in the ICU is defined as:
questions.explanation: Acute renal failure (ARF), now also known as acute kidney injury, is defined as a syndrome characterized by an abrupt deterioration of renal function, leading to the accumulation of metabolic wastes, fluids, and electrolytes, usually followed by a noticeable reduction in urinary output. It is sudden, reversible (in many cases), and distinct from chronic kidney disease.
options: Abrupt deterioration of renal function causing metabolic waste accumulation and reduced urine
Gradual decline in kidney function over months requiring chronic dialysis
Structural kidney damage from long-standing hypertension and diabetes mellitus
Transient reduction in urine output lasting less than 6 hours in a postoperative patient
Mild elevation of serum creatinine incidentally found on routine blood biochemistry

questions.question: A patient with a potentially reversible acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy is best managed in which care setting?
options: Intensive care unit with continuous therapy capability
Home-based care with community nursing support
General medical ward with intermittent dialysis access
Step-down unit without continuous filtration equipment
Outpatient renal clinic with scheduled dialysis sessions
questions.explanation: Continuous renal replacement therapy requires specialised equipment, close haemodynamic monitoring, and rapid response to complications only available in intensive care. The potential reversibility of the injury supports aggressive, intensive management. Ward or outpatient settings lack the capacity for continuous filtration and monitoring.

questions.question: Invasive monitoring in the ICU includes all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Central venous pressure measurement via centrally placed catheter
Respiratory rate monitoring using thoracic impedance on cardiac monitor
Arterial blood pressure monitoring via arterial catheterization
Pulmonary artery pressure measurement via Swan-Ganz catheter
Cardiac output measured by thermodilution via pulmonary artery catheter
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate monitoring using thoracic impedance on a cardiac monitor is a non-invasive method. Invasive monitoring includes arterial blood pressure via arterial catheter, central venous pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, cardiac output, and left atrial pressure — all of which require insertion of intravascular catheters or invasive lines.

Pulse can be palpated at multiple sites including radial, brachial, popliteal, temporal, dorsalis pedis, femoral, posterior tibial, and carotid arteries. The choice of site depends on clinical context and accessibility. The subclavian and pulmonary artery are not palpable, and aortic palpation is not a standard pulse assessment technique.
questions.question: In assessing the pulse in ICU patients, which artery is commonly palpated?
options: Only the femoral artery in sedated and mechanically ventilated ICU patients
Radial, brachial, femoral, carotid, and popliteal arteries among others
The aorta palpated through abdominal assessment in hemodynamically unstable patients
Pulmonary artery accessed via central venous pressure monitoring line
Subclavian artery as the primary site for pulse palpation in ICU

questions.explanation: The Quality of Life quadrant in the Four Quadrants Approach considers how proposed treatments will impact the patient's physical, emotional, and social well-being. It asks: 'How will the intervention affect the patient's future well-being?' This ensures that treatment decisions consider not just survival but the patient's overall experience and quality of life after intervention.
options: The medical treatment options available and their evidence-based effectiveness
The legal, social, and cultural factors influencing the ethical decision-making
How the proposed treatment will impact the patient's physical, emotional well-being
The hospital's capacity to provide the required level of care to the patient
The patient's expressed preferences and documented advance directive wishes
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Quality of Life quadrant in the Four Quadrants Approach?
A nurse notes a mean arterial pressure of 55 mmHg in an ICU patient on a vasopressor infusion. This value is clinically significant primarily because it may indicate:
questions.explanation: A mean arterial pressure below the generally accepted threshold of around 65 mmHg suggests inadequate perfusion to vital organs such as the kidneys and brain. This requires prompt reassessment of fluid status and vasopressor titration. Sustained low perfusion pressure increases the risk of organ dysfunction.
options: Inadequate perfusion pressure to vital organs
An artifact of incorrect cuff size selection
Excessive perfusion pressure requiring immediate reduction
Improved cardiac output from vasopressor therapy
A normal finding requiring no further action

questions.explanation: Sudden cardiac arrest occurs when the heart abruptly begins to beat in an abnormal or irregular rhythm (arrhythmia). Without organized electrical activity, ventricular contractions are absent or ineffective, resulting in inability to generate adequate cardiac output. This is the final common pathway regardless of the underlying cause.
questions.question: Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) and sudden cardiac death (SCD) occur when:
options: The heart abruptly begins beating in an abnormal or irregular rhythm (arrhythmia)
A cardiac valve becomes acutely incompetent causing regurgitation and failure
The heart muscle gradually weakens leading to progressive pump failure over time
A coronary artery becomes completely blocked preventing myocardial oxygen delivery
Blood pressure drops suddenly causing insufficient cardiac output to the brain

questions.question: Emergency nurses are at particularly high legal risk because:
options: They make more medication errors than nurses in other clinical specialties
Emergency departments lack clear protocols to guide nursing management decisions
Legal standards for emergency nursing are higher than for any other nursing specialty
Emergency nurses are less qualified than nurses working in specialized ICU settings
They must make life-and-death priority decisions quickly under significant time pressure
questions.explanation: Emergency nurses are at high legal risk because they must make life-and-death decisions quickly based on sound knowledge and judgment, often with limited information and under time pressure. Triage decisions must be made to expedite care. The rapid, high-stakes nature of emergency nursing combined with the need for accurate, swift prioritization creates significant legal vulnerability.

questions.question:
An unconscious ICU patient with a depressed level of consciousness is found to have one pupil dilated and not reacting to light, while the other pupil is normal and reactive.
(a) Identify the condition or problem indicated.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Unilateral pupil dilatation and non-reactivity with a depressed level of consciousness suggests impaired brainstem function.
• Unequal pupils in an unconscious patient is also an acute-onset physical finding that supports ICU admission.

(b)
• Pathophysiology: equal, normal and reactive pupils imply that the upper brainstem and the third cranial nerve are intact; loss of this pattern indicates that this pathway is impaired.
• Neurologic conditions that warrant ICU admission include acute stroke with altered mental status, coma (metabolic, toxic or anoxic), intracranial haemorrhage with potential for herniation, status epilepticus and progressive neuromuscular dysfunction requiring respiratory support.

(c)
• Observe pupillary reaction closely, as it is essential in patients with neurological problems; monitor level of consciousness with the Glasgow Coma Scale (total 3-15: eye opening 1-4, best verbal response 1-5, best motor response 1-6).
• Assess airway, breathing, circulation and neurological disability (Glasgow Coma Scale) as in the primary survey; ICU patients are mostly intubated, so monitor the respiratory pattern for CO2 retention, secretions in the tube and tube dislodgement.
• Continue monitoring vital signs, end-tidal CO2 (35-45), oxygen saturation (90-100%), arterial blood gases and hourly urine output (0.5-1 ml/kg/hr).

options: Perform a thorough oral examination with a tongue depressor
Encourage the patient to lie flat for comfort measures
Delay escalation until swelling visibly worsens further
Avoid airway manipulation and prepare for emergency airway support
Administer oral fluids immediately to prevent dehydration
questions.explanation: In suspected epiglottitis, avoiding oral examination or airway manipulation is critical because it can precipitate complete airway obstruction, so the priority is to keep the patient calm in a position of comfort and prepare emergency airway equipment. Lying flat or attempting oral fluids can worsen obstruction. This is a recognised paediatric and adult airway emergency requiring specialist involvement.
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with suspected epiglottitis presenting with drooling, stridor, and a tripod positioning. The priority nursing action is to:
An ethical dilemma in critical care occurs when:
options: A situation involves two conflicting moral principles where any choice violates one
A patient's condition suddenly deteriorates requiring immediate emergency response
The physician and nurse disagree about the nursing management of a patient
There is a shortage of nursing staff requiring reallocation of patient assignments
A nurse is uncertain about the clinical diagnosis of a complex patient
questions.explanation: An ethical dilemma occurs when a nurse faces a situation involving two or more conflicting ethical principles where choosing one course of action would violate another. It is characterized by moral conflict rather than clinical uncertainty, staffing issues, or professional disagreements. Classic examples include conflicts between patient autonomy and beneficence.

options: Individual immune defenses explain why some exposed persons become infected and others do not
Only elderly patients with multiple co-morbidities have significant susceptibility
Patients in private rooms have higher susceptibility than those in shared wards
All ICU patients are equally susceptible due to their critical illness state
Susceptibility depends entirely on the virulence of the infecting organism only
questions.question: Which of the following best explains individual variation in susceptibility to nosocomial infection?
questions.explanation: Individual variation in susceptibility to infection is explained by individual immune defenses. Some people become infected upon exposure while others, despite similar exposure, do not. This explains why nosocomial infection rates vary among patients even in the same ICU environment. Susceptibility is not equal for all patients, nor is it determined solely by virulence.

options: Local skin temperature change from room conditions
An isolated finding unrelated to systemic perfusion
Normal peripheral vascular tone for the patient
Improved circulatory status following recent treatment
Peripheral hypoperfusion possibly from evolving shock
questions.question: An ICU nurse notices that a patient's capillary refill time has increased to over three seconds along with cool peripheries. This clinical sign most strongly suggests:
questions.explanation: Delayed capillary refill and cool peripheries are classic signs of peripheral hypoperfusion, which can be an early indicator of shock even before blood pressure drops. This finding should prompt further haemodynamic assessment rather than being dismissed as incidental. Early recognition supports timely resuscitation.

questions.question:
Describe informed consent in critical care nursing:
(a) definition and elements
(b) how it applies when patients lack capacity.
(c) Explain how it guides nursing decisions.
(d) Explain why it may fail or cause harm in critical care, and how this is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Informed consent ensures the patient has sufficient information to decide - risks, benefits and alternatives of treatment - and respects autonomy and self-determination; it is a cornerstone of autonomy.
• Elements: disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness and competence; the patient must be able to ask questions and consent willingly.

(b)
• Critical care patients may be unconscious, heavily sedated or lack capacity; decisions then rely on advance directives (a legal document outlining care preferences if the person cannot communicate) and surrogate decision-makers (next of kin or legally appointed proxies).
• With no advance directive, emergency treatment principles permit life-saving interventions without consent, guided by beneficence.

(c)
• For unconscious patients autonomy is upheld by respecting advance directives or consulting surrogate decision-makers.
• Nurses advocate by facilitating communication, clarifying treatment goals and resolving conflicts through ethics consultation, balancing ethics and advocacy.

(d)
• Surrogates may not fully understand the implications of treatment, may delay or refuse decisions through emotional distress, or decide against medical recommendations or the patient's perceived preferences.
• Emergency interventions such as intubation often proceed without explicit consent, raising questions of overriding autonomy; cultural or religious beliefs (for example rejecting blood transfusion) may conflict with care.
• A patient's religious belief on blood must be respected: giving blood without their knowledge is an assault; if unconscious or a child, blood may be given against relatives' decision because of the fundamental right to life.
• Prevention: educate surrogates, follow institutional policies for emergency interventions, use ethics consultation and encourage documentation of advance directives.
• Cultural competence and open communication help nurses respect beliefs while advocating patient well-being.
• Family meetings with the interdisciplinary team support shared decision-making.

questions.question: Which of the following exemplifies an exogenous source of nosocomial infection?
options: Aspiration of the patient's own oral flora leading to pneumonia
Infection from pathogens transmitted via contaminated staff hands
Bacteremia arising from the patient's own gastrointestinal microbiome
Wound infection caused by the patient's own skin flora colonization
Urinary tract infection from the patient's own commensal bacteria
questions.explanation: Exogenous sources of nosocomial infection originate outside the patient, such as pathogens transmitted via contaminated staff hands, equipment, or the environment. Endogenous infections arise from the patient's own flora – aspiration of oral flora, commensal urinary bacteria, skin colonization, or GI microbiome – are endogenous sources.

questions.question: A serum sodium level that triggers ICU admission under Objective Parameters is:
options: Less than 130 mEq/L or greater than 150 mEq/L in elderly patients
Less than 125 mEq/L or greater than 155 mEq/L on repeat check
Less than 120 mEq/L or greater than 160 mEq/L at any presentation
Less than 135 mEq/L or greater than 145 mEq/L outside normal range
Less than 110 mEq/L or greater than 170 mEq/L newly discovered
questions.explanation: The Objective Parameters specify serum sodium less than 110 mEq/L or greater than 170 mEq/L as ICU thresholds. These extreme values represent life-threatening hyponatremia or hypernatremia with risk of cerebral complications. The values of 120/160, 125/155, or 130/150 are not the stated objective ICU parameters in the document.

questions.question: During the diuresis phase (Stage 3) of ARF, the urine output is:
options: Exactly 1,500 ml per day representing the normal adult daily urine volume
Between 400 ml and 1,000 ml per day reflecting gradual renal function recovery
Between 3 and 6 liters per day representing the diuretic or polyuric phase
Less than 400 ml per day indicating ongoing oliguric phase continuation
Greater than 8 liters per day indicating complete renal function restoration
questions.explanation: The diuresis or polyuric phase (Stage 3) of ARF is characterized by urine output of 3-6 liters per day. This represents recovering renal tubular function with return of glomerular filtration. Despite the high urine output, tubular reabsorption is still impaired, creating a risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance that requires careful monitoring and replacement.

When a patient has mental capacity and refuses ICU admission, this is a valid reason to preclude critical care. Respect for patient autonomy is a core ethical principle. The other options — respiratory failure, hemodynamic instability, arrhythmias, and multi-organ dysfunction — are all indications FOR, not against, ICU admission.
questions.question: A factor that may PRECLUDE admission to critical care is when:
options: The patient has mental capacity and refuses critical care admission
The patient has hemodynamic instability requiring vasoactive drugs
The patient develops complex arrhythmias after myocardial infarction
The patient has multi-organ dysfunction requiring intensive monitoring
The patient has acute respiratory failure needing ventilator support

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Unconsciousness within seconds and no response to tapping the shoulders or asking if the person is all right; absence of normal breathing - apnoea or last gasps 1-3 minutes after arrest.
• No pulse on a large artery (carotid or femoral; check for no more than 10 seconds); changed appearance (colour change, blue-tinged skin); dilated pupils and convulsions may occur.

(b)
• Kneel beside the victim, shake the shoulders and ask 'Are you all right?'; if unresponsive shout for help, open the airway, then look, listen and feel for normal breathing (apnoea or gasps).
• Check for signs of functional circulation: breathing, coughing, movement, skin condition, responsiveness and pulse.

(c)
• If the person responds: leave as found, find out what is wrong and reassess regularly.
• If unresponsive and not breathing normally: call 112, give 30 chest compressions, then 2 rescue breaths, and continue 30:2 until help arrives.
• Loss of consciousness is the most immediate and crucial sign; early action limits brain damage, since cortex cells are irreversibly damaged after 3-5 minutes without perfusion.

(d)
• Pupil dilatation (mydriasis) is not reliable.
• Agonal breathing (barely, heavy, noisy or gasping breathing) occurs in up to 40% of arrests and must be recognised as a sign of arrest, not confused with normal breathing.
• Checking for a pulse is for experienced rescuers only and limited to 10 seconds; time estimates under stress are not precise (arrest witnessed 15 or more minutes earlier).
• Stressing conditions can lead to an inadequate situation assessment; the signs of ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are identical and differentiated only by ECG.
questions.question:
Describe the assessment and recognition of cardiac arrest:
(a) the signs of cardiac arrest
(b) the initial assessment sequence.
(c) Explain how the findings guide nursing decisions and actions.
(d) Explain why the assessment may fail or be misinterpreted, and how this is prevented.

options: Mild tension headache with photophobia and nausea in a young adult
Peripheral neuropathy causing mild weakness in the lower extremities
Intracranial hemorrhage with potential for cerebral herniation
Simple febrile seizure in a child with no neurological deficit
Stable migraine with aura requiring oral analgesia and hydration
questions.explanation: Intracranial hemorrhage with potential for herniation is a neurological indication for ICU admission under the Diagnosis Model. Other examples include stroke with altered mental status, coma, status epilepticus, and progressive neuromuscular dysfunction. Mild headaches, peripheral neuropathy, simple febrile seizures, and stable migraines do not meet ICU criteria.
questions.question: Which neurological condition is listed as an ICU admission indication under the Diagnosis Model?

options: Refer the patient to a different hospital that accommodates their cultural needs
Respect cultural beliefs while advocating for patient well-being through dialogue
Document the conflict and take no action to avoid offending the patient
Override the cultural beliefs to ensure evidence-based care is provided
Inform the patient that cultural practices have no place in evidence-based medicine
questions.question: When a patient’s cultural beliefs conflict with medical recommendations, the nurse should:
questions.explanation: When cultural beliefs conflict with medical recommendations, the nurse should respect cultural beliefs while advocating for the patient's well-being through open, respectful dialogue. Cultural competence and ethical frameworks like principlism help balance autonomy and non-maleficence to support culturally sensitive care while minimizing harm. Overriding cultural beliefs unilaterally violates autonomy.

options: Prioritizing patients based on social status and economic contribution to society
Allocating resources based solely on the order in which patients were admitted
Maximizing the greatest good for the greatest number when resources are limited
Restricting all resources to patients over 60 years to prevent youth mortality
Treating each patient as equally valuable regardless of survival probability
questions.question: Utilitarianism in the context of ICU resource allocation during scarcity involves:
questions.explanation: Utilitarianism in ICU resource allocation during scarcity seeks to maximize the greatest good for the greatest number. This means allocating resources to those with the greatest chance of survival or benefit. While ethically useful, utilitarian decisions are emotionally taxing and may conflict with individual patient rights, requiring careful ethical justification.

questions.question: The Brugada Syndrome is classified as which type of cardiac condition?
questions.explanation: Brugada Syndrome is one of the arrhythmic syndromes not due to structural heart disease that is associated with sudden cardiac death. Along with Long QT syndrome, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, it represents an inherited channelopathy causing life-threatening arrhythmias without structural cardiac abnormality.
options: A cardiomyopathy causing progressive right ventricular systolic dysfunction
A coronary artery disease variant causing right bundle branch ischemia
A valvular disorder causing right-sided heart failure with arrhythmia risk
An arrhythmic syndrome not due to structural disease, associated with SCD
Structural heart disease due to right ventricular outflow tract obstruction

questions.explanation: Recognized nosocomial pathogens in the ICU include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species, Proteus species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Aerobacter species. These are typically gram-negative bacteria that thrive in healthcare environments. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, influenza virus, and malaria parasites are not typical ICU nosocomial pathogens.
questions.question: Which of the following organisms is a recognized cause of nosocomial infections in the ICU?
options: Mycobacterium tuberculosis acquired on the general medical ward
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae only
Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Plasmodium falciparum transmitted through mosquito bites in ICU
Influenza A virus acquired through community respiratory exposure
The ability of a microorganism to evade antibiotic therapy regimens
The prevalence of antibiotic-resistant strains in a specific hospital unit
The capacity of an organism to survive on ICU surfaces for long periods
The severity of infection produced by a microorganism in an immune host
An individual's ability to be infected when exposed to a causative pathogen
questions.explanation: Susceptibility is the ability of an individual to become infected when in contact with a causative pathogen. It depends on individual immune defenses. Some people become infected upon exposure while others do not, explaining individual variation in infection rates even in the same environment. This is distinct from virulence or antibiotic resistance.
questions.question: Susceptibility to nosocomial infection refers to:

options: Safe use and proper disposal of sharp objects and clinical waste
Maintaining hospital environmental hygiene and cleanliness standards
Use of personal protective equipment during patient care activities
Administering prophylactic antibiotics to all patients upon ICU admission
Regular and appropriate hand washing by all healthcare personnel
questions.explanation: Standard infection control principles include environmental hygiene, hand washing, use of PPE, and safe sharps disposal. Routine prophylactic antibiotics for all ICU patients on admission are NOT a standard infection control principle and could contribute to antibiotic resistance. Targeted antibiotic prophylaxis may be used for specific procedures or conditions.
questions.question: Standard infection control principles in the ICU include all of the following EXCEPT:

options: One hundred percent oxygen via a non-rebreather mask
A level determined solely by bed availability pressures
Any concentration provided the patient appears comfortable
The maximum concentration deliverable by ward equipment
An oxygen concentration in the low-to-moderate range only
questions.explanation: Patients stepped down from ICU should have oxygen requirements low enough to be safely managed with standard ward monitoring, not high-concentration support. A patient still needing 50% oxygen suggests ongoing instability that may not be safe for ward-level care. This threshold protects against undetected deterioration after transfer.

A nurse caring for an unconscious, critically ill patient with no advance directive and no available family must make an urgent treatment decision. The ethical principle most relevant here is:
questions.explanation: When a patient cannot express preferences and no surrogate is available, healthcare providers act under the principle of beneficence, making decisions believed to be in the patient's best medical interest. Autonomy cannot be directly applied when the patient's wishes are unknown and unexpressed. This default standard guides urgent decision-making while efforts continue to identify a surrogate or advance directive.
options: Autonomy, since the patient can express no preference
Veracity, requiring disclosure of information to no one
Beneficence, acting in the patient's best interest
Fidelity, based on a prior promise to the patient
Justice, focused solely on resource allocation issues

questions.question: A nurse is teaching about the significance of a prolonged QT interval on ECG. The primary clinical concern with this finding is increased risk of:
questions.explanation: A prolonged QT interval increases susceptibility to torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death. This is why QT-prolonging medications and electrolyte disturbances are closely monitored. Recognising this risk guides careful medication review and electrolyte correction.
options: Sinus bradycardia with no further risk implications
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Torsades de pointes, a life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmia
Benign early repolarisation with no clinical significance

questions.explanation: Identified reservoirs for nosocomial microbes in the ICU include patients' wounds, hands and clothes of staff, tracheal tubes, urinary bags and catheters, bladder irrigation solutions, sinks and sink traps, patients' linens, and visitors' apparel. Fresh intravenous fluids prepared under strict aseptic conditions

questions.explanation: Patients with decision-making capacity have the right to refuse medical interventions, even when refusal may lead to adverse outcomes or death. Overriding a competent refusal without legal justification violates patient autonomy.

Refusal is only valid when the patient is fully recovered from critical illness
The physician can override the refusal if they believe treatment is beneficial
The nurse should administer the treatment anyway to protect the patient's life

questions.question: A nurse notes that a patient in early compensated shock has a normal blood pressure but a rising heart rate and mild anxiety. This stage is significant because:
questions.explanation: In early or compensated shock, the body's sympathetic response maintains blood pressure within normal limits despite reduced perfusion, making subtle signs such as tachycardia and anxiety important early warning indicators. Waiting for hypotension to appear means intervening only once compensatory mechanisms begin to fail. Early recognition at this stage allows for timely intervention before decompensation.
options: This stage indicates the shock has already resolved
Blood pressure changes always precede other symptoms
Compensatory mechanisms are still maintaining perfusion
The patient is not experiencing any shock process
No further monitoring or intervention is required
Increase oral fluid intake and repeat observations tomorrow
Discharge the patient home with outpatient follow-up
Document the trend and review during the next round
Wait for the consultant's routine ward review time
Review the patient promptly and reassess for ICU transfer
questions.question: A ward nurse calls the ICU outreach team because a patient's early warning score has risen sharply over two hours. The most appropriate immediate action by the outreach team is to:
questions.explanation: A rapidly rising early warning score signals clinical deterioration that requires urgent bedside review, not delayed documentation. Outreach teams exist to intervene early and determine whether escalation to critical care is needed. Prompt reassessment can prevent cardiac arrest or further deterioration.

questions.question:
Describe ethics in critical care nursing under the following headings:
(a) definition of ethics
(b) the core principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, fidelity)
(c) veracity, accountability, privacy and confidentiality.
(d) Explain why ethical consideration is essential in critical care.
(e) Distinguish between autonomy and paternalism.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ethics is the branch of philosophy dealing with the principles of right and wrong behaviour; the rules or code of conduct used to decide whether an action is acceptable; in nursing, the moral principles and values guiding practice.

(b)
• Autonomy: the right to make informed, uncoerced decisions, supported by informed consent (disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, competence). Beneficence: actively promoting well-being and preventing or removing harm.
• Non-maleficence: do no harm, balancing risks and benefits and minimising harm (e.g. double checking doses, speaking up against unsafe practice). Justice: fairness and equity in care and resource allocation, regardless of background.
• Fidelity: loyalty, trustworthiness, keeping promises, confidentiality and patient advocacy.

(c)
• Veracity: the obligation of truth-telling, giving honest information on diagnosis, prognosis and options, balanced with compassion. Accountability: taking responsibility for actions and outcomes and acknowledging errors.
• Privacy: the right to control access to personal information; confidentiality: the duty to protect information from unauthorised disclosure without consent or legal justification.

(d)
• The high-stakes nature of life-saving interventions demands respect for patient autonomy and dignity.
• Respecting informed decisions fosters trust and upholds dignity even in life-threatening conditions; this includes advocating the choice to decline interventions.
• Common issues: end-of-life care, informed consent, futile treatments, confidentiality, resource allocation and moral distress.

(e)
• Autonomy honours a person's right to decide for themselves, even when choices differ from professional recommendations.
• Paternalism limits a person's autonomy for their perceived best interest; it is common when providers override patient preferences and is justified as acting in the patient's best interest.
• Balancing autonomy and beneficence is a recognised challenge in implementation.

questions.question: Prevention of nosocomial infection in the ICU requires a combination of:

Antibiotic prophylaxis for all patients, universal isolation, mass weekly screening, or antibiotics for staff are not standard preventive measures.
