Describe veracity (truth-telling) in critical care nursing:
(a) definition and basis
(b) situations in which it applies.
(c) Explain how it guides nursing decisions and communication.
(d) Explain why it may fail or cause harm, and how this is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Veracity is the ethical obligation of truth-telling in the patient-caregiver relationship, grounded in respect for patient autonomy so individuals can make informed decisions.
• In critical care it means honest, transparent information on diagnoses, prognoses and treatment options, even when the news is difficult; it builds trust.

(b)
Breaking bad news (life-altering or terminal diagnoses such as organ failure or advanced cancer); disclosing medical errors (medication mistakes, procedural complications) to the patient or family; end-of-life decisions; futility conversations.

(c)
• Deliver the truth compassionately, considering the patient's emotional readiness and cultural values; balance veracity with compassion to maintain trust and address emotions.
• Give accurate information about the benefits, risks and likelihood of success of CPR or artificial ventilation so decisions to continue or withdraw treatment are informed.
• When treatment cannot help (e.g. irreversible multi-organ failure) communicate this clearly; nurses acknowledge errors and take corrective action transparently, which supports accountability and patient safety.

(d)
• Veracity can conflict with beneficence or non-maleficence; white lies told to protect feelings or prevent harm erode trust, and overuse leads to a slippery slope of dishonesty.
• Some cultures prefer an indirect approach to sharing grim prognoses, which can conflict with veracity.
• Fear of litigation or damaged trust may cause hesitancy in full disclosure; families with unrealistic expectations or in denial make futility discussions difficult.
• Prevention: transparency and open communication that strengthen trust and accountability; cultural competence training, active listening and open-mindedness; incident reporting systems for learning-focused error management.
• Regular training and professional development, clear policies and protocols, and adherence to legal and ethical nursing codes.
• Family meetings with the interdisciplinary team to explain prognosis compassionately.

questions.explanation: Non-invasive ventilation requires the patient to be able to protect their own airway and cooperate with the mask interface, so a decreased level of consciousness is a contraindication due to aspiration risk. questions.explanation: The aim of ICU monitoring is to identify deviations from the limits compatible with life and to institute corrective measures promptly. questions.explanation: Cardiac arrest is defined as a sudden loss of blood flow resulting from the failure of the heart to effectively pump. This is distinct from a heart attack, which is caused by coronary artery blockage. In cardiac arrest, the electrical malfunction prevents effective ventricular contraction, causing cessation of perfusion to all organs.
questions.question: Cardiac arrest is best defined as:

A blockage of a coronary artery preventing blood supply to heart muscle
A rhythm disturbance causing intermittent loss of consciousness in a patient

questions.question: A nurse finds a patient unresponsive and not breathing normally in the ICU. After calling for help, the immediate next action should be to:

Wait for the physician to arrive first
Begin high-quality chest compressions without delay
Search for the patient's advance directive first
Obtain a full set of vital signs first
questions.explanation: Once unresponsiveness and absent normal breathing are confirmed and help is called, high-quality chest compressions should begin immediately to maintain circulation to vital organs. Delaying compressions to search for documents or gather full vitals worsens outcomes. Early, uninterrupted compressions are central to effective resuscitation.

questions.question: An endocrine condition requiring ICU admission under the Diagnosis Model is:
questions.explanation: Thyroid storm with hemodynamic instability is an endocrine indication for ICU admission. Other examples include diabetic ketoacidosis with hemodynamic or mental status changes, myxedema coma, and severe electrolyte disturbances with dysrhythmias. Stable type 2 diabetes, mild hypothyroidism, asymptomatic hypercalcemia, and pre-diabetes do not require ICU care.

questions.question: Left ventricular hypertrophy as a cause of sudden cardiac death most commonly results from:
questions.explanation: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) as a cause of sudden cardiac death is most commonly the result of longstanding high blood pressure, which has caused secondary damage to the wall of the left ventricle. questions.answerText:
(a)
Comatose patients and other critically ill patients unable to maintain volitional intake need nutrition support by the safest, simplest, most effective route.

(b)
Enteral nutrition via nasogastric tube (PEG/gastrostomy for long-term feeding; jejunal feeding is an alternative); enteral feeding preserves intestinal mucosal structure and function, is more physiological and reduces infectious complications.

(c)
• Before: screen for malnutrition (MUST), take the history and weight; the dietitian calculates the prescription - about 25 kcal/kg/day initially, protein 1.25 g/kg/day, fluid 30 ml/kg/24 hours.
• During: keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees because of aspiration risk in ICU; do not start the feed at night; watch for tube displacement and high aspirates.
• After: monitor U&Es, phosphate, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs, fluid balance, haematology and weight.

(d)
Complications: aspiration, displacement, high aspirates and inadequate calories, constipation, diarrhoea, ileus, intolerance (?sepsis); manage with prokinetics, nasojejunal feeding or drugs, avoid opioids in ileus, and avoid overfeeding.

(e)
Nurses, doctors and dietitians share the roles of history, weight, optimising intake and monitoring.

(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after the therapy.
(d) State the safety checks and complications to watch for.
(e) State the documentation and communication/escalation required.
Nosocomial infection in the ICU is best defined as:
options: Community-acquired infections treated in the intensive care unit
Infections caused exclusively by antibiotic-resistant organisms in wards
Hospital-acquired infections contracted during the course of healthcare
Surgical site infections resulting from poor intraoperative sterile technique
Any infection present at the time of the patient's initial admission
questions.explanation: Nosocomial infections, also called hospital-acquired infections, are infections contracted during the course of healthcare that were not present at the time of admission. They represent a major problem in the ICU. Community-acquired infections and pre-existing infections at admission do not qualify as nosocomial infections.

Once a properly conducted, ethically sound decision has been reached to withdraw life-sustaining treatment, the nurse's role is to ensure the process is carried out with dignity, comfort, and compassionate care for the patient and family. Refusing to participate without a recognised conscientious objection process, or withholding comfort measures, would be ethically inappropriate. Supporting a peaceful, dignified process reflects core nursing values during end-of-life care.
questions.question: A nurse is asked to participate in withdrawing life-sustaining treatment from a patient after a properly conducted family and team discussion concluded further treatment was not in the patient's interest. The nurse's ethical role in this process is to:
options: Provide compassionate, dignified care throughout the process
Refuse to participate in any aspect of the process
Withhold comfort measures during the withdrawal process
Rush the process to reduce the nurse's own discomfort
Independently reverse the team's documented decision
Inadequate intravascular volume requiring more fluids
Normal physiological response to any fluid therapy
Arterial line malfunction unrelated to venous pressure
Improved cardiac output from effective resuscitation
Fluid overload or reduced cardiac function
questions.explanation: An unexpectedly high central venous pressure during fluid resuscitation suggests the heart cannot effectively handle the additional volume, indicating fluid overload or impaired cardiac function. This should prompt reassessment of fluid therapy rather than continued aggressive administration. Recognising this pattern helps prevent pulmonary oedema.
questions.question: A central venous pressure reading is significantly higher than expected in a patient receiving fluid resuscitation. This finding most likely indicates:

options: Requiring written consent before any family presence
Ignoring the request without any team communication
Offering family presence with a support person available
Allowing family to participate directly in compressions
Automatically excluding all family members without discussion
questions.explanation: Current resuscitation guidance generally supports offering family the option to be present during resuscitation, accompanied by a staff member who can explain events and offer support. This respects family-centred care while maintaining team focus on the patient. It does not mean family members participate in clinical interventions.
questions.question: A nurse notes that a family member wishes to remain in the room during resuscitation of their relative. Current recommended practice generally supports:
Aerobacter and Proteus species are recognized as nosocomial pathogens because:
questions.explanation: Aerobacter and Proteus species are listed among the microorganisms that cause nosocomial infections in the ICU, thriving in hospital environments and causing infections in susceptible patients. They are gram-negative organisms, not gram-positive, and their modes of transmission and infection sites are varied, not limited to blood products or respiratory only.
options: They thrive in hospital environments and cause infections in ICU patients
They colonize the respiratory tract and cause ventilator-associated pneumonia only
They are gram-positive organisms resistant to all common beta-lactam antibiotics
They are transmitted exclusively through contaminated blood transfusion products
They are the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea in the ICU

questions.question: Which of the following is identified as a reservoir for nosocomial infection in the ICU?
questions.explanation: Bladder irrigation solutions and sinks and sink traps are listed as reservoirs for nosocomial microbes in the ICU. Other reservoirs include patients' wounds, tracheal tubes, urinary bags, catheters, patients' linens, and visitors' and staff apparel. Properly stored sterile equipment and sealed packaged lines are not recognized reservoirs.
options: Clean utility rooms with separately stored medical and cleaning supplies
Freshly laundered bed linen stored in sealed plastic packaging
Negative pressure isolation rooms with HEPA filtration systems
Sealed pre-packaged intravenous lines awaiting patient administration
Bladder irrigation solutions and sink traps in the ICU environment

questions.question: The primary nursing role in ARF prevention for high-risk ICU patients involves:
questions.explanation: The primary nursing role in ARF prevention includes educating patients about risk factors, monitoring for potential issues (e.g., decreased urine output, rising creatinine, nephrotoxic drug use), and advocating for early intervention when necessary. Nurses play a key role in surveillance for early signs of ARF, enabling prompt treatment that can prevent progression to established renal failure.
options: Educating patients and monitoring for risk factors to enable early intervention
Initiating dialysis prophylactically before any signs of renal impairment appear
Restricting all patient oral fluid intake to less than 500 ml per 24 hours
Performing bedside ultrasound daily to detect early renal parenchymal changes
Prescribing nephroprotective medications to prevent renal tubular injury

questions.question: Moral distress in critical care nursing is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: Moral distress occurs when nurses know the ethically appropriate action but are constrained from taking it by institutional policies, authority, or other systemic factors. It leads to frustration, guilt, and professional dissatisfaction. Common triggers include providing treatments nurses believe are futile or not in the patient's best interest due to family or system pressure.
options: Psychological distress from the physical demands of nursing critically ill patients
Anxiety resulting from uncertainty about clinical diagnoses in complex cases
Distress when institutional constraints prevent nurses from acting on ethical beliefs
Emotional fatigue from delivering news of poor prognosis to patient families
Frustration from poor hospital management, underfunding, and understaffing

questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome involves pulmonary infiltrates and vaso-occlusion in the lung vasculature, which can progress rapidly to significant hypoxaemia and respiratory failure, requiring close respiratory monitoring. It is a recognised, serious complication of sickle cell disease rather than a benign or self-limiting event. Early recognition supports timely oxygen therapy, transfusion, and escalation of care as needed.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease should prioritise monitoring for which respiratory complication?
options: Immediate resolution without any respiratory monitoring
No risk of respiratory compromise in this condition
Chronic airway remodelling occurring over several years
Pneumothorax as the primary expected complication
Progressive hypoxaemia from pulmonary infiltrates and vaso-occlusion

questions.question: Crush syndrome is the combination of:
questions.explanation: Crush syndrome is the combination of compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). It represents the systemic manifestation of prolonged crush injury and is a life-threatening condition. Management requires addressing all three components: fasciotomy for compartment syndrome, aggressive hydration and dialysis for rhabdomyolysis, and supportive care for SIRS.
options: Pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, and cardiac tamponade
Burns, electrolyte imbalance, and respiratory failure from inhalation injury
Compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome
Hypovolemia, sepsis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation
Acute kidney injury, liver failure, and cerebral edema from multi-organ failure

questions.question: Effective communication in managing ethical dilemmas in critical care is described as:
questions.explanation: Effective communication involves transparent, honest, and compassionate dialogue with patients and families to ensure understanding of the clinical situation and treatment options. It is a crucial strategy for managing ethical dilemmas, building trust, and facilitating informed decision-making. This is especially important in emotionally charged situations such as end-of-life care decisions.
options: Restricting information to protect families from distressing clinical details
Using technical medical language to maintain professional authority in decisions
Delegating all family communication to the social worker to protect nursing staff
Communicating only positive developments to maintain patient and family hope
Transparent, honest, and compassionate dialogue with patients and families
Document the request and take no further action
Explore the family's concerns and clarify risks of leaving
Immediately allow discharge without further discussion
Refuse to discuss the matter and call security
Insist the family sign forms without any explanation
questions.explanation: When a family requests discharge against advice for a potentially recoverable patient, the nurse should first understand their reasons and clearly explain the risks involved. This respects patient and family autonomy while ensuring an informed decision is made. Immediate compliance or refusal without discussion fails to address the underlying concerns.
questions.question: A nurse observes that a patient meets criteria for 'potentially recoverable' status but the family requests discharge against medical advice. The nurse's most appropriate first action is to:

questions.explanation: Hemodynamically unstable drug ingestion is listed as an ICU admission indication under the Diagnosis Model category of drug ingestion and overdose. All patients are treated based on clinical need, not the cause of illness. Conscious drug overdose with hemodynamic stability is actually a Priority 4A example, but instability changes the classification.
options: A Priority 2 case requiring only monitoring without treatment limits
A ward-level management case with close nursing observation only
An ICU indication under drug ingestion and overdose in Diagnosis Model
A contraindication for ICU due to the patient's role in own illness
Priority 4 Category A because drug overdose is self-inflicted illness
questions.question: A patient with hemodynamically unstable drug ingestion should be classified as:
A nurse is asked why addressing ethical dilemmas proactively in critical care nursing is important. The most accurate explanation is that unresolved dilemmas can:
questions.explanation: Unresolved ethical dilemmas can contribute to significant moral distress among nursing staff, which in turn can affect staff wellbeing, retention, and ultimately the quality of patient care delivered. Proactive, structured approaches to ethical discussion help mitigate this distress. This connection between ethics, staff wellbeing, and care quality underscores the importance of addressing dilemmas rather than avoiding them.
options: Resolve automatically without any structured team input
Have no impact on nursing staff or patient outcomes
Only affect hospital administrative processes and budgets
Improve staff morale by avoiding difficult conversations
Contribute to moral distress affecting staff and care quality

questions.question: A nurse caring for a COPD patient in ICU must be cautious with high-concentration oxygen therapy primarily because it may:
questions.explanation: In some patients with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, the hypoxic drive can be a significant stimulus to breathe, and high-concentration oxygen may blunt this drive, worsening carbon dioxide retention. Careful, titrated oxygen therapy with monitoring is preferred in this population. This risk requires cautious rather than liberal oxygen administration.
options: Improve carbon dioxide clearance more efficiently
Have no effect on this patient's breathing pattern
Immediately cause irreversible lung tissue damage
Blunt the hypoxic respiratory drive and worsen hypercapnia
Cause instant cardiac arrest regardless of dose

questions.explanation: The recommended rate for chest compressions in CPR is 100-120 compressions per minute. Compressions should be hard and fast in the center of the chest. Rates below 100 bpm are too slow to maintain adequate perfusion, and rates above 120 bpm may compromise compression depth and recoil. This rate is specified in current CPR guidelines.
questions.question: The recommended rate of chest compressions in CPR is:
options: Greater than 140 compressions per minute in patients in ventricular fibrillation
Between 120 and 140 compressions per minute for maximum circulation
Between 100 and 120 compressions per minute as per current guidelines
Between 60 and 80 compressions per minute to prevent fatigue
Between 80 and 100 compressions per minute in basic life support

questions.explanation: A valid do-not-attempt-resuscitation order reflects a prior documented decision and should be honoured by withholding chest compressions and defibrillation, focusing instead on comfort and dignity. Initiating resuscitation against a valid order disregards patient autonomy and prior consent. The nurse's role is to respect the documented wishes while supporting the patient and family.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order in place witnesses the patient go into cardiac arrest. The appropriate nursing action is to:
options: Wait for family permission before making any decision
Begin chest compressions immediately regardless of the order
Call for a full resuscitation team response at once
Withhold chest compressions and provide comfort care
Perform resuscitation only if witnessed by other staff

questions.explanation: A narrowing pulse pressure, where systolic and diastolic pressures move closer together, often reflects increasing peripheral vasoconstriction as the body compensates for falling cardiac output in progressing shock. This subtle change can occur before overt hypotension develops. Recognising this trend supports earlier identification of clinical deterioration.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with signs of shock notes a persistently narrowing pulse pressure. This finding most likely indicates:
options: A benign finding unrelated to circulatory status
An expected finding with no monitoring implications
Resolution of the underlying shock process
Worsening compensatory vasoconstriction as shock progresses
Improving cardiac output with no clinical concern

questions.question: A serum glucose level that meets the Objective Parameters for ICU admission is:
options: Serum glucose greater than 600 mg/dl with mild clinical symptoms
Serum glucose greater than 300 mg/dl with ketones in the urine
Serum glucose greater than 800 mg/dl as a newly found laboratory value
Serum glucose greater than 400 mg/dl in a known diabetic patient
Serum glucose greater than 500 mg/dl with normal mental status
questions.explanation: The Objective Parameters specify serum glucose greater than 800 mg/dl as an ICU admission criterion. This extreme level of hyperglycemia is associated with severe metabolic derangement requiring intensive management. Values of 300-600 mg/dl may be clinically significant but do not meet the stated objective threshold.

options: Between 60 and 90 beats per minute under normal resting conditions
Between 70 and 100 beats per minute in all adult age groups
Between 90 and 120 beats per minute in healthy critically ill adults
Between 80 and 110 beats per minute in most adult patients
Between 50 and 80 beats per minute at complete rest
questions.question: The normal heart rate for an adult of 13 years and above in the ICU is:
questions.explanation: The normal heart rate for patients aged 13 years and above is 60-90 beats per minute. For infants 0-12 months, it is 120-160 bpm; 1-3 years: 90-140 bpm; 3-5 years: 80-110 bpm; 5-12 years: 75-100 bpm. Correct age-specific ranges are essential for accurate interpretation of vital signs in ICU patients.

questions.question: Cultural competence in nursing is best defined as:
options: The ability to speak multiple languages to communicate with diverse patients
Knowledge of only the most common cultural groups seen in a particular hospital
Avoiding all discussions of culture to prevent discrimination in patient care
The ability to deliver services meeting the social, cultural, and linguistic needs of patients
Applying identical treatment protocols regardless of a patient's cultural background
questions.explanation: Cultural competence is the ability of healthcare providers and organizations to deliver services that meet the social, cultural, and linguistic needs of diverse patients. It involves respecting cultural differences, being aware of one's own biases, and adapting care to align with patients' values, traditions, and preferences. It promotes equity and reduces health disparities.

questions.question: Why is the ethical dimension of critical care considered uniquely challenging?
options: Because critical care involves simpler clinical decisions than other nursing specialties
Because ethical guidelines in critical care are frequently contradictory and unclear
Because nurses in critical care receive less training in ethics than other specialties
Because nurses must integrate clinical expertise with ethical judgment under pressure
Because critical care patients are always able to communicate clearly with their nurses
questions.explanation: Critical care nursing is both demanding and ethically complex because nurses must integrate clinical expertise with ethical judgment, often under time pressure and with incomplete information, in high-stakes life-or-death situations. This dual requirement — making rapid clinical decisions while simultaneously navigating complex ethical dimensions — makes critical care nursing uniquely challenging.

Equal and normally reactive pupils imply that the upper brainstem and third cranial nerve are intact. Unilateral dilatation and non-reactivity with depressed level of consciousness suggest impaired brainstem function. Pupillary reaction is specifically an assessment of brainstem and cranial nerve function, not overall consciousness or GCS score.
questions.question: Normal pupillary reaction in the ICU implies which of the following?
options: No intracranial pathology is present regardless of other clinical findings
The patient's Glasgow Coma Scale score is within the normal expected range
The upper brain stem and third cranial nerve are intact and functioning
The patient is fully conscious and aware of their surrounding environment
The patient does not require neurological monitoring or further assessment

questions.question: A nurse notes that a ventilated patient's chest rises asymmetrically and breath sounds are diminished on the right side after a recent tube reposition. This finding most likely indicates:
options: Improved ventilation to both lungs equally
Right mainstem bronchus intubation from tube migration
Left-sided pneumothorax unrelated to tube position
Expected finding after any tube repositioning
Normal anatomical variation requiring no action
questions.explanation: Asymmetrical chest rise with diminished breath sounds on one side after tube manipulation suggests the endotracheal tube has migrated into the right mainstem bronchus, ventilating only one lung. This requires prompt tube repositioning and confirmation of correct placement. Left uncorrected, it causes atelectasis of the unventilated lung and hypoxia.

options: The family insists on intensive care regardless of clinical prognosis
The patient has irreversible brain damage with no organ donation option
The patient's diagnosis is chronic and requires regular monitoring
The condition requires monitoring unavailable in high-dependency units
The patient's condition is potentially reversible and survival is expected
questions.explanation: ICU admission is appropriate when the condition is potentially reversible and the patient can reasonably survive the admission. The reversibility of the condition and realistic survival expectation are key criteria. Family insistence alone, irreversible damage, or monitoring needs that could be met at a lower level are not primary indicators.
questions.question: Critical care admission is generally appropriate when:
The recovery phase of ARF (Stage 4) is characterized by:
options: Rapid complete renal recovery within 24-48 hours with normal creatinine
Development of chronic kidney disease requiring permanent renal replacement therapy
Slow recovery of kidney function requiring up to one year for full resolution
Return to pre-illness renal function within 72 hours with appropriate treatment
Persistent oliguria with slowly declining serum creatinine and urea levels
questions.explanation: The recovery phase of ARF is characterized by slow recovery of kidney function that may require up to one year for complete resolution. During this phase, renal function gradually improves, and the patient requires ongoing monitoring. While most cases of ARF are reversible, some patients — particularly those with severe intrarenal injury — may develop chronic kidney disease.

questions.question: Paternalism in healthcare ethics occurs when:
questions.explanation: Paternalism occurs when healthcare providers override or disregard patient preferences on the grounds that they know what is best for the patient. While sometimes intended beneficently, paternalism conflicts with patient autonomy. Modern ethics emphasizes shared decision-making and informed consent rather than unilateral paternalistic decisions by healthcare providers.
options: Healthcare providers override patient preferences for the patient's perceived good
Patients make uninformed decisions that conflict with medical advice given
Families insist on aggressive care that the clinical team considers futile treatment
Patients request more information than the clinical team considers necessary
Nurses follow physician instructions rather than independent clinical judgment

questions.question: In approximately 50% of cardiac arrest victims, the condition is preceded by:
questions.explanation: Cardiac arrest is preceded by no warning symptoms in approximately 50% of people. This makes early recognition of cardiac arrest itself critical, as prevention may not always be possible. The sudden and unpredictable nature of cardiac arrest in half of cases reinforces the importance of public training in CPR and availability of defibrillators.
options: No warning symptoms, making early recognition crucial for survival
Documented episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia on monitoring
Severe chest pain lasting more than 30 minutes with radiation to the arm
Sudden onset of profound hypotension and circulatory collapse symptoms
Prolonged palpitations and dizziness lasting more than one hour before arrest

questions.explanation: Hospital environmental hygiene reduces the environmental reservoir of pathogens, decreasing opportunities for pathogen-patient contact. It is one component of standard infection control principles. However, it does not replace hand hygiene, PPE, or aseptic technique — each plays a distinct and complementary role in preventing nosocomial infections.
options: Replacing the use of PPE since clean surfaces prevent pathogen exposure
Ensuring patients are never exposed to any microorganism during their stay
Reducing the virulence of organisms without preventing their transmission
Reducing the environmental reservoir of pathogens that may infect patients
Eliminating the need for hand hygiene if surfaces are regularly cleaned
questions.question: Hospital environmental hygiene in the ICU contributes to infection control by:

questions.explanation: On the steep part of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve, small drops in saturation correspond to larger drops in PaO2, meaning a saturation of 92% can reflect significant underlying hypoxaemia. This relationship explains why relying on saturation alone can underestimate severity. Correlating both values gives a fuller picture of oxygenation status.
questions.question: A nurse notes that a patient's oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry is 92% while the arterial blood gas PaO2 is 58 mmHg. Applying the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve, the nurse should understand that:
options: This combination is impossible and requires no action
PaO2 values are irrelevant once saturation is known
Small saturation changes reflect large PaO2 changes here
The pulse oximeter reading must be a device error
Saturation and PaO2 change proportionally at all levels

questions.question: A nurse preparing to interpret an arterial blood gas should recognise that the normal PaO2 range used as a reference for ICU patients is generally:
options: Approximately 35 to 45 mmHg on room air
Approximately 100 to 120 mmHg on room air
Approximately 80 to 100 mmHg on room air
questions.explanation: The normal PaO2 range on room air is generally accepted as approximately 80 to 100 mmHg, reflecting adequate arterial oxygenation. This differs from the normal ranges for PaCO2, bicarbonate, and pH, which measure different aspects of gas exchange and acid-base balance. Knowing this range allows the nurse to recognise hypoxaemia promptly.

options: Assume equipment failure and ignore the reading
Reduce sedation to assess patient wakefulness first
Assess for accidental extubation or circuit disconnection
Document the value and continue routine care
Increase the ventilator tidal volume immediately
questions.question: A nurse caring for a mechanically ventilated ICU patient observes a sudden drop in end-tidal carbon dioxide readings toward zero. The priority action is to:
questions.explanation: A sudden fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide toward zero is a critical alarm suggesting accidental extubation, circuit disconnection, or complete airway obstruction, all of which are immediately life-threatening. The nurse must assess the airway and circuit first before any other action. Delayed recognition can rapidly lead to hypoxia and cardiac arrest.

ICU admission decisions must be based on objective, ethical, and transparent decision-making processes. This ensures fairness, reproducibility, and protection of patient rights. Decisions based solely on seniority, bed capacity, finances, or social value are inconsistent with established ethical and clinical guidelines.
options: Objective, ethical, and transparent decision-making processes
Exclusively on the capacity of the ICU at the time of presentation
The patient's social value to the community as assessed by the team
The family's financial contribution to the hospital administration
Seniority of the admitting physician and hospital policy alone
questions.question: The decision to admit or withhold ICU care should be based on:
The significance of ARF in critically ill ICU patients is primarily that it:
options: Is prevented in all cases by optimal hemodynamic management in the ICU
Is a benign self-limiting condition that always resolves without intervention
Is a serious condition that significantly increases morbidity and mortality in ICU
Only occurs as a complication of sepsis and not from other clinical conditions
Occurs only in patients with pre-existing renal disease before ICU admission
questions.explanation: ARF is a serious condition in the ICU that significantly increases morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients. Nurses play a vital role in identifying, managing, and preventing ARF. It can arise from multiple causes in the ICU (sepsis, nephrotoxins, reduced perfusion), is not always preventable, and may be difficult to treat once established, underscoring the importance of early recognition.

options: Directly compress the heart to restore circulation
Help stabilise the cardiac rhythm after defibrillation attempts
Replace the need for further defibrillation attempts
Sedate the patient during ongoing chest compressions
Treat the underlying cause of the cardiac arrest
questions.explanation: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic given during resuscitation from refractory shockable rhythms to help stabilise the cardiac rhythm and improve the chance of successful defibrillation. It does not replace the need for shocks or compressions and does not treat the underlying cause. It is used as an adjunct within the overall resuscitation algorithm.
questions.question: A nurse is asked about the role of amiodarone during resuscitation from refractory ventricular fibrillation. It is administered primarily to:
An ICU nurse is trending a patient's lactate levels every few hours during resuscitation. A persistently rising lactate despite treatment most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: Persistently rising lactate despite treatment reflects ongoing tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism, signalling that current resuscitation is inadequate. Trending lactate helps guide the adequacy of shock treatment over time. A rising trend should prompt reassessment of the treatment plan rather than reassurance.
options: Successful resolution of the underlying shock state
Ongoing tissue hypoperfusion requiring further intervention
A laboratory error unrelated to clinical status
Adequate response to current fluid resuscitation
Normal metabolic variation with no clinical meaning

questions.question: Non-trauma related causes of crush injury include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Rapid deceleration motor vehicle accident is a trauma-related cause of crush injury, not a non-trauma cause. Non-trauma causes include immobility against a firm surface for more than one hour, drug overdose causing prolonged positioning on a limb, MAST pants, stroke/CVA, carbon monoxide poisoning, elderly patients with hip fractures, and intoxication causing prolonged immobility.
options: Prolonged immobility against a firm surface lasting more than one hour
Drug overdose causing an unconscious patient to lie on a limb for hours
Stroke or CVA causing immobility with body weight compressing a body part
Rapid deceleration motor vehicle accident causing blunt traumatic injury
Pneumatic antishock garment (MAST pants) causing compartmental compression

questions.question: In the case study of a 68-year-old COPD patient with an advance directive refusing aggressive care, the ethical priority is:
questions.explanation: The ethical priority in this case is honoring the patient's advance directive, which clearly documented a preference for comfort care and refusal of life-sustaining measures. This upholds the principle of autonomy — respect for self-determination. The healthcare team organized a family meeting to explain the prognosis and facilitate transition to palliative care in alignment with the patient's wishes.
options: Continuing mechanical ventilation until the patient shows clear deterioration
Administering maximum treatment and revisiting the directive after 72 hours
Consulting the ethics committee to override the patient's documented preferences
Honoring the patient's advance directive and providing comfort-focused care
Following family wishes for aggressive care to preserve the patient's life

questions.question: Under bed-shortage conditions, an ICU consultant must choose between admitting a reversible cardiac case and continuing to manage a chronic ventilator-dependent patient already occupying a bed. This scenario best illustrates:
questions.explanation: Choosing between two patients who both need a limited ICU bed is a genuine ethical dilemma involving competing claims to a scarce resource. It requires weighing reversibility, prognosis, and fairness rather than a straightforward administrative fix. Such dilemmas are a recognised consequence of critical care bed shortages.
options: A simple triage error needing disciplinary review
A routine staffing rotation decision within the unit
A billing dispute requiring administrative resolution
An ethical dilemma created by scarce critical care resources
A scheduling conflict resolved by hospital policy alone

questions.explanation: Signs of increased work of breathing, accessory muscle use, and tachycardia during a spontaneous breathing trial indicate the patient is not tolerating reduced ventilator support and the trial should be stopped. Proceeding to extubation in this state risks acute respiratory failure. Recognising weaning failure prevents unsafe premature extubation.
options: A normal expected response to any breathing trial
Improved respiratory muscle strength and endurance
Successful weaning progress requiring immediate extubation
No clinical significance requiring continued observation only
Weaning failure requiring return to fuller ventilator support
questions.question: A patient is being weaned from mechanical ventilation. The nurse notes increasing respiratory rate, use of accessory muscles, and rising heart rate during a spontaneous breathing trial. This most likely indicates:

An ICU patient's gastrointestinal tract is not functioning adequately, enteral feeding has been optimised without success, and total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central line is prescribed.
(a) Identify the condition and the indication for the therapy.
(b) Name the therapy and the access routes.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after the therapy.
(d) State the safety checks and complications to watch for.
(e) State the documentation and communication/escalation required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications for TPN: the GI tract is not functional, cannot be accessed, or GI feeding is inadequate; it is adopted only when absolutely necessary, optimising enteral feeding first.
• If the patient is not absorbing, start TPN on day 3-7 depending on nutritional state.

(b)
Total parenteral nutrition; usually a central line in ICU (keep a clean port, 5-lumen); short term - PIC or PICC (needs a different formula); long term - tunnelled subclavian (Hickman) catheter or subcutaneous port.

(c)
• Before: the doctor decides the patient needs it; the dietitian sees the patient and decides the regime; the bag is ordered from pharmacy and made up aseptically to requirements; screen nutrition status and weigh the patient.
• During: start low and build up; observe strict asepsis when handling the lines.
• After: monitor bloods - U&Es, phosphate, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs, fluid balance, haematology, weight, and trace elements if long term.

(d)
• Complications: line sepsis; overfeeding with lactic acidosis, hyperglycaemia, increased infections, liver impairment (alkaline phosphatase, ALT, GGT, acalculous cholecystitis) and persistent pyrexia.
• Avoid overfeeding.

(e)
Communication: doctors and nurses identify history; nurses weigh; doctors, dietitians and nurses optimise intake and monitor - nursing collaboration with the nutrition team.

options: Acute metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Fully compensated mixed acid-base disturbance overall
Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory response
Acute respiratory acidosis without renal compensation
Chronic respiratory acidosis with full renal compensation
questions.explanation: A low pH with a high PaCO2 and a bicarbonate that remains normal indicates an acute respiratory acidosis, since the kidneys have not yet had time to compensate by retaining bicarbonate. Chronic respiratory acidosis would show an elevated bicarbonate reflecting renal compensation. This pattern points to acute hypoventilation requiring prompt airway or ventilatory support.
questions.question: An arterial blood gas from an ICU patient shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 60 mmHg, and normal bicarbonate. This pattern is best interpreted as:

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support is a Priority 1 ICU admission: critically ill, unstable, needing intensive treatment and monitoring that cannot be provided outside the ICU, with no limits on therapy.

(b)
Ventilatory support through an endotracheal (tracheal) tube; most ICU patients are intubated, which calls for more vigilance.

(c)
• Before/on admission: take baseline arterial blood gases 5-10 minutes after admission with the initial FiO2.
• During: monitor the respiratory pattern, end-tidal CO2 (normal 35-45) and oxygen saturation (90-100%); repeat ABG 30 minutes after changing ventilator parameters and 30 minutes after suctioning; check electrolytes 4-hourly.
• After extubation: ABG 45 minutes to 1 hour afterwards.

(d)
• Watch for retention of CO2, secretions in the tube and tube dislodgement; maintain asepsis because tracheal tubes are reservoirs for microbes.
• Infection safeguards: change suction tubing and oxygen tubing on alternate days, ventilator tubing every fifth day, suction bowls daily; oral toileting three times daily for intubated patients.
questions.question:
A patient with acute respiratory failure is admitted to the ICU and requires ventilatory support through a tracheal tube.
(a) Identify the condition and the priority of admission.
(b) Name the therapy/equipment involved.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities before, during and after the therapy.
(d) State the safety checks and complications to watch for.

questions.explanation: Fulminant hepatic failure is listed as a gastrointestinal ICU indication. Other GI indications include life-threatening GI bleeding with hypotension or comorbidities, severe acute pancreatitis, and esophageal perforation with mediastinitis. Mild peptic ulcer disease, reflux, constipation, and stable IBD in remission do not require ICU-level care.
questions.question: Under the Diagnosis Model, gastrointestinal disorders warranting ICU admission include:
options: Inflammatory bowel disease in remission with normal endoscopy findings
Gastroesophageal reflux disease causing nocturnal respiratory symptoms
Mild peptic ulcer disease managed on proton pump inhibitor therapy
Constipation and incomplete bowel evacuation in a post-operative patient
Fulminant hepatic failure with potential for rapid clinical deterioration

questions.question: An ICU nurse is drawing an arterial sample for blood gas analysis and must first perform which safety check to avoid compromising distal circulation?
questions.explanation: Before radial arterial puncture or catheter insertion, the Allen test is performed to confirm adequate collateral circulation from the ulnar artery in case the radial artery becomes compromised. This reduces the risk of ischaemic complications to the hand. It is a standard safety step before arterial sampling.
options: Allen test to confirm adequate collateral hand circulation
Babinski reflex test for neurological function
Homan's sign assessment for deep vein thrombosis
Capillary refill test on the opposite unaffected limb
Chvostek's sign test for calcium related irritability

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with new-onset atrial fibrillation should prioritise assessment for which major associated risk?
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes ineffective atrial contraction, allowing blood to stagnate and form clots that can embolise and cause stroke, making thromboembolic risk assessment a priority. It does not typically progress directly to ventricular fibrillation or resolve spontaneously without monitoring. Anticoagulation consideration is a key part of managing this dysrhythmia.
options: Guaranteed progression to ventricular fibrillation soon
Spontaneous conversion with no clinical monitoring needed
Thromboembolism and stroke from atrial stasis
Complete resolution without any further evaluation
Immediate cardiac arrest within the first hour

questions.explanation: The oliguric phase (Stage 2) of ARF is defined by urine output less than 400 ml in 24 hours. This follows the initiation phase (Stage 1, onset of injury). Stage 3 is the diuretic or polyuric phase where urine output rises to 3-6 liters per day. Stage 4 is the recovery phase, which is slow and may require up to one year for full recovery.
questions.question: The oliguric phase of ARF is defined by a urine output of:
options: Less than 400 ml in 24 hours representing the second stage of ARF
Less than 100 ml in 24 hours indicating complete renal shutdown
Less than 200 ml in 24 hours representing near-complete renal shutdown
Between 400 ml and 1000 ml per 24 hours indicating partial renal function
Less than 600 ml in 24 hours indicating moderate renal function impairment

questions.explanation: Continuing aggressive treatment when there is no realistic prospect of meaningful recovery raises the ethical concern of medical futility, which can cause unnecessary suffering and inappropriate use of limited resources. Recognising futility requires careful, collaborative discussion among the team, patient, and family rather than automatic continuation of treatment. This is a recognised ethical dilemma in critical care, not a straightforward legal matter.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a critically ill patient recognises that continuing aggressive treatment with no realistic chance of recovery may constitute:
options: A legal requirement with no ethical consideration
Standard best practice regardless of prognosis
A decision requiring no further team discussion
Medically futile care raising an ethical concern
An appropriate use of critical care resources
Kinking of the ventilator tubing itself
Circuit disconnection or a significant air leak
Biting down on the endotracheal tube
Airway obstruction from thick secretions present
questions.explanation: A low-pressure alarm typically indicates a disconnection or leak in the ventilator circuit, cuff, or connections, allowing delivered volume to escape. This differs from a high-pressure alarm, which suggests obstruction or resistance. Prompt identification of the leak source restores effective ventilation.
questions.question: A ventilated patient's low-pressure alarm sounds continuously. The nurse should first check for:

options: Legal guidelines prevent nurses from implementing the most ethical solutions
Healthcare systems lack the resources to implement the ethically correct solution
Family conflict always overrides ethical reasoning in critical care situations
Nursing education does not adequately prepare nurses for ethical decision-making
Each available choice violates at least one ethical principle, creating inevitable moral loss
questions.explanation: Ethical dilemmas are defined as situations where each available choice violates at least one ethical principle — any decision results in some form of moral loss. This is what makes dilemmas different from ordinary clinical challenges. There is no perfect solution; the goal is to choose the option that best honors the most relevant ethical principles given the specific circumstances.
questions.question: The reason ethical dilemmas are described as involving unavoidable moral loss is that:

questions.explanation: While SBAR is primarily a communication tool, its ethical significance lies in promoting clear, structured, and transparent communication that ensures patient safety and reduces errors. Effective communication is a key strategy for managing ethical dilemmas in critical care and is essential for honoring patient-centered care and interdisciplinary collaboration.
questions.question: In the SBAR communication tool, the ethical significance lies primarily in:
options: Limiting the amount of information nurses share with physicians during handover
Promoting clear, structured, and transparent communication about patient status
Ensuring that all documentation is completed in a standardized legal format
Allowing nurses to express personal opinions about physician care decisions
Standardizing medication documentation to prevent pharmacological errors only
Approximately 10-20% of people who survived cardiac arrest events
Approximately 50% of all survivors who receive advanced cardiac life support
Approximately 30-40% of survivors particularly in out-of-hospital settings
Greater than 60% of long-term cardiac arrest survivors after neurological recovery
Less than 5% of all survivors of both in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrest
questions.explanation: Near-death experiences are reported by 10-20% of people who survived cardiac arrest. This is a significant proportion, raising important psychological and spiritual considerations in post-arrest care. The prevalence of near-death experiences is well below the unrealistically high 67% survival rates often depicted on television.
questions.question: Near-death experiences are reported by what proportion of cardiac arrest survivors?

options: Hypokalaemia causing flattened T waves instead
Hypercalcaemia causing a shortened QT interval
Normal ECG variant requiring no further evaluation
questions.question: A nurse notes peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex on a patient's ECG who has a history of renal failure. This pattern should raise suspicion for:
questions.explanation: Peaked T waves with a widening QRS complex are classic ECG changes associated with hyperkalaemia, a common and dangerous complication in renal failure that can progress to life-threatening dysrhythmias. Hypokalaemia would show different changes such as flattened T waves and U waves. Prompt recognition allows urgent treatment to stabilise the myocardium.

The Four Quadrants Approach evaluates Medical Indications (appropriate treatments), Patient Preferences (wishes and autonomy), Quality of Life (impact of treatments on well-being), and Contextual Features (legal, social, or cultural factors). This structured model ensures that ethical decisions are clinically appropriate, morally sound, patient-centered, and contextually sensitive.
questions.question: The Four Quadrants Approach to ethical conflict resolution in critical care evaluates:
options: Diagnosis, prognosis, treatment options, and discharge planning requirements
Medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life, and contextual features
Legal, financial, administrative, and clinical aspects of the ethical problem
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice as the four components
Nursing assessment, physician judgment, family wishes, and hospital policy

questions.explanation: In BLS, checking for responsiveness involves gently shaking or tapping the person and asking loudly if they are okay. This rapid assessment distinguishes the unconscious cardiac arrest victim from a sleeping or unresponsive-but-breathing person. Advanced assessment tools like monitors and auscultation are not required for initial responsiveness assessment.
questions.question: In performing BLS, checking for responsiveness should be done by:
options: Examining the patient's pupils for light reactivity and corneal reflex
Gently shaking or tapping the person and asking loudly if they are okay
Attaching a pulse oximeter and cardiac monitor to assess vital function
Auscultating the chest for heart sounds and breath sounds bilaterally
Measuring blood pressure and heart rate using electronic monitoring devices

questions.explanation: Compartment syndrome is a complication of crush injuries where internal swelling creates pressure within a confined muscle compartment that may cause tissue ischemia and necrosis. It is identified by the 5 Ps: pain out of proportion, pallor, paresthesias, paralysis, and pulselessness. However, these signs are not reliable in patients with decreased consciousness, making invasive pressure monitoring important.
questions.question: Compartment syndrome as a complication of crush injury involves:
options: Venous thrombosis causing pulmonary embolism in the post-injury period
Nerve compression causing permanent paralysis distal to the injury site
Internal swelling creating pressure within the muscle compartment causing ischemia
Bacterial infection of the crushed tissue leading to systemic septicemia
Excessive bleeding into joint spaces causing hemarthrosis and joint destruction

questions.explanation: The best initial management of Clostridium difficile (C. diff) infection is to stop the causative antibiotic, as C. diff is commonly triggered by antibiotic-associated disruption of gut flora. Continuing or broadening antibiotics worsens the condition. C. diff is transmitted through feces and contaminated surfaces, not through blood or IV catheters.
questions.question: Clostridium difficile infection in the ICU is best managed by:
options: Increasing the dose of the current antibiotic to overcome the resistance
Continuing all current antibiotics while adding targeted antifungal agents
Stopping the causative antibiotic as the primary management strategy
Administering broader-spectrum antibiotics to cover all organisms present
Applying topical antiseptics to the perianal area to reduce spore load
Reduce the need for any sedation medication
Replace the need for ongoing haemodynamic monitoring
Eliminate the requirement for positive pressure ventilation
Prevent all future episodes of pneumonia entirely
questions.explanation: Prone positioning in ARDS improves oxygenation by promoting more uniform lung aeration and better ventilation-perfusion matching, particularly in the previously dependent lung regions. It is a recognised adjunct therapy for severe hypoxaemia, not a replacement for ventilator support or a preventive measure against infection. Careful monitoring is required during and after repositioning due to risks such as line dislodgement.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a mechanically ventilated patient with ARDS notes the physician has ordered prone positioning. This intervention primarily aims to:
Continuous heart beat monitoring in the ICU is most accurately achieved by:
options: Repeated manual palpation of the radial pulse every 15 minutes
Pulse oximetry waveform analysis to determine cardiac rhythm patterns
End-tidal CO2 monitoring with capnographic waveform analysis
Non-invasive blood pressure cuff cycling automatically every hour
Electrodes attached to the patient connected to a bedside cardiac monitor
questions.explanation: Continuous heart beat monitoring in the ICU is achieved through electrodes attached to the patient and connected to a cardiac monitor. This provides continuous ECG waveform monitoring. Manual pulse palpation, BP cycling, EtCO2 monitoring, and pulse oximetry waveform are supplementary tools, not the primary method of continuous cardiac monitoring.

options: Transfer the patient to ICU regardless of prior agreement
Call for emergency intubation without consulting the team
Manage symptoms on the ward per the agreed treatment ceiling
Ignore the ceiling and initiate advanced life support
Delay all interventions until the family arrives
questions.explanation: A pre-agreed treatment ceiling reflects a documented, discussed decision about the limits of escalation and should guide care during deterioration. Overriding it without new discussion disregards patient autonomy and prior clinical consensus. The nurse should provide appropriate symptom management within the agreed plan and alert the medical team.
questions.question: A patient with a known treatment ceiling of 'ward-based care only' deteriorates overnight. The nurse's most appropriate action, consistent with ICU admission ethics, is to:

questions.explanation: WHO guidelines on hand hygiene are relevant because clean hands significantly reduce the risk of transmitting nosocomial pathogens in clinical settings. Hand hygiene is the single most effective infection control intervention but is part of a comprehensive approach that includes PPE, aseptic technique, and environmental hygiene. It is not the sole sufficient measure.
options: WHO mandates hand hygiene as the only required infection control measure
Hand hygiene is sufficient without the need for PPE or aseptic technique
Clean hands reduce the risk of transmission of nosocomial pathogens significantly
Hand hygiene prevents all types of healthcare-associated infections globally
Hand hygiene is only required before performing surgical procedures
