questions.question:
A. Describe the principles of drug use in breastfeeding under the following headings: (i) background and safety; (ii) factors affecting drug concentration in milk; (iii) oral bioavailability, maternal pharmacogenomics and milk volume; (iv) factors determining risk to the infant; (v) drugs contraindicated.
B. Relate the principle to the following examples: (i) codeine; (ii) sertraline and protein-bound drugs; (iii) other drugs (metronidazole, valproate, azathioprine, citalopram, omeprazole, gentamicin); (iv) galactogogues and social drugs.
C. (i) Explain how these principles improve patient outcomes; (ii) state the limitation; (iii) state the trade-off.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Most commonly used drugs are relatively safe for breastfed babies because the dose via milk is generally small and much less than known safe doses given directly to infants; few adverse effects occur and it is generally not necessary to suspend breastfeeding.
A(ii)
Passive diffusion is the primary pathway; factors are maternal plasma concentration (high Vd lowers it), protein binding (free drug diffuses), molecular size (heparins and insulin are too large), ionisation (milk pH 7.2 traps weak bases such as oxycodone and codeine) and lipid solubility (citalopram).
A(iii)
The infant gut may degrade the drug (omeprazole) or poorly absorb it (gentamicin); CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers convert codeine to morphine; the estimated intake of an exclusively breastfed baby is 150 mL/kg/day; a relative infant dose of 10% or more is the notional level of concern.
A(iv)
Timing of the dose (feed before the dose; not for long half-life drugs such as diazepam), infant age (most adverse effects occur in newborns under two months, with capacity at birth about a third of that at 7 to 8 months) and premature babies and neonates' poor metabolism and excretion.
A(v)
Contraindicated: amiodarone, antineoplastics, gold salts, iodine (high doses above 150 µg daily), lithium (feasible only with rigorous monitoring), radiopharmaceuticals and oral retinoids.
B(i)
Codeine should be avoided (up to 10% of Western Europeans and up to 30% of North Africans are ultra-rapid metabolisers, with potential CNS depression and infant death); use paracetamol or ibuprofen.
B(ii)
Sertraline (98% protein bound, high Vd) is minimally transferred, venlafaxine has lower binding and more drug in milk, and ibuprofen and warfarin (99% bound) transfer little.
B(iii)
Metronidazole is safe short term; valproate is regarded as safe, especially as monotherapy (monitor infant liver and platelets); azathioprine is excreted as 6-mercaptopurine (monitor the infant); citalopram needs infant drowsiness monitoring; omeprazole is degraded in the infant gut; gentamicin is poorly absorbed orally.
B(iv)
Domperidone and metoclopramide have limited evidence for boosting milk; non-drug measures are preferred; advise delaying alcohol until after a feed and waiting two hours; nicotine replacement is preferable to smoking; high caffeine causes irritability and poor sleep; cannabis may impair motor development.
C(i)
Accurate advice promotes breastfeeding (NHMRC recommends exclusive breastfeeding for around six months), reduces maternal anxiety from negative product information, and protects vulnerable infants through practice points such as lowest effective dose, short half-life drugs (sertraline rather than fluoxetine) and alternative routes.
C(ii)
Neonates and premature infants have limited capacity, prior in-utero exposure adds to levels and long half-life drugs do not follow the timing rule.
C(iii)
Suspending breastfeeding (and expressing milk) is needed for toxic drugs such as cytotoxics, with reinstatement set by half-life, and continuing breastfeeding may not be possible if lengthy toxic treatment is needed.

questions.question:
A. Describe allopurinol clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) interactions; (viii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for selection and for the starting dose; (ii) state the rationale for flare prophylaxis and combination therapy.
C. (i) Explain the basis of its toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of therapeutic failure and the alternatives.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Allopurinol is the first-line xanthine oxidase inhibitor for long-term prevention of recurrent gout attacks, used after two or more attacks a year, tophi, kidney disease or uric acid urolithiasis.
A(ii)
Oral; start at no more than 100 mg daily with normal kidney function and no more than 50 mg/day in stage 4 or worse CKD; titrate every 2 to 5 weeks up to a maximum of 800 mg/day until the target serum uric acid is reached.
A(iii)
It lowers uric acid in a dose-dependent manner.
A(iv)
It reduces uric acid by impairing conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid.
A(v)
Mild: skin rash, leukopenia, GI problems, headache, urticaria; severe: allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (toxic epidermal necrolysis, erythema multiforme or exfoliative dermatitis, hepatitis, interstitial nephritis, eosinophilia), rare but with 20% to 25% mortality.
A(vi)
Low starting dose is a precaution against hypersensitivity syndrome and flares; stage 4 CKD needs a lower start.
A(vii)
It can be combined with a drug having uricosuric properties (probenecid, losartan or fenofibrate) in refractory cases, and a combination product exists with lesinurad (Duzallo 200/200 mg for CrCl 45 to 59 and 200/300 mg for CrCl above 59 mL/min).
A(viii)
Serum uric acid, with a goal below 6 mg/dL (357 µmol/L) and preferably below 5 mg/dL (297 µmol/L) in severe gout; therapy is long term.
B(i)
Xanthine oxidase inhibitors work in both overproducers and underexcretors and are the most widely prescribed; a low start avoids hypersensitivity and flares.
B(ii)
Rapid mobilisation of urate deposits can trigger attacks, so give colchicine or an NSAID for at least the first 8 weeks; combination with a uricosurics-type drug is suggested in refractory cases.
C(i)
Toxicity arises as hypersensitivity, with higher risk at high starting doses and in kidney disease.
C(ii)
Failure is addressed by combining with a uricosuric, switching to febuxostat (second line because of cardiovascular mortality warnings and cost) or using pegloticase 8 mg IV every 2 weeks in refractory gout.

A(i)
They are oral long-acting insulin secretagogues for type 2 diabetes with intact, functioning β-cells; second-generation agents are glyburide/glibenclamide, glipizide and glimepiride; first-generation agents (acetohexamide, chlorpropamide, tolazamide, tolbutamide) are seldom used.
A(ii)
Oral (for example, glibenclamide 5 mg twice daily).
A(iii)
They act within hours; the half-life of chlorpropamide rises from 25 to 48 hours to about 99 hours in the elderly.
A(iv)
They bind the sulfonylurea receptor on the β-cell, directly increasing insulin secretion and decreasing glucagon release, with pancreatic and extra-pancreatic effects.
A(v)
Hypoglycaemia and weight gain; less common rash, photosensitivity, dyspepsia and nausea; efficacy: A1c lowering 1% to 2%, reducing both fasting and postprandial glucose.
A(vi)
Contraindicated in diabetic ketoacidosis, type 1 diabetes, severe liver or kidney disease and hypoglycaemic unawareness; glipizide is the sulfonylurea of choice in renal insufficiency.
A(vii)
Alcohol raises the risk of hypoglycaemia in patients on antidiabetic drugs.
A(viii)
Blood glucose and HbA1c, weight and signs of hypoglycaemia; self-monitoring is advised.
B(i)
Advantages are quick action (within hours), high initial response rate and low cost; glipizide is selected in renal insufficiency.
B(ii)
They are avoided in hypoglycaemic unawareness (neuroglycopenia), as secretagogue use is best avoided there, and in patients with limited β-cell function after long disease duration.
C(i)
Toxicity arises from excess insulin secretion causing hypoglycaemia, with weight gain.
C(ii)
Eventual treatment failure occurs, as β-cell function declines with disease duration; the sulfonylureas are useful only with functioning β-cells.
questions.question:
A. Describe the sulfonylureas clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) interactions; (viii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for selection of an agent; (ii) state the rationale for avoiding them in some patients.
C. (i) Explain the basis of toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of therapeutic failure.

A patient has had phenytoin 300 mg daily orally for 30 days with a steady-state concentration of 7.9 mg/L. When the dose was raised to 450 mg/day, the steady-state concentration 35 days later was 30 mg/L. Assume oral bioavailability of 1.
(i) Interpret the two concentrations against the therapeutic range and the expected dose-concentration relationship.
(ii) Explain the pharmacokinetic reasoning.
(iii) Calculate Km and Vmax with the equations.
(iv) Calculate the daily dose needed for a steady-state concentration of 15 mg/L.
(v) State the clinical significance of the Km value.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The therapeutic range is 10 to 20 mg/L: 7.9 mg/L is below it, while a 50% dose increase (300 to 450 mg) raised the level about four-fold to 30 mg/L, above the range; a proportional (linear) rise would not be expected.
(ii)
Phenytoin shows capacity-limited (Michaelis-Menten) elimination, so the dose-Css ratio is not constant and clearance falls as concentration rises; elimination rate = Vmax × C / (Km + C); when Cp is large relative to Km the enzymes saturate and concentrations rise disproportionately.
(iii)
R₁/Css₁ = 300/7.9 = 38 L/day and R₂/Css₂ = 450/30 = 15 L/day; Km = (D₂ - D₁) / [(D₁/C₁) - (D₂/C₂)] = 150 / (37.97 - 15.00) = 6.5 mg/L; Vmax = D₁ + Km × (D₁/C₁), or from D = Vmax × C / (Km + C): 300 = Vmax × 7.9 / (6.5 + 7.9), giving Vmax of about 546.8 mg/day.
(iv)
D = Vmax × Css / (Km + Css) = about 548 × 15 / (6.5 + 15) = about 382 mg/day.
(v)
In practice Km ranges from 1 to 15 mg/L and Vmax from 100 to 1000 mg/day; patients with a low Km show greater concentration changes with dose adjustments, so avoid dosing near enzyme saturation; Michaelis-Menten kinetics becomes clinically important as Km approaches the therapeutic concentration.

questions.question:
An 80-kg adult with newly established type 1 diabetes has polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and blurred vision, with glucose in the urine and blood.
(i) Identify the condition, its pathophysiology and the confirmatory glucose criteria.
(ii) Select an insulin regimen and justify the choice.
(iii) Calculate the total daily dose and the basal and bolus doses.
(iv) State how the mealtime dose can be matched to carbohydrate intake.
(v) State the monitoring and glycaemic targets.
(vi) State the acute complications and their treatment.
(vii) State the counselling points on devices and injection technique.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (5 to 10% of diabetes) results from cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells with absolute insulin deficiency; diagnosis requires classic symptoms plus fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more (no caloric intake for 8 to 12 hours), or a 2-hour OGTT (75 g glucose) value of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or more, confirmed by repeat testing if unequivocal hyperglycaemia is absent.
(ii)
Insulin is required for survival, so multiple daily injections with analogues are used: basal insulin (glargine, detemir) lowers fasting glucose production and meets about 50% of daily needs; bolus insulin (aspart, glulisine, lispro) limits postprandial hyperglycaemia and each meal needs 10 to 20% of the daily requirement.
(iii)
Daily dose is 0.5 unit/kg = 40 units; 50% basal = glargine (or detemir) 20 units daily; 50% bolus split into three mealtime doses: aspart (or glulisine, lispro) 6 units pre-breakfast, 7 units pre-lunch and 7 units pre-dinner; titrate to blood glucose target.
(iv)
Insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (rule of 500) = 500 / total daily insulin dose (for example 500/50 = 10, i.e. 1 unit per 10 g of carbohydrate); it needs extensive patient education on carbohydrate counting; rapid-acting insulin has onset of 5 to 15 minutes, peak at 45 to 75 minutes and lasts 3 to 5 hours.
(v)
Self-monitoring of blood glucose at least three or four times a day in type 1 diabetes; targets: HbA1c below 7%, pre-prandial glucose 70 to 130 mg/dL, 2-hour post-prandial below 180 mg/dL (individualised); HbA1c reflects glycaemia over the preceding 2 to 3 months.
(vi)
Hypoglycaemia: if conscious give 15 g of carbohydrate, then a long-acting carbohydrate, and recheck in 15 minutes (repeat if below 70 mg/dL or still symptomatic); if unconscious give glucagon 1 mg subcutaneously or intramuscularly and look for causes; diabetic ketoacidosis (commoner in type 1 with poor control): fluid and electrolyte replacement, IV regular insulin, potassium and phosphate replacement and bicarbonate, with close monitoring.
(vii)
Teach safe use of pens, pumps and syringes, site rotation and site care, needle length, skinfolds, priming, storage and device disposal; pens give more accurate dosing, easier dose setting and better adherence but cost more; hypoglycaemia is largely prevented by taking medication properly, regular meals and regular glucose checks.

questions.question:
A. Describe the following pharmacokinetic principle: the effect of renal impairment on drug dosing, under these headings: (i) causes and effects of kidney failure on pharmacokinetics; (ii) the basis of dose adjustment for loading and maintenance doses; (iii) the approaches to adjustment; (iv) the assumptions made; (v) the markers of glomerular filtration.
B. Relate the principle to examples: (i) creatinine clearance equations for adults; (ii) equations for unstable renal function; (iii) equations for children; (iv) removal of drugs by dialysis and related techniques.
C. (i) Explain how the principle improves patient outcomes; (ii) state the limitations; (iii) state the trade-off between dose and interval changes.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Causes include pyelonephritis, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, nephrotoxic drugs and metals (aminoglycosides, phenacetin, mercury, lead), hypovolaemia and nephroallergens; glomerular filtration and active secretion fall, prolonging half-lives, and bioavailability, distribution (Vd, protein binding) and elimination may change, with altered drug sensitivities.
A(ii)
The loading dose is based on Vd (LD = Cp × Vd), which is generally not significantly altered, so it equals the dose in non-uremic patients; the maintenance dose is based on clearance, which falls, estimated from the fraction of normal renal function remaining (from creatinine clearance), using MD = CLT × Cssav × T / (S × F).
A(iii)
Dose can be reduced with the same frequency (Du = Dn × CLTu/CLTn, or Du = Dn × ku/kn), or the interval lengthened with unchanged dose, or both; with the ku approach the non-renal rate constant is assumed unchanged and the renal rate constant to fall in proportion to creatinine clearance (k = knr + kr).
A(iv)
Assumptions: creatinine clearance accurately measures impairment; dose-independent kinetics; non-renal elimination unchanged; constant absorption; clearance declines linearly with creatinine clearance; unaltered protein binding; and constant target concentration; each may be violated (for example uraemic accumulation alters protein binding, and potassium changes affect digoxin sensitivity).
A(v)
An ideal marker is freely filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted, not metabolised, not protein bound, non-toxic and does not alter filtration; inulin fulfils most criteria but is time-consuming; creatinine is the most used (small tubular secretion); blood urea nitrogen (normal 10 to 20 mg/dL) is not a quantitative measure of kidney function.
B(i)
Cockcroft-Gault (stable function): males CLcr = (140 - age) × weight (kg) / (72 × Scr in mg/dL), with 85% for females; (140 - age) × weight / Scr (µmol/L) in SI form; the urine method is CLcr = Cu × V × 100 / (Ccr × 1440); in obesity use ideal or adjusted body weight (AjBW = IBW + 0.4 × (TBW - IBW) when TBW exceeds 120% of IBW).
B(ii)
The Brater, Jelliffe and Chiou equations apply when renal function is unstable; if the time difference between values is less than one day, ignore the Jelliffe and Brater results and use only the Chiou equation.
B(iii)
Schwartz: CLcr = 0.55 × body length (cm) / Scr; Traub and Johnson used a nomogram based on height and serum creatinine in children aged 6 to 12 years; Siersback-Nielsen's nomogram is comparable with Cockcroft-Gault in adults.
B(iv)
Dialysis, hemoperfusion (passing blood over an adsorbent) and haemofiltration (convection across a semipermeable membrane) remove toxic substances; the extent of drug removal is determined by drug properties (for digoxin, insignificant amounts are removed because of its large Vd).
C(i)
Individualising dose to residual renal function prevents accumulation and severe or fatal effects from doses that are safe in normal function, especially for drugs mainly excreted by the kidney with narrow therapeutic windows.
C(ii)
Creatinine-based estimates may be biased and should be verified by physical diagnosis and clinical tests; in elderly or emaciated patients creatinine production is low so values may appear normal despite dysfunction; the risk of retention concerns only drugs mainly excreted by the kidney.
C(iii)
Lengthening the interval keeps the dose but gives larger fluctuations, whereas reducing the dose with the same interval keeps the frequency; either method or a series of compromises between them may be used.

(i)
Hepatic clearance depends on hepatic blood flow and the extraction ratio; for high extraction drugs (for example morphine, propranolol) elimination is limited by hepatic perfusion, oral bioavailability may increase because of decreased first-pass effect, and protein binding may change because of reduced albumin synthesis.
(ii)
Amount eliminated non-renally is (1 - fe); assuming linear kinetics and no deterioration of renal clearance, D hepatitis / D normal = RL × (1 - fe) + fe, where RL is the residual liver function and fe the fraction excreted unchanged.
(iii)
Drugs with low fe are more affected; drugs less than 20% eliminated by the liver are unlikely to be affected, and drugs eliminated mainly by renal routes are least affected; wide therapeutic range drugs are less affected by moderate impairment; metabolism of high intrinsic clearance drugs may be impaired; biliary obstruction may impair excretion of glucuronide metabolites; for example hepatic disease has little influence on digoxin clearance so no adjustment is needed.
(iv)
Child-Pugh classification: groups A, B and C (mild, moderate, severe) correspond to scores of 5 to 6, 7 to 9 and 10 to 15 (a normal liver scores 5, so there is no zero score); serum albumin, prothrombin time and bilirubin are encouraged markers; exogenous markers (antipyrine, MEGX from lidocaine, indocyanine green, galactose) may be used in parallel.
(v)
AST and ALT detect liver cell damage rather than function (ALT is liver specific; AST/ALT of 1 or less suggests acute liver injury and 2 or more alcoholic hepatitis); no single test accurately assesses liver function, so lab tests are used to relate severity to expected pharmacokinetic change.
questions.question:
A patient with chronic liver disease (cirrhosis after chronic hepatitis B or C or alcohol) needs a drug that is eliminated mainly by hepatic metabolism and has a high extraction ratio, such as propranolol.
(i) Predict the effect of liver disease on the pharmacokinetics of this drug.
(ii) State the equation for dose adjustment based on residual liver function.
(iii) State the factors that determine whether a drug is more or less affected by liver disease, and name the safer type of agent.
(iv) State how the degree of hepatic impairment is assessed.
(v) Justify the monitoring plan.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Acute gout (podagra): monoarticular, rapid-onset attack, often beginning at night, with erythematous, warm, swollen joint, fever and leukocytosis; definitive diagnosis is intracellular monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid leukocytes; urate crystal deposition causes inflammation, vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and neutrophil chemotaxis; alcohol is a recognised precipitant; untreated attacks last 3 to 14 days.
(ii)
NSAIDs, corticosteroids or colchicine are used and treatment should begin as soon as possible after onset; NSAIDs have excellent efficacy and minimal toxicity short term (indomethacin, naproxen and sulindac are approved); corticosteroids are equivalent in efficacy to NSAIDs; colchicine is highly effective if started early.
(iii)
NSAID: start within 24 hours and continue until complete resolution (usually 5 to 8 days); prednisone or prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg daily for 5 to 10 days then stop, or for 2 to 5 days then taper over 7 to 10 days; triamcinolone acetonide 20 to 40 mg intra-articular if one or two joints; colchicine 1.2 mg initially then 0.6 mg 1 hour later (use within 36 hours of onset), and the ACR suggests 0.6 mg once or twice daily from 12 hours later until resolution.
(iv)
Monitor pain, joint inflammation and response (two-thirds respond within hours when colchicine is started within 24 hours); monitor renal and hepatic function and blood pressure in NSAID users.
(v)
NSAIDs: GI (gastritis, bleeding, perforation), renal (papillary necrosis, reduced GFR), cardiovascular (raised BP, sodium and fluid retention) and CNS effects; corticosteroids are well tolerated short term but caution in diabetes, GI problems, bleeding disorders, cardiovascular and psychiatric disorders; colchicine causes dose-dependent nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, neutropenia and axonal neuromyopathy.
(vi)
Colchicine levels rise with P-glycoprotein or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (for example clarithromycin) so dose reduction may be required, and myopathy risk rises with other myopathic drugs such as statins; use caution in renal or hepatic impairment.
(vii)
Local ice application is the most effective adjunctive treatment; dietary supplements (flaxseed, cherry, celery root) are not recommended; limit alcohol (avoid during frequent attacks), lose weight through caloric restriction and exercise, limit purine-rich foods (organ meats, some seafood) and high-fructose corn syrup, and encourage vegetables and low-fat dairy; prophylactic urate-lowering therapy is considered after two or more attacks a year.
questions.question:
A man is woken at night by excruciating pain, swelling, redness and warmth of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, with fever, after alcohol ingestion; synovial fluid aspiration shows intracellular monosodium urate crystals.
(i) Identify the condition and explain the supporting findings and mechanism.
(ii) Select drug therapy for the acute attack and justify the choice.
(iii) State the dose, route and duration for each option.
(iv) State the monitoring parameters.
(v) State the key adverse effects and cautions.
(vi) State the interactions.
(vii) State the counselling and non-drug measures.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Rapid sequence intubation to relax muscles and facilitate endotracheal intubation, muscle relaxation for surgery, and as an anaesthesia adjunct enhancing other anaesthetics.
A(ii)
Intravenous.
A(iii)
Onset in 30 to 60 seconds and metabolism within 3 to 5 minutes by plasma cholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) into succinylmonocholine, then succinic acid and choline; paralysis normally lasts 4 to 6 minutes (2 to 6 minutes); 90% to 95% of an IV dose is hydrolysed before reaching the junction.
A(iv)
It is a depolarising muscle relaxant; the remaining 5% to 10% acts as an acetylcholine receptor agonist at the neuromuscular junction, causing prolonged depolarisation of the motor end plate.
A(v)
Prolonged paralysis and apnoea, respiratory failure and protracted paralysis in BChE variants.
A(vi)
Avoid in people with BChE deficiency (atypical, silent and other variants); a normal dose can cause apnoea; mivacurium is similarly affected.
A(vii)
Monitor ventilation and vital signs; dibucaine number (normal 70 or more) classifies genotype; genetic testing after an event and testing of family members.
B(i)
Rapid onset and short duration make onset and offset predictable for controlled anaesthesia.
B(ii)
After an apnoea event, test for BChE deficiency, test family members and use alternative muscle relaxants.
C(i)
Toxicity: with a mutated enzyme an excess reaches the junction producing protracted paralysis (4 to 8 hours in homozygous atypical, up to 10 hours reported), and homozygotes for atypical or silent variants are certain to have prolonged apnoea.
C(ii)
Variants alter response: the K-variant lowers activity 30%, the J-variant lowers circulating enzyme by two-thirds, the fluoride-resistant variant mildly to moderately prolongs the block, and the C5 variant (about 30% higher activity) shortens the duration of action.
questions.question:
A. Describe succinylcholine clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) route of administration; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for its selection; (ii) state the rationale for genetic testing and dose or drug change.
C. (i) Explain the basis of its toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of altered response and therapeutic failure.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Non-linear pharmacokinetics (capacity-limited, dose-dependent or saturation kinetics) occurs when an enzyme- or carrier-mediated process (absorption, distribution, biotransformation or excretion) becomes saturated; at low doses kinetics are first order, at higher doses mixed order and at very high doses may approach zero order.
A(ii)
AUC is not proportional to the bioavailable dose, urinary excretion is not proportional to dose, elimination is not first order, half-life changes with dose and metabolite ratios may change with dose.
A(iii)
Determine Css at different doses (proportional means linear), or determine F, t½ and total clearance at different doses; a change in normally constant parameters indicates non-linearity.
A(iv)
Absorption (solubility-limited griseofulvin, carrier-mediated riboflavin and ascorbic acid, saturable first-pass for propranolol); distribution (saturable protein binding such as phenylbutazone, tissue binding such as imipramine); metabolism (enzyme saturation, induction, hepatotoxicity); excretion (active secretion, active reabsorption, urine pH).
A(v)
Elimination rate = Vmax × Cp / (Km + Cp), where Km is the concentration at which elimination is half maximal and is not an elimination constant; when Cp is much larger than Km (phenytoin) enzymes saturate, and when Cp is small relative to Km saturation occurs only at supratherapeutic doses (paracetamol); Vd is not involved.
B(i)
Saturated absorption lowers bioavailability with dose; saturated protein binding (phenylbutazone) increases free drug and Vd, while saturated tissue binding (imipramine) decreases Vd.
B(ii)
Phenytoin, theophylline and alcohol show capacity-limited metabolism (higher Css, lower CL); carbamazepine induction lowers concentration on repeated dosing; penicillin secretion decreases renal clearance while vitamins and glucose reabsorption increases it.
B(iii)
Phenytoin Css was 7.9 mg/L on 300 mg/day and 30 mg/L on 450 mg/day; Km = (D₂ - D₁) / [(D₁/C₁) - (D₂/C₂)] = 6.5 mg/L and Vmax about 546.8 mg/day, or the plot of R against R/Css.
B(iv)
For Css of 15 mg/L (range 10 to 20), D = Vmax × Css / (Km + Css) = about 382 mg/day.
C(i)
It helps avoid dosing near enzyme saturation and allows doses to be set from individual Km and Vmax, preventing disproportionate concentration rises.
C(ii)
Predicting a blood concentration from a single dose is difficult because the apparent elimination constant changes with dose, and concentrations rise rapidly once elimination is saturated.
C(iii)
Km in patients ranges 1 to 15 mg/L and Vmax 100 to 1000 mg/day; patients with a low Km show greater changes in concentration with dose adjustments, and Michaelis-Menten kinetics becomes clinically important as Km approaches the therapeutic concentration.
questions.question:
A. Describe non-linear (capacity-limited) pharmacokinetics under the following headings: (i) definition and concept; (ii) characteristics; (iii) tests to detect it; (iv) causes; (v) Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
B. Relate the principle to examples: (i) absorption and distribution examples; (ii) metabolism and excretion examples; (iii) determination of Km and Vmax from a worked phenytoin example; (iv) estimation of the dosing rate.
C. (i) Explain how knowledge of the principle improves patient outcomes; (ii) state its limitation; (iii) state the trade-off with Km.

An elderly patient (above 65 years) with several diseases and polypharmacy is to receive digoxin, gentamicin, diazepam and an NSAID for knee osteoarthritis.
(i) Predict the changes in absorption and distribution with ageing.
(ii) Predict the changes in metabolism and excretion.
(iii) State the dose adjustment and precautions for narrow-therapeutic-window drugs.
(iv) Name safer alternative approaches.
(v) Justify the monitoring plan.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Absorption may fall with reduced saliva and gastric secretion, raised gastric pH, intestinal epithelial atrophy, reduced splanchnic blood flow and reduced active transport (levodopa is the exception); subcutaneous and intramuscular absorption may be slower; body fat increases while body water and muscle mass fall, albumin falls and α₁-acid glycoprotein rises, so fat-soluble drugs such as diazepam have larger Vd and longer action, and water-soluble drugs have lower Vd and higher plasma levels (digoxin Vd falls with reduced muscle).
(ii)
Hepatic blood flow and metabolic capacity fall, giving reduced metabolism and longer half-life; reduced first-pass effect raises bioavailability of propranolol, nifedipine, labetalol and verapamil; renal function declines (kidney size down about 20% and about 30% of glomeruli lost between 20 and 80 years), so chlorpropamide half-life rises from 25 to 48 hours to about 99 hours.
(iii)
Gentamicin and digoxin have narrow therapeutic windows and need dose adjustment to avoid accumulation and toxicity; elderly patients have a higher risk of ADRs from polypharmacy, multiple diseases, reduced elimination and increased sensitivity (especially CNS drugs).
(iv)
For osteoarthritis, topical NSAIDs are preferred over oral NSAIDs in patients older than 75 years (similar pain relief, fewer GI events, no linked CV risk); acetaminophen is first-line.
(v)
Use Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance rather than serum creatinine, which may stay normal despite reduced renal function because creatinine production also falls; acute illnesses such as congestive cardiac failure or infection reduce theophylline elimination; low albumin raises toxicity of acidic drugs such as NSAIDs, furosemide, cimetidine and sulfonylureas, but free phenytoin and warfarin are cleared so dose reduction may not be needed.

(i)
Nausea and vomiting may reduce oral absorption; gastric acid falls and gastric pH rises, increasing ionisation and reducing absorption of weak acids (aspirin) while weak bases (caffeine) diffuse more readily (no confirmatory evidence); maternal blood volume rises 40 to 50% and total body water by 6 to 8 L, reducing Cmax of many hydrophilic drugs with small volume of distribution.
(ii)
CYP3A4 abundance and activity rise, so clearance of substrates such as nifedipine, carbamazepine and midazolam increases and dose adjustment is required; increased UGT1A4 activity increases oral clearance of lamotrigine.
(iii)
GFR is 50% higher by the first trimester and rises until the last week; renal clearance parallels GFR for drugs cleared only by filtration (cefazolin, clindamycin), but tubular transport differences vary: lithium clearance doubles in the third trimester, digoxin (80% renally cleared) is only 20 to 30% higher than postpartum, and atenolol only 12% higher.
(iv)
Plasma iodide falls with fetal use and increased maternal iodide clearance; patients on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism should increase the dose by 30% early in pregnancy, be monitored, and decrease the dose postpartum.
(v)
Digoxin crosses the placenta and has been used for maternal and fetal indications without reported fetal harm or teratogenicity, so there is no contraindication in pregnancy or lactation.
(vi)
Monitoring should be done during pregnancy (explicitly for levothyroxine, with dose reduction postpartum).
questions.question:
A pregnant woman in her third trimester with hypothyroidism needs levothyroxine and is also taking lamotrigine, nifedipine, lithium and digoxin.
(i) Predict the effect of pregnancy on the absorption and distribution of her drugs.
(ii) Predict the effect on metabolism by CYP3A4 and UGT1A4 with examples.
(iii) Predict the effect on renal elimination, with examples.
(iv) State the dose adjustment for levothyroxine and the reason.
(v) State precautions in pregnancy for digoxin.
(vi) State the monitoring plan.

A neonate with sepsis needs gentamicin, a water-soluble aminoglycoside, and the prescriber asks how paediatric patients differ from adults in dose calculation.
(i) Predict the effect of neonatal physiology on absorption and distribution.
(ii) Predict the effect on metabolism and renal elimination.
(iii) State the dose adjustment and precautions for the aminoglycoside.
(iv) State the dose-calculation methods for children and which is most reliable.
(v) State rules to use when weight is unknown.
(vi) Justify the monitoring plan.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Neonates are relatively achlorhydric (acid production comparable to older infants only after the 6th week), gastric emptying reaches adult rate around 6 to 8 months, bile salt production is about 50% of adult and lipase levels are low; albumin and α₁-acid glycoprotein are reduced so more free drug is present; extracellular fluid is about 40% at birth (total body water 80% at birth), so water-soluble drugs have a large volume of distribution, and body fat is 12 to 16% in full-term neonates.
(ii)
CYP activity is about 50% of adult at birth and rises over weeks; glucuronidation reaches adult level at 3 to 4 years and acetylation is significantly reduced at birth; glomerular filtration in full-term neonates is 30 to 50% of adults and matures between the 3rd and 5th month (pre-term infants lower), so half-lives are longer.
(iii)
Polar drugs distributed into extracellular fluid, such as aminoglycosides, require a loading dose in neonates; dosing intervals may increase in neonates because of reduced renal and hepatic function; children are not smaller adults and weight or age based dosing is not reliable.
(iv)
Methods include Young's rule (age/(age + 12) × adult dose, over 2 years), Dilling's formula (age/20 × adult dose, 4 to 20 years), Fried's rule (age in months × adult dose / 150, up to 1 to 2 years), Clark's rule (weight in pounds × adult dose / 150), mg/kg dosing, Salisbury rule and body surface area dosing (child BSA / 1.73 m² x adult dose); BSA-based dosing is the most reliable and Mosteller BSA = square root of (height cm × weight kg / 3600).
(v)
If weight is unknown, (4 × age) + 20 gives the best fit to the BSA curve for normal-sized children; the Salisbury rule gives (weight × 2) per cent of adult dose below 30 kg and (weight + 30) per cent above 30 kg.
(vi)
Always confirm with paediatric references; convert pounds to kilograms (1 kg = 2.2 lb), write orders in mg rather than mL, and clarify orders written as mg/kg/d.

(i)
IBW (male) = 50 + 0.9 × (180 - 152) = 75.2 kg; ABW/IBW = 140/75.2 = 1.86, which is above 1.2, so adjusted body weight is used: IBW + 0.4 × (ABW - IBW) = 101.12 kg.
(ii)
Vd = 0.25 L/kg × 101.12 kg = 25.28 L; CrCl = (140 - 50) × 101.12 × 1.23 / 110 = 101.76 mL/min (Cockcroft-Gault form with 1.23 for males and creatinine in µmol/L).
(iii)
CLamg = CrCl × 60 / 1000 = 6.105 L/hr; Ke = CLamg / Vd = 6.105 / 25.28 = 0.241 per hour; t½ = 0.693 / 0.241 = 2.87 hours.
(iv)
Interval = (ln 30 - ln 2) / Ke = 11.2 hours, rounded to a practical 12 hours.
(v)
Initial dose = target Cmax × Vd × (1 - e^(-Ke × τ)) = 30 × 25.28 × 0.945 = 716 mg, rounded to about 700 mg; expected Cmax = 700 / (25.28 × 0.945) = 29.31 mg/L; expected Cmin = Cmax × e^(-Ke × τ).
(vi)
With patient levels: Ke = (ln C₂ - ln C₁) / (τ - (t₂ - t₁)); Cmax = Cpost × e^(Ke × τ'), where τ' is the time from end of infusion to the post sample; Cmin = Cmax × e^(-Ke × τ); Vd = Dose / [Cmax × (1 - e^(-Ke × τ))]; new dose = Cmax × Vd × (1 - e^(-Ke × τ)); sampling is pre-dose and 30 minutes after the end of an IV infusion.
questions.question:
Mr Ali, a 50-year-old man (180 cm, 140 kg), has septic shock from prolonged hospital-acquired pneumonia with Pseudomonas spp.; IV cefuroxime was started and the physician wants to add IV amikacin. Serum creatinine is 110 µmol/L, population Vd is 0.25 L/kg, and the target range is Cmax 30 mg/L and Cmin 2 mg/L.
(i) Select the dosing weight.
(ii) Estimate volume of distribution and creatinine clearance.
(iii) Estimate aminoglycoside clearance, elimination rate constant and half-life.
(iv) Estimate the dosing interval.
(v) Calculate the initial dose and the expected Cmax, and state the expression for the expected Cmin.
(vi) State how the regimen is individualised after measured concentrations.

A patient given a standard intravenous dose of succinylcholine for rapid sequence intubation remains paralysed with no spontaneous breathing far longer than the usual few minutes, and the family history suggests an inherited enzyme defect.
(i) Identify and classify the drug-related problem.
(ii) Explain the mechanism, including the normal metabolism of succinylcholine and the effect of the genetic defect.
(iii) Name the enzyme variants and the expected duration of paralysis for the homozygous and heterozygous atypical genotypes.
(iv) State how the dibucaine number classifies the genotype.
(v) State the immediate management.
(vi) State prevention, follow-up testing and the multidisciplinary approach.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Succinylcholine apnoea (scoline apnoea or post-anaesthetic apnoea): abnormal prolongation of action of succinylcholine because the body fails to metabolise it, causing sustained paralysis and a prolonged pause in breathing; it is a pharmacogenetic disorder involving the BCHE gene.
(ii)
Succinylcholine is a depolarising muscle relaxant normally hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase, BChE) to succinylmonocholine and then succinic acid and choline, so about 90 to 95% is inactivated before reaching the neuromuscular junction; with a mutated or deficient enzyme an excess reaches the nerve-muscle junction and produces protracted paralysis; mivacurium is affected similarly.
(iii)
Variants include atypical, fluoride-resistant, silent, K, J and C5; normal paralysis lasts 3 to 5 minutes (about 4 to 6 minutes), but in atypical BChE it can last up to 2 hours, and effects can last up to 10 hours; homozygous atypical (E1aE1a) gives a prolonged block of 4 to 8 hours and heterozygous atypical (E1uE1a) an intermediate block of 1.5 to 2 times normal.
(iv)
Dibucaine number: normal (E1uE1u) 70 or more; heterozygous atypical (E1uE1a) 40 to 60; homozygous atypical (E1aE1a) below 30; people homozygous for atypical (D70G) or silent BChE are certain to have prolonged apnoea with standard doses.
(v)
Quick recognition and intervention are critical to prevent life-threatening hypoxia; mechanical ventilation is the cornerstone, with ventilation settings monitored closely until the drug wears off; patients are awake but unable to breathe; give supportive care (vital signs monitoring and treatment of complications).
(vi)
Genetic testing for BChE deficiency is recommended after an event, and family members may also benefit from testing; avoid succinylcholine in future and use alternative muscle relaxants once BChE deficiency is identified; anaesthesiologists, geneticists and nurses must collaborate.

A(i)
Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM, or protein-calorie malnutrition) is the most common form of malnutrition worldwide: a continuum of consuming too little protein, energy or both, with kwashiorkor at one end and marasmus at the other.
A(ii)
Poverty and chronic hunger, early weaning to diluted bottle formula prepared with unsafe water (marasmus), weaning from protein-rich breast milk to a low-protein carbohydrate source (kwashiorkor), and illness or prolonged IV glucose, eating disorders, cancer, AIDS and malabsorption in hospitalised patients.
A(iii)
Poor hygiene and continued depletion cause a vicious cycle of gastroenteritis and deterioration of the gut lining that impairs nutrient absorption and reduces resistance to infection.
A(iv)
Marasmus: extreme underweight, loss of subcutaneous fat, "skin and bones", profound weakness and infections; kwashiorkor: swollen belly from oedema, weakness, poor growth, apathy, hair discoloration, dry peeling skin with unhealed sores, enlarged fatty liver; weight loss may be masked by oedema.
B(i)
Resolve life-threatening conditions, restore nutritional status quickly and safely, and ensure long-term nutritional rehabilitation.
B(ii)
Correct fluid and electrolyte imbalances and infections first; rapid weight gain can occur in one to two weeks; then continued nutritional rehabilitation; speed and success depend on severity, timeliness of treatment and adequacy of ongoing support.
B(iii)
Life-threatening problems are addressed first because untreated marasmus may end in death from starvation or heart failure; prompt restoration limits harm, since starvation in the first year may reduce brain growth.
C(i)
Kwashiorkor is severe protein deficiency with oedema and little muscle or fat wasting possible; marasmus is absolute food deprivation with grossly inadequate energy and protein, and loss of fat.
C(ii)
Undernutrition is insufficient food to meet energy needs (weight loss, failure to thrive, wasting); malnutrition is impaired function from prolonged deficiency or excess of energy or specific nutrients (protein, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals).
C(iii)
Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia; vitamin D, rickets; thiamin, beriberi; niacin, pellagra; vitamin C, scurvy; iron, anaemia; iodine, goitre and cretinism, each with food sources such as liver, fortified milk, pork, whole grains, citrus fruits, meat and iodised salt.
questions.question:
A. Describe protein-energy malnutrition under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) aetiology and risk factors; (iii) pathophysiology; (iv) clinical presentation.
B. (i) State the treatment goals; (ii) state the nutritional and non-pharmacological management; (iii) give the rationale for each component.
C. Distinguish between: (i) kwashiorkor and marasmus; (ii) malnutrition and undernutrition; (iii) the main micronutrient deficiency diseases.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Osteoarthritis (OA) is a common progressive disorder primarily affecting weight-bearing diarthrodial joints, characterised by pain, disability, deformity, limitation of motion, osteophyte formation and progressive destruction of articular cartilage.
A(ii)
Primary (idiopathic) OA has no known cause; secondary OA follows inflammation, trauma, metabolic or endocrine disorders or congenital factors; risk factors are increasing age, obesity, sex, certain occupations and sports, joint injury or surgery and genetic predisposition.
A(iii)
Cartilage damage (injury, overloading from obesity, instability) increases chondrocyte repair activity but the balance of breakdown and resynthesis is lost; subchondral bone releases vasoactive peptides and matrix metalloproteinases, with neovascularisation and chondrocyte apoptosis; osteophytes form at joint margins; IL-1, PGE₂, TNF-α and nitric oxide contribute to inflammation and effusion.
A(iv)
Deep aching pain with joint activity that decreases with rest; DIP and PIP joints, first carpometacarpal joint, knees, hips, spine and first MTP joint; limited motion, stiffness under 30 minutes on rising, crepitus, deformity; warm, red tender joints suggest inflammatory synovitis.
A(v)
Diagnosis is by history, examination, radiology (osteophytes, joint space narrowing) and laboratory tests; ACR criteria require pain, bony changes, normal ESR and radiographic changes (ESR may be slightly raised with inflammation); rheumatoid factor is negative and synovial fluid shows high viscosity with fewer than 2000 WBC/mm³.
B(i)
Educate the patient and caregivers, relieve pain and stiffness, maintain or improve joint mobility, limit functional impairment and maintain quality of life.
B(ii)
Education, dietary counselling, exercise and weight loss, physical therapy with heat or cold, assistive and orthotic devices (canes, walkers, braces, heel cups, insoles) and surgery (osteotomy, arthroplasty, fusion) for functional disability or severe pain unresponsive to conservative therapy.
B(iii)
Knee and hip: acetaminophen first line, then topical NSAIDs (knee), oral NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors, intra-articular corticosteroids, tramadol, duloxetine (knee only) and opioids; hand: topical NSAIDs, oral NSAIDs, tramadol and capsaicin cream (about 50% pain reduction in small trials); systemic corticosteroids and routine hyaluronic acid are not recommended.
B(iv)
Drug therapy targets pain with a conservative, individualised approach because OA often occurs in older people with comorbidities; acetaminophen has lower serious GI and CV risk than oral NSAIDs; each step is chosen when the previous one fails or is unsuitable, and non-drug therapies continue throughout.
C(i)
Primary OA is idiopathic and more common; secondary OA has an identifiable cause such as inflammation, trauma, metabolic or endocrine disorders or congenital factors.
C(ii)
Topical NSAIDs give similar relief with fewer GI events, are not linked to CV risk and are preferred above 75 years, with application-site reactions; oral NSAIDs cause GI ulcers and bleeding, CV events, kidney disease and interactions; patients on topical products should avoid oral NSAIDs.
C(iii)
Tramadol (after failed acetaminophen and topical NSAIDs) has no GI bleeding, CV or renal failure risk but seizures and dependence; opioids are for non-responders or high surgical risk, at the lowest dose with review every 3 months; duloxetine is adjunctive for knee OA, takes about 4 weeks and shares serotonin syndrome risk with tramadol.
questions.question:
A. Describe osteoarthritis under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) aetiology and risk factors; (iii) pathophysiology; (iv) clinical presentation; (v) diagnosis.
B. (i) State the treatment goals; (ii) state the non-pharmacological management; (iii) describe the pharmacotherapy for knee and hip OA and for hand OA; (iv) give the rationale for each choice.
C. Distinguish between: (i) primary and secondary osteoarthritis; (ii) topical and oral NSAIDs; (iii) tramadol and opioids or duloxetine in their place.

A patient has just started carbimazole for thyrotoxicosis and asks how long treatment lasts, what side effects to report, and whether radioactive iodine or surgery are alternatives; she may become pregnant.
(i) Identify the patient's needs and risks.
(ii) State the pharmacist's interventions.
(iii) State the counselling and adherence points.
(iv) State the alternatives.
(v) State follow-up and referral criteria.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Needs: understanding the long course (minimum 12 to 18 months, with euthyroidism usually after 4 to 8 weeks); risks: thionamide toxicity (rash, bone marrow suppression, hepatic effects), relapse or treatment failure from non-compliance or under-dosing, thyroid storm if therapy stops abruptly, and fetal risk with pregnancy.
(ii)
Confirm the dose (carbimazole 15 to 40 mg/day initially, maintenance 5 to 15 mg), advise that propranolol (20 to 40 mg every 6 or 8 hours) only relieves symptoms and does not treat the disease, and flag that PTU is the thionamide of choice in pregnancy and lactation and that RAI is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
(iii)
Report immediately sore throat, mouth ulcers, fever, malaise or other non-specific illness; a pruritic rash occurs in 1 to 5% and another thionamide can be substituted; do not stop the drug abruptly; take the full course to raise remission rate.
(iv)
RAI (iodine-131) is effective, quick and painless and is the treatment of choice in elderly patients with cardiac disease and toxic multinodular goitre, but hypothyroidism is the major complication; surgery suits large goitres causing disfigurement or breathing or swallowing difficulty, suspected malignancy or when other options are contraindicated, with hypothyroidism 6 months to 3 years later.
(v)
Failure to resolve symptoms in the expected time should prompt review of adherence, dose and interval; thyroid storm (high fever, tachycardia, vomiting, agitation, shock) is an emergency.

(i)
HbA1c above 7% (normal 4 to 7%) shows poor control over the preceding 2 to 3 months; fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more and random of 200 mg/dL or more fit diabetes; targets are HbA1c below 7%, pre-prandial 70 to 130 and 2-hour post-prandial below 180 mg/dL; microalbuminuria (30 to 299 mg/24 hours) indicates early nephropathy and calls for an ACE inhibitor or ARB; BP goal is below 130/80 mmHg and HDL goal above 50 mg/dL in women, TG below 150 mg/dL and LDL-C below 100 mg/dL; classic symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia and nocturia persist.
(ii)
Sulfonylureas lower HbA1c by 1 to 2% only with functioning β-cells but cause weight gain and eventual failure; weight gain exacerbates glucose, BP and lipid control; as β-cell function declines with duration, secretagogues become less useful; BP and lipids are not at goal on current therapy.
(iii)
Options: add metformin 500 mg once or twice daily with food, increase by 500 mg/day weekly, maximum 2550 mg/day (avoid if serum creatinine is 1.4 to 1.5 mg/dL or more or CrCl below 50 mL/min; here creatinine is 0.8); prefer weight-neutral or weight-loss agents (DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 analogues; SGLT2 inhibitors second or third line); glucose of 250 mg/dL or more typically requires insulin initially, so basal insulin (10 to 20 units at bedtime) is possible; intensify BP therapy (ACEI or ARB) and lipid therapy.
(iv)
Monitor HbA1c, fasting and post-prandial glucose by self-monitoring, weight, BP, lipids, serum creatinine and urinary albumin at least annually, annual eye and neuropathy screening and foot inspection; adverse effects (hypoglycaemia on sulfonylurea, GI effects and B12-related macrocytic anaemia with metformin).
questions.question:
JK, a 45-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for six months, takes glibenclamide 5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg, enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg and pravastatin 40 mg. She has gained 10 kg, weighs 109 kg, BP is 165/90, home glucose is 210 to 270 mg/dL, average fasting glucose 175 mg/dL, random glucose 232 mg/dL, HbA1c 9% (8.9% a month earlier), HDL 36, triglycerides 223 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, urinalysis 1+ protein with microalbuminuria; she has daily nocturia, polyuria and polydipsia and exercises once a week.
(i) Interpret the laboratory values against the targets.
(ii) Explain the pharmacological reasoning for the drug therapy problems.
(iii) State the regimen adjustment options.
(iv) State the follow-up monitoring and outcome assessment.

A. Describe digoxin clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) interactions; (viii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for the choice of therapeutic range and loading method; (ii) state the rationale for dose adjustment in special situations.
C. (i) Explain the basis of digoxin toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of interaction and of therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Digoxin is used for heart failure due to systolic dysfunction and for controlling ventricular response in supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, mainly atrial fibrillation and flutter; it is the only cardiac glycoside available in most countries (digitoxin has not been widely available since the 1980s).
A(ii)
Slow oral loading: maintenance 0.125 to 0.25 mg daily (steady state in 7 to 10 days); rapid IV loading: 0.25 to 0.5 mg over several minutes then 0.25 mg every 6 hours to a total of 0.75 to 1.5 mg; rapid oral: 0.5 mg then 0.25 mg every 6 hours to 0.75 to 1.5 mg; maintenance 0.125 to 0.25 mg daily; forms are injection, tablets and elixir.
A(iii)
Oral bioavailability 70 to 80% for tablets and 75 to 85% for elixir (not affected by heart failure); half-life 33 to 50 hours with normal renal function; volume of distribution 4 to 7 L/kg; about 70 to 80% excreted unchanged in urine; IV onset 15 to 30 minutes, peak 1 to 5 hours.
A(iv)
Inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase pump gives positive inotropic effect; it also alters neurohormonal systems through the autonomic nervous system (sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodal effects and increased baroreceptor sensitisation) and reduces sympathetic activation.
A(v)
Digoxin-related cardiac arrhythmias and extracardiac symptoms occur and may arise at therapeutic or subtherapeutic levels; a change from single junctional escapes to periodic junctional rhythm signifies toxicity.
A(vi)
Reduce the dose in renal impairment, low body weight and with interacting drugs; hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypoxia and hypothyroidism increase sensitivity.
A(vii)
P-glycoprotein inhibitors (amiodarone, dronedarone, propafenone, quinidine, verapamil) raise levels; inducers (phenytoin, rifampin) lower them; cholestyramine and antacids reduce absorption by 20 to 35%; bupropion lowers levels by 60%; diuretics increase toxicity; tetracycline and erythromycin raise levels in about 10% of patients; high-dose biotin gives falsely high assay results.
A(viii)
Monitor serum digoxin (narrow therapeutic window) at least 6 hours, optimally 12 hours, after a dose, and 12 to 24 hours in advanced kidney disease; ranges are 0.5 to 0.9 mcg/L in CHF and 0.8 to 2 mcg/L in AF; check electrolytes and renal function; in AF levels are used more as a guide to toxicity.
B(i)
Positive inotropic effects occur at low concentrations and most CHF patients gain no extra benefit from higher levels, hence the lower range in CHF; the goal in AF is rate control so higher concentrations are needed; slow loading is generally preferred, and rapid loading is rarely needed unless alternative drugs are contraindicated or ineffective.
B(ii)
Renal impairment (both loading and maintenance doses reduced; 0.0625 mg every 48 hours in stage 5 CKD or dialysis), low body weight (50% of the loading dose below 45 kg), low lean body weight, concurrent hypokalaemia or hypothyroidism (lower loading dose) and interacting drugs; obese patients use normal non-weight-based loading doses, or lean weight if weight-based.
C(i)
The therapeutic window is narrow with substantial overlap between therapeutic and toxic levels; renal insufficiency lowers elimination and volume of distribution, raising levels; hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia (from diuretics) promote arrhythmias; toxicity is a clinical diagnosis irrespective of levels.
C(ii)
Interactions occur through P-glycoprotein inhibition or induction, reduced intestinal absorption (cholestyramine, antacids) and altered hydrolytic metabolism (tetracycline, erythromycin); therapeutic failure in AF arises because digoxin is less effective than β blockers or calcium channel blockers, poorly controls rate during exercise, cannot terminate the arrhythmia and often does not slow recurrent AF.

A(i)
Cardiac output rises 30 to 50% (4 to 6 L/min), uterine blood flow rises 10-fold and renal blood flow 50%, and blood volume rises 40 to 50% from 6 to 8 weeks to 32 weeks; progesterone raises minute ventilation by 30 to 50% and the diaphragm rises 4 to 5 cm with 10 to 20% falls in FRC and total lung capacity; GFR rises, with sodium and water retention (total body water up 6 to 8 L).
A(ii)
Estrogen raises binding globulins (thyroid-binding and cortisol-binding globulin), cholesterol and clotting factors; drug-metabolising enzymes in phase I and II change; plasma iodide falls and the thyroid enlarges in almost 15% of women.
A(iii)
Nausea and vomiting may decrease drug available for absorption; gastric acid falls and mucus rises, raising gastric pH (weak acids such as aspirin ionise more, weak bases such as caffeine diffuse more); motility slows, but confirmatory evidence is lacking (β-lactams showed no bioavailability difference late in pregnancy), and higher cardiac output and intestinal blood flow may increase absorption; inhaled steroids may be absorbed more readily.
A(iv)
Vd depends on tissue perfusion, tissue binding, lipid solubility and protein binding and determines the loading dose; expanded volume reduces Cmax of hydrophilic drugs with small Vd; most xenobiotics cross the placenta by simple diffusion, and small, lipid-soluble, ionised, poorly protein-bound molecules cross easily; syncytiotrophoblast transporters (P-gp, BCRP, MRP and others) also mediate transport.
A(v)
CYP3A4 and UGT1A4 activity increase, raising clearance of their substrates; GFR is 50% higher by the first trimester and keeps rising until the last week, so renal clearance of drugs cleared only by filtration parallels GFR; tubular secretion and reabsorption differences produce varying effects.
B(i)
CYP3A4 substrates (nifedipine, carbamazepine, midazolam, saquinavir, indinavir, lopinavir, ritonavir) show increased clearance requiring dose adjustment; increased UGT1A4 raises oral clearance of lamotrigine.
B(ii)
Cefazolin and clindamycin show increased renal elimination; lithium clearance doubles in the third trimester; digoxin (80% renally cleared) is only 20 to 30% higher than postpartum; atenolol clearance is only 12% higher.
B(iii)
Women needing levothyroxine for hypothyroidism should increase the dose by 30% early in pregnancy, be monitored during pregnancy and have the dose decreased postpartum.
B(iv)
Placental transporters include MRPs, P-gp, BCRP, OAT, OCT, OATP2B, MATE and PEPT; they transport endogenous substrates (cytokines, nucleoside analogues, steroid hormones) and exogenous compounds of similar structure.
C(i)
Understanding drug-specific properties and gestation-specific variations allows improved treatment and dosing strategies, improving efficacy and limiting maternal and fetal risks.
C(ii)
Pregnant women are orphan populations, rarely included in trials, so most drugs are prescribed off-label using doses based on men or non-pregnant women plus clinical judgment; the module focuses on clinical relevance rather than mathematical estimation.
C(iii)
Higher doses may be needed for rapidly cleared substrates, while concerns persist about teratogenic exposure in early pregnancy and fetal exposure.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
COPD is a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties, including emphysema (damage to the air sacs) and chronic bronchitis (long-term airway inflammation); it is progressive and mainly affects middle-aged or older smokers.
A(ii)
The main cause is smoking, with risk rising with the amount and duration of smoking; others are long-term exposure to harmful fumes or dust and a rare genetic problem that makes the lungs more vulnerable.
A(iii)
The lungs become inflamed, damaged and narrowed, and the damage is permanent.
A(iv)
Breathlessness (especially on activity), persistent chesty cough with phlegm ("smoker's cough"), frequent chest infections and persistent wheezing, worsening gradually, with sudden periods of worsening called flare-ups or exacerbations; many people do not realise they have it.
B(i)
Slow progression of the disease and control of symptoms, as there is no cure; stopping smoking is the most important step.
B(ii)
Stopping smoking (it is never too late), pulmonary rehabilitation (2 or more group sessions a week for at least 6 weeks with exercise, education, dietary advice and psychological support), electrical muscle stimulation during bad flare-ups, and surgery or lung transplant for a very small number of people.
B(iii)
Short-acting β-2 agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline) or antimuscarinics (ipratropium) first; long-acting β-2 agonists (salmeterol, formoterol, indacaterol) or antimuscarinics (tiotropium, glycopyronium, aclidinium), or combinations; steroid inhalers in combination inhalers; theophylline or aminophylline; carbocisteine or acetylcysteine mucolytics; steroid tablets and antibiotics for flare-ups.
B(iv)
Bronchodilators relax and widen the airways to ease breathing; long-acting agents are added when symptoms or exacerbations persist on short-acting ones; steroid inhalers reduce airway inflammation when breathlessness or exacerbations continue; theophylline is added when inhalers fail (blood levels checked); mucolytics thin thick phlegm; antibiotics for signs of chest infection.
C(i)
Short-acting inhalers are used when breathless, up to 4 times a day; long-acting ones last at least 12 hours and are used once or twice daily.
C(ii)
Emphysema is damage to the air sacs of the lungs; chronic bronchitis is long-term inflammation of the airways.
C(iii)
Stable disease is managed with regular inhalers, tablets and rehabilitation; flare-ups may need a 5-day steroid tablet course (long-term use causes weight gain, mood swings and osteoporosis) and a short antibiotic course when phlegm colour or thickness changes or breathlessness increases.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Metformin (biguanide, insulin sensitiser) is an oral antidiabetic for type 2 diabetes, used in dual and triple combinations in the glycaemic algorithm; A1c lowering is 1% to 2%.
A(ii)
Oral: 500 mg once or twice daily with food to start, increased by 500 mg/day at weekly intervals; maximal dose 2550 mg/day.
A(iii)
Renal clearance of metformin is reduced by cimetidine from 527 to 378 mL/min.
A(iv)
It primarily inhibits hepatic glucose production, secondarily enhances insulin action and reduces peripheral insulin resistance, and may decrease intestinal glucose absorption.
A(v)
Common: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea (especially early); uncommon: macrocytic anaemia (vitamin B12 deficiency) and life-threatening lactic acidosis; primarily reduces fasting glucose, with a 5% to 10% per year secondary failure rate.
A(vi)
Contraindicated with serum creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL or more in men or 1.4 mg/dL or more in women, creatinine clearance below 50 mL/minute, and severe hepatic, pulmonary or cardiac disease.
A(vii)
Cimetidine, an inhibitor of the organic cation transporter, reduces renal clearance and raises exposure.
A(viii)
Renal function (serum creatinine and creatinine clearance) and fasting blood glucose.
B(i)
It targets hepatic glucose output and is chosen as monotherapy or with other agents; starting low with food and titrating weekly decreases GI adverse effects.
B(ii)
Dose is limited to 2550 mg/day and the drug is avoided when creatinine or clearance thresholds are crossed, because accumulation raises lactic acidosis risk.
C(i)
Toxicity: lactic acidosis in the setting of renal, hepatic, pulmonary or cardiac disease, and B12-related macrocytic anaemia; GI effects are dose related and early.
C(ii)
Cimetidine blocks the renal organic cation transporter; therapeutic failure is a secondary failure rate of 5% to 10% per year, requiring add-on therapy.

A. Describe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) aetiology and risk factors; (iii) pathophysiology; (iv) clinical presentation; (v) diagnosis.
B. (i) state the non-pharmacological and supportive management; (ii) describe the pharmacotherapy; (iii) give the rationale for each choice.
C. Distinguish between: (i) paediatric ARDS and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome; (ii) dobutamine, dopamine and epinephrine; (iii) ECMO and extracorporeal CO₂ removal.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
ARDS is a life-threatening lung injury in which fluid leaks into the lungs, making breathing extremely difficult, with critically low oxygen levels.
A(ii)
About 20% have no identified risk factor; sepsis is the commonest, with direct lung injury (aspiration, pneumonia), COVID-19, trauma, burns, massive transfusion, drug overdose, near drowning, pancreatitis and fat embolism; risk increases with advanced age, smoking, alcohol, severity of illness (APACHE) and genetic factors.
A(iii)
Increased alveolar-capillary permeability to fluid, proteins, neutrophils and red cells is the hallmark; hypoxaemia arises from ventilation-perfusion mismatch and right-to-left shunting, and impaired CO₂ excretion and increased dead space occur; type II cells' surfactant and fluid reabsorption are disrupted.
A(iv)
Shortness of breath, cough with purulent sputum if pneumonia is the cause, fast breathing, tachycardia, increased work of breathing, cyanosis and reduced oxygen saturation; deterioration may be hyperacute (as in TRALI) or develop over hours to days.
A(v)
Diagnosis uses the Berlin criteria, exclusion of mimics (acute eosinophilic pneumonia, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, acute interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organising pneumonia, acute exacerbation of pulmonary fibrosis, acute heart failure) and bronchoscopy with lavage if no risk factor is evident; chest radiograph interpretation is subjective and the Kigali modification applies where resources are limited.
B(i)
Fluid management with a fluid-conservative approach after shock resolves increased ventilator-free days and improved oxygenation; low tidal volume ventilation and modes such as airway pressure release ventilation may improve oxygenation and reduce sedation need; rescue therapies include veno-venous ECMO.
B(ii)
Adrenergic agents (dobutamine, dopamine, epinephrine) and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor milrinone for haemodynamic support; corticosteroids (no benefit for prevention; evidence insufficient in paediatric ARDS); aerosolised budesonide with formoterol improved oxygenation in a small trial; exogenous surfactant has insufficient evidence in paediatric ARDS.
B(iii)
Adrenergic agents increase cardiac output and improve haemodynamics affected by high airway pressures, sedation and multi-organ failure; milrinone raises cAMP for inotropy, vasodilation and cardiac output; ECMO is for very severe ARDS when gas exchange cannot be corrected with lung-protective ventilation.
C(i)
Paediatric ARDS lacks evidence for corticosteroids and surfactant, whereas neonatal RDS (hyaline membrane disease) occurs almost exclusively in premature infants, inversely related to gestational age, and is helped by antenatal steroids, early CPAP and early surfactant.
C(ii)
Dobutamine is predominantly β-1 with β-2 effects (inotropy, chronotropy, vasodilation; tachycardia and raised myocardial oxygen need); dopamine acts on dopaminergic receptors at 2 to 5, β receptors at 5 to 15 and α receptors at 15 to 20 mcg/kg/min; epinephrine stimulates β-1 and, at higher doses, α receptors.
C(iii)
ECMO circulates blood outside the body for oxygenation and suits very severe ARDS in the first week without multiple organ failure; extracorporeal CO₂ removal uses 0.5 to 1 L/min blood flow, permits very low tidal volume (3 to 4 mL/kg PBW) and carries bleeding risk.

(i)
Protein-energy malnutrition: kwashiorkor (severe protein deficiency, swollen belly from oedema, weakness, poor growth, apathy, hair discoloration, peeling skin and sores that fail to heal, enlarged fatty liver, susceptibility to infection and fatal diarrhoea) and marasmus (absolute food deprivation with inadequate energy and protein, extreme underweight, loss of subcutaneous fat, weakness, infections, possible death from starvation or heart failure); in the first year starvation may reduce brain growth.
(ii)
Treatment has three components: resolve life-threatening conditions (fluid and electrolyte imbalance and infection); restore nutritional status as quickly and safely as possible (rapid weight gain can occur in one to two weeks); then long-term nutritional rehabilitation, with speed of recovery depending on severity, timeliness of treatment and adequacy of support.
(iii)
Marasmus often follows early weaning to diluted formula made with unsafe water; poor hygiene and gastroenteritis lead to a vicious cycle of malabsorption and infection, so safe water, hygiene and adequate protein and energy are needed; kwashiorkor occurs when the child is weaned from protein-rich breast milk to an insufficient-protein carbohydrate source.
(iv)
Vitamin A (xerophthalmia; liver, fortified milk, sweet potatoes, spinach, carrots); vitamin D (rickets; fortified milk, fish oils, sun exposure); thiamin (beriberi; pork, whole grains, dried beans); niacin (pellagra; tuna, chicken, beef, peanuts); vitamin C (scurvy; citrus fruits, strawberries, broccoli); iron (iron-deficiency anaemia; meat, spinach, seafood); iodine (goitre and cretinism; iodised salt, saltwater fish).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A group of metabolic disorders characterised by chronic hyperglycaemia with abnormal carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism resulting from absolute or relative insulin deficiency, insulin action defects or both, and possibly high glucagon and other counter-regulatory hormones.
A(ii)
Primary forms are type 1 (5 to 10%) and type 2 (90 to 95%), plus gestational diabetes and other specific types (genetic β-cell defects such as MODY, defects of insulin action, exocrine pancreatic disease, endocrinopathies, drug- or chemical-induced, infections); risk factors include obesity, family history, age over 40, ethnicity, high-calorie high-fat low-fibre diet, inactivity, hypertension and gestational diabetes.
A(iii)
Type 1 results from cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells with absolute insulin deficiency; type 2 ranges from predominantly insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency to a predominantly secretory defect with insulin resistance; pre-diabetes (IFG and IGT) lies between normal and diabetes.
A(iv)
Polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia with weight loss, blurred vision, susceptibility to infection, tingling and numbness of feet, slow wound healing, itching, drowsiness and irritability; type 2 often has no symptoms; acute consequences are ketoacidosis (type 1) and hyperosmolar non-ketotic syndrome (type 2).
A(v)
Fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more, 2-hour OGTT (75 g) of 200 mg/dL or more, or random glucose of 200 mg/dL or more (repeat if no unequivocal hyperglycaemia); pre-diabetes is fasting 100 to 125 or 2-hour 140 to 199 mg/dL; HbA1c above 7% indicates high glucose but is mainly for monitoring.
B(i)
Eliminate symptoms, prevent hypoglycaemia, ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar state and long-term complications, and attain glycaemic goals (HbA1c below 7%, pre-prandial 70 to 130 mg/dL, post-prandial below 180 mg/dL), individualised (for example below 6.5% in a healthy 50-year-old and below 8% in a 75-year-old post-MI patient on insulin).
B(ii)
Three-stage patient education, weight control (5 to 10% loss brings benefit), medical nutrition therapy (fat 25 to 35% of calories, carbohydrate 50 to 60%, fibre, restricted salt), alcohol limits, at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week, BP below 130/80 mmHg, tobacco cessation and aspirin for those at increased CV risk.
B(iii)
Parenteral: insulin (rapid, short, intermediate, long-acting, premixed), amylin analogue and GLP-1 incretin mimetics; oral: sulfonylureas, meglitinides, metformin, α-glucosidase inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, colesevelam and bromocriptine; plant-based chromium and vanadium supplements are listed as alternative medicines.
B(iv)
Choice depends on baseline HbA1c or glucose (250 mg/dL or more typically needs insulin), organ function, contraindications, duration of disease, self-monitoring ability, hypoglycaemic unawareness, weight, route, cost and combination therapy; metformin is a first option and the stepwise approach escalates to dual and triple therapy as HbA1c rises.
C(i)
Type 1: autoimmune β-cell destruction with absolute insulin deficiency, 5 to 10% of cases (formerly juvenile-onset); type 2: insulin resistance with relative deficiency, 90 to 95% of cases.
C(ii)
Type 1 usually shows the classic triad with high glucose in urine and blood and is easy to diagnose; type 2 often lacks classic symptoms, may be found on routine testing and may already show complications at diagnosis.
C(iii)
Ketoacidosis is much commoner in type 1 with poor control (type 2 patients usually make enough insulin, but stress, infection and non-compliance can precipitate it); hyperosmolar non-ketotic syndrome typically occurs in type 2 patients who are non-adherent, dehydrated, stressed or on steroids; hypoglycaemia can occur with treatment in both.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Inter-patient variability in response is the rule, not the exception; the "one dose fits all" and trial-and-error approach leaves only about 50% of patients responding to major drug groups, so therapy is individualised ("personalised medicine") using knowledge, logic and equations.
A(ii)
Genetic, environmental and physiological factors (exposure to drugs, toxins and pollutants, diet, disease, age, weight, gender and hormones, exercise) acting on absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, target interaction and drug-drug interactions.
A(iii)
Altered by GI disease (colitis, Crohn's, cystic fibrosis, malnutrition, achlorhydria with dose dumping of enteric-coated products), permeability, motility, active transporters and metabolic enzymes, and by diet and herbal products.
A(iv)
Changes in plasma proteins (low albumin decreases binding and raises Vd for NSAIDs; α₁-acid glycoprotein for propafenone and propranolol), obesity (fat-soluble drugs), pregnancy, age and altered blood-brain barrier permeability.
A(v)
Environmental toxins, food, drugs, disease, age and pregnancy affect hepatic and renal elimination; smoking and charcoal broiling induce P450s (increased clearance of theophylline), high protein diet and alcohol alter clearance, and red wine alters cyclosporin A levels.
B(i)
Grapefruit juice inhibits gut CYP3A4 and P-gp (up to 3-fold higher concentrations of cyclosporin A, felodipine, midazolam) and reduces OATP-mediated fexofenadine uptake (bioavailability halved); St John's wort induces intestinal CYP3A and P-gp, reducing cyclosporin, indinavir and digoxin and oral contraceptive effectiveness.
B(ii)
Inducers: CYP1A2 (smoke, omeprazole, phenobarbitone), CYP2E1 (ethanol, isoniazid), CYP3A (barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin); inhibitors: CYP1A2 (cimetidine, fluoroquinolones), CYP2D6 (fluoxetine, quinidine, paroxetine), CYP3A (HIV protease inhibitors, clarithromycin, erythromycin, ketoconazole).
B(iii)
Quinidine reduces biliary and renal clearance of digoxin by 50% to 60%; gemfibrozil doubles pravastatin AUC and cyclosporin A raises cerivastatin and rosuvastatin AUC; probenecid raises cephradine AUC 2.4-fold; cimetidine lowers renal clearance of procainamide (347 to 196 mL/min) and metformin (527 to 378 mL/min).
B(iv)
Metabolism and secretion fall in inflammatory states (infection, arthritis, Crohn's disease, renal disease, cancer, shown by reduced CYP3A activity in cancer patients), and bacterial infection alters P-gp substrate disposition.
C(i)
Understanding variability allows drug and dose selection tailored to the patient, as shown for warfarin where CYP2C9, VKORC1, age, gender, body weight, race, drugs and diet affect dose requirement.
C(ii)
Many contributing factors remain unknown (the "unknown" component in warfarin dose requirement), and pharmacogenetic knowledge is still progressing.
C(iii)
Individualisation requires more testing and calculations than a fixed dose.
