A. Describe phenytoin clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) adverse effects; (v) contraindications and precautions; (vi) interactions; (vii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for dose calculation and the formulation factors; (ii) state the rationale for correcting levels in low albumin.
C. (i) Explain the basis of its toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of its unpredictable concentrations.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Status epilepticus and anticonvulsant therapy, with a recommended therapeutic range of 10 to 20 mg/L.
A(ii)
Oral (capsule, suspension or chew tablet) or IV; the loading dose = Cp desired × Vd × BW / (S × F), the maintenance dose = Vmax × BW × Cp / [S × F × (Km + Cp)], and in the worked example 900 mg IV was given for status epilepticus, then 100 mg three times daily.
A(iii)
Half-life 22 hours orally (range 7 to 42) and 10 to 15 hours IV; Vd 0.65 to 0.7 L/kg (adult) and 0.7 to 0.8 L/kg (infants); F is 1 (IV, capsule and suspension about 1); salt factor S is 0.92 (IV and capsule) or 1 (suspension and chew tablet); population Vmax 7 mg/kg/day and Km 4 mg/L in adults (infants 10 to 14 mg/kg/day and 6 mg/L); elimination is capacity-limited.
A(iv)
At 40 mg/L: lethargy, slurred speech and nystagmus.
A(v)
Check renal profile, albumin and other drug interactions before incremental loading; low albumin below 25 g/L or CrCl below 10 mL/minute needs corrected levels; neonates have reduced albumin and more free drug, increasing activity and toxicity.
A(vi)
Drug interactions with phenytoin are partly covered: colesevelam may interact with phenytoin, phenytoin is among CYP3A inducers and can impair insulin action (drug-induced hyperglycaemia), and it lowers digoxin levels by P-glycoprotein induction; shankhapushpi herbal interaction is cited for TDM.
A(vii)
Serum concentration (TDM): phenytoin's long half-life means timing is not critical, saliva gives unbound concentration, and levels are needed because the dose-concentration relationship is unpredictable.
B(i)
Salt factor and bioavailability differ by formulation, Vd determines the loading dose (incremental LD = (Cp desired - Cp measured) × Vd × BW / (S × F)), and Km and Vmax from two steady-state doses individualise the maintenance dose.
B(ii)
Albumin correction (measured level / [0.9 × albumin/44 + 0.1]) estimates the concentration at normal binding, because TDM assays measure bound plus unbound drug while only unbound drug is active.
C(i)
Phenytoin undergoes saturable metabolism at therapeutic concentrations, so a small dose increase produces a large concentration rise (300 mg to 450 mg raised the level from 7.9 to 30 mg/L), leading to toxicity; the time to withhold is calculated from Km, Vd and Vm.
C(ii)
Unpredictable concentrations arise from capacity-limited kinetics (non-proportional Css), changed protein binding and altered Km and Vmax between patients (Km 1 to 15 mg/L; Vmax 100 to 1000 mg/day).

(i)
The level is double the desired concentration; it is valid only if drawn at least 6 hours (optimally 12 hours) after the dose, at steady state (five half-lives, about 7 to 10 days) and with stable renal function; levels above 1 ng/mL (1.3 nmol/L) should be avoided in rate control to reduce toxicity risk, and the reference ranges are 0.5 to 0.9 mcg/L in CHF and 0.8 to 2 mcg/L in AF, with values above 1.2 mcg/L in AF associated with increased all-cause mortality.
(ii)
With correct timing, steady state and stable renal function there is a linear relationship between digoxin dose and serum concentration (the half-life is 33 to 50 hours with normal renal function and about 70 to 80% is renally eliminated).
(iii)
Reduce the dose by 50%, from 0.25 mg daily to 0.125 mg daily; the same linear relationship applies when a dose increase is needed for a concentration below the target.
(iv)
In AF the level is checked periodically, but concentration often does not correlate with rate control and is used more as a guide to toxicity; assess ventricular rate response and ECG (junctional escape beats are common when the rate is controlled; periodic junctional rhythm signifies toxicity); toxicity is a clinical diagnosis even at therapeutic levels; recheck electrolytes (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) and renal function; digoxin is less effective than β blockers or calcium channel blockers for rate control, so those may need adding.

(i) Interpret the value and state the conditions for a valid sample.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Asthma is a common long-term lung condition causing occasional breathing difficulties, affecting all ages and often starting in childhood; there is no cure.
A(ii)
It is caused by inflammation of the breathing tubes; it may occur randomly or after triggers: allergies (house dust mites, animals, pollen), smoke, pollution, cold air, exercise and infections like colds or flu; occupational asthma is linked to the job.
A(iii)
The inflamed breathing tubes carrying air in and out of the lungs become highly sensitive and temporarily narrow.
A(iv)
Wheezing, breathlessness, a tight chest and coughing, which can temporarily worsen into an asthma attack; badly controlled asthma causes tiredness, absence from work or school, anxiety or depression, pneumonia and growth delay in children.
A(v)
A doctor usually diagnoses asthma from symptoms and simple tests; similar conditions exist, so a proper diagnosis is important.
B(i)
Control symptoms so the person can live a normal active life, prevent attacks and use a personal action plan.
B(ii)
Identify and avoid triggers; breathing exercises (Papworth, Buteyko) may improve symptoms but must not replace medicine; protective measures at work (remove the substance, redeploy or provide protective breathing equipment); other complementary therapies have little evidence.
B(iii)
Reliever inhalers (usually blue), preventer inhalers (steroid), combination inhalers; leukotriene receptor antagonists, theophylline and steroid tablets; biologic injections every few weeks; bronchial thermoplasty for severe disease.
B(iv)
Relievers act within minutes when symptoms occur; a preventer is used daily even without symptoms to reduce airway inflammation; combinations are used when both fail; tablets are added if inhalers alone do not control symptoms; thermoplasty applies heat to airway muscles to stop narrowing.
C(i)
Relievers treat symptoms quickly (shaking or fast heartbeat for minutes); preventers are used daily and may cause oral thrush, hoarse voice and sore throat (reduced with a spacer and mouth rinsing).
C(ii)
Asthma often starts in childhood and may improve in the teens, with inflammation of the breathing tubes; COPD mainly affects middle-aged or older smokers, has permanent lung damage and gets progressively worse.
C(iii)
Tablets (LTRAs with tummy aches or headaches, theophylline with headaches and sickness, steroids with weight gain, bruising and osteoporosis) are taken orally; biologic injections are specialist-prescribed with discomfort at the injection site; thermoplasty is done under general anaesthetic with no serious safety concerns.

A patient with recurrent gout (two or more attacks per year) taking a thiazide diuretic and low-dose aspirin is started on allopurinol 100 mg daily, then has an acute gout attack and later a skin rash.
(i) Identify and classify the drug-related problems.
(ii) Explain the mechanism of each.
(iii) State the management and the correct allopurinol approach.
(iv) State the target and the flare prophylaxis.
(v) State how the problem is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Drug-induced hyperuricaemia (thiazide), an initiation-related gout flare during urate-lowering therapy, and a possible allopurinol hypersensitivity reaction (rash).
(ii)
Thiazides and loop diuretics, nicotinic acid, low-dose salicylates, ethanol, pyrazinamide, levodopa, ethambutol, cyclosporine and cytotoxic drugs decrease renal uric acid clearance; rapid lowering of serum uric acid and mobilisation of urate deposits during initiation precipitate acute attacks; allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (severe rash such as toxic epidermal necrolysis, hepatitis, interstitial nephritis, eosinophilia) is rare but has 20 to 25% mortality.
(iii)
Eliminate non-essential urate-raising drugs where feasible (thiazide and loop diuretics, cyclosporine, niacin); continue low-dose aspirin for CV prevention because it has a negligible effect on uric acid; start allopurinol at no more than 100 mg daily with normal kidney function (no more than 50 mg/day in stage 4 or worse CKD) and titrate every 2 to 5 weeks up to 800 mg/day; mild effects include rash, leukopenia, GI problems, headache and urticaria.
(iv)
Target serum uric acid is below 6 mg/dL (357 µmol/L) and preferably below 5 mg/dL (297 µmol/L) in severe gout; give colchicine or an NSAID for at least the first 8 weeks to prevent flares; urate lowering is long term; febuxostat is second-line, and uricosurics are for those intolerant of xanthine oxidase inhibitors (CrCl above 45 to 50 mL/min).
(v)
Prevention is by gradual titration, flare prophylaxis and review of the medication list.

A(i)
Hepatic clearance is determined by hepatic blood flow and the extraction ratio of the drug, caused by metabolic transformation by hepatic microsomal enzymes and biliary excretion; systemic clearance is the sum of the clearances by various organs, and hepatic disease can alter drug clearance.
A(ii)
Hepatitis A, B and E cause acute liver failure (also Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus); worldwide chronic hepatitis B or C is the commonest cause of chronic liver disease, and in the western world chronic excessive alcohol; others are primary biliary cirrhosis, primary sclerosing cholangitis and autoimmune hepatitis; ongoing destruction leads to cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
A(iii)
AST and ALT detect liver cell damage rather than function and no single test accurately assesses liver function; markers include antipyrine, indocyanine green, monoethylglycine-xylidide, galactose, albumin, bilirubin and prothrombin time, and a marker may correlate well with clearance of one drug but poorly with substrates of a different enzyme.
A(iv)
Child-Pugh groups A, B and C (mild, moderate, severe) correspond to scores of 5 to 6, 7 to 9 and 10 to 15; no zero score exists; albumin falls with decreased synthesis, bilirubin is an insensitive marker (large reserve), and prothrombin time rises with decreased factor synthesis or vitamin K deficiency; the system is used until optimal markers are found.
A(v)
Consider nature and severity of disease, extent of hepatic elimination (below 20% less affected), route (oral bioavailability may rise from decreased first pass), protein binding, hepatic blood flow, intrinsic clearance, biliary obstruction, pharmacodynamic changes and therapeutic range (wide range drugs are less affected).
B(i)
High extraction ratio drugs (morphine, propranolol) are limited by hepatic perfusion, whereas low extraction ratio drugs (diazepam, fluoxetine, caffeine) are limited by intrinsic metabolic capacity and unbound fraction and change little with perfusion.
B(ii)
With linear kinetics and no renal change, CLh = CLT × (1 - fe), and D hepatitis / D normal = RL × (1 - fe) + fe, where RL is the residual hepatic function; drugs with low fe are more affected by liver disease.
B(iii)
Hepatic disease has little influence on digoxin metabolism or clearance, so no dose adjustment is needed (about 70 to 80% is renally eliminated).
B(iv)
AST/ALT of 1 or less suggests acute liver injury and 2 or more alcoholic hepatitis; exogenous markers (antipyrine, MEGX, ICG, galactose) can be used in parallel with Child-Pugh.
C(i)
Adjusting doses to residual liver function and drug properties prevents accumulation and toxicity and supports predicting changes in the pharmacokinetic profile.
C(ii)
Elimination of a specific drug in hepatic disease is unpredictable; the high capacity of the liver means that even with cirrhosis residual metabolic function may be well preserved for years; markers are drug-specific.
C(iii)
Using a marker or score approximates impairment but none is specific; drugs with wide therapeutic range may tolerate moderate impairment, whereas narrow-range or high intrinsic clearance drugs are riskier.
questions.question:
A. Describe the following principle: the effect of hepatic impairment on drug elimination and dosing, under these headings: (i) role of the liver in elimination; (ii) causes of hepatic disease; (iii) liver function tests and markers; (iv) Child-Pugh classification; (v) considerations in dosing.
B. Relate the principle to examples: (i) high and low extraction ratio drugs; (ii) the dose adjustment equation; (iii) the example of digoxin; (iv) AST and ALT interpretation and exogenous markers.
C. (i) Explain how the principle improves patient outcomes; (ii) state the limitations; (iii) state the trade-off.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis, a progressive disorder of weight-bearing joints with pain, deformity, limited motion, osteophytes and progressive loss of articular cartilage; damage to cartilage, excessive joint loading from obesity or joint instability upsets the balance between breakdown and resynthesis, with subchondral bone changes, inflammatory mediators (IL-1, PGE₂, TNF-α, nitric oxide) and synovial effusion; ESR is normal or slightly raised and rheumatoid factor is negative.
(ii)
Acetaminophen is preferred first-line (lower GI and CV risk than oral NSAIDs but may be less effective); if it fails, topical NSAIDs for knee OA, or nonselective NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib; intra-articular corticosteroids when analgesia is suboptimal; tramadol after failed acetaminophen and topical NSAIDs; duloxetine as adjunct for knee OA; opioids if other therapy fails; systemic corticosteroids are not recommended; intra-articular hyaluronic acid is not routinely recommended.
(iii)
Intra-articular corticosteroids should not be given more often than once every 3 months (relief starts in 24 to 72 hours, peaks at 7 to 10 days and lasts 4 to 8 weeks); opioids at the lowest effective dose and smallest quantity.
(iv)
Assess opioid use at least every 3 months; response of pain, stiffness and function; duloxetine pain reduction occurs after about 4 weeks; local adverse effects after injection (infection, osteonecrosis, tendon rupture, skin atrophy).
(v)
Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in overdose (avoid in chronic alcohol use or liver disease); NSAID GI, CV, renal effects and interactions with lithium, warfarin, oral hypoglycaemics, methotrexate and antihypertensives; tramadol seizures and serotonin syndrome with duloxetine.
(vi)
Education about the disease, dietary counselling, exercise and weight loss, physical therapy with heat or cold, assistive devices (canes, walkers, braces, insoles), and surgery (osteotomy, arthroplasty, joint fusion) for disability or severe pain unresponsive to conservative therapy.
questions.question:
A patient has knee osteoarthritis with deep aching pain on joint activity that eases with rest, morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes, crepitus and bony enlargement; the patient is overweight.
(i) Identify the condition and its pathophysiology.
(ii) Select drug therapy and justify the stepwise choices.
(iii) State the dose, route and frequency constraints.
(iv) State the monitoring parameters.
(v) State the key adverse effects and interactions.
(vi) State the counselling and non-drug measures.

A. Describe the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) interactions; (viii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for selection (oral, topical, COX-2 selective); (ii) state the rationale for risk reduction.
C. (i) Explain the basis of toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of interaction and therapeutic failure.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Osteoarthritis (second-line after acetaminophen in knee and hip OA, first-line topical in hand OA), acute gout (indomethacin, naproxen and sulindac are approved) and bridging in rheumatoid arthritis.
A(ii)
Oral or topical; in gout start within 24 hours and continue until resolution (usually 5 to 8 days).
A(iii)
NSAIDs inhibit platelet thromboxane reversibly, with platelet function normalising 1 to 3 days after stopping.
A(iv)
They inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX-1-dependent thromboxane production in platelets); celecoxib is COX-2 selective.
A(v)
GI complaints (nausea, dyspepsia, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhoea), gastric and duodenal ulcers and bleeding, hypertension, stroke, MI and death, kidney disease (papillary necrosis, reduced GFR), hepatitis, hypersensitivity, rash and CNS effects (drowsiness, dizziness, headache, depression, confusion, tinnitus); topical forms cause dry skin, pruritus and rash.
A(vi)
Avoid in late pregnancy (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus); ulcer risk rises with longer duration, higher dose, age over 60, peptic ulcer history, alcohol, and glucocorticoids or anticoagulants.
A(vii)
Serious interactions with lithium, warfarin, oral hypoglycaemics, methotrexate, antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, β-blockers and diuretics; aspirin reduces the GI advantage of COX-2 inhibitors; patients using topical products should avoid oral NSAIDs.
A(viii)
Monitor GI symptoms, blood pressure, renal and hepatic function and clinical response.
B(i)
Topical NSAIDs are preferred above 75 years and give similar relief with fewer GI events and no linked CV risk; nonselective NSAIDs or celecoxib follow acetaminophen failure; COX-2 inhibitors pose less GI risk.
B(ii)
Use the lowest dose when needed, add misoprostol four times daily or a PPI or H₂-receptor antagonist daily, and consider tapering after gout resolution if comorbidities make prolonged therapy undesirable.
C(i)
GI toxicity arises by direct (topical) and indirect (systemic) mechanisms, and CV and renal effects arise from the class effect; bleeding risk arises from COX-1 inhibition of platelets.
C(ii)
Interactions affect antihypertensive, anticoagulant and hypoglycaemic therapy; therapeutic failure of acetaminophen leads to NSAIDs, and NSAIDs do not slow RA progression.

(i)
About 70 to 80% of digoxin is eliminated unchanged in urine, so the half-life (33 to 50 hours with normal renal function) is prolonged; renal insufficiency also decreases the extravascular volume of distribution (normally 4 to 7 L/kg), and both effects raise plasma levels.
(ii)
In severe chronic renal insufficiency the loading dose is reduced by about one-third to one-half or more (in end-stage kidney disease one-half to two-thirds of normal); for stage 5 CKD or dialysis a reduced loading dose of 3 to 5 mcg/kg (0.25 to 0.375 mg) is recommended, followed by maintenance of 0.0625 mg every 48 hours (about 10 to 25% of the usual dose given every 48 hours).
(iii)
No supplemental dose is needed because haemodialysis, CAPD and CRRT remove only insignificant amounts of digoxin owing to its large volume of distribution.
(iv)
β blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers may be preferred for heart rate control in stage 5 CKD or dialysis patients.
(v)
Take the sample at least 12 to 24 hours after the previous dose in advanced kidney disease or haemodialysis (otherwise at least 6 hours, optimally 12 hours), as earlier samples may be falsely elevated; check electrolyte and renal status before starting and periodically, and monitor levels until potassium and magnesium normalise.
(vi)
Increased levels: P-glycoprotein inhibitors (amiodarone, dronedarone, propafenone, quinidine, verapamil; halve the digoxin dose with dronedarone if it cannot be stopped); decreased levels: P-glycoprotein inducers (phenytoin, rifampin), cholestyramine and antacids (20 to 35% less absorption), bupropion (60% lower); hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypoxia and hypothyroidism increase sensitivity.
(vii)
Toxicity is a clinical diagnosis irrespective of circulating levels because arrhythmias and extracardiac symptoms can occur at therapeutic or even subtherapeutic concentrations; a change from single junctional escapes to periodic junctional rhythm usually signifies digoxin toxicity.
questions.question:
A patient with heart failure and atrial fibrillation has stage 5 chronic kidney disease (GFR below 15 mL/minute) and is on intermittent haemodialysis. Digoxin is being considered for heart rate control.
(i) Predict the effect of renal impairment on digoxin elimination, half-life and volume of distribution.
(ii) State the loading and maintenance dose adjustments.
(iii) State whether a supplemental dose after dialysis is needed.
(iv) Name the alternative agents that may be preferred.
(v) State the correct sampling time and the monitoring plan, including electrolytes.
(vi) Name the interacting drugs and conditions that increase sensitivity to digoxin.
(vii) State how digoxin toxicity is recognised.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The geriatric population is arbitrarily defined as patients aged over 65 years (young old 65 to 75, old 75 to 85, old old above 85); ageing raises blood and tissue drug levels through reduced elimination and increases sensitivity to many drugs, particularly CNS drugs, with poorer homeostatic mechanisms.
A(ii)
Reduced saliva and gastric secretion, raised gastric pH, intestinal epithelial atrophy, decreased splanchnic and mesenteric blood flow and decreased active transport reduce absorption (levodopa is the exception because of reduced dopa-decarboxylase activity); SC and IM absorption fall as muscle is replaced by fat and connective tissue.
A(iii)
Increased adipose tissue, reduced body water and muscle mass, increased α₁-acid glycoprotein and decreased albumin, reduced cardiac output with raised peripheral resistance, and increased blood-brain barrier permeability.
A(iv)
Reduced hepatic blood flow gives reduced delivery, reduced metabolism and a longer half-life; four processes matter (first pass, hepatic blood flow, extraction and metabolic capacity); reduced first-pass raises bioavailability of propranolol, nifedipine, labetalol and verapamil.
A(v)
Kidney size falls about 20% and about 30% of glomeruli are lost between ages 20 and 80; this affects renally excreted drugs, and narrow-window drugs such as gentamicin and digoxin need dose adjustment.
B(i)
Low Vd drugs (warfarin, gentamicin) are not widely distributed while digoxin and amiodarone have large Vd; fat-soluble drugs such as diazepam have increased Vd and longer action, and water-soluble drugs have decreased Vd; digoxin Vd falls with reduced muscle.
B(ii)
Decreased albumin, which binds acidic drugs (NSAIDs, furosemide, cimetidine, sulfonylureas), may cause toxicity; highly bound phenytoin and warfarin have a higher free fraction, but free drug is cleared so dose reduction may not be needed.
B(iii)
Reduced blood flow lowers metabolism of hypnotics and antipsychotics; reduced metabolic capacity raises levels of NSAIDs and phenytoin.
B(iv)
Chlorpropamide half-life rises from 25 to 48 hours to about 99 hours; tramadol and furosemide levels rise with reduced creatinine clearance; Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance predicts renal function better than serum creatinine, which stays normal because creatinine production also falls; acute illness such as CHF reduces theophylline elimination.
C(i)
Adjusting doses and choosing agents using these changes avoids accumulation and toxicity, especially of narrow-window drugs.
C(ii)
Elderly patients have increased ADR risk through polypharmacy, multiple diseases, increasing severity of illness, reduced elimination and increased sensitivity.
C(iii)
Reduced clearance of bound drug may offset higher free fractions, so dose reduction is not always needed, whereas lipid-soluble drugs persist longer.
questions.question:
A. Describe the pharmacokinetics of drugs in the elderly under the following headings: (i) definition and the effect of the ageing process; (ii) absorption; (iii) distribution; (iv) metabolism; (v) excretion.
B. Relate the principle to the following examples: (i) volume of distribution examples; (ii) protein binding examples; (iii) hepatic first-pass and blood flow examples; (iv) renal examples.
C. (i) Explain how knowledge of these changes improves patient outcomes; (ii) state the limitation; (iii) state the trade-off.

A middle-aged smoker has breathlessness on activity, a persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and persistent wheezing, and is diagnosed with COPD.
(i) Identify the condition and its components.
(ii) Select first-line and step-up drug therapy and justify the choices.
(iii) State the dose frequency and duration for each option.
(iv) State the monitoring parameters.
(v) State the key adverse effects.
(vi) State the counselling and non-drug management.
questions.answerText:
(i)
COPD is a group of lung conditions that includes emphysema (damage to the air sacs) and chronic bronchitis (long-term airway inflammation); the lungs become inflamed, damaged and narrowed, mainly from smoking, with some cases from long-term exposure to fumes or dust or a rare genetic problem; the damage is permanent but progression can be slowed; there is no cure.
(ii)
Stopping smoking is the most important step; short-acting bronchodilators are first treatment: β-2 agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline) or antimuscarinics (ipratropium); if symptomatic or having exacerbations, add a long-acting β-2 agonist (salmeterol, formoterol, indacaterol) or antimuscarinic (tiotropium, glycopyronium, aclidinium), or a combination of both; add a steroid inhaler (usually in a combination inhaler) if still breathless or frequent exacerbations.
(iii)
Short-acting inhalers are used when breathless up to a maximum of 4 times a day; long-acting inhalers last at least 12 hours so are used once or twice daily; theophylline is usually taken twice daily; carbocisteine 3 or 4 times daily (acetylcysteine powder if it fails); a 5-day course of steroid tablets for a bad flare-up; short antibiotic courses for signs of chest infection (more breathless, more cough, change in colour or thickness of phlegm).
(iv)
Regular blood tests for theophylline levels to set the dose and reduce side effects; closely monitor patients on long steroid courses (lowest effective dose, specialist prescribed); monitor for chest infection signs.
(v)
Theophylline: nausea, vomiting, headache, insomnia, palpitations; steroid tablets long term: weight gain, mood swings, osteoporosis; unpleasant egg-like smell of acetylcysteine powder (disappears on mixing).
(vi)
Pulmonary rehabilitation (2 or more group sessions a week for at least 6 weeks: exercise, education, dietary advice, psychological support); electrical muscle stimulation during bad flare-ups; surgery or lung transplant for a very small number of people; stopping smoking is never too late; COPD is largely preventable by avoiding smoking.

A(i)
Gout involves hyperuricaemia, recurrent acute arthritis with monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid leukocytes, tissue deposits of MSU crystals (tophi), interstitial kidney disease and uric acid nephrolithiasis.
A(ii)
Uric acid is the end product of purine degradation; the urate pool rises by overproduction (increased PRPP synthetase activity, HGPRT deficiency, tissue nucleic acid breakdown in myeloproliferative disorders, cytotoxic drugs) or underexcretion (diuretics, nicotinic acid, low-dose salicylates, ethanol, pyrazinamide, levodopa, ethambutol, cyclosporine); dietary purines are insignificant without a derangement in metabolism or elimination.
A(iii)
Urate crystal deposition in synovial fluid causes inflammation, vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, complement activation and neutrophil chemotaxis; phagocytosis lyses leukocytes and releases proteolytic enzymes; about 10% of patients form uric acid stones (acidic urine below pH 6, concentrated urine), and acute or chronic urate nephropathy and late tophi can occur.
A(iv)
Acute attacks have rapid onset of excruciating pain, swelling and inflammation, typically monoarticular, most often the first MTP joint (podagra), starting at night, with erythema, warmth, fever and leukocytosis; untreated attacks last 3 to 14 days and are precipitated by stress, trauma, alcohol, infection, surgery, rapid lowering of uric acid and urate-raising drugs.
A(v)
Definitive diagnosis needs aspiration of synovial fluid showing intracellular MSU monohydrate crystals in leukocytes; when aspiration is not feasible, a presumptive diagnosis is based on characteristic signs and symptoms and response to treatment.
B(i)
Terminate the acute attack, prevent recurrent attacks and prevent complications of chronic urate crystal deposition.
B(ii)
Local ice is the most effective adjunct; supplements (flaxseed, cherry, celery root) are not recommended; weight loss by caloric restriction and exercise, alcohol restriction, limiting purine-rich foods and high-fructose corn syrup, encouraging vegetables and low-fat dairy (the DASH diet may lower uric acid by about 1 mg/dL), and eliminating non-essential urate-raising drugs.
B(iii)
Acute: NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen, sulindac) started within 24 hours for 5 to 8 days, corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily or intra-articular triamcinolone) or colchicine 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg an hour later; hyperuricaemia: xanthine oxidase inhibitors first line, uricosurics for intolerance, combination or pegloticase in refractory cases, aiming for serum uric acid below 6 mg/dL (below 5 if severe).
B(iv)
NSAIDs, corticosteroids and colchicine are equally effective if started early; start urate-lowering therapy after two or more attacks a year, or with tophi, kidney disease or urolithiasis, and give anti-inflammatory prophylaxis (colchicine or an NSAID for at least 8 weeks) because urate mobilisation triggers flares.
C(i)
Xanthine oxidase inhibitors impair conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid, work in both overproducers and underexcretors and are first line; uricosurics (probenecid, lesinurad) increase renal clearance by inhibiting proximal tubule reabsorption, need CrCl above 45 to 50 mL/min, are avoided in urolithiasis and are second line.
C(ii)
Allopurinol is started at no more than 100 mg/day (50 mg in stage 4 CKD) and titrated to 800 mg/day, with rare hypersensitivity syndrome; febuxostat starts at 40 mg (80 mg if target not met after 2 weeks), needs no renal or hepatic adjustment but carries increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality warnings and is second line.
C(iii)
Colchicine works best within 24 hours (about two-thirds respond within hours; use within 36 hours) and has dose-dependent GI effects, neutropenia, neuromyopathy and interactions with P-glycoprotein or CYP3A4 inhibitors, whereas NSAIDs bring GI, renal, CV and CNS effects and corticosteroids are well tolerated short term but are limited by long-term effects.
questions.question:
A. Describe gout under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) aetiology; (iii) pathophysiology; (iv) clinical presentation; (v) diagnosis.
B. (i) State the treatment goals; (ii) state the non-pharmacological management; (iii) describe the pharmacotherapy of acute gout and of hyperuricaemia; (iv) give the rationale for each choice.
C. Distinguish between: (i) xanthine oxidase inhibitors and uricosurics; (ii) allopurinol and febuxostat; (iii) colchicine and the NSAIDs and corticosteroids in acute gout.

A patient stable on digoxin for atrial fibrillation (loading and maintenance already established) is started on amiodarone and also takes an antacid and a diuretic; later bupropion is added and the patient is taking high doses of biotin before a serum digoxin measurement.
(i) Identify and classify the drug-related problems.
(ii) Explain the mechanism of each.
(iii) State the management and dose adjustment.
(iv) State how the problems are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Pharmacokinetic drug interactions: amiodarone (P-glycoprotein inhibitor) raising levels; antacid reducing absorption; diuretic-related toxicity risk; bupropion lowering levels; and an analytical (assay) interference from biotin giving an artificially high result.
(ii)
P-glycoprotein inhibitors (amiodarone, dronedarone, propafenone, quinidine, verapamil) increase serum digoxin; antacids and cholestyramine decrease intestinal absorption by 20 to 35%; diuretics increase toxicity by decreasing glomerular filtration rate and causing electrolyte abnormalities, especially hypokalaemia; bupropion can decrease digoxin levels by 60%; high-dose biotin can raise measured concentration by up to 0.25 ng/mL (0.3 nmol/L) on the luminescent oxygen channeling immunoassay, which is not a true increase.
(iii)
Give digoxin 1 hour before or 2 to 3 hours after antacids or cholestyramine (the daily dose may need to rise); with dronedarone halve the digoxin dose if it cannot be stopped; monitor serum digoxin and clinical status with bupropion; correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia and monitor levels until they normalise.
(iv)
Prevention: ascertain electrolyte and renal status before and during treatment and check interactions (for example with the Lexicomp program); levels above 1 ng/mL (1.3 nmol/L) should be avoided in rate control to reduce toxicity; digoxin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis irrespective of levels.

questions.question:
An older patient (over 60 years) with knee osteoarthritis has taken a nonselective NSAID for months, has a past history of peptic ulcer disease and uses alcohol, and also takes a glucocorticoid, warfarin and an ACE inhibitor; the patient now has dyspepsia and a rise in blood pressure.
(i) Identify and classify the drug-related problems.
(ii) Explain the mechanism or cause of each problem.
(iii) State the management and the ways to lower the risk.
(iv) State the safer alternatives for osteoarthritis pain.
(v) State how the problem is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i)
NSAID-associated GI toxicity (ulcer or bleeding risk) and cardiovascular toxicity (hypertension, with risk of stroke, MI and death), plus clinically important interactions of NSAIDs with warfarin, ACE inhibitors and glucocorticoids.
(ii)
NSAIDs cause ulcers and bleeding through direct (topical) or indirect (systemic) mechanisms; risk factors present are age over 60, past peptic ulcer disease, alcohol use and concomitant glucocorticoid or anticoagulant; NSAIDs inhibit COX-1-dependent platelet thromboxane production, increasing bleeding risk (reversible, with platelet function normalising 1 to 3 days after stopping); NSAIDs may also cause kidney disease, hepatitis, hypersensitivity, rash and CNS effects.
(iii)
Use the lowest dose possible only when needed, and add misoprostol four times daily, or a PPI or H₂-receptor antagonist daily; COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) pose less GI risk but this advantage is substantially reduced with aspirin and they also raise CV risk; serious interactions occur with lithium, warfarin, oral hypoglycaemics, methotrexate, antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, β-blockers and diuretics.
(iv)
Acetaminophen is the preferred first-line therapy for knee and hip OA (lower GI and CV risk but hepatotoxic in overdose; avoid in chronic alcohol users or liver disease); topical NSAIDs are recommended for knee OA if acetaminophen fails and are preferred over oral NSAIDs above 75 years (similar relief, fewer GI events, no linked CV risk; avoid oral NSAIDs with them); intra-articular corticosteroids, tramadol, duloxetine and opioids are further options.
(v)
NSAIDs should be avoided in late pregnancy (premature closure of ductus arteriosus).

questions.question:
A patient with type 2 diabetes who is already on an oral agent is about to start a single bedtime basal insulin dose, and has hypertension and a history of poor adherence to lifestyle measures.
(i) Identify the patient's needs and risks.
(ii) State the pharmacist's interventions for starting insulin and titration.
(iii) State the counselling on monitoring, hypoglycaemia and injection devices.
(iv) State the counselling on diet, exercise, alcohol and smoking.
(v) State the screening and cardiovascular risk-reduction measures.
(vi) State follow-up and referral criteria.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Needs: control of fasting glucose, prevention of acute complications (hypoglycaemia, ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar state) and chronic microvascular and macrovascular complications; a patient starting insulin must self-monitor glucose to adjust doses and reduce hypoglycaemia risk; weight gain worsens glucose, BP and lipid control.
(ii)
Continue oral agents at the same dose initially (a secretagogue may eventually be reduced or stopped); add a single bedtime basal dose (glargine, detemir or NPH) of 10 to 20 units or 0.1 to 0.2 unit/kg; adjust to fasting glucose (target 80 to 100 mg/dL) every 3 to 4 days: +2 units if 100 to 140, +4 if 141 to 180, +6 if 181 to 220, +8 if above 200 mg/dL; return to the previous dose immediately if fasting glucose falls below 80 mg/dL.
(iii)
Teach self-monitoring, recognition of hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion) and its treatment (15 g carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes), and device skills (pen or syringe use, site rotation, needle length, priming, storage, disposal); alcohol raises hypoglycaemia risk.
(iv)
Dietary control is the cornerstone: low saturated fat, moderate carbohydrate from whole grains, fibre, restricted salt, evenly distributed meals; weight loss of 5 to 10% brings profound benefit; at least 150 minutes of moderate (or 90 minutes of vigorous) aerobic activity per week over at least 3 days with no more than 2 consecutive inactive days; alcohol limited to 1 drink (women) or 2 (men) per day; advise every tobacco user to quit.
(v)
Annual comprehensive eye examination, serum creatinine and urine albumin at least annually, annual neuropathy screening and daily foot inspection; BP goal below 130/80 mmHg with an ACE inhibitor or ARB; statin with LDL-C below 100 mg/dL; aspirin 75 to 162 mg/day for those at increased CV risk (not for those under 21, with aspirin allergy, bleeding tendency, anticoagulation, recent GI bleeding or active liver disease).
(vi)
Targets: HbA1c below 7% (individualised), pre-prandial 70 to 130 mg/dL and 2-hour post-prandial below 180 mg/dL; education should be repeated in three stages (initial, in-depth, continuing).

questions.question:
A patient with knee osteoarthritis has partial pain relief on acetaminophen and tramadol and is considered for duloxetine; the patient then develops symptoms attributed to excess serotonergic activity.
(i) Identify and classify the drug-related problem.
(ii) Explain the mechanism.
(iii) State the management.
(iv) State the other adverse effects and regulatory status of the drugs.
(v) State how the problem is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A pharmacodynamic drug interaction between tramadol and duloxetine with increased risk of serotonin syndrome.
(ii)
Both tramadol and duloxetine increase serotonin concentration, so concomitant use with other serotonergic medicines raises the risk.
(iii)
Duloxetine is adjunctive treatment only for knee (not hip) OA with partial response to first-line analgesics, and tramadol should be recommended only after failure of full-dose acetaminophen and topical NSAIDs where oral NSAIDs and intra-articular steroids are unsuitable.
(iv)
Tramadol causes nausea, vomiting, dizziness, constipation, headache and somnolence, seizures are the most serious adverse event, it carries potential for dependence, addiction and diversion (Schedule IV controlled substance), but is not linked with GI bleeding, CV events or renal failure; duloxetine causes nausea, dry mouth, constipation, anorexia, fatigue, somnolence and dizziness, with rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome and liver failure, and pain relief takes about 4 weeks.
(v)
Prevention: avoid combining serotonergic medicines unless necessary; opioid use should be assessed at least every 3 months for functional goals, harm and adverse effects, at the lowest effective dose.

A(i)
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, progressive autoimmune condition that primarily affects joints and the synovium but can have systemic manifestations.
A(ii)
It results from genetic susceptibility, non-genetic factors and a triggering event, with an unknown infectious process thought to be the primary trigger.
A(iii)
Antigen-presenting cells activate T cells, which stimulate B cells to produce autoantibodies (rheumatoid factor, ACPA) and proinflammatory cytokines (TNF, interleukins); synovial hypertrophy and angiogenesis form a pannus that invades cartilage and bone; cytokines increase chondrocyte catabolism and RANKL-driven osteoclast activity; chronic inflammation causes vasculitis, fibrosis, anaemia and renal amyloidosis.
A(iv)
Prodromal fatigue, weakness, low-grade fever, anorexia and joint pain; symmetric involvement of small joints of hands, feet, wrists and ankles; morning stiffness exceeding 30 minutes; soft warm swollen joints; erosions and deformities (swan neck, boutonniere, ulnar deviation); extra-articular features (nodules, interstitial lung disease, pleural effusion, vasculitis, pericarditis, ocular disease).
A(v)
The 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria score joint involvement, serology (RF, anti-CCP), acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) and duration (6 weeks or more); a score of 6 or more out of 10 indicates definite RA; RF is found in 70 to 80%, ANA in 25%, and synovial fluid shows high white cells without crystals or infection.
B(i)
The ultimate goal is complete remission or low disease activity (treat to target), reducing inflammation and symptoms, maintaining function, slowing joint destruction and delaying disability.
B(ii)
Patient education, physical and occupational therapy, exercise, assistive devices and orthoses, weight loss and surgery such as joint replacement for severe cartilage loss.
B(iii)
Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine), biologic DMARDs (TNF inhibitors and non-TNF biologics) and JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib), with NSAIDs, glucocorticoids and acetaminophen as bridge therapy.
B(iv)
Start a conventional DMARD (methotrexate preferred) in treatment-naive patients; monotherapy for low activity, double or triple therapy for moderate or high activity; add a biologic or JAK inhibitor if activity stays moderate or high; low-dose glucocorticoid for the shortest time; taper but never stop DMARD therapy fully once in remission.
C(i)
Conventional DMARDs are cheaper small molecules; biologics are genetically engineered proteins (TNF or non-TNF), more expensive, raise infection risk, need TB and hepatitis B screening and cannot be combined with each other.
C(ii)
RA is autoimmune with symmetric small-joint disease, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, raised ESR and CRP and RF positivity; OA is a degenerative disorder of weight-bearing joints with stiffness under 30 minutes, normal or slightly raised ESR and negative RF.
C(iii)
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, is preferred and teratogenic with benefit in 3 to 6 weeks; hydroxychloroquine is mainly used with other DMARDs (monotherapy for mild cases), needs no frequent routine laboratory monitoring, can be continued in pregnancy, is excreted in breast milk and requires periodic eye examinations.
questions.question:
A. Describe rheumatoid arthritis under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) aetiology; (iii) pathophysiology; (iv) clinical presentation; (v) diagnosis.
B. (i) State the treatment goals; (ii) state the non-pharmacological management; (iii) describe the pharmacotherapy; (iv) give the rationale for the stepwise choices.
C. Distinguish between: (i) conventional and biologic DMARDs; (ii) rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis; (iii) methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine.

A. Describe the pharmacokinetics of drugs in children under the following headings: (i) age classification and the principle that children are not small adults; (ii) absorption; (iii) distribution; (iv) metabolism; (v) elimination.
B. Relate the principle to the dose-calculation examples: (i) age and weight-based rules; (ii) body surface area dosing; (iii) rules when weight is unknown; (iv) practical prescribing rules.
C. (i) Explain how these approaches improve outcomes; (ii) state the limitation; (iii) state the trade-off between simplicity and accuracy.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Classification: neonate (birth to 28 days), infant (28 days to 23 months), young child (2 to 5 years), older child (6 to 11), adolescent (12 to 18); children are not smaller adults, and weight or age-based dosing is not reliable.
A(ii)
Neonates are relatively achlorhydric until about the 6th week; bile salts are about 50% of adult and lipase low (affecting vitamin D, chloramphenicol palmitate and lipid-soluble drugs); gastric emptying reaches adult rate around 6 to 8 months; skin absorption is increased in premature infants and intramuscular absorption is erratic in them.
A(iii)
Albumin and α₁-acid glycoprotein are reduced (more free phenytoin, phenobarbital, chloramphenicol, penicillin); ECF is about 40% at birth falling to 20% by 12 years (loading dose for aminoglycosides); total body water is 80% at birth; fat is 12% to 16% in term neonates; bilirubin displacement can cause kernicterus.
A(iv)
CYP activity is about 50% of adult at birth, reaching adult level or higher by 1 to 5 years and declining to adult level at puberty; glucuronidation reaches adult level at 3 to 4 years, acetylation is reduced at birth, sulfate conjugation is well developed and glycine conjugation matures by 6 months.
A(v)
GFR in full-term neonates is 30% to 50% of adult and matures between the 3rd and 5th month (pre-term reach term levels at about 4 weeks); renal clearance is about 50% of adult and reaches adult values at about 6 months; dosing intervals may increase in neonates but older children may need shorter intervals.
B(i)
Young's rule = age/(age + 12) × adult dose (over 2 years); Dilling = age/20 × adult dose (4 to 20 years); Fried = age in months × adult dose / 150 (up to 1 to 2 years); Clark = weight in pounds × adult dose / 150.
B(ii)
Child's dose = child BSA / adult BSA (1.73 m²) × adult dose; Mosteller BSA = square root of (height cm × weight kg / 3600), DuBois uses 0.20247 × height(m)^0.725 × weight(kg)^0.425; average BSA is 0.25 m² (neonate), 0.5 (2 years), 1.07 (9 years), 1.33 (12 to 13 years).
B(iii)
If weight is unknown, (4 × age) + 20 fits the BSA curve for normal-sized children; the Salisbury rule gives (weight × 2) per cent of the adult dose below 30 kg and (weight + 30) per cent above 30 kg, close to the BNF rule.
B(iv)
Doses are mg/kg, mg/m² or by age; convert pounds to kilograms (1 kg = 2.2 lb); orders written mg/kg/d need clarification; write orders in mg rather than mL; dosing varies by indication; use references for children.
C(i)
BSA-based dosing mitigates variation in patient size, improves efficacy, minimises toxicity and accounts for some pharmacokinetic changes.
C(ii)
Weight varies with age up to about 13 years, so age-based rules may be highly unreliable.
C(iii)
The Salisbury rule is simple and approximately correct, whereas the other rules are not both simple and accurate enough for clinical use; Dubois and Mosteller formulae suit extremes of weight and height (for example chemotherapy).

(i)
The recommended range for status epilepticus or anticonvulsant therapy is 10 to 20 mg/L, so 7.96 mg/L is subtherapeutic (and below the expected 15.0 mg/L), consistent with continued fitting.
(ii)
Check the renal profile, albumin level and other drug interactions before considering an incremental loading dose; here albumin and creatinine clearance are normal, so another incremental loading dose is given.
(iii)
Incremental LD = (Cp desired - Cp measured) × Vd × BW / (S × F); with population adult Vd 0.70 L/kg, S = 0.92 for IV phenytoin and F = 1: (15 - 7.96) × 0.70 × 62 / (0.92 × 1) = 305.5 / 0.92 = about 332, rounded to about 330 mg.
(iv)
An incremental loading dose of IV phenytoin 300 mg stat is appropriate if she is still fitting, and she continues the maintenance dose of IV phenytoin 100 mg three times daily.
(v)
Maintenance dose (mg/day) = Vmax × BW × Cp desired / [S × F × (Km + Cp desired)]; Cpss = Km × S × F × Dose / (Vmax × BW - S × F × Dose); the worked examples use population Vmax 7 mg/kg/day and Km 4 mg/L.
(vi)
If albumin is low (below 25 g/L), correct the measured concentration to the value for normal protein binding: measured concentration divided by [0.9 × (albumin/44) + 0.1]; if albumin is low and creatinine clearance is below 10 mL/minute a second equation with a factor of 0.48 is used.
(vii)
Useful pharmacokinetic reference data: half-life 22 hours orally (range 7 to 42) and 10 to 15 hours IV.
questions.question:
BJ, a 30-year-old woman (62 kg), was admitted after status epilepticus. She received IV phenytoin 900 mg stat and was prescribed IV phenytoin 100 mg three times daily. The next day her phenytoin concentration was 7.96 mg/L, whereas 15.0 mg/L was expected from population data. Her liver and renal profiles are normal and she is still fitting.
(i) Interpret the measured concentration against the therapeutic range.
(ii) State what must be checked before giving more drug.
(iii) Calculate the incremental loading dose using population volume of distribution and show the equation.
(iv) State the dose, route and the maintenance regimen to continue.
(v) State the equations for maintenance dose and for predicting steady-state concentration.
(vi) State when and how the measured level is corrected for low albumin.
(vii) State the pharmacokinetic reference data.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
TDM is the clinical laboratory measurement of a chemical parameter that, with appropriate medical interpretation, directly influences prescribing; it uses drug concentrations in body fluids as an aid to managing therapy and aims to individualise regimens for optimal patient benefit.
A(ii)
It is based on a close relationship between plasma level and clinical effect; if no such relationship exists TDM is of little value, and its value depends on how precisely the treatment outcome can be defined (it helps most when a precise therapeutic end point is hard to define).
A(iii)
The therapeutic range is the plasma concentration range where the drug is efficacious without toxicity in most people, but it introduces uncertainty about the dose and assumes all concentrations in range are equally desirable; the target concentration is linked to a specific dose for an individual, chosen from the concentration-effect relationship to balance desired and undesired effects.
A(iv)
Indications include unpredictable dose-concentration relationship (phenytoin), narrow therapeutic window (lithium, phenytoin, digoxin), steep dose-response curve (theophylline), saturable metabolism (phenytoin), difficulty interpreting clinical effects (nausea in digitalis toxicity versus heart failure), poorly defined end point (immunosuppressants), renal disease, drug interactions (thiazide with lithium), suspected toxicity or drug abuse, evaluating compliance and guiding withdrawal of therapy.
A(v)
Unsuitable drugs include those with a wide therapeutic index or no realistic toxicity concern (penicillin), those whose effects are measured by functional tests or whose concentration is not predictably related to effect (anticoagulants), those with undefined concentration-effect relationship (antidepressants) and hit-and-run drugs (omeprazole, MAO inhibitors).
B(i)
Established drugs: cardioactive drugs (amiodarone, digoxin, disopyramide, lignocaine, procainamide, propranolol, quinidine); aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin); lithium and tricyclic antidepressants; antiepileptics (phenytoin, phenobarbitone, benzodiazepines, carbamazepine, valproic acid, ethosuximide); theophylline; methotrexate; cyclosporine and tacrolimus.
B(ii)
Digoxin at least 6 hours after the dose; phenytoin has a long half-life so timing is not critical; carbamazepine ideally a trough just after a dose plus a peak 3 hours later; lithium a 12-hour sample; gentamicin a peak 0.5 hour after IV (1 hour after IM) infusion and a pre-dose trough; theophylline slow-release preparations are sampled at trough.
B(iii)
Cyclosporine needs whole blood (it binds red cells) in an EDTA tube; trough (C₀) correlates with nephrotoxicity but not acute rejection, which correlates better with AUC; the 2-hour level (C₂) is a surrogate of absorption and exposure; levels are checked every 2 to 3 days in the first 4 weeks post-transplant, then monthly after 3 months.
B(iv)
Lower than anticipated: non-compliance, dosage error, rapid elimination, sample timing, changing hepatic blood flow, poor bioavailability and reduced plasma binding; higher than anticipated: dosage error, rapid bioavailability, slow elimination, increased protein binding and decreased renal or hepatic function.
C(i)
The target concentration strategy selects a target, predicts clearance and volume of distribution from population values and patient characteristics, calculates loading and maintenance doses, measures concentrations, refines individual parameters and revises the dose, so doses are tailored to avoid toxicity and treatment failure.
C(ii)
Factors include pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, dose, sampling time and matrix, assay method, genetic polymorphisms, smoking, formulation, circadian effect, herbal medicines, protein binding, active metabolites, steady state and turnaround time.
C(iii)
Therapeutic ranges are not absolutes (the lower limit gives about 50% of maximum effect and the upper limit is set by toxicity), assays usually measure bound plus unbound drug although only unbound drug acts, and specialised assays may delay results, so expert clinical interpretation is needed.
questions.question:
A. Describe therapeutic drug monitoring under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) concept and underlying principle; (iii) therapeutic range versus target concentration; (iv) indications; (v) drugs unsuitable for monitoring.
B. Relate the principle to examples: (i) established drugs monitored; (ii) sampling times for digoxin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, lithium, gentamicin and theophylline; (iii) the example of cyclosporine; (iv) causes of lower or higher than anticipated concentrations.
C. (i) Explain how monitoring improves patient outcomes; (ii) state the factors that affect interpretation; (iii) state the limitation or trade-off.

A. Describe insulin therapy clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) interactions; (viii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for basal and bolus insulin and for the type of regimen; (ii) state the rationale for dose titration.
C. (i) Explain the basis of hypoglycaemia and of treatment failure; (ii) explain the basis of premixed insulins and the choice of device.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Type 1 diabetes (insulin requiring for survival), type 2 diabetes when insulin is needed for control, severe hyperglycaemia, a baseline glucose of 250 mg/dL or more, and DKA (IV regular insulin).
A(ii)
Subcutaneous (pens, pumps, syringes) or IV in DKA; type 2: continue oral agents and add a bedtime basal dose of 10 to 20 units or 0.1 to 0.2 unit/kg; type 1: 0.5 unit/kg/day, 50% basal and 50% bolus split into three meals; insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio = 500 / total daily dose.
A(iii)
Onset, peak and duration: rapid-acting 5 to 15 minutes, 45 to 75 minutes, 3 to 5 hours; short-acting 30 to 60 minutes, 2 to 4 hours, 6 to 8 hours; intermediate about 2 hours, 4 to 12 hours, 18 to 26 hours; long-acting glargine and detemir onset 3 to 4 hours, durations in the range of 10 to 20 hours; premixed 10 to 16 hours duration.
A(iv)
Insulin replaces the absolute or relative deficiency in insulin secretion or action; basal insulin lowers fasting glucose production and bolus insulin limits postprandial hyperglycaemia.
A(v)
Hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion).
A(vi)
Know when not to use a therapy; patients who start insulin must self-monitor to adjust doses and reduce hypoglycaemia; hypoglycaemic unawareness calls for caution and higher A1c targets (about 8%); some patients refuse parenteral therapy.
A(vii)
Alcohol increases hypoglycaemia risk; glucocorticoids, thiazides and other drugs can impair insulin action.
A(viii)
Self-monitoring of blood glucose (at least three or four times daily in type 1); titrate every 3 to 4 days to fasting glucose of 80 to 100 mg/dL and cut back if below 80 mg/dL; HbA1c below 7%.
B(i)
Basal insulin (detemir, glargine, NPH) gives constant levels for about 50% of needs, mostly preferred for fasting hyperglycaemia; bolus insulin (regular, aspart, glulisine, lispro) needs an immediate peak and provides 10% to 20% per meal; "fix the fasting first" in type 2.
B(ii)
Increase by 2, 4, 6 or 8 units according to fasting glucose bands (100 to 140, 141 to 180, 181 to 220, above 200 mg/dL) every 3 to 4 days, to avoid hypoglycaemia while reaching the target.
C(i)
Hypoglycaemia follows excess dose, missed or delayed meals, extra exercise or alcohol; treatment failure arises from non-adherence, poor monitoring or insufficient titration.
C(ii)
Premixed products (for example 70% NPH/30% regular, 75% lispro protamine/25% lispro, 70% aspart protamine/30% aspart) combine two insulins in one injection; pens give more accurate dosing, easier dose setting and better adherence than syringes but cost more.

(i)
The trough (pre-dose) is 1.6 mg/L and the peak 10 mg/L; the pre-sample falls 22.5 hours after the post-sample (24 hours less 1.5 hours), allowing Ke to be derived from the two points.
(ii)
Ke = (ln 10 - ln 1.6) / (24 - 1.5) = 1.83 / 22.5 = about 0.08 per hour; t½ = 0.693 / 0.081 = about 8.66 hours.
(iii)
Cmax = 10 × e^(-0.08 × 0.5) = 9.60 mg/L; Cmin = 9.60 × e^(-0.08 × 24) = 1.40 mg/L.
(iv)
Vd = Dose / [Cmax × (1 - e^(-Ke × τ))] = 13 / [9.60 × (1 - e^(-0.08 × 24))] = 13 / 8.198 = 1.58 L.
(v)
New dose = target Cmax × Vd × (1 - e^(-Ke × τ)) = 10 × 1.58 × 0.944 = about 14.9 mg; expected Cmin = 10 × e^(-0.08 × 36) = 0.56 mg/L.
(vi)
Give about 14 mg IV gentamicin every 36 hours; as a general rule, take the peak sample 30 minutes after the end of an IV infusion and the trough before the dose.
questions.question:
A newborn (20 days old, 55 cm, 4.2 kg) is treated for neonatal sepsis with IV C-penicillin twice daily and IV gentamicin 13 mg once daily. The first gentamicin dose was given at 12 pm on day 1. On the second dose the pre-sample at 11:30 am was 1.6 mg/L and the post-sample at 1:00 pm is taken as the target Cmax of 10 mg/L (peak assumed 30 minutes into the infusion). A dosing interval of 36 hours is suggested.
(i) Interpret the measured values.
(ii) Calculate the elimination rate constant and half-life.
(iii) Calculate the actual peak and trough.
(iv) Calculate the volume of distribution.
(v) Calculate the new dose and expected trough for the 36-hour interval.
(vi) State the follow-up and the regimen recommended.

A breastfeeding mother of a newborn asks whether her medicines are safe; she has been prescribed codeine for pain, takes sertraline, occasionally drinks alcohol, smokes, and wants to boost her milk supply.
(i) Identify the mother's needs and the infant's risks.
(ii) State the pharmacist's interventions on the codeine and sertraline.
(iii) State the counselling on timing of doses and feeds.
(iv) State the counselling on alcohol, nicotine, caffeine and other substances.
(v) State the advice on milk-boosting drugs and information sources.
(vi) State follow-up and when to stop or suspend breastfeeding.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Most commonly used drugs are relatively safe for breastfed babies; risk is greatest in newborns under two months and in premature babies, who metabolise and excrete drugs poorly (an infant's capacity at birth is about one-third that at 7 to 8 months); transfer is mainly by passive diffusion and depends on maternal plasma concentration, protein binding, molecular size, ionisation, lipid solubility, oral bioavailability and milk volume.
(ii)
Codeine should be avoided because ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolisers (up to 10% of Western Europeans and up to 30% of North Africans) make significant morphine, which may cause CNS depression and potentially infant death; alternative analgesia is paracetamol or ibuprofen; sertraline is highly protein bound (98%) and has a high volume of distribution, so minimal transfer, and a short half-life drug such as sertraline is preferred over fluoxetine.
(iii)
Feed the baby just before the mother takes the medicine so milk concentration is lowest, and reassure that the drug does not store in the milk; this does not apply to long half-life drugs such as diazepam, whose need should be reassessed; prescribe at the lowest effective dose and consider alternative routes or products to minimise maternal systemic exposure.
(iv)
Delay a glass of alcohol until after a feed and wait two hours before the next feed; nicotine replacement is not an absolute contraindication and is preferable to smoking (short-acting forms); smoking, including passive, is associated with sudden infant death syndrome; high maternal caffeine is linked to infant irritability and poor sleep; cannabis may impair motor development, so stop it and avoid second-hand smoke.
(v)
Domperidone and metoclopramide have been used off-label to stimulate prolactin but have limited efficacy evidence; non-drug approaches (correct advice, support, more frequent breastfeeding) are preferred; sources include state obstetric drug information services, LactMed and the Australian Medicines Handbook.
(vi)
Contraindicated drugs include anticancer drugs, lithium, oral retinoids, iodine, amiodarone, gold salts and radiopharmaceuticals; temporarily suspend breastfeeding and express milk for potentially toxic drugs such as cytotoxics and radiopharmaceuticals, with resumption determined by half-life; a relative infant dose of 10% or more is the notional level of concern; monitoring the infant for drowsiness or other signs is advised for some drugs.

questions.question:
A patient is given gentamicin; the maintenance dose is 80 mg four times daily with normal renal function. The patient is now uraemic with a creatinine clearance of 55 mL/min (normal 110 mL/min) and gentamicin is 100% excreted by the kidney.
(i) Predict the effect of renal impairment on the drug and its dosing.
(ii) State the dose adjustment equations and calculate the new dose.
(iii) State the alternative adjustment by interval.
(iv) State how to estimate renal function in this patient.
(v) Justify the monitoring plan.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Glomerular filtration and active secretion are impaired, so renal excretion falls and elimination half-lives lengthen; the loading dose depends on Vd, which is generally not significantly altered, so the loading dose is the same as in non-uremic patients, while the maintenance dose depends on clearance and must be reduced; doses of narrow-window drugs should be reduced, especially if the drug has accumulated.
(ii)
To keep the same average steady-state concentration with the same interval, Du = Dn × (CLTu / CLTn); with 100% renal excretion and clearance proportional to creatinine clearance, Du = 80 × (55/110) = 40 mg four times daily (equivalently Du = Dn × ku/kn).
(iii)
Either decrease the maintenance dose or increase the dosage interval without changing the dose, or change both.
(iv)
Cockcroft-Gault (stable renal function): CLcr = (140 - age) × weight (kg) / (72 × serum creatinine in mg/dL) for males (use 85% for females), or (140 - age) × weight / serum creatinine in µmol/L; for unstable renal function use the Brater, Jelliffe or Chiou equations; serum creatinine or creatinine clearance assumes a linear relation with drug clearance, which should be verified clinically.
(v)
Monitoring should verify renal impairment by physical diagnosis and other clinical tests, as creatinine-based estimates may be biased (for example in elderly or obese patients, where adjusted body weight is used above 120% of ideal body weight).

(i)
Rheumatoid arthritis: a chronic progressive autoimmune disease in which antigen presentation drives T and B cell activation, autoantibodies (RF, ACPA) and cytokines (TNF, interleukins) cause synovial hypertrophy, angiogenesis and pannus that invades cartilage and bone; the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria score joint involvement, serology, acute-phase reactants and duration (6 weeks or more), and a score of 6 or more out of 10 indicates definite RA; RF and ACPA positivity predict a more aggressive course.
(ii)
Start a conventional DMARD irrespective of disease activity in treatment-naive patients; methotrexate is preferred unless contraindicated; for moderate or high disease activity double or triple DMARD therapy is recommended, or a biologic with or without a DMARD.
(iii)
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; SC or IM methotrexate has higher bioavailability than oral and is better tolerated (oral doses above 15 mg weekly may add no benefit); benefit appears 3 to 6 weeks after starting; DMARDs take weeks to months, so NSAIDs, glucocorticoids and acetaminophen can bridge, and low-dose prednisone (10 mg/day or less) can be added for the shortest time.
(iv)
Add or switch to a TNF inhibitor (adalimumab, certolizumab, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab), a non-TNF biologic (abatacept, sarilumab, tocilizumab, rituximab, anakinra) or a JAK inhibitor (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib); avoid dual biologic therapy because of infection risk.
(v)
Before a biologic obtain a tuberculin skin test or IGRA and screen for hepatitis B (reactivation risk); hydroxychloroquine needs periodic ophthalmologic examinations (retinal toxicity).
(vi)
Methotrexate has numerous adverse effects; concomitant folic acid 1 to 5 mg/day may reduce some; biologics increase infection risk; TNF inhibitors increase serious infection and malignancy risk and may exacerbate demyelinating disorders; glucocorticoids and NSAIDs are less desirable long term.
(vii)
Methotrexate is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy, nursing, chronic liver disease, immunodeficiency and pre-existing haematological disorders, and excretion falls in renal impairment; TNF inhibitors should not be used in NYHA class III or IV heart failure; live vaccines must not be given with biologics.
(viii)
Patient education, physical and occupational therapy, exercise, assistive devices, weight loss and (in severe cartilage loss) joint replacement; patients on biologics should report infection or planned major surgery; contraception is needed on methotrexate and the drug stopped if conception is planned.
questions.question:
A patient has symmetric pain and swelling of the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet with morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, fatigue and low-grade fever for several weeks; rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies are positive, ESR and CRP are raised, and symptoms have lasted 6 weeks or more. The patient has not been treated before and disease activity is moderate to high.
(i) Identify the condition, its pathophysiology and the classification score.
(ii) Select drug therapy and justify the choice.
(iii) State the route and onset for the first-line drug and the bridging therapy.
(iv) State the escalation options if the response is inadequate.
(v) State the monitoring and screening before biologics.
(vi) State the key adverse effects.
(vii) State the interactions and precautions.
(viii) State the counselling and non-drug measures.

A. Describe the basic clinical pharmacokinetic principles of dose individualisation under the following headings: (i) goal of therapeutics; (ii) clearance; (iii) volume of distribution and loading dose; (iv) half-life; (v) elimination kinetics and bioavailability.
B. Relate the principle to the following examples: (i) the digoxin loading dose; (ii) the maintenance dose-rate; (iii) the time to steady state; (iv) the choice of dosing interval.
C. (i) Explain how these principles improve patient outcomes; (ii) state the limitation; (iii) state the trade-off.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The goal is the desired beneficial effect with minimal adverse effects, by keeping plasma concentration above the minimal effective concentration and below the minimal toxic concentration (the therapeutic window), so the clinician must determine the dose that achieves this.
A(ii)
Clearance is the single most important parameter: the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time, a constant relating elimination rate to Cp (rate = CL × Cp); total CL = renal + hepatic + other; CL = Dose/AUC (F × Dose/AUC orally) or 0.693 × Vd / t½.
A(iii)
Vd is a proportionality constant relating Cp to the amount of drug in the body (Ab = Vd × Cp), an apparent volume (heparin 5 L, gentamicin 15 L, digoxin 500 L, quinacrine 20,000 L); Vd determines the loading dose (LD = Vd × target Cp).
A(iv)
Half-life is the time for concentration to halve; it determines time to steady state and the dosing interval; t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL and k = 0.693 / t½.
A(v)
Zero-order elimination (rare, such as ethanol at about 15 mg/100 mL/h) versus first-order elimination (rate proportional to Cp, most drugs); oral bioavailability F is the fraction reaching the systemic circulation, from the AUC after oral versus IV dosing.
B(i)
For a target digoxin Cp of 1.5 µg/L and Vd about 500 L, LD = 500 × 1.5 = 750 µg.
B(ii)
Maintenance dose-rate = CL × Cpss (rate of administration equals rate of elimination at steady state), so CL determines the maintenance dose.
B(iii)
Steady state or 90% of a new steady state is reached after four half-lives; a loading dose of Vd × (Cpss₂ - Cpss₁) reaches a higher level faster; after stopping an infusion, concentration falls to 10% after four half-lives.
B(iv)
The interval keeps concentrations above MEC and below MTC, and considers therapeutic index and compliance (once or twice daily is best); with decreased CL in renal impairment a three or four times daily drug may be given twice or once daily.
C(i)
Using CL, Vd and t½ allows rational regimens tailored to the individual patient, achieving concentrations quickly (loading) and maintaining them (maintenance).
C(ii)
Vd is an apparent volume with no anatomical meaning, clearance applies only to first-order kinetics, and the concentration at the site of action is difficult to measure so plasma concentration is used.
C(iii)
A loading dose gives speed but needs the Vd; a longer interval improves compliance but widens fluctuation (determined by t½).

questions.question:
SJ, a 30-year-old man (60 kg) with epilepsy took 300 mg of capsule phenytoin and suddenly became lethargic with slurred speech and mild nystagmus. A random serum concentration is 40.0 mg/L (population target 15 mg/L).
(i) Identify and classify the drug-related problem.
(ii) Explain the mechanism.
(iii) State the management and the equation used to estimate how long to withhold the next dose.
(iv) State the parameters used in that equation.
(v) State how the problem is prevented.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Dose-related phenytoin toxicity (an adverse drug reaction from supratherapeutic concentration): 40 mg/L is far above the 10 to 20 mg/L therapeutic range, with nystagmus, slurred speech and lethargy.
(ii)
Phenytoin undergoes saturable (Michaelis-Menten) metabolism at therapeutic concentrations, so once the enzyme is saturated drug concentrations rise rapidly and disproportionately and clearance falls (Cp much greater than Km); a small dose increase can produce a large concentration rise.
(iii)
Withhold further doses until the concentration falls toward the desired level; time to withhold T = [Km × ln(Cp measured / Cp desired) + (Cp measured - Cp desired)] × Vd (L) / Vm (mg/day).
(iv)
Population values used: Km 4 mg/L, Vmax 7 mg/kg/day, Vd 0.7 L/kg, Cp desired 15 mg/L and body weight 60 kg.
(v)
Prevention is by individualising the dose with Km and Vmax and monitoring levels, avoiding dosing near saturation; phenytoin has a therapeutic range of 10 to 20 mg/L.

questions.question:
A patient who has recently been diagnosed with asthma has wheezing, breathlessness, a tight chest and cough, uses a reliever inhaler 3 or more times a week, and is worried about steroid inhalers.
(i) Identify the patient's needs and the risks of poor control.
(ii) State the pharmacist's interventions on the inhaler types and when each is used.
(iii) State the counselling on inhaler side effects and how to prevent them.
(iv) State the add-on tablets and other treatments for severe disease with their side effects.
(v) State the counselling on triggers, non-drug measures and the personal action plan.
(vi) State the follow-up and referral criteria.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Asthma is inflammation of the breathing tubes that makes them highly sensitive so they temporarily narrow; there is no cure but symptoms can be controlled; poorly controlled asthma causes constant tiredness, missed work or school, stress, anxiety or depression, unplanned GP or hospital visits, pneumonia, delayed growth or puberty in children, and risk of life-threatening attacks.
(ii)
The reliever inhaler (usually blue) is used when needed and relieves symptoms within minutes; a preventer inhaler (contains a steroid) is used every day, even without symptoms, to reduce inflammation and sensitivity of the airways; a combination inhaler is used daily if reliever plus preventer do not control the asthma.
(iii)
Reliever side effects are shaking or a fast heartbeat for a few minutes; preventer side effects are oral thrush, hoarse voice and sore throat, which can be prevented by using a spacer and rinsing the mouth after use.
(iv)
Leukotriene receptor antagonists daily (tummy aches, headaches); theophylline (headaches, feeling sick); steroid tablets (weight gain from appetite, easy bruising, mood changes, osteoporosis, high blood pressure, with regular monitoring); biologic injections every few weeks (specialist only; discomfort at the injection site) and bronchial thermoplasty for severe asthma.
(v)
Identify and avoid triggers (allergies such as house dust mites, animals, pollen; smoke, pollution, cold air; exercise; infections like colds or flu); breathing exercises (Papworth, Buteyko) may reduce symptoms and reliever use but must not replace medicine; a personal action plan covers medicines, monitoring and what to do in an attack; return used inhalers to a pharmacy for disposal.
(vi)
Tell the GP or asthma nurse if the reliever is needed 3 or more times a week or if symptoms continue on a preventer; occupational asthma is referred to a specialist (employer and occupational health informed); severe asthma needing biologics or thermoplasty needs a specialist.

(i)
Thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism), most likely Graves' disease, which is the most common cause, predominantly affects females (male:female 1:5), peaks at ages 30 to 40 and has strong familial predisposition; supporting findings are palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss with increased appetite, loose stools, hair thinning, irritability, tachycardia, low TSH with raised T4, T3 and free thyroxine index.
(ii)
A thionamide is selected: carbimazole is the most commonly used, and propylthiouracil (PTU) is used if the patient has sensitivity reactions to carbimazole; they act by interfering with thyroid hormone synthesis (inhibiting oxidative binding of iodide and its coupling to thyroxine residues).
(iii)
Thionamides are preferred over RAI and surgery in uncomplicated hyperthyroidism because they do not destroy the gland and control the disease until remission; carbimazole is started at 15 to 40 mg/day orally, as a single daily dose or in divided doses, until euthyroid (usually 4 to 8 weeks), then reduced gradually to a maintenance dose of 5 to 15 mg; treat for a minimum of 12 to 18 months to increase remission rate; carbimazole is 10 times more potent than PTU (100 mg PTU = 10 mg carbimazole).
(iv)
Propranolol 20 to 40 mg orally every 6 or 8 hours relieves symptoms (it does not affect the underlying disease and is only an adjunct); diltiazem is a useful alternative when β-blockers are contraindicated (for example in asthma).
(v)
Monitor thyroid function and clinical response; the best predictor of remission is reduction of goitre size to normal (euthyroid) during therapy; if symptoms do not resolve, consider non-compliance, insufficient dosage or inadequate dosing interval.
(vi)
Pruritic maculopapular rash (1 to 5% of patients; it may disappear spontaneously or another thionamide can be substituted because cross-sensitivity does not seem to exist); carbimazole may also cause GI and taste disturbances, headache, fever, malaise, alopecia and bone marrow suppression; hepatocellular damage is most prevalent with PTU and obstructive jaundice with carbimazole.
(vii)
PTU is the thionamide of choice in pregnancy and lactation, and RAI is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta and destroys the fetal thyroid.
(viii)
Counsel her to report immediately sore throat, mouth ulcers, fever, malaise or other non-specific illness, and not to stop the drug abruptly (abrupt discontinuation of antithyroid medication can precipitate thyroid storm); if thionamides fail or cause toxicity, RAI (iodine-131, half-life 8 days; main complication hypothyroidism, commonest in the first year) or thyroidectomy (hypothyroidism within 6 months to 3 years) are options.
questions.question:
TY, a 25-year-old woman, presents with palpitations that have become almost daily over the past week, a fine tremor for about 3 weeks, loose stools, a 5-kg weight loss over 6 months despite good appetite, heat intolerance, heavy sweating, hair loss and irritability. Her mother and aunt had Graves' disease. Pulse is 120 bpm, temperature 38.1 °C, weight 48 kg; total T4 is 24 mcg/dL, total T3 550, TSH 0.02 mIU/L and free thyroxine index 28.7. She takes drospirenone (ethylestradiol) daily and smokes.
(i) Identify the condition and its most likely form, citing the findings that support it.
(ii) Select drug therapy and justify the choice.
(iii) State the dose, route and duration, and the expected time to the euthyroid state.
(iv) State the adjunct for symptom control, with dose and a alternative if it is contraindicated.
(v) State the monitoring parameters and the best predictor of remission.
(vi) State the key adverse effects of the selected drug.
(vii) State the special precautions.
(viii) State the counselling points and the options if drug therapy fails.

A. Describe thyrotoxicosis under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) aetiology and forms; (iii) pathophysiology; (iv) clinical presentation; (v) diagnosis.
B. (i) State the treatment goals; (ii) state the factors that guide the choice of treatment; (iii) describe the pharmacotherapy (thionamides, adjuncts, iodides, lithium); (iv) give the rationale for radioactive iodine and surgery.
C. Distinguish between: (i) carbimazole and propylthiouracil; (ii) thionamide therapy and radioactive iodine; (iii) radioactive iodine and thyroidectomy in their main complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism) is a syndrome of increased metabolism of all body systems from excessive quantities of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4).
A(ii)
