Major forms are Graves' disease (toxic diffuse goitre, the commonest, with female predominance 1:5, peak onset 30 to 40 years and strong familial predisposition), toxic nodules (single or multinodular) and Jod-Basedow (iodine-induced) disease; rare causes are factitious hyperthyroidism, tumours secreting thyroid-stimulating substance, subacute thyroiditis, Hashitoxicosis and T3 toxicosis.
A(iii)
Hormone synthesis is regulated by negative feedback between the gland and the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (low hormone releases TRF and TSH, raising iodide trapping and synthesis; high hormone shuts off TRF, TSH and synthesis); loss of this feedback can cause hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.
A(iv)
Heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, sweating, thin fine hair, eye prominence and lid retraction, soft diffuse goitre, palpitations with raised pulse and systolic pressure, diarrhoea, amenorrhoea, warm moist skin, tremor, weakness, nervousness, irritability and insomnia; Graves' triad is thyrotoxicosis, diffuse goitre and infiltrative ophthalmopathy and dermopathy.
A(v)
Diagnosis rests on history, thyroid examination, medication history and thyroid function tests: circulating T3 and T4, radioactive iodine uptake (adjunct only), serum TSH and the TRH stimulation test (when other indices are not confirmatory), and autoimmunity tests (antithyroglobulin and antimicrosomal antibodies in Graves' or Hashimoto's disease).
B(i)
The carbimazole dose is continued until the patient is euthyroid and the disease is controlled until remission occurs.
B(ii)
Treatment must be individualised according to the type of hyperthyroidism, patient age, severity, thyroid and non-thyroid complications, and social and economic issues; the major modalities are thionamides, radioactive iodine and surgery.
B(iii)
Carbimazole 15 to 40 mg/day (maintenance 5 to 15 mg) or PTU for 12 to 18 months; propranolol 20 to 40 mg every 6 or 8 hours as adjunct (diltiazem if β-blockers are contraindicated); iodides (Lugol's solution) give rapid relief in 2 to 7 days but are not for use before RAI; lithium 800 to 1200 mg/day is reserved for when iodides and β-blockers are contraindicated.
B(iv)
RAI is indicated in adults with prior thyroid surgery, poor surgical risk, Graves' ophthalmopathy, or thionamide failure or toxicity, and is the choice in elderly cardiac patients and toxic multinodular goitre; thyroidectomy suits patients in whom RAI or thionamides are contraindicated, large goitres with disfigurement or respiratory or swallowing difficulty, suspected malignancy and selected pregnant and paediatric patients.
C(i)
Carbimazole is the most commonly used thionamide and is 10 times more potent than PTU (10 mg carbimazole = 100 mg PTU); PTU is used if carbimazole sensitivity occurs and is the thionamide of choice in pregnancy and lactation; hepatocellular damage is most prevalent with PTU and obstructive jaundice with carbimazole.
C(ii)
Thionamides inhibit hormone synthesis, do not destroy the gland and control disease until remission (preferred in uncomplicated cases), whereas RAI (iodine-131, half-life 8 days, deep to 2 mm) destroys thyroid tissue, is effective, quick and painless, and is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
C(iii)
The major complication of both RAI and thyroidectomy is hypothyroidism: with RAI it is commonest in the first year and carcinogenesis and genetic damage are the major concerns; after thyroidectomy it occurs in the first 6 months to 3 years, is inversely related to the remnant of thyroid tissue left, and surgery also carries expense, hospitalisation, anaesthesia and post-operative risks.

A(i)
TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, certolizumab, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab) are used in rheumatoid arthritis when disease activity remains moderate or high despite conventional DMARD therapy.
A(ii)
Selection of a particular TNF inhibitor depends on cost and patient preference for route and frequency of administration.
A(iii)
Biologic agents are genetically engineered proteins; it may take several weeks for clinical benefit and up to 3 months for full benefit.
A(iv)
They block the proinflammatory cytokine TNF-α.
A(v)
They increase the risk of serious infection and malignancies (lymphoma, skin cancers), may cause new-onset or worsening heart failure, and have been associated with new-onset or exacerbation of demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis; they are considerably more expensive than conventional DMARDs.
A(vi)
They should not be used in moderate-to-severe heart failure (NYHA class III or IV); live vaccines should not be given; patients should report infection or planned major surgery, and treatment may be held until post-surgical healing or resolution of infection.
A(vii)
They can be used with conventional DMARDs; in patients on TNF inhibitor monotherapy with moderate or high disease activity, one or two conventional DMARDs can be added; multiple biologics should not be used together because of additive immunosuppression.
A(viii)
Obtain a tuberculin skin test or IGRA blood test before starting to detect latent or active tuberculosis and screen for hepatitis B (reactivation risk).
B(i)
They are added when conventional DMARDs fail to achieve adequate control, in patients with moderate or high disease activity, either as monotherapy or with conventional DMARDs.
B(ii)
If switching from one biologic to another, the new agent should be started when the patient is due for a dose of the previous biologic; dual biologic therapy should be avoided because of infection risk.
C(i)
Toxicity stems from immunosuppression (infection, TB and hepatitis B reactivation, malignancy), effects on cardiac function in heart failure and demyelinating disease.
C(ii)
If activity remains moderate or high on a TNF inhibitor, a non-TNF biologic can replace it (recommended over a JAK inhibitor), or the therapy can be switched to another non-TNF biologic; a JAK inhibitor may be started if activity persists despite multiple TNF inhibitors and non-TNF biologics are not an option; a glucocorticoid can be added for flares.
questions.question:
A. Describe the TNF-α inhibitors clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) interactions; (viii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for their selection in rheumatoid arthritis; (ii) state the rationale for dose timing when switching and for avoiding combinations.
C. (i) Explain the basis of their toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of therapeutic failure and the next options.

A. Describe methotrexate clinically under the following headings: (i) indications; (ii) dose and route; (iii) pharmacokinetics; (iv) mechanism of action; (v) adverse effects; (vi) contraindications and precautions; (vii) monitoring.
B. (i) State the rationale for selecting methotrexate and for changing its route; (ii) state the rationale for adding folic acid and for dose reduction.
C. (i) Explain the basis of methotrexate toxicity; (ii) explain the basis of therapeutic failure and how it is managed.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Methotrexate is the preferred conventional DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis unless contraindicated, started irrespective of disease activity in treatment-naive patients.
A(ii)
It may be given orally, subcutaneously or intramuscularly; oral doses above 15 mg weekly may add no clinical benefit and a switch to SC may increase bioavailability and benefit.
A(iii)
Injectable (SC or IM) methotrexate has higher bioavailability than oral; excretion is reduced in renal impairment; clinical benefit is seen 3 to 6 weeks after starting.
A(iv)
It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, thereby inhibiting DNA synthesis and repair and cellular replication.
A(v)
It has numerous adverse effects, including GI side effects (less with the injectable form).
A(vi)
It is teratogenic (contraception is needed and the drug stopped if conception is planned) and contraindicated in pregnant and nursing women, chronic liver disease, immunodeficiency and pre-existing haematological disorders (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia); renal impairment may require dose reduction or discontinuation.
A(vii)
Clinical response (3 to 6 weeks), renal function (excretion falls in impairment) and screening for contraindications are indicated.
B(i)
Guidelines recommend a conventional DMARD first and prefer methotrexate; in early RA with low disease activity DMARD monotherapy is used, and injectable methotrexate is better tolerated with higher bioavailability and superior efficacy, so changing to SC is a response to oral doses above 15 mg weekly.
B(ii)
Folic acid 1 to 5 mg/day may reduce some adverse effects without loss of efficacy; renal impairment reduces excretion so the dose may need to be reduced or the drug discontinued in some cases.
C(i)
Toxicity arises from interference with DNA synthesis and cellular replication (haematological effects) and teratogenicity, and from reduced renal excretion in renal impairment.
C(ii)
If disease activity stays moderate or high on monotherapy, add or switch to combination conventional DMARDs, a biologic DMARD or a JAK inhibitor; DMARDs take weeks to months, so NSAIDs, glucocorticoids (low-dose prednisone 10 mg/day or less, for the shortest time) and acetaminophen provide bridging.

questions.question:
A. Describe the acute complications of diabetes mellitus under the following headings: (i) definition; (ii) aetiology and risk factors; (iii) pathophysiology; (iv) clinical presentation; (v) diagnosis.
B. (i) State the treatment goals; (ii) state the non-pharmacological and preventive management; (iii) describe the treatment of each complication; (iv) give the rationale for each.
C. Distinguish between: (i) diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar non-ketotic syndrome; (ii) initial and advanced hypoglycaemic symptoms; (iii) micro-vascular and macro-vascular complications in their response to glucose control.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Acute complications are short-term complications from sustained blood glucose elevation or its treatment: diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar non-ketotic syndrome (HHNKS) and hypoglycaemia (FBG below 40 mg/dL).
A(ii)
DKA occurs with absolute or relative lack of insulin or elevated counter-regulatory hormones, mostly in poorly controlled type 1 (risk factors: extremes of age, poor control, poor socioeconomic status, non-adherence; type 2 with stress, infection, non-compliance); HHNKS occurs in non-adherent, dehydrated or stressed type 2 patients or those on steroids; hypoglycaemia follows excess antidiabetic drugs, missed or delayed meals, extra exercise or alcohol.
A(iii)
DKA: uncontrolled hyperglycaemia builds up acidic ketones in blood secondary to insulin deficit; HHNKS: severe hyperglycaemia, dehydration and hyperosmolarity without severe ketosis; hypoglycaemia: abnormally low glucose.
A(iv)
DKA: nausea, vomiting, polydipsia, polyuria, abdominal pain, visual disturbance, somnolence, tachycardia, postural hypotension, dehydration, hyperpnoea, fruity ketone smell, coma; HHNKS: dehydration, lethargy, confusion, convulsion, coma and stroke-like deficits with slow onset; hypoglycaemia: sweating, tremor, hunger, mood change, then confusion, poor coordination, headache, double vision.
A(v)
Hypoglycaemia is defined as FBG below 40 mg/dL, and treatment requires frequent assessment of vital signs, fluid balance and serum electrolytes.
B(i)
Prevent short-term complications (hypoglycaemia, DKA/HHNKS), eliminate symptoms and prevent long-term complications.
B(ii)
Hypoglycaemia is largely prevented by taking antidiabetes medication properly, eating regular meals and regular glucose checks; patients should know how to cope with emergencies (illness, hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemic crisis); alcohol should be avoided because it raises hypoglycaemia risk.
B(iii)
DKA: fluid and electrolyte replacement, IV regular insulin, potassium and phosphate replacement and plasma bicarbonate; hypoglycaemia: 15 g carbohydrate if conscious, then long-acting carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes (repeat if below 70 mg/dL or symptomatic), glucagon 1 mg SC or IM if unconscious.
B(iv)
Close monitoring is needed because DKA is life-threatening; repeated hypoglycaemia calls for a search for causes and insulin dose adjustment.
C(i)
DKA is common in type 1 diabetes and involves ketosis and acidosis; HHNKS is typical of type 2, has slow subtle onset and hyperosmolarity without severe ketosis.
C(ii)
Initial symptoms are sweating, tremulousness, nausea and vomiting, dizziness, mood change, hunger and weakness; intermediate and advanced symptoms are confusion, poor coordination, headache and double vision.
C(iii)
Micro-vascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) can be prevented by intensive glucose control, which may not reverse them once established; macro-vascular disease (coronary, cerebrovascular, peripheral arterial) is not effectively prevented by glucose control alone.

questions.question:
A teenager attends a community pharmacy with nasal itch, paroxysmal sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea and nasal congestion, with ocular irritation; symptoms are worse in the morning and evening and in hot, humid weather, and there is a family history of atopy.
(i) Identify the patient's needs and the likely diagnosis and classification.
(ii) State the pharmacist's interventions in reaching a differential diagnosis.
(iii) State the treatment approach available in the pharmacy.
(iv) State the counselling on prevention and non-drug measures.
(v) State follow-up and referral criteria.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Likely intermittent allergic rhinitis (hay fever), inflammation of the nasal lining with the four classical symptoms of itch, paroxysmal sneeze, watery rhinorrhoea and congestion, possibly with allergic conjunctivitis; ARIA classifies it as intermittent (fewer than 4 days per week and fewer than 4 weeks) or persistent, each mild or moderate-severe; it commonly affects school-aged children, with mean onset about 10 years and peak incidence at 13 to 19 years.
(ii)
Diagnosis depends on family history of atopy, clinical symptoms and when they worsen; symptom-specific questions help establish a differential diagnosis, and conditions such as viral infection or colds must be eliminated; the underlying mechanism is allergen activation of IgE on mast cells releasing histamine, leukotrienes, kinins and prostaglandins, with an early-phase reaction and a late-phase reaction 4 to 12 hours later (mainly congestion).
(iii)
Management falls broadly into systemic and topical categories and most sufferers can be managed in the pharmacy.
(iv)
Prevent by avoiding allergens (pollen, dust, pet dander), good hygiene such as regular handwashing, proper ventilation and air purification, smoking cessation and limiting pollutants, and regular exercise and a balanced diet to support immune function.
(v)
Consultation with a healthcare professional gives personalised preventive advice; nasal priming explains why symptoms worsen the longer the season goes on.

questions.question: Toluidine blue is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Toluidine blue is a basic (cationic) dye that binds to acidic tissue components like glycosaminoglycans. Its positive charge enables electrostatic attraction to negatively charged cellular structures. This basic nature makes it ideal for staining acidic mucopolysaccharides.

questions.question: How many total chains per hemoglobin molecule?
questions.explanation: A complete hemoglobin molecule contains four globin chains total (a tetramer). The typical combination is two alpha and two non-alpha chains. Each chain carries one heme group for a total of four oxygen-binding sites.

questions.question: What is the primary indication for volume-reduced platelets
questions.explanation: Volume-reduced platelets prevent hemolytic reactions by removing ABO-incompatible plasma. This also prevents volume overload in at-risk patients. The procedure concentrates platelets while removing most supernatant plasma.

questions.question: What phenomenon do all Rh antibodies except anti-D characteristically display?
questions.explanation: All Rh antibodies except anti-D display dosage effect, meaning they react more strongly with red cells homozygous for an antigen (e.g., EE) than with cells heterozygous for that antigen (e.g., Ee). This phenomenon occurs because homozygous cells express more antigen sites than heterozygous cells. Anti-D does not show dosage because the d antigen is an amorph with no corresponding antigenic product.

questions.question: The importance of maintaining proper pH buffer in Romanowsky staining is to:
questions.explanation: Proper pH buffer is essential for maintaining the characteristic dye colors and their binding properties in Romanowsky staining. pH alterations change the ionization states of both acidic and basic dye components, affecting color development. Buffer maintenance ensures reproducible and diagnostic staining quality across specimens.

options: Any antibody detected in patient serum
Antibodies causing decreased RBC survival, HTR, or HDFN
questions.question: What defines a clinically significant antibody in transfusion medicine?
questions.explanation: Clinically significant antibodies are those associated with decreased red blood cell survival, causing hemolytic transfusion reactions (HTR) and/or hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN). These antibodies are usually IgG class, react best at 37 C and the antiglobulin phase (IAT), and can cause red cell destruction in vivo. Not clinically significant antibodies do not cause red cell destruction despite being detectable in testing.

questions.question: Which growth factors besides TPO support megakaryopoiesis?
questions.explanation: SCF, GM-CSF, IL-1, IL-3, IL-6, and IL-11 support megakaryopoiesis synergizing with thrombopoietin. These factors promote progenitor proliferation and precursor maturation. Multiple growth factor interactions ensure adequate platelet production under various physiological conditions.

questions.question: At what temperature range must whole blood be stored
questions.explanation: Whole blood storage at 1-6 degrees C preserves red cell viability while slowing metabolic processes. However, this cold temperature irreversibly damages platelet function. Coagulation factors, particularly factors V and VIII, also deteriorate progressively during refrigerated storage.

Monocytes measure 12-20 micrometers in diameter, making them the largest circulating leukocytes. Their size accommodates abundant cytoplasm containing lysosomes and an indented kidney-shaped nucleus. This large size reflects their role as precursors to tissue macrophages.

How many times greater is haemoglobin's affinity for carbon monoxide compared to oxygen?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin's affinity for carbon monoxide exceeds that for oxygen by approximately 200-fold, causing carboxyhaemoglobin formation even at low CO concentrations. This competitive binding explains carbon monoxide poisoning severity and its cherry-red appearance. The binding is reversible but requires high oxygen concentrations for displacement.

Thrombopoietin levels are inversely regulated by platelet mass through receptor-mediated clearance. Platelets express TPO receptors that bind and remove circulating TPO. When platelet counts fall, less TPO is cleared, allowing levels to rise and stimulate megakaryopoiesis in a negative feedback loop.

questions.question: What is the fundamental characteristic that distinguishes the ABO blood group system from other blood group systems?
questions.explanation: The ABO system is unique because individuals naturally possess antibodies (anti-A and/or anti-B) in their serum against the antigens they lack on their red cells, without prior sensitization. This naturally occurring antibody production begins around 3-6 months after birth and distinguishes ABO from other blood group systems. These antibodies are responsible for making ABO incompatibility the leading cause of fatal hemolytic transfusion reactions.

questions.explanation: Bernstein's laws of heredity for ABO state that a parent of group AB cannot produce an offspring of group O, and conversely, a parent of group O cannot give rise to a child of group AB. This is because AB individuals must pass either an A or B gene to offspring, never O, while O individuals can only pass O genes. Offspring can only possess A or B antigens inherited from one or both parents, never de novo.

LAP stain helps differentiate CML from other:
questions.explanation: LAP staining distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders like polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia. Different myeloproliferative conditions show varying LAP scores, aiding classification. The enzyme pattern provides functional characterization beyond morphological assessment.

Excessive RBC destruction in hemolytic conditions produces more bilirubin than the liver can conjugate and excrete. This causes unconjugated bilirubin accumulation in blood. The yellow pigment deposits in tissues causing jaundice.
questions.question: What causes jaundice in hemolytic conditions?
options: Excessive RBC destruction producing more bilirubin than liver can process

questions.explanation: Normal white blood cell count ranges from 4,000 to 11,000 cells per microliter of blood. Counts above this range indicate leukocytosis, while counts below indicate leukopenia. These parameters help assess immune system status and detect infections or haematological disorders.
questions.question: What is the normal white blood cell count range per microliter?
What enzyme catalyzes uroporphyrinogen III conversion to coproporphyrinogen III?
questions.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase removes acetate side chains through decarboxylation, converting uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III in the cytoplasm. This enzyme deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda. The modification prepares the molecule for mitochondrial re-entry.

The Le (FUT3), Se (FUT2), and H (FUT1) genes are all located on chromosome 19, with Le and Se being closely linked. The ABO genes are located separately on chromosome 9. This chromosomal linkage explains the genetic relationship between Lewis and secretor phenotypes, as these genes are often inherited together and their products interact to determine the final Lewis antigens expressed.
questions.question: On which chromosome are the Lewis (Le), Secretor (Se), and H genes located?
On which non-erythroid cells are Duffy antigens also expressed?
options: Endothelial and epithelial cells of various organs
questions.explanation: Fya and Fyb antigens are present on both erythroid and non-erythroid cells, including endothelial cells and epithelial cells in various organs such as brain, kidneys, spleen, heart, lungs, pancreas, and placenta. This widespread tissue expression of DARC reflects its role in chemokine regulation and inflammatory responses beyond red blood cells. The presence on endothelial cells particularly suggests involvement in leukocyte trafficking and vascular inflammation.

questions.question: The basic component of Romanowsky stains that binds to acidic nuclei is:
questions.explanation: Azure dyes are basic components that specifically bind to acidic structures like nuclei, producing blue-purple coloration. This electrostatic attraction between basic dyes and acidic nucleoproteins is fundamental to Romanowsky staining mechanism. The azure-nucleic acid interaction enables clear visualization of nuclear chromatin patterns.

questions.question: Which extracellular matrix component is secreted by bone marrow stromal cells?
questions.explanation: Stromal cells secrete fibronectin along with collagen, thrombospondin, hyaluronic acid, and chondroitin derivatives forming the extracellular matrix. This matrix provides structural support and creates microenvironmental niches where stem and progenitor cells reside. The ECM also binds and presents growth factors to haematopoietic cells in locally high concentrations.

questions.question: What is the molecular weight of haemoglobin in Daltons?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is a chromoprotein with a precise molecular weight of 64,458 Daltons. This molecular weight reflects its complex quaternary structure consisting of four globin chains and four haem groups. The specific molecular weight is important for calculating oxygen-carrying capacity and understanding haemoglobin concentration measurements.

TGF-beta supports plasma cell development, germinal center formation, and regulates B cell proliferation. It has context-dependent effects promoting or inhibiting B cell responses depending on activation state. TGF-beta also influences immunoglobulin class switching.
options: Plasma cell development and germinal center regulation
questions.question: What role does TGF-beta play in B lymphocyte development?

questions.explanation: Pronormoblast is the first morphologically identifiable erythroid cell measuring 12-20 micrometers with deep blue cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. It arises from CFU-E progenitors activated by erythropoietin and begins the sequence of normoblastic maturation. Before the pronormoblast stage, committed erythroid progenitors are morphologically indistinguishable from other progenitors.
questions.question: Which cell represents the earliest morphologically recognizable erythroid precursor in bone marrow?

questions.explanation: The nucleus is lost in mammalian red blood cells through pyknosis (nuclear condensation and extrusion). This process occurs during RBC maturation in bone marrow. Birds and other species retain their RBC nuclei.
questions.question: What happens to the nucleus in mammalian RBCs?
What is the normal lifespan of human red blood cells?
questions.explanation: Normal human erythrocytes survive approximately 120 days in circulation before senescence signals trigger macrophage recognition and phagocytosis. This lifespan reflects accumulated oxidative damage and metabolic decline. Shortened survival characterizes hemolytic anaemias while prolonged survival rarely occurs.

questions.question: What is considered universal donor plasma for emergency situations
questions.explanation: Group AB plasma is universal donor plasma because it lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies. It can be given to any ABO group in emergencies. This is opposite to red cell transfusion where O is universal.

questions.question: What distinguishes precursor cells from progenitor cells morphologically?
questions.explanation: Precursor cells (blasts) display morphologically recognizable features indicating their lineage, while progenitors remain indistinguishable from stem cells. Myeloblasts, lymphoblasts, erythroblasts, and megakaryoblasts can be identified microscopically. This morphological distinction marks the transition to committed differentiation.

questions.question: Which antibody is sometimes associated with infectious mononucleosis?
questions.explanation: Anti-i antibodies are rare and sometimes associated with infectious mononucleosis (caused by Epstein-Barr virus). These antibodies react with the linear i antigen that predominates on cord cells and is present in small amounts on adult cells. Unlike anti-I which is common, anti-i is clinically unusual and its presence may prompt investigation for underlying infectious mononucleosis or lymphoproliferative disorders.

questions.question: The unique ability of Romanowsky stains to produce various hues is called:
questions.explanation: Metachromasia, also known as the Romanowsky effect, describes the ability to produce multiple color shades from a single stain mixture. This phenomenon enables differentiation of various cellular components through distinct color patterns. The metachromatic property is what makes Romanowsky stains uniquely valuable for blood cell identification.

Blood group O individuals have both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in their serum. This is because they lack both A and B antigens on their RBCs. Having both antibodies makes group O the universal donor for RBCs but limits compatible plasma.
questions.question: Which antibodies are found in blood group O individuals?
What happens when haematopoietic growth factor receptors dimerize?
questions.explanation: Receptor dimerization activates associated tyrosine kinase domains initiating phosphorylation cascades. These kinases phosphorylate intracellular signaling proteins including STATs, MAPKs, and PI3K pathway components. The cascade transmits signals to the nucleus changing gene expression.

questions.question: How many functional globin genes do humans normally carry?
questions.explanation: Humans possess 8 functional globin genes arranged in two clusters: the β-like cluster on chromosome 11 and the α-like cluster on chromosome 16. These genes code for six different globin chains (α, β, γ, δ, ε, ζ). Proper gene expression ensures appropriate haemoglobin production throughout development.

Rh antibodies rarely bind complement, so RBC destruction occurs via macrophages in the spleen causing extravascular hemolysis. The antibody-coated cells are recognized and phagocytosed by splenic macrophages. This process is slower than complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.
questions.question: How do Rh antibodies primarily cause RBC destruction?
Within what time period should alkaline haematin matching be completed after boiling?
questions.explanation: Alkaline haematin colour comparison must be completed within 30 minutes following boiling to ensure accurate results before colour degradation occurs. Extended delays produce falsely low readings due to colour fading. Timely measurement maintains consistency and reliability in haemoglobin determination.

questions.question: What happens to globin after red cell phagocytosis?
questions.explanation: Globin chains are degraded to constituent amino acids that re-enter the body's amino acid pool for protein synthesis. This recycling conserves valuable amino acids. Meanwhile, haem undergoes separate catabolism to bilirubin with iron recovery and recycling.

questions.question: What blood volume is added to Drabkin's solution in cyanmethaemoglobin method?
questions.explanation: Twenty microliters of well-mixed anticoagulated venous blood is added to Drabkin's reagent, requiring careful pipetting technique for accuracy. The pipette must be rinsed with reagent to ensure complete blood transfer. Pipetting errors directly affect final haemoglobin concentration calculations.

questions.question: What percentage of methaemoglobin is considered normal in blood?
questions.explanation: Normal methaemoglobin concentration ranges from 1-2% of total haemoglobin, representing oxidized iron in the ferric state. This form cannot reversibly bind oxygen and appears dark brown in colour. Higher concentrations cause clinical methemoglobinemia requiring intervention.

Primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus) support antigen-independent lymphocyte development and maturation. Secondary lymphoid organs (spleen, lymph nodes) provide sites for antigen-dependent activation and immune responses. This division of labor optimizes lymphocyte development and function.
questions.question: What distinguishes primary from secondary lymphoid organs?

questions.explanation: The majority of Rh antibodies are of the IgG type, which can cross the placenta. This characteristic makes Rh antibodies particularly significant in hemolytic disease of the newborn. IgG antibodies also persist longer than IgM antibodies.
questions.question: What is the typical immunoglobulin class of Rh antibodies?

options: Blood density proportional to haemoglobin content
questions.question: What principle underlies the copper sulphate specific gravity method?
questions.explanation: Specific gravity method assumes blood density correlates directly with haemoglobin concentration since haemoglobin represents the largest single blood constituent. When blood drops into copper sulphate solutions, sinking or floating indicates density relative to solution. This principle allows rapid haemoglobin screening despite limited accuracy.

questions.question: Which interleukin combination helps derive T lymphocytes from precursor cells?
questions.explanation: IL-1, IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, and IL-9 support T lymphocyte derivation from precursor lymphoid cells in marrow. These interleukins promote T cell lineage commitment, proliferation, and survival. IL-7 is particularly critical for T cell development and homeostasis.

Electronic tube sealers create hermetic seals in blood bag tubing, maintaining sterile closed systems. This prevents contamination during component separation. Closed systems extend component shelf life compared to open systems.
questions.question: What is the purpose of an electronic tube sealer in component preparation
How severe is hemolytic disease of the newborn in ABO incompatibility?
questions.explanation: Hemolytic disease of the newborn is always a mild condition when due to ABO incompatibility. This is because ABO antibodies are IgM and don't cross the placenta readily. When IgG ABO antibodies do form, they cause less severe hemolysis than Rh antibodies.

questions.question: What triggers initial B cell activation at secondary lymphoid organs?
questions.explanation: B cell activation begins when surface BCR binds cognate antigen at secondary lymphoid organs. This binding triggers intracellular signaling cascades and receptor clustering. Additional signals from T helper cells and cytokines complete the activation process.

questions.question: Which combination forms the basis of Romanowsky stains?
questions.explanation: Romanowsky stains are composed of oxidized methylene blue (azure) dyes combined with eosin Y as the neutral stain mixture. This specific combination creates the characteristic polychromatic effect essential for blood cell differentiation. The azure-eosin interaction produces the distinctive color patterns that identify various cellular components.

Drabkin's reagent requires storage at room temperature in brown borosilicate glass bottles protected from direct sunlight to prevent photodegradation and ferricyanide reduction. Freezing causes decolorization and loss of activity. Proper storage maintains reagent stability for extended periods.
options: Room temperature in brown borosilicate glass
questions.question: How should Drabkin's reagent be stored to maintain stability?

questions.explanation: Reticulocytes appear polychromatic (gray-blue) with Romanowsky stains because they contain both residual RNA (basophilic) and hemoglobin (acidophilic). This mixed staining distinguishes them from mature pink erythrocytes. The term polychromatophilic erythrocyte refers to reticulocytes in blood films.
options: Mixture of residual RNA and accumulated hemoglobin
questions.question: What causes the polychromatic appearance of reticulocytes with Romanowsky staining?

options: Clerical error with ABO incompatible blood
questions.explanation: Clerical errors leading to transfusion of ABO incompatible blood remain the most common cause of transfusion-related deaths. These errors occur despite established safety protocols and checking procedures. The immediate hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility can be rapidly fatal.
questions.question: What is the most common cause of death from blood transfusion?
What quality control measure involves running known value samples?
questions.explanation: Running haemolysates with predetermined haemoglobin values alongside test samples provides ongoing quality control, detecting systematic errors, reagent deterioration, or instrument malfunction. Control values must fall within acceptable ranges for result validation. Regular control testing ensures consistent measurement accuracy.

questions.question: After Kleihauer-Betke staining, cells containing HbA appear:
questions.explanation: Erythrocytes containing adult hemoglobin (HbA) appear unstained as ghost cells after acid treatment in Kleihauer-Betke staining. The acidic buffer dissolves HbA, leaving only the red cell membrane visible. This creates stark contrast with HbF-containing cells that retain their hemoglobin.

Adult monocyte counts normally range from 0.2 to 0.8 x 10^9/L, representing absolute numbers rather than percentages. Children have higher counts ranging from 0.6 to 1.5 x 10^9/L reflecting more active immune development. These reference ranges help detect monocyte disorders.
questions.question: What is the normal monocyte count in adult blood?

questions.explanation: McLeod syndrome results from absence of the Kx protein (encoded by XK1 gene on the X chromosome), which causes marked reduction of Kell antigens on red cells. This X-linked condition occurs almost exclusively in males and is associated with morphologic and functional red cell abnormalities including acanthocytes (spur cells), decreased deformability, and reduced red cell survival. It is also associated with chronic granulomatous disease.
options: Complete absence of all Kell antigens
Enhanced expression of all Kell antigens
Normal Kell antigens with absent Kx
Marked reduction of Kell antigens due to absent Kx protein
questions.question: What characterizes McLeod syndrome regarding Kell antigen expression?

questions.explanation: Alkaline haematin method requires boiling the blood-alkali mixture for exactly 4 minutes to ensure complete haemoglobin denaturation. The standard solution must be boiled simultaneously for accurate comparison. Insufficient boiling produces incomplete conversion while excessive heating may alter colour intensity.
questions.question: How long must the alkaline haematin solution be boiled?

questions.explanation: Sahli's method converts haemoglobin to acid haematin using N/10 hydrochloric acid, producing a brown colour compared against standard glass blocks. The intensity correlates directly with haemoglobin concentration. This technique, while outdated, provided foundational understanding for modern spectrophotometric methods.
questions.question: What is the principle of Sahli's haemoglobin estimation method?
What factor distinguishes T cell-dependent from T cell-independent B cell activation?
options: Requirement for T helper cell interaction
questions.explanation: T cell-dependent activation requires direct interaction between B cells and cognate T helper cells providing essential co-stimulatory signals. T cell-independent activation occurs without T cell help, typically in response to polysaccharide antigens. T-dependent responses generate higher affinity antibodies and memory.

Mature megakaryocytes show 2N to 16N ploidy, with most cells being 8N or 16N. Higher ploidy correlates with larger cell size and greater platelet production capacity. Thrombopoietin regulates both ploidy level and megakaryocyte number.
questions.question: What ploidy range characterizes mature megakaryocytes?
Which haemoglobin derivative is NOT converted to cyanmethaemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Sulphaemoglobin remains the only haemoglobin derivative not converted to cyanmethaemoglobin, representing a minor limitation since sulphaemoglobin rarely exceeds 1% of total haemoglobin. All other major derivatives undergo complete conversion. This comprehensive conversion capability makes the method highly reliable.

Duffy antigens (Fya and Fyb) and MNSs antigens (M, N, S, s) are destroyed by proteolytic enzyme treatment because these antigens are located on glycophorins which are cleaved by enzymes. This enzyme sensitivity is diagnostically valuable: antibodies to these antigens will not react with enzyme-treated cells, helping distinguish them from antibodies to enzyme-resistant or enzyme-enhanced antigens like Rh, Kidd, and Lewis.
options: Duffy (Fya, Fyb), M, N, S, s
questions.question: Which blood group antibodies are characteristically destroyed by enzyme treatment?

questions.explanation: Growth factor binding induces receptor dimerization bringing together intracellular domains that activate tyrosine kinase signaling. This dimerization initiates a cascade of phosphorylation events transmitting signals to the nucleus. The biochemical cascade ultimately changes gene expression patterns controlling cell fate decisions.
questions.question: What molecular event occurs immediately after growth factor binding to its receptor?

questions.explanation: Direct spectrometry dilutes blood 1:250 with cyanide-ferricyanide reagent, measuring absorbance at 540 nm against properly calibrated spectrophotometers without requiring standards. The calculation incorporates haemoglobin's molecular weight and extinction coefficient. Instrument calibration accuracy is critical for reliable results.
questions.question: What dilution factor is used in direct spectrometry without standards?
What explains the mild nature of ABO HDN compared to Rh HDN?
options: ABO antigens weaker than Rh antigens
ABO antibodies mainly IgM which don't cross placenta readily
questions.explanation: ABO antibodies are mainly IgM class which cannot readily cross the placenta due to large size. When IgG ABO antibodies do form and cross, they cause milder hemolysis. Additionally, fetal ABO antigen expression is weaker than in adults.

questions.question: PAS staining is most useful in diagnosing which type of leukemia?
questions.explanation: PAS staining provides valuable diagnostic information in acute lymphoblastic leukemia where lymphoblasts show characteristic block positivity. This staining pattern, combined with morphology and other markers, aids in leukemia classification. PAS positivity helps distinguish ALL from acute myeloid leukemias.

T2 transitional B cells differentiate into follicular (FO) B cells or marginal zone (MZ) B cells depending on signals received. FO B cells recirculate through blood and lymphoid organs, while MZ B cells remain in the splenic marginal zone. These subsets have different functional characteristics and antigen responses.
questions.question: What B cell subsets emerge from T2 transitional B cells in the spleen?
options: Follicular and marginal zone B cells

questions.question: Leukemoid reactions show which LAP pattern?
questions.explanation: Leukemoid reactions demonstrate elevated LAP scores, contrasting sharply with the low scores in CML. This elevation reflects the reactive nature of neutrophils responding to physiological stress or infection. High LAP scores help identify benign reactive causes of leukocytosis.

The gallbladder excretes conjugated bilirubin through bile into the intestinal tract. Bile serves as the vehicle for eliminating bilirubin from the body. This excretion pathway is the primary route for bilirubin elimination.
questions.question: What organ excretes conjugated bilirubin?

questions.explanation: Myeloperoxidase staining identifies monocytic cells which show weak to moderate enzyme activity, distinguishing them from peroxidase-negative lymphocytes. The intensity of peroxidase positivity helps classify acute leukemias into myeloid and monocytic lineages. This enzyme marker complements morphological and immunophenotypic analysis.
questions.question: Monocytic leukemia can be differentiated from lymphocytic leukemia using:
How are the A and B antigens inherited relative to O?
questions.explanation: A and B antigens are inherited codominantly over O, meaning both can be expressed equally when present. This inheritance pattern explains why individuals with AB blood type express both antigens. The O allele is recessive and only expressed in the OO genotype.
options: A is dominant, B is recessive
B is dominant, A is recessive

questions.question: What filter is used for colorimetric reading in acid-alkali method?
questions.explanation: Acid-alkali method employs a yellow-green filter for photoelectric colorimetry against Gibson and Harrison's standard, matching the absorption characteristics of alkaline haematin. Filter selection optimizes sensitivity and accuracy for the measured compound. Incorrect filter wavelength produces unreliable measurements.

questions.question: What stimulates proliferation of myeloblasts, promyelocytes, and myelocytes?
questions.explanation: GM-CSF and G-CSF stimulate proliferation of myeloblasts, promyelocytes, and myelocytes during granulopoiesis. These colony-stimulating factors promote both cell division and maturation through granulocyte developmental stages. They are clinically used to accelerate neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy.

questions.question: What is thought to be the composition of the Rh complex?
questions.explanation: The Rh system complex is thought to be a tetramer consisting of four protein molecules. It contains two molecules of Rh-associated glycoprotein (RhAG) and two Rh proteins. This tetrameric structure is essential for proper expression of Rh antigens.

questions.question: What is the primary physiologic function of the Kidd blood group antigen-carrying molecule?
questions.explanation: The Kidd antigen-carrying molecule functions as the human urea transporter 11 (HUT11), serving as the primary urea transporter on red blood cells. This transporter is encoded by the SLC14A1 (Solute Carrier Family 14 Member 1) gene located on chromosome 18. The physiologic role in urea transport explains why Jk(a-b-) red cells show increased resistance to lysis in 2M urea solutions.

questions.question: What temperature range is used for thawing plasma products before transfusion
questions.explanation: Plasma thaws at 30-37 degrees C in approximately 20 minutes, preserving coagulation factor activity. Lower temperatures require excessive time while higher temperatures may denature proteins. Thawed plasma is then refrigerated if not immediately transfused.

questions.question: What is the storage temperature and maximum shelf life for cryoprecipitate
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate stores at -18 degrees C or colder for up to one year. This frozen storage maintains coagulation factor stability. Thawing at 30-37 degrees C takes approximately 15-20 minutes before transfusion.

The biconcave shape maximizes surface area to volume ratio optimizing oxygen exchange efficiency. This configuration allows rapid oxygen loading in lungs and unloading in tissues. The shape also provides deformability for squeezing through capillaries narrower than the cell diameter.
questions.question: What is the primary function of erythrocyte biconcave shape?

questions.explanation: Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetal-maternal hemorrhage by counting HbF-containing cells in maternal blood. The test determines the volume of fetal blood in maternal circulation, guiding Rh immunoglobulin dosage. This application is critical in preventing hemolytic disease of the newborn.
questions.question: Kleihauer-Betke test is clinically used to assess:
What precursor cells develop from CFU-Meg during thrombopoiesis?
questions.explanation: CFU-Meg differentiates into megakaryoblasts, the earliest morphologically recognizable megakaryocyte precursors. Megakaryoblasts mature through promegakaryocyte to megakaryocyte stages with increasing size and ploidy. This maturation sequence occurs in bone marrow near sinusoids.

questions.question: What happens to HbF levels shortly after birth?
questions.explanation: Shortly after birth (3-6 months), HbF levels fall as adult hemoglobin (HbA) production increases. This switch represents a normal developmental transition. By one year, HbA becomes the predominant hemoglobin type.

Spectrophotometric methods apply Beer-Lambert's law, stating that optical density relates directly to coloured material concentration and path length through solution. With constant 1 cm cuvette path length, absorbance varies proportionally with haemoglobin concentration. This fundamental principle enables accurate quantitative measurements.
questions.question: Which law forms the basis for spectrophotometric haemoglobin estimation?

questions.explanation: The SLAM family marker combination CD150+ CD48CD41identifies the most primitive long-term repopulating HSCs. These surface markers correlate with stem cell primitiveness and functional capacity. SLAM markers enable HSC identification and purification for research and therapy.
questions.question: Which molecular marker combination identifies the most primitive haematopoietic stem cells?

questions.explanation: Anti-Fya is approximately 20 times more common than anti-Fyb, likely due to population demographics where many individuals of African descent lack both antigens (Fy(a-b-)) and are more likely to be exposed to Fya-positive blood than Fyb-positive blood. Additionally, the relatively high frequency of Fya-positive donors increases exposure opportunities. Both antibodies are IgG, clinically significant, and stimulated by transfusion or pregnancy.
questions.question: Which antibody in the Duffy system is more commonly encountered and why?
options: Anti-Fyb because Fyb is more immunogenic
Anti-Fya because Fya is less common
Anti-Fya is 20 times more common than anti-Fyb

questions.question: What process allows B cells to change from producing IgM to other immunoglobulin classes?
questions.explanation: Class switch recombination allows activated B cells to switch from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE production while maintaining antigen specificity. This DNA rearrangement changes the constant region gene used with the same variable region. Class switching optimizes antibody effector functions.

The biconcave disc shape with thinner center and thicker rim creates central pallor visible microscopically. This shape maximizes surface area to volume ratio enhancing gas exchange efficiency. The biconcave configuration also provides deformability for passage through narrow capillaries.
questions.question: What structural feature creates the central pallor in mature erythrocytes?
Why should reagents and samples not be poured undiluted into sinks?
questions.explanation: Potassium cyanide in cyanmethaemoglobin reagents releases toxic hydrogen cyanide gas when acidified, posing serious safety risks if undiluted reagents contact acidic sink environments. Gas accumulation in plumbing creates explosion and inhalation hazards. Disposal protocols mandate dilution with copious running water.

Rh antigens are inherited as codominant alleles, meaning both alleles can be expressed simultaneously. Each parent contributes one Rh gene to their offspring. This inheritance pattern creates diverse Rh phenotype combinations.
questions.question: How are Rh antigens inherited?
What is the principle of the elution technique in blood banking?
questions.explanation: Elution removes antibodies bound to red blood cells (either in vivo or in vitro) so they can be tested against a panel of cells for identification. Various methods (heat, acid, organic solvents) disrupt antibody-antigen bonds without destroying antibody specificity. Eluates are crucial for identifying antibodies in cases of positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT), hemolytic transfusion reactions, HDFN, and autoimmune hemolytic anemia where antibodies coat the patient's cells.
options: Removing bound antibodies from red cells for identification

questions.explanation: Sudan Black B is a lysochrome dye that dissolves in lipids, staining lipid-containing structures black. The dye preferentially accumulates in phospholipids and neutral fats within myeloid granules. This lipid solubility principle makes it specific for lipid-rich cellular components.
questions.question: The staining principle of Sudan Black B involves:
Which antibodies are present in a group A individual?
questions.explanation: A group A individual will have anti-B antibodies in their serum against the missing B antigen. These antibodies develop naturally through environmental exposure to B-like antigens. The immune system recognizes B antigen as foreign since it's not present on their own cells.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of washing red blood cells
questions.explanation: Washing removes plasma proteins that cause severe allergic or anaphylactic reactions. This modification benefits IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA antibodies. Multiple saline washes effectively eliminate plasma while preserving red cell function.

questions.question: The major difference between Wright-Giemsa and May-Grunwald-Giemsa stains is:
questions.explanation: May-Grunwald-Giemsa stain produces more intense coloration but requires longer processing time than Wright-Giemsa stain. Both stains use similar chemical principles but differ in their practical application characteristics. The choice between them often depends on laboratory workflow requirements and desired color intensity.

AB positive individuals are considered universal recipients for red cell transfusions because they have no ABO antibodies (their cells express A and B antigens) and no anti-D (they are Rh-positive). Therefore, they can theoretically receive red cells from any ABO/Rh type. However, this doesn't account for other blood group antibodies they might possess, so compatibility testing is still essential. The universal recipient concept applies only to red cells, not to plasma or whole blood.
questions.question: What blood type is considered the "universal recipient" for red blood cell transfusions?

questions.explanation: Lymphoblasts characteristically lack myeloperoxidase enzyme, showing negative reactions in ALL. This absence of peroxidase is a defining feature distinguishing lymphoid from myeloid leukemias. Peroxidase negativity, combined with other markers, confirms lymphoblastic lineage.
questions.question: Lymphoblasts in acute lymphocytic leukemia are:

questions.explanation: Anti-D antibody causes the most severe form of hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN). It was historically a major cause of fetal death before prophylaxis became available. Anti-D remains clinically significant despite preventive measures.
questions.question: Which Rh antibody causes the most severe hemolytic disease of newborn?

questions.explanation: Proerythroblasts demonstrate granular PAS positivity reflecting glycogen distribution in early red cell precursors. This granular pattern differs from the homogenous positivity seen in more mature normoblasts. The PAS staining pattern helps identify and classify erythroblast maturation stages.
questions.question: Proerythroblasts show which type of PAS positivity?
What color does polychromatophilic normoblast cytoplasm display on Romanowsky staining?
questions.explanation: Polychromatophilic normoblast cytoplasm appears gray-blue to pink reflecting both residual RNA basophilia and accumulating hemoglobin acidophilia. This mixed staining represents the transition from RNA-rich early stages to hemoglobin-rich late stages. The nucleus becomes smaller and reddish-purple with condensing chromatin.

questions.question: What agent is commonly used during granulocyte collection to improve sedimentation
questions.explanation: Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) enhances RBC sedimentation during granulocyte apheresis, improving collection efficiency. Combined with G-CSF and corticosteroids, HES increases granulocyte yields. However, HES use has declined due to adverse effects.

HemoCue cuvettes require storage between 15-30 C in containers with desiccant to maintain reagent stability and prevent moisture absorption. Temperature excursions outside this range compromise reagent activity and measurement accuracy. Proper storage ensures reliable results throughout the cuvette shelf life.
questions.question: What temperature range must HemoCue cuvettes be stored within?
What connects the ABO system with Lewis and Hh blood groups?
questions.explanation: Some enzymes involved in earlier stages of ABO antigen synthesis are also involved in producing Hh and Lewis blood group antigens. The biosynthetic pathways share common precursor molecules and enzymes. This explains why these systems interact genetically and biochemically.
options: Enzymes overlap in antigen synthesis pathways

questions.explanation: Secretor status testing is used in forensic pathology for typing blood and semen stains at scenes of violent crime. Since approximately 80% of individuals are secretors, their ABO type can be determined from dried secretions. This can help include or exclude suspects and victims at crime scenes. Secretor testing of saliva, semen, or other body fluid stains provides valuable evidence when red blood cells are not available for typing.
options: It types blood and semen stains at crime scenes
questions.question: How can secretor status testing be useful in forensic pathology?
What plasma derivative is used for Rh immunization prevention
questions.explanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin (RhIg) prevents maternal Rh antibody development from fetomaternal hemorrhage. Administration within 72 hours of exposure prevents sensitization. This prevents hemolytic disease in subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies.

Pooled cryoprecipitate in an open system must be transfused within 4 hours due to loss of sterility. Closed system pooling extends this to 6 hours. Rapid transfusion ensures optimal factor activity and prevents bacterial growth.
questions.question: What is the maximum time allowed for cryoprecipitate transfusion after pooling in an open system

questions.explanation: Other blood cells like T cells, B cells, and platelets acquire ABO antigens by adsorption from plasma. Unlike RBCs, these cells do not intrinsically synthesize ABO antigens. The antigens passively attach to cell membranes from surrounding plasma.
questions.question: How do T cells, B cells, and platelets acquire ABO antigens?

questions.explanation: The ABO locus has three main allelic forms: A, B, and O, which determine blood group phenotypes. Each parent contributes one allele to their offspring, creating various combinations. These three alleles account for all possible ABO blood group genotypes.
questions.question: How many allelic forms does the ABO locus have?

questions.explanation: Leukoreduction removes white blood cells that release pyrogenic cytokines causing febrile reactions. Modern filters remove >=99.99% of WBCs. This modification also prevents HLA alloimmunization and CMV transmission.
questions.question: Which modification prevents febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions most effectively
Which growth factors act on the earliest pluripotent stem cells?
questions.explanation: SCF, IL-1, IL-3, IL-6, and IL-11 are early-acting factors that stimulate pluripotent stem cells to enter differentiation pathways. These factors support stem cell survival and promote commitment to multilineage progenitors. Later-acting factors then drive lineage-specific development.

questions.question: What is the non-alpha chain in fetal hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: The fetus has a distinct non-alpha globin chain called gamma that pairs with alpha. Two alpha and two gamma chains form fetal hemoglobin (HbF). Gamma chains have different oxygen-binding characteristics than beta chains.

questions.question: Which enzyme is directly responsible for converting precursor substance to H substance on red blood cell membranes?
questions.explanation: The H gene codes for α2-fucosyltransferase (also called α2-L-fucosyltransferase), which adds fucose to the precursor substance to form H substance. This H substance then serves as the foundation upon which A and B antigens are subsequently built through the addition of specific sugars. Without this enzyme, as seen in Bombay phenotype (hh), no H substance forms and consequently no A or B antigens can develop.

HemoCue measures absorbance at 565 nm, optimizing detection of azidemethaemoglobin formed when sodium nitrite and sodium azide react with haemoglobin in the cuvette. This wavelength selection maximizes sensitivity and minimizes interference from other blood components. Proper wavelength calibration ensures accurate measurements.
questions.question: What wavelength does the HemoCue system use for absorbance measurement?
What makes group O serum unique regarding its antibody composition?
options: It contains anti-A, anti-B, and inseparable anti-AB
questions.explanation: Group O serum contains anti-A, anti-B, and anti-AB, with the anti-AB component being a separate cross-reacting antibody that cannot be separated into pure anti-A or anti-B specificity through absorption. The anti-AB in group O individuals is usually IgG, making it particularly dangerous as it can cross the placenta. This potent antibody combination explains why group O donors are considered "dangerous" in cases of ABO-incompatible transfusions.

questions.question: What evidence confirms inheritance of the A, B, H, and Se genes?
questions.explanation: Demonstration of A, B, and H substances in saliva is evidence that the A gene, B gene, H gene, and Se gene have all been inherited. Saliva testing reveals secretor status and confirms the genetic inheritance pattern. This testing is particularly useful when red cell antigens are poorly developed (as in newborns or certain disease states) or when establishing true ABO group in cases with weak or anomalous red cell typing results.
options: Presence of antigens on red cells only
Demonstration of A, B, and H substances in saliva

questions.question: What is the normal haemoglobin range for adult females?
questions.explanation: Adult females maintain haemoglobin levels between 11-16 gm/dl, lower than males due to menstrual blood loss and reduced androgen stimulation. Pregnancy further decreases these values through haemodilution. Appropriate reference ranges prevent overdiagnosis or underdiagnosis of anaemia in women.

Blood drops maintain intrinsic density for approximately 15 seconds after entering copper sulphate solution before diffusion and osmotic effects alter specific gravity. Observations must occur within this critical time window. Rapid reading ensures accurate density determination before blood equilibrates with surrounding solution.
questions.question: How long does a blood drop maintain its density in copper sulphate solution?
What is the primary indication for washing blood components
options: Remove plasma proteins causing severe allergic reactions
questions.explanation: Washing removes plasma proteins that cause severe allergic or anaphylactic reactions. Multiple saline washes eliminate IgA and other allergenic proteins. This benefits IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA antibodies.

Alkaline haematin method successfully converts carboxyhaemoglobin and sulphaemoglobin, overcoming Sahli's method limitations for measuring these derivatives. This broader conversion capability improves accuracy in patients with carbon monoxide exposure or drug-induced sulphaemoglobin formation. The alkaline environment facilitates more complete haemoglobin derivative denaturation.
questions.question: Which haemoglobin derivatives are converted in alkaline haematin method but not in Sahli's?

questions.explanation: Granulocytes have only a 24-hour shelf life due to rapid function deterioration. These cells should be transfused as soon as possible after collection. Storage occurs at room temperature without agitation.
questions.question: What is the shelf life of granulocyte products
What enzyme catalyzes the first step of haem synthesis?
questions.explanation: δ-Aminolaevulinic acid synthetase catalyzes the condensation of succinyl CoA and glycine, representing the rate-limiting enzyme controlling overall haem synthesis. This enzyme's activity is regulated by haem concentration through negative feedback. Synthesis of the enzyme itself is inhibited by free haem.

ALA dehydratase (also called porphobilinogen synthase) catalyzes cytoplasmic dimerization of two δ-aminolaevulinic acid molecules to form porphobilinogen, the pyrrole ring compound. This enzyme is inhibited by lead, explaining lead poisoning's haematological manifestations. The reaction represents the second step in haem synthesis.
questions.question: What enzyme converts ALA to porphobilinogen?

questions.explanation: ABO antibodies are usually IgM class immunoglobulins, which are characteristically cold reacting. IgM antibodies are large pentameric molecules that cannot cross the placenta. Their size and ability to bind complement make them highly effective at causing agglutination.
questions.question: What is the typical immunoglobulin class of ABO antibodies?

questions.explanation: ABO antibody production happens at an early age because sugars identical or similar to ABO antigens are found in nature. Exposure to these environmental antigens through food and microorganisms stimulates antibody development. By six months of age, most infants have detectable ABO antibodies.
questions.question: At what age does ABO antibody production typically begin?

questions.explanation: Cytoplasm changes from deep blue to pink reflecting progressive hemoglobin accumulation and simultaneous RNA reduction. The basophilia from RNA-rich cytoplasm gives way to acidophilia as hemoglobin content increases. This color transition on Romanowsky staining provides visual evidence of erythroid maturation.
questions.question: What progressive change characterizes cytoplasmic maturation during erythropoiesis?

questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate preparation uses 4170 x g for 10 minutes to separate the cold precipitate from supernatant plasma. This moderate force adequately concentrates the cryoprecipitate. The supernatant becomes cryoprecipitate-reduced plasma.
questions.question: What centrifugation parameters are used for cryoprecipitate preparation

questions.explanation: Clinically significant Kidd antibodies are mainly IgG, though rarely IgM forms occur. Some Kidd antibodies may bind complement, which can contribute to both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis. Being predominantly IgG, these antibodies react at 37 C and in the antiglobulin phase, can cross the placenta (though HDFN is usually mild), and cause significant delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions upon re-exposure.
questions.question: What is the immunoglobulin class of clinically significant Kidd antibodies?

questions.explanation: Adult haemoglobin A (α2β2) normally constitutes 96-98% of total haemoglobin after the first year of life, representing the predominant oxygen carrier. The remainder comprises Hb A2 (1.5-3.2%) and Hb F (0.5-0.8%). Altered percentages indicate haemoglobinopathies or thalassaemias.
questions.question: What is the normal percentage of Hb A in adults?
What antibodies are present in blood group AB individuals?
questions.explanation: Blood group AB individuals have neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies in their serum. This is because they express both A and B antigens on their cells. The absence of these antibodies makes AB individuals universal plasma donors.

The Rh complex is only expressed in cells of the erythroid lineage, making Rh antigens RBC-specific. This restricted expression distinguishes Rh from ABO antigens which appear on multiple tissues. Rh antigens appear during red cell development in bone marrow.
questions.question: Where is the Rh complex exclusively expressed?
Perls' stain is used to identify sideroblastic iron in:
questions.explanation: Perls' stain identifies iron deposits (sideroblastic iron) in nucleated red blood cells during erythropoiesis. Abnormal ringed sideroblasts with perinuclear iron accumulation indicate specific disorders. The presence and pattern of sideroblastic iron have diagnostic significance in anemia classification.

questions.question: Which colony-stimulating factor specifically promotes neutrophil production and maturation?
questions.explanation: G-CSF specifically stimulates neutrophil progenitor proliferation, maturation, and survival, promoting rapid recovery of neutrophil counts. It acts on committed granulocyte progenitors and also enhances mature neutrophil function including phagocytosis and killing. G-CSF is clinically used to treat neutropenia and mobilize stem cells.

The Rh system genes (C/c, D/d, and E/e) are located on chromosome 1 as a single gene complex with three alternative antigens positioned close together. These genes are inherited as a unit and behave as a single gene (haplotype). The close linkage of these genes on the same chromosome explains why certain Rh antigen combinations are commonly inherited together, such as CDe (R1) or cDE (R2).
questions.question: On which chromosome is the Rh gene complex located?

options: Cell-cell contact, matrix production, and growth factor secretion
questions.explanation: Bone marrow stroma provides support through direct cell-cell contact, extracellular matrix production, and growth factor secretion. Stromal cells create microenvironmental niches where stem cells reside and receive appropriate signals. This three-dimensional architecture organizes haematopoietic cell development.
questions.question: How does bone marrow stroma support haematopoiesis?

questions.explanation: Washing platelets removes plasma proteins causing severe allergic or anaphylactic reactions. Multiple washes with saline eliminate allergenic proteins while preserving platelet function. This benefits IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA antibodies.
questions.question: What modification prevents recurrence of severe allergic reactions to platelet transfusion
What signaling pathway is commonly activated by growth factor receptors?
questions.explanation: Growth factor receptor activation commonly triggers the JAK-STAT signaling pathway where Janus kinases phosphorylate STAT transcription factors. Phosphorylated STATs dimerize and translocate to the nucleus regulating gene expression. This pathway mediates proliferation, differentiation, and survival responses.

Clostridium difficile is a gastrointestinal pathogen diagnosed through stool toxin assays, not blood film examination with Giemsa. Giemsa stain is specifically used for blood-borne parasites, spirochetes, and certain intracellular organisms visible in blood or tissue. The other listed organisms are appropriately diagnosed using Giemsa staining techniques.
questions.question: Which organism is NOT typically diagnosed using Giemsa stain?

questions.explanation: Naturally occurring antibodies (remembered by mnemonic LIiPMABHN) include anti-Lea, anti-Leb, anti-I, anti-i, anti-P1, anti-M, anti-A, anti-B, anti-H, and anti-N. These antibodies develop without prior transfusion or pregnancy exposure, are typically IgM, cold-reacting, and generally not clinically significant. ABO antibodies are the most clinically important naturally occurring antibodies due to their prevalence and ability to cause severe reactions.
options: Anti-Lea, anti-Leb, anti-I, anti-P1, anti-M, anti-A, anti-B, anti-H, anti-N
questions.question: Which antibodies are considered naturally occurring?

questions.explanation: Female blood donor screening employs copper sulphate specific gravity 1.053, representing approximately 12 g/dl haemoglobin with 7.0 g/dl serum protein assumption. This lower threshold acknowledges physiological gender differences in haemoglobin levels. Appropriate screening prevents donation-related anaemia complications.
questions.question: What specific gravity corresponds to 12 g/dl haemoglobin for female blood donors?
What problem results from inadequate EDTA mixing after venous collection?
questions.explanation: Insufficient mixing of venous blood with EDTA anticoagulant allows microclot formation, causing inaccurate cell counts and haemoglobin measurements when clots trap erythrocytes. Immediate gentle inversion mixing prevents clotting. Clotted samples require recollection as they yield unreliable results.

questions.question: What type of proteins are Rh antigens structurally?
questions.explanation: Rh antigens are transmembrane polypeptides that span the RBC membrane multiple times. They are integral membrane proteins firmly embedded in the lipid bilayer. This structural characteristic makes them highly stable and resistant to removal.

questions.question: What happens to extruded normoblast nuclei in bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow macrophages phagocytose extruded normoblast nuclei during erythrocyte maturation. These macrophages also transmit iron to developing erythroblasts for hemoglobin synthesis. Macrophages form central components of erythroblastic islands supporting red cell production.

Toluidine blue produces strongly positive staining of basophil granules due to their high heparin and histamine content. The metachromatic properties of basophil granules cause color shift to purple-red. This specific staining helps identify and quantify basophils in blood smears.
questions.question: Toluidine blue staining demonstrates strong positivity in:

questions.explanation: The i antigen (linear precursor chains) converts to I antigen (branched chains) at approximately 18 months of age as the child matures. Newborns predominantly express i antigen, while adults predominantly express I antigen. This developmental change reflects the maturation of glycosyltransferases that create branched carbohydrate structures on the red cell membrane, with the precursor chain becoming increasingly branched over time.
questions.question: At what approximate age does the i antigen convert predominantly to I antigen?
What is unique about Lutheran antigen expression on cord blood cells?
options: They are weakly expressed compared to adult cells
They are only on white cells
questions.explanation: Lutheran antigens are weakly expressed on cord blood cells compared to adult red cells, reaching full expression as the infant matures. This developmental pattern is similar to other blood group antigens like Lewis, though less pronounced. The weak expression on fetal cells may contribute to the generally mild nature of Lutheran-associated hemolytic disease of the newborn when it does occur.

questions.question: Specific esterase staining produces red coloration in:
questions.explanation: Specific esterase (naphthol AS-D chloroacetate esterase) produces red coloration specifically in neutrophils and mast cells. This enzyme is present in primary and secondary granules of granulocytes. The specificity for neutrophils helps differentiate myeloid from monocytic lineages.

questions.question: What is the relationship between ABO blood groups and H antigen expression?
questions.explanation: H antigen expression is highest in group O individuals (who lack A and B transferases to convert H), intermediate in groups A and B (where some H is converted to A or B), and lowest in group AB (where H is converted to both A and B antigens). This differential H expression explains why anti-IH antibodies show varying reaction strengths with different ABO group cells, reacting strongest with O cells and weakest with AB cells.
options: H antigen is highest in group AB, lowest in group O
H antigen is highest in group O, progressively less in A, B, and AB
H antigen is absent in all ABO groups
Only group B has H antigen

questions.explanation: ABO antibodies, particularly in group O individuals, are most associated with acute hemolytic transfusion reactions (AHTR), which can be fatal. These naturally occurring IgM antibodies activate complement efficiently, causing rapid intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and potential renal failure and DIC. ABO incompatibility due to clerical errors remains the leading cause of transfusion-related deaths, emphasizing the critical importance of proper patient identification and blood typing.
questions.question: Which blood group system antibodies are most associated with acute hemolytic transfusion reactions?
Which class of stains is primarily used for differential blood cell counts in routine haematology?
questions.explanation: Romanowsky stains are the routine haematological stains specifically designed for differential blood cell counting. They provide excellent morphological differentiation of blood cells through their unique polychromatic staining properties. These stains form the foundation of basic haematological examination in diagnostic laboratories.

questions.question: What platelet count threshold generally requires prophylactic transfusion in asymptomatic patients
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic patients with severe thrombocytopenia (<10,000/muL) typically receive prophylactic platelets to prevent spontaneous bleeding. Higher thresholds apply for bleeding patients or surgical procedures. Clinical judgment considers individual risk factors.

questions.question: What is the immediate precursor cell that gives rise to monocytes?
questions.explanation: Promonocytes are the immediate precursors that divide to form monocytes in bone marrow. Promonocytes develop from monoblasts, the earliest recognizable monocytic precursor. This maturation sequence occurs in bone marrow before monocytes enter circulation.

questions.question: What property do haematopoietic growth factors share regarding their production sites?
questions.explanation: Haematopoietic growth factors are produced by many cell types including stromal cells, T lymphocytes, monocytes, and endothelial cells. This distributed production allows local and systemic regulation of haematopoiesis. Different cell types produce different factor combinations coordinating responses.
options: Made by many different cell types

questions.question: What converts coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX?
questions.explanation: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase transforms coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX. This mitochondrial enzyme removes carboxyl groups and oxidizes the molecule. The reaction is the sixth step in heme synthesis.

Once thawed, FFP must be transfused within 24 hours or reclassified as thawed plasma. This timeframe balances clinical utility with maintaining adequate factor levels. After 24 hours, labile factors decline significantly.
questions.question: What is the maximum time FFP can be stored after thawing before it becomes classified as thawed plasma
What is the Rosenfield terminology based on?
questions.explanation: Rosenfield and coworkers developed an alphanumeric terminology system for Rh antigens. This system uses "Rh" followed by numbers to designate different antigens. It's particularly useful for describing rare Rh phenotypes and new discoveries.

questions.question: What special testing approach helps detect Kidd antibodies?
options: Use of enzyme reagents, LISS, and polyethylene glycol
questions.explanation: Kidd antibody detection is aided by use of enzyme reagents (which enhance reactivity because Kidd antigens are not destroyed by enzymes), low ionic strength saline (LISS), and polyethylene glycol (PEG) as potentiators. These enhancement techniques are necessary because Kidd antibodies tend to be weak and their reactivity deteriorates rapidly. Without these enhancements, clinically significant Kidd antibodies may be missed in routine blood crossmatches.

questions.question: What distinguishes Rh antibodies from ABO antibodies regarding pregnancy?
options: Rh antibodies are always IgM type
Rh IgG antibodies cross placenta causing severe HDN
ABO antibodies cause worse HDN than Rh
questions.explanation: Rh antibodies are IgG class and cross the placenta, potentially causing severe hemolytic disease of newborn. ABO antibodies are mainly IgM which cannot cross placenta, causing milder HDN. Anti-D can cause life-threatening fetal anemia and hydrops.

questions.question: Which bone marrow niche maintains haematopoietic stem cells in their most quiescent state?
