Describe the routes of drug administration and their effects on absorption.
A(i) Intravenous bolus. A(ii) Intravenous infusion. A(iii) Intramuscular. A(iv) Subcutaneous. A(v) Oral. A(vi) Buccal, sublingual and rectal. A(vii) Transdermal and inhalation.
B(i) Relate to specific drug examples. B(ii) Relate to gastrointestinal factors.
C(i) How routes improve safety and efficacy. C(ii) What limitations or trade-offs result.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
IV bolus: 100% bioavailability, immediate; increased chance of adverse reaction and possible anaphylaxis.
A(ii)
IV infusion: 100%, precisely controlled plasma levels, large volumes, suits poorly lipid-soluble or irritating drugs; needs skill, risks tissue damage at the site.
A(iii)
IM: rapid from aqueous, slow from non-aqueous solutions; easier than IV; irritating drugs painful; rate varies with muscle group and blood flow.
A(iv)
SC: prompt from aqueous solution, slow from repository formulations; rate depends on blood flow and volume.
A(v)
Oral: safest and easiest; slower than IV or IM; absorption may vary, some drugs are erratic, unstable in the GI tract, or metabolized by the liver first.
A(vi)
Buccal/sublingual: rapid for lipid-soluble drugs with no first-pass effect; rectal: useful when the patient cannot swallow; absorption erratic.
A(vii)
Transdermal: slow and easy, for low-dose, low-molecular-weight lipid-soluble drugs, with variable permeability and irritation; inhalation: rapid, local or systemic, with variable dose absorbed and possible cough reflex.
B(i)
The SC route is generally used for insulin; salicylic acid is absorbed from the stomach and quinidine poorly.
B(ii)
Small intestine transit takes 3-4 hours; duodenum is the main absorption site; stomach pH is about 1.5-2 with food; colon absorption is limited and erratic.
C(i)
Route choice allows rapid onset, precise control or local effect; first-pass avoidance via sublingual route.
C(ii)
IV carries anaphylaxis and tissue damage risk; oral absorption variable; transdermal slow; inhalation dose variable.

questions.question:
A migraine patient takes sumatriptan after ergotamine taken earlier the same day, has taken an MAOI within the last two weeks, and has a history of angina.
(i) Identify the interacting drugs and conditions.
(ii) Explain the mechanism and clinical consequence.
(iii) Classify the severity.
(iv) Recommend management.
(v) Give the counselling advice.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Sumatriptan with ergotamine derivatives (within the previous 24 hours) and with MAOIs (within 2 weeks), plus ischaemic heart disease or angina; ergotamine with a β-blocker or methysergide also carries vasospasm risk.
(ii)
Sumatriptan stimulates 5-HT1D and 5-HT1B receptors with direct vasoconstrictive effect; ergotamine stimulates presynaptic 5-HT1 receptors. Ergotism: nausea, diarrhoea, thirst, pruritus, vertigo, muscle cramps, paraesthesias, cold skin, reduced peripheral pulses.
(iii)
Sumatriptan is contraindicated in these situations.
(iv)
Do not give sumatriptan within 24 hours of ergotamine or within 2 weeks of an MAOI, nor in ischaemic heart disease, angina, MI or uncontrolled hypertension. Alternatives: aspirin, paracetamol, NSAIDs, or Midrin if sumatriptan and ergotamine cannot be used.
(v)
Titrate ergotamine strictly, avoid frequent dosing above the maximum (6 tablets/day or 10/week) to prevent dependency, withdrawal (severe headache, nausea, vomiting) and ergotism.

questions.question:
Describe the mechanisms by which drugs cross cell membranes.
A(i) Passive diffusion. A(ii) The pH-partition hypothesis. A(iii) Active transport. A(iv) Facilitated diffusion. A(v) Vesicular transport. A(vi) Pore transport and ion-pair formation.
B(i) Relate each to examples. B(ii) Explain the role of tissue binding.
C(i) Explain what limits or complicates these processes. C(ii) State the implications for absorption.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Net movement from high to low concentration, no energy; the major mechanism for most drugs; Fick's law: rate depends on diffusion coefficient, partition coefficient, membrane area and thickness, and concentration difference; lipid-soluble drugs cross more easily.
A(ii)
The ionized form is more water soluble and the non-ionized form more lipid soluble; the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relates ionization to pKa and pH; the compartment where the drug is more ionized holds the greater total drug concentration.
A(iii)
Carrier-mediated movement against a concentration gradient, using energy; selective and saturable; structurally similar drugs compete.
A(iv)
Carrier-mediated movement along a concentration gradient with no energy; saturable and competitive; minor role in absorption.
A(v)
Pinocytosis and phagocytosis engulf material; endocytosis and exocytosis move macromolecules in and out of the cell.
A(vi)
Very small molecules (urea, water, sugars) cross through pores; strong electrolytes form neutral ion pairs that diffuse more easily.
B(i)
Salicylic acid (pKa 3.0) is mostly non-ionized at gastric pH 1.2 and absorbed from the stomach, quinidine (weak base) poorly; 5-fluorouracil by active transport; insulin by exocytosis; sabin polio vaccine by vesicular transport; propranolol with oleic acid and quinine with hexylsalicylate by ion pairs.
B(ii)
Binding to proteins (dicumarol), fat (chlordane) or bone and teeth (tetracycline-calcium) prevents drug moving back across the membrane; specific uptake (iodide in thyroid) also concentrates drugs.
C(i)
Lipid bilayer theory cannot explain diffusion of water, small molecules and charged ions; carrier systems saturate; the blood-brain barrier slows diffusion into the brain.
C(ii)
Duodenum has the fastest absorption because of villi and microvilli; the plasma sink maintains the gradient; carrier-mediated absorption plateaus.

A(i)
Recurrent, unprovoked seizures with no identifiable intracranial or metabolic cause; seizures are transient paroxysmal uncontrollable neuronal discharges.
A(ii)
Idiopathic (genetic link, most common), cryptogenic, symptomatic; ILAE: genetic, structural-metabolic, unknown; causes vary by age (birth injury, febrile convulsion, trauma, infection, tumour, cerebrovascular disease over 50 years).
A(iii)
Neuronal injury replaces low-frequency discharge with high-frequency bursts by a population of neurones, arising from an epileptic focus.
A(iv)
Depends on focus location; tonic-clonic (stiffness, falls, convulsion, cyanosis, tongue biting, post-ictal drowsiness), absence, myoclonic, atonic, simple and complex partial seizures.
A(v)
Patient and eyewitness report; EEG; MRI; PET and SPECT; CAT scan.
B(i)
In status epilepticus the goals are aggressive supportive care and prompt termination of electrical seizure activity; surgery aims to abolish or reduce seizures with minimal neurosurgical or cognitive risk.
B(ii)
Counselling, psychosocial assistance, rehabilitation; surgery for 30-40% uncontrolled by drugs; vagus nerve, responsive neurostimulation and deep brain stimulation; dietary therapy.
B(iii)
First aid (loosen clothing, protect head, roll to side, do not force mouth open); diazepam 10-20 mg IV in adults (or rectal in children) if seizure exceeds 10 minutes; status epilepticus: IV access, dextrose 50 mL of 50% and thiamine 100 mg, diazepam 0.15 mg/kg or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg then fosphenytoin 15-20 mg PE/kg.
B(iv)
Drugs can be withdrawn after 2-5 years seizure-free in about 70% of children and 60% of adults; about 25% of cases are preventable (prevent head injury, perinatal care, fever control, stroke risk reduction, parasite elimination).
C(i)
Generalized (tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, atonic) with impaired consciousness from onset; partial (simple, complex, secondarily generalized) with localized discharge.
C(ii)
Seizure during a high fever, mostly in children 6 months to 5 years; managed with rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg, antipyretics, airway care, oxygen; preventive treatment is generally not warranted.
C(iii)
Life-threatening seizures in pregnancy with sudden blood pressure rise; treated in hospital with magnesium sulphate (loading 4-6 g slow IV over 5 minutes, then 1-2 g per hour) and labetalol; no further seizures usually after pregnancy.

A patient with myasthenia gravis on neostigmine develops increased sweating and salivation, abdominal cramps, slow pulse, and worsening muscle weakness with breathing difficulty.
(i) Identify the causative drug and the type of reaction.
(ii) Explain the mechanism and risk factors.
(iii) Outline management.
(iv) State the preventive strategy.
(v) State the alternative therapy.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Neostigmine (an indirectly acting cholinomimetic): muscarinic adverse effects, and possibly cholinergic crisis from anticholinesterase overdose; myasthenic crisis and cholinergic crisis both cause severe weakness and breathing difficulty.
(ii)
Anticholinesterases inhibit acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine levels and duration; neostigmine has pronounced muscarinic action; excessive dosage impairs neuromuscular transmission by a depolarizing block. Muscarinic effects: sweating, salivary and gastric secretions, GI and uterine motility, bradycardia. There is no fixed dose because symptoms vary with stress and weather.
(iii)
Atropine 0.4-0.6 mg per day orally (or propantheline) is given as adjunct to reverse muscarinic effects.
(iv)
Titrate doses to muscle strength (neostigmine oral 15-30 mg every 3-4 hours, maximum tolerable 180 mg daily); give atropine or propantheline with neostigmine; avoid triggers (emotional stress, extreme temperatures).
(v)
Pyridostigmine (long acting, less powerful, slower, smoother, less frequent dosing); prednisolone from 5 mg daily raised in 5 mg steps to 60-80 mg daily; thymectomy; plasmapheresis; IVIG.

questions.question:
A patient on a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor is prescribed simvastatin, also takes St John's wort and uses an antacid and fluticasone.
(i) Identify the interacting drugs.
(ii) Explain the mechanism and clinical consequence.
(iii) Classify the severity or significance.
(iv) Recommend management.
(v) Give the counselling advice.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Protease inhibitor (boosted with ritonavir) with simvastatin; other listed interacting items are prescription drugs, OTCs such as antacids and fluticasone, and herbal supplements such as St John's wort.
(ii)
Low-dose ritonavir blocks intestinal and hepatic 3A metabolism; PIs increase statin levels in the body, raising the risk of muscle pain and kidney damage.
(iii)
Simvastatin and lovastatin are contraindicated with all PIs.
(iv)
Do not combine simvastatin with the PI.
(v)
Relevant points: PIs can cause lipodystrophy, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes and kidney stones, and adherence is critical to effectiveness of HIV medicines.

questions.question:
Discuss antiparkinsonian drug classes other than levodopa under the following headings.
A(i) Classification. A(ii) Mechanism of action. A(iii) Indications. A(iv) Adverse effects.
B(i) Rationale for non-ergot agonists. B(ii) Role of carbidopa and benserazide. B(iii) Place of anticholinergics. B(iv) Place of amantadine.
C(i) Distinguish bromocriptine from ropinirole. C(ii) Distinguish selegiline from COMT inhibitors. C(iii) Distinguish ergot from non-ergot agonists.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Dopamine agonists (ergot: bromocriptine, cabergoline, pergolide; non-ergot: rotigotine, ropinirole, apomorphine), MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors, antimuscarinics, amantadine.
A(ii)
Agonists act directly on dopamine receptors; MAO-B inhibitors block dopamine breakdown; COMT inhibitors block enzymatic degradation; antimuscarinics suppress cholinergic overactivity.
A(iii)
Agonists and others used alone or with levodopa; selegiline as adjunct in response fluctuation; COMT inhibitors as adjunct in prolonged levodopa; anticholinergics for drug-induced parkinsonism with cognitive impairment.
A(iv)
Agonists: sleepiness, hypotension; selegiline: insomnia, hallucination, headache; COMT inhibitors similar to levodopa; anticholinergics have numerous side effects.
B(i)
Ergots have numerous side effects; non-ergot agents are preferred though relatively expensive.
B(ii)
Dopa decarboxylase inhibitors do not cross the BBB; they raise plasma levodopa, prolong half-life and allow more to reach the brain.
B(iii)
Avoided in mild to moderate PD because of side effects.
B(iv)
Antiviral with antiparkinsonian properties used in early PD to delay levodopa.
C(i)
Bromocriptine is ergot-derived, D2-agonist, 7.5-30 mg daily; ropinirole is non-ergot, D2/D3-specific, started at 750 µg daily.
C(ii)
Selegiline blocks dopamine breakdown, little benefit alone; COMT inhibitors (entacapone, tolcapone) block neurotransmitter degradation and have side effects like levodopa.
C(iii)
Ergot agonists are used when levodopa fails in severe disability; non-ergot agonists include rotigotine, ropinirole, apomorphine.

A(i)
Disorders of emotional state with long periods of extreme happiness, sadness or both, lasting several weeks or longer.
A(ii)
Exact cause unknown; genetic, biological, environmental, socioeconomic and endocrine factors; family history, trauma, stress, physical illness, medications.
A(iii)
Excess or deficiency of dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine and GABA is implicated.
A(iv)
Mania: elevated, expansive or irritable mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, flight of ideas; depression: at least 5 of 9 symptoms nearly every day for 2 weeks.
A(v)
No medical tests; history, mental status examination, scales (Beck, Hamilton), and medical evaluation to rule out organic causes.
B(i)
Therapy combines medication and psychotherapy and reduces relapse.
B(ii)
Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, TCAs, MAOIs), mood stabilizers (lithium first-line; valproic acid, lamotrigine, carbamazepine), atypical antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, vitamin D.
B(iii)
Behavioural, cognitive, interpersonal, social rhythm, problem-solving, family therapy.
B(iv)
ECT (response rate 90%; 6-12 sessions); rTMS after failing an antidepressant; light therapy 20-60 minutes each morning for seasonal disorder.
C(i)
Bipolar I: manic and often major depressive episodes, most severe; bipolar II: major depression with at least one hypomanic episode, less extreme.
C(ii)
Major depression: persistent dysphoric mood; dysthymia: chronic milder mood over 2 years best treated by psychotherapy; cyclothymia: over 2 years of depression and hypomania.
C(iii)
Seasonal affective disorder, double depression, delusional depression, atypical depression, rapid cycling.
questions.question:
Discuss mood disorders under the following headings.
A(i) Definition. A(ii) Aetiology and risk factors. A(iii) Pathophysiology. A(iv) Clinical features. A(v) Diagnosis.
B(i) Goals of therapy. B(ii) Pharmacological management. B(iii) Psychotherapy. B(iv) Brain stimulation and light therapy.
C(i) Distinguish bipolar I from bipolar II. C(ii) Distinguish major depression, dysthymia and cyclothymia. C(iii) Other types.

A woman with HIV, never on antiretrovirals and with a CD4 count between 250 and 350 cells/mm³, is started on a nevirapine-containing regimen at the same time as co-trimoxazole and develops a rash.
(i) Identify the likely causative drug and the type of reaction.
(ii) Explain the risk factors.
(iii) Outline management.
(iv) State the preventive strategy.
(v) State the alternative therapy.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Nevirapine: rash that may be severe and life-threatening (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and a rare but potentially life-threatening risk of hepatotoxicity.
(ii)
Higher incidence in women and in antiretroviral-naive women with CD4 above 250 cells/mm³; co-initiation with other rash-causing drugs such as co-trimoxazole; use with hepatotoxic medications.
(iii)
In severe hepatic or skin reactions nevirapine should be permanently discontinued.
(iv)
Use with caution in women with CD4 250-350; careful monitoring during the first 12 weeks; avoid starting together with co-trimoxazole where possible; avoid in patients using hepatotoxic drugs.
(v)
Efavirenz (once daily at bedtime on an empty stomach; CNS toxicity, teratogenicity, rash; avoid in severe psychiatric illness, with potential for pregnancy and in first trimester; drug of choice with rifampicin-based TB therapy). Nevirapine is the preferred NNRTI if pregnancy is possible. Dolutegravir plus an NRTI backbone is WHO preferred first line, more effective with fewer side effects and a high barrier to resistance.

questions.question:
Discuss systemic lupus erythematosus under the following headings.
A(i) Definition and epidemiology. A(ii) Aetiology. A(iii) Pathogenesis. A(iv) Clinical features. A(v) Investigations.
B(i) Goals of therapy. B(ii) Mild disease. B(iii) Severe disease. B(iv) General advice.
C(i) Distinguish joint disease from rheumatoid arthritis. C(ii) Distinguish drug-induced lupus. C(iii) Triggers of flares.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Inflammatory multisystem disorder, about nine times commoner in women, peak onset 20-40 years; arthralgia and rashes most common, cerebral and renal disease most serious.
A(ii)
Unknown; hereditary, HLA genes, complement deficiency, sex hormones, immunological loss of self tolerance, drugs and UV light.
A(iii)
Widespread vasculitis, fibrinoid along vessels and joints with immune complexes, haematoxylin bodies.
A(iv)
Joints 90%, skin 75% with butterfly erythema, lungs, heart 25%, kidneys about 40%, nervous system up to 60%, eyes, fever and malaise.
A(v)
FBC (anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia), raised ESR, ANA, rheumatoid factor, low complement, false-positive syphilis test, raised immunoglobulins, biopsy, CT and MRI.
B(i)
Drug therapy is for active disease, with no evidence that treatment in remission alters progression.
B(ii)
NSAIDs for arthralgia, arthritis, fever, serositis; chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine for mild skin disease, fatigue and arthralgias.
B(iii)
Oral corticosteroids or high-dose IV boluses and/or azathioprine or cyclophosphamide for glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, cerebral disease, blood dyscrasias.
B(iv)
A caring approach, discuss the good prognosis, avoid excessive sunlight.
C(i)
Joints are painful but appear normal, deformity and bony erosions are rare.
C(ii)
Hydralazine, methyldopa, isoniazid and D-penicillamine can induce lupus not associated with anti-dsDNA.
C(iii)
Contraceptive pill, HRT and ultraviolet light.

questions.question:
Describe the treatment of Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease.
A(i) First-line therapy. A(ii) Second-line therapy. A(iii) Alternatives. A(iv) Duration.
B(i) How eradication is confirmed. B(ii) Assessment of response and ulcer healing. B(iii) Expected eradication rates. B(iv) Factors affecting adherence.
C(i) Management of complicated ulcers. C(ii) Management of NSAID-induced ulcers. C(iii) Management of treatment failure and refractory ulcers. C(iv) Complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
PPI-based triple therapy: PPI (e.g. omeprazole 20 mg BID or lansoprazole 30 mg BID) with amoxicillin 1 g BID and clarithromycin 500 mg BID.
A(ii)
Quadruple therapy for failure of standard treatment: bismuth subsalicylate 525 mg QID, metronidazole 250 mg QID, tetracycline QID plus a PPI or ranitidine BID.
A(iii)
Metronidazole replaces amoxicillin in penicillin-allergic patients only; PPIs, H2RAs, sucralfate and misoprostol are other agents.
A(iv)
7-14 days, with 14 days recommended as more effective; uncomplicated ulcers treated for 14 days.
B(i)
Urea breath test is suited to confirm eradication; false negatives occur with PPIs, antibiotics or bismuth; serology, stool PCR and invasive tests also exist.
B(ii)
Goals: relieve symptoms, reduce acid, promote healing, prevent complications and recurrence; endoscopy confirms ulcers in at least 95%.
B(iii)
Triple therapy 85-90% cure; quadruple regimens above 90%; target at least 90% per-protocol.
B(iv)
Many drugs, frequent dosing, long duration and side effects (taste disturbance, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea).
C(i)
In complicated H. pylori ulcers continue the PPI beyond the 14-day antibiotic course until eradication is confirmed.
C(ii)
Stop the NSAID and give a PPI; if unavoidable use the lowest dose with a PPI or misoprostol, or a COX-2 inhibitor; prophylaxis for age over 60, prior PUD, steroids or anticoagulants.
C(iii)
Refractory: not healed by 8 weeks (duodenal) or 12 weeks (gastric); re-evaluate with repeat endoscopy, biopsy, serum gastrin, compliance and recent NSAID use; surgery only if medical therapy fails. Persistent infection may reflect reinfection, non-adherence or resistance.
C(iv)
Haemorrhage, perforation, obstruction, refractory ulcer.

questions.question:
Discuss Parkinson disease under the following headings.
A(i) Definition. A(ii) Aetiology. A(iii) Pathophysiology. A(iv) Clinical features. A(v) Diagnosis and staging.
B(i) Goals of therapy. B(ii) Non-pharmacological management. B(iii) Pharmacological management. B(iv) Surgical options.
C(i) Distinguish idiopathic from secondary parkinsonism. C(ii) List the secondary types. C(iii) Distinguish drug-induced parkinsonism.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A slow, chronic, progressive, degenerative neurological disease of the extrapyramidal system.
A(ii)
Depletion or decrease of brain dopamine, shifting the acetylcholine-dopamine balance toward dopamine depletion; idiopathic (cause unknown) is most common.
A(iii)
The syndrome results from dopamine depletion, through inhibition (e.g. antipsychotic-induced) or otherwise.
A(iv)
Resting tremor (pill-rolling), rigidity, bradykinesia (the most important), postural instability, shuffling gait; also dysphagia, hypophonia, micrographia, constipation, orthostatic changes.
A(v)
Clinically based; Hoehn and Yahr stages 0 to V.
B(i)
Drugs do not prevent progression but improve quality of life; start only once functional difficulty occurs (mostly stage 3).
B(ii)
Speech and language therapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, educational and nutritional advice.
B(iii)
Levodopa with carbidopa or benserazide (Sinemet 25/100 mg 3 times daily); dopamine agonists; MAO-B inhibitors; COMT inhibitors; antimuscarinics; amantadine.
B(iv)
Deep brain stimulation, thalamotomy, pallidotomy, carbidopa/levodopa enteral suspension.
C(i)
Idiopathic (primary) has unknown cause; secondary forms have identifiable causes and are a smaller percentage.
C(ii)
Atherosclerotic, chemical-induced, drug-induced, trauma-induced, post-encephalitic, infection-induced, tumour-induced.
C(iii)
Extrapyramidal effects of dopamine antagonists such as phenothiazines (fluphenazine, prochlorperazine) and metoclopramide.

questions.question:
A patient with schizophrenia recently started on a first-generation antipsychotic such as haloperidol develops fixed upward gaze, neck twisting, clenched jaw and tongue protrusion.
(i) Identify the likely causative drug class and the type of reaction.
(ii) Explain the mechanism and risk factors.
(iii) Outline management, including drugs, doses and expected onset of relief.
(iv) Distinguish it from the other extrapyramidal reactions.
(v) State the preventive strategy.
(vi) State the alternative therapy.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Acute dystonic reaction (an extrapyramidal side effect) from a first-generation antipsychotic; features are oculogyric crisis, torticollis, trismus, tongue protrusion, and pharyngeal or laryngeal dystonia.
(ii)
EPS are thought to relate to dopamine antagonism in the dorsal striatum. Dystonia occurs primarily with FGAs and can be life-threatening if pharyngeal or laryngeal; EPS are the most significant adverse effect in frequency and a major reason for non-adherence.
(iii)
Treatment of choice: IM or IV anticholinergic, benztropine 2 mg or benzhexol 5 mg; or diphenhydramine 50 mg IM/IV; alternative diazepam 5-10 mg by slow IV push. Relief is typically within 15-20 minutes of IM injection and within 5 minutes of IV injection.
(iv)
Pseudoparkinsonism (D2 antagonism in the nigrostriatum): akinesia/bradykinesia, resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, postural instability, treated with anticholinergics or amantadine. Akathisia: inner restlessness, treated by dose reduction or switching as it responds poorly to anticholinergics. Tardive dyskinesia: late-onset, buccal-linguo-masticatory movements, may be irreversible, worsened by anticholinergics.
(v)
Lower initial doses of the FGA minimize the risk of dystonic reactions.
(vi)
Second-generation antipsychotics have lower risk of neurological effects but more metabolic effects (weight gain, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes); choice is individualized by past response and adverse effects, patient attitude and adverse-effect profile. A self-rated side-effect scale helps because many patients do not report side effects.

questions.question:
A child under 5 years living where yams and cassava are the staple foods presents with stunted growth, sparse, brittle, unnaturally blond hair, discoloured patches of skin, pitting oedema of the legs and feet, an enlarged liver, and apathy with irritability.
(i) Identify the likely condition, its type and its classification.
(ii) State the pathophysiological basis of the presentation.
(iii) Outline the goals of treatment.
(iv) Recommend the first-line pharmacological and non-pharmacological management.
(v) State the monitoring parameters.
(vi) State the key counselling points.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Kwashiorkor, a form of protein-energy malnutrition: diet more deficient in protein than energy, staples low in protein and high in carbohydrate; primary PEM (inadequate intake) vs secondary PEM (disorders or drugs); marasmic kwashiorkor shows both oedema and wasting.
(ii)
Adequate carbohydrate with low protein reduces visceral protein synthesis; hypoalbuminaemia contributes to extravascular fluid accumulation; cell membranes leak fluid and protein causing peripheral oedema; impaired β-lipoprotein synthesis causes fatty liver; cell-mediated immunity is impaired, so infections are common.
(iii)
Goals by WHO phase: Phase 1 resuscitate, rehydrate, treat infection, prevent sepsis and avoid treatment complications; Phase 2 raise caloric intake, treat occult infections, complete vaccination, involve family, stimulate psychomotor activity; Phase 3 prevent relapse.
(iv)
• Phase 1 (about 1 week): rehydrate, antibiotics if infection suspected (even without fever), keep warm; feed slowly at 60% to 80% of caloric requirement for age; thiamine and oral phosphate; continuous NG feeding or small frequent meals including at night to avoid hypoglycaemia.
• Phase 2 (2 to 6 weeks): 120% to 140% of estimated caloric requirement, 150-220 kcal/kg/day, protein 4-6 g/kg/day, target weight gain at least 10 g/kg/day; continue micronutrients; start iron after the first week; psychosocial stimulation.
(v)
• Phase 1: serum phosphate, potassium, magnesium; watch for refeeding syndrome (sweatiness, muscle weakness, tachycardia, heart failure). Phase 2: weight gain, resolution of oedema, overall improvement, persistent diarrhoea or poor weight gain. Phase 3: weight, height, appetite, developmental milestones, general health.
• Follow-up visits start within the first week after discharge and continue monthly for at least six months.
(vi)
• Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then timely complementary feeding from 6 months; hygiene to prevent infections; regular growth monitoring and immunization; routine deworming and vitamin A per national guidelines; link families to food support programmes.
• Pharmacist: nutrition-focused medication management, early detection and referral, caregiver education, correct administration of therapeutic feeds.

(i)
GERD (typical symptoms: heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia). Types: physiologic reflux (NERD), pathologic reflux or GERD (erosive esophagitis), and secondary reflux.
(ii)
Transient LES relaxation, low resting LES pressure or transient increase in abdominal pressure; damage depends on acid and pepsin amount over 24 hours, duration in the esophagus and mucosal sensitivity. Triggers: coffee, alcohol, chocolate, fatty meals, nicotine, hormones, and drugs (β-agonists, nitrates, CCBs, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics).
(iii)
Control symptoms, heal esophagitis, prevent recurrent esophagitis and other complications.
(iv)
• Lifestyle: lose weight, avoid trigger foods and large meals, wait 3 hours after meals before lying down, raise the bed head 8 inches, avoid bending. Drugs: antacids for mild symptoms (after each meal and at bedtime); H2RAs first-line for mild-moderate symptoms (healing mild esophagitis in 70-80%); PPIs most powerful, e.g. omeprazole 20 mg or esomeprazole 40 mg daily, 30-60 mins before eating, twice daily for nocturnal symptoms; erosive esophagitis healed with omeprazole 20 mg or equivalent for up to 12 weeks.
• Prokinetics help only mild symptoms and long-term use is discouraged; antireflux surgery is an option.
(v)
Laboratory tests are seldom useful; manometry and pH monitoring are essential before antireflux surgery; PPIs: headache, diarrhoea, abdominal pain; cimetidine: blood disorders; H2RA tolerance.
questions.question:
A patient is overweight, smokes, drinks coffee and takes a calcium channel blocker, and has burning chest pain after eating that worsens when lying down, with regurgitation and heartburn more than twice a week.
(i) Identify the likely condition and its classification.
(ii) State the pathophysiological basis.
(iii) Outline the treatment goals.
(iv) Recommend first-line pharmacological and non-pharmacological management.
(v) Give the monitoring parameters.

A patient with Parkinson disease has been on levodopa for 2 to 3 years and now swings abruptly between being symptom-free and having full-blown parkinsonism, each phase lasting minutes to hours.
(i) Identify the problem with the current therapy.
(ii) Explain its basis, including why dyskinesia is more likely with levodopa.
(iii) Recommend suitable alternatives or adjustments.
(iv) Justify the choice (efficacy, safety, patient factors).
(v) State the dose adjustments or precautions.
(vi) State the monitoring plan.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The 'on-off' (wearing-off, end-of-dose deterioration, response fluctuation) phenomenon, the most common medication-use problem in long-term levodopa therapy; a motor complication usually after 2 to 3 years.
(ii)
Attributed to decreased sensitivity of dopamine receptors, or a decrease in receptors, with prolonged therapy. Dyskinesia is more likely because levodopa activates both D1 and D2 receptors: D2 activation is useful in PD, while simultaneous D1 activation accounts for dyskinesia.
(iii)
More frequent levodopa dosing; a sustained-release levodopa/dopa decarboxylase inhibitor (Sinemet CR is for response fluctuations); substitute a direct-acting dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine; or add the MAO-B inhibitor selegiline. COMT inhibitors (entacapone, tolcapone) are adjuncts in prolonged levodopa therapy.
(iv)
Non-ergot dopamine agonists are preferred to ergot-derived ones because of the many side effects of ergots, but are relatively expensive; bromocriptine is reserved for severely disabled patients no longer responding to levodopa alone or with intolerable effects; selegiline is used mainly as adjunct in response fluctuations but has little benefit alone and can enhance levodopa adverse effects.
(v)
• Selegiline 10 mg in the morning or 5 mg at breakfast and mid-day; bromocriptine 7.5-30 mg daily in PD; ropinirole 750 µg daily in 3 divided doses, and levodopa may be reduced by about 20% when ropinirole is added; Sinemet 25/100 mg 3 times daily, gradually increased.
• Precautions: dopamine agonists cause excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden onset of sleep and hypotension (especially in the first days); selegiline causes insomnia, hallucination, headache, GI upset, vertigo.
(vi)
Monitoring parameters include response fluctuations, dyskinesia, sleepiness, hypotension and other side effects, with severity staged by Hoehn and Yahr.

questions.question:
A patient with known epilepsy continues to have seizures despite drug treatment and now arrives with a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes without recovery of consciousness.
(i) Identify the likely reasons for treatment failure.
(ii) State the parameters to assess.
(iii) Recommend changes to therapy and emergency management.
(iv) State the criteria for escalation to non-drug options.
(v) Give the adherence and patient-education measures.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Status epilepticus; the most common cause in a patient with known epilepsy is non-compliance, so assume non-compliance. Also 30-40% of patients with epilepsy have seizures not adequately controlled by drugs (intractable epilepsy).
(ii)
Vital signs and respiratory function (intubate for respiratory insufficiency), cardiac and haemodynamic monitoring; phenytoin level (therapeutic 10-20 µg/mL, but 20-30 µg/mL appears more effective in stopping seizures), though treatment should not wait for the level.
(iii)
Secure IV access in a large vein; 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV and 100 mg thiamine; add naloxone 0.4-2.0 mg IV where drug intoxication is likely; if seizure continues beyond 4-5 minutes give diazepam 0.15 mg/kg or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, then fosphenytoin 15-20 mg PE/kg at not more than 150 mg PE/min (preferred) or phenytoin. Give the phenytoin loading dose regardless of prior phenytoin use.
(iv)
Intractable seizures (30-40%) lead to surgery, aimed at abolishing or reducing seizures with low neurosurgical or cognitive risk; electrical stimulation (vagus nerve, responsive neurostimulation, deep brain stimulation) and dietary therapy are also options.
(v)
Counselling, psychosocial assistance and rehabilitation are part of care; seizure first aid for family (protect head, roll onto side, do not force mouth open, no food or drink until alert, reassure). After 2 to 5 years seizure-free, drugs can be withdrawn in about 70% of children and 60% of adults without relapse.

questions.question:
Explain the principles of drug interactions with agents used in GERD and peptic ulcer disease.
A(i) Antacids. A(ii) H₂-receptor antagonists. A(iii) Proton pump inhibitors. A(iv) Sucralfate. A(v) Misoprostol and bismuth.
B(i) Relate to examples of absorption interactions. B(ii) Relate to metabolic interactions. B(iii) Relate to spacing advice.
C(i) How this improves safety and efficacy. C(ii) How it affects adherence. C(iii) What limitations result.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Antacids alter gastric pH and bind drugs, so interaction potential is high; they can destroy enteric coatings.
A(ii)
Cimetidine inhibits hepatic CYP450 and reduces hepatic blood flow; H2RAs with azoles reduce efficacy.
A(iii)
Omeprazole affects diazepam, warfarin and phenytoin metabolism; PPIs may reduce clopidogrel antiplatelet activity (significance unclear); reduced bioavailability of ketoconazole, ampicillin esters and iron.
A(iv)
Sucralfate may interfere with absorption of digoxin, tetracycline, phenytoin, iron, ciprofloxacin and cimetidine.
A(v)
Misoprostol has no reported interactions; bismuth subsalicylate in high doses causes salicylism.
B(i)
Antacids bind tetracycline and fluoroquinolones; reduce absorption of cimetidine, ranitidine, digoxin, isoniazid, iron, ketoconazole and phenothiazines.
B(ii)
Cimetidine with phenytoin, theophylline, phenobarbital, lidocaine, warfarin, imipramine, diazepam, propranolol.
B(iii)
Antacids 1 hr apart from cimetidine and ranitidine; 30-60 mins apart from sucralfate.
C(i)
Recognizing these interactions prevents loss of efficacy of antibiotics and toxicity of narrow-range drugs.
C(ii)
Frequent dosing and many drugs reduce adherence (stated for H. pylori therapy).
C(iii)
Clinical significance is unclear for some (clopidogrel).

questions.question:
A patient with first-episode schizophrenia has shown inadequate improvement after a trial of a single antipsychotic.
(i) Identify the likely reasons for failure.
(ii) State the parameters to assess.
(iii) Recommend changes to therapy.
(iv) State the criteria for escalation.
(v) Give the adherence and patient-education measures.
questions.answerText:
(i)
EPS are the main reason for non-adherence and the patient's attitude toward a drug may affect compliance.
(ii)
History of drug response and adverse effects; side effects by a patient-rated scale; EPS, weight, glucose, QTc prolongation, orthostatic hypotension, prolactin effects; WBC regularly if clozapine is used.
(iii)
Stage 2: trial of an alternative SGA or FGA monotherapy (excluding clozapine); Stage 3: clozapine monotherapy (delayed because of safety concerns and WBC monitoring; superior for suicidal behaviour).
(iv)
Stage 4: clozapine plus FGA, SGA or ECT; Stage 5: single agent not previously tried; Stage 6: combinations (not evidence-based; stop if no improvement). Hospitalization if severe, danger to self or others, or unable to self-care.
(v)
CBT, family interventions, social support, psychosocial rehabilitation; recovery may take weeks or months; some need medication indefinitely at the lowest possible dose.

questions.question:
A patient with cluster headache has severe unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation, nasal stuffiness and ptosis, and has not responded to oxygen, sumatriptan, verapamil or lithium; the pain is partly bilateral with residual headache between attacks.
(i) Identify the likely reasons for failure.
(ii) State the parameters to assess.
(iii) Recommend changes to therapy.
(iv) State the criteria for referral or escalation.
(v) Give the patient-education measures.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Atypical features (no periodic pattern, residual headache, bilaterality, incomplete response) suggest a structural lesion; sumatriptan has a long onset of action; precipitants such as alcohol and tobacco may persist.
(ii)
Pattern and periodicity, attack frequency (one every other day to eight per day), duration (15-180 minutes), autonomic signs, lateralizing findings.
(iii)
Abortive: 100% oxygen at 7 L/min for 10-15 minutes, ergotamine IV for 3-7 days. Prophylaxis: verapamil 240-360 mg/day, lithium 660-900 mg/day, ergotamine 1-2 mg, methysergide 4-8 mg/day. Refractory: prednisolone 40-60 mg/day tapered over about 3 weeks; others valproic acid, transdermal clonidine, intranasal capsaicin, leuprolide, bright light.
(iv)
A structural lesion should be suspected if the presentation is atypical.
(v)
Avoid alcohol and tobacco and precipitants (hot weather, nitroglycerin, stress, glare, allergic rhinitis, sexual activity).

(i)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (inflammatory multisystem disorder; arthralgia and rashes most common, cerebral and renal disease most serious).
(ii)
Widespread vasculitis (capillaries, arterioles, venules); loss of self tolerance (B cell activation, immune complexes, impaired T cell regulation, abnormal cytokines). Predisposing: hereditary, HLA genes, complement deficiency, sex hormones, drugs (hydralazine, methyldopa, isoniazid, D-penicillamine), UV light.
(iii)
Prognosis is good and drug therapy is for active disease, with no evidence that treatment in remission alters progression.
(iv)
NSAIDs for arthralgia, arthritis, fever, serositis; chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine for mild skin disease, fatigue and arthralgias uncontrolled by NSAIDs; oral corticosteroids or high-dose IV boluses and/or azathioprine or cyclophosphamide for severe disease (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, cerebral disease, blood dyscrasias). Avoid excessive sun.
(v)
FBC, ESR (rises with activity), ANA, serum complement (reduced in active disease), immunoglobulins, proteinuria; biopsies and imaging as needed.
(vi)
Discuss the disease and management with a caring approach; avoid sun exposure; flares can be induced by the contraceptive pill and HRT.
questions.question:
A woman aged 30 presents with fever, marked malaise, painful symmetrical small-joint pains with normal-looking joints, butterfly-distribution facial erythema worsened by sun, proteinuria above 1 g per 24 hours, anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia and positive antinuclear antibodies.
(i) Identify the likely condition.
(ii) State the pathophysiological basis and aetiology.
(iii) Outline the treatment goals.
(iv) Recommend first-line pharmacological and non-pharmacological management.
(v) Give the monitoring parameters.
(vi) Give the counselling points.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Misoprostol is contraindicated in pregnancy because of its abortifacient property and should not be used in women with childbearing potential unless NSAID therapy is needed and the risk of gastric ulcer complications is high; patients must be warned not to give it to others.
(ii)
Prophylaxis with a PPI (omeprazole 20-40 mg daily or lansoprazole 15-30 mg daily), using the lowest effective NSAID dose, switching to a COX-2 inhibitor such as celecoxib, or acetaminophen where possible.
(iii)
PPI or prostaglandin-analog regimens dramatically reduce NSAID ulcer risk; COX-2 inhibitors cause fewer ulcers; NSAIDs injure the mucosa by reducing PGE₂ and PGI₂ synthesis; prophylaxis suits those with prior PUD or GI bleeding, age over 60, or steroids or anticoagulants.
(iv)
Misoprostol 200 mcg QDS with food (100 mcg QDS if not tolerated), for the duration of NSAID therapy, with no routine renal adjustment; PPIs in the morning 30-60 mins before eating.
(v)
Diarrhoea (14-40%) and abdominal pain (13-20%) with misoprostol, needing stoppage in about 2%; for active NSAID ulcers use a PPI and stop the NSAID; ulcers not healed by 8 weeks (duodenal) or 12 weeks (gastric) are refractory.
questions.question:
A woman of childbearing age with a history of NSAID-induced gastric ulcer requires chronic daily NSAID therapy and is proposed for misoprostol prophylaxis.
(i) Identify the problem with the proposed therapy.
(ii) Recommend a suitable alternative.
(iii) Justify the choice.
(iv) State the dose adjustments or precautions.
(v) State the monitoring plan.

questions.answerText:
(i)
HRT should be avoided in women with blood clots (also breast, uterine or endometrial cancer, heart or liver disease, suspected pregnancy, stroke); HRT carries higher risk of cardiovascular disease, breast and endometrial cancer, venous thromboembolism and gallbladder disease.
(ii)
Lifestyle changes (exercise, weight control, smoking cessation, healthy diet); vaginal lubricants for dryness; antidepressants sometimes prescribed for hot flushes.
(iii)
Antidepressants offer benefits similar to low-dose estrogen without the risks (study cited); aerobic and strength exercise and a balanced diet help maintain bone strength.
(iv)
If HRT is otherwise used: lowest dose, shortest time; risks of clots, breast cancer and stroke increase after 5 years; in an intact uterus estrogen alone raises endometrial cancer risk, so progestogen is added.
(v)
Women should contact the doctor for bloating, breast swelling or tenderness, headaches, mood changes, nausea or vaginal bleeding; menopausal symptom therapy can be stopped after about 2-3 years.
questions.question:
A menopausal woman with hot flushes, night sweats and vaginal dryness has a history of blood clots and is being considered for hormone replacement therapy.
(i) Identify the problem with the proposed therapy.
(ii) Recommend suitable alternatives.
(iii) Justify the choice.
(iv) State the dose adjustments or precautions.
(v) State the monitoring plan.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Identify signs and symptoms such as fatigue, pallor and poor wound healing; early detection and referral in malnutrition.
A(ii)
Educate and counsel patients and caregivers on diet and supplements; PEM counselling: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, complementary feeding from 6 months, hygiene, growth monitoring, immunization.
A(iii)
Recommend and dispense oral supplements or injectables; ensure proper administration of therapeutic feeds; manage the supply chain.
A(iv)
Repeat blood tests, adjust doses, monitor toxicity (especially fat-soluble vitamins and minerals); manage drug-nutrient interactions; public health and preventive care.
B(i)
Vitamin A (night blindness, malnourished children), D (rickets, elderly), B12 (megaloblastic anaemia, vegans), folic acid (neural tube defects, pregnancy), C (scurvy, smokers), iron (reproductive-age women, infants), iodine (goitre), zinc, magnesium.
B(ii)
Antacids (B12, iron, calcium), diuretics (K, Mg, Zn), metformin (B12), antibiotics (vitamins K and B), isoniazid (B6), bariatric surgery.
B(iii)
PEM: nutrition-focused medication management; follow-up visits in the first week and monthly for 6 months; counselling for at-risk adults on supplementation and adherence to therapeutic nutrition.

Monitoring for toxicity and addressing drug-nutrient interactions prevents harm; thiamine and phosphate during refeeding prevent complications.
C(ii)
Correcting the underlying cause with supplementation and dietary change with monitoring improves outcomes; community nutrition programmes support adherence.

Treatment depends on the specific nutrient, severity and underlying cause.
questions.question:
Describe the role of the pharmacist in managing vitamin and mineral deficiencies and protein-energy malnutrition.
A(i) Patient assessment and screening. A(ii) Patient education and counselling. A(iii) Supplement recommendation and dispensing. A(iv) Monitoring, follow-up and drug-nutrient interaction management.
B(i) Relate to examples of at-risk groups and deficiency signs. B(ii) Relate to drug-induced causes. B(iii) Relate to PEM counselling and follow-up.
C(i) How it improves safety. C(ii) How it improves efficacy and adherence. C(iii) What limitations result.

A patient takes metformin, an antacid and a diuretic long term and complains of fatigue, pallor and poor wound healing.
(i) Identify the drugs and nutrients involved.
(ii) Explain the mechanism and clinical consequence.
(iii) Recommend management.
(iv) Give the counselling advice.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Metformin (vitamin B12), antacids (B12, iron, calcium), diuretics (potassium, magnesium, zinc).
(ii)
These drugs interfere with nutrient absorption or increase losses. B12 deficiency: megaloblastic anaemia and neuropathy; iron: microcytic hypochromic anaemia, fatigue, pallor; magnesium: neuromuscular irritability, arrhythmias; zinc: delayed wound healing, growth retardation, taste changes.
(iii)
Identify and address the cause, adjust medications that interfere; oral supplements, or injectables if oral absorption is poor or rapid correction is needed; dietary modification; repeat blood tests, adjust doses, monitor for toxicity.
(iv)
Pharmacist roles: assess signs (fatigue, pallor, poor wound healing), educate and counsel, recommend and dispense supplements, monitor and follow up, manage drug-nutrient interactions.

(i)
Double depression: dysthymia (chronic mood disturbance longer than 2 years) with a superimposed major depressive episode; up to 20% of patients hospitalized for a major episode have underlying dysthymia. The patient may wrongly be viewed as a partial responder.
(ii)
An adequate history to set a realistic therapeutic end point; past antidepressants used, which worked, adverse effects and patient views; rating scales (Beck Depression Inventory, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale); medical evaluation to rule out organic causes.
(iii)
Stop escalating doses or switching drugs; dysthymia is often unresponsive to antidepressants and the most effective treatment is non-drug psychotherapy (behavioural, cognitive, interpersonal and others).
(iv)
Escalation: add an antipsychotic if delusions; ECT for drug-resistant depression; rTMS for those not responding to at least one antidepressant. Step-down: continuation about 6 months, symptom-free 16-20 weeks before stopping, reduce maintenance dose by 30-50%, taper by no more than 25% every 1-2 weeks; highest relapse risk in first 8 weeks after stopping.
(v)
Take antidepressants as prescribed and continue when feeling better; onset takes 4-6 weeks; counsel on expected adverse effects and withdrawal effects; avoid routine one-month supplies because of overdose toxicity; psychotherapy improves psychosocial function while maintenance drugs reduce relapse.
questions.question:
A patient hospitalized for a major depressive episode responded to an antidepressant but returned to a chronic mild depressed baseline; the clinician keeps increasing the dose and changing drugs.
(i) Identify the likely reasons for failure.
(ii) State the parameters to assess.
(iii) Recommend changes to therapy.
(iv) State the criteria for escalation or step-down.
(v) Give the adherence and patient-education measures.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
SSRIs (citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline, fluoxetine, paroxetine); SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine); bupropion; TCAs, MAOIs, tetracyclics.
A(ii)
Most are potent inhibitors of norepinephrine and/or serotonin reuptake and also antagonize histamine-1, muscarinic, α-1 and dopamine-2 receptors.
A(iii)
Depression; bupropion also for seasonal affective disorder; TCAs for prophylaxis in frequent relapse.
A(iv)
Sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, reduced cardiac conduction, sexual dysfunction, weight gain; overdose causes CNS, cardiovascular and anticholinergic toxicity.
A(v)
Precautions include TCA orthostatic hypotension in cardiac conduction defects, antihypertensives; bipolar patients may switch to mania; bupropion can exacerbate psychosis.
B(i)
Past history of response and adverse-effect profile; no difference in overall efficacy or onset except atypical and delusional depression.
B(ii)
Start with small divided doses, assessing tolerance, sedation and orthostatic hypotension.
B(iii)
More conservative initial dosing and slower titration because elderly are more sensitive to therapeutic and toxic effects.
B(iv)
A lag of 4-6 weeks before effect.
C(i)
MAOI to TCA needs a 2-week washout; TCA to MAOI can be done without washout because TCA reuptake blockade is immediate while MAOI blockade develops over weeks.
C(ii)
SSRIs and SNRIs act by reuptake inhibition; bupropion works differently, treats depression and seasonal affective disorder.
C(iii)
Orthostatic hypotension is common with TCAs (except nortriptyline) and more frequent with MAOIs; fluoxetine and bupropion cause none and no continued weight gain.
questions.question:
Discuss antidepressants under the following headings.
A(i) Classification. A(ii) Mechanism of action. A(iii) Indications. A(iv) Adverse effects. A(v) Contraindications and precautions.
B(i) Rationale for selection. B(ii) Initiation. B(iii) Use in the elderly. B(iv) Onset of action.
C(i) Distinguish switching between MAOIs and TCAs. C(ii) Distinguish SSRIs/SNRIs from bupropion. C(iii) Distinguish effects on orthostatic hypotension and weight.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Simple analgesics for mild infrequent migraine; aspirin the drug of choice, paracetamol if aspirin is contraindicated, caffeine to aid absorption.
A(ii)
Ibuprofen 400-600 mg; ergotamine 1 mg with caffeine 100 mg (max 6 tablets/day or 10/week); sumatriptan 25 mg repeated at 2 hours (max 300 mg/day), rizatriptan 5-10 mg (max 30 mg/day).
A(iii)
Midrin when sumatriptan or ergotamine cannot be used; prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine; metoclopramide 10 mg 15-30 minutes before; short corticosteroid courses.
A(iv)
Propranolol, amitriptyline, methysergide, valproic acid, verapamil; started at low doses and raised slowly; continue at least 6 months after improvement then taper.
B(i)
Attacks more than 2-3 per month, severe or prolonged with impairment, symptomatic therapy failed or caused serious effects, patient unable to cope, or predictable pattern such as menstrual migraine.
B(ii)
A trial of 2-3 months is needed to judge each prophylactic drug.
B(iii)
Simple analgesics and NSAIDs acutely; amitriptyline prevention when attacks occur more than 2 days a week; biofeedback, CBT, relaxation.
B(iv)
Oxygen 100% at 7 L/min for 10-15 minutes; sumatriptan; verapamil 240-360 mg/day, lithium 660-900 mg/day; prednisolone 40-60 mg/day for refractory.
C(i)
Status migrainosus (over 72 hours despite treatment) and migrainous infarction.
C(ii)
Pregnant patients can use non-pharmacological options; in elderly new-onset headache obtain ESR and consider biopsy to exclude temporal arteritis.
C(iii)
Frequent ergotamine dosing causes dependency, withdrawal, ergotism; frequent combination analgesic use reduces relief; failed symptomatic therapy is an indication for prophylaxis.
questions.question:
Describe the therapeutic approach to migraine, cluster and tension-type headache.
A(i) Abortive therapy. A(ii) NSAIDs, ergotamine and triptans. A(iii) Miscellaneous agents. A(iv) Prophylaxis and duration.
B(i) When prophylaxis is started. B(ii) Criteria for assessing response. B(iii) Tension-type treatment. B(iv) Cluster treatment.

Describe the hormone replacement therapy regimens for menopause.
A(i) Estrogen alone. A(ii) Continuous cyclic (sequential). A(iii) Continuous combined. A(iv) Continuous long-cycle. A(v) Intermittent combined.
B(i) Response in vasomotor symptoms. B(ii) Bleeding patterns as a response criterion. B(iii) Duration and stopping.
C(i) Risks and populations to avoid. C(ii) Management of unpredictable bleeding. C(iii) Benefits for bone and vagina. C(iv) Treatment failure and alternatives.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Low-dose estrogen suggested for women who have had a hysterectomy.
A(ii)
Daily estrogen with a progestogen for at least 12-14 days of a 28-day cycle; withdrawal bleeding in about 90%.
A(iii)
Daily estrogen and progestogen; endometrial atrophy and no bleeding; reserved for women at least 2 years post-menopause.
A(iv)
Daily estrogen with progestogen 6 times a year for 12-14 days; endometrial protection unclear.
A(v)
3 days estrogen alone then 3 days estrogen plus progestogen repeated; endometrial protection undetermined.
B(i)
Estrogens diminish hot flushes in most women with a dose-dependent effect; younger women may need higher doses.
B(ii)
Bleeding about 1-2 days after the last progestogen dose in cyclic therapy; spotting resolving within 6-12 months in continuous combined.
B(iii)
Therapy for symptoms can stop after about 2-3 years; use the lowest dose for the shortest time; risks increase after 5 years.
C(i)
Higher risks of cardiovascular disease, breast and endometrial cancer, thromboembolism and gallbladder disease; avoid in blood clots, cancers, heart or liver disease, pregnancy, stroke.
C(ii)
Decrease estrogen or increase progestogen; occasionally a drug-free period of 1-2 weeks.
C(iii)
Prevents bone loss while treatment continues; local or systemic estrogen for vaginal atrophy.
C(iv)
Lifestyle changes, vaginal lubricants and antidepressants are alternatives.

questions.question:
A patient being treated for GERD and ulcer disease takes cimetidine together with phenytoin and warfarin, takes an antacid at the same time as tetracycline, and takes sucralfate together with ciprofloxacin.
(i) Identify the interacting drugs.
(ii) Explain the mechanism and clinical consequence of each interaction.
(iii) Classify the severity or significance.
(iv) Recommend management (substitution, spacing, dose change, monitoring).
(v) Give the counselling advice.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Cimetidine with phenytoin and warfarin; antacid with tetracycline; sucralfate with ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone). Other listed antacid interactions include digoxin, isoniazid, iron, ketoconazole, phenothiazines, cimetidine and ranitidine.
(ii)
Cimetidine binds the hepatic cytochrome P450 system (hepatic enzyme inhibitor) and interferes with metabolism of phenytoin, warfarin, theophylline, phenobarbital, lidocaine, imipramine, diazepam, propranolol; it also decreases hepatic blood flow, reducing clearance of propranolol and lidocaine. Antacids bind tetracycline and fluoroquinolones, inhibiting absorption and reducing efficacy. Sucralfate may interfere with absorption of tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, digoxin, phenytoin, iron and cimetidine if given simultaneously.
(iii)
Antacids are described as having a high potential for drug interactions because they alter gastric pH.
(iv)
Antacids should be given 1 hr apart from cimetidine or ranitidine; antacids and sucralfate 30 to 60 mins apart; omeprazole also interferes with CYP450 metabolism of diazepam, warfarin and phenytoin.
(v)
Timing advice: antacids after each meal and at bedtime, PPIs 30 to 60 mins before eating.

A(i)
Indirectly acting cholinomimetics: edrophonium (short-acting), neostigmine (intermediate), pyridostigmine (long-acting).
A(ii)
They inhibit acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine levels and duration and enhancing neuromuscular transmission.
A(iii)
First-line in MG, most useful for ocular MG or as adjunct to immunosuppressants in generalized MG; edrophonium for diagnosis; neostigmine for long-term therapy.
A(iv)
Mostly muscarinic: sweating, increased salivary and gastric secretions, GI and uterine motility, bradycardia; edrophonium causes lacrimation, cramps, diarrhoea, miosis and bradycardia, gone in about 5 minutes.
B(i)
Neostigmine is the drug of choice but has pronounced muscarinic action; pyridostigmine is preferred for smoother action and fewer doses.
B(ii)
No fixed dose because symptoms vary daily; neostigmine 15-30 mg orally every 3-4 hours, max 180 mg daily, 1.5 mg IM or 0.5 mg IV for severe dysphagia; titrated to muscle strength.
B(iii)
Atropine 0.4-0.6 mg daily orally or propantheline counteracts muscarinic effects.
B(iv)
Adjunct to immunosuppressant therapy such as corticosteroids.
C(i)
Edrophonium: short-acting, diagnostic (2 mg IV, max 10 mg); neostigmine: intermediate, therapeutic and diagnostic (1.5 mg IM with 0.6 mg atropine).
C(ii)
Pyridostigmine is long-acting, less powerful and slower, preferred in patients weak on walking.
C(iii)
Excessive dosage causes cholinergic crisis through a depolarizing block, whereas myasthenic crisis is worsening disease; both show severe weakness and breathing difficulty.
questions.question:
Discuss anticholinesterase drugs used in myasthenia gravis under the following headings.
A(i) Classification. A(ii) Mechanism of action. A(iii) Indications. A(iv) Adverse effects.
B(i) Rationale for choosing a drug. B(ii) Dosing approach. B(iii) Role of atropine and propantheline. B(iv) Place alongside other therapy.

questions.question: Evasion of host immune system is accomplished by:
questions.explanation: Immune evasion mechanisms include capsule production, antigenic variation, intracellular survival, and immunosuppressive factors that help bacteria avoid or survive immune attacks. Successful pathogens must evade at least some immune defenses to establish infection. Multiple evasion strategies often work synergistically.

Tuberculosis can be transmitted through contaminated unpasteurized milk from infected cattle. Pasteurization effectively kills Mycobacterium tuberculosis along with other milk-borne pathogens. This public health measure has dramatically reduced milk-borne disease transmission.
questions.question: Which zoonotic disease does pasteurization prevent transmission of?

questions.explanation: Mutualism involves symbiotic interactions where both host and bacteria benefit from the association, representing ideal host-microbe relationships. The host gains nutrition, immune stimulation, and pathogen protection, while bacteria gain nutrients and habitat. Mutualistic relationships promote health and resist disruption.
questions.question: In mutualism, the interaction benefits:
Which Aspergillus species most commonly causes disease?
questions.explanation: Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common Aspergillus species causing human disease due to optimal growth at body temperature. Small conidia enable deep lung penetration. This thermotolerant species accounts for majority of aspergillosis cases.

Erythromycin has a relatively short half-life of 1.4 hours, requiring frequent dosing for maintaining therapeutic levels. This rapid elimination results from hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion. The short duration limits its convenience compared to newer macrolides.
questions.question: What is erythromycin's half-life?

questions.explanation: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis represents the most common presentation, beginning in paranasal sinuses and potentially extending to brain. Diabetic ketoacidosis particularly predisposes to this fulminant infection. Rapid diagnosis and treatment are essential.
questions.question: What is the most common form of mucormycosis?
Why are viable counts required for antibiotic susceptibility testing?
questions.explanation: Antibiotic susceptibility testing measures growth inhibition of viable organisms by antimicrobial agents. Dead organisms cannot demonstrate susceptibility or resistance. Viable cells must grow in control conditions to validate results.
options: Only living organisms can exhibit growth inhibition
Dead cells respond to antibiotic treatment

questions.question: What critical step must follow ethylene oxide sterilization?
questions.explanation: Ethylene oxide residues are toxic and must be removed through prolonged aeration before item use. This off-gassing period allows residual gas to dissipate to safe levels. Aeration time depends on material type and sterilization conditions.
options: Immediate heating to activate residual gas
Water rinsing to dissolve remaining chemicals
Exposure to ultraviolet radiation for activation

questions.question: Where are antimicrobial enzymes commonly utilized?
questions.explanation: Antimicrobial enzymes enhance detergent cleaning effectiveness and extend food product shelf life. These enzymes break down biofilms, proteins, and other organic matter harboring microorganisms. Industrial applications exploit enzymatic specificity and environmental compatibility.
options: Detergents for cleaning and food preservation

questions.explanation: Solar disinfection targets waterborne pathogenic bacteria, viruses, and protozoa that cause diarrheal diseases. The method provides low-cost water treatment in resource-limited settings. However, it cannot remove chemical contaminants or turbidity.
questions.question: Which organisms are targeted by solar water disinfection?

questions.explanation: Aflatoxin produced by Aspergillus flavus in contaminated nuts and grains causes hepatotoxicity and is carcinogenic. This potent mycotoxin accumulates in improperly stored foods. Aflatoxin exposure poses serious health risks.
questions.question: Which toxin causes hepatotoxicity from Aspergillus flavus?

questions.explanation: Fungi naturally inhabit soil or water containing decaying organic material, serving as primary decomposers. These environments provide abundant nutrients from dead plant and animal matter. The ubiquitous presence in soil explains environmental acquisition of many fungal infections.
options: Soil or water with decaying matter
questions.question: Where is fungi's natural habitat primarily located?

questions.explanation: Duodenal aspiration or string test (Enterotest) can detect Giardia lamblia trophozoites when stool examinations are negative, as the organism inhabits the duodenum and proximal jejunum. The capsule with string is swallowed and retrieved, bringing duodenal contents containing trophozoites. This is particularly useful in symptomatic patients with negative stool examinations.
questions.question: Duodenal aspirate is most useful for diagnosing which parasitic infection?

questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is commonly found in the nose and nasopharynx as part of normal flora, along with Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and others. Despite being normal flora, S. aureus can cause serious infections if it enters normally sterile sites or if host immunity is compromised. Approximately 30% of healthy individuals carry S. aureus in their nasal passages.
questions.question: Staphylococcus aureus is commonly found as normal flora in the:

questions.explanation: Beta-lactam antibiotics form covalent bonds with penicillin binding proteins through acylation reactions. This irreversible binding permanently inactivates the target enzyme. The covalent nature of this interaction explains the bactericidal activity of beta-lactams.
questions.question: How do beta-lactam antibiotics bind to their target enzymes?
Dynamic equilibrium between human body and microbes is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium involves active interaction between human body and microbes rather than mutual indifference, with both deriving benefits. This relationship constantly adjusts to maintain balance despite environmental and physiological changes. The dynamic nature allows adaptation to varying conditions while maintaining overall stability.

questions.question: What problem results from storing media where it's too cold?
questions.explanation: Excessive cold causes chemical instability and may freeze aqueous media, damaging component structure. Freezing destroys agar gel integrity through ice crystal formation. Storage requires cool but non-freezing temperatures within specified ranges.

questions.question: What is tigecycline's half-life range?
questions.explanation: Tigecycline has an exceptionally long half-life ranging from 37 to 67 hours. This extended duration allows less frequent dosing but requires careful monitoring. The large volume of distribution contributes to the prolonged elimination.

Autoclaves must maintain at least 15 psi pressure to achieve the 121°C temperature required for sterilization. Pressure and steam together ensure heat penetration throughout media volumes. Lower pressure results in inadequate temperature
questions.question: What pressure must autoclaves maintain for sterilization?
Xenodiagnosis is specifically employed for detecting which parasitic infection?
questions.explanation: Xenodiagnosis for Trypanosoma cruzi involves allowing laboratory-reared triatomine bugs to feed on suspected patients, then examining the bugs' intestinal contents weeks later for parasites. This technique is useful in chronic Chagas disease when blood parasitemia is extremely low and direct detection methods fail. The bugs concentrate parasites in their gut.

Transfer intervals vary with bacterial species, culture medium used, and storage temperature requirements. Different organisms have different survival rates and growth characteristics necessitating individualized schedules. Optimal intervals balance viability maintenance with workload management.
questions.question: Which factor determines transfer intervals in periodic subculturing?
Loeffler syndrome characterized by pulmonary eosinophilia is caused by which larval migration?
questions.explanation: Loeffler syndrome occurs when helminth larvae (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides) migrate through pulmonary tissue during their life cycle, causing transient pneumonitis with eosinophilia. The inflammatory response to larval passage through alveoli produces cough, dyspnea, and fleeting pulmonary infiltrates on X-ray. This represents an immunological response to the migrating larvae.

Outbreak investigations require isolating and characterizing viable pathogens to determine sources and transmission routes. Only culture-based viable counting provides isolates for typing and molecular epidemiology. Pathogen identification is impossible without viable organisms.
questions.question: Which count type is essential for outbreak investigation?

questions.explanation: Heat-sensitive substances including sera, antibiotics, and vitamins require filtration sterilization to avoid thermal degradation. These biological and pharmaceutical products maintain activity when filter-sterilized. The method preserves molecular structure and biological function.
options: Heat-labile substances like sera and antibiotics
questions.question: For which materials is filtration sterilization most appropriate?

options: Two growth forms dependent on conditions
questions.question: What defines dimorphic fungi?
questions.explanation: Dimorphic fungi exist in two morphological forms: mold phase at environmental temperatures (25°C) and yeast phase at body temperature (37°C). This temperature-dependent transformation is critical for pathogenesis. Most systemic mycosis agents exhibit thermal dimorphism.

questions.question: Normal flora are found mostly in all areas EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Normal flora inhabit eyes, upper respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, vagina, external ear, and skin, but blood and cerebrospinal fluid remain sterile in health. Surface tissues exposed to environment harbor microorganisms, while internal sterile sites are protected by barriers and immune defenses. This distribution reflects accessibility to environmental microbes.

options: Production of toxins causing host damage
questions.question: Toxigenicity refers to:
questions.explanation: Toxigenicity is the ability to produce toxins (exotoxins or endotoxins) that cause host damage, representing a major virulence mechanism. Some bacteria cause disease primarily through toxin production without tissue invasion. Toxin neutralization with antitoxins can prevent or treat these diseases.

questions.question: Leishmania donovani causes which systemic disease presentation?
questions.explanation: Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with massive hepatosplenomegaly, fever, weight loss, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia as parasites multiply in reticuloendothelial cells throughout the body. Without treatment, it is fatal. This differs from cutaneous species like L. major and mucocutaneous species like L. braziliensis.

questions.question: Paragonimus westermani metacercariae are found in which intermediate host?
questions.explanation: Paragonimus westermani uses freshwater crabs and crayfish as second intermediate hosts where metacercariae encyst in tissues. Humans acquire infection by eating raw, pickled, or undercooked crustaceans in endemic areas of Asia. After ingestion, metacercariae penetrate intestine, migrate through diaphragm, and settle in lungs forming cystic lesions.

questions.question: What is the most common use of sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim combination?
questions.explanation: Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim combination is most commonly used for urinary tract infections. Both components concentrate in urine, achieving high local levels. The synergistic activity provides effective coverage against common uropathogens.

Microaerophiles like Campylobacter and Helicobacter require low oxygen concentrations (typically 5-10%), being damaged by both atmospheric oxygen and anaerobiosis. They require specialized incubation conditions with reduced oxygen and increased carbon dioxide. Microaerophiles occupy an environmental niche between aerobes and anaerobes.
questions.question: Microaerophiles require:

questions.explanation: Second and third-generation cephalosporins demonstrate effectiveness in treating community-acquired pneumonia. Their spectrum covers common respiratory pathogens including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Oral and parenteral formulations provide treatment flexibility.
questions.question: For which infections are second and third-generation cephalosporins effective?

questions.explanation: At refrigeration temperature (5°C), E. histolytica cysts can survive in water for up to 42 days, providing extended transmission potential. At room temperature, survival in water is approximately 10 days, while in feces it ranges 14-40 days. Cool, moist conditions maximize cyst viability.
questions.question: How long can E. histolytica cysts survive in water at 5°C?

questions.explanation: G. lamblia is generally believed to be pathogenic, with clinicians agreeing it may cause diarrhea, steatorrhea, or symptoms referable to gallbladder or duodenum. Heavy infections can interfere with intestinal absorption and cause malabsorption syndrome. Some infected individuals remain asymptomatic carriers.
questions.question: What is the general consensus about Giardia lamblia pathogenicity?
What is the primary purpose of culture preservation methods?
questions.explanation: Culture preservation maintains organism viability and purity free from contamination throughout storage. Proper preservation prevents genetic drift and phenotypic changes during maintenance. Multiple preservation methods suit different organism types and storage durations.

questions.question: Which media require refrigerator storage immediately after preparation?
questions.explanation: Media containing blood, antibiotics, or other heat-labile components require immediate refrigerator storage to prevent degradation. These sensitive ingredients lose activity at room temperature or in warm conditions. Proper cold storage preserves antimicrobial activity and growth factors.

questions.question: Approximately how many non-human genes exist in the human body for every human gene?
questions.explanation: There are approximately 300 non-human genes (from microbiota) for every human gene in the body, highlighting the massive genetic contribution of the microbiome. The human genome contains approximately 20,000-23,000 genes, while the human microbiome contains 5,000,000-10,000,000 genes from over 1000 species. This demonstrates the significant role microbiota play in human physiology.

questions.question: How does dry heat sterilization destroy microorganisms?
questions.explanation: Dry heat causes protein denaturation, oxidative free radical damage, and cellular desiccation leading to microbial death. Unlike moist heat, dry heat requires higher temperatures and longer exposure times. The absence of moisture means heat must directly damage cellular components.
options: By promoting rapid bacterial spore germination
Through protein denaturation and oxidative damage
Through enhanced metabolic activity leading to death
By stimulating production of toxic metabolites

questions.question: Why are aminoglycosides only available parenterally?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides' polar nature prevents significant gastrointestinal absorption, necessitating parenteral administration. The multiple charged groups cannot cross lipid membranes efficiently. This limitation restricts their use to injectable formulations.

questions.question: What disease results from ergot alkaloids in grain?
questions.explanation: Ergotism results from consuming grain contaminated with Claviceps purpurea ergot alkaloids. Historical epidemics caused gangrenous and convulsive symptoms. Modern grain processing reduces ergotism incidence.

T. hominis resides in the lumen of the colon and cecum, inhabiting the large intestine. Unlike Giardia which lives in the small intestine, Trichomonas hominis colonizes the lower intestinal tract. It lives as a commensal without causing disease.
questions.question: Where does Trichomonas hominis primarily reside?

questions.explanation: In schistosomes, miracidia (hatched from eggs in water) penetrate snails where they undergo asexual multiplication and development into cercariae, the infective stage for humans. The snail serves as the intermediate host essential for completing the life cycle. Different Schistosoma species require specific snail genera as intermediate hosts.
questions.question: In schistosomiasis transmission, snails serve as hosts for which larval stage?
When normal flora neither help nor harm the host, the relationship is:
questions.explanation: Commensalism describes relationships where normal flora neither hurt, harm, nor benefit the carrying host, representing a neutral association. One organism benefits (the bacteria) while the other (host) is unaffected. Many normal flora maintain commensal relationships under normal circumstances.

questions.question: In the relationship between Entamoeba gingivalis and humans, which type of symbiosis is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Entamoeba gingivalis is a commensal parasite found in the mouth where it feeds on bacteria, food particles, and dead epithelial cells without causing harm to the host. In commensalism, one organism benefits while the other remains unaffected, which accurately describes this relationship. This organism does not produce disease in immunocompetent individuals.

When pressurized steam condenses on surfaces, it releases latent heat that rapidly denatures proteins and kills microorganisms. This heat transfer is more efficient than dry heat at the same temperature. The combination of moisture and heat provides superior microbial destruction.
questions.question: Which principle explains the superior effectiveness of moist heat sterilization?
options: Moisture reduces the boiling point of water
Steam cannot penetrate into contaminated materials
Moist heat works only on vegetative cells
Steam under pressure delivers latent heat upon condensation

questions.explanation: Tyndallisation relies on cycles of heating to kill vegetative cells, followed by incubation allowing spores to germinate, then reheating to kill the germinated cells. This repetitive process eventually eliminates all spores without using destructive high temperatures. The method exploits the spore germination cycle for effective sterilization.
options: To allow complete evaporation of moisture
To gradually increase bacterial resistance to heat
To accommodate laboratory scheduling constraints only
To enhance sugar caramelization for media color
To permit spore germination between heating cycles
questions.question: Why is tyndallisation performed on three successive days?
How many flagella do Trichomonas species typically possess?
questions.explanation: Trichomonas species typically possess four anterior flagella extending from the anterior end. One flagellum extends posteriorly along the undulating membrane. The flagellar number and arrangement characterize the genus Trichomonas.

options: As few as 10-100 cells for highly virulent organisms
questions.explanation: Infectious dose varies widely; highly virulent organisms like Shigella require as few as 10-100 cells to cause infection, while others need millions. This variation reflects differences in virulence mechanisms, survival capability, and host defenses. Low infectious doses facilitate transmission and increase epidemic potential.
questions.question: The infectious dose varies among pathogens with some requiring:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa requires which atmospheric condition?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an obligate (strict) aerobe requiring oxygen for growth and energy generation through aerobic respiration. It cannot grow anaerobically and requires efficient oxygen utilization. This oxygen requirement influences its ecological niches and infection sites.

questions.question: Which describes tetrathionate broth's primary function?
questions.explanation: Tetrathionate broth selectively enriches Salmonella species by inhibiting coliforms and other intestinal bacteria. The tetrathionate acts as selective agent favoring Salmonella multiplication. It's used before plating fecal specimens on selective solid media.

questions.question: Toxocara canis causing visceral larva migrans in humans represents which classification?
questions.explanation: Accidental parasites attack unusual hosts where they would not normally complete their life cycle, as seen with Toxocara canis (dog roundworm) infecting humans. In humans, the larvae migrate through tissues causing visceral or cutaneous larva migrans but cannot mature to adult worms. Dogs are the natural definitive hosts for this parasite.

questions.question: How many nuclei do mature Endolimax nana cysts contain?
questions.explanation: Mature E. nana cysts characteristically contain four nuclei, similar to E. histolytica but distinguishable by nuclear morphology. The nuclei have small, central karyosomes rather than peripheral chromatin. Nuclear number and structure are critical for species differentiation among intestinal amebae.
