What percentage of the body's calcium is found in bones?
questions.explanation: Bones contain approximately 99% of the body's total calcium content, primarily as hydroxyapatite crystals. This massive concentration necessitates effective decalcification methods for histological examination. The remaining 1% circulates in blood and soft tissues.

courses.title: Exercise Physiology II
courses.objectives:
Muscle Structure, Contraction and Energy Systems: Q1–10
Acute Responses to Exercise and Factors Modifying Them: Q11–21
Chronic Adaptations, Detraining and Inactivity: Q22–29
Fitness Testing, Body Composition and Exercise Prescription: Q30–40

questions.question:
A 45-year-old client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus is referred to physiotherapy to begin an exercise programme.
(i) Identify the exercise-related condition affecting this client.
(ii) Explain the physiological basis of this condition in relation to exercise.
(iii) State the risk factors and possible complications this client may experience during exercise.
(iv) Discuss the exercise management or modification options available, and justify one of them.
questions.answerText:
(i) The client has diabetes mellitus (type 2), a metabolic disorder in which the body is unable to regulate blood glucose, caused by poor sensitivity to insulin (insulin resistance) or inadequate insulin production; exercise is one of the first management strategies advised for newly diagnosed patients, together with diet and behaviour modification.
(ii) Exercise facilitates the transport of glucose into the muscle cell and glycolysis, reduces insulin resistance and helps regulate blood glucose; it lowers uric acid and triglycerides and increases the HDL/LDL cholesterol ratio.
- Because exercise facilitates injected insulin absorption via increased blood flow to muscle, exercise can precipitate hypoglycemia in insulin-treated patients, and the insulin response to exercise differs from one patient to another, requiring individual evaluation.
(iii) Risk factors/complications: hypoglycemia, worsened if the injection site is a limb/muscle about to be exercised; individuals with proliferative retinopathy are at increased risk of haemorrhage with high-intensity exercise.
- Patients with peripheral neuropathy may have balance problems and a risk of falling and of foot injury; those with autonomic neuropathy or dehydration may develop postural hypotension.
- Patients with a history of, or suspected, coronary artery disease need specialist consultation before starting; solitary sports such as mountain climbing or diving should be avoided if hypoglycemia is uncontrolled.
(iv) Management/modification options include moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (e.g., walking briskly, cycling, swimming) and resistance exercise; using the "talk test" or a target-heart-rate method to regulate intensity; checking blood sugar before and after exercise and eating a small snack if it is below 100 mg/dL; avoiding insulin injection into a limb about to be exercised; and wearing cotton socks and proper athletic shoes, checking the feet after exercise for sores or blisters.
- Of these, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise such as brisk walking is justified as the exercise of choice because it is cheap, easy to perform, helps lower blood glucose, boosts insulin sensitivity and counters insulin resistance, while carrying a lower hypoglycemia and cardiovascular risk than high-intensity exercise.

questions.question:
A classmate who does not routinely engage in sports or exercise runs an 800-metre race as fast as possible, taking a little under 3 minutes to finish.
(i) Identify the energy system(s) primarily supplying ATP for this effort.
(ii) Explain the underlying mechanism of ATP production for this system.
(iii) Describe the acute responses of the body systems during and immediately after the race.
(iv) State the practical implication of this energy system for prescribing training for an event of this duration.
questions.answerText:
(i) The event lasts from about 30 seconds up to 2 minutes-plus of near-maximal effort, so the glycolytic (lactic acid/anaerobic glycolysis) system is the primary contributor, since people running an 800m event use this pathway the most, with the ATP-PCr system contributing at the start and the oxidative system contributing increasingly as the race progresses.
(ii) In the glycolytic system, glucose or glycogen is broken down to pyruvic acid and, because oxygen demand exceeds supply at this intensity, further to lactic acid, generating ATP anaerobically; this pathway yields about 4 molecules of ATP.
- Its major limitation is that it produces lactate, which lowers the pH of muscle and blood; once pH drops below about 6.4 to 6.6, enzymes critical for energy production can no longer function and ATP production stops.
(iii) During the race: heart rate, cardiac output, systolic blood pressure and pulmonary ventilation all rise steeply; blood lactate concentration rises well above resting levels once the athlete's lactate threshold is exceeded; blood flow is redistributed toward the active skeletal muscle.
- Immediately after the race: because this untrained classmate is not adapted to this exercise, the physiological strain (elevated heart rate, ventilation and blood lactate) will take longer to return to resting levels than in a trained athlete, and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption will occur as the body restores pre-exercise conditions.
(iv) Because the glycolytic system predominates for this duration and its capacity is limited by falling pH and lactate accumulation, training for an 800m-type event should include repeated near-maximal efforts of about 30 seconds to 2 minutes with sufficient recovery to allow lactate clearance, to progressively improve the athlete's tolerance of, and capacity to buffer, high blood lactate levels.

questions.question:
A previously well-conditioned athlete who had been training six times per week stops all exercise training completely for 2 weeks because of a minor injury, and on reassessment shows a significant reduction in VO₂max and a decrease in plasma volume, although his muscular strength appears largely unchanged.
(i) Name the phenomenon illustrated by this scenario.
(ii) Explain the contributing factors and underlying physiology.
(iii) State the management/training implication of this finding.
questions.answerText:
(i) This illustrates detraining, the loss of training-induced physiological efficiency and capacity that occurs with removal of the training stimulus.
(ii) With complete cessation of exercise training, a significant reduction in VO₂max and a decrease in plasma volume occur within 2 weeks, and all prior functional gains are dissipated within 2 to 8 months, even if routine low- to moderate-intensity physical activity replaces training.
- Muscular strength and power, however, are reduced at a much slower rate than VO₂max, particularly during the first few months after an athlete discontinues resistance training; no decrement in either strength or power may occur for the first 4 to 6 weeks after training ends.
- Even after 12 months, almost half of the strength gained might still be retained if the athlete remains moderately active.
(iii) Because VO₂max/cardiorespiratory fitness is lost much faster than muscular strength once training stops, this athlete's return-to-training plan should prioritise re-establishing his aerobic/cardiorespiratory conditioning promptly, while recognising that his strength gains are likely to be largely preserved over this short a period and will not require the same urgency of retraining.

questions.question:
A(i) Define a motor unit and describe its organisation, including innervation ratio.
A(ii) Describe the neuromuscular junction and the process of excitation-contraction coupling.
A(iii) Describe the size principle of motor unit recruitment.
B(i) Explain the functional/clinical significance of motor unit recruitment for grading of muscle force.
C(i) Distinguish between a single twitch and tetanus.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A motor unit consists of a group of muscle fibres that are innervated by the same motor neuron; motor units can consist of only a few muscle fibres (e.g., the optic muscles) or up to about 2,000 muscle fibres (e.g., the gastrocnemius).
- The size of a motor unit is described by its innervation ratio (IR), the number of muscle fibres innervated by a given motor neuron, which ranges from less than a dozen for the extraocular muscles to over a thousand for motor units of large limb muscles, and is a major factor governing the motor unit's force output.
A(ii) The neuromuscular junction is the synapse/gap between a motor nerve and a muscle fibre, where communication between the nervous and muscular systems occurs; when a nerve impulse arrives at the axon terminals, acetylcholine is released and binds to receptors on the sarcolemma, creating an electric charge transmitted along the muscle fibre (depolarization), generating an action potential.
- This wave of depolarization spreads to the muscle membrane as calcium ions are released into the area surrounding the myofibrils, promoting cross-bridge formation between actin and myosin; when stimulation stops, the ions are actively removed from around the myofibrils, releasing the cross-bridges; this sequence is termed excitation-contraction coupling.
A(iii) Muscle force can be increased by recruiting increasingly larger motor units; the sequence of motor unit recruitment usually follows the size principle, whereby small, slow-twitch motor units are recruited first, followed by fast-twitch oxidative units, and finally the large, fast-twitch glycolytic motor units.
- After a motor unit is recruited it remains active until force declines, at which point motor units are deactivated in reverse order, with the large motoneurons going first.
B(i) Because increasing muscle force requires an increase in the number of motor units activated, and because recruitment proceeds from small to large motoneurons (fatigue-resistant to fatigable), this size-principle pattern allows fine, low-force movements to be produced by small motor units while reserving the large, powerful but easily fatigable motor units for near-maximal efforts.
C(i) A single action potential that activates a fibre causes the force to increase and then decrease; this is a twitch; if a second stimulus occurs before the initial twitch has subsided, another twitch builds on the first, and with subsequent high-frequency stimulation, force continues to build to a state called unfused tetanus.
- When the force builds to a level at which there is no further increase in muscle force despite continued stimulation, the force level has reached (fused) tetanus.

questions.question:
An athlete performs a session of downhill running with repeated eccentric loading of the quadriceps, and 24 to 48 hours later reports significant soreness and stiffness in the thighs that limits activity.
(i) Name the phenomenon illustrated by this scenario.
(ii) Explain the contributing factors and underlying physiology.
(iii) State the training implication of this finding.
questions.answerText:
(i) This illustrates delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS).
(ii) During both aerobic and resistance exercise, active muscles can undergo changes that lead to muscle soreness; some soreness is felt immediately after exercise, but delayed-onset muscle soreness occurs 24 to 48 hours following exercise and is a more limiting soreness.
- It is primarily associated with eccentric-type muscle action, during which the muscle exerts force while lengthening, as can happen when a person runs down a steep hill or lowers a weight from a fully flexed to a fully extended position.
- Delayed-onset muscle soreness results from structural damage to the muscle and appears to result in an inflammatory response; in its most severe form it may include rupture of the cell membrane and disruption of the contractile elements of individual muscle fibres.
(iii) Because this delayed soreness is associated with eccentric muscle action and structural damage, whereas the milder soreness felt immediately after exercise is generally not physically limiting and dissipates rapidly, training programmes that introduce or increase eccentric loading (such as downhill running) should be progressed gradually rather than abruptly, to allow the muscle to adapt and to reduce the degree of structural damage and inflammatory response produced by each session.

(i) The thermoregulatory (heat-dissipation) mechanism is most affected, and it differs between children and adults because children have a higher body-surface-area-to-body-mass ratio, which facilitates heat loss when environmental temperature is below skin temperature, but becomes a disadvantage (an avenue of heat gain) when environmental temperature exceeds skin temperature.
(ii) As core body temperature rises during exercise, blood vessels in the skin dilate to divert blood to the body's surface for heat loss, and evaporation of sweat aids heat loss, though this becomes limited as humidity increases.
- Children also have a lower rate of sweat production than adults, because even though they have more heat-activated sweat glands, each gland produces considerably less sweat than an adult's.
- The inability to maintain core temperature can lead to heat disorders ranging from heat cramps (severe cramping of active skeletal muscle, the least severe), to heat exhaustion (extreme fatigue, breathlessness, dizziness, vomiting, fainting, cold and clammy or hot and dry skin, hypotension, and a weak rapid pulse), to heatstroke (core temperature of 40°C/104°F or higher, cessation of sweating, hot dry skin, rapid pulse and respiration, hypertension, and confusion or unconsciousness, which if untreated can lead to coma and death).
(iii) Because children are less resistant to the adverse effects of heat during exercise than adults, due to their lower sweat production and the disadvantage of a high surface-area-to-mass ratio once environmental temperature exceeds skin temperature, the child is at greater risk of heat-related injury than the adult performing the identical session.
(iv) Special attention should be given to protect children when they exercise in the heat, including providing them with extra fluids to drink; more generally, a person should drink enough fluid to try to match what is lost through sweating, avoid extreme heat, and reduce the intensity of activity in hot weather.
- If heat-related injury is suspected, the person should be taken to a shady area, cooled by whatever means available, given non-alcoholic beverages if conscious, and medical assistance sought; the physiotherapist should therefore reduce the intensity/duration of the child's session, ensure extra hydration, and monitor the child closely, more so than would be required for the adult in the same conditions.
questions.question:
A physiotherapist supervises a 9-year-old child and, separately, an adult performing the same moderate-intensity exercise session outdoors in hot weather.
(i) Identify the mechanism most affected by this environmental condition, and how it differs between the child and the adult.
(ii) Explain the changes in thermoregulatory function that occur.
(iii) Compare the child's response with the adult's response.
(iv) Give the reasoning for how the physiotherapist should modify the exercise session for the child in these conditions.

A(i) Describe the major changes in the respiratory system that result from endurance training, under the headings: maximal pulmonary ventilation and pulmonary diffusion.
B(i) State the factors that determine the magnitude of these respiratory adaptations.
C(i) Explain the difference in ventilatory capacity between an endurance-trained person and an untrained person.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Maximal pulmonary ventilation: the major change is an increase in the maximal rate of pulmonary ventilation, resulting from increases in both tidal volume and respiration rate.
A(ii) Pulmonary diffusion: an increase in pulmonary diffusion occurs at maximal rates of work, primarily because of increases in pulmonary blood flow, particularly to the upper regions of the lung.
B(i) The magnitude of these adaptations largely depends on the person's initial fitness level; on the mode, intensity, duration and frequency of exercise; and on the length of training (weeks, months or years).
C(i) In a hypothetical example of a sedentary man before and after 6 months of endurance training, compared with an elite endurance runner, maximal ventilation rose from 110 L/min pretraining to 135 L/min post-training, and was 195 L/min in the elite runner.
- Maximal tidal volume rose from 2.75 L to 3.0 L post-training and was 3.9 L in the runner.
- Maximal respiratory rate rose from 40 to 45 breaths/min post-training and was 50 breaths/min in the runner, illustrating that the trained/elite person achieves a substantially greater ventilatory capacity at maximal exercise than the untrained person.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old previously sedentary woman is referred to physiotherapy to begin a supervised exercise programme, and her cardiorespiratory response is compared with that of a young, trained adult performing the same absolute submaximal work rate.
(i) Identify the system most affected by her age.
(ii) Explain the changes in function that occur with ageing.
(iii) Compare her expected response with that of a younger or an active older adult.
(iv) Give the reasoning for how the physiotherapist should plan her exercise programme.
questions.answerText:
(i) The cardiovascular system is most affected, with a resulting decrease in maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max).
(ii) With ageing, maximal heart rate and maximal stroke volume decrease, so maximal cardiac output decreases, resulting in a lower VO₂max than in a young adult.
- At the same absolute submaximal rate of work, an older person's stroke volume is generally lower and heart rate higher (in an attempt to maintain cardiac output); because this attempt is generally insufficient, the arterial-mixed venous oxygen difference must increase to provide the same submaximal oxygen uptake.
- VO₂max declines by approximately 0.40 to 0.50 ml/kg/min per year in men, at a somewhat lesser rate in women; this deterioration with ageing is almost identical to the change that accompanies inactivity, caused by a combination of reduced physical activity and the ageing process itself.
(iii) Compared with a young or active older adult, this sedentary 68-year-old will show a lower VO₂max and a more exaggerated heart-rate response for the same absolute work rate.
- Through training, older men and women can increase their VO₂max values by approximately the same percentage as seen in younger adults; in one study, a 10-week progressive resistance programme produced a 113% increase in strength in elderly men and women with a mean age of 87 years, along with increases in thigh muscle area, stair-climbing power and gait velocity.
(iv) Because deterioration in physiological function with ageing largely reflects reduced physical activity rather than ageing alone, and because both endurance and resistance training can produce meaningful gains even at advanced age, the physiotherapist should plan a progressive programme combining aerobic and resistance exercise, starting at a level appropriate to her current sedentary status and progressing gradually, since increasing endurance and strength in the elderly contributes to their ability to live independently.

(i) The client has obesity; obesity and overweight are two words often used interchangeably in relation to body composition, but overweight refers to a body mass index of 25-29.9, while obesity refers to a BMI of 30 and over, reflecting a greater excess of storage fat.
(ii) Body Mass Index is calculated as body mass divided by the square of height in metres, and is positively associated with body fat, though it cannot itself distinguish fat mass from lean mass.
- The lowest mortality risk is in the BMI range of 20-25, and risk increases as BMI rises, with the highest risk at a BMI over 40.
- Storage fat (accumulated in adipose tissue, both visceral and subcutaneous) normally makes up about 12% of body mass in men and 15% in women, and obesity reflects an excess of this storage fat.
(iii) As BMI increases, the risk increases for cardiovascular complications, including hypertension, diabetes and renal disease.
(iv) Modes of exercise training that can be used to effect weight reduction include aerobic exercise (e.g., brisk walking, jogging, cycling, swimming) and resistance training.
- Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise performed regularly is justified as an appropriate mode because it increases energy expenditure and, through regular practice, changes body composition; a combination of exercise with dietary and lifestyle modification is generally required, since weight loss obtained from exercise alone tends to be modest.
questions.question:
A 38-year-old client with a body mass index in the obese range is referred to physiotherapy to lose weight and reduce her cardiovascular risk.
(i) Identify the condition affecting this client and describe its relationship to a related term she has heard used interchangeably with it.
(ii) Explain the physiological basis of this condition and its relationship to body composition.
(iii) State the complications/risk factors associated with this condition.
(iv) Discuss the modes of exercise training that can be used to effect weight reduction in this client, and justify one of them.

A(i) Explain the principle of the skinfold thickness method of assessing body composition.
A(ii) State the method/equipment used and how percentage body fat is derived from the raw skinfold values.
A(iii) State the common anatomical sites used in skinfold assessment.
B(i) State the applications and limitations of the skinfold method.
C(i) Distinguish the skinfold method from underwater (hydrostatic) weighing/densitometry as methods of assessing body composition.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The skinfold method is based on the principle that fat is of a known density, and that by summing measurements of subcutaneous fat thickness across the body, total and regional body fat can be estimated; it is the most widely adopted field method for assessing body fat.
A(ii) It is measured using a caliper and a non-stretchable tape to locate anatomical sites; raw skinfold values (in mm) act as reliable indices of regional fatness and can also be converted into percentage body fat using population-specific or generalised equations derived from empirical relationships between skinfold thickness and body density.
- Many equations first calculate body density and then require an additional calculation (e.g., the Siri or Brozek equations) to convert density into percentage body fat.
A(iii) Common sites include triceps, biceps, subscapular, supra-iliac, abdomen, thigh and chest; the subscapular and triceps skinfolds are the most commonly used, and the triceps site alone is the most common single-site measurement, though no equation exists for estimating body fat from a single site.
B(i) Applications: skinfold measurement is quick and simple to obtain in most age groups, is used in large-scale population studies or screening where portable field methods are desirable, and is the most widely used method of indirectly estimating percentage body fat, especially in infants and children.
- Limitations: intraobserver and interobserver error, while generally low compared with between-subject variability, are poorer in obese children; results should not be taken after exercise, since increased body heat shifts fluid to the skin and inflates skinfold size; and the equation chosen must match the demographics of the population being assessed, or it will bias results.
C(i) The skinfold method is an indirect field measurement of regional subcutaneous fat thickness using a caliper, requiring conversion via a population-specific equation to estimate percentage body fat.
- Underwater (hydrostatic) weighing/densitometry, by contrast, is an indirect laboratory method that distinguishes fat mass and fat-free mass by measuring total body density (body mass/body volume), assuming specific densities of fat and fat-free mass, and is less portable and more technically demanding than the skinfold method.

(i) His waist-to-hip ratio is 98/108 = 0.91, which falls in the "average" category for a male (0.90-0.95), below the "high" (0.95-1.00) and "very high" (>1.00) categories, indicating a moderate rather than markedly elevated risk of coronary heart disease from central fat distribution, although his waist girth alone (98 cm) is close to the guideline of greater than 102 cm for men that indicates increased risk.
(ii) The test used is the waist-to-hip ratio (a girth/circumference measurement), whose purpose is to determine the ratio of waist girth to hip girth, as this has been shown to relate to the risk of coronary heart disease.
(iii) It measures central (abdominal) fat distribution relative to gluteal/hip size.
- It is performed using a tape measure that is not too tight or too loose, lying flat and horizontal; the waist is measured at the visually narrowest level (or midway between the lowest rib and the iliac crest if no narrowing is visible), with the client looking straight ahead and breathing normally; the hip is measured over minimal clothing at the level of greatest gluteal protrusion, with weight evenly distributed and the gluteal muscles relaxed.
(iv) Tape tension (too tight or too loose), whether the tape is kept horizontal, breathing pattern at the moment of measurement, and tensing of the gluteal muscles during the hip measurement.
(v) Girth measurements as a predictor of body fat are best suited to individuals with average or above-average body fat, since girths tend to increase significantly when a person is already fat but do not decrease significantly when the person is already lean; the measurement can also be embarrassing for some clients.
questions.question:
A physiotherapist measures a 50-year-old man's waist girth at the visually narrowest point (98 cm) and his hip girth at the level of greatest gluteal protrusion (108 cm) using a tape measure, and calculates his waist-to-hip ratio.
(i) Interpret this client's waist-to-hip ratio finding.
(ii) Name the test/measurement used.
(iii) State what this test measures and describe how it is performed.
(iv) State the factors that can influence the result.
(v) State the limitations of this test.

A(i) Describe the pattern of decline in cardiorespiratory fitness (VO₂max) that occurs with detraining.
A(ii) Describe the pattern of decline in muscular strength and power that occurs with detraining.
B(i) State the factors that determine the rate/magnitude of these declines.
C(i) Explain the difference between the rate of loss of cardiorespiratory fitness and the rate of loss of muscular strength with detraining.
questions.answerText:
A(i) With complete cessation of exercise training, a significant reduction in VO₂max and a decrease in plasma volume occur within 2 weeks; all prior functional gains in VO₂max are dissipated within 2 to 8 months, even if routine low- to moderate-intensity physical activity has taken the place of training.
A(ii) Muscular strength and power are reduced at a much slower rate than VO₂max, particularly during the first few months after an athlete discontinues resistance training; no decrement in either strength or power may occur for the first 4 to 6 weeks after training ends, and after 12 months, almost half of the strength gained might still be retained if the athlete remains moderately active.
- In previously untrained persons, gains in muscular strength can be sustained by as little as a single session per week of resistance training, provided the intensity is not reduced.
B(i) The magnitude and rate of decline are determined by whether training is completely stopped or merely reduced: a reduction in training intensity of as little as one-third can produce a substantial reduction in VO₂max over the following 15 weeks, whereas a reduction in session duration by up to two-thirds can still retain a substantial part of the gain provided intensity remains at least about 70% of VO₂max.
- The frequency of maintenance training performed also determines the magnitude of loss.
C(i) Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO₂max) declines rapidly, with significant reductions evident within 2 weeks of complete training cessation and all gains lost within 2 to 8 months.
- Muscular strength and power decline much more slowly, with little or no loss in the first 4-6 weeks and up to half the strength gain still retained after 12 months in a moderately active person, showing that the cardiovascular/metabolic adaptations underlying VO₂max are less durable than the neuromuscular/structural adaptations underlying strength.

(i) The cardiovascular system's stroke volume and oxygen-carrying capacity are responsible for this observed sex difference.
(ii) At the same absolute rate of exercise, women have a higher heart rate response than men, primarily because of a lower stroke volume, which is a function of smaller heart size and smaller blood volume.
- In addition, women have less potential to increase the arterial-mixed venous oxygen difference because of lower haemoglobin content; these differences, together with greater fat mass, result in a lower VO₂max in women, even when normalised for size and level of training.
(iii) For the most part, women and men who participate in exercise training have similar responses in cardiovascular, respiratory and metabolic function, provided size and activity level are normalised; relative increases in VO₂max with aerobic endurance training are equivalent for women and men, and women show similar gains in strength from resistance training as men, although women gain less fat-free mass due to less muscle hypertrophy.
- Some evidence suggests older women accomplish increases in VO₂max mainly through an increase in the arterial-mixed venous oxygen difference, whereas younger women and men show substantial increases in stroke volume.
(iv) Because the female client will show a higher heart-rate response than a male at the same absolute workload (due to lower stroke volume and haemoglobin content), the physiotherapist should prescribe and monitor her exercise intensity using relative measures (such as percentage of her own heart-rate reserve) rather than comparing her heart rate directly to values used for male clients, while recognising that she can expect similar relative (percentage) gains in VO₂max and strength from an appropriately progressed training programme.
questions.question:
A female client and a male client of similar age and training status both perform the same absolute rate of exercise on a cycle ergometer, and the physiotherapist notes that the female client has a higher heart rate response than the male.
(i) Identify the mechanism responsible for this observed sex difference.
(ii) Explain the changes in function responsible for this difference.
(iii) Compare the female response with the male response and with the response expected after training.
(iv) Give the reasoning for how the physiotherapist should account for this difference when planning her exercise programme.

A(i) Describe the acute response of the cardiovascular system to a single episode of exercise, under the headings: heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, blood pressure and blood flow distribution.
B(i) State the factors that influence the magnitude of this cardiovascular response.
C(i) Explain how the response differs between dynamic (aerobic) exercise and resistance exercise.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Heart rate increases from resting values (about 60-80 beats/min) and rises further with exercise intensity; an anticipatory rise occurs before exercise even begins, caused by the release of catecholamines.
A(ii) Stroke volume, the volume of blood ejected per beat, increases with exercise intensity but plateaus at about 40-60% of maximal oxygen uptake in untrained persons, though it may continue to increase up to near-maximal work rates in highly trained persons.
A(iii) Cardiac output, the product of heart rate and stroke volume, increases in a nearly linear manner with rate of work up to its maximal capacity.
A(iv) Blood pressure: mean arterial pressure increases, largely from a rise in systolic pressure, which can reach peak values of 200-240 mmHg in normotensive persons, while diastolic pressure remains near resting levels during dynamic exercise.
A(v) Blood flow distribution: blood is redistributed away from areas of low demand (e.g., splanchnic organs) toward active skeletal muscle and, as body temperature rises, to the skin.
- At rest, skeletal muscle and skin receive about 15-20% of cardiac output, but this can rise to about 80-90% during vigorous exercise, through vasodilation in active muscle and vasoconstriction elsewhere.
B(i) Intrinsic factors influencing the response include the type, intensity and duration of exercise, environmental conditions and emotional state.
- Extrinsic factors include body size, gender, genetics, age and training status.
C(i) During dynamic (aerobic) exercise, systolic blood pressure rises while diastolic pressure barely changes.
- During resistance exercise, both systolic and diastolic blood pressure rise, and there is an exaggerated blood pressure response because the high, isolated force generated compresses the smaller arteries, causing a substantial increase in total peripheral resistance.

questions.question:
A powerlifter performs a single maximal back-squat lift that takes about 6 seconds to complete.
(i) Identify the energy system(s) supplying ATP for this lift.
(ii) Explain the underlying mechanism by which this system generates ATP.
(iii) Describe the acute muscular response occurring during this maximal effort.
(iv) State the practical implication of this energy system for prescribing this athlete's resistance-training programme.
questions.answerText:
(i) The ATP-PCr (phosphocreatine) system supplies ATP for this brief, maximal lift, since it operates during the first 5-8 seconds of exercise and can sustain high-intensity, short-duration exercise such as powerlifting.
(ii) Stored phosphocreatine in the muscle breaks down, freeing an inorganic phosphate that combines with ADP to reform ATP (ADP + CP → ATP + Creatine, phosphorylation of ATP); this system operates majorly without oxygen (anaerobic), and produces energy at the highest rate of the three systems (36 kcal/min), sufficient to maintain muscular contraction for only a few seconds.
(iii) During the lift, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and cross-bridges form rapidly between actin and myosin via the sliding filament mechanism.
- Because a maximal force is required, motor unit recruitment proceeds through the size principle up to the large, fast-twitch glycolytic motor units, and all motor units are activated when the muscle is producing its maximal force.
(iv) Because ATP-PCr stores are depleted within 10-20 seconds and this system has the highest rate but lowest capacity of ATP production, this athlete's resistance-training programme should use brief, maximal or near-maximal efforts with adequate rest intervals between sets (sufficient to allow phosphocreatine resynthesis) rather than continuous, prolonged sets, to train this predominant energy pathway specifically.

(i) Because the exercise lasts longer than 3 minutes at low-to-moderate intensity, the oxidative system (Krebs cycle/aerobic system) is the primary energy system used.
(ii) The oxidative process consists of four processes to produce ATP: slow glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, and β-oxidation.
- Slow glycolysis's end product is pyruvic acid, which produces acetyl-CoA used in the Krebs cycle to produce energy; the electron transport chain is aerobic and produces 34 ATP; β-oxidation uses fat and carbohydrate to produce ATP.
- This system is the slowest but the most efficient, and uses fat as its primary energy substrate to produce ATP for sustained activity such as jogging.
(iii) Cardiovascular: heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output rise and are sustained at an elevated but steady-state level appropriate to the work rate, with blood flow redistributed toward the active muscle.
- Respiratory: pulmonary ventilation rises and is sustained at a steady state where the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide meet the demands of the exercise, with breathing rate and tidal volume both contributing to the increase.
(iv) Because the oxidative system has the highest energy capacity but the lowest rate of ATP production (about 10 kcal/min, compared with 36 kcal/min for ATP-PCr and 16 kcal/min for glycolysis), and because at least about 20 minutes of continuous exercise is generally needed for adequate muscle and vascular adaptation, endurance-training sessions for this client should be prescribed as continuous, sustained, low-to-moderate intensity activity of adequate duration (well beyond 20 minutes) to develop the oxidative capacity that supports this type of exercise.
questions.question:
A trained 35-year-old man goes for a steady jog lasting 50 minutes at a low-to-moderate, conversational pace.
(i) Identify the energy system primarily supplying ATP for this effort.
(ii) Explain the underlying mechanism of ATP production for this system.
(iii) Describe the acute responses of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems during this sustained effort.
(iv) State the practical implication of this energy system for exercise prescription in an endurance-training programme.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The metabolic rate at rest is defined as 1 metabolic equivalent (MET); a 4-MET activity thus represents an activity that requires four times the resting metabolic rate; the use of METs to quantify physical activity intensity is the basis of the absolute intensity scale.
- One MET represents 3.5 mL of oxygen uptake per kilogram of body weight per minute, and is considered the metabolic rate of an individual at rest.
A(ii) METs are determined from the oxygen cost of an activity relative to resting oxygen consumption; for example, playing golf or walking at 4.5-6 km/hr is equal to about 3-5 METs.
- Playing tennis against a partner is about 5-7 METs; heavy occupational activity or walking/running at 9-10 km/hr is about 9 METs; moderate-intensity exercise is generally considered to be about 3-6 METs.
B(i) Applications: METs allow exercise intensity to be quantified and compared across different activities, using a common, absolute unit related to resting metabolic rate; this is useful in exercise prescription for patients with chronic disease such as diabetes.
- Limitations: because 1 MET is defined relative to resting metabolic rate under highly controlled resting conditions (following a 12-hour fast and a good night's sleep), the MET value of an activity is an approximation and does not account for individual variation in fitness, body composition or efficiency of movement in the way a relative measure does.
C(i) The MET method expresses exercise intensity as an absolute multiple of resting metabolic rate, the same for everyone regardless of fitness level.
- The target-heart-rate method (e.g., using 220 minus age to estimate maximum heart rate, or the simpler "talk test", which refers to an intensity that allows a person to still talk to a partner without dyspnoea) expresses and regulates intensity relative to the individual's own physiological capacity and is more practical for a novice exerciser to self-monitor without equipment, since it is difficult to measure heart rate during exercise without a portable heart-rate monitor.
questions.question:
A(i) Explain the principle of the metabolic equivalent (MET) as a unit of exercise intensity.
A(ii) State how METs are determined/measured and give examples of activities at different MET levels.
B(i) State the applications and limitations of using METs to prescribe exercise intensity.
C(i) Distinguish the MET method of prescribing exercise intensity from the target-heart-rate ("talk test") method.

questions.answerText:
(i) This illustrates the long-term cardiovascular adaptation to endurance training, seen as resting bradycardia together with an increased resting stroke volume; in a hypothetical 6-month endurance training example, resting heart rate fell from 71 to 59 beats/min while resting stroke volume rose from 65 to 80 ml, maximal cardiac output rose from 22.2 to 25.6 L/min, and VO₂max rose from 40.5 to 49.8 ml/kg/min.
(ii) Endurance training increases plasma volume by approximately the same percentage that it increases stroke volume, increasing venous return and end-diastolic volume; this acute increase in end-diastolic volume stretches the ventricular wall, producing more elastic recoil.
- Long-term adaptation includes hypertrophy of cardiac muscle fibres, increasing ventricular muscle mass and the thickness of the posterior and septal walls, permitting a more forceful contraction and greater stroke volume.
- Because more blood is ejected per beat, fewer beats per minute are required at rest and during submaximal exercise to meet the body's demand, explaining the resting and submaximal bradycardia; maximal heart rate itself is usually unchanged with training.
(iii) Because gains in VO₂max obtained through cardiorespiratory exercise performed six times per week can be maintained with as little as two to four times per week of training, provided intensity remains at about 70% of VO₂max or more, the training frequency for this client can be reduced for maintenance once the adaptation is achieved, without reducing training intensity, since reducing intensity by as little as one-third can produce a substantial decline in VO₂max over the following weeks.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old man who has cycled for endurance six times a week for 6 months is found to have a resting heart rate of 59 beats/min (previously 71 beats/min) and a resting stroke volume of 80 ml (previously 65 ml), compared with an untrained peer.
(i) Name the response/adaptation illustrated by this scenario.
(ii) Explain the contributing factors and underlying physiology of this adaptation.
(iii) State the training/management implication of this finding.

questions.answerText:
(i) The client's hypertension creates a particular exercise-related concern because resistance exercise, more than aerobic exercise, produces an exaggerated blood pressure response.
(ii) Cardiovascular responses to resistance exercise are mostly similar to those of endurance exercise, with one notable exception: resistance exercise usually involves muscle mass that develops considerable, high, isolated force, which compresses the smaller arteries and results in substantial increases in total peripheral resistance.
- During resistance exercise there is an increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure, unlike dynamic aerobic exercise where diastolic pressure barely changes.
(iii) High-intensity resistance training poses a potential risk to hypertensive patients and to those with cardiovascular disease because of this exaggerated blood pressure response; however, hypertensive persons may still benefit from resistance training, and research data suggest that the associated risk is relatively low.
(iv) Management/modification options include using moderate rather than high-intensity resistance loads to limit the blood pressure response; combining resistance training with aerobic (dynamic) exercise, which after endurance training tends to lower resting blood pressure (with a greater decrease, about -10/-8 mmHg, seen in hypertensive persons); and ensuring appropriate technique to avoid excessive strain.
- Of these, prescribing moderate-intensity resistance training is justified because the risk of an exaggerated blood pressure response is directly related to the magnitude of the isolated force generated, and hypertensive persons may still gain the benefits of resistance training, including improved strength, while research indicates this risk is relatively low at appropriate intensities.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension wishes to begin a resistance (weight) training programme under physiotherapy supervision.
(i) Identify the exercise-related concern affecting this client's suitability for resistance training.
(ii) Explain the physiological basis of this concern.
(iii) State the risk factors and possible complications this client may experience during resistance exercise.
(iv) Discuss the exercise management or modification options available, and justify one of them.

questions.answerText:
(i) The development of chest pain during graded exercise suggests an ischaemic manifestation, indicating a possible cardiac abnormality provoked by the increasing exercise intensity; this is the kind of manifestation graded exercise testing is designed to detect, and the test is symptom-limited, meaning it is stopped when the person develops abnormal symptoms that signal termination.
(ii) The test being performed is graded exercise testing (GXT)/stress testing.
(iii) It is a non-invasive physiological test that describes the systematic use of exercise for observing cardiac rhythm abnormalities during exercise and for assessing physiological adjustment to exercise; the most common modes are multistage testing using a bicycle or treadmill.
- The test is graded for exercise intensity and uses sub-maximal exercise of three to five minutes duration at each stage, progressing up to self-imposed fatigue or a symptom-limited endpoint (the test need not be maximal but may go up to 85% of the person's target heart rate); a resting ECG usually precedes the GXT as a baseline.
(iv) Ambient temperature and relative humidity, the subject's sleep state, emotional state, medication, time of day, caffeine intake, the testing environment, time since the last meal, and time since the last exercise session.
(v) Absolute contraindications include a resting ECG suggestive of acute cardiac disease, recent complicated myocardial infarction, unstable angina pectoris, uncontrolled ventricular or atrial arrhythmia compromising cardiac function, acute congestive heart failure, severe aortic stenosis, and active or suspected myocarditis, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism or acute infection.
- Relative contraindications include resting diastolic blood pressure greater than 115 mmHg or systolic ≥200 mmHg, moderate valvular disease, electrolyte abnormalities, ventricular aneurysm, uncontrolled metabolic disease, chronic infectious disease, pregnancy, psychological distress, and neuromuscular disorders; informed consent is required before testing.
questions.question:
During a symptom-limited graded exercise test on a treadmill using a standard multistage protocol, a 52-year-old man develops chest pain at the fifth stage of the test, prompting the supervising clinician to stop the test.
(i) Interpret this finding.
(ii) Name the test/measurement being performed.
(iii) State what this test measures and briefly describe how it is performed.
(iv) State the factors that can influence the physiological response to this test.
(v) State the precautions/contraindications relevant to this test.

A physiotherapist measures the triceps, biceps, subscapular and supra-iliac skinfolds of a 28-year-old woman using a caliper, obtaining a sum of skinfolds that is substituted into a 4-site skinfold equation to estimate her percentage body fat.
(i) Explain what the resulting percentage body fat value tells the physiotherapist about this client.
(ii) Name the test/measurement technique used.
(iii) State what this test measures and briefly describe how it is performed.
(iv) State the factors that can influence the result.
(v) State the limitations or precautions associated with this test.
questions.answerText:
(i) The percentage body fat value indicates the client's relative body "fatness", derived from the estimated body density calculated from the sum of her skinfolds using an equation appropriate to her age, sex and population; it can be compared with reference values to judge whether her body composition falls within a normal range or represents an overweight/obesity risk.
(ii) The technique used is the skinfold (caliper) method of body composition assessment.
(iii) It measures subcutaneous fat thickness at specific anatomical sites, based on the principle that fat has a known density and that summing skinfold thicknesses across regions of the body estimates total and regional fatness.
- It is performed by firmly grasping the skinfold with the thumb and index finger about 1 cm proximal to the site and pulling it away from the body, applying the caliper perpendicular to the fold with the tip 1 cm distal to the fingers, and reading the dial about 4 seconds after releasing pressure.
- Three measurements are taken to the nearest 0.2 mm, and remeasured if consecutive readings differ by more than 1 mm.
(iv) Hydration status (measurements are best taken in a hydrated state); recent exercise (measurements should not be taken after exercise, because increased body heat shifts fluid to the skin and inflates skinfold size); which equation is selected, since it must match the demographics (race, age, gender) of the person; and periodic calibration of the caliper against a calibration block.
(v) Intraobserver and interobserver error, although generally low compared with between-subject variability, are poorer in obese individuals.
- The Jackson & Pollock and Durnin & Womersley equations have both been shown to underestimate body fat compared with the criterion 4-component model, especially in larger individuals (mean bias of about -6.6% and -2% respectively).
- No equation is available for estimating body fat from a single skinfold site alone.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the effect of moderate-intensity exercise on the immune system.
A(ii) Describe the effect of high-intensity, prolonged, or excessive exercise (overtraining) on the immune system.
B(i) State the factors that influence whether exercise bolsters or impairs immune function.
C(i) Explain the significance of this dual effect of exercise on the immune system.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Moderate exercise has been shown to bolster the function of certain components of the human immune system, such as natural killer cells, circulating T- and B-lymphocytes, and cells of the monocyte-macrophage system, thereby possibly decreasing the incidence of some infections and perhaps of certain types of cancer.
A(ii) Exercise of high intensity and long duration, or exercise that involves excessive training, may have adverse effects on immune function; in general, a high-intensity, single episode of exercise results in a marked decline in the functioning of all major cells of the immune system.
- In addition, overtraining may reduce the response of T-lymphocytes to mutagenic stimulation, decrease antibody synthesis and plasma levels of immunoglobulins and complement, and impair macrophage phagocytosis.
B(i) The immune system is a complex adaptive system that interacts with neural and endocrine factors and influences the body's overall response to exercise; the reduced plasma glutamine levels that occur with high-intensity exercise or excessive training are postulated to contribute to these adverse immune effects.
- This indicates that exercise intensity, duration, and whether training is excessive (overtraining) are key factors determining whether the immune response is beneficial or adverse.
C(i) A growing body of literature indicates that the incidence of some infections may be influenced by a person's exercise history; because moderate exercise appears protective while high-intensity or excessive exercise appears to suppress immune function, this dual effect has practical significance for prescribing exercise intensity and monitoring training load in clients, particularly to avoid excessive or high-intensity training that could increase susceptibility to infection.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the structure of the sarcomere under the headings: Z disk, I band, A band, and H zone.
A(ii) Describe the length-tension relationship of skeletal muscle.
B(i) Explain the clinical/functional significance of the length-tension relationship for muscle force production.
C(i) Distinguish between passive tension, total tension and active tension.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Z disk: two adjacent Z disks along the myofibril mark the boundaries of a single sarcomere and are the attachment sites for the thin (actin) filaments; when a muscle fibre contracts, the Z disks of a sarcomere move closer together and the sarcomere shortens.
- I band: the lightest region of the sarcomere, occupied by thin filaments only, and it shortens as the muscle contracts.
- A band: the entire length of the thick (myosin) filament, the darkest region where thick and thin filaments overlap; the centre of the A band does not change as the muscle contracts.
- H zone: the centre of the A band where there is no overlap between thick and thin filaments (thick filaments only); it becomes smaller as the muscle contracts because the overlap between thick and thin filaments increases.
A(ii) The amount of tension developed by a muscle is directly proportional to the overlap between the thick and thin filaments; the greater the number of myosin heads that interact with actin, the greater the tension the muscle can produce.
- If a muscle is stretched so there is very little overlap between filaments, little tension can be developed; if the muscle shortens to the point where thin filaments from opposite Z disks collide, this also reduces the number of thin filaments that can interact with myosin heads, again reducing tension.
- There is therefore an optimum length at which the muscle produces maximum tension, and at rest, most skeletal muscles are near this optimum length (average resting sarcomere length about 2.15 micrometres).
B(i) Because tension developed depends on the degree of overlap between actin and myosin filaments, a muscle's ability to produce force varies with its length; this has significance in physiotherapy practice, since positioning a muscle at, near, or away from its optimum resting length will influence how much active tension/force it is capable of generating during assessment or exercise.
C(i) Tension developed by muscle tissue at rest is called passive tension; tension generated during isometric contraction is called total tension.
- The difference between the total tension and the passive tension is called the active tension, and it is the real tension developed during contraction.

questions.question:
A physiotherapist asks a 24-year-old healthy client to walk/run/jog as fast as possible for 12 minutes on a track, and afterwards uses the client's age, body weight, sex, distance/time and heart response to estimate the client's VO₂max.
(i) Explain what this estimated VO₂max value tells the physiotherapist about the client.
(ii) Name the test/measurement used.
(iii) State what this test measures and describe how it is performed.
(iv) State the factors that can influence the result.
(v) State the limitations of this test compared with a laboratory method.
questions.answerText:
(i) The estimated VO₂max value gives an indication of the client's cardiorespiratory (aerobic) fitness, i.e., how well the body can supply fuel during physical activity via the circulatory and respiratory systems; a higher value indicates better cardiorespiratory endurance.
(ii) The test used is a field test of physical fitness/cardiorespiratory fitness, specifically the 12-minute walk/run test (related field tests include the 1.5-mile and 1-mile walk/run tests).
(iii) It measures cardiorespiratory endurance, assessed by having the individual walk, run or jog as fast as possible for 12 minutes (or cover 1.5 miles).
- The person's age, body weight, sex, the time taken to complete the distance, and heart-rate response are then used to calculate/estimate VO₂max.
(iv) The client's age, body weight, sex, effort/pacing during the test, and their heart-rate response to the exertion.
(v) As a field method, this is a derived approximation of VO₂max rather than a directly measured value, unlike laboratory methods such as treadmill or ergometer testing with direct gas analysis; its accuracy therefore depends on the client giving a genuine maximal pacing effort and on the accuracy of the prediction method used to convert time/distance/heart-rate data into an estimated VO₂max.

A(i) Ligaments and tendons become stronger with prolonged, high-intensity exercise, through an increase in the strength of the insertion sites between ligaments, tendons and bones, and an increase in the cross-sectional areas of ligaments and tendons.
- Bones increase their mineral density over time to manage increasing load, and even small increases in bone mass gained from endurance or resistance training can help prevent or delay osteoporosis.
B(i) The magnitude of these adaptations depends on the type of exercise (mechanical/metabolic overload), the intensity, frequency and duration of exercise, the person's initial level of fitness, and genetic factors influencing responsiveness to training.
C(i) The increases in bone mass that result from either endurance or resistance training are relatively small, and the role of resistance training in increasing or maintaining bone mass is not well characterised; endurance training has little demonstrated positive effect on bone mineral and mass, although persons who are sedentary generally have less bone mass than those who exercise.
- By contrast, ligaments and tendons become weaker and smaller with several weeks of immobilisation, which can have important implications for musculoskeletal performance and risk of injury.
- Prolonged immobilisation also results in a progressive decrease in bone mineral density approximately proportional to its duration, with the muscle groups most affected being the antigravity postural muscles of the lower extremities.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the adaptations of bone, ligaments and tendons to chronic exercise training.
B(i) State the factors that determine the magnitude of these adaptations.
C(i) Explain the difference between the effects of resistance/endurance training and immobilisation on bone, ligament and tendon strength.

A(i) Describe the acute response of the respiratory system to a single episode of exercise, under the headings: pulmonary ventilation, tidal volume, respiratory rate, and diffusion.
B(i) State the factors that influence the magnitude of this respiratory response.
C(i) Explain how the pattern of ventilatory increase differs between low work intensities and higher work intensities.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pulmonary ventilation increases almost immediately with exercise, largely through stimulation of the respiratory centres in the brain stem from the motor cortex and through feedback from proprioceptors in the muscles and joints of the active limbs.
- In normal-sized, untrained adults it can rise from about 10 L/min at rest to more than 100 L/min at maximal rates of work, and to more than 200 L/min in large, highly trained male athletes.
A(ii) Tidal volume (the depth of breathing) increases from about 0.5 L per breath at rest to a maximum of several litres per breath during exercise.
A(iii) Respiratory rate (breathing frequency), usually around 12-15 breaths per minute at rest, increases toward a maximum during exercise.
A(iv) Diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide occurs at the alveoli of the lungs and at the muscle capillaries, moving from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration, increasing the volume of oxygen diffused into the blood and transported to the working muscles.
B(i) During prolonged exercise or at higher rates of work, increases in carbon dioxide production, hydrogen ion concentration, and body and blood temperature stimulate further increases in pulmonary ventilation.
C(i) At low work intensities, the increase in ventilation is mostly the result of increases in tidal volume.
- At higher intensities, the respiratory rate also increases, so ventilation rises through a combination of a deeper and a faster breathing pattern.

(i) The mechanism primarily affected is oxygen delivery, because as altitude increases, barometric pressure decreases and the partial pressure of inhaled oxygen decreases proportionally.
(ii) A decreased partial pressure of oxygen reduces the driving force to unload oxygen from air to blood and from blood to muscle, compromising oxygen delivery; VO₂max is significantly reduced at altitudes greater than 1,500 metres, impairing endurance performance.
- Within the first 24 hours of altitude exposure the body makes short-term adaptations: an increased cardiac output at rest and during submaximal exercise, and increased ventilatory volumes.
- Over several weeks, a reduction in plasma volume increases the concentration of red blood cells (hemoconcentration), and red blood cell mass increases through stimulation of the bone marrow by erythropoietin, providing more oxygen-carrying capacity.
(iii) At sea level, in her trained state, her VO₂max and oxygen delivery to working muscle are higher for the same work rate; at altitude, for the same absolute rate of work, her oxygen delivery is compromised, so cardiac output and ventilation are increased relative to sea level as a short-term compensation, and her exercise capacity is reduced until the longer-term adaptation of increased red blood cell mass occurs over several weeks.
(iv) Because VO₂max and endurance performance are reduced at altitude, and full adaptation takes several weeks, the physiotherapist should reduce the intensity and/or duration of her usual jogging routine initially, allow a period of acclimatization, and progress the programme gradually as short-term (cardiac output/ventilation) and longer-term (hemoconcentration, red cell mass) adaptations occur.
questions.question:
A physiotherapy client who normally trains at sea level travels to a location at 2,000 metres above sea level and attempts her usual jogging routine within the first day of arrival.
(i) Identify the mechanism primarily affected by this change in environment.
(ii) Explain the changes in function that occur.
(iii) Compare this response with her normal sea-level (trained) state.
(iv) Give the reasoning for how a physiotherapist should plan her exercise programme under these conditions.

A(i) Describe Type I (slow-twitch) muscle fibres under the headings: speed of contraction, metabolism, and fatigue resistance.
A(ii) Describe Type IIa muscle fibres under the same headings.
A(iii) Describe Type IIb muscle fibres under the same headings.
B(i) Explain the functional significance of fibre-type composition for athletic performance.
C(i) Distinguish between slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibres in terms of colour and mitochondrial/capillary characteristics.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Type I fibres: slow twitch, well suited for prolonged low-intensity work; metabolism is oxidative in nature; they are highly resistant to fatigue and suitable for sustained contraction under aerobic conditions.
A(ii) Type IIa fibres: fast twitch, known as intermediate fast-twitch because they can sustain activity for a long period, also contracting with a burst of force before fatiguing; metabolism is oxidative and glycolytic; they have fairly high resistance to fatigue and are suitable to function under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions.
A(iii) Type IIb fibres: fast twitch, providing rapid force production; metabolism is glycolytic; they fatigue easily and are suitable for short bursts of anaerobic exercise.
B(i) Sprinters and athletes have a great concentration of fast-twitch fibres, especially in muscles such as the gastrocnemius, while distance runners have a high concentration of slow-twitch fibres.
- In most marathon runners, slow-twitch fibres account for up to or more than 90% of the total fibres in the leg muscles, while in sprinters the leg muscles are often more than 80% fast-twitch, reflecting the direct relationship between fibre-type composition and performance in different sports.
C(i) Slow-twitch (Type I) fibres are red in colour owing to their high myoglobin content, and are associated with many mitochondria and a rich capillary supply.
- Fast-twitch fibres (Type IIa/IIb) are white in colour, with Type IIb fibres in particular having relatively sparse mitochondria and lower capillary/blood-flow capacity than Type I fibres.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the acute responses of the muscular system to a single episode of exercise, under the headings: arteriovenous oxygen difference, motor unit recruitment, temperature, and energy substrate levels.
B(i) State the factors that influence these acute muscular responses.
C(i) Explain how oxygen uptake changes from the start of exercise (oxygen deficit) through to recovery (oxygen debt/EPOC).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Arteriovenous oxygen difference (a-vO₂ diff): increases, reflecting the difference in oxygen concentration between arterial and venous blood as more oxygen is extracted by the working muscle.
A(ii) Motor unit recruitment: increases, with increased motor neuron firing and recruitment of the muscle fibres each motor neuron innervates; more motor units recruited produces greater force.
A(iii) Temperature: increases (a change in internal body temperature), with mechanisms such as sweating working to prevent an excessive rise in core body temperature.
A(iv) Energy substrate levels: decrease, as the chemicals required to resynthesise ATP (phosphocreatine, glycogen and triglycerides) are used up.
B(i) These responses are influenced by the intensity, duration and type of exercise being undertaken; acute responses only occur for the duration of exercise and recovery, and involve the respiratory, cardiovascular and muscular systems working together to supply more energy/ATP and oxygen to the working muscles and to remove waste products.
C(i) At rest the body easily takes in the oxygen it requires; as exercise begins, oxygen demand rises faster than the body can meet it, creating an oxygen deficit during which ATP is produced mainly anaerobically.
- During steady state, oxygen supply meets demand and ATP is produced aerobically; oxygen deficit occurs mainly at the start of exercise and when intensity rises rapidly, and is met largely by anaerobic energy systems.
- At the completion of exercise, excess oxygen is taken in during recovery (oxygen debt/excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, EPOC) to return the body to pre-exercise levels, a process that is largely aerobic.

questions.question:
A(i) Explain the principle behind the Body Mass Index (BMI) as a measurement, including its formula.
A(ii) State how BMI is interpreted, including the standard adult cut-off categories.
B(i) State the applications and limitations of BMI in assessing body composition.
C(i) Distinguish BMI from skinfold thickness measurement as methods of assessing body composition.
questions.answerText:
A(i) BMI is calculated as body mass divided by the square of height in metres (BMI = body mass / height squared); for children and adolescents, BMI is calculated in percentiles rather than by a single adult formula.
A(ii) The standard adult BMI cut-offs are: below 18.5 = underweight; 18.5-24.9 = normal weight; 25-29.9 = overweight; 30 and over = obesity.
- The lowest mortality risk is found in the range of 20-25, with risk increasing as BMI rises and the highest risk at a BMI over 40; an ideal BMI is cited as 21.9-22.4 for men and 21.3-22.1 for women.
B(i) Applications: BMI is positively associated with body fat, and its importance lies in its curvilinear relationship to all-cause mortality risk, being widely used by clinicians and researchers to evaluate the normalcy of a person's body weight relative to stature.
- Limitations: BMI does not distinguish between fat mass and fat-free (lean) mass, so it can be misleading, for example in very muscular individuals such as athletes, where BMI may overestimate fatness.
C(i) BMI is derived only from body mass and height and gives a global index of nutritional status but cannot separate fat from lean tissue.
- Skinfold thickness measurement directly measures subcutaneous fat at specific anatomical sites using a caliper and, combined with population-specific equations, can be converted into an estimate of percentage body fat, giving more direct information about regional and total body fatness than BMI alone.

questions.question:
A(i) Explain the principle of maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max) as a measurement.
A(ii) State the method by which VO₂max is determined and the point during exercise at which it is defined.
A(iii) State the units in which VO₂max is expressed and how it should be interpreted.
B(i) State the applications and limitations of VO₂max as a measure of fitness.
C(i) Distinguish VO₂max from the lactate threshold.
questions.answerText:
A(i) VO₂max is defined as the point at which a person's oxygen uptake (VO₂) is no longer able to increase despite further increases in the rate of work; VO₂ increases in direct proportion to the rate of work until this maximal point is reached, and VO₂max is considered the best estimate of a person's cardiorespiratory fitness or aerobic power.
A(ii) It is determined during a progressively increasing rate-of-work test (e.g., on a cycle ergometer or treadmill), by measuring oxygen uptake as work rate rises until VO₂ plateaus despite further increases in work rate; VO₂max is in part genetically determined and can be increased through training up to the genetically possible maximum.
A(iii) VO₂max is expressed in millilitres of oxygen per kilogram of body weight per minute (ml.kg-1.min-1), or in litres per minute; for example, a hypothetical sedentary man's VO₂max was 40.5 ml/kg/min before training, 49.8 ml/kg/min after 6 months of endurance training, while an elite endurance runner's was 76.5 ml/kg/min.
- A higher VO₂max value reflects greater aerobic power/cardiorespiratory fitness.
B(i) VO₂max is used as the best estimate of cardiorespiratory fitness/aerobic power; increases of 15-20% are typically seen following a 6-month endurance training programme, although individual variation is considerable (0-43% in one study of older men and women).
- Its limitation is that testing to true maximum requires an all-out, symptom-limited effort, which may not be appropriate for all individuals, and the value obtained is influenced by genetics, age, sex, training status and initial fitness level.
C(i) VO₂max is the point at which oxygen uptake can no longer increase with rising work rate, whereas the lactate threshold is the point at which blood lactate concentration begins to increase above resting levels, because the rate of lactate entry into the blood exceeds its rate of removal.
- Distance runners set their race pace at or slightly above the lactate threshold rather than at VO₂max, and the lactate thresholds of highly trained endurance athletes occur at a much higher percentage of VO₂max than in untrained persons, which is what allows endurance athletes to perform at a faster pace.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the hormonal (endocrine) response to a single episode of exercise, under the headings: catecholamines, growth hormone, ACTH-cortisol, and insulin/glucagon.
B(i) State the factors that influence the magnitude of these hormonal responses.
C(i) Explain how the hormonal response to exercise differs between an intense bout of exercise and a lower-intensity bout.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Catecholamines increase during exercise, with norepinephrine increasing more than epinephrine; their probable importance is increased blood glucose and increased skeletal muscle and liver glycogenolysis and lipolysis.
A(ii) Growth hormone (GH) increases during exercise, and increases more in untrained persons, declining faster in trained persons.
A(iii) Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-cortisol increases during exercise, with the probable importance of increased gluconeogenesis in the liver and increased mobilisation of fatty acids.
A(iv) Insulin secretion decreases during exercise (decreasing less after training), reducing the stimulus to use blood glucose, while glucagon increases during exercise (increasing less after training), raising blood glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
B(i) The magnitude of these hormonal changes is influenced by exercise intensity, with greater increases seen with more intense exercise, and by training status, since most of these hormonal responses (catecholamines, ACTH-cortisol, glucagon) increase less for a given submaximal workload after training has occurred.
C(i) Catecholamines and ACTH-cortisol show a greater increase with more intense exercise than with lower-intensity exercise, whereas growth hormone increases more in untrained persons than in trained persons for a comparable bout.
- Overall, the endocrine system integrates these physiologic responses to maintain homeostatic conditions during exercise, and the degree of hormonal change generally scales with how intense and how unfamiliar (untrained) the exercise is for the individual.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the metabolic adaptations that occur in skeletal muscle in response to endurance training, under the headings: mitochondria, myoglobin, glycogen storage, and fat utilisation.
B(i) State the factors that determine the magnitude of these metabolic adaptations.
C(i) Explain how these metabolic adaptations differ from those produced by resistance training.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Mitochondria: both the size and number of mitochondria increase substantially with endurance training, as does the activity of oxidative enzymes, greatly enhancing the oxidative capacity of the trained muscle.
A(ii) Myoglobin: myoglobin content in the muscle can be augmented, increasing the amount of oxygen stored within individual muscle fibres, although this effect is variable between individuals.
A(iii) Glycogen storage: endurance training increases the capacity of skeletal muscle to store glycogen.
A(iv) Fat utilisation: the ability of trained muscle to use fat as an energy source is improved, resulting from an enhanced ability to mobilise free fatty acids from fat depots and an improved capacity to oxidise fat, owing to increases in the muscle enzymes responsible for fat oxidation; this greater reliance on fat spares glycogen stores.
B(i) The magnitude of these metabolic adaptations depends on the type, intensity, frequency and duration of exercise, as well as the person's initial level of fitness and genetic factors that determine responsiveness to a given training stimulus.
C(i) Endurance training primarily produces these metabolic/oxidative adaptations (increased mitochondria, capillary density, glycogen storage and fat oxidation capacity), together with only a small increase in the cross-sectional area of slow-twitch fibres.
- Resistance training, by contrast, primarily produces increases in muscle fibre size (hypertrophy) and increased muscle fibre recruitment, allowing considerably more force to be exerted, with the metabolic adaptations of resistance training being less pronounced than those of endurance training.

A(i) Graded exercise testing (GXT) is a non-invasive physiological test that systematically uses exercise to observe cardiac rhythm abnormalities during exercise and to assess physiological adjustment to exercise; the graded nature of the testing allows detection of ischaemic manifestations and rhythm disorders with small increments in exercise intensity, and the test can provide a reliable, quantitative index of a person's level of functional impairment.
A(ii) The most common modes are the multistage treadmill or bicycle ergometer test, using sub-maximal exercise of three to five minutes duration per stage, progressing up to self-imposed fatigue.
- A maximal test continues until the person decides to stop or develops abnormal symptoms that signal termination (symptom-limited); a submaximal test is preferred and, though it cannot give maximal VO₂ directly, is as good as a maximal test at giving physiological information, and VO₂max can instead be calculated rather than requiring the stress of an all-out effort.
- Protocols include the modified Naughton (for very sedentary persons), modified Balke (normal sedentary), and modified Bruce (young/active) treadmill protocols, as well as bicycle and arm-cranking ergometer tests.
B(i) Applications: GXT can detect heart disease, reproduce and assess exercise-related chest symptoms, screen candidates for preventive and rehabilitative exercise programmes, detect abnormal blood pressure response, monitor response to therapeutic interventions, and define functional aerobic capacity.
- Limitations/precautions: informed consent is required, covering explanation of the test, risks and discomforts, participant responsibility, expected benefits, and freedom of consent; the test has absolute contraindications (e.g., acute cardiac disease on resting ECG, recent complicated myocardial infarction, unstable angina, uncontrolled arrhythmia, acute heart failure, severe aortic stenosis, active myocarditis/pericarditis) and relative contraindications (e.g., severe hypertension, moderate valvular disease, electrolyte abnormalities, uncontrolled metabolic disease, pregnancy).
- The physiological response can also be influenced by ambient temperature/humidity, sleep state, emotional state, medication, time of day, caffeine intake, and time since the last meal or exercise.
C(i) GXT is a laboratory-based, clinically supervised, multistage test performed on a treadmill, bicycle or arm ergometer, with continuous monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure and ECG, used mainly to detect cardiac abnormalities and to define functional capacity under medical supervision.
- A field test such as the 12-minute walk/run test is a simple, non-laboratory test in which the person covers as much distance as possible in a fixed time, with age, body weight, sex, time and heart response used to estimate VO₂max, making it a more accessible but less diagnostically detailed (no ECG monitoring) method of assessing cardiorespiratory fitness.
