questions.answerText:
(i) The ATP-PCr (phosphocreatine) system supplies ATP for this effort; it operates during the first 5-8 seconds of exercise and can sustain high-intensity, short-duration exercise such as a 50m dash, lasting up to about 10-15 seconds before another system must take over.
(ii) Stored phosphocreatine in the muscle cells breaks down, freeing an inorganic phosphate that combines with ADP to form ATP; this is described as phosphorylation of ATP (ADP + CP → ATP + Creatine); the system operates mainly without oxygen (anaerobic) and produces energy sufficient to maintain contraction for only a few seconds (about 15 seconds), at the highest rate of production (36 kcal/min) of the three systems.
(iii) Muscular: calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, cross-bridges form rapidly between actin and myosin (sliding filament mechanism), and motor units are recruited according to the size principle to generate maximal force.
- Cardiovascular: heart rate rises quickly (an anticipatory rise occurs even before exercise begins) and blood is redistributed toward the active muscle.
- Respiratory: pulmonary ventilation increases almost immediately through stimulation of respiratory centres in the brain stem and feedback from proprioceptors in the active limbs.
(iv) Because ATP-PCr stores are depleted within 10-20 seconds, training or rehabilitation for this type of effort should use very short, maximal-intensity bouts (e.g., short sprints or single maximal lifts) with adequate rest between bouts to allow phosphocreatine resynthesis, rather than prolonged continuous activity.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) Heart rate: decreased at rest and during submaximal exercise following training, and usually unchanged at maximal rates of work.
A(ii) Stroke volume: increased at rest, during submaximal exercise and during maximal exercise; this increase is the dominant change explaining most of the improvement in cardiac output.
A(iii) Cardiac output: essentially unchanged at rest and during submaximal exercise, but increased substantially (up to 30% or more) at or near maximal rates of work.
A(iv) Cardiac structure: adaptation includes hypertrophy of cardiac muscle fibres (increase in fibre size), increasing ventricular muscle mass, and ventricular dilatation that increases end-diastolic volume without excessive stress on the ventricular walls, together with increased thickness of the posterior and septal walls of the left ventricle.
A(v) Blood pressure: resting, submaximal and peak blood pressure show a slight decline in normotensive persons (about -3/-3 mmHg), with a greater decline in hypertensive persons (about -10/-8 mmHg).
B(i) The magnitude of these adaptations depends on the person's initial fitness level; on the mode, intensity, duration and frequency of exercise; and on the length of training (weeks, months or years).
C(i) At the same absolute submaximal rate of work, the endurance-trained person has a lower heart rate and a higher stroke volume than the untrained person, because the increase in plasma volume and end-diastolic volume, together with cardiac hypertrophy, allow more blood to be ejected per beat.
- The trained person can therefore perform at considerably higher rates of work before reaching maximal capacity, and their lactate threshold occurs at a higher percentage of VO₂max than in the untrained person.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) ATP-PCr system: breakdown of phosphocreatine stored in the muscle cell frees an inorganic phosphate that combines with ADP to form ATP (phosphorylation of ATP); it operates during the first 5-8 seconds of exercise, with stores depleted within 10-20 seconds, producing energy for only a few seconds but at the highest rate of production (36 kcal/min).
- It can operate aerobically or anaerobically but is majorly anaerobic, sustaining high-intensity, short-duration exercise such as a 50m dash or powerlifting.
A(ii) Glycolytic system: the breakdown of glucose or glycogen to pyruvic acid and, if fast/anaerobic, eventually to lactic acid; contribution increases after the first 10-15 seconds of exercise and its power input declines after about 45 seconds; it yields 4 molecules of ATP anaerobically, producing about 16 kcal/min.
- Fast/anaerobic glycolysis (final product lactic acid) predominates in events such as an 800m run, while slow/aerobic glycolysis (final product pyruvate) feeds into the oxidative system.
A(iii) Oxidative system: consists of slow glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain and β-oxidation, using oxygen within the mitochondria; slow glycolysis's end product, pyruvic acid, produces acetyl-CoA used in the Krebs cycle; the electron transport chain (aerobic) produces 34 ATP, and β-oxidation uses fat and carbohydrate to produce ATP.
- It is used for exercise lasting longer than 3 minutes, is the slowest system but has the highest energy capacity (about 10 kcal/min), and uses fat as its primary energy substrate for activities such as biking or jogging long distances.
B(i) The three energy systems do not work independently of one another; from very short, very intense exercise to very light, prolonged activity, all three systems make a contribution, although one or two usually predominate depending on exercise intensity and duration, allowing the body to supply ATP across the whole range of exercise demands.
C(i) Fast/anaerobic glycolysis breaks down glucose or glycogen to lactic acid without oxygen, sustains all-out exercise for about 20-40 seconds, and yields far fewer ATP molecules (about 4) than the aerobic pathway.
- Aerobic glycolysis/oxidative phosphorylation breaks down glucose or glycogen (via pyruvic acid) using oxygen within the mitochondria, can be used for prolonged muscular events, and yields far more ATP (about 40 molecules), though at a slower rate of production.

A(ii) Describe the glycolytic energy system under the same headings.
A(iii) Describe the oxidative (aerobic) energy system under the same headings.
B(i) Explain the functional significance of having three energy systems working together during exercise.

questions.answerText:
(i) The client is affected by the physiological decrements of prolonged inactivity/bed rest, including cardiorespiratory deconditioning, skeletal muscle disuse atrophy, and reduced bone mineral density.
(ii) Results of bed rest studies show numerous physiological changes proportional to the duration of bed rest, including reversible glucose intolerance and hyperinsulinemia, reduced total energy expenditure, negative nitrogen balance (reflecting loss of muscle protein), negative calcium balance (reflecting loss of bone mass), and a substantial decrease in plasma volume that affects aerobic power.
- A decline in VO₂max of about 15% was evident within 10 days of bed rest, progressing to 27% within 3 weeks (about 0.8% per day), resulting from a decrease in maximal cardiac output consequent to a reduced stroke volume, itself reflecting reduced end-diastolic volume from decreased blood/plasma volume.
- One month of bed rest in healthy young men resulted in a 10-20% decrease in muscle fibre cross-sectional area and a 21% reduction in peak isokinetic torque of the knee extensors, while causing only a 0.3-3% reduction in lumbar spine bone mineral density and 1.5% at the heel over a similar period, showing that muscle atrophies faster than bone loses density.
(iii) Risk factors/complications include orthostatic intolerance and reduced exercise tolerance due to decreased plasma volume and stroke volume; increased fracture/injury risk from reduced bone mineral density, particularly in the heel and spine (loss of normal mechanical strain from antigravity postural muscles of the lower extremities); and muscle weakness/atrophy limiting his ability to perform activities safely.
(iv) Management/modification options include a graded return to weight-bearing and resistance activity to restore muscle strength and bone loading; low-intensity aerobic reconditioning progressed gradually to rebuild plasma volume and cardiorespiratory capacity; and close monitoring given his reduced tolerance.
- Of these, a graded, progressive weight-bearing and resistance programme is justified because reversibility of the cardiorespiratory, metabolic and muscle decrements from bed rest is fairly rapid (within days to weeks) once normal activity resumes, whereas reversal of the bone mineral density decrement requires weeks to months, so weight-bearing loading should be introduced as early and as safely as possible.

questions.answerText:
(i) This illustrates the cardiovascular response to prolonged exercise in the heat, in which stroke volume declines over time and heart rate increases to try to maintain cardiac output.
(ii) As core body temperature rises during exercise, blood vessels in the skin dilate, diverting more blood to the body's surface for heat loss; this increased skin blood flow competes with the active muscles for a large percentage of cardiac output.
- When a person exercises for prolonged periods in the heat, stroke volume generally declines over time as a consequence of dehydration (from sweating) and the increased blood flow directed to the skin; heart rate increases substantially to try to maintain cardiac output to compensate for the reduced stroke volume.
- Evaporation of sweat aids heat loss, but as humidity increases, evaporation becomes limited, further stressing the cardiovascular system.
(iii) The runner should be encouraged to drink enough fluid to try to match what is lost through sweating, avoid exercising in extreme heat where possible, and reduce the intensity of activity in hot weather.
- Because children have a higher surface-area-to-mass ratio and lower sweat production than adults, comparable precautions and closer monitoring are especially important for younger or more heat-vulnerable clients.

A(i) Define the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
A(ii) Describe the mechanism of cross-bridge formation and the power stroke.
A(iii) State the role of calcium in regulating this process.
B(i) Explain the functional significance of the sliding filament mechanism for force generation in skeletal muscle.
C(i) Distinguish between isotonic and isometric muscle contraction.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The sliding filament theory explains how muscle fibres (sarcomeres) shorten or contract; when calcium is released into the muscle through neurochemical stimulation, the myosin filament "walks" along the actin filament, forming cross-bridges between the myosin head and a prepared site on actin, causing the filaments to slide over one another.
A(ii) When contraction is initiated by a muscle fibre action potential, calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to troponin, uncovering binding sites on actin, and cross-bridges form.
- Once activated, the myosin head tilts toward the arm of the cross-bridge (the power stroke), dragging the actin and myosin filaments in opposite directions, so the muscle shortens and tension is generated.
- The myosin head then releases ADP and phosphate, ATP attaches to myosin, and the head returns to its original position (the recovery stroke), repeating the cycle until the ends of the myosin filament reach the Z disk.
A(iii) Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to troponin, which lifts tropomyosin off the active sites on actin, exposing the myosin-binding sites.
- Cross-bridge formation can occur only when calcium concentration is high; at rest, when calcium concentration is low, cross-bridges do not form.
B(i) The overlap between thick and thin filaments produced by this mechanism determines the tension a muscle can generate (the length-tension relationship); the greater the number of myosin heads interacting with actin, the greater the tension produced.
- The shortening of many sarcomeres, myofibrils and fibres in series develops the overall tension that is transmitted through the muscle and to the bone at both ends to create movement, with force proportional to the number of cross-bridges formed.
C(i) Isotonic contraction is the type of contraction in which tension remains the same while the length of the muscle fibre changes to produce movement, with two subtypes: concentric contraction (shortening) and eccentric contraction (actively controlled lengthening).
- Isometric contraction is the type in which the length of the muscle fibres remains the same while tension increases, with no movement occurring; this is useful for maintaining upright posture.

questions.question:
A chest X-ray shows a well-defined, rounded opacity in the right upper zone that has remained unchanged on serial films over two years. It measures approximately 1 cm in diameter. The margins are well defined, calcification is visible within the lesion, and it is in the upper zone.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis for this solitary pulmonary nodule in an African patient, and how does the likely cause differ from that expected in a United Kingdom patient?
(ii) List all the causes of a solitary pulmonary opacity on the chest X-ray, and for each, describe the distinguishing radiological feature.
(iii) List all the causes of multiple pulmonary opacities/nodules, and describe the specific feature that suggests squamous cell tumour or sarcoma metastases among multiple nodules.
(iv) A different patient presents with a similar CXR showing a solitary pulmonary nodule that has grown rapidly on serial X-rays, has irregular spiculated borders, and is associated with hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how else can primary lung cancer present on the chest X-ray?
(v) What is the mechanism of tension pneumothorax as a recognised complication in a patient with osteogenic sarcoma who develops pulmonary metastases, and which specific malignancy has a high incidence of pneumothorax as a complication?
questions.answerText:
(i)
In Africa, the most likely cause of a solitary pulmonary opacity with calcification, well-defined margins, small size (~0.5–1 cm), and no change on serial X-rays in the upper or mid zones is a tuberculoma. In the United Kingdom, the commonest cause of a solitary pulmonary opacity would be a lung carcinoma (primary or secondary).

(ii)
Causes of solitary pulmonary opacity and distinguishing features:
• Bronchial carcinoma: rapid growth on serial CXR; usually irregular borders (occasionally smooth); may cavitate; associated hilar or mediastinal adenopathy
• Solitary metastasis: usually well defined; lower lobe commoner than upper lobe
• Tuberculoma: calcification common; well-defined margins; usually 0.5–1 cm in diameter; unchanged on serial X-rays; usually upper or mid zones
• Benign tumour (bronchial adenoma/carcinoid): rare; may calcify
• Hamartoma: well defined; lobulated; usually less than 4 cm; calcification may occur in larger lesions; uncommon
• Arterio-venous malformation: feeding vessels may be seen leading into the mass; not common
• Loculated effusion in a fissure: common
• Hydatid cyst: smooth; no surrounding lung reaction; may contain a fluid level; rare
• Lung abscess

(iii)
Causes of multiple pulmonary opacities/nodules:
• Metastases: usually well defined; nodules of varying size; more common in lower lobes; cavitation may be seen in squamous cell tumours and sarcomas; the commonest cause of multiple lung nodules
• Abscesses: staphylococcal infection; usually one or more will show evidence of cavitation
• Hydatid cysts: often large
• Rheumatoid nodules: associated with rheumatoid arthritis
• Wegener's granulomatosis: cavitation common; associated paranasal sinus disease
• Multiple arterio-venous malformations (rare)
Cavitation in multiple nodules suggests squamous cell tumours or sarcomas.

(iv)
Primary lung cancer. Primary lung cancer can also present as: a hilar mass; collapse of a lobe due to bronchial obstruction; pneumonia distal to partial bronchial occlusion; a well-defined or irregular spiculated opacity; a cavitating mass; an apical opacity; involvement of the phrenic nerve with elevation of the diaphragm due to paralysis.

(v)
Tension pneumothorax mechanism: a tear in the visceral pleura acts as a ball valve, allowing air to enter the pleural cavity during inspiration but none to escape during expiration, leading to progressive positive pressure buildup and mediastinal displacement. Malignancy specifically associated with high incidence of pneumothorax: osteogenic sarcoma (metastases).

A(i)
Oncology is a branch of medicine that specialises in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Three primary disciplines:
• Medical oncology: uses drugs like chemotherapy and hormones
• Surgical oncology: uses surgery and surgical procedures
• Radiation oncology: uses therapeutic radiation

A(ii)
Subspecialties by country:
• USA: Medical Oncology; Radiation Oncology; Surgical Oncology
• UK: Clinical Oncology; Radiation Oncology; Surgical Oncology (Specific training not yet available in Nigeria for some subspecialties)
• Nigeria: Clinical Oncology (Radiation and Clinical Oncology)
Postgraduate training in Nigeria:
• West African College of Surgeons, Faculty of Radiology
• National Postgraduate College of Nigeria, Faculty of Radiology
• Duration: 6 years total (Part I: 3 years; Part II: 3 years)
• Primaries in Radiology are the same primary exams as for diagnostic radiology

B(i)
Basic sciences underpinning oncology:
• Anatomy
• Physics
• Communication skills
• Research and evidence-based oncology
• Tumour biology
• Radiobiology
• Clinical pharmacology
• Palliative care and survivorship

B(ii)
Tumour biology and radiobiology provide the scientific basis for understanding how tumours grow, how radiation kills cancer cells (by targeting DNA — directly by producing electrons, and indirectly by producing radicals through ionisation of water), and why specific doses and schedules are used. These sciences explain why radiation oncology requires separate specialist training.

C(i)
Core oncology team members:
• Oncologist
• Surgeons
• Pathologist
• Radiologist
• Oncology nurse

C(ii)
General principles of cancer management:
• Establish diagnosis: history, clinical examination, investigations (diagnostic, baseline, specific)
• Stage the cancer: to determine goal of treatment, prognosis, and type of treatment; using UICC TNM and group staging
• Determine goal of treatment/modality of treatment: curative/radical or palliative; modalities — surgery, radiotherapy, systemic therapy (hormones, immunotherapy, chemotherapy)
• Treatment: multimodality and multidisciplinary; sequence (adjuvant, neoadjuvant, concurrent)
• Follow-up plan: to detect and manage complications of treatment, monitor compliance, detect and manage recurrence
• Survivorship plan: psychosocial, occupational, fertility, and legal issues

B(ii) Describe the approach to reading a chest radiograph: reading environment, reading sequence, reporting, and observer error

C. Distinguish the following uncommon respiratory abnormalities demonstrated on imaging:

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Plain radiography — Basic view: PA-erect. Additional views: AP-erect, supine, semi-erect. Supplementary views: oblique (for rib lesions and some pneumothoraces); lateral decubitus; inspiratory/expiratory (for air trapping); lateral; thoracic inlet; apical/lordotic (for apical lesions).

A(ii)
Fluoroscopy: used for barium swallow (to demonstrate presence of vascular rings and chamber enlargement as indirect signs) and for tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TEF). Types of TEF demonstrable: H-type, type E, type C.

A(iii)
CT and CTA: cross-sectional imaging using X-rays; demonstrates anatomy as well as function especially LV function analysis; CTA (CT angiography) demonstrates pulmonary vasculature and coronary vessels.

B(i)
Imaging modalities in respiratory imaging:
• Conventional: X-ray, fluoroscopy, tomographic studies, ultrasound (2–20 MHz), computerised tomography, MRI (electromagnetic signal/RF pulse)
• Contrast examinations: barium swallow (TEF), bronchography, pulmonary angiography
• Radionuclide studies: V/Q scintigraphy, PET/SPECT
• Fusion studies: USS/MRI, USS/CT, PET-CT

B(ii)
Principles of interpretation include: Reading Environment (appropriate conditions); Reading Sequence (systematic approach to avoid missing lesions); Reporting (formal documentation); Observer error (awareness of the tendency to miss lesions, particularly in review areas).

B(iii)
Competencies:
• Must Know: identify different views of the CXR; identify radiological patterns of common pulmonary abnormalities on CXR
• Should Know: identify radiological patterns of less common pulmonary abnormalities on CXR
• May Know: positioning and technique for CXR views

C(i)
Diaphragmatic abnormalities: congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is demonstrated by barium/fluoroscopy as the imaging modality of choice.

C(ii)
Virtual bronchoscopy: used for tracheal abnormalities; allows non-invasive internal view of the tracheal lumen and airways.

C(iii)
Bone scintigraphy (radionuclide scan) using Tc-99m is the most sensitive modality for bone/rib abnormalities but is non-specific.

questions.question:
A. Describe the radiological imaging evaluation of the spine:
A(i) List all the anatomical elements to evaluate on a spinal plain X-ray (curvature, alignment, vertebral bodies, pedicles, disc spaces, posterior elements, transverse processes, adjacent soft tissue)
A(ii) State how the musculoskeletal radiology request form helps with radiological interpretation, listing all the clinical details required on a request form

B. Describe the principles of plain X-ray diagnosis for arthritis:
B(i) State how arthritis affects bones relative to the joint space (both sides of the joint and joint space narrowing)
B(ii) For each type of hypertrophic arthritis (primary DJD, secondary DJD, and Charcot joint), describe the underlying pathological mechanism and give specific examples of conditions causing secondary DJD and Charcot joint

C. Describe the features that help distinguish bone tumours from infections on plain radiography:
C(i) Describe how the radiological pattern of periosteal reaction differs between solid (chronic osteomyelitis) and lamellated/onion-skin (Ewing's sarcoma) and sunburst (osteosarcoma), and explain what the zone of transition indicates about the aggressiveness of a lesion
C(ii) Describe the plain radiograph features of acute osteomyelitis at different time points (first 1–2 weeks vs later), and state the early imaging modalities of choice and why
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Anatomical elements to evaluate on spinal plain X-ray:
• Curvature
• Vertebral alignment
• Vertebral bodies
• Pedicles
• Disc spaces
• Posterior elements
• Transverse processes
• Adjacent soft tissue

A(ii)
Clinical details required on musculoskeletal request form:
• Age
• Sex
• Presenting complaints (type, duration)
• Mechanism of injury
• Past medical history (PMH): incidental findings, healed fracture, deformity, previous surgery (important for MRI)
• Allergies: especially for contrast studies
The request form helps with differentials by providing clinical context.

B(i)
Arthritis affects bones on both sides of the joint and narrows the joint space in between. This is the fundamental radiological definition of arthritis.

B(ii)
Types of hypertrophic arthritis:
• Primary DJD: intrinsic degeneration of articular cartilage; excessive wear and tear; affects knee, hip, shoulder, elbow; radiological signs: narrowing of joint space, marginal osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts
• Secondary DJD: another process destroys articular cartilage, leading to secondary degenerative changes; presents at atypical age, with unusual appearance (unilateral, atypical location); causes: trauma, infection, AVN, rheumatoid arthritis, haemophilia
• Charcot joint: abnormal sensation leads to microfractures that accumulate unperceived, resulting in joint destruction; causes: syringomyelia (upper limb), diabetes mellitus, syphilis; X-ray: joint destruction, soft tissue swelling, bony fragmentation, sclerosis, osteophytes

C(i)
Periosteal reaction patterns:
• Solid: seen in chronic osteomyelitis; indicates a slow, controlled, chronic process; relatively benign
• Lamellated/onion-skin: seen in Ewing's sarcoma; indicates rapidly alternating periods of tumour growth and attempted periosteal healing; associated with aggressive malignancy
• Sunburst: seen in osteosarcoma; indicates very rapid, aggressive tumour infiltrating periosteum outward; characteristic of malignant bone tumours
Zone of transition: a narrow zone of transition indicates a slow-growing, less aggressive (likely benign) process (geographic pattern). A wide zone of transition indicates rapid growth and an aggressive (likely malignant) process (permeative pattern).

C(ii)
Acute osteomyelitis:
• First 1–2 weeks: plain X-ray is negative; 30% of bone destruction must occur before changes are visible on plain X-ray
• Later: irregular lucencies/osteolytic areas; periosteal reaction; loss of cortico-medullary differentiation
Early imaging modalities of choice:
• Bone scan (hot spot — increased uptake with increased osteoblastic activity in response to infection): sensitive and detects early changes before plain X-ray
• MRI: superior soft tissue detail and bone marrow evaluation; can detect early marrow oedema and soft tissue extension before plain X-ray becomes positive

questions.question:
A 36-year-old male on CT following head trauma has a depressed fracture in the left temporal region with underlying haemorrhagic contusions, a frontal aerocele with a frontal fracture connecting to the top of the frontal sinus, and diffuse axonal injury.

(i) Diffuse brain damage is classified into four types — list all four.
(ii) What is the prevalence of diffuse brain damage without obvious mass lesions?
(iii) List all six post-traumatic sequelae.
(iv) CSF fistula is a post-traumatic sequela — what are the two clinical forms named?
(v) Five radiographic densities are recognised on plain x-rays — list them in order from least to most dense.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Four types of diffuse brain damage:
• Multiple petechial haemorrhages
• Diffuse axonal injury
• Brain swelling
• Hypoxic brain damage

(ii)
About 50% of patients who suffer immediate prolonged unconsciousness following a head injury have no obvious mass or focal lesions of the types described; this is true of about one-third of fatal cases.

(iii)
Six post-traumatic sequelae:
• Cerebral infarction
• Cerebral atrophy
• Hydrocephalus
• Aerocele
• Infections
• CSF fistula

(iv)
Two clinical forms: rhinorrhoea (CSF leak from the nose) and otorrhoea (CSF leak from the ear).

(v)
Five radiographic densities (least to most dense):
• Air/gas (black)
• Fat (dark grey)
• Soft tissues/water (light grey)
• Bone (off white)
• Contrast material/metal (bright white)

A(i)
IMRT is an advanced form of 3DCRT that conforms radiation dose more precisely to the 3D shape of the tumour by modulating — or controlling — the intensity of the beam in multiple small volumes. It utilises the multi-leaf collimators (MLC) on a LINAC to vary the radiation beam intensity. The shape, intensity and direction of the radiation beams may change hundreds of times during the course of treatment, resulting in radiation sculpted in 3 dimensions around the tumour.

A(ii)
DMLCs use up to 120 movable "leaves" to conform the beam to tumour shape from any angle. With DMLCs, the dose of radiation can vary within a single beam. Variation of radiation dose is accomplished by "sliding windows" of radiation beams across the target cancerous area.

A(iii)
In IMRT, the physician designates specific doses of radiation (constraints) that the tumour and OAR should receive. The physics team then uses a sophisticated computer program to develop an individualised plan to meet the constraints. This process is termed "inverse treatment planning."

B(i)
SRT is a technique that allows for pin-point, sub-millimetre accuracy when targeting a tumour volume. Nomenclature: stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT); stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS); stereotactic brain radiosurgery; Gamma Knife™; CyberKnife™.

B(ii)
Major Cyberknife components: a compact linear accelerator mounted on a robotic arm; a treatment couch with motions not possible with conventional couches; a pair of diagnostic x-ray sources directed at corresponding amorphous silicon image detectors; infrared cameras for the Synchrony system. Synchrony system: continuously monitors respiratory motion using infrared diodes on a vest tracked by infrared cameras, used in conjunction with internal fiducials tracked with real-time x-ray images every few seconds.

B(iii)
IGRT is the use of a variety of imaging techniques alongside radiotherapy to enable patient position and tumour to be tracked and confirmed. Image guidance is necessary because tumour and normal tissues move with time. Three types of movement: periodic and predictable (like respiratory motion); irregular (like peristalsis); permanent (like tumour shrinkage).
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(i)
The kidney has a cortex, of even thickness (around 2cm), surrounding the medulla and papillae.
The papillae drain into the calyces and renal pelvis, forming the pelvicalyceal system.

(ii)
The cortex is affected in acute and chronic nephritis, causing increased echogenicity.
The cortex is also affected in chronic pyelonephritis, showing scarring most commonly at the poles.
In chronic pyelonephritis the cortex is pulled inwards towards a distorted calyx.
The papillary/medullary region is affected in nephrocalcinosis, with calcifications clustered in the papillary regions.
Nephrocalcinosis is associated with renal tubular acidosis, hyperparathyroidism, or medullary sponge kidneys.
The papillary region is also affected in papillary necrosis, a complication of diabetes, sickle cell disease, or excess paracetamol.
The pelvicalyceal system is the site of calculi, tuberculosis, and transitional cell tumours.

(iii)
Chronic pyelonephritis causes progressive renal cortical scarring, and if bilateral this leads to chronic renal disease.
Long-standing obstruction of the pelvicalyceal system causes progressive cortical atrophy.
In severe, long-standing obstruction the cortex may be completely destroyed, leaving a non-functioning kidney.
questions.question:

A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back, diaphoresis, and hypertension. A chest X-ray is urgently performed. The radiograph shows widening of the mediastinum and prominence of the thoracic aorta.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis based on these radiological findings, and which imaging modality offers the highest temporal and spatial resolution for definitive evaluation of this condition?
(ii) What are the changes of the aorta that can be identified on a chest radiograph, and which of these constitutes a medical emergency?
(iii) What are the principles of initial management, including the goal of radiotherapy/imaging-guided intervention in this setting?
(iv) Which invasive imaging technique is currently the primary tool for detailed study of the aorta and integral to most cardiac interventional techniques, and what specific procedure would be performed to outline the aortic anatomy with contrast?
(v) What is the definitive imaging-guided or surgical approach, and what are the main complications of the condition if left untreated?
questions.answerText:
(i)
The most likely diagnosis is aortic dissection. Angiography offers the highest temporal and spatial resolution of all cardiac imaging techniques and is currently the primary tool for detailed cardiac study.

(ii)
Changes of the aorta identifiable on chest radiograph include:
• Elongation/distortion
• Calcification
• Dissection (medical emergency)
• Aneurysm (graded by size: 5, 4, 3, 2 cm)
Aortic dissection is the medical emergency among these changes.

(iii)
Initial management follows general principles of cancer/cardiac management: establish diagnosis, determine goal of treatment. In imaging, the goal is to give optimal information about tumour (or in this context, aortic) extent with minimal harm. The imaging approach is to use the most appropriate technique considering diagnostic appropriateness, cost, availability, associated hazards, and accuracy.

(iv)
Angiography — specifically aortography — is the primary invasive imaging tool. Aortography outlines the aortic lumen with contrast. Coronary angiography can also be performed as part of the workup and is used in percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA).

(v)
Definitive management involves interventional or surgical repair. If untreated, aortic dissection leads to progressive widening of the mediastinum on serial chest films, haemorrhage into the mediastinum, and death from rupture. Bleeding into the mediastinum will cause widening of the mediastinum; a normal mediastinum may appear wider on supine films, making it more difficult to assess.

questions.question:
A. Describe the palliative care approach under the following headings:
(i) The WHO definition of palliative care
(ii) All six principles of palliative care
(iii) The four settings where palliative care can be given

B. (i) State the estimated global number of people needing palliative care annually and the percentage who currently receive it.
(ii) List all disease categories with their proportion of patients needing palliative care.
(iii) List all professionals who are members of the palliative care team.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Palliative care is an approach that improves the quality of life of patients (adults and children) and their families who are facing problems associated with life-threatening illness. It prevents and relieves suffering through the early identification, correct assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, whether physical, psychosocial or spiritual.

A(ii)
Six principles:
• Affirm life and regards dying as a normal process
• Neither hastens nor postpones death
• Provides relief from pain and other distressing symptoms
• Integrates the psychological and spiritual aspects of care
• Offers a support system to help patients live as actively as possible until death
• Offers a support system to help patients' families cope during the patient's illness and in their own bereavement

A(iii)
Four settings: Home; Hospice; Hospital; Aged care facility.

B(i)
An estimated 56.8 million people, including 25.7 million in the last year of life, are in need of palliative care annually. Worldwide, only about 14% of people who need palliative care currently receive it.

B(ii)
Proportions:
• Cardiovascular diseases: 38.5%
• Cancer: 34%
• Chronic respiratory diseases: 10.3%
• AIDS: 5.7%
• Diabetes: 4.6%
• Others (kidney failure, liver failure): 6.9%

B(iii)
Professionals: physicians, nursing, support workers, paramedics, pharmacists, physiotherapists, and volunteers.

(i)
Perforated abdominal viscus (commonly a perforated peptic ulcer), with resulting pneumoperitoneum (free intraperitoneal air); the most common cause of free gas is perforation of a peptic ulcer.

(ii)
Pneumoperitoneum refers to disruption of the wall of a hollow viscus, allowing gas to enter the peritoneal cavity.

(iii)
Patients with such conditions need urgent surgery. An exception exists: occasionally patients with vague abdominal symptoms have unequivocal features of pneumoperitoneum but little clinical evidence of peritonism (pneumoperitoneum without peritonitis); these are treated expectantly and do not require surgery.

(iv)
Rigler's sign (the double wall sign, where air is present on both the luminal and peritoneal sides of the bowel wall) and the football sign (a massive pneumoperitoneum outlining the whole peritoneal cavity, likened to an American football) are additional signs.
questions.question:
A patient presents with sudden severe epigastric pain and a rigid abdomen. An erect chest film is requested.
(i) What is the most likely underlying diagnosis and abnormal finding expected on the film?
(ii) What is the pathological basis for this radiographic finding?
(iii) What immediate management is required, and is there an exception in which surgery is not needed?
(iv) List two additional radiographic signs that could support the diagnosis if the amount of free gas were large.

questions.answerText:
(i)
An immediate film shows contrast in the tubules of the kidney.
This causes the whole kidney to be slightly denser, with the renal outlines easier to see.
This early stage is called the nephrogram phase.
The 5-10 minute film shows the calyces, renal pelvis and parts of the ureters outlined with contrast.
This later stage is called the pyelogram phase.

(ii)
If the kidneys are excreting normally, ureteric compression is applied, if available.
This compression helps to distend the calyces and demonstrate any calyceal abnormality.
A film of the renal areas is then taken at 15 minutes to show calyceal detail.

(iii)
An obstructing lesion shows persistent contrast outlining the renal cortex, a delayed nephrogram.
This occurs because the obstruction slows passage of contrast out of the renal tubules.
Other signs of obstruction include delayed uptake of contrast and delayed appearance of contrast in the collecting system.
A dilated collecting system above the level of the obstructing lesion is also seen.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the course taken by intravenous contrast through the kidney during intravenous pyelography, naming the phases seen.
(ii) State the technique used during the procedure to improve demonstration of calyceal detail.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of a delayed nephrogram as a sign of obstruction.

(i) Describe the vessels involved in cerebral angiography, including the site of vascular access, the vessels catheterised, and the vascular site from which most intracranial aneurysms arise.
(ii) State the standard/safe site used for catheter access in cerebral angiography.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis for the pattern of blood distribution seen on CT following rupture of an intracranial aneurysm.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Cerebral angiography is nowadays performed via the femoral artery.
Selective catheterisation of the internal carotid artery (ICA) or vertebral artery (VA) is used.
Most aneurysms arise from the circle of Willis.
An arch aortogram may also be performed if stenosis at the origin of an arch vessel is suspected.
Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is now taking over from conventional angiography for detecting berry aneurysms.

(ii)
The femoral artery is the standard site of vascular access used for cerebral angiography.

(iii)
On CT after subarachnoid haemorrhage, blood fills the basal cisterns and subarachnoid space.
The blood appears white, i.e. of high density, on the scan.
The blood is usually larger in amount near the site of the aneurysm.
Its distribution may therefore indicate which vessel the aneurysm is arising from.
This reflects the proximity of the bleeding point to the site of pooling of blood.
Rarely, the aneurysm or an angioma may itself be demonstrated on the scan.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man presents with lower back pain and right hip pain. A plain radiograph of the pelvis shows narrowing of the right hip joint space, marginal osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and subchondral cysts on both sides of the joint. He has a history of a road traffic accident 5 years ago injuring the same hip.

(i) What type of arthritis is this, and how does it differ from primary degenerative joint disease (DJD) in terms of age, appearance, laterality, and causes?
(ii) Describe the plain radiograph features of primary osteoarthritis/DJD, listing all four signs.
(iii) What is Charcot joint, what conditions cause it, and what are all the plain radiograph features of Charcot joint?
(iv) Describe the types of erosive arthritis, and the mechanism by which erosive arthritis destroys bone.
(v) What is the difference between the arthritis caused by rheumatoid arthritis and gout in terms of the joints affected, and which seronegative rheumatoid arthritis variants are recognised?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Secondary degenerative joint disease (secondary DJD/secondary osteoarthritis). Differences from primary DJD:
• Age: secondary DJD presents at an atypical (younger) age
• Appearance: may be atypical/unusual radiological features
• Laterality: may be unilateral (primary is typically bilateral and symmetrical)
• Causes of secondary DJD: trauma, infection, AVN (avascular necrosis), rheumatoid arthritis, haemophilia, etc.
Primary DJD: intrinsic degeneration of articular cartilage; excessive wear and tear; affects both sides of the joint; typical sites: knee, hip, shoulder, elbow.

(ii)
Plain radiograph features of primary DJD:
• Narrowing of the joint space
• Marginal osteophytes
• Subchondral sclerosis
• Subchondral cysts

(iii)
Charcot joint: caused by abnormal sensation leading to microfractures that go unperceived and accumulate, resulting in joint destruction.
Conditions causing Charcot joint: syringomyelia (upper limb), diabetes mellitus, syphilis.
Plain radiograph features:
• Joint destruction
• Soft tissue swelling
• Bony fragmentation
• Sclerosis
• Osteophytes

(iv)
Erosive arthritis: caused by synovial proliferation (pannus formation) and inflammation, causing erosions in small joints especially; destroys part of the cortex.
Types:
• Rheumatoid arthritis
• Gout
• Haemophilia
• RA variants: ankylosing spondylitis
• Seronegative RA: psoriatic arthritis, Reiter's syndrome
• Connective tissue diseases: scleroderma, sarcoid, SLE

(v)
Rheumatoid arthritis predominantly affects small joints (especially hands and feet) through synovial proliferation and pannus formation causing erosions. Gout also causes erosive arthritis from urate crystal deposition.
Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis variants listed:
• Psoriatic arthritis
• Reiter's syndrome

(i)
Iodine-131 is taken up by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), depending on TSH stimulation and iodine load.
It is then retained in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland.
Its biodistribution to other organs includes the salivary gland, stomach, breast, kidney, bladder, and intestine.

(ii)
Usually 3-10mCi of I-131 is administered orally on an outpatient basis.
A huge multinodular goitre may require up to 15mCi.
Above 15mCi, admission of the patient becomes necessary.

(iii)
The path length of the beta energy of I-131 is only 0.5mm.
This means the therapeutic effect is limited to the thyroid gland itself.
The principal gamma photon energy is 364 keV, with 81% abundance.
This gamma emission is used for scintigraphy and measurement of uptake.
However, this gamma emission also causes unwanted whole-body irradiation.
This whole-body irradiation is the possible unwanted effect of the therapy.

A patient receiving CT contrast medium develops signs of contrast reaction. The radiologist is also concerned about contrast-induced nephropathy.

(i) CT intravenous contrast contains a specific element — what is it and what is its effect on x-rays?
(ii) What are the two contraindications for CT IV contrast use related to the kidneys?
(iii) What specific risk is associated with hyperacute renal failure regarding creatinine?
(iv) MRI contrast contains a different agent — what is it and what is its effect on MRI signal?
(v) In what specific condition of renal failure is MRI contrast (gadolinium) contraindicated, and what is the named risk?
questions.answerText:
(i)
CT IV contrast contains iodine, which attenuates x-rays; it is power-injected and causes vasovagal reactions.

(ii)
CT IV contrast is contraindicated in: acute renal failure and chronic renal failure, because of the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.

(iii)
In hyperacute renal failure, the creatinine has not risen yet — decreased urine output or anuria is acute renal failure regardless of the creatinine level.

(iv)
MRI IV contrast contains gadolinium chelated to a carrier molecule; it acts as a paramagnetic molecule, which increases signal on T1 images.

(v)
MRI gadolinium contrast is contraindicated in acute renal failure and particularly ESRD (end-stage renal disease), because of the risk of NSF (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis).

questions.question:
On barium meal of a 50-year-old patient, a benign gastric ulcer is identified. The radiologist notes a thin radiolucent line around the ulcer crater and oedematous submucosal tissue surrounding the crater.

(i) Name the two specific signs for a benign gastric ulcer.
(ii) Along which anatomical surface do most benign gastric ulcers occur?
(iii) Benign gastric ulcers of one particular curvature are unusual and often associated with a specific drug — state both.
(iv) What is the relationship between duodenal ulcers and malignancy?
(v) Along which surface of the duodenal cap do most duodenal ulcers occur?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Hampton line: non-ulcerated mucosa around the ulcer crater (thin radiolucent line). Ulcer mound: oedematous submucosal tissue surrounding the ulcer crater.

(ii)
Most gastric ulcers occur along the lesser curvature or posterior wall of the body or antrum.

(iii)
Benign gastric ulcers of the greater curvature are unusual and often associated with aspirin ingestion.

(iv)
Duodenal ulcers alone are rarely malignant.

(v)
Most duodenal ulcers occur along the anterior surface of the cap.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the composition of breast tissue as seen on mammography, and how this composition changes with age.
(ii) State how the tissue composition/site within the breast relates to common benign and malignant pathologies.
(iii) Explain how breast carcinoma may spread to distant structures and produce a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A post-menopausal breast shows very little glandular breast tissue on mammography, being predominantly fatty.
Younger women have denser, more glandular breasts.
This makes mammograms more difficult to interpret in the younger, denser breast.

(ii)
Benign lesions such as cysts and fibroadenomas are common in younger women.
They often occur in dense breasts associated with fibrocystic disease.
They are usually well-defined, of low density, and are often multiple, aiding diagnosis.
Carcinoma may show as a spiculated mass, which is the most characteristic sign of malignancy.
Carcinoma may also show as a dense mass without spiculation, a vague density, or an area of distortion.
Microcalcification of variable particle size/shape with segmental distribution is also suspicious for carcinoma.
Carcinoma is more difficult to detect within a dense breast than a fatty one.

(iii)
Breast carcinoma commonly metastasises to bone, from which secondary deposits occur in about two-thirds of women with the disease.
Breast carcinoma also metastasises to the brain, where lesions show ring enhancement with marked surrounding oedema on CT, causing focal neurological deficit.

(i)
Fibroids may be intramural, subserosal, or subendometrial (submucosal) in location.
Occasionally fibroids are pedunculated, lying away from the uterus.

(ii)
Pedunculated fibroids are often confused with an ovarian or other pelvic mass.
Fibroids in the cervix are less common than those in the body of the uterus.
On ultrasound, fibroids cause enlargement and distortion of the uterine outline.
They appear as a round or lobulated mass of variable echogenicity.
They cause distortion and displacement of the endometrial echo.

(iii)
Carcinoma of the cervix can occlude the cervical canal.
This occlusion results in a fluid collection within the uterine cavity, known as haematometra.
Ultrasound may also detect hydronephrosis secondary to cervical carcinoma.
Ultrasound may also detect spread to the iliac nodes secondary to cervical carcinoma.
This shows how a cervical lesion can obstruct the ureters and impair renal function, a functional deficit distant from the primary site.

(ii) State how the site of a fibroid relates to its clinical/imaging presentation.
(iii) Explain how disease of the cervix may cause a distant functional deficit affecting another organ system.

The mass is growing into the 4th ventricle, causing hydrocephalus due to obstruction of CSF flow.

(ii)
Medulloblastoma is the commonest cerebellar tumour in children; on CT it shows as a hyperdense central mass growing into the 4th ventricle, with intense enhancement after contrast.

(iii)
Ependymoma is the next commonest cerebellar tumour to consider in this age group.

The temporal horns of the lateral ventricles are dilated due to hydrocephalus, and MRI is better than CT for imaging the posterior fossa. Subarachnoid haemorrhage — non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense lesion in the basal cisterns, sylvian fissure, and interhemispheric cleft.

(ii)
Non-contrast enhanced CT scan of an intraparenchymal bleed with surrounding oedema.

questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(i)
Barium enema demonstrates: diverticulosis; diverticulitis; abnormal colon movement; dilation (widening) of the colon; polyps and cancers of the colon and rectum.

(ii)
Polyps and small cancers are more readily found on the air contrast barium enema or double-contrast barium enema.

(iii)
Oral contrast: dilute barium or dilute gastrografin — used to outline the stomach and bowel, enabling differentiation from other structures. Intravenous contrast: used to differentiate normal blood vessels from abnormal masses, to make an abnormality more apparent, and to demonstrate the vascular nature of a mass.

(iv)
One head CT scan gives a dose equivalent to 115 chest x-rays.

(v)
Hounsfield values:
• Water: 0 HU
• Air: −1000 HU
• Fat: −20 to −200 HU
• Fluid: 0–15 HU
• Soft tissue: 20–60 HU
• Calcification: 150–200 HU
• Bone: +1000 HU

A barium enema shows an apple-core sign in the descending colon of a 65-year-old patient. The radiologist also notes diverticulosis, dilation of the colon, and polyps on the same examination.

(i) List all the pathologies that a barium enema can demonstrate.
(ii) What distinguishes the air contrast barium enema from a standard barium enema in terms of sensitivity for lesions?
(iii) For CT scanning of the abdomen, what oral contrast agent and what intravenous contrast are used, and why is each used?
