A. Describe the imaging of bone tumours using the pattern of bone destruction and tumour matrix:
A(i) Describe osteoblastic tumour matrix appearance and what it indicates about tumour origin
A(ii) Describe cartilaginous (chondroid) tumour matrix appearance and give an example of a tumour with this matrix
A(iii) State which tumour shows a sunburst periosteal reaction and which shows a lamellated (onion-skin) periosteal reaction

B. Describe fractures in children and adults:
B(i) Define a fracture, distinguish complete from incomplete fractures, and describe all types of incomplete fractures specific to children (greenstick, torus/buckle, and pathological)
B(ii) Describe how to classify any fracture radiologically, listing all four descriptors (direction, relation of fragments, number of fragments, and external communication) with subcategories for each

C. Describe bone tumours by their clinical characteristics:
C(i) State the factors to consider when classifying any bone tumour (number, location, soft tissue involvement, age, sex, matrix, periosteal reaction, and zone of transition)
C(ii) Define what "bone in bone" appearance indicates, and in which condition it occurs
C(iii) Distinguish between a benign periosteal reaction and an aggressive/malignant periosteal reaction in terms of the types seen for each category
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Osteoblastic tumour matrix: fluffy, cotton cloud, bone formation appearance on X-ray. Indicates osteoblastic/bone-forming tumour origin — characteristic of osteosarcoma.

A(ii)
Cartilaginous (chondroid) tumour matrix: comma, punctate, popcorn calcification pattern on X-ray. Example: chondrosarcoma.

A(iii)
Sunburst periosteal reaction — osteosarcoma. Lamellated/onion-skin periosteal reaction — Ewing's sarcoma.

B(i)
A fracture is a disruption in all or part of the cortex. Complete fracture: all cortices disrupted. Incomplete fractures (specific to children):
• Greenstick fracture: fracture through one cortex only
• Torus (buckle) fracture: buckling of the cortex/bucket handle appearance
• Pathological fracture: fracture through an area of underlying bone abnormality

B(ii)
Fracture classification:
• Direction: transverse, oblique, spiral, longitudinal
• Relation of fragments (distal to proximal): displacement, angulation, shortening/overlap
• Number of fragments: simple (2 fragments); comminuted (>2 fragments)
• External communication: closed fracture; open/compound fracture

C(i)
Factors to consider when classifying any bone tumour:
• Number: solitary or multiple
• Location: flat or tubular bones
• Soft tissue involvement
• Age
• Sex
• Matrix (osteoblastic vs cartilaginous)
• Periosteal reaction (benign vs malignant type)
• Zone of transition (narrow vs wide)

C(ii)
"Bone in bone" appearance: a bone density seen within the outline of another bone; it occurs in chronic osteomyelitis.

C(iii)
Benign periosteal reaction: none, or solid periosteal reaction (e.g. solid — chronic osteomyelitis).
Aggressive/malignant periosteal reaction: lamellated/onion-skin (e.g. Ewing's sarcoma); sunburst (e.g. osteosarcoma). Malignant tumours may show no periosteal reaction or only aggressive patterns; benign lesions show none or solid.

questions.question:
A stroke patient undergoes imaging assessment. On non-contrast CT, a large acute infarction in the MCA territory is identified involving the lateral surfaces of the left frontal, parietal and temporal lobes, with mass effect and rightward midline shift. A dense MCA sign is also noted on CT angiography.

(i) What does the dense MCA sign on CT represent?
(ii) What does CT angiography show in this patient?
(iii) Stroke is classified into two major categories — name them, state their relative frequency, and explain the difference.
(iv) What is haemorrhagic transformation?
(v) List all imaging modalities used for stroke assessment.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The dense MCA sign represents occlusion of the MCA visible on CT angiography; it is the hyperdense appearance of thrombus within the MCA on non-contrast CT.

(ii)
CT angiography shows occlusion of the left MCA at the proximal segment.

(iii)
Ischaemic strokes: caused by interruption of blood supply to the brain; account for about 80–87% of strokes. Haemorrhagic strokes: result from rupture of a blood vessel or an abnormal vascular structure; account for about 20% of strokes.

(iv)
Bleeding can develop inside areas of ischaemia, a condition known as "haemorrhagic transformation."

(v)
Imaging modalities:
• Computed tomography: unenhanced imaging, CT angiography, and perfusion imaging
• Magnetic resonance imaging and MRA — including diffusion and perfusion studies, MR spectroscopy
• Ultrasonography — B-mode, Doppler, transcranial
• Echocardiography
• PET, SPECT
• Conventional angiography/interventional
• Plain films — skull and chest x-ray

(i)
Position: the pituitary fossa is a rounded depression in the middle of the skull base lying above the sphenoid sinus.
Boundaries: it is bounded by the bony anterior and posterior clinoid processes.
Lining: it is lined by a thin white line called the lamina dura.

(ii)
Erosion of the dorsum sellae occurs with a local tumour or with raised intracranial pressure.
It shows firstly as loss of the white line of the lamina dura lining the floor of the fossa.
This makes it a useful early sign of underlying pituitary or intracranial pathology.

(iii)
Pituitary microadenomas cause hyperprolactinaemia and are usually less than 1cm in size.
Small pituitary tumours will not show changes on plain film; high resolution CT or MRI is needed to demonstrate them.
Craniopharyngiomas occur in childhood or adolescence and show calcification in 80% of cases.
Some craniopharyngiomas can be diagnosed purely from midline calcification above the pituitary fossa on plain film.
15% of craniopharyngiomas grow into the pituitary fossa causing enlargement, and they are related to the floor of the 3rd ventricle.
On CT, craniopharyngiomas are cystic or partially cystic, with enhancement of the solid parts after contrast, making surgical removal difficult.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the pituitary fossa under the following headings: position, boundaries, and lining.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis of why erosion of the dorsum sellae is a significant radiographic finding.
(iii) Distinguish between a pituitary microadenoma and a craniopharyngioma in terms of age of occurrence, calcification, and radiological behaviour.

A. Describe the components of cancer control and the levels of prevention:
A(i) Define disease control, disease elimination, and disease eradication using the WHO definitions
A(ii) List all four components of cancer control in the correct order

B. Describe the levels of prevention in cancer control:
B(i) Primary prevention: define it and list all four primary prevention strategies, with examples of each
B(ii) Secondary prevention: define it and list all the screening and early detection methods
B(iii) Tertiary prevention: define it and list all the tertiary prevention measures

C. Describe screening as a tool in cancer control:
C(i) Define screening and state what types of individuals it targets
C(ii) State the screening tests used for prostate cancer, breast cancer, and cervical cancer
C(iii) Explain the clinical basis for why screening for cervical cancer is important in Nigeria — include the proportion diagnosed at advanced stage and the incidence figure at the University College Hospital
questions.answerText:
A(i)
WHO definitions:
• Disease Control: reduction in the incidence, prevalence, morbidity, or mortality of a disease to a locally acceptable level
• Disease Elimination: reduction to zero of the incidence of disease or infection in a defined geographical area
• Disease Eradication: permanent reduction to zero of the worldwide incidence of the disease

A(ii)
Four components of cancer control (in order):
• Prevention
• Early detection
• Treatment
• Palliative care

B(i)
Primary prevention (prevent development):
• Vaccination (e.g. against HPV)
• Health education and promotion
• Prophylactic surgery
• Chemoprevention

B(ii)
Secondary prevention (prevent progression):
• Screening: e.g. Pap smear, mammography
• Treatment: cryotherapy, surgery, systemic therapy, radiotherapy

B(iii)
Tertiary prevention (prevent suffering):
• Pain control
• Other symptom control
• Psychosocial support

C(i)
Screening is a test carried out on asymptomatic individuals (apparently healthy persons) to detect the presence of a disease. It targets apparently healthy/asymptomatic individuals. It can be a lab test or clinical examination.

C(ii)
Screening tests:
• Prostate cancer: PSA (prostate-specific antigen) and DRE (digital rectal examination); all men should undergo yearly screening beginning at age 40
• Breast cancer: BSE (breast self-examination), mammography
• Cervical cancer: Pap smear

C(iii)
Cervical cancer screening is critically important in Nigeria because:
• It is the 2nd most common malignancy of women in Nigeria
• 70% of cases are diagnosed at advanced stages (III–IV)
• Over 1000 new cases are diagnosed annually at UCH (University College Hospital)
• It usually affects women around 45 years, but about 20% are seen at ages less than 30 years
• Incidence is substantially higher among low socioeconomic classes
• Early detection via Pap smear allows treatment at a curable stage (secondary prevention)

questions.question:
A 20-year-old presents with pain and swelling around the knee. X-ray shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion with periosteal new bone formation and a soft tissue mass.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the typical age group and site of predisposition?
(iii) What is the underlying pathophysiology producing the radiographic appearance, including the classic periosteal sign?
(iv) What is the significance of lung involvement in this disease?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Osteogenic sarcoma, the commonest primary malignant bone tumour.

(ii)
It is a bone-forming tumour affecting the metaphysis in children and young adults, particularly around the knee.

(iii)
It presents with a variety of appearances: an irregular destructive lesion involving the medulla, cortical destruction, a soft tissue mass displacing tissue planes, and new bone formation. Elevation of the periosteum associated with new bone formation produces the classic "Codman's triangle."

(iv)
Lung metastases develop early in osteogenic sarcoma and may be bone-producing, causing very dense nodular opacities in the lungs.

questions.question:
A. Describe the head and neck cancers as a group:
A(i) Define head and neck (HN) cancers and list the specific sites and subsites included under this category, including those that are NOT classified as HN cancers
A(ii) State the global and regional incidence proportions and demographic characteristics (sex, age, social class) for HN cancers

B. Describe the aetiology of head and neck cancers:
B(i) State the major risk factors for HN cancer development and the specific proportion of HN cancers linked to tobacco use
B(ii) List all other aetiological factors including specific viral associations, environmental/occupational exposures, and systemic factors

C. Describe the clinical presentation of head and neck cancers and the approach to treatment:
C(i) List all the common symptoms of HN cancers, organised by anatomical category (swelling, swallowing, ulcers, voice, bleeding, pain, blockage, weight)
C(ii) Describe the treatment approach for HN cancers including screening, diagnosis, investigations, the role of the multidisciplinary team, all treatment modalities, and for each modality state what type of disease it is most suited for
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Head and neck cancers are malignant tumours arising from the head or the neck region. They include:
• Tumours of the oral cavity: cancer of the lips, anterior two-thirds of the tongue, buccal mucosa, gingiva, floor of the mouth, and hard palate
• Tumours of the nasopharynx, oropharynx (tonsils, base of tongue, and soft palate), and hypopharynx
• Tumours of the parotid glands and other minor salivary glands in the floor of the mouth
• Tumours of the paranasal sinuses (maxillary sinus) and the nasal cavity
• Tumours of the larynx
NOT classified as HN cancers: primary tumours of the eye, brain, thyroid, scalp, skin, muscle, and bones of the head and neck region.

A(ii)
Head and neck cancers account for 5–50% of cancers globally; 5–8% of cancers in Europe and America; more common in males than females; 10th most common cancer in the world. Incidence is on the increase, with a peak amongst the active working class.

B(i)
Major risk factors: tobacco and alcohol. The use of both tobacco and alcohol carries higher risk than use of either alone. 85% of HN cancers are linked to tobacco use.

B(ii)
Other aetiological factors:
• Infection: HPV (oral tumours), EBV (Epstein-Barr virus — nasopharyngeal tumours)
• Radiation including sun exposure
• Environmental pollution: asbestos, fumes, chemicals, wood dust, dyes
• Poor oral hygiene
• Nutritional deficiencies
• Depressed immunity

C(i)
Common symptoms:
• Swelling/lumps
• Odynophagia/dysphagia
• Ulcers/sores that do not heal
• Hoarseness
• Bleeding
• Pain including headache/ear ache
• Discharge
• Blockage/obstruction
• Weight loss

C(ii)
Treatment approach:
• Screening for early diagnosis
• Diagnosis
• Investigations to aid treatment
• Multidisciplinary assessment/joint clinic of specialists: surgeons, clinical/medical oncologists/haematologists, radiation oncologists, palliative care physicians/team, oncology nurses, medical social workers, occupational therapists
Treatment modalities and their applications:
• Surgery: for localised cases
• Radiotherapy: for localised tumours and tumours confined to regions
• Chemotherapy/immunotherapy/targeted therapy: for metastasised cases
• Hormone therapy
• Support services (appropriate for each disease/patient)
There are overlaps in management, which is why each case should be discussed at multidisciplinary rounds.

questions.question:
A. Describe the Cobalt-60 telecobalt unit under the following headings:
(i) Historical significance: when and where the first patient was treated
(ii) How Cobalt-60 is produced and the source specifications
(iii) How Cobalt-60 decays and the energies of photons emitted

B. (i) State three advantages of the cobalt unit over orthovoltage therapy.
(ii) Explain why low-energy x-rays are disadvantaged for treating deep-seated tumours (list all four disadvantages).
(iii) State which unit is the most widely used treatment unit in developing countries and why.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The first patient with a telecobalt unit was treated at the London Regional Cancer Centre, London, Ontario, Canada on 27 October 1951.

A(ii)
Cobalt-60 is produced by bombardment of Co-59 with neutrons: ⁵⁹Co + ⁰n¹ → ⁶⁰Co + Q (energy released). The source usually houses 10,000 Ci; source size is 1.5 to 2 cm diameter capsule.

A(iii)
Cobalt-60 emits beta and gamma radiation. Energy of gamma photons: 1.17 MeV and 1.33 MeV; average energy 1.25 MeV.

B(i)
Three advantages over orthovoltage:
• Higher energy — higher build-up depth; maximum dose at 5 mm depth
• Skin-sparing effect
• Higher penetration; useful to treat deep-seated tumours; less maintenance of equipment

B(ii)
Four disadvantages of low-energy x-rays:
• Higher dose to bone — photoelectric absorption
• Maximum dose on the surface, hence higher skin dose
• Treatment to a depth of only a few centimetres possible
• Low energy, hence high scattered radiation and larger penumbra

B(iii)
The telecobalt unit is the most widely used treatment unit in developing countries; Cobalt-60 is the source of radiation.

questions.question:
A. Describe the imaging modalities available for examination of the cardiovascular system:
A(i) Plain radiography: views used, what it demonstrates, and its specific advantages as a first-line investigation
A(ii) Echocardiography: the modalities available (two-dimensional, M-mode, Doppler), the two approaches (transthoracic and transoesophageal), and the indications for each approach
A(iii) Computed tomography: the technology used, what specific vascular and cardiac structures it demonstrates, and its limitation

B. Describe radionuclide imaging of the cardiovascular system:
B(i) Blood pool imaging: how it is performed and what information it provides
B(ii) Myocardial perfusion imaging: name the two techniques used including PET and what each demonstrates

C. State and explain the specific radiological features of the following conditions on plain chest radiograph, distinguishing between them:
C(i) Pericardial effusion
C(ii) Constrictive pericarditis
C(iii) Acute myocardial infarction
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Plain radiography (chest X-ray): views used — PA, lateral, AP (supine or semi-erect for ill patients). It demonstrates cardiac size and contour, chamber enlargement, lung fields giving clues to cardiac function, metallic implants, calcification, and bony anomalies. It remains a valuable and readily available imaging modality; it provides important physiologic as well as anatomic information; it uses ionising radiation (X-rays). It is the first-line investigation for cardiac and pulmonary assessment.

A(ii)
Echocardiography utilises high frequency sound waves to demonstrate anatomy and dynamic function. Modalities: two-dimensional, M-mode, pulse and continuous wave, and colour flow Doppler studies. Two approaches — transthoracic and transoesophageal.
Indications for transthoracic ECHO: assessment of left ventricular function; determination of the cause of cardiac failure; evaluation of a patient with cardiac murmur; assessment of known or suspected cardiac valve disease and congenital heart disease; evaluation of abnormal CXR and follow-up.
Indications for transoesophageal ECHO (more complex, requires topical anaesthetics and mild sedation): assessment of the left atrium, mitral valve, interatrial septum and aortic valve; diagnosis of dissection of the thoracic aorta; assessment of some right-sided cardiac lesions and left ventricular function; perioperatively.

A(iii)
CT uses spiral multislice technology with contrast study. It demonstrates coronary vessels, pulmonary artery and its major branches; used for assessment of the thoracic aorta and masses in or near the heart; also demonstrates anatomy as well as function especially LV function analysis. Limitation: associated with high doses of radiation.

B(i)
Blood pool imaging: performed by ECG-gated pool scan at rest and under stress conditions. It gives valuable data on overall and regional left ventricular function.

B(ii)
Myocardial perfusion imaging:
• Radionuclide scanning: for assessment of myocardial perfusion and viability
• Positron emission tomography (PET): gives detailed insight to complex phenomena such as hibernating, infarcted, or stunned myocardium

C(i)
Pericardial effusion: massive enlargement of the cardiac shadow with rounded globular appearance; the lung fields are usually clear; rapidly enlarging heart on serial films. Causes include viral pericarditis, collagen-vascular disease (e.g. lupus), uraemia, TB, trauma, post-myocardial infarction, metastasis.

C(ii)
Constrictive pericarditis: the heart is not enlarged; there is roughening of the cardiac outline.

C(iii)
Acute myocardial infarction: features of pulmonary oedema (lower zone haziness, clouding of the perihilar and peripheral parenchyma and septal lines); pleural effusion; progressive enlargement of the heart on serial CXR. Stable angina may also show coronary and aortic calcification and calcified atheromatous plaques on CXR.

questions.question:
A. Describe the general principles of cancer management:
A(i) List all the steps in the general principles of cancer management in the correct sequence
A(ii) Describe what is meant by "cure" in oncology, including the time-based definitions used
A(iii) Describe what "palliation" means in the context of cancer treatment

B. Describe the staging of cancer:
B(i) State the aims of staging cancer and list all three components of the UICC TNM staging system, stating what each letter stands for and what it assesses
B(ii) Name two alternative or site-specific staging systems used for gynaecological and paediatric malignancies

C. Describe the follow-up plan and survivorship plan after cancer treatment:
C(i) State the aims of follow-up in oncology (three aims)
C(ii) List all the survivorship issues that must be addressed after cancer treatment
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Steps in general principles of cancer management:
• Establish diagnosis
• Stage the cancer
• Determine goal of treatment/modality of treatment
• Treatment (multimodality, multidisciplinary, sequence of treatment)
• Follow-up plan/survivorship plan

A(ii)
Cure in oncology: Five-year survival or 10-year survival is used as the definition. A patient is considered cured if they survive disease-free for these defined periods. The goal is curative/radical treatment.

A(iii)
Palliation: treatment aimed not at curing the cancer but at relieving symptoms, improving quality of life, and reducing suffering. It includes pain control, other symptom control, and psychosocial support (tertiary prevention — preventing suffering).

B(i)
Aims of staging: to determine the goal of treatment; to determine prognosis; to determine the type of treatment.
UICC TNM staging:
• T = Tumour: extent and size of the primary tumour
• N = Nodes: presence and extent of regional lymph node involvement
• M = Metastasis: presence of distant metastases

B(ii)
Alternative staging systems:
• FIGO staging: for gynaecological malignancies (e.g. cervix, ovary)
• International Retinoblastoma Staging System (IRSS): for retinoblastoma (paediatric)

C(i)
Aims of follow-up:
• To detect and manage complications of treatment
• To monitor compliance to ongoing treatment
• To detect and manage recurrence

C(ii)
Survivorship issues:
• Psychosocial issues
• Occupational issues
• Fertility issues
• Legal issues

(i)
The carpus shows normal arcs on the AP view, which should not be disrupted.
The lateral view shows a specific normal relationship between the carpal bones.
This relationship is particularly important between the lunate and the capitate.

(ii)
A scaphoid fracture may be difficult to see immediately after the injury.
The fracture line may only become clearly visible after 7-10 days.
This delay is due to some widening of the fracture line from bone resorption.
If suspected but not seen, the wrist should be immobilised in plaster.
The film should then be repeated after 10 days.
Failure to diagnose the fracture may result in avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
This avascular necrosis may lead to subsequent osteoarthritis.
A missed scaphoid fracture is one of the commonest causes of litigation.

(iii)
In lunate dislocation, the lunate is displaced (anteriorly, tilted forward) and no longer articulates with the capitate, while other carpal bones remain normally positioned; in a perilunar dislocation, the lunate stays in its normal position, but all the other carpal bones are dislocated around it.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the normal arrangement of the carpal bones as assessed on plain film, including the normal "arcs" of the carpus.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis of why a scaphoid fracture is particularly important not to miss.
(iii) Distinguish between dislocation of the lunate and a perilunar dislocation.

A 68-year-old Nigerian man presents with a 6-month history of progressive difficulty in initiating urination, weak stream, hesitancy, nocturia, and low back pain. Digital rectal examination reveals a hard, irregular prostate. His PSA is markedly elevated.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the most common histological type of this cancer?
(ii) List all the risk factors for this condition, including age-related findings from autopsy studies, gonadal factors, dietary factors, familial factors, and occupational exposures.
(iii) Describe the full clinical presentation of this condition, covering local disease signs, locally advanced signs, and signs of metastases including bone, cerebral, and organ failure features.
(iv) Describe the pathological zones of origin of this cancer, the significance of premalignant lesions, and the molecular/genetic alterations for this condition.
(v) What are the staging system used for this cancer, the sequence of treatment options (adjuvant, neoadjuvant, concurrent), and what is the follow-up aim?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Prostate cancer (adenocarcinoma). Adenocarcinoma constitutes >85% of prostatic cancer.

(ii)
Risk factors:
• Age: most powerful risk factor; autopsy studies found 40% of men dying after age 50 with no clinical evidence of prostate cancer have histologically recognisable cancer; <20% in their 30s
• Gonadal function: testicular function and plasma sex steroid hormone play a major role; prostate cancer is rare in eunuchs; in men with chronic liver disease, rate is disproportionately low due to elevated oestrogen suppressing testicular androgen
• Married men and men with many children have higher risk; men who become sexually active early or have multiple partners have higher risk
• Dietary: higher fat content increases risk; vegetarians have lower incidence; diet high in saturated fat and low in selenium, Vitamin E, and Vitamin D increases risk
• Familial: 1st degree relatives of men with prostate cancer have 2–3 fold higher risk; BRCA1 and BRCA2 implicated
• Occupational: higher rates in workers exposed to cadmium, farmers, chemists, textile workers, painters, rubber and tyre workers
• Infection: herpes simplex type-2 virus implicated (not widely accepted)

(iii)
Clinical presentation:
• Asymptomatic/incidental: discovered on routine DRE or PSA (~10%)
• Local disease: outflow obstruction (weak stream, hesitancy, incomplete voiding, straining); irritative signs (urgency, frequency, nocturia, urge incontinence)
• Locally advanced: haematuria, dysuria, urinary incontinence, perineal or suprapubic pain, erectile dysfunction, haemospermia, rectal signs
• Metastases (>40%): low back pain and sciatica from spinal metastases, pathological fracture, paraplegia; cerebral mets: headache, vomiting, drowsiness, disorientation, seizure
• Organ failure: kidney (uraemia), bone marrow infiltration (anaemia)

(iv)
>70% arise from peripheral zone (felt posteriorly on DRE); 20% from transition zone; <10% from central zone. Tumour volume of 0.5ml is clinically significant. Adenocarcinoma of prostate is multifocal with 2–3 foci in >90% of cases. Premalignant lesion: Prostatic Intraepithelial Neoplasm (PIN); PIN-1 is indistinguishable from BPH; PIN-2 and PIN-3 associated with carcinoma in 30–50% of subsequent biopsies; when high-grade PIN is found, TRUS-guided prostatic biopsy should be done. Molecular alterations include: gain at 7p, 7q, 8q, Xp; loss of chromosomes 8q, 17p, 10q, 16q; alteration in P53 gene, pRB, PTEN; overexpression of EGF, PDGF, TGFR; increase in HER-2.

(v)
Staging: UICC TNM (T-Tumour, N-Nodes, M-Metastasis) and group staging. Sequence of treatment: neoadjuvant (before primary treatment), adjuvant (after primary treatment), concurrent. Follow-up aims: to detect and manage complications of treatment; monitor compliance to ongoing treatment; to detect and manage recurrence.

questions.question:
A patient after head trauma presents with clear fluid leaking from the ear.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and why may it not be visible on a standard skull X-ray?
(ii) What is the pathological basis for a fluid level sometimes seen on a lateral skull film in this condition?
(iii) What immediate risk/complication must be watched for, and what positioning is used to obtain useful films?
(iv) What associated finding may be seen if the fracture involves the nasal sinuses/orbit?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Basal skull fracture; it will not be seen on skull X-ray due to overlapping structures at the base of the skull, but bleeding from the ear or cerebrospinal fluid leakage indicates its presence.

(ii)
If there is a fracture involving an air sinus or mastoid air cells, air may leak into the cranial cavity producing a fluid level with the cerebrospinal fluid; alternatively CSF may leak into a sinus producing a fluid level in the sphenoid or frontal sinus.

(iii)
There is a danger of meningitis in these patients. A lateral skull film following trauma should be taken with a horizontal beam while the patient lies supine, in order to demonstrate these fluid levels.

(iv)
Fractures of the nasal sinuses may allow air to pass into the orbit, especially on nose blowing, causing orbital emphysema seen as a dark area in the upper orbit below the supraorbital ridge.

questions.question:
A. Describe ultrasound wave production and propagation under the following headings:
(i) Definition of medical ultrasound and the frequency range used
(ii) The mechanism of ultrasound generation in the transducer (name the effect and its discoverer and year)
(iii) The assumed average speed of sound in soft tissue and how this is used clinically

B. (i) Define acoustic impedance and state its formula.
(ii) Explain what determines the degree of reflection at a tissue interface.
(iii) Distinguish specular reflection from scattering (diffuse reflection).
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Ultrasound is a form of mechanical sound energy that travels through a conducting medium as a longitudinal wave. Medical ultrasound commonly operates in the 2.5–15 MHz range; this is above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), the upper limit of human hearing.

A(ii)
Ultrasound is generated when an electric field is applied to an array of piezoelectric crystals on the transducer surface, causing mechanical distortion and vibration. The conversion of electrical to mechanical (sound) energy is called the converse piezoelectric effect (Gabriel Lippmann, 1881).

A(iii)
The average speed of sound in soft tissue is assumed to be 1,540 m/sec. This constant value is used to calculate the depth of a reflecting structure from the time the echo takes to return to the transducer.

B(i)
Acoustic impedance is the resistance of a tissue to the passage of ultrasound. Formula: Z = Density × Velocity.

B(ii)
The degree of reflection at an interface depends on the differences in acoustic impedance between the two adjacent tissues.

B(iii)
Specular reflection occurs at flat, smooth interfaces where the transmitted wave is reflected in a single direction depending on the angle of incidence. Scattering (diffuse reflection) occurs when the incident wave encounters an interface that is not perfectly smooth, or when the wavelength is larger than the dimensions of the reflective structure (e.g. red blood cells).

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy and radiological anatomy of the musculoskeletal system imaging approach:
A(i) State the principal imaging modality for cortical bone evaluation, including the rationale for using two views at right angles
A(ii) Describe the advantages and specific indications of CT scan, MRI, ultrasound, bone scintigraphy, and arthrography in musculoskeletal imaging

B. Describe the terminology and diagnostic checklist for musculoskeletal radiology:
B(i) List the density-related terms and the structural elements to assess in any bone (periosteum, cortex, medulla, texture, length/tubulation)
B(ii) List the parts of the bone from epiphysis to diaphysis including the zone of provisional calcification, and the joint assessment checklist

C. Explain how pattern of bone destruction helps classify the aggressiveness of bone lesions:
C(i) Describe geographic, moth-eaten, and permeative patterns with examples of diseases causing each
C(ii) Describe the periosteal reactions associated with benign versus malignant lesions, and name the specific periosteal pattern and disease associated with sunburst, lamellated (onion-skin), and solid periosteal reactions
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Plain X-ray (PXR) is the first choice for cortical bone evaluation. Two views at right angles are used as a standard for assessment to ensure full visualisation of the bone, as a lesion visible in only one plane may be missed in the orthogonal view.

A(ii)
Imaging modalities in MSK:
• CT scan: better cortical bone evaluation; supplements PXR; indicated for complex anatomy (spine, pelvis, wrist, ankle, foot) and tumours (bone and soft tissue)
• MRI: better soft tissue definition; bone marrow evaluation; distinguishes tissues — muscle, fat, fluid, tendon, ligaments, cartilage; not suitable for cortical bone (signal void); indicated for infants/CDH and joint effusion in children
• Ultrasound (USS): soft tissue and fluid; infants and children for CDH; joint effusion; superficial joints (joint/tendon/ligament injury); FNAC/biopsy guidance; intervention/drainage
• Bone scintigraphy: Tc-99m; uptake with increased osteoblastic activity; used for metastases, inflammation, and tumours; entire skeleton imaged; bilateral for comparison
• Arthrography: used for shoulder, hip, knee (ligaments, menisci tears, wrist); replaced by MRI/arthroscopy; CT arthrography for double contrast, intra-articular bodies, labrum tears

B(i)
Density-related terms: sclerosis; osteopenia/lucency. Structural elements: texture (trabeculae), periosteum, cortex, medulla, bone length/tubulation.

B(ii)
Parts of the bone: epiphysis, physis (epiphyseal plate), zone of provisional calcification, metaphysis, diaphysis.
Joint assessment checklist: bony articular surfaces; alignment; joint space; adjacent soft tissue; fat planes.

C(i)
Patterns of bone destruction:
• Geographic: sharply defined border; narrow zone of transition; less aggressive; slow growing; benign — examples: non-ossifying fibroma, eosinophilic granuloma
• Moth-eaten: ragged borders; more rapid growth; likely malignant — examples: multiple myeloma, metastases, lymphoma, Ewing's sarcoma
• Permeative: ill-defined; multiple worm holes; marrow spread; wide zone of transition; aggressive malignancy — examples: leukaemia, lymphoma, Ewing's sarcoma, osteomyelitis

C(ii)
Periosteal reactions:
• Benign: none, or solid periosteal reaction — seen in chronic osteomyelitis
• More aggressive/malignant: lamellated/onion-skin — seen in Ewing's sarcoma
• Sunburst periosteal reaction — seen in osteosarcoma
Malignant tumours also show no periosteal reaction or only aggressive patterns; benign lesions show none or solid.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman is referred for a mammogram. She has no symptoms. The mammogram shows a spiculated, poorly defined opacity in the left upper outer quadrant with associated microcalcification, skin thickening, and nipple retraction. There is also venous engorgement and a wide halo around the opacity.

(i) What is the mammographic diagnosis, and list all the mammographic features of this condition.
(ii) Using ultrasound as a complementary imaging tool, state all the indications for ultrasound over mammography in breast imaging, and all the specific advantages of mammography over ultrasound.
(iii) What is the role of mammography as both a screening and diagnostic tool, and what does it help detect in early breast cancer?
(iv) Describe the sagittal anatomy of the breast, naming all the labelled structures from the pectoralis minor (B) to the surface of the breast, including the retromammary space and Cooper's ligaments in relation to the pectoralis major muscle.
(v) What are the views used in mammography, and what is the biomechanical purpose of compression in mammography? Also, describe the mammographic appearances of a lipoma and an intramammary lymph node for comparison with carcinoma.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Breast carcinoma. Mammographic features of carcinoma:
• Spiculated/poorly defined mass
• Microcalcification
• Distortion of adjacent tissues
• Skin retraction
• Nipple retraction
• Oedema
• Ductal dilatation
• Venous engorgement
• Wide halo around the opacity

(ii)
Indications for ultrasound over mammography:
• Dense parenchyma in young women
• Breast tenderness (compression for mammography not possible)
• Breast implant (mammography not helpful)
• Equivocal mammography or biopsy
• Localisation guidance in biopsy
• Non-ionising radiation (ultrasound)
Advantages of mammography over ultrasound:
• Demonstrates calcifications very well
• Demonstrates small sized masses that can be missed on USS
• Also useful in biopsy guidance
• Used as both diagnostic and screening tool
• Useful for early detection of breast cancer

(iii)
Mammography is used as both a diagnostic tool (for symptomatic patients) and a screening tool (for asymptomatic women). It is useful for early detection of breast cancer, detecting small masses and microcalcifications before they become palpable.

(iv)
Sagittal anatomy of the breast (from posterior to anterior):
• Rib (A)
• Pectoralis minor muscle (B)
• Pectoralis major muscle (C)
• Retromammary space (D): penetrated by deep fascia and epithelium forming Cooper's ligaments (E) into the pectoralis major muscle
• Suspensory ligaments of Cooper (E): run from the deep fascia through the breast to the skin providing support
• Acinar lobule (F)
• Adipose tissue (G): supports the lobes

(v)
Mammographic views: craniocaudal (CC) image and mediolateral oblique (MLO) view. Compression: used in mammography to: maximise differences in soft tissue density by reducing thickness of breast tissue; shorten exposure time; and improve image quality with high-quality screen-film equipment.
Lipoma on mammography: large, rounded, radiolucent, well-defined with compression of adjacent parenchyma.
Intramammary lymph node: identified by a central lucency (fatty hilum).
Comparison with carcinoma: carcinoma is spiculated/poorly defined with microcalcification, while lipoma is radiolucent and well-defined, and lymph node has a central lucency.

questions.question:
A child with sickle cell disease presents with fever, bone pain and swelling for three weeks. X-ray shows a destructive lesion with periosteal reaction.
(i) What risk factor for infection is recognised in this group, and what is the usual causative organism?
(ii) What complication may develop in the acute stage if the process is extensive?
(iii) What chronic complications/appearances may occur?
(iv) What diagnostic difficulty is noted in this risk group, and what is the recommended assessment for the hip?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Patients with sickle cell disease are at risk of infection, commonly due to Salmonella.

(ii)
If osteomyelitis is extensive in the acute stage, pathological fracture may occur.

(iii)
Chronic osteomyelitis shows increased bone density, widening and irregularity of the cortex, and a central density which is a sequestrum; a cloacum (a hole in the cortex through which pus drains and sequestra are extruded) may also be seen.

(iv)
In patients with sickle cell disease, it is often difficult to differentiate bone infarction from osteomyelitis, as the radiological appearances are identical. In the hip, ultrasound may show an effusion which can be aspirated for cytology and culture; the hip must also be differentiated from the "irritable hip" and Perthes disease.

A(i)
The barium swallow is a contrast study of the gastrointestinal tract involving administration of barium to the GIT under fluoroscopic screening, with spot films acquired; used specifically to examine the oesophagus.

A(ii)
Upper oesophagus impressions: Hyoid bone; Cricoid cartilage; Cricopharyngeus muscle; Oesophagus.

A(iii)
Mid-oesophagus impressions: Aortic arch; Left main bronchus.

A(iv)
Distal oesophagus normal structures: Cardiac impression; A ring; B ring; Vestibule; Diaphragmatic hiatus; Oesophageal mucosal folds; Oesophagogastric junction; Diaphragm.

B(i)
Single contrast uses barium alone; double contrast uses barium plus air. Barium is the positive contrast; air is the negative contrast.

B(ii)
Double contrast is more commonly performed; it is needed to assess the GIT mucosa.
questions.question:
A. Describe the barium swallow examination under the following headings:
(i) Definition and purpose
(ii) Normal anatomical impressions seen on the upper oesophagus
(iii) Normal anatomical impressions on the mid-oesophagus
(iv) Normal structures identified on the distal oesophagus

B. (i) Distinguish between single contrast and double contrast barium studies, stating which contrast agent is positive and which is negative.
(ii) Explain which technique is more commonly performed and why.

A. Describe the principles of Computed Tomography under the following headings:
(i) The basic principles of how CT produces an image
(ii) Define Hounsfield units and state the reference value for water and air
(iii) Define window width and window level

B. (i) List all uses of CT (include all organ systems and applications).
(ii) State three safety precautions for CT.
(iii) List three limitations of CT, and for each state which modality is recommended instead.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A CT scanner emits a narrow collimated fan of x-ray beams through the human body and falls on a bank of well-collimated detectors on the opposite side of the x-ray source. The x-ray tube and collimators are fixed to a common frame. The detectors measure the linear attenuation coefficient between the tube and detectors. Data is transmitted to a computer, which builds up a 3D cross-sectional picture and displays it as absorption coefficients of various substances within each square millimetre of the slice with respect to water, to an accuracy of ¼%.

A(ii)
Hounsfield units (HU) are the values of absorption coefficients displayed on the CT image. Water = 0 HU; Air = −1000 HU.

A(iii)
Window width: the total range of CT numbers selected for grey-scale interpretation. Window level: the CT number selected for the centre of the range of numbers displayed on the image.

B(i)
Uses of CT:
• Brain tumours; bone conditions; injuries to internal organs (kidneys, liver, spleen); heart (with some caution); lungs, vessels, bowel in trauma
• Guided biopsies, abscess drainages, minimally invasive tumour treatments
• Plan and assess results of surgery (organ transplants, gastric bypass)
• Stage, plan and administer radiation treatments; monitor response to chemotherapy
• Measure bone mineral density for detection of osteoporosis

B(ii)
Three safety precautions:
• CT cannot be routinely recommended for pregnant women because of radiation risk which could harm the unborn baby
• Children are more at risk of developing a build-up of radiation than adults; CT only recommended if child has a serious condition
• CT scans are only used when there is a clear medical benefit

B(iii)
Three limitations and recommended alternatives:
• Soft-tissue details in brain, internal pelvic organs, and joints often better evaluated with MRI
• In pregnant women, ultrasound or MRI are preferred if likely to be as good as CT
• A very large person (usually over 200 kilograms) may not fit or may be over the weight limit

questions.question:
A 57-year-old male with a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage undergoes cerebral angiography. The lateral projection demonstrates a narrow-necked aneurysm arising off the posterior aspect of the distal supraclinoid left ICA. Follow-up angiography after treatment shows multiple coils placed with sequential occlusion of the aneurysm.

(i) What interventional radiology procedure was performed to treat this aneurysm?
(ii) What is the appearance after coil placement?
(iii) On a non-contrast CT of the head, what would be the expected appearance of an acute extradural (epidural) haematoma in terms of shape and density?
(iv) Name the vessel most likely responsible for an extradural haematoma.
(v) What is the typical CT appearance of a large intraventricular bleed?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Coil embolisation (multiple coils were placed with sequential occlusion of the aneurysm).

(ii)
After coil placement, a small amount of residual filling is noted at the proximal neck of the aneurysm, which may thrombose over time.

(iii)
A large left-sided parietal extradural haematoma appears: between the cranium and the dural membrane, biconvex in shape, and hyperdense on CT.

(iv)
The haematoma is most likely due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery.

(v)
A large intraventricular bleed: blood can be seen in the third ventricle and in the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles.

A cannula or catheter is placed within the cervical canal.
10-20ml of contrast is injected to outline the uterine cavity and tubes.
If the tubes are patent, contrast fills them and then spills into the peritoneal cavity.
This peritoneal spill on both sides indicates tubal patency.

(ii)
The examination is best performed around day 10 of the cycle, when tubal filling is most likely.
In practice it is performed within the first half of the cycle, after menstruation has ceased and before fertilisation.
It is contraindicated during pregnancy, infection, or menstruation.

(iii)
A patent tube shows satisfactory filling with contrast and peritoneal spill on both sides.
Hydrosalpinx is dilatation of the fallopian tube.
Hydrosalpinx is commonly associated with tubal occlusion.
However, a hydrosalpinx may also be seen in a tube that is otherwise patent.
Dilatation and patency of the tube are therefore not the same anatomical finding.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the course of contrast during hysterosalpingography, from injection to its final distribution when the tubes are patent.
(ii) State the recommended timing in the menstrual cycle for performing this procedure.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the difference between the appearance of a patent tube and a hydrosalpinx.

A. Describe the nuclear medicine radiopharmaceutical under the following headings:
(i) Definition of a radiopharmaceutical and how it is formed
(ii) Routes of administration
(iii) The principle that determines radiopharmaceutical design

B. (i) Describe how Nuclear Medicine differs from other imaging modalities (ultrasound, MRI etc.) — list all seven distinguishing features.
(ii) State the absolute contraindication and all relative contraindications to nuclear medicine scans.
(iii) Distinguish SPECT from PET cameras.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A radiopharmaceutical is formed by combining a carrier molecule (drug or tracer) with a radionuclide. The labeled radionuclide-drug complex is called a radiopharmaceutical. Examples of carrier molecules: antibody, drug, peptide. Examples of radionuclides: Technetium, Fluorine-19, Lutetium-177.

A(ii)
Routes of administration: inhalation; injection (intravenous, intradermal, subcutaneous, intralesional); swallowing (oral); instillation (radionuclide voiding cystography).

A(iii)
"Design of radiopharmaceuticals is based solely on the physiology of the target organ."

B(i)
Seven distinguishing features of nuclear medicine:
• Uses gamma rays for imaging
• Patient is the source
• Emitted continuously
• Decaying all the time
• Use of radiopharmaceuticals
• Provides physiological information
• Same agent may be used to diagnose and treat (THERAGNOSTICS)

B(ii)
Absolute contraindication: pregnancy. Relative contraindications: breastfeeding; recent nuclear medicine scan or therapy; bone marrow suppression; radiation safety.

B(iii)
SPECT: Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography; may be single, double or triple head. PET: Positron Emission Tomography cameras. Hybrid cameras include SPECT/CT, PET/CT, or PET/MRI.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomical zones of a growing long bone (diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis, and growth plate) and how they ossify.
(ii) State how specific pathologies are related to specific zones of the long bone.
(iii) Explain why injury or disease at the growth plate can produce a lasting functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Bones develop and grow through primary and secondary ossification centres.
The part of bone ossified from the primary centre is the diaphysis, forming most of the shaft.
The secondary centre at the end of a long bone is the epiphysis, separated from the shaft by the epiphyseal growth plate.
The metaphysis is the part of the bone between the diaphysis and the growth plate.
Longitudinal bone growth occurs at the metaphysis, while periosteal activity along the diaphysis gives circumferential growth.

(ii)
Osteomyelitis, osteogenic sarcoma, and acute leukaemia characteristically involve the metaphysis.
Giant cell tumour occurs only after the epiphyses have fused, at the end of long bones.
Tuberculous osteomyelitis in long bones begins in the metaphysis and soon crosses the epiphyseal line.
Rickets produces its most obvious changes at the metaphysis, where growth is most rapid.

(iii)
Salter-Harris fractures involving the epiphyseal growth plate are difficult to detect as the bones remain intact.
Types 1 and 5 are the most difficult to recognise of the Salter-Harris types.
These fractures may lead to problems with growth of the bone, resulting in limb shortening.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with known ischaemic heart disease presents for evaluation of his coronary arteries. He is being prepared for an imaging procedure that will outline the coronary artery anatomy and allow potential percutaneous transluminal intervention.

(i) What is the name of this imaging procedure, and under which major imaging modality for the cardiovascular system does it fall?
(ii) What specific cardiac anatomy does this procedure demonstrate, and what interventional procedure can be performed using the same technique?
(iii) What is left ventricular angiography, what does it demonstrate, and what specific functional measurements can be obtained from it?
(iv) What are the other angiographic procedures for the cardiovascular system used alongside coronary angiography?
(v) What are the advantages of cardiac MRI over conventional angiography in terms of multiplanar capability, soft tissue characterisation, and the ability to assess ventricular function, and what are its disadvantages?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Coronary angiography. It falls under angiography, which offers the highest temporal and spatial resolution of all cardiac imaging techniques.

(ii)
Coronary angiography shows coronary artery anatomy. Using the same technique, percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) can be performed as an interventional procedure.

(iii)
Left ventricular angiography outlines the left ventricle with contrast. It demonstrates: the overall movement of the endocardium; myocardial infarction; ventricular function; left ventricular volume; and ejection fraction.

(iv)
Other angiographic procedures for the cardiovascular system include:
• Aortography
• Right heart catheterisation
• Angiocardiography (demonstrates anatomy and function of individual cardiac chambers and great vessels)
• Cardiac catheterisation (provides information regarding pressure and oxygenation within selected chambers and great vessels)

(v)
Advantages of cardiac MRI: demonstrates cardiac anatomy without the use of ionising radiation; multiplanar capability; excellent soft tissue characterisation; can assess ventricular function; defines cardiac chambers very accurately; perfusion studies are becoming possible; can be used for flow studies; potentially the most comprehensive cardiac imaging modality; allows imaging in any spatial orientation, suited for complex, variable, and asymmetrical cardiac anatomy.
Disadvantages of MRI: presence of metals in body is a contraindication; claustrophobia; high cost of examination; relatively long examination time; still limited in both spatial and temporal resolution.

(i)
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

(ii)
Idiopathic thickening of the gastric pyloric musculature resulting in progressive outlet gastric obstruction.

(iii)
Male to female ratio is 4:1.

(iv)
Manifests 2–8 weeks of life.

(v)
Barium meal signs:
• Delayed gastric emptying
• Elongated pylorus with narrowing of lumen (String sign), which may appear duplicated — puckering of the mucosa (Double track sign)
• Indentation of the contrast-filled antrum (Shoulder sign) or base of the duodenal cap (Mushroom sign)
• Entrance of the pylorus may be beak-shaped (Beak sign)
questions.question:
A 3-week-old male infant presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting after every feed. He is hungry immediately after vomiting. On barium meal examination the radiologist identifies a delayed gastric emptying, an elongated pylorus with narrowing of the lumen, a double track sign, a shoulder sign on the contrast-filled antrum, and a mushroom sign at the base of the duodenal cap.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the underlying pathological basis of this condition?
(iii) What is the sex distribution for this condition?
(iv) At what age does this condition typically manifest?

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Right border of the heart on PA view:
• In older adults: aorta (ascending)
• In youth: SVC (superior vena cava)
• Right atrium (forms the main right border)

A(ii)
Left border of the heart on PA view (top to bottom):
• Aortic bulb/aortic knob (aortic arch)
• Pulmonary artery segment/main pulmonary artery
• Left ventricle (forms the main left border inferiorly)
• (Left atrium contributes a small portion superiorly)

A(iii)
Lateral view:
• Anterior border: ascending aorta, anterior border of the right ventricle
• Posterior border (superior): left atrium
• Posterior border (inferior): left ventricle

B(i)
Normal pulmonary vasculature: Right descending pulmonary artery (RDPA) <17 mm in diameter; distribution lower > upper; central vessels gradually taper to periphery.

B(ii)
Pulmonary venous hypertension: RDPA >17 mm; cephalisation (upper lobe vessels become more prominent than lower lobe vessels); visible lymphatic channels (Kerley B lines); mild haziness in lower zones.

B(iii)
Pulmonary arterial hypertension: MPA (main pulmonary artery) projects beyond the tangent line; RDPA >17 mm; pruning (rapid cut-off in size of peripheral vessels relative to size of central vessels).

B(iv)
Increased pulmonary flow: RDPA >17 mm; all blood vessels bigger than normal.

B(v)
Decreased pulmonary flow: fewer than normal blood vessels visible.

C.
Cardiomegaly with normal vasculature — causes:
• Viral myocarditis
• Endocardial fibroelastosis
• Aberrant left coronary artery
• Cystic medial necrosis
• Diabetic mother
(Also: cardiomyopathy, pericardial effusion, multiple valve disease)
Cyanosis with decreased vascularity — causes:
• Tetralogy of Fallot
• Truncus-type IV
• Tricuspid atresia
• Transposition
• Ebstein's anomaly
questions.question:
A. Describe the normal cardiac silhouette and contour on the chest radiograph (PA view and lateral view):
A(i) Right border of the heart on PA view: name all contributing structures in both youth and older adults
A(ii) Left border of the heart on PA view: name all contributing structures from top to bottom
A(iii) Anterior and posterior borders of the heart on lateral view: name contributing structures

B. Describe the five states of the pulmonary vasculature as seen on the chest radiograph and state the diagnostic criteria for each:
B(i) Normal pulmonary vasculature
B(ii) Pulmonary venous hypertension
B(iii) Pulmonary arterial hypertension
B(iv) Increased pulmonary flow
B(v) Decreased pulmonary flow

C. Distinguish between cardiomegaly with normal vasculature and cyanosis with decreased vascularity on the plain chest radiograph, listing the causes of each.

A. Describe X-ray production in the x-ray tube under the following headings:
(i) The two processes by which x-rays are generated
(ii) Definition of bremsstrahlung radiation and factors that increase its production
(iii) Definition and mechanism of characteristic radiation, including the voltage threshold for tungsten and for molybdenum

B. (i) State the definition of the focal spot and the phenomenon called blooming.
(ii) Explain the line focus principle and what happens as the anode angle is made steeper.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
X-rays are generated by two processes: Bremsstrahlung (braking) radiation and Characteristic radiation.

A(ii)
Bremsstrahlung: radiation produced when incident electrons interact with nuclear electric fields, which slow them down (brake) and change their direction. Production increases with:
• the accelerating voltage (kV)
• atomic number (Z) of the anode.

A(iii)
Characteristic radiation results from ionisation and is produced when inner-shell electrons of the anode target are ejected by incident electrons. The resultant vacancy is filled by an outer-shell electron and the energy difference is emitted as characteristic radiation. For tungsten, K-shell characteristic x-rays are only produced when applied voltage exceeds 69.5 kV. For molybdenum, this occurs when applied voltage exceeds 20 kV.

B(i)
The focal spot is the location on the anode and apparent source of x-rays in the tube. Blooming is the enlargement of the focal spot size as milliamperes increase, owing to repulsion of adjacent electrons.

B(ii)
The line focus principle permits larger heat loading while minimising the size of the focal spot by orienting the anode at a small angle. The steeper the anode target, the smaller the effective focal spot; the steeper the target, the larger the actual focal spot and target heat rating; the steeper the target, the narrower the useful x-ray beam and the smaller the field covered.

questions.question:
A. Describe MRI physics under the following headings:
(i) The behaviour of hydrogen protons when placed in an external magnetic field
(ii) The definition and significance of Larmor frequency
(iii) Define T1 relaxation and T2 relaxation, distinguishing the axis and mechanism of each

B. (i) List all tissues/substances that appear bright on T1 (high intensity) and all that appear dark on T1 (hypointense).
(ii) List all substances that appear bright on T2 (hyperintense) and all that appear dark on T2.
(iii) List the five basic MRI sequences.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
When placed in an external magnetic field, protons align in a direction either parallel or anti-parallel to the strong external field. A greater proportion align in the parallel direction so that the net vector of their alignment — and therefore the net magnetic vector — will be in the direction of the external field. Though aligned, the hydrogen nuclei do not lie motionless but each nucleus spins (precesses) around the line of the field.

A(ii)
Larmor frequency is the number of times per second that the axis of the magnet revolves about the magnetic field direction (the z direction). Larmor frequency is directly proportional to the magnetic field strength.

A(iii)
T1 (longitudinal relaxation, spin-lattice relaxation): refers only to magnetisation in the direction of precession (z axis in B₀ direction); the relaxation curve is of the form (1 − e⁻ᵗ/T1). T2 (transverse relaxation, spin-spin relaxation): refers to magnetisation in the x-y direction; T1 value is much greater than T2.

B(i)
Bright on T1: Fat; Subacute haemorrhage; Melanin; Protein-rich fluid; Slow-flowing blood; Paramagnetic substances (gadolinium, Cu, Mn).
Dark on T1: Oedema; Tumour; Infection; Inflammation; Haemorrhage (chronic and hyperacute); Calcification; Flow void.

B(ii)
Bright on T2: Oedema; Tumour; Infection; Inflammation; Subdural collection; Methaemoglobin in late subacute haemorrhage.
Dark on T2: Calcification; Fibrous tissue; Protein-rich fluid; Flow void.

B(iii)
Five basic sequences: T1W; T2W; PD (proton density); FLAIR; STIR.

questions.question:
A. Describe radiation protection principles under the following headings:
(i) The three types of exposure
(ii) The three key principles of radiological protection, with a definition of each
(iii) The three methods of controlling radiation exposure, with a brief explanation of each

B. (i) State the annual dose limits for occupational workers (effective dose) and for the public (effective dose).
(ii) Distinguish between stochastic and non-stochastic (deterministic) effects, giving two examples of each.
(iii) State the quality factor (Q) for x-rays/gamma rays, neutrons/protons, and alpha particles.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three types of exposure:
• Occupational exposure: exposure incurred by workers in the course of their work, except medical exposure and local natural background radiation.
• Medical exposure: exposure incurred by patients as part of their own medical or dental diagnosis or treatment; by persons other than those occupationally exposed, caregivers, and by volunteers in biomedical research.
• Public exposure: exposure incurred by members of the public from radiation sources, excluding occupational, medical, and normal natural background radiation.

A(ii)
Three principles:
• Justification: the use of radiation gives benefit to the individual and society; the benefit must outweigh the cost and any harm it causes.
• Optimisation: the likelihood of incurring exposure, the number of people exposed, and the magnitude of individual doses should be kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), taking economic and societal factors into account.
• Limitation: the dose received by individuals from all practices should not exceed the recommended limit.

A(iii)
Three methods: Time — dose = dose rate × time; longer exposure = higher dose. Distance — exposure rate decreases with increasing distance from the source; radiation dose increases as the square of the distance decreases from the source. Shielding — physical barriers between worker and source.

B(i)
Occupational effective dose: 20 mSv/year averaged over 5 years; 50 in any 1 year. Public effective dose: 1 mSv/year.

B(ii)
Stochastic: no dose threshold; probability but not severity increases with dose; examples: cancer, genetic mutation. Non-stochastic (deterministic): threshold dose; severity increases above threshold; examples: skin erythema, hair loss, infertility, cataract, fibrosis.

B(iii)
Q values: X-rays, gamma rays, electrons, beta: Q ≈ 1. Neutrons and protons: Q ≈ 10. Alpha particles: Q ≈ 20.

questions.question:
A patient is prepared for Intensity Modulated Radiotherapy (IMRT).

(i) List all the operation steps for IMRT preparation.
(ii) State the estimate of patient benefit from IMRT.
(iii) What are the two merits of IMRT in terms of side effects and toxicity?
(iv) Describe the WHO Analgesic Ladder for pain management, and state what is known about its effectiveness.
(v) List all the advantages of pain treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i)
IMRT preparation steps:
• Physical examination/medical history review
• CT, with or without additional scanning procedures (PET, MRI) required for IMRT planning; the latter can be merged with the former for precise tumour location
• The patient may follow a certain bowel and bladder preparation regimen prior to simulation
• Intravenous contrast material may be injected during the CT scan
• Prior to treatment, the patient's skin may be marked or tattooed
• A special device will be moulded for reproducibility of position

(ii)
An estimated 1 in 3 patients having radiotherapy could benefit from IMRT.

(iii)
Two merits: Fewer side effects — ratio of normal tissue dose to tumour dose is reduced to a minimum. Potential to reduce treatment toxicity — even when doses are not increased.

(iv)
The WHO Analgesic Ladder is extremely effective for patients with acute pain, cancer pain, and neuropathic pain (nerve pain); 80–90% of people are effectively treated.

(v)
Advantages of pain treatment:
• Improves compliance to curative treatment
• Extends survival for some patients
• Improves quality of life
• Improves patient–physician relationship
• Reduces unnecessary prolonged admission

questions.question:
A. Describe the principles of nuclear medicine bone scanning under the following headings:
(i) The radiopharmaceutical used and its mechanism of attachment to bone
(ii) The three phases of a three-phase bone scan and what each phase assesses
(iii) State the sensitivity of bone scan compared to radiographs in detecting skeletal metastases and explain why this difference exists

B. (i) List four established clinical indications for bone scanning.
(ii) State two sources of false negative results on bone scan.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Technetium-MDP (Methylene diphosphonate) is the agent used for bone imaging. It affixes to the bone surface by chemisorption, attaching to hydroxyapatite crystals in bone and calcium crystals in mitochondria (or heterotopic calcium crystal deposition).

A(ii)
Three phases:
• Phase 1 (Immediate scans): assesses blood flow to bone
• Phases 2 and 3 (Delayed scans): assesses bone metabolic activity
About 40–50% of the compound is affixed to bone by 3 to 4 hours after injection.

A(iii)
Bone scan is 50 to 80% more sensitive than radiographs in detecting skeletal metastases. This is because about 30–75% of the bone mineral content must be lost before a metastasis is evident on a radiograph; in contrast, as little as a 5–10% change in the ratio of the lesion to normal bone is required to detect an abnormality on bone scan.

B(i)
Established indications:
• Osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, soft tissue infections, painful prosthesis
• Occult fractures, stress fractures, insufficiency fractures, multiple trauma
• Primary and secondary bone tumours
• Metabolic bone disease (Paget, hyperparathyroidism)

B(ii)
False negatives:
• Lytic lesions (e.g. myeloma or very lytic aggressive lesions such as lymphoma — bone scan is less sensitive for these).
• Homogeneously increased bony activity (reporting error).

questions.question:
A child presents with recurrent urinary tract infections. Intravenous pyelography shows a duplex collecting system on one side.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What complication may affect the ureter draining the upper moiety, and what is its typical imaging appearance?
(iii) What complication affects the ureter draining the lower moiety, and what is its consequence?
(iv) What other congenital renal variants are named alongside duplex systems?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Duplex kidney and double ureter, the commonest congenital variant seen on intravenous pyelography (IVP).

(ii)
The ureter draining the upper moiety may be obstructed by a ureterocoele or may have an ectopic insertion, sometimes draining into the vagina or male urethra instead of the bladder, causing urinary incontinence. This produces loss of renal cortex in the upper pole and a "drooping flower" appearance of the lower pole calyces.

(iii)
The ureter draining the lower moiety commonly exhibits reflux, resulting in scarring of the lower pole.

(iv)
Other related congenital malformations named alongside duplex systems are horseshoe kidney and crossed ectopia.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and heavy alcohol use presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea. A chest X-ray shows: cardiomegaly with a CTR of 0.6; bilateral basal shadowing described as 'bat wings'; Kerley B lines at the bases; dilated prominent upper lobe vessels; and bilateral pleural effusions.

(i) What is the radiological diagnosis, and what do the ABCDE features of cardiac failure on CXR stand for?
(ii) List all the causes of congestive heart failure (CHF), and specify which imaging modalities are the choice for evaluating heart failure.
(iii) Describe the echocardiographic parameters used to assess cardiac failure: what is the ejection fraction, and what is the difference between pressure overload (stenosis) and volume overload at the valve level?
(iv) Describe the radiological features of pulmonary interstitial oedema and pulmonary alveolar oedema on a chest X-ray, listing each feature separately.
(v) Using the plain radiograph algorithm for cardiac disease, list all causes of increase in left atrial size and all causes of an enlarged main pulmonary artery that can produce an abnormal cardiac contour similar to that seen in this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Congestive cardiac failure (CCF) with pulmonary oedema. ABCDE features on CXR:
• A = Alveolar oedema (bat wings/fan-shaped parahilar bilateral opacities)
• B = Kerley B lines (interstitial oedema — short horizontal lines at lung bases)
• C = Cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5)
• D = Dilated prominent upper lobe vessels (cephalisation)
• E = Effusion (pleural effusion)

(ii)
Causes of congestive heart failure:
• Coronary artery disease
• Hypertension
• Cardiomyopathy
• Valvular lesions (aortic stenosis, mitral stenosis)
• Left-to-right shunts
• Fluid overload
Imaging modalities of choice for heart failure: CXR (PA/AP) and echocardiography.

(iii)
Echocardiographic parameters:
• Ejection fraction (EF) = (EDV − ESV)/EDV × 100, where EDV = end diastolic volume and ESV = end systolic volume
• Pressure overload (stenosis): increased pressure work on the ventricle
• Volume overload: increased volume work on the ventricle
• Echocardiography also assesses valvular malfunction, tumours, size and wall thickness of ventricles, and function

(iv)
Pulmonary interstitial oedema:
• Thickening of the interlobular septa (Kerley B lines, Kerley A lines)
• Peribronchial cuffing or blurring (thickening of the bronchial wall, normally hairline thin)
• Thickening of the fissures
• Fluid in the subpleural space in continuity with interlobular septa (subpleural oedema)
• Perivascular blurring or cuffing in the parahilar regions
• Pleural effusions
Pulmonary alveolar oedema:
• Fan-shaped parahilar bilateral opacities (patchy, mottled, homogeneous — "bat wings")
• Air bronchogram
• Loss of cardiac and mediastinal contour

(v)
Causes of enlarged left atrium:
• CHF
• Mitral stenosis
• Mitral regurgitation
• Prolapsed mitral valve
• Papillary muscle dysfunction
• Left atrial myxoma
Causes of enlarged main pulmonary artery:
• Left-to-right shunt
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension
• Pulmonic stenosis
• Idiopathic dilatation of the pulmonary artery

questions.question:
A patient is referred for a barium enema after presenting with colicky abdominal pain. The examination demonstrates diverticulosis, abnormal colon movement, dilation of the colon, polyps and cancers of the colon and rectum.

(i) What type of barium enema more readily finds polyps and small cancers?
(ii) One barium enema technique uses air — what is this technique called?
(iii) A hysterosalpingogram (HSG) is requested for a different patient presenting with infertility. What is the purpose of an HSG?
(iv) What does an arthrogram involve and what is its purpose?
(v) What is an IVU/IVP and what does it examine?
questions.answerText:
(i)
The air contrast barium enema or double-contrast barium enema is stated to more readily find polyps and small cancers.

(ii)
The technique is called the air contrast barium enema or double-contrast barium enema.

(iii)
HSG is an x-ray of the uterus and fallopian tubes; usually done in diagnosing infertility to see if there are any blockages.

(iv)
An arthrogram is an x-ray of a joint after the injection of a contrast medium to more clearly visualise the joint.

(v)
An IVU/IVP is an x-ray examination of the kidneys, their drainage to the bladder, and the bladder.

(i)
A solid renal mass (malignant tumour); malignant tumours are usually dark (hypoechoeic) and heterogeneous (uneven) in texture, whereas a cyst is anechoeic (no internal echoes) with acoustic enhancement, features readily distinguished by ultrasound.

(ii)
Involvement of the renal vein or inferior vena cava by tumour should be assessed.

(iii)
Enlarged nodes, liver metastases, and local spread outside the kidney should be looked for.

(iv)
Tumour in the contralateral kidney is not uncommon and should be considered. On intravenous pyelography, a renal mass may show as a space-occupying lesion displacing the renal pelvis and calyces (for example downwards, like a "drooping flower," in an upper pole mass, or producing calyces with a concave appearance), reflecting how the tumour's location within the kidney determines the pattern of distortion of the collecting system.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Acute osteomyelitis. Plain X-ray is negative for the first 1–2 weeks because 30% of bone destruction must occur before it becomes visible on plain X-ray. Early imaging of choice is bone scan (hot spot) or MRI.

(ii)
Organisms: usually Staphylococcus aureus (rapid course); Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes a prolonged course. Healing with ankylosis is common. Infective arthritis causes local trauma from surgery or RTA; usually affects one joint; caused by human bites, DM, SCD.

(iii)
Causes of infective arthritis: local trauma (surgery or RTA); usually affects one joint; human bites, DM, SCD. It usually causes destruction of articular cartilage and cortex, more in adults. Distinguishing from DJD: DJD (primary) shows: narrowing of joint space; marginal osteophytes; subchondral sclerosis; subchondral cysts; affects both sides of joint; typically knee, hip, shoulder, elbow. Infective arthritis: rapid destruction; involves one joint; systemic features.

(iv)
Radiological features of chronic osteomyelitis:
• Lytic/radiolucent areas — cloaca (holes in the involucrum through which pus drains)
• Sclerosis
• Sinus tracts
• Sequestrum (dead bone fragment within cavity)
• Involucrum (periosteal new bone surrounding the sequestrum)
• Cortical thickening and irregularity
• Loss of cortico-medullary differentiation
• Bone in bone appearance

(v)
Complications of rib fractures: flail chest; pneumothorax; haemothorax; surgical emphysema; pulmonary contusion. Fractures of the upper 3 ribs are associated with major intrathoracic injuries. Fractures of the lower 3 ribs may be associated with upper abdominal injury, e.g. ruptured spleen. Air in the soft tissues may spread widely along the chest wall into the neck. Haemothorax appearances are identical to a pleural effusion.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Cervical cancer. In Nigeria, it usually affects women around 45 years of age; about 20% are seen at ages less than 30 years.

(ii)
Risk factors:
• It is the 2nd most common malignancy of women in Nigeria; 70% diagnosed in advanced stages (III–IV)
• Incident substantially higher among low socioeconomic classes
• Sexual activity and parity appear to affect incidence
• Uncommon in nulliparous women
• Association of prenatal exposure to diethylstilboestrol and development of clear cell adenocarcinoma of the cervix has been reported
• HPV (human papillomavirus) association (Boon and associates suggested HPV in cervical cancer, with men as vectors)
• Efforts are now geared towards vaccination against HPV exposure

(iii)
Clinical presentation:
• Post-menopausal bleeding
• Post-coital bleeding
• Inter-menstrual bleeding
• Menorrhagia may occur
• Foul-smelling yellowish vaginal discharge
• Lower abdominal pain
• Weakness and fatigue from anaemia
• In very advanced stage: VVF (vesico-vaginal fistula), RVF (recto-vaginal fistula)

(iv)
Staging: FIGO for gynaecological malignancies; UICC TNM (T-Tumour, N-Nodes, M-Metastasis). Staging aims to determine goal of treatment, prognosis, and type of treatment.
Screening: Pap smear (cervical smear). Primary prevention strategies: vaccination against HPV; health education and promotion; prophylactic surgery; chemoprevention (secondary prevention includes screening e.g. pap smear, mammography; tertiary prevention includes pain control, other symptom control, psychosocial support).

(v)
Treatment modalities: surgery, chemotherapy/immunotherapy/targeted therapy, hormone therapy, radiation therapy.
Radiotherapy:
• Goal: to give optimal tumour dose and minimal dose to normal tissues; radiotherapy does not differentiate between tumour and normal tissues; the radiation oncologist's main responsibility is to delineate the tumour volumes
• Types: Teletherapy (long distance from source to tumour; cobalt-60 is an older machine; linear accelerators are modern types); Brachytherapy (brachy = short distance; intracavitary e.g. for cervix; interstitial e.g. for prostate; topical/superficial)
• For cervical cancer: intracavitary brachytherapy is specifically used

(i)
Right upper lobe collapse (likely due to a proximal bronchial carcinoma). The collapse pattern of the right upper lobe is specific: the lesser (horizontal) fissure moves upwards, pivoted at the right hilum in both PA and lateral projections. The collapsed lung assumes increased density at the right apex; its lower border is sharply defined by the horizontal fissure, which may be bowed. The hilum is usually distorted and pulled up. On lateral view, the upper lobe collapses upwards, anteriorly, and towards the mediastinum and may be invisible as shadowing blends with the mediastinal shadow.

(ii)
Causes of solitary pulmonary opacity with irregular borders or hilar adenopathy (relevant causes):
• Bronchial carcinoma (rapid growth on serial CXR; irregular borders; may cavitate; associated hilar or mediastinal adenopathy)
• Solitary metastasis (usually well defined; lower lobe commoner)
• Tuberculoma (calcification common; well-defined margins; unchanged on serial X-rays; upper/mid zones)
• Lung abscess (may cavitate)
• Benign tumour (rare; may calcify)

(iii)
Primary lung cancer presentations on CXR:
• Hilar mass
• Lung opacity (well defined or irregular/spiculated)
• Collapse of a lobe due to bronchial obstruction
• Pneumonia distal to partial bronchial occlusion
• Cavitating mass
• Apical opacity
• Involvement of the phrenic nerve with elevation of the diaphragm due to paralysis
Phrenic nerve paralysis confirmation: by fluoroscopy (the normal diaphragm changes position between inspiration and expiration, whereas the paralysed one does not). If fluoroscopy is unavailable, two exposures (inspiratory and expiratory) on the same film can be taken to demonstrate the unmoving paralysed diaphragm.

(iv)
Causes of prominence of the thoracic aorta:
• Hypertension (entire aorta)
• Atherosclerosis (entire aorta)
• Aortic insufficiency (entire aorta)
• Aortic stenosis (ascending aorta)
• Aneurysm (ascending or entire aorta)
• Coarctation of the aorta (ascending aorta)
• Aortitis (ascending or entire aorta)
Types of left-to-right shunts:
• Atrial septal defect (ASD)
• Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
• Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
• Anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)
• AV communis
• Anomalous origin of left coronary artery from pulmonary artery

(v)
CT of the thorax demonstrates: coronary vessels; pulmonary artery and its major branches; thoracic aorta and its anatomy; masses in or near the heart; complex anatomy (spine, pelvis); soft tissue tumours. These are not visible or fully assessable on the plain CXR.
Major limitation of CT compared to MRI: CT is associated with high doses of ionising radiation; MRI demonstrates cardiac anatomy without ionising radiation, has multiplanar capability, excellent soft tissue characterisation, can assess ventricular function, and define cardiac chambers very accurately. However MRI is limited in spatial and temporal resolution and has contraindications (metals, claustrophobia, high cost, long examination time).
