questions.answerText:
A(i)
Teletherapy implies that the source of radiation used for treatment is at a distance from the area of the body being treated. The energy of radiation used in treatment is in the megavoltage range from either a Cobalt-60 machine or linear accelerator.

A(ii)
In brachytherapy the radiation source is in very close proximity to the area being treated. Two main types: Interstitial brachytherapy — the radioactive sources are inside the tumour; Contact brachytherapy (plesiobrachytherapy) — radioactive sources are close to the tumour, e.g. intracavitary, intraluminal, endovascular, and surface brachytherapy.

A(iii)
Systemic radiotherapy uses unsealed radiopharmaceuticals. Examples: Iodine-131 capsule (oral, for thyroid); Strontium-89 (intravenous, for pain palliation in metastatic bone disease); Yttrium-90 (intraperitoneal, intrapleurally, or intra-articular, for treatment of malignant effusions and arthritis).

B(i)
In conventional fractionation, radiation treatment is given as 2 Gy daily, five days a week.

B(ii)
The five Rs: Radiosensitivity (intrinsic); Repair of sublethal damage; Re-oxygenation; Repopulation; Redistribution.

(i)
Rickets (due to vitamin D deficiency), commonest in small children.

(ii)
There are many causes of rickets, ranging from malabsorption to renal failure.

(iii)
The changes are due to failure of osteoid to calcify. As the metaphysis is where the most rapid growth is occurring, the earliest sign is loss of the white line of provisional calcification, followed by widening of the growth plate, an indistinct metaphyseal margin, fraying and splaying (cupping) of the metaphyses from weight bearing on unossified bone, a thin bony spur at the metaphyseal corner, and an indistinct cortex due to uncalcified subperiosteal osteoid.

(iv)
Later deformities include bowing of the legs, a triradiate pelvis, scoliosis, biconcave vertebral bodies, cupping of the anterior rib ends, and indrawing of the lower chest wall (Harrison's sulcus), all from weight bearing on softened bone. Rickets may be confused with Blount's disease, a developmental abnormality of the upper tibial metaphysis with a medial bony "beak" and genu varus, but without the fraying or cupping seen in rickets.

In posterior dislocation the humeral head passes upwards and backwards, whereas in anterior dislocation it passes downwards and forwards, reflecting the differing mechanical direction of displacement relative to the glenoid.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Complete (whole lung) collapse, or in the context of trauma, a massive haemothorax. The principal radiological finding in complete lung collapse is: complete opacity of the hemithorax with displacement of the mediastinum to the side of the opacity (towards the collapsed lung). In massive pleural effusion, the mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side; if there is no mediastinal shift with a massive effusion, this suggests complete collapse of the underlying lung.

(ii)
Three main causes of collapse:
• Obstruction of a bronchus by a foreign body, tumour, mucus plug, aspiration, or a stricture
• Compressive collapse due to air or fluid in the pleural cavity
• Cicatrisation collapse due to scarring (commonly following pulmonary tuberculosis)
Lobe collapse direction:
• Upper lobes: collapse upwards, medially, and anteriorly
• Middle lobe: collapses downwards and medially
• Lower lobes: collapse posteriorly, medially, and downwards

(iii)
Radiological signs of lobar collapse:
• Increased density due to loss of aeration
• Crowding of the blood vessels
• Displacement of the hilum (upwards or downwards)
• Displacement of a fissure, which may be bowed
• Shift of the mediastinum and trachea towards the collapsed part of the lung
• Elevation of the diaphragm
• Silhouette sign
• Remainder of the lung may be overexpanded and hypertranslucent with fewer vessels

(iv)
Tension pneumothorax: a tear in the visceral pleura acts as a ball valve, allowing air to enter the pleural cavity during each inspiration but none to escape during expiration. Positive pressure builds up, resulting in shift of the mediastinum to the opposite side. This is a medical emergency as death may ensue from respiratory distress and diminished cardiac output. On CXR: absent lung markings on affected side, depression of the diaphragm, mediastinal displacement away from the affected side.

(v)
Causes of pneumothorax:
• Spontaneous: rupture of a small congenital pleural bleb; usually young males and often smokers
• Iatrogenic: following pleural tap, lung biopsy
• Trauma
• Emphysema
• Asthma
• Malignancy (high incidence in osteogenic sarcoma metastases)
• Lung disease: pneumocystis carinii, tuberculosis, honeycomb lung
Radiological features — erect PA: lung edge visible as lung retracts towards hilum; absent lung markings between lung edge and chest wall; increased translucency of affected hemithorax; mediastinal displacement with depression of diaphragm if tension develops.
Supine features: pleural air lies anteriorly and medially; mediastinal structures sharply outlined by adjacent free pleural air; upper abdomen appears lucent; basal hyperlucency; deepening of the lateral costophrenic angle; double diaphragm sign.

A 10-year-old child is brought with sudden onset of coughing, wheezing, and breathlessness after eating peanuts. A chest X-ray shows the left hemithorax appearing darker than the right, with visible vascular lung markings within the dark lung. The left hemithorax does not deflate on an expiratory film.

(i) What is the radiological diagnosis, and what is the mechanism by which the affected lung appears hyperinflated rather than collapsed in this situation?
(ii) Describe all the causes of bilateral lung transradiancy with over-expansion of the lungs, including the CXR features of the diaphragm, heart, and lung fields in each.
(iii) How does unilateral transradiancy differ from bilateral transradiancy on the chest X-ray, and what is the value of an expiratory film in confirming bronchial obstruction from an inhaled foreign body?
(iv) What happens when a foreign body causes complete (rather than partial) obstruction of a bronchus, and which lobe collapses in which direction in each case (upper, middle, and lower lobe collapse)?
(v) In children, what are the specific features of pneumothorax on a CXR that differ from adults, including herniation, mediastinal displacement, and the specific conditions in which pneumothorax commonly complicates childhood infections?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Inhaled foreign body (peanut) with partial bronchial obstruction of the left main bronchus, causing air trapping (obstructive emphysema). Mechanism: the foreign body acts as a ball valve, allowing air in during inspiration but preventing expiration from the left lung. Air builds up beyond the obstruction, causing the lung to balloon and appear hyperinflated and hyperlucent.

(ii)
Causes of bilateral lung transradiancy with over-expansion:
• Chronic obstructive emphysema
• Asthma
• Acute bronchiolitis
• Laryngeal or tracheal narrowing (due to mucus plug or foreign body)
CXR features common to all: diaphragms are low and flat; heart appears small (long and narrow); lungs appear darker than normal with paucity of peripheral pulmonary vessels. In emphysema, cyst-like spaces or bullae may develop from rupture of distended alveoli, seen as thin curvilinear hairline shadows.

(iii)
Unilateral transradiancy: one hemithorax appears darker than the other; vascular lung markings should be visible within the dark lung (confirming it is not a pneumothorax); must not be due to patient rotation (check clavicles equidistant from spinous processes). Expiratory film: the normal lung deflates (becomes smaller and denser) on expiration, but the affected lung with air trapping does not deflate; this makes the asymmetry more obvious and confirms the presence of air trapping.

(iv)
Complete obstruction by a foreign body causes collapse of the lung beyond it (compressive collapse). Collapse directions:
• Upper lobes: collapse upwards, medially, and anteriorly
• Middle lobe: collapses downwards and medially; produces triangular opacity anteriorly on lateral view; density lateral to the right heart border on PA
• Lower lobes: collapse posteriorly, medially, and downwards; left lower lobe shows triangular opacity projected through the heart shadow; right lower lobe may collapse with middle lobe

(v)
Pneumothorax in children: specific features differ from adults:
• Pockets of free air collect anteriorly and medially (the lung edge is usually not visible)
• Pleural air also in costophrenic areas with absence of pulmonary vascular markings peripherally above the diaphragms
• Mediastinum displaces readily in children with herniation of the pneumothorax across the midline
• The herniated pneumothorax can be seen on the opposite side (arrows on CXR)
• In children, pneumothorax is a common complication of staphylococcal pneumonia; if a pleural collection is present, a hydro- or pyopneumothorax will be seen

questions.question:
A patient undergoing preparation for radiation therapy has their full blood count checked. Specific parameters must be met before commencing radiotherapy.

(i) What is the PVC (haematocrit) threshold before radiotherapy commences?
(ii) What is the WBC threshold and what does a raised WBC signify in this context?
(iii) What action is taken if a patient is anaemic?
(iv) Why is pain control important before radiotherapy, and what percentage of cancer patients present with pain?
(v) When chemotherapy is given concurrently with radiotherapy, what is this regimen called, and what is involved in patient counselling before chemotherapy?
questions.answerText:
(i)
PVC should be greater than or equal to 30%.

(ii)
WBC should be greater than or equal to 3000/mm³. A raised WBC might signify infection, which must be treated with appropriate antibiotics before commencement of radiotherapy.

(iii)
If a patient is anaemic, blood transfusion will be done before the treatment, since radiation will not be effective in an anaemic patient.

(iv)
About 60–70% of cancer patients present with pain. When pain is well controlled, patients are more likely to comply with treatment regimen planned for them.

(v)
The regimen is called Chemo-Radiotherapy. Patients are counselled prior to chemotherapy; possible side effects are explained to the patients; they are taught some self-care procedures to follow at home while on chemotherapy.

(i)
Indications for palliative radiotherapy:
• To relieve pain
• Pathological fractures (+/- severe pain): to relieve pain and avert fracture
• To stop bleeding from tumours
• To reduce foul-smelling discharge from tumours
• To debulk large "ugly" masses
• To reduce raised intracranial pressure of brain metastasis
• To relieve airway obstruction due to tumour

(ii)
Radiation doses:
• Bone metastases (extremities): 8–10 Gy single fraction
• Brain metastasis: 30 Gy in 10 fractions
• Spinal cord compression: 30 Gy in 10 fractions
• SVCO: 25 Gy in 6 fractions

(iii)
80% of advanced cancer present with pain. The pain arises from tissue and bony infiltration, compression of neighbouring normal tissue.

(iv)
Total pain encompasses: Physical; Psychological; Emotional; Spiritual. Patients experience pain on several levels and effective treatment requires a holistic assessment.

(v)
Weak opioids: Codeine; Tramadol; Dihydrocodeine. Strong opioids: Morphine; Fentanyl; Oxycodone; Hydrocodone; Buprenorphine; Methadone.

(ii) The three components of the x-ray generator
(iii) Types of transformers — define each type and give the mathematical relationship between primary and secondary coils

B. (i) Define rectification and distinguish half-wave from full-wave rectification.
(ii) Define waveform ripple and state the ripple percentage for: single-phase half/full-wave; three-phase six-pulse; and 12-pulse systems.
(iii) State three exposure factors controlled by the generator and what each affects.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The generator is the set of equipment that provides power to the x-ray tube and permits control of the exposure factors. Functions:
• Increases the voltage and rectifies the waveform from AC to direct current (DC)
• Permits x-ray operators to control three key parameters of x-ray operation (exposure factors).

A(ii)
Three components: High-voltage transformer; Filament transformer; Rectifier circuits.

A(iii)
Types of transformers: Step-up transformers increase the voltage (e.g. 240 V to 70 kV for x-ray production). Step-down transformers decrease the voltage (e.g. 240 V to 10 V for the filament). Mathematical relationship: Np/Ns = Vp/Vs (number of turns in primary/secondary coils proportional to voltages).

B(i)
Rectification changes the AC voltage into DC voltage across the x-ray tube. Half-wave rectification eliminates one direction of current. Full-wave rectification (using a minimum of four diodes) produces two pulses per cycle.

B(ii)
Waveform ripple is the maximum voltage minus the minimum voltage per cycle, expressed as a percentage of the maximum voltage. Single-phase half- and full-wave: 100% ripple. Three-phase six-pulse: 14% ripple. 12-pulse systems: 4% ripple.

B(iii)
Three exposure factors: X-ray tube voltage (kV) — affects x-ray energy; Tube current (mA) — affects radiation quantity; Exposure time (seconds).

(i)
The mandible behaves as a rigid ring.
It is connected at each end by a firm joint, the temporomandibular joint.

(ii)
Because the mandible behaves as a rigid ring connected by joints at each end, a double fracture usually occurs.
This may be in the region of the angle and the opposite condylar neck, or both condylar necks.
If one fracture is found, the second fracture should always be sought.

(iii)
Floating teeth result from destruction of the supporting bone leaving teeth unsupported.
Floating teeth may occur in histiocytosis, metastatic disease, and Burkitt's lymphoma.
A related sign, absence of the lamina dura (the white line around the tooth roots), may also be seen.
Absence of the lamina dura may be seen in osteoporosis, and in rickets and osteomalacia.
It may also be seen in leukaemia, histiocytosis, multiple myeloma, and Burkitt's lymphoma.
These conditions therefore overlap considerably in their radiographic dental signs.
The distinguishing feature between them is not resolvable on plain film alone; biopsy is usually required.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH); computed tomography (CT) of the brain is the imaging method of choice and is positive in over 80% of cases. Magnetic resonance imaging is not reliable and will not show small amounts of blood.

(ii)
Most cases are due to rupture of a berry aneurysm, though rupture of an angioma, acute leukaemia, or anticoagulants may also be responsible. Most aneurysms arise from the circle of Willis, and blood is usually larger in amount near the site of the aneurysm.

(iii)
A negative CT scan does not exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage, as very small leaks may not show; if strongly suspected, a lumbar puncture should be performed. Hydrocephalus occurs in 50% of cases within 24 hours due to obstruction of CSF flow by blood, and must be watched for.

(iv)
Cerebral angiography, performed via the femoral artery with selective catheterisation of the ICA or VA, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), is used to localise the aneurysm prior to surgery.

(i) A 50-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life, vomiting, and neck stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis and the imaging investigation of choice?

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the heart under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and location
A(ii) Relations (anterior, posterior, superior, inferior, lateral)
A(iii) Surfaces and borders (list each surface and each border with its constituents)

B. Using the cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) as a reference:
B(i) Explain the radiological basis for measuring cardiac size on a PA chest radiograph, including the normal values for adults and neonates and the formula used.
B(ii) Explain why body type, age, and patient position each influence the appearance of the normal cardiac shadow on a chest radiograph.

C. Distinguish between left ventricular enlargement and right ventricular enlargement on the plain chest radiograph, describing the characteristic radiological features of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The heart is a hollow, muscular organ of the middle mediastinum, designed to pump oxygenated blood around the systemic circulation and de-oxygenated blood around the pulmonary circulation. It lies obliquely in the chest with 1/3rd of its mass lying to the right and 2/3rd to the left.

A(ii)
Relations:
• Anteriorly: body of the sternum, adjoining costal cartilage, left lungs and pleura
• Posteriorly: oesophagus, descending thoracic aorta, azygos and hemi-azygos veins, thoracic ducts
• Superiorly: bifurcation of the main pulmonary trunk
• Inferiorly: diaphragm
• Laterally: lungs, pleura

A(iii)
Surfaces: Posterior (base) — mainly left atrium and a little right atrium; Apex — formed by the left ventricle; Anterior (sternocostal) — mainly right ventricle, inferiorly and superiorly by the atria; Inferior (diaphragmatic) — formed by the ventricles, resting on the central tendon of the diaphragm; Right surface — mainly right atrium; Left pulmonary surface — mainly left ventricle and a little superiorly by the atrium.
Borders: Right — IVC, right atrium, SVC; Left — left ventricle, left atrium, pulmonary trunk, arch of aorta; Anterior — right ventricle; Superior — right and left atria, SVC, ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

B(i)
Cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) = widest heart diameter / widest internal inter-thoracic diameter. Normal value: ≤50% (0.5) in adults; 0.6 in neonates. A CTR greater than these values indicates cardiomegaly. The cardiopulmonary ratio (CPR) uses the transverse cardiac measurement of the horizontal distance of the most lateral aspects of right and left margins, divided by the internal diameter of the thoracic cavity at the level of the right diaphragm.

B(ii)
Body type: oblique, transverse, or vertical build affects cardiac orientation. Age: with age the heart grows and its position changes from globular to oblique to horizontal. Respiration: on inspiration, normal heart shadow appears; on expiration, heart shadow becomes horizontal. Patient position: erect position gives an elongated heart shadow; supine position gives apparent enlargement of the cardiac shadow.

C.
Left ventricular enlargement: increased cardiothoracic/cardiopulmonary ratio; curvature of the left heart border takes on a larger radius; apex is displaced laterally and inferiorly.
Right ventricular enlargement: lateral displacement of the left heart border (higher in the left border); apex is also displaced laterally, but not inferiorly.

questions.question:
(i) A 14-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of severe scrotal pain and swelling of less than one hour's duration. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what ultrasound finding would support it?
(ii) What condition closely mimics this diagnosis on ultrasound, and how are the two differentiated?
(iii) What is the appropriate management, and why should imaging not delay it?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Testicular torsion. Ultrasound abnormality develops within one hour; the testis becomes enlarged and uniformly darker (hypoechoeic) than normal, the epididymis may be enlarged, and a hydrocele is often associated.

(ii)
Epididymo-orchitis produces very similar appearances (an enlarged, echo-poor epididymis with an associated hydrocele), and the two conditions can only be differentiated with colour Doppler ultrasound.

(iii)
Surgery should not be delayed by asking for a scan, since ultrasound changes develop within an hour and this is a time-critical surgical emergency.

questions.question:
A. Describe the mechanism of radiation injury to mammalian cells under the following headings:
(i) The three phases of biological damage by ionising radiation, including the time scale for each
(ii) The specific target of radiation damage in mammalian cells
(iii) Distinguish direct interaction from indirect interaction, stating which is the most important in radiotherapy

B. (i) Define the Oxygen Enhancement Ratio (OER).
(ii) Explain why cells irradiated under well-oxygenated conditions are more radiosensitive than those under hypoxic conditions.
(iii) State the Law of Bergonie and Tribondeau.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three phases:
• Physical phase (10⁻¹⁸ s): Energy deposition phase. Photons interact with orbital electrons causing excitation or ionisation.
• Chemical phase (10⁻³ s): The ionised or excited atoms interact, leading to breakage of chemical bonds through formation of free radicals (directly or indirectly).
• Biological phase (seconds to years): The cells react to the inflicted chemical damage. Cell death usually occurs during the next cell division.

A(ii)
The specific target is the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) molecule.

A(iii)
Direct interaction: direct damage to the DNA molecule (single or double strand break); most lethal is the double strand break; high-LET radiation usually causes direct interaction. Indirect interaction: the most important mode of interaction in radiotherapy; DNA molecular damage is by radiation-induced free radicals; when radiation interacts with water in the tissue, free radical ions are produced: H₂O → H₂O⁺ + e⁻; H₂O⁺ → H⁺ + OH• (unpaired electron on hydroxyl ion).

B(i)
OER is defined as the ratio of doses needed for a given biological effect in the presence or absence of oxygen.

B(ii)
Oxygen molecules react with free radicals to produce chemically unrepairable peroxy radicals, making oxygenated cells more radiosensitive.

B(iii)
Mammalian cell sensitivity to ionising radiation increases when cells are rapidly dividing, undifferentiated, and have a high mitotic figure.

(i)
Breast carcinoma. Most breast cancers present as a painless lump/mass.

(ii)
Risk factors:
• Increasing age (mean age is 48 years in the Nigerian environment)
• Family history of breast cancer
• Oestrogen exposure
• Use of oral contraceptive pills
• First pregnancy after thirty years of age
• Nulliparity
• Previous benign breast lump/disease
• Stress
• Increased dietary fat intake
• Obesity (postmenopausal women)
• High alcohol consumption
• Smoking/passive smoking
• Use of hormone replacement therapy
• Radiation exposure in teenagers

(iii)
Symptoms and signs:
• No symptom (very early detection)
• Painless or painful breast lump/mass
• Axillary lump/mass
• Nipple retraction, puckering, skin tethering, ulceration
• Bloody nipple discharge
• Symptoms from spread: bone pain, fractures, headache, cough, breathlessness

(iv)
Treatment modalities:
• Surgery (for localised cases)
• Chemotherapy/immunotherapy/targeted therapy
• Hormone therapy
• Radiation therapy
• Support services (appropriate for each disease/patient)
Each case should be discussed at multidisciplinary rounds among Medical, Surgical, and Radiation Oncologists because there are overlaps in management; the most appropriate and beneficial treatment requires joint assessment of all options.

(v)
In the developed world with advanced medical care, the 5-year survival of all cases is about 50%. In the developing world it is less than 20%, because of late presentation (70%) and inadequate medical facilities. In our environment, 70–80% of patients present with advanced (stage 3–4) disease.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with a painless, firm lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. She is nulliparous, had her first pregnancy after age 30, and has a family history of breast cancer. Mammography shows a spiculated, poorly defined opacity with microcalcification, skin retraction, and nipple retraction.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis, and what is the most common presentation of this condition?
(ii) List all the risk factors for this condition, including age, parity, hormonal, dietary, lifestyle, and radiation-related factors.
(iii) List all the symptoms and signs by which this condition can present, including those from spread of disease.
(iv) Describe the full range of treatment modalities available for this condition and explain why each case should be assessed in a multidisciplinary setting.
(v) What are the five-year survival rates in developed and developing countries, and what accounts for the difference in outcome?

questions.answerText:
(i)
Right-sided pleural effusion. A minimum of 100–200 cc of fluid must be present before it becomes visible on a PA chest radiograph.

(ii)
Radiological appearances of pleural effusion on erect PA CXR:
• First sign: blunting of the costophrenic angle (normally acute angle fills in with fluid)
• Larger collection: homogeneous opacity devoid of lung markings; concave upper border higher laterally than medially; loss of the diaphragm (silhouette sign)
• Large effusions displace the mediastinum to the opposite side
• As effusion increases, the underlying lung retracts to the hilum
• A massive effusion causing complete opacity of the hemithorax with no mediastinal shift suggests complete collapse of the underlying lung

(iii)
Variations:
• Subpulmonary collection: fluid between the diaphragm and inferior part of the lung; upper margin parallel to the diaphragm; may be mistaken for an elevated diaphragm
• Encysted/loculated in fissures: fluid in the lesser fissure may simulate a mass lesion; fluid encysted in the oblique fissure also simulates a mass; common in heart failure
• Loculated collection: common in empyema with adhesions; may have a convex inner border
• Supine film: appears as a homogeneous haze covering the entire hemithorax; small amounts difficult to detect; shows first on a lateral film

(iv)
Pleural effusion vs consolidation:
• Pleural effusion: concave upper border; no air bronchogram; silhouette sign present (loss of diaphragm); fluid may not always be visible in both projections equally; lateral film shows fluid in the posterior costo-phrenic recess first
• Consolidation/pneumonia: always visible in both PA and lateral projections unlike collapse; air bronchogram may be present; silhouette sign relates to which lobe is consolidated; increased density with preserved or increased volume
• Collapse: there is no air bronchogram unless consolidation also present; loss of lung volume causes displacement of adjacent structures (diaphragm, hilum, mediastinum, fissures); increased density due to loss of aeration

(v)
Causes of pulmonary venous hypertension (associated with pleural effusion):
• Coarctation of aorta
• Aortic stenosis
• Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
• Mitral stenosis (acquired or congenital)
• Left atrial myxoma
• Cor triatriatum
• TAPVR from below diaphragm
• Congestive heart failure (CHF)
Kerley B lines: represent thickening of the interlobular septa due to lymphatic engorgement in pulmonary interstitial oedema; they are short horizontal lines at the lung bases, seen in pulmonary venous hypertension.
questions.question:
A chest X-ray of a 55-year-old woman shows a homogeneous opacity in the right lower zone with a concave upper margin that is higher laterally than medially, blunting of the right costophrenic angle, and a silhouette sign with loss of the right diaphragm. There is no air bronchogram.

(i) What is the radiological diagnosis, and what is the minimum volume of fluid that must be present before it becomes visible on a PA chest radiograph?
(ii) Describe the full radiological appearances of this condition on an erect PA chest X-ray, including the first sign, the appearance of larger collections, and the effects on adjacent structures.
(iii) What are the variations in appearance of this condition, including subpulmonary collection, encysted/loculated fluid in fissures, and the difference between a supine and erect film appearance?
(iv) Distinguish between a pleural effusion and pulmonary consolidation on the chest X-ray, with reference to the presence or absence of the silhouette sign, air bronchogram, and visibility on both PA and lateral views.
(v) Using the chest radiograph findings, what are the causes of pulmonary venous hypertension as a recognised condition associated with pleural effusion, and how do Kerley B lines arise in this context?

A. Describe the aetiology of cancer:
A(i) State the fundamental genetic basis from which cancer arises, listing all the cellular properties acquired as a result of genetic alterations
A(ii) List all the environmental, lifestyle, and hereditary risk factors for cancer development

B. Explain carcinogenesis at the molecular level:
B(i) Define a mutation and list all the mechanisms by which mutations can arise
B(ii) Distinguish between germline mutations and somatic mutations in terms of their origin and heritability
B(iii) Explain why most cancers are monoclonal, and describe the sequence of events from unrepaired DNA damage to clinical cancer

C. Describe the cell cycle and explain the modes of cancer spread:
C(i) Name all phases of the cell cycle and all stages of mitosis
C(ii) List the three primary ways tumours can spread to distant organs, naming each pathway
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cancer arises from a series of genetic alterations that promote:
• Self-sufficiency in growth
• Escape from cell cycle exit
• Resistance to apoptosis
• Cellular immortalisation
• Acquisition of properties that facilitate angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis

A(ii)
Risk factors:
• Environmental:
• Physical: e.g. UV radiation
• Biological: e.g. HPV
• Lifestyle: smoking, alcohol, obesity, sedentary lifestyle
• Genetics and hereditary: BRCA1, BRCA2; MSI (microsatellite instability)

B(i)
A mutation is a change in a DNA sequence. Mutations can result from:
• DNA copying mistakes made during cell division
• Exposure to ionising radiation
• Exposure to chemicals called mutagens
• Infection by viruses

B(ii)
Germline mutations: occur in the eggs and sperm; can be passed on to offspring.
Somatic mutations: occur in body cells; are not passed on.

B(iii)
Most cancers are monoclonal: they arise from a single cell. Damaged DNA is usually repaired during cell division; however, sometimes it is not. When this unrepaired damaged DNA persists, abnormal cell growth occurs. The clone accumulates mutations and acquires phenotypes that make it evade the body's immune system, and then acquires the ability to invade and metastasise.

C(i)
Cell cycle phases: G1, S, G2, G2, and Mitosis. Stages of mitosis: Prophase, Prometaphase, Metaphase, Anaphase, and Telophase.

C(ii)
Three primary ways tumours spread to distant organs:
• Through the circulatory (blood) system — haematogenous spread
• Through the lymphatic system
• Through the body wall into the abdominal and chest cavities — transcoelomic spread

A(i)
Response may depend on:
• Histologic type: e.g. Hodgkin's lymphoma and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma respond differently
• Grade: poorly differentiated versus well differentiated
• Receptor status: ER (oestrogen receptor), PR (progesterone receptor), HER2

A(ii)
Routes of administration of chemotherapy:
• Intravenous (most common)
• Oral (e.g. Xeloda/capecitabine)
• Intrathecal
• Intra-arterial
• Intra-peritoneal

A(iii)
Principles of combination chemotherapy:
• Each drug should have activity against the tumour when used alone; drugs with maximal efficacy are most preferable
• Drugs should have different mechanisms of action
• Drugs should have minimal overlapping toxicities; when several drugs of a class are available, a drug with minimal overlapping toxicity should be selected; although this leads to a greater range of side effects, it decreases the risk of potentially life-threatening cumulative toxicity to the same organ system
• Each drug in a combination should be used in its optimal dose and schedule
If a drug is omitted: may allow overgrowth of a cell clone that is sensitive to that drug alone but resistant to the other drugs in the combination.
If too many drugs are added: the doses of some or all of the component drugs may be reduced below the threshold of efficacy, thereby decreasing activity of the regimen.

B(i)
Sequencing:
• Neoadjuvant: given before primary treatment
• Adjuvant: given after primary treatment
• Concurrent: given at the same time as primary treatment

B(ii)
Cycle durations: 4 weeks; 3 weeks; weekly.
Course day patterns: Day 1; Day 1–3; Day 1–5.

C(i)
The main target of radiotherapy is the DNA.

C(ii)
Radiation can damage DNA:
• Directly: by producing electrons to damage the DNA
• Indirectly: by producing radicals through ionisation of water (free radicals that then damage DNA)

C(iii)
Radiotherapy does not differentiate between tumour and normal tissues. The goal of radiotherapy is to give optimal tumour dose and minimal dose to normal tissues. The radiation oncologist's main responsibility is to delineate the tumour volumes.

A(ii) Routes of administration of chemotherapy: list all routes

A young adult presents with right iliac fossa pain, fever, and leucocytosis.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what imaging modalities are used to confirm it?
(ii) What CT features support the diagnosis?
(iii) What is the role of imaging in reducing unnecessary surgery in this condition?
(iv) What is the surgical procedure for this diagnosis?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Acute appendicitis, presenting with right lower quadrant (RLQ) pain, fever and leucocytosis; CT and ultrasound are increasingly used to confirm the clinical suspicion.

(ii)
General CT features of appendicitis include a dilated appendix greater than 6mm, or visualisation of an appendicolith with an appendix of any size, and peri-appendiceal fat stranding.

(iii)
CT and ultrasound are used more often to confirm clinical suspicion and reduce the number of unnecessary laparotomies.

(iv)
The surgical treatment is laparotomy (for appendicectomy).

(i)
Ovaries appear as oval structures lateral to the uterus.
They are recognised by the follicles within them, small dark rounded structures.
They can be found anywhere between the lower pole of the kidney and the pouch of Douglas.
Normally they lie just anterior and medial to the iliac vessels on the pelvic side wall.
The ovaries may not be symmetrical in position.

(ii)
Malignancy should be suspected if there are thick irregular septations in a cystic mass.
Malignancy is also suspected with nodules in the septations, or solid tissue within cystic spaces.
A thick irregular cystic wall, or pelvic ascites, also raise suspicion of malignancy.
The size of the cyst is not an indicator of malignancy.

(iii)
A simple functional cyst (follicular cyst) is usually less than 6cm in diameter.
It is dark and clear, with a thin wall and acoustic enhancement, and disappears after an interval.
A benign cystadenoma contains internal strands or septations, does not show acoustic enhancement, is persistent, and increases in size, though it has malignant potential.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the normal appearance and location of the ovary on ultrasound.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis (ultrasound features) that raise suspicion of malignancy in an ovarian cystic mass.
(iii) Distinguish a simple functional ovarian cyst from a benign cystadenoma.

A patient presents with loin pain radiating to the groin. Ultrasound shows hydronephrosis with echogenic debris in the calyces.
(i) What are the recognised associations of nephrocalcinosis?
(ii) What complication has occurred here, and what is its ultrasound appearance?
(iii) What further complication may occur if the obstruction is longstanding?
(iv) What imaging combination is recommended for initial assessment of suspected renal colic, and what further study confirms the site and cause?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Nephrocalcinosis (multiple calcifications within the renal parenchyma rather than the pelvicalyceal system) is associated with renal tubular acidosis, hyperparathyroidism, and medullary sponge kidneys.

(ii)
Pyonephrosis, a complication of obstructive hydronephrosis due to infection; on ultrasound the urine is no longer anechoeic but contains echoes (turbid urine), and in severe cases the calyces become filled with debris, sometimes mistaken for a renal mass.

(iii)
If the obstruction is longstanding, the renal cortex atrophies and appears narrow on ultrasound; in severe, longstanding obstruction the cortex may be completely destroyed and the kidney non-functioning, so an intravenous pyelogram will usually be unhelpful.

(iv)
An ultrasound scan plus a plain film is the recommended initial imaging for suspected renal colic, the plain film demonstrating calculi and ultrasound demonstrating any hydronephrosis. An intravenous pyelogram (IVP) may be needed for confirmation or further assessment of the site and cause.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the spinal canal and its relations, and state the three anatomical compartments used to classify a spinal mass lesion.
(ii) Explain the clinical basis of why the pedicles are particularly important when assessing a vertebral body on plain film.
(iii) Distinguish between an extradural mass and an intradural mass in terms of their effect on the spinal cord and nerve roots, and give examples of each.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The spinal canal contains the cord, surrounded by dura, with nerve roots passing through it.
Mass lesions in the spinal canal are classified by location as extradural, intradural, or intramedullary.

(ii)
The pedicles are a common site of erosion by metastasis or myeloma.
A missing/absent pedicle on plain film may be the only clue to the presence of such a lesion.
Thinning of the pedicles with increased distance between them suggests a slow-growing intraspinal lesion.
Such thinning may indicate a benign tumour or syringomyelia rather than a rapidly growing lesion.

(iii)
An extradural mass lies outside the dura.
It displaces the theca away from the bony margins of the spinal canal.
It compresses the theca and nerve root sheaths, so nerve roots show a "bunched up" appearance.
Examples include prolapsed disc, metastasis, myeloma, lymphoma, neurofibroma, meningioma, haematoma, and abscess.
An intradural mass lies within the dura but outside the cord and displaces the cord and nerves smoothly around it.
Examples include meningioma, neurofibroma, metastasis from a CNS primary or lymphoma, and subdural empyema.

questions.question:
A patient with liver cancer and bile duct cancer undergoes imaging which reveals obstruction of the bile ducts. The interventional radiologist plans a percutaneous procedure.

(i) Name the two percutaneous procedures performed by interventional radiologists for bile duct obstruction.
(ii) Name both techniques used in the spinal procedure for vertebral fractures, and describe what is injected.
(iii) Regarding stone disease, percutaneous nephrolithotomy is used for large kidney stones — what three steps are involved?
(iv) For uterine fibroids causing heavy menstrual bleeding, what interventional procedure is used and what is its mechanism?
(v) What treatment is used for dilated veins (varicose veins) by interventional radiologists?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) to image the obstructions; and percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD), wherein catheters or stents are placed through the skin into the bile ducts to drain the bile.

(ii)
Vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty: the percutaneous injection of biocompatible cement into fractured vertebrae.

(iii)
Three steps for percutaneous nephrolithotomy:
• Creating a tunnel into the kidney through a small skin incision
• Passing an endoscope directly into the kidney
• Breaking the stone with special instruments and pulling the fragments out

(iv)
Uterine fibroid embolisation (UFE): blocking blood vessels supplying the fibroids, which leads to shrinkage.

(v)
Varicose veins are treated by blocking the vein by heat treatment (laser or microwave) or by the use of irritant drugs and embolisation techniques.

(i)
A tripod (punch) injury is so-called because the zygoma is separated at three attachments.
These attachments are the fronto-zygomatic suture, the lateral wall of the maxillary antrum, and the zygomatic arch.

(ii)
Three lines should be examined carefully to make sure they are intact following trauma.
Interpretation is helped by drawing a line along the outer border of the antrum and the lower zygomatic arch.
This line takes the shape of an "elephant's trunk" in the normal state.
If this shape is altered, or the line interrupted, a fracture should be suspected.

(iii)
A blow-out fracture is a fracture through the floor of the orbit at its weakest part.
It is typically caused by a blow to the eye, such as by a tennis ball.
The increased pressure in the orbit causes the floor to rupture further back than the orbital margin.
The orbital margin itself therefore remains intact on plain films.
This allows soft tissue from the orbit to prolapse into the upper part of the maxillary antrum.
This produces an opacity in the upper antrum shaped like a "tear drop".
questions.question:
(i) Describe the course of the fracture lines seen in a tripod (zygomatic) fracture.
(ii) State the key sites/lines that must be carefully examined on the occipito-mental (OM) view following facial trauma.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and radiographic appearance seen in a blow-out fracture of the orbit.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A good PA chest X-ray requires:
• No rotation: anterior ends of clavicles equidistant from spinous processes
• Full inspiration: top of right diaphragm should lie below the anterior end of the 6th right rib
• Ribs should be sloping, not horizontal; anterior end of first rib should lie just below the clavicle
• Scapulae should not overlay the lung fields
• Spinous processes should be faintly visible through the heart shadow
• Whole of the lung fields fully included, including costophrenic angles and apices

A(ii)
Normal structures:
• Soft tissues and bones: breast shadows, ribs, clavicles, spine, shoulders
• Diaphragms: smooth, convex upwards; right dome 1–2 cm higher than left; at or below level of 10th posterior rib or 6th anterior rib; costophrenic angle should be acute and clear
• Fissures: horizontal fissure at level of 4th anterior rib, runs horizontally to hilum; oblique fissures seen on lateral CXR
• Lung hilae: left hilum lies 0.5–1.5 cm higher than right; similar density and size; concave borders; composed of pulmonary arteries and veins
• Mediastinum: trachea central; subcarinal angle 60–70 degrees; heart size ≤50% of thorax transverse diameter; right border visible to the right of the spine; aorta descends just to the left of the spine
• Paraspinal line: thin white line parallel to spine, should lie within 1 cm of lateral border of spine unless aortic unfolding
• Lung markings: pulmonary vessels and fissures; bronchi normally only visible near the hilae; lower zone vessels larger than upper in erect film

B(i)
Silhouette sign: it is only possible to see the outline of any tissue in the chest because there is air in the lung adjacent to or surrounding it. If the air space is filled by fluid or tumour, borders become obliterated. The right heart border disappears with collapse or consolidation of the right middle lobe. The right aortic border is lost with opacity in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe and middle lobe. The outline of the diaphragms is lost when there is consolidation in the lower lobe or fluid adjacent to the diaphragm.

B(ii)
Air bronchogram: bronchi are normally invisible because surrounded by air-filled alveoli. They become visible when: bronchi are filled with fluid/pus and walls are visible; walls are thickened; surrounding alveoli are filled with fluid (oedema or pus) but bronchi remain clear and filled with air, appearing as darker lines within lung shadowing. The air bronchogram is a feature of alveolar shadowing (not interstitial shadowing); there is no air bronchogram in collapse unless consolidation is also present.

C.
Review areas are those where lesions are more likely to be overlooked:
• Apices: overlying ribs cause difficulty; an apical tumour may only show as a subtle opacity with rib destruction
• Retrocardiac and retrodiaphragmatic areas: the lung dips behind the diaphragm and behind the heart; lesions in these areas may be hidden by overlying structures; a lateral view or CT may be needed
• Mediastinum and hilae: subtle adenopathy or mass may blend with normal mediastinal contours
• Bones: rib deposits may only show as a peripheral opacity related to the rib
Example: A nodule in the right lower lobe lying behind the diaphragm is a common miss; it was confirmed on lateral view as a metastasis.
questions.question:
A. Describe the radiological anatomy of the normal chest X-ray (PA view) under the following headings:
A(i) Criteria for a technically satisfactory PA chest X-ray (rotation, inspiration, scapular position, vertebral visibility, lung field inclusion)
A(ii) Normal structures to evaluate systematically: soft tissues and bones, diaphragms, fissures, lung hilae, mediastinum, paraspinal line, and lung markings

B. Explain the following interpretive principles:
B(i) The silhouette sign: what it is, how it occurs, and how it helps localise pulmonary abnormalities — with specific examples of which structures are lost in which lobe abnormalities
B(ii) The air bronchogram: describe the conditions under which bronchi become visible, and explain what this sign indicates about the nature of the shadowing (alveolar vs interstitial)

C. Explain why the apices, retrocardiac area, retrodiaphragmatic area, mediastinum, hilae, and bones are designated "review areas" on the chest X-ray, and give an example of a lesion likely to be overlooked in one of these areas.

(i) Describe the patterns of thyroid gland enlargement relevant to nuclear medicine imaging (diffuse versus nodular).
(ii) State how each pattern relates to a specific disease state.
(iii) Explain how thyroid disease may produce a distant/extrathyroidal manifestation causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The thyroid may show diffuse enlargement (a goitre) as one pattern.
It may alternatively show nodular enlargement, with single or multiple nodules, as another pattern.

(ii)
A thyroid scan in hyperthyroidism shows increased diffuse, uniform uptake in an enlarged gland.
This diffuse pattern, with or without retrosternal extension, is seen in Graves' disease and diffuse toxic goitre.
Toxic nodular goitre and toxic multinodular goitre are variants showing a nodular pattern of increased uptake ("hot" nodules).
Euthyroid goitre is due to a fall in T4 with increased TSH stimulation causing cellular hyperplasia, usually from iodine deficiency.

(iii)
Graves' disease is an autoimmune thyroid disease in which thyroid-stimulating antibodies bind to the TSH receptor.
It is characterised by exophthalmos, due to lymphocytic infiltration and swelling of the retro-orbital tissue of the eyes.
Exophthalmos is an extrathyroidal manifestation that can cause a visual/functional deficit distant from the gland itself.
Pretibial myxoedema, local thickening of subcutaneous tissue over the shin, is another extrathyroidal manifestation described.

questions.question:
A chest X-ray of a 58-year-old woman with known mitral stenosis shows: a double density at the right heart border, straightening and convexity of the left heart border, elevation of the left main bronchus, and a calcified mitral annulus.

(i) What chamber enlargement is demonstrated, and what are the CXR findings specific to this chamber enlargement?
(ii) Explain the physiological mechanism linking mitral stenosis to the CXR abnormalities visible in this case, and describe the corresponding pulmonary vascular changes expected on CXR.
(iii) What are all the causes of left atrial enlargement, and what is the difference between the CXR appearances of left atrial enlargement and left ventricular enlargement?
(iv) How does the right atrial enlargement in tricuspid valve stenosis appear differently from left atrial enlargement on the CXR, and how does right ventricular enlargement differ from left ventricular enlargement in terms of apex displacement?
(v) What are the five types of X-ray features to evaluate on the CXR in any cardiac patient, and how does echocardiography add functional information that the plain CXR cannot provide?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Left atrial enlargement (LAE). CXR findings specific to LAE:
• Double density/double right heart border (two shadows overlapping each other — the normal right heart border and the enlarged left atrium projecting through it)
• Elevation of the left main bronchus (and splaying of the carina)
• Straightening of the left heart border
• Convexity of the left heart border
• Convexity of the left atrial appendage
• "Indentation" for left atrium
• Calcified mitral annulus may be seen

(ii)
Mitral stenosis obstructs flow from left atrium to left ventricle, causing left atrial pressure to rise (left-sided cardiac outflow obstruction). This leads to pulmonary venous hypertension. CXR pulmonary vascular changes: RDPA >17 mm; cephalisation (upper lobe vessels become more prominent than lower lobe); visible lymphatic channels (Kerley B lines); mild haziness in lower zones; attenuation of vessels; slight loss of definition of heart and mediastinal contour.

(iii)
All causes of left atrial enlargement:
• CHF
• Mitral stenosis
• Mitral regurgitation
• Prolapsed mitral valve
• Papillary muscle dysfunction
• Left atrial myxoma
Difference between LAE and LVE on CXR:
• LAE: double right heart border; elevation of left main bronchus; straightening/convexity of left heart border; no significant displacement of apex
• LVE: increased CTR; curvature of left heart border takes on a larger radius; apex displaced laterally and inferiorly

(iv)
Right atrial enlargement (e.g. in tricuspid stenosis): lateral prominence of the right heart border with associated increased convexity.
Right ventricular enlargement: lateral displacement of the left heart border (higher in the left border); apex displaced laterally but NOT inferiorly.
Left ventricular enlargement: apex displaced laterally AND inferiorly.

(v)
Five CXR features to evaluate in cardiac patients:
• Cardiac size (CTR)
• Cardiac contour
• Pulmonary vasculature
• Lung fields (interstitial/alveolar oedema; Kerley lines A, B, and C; pleural effusion)
• Rib cage (e.g. rib notching in coarctation of the aorta)
Echocardiography adds: real-time dynamic assessment of valve function (stenosis, regurgitation), ejection fraction, end diastolic and end systolic volumes, wall thickness, wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, and intracardiac masses — none of which can be fully assessed on the static plain CXR.

questions.question:
A 12-month-old with sickle cell disease presents with painful, swollen hands and feet.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the predisposing condition and typical age group?
(iii) What is the underlying pathophysiology?
(iv) What is the radiographic appearance, and what diagnostic pitfall is noted?
questions.answerText:
(i)
Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome).

(ii)
It occurs in children with sickle cell disease aged 6-24 months.

(iii)
It is caused by vascular occlusion due to sickling, resulting in bone infarction.

(iv)
There is soft tissue swelling with patchy lucency and sclerosis of the shaft with periosteal reaction, seen in the metacarpals or phalanges. In many cases the X-ray appears normal at presentation, as it takes 1-2 weeks for radiological changes to occur, and the appearances are identical to those of infection.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the breast as a glandular structure under the following headings:
A(i) Position and surface markings, including the relationship to the ribs, and the location of the nipple in the non-pendulous breast
A(ii) Internal structure: Cooper's ligaments, number of lobes, and the drainage system to the nipple
A(iii) Blood supply: name all three arterial sources
A(iv) Venous drainage and lymphatic drainage: name the primary lymphatic drainage and the percentage draining to each chain

B. Explain the basis of mammography as an imaging technique:
B(i) Describe the type of X-ray beam used and why it maximises soft tissue contrast
B(ii) Describe how the relative composition of ductal, fatty, fibrotic, or glandular tissue affects mammographic appearances of the breast, including the course of ducts and blood vessels

C. Distinguish between the mammographic appearances of fibroadenoma, carcinoma, and cystosarcoma phylloides.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The breast overlies the 2nd to 6th ribs on the anterior chest wall. It has an axillary tail. The nipple overlies the 4th intercostal space in the non-pendulous breast.

A(ii)
The breast consists of fat and a variable amount of glandular tissue. Cooper's ligaments run through the breast providing a supportive framework and attach it to anterior and posterior structures. The breast contains 15–20 lobes which drain into the lactiferous ducts that open onto the nipple.

A(iii)
Arterial blood supply:
• Branches of the internal mammary (thoracic) artery
• Lateral thoracic branch of the axillary artery
• Perforating branches of the anterior intercostal arteries

A(iv)
Venous drainage accompanies the arteries to the axillary and subclavian veins and the azygos system. Lymphatic drainage: the majority of drainage is to the axillary chain, with less than 5% draining to the internal mammary chain.

B(i)
Mammography uses a low energy X-ray beam to maximise differences in soft tissue density and demonstrate the internal architecture of the breast. Compression, a short exposure time, and the use of high-quality screen-film equipment improve image quality.

B(ii)
When fat predominates, the ducts may be seen. When fibrotic and glandular tissue predominate, the ducts are difficult to see. The ducts radiate out from the nipple and may be seen centrally if dilated; they increase in calibre as they converge onto the nipple. Blood vessels may be distinguished from ducts as they run more haphazardly through the breast and have a more uniform calibre.

C.
• Fibroadenoma: rounded/lobulated, well-defined soft tissue opacity.
• Carcinoma: spiculated/poorly defined; microcalcification; distortion of adjacent tissues; skin and nipple retraction; oedema; ductal dilatation; venous engorgement; wide halo around opacity.
• Cystosarcoma phylloides: usually large; may be benign but has malignant potential.

options: continue using the vaccines without any action
increase the refrigerator temperature and discard the vaccine records
remove the affected vaccines from use and report the temperature excursion
use only half the standard dose to compensate
freeze the vaccines further to preserve them
questions.question: A nurse discovers that vaccines in the clinic refrigerator are stored at 0 degrees Celsius, below the recommended range. The appropriate action is to:
questions.explanation: Vaccines exposed to freezing temperatures, particularly those such as pentavalent or pneumococcal vaccine that are damaged by freezing, must be removed from use and the temperature excursion reported, as administering compromised vaccine gives false reassurance of protection without genuine immunity. Proper documentation and investigation of the cold chain failure help prevent recurrence. This vigilance protects the effectiveness of the entire immunisation programme.

The uterosacral ligaments pass backwards from the cervix to the sacrum, providing posterior support to the uterus and helping maintain its position over the bladder. They contain smooth muscle and fibrous tissue along with autonomic nerves. Presacral neurectomy, which involves cutting these ligaments, has been used to treat severe dysmenorrhoea, though this may cause bladder or bowel dysfunction as a side effect.
questions.question: The uterosacral ligaments provide uterine support by passing backwards from the cervix to which bony structure?

questions.explanation: The arbor vitae pattern of folds increases the surface area of the endocervical mucosa available for mucus secretion. This mucus changes character across the cycle to either block or facilitate sperm passage. The folded architecture is unrelated to menstrual flow control.
questions.question: A pathologist examining a hysterectomy specimen notes the endocervical mucosa arranged in branching folds. This arrangement, called arbor vitae, primarily functions to:
options: anchor the cervix to the vagina

questions.explanation: Lymph from the uterine body drains to the internal iliac glands, while lymph from the cervical area drains to multiple other pelvic lymph glands. This dual drainage provides an effective defence against uterine infection but also means that uterine cancer can spread through multiple lymph node groups. Surgical staging of uterine malignancies requires systematic sampling of relevant pelvic and para-aortic nodes.
questions.question: Lymphatic drainage from the uterine body flows primarily to which group of lymph nodes?

options: resting with the upper body slightly elevated
lying flat on the back at all times
remaining in a strict left lateral position only
questions.explanation: Encouraging positions that use gravity, such as periods of prone lying or a slightly elevated upper body when resting, can aid drainage of lochia and reduce the risk of pooling that predisposes to infection. Prolonged immobility in a single position should be avoided. This advice forms part of routine postnatal self-care education.
questions.question: A midwife advises a postnatal mother on positioning to aid drainage of lochia from the uterus and vagina. The most appropriate recommendation is:

options: Nutritional status and adipose tissue distribution pattern
Brain growth and detect microcephaly or macrocephaly
Skeletal maturation and bone density in the cranial vault
Degree of hydration and fluid balance in the neonate
Adequacy of fontanelle closure at scheduled health visits
questions.question: Head circumference (HC) measurement is used in growth monitoring primarily to assess:
questions.explanation: Head circumference measurement is used to monitor brain growth and detect abnormalities of cranial growth including microcephaly (abnormally small head) and macrocephaly (abnormally large head). The head grows rapidly in the first 2 years of life, reflecting rapid brain development. Average neonatal HC is 33-35 cm, reaching approximately 47 cm at 12 months. Serial HC measurements plotted on WHO charts enable early detection of conditions including hydrocephalus and microcephaly.

options: Prevent urine from pooling around the abdominal area
Keep cord from rubbing and allow air circulation to dry it
Ensure cord is protected from contamination with faeces
Allow visual inspection of cord stump at each nappy change
Prevent pressure on the cord from tight diaper waistband
questions.question: The diaper positioning technique during cord stump care requires folding the diaper below the stump in order to:
questions.explanation: The diaper should be folded below the cord stump to keep it from rubbing against the stump and to allow air circulation that promotes drying of the stump. Friction from the diaper edge against a moist stump can delay natural separation and create conditions for infection. Air circulation is essential for the drying process that leads to normal cord separation within 7-14 days of birth.

options: Be refrigerated and used within 48 hours of thawing
Be left at room temperature to slowly reach feeding temperature
Never be refrozen and discarded if any remains after feeding
Be warmed in a microwave for quick and safe preparation
Be kept at room temperature for up to 4 hours after thawing
questions.explanation: Thawed breast milk should never be refrozen. It should be thawed in a cup or bowl of warm water (not left to cool at room temperature). After feeding, any milk remaining in the feeding container should be discarded and not saved for a later feeding. Breast milk that is refrigerated should not be left to cool at room temperature but thawed in warm water to maintain nutritional and immunological properties.
questions.question: A breastfeeding mother asks about storing expressed breast milk. The nurse should advise that thawed breast milk should:

options: Stabilises neonatal temperature through heat transfer
Promotes initiation and duration of breastfeeding
Prevents neonatal jaundice in all neonates
Facilitates maternal-infant bonding and oxytocin release
questions.question: Skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care) immediately after birth between the newborn and mother has multiple evidence-based benefits. Which of the following is NOT a recognised benefit of immediate skin-to-skin contact?
questions.explanation: Skin-to-skin contact (SSC) or kangaroo care immediately after birth has many evidence-based benefits: it stabilises neonatal temperature (the maternal chest acts as a 'biological incubator'), promotes breastfeeding initiation and duration, reduces neonatal pain perception during procedures, facilitates maternal-infant bonding, and stimulates oxytocin release in the mother, supporting uterine involution. However, SSC does not prevent neonatal jaundice - physiological jaundice is caused by fetal haemoglobin breakdown after birth and is not preventable by SSC alone.

options: be given sponge baths, keeping the stump area dry
be fully immersed in bath water daily regardless of stump status
never be bathed until six weeks of age
have the stump soaked deliberately to soften it
be bathed only in cold water for stump health
questions.question: A mother asks whether she can bathe her newborn normally while the cord stump is still attached. The midwife's correct advice is that the baby should:
questions.explanation: While the cord stump remains attached, sponge bathing is generally recommended to keep the stump area dry and reduce the risk of infection, rather than fully immersing the baby in bath water. Once the stump has separated and the area has healed, normal immersion bathing can resume. This precaution supports the natural drying process necessary for timely cord separation.

Stunting refers to low height-for-age, typically defined as more than two standard deviations below the WHO growth reference median, and reflects the cumulative effect of chronic or recurrent undernutrition over time. It differs from wasting, which reflects acute malnutrition through low weight-for-height. Recognising stunting early allows targeted nutritional intervention, though its effects on linear growth can be difficult to fully reverse once established.
questions.question: A nurse assesses a child's height for age and finds it significantly below the expected reference range for age. This finding, reflecting chronic malnutrition, is termed:

questions.explanation: Magnesium sulphate is used in obstetrics primarily for: (1) treatment and prophylaxis of eclamptic seizures in severe preeclampsia - it is superior to phenytoin and diazepam for this indication; and (2) fetal neuroprotection before preterm birth before 32 weeks of gestation, reducing the risk of cerebral palsy. It also has tocolytic properties but is not first-line for tocolysis. Monitoring for magnesium toxicity (absent deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression) is essential during infusion.
questions.question: Magnesium sulphate is used in obstetrics for two primary indications. These are:
options: Eclamptic seizure treatment and prophylaxis, and fetal neuroprotection before preterm birth
Tocolysis in all preterm labour cases and antihypertensive treatment
Remove all decidual tissue from the uterine cavity
Avoid uterine perforation during the procedure
Identify organisms causing the polymicrobial infection
Stimulate uterine contractions to aid involution
Collect material for histopathological analysis only
questions.explanation: Therapeutic curettage for delayed uterine atony or retained products is performed with blunt instruments under ultrasound guidance specifically to avoid uterine perforation. The material obtained from uterine curettage should undergo histopathological analysis to exclude trophoblastic neoplasia. Prophylactic antibiotic administration in the absence of signs of infection remains controversial, and uterotonic drugs or prostaglandins may be administered as adjuncts.
questions.question: In management of puerperal endometritis via curettage, blunt instruments are used under ultrasound guidance specifically to:

questions.explanation: The booking visit should ideally occur before 12 weeks of gestation to allow timely first-trimester combined screening (nuchal translucency and biochemistry), early detection and management of pre-existing conditions, initiation of folic acid and other supplementation, baseline blood pressure and urinalysis, and early identification of high-risk pregnancies. Late booking (after 20 weeks) significantly reduces the opportunity for preventive interventions and early identification of complications.
questions.question: The first antenatal visit (booking visit) should ideally take place before which gestational week to allow maximum benefit from early pregnancy care?
Methyldopa is a preferred antihypertensive in pregnancy. Its mechanism of action is:
options: Central alpha-2 agonism reducing sympathetic outflow
questions.explanation: Methyldopa (alpha-methyldopa) acts as a central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, reducing sympathetic nervous system outflow and thereby lowering blood pressure. It has the most extensive long-term safety data in pregnancy with no evidence of fetal harm. It is first-line for non-severe chronic hypertension in pregnancy in many national guidelines. Side effects include sedation, dry mouth, and hepatotoxicity with prolonged use. It is given orally two to four times daily and takes 2-3 days for full effect.

options: omphalitis, a potentially serious cord infection
expected colour change of the stump
questions.explanation: Redness, swelling, purulent discharge, and foul odour around the umbilical stump are signs of omphalitis, a bacterial infection of the cord stump that can rapidly progress to systemic sepsis in the vulnerable newborn. Immediate medical evaluation and treatment, often with antibiotics, are required. Educating caregivers to recognise these warning signs supports early presentation and treatment.
questions.question: A mother notices redness, swelling, and pus discharge around her newborn's cord stump, along with a foul odour. This presentation is a warning sign requiring immediate medical attention because it suggests:
The cavity of the uterus is described as triangular in shape with the base being uppermost. This base corresponds anatomically to:
questions.explanation: The triangular uterine cavity has its base uppermost, corresponding to the fundal wall between the cornual angles where the uterine tubes join. The apex of the triangle points downward towards the internal os. This shape is assessed during hysteroscopy and on hysterosalpingography to detect intrauterine pathology such as polyps, fibroids, or congenital anomalies that distort the normal triangular contour.

questions.question: Which practice during complementary feeding is associated with increased risk of dental caries?
options: Offering soft fruits as complementary foods after 6 months
Providing iron-fortified complementary cereals at mealtimes
Sweetening porridges and weaning foods with added sugars
Offering boiled cooled water between complementary meal times
Including dairy products like yoghurt in complementary foods
questions.explanation: Sweetening complementary foods and porridges with added sugars, honey, or syrups is associated with increased risk of early childhood dental caries (tooth decay) and establishes a preference for sweet foods that persists into later childhood. Added sugars should be completely avoided in foods for infants under 12 months and minimised in toddlers. Natural sweetness from fruits and vegetables is the appropriate and safe source of sweet taste during complementary feeding.

questions.question: Superimposed preeclampsia occurs in a woman with chronic hypertension. It is characterised by which new finding after 20 weeks?
options: Stable blood pressure with new jaundice
Worsening or resistant hypertension and new proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction
Reduction in blood pressure with oedema
questions.explanation: Superimposed preeclampsia is characterised by worsening or resistant hypertension (especially acutely), new onset of proteinuria or sudden increase in proteinuria, and/or development of significant new end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks in a woman with pre-existing chronic hypertension. Women with chronic hypertension typically have no proteinuria, so new proteinuria is a key indicator of superimposed preeclampsia. Serum urate elevation also supports this diagnosis.

options: is the commonest site of cervical dysplasia
questions.question: A colposcopist identifies the junction where squamous epithelium of the ectocervix meets the columnar epithelium of the endocervical canal. This transformation zone is clinically significant because it:
questions.explanation: The squamo-columnar junction is a site of active cellular metaplasia and is the region most vulnerable to human papillomavirus infection and subsequent dysplastic change. Its position shifts with age, parity, and hormonal status. Colposcopic sampling therefore targets this transformation zone during cervical screening.

options: 36.5°C as the lower limit of normal neonatal temperature
35.0°C as the severe hypothermia threshold for neonates
36.0°C as the lower limit of axillary normal temperature
35.5°C as the threshold for mild neonatal hypothermia
37.0°C as the accepted neonatal temperature lower limit
questions.question: IMCI assessment for the young infant (0-2 months) includes measuring temperature. Hypothermia in this age group is defined as axillary temperature below:
questions.explanation: IMCI defines hypothermia in young infants (0-2 months) as an axillary temperature below 36.0°C. Hypothermia in neonates is a sign of serious illness (including possible serious bacterial infection or birth asphyxia sequelae) and is classified as 'Possible Serious Bacterial Infection' in IMCI, requiring urgent referral. Neonates have immature thermoregulation and are highly susceptible to heat loss; skin-to-skin care, warm environment, and breastfeeding are critical preventive measures.

questions.question: A woman using the symptothermal method wants to know when her pre-ovulatory infertile phase ends. The midwife explains that this phase ends as soon as which event first occurs?
questions.explanation: The pre-ovulatory infertile phase ends as soon as the earliest indicator of approaching fertility appears, whether this is the first sign of fertile-type cervical mucus or an early temperature shift. Because ovulation timing varies between cycles, this phase cannot be fixed to a specific calendar day. Careful daily observation is therefore required rather than relying on assumed regularity.
options: the twelfth day of every cycle
a full week after menstruation ends
the first day of the cycle
the first sign of fertile mucus

questions.question: A midwife explains respiratory changes during the puerperium. Full ventilatory capacity is restored relatively quickly after delivery mainly because:
questions.explanation: Once the uterus is delivered, the diaphragm is no longer displaced upward by the enlarged pregnant uterus, allowing full descent and restoration of normal lung volumes and ventilatory capacity. This relatively rapid respiratory recovery contrasts with the slower resolution of some other pregnancy-related changes. Improved ventilation contributes to overall improved maternal comfort in the early puerperium.

questions.question: A woman with chronic hypertension shows worsening blood pressure after 20 weeks. Which laboratory finding would most support a diagnosis of superimposed preeclampsia rather than chronic hypertension alone?
questions.explanation: New-onset significant proteinuria in a woman with pre-existing chronic hypertension strongly suggests superimposed preeclampsia rather than isolated chronic hypertension. Other supportive findings include rising liver enzymes, falling platelets, or worsening renal function. These markers guide the need for closer surveillance and possible early delivery.

questions.question: During the mechanism of normal labour for a vertex presentation, which movement immediately follows internal rotation of the fetal head?
questions.explanation: After internal rotation brings the occiput anteriorly under the symphysis pubis, the head extends as it passes beneath the pubic arch, allowing the face, brow, and vertex to be born in sequence. This extension is a critical step in the mechanism of normal labour for vertex presentations. It is followed by restitution, where the head realigns with the shoulders.

questions.question: The fourth T cause of PPH is Thrombin, referring to blood coagulation defects. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) as a cause of PPH can be precipitated by:
options: Placental abruption and amniotic fluid embolism
Prolonged first stage of labour alone
questions.explanation: DIC (Thrombin component of the 4Ts) can be precipitated in PPH by placental abruption (which releases thromboplastins), amniotic fluid embolism (which introduces fetal material into maternal circulation triggering coagulation cascade), severe preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome, and intrauterine fetal death. DIC causes consumption of clotting factors and platelets, resulting in paradoxical bleeding from multiple sites that does not respond to uterotonics alone.

options: performing a full blood count immediately
asking about the problem and checking danger signs
taking a chest X-ray as a first step
questions.explanation: The IMCI 'Ask, Look, Listen, Feel' approach begins with asking the caregiver about the presenting problem and checking for general danger signs, before proceeding through the systematic assessment of the main symptom areas. This structured sequence ensures no critical warning sign is missed early in the encounter. The approach is designed to be feasible without reliance on laboratory or imaging investigations, appropriate for first-level health facilities.
questions.question: A nurse follows the IMCI 'Ask, Look, Listen, Feel' approach when assessing a sick child. This structured approach means that assessment of every sick child always begins with:

questions.explanation: A child is classified as underweight when their weight-for-age z-score falls below -2 standard deviations from the WHO Child Growth Standards median. Severe acute malnutrition is classified as below -3 standard deviations. Weight-for-age reflects both current nutritional status (wasting) and longer-term nutritional history (stunting), making it a composite measure. Regular growth monitoring with plotting on WHO charts enables early identification of children crossing centile lines downward.
questions.question: The weight-for-age z-score below which a child is classified as underweight is:
options: Below -1 standard deviation from the mean for age
Below -3 standard deviation indicating severe underweight
Below -2 standard deviation from the WHO reference median
Below the 5th centile of the WHO growth reference charts
Below -2.5 standard deviation as an intermediate threshold

questions.explanation: High-dose fluconazole, particularly with prolonged use, has been associated with a pattern of congenital malformations resembling fluconazole embryopathy. Single low-dose use for uncomplicated candidiasis carries a lower theoretical risk, but caution and topical alternatives are generally preferred in pregnancy. This risk profile guides prescribers toward safer topical antifungal agents where possible.
options: congenital malformation with prolonged high-dose use
questions.question: A pregnant woman with recurrent vaginal candidiasis is prescribed high-dose fluconazole. This has been associated with which fetal risk when used at doses of 150 mg or more?
The Mons pubis is defined anatomically as:
questions.explanation: The Mons pubis is the rounded pad of adipose tissue that lies anterior to the symphysis pubis and is covered with pubic hair from the time of puberty. It forms the uppermost part of the external genitalia (vulva) and provides cushioning during sexual intercourse. Its size is influenced by hormonal status and body fat distribution, and it may become more prominent during pregnancy due to oedema and fat deposition.
options: Two folds of fat covering the labia minora
A rounded pad of fat anterior to the symphysis pubis
The frenulum between the labia minora

questions.explanation: Preeclampsia typically presents with the combination of hypertension and proteinuria, so an elevated creatinine occurring without these accompanying features is atypical and should prompt evaluation for alternative diagnoses such as haemolytic uraemic syndrome. This pattern recognition helps direct further specific testing, including complement studies. Early differentiation guides whether delivery alone will resolve the renal impairment.
questions.question: A woman has an elevated serum creatinine without significant hypertension or proteinuria in the third trimester. This finding pattern should raise suspicion for a renal thrombotic microangiopathy rather than typical preeclampsia because:
options: preeclampsia rarely causes isolated renal impairment
preeclampsia always causes isolated renal failure
creatinine is never elevated in preeclampsia
proteinuria always precedes hypertension in preeclampsia
renal impairment excludes any pregnancy complication

questions.explanation: A skin pinch that returns very slowly, taking more than two seconds, is a key IMCI sign indicating severe dehydration, reflecting significant fluid deficit affecting tissue turgor. This finding, combined with other signs such as lethargy or inability to drink, guides classification and the urgency of fluid replacement therapy, typically Plan C. Rapid recognition of severe dehydration signs is critical to prevent progression to hypovolaemic shock.
questions.question: A nurse performs a skin pinch test on a dehydrated child and finds that the skin returns very slowly, taking more than two seconds. This finding within IMCI dehydration assessment indicates:

questions.explanation: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) is the WHO and Nigeria-recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in children. Current Nigerian guidelines recommend Artemether-Lumefantrine (AL) given over 3 days (6 doses) as the first-line ACT. ACT replaced chloroquine and SP due to widespread resistance. Pre-referral treatment for severe malaria includes parenteral artesunate. The 3-day ACT course ensures parasitological cure and prevents recrudescence.
questions.question: The IMCI recommended treatment for uncomplicated malaria in Nigeria is:
options: Chloroquine 25mg/kg over 3 days as per older guidelines
Quinine 10mg/kg three times daily for 7 days orally
Artesunate plus amodiaquine for 5 days total treatment
six weeks exactly with no earlier change
questions.explanation: Cardiac output, which rises during pregnancy, begins to fall after delivery and generally returns close to pre-pregnancy values within about two weeks postpartum, reflecting resolution of the increased blood volume and cardiac workload of pregnancy.
