options: No water is needed as breast milk provides all fluid requirements
250-500ml of boiled, cooled water is required daily for hydration
Small amounts of boiled cooled water can be offered with meals
Commercial mineral water is the safest option for infant hydration
Fruit juices can replace water as a healthier beverage choice
questions.explanation: For infants aged 6-12 months, small amounts of boiled, cooled water can be offered with meals as a complementary drink. Breast milk or formula continues to provide the majority of fluid requirements at this age. Fruit juices are not recommended for infants under 12 months as they provide excess sugar without fibre. Commercial mineral water may have inappropriate mineral content for infants. Water offered should always be boiled and cooled to eliminate pathogens.

questions.question: Colostrum has a laxative action on the newborn because of:
options: Its high content of carbohydrate and soluble fibre
Large fat molecules that facilitate meconium passage
High potassium concentration stimulating bowel motility
Alkaline pH that neutralizes gastric acid in the gut
Low protein levels reducing osmolarity of intestinal fluid
questions.explanation: Colostrum has a laxative action on the newborn because of the large fat molecules it contains, which facilitate the passage of meconium from the newborn's bowel. This laxative effect is beneficial as it helps clear meconium from the gut in the early days of life, reducing the risk of jaundice and intestinal obstruction.

options: Kwashiorkor (severe acute malnutrition) with nutritional oedema
Normal developmental finding in infants under 12 months
Marasmus with severe muscle wasting and fat depletion
Mild malnutrition without significant risk of mortality
Cardiac failure from congenital heart disease in infants
questions.explanation: Bilateral pitting oedema of the feet in a child assessed using IMCI indicates kwashiorkor (a form of severe acute malnutrition characterised by protein deficiency causing hypoalbuminaemia and fluid accumulation in tissues). Kwashiorkor requires urgent referral for therapeutic feeding and management of complications. The oedema starts from the feet and may extend to the legs and face (moon face), and distinguishes kwashiorkor from marasmus, which presents with severe wasting without oedema.
questions.question: IMCI assessment for malnutrition includes checking for oedema of the feet, which when present indicates:

options: Giving ACT empirically because all fevers are malaria in Nigeria
Treating for bacterial infection only with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Assessing for other causes of fever and managing appropriately
Repeating the RDT after 48 hours before giving any treatment
Referring all RDT-negative febrile children to hospital urgently
questions.explanation: A child with fever from a high malaria area who has a negative malaria RDT should not be treated empirically with antimalarials. Instead, the IMCI approach is to assess for other causes of fever - pneumonia (check respiratory rate), ear infection (check ears), skin infection, urinary tract infection, or other bacterial infections - and manage the identified cause appropriately. This RDT-guided approach prevents unnecessary antimalarial use while ensuring the true cause of fever is identified and treated.
questions.question: IMCI management of a child with fever from a high malaria area who has a negative RDT test includes:
An 'adverse event following immunization' (AEFI) that is classified as a programme error includes:
questions.explanation: A programme error AEFI results from errors in vaccine preparation, handling, or administration - including wrong dose, wrong site, wrong vaccine, reconstitution with wrong diluent, failure to sterilise equipment, or subcutaneous injection of BCG instead of intradermal. These AEFIs are preventable through training, supervision, and adherence to protocols. They are distinguished from vaccine reactions (expected physiological responses), coincidental events (unrelated to vaccination), and injection reactions (responses to the act of injection).
options: Fever and local swelling that are known vaccine reactions
Rare idiosyncratic reactions independent of vaccine quality
Injection of vaccine with incorrect dose or wrong site
Anaphylaxis occurring minutes after vaccine administration
BCG adenitis occurring weeks after correct BCG administration

questions.question: A surgeon ligating the ovarian and uterine vessels notes their point of anastomosis. This union occurs within which structure?
questions.explanation: The uterine artery ascends within the broad ligament and anastomoses with the ovarian artery, ensuring collateral blood supply to the uterus and ovary. This anastomosis explains why uterine artery ligation alone rarely causes ovarian ischaemia. Surgeons must identify this relationship to avoid inadvertent vascular injury.

questions.question: The calendar rhythm method of fertility awareness requires a woman to track her cycles for at least how many months to estimate her fertile window?
questions.explanation: The calendar (Ogino-Knaus) rhythm method requires a woman to record her menstrual cycle lengths for at least 6 months to identify her shortest and longest cycles. The fertile window is then calculated using the formula: fertile period starts on (shortest cycle - 18 days) and ends on (longest cycle - 11 days). This method is less reliable for women with irregular cycles and has a higher failure rate compared to modern long-acting reversible contraceptives.

questions.question: The internationally accepted growth reference charts used for monitoring children under 5 years globally are:
questions.explanation: The WHO Child Growth Standards, published in 2006 and derived from the Multicentre Growth Reference Study (MGRS), are the internationally accepted reference charts for monitoring children under 5 years. The MGRS enrolled children from Brazil, Ghana, India, Norway, Oman, and the United States who were raised in optimal conditions (breastfed, non-smoking environment, adequate healthcare). These charts represent how children should grow under optimal conditions rather than descriptive norms.
options: UK 1990 reference charts based on British population data
CDC 2000 growth charts developed from US population surveys
WHO Child Growth Standards developed from MGRS multicentre study
NCHS reference charts from the 1970s United States surveys
Fenton preterm charts adapted for term infant monitoring

questions.explanation: In preeclampsia, complement levels are usually normal or increased, unlike SLE flares where hypocomplementaemia (low C3/C4) is characteristic. This distinction is clinically useful because SLE flares may require immunosuppressive therapy while preeclampsia is managed with blood pressure control and delivery. However, SLE and preeclampsia can coexist, making simultaneous evaluation of complement levels, anti-DNA antibodies, and standard preeclampsia markers necessary.
questions.question: When evaluating a pregnant woman with hypertension and proteinuria who has systemic lupus erythematosus, complement levels help distinguish SLE flare from preeclampsia because in preeclampsia complement levels are usually:
A woman using an ovulation predictor kit to time intercourse for conception is informed that the kit detects a urinary surge of which hormone?
questions.explanation: Ovulation predictor kits detect the urinary surge of luteinising hormone, which occurs shortly before ovulation and signals the optimal time for intercourse to achieve conception. This urinary test offers a convenient, objective way to identify the fertile window compared with subjective symptom tracking alone. It is used both for achieving and, less commonly, for avoiding pregnancy.

Breast engorgement is described as excessive swelling and overfilling of the breast and areola and is a physiological response to an increase in blood flow and an increase in milk production. The areolae become very firm and the nipples may flatten, making it difficult for the infant to latch on. Management includes frequent breastfeeding lasting 15-20 minutes on each breast with gentle massage and warm compresses.
options: Mastitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus infection
Inadequate emptying of milk leading to ductal blockage
Physiological response to increased blood flow and milk production
Retained products causing hormonal stimulation of lactation
Incorrect positioning leading to ineffective milk removal only
questions.question: Breast engorgement is described as excessive swelling of the breast and areola resulting from:

questions.explanation: The post-ovulatory infertile phase is considered to begin reliably once basal body temperature has remained elevated above the cover line for three consecutive days, confirming that ovulation has already occurred. A single elevated reading is insufficient because temperature can fluctuate for other reasons. This three-day rule increases confidence that the fertile window has passed.
questions.question: A midwife counselling on fertility awareness explains that the post-ovulatory infertile phase begins reliably once which sign has persisted for a set number of days?
options: three consecutive days of sustained temperature rise
Safe for use with no special precautions
Acceptable when benefits outweigh risks, though avoided in the very first trimester in some guidelines
A Category X drug in all countries
Freely substitutable with tetracycline in pregnancy
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is generally considered acceptable for use in pregnancy when clinically indicated, as current evidence does not demonstrate teratogenicity. Some historical concerns about mutagenicity (from animal studies) led to avoidance in early pregnancy in certain guidelines, but human data do not support increased birth defect risk. Bacterial vaginosis is associated with preterm labour, making treatment appropriate when diagnosed. High-dose regimens should be avoided and treatment decisions made weighing benefits against theoretical risks.
questions.question: Metronidazole is used for bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis in pregnancy. Its use in the FIRST trimester has historically been debated, though current evidence generally considers it:

options: The surface of the cervix on speculum contact
Pooled blood in the posterior fornix
questions.explanation: Bleeding from the surface of the cervix caused by contact with the speculum (contact bleeding) may indicate cervicitis or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), while bleeding from a cervical tumour or ulcer may indicate infiltrating carcinoma. These local causes are distinguished from placental causes because they originate at the cervical surface rather than from the placental bed. Speculum examination is essential for making this clinical distinction.
questions.question: Local causes of APH, such as cervical infection or tumour, are identified when bleeding comes from which finding?

questions.question:
A patient on antidepressant medication complains of a persistent sensation of dry mouth.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
(i) Xerostomia (dry mouth).
(ii) Predisposing factors include radiation therapy to the head and neck region (which directly damages the integrity of the salivary gland), medication side effects (anticholinergic drugs like atropine; tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline, which have antagonistic effects at muscarinic receptors; and antihypertensive medications like terazosin, clonidine, atenolol and propranolol), infections like mumps, and normal age-related changes.
(iii) Xerostomia is the subjective sensation of dry mouth, i.e. decreased salivation; failure to produce normal amounts of saliva (from these causes) leads to dental caries.

(i) Autonomic neuropathy impairs the autonomic mechanisms (central command and local muscle mechano- and chemoreceptors) that drive sympathetic activity, preventing adequate increases in heart rate and cardiac output during exercise.
(ii) Compensatory mechanisms maintaining stroke volume during exercise despite increased HR:
- Increased venous return via abdominothoracic and muscle pumps.
- Venous constriction.
- Increased atrial inotropy.
- Increased ventricular inotropy.
- Enhanced ventricular lusitropy.
- Concomitant reduction in sympathetic adrenergic and increased sympathetic cholinergic stimulation of cutaneous vessels influenced by thermoregulatory centres in the hypothalamus.
(iii) Four factors influencing cardiovascular response to exercise:
- Type of exercise: dynamic (running, jogging, swimming) vs. isometric/static (weight lifting, press-ups).
- Body posture: effect of gravity on venous return and CVP; supine vs. erect position.
- Physical conditioning: active vs. sedentary lifestyle.
- Environmental conditions: high altitude decreases maximal SV and HR; temperature and humidity.
(iv) Maximal HR = 220 − individual age. For this 45-year-old patient: Maximal HR = 220 − 45 = 175 beats/min.
(v) Pregnancy alters CVS response to exercise because CO is already elevated at rest (30–50% above normal); compression of inferior vena cava reduces venous return; supine hypotensive syndrome may occur. In pregnancy, ABP generally falls due to disproportionate fall in SVR. Maximal CO is about 25% less in females generally.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old male with autonomic neuropathy from type II diabetes complains of weakness and lightheadedness when mowing his lawn. He is unable to perform normal physical activities.
(i) Identify the cardiovascular mechanism impaired by autonomic neuropathy during exercise.
(ii) Describe the compensatory mechanisms that normally maintain stroke volume during exercise despite increased heart rate.
(iii) List four factors that influence the cardiovascular response to exercise.
(iv) State the formula for calculating maximal heart rate and apply it to this patient.
(v) Describe how pregnancy alters the cardiovascular response to exercise.

A 22-year-old poorly controlled type 1 diabetic is brought in unconscious. Arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.10, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 8 mEq/L, glucose 480 mg/dL. Breathing is deep and laboured.
(i) Identify the primary acid-base disturbance and state the factors that decrease body pH that are relevant here.
(ii) Explain the compensatory respiratory mechanism and describe the pattern of breathing observed.
(iii) Describe the role of the kidneys in correcting this acid-base disturbance under the following headings: reabsorption of bicarbonate, phosphate mechanism, and ammonia mechanism.
(iv) State the three main buffers used by the body to defend against the acid load in this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Primary acid-base disturbance: Metabolic acidosis (low pH 7.10, low HCO3- 8 mEq/L). Relevant factors that decrease body pH in this patient: production of aceto-acetic acid and beta-hydroxybutyric acids as may occur in poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. (Other factors that decrease body pH include: production of CO2 from metabolic processes, metabolism of sulphur-containing amino acids, production of lactic acid or pyruvic acid as may occur in exercise.)
(ii) Compensatory respiratory mechanism: When there is excess acid in the body, pH falls. H+ stimulates the respiratory centres in the medulla, increasing the rate and depth of respiration, leading to elimination of excess CO2. The pH therefore rises back toward normal. Pattern of breathing: deep and laboured breathing (Kussmaul breathing) — this is the clinical manifestation. The low PaCO2 (28 mmHg) in this patient confirms active respiratory compensation.
(iii) Renal role in correcting acidosis:
- Reabsorption of bicarbonate: in acidosis, there is 100% reabsorption of HCO3- in the kidneys. The kidneys prevent loss of bicarbonate in the urine by reabsorbing approximately 4320 mEq of bicarbonate filtered daily.
- Phosphate mechanism: secreted hydrogen ion is excreted through the phosphate mechanism. Phosphate becomes greatly concentrated in the tubules, increasing buffering power. H+ secreted combines with HPO4(2-) to form H2PO4- for excretion.
- Ammonia mechanism: H+ is secreted into the renal tubules; production of ammonia is increased several-fold to buffer the hydrogen ion secreted into the tubular lumen. In the PCT and TAL, formation of NH4+ (secreted and eliminated) and new HCO3- (reabsorbed into blood) occurs. In the collecting tubules, H+ secreted by hydrogen pump combines with ammonia to form ammonium ion which is excreted.
(iv) Three main buffers:
a) NaHCO3/H2CO3 buffer — the most important buffer due to its relatively high concentration and the ability to vary PCO2.
b) Na2HPO4/NaH2PO4 buffer — pK value is 6.8; especially important in the tubular fluids of the kidneys and in buffering ICF.
c) Protein buffer system — the most plentiful buffer of the body; proteins contain both acid and base groups that can give up or take up H+.

(i) Cardiac output = SV × HR = 50 ml/beat × 95 beats/min = 4,750 ml/min.
(ii) Three variables regulate stroke volume:
- End diastolic volume (EDV): volume of blood in the ventricles at end of diastole (preload); stroke volume increases with increased EDV.
- Total peripheral resistance: frictional resistance in the arteries; inversely related to stroke volume (afterload).
- Contractility: strength of ventricular contraction; stroke volume increases with contractility.
(iii) Ejection fraction (EF) is the percentage of the EDV ejected per cardiac cycle. EF% = (SV/EDV) × 100. Normal ejection fraction is about 50–65%.
(iv) Pathological conditions causing decreased cardiac output: hypothyroidism, hypovolaemia, haemorrhage, myocardial infarction.
(v) Intrinsic control is based on the Frank-Starling mechanism/law. The initial length of muscle fibre is decided by the condition of the muscle before contraction, affected by end-diastolic volume. Factors affecting end-diastolic volume include the respiratory pump, cardiac pump, muscle pump, blood volume, sympathetic discharge, standing body position, and resistance to venous return.
questions.question:
A 38-year-old male presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea. On examination his heart rate is 95 beats/minute, and his stroke volume is estimated at 50 ml/beat. His cardiac output is calculated, and his ejection fraction is noted to be reduced.
(i) Calculate his cardiac output from the given values.
(ii) State the three variables that regulate stroke volume, and explain how each relates to stroke volume.
(iii) Define ejection fraction and state its normal range.
(iv) List four pathological conditions that can cause a decrease in cardiac output.
(v) Describe the Frank-Starling intrinsic control mechanism of cardiac output.

questions.answerText:
(i) Hypopituitarism presenting as dwarfism, due to deficiency of growth hormone during childhood.
(ii) Growth hormone deficiency during childhood gives proportionate dwarfism (short stature); features of the body are proportionate to each other, but the rate of development is decreased, so a patient at age 20 may have the body development of a 10-year-old.
- There is no thyroid deficiency.
- There is no adrenocortical deficiency.
- There is no mental retardation (a wise person of small stature).
(iii) Synthetic growth hormone.
questions.question:
A child is observed to have short stature in which all body features are proportionate to one another, but the rate of development is delayed; at 20 years of age the body development is that of a 10-year-old child. Thyroid function and adrenocortical function are normal, and there is no mental retardation.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of the condition.
(iii) State the definitive treatment.

questions.answerText:
C(i) Classification of cell membrane receptors:
- Ion channel-linked (ionotropic) receptors: coupled directly to ligand-gated ion channels (e.g. nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, ionotropic glutamate receptors, GABA-A receptors).
- Catalytic receptors: possess a cytoplasmic catalytic region (usually tyrosine kinase).
- G-protein-linked receptors: coupled to GTP-activated proteins.
C(ii) Types of intercellular junctions:
- Adherent junctions: hold epithelial and cardiac muscle cells together; connect cytoskeletal elements.
- Tight (occluding) junctions: segregate apical and basolateral domains; prevent pericellular diffusion of water and ions (barrier function).
- Gap (communicating) junctions: allow intercellular diffusion of ions and signalling molecules; composed of hexagonal arrays of connexins (central pore ≈1.5 nm); permit electrical coupling.
D. Membrane fluidity is determined by the degree of unsaturation of constituent fatty acids. Lipids and proteins can undergo rotational and lateral movement. Membranes are structurally and functionally asymmetrical due to asymmetrical orientation of integral and peripheral membrane proteins laterally and transversely. Membranes are also electrically polarised (inside negative relative to exterior). Asymmetry is important for directed cell movement, signal transduction, and transport selectivity.
questions.question:
Describe the structure of the cell membrane under listed headings; explain the clinical basis for membrane transport disorders; and distinguish between integral and peripheral membrane proteins.
A. Describe the composition and structure of the cell membrane including the fluid mosaic model.
B. Classify membrane transport mechanisms and describe each type.
C(i) . Classify cell membrane receptors with examples.
C(ii) . Describe the types of intercellular junctions and their functions.
D. Explain how membrane fluidity is determined and why asymmetry is important.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas.
(ii) State how the endocrine (islet) cell types of the pancreas relate to common pathologies.
(iii) Explain how disease of the pancreatic islets acts on distant structures/tissues to cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pancreas is a triangular gland with both exocrine (acinar) and endocrine (islet) cells; it lies retroperitoneally, posterior to the stomach, and has a head, body, and tail.
- Acinar cells produce an enzyme-rich juice used for digestion (exocrine product); pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) produce hormones that regulate fuel storage and use.
- Islets are ovoid collections of cells; humans have 1-2 million islets, forming 1-2% of the pancreatic mass, more toward the tail of the pancreas.
(ii) Based on staining, cells are grouped into: A/Alpha cells (produce glucagon), B/Beta cells (produce insulin), D/Delta cells (produce somatostatin), and F cells (produce pancreatic polypeptide).
- Destruction of beta cells with loss of insulin production causes Type 1 diabetes mellitus; insulin resistance that keeps blood glucose too high underlies Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
(iii) In insulin deficiency, the liver, muscle, and adipose tissue show organ/tissue responses of increased glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; insulin normally increases glucose uptake, glucose use, glycogenesis, and fatty acid/protein synthesis in these same tissues, so its deficiency produces distant functional deficits: reduced glucose uptake in most cells, reduced protein and fat synthesis, and the cardinal features of diabetes mellitus (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia), with chronic complications of atherosclerosis, renal failure and blindness.

questions.question:
A patient presents with hypertension and edema, together with muscle weakness and non-responsiveness of neurons (paralysis) attributed to excessive potassium loss.
(i) State the risk factor/cause.
(ii) State the complications.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hypersecretion of aldosterone (aldosteronism).
(ii) Hypertension and edema; excessive loss of potassium can cause muscle weakness and non-responsiveness of neurons (paralysis).

questions.question:
A young patient presents in a chronic fasted state with marked weight loss ('melting flesh'), ketosis, acidosis, glucose in the urine, and increased urine output, progressing toward coma.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of the condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diabetes Mellitus Type I.
(ii) Beta cells are destroyed so that no insulin is produced, resulting in a chronic fasted state with 'melting flesh', ketosis, acidosis, glucosurea (glucose in urine), diuresis, and coma.
- The three cardinal signs of diabetes mellitus are polyuria (huge urine output), polydipsia (excessive thirst), and polyphagia (excessive hunger and food consumption); diabetes mellitus is a serious disorder of carbohydrate metabolism resulting from hyposecretion or hypoactivity of insulin.

questions.question:
A patient presents with excessive urine output and, on evaluation, is found to have either a partial/complete absence of vasopressin secretion from the hypothalamus, or resistance of the nephrons to vasopressin. There is a risk of dehydration and hypernatremia if water intake is inadequate.
(i) State the diagnosis (both forms).
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of each form.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diabetes insipidus - central (cranial) diabetes insipidus and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
(ii) Central diabetes insipidus: partial or complete absence of vasopressin secretion by the hypothalamus, leading to excessive free water clearance.
- Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: resistance of vasopressin at the level of the nephrons.
- Both result in dehydration and hypernatremia if there is inadequate water intake to compensate for the loss of water.

(i) A typical neuron is divided into three parts: the soma or cell body, dendrites, and the axon; the soma is usually compact, while the axon and dendrites are filaments that extrude from it, and the axon is usually surrounded by an insulating protecting layer, the myelin sheath.
(ii) The axon carries nerve signals away from the soma (and also carries some types of information back to it); many neurons have only one axon, and axons undergo extensive branching to communicate with many target cells.
The part of the axon where it emerges from the soma is called the axon hillock; it has the greatest density of voltage-dependent sodium channels and the most negative action potential threshold, and the axon terminal contains synapses.
(iii) Based on direction: afferent neurons convey information from tissues and organs into the CNS (sensory neurons); efferent neurons transmit signals from the CNS to effector cells (motor neurons); interneurons connect neurons within the CNS.
Clinical basis: demyelination, e.g. in Guillain-Barré syndrome, is listed as a clinical relevance of the neuron, and it leads to certain neurodegenerative disorders like multiple sclerosis and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
Because the myelin sheath is the insulating layer around the axon that normally supports nerve signal conduction away from the soma, its loss (demyelination) is consistent with the impaired conduction underlying these demyelinating disorders.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy), a heterogeneous inherited disorder of nerves, is characterized by loss of muscle tissue and touch sensation, consistent with dysfunction of the neurons/nerves affected.
Distinguishing feature 1: afferent neurons convey information from tissues and organs into the CNS, i.e. they are sensory neurons.
Distinguishing feature 2: efferent neurons transmit signals from the CNS to the effector cells, i.e. they are motor neurons.
Both are distinguished from interneurons, which connect neurons within the CNS rather than carrying signals into or out of it.
This functional classification by direction is one of several ways neurons are classified, alongside classification by polarity (unipolar, bipolar, multipolar) and by discharge pattern (tonic, phasic, fast spiking).

A. Describe the factors that control interstitial fluid volume under the following headings:
A(i) Capillary pressure
A(ii) Interstitial fluid pressure
A(iii) Oncotic pressure
A(iv) Capillary filtration coefficient and number of active capillaries
A(v) Lymph flow
B. State all the mechanisms by which interstitial fluid is increased, leading to oedema, classifying them into at least four categories.
C. Explain the anatomical and physiological basis of lymphoedema (elephantiasis) and distinguish it from cardiac oedema with respect to its underlying mechanism.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Capillary pressure: Increased capillary pressure raises filtration at the arterial end and reduces reabsorption, increasing interstitial fluid. Causes: arteriolar dilation, venular constriction, increased venous pressure (heart failure, incompetent valves, venous obstruction, increased total ECF, effect of gravity).
A(ii) Interstitial fluid pressure: Changes in interstitial fluid pressure alter the balance between filtration and reabsorption; abnormal retention contributes to oedema formation.
A(iii) Oncotic pressure: Decreased plasma protein level reduces osmotic reabsorption at the venous end, and accumulation of osmotically active substances in the interstitial space draws fluid into the interstitium.
A(iv) Capillary filtration coefficient and number of active capillaries: Increased capillary permeability (from Substance P, histamine, kinins) allows more fluid to leak out. More active capillaries increase the surface area for filtration.
A(v) Lymph flow: Inadequate lymph flow allows interstitial fluid to accumulate.
B. Mechanisms of oedema:
1. Increased filtration pressure (arteriolar dilation, venular constriction, increased venous pressure).
2. Decreased osmotic pressure gradient across capillary (decreased plasma protein, accumulation of osmotically active substances in interstitial space).
3. Increased capillary permeability (Substance P, histamine, related substances, kinins).
4. Inadequate lymph flow.
5. Increased capillary pressure from excessive kidney retention of salt and water (mineralocorticoid excess, acute/chronic salt and water retention).
6. Increased capillary pressure due to decreased arteriolar resistance (excessive body heat, insufficiency of sympathetic vasodilators).
C. Lymphoedema (elephantiasis): Results from inadequate lymphatic flow or obstruction. Without drainage, interstitial fluid accumulates. It can cause compression of local blood vessels and subsequent tissue damage. Cardiac oedema differs: its mechanism is increased venous pressure (from heart failure, incompetent valves) which raises capillary hydrostatic pressure. In lymphoedema the hydrostatic pressure is normal but lymphatic return is obstructed.

(i) Diagnosis: Polycythaemia — an abnormal excess of erythrocytes that increases the viscosity of the blood.
Common causes:
- Bone marrow cancer.
- A response to reduced availability of oxygen at high altitudes.
(ii) Pathophysiological mechanism: A drop in renal blood oxygen level stimulates renal cells to produce erythropoietin, a glycoprotein hormone. Erythropoietin stimulates erythrocyte production in the red bone marrow. Increased RBC production raises haematocrit and RBC mass. This is the same mechanism as the physiological high-altitude response but is exaggerated or pathological in polycythaemia vera (bone marrow cancer).
(iii) Direct consequence on blood rheology: Polycythaemia increases viscosity of the blood, causing it to sludge or flow sluggishly. The normal relative viscosity of whole blood to water is 4.5-5.5; excess RBCs raise this further.
(iv) Difference from athlete training: Legal method — raise RBC count by training athletes at high altitude (stimulates erythropoietin via reduced oxygen tension). Illegal method — use erythropoietin, androgen, or their analogs directly. The physiological mechanism (reduced O2 → erythropoietin → increased RBC production) is the same, but direct hormone/drug administration bypasses the natural stimulus.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: A countercurrent system is a system in which the inflow runs parallel to, counter to, and in close proximity to the outflow over some distance. In the kidney, the structures forming the countercurrent system are the loop of Henle and the vasa recta.
A(ii) Countercurrent multiplier: The loop of Henle of juxtamedullary nephrons is the countercurrent multiplier. The high permeability of the thin descending limb to water (via aquaporin-1) allows water to leave as osmolarity increases going deeper. Active transport of Na+ and Cl- out of the thick ascending limb (which is impermeable to water) concentrates the medullary interstitium. The major cause of hyperosmolarity of medullary interstitial fluid is active reabsorption of sodium and chloride from the ascending limb.
A(iii) Countercurrent exchanger: The vasa recta is the countercurrent exchanger. Being fenestrated, as blood flows from the corticomedullary junction into deeper layers of medulla, it passes through areas of increasing osmolarity; the vasa recta gains solutes and loses water, becoming progressively concentrated. At the level of the papilla, osmolarity of blood in the vasa recta is 1200 mOsm/L. As blood flows back, it passes through areas of decreasing osmolarity, gaining water from the medulla and losing most solutes gained on entry. By giving up most solutes on exit, the countercurrent exchanger maintains the medullary gradient set up by the CC multiplier and prevents supersaturation in the interstitium.
A(iv) Role of urea: Urea is filtered in the glomeruli. The PCT and inner medullary collecting duct (MCD) are permeable to urea (via urea transporters). Urea is partly passively reabsorbed in the PCT; its concentration increases as water moves out of the tubules. At the inner MCD, urea diffuses into the interstitium where it contributes to hyperosmolarity there. The inner medullary region has higher osmolarity than the outer medullary region because it is the site of urea recycling.
B. Three types of diuresis:
caused by lack of secretion of ADH due to intake of large volume of hypotonic fluid. Osmolarity of urine <250 mOsm/L. Alcohol also suppresses release of ADH. Complication: water intoxication.
due to presence of unreabsorbed osmotically active compounds in the tubular lumen. Urine osmolarity is 300-400 mOsm/L. Results in dehydration, polydipsia, and polyuria — seen in diabetes mellitus.
increased urinary excretion of water when arterial pressure increases; a compensatory mechanism to maintain blood pressure. Increase in blood flow in the medulla due to lack of renal autoregulation in the medulla leads to dissipation of medullary hyperosmolarity and increased urine production.
C. Role of ADH: Stimulus for release: increase in plasma osmolarity. Cellular mechanism: ADH causes aquaporin 2 to insert at the late distal convoluted tubules and collecting tubules, making them permeable to water. Facultative reabsorption of water occurs in addition to obligatory reabsorption, reducing urine volume. In the absence of ADH: urine concentration cannot occur; the DCT and collecting duct remain impermeable to water; a large volume of dilute urine is excreted (water diuresis).

C(ii) . List four factors that alter pulmonary circulation and state the direction of change.
D. Explain the concept of V/Q ratio and the effect of its increase and decrease on alveolar gas tensions.
questions.answerText:
C(i) Pulmonary circulation characteristics:
- Output = systemic circulation = 5 L/min.
- Low pressure: 25/10 mmHg (vessels distensible).
- Low pressure prevents fluid exudation into alveoli (capillary pressure 10 mmHg < plasma osmotic pressure 25 mmHg).
- Reservoir: contains about 1 L of blood at any time.
C(ii) Four factors altering pulmonary circulation:
- Increase in alveolar pressure → decreases flow.
- Rise in pulmonary arterial pressure → increases flow.
- Hypoxia → pulmonary vasoconstriction (unique — opposite to systemic).
- Hypercapnia and acidosis → increased pulmonary resistance, reduced flow.
D. V/Q ratio: average V ≈ 4 L/min; CO ≈ 5 L/min; overall V/Q = 0.8.
- Increased V/Q: PAO₂ rises, PACO₂ falls (wasted/dead space ventilation — upper lung segments, zone I).
- Decreased V/Q: PAO₂ falls, PACO₂ rises (shunted blood — lower lung segments, zone III).

questions.question:
A. Describe the body fluid compartments under the following headings:
A(i) Total body water — volume and percentage of body weight in a lean adult male
A(ii) Extracellular fluid — its two main subdivisions, volumes, and approximate percentage of body weight each occupies
A(iii) Intracellular fluid — volume and percentage of body weight
A(iv) Transcellular fluid — definition, examples, and total volume
B. Explain how the volume of each compartment is measured, stating the indicator used for each.
B(i) Total body water
B(ii) Extracellular fluid
B(iii) Plasma volume
B(iv) Intracellular fluid and interstitial fluid (state how each is derived)
C. Distinguish between plasma and interstitial fluid with respect to their electrolyte and protein content.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Total body water (TBW): 60% of body weight in a lean adult male, approximately 42 L.
A(ii) Extracellular fluid: 20% of body weight, approximately 14 L.
- Interstitial fluid: three-quarters of ECF, approximately 11 L (25% of TBW; 15% of body weight).
- Plasma: one-quarter of ECF, approximately 3 L (7-8% of TBW; 4% of body weight).
- Transcellular fluid: 1-2 L, usually included as a specialised type of ECF.
A(iii) Intracellular fluid: 40% of body weight, approximately 28 L (two-thirds of TBW).
A(iv) Transcellular fluid: a specialised type of ECF in synovial, peritoneal, pericardial, intraocular spaces, and cerebrospinal fluid; total approximately 1-2 L.
B(i) TBW: measured with radioactive water (tritiated water, 3H2O), heavy water (deuterated water, 2H2O), or antipyrine.
B(ii) ECF: measured using radioisotopes of Na+, Cl-, SO4(2+), Br-, or non-metabolisable saccharides such as inulin, manitose, raffinose.
B(iii) Plasma volume: measured using indicators that do not penetrate the capillary membrane, such as Evans blue (T-1824) or iodinated albumin (131I-albumin).
B(iv) ICF = TBW minus ECF (calculated mathematically). Interstitial fluid = ECF minus plasma (calculated mathematically).
C. Plasma vs interstitial fluid:
- Protein content: plasma contains 16 mEq/L of protein; interstitial fluid contains only 2 mEq/L. This difference generates the oncotic (colloidal osmotic) pressure of approximately 25 mmHg.
- Na+: plasma 152 mEq/L; interstitial fluid 143 mEq/L.
- K+: plasma 5 mEq/L; interstitial fluid 4 mEq/L.
- All other electrolyte concentrations are similar between the two compartments.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea. The mother reports reduced urine output and the child appears lethargic. Examination reveals sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and poor skin turgor.
(i) State the diagnosis and identify the type of fluid and electrolyte disturbance occurring.
(ii) List the risk factors and precipitating causes relevant to this presentation as stated for diarrhoea.
(iii) Describe the immediate complications arising from the electrolyte imbalance.
(iv) Justify the most appropriate management option to correct the fluid disturbance.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute diarrhoea with dehydration and hypovolaemia. The disturbance involves loss of large amounts of Na+, K+, and water from the colon in diarrhoeal stools. The resulting electrolyte imbalance causes osmotic flow of water into the stool, producing dehydration, hypovolaemia, and shock.
(ii) Precipitating causes:
- Enteric infection: infection caused by bacteria or virus in the intestinal tract.
- Psychogenic: nervous tension.
- Ulcerative colitis.
(iii) Immediate complications:
- Dehydration due to osmotic loss of water into the stool.
- Hypovolaemia from reduced plasma volume.
- Shock from cardiovascular compromise.
- Cardiovascular collapse if fluid replacement is not initiated.
(iv) Immediate management: Rehydration — oral or intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement to reverse dehydration, hypovolaemia, and shock. Restoring Na+, K+, and water corrects the osmotic imbalance that drives water into the stool and re-establishes normal plasma volume.

(i) Most likely diagnosis: hypoglycaemia secondary to insulin excess. Cell type involved: B/Beta (β) cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, which produce insulin. Note: no insulin is produced when plasma glucose is below 50 mg/dl; threshold of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion is 100 mg/dl.
(ii) Structure and synthesis of insulin:
- Polypeptide of two amino acid chains linked by disulfide bonds.
- Synthesised as proinsulin (86 AA), then excised releasing functional insulin (51 AA) and C peptide (29 AA).
- Half-life 5 minutes; destroyed by proteases in endosomes.
- Chain A (21 AA) and chain B (30 AA) with 3 disulfide bonds; MW 6000.
(iii) Mechanism of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion:
- Glucose enters the beta cell via GLUT2 transporter; glycolysis and citric acid cycle produce ATP.
- Increased ATP closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels → less K⁺ leaves cell → cell depolarises.
- Depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → Ca²⁺ entry.
- Ca²⁺ entry triggers exocytosis of insulin storage granules → insulin secretion.
(iv) Stimulators of insulin secretion: raised serum amino acids, raised serum free fatty acids, gastroinhibitory peptide (GIP), glucagon, parasympathetic nervous system stimulation.
Inhibitors: somatostatin, epinephrine (α-receptor), sympathetic nervous system stimulation.
(v) Actions of insulin:
Liver: ↑ glucose uptake, ↑ glycogenesis, ↓ glycogenolysis, ↑ glycolysis, ↓ gluconeogenesis, ↑ fatty acid synthesis and VLDL formation, ↓ ketogenesis.
Muscle: ↑ glucose uptake (GLUT-4), ↑ glycogenesis, ↓ glycogenolysis, ↑ glycolysis, ↑ amino acid uptake, ↑ protein synthesis, ↓ proteolysis.
Adipose tissue: ↑ glucose uptake (GLUT-4), ↑ glycolysis, ↑ α-glycerol phosphate production, ↑ esterification of fats, ↓ lipolysis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Mechanoreceptors (detect mechanical compression/stretching): free nerve endings, Merkel's discs, Meissner's corpuscles, muscle spindles, Golgi tendon receptors, vestibular receptors, baroreceptors.
- Thermoreceptors (temperature change), nociceptors (pain, injury), electromagnetic receptors (light on the retina, e.g. rods and cones), osmoreceptors (solute concentration in ECF), and chemoreceptors (taste, smell, arterial O2, blood CO2, glucose - taste buds, olfactory epithelium, aortic and carotid bodies, hypothalamic receptors).
- Differential sensitivity: each receptor type is highly sensitive to one designated stimulus and almost non-responsive to others.
- Receptor potentials can be elicited by mechanical deformation, chemical change, temperature change, or electromagnetic radiation; maximum receptor potential amplitude is about 100 millivolts in most receptors.
- Adaptation varies by type: non-adapting receptors (chemoreceptors, pain receptors), slowly adapting receptors (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon apparatus), and rapidly adapting receptors (Pacinian corpuscle).
(ii) Lesions involving peripheral nerves produce symptoms that differ depending on whether the damaged nerve carries sensory fibres and which fibres are involved, e.g. paresthesia, anesthesia, allodynia, hyperalgesia; dorsal root and spinal nerve lesions are usually revealed in a segmental distribution.

questions.answerText:

(ii) Mass effect from a pituitary lesion causes headaches and peripheral vision changes.
(iii) Physiological causes: nursing/suckling, pregnancy.
- Pharmacological causes: phenothiazines, haloperidol, metoclopramide, and other listed agents.

(iv) The listed symptoms of hyperprolactinemia include, from mass effect: headaches and peripheral vision changes; in males: decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and gynaecomastia; in females: menstrual irregularities, secondary amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and infertility - reflecting both the local mass effect of the pituitary lesion and the systemic hormonal effect of excess prolactin.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the parasympathetic nerve supply to the salivary glands.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity/change following injury to this nerve supply.
questions.answerText:
(i) Origin: salivary flow is dependent on parasympathetic nerves, specifically the glossopharyngeal and facial nerves.
Course: these parasympathetic nerves supply the glands as a discrete pathway; severing them produces a specific effect, described below.
Distribution: when stimulated, the parasympathetic supply increases blood flow, which increases ultrafiltrate secretion into the acini; the salivatory nucleus in the brainstem also transduces a sensory (CNS) effect, for example when visual or olfactory input stimulates salivation.
(ii) If the parasympathetic nerves are severed, salivation decreases significantly and the glands atrophy, since this follows directly from loss of the parasympathetic drive that normally increases blood flow and acinar ultrafiltrate secretion; without this drive the secretory tissue is not maintained.
By contrast, the sympathetic nerves innervate the blood vessels around the glands and the myoepithelial cells in the acini; sympathetic stimulation (e.g. during stress) reduces blood flow but contracts the myoepithelial cells, releasing preformed mucous saliva, after which flow decreases, resulting in dry mouth. This distinguishes the consequence of losing parasympathetic supply (gland atrophy from loss of trophic blood flow and secretion) from the effect of sympathetic activity (transient reduction of flow and dry mouth without atrophy).

(i) Tumour of the salivary gland (most likely of the parotid gland).
(ii) Salivary gland tumours usually occur in the major salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, and sublingual); approximately 80% of salivary gland tumours are benign, and most originate in the parotid gland, which is the largest gland, located in the infratemporal region, anterior to the ears.

questions.answerText:
(i) The thyroid gland is the largest, butterfly-shaped endocrine gland, located at the base of the neck immediately below the larynx, on each side of and anterior to the trachea; it consists of two lobes joined in the middle by the isthmus. It has one of the highest rates of blood flow per gram of tissue, and in a normal adult male weighs 15-20 g.
- The functional unit is the follicle (acinus), composed of cuboidal follicular epithelial cells arranged around vesicles filled with a glycoprotein colloid (thyroglobulin); there are about 3 million follicles in an adult human thyroid gland.
(ii) Follicular cells secrete thyroid hormone (T3, T4); C cells secrete calcitonin, an important hormone of calcium metabolism.
- Chronic rise of TSH causes thyroid hypertrophy or goitre (increase in size and number of follicles); clinical correlates listed include hypothyroidism (myxedema in adults), cretinism in children, thyroid hormone resistance, and iodine deficiency.
(iii) The widespread effects of thyroid hormones in the body are secondary to stimulation of oxygen consumption (calorigenic action); other effects on distant tissues include: chronotropic and inotropic effects on the heart (increased beta-adrenergic receptor number, increased response to catecholamines); catabolic effects on adipose tissue (stimulates lipolysis, lowers circulating cholesterol) and muscle (increased protein breakdown); developmental/anabolic effects on bone (growth, skeletal maturation) and the nervous system (normal brain development); metabolic effects on the gut (increased carbohydrate absorption) and on lipoproteins (stimulates LDL receptor formation).

questions.answerText:
A(i) A buffer system is a solution that will accept hydrogen or hydroxyl ions without an appreciable change in its pH. It consists of a weak base and its salt, or a weak acid and its salt. The general equation: H+ + Buffer- = H-Buffer.
A(ii) NaHCO3/H2CO3 buffer: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK + log [Base]/[Acid]. The pK of the system is 6.1 (1.3 units less than the pH of ECF). However, the system buffers well because PCO2 can be regulated by changes in alveolar ventilation, providing an 11-fold increase in efficiency. This is the most important buffer due to its relatively high concentration and ability to vary PCO2. HCl + NaHCO3 → NaCl + H2CO3 → NaCl + H2O + CO2. NaOH + H2CO3 → NaHCO3 + H2O.
A(iii) Na2HPO4/NaH2PO4 buffer: pK value is 6.8 (closer to pH 7.4 than the pK of 6.1 of the HCO3 buffer), allowing the system to operate near its maximum buffering power. However, its concentration in the extracellular fluid is low — only about 8% of the concentration of the bicarbonate buffer — so total buffering power in ECF is much less than bicarbonate. Most important in: (1) tubular fluids of the kidneys — phosphate becomes greatly concentrated in tubules, increasing buffering power, and tubular fluid has lower pH, bringing the operating range closer to pK 6.8; (2) intracellular fluid — because of its high concentration in ICF and because ICF pH is lower than ECF pH.
A(iv) Protein buffer: The most plentiful buffer of the body. Proteins are excellent buffers because they contain both acid and base groups that can give up or take up H+. Proteins and their component amino acids have acidic COOH group and basic NH2 group. The COOH group acts as H+ donor and ionises as COO- in basic environments. The NH2 group accepts H+ to become NH3+ in acidic environments.
B. Three lines of defence:
1. Buffer systems (immediate, seconds): chemical buffers in ECF and ICF instantaneously bind or release H+ to minimise pH change.
2. Lungs (minutes): the second line of defence. When pH falls, H+ stimulates respiratory centres in the medulla, increasing rate and depth of respiration, eliminating excess CO2 and raising pH. CO2 produced in the body of an adult man in a day is equivalent to about 15 litres of normal HCl.
3. Kidneys (hours to days): the third line of defence. Kidneys control acid-base balance by excreting either acidic or alkaline urine through reabsorption of bicarbonate, excretion of non-volatile acids, and secretion of hydrogen ion via phosphate and ammonia mechanisms.
C. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pK + log [Base]/[Acid]. To maintain a constant body pH, the ratio of base to acid must be kept constant. Body pH is 7.4 ± 0.04. Two factors that decrease body pH (cause acidosis): production of aceto-acetic acid and beta-hydroxybutyric acids as may occur in poorly controlled diabetes mellitus; production of lactic acid or pyruvic acid as may occur in exercise.

A semen analysis in a man shows a sperm count under 20 million/mL.
(i) Name this finding, the terms for absent sperm and absent semen, and the normal values.
(ii) Identify the structures that contribute to semen and the function of the seminal vesicle and prostate secretions.
(iii) List the factors that impair spermatogenesis.
(iv) Explain the hormonal regulation and Sertoli cell functions that support sperm production and maturation.
questions.answerText:
(i) A count under 20 million/mL is oligozoospermia; azoospermia is lack of sperm; aspermia is lack of semen.
(i) Normal: ejaculate volume 2.5-3.5 mL after several days of abstinence; concentration about 100 million sperms/mL.
(ii) Semen contains sperms and secretions of the seminal vesicles, prostate, Cowper's glands and urethral glands (mixed with bulbourethral mucus in the internal urethra).
(ii) Seminal vesicles: fructose nourishes spermatozoa; fibrinogen converts to fibrin so semen forms a coagulum after ejaculation.
(ii) Prostate: alkaline secretion neutralizes the low vaginal pH to enhance sperm motility; clotting enzyme converts fibrinogen to fibrin; fibrinolysin dissolves the coagulum so sperm become motile.
(iii) Increased temperature (cryptorchidism) and infectious diseases such as mumps.
(iv) FSH acts on Sertoli cells; LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone; FSH, LH and testosterone are essential to initiate spermatogenesis; growth hormone and inhibin are also regulators.
(iv) Sertoli cells support, protect and nourish germ cells and secrete androgen-binding protein, oestrogen and inhibin.
(iv) Spermatid maturation depends on FSH and androgen acting on Sertoli cells; sperm gain motility only after time in the epididymis and stay immotile until ejaculation.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney under the headings below, explain how its zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why disease may spread to cause functional deficits.
A. Macroscopic structure (location, shape, dimensions, hilus, renal sinus, calices)
B. Microscopic structure (nephron types, proportions, components)
C. Blood supply (arterial pathway from aorta to capillaries)
A(i) Explain the basis of cortical versus juxtaglomerular nephron differences
A(ii) State how a reduction in GFR could lead to uraemia
questions.answerText:
A(i) Cortical nephrons have shorter loops of Henle; juxtaglomerular nephrons have longer loops important for the countercurrent multiplier system concentrating urine.
A(ii) Reduced GFR means less filtration of waste products such as urea, creatinine, and uric acid. Since these are poorly reabsorbed, their accumulation in the blood causes uraemia.

questions.question:
A. Describe the process of blood clotting (coagulation) under the following headings:
A(i) Intrinsic pathway — initiating event and the sequence of factor activation up to Factor X
A(ii) Extrinsic pathway — initiating event and the sequence of factor activation up to Factor X
A(iii) Common pathway — events from Factor X activation to fibrin clot formation
B. Explain fibrinolysis and antithrombotic mechanisms under the following headings:
B(i) Role of antithrombin III
B(ii) Role of thrombomodulin and protein C
B(iii) Role of plasmin (fibrinolysin)
C. Explain the clinical basis for why Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease impairs coagulation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Intrinsic pathway: Initiated by conversion of inactive Factor XII to active Factor XII (XIIa), catalysed by HMW kininogen and kallikrein. Active Factor XII activates Factor XI; active Factor XI activates Factor IX. Active Factor IX forms a complex with active Factor VIII (activated when separated from vWF). The complex of IXa and VIIIa activates Factor X. Phospholipids from aggregated platelets and Ca2+ are necessary for full activation of Factor X.
A(ii) Extrinsic pathway: Triggered by release of tissue thromboplastin that activates Factor VII. Tissue thromboplastin and Factor VII activate Factors IX and X. In the presence of phospholipid, Ca2+, and Factor V, activated Factor X catalyses conversion of prothrombin to thrombin. Clot can form in 10 to 15 seconds.
A(iii) Common pathway: Starts from activation of Factor X. In the presence of phospholipid (PL), Ca2+, and Factor V, activated Factor X catalyses conversion of prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin catalyses conversion of fibrinogen (Factor I) to fibrin monomers. Polymerisation of fibrin monomers results in cross-linked fibrin strands. The resulting clot traps erythrocytes and other blood cells, bridges the opening in the vessel wall, and secures platelets in position. Clot retraction pulls damaged edges of the vessel together, squeezing out clear serum.
B(i) Antithrombin III: A protease inhibitor that binds to serine proteases in the coagulation system, blocking their activity as clotting factors. This binding is facilitated by heparin, a naturally occurring anticoagulant. Factors inhibited include the active forms of Factors IX, X, XI, and XII.
B(ii) Thrombomodulin and protein C: All endothelial cells except those in the cerebral microcirculation produce thrombomodulin on their surfaces. When thrombin binds to thrombomodulin, it becomes an anticoagulant. Thrombomodulin-thrombin complex activates protein C. Activated protein C (APC), along with cofactor protein S, inactivates Factors V and VIII. APC also inactivates an inhibitor of tissue plasminogen activator, increasing plasmin formation.
B(iii) Plasmin (fibrinolysin): Tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) causes activation of plasminogen. Plasminogen becomes plasmin. Plasmin degrades proteins within the clot. Plasmin lyses fibrin and fibrinogen with production of fibrinogen degradation products (FDP) that inhibit thrombin.
C. Clinical basis: Many clotting factors are produced in the liver and are Vitamin K dependent. Vitamin K deficiency (e.g., from broad-spectrum antibiotics killing colonic bacteria, drugs blocking Vitamin K use, or fat absorption problems) or liver disease impairs synthesis of these factors, preventing formation of a proper coagulation cascade and leading to bleeding disorders.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency unit having sustained third-degree burns covering over 75% of his total body surface area in a house fire. On arrival he is confused, hypotensive, and tachycardic.
(i) State the diagnosis and identify the immediate life-threatening physiological consequence of this injury.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological basis of his circulatory compromise, citing the specific compartment most affected and the mechanism of fluid loss.
(iii) Outline the principles of immediate fluid resuscitation required to stabilise this patient.
(iv) State the definitive management goal for restoring plasma volume and preventing cardiovascular collapse.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Third-degree burns with hypovolemic shock. The immediate life-threatening consequence is loss of plasma from the denuded area of the body with marked reduction in plasma volume.
(ii) The fluid loss occurs through: loss of plasma from the denuded area of the body. This results in increased plasma viscosity, marked reduction in blood flow, and reduction in cardiac output. The plasma compartment (approximately 3 L, 4% of body weight) is most critically affected. The consequence is hypovolemic shock and cardiovascular collapse.
(iii) Immediate fluid resuscitation principles:
- Restore plasma volume to counteract hypovolemic shock
- Intravenous fluid replacement is required urgently
- Prevent cardiovascular collapse by maintaining blood pressure and cardiac output
(iv) Definitive management goal: Restoration of plasma volume to prevent the progression from hypovolemic shock to cardiovascular collapse, thereby restoring adequate blood flow and cardiac output.

A(i) Parturition is expulsion of the foetus from the uterus; the process is labour, caused by true uterine contractions, cervical dilatation and opening of the vagina; true contractions are preceded by weak, irregular, short, painless Braxton Hicks contractions.
A(ii) The mechanism of onset is uncertain; progressive hormonal changes increase uterine excitability and progressive mechanical changes also occur.
A(ii) Rising oestrogen and falling progesterone: progesterone inhibits uterine contractility, oestrogen increases it (more gap junctions between myometrial cells, more prostaglandins, more oxytocin receptors).
A(ii) Oxytocin receptors increase through oestrogen and late uterine distension; plasma oxytocin in pre-labour and early labour do not differ, but once uterine stretching starts a neurogenic reflex raises oxytocin secretion.
A(ii) Foetal hormones: the foetal pituitary secretes increasing oxytocin; foetal hypothalamic CRH rises (augmented by placental CRH), increasing cortisol that may stimulate the uterus.
A(iii) Stretch of the uterine muscle (e.g. from foetal movements) and stretch of the cervix increase contractility.
B(i) Cervical stretch by the foetal head initiates a strong reflex increasing contractility of the uterine body; contraction pushes the baby forward, stretching the cervix more and starting more feedback, repeated until the baby is expelled.
B(i) The mechanism involves increased oxytocin receptors, prostaglandins produced in the decidua, cervical stretch with vaginal dilatation, and plasma oxytocin rising from a neurogenic reflex.
B(ii) Stage one (latent phase): true contractions begin, mucous plug lost, cervix dilates (1-3 cm) and the stage ends at 10 cm.
B(ii) Stage two (active phase): cervix 10 cm, membranes rupture, baby expelled; 1 minute in multiparous women to 30 minutes or more in nulliparous women.
B(ii) Stage three: continued contractions with shearing between uterus and placenta, placental separation, bleeding from placental sinuses.
B(ii) The placenta is expelled 10-45 minutes after the baby is born.

Describe the origin, course, relations, branches, and distribution of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS); state the safe therapeutic target; and explain the anatomical basis of blood pressure-regulating deficits after injury to the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
A. Describe the structure of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) and its components.
B. State the stimuli for renin secretion and describe the full cascade from renin release to aldosterone action.
C(i) . Describe the role of ADH in water balance and its mechanism of action on the collecting duct.
C(ii) . Distinguish between ADH deficiency and RAAS activation in terms of urine output and concentration.
D. State the actions of angiotensin II and explain how ACE inhibition reduces blood pressure.
questions.answerText:
C(i) ADH: principal function is water retention by kidney; increases permeability of distal tubules and collecting ducts to water. Deficiency leads to diabetes insipidus (large volume of hypotonic urine, net water loss). In large doses: peripheral vasoconstriction (hypertensive effect).
C(ii) ADH deficiency: large volume, hypotonic (dilute) urine.
RAAS activation (aldosterone): sodium reabsorption increased → water follows → reduced urine volume; urine more concentrated with less sodium.
D. Actions of angiotensin II: powerful vasoconstrictor; stimulates zona glomerulosa to produce aldosterone; stimulates ADH secretion and release; stimulates thirst; increases ACTH secretion; decreases sensitivity of baroreceptors (potentiating pressor effect).
ACE inhibition reduces BP by blocking conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, thereby reducing vasoconstriction, reducing aldosterone release (reducing sodium and water retention), and reducing ADH release.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, and distribution of the somatosensory ascending pathways (the anterolateral system and the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway).
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the sensory deficit that follows a lesion of these pathways.
questions.answerText:
(i) The 1st order (primary afferent) neuron has its cell body in a peripheral (spinal or cranial) ganglion; its peripheral axon innervates somatosensory receptors, and its central process synapses with a 2nd order afferent neuron in the spinal cord or brainstem nucleus.
- The 2nd order afferent may synapse with a 3rd order neuron in the spinal cord or ascend to synapse with it in the thalamus; there is decussation (crossing to the opposite side) below the level of the thalamus in every somatosensory pathway.
- The anterolateral system comprises the spinothalamic, spinoreticular, spinomesencephalic, spinotectal, and spinohypothalamic tracts, relaying pain, temperature, and non-discriminative touch/pressure/some proprioception.
- The dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway includes the fasciculus gracilis, fasciculus cuneatus, and medial lemniscus, relaying discriminative (fine) touch, vibratory sense, and position sense.
- All somatosensory pathways include a thalamic nucleus; thalamic neurons send axons in the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the cerebral cortex, and most pathways terminate in the parietal lobe.
(ii) Dorsal root and spinal nerve lesions are usually revealed in a segmental distribution; lesions affecting different levels or parts of the pathways result in varying sensory dysfunctions, e.g. paresthesia, anesthesia, allodynia, and hyperalgesia, depending on which fibres are involved; neuropathic pain is pain caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system, and referred pain is pain perceived at a location other than the site of the painful stimulus.

questions.question:
A woman who is breastfeeding has not resumed menstruation and asks about contraception.
(i) Name the phenomenon and explain its hormonal basis.
(ii) Explain how milk secretion is initiated and how milk is ejected.
(iii) Describe the natural, barrier and chemical methods of contraception with their mechanisms and disadvantages.
(iv) List the other and more definitive methods.
questions.answerText:
(i) Lactational amenorrhea: nursing stimulates prolactin, which inhibits GnRH and so antagonizes gonadotropin production; ovulation is inhibited, ovaries are inactive and oestrogen and progesterone fall to low levels, so lactation may cause contraception.
(ii) Prolactin promotes milk secretion (secreted from the fifth week of pregnancy till birth) and hCS is also lactogenic; in pregnancy oestrogen inhibits milk secretion; after parturition oestrogen and progesterone fall and prolactin assumes its role; GH, insulin, cortisol and parathyroid hormones are also needed; milk is secreted into alveoli but does not flow into ducts.
(ii) Ejection: suckling sends somatic afferent impulses from the nipple to the spinal cord and hypothalamus, releasing oxytocin, which contracts myoepithelial cells so milk is expressed into the ducts at +10 to 20 mm Hg.
(iii) Natural: abstinence (100% effective); rhythm/calendar (unreliable if cycles irregular and ovulation variable); withdrawal (penis removed from vagina before ejaculation).
(iii) Physical barrier: condom, diaphragm, cervical cap; cheap, no medical consultation; failure may be from displacement; diaphragm and cap may cause cervicitis.
(iii) Chemical barrier: foam tablets, pastes, creams, jellies, vaginal sponges (spermicides containing ricinoleic acid, nonoxynol-9 or octoxynol-3); inexpensive, well tolerated, but messy and may irritate.
(iii) Steroidal: oral contraceptives (combined, sequential, minipill, postcoital) whose high oestrogen and progesterone suppress gonadotropins and prevent ovulation; very effective, but may cause hypertension, metabolic disorders, thromboembolic disease, carcinogenic effect; also injectables, subdermal implants, vaginal rings.
(iii) Non-steroidal: intrauterine contraceptive devices (non-medicated and medicated); mechanism unsettled but seem to prevent sperm fertilizing ova; copper ones are spermicidal; progesterone/progestin-releasing ones also thicken cervical mucus.
(iv) Other methods: tubal ligation, laparoscopic occlusion, vasectomy, medical termination of pregnancy and pregnancy vaccines (under trial).

(i) Cortisol excess, causing Cushing's disease or syndrome.
(ii) May be due to a tumour of the pituitary or the adrenal cortex.
(iii) Cortisol (a glucocorticoid from the zona fasciculata) helps the body resist stress; it causes protein catabolism, promotes hyperglycemia and gluconeogenesis, and depresses inflammatory and immune responses. Cortisol excess produces symptoms including hyperglycemia, losses in muscle and bone protein, a swollen moon face, and fat redistribution to the abdomen and posterior neck (causing a buffalo hump). Cortisol secretion is normally regulated through a negative feedback system, under the control of ACTH, which is itself under the control of CRH released from the hypothalamus.
questions.question:
A patient is noted to have a swollen 'moon' face, fat redistribution to the abdomen and posterior neck, hyperglycemia, and loss of muscle and bone protein.

A patient has fatty, malabsorbed stools, found to be caused by a deficiency of a specific digestive enzyme.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiologic basis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Steatorrhoea.
(ii) Steatorrhoea is a condition caused by deficiency of pancreatic lipase, resulting in malabsorption of fat.

(i) Motility is regulated by the enteric nerves, the autonomic nerves, and hormones; the enteric nerves respond to luminal receptors sensing the presence and composition of chyme, as well as to signals from the ANS and hormones. Cranial nerve X (vagus) is specifically named as coordinating primary peristalsis in the oesophagus, emerging from the medulla; parasympathetic nerve fibres are also described as supplying the descending colon, sigmoid, rectum and anus. The parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) primarily promotes motility, whereas the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) slows or stops motility. In the colorectal region, parasympathetic stimulation intensifies the peristaltic waves and relaxes the internal anal sphincter, making the intrinsic myenteric defecation reflex more effective. A general rule is that most GI hormones inhibit gastric motility and/or emptying, allowing the duodenum to process the chyme released; gastrin is an exception, tending to stimulate gastric motility and antral cycle activity, increasing gastric emptying.
(ii) Because the PNS promotes motility and intensifies peristalsis/relaxes the internal anal sphincter (via the myenteric defecation reflex), and the SNS instead slows or stops motility, a shift in the balance of this autonomic input alters motility accordingly. Loss of the intrinsic enteric nervous system itself (as in Hirschsprung's disease, affecting the distal colon and internal anal sphincter) prevents the normal defecation reflex and causes faecal build-up and colonic dilation; this is a lesion of the enteric (intrinsic) nervous system rather than of the extrinsic autonomic nerve supply.
questions.question:

(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the change in motility following loss or overactivity of this nerve supply.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Innate immunity is the inborn, non-specific (natural) capacity to resist pathogens (viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoans, worms); it gives the initial response to a pathogen or injury.
A(i) Components: epithelial barriers (skin, GI and respiratory tracts), phagocytic cells (macrophages, neutrophils, monocytes), natural killer cells (kill virally infected cells and tumours) and complement proteins (>30 blood proteins that complement antibody in killing bacteria).
A(ii) The skin and the mucous membranes of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts are the first line of defence against invasion by microbes or parasites; the skin's tough outer cell layer is a mechanical barrier.
A(ii) Skin glands secrete oily substances such as oleic acid (kills some bacteria) and lysozyme (also in tears and saliva; breaks down the outer wall of certain bacteria).
A(iii) Mucous membranes form a mechanical barrier of cells; respiratory lining cells secrete mucus (phlegm) that traps small particles, and cilia sweep the mucus and particles up and out of the throat and nose.
A(iii) The mucus has protective antibodies, and stomach hydrochloric acid also protects against microbes.
A(iv) Transferrin transports iron in bound form and protects against bacteria by making free iron unavailable for their growth.
A(iv) Antimicrobial proteins: complement (works with other defences) and interferons (inhibit viral replication); bacteria in the small and large intestines secrete proteins that inhibit invading bacteria.
A(v) Scavenger cells (WBC, neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages) attack infectious agents directly; natural killer cells destroy body cells harbouring infectious organisms; phagocytic cells engulf and destroy microbes.
B(i) Innate immunity is possessed at birth as an essential characteristic and is non-specific.
B(i) Adaptive immunity is resistance developed against a specific foreign body (specific and acquired), made of highly specialized systemic cells and processes.
B(i) Adaptive components: humoral (B cells secrete antibodies) and cellular (CD8+ cells direct killing, CD4+ cells recruit immune cells).

questions.question:
A patient has a joint showing redness, swelling, pain and stiffness.
(i) Identify the process, state its functions and its cardinal signs.
(ii) Identify the structures affected in arthritis.
(iii) Name the differential arthritic pathologies.
(iv) Explain the clinico-immunological reasoning linking the signs to the cells involved.
questions.answerText:
(i) The process is inflammation.
(i) Functions: to eliminate the initial cause of cell injury, to remove necrotic cells and damaged tissues, and to initiate tissue repair.
(i) Signs: redness, swelling, pain (e.g. joint pain) and loss of function such as stiffness of a joint.
(ii) Arthritis is inflammation in the joint; rheumatoid arthritis is illustrated by worn-down cartilage, a narrowed joint, and growth of synovial (joint) membrane that invades the bone.
(iii) Differential: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and gouty arthritis.
(iv) CD4+ T cells help recruit other immune cells (inflammatory response), and Th1 cells stimulate macrophage activation.

(i) Crohn's disease - inflammation of the small intestine (enteritis, inflammatory bowel disease/IBD).
(ii) Crohn's disease usually affects the ileum.
