A girl is brought to a clinic with breast development and pubic hair growth before the age of 7 years.
(i) State the diagnosis and the age criteria used in girls and boys.
(ii) List the categories of cause.
(iii) Explain the normal mechanisms that control the onset of puberty (hormonal and genetic).
(iv) Describe the sequence of normal pubertal changes in girls.
questions.answerText:
(i) Precocious puberty: onset of signs of puberty before age 7/8 in girls and before age 9 in boys.
(ii) Causes: central and peripheral.
(iii) Gonadotropins are high in the newborn, fall a few weeks after birth and stay low until puberty; in childhood the hypothalamus secretes little GnRH because even slight sex steroid strongly inhibits it.
(iii) Onset is marked by rising FSH followed by LH, from programmed maturational brain changes increasing GnRH plus decreased sensitivity of gonadotropin secretion to sex steroid negative feedback.
(iii) Hormonal: leptin activates hypothalamic GnRH release; about 17% body fat is needed for menarche and about 22% for regular cycles; menarche is later in very active girls.
(iii) Genetic: KiSS1 gene produces kisspeptins that activate GPR54, which signals the brain to initiate puberty; leptin acts via the leptin-melanocortin-kisspeptin pathway.
(iv) Stage 1 (about 8-11 y): ovaries enlarge, hormone production starts. Stage 2 (about 8-14 y): thelarche (usually first external sign), pubic hair, height and weight increase.
(iv) Stage 3 (about 9-15 y): breast growth continues, coarser darker pubic hair, whitish vaginal discharge, menarche may occur. Stage 4 (about 10-16 y): areolar mound, adult triangular pubic hair, menarche if not yet occurred, irregular (anovulatory) ovulation.
(iv) Stage 5 (about 12-19 y): full height, regular ovulation, pubic hair filled in, breasts fully developed.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old male patient is admitted to the cardiology ward with progressive heart failure. His resting cardiac output is markedly reduced, his peripheral oedema is severe, and he has signs of both left and right heart failure.
(i) Describe the functional anatomy of the heart: its location, layers, chambers, and valves.
(ii) Describe the blood flow through the heart and distinguish between the pulmonary and systemic circulations in terms of pressure.
(iii) Explain how the lymphatic system relates to the cardiovascular system.
(iv) Describe the local regulation of blood flow by tissue factors and paracrine hormones.
(v) Describe how the endothelium regulates vascular tone, naming specific substances and their effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Functional anatomy of the heart:
- Location: thoracic cage, middle mediastinum; size of a clenched fist; weighs about 150 g.
- Shape: inverted cone; apex inferiorly, base superiorly.
- Layers: epicardium (outermost), myocardium (middle), endocardium (innermost); surrounded by double-layered pericardial sac (fibrous and serous pericardium).
- Chambers: 2 atria (collect blood, deliver to ventricles); 2 ventricles (pump to pulmonary and systemic circulation); separated by interatrial septum and interventricular septum.
- Valves: AV valves (tricuspid and bicuspid/mitral) between atria and ventricles; semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) at bases of pulmonary trunk and aorta; supported by suspensory ligaments and papillary muscles.
(ii) Blood flow and circulation pressures:
- Pulmonary (right pump): right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium; low-pressure circulation.
- Systemic (left pump): left ventricle → aorta → whole body → superior and inferior vena cavae → right atrium; high-pressure circulation.
- Two pumps work in series; normal ABP = 120/80 mmHg.
(iii) Lymphatic system: contains no blood; carries tissue fluid (lymph); returns it to circulation via lymphatic ducts emptying into large veins.
(iv) Local regulation of blood flow:
- Tissue factors: adenosine, inorganic phosphate, CO₂, hydrogen ions, potassium ions, oxygen levels, osmolarity.
- Paracrine hormones: histamine, bradykinin, products of arachidonic acid metabolism (PGE₂, thromboxanes, leukotrienes).
(v) Endothelial regulation of vascular tone:
- Nitric oxide (NO): vasodilator.
- Prostacyclin: vasodilator.
- EDHF (endothelium-derived hyperpolarising factor): vasodilator.
- Endothelin: vasoconstrictor.
Smooth muscle myogenic mechanism: increased intraluminal pressure stretches VSM → depolarisation → contraction → increased resistance, counteracting the pressure increase; usually overridden by metabolic mechanisms.

(i) Diagnosis: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) of the inferior wall — due to occlusion of the right coronary artery.
(ii) Anatomical distribution of the right coronary artery: supplies most of the right ventricle as well as the posterior part of the left ventricle. Therefore, structures most at risk include the right ventricular myocardium and the posterior left ventricular wall. The inferior wall of the heart (supplied by the RCA) is the territory of infarction.
(iii) Sudden vs. gradual occlusion: In normal human hearts, there are virtually no functional intercoronary channels (anastomoses). Hence, occlusion of a coronary artery or one of its branches leads to ischaemic necrosis and eventual fibrosis of the area supplied by the vessel. However, if a coronary vessel narrows slowly over time, collateral vessels develop and may furnish sufficient blood to ischaemic myocardium to prevent or reduce the extent of the necrosis. Therefore sudden occlusion allows no time for collateral development, producing immediate infarction.
(iv) Phasic changes in coronary blood flow:
- During systole: left ventricular vascular blood flow is markedly reduced due to the strong compression of left ventricular muscle around the intramuscular vessels.
- During diastole: blood flow is rapid as the initial obstruction caused by compression of vessels by ventricular muscle is removed.
- Coronary blood flow occurs mainly during cardiac diastole. Diastole is the most critical phase for coronary perfusion because it is when the intramyocardial pressure is low enough to allow flow.
questions.question:
A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertension and smoking presents with sudden-onset severe chest pain radiating to the left arm. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Emergency coronary angiography reveals 100% occlusion of the right coronary artery.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Describe the anatomical distribution of the right coronary artery and the structures most at risk from its occlusion.
(iii) Explain why sudden occlusion of a coronary artery leads to necrosis even though gradual narrowing may not, using the anatomical characteristic of coronary vasculature.
(iv) Explain the phasic changes in coronary blood flow during the cardiac cycle, and state which phase is most critical for coronary perfusion.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the adrenal gland.
(ii) State how the zones/parts of the gland relate to common endocrine pathologies.
(iii) Explain how disease of this gland may act on distant structures to cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) Adrenal (suprarenal) glands are paired, pyramid-shaped endocrine organs located on the upper poles of each kidney.
- Each gland has two parts: an inner adrenal medulla, constituting 20% of the gland, and an outer adrenal cortex, constituting 80% of the gland.
- The adrenal cortex is divided into three layers: zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis; hormones of the adrenal cortex are steroid hormones (corticosteroids) synthesized from cholesterol.
(ii) Zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); hypersecretion is called aldosteronism, causing hypertension and edema, and excessive potassium loss causing muscle weakness and paralysis.
- Zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol); excess causes Cushing's disease/syndrome (due to a tumour of the pituitary or adrenal cortex), while deficiency of adrenal cortex hormones causes Addison's disease.
- Zona reticularis secretes sex hormones, mainly androgens (DHEA, converted to testosterone and dihydrotestosterone) and small amounts of estrogens; hypersecretion causes masculinization or virilization.
(iii) Cortisol excess (from the zona fasciculata) causes protein catabolism, promotes hyperglycemia and gluconeogenesis, and depresses inflammatory and immune responses; excess produces losses in muscle and bone protein, a swollen moon face, and fat redistribution to the abdomen and posterior neck (buffalo hump), illustrating how a hormone from this gland acts on distant tissues (muscle, bone, immune system, adipose tissue) to produce a functional deficit.
- Addison's disease (deficiency of adrenal cortex hormones) similarly produces distant effects: loss of weight, dehydration, hypotension, and hypoglycemia.

questions.question:
A. Describe the male sexual act under the following headings:
A(i) the phases and their features;
A(ii) neural control of erection;
A(iii) emission and ejaculation.
B.
B(i) Explain the mechanism of resolution.
B(ii) Distinguish between emission and ejaculation.
B(iii) Describe the composition of semen.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The male sexual act (sexual response, coitus, copulation) results from a complex neurovascular mechanism; phases are excitement (erection, glandular secretion), orgasm (emission, ejaculation) and resolution (detumescence).
A(i) Excitement also brings vasocongestion, myotonia, and increased heart rate, blood pressure, ventilation and glandular secretion; it can be started by psychic or physical stimuli or both.
A(ii) Erection is caused by parasympathetic fibres from S2-S4 via the pelvic nerves to penile arteries and erectile tissue, releasing nitric oxide, acetylcholine and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide.
A(iii) Orgasm (climax) lasts 3-15 seconds, usually with discharge of semen; heart rate rises to as high as 180 beats/min and respiratory rate to as high as 40 breaths/min, with proportional blood pressure rise.
A(iii) Emission and ejaculation are initiated by sympathetic impulses from T12-L2; smooth muscle of the vas deferens, ampulla, prostate and seminal vesicles contracts, expelling secretions into the internal urethra, where they mix with bulbourethral mucus to form semen.
A(iii) In ejaculation, sympathetic signals further increase prostate and seminal vesicle secretions and compress the internal urethral sphincter to retain urine in the bladder.
A(iii) Somatic signals go to the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus; the bulbospongiosus undergoes five or six spasmodic contractions compressing the urethra, while pelvic and trunk muscles cause thrusting.
B(i) Erection ceases within 1-2 minutes after ejaculation; sympathetic stimulation constricts the internal pudendal artery, reducing inflow, and contracts trabecular muscles that squeeze blood from the lacunae, so the penis becomes soft and flaccid (detumescence).
B(ii) Emission is the forerunner of ejaculation (secretions expelled into the internal urethra).
B(ii) Ejaculation is the propulsion of semen out of the urethra at orgasm.
B(iii) Semen contains sperms and secretions of the seminal vesicles, prostate, Cowper's and urethral glands; average volume 2.5-3.5 mL after several days of abstinence; about 100 million sperms/mL.
B(iii) Seminal vesicle secretion has fructose and fibrinogen; prostatic secretion is alkaline with a clotting enzyme and fibrinolysin.

(i) Diagnosis: achalasia. Mechanism: the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) fails to relax during swallowing due to damage in the myenteric plexus in the lower two-thirds of the oesophagus, with loss of 'receptive relaxation'. This leads to progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, proximal oesophageal dilatation, and distal stenosis ('bird's beak' on barium swallow).
(ii) Normal phases of deglutition:
food squeezed by tongue up and back against soft palate into oropharynx, triggering the pharyngeal phase.
2. Pharyngeal stage (swallowing reflex): tactile receptors in posterior mouth and pharynx → cranial nerves → swallowing centre in medulla and lower pons → automatic pharyngeal muscle contractions.
primary peristaltic wave (continuation of pharyngeal wave, centrally coordinated) and secondary peristaltic waves (from oesophageal distension); receptive relaxation of LES allows propulsion into stomach.
(iii) Types of dysphagia:
- Oral obstructive: peritonsillar abscess; tumours (tonsils, tongue).
- Pharyngeal neurological: stroke; Parkinson's disease (80% of cases); multiple sclerosis.
- Oesophageal neurological: stroke, Parkinson's disease, achalasia.
- Oesophageal obstructive: oesophageal stricture (post acid/corrosive fluid); oesophageal cancer.
(iv) Barrett's oesophagus: caused by chronic acid reflux (weakened LES). Results in reversible substitution of normal stratified squamous epithelium of lower oesophagus with simple columnar epithelium (metaplasia). Untreated chronic metaplasia can become irreversible — adenocarcinoma.
(v) Mastication reflex: afferent — sensory impulses from teeth, jaw, and oral mucosa. Integrating centre — motor cortex (via corticobulbar projections) and brain stem centre. Motor response — CN V (trigeminal, V3) innervates temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid muscles; CN VII (facial) controls lips and cheeks; CN XII (hypoglossal) controls tongue.

(i) Describe the origin, course, and relations of the neurosecretory pathway that produces antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin, and state the structures to which these hormones are distributed.
(ii) Explain the functional/anatomical basis of the deformity/dysfunction that follows injury to this pathway.
questions.answerText:
(i) ADH (vasopressin) originates from neurons of the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus; oxytocin originates from neurons of the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus.
- The posterior pituitary is an extension of the hypothalamus; the hormones are carried along axons of these hypothalamic neurons (pituicytes/axons) down to the posterior pituitary.
- The hormones are stored in and released from the posterior pituitary gland (neurohypophysis), which lies in structural relationship with the anterior pituitary.
- ADH acts on the distal tubule of the nephron (increases water permeability), causes arteriolar vasoconstriction in high dose, stimulates renal mesangial cell contraction, inhibits renin secretion, and stimulates ACTH secretion, especially in stress. Oxytocin acts on uterine smooth muscle and mammary myoepithelial cells.
(ii) Partial or complete absence of vasopressin secretion by the hypothalamus (central diabetes insipidus) leads to excessive free water clearance; resistance of vasopressin at the level of the nephrons (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) has the same functional result; both cause dehydration and hypernatremia if there is inadequate water intake to compensate for the loss of water.

(i) Menopause: cessation of ovarian activity and menstruation; end of female reproductive life; occurs at about 50 years (about 45-55 years of age).
(i) Cause: ovaries are depleted of follicles, stop secreting estradiol and inhibin, so negative feedback is lost and pituitary FSH and LH secretion is elevated.
(ii) Vasomotor disturbances (hot flashes/flushes): a fall in core body temperature is followed by feelings of heat and profuse perspiration.
(ii) Urogenital atrophy: atrophy of the urethra, vaginal wall and vaginal glands, with loss of lubrication.
(ii) Cardiovascular: oestrogen increases the HDL/LDL cholesterol ratio (helps clear arteries of LDL that contributes to atherosclerotic plaque) and keeps vessel lining strong and pliable, so its loss increases atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk.
(ii) Bone: osteoporosis weakens bones and increases risk of sudden, unexpected fractures; oestrogen normally inhibits osteoclastic activity and prevents bone resorption. Irritability and depression also occur.
(ii) Source of oestrogen: the only oestrogen in the blood is the weak oestrone, formed by mesenchymal cells in adipose tissue from weak adrenal androgens (androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone); women with more adipose tissue have higher oestrogen and less propensity to osteoporosis.
(iii) Aim of treatment is to improve quality of life.
(iii) Hormonal option: oestrogen replacement therapy; disease risks listed are coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, cancer and death.
(iii) Nonhormonal option: paroxetine mesylate (Brisdelle).

questions.answerText:
(i) From the mouth to the anus, the digestive canal is lined by a mucous membrane (mucosa); in the mouth, oesophagus and anus the epithelial layer is stratified squamous, about 10-15 cells thick, while in the region of absorption and secretion a single-layered columnar epithelium is found, with folding and finger-like projections (villi).
The mucosa also contains lymph nodules for protection against disease, and external to the lamina propria is a thin layer of smooth muscle, the muscularis mucosae, responsible for numerous small folds that increase absorptive surface area; specialized goblet cells in the mucosa secrete mucus throughout most of the GI tract.
(ii) The submucosa is a highly vascular layer of connective tissue that serves the mucosa; absorbed molecules passing through the columnar epithelial cells of the mucosa enter the blood and lymphatic vessels of the submucosa.
It contains glands and nerve plexuses, the submucosal plexus (Meissner's plexus), which provides an autonomic nerve supply to the muscularis mucosae.
(iii) The layers of the gastrointestinal tract, from the figure, are (from outside in): serosa, longitudinal muscle, myenteric plexus, circular muscle, submucosa, submucosal plexus, and muscularis mucosae, with the mesentery attached externally.
The myenteric plexus lies between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers of the muscularis externa.
Clinical basis: motility is regulated by the enteric nerves (intrinsic nervous control, comprising the myenteric and submucosal plexuses), the autonomic nerves, and hormones, and can act independently, involving local reflexes confined to the gut wall, such as the peristaltic reflex.
Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital disease that involves the loss of the enteric nervous system in the distal part of the colon and always involves the internal anal sphincter; the normal defecation reflex, mediated by the myenteric plexus, does not occur, so faeces build up and the colon dilates.
This shows why loss of the intrinsic (enteric) nerve supply particularly affects the distal colon: the myenteric plexus in that segment is required for the defecation reflex, and its loss blocks the normal propulsive/relaxation response.
Distinguishing feature 1: the myenteric plexus consists mostly of a linear chain of interconnecting neurons, and when stimulated its principal effects include increased tonic contraction, increased intensity of rhythmical contractions, increased rate of the rhythm of contraction, and increased velocity of conduction of excitatory waves along the gut wall.
Distinguishing feature 2: the submucosal plexus is concerned with local intestinal secretion, local absorption, and local contraction of the submucosal muscle, involving many sensory receptors within the gastrointestinal epithelium.
The myenteric plexus thus principally controls the motility of the gut, while the submucosal plexus principally controls local secretory and absorptive function of the mucosa.

(i) Describe the gross structure of the anterior and posterior pituitary gland.
(ii) State how the cell types/parts of the pituitary relate to common endocrine pathologies.
(iii) Explain how pituitary hormones act on distant structures to produce a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pituitary gland is made of the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) and the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis), located in the sella turcica (Turkish saddle) of the sphenoid bone. The anterior pituitary consists of the pars distalis, pars intermedia, and pars tuberalis, and is derived from Rathke's pouch (ectodermal, from the primitive oropharynx); the posterior pituitary is an extension of the hypothalamus, containing pituicytes and axons from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei.
(ii) Somatotrophs (acidophilic) produce growth hormone - excess causes gigantism/acromegaly, deficiency causes dwarfism.
- Lactotrophs (acidophilic) produce prolactin - excess causes hyperprolactinemia.
- Corticotrophs (basophilic) produce ACTH - excess drives Cushing's disease.
- Thyrotrophs (basophilic) produce TSH; gonadotrophs (basophilic) produce FSH and LH.
- The posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH (deficiency causes central diabetes insipidus) and oxytocin.
(iii) TSH stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion, and chronic TSH rise causes thyroid hypertrophy/goitre, illustrating action on a distant gland; ACTH is involved in every step of production and release of cortisol from the adrenal gland, and stimulates lipoprotein uptake and steroidogenic enzyme transcription in the adrenal cortex; GH acts partly through IGFs (produced in the liver) to increase cartilage and long bone growth, and alters carbohydrate and fat metabolism in distant tissues (muscle, adipose tissue, liver); FSH and LH act on the gonads to stimulate follicle growth/estrogen secretion or spermatogenesis and testosterone production.

(i) Iodine uptake is facilitated by the iodide pump, the Na+/I- symporter (NIS), at the basolateral membrane of the follicular cell; this is secondary active transport, energized by the gradient maintained by the sodium-potassium pump, producing an iodide concentration in the colloid 20-40 times greater than in plasma.
- Iodide ion is oxidized to form nascent iodine (I0) or I2-, catalysed by thyroperoxidase (peroxidase) and hydrogen peroxidase, located in the apical membrane of the cell.
- Addition of iodide to tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin: tyrosine + 1 iodine = monoiodotyrosine (MIT); tyrosine + 2 iodines = di-iodotyrosine (DIT).
- Coupling of 2 iodinated tyrosine molecules forms thyroid hormone: DIT + DIT = thyroxine (T4); DIT + MIT = tri-iodothyronine (T3). Coupling does not occur between two MIT molecules.
- About 30% of the mass of the thyroid gland is thyroglobulin, representing about a 2-3 month supply of hormone.
- On stimulation, follicular cells internalize thyroglobulin-hormone complex by phagocytosis as endocytic vesicles; these fuse with lysosomes, which release enzymes splitting off T3 and T4 as well as inactive MIT and DIT; the lipophilic thyroid hormones then pass freely into the blood.
(ii) Iodide must be obtained from dietary intake (about 150 micrograms/day is needed), so a lack of dietary iodine limits the substrate needed for organification and coupling, and iodine deficiency is listed as a clinical correlate of thyroid dysfunction.
(iii) About 93% of secreted hormone is T4 while 7% is T3, though almost all T4 is ultimately converted to T3; T3 is about 4 times as potent as T4 and has greater biological activity, but is present in blood in smaller quantities and for a shorter time. T3 has less affinity for plasma proteins and releases quickly (acts on target cells immediately, shorter latent period of 6-12 hours), while T4 has more affinity and binds strongly, so it is released slowly (prolonged latent period of 2-3 days, action may persist for 6 weeks to 12 months); T4 has a half-life of 7 days versus up to 1 day for T3.

questions.answerText:
C(i) Cystometrogram — plot of intravesical pressure vs. volume:
- Ia: initial slight rise in pressure.
- Ib: long, nearly flat segment (Law of Laplace: P = 2T/r).
- II: sudden sharp rise — micturition reflex triggered.
Volume thresholds: first sensation 100–150 mL; first desire to void 150–250 mL; uncomfortable fullness 350–400 mL; reflex contraction at 300–400 mL; pain and loss of control at 700 mL.
C(ii) Micturition reflex: stretch receptors → spinal cord → parasympathetic efferent discharge → micturition contractions (self-regenerative). Higher centres: normally keep reflex inhibited; cortical centres can facilitate sacral micturition centres and allow voluntary relaxation of external sphincter when convenient.
D. In young children, micturition is purely reflex (myelination incomplete), occurring whenever bladder is sufficiently distended. At about 2½ years, cortical control begins. In adults, micturition is under voluntary cortical control.

C(i) Lung compliance: change in lung volume per unit change in alveolar pressure (δV/δP). Normal value: 200 ml/cm H₂O. Total pulmonary compliance: 120 ml/cm H₂O.
C(ii) Conditions decreasing compliance: pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary oedema, respiratory distress syndrome, reduced surfactant synthesis, lung collapse, increased pulmonary venous pressure.
Conditions increasing compliance: old age, emphysema.

A pregnant woman is found to have a cervix plugged by mucus, a larger and more vascularized vagina with a wider introitus, darkened areola and nipple, and a total weight gain of about 12 kg.
(i) Identify the reproductive organ changes and account for the weight gain by component.
(ii) Explain the endocrine changes involved.
(iii) State the possible complications and deficiencies.
(iv) Describe the metabolic and haematological changes.
questions.answerText:
(i) Ovaries: follicular development is replaced by corpus luteum; uterus: volume, size, weight and shape changed; cervix plugged by mucus; vagina bigger and more vascularized with wider introitus; breast: new ducts and alveoli, fat deposited, areola and nipple darken.
(i) Weight gain (about 12 kg): foetus about 3.5 kg; placenta, amniotic fluid and membranes about 2.0 kg; uterus about 1.0 kg; breast about 1.0 kg; blood and extracellular fluid about 3.0 kg; maternal fat about 1.5 kg.
(ii) Pituitary: anterior pituitary enlarges, ACTH, TSH and prolactin rise, FSH and LH fall to almost zero. Adrenal cortex enlarges: cortisol and aldosterone rise under ACTH; cortisol makes glucose and amino acids available to the foetus; aldosterone raises sodium and water retention.
(ii) Thyroid enlarges, thyroxine rises (prepares mammary gland for lactation); parathyroids enlarge, parathormone rises to increase calcium retention for the foetus; pregnancy hormones are hCG, oestrogen, progesterone, hCS and relaxin.
(iii) Aldosterone-driven sodium and water retention occasionally may lead to pregnancy-induced hypertension; nutritional deficiency may occur if the diet lacks appropriate elements, especially calcium, phosphates, iron and vitamins.
(iv) Metabolic: basal metabolic rate rises about 15% (increased thyroxine, adrenocortical and sex hormones), more heat is produced, glucose, protein and fat are mobilised from mother to foetus, and food consumption increases.
(iv) Haematological: blood volume increases; plasma volume rises through aldosterone and oestrogen; bone marrow is more active and forms additional blood cells if nutrition matches requirements.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old hypertensive male is found collapsed at home. His blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg and there is evidence of significant blood loss. His kidneys are producing very little urine.
(i) Identify the type of shock present and the mechanism of renal hypoperfusion.
(ii) Describe the factors that affect GFR in terms of the filtration pressure equation.
(iii) Explain the three processes involved in urine formation.
(iv) Describe what happens to glucose reabsorption when plasma glucose exceeds the transport maximum.
(v) State the endocrine functions of the kidney and describe the action of each hormone produced.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hypovolaemic (haemorrhagic) shock. Mechanism of renal hypoperfusion: decreased blood volume → decreased CO → decreased ABP → decreased renal perfusion pressure → decreased RBF → decreased GFR → oliguria. ABP = CO × SVR; decrease in CO decreases ABP.
(ii) Factors affecting GFR — filtration pressure equation:
GFR = Kp [PH − (PO + PB)].
- Kp = glomerular capillary filtration coefficient (product of capillary wall permeability × effective filtration surface area); direct relationship with GFR.
- PH = glomerular hydrostatic pressure (~60 mmHg); increased PH → increased GFR.
- PO = glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure (~25 mmHg); increased PO → decreased GFR.
- PB = Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure/tissue resistance (~10 mmHg); increased PB → decreased GFR.
- Net filtration pressure = 60 − 25 − 10 = 25 mmHg.
(iii) Three processes in urine formation:
- Glomerular filtration (GF): filtering of blood into tubule forming primitive urine.
- Tubular reabsorption (TR): absorption of substances needed by body from tubule to blood.
- Tubular secretion (TS): secretion of substances to be eliminated from blood into tubule.
Urinary excretion = GF − TR + TS.
(iv) Glucose reabsorption: normally all glucose is reabsorbed in early PCT by secondary active transport (co-transport with Na⁺). Amount reabsorbed is proportional to plasma glucose × GFR up to the transport maximum (TmG): ~375 mg/min in men; ~300 mg/min in women. When TmG is exceeded, glucose appears in the urine (glucosuria).
(v) Endocrine functions of the kidney (3 hormones):
- Renin: secreted by juxtaglomerular cells; converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → angiotensin II (via ACE) → vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, ADH release, thirst stimulation — all raising ABP.
- Erythropoietin: 90% produced by interstitial fibroblasts; stimulated by hypoxia; increases erythropoietin-sensitive stem cells in bone marrow to produce more RBCs; half-life 5 hours.
- 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol: active vitamin D3; produced by 1α-hydroxylase in kidney proximal tubule. Functions: increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption from intestine; facilitates Ca²⁺ reabsorption in kidney; mobilises Ca²⁺ from bone; stimulates differentiation of immune cells.

(i) The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord, protected by the skull and housed with the spinal cord in the triple-layered meninges. The three major parts of the brain are the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem; other parts include the thalamus, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, basal ganglia, limbic system, ventricles, CSF, and 12 cranial nerves.
- The cerebrum is separated into four lobes: temporal, occipital, parietal, and frontal.
(ii) Temporal lobe: processes sensory input, assigns emotional meaning, lays down long-term memories, houses part of language perception.
- Occipital lobe: visual processing, houses the visual cortex.
- Parietal lobe: integrates touch, spatial awareness, navigation, and is important in language processing.
- Frontal lobe: attention, reward, short-term memory, motivation, and planning; contains the majority of dopamine-sensitive neurons.
- Cerebellum: precise motor control, language, and attention; damage causes ataxia. Broca's area: important in language processing; damage causes difficulty speaking with preserved understanding.
(iii) The hypothalamus sits just above the brainstem, is roughly the size of an almond, and secretes a number of neurohormones, influencing body temperature control, thirst, and hunger; the hypothalamic hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, GHIH, PIH) regulate secretion of anterior pituitary hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH/LH, GH, prolactin), which in turn act on distant target glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads) - demonstrating how the hypothalamus, a CNS structure, influences endocrine function throughout the body via the pituitary.

questions.answerText:
(i) Tetany (hypocalcemic tetany) - a state of spastic contraction of skeletal muscles due to increased neuromuscular excitability from decreased calcium below the normal level (9-11 mg%).
- Latent tetany: calcium level 7-9 mg%, symptoms absent at rest but appear with emotional stress, pregnancy and lactation.
- Manifest tetany: plasma calcium level drops below 7 mg%.
(ii) Emotional stress, pregnancy, and lactation (for latent tetany); a fall of plasma calcium below normal levels.
(iii) When extracellular calcium falls below normal, the nervous system becomes progressively more excitable because of increased permeability of neuronal membranes to sodium; this hyperexcitability causes tetanic contractions.
- In children, chronic hypocalcemia causes rickets; in adults it causes osteomalacia.

questions.answerText:
C(i) RV cannot be measured by spirometry because the lungs can never be fully emptied and residual volume cannot be exhaled. Measured by helium dilution or body plethysmography. FRC similarly measured by helium dilution or body plethysmography.
C(ii) FEV₁ (forced expiratory volume in 1 second): fraction of VC expired in 1 second. Normal: FEV₁ = 83% of VC; FEV₂ = 91%; FEV₃ = 97%.
Obstructive disease: FEV₁ markedly reduced proportionally more than VC; FEV₁/VC ratio decreased; TLC may increase (air trapping).
Restrictive disease: both FEV₁ and VC reduced proportionally; FEV₁/VC ratio normal or increased; TLC decreased.
D. Alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space volume) × respiratory rate (RR).
Pulmonary ventilation = TV × RR.
Anatomical dead space (ADS) = 0.15 L (airways above respiratory bronchioles).
Physiological dead space = ADS + volume of unperfused but ventilated lung. In normal lung, physiological dead space equals anatomical dead space.

A. Describe erythropoiesis under the following headings:
A(i) Sites of erythropoiesis during embryonic life (first, second, and third trimesters)
A(ii) Sites of blood formation from birth through adulthood
A(iii) The stages of erythropoiesis from proerythroblast to mature RBC, stating the important event, size, and staining pattern at each stage
B. Describe the dietary requirements for erythropoiesis and the specific anaemia resulting from deficiency of each.
C. Explain the feedback regulation of erythropoiesis, identifying the hormone responsible, its site of production, the stimulus for its release, and its target.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Embryonic erythropoiesis:
- First trimester: yolk sac.
- Second trimester: liver and spleen.
- Third trimester until 5 years of age: bone marrow of all bones.
A(ii) Blood formation from birth through adulthood:
- 5-20 years: long bone marrow.
- 20 years upward: marrow of membranous bones — vertebrae, ribs, sternum, skull, pelvis.
A(iii) Stages of erythropoiesis:
- Proerythroblast: synthesis of haemoglobin starts; approximately 20 µm; stains basophilic.
- Early normoblast: nucleoli disappear; approximately 15 µm; basophilic staining.
- Intermediate normoblast: haemoglobin starts appearing; approximately 10-12 µm; polychromophilic staining.
- Late normoblast: nucleus disappears; approximately 8-10 µm; acidophilic staining.
- Reticulocyte: reticulum is formed; cell enters capillary from site of production; slightly bigger than RBC; basophilic (organelle remnants).
- Matured RBC: reticulum disappears; cell attains biconcavity; 7.2 µm; acidophilic.
B. Dietary requirements and resulting deficiency anaemias:
- Iron: deficiency results in iron deficiency anaemia (microcytic anaemia).
- Folic acid or Vitamin B12: deficiency results in megaloblastic anaemia.
- Intrinsic factor (from stomach secretions): inability to absorb Vitamin B12 as a result of a lack of intrinsic factor results in pernicious anaemia.
C. Feedback regulation:
- Hormone: erythropoietin, a glycoprotein hormone.
- Site of production: produced by renal cells.
- Stimulus for release: decreased renal blood oxygen content — from reduced numbers of RBCs (haemorrhage or excess RBC destruction), reduced availability of oxygen (high altitudes or pneumonia), or increased demands for oxygen (aerobic exercise).
- Target: erythropoietin stimulates erythrocyte production in the red bone marrow.

questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, relations, branches, and distribution of the renal clearance technique; state the safe substance for measuring GFR; and explain the anatomical basis of why PAH but not inulin can be used to measure renal plasma flow.
A. Define renal plasma clearance and write its mathematical expression.
B. Describe the properties required of a substance to measure GFR and identify the substance used clinically.
C(i) . Explain why creatinine is preferred clinically over inulin.
C(ii) . Distinguish between ERPF and TRPF and state the formula to calculate TRPF.
D. Explain why a substance used to measure RPF must be secreted in addition to being filtered.
questions.answerText:
C(i) Creatinine is preferred clinically because it is endogenously produced (by-product of muscle metabolism) — no continuous infusion needed. A small amount is secreted (excretion exceeds filtration by 5–10%) but this is offset by slight overestimation of plasma creatinine, making creatinine clearance a reasonable estimate of GFR.
C(ii) ERPF (effective renal plasma flow) = clearance of PAH = Upah × V / Ppah.
TRPF (total renal plasma flow) = ERPF ÷ extraction ratio of PAH (≈90%).
Formula: TRPF = ERPF × (100/90).
D. GFR is only 20% of total plasma flow; a substance cleared only by filtration cannot be completely removed in one circulation through the kidneys. The substance used to measure RPF must also be secreted to achieve near-complete clearance in a single pass through the kidney. PAH is about 90% cleared from plasma in one circulation and is used to approximate renal plasma flow.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents with recurrent spontaneous haemarthroses (bleeding into joints) and prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. His mother has two brothers with similar complaints. Coagulation studies show a markedly prolonged APTT with a normal PT. Factor VIII activity is severely reduced.
(i) State the specific diagnosis and its mode of inheritance.
(ii) Identify the coagulation pathway that is defective and describe the normal role of Factor VIII in that pathway.
(iii) State two other disorders of haemostasis mentioned alongside this condition, naming the specific factor deficient in each.
(iv) Explain the role of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in haemostasis and why its deficiency causes a related but distinct bleeding disorder.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Haemophilia A (Classical haemophilia). Mode of inheritance: genetically transmitted (sex-linked).
(ii) The intrinsic pathway is defective. Normal role of Factor VIII: activated Factor IX (IXa) forms a complex with active Factor VIII (VIIIa), which has been activated when separated from von Willebrand factor. The complex of IXa and VIIIa activates Factor X. Phospholipids from aggregated platelets and Ca2+ are necessary for full activation of Factor X.
(iii) Other haemostasis disorders:
- Haemophilia B (Christmas disease): characterised by failure of Factor IX; it is sex-linked.
- Haemophilia C: characterised by failure of Factor XI (plasma thromboplastin antecedent).
- Hypofibrinogenaemia: deficiency of fibrinogen; can be congenital or acquired due to severe liver damage.
- Von Willebrand disease: deficiency of von Willebrand factor, which forms a complex with Factor VIII, regulating plasma level of Factor VIII.
(iv) Von Willebrand factor (vWF) forms a complex with Factor VIII, regulating the plasma level of Factor VIII. Deficiency of vWF leads to von Willebrand disease. This differs from Haemophilia A because vWF deficiency primarily impairs platelet plug formation (primary haemostasis) by preventing platelet adhesion to the damaged vessel wall, and secondarily reduces Factor VIII levels. Haemophilia A is a pure coagulation cascade defect.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy from a malaria-endemic region is brought in with yellow discolouration of the sclera, dark urine, and pale stools. Laboratory results show elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and the absence of urobilinogen in the stool.
(i) Identify the type of jaundice and its underlying cause.
(ii) State the normal plasma bilirubin level and the level at which jaundice becomes detectable.
(iii) Describe all three types of jaundice and their specific causes.
(iv) Explain why malaria parasitaemia is associated with a different type of jaundice, identifying the mechanism.
questions.answerText:
(i) Type of jaundice: Obstructive jaundice (post-hepatic). Underlying cause: obstruction to the bile ducts prevents excretion of conjugated bilirubin into the intestine. Elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin spills into urine (dark urine), while absent bile in the intestine causes pale stools and absence of urobilinogen.
(ii) Normal plasma bilirubin level: 0.3-1.0 mg/dL (5-18 µmol/L). Jaundice becomes detectable when plasma bilirubin is greater than 2 mg/dL (34 µmol/L).
(iii) Three types of jaundice and their specific causes:
1. Haemolytic jaundice (pre-hepatic): caused by excessive breakdown of red blood cells. Excess bilirubin results from excessive haemolysis.
caused by failure of the liver to excrete bilirubin. The liver itself is diseased and cannot process bilirubin normally.
3. Obstructive jaundice (post-hepatic): caused by obstruction to the bile ducts. Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the intestine.
(iv) Malaria and jaundice: Heavy malaria parasitaemia causes haemolytic anaemia — excessive haemolysis of RBCs infected by the parasite. This releases large quantities of haemoglobin, which is catabolised to unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. This overwhelms the liver conjugation capacity, producing pre-hepatic (haemolytic) jaundice with elevated unconjugated bilirubin — not obstructive jaundice.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy and function of the large intestine, including its absorbing and storage portions.
(ii) State how its regions relate to the pathologies that can occur.
(iii) Explain how disease/function of the large intestine may affect a distant structure and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) About 1500 mL of chyme normally passes through the ileocaecal valve into the large intestine each day; most of the water and electrolytes in this chyme are absorbed in the colon, usually leaving less than 100 mL of fluid to be excreted in the faeces. Most absorption in the large intestine occurs in the proximal half of the colon, giving this portion the name 'absorbing colon', whereas the distal colon functions principally for faeces storage until a propitious time for excretion, and is therefore called the 'storage colon'.
The large intestine has a high capability for active absorption of Na+, and the electrical potential gradient created by absorption of sodium causes Cl- absorption; the mucosa of the large intestine also secretes bicarbonate while simultaneously absorbing an equal number of chloride ions, and this bicarbonate helps neutralize the acidic end-products of bacterial action; absorption of Na+ and Cl- creates an osmotic gradient across the large intestinal mucosa, which causes absorption of water. About 5 to 8 litres of fluid and electrolytes is absorbed by the large intestine each day; numerous bacteria, especially colon bacilli, are present even normally in the absorbing colon. Bacterial activity forms vitamin K, vitamin B12, thiamine, riboflavin, and various gases that contribute to flatus (especially carbon dioxide, hydrogen gas and methane).
(ii) Hirschsprung's disease involves loss of the enteric nervous system in the distal part of the colon and always involves the internal anal sphincter, causing faecal build-up and colonic distension; diarrhoea results when abnormal motility causes faecal matter to move through the colon with minimal absorption.
(iii) The bacterially-formed vitamin K is especially important, because the amount of this vitamin in the daily ingested food is normally insufficient to maintain adequate blood coagulation; this is a direct example of a function of the large intestine (bacterial vitamin K synthesis) whose disruption would cause a functional deficit in a distant system (impaired blood coagulation). Toxins from cholera or certain other bacterial infections can cause the crypts in the terminal ileum and in the large intestine to secrete 10 or more litres of fluid each day, leading to severe and sometimes lethal diarrhoea, which in turn can cause dehydration and, through loss of bicarbonate and potassium, metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia.

questions.question:
A person develops sneezing, itching and skin rashes on exposure to a substance, having had no reaction on the first exposure to it.
(i) Identify the condition, define it and explain why the first exposure produced no response.
(ii) Classify the common allergens (predisposing agents).
(iii) State the symptoms, the potential severity and the common allergic conditions.
questions.answerText:
(i) Allergy (hypersensitivity): an abnormal immune response to a chemical or physical agent (allergen); the allergic reaction is the inflammatory response to subsequent exposure to a particular allergen (immunological hypersensitivity reaction).
(i) On first exposure to an allergen there is no immune response; the reaction occurs on subsequent exposure.
(ii) An allergen may be an antigen, a protein or any other type of substance.
(ii) Food substances: wheat, egg, milk, chocolate. Inhalants: pollen grains, fungi, dust, smoke, perfumes, disagreeable odour. Contactants: chemical substances, metals, animals, plants.
(ii) Infectious agents: parasites, bacteria, viruses, fungi. Drugs: aspirin, antibiotics. Physical agents: cold, heat, light, pressure, radiation.
(iii) Symptoms include sneezing, itching and skin rashes; in some persons symptoms may be severe.
(iii) Common allergic conditions: food allergy, allergic rhinitis, bronchial asthma, urticaria.

questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, relations, branches and distribution of the conduction system of the heart; state the safe site for ECG recording; and explain the anatomical basis of ECG waveform abnormalities after injury to specific components.
A. Describe the components of the conduction system and their conduction rates.
B(i) . Describe the action potential phases of ventricular cardiac muscle.
B(ii) . Distinguish between absolute and relative refractory periods.
C. Explain each component of the normal ECG waveform and its normal time range.
questions.answerText:
B(i) Phases of ventricular action potential:
- Phase 4: RMP stable at –90 mV; Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels closed; open K⁺ rectifier channels.
- Phase 0: rapid Na⁺ influx through fast Na⁺ channels (depolarisation).
- Phase 1: transient K⁺ channels open; K⁺ efflux returns TMP to 0 mV.
- Phase 2 (plateau): influx of Ca²⁺ through L-type Ca²⁺ channels electrically balanced by K⁺ efflux through delayed rectifier K⁺ channels.
- Phase 3: Ca²⁺ channels close; delayed rectifier K⁺ channels remain open; TMP returns to –90 mV.
B(ii) Absolute refractory period: no stimulus, no matter how strong, will depolarise the cell. Relative refractory period: a sufficiently strong stimulus will depolarise the myocardium.
C. ECG waveform components and normal ranges:
- P wave: depolarisation of atria in response to SA node triggering.
- PR interval: delay at AV node to allow ventricular filling; normal: 0.12–0.20 s.
- QRS complex: ventricular depolarisation (triggers contraction); normal: 0.07–0.12 s.
- ST segment and T wave: ventricular repolarisation; normal QT: 0.327–0.44 s.

questions.question:
Endoscopic biopsy of the lower oesophagus in a patient with a weakened lower oesophageal sphincter and chronic burning chest pain shows reversible substitution of the normal stratified squamous epithelium for simple columnar epithelium.
(i) Identify the organ/structure affected.
(ii) State the differential pathologies.
(iii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for this finding.
questions.answerText:
(i) The lower oesophagus, specifically its epithelial lining (Barrett's oesophagus).
(ii) Gastro-oesophageal reflux (a weakened lower oesophageal sphincter, causing burning chest pain) as a simple entity, Barrett's oesophagus (chronic acid reflux resulting in the described metaplasia), and, if untreated, progression to adenocarcinoma, are the pathologies described in this sequence.
(iii) Gastro-oesophageal reflux is caused by a weakened lower oesophageal sphincter, producing chest pain of a burning nature.
Chronic acid reflux (Barrett's oesophagus) results in reversible substitution of the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus for simple columnar epithelium (metaplasia); untreated, chronic metaplasia can become irreversible and progress to adenocarcinoma.

A(i) Appearance and shape: Erythrocytes have a biconcave disc shape, which is suited for gas exchange. The shape is flexible so that RBCs can pass through the smallest blood vessels (capillaries). The biconcave shape maximises surface area for diffusion.
A(ii) Primary cellular content: haemoglobin, the protein that binds oxygen and carbon dioxide. RBCs have no nucleus nor mitochondria. Haemoglobin consists of globin and heme pigment. Structure was first unravelled by Max Perutz in 1959 using X-ray crystallography.
A(iii) Haemoglobin types:
- HBA: 2 alpha and 2 beta subunits.
- HBF: 2 alpha and 2 gamma subunits.
Each subunit binds to a heme group. Each heme group bears an atom of iron, which binds reversibly with one molecule of oxygen; haemoglobin carries four molecules of oxygen.
A(iv) Forms of haemoglobin:
- Oxyhaemoglobin: bound with oxygen; red.
- Deoxyhaemoglobin: free of oxygen; dark red.
- Carbaminohaemoglobin: 20% of carbon dioxide in the blood binds to the globin part of haemoglobin.
- Carboxyhaemoglobin: carbon monoxide competes with oxygen for haem binding with a much higher affinity, causing deoxygenation of haemoglobin. Treatment: hyperbaric oxygen chamber.
B(i) MCV: Mean Corpuscular Volume is the average volume of a single RBC expressed in cubic microns (cu µ). Normal MCV is 90 cu µ (78 to 90 cu µ). When MCV is normal, the RBC is called a normocyte.
B(ii) MCH: Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin is the quantity or amount of haemoglobin present in one RBC. Expressed in picograms (pg). Normal value of MCH is 30 pg (27 to 32 pg).
B(iii) MCHC: Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration is the concentration of haemoglobin in one RBC — the amount of haemoglobin expressed in relation to the volume of one RBC. Normal value of MCHC is 30% (30% to 38%). When MCHC is normal, the RBC is normochromic. When MCHC decreases, the RBC is hypochromic. A single RBC cannot be hyperchromic.
B(iv) Colour Index (CI): the ratio between the percentage of haemoglobin and the percentage of RBCs in the blood; the average haemoglobin content in one cell of a patient compared to the average haemoglobin content.
C. Primary function: transport oxygen from the lung to tissue cells and carbon dioxide from tissue cells to the lung. Secondary function: buffer blood pH.

questions.answerText:
(i) In the region of absorption and secretion (as opposed to the mouth, oesophagus and anus, which have stratified squamous epithelium), a single-layered columnar epithelium is found, characterized by folding and finger-like projections called villi. About 2 L/day of fluid is secreted by the small intestine, mostly mucus, from Brunner's glands within the duodenum and goblet cells within the intestinal crypts of Lieberkuhn; enzymes capable of breaking down small peptides and disaccharides (e.g. aminopeptidases, amylases, sucrase, maltase) are located on the brush border of the epithelial cells, along with secretion of water and electrolytes.
Enterocytes absorb glucose and galactose through an Na-dependent secondary active transport process (SGLT-1), while fructose is absorbed by facilitated transport; ionic iron is transported into mucosal cells where it binds to ferritin, and Ca2+ absorption is related to blood levels of ionic calcium and is regulated by vitamin D and parathyroid hormone (PTH). In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases cleave the R proteins carrying vitamin B12, allowing B12 to bind intrinsic factor (secreted by the gastric parietal cells), which protects it until it is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
(ii) Crohn's disease is inflammation of the small intestine (enteritis, IBD), usually affecting the ileum, caused by the immune system reacting to an infection (viral or bacterial); coeliac disease is an autoimmune disorder resulting in damage of the mucosa and atrophy of villi, causing impaired digestion and absorption; steatorrhoea is caused by deficiency of pancreatic lipase, resulting in malabsorption of fat.
(iii) If any part of the B12-intrinsic factor pathway is lost, B12 cannot be absorbed in the terminal ileum, and because B12 is critical for maturation of red blood cells, pernicious (macrocytic) anaemia develops - a deficit at a distant site (the blood/bone marrow) caused by failure of absorption in the small intestine. Because glucose is absorbed into enterocytes by SGLT-1 transporters, rapid glucose absorption facilitates sodium, chloride and water absorption; this is the basis of oral rehydration therapy for enteric diseases such as cholera, showing how the absorptive function of the small intestine can be exploited to correct a distant, systemic problem (dehydration) when its normal fluid-handling capacity elsewhere (the colon) is overwhelmed.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Glomerular filtration barrier — three layers:
pores 50-100 nm in diameter; prevents filtration of blood cells but allows all components of blood plasma to pass through.
2. Glomerular basement membrane (basal lamina): does not contain visible gaps; surrounded by polyanions; prevents filtration of larger proteins.
3. Epithelial cell slit membrane (pedicels of podocytes): slits approximately 25 nm wide; prevents filtration of medium-sized proteins.
A(ii) Glomerular filtrate: Barrier permits free passage of neutral substances up to 4 nm in diameter and almost totally excludes those greater than 8 nm. The membrane provides structural and electrical barriers. Order of filtration: cationic > neutral > anionic. Protein, cellular elements (RBCs, WBCs, platelets), fatty acids, about 50% of Ca2+ and substances dependent on plasma protein are NOT filtered. Electrolytes, glucose, water, and urea ARE filtered. GF is an ultrafiltrate of plasma that does not contain protein.
A(iii) Tubular reabsorption: Transfer of substances from the lumen into peritubular capillaries. Daily averages: water — 180 L filtered, 1.8 L excreted, 99% reabsorbed; sodium — 630 g filtered, 3.2 g excreted, 99.5% reabsorbed; glucose — 180 g filtered, 0 g excreted, 100% reabsorbed; urea — 54 g filtered, 30 g excreted, 44% reabsorbed.
A(iv) Tubular secretion: Transfer of substances from peritubular capillaries into the lumen. K+ or H+ is secreted in the distal tubules in exchange for reabsorbed sodium. The kidney also secretes large numbers of organic ions such as creatinine and foreign chemicals such as penicillin.
A(v) Tubular cell metabolism: Kidney cells synthesise NH3 added to luminal fluid and excreted. Cells also catabolise certain organic substances (e.g., peptides) taken up from tubular lumen or peritubular capillaries, eliminating them from the body.
B. Sodium reabsorption by segment:
- Proximal convoluted tubules: 60%; transporters — Na-H exchanger, Na-Glucose co-transporter, Na-Pi co-transporter, Na-Lactate co-transporter, Na-Amino acid co-transporter at apical membrane; Na-K pump at basolateral membrane.
- Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle: 30%; transporter — Na-2Cl-K co-transporter, Na-H exchanger at apical; Na-K pump at basolateral.
- Distal convoluted tubules: 7%; transporter — Na-Cl co-transporter at apical; Na-K pump at basolateral.
- Collecting tubules: 3% (depends on aldosterone); ENaC channels at apical; Na-K pump at basolateral.
C. Water reabsorption by segment:
- PCT: 60-70% reabsorption facilitated by aquaporin 1 in apical and basolateral membrane.
- Descending limb of loop of Henle: 15% reabsorption facilitated by aquaporin 1.
- DCT and CT: about 10% reabsorption facilitated by aquaporin 2 (under ADH influence) in vesicles inside cells; aquaporins 3 and 4 at basolateral membrane. Over 4% may be reabsorbed in inner medullary collecting duct under ADH influence.

Describe the neuromuscular junction under the following headings:
(i) its components
(ii) the steps of neuromuscular transmission
(iii) the mechanism of calcium-triggered neurotransmitter release.
Explain the clinical basis of myasthenia gravis at this junction.
Distinguish the neuromuscular junction from a general/interneuronal CNS synapse.
questions.answerText:
(i) The components of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) are: the presynaptic membrane (motor nerve), the postsynaptic membrane (muscle cell), synaptic vesicles, the synaptic cleft, the neurotransmitter (acetylcholine), and the receptors (acetylcholine receptors, which are ligand-gated channels).
(ii) The steps in neuromuscular transmission are: arrival of the action potential at the presynaptic membrane; opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; influx of Ca2+ into the cell; Ca2+ signalling to the vesicles; movement of vesicles to the membrane; release of neurotransmitter by exocytosis; diffusion of the neurotransmitter across the synaptic cleft; and binding to the postsynaptic membrane.
(iii) Depolarization caused by an action potential transiently opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and increases Ca2+ conductance; Ca2+ flows down its electrochemical gradient into the axon terminal at a high rate, but this rise is short-lived because Ca2+-binding proteins and Ca2+ pumps (e.g. the Na/Ca antiporter) rapidly remove it, so the terminal is quickly ready to transmit again.
The Ca2+ influx triggers an interaction of contractile proteins attached to the presynaptic membrane with the synaptic vesicles; the vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and discharge their contents into the cleft by exocytosis, restricted to specialized 'active zones' exactly opposite the postsynaptic receptors; the discharged vesicle membrane is then retrieved by endocytosis.
An axon terminal at the NMJ typically releases a few hundred of its many thousands of synaptic vesicles in response to a single action potential; the time for calcium channels to open in response to depolarization is the major component of synaptic delay.
Clinical basis: myasthenia gravis is a condition associated with severe muscular weakness due to a decrease in the number of acetylcholine receptors in the muscle cell (the postsynaptic component of this junction); inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (e.g. neostigmine) are used to treat it, increasing the availability of acetylcholine at the junction to compensate for the reduced receptor number.
Distinguishing feature 1: neuromuscular junctions are specific chemical synapses between the axons of motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres, also known as 'motor end-plates'.
Distinguishing feature 2: at the NMJ, the motor nerve loses its myelin sheath and divides into fine terminal branches lying in synaptic troughs on the muscle cell surface, with the postsynaptic muscle membrane thrown into numerous junctional folds where acetylcholine receptors are concentrated near the mouths of the folds, and acetylcholinesterase evenly distributed on the external postsynaptic surface.
The NMJ possesses all the common characteristics of CNS synapses and was among the first synapses studied, and is often used as the model for the general (interneuronal) chemical synapse, which likewise has its own presynaptic membrane, postsynaptic membrane, synaptic cleft, synaptic vesicles and neurotransmitters.

questions.question:
Three patients each pass a large volume of urine. Patient 1 has taken a large volume of hypotonic fluid. Patient 2 has diabetes mellitus and presents with dehydration, polydipsia and polyuria. Patient 3 has an increase in arterial pressure.
(i) Name the type of diuresis in each patient.
(ii) Explain the mechanism and urinary osmolarity in each type.
(iii) State the causes and complications of each type.
(iv) State the compensatory significance of the third type.
questions.answerText:
(i) Patient 1: water/fluid diuresis; Patient 2: solute/osmotic diuresis; Patient 3: pressure diuresis (diuresis = excretion of a large volume of urine).
(ii) Water diuresis: lack of ADH secretion after a large intake of hypotonic fluid; water reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule is normal; maximum urine production rate is stated as 16 L/min; urine osmolarity <250 mOsm/L.
(ii) Osmotic diuresis: unreabsorbed osmotically active compounds in the tubular lumen retain water; urine osmolarity >300 mOsm/L.
(ii) Pressure diuresis: increased urinary water excretion when arterial pressure rises; medullary blood flow increases because the medulla lacks renal autoregulation, dissipating medullary hyperosmolarity and increasing urine production.
(iii) Water diuresis causes: large hypotonic fluid intake; tea (theobromine dilates renal vessels and increases blood flow); alcohol (suppresses ADH release); diabetes insipidus (neurogenic and nephrogenic). Complication: water intoxication.
(iii) Osmotic diuresis results in dehydration, polydipsia and polyuria, as seen in diabetes mellitus.
(iii) Pressure diuresis: cause is a rise in arterial pressure with increased medullary blood flow.
(iv) Pressure diuresis is a compensatory mechanism to maintain blood pressure within the normal range.

(i) Myasthenia gravis.
(ii) It is a condition associated with severe muscular weakness due to a decrease in the number of acetylcholine receptors in the muscle cell; it is also described as a neuromuscular disease leading to fluctuating muscle weakness and fatigability during simple activities, caused by circulating antibodies that block acetylcholine receptors at the post-synaptic neuromuscular junction, and is classified as a synaptopathy.
(iii) Inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) are used to treat patients with myasthenia gravis, e.g. neostigmine.

questions.answerText:

- Fraction of body weight: 8%.
- Volume: female 4-5 L; male 5-6 L.

A(iii) Haematocrit:
- Female: 37%-48%.

A(iv) :
- Haemoglobin: female 12-16 g/100 mL; male 13-18 g/100 mL.
- Mean RBC count: female 4.8 million/µL; male 5.4 million/µL.
- Platelet count: 130,000-360,000/µL.
- Total WBC count: 4,000-11,000/µL.
B(i) Composition of plasma:
- Water: 92% by weight.
- Total protein: 6-9 g/100 mL.
- Albumin: 60% of total plasma protein.
- Globulin: 36% of total plasma protein.
- Fibrinogen: 4% of total plasma protein.
B(ii) Key electrolytes:
- Sodium: 135-145 mEq/L.
- Potassium: 3.5-5.0 mEq/L.
- Calcium: 9.2-10.4 mEq/L.
- Chloride: 90-106 mEq/L.

C. Plasma vs serum: Serum = Plasma minus fibrinogen (clotting proteins). Plasma is a straw-coloured clear liquid part of blood containing 91-92% water and 8-9% solids. Serum is the fluid obtained after clotting has occurred and the clot has been removed.
Three major functions of blood:
oxygen from lungs to body cells; carbon dioxide from body cells to lungs; nutrients from GI tract to body cells; hormones from glands to body cells; waste products to excretory organs.
2. Regulation (maintenance of homeostasis): maintenance of normal body pH (bicarbonate system); exchange of water, electrolytes, and hydrogen ions between body compartments; maintenance of temperature.
humoral antibodies, chemical agents, enzymes, and cellular elements important in defence of the body against infection or invasion by foreign tissue/organism.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Erythroblastosis fetalis (haemolytic disease of the newborn) — Rh incompatibility.
First pregnancy spared: In the first pregnancy, the foetus is protected by the placenta-blood barrier, preventing transfer of foetal Rh-positive RBCs into the maternal circulation (or transfer is minimal). No anti-Rh antibody is present in the mother at the time of the first pregnancy, so no haemolysis occurs.
(ii) Mechanism in second pregnancy: Infusion of Rh-positive blood (from the foetus) into the Rh-negative mother (during the first delivery or during the second pregnancy via placental breaches) leads to development of anti-Rh antibody in the mother. On second experience of Rh-positive foetal RBCs, maternal anti-Rh antibody crosses the placenta, destroys Rh-positive foetal RBCs, and causes Rhesus haemolytic disease of the newborn — erythroblastosis fetalis.
(iii) Risk factors determining severity: The Rh antigen (D antigen) was first discovered on the blood of the rhesus monkey. About 85% of white people are Rh-positive and 15% are Rh-negative. In African blacks, the percentage of Rh-positives is virtually 100%. The corresponding antibody is not naturally present in plasma of Rh-negative individuals — antibody only forms after exposure. Severity is related to the degree of immunisation of the mother (antibody titre) and the number of sensitising exposures.
(iv) Prevention: Administration of Rh immunoglobulin (anti-D immunoglobulin) to the Rh-negative mother after delivery of the first Rh-positive infant (or after any sensitising event). This prevents the mother from producing anti-Rh antibodies, protecting future Rh-positive pregnancies from haemolytic disease.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy/organization of the hypothalamus, including its prominent nuclei.
(ii) State how these nuclei relate to their physiological functions.
(iii) Explain how the hypothalamus acts on the distant pituitary gland to control secretion, and the functional consequence of dysfunction.
questions.answerText:
(i) The hypothalamus is the portion of the brain linking the nervous system to the endocrine system; it is located below the thalamus, is part of the limbic system, is present in all vertebrates, and is about the size of an almond.
(ii) Preoptic area: sleep, care of young, mating.
- Suprachiasmatic nucleus: circadian rhythm.
- Anterior hypothalamus: thermoregulation.
- Paraventricular nucleus: pituitary hormone release, thirst (also the source of oxytocin).
- Supraoptic nucleus: thirst, milk ejection (also the source of ADH).
- Lateral hypothalamus: thirst, hunger, sleep.
- Arcuate nucleus: feeding (also source of GHRH).
- Ventromedial nucleus: satiety, mating (also source of GHIH/somatostatin).
- Posterior hypothalamus: thermoregulation; mammillary bodies: memory.
(iii) The hypothalamus produces hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, GHIH, PIH/dopamine) that regulate secretion of the anterior pituitary via the portal circulation, and produces ADH and oxytocin, which travel along axons to be stored in and released from the posterior pituitary. Dysfunction of these hypothalamic nuclei/hormones has distant functional consequences: e.g. TRH deficiency reduces TSH and thyroid hormone secretion; CRH deficiency reduces ACTH and cortisol; GnRH deficiency reduces FSH/LH and gonadal hormone secretion; GHRH/GHIH imbalance alters GH secretion; and absence of vasopressin secretion by the hypothalamus causes central diabetes insipidus.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the neuromuscular junction, including its components and characteristics.
(ii) State how its components relate to the disease that can occur when they are affected.
questions.answerText:
(i) Neuromuscular junctions are specific chemical synapses, between the axons of motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres, also known as 'motor end-plates'; they possess all common characteristics of CNS synapses and have been among the first synapses studied.
Components: the presynaptic membrane (motor nerve), the postsynaptic membrane (muscle cell), synaptic vesicles, the synaptic cleft, the neurotransmitter (acetylcholine), and the receptors (acetylcholine receptors, which are ligand-gated channels).
Characteristics: the motor nerve loses its myelin sheath and divides into fine terminal branches lying in synaptic troughs on the muscle cell surface; the plasma membrane of the muscle cell lining the trough is thrown into numerous junctional folds; the axon terminals contain many synaptic vesicles containing acetylcholine; acetylcholine receptors are concentrated near the mouths of the junctional folds, and acetylcholinesterase is evenly distributed on the external surface of the postsynaptic membrane. Transmission occurs when a quantum of acetylcholine from the nerve ending is released and binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the post-junctional muscle membrane.
(ii) Myasthenia gravis is a condition of severe muscular weakness due to a decrease in the number of acetylcholine receptors in the muscle cell. Inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (e.g. neostigmine) are used to treat it, increasing the availability of acetylcholine at the junction to compensate for the reduced receptor number.

questions.question:
During a cystometrogram in a healthy adult, the bladder is filled progressively with urine.
(i) Describe the pressure-volume changes recorded at about 50 mL, 200-300 mL, about 400 mL and beyond 600-700 mL.
(ii) Name each component of the micturition reflex arc.
(iii) State the roles of the sympathetic and pudendal nerves and explain the period of inhibition after a reflex that fails to empty the bladder.
(iv) Describe the events of micturition and how voluntary micturition is facilitated.
questions.answerText:
(i) The cystometrogram records intravesical pressure as the bladder fills; an empty bladder has zero pressure.
(i) About 50 mL: pressure rises sharply to about 5 cm H2O; a further 200-300 mL adds little pressure because detrusor relaxation increases the radius (Law of Laplace, P=2T/r).
(i) About 400 mL: detrusor contraction becomes intense with urge to void and voluntary control is still possible; beyond 600-700 mL voluntary control fails and micturition occurs spontaneously.
(ii) Micturition contractions are a stretch reflex: stimulus is bladder filling/stretch; receptors are stretch receptors in the bladder wall; afferent is via the pelvic nerves; centre is the sacral spinal cord; efferent is parasympathetic; effector is detrusor contraction with relaxation of the internal sphincter.
(iii) In a partly filled bladder contractions relax and pressure returns to baseline, mediated by sympathetic stimulation (detrusor relaxes, internal sphincter contracts).
(iii) A reflex that fails to empty the bladder is followed by inhibition lasting a few minutes to 1 hour or more; with more filling reflexes become more frequent and more potent.
(iii) A powerful reflex passes through the pudendal nerves to inhibit the external sphincter; urination occurs if this is more potent than voluntary constrictor signals to the external sphincter.
(iv) Process: abdominal pressure rises (diaphragm descends, abdominal muscles contract), perineal muscles relax, the detrusor contracts, both sphincters relax and urine passes out through the urethra.
(iv) Voluntary micturition: voluntary abdominal contraction raises abdominal pressure, allowing extra urine into the bladder and raising bladder pressure, which stimulates stretch receptors to initiate the micturition reflex.

A(i) Splanchnic circulation includes blood flow through the gut itself and the flow through the spleen, pancreas, and liver. The system is designed so that all the blood that courses through the gut, spleen, and pancreas then flows immediately into the liver by way of the portal vein (portal circulation). In the liver, it passes through liver sinusoids and empties into hepatic veins that empty into the vena cava. This pattern allows reticuloendothelial cells lining the liver sinusoids to remove bacteria and other particulate matter that might enter the blood from the gastrointestinal tract.
A(ii) Blood flow in each area of the gastrointestinal tract, as well as in each layer of the gut wall, is directly related to the level of local activity. Blood flow in the muscle layers of the intestinal wall increases with increased motor activity in the gut. Arterial blood supply includes the superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries, which supply the walls of the small and large intestines by way of an arching arterial system.
A(iii) Countercurrent exchange in intestinal villi: The direction of blood flow in the capillaries and venules is opposite that in the main arteriole — countercurrent exchange system. This effective countercurrent system permits diffusion of oxygen from arterioles to venules. At low blood flow, shunting of oxygen may cause necrosis of intestinal villi tips.
B(i) Nervous control:
- Parasympathetic: stimulation of parasympathetic nerves going to the stomach and lower colon increases local blood flow at the same time that it increases glandular secretion. Increased flow results secondarily from the increased glandular activity and not as a direct effect of the nervous stimulation.
- Sympathetic: stimulation acting via alpha adrenergic receptors has a direct effect causing intense vasoconstriction of the arterioles with greatly decreased blood flow. Vasoconstriction is however a temporary effect; local metabolic vasodilator mechanisms that are elicited by ischaemia become prepotent over sympathetic vasoconstriction, therefore redilating the arterioles, causing return of necessary nutrient blood flow to gastrointestinal glands and muscle.
B(ii) Local control:
- Vasodilator substances (CCK, VIP, Gastrin, and Secretin) are released from the mucosa of the intestinal tract during the digestive process.
- Release of kallidin and bradykinin follows gastrointestinal gland secretions; these kinins are powerful vasodilators causing much of the increased mucosal vasodilation that occurs along with secretion.
- Decreased oxygen concentration in the gut wall increases intestinal blood flow at least 50-100%. The decrease in oxygen can also lead to as much as a fourfold increase of adenosine, a vasodilator responsible for much of the increased flow.
C(i) Primary function of cutaneous blood flow: to maintain a constant body temperature (not primarily to supply oxygen and nutrients). The skin undergoes wide fluctuations in blood flow depending on the need to conserve heat or lose it. Two resistance vessels: arterioles and arteriovenous anastomoses (which shunt blood from arterioles to venules and venous plexus).
C(ii) Neural control of AV anastomoses: AV anastomoses have walls richly supplied with nerves and are almost exclusively under sympathetic neural control. They dilate maximally when their nerve supply is interrupted. Sympathetic stimulation causes constriction and may obliterate the vascular lumen. AV anastomoses are highly sensitive to vasoconstrictor agents such as adrenaline and noradrenalin.
C(iii) Difference in control:
- AV anastomoses: not under metabolic control; they do not exhibit reactive hyperaemia or autoregulation of blood flow. Regulation is mainly governed by the nervous system in response to reflex activation by temperature receptors or from higher centres in the CNS.
- Arterioles supplying the skin: responsive to autoregulation and reactive hyperaemia. Parasympathetic vasodilator nerve fibres do not innervate cutaneous blood vessels. Stimulation of the sweat glands (innervated by parasympathetic cholinergic fibers) dilates the skin's resistance vessels.

(i) Describe the organization of the hypothalamo-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis, from hypothalamic hormone to thyroid hormone, including the structures involved.
(ii) Explain the anatomical/functional consequence of chronic overstimulation of this axis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH) is manufactured in the hypothalamus and transported via the portal circulation to the pituitary, where it leads to exocytosis of TSH; TRH is a modified tripeptide synthesized as a prohormone by peptidergic hypothalamic nuclei.
- TRH stimulates TSH synthesis and secretion by binding to receptors on pituitary thyrotroph cell membranes linked to phospholipase C; TSH then stimulates thyroid hormone (T3/T4) synthesis and secretion by the thyroid gland by influencing iodide trapping, iodide binding, synthesis of T3/T4, secretion of thyroglobulin into the colloid, and endocytosis of colloid.
- TSH also increases blood supply to the thyroid gland and increases the size and number of follicles.
(ii) A chronic rise of TSH causes thyroid hypertrophy or goitre, i.e. an increase in the size and number of thyroid follicles, illustrating the anatomical/functional consequence of sustained overstimulation of this axis.

(ii) Disequilibrium in synthesis and resorption, or obstruction of circulation, results in CSF accumulation and raised intracranial pressure called hydrocephalus; composition of CSF is closely regulated and any variation can be used for diagnostic purposes, examined clinically through a lumbar puncture.
(iii) The choroid plexus, located in the lateral, third and fourth ventricles, is the structure that predominantly secretes/produces CSF, whereas the arachnoid villi are out-pouchings of the arachnoid mater (arachnoid granulations) responsible for resorption of CSF into the dural venous (superior sagittal) sinus and act as one-way valves.

(i) Origin: the sympathetic nerves are described alongside the parasympathetic (glossopharyngeal and facial) supply as innervating the salivary glands.
Course: the sympathetic nerves innervate the blood vessels around the glands, as well as the myoepithelial cells in the acini.
Distribution: sympathetic stimulation (e.g. during stress) reduces blood flow to the glands but contracts the myoepithelial cells, releasing preformed mucous saliva.
(ii) After this initial release of preformed mucous saliva, flow decreases, resulting in dry mouth. This follows from the dual action described: contraction of the myoepithelial cells around the acini squeezes out stored mucous saliva, giving an initial release, but the accompanying reduction in glandular blood flow (in contrast to the parasympathetic effect of increasing blood flow) then limits further ultrafiltrate secretion, so flow subsequently falls. This is distinguished from parasympathetic stimulation, which instead increases blood flow and acinar ultrafiltrate secretion into the acini, and whose loss (by nerve section) causes glandular atrophy rather than a transient dry mouth.

A(i) Normal values:
- Total proteins: 7.3 g/dL (range 6-9 g/dL).
- Serum albumin: 4.7 g/dL.
- Serum globulin: 2.3 g/dL.
- Fibrinogen: 0.3 g/dL.
- A/G ratio: 2:1 (normal range 0.8-2.0).
A(ii) Molecular weights:
- Albumin: 69,000.
- Globulin: 156,000.
- Fibrinogen: 400,000.
A(iii) Sites of synthesis:
- Albumin, fibrinogen, and prothrombin: formed in the liver.
- Immunoglobulins (gamma globulins): formed in lymphoid tissues.
B. Functions of plasma proteins:
fibrinogen is essential for coagulation of blood.
gamma globulins act as antibodies (immunoglobulins) in defence of the body.
albumin transports calcium and bilirubin; alpha globulins transport iron (transferrin), cholesterol, lipids, insulin, and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, and K.
4. Maintenance of osmotic (oncotic) pressure: approximately 25 mmHg; pulls water from tissue spaces into blood.
albumin contributes 15% of buffering capacity of blood.
albumin provides maximum viscosity; important in maintaining blood pressure.
globulin and fibrinogen accelerate rouleaux formation, responsible for ESR.
C. Oedema mechanism: Plasma proteins are responsible for oncotic (colloidal osmotic) pressure of approximately 25 mmHg. This pressure pulls water from tissue spaces into blood. In liver disease, reduced synthesis of albumin lowers oncotic pressure. In nephrotic syndrome, urinary protein loss reduces plasma protein levels. In both cases, the reduced oncotic pressure cannot draw fluid back from interstitial spaces into capillaries, leading to accumulation of fluid in the interstitium — peripheral oedema.
