questions.answerText:
(i) The causative agent is the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, which is contracted in a faecal-oral manner, usually through ingestion of contaminated water.
(ii) This is a secretory diarrhoea, caused specifically by increased secretion of solutes into the lumen of the gut; toxins from cholera often cause the crypts in the terminal ileum and the large intestine to secrete 10 or more litres of fluid each day, leading to severe and sometimes lethal diarrhoea.
Chronic diarrhoea can result in dehydration, and the loss of bicarbonate and potassium can lead to metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia (low plasma potassium).
(iii) Because glucose is absorbed into the enterocytes by SGLT-1 transporters, the rapid absorption of glucose facilitates sodium absorption, and hence chloride and water absorption; this is the principle behind oral rehydration therapy (ORT) for dehydration or enteric diseases such as cholera.
Justification: oral rehydration therapy is justified because it exploits the SGLT-1-coupled glucose-sodium co-transport that remains intact in cholera, so that glucose-driven sodium absorption in turn drives chloride and water absorption, correcting the dehydration produced by the massive crypt fluid secretion.

questions.answerText:
(i) Venous return and facilitating factors:
- Veins are capacitance vessels; hold 2/3 of total blood volume; high compliance; lower pressure than arteries.
Factors:
- Pressure difference between arteries and veins (about 10 mmHg).
- Pressure gradient in venous system (highest in venules, lowest in vena cava).
- Sympathetic nerve activity to stimulate smooth muscle contraction, lower compliance.
- Pressure difference between abdominal and thoracic cavities (respiration).
- Blood volume.
(ii) Venous return determines end-diastolic volume (preload). Increased venous return increases EDV, which by the Frank-Starling mechanism stretches ventricular muscle fibres, increasing force of contraction and therefore stroke volume.
(iii) Physiological variations of cardiac output:
- Age: greater in adults than children (more blood volume).
- Gender: greater in males than females.
- Altitude: increases at high altitude.
- Pregnancy: increases during pregnancy.
- Exercise: increases during exercise.
- Emotion: increases during emotional expressions.
Cardiac reserve: adults 300–400%; athletes 500–600%; old age 200–250%.
(iv) Fick principle: amount of substance taken up by an organ per unit time (Q) = (arterial level − venous level) × blood flow. Applied to pulmonary blood flow: CO = O₂ consumed / (arterial O₂ − venous O₂). Direct method: blood samples from peripheral artery and pulmonary artery for O₂ content; invasive (risk of infection, haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation). Indirect method: spirometer determines O₂ consumption; less invasive.
(v) Three other methods:
- Dilution methods (e.g. Evan's blue dye): known amount injected into right atrium; mean concentration of first passage through an artery determined; CO = Q/(C × t) × 60.
- Thermodilution: same principle as dye dilution but cold saline is used; change in blood temperature in pulmonary artery is determined; results in CO calculation.
- Doppler echocardiography: B-scan ultrasound at 2.25 MHz; measures EDV, ESV, CO, and valvular defects non-invasively.

A patient with a chronic autoimmune condition destroying the gastric mucosa is found to have a macrocytic anaemia.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pernicious anaemia (macrocytic anaemia due to loss of intrinsic factor).
(ii) Achlorhydria, described as a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by destruction of the gastric mucosa, is the predisposing condition; this destroys the parietal (oxyntic) cells, which are located in the body of the stomach and secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
(iii) Intrinsic factor is a glycoprotein secreted by the gastric parietal cells that binds to vitamin B12 and is essential for B12 absorption in the distal ileum; in the duodenum, pancreatic proteases cleave the R proteins carrying B12, allowing B12 to bind intrinsic factor, which protects it until it is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
If any part of this pathway, especially intrinsic factor, is lost, B12 cannot be absorbed, and because B12 is critical for maturation of red blood cells, macrocytic (pernicious) anaemia develops.

questions.question:
An adult patient, while awake, has an electroencephalogram (EEG) that shows a persistent low-frequency wave pattern (1-3.5 cycles/sec).
(i) Identify the wave/pattern recorded.
(ii) State the structures generating this wave pattern.
(iii) State the differential clinical interpretations for abnormal EEG patterns in general.
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for the significance of this finding.
questions.answerText:
(i) A delta wave.
(ii) Delta waves are emitted generally from the cerebral cortex, with a frequency between 1-3.5 cycles/sec (<4).
(iii) Deviations from normal EEG patterns can be used clinically to diagnose epilepsy and localize brain tumours; the absence of EEG tracings can be used to detect brain death.
(iv) Delta waves are common in slow wave sleep in adults and in awake infants; presence of delta waves in an awake adult indicates brain damage, so this EEG finding in an awake adult is clinically significant, reflecting abnormal cortical electrical activity generated by synaptic potentials at the cell bodies and dendrites of the cerebral cortex.

(i) Blood group O must be given (universal donor). Immunological basis: type O RBCs carry neither A nor B agglutinogen (antigen) on their surface. Since they carry no A or B antigens, they will not be attacked by anti-A or anti-B agglutinins (preformed antibodies) present in any recipient's plasma regardless of the recipient's blood group. Agglutinogens are specific glycoproteins on red blood cell membranes.
(ii) Universal recipient: blood group AB. Type AB individuals carry both A and B agglutinogens on their RBCs and have no preformed agglutinins (neither anti-A nor anti-B) in their plasma. Therefore, they will not produce an agglutination reaction against donor RBCs of any ABO blood group. They can receive blood from all ABO groups.
(iii) Inheritance of blood group B: Agglutinogen A and B are inherited according to Mendelian theory of inheritance. Blood group B may have inherited group B antigen from one parent and O antigen from the other parent. Thus an individual whose phenotype is B may have a genotype BB (homozygous) or genotype BO (heterozygous).
(iv) ABO blood group distribution in Nigeria:
- Group A: 20%
- Group B: 23%
- Group AB: 5%
- Group O: 52%

A. Describe each type of leukocyte under the following headings for each cell:
A(i) Neutrophils — percentage, nucleus, size, development period, life span, and function
A(ii) Eosinophils — percentage, nucleus, size, development period, life span, and function
A(iii) Basophils — percentage, size, development period, life span, and function
A(iv) Lymphocytes — percentage, nucleus, size, development period, life span, and function
A(v) Monocytes — percentage, nucleus, size, development period, life span, and function
B. Describe the three-step process by which leukocytes are deployed to sites of infection outside blood vessels.
C. Explain the clinical basis of leukopenia occurring as a side effect of chemotherapy, identifying which other fast-growing normal cells are similarly affected.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Neutrophils: 40-70% of WBCs. Nucleus multilobed (up to six lobes). Approximately 12-14 µm in diameter. Development: 6-9 days. Life span: 6 hours to a few days. Function: phagocytise bacteria.
A(ii) Eosinophils: 1-4% of WBCs. Nucleus bilobed; approximately 12-14 µm in diameter. Development: 6-9 days. Life span: 8-12 days. Function: (1) kill parasitic worms; (2) destroy antigen-antibody complexes; (3) inactivate some inflammatory chemicals of allergy.
A(iii) Basophils: 0.5% of WBCs. Do not always have a lobed nucleus; approximately 10-12 µm in diameter. Development: 3-7 days. Life span: a few hours to a few days. Function: (1) release histamine and other mediators of inflammation; (2) contain heparin, an anticoagulant.
A(iv) Lymphocytes: 20-45% of WBCs. Nucleus spherical or indented. Principal ones are small (10 µm); larger ones in tissues approximately 20 µm. Development: days to weeks. Life span: hours to years. Function: mount immune response by direct cell attack (T cells) or via antibodies (B cells).
A(v) Monocytes: 4-8% of WBCs. Nucleus U-shaped. Largest of the circulating cells (16-22 µm in diameter). Development: 2-3 days. Life span: months. Function: phagocytosis; develop into macrophages in tissues.
B. Three-step deployment process:
migration of the WBCs toward the endothelium during blood flow.
leukocytes slip out of the capillary blood vessels.
gather in large numbers at areas of tissue damage and infection by following the chemical trail of molecules released by damaged cells or other leukocytes.
C. Clinical basis of chemotherapy-induced leukopenia: Cancerous cells grow fast, which distinguishes them from most normal cells. Chemotherapy is designed to kill fast-growing cells by interrupting mitotic cell division. Chemotherapy also kills a few normal fast-growing cells including leukocytes, hair cells, and intestinal epithelial cells.

questions.question:
Describe the synapse under the following headings:
(i) its components/structure
(ii) the steps of synaptic transmission
(iii) postsynaptic stimulation (EPSP and IPSP).
Explain the clinical basis of a synaptopathy such as myasthenia gravis.
Distinguish between a chemical synapse and an electrical synapse.
questions.answerText:
(i) The components/structure of a synapse are: the presynaptic membrane (part of the synapse belonging to the initiating neuron), the postsynaptic membrane (part belonging to the receiving neuron), the synaptic cleft (the space between the two, approximately 20 nm wide), synaptic vesicles (storage vesicles in the presynaptic terminals), and neurotransmitters (chemical substances stored in the vesicles that mediate postsynaptic changes).
(ii) The steps are: arrival of the action potential at the presynaptic neuron; neurotransmitter release; action of the neurotransmitter on the postsynaptic membrane via receptors; and inactivation of the neurotransmitter.
In sequence: the AP signal arrives at the axon terminal, local depolarization opens Ca2+ channels, Ca2+ enters the presynaptic neuron and, by binding calmodulin, causes neurotransmitter-filled vesicles to migrate to and merge with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitter into the cleft by exocytosis; the neurotransmitter then diffuses across the cleft and binds receptor channels on the pre- and postsynaptic membranes.
(iii) Once the postsynaptic ion channel opens, the effect can be excitatory (EPSP) or inhibitory (IPSP): EPSP ion channels are permeable to Na+ and K+, with more Na+ entering than K+ leaving, causing local depolarization that, if sufficient, generates an action potential.
IPSP ion channels are permeable to Cl- and K+, with Cl- entering and K+ leaving, causing local hyperpolarization that makes it more difficult to reach threshold, making an action potential less likely.
Clinical basis: synaptopathy is listed as a clinical relevance of synaptic transmission, with myasthenia gravis given as an example.
Myasthenia gravis is described elsewhere as a condition of severe muscular weakness due to a decrease in the number of acetylcholine receptors on the muscle cell, i.e. a defect at the postsynaptic membrane/receptor level of this synapse-like junction, consistent with its classification as a synaptopathy.
Distinguishing feature 1: a chemical synapse has a space (the synaptic cleft) between the axon terminus and the adjacent neuron; as the action potential reaches the presynaptic neuron's end, a neurotransmitter is released that travels across the cleft to alter the postsynaptic neuron's electric potential; this is the most common type in the human CNS.
Distinguishing feature 2: an electrical synapse is characterized by direct open channels (gap junctions) that conduct electricity from one neuron to the other, so depolarization continues directly across the membrane to the postsynaptic neuron; these are few in the CNS.
Thus a chemical synapse relies on neurotransmitter release and diffusion across a cleft, while an electrical synapse relies on direct ionic continuity through gap junctions.
Both types, however, mediate communication between one neuron and another (inter-neuronal communication), which is the general process described for synaptic transmission.

questions.question:
A patient presents with progressive weakness of skeletal muscles.
(i) Name the group of disorders and list the other abnormalities of muscle and its contraction.
(ii) Explain the normal contractile mechanism that these disorders disturb.
questions.answerText:
(i) Myopathies: muscular dystrophies are diseases characterised by progressive weakness of skeletal muscles.
(i) Other abnormalities: spasms (e.g. seizure, convulsion) and cramps (painful spasms); muscle strain (muscle or tendon overstretched or torn); denervation hypersensitivity; drugs that enhance or block transmission at the neuromuscular junction.
(ii) Motor nerve action potential opens Ca channels, ACh is released, binds end plate receptors, Na channels open and an action potential forms on the fibre; the action potential releases Ca from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca binds troponin and tropomyosin uncovers the actin sites.
(ii) Cross-bridges bind and deliver a power stroke; ATP breaks the actin-myosin bond and re-energizes the cross-bridge; Ca returns to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and contraction ceases.
(ii) The contractile proteins are myosin II, actin, tropomyosin and troponin I, T and C (others: actinin, titin, desmin).

questions.question:
A middle-aged patient is found to have blood glucose that remains too high because of insulin resistance; the patient belongs to an ethnic group in which this condition is more common.
(i) State the risk factor for this condition.
(ii) State the complications of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) The condition (Diabetes Mellitus Type II) is more common in some ethnic groups; insulin resistance keeps blood glucose too high.
(ii) Chronic complications include atherosclerosis, renal failure, and blindness.
- Associated symptoms of diabetes mellitus generally include hyperglycemia, polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, ketoacidosis, hyperlipidemia, muscle wasting, and electrolyte depletion.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the kidneys' water and electrolyte regulation system under the listed headings; explain how each mechanism maintains homeostasis; and distinguish between the actions of ADH, RAAS, and ANP.
A. Describe the sources of body water intake and routes of output with values.
B. Describe the role of ADH in regulating body fluid balance and the consequences of its deficiency.
C(i) . Describe the full RAAS cascade from stimulus to final effector action.
C(ii) . Describe the role of ANP in electrolyte regulation and distinguish its action from aldosterone.
D. Describe the functions of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol produced by the kidney.
questions.answerText:
C(i) RAAS cascade:
Stimulus: fall in NaCl, extracellular fluid volume, or arterial blood pressure → juxtaglomerular apparatus → renin secretion → renin acts on angiotensinogen (liver) → angiotensin I (10 aa polypeptide) → ACE in lungs → angiotensin II (octapeptide) → adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa) → aldosterone → increased sodium reabsorption from collecting tubules → increased water retention → correction of volume/pressure deficit.
Additional actions of Ag II: arteriolar constriction (increases BP); increases water intake; increases vasopressin (ADH) release; increases ACTH secretion; decreases baroreceptor sensitivity (potentiating pressor effect).
C(ii) ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide):
- Stimulates salt excretion (natriuresis).
- Increases rate of GFR when present in blood.
- Has opposite effect to aldosterone — stimulates salt excretion rather than retention.
- Different mechanism of action from RAAS.
D. Functions of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol:
- Steroid hormone; active form of vitamin D3.
- Synthesis: vitamin D3 → (liver, 25-hydroxylation) → 25-hydroxycholecalciferol → (kidney proximal tubule, 1α-hydroxylase) → 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol.
- Functions: increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption from intestine; facilitates Ca²⁺ reabsorption in kidney; mobilises Ca²⁺ from bone; stimulates differentiation of immune cells. Low Ca²⁺ level stimulates its release.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the salivary glands, including the major and minor glands and their secretory units.
(ii) State how the individual glands relate to the pathologies that can occur.
questions.answerText:
(i) There are three major paired salivary glands - the parotid gland (the largest, located in the infratemporal region, anterior to the ears), the submandibular gland (in the submandibular triangle of the neck), and the sublingual gland (the smallest) - plus minor salivary glands in the submucosa of the oral cavity, which empty directly into the cavity via short buccal, labial, lingual and palatine ducts.
The basic secretory unit is the acinus (the 'salivon'), a blind sac of secretory cells; serous acini secrete a protein-rich isotonic fluid, and mucous acini secrete the lubricant mucin; myoepithelial cells are found at the basal aspect of the acinar secretory cells and ducts. The parotid gland is serous and its serous secretion contains alpha-amylase; the submandibular gland is mixed, mainly serous; the sublingual gland and the buccal glands are mucous, with mucus secretion containing mucin. The duct system includes intercalated ducts, striated ducts and excretory ducts, and saliva secretion has a primary stage (acinar secretion, isosmotic like plasma) and a secondary/modification stage (reabsorption of Na+ and Cl-, secretion of K+ and HCO3-).
(ii) Tumours of the salivary glands usually occur in the major salivary glands (parotid, submandibular and sublingual); approximately 80% of salivary gland tumours are benign, and most originate in the parotid gland. Mumps (parotitis) is listed among the causes of failure to produce normal amounts of saliva; xerostomia (dry mouth) can result from irradiation of the salivary glands, anticholinergic drugs, mumps, or age-related change; sialorrhea is excessive salivary secretion.

(i) Cardiovascular changes during pregnancy:
- CO increases by 30–50% in the 1st and 2nd trimester, plateauing in the 3rd trimester.
- In the first half, increased CO is due to increased SV (consequent on increased blood volume — about 50% increase by end of 3rd trimester), mainly due to effect of oestrogen on the renin-angiotensin system.
- By the 3rd trimester, increased HR (10–20 beats/min above normal) is the main driver of increased CO.
(ii) Despite increased CO, ABP generally falls because there is a disproportionate fall in SVR. This is caused partly by hormonal changes dilating blood vessels and mainly by development of a low-resistance uterine circulation. Since ABP = CO × SVR, a fall in SVR outweighs the rise in CO. Diastolic pressure falls more than systolic pressure, leading to increased pulse pressure.
(iii) Complications affecting CVS response to exercise during pregnancy: elevated CO at rest (less reserve); compression of inferior vena cava reducing venous return; supine hypotensive syndrome.
(iv) Significance of RBF autoregulation: normally, a decrease in arterial pressure to as low as 60 mmHg or an increase to as high as 180 mmHg changes RBF by only a few percentage points. Autoregulation of RBF runs in parallel with GFR, maintaining constant filtration independent of systemic pressure fluctuations.
(v) Two hypotheses of RBF autoregulation:
- Myogenic hypothesis: increased systemic arterial pressure stretches afferent arterioles, stimulating them to contract and increasing resistance, maintaining constant RBF.
- Tubuloglomerular feedback: increased RBF → increased GFR → increased NaCl at macula densa → adenosine released → afferent arteriole constricts, efferent arteriole dilates → GFR and RBF normalised.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman in her 32nd week of pregnancy is noted to have a heart rate of 88 beats/min and is told her cardiac output has increased significantly. Routine physical examination reveals mild ankle oedema.
(i) Describe the cardiovascular changes that occur during pregnancy and the mechanisms responsible.
(ii) Explain why arterial blood pressure generally falls despite increased cardiac output during pregnancy.
(iii) State three complications that can affect the cardiovascular response to exercise during pregnancy.
(iv) Describe the physiological significance of autoregulation of renal blood flow and how it is maintained.
(v) State the two hypotheses describing autoregulation of renal blood flow.

Describe the gross anatomy of the cell membrane under listed headings; explain the clinical basis for membrane transport disorders; and distinguish between integral and peripheral membrane proteins.
A. Describe the composition and structure of the cell membrane including the fluid mosaic model.
B. Classify cell membrane receptors with examples of each type.
C(i) . Describe the types of intercellular junctions and their functions.
C(ii) . Distinguish between endocrine, paracrine, and autocrine cell-to-cell signalling.
D. List the functions of cell adhesion molecules and classify them by mechanism.
questions.answerText:
C(i) Types of intercellular junctions:
- Adherent junctions: hold epithelial and cardiac muscle cells together; connect cytoskeletal elements.
- Tight (occluding) junctions: segregate apical and basolateral domains; prevent pericellular diffusion of water and ions (barrier function).
- Gap (communicating) junctions: allow intercellular diffusion of ions and signalling molecules; composed of hexagonal arrays of connexins; central pore ≈1.5 nm; permit electrical coupling between cells.
C(ii) Cell-to-cell signalling mechanisms:
- Endocrine: inter-glandular; hormones produced by an endocrine gland act on target cells at a distant body site.
- Paracrine: local intercellular; act on neighbouring target cells.
- Autocrine: intracellular; act on the cell responsible for production.
D. Functions of cell adhesion molecules: cell–cell recognition; cell signalling; cell growth; cell migration; embryogenesis; information transfer from extracellular matrix to cell; establishment of the blood–brain barrier; cancer metastasis.
Classification by mechanism: calcium-dependent (cadherins — homophilic adhesion); calcium-independent (immunoglobulin superfamily including ICAMs and N-CAMs); cell to cell surface carbohydrate ligand-binding proteins (selectins — divalent cation-dependent); cell to extracellular matrix (integrins — non-covalently attached heterodimeric glycoproteins).

(i) The type is anaemic hypoxia. The patient has decreased or abnormal haemoglobin (reduced oxygen-carrying capacity) but arterial PO₂ is normal, which is the defining feature of anaemic hypoxia.
(ii) Five clinical types of hypoxia:
- Anaemic (low Hb): decreased oxygen-carrying capacity; arterial PO₂ normal, Hb reduced.
- Hypoxaemic/hypoxic: O₂ available to RBCs from atmosphere is reduced (low PO₂).
- Histotoxic: inability of tissues to utilise available oxygen due to toxic agents.
- Circulatory/ischaemic/stagnant: decrease in cardiac output causes low BP and prolonged systemic transit time.
- Hypermetabolic: large increases in metabolism (e.g. extensive burns) require supplemental O₂.
(iii) Causes of anaemic hypoxia: anaemia (blood loss/hypochromic), methemoglobinaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, sickle cell anaemia.
(iv) Effects on brain in temporal sequence:
- Functional disturbance in 5 seconds.
- Unconsciousness in 15 seconds.
- Irreversible cell damage in about 2 minutes.
- Cell death in 4–5 minutes.
- Secondary polycythaemia, acute pulmonary oedema, acute cerebral oedema, and reduced muscular activities can also result.
(v) Treatment of anaemic hypoxia: blood transfusions, hyperbaric chamber, bone marrow transplant.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old female develops progressive weakness and lightheadedness on exertion. Investigation reveals a reduced haemoglobin level. Arterial PO₂ is reported as normal.
(i) Identify the type of hypoxia present and justify your diagnosis.
(ii) List all five recognised clinical types of hypoxia with their defining mechanism.
(iii) State the causes of the specific type diagnosed in this patient.
(iv) Describe the effects of hypoxia on brain tissue in temporal sequence.
(v) Outline the treatment of the type of hypoxia identified.

questions.answerText:
(i) Control of the swallowing mechanism, including the oropharynx and the upper oesophageal sphincter (UES), is largely under the control of the swallowing centre in the medulla, acting through cranial nerves V (trigeminal), IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus) and XII (hypoglossal). Primary peristalsis in the oesophagus is initiated by swallowing and is coordinated by vagal fibres emerging from the medulla.
The lower oesophageal sphincter has a high resting muscle tone to prevent reflux of gastric acid; this basal tone is maintained by enteric nerves, hormones, and vagal cholinergic fibres, and can be increased by sympathetic stimulation. As the bolus nears the lower oesophageal sphincter, noncholinergic vagal fibres acting on inhibitory interneurons release VIP and nitric oxide, causing relaxation of the sphincter, so the bolus can pass into the stomach. In the stomach, inhibition of the excitatory signal from the vagus nerve is one of the mechanisms involved in receptive relaxation of the stomach.
(ii) The condition that illustrates loss of this inhibitory control is achalasia, in which the enteric nervous system of the lower oesophagus (rather than the vagus itself) is lost: this relatively uncommon condition causes difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and a dilated oesophagus proximal to a narrowed, tapered area at the gastro-oesophageal junction, because the aganglionic region cannot stimulate contractions or transduce the signal to relax the lower oesophageal sphincter. This produces the same functional endpoint (failure of receptive LOS relaxation) that would also result from loss of the inhibitory vagal (noncholinergic) pathway described above.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the vagal (parasympathetic) nerve fibres to the oesophagus and stomach.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the dysfunction that follows loss of the lower oesophageal sphincter's normal inhibitory control.

questions.answerText:
(i) Gas exchange mechanisms:
- External respiration: gas exchange between pulmonary capillaries and alveoli. Quantity of O₂ and CO₂ exchanged per minute = respiratory exchange ratio (RR). Under normal conditions RR = RQ.
- Internal respiration: gas exchange between systemic capillaries and body cells.
- About 250 mL O₂ consumed by tissues per minute; cells produce about 200 mL CO₂. Respiratory quotient (RQ) = CO₂ produced / O₂ consumed = 200/250 = 0.8 normally.
- Average alveolar ventilation ≈ 4 L/min; cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min; V/Q = 0.8.
(ii) Herring-Breuer reflex:
- An inflation and deflation reflex that helps regulate rhythmic ventilation of the lungs.
- Limits degree of inspiration and prevents over-distension and extreme deflation.
- Infants: plays a role in regulating basic rhythm of breathing and preventing over-inflation of lungs.
- Adults: important only when tidal volume is large, as in exercise.
(iii) Disorders diminishing pulmonary perfusion cause affected lung areas to receive little or no blood flow in relation to ventilation, thereby increasing the V/Q ratio. This leads to wasted or dead space ventilation — ventilation of alveoli that are not perfused and therefore cannot participate in gas exchange. Physiologically, high V/Q means PAO₂ rises and PACO₂ falls in affected areas.
(iv) Vital capacity (VC): maximum air expired after maximum inspiration = IRV + TV + ERV; 4800 mL (males).
FEV₁: fraction of VC expired in 1 second; normal = 83% of VC.
FRC: air remaining in lungs after normal expiration = ERV + RV; 2200 mL (males).
Obstructive disease: FEV₁ markedly reduced; VC relatively preserved; FEV₁/VC ratio decreased; TLC may increase (air trapping).
Restrictive disease: both FEV₁ and VC reduced proportionally; FEV₁/VC ratio normal or increased; TLC decreased.
(v) Work of breathing: energy expended in expanding elastic structures of lungs and chest wall, and overcoming airway resistance.
Six conditions that increase work of breathing: exercise, emphysema, asthma, lung oedema, reduced surfactant, congestive heart failure, and rapid breathing with turbulent airflow.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old male ex-smoker presents with progressive dyspnoea at rest and on exertion. Pulmonary function tests show a markedly reduced FEV₁ with an increased total lung capacity.
(i) Describe the mechanisms of gas exchange using the concepts of the respiratory exchange ratio and respiratory quotient.
(ii) Describe the Herring-Breuer reflex: its function, afferent pathway, and clinical relevance in adults and infants.
(iii) Using the V/Q ratio, explain why disorders diminishing pulmonary perfusion lead to dead space ventilation.
(iv) Define vital capacity, FEV₁, and FRC; state how they change in obstructive versus restrictive disease.
(v) State the work of breathing and list six conditions that increase it.

A woman at term has true labour contractions that start at the fundus and move down the uterus, loss of the cervical mucous plug, and cervical dilatation of 1-3 cm.
(i) Identify the stage of labour and describe its features.
(ii) Explain why labour continues to progress.
(iii) Describe the next stages of labour, including the events of the third stage.
questions.answerText:
(i) First stage, latent phase: true contractions begin (preceded by weak, irregular, short, painless Braxton Hicks contractions), the mucous plug is lost, contractions start at the fundus and move down the body.
(i) Contractions occur from once every 30 minutes to once every 1-3 minutes, push the baby down with the head against the cervix; cervix dilates (1-3 cm), vaginal canal opens; duration variable; stage ends at 10 cm cervical dilatation.
(ii) Positive feedback: cervical stretch by the foetal head initiates a strong reflex increasing contractility of the uterine body; the contraction pushes the baby forward, stretching the cervix more and giving more feedback, repeated until the baby is expelled.
(ii) Stretch of the cervix or uterine muscle (e.g. from foetal movements) increases contractility; oxytocin rises through a neurogenic reflex once uterine stretching starts.
(iii) Second stage (active phase): cervix 10 cm; foetal membranes rupture and amniotic fluid is lost; head moves rapidly into the birth canal and the baby is expelled through cervix and vagina.
(iii) Second stage lasts as little as 1 minute in multiparous women to 30 minutes or more in nulliparous women.
(iii) Third stage: uterine contractions continue, shearing between uterine wall and placenta separates the placenta from the implantation site, with bleeding from opened placental sinuses.
(iii) The placenta is expelled through the cervix and vagina 10-45 minutes after the baby is born.

questions.question:
A. Describe the nerve supply of the urinary bladder and its sphincters:
A(i) sympathetic supply;
A(ii) parasympathetic supply;
A(iii) somatic supply,
stating for each the spinal segments, named nerve, and action on the bladder body and sphincters.
B.
B(i) Describe the higher centres that regulate the spinal centres of micturition.
B(ii) Explain the effect of a brain stem lesion that interrupts most inhibitory signals.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Sympathetic: L1-L3 segments, through the sympathetic chain and hypogastric ganglion to the hypogastric nerves.
A(i) Action: inhibitory to the bladder body and excitatory to the internal sphincter.
A(ii) Parasympathetic: S2-S4 segments via the pelvic nerves.
A(ii) Action: excitatory to the bladder and relaxes the internal sphincter.
A(iii) Somatic: S2-S4 segments via the pudendal nerves to the external sphincter (skeletal muscle at the urogenital diaphragm).
A(iii) Action: excitatory to the external sphincter.
A(iii) Sensory (afferent) signals from bladder wall stretch receptors travel through the pelvic nerves to the sacral cord.
B(i) Spinal centres of micturition lie in the sacral and lumbar segments and are regulated by higher centres in the brain.
B(i) Facilitatory area in the pontine region; inhibitory areas in the midbrain and cerebral cortex.
B(i) The higher centres keep micturition partially inhibited.
B(ii) A lesion in parts of the brain stem interrupts most of the inhibitory signals, so the spinal micturition centres are continuously excited by the higher centres.
B(ii) Result: uncontrollable micturition; even a small quantity of urine elicits the reflex and micturition frequency increases (uninhibited neurogenic bladder).

questions.question:
A person is to be protected against an infectious disease such as measles.
(i) Define immunization and vaccination and state what a vaccine consists of.
(ii) Explain how a vaccine induces immunity through the humoral and cellular pathways.
(iii) List the diseases that can be prevented by vaccination.
questions.answerText:
(i) Immunization is the process by which a person is made immune or resistant to an infectious disease by administration of a vaccine; vaccination is a type of immunization.
(i) A vaccine is a substance introduced into the body to prevent disease produced by a certain pathogen; it consists of dead or weakened live organisms that cause the disease.
(ii) Vaccines induce immunity by production of antibodies or activation of T cells.
(ii) Humoral: antigen activates a dormant B cell through its surface receptor; the B cell engulfs, processes and presents antigen to helper T cells, which produce cytokines; the B cell enlarges into a plasma cell that makes antibodies at a very rapid rate until the antigen is destroyed; without helper T cells the antibody quantity is small.
(ii) Cellular: T cells cannot recognise free antigen and need it presented as peptides by antigen presenting cells; CD8+ cells (MHC-I) are cytotoxic; CD4+ Th1 cells (MHC-II) activate macrophages; CD4+ Th2 cells (MHC-II) activate B cells to produce antibody.
(iii) Diseases: measles, tuberculosis, tetanus, smallpox, polio, rabies, yellow fever, typhoid fever.

questions.question:
A. Describe the lymphatic circulation under the following headings:
A(i) How lymph is formed and the average daily volume of lymph flow
A(ii) The pathway of lymph flow from the lower body and from the right side of the neck and head to the bloodstream
A(iii) The two categories of lymphatic vessels and their structural differences
A(iv) Forces that aid lymph flow
B. Compare and contrast lymph and plasma under the following headings: composition, protein content, coagulation properties, and function.
C. Explain what oedema is, how it develops when lymph flow is inadequate, and the potential consequences.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Lymph formation and volume: Lymphatic fluid is formed by the slight mismatch between filtration and absorption in the capillaries. Approximately 85% of the fluid lost at the arterial end of the capillary bed is reclaimed into the blood at the venous end. The remaining 15% is added to the interstitial fluid and enters lymphatic vessels. Total lymph flow averages 120 mL/hour or 2-3 litres per day.
A(ii) Pathway of lymph flow:
- Lymph from lower body: flows up the thoracic duct and empties into the left internal jugular vein and subclavian vein.
- Lymph from left head, left arm, and parts of chest: drain into the thoracic duct.
- Lymph from right side of neck and head, right arm, and parts of the thorax: drain into the right lymph duct, which empties into the right subclavian and internal jugular vein.
A(iii) Two categories of lymphatic vessels:
lack valves and smooth muscle in their walls; found in regions such as the intestine or skeletal muscle. Movement of lymph is mediated by contraction of associated muscle and contraction of associated arterioles and venules.
have valves and smooth muscle in their walls and contract in a peristaltic manner, propelling lymph along the vessels.
A(iv) Forces aiding lymph flow: movement of skeletal muscle, negative intrathoracic pressure (inspiration), and suction pressure caused by venous flow that the lymphatics drain into.
B. Lymph vs Plasma:
- Plasma: cell-free part of blood; contains salt, considerable amount of proteins, and more or less all constituents of the body. Flows within blood vessels. Can coagulate because it contains fibrinogen and prothrombin. Function: takes part in nutrition, excretion, respiration by transporting various materials and defence mechanism by producing antibodies.
- Lymph: modified tissue fluid; contains cells like lymphocytes and monocytes, and small amounts of proteins and salts. Flows within lymphatic vessels. Can coagulate but very slowly because it contains fibrinogen and prothrombin only in small quantities. Function: supplies nutrition to tissue devoid of blood supply; takes part in fat absorption and defence mechanism.
C. Oedema: accumulation of fluid in abnormal quantities. It develops when lymph flow is inadequate to drain the excess interstitial fluid. Without adequate drainage, excess interstitial fluid accumulates in the tissues, leading to swelling (oedema) and, potentially, compression of local blood vessels and subsequent tissue damage.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman with severe sepsis develops simultaneous bleeding from venepuncture sites, skin petechiae, and oozing from the gums. Laboratory results show low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, and elevated FDP.
(i) State the diagnosis and describe the four major components of normal haemostasis.
(ii) Explain the physiological mechanisms that normally prevent clotting inside blood vessels, citing the role of prostacyclin, antithrombin III, and protein C.
(iii) Describe how failure of these anticoagulant mechanisms in the context of sepsis leads to the laboratory picture described.
(iv) State the role of fibrinolysis in the resolution of clots, including the specific enzyme and its precursor.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in the context of sepsis.
Four major components of haemostasis:
damage to the wall of a blood vessel leads to rapid smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction of the vessel), mediated by release of serotonin and other vasoconstrictors from platelets.
platelets are attracted and adhere to the vessel wall when exposed to tissue collagen following vascular damage; aggregation follows, facilitated by release of ADP and thromboxane A2.
3. Clotting (coagulation): platelet plugs are secured by formation of a fibrin clot. Depends on plasma clotting factors (many produced in the liver and vitamin K dependent). Clotting factors are normally present as inactive proenzymes; once activated, each factor activates the next in the coagulation cascade.
4. Fibrinolysis and clot degradation.
(ii) Anticoagulant mechanisms:
- Prostacyclin: anti-aggregating effect of prostacyclin produced by endothelial cells, which reduces intracellular Ca2+ via activation of adenyl cyclase, leading to inhibition of platelet aggregation and platelet relaxation.
- Antithrombin III: a protease inhibitor that binds to serine proteases (active forms of Factors IX, X, XI, XII) in the coagulation system, blocking their activity. This binding is facilitated by heparin.
- Protein C: all endothelial cells except those in the cerebral microcirculation produce thrombomodulin. Thrombomodulin-thrombin complex activates protein C. Activated protein C (along with cofactor protein S) inactivates Factors V and VIII; APC also inactivates an inhibitor of tissue plasminogen activator, increasing plasmin formation.
(iii) DIC mechanism: In severe sepsis, systemic activation of coagulation overcomes anticoagulant mechanisms. Widespread coagulation consumes clotting factors and platelets, causing simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding. Low fibrinogen reflects consumption; elevated FDP reflects activation of fibrinolysis.
(iv) Fibrinolysis: Tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) causes activation of plasminogen. Plasminogen becomes plasmin (fibrinolysin). Plasmin lyses fibrin and fibrinogen with production of fibrinogen degradation products (FDP) that inhibit thrombin, forming a negative feedback that limits further clotting.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man with head trauma develops polyuria — passing 8 litres of pale, dilute urine per day. His serum osmolarity is elevated at 315 mOsm/L, and urine osmolarity is only 80 mOsm/L. He has intense thirst.
(i) Identify the underlying physiological defect and the specific urine formation problem.
(ii) Explain the normal regulation of body water when osmolarity is increased, detailing the complete cascade of events from osmoreceptor stimulation to reduced urine volume.
(iii) State the obligatory urine volume and explain how it is calculated from the solute load and maximal concentrating ability.
(iv) Describe the two main pathways by which the body gains and loses water daily (state volumes), explaining how the kidneys maintain balance.
questions.answerText:
(i) Physiological defect: Lack of secretion of ADH (antidiuretic hormone). Urine formation problem: water diuresis — caused by lack of secretion of ADH, producing dilute urine with osmolarity below 250 mOsm/L. Without ADH, the DCT and collecting duct remain impermeable to water; a large volume of dilute urine is excreted. The elevated serum osmolarity confirms dehydration; the dilute urine confirms inability to concentrate urine.
(ii) Normal regulation when osmolarity is increased: Increased osmolarity → osmoreceptors are sensitised → thirst is activated (increased intake of water) → ADH is released → aquaporin 2 inserts at the late distal convoluted tubules and collecting tubules → facultative reabsorption of water in addition to obligatory reabsorption → urine volume is reduced.
(iii) Obligatory urine volume: 600 milliosmoles of solute must be excreted each day. Maximal urine concentrating ability is 1200 mOsm/L. The minimal volume of urine that must be excreted to rid the body of 600 milliosmoles of solute is 500 mL (calculated as 600 mOsm ÷ 1200 mOsm/L = 0.5 L). This volume is called the obligatory urine volume.
(iv) Daily water balance:
Water gain — body can gain water by:
- Ingestion of liquids and water in food: 2100 mL/day.
- Metabolic synthesis of water during cellular respiration (oxidation of carbohydrate): 200 mL/day.
- Total water gained: approximately 2300 mL/day.
Water loss — body loses water through:
- Insensible water loss: evaporation from skin (300-400 mL/day) and lungs (300-400 mL/day).
- Faeces: 100 mL/day (can increase to several litres in diarrhoea).
- Sweat: 100 mL/day (can increase to 1-2 L/hour).
- Kidneys: 1400 mL/day (can be as low as 0.5 L/day and as high as 20 L/day).
- Total: approximately 2300 mL/day.
The kidneys maintain balance as the most important way — by controlling the rate of renal excretion.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old Nigerian woman presents with lifelong episodic bone pain, recurrent infections, and mild jaundice. Peripheral blood film shows sickle-shaped red cells. Haemoglobin electrophoresis confirms HbS.
(i) Identify the specific type of haemoglobin abnormality and state the precise molecular defect.
(ii) Describe the altered red blood cell shape seen and the conditions under which it develops.
(iii) State three other abnormal haemoglobin types and the key characteristic of each.
(iv) Explain the pathophysiological basis of haemolytic anaemia and how it differs from aplastic anaemia and blood loss anaemia.
questions.answerText:
(i) Haemoglobinopathy: Haemoglobin S (HbS) — found in sickle cell anaemia. The alpha-chains are normal; the beta-chains are abnormal. This is a genetic disorder caused by abnormal polypeptide chains of haemoglobin.
(ii) Altered shape: Sickle cell — crescentic shape as in sickle cell anaemia. The abnormal beta-chains cause the haemoglobin to polymerise under deoxygenated conditions, deforming the cell into the characteristic sickle shape.
(iii) Other abnormal haemoglobin types:
- Haemoglobin C: beta-chains are abnormal; characterised by mild haemolytic anaemia and splenomegaly.
- Haemoglobin E: beta-chains are abnormal; present in people with haemoglobin E disease.
- Haemoglobin M: abnormal haemoglobin present in the form of methemoglobin; occurs due to mutation of genes of both alpha and beta chains, resulting in abnormal replacement of amino acids — causes Blue Baby Syndrome in children.
(iv) Classification comparison:
- Haemolytic anaemia: caused by excessive haemolysis of RBCs. Can occur in congenital spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, heavy malaria parasitaemia, transfusion reactions, certain drugs, and Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
- Aplastic anaemia: caused by destruction of bone marrow (e.g., radiation, viruses, drugs) leading to failure of RBC production.
- Blood loss anaemia (haemorrhagic anaemia): due to blood loss from trauma or ulcer.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, pallor, and mild jaundice. Peripheral blood film shows large, oval-shaped red cells with hypersegmented neutrophils. Her serum Vitamin B12 level is markedly low, and gastric biopsy reveals atrophic gastritis.
(i) State the specific diagnosis.
(ii) Identify the predisposing factor unique to this condition that distinguishes it from dietary B12 deficiency.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiological mechanism that leads to the haematological picture.
(iv) State the management approach implied by the pathophysiological defect identified in (ii).
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Pernicious anaemia — megaloblastic anaemia resulting from inability to absorb Vitamin B12 due to a lack of intrinsic factor from stomach secretions.
(ii) Predisposing factor unique to pernicious anaemia: deficiency of intrinsic factor from stomach secretions. Atrophic gastritis destroys parietal cells, eliminating intrinsic factor. Without intrinsic factor, oral Vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed. This is the key distinction from dietary B12 deficiency where intrinsic factor is present.
(iii) Pathophysiological mechanism: Without Vitamin B12, DNA synthesis is impaired in rapidly dividing erythroid precursors. Cells undergo nuclear maturation failure, producing oversized (megaloblastic) red cells (macrocytic) with defective function. Folic acid deficiency produces the same nuclear maturation failure. Haemolysis of abnormal cells causes mild jaundice. Hypersegmented neutrophils reflect the same nuclear maturation defect in granulocyte precursors.
(iv) Management: Because the defect is lack of absorption of oral B12 (not dietary deficiency), the treatment requires parenteral (intramuscular) administration of Vitamin B12, bypassing the gastrointestinal absorption pathway that depends on intrinsic factor.

questions.question:
Below the level of a spinal cord lesion, stimulation produces flexor muscle spasms, incontinence of urine and feces, priapism, hypertension, and profuse sweating.
(i) Identify the structure/level responsible.
(ii) State the structures/pathways affected below this level.
(iii) State the differential findings in relation to spinal cord injury.
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for this presentation.
questions.answerText:
(i) A spinal cord (SC) lesion; the phenomenon described is the mass reflex.
(ii) Stimulation below the level of the SC lesion affects the reflex arcs and autonomic pathways of the spinal cord segments below the lesion.
(iii) In the 'spinal animal' model, prior section of the spinal cord with stimulation of the hind limb results in withdrawal of the limb, extension of the opposite hind limb and ipsilateral forelimb, and flexion of the contralateral forelimb.
(iv) The mass reflex is a marked central excitatory potential that results in stimulation of other areas; stimulation below the level of an SC lesion results in flexor muscle spasms, incontinence of urine and feces, priapism, hypertension, and profuse sweating, reflecting loss of the normal descending control over reflex and autonomic pathways below the lesion.

A(i) The bladder is a smooth muscle chamber of two parts: the body, where urine collects (epithelium has folds called rugae), and the neck, a funnel-shaped extension passing inferiorly and anteriorly into the urogenital triangle to join the urethra.
A(ii) The smooth muscle is called detrusor muscle and is arranged in spiral, longitudinal and circular bundles.
A(ii) Its cells fuse with one another, allowing an electrical pathway from one cell to another.
A(iii) The trigone is a small triangular area on the posterior wall above the neck; the ureters enter at its uppermost part and the bladder opens into the urethra at its lowermost part.
A(iii) Its mucosa is smooth (unlike the rest of the bladder); each ureter passes obliquely into the detrusor and runs a further 1-2 cm beneath the mucosa before emptying.
A(iv) The urethra extends from the bladder to the exterior, passes through the urogenital diaphragm (external urinary sphincter), and differs in length and function in males and females.
B(i) Empty bladder pressure is zero; about 50 mL raises it sharply to about 5 cm H2O and a further 200-300 mL adds only a small increase.
B(i) Tension rises with filling but the radius also rises because the detrusor relaxes (Law of Laplace, P=2T/r), so pressure rise is almost nil until the bladder is relatively full.
B(i) At about 400 mL detrusor contraction becomes intense with urge to void (voluntary control still possible); beyond 600-700 mL voluntary control fails and micturition occurs spontaneously.
B(ii) Internal sphincter: smooth muscle, located where the bladder neck has a large amount of elastic tissue.
B(ii) External sphincter: skeletal muscle, located at the urogenital diaphragm.
B(ii) Internal sphincter is excited by sympathetic (hypogastric) and relaxed by parasympathetic supply; external sphincter is excited by the somatic pudendal nerves.

questions.question:
A patient has progressive difficulty swallowing solids and liquids, and is found to have loss of the enteric nervous system in the lower part of the oesophagus, always involving the lower oesophageal sphincter.
(i) State the risk factors for this condition.
(ii) State the complications of this condition.
(iii) State the management options, and justify one.
questions.answerText:
(i) The aetiology of achalasia is unknown.
(ii) Achalasia is associated with difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and a dilated oesophagus proximal to a narrowed, tapered area at the gastro-oesophageal junction; surgically cutting the sphincter (oesophagomyotomy) allows food and fluids to pass through the lower oesophageal sphincter into the stomach but usually produces gastric reflux, so patients must then be treated with oral medication for GERD (gastro-oesophageal reflux disease).
(iii) Pharmacologic intervention with nitrites (isosorbide dinitrate) or calcium channel blockers (nifedipine or verapamil) is used but has limited efficacy; primary treatment is by balloon dilation or surgically cutting the sphincter (oesophagomyotomy).
Justification: oesophagomyotomy is described as the primary treatment because it directly divides the aganglionic, non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter, allowing food and fluids to pass through into the stomach, whereas pharmacologic treatment (nitrites or calcium channel blockers) only has limited efficacy and only partially alleviates the problem.

(i) The stretch reflex is a contraction of a muscle in response to stretching of the attached tendon or of the muscle itself; the receptors involved are the muscle spindles.
- It is a monosynaptic reflex - the simplest reflex arc, with a single synapse between the afferent and efferent neurons; afferents are Ia fibres and efferents are gamma motor neurons, producing a fast reflex with fast onset and offset.
- In the knee-jerk reflex, stretching of the quadriceps produces contraction of the quadriceps muscle; reaction time for a stretch reflex in humans is usually 19-24 ms, with a central delay of 0.6-0.9 ms.
(ii) The reflex is elicited by tapping the patellar tendon.
(iii) Reflex testing is an important diagnostic tool to assess the condition of the nervous system; distorted, exaggerated, or absent reflex responses may indicate pathology of portions of the nervous system, and abnormal reflexes often occur before other signs are apparent. Reflex tests can indicate the area of spinal cord injury, since afferent neurons enter via the dorsal roots (cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia) and efferent fibres leave via the ventral roots at specific spinal levels.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, and distribution of the fibres involved in the monosynaptic stretch (knee-jerk) reflex.
(ii) State the site used to elicit this reflex clinically.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis for the clinical usefulness of reflex testing after injury.

A boy shows growth of the testis and scrotum (but not the penis), a little pubic hair at the base of the penis, darkening of the areola, and an increase in height.
(i) Identify the stage of puberty and its usual age range.
(ii) Explain the hormonal events driving these changes.
(iii) Describe the mechanisms that control the onset of puberty.
(iv) Describe the changes of the remaining male stages.
(v) State the first external sign of puberty in girls and the sex difference in the growth spurt.
questions.answerText:
(i) Male stage two (about 9-15 years): body shape changes and height increases, muscle and fat develop, areola darkens and enlarges, testis and scrotum (not penis) grow, a little pubic hair appears at the base of the penis; puberty occurs at about 12-16 years in males.
(ii) Late puberty brings pulsatile gonadotropin secretion, which stimulates a rise in sex steroid secretion; increased testosterone from the testes produces the secondary sex characteristics.
(iii) Gonadotropins are high in the newborn, fall low after a few weeks; in childhood little GnRH is secreted because slight sex steroid strongly inhibits it; onset is marked by rising FSH then LH.
(iii) Causes: programmed maturational brain changes increasing GnRH (children without gonads show FSH rise at the normal time) and decreased sensitivity to negative feedback; leptin activates GnRH release; KiSS1 kisspeptins activate GPR54; leptin-melanocortin-kisspeptin pathway.
(iv) Stage 1 (about 9-12 y): male hormones more active, often no visible signs, sometimes a growth spurt begins.
(iv) Stage 3 (about 11-16 y): penis grows in length, pubic hair darker and coarser, height continues to increase, facial hair begins, shoulders broaden, muscle increases, voice starts to deepen.
(iv) Stage 4 (about 11-17 y): penis grows in width, testis and scrotum continue to grow, anal hair may appear, underarm and facial hair increase, skin oilier, voice continues to deepen.
(iv) Stage 5 (about 14-18 y): full adult height, pubic hair and genitals reach adult proportions; some continue to grow into their twenties.
(v) In girls thelarche (breast development) is usually the first external sign (stage two, about 8-14 y); the growth spurt begins at an earlier age in girls than boys.

questions.answerText:
(i) The sensory receptor reacts to a stimulus.
- The sensory neuron conducts impulses to the CNS; afferent neurons enter via the dorsal or cranial nerves and have their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia or similar ganglia in cranial nerves.
- The integration centre consists of one or more synapses in the CNS.
- The motor neuron conducts impulses from the integration centre to an effector; efferent fibres leave via the ventral roots or corresponding motor cranial nerves.
- The effector responds to the impulses by contracting or secreting a product.
(ii) Reflex testing is an important diagnostic tool to assess the condition of the nervous system; distorted, exaggerated, or absent reflex responses may indicate pathology of portions of the nervous system, abnormal reflexes often occur before other signs are apparent, and reflex tests can indicate the area of spinal cord injury.
(iii) A monosynaptic reflex arc is the simplest reflex arc, with a single synapse between the afferent and efferent neurons (e.g. the stretch reflex, using muscle spindle receptors). A polysynaptic reflex arc has interneurons between the afferent and efferent neurons, with paths that branch in a complex fashion; branches with fewer synapses produce faster activity, and prolonged stimulation of the motor neuron from a single stimulus can give prolonged responses (e.g. the withdrawal reflex, which produces flexor muscle contraction with inhibition of extensors and a crossed extensor response in the opposite limb).

questions.answerText:
(i) The swallowing reflex consists of afferent pathways, central integration, and efferent pathways; impulses from tactile receptors in the posterior mouth and pharynx initiate the pharyngeal stage and are transmitted through cranial nerves. The integration centre is the deglutition/swallowing centre in the medulla and the lower portion of the pons.
Control of the swallowing mechanism, including the oropharynx and the upper oesophageal sphincter, is largely under control of the swallowing centre in the medulla, acting through cranial nerves V (trigeminal), IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus) and XII (hypoglossal); respiration and deglutition are closely integrated, with the upper oesophageal sphincter closed during inspiration (diverting air to the glottis) and, during swallowing, the glottis closes, respiration is inhibited, and the upper oesophageal sphincter relaxes. Motor impulses from the swallowing centre to the pharynx and upper oesophagus, transmitted to initiate a series of automatic pharyngeal muscle contractions, cause swallowing.
(ii) Dysphagia is difficulty with swallowing of solid or liquid, due to structural defects (obstructive) or a propulsive/motility abnormality (neurological), including inability to initiate the swallowing reflex, or food stuck in the oesophagus/throat/chest/behind the breastbone. Any defect or disorder along the reflex arc can cause a potential delay or impairment in swallow function. Dysphagia is classified by site: oral (e.g. peritonsillar abscess, tumours of tonsils/tongue), pharyngeal (neurological), and oesophageal, which may be neurological (stroke, Parkinson's disease [80% of cases], multiple sclerosis, achalasia) or obstructive (oesophageal stricture from post-acid/corrosive fluid consumption, or oesophageal cancer). Because the reflex arc depends on intact afferent input, an intact medullary/pontine integration centre, and intact motor output via cranial nerves V, IX, X and XII, a lesion anywhere along this arc manifests as dysphagia, with the site of the lesion determining whether it is classified as oral, pharyngeal, or oesophageal in type.

A(i) The immune response is how the body recognises and defends itself against infectious microbes through antigens on the surface of cells, viruses, fungi or bacteria.
A(i) Adaptive immunity is specific and acquired: resistance against a specific foreign body by specialized systemic cells; components are humoral (B cells secrete antibodies) and cellular (CD8+ direct killing, CD4+ recruit other immune cells).
A(ii) An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein on the surface of B cells or free in the blood that neutralises antigen by binding specifically; humoral immunity acts against extracellular microbes and antibodies are secreted into mucosal lumens, blood and interstitial fluids.
A(ii) Sequence: dormant B cell is activated by antigen through its receptor, engulfs and presents processed antigen to helper T cells, which produce cytokines; the B cell becomes a plasma cell producing antibodies rapidly until the antigen is destroyed; without helper T cells the antibody quantity is usually small.
A(iii) T cells lack surface immunoglobulin receptors for antigen; antigen must be presented to them as specific peptides by antigen presenting cells.
A(iii) Cellular immunity is mediated via T cells: CD8+ stimulated leads to direct killing; Th1 leads to macrophage activation; Th2 leads to B cell activation.
B(i) General APCs: all body cells undergoing self-cleansing; they present antigen found within (viral protein, cellular debris) on MHC-I to a CD8+ T cell.
B(i) Professional APCs: B cells, macrophages and dendritic cells; they take up extracellular proteins (self or foreign) by endocytosis, break them into peptides, attach them to MHC-II and present to a CD4+ T cell.
B(ii) Humoral: antibody production by B cells.
B(ii) CD8+ T cells (MHC-I) are cytotoxic.
B(ii) CD4+ Th1 cells (MHC-II) activate macrophages.
B(ii) CD4+ Th2 cells (MHC-II) activate B cells to produce antibody.

Describe the structure of the cardiac muscle cell; state how its physiological properties underpin normal heart function; explain the clinical basis for arrhythmias; and distinguish between the conducting and contractile cells.
A. Describe the structure and components of the cardiomyocyte.
B. List the four physiological properties of cardiac muscle and define each.
C(i) . Describe the conducting system of the heart and how the impulse is timed through the heart.
C(ii) . Explain the clinical basis of heart block using conduction rates.
D. Distinguish between the action potential of ventricular muscle and that of SA/AV nodal pacemaker cells.
questions.answerText:
C(i) Conducting system:
- SA node → atrial pathways → AV node → Bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular muscle.
- Impulse slows at AV node (0.05 m/s) to allow atria time to finish filling ventricles — seen as flat PR segment on ECG.
- Purkinje system conducts fastest (4 m/s), rapidly activating ventricular muscle synchronously.
C(ii) Heart block: AV node has the slowest conduction rate (0.05 m/s). If AV nodal conduction is impaired, PR interval is prolonged beyond 0.20 s (first-degree block); complete failure to conduct = complete heart block with ventricular escape rhythm.
D. Ventricular muscle action potential: 5 phases (0–4) including plateau phase (phase 2, Ca²⁺ influx) producing a prolonged action potential duration; RMP stable at −90 mV.
SA/AV nodal pacemaker cells: unstable resting membrane potential (prepotential/pacemaker potential) — spontaneous slow depolarisation during phase 4 — basis of automaticity and rhythmicity. They lack a fast sodium channel-driven phase 0; depolarisation is slower via Ca²⁺ and funny current channels.

(i) First heart sound (S₁): caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at onset of ventricular systole.
- Mitral valve closure: best heard at the apex.
- Tricuspid valve closure: best heard at lower left sternal border.
Second heart sound (S₂): during diastole, blood in blood vessels tries to flow back to ventricles; semilunar valves bulge; elastic recoil of arteries bounces blood forward, vibrating blood, valves, and ventricular walls. Best heard at the base.
(ii) Third heart sound (S₃): low-pitched early diastolic sound; best heard with the bell at the apex; coincides with rapid ventricular filling immediately after AV valve opening; heard 0.12–0.18 seconds after S₂ as 'lub-dub-dum'.
Physiological: in children, young adults, and pregnancy. In this patient (over 40), it is pathological — most common causes are left ventricular failure and mitral regurgitation.
(iii) Fourth heart sound (S₄): soft, low-pitched; best heard with the bell at the apex; occurs 0.11 seconds prior to S₁ (heard as 'da-lub-dub'). It is always pathological; caused by forceful atrial contraction against a non-compliant or stiff ventricle.
(iv) Eight phases of the cardiac cycle in order:
1. Atrial systole.
2. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
3. Rapid ventricular ejection.
4. Reduced ventricular ejection.
5. Protodiastole.
6. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation.
7. Rapid ventricular filling.
8. Reduced ventricular filling (diastasis).
(v) Total duration of cardiac cycle at 70 beats/min = 0.8 seconds.
Ventricular systole (total 0.27 s): isometric contraction = 0.05 s; ejection period = 0.22 s.
Ventricular diastole (total 0.53 s): protodiastole = 0.04 s; isometric relaxation = 0.08 s; rapid filling = 0.11 s; slow filling = 0.19 s; last rapid filling = 0.11 s.

questions.answerText:
A(i) An action potential travels along a motor nerve to its ending on muscle fibres, activating voltage-gated Ca channels on the axon; Ca enters, ACh vesicles fuse with the membrane and ACh is released into the synaptic cleft.
A(i) ACh diffuses across the cleft, binds receptors on the motor end plate, opens Na channels, causing depolarization and an action potential on the muscle fibre.
A(ii) Sarcotubular system: vesicles and tubules around the fibrils that facilitate action potential transmission; T system (transverse tubules continuous with the sarcolemma) and sarcoplasmic reticulum (irregular curtain around each fibril).
A(ii) The action potential causes Ca release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca binds troponin on the actin filaments.
A(iii) Proteins: myosin II, actin, tropomyosin and troponin; troponin T binds tropomyosin, troponin I inhibits myosin-actin interaction, troponin C binds Ca; others are actinin, titin, desmin.
A(iii) Tropomyosin blocks cross-bridge binding sites; Ca-bound troponin moves tropomyosin out of the way, unblocking them.
A(iv) The cross-bridge binds the uncovered sites and delivers a power stroke; ATP binding breaks the actin-myosin bond and a second ATP is split to re-energize the cross-bridge.
A(iv) Ca is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum and stored until a new action potential arrives, so contraction ceases.
B(i) Involuntary movements: spasms (e.g. seizure, convulsion) and cramps (painful spasms).
B(i) Injury: muscle strain (muscle or tendon overstretched or torn) and denervation hypersensitivity.
B(i) Myopathies: muscular dystrophies, diseases with progressive weakness of skeletal muscles.
B(ii) Drugs can enhance or block transmission at the neuromuscular junction.

(i) Describe the organization of the sympathetic and parasympathetic (autonomic) nervous systems, including their neurotransmitters and the structures to which they are distributed.
(ii) Explain the functional basis of the impairment that follows dysfunction of these systems.
questions.answerText:
(i) The sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems are the two major divisions of the autonomic nervous system (ANS), mainly responsible for homeostasis; they supply innervation to all other organs except skeletal muscle.
- Cholinergic neurons release acetylcholine (ACh): all sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic neurons, sympathetic postganglionic neurons to most sweat glands, and all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons.
- Adrenergic neurons release norepinephrine (and epinephrine): most sympathetic postganglionic neurons are adrenergic.
- Receptors are broadly grouped into cholinergic receptors (nicotinic and muscarinic) and adrenergic receptors (alpha and beta, with subtypes).
- Nerve terminals of the ANS are located in smooth muscle (blood vessels, gut wall, urinary bladder), cardiac muscle, and glands (sweat, salivary glands).
(ii) Impaired function of the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems results in inability to adapt to environmental stressors and other challenges; the receptors of these systems are targets for treatment of diseases affecting the systems, e.g. myasthenia gravis, asthma, and hypertension.

(i) Gastric secretion is watery, acidic (pH 1-3), and daily secretion is about 2 L, containing water, HCl and the enzyme pepsinogen. Histologically, the stomach is divided into three regions based on the types of glands: the cardiac region (cardia), near the oesophageal orifice, containing cardiac glands; the fundic region (fundus), situated between cardia and pylorus and the largest part, containing fundic (gastric/oxyntic) glands; and the pyloric region (pylorus), the distal funnel-shaped region proximal to the pyloric sphincter, containing pyloric glands.
Oxyntic (fundic/gastric) glands are located on the inside surfaces of the body of the stomach and secrete hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, and mucus; pyloric glands, located in the antral portion, secrete mucus and gastrin.
The cell types are mucous cells (surface mucous cells and mucous neck cells, secreting mucus), parietal (oxyntic) cells (secreting HCl and intrinsic factor), chief cells (secreting pepsinogen, and a weak lipase), enteroendocrine cells (including G cells secreting gastrin, concentrated in the pyloric antrum; enterochromaffin-like/ECL cells secreting histamine; and D cells secreting somatostatin under the influence of HCl, which inhibits G cells), and stem cells found in the isthmus of the gland.
(ii) Achlorhydria is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by destruction of the gastric mucosa (parietal cells); gastritis is inflammation, erosion is breakdown of the superficial mucosa not involving the submucosa, and ulceration is damage to the muscularis mucosa and deeper layers; ulcers are linked to H. pylori, smoking, NSAIDs and gastrinomas (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, arising from the gastrin-related cell population).
(iii) Intrinsic factor, secreted by the parietal cells, is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the distal ileum; loss of intrinsic factor (as in achlorhydria) means B12 cannot be absorbed, and because B12 is critical for maturation of red blood cells, macrocytic (pernicious) anaemia develops. This is a direct example of disease confined to the stomach (destruction of parietal cells) producing a functional deficit at a distant site (the blood/bone marrow).

questions.answerText:
(i) Five types of transport processes in renal tubule:
1. Passive transport (simple diffusion): movement along electrochemical gradient without energy expenditure.
aided by carrier proteins in direction of electrochemical gradient.
energy-requiring (ATP); e.g. Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase on basolateral membrane.
4. Secondary active transport (co-transport/counter-transport): uses Na⁺ gradient created by primary active transport; symport (Na⁺ + glucose/amino acids) and antiport (Na⁺-H⁺ exchange).
5. Pinocytosis and solvent drag.
(ii) Na⁺ reabsorption in PCT:
- Basolateral Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase pumps Na⁺ out, creating low intracellular Na⁺ concentration.
- In first half of PCT: Na⁺ reabsorbed by co-transport with glucose, amino acids, phosphate (secondary active transport — symport).
- In second half: Na⁺ reabsorbed mainly with chloride ions.
- Electrical gradient draws Cl⁻ across; water follows Na⁺ by osmotic force.
- 65% of water and sodium reabsorption occurs in PCT; 90% of bicarbonate, calcium, K⁺; 99% of glucose and amino acids.
(iii) K⁺ handling:
- PCT: 90% of filtered K⁺ actively reabsorbed; largely passive, following Na⁺ and fluid movement.
- Cortical collecting duct (principal cells): K⁺ secretion via active transport of K⁺ across basolateral membrane and passive exit across apical membrane into tubular fluid.
- Small change in plasma K⁺ from 4 to 5.5 mmol/L = hyperkalaemia → ventricular fibrillation → death.
(iv) Loop of Henle absorption:
- Descending limb: water-permeable; absorbs 25% of filtered water; impermeable to NaCl.
- Thin ascending limb: impermeable to water; permeable to NaCl; passive NaCl reabsorption.
- Thick ascending limb: impermeable to water; Na-K-2Cl co-transport.
(v) Composition of glomerular filtrate: same as plasma except no proteins. Contains Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, PO₄, SO₄²⁻, amino acids, glucose — all at same concentrations as found in plasma.
