A. Describe the gross and microscopic anatomy of a lymph node under the following headings:
A(i) External structure: capsule, trabeculae, and afferent/efferent vessels
A(ii) Outer cortex: cellular composition and the significance of germinal centres
A(iii) Inner cortex: cellular composition
A(iv) Medulla: cellular composition and function
B. State the primary and secondary lymphoid organs, giving the specific location and function of each.
B(i) Primary lymphoid organs (two)
B(ii) Secondary lymphoid organs (two)
C. Explain how disease in the lymph node may lead to failure of body defence, and how this relates to the structural interaction between macrophages and lymphocytes within the node.
questions.answerText:
A(i) External structure: Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures found clustered at specific locations throughout the body. Each node is surrounded by a fibrous capsule that forms a protective outer sheath with trabeculae extending periodically into the node, subdividing it into small compartments.
A(ii) Outer cortex: Just inside the capsular margin, the outer cortex consists of numerous follicles rich in B-cells. When pathogens are present, follicles expand to reveal prominent germinal centres containing actively dividing, antibody-secreting B-cells.
A(iii) Inner cortex: Just below the outer cortex; particularly rich in T-cells, which continually circulate throughout most regions of the node.
A(iv) Medulla: The central inner portion containing large numbers of fixed phagocytic macrophages that continually monitor lymph for potentially pathogenic foreign material to phagocytose on contact. Medullary cords contain lymphocytes and plasma cells.
B(i) Primary lymphoid organs:
- Red bone marrow: located diffusely in flat bones (ribs, sternum, pelvis, vertebrae) and epiphyses of long bones. Function: acts as the major haemopoietic tissue, producing all formed elements of blood including erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes.
- Thymus gland: a small, butterfly-shaped gland on the superior surface of the heart. Function: plays a key role in programming the immune system to recognise 'self' and provides the site for maturation of T-lymphocytes.
B(ii) Secondary lymphoid organs:
- Spleen: the largest lymphoid organ, lobular, located on the left side of the abdomen between the diaphragm and the fundus of the stomach. Function: helps trap foreign material, removes damaged and aged erythrocytes, and stores platelets.
- Lymph nodes: small, bean-shaped organs clustered at cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions. Function: primarily filter lymph, trapping foreign material such as bacterial and viral particles.
C. Disease mechanism: Phagocytic macrophages in the medulla trap pathogenic material; this material is presented to lymphocytes so antibodies can be generated. If macrophage function is impaired or lymphocytes are depleted, antigen presentation fails, antibody production is reduced, and body defence is compromised. The tight interaction between fixed macrophages and B/T-cell populations is essential; disruption at any point in this interaction leads to failure of immune responses.

questions.question:
A. Describe the coronary circulation under the following headings:
A(i) Arterial supply: origin and distribution of the right and left coronary arteries
A(ii) Venous drainage: pathways by which coronary venous blood returns to the heart
A(iii) Characteristics of the coronary circulation — list all eight characteristics
B. Describe the regulation of coronary blood flow under the following headings:
B(i) Nervous factors: effect of sympathetic and parasympathetic stimulation
B(ii) Metabolic/chemical factors: the role of oxygen lack, carbon dioxide, potassium, lactic acid, and adenosine
B(iii) Mechanical factors: effect of systole and diastole on coronary blood flow
C. Explain the subendocardial vulnerability to ischaemia and infarction, stating its anatomical and physiological basis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Arterial supply: Right and left coronary arteries arise from the root of the aorta. The left coronary artery supplies the anterior and left lateral portions of the left ventricle. The right coronary artery supplies most of the right ventricle as well as the posterior part of the left ventricle.
A(ii) Venous drainage: Arterial blood traverses through the capillary bed and is returned to the right atrium through the capillary sinus (coronary sinus). Coronary venous blood also reaches the right atrium through the anterior coronary veins. The myocardial vessels are also in direct communication with the cardiac chambers through arteriosinusoidal, arterioluminal, and thebesian vessels.
A(iii) Eight characteristics of coronary circulation:
1. Very short and very rapid (essential to the heart).
2. Blood flow occurs mainly during cardiac diastole.
3. No efficient anastomoses between the coronary vessels.
4. Rich circulation — 5% of cardiac output, while the heart weighs 300 g. Resting coronary blood flow averages 225 mL/min.
5. Regulation is mainly by metabolites and not neural.
6. Capillary permeability is high (cardiac lymph is rich in protein).
7. Coronary vessels are susceptible to degeneration and atherosclerosis.
the subendocardial myocardial layer in the left ventricle receives less blood due to more myocardial compression but is normally compensated during diastole.
B(i) Nervous factors: Sympathetic stimulation → increased cardiac metabolism → coronary vasodilation → increased CBF. Parasympathetic stimulation → decreased cardiac metabolism → coronary vasoconstriction → decreased CBF. The effect of autonomic nerves is indirect through their effect on cardiac metabolism.
B(ii) Metabolic/chemical factors: Increased cardiac metabolism → decreased O2 tension (local hypoxia), increased CO2, increased K+, lactic acid, and adenosine → coronary vasodilation → increased CBF. O2 lack (hypoxia) is the most effective coronary vasodilator. It produces coronary vasodilation through direct action on coronary blood vessels and release of adenosine (from ATP), which is a potent coronary vasodilator.
B(iii) Mechanical factors: Ventricular systole → increased intramyocardial pressure → compression of coronary vessels → decreased CBF mainly in the left coronary artery (due to stronger contraction of the left ventricle). CBF increases during ventricular diastole (maximal at the end of isometric relaxation).
C. Subendocardial vulnerability: There is evident regional distribution — the subendocardial myocardial layer in the left ventricle receives less blood due to more myocardial compression. This renders this area more liable to ischaemia and infarction. It is normally compensated during diastole by vasodilation, but when diastole is reduced (e.g., in tachycardia) or when coronary disease is present, this compensatory vasodilation is insufficient.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old patient receives a blood transfusion during elective surgery. Shortly after transfusion begins, she develops fever, chills, flank pain, and haemoglobinuria. The recipient is blood group A and the administered blood was blood group B.
(i) State the diagnosis and explain the immunological mechanism responsible.
(ii) Identify the specific agglutinogen-agglutinin mismatch that caused this reaction, citing the normal ABO blood group composition.
(iii) State the complication of transfusing Rh-positive blood into an Rh-negative recipient on a second exposure.
(iv) State the correct universal donor blood group and explain why it can be given to all ABO types.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction due to ABO incompatibility. Mechanism: Blood type is determined by agglutinogens — specific glycoproteins on red blood cell membranes. All RBCs in an individual carry the same specific type of agglutinogens. Agglutinins are preformed antibodies in plasma that bind to agglutinogens not carried by host RBCs, causing agglutination (aggregation and lysis of incompatible RBCs).
(ii) Mismatch: Type A recipient carries agglutinogen A on RBCs and preformed agglutinin B (anti-B antibody) in plasma. Type B donor RBCs carry agglutinogen B. The recipient's anti-B agglutinin binds agglutinogen B on transfused cells, causing agglutination and lysis.
ABO composition:
- Type A: agglutinogen A, agglutinin B.
- Type B: agglutinogen B, agglutinin A.
- Type O: no A nor B agglutinogen, agglutinins A and B.
- Type AB: agglutinogens A and B, no agglutinins.
(iii) Rh complication on second exposure: Infusion of blood from an Rh-positive individual into an Rh-negative individual leads to development of anti-Rh antibody. Second exposure to Rh-positive blood leads to destruction of Rh-positive RBCs. This is also the mechanism of Rhesus haemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis).
(iv) Universal donor: Blood group O (no A nor B agglutinogen on RBCs). The person can donate to all ABO types because their RBCs carry no agglutinogens that would be attacked by anti-A or anti-B agglutinins in any recipient's plasma.

A(i) The shaft has three erectile columns (two corpora cavernosa and a corpus spongiosum) plus fascial layers, nerves, lymphatics and blood vessels, all covered by skin.
A(i) Erectile tissue consists of large sinusoids, normally relatively empty, that dilate greatly when arterial blood enters rapidly under pressure while venous outflow is partially occluded; the corpora cavernosa are surrounded by a strong fibrous band.
A(ii) The internal pudendal (penile) artery, from each internal iliac artery, enters the root of the penis and divides: the dorsal artery (runs dorsally not far beneath the skin), the deep artery (runs through the corpus cavernosum core) and the bulbourethral artery (supplies the corpus spongiosum).
A(ii) The deep artery gives off helicine arteries that penetrate the trabeculae and empty into the lacunae.
A(iii) The corpus cavernosum spaces drain by the deep dorsal vein into the prostatic venous plexus; the superficial dorsal veins drain skin and cutaneous tissues.
A(iv) The penis is richly innervated by sensory and motor fibres with abundant tactile, pressure and temperature receptors.
B(i) Stimuli: psychic (sexual thoughts or dreaming) and/or physical (tactile stimulation of the glans is most important; impulses may also enter the cord from perineal structures and internal organs).
B(i) Parasympathetic fibres from S2-S4 via the pelvic nerves to penile arteries and erectile tissue release nitric oxide, acetylcholine and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide as cotransmitters.
B(i) Nitric oxide especially relaxes the arteries and the erectile tissue of the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum.
B(i) Arteries and arterioles dilate, erectile tissue relaxes, blood flow increases (with increased cardiac output), and filling compresses veins, blocking outflow and adding to turgor.
B(ii) When flaccid, most blood supply comes from the dorsal arteries.
B(ii) The penis becomes erect when the deep artery dilates, filling the lacunae with blood.

questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, relations, branches, and distribution of the venous return system; state the safe site for venous access; and explain the anatomical basis of orthostatic hypotension and compensatory mechanisms.
A. Describe venous return and all factors that facilitate it.
B. Describe the Frank-Starling mechanism in the context of venous return and preload.
C(i) . Describe all physiological variations of cardiac output and the contributing factors.
C(ii) . Describe the cardiac reserve and state its normal values across age groups.
D. Describe the Fick principle and all methods used to measure cardiac output.
questions.answerText:
C(i) Physiological variations of cardiac output:
- Age: greater in adults than children (more blood volume).
- Gender: greater in males than females.
- Altitude: increases at high altitude places.
- Pregnancy: increases during pregnancy.
- Exercise: increases during exercise.
- Emotion: increases during emotional expressions.
Cardiac index = CO / body surface area; normal value 3.2 L/min/m².
C(ii) Cardiac reserve: maximum increase in cardiac output above normal value; expressed as percentage.
- Adults: 300–400%.
- Old age: 200–250%.
- Athletes: 500–600%.
D. Fick principle: amount of substance taken up by an organ per unit time (Q) = (arterial level − venous level) × blood flow.
Methods to measure CO:
1. Fick principle (direct and indirect): CO = O₂ consumed / (arterial O₂ − venous O₂).
2. Dilution methods (e.g. Evan's blue dye): known dye amount injected; CO = Q/(C × t) × 60.
cold saline injected; change in blood temperature in pulmonary artery measured.
B-scan ultrasound at 2.25 MHz; measures EDV, ESV, CO, and valvular defects.
graphical record of pulsations created due to ballistic recoil of the pumping heart.

A(i) The breast has secretory lobules, alveoli and lactiferous ducts that constitute the mammary glands.
A(i) Development: oestrogen is primarily responsible for proliferation of stromal cells and ducts and fat deposition; growth hormone, glucocorticoid, insulin and prolactin aid ductal growth; progesterone is primarily responsible for the lobule-alveoli system.
A(ii) Prolactin promotes milk secretion (secreted from the fifth week of pregnancy till birth); human chorionic somatomammotropin is also lactogenic; in pregnancy oestrogen inhibits milk secretion so only a few mL is secreted.
A(ii) After parturition oestrogen and progesterone fall and prolactin assumes its milk-promoting role; growth hormone, insulin, cortisol and parathyroid hormones must be adequate; milk is secreted into alveoli but does not flow into the ducts.
A(iii) Suckling sends impulses via somatic afferents from the nipple to the spinal cord and hypothalamus, releasing oxytocin, which is carried in blood to the breasts and contracts myoepithelial cells.
A(iii) Milk is expressed from the alveoli into the ducts at a pressure of +10 to 20 mm Hg (milk ejection/let-down reflex, a neuro-hormonal reflex).
B(i) Colostrum is the milk of the last few days of pregnancy and first few days after parturition: full of antibodies and white blood cells, acting as the child's first immunization; cloudy yellowish; secreted at about 1/100 of the later milk production rate.
B(i) It has more protein but less sugar and fat than transitional milk; per deciliter, colostrum has protein 2.7 g, lactose 5.3 g, fat 2.9 g versus human milk protein 1.2 g, lactose 6.8 g, fat 3.8 g.
B(i) Colostrum also has more sodium (92 mg versus 15 mg) and chloride (117 mg versus 43 mg) than human milk per deciliter.
B(ii) Breastfeeding causes lactational amenorrhea: nursing stimulates prolactin, which inhibits GnRH and antagonises gonadotropin production.
B(ii) Ovulation is inhibited and the ovaries are inactive, so oestrogen and progesterone output falls to low levels.
B(ii) Thus lactation may cause contraception.
questions.question:
A. Describe lactation under the following headings:
A(i) the breast and its development;
A(ii) initiation of milk secretion;
A(iii) the milk ejection reflex.
B.
B(i) Describe colostrum and how its composition differs from that of later milk.
B(ii) Explain the effect of lactation on the menstrual cycle.

Describe the origin, course, relations, branches, and distribution of the major divisions of the cardiovascular system responsible for regional circulation; state the safe site for measuring cerebral blood flow; and explain the anatomical basis of autoregulation.
A. Describe the anatomy and blood supply of the coronary circulation.
B. Describe the anatomy of the cerebral circulation, including the circle of Willis.
C(i) . Define autoregulation of blood flow and state the perfusion pressure range over which it operates.
C(ii) . Distinguish between reactive and active hyperaemia.
D. State the special features of the blood-brain barrier and its functional significance.
questions.answerText:
C(i) Autoregulation: intrinsic ability of an organ to maintain constant blood flow despite changes in perfusion pressure (F = (Pa − Pv)/R). Operates within perfusion pressure range of 60–170 mmHg. Coronary, cerebral, and renal circulations show highest autoregulation; skeletal and GI show moderate; cutaneous shows none.
C(ii) Reactive hyperaemia: transient increase in organ blood flow following a brief period of ischaemia (temporary arterial occlusion); due to hypoxia and build-up of vasoactive metabolites.
Active hyperaemia: increase in organ blood flow associated with increased metabolic activity (muscular exercise, increased cardiac activity, increased GIT activity).
D. Blood-brain barrier: tight junctions between endothelial cells of cerebral capillaries prevent movement of destructive substances from blood to brain. Interconnecting network from Circle of Willis provides a safety mechanism — if one artery is partly occluded, flow increases through other interconnecting arteries.

A(i) A series of periodic changes in the reproductive system of post-pubertal females preparing for fertilization and pregnancy; length 28 +/- 7 days; two concurrent cycles (ovarian and uterine), ovarian hormonal changes producing uterine changes.
A(ii) Follicular phase (days 1 to about 14): primordial follicle (ovum with single granulosa layer); after puberty FSH and LH make some follicles grow; 6-12 become primary follicles (ovum enlarges 2-3 fold, more granulosa layers); granulosa cells secrete increasing oestrogen.
A(ii) Theca forms from ovarian interstitium spindle cells: theca interna secretes oestrogen and progesterone (testosterone precursor for oestrogen), theca externa is a vascular connective tissue capsule; secondary follicles form fluid-filled vesicles.
A(ii) One follicle forms an antrum and becomes the dominant Graafian follicle (about day 6; coverings theca externa, theca interna, granulosa); others regress as atretic follicles; primary oocyte completes meiosis I (secondary oocyte plus polar body); meiosis II arrests at metaphase II and completes after fertilization.
A(iii) Rising oestrogen from the dominant follicle triggers an LH surge (positive feedback); the follicle wall ruptures 24-36 hours later (about day 14), releasing the secondary oocyte with zona pellucida and corona radiata.
A(iii) Normally one ovum is released per cycle; only about 400 of about 400,000 viable oocytes ovulate in a lifetime and the rest die by apoptosis.
A(iv) Luteal phase (second half): ovulated follicle becomes corpus haemorrhagicum then corpus luteum, secreting oestrogen, progesterone and possibly inhibin.
A(iv) If no fertilization: oocyte disintegrates about 12-24 hours after ovulation; corpus luteum regresses (about 4 days to end of cycle) to corpus albicans; oestrogen and progesterone fall causing menstruation; less negative feedback raises FSH and LH and a new cycle begins.
B(i) Menstrual phase (about first 3-5 days): orderly sloughing of the stratum functionale with bleeding (stratum basale intact) due to corpus luteum regression; mean blood loss about 30 mL (10-80 mL).
B(i) Proliferative (preovulatory) phase (about days 5-14): stratum functionale restored by glandular and vascular outgrowths from the stratum basale under oestrogen from the follicles.
B(i) Secretory (progestational) phase (after ovulation): endometrium highly vascularised with secretory glands, under oestrogen and progesterone from the corpus luteum.
B(ii) Inhibin from the corpus luteum has a negative feedback effect on gonadotropins; its inhibition of FSH retards development of new follicles, so there are no multiple ovulations or pregnancies in the same cycle.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the digestive system; explain how mastication prepares food; and explain the pathophysiology of common swallowing disorders and oesophageal disease.
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the digestive system and its major functions.
B. Describe the function of each type of tooth and the muscles of mastication with their nerve supply.
C(i) . Describe the mastication reflex in full (motor cortex, brainstem, cranial nerve supply).
C(ii) . List five problems that impair mastication.
D. Describe the two types of peristalsis in the oesophageal stage and the role of receptive relaxation of the LES.
questions.answerText:
C(i) Mastication reflex:
- Primary motor cortex: initiates and controls mandibular movement via descending corticobulbar projections to brain stem nuclei.
- Brain stem centre: integrates the reflex.
- Cranial nerve supply: CN V (trigeminal V3) — muscles of mastication; CN VII (facial) — lips and cheek muscles; CN XII (hypoglossal) — tongue muscles.
C(ii) Problems impairing mastication: mouth, gum, tooth, head or neck surgery; gum disease; reduced saliva; tooth decay or tooth loss; stroke (weak muscles, weak bite force).
D. Oesophageal peristalsis:
- Primary peristaltic wave: caused by intentional swallowing; coordinated via central innervation; continuation of the peristaltic wave beginning in the pharynx.
- Secondary peristaltic waves: caused by oesophageal distension; not dependent on swallowing initiation.
- Receptive relaxation of the LES occurs ahead of the peristaltic wave, allowing easy propulsion of swallowed food into the stomach. In achalasia, this relaxation is lost.

questions.question:
A patient presents with features of raised intracranial pressure. Disequilibrium of CSF synthesis and resorption, or obstruction of its circulation, is suspected.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Name the procedure used clinically to examine CSF.
(iii) State the anatomical landmarks of the CSF pathway relevant to this condition.
(iv) State the structure at risk of obstruction/dysfunction in this pathway.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hydrocephalus - disequilibrium in synthesis and resorption, or obstruction of circulation of CSF, resulting in CSF accumulation and raised intracranial pressure.
(ii) A lumbar puncture, used to examine CSF clinically and help create a differential diagnosis.
(iii) The choroid plexus (in the lateral, third and fourth ventricles), the interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro), the cerebral aqueduct (Aqueduct of Sylvius), the foramina of Luschka and the foramen of Magendie, the subarachnoid space, the superior sagittal sinus, and the arachnoid villi.
(iv) The arachnoid villi (site of resorption of CSF into the dural venous sinuses) or any part of the ventricular pathway listed above may be the site of obstruction/dysfunction;

questions.question:
A. Describe the hormones of pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) human chorionic gonadotropin;
A(ii) oestrogen and progesterone;
A(iii) human chorionic somatomammotropin and relaxin.
B.
B(i) Explain the role of the corpus luteum of pregnancy and the takeover by the placenta.
B(ii) State the other placental hormones.
questions.answerText:
A(i) hCG is secreted early in pregnancy by the syncytial trophoblast and later by the placenta; it is detectable in blood as early as 8-9 days after ovulation; it is primarily luteinizing and luteotropic with little FSH activity.
A(i) Functions: prevents involution of the corpus luteum (which becomes twice its size), makes it secrete larger quantities of steroid hormones, prevents the menstrual cycle, and stimulates foetal Leydig cells to release testosterone.
A(ii) Oestrogen: enlarges the uterus, genitalia and breast (with ductal growth), causes relaxation of the pelvic ligament and maintains the rate of foetal growth.
A(ii) Progesterone: necessary for development of decidual cells, decreases uterine contractility (preventing spontaneous abortion) and helps prepare the breast for lactation.
A(iii) hCS: secretion begins at about the 5th week from the syncytial trophoblast and increases throughout pregnancy; large amounts in maternal blood; involved in metabolism and foetal growth.
A(iii) Relaxin: secreted by the corpus luteum and placental tissues, increased by hCG stimulation; helps maintain pregnancy by inhibiting myometrial contractions, may relax the pelvic ligament, and is claimed to soften the cervix at delivery.
B(i) Pregnancy lasts about 270 days from fertilization; the corpus luteum present at fertilization does not regress but serves the function of the placenta before its development, secreting oestrogen, progesterone and relaxin.
B(i) In the first trimester the chorion is the source of a gonadotropin that maintains steroid production by the corpus luteum.
B(i) The placenta takes over the secretory activities at the sixth week; the corpus luteum declines after eight weeks but persists throughout pregnancy.
B(i) By the end of the first trimester the placenta is more fully developed, with a nutritive/exchange relationship between maternal and foetal circulations and steroid products giving hormonal support to the uterus.
B(ii) Other placental hormones (identical to hypothalamic counterparts): GnRH, inhibin, proopiomelanocortin (POMC), CRH, beta-endorphin, alpha-MSH, dynorphin A, leptin and prolactin.

A(i) Muscles are excitable tissues with myosin (contractile) and actin (cytoskeletal) as key proteins; three types: skeletal, smooth and cardiac; contraction may be voluntary or involuntary (autonomic).
A(ii) Muscle is made of fibres (lined by endomysium); fibres are bound by perimysium into fascicles; fascicles form the muscle lined by epimysium; each fibre has myofibrils containing sarcomeres of actin and myosin filaments.
A(ii) Skeletal muscle: discrete groups anchored by tendons to bone; multinucleated cells with peripheral nuclei; striated.
A(iii) Smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, one nucleus, no striations, in walls of organs; unitary/visceral and multiunit subdivisions.
A(iv) Cardiac muscle: striated, one nucleus, many elongated mitochondria, branching interdigitating fibres, found only in the heart, capable of spontaneous contraction.
A(v) Type I (slow oxidative, red): many capillaries, mitochondria and myoglobin; sustains aerobic activity. Type IIa: aerobic, red. Type IIb: anaerobic, glycolytic, white. Type IId: fastest in humans, more force but only short anaerobic bursts before painful contraction.
B(i) Slow (type I) versus fast (IIa/IIb): glycogen low/intermediate-high; fatigue slow/intermediate-fast; ATPase activity low/high; fibre diameter small/intermediate-large.
B(i) Motor unit size small/intermediate-large and innervation by small/intermediate-large neurons respectively (motor unit = one motor neuron and the fibres it innervates).
B(ii) Isometric: muscle does not shorten, no sliding of myofibrils (e.g. holding an object up without moving it).
B(ii) Isotonic: muscle length changes, more energy is used and contraction lasts longer.
B(ii) Isotonic divides into concentric (fibres shorten, e.g. up phase of a biceps curl) and eccentric (fibres lengthen while contracting, e.g. lowering a load gently).
B(ii) A twitch is a brief contraction followed by relaxation from a single action potential.

A(i) Puberty (Latin pubertas = age of maturity) is the stage of physical maturation in which an individual becomes physiologically capable of sexual reproduction; it occurs at about 10-14 years in females and about 12-16 years in males.
A(ii) Gonadotropin secretion is high in the newborn, falls to very low levels a few weeks after birth and stays low until puberty; in childhood the hypothalamus secretes little GnRH because even slight sex steroid strongly inhibits it; onset is marked by rising FSH followed by LH.
A(ii) The rise results from programmed maturational brain changes increasing GnRH and from decreased sensitivity of gonadotropin secretion to sex steroid negative feedback; in late puberty pulsatile gonadotropins raise testosterone (testes) and estradiol-17-beta (ovaries), producing secondary sex characteristics and a growth spurt that starts earlier in girls.
A(iii) Hormonal: leptin activates hypothalamic GnRH release and acts peripherally on the gonads; timing relates to body fat and physical activity; about 17% body fat is needed for menarche and about 22% for regular cycles; menarche is later in very active girls.
A(iii) Genetic: KiSS1 gene produces kisspeptins that activate GPR54, which signals the brain to start puberty; leptin acts through the leptin-melanocortin-kisspeptin (metabolic) pathway.
B(i) Stage 1 (about 8-11 y): ovaries enlarge and hormone production starts. Stage 2 (about 8-14 y): thelarche (first external sign), pubic hair, height and weight increase.
B(i) Stage 3 (about 9-15 y): breast growth continues, coarser pubic hair, whitish vaginal discharge, menarche may occur.
B(i) Stage 4 (about 10-16 y): areolar mound, adult triangular pubic hair, menarche if not yet occurred, ovulation may occur but irregular (anovulatory cycles).
B(i) Stage 5 (about 12-19 y): full height reached, regular ovulation, pubic hair filled in, breasts fully developed.
B(ii) Precocious puberty is onset of signs of puberty before age 7/8 in girls and age 9 in boys.
B(ii) Its causes are central and peripheral.
questions.question:
A. Describe puberty under the following headings:
A(i) definition and age of occurrence in each sex;
A(ii) hormonal changes at onset;
A(iii) factors implicated in the timing of onset.
B.
B(i) Describe the stages of female puberty with approximate ages.
B(ii) Distinguish precocious puberty from normal puberty.

A 35-year-old male presents with chest tightness and palpitations after exertion. ECG reveals a prolonged PR interval of 0.28 s. He is noted to have heart block.
(i) Describe what the ECG records and the principle by which it does so.
(ii) List all clinical uses of the ECG.
(iii) State the two types of ECG leads, name the specific limb leads in each category, and explain Einthoven's equation.
(iv) Describe how the cardiac cycle relates to ECG waveform events.
(v) Explain what a prolonged PR interval represents mechanistically.
questions.answerText:
(i) The ECG is a measure of how electrical activity of the heart changes over time as action potentials propagate throughout the heart during each cardiac cycle. It is not a direct measure of cellular depolarisation and repolarisation but reflects the relative, cumulative magnitude of populations of cells eliciting changes in their membrane potentials at a given time. The human body acts as a large volume conductor; dipoles created by depolarised and polarised cells cause current flow in body fluids detectable by surface electrodes. Amplitude is proportional to the mass of tissue involved.
(ii) Clinical uses of ECG:
- To assess cardiac functions (rate, rhythm, conduction).
- To diagnose cardiac rhythm disorders (e.g. heart block).
- To diagnose cardiac diseases (e.g. myocardial infarction).
- To detect electrolyte imbalance (e.g. hyperkalaemia).
- To evaluate effects of treatments (e.g. cardiac drugs).
(iii) Two types of leads:
- Bipolar (standard limb) leads: Lead I = LA − RA; Lead II = LL − RA; Lead III = LL − LA.
- Unipolar leads: limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF), chest leads, oesophageal leads.
Einthoven's equation: Lead I + Lead III = Lead II.
(iv) Cardiac cycle and ECG events:
- P wave: atrial depolarisation (SA node triggering).
- PR interval: AV node delay (allows atria to fill ventricles).
- QRS complex: ventricular depolarisation (triggers contraction).
- ST segment and T wave: ventricular repolarisation.
(v) A prolonged PR interval (>0.20 s) indicates delayed conduction through the AV node. Normally the AV node has the slowest conduction rate (0.05 m/s), creating a physiological delay for ventricular filling. Prolongation beyond 0.20 s indicates impaired AV nodal transmission (heart block).

questions.question:
A patient presents with progressive weakness and sensory changes, and nerve conduction studies show loss of the insulating myelin sheath around peripheral axons.
(i) Identify the structure affected.
(ii) State the differential pathologies.
(iii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for this finding.
questions.answerText:
(i) The myelin sheath of the axon (the insulating, protecting layer surrounding the axon).
(ii) Demyelination is exemplified by Guillain-Barré syndrome, and leads to certain neurodegenerative disorders like multiple sclerosis and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy), a heterogeneous inherited disorder of nerves characterized by loss of muscle tissue and touch sensation, is a further listed nerve disorder for comparison.
(iii) The axon is usually surrounded by an insulating protecting layer, the myelin sheath; because this sheath supports the conduction of nerve signals away from the soma, its loss (demyelination), as in Guillain-Barré syndrome, multiple sclerosis, and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, is consistent with the progressive weakness and sensory change described.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old Nigerian boy presents to the emergency department with acute severe pain in the hands, feet, and lower back. He has a known history of sickle cell anaemia. His SpO2 on room air is 90%. On examination his spleen is not palpable.
(i) State the molecular basis of sickle cell disease, identifying the specific polypeptide chain affected and the type of haemoglobin abnormality.
(ii) Describe how the RBC shape changes in sickle cell disease and under what conditions it is triggered.
(iii) Describe the other shapes that RBCs can assume in various conditions, giving the specific condition associated with each.
(iv) Explain why his spleen is not palpable despite this being a haemolytic condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Molecular basis: Sickle cell anaemia is a haemoglobinopathy — a genetic disorder caused by abnormal polypeptide chains of haemoglobin. In haemoglobin S (HbS), the alpha-chains are normal and the beta-chains are abnormal. This is an abnormality of the polypeptide chain structure of haemoglobin.
(ii) RBC shape change: Sickle cell — crescentic shape as in sickle cell anaemia. The condition is triggered by deoxygenation (reduced oxygen tension), acidosis, dehydration, and other hypoxic states that cause the abnormal beta-chains to interact and cause the cell to deform into a sickle shape.
(iii) Other RBC shapes:
- Crenation: shrinkage as in hypertonic conditions.
- Spherocytosis: globular form as in hypotonic conditions.
- Elliptocytosis: elliptical shape as in certain types of anaemia.
- Poikilocytosis: unusual shapes due to deformed cell membrane; the shape will be of flask, hammer, or any other unusual shape.
(iv) Non-palpable spleen: In sickle cell anaemia, repeated episodes of splenic infarction (due to sickle cells occluding splenic microvasculature) lead to gradual destruction and shrinkage of the spleen (autosplenectomy). By adolescence, the spleen is often fibrosed and no longer palpable, despite the ongoing haemolytic process. Haemolytic anaemia in sickle cell disease is caused by excessive haemolysis of RBCs as a result of the hereditary haemoglobin defect.

questions.question:
A woman with a cycle length of 28 +/- 7 days has bleeding during the first 3-5 days of her cycle.
(i) Identify the phase and state what is shed and what is retained.
(ii) Explain the hormonal basis and the normal blood loss.
(iii) Describe the two uterine phases that follow and the hormones responsible.
(iv) Explain how the next cycle begins.
questions.answerText:
(i) Menstrual phase (about the first 3-5 days): cyclic, orderly sloughing of the endometrium with bleeding and shedding of the superficial stratum functionale, leaving the deeper stratum basale intact.
(ii) It occurs due to regression of the corpus luteum, so oestrogen and progesterone fall by about the last day of the cycle; the sloughing responds to interactions of hypothalamic, pituitary and ovarian hormones.
(ii) Mean blood loss is about 30 mL (range 10-80 mL).
(iii) Proliferative (preovulatory) phase (about days 5-14): stratum functionale restored by glandular and vascular outgrowths from the stratum basale, due to oestrogen from the follicles.
(iii) Secretory (progestational) phase (last half, after ovulation): endometrium highly vascularised and glands secretory, due to oestrogen and progesterone from the corpus luteum.
(iv) The corpus luteum regresses to the corpus albicans (about 4 days to end of cycle); the lessened negative feedback increases FSH and LH secretion and another cycle begins.

questions.question:
A. Describe spermatogenesis under the following headings:
A(i) site and origin of the germ cells;
A(ii) the four stages;
A(iii) chromosome number at each step.
B.
B(i) State the functions of the Sertoli cells.
B(ii) Explain the hormonal regulation of spermatogenesis.
B(iii) State the factors that impair spermatogenesis and how sperm acquire motility.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Spermatogenesis (onset is the most significant event of puberty in males) is the change of diploid spermatogonia into haploid spermatozoa inside the seminiferous tubules, which form when sex cords acquire a lumen shortly before puberty.
A(i) Primordial germ cells migrate along the yolk sac wall in the 5th-6th week into the gonadal ridges and lie at the periphery of the sex cords, outside the blood-testis barrier.
A(ii) Proliferation: spermatogonial stem cells form type A spermatogonia (initiating spermatogenesis), which multiply as a clone and end as type B spermatogonia that migrate nearer the lumen.
A(ii) Growth: type B spermatogonia become enlarged primary spermatocytes, pass through the blood-testis barrier toward the lumen and are shielded from blood-borne agents such as antibodies by tight junctions.
A(ii) Maturation: prolonged prophase (average 22 days), then meiosis I gives two secondary spermatocytes and meiosis II gives spermatids (four per spermatogonium).
A(ii) Transformation: spermiogenesis (acrosome with enzymes for egg penetration, nuclear condensation, neck/middle piece/tail, loss of excess cytoplasm) then spermination; about 74 days from spermatogonium to mature spermatozoon.
A(iii) Spermatogonium: 23 pairs (22 autosomal pairs plus one sex pair, one of each pair from each parent); primary spermatocyte: 23 double-stranded pairs; secondary spermatocyte: 23 double-stranded chromosomes (22 autosomes plus X or Y); spermatid: 23 single-stranded.
B(i) Sertoli cells support, protect and nourish germ cells (which stay embedded in their recesses) and help release spermatozoa; they secrete androgen-binding protein, oestrogen, inhibin, and Mullerian regression factor in fetal testes.
B(ii) FSH acts on Sertoli cell receptors so they grow and secrete spermatogenic substances; LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which acts strongly on Sertoli cells; FSH, LH and testosterone are essential to initiate spermatogenesis (growth hormone and inhibin are also listed regulators).
B(ii) Spermatogonia-to-spermatid stages appear androgen-independent; maturation of spermatids depends on FSH and androgen acting on Sertoli cells.
B(iii) Impairing factors: increased temperature (cryptorchidism) and infectious diseases such as mumps.
B(iii) Sperm gain motility and fertilizing ability after time in the epididymis (CatSper activation in the tail) but are kept immotile by inhibitory epididymal proteins until ejaculation.

(i) Peptic ulcer disease (duodenal ulcer), occurring most commonly in the first part of the duodenum, called the duodenal bulb; the secondary site of occurrence is along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
(ii) Causes include infection by H. pylori (which secretes urease and proteases that break down mucus), tobacco smoking, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications (which inhibit prostaglandins), and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma).
These result in loss of mucosal protection or an increase in acid secretion, leading to inflammation; the inflamed mucous membrane may become necrotic, leaving a sore or ulcer.
Ulceration is damage to the muscularis mucosa and deeper layers (in contrast to erosion, which is breakdown of the superficial mucosa not involving the submucosa); ulcers may penetrate the submucosa, muscularis externa and serosa.
Major complications include bleeding (erosion of vessels at the base of an ulcer), perforation, and peritonitis secondary to perforation.
(iii) Treatment includes proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole), antibiotics against H. pylori bacteria, histamine 2 (H2) receptor antagonists (e.g. ranitidine), local antacids, and lifestyle changes.
questions.question:
A patient presents with epigastric pain that is relieved by eating, and endoscopy shows a lesion in the first part of the duodenum with damage extending to the muscularis mucosa and deeper layers.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis of this condition.
(iii) State the definitive treatment.

questions.answerText:
(i) In the primary stage of secretion, acini cells produce a secretion with an initial electrolyte composition similar to plasma (isosmotic).
(ii) In the secondary/modification stage, there is reabsorption of Na+ and Cl-, and secretion of K+ and HCO3-; the eventual composition of saliva is influenced by the rate of flow.
(iii) Functions of saliva include lubrication of food during chewing and formation of the bolus; moistening dry foods to aid swallowing; digestion of food via amylase and lipases; buffering the contents of the oral cavity because of its high bicarbonate concentration; and providing calcium and phosphate essential for the mineralization of teeth; saliva also dilutes regurgitated HCl or bile, protects the mouth and GI tract by cooling hot foods, protects the tract through the antimicrobial action of white blood cells, IgA and opsonins, and aids coagulation by secreting platelet-activating factor.
Clinical basis: saliva provides oral hygiene by buffering and cleansing the oral cavity - swallowing and spitting allow removal of bacteria, whereas low flow (e.g. while asleep) allows bacteria to accumulate, causing halitosis (bad breath).
This shows that the modification/clearance function of normal salivary flow is what keeps bacterial accumulation, and hence halitosis, in check; when flow is low, this clearance is reduced.
Distinguishing feature 1: the primary stage occurs in the acini and produces an isosmotic secretion resembling plasma electrolyte composition.
Distinguishing feature 2: the secondary/modification stage occurs as the primary secretion passes along the duct system, where Na+ and Cl- are reabsorbed and K+ and HCO3- are secreted, altering the final composition.
Because this ductal modification is what determines the eventual, flow-rate-dependent composition of saliva, the primary acinar secretion and the final (duct-modified) saliva are not the same fluid.
Control of secretion is via autonomic nervous system reflexes and salivary reflexes elicited by thought, aroma and taste.
Disorders of salivary secretion described include xerostomia (the subjective sensation of dry mouth) and sialorrhea (salivary hyper-secretion, clinically diagnosed by quantitative sialometry).
These disorders reflect abnormalities of the overall secretory process described above (either reduced net secretion/flow, or excess), rather than a stated defect confined to only the primary or only the secondary stage.
questions.question:
Describe salivary secretion under the following headings:
(i) the primary (acinar) stage of secretion
(ii) the secondary/modification (ductal) stage of secretion
(iii) the functions of saliva.
Explain the clinical basis of halitosis in relation to salivary flow.
Distinguish between the primary stage and the secondary/modification stage of salivary secretion.

After destruction of the sensory nerve fibres from the urinary bladder, a patient's bladder fills to capacity and overflows a few drops at a time through the urethra.
(i) Identify the condition and explain its mechanism.
(ii) Name the reflex components that are disrupted and the nerves involved.
(iii) Describe the other abnormalities of micturition, with their causes.
(iv) Explain the higher-centre control that is lost or interrupted in these conditions.
questions.answerText:
(i) Atonic bladder: destruction of sensory fibres abolishes reflex contractions of the bladder; the muscle loses tone (hypotonic, flaccid), fills to capacity and overflows a few drops at a time (overflow incontinence/dribbling).
(ii) The micturition reflex arc: stretch receptors in the bladder wall, afferent signals via the pelvic nerves, integrating centre in the sacral spinal cord, parasympathetic efferents, effector detrusor and internal sphincter; pudendal (somatic) nerves supply the external sphincter.
(iii) Automatic (spastic neurogenic) bladder: loss of higher centre control over the spinal centre, so the bladder empties automatically whenever some urine has collected.
(iii) Uninhibited neurogenic bladder: a lesion in parts of the brain stem interrupts most inhibitory signals; continuous excitation of the spinal centres gives uncontrollable micturition, and even a small volume elicits the reflex.
(iii) Nocturnal micturition (bed wetting): normal in infants and children below 3 years, due to incomplete myelination of the motor nerve fibres of the bladder with loss of voluntary control.
(iv) Higher centres regulate the sacral and lumbar spinal centres: a facilitatory area in the pons, inhibitory areas in the midbrain and cerebral cortex; they keep micturition partially inhibited.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old child is brought to a clinic with repeated episodes of involuntary urination, especially at night. The mother reports the child was previously continent but recently had regression. On assessment the bladder is found to function normally.
(i) Describe the developmental basis of micturition control in children compared to adults.
(ii) Describe the higher centres for micturition and distinguish between facilitatory and inhibitory areas.
(iii) Describe the self-regenerative nature of the micturition reflex.
(iv) Outline the physiology of bladder filling: first sensation, first desire to void, and initiation of the reflex contraction.
(v) Explain how the external sphincter can voluntarily prevent micturition even when the reflex occurs.
questions.answerText:
(i) In young children, micturition is purely reflex — it occurs whenever the bladder is sufficiently distended (myelination not complete). At about 2½ years, micturition begins to come under cortical control. In adults, it is a complex act involving both autonomic and somatic nerve pathways with reflexes that can be inhibited or facilitated by higher centres in the brain.
(ii) Higher centres for micturition:
Facilitatory areas: pons, posterior hypothalamus.
Inhibitory areas: cerebral cortex, midbrain.
The higher centres keep the micturition reflex partially inhibited except when desired. Cortical centres can facilitate sacral micturition centres when urination is convenient.
(iii) Self-regenerative nature of the micturition reflex:
- Stretch receptors in bladder wall → spinal cord → parasympathetic efferent discharge → micturition contractions.
- Initially contractions die out immediately; with increasing bladder pressure they become stronger, last longer, and are more frequent.
- The reflex may become inhibited for a few minutes to one hour before another reflex occurs.
- This pattern is described as 'self-regenerative'.
(iv) Physiology of bladder filling:
- First sensation of filling: at 100–150 mL.
- First desire to void: at 150–250 mL.
- Uncomfortable awareness of full bladder: at 350–400 mL.
- Volume initiating reflex contraction: approximately 300–400 mL.
- Increase to 700 mL creates pain and loss of control.
(v) The higher centres can prevent micturition even when the reflex occurs by tonic contraction of the external sphincter via pudendal nerves (somatic control). When convenient, cortical centres facilitate sacral micturition centres to allow relaxation of the external sphincter and voluntary initiation of voiding.

(i) The likely emergency is hypertensive crisis with possible aortic dissection. Physiological derangement: severely elevated ABP (ABP = CO × SVR), reflecting markedly elevated systemic vascular resistance and/or cardiac output.
(ii) Baroreceptor mechanism following acute blood loss:
- Decreased ABP → reduced stretch of baroreceptors → reduced baroreceptor firing → reduced inhibition of vasomotor centre → increased sympathetic outflow → increased HR, increased contractility, vasoconstriction → restoration of ABP.
- Humoral mechanisms: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is also activated following acute blood loss.
(iii) ABP = CO × SVR. Compensation for haemorrhagic hypotension:
- Baroreceptor activation → sympathetic stimulation → increased HR, increased contractility, vasoconstriction.
- Renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone → sodium and water retention.
- Fluid shift from interstitial to intravascular space.
- ADH release → water retention by collecting ducts.
(iv) Physiological basis for therapeutic intervention in hypovolaemic hypotension:
- Cause is decreased blood volume; treatment = increasing blood volume via blood or fluid transfusion.
- Occasionally accompanied by administration of pressor agents (e.g. alpha-adrenoceptor agonists such as norepinephrine).
(v) Compensatory mechanisms maintaining SV during exercise: increased venous return (abdominothoracic and muscle pumps), venous constriction, increased atrial and ventricular inotropy, enhanced ventricular lusitropy, concomitant reduction in sympathetic adrenergic and increased sympathetic cholinergic stimulation of cutaneous vessels. The limiting point is when increased HR begins to decrease SV; this varies with age, health status, and physical conditioning.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old male with known hypertension presents with sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back. Blood pressure is 180/110 mmHg. He is sweating profusely and in distress.
(i) Identify the likely cardiovascular emergency and the immediate physiological derangement.
(ii) Describe the baroreceptor mechanism activated following acute blood loss/hypotension.
(iii) State the formula for arterial blood pressure and describe the mechanisms by which hypotension caused by haemorrhage is compensated.
(iv) Describe the physiological basis for therapeutic intervention in hypovolaemic hypotension caused by haemorrhage.
(v) Describe the compensatory mechanism for maintaining stroke volume during exercise and the factors that may limit it.

A. Describe the immune system under the following headings:
A(i) definition and immune response;
A(ii) organs and their roles;
A(iii) cells of the system.
B.
B(i) Describe the five types of white blood cell with their proportions and functions.
B(ii) Describe the types of lymphocyte and how they relate to the two types of adaptive immunity.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The immune system is made of cells, tissues and molecules that defend the body against infectious microbes; the coordinated reaction against infections (and other foreign substances) is the immune response.
A(ii) Organs: bone marrow; thymus (site of T cell maturation); spleen and lymph nodes (immunologic filters).
A(iii) Cells: T cells (CD4+ and CD8+), natural killer cells, B cells, granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and macrophages.
A(iii) Natural killer cells are lymphocytes that kill virally infected cells and tumours; phagocytic cells include macrophages, neutrophils and monocytes.
B(i) Neutrophils (60%) kill bacteria.
B(i) Eosinophils (2%): allergic response and parasite killing; basophils (1%): allergic reactions.
B(i) Monocytes (4%) become macrophages; lymphocytes (33%) direct the immune system.
B(ii) Lymphocytes are responsible for the two types of adaptive immunity.
B(ii) T cells are thymus derived: natural killer cells (innate immunity), CD4+ helper cells and CD8+ cytotoxic cells; B cells are bone marrow derived.
B(ii) Humoral immunity involves B cells that secrete antibodies; cellular immunity involves CD8+ cells (cellular killing) and CD4+ cells (recruitment of other immune cells; Th1 stimulate macrophage activation, Th2 stimulate B cell activation).

questions.question:
A patient develops yellowish discolouration of the blood and tissue, with build-up of the pigments normally responsible for the golden yellow colour of bile.
(i) Identify the structure/system affected.
(ii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for this finding.
questions.answerText:
(i) The biliary secretion system (bile pigments).
(ii) Bile pigments, bilirubin and biliverdin, are responsible for the golden yellow colour of bile; if not secreted, they build up in the blood and tissue, producing jaundice.
