options: Two vessels, comprising one artery and one vein
Three vessels, comprising two arteries and one vein
Four vessels, comprising two arteries and two veins
One vessel only, functioning as a combined conduit
Five vessels, comprising three arteries and two veins
questions.question: A midwife examines a term neonate's umbilical cord shortly after birth as part of routine assessment. How many blood vessels should normally be present within the cord?
questions.explanation: A normal umbilical cord contains three vessels: two umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, and one umbilical vein carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. The presence of only two vessels, a single umbilical artery, is associated with an increased risk of congenital anomalies and warrants further neonatal assessment. Documenting vessel number at birth is a routine part of newborn examination.

questions.question: A woman taking sodium valproate for epilepsy becomes pregnant and requires a higher folic acid dose than usual due to her medication's known effect. What is the standard recommended dose in this situation?
questions.explanation: Women taking anticonvulsant medications such as sodium valproate, which act as folate antagonists and increase the risk of neural tube defects, are recommended a higher folic acid dose of five milligrams daily rather than the standard four hundred microgram dose used in low-risk pregnancies. This higher dose should ideally begin preconceptionally and continue through the first trimester. Close liaison with neurology is also important to review the anticonvulsant regimen itself.
options: Four hundred micrograms of folic acid daily
One milligram of folic acid daily
Five milligrams of folic acid daily
Ten milligrams of folic acid daily
Two hundred micrograms of folic acid daily

questions.question: A woman at 38 weeks with gestational diabetes is on insulin. Her fasting blood glucose should ideally be maintained within which range?
questions.explanation: For women with gestational diabetes (or pre-existing diabetes in pregnancy), the recommended blood glucose targets are: fasting =5.3 mmol/L; 1-hour post-meal =7.8 mmol/L; 2-hour post-meal =6.4 mmol/L. These targets are set by NICE and WHO to prevent macrosomia, birth trauma, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and other adverse perinatal outcomes. Insulin is titrated to achieve these targets. In labour, blood glucose is maintained at 4-7 mmol/L with a variable rate IV insulin infusion (VRIII).
options: 3.0–4.0 mmol/L — tight control to prevent macrosomia
5.3 mmol/L or below for fasting glucose in GDM
7.0–8.0 mmol/L — to avoid hypoglycaemia in labour
Abdominal bloating occurring after implantation in early pregnancy
Lower back pain occurring on the first day of menstruation
Mid-cycle unilateral pelvic pain at or around the time of ovulation
Bilateral pelvic cramps lasting throughout the follicular phase
Breast tenderness occurring in the late luteal phase premenstrually
questions.explanation: Mittelschmerz (German: "middle pain") is a mid-cycle unilateral pelvic pain or discomfort occurring at or around ovulation (approximately day 14 in a 28-day cycle). It is believed to result from follicle rupture, the release of follicular fluid and blood into the peritoneal cavity causing peritoneal irritation, and distension of the follicle before rupture. It may last a few hours to 1-2 days and can alternate sides each cycle. It is a useful but inconsistent fertility indicator.
questions.question: The mittelschmerz phenomenon can be used as a fertility sign. What is it and when does it occur?
Why has X-ray pelvimetry been largely abandoned in modern obstetrics?
questions.explanation: X-ray pelvimetry has been largely abandoned because it exposes the fetus to ionising radiation, and studies have shown it does not improve labour outcomes or reduce caesarean section rates. The ultimate test of pelvic adequacy is a trial of labour. When pelvimetry is clinically indicated, MRI (no ionising radiation) is preferred.
options: It exposes the fetus to ionising radiation with little benefit
MRI is superior but not widely available in low-resource settings
It is inaccurate in measuring the true conjugate
CT pelvimetry is too expensive for routine antenatal use
Ultrasound now provides all necessary pelvic measurements

questions.explanation: In the Schultz mechanism, the placenta separates centrally, and a retroplacental haematoma assists in pushing it down. The placenta descends with the shiny fetal surface (covered by amnion) presenting first - the "shiny Schultz." In the Matthews Duncan mechanism, the placenta separates from the margin, sliding out with the rough maternal cotyledon surface first.
questions.question: In the Schultz mechanism of placental delivery, what is the characteristic appearance?
options: Mixed cotyledon and membrane presentation simultaneously
The membranes delivering before the placental disc
The umbilical cord presenting first before the placental disc

questions.explanation: Each innominate (hip) bone is formed by fusion of three bones: the ilium (superior), ischium (posterior-inferior), and pubis (anterior-inferior). The three bones meet at the acetabulum. The two innominate bones, the sacrum, and coccyx form the bony pelvis. Fusion is complete by approximately 16 years of age.
questions.question: Which component of the bony pelvis is formed by fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis?
options: Innominate bone, the lateral composite hip bone
Coccyx, the terminal segment of the vertebral column
Obturator foramen, the anterior pelvic membrane gap
Sacrum, which forms the posterior pelvic wall
Acetabulum, which is only the hip socket itself

questions.explanation: Uterine inversion is a third-stage emergency causing profound haemorrhage and neurogenic shock. The O'Sullivan hydrostatic method infuses warm saline (2-3 litres) into the vagina to create hydraulic pressure that repositions the uterus. Johnson's manual replacement is an alternative. Oxytocics are withheld until after replacement, as they can make reduction impossible by contracting the cervical ring.
options: Immediate manual removal of the placenta then uterine replacement
Aggressive fundal pressure to assist placental delivery
IV ergometrine to contract the uterus around the inversion
Caesarean hysterectomy as the definitive first-line treatment
Hydrostatic replacement using warm saline infusion into the vagina
questions.question: The O'Sullivan technique for managing uterine inversion involves which intervention?

questions.explanation: At 28 weeks, all Rh-negative unsensitised women should receive: (1) routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis (500 IU IM or 1500 IU depending on local guidelines); and (2) an indirect Coombs test (antibody screen/MSAFP/red cell alloantibody screen) to ensure the woman has not already become sensitised. If alloantibodies are detected, anti-D will not help and specialist monitoring for haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) is initiated. Both are essential components of the 28-week antenatal visit.
options: Indirect Coombs test (antibody screen) for alloimmunisation
Both anti-D administration and indirect Coombs test
Complete blood count and serum ferritin assessment
questions.question: During antenatal care, which investigation is performed routinely at the 28-week visit for all Rh-negative women?

questions.explanation: The blastocyst has an inner cell mass (embryoblast), which differentiates into the epiblast and hypoblast, and the outer trophoblast. The inner cell mass gives rise to all embryonic tissues (and eventually the fetus). The epiblast will form the three primary germ layers - ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm - via gastrulation in the third week. The trophoblast forms the placenta.
options: Syncytiotrophoblast — the invasive outer cellular layer
Cytotrophoblast — the inner cellular trophoblast layer
Epiblast (inner cell mass/embryoblast) — the embryonic layer
questions.question: The blastocyst has two distinct cell populations. Which layer will form the fetus itself?

options: Mastitis, an infection localised to the breast tissue
Urinary tract infection, unrelated to the uterus itself
Deep vein thrombosis, presenting with leg swelling
Puerperal sepsis, an infection of the reproductive tract
Postpartum psychosis, presenting with behavioural changes
questions.explanation: Puerperal sepsis is characterised by fever of at least 38 degrees Celsius, offensive or purulent lochia, and uterine tenderness, reflecting infection of the reproductive tract following childbirth, most commonly caused by ascending bacterial infection. Prompt recognition and treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics are essential to prevent progression to severe sepsis or septic shock. This condition remains an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality globally.
questions.question: A midwife caring for a postpartum woman identifies fever, offensive lochia, and uterine tenderness as key features of a specific postpartum complication. Which condition does this triad describe?

options: Glucose tolerance test, full blood count, and biophysical profile
Urine culture, vaginal swab for GBS, and thyroid function tests
Cervical smear, serum folate, and hepatitis B surface antigen
Blood group, Rhesus factor, haemoglobin, VDRL/RPR, and HIV screening
Urea and electrolytes, LFTs, and thrombophilia screen
questions.explanation: At the booking visit, routine investigations include: ABO blood group and Rhesus factor; haemoglobin (Hb) for anaemia; VDRL or RPR for syphilis (a cause of congenital infection); HIV screening (with pre-test counselling); hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg); urinalysis for protein and glucose; and malaria parasite testing in endemic areas. These investigations follow the NMCN and Nigerian National Guidelines for Antenatal Care and are essential for identifying risks that can be addressed to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes.
questions.question: Which investigation is routinely performed at the first antenatal (booking) visit for all pregnant women in Nigeria?

options: Immediate administration of oxytocin and fluid resuscitation only
Manual removal of the placenta and uterine packing
Emergency caesarean section after maternal stabilisation
Insertion of a Bakri balloon for tamponade
Application of a B-Lynch suture to compress the uterus
questions.question: A woman at 34 weeks with known placenta praevia experiences a sudden massive haemorrhage with maternal shock. What is the definitive treatment?
questions.explanation: Massive haemorrhage from placenta praevia with maternal shock requires emergency caesarean section as the definitive treatment. Simultaneous resuscitation (IV fluids, blood transfusion, oxygen) is initiated immediately. The surgical team, anaesthetist, neonatal team, and blood bank must be alerted. Caesarean section stops the haemorrhage by delivering the placenta. Balloon tamponade and compression sutures may be used intraoperatively if postpartum atony occurs.

options: Induction of labour at 37 weeks to prevent haemorrhage
Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity before delivery
Outpatient management with weekly ultrasound surveillance
Immediate emergency caesarean section regardless of stability
Conservative inpatient management with steroids and blood cross-matching
questions.explanation: A stable woman with major placenta praevia at 36 weeks without active haemorrhage should be managed conservatively in hospital (inpatient): corticosteroids (betamethasone) to accelerate fetal lung maturity, blood group and cross-match, IV access, and planned elective caesarean section at 37-38 weeks. Emergency CS is reserved for uncontrolled haemorrhage or fetal compromise. Outpatient management is only considered for minor praevia in selected stable women after thorough risk assessment.
questions.question: A primigravida at 36 weeks has a major placenta praevia diagnosed on ultrasound. She is clinically stable with no active bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?

options: 6 weeks — the period of return to the pre-pregnant state
2 weeks — return of menstruation marks the end
4 weeks — uterine involution is fully complete
12 weeks — the extended WHO postpartum definition
questions.explanation: The puerperium is defined as the 6 weeks (approximately 42 days) following delivery, during which the reproductive organs and maternal physiology return to their pre-pregnant state. Key processes include uterine involution, cervical competence restoration, healing of perineal trauma, resumption of ovarian function, and establishment of lactation. Complications include PPH, puerperal sepsis, DVT/PE, and postpartum depression.
questions.question: The puerperium (postpartum period) lasts how long?

options: From anteroposterior to the transverse diameter
From the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior
From the direct OA to the direct OP position
From the oblique diameter to the transverse diameter
From OP to the transverse and then to OA
questions.explanation: Internal rotation involves the occiput rotating from the transverse (or oblique) diameter of the mid-pelvis to the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet, so the occiput comes to lie beneath the symphysis pubis (direct OA). This rotation is guided by the levator ani and pelvic floor slope, converting transverse engagement to the AP orientation matching the widest outlet diameter.
questions.question: Internal rotation in vertex presentation involves the occiput rotating from which position to which?

questions.explanation: Secondary PPH (abnormal vaginal bleeding from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum) most commonly occurs between days 7-14 after delivery. The most common causes are retained products of conception (RPOC) causing subinvolution, and endometritis (puerperal sepsis). Women typically present with offensive lochia, uterine tenderness, fever, and heavy bleeding. Ultrasound identifies RPOC; treatment is surgical evacuation ± antibiotics.
options: 4–6 weeks postpartum, as lactation is established
24–72 hours after delivery, the immediate postpartum period
6–12 weeks postpartum, at the late puerperium
Within 24 hours of delivery (primary PPH period)
Days 7–14 after delivery, the most common secondary PPH period
questions.question: Secondary PPH most commonly occurs between which timeframe?
A woman with suspected cervical incompetence and a history of recurrent mid-trimester loss is considered for cervical cerclage. At what point in pregnancy is this procedure typically performed?
options: After twenty-eight weeks gestation, as an emergency
Between twelve and fourteen weeks gestation, electively
In the first trimester, before six weeks gestation
Only in labour, once contractions have begun
Immediately postpartum, to prevent future incompetence
questions.explanation: Elective cervical cerclage, using techniques such as the McDonald or Shirodkar suture, is typically performed between twelve and fourteen weeks gestation in women with a history suggestive of cervical incompetence, aiming to provide mechanical support to the cervix before significant dilatation can occur. Emergency cerclage may be considered later if cervical shortening or dilatation is detected on surveillance. Careful patient selection based on obstetric history improves outcomes from this intervention.

questions.question: Labetalol is used for acute management of severe hypertension in pregnancy. What is its mechanism of action?
options: It acts as a central sympatholytic reducing noradrenaline release
It acts as a combined non-selective alpha and beta adrenergic blocker
It acts as a selective beta-1 adrenergic receptor blocker
It acts as a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blocker
It acts as a calcium channel blocker reducing vascular tone
questions.explanation: Labetalol is a combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta-adrenergic receptor blocker. By blocking both receptors, it reduces systemic vascular resistance (alpha-1 blockade) and heart rate and cardiac output (beta-blockade), thereby lowering blood pressure. For acute severe hypertension in pregnancy: IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, then 40 mg, then 80 mg at 10-20 minute intervals (maximum 300 mg total). Oral labetalol 200 mg twice to three times daily is used for maintenance.

questions.question: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is distinguished from HELLP syndrome primarily by which laboratory finding?
options: Elevated liver transaminases in AFLP but normal in HELLP
Hypoglycaemia and reduced fibrinogen (<300 mg/dL) in AFLP
Severe thrombocytopaenia present in AFLP but not HELLP
Elevated bilirubin in HELLP only, not in AFLP
Elevated creatinine only in AFLP and not in HELLP
questions.explanation: While HELLP and AFLP can be clinically similar, key distinguishing features of AFLP include: hypoglycaemia (due to acute hepatic failure), markedly reduced fibrinogen (<300 mg/dL - indicative of hepatic synthetic failure), elevated ammonia, and features of encephalopathy. In HELLP, fibrinogen is usually normal or mildly elevated (as it is an acute-phase reactant) unless DIC supervenes. AFLP occurs in the third trimester and carries very high maternal and fetal mortality without urgent delivery.

options: Tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menstruation
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen
Combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress ovulation
Paracetamol 1 g four times daily for mild dysmenorrhoea
Mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
questions.question: A woman presents with primary dysmenorrhoea and is not planning pregnancy. Which first-line pharmacological treatment is recommended?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, naproxen, mefenamic acid) are first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea. They inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX), reducing prostaglandin synthesis in the endometrium. Elevated PGF2a and PGE2 in the menstrual fluid cause uterine hyperstimulation and ischaemia - the cause of primary dysmenorrhoea. NSAIDs should be started 1-2 days before expected menstruation for maximum benefit. The combined oral contraceptive pill is a second-line option.

questions.question: A labouring woman's partograph shows the plotted cervical dilatation crossing to the right of the action line. What does this finding require?
questions.explanation: The action line on the WHO partograph is set four hours to the right of the alert line, and crossing it signals that labour has deviated significantly from the expected progress, warranting prompt clinical review. This may lead to interventions such as amniotomy, oxytocin augmentation, or caesarean section depending on the underlying cause. Timely response at this stage helps prevent obstructed labour and its complications.
options: Routine continuation of expectant midwifery care
Discharge home to await spontaneous labour onset
Immediate delay of all further vaginal examinations
Prompt clinical review and consideration of intervention
Reassurance only, since dilatation is still progressing
Polycystic ovary syndrome, with anovulatory cycles
Premature ovarian insufficiency, with early menopause
Mullerian agenesis, with absent uterus and upper vagina
Turner syndrome, with associated short stature
questions.question: A woman presents with primary amenorrhoea at seventeen years of age, and examination reveals a blind-ending vagina with normal secondary sexual characteristics. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Mullerian agenesis, also known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome, presents with primary amenorrhoea due to congenital absence of the uterus and upper vagina, while normal secondary sexual characteristics develop because ovarian function and hormone production remain intact. A blind-ending vagina on examination is a classic finding. Karyotyping and imaging help confirm the diagnosis and guide further management.

questions.question: Risk factors specifically associated with the development of pre-eclampsia include which combination?
questions.explanation: Well-established risk factors for pre-eclampsia include: nulliparity (3× risk); previous pre-eclampsia; multiple pregnancy; obesity (BMI >35); advanced maternal age (>40); pre-existing hypertension; diabetes (pre-gestational); renal disease; antiphospholipid syndrome; and family history of pre-eclampsia. Low-dose aspirin (150 mg nocte) from 12 weeks reduces the risk by approximately 20% in high-risk women.
options: Nulliparity, low folate intake, anaemia, and urinary tract infection
Multiparity, BMI <18.5, thrombophilia, and male fetus
Nulliparity, BMI >35, age >40, multiple pregnancy, and previous pre-eclampsia
Multiparity, diabetes without hypertension, and iron deficiency
Multiparity, young maternal age, low BMI, and smoking

questions.question: Thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid primarily requires which action at delivery?
questions.explanation: Thick meconium (pea-soup consistency) is associated with meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). Current guidelines recommend the paediatric/neonatal team attend delivery for thick MSAF, with preparation for airway suctioning if the baby is non-vigorous at birth. Vigorous babies with MSAF do not require routine tracheal suctioning. Thin meconium with normal CTG can be managed expectantly with close monitoring.
options: Paediatric presence at delivery for active airway management
Thin meconium only requires oxytocin augmentation to speed delivery
It requires immediate caesarean section to prevent aspiration
It confirms fetal death and necessitates immediate delivery
It confirms that labour has been prolonged beyond 42 weeks
The anterior shoulder descending beneath the symphysis
The head rotating back to its original pre-rotation position
The posterior shoulder being delivered over the perineum
The head extending under the pubic symphysis
The fetal head flexing to reduce the presenting diameter
questions.question: Restitution is the movement of the fetal head immediately after delivery of the head. What does it describe?
questions.explanation: Restitution is the movement immediately after the head is delivered. The delivered head rotates approximately 45° back to its original position (untwisting the neck), as the shoulders are still oblique in the pelvis. This aligns the sagittal suture with the maternal transverse diameter again. External rotation follows as the shoulders complete internal rotation to the AP diameter.

questions.question: A woman with sharp groin pain in the third trimester is reassured this is common in pregnancy. Stretching of which structure explains this pain?
options: Broad ligament, compressed by the enlarging fetus
Round ligament, hypertrophied and stretched by the growing uterus
Uterosacral ligament, pulled posteriorly toward the sacrum
Ovarian ligament, tethered near the pelvic sidewall
Cardinal ligament, stretched at the cervix
questions.explanation: The round ligament runs from the uterine cornua through the inguinal canal to the labium majus, and hypertrophies during pregnancy to help support the anteverted uterus. Rapid stretching, especially with sudden movement, causes sharp groin or lower abdominal pain. This round ligament pain is benign and self-limiting.

The calendar (Ogino-Knaus/rhythm) method calculates the fertile window based on recorded cycle lengths over at least 6-12 months: first fertile day = (shortest cycle - 18 days); last fertile day = (longest cycle - 11 days). For example, with cycles ranging from 26-32 days: fertile days = 8th to 21st. Women are advised to avoid unprotected intercourse during this window. It has a high failure rate (9-20% typical use) as it relies on cycle regularity.
options: Day 10 to day 17 for all women with regular cycles
Day 12 to day 15 regardless of the cycle length
Shortest cycle minus 18 days to the longest cycle minus 11 days
Shortest cycle plus 7 days to the longest cycle plus 3 days
Longest cycle minus 20 days to the shortest cycle minus 10 days
questions.question: The calendar (rhythm) method of natural family planning requires the woman to track her cycles and avoid intercourse during the fertile window. This method estimates the fertile period based on which calculation?

options: Deep femoral nodes running along the femoral vessels
External iliac nodes positioned lateral to the iliac vessels
Superficial inguinal nodes located in the femoral triangle
Internal iliac nodes draining the deep pelvic organs
Para-aortic nodes situated at the level of L1 to L2
questions.question: The lymphatic drainage of the vulva passes primarily to which lymph node group?
questions.explanation: The vulva drains primarily to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes in the femoral triangle. From there, lymph passes to the deep inguinal then external iliac nodes. This pathway is clinically important in vulvar carcinoma, where inguinal lymphadenopathy is an early sign of metastasis. The clitoris may additionally drain to deep nodes.

questions.question: In the modified Ritgen manoeuvre, how are the midwife's hands positioned?
options: Both hands cup the sides of the fetal head to prevent moulding
One hand on the perineum and one on the fundus
One hand under the chin through the perineum; one on the occiput
Both hands on the occiput controlling the rate of extension
One hand supports the perineum; the other controls the occiput
questions.explanation: The modified Ritgen manoeuvre involves one hand applying gentle pressure to the fetal occiput to slow delivery, while the other hand applies upward pressure toward the fetal chin through the posterior perineum - promoting flexion and protecting the perineum. This allows controlled delivery of the head under flexion, reducing the presenting diameter and minimising perineal trauma.

Dystocia (Greek: "dys" = difficult, "tokos" = birth) refers to abnormal, slow, or obstructed labour progress. It encompasses: failure to progress (slow cervical dilatation or descent); cephalopelvic disproportion; malpresentation/malposition; inadequate uterine contractions (uterine inertia); and soft tissue obstruction. Dystocia is the most common indication for emergency caesarean section. Management depends on the cause: augmentation (for uterine inertia), repositioning, or caesarean section (for CPD or malpresentation).
questions.question: The term "dystocia" in obstetrics refers to which condition?
options: The passage of meconium-stained liquor in labour
Abnormal or difficult labour due to obstructed or slow progress
Rupture of membranes more than 18 hours before labour
Failure of the fetal head to engage before labour begins

questions.question: A midwife palpates the uterine fundus at the level of the umbilicus. At approximately what gestational age does this correspond?
options: 24 weeks, when fundus has risen above the umbilicus
20 weeks, when fundus reaches the level of the umbilicus
16 weeks, when fundus has just reached the symphysis
32 weeks, when fundus is approaching the costal margin
28 weeks, when fundus is midway toward the xiphisternum
questions.explanation: The uterine fundus reaches the level of the umbilicus at approximately 20 weeks of gestation. Before 20 weeks, fundal height in centimetres approximates gestational age in weeks. At 12 weeks, the uterus just becomes palpable above the symphysis pubis. This clinical correlate is routinely used to assess fetal growth during antenatal visits.
