questions.question: A woman undergoing pelvic examination is found to have an anteverted, anteflexed uterus. How should the midwife document this normal finding?

options: Clitoris, providing lubrication during sexual arousal
Labia minora, along their medial surface
Urethral meatus, situated just below the clitoris
Vestibule, on either side of the vaginal introitus
Vaginal fornix, at the lateral vault angles
questions.question: Bartholin's glands (greater vestibular glands) open into which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation: Bartholin's glands are a pair of pea-sized mucous glands whose ducts open into the vestibule between the hymen and labia minora. They secrete mucus that lubricates the vestibule during sexual arousal. Bartholin's cysts and abscesses form when the duct becomes obstructed.

questions.question: A woman presents with oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne, and obesity. Ultrasound shows polycystic ovaries. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis of PCOS?
questions.explanation: PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria (2003), requiring at least 2 of 3 features: (1) oligo-anovulation (irregular or absent periods); (2) clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, elevated testosterone); and (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (=12 follicles per ovary or ovarian volume >10 mL). Other causes of hyperandrogenism (Cushing's syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumours) must be excluded.
options: Fasting insulin level greater than 20 mIU/L confirming insulin resistance
Serum LH:FSH ratio greater than 2:1 with elevated androgens
At least two of three Rotterdam criteria (oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on USS)
Serum FSH level above 10 IU/L confirming ovarian insufficiency
Serum oestradiol greater than 400 pmol/L with low progesterone
Fetal head pressure on the pelvic floor initiating pushing urge
Stretch receptors in the vagina and LUS triggering oxytocin release
Cervical dilation triggering cortisol from fetal adrenals
Stretch receptors in the cervix triggering FSH release
Placental CRH triggering PGE2 release from the decidua
questions.question: The Ferguson reflex is triggered by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: The Ferguson reflex is a neuroendocrine reflex in which distension of the lower uterine segment and vagina by the presenting part stimulates stretch receptors. Signals travel via the spinal cord to the hypothalamus, triggering an oxytocin surge from the posterior pituitary. This intensifies uterine contractions in the second stage and stimulates the mother's involuntary urge to push. Epidural anaesthesia can blunt this reflex.

options: Mixed gynecoid-anthropoid with a moderate arch angle
Gynecoid pelvis where the subpubic arch is >90 degrees
Anthropoid pelvis with a wide obtuse subpubic angle
Platypelloid pelvis with a very wide subpubic arch
Android pelvis with a narrow acute subpubic arch
questions.question: A woman in advanced labour is found to have a narrow acute subpubic arch. This is most consistent with which pelvic type?
questions.explanation: The android pelvis typically has a narrow, acute subpubic arch (less than 90°), compared to the gynecoid where it is 90° or greater. A narrow subpubic arch forces the fetal head posteriorly toward the sacrum, reducing the usable outlet diameter. This increases the risk of perineal trauma, instrumental delivery, and caesarean section.

questions.question: A woman with endometriosis is being counselled on how this condition can contribute to infertility. Through which mechanisms does endometriosis primarily impair fertility?
questions.explanation: Endometriosis causes infertility primarily through pelvic inflammation, adhesion formation, and distortion of normal tubo-ovarian anatomy, which impair oocyte release, tubal transport, and fertilisation. Endometriomas can also directly reduce ovarian reserve. Management of infertility in endometriosis may involve surgical treatment of adhesions or assisted reproduction depending on severity.
options: Direct destruction of ovarian follicular reserve alone
Pelvic adhesions and distorted tubo-ovarian anatomy
Complete obstruction of the cervical canal alone
Autoimmune destruction of sperm within the uterus

questions.question: A primigravida has been pushing for two hours in the second stage with inadequate progress, though the fetal head is visible at the introitus. What is the most appropriate next action?
questions.explanation: A prolonged second stage with a visible head at the introitus but inadequate progress is an indication for assisted vaginal delivery using vacuum extraction or forceps by a skilled practitioner, since the head is low enough for safe instrumental delivery. Continued unassisted pushing risks maternal exhaustion and fetal compromise. Fundal pressure is discouraged due to risk of uterine rupture and fetal injury.
options: Refer promptly for assisted vaginal delivery
Continue expectant pushing for another two hours
Perform immediate caesarean section without further assessment
Administer intravenous oxytocin to strengthen contractions
Apply fundal pressure to hasten expulsion

questions.explanation: A retained placenta is defined as failure of the placenta to deliver within thirty minutes after birth when active management has been used, or within sixty minutes with expectant management. This classification prompts further assessment and consideration of manual removal to prevent haemorrhage and infection. Prompt recognition avoids unnecessary delay in appropriate intervention.
options: Normal third stage, still within expected time
Placenta accreta, confirmed without further assessment
Retained placenta, as delivery has exceeded thirty minutes
questions.question: A woman's placenta has not delivered thirty-five minutes after birth despite active management. How should this delay be classified according to standard obstetric definitions?

questions.explanation: The Billings ovulation method (BOM) relies on the woman observing and recording the characteristics of cervical mucus (vaginal discharge) throughout her menstrual cycle. In the periovulatory period, oestrogen causes the cervical mucus to become clear, slippery, stretchy (Spinnbarkeit), and abundant - like raw egg white - indicating the fertile window. After ovulation, progesterone transforms mucus to thick, cloudy, and scant (infertile). Correct use requires daily observation and charting, with trained counselling.
options: Counting cycle days from the first day of menstruation
Observing the characteristics of cervical mucus throughout the cycle
Monitoring basal body temperature rise after ovulation
Measuring urinary LH levels to detect the preovulatory surge
questions.question: The Billings ovulation method (cervical mucus method) of fertility awareness is based on which physiological observation?
The posterior fontanelle (lambda) has which shape and closes at what age?
questions.explanation: The posterior fontanelle (lambda) is triangular, formed at the junction of the sagittal suture and two lambdoid sutures. It is present at birth and closes at approximately 6-8 weeks of age. It is palpated during vaginal examination to determine fetal head position. The anterior fontanelle (bregma) is diamond-shaped and closes at 12-18 months.
options: Circular, closing at birth as sutures fuse
Square-shaped, closing at the end of the neonatal period
Triangular, closing at 6–8 weeks after birth

questions.question: Which drug is commonly used in medical management of fibroids to reduce uterine volume and fibroid size before surgery?
questions.explanation: GnRH agonists (leuprorelin, goserelin) are used pre-operatively to induce a hypo-oestrogenic state (medical menopause), causing fibroid volume reduction of 30-60% over 3-6 months. This reduces intraoperative blood loss during myomectomy or hysterectomy, can correct preoperative anaemia, and may allow a laparoscopic rather than open approach. Newer selective progesterone receptor modulators (ulipristal acetate) were also used but have been restricted due to hepatotoxicity. GnRH agonists cannot be used long-term due to bone loss.
options: Clomiphene citrate 50 mg orally to stimulate ovulation
Tranexamic acid to reduce menstrual blood loss
Norethisterone 10 mg three times daily as progestogen
Mifepristone 5 mg daily as a progesterone antagonist
GnRH agonist (e.g., leuprorelin) to induce a hypo-oestrogenic state

questions.question: A woman with a suspected ovarian mass is being investigated, and the nurse explains the role of a specific tumour marker used in monitoring epithelial ovarian conditions. Which marker is this?
questions.explanation: CA-125 is commonly used as a tumour marker in the assessment and monitoring of epithelial ovarian masses, though it lacks specificity as it can also be elevated in benign conditions such as endometriosis and fibroids. It is most useful when interpreted alongside imaging findings and clinical risk assessment tools. Other markers such as alpha-fetoprotein are more relevant to germ cell tumours rather than epithelial ovarian disease.
options: CA-125, a non-specific marker used in ovarian monitoring
Alpha-fetoprotein, specific to germ cell tumours
Human chorionic gonadotrophin, specific to trophoblastic disease
Prostate-specific antigen, specific to male reproductive tissue
Carcinoembryonic antigen, specific to gastrointestinal malignancy

questions.question: A midwife explains to a new mother that her fundus should be at approximately the level of the umbilicus immediately after birth and will progressively descend. Over what period does the uterus typically involute back to its pre-pregnancy size?
options: Approximately six weeks, the duration of the puerperium
questions.explanation: The puerperium, the period during which the reproductive organs return to their pre-pregnancy state, lasts approximately six weeks, during which the uterus undergoes progressive involution from its immediate postpartum size back to its normal weight and dimensions. Delayed involution beyond this expected timeframe may suggest retained products or infection requiring further assessment. Regular fundal height assessment in the early postnatal period tracks this normal process.

questions.question: Which cells surrounding the primary follicle express aromatase activity to produce oestrogen?
options: Luteal cells from the granulosa layer after ovulation
Stromal cells producing inhibin B to suppress FSH
Theca externa cells providing structural support
Theca interna cells secreting androgens from cholesterol
Granulosa cells expressing aromatase to convert androgens to oestrogen
questions.explanation: Granulosa cells express the enzyme aromatase (CYP19A1), which converts androgens (produced by theca interna cells) to oestrogens (oestradiol). This is the "two-cell, two-gonadotrophin" theory: LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens, while FSH acts on granulosa cells to upregulate aromatase. The resulting oestradiol drives endometrial proliferation and the positive feedback LH surge.

options: Short-acting beta-agonists, used for acute relief
Inhaled corticosteroids, used for maintenance therapy
Non-selective beta-blockers, which can worsen bronchospasm
Oral corticosteroids, used for severe exacerbations
Oxygen therapy, used to correct hypoxaemia
questions.explanation: Non-selective beta-blockers can precipitate or worsen bronchospasm in patients with asthma by blocking bronchodilating beta-2 receptors, and should generally be avoided when safer alternatives exist. Short-acting beta-agonists, inhaled and oral corticosteroids, and oxygen remain standard components of acute asthma management in pregnancy. Careful drug selection ensures effective asthma control without compromising respiratory function.
questions.question: A woman at 28 weeks with known asthma develops acute breathlessness and audible wheeze. Which category of drug should be avoided in her acute management if possible?

questions.explanation: LOA stands for Left Occipito-Anterior, meaning the occiput (denominator in vertex presentation) is directed toward the left anterior quadrant of the maternal pelvis. LOA is the most common and favourable position for delivery, allowing the head to rotate anteriorly to direct OA for delivery. Other presentation denominators: face (mentum), brow (sinciput), breech (sacrum).
options: Left Oblique Axis — direction of the sagittal suture
Left Occipital-Angle — position of the head at the pelvic brim
Lower Occipito-Anterior — position in the mid-pelvic cavity
Left Occipito-Anterior — occiput directed to the left-anterior quadrant
Left Occiput-Apex — relationship of vertex to the pelvis
questions.question: In vertex presentation, the position described as LOA means the occiput is directed where?

questions.explanation: A personal history of venous thromboembolism is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraceptives, as the oestrogen component further increases clotting risk in women already predisposed to thrombosis. Progestogen-only methods are generally considered safer alternatives in this context. Thorough risk assessment before prescribing hormonal contraception helps prevent recurrent thrombotic events.
questions.question: A woman using combined oral contraceptives has a strong personal history of deep vein thrombosis. Which pregnancy-related condition would also make oestrogen-containing contraception absolutely contraindicated?
options: A previous uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery
A personal history of any venous thromboembolism
A previous pregnancy affected by mild anaemia
A previous pregnancy with mild nausea and vomiting
A family history of migraine without aura

questions.explanation: Placenta accreta spectrum disorders include: placenta accreta (villi attach to the myometrium without invasion - most common, 75%); placenta increta (villi invade the myometrium); and placenta percreta (villi penetrate through the full thickness of the uterine wall and may invade the bladder or bowel - most severe). PAS is strongly associated with previous uterine surgery (especially previous caesarean section) and major placenta praevia.
questions.question: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) describes abnormal placental implantation. Which degree involves invasion through the uterine wall into adjacent organs?
options: Placenta accreta — superficial attachment without invasion
Placenta percreta — invasion through the serosa into adjacent organs
Placenta praevia accreta — combination of low lying and invasive placenta
Velamentous insertion — cord inserted into membranes
Placenta increta — invasion into the myometrium

questions.explanation: WHO's Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour (AMTSL) consists of three components: (1) uterotonic drug administration - oxytocin 10 IU IM (preferred) immediately after delivery of the baby (or anterior shoulder); (2) controlled cord traction (CCT) with counter-pressure (Brandt-Andrews technique) after signs of placental separation; and (3) uterine massage after delivery of the placenta to encourage continued uterine contraction. Early (within 1-3 minutes) cord clamping is also recommended unless delayed cord clamping is indicated.
questions.question: The standard regimen for active management of the third stage of labour as recommended by WHO includes which three components?
options: Ergometrine + controlled cord traction + fundal pressure
Misoprostol + delayed cord clamping + uterine massage
Oxytocin + controlled cord traction + uterine massage
Below 12 g/dL in the first and third trimesters
Below 9 g/dL in the second trimester only
Below 10 g/dL in any trimester of pregnancy
Below 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester
Below 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters
questions.explanation: The WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as haemoglobin below 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, and below 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester (due to physiological haemodilution). Iron deficiency anaemia is the most common cause. Management includes oral ferrous sulphate 200 mg three times daily; IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) is used if oral iron is not tolerated or in severe cases. Blood transfusion is reserved for Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms or <6 g/dL.
questions.question: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy is defined as haemoglobin below which threshold?
A woman is found to have a blood pressure reading of 165/115 mmHg at 32 weeks gestation with significant proteinuria. How should this finding be classified?
questions.explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia is indicated by a blood pressure of at least 160/110 mmHg accompanied by significant proteinuria, distinguishing it from milder gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia. This classification triggers closer monitoring, antihypertensive therapy, and consideration of timing of delivery based on gestational age and maternal-fetal status. Recognising severity accurately guides the urgency of management.
options: Severe pre-eclampsia, given the markedly elevated readings
Mild pre-eclampsia, within an acceptable range
White coat hypertension requiring repeat measurement only

questions.question: Two hours after a normal delivery, a midwife finds the uterus soft, relaxed, and boggy with continued vaginal bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Retained products of conception without atony
Cervical laceration with a firm uterus
Uterine inversion with a palpable fundus
Uterine atony causing primary postpartum haemorrhage
questions.explanation: A soft, boggy, relaxed uterus with ongoing bleeding is the hallmark of uterine atony, the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage, as the myometrium fails to compress the spiral arterioles at the placental site. Immediate uterine massage and uterotonic administration are the priority interventions. If the uterus were firm despite bleeding, a genital tract laceration would be more likely.

questions.question: Which sign indicates a woman is no longer in the latent phase of labour and has entered active labour?
questions.explanation: The transition from latent to active phase of labour is defined by cervical dilatation reaching 4-5 cm (WHO/NICE now use 5 cm as the threshold for confirmed active labour in most guidelines) with regular, progressive, painful contractions. Bloody show and membrane rupture can occur in the latent phase and are not reliable indicators of active labour onset. Cervical effacement alone without adequate dilatation does not confirm active labour.
options: Regular contractions occurring at least every 10 minutes
Cervical dilatation of 4–5 cm with regular painful contractions
Spontaneous rupture of membranes with liquor drainage
Cervical effacement of 50% with the presenting part engaged
Bloody show with blood-stained mucus discharge
Triangular with convergent sidewalls and narrow outlet
Round or slightly oval (gynecoid) with adequate diameters
Heart-shaped (android) with a prominent sacral promontory
Oval transversely (platypelloid) with a flat reduced inlet
Long oval anteroposteriorly (anthropoid) with narrow sides
questions.question: The gynecoid pelvis is the most favourable pelvic type for vaginal delivery. What shape is its inlet?
questions.explanation: The gynecoid pelvis has a rounded or slightly oval inlet with adequate transverse (13 cm) and anteroposterior (11 cm) diameters, straight sidewalls, a broad sacrum, and a wide subpubic arch (>90°). Approximately 50% of women have this pelvic type. Its proportionate dimensions favour engagement, descent, and rotation of the fetal head, making it most suitable for spontaneous vaginal delivery.

courses.objectives:
Oral Mucosal Diseases & Infections: Q1–65
Oral Candidiasis & Fungal Infections: Q66–117
Dental Radiology & Imaging: Q118–180
Oral Pathology: Investigations & Biopsy Techniques: Q181–216
Dental Caries: Etiology, Pathology & Prevention: Q217–287
Tooth Preparation Principles & Restoration Fundamentals: Q288–317
Direct Restorative Materials: Q318–370
Indirect Restorative Materials & Prosthodontics: Q371–405

Temporomandibular Joint: Anatomy & Disorders: Q618–669

questions.question: Which statement about antibiotic use in primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is CORRECT?
options: Antibiotics are unnecessary; superinfection is rare
Steroids plus antibiotics are first-line therapy
questions.explanation: Secondary bacterial infection in primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is very rare, making routine antibiotic use unnecessary. Treatment is primarily symptomatic using antipyretics, topical anesthetics, and adequate fluid intake. Steroids are specifically contraindicated as they can exacerbate the viral infection.

questions.question: Intraarticular TMJ ankylosis leads to obliteration of the joint cavity and fusion of the mandible to:
options: The coronoid process of the opposite side
questions.explanation: In intraarticular TMJ ankylosis, the joint cavity is obliterated, and the mandible fuses — through fibrous or bony union — to the base of the skull (temporal bone). This prevents any condylar movement, resulting in limited or absent mouth opening. The severity of functional impairment, facial deformity, and management complexity depends on whether the ankylosis is fibrous or bony and whether it is unilateral or bilateral.

Light-cured composite resin sets through polymerisation, initiated by a photoinitiator (commonly camphorquinone) that is activated by blue light, converting the resin monomers into a hardened, cross-linked polymer network. Some composites are chemically (self) cured or dual-cured, using a chemical initiator instead of or in addition to light. Correct curing technique and adequate light exposure are essential for achieving optimal mechanical properties.
questions.question: A composite resin restoration is placed and hardened using a blue light source that initiates a chemical reaction converting monomers into a cross-linked polymer network. This setting mechanism is termed:
The etching liquid used in the composite resin system is typically:
questions.explanation: The standard etchant for composite resin bonding is 37% (approximately) phosphoric acid, applied for 15–30 seconds on enamel and 10–15 seconds on dentine. Etching creates micropores in enamel rods and demineralises the superficial dentine, allowing resin monomers to infiltrate and form the hybrid layer after bonding agent application. Hydrofluoric acid is used only for ceramic etching.

options: Colour stability superior to composite resin
Continuous fluoride release with anticariogenic effect
Ability to bond only to enamel rods
questions.question: Which property of GIC makes it PARTICULARLY suitable for patients at high caries risk?
questions.explanation: Glass ionomer cement's defining clinical advantage for high-caries-risk patients is its continuous slow release of fluoride ions, which creates an anticariogenic reservoir that inhibits demineralisation and promotes remineralisation at the tooth-restoration interface. This property is especially valuable in root caries management, xerostomic patients, and individuals with special needs who have limited ability to maintain oral hygiene. No other direct restorative material shares this intrinsic sustained fluoride release property.

options: Evading immune detection by varying surface antigens
Resistance to all classes of antifungal drugs simultaneously
Formation of endospores resistant to heat and desiccation
Horizontal transfer of virulence genes to bacteria
Production of toxins that directly lyse immune cells
questions.question: Candida's ability to shift between different phenotypes reversibly is considered a virulence factor because it allows:
questions.explanation: Candida's phenotypic switching — reversible transitions between distinct colony morphologies (white-opaque switching in C. albicans) — varies the expression of surface antigens, adhesins, and virulence determinants, enabling the organism to evade immune recognition and adapt to different host microenvironments. This plasticity is a sophisticated immune evasion strategy that contributes to Candida's success as an opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised hosts.

options: Bilateral mandibular excess with anterior crossbite
Vertical maxillary excess with downward cant of the palatal plane
Denture bases (jaw bases) in harmony without significant sagittal discrepancy
questions.question: A Class I flat facial profile indicates which jaw base relationship?
questions.explanation: A flat (straight) facial profile corresponds to a Class I skeletal pattern where the maxillary and mandibular bases are in sagittal harmony, with the mandible positioned appropriately relative to the maxilla. This profile is considered the aesthetic and functional ideal in orthodontic assessment. Deviations — convex (Class II) or concave (Class III) — indicate sagittal jaw discrepancies requiring orthodontic or surgical correction to restore balance.

Long-standing amalgam restorations can produce marginal staining and greyish discolouration of adjacent tooth structure due to corrosion products from the metallic material diffusing into the surrounding dentin and enamel over time. This is a recognised, generally benign aesthetic change rather than a sign of active disease, although the margins should still be checked clinically for recurrent caries. This staining is a distinct phenomenon from fluorosis or allergic reactions.
options: An allergic reaction to the composite resin
Corrosion products from the metallic amalgam diffusing into adjacent tooth structure
Normal, expected tooth colour with no pathological cause
questions.question: A patient with a large amalgam restoration that has been in place for over 15 years develops marginal staining and slight discolouration of the surrounding tooth structure. This staining is best explained by:

An elderly patient on chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma develops a unilateral vesicular rash following the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, with severe pain preceding the rash. What is the underlying pathogenesis?
questions.explanation: Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus residing in sensory ganglia, commonly the trigeminal ganglion when facial dermatomes are involved. Immunosuppression, as in lymphoma or chemotherapy, greatly increases the risk of reactivation. Pain characteristically precedes the vesicular eruption along the affected dermatome.

The three main dental notation systems used for identifying teeth in tooth replacement planning are: FDI (two-digit system), Zsigmondy-Palmer (quadrant grid system), and Universal notation (a sequential numbering system used primarily in the USA). Familiarity with all three systems is important for interpreting referral letters and international dental literature.
questions.question: The universal (USA) dental notation system is the THIRD notation system described for tooth replacement treatment planning, alongside:

During Class II amalgam cavity preparation, a dentist creates slightly convergent occlusal walls and undercuts in the dentin to mechanically lock the restoration in place. This design feature primarily provides:
questions.explanation: Retention form refers to specific design features of a cavity preparation, such as convergent walls or dentinal undercuts, that mechanically prevent the restoration from being displaced or dislodged under function. It is distinct from resistance form, which relates to fracture resistance rather than displacement. Both forms work together to ensure restoration longevity.

Dental amalgam sets through amalgamation, a reaction in which liquid mercury combines with the silver-tin (and other metal) alloy powder during trituration, forming a plastic mass that subsequently hardens. This differs fundamentally from the polymerisation reaction that hardens composite resin, or the acid-base reaction of glass ionomer cement. Understanding the specific setting mechanism informs correct handling and manipulation of the material.
questions.question: A dentist explains that dental amalgam achieves its final set through a specific chemical reaction between mercury and an alloy powder. This reaction is termed:
Management of dental caries at the stage of deep dentinal involvement with pulpal symptoms typically requires:
questions.explanation: When dental caries has involved the pulp causing irreversible pulpitis or pulp necrosis, root canal treatment (RCT) is required for a restorable tooth. Direct restoration alone is no longer adequate at this stage. In primary teeth, pulpotomy or pulpectomy may be performed. Where the tooth is unrestorable or the patient opts for removal, extraction is the alternative.
options: Extraction as the only treatment option
Root canal treatment or pulp therapy
Surgical procedures that are performed to re-implant teeth that were avulsed
A biomaterial placed in a prepared tooth to repair it
Chemical treatments to remineralise early caries
questions.question: Dental restorations are defined as:
questions.explanation: Dental restorations involve placement of a biomaterial in an adequately prepared tooth to repair damaged, injured, diseased, or discoloured teeth. The aim is to retain the tooth as a functional and aesthetically acceptable unit of the dental arch. Restorations do not last indefinitely and replacement may be necessary several times during a patient's lifetime.

Class III malocclusion is called mesioclusion because the mandible is in an abnormal mesial (forward) relationship to the maxilla. The mandibular anterior teeth protrude in front of the maxillary anterior teeth, producing an anterior crossbite or 'underbite.' Class II is distoclusion (mandible too far back) and Class I is neutrocclusion (normal relationship).
questions.question: In orthodontics, Class III malocclusion is also referred to as:

questions.explanation: A radicular cyst typically presents radiographically as a unilocular, well-defined periapical radiolucency with a corticated (sclerotic) margin associated with the root apex of a non-vital tooth. The corticated margin indicates a slow-growing, non-aggressive lesion. As it enlarges, it may cause root divergence and displacement. Loss of the corticated margin suggests secondary infection or, in rare cases, conversion to a malignant lesion requiring biopsy.
options: A multilocular radiolucency with a scalloped margin
A diffuse ill-defined radiolucency without corticated margins
A mixed radiolucent-radiopaque lesion containing calcifications
A lesion expanding from the alveolar crest with a horizontal bone loss pattern
A unilocular well-defined periapical radiolucency associated with a non-vital tooth root
questions.question: On radiographic examination, a radicular cyst is expected to appear as:

questions.explanation: A pseudo-pocket forms when there is coronal displacement of the gingival margin due to swelling or hyperplasia without actual apical migration of the junctional epithelium or loss of periodontal attachment. This differs from a true periodontal pocket, which involves genuine attachment loss. Distinguishing between the two is essential for correct diagnosis and treatment planning.
questions.question: A patient develops localised gingival swelling that mimics a true periodontal pocket, but on probing there is no apical migration of the junctional epithelium or loss of attachment. This is best described as a:

options: Remove debris and necrotic tissue from the exposed socket
Immediately restore a blood clot chemically
Permanently seal the socket from further exposure
Eliminate the need for any analgesia
questions.explanation: Irrigation of a dry socket with warm saline is performed primarily to gently remove food debris and necrotic tissue from the exposed, painful socket before placement of a soothing, often eugenol-containing, medicated dressing to relieve symptoms while natural healing occurs. This is a symptomatic management approach rather than a curative one, as dry socket generally resolves with time and appropriate supportive care. Antibiotics are not routinely required unless there is evidence of associated infection.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected dry socket three days after a lower molar extraction is examined and the socket is gently irrigated with warm saline before placement of a medicated dressing. The primary purpose of this irrigation step is to:

questions.explanation: An eruption cyst is a soft tissue lesion that develops when fluid or blood accumulates within the follicular space overlying an erupting tooth, presenting as a bluish, fluctuant swelling of the gingiva. It typically resolves spontaneously as the tooth erupts through the mucosa, and intervention is rarely required. This differs from odontogenic cysts arising from deeper bony structures such as dentigerous or radicular cysts.
questions.question: A 2-week-old infant is noted to have a bluish, fluctuant swelling overlying the site of an erupting primary tooth, caused by blood or fluid trapped beneath the oral mucosa above the erupting crown. This is best described as a(n):

questions.explanation: Gingivitis is defined as inflammation of the gingiva that occurs without loss of connective tissue attachment or alveolar bone, distinguishing it from periodontitis, in which attachment and bone loss have occurred. This distinction is fundamental to periodontal diagnosis and prognosis. Gingivitis is generally reversible with appropriate plaque control, whereas attachment loss in periodontitis is largely irreversible.
questions.question: A patient's chart records inflammation confined to the gingival tissues, with no radiographic evidence of bone loss or clinical attachment loss on probing. This finding is most consistent with:

questions.explanation: Angle's Class III malocclusion, also called mesiocclusion, occurs when the mandibular arch and molars are positioned mesially relative to the maxillary arch, in contrast to Class II (distoclusion), where the mandible is positioned distally. This classification is based on the relationship of the mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar to the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar. Correct classification guides orthodontic treatment planning.
questions.question: A patient presents with the mandibular first molar occluding one full cusp width mesial to its normal relationship with the maxillary first molar, indicating a mesial position of the mandibular arch relative to the maxilla. This malocclusion is classified as:

A patient presents after facial trauma with a 'battle sign' (bruising over the mastoid process) and clear fluid draining from the ear. These findings raise clinical suspicion for which underlying injury?
questions.explanation: Battle's sign, bruising over the mastoid process, combined with clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) otorrhoea, are clinical signs raising strong suspicion for a base of skull fracture, a serious injury requiring urgent further assessment and neurosurgical or ENT input. Recognising these signs during initial trauma assessment is critical, as they indicate injury extending well beyond simple dentoalveolar or mandibular trauma. Prompt recognition ensures the patient receives appropriately escalated, multidisciplinary emergency care.

questions.question: Amalgam and composite resin restorations are classified as:
questions.explanation: Amalgam and composite restorations are direct intra-coronal restorations placed within a cavity prepared in the crown of a tooth and placed directly at the chairside without laboratory fabrication. Indirect intra-coronal restorations (inlays) are fabricated in the dental laboratory from an impression. Extra-coronal restorations (crowns, veneers) are placed around the outside of the tooth.

Periodontitis associated with Down syndrome is classified within the group of periodontal diseases linked to genetic or systemic disorders, reflecting the altered host immune and connective tissue response characteristic of the condition. This classification highlights the need for tailored, often more intensive, periodontal management in affected individuals. Early onset and rapid progression are common features in this population.
questions.question: A patient with Down syndrome develops early, severe periodontal destruction disproportionate to plaque levels, attributed in part to altered host immune function associated with the syndrome. This form of periodontitis is classified under which broad group?
A patient with plaque-induced gingivitis, present for many years with a slow, insidious onset and minimal symptoms, is best described using which chronological classification?
questions.explanation: Plaque-induced gingivitis with a slow onset, long duration, and typically painless course is classified as chronic, in contrast to acute gingival conditions such as necrotizing gingivitis, which have a rapid onset and pronounced symptoms. This chronological classification helps guide clinical expectations regarding presentation and management approach. Chronic gingivitis, while less dramatic in presentation, still requires appropriate intervention to prevent progression.

questions.question: The PRIMARY function of silver in dental amalgam alloy is to:
options: Act as a scavenger and prevent oxidation
The major element, increasing strength, reducing creep
questions.explanation: Silver is the major reactive element in dental amalgam, contributing to the amalgamation reaction, increasing strength, decreasing creep, and whitening the alloy. Zinc acts as the scavenger (deoxidizer), copper increases hardness and expansion, and tin controls the reaction speed. Understanding each element's role is critical for predicting amalgam behaviour clinically.

options: Maximise removal of healthy tooth structure
Avoid any consideration of pulp health
Remove disease and create form that receives and retains the restoration
Achieve the widest possible cavity outline
Preserve all carious tissue to save time
questions.explanation: The primary objective of tooth preparation is to remove diseased or damaged tissue and create a cavity form that will receive, support, and retain the chosen restorative material while preserving as much healthy tooth structure and pulp vitality as possible. This objective underlies all more specific principles such as resistance form, retention form, and outline form. Balancing disease removal against conservation of tooth structure is central to modern minimally invasive dentistry.
questions.question: A dentist explains to a patient that the primary objective of tooth preparation, regardless of the restorative material chosen, is to:

questions.explanation: A periapical radiograph is designed to display the entire tooth, from crown to root apex, along with the surrounding periapical bone, making it the ideal projection to assess periapical pathology such as an abscess. Bitewings do not adequately capture the root apex. This localised projection provides the detail required for periapical diagnosis.
questions.question: A dentist wants to visualise the entire root and surrounding periapical bone of a single tooth to assess a suspected periapical abscess. Which radiograph is indicated?

questions.explanation: The primary goal of asepsis in oral and maxillofacial surgery is to prevent introduction of pathogenic microorganisms into the surgical site, thereby reducing the risk of postoperative infection and promoting uncomplicated healing. This encompasses instrument sterilisation, proper draping, and careful surgical technique. While it may reduce the need for antibiotics in some cases, asepsis does not eliminate the requirement for antibiotics when otherwise clinically indicated.
questions.question: A dental surgical team implements strict aseptic technique before an implant placement procedure, including sterilisation of instruments and use of a no-touch technique for critical surfaces. The primary goal of asepsis in this surgical context is to:
options: Improve the aesthetic outcome of the surgery
Eliminate the need for postoperative antibiotics in every case
Increase patient comfort during the procedure
Prevent introduction of pathogenic microorganisms into the surgical site
Local anaesthesia syringe, needle, and anaesthetic ampoule
questions.explanation: A simple (uncomplicated) intra-alveolar extraction requires an examination set, local anaesthetic equipment, extraction forceps, elevators, sterile gauze, suction tip, and artery forceps. A bone rongeur and periosteal elevator are instruments used in surgical (trans-alveolar) extraction when bone removal or flap reflection is needed — they are not standard equipment for simple closed-technique extractions.
questions.question: The sterile instruments required for a simple intra-alveolar extraction include all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Reversible pulpitis affecting only the tooth itself
Cellulitis or space infection, e.g. Ludwig's angina
questions.explanation: Untreated dental caries can progress through pulpitis, apical periodontitis, periapical abscess, and dentoalveolar abscess to cellulitis and spread of infection to fascial spaces such as Ludwig's angina. This represents the most severe sequela and can be life-threatening if the infection involves the airway. Mortality from unmanaged dental infections has been reported, highlighting the importance of timely treatment.
questions.question: The sequela of untreated dental caries that involves spread of infection to fascial spaces is:

questions.explanation: A traumatic ulcer that persists beyond two weeks despite removal of the causative agent should raise suspicion for malignancy or another chronic disease process, and an incisional biopsy is indicated. Persistence beyond the expected healing time is a red flag in oral mucosal lesions. Early biopsy prevents delayed diagnosis of a potentially malignant lesion.
options: Reassure and review in one month
Prescribe a further course of antibiotics
questions.question: A chronic traumatic ulcer on the buccal mucosa fails to heal two weeks after the sharp cusp causing it has been smoothed. What is the most appropriate next step?

questions.explanation: Acyclovir and its analogues (valacyclovir, famciclovir) must be initiated within 48 hours of onset of symptoms to be effective. They reduce viral replication by inhibiting DNA polymerization or interfering with viral-epithelial interaction. Delaying treatment beyond 48 hours markedly reduces the benefit of antiviral therapy.
questions.question: Antiviral therapy for HSV infection is MOST effective when initiated within:

questions.explanation: NUG produces a characteristic fetid offensive odour (halitosis) that is one of its distinguishing clinical features alongside gingival bleeding and soreness. Additional signs include difficulty eating, drooling of saliva, poor oral hygiene, and signs of malnutrition. Complications include cancrum oris and osteomyelitis.
questions.question: The characteristic offensive odour (halitosis) in NUG is described as:

options: Inferior alveolar nerve injury during extraction
questions.explanation: Radiographic signs suggesting close proximity between the roots of an impacted mandibular third molar and the inferior alveolar canal, such as darkening of the root or interruption of the canal's cortical white lines, are assessed preoperatively to anticipate and reduce the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury during surgical removal. Identifying high-risk cases may prompt modified surgical technique, such as coronectomy, to minimise this risk. Careful preoperative planning is essential in surgery involving teeth close to vital neurovascular structures.
questions.question: A surgeon planning removal of an impacted mandibular third molar assesses the relationship of the roots to the inferior alveolar canal using radiographic signs, such as darkening of the root or interruption of the canal's white lines. This assessment is performed primarily to reduce the risk of:

questions.explanation: A bitewing radiograph is a lateral view of the posterior jaw regions demonstrating the crowns of the teeth and alveolar crestal bone of the premolar and molar regions of both the maxilla and mandible simultaneously. It is primarily used for detecting proximal caries and assessing crestal bone levels. The bitewing was invented by Howard Raper in 1927.
questions.question: In which radiographic view are the crowns of posterior teeth and alveolar crestal bone of both arches simultaneously visible?

questions.explanation: Among common odontogenic cysts, the radicular cyst has the lowest recurrence rate following adequate treatment, the dentigerous cyst has a low to moderate recurrence rate, and the odontogenic keratocyst has the highest recurrence rate due to its thin, friable lining and potential satellite cysts. This hierarchy informs both surgical planning and the intensity of long-term follow-up required for each lesion type. Recognising differing recurrence potential helps set realistic patient expectations regarding prognosis.
questions.question: Comparing the recurrence potential of common odontogenic cysts, a clinician ranks radicular cyst, dentigerous cyst, and odontogenic keratocyst in order of increasing likelihood of recurrence after treatment. Which ranking correctly reflects this order?
options: Radicular cyst, dentigerous cyst, odontogenic keratocyst
Dentigerous cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, radicular cyst
Radicular cyst, odontogenic keratocyst, dentigerous cyst
Odontogenic keratocyst, dentigerous cyst, radicular cyst
All three cysts share an identical recurrence rate

questions.explanation: Moyers' classification of malocclusion aetiology includes seven categories: heredity, developmental defects of unknown origin, trauma, physical agents, habits, diseases, and malnutrition. This comprehensive framework captures both biological and environmental causes. Moyers' work remains foundational to orthodontic aetiological thinking alongside Graber's and Salzman's classifications, each offering complementary perspectives.
questions.question: According to Moyers' classification, which of the following is listed as an aetiological factor for malocclusion?
options: Only the congenital and acquired skeletal factors listed
Heredity, defects, trauma, agents, habits, disease, malnutrition
Systemic diseases and fluoride intake only

questions.question: According to the thermal dimorphism of important pathogenic fungi, at BODY temperature they predominantly exist as:
questions.explanation: Thermally dimorphic pathogenic fungi exist as hyphal forms at room temperature (approximately 25°C) and as yeast forms at body temperature (37°C). This thermal dimorphism is a key virulence property as the yeast form is better adapted for tissue invasion and evasion of host defences. Candida albicans, while technically a diamorphic fungus, also exhibits this temperature-dependent morphological shift relevant to its pathogenicity.

questions.question: Condylar hyperplasia as a developmental TMJ condition most typically presents as:
questions.explanation: Condylar hyperplasia is a developmental condition of unilateral or occasionally bilateral excessive condylar growth, presenting as progressive facial asymmetry — with the affected side showing a longer face, mandibular deviation to the contralateral side, and a cant of the occlusal plane. It typically becomes apparent during puberty. Management includes condylectomy to halt growth and subsequent orthognathic surgery to correct the established deformity.
options: Bilateral joint ankylosis from calcium deposits
Anterior disc displacement with restricted opening
Acute pain and trismus without radiographic change
Progressive asymmetry from unilateral condylar overgrowth

questions.explanation: Koplik's spots are the oral manifestation of measles, appearing 2–3 days before the characteristic skin rash on the buccal mucosa as white flecks with red margins. Other oral management includes a soft diet, cold foods, and orabase paste to provide mucosal protection and pain relief. Systemic complications of measles include encephalitis, otitis media, and bronchial pneumonia.
questions.question: Which complication of measles infection specifically affects the oral cavity?
options: Otitis media of the middle ear
Koplik's spots before the skin rash

questions.explanation: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause local immunosuppression of the oral mucosa where they are deposited, reducing local defence mechanisms and predisposing to opportunistic Candida overgrowth, particularly if the mouth is not rinsed after use. Advising patients to rinse their mouth with water after each use of a corticosteroid inhaler is a simple, effective preventive measure. This illustrates how even topically or locally acting medications can have significant oral mucosal effects.
questions.question: A patient using a corticosteroid inhaler for asthma without rinsing the mouth afterward develops white patches on the palate and buccal mucosa. The mechanism by which inhaled corticosteroids predispose to oral candidiasis is primarily through:
options: Mechanical abrasion of the mucosa by the inhaler device
Direct fungicidal activity being paradoxically stimulatory
Local immunosuppression of oral mucosal tissue
Increased salivary flow displacing normal flora
Systemic hyperglycaemia from a single inhaled dose

questions.question: A dentist restoring a deep proximal lesion widens the cavity access at the occlusal aspect specifically to allow better visibility and instrumentation during cavity preparation and restoration placement. This design consideration is called:
questions.explanation: Convenience form refers to shaping the cavity preparation to allow adequate visibility, access, and ease of instrumentation during cavity preparation and restoration placement. This is distinct from outline form, which defines the extent of the cavity margins on the tooth surface. Adequate convenience form facilitates a technically sound restoration.

questions.question: A patient with a fractured maxillary central incisor from trauma presents with the fracture line passing through the coronal half of the crown, with pulp exposure and a poor long-term restorative prognosis. This is listed as an indication for extraction primarily because:
questions.explanation: A fracture through the coronal half of a tooth with pulp exposure often leaves insufficient remaining tooth structure to support a predictable, functional restoration, making extraction a reasonable option when restorative or endodontic treatment is not feasible or has a poor long-term prognosis. This decision depends on the extent of remaining structure and the patient's overall treatment goals. Preserving a tooth is generally preferred when restorability and prognosis are favourable.
options: The remaining tooth structure is insufficient to support a restorable, functional tooth
Orthodontic movement can always resolve the fracture
The adjacent teeth are automatically also indicated for extraction
The tooth is always asymptomatic in this scenario

questions.question: The aim of exodontia specifically states that the wound should heal:
questions.explanation: The definition of exodontia specifically states that the procedure should achieve painless removal of tooth or root with minimal trauma to investing tissues, so that the wound heals uneventfully and with no postoperative pre-prosthetic problems. This goal emphasises the importance of atraumatic technique in preserving alveolar ridge morphology for future prosthetic rehabilitation. SUBTOPIC 7: TOOTH REPLACEMENT, ORTHODONTICS & ORAL CONDITIONS IN CHILDREN
options: With a stable blood clot that must not be disturbed for 4 weeks
Uneventfully, with no postoperative pre-prosthetic problems
Rapidly requiring sutures in all cases

questions.explanation: Transverse plane jaw discrepancies produce crossbites: mandibular deficiency or maxillary excess results in a posterior crossbite, while the reverse (mandibular excess or maxillary deficiency) produces a scissors bite. Understanding the plane of deformity is essential for accurate diagnosis and determining whether orthodontic, orthopaedic, or surgical correction is required.
options: The vertical plane, causing an anterior open bite
Transverse plane, mandibular deficiency or maxillary excess
questions.question: Mandibular deficiency in the transverse plane leading to posterior crossbite is an example of a defect in the:

questions.explanation: Exfoliative cytology involves collection of surface cells that have been scraped or exfoliated from a mucosal lesion, providing a rapid, minimally invasive screening test. It does not sample deeper tissue architecture, limiting its diagnostic accuracy compared with biopsy. It is most useful as an adjunct screening tool rather than a definitive diagnostic method.
questions.question: A clinician gently scrapes the surface of a suspicious white oral lesion with a wooden spatula to collect surface cells for microscopic examination without local anaesthesia. This technique is best described as:
A dentist examining a patient's gingiva notes small pinpoint depressions on the attached gingiva resembling an orange peel texture. This normal surface feature is produced by:
options: Fusion of collagen bundles pulling the epithelium at intervals
questions.explanation: Stippling of the attached gingiva is produced by the fusion of underlying collagen bundles that pull the epithelium inward at regular intervals, creating an orange-peel-like surface texture in health. Loss of stippling is often an early sign of gingival inflammation. Its presence is generally considered a sign of healthy, well-keratinised gingiva.

options: The patient has refused periodontal treatment specifically
It is more economical to extract than restore all carious teeth
Multiple unrestorable teeth representing a significant infectious focus require removal
The patient is preparing for orthodontic treatment requiring space creation
Pain from multiple teeth cannot be managed conservatively
questions.explanation: Grossly neglected dentition involves multiple teeth that are unrestorable due to the extent of caries, periodontal disease, and accumulated destruction. These represent significant infectious foci that can cause systemic complications, particularly in medically compromised patients. Comprehensive extraction to eliminate this infectious burden — followed by appropriate rehabilitation — is therefore clinically justified. The decision requires careful assessment of restorability, patient motivation, and medical status.
questions.question: Grossly neglected dentition is listed as an indication for extraction because:
Tooth preparation for radiotherapy is an indication for extraction because radiation reduces:
options: Blood supply to bone, risking osteoradionecrosis after extraction
The sensitivity of the teeth to pain stimuli
questions.explanation: Teeth in or adjacent to the radiation field should be extracted before radiotherapy because post-irradiation, reduced blood supply to the bone creates a risk of osteoradionecrosis if extraction is attempted — a severe, difficult-to-treat complication. Pre-irradiation dental clearance prevents this life-altering complication. Extractions must be completed with adequate healing time before radiation begins, typically 2–3 weeks minimum.

Outline form refers to the shape of the cavosurface margin of the cavity, which should consist of smooth flowing curves determined by the size and location of the carious lesion. The margins should be placed on sound tooth structure and in areas that allow adequate access for finishing and polishing. Irregular or sharp corners in the outline form can create stress concentrations predisposing to fracture.
questions.question: Outline form in cavity preparation refers to:
options: The depth of the preparation floor
The internal configuration of all preparation walls
The angle of the bur during cutting
The retention features within the preparation
The cavosurface margin's shape, comprising smooth curves
A high-speed drill with bone rongeurs
Forceps and elevators, no flap raised
questions.question: In exodontia, 'intraalveolar approach' uses which instruments?
questions.explanation: The intraalveolar approach (simple extraction) uses forceps and elevators without raising a mucoperiosteal flap. It is applicable when the tooth has sufficient crown remaining for forcep engagement and the roots are not unusually curved, divergent, or hypercementosed. The transalveolar approach (surgical extraction) additionally requires flap elevation and bone removal with drills or chisels.

questions.question: Gout as a metabolic disease affecting the TMJ produces joint damage primarily through:
questions.explanation: Gout affects the TMJ through deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the synovial membrane and articular cartilage, triggering acute inflammatory arthropathy characterised by acute pain, swelling, and restricted opening. While the peripheral joints (first metatarsophalangeal joint) are more classically affected, the TMJ can be involved in tophaceous gout. Diagnosis is confirmed by synovial fluid analysis and serum uric acid levels.
options: Bony ankylosis of the articular surfaces
Urate crystal deposition causing inflammatory arthropathy
Condylar hyperplasia from excess growth hormone
Attachment of gingival fibres to bone
Vascular proliferation in the lamina propria
questions.explanation: Stippling, the orange-peel texture of healthy attached gingiva, results from the attachment of gingival fibres to the underlying alveolar bone. Loss of stippling, producing a smooth and shiny surface, is a hallmark of gingivitis due to destruction of these fibres by inflammation. It is an early and reliable clinical sign of disease.
questions.question: Stippling of the attached gingiva is produced by:
A dentist explains that the alveolar bone forms part of the periodontium and serves a key functional role. This primary function is to:
options: Provide bony support and attachment for the periodontal ligament fibres of the tooth
Serve as the primary site of taste perception
questions.explanation: The alveolar bone's primary function within the periodontium is to provide bony housing and attachment for the periodontal ligament fibres (via Sharpey's fibres), thereby supporting and anchoring the tooth. It undergoes continuous remodelling in response to functional and pathological stimuli, including periodontal disease. Loss of alveolar bone height is a hallmark radiographic sign of periodontitis.

Edentulism is the medical term describing the condition of missing teeth, either complete (all teeth missing) or partial (one or more teeth missing). Complete edentulism refers to absence of all teeth in one or both arches, while partial edentulism refers to absence of one or several teeth. Hypodontia, oligodontia, and anodontia specifically refer to developmental absence of varying numbers of teeth.
questions.question: The medical term describing the condition of missing teeth is:

questions.explanation: Dentigerous cysts are the second most common jaw cysts, accounting for 15–18% of all jaw cysts. They are always associated with the crown of an unerupted or impacted tooth, typically the mandibular third molar, maxillary canine, or maxillary third molar. Early diagnosis and enucleation with extraction of the associated tooth are the standard management.
questions.question: The dentigerous cyst accounts for approximately what percentage of all jaw cysts?
The thoracic dermatome is the MOST frequently affected site in herpes zoster, accounting for approximately:
questions.explanation: Thoracic dermatomes are involved in approximately 45% of herpes zoster cases, making them the most commonly affected region. Cervical dermatomes account for 23% and the trigeminal nerve for 15% of cases. The rash characteristically does not cross the midline, remaining strictly unilateral.

questions.question: Which radiographic investigation is MOST useful for detecting proximal caries?
questions.explanation: Bitewing radiographs are the investigation of choice for detecting proximal (interproximal) caries as they provide a clear view of the contact areas of posterior teeth in both arches simultaneously. They are highly sensitive for early caries that may not be clinically detectable. A combination of clinical examination and bitewing radiography provides the most comprehensive caries assessment.

Intraoral periapical radiographs provide superior fine detail and spatial resolution for localized lesions compared with panoramic radiographs, which offer a broader survey at the expense of detail due to inherent distortion and overlap. For a single, well-localized lesion, this higher resolution is diagnostically valuable. Panoramic views remain useful for broader screening rather than fine anatomical detail.
questions.question: A dental surgeon requests a radiograph specifically to assess the internal bony architecture and cortical outline of a jaw lesion before biopsy, choosing intraoral periapical film over an extraoral panoramic view for a localized single-tooth lesion. Which factor MOST justifies this choice?
options: Superior fine detail and resolution of intraoral films for localized lesions
Panoramic radiographs cannot show any bony detail
Intraoral films always show the whole jaw
Lower equipment cost of panoramic units

questions.question: A surgeon performing a coronectomy on a mandibular third molar with roots intimately related to the inferior alveolar canal deliberately leaves the roots in situ rather than fully extracting them. This modified surgical approach is chosen specifically to:
questions.explanation: Coronectomy involves intentional removal of only the crown of a tooth while leaving the roots in situ, specifically employed when roots are intimately related to the inferior alveolar canal, to reduce the risk of nerve injury that could occur with complete root removal. This technique requires careful patient selection and long-term follow-up, as retained roots can occasionally require later removal if complications arise. It represents an example of modifying standard surgical technique to prioritise preservation of nerve function.
options: Increase the risk of postoperative infection deliberately
Eliminate the need for any postoperative follow-up
Reduce the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury associated with complete root removal
Avoid any need for local anaesthesia
Achieve faster healing than complete extraction in all cases

questions.question: A 6-year-old with fever, oral ulcers, and vesicular lesions on the palms and soles is diagnosed clinically. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Hand, foot and mouth disease is caused by Coxsackievirus A16, an enterovirus that produces oral ulcers together with a characteristic vesicular rash on the palms, soles, and buttocks. It is common in young children and is usually self-limiting. The oral lesions may be mistaken for herpetic stomatitis but the skin distribution clarifies the diagnosis.

options: Portion of the tooth visible in the mouth
The full length of the root within bone
questions.question: The clinical crown differs from the anatomic crown in that it is defined by the:
questions.explanation: The clinical crown is that portion of the tooth visible above the gingival margin in the oral cavity, while the anatomic crown is defined by the extent of enamel coverage. The clinical crown changes with gingival recession or overgrowth, making it a dynamic measurement with direct implications for aesthetics and dentinal hypersensitivity.

questions.question: Tooth preparation for an amalgam Class II restoration requires a pulpal floor depth of at least:
questions.explanation: A minimum pulpal floor depth of 2 mm is required for amalgam restorations to provide adequate resistance form and allow for sufficient bulk of amalgam to withstand occlusal forces without fracture. Shallower preparations result in thin amalgam that is prone to fracture. This depth requirement differs from composite preparations where the adhesive mechanism provides retention without the need for specific depth requirements.

options: Identifying and removing infected carious dentine
Indicate the depth of the pulp chamber
Increase the retention of the restoration
Mark the cavity margins for ease of finishing
questions.explanation: Caries detecting dyes selectively stain infected, softened carious dentine red while leaving sound, slightly demineralised (affected) dentine unstained. They guide the clinician to remove infected dentine without over-cutting into healthy structure. Their use supports the minimally invasive approach to cavity preparation by distinguishing infected from affected dentine.
questions.question: Caries detecting dyes are used during cavity preparation to:
Clinical assessment of gingiva includes which of the following parameters?
questions.explanation: The six standard parameters for clinical gingival assessment are colour, contour, consistency, size, surface texture, and position. Each parameter has characteristic normal and diseased presentations that assist the clinician in diagnosing and staging periodontal disease. Comprehensive gingival assessment precedes any periodontal treatment planning.
options: Colour, contour, consistency, size, surface texture, and position
Colour, bone density, root length, and mobility
Probing depth, bone height, furcation involvement only
Colour, pH of saliva, bacterial count, and mobility
Contour, caries index, plaque score, and calculus

questions.explanation: The articular disc of the temporomandibular joint is positioned between the mandibular condyle inferiorly and the articular (glenoid) fossa of the temporal bone superiorly, dividing the joint into upper and lower compartments and allowing both rotational and translational movements. This anatomical relationship is fundamental to normal joint function. Disruption of normal disc position or morphology underlies many common TMJ disorders.
options: The mandibular condyle and the articular (glenoid) fossa of the temporal bone
The lateral pterygoid muscle and the medial pterygoid muscle
The mandibular ramus and the maxillary tuberosity
The mental foramen and the mandibular foramen
The coronoid process and the zygomatic arch
questions.question: A dentist examining a patient's temporomandibular joint palpates the lateral pole of the condyle during opening and closing to assess joint movement and detect clicking or crepitus. The articulating disc of the TMJ is positioned primarily between which two structures?

questions.explanation: Malocclusion may manifest in any or all three planes of space: vertical (anterior open bite, deep bite), transverse (crossbite, scissors bite), and sagittal (antero-posterior Class II or Class III relationship). Multi-planar malocclusions are common and require three-dimensional assessment for diagnosis and treatment planning, particularly in orthognathic surgery cases.
questions.question: Malocclusion can occur in which planes of human anatomy?

questions.explanation: An eruption cyst is a localised, dome-shaped, fluctuant benign swelling overlying an erupting tooth, representing fluid accumulation in the follicular space. It is tender only if inflamed. Management is usually conservative (no treatment needed) as the cyst resolves spontaneously with tooth eruption. It may be excised if symptomatic or if eruption is delayed.
questions.question: An eruption cyst in a child is BEST described as:
options: A localised dome-shaped fluctuant swelling overlying an erupting tooth requiring urgent surgery
A localised dome-shaped fluctuant benign swelling usually requiring no treatment
A retention cyst from blocked minor salivary glands

questions.question: A radicular cyst arises by epithelial proliferation in which pre-existing lesion?
questions.explanation: Radicular cysts arise from inflammatory stimulation and proliferation of the epithelial rests of Malassez within an apical granuloma. The granuloma precedes the cyst; without a non-vital tooth and associated periapical inflammation, the rests remain dormant. This sequential development from pulp necrosis ? apical granuloma ? radicular cyst is the hallmark pathogenesis of this most common jaw cyst.

Streptococcus mutans is the primary cariogenic bacterium harboured in dental plaque, converting sucrose to organic acids and extracellular polysaccharides. Lactobacilli are more important in the progression of established dentinal caries. S. mutans produces glucans (from sucrose) and fructans (from fructose), which promote adherence to tooth surfaces and create barriers that trap organic acids.
questions.question: The PRIMARY microbial factor in caries initiation and progression is:

questions.explanation: Condylar agenesis refers to the failure of normal development of the mandibular condyle, commonly seen in conditions such as hemifacial microsomia, resulting in significant facial asymmetry and malocclusion due to the absent growth centre on the affected side. This contrasts with condylar hyperplasia, which involves excessive rather than absent growth. Comprehensive, often staged, surgical and orthodontic management is typically required in affected patients as they grow.
questions.question: A child with hemifacial microsomia presents with an absent or underdeveloped mandibular condyle on one side, resulting in facial asymmetry and malocclusion. This developmental absence of the condyle is termed:

questions.explanation: Dental plaque is correctly described as a biofilm, a structured, organised community of bacteria embedded within a self-produced extracellular matrix that adheres firmly to the tooth surface, distinguishing it from materia alba, which is a loosely adherent, unstructured mass of bacteria and debris that can be easily rinsed away. Understanding plaque as a true biofilm has important implications for its resistance to mechanical removal and antimicrobial agents. This concept underlies modern approaches to plaque control and periodontal disease management.
questions.question: A dentist explains that dental plaque is a structured, organised community of bacteria embedded within an extracellular matrix adherent to the tooth surface, distinguishing it from loosely adherent food debris. This organised bacterial community is best described using which term?

questions.explanation: The scope of knowledge required in oral radiology includes radiation physics, radiographic technique, normal anatomy, and recognition of pathological changes relevant to the maxillofacial region, but does not extend to unrelated fields such as long bone orthopaedic surgical techniques. Recognising the boundaries of the specialty helps focus training appropriately. This distinguishes oral radiology from general medical radiology practice.
questions.question: A dentist explains that the range of knowledge required in oral radiology extends beyond physics and technique to include interpretation of pathology. Which of the following would NOT typically be included in this required knowledge base?
options: Advanced orthopaedic surgical techniques of the long bones

questions.explanation: Caries-detecting dyes selectively stain carious, bacterially infected dentin, helping the operator distinguish it from sound or merely affected dentin during cavity preparation, thereby guiding conservative removal of only diseased tissue. This minimises unnecessary removal of healthy tooth structure while ensuring complete removal of infected tissue. It is a chairside adjunct rather than a diagnostic test for other conditions.
options: Guide selective removal of infected dentin during preparation
questions.question: A dentist applies a caries-detecting dye during cavity preparation that selectively stains carious, infected dentin a deep red while leaving sound, mineralised dentin unstained. The primary purpose of this dye is to:

questions.explanation: Marsupialisation involves creating a surgical window into the cystic cavity, allowing it to communicate with the oral cavity and gradually decompress and shrink over time, which is a useful conservative approach for large cysts in young patients, helping to preserve adjacent developing teeth or vital structures. This contrasts with enucleation, which removes the entire cystic lining in a single procedure. Definitive removal may still be undertaken later once the cyst has reduced sufficiently in size.
questions.question: A large dentigerous cyst associated with an impacted mandibular canine in a young patient is managed initially by creating a surgical window to allow the cyst to decompress and gradually reduce in size, rather than immediate complete removal, to preserve the developing dentition. This conservative surgical approach is termed:

A young adult presents with a well-defined radiolucency between the roots of the mandibular canine and lateral incisor, with both teeth testing vital, discovered incidentally on routine radiograph. This developmental cyst, typically found in this specific location, is MOST likely:
questions.explanation: The lateral periodontal cyst is a developmental odontogenic cyst that typically presents as a well-defined radiolucency lateral to the root of a vital tooth, most commonly in the mandibular canine-premolar region, distinguishing it from a radicular cyst that arises secondary to pulp necrosis. Vitality of the adjacent teeth is a key distinguishing feature. It is usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on routine radiographic examination.

Surgical asepsis refers to the comprehensive set of measures aimed at preventing microorganisms from gaining access to surgically created wounds. Although the oral cavity contains normal flora, introduction of exogenous organisms can cause infection. Universal precautions include instrument sterilisation, operatory disinfection, and appropriate surgical staff preparation (hand washing, sterile gowning, and gloving).
options: Sterilisation of the oral cavity with chlorhexidine only
Using disposable gloves without hand washing
Prevents microbes from entering surgical wounds
questions.question: Asepsis in oral surgery refers to:

questions.explanation: Periodontal disease is the leading cause of tooth loss in adults, with aggressive periodontitis also affecting teenagers. In children, dental caries and its sequelae are the more common causes of tooth loss. Adults with uncontrolled periodontal disease progressively lose alveolar bone support, leading to tooth mobility and eventual loss.
questions.question: Periodontal (gum) disease is the LEADING cause of tooth loss in:

options: Lower radiation dose than a single periapical film
Three-dimensional volumetric imaging of anatomical structures
Elimination of the need for any patient positioning
Only soft tissue imaging with no bone detail
questions.explanation: CBCT provides three-dimensional volumetric imaging of anatomical structures, allowing assessment of spatial relationships, bone architecture, and pathology in all three planes, which conventional two-dimensional radiography cannot achieve. This makes it valuable for complex diagnostic and surgical planning scenarios. However, its radiation dose is generally higher than conventional intraoral films, requiring judicious use.
questions.question: A dentist explains that Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT), compared with conventional two-dimensional radiography, provides which additional diagnostic capability?

questions.explanation: The zone closest to the pulp in dentinal caries is the affected (demineralised) dentin, which is softened and demineralised but retains a largely intact collagen matrix and viable structure, making it potentially remineralisable and distinguishable from the more superficial, bacterially infected and irreversibly damaged dentin. This distinction is clinically important because affected dentin can be preserved during cavity preparation. Only the outer infected dentin needs to be removed.
questions.question: Histological examination of a deep dentinal carious lesion closest to the pulp reveals viable but demineralised dentin with intact collagen matrix, distinguishable from the more superficial infected zone. This innermost zone is termed the zone of:
options: Affected (demineralised but not yet infected) dentin
Sit entirely within the confines of the tooth crown
Cover the external surfaces of the remaining tooth structure
Only be used on anterior teeth
questions.question: A dentist explains that an extra-coronal restoration, unlike an intra-coronal restoration, is designed to:
questions.explanation: Extra-coronal restorations, such as crowns, cover the external surfaces of the remaining tooth structure, providing protection and reinforcement to a weakened tooth, whereas intra-coronal restorations, such as fillings, sit within the confines of the prepared cavity inside the tooth. This distinction determines the amount of tooth reduction and retention design required. The choice between the two depends on the extent of tooth damage.

An incisional biopsy is a procedure in which a small representative area of tissue is removed to identify the composition of a lesion or abnormality. It is preferred for large lesions where complete removal is not feasible or would cause significant morbidity. It provides histological diagnosis without committing to definitive surgical management.
options: Removal of a small representative tissue sample
Aspiration of cystic fluid with a syringe
Scraping cells from the mucosal surface
Endoscopic examination of the oral cavity
questions.question: An incisional biopsy involves:

A patient with cyclic neutropenia presents with recurrent, severe periodontal destruction disproportionate to plaque levels, attributed to an underlying haematological disorder. Periodontitis occurring as a manifestation of such systemic disease is classified under which category?
questions.explanation: Periodontitis occurring in association with systemic haematological disorders, such as cyclic neutropenia or leukaemia, is classified as periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, reflecting impaired host defence against the periodontal bacterial challenge. This differs from simple plaque-induced chronic periodontitis, which occurs in an otherwise systemically healthy individual. Recognising this association is important because management requires addressing both the periodontal and systemic conditions.
options: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease

questions.question: A patient who smokes heavily has more severe periodontal destruction than a non-smoker with similar plaque levels. Tobacco smoking is significant as a host factor in periodontitis primarily because it:
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoking impairs host immune and vascular responses in the periodontium, reducing gingival bleeding (masking a key clinical sign of inflammation) while simultaneously worsening underlying tissue destruction and impairing healing after periodontal therapy. This combination makes smoking a major modifiable risk factor for both the development and progression of periodontitis. Smoking cessation is an important component of comprehensive periodontal management.
options: Impairs host immune and vascular response, masking clinical signs while worsening destruction
Only affects the aesthetic appearance of teeth
Improves wound healing after periodontal therapy
Directly increases gingival bleeding on probing
Has no effect on periodontal tissues
Fibrinolysis: trauma activates plasminogen, destroying the clot
