Bacterial invasion of the now empty socket space
Direct osteomyelitis of the socket walls
questions.explanation: Birn's hypothesis proposes that trauma and infection cause bone marrow inflammation, releasing tissue activator. This activator converts plasminogen in the blood clot to plasmin, a fibrinolytic agent, which destroys the clot. The displaced clot releases kinins from kininogen, causing intense pain. The condition is clinically characterised by a painful empty socket with exposed bone and no clot.
questions.question: The Birn's hypothesis of dry socket involves which pathological process?
A Class II sagittal skeletal relationship results from which combination of jaw discrepancies?
questions.explanation: A Class II skeletal pattern (retrognathic or retrusive profile) results from maxillary excess (protrusive maxilla) and/or mandibular deficiency (retrusive mandible). The reverse — mandibular excess or maxillary deficiency — produces a Class III pattern with a prognathic or concave profile. Accurate identification of the contributing jaw(s) is essential for planning orthodontic versus surgical treatment.

questions.question: Class II malocclusion (distoclusion) occurs when:
questions.explanation: Class II malocclusion occurs when the body of the mandible is in an abnormal distal relationship to the maxilla, causing the maxillary anterior teeth to protrude over the mandibular anterior teeth. It is also called distoclusion. Class III (mesioclusion) is the opposite: the mandible is in mesial relationship causing the lower anteriors to protrude in front of the upper.
options: The mandibular first molar occludes mesially to the maxillary first molar
There is excessive vertical overlap of the incisors only
The mandible protrudes in front of the maxilla
Upper and lower arches are in ideal occlusion
Mandible distally placed, causing upper anteriors to protrude

questions.question: The two basic necessities for performing any surgical procedure are:
options: Adequate lighting and a qualified anaesthetist
Radiographic assessment and blood pressure monitoring
Sterilised instruments and a dental nurse only
questions.explanation: Adequate visibility and appropriate assistance are the two fundamental necessities for any surgical procedure. Visibility depends on adequate access, sufficient lighting, and a surgical field clear of blood and fluids. Assistance ensures safe retraction, suction, and instrument handling. These principles apply equally to minor dental procedures and complex maxillofacial operations.

Angular stomatitis (angular cheilitis) in children is typically associated with reduced (not excess) vertical dimension of occlusion, causing pooling of saliva at the oral commissures, along with nutritional deficiencies such as vitamin B, candidal or bacterial infection, and habits such as lip licking. Excess vertical dimension would not typically cause this pooling effect. Recognising the correct associated factors guides appropriate management, including nutritional and infective causes.
questions.question: A child presents with painful fissuring and erythema at the corners of the mouth. Which of the following is NOT typically associated with this presentation of angular stomatitis?

options: A right angle technique that uses cone beam imaging device
A tab/eye alignment, or film holder with beam-aiming device
questions.explanation: The two main techniques for bitewing radiography positioning are: using a tab attached to the film packet and aligning the X-ray tubehead by eye, or using a film packet holder with beam-aiming device to facilitate positioning and alignment. The film holder method is more reproducible and reduces geometric distortion. Both methods require careful horizontal and vertical angulation to avoid overlapping of contacts.
questions.question: The two main positioning techniques for bitewing radiography are:
Before extraction, orthodontic assessment may indicate tooth removal primarily for:
questions.explanation: Orthodontic extraction — the planned removal of specific teeth to create space for the alignment of crowded or displaced teeth — is one of the most common indications for tooth extraction in orthodontic practice. The most frequently extracted teeth for this purpose are maxillary and mandibular first or second premolars. The decision is guided by cephalometric analysis, arch length discrepancy assessment, and the patient's growth pattern and facial profile.
options: Reducing periodontal pocket depth adjacent to the tooth
Creating space to allow alignment of crowded teeth
Managing temporomandibular joint pain from the occlusion
Treating a dentigerous cyst associated with the tooth

questions.question: A patient develops trismus and difficulty swallowing several days after extraction of an infected lower third molar, with swelling extending into the pterygomandibular and parapharyngeal spaces. This spread of infection into deep fascial spaces illustrates the importance of which surgical principle?
questions.explanation: Spread of odontogenic infection into deep fascial spaces such as the pterygomandibular and parapharyngeal spaces represents a serious complication requiring early recognition and prompt management, including drainage, antibiotics, and airway monitoring, given the potential for life-threatening progression. This underscores the importance of vigilant postoperative assessment following extraction of infected teeth. Delayed recognition of spreading infection significantly increases morbidity and risk of serious complications.
options: Early recognition and management of spreading odontogenic infection
Delayed antibiotic therapy until symptoms resolve spontaneously
Avoidance of any radiographic assessment before extraction
Avoidance of local anaesthesia in all extractions
Routine coronectomy for all third molars

questions.question: In the FDI (Fédération Dentaire Internationale) notation, the number assigned to the upper right permanent quadrant is:
questions.explanation: In FDI notation, the four permanent dentition quadrants are assigned numbers 1–4 starting from the upper right (1), upper left (2), lower left (3), and lower right (4). The deciduous quadrants are assigned 5–8 in the same sequence. The quadrant number precedes the tooth number, so tooth 11 is the upper right central incisor.

A periodontal abscess is classified as a distinct category within the periodontal disease classification, presenting as a localized, often painful, purulent lesion arising within a pre-existing periodontal pocket. It requires prompt drainage and management, distinct from the more diffuse, chronic presentation of gingivitis or established periodontitis. Its acute nature necessitates urgent attention to prevent further spread of infection.
questions.question: A patient develops a painful, localized, dome-shaped swelling of the gingiva with purulent discharge from a periodontal pocket in a tooth with pre-existing periodontal disease. This acute lesion is classified under which category of the periodontal disease classification?
Oblique lateral radiography demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Oblique lateral radiography demonstrates large areas of the maxilla or mandible, with the region imaged dependent on the specific technique chosen. It is an extra-oral projection that provides information on areas not easily assessed with intraoral films. Dental panoramic radiography (DPR), oblique lateral radiography, and cephalometry are the most frequently requested extra-oral projections.
options: Large areas of the maxilla or mandible
Both arches simultaneously on panoramic film
Detailed view of a single tooth and its apex
The nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses

questions.question: The most critical period for preventing facial growth disruption from unilateral TMJ ankylosis is:
options: As early as possible, releasing it for catch-up growth
During puberty when peak growth velocity occurs
In adulthood, when surgical correction tends to work most effectively
Between ages 16–18 when growth plates close
Only after secondary dentition has fully erupted
questions.explanation: Early surgical release of TMJ ankylosis in childhood is critical because the condyle is the primary growth centre for the mandible; every year of ankylosis during the growth period results in progressively greater growth deficiency and facial deformity. Early gap arthroplasty or costochondral rib graft reconstruction — ideally performed as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed — allows the mandible to resume growth with physiotherapy to prevent re-ankylosis. Delayed treatment requires more complex orthognathic surgical correction in adulthood.

Haemophilia represents an absolute systemic contraindication to extraction without appropriate medical liaison and haematological preparation because of life-threatening haemorrhage risk. Absolute systemic contraindications include leukaemia, renal failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and cardiac failure. Most other systemic conditions represent relative contraindications that can be modified by the clinician.
questions.question: Which of the following is an ABSOLUTE systemic contraindication to dental extraction?
options: Pregnancy occurring during the second trimester
Haemophilia on anticoagulants without medical liaison

questions.explanation: Current caries science recognises that demineralisation by organic acids of microbial origin and remineralisation by salivary components (or therapeutic agents like fluoride) occur simultaneously. Whether caries progresses depends on which process prevails in the oral environment over time. This dynamic model has replaced earlier static theories and forms the basis for modern preventive and minimally invasive dentistry.
questions.question: In the current dynamic concept of caries, the disease represents a balance between:
options: Demineralisation by acids versus salivary remineralisation
Acid production and buffering by plaque

questions.explanation: Riga-Fede disease is a traumatic ulcer located on the anterior portion of the tongue in infants who have natal (present at birth) or neonatal teeth. Repeated trauma from the sharp incisal edges of natal teeth causes the characteristic ulceration. Management involves smoothing the sharp tooth edges or extraction if conservative measures fail.
questions.question: Riga-Fede disease is a traumatic ulcer affecting specifically:
options: The soft palate of elderly denture wearers
The lip mucosa after chemical burns
The buccal mucosa following cheek biting
Anterior tongue of infants with natal teeth

questions.question: The MAIN disadvantage of dental amalgam compared to composite resin is:
options: Colour does not match tooth structure
Poor wear resistance on occlusal surfaces
Inability to be used in Class II cavities
questions.explanation: The primary clinical disadvantage of dental amalgam is its silver-grey colour, which does not match tooth structure — an unacceptable aesthetic limitation for visible teeth. Amalgam has excellent compressive strength, wear resistance, and longevity. Its disadvantages also include galvanic shock, corrosion potential, and mercury-related concerns, but aesthetics remains the most clinically relevant limitation.

questions.question: The maxillofacial region is demarcated superiorly by the hairline and inferiorly by:
questions.explanation: The maxillofacial region is demarcated by the hairline superiorly and the chin inferiorly, with two auricles laterally. It can be divided into three thirds: the upper third (eyebrow and above), the middle third (eyebrow to upper occlusal level), and the lower third (lower occlusal level to the chin). This region is uniquely associated with vital functions of daily life including sight, smell, hearing, mastication, and speech.

questions.question: A dentist compares the marginal fit and internal adaptation of a cast metal crown fabricated using the lost-wax technique with a directly fabricated restoration. Achieving a well-fitting indirect restoration primarily depends on:
questions.explanation: Achieving a well-fitting indirect restoration, such as a cast metal crown, depends critically on accurate impression taking to capture precise tooth preparation detail, combined with meticulous laboratory fabrication technique, including accurate model pouring and casting procedures. Errors introduced at any stage of this multi-step indirect process can compromise the final marginal fit and clinical success of the restoration. This contrasts with direct restorations, which are fabricated and adjusted chairside in a single visit.
options: Only the speed of chairside placement
Elimination of any need for a try-in appointment
Only the colour of the restorative material
Accurate impression taking and precise laboratory fabrication technique

questions.explanation: Inlays and onlays are indirect intra-coronal restorations fabricated in the dental laboratory from an impression of the prepared tooth and later cemented into the prepared cavity. They are used when direct restorations are inadequate due to large cavity size or when superior mechanical properties are required. Gold, ceramic, and composite inlays/onlays are available.
questions.question: Inlays and onlays are examples of:
A patient with suspected sialolithiasis of the submandibular duct requires imaging of the salivary gland ductal system using a contrast medium. Which radiographic technique is specifically indicated?
questions.explanation: Sialography is a specialised radiographic technique that involves injecting a radiopaque contrast medium into a salivary gland duct to visualise the ductal system and detect obstructions such as sialoliths. It is not used for routine dental hard tissue evaluation. This makes it the specific investigation of choice for suspected salivary duct pathology.

The nasolabial cyst is a non-odontogenic soft tissue cyst arising from remnants of the nasolacrimal duct epithelium, located in the soft tissues of the nasolabial fold — external to the jaw bone and therefore not producing a radiographic intraosseous radiolucency. It presents as a fluctuant swelling elevating the ala of the nose. This extrabony location distinguishes it from all odontogenic and other jaw cysts that are intraosseous lesions.
options: Within the nasopalatine canal in the midline anterior maxilla
In the nasolabial fold's soft tissue, outside the jaw
Within the mandibular symphysis at the midline
Adjacent to the maxillary sinus wall
At the apices of maxillary lateral incisors
questions.question: The nasolabial cyst is classified as a non-odontogenic cyst and is characteristically located:
The consistency of a large radicular cyst may be described as which of the following upon palpation?
options: Ranges from bony hard to soft and fluctuant
Always remaining tender and quite painful upon palpation
Rubbery and resilient in all cases
questions.explanation: As a radicular cyst grows, its consistency evolves. Early lesions surrounded by thick bone are bony hard; as bone thins, egg-shell cracking and ping-pong ball consistency develop; at the largest sizes, the wall becomes soft and fluctuant. This progression of consistencies is a clinical hallmark that helps clinicians gauge lesion size and guide their investigation and surgical approach.

questions.question: Mumps is defined as an acute viral infection primarily of which gland?
questions.explanation: Mumps is an acute viral infection of the salivary glands, most commonly affecting the parotid gland, making it the commonest cause of parotid swelling in children. It is highly infectious with an incubation period of approximately 21 days. Extra-glandular involvement can include the testes (orchitis) and ovaries (ovaritis), potentially causing infertility.

questions.question: A dentist evaluates a chronic carious lesion that has become hard, dark, and shiny, with no evidence of active progression on repeat examination over several months. This lesion is best described as:
questions.explanation: Arrested caries describes a lesion in which the carious process has stopped progressing, often becoming hard, dark, and shiny due to surface remineralisation and loss of the cariogenic biofilm, distinguishing it from active progressive caries, which remains soft and continues to advance. Recognising arrested lesions is important because they may not require immediate restorative intervention. Active lesions, in contrast, warrant timely treatment to prevent further progression.

questions.question: A patient with a single missing tooth and adequate bone volume is offered dental implant treatment as an alternative to a conventional bridge. The main advantage of an implant-supported restoration in this scenario, compared with a tooth-supported bridge, is that it:
questions.explanation: The main advantage of an implant-supported restoration for a single missing tooth is that it avoids the need to reduce and potentially compromise adjacent healthy teeth, which is required for a conventional tooth-supported bridge. This preserves the structural integrity of neighbouring teeth. However, implant treatment requires adequate bone volume and quality, a healing period for osseointegration, and diligent oral hygiene to prevent peri-implant disease.
options: Requires no healing period whatsoever before restoration
Eliminates the need for any oral hygiene maintenance
Is always less costly than a conventional bridge
Avoids the need to prepare and potentially compromise adjacent healthy teeth
Is suitable in all patients regardless of bone quality or quantity

questions.explanation: Hybrid composite resins combine both conventional macro-fillers and microfine fillers to achieve better surface smoothness than conventional composites while maintaining mechanical properties equivalent to conventional composites. This makes hybrids the most versatile composite type, suitable for both anterior aesthetic restorations and posterior load-bearing restorations — effectively combining the advantages of both conventional and microfilled composites.
questions.question: Hybrid composite resin differs from microfilled composite primarily in that it has:
options: Only micron-sized fillers without any submicron particles
Lower wear resistance than microfilled composites
No coupling agent between filler and matrix
Equal properties to conventional composite, smoother surface
Only chemical activation and no light-cure option
The inferior border of the mandibular ramus
The neck of the condyle at the sigmoid notch
The anterior border of the ramus only
The articular margin of the condyle
The mandibular notch between coronoid and condyle
questions.explanation: The TMJ joint capsule attaches high up on the neck of the mandible around the articular margin of the condyle. Despite being described as lax, it provides sufficient containment for joint stability during function. The laxity accommodates the wide range of mandibular movements. The disc is attached around its periphery to the inside of the capsule, creating the upper and lower joint compartments.
questions.question: The TMJ capsule is described as lax but strong, attaching high up on the neck of the mandible around:

options: Stain dental plaque for oral hygiene assessment
Identify potentially malignant or malignant oral lesions
questions.explanation: Toluidine blue is a vital stain used as a chair-side investigation to identify potentially malignant or malignant oral mucosal lesions. It stains nucleic acids in rapidly dividing cells (as found in dysplastic or malignant tissue) a deep blue colour. A positive toluidine blue stain indicates areas warranting biopsy, though false positives with inflammation can occur.
questions.question: Toluidine blue (vital) staining in oral pathology is used to:

questions.explanation: Rotational force during forceps extraction is particularly useful for teeth with a single conical root (such as upper central incisors and lower premolars) because rotation causes internal expansion of the socket all around the root circumference. Teeth with multiple divergent roots, curved roots, or widely separated roots cannot be rotated without risk of root fracture. Understanding root morphology guides the extraction movement strategy.
questions.question: Rotational force during forceps extraction is particularly useful for teeth with:

A researcher proposes that periodontitis does not progress at a constant, continuous rate but instead advances through short, episodic periods of active tissue destruction interspersed with longer periods of quiescence. This model is known as the:
questions.explanation: The random burst theory of periodontitis progression proposes that the disease advances through episodic bursts of active destruction, occurring unpredictably at different sites, rather than through a slow, continuous, linear process. This concept has important implications for monitoring and timing of periodontal maintenance therapy. It contrasts with earlier models that assumed uniform, gradual progression across all affected sites.

Riga-Fede disease is a traumatic ulceration of the ventral tongue in infants, caused by repetitive friction against natal or neonatal teeth during suckling. It typically resolves once the traumatic cause, such as smoothing or extracting the offending tooth, is removed. It is a specific eponymous variant of traumatic oral ulceration in infancy.
questions.question: A toddler who is still bottle-fed presents with a persistent ulcer on the ventral surface of the tongue caused by repeated trauma from the natal incisors during sucking. This traumatic ulcer is specifically termed:

questions.explanation: The globulomaxillary cyst was historically thought to arise from entrapped epithelium at the fusion of the globular and maxillary embryonic processes, presenting radiographically as a radiolucency between the lateral incisor and canine, though modern understanding suggests most such lesions are actually odontogenic in origin (e.g., radicular or lateral periodontal cysts) rather than representing a distinct fissural cyst entity. This evolving understanding illustrates how classification systems in oral pathology continue to be refined. Correct diagnosis relies on vitality testing and histological examination rather than location alone.
questions.question: A radiograph shows a well-defined unilocular radiolucency between the roots of the maxillary lateral incisor and canine, initially considered as arising from fusion of embryonic processes, though this theory has since been largely discredited in favour of an odontogenic origin. This historically named cyst is the:
A patient with a peg-shaped maxillary lateral incisor requests improved appearance. Restorative build-up of this tooth would primarily be classified under which indication for restoration?
questions.explanation: A peg-shaped lateral incisor represents a developmental morphological anomaly rather than caries, trauma, or restoration failure, so restorative build-up in this case is indicated primarily for aesthetic and morphological improvement. Composite bonding or veneers are commonly used to reshape such teeth. This illustrates that not all restorative indications relate to disease.
options: Replacement of missing tooth structure due to caries
Restoration of fractured tooth from trauma
Correction of a failed prior restoration

questions.question: A patient reports that several posterior teeth on the working side make simultaneous contact and share the load during lateral excursive movement, rather than the canine alone providing guidance. This occlusal scheme is termed:
questions.explanation: Group function occlusion is an occlusal scheme in which multiple posterior teeth on the working side make simultaneous contact and share the functional load during lateral excursive movement, rather than the canine alone providing disengagement of the posterior teeth as in canine-guided occlusion. Both schemes are considered physiologically acceptable occlusal patterns, and the specific scheme present in a given patient can inform restorative and prosthodontic treatment planning to maintain harmonious function. Recognising a patient's natural occlusal scheme helps guide restoration design to preserve existing occlusal harmony.

questions.question: 'Retention form' in tooth preparation refers to the preparation's ability to:
questions.explanation: Retention form is the ability of the prepared tooth to resist displacement or removal of the restoration by occlusally directed forces. For amalgam preparations, the cavity walls should converge occlusally (occlusally convergent) with retentive features such as undercuts, grooves, and locks. Insufficient retention form results in restoration dislodgement.
options: Protect the pulp from thermal stimuli
Anxiety, medical health, tooth evaluation, and radiographs
Age, weight, blood group, and medication history
Blood pressure, blood glucose, clotting time, and ECG
Pain threshold, dental history, social history, and financial capacity
Medical history, allergy status, last meal time, and ASA classification
questions.question: Pre-operative assessment for exodontia includes evaluation of which four components?
questions.explanation: Pre-operative assessment for exodontia includes: (1) evaluation of the patient's anxiety level, (2) general and medical health status, (3) clinical evaluation (crown, root, surrounding structures), and (4) radiological evaluation. Thorough pre-operative assessment identifies contraindications, guides anaesthetic choice (LA, sedation, GA), and ensures informed consent for the surgical procedure.

questions.question: Which clinical gingival parameter is evaluated through probing during a periodontal examination?
questions.explanation: Probing assesses the position of the gingival margin and the base of the sulcus or pocket, determining pocket depth and attachment level. Colour, surface texture, contour, and consistency are assessed by inspection and palpation. Probing depth measurement is the cornerstone of periodontal disease staging.

options: Elevated salivary and mucosal glucose levels favouring fungal growth
questions.question: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and dry mouth develops recurrent oral candidiasis. Which of the following diabetes-related factors MOST directly predisposes to this fungal overgrowth?
questions.explanation: Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus predisposes to oral candidiasis in part because elevated glucose levels in saliva and oral mucosal tissues provide a favourable environment for fungal growth, combined with impaired immune function and reduced salivary flow often seen in diabetic patients. This multifactorial predisposition explains the increased prevalence of candidiasis in this population. Optimising glycaemic control is an important adjunct to direct antifungal treatment.

questions.question: Which vitamin deficiencies reduce tissue resistance and predispose to NUG in children?
questions.explanation: Deficiency of essential vitamins A, B, and C reduces tissue resistance and immune defence, predisposing children to NUG. Nutritional deficiency is among the systemic predisposing factors, alongside debilitating illnesses that decrease immunological defence and psychosomatic stressors such as child neglect. Adequate nutrition is therefore fundamental in prevention and management.

options: A diamorphic, commensal fungus that is native to the oral cavity
Thermally dimorphic: hyphal at room temperature, yeast at body heat
An obligate intracellular virus-like fungal parasite
A permanently hyphal fungus in all host environments
questions.explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum is a classic example of a thermally dimorphic fungus: it exists as septate hyphal form in the environment (room temperature) and converts to yeast form at body temperature (37°C) within the host. This thermal dimorphism is a key virulence determinant — the yeast form is adapted for intramacrophage survival and systemic dissemination. Geographic exposure in endemic regions (Mississippi and Ohio river valleys) determines infection risk in immunocompetent individuals.
questions.question: Histoplasma capsulatum is an example of which category of fungal pathogen?

questions.explanation: Immunologically mediated oral ulcers include Reiter's syndrome and Behcet's syndrome, both characterized by immune-mediated tissue destruction. Behcet's disease is a multisystem vasculitic disorder with recurrent oral ulcers as a major feature. Drug-induced ulcers such as erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome constitute a separate category.
questions.question: Oral ulcers classified under 'Immunologic' causes include:
The 'early lesion' in the histopathological progression of gingivitis is characterised by predominance of:
options: T-lymphocytes with more collagen loss than initially
Osteoclasts and osteoblasts present in equal numbers
questions.explanation: The early lesion, developing after approximately 4–7 days of plaque accumulation, is characterised by a predominance of T-lymphocytes and is associated with increasing collagen loss in the connective tissue. It represents the transition from the acute neutrophilic initial lesion toward the adaptive immune response. If plaque is removed at this stage, the lesion is still fully reversible without permanent tissue damage.

questions.question: A patient who has undergone maxillectomy for a tumour requires a removable prosthesis to close a palatal defect and restore speech and swallowing function. This specific type of prosthesis is called a(n):
questions.explanation: An obturator denture is specifically designed to close a congenital or acquired defect of the palate, such as following maxillectomy, restoring separation between the oral and nasal cavities to improve speech, swallowing, and prevent nasal regurgitation. This differs from conventional complete or partial dentures, which simply replace missing teeth. Obturators require specialised design considerations for retention given the altered anatomy.

Pemphigus vulgaris is a mucocutaneous autoimmune disease in which oral erosions and ulcers frequently precede skin involvement. These ulcers are classified as secondary to systemic disease rather than local trauma. Recognition is important because delayed diagnosis can result in significant morbidity from widespread blistering.
questions.question: A patient with pemphigus vulgaris presents with widespread painful oral erosions that were the first manifestation of the disease. These oral lesions are best classified as ulcers occurring:

questions.explanation: The principal clinical limitation of conventional glass ionomer cement as a posterior direct restorative material is its poor fracture toughness and abrasion resistance compared to composite resin and amalgam. In high-load-bearing posterior sites, conventional GIC restorations are prone to surface wear and bulk fracture. Resin-modified GIC (RMGIC) and glass carbomer modifications have partially addressed this limitation while retaining fluoride release.
questions.question: The MAIN limitation of glass ionomer cement as a posterior restorative material is its:
options: High thermal conductivity causing pulp sensitivity
Inability to release fluoride under occlusal loading
Lack of any bonding to dentine
Poor fracture and abrasion resistance versus composite

questions.question: A patient requires crown lengthening surgery to expose additional sound tooth structure before restorative treatment of a subgingivally fractured tooth. This procedure primarily achieves its goal by:
questions.explanation: Crown lengthening surgery achieves its goal by surgically removing gingival tissue and, when necessary, a portion of the underlying alveolar bone, to expose additional sound tooth structure coronal to the existing gingival margin, facilitating subsequent restorative procedures such as crown placement. This differs fundamentally from procedures aimed at covering exposed roots, such as root coverage grafting. Adequate biological width must be respected during this procedure to maintain periodontal health.
options: Surgically removing gingival and, if needed, alveolar bone to expose more tooth structure
Adding gingival tissue to cover exposed roots
Regenerating lost alveolar bone using a membrane

questions.explanation: Pre-operative assessment for exodontia includes evaluation of the patient's medical history, dental history, radiographic findings, and relevant social or psychological factors that may affect the procedure or recovery. This comprehensive approach ensures that systemic, local, and patient-related risk factors are identified before proceeding. Omitting any component risks missing a contraindication or complicating factor.
questions.question: Before extracting a tooth, a dentist performs a comprehensive pre-operative assessment. Which four components are specifically evaluated in this assessment?
options: Only the patient's age and occupation
Medical, dental, radiographic, and social history/assessment

questions.question: Treatment of chronic traumatic ulcers that fail to respond within 2 weeks of cause removal should include:
questions.explanation: Chronic ulcers strongly suspected to be traumatic in origin should have their cause identified and be observed for 2 weeks using bland rinses. If there is no improvement or the lesion increases in size, biopsy must be performed to exclude malignancy. Failing to biopsy a non-healing ulcer risks missing an early squamous cell carcinoma.
options: Immediate extraction of all adjacent teeth
Large enough to admit working instruments
The cavity is deep enough for adequate material thickness
All caries is removed without over-extension
The pulp is completely protected from thermal insults
The margins are placed in self-cleansing areas
questions.explanation: Convenience form ensures the prepared cavity is sufficiently large to admit the instruments used in the operative procedure, including placement and condensation instruments. Without adequate convenience form, instruments cannot be properly manipulated within the cavity, compromising the quality of the restoration. It may require slight extension of the cavity outline beyond the minimum needed for caries removal.
questions.question: Convenience form in cavity preparation ensures that:

options: Nystatin is more effective against all Candida species including resistant ones
Azoles cause renal toxicity that is poorly tolerated in pregnancy
Poorly absorbed orally, acting locally with no fetal effect
Nystatin has a broader spectrum including antiviral activity
Azoles are excreted in large amounts in breastmilk only
questions.explanation: Nystatin is the preferred antifungal for oral candidiasis in pregnancy because it is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract when swallowed, acting topically on the oral and gastrointestinal mucosa without clinically significant systemic absorption — thus posing no risk to the fetus. Systemic azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole) are teratogenic in animal studies and are contraindicated in pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester. Topical nystatin rinses or lozenges are both safe and effective for mucosal candidiasis.
questions.question: In the management of oral candidiasis, nystatin is preferred over systemic azoles in pregnancy because:

questions.explanation: An oro-antral communication (which may become a fistula if not managed promptly) can occur following extraction of a maxillary molar with close root proximity to a pneumatised maxillary sinus, resulting in an abnormal connection between the oral cavity and the sinus, often confirmed clinically by a positive nose-blowing (Valsalva) test. Prompt recognition and appropriate management, ranging from conservative measures for small communications to surgical closure for larger or persistent defects, is important to prevent chronic sinus infection. This complication highlights the importance of preoperative radiographic assessment of root-sinus relationships.
questions.question: A patient undergoing extraction of a maxillary molar with a large, pneumatised maxillary sinus develops a persistent communication between the oral cavity and the sinus after the procedure, confirmed by a positive nose-blowing test. This complication is termed an:

A radiograph of an impacted mandibular third molar reveals a multilocular radiolucent lesion with cystic and solid components. Histological examination confirms ameloblastomatous epithelium lining a cystic cavity. This lesion, showing features of both a cyst and a benign but locally aggressive neoplasm, is termed:
questions.explanation: Unicystic (cystic) ameloblastoma presents radiographically similar to a dentigerous cyst but shows ameloblastomatous epithelium on histological examination, reflecting its more locally aggressive, neoplastic nature compared with a simple dentigerous cyst. This distinction is crucial because management and recurrence risk differ significantly from a benign developmental cyst. Accurate histological diagnosis therefore guides the extent of surgical treatment required.

options: Soft tissue, nerve, and vascular involvement
Degree of calcification present within lesions
questions.explanation: MRI provides superior soft tissue characterisation compared to CT and is therefore preferred for evaluating extent of soft tissue involvement, perineural spread, vascular involvement, and temporomandibular joint disc position. It does not use ionising radiation. CT remains superior for evaluating bony cortical integrity, calcification, and complex three-dimensional bone anatomy.
questions.question: MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) in oral pathology is superior to CT for evaluating:

questions.explanation: Silicate cement has largely been superseded for permanent restorations because of its high solubility in oral fluids, loss of anatomic contour, and marginal degradation over time. It is now used only as a temporary restorative material. Despite its anticariogenic properties and good compressive strength, its clinical longevity is unacceptably limited for definitive restorations.
options: Permanent aesthetic restoration for anterior teeth
Temporary restoration, due to high solubility
questions.question: Silicate cement is NOW used primarily as a:

questions.explanation: Chronic, refractory mucocutaneous candidiasis affecting multiple sites from early childhood should prompt investigation for an underlying primary immunodeficiency, as persistent, treatment-resistant fungal infection can be an important clinical marker of significant systemic immune dysfunction. This differs from typical, transient, or localized candidiasis related to common predisposing factors such as antibiotics or dentures. Early recognition allows appropriate referral for immunological assessment and management.
options: Caused only by external environmental exposure
Exclusively related to poor oral hygiene alone
Always a benign, self-limiting condition needing no further workup
A marker of an underlying primary immune defect requiring further systemic investigation
Never associated with any systemic disease
questions.question: A patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis has persistent, refractory oral and nail infections since early childhood, associated with an underlying primary immunodeficiency. This presentation illustrates that Candida infections can be:

questions.explanation: Active herpetic gingivostomatitis increases systemic debilitation and oral pain, complicating the drainage and treatment of a concurrent dental abscess. Stress and systemic illness can trigger HSV reactivation, and vice versa, the infection lowers immune defence. Management requires careful sequencing: supportive HSV care first, while ensuring the dental infection is appropriately addressed with antibiotics and drainage.
options: The HSV infection simply means the child needs GA only
Active HSV worsens with stress; the abscess adds systemic strain
Abscess treatment requires the same antiviral drugs
HSV causes bone destruction similar to abscess
The child cannot receive antibiotics during active HSV
questions.question: A primary herpetic gingivostomatitis in a child with a dento-alveolar abscess would MOST complicate management because:
TMJ ankylosis is derived from the Greek word meaning:
questions.explanation: Ankylosis derives from the Greek 'ankylos' meaning stiff (or bent/crooked). In the context of the TMJ, ankylosis refers to the abnormal immobility and consolidation of the joint due to either intra-articular (true ankylosis — obliteration of the joint space with bony or fibrous union) or extra-articular changes (pseudo-ankylosis). Knowing the Greek origin helps remember the defining clinical feature: a stiff, immobile joint.

questions.question: Composite resin restorative materials are composed of which three main components?
options: Resin matrix, filler particles, and coupling agent
Calcium hydroxide, zinc oxide, and eugenol mix
Glass powder, polyacrylic acid, and water
Phosphoric acid, methyl methacrylate, and silicate
questions.explanation: Composite resin consists of a resin matrix (Bis-GMA or UDMA), inorganic filler particles (quartz, colloidal silica, or metal glasses), and a silane coupling agent that bonds the filler to the resin. The ratio of filler to resin determines physical properties such as wear resistance and polymerisation shrinkage. All three components are essential for clinical performance.

questions.question: Scissors bite malocclusion in the transverse plane results from which jaw discrepancy?
questions.explanation: Scissors bite (Brodie syndrome) occurs when the mandibular buccal cusps occlude completely outside the maxillary buccal cusps — the reverse of a crossbite. This results from transverse mandibular excess (or maxillary deficiency), where the lower arch is wider than the upper. In a standard crossbite, the mandibular teeth occlude inside (palatal to) the maxillary teeth; in scissors bite, they occlude outside (buccal to) the maxillary teeth. Correction typically requires transverse jaw narrowing.
options: Mandibular deficiency in the transverse plane (or maxillary excess)
Mandibular excess in the transverse plane (or maxillary deficiency)
Vertical anterior excess producing excessive overbite
Sagittal mandibular excess producing reverse overjet
Bilateral constriction of both arches equally

questions.explanation: Common investigations in oral pathology include radiography, biopsy, chair-side investigations, and haematological investigations (FBC, WBC differentials, FPG, clotting profile, retroviral screening). Dental chair ergonomics is not a diagnostic investigation. Correct selection and interpretation of these investigations is fundamental to establishing a definitive oral pathological diagnosis.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised category of common investigation in oral pathology?
Which of the following is NOT typically classified as an indirect restorative material?
questions.explanation: Dental amalgam is a direct restorative material placed and shaped intraorally. Indirect restorative materials — including gold alloy, base metal alloy, porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM), composite resins, and ceramics — are fabricated in the laboratory and cemented onto the tooth. This fundamental distinction determines which restoration types require laboratory fabrication and a second clinical visit.

questions.question: The preventive measure of using xylitol for caries prevention works because:
questions.explanation: Xylitol, a sugar alcohol, cannot be fermented by Streptococcus mutans to produce acid, making it non-cariogenic and potentially anticariogenic. Unlike sucrose, xylitol is taken up by S. mutans but cannot be metabolised, resulting in a futile energy expenditure cycle that may inhibit bacterial growth. Regular xylitol use reduces S. mutans counts in plaque and saliva.
options: It increases fluoride uptake into the enamel
S. mutans cannot ferment it to acid
It chelates calcium from plaque bacteria

questions.explanation: Provisional (temporary) restorative materials are specifically formulated to offer adequate short-term strength, aesthetics, and marginal seal while protecting the prepared tooth and maintaining function until the permanent indirect restoration is fabricated and cemented. They are designed for easy removal without damaging the underlying tooth preparation. Selecting an inappropriate permanent material for a temporary role could complicate later removal and permanent restoration placement.
questions.question: A patient requires a temporary (provisional) restoration while awaiting a permanent indirect crown. The material chosen must provide adequate strength and aesthetics for a short period while being easily removable without damaging the prepared tooth. Which class of material is specifically designed for this purpose?
options: Glass ionomer luting cement used as a permanent restoration
Is caused by different bacteria entirely
Is more common in children than adults
Affects cementum and dentine of exposed roots
Requires a different type of bur for removal
questions.question: Root (cemental) caries differs from coronal caries in that it:
questions.explanation: Root caries (also called cemental or cervical caries) affects the cementum and exposed dentine of root surfaces, which become exposed through gingival recession common in older adults or periodontal disease. Cementum has lower mineral content and is more susceptible to cariogenic acid attack than enamel. It requires modified restorative approaches due to the proximity to the pulp and the challenging cavity access.

options: Facial deformity due to restricted mandibular growth
Normal facial growth with compensatory mechanisms
Bilateral facial symmetry maintained by adaptive remodelling
Superior condylar displacement without growth effects
questions.question: TMJ ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint, if occurring during the period of growth, causes:
questions.explanation: TMJ ankylosis during growth causes severe facial deformity because the fused joint prevents normal condylar translation and rotation, which are essential for mandibular growth. Unilateral ankylosis results in facial asymmetry with mandibular deviation to the affected side; bilateral ankylosis produces a 'bird-face' deformity (micrognathia). Early surgical release and gap arthroplasty are essential to allow catch-up growth.

S. mutans converts sucrose to glucans and fructose to fructans—high-molecular-mass polymers that aid adherence of microorganisms to the tooth surface, are water-insoluble acting as diffusion barriers that trap organic acids on the tooth, and increase plaque thickness to retain acid. These mechanisms collectively amplify the cariogenic potential of sucrose above all other dietary sugars.
questions.question: Streptococcus mutans converts sucrose and fructose to extracellular polysaccharides that:
options: Promote remineralisation of the enamel surface
Aid adherence, trap acids, thicken plaque
Rate of progression of caries in filled teeth
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is not a direct determinant of restoration lifespan. Factors affecting restoration longevity include patient age, properties of the restorative material (wear resistance, marginal adaptation), rate of caries progression, occlusal load, moisture control during placement, and operator expertise. Understanding these factors helps in material selection and treatment planning.
questions.question: The longevity of a dental restoration is influenced by all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Normally, the gingival margin is positioned approximately 1 mm coronal to (above) the cemento-enamel junction. This relationship is determined by the position of the tooth in the arch. Apical migration signals recession, while coronal placement may indicate pseudo-pocket formation or gingival overgrowth.
questions.question: In health, the position of the gingival margin relative to the cemento-enamel junction (CEJ) is approximately:

options: Advanced bone loss making the tooth non-restorable
Localised gingival bleeding on probing only
Gingival recession limited to one tooth surface
questions.explanation: Advanced periodontal disease is an indication for extraction only when bone loss is so severe that the tooth cannot be retained even with comprehensive periodontal treatment — typically assessed by unfavourable crown-to-root ratio, poor furcation involvement classification, or hopeless prognosis despite treatment. The extraction decision must always weigh the strategic value of the tooth, the patient's oral hygiene potential, and the prosthetic replacement plan.
questions.question: Advanced periodontal disease is an indication for extraction when it has produced:
In dental amalgam, tin primarily functions to:
options: Whiten the alloy and increase strength
Acting as the main scavenger that helps prevent oxidation
Controls the silver-mercury reaction, lowering strength and corrosion resistance
questions.explanation: Tin controls the rate of the amalgamation reaction between silver and mercury — without tin, the reaction would be too rapid with unacceptable expansion. However, tin reduces the strength, hardness, and resistance to tarnish and corrosion of the set amalgam, making it one of the elements whose proportion requires careful balancing. Alloys with reduced tin content (high-copper amalgams) were developed to improve corrosion resistance while maintaining the setting control.

Cancrum oris is a devastating gangrenous infection affecting malnourished young children who are recovering from a serious debilitating illness. It causes well-demarcated gangrene affecting the gum, oral mucosa, and facial soft tissue. Predisposing illnesses include measles, malaria, diarrhoea, typhoid, tuberculosis, and Burkitt lymphoma.
options: Malnourished children recovering from debilitating illness
Immunocompetent teenagers with poor oral hygiene
questions.question: Cancrum oris (noma) characteristically affects:

questions.explanation: Crouzon syndrome is a craniosynostosis syndrome caused by FGFR2 mutations, characterised by premature fusion of cranial sutures producing midface hypoplasia (maxillary deficiency) and a normal or relatively prognathic mandible — resulting in a Class III skeletal pattern with anterior crossbite and midface retrusion. Exorbitism and beaked nose complete the characteristic facies. Management requires Le Fort III or monobloc midface advancement as part of a staged craniofacial surgical approach.
questions.question: A Crouzon syndrome patient presenting with malocclusion is MOST likely to exhibit which skeletal pattern?
options: Class II from mandibular prognathism alone
Open bite from vertical maxillary excess only
Class I with bilateral posterior crossbite only
Class III from midface deficiency and maxillary hypoplasia
Symmetric Class II from mandibular deficiency without midface involvement

questions.question: During extraction of a maxillary first molar with widely divergent buccal roots, which specific forceps movement is particularly useful to disengage the tooth from the alveolar bone?
options: Rotational movement is generally avoided; buccal and palatal expansion is favoured
No force is required for multi-rooted teeth
Rotational force is the primary technique for all multi-rooted teeth
questions.explanation: Teeth with divergent or multiple roots, such as the maxillary first molar, are generally not suited to rotational forceps movement because the roots would resist rotation and risk fracture; buccal and palatal (lingual) expansion movements are favoured instead. Rotational force is more useful for single-rooted, conical teeth like incisors and canines. Selecting the correct movement for root morphology reduces the risk of root fracture during extraction.

The neutral zone is the potential space in the dental arch where the outward pressure of the tongue is balanced by the inward pressure of the lips and cheeks. Teeth naturally migrate to this zone. Disruption of the balance — by tongue postural changes, tongue thrust, altered lip tone, or enlarged tonsils — displaces teeth beyond the neutral zone, producing characteristic malocclusions such as anterior open bite or proclination.
questions.question: The 'neutral zone' in the context of malocclusion soft tissue factors refers to:
options: The area of optimal bone density in the alveolar process
The neutral occlusal plane between arches
The arch zone where tongue and lip/cheek pressures balance
The zone free of periodontal pathogens
The relaxed position of the mandible at rest

questions.question: Nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, causes which gingival change?
questions.explanation: Nifedipine is a well-documented cause of drug-induced gingival enlargement, characterised by an increase in fibrous connective tissue. The mechanism involves alteration of fibroblast activity and reduced collagen degradation. Other common culprits include phenytoin and cyclosporin. Good oral hygiene can minimise severity.

options: Observation only, without any surgical intervention
Peripheral ostectomy or chemical treatment (e.g. Carnoy's solution) of the bony cavity
No follow-up is required after simple enucleation
Systemic antibiotics alone as definitive treatment
questions.explanation: Odontogenic keratocysts have a notably higher recurrence rate than most other odontogenic cysts, related to the thin, friable lining and potential for satellite (daughter) cysts, prompting many surgeons to combine enucleation with adjunctive treatment such as peripheral ostectomy or chemical fixation of the bony cavity using Carnoy's solution. This combined approach aims to reduce the likelihood of recurrence compared with enucleation alone. Long-term follow-up remains important given the recurrence potential.
questions.question: A large odontogenic keratocyst is planned for surgical management. Compared with simple enucleation alone, the recurrence rate of odontogenic keratocysts is notably higher, prompting many surgeons to also employ which adjunctive treatment?

questions.explanation: Abrasion refers to tooth surface loss caused by mechanical wear from an external object or substance, such as aggressive toothbrushing with a hard-bristled brush, typically producing characteristic wedge-shaped notches at the cervical margin, often more pronounced on the side corresponding to the patient's dominant brushing hand. This differs from attrition, which results from direct tooth-to-tooth contact, and erosion, which results from chemical acid dissolution. Modifying the causative brushing technique and material is central to preventing further progression of abrasion lesions.
questions.question: A patient with a habit of aggressive horizontal toothbrushing using a hard-bristled brush develops wedge-shaped notches at the cervical margins of several teeth on the side of their dominant hand. This specific pattern of tooth surface loss is best classified as:
Psoriatic arthritis of the TMJ is classified under which disease category?
questions.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis is classified among the infective/inflammatory arthritides affecting the TMJ, alongside ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, and osteoarthritis. While not primarily infectious, these conditions share inflammatory pathogenesis affecting synovial joints including the TMJ. The sero-negative spondyloarthropathies (including psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis) are associated with HLA-B27 and can produce significant TMJ inflammation, pain, restricted opening, and in severe cases, ankylosis.

Cephalometric radiography uses a standardised, reproducible head position to allow precise measurement of skeletal and dental relationships, which is essential for orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. This standardisation allows comparison of pre- and post-treatment films. It is not used for detecting individual tooth pathology such as caries.
questions.question: An orthodontist requires a standardized lateral radiograph of the skull to assess skeletal relationships and plan treatment for a Class III malocclusion. Which technique is specifically indicated?

options: It reduces salivary flow and promotes candidiasis
It suppresses immunity, worsening viral spread
questions.explanation: Steroids are contraindicated in HSV infections because they suppress both innate and adaptive immunity, removing the host defences needed to control viral replication. This can lead to widespread dissemination of the herpes infection, particularly dangerous in immunocompromised patients. Treatment is supportive with antipyretics, topical anaesthetics, and adequate hydration.
questions.question: Steroid therapy is contraindicated in herpetic stomatitis because:
Which virus is the MOST frequent cause of viral infection of the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) is the most frequent cause of viral infection of the oral cavity. It exists in two serotypes; HSV-1 predominantly causes oral and skin lesions while HSV-2 causes genital infections. HSV-1 primary infection in children most commonly presents as herpetic gingivostomatitis.

questions.question: Before extracting several teeth in a patient on long-term warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation, which single investigation is MOST critical to obtain preoperatively?
questions.explanation: In a patient on warfarin, the clotting profile, specifically the International Normalised Ratio (INR), is the most critical preoperative investigation, as it determines whether anticoagulation is within a safe therapeutic range for extraction. Extracting teeth without knowledge of the INR risks uncontrolled haemorrhage. This test directly guides whether surgery can proceed safely or requires medical liaison first.

questions.question: 'Resistance form' in tooth preparation means the preparation provides:
options: Ability of the restoration to withstand obliquely directed forces without fracture
Ability of the restoration to resist being removed by displacing forces
Adequate space for instrument access during preparation
questions.explanation: Resistance form ensures that both the tooth and the restoration can withstand obliquely directed occlusal forces without fracturing. For amalgam restorations, a smooth flat floor and minimum depth of 2 mm is required for adequate resistance. Without adequate resistance form, restorations or remaining tooth structure can fracture under functional loading.

options: Composite resin or glass ionomer cement
A zinc oxide eugenol temporary dressing material
questions.explanation: For a Class V cavity on a visible maxillary canine where aesthetics is a priority, tooth-coloured direct restorative materials — composite resin or glass ionomer cement — are the appropriate choices. Composite offers superior aesthetics and strength; GIC provides the added benefit of fluoride release and chemical adhesion without etching. Amalgam is inappropriate due to its metallic colour; direct filling gold requires specialised technique and poor aesthetics.
questions.question: A patient requires restoration of a Class V cavity on a maxillary canine where aesthetics is important. The MOST appropriate direct restorative material is:

questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve, which exits through the infraorbital foramen and provides sensation to the cheek, lateral nose, and upper lip, is commonly affected in zygomatic complex fractures due to its close anatomical relationship with the orbital floor and zygomatic bone, resulting in altered or reduced sensation in its distribution. This finding, combined with cheek flattening and restricted mouth opening from impingement on the temporalis or masseter, supports clinical suspicion of a zygomatic complex fracture. Recognising the specific nerve involved helps localise the likely fracture site.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected zygomatic complex fracture following facial trauma presents with flattening of the cheek, restricted mouth opening, and altered sensation over the cheek and upper lip. The altered sensation in this presentation is most likely attributable to involvement of which nerve?
An eruption cyst is classified as which type of odontogenic cyst?
questions.explanation: The eruption cyst is a developmental odontogenic cyst that forms in the soft tissue overlying the crown of an erupting tooth. It appears as a bluish-purple swelling of the alveolar mucosa in children. Most eruption cysts resolve spontaneously as the tooth erupts; surgical intervention (marsupialization) is rarely needed unless infection or delayed eruption occurs.

Asymptomatic developmental enamel pits in a completely caries-free patient do not by themselves constitute an indication for restoration. Indications for restoration include carious destruction, replacement of defective restorations, fractured teeth, congenitally malformed teeth, aesthetic desires, tooth wear lesions, and as part of bridge construction. Clinical judgment determines when to observe versus intervene.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an indication for dental restoration?

questions.explanation: Cementum is a calcified tissue that covers the root surface, providing the attachment site for Sharpey's fibres of the periodontal ligament. Unlike bone, cementum lacks vascularisation and is not normally resorbed. Its preservation is critical to periodontal attachment; its loss during periodontitis contributes to tooth mobility and pocket deepening.
questions.question: Cementum forms which part of the periodontium?
options: The outer covering of the anatomic crown
The calcified covering of the root surface
The lining of the alveolar socket
The soft tissue attachment to enamel
The periosteum of the alveolar bone

questions.question: A dentist explains to a parent that fissure sealants prevent caries primarily by which mechanism?
options: Physically blocking bacteria and food debris from colonising the fissure
Directly killing all cariogenic bacteria in the mouth
questions.explanation: Fissure sealants prevent caries primarily by creating a physical barrier that blocks bacteria and food debris from colonising the vulnerable pits and fissures of posterior teeth, thereby preventing the substrate and bacterial interaction needed for caries initiation. Some sealants also contain fluoride for an additional preventive effect, but the primary mechanism is mechanical protection. This makes sealants particularly effective in newly erupted, caries-susceptible posterior teeth.

Lichen planus is classified among mucocutaneous diseases that produce oral ulcers secondary to systemic involvement, alongside pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigoid, and erythema multiforme. It is an immune-mediated condition producing reticular white striae or erosive ulcers most commonly on the buccal mucosa. Gastrointestinal diseases such as Crohn's disease and coeliac disease form another systemic category.
questions.question: Which mucocutaneous disease is classified under oral ulcers secondary to systemic disease?
A cyst is pathologically defined as:
questions.explanation: A cyst is defined as a pathological cavity containing fluid, semi-fluid, or gaseous material (but NOT pus), that is frequently but not always lined by epithelium and surrounded by a connective tissue wall. The presence of pus defines an abscess. This distinction is fundamental, as the pathological contents, lining, and relationship to adjacent structures guide diagnosis and management.
options: A solid tumour surrounded by bone
A pathological cavity that contains pus, lined by epithelium
A benign neoplasm arising from the jaw bone
An inflammatory granuloma without epithelial lining
A pathological cavity with fluid or gas, often epithelium-lined

questions.question: A public health dentist wants a chairside clinical method to detect proximal caries without radiographs during a community screening programme with limited resources. Clinical examination for caries in this setting would rely on all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sialography is a specialised radiographic technique for imaging the salivary gland ductal system and is not a method used in routine clinical caries examination, which instead relies on visual inspection, careful probing, drying of the tooth surface, and transillumination. Understanding which techniques are appropriate for caries detection versus unrelated investigations avoids inappropriate resource use. Radiographs, where available, remain valuable adjuncts but sialography specifically has no role in caries detection.

options: Lip and cheek muscles directly determine arch length and breadth through bone remodelling
Counterbalance tongue pressure, helping define the neutral zone
They provide the primary masticatory force determining occlusal wear patterns
They determine tongue posture by their resting tone only
They have no significant influence on arch form once teeth have erupted
questions.explanation: The lips and cheeks exert inward (lingual) pressure on the teeth, which is balanced against the outward (buccal) pressure of the tongue to define the neutral zone — the region where teeth are stable. Altered lip tone (e.g., lip incompetence, lower lip trap in Class II division 1), reduced cheek pressure, or exaggerated circumoral muscle activity can shift the equilibrium and produce characteristic malocclusion patterns. This concept underpins myofunctional therapy in orthodontics.
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the DIRECT relationship between the lip and cheek muscles and dental arch form?

options: Magnification, colour enhancement, and contrast adjustment
Increased radiation exposure for better contrast
Three-dimensional reconstructions directly from standard sensors
questions.question: In digital radiography, radiographic images can be manipulated to provide:
questions.explanation: Digital radiography allows image manipulation including magnification, colour enhancement, and contrast adjustment after image acquisition. This enables the clinician to improve diagnostic yield without additional radiation exposure. Instant image availability, elimination of darkroom and chemical processing, and the ability to store and transmit images electronically are further major advantages. SUBTOPIC 3: ORAL PATHOLOGY INVESTIGATIONS

options: Direct mechanical clasping onto remaining natural teeth
Chemical bonding of acrylic resin to oral mucosa
Adhesion and cohesion via a thin saliva film between the denture base and mucosa
Screw retention into the underlying alveolar bone
Osseointegration of the denture base into bone
questions.question: A patient wearing a new complete denture reports excessive movement and instability during function, despite an accurate impression and good extension of the denture base. Denture retention is primarily achieved through which physical mechanism in a well-fitting complete denture?
questions.explanation: Retention of a complete denture is primarily achieved through physical forces of adhesion (attraction between the saliva film and both the denture base and the mucosa) and cohesion (attraction between saliva molecules themselves), requiring a well-adapted denture base and adequate extension to maximise contact area. This differs fundamentally from partial dentures, which can additionally use mechanical clasps on remaining natural teeth for retention. Poor denture fit or inadequate extension compromises this thin-film retention mechanism, leading to instability.

questions.question: Which of the following gingival features is described as 'knife-edged' in a healthy state?
questions.explanation: The contour of healthy gingiva is scalloped with a knife-edged margin, shaped by the underlying tooth anatomy and arch alignment. In chronic gingivitis, inflammatory changes cause the margin to become blunted and rolled. Recognising contour changes is an essential clinical diagnostic skill.

options: Upper right second and third molars
Lower right second and third molars
Lower left second premolar and first molar
Upper left second and third molars
Lower left second and third molars
questions.question: Using FDI notation, the designation '37, 38' refers to:
questions.explanation: In FDI notation, quadrant 3 is the lower left, and teeth 7 and 8 are the second and third molars respectively. Therefore 37 and 38 refer to the lower left second and third molars. FDI notation is preferred by some clinicians because it reduces typographical errors that can occur with the Palmer grid system.

questions.question: Periodontitis is clinically differentiated from gingivitis specifically by the finding of:
questions.explanation: Clinical attachment loss (CAL) is the definitive distinguishing feature between periodontitis and gingivitis. Measured from the CEJ to the base of the pocket, CAL indicates permanent loss of the supporting apparatus. Bleeding, colour change, and plaque are features of both conditions; only CAL confirms irreversible disease and drives periodontitis diagnosis and staging.

options: A structure that only affects tooth eruption, not jaw growth
A purely functional structure unrelated to growth
A structure unrelated to facial symmetry
An area with no growth potential
questions.explanation: The mandibular condyle acts as a primary growth centre during childhood and adolescence, and ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint in early childhood can severely restrict growth on the affected side, leading to facial asymmetry and mandibular retrognathia. This underscores the clinical importance of early diagnosis and management of TMJ ankylosis to minimise long-term growth disturbance. Early surgical intervention combined with physiotherapy aims to restore joint function and support more normal subsequent growth.
questions.question: A patient with ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint occurring in early childhood presents with severe facial asymmetry and mandibular retrognathia on the affected side. This is best explained by the role of the condyle as:
Intrinsic dietary sugars are considered:
questions.explanation: Extrinsic sugars (free sugars added to foods or naturally present in fruit juices and honey) are considered more cariogenic than intrinsic sugars (those naturally contained within cellular food structures such as whole fruits and vegetables). Extrinsic sugars are more freely available for fermentation by cariogenic bacteria. This distinction informs dietary advice in caries prevention.
options: More cariogenic only for root caries

questions.explanation: The septate versus aseptate distinction is clinically critical: Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus — aseptate, broad hyphae) cause mucormycosis, an angioinvasive, rapidly progressive infection requiring urgent surgical debridement combined with amphotericin B because the aseptate hyphae occlude blood vessels causing tissue necrosis. Aspergillus (narrow, septate hyphae) causes aspergillosis managed differently. Histological identification of hyphal morphology on tissue biopsy is therefore essential for guiding emergency surgical and antifungal management.
questions.question: The 'hyphae may be septate or aseptate' distinction in fungi is clinically important because:
options: Aseptate fungi like Mucor require surgical debridement while septate fungi do not
Septate fungi are always more pathogenic than aseptate fungi
Aseptate hyphae are characteristic of Candida and septate of Aspergillus, guiding antifungal selection
Septation determines whether hyphae form budding yeast in tissue
Septation determines if fungi are dimorphic or monomorphic

questions.explanation: Pierre Robin syndrome is a congenital skeletal cause of malocclusion, characterised by micrognathia (underdeveloped mandible), glossoptosis, and often cleft palate, causing a characteristic Class II skeletal pattern. Other congenital skeletal causes include Crouzon syndrome, cleft lip and palate, and sickle cell disease. These intrinsic factors contrast with acquired environmental causes such as habits and trauma.
questions.question: Which of the following is a SKELETAL congenital cause of malocclusion?

questions.explanation: Postoperative pain and hypersensitivity after amalgam placement most commonly occurs in unlined cavities where the thickness of remaining pulpal dentin is less than 1 mm, causing thermal stimulation of the pulp. Adequate cavity lining with a base material (e.g., zinc oxide eugenol or glass ionomer) prevents this complication by insulating the pulp from thermal changes.
questions.question: Postoperative pain and hypersensitivity following amalgam restoration is MOST commonly due to:
options: Incorrect occlusal contact found on the restoration
Unlined cavities with under 1mm pulpal dentin

questions.question: A dentist plans the outline of a cavity preparation to include all carious tissue while extending margins to sound, cleansable, self-supporting enamel. According to the principle of outline form, cavity margins should ideally be placed:
options: In areas of self-cleansing or easily cleaned tooth surface
As far into the pulp as possible
Randomly, since margin location has no clinical significance
Only on occlusal surfaces regardless of caries extent
questions.explanation: The principle of outline form dictates that cavity margins should be placed in areas of the tooth that are self-cleansing or can be easily kept clean by the patient, reducing the risk of recurrent caries at the margin. Margins placed in stagnation areas are more prone to plaque accumulation and secondary caries. This principle guides both the extent and location of cavity outline design.

questions.question: A patient presents with a rapidly spreading bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental space infection following a lower molar dental abscess, causing airway compromise. This life-threatening infection is specifically termed:
questions.explanation: Ludwig's angina is a severe, rapidly spreading cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces bilaterally, most commonly originating from an infected lower molar, and poses a risk of airway obstruction. It is a surgical and medical emergency requiring urgent airway management, antibiotics, and often surgical drainage. Early recognition is critical given its potential for rapid deterioration.

options: Directly sealing pits and fissures mechanically
Acting as a mechanical abrasive during brushing
Promoting remineralisation and forming acid-resistant fluorapatite
Preventing plaque formation entirely on all surfaces
Eliminating the need for any dietary modification
questions.explanation: Fluoride's role in caries prevention includes promoting remineralisation of early carious lesions and forming fluorapatite, which is more resistant to acid dissolution than normal hydroxyapatite, as well as some inhibitory effects on bacterial metabolism. It does not act as a mechanical sealant or replace the need for good dietary and hygiene practices. Its multiple mechanisms make it a cornerstone of modern caries prevention.
questions.question: A dentist explains the role of fluoride in caries prevention to a patient. Which of the following mechanisms is included in fluoride's protective action?

questions.explanation: The cornerstone of treating chronic marginal gingivitis is elimination of the primary aetiological agents — bacterial plaque and calculus — through comprehensive oral hygiene instruction (OHI) to empower the patient's daily plaque control, combined with professional scaling and polishing to remove supra- and subgingival deposits. This cause-related phase of therapy must precede any surgical considerations, as gingivitis is fully reversible with adequate plaque control.
options: Eliminating plaque and calculus through OHI and scaling
Surgical pocket elimination done as the first step
Systemic antibiotic therapy before any other treatment
Immediate extraction of all affected teeth
Occlusal adjustment to reduce traumatic forces
questions.question: The most important goal of periodontal treatment in a patient with chronic marginal gingivitis is:
The theoretical basis of the bisecting angle technique employs which geometrical principle?
questions.explanation: The bisecting angle technique applies the geometrical principle of similar triangles: the actual tooth length in the mouth equals the image length on the film when the central ray is directed at right angles to the line that bisects the angle between the long axis of the tooth and the film. The film is placed as close to the tooth as possible without bending and the bisecting line is mentally visualised.

According to the specific plaque hypothesis, periodontitis is initiated by gram-negative anaerobic or micro-aerophilic bacteria colonising the subgingival environment. Key pathogens include Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans. These organisms produce enzymes and toxins that directly and indirectly destroy periodontal tissues.
questions.question: Periodontitis is initiated and perpetuated primarily by which group of bacteria?

options: An underlying herpes simplex virus infection
questions.explanation: Chronic marginal gingivitis results primarily from the accumulation of bacterial plaque and calculus along the gingival margin. The bacterial biofilm initiates and perpetuates the inflammatory response. Treatment centres on oral hygiene instruction and professional scaling and polishing to eliminate the aetiological agents and resolve inflammation.
questions.question: Chronic marginal gingivitis is MOST commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: In the vertical plane, anterior deficiency (insufficient vertical overlap or negative overbite) results in an anterior open bite, where the anterior teeth do not meet when the posterior teeth are in occlusion. The reverse — posterior vertical excess — also contributes to anterior open bite. Vertical anterior excess produces a deep bite. Accurate plane-of-space diagnosis drives the choice of orthodontic or orthognathic correction.
questions.question: Malocclusion associated with an anterior vertical plane deficiency is classified as which type?
Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining is routinely used in which investigation?
options: Fine needle aspiration cytology smear only
questions.explanation: Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining is the standard histological stain used on paraffin-embedded tissue sections from biopsy specimens. Haematoxylin stains cell nuclei blue/purple while eosin stains cytoplasm and extracellular matrix pink/red. Together they allow evaluation of tissue architecture, cell morphology, inflammatory infiltrate, and features of malignancy.

questions.question: Sequelae of dental caries, listed in order of severity from least to most severe, progresses as:
options: Reversible pulpitis ? irreversible ? periodontitis ? abscess ? osteomyelitis
Gingivitis ? periodontitis ? bone loss ? final tooth loss
questions.explanation: The sequelae of untreated dental caries follows a predictable progression: reversible pulpitis ? irreversible pulpitis ? apical periodontitis (granuloma/cyst) ? periapical abscess ? dentoalveolar abscess ? cellulitis/space infection (e.g. Ludwig's angina) ? osteomyelitis, and potentially death in extreme cases. Each stage represents increasing severity and complexity of management.

questions.question: Flap design principles in OMFS are critical to prevent all of the following EXCEPT:
