Crown lengthening surgery is often required to correct this violation and restore adequate biological width before or during restorative treatment. Respecting this principle is essential for long-term periodontal health around restored teeth.
options: Enhanced restoration retention with no downside
Chronic gingival inflammation and potential attachment loss

questions.question: Smoking specifically INCREASES Candida carriage rate by which mechanism?
options: Reducing salivary flow, causing dry mouth
Suppressing local mucosal immunity and altering oral flora
Reducing oral pH to below 5 creating a fungal environment
questions.explanation: Cigarette smoking increases oral Candida carriage rate by suppressing local mucosal immune defences — including secretory IgA levels and mucosal macrophage function — and by altering the oral microbiota, creating an environment more favourable to Candida colonisation. Heat and tobacco constituents also cause mucosal changes (hyperkeratosis, altered epithelial turnover) that may enhance Candida adherence. Smokers with dentures face compounded risk from both smoking and denture-related factors.

TMJ dislocation occurs when the mandibular condyle moves anterior to the articular eminence and becomes unable to return to the glenoid fossa, typically following an event such as excessive yawning or wide mouth opening, resulting in an acute inability to close the mouth. This is a distinct acute event, differing from ankylosis, which represents a more chronic, often bony, restriction of movement. Manual reduction is usually required to reposition the condyle and restore normal occlusion.
questions.question: A patient presents with acute inability to close the mouth following excessive yawning, with the mandibular condyle displaced anterior to the articular eminence and unable to return to the fossa. This acute condition is termed:

questions.explanation: Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is classically associated with a fusospirochetal complex, particularly fusiform bacilli and spirochetes, in a background of poor oral hygiene and reduced host resistance. Malnutrition and vitamin deficiency predispose children to this condition. The characteristic punched-out papillae and foul odour help distinguish it from simple gingivitis.
questions.question: A malnourished child presents with painful, bleeding, ulcerated interdental papillae, a grey pseudomembrane, and profound halitosis. Gram staining of the lesion is most likely to reveal a combination of which organisms?

options: Permanent deformation of the disc during protrusion
Prevention of all lateral condylar excursions
Restriction of mandibular opening beyond 30 mm
Fixation of the condyle in the glenoid fossa at all times
Accommodation of condylar movement without disc perforation
questions.question: The fibers of the TMJ capsule can elongate and recoil, and the disc has an undulating contour. This arrangement PRIMARILY allows:
questions.explanation: The elastic properties of the capsular fibres and the undulating contour of the TMJ disc allow the joint to accommodate the complex three-dimensional condylar movements during function without trauma to the disc or capsule. The undulating (folded) contour provides reserve length that unfolds during condylar translation, preventing disc perforation or tearing. Disruption of this architecture — through trauma or degeneration — produces internal derangements with clicking, crepitus, or locking.

Surveys repeatedly confirm that when choosing a restoration for their own posterior teeth, dentists most frequently select gold, citing its durability, minimal tooth preparation requirements, excellent marginal fit, and biocompatibility. Despite patient preferences for tooth-coloured options, gold remains the material of choice among informed clinicians for their own high-load posterior restorations.
questions.question: Which indirect restorative material would a dentist most likely choose for their OWN posterior tooth if given a free choice, based on current evidence?

A patient has occlusal and proximal caries affecting a molar tooth with cavitation on the mesial surface extending to involve the occlusal fissure system. According to G.V. Black's classification, this lesion pattern is best classified as:
questions.explanation: G.V. Black's Class II cavities specifically involve the proximal surfaces of posterior teeth, often in combination with the occlusal surface, as seen in this molar with mesio-occlusal caries. Class I lesions are confined to pits and fissures alone. Correct classification guides appropriate cavity design and restorative material selection.

questions.question: Achondroplasia, if it were to affect mandibular condylar growth, would produce malocclusion through which mechanism?
options: Defective ossification reducing condylar growth, retrognathia
Excessive endochondral ossification expanding the condyle beyond normal
Intramembranous bone formation defect affecting only the mandibular body
Abnormal periosteal bone deposition causing mandibular prognathism
Selective cartilage hypertrophy without any bone formation
questions.explanation: Achondroplasia results from gain-of-function mutations in FGFR3 that inhibit endochondral ossification. Since condylar growth relies on endochondral ossification at the condylar cartilage, achondroplasia could in principle impair condylar growth, reducing mandibular length and producing mandibular retrognathia and Class II malocclusion. This mechanism illustrates how systemic skeletal dysplasias affecting endochondral bone formation can secondarily impact dentofacial growth and occlusal development.

questions.question: An obturator denture is specifically used to:
options: Covers an oronasal fistula to aid speech and eating
Replace all missing teeth in a completely edentulous patient
Support implants in the lower jaw
Maintain space after premature loss of primary teeth
questions.explanation: An obturator prosthesis covers an oronasal fistula or defect in the palate, providing the patient with a removable roof of the mouth that aids speech, eating, and proper air flow. Such defects may result from cleft palate, tumour resection, or gunshot trauma. The obturator is a specialised type of dental prosthesis within the scope of maxillofacial prosthodontics.

Streptococcus mutans is the primary cariogenic organism implicated in caries initiation, converting sucrose and fructose into extracellular polysaccharides that promote bacterial adhesion, plaque matrix formation, and acidogenic potential. Its acidogenic and aciduric properties allow it to thrive and dominate in a cariogenic biofilm. This makes it central to the microbial aetiology of dental caries.
questions.question: A microbiologist identifies an organism from dental plaque that metabolises dietary sucrose into extracellular polysaccharides, promoting bacterial adhesion and plaque matrix formation. This organism is most likely:

options: Loss of the buffering and remineralising capacity of saliva
Reduced bacterial colonisation of the mouth
questions.explanation: Xerostomia promotes caries because saliva normally provides buffering capacity, clears food debris, and supplies calcium and phosphate ions essential for remineralisation; when salivary flow is reduced, these protective mechanisms are lost. This creates a highly cariogenic environment even with unchanged dietary habits. Management includes saliva substitutes, fluoride, and frequent dental review in affected patients.
questions.question: A patient with severe xerostomia following head and neck radiotherapy develops multiple new carious lesions within months. The mechanism by which reduced salivary flow promotes caries is best explained by:

questions.explanation: Excessive tension on sutures during flap closure risks compromising blood supply to the flap margins, leading to wound dehiscence, delayed healing, and increased risk of infection. Achieving tension-free closure, sometimes requiring adequate flap design and periosteal releasing incisions, is a fundamental principle of successful surgical wound management. Proper suturing technique complements good flap design to optimise healing outcomes.
questions.question: A surgeon closing a mucoperiosteal flap places sutures to reposition the tissue precisely over its original bony bed without tension. Excessive tension on sutures during flap closure is avoided primarily because it risks:
options: Improved blood supply to the flap margins

questions.explanation: Cystic ameloblastoma (along with the calcifying odontogenic ghost cell cyst) falls under neoplastic odontogenic cysts — cystic jaw lesions arising from odontogenic epithelium that exhibit neoplastic behaviour. Unlike simple developmental cysts, ameloblastomas are locally aggressive, require wider surgical resection, and have significant recurrence rates, demanding a fundamentally different management approach.
questions.question: Cystic ameloblastoma is classified under which category of jaw cysts?

questions.explanation: Periodontitis is primarily initiated and perpetuated by anaerobic, Gram-negative bacteria within the subgingival biofilm, including organisms such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, which possess virulence factors that promote tissue destruction and immune evasion. This differs from the more mixed, aerobic Gram-positive flora associated with early supragingival plaque and gingivitis. Understanding this microbial shift underlies the rationale for mechanical and, where indicated, antimicrobial periodontal therapy.
questions.question: A microbiologist analysing subgingival plaque from a patient with periodontitis identifies a predominance of anaerobic, Gram-negative organisms associated with disease initiation and progression. Periodontitis is primarily initiated and perpetuated by which group of bacteria?

options: Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis and necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis
Periodontitis as a manifestation of Down syndrome
Chronic periodontitis with secondary occlusal trauma
questions.explanation: Necrotizing periodontal diseases are classified as necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG) and necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis (NUP). These conditions share distinct features including tissue necrosis, punched-out papillae, pain, and halitosis. NUP involves loss of the supporting structures, distinguishing it from NUG which remains confined to the gingival tissues.
questions.question: Which of the following is classified under 'Necrotizing Periodontal Diseases'?

questions.explanation: Amalgam is defined as a special type of alloy in which mercury is one of the components. In dental amalgam, mercury reacts with the alloy powder (primarily silver, tin, copper, and zinc) through trituration to form a setting amalgam. The liquid mercury wets all alloy particle surfaces to initiate the amalgamation reaction.
questions.question: Dental amalgam is defined as an alloy in which one of the components is:

questions.explanation: Polyene antifungals — including amphotericin B and nystatin — exert their antifungal action by binding directly to ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that cause irreversible leakage of intracellular ions and fungal cell death. Because mammalian cell membranes contain cholesterol rather than ergosterol, polyenes have selective toxicity for fungi. This selectivity is the basis for nystatin's safety profile, though amphotericin B's affinity for cholesterol contributes to its nephrotoxicity.
questions.question: The function of the ergosterol-containing cell membrane in fungi, distinct from the cholesterol-containing membrane of mammalian cells, is clinically exploited by:
options: Quinolone antibiotics that target fungal DNA gyrase enzymes
Polyene antifungals binding ergosterol, e.g. amphotericin B

questions.explanation: Cancrum oris (noma) is an opportunistic gangrenous infection that typically affects severely malnourished, immunocompromised children and causes rapid destructive necrosis of orofacial tissue. It often begins as untreated necrotizing gingivitis that spreads to the cheek. Mortality is high without urgent nutritional and antimicrobial intervention.
questions.question: A severely malnourished child in a resource-poor setting develops a rapidly progressive, foul-smelling gangrenous lesion of the cheek that perforates, exposing the underlying teeth. This condition is best classified as:

questions.explanation: Active caries progresses rapidly with soft, lighter-coloured dentine, while arrested (inactive) caries has been remineralised—becoming hard, dark brown or black, and glossy—after the cariogenic challenge has been removed. Chronic caries progresses slowly compared to the acute form. Understanding lesion activity status informs whether surgical intervention or monitoring is more appropriate.
options: Progresses more rapidly than acute caries
Shows surface remineralisation and becomes hard and dark brown
Is associated with higher bacterial counts
Is found exclusively in elderly patients
questions.question: Active arrested caries differs from chronic progressive caries in that it:

questions.explanation: Base metal alloys (nickel-chromium, cobalt-chromium) are used as alternatives to gold in indirect restorations primarily because of their significantly lower cost. While they are harder and less ductile than gold (making precise marginal adaptation more challenging), their cost advantage is substantial. Concerns about nickel hypersensitivity in some patients and inferior biocompatibility compared to gold are their main clinical disadvantages.
options: They have superior biocompatibility to gold
They offer better marginal adaptation than gold
They bond chemically to all ceramic systems
They are significantly less expensive than gold
questions.question: Base metal alloys used in indirect restorations are preferred over gold in some situations PRIMARILY because:

questions.explanation: A radiograph is the recorded image produced by X-rays on photographic film or a digital sensor. The term 'radiography' denotes the use of radiation for diagnostic purposes, while 'radiology' refers to the science of radiation as used in medicine. These terms are sometimes used interchangeably in clinical practice, though strictly they describe the image and the science respectively.
questions.question: An image produced by X-rays on a photographic film is called a:

options: The handle, above the hinge, and the beaks below
The shaft and the working end of the instrument
questions.question: Extraction forceps are composed of which two essential parts?
questions.explanation: Each extraction forceps consists of the handle (above the hinge), through which force is applied, and the beaks (below the hinge), which are the functional components that grasp the tooth at the cervical region. The hinge articulates the two components. Beak design varies by tooth anatomy — specific forceps are manufactured for each tooth type to match root morphology and access requirements.

The orthopantomogram (OPG) is an extra-oral projection where the film is placed outside the mouth. The three main intraoral projections are bitewing, periapical, and occlusal radiography. Extra-oral projections place the film outside the mouth on the opposite side of the head from the X-ray source and include panoramic, cephalometric, and CBCT.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an intraoral radiographic projection?

questions.explanation: The orthopantomogram (OPG) is an extra-oral panoramic radiograph that captures both jaws and their dentitions on a single film using rotational tomography. It is extremely versatile, used for assessing the entire dentition, impacted wisdom teeth, jaw cysts, fractures, and orthodontic assessment. Its limitation is that it lacks the fine detail of intraoral periapical films for specific teeth.
questions.question: The orthopantomogram (OPG) is classified as which type of radiograph?

questions.explanation: Unlike composite resin, glass ionomer cement bonds to tooth structure through an intrinsic ion-exchange mechanism without requiring acid etching with phosphoric acid. GIC's polyalkenoate chains interact directly with calcium and phosphate in hydroxyapatite. However, cavity conditioning with polyacrylic acid (10–20%) is recommended to clean the smear layer and improve bond strength, which is fundamentally different from the aggressive 37% phosphoric acid etching used for composite.
questions.question: Glass ionomer cement (GIC) bonding to tooth structure does NOT require which step that composite resin bonding requires?
The aetiology of malocclusion according to Graber's classification divides causes into:
questions.explanation: Graber's classification divides aetiological factors of malocclusion into general (extrinsic) factors — including heredity, congenital defects, environment, diet, habits, posture, and trauma — and local (intrinsic) factors — including anomalies of tooth number, size, shape, and position, premature tooth loss, and supernumerary teeth. This two-tier framework remains influential in orthodontic teaching and treatment planning.
options: Dental factors and skeletal factors only considered

questions.question: A surgeon suspects a soft tissue lesion, such as a tumour of the parotid gland, and requires superior soft tissue contrast without ionising radiation. Which imaging modality is most appropriate compared with CT?
questions.explanation: MRI provides superior soft tissue contrast compared with CT and does not use ionising radiation, making it the preferred modality for evaluating soft tissue lesions such as salivary gland tumours or TMJ disc pathology. CT remains superior for evaluating bony detail. Choosing the appropriate modality depends on whether soft tissue or bone detail is the primary diagnostic concern.

Composite resins do not chemically bond to tooth structure on their own; they rely on micromechanical retention achieved through acid etching of enamel (creating microporosities) and the application of bonding agents on dentine. This hybrid layer of resin infiltrating etched tooth surfaces provides the mechanical retention. This technique-sensitive process determines the longevity of composite restorations.
questions.question: Composite resin restorations achieve retention primarily through:
options: Chemical bonding to calcium in hydroxyapatite
Micromechanical retention via bonding and etching
Fluoride release that prevents marginal leakage
Directly stimulate Candida adhesion to mucosa
Inhibit white cell production in bone marrow
Cause xerostomia as a side effect
Eliminate competing oral bacteria, allowing Candida overgrowth
Increase oral pH favouring fungal growth
questions.question: Prolonged use of broad-spectrum antibiotics predisposes to oral candidiasis because they:
questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum antibiotics eliminate the normal bacterial flora of the oral cavity, which normally competes with Candida for adhesion sites and nutrients, keeping candidal populations in check. This disruption of ecological balance allows Candida to proliferate and cause symptomatic candidiasis, a process known as antibiotic-associated candidiasis. Prophylactic antifungal therapy is recommended during prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic courses in susceptible patients.

The management of a dento-alveolar abscess includes antibiotics for systemic spread, incision and drainage to release pus, and extraction of the non-restorable affected tooth. The dento-alveolar abscess results from death of the pulp following neglected caries or trauma, with infection extending through the apical foramen into periradicular tissues. Early management prevents spread to spaces and bone.
questions.question: The management of a dento-alveolar abscess in a child includes:

questions.explanation: Mucormycosis (caused by Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia spp.) is characterised by broad, ribbon-like, aseptate (coenocytic) hyphae with irregular branching — a key histological feature distinguishing it from Aspergillus (narrow, regular, septate, dichotomously branching hyphae). Mucormycosis causes angioinvasive, necrotising infections particularly in diabetics and immunocompromised patients, presenting as rhinoorbital or rhinocerebral infection requiring urgent surgical debridement and antifungal therapy.
options: Narrow, regular septate hyphae with dichotomous branching
Thin, heavily branched septate hyphae forming fruiting bodies
Broad, ribbon-like aseptate (coenocytic) hyphae with irregular branching
Yeast forms at all temperatures without hyphal conversion
questions.question: Mucormycosis as listed in the fungal diseases category is characterised by which distinguishing feature of its hyphae?

A clinician removes an entire small, discrete pigmented lesion of the lip along with a margin of normal tissue for histological diagnosis, rather than sampling only part of it. This procedure is best described as:
questions.explanation: An excisional biopsy involves complete removal of a small lesion, including a margin of surrounding normal tissue, and is both diagnostic and potentially curative. This differs from an incisional biopsy, which samples only a representative portion of a larger lesion. Excisional biopsy is preferred for small, well-circumscribed lesions where complete removal is feasible.

The occipito-mental radiograph is also called the Waters view or sinus view. It is an extra-oral projection used for visualising the paranasal sinuses, particularly the maxillary antra. It is valuable in diagnosing sinusitis, detecting sinus opacification following dentoalveolar infection, and assessing fractures of the middle third of the face.
questions.question: The occipito-mental radiograph is also known as the:

questions.explanation: Candida albicans is a diamorphic fungus (capable of existing as both yeast and hyphal forms) that normally exists as a commensal organism in the mouth, vagina, throat, and large bowel of about 20% of the healthy population. It becomes pathogenic only in the presence of predisposing local or systemic factors. Its ability to shift between phenotypes contributes significantly to its virulence and adaptability.
options: A diamorphic fungus, both commensal and pathogenic
A DNA virus that shows oral tropism
questions.question: Candida albicans is best described as:

questions.explanation: Histological examination provides microscopic analysis of tissue architecture and cellular morphology following biopsy. It is the gold standard for definitive diagnosis of oral lesions, distinguishing benign from malignant pathology, identifying specific disease entities (e.g., pemphigus, lichen planus), and guiding further management. Both incisional and excisional biopsies are submitted for histological processing.
options: Microscopic exam of tissue and cell structure
Real-time imaging of soft tissue blood vessels
Serum antibody levels to specific pathogens
questions.question: Histology in oral pathology provides:

options: Within the carious lesion for ease of access
Deep into the dentine for resistance form
Over the pulp horns for maximum retention
In self-cleansing areas on sound structure, finishable margins
questions.explanation: Outline form requires cavity margins to be placed on sound tooth structure in self-cleansing areas that are accessible for finishing and polishing instruments. Margins left on soft, unsound enamel rods are prone to fracture and microleakage. The extension should be the minimum required to include all the carious lesion plus a small preventive extension into susceptible adjacent areas.
questions.question: The principle of 'outline form' dictates that margins of a cavity should ideally be placed:

questions.explanation: Radicular (periodontal) cysts are the most common jaw cysts, accounting for 65–70% of all jaw cysts. They arise from inflammatory stimulation of epithelial rests of Malassez in an apical granuloma at the root apex of a non-vital tooth. Their predominance reflects the high prevalence of dental caries and pulp necrosis as triggering conditions in the population.
questions.question: The MOST common type of jaw cyst is the:

questions.explanation: Digital radiography eliminates the need for film, chemical processing, and a darkroom, providing instant images. It also allows image manipulation including magnification, contrast adjustment, and colour enhancement. Digital systems generally reduce radiation exposure compared to conventional film, making longer exposure times an incorrect advantage—digital imaging uses equal or shorter exposures.
questions.question: The digital radiography of the future as described offers all of the following advantages EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Factitious ulcers are self-inflicted lesions resulting from habits such as lip or cheek biting, often related to underlying psychological stress or habit disorders. They characteristically have an irregular shape corresponding to the pattern of the habit. Management includes habit-breaking counselling in addition to local wound care.
questions.question: A young patient presents with a chronic, irregular, self-inflicted ulcer on the labial mucosa related to habitual lip biting during periods of stress. This type of ulcer is best classified as:

questions.explanation: Birn's hypothesis proposes that dry socket results from excessive fibrinolysis within the blood clot, mediated by tissue and bacterial plasminogen activators, leading to premature clot breakdown and exposure of the underlying bone. This explains the characteristic severe pain and malodour seen in the condition. Management focuses on socket irrigation, dressing, and analgesia rather than antibiotics alone.
questions.question: A patient develops severe pain in the extraction socket three days after a lower molar extraction, with a foul odour and an exposed bony socket lacking a blood clot. This presentation, attributed to loss of the fibrinolytic-stable clot, is best explained by which hypothesis of dry socket pathogenesis?

A patient with a missing maxillary central incisor requests a fixed restoration using adjacent teeth as support rather than a removable prosthesis. For this bridge (fixed partial denture) to succeed, the abutment teeth must be:
options: Absent, as bridges require no abutments
Sound, well-supported, and capable of bearing additional load
Mobile with significant periodontal bone loss
questions.explanation: Successful fixed bridge (partial denture) therapy requires abutment teeth that are sound, adequately supported by healthy periodontium, and capable of withstanding the additional functional load of the pontic. Compromised abutments with mobility or periodontal disease jeopardise the longevity of the prosthesis. Careful abutment selection and evaluation is essential before bridge fabrication.

The paralleling technique is also known as the long cone technique because it typically employs a longer focus-to-film distance, which reduces image magnification and distortion by using a more parallel beam of radiation. This is in contrast to the bisecting angle technique, which often uses a shorter cone. The long cone paralleling technique generally produces images with less distortion and geometric accuracy superior to the bisecting angle method.
questions.question: A radiographer explains that the paralleling technique is also referred to by an alternative name that reflects the length of the X-ray cone or tube used to reduce image distortion. This alternative name is the:

During periapical radiography, a clinician positions the film parallel to the long axis of the tooth with the X-ray beam directed perpendicular to both the film and the tooth. Which technique is being used?
questions.explanation: The paralleling (long cone) technique requires the film to be positioned parallel to the long axis of the tooth, with the central X-ray beam directed at right angles to both the tooth and the film to minimise distortion. This produces images with minimal magnification and geometric accuracy. It is generally preferred over the bisecting angle technique for image quality.

Erosion is tooth surface loss resulting from chemical, non-bacterial acid dissolution of tooth structure, such as from chronic exposure to gastric acid in recurrent vomiting or gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, distinguishing it from attrition (tooth-to-tooth wear), abrasion (mechanical wear from an external object such as a toothbrush), and abfraction (wear attributed to flexural, occlusal loading forces). Correct identification of the type and likely cause of tooth surface loss is essential for appropriate management, which may include addressing the underlying acid source alongside restorative treatment. Multiple types of tooth surface loss can coexist in the same patient.
questions.question: A patient with generalised tooth wear attributed to chronic exposure of the dentition to gastric acid from recurrent vomiting, without evidence of mechanical attrition or abrasion, is diagnosed with which specific type of tooth surface loss?

questions.explanation: Primary HSV-1 infection is most commonly transmitted through direct contact with infected saliva, such as through kissing or shared utensils, particularly from an asymptomatic carrier. This explains the common childhood acquisition of the virus. Vertical or blood-borne transmission is not the typical route for oral HSV-1.
questions.question: A dental student wants to know how primary HSV-1 infection is most commonly acquired in early childhood. Which route of transmission is correct?

questions.explanation: The Palmer (Zsigmondy) notation system uses a cross-shaped diagram formed by four right-angle bracket symbols to represent the four quadrants of the mouth, with the tooth number placed within the appropriate bracket. This visual method quickly conveys both the tooth number and quadrant location. It differs fundamentally from the purely numeric FDI two-digit system.
options: A cross-shaped diagram of four right-angle symbols
questions.question: A chart uses the Palmer (Zsigmondy) notation system with a right-angle bracket symbol to denote a tooth's quadrant. What visual convention does this system rely upon?

questions.explanation: Pit and fissure surfaces are more susceptible to caries because their anatomy creates stagnation areas that accumulate plaque, are inaccessible to toothbrush bristles, and have reduced salivary access for buffering and remineralisation. Smooth surface caries develops more slowly because saliva and mechanical cleaning can access these surfaces more effectively. Fissure sealants exploit this by eliminating the anatomical susceptibility.
options: They are closer to the pulp
They lack an enamel rod structure
Less saliva contact allows plaque to accumulate
They are exposed to more dietary sugar
questions.question: Pit and fissure surfaces are MORE susceptible to caries than smooth surfaces because:

questions.explanation: Onlays are extra-coronal restorations that cover one or more cusps and are fabricated indirectly outside the mouth before being cemented in place, distinguishing them from intra-coronal restorations such as fillings and from direct restorations placed and set within the mouth. This indirect approach allows superior control over contour and material properties for larger restorations. Inlays are a related but intra-coronal indirect restoration.
questions.question: A dentist chooses an indirect ceramic onlay rather than a direct filling for a large cavity fabricated outside the mouth on a model and later cemented in place. This is an example of which category of restoration?

A patient with sickle cell anaemia presents with recurrent, painful, punched-out oral ulcers unrelated to trauma. This finding illustrates that oral ulcers can arise secondary to which category of underlying disease?
questions.explanation: Certain blood disorders, including sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies or cytopenias, can predispose to oral ulceration through impaired tissue perfusion and reduced host defence. Recognising a systemic haematological cause is important because local treatment alone will not resolve the underlying problem. Management should address the systemic disease alongside symptomatic oral care.

options: The patient's specific malocclusion, crowding, and overall treatment goals
The type of toothbrush the patient currently uses
The patient's age at the time of the initial dental visit alone
The season in which the tooth was originally lost
The colour of the patient's remaining teeth alone
questions.question: A patient with a missing permanent tooth due to early loss requires orthodontic space closure rather than prosthetic replacement. This decision to close rather than maintain and restore the space depends significantly on which factor?
questions.explanation: The decision to orthodontically close a space from a missing tooth versus maintaining the space for prosthetic replacement depends on a comprehensive assessment of the patient's specific malocclusion, degree of crowding elsewhere in the arch, occlusal relationships, and overall treatment goals, rather than any single isolated factor. This individualised treatment planning approach ensures the chosen strategy achieves the best overall functional and aesthetic outcome. Multidisciplinary input, including restorative dentistry, may be required for complex cases.

options: Full blood count and haemoglobin level
questions.question: Before performing oral surgical procedures in a patient on warfarin, the MOST important haematological test is:
questions.explanation: In a patient on warfarin (anticoagulant therapy), the International Normalised Ratio (INR) as part of the clotting profile is the most critical pre-operative investigation to quantify bleeding risk. An INR above safe limits requires medical liaison for dose adjustment before elective oral surgery. Uncontrolled anticoagulation without pre-operative assessment risks life-threatening haemorrhage.

options: The patient's active growth (pubertal growth spurt) period
After growth has completely ceased in adulthood
Only in patients over 40 years of age
Regardless of growth status, with no difference in effectiveness
questions.question: An orthodontist uses a functional appliance in a growing child with a Class II skeletal pattern to harness and modify the pattern of mandibular growth, aiming to reduce the skeletal discrepancy. This treatment approach is MOST effective when applied during which period?
questions.explanation: Functional appliances are most effective when used during a patient's active growth period, particularly around the pubertal growth spurt, as they aim to harness and modify the pattern and amount of mandibular growth to help correct an underlying skeletal Class II discrepancy. Their effectiveness diminishes significantly once growth has ceased, at which point orthognathic surgery may instead be required to correct significant skeletal discrepancies. Timing of intervention is therefore a critical factor in the success of functional appliance therapy.

questions.question: Plaque-induced gingivitis can best be described as which chronological type when it has a slow onset, long duration, and is usually painless?
questions.explanation: Chronic gingivitis is the most common form of plaque-induced gingivitis, characterised by slow onset, long duration, and absence of pain. This painless nature often leads to delayed presentation and underdiagnosis. Acute gingivitis is sudden, painful, and short-lived, while recurrent gingivitis reappears after treatment or spontaneous resolution.

questions.question: A patient develops sensitivity around a newly placed amalgam restoration adjacent to a gold crown on the neighbouring tooth, experiencing a metallic taste and mild discomfort on biting. This phenomenon, caused by an electrochemical reaction between the two dissimilar metals in the presence of saliva, is termed:
questions.explanation: Galvanic shock (galvanism) occurs when two dissimilar metallic restorations, such as amalgam and gold, are in direct or close contact in the presence of saliva acting as an electrolyte, generating a small electrical current that can cause a sharp pain or metallic taste sensation. This phenomenon usually resolves once the amalgam surface oxidises and stabilises. Understanding galvanism helps reassure patients about this typically self-limiting, benign occurrence.

HIV/AIDS causes progressive depletion of CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes (measured as CD4 count), progressively impairing cell-mediated immunity. Oral candidiasis typically appears when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/µL and is one of the most common early AIDS-defining illnesses. The predisposition to Candida reflects the central role of Th1 and Th17 T-cell responses in mucosal immunity against fungi. Oral candidiasis in an HIV-negative patient should prompt investigation of other causes of immunodeficiency.
options: Deficiency of B-lymphocytes and IgA production
Deficiency of neutrophils from bone marrow failure
Reduced salivary gland secretion from HIV-associated sialadenitis
CD4+ T-cell depletion reducing cellular immunity
Excess TNF-alpha production causing mucosal destruction
questions.question: In a patient with HIV/AIDS, oral candidiasis is most commonly attributable to which specific immune defect?

options: Extract under general anaesthesia without delay
Defer elective extraction and liaise with the physician
Ignore the cardiac history since the tooth is infected
Refer directly for extraction the same day regardless of cardiac status
questions.question: A patient with a recent history of myocardial infarction three weeks ago requires an urgent extraction for a grossly infected tooth. Considering absolute systemic contraindications, the MOST appropriate course of action is to:
questions.explanation: A recent myocardial infarction, particularly within the last few weeks to months, is considered an absolute systemic contraindication to elective extraction due to the high risk of cardiovascular complications under stress. Deferral and medical liaison, with only true emergency intervention under careful monitoring if unavoidable, is the safest course of action. This illustrates why systemic health assessment precedes any exodontia procedure.

questions.question: An orthodontist selects a removable appliance for a young patient requiring simple tipping movement of a single tooth, understanding this appliance type relies significantly on patient compliance for effectiveness. Compared with fixed appliances, the main disadvantage of removable orthodontic appliances is:
questions.explanation: Removable orthodontic appliances rely heavily on patient compliance for adequate wear time to be effective, and are generally limited to simple tooth movements such as tipping, in contrast to fixed appliances, which can achieve more complex, three-dimensional tooth movements independent of patient removal. This trade-off is an important consideration in appliance selection based on the complexity of the malocclusion and the patient's likely compliance. Fixed appliances, while offering greater control, require more chairside time and cannot be removed by the patient for hygiene.
options: Higher cost than fixed appliances in every situation
Reliance on patient compliance and limited ability to achieve complex tooth movements
Complete inability to correct any malocclusion
Inability to be removed for oral hygiene

questions.explanation: Farmers, pest control workers, poultry keepers, landscapers, bird population monitors, archaeologists, and geologists are at risk of serious fungal infections (particularly histoplasmosis and blastomycosis) through occupational exposure to soil and bird/bat droppings containing fungal spores (Histoplasma capsulatum). These dimorphic fungi are endemic in specific geographic regions and cause respiratory and disseminated infections in immunocompetent as well as immunocompromised individuals.
questions.question: Which occupational group is listed as being at RISK of histoplasmosis or similar serious fungal infection?
options: Laboratory scientists working with cell cultures
Dental professionals exposed to aerosols only
Farmers, pest control workers, poultry keepers
Increased dietary sugar intake as the sole cause
Profound immunosuppression impairing normal antifungal host defence
Direct antifungal drug resistance unrelated to immune status
questions.question: A patient with untreated HIV infection and a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ develops extensive, persistent oral candidiasis resistant to conventional topical therapy. The severity of candidiasis in this patient is best explained by:
questions.explanation: Severe, persistent, and treatment-resistant oral candidiasis in a patient with advanced HIV infection and low CD4 count is primarily explained by profound immunosuppression, which impairs the normal cell-mediated immune defence against Candida overgrowth. This presentation may prompt further HIV-related evaluation if not already diagnosed, and can indicate advanced immunosuppression requiring urgent antiretroviral therapy. Recognising oral candidiasis as a potential marker of underlying immunosuppression is clinically important.

Psychosomatic and psychosocial stress factors are recognised contributors to the development of NUG in children, alongside poor nutrition and reduced immune resistance. Stress may impair local and systemic host defences, facilitating overgrowth of the fusospirochetal flora. Addressing the underlying psychosocial situation is part of comprehensive management.
questions.question: A child from a home with significant psychosocial stress and poor supervision presents with necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis. Beyond nutrition, which factor is recognised as a specific predisposing element in paediatric NUG?

options: Predisposing factors including stress and malnutrition
questions.question: Acute ulcerative gingivitis (AUG) is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: AUG is characterised by an acute, painful presentation with punched-out ulceration of the interdental papillae, halitosis, metallic taste, and bleeding. A chronic painless course is characteristic of chronic marginal gingivitis, not AUG. Predisposing factors include malnutrition, stress, smoking, and impaired host immunity, particularly in children and adolescents.

options: Purely genetic factor with no environmental contribution
Purely traumatic factor unrelated to any congenital condition
questions.question: A patient with cleft lip and palate presents with significant maxillary hypoplasia and a Class III malocclusion, attributed in part to scarring from surgical repair restricting normal maxillary growth. This aetiological factor is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Cleft lip and palate is a congenital developmental anomaly, and the resulting malocclusion often has an additional iatrogenic component from surgical scarring that restricts normal maxillary growth following cleft repair. This combination of congenital and treatment-related factors illustrates the complex, multifactorial nature of malocclusion in such patients. Comprehensive, often lifelong, multidisciplinary management is typically required in these cases.

options: Mental retardation along with heart defects
Defects of hair, skin, and nails
questions.explanation: Ectodermal dysplasia involves defects of ectodermal-derived structures including hair, skin, nails, and teeth—hence the characteristic hypodontia and/or anodontia. Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) involves mental retardation, mongoloid face, macroglossia, and delayed eruption. Cleft lip and palate is a separate congenital condition that can be associated with hypodontia.
questions.question: Ectodermal dysplasia is a systemic condition associated with hypodontia that also involves:

options: Only unfilled resin with zero particles
Particle size has no bearing on polishability
questions.question: A dentist explains to a patient that composite resin filler particles, in addition to providing strength, also influence the polishability and wear resistance of the material. Which filler particle size range is specifically associated with achieving a very high surface polish, as used in microfilled composites?
questions.explanation: Microfilled composites use very small, submicron-sized filler particles, which allow for a very high surface polish and excellent aesthetic result, making them well suited for restorations in highly visible anterior areas. However, their smaller filler content generally reduces mechanical strength compared with hybrid or nanofilled composites used in posterior, higher-stress situations. Filler particle size and content are therefore key determinants of both aesthetic and mechanical performance.

Shillingburg's principles of tooth preparation for extra-coronal restorations emphasise achieving a balance between conserving as much tooth structure as possible while still meeting mechanical requirements for retention, resistance, and structural durability, alongside biological considerations such as pulp protection and periodontal health. Over-reduction risks pulpal damage while under-reduction compromises restoration strength. This balance is central to successful crown preparation.
options: Conservation of tooth structure and mechanical/biological requirements
questions.question: A dentist preparing a full crown must balance adequate tooth reduction for restorative material bulk against preservation of pulp vitality and retention. According to Shillingburg's principles, this balance in extra-coronal tooth preparation is primarily between:

questions.explanation: Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is characterised by irregular, well-demarcated erythematous patches with a slightly raised white or yellow border that migrate and change pattern over time. It is a benign, usually asymptomatic condition of unknown cause. Reassurance is generally sufficient, as no treatment is required unless the patient reports discomfort.
questions.question: A patient presents with an asymptomatic tongue lesion showing irregular red patches with white, slightly raised borders that change shape and location over successive visits. This is most consistent with:
Restorations placed as part of a dental bridge are primarily classified under:
questions.explanation: Restorations placed 'as part of other restorative needs, e.g. in a bridge' is a specific listed indication for dental restoration. Crown preparations on abutment teeth are examples of restorations integral to fixed prosthodontic construction. Without adequately prepared and restored abutments, the bridge cannot be retained or function effectively. SUBTOPIC 6: EXODONTIA & ORAL AND MAXILLOFACIAL SURGERY

The calcifying odontogenic cyst (Gorlin cyst or ghost cell cyst) is classified as a neoplastic odontogenic cyst, alongside cystic ameloblastoma, due to its proliferative epithelial lining with locally aggressive behaviour. It is characterised histologically by 'ghost cells' — epithelial cells that retain their cellular outline but lose their nuclei — and may show calcification. Its neoplastic classification reflects its growth potential and variable recurrence after treatment.
questions.question: The calcifying odontogenic cyst (ghost cell cyst) is classified under which category?

options: Assessing both arches for bone loss simultaneously
Measuring root length before endodontic therapy
questions.explanation: Periapical radiography is specifically indicated for measuring the length of tooth roots before endodontic therapy, alongside detecting apical infection, assessing periodontal status, evaluating root morphology before extractions, and monitoring implants. It provides the detailed apical region view that other projections cannot supply. Bitewing radiography, not periapical, is used for simultaneous crest bone assessment in both arches.
questions.question: Which of the following represents an indication for periapical radiography?

questions.explanation: Healthy gingiva is classically described as coral pink, attributable to its vascular supply and degree of keratinisation. Brown racial pigmentation is a normal variation. Any deviation toward red, blue, or purple indicates inflammatory changes affecting the microvasculature and tissue fluid balance.
questions.question: The colour of healthy gingiva in a non-pigmented individual is best described as:

options: Detecting proximal caries in the primary molars
Routine screening of the permanent dentition
Periapical assessment of upper anteriors and trauma
Assessing bone levels in periodontal disease
questions.explanation: The main clinical indications for occlusal radiography include periapical assessment of upper anterior teeth especially in children, detection of unerupted canines and supernumeraries, evaluation of lesions in the anterior maxilla, and assessment of anterior tooth and alveolar bone fractures after trauma. Its ease of film placement makes it particularly useful in children following trauma.
questions.question: The main clinical indication for occlusal radiography in children is:

options: A well-controlled case of diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Teeth in patients with haemophilia (and other coagulopathies) may require extraction to eliminate a chronic septic focus that could precipitate haemarthrosis or life-threatening systemic infection. However, extraction in haemophilia itself requires careful perioperative haematological management (factor replacement, antifibrinolytics, local haemostatics) to prevent life-threatening haemorrhage. The indication therefore balances risk against benefit.
questions.question: For which systemic condition is extraction considered an indication due to risk of life-threatening complications?

questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus predisposes to oral candidiasis through multiple mechanisms: elevated blood and salivary glucose provides an enhanced carbon source supporting Candida proliferation; hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and intracellular killing; and salivary secretory IgA may be reduced. Additionally, poorly controlled DM causes dry mouth. The combination of substrate enrichment and immune impairment makes candidiasis significantly more prevalent and severe in poorly controlled diabetics.
options: Reduced salivary lactoferrin production from parotid gland atrophy
Increased saliva flow washing organisms onto the mucosa
Altered bone marrow production reducing lymphocyte numbers
High glucose feeding Candida growth, plus impaired immunity
questions.question: DM (diabetes mellitus) as a systemic predisposing factor for oral candidiasis operates PRIMARILY through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Median rhomboid glossitis is a chronic form of oral candidiasis presenting as a well-demarcated, red, depapillated, rhomboid-shaped area on the midline posterior dorsum of the tongue, often asymptomatic and persistent over time. It differs from geographic tongue, which is migratory and typically has raised white borders, and is associated with chronic candidal colonisation rather than an idiopathic inflammatory process. Recognising this presentation avoids unnecessary biopsy in a classic, benign case.
questions.question: A patient presents with a chronic, painless, red, depapillated area on the midline of the dorsum of the tongue, asymptomatic and unchanged over years. This lesion, associated with chronic candidal infection, is termed:

questions.explanation: CAD/CAM (Computer-Aided Design/Computer-Aided Manufacturing) uses digital information from computerised surface digitisation of the tooth preparation to design a restoration on a computer monitor, then translates this into milling instructions to cut the restoration from a ceramic or composite block. It allows single-visit restorations without conventional laboratory procedures. Copy milling uses a physical replica as the guide.
questions.question: CAD/CAM milling in dental restorations uses:
options: Digital surface data to design and mill restorations
A plaster replica as physical guide for milling
Casting of molten metal into an invested pattern
Press-sintering of ceramic powders by hand

questions.question: A patient with multiple odontogenic keratocysts, bifid ribs, and characteristic facial features suggestive of an inherited syndrome undergoes genetic assessment. This constellation of findings is characteristic of which syndrome?
questions.explanation: Basal cell nevus (Gorlin-Goltz) syndrome is characterised by multiple odontogenic keratocysts, skeletal abnormalities such as bifid ribs, and characteristic facial features, along with a predisposition to basal cell carcinomas. Recognition of multiple keratocysts in a patient should prompt evaluation for this underlying syndrome. Genetic counselling and long-term multidisciplinary follow-up are important components of managing affected individuals.

questions.question: A patient develops transient facial nerve palsy immediately following an inferior alveolar nerve block injection, with drooping of the eyelid and corner of the mouth on the injected side. This complication is best explained by:
questions.explanation: Transient facial nerve palsy following an inferior alveolar nerve block can occur if the anaesthetic solution is inadvertently deposited too far posteriorly, entering the substance of the parotid gland and diffusing to affect the facial nerve as it passes through the gland, resulting in temporary facial weakness that resolves as the anaesthetic wears off. This differs from permanent nerve injury, which would not be expected from correct injection technique. Recognising this transient, self-limiting complication helps reassure the patient while emphasising the importance of correct injection technique to avoid it.
options: A normal, expected effect of the injection
Inadvertent deposition of anaesthetic into the parotid gland affecting the facial nerve
An allergic reaction to the anaesthetic
Direct damage to the trigeminal ganglion
Open surgical removal of a lymph node
Removal of a core of tissue using a large cutting needle
Applying liquid nitrogen to lesional tissue
Aspiration of cells from a lesion using a fine needle
questions.explanation: FNAC involves aspiration of cells from a lesion using a fine needle attached to a syringe. It provides a cytological specimen for analysis without the need for open surgery. It is particularly useful for assessing cervical lymphadenopathy, salivary gland masses, and other head and neck swellings.
questions.question: Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) involves:
When performing the lower true occlusal projection, the X-ray beam is directed:
options: Through the symphysis at ninety degrees
questions.explanation: For the upper standard occlusal, the X-ray tubehead is positioned above the patient in the midline, aiming downward at an angle of 65–70° to the film packet through the bridge of the nose. The film packet is placed flat on the occlusal surfaces of the lower teeth and the patient bites gently to hold it. The film long axis is placed crossways in adults and anteroposteriorly in children.

options: A case of diabetes mellitus, type 2
Ankylosing spondylitis and juvenile rheumatoid arthritis
questions.explanation: Infective (inflammatory) arthritis of the TMJ can be caused by conditions including ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis, and direct infective arthritis. These systemic inflammatory arthropathies target synovial joints throughout the body, including the TMJ. Their management requires systemic disease control in addition to local joint treatment.
questions.question: Which systemic disease is listed as a cause of infective arthritis of the TMJ?

questions.explanation: CBCT provides three-dimensional imaging that allows precise localisation of structures such as an impacted tooth in relation to adjacent roots and vital structures, information that conventional two-dimensional radiographs cannot provide. This makes it especially valuable for complex surgical and implant planning. The trade-off is a higher radiation dose compared with conventional intraoral films.
questions.question: A maxillofacial surgeon requires a three-dimensional image to precisely evaluate the buccolingual position of an impacted canine relative to adjacent roots before surgical exposure. Which imaging modality provides this level of detail?

questions.explanation: Appendicitis is not listed among the predisposing illnesses for cancrum oris. Recognised predisposing illnesses include measles, malaria, diarrhoea and vomiting, smallpox, typhoid fever, tuberculosis, chickenpox, whooping cough, and Burkitt lymphoma. These debilitating systemic illnesses severely compromise nutritional status and immune function in affected children.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a predisposing illness for cancrum oris (noma)?

options: Prokaryotic nucleus, cell wall of peptidoglycan, no organelles
No cell wall, only a lipid bilayer membrane
Single circular DNA chromosome without a nucleus
Viral-like replication inside host cell nucleus
Eukaryotic nucleus, chitin-containing cell wall, ergosterol-containing cell membrane
questions.explanation: Fungi are eukaryotes — they possess a true membrane-bound nucleus — distinguished from bacteria which are prokaryotes. Their cell wall contains chitin (not peptidoglycan as in bacteria), and their cell membrane contains ergosterol (not cholesterol as in mammals). These unique features are exploited by antifungal drugs: polyenes target ergosterol, azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis, and echinocandins target beta-glucan in the fungal cell wall.
questions.question: Fungi are characterised by possessing which unique cellular features that distinguish them from bacteria?
When plaques of oral candidiasis are stripped from the mucosal surface, the underlying tissue appears:
questions.explanation: When the white plaques of candidiasis are stripped from the mucosal surface, the underlying tissue appears raw and bleeding. This feature helps distinguish thrush from other white lesions such as leukoplakia, which cannot be wiped off. The condition predominantly affects the buccal mucosa and tongue, though the palate, gingiva, and floor of the mouth may also be involved.

A radiograph is the general term for the image produced when X-rays pass through tissue and interact with a photographic film or digital sensor, creating an image based on differential absorption of radiation by tissues of varying density. Specific types of radiographs, such as sialograms or cephalograms, are named according to their specific technique or purpose. Understanding this general terminology underlies communication in radiology.
questions.question: A patient asks a dentist to explain what image is produced when X-rays pass through tissue and strike a photographic film, creating varying degrees of blackening based on tissue density. This resulting image is called a:
A surgeon designing a mucoperiosteal flap for surgical removal of an impacted tooth ensures the base of the flap is wider than its free margin. This principle is applied primarily to ensure:
questions.explanation: Designing a flap with a base wider than its free margin ensures an adequate blood supply is maintained to the flap, as blood vessels typically enter from the base; a narrow base relative to the flap length risks compromising perfusion and can lead to flap necrosis. This principle is fundamental to safe and successful flap design in oral surgery. Ignoring this principle risks poor healing and increased postoperative complications.
options: Adequate blood supply to the flap

questions.question: Trituration in dental amalgam refers to the process of:
questions.explanation: Trituration is the mechanical mixing process that wets all surfaces of the alloy particles with mercury to initiate the amalgamation (setting) reaction. It can be performed manually with a mortar and pestle or, preferably, mechanically with an amalgamator. Mechanical trituration offers shorter mixing time, more standardised procedure, and less mercury exposure compared to manual mixing.
options: Packing the mixed amalgam into the prepared cavity
Condensing the amalgam to eliminate voids
Mixing alloy and mercury to start the reaction

questions.question: The innermost zone of dentinal caries, closest to the pulp, is microscopically described as:
questions.explanation: The translucent zone is the innermost part of the dentinal caries lesion, located closest to the pulp, representing the advancing front of acid demineralisation. The dark zone is the second layer, followed by the body of the lesion (area of maximum demineralisation), and the surface zone (which shows only about 10% mineral loss). Understanding these zones informs decisions about caries removal.

The wedge principle describes the mechanical action of an elevator blade being driven between the tooth root and surrounding bone, using the wedge shape to displace and loosen the tooth from its socket. Elevators may also use lever and wheel-and-axle principles depending on their design and application. Understanding these mechanical principles guides safe and effective elevator use during extraction.
questions.question: A dental elevator is inserted between the tooth root and alveolar bone, and the wedge-shaped blade is advanced to displace the tooth by mechanical advantage. This principle of elevator use is termed the:

questions.explanation: Tooth preparation aims to remove all defects/caries, protect the underlying pulpal tissue, provide necessary resistance and retention form, and extend the restoration as conservatively as possible while maintaining structural strength. No friable tooth structure should remain after preparation. The restored tooth and restoration must withstand masticatory forces without fracture or displacement.
questions.question: The primary objective of tooth preparation for restorations is to:
options: Maximise the amount of tooth tissue removed
Remove all enamel and expose dentine
Create as deep a preparation as possible for better retention
Remove defects, protect pulp, provide retention
Expose the cemento-enamel junction in all cases

questions.question: Herpes zoster affecting the trigeminal nerve is caused by reactivation of:
questions.explanation: Herpes zoster (shingles) is caused by reactivation of Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV), a ubiquitous double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the alpha herpesvirus subfamily. After primary varicella infection, VZV remains latent in dorsal root ganglia and can reactivate. The trigeminal nerve is affected in approximately 15% of cases.

options: It must be removed for cleaning
It cannot replace more than one missing tooth
Abutment teeth are irreversibly trimmed and weakened
It always requires general anaesthesia for placement
It is uncomfortable and requires adhesive
questions.question: The MAIN disadvantage of a dental bridge compared to dentures is:
questions.explanation: The main disadvantage of a bridge is that the natural abutment teeth must be irreversibly trimmed (prepared), which can weaken the teeth, risk pulp damage, or cause pulp death. Bridges are also relatively costly compared to dentures. Loose crown margins can predispose abutment teeth to decay if not fitted well.

questions.question: A surgeon requires a single extraoral image displaying the entire maxillary and mandibular dental arches, sinuses, and TMJs to plan management of multiple impacted third molars. Which technique is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Dental panoramic radiography (orthopantomography) is an extraoral technique that produces a single image of the entire maxilla, mandible, and associated structures, making it ideal for surveying multiple impacted teeth and assessing overall jaw pathology. It offers a broad overview but with less fine detail than intraoral films. This makes it the technique of choice for comprehensive assessment before third molar surgery.

Anterior disc displacement with reduction is characterised by an audible or palpable click during opening, corresponding to the displaced disc 'reducing' or returning to a more normal position relative to the condyle, with a second click sometimes occurring on closing as the disc redisplaces. This differs from disc displacement without reduction, in which the disc remains persistently displaced, typically causing limited opening without a reciprocal click. Accurate diagnosis of the specific disc disorder guides appropriate conservative or surgical management.
questions.question: A patient reports a clicking sound in the TMJ during mouth opening, which corresponds to the articular disc returning to a normal position relative to the condyle after having been anteriorly displaced at rest. This finding is characteristic of:
options: Osteoarthritis of the TMJ without disc involvement

questions.explanation: Ongoing radio- and/or chemotherapy represents a systemic contraindication to extraction due to risks of post-radiation osteonecrosis, impaired wound healing, and myelosuppression-related infection and bleeding. Other systemic contraindications include haemophilia, uncontrolled metabolic diseases (uncontrolled diabetes, uraemia), uncontrolled hypertension and cardiac diseases, and patients on anticoagulants, cancer medications, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants.
questions.question: Which of the following systemic conditions is listed as a systemic contraindication to extraction?
Which component of the periodontium is responsible for the principal attachment of the tooth to alveolar bone via Sharpey's fibres?
questions.explanation: The periodontal ligament (PDL) is a specialised connective tissue that attaches the tooth root (via cementum) to the alveolar bone through bundles of collagen fibres called Sharpey's fibres. The PDL also provides proprioception, nutrient supply, and remodelling capacity. Its destruction leads to pocket formation and eventual tooth mobility.

questions.question: The MOST common contributor to malocclusion from malaligned teeth is:
questions.explanation: Crowding is the most common contributor to malocclusion, occurring when one or many teeth are misplaced due to arch-tooth size discrepancy. Overjet is excessive horizontal protrusion of upper incisors, overbite is excessive vertical overlap, open bite is lack of vertical overlap, and crossbite is improper alignment with opposing teeth. All represent types of malalignment but crowding is most prevalent.

questions.question: A patient with poorly controlled leukaemia and severe thrombocytopenia requires extraction of a symptomatic tooth. Which systemic factor listed as a contraindication to extraction is most relevant in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled bleeding disorders, such as severe thrombocytopenia associated with leukaemia, represent a significant systemic contraindication to extraction because of the high risk of uncontrollable haemorrhage. Extraction in such cases requires careful haematological optimisation and often specialist liaison before proceeding. Well-controlled chronic conditions, in contrast, generally do not preclude extraction.

questions.question: Osteomyelitis of the TMJ causing malocclusion is specifically noted in YOUNG patients because:
options: The condyle is a growth centre; damage impairs growth
Children are more susceptible to all bacterial infections than adults
Young patients receive higher doses of antibiotics that alter bone healing
Deciduous teeth adjacent to the joint contribute to infection spread
Immune immaturity in children prevents any bone repair after infection
questions.explanation: In young patients, the condyle is the primary growth centre for the mandible. Osteomyelitis destroying the condyle eliminates this growth centre, resulting in ipsilateral mandibular growth failure, progressively worsening facial asymmetry, and Class II deviation to the affected side. The younger the age of condylar destruction, the more severe the resulting deformity. This is why early recognition and aggressive treatment of TMJ infections in children is critical to prevent growth disturbance.

questions.question: Indirect composite resin restorations were primarily found beneficial for:
options: Anterior veneers built on a metal substructure
Inlays and onlays nearing porcelain's properties
questions.explanation: Indirect composite restorations, developed from the 1980s, demonstrated physical properties approximating those of porcelain, making them particularly useful for inlay and onlay restorations. They were typically less expensive for the laboratory to fabricate than ceramic options. Long-term studies (e.g., on BelleGlass by Kerr) confirmed their viability as an alternative to gold or ceramic for conservative indirect restorations.

Xerostomia (dry mouth from reduced salivary flow) promotes caries by removing all major salivary protective functions: buffering of acids, mechanical clearance of sugars, antibacterial activity, and supply of calcium and phosphate for remineralisation. It is a major risk factor for rampant caries and is commonly caused by medications (antihistamines, antidepressants), radiotherapy, and Sjögren's syndrome.
questions.question: Xerostomia promotes caries by:

questions.explanation: Light-activated (photopolymerized) composite resins cure upon exposure to a specific wavelength of visible blue light (approximately 470 nm), which activates the photoinitiator camphorquinone, initiating free-radical polymerization. This on-command curing gives the clinician working time for precise placement and contouring before initiating set — a major clinical advantage over chemically-activated systems.
options: Chemical reaction between base and catalyst paste
Heat from the dental unit light
Exposure to visible light activating a photoinitiator
questions.question: The setting of light-activated composite resin is initiated by:

questions.explanation: PFM restorations are suited only for crown and bridge (fixed partial denture) fabrication; they cannot be used for conservative restorations such as inlays and onlays due to the inherent design requirements of the metal-ceramic system. All-ceramic and indirect composite materials offer the flexibility to fabricate both crowns and conservative inlay/onlay restorations, expanding their indication range.
questions.question: A significant drawback of PFM restorations beyond aesthetics is that they are limited to:
options: Single unit crowns only with no bridge capability
Posterior teeth only due to low strength
Crown and bridge restorations, excluding inlays and onlays
Short-span bridges with not more than two units
Improving denture hygiene and removing the denture at night
Increasing denture wear time to 24 hours per day
Applying antifungal cream only to the denture base without addressing hygiene
questions.explanation: Effective long-term management of denture stomatitis requires addressing the underlying predisposing factors, including improving denture hygiene and removing the denture at night to allow the mucosa to rest and recover, in addition to antifungal medication to treat the active infection. Antifungal therapy alone, without correcting these contributing factors, often results in recurrence. This comprehensive approach reflects the multifactorial nature of denture-associated candidiasis.
questions.question: A patient with untreated denture-related candidiasis (denture stomatitis) is advised on management. Beyond antifungal medication, which additional measure is essential for effective long-term resolution?

questions.explanation: Neoplasms listed as affecting the TMJ include chondroma and osteoma. Haemarthrosis — bleeding into the joint space — is classified as a traumatic TMJ condition, not a neoplasm. Ameloblastoma affects the jaw bone rather than the TMJ specifically. This distinction between the traumatic, infective, metabolic, neoplastic, developmental, and genetic categories of TMJ disease is fundamental to the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with jaw pain and dysfunction.
questions.question: Neoplasms that may affect the TMJ and are listed include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Both chondroma and osteoma are listed

questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament attaches to the axis of rotation of the mandible and, uniquely, remains constant in length and tension throughout all positions of the mandible — opening, protrusion, lateral excursion. This means it does not limit any specific movement but instead acts as a stabiliser. In contrast, the temporomandibular ligament tightens specifically during retrusion and protrusion.
questions.question: The sphenomandibular ligament is clinically significant because it:
options: Limits protrusion by tightening during forward translation
Prevents posterior displacement of the condyle only
Stays constant in length whatever the jaw position
Connects the disc to the lateral pterygoid muscle
Is the primary ligament that guides lateral excursion

questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with fever, drooling, and numerous small vesicles on the gingiva and hard palate that have ruptured into painful ulcers, with markedly swollen erythematous gingiva. Which management step is CONTRAINDICATED?
questions.explanation: Systemic steroids are contraindicated in primary herpetic gingivostomatitis because they suppress the immune response and can promote viral dissemination. Supportive care, hydration, and early antiviral therapy are the mainstay of management. Steroids may worsen the course and prolong healing time in an active viral infection.

Glass ionomer cement bonds to tooth structure via an ion-exchange mechanism between its polyalkenoate chains and the calcium and phosphate ions of hydroxyapatite in both enamel and dentine. This chemical bonding is intrinsic and does not require acid etching, distinguishing GIC from composite resin. The result is a clinically useful, if not highly strong, adhesive interface.
options: Micromechanical retention via acid etching only
Physical adherence without any chemical interaction
Bonding only to enamel via silane coupling agents
Covalent bonding through photoactivated resin bridges
Chemical bonding via ion exchange with tooth minerals
questions.question: Which statement BEST describes the bonding mechanism of glass ionomer cement to tooth structure?

A patient requests a thin layer of tooth-coloured material bonded to only the labial surface of an anterior tooth to mask discolouration, without full coverage of the tooth. This restoration is classified as a:
questions.explanation: A veneer is a thin layer of restorative material, typically composite or ceramic, bonded to the facial (labial) surface of a tooth to improve aesthetics while preserving most of the underlying tooth structure. It is more conservative than a full crown, which covers the entire clinical crown. Veneers are commonly indicated for discolouration, minor malalignment, or diastema closure.

CAD/CAM (Computer-Aided Design/Computer-Aided Manufacturing) milling uses digital scanning and computer-guided cutting of a ceramic or composite block to fabricate a restoration, offering precision and often same-day delivery compared with traditional laboratory techniques. This technology has become widely used for inlays, onlays, and crowns. It reduces reliance on conventional impression and casting methods.
questions.question: A laboratory technician uses a computer-guided milling machine to fabricate a ceramic onlay from a digital scan of a prepared tooth, rather than using traditional wax-up and casting techniques. This fabrication method is known as:

A dentist explains that certain restorative materials, such as glass ionomer, demonstrate anticariogenic potential at the restoration margin through sustained release of a specific ion over time. This ion is:
questions.explanation: Glass ionomer cement demonstrates anticariogenic potential through sustained release of fluoride ions over time, which can be taken up by adjacent tooth structure to promote remineralisation and inhibit demineralisation at the restoration margin, an effect sometimes referred to as a 'battery effect' when fluoride is later recharged from external sources such as fluoride toothpaste. This property is a distinguishing advantage of glass ionomer over materials such as composite resin or amalgam, which do not offer comparable sustained fluoride release. This makes it particularly valuable in caries-prone patients.

questions.question: A patient undergoing head and neck radiotherapy for oropharyngeal cancer develops painful oral ulcerations several weeks into treatment. These mucosal ulcers typically become apparent once cumulative radiation doses reach approximately:
questions.explanation: Radiation-induced oral mucositis and ulceration typically become clinically apparent once cumulative doses reach around 2000 cGy (20 Gy), as the rapidly dividing basal mucosal cells are damaged. Ulceration worsens as treatment progresses and often necessitates supportive oral care. This is an important consideration in planning dental care before radiotherapy.

questions.question: Histologically, acute oral ulcers show:
questions.explanation: Acute oral ulcers microscopically show loss of surface epithelium replaced by a fibrin network containing predominantly neutrophils. The ulcer base contains dilated capillaries, and with time granulation tissue forms while epithelial regeneration begins at the margins. Chronic ulcers show a mixed inflammatory infiltrate rather than predominantly neutrophils.
options: Dense collagen fully replacing the lost epithelium
Surface lost, replaced by fibrin and neutrophils
Spongiosis and acantholysis of epithelial cells

questions.question: A patient with a persistent thumb-sucking habit beyond the age of normal cessation develops an anterior open bite and proclined maxillary incisors. This malocclusion is best classified under which category of aetiological factor?
questions.explanation: Persistent thumb-sucking is classified as a local, habit-related environmental factor contributing to malocclusion, producing characteristic changes such as anterior open bite and proclined maxillary incisors due to the sustained pressure of the habit on the developing dentition and alveolar bone. This differs from genetic or skeletal factors, which are inherent to the individual's growth pattern rather than acquired through behaviour. Early habit cessation can allow significant self-correction of the resulting malocclusion in younger patients.

Dental plaque is a colourless, soft, sticky coating that tenaciously adheres to teeth and forms almost immediately after toothbrushing. It resists removal by tongue movements, water rinsing, or water spray, and concentrates millions of microorganisms on the tooth surface including the primary cariogenic bacteria S. mutans and Lactobacilli. Its removal through mechanical oral hygiene is the fundamental caries prevention strategy.
options: A loose, easily removable layer of food debris
A calcified deposit on tooth surfaces
An extrinsic stain from tobacco use
A pigmented film from dietary staining
A colorless, sticky film adherent to teeth
questions.question: Dental plaque is BEST described as:
