A patient requires a fixed bridge to replace a missing premolar, and the dentist selects a design in which the pontic (artificial tooth) is retained by a full crown on the tooth immediately mesial to the space, with no retainer on the distal abutment. This bridge design is termed a:
questions.explanation: A cantilever bridge is retained by an abutment (or abutments) on only one side of the pontic, unlike a conventional fixed-fixed bridge, which is retained by abutments on both sides of the missing tooth space. This design can be advantageous when only one adjacent tooth is a suitable abutment, but it generates different, potentially higher, leverage forces on the retaining abutment that must be carefully considered during treatment planning. Case selection is important to ensure the chosen abutment can withstand these forces long-term.

questions.question: A radiograph of a non-vital, grossly carious mandibular molar reveals a well-defined, unilocular radiolucency at the root apex, consistent with chronic periapical inflammation. This is the MOST common odontogenic cyst and is termed:
questions.explanation: The radicular (periapical) cyst is the most common odontogenic cyst, arising from proliferation of epithelial rests of Malassez within a pre-existing periapical granuloma secondary to pulp necrosis, typically from a non-vital tooth. It is well-defined and unilocular, attached to the root apex of the offending tooth. Its treatment usually involves root canal therapy and/or extraction with enucleation of the cystic lining.

Serum antibody titre for S. mutans is not a clinical investigation for caries detection. Clinical examination combines visual inspection, mirror, and caries explorer, while investigation adds radiographs (periapical and bitewing), caries-detecting dyes, fiberoptic transillumination, electronic caries monitors, and laser fluorescence devices (Diagnodent). Dietary history is also a key part of caries management assessment.
questions.question: Clinical examination for caries uses all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Visual inspection using a dental mouth mirror
Serum antibody titre for S. mutans
Assessment of tooth mobility status alone
Presence of pus and tissue consistency
questions.question: During gingival examination, palpation is performed primarily to assess:
questions.explanation: Digital palpation of the gingiva allows assessment of tissue consistency (firm versus oedematous) and detection of suppuration from periodontal pockets. Pus expressed through a pocket on digital pressure indicates an acute exacerbation of periodontitis. It is a simple but important complement to inspection and probing.

questions.question: A patient's gingival biopsy shows an area of dense fibrous connective tissue with a marked reduction in cellularity, seen clinically as a firm, pink, enlarged gingiva that does not bleed easily. This is MOST characteristic of which type of gingival enlargement?
questions.explanation: Fibrotic (chronic) gingival enlargement is characterised histologically by increased dense fibrous connective tissue with reduced cellularity, presenting clinically as firm, pale pink tissue that bleeds less readily than acutely inflamed gingiva. This contrasts with oedematous enlargement, which is soft, red, and bleeds easily due to vascular engorgement and inflammatory infiltrate. Recognising the type of enlargement helps guide appropriate management, whether through improved hygiene or surgical recontouring.
options: Haemorrhagic enlargement from a bleeding disorder

questions.question: The condylar head's articular surface is covered by which tissue type that differs from most other synovial joints?
questions.explanation: The TMJ condylar head and articular eminence are covered by fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage as found in most other synovial joints. This fibrocartilaginous covering is more resistant to compressive loading and has greater regenerative capacity than hyaline cartilage. However, it is also less resilient to excessive loading and injury — explaining the susceptibility of the TMJ to degenerative osteoarthritis with advancing age or parafunction.
options: Hyaline cartilage identical to other synovial joints
Elastic cartilage similar to the ear auricle
Fibrocartilage, unlike most joints' hyaline cartilage
Compact bone with no intervening cartilage
Synovial membrane directly covering the condylar head

questions.explanation: Herpes labialis, also called fever blisters or orolabial herpes, is the recurrent manifestation of Herpes Simplex Virus type 1. After primary infection the virus lies dormant in epithelial cells and reactivates to produce recurrent lesions at the corner of the mouth (commissure). It is distinct from the primary disease which manifests as herpetic gingivostomatitis.
questions.question: Herpes labialis is the recurrent form of infection caused by:
options: Reactivation of the Varicella Zoster Virus

questions.explanation: A gold crown (full gold crown or full cast metal crown) covers the entire anatomic crown of the tooth. A gold inlay restores only an intracoronal defect without covering cusps; a gold onlay covers one or more cusps for reinforcement; a veneer covers only the facial surface; and a pontic is the suspended unit of a fixed partial denture. These precise terminology distinctions reflect different preparation designs and restoration geometries.
questions.question: A full coverage indirect restoration made from gold that covers the entire anatomic crown is MOST accurately termed a:

A radiograph of an unerupted mandibular third molar shows a well-defined unilocular radiolucency surrounding the crown, attached at the cemento-enamel junction. This cyst, arising from the reduced enamel epithelium of an unerupted tooth, is termed:
questions.explanation: A dentigerous cyst arises from the reduced enamel epithelium surrounding the crown of an unerupted tooth, characteristically presenting radiographically as a well-defined radiolucency attached at the cemento-enamel junction and enclosing the crown. It is the second most common odontogenic cyst after the radicular cyst. Management typically involves enucleation with removal of the associated unerupted tooth, or marsupialisation in select cases.

questions.question: A radiograph reveals a well-defined unilocular radiolucent lesion in the mandible with no epithelial lining on histological examination and no fluid content on aspiration, described as an 'empty' cavity within bone found incidentally in an adolescent. This lesion is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: A solitary (simple/traumatic) bone cyst is an empty or fluid-scant intraosseous cavity lacking an epithelial lining, often discovered incidentally in adolescents, and is technically classified as a pseudocyst rather than a true cyst. It is thought to be related to intramedullary haemorrhage, though the exact aetiology remains uncertain. Surgical exploration and curettage typically promotes bone healing, often the sole treatment required.

questions.question: A solitary bone cyst of the jaw is classified as a pseudocyst because:
questions.explanation: A solitary (simple) bone cyst is a pseudocyst — a cystic cavity lacking an epithelial lining. On surgical exploration, the cavity is often found to be empty or contain only a small amount of serous fluid or blood. Its pathogenesis is debated, with trauma and intramedullary haemorrhage proposed as causes. Treatment is surgical exploration (which often induces bleeding and healing), with a low recurrence rate compared to true epithelium-lined cysts.
options: It contains pus rather than cyst fluid
It is lined by stratified squamous epithelium
It is a neoplastic lesion rather than a cyst
It contains tooth-bearing structures within the lumen

questions.explanation: The lateral cephalometric radiograph is an extra-oral projection placed outside the mouth, used for orthodontic, orthognathic surgery, and implant treatment planning. It provides standardised measurements of the skeletal pattern, dental relationships, and soft tissue profile. Serial cephalometric records track treatment changes in orthodontic patients over time.
questions.question: Which radiographic modality is classified as extra-oral and used for orthodontic planning?
Orofacial infections are defined as diverse diseases of which origin?
questions.explanation: Orofacial infections encompass diverse diseases of bacterial, fungal, or viral origin affecting the oral cavity and adjacent facial structures. The oral cavity may be the primary site of involvement or may show manifestations of systemic infection. Routes of infection include airborne transmission, direct contact, and transfer via hands or objects.

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY function of the beaks of an extraction forceps?
options: To deliver the anaesthetic solution periapically
To grasp the tooth cervically and remove it
To rotate the tooth before its final delivery
To retract the gingival tissue during extraction
To hold the neighbouring teeth during removal
questions.explanation: The beaks of extraction forceps function to grasp the tooth at the cervical region (below the gingival margin), applying controlled forces to luxate the tooth from its periodontal attachments and remove it from the alveolar socket. Beaks must be placed as apically as possible to maximise leverage and minimise risk of crown fracture. Beak design is tooth-specific to match individual root anatomy.

Host modifying factors — particularly tobacco smoking and genetic predisposition — can outweigh the bacterial load as determinants of periodontitis severity and clinical outcome. Smoking impairs neutrophil and macrophage function, reduces vascularity, and masks clinical signs of inflammation, making disease harder to detect and treat. This concept is central to contemporary periodontal risk assessment.
options: Reduce gingival crevicular fluid flow rate
May outweigh bacteria in disease severity
questions.question: Host factors such as tobacco smoking in periodontitis are significant because they:

questions.explanation: Denture wearing alone increases Candida carriage; the risk is compounded significantly when combined with poor denture hygiene (failure to remove and clean the denture daily) and leaving dentures in continuously, including overnight. The fitting surface of a denture creates an anaerobic, warm, moist environment that promotes Candida biofilm formation (denture plaque). Denture-related stomatitis (atrophic candidiasis) is the most common form of oral candidiasis in older denture-wearing patients.
options: The regular use of a fluoride-containing toothpaste daily
Poor hygiene plus leaving dentures in overnight
questions.question: Denture wearing as a predisposing factor for oral candidiasis is MOST significant when combined with:
Fungi can grow either as budding yeast cells OR as:
questions.explanation: Fungi can grow in two principal morphological forms: as budding yeast cells (unicellular, spherical) or as slender filamentous hyphae (multicellular, tubular structures). The hyphae may be septate (with cross-walls dividing the hyphae into compartments) or aseptate (coenocytic, lacking cross-walls). This morphological flexibility — particularly the yeast-to-hyphae transition — is a critical virulence determinant in organisms such as Candida albicans.

options: Cantilever bridge with full crown retainer
Fixed-fixed conventional bridge with full crown retainers
questions.question: A patient requires replacement of a missing maxillary lateral incisor and desires a minimally invasive option that avoids significant reduction of the adjacent healthy abutment teeth. The dentist recommends a bridge design bonded primarily to the palatal/lingual surface of the abutment teeth using a metal or ceramic wing, with minimal tooth preparation. This conservative bridge design is termed a:
questions.explanation: A resin-bonded (Maryland) bridge uses a metal or ceramic wing bonded primarily to the palatal or lingual surface of adjacent abutment teeth, requiring minimal tooth preparation compared with a conventional bridge that uses full crown retainers, making it a more conservative option for suitable cases. Case selection depends on factors such as occlusion, available bonding surface, and the specific clinical situation. This design offers a reversible, minimally invasive alternative when abutment teeth are otherwise sound and unrestored.

The temporomandibular ligament, a stout band of fibrous tissue running from the lower border of the zygomatic arch to the posterior border of the mandibular ramus, tightens specifically during retrusion and protrusion of the condyle. It acts to limit these movements and guide condylar path. The sphenomandibular ligament, by contrast, remains constant in length and tension in all positions of the mandible.
options: Rotation of the condyle in the lower compartment
Retrusion and protrusion of the mandible
questions.question: The Temporomandibular ligament specifically tightens during which mandibular movements?
Oral candidiasis associated with Sjögren's syndrome predominantly relates to which predisposing mechanism?
options: Increased carbohydrate intake in Sjögren's patients
Excess salivary flow washing oral Candida
Xerostomia causing reduced salivary antimicrobial activity
Steroid therapy for joint manifestations only
questions.explanation: Sjögren's syndrome causes xerostomia (dry mouth) by immune-mediated destruction of salivary gland acinar cells. Saliva provides critical antimicrobial protection through lactoferrin, lysozyme, salivary IgA, and mechanical cleansing. Xerostomia dramatically increases Candida carriage rate and oral candidiasis risk. Radiotherapy-induced xerostomia carries the same risk. Adequate salivary substitution and antifungal therapy are key management strategies.

A true cyst is defined pathologically as a pathological cavity lined by epithelium; lesions lacking an epithelial lining, such as the solitary bone cyst or aneurysmal bone cyst, are more correctly termed pseudocysts despite their cyst-like clinical and radiographic appearance. This distinction has important implications for both diagnosis and management, as pseudocysts often respond well to simple surgical exploration and curettage. Understanding this terminology avoids confusion when comparing different types of jaw lesions.
questions.question: A cystic lesion of the jaw is examined and found to lack any epithelial lining on histological section, despite having a defined cavity within bone. According to strict pathological definition, this lesion should more correctly be termed a:

questions.explanation: Bifid condyle is a rare developmental anomaly involving congenital or acquired division of the condylar head into two distinct portions (mediolateral or anteroposterior bifurcation), usually discovered incidentally on radiographs. It may be asymptomatic or associated with reduced range of motion. It must be distinguished from condylar fracture, condylar hyperplasia, and condylar hypoplasia in the differential diagnosis of condylar morphology abnormalities.
questions.question: Bifid condyle as a developmental TMJ condition refers to:
options: Overgrowth of one condyle, causing facial asymmetry there
Fusion of both condyles producing bilateral ankylosis
Congenital splitting of the condylar head in two

questions.question: Regarding traumatic oral ulcers, which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.explanation: Traumatic ulcers are the most common soft tissue lesions and a cause-and-effect relationship is usually obvious from history. They result from accidental mechanical trauma at regions easily trapped between the teeth, such as the lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa. Broken teeth and poorly designed prostheses are also common causes.
options: They are the least common soft tissue lesions
They are always the result of chemical injury
Biopsy is routinely required within 7 days
They predominantly affect the dorsum of tongue
A cause-and-effect relationship is usually obvious

questions.explanation: Amalgam and composite resin are classified as direct restorative materials because they are placed directly into the prepared cavity and set or cured in situ within the mouth, without a laboratory fabrication step. This differs from indirect restorations, such as crowns or inlays, which are fabricated outside the mouth before cementation. Direct materials generally allow single-visit restoration of teeth.
questions.question: A dentist explains to a patient that amalgam and composite resin restorations, placed directly into a prepared cavity and set or hardened within the mouth, belong to which broad category of dental restorative materials?

A patient's silver amalgam restoration, more than two decades old, remains functionally intact with minimal wear despite constant occlusal loading. This long clinical longevity is primarily attributed to amalgam's:
questions.explanation: Dental amalgam's long clinical longevity in posterior, load-bearing restorations is primarily attributed to its high compressive strength and good wear resistance under sustained occlusal function, despite lacking adhesive bonding to tooth structure and tooth-coloured aesthetics. This mechanical durability has made it a long-standing, reliable choice, particularly in areas where aesthetics are less critical. Newer materials aim to combine similar durability with improved aesthetics and adhesive bonding.
options: High compressive strength and wear resistance under load
Ability to chemically bond to enamel and dentin

questions.question: Dental ceramics as a DIRECT restorative material are valued for their superior aesthetic properties, but their critical drawback is:
questions.explanation: Dental ceramics offer outstanding aesthetic properties, hardness, and colour stability, but their inherent brittleness is their critical clinical limitation. Ceramic restorations are susceptible to fracture from tensile and shear stresses, requiring careful cementation to dissipate stress and strong adhesive bonding to tooth structure for support. Proper tooth preparation, accurate fit, and appropriate cementation technique are all essential to prevent ceramic fracture in function.
options: High thermal conductivity causing post-operative sensitivity
Inability to bond to composite luting cements

questions.explanation: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a hereditary developmental condition affecting enamel formation, resulting in generalised hypoplastic or hypomineralised, discoloured, and structurally weak enamel across the entire dentition from eruption. It is distinct from acquired or localized causes such as fluorosis or illness-related hypomineralisation. Affected patients often require comprehensive, often full-mouth, restorative management.
questions.question: A patient presents with generalised hypoplastic, discoloured, and structurally weak enamel affecting all teeth since eruption, with no history of trauma or systemic illness during tooth development. This developmental condition affecting enamel formation is:
Oral Candida carriage rate in the healthy population is approximately:
questions.explanation: Oral Candida carriage rate in the healthy general population is approximately 20%, meaning about one in five healthy individuals harbour Candida as a commensal organism without clinical disease. Predisposing factors — dentures, diabetes, dry mouth, immunosuppression — increase this carriage rate and tip the balance toward symptomatic candidiasis. Carriage alone is not pathological and does not require antifungal treatment.

A dental implant is a metal rod (usually titanium) surgically placed in the jaw bone, into which an artificial tooth (crown), bridge, or denture can be screwed. Implants provide superior aesthetics, function, and preservation of alveolar bone compared to conventional dentures. They require adequate healthy bone volume and are more expensive than conventional prostheses.
options: A metal rod in bone supporting an artificial tooth
A removable acrylic prosthesis that is held by suction
A fixed ceramic bridge supported by natural teeth
A bone graft procedure for ridge augmentation
questions.question: A dental implant is defined as:

questions.explanation: Modified tooth preparations for bonded restorations (composite, GIC) use more shallow, non-uniform depths with no strict requirement for resistance/retention form features (locks, slots, grooves, undercuts) because the adhesive bond itself provides retention. Greater variability, marginal angles of 90° or greater, and more enamel bevel are characteristic. This approach conserves significantly more tooth structure than conventional preparations.
options: More shallow, with no strict geometry
Extended to include all fissures prophylactically
questions.question: In modified tooth preparation for bonded composite restorations, compared to conventional amalgam preparation, the depth is:

questions.explanation: An envelope flap consists of a horizontal incision along the gingival margin without any vertical releasing incisions, providing adequate access for straightforward procedures while minimising surgical trauma. This contrasts with triangular or trapezoidal flaps, which include one or two vertical releasing incisions respectively for improved access in more complex procedures. Flap design is selected based on the complexity and extent of the planned surgical procedure.
questions.question: A surgeon uses a curved incision that follows the gingival margin around the necks of teeth without any vertical releasing incisions for a straightforward extraction. This design is best described as a:

A patient requires retention following completion of active orthodontic treatment to prevent relapse of the corrected tooth position. The dentist explains that periodontal ligament fibres, particularly the more slowly reorganising fibres, require a period of stabilisation. This principle underlies the need for:
questions.explanation: Following active orthodontic tooth movement, a period of retainer wear is required because periodontal ligament fibres, particularly the more slowly reorganising supracrestal (gingival) fibres, take time to stabilise in the new tooth position, and premature discontinuation of retention risks relapse toward the original malposition. This principle underlies the standard practice of prescribing retainers, whether removable or fixed, following completion of active orthodontic treatment. Long-term or even permanent retention is often required to maintain stability, particularly in cases with significant rotational correction.
options: Avoidance of any further dental review
A period of retainer wear following active orthodontic treatment
Immediate discontinuation of all appliances without any retention phase
Repeating the entire course of active orthodontic treatment
Extraction of the previously treated teeth

questions.explanation: Universal precautions to prevent surgical sepsis are organised under three headings: instrument sterilisation (autoclaving all reusable instruments), operatory disinfection (cleaning and disinfecting all surfaces and equipment in the surgical environment), and surgical staff preparation (hand and arm washing followed by clean or sterile technique with appropriate protective equipment). These three pillars collectively create a controlled aseptic surgical environment.
options: Antibiotic prophylaxis, sterile draping, and rubber dam isolation
Instrument sterilisation, operatory disinfection, and surgical staff preparation
Patient consent, blood pressure monitoring, and post-op antibiotics
Hand washing, face mask use, and post-operative analgesics
questions.question: Universal precautions in oral surgery to prevent sepsis are organised under which three headings?

options: Rotation of the condyle around a transverse axis
Lateral excursion of the condyle only
Translational (gliding) movement of the condyle-disc unit
Elevation and depression without any translation
questions.explanation: The upper compartment (superior synovial cavity) of the TMJ between the articular disc and the articular surface of the temporal bone allows translational (gliding) movement as the condyle-disc complex slides anteriorly down the articular eminence during wide opening and protrusion. The lower compartment (between condyle and disc) allows rotation. Both compartments must function harmoniously for full, pain-free mandibular range of motion.
questions.question: In the TMJ, the upper joint compartment (between disc and temporal bone) primarily allows which movement?

options: Patient's diet and degree of fluoride exposure
Material properties, moisture control, operator skill
questions.explanation: Operator-related factors affecting restoration longevity include the type and physical properties of the material, quality of moisture control during placement, anaesthesia adequacy, and the operator's expertise and training. These are distinct from patient factors (diet, fluoride, general health, parafunctional habits) and tooth factors (location, cavity design, occlusal load). All three categories must be considered for treatment planning.
questions.question: Factors related to the operator and restoration process that influence restoration longevity include:
The proposed 'random burst' theory of periodontitis progression suggests that:
questions.explanation: The random burst theory proposes that periodontitis progresses episodically, with unpredictable bursts of attachment loss occurring at different sites at different times, rather than as a continuous or uniform process. This theory contrasts with the continuous model and has implications for monitoring intervals and targeted treatment of active sites in periodontal maintenance.
options: All sites progress simultaneously at a constant rate
Attachment loss occurs continuously at all affected sites
Only posterior teeth are affected in bursts
Destruction occurs randomly at different sites and times
Disease follows a predictable apico-coronal spread

questions.explanation: Glass ionomer cement is relatively more tolerant of moisture contamination during placement compared with composite resin, which requires a meticulously dry field for effective bonding, making glass ionomer advantageous in situations with limited moisture control such as young or uncooperative children. This property, combined with fluoride release, supports its common use in paediatric and high-caries-risk restorative situations. Composite generally offers superior aesthetics and strength when moisture control is achievable.
options: Amalgam requiring completely dry field for bonding
questions.question: A patient requires a posterior restoration in a high-caries-risk area with limited moisture control, such as a young child unable to fully cooperate for rubber dam placement. Which material's relative tolerance of moisture contamination makes it advantageous in this situation?

questions.explanation: Direct restorative materials are placed, shaped, and finished directly within the prepared tooth cavity during a single clinical appointment, without laboratory involvement. This contrasts with indirect restorations, which are fabricated outside the mouth in a laboratory and later cemented. Direct restorations include amalgam, composite resin, glass ionomer cement, and direct filling gold.
questions.question: Direct restorative materials are characterised by being:
options: Fabricated in a dental laboratory before placement
Inserted and shaped directly in the clinic

questions.explanation: Dental caries is a localised, progressive destruction of the hard tissue of teeth starting from the external surface, caused by demineralisation from acidogenic bacteria. It is a multifactorial disease and a dynamic condition involving competing processes of demineralisation and remineralisation. It affects anyone with teeth regardless of age or gender.
options: An acute bacterial infection limited to the enamel
A viral disease causing dissolution of the organic matrix
Multifactorial, progressive destruction of hard tissue from the surface
A purely genetic condition of demineralisation
A nutritional deficiency disorder of dental enamel
questions.question: Dental caries is BEST defined as:

options: The genetic basis for dentofacial malocclusion patterns
The neutral zone theory of tooth position
questions.question: The concept that heredity determines a 'blueprint for dentofacial development that may be masked but not really changed except by surgery' was proposed in relation to:
questions.explanation: This concept, central to orthodontic thinking, states that each individual has a genetically determined blueprint for dentofacial development that may be influenced but not fundamentally altered by environmental factors — only surgery can produce permanent architectural skeletal changes. This explains why orthodontic treatment in growing patients attempts to work with and optimise the genetically determined growth pattern rather than fundamentally alter it.

Toluidine blue (vital) staining is a chairside investigation that preferentially stains areas of increased nucleic acid content, such as dysplastic or malignant epithelium, helping to identify the most appropriate site for biopsy in a large or heterogeneous lesion. It does not replace histological diagnosis but guides biopsy site selection. False positives can occur with areas of inflammation or ulceration.
questions.question: A clinician applies a dye to a suspicious oral mucosal lesion to preferentially highlight areas of increased nuclear content that may indicate dysplasia, guiding the site for biopsy. Which chairside investigation is being used?
Which classification group of periodontal disease includes periodontitis associated with Down syndrome?
options: Chronic periodontitis with added secondary occlusal trauma
Periodontitis as a systemic manifestation, genetic disorders
questions.explanation: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is listed under periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic diseases — specifically genetic disorders — because individuals with Down syndrome exhibit an increased susceptibility to severe, early-onset periodontitis. This is partly attributable to impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and function. This classification underscores the need for intensive preventive periodontal care in this patient group from an early age.

questions.question: A patient with chronic untreated dental infection develops persistent bone pain, swelling, and radiographic evidence of bony destruction and sequestrum formation in the mandible. This serious sequela is recognised as:
questions.explanation: Osteomyelitis of the jaw is a recognised, serious sequela of untreated dental caries and its complications, characterised by bony infection, destruction, and sequestrum formation, often requiring both surgical and prolonged antimicrobial management. It represents one of the more severe outcomes in the natural progression of untreated dental disease. Early treatment of caries and its immediate complications helps prevent this outcome.

questions.question: Glass ionomer cement (GIC) is characterised by its unique property of:
questions.explanation: A defining property of glass ionomer cement is its slow and continuous release of fluoride ions, which provides an anticariogenic effect by inhibiting demineralisation and promoting remineralisation at the cavity margins. GIC also bonds chemically to both enamel and dentine through an ion-exchange mechanism, without requiring acid etching, making it clinically versatile.
options: Setting by polymerization under visible light only
High compressive strength superior to amalgam
Slow and continuous release of fluoride ions
Complete opacity matching all tooth shades
Bonding exclusively to enamel and not dentine
Class I with an anterior open bite
questions.explanation: Angle's Class II division 2 malocclusion is characterised by a distal (Class II) molar relationship with retroclined maxillary central incisors, often with proclined lateral incisors, and an associated deep overbite. This contrasts with Class II division 1, in which the central incisors are proclined rather than retroclined. Recognising this specific subtype is important because treatment approach and biomechanics differ from Class II division 1 management.
questions.question: A patient presents with a Class II molar relationship, retroclined and overlapping maxillary central incisors, a deep overbite, and proclined lateral incisors. This specific presentation is classified as:

options: Direct bony extension of the abscess
Drainage of infection via lymphatic channels
questions.question: The submandibular lymphadenopathy seen in children with dento-alveolar abscess is caused by:
questions.explanation: Submandibular lymphadenopathy in children with dento-alveolar abscess results from lymphatic drainage of the intra-oral infective source through the regional lymph nodes of the head and neck. The submandibular nodes receive drainage from the lower lip, floor of mouth, anterior tongue, and lower anterior teeth. Management addresses the primary dental source (antibiotics, incision and drainage, extraction).

questions.question: A denture-wearing elderly patient presents with erythema and white plaques localised almost exclusively to the palate beneath the denture base. This is most consistent with candidiasis occurring at which oral site preferentially?
questions.explanation: Oral candidiasis commonly localises to the denture-bearing palatal mucosa in denture wearers, a condition known as denture stomatitis, due to a warm, moist, plaque-retentive environment beneath ill-fitting appliances. Poor denture hygiene and continuous wear further predispose to this site-specific infection. Removing the denture at night and improving hygiene are key management steps.

options: As a primary pathogen in all healthy individuals equally
Only in patients with neutrophil counts below 500 cells/µL
When local or systemic factors weaken host defences
Exclusively in patients receiving organ transplants
Only in populations living in tropical climates
questions.question: Candidiasis classified as a 'common opportunistic mycotic disease' implies that it develops primarily:
questions.explanation: Candidiasis is termed an opportunistic mycosis because Candida lacks the inherent pathogenicity to cause disease in a fully intact immune host; it requires predisposing local or systemic factors that compromise host defences to establish infection. These may be local (dentures, antibiotics, mucosal trauma) or systemic (immunodeficiency, diabetes, extremes of age, immunosuppressive drugs). This opportunistic nature explains why Candida is a commensal in 20% of healthy individuals without producing disease.

options: Standard periapical film using paralleling technique
questions.question: A radiology student is asked to identify which of the following is NOT classified as an intraoral radiographic projection.
questions.explanation: The dental panoramic radiograph is an extraoral technique, as the film or sensor and X-ray source are positioned outside the mouth, unlike periapical, bitewing, and occlusal radiographs, which are all intraoral techniques requiring film placement inside the mouth. Recognising this distinction is essential for correctly categorising radiographic techniques. Extraoral and intraoral techniques serve complementary diagnostic purposes.

options: Spring tension, bending force, and gravity
questions.explanation: The three mechanical principles applied in tooth extraction are: the lever (primarily a first-order lever where the fulcrum is between effort and resistance, used in elevators), the wedge (the elevator forced between the root and alveolar bone parallel to the root), and the wheel and axle (a modification of the lever principle used with handle-type elevators). These physical principles are exploited through elevators and forceps.
questions.question: The mechanical principles applied during tooth extraction from physics include:

questions.explanation: Root coverage (mucogingival) surgery, such as a connective tissue graft, is specifically indicated to treat localized gingival recession by covering the exposed root surface, improving both aesthetics and reducing root sensitivity. This differs from procedures aimed at reducing pocket depth or exposing tooth structure, such as gingivectomy or crown lengthening. Case selection depends on factors such as recession classification and the quality and quantity of surrounding periodontal tissue.
options: Guided tissue regeneration for a furcation defect
questions.question: A patient with localized gingival recession on a single tooth, with adequate keratinised tissue on adjacent areas, is treated with a graft procedure to cover the exposed root surface and improve aesthetics. This procedure is best classified as:
Acute oral candidiasis (thrush) is caused by:
questions.explanation: Acute oral candidiasis (thrush) is caused by Candida albicans, a yeast-like fungus that is normally a commensal of the oral cavity and gastrointestinal tract. Disease occurs when actual penetration of the tissues occurs under altered conditions such as immunosuppression, steroid use, or antibiotic therapy. Clinically it presents as soft white slightly elevated plaques most frequently on the buccal mucosa and tongue.

questions.question: A pathology laboratory processes a biopsy specimen and stains the tissue sections with a routine dye combination that highlights nuclei in blue-purple and cytoplasm/connective tissue in pink, allowing assessment of tissue architecture. This staining technique is:
questions.explanation: Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining is the routine staining technique used in histopathology, with haematoxylin staining nuclei blue-purple and eosin staining cytoplasm and connective tissue pink, allowing detailed assessment of tissue architecture. It is the standard stain used in histological investigation of biopsy specimens. Other special stains may be added for specific diagnostic purposes.

questions.question: A child presents with dome-shaped vesicles approximately 2–3 mm in size on the hard palate that rupture to form sharply defined ulcers with erythematous margins. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis characteristically produces dome-shaped vesicles of 2–3 mm that rupture to form circular ulcers with yellowish or grayish floor and erythematous margins. The hard palate and dorsum of tongue are favored sites. Associated features include swollen gingiva, lymphadenopathy, and systemic fever.

The typical progression of untreated dental caries proceeds from reversible pulpitis, to irreversible pulpitis, to periapical abscess formation, and finally to more severe complications such as osteomyelitis or spreading fascial space infection if left unaddressed. Understanding this sequence helps clinicians recognise the urgency of intervention at each stage. Early treatment interrupts this progression and prevents severe systemic complications.
questions.question: A dentist explains the sequelae of untreated dental caries to a patient, describing the progression from least to most severe. Which of the following correctly reflects this typical order of increasing severity?
options: Reversible pulpitis, irreversible pulpitis, periapical abscess, osteomyelitis/fascial space infection
Fascial space infection, reversible pulpitis, periapical abscess, irreversible pulpitis
Osteomyelitis, reversible pulpitis, irreversible pulpitis, periapical abscess
Periapical abscess, osteomyelitis, reversible pulpitis, irreversible pulpitis
Irreversible pulpitis, reversible pulpitis, osteomyelitis, periapical abscess
Only genetic susceptibility, regardless of diet
The frequency of acid challenges to the tooth surface from repeated sugar exposure
Only the pH of drinking water
Only the total daily caloric intake
Only the total volume of saliva produced
questions.explanation: Frequency of sugar consumption is important in caries risk because each exposure to fermentable carbohydrate triggers a period of acid production and reduced plaque pH, and frequent exposures do not allow adequate time for salivary buffering and remineralisation between challenges. This is why frequent snacking on sugary foods is more cariogenic than the same total sugar consumed in a single sitting. Dietary counselling therefore emphasises reducing frequency, not just total quantity.
questions.question: A dentist reviewing a patient's diet history is more concerned about the frequency of sugar intake throughout the day than the total quantity consumed at one sitting. This concern reflects the understanding that caries risk is influenced primarily by:

options: Whether orthodontic treatment is covered by dental insurance
Which dental specialist manages the patient — orthodontist or oral surgeon only
The appropriate shade selection for restorative treatment of affected teeth
Whether the patient requires dental extractions or not in all cases
Whether interceptive treatment or surgical correction alone is feasible
questions.explanation: Distinguishing innate (genetic/intrinsic) from environmental (acquired) aetiological factors determines treatment feasibility and timing. Environmental factors — habits, premature tooth loss, trauma — may be intercepted and corrected during the developmental period, potentially preventing malocclusion or reducing its severity. Innate skeletal factors may require orthognathic surgery for correction in severe cases, as orthodontic forces cannot alter the genetically determined skeletal blueprint. This triage guides early versus late treatment decisions.
questions.question: The concept that 'malocclusion aetiological factors may be innate or environmental' is fundamental because it determines:

questions.explanation: The paradental cyst is an inflammatory odontogenic cyst that develops adjacent to a partially erupted or erupting tooth, most commonly the mandibular first permanent molar in children, associated with pericoronal inflammation during eruption. This differs from a dentigerous cyst, which arises from the reduced enamel epithelium of an unerupted tooth without necessarily involving inflammation. Recognising the inflammatory, eruption-related aetiology helps distinguish this cyst from purely developmental cysts.
questions.question: A patient develops a cyst arising adjacent to an erupting tooth in the alveolar mucosa, following minor trauma or inflammation during eruption, most commonly seen around erupting mandibular first permanent molars in children. This cyst is termed the:
Intracapsular TMJ fracture is classified as which type of TMJ disease?
questions.explanation: Intracapsular TMJ fracture — a fracture through the condylar head within the joint capsule — is classified as a traumatic TMJ disease, alongside birth injury and haemarthrosis. These injuries typically result from direct mandibular trauma or indirect force transmitted through the symphysis. Intracapsular fractures in children are particularly significant because they may damage the condylar growth centre, leading to growth disturbance, ankylosis, and facial asymmetry if unmanaged.

Malocclusion arising from TMJ ankylosis results from disruption of condylar growth due to trauma or infection — both skeletal aetiological factors. The resulting mandibular growth failure and facial asymmetry are skeletal in origin. Under Graber's classification, these fall under 'skeletal factors' including traumatic and infectious subcategories. Treatment requires both surgical release of the ankylosis and orthognathic surgery to correct the established skeletal discrepancy and malocclusion.
options: Soft tissue factors — neutral zone disruption
Skeletal factors — traumatic/infective jaw growth disruption
questions.question: A malocclusion caused by TMJ ankylosis is classified under which aetiological category?

questions.explanation: Peptic ulcer disease is not classified among gastrointestinal causes of oral ulcers. Recognised gastrointestinal diseases causing oral ulcers include Crohn's disease, coeliac disease, and ulcerative colitis. In Crohn's disease, oral lesions may include cobblestone mucosal thickening, linear ulcers, and lip swelling in addition to aphthous-type ulcers. SUBTOPIC 2: DENTAL RADIOLOGY & RADIOGRAPHIC TECHNIQUES
questions.question: Gastrointestinal diseases known to produce oral ulcers include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: HSV-1 is transmitted primarily by droplet spread or direct contact with an active lesion or infected secretions. Primary infection is common and more predominant in children, often presenting subclinically or as mild pharyngitis. The virus can be shed asymptomatically in saliva, making transmission possible even without visible lesions.
questions.question: Which route of transmission is MOST associated with primary HSV-1 infection?
Ludwig's angina is a specific type of:
questions.explanation: Ludwig's angina is a life-threatening bilateral cellulitis involving the submandibular and sublingual spaces, which can rapidly spread to the mediastinum causing airway compromise and death. It is typically of odontogenic origin (most commonly from lower molar infections). Early recognition, airway management, hospitalisation, intravenous antibiotics, and surgical drainage are essential.
options: Herpes zoster of the trigeminal nerve
Dental abscess limited to the alveolar bone
Life-threatening infection of bilateral submandibular/sublingual spaces

questions.question: Glass ionomer cement (GIC) restorations are categorised as:
questions.explanation: Glass ionomer cement is categorised among tooth-coloured intra-coronal restorations, alongside composite and ceramic inlays. GIC has the unique property of bonding chemically to tooth structure and releasing fluoride, making it particularly valuable in high caries-risk patients and for cervical lesions. Compomers are hybrid materials combining GIC and composite properties.

questions.question: The predisposing metabolic climate and disease listed under Graber's hereditary causes of malocclusion refers specifically to:
questions.explanation: Under Graber's general aetiological factors, 'predisposing metabolic climate and disease' refers broadly to systemic conditions — including endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, acromegaly), nutritional deficiencies (rickets, vitamin D deficiency), and metabolic diseases — that alter the biological environment for dentofacial growth and development. These conditions modify the expression of the genetic blueprint for jaw and tooth development, producing secondary dentofacial deformities and malocclusions.
options: Only diabetes mellitus and thyroid disorders
Only hypercementosis and root resorption from local metabolic disease
Bone mineral density changes from osteoporosis affecting arch form
Temporomandibular joint degeneration from gout exclusively
Endocrine, metabolic, and nutritional factors altering growth
Blanched with a white lace pattern
questions.explanation: In primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, the gingiva becomes diffusely erythematous, oedematous, and friable, often bleeding on gentle contact, distinguishing it from localized recurrent lesions. This diffuse gingival involvement is a hallmark that helps differentiate the primary infection from recurrent herpes labialis. The gingival changes typically resolve as the systemic illness subsides.
questions.question: On examination of a child with primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, the gingiva is expected to appear:

questions.explanation: The vesicular rash of herpes zoster is strictly unilateral and does not cross the midline, a distinguishing feature from other vesiculobullous conditions. This unilateral distribution corresponds to the dermatomal territory of the affected nerve. Associated features include regional lymph node enlargement and tenderness, along with the prodromal stage of tingling, burning, and itching.
options: Confined to the oral mucosa only
questions.question: In herpes zoster, the characteristic rash is described as:

questions.explanation: Bisphosphonate medications, used in the management of osteoporosis and certain malignancies, are associated with a risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw following invasive dental procedures such as extraction, due to their effect on bone remodelling and healing capacity. Risk varies depending on factors such as the specific medication, duration of use, and route of administration (oral versus intravenous). Careful risk assessment, and where appropriate, liaison with the prescribing physician, is important before undertaking invasive dental treatment in these patients.
questions.question: A patient taking a bisphosphonate medication for osteoporosis requires extraction of a symptomatic tooth. The dentist is aware of an important potential complication associated with extractions in patients on this medication class. This complication is:
options: Complete inability to achieve local anaesthesia

questions.question: Stillman's cleft is a pathological change in the:
questions.explanation: Stillman's cleft is a slit-like recession defect in the gingival contour, associated with toothbrush trauma or localised inflammation. It differs from physiological scalloping of the healthy gingival contour. Recognising this cleft is important as it may be misdiagnosed as a developmental groove or a root fracture line.

options: Cleft lip and palate, a congenital condition
Abnormal number, size, or position of teeth
questions.explanation: Local (intrinsic) factors in malocclusion according to Graber include anomalies of teeth: abnormal number (hyperdontia, hypodontia), size (microdontia, macrodontia), shape, position, and premature loss of deciduous teeth. These factors act directly on the developing dentition. General (extrinsic) factors — heredity, environment, systemic disease, nutrition, habits — influence the dentoalveolar and skeletal development more broadly.
questions.question: Which of the following constitutes a LOCAL factor in the aetiology of malocclusion according to Graber?
Radiation-associated oral ulcers are typically seen when radiation doses reach the range of:
questions.explanation: Radiation-associated ulcers in head and neck cancer patients are typically seen when large doses in the range of 60–70 Gy are delivered. Both radiation and chemotherapy-induced ulcers result from reduction in basal cell renewal, leading to mucosal atrophy and ulceration. Tissues within the direct path of the radiation beam are most affected.

options: Each intake causes a prolonged drop in pH
Higher frequency raises the total sugar mass consumed
More frequent intake increases salivary flow more
Sugar frequency determines type of bacteria present
questions.explanation: Each intake of fermentable carbohydrate triggers an acid attack by plaque bacteria, lowering oral pH below the critical 5.5 needed for enamel dissolution. With frequent sugar intake, the oral pH remains below the critical level for extended periods, preventing adequate remineralisation between attacks. Reducing the frequency of sugar intake, not merely total amount, is therefore fundamental to caries prevention.
questions.question: The frequency of sugar consumption is important in caries because:

questions.explanation: Peg-shaped lateral incisors are congenitally malformed teeth (microdontia of the upper lateral incisor) that require restoration to restore proper form, function, and aesthetics. Like amelogenesis imperfecta, this represents a developmental indication for restoration. Options include direct composite build-up, porcelain veneers, or crowns depending on the severity and patient requirements.
questions.question: Peg-shaped lateral incisors are classified as which indication for restoration?

questions.explanation: Exodontia is the painless removal of a whole tooth or tooth root with minimal trauma to the investing tissues, ensuring uneventful wound healing and no postoperative pre-prosthetic problems. It is the most frequent oral surgical procedure worldwide, ranging from technically simple to highly challenging. It is irreversible and should be employed only when all treatment alternatives have been excluded.
options: Painless removal of a tooth or root, healing uneventfully
Surgical removal of the impacted third molars only and alone
Orthodontic extraction of teeth for space creation
questions.question: Exodontia is BEST defined as:

Before performing a simple forceps extraction, a surgeon confirms that adequate local anaesthesia has taken full effect, testing soft tissue and bone anaesthesia around the tooth. This preparatory step must be completed FIRST primarily because:
options: It replaces the need for any radiographic assessment
Adequate anaesthesia ensures a pain-free, cooperative patient throughout the procedure
It eliminates the need for post-operative instructions
It guarantees the tooth will not fracture
It has no bearing on the outcome of the extraction
questions.explanation: Confirming adequate local anaesthesia before beginning a forceps extraction is essential to ensure the patient remains pain-free and cooperative throughout the procedure, allowing the surgeon to perform controlled, deliberate movements without patient movement due to pain. Proceeding without confirmed anaesthesia risks patient distress and procedural complications. This preparatory step is a fundamental prerequisite before any extraction technique is applied.

Saliva promotes remineralisation through its calcium, phosphate, and buffering capacity, which neutralise organic acids and supply mineral ions needed to replenish enamel mineral lost during demineralisation. Salivary flow dilutes and clears fermentable carbohydrates from the oral cavity. Reduced salivary flow (xerostomia) dramatically increases caries risk by removing these protective mechanisms.
questions.question: Which salivary property is MOST important for remineralisation of early carious lesions?
The resin matrix of conventional composite resin is MOST commonly composed of:
questions.explanation: The resin matrix of conventional composite resin is most commonly Bis-GMA (bisphenol A-glycidyl methacrylate) or urethane dimethacrylate (UDMA). These high-molecular-weight dimethacrylates provide the structural backbone of the set resin. Diluting monomers such as TEGDMA are added to adjust viscosity. The choice of resin matrix influences polymerisation shrinkage, water sorption, and biocompatibility of the final restoration.

Microfilled composites contain extremely small filler particles that produce a superior surface finish after polishing, making them ideal for anterior aesthetic restorations in low-stress areas. However, their mechanical properties (strength, modulus) are inferior to conventional and hybrid composites. They are not suitable for high-stress posterior load-bearing restorations.
options: Larger filler particle size and better wear resistance
Higher strength and better marginal integrity
Equivalent mechanical properties but darker shades
Better surface smoothness but inferior mechanical properties
Faster polymerization with chemical activation only
questions.question: Microfilled composite resins differ from conventional composites in having:
Caries progression on smooth surfaces from incipient lesion to clinically visible cavitation typically takes:
options: Only days in rampant caries regardless of host
questions.explanation: Incipient caries progresses to clinically visible cavitation on smooth surfaces in approximately 18 months (±6 months) in healthy individuals. Poor oral hygiene and frequent sucrose exposure can produce incipient lesions in as little as 3 weeks, while caries development in healthy individuals is generally slower than in compromised hosts. This progression timeline informs review intervals and treatment timing decisions.

questions.question: A patient with suspected midface fractures requires a radiograph also known as 'Waters' view' to assess the maxillary sinuses and orbital floors. This corresponds to which projection?
questions.explanation: The occipito-mental radiograph, also known as Waters' view, is specifically used to assess the maxillary sinuses, orbital floors, and midface for fractures, as the projection angle clears the petrous temporal bones from overlapping the sinuses. This makes it valuable in trauma assessment of the middle third of the face. It differs from the submentovertex view, which is oriented for the zygomatic arches and skull base.

Chronic marginal gingivitis is most commonly caused by the accumulation of bacterial plaque at the gingival margin, which triggers a local inflammatory response in the absence of adequate oral hygiene. While systemic and hormonal factors can modify the inflammatory response, plaque remains the primary aetiological factor. Effective plaque control is therefore central to both prevention and treatment.
questions.question: A patient with long-standing, slowly progressing, painless gingival inflammation related to accumulated plaque is diagnosed with chronic marginal gingivitis. The MOST common cause of this condition is:

questions.explanation: Dental amalgam is principally indicated for Class I (pits and fissures on occlusal surfaces) and Class II (proximal surface of posterior teeth) cavities, and for Class V cavities where aesthetics is not a concern. Its strength and wear resistance make it ideal for load-bearing posterior restorations. Amalgam is contraindicated in anterior teeth where aesthetics is a priority.
questions.question: Which classification of cavity best describes the TYPICAL indications for dental amalgam?
options: Class III and Class IV only
Class I and II, plus Class V where looks don't matter
Class I cavities in the posterior teeth, plus Class VI lesions
Class II and Class IV only

questions.question: The cavosurface angle (CSA) is defined as:
questions.explanation: The cavosurface angle (CSA) is the angle formed by the junction of a prepared wall and the external surface of the tooth. The actual junction is called the cavosurface margin (CSM). The CSA is named according to the tooth surface it is adjacent to (e.g. buccal CSA). Proper CSA design is critical for marginal integrity and resistance to microleakage at the restoration-tooth interface.
options: The depth of the preparation floor
The outline form of the cavity margin
The angle of the bur during cavity preparation
The taper of the crown preparation
Angle between a prepared wall and tooth surface

questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve block is a technique that deposits local anaesthetic solution near the mandibular foramen to anaesthetise the inferior alveolar nerve (and often the lingual nerve given their close proximity), providing profound anaesthesia of the mandibular teeth, associated bone, and soft tissue on that side, commonly supplemented with a long buccal nerve injection for buccal soft tissue anaesthesia in posterior extractions. This is one of the most commonly used mandibular anaesthesia techniques in oral surgery and general dentistry. Correct technique and anatomical knowledge are essential to achieve reliable anaesthesia and avoid complications such as nerve injury.
questions.question: A patient requires extraction of a tooth under local anaesthesia using a nerve block technique that anaesthetises the inferior alveolar, lingual, and long buccal nerves via a single injection near the mandibular foramen. This specific technique is termed the:

questions.explanation: The TMJ is the articulation between the mandibular condyle and the squamous portion (articular fossa and articular eminence) of the temporal bone. It is a synovial joint separated into upper and lower cavities by a fibrocartilaginous disc (meniscus). Its unique dual-cavity design allows both rotation (lower compartment) and translation (upper compartment), enabling the complex movements of mandibular function.
questions.question: The temporomandibular joint is the articulation between the condyle of the mandible and:
options: The coronoid process and the zygomatic arch
The squamous portion of the temporal bone
The mastoid process of the temporal bone
The styloid process and the hyoid bone
The petrous portion of the temporal bone

questions.question: The MOST widely accepted theory of caries formation is the:
questions.explanation: The acidogenic (chemico-parasitic) theory is the most well-accepted theory of caries formation. It proposes that acid produced by microorganisms acting on sucrose dissolves the organic matrix and mineral content of the tooth through decalcification and dissolution of the softened residue. Other theories including the worm, proteolytic, and proteolysis-chelation theories are of historical interest only.

questions.question: A gingival enlargement where there is an increase in fibrous tissue and decrease in cells is MOST characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis is characterised by a marked increase in collagen fibres (fibrous tissue) and a relative decrease in cellular content, distinguishing it from inflammatory enlargements. Drug-induced and inflammatory enlargements also show fibrosis but with more cellular infiltrate. Biopsy is the definitive diagnostic tool.

Panoramic radiography provides a broad overview of the jaws but has inherent image distortion and overlapping of proximal surfaces, particularly in the premolar region, reducing its reliability for detecting interproximal caries. This is a well-recognised limitation that necessitates supplementary bitewing or periapical films when caries detection is the specific goal. Understanding this trade-off guides appropriate radiographic selection.
questions.question: A dentist reviewing an OPG notices the film reveals overlapping proximal surfaces of the premolars, limiting caries detection at that site, despite good overall image quality of the jaws. This limitation is an inherent trade-off of which imaging technique?

questions.explanation: Amalgam restorations require adequate bulk of material to resist fracture under occlusal load, and the accepted minimum pulpal floor depth for a Class II amalgam preparation is approximately 1.5-2 mm into dentin. Insufficient depth predisposes the restoration to marginal fracture and isthmus failure. This requirement reflects amalgam's relatively brittle nature compared with bonded composite materials.
questions.question: A dentist evaluates a Class I amalgam restoration that repeatedly fractures at the isthmus. Reviewing preparation depth, the dentist notes the pulpal floor was prepared with insufficient bulk. According to accepted principles, the minimum recommended pulpal floor depth for an amalgam Class II restoration is approximately:

questions.explanation: Retroviral screening for HIV is indicated in patients presenting with features suggestive of immunosuppression, such as recurrent infections, unexplained weight loss, or oral manifestations like persistent candidiasis, before undertaking invasive procedures. Identifying an underlying immunosuppressive state allows appropriate precautions and management planning. It also has implications for wound healing and postoperative infection risk.
questions.question: A patient scheduled for multiple extractions has a history of recurrent infections and unexplained weight loss. The clinician wishes to screen for underlying immunosuppressive disease before proceeding. Which investigation is specifically indicated?

questions.explanation: A denture is a dental prosthesis that replaces one or more missing teeth or the entire dentition and associated structures in the maxillary or mandibular arch or both. It can be partial (replacing some teeth) or complete (replacing all teeth). Dentures restore mastication, aesthetics, phonetics, and prevent drifting of adjacent and opposing teeth.
questions.question: A dental prosthesis that replaces one or more missing teeth and associated structures in one or both arches is called:

options: An imbalance between demineralisation and remineralisation
An isolated bacterial infection unrelated to diet
questions.question: Caries is best conceptually defined, according to the modern dynamic understanding of the disease process, as resulting from:
questions.explanation: The current dynamic concept of caries describes the disease as a continuous imbalance between demineralisation, driven by bacterial acid production, and remineralisation, supported by saliva and fluoride. When demineralisation exceeds remineralisation over time, net mineral loss and cavitation occur. This concept underlies modern preventive strategies aimed at shifting the balance toward remineralisation.

questions.question: Which Candida species OTHER than C. albicans is commonly associated with clinical infection?
options: Candida auris and Candida tropicalis only
Candida glabrata, Candida krusei, and Candida parapsilosis
Candida stellatoidea and Candida lusitaniae only
Candida famata and Candida guilliermondii only
Only C. albicans causes clinical infection in humans
questions.explanation: While C. albicans is the principal species associated with infection in immunocompromised patients, other clinically important Candida species include C. glabrata, C. krusei, and C. parapsilosis. C. krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole, making species identification clinically critical for antifungal selection. C. glabrata shows reduced susceptibility to azoles. Non-albicans Candida species have increased in frequency with greater use of azole prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients.

questions.question: A patient with disseminated herpes zoster involving the trigeminal dermatome is noted to have a rash that is best described on examination as:
options: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
questions.explanation: Herpes zoster classically presents as grouped (clustered) vesicles on an erythematous base, distributed unilaterally along a single dermatome, distinguishing it from other vesiculobullous conditions. The unilateral, dermatomal pattern is a key diagnostic clue. Lesions progress through vesicle, pustule, and crust stages before healing.

options: Routine pre-extraction workup in all patients
questions.question: Clotting profile investigations before oral surgical procedures are indicated for:
questions.explanation: Clotting profile (including PT, aPTT, INR, platelet count) is ordered for patients with suspected or confirmed bleeding disorders as a baseline investigation before any surgical procedure. Without establishing baseline haemostatic parameters, post-extraction haemorrhage risk cannot be adequately managed. Patients on anticoagulant therapy also require clotting profile assessment.

In FDI notation, the first digit denotes the quadrant, with '3' representing the lower left quadrant, and the second digit denotes the tooth position, with '7' being the second molar and '8' the third molar. Therefore, '37, 38' refers to the lower left second and third molars. This system avoids ambiguity present in other notation systems.
options: Lower left second and third molars
Upper left second and third molars
Lower right second and third molars
Upper right second and third molars
Lower left first and second molars
questions.question: Using FDI two-digit notation, a radiograph report describes findings on teeth '37' and '38'. These numbers correspond anatomically to:

A patient with an untreated carious molar develops a spreading facial swelling extending into the buccal and submandibular spaces, attributed to bacterial spread beyond the tooth. This sequela of untreated caries, involving spread of infection into adjacent soft tissue spaces, is termed:
questions.explanation: Untreated dental caries can progress through pulpitis and periapical infection to spread beyond the confines of the tooth into adjacent fascial spaces, resulting in cellulitis or abscess formation such as buccal or submandibular space infection. This represents a serious sequela requiring prompt drainage and antimicrobial therapy. Left untreated, such spread can progress to life-threatening complications such as Ludwig's angina.
options: Simple pulpitis confined to the tooth

questions.explanation: Innate immunity and T-cell responses are most critical in protecting against superficial mucosal candidal infections. Neutrophils and mononuclear phagocytes play the dominant role in deep systemic infections. Patients with defects in Th17 lymphocyte responses (e.g., STAT3 mutations causing hyper-IgE syndrome) are particularly susceptible to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, demonstrating the importance of T-cell immunity for mucosal protection.
options: Candidal osteomyelitis of the jaw bone
Candidal endocarditis from IV drug use
questions.question: The innate and Tcell immune responses are particularly important in which type of candidal infection?

options: Supersaturation with calcium and phosphate ions
questions.explanation: Saliva supersaturated with calcium and phosphate ions is essential for remineralisation of early carious lesions, as these ions diffuse into the demineralised enamel to restore mineral content, particularly when supported by fluoride presence. A low flow rate or acidic resting pH would instead promote further demineralisation rather than repair. This property underlies the rationale for saliva stimulation and substitutes in patients with hyposalivation.
questions.question: A dentist explains to a patient that the caries process depends not only on bacteria and diet but also on host-related salivary factors. Which specific salivary property is MOST important for remineralisation of an early carious lesion?

options: Reducing sucrose concentration in the diet
questions.explanation: Fluoride promotes remineralisation of early caries lesions and incorporates into the enamel crystal structure (forming fluorapatite), which is more resistant to acid dissolution than hydroxyapatite. It also inhibits certain enzymatic processes in cariogenic bacteria. Fluoride can be delivered topically (toothpaste, varnish, gels) or systemically (fluoridated water, supplements).
questions.question: The role of fluoride in caries prevention includes:
Periodontal abscess is classified under which category of the periodontal disease classification?
questions.explanation: The periodontal abscess is classified under 'Abscesses of the Periodontium,' which includes gingival abscess, periodontal abscess, and pericoronal abscess. A periodontal abscess arises within a pre-existing periodontal pocket and is characterised by acute localised pain, swelling, and suppuration. Prompt diagnosis and drainage are critical to prevent local and systemic spread.

questions.question: Which systemic disease is associated with periodontitis as a manifestation of a haematological disorder?
questions.explanation: Periodontitis can manifest as a feature of haematological disorders such as acquired neutropenia and leukaemias, where deficiency or dysfunction of neutrophils impairs the host's first line of defence against periodontal pathogens. Clinicians should consider a haematological workup in young patients presenting with severe periodontitis disproportionate to local factors.

questions.question: A patient with a high, malpositioned restoration develops periodontal breakdown at that specific tooth, occurring on a background of pre-existing periodontal disease at that site. This is best described as:
options: Chronic marginal gingivitis unrelated to occlusion
questions.explanation: Secondary occlusal trauma refers to periodontal injury resulting from normal or abnormal occlusal forces applied to a tooth whose periodontal support has already been compromised by pre-existing periodontal disease. This differs from primary occlusal trauma, which occurs in a periodontium with normal support subjected to excessive forces. Recognising this distinction is important for appropriate management, which may include occlusal adjustment alongside periodontal therapy.

questions.question: In oral pathology investigation, WBC with differentials is specifically useful for detecting:
options: Leukaemia and agranulocytosis of oral tissues
Renal failure affecting drug metabolism rate
questions.explanation: WBC with differential count identifies abnormalities in individual white cell lines, enabling detection of leukaemia (elevated blast cells), neutropenia/agranulocytosis (reduced neutrophils), and other haematological disorders that cause gingival changes and oral ulcers. In acute leukaemia, gingival infiltration by leukaemic cells may be the presenting feature alerting the dentist to the systemic diagnosis.

questions.question: Anterior disc displacement WITH reduction in the TMJ is characterised clinically by:
questions.explanation: Anterior disc displacement with reduction produces a characteristic reciprocal clicking: a click on opening (as the condyle recaptures the anteriorly displaced disc) and a click on closing (as the disc re-displaces anteriorly). The mouth can open fully. In anterior disc displacement without reduction ('closed lock'), the disc does not recapture, producing restricted opening and no click — a more serious condition requiring active management.
options: Severe restriction of opening with no joint sounds at all
Crepitus throughout the full range of movement only
Acute locking with the mouth half-open
Bilateral condylar hyperplasia causing progressive open bite
Clicking on opening and closing as the disc reduces

questions.explanation: Mumps is an acute viral infection that primarily targets the parotid gland, producing characteristic painful bilateral or unilateral swelling. It is caused by a paramyxovirus and spreads via respiratory droplets. Complications can include orchitis, pancreatitis, and rarely sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.question: A child presents with painful bilateral parotid swelling, fever, and difficulty chewing. Which gland is primarily affected in this classic presentation?
Which investigation tool uses laser-induced fluorescence to detect caries?
questions.explanation: Diagnodent uses laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) to detect caries by measuring the fluorescent light emitted by bacterial porphyrins in carious lesions. It is particularly useful for detecting early occlusal caries and sub-surface lesions not yet visible clinically or radiographically. It provides a numerical reading, helping clinicians decide on active monitoring versus surgical intervention.

Salivary cytological examination is an example of exfoliative cytology, collecting cells that have naturally shed or been scraped from epithelial surfaces. As with all cytology, it is an adjunct to rather than a replacement for biopsy-based histological diagnosis. It is non-invasive and can be repeated easily for monitoring purposes. SUBTOPIC 4: DENTAL CARIES – ETIOLOGY, PATHOLOGY & MANAGEMENT
questions.question: In oral pathology, cytological examination of saliva is an example of:

questions.explanation: Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and 2-hour post-prandial glucose (2HPP) are ordered in suspected diabetes mellitus cases presenting with oral manifestations, or in poorly controlled diabetics with recalcitrant oral infections. Uncontrolled diabetes impairs immune function, wound healing, and promotes candidal infections. Identifying glycaemic control status is essential before oral surgical procedures.
questions.question: Haematological investigation with FPG + 2HPP is specifically ordered when:

questions.explanation: A white blood cell count with differential is particularly useful for detecting leukaemia, as abnormal blast cells and altered lymphocyte counts may be first identified through this simple, widely available test. Oral manifestations of leukaemia, such as gingival enlargement or spontaneous bleeding, may prompt this investigation. Early detection allows timely referral for definitive haematological diagnosis and management.
questions.question: A patient's white blood cell count with differential shows marked lymphocytosis with abnormal blast cells, prompting further haematological workup. Which oral pathology finding would this investigation be MOST useful for detecting?

options: Only a different type of forceps
Bone removal or tooth sectioning after flap elevation
Administration of intravenous antibiotics before the procedure
Use of rotary instruments for cavity preparation only
questions.explanation: Surgical (transalveolar) extraction involves elevation of a mucoperiosteal flap, removal of overlying alveolar bone, and/or tooth sectioning to facilitate removal of teeth that cannot be extracted by simple closed-technique forceps methods alone. Indications include impacted teeth, dilacerated roots, hypercementosis, ankylosis, and grossly broken-down roots. The approach allows controlled tooth removal with preservation of adjacent structures.
questions.question: A surgical (transalveolar) extraction differs from a simple intra-alveolar extraction in that it requires:
Ankyloglossia (tongue tie) is treated by:
questions.explanation: Ankyloglossia (tongue tie) results from a short lingual frenum or anterior attachment of the frenum to the tip of the tongue, present at birth. It does not prevent speech entirely but affects articulation quality. Treatment is frenectomy—surgical release of the lingual frenum—which improves tongue mobility. Referral is typically to an oral surgeon or paediatric dentist.
options: Orthodontic expansion of the lower arch
Frenectomy (surgical release of the lingual frenum)
Watchful waiting until adult life in all cases

questions.question: A patient with long-standing, untreated TMJ ankylosis from childhood trauma presents as an adult with severe limitation of mouth opening and facial asymmetry. Management of established bony ankylosis in this patient would MOST likely require:
questions.explanation: Established bony TMJ ankylosis, particularly of long duration, typically requires surgical intervention such as gap arthroplasty or interpositional arthroplasty to restore joint mobility, combined with aggressive postoperative physiotherapy to maintain the surgically achieved range of motion and prevent reankylosis. Conservative measures alone are generally insufficient once true bony fusion has occurred. Early diagnosis and management of the underlying cause in childhood can help prevent this severe long-term complication.
options: Conservative management with soft diet alone
Surgical intervention (e.g. gap arthroplasty) with postoperative physiotherapy
Occlusal splint therapy alone without surgery

questions.question: Which class of restoration by G.V. Black specifically addresses caries on the proximal surfaces of posterior teeth?
questions.explanation: Class II restorations address caries on the proximal (mesial and/or distal) surfaces of posterior teeth (premolars and molars). They are among the most technically demanding restorations due to the need to restore interproximal contact and contour. Class I involves pits and fissures, Class III involves proximal surfaces of anteriors, Class IV adds the incisal angle, and Class V involves the cervical third of all teeth.

questions.question: A patient presents after facial trauma with suspected fracture of the zygomatic arch and orbital floor. The clinician requests a radiograph that is also known as the 'jug-handle view'. This corresponds to which projection?
