Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology is the dental specialty concerned with the production and interpretation of images of the teeth, jaws, and surrounding orofacial structures, both intraorally and extraorally, to aid diagnosis and treatment planning. It underpins nearly every other dental specialty by providing essential diagnostic information. Its scope includes both conventional and advanced imaging modalities.
questions.question: A dentist explains that oral and maxillofacial radiology, as a dental specialty, is primarily concerned with which scope of practice?
options: Production and interpretation of images of the teeth, jaws, and orofacial structures
Only the treatment of jaw fractures surgically
Only the fabrication of dental prostheses

questions.explanation: Smoking cessation is associated with improved response to periodontal therapy and reduced further disease progression, as the harmful vascular and immune effects of tobacco on periodontal tissues are reduced once smoking stops, even though it does not reverse pre-existing attachment or bone loss. This makes smoking cessation counselling an important component of comprehensive periodontal management in patients who smoke. Combining behavioural counselling with periodontal therapy improves overall long-term outcomes.
options: Complete reversal of all pre-existing attachment loss
Worsened periodontal healing compared with continued smoking
Improved response to periodontal therapy and reduced disease progression
Immediate regrowth of lost alveolar bone
No measurable difference in periodontal healing
questions.question: A patient with chronic periodontitis has been advised that smoking significantly worsens both disease severity and treatment outcomes. When counselling this patient, the dentist explains that smoking cessation is associated with:

options: Iatrogenic chemical burns from dental materials
questions.explanation: Factitious ulcers are not very common and are typically a consequence of a disturbed mental state, often representing a 'call for attention.' They may on rare occasions be a prelude to suicidal behaviour. Clinical features suggesting a factitious ulcer include bizarre configuration with sharp outlines, lack of correspondence with any recognizable disease pattern, and location in areas accessible to the patient.
questions.question: Factitious oral ulcers are most commonly a consequence of:

options: When the permanent successor is in a good position to erupt
When the patient prefers a removable partial denture
When the deciduous tooth is still firmly retained with no pathology
At any age the patient requests it regardless of successor status
Only when the deciduous tooth is grossly carious with pulp exposure
questions.explanation: A retained deciduous tooth is indicated for extraction when its permanent successor is in a good position to erupt and the retained deciduous tooth is preventing or delaying this eruption. Extraction in this context facilitates normal dental development and prevents the successor from erupting ectopically. If there is no permanent successor, the retained deciduous tooth may serve a valuable function and be preserved as long as possible.
questions.question: Which of the following is an indication for extracting a retained deciduous tooth?
A paradental cyst falls under which subcategory of the odontogenic cyst classification?
questions.explanation: The paradental cyst is classified as an inflammatory odontogenic cyst, alongside the radicular cyst. It typically occurs adjacent to the crown of a partially erupted or impacted mandibular third molar and is associated with pericoronitis. Unlike the radicular cyst which arises from the root apex, the paradental cyst forms laterally or distally to the crown from inflammatory stimulation of the reduced enamel epithelium.

Fissure sealants prevent caries by physically occluding the pits and fissures, eliminating the anatomical stagnation areas where plaque accumulates. This converts an inaccessible caries-prone surface into a smooth, cleansable surface. Resin-based sealants may also release small amounts of fluoride, but their primary preventive mechanism is physical occlusion of susceptible morphology.
questions.question: Fissure sealants prevent caries by:
options: Releasing fluoride into the enamel continuously
Increasing salivary flow to the posterior teeth
Physically occluding the pit and fissure areas
Remineralising the enamel beneath the sealant
Complete absence of any technique sensitivity
Lower cost compared with all other ceramic systems
Inability to be milled using CAD/CAM technology
Superior natural translucency compared with feldspathic porcelain
Superior fracture resistance under high occlusal load
questions.question: A patient requires a full crown, and the dentist selects a zirconia-based ceramic material due to its high flexural strength. Compared with feldspathic porcelain, zirconia is generally favoured for posterior crowns primarily because of its:
questions.explanation: Zirconia-based ceramics are favoured for posterior crowns, which experience high occlusal loads, primarily due to their superior flexural strength and fracture resistance compared with more traditional feldspathic porcelain, which is more prone to brittle fracture under heavy load. Feldspathic porcelain, in contrast, often offers superior translucency and is generally preferred for highly aesthetic anterior restorations where load is lower. Material selection therefore balances strength requirements against aesthetic demands depending on the restoration's location.

options: Only tooth colour and enamel thickness
Only jaw bone density and eruption timing
Tooth size, arch size, muscle and tongue shape
Salivary flow rate and oral pH levels only
questions.question: Heredity influences which specific dental characteristics that may lead to malocclusion?
questions.explanation: Heredity directly influences tooth size, arch length and width, height of the palatal vault, position and configuration of muscles, tongue size and shape, character of the oral mucosa, and tendency for crowding, spacing, overbite, and overjet. These heritable traits collectively determine the dentofacial architectural blueprint. Racial and familial characteristics repeat across generations, making family history an important component of orthodontic diagnosis.

questions.question: Black's classification of dental caries is based primarily on:
options: The tooth surface and anatomy affected
The rate of progression of the lesion
questions.explanation: G.V. Black's classification (Class I–V, with some sources adding Class VI) categorises caries by the tooth surface and anatomical site of the lesion. Class I affects pits and fissures; Class II affects the mesial or distal surfaces of posterior teeth; Class III affects proximal surfaces of anterior teeth; Class IV adds the incisal angle; Class V affects the cervical third of all teeth. This classification underpins cavity design principles for restorations.

options: Degrading cell walls of host epithelium
Aiding survival inside cells, resisting oxidative killing
Producing haemolysins that lyse red blood cells
questions.question: Candida produces catalases that specifically aid its pathogenicity by:
questions.explanation: Catalases produced by Candida protect the organism from oxidative killing by neutrophils and macrophages, enabling intracellular survival and persistence within phagosomes. Candida also produces adenosine that blocks neutrophil oxygen radical production and degranulation, and proteinases that encourage tissue invasiveness. These combined virulence mechanisms explain why predisposing factors that impair phagocyte function dramatically increase candidiasis risk.

In modified tooth preparation for bonded composite restorations, the cavity depth is generally shallower than in conventional amalgam preparation because the adhesive bond to enamel and dentin reduces the need for mechanical retention features such as depth-dependent undercuts. This allows for more conservative removal of tooth structure. Amalgam, lacking adhesive bonding, relies more heavily on mechanically retentive cavity geometry.
questions.question: A dentist preparing a cavity for a bonded composite restoration, compared with the classical preparation for amalgam, typically prepares the cavity depth to be:
options: Deeper, to compensate for weaker material strength
Shallower, since bonding does not require mechanical retention depth

questions.explanation: Resistance form refers to the shape given to a cavity preparation that enables both the tooth structure and the restorative material to withstand occlusal forces without fracture. Adequate depth and flat pulpal/gingival floors are features that provide resistance form. This differs from retention form, which specifically prevents displacement or dislodgement of the restoration.
questions.question: A dentist prepares a Class II amalgam cavity and ensures the pulpal floor is at least 0.5-1mm into dentin to provide adequate bulk for the restorative material to resist fracture under occlusal load. This principle of cavity preparation is termed:

questions.explanation: Condylar agenesis — the complete absence of the mandibular condyle — is classified as a developmental TMJ condition, alongside condylar hyperplasia, condylar hypoplasia, and bifid condyle. These conditions arise from disruptions in embryonic or post-natal development of the condyle rather than trauma, infection, or systemic disease. Condylar agenesis produces severe facial asymmetry, malocclusion, and functional impairment requiring complex orthognathic and prosthetic rehabilitation.
questions.question: Condylar agenesis (absence of the condyle) represents which category of TMJ developmental condition?

questions.explanation: Fasting plasma glucose combined with a two-hour postprandial glucose (FPG + 2HPP) is specifically ordered when diabetes mellitus is suspected, such as in a patient with recurrent candidiasis, polyuria, and polydipsia. Undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes increases the risk of delayed healing and infection following extraction. Identifying this metabolic disorder preoperatively allows better perioperative glycaemic control.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent oral candidiasis, polyuria, and polydipsia is being worked up before extraction of a grossly carious tooth. Which haematological investigation, including a two-hour postprandial value, would specifically be ordered?
options: Fasting plasma glucose plus 2-hour postprandial glucose
At 45 degrees to the epithelial surface
At 30 degrees to enable bevelled edges
At any angle convenient to the surgeon
questions.question: When making intraoral incisions, the blade should be applied to the tissue at which orientation?
questions.explanation: Incisions should be made perpendicular to the epithelial surface to produce vertical incision walls that align accurately during closure, promote primary healing, and reduce scarring. Bevelled incisions produce wound edges of unequal thickness that are difficult to appose and heal poorly. Using a sharp blade with firm continuous strokes further minimises tissue trauma and promotes predictable healing.

questions.question: A patient with a severely retrognathic mandible and a Class II skeletal relationship is noted to have a convex facial profile. This facial profile finding corresponds MOST closely to which skeletal classification?
options: Bimaxillary protrusion unrelated to skeletal class
questions.explanation: A convex facial profile, where the mandible is retrognathic relative to the maxilla, corresponds to a Class II skeletal relationship, in which the mandible lies posterior to its ideal position relative to the maxilla. A Class III relationship typically produces a concave profile due to mandibular prognathism. Assessing facial profile is a rapid clinical method of estimating underlying skeletal classification.

questions.question: Dental panoramic radiography is an extra-oral technique that produces:
questions.explanation: Dental panoramic radiography (OPG/orthopantomogram) is an extra-oral projection that produces an image of both jaws and their respective dentitions on a single extra-oral film. It provides a broad overview of the entire dentition, supporting structures, and surrounding anatomy. It is widely used for assessment of impacted teeth, cysts, fractures, and pathology of the jaws.
options: Separate images of each dental arch shown on individual films
Cross-sectional views of alveolar bone only
A lateral skull projection for cephalometric analysis
An image of both jaws and dentitions on one film

questions.question: A radiographer describes two techniques for positioning bitewing film in the mouth. These two main positioning techniques for bitewing radiography are:
questions.explanation: The two main positioning techniques for bitewing radiography are the simple tab (bite-tab) technique, where the patient bites on a paper or plastic tab attached to the film, and the film-holder technique, which uses a dedicated holder for more precise, reproducible positioning. Both aim to position the film parallel to the crowns of the posterior teeth. Film-holders generally provide more consistent, reproducible image geometry.
options: Paralleling and bisecting angle techniques only
The anterior disc moves forward with the condyle via lateral pterygoid fibres
The disc is static and does not move during any mandibular movement
The posterior band bears all compressive forces during biting
The anterior band provides all proprioceptive feedback to the trigeminal sensory system
The posterior band tears first in all cases of disc displacement
questions.question: The posterior of the TMJ disc is less dense and attaches nearer the temporal bone, while anteriorly it is attached near the condyle. The clinical consequence of this architecture is that:
questions.explanation: The anterior margin of the TMJ disc and adjoining capsule receive the insertion of the upper fibres of the lateral pterygoid muscle, meaning the anterior disc moves forward with the condyle during protrusion and wide opening. The posterior disc attachment to the temporal bone restricts its posterior freedom but the bilaminar zone's elasticity allows controlled posterior displacement during closing. This architectural arrangement ensures the disc remains interposed between condyle and temporal bone throughout function.

questions.question: A patient presents with a firm, deep swelling in the parotid region. To obtain cells for cytological diagnosis without open surgery, the clinician inserts a fine needle into the mass and applies suction to collect cellular material. This procedure is:
questions.explanation: Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) involves inserting a fine needle into a deep-seated mass and applying suction to aspirate cellular material for cytological examination, avoiding the need for open surgical biopsy. It is particularly useful for deep swellings such as salivary gland or lymph node masses. It is less invasive but provides less architectural information than a tissue biopsy.

Clinical attachment level is measured from a fixed anatomical reference point, the cemento-enamel junction, to the base of the periodontal pocket, providing a more accurate reflection of true periodontal attachment loss compared with probing depth alone, which can be confounded by gingival swelling or recession affecting the position of the gingival margin. This makes clinical attachment level a more reliable indicator of disease severity and progression over time. It is essential for accurate periodontal diagnosis and monitoring.
questions.question: A dentist measures periodontal destruction using the cemento-enamel junction as a fixed reference point rather than the gingival margin, which can be affected by swelling or recession. This measurement is termed:

A dentist requests investigation for a suspected mandibular fracture that requires assessment of the whole width of the mandible from front to back, viewed directly from behind the patient. Which radiograph best serves this purpose?
questions.explanation: The postero-anterior (PA) view of the jaws is used to assess the width and symmetry of the mandible and detect displaced fractures, as the X-ray beam passes from behind the patient's head through to the front. It provides a frontal perspective that complements lateral views in trauma assessment. This makes it useful for evaluating conditions such as mandibular asymmetry or fractures.

In the bisecting angle technique, the X-ray beam is directed perpendicular to an imaginary line that bisects the angle formed between the long axis of the tooth and the plane of the film, based on the geometric principle of equal triangles. This technique is used when the paralleling technique is not feasible due to anatomical limitations, such as a shallow palate. It is more prone to image distortion than the paralleling technique.
options: The tooth's long axis only, regardless of film position
The film only, regardless of tooth angulation
The imaginary bisector between the tooth's long axis and the film
questions.question: A dentist compares the bisecting angle technique to the paralleling technique for periapical radiography. In the bisecting angle technique, the X-ray beam is directed at right angles to:
Oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMFS) is defined as the branch of surgery dealing with:
questions.explanation: Oral and maxillofacial surgery is defined as the surgical specialty dealing with conditions of the face, jaws, and oral cavity, encompassing extractions, dentoalveolar surgery, facial trauma, pathology, orthognathic surgery, and oncological reconstruction. It is a discipline at the interface of dentistry and medicine, requiring both dental and medical training in many countries.
options: Skin and soft tissue of the neck only
Orthopaedic conditions of the temporomandibular joint only
Reconstructive surgery of the salivary glands only
Surgical conditions of the face, jaws, oral cavity

questions.question: TMJ osteomyelitis in a YOUNG patient is specifically listed as an infectious cause of malocclusion because it can:
questions.explanation: TMJ osteomyelitis in children and young patients can destroy the growing condyle, eliminating the primary growth centre for the mandible on the affected side. This results in reduced mandibular growth and consequent malocclusion — typically Class II deviation to the affected side with facial asymmetry. Early treatment of TMJ infections and careful long-term orthodontic and surgical management of the resulting malocclusion are essential.
options: Causes condylar destruction, affecting mandibular growth
Directly kill Candida colonising the oral cavity
Produce ipsilateral enlargement of the condyle only

questions.explanation: A strong familial pattern of similar skeletal relationships, such as mandibular prognathism observed across generations, is best classified as a genetic (hereditary) factor contributing to malocclusion, reflecting inherited growth patterns of the jaws. This differs from local environmental factors such as habits or premature tooth loss, which are acquired rather than inherited. Recognising a genetic component has implications for prognosis and the likely stability of orthodontic or orthognathic treatment outcomes.
questions.question: A patient with a Class III skeletal pattern is noted to have both parents with similarly prognathic mandibles, suggesting a strong familial pattern. This aetiological factor for the patient's malocclusion is best classified as:
Cleft lip and palate as a congenital skeletal cause of malocclusion produces which SPECIFIC dental effect?
options: Microdontia or missing lateral incisor near the cleft
A Class III malocclusion from mandibular prognathism alone
Supernumerary teeth remote from the cleft site
Generalised enamel hypoplasia of all permanent teeth
Mandibular torus formation on the lingual aspect
questions.explanation: Cleft lip and palate (CLP) characteristically affects the maxillary lateral incisor adjacent to the cleft — it may be absent (congenitally missing), microdont (peg-shaped), or duplicated as a supernumerary tooth. This dental anomaly arises from the disruption of the dental lamina in the cleft zone. Comprehensive management of CLP requires a multidisciplinary team including orthodontists, oral surgeons, and prosthodontists to address these dental sequelae alongside the structural cleft repair.

options: Only the mandible from the maxilla
Only the zygomatic arch from the maxilla
The lower maxilla (tooth-bearing segment) from the rest of the midface
The entire maxilla from the cranial base at the highest level
Only the nasal bones from the frontal bone
questions.question: A patient presents with a Le Fort I level maxillary fracture following high-impact facial trauma. This fracture pattern is characterised by a fracture line that separates:
questions.explanation: A Le Fort I fracture is characterised by a horizontal fracture line that separates the lower maxilla, including the tooth-bearing alveolar segment and hard palate, from the rest of the midface, resulting in a mobile 'floating' maxillary segment on clinical examination. This is the lowest level of the three classic Le Fort fracture patterns, with Le Fort II and III involving progressively higher and more extensive fracture lines through the midface and cranial base respectively. Correct classification guides appropriate surgical fixation planning.

questions.question: The most common soft tissue oral lesion overall is:
questions.explanation: Traumatic ulcers are the most common soft tissue oral lesions and a clear cause-and-effect relationship is usually identifiable. They most frequently result from accidental trauma to regions easily trapped between the teeth such as the lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa. Unlike recurrent aphthous stomatitis, they do not recur once the causative trauma is removed.

questions.question: A clinician notes that digital radiography allows post-acquisition adjustment of brightness, contrast, and magnification without repeating the exposure. This capability is an example of which advantage of digital imaging?
questions.explanation: In digital radiography, radiographic images can be manipulated electronically to adjust brightness, contrast, and magnification after acquisition, improving diagnostic yield without the need for repeat exposures. This is a key advantage over conventional film, which cannot be altered once processed. Other advantages include instant availability and easy digital storage and transfer.

questions.question: A patient on long-term nifedipine for hypertension develops generalised, fibrous enlargement of the interdental papillae without significant inflammation. This gingival change is best attributed to:
questions.explanation: Nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, is a recognised cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth, characterised by fibrous enlargement of the interdental papillae, similar to changes seen with phenytoin and cyclosporine. This overgrowth can be exacerbated by co-existing plaque-induced inflammation but has a distinct pharmacological aetiology. Management includes improved oral hygiene and, if severe, surgical recontouring or medication review with the physician.
options: Scorbutic gingivitis from vitamin C deficiency

questions.question: Before performing a simple forceps extraction, the surgeon must ensure which preparatory step is completed FIRST?
questions.explanation: Pre-operative assessment is the essential first step, encompassing presurgical medical assessment (relevant systemic conditions, medications, allergies), general patient assessment (biodata, demeanour, vital signs), and clinical evaluation of the tooth (access, mobility, crown condition) and radiographic review. Skipping this step risks complications from unrecognised medical conditions or surgical difficulties that could have been anticipated.

Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the tissues surrounding a dental implant, characterised by bleeding on probing, increased probing depth, and progressive loss of supporting bone, closely analogous to periodontitis affecting a natural tooth, though the surrounding biological tissues differ somewhat in structure. Both conditions are driven by bacterial biofilm accumulation and require appropriate mechanical and, where indicated, surgical management to arrest progression. Regular maintenance and early detection are key to managing peri-implant disease effectively.
questions.question: A patient develops peri-implantitis around a previously well-integrated dental implant, presenting with bleeding on probing, increased probing depth, and radiographic bone loss around the implant. This condition is best understood as analogous to which natural tooth condition?
options: Simple gingivitis without any bone involvement

questions.explanation: In the lower true occlusal projection, the X-ray beam is directed vertically downward through the floor of the mouth onto the occlusal film, producing a cross-sectional view of the mandible useful for assessing buccolingual position of structures such as impacted teeth or sialoliths in the submandibular duct. This differs from oblique occlusal projections that angle the beam. Understanding beam direction is key to interpreting this projection correctly.
questions.question: A general dentist wants a projection to assess the transverse relationship of an impacted canine relative to the floor of the nose in the mandible, using a technique in which the beam is directed vertically downward through the tongue toward the film placed on the occlusal surface. This describes the:

options: Technique sensitivity and lengthy placement time
questions.question: A dentist selects direct filling gold for a small Class I cavity in a patient wanting maximum longevity, understanding this material requires meticulous, time-consuming, layer-by-layer condensation technique. Compared with amalgam, direct filling gold's main disadvantage in modern practice is:
questions.explanation: Direct filling gold offers excellent biocompatibility, marginal adaptation, and longevity, but its main disadvantage in modern practice is the significant technique sensitivity and lengthy chairside time required for meticulous, incremental condensation, making it far less commonly used today compared with amalgam or composite. Despite these excellent physical properties, practical constraints have limited its contemporary use. It remains valued in select, small, low-stress cavity situations where cost and time are not limiting factors.

questions.question: Retroviral screening in oral pathology is indicated when patients present with:
questions.explanation: Retroviral screening is indicated in suspected cases presenting with a combination of features such as oral candidiasis, bilateral parotid gland enlargement, and recalcitrant extensive oral aphthous ulcerations—features suggestive of HIV infection. HIV compromises cell-mediated immunity, predisposing to opportunistic oral infections. Early identification enables appropriate antiretroviral management and prevention of transmission.
options: Bilateral parotid swelling with candida and aphthous sores
Traumatic ulcers affecting only the lateral tongue surface
Surgical field free of blood and other fluids
questions.explanation: Adequate surgical visibility depends on mouth opening (access), surgical exposure (incision and flap), retraction (maintaining access), adequate lighting, and a blood-free operative field. Radiographic magnification provides pre-operative diagnostic information but does not constitute an intraoperative visibility requirement. Failure to achieve any of the first four components compromises the surgeon's view and significantly increases the risk of procedural complications.
questions.question: Adequate access for surgical visibility depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
The paralleling (long cone) technique for periapical radiography requires the film to be:
questions.explanation: In the paralleling technique, the film packet is placed in a holder parallel to the long axis of the tooth, and the X-ray tubehead is aimed at right angles (vertically and horizontally) to both the tooth and the film packet. A long cone of 12 inches is used. The use of a film holder with fixed positions makes this technique reproducible.
options: Placed close to the tooth and angled at 45°
Parallel to the tooth's axis, beam at right angles
Touching directly against the lingual surface of the tooth
Positioned outside the mouth opposite the X-ray source
Placed on the occlusal surfaces of adjacent teeth

questions.explanation: An indirect restorative material is fabricated outside the patient's mouth in a dental laboratory from an impression, and is subsequently cemented or bonded to the prepared tooth in the clinic. This contrasts with direct materials that are placed and shaped intraorally. Indirect restorations include crowns, inlays, onlays, and fixed partial dentures using gold, porcelain, ceramic, or composite.
questions.question: An indirect restorative material differs from a direct one in that it is:
options: Placed directly into the tooth at chairside
Used only as a temporary restoration
Fabricated outside the mouth, cemented in clinic
Mixed and set in the patient's mouth

questions.question: A pregnant patient in her second trimester develops localized, erythematous, easily bleeding gingival enlargement despite reasonable oral hygiene. This exaggerated gingival response to plaque during pregnancy is primarily attributed to:
questions.explanation: Pregnancy gingivitis results from elevated levels of pregnancy-associated hormones, such as progesterone and oestrogen, which alter vascular permeability and exaggerate the gingival inflammatory response to existing bacterial plaque, even when plaque levels are relatively low. Plaque remains a necessary co-factor, as the condition does not occur in the complete absence of plaque. Meticulous plaque control during pregnancy helps minimise the severity of this hormonally influenced gingival response.
options: Elevated pregnancy hormone levels altering the gingival inflammatory response to plaque
Direct fetal antigen deposition in the gingiva
Complete absence of any bacterial plaque involvement

questions.explanation: Following transmission of HSV-1, the virus replicates for about 5 days before prodromal symptoms of malaise and fever develop. One to two days after prodromal symptoms, numerous small vesicles appear on the oral mucosa. The lesions typically heal within 10 days without scarring.
questions.question: In primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, the incubation period before prodromal symptoms appear is approximately:

questions.explanation: Jaw cysts are identified as the most common cause of chronic jaw swellings. Their slow-growing, asymptomatic nature — particularly radicular and dentigerous cysts — means they often present as unexplained swelling without acute symptoms. This clinical pattern should prompt radiographic investigation whenever a chronic, painless jaw swelling is encountered, as cysts are far more common in the jaws than in any other bone due to the unique persistence of odontogenic epithelial rests.
options: Gingival recession adjacent to involved teeth
questions.question: Cysts are stated to be the most common cause of which clinical finding in the jaw?

questions.explanation: Chronic gingivitis is fully reversible upon meticulous plaque removal, resulting in complete resolution of gingival inflammation without residual tissue destruction. This reversibility distinguishes gingivitis from periodontitis, where attachment loss is permanent. Oral hygiene instruction combined with professional scaling is the definitive treatment for chronic marginal gingivitis.
questions.question: Meticulous removal of dental plaque in a patient with chronic gingivitis will typically result in:
options: Resolution of inflammation without tissue destruction
Permanent pocket elimination only with surgery
No change due to established fibrosis

questions.explanation: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a genetic condition affecting enamel formation, resulting in hypoplastic, hypomature, or hypocalcified enamel that is structurally abnormal and may be discoloured. It can affect the entire dentition in both the primary and permanent dentitions. Restoration of affected teeth is indicated to restore function and aesthetics, with treatment complexity varying with severity.
questions.question: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a condition affecting:

questions.explanation: Pseudomembranous candidiasis presents as white plaques composed of fungal hyphae, desquamated epithelium, and debris that can be wiped off, revealing an underlying erythematous, sometimes bleeding, mucosal surface. This distinguishes it from leukoplakia, which cannot be scraped off. It typically affects infants, the immunocompromised, or antibiotic users.
questions.question: A 3-year-old presents with generalised oral candidiasis. On attempting to wipe away the white plaques with a gauze swab, the clinician notes bleeding points underneath. This finding is most consistent with:

questions.explanation: Submandibular lymphadenopathy in a child with a dento-alveolar abscess results from reactive lymph node enlargement as the regional lymphatic system drains and responds to the localized dental infection. This is a normal immunological response to a nearby infective source rather than a separate systemic disease process. Resolution of lymphadenopathy is typically expected following successful treatment of the underlying dental infection.
questions.question: A child with a dento-alveolar abscess presents with tender, palpable, enlarged lymph nodes beneath the mandible. This submandibular lymphadenopathy is best explained by:
options: Normal physiological lymph node size in children
Reactive drainage of infection from the affected tooth via regional lymphatics
Direct viral infection of the lymph nodes unrelated to the abscess

questions.question: An orthodontist plans treatment for a patient with moderate crowding requiring controlled, complex three-dimensional tooth movement including rotation and torque, which cannot be reliably achieved with a removable appliance alone. This treatment need is best addressed using:
questions.explanation: Fixed orthodontic appliances, using brackets bonded to teeth connected by archwires, allow precise, complex three-dimensional control of tooth movement, including rotation, torque, and bodily movement, which cannot be reliably achieved with removable appliances alone. This makes fixed appliances the treatment of choice for more complex malocclusions requiring controlled multi-planar tooth movement. Removable appliances remain useful for simpler cases or specific adjunctive purposes, such as retention or habit-breaking.

The odontogenic keratocyst is characterised histologically by a thin, uniform parakeratinised epithelial lining with a corrugated surface, and is notable for its aggressive behaviour and relatively high recurrence rate if not completely removed, distinguishing it from the more common radicular and dentigerous cysts. Its association with basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome when multiple is a recognised clinical feature. Treatment often requires more extensive surgical management than a simple radicular or dentigerous cyst.
questions.question: Histological examination of a jaw cyst reveals a thin, uniform parakeratinised epithelial lining with a corrugated surface and a characteristic tendency for aggressive local recurrence if incompletely removed. This cyst is:

options: Trauma from bruxism on healthy periodontium
Forces on a tooth with reduced healthy periodontium
Injury to the TMJ from excessive loading forces
questions.explanation: Secondary occlusal trauma involves normal or even reduced occlusal forces acting on a tooth with a diminished periodontium — already compromised by periodontal disease. It differs from primary occlusal trauma, where excessive forces act on a healthy periodontium. Management involves reducing force magnitude and treating the underlying periodontal disease to restore tissue support.
questions.question: Secondary occlusal trauma refers to:

questions.explanation: Canine-guided occlusion is an occlusal scheme in which the canine teeth alone provide guidance and disengagement of the posterior teeth during lateral excursive movements, distributing lateral forces onto a single, strong-rooted tooth away from the posterior teeth. This contrasts with group function occlusion, in which several teeth on the working side share contact and guidance during lateral movement. Understanding these occlusal schemes is important when planning restorative or orthodontic treatment that may alter a patient's existing occlusal relationships.
questions.question: A dentist evaluating a patient's occlusion notes that during lateral excursive movement, the working-side canine alone contacts and disengages the posterior teeth, while all other teeth pass out of contact. This specific occlusal scheme is termed:
Gingivitis is defined as inflammation of the gingivae that occurs WITHOUT:
questions.explanation: Gingivitis, by definition, is confined to the gingival tissues without involvement of the periodontal ligament, alveolar bone, or cementum. The inflammation is reversible with adequate plaque removal. Once the underlying supporting structures become involved, the diagnosis escalates to periodontitis, which involves irreversible structural loss.

A bifid condyle is a rare developmental anomaly in which the mandibular condylar head is divided into two distinct articulating surfaces rather than the normal single smooth convex head, often discovered incidentally on imaging without associated symptoms. It is generally considered a developmental variant rather than a disease process. Recognising this anomaly avoids unnecessary concern or misdiagnosis as a pathological condition when identified incidentally.
questions.question: A patient presents with a rare developmental anomaly in which the mandibular condylar head is divided into two distinct articulating surfaces rather than a single smooth head, discovered incidentally on imaging. This developmental variant is termed:
Which direct restorative material is described as 'the most noble of metals' and is malleable?
questions.explanation: Direct filling gold is described as the most noble of metals and is malleable, meaning it can be condensed and welded directly into the prepared cavity without a laboratory step. Its nobility confers excellent biocompatibility and corrosion resistance. However, its technique sensitivity, limited indications, and the availability of superior aesthetic alternatives have dramatically reduced its clinical use in contemporary dentistry.

options: Local factor (premature loss of a primary tooth)
questions.question: A child loses a primary second molar prematurely due to extensive caries, resulting in mesial drift of the permanent first molar and subsequent space loss for the succeeding premolar. This cause of malocclusion is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Premature loss of a primary tooth, such as a second molar lost early due to caries, is classified as a local factor contributing to malocclusion, as it disrupts the normal sequence of eruption and can lead to space loss and subsequent crowding or malalignment of the succeeding permanent tooth. This differs from genetic or systemic factors, which relate to inherent growth or hormonal influences rather than a localized dental event. Space maintainers are often used to prevent this complication following early primary tooth loss.

options: Using the tooth as the fulcrum to lever the adjacent tooth
Engaging the tooth with beaks of the forceps apically
Applying a twisting motion to fracture the periodontal ligament
Creating a lever of the third order
Forcing the elevator between root and bone, parallel to the root
questions.question: The wedge principle used with dental elevators involves:
questions.explanation: The wedge principle involves forcing the elevator between the root of the tooth and the surrounding investing bone, parallel to the root, creating a force that displaces the root from its socket. It is used alone or in combination with the lever principle. The wedge principle is particularly useful for loosening roots after coronal crown removal.

A habit-breaking appliance is specifically designed with features, such as a palatal rake or crib, to discourage persistent oral habits like digit or thumb sucking by disrupting the pleasurable sensation associated with the habit, thereby helping to eliminate the habit and allow potential self-correction of the resulting malocclusion. This differs from functional appliances, which are designed to modify skeletal growth patterns. Timely habit cessation, particularly before permanent dentition is established, improves the likelihood of favourable spontaneous correction.
options: Functional appliance for Class II correction
questions.question: A patient with an anterior open bite due to a persistent digit-sucking habit is fitted with an appliance incorporating a palatal component specifically designed to discourage the habit by removing the associated pleasurable sensation. This type of appliance is termed a:
For extra-coronal restorations (crowns), the principles of preparation described by Shillingburg include the need for balance between:
questions.explanation: Shillingburg's principles of crown preparation require a balance between conserving tooth structure/pulp health and achieving an aesthetically pleasing and mechanically strong crown. These include adequate reduction, taper, margin design, and surface area. The principles are not applied in isolation but must be balanced against each other in clinical decision-making.
options: Speed of preparation versus the comfort of the patient
Conserving tooth and pulp while keeping the crown strong
Occlusal coverage and aesthetic appearance only

questions.explanation: McCoy and Shepard's 1956 classification divides malocclusion aetiology into direct (determining) factors — which directly produce the malocclusion — and indirect (predisposing) factors — which create conditions favouring but not inevitably causing malocclusion. This fundamental distinction between direct causation and predisposition parallels concepts in medical epidemiology and remains pedagogically useful in orthodontic teaching alongside later, more detailed classifications.
options: Skeletal, dental, and soft tissue factors
questions.question: McCoy and Shepard's (1956) classification of malocclusion causes divides aetiological factors into:

questions.explanation: Composite resin undergoes volumetric shrinkage during polymerization (typically 1–5%), generating contraction stress at the tooth-restoration interface. If this stress exceeds the adhesive bond strength, marginal gaps form, allowing microleakage of oral fluids, bacteria, and stains — leading to secondary caries and postoperative sensitivity. Incremental placement technique reduces the effects of polymerization shrinkage.
questions.question: Polymerization shrinkage of composite resin is clinically significant because it can lead to:

options: Is always associated with poor oral hygiene
Shows rapid loss disproportionate to local factors
Does not involve alveolar bone resorption
questions.explanation: Aggressive periodontitis (localized or generalized) is characterised by rapid loss of attachment and alveolar bone that is disproportionate to the amount of local factors (plaque, calculus) present. It commonly affects younger individuals and may have familial clustering suggesting genetic susceptibility. Early diagnosis and aggressive treatment are essential to prevent tooth loss.
questions.question: Aggressive periodontitis differs from chronic periodontitis primarily in that it:
The primary indication for extraction of a grossly carious tooth is when:
options: Restoration is impractical due to the extent of destruction
The patient has mild sensitivity to cold only
The adjacent tooth has early proximal caries
The tooth has a fracture limited to the enamel only
The tooth is Class I mobility without pathology
questions.explanation: Extraction of a grossly carious tooth is indicated when the extent of destruction renders restoration impractical — insufficient sound tooth structure remains to support a direct or indirect restoration. Clinical judgement considers restorability (crown-to-root ratio, remaining tooth structure, ability to achieve isolation), patient factors, and strategic importance of the tooth before making this irreversible decision.

options: Provide the socket that supports the tooth root
Act as the source of dental pulp cells
questions.question: The alveolar bone's primary function in the periodontium is to:
questions.explanation: The alveolar bone forms the bony socket (alveolus) that houses and supports each tooth root. It is the most dynamic component of the periodontium, capable of resorption and apposition in response to occlusal forces and inflammatory processes. Alveolar bone loss is the defining feature that distinguishes periodontitis from gingivitis.

options: The tooth has a recent successful root canal treatment
It is a maxillary tooth rather than a mandibular one
It is needed for stabilisation of the fracture
A removable partial denture is being planned
questions.explanation: Teeth in the fracture line are generally extracted to prevent infection and delayed union, except when the tooth is needed for stabilisation of the fracture — for example, when it serves as an abutment for intermaxillary fixation or splinting. In such cases, careful monitoring and antibiotics are used, and the tooth may be extracted once the fracture has healed sufficiently.
questions.question: When a tooth is in the fracture line of a jaw fracture, it is generally extracted EXCEPT when:

questions.explanation: Periodontal flap surgery is indicated when non-surgical therapy, such as scaling and root planing, has failed to adequately resolve deep periodontal pockets, allowing direct surgical access for more thorough debridement of the root surface and, where appropriate, osseous recontouring. This represents a step-wise approach to periodontal management, escalating to surgical intervention only when conservative measures are insufficient. Regular periodontal maintenance is essential following either non-surgical or surgical therapy to sustain treatment outcomes.
options: Only superficial gingivitis without any pocketing is present
Non-surgical therapy has failed to adequately resolve deep pockets
No periodontal pockets are present at all
The patient declines all forms of periodontal treatment
The patient has completely healthy periodontal tissues
questions.question: A patient with residual periodontal pockets after initial non-surgical therapy is considered for surgical management, including access flap surgery to allow direct visualisation of the root surface for thorough debridement. This surgical approach is primarily indicated when:
A convex facial profile in the context of skeletal classification corresponds MOST closely to which type?
options: Class II with protrusive maxilla or retrusive mandible
Class I with harmonious jaw bases
An open bite with vertical maxillary excess present
questions.explanation: A convex facial profile is associated with a Class II skeletal pattern, resulting from a protrusive maxilla (maxillary excess), a retrusive mandible (mandibular deficiency), or both — and also from Class I bimaxillary protrusion. A concave profile indicates Class III; a flat profile indicates Class I with harmonic jaw bases. Profile assessment is a fundamental component of orthodontic and orthognathic surgical diagnosis.

options: Plaque-induced inflammatory diseases affecting the marginal periodontium
All diseases of the oral mucosa
Any pathological condition of the alveolar bone alone
Non-bacterial diseases of the gingiva exclusively
Only fungal infections of the gingival sulcus
questions.explanation: The term 'periodontal disease' in clinical usage refers specifically to plaque-induced inflammatory diseases affecting the marginal periodontium, namely gingivitis and periodontitis. While the periodontium can be affected by many pathological conditions, this narrower clinical definition guides diagnosis, treatment, and public health measures in dental practice.
questions.question: Periodontal disease, as commonly used clinically, refers specifically to:

options: Immediate catastrophic fracture of the restoration
Elimination of the need for bonding agents
Improved marginal seal compared with amalgam
questions.explanation: Polymerisation shrinkage in composite resin can generate stress at the tooth-restoration interface, potentially resulting in marginal gap formation, microleakage, postoperative sensitivity, and increased risk of secondary caries if not properly managed. Techniques such as incremental layering and appropriate bonding protocols help minimise this effect. Understanding this limitation is essential for successful composite restoration placement, particularly in deep or large cavities.
questions.question: A dentist explains that composite resin restorations, unlike amalgam, undergo polymerisation shrinkage during setting. This shrinkage is clinically significant primarily because it can lead to:

A cystic lesion is aspirated and examined histologically after excision. The overall histological report describing tissue architecture, cellular detail, and definitive diagnosis is generated from which type of investigation?
questions.explanation: Histology involves microscopic examination of tissue sections, preserving architecture and cellular relationships, and provides the definitive diagnosis for most oral lesions. This differs from cytology, which examines individual cells without tissue architecture. Histology remains the gold standard investigation in oral pathology diagnosis.

options: The long axis of the tooth being radiographed
The line bisecting tooth and film axes
The curvature of the dental arch
questions.question: In the bisecting angle technique, the X-ray beam is directed at right angles to:
questions.explanation: In the bisecting angle technique, the clinician mentally bisects the angle between the long axis of the tooth and the long axis of the film packet, then directs the X-ray central ray at right angles to this bisecting line. This applies the principle of similar triangles so that the image length equals the actual tooth length. The film is placed as close to the tooth as possible without bending.

questions.question: A dental hygienist recommends mechanical plaque control through toothbrushing and interdental cleaning as a caries prevention strategy. This approach targets caries prevention primarily by:
options: Physically disrupting and removing the cariogenic bacterial biofilm
Eliminating the need for fluoride use
questions.explanation: Mechanical plaque control through toothbrushing and interdental cleaning targets caries prevention by physically disrupting and removing the cariogenic bacterial biofilm before it can produce sustained acid challenges to the tooth surface. This approach complements chemical strategies such as fluoride use and dietary modification. Consistent, effective mechanical plaque control remains a cornerstone of comprehensive caries prevention.

questions.question: A patient requiring a large post-endodontic restoration in a molar with minimal remaining coronal tooth structure is advised that a cuspal-coverage restoration, such as an onlay or crown, is preferable to a simple direct filling. This recommendation is primarily based on the principle that:
options: Cuspal coverage restorations require less tooth reduction than direct fillings
Direct restorations bond better to endodontically treated dentin in all cases
Direct fillings are always stronger than any indirect restoration
Endodontically treated teeth are structurally identical to vital teeth
Unsupported cusps without cuspal coverage are at high risk of fracture under occlusal load
questions.explanation: Endodontically treated teeth with extensive loss of coronal tooth structure are at significantly increased risk of cuspal fracture under normal occlusal function if unsupported cusps are left uncovered, making cuspal-coverage restorations such as onlays or crowns preferable to protect the remaining tooth structure and distribute occlusal forces more favourably. This principle reflects the altered structural integrity of endodontically treated teeth compared with vital, intact teeth. Appropriate restoration selection is therefore critical to the long-term survival of heavily restored, root-treated teeth.

options: A purely traumatic TMJ disorder category
Pain dysfunction syndrome, a separate category
questions.question: The Pain Dysfunction Syndrome of the TMJ is classified under which broad disease category?
questions.explanation: Pain Dysfunction Syndrome (PDS), also known as myofascial pain-dysfunction syndrome or temporomandibular disorder (TMD), is listed as its own distinct category among TMJ diseases, separate from traumatic, infective, metabolic, developmental, and genetically determined diseases. It is characterised by muscle-based pain, clicking, and restricted movement without significant radiographic joint changes, and is managed conservatively with splints, physiotherapy, and behaviour modification.

Scorbutic gingivitis results from severe vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), causing impaired collagen synthesis, which leads to swollen, haemorrhagic gingiva alongside other systemic features such as poor wound healing and perifollicular skin haemorrhages. This distinguishes it from ordinary plaque-induced gingivitis, which lacks these systemic nutritional deficiency features. Recognising this association allows appropriate systemic nutritional correction alongside local periodontal care.
questions.question: A patient presents with generalised gingival bleeding, poor wound healing, and perifollicular haemorrhages on the skin, in addition to swollen, haemorrhagic gingiva, attributed to a dietary deficiency. This gingival condition is best classified as:
Sialography is a radiographic technique specifically used to image:
questions.explanation: Sialography is a contrast-enhanced radiographic technique used to image the salivary glands and their ductal system. It involves injecting a radiopaque contrast medium into the salivary duct. It is used to diagnose salivary gland obstructions, calculi, strictures, and ductal anomalies including Sjögren's syndrome features.

The paralleling technique is also called the long cone technique or right-angle technique because it uses a 12-inch long cone and directs the X-ray beam at right angles to both the film and the long axis of the tooth. Film holders that keep the film parallel to the tooth axis are used. This technique produces more accurate images with less geometric distortion compared to the bisecting angle technique.
options: The bisecting angle technique by name
questions.question: The paralleling technique is also known as:

questions.explanation: Blood disorders including anaemia, leukaemia, neutropenia, cyclic neutropenia, and haematinic deficiencies are recognised causes of oral ulcers secondary to systemic disease. Haematological workup is therefore important in patients with recurrent or atypical oral ulcers. Leukaemia in particular can manifest with gingival infiltration and ulceration as initial presentation.
questions.question: Which of the following blood disorders can cause oral ulcers?

options: Assessing proximal caries and bone crest levels
Detecting cysts in the posterior mandible region
Evaluating fractures of posterior alveolar bone
questions.explanation: Bitewing radiographs are the primary tool for detecting proximal (interproximal) caries and assessing alveolar crestal bone levels in both the maxilla and mandible simultaneously. They show the crowns of posterior teeth in both arches on a single film. The paralleling film holder technique with a beam-aiming device improves accuracy of the bitewing projection.
questions.question: Bitewing radiographs are indicated for:

options: The plaque index and the bleeding score, both recorded
Root shape, surrounding bone, and vital structures nearby
questions.question: Radiographic examination before extraction is performed to assess which of the following?
questions.explanation: Pre-extraction radiographic examination is essential to assess root number, morphology and configuration (curved, dilacerated, or hypercementosed roots), condition of surrounding bone (bone density, pathology), and proximity to vital structures (inferior alveolar nerve, maxillary sinus). This information directly influences the choice of technique, instruments, and whether referral to a specialist is warranted.

options: The abscess will resolve spontaneously without treatment due to the viral infection
Herpetic infection has no bearing on dental abscess management
The two conditions never occur together clinically
Diffuse painful gingival and mucosal inflammation limits oral examination, hygiene, and local anaesthesia
Antibiotics for the abscess will cure the viral infection simultaneously
questions.question: A child with a dento-alveolar abscess also develops primary herpetic gingivostomatitis simultaneously. Management of the abscess is MOST complicated in this scenario because:
questions.explanation: Concurrent primary herpetic gingivostomatitis complicates management of a dento-alveolar abscess because the diffuse painful gingival and oral mucosal inflammation limits the child's ability to tolerate examination, local anaesthesia, and oral hygiene measures needed for definitive dental treatment. Systemic illness from the viral infection may also affect the child's overall condition and cooperation. Coordinated, gentle management of both conditions is required for optimal outcomes.

questions.question: Innate immunity to Candida in the oral mucosa is mediated PRIMARILY through which cells at the mucosal surface?
options: Neutrophils migrating through the junctional epithelium only
Pattern receptors on epithelium and macrophages sensing Candida
Mast cells releasing histamine on candidal contact
Natural killer cells recognising MHC-I loss on Candida
questions.explanation: Innate mucosal immunity to Candida is initiated by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) — including Toll-like receptors (TLR2, TLR4) and C-type lectin receptors (Dectin-1, Dectin-2) — expressed on oral epithelial cells and tissue macrophages, which detect conserved fungal cell wall components (beta-glucan, mannan). Dectin-1 recognition of beta-glucan is particularly critical for triggering anti-Candida inflammation. This innate recognition system activates downstream signalling cascades leading to cytokine production and neutrophil recruitment.

questions.question: The 'initial lesion' in the histopathological progression of gingivitis is characterized by:
options: Plasma cell dominance with antibody production
Acute exudative response with neutrophilic infiltration
T-lymphocyte infiltration and early collagen loss
questions.explanation: The initial lesion appears within 2–4 days of plaque accumulation as an acute exudative inflammatory response in the connective tissue beneath the junctional epithelium, characterised by vascular changes and neutrophilic infiltration. Neutrophils migrate into the sulcus to combat bacteria. This initial vascular and cellular response is the first histological sign of gingivitis.

questions.question: The nasopalatine cyst is categorised as which type of jaw cyst?
questions.explanation: The nasopalatine cyst is a non-odontogenic (fissural) developmental cyst arising from epithelial remnants in the nasopalatine canal in the anterior maxilla. It accounts for approximately 5–10% of all jaw cysts and presents as a well-defined radiolucency in the midline of the anterior maxilla. Treatment is surgical enucleation with low recurrence rates.

options: Generalised joint hypermobility leading to recurrent TMJ dislocation
Condylar agenesis as part of the syndrome
Fusion of disc and condyle producing closed lock
questions.question: Which Ehlers-Danlos syndrome finding makes it a disease affecting the TMJ?
questions.explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a connective tissue disorder characterised by hyperextensible skin, fragile tissues, and — most relevant to the TMJ — generalised joint hypermobility. Hyperlaxity of the joint capsule and ligaments predisposes to recurrent TMJ dislocation and internal derangement. It is listed among genetically determined diseases affecting the TMJ. Management involves physiotherapy, splints, and occasionally surgical stabilisation.

options: Bacteraemia-induced infective endocarditis in susceptible patients
questions.question: A patient with a history of infective endocarditis risk requires antibiotic prophylaxis before certain invasive dental procedures according to current guidelines. The primary rationale for this prophylaxis is to reduce the risk of:
questions.explanation: Antibiotic prophylaxis before certain invasive dental procedures in patients at risk of infective endocarditis aims to reduce the risk of transient bacteraemia, arising from the procedure, seeding susceptible damaged or prosthetic heart valves and causing infective endocarditis. Current guidelines have become more selective regarding which patients and procedures warrant prophylaxis compared with historical practice. Understanding this rationale helps ensure prophylaxis is applied appropriately, avoiding both under- and over-prescription of antibiotics.

questions.question: A dentist choosing a luting (cementation) agent for a zirconia crown considers the material's bonding mechanism to both the tooth structure and the ceramic surface. Resin cement is often preferred over conventional glass ionomer luting cement for this indication primarily because resin cement offers:
questions.explanation: Resin luting cements generally offer superior bond strength compared with conventional glass ionomer luting cements, particularly when the ceramic surface is appropriately treated (such as with sandblasting or a primer for zirconia), enhancing micromechanical and chemical retention of the restoration. This superior bonding is especially valuable for restorations requiring maximum retention, such as veneers or crowns with reduced preparation. Selection of luting cement depends on the specific ceramic material and clinical retention requirements.
options: Reduced retention compared with zinc phosphate cement
Superior bond strength, particularly with appropriately treated ceramic surfaces
No requirement for any surface treatment of the ceramic
Lower cost than glass ionomer luting cement
Inferior aesthetics compared with glass ionomer
