questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and composition of von Willebrand factor, including its identifying features.
(b) State the standard functions/setting in which von Willebrand factor operates.
(c) State how a deficiency of von Willebrand factor is reflected in standard test results.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind considering both the bleeding time and the APTT/Factor VIII level together when a defect of platelet adhesion is suspected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Von Willebrand factor is a large adhesive glycoprotein with a base polypeptide chain of about 220,000 molecular weight.
• Its base structure is a dimer, and it can form multimers of as many as 20 linked dimers joined by disulfide bridges.
(b)
• It is synthesised in endothelial cells and megakaryocytes, with both constitutive and stimulated secretion, and its large multimers are stored in Weibel-Palade bodies.
• Its two main functions are to stabilise Factor VIII and to mediate platelet adhesion to the vessel wall.
(c)
• Because von Willebrand factor mediates platelet adhesion, disorders of adhesion such as von Willebrand disease are associated with a prolonged bleeding time.
• Since it also stabilises Factor VIII, von Willebrand disease is also associated with a low Factor VIII level and a prolonged APTT.
• Von Willebrand disease can be congenital or acquired and causes mucocutaneous bleeding.
(d)
• Because von Willebrand factor affects both platelet adhesion (primary haemostasis) and Factor VIII stability (secondary haemostasis), a deficiency can abnormally affect both the bleeding time and the APTT.
• Relying on only one of these tests when von Willebrand disease is suspected could therefore miss part of the abnormality.
• Both the bleeding time and the coagulation factor pathway should be considered together when investigating suspected defects of platelet adhesion.
• This combined consideration reduces the risk of an incomplete or inaccurate assessment of the patient's haemostatic defect.
• Accurate recognition of von Willebrand factor's dual role therefore guides the correct selection of confirmatory tests.

(a)
The procedure should be discontinued and pressure applied to the wound site.
(b)
If the bleeding time is repeated on the other arm and again does not cease within 15 minutes, the result is reported as >15 minutes.
(c)
A bleeding time >15 minutes is considered critical and indicates a significant abnormality of platelet plug formation or capillary integrity, such as may be seen in thrombocytopenia, hereditary or acquired platelet dysfunction, von Willebrand's disease, afibrinogenaemia, severe hypofibrinogenaemia, or a vascular bleeding disorder.
(d)
After ensuring bleeding has stopped and bandaging the site, the abnormal result should prompt further investigation, and the patient's history should be reviewed for recent aspirin or blood thinner use, which can also cause a falsely prolonged result.
questions.question:
(a) During a bleeding time test, bleeding has not ceased after 15 minutes. State the required action.
(b) State how the result should be recorded.
(c) State what this result indicates.
(d) State the follow-up.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The thromboplastin reagent used in the PT test contains recombinant human tissue factor combined with synthetic phospholipids.
• Calcium chloride (CaCl2) is included as part of the reagent, or added separately at 0.025 mol/l if the thromboplastin reagent does not already contain it.
(b)
• The reagent is identified by its ability to recalcify citrated plasma and provide tissue factor, allowing a visible fibrin clot to form.
• It is supplied alongside the patient's platelet-poor plasma and a normal/control plasma for comparison.
(c)
• In the standard PT procedure, 200 µl of the thromboplastin-with-calcium reagent is added to 100 µl of pre-warmed plasma, and the time to visible clot formation is recorded.
• The same reagent, using recombinant human thromboplastin, is also used in the one-stage assay of Factor VII, where it helps yield results that more closely reflect the patient's actual Factor VII activity.
• The reagent must be used together with a water bath set at 37°C and appropriate micropipettes and stopwatches for accurate timing.
(d)
• The sensitivity of the PT test is influenced by the specific reagent and technique used.
• For this reason, a reference range for the PT must be established locally for the reagent in use.
• Using a reagent without establishing a corresponding local reference range risks misinterpreting a normal or abnormal result.
• This precaution ensures that PT results are correctly compared against an appropriate normal range for that laboratory's reagent system.
• Consistent reagent quality and calibration are therefore essential to reliable interpretation of PT results.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the thromboplastin reagent used in the PT test, including its identifying features.
(b) State how this reagent is supplied and used with other materials.
(c) State the standard use of this reagent in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind establishing a local reference range for this reagent.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Platelet-poor plasma (PPP) is plasma obtained from citrated whole blood by centrifugation, containing fewer than 10 × 10⁹/L platelets.
• It is prepared by centrifuging the sample at a minimum of 1700 rpm for at least 10 minutes, or 2500 rpm for 15 minutes, preferably at 4°C in a refrigerated centrifuge.
(b)
• After centrifugation, the samples are opened at room temperature and the plasma is separated and stored at 4°C as quickly as possible.
• PPP is identified as the clear supernatant plasma layer remaining above the sedimented cells after this centrifugation step.
(c)
• PPP is the specimen used for all the standard screening tests of blood coagulation, namely PT, APTT, TT and the fibrinogen concentration assay, as well as for individual coagulation factor assays.
• For factor assays specifically, the resulting PPP is stored at 4°C prior to testing, whereas PPP for screening tests and the Factor VII assay is kept at room temperature to avoid cold activation.
• Samples should be tested within 4 hours of collection where possible, since longer storage should be avoided for screening tests and clotting factor assays.
(d)
• When room temperature exceeds 25°C, the labile coagulation proteins in the plasma may be affected.
• For this reason, a refrigerated (4°C) centrifuge should be used to prepare PPP under such conditions.
• Using an unrefrigerated centrifuge in a warm environment risks degrading labile factors and producing a falsely prolonged screening test result.
• Prompt separation and cold storage of the plasma after centrifugation similarly protects the integrity of the labile clotting factors.
• Correct preparation of PPP is therefore essential for obtaining reliable coagulation screening and factor assay results.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the preparation and composition of platelet-poor plasma (PPP), including its identifying features.
(b) State how PPP is handled immediately after preparation.
(c) State the standard use of PPP in the coagulation laboratory.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind using a refrigerated centrifuge when room temperature is high.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A mixture value of 42 seconds, close to the control of 35 seconds, represents a good correction of the prolonged APTT, suggesting a factor deficiency.
(b)
A mixture value of 52 seconds, still substantially prolonged compared with the control, represents a poor correction, suggesting the presence of an inhibitor rather than a simple deficiency.
(c)
Both results are recorded as the clotting time of the 50:50 mixture in seconds, together with a statement of whether correction occurred.
(d)
Good correction should be followed by specific one-stage factor assays (e.g., for Factor VIII, based on the APTT) to identify and quantify the deficient factor, while poor correction should prompt further investigation for an inhibitor.
questions.question:
(a) A patient's APTT is 60 seconds against a control of 35 seconds. After a 50:50 mix of patient and control plasma, the APTT is 42 seconds. Interpret this result.
(b) A second patient's 50:50 mix instead gives 52 seconds. Interpret this result.
(c) State how each result should be recorded.
(d) State the action that follows each interpretation.

(a) Classify the needles used for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.
(b) State how each type of needle is used.
(c) State how the needle type is selected for a given clinical requirement.
(d) Explain how using the wrong needle type for the required investigation can lead to an inadequate bone marrow examination.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Needles used for bone marrow aspiration include the Salah, Klima and Islam's aspiration needles.
• Needles used for bone marrow biopsy (trephine) include the Jamshidi needle.
(b)
• Aspiration needles are used with a needle and syringe technique to withdraw a small amount of bone marrow fluid.
• Biopsy needles are inserted with a to-and-fro rotation to obtain a solid core of bone marrow tissue, and such needles are both reusable and disposable.
(c)
• Aspiration needles are selected when fine cytological detail, cytochemical stains, flow cytometry, or cytogenetic and molecular studies are required.
• Biopsy needles are selected when assessment of marrow cellularity and architecture, or detection of lesions such as in aplastic anaemia or metastasis, is required, particularly if aspiration alone yields a dry tap.
• The choice between aspiration and biopsy needles also depends on whether a needle or trephine biopsy is required in addition to aspiration.
(d)
• Using an aspiration needle where a solid core of tissue is actually required, for example to assess marrow architecture, would fail to provide the structural information a biopsy needle is designed to yield.
• Conversely, relying only on a trephine biopsy needle when fine cytological detail, immunophenotyping, or cytogenetic and molecular studies are needed would not provide the material that an aspiration needle offers.
• Such a mismatch between needle type and the clinical information required can result in an inadequate sample being obtained.
• This can, in turn, lead to an incomplete or non-diagnostic bone marrow examination.
• Correct selection of needle type according to the information required is therefore necessary for a satisfactory bone marrow examination.

(a)
• The one-stage assay of Factor VIII is based on the APTT, following the bioassay principle, and compares dilutions of the patient's and standard plasma for their ability to correct the APTT of a Factor VIII-deficient (substrate) plasma.
• Reagents are the patient's platelet-poor plasma, standard/reference plasma, Factor VIII-deficient substrate plasma, barbitone buffered saline, the APTT reagent, plastic tubes and an ice bath.
(b)
The APTT reagent and calcium chloride are placed at 37°C while the patient's, standard's and substrate plasma are kept in an ice bath until used.
(c)
• Make 1 in 10 dilutions of the test and standard plasma in buffered saline in plastic tubes in the ice bath, then use 0.2 ml volumes to make doubling dilutions to obtain 1 in 20 and 1 in 40 dilutions.
• Place 0.1 ml of each of the three dilutions in glass tubes, add 0.1 ml of freshly reconstituted or thawed substrate plasma to each, warm to 37°C, and perform APTTs according to laboratory protocol, testing dilutions at 2-minute intervals on the master watch.
(d)
Reduced Factor VIII concentration is found in Haemophilia A, Von Willebrand disease types I and III and some cases of type II, congenital combined deficiency of Factors VIII and V, and DIC.
(e)
The normal range is 45–158 IU/dL, and if a test sample gives, for example, 7% of the standard's concentration, and the standard is 85 IU/dL, the test sample's concentration is calculated as 85 × 7% = 6 IU/dL.
(f)
• This assay is used to quantify the actual level of circulating Factor VIII when a deficiency such as Haemophilia A or Von Willebrand disease is suspected.
• The Factor VII assay, similarly based on the PT rather than the APTT, compares dilutions of the patient's and standard plasma for their ability to correct the PT of a Factor VII-deficient substrate plasma, and can easily be adapted for the prothrombin, Factor V or Factor X assays.
(g)
• The Factor VIII assay is APTT-based (intrinsic pathway) and uses a Factor VIII-deficient substrate plasma, whereas the Factor VII assay is PT-based (extrinsic pathway) and uses a Factor VII-deficient substrate plasma.
• The normal range for the Factor VIII assay is 45–158 IU/dL, compared with 50–150 iu/dl for the Factor VII assay, and results for Factor VII are plotted as clotting times of test and standard against factor concentration on graph paper.
• Therapeutic options following a low Factor VII result include fresh frozen plasma, prothrombin complex concentrates and recombinant Factor VIIa, and plasma Factor VII levels of at least 20% are considered sufficient for major surgery.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the one-stage Factor VIII assay.
(b) List the reagents required.
(c) Describe the procedure for performing the assay.
(d) State the conditions associated with a reduced result.
(e) State the normal range and how the result is calculated.
(f) Explain why this assay is used in the investigation of bleeding disorders.
(g) Distinguish the one-stage Factor VIII assay from the one-stage Factor VII assay.

(a) Describe the structure and composition of a platelet, including its identifying features.
(b) State the standard method or setting in which platelets are assessed in practice.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of avoiding EDTA when a false platelet count is suspected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Platelets have three structural zones: peripheral, sol-gel and organelle zones.
• The peripheral zone contains the glycocalyx and plasma membrane and is responsible for adhesion and aggregation.
• The sol-gel zone provides structure and support through microfilaments, thrombosthenin, the open canalicular system and dense tubular system.
• The organelle zone is responsible for secretion and storage and contains alpha granules, dense granules, glycogen, mitochondria and lysosomes.
• Identifying glycoproteins include GPIb, the receptor site for von Willebrand factor, and the GPIIb/IIIa complex, which becomes the receptor site for fibrinogen.
• Dense granules contain ATP, ADP, calcium, magnesium, serotonin and epinephrine, while alpha granules contain fibrinogen, Factor V, von Willebrand factor, plasminogen and PAI-1 among other proteins.
(b)
• Platelets and their function are assessed in practice through the platelet count and blood film, and through platelet function studies of adhesion, aggregation and release.
• A normal platelet count is 150,000–400,000 cells/mm3, with counts below 100,000 indicating thrombocytopenia and below 50,000 indicating severe thrombocytopenia.
(c)
• Pseudothrombocytopenia may occur due to platelet clumping in samples anticoagulated with EDTA.
• For this reason, heparin should be used instead of EDTA when performing platelet counts to avoid a falsely low result.
• Failure to observe this precaution can give a spuriously low platelet count that does not reflect the patient's true platelet status.
• Blood counts and films also reveal platelet morphology and any associated blood disorder such as leukaemia.

(a)
• The principle of the fibrinogen assay (Clauss technique) is that diluted plasma is clotted with a strong thrombin solution, and a standard curve is prepared by recording the clotting time for each serial dilution of a calibration plasma.
• The plasma is diluted to give a low level of any inhibitors present, such as FDPs and heparin, and a strong thrombin solution is used so that clotting time over a wide range is independent of the exact thrombin concentration.
(b)
Reagents are calibration plasma (with a known fibrinogen level calibrated against an International Reference Standard), platelet-poor plasma, thrombin solution and buffer.
(c)
• Dilutions of the calibration plasma are made in veronal buffer (1 in 5, 1 in 10, 1 in 20 and 1 in 40); 0.2 ml of each dilution is warmed to 37°C, 0.1 ml of thrombin solution is added, and the clotting time is measured.
• A calibration curve is prepared by plotting clotting time in seconds against fibrinogen concentration in g/l, and this curve is used to read off the patient's fibrinogen concentration from their clotting time.
(d)
Care must be taken to dilute the plasma sufficiently to minimise the effect of inhibitors such as FDPs and heparin on the clotting time.
(e)
The normal fibrinogen range is approximately 1.8–3.6 g/l, and results are reported as a concentration in g/l read from the calibration curve.
(f)
• Low fibrinogen levels are seen in hypofibrinogenaemia/afibrinogenaemia, inherited dysfibrinogenaemia, DIC and liver disease, so the assay is used to quantify fibrinogen when these conditions are suspected.
• Because the plasma is diluted before testing, the effect of inhibitors on the measured clotting time is minimised, allowing a more specific estimate of the fibrinogen level itself.
(g)
• The thrombin time (TT) measures the clotting time of undiluted plasma after thrombin is added and is markedly affected by inhibitors such as heparin, FDPs and dysfibrinogenaemia.
• The fibrinogen assay instead uses diluted plasma compared against a calibration curve, which reduces the influence of such inhibitors and allows an actual fibrinogen concentration to be calculated rather than only a clotting time.
• The TT is therefore a screening test for an abnormality affecting fibrin formation, while the fibrinogen assay is a quantitative test for the fibrinogen concentration itself.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the fibrinogen assay (Clauss technique).
(b) List the reagents required.
(c) Describe the procedure for performing the assay.
(d) State the precautions to be observed.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the fibrinogen assay is used in the investigation of bleeding disorders.
(g) Distinguish the fibrinogen assay from the thrombin time (TT) test.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The agglutination indicates the presence of fibrin degradation products (FDPs) in the patient's serum.
(b)
FDPs are fragments produced by proteolytic digestion of fibrinogen or fibrin by plasmin; when present, they cause the latex particles coated with anti-fibrinogen antibodies to agglutinate.
(c)
Blood for this test is collected in a tube containing thrombin (to remove all fibrinogen by converting it into a clot) and soybean trypsin inhibitor (to inhibit plasmin and thus prevent in vitro breakdown of fibrin), ensuring the FDP level measured reflects what was present in vivo rather than artefactual breakdown.
(d)
Increased FDP levels occur in DIC, deep vein thrombosis, severe pneumonia and recent myocardial infarction, so a positive finding should prompt clinical correlation and, where DIC is suspected, further coagulation screening (e.g., platelet count, PT, APTT, fibrinogen).
questions.question:
(a) In an FDP assay, latex particles linked to anti-fibrinogen antibodies are mixed with dilutions of a patient's serum on a glass slide, and agglutination is observed. Identify the finding.
(b) State the principle behind this finding.
(c) Describe how the specimen for this test should be collected and why.
(d) State the clinical significance and any follow-up.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The haemoglobin sickling test (dithionite solubility test) is based on sodium dithionite removing an oxygen molecule from the iron atom of the haem group, converting oxyhaemoglobin to deoxyhaemoglobin, causing HbS-containing red cells to form the typical sickle shape.
• It requires an anticoagulated peripheral blood sample.
(b)
Materials are a 10% sodium dithionite solution in phosphate buffer (pH 6.8), a Pasteur pipette, microscope slides and coverslips, and petroleum jelly-paraffin wax or depex.
(c)
A drop of dithionite solution and a drop of anticoagulated blood are mixed in a test tube; a drop of the mixture is placed on a slide, covered with a coverslip avoiding air bubbles, the edges sealed with petroleum jelly-paraffin wax or depex, and the slide observed under the microscope.
(d)
In HbS disease, sickling can appear immediately or near-immediately, whereas in the HbS trait, clear sickling within an hour at 37°C may not be conclusive and may require additional time or altered oxygen tension.
(e)
The result is reported as sickling positive or negative based on the presence of sickle-shaped cells.
(f)
• This test is used because it directly demonstrates, under the microscope, the characteristic morphological change of red cells containing HbS when deoxygenated.
• It provides a first-line, low-cost method for detecting the presence of HbS in a blood sample.
(g)
• The sickle solubility test instead mixes blood with a phosphate buffer containing saponin (to cause haemolysis) and sodium dithionite (to induce deoxygenation), and reads the result as turbidity against a white card with black lines rather than as a microscopic morphological change.
• In the sickle solubility test, an opaque or turbid solution (through which the lines cannot be seen) is read as positive for HbS, because insoluble HbS crystals refract light.
• The sickling test directly visualises sickle-shaped red cells under the microscope, whereas the sickle solubility test is a macroscopic turbidity test based on the solubility properties of deoxygenated HbS.
• Both tests rely on deoxygenation by sodium dithionite, but they differ in their reagents (dithionite alone versus dithionite with saponin) and in how the result is read (microscopic morphology versus tube turbidity).
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the haemoglobin sickling test.
(b) List the materials required.
(c) Describe the procedure for the sickling test.
(d) State how the interpretation differs between HbS disease and HbS trait.
(e) State how the result is reported.
(f) Explain why the sickling test is used in the investigation of haemoglobinopathies.
(g) Distinguish the sickling test from the sickle solubility test.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The next step is screening of the sample for transfusion-transmissible infections (TTIs), namely HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, syphilis, malaria and Zika virus.
(b)
The principle/purpose is to ensure blood safety by identifying donations that could transmit infection to a recipient before the blood is released for use.
(c)
If a blood sample tests positive for any TTI, the tests are repeated in duplicate, complete confidentiality is maintained about the results, only the donor is informed and counselled and encouraged for further testing and treatment, and referrals to health experts are provided along with follow-up.
(d)
This step matters because ensuring blood safety requires strict donor screening, testing of collected blood, safe storage, and strict crossmatching, all working together to protect the recipient from transfusion-transmissible infection.
questions.question:
(a) A unit of blood is collected from a donor at the blood bank and placed aside in the correct specimen bottle. Identify the next step and list the infections it screens for.
(b) State the principle/purpose of this step.
(c) Describe what happens if a sample tests positive (reactive).
(d) State why this step matters for blood safety.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The screening tests of blood coagulation are the prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), thrombin time (TT), fibrinogen concentration assay, and mixing studies (50:50 mix).
• The PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways, the APTT measures the intrinsic and common pathways, the TT measures fibrinogen conversion in the common pathway, the fibrinogen assay quantifies fibrinogen concentration, and mixing studies distinguish a factor deficiency from an inhibitor.
(b)
• The PT evaluates deficiencies of Factors I, II, V, VII and X and is used to monitor anticoagulant therapy.
• The APTT evaluates contact factors and Factors VIII, IX, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen, and is also sensitive to heparin and inhibitors.
(c)
• Each test is selected according to the pathway suspected of being abnormal: PT for extrinsic pathway disorders, APTT for intrinsic pathway disorders, TT and the fibrinogen assay for suspected fibrinogen abnormalities, and mixing studies once a screening test is found to be prolonged.
• All these tests require citrated whole blood processed into platelet-poor plasma, obtained by centrifugation at a minimum of 1700 rpm for at least 10 minutes, preferably at 4°C.
• Samples for these screening tests should be tested within 4 hours of collection and, for screening tests and the Factor VII assay specifically, kept at room temperature to avoid cold activation.
(d)
• If a sample is not tested within the recommended time, or is stored at the wrong temperature, labile coagulation proteins may be affected, leading to falsely prolonged results.
• Freezing and thawing of plasma before an APTT determination can also affect the result and should be avoided.
• If the volume of anticoagulant added is not correctly adjusted to the patient's haematocrit using the stated formula, the citrate-to-blood ratio will be wrong and can distort the clotting times obtained.
• Failure to run tests in duplicate, as specified for PT, APTT and TT, also risks an unrecognised technical error going unnoticed.
• Such handling or technique errors can produce an inaccurate screening result that misrepresents the patient's true coagulation status.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the screening tests used for blood coagulation.
(b) State what each type of test evaluates.
(c) State how each test is applied or selected in the laboratory.
(d) Explain how a basic handling or technique error can lead to an inaccurate coagulation screening result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Whole blood clotting time (CT) refers to the time interval between the entry of blood into a glass capillary tube or syringe and the formation of fibrin threads.
• It is a test of the ability of whole blood, rather than plasma alone, to form a fibrin clot.
(b)
Apparatus required is a 10–12 cm long glass capillary tube of uniform diameter and a stopwatch.
(c)
Methods for performing the test include Wright's capillary glass tube method, Duke's drop method, and the Lee and White test-tube method.
(d)
Because the test uses a capillary tube of specified length and diameter, consistent apparatus is needed to obtain a comparable, reproducible clotting time.
(e)
The normal clotting time by Wright's method is 3–6 minutes, and results are reported as the time in minutes for fibrin threads to form.
(f)
• The whole blood clotting time is used as a simple bedside or basic laboratory assessment of the overall clotting ability of blood, complementing the plasma-based screening tests such as PT and APTT.
• It is one of the older, simple methods for detecting a gross abnormality of coagulation before more specific plasma-based tests are performed.
(g)
• Hess's test (the capillary resistance test), by contrast, assesses vascular integrity rather than clot formation: an area 5 cm in diameter is marked on the antecubital fossa and a sphygmomanometer is inflated to 80 mm Hg for 5 minutes.
• In Hess's test, normally 3–5 purpuric eruptions appear in the marked area, reflecting the resistance of small vessels rather than the time for a fibrin clot to form.
• The whole blood clotting time therefore evaluates the coagulation system directly by timing clot formation, whereas Hess's test evaluates the vascular component of haemostasis by observing capillary fragility under pressure.
• Both tests are simple bedside procedures, but they investigate different components of the haemostatic mechanism.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of whole blood clotting time (CT).
(b) List the apparatus required.
(c) State the methods used to perform the test.
(d) State the reasoning behind using standardised apparatus for this test.
(e) State the normal value and how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the whole blood clotting time is used in practical haematology.
(g) Distinguish the whole blood clotting time from Hess's test (capillary resistance test).

(a) Describe the apparatus and materials used for the bleeding time test, including their identifying features.
(b) State the standard method/setting in which this apparatus is used.
(c) State how this apparatus is used across the different bleeding time methods.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precautions concerning drug history and alcohol drying before the test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The apparatus required for the bleeding time test includes a blood pressure cuff, a sterile disposable blood lancet capable of making a puncture 5 mm wide and 1 mm deep, and a stopwatch.
• Other materials are Whatman No. 1 circular filter paper, alcohol pads, gloves and a butterfly bandage.
(b)
• These items identify the apparatus as belonging to the Simplate/Surgicutt method, in which the device has a spring-activated surgical steel blade housed in a plastic unit with a depth of 1.0 mm and a width of 5.0 mm.
• The filter paper is used to blot, not wipe, the blood at the puncture site at regular 30-second intervals without touching the wound.
(c)
• This apparatus is used in the standard Simplate/Surgicutt bleeding time procedure, where a blood pressure cuff is inflated to 40 mm Hg on the upper arm, a standardised puncture is made on the forearm, and the time to cessation of bleeding is recorded to the nearest 30 seconds.
• It is also used generally in the Duke, Ivy and Mielke bleeding time methods, which likewise require a lancet or blade and a stopwatch to time bleeding cessation.
(d)
• Before the test, the patient must be asked whether they have taken aspirin, aspirin-containing compounds, or blood thinners such as heparin or coumadin recently.
• These drugs cause a falsely abnormal (prolonged) bleeding time, so the test should not be performed if the patient has taken them within the last 7–10 days.
• The alcohol used to cleanse the puncture site must be allowed to dry completely before the puncture is made.
• If residual alcohol remains on the puncture site, the bleeding time will be erroneously prolonged.
• If the filter paper is allowed to touch the wound, the platelet clot may be dislodged, causing falsely elevated results.
• The stopwatch used must be properly calibrated, as an uncalibrated stopwatch will keep incorrect time and affect the result.

questions.question:
(a) In a one-stage Factor VIII assay, the test sample gives a result equivalent to 7% of the standard plasma, and the standard has a concentration of 85 IU/dL. Calculate the Factor VIII concentration of the test sample.
(b) State how this result should be recorded.
(c) State what this result indicates.
(d) State the relevance of this finding.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The test sample's Factor VIII concentration is 85 IU/dL × 7% = 6 IU/dL.
(b)
The result is recorded as a concentration in IU/dL, compared with the normal range of 45–158 IU/dL.
(c)
A value of 6 IU/dL is markedly below the normal range, indicating a severe reduction in Factor VIII concentration.
(d)
Reduced Factor VIII concentration is found in Haemophilia A, Von Willebrand disease (types I and III, and some cases of type II), congenital combined deficiency of Factors VIII and V, and DIC, so this result would prompt clinical correlation with these conditions.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of mixing studies.
(b) State which samples are investigated by this method.
(c) Describe the procedure for mixing studies, including a worked example.
(d) State how the results are interpreted.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why mixing studies are used in the investigation of bleeding disorders.
(g) Distinguish mixing studies from an individual (one-stage) coagulation factor assay.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mixing studies, also called correction tests or 50:50 mixing experiments, use a 50:50 mix of the patient's plasma with normal plasma, after which the PT or APTT is repeated on the mixture.
• Reagents used are the PT or APTT reagents together with the patient's plasma and normal plasma.
(b)
Plasma samples with an abnormal screening test result (prolonged PT or APTT) are the ones investigated further by this method.
(c)
• If PT, APTT or TT is prolonged, the patient's plasma is mixed with an equal volume of normal plasma and the relevant test is repeated on the mixture.
• In the interpretation example given, an APTT control of 35 seconds and a patient/test value of 60 seconds that corrects to 42 seconds on 50:50 mixing represents good correction, while a mixture value of 52 seconds represents poor correction.
(d)
Correction of the prolonged time indicates a possible factor deficiency, whereas failure to correct suggests the presence of an inhibitor.
(e)
Results are reported as the corrected clotting time of the mixture, together with a statement of whether correction occurred (suggesting deficiency) or did not occur (suggesting an inhibitor).
(f)
• Mixing studies are used to distinguish between a factor deficiency and a factor inhibitor as the cause of a prolonged PT or APTT.
• This distinction guides whether further investigation should proceed to individual factor assays (for a deficiency) or to inhibitor-specific testing.
(g)
• An individual (one-stage) factor assay, in contrast, compares the ability of dilutions of a standard or reference plasma and of the test plasma to correct the PT or APTT of a plasma that is known to be totally deficient in the specific factor being measured.
• Where a mixing study simply shows whether correction occurs, a one-stage factor assay quantifies the actual level of the deficient factor, for example by plotting clotting times of the test and standard plasma dilutions against known factor concentration.
• Mixing studies are therefore a preliminary distinguishing test, while individual factor assays provide a specific, quantitative measurement of a given clotting factor.

questions.question:
(a) A dried blood stain is submitted for determination of its ABO blood type. Identify the technique that would be used and the reagent involved in its first step.
(b) State the principle of this first step.
(c) Describe the procedure of this first step.
(d) State what further step follows.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The absorption elution technique would be used; the reagent used in its first step (absorption) is antiserum containing A, B and AB antibodies.
(b)
The principle of absorption is that the antibodies in the antiserum bind to their specific antigen on the dried red cells, forming an antibody-antigen complex; for example, in an A-type sample, A-antibodies combine with the A-antigens present.
(c)
Antiserum is added to the dried blood sample, allowing the antibodies to bind to their specific antigen; the sample is then washed with a solvent to remove any unbound antibodies, leaving only the antibody-antigen complexes that have formed.
(d)
The second step, elution, involves using a solvent to remove or extract the bound antibody from the red cells before identification; the antigens on the red cells determine the individual's blood type (A, B, AB, or O, based on which antigens are present).

(a)
• Crossmatch procedures are classified as the full crossmatch, the emergency crossmatch, and uncrossmatched release of blood.
• The full crossmatch is the complete, staged procedure of washing donor cells, mixing with patient serum in four tubes, and checking for agglutination at room temperature, at 37°C, with albumin, and after AHG addition, with centrifugation.
(b)
• The emergency crossmatch is a full crossmatch completed within 1 hour.
• The uncrossmatched procedure involves blood grouping, dispatch of the blood, and immediate commencement of the full crossmatch afterwards.
(c)
• The full crossmatch is selected when time allows for the complete staged procedure to be carried out before transfusion.
• The emergency crossmatch is selected when a patient needs blood urgently but there is still time to perform the full crossmatch within an hour.
• Uncrossmatched blood is selected in situations requiring the most urgent release of blood, where grouping and dispatch occur first and the full crossmatch is only commenced afterwards.
(d)
• If uncrossmatched blood is dispatched without subsequently commencing and completing the full crossmatch, an incompatibility between donor and patient could go undetected.
• Similarly, if an emergency crossmatch omits any of the required phases (room temperature, 37°C incubation, albumin phase, or AHG phase) in order to finish within an hour, an incompatibility detectable only at a later phase could be missed.
• Selecting the uncrossmatched or emergency option when there is, in fact, time to perform a full crossmatch unnecessarily increases the risk of an undetected incompatibility.
• Any failure to complete every stage of the crossmatch procedure appropriate to the clinical urgency can therefore result in the release of incompatible blood.
• This can lead to a transfusion reaction, ranging from mild reactions such as shivering and urticarial rash to severe reactions such as haemolysis, haematuria, renal damage, other organ damage, and death without immediate treatment.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the crossmatch procedures used in compatibility testing.
(b) State what each type of crossmatch involves.
(c) State when each type of crossmatch is selected.
(d) Explain how omitting or shortening any stage of these procedures can lead to the release of incompatible blood.

(a) A blood film prepared from an EDTA sample shows clumps of platelets, and the automated platelet count is unexpectedly low. Identify the phenomenon.
(b) State why this occurs.
(c) State the corrective step for the specimen.
(d) State how the finding should be recorded/followed up.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is pseudothrombocytopenia.
(b)
It occurs because platelets clump together in samples anticoagulated with EDTA.
(c)
The platelet count should be repeated using a sample anticoagulated with heparin instead of EDTA.
(d)
The blood film finding of platelet clumping should be recorded and correlated with the repeat count, so that the true platelet count (and any true blood disorder shown on the film, such as leukaemia) is not confused with this artefact.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the method of preparing bone marrow films, including particle/crush smears.
(b) State how the films are fixed and stained.
(c) State how the film is reported.
(d) Explain why this method of preparation is used for bone marrow.
(e) Distinguish bone marrow film preparation from ordinary peripheral blood film preparation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bone marrow films are prepared by delivering single drops of aspirate onto two slides about 1 cm from one end, then quickly removing most of the blood with a pipette applied to the edge of each drop, or by placing the slides on a slope to allow the blood to drain away.
• The irregularly shaped marrow fragments tend to adhere to the slide, so most of them are left behind after the blood drains or is removed.
• Films are then prepared using three-quarters of a glass slide of the marrow fragments and the remaining blood, using a smooth-edged glass spreader of not more than 2 cm in width.
• The marrow fragments are dragged behind the spreader, leaving a trail of cells; differential counts are made in these cellular trails, starting from the marrow fragments and working back towards the head of the film.
• The preparation is considered satisfactory only when marrow particles and free marrow cells can be seen in the stained films; particle/crush smears can also be made as isolated crush preparations by gentle pressure of a second slide combined with sliding the two slides apart, giving preparations of authentic marrow cells.
(b)
• The films are fixed and stained with Romanowsky dyes as used for peripheral films, but a longer fixation time of at least 20 minutes in methanol is essential for high-quality staining, and the staining time should be increased if the marrow is hypercellular.
• Squashing and smearing the particles too firmly causes disruption and distortion of the cells, and the resultant thick preparations are difficult to stain well.
(c)
The film is reported with reference to the marrow particles visible mainly at the tail of the film, along with the differential count made from the cellular trails.
(d)
This method is used because it concentrates the marrow fragments and their trailing cells at the expense of the more dilute peripheral blood, allowing a meaningful differential count of marrow cells rather than mainly peripheral blood cells.
(e)
• Bone marrow film preparation differs from ordinary peripheral blood film preparation mainly in its longer fixation time (at least 20 minutes in methanol, increased further if hypercellular) and its reliance on marrow particles and fragment trails for the differential count.
• Peripheral blood films, by comparison, are stained with the same Romanowsky dyes but do not involve marrow fragments or particle-trail differential counting.
• The bone marrow method is therefore adapted specifically to concentrate and preserve marrow particles, unlike a routine peripheral blood film.

(a)
• Antihuman globulin (AHG) is the reagent added in the Coombs (antihuman globulin) techniques, namely the direct antiglobulin test (DAT) and the indirect antiglobulin test (IAT).
• In the DAT, 4–8 drops of AHG are added to washed red cells to detect agglutination.
(b)
• In the IAT, AHG is added after incubating patient serum with standard cells and washing the mixture three times.
• AHG is identified by its role in producing visible agglutination when it binds antibody or complement already coating the red cells.
(c)
• In the standard DAT procedure, whole blood is collected in plain tubes, red cells are washed three times and suspended in 3–5% saline, and 4–8 drops of AHG are added to 2–4 drops of the washed cells before checking for agglutination macroscopically and microscopically.
• In the standard IAT procedure, patient serum is incubated with standard O Rh D-positive cells at 37°C for 1 hour, checked for agglutination, washed three times, and AHG is then added before a second check for agglutination.
• Agglutination in the DAT indicates that sensitisation of the red cells occurred in vivo, whereas agglutination in the IAT indicates sensitisation occurred in vitro.
• AHG is also used in the fourth tube of the full crossmatch procedure, where donor cells are washed and AHG is added before centrifuging and checking for agglutination.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the antihuman globulin (AHG) reagent and its role in the Coombs techniques, including its identifying features.
(b) State how it is used in each technique.
(c) State the standard procedures in which AHG is used, including in compatibility testing.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• PT measures the time required for plasma to clot after an excess of thromboplastin and an optimal calcium concentration have been added to citrated plasma.
• It measures the function of the extrinsic coagulation pathway and is sensitive to Factors I, II, V, VII and X.
(b)
• Reagents include the patient's platelet-poor plasma, normal/control plasma, and thromboplastin reagent (which may already contain calcium chloride) plus calcium chloride 0.025 mol/l if required.
• Other requirements are glass tubes, automatic micropipettes of 100 µl, a water bath set at 37°C, stopwatches and a table lamp.
(c)
• Add 100 µl of plasma to a pre-warmed glass tube, add 200 µl of thromboplastin with calcium, mix and immediately start timing until a visible clot forms; repeat in duplicate.
• If PT is prolonged, mix 100 µl of abnormal plasma with 100 µl of normal plasma and repeat the thromboplastin/calcium clot test as a mixing study.
(d)
The test's sensitivity is influenced by the reagent and technique used, so the reference range should be established locally.
(e)
Results are expressed as the mean of duplicate recordings in seconds (normal value 11–16 seconds), as a prothrombin ratio, or as the INR, with a normal INR of 0.8–1.1.
(f)
• The PT evaluates patients suspected of having an inherited or acquired deficiency of the extrinsic/common pathway factors and is used to control oral anticoagulant therapy.
• Prolonged PT occurs in oral anticoagulant therapy, obstructive jaundice, liver disease, DIC, malabsorption, vitamin K deficiency and hereditary factor deficiency.
(g)
• The PT measures the extrinsic pathway using thromboplastin, whereas the APTT measures the intrinsic pathway after activating contact factors without adding tissue thromboplastin.
• The PT is sensitive to Factors I, II, V, VII and X, while the APTT depends on contact factors, Factors VIII, IX, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the prothrombin time (PT) test.
(b) List the reagents required for the PT test.
(c) Describe the procedure for performing the PT test.
(d) State the precautions to be observed when performing the PT test.
(e) State how PT results are reported.
(f) Explain why the PT test is used in the investigation of bleeding disorders.
(g) Distinguish the PT test from the APTT test.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Haemoglobin electrophoresis is a separation technique that identifies haemoglobin variants based on charge and molecular weight, commonly using an agarose medium.
• Variants of haemoglobin have different amino acids and therefore slightly different charges, which is the basis for their separation.
(b)
Haemoglobin standards are used to mark the migration of known variants, and variants can be identified on cellulose acetate/agarose at alkaline pH or citric agar/agarose at acidic pH.
(c)
• At alkaline pH, haemoglobin is negatively charged and migrates towards the anode, with separation based on charge; at acidic pH, the test is used as confirmation, since various haemoglobins carry different charges and interact differently with the agarose.
• The gel is positioned in the chamber agarose side down, aligning the positive and negative sides of the gel with the tank (bending the gel carefully into an inverted U), and run for 30 minutes at 50 V.
(d)
Migration patterns of the samples are compared to the standard sample to see how far and into how many bands each sample has separated.
(e)
The likely haemoglobin type for each patient is reported based on comparison of the sample's migration pattern and number of bands with the standard.
(f)
• Electrophoresis is used because separation based on charge and interaction with the agarose medium allows different haemoglobin variants to be visually distinguished and identified against known standards.
• Running the test at both alkaline and acidic pH allows the acidic-pH run to serve as confirmation of a variant tentatively identified at alkaline pH.
(g)
• High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is a broad analytical chemistry technique for separating compounds in a chemical mixture and can confirm the identity and quantify haemoglobin types.
• For most HPLC analyses, peak areas are used for quantitative calculation, although in most cases equivalent results can be achieved using peak height instead.
• Electrophoresis identifies haemoglobin variants mainly by their pattern of migration on a gel compared with standards, whereas HPLC separates and quantifies the haemoglobin types based on their chromatographic peaks.
