(a) State the principle of haemoglobin electrophoresis.
(b) State the media and pH conditions used.
(c) Describe the procedure for running the electrophoresis.
(d) State how the gel is read.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why electrophoresis is used in the investigation of haemoglobinopathies.
(g) Distinguish haemoglobin electrophoresis from high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).

(a) Less than 0.5 ml of marrow fluid, together with some blood, is obtained from an iliac crest aspiration and delivered for smear preparation. Identify the appropriate next step and the apparatus that would be used.
(b) State the principle behind the film preparation method.
(c) Describe the procedure.
(d) State the criterion for a satisfactory preparation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The next step is to prepare bone marrow films/smears immediately following aspiration, using two slides, a pipette to remove excess blood (or a sloped surface to drain it), and a smooth-edged glass spreader not more than 2 cm wide.
(b)
The principle is that the irregularly shaped marrow fragments adhere to the slide while much of the diluting blood is removed, and dragging the fragments with a spreader leaves a trail of cells suitable for a differential count concentrated at the tail of the film.
(c)
Single drops of aspirate are delivered onto two slides about 1 cm from one end; most of the blood is removed with a pipette applied to the edge of the drop, or the slides are placed on a slope to drain the blood; films are then made using three-quarters of the slide of marrow fragments and remaining blood with the spreader; the films are fixed and stained with Romanowsky dyes, using a fixation time of at least 20 minutes in methanol (longer if the marrow is hypercellular).
(d)
The preparation is considered satisfactory only when marrow particles and free marrow cells can be seen in the stained films.

questions.question:
(a) In a direct antiglobulin test, red cells washed three times and suspended in 3–5% saline show agglutination on microscopic and macroscopic examination after antihuman globulin is added. Identify the finding.
(b) State the principle behind this finding.
(c) Describe how the test producing this finding is performed.
(d) State how this finding should be recorded and any follow-up.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The agglutination is a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) result, indicating in vivo sensitisation of the patient's red cells.
(b)
Agglutination occurs because antihuman globulin binds to antibody or complement already coating the patient's red cells, cross-linking the cells together.
(c)
Whole blood is collected in plain tubes, about 0.5 ml is picked from the clotted, dislodged blood, the red cells are washed three times, suspended in 3–5% saline, and 2–4 drops of the washed cells are mixed with 4–8 drops of antihuman globulin before checking for agglutination macroscopically and microscopically.
(d)
The result is recorded as DAT positive, indicating in vivo sensitisation of the red cells, and this finding is relevant to further investigation of conditions such as haemolytic disease of the newborn or a transfusion reaction.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the APTT reagent, including its identifying features.
(b) State how this reagent is used in practice.
(c) State the standard procedure in which this reagent is applied.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind shaking the reagent before use and being aware of interferences such as lipaemia.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The APTT reagent contains an activator such as kaolin (5 g/l, i.e., 0.5 g in 100 ml of barbitone buffered saline, pH 7.4), although silica, celite or ellagic acid may also be used.
• It also contains phospholipid, and calcium chloride at 0.025 mol/l is added separately during the test.
(b)
• The activator initiates the intrinsic pathway of coagulation by contact activation, after which phospholipid and calcium are added and the clotting time is measured.
• The reagent is used together with the patient's platelet-poor plasma to perform the test.
(c)
• In the standard procedure, the APTT reagent is added to pre-warmed plasma and incubated for 3 minutes before calcium solution is added and clotting time is recorded.
• The reagent evaluates the overall efficacy of the intrinsic pathway and is also sensitive to circulating anticoagulants (inhibitors) and heparin.
• It depends on contact factors, Factors VIII, IX, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen being present and functional.
(d)
• The reagent must be shaken vigorously for approximately 15 seconds before use.
• Failure to shake the reagent adequately can affect its activation of the intrinsic pathway and give an inaccurate clotting time.
• Lipaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia can interfere with the detection of clot formation by photo-optical methods.
• These interferences should be recognised so that results in lipaemic or hyperbilirubinaemic samples are interpreted with caution.
• Proper reagent handling and awareness of interferences are therefore necessary for a reliable APTT result.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle and indications of bone marrow aspiration.
(b) List the needles used.
(c) Describe the procedure for bone marrow aspiration.
(d) State the precautions to be observed.
(e) State how the aspirate is reported.
(f) Explain why bone marrow aspiration is used in haematological investigation.
(g) Distinguish bone marrow aspiration from bone marrow biopsy (trephine biopsy).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bone marrow aspiration is a procedure to collect a sample of bone marrow fluid, which is examined under the microscope and checked for abnormal cells, and it is usually simple, safe and relatively painless.
• The appropriate sites in an adult are the posterior iliac crest (preferred), the anterior iliac crest, and the sternum, while the iliac crest is used under 12 years of age and the tibia may be used in infants younger than 18 months.
(b)
Needles used include the Salah, Klima and Islam's aspiration needles.
(c)
• After patient preparation, the needle and stylet are inserted into the iliac crest or spine with a slight rotary motion; when firmly in place, the stylet is removed, a syringe without anticoagulant is attached, and <0.5 ml of bone marrow and blood is aspirated, with smears prepared immediately.
• A second syringe may be attached to draw additional samples for flow cytometry, cytogenetic and molecular studies, microbiology, electron microscopy or bone marrow culture; if a 'dry tap' occurs, the aspiration can be repeated at a slightly different angle or another site.
(d)
• A minimum amount of marrow should be aspirated, since volumes over 0.5 ml will almost certainly be diluted with blood, making processing and interpretation more difficult.
• Bone marrow puncture is prohibited in patients with coagulopathies such as haemophilia or vitamin K deficiency, although thrombocytopenia is not an absolute contraindication.
(e)
The aspirate is assessed and reported for cellularity, differential count, myeloid:erythroid ratio, the erythroid, myeloid, megakaryocyte, lymphoid and plasma cell series, and any abnormal cells or parasites.
(f)
Aspiration provides fine cytological detail and allows cytochemical stains, microbiological culture, flow cytometry, and cytogenetic and molecular studies to be performed, and is indicated for unexplained anaemia, cytopenia or cytosis, abnormal blood film morphology, and diagnosis/staging of haematological malignancies.
(g)
• Bone marrow biopsy (trephine biopsy) instead yields a narrow, cylindrically shaped solid piece of bone marrow, obtained by inserting the biopsy needle with a to-and-fro rotation, and is fixed in 10% formal saline before decalcification, paraffin embedding and sectioning on a microtome.
• While aspiration gives fine cytological detail for cytochemistry, culture and molecular studies, biopsy is used mainly to assess cellularity and architecture, detect lesions, and assess conditions such as aplastic anaemia or marrow metastasis, particularly when aspiration yields a dry tap.
• Biopsy also provides archival material and can proceed immediately at the iliac spine sites even if aspiration alone fails.

questions.question:
(a) A tube containing a mixture of a patient's blood with phosphate buffer, saponin and sodium dithionite is held in front of a white card ruled with narrow black lines, and the lines cannot be seen through the tube. Identify the finding.
(b) State the principle behind this finding.
(c) Describe how the test is performed.
(d) State the follow-up step required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The inability to see the lines through the tube (an opaque/turbid solution) is a positive sickle solubility test, indicating the presence of haemoglobin S.
(b)
Under deoxygenated conditions, HbS becomes insoluble and forms crystals that refract light, causing the turbidity; saponin is used to cause haemolysis of the red cells, while sodium dithionite induces the deoxygenation.
(c)
A phosphate buffer supplemented with saponin and sodium dithionite is mixed with the blood sample; after incubation, the solution is held in front of the white card with narrow black lines and read for turbidity, with turbidity recorded both before and after centrifugation.
(d)
A positive result should be followed up with confirmatory testing such as haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC to identify the specific haemoglobin variant present.

questions.question:
(a) Classify the outcomes of donor screening and the deferral criteria applied.
(b) Classify the types of donor reaction that may occur.
(c) State how deferral criteria and donor reactions are managed in practice.
(d) Explain how failing to apply deferral criteria or manage a donor reaction correctly can lead to an adverse outcome.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Outcomes of donor screening are classified as acceptance, temporary deferral, or permanent deferral.
• Temporary deferral for 6 months applies to donors with HIV/AIDS risk factors such as having sex with more than one partner, having sex with an unknown partner, intravenous drug use, or having sex with a person with these risk factors.
(b)
• Female donors are temporarily deferred during pregnancy, for one year after delivery, when lactating, and during the menstrual period; male donors are deferred if they have consumed alcohol or tobacco in the previous 24 hours.
• Donor reactions are classified as vasovagal reaction, hyperventilation, and hematoma.
(c)
• Temporary deferral criteria are applied through the medical history interview and physical examination stages of donor screening, based on the donor's answers and presentation on the day.
• Vasovagal reaction (sudden fainting due to hypotension) is managed by psychological support through a positive donor-staff relationship and reassurance, along with physical comfort such as appropriate temperature and surroundings.
• Hyperventilation, usually associated with anxiety, is managed by reassuring the donor, asking them to cough to interrupt the breathing pattern, and instructing them to rebreathe expelled air into a small paper bag.
• Hematoma, a mass of usually clotted blood confined to a local region from rupture of a blood vessel, is prevented by effective collection technique and, once it occurs, resolves spontaneously or with an ice pack.
(d)
• Failing to defer a donor with an HIV/AIDS risk factor, or a female donor who is pregnant, postpartum within a year, lactating, or menstruating, or a male donor who has recently used alcohol or tobacco, risks compromising the safety of the donated blood or the wellbeing of the donor.
• Not recognising early signs of a vasovagal reaction, such as apprehension in a first-time donor, could allow the reaction to progress without appropriate support.
• Failing to interrupt hyperventilation appropriately could allow it to progress to hypocalcaemic tetany or syncope in severe cases.
• Poor collection technique that increases the risk of hematoma formation is itself a preventable handling error in the donation process.

questions.question:
(a) Classify the laboratory tests used to investigate the fibrinolytic system.
(b) State the principle/procedure of each type.
(c) State when each test is selected or applied clinically.
(d) Explain how a basic specimen-handling error can lead to an inaccurate fibrinolytic test result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Laboratory investigations of the fibrinolytic system include detection of FDPs by the latex agglutination method, the D-dimer test, and euglobulin clot lysis.
• FDPs (fibrin degradation products) are fragments produced by proteolytic digestion of fibrinogen or fibrin by plasmin.
(b)
• For the FDP assay, blood is collected in a tube containing thrombin (to remove all fibrinogen by converting it into a clot) and soybean trypsin inhibitor (to inhibit plasmin and prevent in vitro breakdown of fibrin); a suspension of latex particles linked to anti-fibrinogen antibodies is mixed with dilutions of the patient's serum, and agglutination indicates FDPs are present.
• For the D-dimer assay, plasma or serum is mixed with latex or polystyrene microparticles coated with a monoclonal antibody to D-dimer, and microparticle agglutination is observed as the result.
(c)
• FDPs are increased in DIC, deep vein thrombosis, severe pneumonia and recent myocardial infarction.
• D-dimer is raised in DIC, intravascular thrombosis (myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism), and during the postoperative period or following trauma.
• These tests are therefore selected when a thrombotic or fibrinolytic disorder, such as DIC or venous thromboembolism, is suspected.
• The reptilase time is a related confirmatory test that assesses fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion specifically in the presence of heparin.
(d)
• If the correct collection tube (containing thrombin and soybean trypsin inhibitor) is not used for the FDP assay, ongoing in vitro breakdown of fibrin could produce a falsely elevated FDP result.
• Using an inappropriate specimen type for the D-dimer test, rather than the accepted plasma or serum sample, could likewise distort the agglutination result obtained.
• Failure to distinguish D-dimer (a specific breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin) from total FDPs could lead to confusion in interpreting which fibrinolytic pathway abnormality is present.
• Such handling or interpretive errors in fibrinolytic testing can result in a result that does not accurately reflect the patient's true fibrinolytic status.

questions.question:
(a) Classify the laboratory investigations used for haemoglobinopathies.
(b) State what each type of investigation detects or provides.
(c) State how these investigations are applied or selected to confirm a haemoglobinopathy.
(d) Explain how a basic error in performing or reading any of these investigations can lead to an inaccurate result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The laboratory methods for investigating haemoglobinopathies are full blood count (FBC) and peripheral blood film reading, the sickling test, the sickle solubility test, haemoglobin electrophoresis, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), DNA analysis (restriction fragment length polymorphism, RFLP), and paternal testing.
• FBC and blood film provide a general screen, including blood film examination and reporting.
(b)
• The sickling test and sickle solubility test detect the presence of HbS through, respectively, microscopic sickling and macroscopic turbidity.
• Electrophoresis and HPLC separate and identify or quantify specific haemoglobin variants, while DNA analysis identifies the underlying genetic defect and is especially important in antenatal diagnosis; paternal testing evaluates parents since haemoglobinopathies are inherited disorders.
(c)
• To confirm a haemoglobinopathy, the investigations performed are FBC and blood film, the sickle solubility test, and HPLC or haemoglobin electrophoresis.
• The sickling test and solubility test are generally used as rapid initial screens, while electrophoresis, HPLC and DNA analysis are used for definitive identification and confirmation of the specific variant or genetic defect.
• Paternal testing is added to the work-up because these disorders are inherited, so testing of parents assists diagnosis.
(d)
• In the sickle solubility test, an error such as reading the result only after centrifugation, rather than recording turbidity both before and after, can give a misleading interpretation.
• In the sickling test, misreading a trait sample too early, before allowing the additional time or altered oxygen tension that a trait sample may need, can lead to a false-negative result.
• In electrophoresis, failure to compare the sample's migration pattern against the standard sample can lead to misidentification of the haemoglobin variant present.
• Errors in any of these methods can therefore result in an incorrect diagnosis of the type or presence of a haemoglobinopathy.
• Using the appropriate combination of these investigations, rather than any single one alone, reduces the risk of such diagnostic error.

(a)
• The thrombin time (TT) is the time required for thrombin to convert fibrinogen to an insoluble fibrin clot when thrombin is added to plasma, bypassing the earlier steps of the coagulation cascade.
• It detects fibrinogen only and does not measure defects in the intrinsic or extrinsic pathways.
(b)
Reagents are platelet-poor plasma and a thrombin solution that induces the clotting of normal plasma in about 15 seconds.
(c)
• Add 100 µl of saline to a glass tube, place it in a 37°C water bath for 3–5 minutes, add 100 µl of plasma and mix well, then add 100 µl of diluted bovine thrombin, mix, and immediately start the stopwatch, stopping it when a visible clot has formed; repeat for the sample.
• If the TT is prolonged, a mixing study is carried out by combining 100 µl of abnormal plasma with 100 µl of normal plasma (50:50 mix) and repeating the test on the mixture.
(d)
The test is affected by abnormal fibrinogen levels, dysfibrinogenaemia, and the presence of antithrombins such as heparin and direct thrombin inhibitors such as hirudin, and by FDPs.
(e)
Results are reported as the time in seconds for a visible clot to form, compared against the normal thrombin solution time of about 15 seconds.
(f)
• Prolonged TT is caused by hypofibrinogenaemia (as in DIC or a congenital defect), raised FDP concentrations, dysfibrinogenaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, and paraproteinaemia.
• Extreme prolongation of the TT is nearly always due to unfractionated heparin, so the TT is a useful screening tool when heparin contamination or therapy is suspected.
(g)
• The reptilase time also assesses the rate of fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion, but does so in the presence of heparin.
• Because the TT is markedly prolonged by heparin while the reptilase time is not similarly affected, the two tests together can help distinguish a heparin effect from a true fibrinogen abnormality.
• This distinction makes the reptilase time a useful confirmatory test when the TT is prolonged and heparin contamination is suspected.
questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the thrombin time (TT) test.
(b) List the reagents required for the TT test.
(c) Describe the procedure for performing the TT test.
(d) State the factors that affect TT results.
(e) State how TT results are reported.
(f) Explain why the TT test is used in the investigation of bleeding disorders.
(g) Distinguish the TT test from the reptilase time.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This represents a film of aspirated bone marrow in which the marrow fragments/particles are visible, indicating a satisfactory preparation.
(b)
It occurs because the marrow fragments are dragged behind the spreader during film preparation and leave a trail of cells, with the fragments concentrated towards the tail of the film.
(c)
A drop of aspirate is placed on a slide, most of the blood is removed with a pipette or drained on a slope so the irregularly shaped fragments adhere to the slide, and a film is then made of three-quarters of the slide using a smooth-edged glass spreader not more than 2 cm wide, before fixing and staining with Romanowsky dyes (with a longer fixation time of at least 20 minutes in methanol).
(d)
Differential counts are made in the cellular trails, starting from the marrow fragments and working back towards the head of the film, and the preparation is only considered satisfactory for reporting when marrow particles and free marrow cells can be seen in the stained film.
questions.question:
(a) A stained bone marrow film shows marrow particles that are easily visible, mostly at the tail of the film. Identify what this represents.
(b) State why this appearance occurs.
(c) Describe how such a film is prepared.
(d) State how the finding is used in reporting.

(a) State the principle of the activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) test.
(b) List the reagents required for the APTT test.
(c) Describe the procedure for performing the APTT test.
(d) State the precautions/interferences relevant to the APTT test.
(e) State how APTT results are reported and interpreted.
(f) Explain why the APTT test is used in the investigation of bleeding disorders.
(g) Distinguish the APTT test from the thrombin time (TT) test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The APTT measures the clotting time of plasma after activation of contact factors and the addition of phospholipid and calcium chloride, without adding tissue thromboplastin.
• It evaluates the overall efficacy of the intrinsic coagulation pathway and depends on contact factors, Factors VIII, IX, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen.
(b)
Reagents include platelet-poor plasma, an activator such as kaolin (5 g/l), silica, celite or ellagic acid, phospholipid, and calcium chloride 0.025 mol/l.
(c)
• Shake the APTT reagent vigorously for about 15 seconds, add 100 µl of it to a pre-warmed tube, add 100 µl of plasma, mix and incubate for 3 minutes, then add 100 µl of calcium solution and immediately start timing until a visible clot forms; repeat in duplicate.
• If the APTT is prolonged, a mixing study is performed by mixing 100 µl of abnormal plasma with 100 µl of normal plasma and repeating the test on the mixture.
(d)
Lipaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia can interfere with the detection of clot formation by photo-optical methods, so this should be borne in mind when interpreting results.
(e)
The normal APTT range is 30–40 seconds, and results are reported in seconds alongside the control value.
(f)
• The APTT evaluates patients suspected of having a deficiency of the intrinsic and common pathway factors and is also sensitive to circulating inhibitors and heparin, so it is used to monitor heparin therapy and investigate causes of bleeding.
• A prolonged APTT with a normal PT suggests a possible deficiency of factor VIII, IX, XI or XII, high molecular weight kininogen, prekallikrein, or the presence of an inhibitor.
(g)
• The APTT measures the intrinsic pathway by activating contact factors without added tissue thromboplastin, whereas the thrombin time (TT) bypasses the earlier steps of the cascade entirely by adding thrombin directly to plasma.
• The APTT is affected by deficiencies of contact factors and Factors VIII, IX, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen, whereas the TT specifically detects fibrinogen and is affected by abnormal fibrinogen levels, dysfibrinogenaemia and antithrombins such as heparin.
• Unlike the APTT, the TT does not measure defects in the intrinsic or extrinsic pathways.

(a)
• In adults, the appropriate sites for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy are the posterior iliac crest (the preferred site), the anterior iliac crest, and the sternum.
• In children under 12 years, the iliac crest is used, and in infants younger than 18 months to 2 years, the proximal anterior portion of the tibia may be used because of the active marrow present in long bones at that age.
(b)
• The sternum is the best site when aspiration only is needed, is the easiest to puncture, and is considered to yield the most cellular samples.
• The anterior or posterior iliac spines have the advantage that if no material is aspirated, a micro trephine biopsy can be performed immediately at the same site.
(c)
• The site is selected according to the age of the patient and whether a needle or trephine biopsy is required in addition to aspiration.
• The sternum's disadvantage is that the patient has a clear view of the procedure, which may cause distress, whereas the iliac spines allow an immediate biopsy if aspiration fails.
• In infants and children, the sternum is naturally thin, so an alternative site is preferred over sternal puncture.
(d)
• Attempting sternal aspiration in an infant or young child, where the sternum is naturally thin, increases the risk of complications such as perforation of underlying structures.
• Using the iliac crest correctly for children under 12 years, or the tibia in very young infants, instead avoids this risk while still obtaining active marrow.
• If the site chosen does not match the patient's age group, the sample obtained could be inadequate or the procedure could result in complications such as haemorrhage or perforation of major vessels.
• In disorders where haemopoietic marrow is replaced by other tissue, choosing a site without allowing for the possibility of a dry tap can waste the attempt rather than proceeding promptly to a needle or trephine biopsy at another site or angle.
• Correct site selection according to age and clinical need therefore reduces the risk of an inadequate sample or a procedural complication.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the sites used for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy according to age.
(b) State the advantages of the sternum and iliac spine sites.
(c) State how the site is selected in practice.
(d) Explain how choosing a site inappropriate for the patient's age can lead to an inadequate sample or complication.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The dithionite reagent used in the haemoglobin sickling test is a 10% sodium dithionite (Na2S2O4) solution in phosphate buffer at pH 6.8.
• Sodium dithionite (also called sodium hydrosulfite) is a potent reducing agent.
(b)
• It is identified by its preparation method: dissolving 10 mg of sodium dithionite in 1 ml of phosphate buffer at pH 6.8, mixed well and used immediately.
• Other materials used alongside it are an anticoagulated peripheral blood sample, a Pasteur pipette, microscope slides and coverslips, and petroleum jelly-paraffin wax or depex.
(c)
• In the standard sickling test procedure, a drop of the dithionite solution is mixed with a drop of anticoagulated blood in a test tube, and a drop of the mixture is placed on a slide, covered and sealed for microscopic examination.
• It removes an oxygen molecule from the iron atom in the haem group, converting oxyhaemoglobin to deoxyhaemoglobin.
• In a deoxygenated state, red cells containing HbS polymerise and form the typical sickle shape.
(d)
• The dithionite solution must be made fresh and used immediately after preparation.
• This precaution is necessary because the reagent's role depends on its reducing (deoxygenating) action, and its usefulness for the test relies on it being freshly prepared.
• Using an old or improperly prepared solution risks failure to adequately deoxygenate the sample.
• Inadequate deoxygenation could result in a false-negative sickling result even in a sample that truly contains HbS.
• Fresh reagent preparation therefore safeguards the reliability of the sickling test result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition and preparation of the dithionite reagent used in the sickling test, including its identifying features.
(b) State the other materials used alongside this reagent.
(c) State the standard method in which this reagent is used.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that the reagent must be freshly prepared and used immediately.

(a) An area 5 cm in diameter is marked on a patient's antecubital fossa, and a sphygmomanometer is inflated to 80 mm Hg for 5 minutes; on release, 3–5 small purpuric spots appear within the marked area. Identify the test and interpret the finding.
(b) State the principle behind the appearance of these spots.
(c) Describe how the test is performed.
(d) State how an abnormal (excessive) result would be interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is Hess's test (the capillary resistance test), and the appearance of 3–5 purpuric eruptions is the normal result.
(b)
The test assesses vascular integrity; sustained pressure on the small vessels of the marked area reveals their resistance to rupture, with a normal vessel wall producing only a few purpuric spots.
(c)
An area 5 cm in diameter is marked on the antecubital fossa, and a sphygmomanometer is inflated to 80 mm Hg for 5 minutes, after which the marked area is examined for purpuric eruptions.
(d)
An excessive number of purpuric eruptions beyond the normal 3–5 would indicate reduced vascular/capillary integrity, consistent with a vascular bleeding disorder or thrombocytopenia/thrombocytopathy affecting capillary resistance.

(a)
• Antenatal serology tests consist of blood grouping of the mother (and father, if available) to determine ABO and Rh group, screening for infectious diseases (HIV I & II, Hepatitis B and C, Zika virus), antibody screening using the indirect antihuman globulin test (IAT) if the woman is Rh D negative, and antibody titration if the IAT is positive.
• A history is taken first, covering gestational age of the pregnancy, previous transfusion and pregnancies, antibody reaction, and history of RhD immunoglobulin, among other details.
(b)
• Blood grouping identifies the ABO and Rh type of the mother and, where available, the father.
• Infectious disease screening detects HIV I & II, Hepatitis B and C, and Zika virus, which are among the complications antenatal serology aims to prevent, along with haemolytic disease of the newborn and transfusion reaction.
(c)
• These tests are performed in a defined sequence: history and blood grouping first, then infectious disease screening, then antibody screening by IAT if the woman is Rh D negative, and finally antibody titration if the IAT is positive, monitored until delivery.
• A high antibody titre on titration indicates severity of the condition and continues to be monitored throughout the pregnancy.
• The purpose of these tests together is to determine the woman's status, prevent prenatal and postnatal complications in the fetus/neonate, and ensure proper management of the mother's condition.
(d)
• If antibody screening by IAT is omitted in a Rh D-negative woman, in vitro sensitisation of red cells could go undetected, missing a risk factor for haemolytic disease of the newborn.
• If antibody titration is not performed and monitored after a positive IAT, a rising or high antibody titre indicating worsening severity could be missed.
• Skipping the infectious disease screening component could leave conditions such as HIV or hepatitis undetected, with consequences for both mother and neonate.
• Omitting the father's blood grouping, where available, could remove information relevant to assessing risk to the fetus.
• Errors or omissions in this sequence of tests can therefore result in an incomplete antenatal assessment and an increased risk of undetected complications.
questions.question:
(a) Classify the tests performed as part of antenatal serology.
(b) State what each type of test determines.
(c) State the order in which these tests are applied and their overall purpose.
(d) Explain how omitting any one of these tests can lead to an increased risk of undetected complications.

(a) Classify the coagulation factors into their groups.
(b) State the characteristics of each group.
(c) State how this classification is applied in interpreting coagulation screening tests.
(d) Explain how a basic error in classifying which factor group is affected can lead to an inaccurate result or interpretation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Coagulation factors are grouped into the fibrinogen group (Factors I, V, VIII and XIII), the prothrombin group (Factors II, VII, IX and X), and the contact group (Factors XI, XII, high molecular weight kininogen (HMWK) and prekallikrein).
• The fibrinogen group factors are the most labile, are consumed during coagulation, and are also found on platelets.
(b)
• The prothrombin group factors are vitamin K dependent and may be affected by coumarin, diet and antibiotics.
• The contact group factors initiate the intrinsic pathway of coagulation as well as fibrinolysis.
(c)
• This grouping helps in interpreting which screening test is likely to be abnormal: deficiencies within the prothrombin group typically prolong the PT, while deficiencies within the contact group typically prolong only the APTT.
• Recognising the fibrinogen group as the most labile factors also guides specimen handling, since these factors are more susceptible to loss during storage or processing.
• Awareness that prothrombin group factors are vitamin K dependent is used to select and interpret testing in patients on oral anticoagulant (vitamin K antagonist) therapy.
(d)
• If a deficiency within the contact group (e.g., Factor XII, HMWK or prekallikrein) is not recognised, the resulting prolonged APTT with a normal PT may be misinterpreted if the grouping is not understood.
• Similarly, failure to appreciate that Factors II, V, VII and X are the prothrombin group can lead to overlooking oral anticoagulant therapy, liver disease, obstructive jaundice, DIC, malabsorption or vitamin K deficiency as possible causes of a prolonged PT.
• Because fibrinogen group factors are the most labile, improper specimen storage can cause an artefactual deficiency that could be mistaken for a true clotting factor disorder.
• Errors in classifying which factor group is affected can therefore misdirect further investigation, such as choosing the wrong specific factor assay.
• Correct classification of coagulation factors by group thus underpins the accurate selection and interpretation of both screening tests and specific factor assays.

(a)
The crescent-shaped red cells indicate a positive sickling test, that is, the presence of haemoglobin S (HbS).
(b)
Sodium dithionite is a potent reducing agent that removes an oxygen molecule from the iron atom of the haem group, converting oxyhaemoglobin to deoxyhaemoglobin; in this deoxygenated state, red cells containing HbS polymerise and form the typical sickle shape.
(c)
A fresh 10% sodium dithionite solution in phosphate buffer (pH 6.8) is mixed with a drop of the patient's anticoagulated blood; a drop of the mixture is placed on a slide, covered with a coverslip avoiding air bubbles, and the edges sealed with petroleum jelly-paraffin wax or depex before microscopic observation.
(d)
• In HbS disease, sickling can appear immediately or near-immediately, whereas in the HbS trait, clear sickling within an hour at 37°C may not be conclusive and may require additional time or altered oxygen tension.
• The result should be recorded as sickling positive or negative, and a positive finding should be followed up with a sickle solubility test or haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC for confirmation.
questions.question:
(a) A blood sample mixed with a reducing reagent under a coverslip sealed with petroleum jelly is examined under the microscope after incubation, and red cells are seen to have assumed a crescent shape. Identify the abnormal finding.
(b) State the principle behind the technique used to detect this finding.
(c) Describe the reagent and procedure used to prepare the slide for this observation.
(d) State how the finding should be recorded and any follow-up step that should be taken.

(a) Describe the calibration plasma and other reagents used in the fibrinogen assay, including their identifying features.
(b) State how the calibration curve is prepared.
(c) State the standard use of the calibration curve in reporting a patient's fibrinogen level.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind diluting the plasma and using a strong thrombin solution.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The calibration plasma used in the fibrinogen assay (Clauss technique) has a known level of fibrinogen calibrated against an International Reference Standard.
• Other reagents are platelet-poor plasma, a strong thrombin solution, and a buffer (veronal buffer).
(b)
• Serial dilutions of the calibration plasma are prepared in veronal buffer, typically 1 in 5, 1 in 10, 1 in 20 and 1 in 40, to give a range of fibrinogen concentrations.
• A calibration curve is prepared by plotting the clotting time in seconds against the fibrinogen concentration in g/l for each dilution.
(c)
• In the standard procedure, 0.2 ml of each dilution is warmed to 37°C, 0.1 ml of thrombin solution is added, and the clotting time is measured and plotted to derive the fibrinogen concentration.
• This calibration curve is then used to read off the fibrinogen concentration of a patient's plasma from its own clotting time.
• The normal range for fibrinogen is approximately 1.8–3.6 g/l.
(d)
• The plasma is diluted so as to give a low level of any inhibitors present, such as FDPs and heparin.
• Diluting the plasma in this way prevents these inhibitors from artificially lengthening the clotting time and distorting the calibration curve.
• A strong thrombin solution must be used so that the clotting time, over the wide range tested, is independent of the exact thrombin concentration used.
• If a weak thrombin solution were used instead, variation in thrombin activity could itself alter the clotting time and invalidate the calibration curve.
• Careful preparation of the calibration curve is therefore essential to obtaining an accurate fibrinogen concentration for the patient's plasma.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the bleeding time test.
(b) List the apparatus required.
(c) Describe the procedure for the bleeding time test methods.
(d) State the precautions to be observed.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the bleeding time test is used in the investigation of bleeding disorders.
(g) Distinguish the bleeding time test from the whole blood clotting time.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The bleeding time test measures the time between a skin puncture and spontaneous, unassisted stoppage of bleeding, reflecting how fast injured small blood vessels and platelets seal the opening.
• It depends on the efficiency of tissue fluid in accelerating coagulation, capillary function, and the number of platelets and their ability to form a plug.
(b)
Apparatus required includes a sterile finger-prick lancet or bleeding-time device, clean filter paper (Whatman No. 1), a blood pressure cuff (for the Ivy-based methods), and a stopwatch.
(c)
• In the preferred Simplate/Surgicutt procedure, a blood pressure cuff is inflated to 40 mm Hg on the forearm, a standardised puncture 5 mm wide and 1 mm deep is made, and the time is recorded by blotting the site with filter paper every 30 seconds without touching the wound until bleeding ceases.
• Other methods include the Duke method (puncture of the ear lobe, blotted every 30 seconds), the Ivy method (forearm puncture under cuff pressure) and the Mielke method (a template incision with a controlled depth blade).
(d)
Precautions include asking about recent aspirin or blood-thinner use, ensuring the alcohol used to clean the site has dried completely, starting the stopwatch simultaneously with the puncture, and not letting the filter paper touch the wound.
(e)
If bleeding continues beyond 15 minutes, the test is discontinued, pressure is applied, and if repeated on the other arm bleeding still has not ceased by 15 minutes, the result is reported as >15 minutes; otherwise, results are reported to the nearest 30 seconds, with a normal range of 1.0–9.0 minutes.
(f)
• The bleeding time is used to evaluate platelet plug formation and capillary integrity, and is performed before surgery or biopsy, during anticoagulant therapy, or when there is a history of bleeding.
• It is prolonged when the platelet count is below 50,000/µL or when platelet dysfunction is present, so it complements the platelet count in assessing primary haemostasis.
(g)
• Whole blood clotting time (CT) instead measures the time interval between blood entering a glass capillary tube or syringe and the formation of fibrin threads, using methods such as Wright's capillary glass tube, Duke's drop method and the Lee and White test-tube method.
• Its apparatus is a 10–12 cm glass capillary tube of uniform diameter and a stopwatch, and its normal value by Wright's method is 3–6 minutes, compared with 1.0–9.0 minutes for the bleeding time.
• While the bleeding time assesses platelet plug formation and capillary function in vivo, the whole blood clotting time assesses the overall ability of whole blood to form a fibrin clot.

questions.question:
(a) A full blood count reports a platelet count of 40,000 cells/mm3. Interpret this result.
(b) State how it should be recorded.
(c) State what it indicates about the patient's haemostasis.
(d) State the appropriate action.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A platelet count of 40,000 cells/mm3 is below the normal range of 150,000–400,000 cells/mm3 and below the 50,000 cells/mm3 threshold, indicating severe thrombocytopenia.
(b)
The result is recorded as the platelet count in cells/mm3, alongside the applicable classification (normal, mild thrombocytopenia [50,000–100,000], or severe thrombocytopenia [<50,000]).
(c)
A count this low indicates a significant reduction in circulating platelets, which is associated with a prolonged bleeding time and platelet dysfunction, since bleeding times are generally prolonged when the platelet count is below 50,000/µL.
(d)
The result should prompt examination of the blood film for platelet morphology and clumping (to exclude pseudothrombocytopenia, which requires repeating the count using a heparin sample instead of EDTA), and consideration of a bleeding time test as part of further investigation.

questions.question:
(a) A patient on warfarin therapy has an INR result of 6.0. Interpret this result.
(b) State how the result should be recorded.
(c) State what this result indicates.
(d) State the appropriate action.
questions.answerText:
(a)
An INR of 6.0 is well above the normal range of 0.8–1.1 and above the target range of 2.0–3.0 for patients on warfarin therapy, and is classified as an INR >5, representing an unacceptably high risk of bleeding.
(b)
The result is recorded as the INR value alongside the corresponding PT and control PT values used to calculate it.
(c)
This result indicates that the patient's coagulation is excessively prolonged relative to what is therapeutically desired, reflecting an increased bleeding risk.
(d)
Given the unacceptably high risk of bleeding indicated by an INR >5, this result should be reported promptly so that the patient's anticoagulant therapy can be reviewed and adjusted.

(a)
• Whole blood for coagulation testing is aseptically collected by venepuncture into 3.2% sodium citrate as the anticoagulant.
• The volume of anticoagulant needed for a 5 ml blood sample is adjusted to the haematocrit, keeping the citrate volume at 0.5 ml and calculating the blood volume added using (60 − haematocrit)/100 × 4.5.
(b)
• The citrated whole blood is centrifuged to obtain platelet-poor plasma, at a minimum of 1700 rpm for at least 10 minutes (or 2500 rpm for 15 minutes), preferably at 4°C in a refrigerated centrifuge, giving a platelet count of <10 × 10⁹/L.
• Samples are opened at room temperature, and the plasma is separated and stored at 4°C as quickly as possible.
(c)
• This platelet-poor plasma specimen is used for the screening tests of blood coagulation, namely PT, APTT, TT and fibrinogen concentration assay.
• Samples for immediate testing should be tested within 4 hours of collection, whereas samples for factor assays are stored at 4°C, and samples for screening tests and the factor VII assay are kept at room temperature to avoid cold activation.
• Samples can be deep-frozen for later testing, with storage at −70°C or lower preferred, −35°C adequate for most tests, and −20°C usually inadequate.
(d)
• When room temperature exceeds 25°C, labile coagulation proteins may be affected, so a refrigerated (4°C) centrifuge should be used instead.
• This precaution prevents degradation of labile clotting factors that would otherwise give a falsely abnormal (prolonged) result.
• Freezing and thawing of plasma is best avoided before APTT determinations, since the results obtained can be affected.
• Double centrifugation should be used if samples are frozen before analysis for a lupus anticoagulant.
• Proper specimen handling therefore protects the accuracy of coagulation screening test results.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the collection and composition of the specimen used for coagulation testing.
(b) State how this specimen is processed to obtain the material used for testing.
(c) State the standard setting/use for this processed specimen in the laboratory.
(d) Explain the reasoning behind the precaution of using a refrigerated centrifuge when room temperature is high.

(a) Classify coagulation disorders.
(b) State the disorders within each class.
(c) State how each class of disorder is recognised and investigated.
(d) Explain how failing to correctly classify a coagulation disorder can lead to an inaccurate diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Coagulation disorders are classified as inherited (hereditary) disorders, where there is a deficiency in a single coagulation factor, and acquired disorders, where there are deficiencies in multiple coagulation factors.
• Inherited disorders include Haemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency), Haemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency), Haemophilia C (Factor XI deficiency), and Von Willebrand disease (deficiency in quality or quantity of von Willebrand factor).
(b)
• Acquired disorders include vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and fibrinolytic defects.
• Haemophilia A and B are sex-linked recessive disorders that usually affect males, whereas Haemophilia C and Von Willebrand disease are inherited but not sex-linked and affect both genders.
(c)
• Inherited disorders are recognised by a deficiency of a single factor and are investigated using the specific factor assay for that factor once screening tests point to it.
• Acquired disorders are recognised by reduced levels of multiple factors together, for example the reduced synthesis of Factors II, VII, IX and X seen in liver disease or vitamin K deficiency.
• Vitamin K deficiency occurs predominantly in babies aged 0–3 months because very little vitamin K is stored in their bodies and they receive insufficient amounts from the placenta.
• DIC involves rapid consumption of both coagulation factors and platelets, bringing a high risk of serious bleeding, and can also cause small clots that block vessels and damage organs such as the liver, brain or kidneys.
(d)
• Mistaking an acquired multi-factor deficiency, such as liver disease, for a single inherited factor deficiency could result in the wrong specific factor assay being requested.
• Failure to recognise that DIC affects both platelets and coagulation factors could lead to an incomplete work-up that checks only the platelet count or only the coagulation screen, not both.
• Similarly, overlooking that liver disease can result in thrombocytopenia and thrombocytopathy in addition to reduced coagulation factors could cause an inaccurate overall assessment of the bleeding disorder.
• Correctly classifying the disorder as inherited or acquired therefore guides which further tests are needed and helps avoid an inaccurate diagnosis.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and composition of the haemoglobin molecule, including its identifying features and variants.
(b) State the genetic basis of these variants.
(c) State the standard method used to identify haemoglobin variants in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind using standards for comparison during this method.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Haemoglobin is a tetrameric protein composed of two pairs of globin chains, one pair alpha-like and the other beta-like, and each red cell contains about 250 million haemoglobin molecules.
• Each polypeptide chain carries a haem group, and each haem group binds one Fe2+ ion, which in turn binds one molecule of oxygen, so each haemoglobin molecule binds four oxygen molecules.
• Haemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues and returns carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs, leaving the lungs about 97% saturated.
(b)
• The major variants are HbA (α2β2), the normal adult haemoglobin; HbA2 (α2δ2), a minor component present at <3% after birth; and HbF (α2γ2), foetal haemoglobin present in small amounts after birth.
• The alpha-like globin genes (ζ and α chains) are on chromosome 16, while the beta-like globin genes (ε, γ, δ and β chains) are on chromosome 11.
• A deficiency of haemoglobin results in anaemia.
(c)
• In practice, haemoglobin and its variants are identified and quantified using haemoglobin electrophoresis and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).
• Haemoglobin standards are used during electrophoresis to mark the migration of known variants for comparison with the patient's sample.
(d)
• Variants of haemoglobin have slightly different amino acids and therefore slightly different charges, which affects how far they migrate during electrophoresis.
• Comparing a sample's migration to that of standards guards against misidentifying one haemoglobin variant as another.
• Without such comparison, samples that migrate similarly could be wrongly reported as the same haemoglobin type.
• Correct identification of haemoglobin variants underpins accurate diagnosis of the different haemoglobinopathies.

(a)
The specimens/reagents involved are the patient's serum and the donor's red cells, which are washed and made into a 3–5% suspension.
(b)
The principle is to determine the compatibility of the donor's blood with the recipient by testing for agglutination between the patient's serum and donor's red cells at different phases (room temperature, 37°C, with albumin, and after antihuman globulin), to prevent complications of transfusion reaction.
(c)
The patient's serum and donor's cells are added in a 2:1 ratio into four tubes; agglutination is checked at room temperature in tube 1; tubes 2–4 are incubated at 37°C for 1 hour and tube 2 is checked; bovine albumin is added to tubes 3 and 4, incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes, and tube 3 is checked; tube 4 is washed, antihuman globulin is added, and after centrifuging at 3400 rpm for 5 minutes, agglutination is checked.
(d)
Absence of agglutination in all four tubes indicates the donor unit is compatible with the patient and may be released for transfusion; agglutination at any stage indicates incompatibility, and that donor unit should not be transfused.
questions.question:
(a) A patient scheduled for transfusion has blood samples sent for compatibility testing along with a selected donor unit. Identify the specimens/reagents involved.
(b) State the principle behind the technique that will be performed.
(c) Outline the procedure.
(d) State the expected result and its interpretation.

(a) Classify the methods of bone marrow specimen collection.
(b) State what each method yields.
(c) State how each method is selected or applied in practice.
(d) Explain how a basic error in technique during bone marrow collection can lead to an inaccurate or inadequate result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bone marrow examination can be performed by bone marrow aspiration, bone marrow biopsy (trephine biopsy), clot section, or biopsy imprint smears.
• Aspiration yields semi-liquid bone marrow examined under a light microscope, or analysed by flow cytometry, chromosome analysis or PCR.
(b)
• Biopsy yields a narrow, cylindrically shaped solid piece of bone marrow, examined microscopically (sometimes with immunohistochemistry) for cellularity and infiltrative processes.
• Samples can also be obtained by percutaneous trephine, or by open surgical biopsy/open trephine requiring full operating theatre practice, though most haematological samples are obtained by aspiration, often combined with needle or trephine biopsy.
(c)
• Aspiration is selected when fine cytological detail, cytochemical stains, microbiological culture, flow cytometry, or cytogenetic and molecular studies are required.
• Biopsy is selected for assessment of cellularity and marrow architecture, detection of lesions, assessment of aplastic anaemia or metastasis, and to provide archival material.
• Each bone marrow procedure is ordered after consideration of the patient's clinical symptoms and peripheral blood findings.
(d)
• If a minimum amount of marrow is not maintained during aspiration, volumes over 0.5 ml will almost certainly be diluted with blood, making processing and interpretation more difficult.
• If no material is aspirated (a 'dry tap'), for example in disorders where haemopoietic marrow is replaced by other tissue, aspiration alone may be difficult or impossible and a needle or trephine biopsy becomes essential.
• Bone marrow puncture performed in a patient with an unrecognised coagulopathy, such as haemophilia or vitamin K deficiency, carries a risk of haemorrhage as a complication.
• Errors of technique in either aspiration or biopsy can therefore lead to inadequate samples, dilution with blood, or complications such as pain, local infection or haemorrhage.
• Choosing the appropriate collection method for the clinical situation, and following correct technique, is therefore necessary for an accurate bone marrow examination.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and composition of bone marrow, including its identifying types.
(b) State how bone marrow structure is assessed in standard practice.
(c) State the standard setting in which this assessment is used.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution against bone marrow puncture in patients with coagulopathies.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bone marrow is a highly cellular, viscous and highly vascular tissue within the hollow cavities of hard bone that supports the proliferation, differentiation and maturation of haematopoietic cells.
• There are two types: red marrow (medulla ossium rubra), the active, haematopoietic portion, and yellow marrow (medulla ossium flava), the inactive portion consisting mainly of fat cells.
• Total marrow volume is normally 3000–4000 ml, of which red marrow accounts for about 1500 ml, and bone marrow constitutes about 4% of total body mass.
(b)
• Structurally, bone marrow consists of a vascular compartment and a haematopoietic compartment containing haematopoietic cells and stromal cells, with no lymphatic channels.
• Stromal cells include fibroblasts, macrophages, adipocytes, osteoblasts, osteoclasts and the endothelial cells that form the sinusoids.
• At birth all marrow is red; with age more is converted to yellow marrow, and in adults red marrow is found mainly in flat bones and the epiphyseal ends of long bones such as the femur and humerus, while yellow marrow occupies the medullary cavity of long bones.
(c)
• Bone marrow structure and cellularity are assessed in practice through bone marrow aspiration and biopsy as part of haematological investigation and diagnosis.
• The haematopoietic compartment produces approximately 500 billion blood cells daily, and the proportion of fatty tissue increases with age, being about 50% in adults and about 70% in the elderly.
(d)
• Bone marrow puncture is prohibited in patients with coagulopathies such as haemophilia or vitamin K deficiency, although thrombocytopenia is not an absolute contraindication.
• This precaution is taken because puncturing the marrow in a patient with a bleeding tendency carries a risk of haemorrhage at the puncture site.
• Careful review of clinical history and coagulation status is therefore required before the procedure is undertaken.
• Observing this precaution helps prevent complications such as haemorrhage during bone marrow examination.

questions.question:
(a) A blood sample is received from a pregnant woman found to be Rh D negative at her antenatal visit. Identify the technique that should be performed and the specimen/reagents needed.
(b) State the principle of this technique.
(c) Describe the procedure.
(d) State the significance of a positive result and the follow-up.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) should be performed; whole blood is collected in a plain tube, and standard O Rh D-positive cells and antihuman globulin (AHG) are the reagents needed.
(b)
The principle is to detect in vitro sensitisation: the patient's serum is incubated with standard cells known to carry the D antigen, and any antibody present in the serum will sensitise these cells, which is then revealed by agglutination after AHG is added.
(c)
Whole blood is collected in a plain tube; 4–8 drops of the patient's serum are added to 2–4 drops of standard O Rh D-positive cells and incubated at 37°C for 1 hour; agglutination is checked macroscopically and microscopically, the mixture is washed three times, AHG is added, and agglutination is checked again.
(d)
Agglutination indicates in vitro sensitisation, meaning the woman has antibody capable of reacting with D-positive cells; if the IAT is positive, antibody titration should be performed and monitored until delivery, since a high titre indicates severity of the condition.

(a)
• The reagent used in the sickle solubility test is a phosphate buffer supplemented with saponin and sodium dithionite.
• Saponin is included to cause haemolysis of the red cells, while sodium dithionite acts as a reducing agent to induce deoxygenation.
(b)
• The reagent is identified by its use with a white card ruled with narrow black lines, against which the tube is read for turbidity after incubation.
• Blood is mixed with the phosphate buffer-saponin-dithionite reagent to make the test suspension.
(c)
• In the standard procedure, the blood-reagent mixture is incubated, then placed in front of the white card with black lines; if the solution is opaque or turbid so that the lines cannot be seen through the tube, the result is read as positive for HbS.
• Under deoxygenated conditions, HbS becomes insoluble and forms crystals that refract light, which is what produces the turbidity in a positive result.
• A pink or colourless solution rather than turbidity is seen when the test is negative.
(d)
• It is important to record the turbidity of the sample before it is centrifuged.
• Results should therefore be captured (observed and recorded) both before and after centrifugation.
• If turbidity is not recorded before centrifugation, information about the true appearance of the uncentrifuged sample may be lost.
• Centrifugation separates the red cell debris from the fluid, which can change the apparent clarity of the tube if it is the only reading taken.
• Recording the result at the correct stage of the procedure therefore avoids a misleading interpretation of the sickle solubility test.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the reagent used in the sickle solubility test, including its identifying features.
(b) State how this reagent is used with the specimen.
(c) State the standard procedure and basis for reading the result.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind recording the result before and after centrifugation.

(a) State the principle of the full crossmatch procedure.
(b) List the reagents/materials required.
(c) Describe the procedure for the full crossmatch.
(d) State the reasoning behind performing each phase in sequence.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the full crossmatch procedure is used before transfusion.
(g) Distinguish the full crossmatch from antibody screening (the IAT).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The full crossmatch procedure determines the compatibility of a donor's red cells with a recipient's serum before transfusion, to prevent transfusion reactions.
• It is part of compatibility testing, which also includes blood grouping to determine blood type and selection of a compatible donor.
(b)
Reagents/materials needed are the donor's red cells, the patient's serum, saline for washing and suspension, bovine albumin, and antihuman globulin (AHG).
(c)
• The donor's cells are washed and made into a 3–5% suspension; the patient's serum and donor's cells are added in a ratio of 2:1 into 4 tubes.
• Agglutination is checked at room temperature in tube 1; tubes 2, 3 and 4 are incubated at 37°C for 1 hour and agglutination checked in tube 2.
• Bovine albumin is added along the side of tubes 3 and 4, which are incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes, and agglutination is checked in tube 3; tube 4 is then washed, AHG is added, and after centrifuging at 3400 rpm for 5 minutes, agglutination is checked.
(d)
Each phase (room temperature, 37°C, albumin, AHG) must be completed and checked in sequence to detect different types of incompatibility.
(e)
Agglutination at any phase is reported as an incompatible crossmatch, while absence of agglutination through all phases is reported as compatible.
(f)
The full crossmatch is used to detect antibodies in the patient's serum that would react with the donor's red cells, thereby preventing complications of transfusion such as shivering, urticarial rash, hyperthermia, haemolysis, haematuria and organ damage.
(g)
• Antibody screening (the IAT) instead tests the patient's serum against standard O Rh D-positive cells, rather than against the specific donor's cells, to detect the presence of an antibody in general, without confirming compatibility with a particular donor unit.
• Emergency crossmatch is simply the full crossmatch completed within 1 hour, while an uncrossmatched release involves only blood grouping and dispatch of blood with the full crossmatch commenced immediately afterwards, showing how the full crossmatch differs from these faster, less complete alternatives.
• The full crossmatch is thus the most complete compatibility test, going beyond the general antibody detection provided by the IAT.

(a)
An APTT of 65 seconds is prolonged, while a normal PT indicates the extrinsic pathway is intact; this pattern suggests a possible deficiency of Factor VIII, IX, XI or XII, high molecular weight kininogen, prekallikrein, or the presence of an inhibitor.
(b)
The APTT result is recorded in seconds together with the control value (normal range 30–40 seconds).
(c)
This combination indicates an abnormality confined to the intrinsic pathway of coagulation, since the common pathway (shared with the PT) appears intact.
(d)
A mixing study should be performed by mixing the abnormal plasma with an equal volume of normal plasma and repeating the APTT; correction of the prolonged time suggests a factor deficiency (to be confirmed and quantified with the relevant one-stage factor assay), while failure to correct suggests an inhibitor.
questions.question:
(a) A patient's APTT is reported as 65 seconds against a normal range of 30–40 seconds, while the PT is within the normal range. Interpret this combination of results.
(b) State how the APTT result should be recorded.
(c) State what this combination indicates about the coagulation pathway.
(d) State the next action.

(a) A whole blood sample collected into 3.2% sodium citrate is delivered to the coagulation section for a patient with a suspected bleeding disorder. Identify the specimen and state how it should be processed before testing.
(b) State the underlying principle of the screening tests that would be performed on the resulting plasma.
(c) Outline the procedure for one of these screening tests.
(d) State the expected result and its interpretation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is a citrated whole blood specimen; it is centrifuged at a minimum of 1700 rpm for at least 10 minutes (or 2500 rpm for 15 minutes), preferably at 4°C, to obtain platelet-poor plasma (PPP) for coagulation testing.
(b)
The screening tests measure the time taken for the plasma to clot after specific reagents are added: the PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways after thromboplastin and calcium are added, while the APTT measures the intrinsic and common pathways after an activator, phospholipid and calcium are added.
(c)
For the PT, 100 µl of plasma is added to a pre-warmed glass tube, 200 µl of thromboplastin with calcium is added, and the time to a visible clot is recorded immediately, in duplicate.
(d)
A result within the normal range (11–16 seconds for PT) indicates normal extrinsic/common pathway function, while a prolonged result indicates a deficiency of Factors I, II, V, VII or X or the presence of an inhibitor such as heparin, and would prompt a mixing study.

questions.question:
(a) Classify the haemoglobin variants.
(b) State the composition and genetic basis of these variants and how haemoglobinopathies themselves are classified.
(c) State how haemoglobin variants are identified and selected for further testing in the laboratory.
(d) Explain how a basic error in reading or classifying a variant can lead to an inaccurate diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The main haemoglobin variants are HbA (α2β2), the normal adult haemoglobin; HbA2 (α2δ2), a minor component (<3%) after birth; and HbF (α2γ2), foetal haemoglobin present in small amounts after birth.
• Embryonic variants include HbGower1 (ζ2ε2), HbGower2 (α2ε2), and HbPortland (ζ2γ2).
(b)
• Each variant is composed of two alpha-like and two beta-like globin chains, with the alpha-like genes on chromosome 16 and the beta-like genes on chromosome 11.
• Haemoglobinopathies themselves are classified as qualitative (affecting structure, e.g., HbS, HbC, HbD, HbOArab, Hb Lepore, HbE) or quantitative (affecting the amount produced, e.g., alpha, beta and delta-beta thalassaemias).
(c)
• Haemoglobin variants are identified in the laboratory using electrophoresis (based on charge and interaction with the agarose medium) or HPLC (based on chromatographic separation), each compared with a known standard.
• Because HbS results from a point mutation causing a structural change (an amino acid substitution in the beta-globin gene), it is classified among the qualitative haemoglobinopathies, whereas thalassaemias, which reduce the quantity of haemoglobin produced, are quantitative.
• The specific variant present is selected for further testing (such as the sickling test or sickle solubility test) when HbS is suspected, based on the initial FBC and blood film findings.
(d)
• If a sample's electrophoretic migration is not compared against known standards, one variant could be mistaken for another with a similar migration pattern.
• Since HbA2 is normally present at <3%, failing to account for this small proportion when reading a gel could result in it being overlooked or misclassified.
• Confusing a qualitative haemoglobinopathy (structural change) with a quantitative one (reduced amount) could lead to the wrong category of confirmatory test being requested.
• Such classification errors can result in an inaccurate diagnosis of the specific haemoglobinopathy present.
• Correct identification of the haemoglobin variant is therefore essential before a definitive diagnosis and appropriate management can be reached.

questions.question:
(a) State the principle of the direct antiglobulin test (DAT).
(b) List the reagents required.
(c) Describe the procedure for performing the DAT.
(d) State the precaution to be observed regarding washing.
(e) State how results are reported.
(f) Explain why the DAT is used in practical haematology.
(g) Distinguish the DAT from the indirect antiglobulin test (IAT).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The direct antiglobulin test (DAT), one of the Coomb's techniques, determines in vivo sensitisation of red cells.
• It works by detecting antibody or complement already bound to the patient's red cells using antihuman globulin (AHG).
(b)
Reagents required are plain collection tubes, saline for washing, 3–5% saline for cell suspension, and antihuman globulin (AHG).
(c)
• Whole blood is collected in plain tubes, about 0.5 ml is picked from the clotted, dislodged blood, and the red cells are washed three times.
• The washed cells are suspended in 3–5% saline; 2–4 drops of the washed cells are picked and 4–8 drops of AHG are added.
• Agglutination is then checked both microscopically and macroscopically.
(d)
The red cells must be washed three times before AHG is added, following the standard procedure for the test.
(e)
Agglutination is reported as a positive result, indicating in vivo sensitisation of the red cells; absence of agglutination is reported as negative.
(f)
• The DAT is used in practice to detect whether a patient's own red cells have already become sensitised in the body, which is relevant in conditions such as haemolytic disease of the newborn and transfusion reaction investigation.
• It forms part of antibody screening (Coomb's techniques) used during antenatal serology.
(g)
• The indirect antiglobulin test (IAT), the other Coomb's technique, instead determines in vitro sensitisation: standard O Rh D-positive cells are incubated with the patient's serum at 37°C for 1 hour, checked for agglutination, washed three times, and AHG is then added before a further check for agglutination.
• The DAT tests the patient's own red cells directly for antibody already attached in vivo, whereas the IAT tests the patient's serum against separately prepared standard cells to detect antibody capable of sensitising cells in vitro.

(a)
• Platelet disorders are classified as quantitative disorders (thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis) and qualitative disorders (a problem with the structure or function of the platelet).
• Quantitative disorders occur when the body either does not make enough platelets or makes enough but they are removed too rapidly, and this is the most common form of platelet disorder.
(b)
• Qualitative disorders can be congenital (such as disorders of adhesion, aggregation, or granule storage) or acquired (such as those caused by drugs like aspirin and heparin, or by systemic disorders such as uraemia).
• Thrombocytopenia can arise from decreased production or increased destruction of platelets, while thrombocytosis can be primary/essential (a myeloproliferative disorder of unknown cause) or secondary/reactive (due to inflammation, infection, iron deficiency or other underlying conditions).
(c)
• The classification guides investigation: a quantitative disorder is assessed mainly through the platelet count, while a qualitative disorder is assessed through platelet function studies such as adhesion, aggregation and release tests.
• Congenital qualitative disorders, such as Bernard-Soulier syndrome (an adhesion defect) or Glanzmann's thrombasthenia (an aggregation defect), are distinguished by which platelet function is missing or defective.
• Acquired qualitative disorders are often drug-induced, with aspirin being the most notable because of its irreversible effect on platelet prostaglandin synthesis.
(d)
• If a platelet count is not checked alongside a suspected qualitative disorder, a coexisting quantitative problem, such as thrombocytopenia in DIC, could be missed.
• A blood sample anticoagulated with EDTA can show pseudothrombocytopenia due to platelet clumping, so heparin should be used instead when accurate platelet counting is required.
• Failure to take a careful drug history (e.g., aspirin, heparin, antibiotics) could lead to an acquired qualitative platelet defect being mistaken for an inherited disorder.
• Not distinguishing primary/essential thrombocytosis from secondary/reactive thrombocytosis could result in an incorrect assessment of the underlying cause of a raised platelet count.
• Correct classification of the platelet disorder present is therefore essential to selecting the right confirmatory tests and avoiding a misleading result.
questions.question:

(b) State the sub-types within each class.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A PT of 28 seconds is prolonged compared with the normal range of 11–16 seconds, indicating a deficiency of Factors II, V, VII or X, or the presence of heparin.
(b)
The result is reported as the mean of duplicate recordings in seconds; it may also be expressed as a prothrombin ratio or as the INR, for which the normal value is 0.8–1.1.
(c)
• A prolonged PT indicates an abnormality of the extrinsic and/or common coagulation pathway.
• This can occur in oral anticoagulant therapy, obstructive jaundice, liver disease, DIC, malabsorption, vitamin K deficiency, or hereditary deficiency of the relevant factors.
(d)
• Because the PT is prolonged, a mixing study should be performed, mixing the abnormal plasma with normal plasma and repeating the thromboplastin/calcium clot test.
• Correction of the prolonged time on mixing suggests a factor deficiency, while failure to correct suggests the presence of an inhibitor.
