questions.question:
A 38-week primigravida presents with rupture of membranes 18 hours ago, confirmed on sterile speculum examination. She now has a temperature of 38.5°C, a fetal heart rate of 175 bpm, uterine tenderness, leucocytosis, and foul-smelling liquor on inspection.
(i) State the specific complication that has developed and list all its clinical signs and common causative organisms.
(ii) Enumerate all the indications for active/aggressive management of PROM.
(iii) Describe the methods of active management available and the supportive care to be given.
(iv) Define cervical incompetence, state its most common causes, and describe the diagnostic criteria and management in pregnancy.
questions.answerText:
(i) Chorioamnionitis. Signs: fetal tachycardia, maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, leucocytosis, fever, foul-smelling liquor. Common organisms: Streptococcus, anaerobes.
(ii) Indications for active/aggressive management: pregnancy ≥ 34 weeks, term pregnancy, pregnancy ≤ 26 weeks, fetal distress, intrauterine fetal death, congenital abnormalities, concomitant maternal illness (pre-eclampsia, diabetes mellitus), chorioamnionitis, abruptio placentae, IUGR.
(iii) Active/aggressive management: delivery of the infant by induction of labour or augmentation. Induction methods: amniotomy, oxytocin infusion. In the presence of chorioamnionitis, effect delivery immediately. Supportive care at expectant stage: bed rest, antibiotics, corticosteroids (< 34 weeks), screen for infection (FBC, urine culture, amniocentesis pool for culture, HVS M/C/S), fetal monitoring (fetal kick count, antenatal CTG, biophysical profile, serial USS for liquor volume).
(iv) Cervical incompetence: the most common cause of recurrent abortion in Sub-Saharan Africa; inability of the cervix to support a pregnancy to term. Typical history: recurrent mid-trimester abortions, painless rupture of membranes, bleeding or expulsion of products of conception in mid or early third trimester. Causes: previous forceful dilatation of the cervix, previous surgery (amputation of cervix — Manchester repair, cone biopsy), cervical laceration at childbirth, congenital weakness, in-utero exposure to DES. Diagnosis: history is typical; during pregnancy — dilated cervix, bulging membranes; ultrasound (cervical os diameter, cervical length); non-pregnant state — HSG (funnel-shaped uterus), retrograde cervical dilatation beginning with size 10, insertion of paediatric Foley's catheter with traction after inflation. Management: encourage conception, confirm normal pregnancy in first trimester, insert a cervical cerclage between 14 and 18 weeks.

questions.question:
A) Describe the gross anatomy of the uterus as it relates to the sources of haemorrhage in postpartum haemorrhage, under the headings:
A(i) The placental site and normal haemostasis
A(ii) Genital tract lacerations
A(iii) The abnormally adherent placenta: types and their relationship to the uterine wall

B) For each of the following causes of PPH, state how the uterine zone or type of placentation directly leads to haemorrhage: uterine atony, genital tract lacerations, and abnormally adherent placenta.

C) Explain why disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) may develop as a distant complication of PPH and abruptio placentae, including the physiological basis of pregnancy hypercoagulability.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Placental site and normal haemostasis:
- Normal haemostasis depends on uterine muscle arrangements and uterine contractions causing intravascular thrombosis at the placental site.
- When the placenta separates, the placental site is the primary source of bleeding.
- Mismanagement of the third stage (passive management with premature attempts to separate the placenta) disrupts this haemostasis.

A(ii) Genital tract laceration sites:
- Vulva.
- Vagina and cervix (the most common sites).
- Uterus.

A(iii) Abnormally adherent placenta types and their uterine relationship:
- Placenta accreta: adherent to the decidua.
- Placenta increta: invades the myometrium.
- Placenta percreta: penetrates through the myometrium.

B) How each cause leads to haemorrhage:
- Uterine atony: failure of uterine contraction means the intravascular thrombosis mechanism at the placental site fails, leaving open sinuses bleeding freely; grandmultiparity causes muscle replacement by fibrosis.
- Genital tract lacerations: tears of the vagina, cervix, or uterus open vessels in the genital tract directly; mismanagement or operative delivery predisposes to these lacerations.
- Abnormally adherent placenta: because the placenta does not separate cleanly, traction causes tearing of the myometrium and its blood vessels, leading to profuse haemorrhage.

C) DIC as a distant complication:
- Pregnancy is associated with hypercoagulability: increased factors V, IX, X; marked increase in fibrinogen (Factor I); no increase in platelets.
- In abruptio placentae, retroplacental blood and thromboplastin released from the placenta enter the circulation, triggering systemic intravascular activation of both intrinsic and extrinsic clotting cascades.
- This leads to consumption of clotting factors and platelets, causing DIC.
- The result is troublesome or catastrophic bleeding from the vagina, venepuncture sites, surgical wounds, and trauma sites.
- Investigations show prolonged PT and PTTK, torn red cells on blood film, reduced platelets and fibrinogen, and elevated fibrinogen degradation products (FDPs).
- Other causes of DIC include septic abortion, eclampsia or preeclampsia, retention of dead fetus (more than three weeks), amniotic fluid embolism, chorioamnionitis, sickle cell disease, prolonged and profound shock, and iatrogenic heparinisation.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant presents with extreme pallor, dyspnoea at rest, and palpitations. Her haemoglobin is 4.8 g/dl and PCV is 15%. Her blood film shows hypochromic microcytic red cells.
(i) What is the diagnosis and how is anaemia defined in this environment?
(ii) What are the physiological changes in blood during pregnancy that predispose to this condition, and what are the three main mechanisms by which anaemia arises in pregnancy?
(iii) What are the compensatory changes the body makes in severe anaemia, and at what haemoglobin level are these compensatory changes likely to be inadequate?
(iv) Outline the resuscitation and immediate management of this patient.
(v) What is the definitive treatment and what are the methods available for correcting anaemia in pregnancy?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is iron deficiency anaemia. In this environment, Hb concentration of 10 g/dl or less defines anaemia. WHO defines it as Hb less than 11 g/dl and haematocrit less than 33%.
(ii) Physiological changes: plasma volume expands by 46–55% and red cell mass expands by only 18–25%, producing dilutional (physiological) anaemia. The three main groups of mechanisms are: (a) inadequate production of new red blood cells (micronutrient deficiency, aplastic causes, erythropoietin deficiency); (b) excessive rapid destruction of red blood cells (malaria, sickle cell, G6PD deficiency, autoimmune); (c) haemorrhage (placenta praevia, abruption, hookworm).
(iii) Compensatory changes: increased plasma volume, increased cardiac output, increased blood flow velocity, decreased peripheral resistance. These are likely to be inadequate (high output cardiac failure) when Hb falls below 5 g/100 ml.
(iv) Resuscitation/immediate management: all anaemic patients should receive antimalaria treatment; treat any identifiable cause (urinary tract infections; hookworm with Albendazole 400 mg stat or Mebendazole 100 mg bd x 3 days); iron supplementation given to all anaemic women in the 2nd and 3rd trimester; for very severe anaemia, blood transfusion with packed cells slowly under Lasix cover.
(v) Definitive treatment: (a) oral haematinics (Fersolate 200 mg tds, folic acid 5 mg daily); (b) parenteral iron; (c) erythropoietin; (d) blood transfusion. Methods of correction depend on severity of anaemia and gestational age. The objective is to correct anaemia before onset of labour.

(i) HELLP syndrome — Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count. It is a severe complication of pre-eclampsia/eclampsia.
(ii) HELLP syndrome occurs in 3–10% of patients with pre-eclampsia. The pathophysiology reflects that of pre-eclampsia, driven by endothelial dysfunction and vasospasm. Vasospasm leads to microangiopathic haemolysis; liver capsule distension from periportal necrosis and subcapsular haematoma causes upper abdominal pain. The underlying process involves failure of trophoblastic invasion, imbalance of prostacyclin/thromboxane, and generalised vasospasm. Risk factors are those of pre-eclampsia: primigravidity, extremes of maternal age, multiple gestations, previous pre-eclampsia, genetic predisposition.
(iii) Maternal complications include: abruptio placentae with DIC; renal insufficiency or failure; pulmonary oedema; hepatic rupture from subcapsular haematoma; cerebral haemorrhage; retinal detachment; severe DIC; and maternal death.
(iv) Management: hospitalise immediately; antihypertensive therapy to control severe hypertension (hydralazine, labetalol, nifedipine); IV MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis and treatment; monitor urine output with indwelling catheter; monitor full blood count, liver enzymes, and coagulation profile; crossmatch blood and platelet concentrates; in most cases, delivery is the definitive management — at 38 weeks, delivery should proceed; corticosteroids (betamethasone/dexamethasone) if preterm; continuous fetal monitoring; low threshold for caesarean section.
(v) Fetal consequences: IUGR; IUFD; premature delivery; fetal asphyxia; placental abruption with poor fetal outcome; respiratory distress syndrome if premature; reduced placental perfusion.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks gestation presents with a 2-day history of nausea, abdominal pain, and decreased fetal movement. On examination, BP is 155/105 mmHg. Investigations show: haemolysis on blood film, platelets 68 × 10^9/L, ALT 420 IU/L, and AST 380 IU/L.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what does the syndrome name stand for?
(ii) What are the risk factors and underlying pathophysiology for this complication?
(iii) What are the maternal complications if this condition is not promptly managed?
(iv) Outline the management of this patient.

A) Define primary and secondary postpartum haemorrhage under the following headings:
A(i) Primary PPH: definition, timing, and the three thresholds stated (volume, haematocrit, and clinical)
A(ii) Secondary PPH: definition and timing

B) For primary PPH, describe the clinical features that allow clinical diagnosis before formal measurement of blood loss.

C) Distinguish between primary and secondary PPH under the headings: most common causes, investigations, and first-line management steps.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Primary PPH – definition, timing, thresholds:
- Definition: excessive bleeding from the genital tract after the birth of the baby, occurring within 24 hours of delivery (0 to less than 24 hours).
- Volume threshold: more than 500 ml after vaginal delivery; more than 1000 ml after caesarean section; less if anaemia was already present.
- Clinical threshold: any amount causing circulatory disturbance.
- Haematocrit threshold: decrease in haematocrit of more than 10% from before to after delivery (ACOG definition).

A(ii) Secondary PPH – definition and timing:
- Excessive bleeding from the genital tract occurring after 24 hours of delivery.
- Usually between the 5th and 10th day postpartum, but can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum.

B) Clinical features of primary PPH before formal measurement:
- Anxiety, air hunger, restlessness, coma (in severe cases).
- Shock: tachycardia, hypovolaemia, oliguria, anuria.
- Accumulation of blood within the uterine cavity: increased fundal height, soft enlarged uterus.
- Pelvic examination: visible bleeding and lacerations.
- Sheehan's syndrome may develop subsequently (anterior pituitary necrosis due to haemorrhagic shock).

C) Distinction – primary vs secondary PPH:
Most common causes:
- Primary PPH: uterine atony (commonest); retained placenta, retained lobe, or blood clot; genital tract lacerations; abnormally adherent placenta; mismanagement of the third stage; uterine overdistension; grandmultiparity; prolonged or obstructed labour.
- Secondary PPH: retained placenta; fibroids; infection (puerperal sepsis); infected slough of the cervix or vaginal laceration; infected caesarean section wound.
Investigations:
- Primary PPH: primarily a clinical diagnosis with urgent action; investigations run concurrently: clotting time, PT, PTTK, blood film, platelet count, fibrinogen, and FDPs if DIC is suspected.
- Secondary PPH: high vaginal swab for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity; ultrasound scan.
First-line management:
- Primary PPH: lie supine, catheterise bladder, insert IV line, administer oxygen, give oxytocics, resuscitate, and proceed to bimanual compression then escalating surgical intervention.
- Secondary PPH: antibiotics; examination under anaesthesia with evacuation of uterine cavity.

questions.question:
A) Describe the gross anatomy of the lower uterine segment as it is relevant to the lower segment caesarean section (LSCS), under the following headings:
A(i) The anatomical structures entered in sequence from skin to uterine cavity
A(ii) The type and direction of incision in the lower segment and why it is preferred over the classical upper segment incision

B) State how the zone of incision relates to the most important remote complication of previous caesarean section, including the rates of scar rupture for LSCS and classical caesarean section.

C) Explain how delayed gastric emptying in labour predisposes to Mendelson's syndrome during general anaesthesia for caesarean section, and describe the full preventive measures.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Structures entered in sequence:
- Skin: entered via a Pfannenstiel or midline infraumbilical incision.
- Doyen's bladder retractor is inserted into the lower end of the wound.
- Peritoneum of the utero-vesical pouch: divided transversely.
- The bladder is gently pushed down from the lower segment.
- A transverse incision is made in the midline of the lower segment and deepened until the membranes bulge.
- Membranes are ruptured and the head is delivered.
Pre-operatively: empty the bladder with a catheter; set up IV line; group and crossmatch 2 units of blood; tilt the operating table laterally 15° to prevent uterine compression of the inferior vena cava.

A(ii) Incision type and preference:
- LSCS uses a transverse incision in the lower uterine segment.
- It is preferred because the classical vertical upper segment incision caused free bleeding, could not be covered with a free layer of loose peritoneum, and gave an insecure scar that might rupture during subsequent pregnancy or labour.
- The LSCS incision is repaired in two layers of catgut or dexon with complete haemostasis.

B) Zone of incision and scar rupture:
- Remote risk: rupture of the uterine scar; rare after LSCS, usually occurs during labour.
- An upper segment (classical) scar is more likely to rupture, including during pregnancy.
- Risk of rupture: classical caesarean section 2.2–4.7%; LSCS 0.5%.
- If the indication for the first section persists (e.g. contracted pelvis), the operation should be repeated.
- If the indication was non-recurrent (e.g. placenta praevia), trial of vaginal birth (VBAC) may be considered; the risk of a second elective CS outweighs the risk of rupture of a lower segment scar.
- More than one previous CS makes the indication for repeat CS stronger.

C) Gastric emptying and Mendelson's syndrome:
- Physiological changes of pregnancy are associated with slight slowing of gastric emptying.
- Opioids such as pethidine and diamorphine used for pain relief in labour delay gastric emptying significantly, increasing the volume of acidic fluid; if gastric fluid pH is less than 2.5 and volume exceeds 0.4 ml/kg, aspiration may lead to potentially fatal pulmonary damage.
- Prevention:
 - Dietary restriction: patients suck ice; IV fluids if required; withhold breakfast.
 - Particulate antacids (magnesium trisilicate) should not be used as aspiration of particulate antacids causes pneumonitis.
 - H2-receptor antagonists: ranitidine 150 mg 6-hourly during labour reduces volume of subsequent gastric secretions and increases pH; alternative: cimetidine 200 mg IM plus 30 ml of 0.3 M sodium citrate orally 5 minutes before induction.
 - Cricoid pressure: must be applied to all obstetric patients requiring GA until the airway is secured by a cuffed tracheal tube; it compresses the oesophagus against the cervical vertebrae to prevent regurgitation into the pharynx.
 - Pass a gastric tube to empty the stomach before anaesthesia; give 15 ml of 0.3 M sodium citrate by mouth and repeat immediately before induction.

(i) Diagnosis: Occipito-posterior position (OPP), specifically right occipito-posterior (ROP).
- In a deflexed OP, the presenting diameter is the occipitofrontal diameter = 11 cm.
- In a flexed OP, the suboccipitofrontal and BPD engage at 10 cm × 9.5 cm.

(ii) Predisposing causes:
- Pendulous abdomen (multiparity).
- Anthropoid pelvic diameter: favours direct OP or direct OA.
- Android pelvic brim: the transverse diameter being near the sacrum encourages the biparietal diameter to accommodate posteriorly.
- Flat sacrum: with a poorly flexed head leads to further deflexion and OP.
- Anterior placenta: tends to encourage the fetus to flex round it.
- Right occipito-lateral position and normal right obliquity and dextrorotation of the uterus favours deflexion and ROP descent, assisted by the pelvic colon in the left posterior quadrant.
- Chance is also an apparent cause.

(iii) Pathophysiology and labour pattern:
- OPP presents a wider diameter (occipitofrontal, 11 cm) to the pelvis and causes poor flexion.
- The ill-fitting presenting part means forewaters are not protected and are forced through an incompletely dilated cervix ("sausage-shaped forewaters").
- Membranes rupture early; cord may prolapse.
- Uterine contractions are irregular and poorly sustained; dilatation may cease temporarily after forewaters rupture.
- Progress: engagement in the transverse or right oblique diameter; descent continues to pelvic floor; further progress depends on flexion of the head.
- Labour is disorganised (not coordinated) especially in primigravida; contractions are sustained and irregular with marked backache.
- Prolonged first and second stages; patient feels urge to bear down before second stage due to pressure on sacrum and rectum.
- 70% correct to occipitoanterior; 20% persistent OP; 10% deliver face to pubis.

(iv) Management:
First stage:
- Good monitoring and allow normal progress.
- Administer pethidine or pentazocine analgesia for pain; epidural anaesthesia gives good relief and shortens labour.
- Augmentation of labour if indicated.
- Encourage patient to lie on the side which the fetus faces to encourage engagement.
- Caesarean section if there is poor progress.
Second stage:
- Allow spontaneous delivery (two-thirds deliver as OA).
- Augmentation of labour.
- Forceps delivery: assisted rotation with Kielland's forceps.
- Vacuum extraction.
- Caesarean section if indicated.
- If delivering face-to-pubis: an extensive episiotomy is required as the perineum is distended by the occipitofrontal diameter.
questions.question:
A primigravida is admitted in active labour. On abdominal examination, her lower abdomen appears flattened, fetal limbs are easily palpable anteriorly, and fetal heart sounds are difficult to locate over the anterior chest wall. The membranes ruptured spontaneously early. On vaginal examination, the anterior fontanelle is readily felt near the ileopectineal eminence, the sagittal suture aims towards the right sacroiliac joint, and there is an oedematous anterior cervical lip. Labour has been prolonged with severe backache.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what does the presenting diameter of the fetal head measure in this position?
(ii) List all the predisposing causes of this malposition.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology and the pattern of labour progression in this position.
(iv) Outline the complete management of this malposition in both the first and second stages of labour.

questions.answerText:
(i) Risks of aspirin in pregnancy: cases of association between congenital malformations and aspirin use in early pregnancy; most concern is from prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor effects on decreasing platelet aggregation; increased incidence of intracranial bleeding; chronic use may cause premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus; use not recommended in the last 3 months of pregnancy; it is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent with analgesic and antipyretic effects.
(ii) FDA Category D: positive evidence of human fetal risks exists, but benefits in certain situations may make use of the drug acceptable despite its risks.
(iii) FDA categories:
- Category A: controlled studies in women have not shown risk to the fetus in the 1st trimester; possibility of fetal harm appears remote.
- Category B: animal studies do not indicate risk to fetus; no controlled human or animal studies show adverse effect on fetus.
- Category C: studies show animal teratogenic or embryocidal effects, but no controlled studies in women; OR no studies available in animals or women.
- Category D: positive evidence of human fetal risks exist, but benefits in certain situations may make use of drug acceptable despite its risks.
- Category X: studies in animals or humans have demonstrated fetal abnormalities OR evidence of risk based on human experience; risk clearly outweighs any possible benefit.
(iv) Analgesic and antipyretic of choice: acetaminophen (paracetamol). Risks: no increase in frequency of congenital abnormalities in babies of women who took it in pregnancy; nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity occur in overdosage in adults; similar complications seen in infants of women who took large therapeutic or toxic doses late in pregnancy.
(v) Principle: drugs ingested during pregnancy can affect the fetus; placental barrier is a contradictory term as the placenta allows several substances to cross; alternatives to drugs are preferable; the risk-benefit ratio should justify use of any drug; the minimal effective dose should be employed.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman at 12 weeks takes aspirin for joint pain without medical advice. Her obstetrician reviews her drug history.
(i) What are the risks of aspirin use in pregnancy?
(ii) What is the FDA category for drugs with positive evidence of human fetal risks but where benefits may justify use?
(iii) List the five FDA categories of drug labelling in pregnancy and their definitions.
(iv) What is the safest analgesic and antipyretic of choice in pregnancy and what are its risks in overdosage?
(v) State the principle governing drug use in pregnancy.

A) Describe obstetric forceps under the following headings:
A(i) General structure and parts of the forceps
A(ii) Classification of forceps delivery by station and the type of forceps used at each level

B) Explain the clinical basis and the prerequisites that must be fulfilled before embarking on a forceps delivery.

C) Distinguish between forceps delivery and vacuum extraction under the headings: anaesthesia requirement, stage of cervical dilatation required, use in preterm delivery, and overall maternal and fetal complication profile.
questions.answerText:
A(i) General structure and parts:
- Forceps are a paired instrument made up of left and right parts (halves) which articulate by crossing at their shanks.
- Parts: the blades (with cephalic and pelvic curves and hollow fenestrations), the shanks, the lock, and the handle.
- Improvements have been made to: locks, length of the shank, pelvic curve, and weight.

A(ii) Classification by station and forceps type:
- Outlet forceps: scalp visible at the introitus without separating the labia between contractions; fetal skull has reached the pelvic floor; sagittal suture in AP diameter or right or left occipital anterior or posterior position. Instrument: Wrigley's forceps (short curved).
- Low forceps: leading point of skull at station +2 cm or more; skull not on pelvic floor. Instrument: Neville-Bands forceps (long curved).
- Mid forceps: head is engaged; leading point of skull above station +2 cm. Instrument: Kielland's forceps (sliding lock, minimal pelvic curve).
- High forceps: application prior to engagement. Not used in modern practice; no place for forceps with an unengaged head.

B) Prerequisites – FORCEPS mnemonic:
- F: Full dilatation of the cervix (the cervix must be fully dilated; temptation to apply forceps with a nearly fully dilated cervix must be avoided).
- O: Outlet must be adequate.
- R: Ruptured membranes.
- C: Contractions must be present.
- E: Engagement of the head necessary; no CPD.
- P: Presenting part must be suitable (vertex, or occasionally after-coming head of breech or face in mento-anterior).
- S: Surrounding structures must be empty (bladder must be empty; episiotomy must be performed; adequate analgesia must be in place; facilities for neonatal resuscitation must be available).

C) Distinction – forceps vs vacuum extraction:
- Anaesthesia: forceps require adequate analgesia (GA, regional, pudendal, or local perineal infiltration); anaesthesia and episiotomy are not always required for vacuum extraction.
- Cervical dilatation required: forceps require full cervical dilatation; vacuum extractor can be used from 8 cm dilatation.
- Preterm delivery: forceps can safely deliver premature infants with birth weight less than 1.5 kg where ventouse is contraindicated; vacuum cannot be used in prematurity below this threshold.
- Complication profile: failed vacuum extraction is associated with fewer complications to mother and baby due to its in-built safety mechanism; overall maternal and fetal or neonatal complications are lower with the ventouse compared to forceps; forceps carry risks of facial nerve damage, skull fractures, supratentorial and subdural haemorrhage, and maternal cervical or uterine lacerations.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman uses a cold and cough medication containing a decongestant and an antihistamine at 24 weeks gestation without informing her doctor. She also applies a scabicide (containing pyrethrin and piperonyl butoxide) to treat lice.
(i) What are the risks of cold and cough medications in pregnancy?
(ii) What are the properties and risks of antihistamines in pregnancy?
(iii) Specifically, what are the risks of Dimenhydrinate and Meclizine hydrochloride?
(iv) What precautions should be taken when using scabicides in pregnancy?
(v) What is the effect of maternal cigarette smoking on the fetus, and why is the use of lobeline for smoking cessation uncertain?
questions.answerText:
(i) Cold and cough medications are usually a combination of decongestants, antitussives, expectorants and mild analgesics. Because of the theoretical risk of vascular-mediated birth defects, maternal hypertension and reduced uterine blood flow, they should be reserved for cases of significant maternal discomfort.
(ii) Antihistamines: useful for treating hayfever; dry nasal secretions and induce drowsiness slightly; not effective in relieving cold symptoms; most have low risk for teratogenicity and such associations are usually not conclusive. Examples: chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, pyrilamine.
(iii) Dimenhydrinate (for motion sickness): possible association with cardiovascular defects and inguinal hernia; can also cause premature labour.
Meclizine hydrochloride: may cause clefting in rodents; malformations of ear or eye in humans.
(iv) Scabicides (pyrethrin and piperonyl butoxide): should be used with caution in pregnancy as there are limited studies on their effects; gloves should be worn during use to minimise systemic absorption.
(v) Cigarette smoking: there are overwhelming evidences of harmful effects of maternal smoking on the fetus. Contributory mechanisms: chronic reduction of placental blood flow by nicotine; fetal hypoxia from carbon monoxide.
Lobeline (plant alkaloid origin): has similar effects to nicotine; may inhibit synthesis of sex steroids when applied to granulosa and testicular cells; therefore, it is unclear whether using lobeline to aid smoking cessation presents a lower risk than use of cigarette; it is reasonable to use non-medication strategies in cigarette cessation therapy, like behavioural modification.

A(i) Levels of maternity service (pyramidal in structure; personnel and equipment vary with level):
Primary health care level: typical facility is the Primary Health Centre; operates at ward level; both rural and urban; available all over the country; supervises women with no risks; provides 24-hour service.
Personnel: Community Health Officers (CHO); Community Health Extension Workers (CHEW); Junior Health Extension Workers (JCHEW); Medical Doctor if available; Pharmacy Technicians; Laboratory Technician.
Functions: health education; immunisation; maternal and child health services including family planning; essential drugs; life-saving skills.
Equipment: delivery couch; autoclave; partograph; IEC materials.
Sub-structure: for every local government—20 Basic Health Clinics (CHEWs/JCHEWs), 4 Primary Health Centres, 1 Comprehensive Health Centre.
Secondary level (District/General Hospital): described as the first referral level; headed by a General Practitioner; provides emergency obstetric care/surgery.
Tertiary level (University Teaching Hospital/Specialist Hospital): multidisciplinary institutions of training and research; highest level of competence; receives referrals from lower levels; all interventions available; high-risk pregnancies managed here.
A(ii) Essential elements at First Referral Level: surgical obstetric care; anaesthesia; medical treatment; blood replacement; manual procedures and monitoring labour; management of women at high risk; family planning support; neonatal special care.
B(i) Deficiencies: poor access to obstetric care; less than 10% of PHCs open 24 hours; wide urban-rural discrepancy in distribution of health facilities/personnel; inadequate infrastructure and manpower; lack of drugs and supplies; poor quality care; ineffective referral system; high rates of maternal and perinatal morbidity/mortality.
B(ii) Initiatives:
- CHEWs: modified life-saving skills training; antenatal risk assessment; partographic monitoring.
- Midwives: life-saving skills training; antenatal risk assessment; partographic monitoring; assisted delivery with vacuum extractor; repair of episiotomy; prevention of PPH.
- Doctors: advanced life-saving skills training; obstetric surgery; assisted/instrumental delivery; management of PPH.

questions.answerText:
(i) Acute pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract infection) in pregnancy. Pregnancy predisposes to this condition through: atony and dilatation of the renal pelves and ureters (hormonal and mechanical factors, mainly progesterone); lateral displacement and kinking of the abdominal portion of the ureters; urinary stasis (greatest between 20th and 24th weeks); increased urinary pH creating a favourable environment for bacterial multiplication; glycosuria and aminoaciduria providing nutrients for bacteria; 50% increase in GFR and renal blood flow overwhelming tubular reabsorptive capacity.
(ii) Predisposing factors for UTI in pregnancy: asymptomatic bacteriuria (20–30% of women with it develop frank UTI); upward massage of organisms during coitus; poor hygiene following defaecation or coitus; urethral catheterisation; trauma of labour; puerperal reduction in bladder tone; urinary retention from perineal pain; vaginitis/cervicitis. Acute pyelonephritis is often associated with structural abnormality of the kidney, hypertension, or anaemia.
(iii) Management: admit stat; investigations — FBC, U&Es, creatinine, blood culture, MSU for microscopy/culture/sensitivity; IV antibiotics (choice based on sensitivity, but started empirically pending results); increase fluid intake; bed rest; monitor urine output; treat pyrexia.
(iv) MSU for MCS should be performed regularly until the end of pregnancy; antibiotics for at least 2 weeks due to substantial risk of re-infection. Intravenous urography after the puerperium is indicated as one-third of women will show abnormalities (structural abnormality of the kidney). A course that eliminates bacteriuria in 70–80% of patients is the goal.
(v) Risks to the fetus include: asymptomatic bacteriuria not treated increases risk of pre-term labour and births, probably because of pyrexia and an irritant effect of the inflamed bladder on the adjacent myometrium; anaemia in pregnancy; spontaneous abortions; pre-eclampsia. Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria does not improve the outlook for the fetus, but preventing progression to upper UTI is important.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definitions:
- Gestation (Pregnancy): the maternal condition of having a fetus in the body.
- Embryo: the human conceptus from fertilization through the eighth week of pregnancy.
- Fetus: the human conceptus from the eighth week until delivery.
- Gestational age: the estimated age of the fetus calculated from the first day of the last (normal) menstrual period (LMP), assuming a 28-day cycle.
- Developmental age: the age of the offspring calculated from the time of implantation.
- Gravidity: the total number of previous pregnancies (normal or abnormal).
- Parity: the state of having given birth to an infant or infants weighing 500 g or more, alive or dead; in the absence of known weight, an estimated duration of gestation of 24 completed weeks or more; a multiple birth is a single parous experience.
A(ii) Gestational age: calculated from the first day of the LMP assuming a 28-day cycle; expressed in weeks; the duration of pregnancy is based on gestational age.
B(i) Conception: in humans, most cells have 46 chromosomes (diploid state); meiosis generates mature (haploid) eggs or sperm containing 23 chromosomes; a diploid primary oocyte undergoes meiosis to produce one haploid mature ovum (and one polar body); the primary oocyte remains in meiotic arrest (metaphase II) and resumes only once fertilization by sperm has occurred (completed in 20 hours); conception is the consequence of complex events including final maturation, transport and fusion of gametes, and assembly of a diploid number of chromosomes (syngamy).
B(ii) The immunobiological events that make it possible for a foreign tissue graft (allograft) to survive maternal immune rejection in utero are not fully understood (viviparous reproduction). The sperm determines the sex of a child.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Placenta praevia — the placenta is wholly or partly situated in the lower uterine segment. Given the history of two previous caesarean sections, transverse lie, high presenting part, and painless bleeding, a major degree (Type III or IV / central) is likely, as the incidence rises from 0.26% in an unscarred uterus to 10% after four caesarean sections (Clark et al 1985).

(ii) Aetiological and predisposing factors:
- Advanced maternal age and high parity (0.2% in nulliparous, 5% in grandmultips)
- Previous uterine surgery: myomectomy, caesarean section, endometriosis, fibroids
- Scarred uterus impairs placental migration (differential growth of lower uterine segment fails in scarred uterus)
- Endometrial damage from D&C, evacuation of retained products, termination of pregnancy (6x risk after first-trimester TOP)
- Large placental surface area (e.g., twin pregnancy)
- Smoking: compensatory placental enlargement due to effects of CO and nicotine
- Membranous, succenturiate, or bipartite placenta

(iii) Initial resuscitation:
- Two peripheral intravenous infusions with large-bore cannulae
- Intravenous infusion with compression cuff
- Blood transfusion (cross-matched blood constantly available)
- Notify relevant staff
- Establish central venous pressure line
- Cardiopulmonary assessment: heart rate, intra-arterial pressure, blood gases

(iv) Definitive delivery:
- Major (central) placenta praevia → Caesarean section (Classical or Lower Segment CS); minor placenta praevia with vertex presentation and adequate pelvis → vaginal delivery may be feasible.
- Double Set-Up (EUA) indications: non-availability of ultrasonography; bleeding in established labour. Prerequisites: cross-matched blood available, surgeon, assistants and patient all scrubbed, paediatric team present. Digital examination of fornices; if placenta felt or bleeding encountered, proceed immediately to CS.

Describe jaundice in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Classification of jaundice by timing and pathophysiology in pregnancy.
A(ii) First-trimester causes of jaundice in pregnancy.
B(i) Hepatitis B in pregnancy: risk of vertical transmission and management.
B(ii) Hepatitis C in pregnancy: risk factors and vertical transmission.
C(i) Acute fatty liver of pregnancy: aetiology, clinical features, pathology, and management.
C(ii) Haemolytic jaundice in pregnancy: causes and liver function test findings.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Jaundice in pregnancy is classified by timing: 1st trimester causes, 2nd/3rd trimester causes, and puerperium causes. By pathophysiology: intrahepatic (viral hepatitis, intrahepatic cholestasis, acute fatty liver, hyperemesis gravidarum), extrahepatic/obstructive (cholelithiasis, cholangitis, Ca head of pancreas), and haemolytic (haemoglobinopathies, malaria, septicaemia). In normal pregnancy, alkaline phosphatase increases 3–4 fold (placental alkaline phosphatase). Elevated ALT suggests possible aetiological factors including viral hepatitis, pre-eclampsia/HELLP, and acute fatty liver.
A(ii) First-trimester causes include: severe pyelonephritis; hyperemesis gravidarum; drug reaction; advanced chronic leaking ectopic pregnancy; haemoglobinopathy; liver cirrhosis; cholelithiasis; cholestatic jaundice; and hepatitis B.
B(i) Hepatitis B: universal screening of pregnant women for HBsAg is recommended to reduce vertical transmission. Risk is proportional to maternal hepatitis B virus DNA levels. Acute hepatitis B virus infection complicating pregnancy: prevalence of neonatal infection depends on gestational age; 1st trimester — neonatal HBV infection is rare; risk increases later. Infants of HBsAg-positive women should receive hepatitis B immune globulin immunoprophylaxis at birth and hepatitis B vaccine at 1 week, 1 month, and 6 months.
B(ii) Hepatitis C: incidence rising most rapidly in those aged 20–45 years. Risk factors include: high viral load (greater than 10^6 copies per ml); HIV-positive status with active hepatitis virus infection. Patients with hepatitis C are more at risk of vertical transmission than those with hepatitis B if viral load is high. No therapy has been shown to influence neonatal transmission of hepatitis C virus.
C(i) Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is rare; associated with 18% maternal and 23% fetal mortality. Most frequently complicates the 3rd trimester; commonly associated with pre-eclampsia (50–100%). The most frequent predisposing factor is deficiency of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase. Symptoms include anorexia, nausea and vomiting, lethargy. Features include coma, renal failure, hypoglycaemia, and fatty infiltration of the liver on pathology. It requires prompt delivery of the fetus.
C(ii) Haemolytic jaundice is due to haemolysis from: haemoglobinopathies; malaria; septicaemia; auto-immune haemolysis; drugs (e.g., chlorpromazine). LFT findings: elevated unconjugated bilirubin (haemolysis leads to elevated bilirubin levels and lactate dehydrogenase); mildly elevated transaminases. In HELLP syndrome associated with pre-eclampsia, there is haemolysis (elevated bilirubin levels, elevated lactate dehydrogenase), moderately elevated transaminases, and low platelet count. Alkaline phosphatase is raised in cholestasis (4th degree, diagnostic in cholestasis of pregnancy) and in cholelithiasis.

A(i) Factors predating pregnancy: premenstrual syndrome (PMS); eating disorders (anorexia nervosa or bulimia); previous personal or family history of psychiatric problems; mood disorders and depression. Because society cherishes pregnancy and motherhood, many women suffer in silence when their experience is less than sublime, making recognition difficult.

A(ii) Baby Blues: affects ~80% of new mothers; occurs between 3rd and 10th day after birth. Symptoms: tearfulness; anxiety; feeling of helplessness; sensitivity to criticism; poor sleep; mood fluctuations and irritability. Management: transient — resolves with understanding, psychological support, and reassurance.

A(iii) PND: about 10–15% of women develop PND; symptoms can emerge at any time during the first year after birth; most cases onset within first 4 months; peak incidence at 3 months postpartum.
Symptoms (SIGE CAPS): Sleep disturbances unrelated to baby's sleep needs; lack of Interest in sex, in life, and loss of confidence and self-esteem; feeling Guilty and inadequate; Energy level/chronic exhaustion; Memory difficulties and loss of concentration; Appetite disturbance, anxiety, fear of being alone; Psychological retardation or agitations (crying spells, irritability, negative obsessive or morbid thoughts); Feelings of self-harm or harm to baby or Suicide.
Risk factors: previous PND; family history of psychiatric illness; stressful life events; history of pre-menstrual tension; difficult marital or family relationships.

B. Puerperal Psychosis: affects 1 in 500 mothers; usually in first 3–4 weeks after delivery; serious condition. Mother may be unaware she is ill — grasp on reality affected. Symptoms: severe mood disturbance (marked elation or depression or fluctuations between them); disturbance in thought processes; bizarre thoughts and affective disorder; depression or hypomania; schizophrenia with delusion and hallucination; insomnia; inappropriate responses to the baby. There is risk to the life of both mother and baby if not recognised and treated.

C. PND can be mild or severe; symptoms may begin during pregnancy (antenatal depression), suddenly after birth, or gradually in the weeks or months following delivery. Women with PND have little control over how they feel; many do not realise PND can occur unexpectedly and typically blame themselves, partners, or baby. Untreated PND impairs mother–infant bonding, childcare, breastfeeding, marital relationship, and the infant's cognitive and emotional development. Practical help with housework and childcare is required alongside medical and psychological treatment.

questions.answerText:
(i) Sociobiological variable: age (teenage/under-aged pregnancy, best 18–24 years). Effects on obstetric outcome: obstructed labour; increased incidence of pre-eclampsia; miscarriages/preterm delivery; pre-labour rupture of fetal membranes; CPD and its sequelae (perinatal death, sepsis, VVF, maternal death, increased operative deliveries); primary PPH; poor motherhood; lack of contraceptive use; short interval between pregnancies; absent or inadequate ANC; unplanned pregnancies.
(ii) Best age range: 18–24 years. Under-aged: obstructed labour; increased complications. Elderly (>35 years): medical problems; hypertension; degenerating changes; fetal problems including chromosomal abnormalities.
(iii) Influence of height: less than 1.5 m is associated with cephalopelvic disproportion; associated with more operative deliveries; associated with small for gestational age infants; short stature classified as high risk pregnancy. Height of a woman is directly proportional to size of her pelvis; shoe size of less than 5 inches may indicate inadequate pelvis.
(iv) Influence of parity:
Primigravida: hypertensive disorders; incoordinate uterine activity; untried pelvis; obstructed labour.
Grand multipara: risk of parity and age combined; congenital abnormality; abnormal fetal lie; medical disorders; uterine rupture; post-partum haemorrhage; increased rate of twinning; higher rates of anaemia (particularly with short inter-birth intervals); abnormal lie/presentations (lax abdominal wall); precipitate labour.
(v) Influence of pregnancy interval: increased fetal loss especially if the interval is less than 3 months after previous delivery.

questions.answerText:
A(i) On the surface of red blood cells, there are many blood group antigens including ABO group antigens, Rhesus, Duffy, Kell, and Kidd antigens. There are 3 pairs of Rh antigens: Dd, Cc, and Ee. The most important is the D antigen. Inheritance follows an autosomal dominant pattern. A complex area of chromosome 1 produces the Rhesus antigen; over 95% of Rh incompatibility is due to the D antigen, inherited by simple Mendelian principles. Clinically significant Rh iso-immunisation is usually against the D antigen; anti-c or anti-Kell antibodies may also cause problems.
A(ii) Caucasians: 15% are Rh-negative. Negroids: 5% are Rh-negative. Haemolytic disease of the newborn is higher in Caucasians; lower incidence in Negroids is partly attributable to the higher prevalence of the trait (more people are Rh-positive), and ABO incompatibility between fetal and maternal blood offers partial protection.
B(i) Unlike the ABO system, individuals who lack Rh antigens do not have circulating antibodies; the antibodies are formed in response to exposure to the antigen. Initial exposure (e.g., at abortion or delivery) triggers IgM antibody production (does not cross placenta). Between 6 weeks and 6 months later, IgG antibodies are produced. In subsequent pregnancies, maternal IgG crosses the placenta, coats fetal Rh-positive RBCs, which are then destroyed by the fetal reticuloendothelial system, causing haemolysis, anaemia, and hydrops fetalis.
B(ii) Repeat indirect Coombs test at 28 weeks, 32 weeks, and 36 weeks in unsensitised women. Once antibodies are detected, they must be measured at least monthly; serum antibody protein levels are of greater predictive value than antibody titres; a rapid increase suggests acute haemolysis. Amniotic fluid bilirubin: spectrophotometry at OD 450 nm; fetal blood sampling under ultrasound guidance for haematocrit.
C(i) Prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin doses and indications: abortion — 50 mg (before 20 weeks) or 100 mg (after 20 weeks); amniocentesis — 300 mg; CVS — 300 mg; antepartum haemorrhage — 300 mg; ECV — 300 mg; after delivery if baby is Rh-positive — 300 mg, within 72 hours. Routine antenatal prophylaxis: anti-D 500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks to Rh-D-negative primigravidae and other previously unsensitised women; this reduces the incidence of Rh sensitisation by at least a factor of 8.
C(ii) The continued occurrence of Rh iso-immunisation is due to: failure to give any anti-D when indicated; failure to give enough anti-D (initial sensitisation has already occurred); failure to recognise a sensitising event; late administration beyond the 72-hour window after delivery or sensitising event.

questions.answerText:
(i) Average gestational age at delivery for twins is 37 weeks; 50% of twins deliver preterm. Neither bed rest nor prophylactic administration of tocolytics is useful in preventing preterm delivery in twins.
(ii) Zygosity can only be determined by DNA fingerprinting; prenatal determination requires invasive procedures — amniocentesis, chorionic villous sampling (CVS), or cordocentesis. Chorionicity is determined by USS: assessment of fetal gender, number of placentae, and characteristics of the inter-twin membrane. Different-sex twins are dizygotic and therefore dichorionic. Two separate placentae indicate dichorionic (but fused placentae are difficult to distinguish). In dichorionic twins, the inter-twin membrane is composed of a central layer of chorionic tissue sandwiched between two layers of amnion — thick and more echogenic; in monochorionic twins, there is no chorionic layer. Lambda sign: extension of placental tissue into the base of the inter-twin membrane is present in dichorionic twins and absent in monochorionic twins; best assessed in the first trimester.
(iii) Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome is a complication unique to monochorionic twinning, arising from vascular anastomoses within the two placental circulations (present in two-thirds of monochorionic twins). In monochorionic twin pregnancy, death of one fetus may result in death or handicap of the co-twin because of complications arising from these placental vascular anastomoses. This does not occur in dichorionic twins (which never have anastomoses between their blood vessels).
(iv) The normal sex ratio at birth (slight male preponderance) is altered to a female preponderance in twins. Epidemiological factors affecting twinning incidence: ethnic group (Caucasian: 1 in 90 twin conception; 5 times higher in certain parts of Africa; half in Asia), maternal age (2% at 35 years), parity (2% after 4 pregnancies), method of conception (20% after ovulation induction), family history, and previous history of multiple delivery. Factors that do NOT vary with maternal age, parity, or method of conception: monozygotic twinning — its incidence is similar in all ethnic groups and is not affected by these factors.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) Haemoglobinopathies are inherited disorders of haemoglobin synthesis (thalassaemias) or structure (sickle cell syndromes), resulting from single amino acid substitutions on the haemoglobin molecule. Haemoglobin has a haem moiety and a globin moiety with 2 pairs of globin chains per molecule. Normal haemoglobins: HbA (alpha and beta chains), HbA2 (alpha and delta chains), HbF (alpha and gamma chains — fetal Hb). Abnormal haemoglobins: S, C, and the thalassaemias (alpha and beta).
A(ii) Hb S results from valine replacing glutamine at position 6 of the β-chain. Hb C results from lysine replacing glutamine also at position 6 of the β-chain. About 25% of Africans are carriers of the Hb S gene but only 2–3% are homozygous. These genes are rare among Caucasians.
B(i) Under low oxygen tension, abnormal red cells change shape (sickle shape) — a reversible reaction. Sickling leads to increased blood viscosity, which causes stasis; stasis causes obstruction, which leads to infarction. Abnormally shaped red blood cells also lyse more easily, causing haemolytic anaemia and jaundice.
B(ii) Abnormal combinations and severity: HbSS — usually fatal; crises are more common; improved clinical status nowadays. HbSC — milder form; outlook better; may be asymptomatic/undiagnosed before pregnancy; often has more severe morbidity in pregnancy. Thalassaemia + S; HbCC; HbSF; HbAS (sickle cell trait). Complications occur in decreasing order of severity: HbSS, HbSC, HbAS, HbAC.
C(i) Prevention: genetic counselling of potential partners about the risks of sickle cell disease; pre-implantation diagnosis (conception by IVF followed by prenatal diagnosis — chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis); public enlightenment; decision as to terminating pregnancy or caring for a child with SCD. Users of hydroxyurea should be on contraception; hydroxyurea should be discontinued when pregnancy is planned.
C(ii) A child with SCD can receive a cord blood transplantation from a later HbAA or HbAS sibling; this serves as a source of haematopoietic stem cells which can cure the disease. It can also be banked for a future affected child if the index baby is not affected. Drawbacks: the chance of HLA match is only 25%; there is risk of graft-versus-host disease.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Respiratory rate: increases in pregnancy due to increased sensitivity of the respiratory centre to CO2, probably related to progesterone. Vital capacity: remains unchanged at 3,200 ml. Tidal volume: increases by approximately 200 ml; combined with increased respiratory rate, this produces an increased minute volume. Residual volume: reduced by approximately 200 ml due to splinting of the diaphragm from raised intra-abdominal pressure. Acid-base consequence: pregnancy changes cause overbreathing or hyperventilation, leading to lower arterial pCO2; compensatory decrease in plasma HCO3− to maintain blood pH — this produces respiratory alkalosis. Anatomical changes: capillary dilatation throughout the respiratory tract leads to engorgement of the nasopharynx, larynx, trachea, and bronchi; CXR shows increased lung markings (vascular); the diaphragm can be elevated by as much as 4 cm; the ribcage is displaced upwards and widens the lower thoracic circumference by up to 6 cm.
A(ii) Pregnancy has no consistent effect on asthma; managed routinely. Drugs that can be used in pregnancy: sympathomimetic bronchodilators (salbutamol, orciprenaline), aminophylline, disodium cromoglycate, steroids. Caution with steroids: decreased labour tolerance with prolonged use; hydrocortisone must be administered during labour. Steroids are indicated in status asthmaticus.
B(i) Pregnancy increases the prevalence of pulmonary TB; the increasing prevalence is attributed to the AIDS pandemic; HIV infection lowers resistance to TB and increases the risk of activation of latent TB in those previously infected. Early disease in pregnancy may mimic physiological changes — increased respiratory rate (already elevated in pregnancy), fatigue (also seen in anaemia of pregnancy), tachycardia, and raised ESR. A high index of suspicion is vital; TB in pregnancy may be asymptomatic. Historical belief (now refuted): from the time of Hippocrates and until the early 20th century, it was believed that the raised diaphragm due to pregnancy helped collapse tuberculous cavities situated in the lower lung regions; this led to the recommendation that young women with TB should marry and become pregnant. This belief was subsequently refuted by controlled studies.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the management of bronchial asthma in pregnancy, including which drugs can be used and the specific steroid management required during labour.

State the role of respiratory physiology in relation to the diaphragm that was historically believed to benefit TB (now refuted).
