A(i) Organisation by level:
Primary level: prayer homes/traditional clinics/health centres/maternity centres/private clinics; personnel: TBAs, auxiliary midwives, midwives, physicians.
Secondary level: midwives and physicians.
Tertiary level: physician-led; multidisciplinary; provides highest level of care; receives referrals; all interventions available.
Aims: screening/prevention of maternal problems; screening/prevention of fetal problems; management of maternal problems; management of fetal problems; preparation of couple for childbirth and childrearing.
A(ii) Activities of pre-conception care:
- Screening for genetic carrier states
- Evaluating for pre-existing medical conditions
- Screening for nutritional deficiencies and providing peri-conceptional vitamin supplementation
- Screening for hepatitis B surface antigens and vaccinating those at high risk
- Screening for rubella antibodies and providing immunization
- Counselling on psychosocial risk factors (alcohol, smoking, exercise, occupational exposure to teratogens, avoidance of environmental toxins)
- Contraceptive advice/provision of effective contraception
- Precise dating of pregnancies through promotion of menstrual calendars
B(i) Potential value of ANC in developing countries: many more women make contact with the health care system at ANC than are delivered by a trained attendant; provides opportunity to reach a larger section of the pregnant population; antenatal visits afford a chance to reach a large proportion of the female population and provide information about other health-related issues (family planning, immunization, child health, nutrition, STIs).
B(ii) Booking visit: comprehensive history (past medical, past obstetric, drug, social history); thorough physical examination; ancillary screening tests; assessment of risk; health promotion/intervention. Subsequent visits detect: anaemia; hypertension; IUGR; malpositions/malpresentations; diabetes mellitus. Also includes: immunisation; screening for Rhesus antibodies (at booking, 16, 28, 32, 36 weeks); iron/folic acid supplementation; antimalarial chemoprophylaxis; pelvic assessment when indicated.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the aims and organisation of antenatal care at different levels, including primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, with the personnel involved at each.
A(ii) Describe the activities of pre-conception care, including screening activities and counselling components.
B(i) Explain the potential value of antenatal care in developing countries.
B(ii) State the standard content of a booking visit (first antenatal visit) and what must be done at the booking visit and subsequent visits to detect complications.

questions.answerText:
(i) Types of breech presentation:
- Frank breech: both hips are flexed and both knees extended. This is the commonest type and is the type in this patient.
- Complete breech: both hips flexed, one or both knees are flexed.
- Incomplete (footling) breech: either hip is extended with foot or knee presenting.

(ii) Procedure: External Cephalic Version (ECV).
Goal: vaginal delivery with cephalic presentation.
Timing: approximately 36 to 37 weeks gestation.
Absolute contraindications: placental abruption, placenta praevia, antepartum haemorrhage (APH), multiple pregnancy, ruptured membranes, severe fetal anomaly, cord completely encircling fetal neck on ultrasound, consent declined.
Relative contraindications: fetal compromise, oligohydramnios, labour, previous caesarean section (?), hypertension, obesity.

(iii) Method and precautions:
- Pressure is applied to the maternal abdomen to turn the fetus to cephalic presentation.
- Ultrasound monitoring is used during the procedure.
- Tocolytics are administered.
- Regional anaesthesia may be used.
- Anti-D is given to Rh-negative mothers.
- Success rate is 35 to 85%.

(iv) Complications of ECV:
- Fetal compromise and fetal death.
- Premature labour.
- Uterine rupture.
- Placental abruption.
- Amniotic fluid embolism.
- Need for emergency caesarean section.

(v) Structural and embryologic fetal variants predisposing to breech at term:
- Structural abnormalities: anencephaly, macrocephaly, neuromuscular disorders.
- Oligohydramnios or polyhydramnios.
- Extended fetal legs.
- Prematurity.
- Short umbilical cord.
- Decreased fetal activity.
- Fetal death.
- Impaired fetal growth.
Placental: placenta praevia, cornual praevia.
questions.question:
A 37-week primigravida attends the antenatal clinic. Ultrasound confirms breech presentation with a frank breech position. The fetal weight is estimated at 3.0 kg, and there are no placental or uterine abnormalities. The attending obstetrician considers external cephalic version (ECV).

(i) Define the types of breech presentation, and identify which type this patient has.
(ii) Name the procedure being considered, state its goal and timing, and list all absolute and relative contraindications.
(iii) Describe the method and precautions for performing ECV, including adjuncts used.
(iv) List all complications of ECV.
(v) State the embryologic or structural fetal variants that predispose to breech presentation remaining at term.

A. Describe abruptio placentae under the following headings:
A(i) Definition
A(ii) Aetiology and predisposing factors
A(iii) Classification (grades) based on maternal haemodynamic status, coagulation profile, and fetal condition

B. Explain the histopathological changes seen in abruptio placentae and how these lead to Couvelaire uterus.

C. Distinguish between the management of Grade I/II (mild-moderate) abruptio placentae from Grade III (severe) abruptio placentae, including indications for expectant management and the role of DIC correction.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: bleeding from the placental site when it is normally situated wholly within the upper uterine segment, due to premature separation of part or the whole of the placenta. Separation causes accumulation of a retroplacental clot from which serum is re-absorbed into the circulation.

A(ii) Aetiology and predisposing factors: hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia — major cause; chronic hypertension); poor transformation of uteroplacental arteries (60%); occlusion of deep myometrial vessels with haemorrhage (33%); decidual haematoma, vessel thrombosis, focal necrosis and recent infarct; congestion of chorionic villi capillaries; severe malnutrition; genetic mutations; smoking; substance abuse; previous abruptio; trauma (though practically never present).

A(iii) Classification based on maternal haemodynamic status, coagulation profile, and fetal condition: Grade I (mild) — 40% of cases; Grade II (moderate) — 45%; Grade III (severe) — 15%. Grade IIIA — no overt coagulopathy; Grade IIIB — overt coagulopathy present.

B. Histopathological changes: widespread haemorrhages in severe cases; focal haemorrhages in ovaries, kidneys, liver, GIT, heart, CNS, and adrenals. Organised infarct and haemosiderin granules (chronic abruption). Pathophysiology: rupture of uteroplacental arteries → extravasation of blood under arterial pressure between myometrial bundles → tracks towards decidua basalis (placental separation, fetal hypoxia) or towards serosal surface → Couvelaire uterus (uteroplacental apoplexy). Blood extravasated throughout the myometrium gives the uterus a bruised, purple, oedematous appearance — Couvelaire uterus.

C. Grade I/II (expectant management when indicated — Combs et al 1992): stable clinically; resolving abruption; no increased uterine activity; reassuring fetal surveillance; premature infant. Components: admit labour ward; monitor vital signs; urinary output >30 ml/hr; CTG; careful speculum examination; bedside clotting time; fluid replacement (crystalloids, fresh whole blood, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, platelet transfusion). Mode of delivery: IUFD → vaginal ± oxytocin augmentation.
Grade III: immediate delivery; correct DIC vigorously before and during delivery; blood transfusion essential; if viable fetus → abdominal delivery (CS or hysterectomy); other treatments: ± Rhesus immunoglobulin; ± heparinisation; ± intravenous protein C; ± renal dialysis. Maternal complications: hypovolaemic shock; DIC; PPH; ischaemic necrosis — ATN, cortical necrosis, Sheehan's syndrome; maternal death; recurrence.

questions.question:
A) Define the following terms:
A(i) Fetal lie
A(ii) Fetal presentation
A(iii) Fetal position
A(iv) Malposition versus malpresentation

B) Under the heading "Diagnosis of transverse lie," describe all the clinical and ultrasound findings for transverse lie, and state the additional findings observed when membranes have ruptured in labour.

C) Distinguish between the management of transverse lie in preterm pregnancy and at term, and explain the anatomical basis for why obstructed labour is "the norm" in transverse lie at term.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Fetal lie: the fetal longitudinal axis relative to the maternal longitudinal axis.

A(ii) Fetal presentation: the part of the fetus presenting at the maternal pelvis, i.e. the most dependent part of the fetus in an erect mother.

A(iii) Fetal position: the place of the fetal occiput in the transverse plane of the maternal pelvis, determined by an imaginary transverse line drawn from pelvic side wall to the other. Types: occipito-anterior, occipito-lateral (transverse), and occipito-posterior.

A(iv) Malposition versus malpresentation:
- Malposition: incorrect positioning of the vertex; includes occipito-posterior position and deflection of the head; the relationship between fetal denominator and maternal pelvis makes spontaneous delivery unfavourable.
- Malpresentation: the presence of a presenting part other than the vertex; includes breech, face, brow, shoulder, and compound presentation.

B) Diagnosis of transverse lie:
Clinical findings:
- Abnormal uterine shape.
- Fundus lower than expected for gestational age.
- Empty lower uterine segment with no fetal pole in the pelvic inlet.
- No fetal pole at the fundus.
In labour with ruptured membranes:
- Empty lower segment.
- Bag of membranes with umbilical cord or fetal limbs may be felt on vaginal examination.
Confirmation: ultrasound scan (and in some cases X-ray, CT scan, or MRI).

C) Management preterm vs at term, and anatomical basis:
Preterm pregnancy:
- Await spontaneous version; most fetuses will revert to longitudinal lie spontaneously before term.
Management at term:
- External cephalic version after 36 weeks by experienced hands (after ruling out CPD or placenta praevia).
- Admit after 37 weeks and await spontaneous version until labour.
- Terminate pregnancy by caesarean section at term.
- In early labour: external cephalic version can be performed if there are no contraindications.
- In prolonged labour with ruptured membranes: caesarean section is mandatory.
Anatomical basis for obstructed labour:
- In transverse lie, the fetal shoulder presents at the pelvic inlet.
- The shoulder cannot engage or descend through the pelvis; no fetal part can negotiate the birth canal in this orientation.
- The uterus continues to contract against an immovable obstruction; the lower uterine segment stretches and thins, leading to imminent uterine rupture.
- Cord or hand prolapse is common because of the ill-fitting presenting part.
- Therefore, obstructed labour with uterine rupture and fetal death is inevitable without surgical intervention.

(i) Acute Renal Failure following septic abortion. The pathogenesis involves: gram-negative septicaemia and endotoxic shock causing hypovolaemia and reduced renal perfusion; microthrombi in renal arterioles from coagulopathy; Clostridium welchii septicaemia, which releases a haemolysin; direct damage to renal tissue from nephrotoxins (e.g., aminoglycosides). Septic abortion is one of the leading aetiological factors in obstetric ARF. The result is either Acute Tubular Necrosis or, in severe cases, Renal Cortical Necrosis.
(ii) Aetiological factors relevant to this case: gram-negative septicaemia and endotoxic shock; Clostridium welchii septicaemia; severe obstetric haemorrhage; disseminated intravascular coagulation; nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, radiographic contrast agents, heavy metals, chemotherapy). Pre-renal causes: sepsis, volume depletion. Intrinsic renal causes: acute tubular necrosis; pyelonephritis; glomerular disease.
(iii) Immediate management: large doses of frusemide to challenge the kidneys, in case it is pre-renal azotaemia where tubular damage has yet to occur. Pre-renal failure is due to renal hypoperfusion with no changes in renal morphology; it is reversible within 24–36 hours with volume restoration and treatment of the precipitating cause. Established ATN does not respond to frusemide in the same way.
(iv) Management of hyperkalaemia: monitor hyperkalaemic effect on the heart by ECG (look for absent P-waves, widening QRS complex to more than 0.2 seconds, and peaking of T-waves — the earliest noticeable sign); ion exchange resins (Resonium A); IV 50 ml of 50% glucose plus 50 IU of soluble insulin; up to 60 ml of 10% calcium gluconate to mute the effect of potassium on the myocardium; dialysis.
(v) Dialysis is indicated in the oliguric phase of ATN and in renal cortical necrosis. Forms: peritoneal dialysis — contraindicated in presence of prosthetic materials in the peritoneal cavity, colostomy, or severe respiratory failure; complications include infection and hyperglycaemia (preventable by adding insulin to dialysate) and peritoneal access problems (heparin added to dialysate). Haemodialysis: useful for removal of rapidly accumulating toxic substances; used when heparinisation is best avoided (e.g., in cardiac disease). RCN ultimately requires dialysis and renal transplantation.
questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation presents with oliguria (urine output 25 ml/hour). She had a septic abortion 3 days ago. Her temperature is 39.5°C, blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, and she is clammy. Blood results show elevated serum creatinine and potassium of 6.5 mmol/L.
(i) What is the diagnosis and the pathogenesis in this obstetric context?
(ii) What are the aetiological factors responsible for ARF after septic abortion?
(iii) What is the immediate management priority, and how is pre-renal failure distinguished from established ATN at this stage?
(iv) Outline the management of the hyperkalaemia in this patient.
(v) What is the role of dialysis in ARF, and what are the forms available?

questions.answerText:
A(i) ANC schedule:
- Booking visit: ideally by 2nd missed period; allows for early losses from chromosomal anomalies; identification of viable fetus on ultrasound; early management or prevention of pregnancy-induced conditions.
- Subsequent visits (standard): 4-weekly until 28 weeks; 2-weekly until 36 weeks; weekly until delivery.
- High-risk women: 2-weekly until 28 weeks; weekly until delivery.
- Focused ANC as an alternative approach.
A(ii) Aims of antenatal care:
- Screening/prevention of maternal problems
- Screening/prevention of fetal problems
- Management of maternal problems
- Management of fetal problems
- Preparation of the couple for childbirth and childrearing
B(i) Risk approach: attempts to screen the entire pregnant population and provide surveillance/treatment to individual women or groups based on level of need; allocates existing resources as a function of need rather than access/demand; effectiveness measured by ability to identify high-risk and low-risk women.
Requisite conditions: whole population must be included in primary screening; conditions screened for must include important causes of maternal morbidity/mortality; when increased risk is detected, appropriate referral or other action must be taken; adequate services must exist at the referral level; women at risk must be able to reach the referral level and be motivated to do so; all care providers must be motivated to implement the system.
B(ii) Problems in Nigeria: only 50% of pregnant women receive antenatal care; long clinic waiting times/overcrowded clinics; expensive service; long distance to clinic; poor communication; poor transportation/road network; late booking. General problems with ANC: irregularly spaced visits; long waiting times; poor feedback to women; little communication between ANC clinics and delivery units; number, timing and content of antenatal visits more a matter of ritual than evidence-based health care.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the antenatal care schedule in Nigeria including the booking visit timing, frequency of subsequent visits for low-risk and high-risk pregnancies, and what constitutes focused ANC.
A(ii) State the aims of antenatal care.
B(i) Describe the risk approach in antenatal care: what it aims to do, the requisite conditions for it to work, and its limitations.
B(ii) What are the characteristics of antenatal care in Nigeria, including the problems with the current delivery of ANC?

A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation is seen in the antenatal clinic. An ultrasound scan confirms a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy. One twin is noted to have excess amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios) while the other has oligohydramnios.

(i) Identify all the risk factors for twinning, and state the incidence of multiple pregnancy in Nigeria and Ibadan specifically.
(ii) Name the complication most likely occurring in this monochorionic twin pair, and explain its mechanism.
(iii) List all the maternal and obstetric complications associated with multiple pregnancy.
(iv) Describe the full intrapartum management for delivery of twin pregnancy, including the second and third stages.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors for twinning:
- Black race.
- Genetic predisposition (inherited as autosomal recessive trait).
- Use of ovulation induction drugs.
- Increasing maternal age.
- Increasing parity.
- Previous or first-degree family history of twinning.
- Diet (?some types of yam).
- Assisted reproduction (ART) increases monozygotic twinning rate by 2–6-fold especially with two-blastocyst transfer.
Incidence: 54/1000 births in Nigeria; 52/1000 births in Ibadan (Nylander, 1971).

(ii) Complication in this monochorionic-diamniotic pair:
- Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS).
- Mechanism: occurs in monochorionic twins due to vascular anastomoses; one twin (the donor) loses blood to the other (the recipient) through these connections; this leads to polyhydramnios in the recipient and oligohydramnios in the donor.
- Seen in up to 30% of cases; mortality can be up to 30%; severe morbidity in survivors.

(iii) Maternal and obstetric complications:
- Increased minor complaints of pregnancy.
- Increased risk of miscarriage.
- Increased anaemia.
- Increased risk of preterm delivery (43.6% born before 37 weeks).
- Hypertension (pre-eclampsia is 5 times more likely in twin pregnancy).
- Antepartum haemorrhage.
- Hydramnios.
- Need for hospitalisation.
- Single fetal death in twins (increased risk of death of surviving twin of 20%).
- Operative delivery and caesarean section.
- Postpartum haemorrhage.
- Cord prolapse due to malposition and malpresentation.
- Premature rupture of membranes.
- Uterine atony after delivery.
- Perinatal mortality up to 10 times higher than singletons.
- Locked twins (leading twin breech, second twin cephalic).

(iv) Full intrapartum management:
- Establish intravenous access; group and crossmatch blood.
- Continuous intrapartum fetal monitoring with cardiotocograph.
- Two obstetricians or midwives and two paediatricians must be present.
- Woman in lithotomy position.
- Deliver leading twin as in normal singleton delivery; clamp the cord but do not attempt placental delivery.
- After first twin delivery: perform abdominal examination to determine lie of second twin; listen to fetal heart; perform vaginal examination to check for membrane, cord, and confirm fetal presentation.
- Await spontaneous uterine contractions or stimulate with pitocin drip.
- If second twin is cephalic: normal delivery. If breech: assisted breech delivery.
- Third stage: active management of the third stage of labour.
- Retained second twin (not delivered within 30 minutes after first twin): management is by caesarean section.
- Management of breech second twin: external cephalic version; internal podalic version for transverse lie and fetal distress; caesarean section.

A(i) There is atony and dilatation of the renal pelves and ureters due to hormonal factors (mainly progesterone) and mechanical factors. The kidneys show increased renal parenchyma and increased intra-renal fluid, resulting in renal enlargement. Dilatation of the calyces, renal pelvis, and ureter is present especially on the right side. Smooth muscle hypertrophy in the ureters (oestrogenic effect) compensates for atony. Lateral displacement and kinking of the abdominal portion of the ureters also occurs.
A(ii) Glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow increase by approximately 50% in pregnancy. The increased GFR overwhelms tubular reabsorptive capacity, allowing more nutrients — glucose and amino acids — to escape into the urine, causing glycosuria and aminoaciduria. Within 1 week of delivery, glucose excretion returns to its non-pregnant pattern.
B(i) Urinary pH increases markedly in pregnancy, creating a more favourable environment for the multiplication of micro-organisms. Glucose and amino acids in urine further support bacterial growth. Causative organisms: Escherichia coli in more than 90%; others include Klebsiella aerogenes, Proteus mirabilis, Streptococcus faecalis, Aerobacter aerogenes, and Staphylococcus aureus.
B(ii) Predisposing factors include: asymptomatic bacteriuria; upward massage of organisms during coitus; poor hygiene following defaecation or coitus; urethral catheterisation; trauma of labour; puerperal reduction in bladder tone; urinary retention from perineal pain after birth; and vaginitis/cervicitis.
C(i) Clinical features of symptomatic UTI: rigors, pyrexia, abdominal pains, loin pains, frequency of micturition, urgency, dysuria, and pyuria. Features are not always apparent until early in the puerperium.
C(ii) Management of lower urinary tract infection: mid-stream specimen of urine for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity; increase fluid intake; acidify urine with high-dose ascorbic acid; bed rest; appropriate antibiotic or urinary antiseptic based on culture/sensitivity results — antibiotics with mist potassium citrate or vitamin C. Management of upper urinary tract infection (acute pyelonephritis): admit stat; investigations — FBC, U&Es, creatinine, blood culture, MSU M/C/S; IV antibiotics. Often associated with structural abnormality of kidney, hypertension, or anaemia. MSU for MCS should be performed regularly until the end of pregnancy; antibiotics for at least 2 weeks due to substantial risk of re-infection. Intravenous urography after the puerperium is indicated as one-third will be abnormal. Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria does not improve the outlook for the fetus.
questions.question:
Describe the anatomy of the urinary tract changes in pregnancy and their clinical relevance under the following headings:
A(i) Structural changes in the kidneys and ureter.
A(ii) The physiological basis of glycosuria and aminoaciduria in pregnancy.
B(i) The effect of urinary pH change on bacterial growth and the bacterial species involved.
B(ii) How predisposing factors combine to make UTI commoner in pregnancy.
C(i) Describe the clinical features of symptomatic UTI in pregnancy.
C(ii) Management of symptomatic UTI in pregnancy, distinguishing lower from upper urinary tract disease.

A(i) Describe the methods of intrapartum fetal monitoring available, and outline the advantages and limitations of continuous electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) compared with intermittent auscultation, as established by the Cochrane Systematic Review.
A(ii) Describe the four components of CTG interpretation, and define the following terms: baseline fetal heart rate (normal and abnormal ranges), baseline variability, accelerations, and the three types of deceleration — early, late, and variable.
B(i) Define sinusoidal pattern, state its causes, and describe the management. State the causes and clinical significance of late decelerations, and outline the intra-uterine resuscitation measures available before delivery.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Methods of intrapartum fetal monitoring: auscultatory monitoring (Pinnard's stethoscope — fetal heart recorded for 30 seconds after a contraction, every 30 minutes in first stage, every 15 minutes in second stage, every 10 minutes in the delivery room), electronic fetal heart rate monitoring (CTG), fetal blood sampling, ultrasonography in labour, review of the clinical scenario, and the partograph. Cochrane Systematic Review conclusions: continuous EFM is associated with increased Caesarean section and operative vaginal delivery; no significant differences in 1-minute Apgar score < 4 or < 7; no difference in intensive neonatal care unit admission, perinatal deaths, or cerebral palsy. The only clinically significant benefit of routine continuous EFM is reduction of neonatal seizures.
A(ii) Four CTG components: baseline rate, baseline variability, accelerations, and decelerations. Normal baseline FHR: 110–160 bpm (some sources state 120–160 bpm). Moderate bradycardia: 100–109 bpm; moderate tachycardia: 161–180 bpm; abnormal bradycardia: < 100 bpm; abnormal tachycardia: > 180 bpm. Baseline variability: FHR fluctuations occurring at 3–5 cycles/min (> 5 bpm between contractions); normal 5–15 bpm. Accelerations: transient FHR rise of > 15 bpm lasting > 15 seconds. Early decelerations: onset at onset of contraction; lowest FHR at peak of contraction; recovers at end of contraction; amplitude ≤ 40 bpm. Late decelerations: uniform repetitive slowing; onset mid to end of contraction; nadir > 20 seconds after peak; ending after contraction. Variable decelerations: variable/intermittent periodic slowing; variable relationship with contraction cycle.
B(i) Sinusoidal pattern: absent beat-to-beat variability with regular oscillation; causes: idiopathic, severe hypoxia, fetal anaemia; management: assessment and immediate delivery. Late decelerations are caused by reduction in uteroplacental blood flow from: placental abruption, maternal hypotension, excessive uterine activity/hypertonic contraction, maternal systemic illness (DM, PET, renal disease), IUGR, prematurity, Rh isoimmunisation, twin-to-twin transfusion. Intra-uterine resuscitation: change maternal position (right/left lateral recumbent or knee-chest), IV infusion, oxygen by face mask, discontinue oxytocics, subcutaneous terbutaline or magnesium sulphate, amnioinfusion (for thick meconium, oligohydramnios, repetitive severe variable deceleration, prolonged deceleration).

A(i) Uterine size: possibly the reason for early delivery in multiple pregnancy and polyhydramnios. Placental steroids: progesterone (inhibitory effect) secretion decreases while oestrogen (stimulatory effect on myometrium — reduces resting membrane potential and increases formation of gap junctions) output increases. Oxytocin: increasing sensitivity of uterine muscle as pregnancy progresses (Ferguson reflex). Fetal adrenal cortisol: involved in onset of labour. Prostaglandins: concentration increases in late pregnancy; those produced by amnion and decidua act as myometrial stimulants, change cervical compliance, reduce cervical resistance, and influence gap junction formation in the myometrium. Cervical ripening: cervix contains 10–15% smooth muscle; hyaluronic acid increases with decrease of chondroitin and dermatan sulphate in last few weeks, attracting water and making collagen looser; increase in cervical collagenases. Activation of myometrium: contraction occurs when actin and myosin combine by phosphorylation by enzyme myosin light kinase to form actinomyosin; requires influx of calcium provoked by oxytocin and prostaglandins (F2 alpha).
A(ii) Components of labour: Power — primary forces: uterine myometrial contractions; secondary forces: voluntary muscles of diaphragm and abdominal walls. Passages: ligaments, fascia, fat, bony pelvis. Passenger(s): fetus(es), placenta, and membranes. Normal uterine action: contraction begins in two pacemakers near the uterotubal junctions; upper segment contracts, relaxes, and retracts; lower segment is passive. Frequency: 3–4 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 40–60 seconds. Intrauterine pressure: resting tone 5–10 mmHg; cervical dilatation occurs at 20 mmHg; discomfort at 25 mmHg; rises by about 75 mmHg above resting pressure later in labour; expulsive bearing down reaches 125 mmHg.
B(i) Hypostimulation (uterine inertia): inadequate uterine activity. Causes: maternal distress, prolonged obstructed labour in primigravida, uterine fibroids, drugs (tocolytics — nifedipine, magnesium sulphate). Treatment: identify cause, rehydration in maternal exhaustion, oxytocics. Hyperstimulation: excessive uterine activity. Causes: drugs (prostaglandins, misoprostol, oxytocin), prolonged obstructed labour in multipara. Treatment: stop induction or augmentation, rehydration (normal saline), oxygen, nurse in left lateral position, tocolytics.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the theories of onset of labour under the following headings: the role of uterine size, placental steroids, oxytocin, fetal adrenal cortisol, prostaglandins, cervical ripening, and activation of the myometrium.
A(ii) Define the components of labour (power, passages, passenger), describe normal uterine action including pace-maker location and normal intrauterine pressure values, and define abnormal uterine action with its causes and treatment.
B(i) Distinguish between hypostimulation (uterine inertia) and hyperstimulation of the uterus: define each, list the causes of each, and state the treatment for each.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Hypertension in pregnancy is defined as a diastolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart, or a rise of at least 30 mmHg systolic and 15 mmHg diastolic from baseline. Significant proteinuria is a total protein excretion of 300 mg or more in a 24-hour urine collection, or two random clean-catch or catheter urine specimens showing 2+ (0.3g albumin/L) when specific gravity is adequate. Reagent strips give an indication of degree; accurate quantification relies on a 24-hour collection.
A(ii) Classification: (1) Gestational hypertension and/or proteinuria — hypertension and/or proteinuria developing after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive, non-proteinuric woman (includes gestational hypertension, gestational proteinuria, gestational proteinuric hypertension/pre-eclampsia, and eclampsia); (2) Chronic hypertension and chronic renal disease — hypertension and/or proteinuria in a woman with these conditions antedating pregnancy; (3) Unclassified hypertension and/or proteinuria — first detected after 20 weeks in a patient with insufficient information to classify. Pre-eclampsia is the second leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide, constituting 12–18% of pregnancy-related maternal deaths.
B(i) Aetiology is poorly understood. Theories include: immunological disorder with prevention of normal trophoblastic invasion of uteroplacental vessels; lack of conversion of myometrial arteries to thin-walled vessels; failure of the second wave of trophoblastic invasion; imbalance of prostacyclin/thromboxane activity; endothelial activation; disseminated intravascular coagulopathy; increased CNS irritability; uterine muscle stretch and ischaemia; abnormal salt and water retention; decreased intravascular volume; genetic predisposition; and excessive maternal immune response to fetal allograft.
B(ii) Cardiovascular: hyperdynamic circulation with increased peripheral resistance; failure of normal physiological plasma volume expansion. Haematological: polycythaemia, thrombocytopaenia, abnormalities in platelet aggregation, DIC, and micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia.
C(i) Fetal consequences include reduced placental perfusion, IUGR, IUFD, premature delivery, respiratory distress syndrome, neonatal jaundice, intraventricular haemorrhage, fetal asphyxia, and placental abruption.
C(ii) Measure blood pressure in the sitting position with the cuff at the level of the heart. Allow the woman to sit quietly for 5–10 minutes before measuring. Record Korotkoff sound I (first sound) as systolic and sound V (disappearance) as diastolic. In about 5% of women an exaggerated gap exists between the fourth (muffling) and fifth (disappearance) sounds. Maternal systolic BP greater than 160 mmHg or diastolic BP greater than 110 mmHg denotes severe disease.
questions.question:
Describe the classification and aetiopathogenesis of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Definition of hypertension and significant proteinuria in pregnancy.
A(ii) Classification of the hypertensive disorders.
B(i) Theories of aetiopathogenesis of pre-eclampsia.
B(ii) Cardiovascular and haematological consequences of gestational hypertension in the mother.
C(i) Fetal consequences of gestational hypertension.
C(ii) The blood pressure measurement technique required for accurate classification.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Afferent fibres from body of uterus and cervix:
- Somatic sensory fibres travel with sympathetic nerves.
- They pass laterally in paracervical tissues to the cervical plexus.
- The fibres pass through the inferior, middle, and superior hypogastric plexuses.
- They enter the sympathetic chain in the lumbar and lower thoracic regions.
- Central connections from the sympathetic chain are via the white rami communicantes of the 11th and 12th thoracic nerves.
- In some women, a proportion of nerve fibres pass through the 1st lumbar nerve.
- There may be an additional afferent pathway from the cervix to S2–4 through the pelvic splanchnic nerve.

A(ii) Afferent fibres from vagina, vulva, perineum:
- Haemorrhoidal and perineal nerves and the dorsal nerve of the clitoris carry impulses through the pudendal nerves to S2–4.
- Some areas of perineal and vulval skin are innervated by the ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, and posterior femoral cutaneous nerves, and by cutaneous branches of S2–4.

B) Anatomical level and landmark for extradural placement:
- The Tuohy needle is inserted at the L2/3 interspace.
- Landmarks traversed: supraspinous ligament, then ligamentum flavum.
- Identification of the extradural space is characterised by a palpable click (loss of resistance technique using a syringe filled with sterile saline).

C) Total spinal block – features and management:
- Occurs when the dose of anaesthetic intended for the extradural space is inadvertently injected into the subarachnoid space.
- Features: arm and hand weakness and advancing sensory loss often precede ventilatory impairment; respiratory distress and cardiovascular collapse.
- Management:
 - Immediate cardiovascular support.
 - IV fluids.
 - IV ephedrine 5–10 mg.
 - Maintain systolic arterial pressure above 90 mmHg.
 - Before marked respiratory distress occurs, administer standard general anaesthesia.
 - Controlled ventilation until recovery (45–60 minutes).
 - Subsequent recovery: spinal headache may occur; treat with extradural blood patch.
questions.question:
A) Describe the afferent nerve supply of the uterus, cervix, vagina, vulva, and perineum under the following headings:
A(i) Fibres from the body of the uterus and cervix: pathway from organ to central connections
A(ii) Fibres from the vagina, vulva, and perineum: named nerves and their spinal levels

B) State the anatomical level for lumbar extradural catheter placement and the landmark for identifying the extradural space.

C) Describe the clinical features of total spinal block, and explain its management including the drug, dose, target blood pressure, and duration of ventilation.

A. Describe heart disease in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Spectrum of cardiac diseases encountered in pregnancy
A(ii) The New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification
A(iii) Investigations used in the diagnosis of cardiac disease in pregnancy

B. Explain the clinical basis for why women with severe cardiac dysfunction may deteriorate before midpregnancy and again peripartum.

C. Distinguish between the antenatal care of a woman with Grade II heart disease and one with Grade IV heart disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Spectrum of cardiac diseases: Rheumatic heart disease — commonest in our environment (reduced incidence in developed countries due to antibiotic use for streptococcal infections; rheumatic fever occurs between ages 5 and 15 years; valvular lesions occur 4–8 years later). Congenital: ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, coarctation of the aorta, pulmonary stenosis, Fallot's tetralogy, Eisenmenger's complex. Cardiomyopathies: peripartal dilated cardiomyopathy (common in Hausa women); endomyocardial fibrosis. Hypertensive heart disease; pulmonary heart disease; syphilitic heart disease; coronary heart disease; anaemic heart failure; infective myocarditis.

A(ii) NYHA Classification: Grade I — cardiac disease but no limitation of physical activity; no complaints. Grade II — slight to moderate limitation of physical activity; ordinary activity causes discomfort; no symptoms at rest. Grade III — marked limitation of activity; dyspnoea or pain on minimal activity. Grade IV — unable to carry out any physical activity without discomfort; orthopnoea; symptoms at rest or with minimal activity.

A(iii) Investigations: ECG (average 15-degree left-axis deviation in pregnancy due to elevated diaphragm; mild ST changes in inferior leads; pregnancy does not alter voltage findings). Chest X-ray (slight cardiomegaly cannot be detected accurately; gross cardiomegaly can be excluded; use lead apron shield to minimise fetal radiation). Echocardiography (allows noninvasive accurate diagnosis of most heart diseases; essential). Fetal echocardiography.

B. Significant haemodynamic alterations are apparent early in pregnancy; CO increases by up to 30–50%; early increase attributed to augmented stroke volume (decreased vascular resistance, diminished BP). Women with severe dysfunction may deteriorate before midpregnancy due to early haemodynamic changes. Hypervolaemia of pregnancy is maximal after 28 weeks → heart failure may develop then. In the majority, failure develops peripartum when additional haemodynamic burdens (autotransfusion from uterine contraction after delivery, relief of IVC compression) can overwhelm physiological capacity for rapid changes in CO.

C. Grade II: Fortnightly antenatal visits; ensure adequate rest and restrict physical activity; prevent anaemia; ensure competent dental care; administer prophylactic penicillin V for dental procedures to protect against streptococcal endocarditis; admit a few days before term; joint management with cardiologist; detect obstetric complications.
Grade IV: In-patient care throughout pregnancy; strict rest; all measures above plus close monitoring for factors promoting cardiac failure (anaemia, respiratory tract infection, pre-eclampsia, tachycardia/arrhythmia, recurrence of rheumatic fever, bacterial endocarditis).

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman known to be Rh-D-negative presents after an amniocentesis at 18 weeks of pregnancy. Her husband is Rh-positive and homozygous. Antibody screen at booking was negative.
(i) What is this patient's risk status, and why is the husband's genotype important?
(ii) What immediate action is required following the amniocentesis?
(iii) How and when should this patient be monitored for sensitisation during the remainder of pregnancy?
(iv) If antibodies are subsequently detected and found to be rising, what investigations are indicated and what do they show?
(v) Describe the intrauterine treatment of a severely affected fetus at 24 weeks gestation.
questions.answerText:
(i) She is at high risk because she is Rh-D-negative and her husband is homozygous Rh-positive; about 75% of fathers of affected children are homozygous, meaning all their children will be Rh-positive and thus at risk of haemolytic disease. The paternal genotype determines whether the fetus must be Rh-positive. If the father were heterozygous, there would be a 50% chance the fetus is Rh-negative and unaffected.
(ii) Amniocentesis is a cause of transplacental haemorrhage and is an indication for anti-D administration. Anti-D 300 mcg (500 IU) should be given to the patient as soon as possible after the procedure, before sensitisation can occur.
(iii) In unsensitised women, check for Rh antibodies at booking, 28, 32, and 36 weeks. Anti-D 500 IU should be given prophylactically at 28 and 34 weeks to Rh-D-negative primigravidae and previously unsensitised women, to reduce the incidence of sensitisation by at least a factor of 8.
(iv) Once antibodies are detected, they must be measured at least monthly thereafter. Serum antibody protein levels are of greater predictive value than antibody titres. A rapid increase suggests that acute haemolysis is occurring in the fetus, and amniotic fluid analysis is necessary. Amniocentesis determines the amount of bilirubin in the liquor; spectrophotometry at OD 450 nm shows a peak directly proportional to bilirubin quantity. The first amniocentesis should be 10 weeks before the earliest previous intrauterine death or delivery of a severely affected infant, but not before 20 weeks gestation. Fetal blood sampling under ultrasound guidance can check fetal haematocrit; it is indicated in patients at risk of severe early disease.
(v) At 24 weeks, the fetus is too premature for delivery; intrauterine transfusion is indicated. O Rh-negative, CMV-negative donor blood, cross-matched with maternal blood (irradiated in some centres), is transfused either intraperitoneally or directly via a fetal vein such as the umbilical cord. A haematocrit at or before 26 weeks warrants transfusion. Transfusion may be repeated as necessary based on gestational age and fetal haematocrit.

questions.question:
A. Describe the comprehensive management framework for diabetes in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Goals of management (glycaemic targets) and the multidisciplinary approach
A(ii) Monitoring of response to therapy — clinical markers, HbA1c targets, and side effects of insulin therapy
A(iii) Antenatal fetal monitoring schedule for diabetic pregnancies

B. Explain the role of oral hypoglycaemic agents in pregnancy and state the alternatives available.

C. Distinguish between the management of a woman with pre-gestational diabetes and one with diet-controlled GDM, from preconception through to the postpartum period.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Goals of management: maintain FBS at 60–95 mg/dl (whole blood); 2-hour post-prandial <120 mg/dl (whole blood); HbA1c <6%. Multidisciplinary: obstetrician, diabetologist/physician, dietitian, neonatologist. Preconception — achieve normoglycaemia before conception; folic acid supplementation; screen for vascular complications. Education crucial to achieve and maintain normoglycaemia. Daily self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG). Dietary treatment — cornerstone of therapy.

A(ii) Monitoring of therapy: clinical — hydramnios, macrosomia, hypoglycaemia. Glycosylated haemoglobin monthly — well controlled = <8.0% (normal 6.0%); poorly controlled = >11.0%; HbA1c >10% indicates most significant risk of malformation. Side effects of insulin therapy: lipoatrophy; hypoglycaemia; allergy. Well-controlled diabetes is defined as HbA1c <8.0%.

A(iii) Antenatal fetal monitoring schedule: 1st trimester USS for accurate dating; 18–22 weeks: anomaly USS and fetal echocardiogram; 24 weeks, 28–32 weeks, 36 weeks: fetal growth assessment; 32 weeks: twice-weekly NST and BPP (can be initiated earlier if poor glycaemic control); elective deliveries 38–40 weeks; fetal lung testing (amniocentesis) if delivery before 38 weeks; elective CS for fetal macrosomia. Urinalysis, urine M/C/S, HVS for candidiasis, FBC, E/U/C, blood sugar profile twice weekly; frequent visits — 2-weekly until 28 weeks, then weekly until delivery.

B. Oral hypoglycaemic agents: use is not universally recommended during pregnancy; however, Glibenclamide/Metformin can be used. Insulin is the most commonly used treatment when dietary therapy fails to maintain desired blood glucose levels in GDM and is indicated for all women with pre-gestational DM. Adjustments in insulin dose are based upon results of serial blood glucose monitoring.

C. Pre-gestational DM:
Preconception: lower HbA1c; screen for vascular complications; contraception until control achieved; folic acid.
Antepartum: insulin required from outset (1st trimester 0.6 u/kg; 2nd 0.7 u/kg; 3rd 0.9 u/kg); 2/3 dose morning (2/3 intermediate + 1/3 soluble), 1/3 evening (1/2 intermediate + 1/2 soluble); fetal surveillance as above.
Postpartum: insulin requirements decreased for ~48–96 hours; monitor FBG and post-prandial; recalculate requirements; encourage breastfeeding.
Diet-controlled GDM:
Antepartum: dietary therapy alone (30/24/12–15 kcal/kg depending on weight; correct macronutrient composition); no insulin initially; if diet fails → add insulin or Glibenclamide/Metformin; fetal monitoring as above.
Postpartum: most will not require further insulin; 98% revert to normoglycaemia; 75 g OGTT at 6–8 weeks, then 3-yearly; lifestyle modification; screen in subsequent pregnancies.

questions.question:
A. Describe the pathophysiology of diabetes mellitus in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Normal maternal-fetal glucose metabolism in pregnancy and the hormonal factors that disturb it
A(ii) How fetal hyperinsulinaemia leads to fetal morbidity (the cascade from maternal hyperglycaemia to fetal hypoxia)
A(iii) The relationship between HbA1c levels and the rate of congenital malformation

B. State the diagnostic criteria for diabetes in pregnancy (WHO and North American criteria) and the screening protocol.

C. Explain how the effect of pregnancy on pre-existing diabetes worsens the mother's condition, including effects on chronic complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Normal pregnancy: pregnant women tend to develop hypoglycaemia (plasma glucose mean 65–75 mg/dL) between meals and during sleep. Levels of placental steroid and peptide hormones (oestrogens, progesterone, chorionic somatomammotropin) rise linearly throughout the second and third trimesters — these antagonise insulin. If the maternal pancreatic insulin response is inadequate, maternal and then fetal hyperglycaemia results. Hormones antagonising insulin (marked in 3rd trimester): human placental lactogen, oestrogen and progesterone, prolactin, cortisol, growth hormone.

A(ii) Cascade: maternal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperglycaemia → episodic fetal hyperinsulinaemia → fetal hypoxia → surges in adrenal catecholamines → hypertension, cardiac remodelling and hypertrophy, stimulation of erythropoietin, red blood cell hyperplasia, increased haematocrit. Macrosomia: birth weight >90th percentile or >4000 g; occurs in 15–45% of diabetic pregnancies (3-fold increase from normoglycaemic controls). Birth injury (shoulder dystocia, brachial plexus trauma) more common among IDMs.

A(iii) Rate of congenital malformation and HbA1c: <7.0% — similar to general population (1–2%); 7.2–9.1% — 14%; 9.2–11.1% — 23%; >11.2% — 25%. HbA1c levels >10% indicate the most significant risk of malformation development. Birth defects occur during the critical period 3–6 weeks after conception.

B. Diagnostic criteria:
WHO: 75 g 2-hour OGTT — FPG ≥126 mg/dl and 2-hour plasma glucose ≥140 mg/dl.
North America: 100 g 3-hour OGTT — fasting >95 mg/dl, 1 hour >180 mg/dl, 2 hours >155 mg/dl, 3 hours >140 mg/dl.
Outside pregnancy: FPG ≥126 mg/dl; random PG ≥200 mg/dl; 200 mg/dl or more at 2 hours following 75 g OGTT; impaired glucose tolerance 140–199 mg/dl at 2-hour OGTT; impaired fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dl.
Screening: 1-hour 50 g glucose challenge test (positive ≥7.8 mmol/l); high-risk women screened at booking; low-risk screened at 24–28 weeks; if positive, proceed to diagnostic test.

C. Effect of pregnancy on diabetes: difficult control due to increasing insulin resistance (hCG, HPL, cortisol, prolactin); increased exogenous insulin requirement; increased risk of acute metabolic complications — DKA, hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma, hypoglycaemia. Worsening chronic complications: gastroparesis; retinopathy (leading cause of blindness in women aged 24–64); nephropathy (increased risk of proteinuria; perinatal complications greatly increased); neuropathy; vascular angiopathy. Diabetic retinopathy — pre-existing retinopathy deteriorates during pregnancy.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old primigravida with mild cephalopelvic disproportion at the pelvic brim requests a trial of labour. Clinical pelvimetry at 36 weeks confirms a diagonal conjugate of 11 cm, a concave sacrum with non-prominent ischial spines, and an obtuse subpubic angle with a mobile coccyx.
(i) Define trial of labour, state the conditions under which it should be conducted, and describe the antenatal preparation required.
(ii) Enumerate all contraindications to trial of labour.
(iii) Describe how a trial of labour should be monitored intrapartum, and list all criteria for terminating a trial of labour.
(iv) State the advantages and disadvantages of trial of labour compared with elective Caesarean section.
questions.answerText:
(i) Trial of labour: originally an attempt at vaginal delivery in a woman with mild to moderate CPD at the pelvic brim; now applied more broadly to numerous clinical situations including trial of vaginal birth after Caesarean (VBAC), trial of pelvic outlet, breech delivery, and others. Conditions for conduct: centre with facilities for adequate monitoring, Caesarean section, and neonatal resuscitation; neonatologist and anaesthetist informed; blood available for emergencies; continuous electronic fetal monitoring (or intermittent every 15 minutes). Antenatal preparation: assess maternal wellbeing (search for medical disease), pelvic assessment to rule out gross disproportion, ensure adequate haemoglobin concentration, ensure blood available, await spontaneous labour, assess fetal age and wellbeing.
(ii) Contraindications: elderly primigravida especially with involuntary infertility, medical conditions (pre-eclampsia, hypertension, cardiac disease, renal disease, diabetes mellitus, haemoglobinopathy, thyrotoxicosis), severe CPD (true conjugate < 9 cm), CPD in breech presentation, CPD with previous Caesarean section, previous difficult vaginal delivery resulting in perinatal death or morbidity, previous failed trial of labour, poor fetal wellbeing, multiple pregnancy.
(iii) Intrapartum monitoring: partograph used to monitor progress (cervical dilatation at least 1 cm/hour, descent of presenting part); labour in primigravida augmented with intravenous oxytocin; monitored with cardiotocographic machine and scalp electrode; intrapartum radiography occasionally to detect level and attitude of the head (e.g., occipitoposterior position); 3–4-hourly vaginal examination; intravenous fluids, patient nil per os; analgesics. Indications for terminating trial of labour: poor progress despite good contractions, maternal distress, fetal distress (FHR abnormality, meconium staining of liquor, fetal blood pH < 7.20), development of Bandl's ring, pain and tenderness over the lower uterine segment.
(iv) Advantages: reduction in number of elective Caesarean sections for disproportion (lower incidence of uterine scar, less limitation on obstetric career), reduces incidence of premature induction of labour to prevent CPD at term. Disadvantages: higher perinatal mortality than elective Caesarean section, increased incidence of emergency Caesarean section (with risks of sepsis in a frightened, anxious, and demoralised woman; raised maternal mortality rate), its failure proves nothing.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks presents with pruritus and mildly elevated bilirubin levels, mildly elevated transaminases, and elevated bile acids. She has no fever, no hypertension, and no proteinuria.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and the trimester in which it typically presents?
(ii) What are the pathophysiological and genetic features of this condition?
(iii) What are the laboratory abnormalities and symptoms expected?
(iv) Outline the management options for this condition.
(v) What are the maternal and fetal outcomes associated with jaundice in pregnancy?
questions.answerText:
(i) Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP). Typically presents in the 3rd trimester (earlier presentations have been reported). It is a pregnancy-specific liver disease.
(ii) The pathophysiology is poorly understood. There is a clear racial and genetic predisposition: incidence of 0.01–0.02% in most populations; highest rates in Chile; rare in black populations; strong family history. Alterations in bromosulfophthalein clearance following oestrogen treatment have been demonstrated in relatives.
(iii) Symptoms: pruritus and jaundice. Laboratory abnormalities: mildly elevated bilirubin levels; minimal to no elevation of transaminases, cholesterol, or triglycerides; mild to moderate steatorrhoea; elevated bile acids. Histology shows dilated bile canaliculi and intrahepatic cholestasis.
(iv) Management options: cholestyramine (Questran) binds bile acids and may improve pruritus; multiple medications may be used. Phenobarbital has not been shown to consistently help. General management of jaundice in pregnancy: rest the liver; bed rest; supplements for substances manufactured by the liver (e.g., vitamin K); low fat diet; normal protein diet.
(v) Maternal outcome: good maternal outcome in mild/moderate jaundice. Fulminant hepatitis complicated by hyperemesis can cause maternal death. Fetal/perinatal outcome: good in mild/moderate jaundice; increased perinatal morbidity/mortality in severe jaundice; intrauterine growth retardation. The following causes of jaundice require prompt delivery of the fetus: acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is rare, with 18% maternal and 23% fetal mortality; it is most frequently associated with pre-eclampsia (50–100%) and is most frequently a complication of the 3rd trimester.

A(i) Definition: A placenta that is wholly or partially situated in the lower uterine segment. Incidence: 0.55% (about 1:200) of all pregnancies at delivery (Penna and Peerce, 1994); range 0.29–1.24%. The different rates largely relate to differences in definition. The lower uterine segment is defined as: the part of the uterus below the uterovestical peritoneum; the part that lies within 7.5 cm of the internal os; the part that forms during the last few weeks of pregnancy between the definitive cervix and definitive myometrium, passively stretches during labour.

A(ii) Classification systems: (1) Dewhurst's/Jauniaux & Campbell: Type I — low lying, within 5 cm of os; Type II — marginal, at margin of os; Type III — partial, partially covering os; Type IV — total, completely covering os. (2) Minor/Major: Major — placenta covers internal os; Minor — placenta encroaches on lower segment but does not cover os. (3) Total PP — entire internal os covered; Low lying — placental edge within 2 cm of internal os (Lauria & Cotton, 2002). (4) Type 'a' — placenta on anterior wall; Type 'b' — on posterior wall (more dangerous; discourages engagement, compresses placenta during labour). Clinical: Minor (Types Ia/b and IIa) — vaginal delivery feasible; Major (Types IIb, III, IV) — CS required.

A(iii) Mechanism of placental migration: differential growth of placental edges; differential growth of the uterus itself (fails in a scarred uterus); relative growth of the lower uterine segment to the placenta — achieves 10 times its size at 20 weeks by the third trimester; difficulty identifying the cervix and cervical canal — especially with inadequately filled bladder. There is a 10× incidence of low-lying or frank PP in the second trimester compared with term.

B. Scarred uterus impairs the differential growth of the lower uterine segment; failure of placental migration. Risk: 0.26% in an unscarred uterus; 0.65% after 1 CS; 10% after 4 CS (Clark et al, 1985). Previous endometrial damage from D&C, STOP, evacuation of retained POC also increases risk by 6× after first-trimester TOP (Barret et al, 1981).

C. Expectant management (Macafee's regime, 1945): employed when fetus is not at term and bleeding is not serious. Goal: allow fetus to mature to an age compatible with life before delivery. Components: admission to hospital; correct anaemia; localization of placenta; exclude incidental causes (gentle speculum exam); constant availability of cross-matched blood; availability of facilities/personnel for CS round the clock; patient remains in hospital until delivery. Asymptomatic minor PP: outpatient management, travel restriction, coital holiday. Asymptomatic major PP: admit from 34 weeks GA.
Active management: immediate delivery indications — profuse bleeding (>500 ml); term pregnancy; major degree → CS; severe/massive haemorrhage → CS; uncertainty with degree and non-life-threatening haemorrhage at term → EUA or immediate CS.
questions.question:
A. Describe placenta praevia under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and incidence
A(ii) All classification systems
A(iii) The mechanism of placental migration and why it may fail

B. Explain the clinical basis for why the incidence of placenta praevia is higher in women with previous caesarean sections, and state the specific risks quoted.

C. Distinguish between expectant (Macafee's regime) management and active management of placenta praevia, stating the criteria for each.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Caloric requirements:
- Daily requirement: 35 kcals multiplied by optimal body weight
- Average non-pregnant woman: 2300 kcals/day
- Additional 300–350 kcals/day during pregnancy
- Additional 300 kcals per fetus in multiple pregnancy
- Additional 500 kcals/day during lactation
Protein requirement: 1 g/kg plus 20 g per day in 2nd trimester; essential for embryonic development.
Total weight gain recommended: 11.5–16 kg (ACOG); average is 12 kg; underweight need to gain more; obese need to gain less.
Contributors to weight gain: fetus 3.5 kg; placenta, uterus and amniotic fluid 650–900 g; interstitial fluid and blood volume 1.2–1.8 kg; breast enlargement 400 g; maternal fat 1.65 kg.
A(ii) Micronutrient requirements:
- Iron: 30–60 mg elemental iron for normal pregnancy and lactation; 60–120 mg in iron deficiency anaemia.
- Folic acid: 400 ug daily; 4 mg per day commenced pre-conceptionally for those with previous neural tube defect pregnancy.
- Calcium: 1200 mg per day required during pregnancy; easily met in dairy products; decreases risk of hypertension, pre-eclampsia, low birth weight and chronic hypertension in children.
- Iodine: iodine deficiency is a preventable cause of mental impairment; supplementation and fortification programs largely successful; form depends on severity of deficiency and availability.
- Vitamin A: supplementation confirmed but confirmatory studies needed.
B(i) Poor nutritional status (particularly micronutrients) predisposes to: congenital malformations; abortions; premature labour; low birth weight; APH due to abruptio placentae; cretinism (iodine deficiency); increased perinatal mortality; increased maternal morbidity.
B(ii) Underweight women and low pregnancy weight gain: associated with low birth weight infants (<2500 g); statistically significant relationship between low maternal weight gain and preterm delivery.
Overweight women and high pregnancy weight gain: increased risk of macrosomia (>4000 g); macrosomia associated with birth injuries and caesarean section; pre-pregnancy obesity associated with hypertension, diabetes and post-operative wound infection.
Maternal weight gain in the 2nd trimester is the most important for fetal growth.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe nutrition in pregnancy under the headings of caloric requirements, protein requirements, total weight gain recommended, and the contributors to maternal weight gain.
A(ii) State the micronutrient requirements in pregnancy including iron, folic acid, calcium, iodine, and Vitamin A.
B(i) Explain why poor nutritional status predisposes to adverse pregnancy outcomes, listing all the consequences of poor micronutrient intake.
B(ii) Describe the importance of maternal weight in pregnancy, distinguishing between the consequences of underweight and overweight.

Describe the prevention of Rhesus disease under the following headings:
A(i) The historical basis for passive immunisation with anti-D.
A(ii) The dose, timing, and indications for anti-D immunoglobulin administration.
B(i) Antenatal monitoring of unsensitised Rh-D-negative women.
B(ii) The investigation of amniotic fluid for bilirubin: method, timing, and interpretation.
C(i) Intrauterine blood transfusion: indication, blood used, and route.
C(ii) Neonatal management after delivery of a potentially affected infant.
questions.answerText:
A(i) With the discovery of the Rhesus factor as the major cause of red cell iso-immunisation, the development of passive immunisation with anti-D has led to a dramatic decrease in the incidence of Rhesus disease. Anti-D immunoglobulin works by clearing fetal Rh-positive red blood cells from the maternal circulation before they can stimulate a primary immune response. Rh iso-immunisation was first described after the discovery of the Rh factor by Landsteiner and Wiener in 1940.
A(ii) Doses and indications: anti-D 50 mcg (50 IU in some formulations) for abortion or sensitising events before 20 weeks; 100 mcg after 20 weeks if abortion or antepartum haemorrhage occurs; 300 mcg (500 IU) for amniocentesis, CVS, antepartum haemorrhage, ECV; 300 mcg after delivery if baby is Rh-positive, within 72 hours of delivery. Routine antenatal prophylaxis: anti-D 500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks to Rh-D-negative primigravidae and other previously unsensitised women; reduces incidence of Rh sensitisation by at least a factor of 8. Additional anti-D is required if any FMT exceeds a specified volume.
B(i) In unsensitised women, check for Rh antibodies at booking, 28, 32, and 36 weeks. Once antibodies are detected, they must be measured at least monthly thereafter; serum antibody protein levels are of greater predictive value than antibody titres.
B(ii) Amniocentesis determines the amount of bilirubin in the liquor. Spectrophotometry at an optical density (OD) of 450 nm shows a peak directly proportional to the quantity of bilirubin; this correlates well with the severity of haemolysis. If a previous pregnancy was complicated by Rh iso-immunisation, the first amniocentesis should be 10 weeks before the earliest previous intrauterine transfusion, intrauterine death, or delivery of a fatally or severely affected infant, but not before 20 weeks gestation. The second should be 3–4 weeks later; bilirubin levels determine the necessity for and interval between subsequent amniocenteses.
C(i) Intrauterine transfusion is indicated in severely affected fetus not mature enough for delivery. Blood used: O Rh-negative, CMV-negative donor blood cross-matched with maternal blood, irradiated in some centres. Route: either intraperitoneal or directly via a fetal vein such as the umbilical cord. Timing: the earliest intrauterine blood transfusion between 28 and 30 weeks if no previous history of severely affected fetus; repeat every 2–3 weeks. A haematocrit at or before 26 weeks warrants transfusion.
C(ii) Neonatal management: cord blood for blood grouping, direct Coombs test, bilirubin, and haemoglobin. Early delivery in severely affected fetus in absence of intrauterine therapy; induction of labour or caesarean section depending on circumstances. After birth: treatment depends on the degree of anaemia and jaundice and may include blood transfusion, exchange transfusion, and phototherapy. Lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio (lung function test) should be assessed if premature delivery is planned.

(i) Dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) twin pregnancy. Ultrasound determinants of chorionicity: (a) fetal gender — different sex indicates dizygotic and therefore dichorionic; (b) number of placentae — two separate placentae indicates dichorionic, but fused placentae are difficult to distinguish from monochorionic; (c) inter-twin membrane characteristics — in dichorionic twins, the membrane is composed of a central layer of chorionic tissue sandwiched between two layers of amnion; it is thick and more echogenic; in monochorionic twins there is no chorionic layer. The lambda (twin peak) sign: extension of placental tissue into the base of the inter-twin membrane is seen in dichorionic twins; this sign is absent in monochorionic twins. Best assessed in the first trimester.
(ii) Complications common to any twin pregnancy: miscarriage and severe preterm delivery, perinatal mortality (PNM rate in twins is six times higher than in singletons, almost entirely due to prematurity-related complications), IUGR (risk that at least one fetus will suffer poor growth is 20% in dichorionic twins, almost double in monochorionic), fetal abnormalities, chromosomal defects, death of one fetus. Complications unique to monochorionic twinning: twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (arising from vascular anastomoses between the two placental circulations). PNM is twice as high in monochorionic as in dichorionic twin pregnancies.
(iii) In monochorionic twins, vascular communications exist within the two placental circulations. Death of one fetus may result in death or handicap of the co-twin because of complications arising from these placental vascular anastomoses. Management of fetal abnormality: expectant or selective foeticide of the abnormal twin; risk is loss of the normal twin from foeticide-related complications; for lethal abnormalities, best to avoid such risk unless the condition threatens the normal twin (e.g., anencephaly, which is associated with polyhydramnios and severe preterm delivery of both twins in > 50% of cases).
(iv) Maternal serum biochemistry tests for detection of trisomy 21 are not effective in multiple gestation. The best method of chromosomal screening in twins is measurement of fetal nuchal translucency thickness in each fetus by ultrasound at 10–14 weeks.
(v) Fetus papyraceous: if one fetus in a monochorionic twin pregnancy dies early and is retained until term, it is compressed and flattened on the membranes, forming a paper-thin structure called fetus papyraceous.
questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman presents for her first antenatal ultrasound at 10 weeks gestation. Two gestational sacs are identified with a thick echogenic inter-twin membrane. A lambda (twin peak) sign is seen at the base of the membrane. No vascular anastomoses are identified between the two placental circulations.
(i) State the type of twinning demonstrated. Describe all determinants of chorionicity detectable by ultrasound, and explain what the lambda sign signifies.
(ii) Enumerate the pregnancy complications specific to this type of twinning and those unique to monochorionic twinning, including the mechanism of perinatal mortality differences between the two types.
(iii) Explain how death of one fetus in a monochorionic twin pregnancy can harm its co-twin, and describe the management of fetal abnormality in a multiple pregnancy.
(iv) Describe the chromosomal screening approach recommended in multiple gestation, and state why standard maternal serum biochemistry is not effective in this setting.
(v) Define fetus papyraceous and explain the circumstance in which it arises.

A(i) Describe CTG under the following headings: definition, when it was introduced, how it records fetal information, its sensitivity and specificity, its relationship to Caesarean section rates, and the conditions it can and cannot prevent.
A(ii) Describe fetal scalp blood sampling: what it measures, the pH value that indicates acidosis, contraindications to the procedure, and its clinical impact on Caesarean section rates and Apgar scores.
B(i) Describe the ancillary tests available for intrapartum fetal assessment beyond fetal scalp blood sampling, including vibroacoustic stimulation/fetal scalp stimulation, fetal lactate levels, fetal pulse oximetry, and fetal ECG monitoring, stating the clinical utility of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) CTG (cardiotocography): electronic monitoring of the fetal heart rate and rhythm, either by external microphone or transducer or by applying an electrode to the fetal scalp, recording the fetal ECG and hence the heart rate; also includes measurement of the strength and frequency of uterine contractions; the graphic print-out is called a cardiotocogram. Introduced in the 1970s; use has been controversial. CTG remains the cornerstone of making a diagnosis of fetal distress but is not available in many hospitals in Nigeria. CTG has a high sensitivity but low specificity. CTG can alert the obstetrician about fetal wellbeing and may prevent intrapartum fetal mortality; however, it does not prevent long-term morbidity such as cerebral palsy or Erb's palsy. CTG has contributed to the rise in the Caesarean section rate, which remains a challenge. The only clinically significant benefit of routine continuous EFM is reduction of neonatal seizures.
A(ii) Fetal scalp blood sampling: invasive ancillary test. Measures pH value. Acidotic pH value: < 7.2. Contraindications: maternal infection (HIV, hepatitis, herpes), fetal bleeding disorders, prematurity (< 34 weeks). Clinical impact: its use has not significantly increased Caesarean section rates for fetal distress; it has not reduced the incidence of low Apgar scores or birth asphyxia. It is declining in clinical application.
B(i) Vibroacoustic stimulation / fetal scalp stimulation: assessment of fetal wellbeing when spontaneous accelerations are absent; good correlation with pH; can be used to assess fetal wellbeing. Fetal lactate levels: measured from fetal scalp blood; predicts neurological disability. Fetal pulse oximetry: questionable clinical utility. Fetal ECG: currently under investigation; not yet established in clinical practice.

A(i) History and risk factors: accurate dating of pregnancy (menstrual history, quickening); risk factors — hypertensive disorders, UTI, diabetes mellitus, anaemia, SCD, malaria, chronic renal disease, substance abuse, alcohol, cigarette smoking, genetic abnormalities, TORCHES, multiple pregnancy, post-term pregnancy, abruptio placentae, placental malformations.
Clinical examination signs: uterus small for dates; SFH less than dates by ≥2 cm (suggestive); SFH less than dates by ≥4 cm (severe IUGR); same SFH measurement on 3 successive examinations; oligohydramnios; static/reducing maternal weight gain; presence of risk factor.

A(ii) Value of ultrasound: early USS — crown-rump length for dating. Second trimester: BPD (±7–11 days accuracy); HC (±3–5 days accuracy). Fetal growth assessment: AC (estimated fetal weight); FL (femur length); amniotic fluid volume. Asymmetrical IUGR: increased HC/AC ratio (brain sparing). Serial growth USS every 2–4 weeks: BPD, HC, AC, FL, amniotic fluid volume. USS is the most accurate method for gestational age assessment.

A(iii) Fetal surveillance methods: fetal kick monitoring; USS for fetal growth 2–4 weekly; non-stress test (NST); contraction stress test (CST); biophysical profile (BPP); Doppler velocimetry; amniocentesis for pulmonary maturity (if delivery contemplated).

B. Doppler velocimetry of the umbilical artery: umbilical artery systolic:diastolic (S:D) blood flow ratio is increased in IUGR. Physiological significance: increased resistance in the placental circulation (due to obliterative pathology in the placental vessels) leads to reduced diastolic flow; elevated S:D ratio reflects increased placental resistance and reduced placental perfusion. In severe cases, absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates critical fetal compromise.

C. Management when cause identified: treat underlying cause specifically (e.g., antihypertensives for hypertension; treat malaria, UTI, anaemia; low-dose aspirin to alter thromboxane:prostacyclin ratio in hypertensive disorders). Anomaly scan; amniocentesis to exclude chromosomal abnormality.
When cause not identified: adequate nutrition; bed rest (no proven benefit); weekly visits; antenatal corticosteroid prior to 34 weeks; fetal surveillance (as above). Delivery: individualise; indications — evidence of fetal maturity; evidence of fetal compromise; at 38 weeks. Mode: electronic fetal monitoring in labour; CS for compromised fetus; neonatologist mandatory. Pharmacological: low-dose aspirin; antenatal corticosteroids before 34 weeks.

A(i) Definition: Episiotomy is an incision on the perineum to enlarge the introitus during the second stage of labour to facilitate delivery of the fetus. It is a second-degree laceration of the vulva, vagina and perineal body made deliberately during the second stage of labour.

A(ii) Indications: Fetal distress in the second stage; preterm delivery; breech delivery; cord prolapse; forceps or vacuum delivery; tight or rigid perineum or imminent perineal tear; previous colpoperineorrhaphy; previous surgery for stress incontinence; previous successful repair of complete perineal tear, prolapse, or fistulae; previous RVF repair; macrosomic babies or shoulder dystocia.

A(iii) Types:
- Mediolateral episiotomy: cut at 45 degrees; the commonest type.
- Midline (central/median) episiotomy: cut in the centre of the perineum separating the bulbocavernosus and superficial transverse perineal muscles.
- J-shaped episiotomy: made tangential to the top of the anus.
- Lateral episiotomy.

B) Clinical basis for choosing mediolateral over midline:
- Mediolateral is preferred because anal extension (through the anal sphincter and rectum) is less common compared to midline episiotomy.
- Midline is preferred when easier repair, less pain, smaller blood loss, and better anatomical outcome are the priorities, since faulty healing is rare and anatomical result is almost always excellent with midline.
- Midline carries a higher risk of extension through the anal sphincter and rectum, making mediolateral the safer choice when the perineum is at risk of deep tear.

C) Distinction – midline vs mediolateral:
- Ease of repair: midline is easy to repair; mediolateral is more difficult.
- Pain: midline causes less perineal pain; mediolateral is more painful.
- Blood loss: midline has smaller blood loss; mediolateral has greater blood loss.
- Risk of anal extension: midline has common extension through anal sphincter and rectum; mediolateral has less common anal extension.
- Anatomical outcome: midline gives an almost always excellent result; mediolateral gives a not-as-satisfactory result in 10% of cases depending on the operator.

A(i) Describe the iron balance in pregnancy, including basal iron loss, expansion of red cell mass, fetal requirement, placental requirement, blood loss at delivery, and iron conserved by amenorrhoea, stating the total additional iron needed per day of absorbed iron.
A(ii) Describe the mechanisms that regulate iron absorption in pregnancy, including the normal absorption rate, the absorption rate in deficiency, and the key enhancers and inhibitors of iron absorption.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Iron balance in average pregnancy (mg):
- Basal iron loss: 280
- Expansion of red cell mass: 570
- Fetus: 200–350
- Placenta: 50–150
- Blood loss at delivery: 100–250
- Iron conserved by amenorrhoea: 240–480
- Difference (net demand): 500–600, requiring 4–6 mg/day of absorbed iron
- Achieved by mobilising iron stores and maximum iron absorption from diet
- Average diet contains about 6 mg of iron per 1000 calories and about 10% of dietary iron is absorbed
A(ii) Normal absorption: 15–30%; in deficiency: 50%; in excessive iron diet: 5–8%.
Absorption enhancers: ascorbic acid, gastric acidity, protein, alcohol, erythropoietic activities (high altitude, haemolysis, haemorrhage).
Absorption inhibitors: phytates, tannates, tea and coffee, calcium, herbal drinks.
B(i) High prevalence in developing countries is due to low bioavailability diets: cereals (rice, maize), negligible meat and ascorbic acid, excessive inhibitors of absorption; absorption as low as 3–4%. In developed countries, varied diets rich in meat, poultry, fish and generous ascorbic acid give high bioavailability.
B(ii) Supplementation: 30–60 mg elemental iron for normal pregnancy and lactation; 60–120 mg elemental iron in iron deficiency anaemia. Specific regimens: Fersolate 200 mg tds; Ferrous fumarate 300 mg daily; or slow-release preparation of ferrous sulphate 150 mg combined with folic acid 0.5 mg. Folic acid 400 ug daily; 4 mg per day pre-conceptionally for those with previous neural tube defect pregnancy.

(i) Presenting part: the face is presenting (face presentation). The denominator is the mentum (chin).
- In the mentoanterior position: presenting diameter is the submentobregmatic diameter = 9.5 cm.
- The diameter distending the vulva is the submentovertical diameter = 11 cm.

(ii) Position: right mentoanterior (RMA) position.
- Expected outcome: mentoanterior positions generally deliver more frequently. Spontaneous delivery with episiotomy or outlet forceps delivery is possible. The perineum is distended by the submentovertical diameter of 11 cm.

(iii) Causes of face presentation:
- Anencephaly.
- Persistently extended head without abnormality.
- Neck tumours: thyroid tumours, cystic hygromas.
- Contracted maternal pelvis.
- Prematurity.
- Several loops of cord.
- Results from persistent occipito-posterior position.
- Associated with multiple pregnancies.
- Multiple loops of cord round the neck, musculoskeletal deformities, or neck tumours in the fetus.

(iv) Complete management:
- Exclude cord prolapse.
- Spontaneous delivery with episiotomy in mentoanterior positions.
- Outlet forceps delivery in mentoanterior positions.
- In mentoposterior position: attempt manual rotation; if unsuccessful, forceps rotation with Kielland's forceps; caesarean section.
- No vacuum extraction in face presentation.
- Monitor second stage; prolonged second stage is expected.
- Perineal tear is common; repair is required.

(v) Clinico-anatomical reasoning for why mentoposterior cannot deliver vaginally:
- In mentoposterior, the chin (mentum) is directed posteriorly towards the sacrum.
- For the face to extend and deliver, the chin must sweep under the pubic arch anteriorly; this requires a mentoanterior position.
- In mentoposterior, the submentovertical diameter (11 cm) would be impacted against the pelvic outlet, and the large diameter cannot negotiate the pelvis.
- Delivery per vaginam would require the head to flex back from full extension to pass through as a vertex, which is mechanically impossible once the face is impacted.
- Therefore, persistent mentoposterior position results in obstructed labour and must be delivered by caesarean section.
