(i) Risk factors present in this patient: BMI >27 kg/m² (BMI 32); previous delivery of a baby >4.0 kg; family history of DM in a first-degree relative; maternal age >35 years; glycosuria on 2 episodes.
Additional risk factors: previous history of unexplained stillbirth; congenital malformation in prior pregnancy; recurrent infections; polyhydramnios; previous history of recurrent abortion; previous perinatal loss; multiparity 4+; high-risk racial group (Asian-Indian, Middle-Eastern, Afro-Caribbean); obesity (>90 kg); previous history of PCOS; previous pregnancy with GDM.

(ii) Classification: (1) Pre-gestational diabetes — Type I (IDDM); Type II (NIDDM). (2) Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) — 90%; glucose level normalises after pregnancy; insulin may or may not be required; 40–60% of GDM develop Type 2 diabetes in 10–20 years.
Modified White Classification: Class A — chemical diabetes managed by diet; Class B — insulin needed, onset after 20 years; Class C — onset 10–19 years or duration 10–19 years; Class D — onset before 10 years, duration >20 years, chronic hypertension or background retinopathy; Class F — renal disease; Class H — coronary artery disease; Class R — proliferative retinopathy; Class T — renal transplant.

(iii) Maternal complications: recurrent spontaneous abortions; infections (UTI, candidal vaginitis); pre-eclampsia; polyhydramnios; preterm labour; ketoacidosis; hyper/hypoglycaemia; thromboembolic disease; progression of nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy; coronary artery disease; increased risk of Type 2 DM later.
Fetal/neonatal complications: major congenital malformations (CVS: transposition of great vessels, PDA, coarctation of aorta; CNS: caudal regression syndrome, neural tube defects; renal: hydronephrosis; GIT: duodenal atresia); fetal macrosomia → CPD, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma; neonatal hypoglycaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, jaundice (polycythaemia); delayed fetal lung maturity → RDS/hyaline membrane disease; intrauterine death; increased perinatal mortality.

(iv) Antepartum management:
- Multidisciplinary team approach; goals: FBS 60–95 mg/dl; 2-hour post-prandial <120 mg/dl; HbA1c <6%.
- Diet: normal-weight ~30 kcal/kg/day; overweight ~24 kcal/kg/day; obese 12–15 kcal/kg/day. Breakfast 25%, lunch 30%, dinner 30%, bedtime snack 15%; carbohydrate 50%, fat 30%, protein 20%; avoid refined sugars.
- Insulin: 1st trimester 0.6 u/kg, 2nd trimester 0.7 u/kg, 3rd trimester 0.9 u/kg; 2/3 total dose in morning, 1/3 evening; morning dose 2/3 intermediate + 1/3 soluble; evening dose 1/2 intermediate + 1/2 soluble.
- Fetal monitoring: 1st trimester USS for dating; anomaly USS + fetal echocardiogram at 18–22 weeks; fetal growth assessment at 24, 28–32, 36 weeks; twice-weekly NST and BPP from 32 weeks; elective delivery between 38–40 weeks; elective CS for macrosomia; fetal lung maturity testing (amniocentesis) if delivery before 38 weeks.

A(i) Definition: anaemia is a condition of low circulating haemoglobin in which the Hb concentration has fallen below a threshold lying at two standard deviations below the median of a healthy population of the same age, sex, and stage of pregnancy (WHO 1996); in this environment, Hb 10 g/dl or less.
Morphological classification (based on RBC size and Hb content):
- Normochromic-normocytic (dilutional anaemia)
- Hypochromic microcytic (e.g. iron deficiency)
- Macrocytic (e.g. folate or Vit B12 deficiency)
- Dimorphic (multifactorial)
Kinetic classification:
1) Excessive blood loss: acute (abruptio placentae), chronic (hookworm)
2) Inadequate/decreased red cell production: nutritional (iron, folate, Vit B12, protein); bone marrow failure (aplastic); infiltration (leukaemia); miscellaneous (endocrine, renal, liver disease)
3) Increased red cell destruction: intrinsic (haemoglobinopathy—sickle cell/thalassaemia; membrane disorder—ellipsocytosis/spherocytosis; enzyme deficiency—G6PD/pyruvate kinase); extrinsic (malaria; antibody-mediated; mechanical—MAHA; chemical/physical agents; hypersplenism)
A(ii) Severity classification:
- Mild: PCV 27–29%
- Moderate: PCV 19–26%, Hb 6.1–8.9 g/dl
- Severe: PCV 12–18%, Hb 4.0–6.0 g/dl
- Very severe/critical: PCV <12%, Hb <4.0 g/dl
B(i) Anaemia is common in pregnancy because: (1) physiological anaemia—plasma volume expands 46–55% while red cell mass expands only 18–25%; (2) increased demand for nutrients; (3) lactation; (4) increased susceptibility to malaria due to altered immunity in nulliparous women; (5) decreased pregnancy interval; (6) also common in grand multiparae, teenage and multiple pregnancy.
B(ii) Hypochromic microcytic anaemia: MCV <76 fl (normal 75–96), central pallor seen in RBC; indicates iron deficiency. Normochromic-normocytic: associated with leucocytosis, toxic granulation, malaria parasite; indicates dilutional or infective cause. Macrocytic/megaloblastic: large red cells; indicates folate or Vit B12 deficiency. Dimorphic: mixed picture; indicates multifactorial aetiology.

A(i) STIs are infections transmitted principally through sexual contact with mucous membranes and/or skin surfaces; their primary route of transmission is sexual contact; caused mainly by bacteria, viruses, or protozoa; bacterial STIs are more common in developing countries. Epidemiology: worldwide distribution; more prevalent in developing countries, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Risk groups: urban residents, adolescents and young adults, young females, undergraduates and street hawkers, commercial sex workers, migrant workers, highly mobile people (long-distance truck drivers), refugees. Major sequelae — Women: cancers (cervical, vulval, vaginal, anal, liver, T-cell leukaemia, Kaposi's sarcoma); reproductive health problems (PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, spontaneous abortion); pregnancy-related problems (preterm delivery, PROM, puerperal sepsis, postpartum infection); neurological problems (neurosyphilis); other (chronic liver disease, cirrhosis). Men: penile cancer, anal cancer, liver cancer, T-cell leukaemia, Kaposi's sarcoma, epididymitis, prostatitis, infertility, neurosyphilis. Infants: stillbirth, low birth weight, pneumonia, neonatal sepsis, acute hepatitis, congenital abnormalities, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, syphilis-associated neurological problems, chronic liver disease, cirrhosis.
A(ii) Gonorrhoea: organism — Neisseria gonorrhoeae, gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Symptoms — usually asymptomatic in women (70–80%), purulent vaginal discharge, dysuria, frequency; progression to vulvovaginitis, cervicitis, PID; disseminated infection (anorectal region, joints and tendons, perihepatic, pharynx). Signs: vaginal discharge, Bartholinitis, disseminated infection (pharyngitis, monoarticular arthritis, conjunctivitis), perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). Investigations: swabs for MCS (endocervical, urethral, rectal, pharyngeal), serology (gonococcal complement fixation test). Treatment: penicillin group, cephalosporin, erythromycin. Prevention: health education, barrier contraception, contact tracing. Syphilis: organism — Treponema pallidum, spirochaete, not stainable by Gram's method. Symptoms/signs: primary — painless genital sore (chancre), painless lymphadenopathy; secondary — bilateral symmetrical squamo-papular eruptions, condyloma acuminata, lymphadenopathy; tertiary — neurosyphilis, alopecia, arthritis. Investigations: dark-field microscopy, silver staining, serological tests (VDRL, Kahn, Wassermann, Hinton, Kleine), specific tests (fluorescent treponema antibody absorption test, micro-haemagglutination assay). Treatment: penicillin group, erythromycin.
B(i) LGV: organism — Chlamydia trachomatis, serovars L1–L3, weakly gram-negative intracellular parasite. Presentation: shallow painless ulcer of vestibule and labia; painful adenopathy in inguinal and peri-rectal areas which suppurates; sinuses and fistulae; elephantiasis; stenosis of anal canal and rectum. Investigations: culture of aspirates, monoclonal antibody test, complement fixation antibody (Frei test). Treatment: tetracycline, erythromycin, sulphonamides, doxycycline, surgery (vulvectomy, manual dilatation of strictures). Chancroid: organism — Haemophilus ducreyi, gram-negative bacilli. Presentation: multiple small shallow painful vulval ulcers, localised lymphadenopathy with suppuration. Investigations: culture on specialised medium by direct inoculation. Treatment: sulfonamide group, streptomycin in resistant cases.

A(i) Normal pelvic diameters and normal presenting diameter:
- Inlet: obstetric conjugate = 10 cm; transverse = 13.6 cm.
- Midcavity: circular = 12 cm.
- Outlet: anteroposterior = 12.5 cm; transverse = 10.5 cm.
- Normal presenting diameter in vertex presentation (occipito-anterior): suboccipitobregmatic diameter = 9.5 cm.

A(ii) Pelvic types and predisposition to OPP:
- Anthropoid pelvis: favours direct OP or direct OA because the anteroposterior diameter is greater than the transverse diameter, encouraging the fetal head to engage in the AP diameter.
- Android pelvis: the transverse diameter of the brim is near the sacrum, which encourages the biparietal diameter to accommodate posteriorly, favouring ROP.
- Flat sacrum: with a poorly flexed head leads to further deflexion and OP; the flat sacrum does not provide the posterior space needed for the occiput to rotate forward.

B) Progression of OPP from engagement to delivery:
Engagement:
- Engagement occurs in the transverse or right oblique diameter of the pelvis, giving the right occipito-posterior (ROP) position.
- The presenting diameter is the occipitofrontal diameter = 11 cm (deflexed OP) or suboccipitofrontal = 10 cm (flexed OP).
Descent:
- Descent continues to the pelvic floor.
- Further progress depends on the flexion of the head.
- Labour tends to be long; contractions become more normal as labour progresses but severe backache demoralises the patient.
Outcomes at the pelvic floor:
- 70% correct to occipitoanterior positions.
- 20% remain as persistent occipitoposterior positions.
- 10% deliver face-to-pubis.
- Deep transverse arrest may occur at the level of the ischial spines.
Delivery face-to-pubis:
- The perineum is distended by the occipitofrontal diameter (11 cm).
- An extensive episiotomy is required.
- Internal rotation may be interrupted by prominent ischial spines or restricted by reduced pelvic diameters in the android pelvis.

C) Complications of OPP and anatomical basis for episiotomy:
Maternal complications:
- Prolonged first and second stages of labour.
- Increased operative interventions (forceps, vacuum, caesarean section).
- Obstructed labour; VVF/RVF (vesicovaginal and rectovaginal fistulae) in neglected cases.
- Puerperal infections.
- Episiotomy.
Fetal complications:
- Perinatal morbidity and mortality.
- Birth asphyxia.
- Sepsis.
- Birth trauma.
Anatomical basis for wide episiotomy in face-to-pubis delivery:
- In face-to-pubis delivery, the presenting diameter is the occipitofrontal diameter of 11 cm.
- This is larger than the normal suboccipitobregmatic diameter of 9.5 cm that distends the perineum in a well-flexed cephalic delivery.
- The additional 1.5 cm of distension would cause a severe spontaneous perineal tear without a deliberately wide (extensive) episiotomy.
- The episiotomy therefore prevents uncontrolled perineal damage to the sphincter and rectum.

questions.answerText:
A(i) FDA drug categories in pregnancy:
- Category A: controlled studies in women have not shown risk to the fetus in 1st trimester; possibility of fetal harm appears remote. (No fetal risk: proven safe for use during pregnancy.)
- Category B: animal studies do not indicate risk to fetus; no controlled human or animal studies show adverse effect. (Fetal risk not demonstrated in animal or human studies.)
- Category C: studies show animal teratogenic or embryocidal effects but no controlled studies in women; OR no studies available. (Fetal risk unknown; no adequate human study.)
- Category D: positive evidence of human fetal risks exist, but benefits may make use acceptable. (Some evidence of fetal risk; may be necessary not to use in pregnancy.)
- Category X: studies in animals or humans have demonstrated fetal abnormalities OR evidence of risk based on human experience; risk clearly outweighs benefit. (Definite risk; use not advisable.)
A(ii) Antacids: used for dyspepsia, constipation or diarrhoea; most contain calcium carbonate, aluminium, sodium bicarbonate, or magnesium. Buffered preparation of sodium carbonate often recommended. Moderate use presents minimal risk and enhances maternal nutrition. Frequent use of sodium bicarbonate-containing antacids (alkaline) can produce metabolic alkalosis. Reproductive toxicity of magnesium carbonate lacks evidence.
B(i) Ibuprofen: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent; limited evidence of reproductive effects; no increase in incidence of congenital abnormalities observed in infants of mothers who took ibuprofen in the first trimester; intrauterine closure of ductus arteriosus demonstrated in rodents but not in humans when used late in pregnancy.
Aspirin: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent; association between congenital malformations and aspirin use in early pregnancy; prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor effects on decreasing platelet aggregation; increased incidence of intracranial bleeding; chronic use in pregnancy may cause premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus; not recommended in the last 3 months of pregnancy.
B(ii) Principles of drug use in pregnancy: a typical pregnant woman takes one to three drugs besides vitamins despite awareness of need to avoid drugs; drugs can expose the fetus to teratogenic agents; many drugs contain both active and inactive ingredients causing confusion; the placental barrier is a contradictory term as the placenta allows several substances to cross; alternatives to drugs are preferable; the risk-benefit ratio should justify use; minimal effective dose should be employed.

A(i) Maternal death (ICD-10, WHO 1993): the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.

A(ii) Direct causes: death resulting from obstetric complications of the pregnant state, labour or puerperium; or from intervention, omission of necessary treatment, incorrect treatment, or a combination of these. Indirect causes: death resulting from previously existing disease or disease that developed during pregnancy, labour or puerperium, not due to pregnancy but aggravated by the physiological changes of pregnancy. Incidental causes: death resulting from accidental or other causes unrelated to the pregnancy.

A(iii) Late maternal death: from direct or indirect causes >42 days but <1 year after termination of pregnancy. Pregnancy-related death: death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination, irrespective of cause; introduced to facilitate identification of maternal mortality when cause of death attribution is inadequate.

B. Maternal mortality ratio: number of maternal deaths during a given year per 100,000 live births; represents obstetric risk. Maternal mortality rate: number of maternal deaths in a given period per 100,000 women of reproductive age (15–49 years); measures both obstetric risk and frequency of exposure. Lifetime risk: takes into account the probability of becoming pregnant and dying as a result, cumulated across reproductive years (MMRate × 35 years OR Total fertility rate × MMRatio). It is technically a ratio — not a rate — because the denominator (live births) is at variance with the numerator (total maternal deaths including abortions and stillbirths); the true denominator for a rate would be total pregnant women during the period.

C. Medical factors: obstetric haemorrhage; pre-eclampsia/eclampsia; obstructed labour; pregnancy-related sepsis; unsafe abortion; HIV/AIDS; anaemia; malaria; cardiac diseases; diabetes.
Socio-cultural/economic factors: low status of women; low education; low income/poverty; harmful traditional practices; cultural norms; gender disparities; poor nutrition in childhood, adolescence, and adulthood; ignorance and illiteracy; religious beliefs acting as barriers.
Three Delays: Type I — delay to seek health care (decision rests with husband; cultural/religious beliefs; lack of formal education; ignorance). Type II — delay to access the facility (lack of adequate transport; no effective referral system; inadequate health care facilities; poor siting). Type III — delay in receiving care at the facility (lack of access to essential obstetric care; health care providers' attitude).

(i) Signs present: Robert's Sign (gas in large fetal veins) and Spalding's Sign (overlapping skull bones). The fixed fetal position on serial films constitutes an abnormal fetal attitude. Diagnosis: intrauterine fetal death (IUFD).

(ii) Plain X-ray signs of fetal death:
- Robert's Sign: presence of gas in the big veins of the fetus; following fetal death, autolysis of protein releases gas.
- Spalding's Sign: third-degree moulding leads to fetal death; skull bones are compressed and seen overriding each other.
- Abnormal attitude/altitude: alteration of fetal position in relation to the mother; in the intrauterine fetus the spine is normally parallel to the maternal spine.
- Lithopaedion: a fetus that has died and calcified; can be intrauterine or extrauterine (usually extrauterine — "womb stone").

(iii) Other fetal abnormalities detectable by plain X-ray: hydrocephalus/microcephaly; spina bifida; achondroplasia; anencephaly; multiple pregnancy; conjoined twins (babies lie the same way when serially filmed); osteogenesis imperfecta (fractures, especially in malpresentation during labour); Bhuddha's sign in Rhesus incompatibility (oedematous thighs kept apart).

(iv) Radiologic dating of pregnancy: positive when fetus is at least 16 weeks (bones first appear). At 32 weeks, jet lines visible in limbs. Ossification centre in lower epiphysis of femur apparent → at least 36 weeks. Ossification in upper limbs → at least 38 weeks. Ossification of calcaneus → at least 40 weeks. Note: radiologic dating is no longer appropriate as the primary method.

(v) Major advantage: permanent record for medico-legal reasons — e.g., HSG showing hydrosalpinges in infertility; tubal blockage co-existing with uterine fibroid.

A(i) Physiological changes in blood during pregnancy:
- Plasma volume expands by 46–55%
- Red cell mass expands by only 18–25%
- This produces physiological (dilutional) anaemia of pregnancy, as the plasma expansion exceeds red cell expansion
A(ii) Additional iron demands during pregnancy:
- Fetus/placenta (x2 in multiple pregnancy): ~500 mg iron
- Red cell increment: ~500 mg
- Postpartum loss: ~180 mg
- Lactation for 6 months: ~180 mg
- Total: ~1,360 mg
- Savings (amenorrhoea): ~350 mg
- Actual extra demand: ~1,000 mg
B(i) Iron metabolism in non-pregnancy: approximately 10% of dietary iron is usually absorbed in the upper small intestine; balances daily loss of iron from skin and intestine; barely compensates for monthly menstrual loss. In iron deficiency, serum iron is decreased and iron binding protein is increased; as much as 20% of ingested iron may be absorbed.
What determines anaemia: the state of iron stores determines whether a pregnant woman becomes anaemic; the smaller her stores, the earlier the anaemia; without treatment the more severe by term; IDA at the start of pregnancy indicates empty iron stores; inadequate storage may reflect dietary lack, excessive menorrhagia, chronic intestinal bleeding (haemorrhoids, hookworm), insufficient interval between pregnancies, or poor utilization of iron by marrow.
B(ii) Follow-up after treatment: following pregnancy and correction of Hb deficit, serum iron and iron binding values return to normal; the small intestine's capacity for iron absorption is again reduced to about 10%; it may take 2 years to fill up iron stores from a good diet with oral iron supplements. Also important to control menorrhagia and treat chronic intestinal blood loss, haemorrhoids or hookworm infestation.
questions.question:

A(ii) State the additional iron demands placed on the body during pregnancy, specifying the amounts for the fetus, placenta (in multiple pregnancy), red cell increment, postpartum loss, and lactation, and the total extra demand after savings.
B(i) Describe iron metabolism in non-pregnancy, including absorption site, the proportion absorbed normally, and what determines whether a pregnant woman becomes anaemic.
B(ii) Explain the follow-up required after treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy, and what it may take to fully replenish iron stores.

A(i) Describe the components of maternity care and define each component.
A(ii) List the objectives of pre-conception care.
B(i) Describe the elements of pre-conception care, the evidence of its benefit, and its advantages.
B(ii) List the indications for mandatory referral for pre-conception care.
B(iii) State the obstacles to pre-conception care.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Components of maternity care:
1. Pre-conception care: specialised form of care for women of reproductive age before the onset of pregnancy, to detect, treat or counsel them about pre-existing medical and social conditions that may militate against safe motherhood and delivery of a healthy offspring.
2. Antenatal care: totality of care for the pregnant woman from conception till delivery; prevention of complications; early detection and prompt treatment; comprehensive health education; reduction of maternal/perinatal morbidity and mortality.
3. Intrapartum care: care during labour and delivery.
4. Postnatal care: care up to 6 weeks after delivery.
A(ii) Objectives of pre-conception care:
- Avoidance of maternal exposure to teratogens during fetal organogenesis
- Checking basic measurements (weight/BP) before pregnancy begins
- Introduction of intending mothers to social and medical interventions at a time when they can have maximal effect on the outcome of pregnancy
B(i) Elements: comprehensive health history (past medical, past obstetric, drug, social history); thorough physical examination; ancillary screening tests; health promotion/intervention.
Evidence of benefit: diabetes mellitus, coagulation disorders, drug abuse.
Advantages: improved pregnancy outcome (improved maternal health, significant reduction in neonatal morbidity/mortality); cost-effectiveness; opportunity for counselling/health promotion.
B(ii) Indications for mandatory referral: pre-existing medical conditions (cardiac disease, systemic hypertension, haematologic disorders, auto-immune diseases, neurological disorders, endocrinopathies, chronic pulmonary disease); advanced maternal age; adverse social history; adverse family history; poor obstetric history.
B(iii) Obstacles: lack of information; poor attitude by womenfolk; high rates of unplanned pregnancies; low level of acceptance by health care providers.

(i) Diagnosis: gastroschisis (para-umbilical defect with no overlying membrane). Exomphalos is a central defect surrounded by a membrane on which the umbilical cord is inserted—this distinguishes it from gastroschisis.
(ii) Soft markers for chromosomal abnormality:
- Nuchal oedema/translucency
- Mild renal pyelectasis
- Hyperechogenic bowel
- Echogenic intracardial foci
- Strawberry-shaped skull
- Mild ventriculomegaly
- Shortened long bones
- Choroid plexus cysts
- Clenched fists
- Rocker bottom feet
- Sandal gap
(iii) Structural malformations associated with chromosomal disease:
- Cystic hygroma
- Cardiac defects
- Exomphalos
- Holoprosencephaly
- Microcephaly
- Diaphragmatic hernia
- Oesophageal/duodenal atresia
- Renal anomalies
- Radial aplasia
- Micrognathia
- Clinodactyly of the fifth finger
- Polydactyly
(iv) Skeletal malformations identifiable prenatally: achondrogenesis; thanatophoric dysplasia; short rib polydactyly syndrome; fibrochondroplasia; homozygous achondroplasia; osteogenesis imperfecta (perinatal type); hypophosphatasia (perinatal type).
(v) potential hazards of ultrasound: childhood cancer; non-right-handedness; delayed speech development; reduced birth weight. However, there is no substantial evidence to prove the above effects.
questions.question:

A(i) Describe the puerperium under the following headings: definition, divisions, and the normal anatomic and physiologic changes that occur in the uterus, cervix, vagina, ovaries, and breasts during this period.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis for lochia, including its changing character from delivery to six weeks, and state when its persistence beyond the normal period becomes clinically significant.
B(i) Distinguish between primary and secondary postpartum haemorrhage in terms of definition, timing, and the principal causes of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Puerperium: the period of approximately 6 weeks (42 days) beginning from delivery of the placenta until the reproductive tract returns to the normal non-pregnant state. Divisions: immediate puerperium (first 24 hours), early puerperium (2nd to 7th day), late puerperium (2nd week to 6th week). Uterus: weighs 1 kg at term; recedes to 50–100 g in 6 weeks; palpable at umbilicus immediately after delivery; non-palpable in the pelvis within 2 weeks; endometrial glands present within 7 days. Cervix: reverts to near pre-pregnancy state but never returns to nulliparous state; os closes within the first week. Vagina: regression occurs; rugae reappear in non-breastfeeding women within 3 weeks; smear is atrophic in breastfeeding mothers. Ovaries: ovulation may return in 27 days in non-breastfeeding women; mean ovulation time 70–75 days (non-lactating) and 190 days (breastfeeding). Breasts: lactogenesis follows placental delivery; prolactin continues; in non-breastfeeding women, prolactin drops in 2–3 weeks.
A(ii) Lochia: the discharge from the genital tract during the puerperium. Days 1–3: red (lochia rubra) — blood and decidual debris. Becomes pink (lochia serosa) — mainly white blood cells, decidual debris, and some red cells. By end of first week: yellowish white (lochia alba) — serous fluid and white blood cells. Average duration is 5 weeks; 15% of women continue lochia after 6 weeks. An increase in bleeding 7–14 days after delivery may be due to sloughing of the eschar at the placental site.
B(i) Primary PPH: blood loss from the genital tract in excess of 500 ml within the first 24 hours after delivery of the baby. Causes: uterine atony, retained products, lacerations, exposure to MgSO4, uterine rupture, uterine inversion, placenta accreta, coagulopathy, haematoma. Secondary PPH: excessive bleeding from the genital tract after 24 hours postpartum and until 6 weeks after birth. Causes: infection, sub-involution of the placental site, retained products of conception, coagulopathy.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the gynaecology clinic with painful vesicles and shallow painful ulcers on the vulva, and difficulty walking. She reports a similar but milder episode 6 months ago that resolved. She also has autonomic symptoms including urinary retention.
(i) State the diagnosis, identify the causative virus and which type causes genital herpes, and list all symptoms and signs.
(ii) Describe the investigations used to confirm the diagnosis and the treatment available.
(iii) Describe non-specific infection/non-gonococcal urethritis: symptoms and signs, investigations, and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Genital herpes simplex infection. Most genital herpes infections are caused by Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2); oral infections are caused by HSV-1. Symptoms and signs: painful vesicles, painful ulcers, herpes pharyngitis (from oral sex), autonomic nervous dysfunction (urinary retention), recurrent infection.
(ii) Investigations: viral culture, indirect immuno-peroxidase test, direct immuno-fluorescent test. Treatment: analgesics, Sitz bath, acyclovir.
(iii) Non-specific infection / non-gonococcal urethritis: symptoms and signs — mucopurulent cervicitis, salpingitis, urethral syndrome, non-gonococcal urethritis in the male. Investigations: tissue culture, serology (ELISA, polymerase chain reaction, direct fluorescent antibody test). Treatment: tetracycline, doxycycline, erythromycin, ofloxacin, and other fluoroquinolones.

(i) Rhesus iso-immunisation (Rh-D sensitisation) in pregnancy. The previous spontaneous abortion at 8 weeks was a significant sensitising event: spontaneous fetomaternal transfusion occurs in 6.7% of women in the 1st trimester, and an abortion (especially following D&C or MVA) is a recognised cause of fetomaternal haemorrhage. She should have received anti-D 50 mcg (before 20 weeks) at that time; failure to administer anti-D is a common reason for the continued occurrence of Rh iso-immunisation.
(ii) At the time of the abortion, fetal Rh-positive red cells entered the maternal circulation. The initial maternal immune response produced IgM antibodies that do not cross the placenta. Subsequently, IgG antibodies were produced between 6 weeks and 6 months later. IgG anti-D antibodies cross the placenta and coat fetal Rh-positive red blood cells, which are then destroyed by the fetal reticuloendothelial system.
(iii) Antibodies, once detected, must be measured at least monthly. Serum antibody protein levels are of greater predictive value than antibody titres. A rapid increase suggests acute haemolysis is occurring in the fetus, and amniotic fluid analysis is necessary. Amniocentesis determines the amount of bilirubin in the liquor; spectrophotometry at OD 450 nm shows a peak directly proportional to the quantity of bilirubin. The first amniocentesis should be 10 weeks before the earliest previous intrauterine death or affected delivery, but not before 20 weeks gestation.
(iv) Severe fetal haemolysis leads to: miscarriage; intrauterine death; birth of a severely hydropic infant with attendant obstetric complications. In the newborn: anaemia; hyperbilirubinaemia; kernicterus (bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia due to rapid rise in unconjugated bilirubin after birth, damaging the brain especially the basal ganglia). Excess bilirubin in the fetus is removed by the placenta; amniotic fluid contains bilirubin.
(v) Treatment plan: monitor antibody levels at least monthly; perform amniocentesis to assess amniotic fluid bilirubin; if severe disease is confirmed and the fetus is not mature enough for delivery, perform intrauterine transfusion with O Rh-negative, CMV-negative donor blood cross-matched with maternal blood, either intraperitoneally or directly via fetal vein (e.g., umbilical cord). A haematocrit at or before 26 weeks warrants transfusion. If the baby is mature, delivery is the treatment of choice. After birth, treatment may include transfusion, exchange transfusion, and phototherapy depending on the degree of anaemia and jaundice.
questions.question:
A 20-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks gestation is found to have no Rhesus D antigen on her red blood cells. She has no history of blood transfusion. Her husband is Rh-positive. She had a spontaneous abortion at 8 weeks 6 months ago, for which she was not given any treatment. Her indirect Coombs test is now positive with an anti-D titre of 1:32.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Low birth weight is when a baby is born weighing less than 2500 g (birth weight measured within one hour of birth), irrespective of gestational age. Normal weight at term is 2500–4000 g. WHO categorisation: LBW <2500 g; VLBW (Very Low Birth Weight) <1500 g; ELBW (Extremely Low Birth Weight) <1000 g. WHO further defines prematurity as delivery at less than 37 completed weeks (259 days).

A(ii) Classification by birth weight relative to gestational age: SGA (Small for Gestational Age / IUGR) — birth weight below 10th percentile for gestational age; AGA (Appropriate for Gestational Age); LGA (Large for Gestational Age). Note: 70% of fetuses with EFW ≤10th percentile are constitutionally small (non-pathological). Non-pathological influences: maternal height, paternal height, parity, ethnicity, fetal sex.

A(iii) Symmetrical IUGR (global restriction): early onset of retardation; normal HC/AC ratio; small brains with permanent neurological sequelae; caused by genetic/chromosomal abnormalities, infection (TORCH), anaemia, maternal substance abuse.
Asymmetrical IUGR: commoner (~70%); onset usually late in pregnancy; restriction of weight followed by length; brain weight only slightly decreased (brain sparing) but lack of subcutaneous fat; increased HC/AC ratio; liver affected — loss of glycogen; caused by pre-eclampsia/eclampsia (major cause), chronic hypertension, severe malnutrition, genetic mutations.

B. Pathophysiology → neonatal complications: Decreased body fat, glycogen, and free fatty acids → hypoglycaemia; decreased total protein and DNA/RNA → impaired organ development; altered body proportions and predisposition to oligohydramnios → reduced pulmonary/renal blood flow → hypoxia/acidosis; high body surface area-to-weight ratio, low brown fat, non-keratinised skin, low glycogen supply → hypothermia (conduction, convection, evaporation, radiation); fluid and electrolyte imbalance (ECF>ICF); apnoea; metabolic acidosis; polycythaemia; meconium aspiration syndrome; neonatal hypocalcaemia.

C. Long-term complications from IUGR: lower IQ; learning and behavioural problems; seizure disorder; cerebral palsy; mental retardation; hypertension and heart disease; obesity; Type II diabetes. LBW is also implicated in adulthood associations with CVD, chronic renal disease, obstructive lung disease, and high cholesterol concentrations.
questions.question:

A(i) Definition, and WHO categorisation with weight thresholds
A(ii) Classification of newborn by birth weight relative to gestational age

B. Explain how pathophysiology of IUGR leads to the immediate neonatal complications seen in these infants.

questions.answerText:
(i) Obstructed labour (in a multigravida). In a multigravida, the abdomen shows the three-tumour sign: (a) oedematous, enlarged bladder (rising out of the pelvis due to urethral compression); (b) distended tender lower uterine segment (elongated and thinned as emptying is prevented); (c) Bandl's ring with a tonically contracted upper uterine segment. The vaginal examination may already show a fully dilated cervix (unlike the primigravida who has a poorly dilated cervix). The multigravida's uterus is at greater risk of rupture than the primigravida's because, in the primigravida, uterine contractions eventually cease (continuous spasm); in the multigravida, the uterus proceeds to rupture.
(ii) Maternal complications: sepsis (septicaemia, osteitis pubis), haemorrhage, obstetric neuropraxia, ruptured uterus, genital tract injuries, vaginal fistulae (vesicovaginal, rectovaginal), secondary amenorrhoea (Sheehan's syndrome), psychological shock. Fetal complications: sepsis, injury, death.
(iii) Investigations: PCV, electrolytes and urea, grouping and crossmatching, urinalysis (protein, sugar, acetone), blood, amniotic fluid, and urine MCS; emergency ultrasound or radiological examination. Resuscitation: intravenous fluids (Hartmann's or Ringer's lactate), parenteral antibiotics, passage of nasogastric tube with instillation of 30 ml magnesium trisilicate, analgesics if indicated, close monitoring of vital signs, fluid input/output, and level of consciousness.
(iv) Prevention at population level: improvement in socioeconomic circumstances (good food, breastfeeding, adequate shelter, good communication network, efficient transportation, education); improvement in health care delivery (early recognition, prompt treatment of childhood and other diseases). Prevention at individual patient level: adequate antenatal care; selection of high-risk patients (short stature, abnormal fetus, pelvic abnormality); prompt referral; adequate intrapartum monitoring; early diagnosis and rapid management of difficult labours.
questions.question:

Abdominal examination reveals a three-tumour abdomen: an oedematous, enlarged bladder, a distended tender lower uterine segment, and a Bandl's ring with a tonically contracted upper uterine segment. Vaginal examination shows a fully dilated cervix.

questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors present in this patient:
- Age greater than 35 years.
- Early marriage (implied by high parity).
- Ignorance and illiteracy (no formal education).
- Poverty and low socioeconomic status.
- Multiple cohorts.
- Socio-cultural practices.
- Religious beliefs that discourage use of contraceptives.
- Poor contraceptive usage.
- Inadequate antenatal supervision.

(ii) Antepartum maternal complications:
- Increased predisposition to hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
- Anaemia (poor nutrition, depletion of haemopoietic stores, inadequate spacing of pregnancies).
- Abnormal lie and malpresentations (lax/pendulous abdomen).
- Antepartum haemorrhage: abruptio placentae and placenta praevia.
- Premature rupture of fetal membranes (PROM).
Intrapartum maternal complications:
- Precipitate labour or premature labour.
- Abnormal lie and malpresentations.
- Abruptio placentae.
- Cord prolapse.
- Fetopelvic disproportion and CPD.
- Obstructed labour.
- Dysfunctional labour, uterine inertia, failure to progress, prolonged labour.
- Higher operative interventions.
- Ruptured uterus.
Postpartum maternal complications:
- Postpartum haemorrhage (uterine atony, cervical lacerations).
- Soft tissue trauma and haemorrhage; anaemia.
- Higher maternal morbidity and mortality.
- Utero-vaginal prolapse.

(iii) Fetal complications:
Antepartum: increased pregnancy loss and abortions; congenital abnormalities including genetic dislocations and mutations; Down's syndrome; multiple pregnancy; macrosomia.
Intrapartum: prematurity; birth asphyxia; birth injuries; higher perinatal morbidity and mortality.

(iv) Intrapartum management:
- Group and crossmatch blood.
- Establish intravenous access line.
- Use oxytocin carefully.
- Administer IV ergometrine or oxytocin at the delivery of the anterior shoulder.
- Paediatrician should be present at delivery.
Justification: IV ergometrine or oxytocin at delivery of the anterior shoulder is the single most important measure because grandmultiparae are at high risk of uterine atony due to replacement of uterine muscle by fibrosis; administering a uterotonic at the moment of the anterior shoulder's delivery initiates uterine contraction before placental separation, directly preventing postpartum haemorrhage from atony.
questions.question:
A 39-year-old woman presents in the antenatal clinic for booking. A. Define perinatal death under the following headings:
A(i) Classical definition and current WHO definition
A(ii) The continuum of fetal and neonatal mortality (stillbirth, early neonatal death, late neonatal death)
A(iii) Perinatal mortality rates in Nigeria

B. State the causes of perinatal deaths (stillbirths and neonatal deaths).

C. Describe the intervention strategies for reducing maternal and perinatal mortality, including Basic and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric Care (EOC), the Three Delays solutions, and Child Survival Strategies.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classical definition: death of a fetus in-utero after the 28th week of gestation OR death of a neonate within 7 days of birth. Current definition: death of a fetus in-utero after the 24th week of gestation OR death of a neonate within 7 days of birth. Some include all neonatal deaths (up to 28th day after birth). In the USA, all fetal deaths from the 20th week of gestation are included.

A(ii) Continuum: Early fetal (0–20/24 weeks); Intermediate fetal (24–28 weeks); Late fetal/stillbirth (28–40 weeks); Early neonatal death (0–7 days after birth); Late neonatal death (7–28 days); WHO definition uses 24-week lower limit; developing country definition uses 28 weeks; US uses 20 weeks.

A(iii) Nigeria perinatal and infant survival: perinatal mortality 100–141/1000 births; child mortality 201/1000 live births; infant mortality rate 71/1000; under-5 mortality rate 140/1000; neonatal mortality rate 35/1000; Nigeria is one of 10 countries with worst child survival; ranks 16th out of 29 sub-Saharan African countries with poor child survival at similar economic development levels.

B. Causes of perinatal deaths: Stillbirths — placental insufficiency (IUGR, hypertensive disorders); infection; congenital malformations; abruptio placentae; placenta praevia. Neonatal deaths — prematurity/LBW (LBW implicated in 50% of all neonatal deaths; accounts for 33% of all deaths of children under 5 years); birth asphyxia; infection/sepsis; congenital malformations; RDS.

C. Intervention strategies:
Basic EOC: parenteral antibiotics; parenteral oxytocic drugs; parenteral sedatives for eclampsia; manual removal of placenta; manual removal of retained products; assisted vaginal delivery.
Comprehensive EOC: above plus blood transfusion services; surgical intervention; anaesthetic facility.
Making Pregnancy Safer (MPS): capacity building; provision of adequate equipment; efficient referral system; partnership and advocacy; resource allocation.
Three Delays solutions: Type 1 — girl-child education; restoring women's decision-making power; awareness of warning signs; birth preparedness. Type 2 — good road network; efficient communication network; community transportation. Type 3 — capacity building for care providers (IPC, LSS); provision of EOC and BOC; infrastructural development; health system financing.
Child Survival Strategies: national immunisation programme; control of diarrhoeal diseases; control of acute respiratory infections; IMCI; breastfeeding and complementary feeding; Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative; growth monitoring.

(i) This patient is classified as high risk: she is a teenage pregnant woman (under 18 years). Contributing factors include: social embarrassment leading to concealment; absence of or inadequate ANC due to late registration, poor attendance and poor compliance; being likely to be single with poor family/partner support; increased incidence of anaemia; increased incidence of pre-eclampsia.
(ii) Complications of teenage pregnancy:
- Complications of unsafe abortion
- Increased incidence of anaemia
- Increased incidence of pre-eclampsia
- Increased risk of premature labour
- Complications in the puerperium: anaemia, inadequate care for baby
- Increased neonatal morbidity
- Increased neonatal mortality
(iii) Complications during labour:
- Cephalo-pelvic disproportion (CPD)
- Vesico-vaginal fistulae (VVF) / recto-vaginal fistula
- Pre-labour rupture of fetal membranes
- Primary postpartum haemorrhage
- Increased operative deliveries
- Perinatal death, sepsis, maternal death
(iv) Management: intensive antenatal care with close monitoring; treatment of anaemia and hypertension; referral to tertiary level care given high-risk status; in presence of CPD or other complications, deliver by caesarean section; multidisciplinary approach required; antimalaria, iron and folic acid supplementation; counselling regarding contraception after delivery to prevent short pregnancy intervals.
questions.question:
A 16-year-old unmarried girl presents at 28 weeks gestation having concealed her pregnancy. She has had no antenatal care. She has increased incidence of anaemia and raised blood pressure on examination.
(i) What is the obstetric risk category of this patient and what are the factors that contribute to her risk?
(ii) List all the complications of teenage pregnancy.
(iii) What complications are specifically associated with teenage pregnancy during labour?

questions.answerText:
(i) Structures felt: the pulsating structure is the prolapsed umbilical cord; the presenting foot indicates an incomplete (footling) breech presentation, in which one hip is extended with the foot presenting.
Types of breech:
- Frank breech: both hips flexed, both knees extended (commonest).
- Complete breech: both hips flexed, one or both knees flexed.
- Incomplete (footling): either hip extended with foot or knee presenting. This is the type in this patient.

(ii) Why cord prolapse is more common in breech:
- The breech is an ill-fitting presenting part; it does not completely fill the lower uterine segment or the pelvic brim.
- This leaves space around the presenting part through which the cord can prolapse when the membranes rupture.
- Prematurity (common with breech) further reduces fetal size relative to the pelvis, increasing the risk of cord prolapse.
- Footling breech in particular leaves the largest gap, as neither buttocks nor thighs fully occupy the lower segment.

(iii) Management:
- Immediate: relieve cord compression by elevating the presenting foot to reduce pressure on the cord; call for senior help and anaesthesia.
- Monitor fetal heart continuously.
- Position the mother to reduce cord compression (knee-chest or left lateral).
- If cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent: proceed with vaginal breech delivery.
- Caesarean section if cervix is not fully dilated (prolapsed cord without full dilatation).

(iv) Maternal complications of breech delivery:
- Risks of prolonged labour.
- Risks of anaesthesia and operative deliveries.
- Uterine rupture.
- Genital tract lacerations.
Fetal complications:
- Cord presentation and prolapse.
- Fractures.
- Damage to nerves.
- Rupture of abdominal viscera.
Baby complications:
- Birth asphyxia.
- Birth injuries.

(v) Essential steps for vaginal breech delivery in order:
- Adequate monitoring of the first stage to ensure normal progress.
- Delivery must be by an experienced obstetrician with paediatrician and anaesthetist present.
- Allow spontaneous delivery to the level of the umbilicus.
- Delivery of fetal legs: Pinard's manoeuvre.
- Rotation of trunk so sacrum is anterior.
- Gentle traction on bony pelvis until scapulae show.
- Delivery of arms: Løvset's manoeuvre.
- Careful manipulation of head and shoulders: Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit manoeuvre or Piper forceps.
- Breech extraction and internal podalic version as indicated.
questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation presents in the labour ward with spontaneous rupture of membranes and sudden onset of variable decelerations on the cardiotocograph. On vaginal examination the midwife feels a pulsating structure alongside what appears to be a presenting foot.

(i) Identify the structures felt on vaginal examination, and state the complete types of breech and the specific type in this patient.
(ii) Explain why cord prolapse is more common in breech presentation, using the relevant obstetric and anatomical reasoning.
(iii) Outline the full management of this patient, distinguishing the steps before and during delivery.
(iv) List all the maternal and fetal complications of breech delivery.

A 28-year-old woman at 36 weeks gestation is brought to the labour ward with sudden onset of abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. The uterus is hard and tender. She is in shock. Following delivery, she is noted to have continued oozing from the IV puncture site, from the episiotomy wound, and from the vagina.

(i) What complication has developed, and what is its definition?
(ii) List all the obstetric causes of this complication.
(iii) State the investigations recommended, and the expected abnormal results in each.
(iv) Describe the full treatment of this complication, including specific fluid and blood product replacements and the conditions under which heparin may be used.
questions.answerText:
(i) Complication: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC).
Definition: systemic (intravascular) activation of both intrinsic and extrinsic clotting cascades with consumption of clotting factors and platelets.

(ii) Obstetric causes:
- Abruptio placentae.
- Septic abortion.
- Eclampsia and preeclampsia.
- Retention of dead fetus (more than three weeks).
- Amniotic fluid embolism.
- Chorioamnionitis.
- Sickle cell disease (pseudotoxaemia of pregnancy).
- Prolonged and profound shock.
- Iatrogenic heparinisation.
- Gram-negative septicaemia.

(iii) Investigations and expected abnormal results:
- Clotting time: prolonged.
- Prothrombin time (PT): prolonged.
- Partial thromboplastin time with kaolin (PTTK): prolonged.
- Blood film: torn (fragmented) red blood cells.
- Platelet count: reduced.
- Fibrinogen: reduced.
- Fibrinogen degradation products (FDPs): elevated.
Differential diagnosis: massive haemorrhage.

(iv) Full treatment:
- Treat the underlying cause: antibiotics for infection; deliver the fetus if a dead fetus is retained.
- Treat hypovolaemia and haemostatic disorder:
 - Insert large cannulae in big veins including cutdowns.
 - Fluids: crystalloids (normal saline, Hartmann's solution); colloids (albumin, fresh frozen plasma – 1 pint for every 4 to 6 pints of blood transfused); clotting factor replacement (FFP, platelets, and cryoprecipitate).
- Heparin: may be indicated only when the uterus is empty and well contracted.
- Deliver through the most rapid and safest method: amniotomy and oxytocin drip, or caesarean section (though bleeding may be troublesome).
- In cases of haemophilia A and B (sex-linked; factors VIII and IX), and von Willebrand's disease (autosomal dominant; factor VIII): replacement therapy and antenatal diagnosis; consider genetic counselling and identification before pregnancy.

A(i) Drug, formulations, and doses:
- Drug: bupivacaine.
- Formulations: bupivacaine 0.5% plain solution; bupivacaine 0.5% hyperbaric solution (in 8% glucose, with different spread characteristics). Majority of anaesthetists prefer hyperbaric solution for caesarean section.
- Dose for caesarean section: 12.5 mg (compared to at least 100 mg of bupivacaine required for extradural block).

A(ii) Onset of action and mechanism of PDPH:
- Onset: subarachnoid block achieves onset of action in approximately 10 minutes; extradural block takes approximately 45 minutes.
- Mechanism of PDPH: the large-bore extradural needle (16–18 G) makes a hole in the dura through which CSF leaks; this reduces intrathecal pressure.
- The headache is low-pressure spinal headache: usually occipital, throbbing, more severe when standing or sitting, relieved by lying down.
- 75% of dural punctures from extradural needles (16–18 G) are followed by severe headache.
- Incidence of PDPH with pencil-point needles: less than 2%, and headache is usually mild.

A(iii) Subarachnoid opioids:
- Morphine: 0.3 mg; associated with delayed-onset respiratory depression; side effects include nausea and itching.
- Fentanyl: 10 µg (0.2 ml); very effective; rare risk of delayed-onset respiratory depression; side effects include nausea and itching.

B) Minimising PDPH:
- Use fine-gauge spinal needles (e.g. 25 G or smaller).
- Pencil-point needles reduce PDPH because they part the longitudinal fibres of the dura and ligamentum flavum without cutting them, producing a small hole that closes more readily when the needle is removed.
- Enforced bed rest is not desirable, effective, or necessary after subarachnoid block.

C) Advantages and disadvantages of subarachnoid vs extradural block:
Advantages of subarachnoid over extradural:
- Faster onset: 10 minutes vs 45 minutes.
- Less bupivacaine required: 12.5 mg vs at least 100 mg.
- Simpler technique with a positive endpoint (detection of CSF).
- Patient discomfort is less.
Disadvantages of subarachnoid over extradural:
- Hypotension is common: approximately 40%; may be severe and rapid in onset requiring rapid and energetic treatment.
- Top-up not possible (single-shot technique).
Management of hypotension with subarachnoid block:
- Infuse at least 500 ml crystalloid immediately before the block.
- Ephedrine infusion is effective in maintaining maternal arterial pressure.

questions.answerText:
(i) Primary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH): blood loss from the genital tract in excess of 500 ml within the first 24 hours after delivery of the baby (WHO 1990). Major PPH: blood loss in excess of 1,000 ml. Causes of primary PPH: uterine atony (the cause in this case), retained products of conception, lacerations, exposure to magnesium sulphate, uterine rupture, uterine inversion, placenta accreta, coagulopathy, haematoma.
(ii) Resuscitation: proper resuscitation with IV fluids; arrangement for blood and blood products. DIC threshold: blood loss of 2–3 litres can lead to DIC; the patient will require coagulation factors.
(iii) Sheehan's syndrome: severe blood loss leading to hypoperfusion of the pituitary gland; results in anterior pituitary necrosis and secondary amenorrhoea. This is a complication of severe PPH. Uterine inversion: occurs in 1:2,500 deliveries. Risk factors: fundal implantation of the placenta, uterine atony, placenta accreta, excessive traction on the cord during the third stage of labour. Diagnosis: fundus attached to the placenta on delivery; bleeding may or may not follow; can lead to vasovagal shock; if there is bleeding it is a serious emergency. Management: stabilise the patient, give a uterine relaxant (e.g., nitroglycerine) before attempting to replace the uterus; if this fails, laparotomy is mandatory.
(iv) Secondary PPH: excessive bleeding from the genital tract after 24 hours postpartum and until 6 weeks after birth (WHO 1990). Common causes: retained placental fragments or blood clots (usually within a few days of delivery), infection (often later), sub-involution of the placental site, retained products of conception, coagulopathy. Diagnosis and management: if bleeding is slight and there is no evidence of infection, keep under observation. Careful evacuation of the uterus under general anaesthesia is indicated if: USS suggests retained products, heavy bleeding persists, or the uterus is larger than expected and tender with an open cervix. Infection treated appropriately.
questions.question:
Following delivery of a 4.2 kg baby to a grand multipara, the midwife notes heavy, continuous bleeding per vaginam. The uterus is palpably soft and poorly contracted. The estimated blood loss is 900 ml and rising. The patient appears pale and tachycardic.
(i) State the diagnosis, define it, and list all the causes of primary postpartum haemorrhage.
(ii) Describe the immediate resuscitation required and state the blood loss threshold above which DIC is likely to occur.
(iii) Describe the complications of PPH, specifically Sheehan's syndrome, and outline the management of uterine inversion if it occurs as a cause of PPH.
(iv) Describe the causes, diagnosis, and management of secondary PPH, and state the difference between primary and secondary PPH in terms of timing.

(i) Three Delays present:
- Type I Delay (decision to seek care): 2 hours spent negotiating with husband; decision to seek health care rested with the husband; cultural/religious beliefs; ignorance about danger signs during labour.
- Type II Delay (access to facility): no ambulances; hospital 50 km away; lack of adequate transport; no effective referral system; poor siting of health care facilities.
- Type III Delay (receiving care at facility): though not explicitly stated, receiving appropriate emergency obstetric care rapidly at the facility is the final barrier (lack of access to essential obstetric care; health care providers' attitude).

(ii) Reproductive health risk factors for maternal death: too young (<18 years — this is a primigravida likely young); primigravida; too old (>35 years); grand multipara; inadequate birth spacing (<2 years); high unmet need for contraception., teenage mothers account for ~1 million births in Nigeria annually with 7 times the MMR of adult mothers.

(iii) Burden of Motherhood: estimated 585,000 women die each year from pregnancy-related causes; equivalent to a fully loaded jumbo jet (250 women) crashing every 4 hours; 99% occurring in developing countries; one maternal death every 90 minutes in developed countries; one maternal death every minute in developing countries. For every woman who dies, 30–50 women suffer injury, infection, or disease; almost 8 million survivors suffer serious morbidity.
Nigeria experience: 54,000 maternal deaths annually (10% of world figure though Nigeria is ~2% of world population); 1,080,000–1,620,000 morbidity annually; higher in northern Nigeria; MMR 1,000–1,500/100,000 live births; 545/100,000 (2008 DHS); varies by state (Borno 727, Enugu 783, Plateau 846, Cross Rivers 2,977, Lagos 3,380, Kano 7,523 per 100,000).

(iv) Basic EOC: parenteral antibiotics; parenteral oxytocic drugs; parenteral sedatives for eclampsia; manual removal of placenta; manual removal of retained products; assisted vaginal delivery. Comprehensive EOC (additional to above): blood transfusion services; surgical intervention (e.g., laparotomy, hysterectomy); anaesthetic facility. Making Pregnancy Safer also requires efficient referral system and provision of adequate equipment.
questions.question:
A 22-year-old primigravida delivers in a village setting attended by a traditional birth attendant. She delivers a live baby but sustains massive postpartum haemorrhage and collapses. Her family spends 2 hours negotiating with the husband before he agrees to take her to hospital. There are no ambulances and the nearest hospital is 50 km away. On arrival she is found to be deeply shocked and moribund.

(i) Using the Three Delays Model, identify each type of delay that occurred in this scenario.
(ii) What are the reproductive health risk factors that would have predisposed this patient to a higher risk of maternal death?
(iii) What is the Burden of Motherhood — global statistics and the Nigerian experience?
(iv) What are the components of Basic and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric Care that could have saved this patient?

(i) Diagnosis: Rheumatic heart disease with mitral incompetence (loud blowing pansystolic murmur conducted to the axilla, maximal at apex) and atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular pulse). NYHA Grade III — marked limitation of activity; dyspnoea on minimal activity. Displaced apex beat indicates cardiomegaly.

(ii) Factors promoting cardiac failure: anaemia; respiratory tract infection; pre-eclampsia; tachycardia/arrhythmia (including atrial fibrillation); recurrence of rheumatic fever (administer antibiotics throughout pregnancy if recurrence in previous 2 years); bacterial endocarditis; the haemodynamic peaks of pregnancy (maximal hypervolaemia after 28 weeks; peripartum autotransfusion from uterine contraction; relief of IVC compression after delivery; ergometrine use aggravates haemodynamic changes).

(iii) Antenatal management: joint management with cardiologist; fortnightly antenatal visits; Grade IV heart disease requires in-patient care (this patient approximates Grade III → close monitoring, consider admission); ensure adequate rest and restrict physical activity; prevent anaemia; ensure competent dental care; prophylactic Penicillin V for dental procedures (protection against streptococcal endocarditis); active infection — admit; detect and treat obstetric complications; fetal surveillance (fetal growth, wellbeing); ECG, echocardiography, CXR, fetal echocardiography.

(iv) Intrapartum/postpartum: labour managed with senior obstetric and anaesthetic input; cardiac output increases with each uterine contraction; avoid ergometrine (aggravates haemodynamic changes); careful fluid balance; antibiotic prophylaxis for delivery. Postpartum: CO returns to normal 2 weeks post-delivery; monitor for heart failure in early puerperium (further rise in CO post-delivery due to relief of caval occlusion and uterine retraction). Peripartal cardiomyopathy may develop in the peripartum period in susceptible women.
questions.question:
A 26-year-old gravida 2 para 1 at 30 weeks of gestation presents with progressive dyspnoea on minimal exertion and orthopnoea. She had rheumatic fever at age 10. On examination, pulse is irregularly irregular, there is a loud pansystolic murmur conducted to the axilla, and the apex beat is displaced. She has bilateral ankle oedema.

(i) What is the diagnosis including the cardiac lesion and NYHA grade? What is the most likely arrhythmia?
(ii) What are the factors in this case that would promote further cardiac failure?
(iii) Outline the principles of antenatal management for this patient.
(iv) What is the definitive intrapartum and postpartum management?

A(i) Describe the physiological changes in the cervix, vagina, perineum, abdominal wall, and ovaries during the puerperium, including the timing of recovery of each structure and the hormonal basis for the delayed return of ovulation in breastfeeding women.
A(ii) Describe the changes at the placental site during the puerperium, including the phases of lochia, the average duration of lochia discharge, what percentage of women continue lochia beyond 6 weeks, and the cause of secondary increase in bleeding 7–14 days postpartum.
B(i) Describe the postnatal management of a woman who has delivered by Caesarean section, including wound care, pain management, rehydration, antibiotic use, and discharge instructions specific to Caesarean delivery.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Cervix: reverts to near pre-pregnancy state but never returns to nulliparous state; by the end of the first week, the os closes and can hardly admit a finger. Vagina: regresses but does not return to pre-pregnancy size; resolution of increased vascularity and oedema occurs in the first 3 weeks; rugae reappear in those not breastfeeding; vaginal smear is atrophic due to low oestrogen in breastfeeding mothers, improving in 6–10 weeks. Perineum: swollen and torn perineum resolves in 1–2 weeks; muscle tone returns in about 6 weeks, but not all tone returns because of injury to muscles, nerves, and connective tissue. Abdominal wall: tone remains poor for weeks depending on maternal exercise. Ovaries: ovulation may return in 27 days in non-breastfeeding women; most women menstruate within 12 weeks postpartum (average 7–9 weeks); in breastfeeding women, half to three-quarters have periods return within 36 weeks — effect of prolactin; breastfeeding induces a reduction in GnRH, LH, and FSH, resulting in amenorrhoea; reduced suckling precipitates the return of ovulation.
A(ii) Changes at placental site: the contraction phase reduces the amount of red blood flowing, giving lochia rubra (red). Lochia then becomes brownish red with watery consistency (lochia serosa), then yellowish (lochia alba). Average duration: 5 weeks; 15% of women continue lochia after 6 weeks. Secondary increase in bleeding 7–14 days postpartum: caused by sloughing of the eschar on the placental site. Sub-involution of the placental site is associated with retained products of conception and other causes.
B(i) Caesarean section care: wound care and pain management are key. Local wound care; observe for signs of wound infection or breakdown. Narcotics for pain control with NSAIDs (for involution pain). Rehydration and antibiotics (prophylaxis may be enough in some cases). Discharge: ≤ 4 days for Caesarean section. Discharge instructions: wound care, activity restrictions — avoid lifting objects heavier than the baby, avoid driving soon. Risk factors for abdominal wound infection include DM, hypertension, treatment with steroids, immunosuppression, anaemia, haematoma, chorioamnionitis, PROM, prolonged labour, prolonged operating time, abdominal twin delivery, and excessive blood loss.

A(i) Pelvic inlet: bounded by the symphysis pubis (upper margin), ileo-pectineal line, ala of sacrum, and promontory of sacrum. Diameters: transverse 13.5 cm, anteroposterior 11 cm. Angle of brim to horizontal: 60° in the erect position (may be 90° in Afro-Caribbean women, which may delay the head entering the pelvis in labour). Mid-cavity: bounded in front by the middle of the symphysis pubis, the pubic bone, obturator fascia, and inner aspect of ischial bone and spines; posteriorly by the junction of the second and third pieces of the sacrum. Diameters: transverse and anteroposterior are similar at 12 cm. Ischial spines are palpable vaginally — landmarks to assess descent of the head (station) and for pudendal block. Pelvic outlet: bounded by the lower margin of symphysis pubis, descending ramus of pubic bone, ischial tuberosity, sacrotuberous ligament, and last piece of sacrum. Diameters: transverse 11 cm, anteroposterior 13.5 cm. The two levator ani muscles form a musculofascial gutter during the second stage. Pelvic types: gynaecoid — most favourable and most common. Android — may be associated with deep transverse arrest. Anthropoid — associated with persistent occipitoposterior position. Platypelloid — associated with obstructed labour.
A(ii) Bones of the vault: parietal bones, parts of the occipital, frontal, and temporal bones. Sutures: four un-ossified membranes joining the bones — sagittal, frontal, coronal, and lambdoidal sutures. Fontanelles: anterior fontanelle (bregma, diamond-shaped) — junction of sagittal, frontal, and coronal sutures; posterior fontanelle (triangular) — junction of sagittal and lambdoidal sutures.
B(i) First stage: from diagnosis of labour to full cervical dilatation. Latent phase: onset of labour to cervical dilatation of 3 cm. Active phase: 3 cm to full dilatation; normal rate approximately 1 cm per hour in primigravida, 2 cm per hour in multigravida. Duration — primipara: 6–18 hours; multipara: 3–10 hours. Second stage: from full cervical dilatation to delivery of the baby; two phases — propulsive and expulsive. Duration — primipara: 2 hours; multipara: 1 hour. Third stage: from delivery of fetus to delivery of placenta; duration: less than 30 minutes. Methods of placental delivery: Schultze.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the female bony pelvis relevant to labour under the following headings: the pelvic inlet (plane, diameters, and angle), the mid-cavity (boundaries and diameters), the pelvic outlet (plane and diameters), and the four pelvic types with their obstetric significance.
A(ii) Describe the fetal skull under the following headings: bones of the vault, sutures, fontanelles, and the significance of moulding and caput succedaneum in labour.
B(i) Define and describe the stages of labour (first, second, third), including the two phases of the first stage with their definitions and the normal duration for primigravidae and multigravidae.

A 25-year-old woman, 4 days postpartum following a normal vaginal delivery, is found crying by her partner. She is tearful, irritable, and says she feels hopeless. Her episiotomy is healing well, her temperature is 36.8°C, haemoglobin is 7.5 g/dl. She reports difficulty sleeping.
(i) State the diagnosis, define it, and describe the factors that prolong this condition.
(ii) Distinguish this condition from postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis, including onset, duration, and features of each.
(iii) Explain how breastfeeding affects ovarian function in the puerperium, including the hormonal mechanism, the timing of return of menstruation, and the contraceptive effect.
(iv) Describe postpartum contraception options available, including which hormonal preparations are preferred and why, and which non-hormonal devices require caution and why.
questions.answerText:
(i) Baby blues (maternity blues). Many women feel weepy and depressed 3–5 days after delivery, but this is usually short-lived. Factors that prolong the baby blues: postpartum pyrexia, anaemia of < 8 g/dl, inadequate sleep, delayed healing of the episiotomy.
(ii) Baby blues (maternity blues): onset 3–5 days postpartum; short-lived and self-limiting; characterised by tearfulness, low mood, irritability; usually resolves without specific treatment. Postpartum depression: a more persistent depressive illness; onset later in the puerperium; features include persistent low mood, inability to cope, and a need for ongoing emotional support and professional assessment. Postpartum psychosis: a severe puerperal psychiatric disorder presenting with agitation, confusion, delusions, or hallucinations; it is a psychiatric emergency requiring urgent specialist referral.
(iii) Breastfeeding induces a reduction in GnRH, LH, and FSH, resulting in amenorrhoea. Reduced suckling precipitates the return of ovulation. During lactation, menses before 6 months are mostly anovulatory, and fertility remains low. The mean ovulation time in non-lactating women is 70–75 days; in breastfeeding mothers it is 190 days. Breastfeeding is an effective contraceptive as long as the baby is having at least 5 feeds per 24 hours. Most women menstruate within 12 weeks postpartum (average 7–9 weeks) if not breastfeeding; half to three-quarters of breastfeeding women have their periods return in 36 weeks (effect of prolactin).
(iv) Postpartum contraception: pelvic rest is advised; intercourse can be resumed at 3 weeks when clear red blood stops, the perineum is well healed, and the woman is emotionally ready. Hormonal: progesterone-only minipill, Norplant, Depot Provera — recommended because they do not decrease milk production; combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP) decreases milk production more than progesterone-only, so women wishing to use OCP should establish lactation before starting it. Non-hormonal: condom is recommended over caps/diaphragm before 6 weeks (prevents STIs; cervix needs time to return to normal to fit diaphragm). IUCD inserted in the immediate postpartum has a high chance of extrusion.

(i) Prerequisites specific to vacuum extraction:
- The cervix must be at least 8 cm dilated (in this case fully dilated – met).
- The membranes must be ruptured (met).
- The vertex must be presenting (met).
- The position of the vertex must be known with certainty (met – right occipito-lateral).
- The fetal head must be engaged (station +2 – met).
- There should be no significant cephalopelvic disproportion.
- The bladder must be empty.
- The operator must have the required experience, or an experienced operator must be present.
- The operator must have the willingness to abandon the procedure when it fails.
- Anaesthesia and episiotomy are not always required.

(ii) Procedure of ventouse delivery:
- Local infiltration only.
- Slip the cup sideways; insert as near the posterior fontanelle as possible.
- Gradual build-up of vacuum: 0.2 kg/cm² at 1-minute intervals, up to 0.8 kg/cm².
- Apply traction during contractions while the mother pushes.
- Natural forces come into play; the mother pushes to assist delivery.

(iii) Fetal and neonatal complications:
- Scalp trauma: scalp abrasions are fairly common with the metal cap.
- Cephalhaematoma: in difficult deliveries; rarely subgaleal haematoma.
- Tentorial tears and intracranial haemorrhage (rare, in difficult deliveries).
- Neonatal asphyxia: noticed with prolonged exhaustion.
- Neonatal jaundice: increased incidence compared to spontaneous delivery and forceps delivery.

(iv) Advantages of ventouse over forceps:
- The technique of vacuum extraction is more easily learnt and the skill more easily acquired.
- The vacuum cap does not occupy space in the maternal pelvis.
- Anaesthesia is not a prerequisite.
- Natural forces come into play; the mother pushes to assist delivery.
- In-built safety mechanism.
- Failed vacuum extraction is associated with fewer complications to mother and baby.
- The ventouse can be used in the first stage of labour (from 8 cm dilatation).
- Overall there are lower maternal and fetal/neonatal complications compared to forceps.
Advantage of forceps over ventouse in severe fetal distress at full dilatation:
- In experienced and skilled hands, forceps effect faster delivery, making them more useful in cases of severe fetal distress or cord prolapse when the cervix is fully dilated and other prerequisites are met.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old primigravida is in the second stage of labour. The fetal heart rate shows late decelerations. On vaginal examination the vertex presents, the position is right occipito-lateral, the head is at station +2, the cervix is fully dilated, and the membranes are ruptured. The obstetrician elects to perform a vacuum extraction.

(i) What are the prerequisites specific to vacuum extraction that must be fulfilled in this patient?
(ii) Describe the procedure of ventouse delivery in the sequence.
(iii) List all the fetal and neonatal complications of vacuum extraction.
(iv) List all the advantages of the ventouse over the forceps as stated, and state the single advantage of forceps over ventouse in cases of severe fetal distress at full dilatation.

A(i) There is atony and dilatation of the renal pelves and ureters due to hormonal and mechanical factors, mainly progesterone. Smooth muscle hypertrophy in the ureters compensates for atony (oestrogenic effect). The kidneys show increased renal parenchyma and increased intra-renal fluid, resulting in renal enlargement. Dilatation of the calyces, renal pelvis, and ureter is present especially on the right side, as early as the first trimester. Urinary stasis is greatest between the 20th and 24th weeks.
A(ii) As pregnancy progresses, ureteric dilatation becomes more marked above the pelvic brim. The asymmetry is due to pressure from the right ovarian vein, which crosses the right ureter. On the left side, the ovarian vein runs parallel to the ureter, so dilatation is less marked on the left. Modern urometry shows an increased tonicity in the upper ureter and no decrease in the frequency of ureteric contractions; the concept of hypotonic ureters with urinary stasis has not been substantiated.
B(i) Glomerular filtration rate and effective renal plasma flow increase by approximately 50% in pregnancy. The increased GFR produces an increased filtered load that exceeds the tubular reabsorptive capacity, allowing glucose and amino acids to escape into the urine. Within 1 week of delivery, glucose excretion returns to its non-pregnant pattern.
B(ii) During pregnancy, there is an increase in total body water of 6–8 litres (mostly extracellular), maximal during the 2nd trimester. A net retention of about 900 mmol of sodium occurs. Plasma osmolality is markedly reduced. The increased circulating hormones contribute to these changes. There is also lateral displacement and kinking of the abdominal portion of the ureters.
C(i) Urinary pH increases markedly in pregnancy, creating a more favourable environment for the multiplication of micro-organisms in the urinary tract. The nutrients (glucose, amino acids) that escape into urine further support bacterial growth.
C(ii) Predisposing factors that are more pronounced in pregnancy include: asymptomatic bacteriuria; upward massage of organisms during coitus; poor hygiene following defaecation or coitus; urethral catheterisation; trauma of labour; puerperal reduction in bladder tone; urinary retention from perineal pain after birth; and vaginitis/cervicitis. The anatomical and physiological changes unique to pregnancy — dilatation, stasis, altered urinary pH, glycosuria — mean UTI is commoner in pregnant than in non-pregnant women.
