A(i) Describe the sociobiological factors that influence obstetric outcome, listing all the variables.
A(ii) Describe the effects of religion and culture on obstetric outcome.
B(i) Describe the influence of female illiteracy and socio-economic status on obstetric outcome.
B(ii) Explain the influence of blood group, Hb genotype, and pre-existing diseases on pregnancy outcome.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Sociobiological variables that affect obstetric outcome:
- Socio-economic status
- Age
- Height and weight
- Parity
- Pregnancy interval
- Multiple pregnancy
- Blood group
- Hb genotype
- Pre-existing diseases
- Religion and culture
- Female illiteracy
These variables affect: maternal morbidity; maternal mortality; mode of delivery; perinatal mortality; perinatal morbidity.
A(ii) Effects of religion and culture:
- Jehovah's Witnesses decline use of blood products
- Some doctrines refuse use of contraception (leading to high parity)
- Certain cultures/religions promote early marriage
- Low status of women; no right of fertility determination
- Husband must give consent to access health care
- Husband must give consent for surgical procedure
- Other harmful traditional practices: female genital cutting; food taboos in pregnancy; aversion to operative delivery
B(i) Female illiteracy: poor obstetric outcome; low economic power; reduced access to health care.
Socio-economic status: associated with inadequate antenatal supervision; reduced utilisation of maternal health services; delayed presentation; worse obstetric outcome.
B(ii) Blood group: ABO incompatibility; Rhesus iso-immunisation.
Hb genotype: haemoglobinopathies (e.g. sickle cell disease) cause haemolytic anaemia in pregnancy.
Pre-existing diseases: increase medical complications during pregnancy; must be optimised before conception (pre-conception care); examples include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, HbSS, HIV.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the complications of induced labour under the following headings: iatrogenic prematurity, cord prolapse, intrapartum bleeding (including its predisposing conditions), precipitate labour, fetal distress, and hyperstimulation.
A(ii) Describe the complications related to the post-delivery period following induction, including primary PPH, amniotic fluid embolism (including its management), sepsis, neonatal jaundice, and feto-maternal death.
B(i) Describe the management of hyperstimulation during induction of labour, and state what precautions should be in place regarding the setting and monitoring for any patient undergoing induction of labour.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Iatrogenic prematurity: delivery of a preterm infant if gestational age is miscalculated or indication is incorrect. Cord prolapse: can occur following amniotomy, particularly if the presenting part is not well engaged; precautions include excluding cord presentation, avoiding dislodging the fetal head, applying fundal/suprapubic pressure during membrane rupture, and monitoring the fetal heart before and immediately after amniotomy. Intrapartum bleeding: causes include vasa praevia (polyhydramnios, high parity), abruptio placentae (high parity). Precipitate labour: induction-to-delivery interval of ≤ 3 hours. Fetal distress: abnormal fetal heart rate patterns related to uterine hyperstimulation. Hyperstimulation: ≥ 6 contractions in 10 minutes; caused by excessive oxytocin or prostaglandins.
A(ii) Primary PPH: bleeding in excess of 500 ml within 24 hours of delivery, following prolonged labour or difficult instrumentation. Amniotic fluid embolism: associated with high parity and intact membranes; may develop DIC; highly fatal; management — high-dose steroids, cardiopulmonary support, fresh blood. Sepsis: following prolonged labour, difficult instrumentation, multiple vaginal examinations. Neonatal jaundice: recognised complication of induced labour. Feto-maternal death: can occur as a result of the above complications.
B(i) Management of hyperstimulation: stop oxytocin infusion immediately, give plain infusion, and may require tocolysis. Setting for induction: labour ward only. Monitoring requirements: one-to-one midwifery care; continuous electronic fetal monitoring, or intermittent monitoring every 15 minutes. Post-delivery: continue oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe how tuberculosis affects pregnancy, including the factors that determine the outcome, the effect of late diagnosis, the clinical presentation of pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB in pregnancy, and the outcome with multi-drug-resistant TB.
A(ii) Describe the diagnosis of pulmonary TB in pregnancy, including investigations specific to the pregnant state, and outline the treatment regimen including first-line and second-line drugs, the initial phase, the continuation phase, and the drugs that are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
B(i) Describe the postnatal management of the mother and infant born to a woman with active TB, including chemoprophylaxis for the infant, BCG vaccination timing, breastfeeding recommendations, and the role of pyridoxine.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Effects of TB on pregnancy depend on: type, site and extent of disease, stage of pregnancy at which management is instituted, nutritional status of mother, presence of concomitant disease, immune status and co-existence of HIV infection, and availability of facilities for early diagnosis and treatment. Pulmonary and extrapulmonary forms affect pregnant women the same way as non-pregnant ones. Late diagnosis/care is associated with a four-fold increase in obstetric morbidity and a nine-fold increase in preterm labour. Co-existing HIV infection augments progression of TB and worsens immunosuppression. Clinical presentation: cough, weight loss, fever, fatigue, haemoptysis; other features include lethargy, abdominal distension, irritability, and skin lesions. Extrapulmonary TB occurs in 20% of cases; lymphadenitis is the most common form; other forms (intestinal, spinal, endometrial, meningeal) are associated with increased maternal disability, IUGR, and infants with low Apgar scores. MDR-TB: as common during pregnancy as in non-pregnant women; increased risk of neonatal complications; more advanced disease with more extensive radiographic changes and longer sputum conversion times.
A(ii) Diagnosis: history (contact, symptoms), tuberculin skin test (Mantoux: > 10 mm significant; ≥ 5 mm significant in HIV-positive), CXR with lead shielding (delay until 12 weeks if asymptomatic; immediate if symptomatic). Other investigations: counselling/testing for HIV, CD4+ count if HIV-positive, serological tests for hepatitis B and C. Treatment: untreated TB is a greater danger than treatment. Goal: render patient sputum-negative at delivery; direct observed therapy (DOT) preferred. Initial phase: INH, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide daily for 2 months. Continuation phase: INH and rifampicin daily or twice weekly for 7 months. Contraindicated drugs: streptomycin, kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin). Treatment monitoring: monthly sputum for AFB, renal function test, liver function test, visual acuity/colour vision if ethambutol used > 2 months (retrobulbar neuritis).
B(i) Mother continues anti-TB treatment postnatally. Infant: given chemoprophylaxis with INH for 3 months, or until mother becomes sputum-negative. BCG vaccination: postpone BCG or give INH-resistant BCG. At 3 months: discontinue INH if mother is sputum-negative and infant has a negative Mantoux; if infant is Mantoux-positive, investigate for pulmonary/extrapulmonary focus — if none, extend INH to 6 months; if present, administer full anti-TB treatment. Breastfeeding: encourage breastfeeding; little risk of toxicity in infant; give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation to mother and infant to prevent peripheral neuritis. Congenital TB: rare; BCG is contraindicated in HIV-positive infants.

questions.question:
A) Describe the anatomical basis of lumbar extradural analgesia under the following headings:
A(i) Spinal levels and the interspace used for catheter placement
A(ii) The ligaments traversed in order from skin to the extradural space, and the landmark that identifies entry
A(iii) The four possible positions of the catheter tip after placement

B) State the safe method to confirm correct catheter placement in the extradural space, and describe the test dose.

C) Explain the anatomical basis and clinical consequences of accidental dural puncture, including the type of headache, its characteristics, and the definitive treatment stated.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Spinal level and interspace:
- The Tuohy needle is inserted at the L2/3 interspace.
- The patient is positioned sitting or in the lateral position.
- The local anaesthetic of choice for labour analgesia is bupivacaine, started at 0.25% solution, 5–9 ml.

A(ii) Ligaments traversed and landmark:
- The needle passes through the supraspinous ligament, then the ligamentum flavum.
- Identification of the extradural space is characterised by a palpable click (loss of resistance technique using a syringe in which the plunger moves freely, filled with sterile saline).

A(iii) Four possible positions of catheter tip:
- Correct siting in the extradural space.
- Intravenous (IV) placement.
- Subarachnoid insertion.
- Subdural placement.

B) Confirming correct placement and test dose:
- Allow fluid from the needle hub onto the back of the hand: extradural space fluid will feel cold or warm relative to skin temperature.
- Dextrostix test: saline and local anaesthetic contain no glucose, whereas CSF does; a positive glucose reading suggests subarachnoid placement.
- IV insertion may be suspected by persistent bleeding into the catheter.
- Test dose: should correctly identify subarachnoid or IV injection.
- Subdural block is difficult to detect: catheter pierces dura but not arachnoid membrane; a patchy and unexpectedly high but not intense block following a top-up injection should arouse suspicion of subdural placement.

C) Accidental dural puncture – anatomical basis and consequences:
- Dural puncture complicates 1–2% of extradural blocks.
- Extradural needles are large (16–18 G); 75% of dural punctures from this diameter are followed by severe headache.
- The headache is a low-pressure spinal headache: usually occipital, characteristically throbbing, more severe when standing or sitting, and relieved by lying down.
- This occurs because the large-bore needle leaves a hole in the dura through which CSF leaks, reducing intrathecal pressure.
- Subsequent management: if the headache is disabling, administer an extradural blood patch (injection of 15–20 ml of autologous blood into the extradural space). The fibrinous plug prevents further escape of CSF; relief occurs within 4–5 hours in 90% of patients.
- After dural puncture, extensive block may occur with subsequent top-up injections, so dermatomal spread must be monitored carefully after each injection.

A(i) Puerperal sepsis: infection of the genital tract after delivery. Incidence: approximately 3% (range 1–8%); accounts for 7% of all direct maternal deaths. Predisposing factors: prolonged labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, multiple vaginal examinations during labour, operative delivery (Caesarean section), prenatal bacterial colonisation of the genital tract, manual removal of the placenta, exploration of the uterus, retained products of conception. Organisms: usually polymicrobial; a mixed flora normally colonises the vagina; ascending infection of organisms from the bowel that colonise the perineum. Most frequently identified organisms: facultative G+ve cocci, especially group B Streptococcus, frequently coexisting with Mycoplasma spp. Exogenous organisms causing major epidemics: haemolytic streptococcus Lancefield Group A and Staphylococcus aureus (transmitted by droplet infection, infected dust, or direct skin contact; toxins cause rapid deterioration into septicaemic shock). Methods of spread: ascending infection from lower genital tract → fallopian tube → ovaries → salpingo-oophoritis → pelvic peritonitis → generalised peritonitis and pelvic abscesses; contiguous spread into myometrium and parametrium; via lymphatics and blood vessels; via uterine veins into IVC via iliac veins; directly via ovarian veins into IVC → septic thrombophlebitis, pulmonary infections, generalised septicaemia, endotoxic shock.
A(ii) Symptoms: malaise, headache, fever, rigors, abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhoea, offensive lochia, secondary PPH. Signs: pyrexia, tachycardia, boggy tender uterus larger than appropriate, infected caesarean and perineal wounds, peritonism, paralytic ileus, indurated adnexae (parametritis), bogginess in pelvis (abscess), purulent offensive vaginal discharge, infected episiotomy wounds. Investigations: FBC, PCV, electrolytes and urea, ECS/HVS M/C/S, pelvic USS (retained products, pelvic abscess, retained foreign body).
B(i) Treatment: broad-spectrum antibiotics pending M/C/S — triple regimen: parenteral ampiclox/augmentin + metronidazole (Flagyl) + gentamycin; in severe infections: cephalosporins (e.g., ceftriaxone); change to appropriate antibiotic when results available. Supportive care: IV fluids (for nausea, vomiting, ileus), minimal curettage (for retained products), posterior colpotomy or laparotomy (for pelvic abscess), blood transfusion (severe anaemia). Complications: salpingitis, pelvic peritonitis, pelvic cellulitis, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, wound infection, necrotising fasciitis, septicaemia, chronic PID, infertility, maternal mortality.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Global/Nigerian data: LBW previously synonymous with prematurity (most important cause of infant deaths at national level). LBW implicated in 50% of all neonatal deaths; accounts for 33% of all deaths in children under 5 years. Mortality increases with decreasing gestational age at delivery/birth weight. Nigerian neonatal mortality rate: 35/1000; under-5 mortality rate: 140/1000; infant mortality rate: 71/1000 (child survival indicators). Nigeria is one of 10 countries with worst child survival. LBW rates higher in developing countries; rates increase with level of development.

A(ii) Implications: Individual — fetal and perinatal mortality and morbidity; inhibited growth and cognitive development; chronic diseases later in life; mental retardation; vision loss; learning difficulties. Growth/neurological development deficits in infancy. Adulthood associations: CVD, hypertension, diabetes, renal damage, obstructive lung disease, high cholesterol. Population — indicator of public health problems (maternal malnutrition, ill health, poor health care in pregnancy). Higher burden of deaths in developing countries (98% of neonatal deaths).

A(iii) WHO internationally recognised cut-off levels for public health concern: IUGR rate >20%; LBW rate >15%.

B. Assessment of gestational age: sonography — most accurate method; patient's recall of LMP; physical examination of uterus size; examination of the neonate. Limitations: poor differentiation between infants born small for GA and those small due to preterm delivery; developing countries — unreliable information about gestational age; inaccuracies in estimating GA; methods may be used alone or in combination.
Assessment of fetal growth: early sonographic estimation; anthropometric evaluation of neonate. Limitation: some normal constitutional small newborns classified SGA; pathology could affect size.

C. Developed countries: most LBW infants are due to preterm delivery (obstetric/neonatal care developments allow premature delivery with survival). Developing countries: most LBW infants are IUGR (chronic maternal malnutrition, infections, hypertensive disorders). Burden is higher in developing countries because: 98% of neonatal deaths occur in developing countries; poor access to adequate obstetric/neonatal care; 36% of Nigerian children underweight for age; inadequate immunisation coverage; less than 35.2% of births delivered by skilled personnel (NDHS 2003); only 58% of mothers received ANC from trained personnel; 25.7% of rural residents had skilled attendants at birth.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Abruptio placentae (Grade III — severe). Features indicating Grade III: shock, woody-hard uterus, inaudible fetal heart, prolonged clotting time. Grade IIIB is distinguished by overt coagulopathy. Grade I (mild) — 40% of cases; Grade II (moderate) — 45%; Grade III (severe) — 15%; IIIA — no overt coagulopathy; IIIB — overt coagulopathy.

(ii) Predisposing factors: hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia is a major cause); chronic hypertension; severe malnutrition; genetic mutations; poor transformation of uteroplacental arteries (60%); occlusion of deep myometrial vessels with haemorrhage (33%); decidual haematoma, vessel thrombosis, focal necrosis; prior abruptio; smoking; substance abuse.

(iii) Pathophysiology: Rupture of uteroplacental arteries → extravasation of blood under arterial pressure between myometrial bundles. Blood tracks: (a) towards decidua basalis → placental separation and fetal hypoxia; (b) towards serosal surface → Couvelaire uterus. Initial event: decidual haemorrhage from maternal decidual arteries → haematoma → compression and obliteration of overlying intervillous space → further placental vessel damage. Infusion of decidual debris rich in thromboplastin into maternal circulation → DIC. Haematoma may be retained (concealed), break into amniotic cavity (port-wine liquor), or track to cervix/vagina (revealed).

(iv) Management principles:
- Admit to labour ward; monitor maternal vital signs and urinary output (>30 ml/hr); monitor FHR and uterine activity by CTG.
- Fluid replacement goals: re-establish haemodynamic stability; correct coagulopathy. Types of fluid: crystalloids; fresh whole blood; fresh frozen plasma; cryoprecipitate; platelet transfusion.
- Two peripheral infusions with large-bore cannulae; CVP line; blood transfusion; notify relevant staff.
- Mode of delivery: if intrauterine fetal death (IUFD) → vaginal delivery ± oxytocin augmentation; if viable fetus → abdominal delivery (CS or hysterectomy). Other treatment: ± Rhesus immunoglobulin; ± heparinisation; ± intravenous protein C; ± renal dialysis.

Bedside clotting time is prolonged.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Presumptive evidence: nausea and/or vomiting; urinary frequency; perception of fetal movement; absent menses; breast changes; changes in vaginal mucosa; skin pigmentation/abdominal striae.
Probable signs: include changes such as Hegar's sign, Chadwick's sign, and Braxton Hicks contractions.
Positive signs: identification of fetal heart; perception of fetal movement by examiner; recognition of embryo/fetus by sonography/radiology.
A(ii) Cutaneous manifestations:
- Chloasma (mask of pregnancy): darkening of the skin over the forehead, bridge of the nose, or cheekbones; occurs to a variable degree in most pregnant women after 16 weeks; most marked in dark-complexioned women.
- Linea nigra: a pigmented streak (darkening of the linea alba) on the lower midline of the abdomen extending from the pubis to the umbilicus; appears about the third month in primigravidae but often earlier in multigravidae; most noticeable in dark-complexioned women.
- Striae (stretch marks): caused by separation of underlying collagen tissue; appear as irregular scars; most noticeable in patients with fair complexion; probably an adrenocorticosteroid response.
- Other changes: acne, oily skin, irregular pigmented areas; increased growth of facial or body hair.
B(i) The basis for pigmentary changes is stimulation of the melanophores by an increase in melanocyte-stimulating hormone.
B(ii) Braxton Hicks contractions: painless uterine contractions as the uterus enlarges; patient may complain of a sensation of tightening or pressure; contractions usually start about the 28th week in primiparae and may occur earlier in succeeding pregnancies; as pregnancy progresses they become more regular but remain relatively painless; relieved by walking and exercises.

(i) Obstetric complications of multiple pregnancy:
- Severe preterm delivery
- Intra-uterine growth restriction (IUGR)
- Fetal abnormalities
- Fetal chromosomal defects
- Death of one fetus
- Complications unique to monochorionic twinning
- APH and PPH
- Malpresentation and malpositioning
- Increased operative deliveries and perinatal death
- Raised MSAFP
- Congenital malformation
- Abnormal lie
- Polyhydramnios
- Cord prolapse
(ii) Perinatal mortality is 6 times more in twin pregnancies than in singleton pregnancy.
(iii) Transverse lie poses risk of cord prolapse and obstructed labour/neglected shoulder; management: this patient is a grand multipara at 28 weeks; requires close supervision; if transverse lie persists at term, delivery by caesarean section; cautious use of oxytocin in multipara.
(iv) Effects of excessive weight loss in pregnancy: amenorrhoea and reduced fecundity; increased risk of miscarriages; preterm delivery; preterm pre-labour rupture of fetal membranes; maternal anaemia; blood transfusion and complications; low birth weight; perinatal and neonatal death.

A(i) Describe the initiation and maintenance of human pregnancy, including the role of hCG, when it is produced, when it is first detectable, and when it peaks.
A(ii) Describe the types of pregnancy tests, including biological tests (historical) and immunological tests, and identify the most sensitive parameter tested.
B(i) List the differential diagnoses of pregnancy.
B(ii) Describe the routine management of a normal pregnancy from booking to delivery, including investigations, immunisation, supplementation, and chemoprophylaxis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Human pregnancy is initiated at fertilization; implantation of the blastocyst begins by the sixth day; maternal recognition of pregnancy is important for maintenance; fetal signals promote maternal recognition.
hCG is produced by the syncytiotrophoblast after 8 days from fertilization; hCG may be detected in maternal serum as early as 9 days; levels peak approximately 65 days after conception.
A(ii) Pregnancy tests measure changes in levels of hCG; testing is more accurate with the beta subunit of hCG.
Biological tests (historical): first described by Aschheim and Zondek in 1928; based on observation of corpora lutea in immature mice injected with urine from pregnant women; based on ovarian response to anterior pituitary hormones; complicated and time-consuming. Other biological tests: rabbit test (Friedman and Hoffman, 1931); rat ovarian hyperaemia test (Aschheim and Zondek, 1941).
Immunological tests: use antibodies against hCG; more rapid and practical.
Most sensitive parameter: beta subunit of hCG.
B(i) Differential diagnosis of pregnancy: haematometra; adenomyosis; contiguous extra-uterine masses; spurious pregnancy; pseudocyesis; undetected tumours (e.g. bronchogenic carcinoma).
B(ii) Routine management:
- Booking examination: history, physical examination, routine investigations
- Antenatal follow-up to detect complications: anaemia, hypertension, IUGR, malpositions/malpresentations, diabetes mellitus
- Immunisation
- Screen for Rhesus antibodies (at booking, 16, 28, 32, 36 weeks)
- Iron/folic acid supplementation
- Antimalarial chemoprophylaxis
- Pelvic assessment when indicated

questions.question:
A 25-year-old primigravida is admitted in active labour at term. On abdominal palpation the head appears disproportionately large and the sinciput and occiput are at the same level. The head is unengaged. On vaginal examination, the forehead is felt; the anterior fontanelle and frontal suture lead to the supra-orbital ridge and the root of the nose; the nose, mouth, and chin cannot be felt. The membranes have ruptured early.

(i) State the diagnosis, the presenting diameter and its measurement, and explain why engagement is not possible in this case with a term baby and average-sized pelvis.
(ii) List all the causes of this presentation.
(iii) Describe the behaviour of this presentation in labour and its spontaneous tendency.
(iv) State the complete management including investigations and the indications for each mode of delivery.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Brow presentation.
- Presenting diameter: mentovertical diameter = 13 cm to 14 cm.
- The largest pelvic diameter is 12.5 cm (anteroposterior outlet diameter).
- Therefore, the mentovertical diameter exceeds the largest available pelvic diameter, making engagement impossible in a term baby of average size with a normal pelvis.
- Delivery of the baby per vaginam is only possible when the baby is small for the pelvis.

(ii) Causes:
- Extension of the fetal head.
- Contracted pelvis.
- Partial extension of the fetal head so that the occiput is higher than the sinciput.

(iii) Behaviour in labour and spontaneous tendency:
- Brow presentation is unstable and tends to convert to an occipital or face presentation as labour progresses.
- It may be primary (before labour) or secondary (during labour at the pelvic brim or lower down, with compression of the mentovertical diameter).
- The head is ill-fitting, and labour progress is poor at the beginning.
- There is a risk of cord prolapse because of the ill-fitting presenting part.
- The forewaters tend to rupture early.

(iv) Complete management:
- Investigations: X-ray and ultrasound, especially in primary cases.
- Management depends on fetal condition and cervical dilatation:
 - If the fetus is alive with a normal-sized baby and pelvis: deliver by caesarean section.
 - If the fetus is dead and the cervix is not fully dilated: deliver by caesarean section.
 - If the fetus is dead and the cervix is fully dilated: deliver by craniotomy. If the health provider is not proficient in craniotomy, deliver by caesarean section.
 - Rarely, vacuum extraction using the occipito-posterior cup may be used in premature or small infants.
- Exclude cord prolapse at all times.
- Brow presentation with a normal-sized term baby and normal pelvis: caesarean section is the delivery of choice because vaginal delivery is impossible with this diameter.

(i) Diagnosis: Asymmetrical IUGR. Justification: onset late in pregnancy; increased HC/AC ratio (brain sparing — brain weight only slightly decreased, but lack of subcutaneous fat and loss of hepatic glycogen); SFH less than dates by ≥4 cm on 3 successive examinations (severe IUGR); oligohydramnios (predisposition to oligohydramnios due to reduced renal blood flow in IUGR); fetal weight below 10th percentile for gestational age. Asymmetrical IUGR is commoner (~70%) and commonly caused by pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, chronic hypertension, severe malnutrition, genetic mutations.

(ii) Maternal causes: hypertensive disorders of pregnancy; UTI; diabetes mellitus/gestational diabetes; pulmonary/heart disease; poor maternal nutrition (pre-pregnancy and during pregnancy); recent pregnancy; anaemia; SCD; malaria; chronic renal disease; substance abuse/drugs; alcohol; cigarette smoking.
Fetoplacental causes: genetic abnormalities (trisomies); congenital malformations; TORCHES; uterine abnormalities; multiple pregnancy; post-term pregnancy; abruptio placentae; placental malformations (circumvallate placenta, placental haemangioma); twin-twin transfusion syndrome.

(iii) Fetal surveillance: fetal kick monitoring; USS for fetal growth 2–4 weekly (BPD, HC, AC, FL, amniotic fluid volume); non-stress test (NST); contraction stress test; biophysical profile (BPP); Doppler velocimetry — umbilical artery systolic:diastolic blood flow ratio is increased (significant finding); amniocentesis for pulmonary maturity.

(iv) Indications for delivery: evidence of fetal maturity; evidence of fetal compromise; at 38 weeks. Mode of delivery: individualise; fetus at risk for intrapartum complications; electronic fetal monitoring; caesarean section for compromised fetus; neonatologist involvement mandatory.
Anticipated neonatal complications: hypoglycaemia; hypocalcaemia; hypoxia/acidosis; hypothermia; meconium aspiration syndrome; polycythaemia; congenital malformations; sudden infant death syndrome.

(i) What is the diagnosis and type? Justify using the clinical and USS findings.

(iii) What are the fetal surveillance methods used to monitor the fetus, and what Doppler finding is significant?

Describe the management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Preconceptional care and counselling.
A(ii) Antenatal care: booking, visit frequency, and prophylaxis.
B(i) Investigations required during antenatal care.
B(ii) Principles of management in labour.
C(i) Early puerperium monitoring and management.
C(ii) Contraception after delivery in women with sickle cell disease, and why certain methods are preferred or avoided.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Preconceptional care: allows counselling and identification of patients at risk; optimise her steady-state; counsel on risky behaviour (hydroxyurea must be stopped before conception; users should be on contraception); review of medication. Genetic counselling of potential partners about the risks of sickle cell disease; pre-implantation diagnosis; prenatal diagnosis options.
A(ii) Early booking after the 2nd missed period; frequent antenatal visits — fortnightly until 28 weeks, then weekly until delivery. Antimalarial prophylaxis: daily proguanil; Intermittent Prophylactic Therapy — 3 doses of SP at least 4 weeks apart from 16 weeks. Haematinics, especially folic acid; iron supplementation; maintenance of PCV at 25%.
B(i) Investigations: FBC; blood film for malaria parasites; urine culture; blood culture; liver function tests; electrolytes and urea. Monitor PCV 4-hourly in labour; group and cross-match blood.
B(ii) Principles in labour: avoid dehydration; avoid infection; avoid hypoxia; prevent prolonged labour. Involve haematologist, anaesthetist, and neonatologist; monitor with partograph; give IV fluids; give prophylactic antibiotics; give supplementary oxygen; cross-match blood; give adequate analgesia; monitor PCV 4-hourly. For operative delivery: local/regional block preferred; if GA, ensure adequate oxygenation; shorten the second stage; minimise vaginal examinations.
C(i) Early puerperium: frequent PCV checks for the first 4 days; monitor vital signs regularly; continue antibiotics and folic acid; keep in labour ward/HDU for 4 days; discharge after 5–7 days; review after 2 weeks. Bone marrow embolism risk is highest in the last 4 weeks of pregnancy, in labour, and in the first 4 days of the puerperium; heparinise if predisposing factors are present.
C(ii) Contraception: barrier methods are suitable; Norplant is preferred as it stabilises red blood cell membranes; permanent sterilisation methods are advised to keep parity low due to the risks; IUCDs are not the best choice due to risk of infection and bleeding. Hydroxyurea users must use contraception and discontinue the drug when pregnancy is planned.

questions.question:
During a teaching ward round, a partograph of a primigravida in active labour is reviewed. At 4 cm cervical dilatation, the alert line is crossed. Cervical dilatation is 0.5 cm/hour despite three contractions in ten minutes. The fetal heart tracing shows repetitive late decelerations with fetal tachycardia.
(i) Describe the partograph: what it is, who developed it, what it records, and what it serves as in clinical management.
(ii) Explain the significance of crossing the alert line on the partograph, and state the minimum rate of cervical dilatation expected in a primigravida in the active phase of labour.
(iii) Interpret the fetal heart findings: identify the pattern, state its most likely cause from the common conditions, and list all causes of late decelerations.
(iv) Describe the criteria for continuous electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) in labour versus intermittent auscultation, and state the accepted standard for the interval between confirmed acute fetal compromise and delivery.
questions.answerText:
(i) The partograph is a graphic recording of the progress of labour and salient features of the mother and fetus. It was developed by Philpott in extensive studies of primigravidae and multigravidae in Southern Africa. It records cervical dilatation, descent of the presenting part, fetal heart rate, uterine contractions, maternal vital signs, fluids, and medications. It serves as an early warning system and assists in early decision-making regarding transfer, augmentation, or termination of labour. It has been used since 1970 to detect labour that is not progressing well, indicate when augmentation is appropriate, and recognise cephalopelvic disproportion long before labour becomes obstructed.
(ii) Crossing the alert line indicates deviation from the normal progress of labour and triggers clinical review. The minimum rate of cervical dilatation in a primigravida in the active phase is 1 cm per hour (some sources state at least 1 cm per hour; others state 2 cm per hour for a multigravida).
(iii) Repetitive late decelerations indicate a non-reassuring (pathological) fetal heart rate pattern. Late decelerations represent reduction in uteroplacental blood flow. Causes: placental abruption, maternal hypotension, excessive uterine activity/hypertonic contraction, maternal systemic illness, diabetes mellitus, pre-eclampsia, renal disease, IUGR, prematurity, Rh isoimmunisation, and twin-to-twin transfusion. Fetal tachycardia exceeding 180 bpm for more than 10 minutes with decreased variability is a non-reassuring pattern.
(iv) Continuous EFM indications: high-risk situations with increased risk of perinatal death, cerebral palsy, or neonatal encephalopathy; oxytocin use (induction/augmentation); pregnancies previously monitored with intermittent auscultation if baseline FHR < 110 or > 160 bpm; pregnancies previously monitored with intermittent auscultation if any intrapartum risk factor develops. Intermittent auscultation: recommended for healthy women with uncomplicated pregnancies; monitor fetal heart after a contraction for a minimum of 60 seconds; at least every 15 minutes in the first stage, every 5 minutes in the second stage; one-on-one nursing. Accepted standard for delivery in confirmed or suspected acute fetal compromise: within 30 minutes.

(i) Classification: weight 1,100 g → VLBW (Very Low Birth Weight, <1500 g); gestational age 30 weeks → preterm (before 37 completed weeks). Also classified as appropriate, small, or large for gestational age depending on percentile. LBW classification thresholds: LBW <2500 g; VLBW <1500 g; ELBW <1000 g.

(ii) Physiological basis of immediate complications:
- Temperature instability/hypothermia: high body surface area-to-body weight ratio; low brown fat; non-keratinised skin; low glycogen supply; heat loss immediately after birth by conduction, convection, evaporation, and radiation.
- Apnoea: immature respiratory centre; insufficient surfactant production at 30 weeks leads to respiratory distress syndrome (lung maturity in normal fetuses occurs around 34–35 weeks; for IDMs not guaranteed until >38.5 weeks).
- Hypoglycaemia: low glycogen supply (glycogen and free fatty acids are decreased in IUGR/prematurity); inability to maintain glucose homeostasis.
- Respiratory distress: insufficient surfactant; fluid and electrolyte imbalance (more fluid ECF > ICF); metabolic acidosis.

(iii) Factors determining good outcome: gestational age (higher is better); sex (female neonates do better); exposure to antenatal corticosteroid (prior to 34 weeks); singleton pregnancy; birth weight.

(iv) Prevention of preterm birth: treatment of UTI; cervical cerclage (for cervical abnormalities); treatment of bacterial vaginosis/trichomoniasis; anti-malarial prophylaxis; regular antenatal appointments; nutrition (balanced diet including calcium, magnesium, folates — even pre-conceptionally). Nutritional interventions for preterm: calcium; fish oil.
Prevention of IUGR: cessation of smoking; anti-malarial prophylaxis especially in primigravidae; balanced protein/energy supplementation; treatment of anaemia; identification/treatment of medical problems. Nutritional interventions for IUGR: balanced energy protein supplementation; magnesium supplementation; calcium supplementation. Treatment once detected: monitor with serial USS; treat underlying cause; antenatal corticosteroid if premature delivery anticipated before 34 weeks; low-dose aspirin to alter thromboxane:prostacyclin ratio.
questions.question:
A neonate is delivered at 30 weeks of gestation following preterm labour and weighs 1,100 g. Within 2 hours of birth, the baby develops temperature instability, apnoea, hypoglycaemia, and respiratory distress.

(i) How is this neonate classified by weight and gestational age?
(ii) Explain the physiological basis for each of the immediate complications that have developed.
(iii) What are the factors that determine a good outcome for a preterm/LBW neonate?
(iv) Outline the preventive interventions for both preterm birth and IUGR, including nutritional interventions.

A 30-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 0 (three previous mid-trimester losses), presents at 16 weeks with a history of painless leakage of fluid and mild cramping. On examination, the cervix is dilated to 3 cm with bulging membranes visible at the os. A transvaginal ultrasound confirms cervical shortening and a widened internal os.
(i) State the diagnosis, define it, and identify all the causes.
(ii) Describe the typical clinical history that should raise suspicion of this condition, and outline all diagnostic methods available in both the pregnant and non-pregnant state.
(iii) Describe the surgical management of this condition in the current pregnancy, and state the general principle of pre-conception management.
(iv) Distinguish between PROM terminology — term PROM, preterm PROM, prolonged PROM, and pre-viable PROM — and state the early-onset complication of PROM that can affect the fetus.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cervical incompetence: the most common cause of recurrent abortion in Sub-Saharan Africa; defined as inability of the cervix to support a pregnancy to term. Causes: previous forceful dilatation of the cervix, previous surgery (amputation of cervix — Manchester repair, cone biopsy), cervical laceration at childbirth, congenital weakness, in-utero exposure to DES.
(ii) Typical history: recurrent mid-trimester abortions, painless rupture of membranes, bleeding or expulsion of products of conception in mid or early third trimester. Diagnosis — during pregnancy: dilated cervix, bulging membranes; ultrasound (cervical os diameter and cervical length). Non-pregnant state: HSG showing a funnel-shaped uterus, retrograde cervical dilatation beginning with size 10; insertion of a paediatric Foley's catheter with traction after inflation (extraction is diagnostic).
(iii) Management: insert a cervical cerclage between 14 and 18 weeks of pregnancy. Pre-conception: encourage the woman to conceive; confirm a normal pregnancy in the first trimester before the cerclage is inserted.
(iv) Terminology: PROM — rupture of the membranes before the onset of labour. Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) — PROM prior to 37 completed weeks. Term PROM (prelabour) — PROM at ≥ 37 weeks, but ≥ 1 hour before onset of labour. Prolonged PROM — 24 hours elapse between rupture of membranes and onset of labour. Pre-viable PROM — PROM occurring at < 26 weeks. Early-onset complication of PROM affecting the fetus: pulmonary hypoplasia and limb positioning defects (from early-onset PROM).

questions.question:
A 28-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks presents with severe headache, blurred vision, right upper quadrant pain, and a blood pressure of 170/115 mmHg. Her urine dipstick shows 3+ proteinuria. She subsequently develops generalised tonic-clonic seizures.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is its classification within hypertensive disorders of pregnancy?
(ii) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(iii) Describe the probable aetiopathogenesis including the vascular and immunological basis.
(iv) What are the serious maternal complications of this condition?
(v) What anticonvulsant agents are used, and what are the signs of imminent eclampsia that indicate their use?
questions.answerText:
(i) Eclampsia, defined as seizure activity or coma unrelated to other cerebral conditions in an obstetric patient with pre-eclampsia. Within the classification of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, it falls under gestational hypertension/proteinuria — hypertension and/or proteinuria developing after 20 weeks of pregnancy in a previously normotensive, non-proteinuric woman. Pre-eclampsia is characterised by hypertension, proteinuria, and new-onset nondependent oedema. Pre-eclampsia is the second leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide, constituting 12–18% of pregnancy-related maternal deaths.
(ii) Risk factors include: previous pre-eclampsia; paternal factors (some men increase risk); genetic and familial history; calcium deficiency; history of spontaneous abortion; African American race (nulliparous only); higher body weight; ovum donation; multiple gestations; molar pregnancy; extremes of maternal age; essential hypertension; hypertensive renal disease; and diabetes mellitus.
(iii) Aetiology is poorly understood. The probable aetiopathogenesis involves an immunological disorder with prevention of normal trophoblastic invasion of uteroplacental vessels; lack of conversion of myometrial arteries to thin-walled vessels; failure of the second wave of trophoblastic invasion of maternal spiral arterioles; failure of normal physiological plasma volume expansion. Resulting placental ischaemia leads to: imbalance of prostacyclin/thromboxane activity; endothelial cell activation; reduced vasodilatory prostacyclin (PGI2) and nitric oxide; abnormal salt and water retention; decreased intravascular volume; and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy with increased CNS irritability.
(iv) Serious maternal complications include: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets); abruptio placentae; pulmonary oedema; acute renal failure; cerebral haemorrhage; visual disturbances and blindness; hepatic lesions; cardiovascular lesions; and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.
(v) Anticonvulsant agents: MgSO4, diazepam, phenytoin, and lytic cocktail. Signs of imminent eclampsia indicating their use: headache, visual disturbances, upper abdominal pains, proteinuria greater than 2 g/24 hours, rapidly developing oedema, oliguria less than 30 ml/hour, hyperreflexia/clonus, and established eclampsia.

questions.question:
Describe the prediction, prevention, and treatment of hypertension in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Methods used to predict pre-eclampsia.
A(ii) Prevention strategies for pre-eclampsia.
B(i) Treatment of mild gestational hypertension.
B(ii) Treatment of severe hypertension in pregnancy.
C(i) The drugs used for antihypertensive therapy in pregnancy, including those to avoid.
C(ii) Monitoring strategies during hospitalisation for gestational hypertension.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Methods used to predict pre-eclampsia: water load excretion test; vascular reactivity (cold pressor test, roll-over test, angiotensin infusion test); biochemistry (uric acid); Doppler ultrasound of umbilical blood flow; family history (7–10 times more likely in a first pregnancy, 4 times more likely in daughters of women with positive history, 7 times more likely in sisters); urine metabolite tests.
A(ii) Prevention strategies: dietary calcium supplementation (in low dietary calcium intake); low-dose aspirin (optimum dosage not confirmed); identification of high-risk groups; preventive measures include management of predisposing factors; cessation of smoking and alcohol.
B(i) Treatment of mild hypertension: monitor maternal/fetal wellbeing until 34 weeks; deliver if BP is uncontrollable; initiate antihypertensive if BP exceeds a defined threshold. Outpatient management with good surveillance; sedatives (diazepam/phenobarbitone); anti-hypertensive therapy as indicated; glucocorticoids (betamethasone/dexamethasone 12 mg, 2 doses at 12-hour intervals, followed by weekly injection until delivery or 34 weeks) for fetal lung maturity when delivery before 34 weeks is anticipated.
B(ii) Treatment of severe hypertension: hospitalisation for monitoring; IV antihypertensive agents — hydralazine, labetalol, nifedipine, diazoxide, sodium nitroprusside, trimethaphan, nitroglycerin; maintain DBP at a safe level to protect the mother from intracranial haemorrhage without compromising placental blood flow.
C(i) Antihypertensive drugs: hydralazine, labetalol, nifedipine, diazoxide, sodium nitroprusside, trimethaphan, nitroglycerin, methyldopa. Methyldopa is generally well tolerated; follow-up studies on offspring for 7 years show acceptable safety. ACE inhibitors (captopril, lisinopril) must be avoided because of the risk of fetal damage. Do not excessively lower BP as this may reduce placental blood flow and adversely affect fetal outcome.
C(ii) Monitoring during hospitalisation: daily — record BP 4 times; monitor urine output and test for proteinuria; daily clinical fetal monitoring (FHS, fundal height, abdominal girth, liquor, fetal movement count, CTG). Ultrasound on admission and as indicated. Weekly — monitoring of biochemical parameters. Look for appearance of ominous features. Fetal surveillance: serial ultrasound, Doppler USS of umbilical blood flow, fetal kick chart, biophysical profile.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the cardiovascular and haematological changes of the puerperium, including changes in blood pressure (timing and pattern), blood volume, and haemoglobin levels in the days following delivery.
A(ii) Describe the benefits of breastfeeding for the infant, the management of breast engorgement in non-breastfeeding women, and the management of mastitis including the distinction between inflammatory mastitis and established abscess.
B(i) Describe the routine postnatal care schedule from hospital discharge to the six-week visit, including the content of the 2-week postnatal visit, the six-week visit findings that lead to clinic discharge, and the vaccines given to the baby at these visits.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Cardiovascular: following delivery, there is a transient rise in both diastolic and systolic blood pressure for the first 4 days; progressive fall in blood pressure thereafter; pre-pregnancy pressures reached by the majority of women by 6 weeks after delivery. Blood volume: falls progressively after delivery. Haemoglobin: initial rise on the first day after delivery (from falling blood volume); followed by a sharp fall to a minimum level on the 4th and 5th days; then rises back to the level of the first day by the 9th day.
A(ii) Benefits of breastfeeding: passive immunity from immunoglobulins in breast milk, fewer gastrointestinal symptoms, fewer neonatal seizures, lower incidence of autoimmune conditions (e.g., juvenile-onset diabetes), reduced risk of sudden infant death syndrome, psychological advantages for the baby, possibly higher IQ. Management of breast engorgement in non-breastfeeding women: ice packs, tight bra, analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs; Bromocriptine (Parlodel) can be prescribed if needed; expression should be avoided; warm bathing of breasts; firm support with a good bra and adequate analgesia. Mastitis: acute inflammatory mastitis is due to failure of milk withdrawal from a lobule; treatment involves getting the baby to empty the breast, cold compresses, and antibiotics if there is no improvement within 24 hours. Infective mastitis may be due to Staph. aureus — treat with a sensitive antibiotic. Established breast abscess: antibiotics are of value only if given early; an established abscess requires surgical drainage.
B(i) Routine care: mothers are discharged 24 hours after SVD (stable and educated on newborn care), 48 hours for SVDs in general, and ≤ 4 days for Caesarean section. Before discharge: counselling on breastfeeding, contraception, and puerperium care; mother discharged on haematinics; babies receive first dose of OPV and BCG vaccine before discharge. First postnatal visit at 2 weeks: baby weighed and fully examined; enquiries about breastfeeding made and counselling given; general examination of the mother with particular emphasis on the genital tract; vaginal examination not necessarily done unless indicated; counselling about contraception emphasised. Six-week visit: general examination of mother and baby; if no problems, both are discharged from the clinic; baby receives second dose of OPV and DPT vaccines. Subsequent immunisations are done at child welfare clinics.

(i) Diagnosis: megaloblastic anaemia due to folate deficiency.
(ii) Causes:
- Low intake: anorexia, nausea, vomiting; goat milk poor in folate; malabsorption syndrome/GIT disease
- High demand: pregnancy; hookworm/chronic anaemia
- Loss: folate excretion high in pregnancy; prolonged cooking destroys folate
- Antifolate drugs: phenytoin, pyrimethamine, trimethoprim
For Vit B12: low intake (vegetarian); intrinsic factor lack (gastrectomy, pernicious anaemia); intestinal causes (ileal diseases and resection, Diphyllobothrium latum infection)
(iii) Clinical features: ill-looking, obvious anaemia and dyspnoea; tongue—painful, with papillary flattening, may be smooth or mapped with dark red patches, apthous ulceration of tongue/mouth; spleen/liver may be enlarged; retinal and subcutaneous petechial haemorrhage (platelet production affected); protracted vomiting, anorexia; little/no weight gain or actual weight loss; history of intermittent/persistent diarrhoea (suggests intestinal malabsorption).
(iv) Investigations: blood film; serum iron, total iron binding capacity, serum folate, serum ferritin; red cell folate; bone marrow aspirations; liver function tests; stool microscopy; urine analysis/MCS; electrophoresis; CXR (with abdominal shield); renal function tests; reticulocyte count; Coombs test.
Treatment: folic acid supplementation; treat any identifiable cause (malaria, UTI, hookworm); blood transfusion if needed based on gestational age and severity.
(v) Fetal cord blood folate is usually higher than maternal values at the time of delivery.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman at 34 weeks presents with pallor, dyspnoea, and palpitations. She is found to have a PCV of 22% and blood film shows macrocytic red cells with a smooth, mapped tongue with dark red patches, papillary flattening, and hepatosplenomegaly. She has protracted vomiting, anorexia, and a history of intermittent diarrhoea.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the causes of this type of anaemia (covering dietary, demand, loss, and drug-related causes)?
(iii) Describe the clinical features of this condition.
(iv) What investigations are needed and what is the treatment?
(v) What is the significance of fetal cord blood folate in relation to maternal levels at delivery?

Describe the pathophysiology, fetal effects, and management of Rhesus haemolytic disease under the following headings:
A(i) Development of Rh antibodies: the initial immune response and its timing.
A(ii) Factors that determine the inborn ability of a mother to respond to Rh antigenic stimulus.
B(i) Fetal and neonatal pathology resulting from haemolysis.
B(ii) Prediction of severity using obstetric history, paternal genotype, and maternal antibody.
C(i) Antenatal management of the sensitised mother: monitoring and intrauterine therapy.
C(ii) Management at and after birth.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Fetomaternal transfusion is the main trigger. Sources of fetomaternal haemorrhage: abortion (especially following D&C and MVA); normal pregnancy, particularly multiple gestation; antepartum haemorrhage; amniocentesis; external cephalic version; trauma. Initial maternal stimulation produces IgM antibodies that do not cross the placenta. IgG antibodies are produced between 6 weeks and 6 months later; they cross the placenta and coat fetal Rh-positive red blood cells.
A(ii) Other determinant factors: the inborn ability of the mother to respond to the Rh antigenic stimulus; ABO incompatibility between fetal and maternal blood (ABO incompatibility offers partial protection against Rh sensitisation, as ABO-incompatible fetal red cells are rapidly cleared from the maternal circulation).
B(i) IgG anti-Rh antibodies cross and coat fetal red blood cells; the fetal reticuloendothelial system destroys the coated cells. Fetal effects: haemolysis of fetal RBCs leading to fetal anaemia; extra-medullary erythropoiesis (compensatory); severe fetal anaemia leading to hydrops fetalis; IUFD. Neonatal effects: kernicterus — rapid rise in unconjugated bilirubin after birth damages the brain, especially the basal ganglia, if bilirubin reaches a critical level. The liver in the immature neonate cannot adequately conjugate bilirubin.
B(ii) Obstetric history: it tends to become more severe in successive pregnancies; if at least one child has died from Rhesus haemolytic disease, the chance of this pregnancy ending successfully is less than 50%. Paternal genotype: about 75% of fathers of affected children are homozygous; if homozygous, all children will be Rh-positive. Maternal antibody: once detected, must be measured at least monthly; serum antibody protein levels of greater predictive value than titres; a rapid increase suggests acute haemolysis.
C(i) In unsensitised women: check for Rh antibodies at booking, 28, 32, and 36 weeks. Amniocentesis: determines amount of bilirubin in the liquor; timing — 10 weeks before the earliest previous IUD, the birth of a severely affected infant, or between 28 and 30 weeks if no previous history; repeat every 3–4 weeks based on bilirubin levels. Intrauterine transfusion: indicated in severely affected fetus not mature enough for delivery; use fresh Rh-negative, ABO-compatible blood; earliest between 28 and 30 weeks if no previous severely affected fetus; repeat every 2–3 weeks as needed.
C(ii) At delivery: cord blood for blood grouping, direct Coombs test, bilirubin, haemoglobin. Early delivery in severely affected fetus in absence of IUT; induction of labour or CS if less than 34 weeks. After birth: treatment depends on degree of anaemia and jaundice; may include transfusion, exchange transfusion, and phototherapy. Anti-D administration: 300 mcg after delivery if baby is Rh-positive, within 72 hours.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 3, presents at 22 weeks gestation with a blood pressure of 152/98 mmHg. Review of her antenatal records shows she was hypertensive before 20 weeks. She has no proteinuria on dipstick. Her urine shows no casts.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what are the causes of this condition?
(ii) What high-risk features increase the risk of superimposed pre-eclampsia?
(iii) What maternal complications are associated with the development of superimposed pre-eclampsia?
(iv) What antihypertensive agents are used in this condition, and which must be avoided and why?
(v) Describe the obstetric management including fetal surveillance and criteria for timing of delivery.
questions.answerText:
(i) Chronic pre-existing hypertension in pregnancy, defined as hypertension occurring prior to pregnancy or before the 20th week of gestation, which persists in the puerperium, or is detected at booking. Causes: essential hypertension is the underlying cause in 90% of cases. Other causes include renal disease (glomerulonephritis, polycystic disease, renal artery stenosis, diabetic nephropathy), collagen vascular disease (SLE, scleroderma), coarctation of the aorta, and phaeochromocytoma. Before diagnosing essential hypertension, these other possibilities must be excluded.
(ii) High-risk features for superimposed PIH: renal disease; maternal age above threshold; diabetes mellitus; connective tissue disease (e.g., SLE); coarctation of the aorta; BP of 160/100 mmHg or more in early pregnancy; duration of hypertension; cardiomyopathy; antiphospholipid syndrome. Superimposed PIH may occur in up to one-third of women with pre-existing hypertension, and is more likely in those with renal disease.
(iii) Maternal complications of superimposed pre-eclampsia: eclampsia; abruption (with severe hypertension, risk is 50%); heart failure and intracranial haemorrhage; fetal morbidity and mortality closely related to degree of severity and gestational age at delivery; placental insufficiency leading to growth restriction.
(iv) Preferred antihypertensives: methyldopa (generally well tolerated; follow-up studies on offspring for 7 years); nifedipine; hydralazine (acts within 15 minutes in emergency). ACE inhibitors (captopril, lisinopril) must be avoided because of the risk of fetal damage. Diuretics should also be avoided. Do not excessively lower BP, as this may reduce placental blood flow and adversely affect fetal outcome.
(v) Obstetric management: continuous fetal monitoring in labour due to growth restriction; low threshold for caesarean section if there is any sign of deteriorating maternal or fetal wellbeing; MgSO4 if signs of pre-eclampsia develop. Fetal surveillance: monthly ultrasound assessment of fetal size from 24 weeks; from weeks 32–34, weekly umbilical artery Doppler; fetal heart rate monitoring and amniotic fluid volume. Admit for more frequent BPP if unsatisfactory fetal growth, abnormalities in liquor volume, or abnormal umbilical artery Doppler. Deliver by 38 weeks to minimise risk of stillbirth; preterm delivery if there is deterioration in renal function or evidence of fetal compromise. Post-natally, maternal BP will often resume pre-pregnancy levels, but careful observation in the first 48 hours because of a persisting risk of eclampsia.

questions.question:
A) Describe the anatomical changes in the uterus and abdominal wall that are characteristic of grandmultiparity, under the following headings:
A(i) The effect on uterine musculature and the consequence for uterine contractility
A(ii) The effect on the abdominal wall and its obstetric consequence for fetal lie

B) For each of the following antepartum complications in grandmultiparity, explain the anatomical or physiological basis: abnormal lie and malpresentations; antepartum haemorrhage from abruptio placentae and placenta praevia; premature rupture of membranes.

C) Explain why grandmultiparity predisposes to utero-vaginal prolapse in the postpartum period, and state all the postpartum management steps including definitive contraception.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Effect on uterine musculature:
- In grandmultiparity, uterine muscles undergo replacement by fibrosis with repeated pregnancies.
- This fibrosis impairs the normal contractility of the uterus.
- Clinically, this results in uterine inertia in labour, failure to progress, dysfunctional labour, and prolonged labour.
- It also predisposes to postpartum haemorrhage due to uterine atony, as the fibrosed uterus cannot contract adequately to achieve haemostasis at the placental site after delivery.

A(ii) Effect on the abdominal wall:
- The abdominal wall becomes lax and pendulous.
- A lax or pendulous abdomen allows the uterus to fall forward, reducing the support of the lower uterine segment.
- This abnormal uterine axis predisposes to abnormal fetal lie (transverse or oblique lie) and malpresentations.

B) Antepartum complications – anatomical and physiological basis:
- Abnormal lie and malpresentations: the lax and pendulous abdomen removes the anterior support of the uterus, allowing the fetus to adopt a transverse or oblique lie rather than longitudinal cephalic.
- Antepartum haemorrhage from abruptio placentae: the poorly contractile uterine muscle and the haemodynamic changes of repeated pregnancies predispose to premature separation of the placenta.
- Antepartum haemorrhage from placenta praevia: repeated pregnancies may cause abnormal placentation in the lower uterine segment, increasing the risk of placenta praevia.
- Premature rupture of membranes (PROM): an ill-fitting presenting part (due to abnormal lie) means forewaters are not protected from uterine contractions and rupture early.

C) Postpartum prolapse and management:
- Grandmultiparity predisposes to utero-vaginal prolapse because repeated deliveries stretch and weaken the pelvic floor musculature and supporting ligaments; fibrosis of the uterine muscle also reduces the structural support.
- Postpartum management:
 - Contraception: bilateral tubal ligation (BTL) – either postpartum or as an interval procedure.
 - Management of existing medical problems identified during pregnancy.
- Prevention of future grandmultiparity:
 - Female education and empowerment.
 - Promotion of contraception and family planning.
 - Increasing access to antenatal care; improving basic and essential obstetric care.
 - Legislation to discourage women from having more than 4 children.

(i) A plasma creatinine of 140 µmol/L places her in the moderate to severe impairment category; women in this group have lost a significant portion of their functional renal tissue. Rates of complications are increased due to worsening renal function, hypertension, and obstetric complications.
(ii) Maternal renal outcomes: 50% experience a reduction in GFR from the antepartum to 6 months postpartum; by 6 months post-delivery, 40% of women have a 25% decline in GFR, mostly from the antenatal period; 10% will have progressed to end-stage renal failure by 1 year; risk is particularly high in women whose initial serum creatinine exceeds a defined threshold. Unlike women with mild renal impairment, pregnancy tends to exacerbate renal injury. Proteinuria increases during pregnancy in 30% of cases.
(iii) Fetal risks include preterm delivery, small-for-gestational-age infant, and premature neonatal mortality (5–9%), lowered by modern neonatal intensive care. Placental insufficiency may lead to growth restriction; abruption is associated with poor outcome.
(iv) Incidence of hypertension in early pregnancy rises to 55% by the 3rd trimester in women with moderate CRD; with severe renal impairment, hypertension rises further. Development of PIH is associated with a decline in GFR during pregnancy; hypertension is an important factor in overall renal deterioration. Superimposed PIH may occur in up to one-third of women with pre-existing hypertension. Nephrotic range proteinuria in moderate/severe renal insufficiency is associated with worse pregnancy outcome; 20% of such women have no proteinuria and remain stable during pregnancy; 30% have proteinuria that increases during pregnancy.
(v) Fetal surveillance: monthly ultrasound assessment of fetal size from 24 weeks; from weeks 32–34, weekly umbilical artery Doppler; FHR monitoring and amniotic fluid volume. Admit for more frequent BPP if unsatisfactory fetal growth, abnormalities in liquor volume, or abnormal umbilical artery Doppler. Deliver by 38 weeks to minimise risk of stillbirth; preterm delivery if there is deterioration in renal function or evidence of fetal compromise.
questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation with known chronic renal disease (CRD) (plasma creatinine 140 µmol/L, underlying diffuse glomerulonephritis) presents for review. Her blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg and she has proteinuria of 1.5 g/24 hours.
(i) Into which severity category of renal impairment does her creatinine level place her, and what does this imply?
(ii) What maternal renal outcomes are expected during and after pregnancy in this severity category?
(iii) What are the fetal risks associated with this severity of renal disease?
(iv) What is the risk of developing superimposed PIH in this category, and what complication is specifically associated with nephrotic range proteinuria?
(v) Outline the fetal surveillance strategy and criteria for preterm delivery in this patient.

questions.answerText:
(i) Eisenmenger's complex components: interventricular septal defect; right ventricular hypertrophy; dextrorotation of the aorta overlying the septal defect. Fallot's Tetralogy = Eisenmenger's complex + pulmonary artery stenosis. Eisenmenger's complex proper refers to reversal of a left-to-right shunt through a VSD due to pulmonary hypertension, producing cyanosis.

(ii) NYHA Grade IV: cardiac disease; unable to carry out any physical activity without discomfort; has orthopnoea; symptoms at rest or with minimal activity. Implications: this is the most severe grade; requires in-patient care throughout pregnancy; maximum restriction of physical activity; multidisciplinary management with cardiologist; close monitoring for all factors promoting cardiac failure. The overall likelihood of a favourable outcome depends on functional cardiac capacity, absence of complications that increase cardiac load, and quality of medical care.

(iii) Congenital heart diseases listed: ventricular septal defect (VSD); patent ductus arteriosus (PDA); coarctation of the aorta; pulmonary stenosis; Eisenmenger's complex; interventricular septal defect; right ventricular hypertrophy; dextrorotation of the aorta; Fallot's tetralogy. Worst prognosis: Eisenmenger's complex and cyanotic heart disease (severe pulmonary hypertension); maternal mortality very high.

(iv) Physiological explanation: CO increases by 30–50% in pregnancy; early increase (first trimester) — augmented stroke volume due to decreased vascular resistance. By 16 weeks (early second trimester), significant haemodynamic alterations are already apparent — women with severe cardiac dysfunction may experience worsening of heart failure before midpregnancy. Later (28 weeks), hypervolaemia of pregnancy is maximal. Increased resting pulse and stroke volume (related to increased diastolic filling from augmented blood volume) further burden an already compromised right ventricle — worsening right-to-left shunt and hypoxaemia.

(v) Antenatal care goals: detect obstetric complications; advise patients on how to avoid aggravating the cardiac condition. Key components: joint management with cardiologist; fortnightly antenatal visits; ensure adequate rest/restrict physical activity; prevent anaemia; competent dental care; Grade IV — inpatient care; admit all patients a few days before term; treat active infection (admit); administer antibiotics throughout pregnancy if rheumatic fever recurred in previous 2 years; prophylactic Penicillin V for dental procedures; fetal surveillance.
questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman with a known ventricular septal defect (VSD) and Eisenmenger's complex presents at 16 weeks of gestation with increasing dyspnoea at rest. On examination, her oxygen saturation is 82% on room air. She has marked cyanosis and clubbing.

(i) What is Eisenmenger's complex? Describe its components.
(ii) What is the NYHA grade of this patient and what are the implications for her management?
(iii) What congenital heart diseases are, and which are associated with the worst prognosis in pregnancy?
(iv) Using the physiological changes of pregnancy, explain why this patient's condition has worsened in the second trimester.
(v) What are the goals and key components of antenatal care for women with heart disease in pregnancy?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Induction of labour: the stimulation of the uterus with the aim of starting labour to ensure delivery of the fetus at an appropriate time when the baby is thought to be safer outside the uterus than within it. Augmentation: enhancing uterine contraction when labour has started. Incidence: 3–25% (range across reports: 9.5–33.7% worldwide). Basic requirements: there must be an indication; contraindications must be excluded; personnel skilled in Caesarean section and facilities for C/S must be readily available; vaginal examination performed prior to commencement of oxytocin infusion; personnel familiar with effects of oxytocin and skilled at identifying complications must be in attendance; monitor as for high-risk patient in active labour. Fetal lie conditions: fetal lie must be longitudinal; adequate pelvis confirmed; previous uterine scars must be excluded — classical scar, hysterotomy, uteroplasty, myomectomy with breached endometrium, cornual resection.
A(ii) Amniotomy: an effective method when the cervix is favourable; labour commences within 12 hours of membrane rupture. Precautions against cord prolapse: exclude cord presentation prior to amniotomy, avoid dislodging the fetal head, fundal/suprapubic pressure while rupturing membranes may reduce risk, monitor fetal heart rate prior to and immediately after procedure. Timing with oxytocin: amniotomy should be performed when feasible prior to commencement of oxytocin infusion; synchronous amniotomy is when the time lag between the two events is ≤ 2 hours.
B(i) Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue. Advantages: cheap, has a long shelf-life, stable in tropical conditions. Routes of administration: oral or vaginal; oral dose is less effective. Dose: 25 mcg administered every 4–6 hours; may be used for cervical ripening and induction of labour. Main risk: more associated with hyperstimulation compared with other prostaglandins. General precaution (applies to all prostaglandins): oxytocin must not be started within 6 hours of prostaglandin administration.
questions.question:
A(i) Define induction of labour. Describe the basic requirements that must be fulfilled before induction is commenced, the conditions the fetal lie must satisfy, and what uterine scars constitute contraindications to certain methods.
A(ii) Describe amniotomy as a method of induction: when it is effective, precautions against cord prolapse, and when it should be performed in relation to oxytocin titration.
B(i) Describe misoprostol as an agent for induction of labour: its pharmacological class, advantages over other oxytocics, routes of administration, dose, interval, and its main risk compared with other prostaglandins.

A) Describe the caesarean section operation under the following headings:
A(i) The definition and gestational age criterion as stated, and how this differs from hysterotomy
A(ii) All the fetal indications for caesarean section
A(iii) All the maternal indications

B) State the rules governing previous caesarean section in subsequent pregnancies, including the risk of scar rupture by type, the principle for recurrent vs non-recurrent indications, and the stated complication rate of post-CS morbidity.

C) Describe classical (upper segment) caesarean section under the headings: indications as stated, the specific disadvantages of the classical incision, and the conditions requiring caesarean hysterectomy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and gestational age criterion:
- Caesarean section: the operation by which the fetus is delivered through an incision in the abdominal wall and the uterus after the 28th week of pregnancy.
- Similar procedure before 28 weeks is called hysterotomy.

A(ii) Fetal indications:
- Fetal malpresentation: best treatment for brow presentation; impacted mentoposterior face presentation; shoulder presentation with the fetus alive; breech presentation (advisable if mother is over 35 years, has been infertile, adverse obstetric history, small or ovoid pelvis, or large fetus; indicated in labour if breech does not descend onto pelvic floor after a few hours of regular contractions).
- Placental insufficiency suspected (inadequate fetal growth, maternal hypertension, or proteinuria).
- Fetal distress (postmaturity, hypertension, prolonged labour).
- Prolapse of the cord when the cervix is not sufficiently dilated to allow immediate vaginal delivery.
- To avoid further hypoxia in a compromised fetus (IUGR, maternal diabetes, preterm breech).
- Post-mortem caesarean section to save the life of the child.

A(iii) Maternal indications:
- Cephalopelvic disproportion: delay in labour with cautious oxytocic augmentation and no cervical progress, regardless of cause; trial of labour failed due to disproportion in a previous pregnancy.
- Previous repair of fistula, or successful treatment of stress incontinence.
- Pelvic tumour: impacted ovarian cyst or fibromyoma in the pelvis.
- Cervical or vaginal stenosis.
- Double uterus with obstruction.
- Antepartum haemorrhage: placenta praevia (major); abruptio placentae with a live fetus and continuing bleeding.
- Cardiac disease, respiratory disease, and most intercurrent medical disorders (when assisted vaginal delivery is not feasible).
- Fulminating pregnancy-induced hypertension when chances of speedy vaginal delivery are small.
- Bad obstetric history.
- Severe or fulminating pre-eclampsia.
- Risky vaginal delivery: placenta praevia, repaired VVF, or prolapse.
- Previous uterine injury: perforation, rupture, hysterotomy, uteroplasty.

B) Previous caesarean section rules:
- Principle: once a caesarean section, always a hospital delivery.
- Recurrent indication (e.g. contracted pelvis): repeat caesarean section.
- Non-recurrent indication (e.g. placenta praevia): trial of vaginal birth (VBAC); risk of second elective CS outweighs risk of rupture of lower segment scar at vaginal delivery.
- More than one previous CS: indication for repeat CS is stronger; usually bilateral tubal ligation for three or more previous caesarean sections.
- Risk of rupture: classical (upper segment) scar 2.2–4.7%; LSCS scar 0.5%.
- Post-CS morbidity (maternal mortality): 0.8 per 1000, which is 10 times that after vaginal delivery.

C) Classical caesarean section:
Indications: transverse lie with arm prolapsed or membranes ruptured; a fibroid preventing access to the lower segment; caesarean section in the presence of carcinoma of the cervix.
Disadvantages of classical incision:
- Free bleeding occurs.
- The incision cannot be covered with a free layer of loose peritoneum.
- It gives an insecure scar that may give way during subsequent pregnancy or labour.
Caesarean hysterectomy indications:
- Rupture of the uterus with gross damage or evidence of severe infection.
- Carcinoma of the cervix.

A(i) Dose, route, and pharmacokinetics:
- Dose: 100–150 mg, frequently given intramuscularly (IM).
- After IM injection there is a rapid increase in maternal serum pethidine concentration, followed by a similar and parallel increase in fetal serum pethidine concentration as the drug crosses the placenta freely.

A(ii) Intravenous administration:
- Single bolus injection.
- Patient-controlled analgesic (PCA) system.

A(iii) Neonatal ventilatory depression and reversal:
- Pethidine may induce ventilatory depression in the neonate.
- The paediatrician must be informed if pethidine was given within 3 hours of delivery.
- Reversal agent: naloxone 20 mg injected into the umbilical cord vein.

B) Cause of pain in each stage of labour:
- First stage: uterine contractions and dilatation of the cervix.
- Second stage: stretching, distension, and tearing of fascia, skin, and subcutaneous tissues; and pressure on the skeletal muscles of the perineum.
Pudendal block is insufficient for mid-cavity or rotational forceps delivery because:
- The block is safe with anaesthesia confined to the vagina.
- It is suitable only for outlet or low-cavity forceps delivery.
- Pain from mid-cavity, rotation, or ventouse deliveries is not relieved by pudendal block because these procedures involve structures above the level of the ischial spines and the upper vagina, which are not anaesthetised by pudendal block.

C) Inhalational analgesia with Entonox:
- Composition: 50% mixture of nitrous oxide and oxygen.
- Onset mechanism: rapid onset of analgesia attributable to the insoluble nature of nitrous oxide in blood; this also means equally rapid elimination.
- Mode of administration: self-administered.
- Why non-cumulative: rapid elimination due to the insolubility of nitrous oxide in blood means it does not accumulate; there are no physiological or biochemical consequences of note at the concentrations and durations used in obstetric practice.
- It provides a high inspired oxygen concentration.
- Usually used in conjunction with pethidine.
questions.question:
A) Describe pethidine as used in obstetric analgesia under the following headings:
A(i) Dose, route of administration, and the pharmacokinetic pattern after intramuscular injection (maternal and fetal serum concentrations)
A(ii) Intravenous administration options
A(iii) The mechanism and timing of neonatal ventilatory depression and the reversal agent, dose, and route

B) State the cause of pain in each stage of labour, and explain why pudendal block is insufficient for mid-cavity or rotational forceps delivery.

C) Describe inhalational analgesia with Entonox under the headings: composition, onset mechanism, mode of administration, and why it is non-cumulative.

A(i) Describe what prenatal diagnosis involves, listing all the abnormalities that can be identified and the three main categories of methods used.
A(ii) Describe the three invasive procedures used in prenatal diagnosis: amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling (CVS), and cordocentesis, including timing, route, and risk.
B(i) Describe the aims of prenatal screening in full.
B(ii) Describe the first trimester screening methods.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Prenatal diagnosis: the identification of chromosomal or structural abnormalities in the baby in-utero.
Abnormalities that can be identified:
- Chromosomal/single gene defects (e.g. SCD, CF)
- Structural defects (e.g. cardiac, CNS, GIT, GUS, MSS)
- Metabolic disorders (e.g. phenylketonuria, hypothyroidism)
Methods: (1) biochemical screening; (2) ultrasound/fetal Doppler's and echocardiography; (3) invasive procedures (amniocentesis, CVS, cordocentesis).
A(ii) Invasive procedures:
- Amniocentesis: previously used to measure amniotic acetylcholinesterase (AchE) for neural tube defects; also used for chromosomal karyotyping.
- CVS: usually performed from 10 weeks gestation; placental biopsy when performed after 1st trimester; more useful when large amounts of DNA are needed for monogenic disorders; can be performed transabdominally using 18–20 gauge needle; transcervical CVS is ideal for posterior low-lying placenta; potential risk for infection and procedure-related fetal loss is higher with transcervical route; direct chromosome preparations allow rapid karyotyping.
- Cordocentesis: fetal blood sampling from the umbilical cord, usually performed after 18 weeks gestation.
B(i) Aims of prenatal screening: reduces perinatal mortality (early detection/pregnancy termination); physical and psychological preparation of parents; facilitates in-utero transfer to specialist facilities; allows in-utero treatments to improve fetal conditions; sensitive test to screen fetuses for chromosomal diseases who may benefit from invasive procedures; reassures parents that the fetus is normal.
B(ii) First trimester screening: AFP was the first biochemical marker identified (1956); in 1974, the association of raised serum AFP and open spinal bifida was demonstrated; AFP is produced by the fetal liver; MSAFP rises from 12–32 weeks; measurement is multiple of the normal mean (MoM) at the relevant gestational age; greatest separation between affected and normal pregnancies is at 16–18 weeks.

questions.question:
Describe Rhesus iso-immunisation in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) The Rhesus factor and the mechanism of sensitisation.
A(ii) Causes of transplacental haemorrhage and timing of sensitisation.
B(i) Clinical features resulting from haemolysis in the affected fetus and newborn.
B(ii) Methods used to predict the severity of haemolysis.
C(i) Prevention using anti-D immunoglobulin.
C(ii) Treatment of the affected fetus and newborn.
