questions.answerText:
A(i) Red cell iso-immunisation with consequent placental transfer of antibodies is most commonly due to sensitisation of a Rhesus-negative mother by red cells positive for the Rhesus antigens (first discovered by Landsteiner and Wiener in 1940). Clinically significant Rhesus iso-immunisation is usually against the D antigen; anti-c or anti-Kell antibodies may also cause problems. A complex area of chromosome 1 produces the Rhesus antigen; over 95% of Rh incompatibility is due to the D antigen, inherited by simple Mendelian principles. About 75% of fathers of affected children are homozygous.
A(ii) Sensitisation may occur antenatally in 1–2% of previously unsensitised Rh-D-negative women in the absence of overt complications. It usually occurs at parturition due to fetomaternal haemorrhage. Other causes include abortions (spontaneous or induced), abruptio placentae, amniocentesis, and external cephalic version. Spontaneous fetomaternal transfusion occurs in 6.7% of women in the 1st trimester, 15.9% in the 2nd, and 28.9% in the 3rd trimester. Incompatible blood transfusion is another cause.
B(i) Depending on the degree of haemolysis, the pregnancy may result in miscarriage, intrauterine death, the birth of a severely hydropic infant with attendant obstetric complications, neonatal anaemia, or jaundice leading to kernicterus. In the newborn: anaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia (immature liver cannot conjugate the excess bilirubin), and kernicterus (bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia due to rapid rise in unconjugated bilirubin after birth). Excess bilirubin in the fetus is removed by the placenta; there is no fetal jaundice. Amniotic fluid contains bilirubin.
B(ii) Severity is predicted using: obstetric history (tends to become more severe in successive pregnancies; if at least one child has died from Rhesus haemolytic disease, the chance of this pregnancy ending successfully is less than 50%); maternal antibody levels (measured at least monthly; serum antibody protein levels of greater predictive value than titres; rapid increase suggests acute haemolysis); amniotic fluid bilirubin (spectrophotometry at OD 450 nm shows a peak directly proportional to bilirubin quantity); and fetal blood sampling under ultrasound guidance to check fetal haematocrit.
C(i) Anti-D 500 IU should be given to Rh-D-negative women as soon as possible after a potentially sensitising event. Doses: 50 mg for abortion before 20 weeks; 300 mg for amniocentesis, CVS, antepartum haemorrhage, and ECV; 300 mg after delivery if baby is Rh-positive, within 72 hours of delivery. Anti-D 500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks should be given to Rh-D-negative primigravidae and previously unsensitised women; this reduces the incidence of Rh sensitisation by at least a factor of 8.
C(ii) Treatment depends on the degree of haemolysis and gestational age. Delivery of a mature affected baby is the treatment of choice. Premature affected babies may require intrauterine transfusion of O Rh-negative, CMV-negative donor blood, cross-matched with maternal blood, irradiated in some centres; transfusion may be intraperitoneal or direct via a fetal vein such as the umbilical cord. After birth, treatment depends on the degree of anaemia and jaundice and may include transfusion, exchange transfusion, and phototherapy.

questions.question:
Describe asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and diagnostic threshold.
A(ii) Frequency of occurrence and populations most affected.
B(i) Importance and complications if left untreated.
B(ii) Bacteriology of the causative organisms.
C(i) Steps in diagnosis.
C(ii) Management.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Asymptomatic bacteriuria is the presence of significant numbers of bacteria in the urine of pregnant women in the absence of symptoms of urinary tract infection. By convention, the occurrence of 100,000 (10^5) or more organisms (colony counts) per millilitre of urine in a clean mid-stream specimen of urine is regarded as asymptomatic bacteriuria.
A(ii) Asymptomatic bacteriuria occurs in 6–10% of all pregnant women. It is commoner in multiparae than in primigravidae, and commoner in older women than in younger ones.
B(i) About 20–30% of affected women will develop frank urinary tract infection during the pregnancy, compared to only 3% of women without asymptomatic bacteriuria. Up to one-third go on to develop chronic urinary tract infections even after pregnancy. Other complications more common in affected women include spontaneous abortions, pre-eclampsia, pre-term labour and births (probably because of pyrexia and an irritant effect of the inflamed bladder on the adjacent myometrium), and anaemia in pregnancy.
B(ii) Escherichia coli is isolated in more than 90% of affected women. Other organisms commonly found include Klebsiella aerogenes, Proteus mirabilis, Streptococcus faecalis, Aerobacter aerogenes, and Staphylococcus aureus.
C(i) Proper specimen collection: swabbing of the introitus before voiding, and clean-catch mid-stream specimen. Prompt analysis (the number of bacteria in a urine sample doubles every 30 minutes at room temperature). Use of dip-sticks or dip-slides impregnated with nitrate-sensitive amines; urine microscopy, culture, and sensitivity tests; concomitant high vaginal/endocervical swabs.
C(ii) Educational hygiene, especially about cleaning the vestibule and introitus after defaecation and after coitus; high fluid intake; antibiotics (often controversial because of high recurrence rates of bacteriuria after treatment). A 7–10-day course of ampicillin or cephalosporins eliminates bacteriuria in approximately 70–80% of patients. Nitrofurantoin may also be used.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman is 38 weeks pregnant, grand multipara (para 6), with a history of previous spontaneous vaginal deliveries. She presents in active labour with a lax abdomen and a fetus in oblique lie.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what are the obstetric problems associated with grand multiparity?
(ii) What complications in labour and the puerperium are specifically for this patient?
(iii) What is the recommended management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) prevention in the grand multipara?
(iv) Name all the structural/anatomical risk factors that contribute to abnormal lie in high parity.
(v) If this patient delivers vaginally, what intrapartum precaution should be taken to prevent PPH, and what are the other methods of correcting obstetric haemorrhage?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: grand multipara at risk of abnormal lie and obstetric complications. Obstetric problems: abnormal lie/abnormal presentations (lax abdominal wall); precipitate labour; ruptured uterus; post-partum haemorrhage (PPH); placenta praevia; placental abruption; higher rates of anaemia (particularly with short inter-birth intervals); increased incidence of medical conditions (hypertension, glucose intolerance).
(ii) Complications in labour: abnormal lie/abnormal presentation; precipitate labour; ruptured uterus; PPH; maternal/fetal distress; perinatal death. Complications in the puerperium: poor lactation; sub-involution of the uterus.
(iii) PPH prevention: administer IV ergometrine after delivery of the anterior shoulder to prevent PPH; cautious use of oxytocin in multipara.
(iv) Structural/anatomical risk factors for abnormal lie: lax abdominal wall from previous pregnancies; increased rate of twinning associated with rising parity (abnormal lie/presentation more common in multiple pregnancy); polyhydramnios (in multiple pregnancy).
(v) Intrapartum precaution: administer IV ergometrine after delivery of the anterior shoulder to prevent PPH. Other methods of correcting obstetric haemorrhage include: blood transfusion (complicated by circulating antierythrocyte antibodies in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia); oral haematinics; parenteral iron; erythropoietin. For AIHA: glucocorticoids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day), coincidental thrombocytopenia corrected by therapy.

(i) Diagnosis: Vasa praevia — bleeding from fetal vessels. Embryological basis: results from velamentous insertion of the cord (the umbilical vessels run through the membranes before reaching the placenta, unsupported by Wharton's jelly, and may overlie the cervical os). When membranes rupture, these vessels rupture → fetal haemorrhage. Rare but significant: occurs in 1:5,000 singleton deliveries (Quek & Tan, 1987).

(ii) Confirmatory tests:
- Kleihauer-Betke test: detects fetal cells in maternal blood by acid elution — fetal haemoglobin is resistant to acid and stains pink while maternal cells appear as ghosts.
- Apt test (bedside): based on the alkali resistance of fetal haemoglobin — blood is mixed with 1% NaOH; if fetal blood, remains pink (HbF); if maternal, turns yellow-brown (HbA denatures).
Both tests confirm the presence of fetal blood in the vaginal loss.

(iii) Prognosis: fetal mortality is very high — 75–100%. Emergency management: immediate caesarean section is required to deliver the fetus urgently; there is no time for expectant management. Neonatologist must be present. Blood transfusion for the neonate.

(iv) Full list of investigations for APH: serial PCV; full blood count; blood grouping and cross-match; clotting time; prothrombin time / PTTK; fibrinogen assay; fibrin degradation products; renal function tests; ultrasonography; radioisotope imaging; arteriography; magnetic resonance imaging; Apt test; Kleihauer-Betke test; maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein.

(v) Differential diagnosis of APH: Placental — placenta praevia; placental abruption; circumvallate placenta. Fetal — rupture of vasa praevia. Pathology of lower genital tract (incidental/extra-placental) — cervical polyp; cervical ectopy/ectropion; cervicitis; cervical carcinoma; vaginitis; friable condylomata. Treatment of incidental causes: trichomoniasis — metronidazole; candidiasis — clotrimazole; cervical carcinoma — therapeutic abortion/conventional treatment (surgery or radiotherapy); cervical polyp — polypectomy; cervical erosion — cautery; cervicitis — antibiotics. Unknown/undetermined: 50% of APH cases.
questions.question:
A primigravida at 37 weeks of gestation presents with sudden, painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding at the time of spontaneous rupture of membranes. The fetal heart rate deteriorates rapidly to a bradycardia of 80 bpm. The blood appears to be of a different colour to maternal blood.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what is its embryological basis?
(ii) What bedside and laboratory investigations confirm the diagnosis, and what is their principle?
(iii) What is the prognosis and what emergency management is required?
(iv) Name the full list of investigations that should be performed in any patient presenting with APH.
(v) Describe the complete differential diagnosis of APH and the non-placental causes of APH (incidental/extra-placental causes).

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: secondary postpartum haemorrhage (secondary PPH).
- Timing: usually between the 5th and 10th day postpartum, but can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum.

(ii) Causes of secondary PPH:
- Retained placenta.
- Fibroids.
- Infection (puerperal sepsis).
- Infected slough of the cervix or vaginal laceration.
- Infected caesarean section wound.

(iii) Complete management:
Investigations:
- High vaginal swab for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity (MCS).
- Ultrasound scan (USS) to identify retained products of conception.
Interventions:
- Antibiotics (specific antibiotic choice based on MCS result).
- Examination under anaesthesia (EUA) with exploration and evacuation of the uterine cavity if retained products are found.

(iv) Prevention by active management of the third stage:
- Active management of the third stage of labour is the cornerstone of preventing primary PPH.
- It entails:
 - Administering IV ergometrine or syntocinon (oxytocin) at the delivery of the anterior shoulder to stimulate uterine contraction before placental separation.
 - Delivering the placenta by controlled cord traction once a sign of separation is noted.
 - Ensuring completeness of the placenta after delivery.
- Prevention during pregnancy also includes: eradicating anaemia (regular PCV checks; treating malaria, UTI, and poor nutrition); treating abnormal labour early; avoiding general anaesthesia with halothane if possible; maintaining IV access and crossmatching blood for high-risk patients (previous PPH, twin pregnancy, grandmultiparae, previous caesarean section).
questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman who had a lower segment caesarean section 8 days ago presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and fever. On examination the uterus is tender and the lochia is offensive. A high vaginal swab has been sent.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and between what days postpartum does this condition typically occur?
(ii) List all the causes of this condition.
(iii) Describe the complete management, including investigations and all interventions stated.
(iv) Explain how primary PPH could have been prevented in the first instance by active management of the third stage, and list what active management entails.

A. Describe antepartum haemorrhage (APH) under the following headings:
A(i) Definition (including the historical evolution of the gestational limit used)
A(ii) Incidence
A(iii) Causes and their relative proportions
A(iv) Classification systems used clinically

B. Explain the clinical basis for the distinction between revealed, concealed, and mixed haemorrhage in abruptio placentae.

C. Distinguish between placenta praevia and abruptio placentae with respect to their clinical presentation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: APH is bleeding from the genital tract from 28 completed weeks of pregnancy to the birth of the baby. Traditionally 28 completed weeks was used; the limit has been revised to 24 completed weeks because of improved survival of infants delivered at 24 weeks (35%), and because FIGO perinatal death statistics include fetuses born after 22 weeks or weighing 500 g. Some definitions (e.g., WHO, Stirrat 2003) use 24 weeks as the lower limit.

A(ii) Incidence: Bleeding during the 2nd and 3rd trimester is relatively common; 6–8% of all pregnancies (Ananth et al, 1997); 2–5% of pregnancies progressing beyond 24 weeks; 1.2–1.8% in Ghana (Kwawukume, 2002). Total incidence of about 3% is not unusual, with cases approximately equally divided among the three clinical categories.

A(iii) Causes and proportions: Placenta praevia — 20%; Abruptio placentae — 30%; Unknown/undetermined aetiology — 50% (Sholl, 1987). Other causes: pathology of lower genital tract (cervical polyp, ectopy, cervicitis, carcinoma, vaginitis, condylomata); fetal — rupture of vasa praevia; circumvallate placenta.

A(iv) Classification: (1) Practical classification (Scott, 1964): Placenta praevia; Placental abruption; Indeterminate APH. (2) Praevia types — Type I (low lying, within 5 cm of os); Type II (marginal, at margin of os); Type III (partial, partly covering os); Type IV (total, completely covering os). Minor degree: Types Ia/b and IIa; Major degree: Types IIb, III, IV.

B. In abruptio placentae the haematoma formed after rupture of uteroplacental arteries may: be retained inside the uterus (concealed haemorrhage); track down to the cervix and vagina (revealed haemorrhage); break into the amniotic cavity (port-wine discolouration of liquor). The most common pattern is mixed bleeding.

C. Placenta praevia: painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding; soft non-tender uterus; abnormal lie (oblique/transverse) or high presenting part; fetal heart audible; no shock disproportionate to visible loss. Abruptio placentae: triad of vaginal bleeding (80–90%), abdominal pain (50%), and abnormal uterine tenderness; hypertonic uterus that fails to relax; fetal parts difficult to palpate; fetal heart may be inaudible; signs of shock may exceed visible blood loss (concealed haemorrhage).

A(i) Primary HIV infection and seroconversion: 2–4-week period of intense viral replication before onset of immune response; 1–2 weeks of acute illness (seroconversion illness) in 53–93% of cases — flu-like illness, neurological, gastrointestinal, and dermatological symptoms; clinical manifestations resolve as antibodies become detectable. Laboratory: first 1–2 weeks — reduction in CD4 and CD8 cells with inversion of CD4:CD8 ratio (normal 2:1), then lymphocytosis, mild thrombocytopenia, elevated CRP and ESR; window period 2–6 weeks (may last up to 3 months, rarely 6–12 months); P24 antigen may be detectable before antibodies. Stages: early immune depletion (CD4 > 500/µl) — low viral load, HIV replication limited to lymph nodes, lasts 5 or more years, persistent generalised lymphadenopathy, usually asymptomatic. Intermediate immune depletion (CD4 200–500/µl) — infections start and persist, especially of skin and mucosal surfaces, reactivation of herpes zoster, Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Advanced immune depletion (CD4 < 200/µl) — case definition of AIDS.
A(ii) Routes of MTCT: in utero (late in pregnancy) — 23–35%; intrapartum (at birth) — 65%; late postpartum (breastfeeding) — 12%. Maternal factors increasing risk: high maternal viral load (> 5,000–10,000 copies/ml), low CD4 count (< 100 cells/mm³), seroconversion during pregnancy, late HIV disease; behavioural factors (cigarette smoking, hard drug use, unprotected sexual intercourse during pregnancy, STIs). Placental factors: Hofbauer cells and possibly trophoblasts express CD4+ cells, chorioamnionitis, placental abruption, placental P. falciparum infestation.
B(i) Specific interventions: screen and treat STIs in pregnant women, avoid unprotected sexual intercourse, drug use, and smoking. All pregnant HIV-positive women are candidates for ARV therapy. AZT/NVP have merit in reducing perinatal transmission; most perinatal transmission occurs at the time of delivery. ACTG 076 study: AZT from 14 weeks decreased risk of MTCT by nearly 70% in non-breastfeeding populations; AZT from 36 weeks reduced risk by 37% (breastfeeding) to 50% (non-breastfeeding) at 6 months. Safe delivery practices: avoid invasive tests, consider Caesarean delivery. Safe infant-feeding practices are essential.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the natural history of HIV infection from primary seroconversion to advanced immune depletion, including the laboratory findings at each stage, the CD4 count thresholds that define each stage, and the case definition of AIDS.
A(ii) Explain the routes and timing of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV, the percentage contribution of each route, and the maternal and placental factors that increase the risk of transmission.
B(i) Describe the specific interventions used to prevent MTCT, including the antiretroviral strategy and the efficacy of zidovudine (AZT) as reported in the ACTG 076 study. State the safe infant-feeding approach.

A 36-year-old woman at 24 weeks gestation with a history of two previous pregnancies complicated by hypertension is found at booking to have a blood pressure of 148/94 mmHg. She has retinal changes on fundoscopy and cardiac enlargement on chest X-ray. She is currently on methyldopa.
(i) What do the retinal and cardiac findings indicate about her hypertensive disease?
(ii) In what way does blood pressure behaviour in mid-pregnancy affect the diagnosis of hypertension in such patients?
(iii) What maternal risks does this patient face if superimposed PIH develops?
(iv) What is the monitoring strategy during her antenatal care?
(v) What postpartum monitoring is required, and why?
questions.answerText:
(i) Retinal changes on fundoscopic examination and cardiac enlargement on chest X-ray and ECG are features seen in chronic hypertension with end-organ involvement. These changes, along with the presence of a known medical disorder, indicate that her hypertensive disease has been longstanding and has already caused end-organ damage. These are 'other changes apart from BP changes seen in chronic hypertension.'
(ii) In mid-pregnancy, BP can be in the normal range in women with severe hypertension prior to pregnancy, because BP falls during the 1st and 2nd trimester in all women. This may lead to a patient appearing normotensive at booking (early pregnancy), masking the diagnosis of chronic hypertension. Caution is required in BP assessment during pregnancy; the patient may appear normotensive at booking but have chronic pre-existing hypertension detected later in pregnancy or in the puerperium.
(iii) Maternal risks if superimposed PIH develops: eclampsia; abruption (with severe hypertension, risk is 50%); heart failure and intracranial haemorrhage; fetal morbidity and mortality closely related to degree of severity and gestational age at delivery; placental insufficiency leading to growth restriction.
(iv) Monitoring strategy during antenatal care: joint care by obstetrician and nephrologist; frequent antenatal visits — fortnightly until 32 weeks, weekly thereafter; daily monitoring of BP (4 times daily), urine output, and testing for proteinuria; fetal surveillance — daily clinical fetal monitoring (FHS, fundal height, abdominal girth, liquor, fetal movement count, CTG); serial ultrasound and Doppler assessment; weekly monitoring of relevant biochemical parameters; close surveillance for signs of superimposed pre-eclampsia.
(v) Post-natal monitoring: maternal BP will often resume its pre-pregnancy level, but careful observation is needed in the first 48 hours because of a persisting risk of eclampsia. Long-term antihypertensive therapy should be reviewed. Women with CRD should also have renal function assessed postpartum.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the physiology of lactation including the hormones involved in mammary growth, the mechanism of milk secretion, and the let-down reflex.
A(ii) State the composition and timeline of breast milk production, including colostrum and the average volumes produced.
B(i) List the benefits of breastfeeding for the infant and mother.
B(ii) Describe the Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI): when it was launched, its aim, the conditions that must not be accepted, and all ten steps to successful breastfeeding.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Physiology of lactation:
Puberty: milk ducts linking nipple to secretory alveoli are stimulated by oestrogen.
Pregnancy: further growth occurs; pre-existing alveoli-lobular structures hypertrophy; new ones also formed; milk collecting ducts undergo branching and proliferation.
Hormones involved in mammary growth: oestrogen, progesterone, prolactin, growth hormone and adrenal steroids.
Minimal milk is formed during pregnancy due to inhibition of lactogenic hormones by high levels of oestrogen and progesterone from the placenta.
Milk secretion: sucking causes release of prolactin; prolactin acts on glandular cells to stimulate secretion.
Milk ejection (let-down) reflex: mediated by oxytocin from posterior pituitary; causes contraction of myoepithelial cells; stimulated by sucking, cry of baby, sight of baby; rapidly inhibited by emotional stress.
A(ii) Colostrum is first secreted and lasts about 4 days; rich in carotenoids and protein. Amount of milk produced: 500 ml by sixth day; 800 ml averagely when lactation is fully established; some produce 2–3 litres per day; can sustain a baby alone for 4–6 months. Adequate maternal nutrition is necessary. Smoking and alcohol affect milk volume.
B(i) Benefits: nutritional benefits; protection against infections; reduced incidences of vomiting and diarrhoea; protection against respiratory tract infections; high lactoferrin content binds iron required for growth by E. coli; encourages growth of non-pathogenic organisms in gut; IgA binds offending organisms; contains polymorphs, lymphocytes and plasma cells; neurological benefit (improved cognition); reduced atopic illnesses; reduced breast cancer among mothers who breastfed; cheap and accessible; reduced juvenile-onset diabetes mellitus, inflammatory bowel disease and neoplastic disease.
B(ii) BFHI: launched in 1991 by WHO and UNICEF; aim is to ensure all maternities become centres of breastfeeding support; consists of ten steps based on scientific evidence; a maternity is designated baby-friendly when it does not accept free or low-cost breast milk substitutes, feeding bottles, teats or pacifiers, and has implemented the 10 steps.
10 Steps: (1) have a written BF policy communicated to all health care providers; (2) train all health care staff; (3) inform all pregnant women about benefits and management of BF; (4) help mothers initiate BF within one half-hour of birth; (5) show mothers how to breastfeed and maintain lactation even if separated from infants; (6) give newborns no food or drink other than breastmilk unless medically indicated; (7) practise rooming-in (mothers and infants together 24 hours a day); (8) encourage breastfeeding on demand; (9) give no artificial teats or pacifiers to breastfeeding infants; (10) foster establishment of BF support groups and refer mothers on discharge.

(i) X-ray pelvimetry is indicated. Specific indications: suspected disproportion (baby is big or there was a difficult previous delivery); previous CS × 1 and contemplating vaginal delivery; breech presentation at 36 weeks or later; pelvic trauma — nutritional (history of rickets in childhood) or RTA involving the pelvis; previous delivery by CS due to CPD, postpartum to confirm.

(ii) Information derived: relationship of the presenting part to the pelvic brim; detection of abnormalities of shape of the pelvis; serves as a permanent record for medico-legal purposes. CT pelvimetry (Computer Assisted Tomography) — used to assess suitability of vaginal delivery in suspected fetopelvic disproportion; taken in AP and transverse views; advantage: detects small masses easily; uses less radiation (~4× less than conventional X-ray).

(iii) Types: A. X-rays — plain film (shows air in lungs and intestine; liquids/fluids in abnormal places; foreign bodies e.g. IUCD); contrast studies (CO₂/room air; oil-based solutions in HSG; water-soluble solutions in IVU, barium studies). B. CT Scan — slices the body into various parts; relatively expensive; not widely available. C. Radioisotope imaging. D. Arteriography. E. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). Advantage of radiology: permanent record for medicolegal reasons (e.g. HSG showing hydrosalpinges, tubal blockage with uterine fibroid).

(iv) Hazards of radiation: possibility of irradiation of the gonads (totipotent cells — small alteration can lead to wide changes in the developing zygote); increased risk of childhood leukaemia; radiation burns to skin, intestine, vaginal walls (X-rays cause endarteritis, resulting ulcers heal slowly); depression of immunity; destruction of stem cells of normal body cells.

(v) Placental localisation techniques: (1) Soft-tissue placentography — inject contrast to outline placental vasculature; if distance between fetal skull and pubic symphysis >2 cm or head >2 cm from sacral promontory, placenta praevia suggested. (2) Aortographic studies — contrast injected into vein; shows hypervascularity at placenta; not done when baby is alive as contrast can cause fetal damage and maternal embolism can be fatal. (3) Amniography — contrast injected into amniotic fluid; not desired for living fetus due to adverse effects. These techniques are largely superseded by USS.
questions.question:
A woman with a previous caesarean section for cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) presents at 36 weeks with a breech presentation. The clinician suspects a contracted pelvis and requests radiological assessment.

(i) What radiological investigation is indicated and what are the specific indications for requesting it?
(ii) What information can be derived from this investigation?
(iii) Name and describe the other types of radiology investigations available in obstetrics and gynaecology, including their advantages and disadvantages.
(iv) What are the hazards of radiation exposure in pregnancy that limit the use of radiology?
(v) What placental localisation techniques using contrast/radiology were described, and what are their limitations?

A 38-year-old woman with known chronic renal disease (plasma creatinine 280 µmol/L) presents at 10 weeks gestation for pre-pregnancy counselling which she delayed. She has diffuse glomerulonephritis, and her blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg.
(i) How should you counsel this patient about her prognosis for renal function during and after this pregnancy?
(ii) What fetal risks must be discussed?
(iii) What antihypertensive changes are required and what must be avoided?
(iv) What is the monitoring strategy for renal function during antenatal care?
(v) What is the criterion and gestational age threshold for delivery in this patient?
questions.answerText:
(i) With moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine 280 µmol/L), she has already lost a significant portion of her functional renal tissue. Rates of complications are markedly increased. Unlike women with mild renal impairment, pregnancy tends to exacerbate renal injury. By 6 months post-delivery, 40% of women in this category have a 25% decline in GFR, mostly from the antenatal period; 10% will have progressed to end-stage renal failure by 1 year; risk is particularly high in women whose initial serum creatinine exceeds a defined threshold. Her underlying pathology (diffuse glomerulonephritis) carries a high risk of long-term deterioration. She must be informed of the risk of serious deterioration, severe hypertension, and adverse perinatal outcome.
(ii) Fetal risks: preterm delivery; small-for-gestational-age infant; premature neonatal mortality (5–9%), lowered by modern neonatal intensive care; placental insufficiency leading to growth restriction; increased risk of stillbirth. Closely related to the degree of severity of maternal disease and the gestational age at delivery.
(iii) Appropriate drugs: methyldopa, nifedipine, and hydralazine. Diuretics should be avoided. If she is on ACE inhibitors (captopril, lisinopril), these must be changed immediately as they cause fetal damage. Her current medication must be reviewed and changed to safer alternatives. Do not excessively lower BP as this may reduce placental blood flow.
(iv) Close surveillance: joint care by obstetrician and nephrologist; assess renal function (plasma creatinine, GFR, proteinuria) at each visit. Monthly ultrasound assessment of fetal size from 24 weeks; from weeks 32–34, weekly umbilical artery Doppler; FHR monitoring and amniotic fluid volume; admit for more frequent BPP if unsatisfactory fetal growth, abnormalities in liquor, or abnormal Doppler.
(v) Deliver by 38 weeks to minimise risk of stillbirth; preterm delivery is indicated if there is deterioration in renal function or evidence of fetal compromise. Continuous fetal monitoring in labour due to risk of growth restriction; low threshold for caesarean section if there is any sign of deteriorating maternal or fetal wellbeing.

A(i) Historical development:
- Edward Rigby (1776): described and distinguished 2 types of 3rd trimester haemorrhage — unavoidable/inevitable and accidental haemorrhage.
- Baudelocque (1819): coined the term 'concealed haemorrhage' for abruptio placentae.
- Hicks (1861): presented 23 cases of concealed haemorrhage before the London Obstetric Society.
- DeLee (1892): coined the term abruptio placentae; postulated a haemophilia-like condition for abruption.
- Holmes (1901): introduced the term ablatio placentae.
- Couvelaire: described uteroplacental apoplexy.
- Williams & Wilson: postulated 'haemorrhagin' from placenta or fetus into maternal circulation causing clotting defect.
- Dieckmann (1936): causal relationship between fibrinogen levels and haemorrhage in premature placental separation.
- Pritchard: elucidated pathogenesis and treatment of the complications of abruptio placentae.

A(ii) Evolution of terms: Rigby (1775) — 'inevitable' (low-lying placenta) vs 'chance/accidental' (normally situated placenta). The term 'accidental' created confusion as it suggested a relationship to trauma, which is practically never present. Couvelaire introduced 'placental abruption.' Practical classification (Scott, 1964): placenta praevia; placental abruption; indeterminate APH. Also previously: True APH (bleeding from placental site) vs False APH (from lower genital tract) — a distinction of no practical importance since every vaginal blood loss before delivery should be assumed to be from the placenta until proven otherwise.

B. Controversies:
1. Cervical cerclage in placenta praevia: Advocate (Arias, 1988); No benefit — RCOG Guidelines 2001.
2. Tocolysis in placenta praevia and abruptio placentae using MgSO₄ or beta-sympathomimetics (e.g., ritodrine): RCOG 2001; Besinger 1995 — controversial, use carefully if benefit of delaying delivery for prematurity outweighs risks.
3. Prophylactic embolisation of uterine artery in patients with placenta praevia (Hansch E et al, 1999).

C. Complications of placenta praevia:
Maternal: postpartum haemorrhage; placenta accreta; haemorrhagic shock.
Fetal: IUGR; prematurity; intrauterine fetal death (IUFD).
Prognosis: good fetal outcome when appropriately managed.
questions.question:
A. Describe the historical development of understanding of antepartum haemorrhage under the following headings:
A(i) Key historical figures and their contributions from 1775 to the modern era
A(ii) How the terms used for the two main types of APH evolved

B. Describe the controversies in the management of placenta praevia and abruptio placentae, stating the arguments for and against each controversial intervention.

C. Summarise the complications of placenta praevia (maternal and fetal) and state the prognosis.

A(i) Describe oxytocin under the following headings: pharmacological properties, mechanism of action on the uterus, uterine response across gestation, and routes of administration.
A(ii) Describe the standard protocol for oxytocin titration, including the starting dose, escalation schedule, goal uterine contractile response, and the definition of hyperstimulation.
B(i) Describe the advantages and limitations of prostaglandins for induction of labour, and state the precaution to observe when prostaglandins and oxytocin are used sequentially.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Oxytocin is an octapeptide with a short half-life of 5–10 minutes. It binds to its receptors in the myometrium, altering the transmembrane ionic current and producing contractions. It also causes contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli, causing milk ejection. Routes of administration: intravenous infusion and nasal spray. Uterine response: increases slowly from 20–30 weeks; remains unchanged from 34 weeks until term; sensitivity increases rapidly at term. Stable-state plasma concentration for a given dose is achieved in 40–60 minutes.
A(ii) Standard dilution: 10 iu in 500 ml normal saline (3 ml/hour = 1 milliunit/min). Using an infusion pump, commence with 1–2 milliunits/min and increase at intervals of 30 minutes: 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 20 milliunits/min; adequate contractions may be established at 12 milliunits/min; maximum dose allowed is 32 milliunits/min. Alternatively: 2 units in 500 ml normal saline at 15 drops/min for 30 min, increasing to 30 drops/min, then 60 drops/min. If contractions are unsatisfactory, increase to 4 units in 500 ml saline starting from 60 drops/min; most women at term do not require more than 4 units. Goal: 3–4 contractions every 10 minutes. Hyperstimulation: ≥ 6 contractions in 10 minutes. Shorter intervals predispose to hyperstimulation.
B(i) Advantages of prostaglandins: produce a smooth and more natural onset of labour; allow ambulation in early labour before amniotomy; cause less salt and water retention (preferred in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia); less associated with hyperstimulation, primary PPH, and uterine rupture; preferred in grand multiparae. Dose: vaginal tablets 3 mg 6-hourly (maximum 6 mg). Limitations: high cost, unavailable in developing countries, frequent need for oxytocin augmentation, may be associated with intrapartum pyrexia, risk of hyperstimulation. Precaution: oxytocin must not be started within 6 hours of the administration of prostaglandins.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman in her fifth pregnancy delivers a 4.2 kg baby after a prolonged labour. Thirty minutes after delivery, the midwife notices continued brisk bleeding from the genital tract, a soft and enlarged uterus, rising fundal height, tachycardia, hypotension, and restlessness.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and how is it defined?
(ii) State the pathologic basis underlying this condition in this patient, covering all the causes listed under uterine atony.
(iii) Describe the immediate resuscitative measures that must be initiated.
(iv) Outline the full stepwise management from bimanual compression to definitive surgical intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Primary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). Defined as excessive bleeding from the genital tract after birth of the baby: more than 500 ml after vaginal delivery (more than 1000 ml after caesarean section), any amount causing circulatory disturbance, or a decrease in haematocrit of more than 10% from before to after delivery.

(ii) Pathologic basis in this patient:
- Uterine atony: the commonest cause; grandmultiparity leads to replacement of uterine muscles by fibrosis, impairing contraction.
- Uterine overdistension from a macrosomic baby (4.2 kg) reduces contractility.
- Mismanagement of the third stage: premature attempts to separate the placenta.
- Prolonged labour contributes to uterine inertia.
- Retained placenta, retained lobe, or blood clot.
- Genital sepsis.
- Prolonged or deep anaesthesia.
- Abruptio placentae (couvelaire uterus).
- Low-lying placenta or placenta praevia.
- Uterine inversion.

(iii) Immediate resuscitation:
- Lie patient supine; catheterise the bladder.
- Insert IV line including cut-down if needed; administer oxygen.
- Administer oxytocics: oxytocin, ergometrine, prostaglandins.
- Resuscitate with colloids, crystalloids, or O-negative blood.
- Raise foot of bed.
- Monitor vital signs: pulse, BP, CVP, PCWP.
- Apply antishock garment (ASG).

(iv) Stepwise management:
- Check whether uterus is soft or hard.
- Deliver placenta by controlled cord traction; ensure completeness.
- Bimanual compression.
- Uterine cavity packing.
- Uterine artery embolisation.
- Ligation of hypogastric (internal iliac) vessels.
- B-Lynch suture.
- Hysterectomy (definitive surgical intervention).

(i) HbA1c significance: HbA1c >10% indicates the most significant risk of malformation development. At 9.2–11.1%: 23% rate of congenital malformation; >11.2%: 25%. Patients with long-standing diabetes (glycohaemoglobin exceeding 11%) have been shown to have miscarriage rates of up to 44%. Periconceptional glycaemic control is the main factor in the genesis of diabetes-associated birth defects, which occur during the critical period 3–6 weeks after conception. Most lesions involve the central nervous and cardiovascular systems.

(ii) Preconception measures: achieve maternal normoglycaemia before conception (poor glycaemic control during organogenesis associated with increased major congenital anomalies and spontaneous abortions); discuss appropriate contraception until adequate metabolic control is achieved; optimise glycaemic control; medical assessment and screening for vascular/chronic complications preconception; educate on dietary therapy; educate on self-monitoring of blood glucose and self-care; lower HbA1c to <6% (target); folic acid supplementation; education — crucial to achieve and maintain normoglycaemia.

(iii) Dietary management (diet is the cornerstone of therapy): goals — maintain normoglycaemia; bring about good fetal health; prevent ketosis. Normal-weight women ~30 kcal/kg/day based on present pregnant weight. Overweight women: fewer calories needed (~24 kcal/kg/day). More obese: 12–15 kcal/kg/day. Distribution: breakfast 25%, lunch 30%, dinner 30%, bedtime snack 15%. Composition: carbohydrate 50%, fat 30%, protein 20%. Avoid concentrated or refined sugars. Moderate physical exercise shown to facilitate normoglycaemia.

(iv) Postpartum risk profile for GDM: almost 98% of women with GDM revert to normoglycaemia after delivery; increased risk for gestational diabetes and type 2 DM later in life; probability that diabetes will recur in each subsequent pregnancy is 70–90%; higher maternal pre-pregnancy weight predicts recurrence; 40–60% of GDM develop Type 2 diabetes in 10–20 years; offspring have higher risk of obesity, glucose intolerance, and metabolic syndrome in childhood and adult life.
Follow-up schedule: 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 6–8 weeks postpartum, then 3-yearly; screen during each subsequent pregnancy. Postpartum — initiate lifestyle modification, weight loss in overweight women, and appropriate contraception counselling.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman with known Type 1 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 10.5%) presents for preconception counselling. She is planning her first pregnancy.

(i) What is the significance of her current HbA1c level? What are the risks to the developing embryo at this level of glycaemic control?
(ii) What preconception measures must be completed before she attempts conception?
(iii) A different patient with GDM is managed with diet alone during pregnancy. Outline the dietary targets and composition to be used in her management.
(iv) What is the postpartum risk profile for a woman who had GDM, and what follow-up schedule is required?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: anencephaly (absent cerebral hemispheres and cranial vault). The additional finding of a second fetus makes this a twin pregnancy.
(ii) Anencephaly can be identified as early as 11–12 weeks.
(iii) Standard views at anomaly scan:
- Transverse section through the fetal head, assessing head shape and internal structures
- Fetal spine: sagittal, coronal and transverse views
- Fetal abdomen: longitudinal and transverse; identifying intra-abdominal organs: stomach, kidneys, bladder, ventral wall integrity and cord insertion
- Transverse section through fetal thorax to examine four-chamber view of the heart
- Limbs: identify three long bones in each limb
Also assessed: fetal viability; number of fetuses; placental site; amniotic fluid volume.
(iv) Cardiac malformations with normal four-chamber view (likely to be missed): tetralogy of Fallot; transposition of the great arteries; small atrial and ventricular septal defects; mild pulmonary or aortic valve stenosis; mild coarctation of the aorta. Overall detection rate for cardiac malformations varies from 6% to 77%.
(v) Structural malformations:
- CNS: anencephaly; spinal bifida (commonest CNS anomaly, failure of ventral fusion; lemon/banana signs); hydrocephalus (enlarged lateral ventricles, anterior displacement of choroid plexus; types: aqueductal stenosis, communicating, Dandy-Walker).
- Thoracic: fetal lungs uniformly echogenic; pleural effusion (chylothorax); bronchogenic cyst; congenital cystic adenomatous malformation of the lung (CCAML—overgrowth of terminal bronchioles at expense of saccular spaces).
- Abdominal wall/GIT: gastroschisis (para-umbilical defect); exomphalos (central defect surrounded by membrane, umbilical cord inserted on it); bladder/cloaca extrophy; fetal ascites; bowel obstruction; meconium peritonitis; many obstructive malformations associated with polyhydramnios.
- Urogenital: renal agenesis (unilateral or bilateral); infantile polycystic kidney disease (bilateral hyperechogenic enlarged kidneys, absent fetal bladder, oligohydramnios); posterior urethral valve; urethral atresia; multicystic dysplastic kidney disease (MDKD).
questions.question:
A woman at 20 weeks gestation undergoes a routine anomaly scan. The report describes an absent cranial vault with no recognisable cerebral cortex, and the cerebellum appears absent on transverse section. A second fetus is also noted.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) At what gestational age can this condition be identified earliest by ultrasound?
(iii) List the standard views that must be obtained at an anomaly ultrasound scan.
(iv) What are the cardiac malformations associated with a normal four-chamber view on ultrasound (i.e., those likely to be missed)?
(v) What other structural malformations should be systematically evaluated at the 18–20 week scan, covering CNS, thoracic, abdominal wall, and urogenital systems?

questions.answerText:
(i) Acute Renal Failure (ARF), presenting as oliguria or anuria. Pathological processes: reduced renal perfusion (hypovolaemia from haemorrhagic or endotoxic shock, or microthrombi in renal arterioles as in pre-eclampsia and coagulopathies) and direct damage to renal tissue (toxic renal parenchymal necrosis). The two main pathological forms are Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) and Renal Cortical Necrosis (RCN).
(ii) Severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia; septic abortion; gram-negative septicaemia and endotoxic shock; Clostridium welchii septicaemia; severe obstetric haemorrhage; disseminated intravascular coagulation; amniotic fluid embolism; nephrotoxins such as methoxyflurane and aminoglycosides.
(iii) Oliguric phase lasts 6–21 days (median 9 days); there is absence of both tubular and glomerular function. ECG monitoring of hyperkalaemic effects shows: absent P-waves, widening of the QRS complex to more than 0.2 seconds, and peaking of T-waves (earliest noticeable sign).
(iv) Meticulous monitoring of fluid input and output via indwelling urethral catheter; avoidance of potassium-containing fluids or food; daily monitoring of plasma potassium and urea; control of intercurrent infections and limitation of protein catabolism; avoidance of nephrotoxic antibiotics; control of hyperkalaemia using ion exchange resins (Resonium A), IV 50 ml of 50% glucose plus 50 IU soluble insulin, and up to 60 ml of 10% calcium gluconate to mute the effect of potassium on the myocardium; dialysis.
(v) Prognosis of ATN is excellent if the patient is managed properly through the different phases. In Renal Cortical Necrosis, the oliguric phase persists beyond 21 days; some respond after as long as 60 days of oliguria; if the renal cortex fails to recover, chronic renal failure ensues; management requires dialysis and renal transplantation; prognosis is poorer than in ATN.
questions.question:
A 26-year-old primigravida presents at 32 weeks gestation with sudden onset oliguria (urine output less than 300 ml over 24 hours), nausea, vomiting, and lethargy. She had been diagnosed with severe pre-eclampsia earlier in the pregnancy.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what pathological processes underlie it?
(ii) What are the aetiological factors that can lead to this condition in obstetric patients?
(iii) How is the oliguric phase recognised, and what are its cardiac monitoring findings?
(iv) Outline the full management of the oliguric phase.
(v) What is the prognosis, and how does it differ from a related but more severe pathological variant?

A primigravida has been in the second stage of labour for 2 hours. The vertex is at the level of the ischial spines with no descent. The sagittal suture is in the transverse diameter of the pelvis. The cardiotocograph shows late decelerations. The cervix is fully dilated, the membranes are ruptured, and the bladder has been emptied.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and where in the OPP progression in labour does this occur?
(ii) Name the specific forceps designed for this situation and its anatomical characteristic that makes it suitable.
(iii) List all the prerequisites for forceps delivery (FORCEPS mnemonic) and confirm which are met in this patient.
(iv) State all the fetal complications of forceps delivery.
(v) Outline the indications that signal a problem with OPP in labour.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: deep transverse arrest.
- This occurs at the level of the ischial spines during the progression of OPP in labour.
- In OPP, possible outcomes are: complete rotation anteriorly; deep transverse arrest (arrest at the level of the ischial spines); and total cessation of progress in labour.

(ii) Specific forceps and anatomical characteristic:
- Kielland's forceps are designed for this situation.
- Anatomical characteristic: Kielland's forceps have a sliding lock and a minimal pelvic curve.
- The sliding lock allows correction of asynclitism, and the minimal pelvic curve allows the blades to be applied to the fetal head in the transverse position and rotated to occipito-anterior before traction.
- The Neville-Bands forceps (long curved) are used for straight traction in the mid cavity but not for rotation.

(iii) Prerequisites – FORCEPS – confirmed in this patient:
- F: Full dilatation of the cervix – MET (cervix fully dilated).
- O: Outlet must be adequate – assumed (no CPD stated).
- R: Ruptured membranes – MET (membranes ruptured).
- C: Contractions must be present – MET (patient in active second stage).
- E: Engagement of the head necessary – station is at the level of ischial spines (station 0; engaged) – MET.
- P: Presenting part must be suitable – MET (vertex).
- S: Surrounding structures must be empty – MET (bladder emptied); episiotomy, analgesia, and neonatal resuscitation facilities must be confirmed.

(iv) Fetal complications of forceps delivery:
- Asphyxia.
- Skull laceration.
- Supratentorial haemorrhage.
- Subdural and subarachnoid haemorrhage following skull fractures and compression.
- Cephalhaematoma.
- Facial abrasion from undue compression or slipping of the forceps.
- Facial nerve damage leading to facial palsy.

(v) Indications signalling a problem with OPP in labour:
- Large fetus.
- Lack of engagement.
- Marked moulding or caput.
- Unduly prominent ischial spines.
- Outlet obstruction.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old woman with essential hypertension (BP 160/100 mmHg on methyldopa 250 mg twice daily) becomes pregnant. She presents at 10 weeks of gestation for booking. Her urine shows no proteinuria. Serum creatinine is 78 µmol/L.
(i) What is the classification of her hypertensive disorder in pregnancy?
(ii) What are the causes of hypertension in pregnancy she must be screened for before attributing her condition to essential hypertension?
(iii) What adjustments, if any, should be made to her antihypertensive medication?
(iv) What maternal surveillance is required throughout pregnancy?
(v) What delivery considerations apply to this patient at term?
questions.answerText:
(i) Chronic pre-existing hypertension in pregnancy — defined as hypertension occurring prior to pregnancy or before the 20th week of gestation, which persists in the puerperium, or is detected at booking. She is on antihypertensives already, confirming pre-existing disease.
(ii) Before attributing her condition to essential hypertension (which is the underlying cause in 90% of cases), the following must be excluded: renal disease (glomerulonephritis, polycystic disease, renal artery stenosis, diabetic nephropathy); collagen vascular disease (SLE, scleroderma); coarctation of the aorta; phaeochromocytoma; adrenal disease.
(iii) Continue methyldopa as it is generally well tolerated, with follow-up studies on offspring for 7 years showing acceptable safety. ACE inhibitors (captopril, lisinopril) must be avoided — these are not part of her current regimen, which is appropriate. Other commonly used agents include nifedipine and hydralazine (in emergency). Diuretics should not be used. Do not excessively lower BP as this may reduce placental blood flow.
(iv) Maternal surveillance: joint care by obstetrician and nephrologist; frequent antenatal visits — fortnightly until 32 weeks, weekly thereafter; assess renal function at each visit; daily BP monitoring (4 times); urine output and testing for proteinuria; weekly biochemical monitoring; regular fundoscopy; fetal surveillance — serial ultrasound, Doppler USS of umbilical blood flow, fetal kick chart, BPP; look for appearance of signs of superimposed PIH.
(v) Delivery considerations: continuous fetal monitoring in labour due to risk of growth restriction; low threshold for caesarean section if there is any sign of deteriorating maternal or fetal wellbeing; MgSO4 if signs of pre-eclampsia develop. Post-natally: careful observation in the first 48 hours because of a persisting risk of eclampsia; maternal BP will often resume its pre-pregnancy level.

questions.question:
A) Describe the pudendal nerve under the following headings:
A(i) Fibres and spinal origin
A(ii) Course and the named structures it passes under and posterior to
A(iii) Branches and areas supplied (motor and sensory)

B) State the safe site for performing a pudendal nerve block, and name the local anaesthetic agent specified.

C) Explain the anatomical basis and the functional deficit that would result from injury to the pudendal nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Fibres and spinal origin:
- The haemorrhoidal and perineal nerves and dorsal nerve of the clitoris carry impulses through the pudendal nerves to S2–4.
- The pudendal nerves therefore originate from S2–4.

A(ii) Course:
- The pudendal nerves pass under and slightly posterior to the ischial spines.
- Impulses from the vagina, vulva, and perineum are carried via the haemorrhoidal and perineal nerves and dorsal nerve of the clitoris through the pudendal nerves to S2–4.
- Some areas of perineal and vulval skin are also innervated by the ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, posterior femoral cutaneous nerves, and cutaneous branches of S2–4.

A(iii) Branches and distribution:
- Motor supply: the pudendal nerves provide the motor supply to the levator ani.
- Sensory supply: they supply the vagina, vulva, and perineum via the haemorrhoidal and perineal nerves and the dorsal nerve of the clitoris.
- Anaesthesia from a pudendal block is confined to the vagina.

B) Safe site for pudendal block:
- Pudendal block is performed via a vaginal approach.
- The pudendal nerves are blocked as they pass under and slightly posterior to the ischial spines.
- Prilocaine 0.5% is the specified local anaesthetic agent, used to minimise the risk of toxic reactions.
- The block is safe with no risk to the fetus.

C) Anatomical basis of functional deficit after pudendal nerve injury:
- Because the pudendal nerve provides the motor supply to the levator ani, injury would result in weakness or paralysis of the levator ani muscle.
- Loss of levator ani function impairs the pelvic floor support mechanism, predisposing to utero-vaginal prolapse.
- Sensory loss over the vagina, vulva, and perineum would also occur.
- The block as performed is suitable only for outlet or low-cavity forceps delivery; pain from mid-cavity, rotational, or ventouse deliveries is not relieved, indicating the limited distribution of the pudendal nerve block.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman presents for her first antenatal visit at 10 weeks gestation. She has been trying to conceive for 5 years (sub-fertility). She has a BMI of 32 kg/m2 and booking blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg.
(i) What is the obstetric classification of this patient and what are her risk factors?
(ii) List all the obstetric problems specifically associated with the elderly primigravida.
(iii) What are the problems in labour for the elderly primigravida and what determines the mode of delivery?
(iv) What are the problems associated with obesity in pregnancy (BMI >26 kg/m2)?
(v) What is the ideal BMI for a successful pregnancy outcome and how is obesity sub-classified?
questions.answerText:
(i) Classification: elderly primigravida—a woman carrying her first pregnancy at 35 years or more. Risk factors here: advanced maternal age (38 years); sub-fertility history; obesity (BMI 32 kg/m2); pre-existing hypertension.
(ii) Obstetric problems of the elderly primigravida:
Psychological problems: previous sub-fertility; unmarried (late marriage); previous pregnancy wastage; anxiety.
Obstetric problems: hyperemesis gravidarum; increased incidence of medical complications (effect of age); pre-eclampsia/essential hypertension; carbohydrate intolerance—gestational diabetes mellitus; poor uterine perfusion.
(iii) Problems in labour: poor progress in labour; maternal/fetal distress; low threshold for CS. Mode of delivery: smooth course in labour if pregnancy is well supervised; mode of delivery dependent on associated problems; vaginal delivery permitted in absence of complications; in presence of complications, deliver by CS.
(iv) Problems associated with obesity in pregnancy:
- Increased risk of oligomenorrhoea and polycystic ovarian syndrome
- Chronic hypertension
- Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia
- Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)
- Venous thrombo-embolism (VTE)
- Difficult labour
- Increased risk of operative deliveries
- Increased risk of PPH
- Increased risk of wound infection and dehiscence
- Increased anaesthetic complications
- Increased incidence of maternal morbidity and mortality
(v) Ideal BMI: 19–26 kg/m2. Sub-classification: BMI >26 kg/m2 = overweight; BMI 30–35 = mild obesity; BMI 36–39 = moderate obesity; BMI >40 = morbid obesity. Booking weights of 85 kg or more and 45 kg or less are detrimental to successful outcome of pregnancies.

A(i) ATN results from hypovolaemia of an intensity that falls just short of what leads to Renal Cortical Necrosis. Pathologically, ATN involves intra-renal obstruction and back-diffusion of glomerular filtrate, and afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. RCN involves glomerulosclerosis and more severe cortical destruction. ATN is reversible; RCN often is not. Pathogenesis includes reduced renal perfusion (hypovolaemia from haemorrhagic or endotoxic shock; microthrombi in renal arterioles as in pre-eclampsia and coagulopathies) and direct damage to renal tissue (toxic renal parenchymal necrosis from nephrotoxins).
A(ii) Onset phase management: large doses of frusemide to challenge the kidneys, in case it is a case of pre-renal azotaemia where tubular damage has yet to occur. This distinguishes reversible pre-renal failure (which responds to fluid and frusemide) from established ATN, allowing appropriate early intervention.
B(i) The oliguric phase lasts 6–21 days (median 9 days) and is characterised by absence of both tubular and glomerular function. Monitoring: indwelling urethral catheter for meticulous monitoring of fluid input and output; daily monitoring of plasma potassium and urea; ECG monitoring for hyperkalaemia (absent P-waves, widening QRS to more than 0.2 seconds, peaking of T-waves — earliest noticeable sign). Treatment: avoidance of potassium-containing fluids or food; control of intercurrent infections and limitation of protein catabolism; avoidance of nephrotoxic antibiotics; control of hyperkalaemia; dialysis.
B(ii) Control of hyperkalaemia: ion exchange resins (Resonium A); IV 50 ml of 50% glucose plus 50 IU of soluble insulin; up to 60 ml of 10% calcium gluconate to mute the effect of potassium on the myocardium; dialysis.
C(i) Early diuretic phase: glomerular function returns but tubular function does not; replace electrolytes as they are lost in the urine due to lack of tubular reabsorption; high potassium diet; monitor and replace urinary fluid loss. Late diuretic phase: tubular reabsorptive function returns; decrease potassium intake; maintain fluid balance; general supportive therapy.
C(ii) ATN prognosis: excellent if the patient is managed properly through the different phases. RCN: initial course similar to ATN but oliguric phase persists beyond 21 days; some respond to treatment after as long as 60 days of oliguria; if the renal cortex fails to recover, chronic renal failure ensues; management requires dialysis and renal transplantation. Prognosis is poorer in RCN than in ATN.
questions.question:
Describe the phases of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) in obstetric patients under the following headings:
A(i) The pathological basis and conditions leading to ATN compared with Renal Cortical Necrosis.
A(ii) The onset phase and the rationale for treatment in this phase.
B(i) The oliguric phase: duration, physiology, monitoring parameters, and treatment.
B(ii) Control of hyperkalaemia in the oliguric phase: all mechanisms and agents.
C(i) The diuretic phases: early and late — their physiological basis and management.
C(ii) Prognosis of ATN compared with Renal Cortical Necrosis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Acute bone pain crisis in sickle cell disease complicating pregnancy. Maternal complications include anaemia, bone pain crises, sequestration crises, infections, pregnancy-induced hypertension, bone marrow embolism, haemolytic crises, increased risk of caesarean section, and increased maternal mortality and morbidity. Fetal complications include intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight infant, preterm contractions/labour, birth asphyxia, increased abortions/perinatal losses, and risk of inheriting the disease if the father has the trait.
(ii) Pregnancy serves as a source of stress to the body, increasing the chances and rates of crises. Precipitating factors include malaria, dehydration, infection, and hypoxia. The risk is highest in the last 4 weeks of pregnancy, in labour, and in the first 4 days of the puerperium.
(iii) Treatment of the precipitating factor (e.g., malaria, dehydration); rehydration; antibiotics; analgesia (NSAIDs, opioids); heparinisation; dialysis if required. Hydroxyurea, which is used in managing vaso-occlusive events, is contraindicated in pregnancy. Users should be on contraception and hydroxyurea should be discontinued when pregnancy is planned.
(iv) The most fatal complication in pregnancy is bone marrow embolism. It is heralded by pseudotoxaemia (systolic hypertension with proteinuria). Bone pain crises are a risk factor. It is most likely to occur between term and the first 4 days post-partum. The occurrence of predisposing factors is an indication for heparinisation, which prevents its occurrence.
(v) Principles in labour: avoid dehydration, avoid infection, avoid hypoxia, and prevent prolonged labour. Involve haematologist, anaesthetist, and neonatologist; monitor with partograph; give IV fluids; give prophylactic antibiotics; give supplementary oxygen; cross-match blood; give adequate analgesia; monitor PCV 4-hourly. For operative delivery, local/regional block is preferred; if general anaesthesia is used, ensure adequate oxygenation. Shorten the second stage of labour and minimise vaginal examinations.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman with known sickle cell disease (HbSS) is now at 28 weeks gestation. She presents with sudden onset severe bone pain and is found to have a haemoglobin of 6 g/dl and a PCV of 20%.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what are the maternal and fetal complications of sickle cell disease in pregnancy?
(ii) What are the predisposing and precipitating factors for her current crisis?
(iii) Outline the management of her acute bone pain crisis.
(iv) What is the most fatal complication in pregnancy for this patient, and how is it prevented?
(v) Outline the principles of management in labour for a woman with sickle cell disease.

A) Describe the prerequisites for forceps delivery under the following headings:
A(i) All conditions relating to the cervix and membranes
A(ii) All conditions relating to the fetal head (position, engagement, weight, CPD)
A(iii) All conditions relating to the mother and the operating environment

B) Describe the concept of "failed forceps" and "trial of forceps" and state when trial of forceps should be abandoned.

C) Distinguish between the maternal complications of forceps delivery and those of vacuum extraction under the headings: perineal and vaginal lacerations, cervical laceration, risk to the bladder, and sepsis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Conditions relating to cervix and membranes:
- The cervix must be fully dilated; the temptation to apply forceps with a nearly fully dilated cervix must be avoided at all costs.
- The membranes must be ruptured.

A(ii) Conditions relating to the fetal head:
- Suitable presenting part: mostly the vertex; infrequently the after-coming head of breech; occasionally face in mento-anterior presentation.
- The position of the vertex must be known with certainty.
- The fetal head must be well engaged.
- There should be no cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD).
- The estimated fetal weight must be less than 4 kg.

A(iii) Conditions relating to the mother and operating environment:
- The bladder must be empty.
- Adequate analgesia: general anaesthesia, regional, pudendal block, or local infiltration of the perineum.
- Episiotomy must be performed.
- There must be adequate facility for neonatal resuscitation.
- The experience and skill of the operator is most crucial.
- Facilities for anaesthesia and caesarean section must be available.
- Written consent must be obtained.
- Patient in lithotomy position.

B) Failed forceps and trial of forceps:
- Failed forceps: unsuccessful attempt at forceps delivery with abandonment of effort in favour of caesarean section. Criteria: fetal head does not advance with each pull; fetus undelivered after 3 pulls with no descent; fetus undelivered after 30 minutes.
- Trial of forceps: tentative, cautious traction with forceps with the aim of abandoning the attempt at delivery if undue resistance is encountered.

C) Maternal complications – forceps vs vacuum:
- Perineal and vaginal lacerations: forceps cause extension of episiotomy and perineal tears, and vaginal lacerations during blade application and traction; vacuum causes periurethral and perineal lacerations from improper technique, and the vaginal wall may be sucked into the cap causing vaginal laceration or haematoma.
- Cervical laceration: forceps can cause cervical laceration with upward extension leading to profuse haemorrhage; vacuum can cause complete avulsion of the cervix during first-stage extraction, with upward extensions into the lower uterine segment.
- Risk to the bladder: forceps can cause bladder damage resulting in vesicovaginal fistula; vacuum extraction is not specifically associated with bladder damage, but cervical avulsion can extend to the lower segment.
- Sepsis: forceps delivery predisposes to sepsis due to prolonged labour and genital tract trauma; vacuum extraction overall has lower maternal complication rates.

(i) Premature (pre-labour) rupture of membranes (PROM), defined as rupture of the membranes before the onset of labour. At 32 weeks (prior to 37 completed weeks), this is specifically termed preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). If more than 24 hours elapse between rupture and onset of labour, it is further classified as prolonged PROM.
(ii) Conditions associated with PROM: maternal infections (UTI, STI), intrauterine infection, cervical incompetence, multiple pregnancy, hydramnios, nutritional deficiency, decreased tensile strength of membranes, family history of PROM, smoking.
(iii) Confirmation of liquor: nitrazine test (yellow paper turns black); red litmus paper turns blue; ferning. Differentials of alkaline pH: vaginal infection, contamination with blood or semen. Differentials of ferning: cervical mucus. Investigations: FBC, urine culture, amniocentesis (fetal lung maturity — L/S ratio, presence of phosphatidyl glycerol, inositol; culture), HVS M/C/S, USS (gestational age, amniotic fluid volume, fetal growth and size). Lung maturity testing at sterile speculum exam.
(iv) Expectant management: admit, bed rest, antibiotics, corticosteroids (< 34 weeks), screen for infection. Infection monitoring: BP, pulse rate, temperature every 4 hours; twice-daily abdominal examination for tenderness; daily inspection of perineal pad; sepsis screen weekly (FBC, urine culture, amniocentesis pool, HVS M/C/S). Fetal monitoring: fetal kick count, antenatal CTG (non-stress test), biophysical profile, serial USS for liquor volume. Indications: term PROM for 6–12 hours; pregnancies between 26 and 34 weeks. Contraindications: chorioamnionitis, fetal distress, absence of liquor.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with sudden gush of fluid per vaginam. She denies uterine contractions. Sterile speculum examination confirms pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix, and a nitrazine test on the fluid turns black. Ferning is observed on air-drying a drop of fluid on a slide. No signs of chorioamnionitis are present at this time.
(i) State the diagnosis and define the specific terminology that applies at this gestational age.
(ii) Enumerate all conditions associated with this presentation.
(iii) Describe the confirmatory investigations, including laboratory and imaging findings used to establish the diagnosis and assess the situation.
(iv) Outline the principles of expectant management, specifying the monitoring for infection and fetal wellbeing, and state the indications and contraindications to this approach.

A 10-week pregnant woman has an ultrasound scan. The report states: "two fetuses in one chorionic sac with separate amniotic sacs." She is concerned about the risks to her babies.

(i) Based on the ultrasound findings, determine the chorionicity and amnionicity of this twin pair, and state what timing of cleavage produced this type.
(ii) Describe how chorionicity is determined with 100% accuracy, and state the USS signs at 6, 8, and 10–14 weeks that distinguish dichorionic from monochorionic twins.
(iii) List all the complications specific to monochorionic twinning, including mortality rates where stated.
(iv) State the management plan for this twin pair, including scan frequency, antenatal monitoring, and aim for mode of delivery.
questions.answerText:
(i) Chorionicity and amnionicity:
- Two fetuses in one chorionic sac with separate amniotic sacs: monochorionic-diamniotic (MC/DA) twins.
- Timing of cleavage: cleavage at 4–8 days after conception produces monochorionic/diamniotic twins.

(ii) Determination of chorionicity with 100% accuracy:
- Chorionicity can be determined with 100% accuracy in the first trimester by counting the constituent layers of the dividing membranes.
At 6 weeks USS:
- One fetus in two chorionic sacs: dichorionic (DC).
- Two fetuses in one chorionic sac: monochorionic (MC).
- Two fetuses in one chorionic sac with one yolk sac: conjoined twins.
At 8 weeks USS:
- Two fetuses in one chorionic sac with separate amniotic sacs: MC/DA.
- Two fetuses in one chorionic sac with one amniotic sac: MC/MA.
At 10–14 weeks:
- "Twin peak" or "Lambda sign": projection of placental tissue into the inter-twin membrane (seen in dichorionic twins).
After 14 weeks:
- Count placentae.
- Determine sex of fetuses.
- Dividing membrane greater than 2 mm (suggests dichorionic).

(iii) Complications specific to monochorionic twinning:
- Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS): occurs in monochorionic twins due to vascular anastomoses; seen in up to 30% of cases; mortality up to 30%; severe morbidity in survivors.
- Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Sequence (TRAP): occurs in monochorionic twinning; results from artery-to-artery anastomosis; mortality approximately 50%.
- Monoamniotic twin complications: cord entanglement is the main cause of mortality; 1% of monozygotic pregnancies; mortality up to 50%.
- Single fetal death in twins: increased risk of death of surviving twin of 20%; chorionicity is very important.
- Increased risk of fetal loss in surviving twin.

(iv) Management plan for monochorionic twins:
- Specialised clinic attendance.
- Fortnightly ultrasound scans (more frequent than dichorionic twins which are scanned monthly).
- Iron and folate supplementation.
- Anticipation of complications and watch out for them.
- Adequate rest.
- Abnormality scan between 16–20 weeks.
- Aim for vaginal delivery.
- In delivery: two obstetricians or midwives and two paediatricians; continuous intrapartum fetal monitoring with cardiotocograph; establish IV access; group and crossmatch blood; active management of the third stage of labour.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old primigravida at 18 weeks gestation has a raised maternal serum AFP (MSAFP) of 3.2 MoM on biochemical screening. Ultrasound is performed.
(i) What conditions cause raised MSAFP and what threshold MoM is used for screening?
(ii) What is the optimum gestational age for MSAFP screening, and what are the detection rates for open spinal bifida and anencephaly at the standard cut-off?
(iii) Name the ultrasonographic features that diagnose spinal bifida, and list the CNS malformations identifiable by ultrasound.
(iv) What invasive procedure was previously used to confirm neural tube defects, and what did it measure?
(v) What are the aims of prenatal screening?
questions.answerText:
(i) Conditions causing raised MSAFP:
- Neural tube defects (anencephaly, open spinal bifida, encephalocele)
- Multiple pregnancy
- Abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, exomphalos, bladder extrophy)
- Congenital nephrosis
- Spontaneous fetal loss
- Pre-eclampsia
- Preterm delivery
- Low birth weight
- Underestimated gestation
- Low maternal weight
- Male fetus
- Afro-Caribbean ethnic origin
- Raised MSAFP in a previous pregnancy
Cut-off: 2.5 MoM.
(ii) MSAFP rises from 12–32 weeks; screening is optimal at 16–18 weeks GA; the separation of distributions is greatest at 16–18 weeks. At a cut-off of 2.5 MoM: 79% of open spinal bifida and 88% of anencephaly are detected.
(iii) Ultrasonographic features of spinal bifida: lemon/banana signs (shape of cerebellum); obvious defect of the spinal vertebrae; associated abnormalities such as hydrocephalus, Arnold Chiari malformation, Dandy Walker Syndrome. Lemon and Banana signs are superior to MSAFP in the diagnosis of spinal bifida; ultrasound detection rate for open spinal bifida is 81%.
CNS malformations identifiable by ultrasound: anencephaly (absent cerebral hemispheres and cranial vault, identifiable as early as 11–12 weeks); spinal bifida (commonest CNS anomaly; failure of ventral fusion); hydrocephalus (enlarged lateral ventricles and anterior displacement of choroid plexus; types: aqueductal stenosis, communicating hydrocephalus, Dandy-Walker syndrome).
(iv) Previously, amniocentesis was used to measure raised amniotic level of acetylcholinesterase (AchE).
(v) Aims of prenatal screening: reduces perinatal mortality (early detection/pregnancy termination); physical and psychological preparation of parents for delivery of malformed baby; facilitates in-utero transfer to facilities for expert management; allows in-utero treatments to improve fetal conditions; sensitive test to screen fetuses with chromosomal diseases who may benefit from invasive diagnostic procedures; reassures parents that the fetus is normal.

(i) Ruptured uterus. Causes during pregnancy: previous classical caesarean section or hysterotomy, LSCS, uterine perforation, myomectomy, tubal reimplantation, external cephalic version, trauma (RTA). Causes during labour: scarred uterus, CPD in multiparous patients especially with injudicious use of oxytocin, malposition and malpresentation, uterine manipulations (internal version, forceps application). Types: complete (involving myometrium and serosa) or incomplete (involving only the myometrium). Sites: usually a transverse rupture on the anterior aspect of the lower uterine segment, vertical tear laterally, transverse posteriorly; lateral ruptures involving uterine vessels may be fatal.
(ii) Risk factors in this patient: grand multiparity (high parity), oxytocin augmentation (injudicious use in a multipara), slow progress in labour (suggesting mechanical difficulty). Oxytocin causes hyperstimulation of the uterus; when the lower uterine segment is already thinned and under stress, continued strong contractions from oxytocin can precipitate rupture.
(iii) Complications: sepsis (septicaemia, osteitis pubis), haemorrhage, obstetric neuropraxia, genital tract injuries, vaginal fistulae, secondary amenorrhoea (Sheehan's syndrome), psychological shock; for the fetus: sepsis, injury, death. Maternal mortality: 40–50%; perinatal mortality: 85–95%. In parts of Africa, incidence is 1 in 100 deliveries; in parts of the USA, 1 in 4,000 deliveries.
(iv) Resuscitation: analgesics, IV fluids, blood transfusion, antibiotics. Surgery: repair alone (if edges are fresh and viable), repair with bilateral tubal ligation (if family complete), subtotal hysterectomy, or total hysterectomy (depending on extent and site). Postoperative care: IV fluids, antibiotics, catheterisation.
questions.question:
A grand multipara (para 6) is in active labour with oxytocin augmentation for slow progress. She suddenly develops severe continuous abdominal pain, collapses, and her uterine contractions cease. On examination, she is in shock, the fetal parts are easily palpable through the abdomen, there is free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, and blood is noted at the urethral meatus.
(i) State the diagnosis and enumerate all the recognised causes of this condition, distinguishing those occurring during pregnancy from those occurring during labour.
(ii) List the risk factors present in this patient and explain how oxytocin contributed.
(iii) Describe the complications of this condition, including maternal and perinatal mortality figures stated for parts of Africa and the USA.
(iv) Outline the surgical management options, specifying the criteria for each.

A 30-year-old woman (para 1) presents in early labour at 39 weeks. Her previous delivery was by lower segment Caesarean section (LSCS) for foetal distress, 2 years ago, with an uncomplicated wound healing. She has had one previous vaginal delivery before the Caesarean section. She requests a trial of scar (VBAC).
(i) State the factors to consider when planning vaginal birth after Caesarean (VBAC), including the type of previous scar, previous uterine rupture, desire for future pregnancy, and facility requirements.
(ii) Describe how VBAC should be monitored intrapartum, including the specific preparations required.
(iii) Describe the signs of imminent and completed uterine rupture, and state the differential diagnoses of completed uterine rupture.
(iv) State the management of uterine rupture including resuscitation, surgical options (specifying criteria for each), and postoperative care.
questions.answerText:
(i) Factors to consider for VBAC: desire for future pregnancy (the more Caesarean sections, the greater the risk); type of previous Caesarean scar — no VBAC for classical Caesarean section; previous uterine rupture (precludes VBAC); previous vaginal delivery (increases success of VBAC); any other indication for Caesarean section; previous post-Caesarean wound infection (decreases scar integrity); facilities for emergency Caesarean section. Vaginal delivery can be safe after Caesarean section performed for a non-recurrent indication.
(ii) VBAC intrapartum monitoring: continuous electronic fetal monitoring; group and cross-match blood; intravenous access secured; early recourse to Caesarean section if necessary. This is managed as high-risk labour; neonatologist and anaesthetist should be informed; blood must be available for emergencies; there must be facilities for emergency Caesarean section.
(iii) Imminent rupture: pain between contractions, tender lower segment, continuous contractions, vaginal bleeding, fetal distress (excessive movements, fetal tachycardia, meconium-stained liquor). Completed rupture: sudden sharp generalised abdominal pain (classical scar) or lower abdominal pain (lower segment scar) becoming generalised; faintness and collapse; absence of contractions; irregular abdominal distension; fetal parts easily palpable; free fluid in peritoneal cavity; bloody urine (if bladder involved).
