The random coil configuration of elastin permits extensive deformation without energy expenditure. These fibers are abundant in arteries, lungs, and skin.
questions.question: Which fiber type in connective tissue is composed primarily of the protein elastin and provides tissue resilience?
What enzyme in adrenal medulla converts norepinephrine to epinephrine?
questions.explanation: PNMT methylates norepinephrine to form epinephrine. This enzyme is induced by cortisol from the adrenal cortex, explaining why the medulla is surrounded by cortex. PNMT expression is unique to adrenal medulla and a few brain regions.

questions.question: Which cell type in connective tissue is derived from bone marrow monocytes and exhibits pronounced phagocytic activity?
questions.explanation: Macrophages originate from circulating monocytes that migrate into tissues and differentiate into resident tissue macrophages. They possess extensive phagocytic capability and play crucial roles in defense, antigen presentation, and tissue remodeling. Various tissue-specific macrophages comprise the mononuclear phagocyte system.

Invasion involves degradation of basement membrane and extracellular matrix by proteases (MMPs, cathepsins), altered cell adhesion, and increased motility. Cancer cells lose E-cadherin and gain mesenchymal characteristics (EMT). This is the first step toward metastasis.
questions.question: What process allows cancer cells to escape local tissue boundaries?

questions.explanation: The proximal tubule reabsorbs ~65% of filtered sodium, water, and virtually all filtered glucose and amino acids. Cells have extensive apical brush border and basolateral membrane infoldings with numerous mitochondria. This high metabolic activity supports active transport.
questions.question: Which segment of the nephron is responsible for most sodium and water reabsorption?
Which protein complex regulates the interaction between actin and myosin in skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: The troponin-tropomyosin complex regulates muscle contraction by controlling myosin-binding sites on actin filaments. Tropomyosin blocks binding sites in resting muscle while troponin acts as the calcium sensor. Calcium binding to troponin C causes conformational changes exposing myosin-binding sites.

options: Facilitate exchange between blood and hepatocytes
questions.explanation: Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium (lacking basement membrane) allows free exchange of plasma and large molecules with hepatocytes across the space of Disse. This enables efficient uptake of nutrients, secretion of proteins, and metabolic exchange. The fenestrations are ~100 nm diameter.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of hepatic sinusoids being fenestrated?

questions.explanation: The submandibular gland produces mixed seromucous secretions with approximately 90% serous acini and 10% mucous tubules capped by serous demilunes. This combination provides both enzymatic activity and lubrication. The mixed secretion contributes significantly to total saliva composition.
questions.question: What composition characterizes submandibular gland secretions?
options: The submandibular produces purely mucous secretions exclusively
The submandibular creates mixed seromucous secretions
The submandibular generates only serous watery saliva
The submandibular manufactures predominantly lipid-rich saliva
The submandibular secretes primarily glycogen-containing fluid

questions.explanation: Regeneration requires stem/progenitor cells, intact tissue framework, appropriate growth factors, and limited injury. Extensive damage, loss of architecture, chronic inflammation, or tissues with poor regenerative capacity (heart, CNS) favor fibrotic scarring over regeneration. AGING
questions.question: What determines whether tissue repair proceeds by regeneration or fibrosis?

options: Lymphatic capillaries have thick muscular walls throughout
Lymphatic capillaries have continuous basement membranes
Lymphatic capillaries are open-ended allowing blood entry
Lymphatic capillaries are closed-ended tubes with valves
Lymphatic capillaries are identical to blood capillaries
questions.question: What characterizes lymphatic capillaries structurally?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended thin-walled tubes with discontinuous basement membrane and loose endothelial junctions, facilitating fluid and macromolecule entry. Larger lymphatic vessels have valves preventing backflow and smooth muscle in their walls. Lymph moves by skeletal muscle compression, arterial pulsation, and vessel wall contractions.

Cholecystokinin (CCK), released from duodenal I cells in response to fats and proteins, stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion from acinar cells and gallbladder contraction. Secretin stimulates bicarbonate secretion from ductal cells. Vagal stimulation also enhances enzyme secretion. These mechanisms coordinate pancreatic function with digestion.
questions.question: What controls pancreatic enzyme secretion?
options: Cholecystokinin from I cells triggers enzyme secretion
Secretin from S cells stimulates enzyme release
Gastrin from G cells promotes enzyme production
Somatostatin from D cells enhances enzyme secretion
Insulin from beta cells controls enzyme release

questions.question: What is the approximate thickness range for paraffin-embedded tissue sections prepared for light microscopy?
questions.explanation: Paraffin sections are typically cut at 1-10 μm thickness using a microtome to allow light transmission while maintaining structural detail. This range provides optimal visualization of cellular components under standard light microscopy. Thinner sections would be too fragile, while thicker ones would prevent adequate light penetration.

questions.question: What distinguishes type A from type B intercalated cells?
options: Type B cells produce carbonic anhydrase exclusively
Type A cells secrete hydrogen ions into tubular fluid
Type A cells respond only to aldosterone stimulation
Type B cells are found only in cortical regions
Type A cells lack mitochondria for energy production
questions.explanation: Type A intercalated cells secrete hydrogen ions and reabsorb bicarbonate, helping maintain acid-base balance during acidosis. Type B cells perform the opposite functions, secreting bicarbonate and reabsorbing hydrogen ions during alkalosis. Both cell types contain abundant carbonic anhydrase and numerous mitochondria to support active transport.

questions.question: What happens to cartilage distribution along the bronchial tree?
options: Cartilage becomes more abundant in distal branches
Cartilage changes from hyaline to elastic type
Cartilage increases in thickness toward periphery
Cartilage persists throughout all bronchiolar branches
Cartilage transforms from rings to irregular plates
questions.explanation: Cartilage progresses from nearly complete rings in main bronchi to irregular crescentic plates in smaller bronchi, eventually disappearing entirely in bronchioles. This structural change parallels the decreasing diameter and the transition from cartilaginous to smooth muscle support. The loss of cartilage makes bronchioles susceptible to collapse during forced expiration.

Intramembranous ossification occurs when mesenchymal cells differentiate directly into osteoblasts and produce bone matrix. This process forms flat bones of the skull and facial bones. Ossification centers develop and expand radially, eventually fusing at suture lines.
questions.question: What type of ossification involves bone formation directly from mesenchymal tissue without a cartilage model?
What structure divides the cytoplasm during animal cell cytokinesis?
questions.explanation: The contractile ring composed of actin and myosin filaments forms at the cell equator and constricts to divide the cytoplasm. This creates a cleavage furrow that deepens until the cell completely divides. The process is coordinated with nuclear division.

Marginal cells in the stria vascularis actively transport ions to maintain endolymph's unique composition. These cells have extensive basolateral membrane infoldings containing numerous mitochondria. The resulting endocochlear potential (~80-100 mV) drives sensory transduction.
questions.question: Which cells in the stria vascularis are responsible for endolymph production?

questions.explanation: Portal triads at lobule vertices contain branches of the hepatic artery (oxygenated blood), portal vein (nutrient-rich blood from GI tract), and bile duct (collecting bile). Lymphatic vessels and nerves also accompany these structures. Blood flows from triads through sinusoids to central veins.
options: Branch of hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct
questions.question: What defines the portal triad in hepatic lobules?

questions.explanation: The spongy (penile) urethra is the longest segment of the male urethra at approximately 15 cm, extending through the corpus spongiosum. This portion is lined initially by pseudostratified columnar epithelium, transitioning to stratified squamous epithelium distally. The prostatic and membranous segments are much shorter at 3-4 cm and 1-2 cm respectively.
options: The prostatic urethra measures approximately 15 centimeters
The spongy urethra spans roughly 15 centimeters
The membranous urethra extends about 15 centimeters
The penile urethra reaches approximately 3 centimeters
The bulbar urethra extends for about 15 centimeters
questions.question: Which portion of the male urethra is longest?

questions.explanation: The corneal stroma comprises 90% of corneal thickness and contains precisely arranged collagen lamellae with uniform fibril spacing. This regular organization minimizes light scattering, maintaining transparency. The keratocytes between lamellae maintain the extracellular matrix.
questions.question: Which layer of the cornea contains regular orthogonally arranged type I collagen bundles critical for transparency?

questions.explanation: Flow cytometry analyzes individual cells passing through laser beams, detecting fluorescence from labeled antibodies. FACS (Fluorescence-Activated Cell Sorting) physically separates cell populations based on markers. This enables phenotyping, cell cycle analysis, and purification of specific populations.
questions.question: Which technique allows cell sorting based on fluorescently labeled surface markers?

questions.explanation: Germinal centers form in cortical lymphoid follicles during antigenic stimulation, containing proliferating B cells (centroblasts and centrocytes). Somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation occur here. Tingible body macrophages phagocytose apoptotic B cells failing selection.
questions.question: What structure in lymph nodes serves as the site of B cell proliferation and antibody production?

options: Enterochromaffin-like cells release histamine stimulating acid
Parietal cells regulate acid through paracrine secretion
Chief cells produce paracrine factors controlling acid
Surface mucous cells regulate acid through paracrine signals
G cells use paracrine mechanisms exclusively for regulation
questions.explanation: Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric fundus release histamine in response to gastrin and vagal stimulation. Histamine acts locally (paracrine) on nearby parietal cells through H2 receptors to stimulate acid secretion. H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) block this pathway, reducing acid production for ulcer treatment.
questions.question: Which cells regulate gastric acid secretion through paracrine mechanisms?
Which cell type presents antigens to T cells in lymphoid tissues?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are professional antigen-presenting cells that capture, process, and present antigens to naïve T cells. They express high levels of MHC class II and co-stimulatory molecules. Langerhans cells in skin and follicular dendritic cells in lymphoid organs are specialized types.

Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid follicles in the ileal submucosa overlaid by specialized follicle-associated epithelium containing M cells. M cells transcytose antigens to underlying antigen-presenting cells, initiating mucosal immune responses. They are important for oral tolerance and IgA production.
questions.question: What specialized lymphoid structures in the ileum sample luminal antigens via M cells?

options: Simple columnar epithelium lines the anal canal
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium covers the anal canal
Transitional epithelium allows anal canal distension
Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium lines it distally
Simple cuboidal epithelium forms the anal lining
questions.explanation: The anal canal transitions from simple columnar rectal epithelium to stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium in the mid-portion, then to keratinized stratified squamous epithelium at the external anal orifice. This reflects the transition from internal mucosa to external skin. The keratinized epithelium provides protection against abrasion.
questions.question: Which epithelium lines the anal canal?
Which layer of the ureter contains the nerve plexus?
options: The mucosa harbors the submucosal nerve plexus
The submucosa contains Meissner's plexus exclusively
The adventitia contains the primary neural elements
The muscularis houses autonomic nerve ganglia
The transitional epithelium integrates nerve endings
questions.explanation: The adventitia of the ureter contains blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerve fibers supplying the organ. Autonomic nerve fibers coordinate the peristaltic contractions that propel urine toward the bladder. The muscularis itself contains nerve plexuses between its muscle layers similar to other hollow viscera.

questions.question: What structure separates hepatic sinusoids from hepatocytes?
questions.explanation: The space of Disse (perisinusoidal space) separates fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium from hepatocyte microvilli. This space allows free exchange of plasma components with hepatocytes while excluding blood cells. Stellate cells and extracellular matrix are present in this space.
options: A thick basement membrane forms this barrier
Dense connective tissue creates this separation
The space of Disse separates these structures
Continuous tight junctions seal this interface
No space exists between sinusoids and hepatocytes

questions.question: What immunoglobulin mediates mucosal immunity?
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA (dimeric with J chain and secretory component) protects mucosal surfaces. It neutralizes pathogens and toxins in respiratory, GI, and urogenital tracts. IgA is produced by plasma cells in lamina propria and transcytosed across epithelium.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) scans specimen surfaces with focused electron beams, detecting secondary electrons to create 3D images. Specimens are typically coated with gold or platinum for conductivity. SEM provides detailed surface topography information.
questions.question: What type of electron microscopy is used to study three-dimensional surface structures?
Which cell type lines the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: The gallbladder is lined by simple tall columnar epithelium with short microvilli that actively absorb water and electrolytes from bile. The cells are joined by tight junctions preventing bile leakage. No goblet cells are present. The epithelium rests on a lamina propria and muscular layer without a muscularis mucosae.
options: Simple columnar epithelium with microvilli lines it
Simple squamous epithelium lines the gallbladder
Stratified columnar epithelium forms the lining
Pseudostratified epithelium with goblet cells lines it

questions.explanation: Dysplasia shows disordered cell growth with abnormal size, shape, and organization. It represents a preneoplastic change with potential for progression to cancer. Grades range from mild to severe based on architectural and cytologic abnormalities.
questions.question: Which process involves abnormal cell growth with loss of normal tissue organization?

questions.explanation: Tight junctions contain claudin and occludin proteins that seal adjacent endothelial cell membranes in brain capillaries. This creates a highly selective barrier regulating molecular passage from blood to brain tissue. The degree of tightness varies depending on the number of junction strands.
questions.question: Which cell junction forms the blood-brain barrier by preventing paracellular movement of molecules?
What is the role of podocyte foot processes?
options: They actively transport substances across the filtration barrier
They create filtration slits for selective permeability
They contract to regulate glomerular blood flow
They secrete basement membrane components continuously
They phagocytose debris trapped in the glomerulus
questions.explanation: Podocyte foot processes (pedicels) interdigitate with those of adjacent podocytes, creating filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms. These specialized cell junctions constitute a crucial component of the glomerular filtration barrier, restricting passage of large proteins. The spacing and structure of these processes directly influence filtration selectivity.

Intercalated ducts are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with few distinguishing features and minimal modification of saliva. These cells can divide and differentiate into secretory or ductal cells, serving as reserve cells. The ducts are surrounded by myoepithelial cells that aid in saliva expulsion.
questions.question: Which cells line the intercalated ducts of salivary glands?
options: Tall columnar epithelial cells with extensive secretory granules
Stratified squamous epithelium for mechanical protection
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Transitional epithelium allowing for ductal distension
Simple cuboidal epithelium with sparse microvilli

questions.question: Which substance causes vasodilation of the afferent arteriole?
options: Angiotensin II dilates the afferent arteriole markedly
Endothelin dilates afferent arterioles increasing GFR
Norepinephrine dilates afferent arterioles under stress
Vasopressin dilates afferent arterioles during dehydration
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins, especially PGE2 and PGI2, cause afferent arteriole vasodilation, helping maintain GFR when renal perfusion is threatened. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, potentially causing acute kidney injury in volume-depleted states by eliminating this protective vasodilation. Prostaglandins counterbalance angiotensin II and sympathetic vasoconstriction.

Juxtaglomerular cells (modified smooth muscle in afferent arterioles) are the sole source of renin in the kidney. Renin release is stimulated by decreased renal perfusion pressure, sympathetic activation, and signals from macula densa. This initiates the RAAS cascade.
questions.question: What structure in the kidney produces renin?
Which dermal cells are resident macrophages important for immune surveillance?
questions.explanation: Histiocytes are tissue macrophages in the dermis derived from blood monocytes. They phagocytose debris, present antigens, and secrete cytokines during inflammation. These cells are part of the skin's innate immune system.

options: Diuretics promote SER growth in hepatocytes
questions.question: What medication can induce smooth endoplasmic reticulum proliferation?
questions.explanation: Barbiturates like phenobarbital induce proliferation of smooth endoplasmic reticulum in hepatocytes by upregulating cytochrome P450 enzyme synthesis. This adaptation increases drug metabolism capacity but can lead to tolerance and enzyme induction. Similar effects occur with other drugs including alcohol.

options: Portal vein, hepatic artery, and central vein together
Hepatic artery, central vein, and bile duct together
Bile duct, portal vein, and central vein together
Portal vein, bile duct, and hepatic artery together
Lymphatic, portal vein, and hepatic artery together
questions.explanation: Portal triads (portal areas) contain branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct surrounded by connective tissue at lobule periphery. Lymphatics and nerves are also present. These structures bring blood and drain bile from hepatic parenchyma. Multiple portal triads surround each hepatic lobule.
questions.question: What composes a portal triad?
Which process describes cancer spread to distant organs?
questions.explanation: Metastasis involves invasion, intravasation into vessels, survival in circulation, extravasation at distant sites, and colonization. Only a small fraction of disseminated cells successfully establish metastases. Specific organ tropism depends on seed-soil interactions.

options: All tidal volume participates in gas exchange
Approximately 30% of tidal volume reaches alveoli
Approximately 90% of tidal volume ventilates alveoli
Less than 10% of tidal volume reaches alveoli
Approximately 70% of tidal volume reaches alveoli
questions.explanation: Approximately 70% of tidal volume (about 350 mL of 500 mL) reaches alveoli for gas exchange. The remaining 30% (150 mL) occupies anatomical dead space in conducting airways without participating in gas exchange. Increasing tidal volume increases alveolar ventilation more efficiently than increasing respiratory rate.
questions.question: What percentage of tidal volume reaches alveoli?

options: Ammonia is directly excreted by the kidneys
Ammonia is converted to urea via the urea cycle
Ammonia is exhaled by the lungs unchanged
Ammonia is stored in hepatocytes indefinitely
Ammonia is secreted into bile for elimination
questions.question: What is the fate of ammonia produced in the liver?
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes convert toxic ammonia (from amino acid deamination and bacterial colonic production) to urea via the urea cycle. Urea is then filtered by glomeruli and excreted in urine. Liver failure impairs urea synthesis causing hyperammonemia, which crosses the blood-brain barrier causing hepatic encephalopathy with altered mental status.

options: The duodenum is the main B12 absorption site
The jejunum absorbs most vitamin B12
The colon absorbs the majority of B12
The terminal ileum is the primary B12 absorption site
Vitamin B12 is absorbed throughout the intestine
questions.question: What is the primary site of vitamin B12 absorption?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed specifically in the terminal ileum through cubilin receptors. Ileal resection or disease (Crohn's disease) causes B12 malabsorption despite adequate intrinsic factor. The ileum is the only site with the specific receptor for the B12-IF complex, making it crucial for B12 absorption.

Approximately 20% of renal plasma flow is filtered at the glomerulus (filtration fraction = GFR/RPF). This balance maintains adequate filtration while preventing excessive protein concentration in post-glomerular blood. Changes in filtration fraction affect tubular reabsorption.
questions.question: What is the filtration fraction in normal kidneys?

questions.explanation: Beta cells are the most abundant cells in pancreatic islets (about 70%), producing and secreting insulin in response to elevated blood glucose. Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, lowering blood glucose levels. Beta cell destruction or dysfunction causes diabetes mellitus.
options: Beta cells in pancreatic islets produce insulin
Alpha cells in islets of Langerhans secrete insulin
Delta cells in islets synthesize and release insulin
PP cells in pancreatic islets generate insulin
Acinar cells produce insulin along with enzymes
questions.question: Which pancreatic cells produce insulin?

questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter consists of skeletal muscle fibers from the pelvic floor musculature surrounding the urethra. This voluntary sphincter provides conscious control over micturition, contrasting with the involuntary smooth muscle internal sphincter. Damage to this sphincter can result in urinary incontinence.
options: Skeletal muscle of the pelvic floor forms it
Smooth muscle of the detrusor creates this sphincter
Cardiac muscle fibers encircle the urethral lumen
Oblique smooth muscle layers compose this structure
Circular cardiac muscle surrounds the urethra
questions.question: What muscle forms the external urethral sphincter?
What creates "chatter" marks on tissue sections?
questions.explanation: Chatter appears as parallel lines across sections caused by blade nicks, loose blade holders, or vibrations during sectioning. Sharp blades, proper blade angle, and stable microtome operation prevent this artifact. Regular blade changes maintain section quality.

Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lining the bladder can stretch considerably as the organ fills with urine. The epithelium appears stratified cuboidal when relaxed but flattens to fewer cell layers during distension. This specialized epithelium is also impermeable to urine components, preventing their reabsorption.
options: Simple columnar epithelium lines the bladder completely
Transitional epithelium allows for bladder distension
Stratified squamous epithelium provides protection throughout
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium moves urine distally
Simple cuboidal epithelium facilitates water reabsorption
questions.question: What characterizes the epithelium of the urinary bladder?

options: The median sulcus divides the tongue symmetrically
The terminal sulcus creates a V-shaped boundary
The lingual frenulum attaches the tongue ventrally
The circumvallate papillae form a linear arrangement
The palatoglossal arch separates these tongue regions
questions.explanation: The sulcus terminalis is a V-shaped groove that demarcates the anterior two-thirds (oral part) from the posterior one-third (pharyngeal part). This developmental boundary represents the fusion line between different embryonic origins of tongue tissue. The pharyngeal portion posterior to this sulcus is characterized by lingual tonsils rather than papillae.
questions.question: Which structure forms the boundary between the oral and pharyngeal portions of the tongue?

options: The olfactory epithelium in the superior nasal conchae
The respiratory mucosa throughout the nasal cavity
The paranasal sinuses lining the frontal bone
The nasopharynx posterior to the nasal cavity
The nasal vestibule at the entrance of nostrils
questions.explanation: The olfactory epithelium is located in the superior nasal conchae and contains bipolar olfactory neurons serving as chemoreceptors. This pseudostratified epithelium also includes supporting cells and basal stem cells. The olfactory neurons are unique among neurons in their ability to regenerate throughout life.
questions.question: Which structure contains olfactory receptor neurons?
What limits the thickness of engineered tissues without vasculature?
questions.explanation: Oxygen and nutrients diffuse only 100-200 μm, limiting unvascularized tissue thickness. Thicker tissues require vascularization through angiogenic factor delivery, pre-vascularization in vivo, or microfluidic channels. This remains a major challenge in tissue engineering.

questions.question: Which cells line the initial portion of pancreatic ducts?
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are pale-staining cells lining the initial portion of intercalated ducts extending into the center of acini, unique to the pancreas. These cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid and are stimulated by secretin. Centroacinar cells distinguish pancreatic from salivary gland acini.
options: Centroacinar cells form the initial duct segment
Columnar cells with extensive secretory granules line them
Squamous cells create the duct lining initially
Goblet cells line the proximal pancreatic ducts
Ciliated cells form the initial duct epithelium

questions.question: What produces the plicae circulares in small intestine?
questions.explanation: Plicae circulares (valves of Kerckring) are permanent circular folds of both mucosa and submucosa that do not flatten with distension. They increase surface area approximately threefold and are most prominent in the jejunum. These folds slow transit time and increase nutrient absorption.
options: Mucosa alone folds to create plicae circulares
Muscularis externa contracts to produce these folds
Villi clustering together form plicae circulares
Mucosa and submucosa together form plicae circulares

questions.explanation: Renal cortical fibroblasts sense tissue hypoxia through HIF (hypoxia-inducible factor) and increase erythropoietin synthesis. Erythropoietin stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity. Chronic kidney disease causes anemia from inadequate erythropoietin production, requiring exogenous hormone supplementation.
options: High oxygen levels stimulate erythropoietin synthesis
Excess iron stores promote erythropoietin release
Elevated red blood cell count stimulates production
Anemia and hypoxia trigger erythropoietin production
Normal oxygen saturation maximizes erythropoietin synthesis
questions.question: What stimulates erythropoietin production by the kidney?
What is the primary purpose of immunohistochemistry?
questions.explanation: Immunohistochemistry uses antibodies to detect specific antigens (proteins) in tissue sections. Primary antibodies bind target proteins while labeled secondary antibodies enable visualization. This technique identifies cell types, tissue origins, and protein expression patterns.

questions.question: Which structure in the cochlea contains the sensory hair cells responsible for hearing?
questions.explanation: The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane within the cochlear duct and contains inner and outer hair cells. These mechanoreceptor cells transduce mechanical vibrations into electrical signals. Supporting cells and the overlying tectorial membrane complete the sensory apparatus.

questions.question: What characterizes corpora amylacea in the prostate?
questions.explanation: Corpora amylacea are rounded, concentrically laminated, eosinophilic bodies found in prostatic alveoli, increasing in number with age. They may undergo calcification and can appear in semen, but their exact composition and significance remain unclear. Their presence becomes particularly prominent after age 50 and may reach 2 mm in diameter.
options: They are crystallized calcium deposits in ductal lumens
They consist of bacterial colonies within prostatic tissue
They are malignant cells indicating prostatic carcinoma
They represent rounded eosinophilic proteinaceous bodies
They represent hypertrophic smooth muscle cell clusters

questions.explanation: Endolymph has high potassium and low sodium concentrations, unlike typical extracellular fluids. It is produced by the stria vascularis and fills the membranous labyrinth. This unique ionic composition creates the endocochlear potential essential for hair cell transduction.
questions.question: What fluid fills the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear?

questions.explanation: NK cells recognize and kill cells with decreased MHC class I expression (tumor cells, virus-infected cells) without prior sensitization. They release perforin and granzymes inducing target cell apoptosis. This "missing self" recognition is part of innate immunity.
options: Kill cells lacking MHC class I
questions.question: What is the function of natural killer (NK) cells?
What type of capillaries have continuous endothelium with tight junctions forming the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Continuous capillaries in the brain have particularly tight junctions between endothelial cells creating a selective barrier. Astrocyte foot processes ensheath capillaries contributing to barrier function. This restricts passage of substances from blood to brain tissue.

questions.question: What pretreatment is often required to expose antigens in formalin-fixed tissues?
questions.explanation: Antigen retrieval reverses formaldehyde-induced protein cross-linking that masks epitopes. Heat-induced (pressure cooker, microwave) or enzymatic (proteinase K, trypsin) methods expose antigenic sites. This significantly improves immunostaining sensitivity in fixed tissues.

questions.question: Which part of the pituitary gland develops from the neural ectoderm as an outgrowth of the diencephalon?
questions.explanation: The neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) develops from a downgrowth of the diencephalon and remains connected via the infundibular stalk. It consists of axons from hypothalamic neurosecretory neurons and pituicytes (specialized glial cells). No hormone synthesis occurs here; it stores and releases ADH and oxytocin.

questions.question: What enzyme synthesizes cAMP from ATP?
questions.explanation: Adenylyl cyclase catalyzes cAMP synthesis from ATP. It's activated by Gs proteins and inhibited by Gi proteins, linking cell surface receptors to intracellular responses. cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates numerous target proteins.

questions.question: What structure at the axon hillock integrates incoming signals to determine if an action potential will be generated?
questions.explanation: The initial segment (trigger zone) at the axon hillock contains high concentrations of voltage-gated sodium channels. This region has the lowest threshold for action potential generation due to its high density of ion channels. Summation of excitatory and inhibitory inputs determines whether threshold is reached.

Sebaceous glands use holocrine secretion where entire cells disintegrate to release lipid-rich sebum. Basal cells continuously proliferate, differentiate filling with lipids, then die releasing contents. This oily secretion lubricates hair and skin.
questions.question: What type of secretion characterizes sebaceous glands?
What prevents premature activation of pancreatic proteases?
options: Protease inhibitors completely block all enzyme activity
Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens
Alkaline pH in pancreas prevents enzyme activation
Lack of substrate prevents protease activation
questions.explanation: Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase) that are activated only after reaching the duodenum. Enteropeptidase in the duodenal brush border activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates other proteases. This prevents pancreatic autodigestion.

Delta (δ) cells comprise ~5% of islet cells and secrete somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion via paracrine effects. Somatostatin also inhibits GH release and GI hormone secretion. This provides negative feedback regulation of islet hormone secretion.
questions.question: Which pancreatic cells secrete somatostatin to inhibit both insulin and glucagon release?
Which layer of blood vessel walls contains smooth muscle cells?
questions.explanation: The tunica media contains circumferentially arranged smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers. Vessel diameter and blood flow are regulated by smooth muscle contraction/relaxation. The media is thickest in arteries, particularly muscular arteries.

Phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 into IP3 (inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol). IP3 releases calcium from ER stores while DAG activates protein kinase C. This signaling pathway mediates many hormone and neurotransmitter responses.
questions.question: Which second messenger is produced by activation of phospholipase C?
Which nerve innervates the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5 nerve roots) provides motor innervation to the diaphragm, the primary muscle of respiration. Phrenic nerve injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory compromise. The diaphragm also receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally.
options: The vagus nerve provides motor innervation
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm
The accessory nerve controls diaphragm contraction
The sympathetic chain innervates the diaphragm

questions.question: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
questions.explanation: Enamel is 96% hydroxyapatite crystals organized into rods (prisms), making it the hardest body tissue. Ameloblasts produce enamel during tooth development but are lost after eruption, preventing regeneration. The remaining organic matrix is primarily amelogenins.

options: Stratified squamous epithelium protects this urethral segment
Simple columnar epithelium characterizes this region
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium forms the lining
Transitional epithelium lines the prostatic portion
Simple cuboidal epithelium covers this urethral part
questions.question: Which epithelium lines the prostatic urethra?
questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) continuous with that of the bladder. This epithelium transitions to pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium in more distal portions. The prostatic ducts open into this segment through numerous small orifices on the posterior wall.

questions.question: What percentage of pancreatic volume comprises endocrine islets?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic islets constitute only 1-2% of pancreatic mass, yet their endocrine products (insulin, glucagon, somatostatin) are crucial for metabolic regulation. The remaining 98-99% is exocrine tissue producing digestive enzymes. Despite small volume, islets have rich vascularization.

Red pulp sinusoids and cords contain macrophages that phagocytose aged or damaged erythrocytes. The tortuous splenic circulation allows macrophages to inspect passing red cells. Hemoglobin iron is recycled while heme is converted to bilirubin.
questions.question: Which splenic compartment removes senescent erythrocytes?

questions.explanation: Clearing agents like xylene are miscible with both dehydrating alcohols and embedding paraffin, facilitating the transition between these steps. The tissue becomes transparent during this process as the refractive index changes. Without proper clearing, paraffin infiltration would be incomplete and inadequate.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the clearing step in tissue processing?

questions.explanation: Sertoli cells form tight junctions creating the blood-testis barrier and provide structural and metabolic support for developing spermatogenic cells. They respond to FSH and testosterone, regulating spermatogenesis. These cells also phagocytose residual bodies and secrete androgen-binding protein.
questions.question: Which cells in seminiferous tubules respond to FSH and support developing germ cells?

questions.explanation: IgE binds high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils. Cross-linking by allergen triggers degranulation releasing histamine and other mediators. This causes immediate hypersensitivity symptoms (allergies, anaphylaxis, asthma). Normal serum IgE levels are very low.
questions.question: Which immunoglobulin is involved in type I hypersensitivity reactions?

options: They are serous glands producing watery secretions
They are endocrine glands secreting hormones locally
They are sebaceous glands releasing oily substances
They are mixed glands with mucous and serous components
They are apocrine glands with protein-rich secretions
questions.question: What type of glands are Bowman's glands?
questions.explanation: Bowman's glands in the olfactory lamina propria are serous glands producing watery secretions that dissolve odorants for receptor access. This continuous fluid flow also cleanses olfactory cilia between stimuli, maintaining receptor sensitivity. The secretion creates the appropriate aqueous environment for olfactory transduction.

questions.question: During which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?
questions.explanation: The S (synthesis) phase is dedicated to DNA replication, during which the entire genome is duplicated. Histone production also peaks during this phase to package newly synthesized DNA. Cells exit S phase with doubled DNA content but maintain the same ploidy level.

questions.question: Which cells in respiratory epithelium function as chemoreceptors?
questions.explanation: Brush cells are chemosensory receptors in the respiratory epithelium with apical microvilli and synaptic contacts with nerve endings. They resemble gustatory cells and likely detect chemical composition of airway fluid. These cells are part of the diffuse neuroendocrine system present in respiratory epithelium.
options: Ciliated columnar cells detect airborne chemical signals
Goblet cells sense irritants and increase mucus production
Basal cells monitor epithelial damage and initiate repair
Brush cells respond to chemical stimuli in airways
Small granule cells detect oxygen and carbon dioxide
Bile flows in the same direction as blood
Bile flows circumferentially around hepatic cords
Bile flow direction varies with feeding state
Bile does not flow through hepatic lobules
Bile flows from central vein toward portal triads
questions.question: In which direction does bile flow through hepatic lobules?
questions.explanation: Bile flows from bile canaliculi between hepatocytes toward the lobule periphery, opposite to blood flow. It drains into bile ductules (canals of Hering) then interlobular bile ducts in portal triads. This countercurrent arrangement optimizes hepatocyte access to both blood-borne and biliary substances.

questions.question: Which ion does aldosterone primarily regulate?
options: Aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
questions.explanation: Aldosterone stimulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the collecting duct by upregulating epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) and Na+/K+-ATPase. This increases blood volume and pressure while maintaining potassium homeostasis. Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalemia; hypoaldosteronism (Addison's disease) causes hypotension and hyperkalemia.

questions.question: What is the repeating contractile unit of skeletal muscle extending from Z-disc to Z-disc?
questions.explanation: The sarcomere is the fundamental contractile unit spanning approximately 2.5 μm between adjacent Z-discs in resting muscle. It contains interdigitating thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments whose sliding generates contraction. The characteristic banding pattern results from filament arrangement and overlap.

questions.question: Which cells are most numerous in the gastric epithelium?
questions.explanation: Surface mucous cells line the entire gastric surface and pits, making them the most numerous gastric epithelial cell type. These simple columnar cells form a continuous protective barrier producing alkaline mucus and bicarbonate. They are replaced every 3-5 days through division of progenitor cells.
options: Parietal cells constitute the most abundant type
Chief cells are the most numerous cells
Enteroendocrine cells are most common overall
Surface mucous cells predominate in the epithelium
Mucous neck cells outnumber all other types

questions.explanation: Contact with zona pellucida proteins (ZP3) triggers the acrosome reaction, releasing enzymes (hyaluronidase, acrosin) that digest the zona. This allows sperm to penetrate the extracellular matrix and fuse with the oocyte plasma membrane. Only capacitated sperm can undergo this reaction.
questions.question: What triggers the acrosome reaction during fertilization?
What characterizes respiratory bronchioles histologically?
options: Respiratory bronchioles contain cartilage in their walls
Respiratory bronchioles are lined entirely by pseudostratified epithelium
Respiratory bronchioles lack any smooth muscle tissue
Respiratory bronchioles have alveoli opening into their walls
Respiratory bronchioles contain abundant goblet cells
questions.explanation: Respiratory bronchioles are transitional structures lined partly by cuboidal epithelium (with Clara cells) and partly by squamous epithelium where alveoli open into their walls. They lack cartilage and have thin smooth muscle. This represents the transition from conducting to respiratory zones where gas exchange begins. Alveoli increase in number along the length of respiratory bronchioles.

The blood-air barrier consists of type I alveolar cells, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium, totaling less than 0.5 micrometers thickness. This minimal barrier facilitates rapid gas diffusion while maintaining separation between air and blood. The total surface area available for gas exchange approximates 70 square meters.
options: Thick connective tissue separating air from blood compartments
Multiple layers of epithelial cells preventing gas passage
Surfactant layer forming an impermeable barrier structure
Alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium with fused basement membranes
Alveolar macrophages creating a defensive cellular barrier
questions.question: What composes the blood-air barrier?
Which cells in olfactory epithelium serve as stem cells?
options: Supporting cells divide to replace all epithelial types
Basal cells generate new olfactory neurons throughout life
Olfactory neurons themselves undergo continuous division
Brush cells proliferate to maintain the epithelium
Bowman's gland cells migrate to replenish surface cells
questions.explanation: Basal cells are stem cells that continuously divide to produce new olfactory receptor neurons, making them unique among neurons in their regenerative capacity. This turnover is necessary because olfactory neurons are directly exposed to environmental insults. The entire olfactory epithelium can regenerate after injury.

questions.question: Which adult tissue contains stem cells capable of differentiating into multiple blood cell lineages?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow contains hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) that are multipotent, giving rise to all blood cell types. HSCs reside in specific niches with supporting stromal cells. They balance self-renewal and differentiation throughout life.

questions.question: Which cells in the olfactory epithelium are bipolar neurons detecting odors?
questions.explanation: Olfactory receptor neurons are bipolar neurons with dendrites extending to the epithelial surface bearing cilia containing odorant receptors. Their axons form the olfactory nerve projecting to the olfactory bulb. These neurons are continuously replaced throughout life from basal stem cells.

Western blotting separates proteins by SDS-PAGE, transfers them to membranes, and detects specific proteins using antibodies. This confirms protein expression, determines molecular weight, and assesses post-translational modifications. It's quantitative when combined with densitometry.
questions.question: What technique separates proteins by molecular weight for analysis?

questions.explanation: Endoderm forms epithelial linings of digestive and respiratory tracts, liver, pancreas, thyroid, and bladder. The gut tube develops from endoderm folding during embryonic body formation. Regional specialization creates organ-specific epithelia.
questions.question: Which germ layer forms the gastrointestinal tract epithelium?

options: The pyloric sphincter regulates emptying into the duodenum
The pyloric sphincter prevents gastric reflux into esophagus
The pyloric sphincter prevents duodenal reflux into stomach
The pyloric sphincter mixes gastric contents thoroughly
The pyloric sphincter produces digestive enzymes
questions.question: What is the main function of the pyloric sphincter?
questions.explanation: The pyloric sphincter, formed by thickened circular smooth muscle, regulates gastric emptying into the duodenum, preventing overwhelming of the small intestine. It opens intermittently in response to gastric distension and closes when duodenal contents are acidic or fatty. This coordination ensures optimal digestion and absorption.

Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) are resident phagocytes in alveolar spaces that remove inhaled particles and microorganisms. They arise from blood monocytes and can migrate to airways for mucociliary clearance. These cells are vital for maintaining sterile alveolar environment.
questions.question: Which immune cells patrol alveoli, phagocytosing inhaled particulates and pathogens?

questions.explanation: The floor of the mouth possesses stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium overlying a highly vascular lamina propria, which permits rapid sublingual drug absorption. This thin epithelium allows medications to bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism by entering the systemic circulation directly. The rich vascularity beneath the non-keratinized surface enhances the rate of drug uptake compared to keratinized regions.
questions.question: Which epithelial type lines the floor of the mouth to facilitate drug absorption?
options: Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Supporting sustentacular cells divide to form new neurons
Bowman's gland cells differentiate into neurons
Olfactory neurons themselves divide after injury
Basal stem cells generate new olfactory receptor neurons
Schwann cells transform into olfactory neurons
questions.question: Which cells replace damaged olfactory neurons?
questions.explanation: Basal cells in olfactory epithelium are stem cells that continuously generate new olfactory receptor neurons throughout life, unique among mammalian neurons. This regenerative capacity allows recovery of smell after toxic injury or infection, though severe damage may overwhelm regeneration causing permanent anosmia. Complete turnover occurs approximately every 30-60 days.

options: The cardia and pylorus lack parietal and chief cells
The fundus contains no parietal or chief cells
The body lacks both these cell types
The greater curvature has no parietal or chief cells
All stomach regions contain parietal and chief cells
questions.question: Which region of the stomach lacks parietal and chief cells?
questions.explanation: The cardia and pylorus contain primarily mucus-secreting glands lacking parietal and chief cells. These regions produce protective mucus rather than digestive secretions. The fundus and body contain typical gastric glands with all cell types including parietal and chief cells.

Filiform papillae are numerous conical structures covering the anterior tongue dorsum that lack taste buds. They increase friction for food manipulation and are heavily keratinized. Their mechanical function contrasts with taste-bearing papillae.
questions.question: Which lingual papillae lack taste buds and function primarily in mechanical processing?
What does FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) primarily detect?
questions.explanation: FISH uses fluorescently labeled DNA probes to detect specific chromosomal regions, gene copy numbers, or chromosomal translocations. It's valuable for diagnosing genetic disorders, identifying gene amplifications in cancer, and chromosome enumeration. Multiple probes with different fluorophores enable simultaneous detection.

questions.question: What control is essential in immunohistochemistry to confirm antibody specificity?
questions.explanation: Comprehensive controls include positive controls (tissues known to express the antigen), negative controls (omitting primary antibody), isotype controls (irrelevant antibody of same class), and internal positive cells. These controls validate specificity and identify nonspecific binding.

questions.question: Which zone of the epiphyseal growth plate contains chondrocytes arranged in longitudinal columns parallel to bone's long axis?
questions.explanation: The proliferative zone contains rapidly dividing chondrocytes stacked in columns aligned with longitudinal bone growth. This mitotic activity is essential for lengthening bones during development. The orderly arrangement ensures directional growth and proper bone formation.

questions.question: Which hepatocyte organelle is most affected by alcohol?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol consumption induces proliferation of smooth endoplasmic reticulum in hepatocytes, increasing cytochrome P450 enzymes for alcohol metabolism. This adaptation increases alcohol tolerance but also enhances metabolism of other drugs and production of toxic metabolites. Mitochondria are also damaged, impairing energy production and fatty acid oxidation.
options: Mitochondria are the primary target of alcohol damage
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum proliferates with chronic alcohol
Lysosomes are destroyed by alcohol exposure
Golgi apparatus undergoes fragmentation from alcohol
Nuclei shrink and condense from alcohol damage

questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole that function as baroreceptors. Decreased stretch from reduced blood pressure triggers renin secretion. These cells contain renin in secretory granules and respond to β-adrenergic stimulation and signals from the macula densa.
options: Mesangial cells release renin when stretched less
Macula densa cells produce renin from reduced stretch
Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin with decreased stretch
Podocytes synthesize renin when stretch decreases
questions.question: Which cells produce renin in response to decreased stretch?

questions.explanation: Aldosterone secretion is primarily stimulated by angiotensin II (via RAAS) and elevated plasma potassium. ACTH has minor effects. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal nephron, regulating blood pressure and electrolytes.
questions.question: What stimulates aldosterone secretion from zona glomerulosa?
Which region of the nephron is impermeable to urea?
options: The proximal tubule is completely impermeable to urea
The thin descending limb blocks all urea passage
The collecting duct prevents all urea movement
The thick ascending limb is impermeable to urea
All nephron segments are permeable to urea
questions.explanation: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to both water and urea, allowing it to actively transport NaCl without losing urea. This helps maintain the medullary urea concentration gradient essential for maximum urine concentration. Other segments have varying urea permeability depending on ADH and location.

The parotid gland has well-developed, easily visible intercalated ducts, the longest among salivary glands. The submandibular gland has very short intercalated ducts, and the sublingual gland's are poorly developed. This structural variation reflects differences in saliva modification among glands.
questions.question: Which salivary gland has the longest intercalated ducts?
options: The submandibular gland has the most extensive ones
The parotid gland possesses the longest intercalated ducts
The sublingual gland contains the longest segments
The minor salivary glands show maximal duct length
All salivary glands have equally short intercalated ducts

questions.question: Which cells form multinucleated giant cells at sites of chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation: Macrophages fuse to form multinucleated giant cells (foreign body type or Langhans type) attempting to phagocytose large foreign materials. This occurs in granulomatous inflammation (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis) and around foreign bodies. These cells can persist for extended periods.

Arcuate arteries run in an arc along the corticomedullary junction, giving rise to interlobular (cortical radial) arteries that extend into the cortex. These arteries do not penetrate the medulla but supply both cortical tissue and the bases of medullary pyramids. Their anatomical position is crucial for cortical blood supply.
questions.question: Which arteries run along the corticomedullary junction?
options: Arcuate arteries arch along the corticomedullary junction
Interlobar arteries course along this boundary region
Segmental arteries parallel this junction throughout
Interlobular arteries extend along this interface
Afferent arterioles travel along this boundary line

questions.question: Which cell type predominates in the interalveolar septum?
questions.explanation: Capillary endothelial cells cover approximately 85-95% of the interalveolar septal surface, facilitating gas exchange. The thin cytoplasm of these cells minimizes the diffusion distance between air and blood. The septa also contain thin type I alveolar cells, sparse fibroblasts, and elastic fibers.
options: Smooth muscle cells provide structural support dominantly
Fibroblasts constitute the majority of septal cells
Type II alveolar cells occupy most septal area
Alveolar macrophages fill the interalveolar septa
Capillary endothelial cells cover most septal surface

questions.question: What specialized structure increases the apical surface area of intestinal absorptive cells by approximately 20-fold?
questions.explanation: Microvilli are finger-like projections containing bundled actin filaments that form the brush border of intestinal epithelial cells. Each cell possesses thousands of microvilli creating a striated appearance under light microscopy. This massive surface area enhancement is critical for efficient nutrient absorption.

options: The main bronchi possess the most extensive cartilage
The terminal bronchioles have the most cartilage support
The respiratory bronchioles contain abundant cartilage plates
The lobar bronchi have maximal cartilaginous reinforcement
The segmental bronchi contain the greatest cartilage amount
questions.explanation: The main (primary) bronchi contain the most extensive cartilage, with nearly complete rings similar to but more irregular than tracheal cartilage. As bronchi branch and decrease in diameter, cartilage becomes progressively more sparse, appearing as irregular plates. Bronchioles lack cartilage completely, relying on smooth muscle and elastic tissue.
questions.question: Which structure contains the greatest amount of cartilage in the bronchial tree?

questions.explanation: Chondroitin sulfate is the major GAG in hyaline cartilage, providing compressive resistance through its high negative charge density. These GAGs are covalently attached to core proteins forming large proteoglycan aggregates. The aggregates interact with hyaluronic acid to create the characteristic gel-like matrix.
questions.question: What is the predominant glycosaminoglycan found in hyaline cartilage matrix?

questions.explanation: Intestinal stem cells reside in the crypt base between Paneth cells, continuously dividing to produce progenitor cells. These progenitors migrate upward, differentiating into absorptive enterocytes, goblet cells, and enteroendocrine cells that populate the villus. Paneth cells migrate downward from the stem cell niche.
options: Stem cells are scattered throughout villus epithelium
Stem cells reside at villus tips exclusively
Stem cells occupy the muscularis mucosae layer
Stem cells are located in the crypt base between Paneth cells
Stem cells distribute randomly in lamina propria
questions.question: Where are intestinal stem cells located?

questions.explanation: The parotid gland produces purely serous saliva rich in enzymes, particularly α-amylase for starch digestion. The acini are composed entirely of serous cells with basophilic cytoplasm and secretory granules. The watery secretion lacks mucus, contrasting with the mixed secretions of other major salivary glands.
options: The submandibular gland secretes only serous fluid
The sublingual gland produces exclusively serous saliva
The minor salivary glands create only serous components
The parotid gland generates purely serous secretions
The buccal glands manufacture strictly serous products
questions.question: Which salivary gland produces purely serous secretions?
What characterizes the sublingual gland secretions?
options: Sublingual secretions are purely serous and watery
Sublingual secretions contain only enzymes without mucus
Sublingual secretions are identical to parotid saliva
Sublingual secretions are predominantly mucous in nature
Sublingual secretions lack any antimicrobial components
questions.explanation: The sublingual gland produces predominantly mucous secretions with mucous tubules outnumbering serous acini. Serous cells are present almost exclusively in demilunes capping mucous tubules. This mucus-rich secretion provides excellent lubrication for mastication and swallowing.

options: Rugae are permanent folds containing all wall layers
Rugae are mucosal projections increasing surface area
Rugae are temporary folds of mucosa and submucosa
Rugae are pathological thickenings of gastric wall
Rugae are smooth muscle bundles in muscularis
questions.question: What characterizes rugae in the gastric mucosa?
questions.explanation: Rugae are longitudinal folds of gastric mucosa and submucosa that flatten when the stomach distends with food. They allow stomach expansion without rupture and increase surface area in the empty state. Rugae are most prominent along the lesser curvature and in the body.

options: They are well-developed and prominent throughout adult life
They contain the most abundant taste buds in adults
They increase in size and number with aging
They are rudimentary or absent in adult humans
They migrate to different tongue locations in adulthood
questions.explanation: Foliate papillae are located on the lateral tongue margins and are well-developed in some animals but rudimentary or absent in adult humans. They appear as parallel ridges and furrows containing taste buds in their walls. These papillae are more prominent in children than adults.
questions.question: What distinguishes foliate papillae in adults?

questions.explanation: Alveoli are the primary sites of gas exchange, with thin walls (type I cells, fused basement membranes, capillary endothelium) minimizing diffusion distance. The enormous alveolar surface area (~160 m²) and rich capillary network maximize gas exchange efficiency. Respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts contribute minor gas exchange.
questions.question: What is the primary site of gas exchange?
options: Terminal bronchioles are the main gas exchange sites
Respiratory bronchioles provide some gas exchange
Alveolar ducts are the primary exchange location
Alveolar sacs perform all gas exchange
Alveoli are the principal gas exchange structures

questions.question: What is the primary function of esophageal muscularis externa?
questions.explanation: The esophageal muscularis externa produces primary peristalsis (initiated by swallowing) and secondary peristalsis (clearing retained material), propelling food to the stomach. The muscle transitions from skeletal (upper third) to smooth muscle (lower third), reflecting progression from voluntary to involuntary control. Achalasia results from impaired peristalsis.
options: The muscularis secretes protective mucus throughout
The muscularis generates peristaltic waves propelling food
The muscularis absorbs nutrients from swallowed food
The muscularis produces digestive enzymes for breakdown
The muscularis regulates lower esophageal sphincter tone only

questions.explanation: Developmental apoptosis sculpts structures (interdigital webbing removal, hollow organ formation, nervous system refinement) and eliminates excess or inappropriate cells. This programmed death differs from pathological necrosis. Caspase cascades execute the death program.
questions.question: What developmental process involves programmed cell death shaping tissues?
What is the primary absorptive cell type in the small intestinal epithelium?
questions.explanation: Enterocytes (columnar absorptive cells) have extensive apical microvilli forming a brush border, greatly increasing surface area. They possess enzymes for terminal carbohydrate and peptide digestion and transport systems for nutrient absorption. Tight junctions between cells regulate paracellular transport.

The parotid gland produces purely serous saliva with the highest α-amylase concentration, initiating starch digestion in the mouth. The enzyme remains active in the stomach until inactivated by acid. Submandibular saliva also contains amylase but is diluted by mucous secretions. Amylase deficiency is rare and usually asymptomatic.
questions.question: Which cells produce saliva with the highest amylase content?
options: Parotid gland serous cells produce highest amylase
Submandibular gland cells produce most salivary amylase
Sublingual gland cells generate most amylase
Minor salivary glands produce highest amylase concentration
All salivary glands produce equal amylase amounts

questions.question: What percentage of total saliva volume comes from minor salivary glands?
questions.explanation: Minor salivary glands scattered throughout the oral mucosa contribute approximately 10% of total saliva volume but account for 70% of mucus secreted. These small glands provide continuous baseline secretion maintaining oral moisture. The major salivary glands contribute the remaining 90% of volume.
options: Minor salivary glands contribute approximately 5 percent
Minor salivary glands generate roughly 25 percent volume
Minor salivary glands secrete around 50 percent total
Minor salivary glands account for about 70 percent
Minor salivary glands produce about 10 percent total

questions.question: What protein complex connects keratinocytes via desmosomes?
questions.explanation: Desmosomes contain desmogleins and desmocollins (cadherin family) that bind adjacent cells, providing mechanical strength. Intracellularly, they connect to keratin intermediate filaments via desmoplakin and plakoglobin. Autoantibodies against these proteins cause pemphigus.

questions.question: What structure in thick skin is absent from thin skin?
questions.explanation: The stratum lucidum is a thin, clear layer present only in thick skin (palms, soles) between stratum granulosum and corneum. It consists of dead, flattened cells with densely packed keratin filaments. This additional layer enhances protection in high-friction areas.

Cancer cells employ multiple immune evasion strategies: reducing MHC I (avoiding CD8+ T cells), expressing checkpoint ligands (PD-L1 inhibiting T cells), secreting immunosuppressive cytokines (TGF-β, IL-10), and recruiting immunosuppressive cells. Immunotherapy targets these mechanisms.
questions.question: What mechanism allows cancer cells to evade immune destruction?
Which structure marks the transition from proximal to distal tubule?
options: The juxtaglomerular apparatus signals this transition point
The vascular pole indicates the tubular transition zone
The macula densa represents the beginning of distal tubule
The urinary pole marks where tubules change function
The glomerular capsule space defines tubular boundaries
questions.explanation: The macula densa, a specialized region of the thick ascending limb, marks where the nephron contacts its parent glomerulus and transitions to the distal convoluted tubule. These densely packed cells detect sodium chloride concentration in tubular fluid and regulate renin secretion. This anatomical landmark is crucial for tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms.

Satellite cells are muscle-specific stem cells located between sarcolemma and basal lamina. After injury, they activate, proliferate, and differentiate to regenerate muscle fibers. Their limited regenerative capacity decreases with age.
questions.question: What are satellite cells in skeletal muscle?

options: Simple columnar epithelium lines most esophageal length
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium covers most esophagus
Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium predominates throughout
Simple cuboidal epithelium forms most esophageal lining
questions.question: What type of epithelium lines most of the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The esophagus is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium that protects against mechanical abrasion from swallowed food. This epithelium extends from the pharynx to near the gastroesophageal junction where it transitions abruptly to simple columnar gastric epithelium. Keratinization can occur with chronic acid exposure.

questions.question: What characterizes the hepatic acinus of Rappaport?
questions.explanation: The hepatic acinus is a diamond-shaped functional unit with portal triads at the narrow ends and central veins at the wide ends. It is divided into three zones based on oxygen and nutrient gradients from portal blood. This model best explains patterns of hepatic injury and metabolic zonation.
options: The acinus is centered on a central vein
The acinus is identical to the classical lobule
The acinus has no relevance to liver pathology
The acinus is a diamond-shaped unit between portal triads and central veins
The acinus is purely a theoretical construct

questions.explanation: The zona glomerulosa is the outermost cortical layer producing aldosterone in response to angiotensin II and hyperkalemia. Aldosterone regulates sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in distal nephron. These cells lack 17α-hydroxylase, preventing glucocorticoid synthesis.
questions.question: Which zone of the adrenal cortex produces mineralocorticoids, primarily aldosterone?
What does PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff) stain detect?
questions.explanation: PAS stains carbohydrates (glycogen, mucins, basement membranes) magenta due to periodic acid oxidation of vicinal diols creating aldehydes that react with Schiff reagent. This demonstrates basement membranes, goblet cell mucin, and glycogen stores.

questions.question: Which glands protect the esophagus from acid reflux?
questions.explanation: Esophageal cardiac glands in the lamina propria near the stomach produce mucus similar to gastric cardiac glands. This alkaline mucus protects the esophageal mucosa from acid reflux damage. These glands are more prominent in individuals with chronic reflux disease.
options: Brunner's glands neutralize acid in the esophagus
Esophageal cardiac glands produce alkaline mucus
Von Ebner's glands secrete protective enzymes
Pyloric glands extend into the distal esophagus
Fundic glands provide esophageal acid protection
Simple squamous epithelium lines collecting ducts
Stratified columnar epithelium forms duct lining
Pseudostratified epithelium with cilia lines ducts
Cuboidal epithelium with principal and intercalated cells
questions.explanation: Collecting ducts are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium consisting of pale-staining principal cells (involved in Na+/K+ exchange and water reabsorption) and darker intercalated cells (involved in acid-base balance). Cell boundaries are distinct unlike in proximal tubule. The epithelium becomes taller (columnar) in larger collecting ducts.
questions.question: What cells line the collecting ducts in the kidney?

questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages attached to sinusoidal endothelium or free in the lumen, comprising about 15% of liver cells. They phagocytose aged erythrocytes, bacteria from the portal blood, and other debris. Kupffer cells are most numerous in periportal regions where they first encounter portal blood.
questions.question: Which cells in liver sinusoids are phagocytic?
options: Hepatocytes perform phagocytosis in the sinusoids
Kupffer cells are macrophages in sinusoid lumens
Stellate cells remove debris from sinusoidal blood
Endothelial cells phagocytose particles passing through
Bile duct cells ingest foreign material actively

questions.question: Which blood vessel directly follows the glomerulus?
questions.explanation: The efferent arteriole drains the glomerular capillary network and has a smaller diameter than the afferent arteriole. This unique arterial arrangement maintains high glomerular pressure for filtration while providing blood for the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta. The efferent arteriole's resistance helps regulate glomerular filtration rate.
options: The peritubular capillaries receive blood from glomerulus
The arcuate artery transports blood from glomerular tuft
The interlobular vein drains the glomerular capillary bed
The vasa recta directly continue from glomerular vessels
The efferent arteriole carries blood away from glomerulus

questions.question: Which cell junction maintains the blood-testis barrier?
questions.explanation: Tight (occluding) junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells create the blood-testis barrier, dividing the seminiferous tubule into basal and adluminal compartments. This barrier protects developing sperm from immune attack and creates a specialized microenvironment for spermatogenesis. The barrier must briefly open to allow preleptotene spermatocytes to pass.
options: Gap junctions between Sertoli cells form this barrier
Desmosomes between Sertoli cells create the barrier
Tight junctions (occluding junctions) between Sertoli cells
Adherens junctions maintain the blood-testis barrier
Hemidesmosomes anchor Sertoli cells forming barrier

questions.question: Which cell type is most resistant to ischemic damage?
options: Neurons are most resistant to ischemic injury
Cardiac myocytes tolerate prolonged ischemia best
Skeletal muscle fibers resist ischemia maximally
Fibroblasts and connective tissue cells resist ischemia best
questions.explanation: Fibroblasts and connective tissue cells with low metabolic rates tolerate ischemia better than highly metabolically active cells (neurons, cardiac myocytes). Neurons suffer irreversible damage within minutes of complete ischemia. Cardiac myocytes undergo infarction after 20-40 minutes. Skeletal muscle survives longer (hours) than cardiac muscle but less than connective tissue.

questions.question: What is the primary cell type in the parietal epithelium of Bowman's capsule?
questions.explanation: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule consists of simple squamous epithelium that provides a thin barrier separating the urinary space from surrounding interstitium. This epithelium is supported by a basement membrane and thin connective tissue layer. At the urinary pole, it transitions to the cuboidal epithelium of the proximal tubule.
options: Simple squamous cells form the parietal layer
Podocytes with extensive foot processes characterize it
Cuboidal epithelial cells line this capsular region
Columnar cells with microvilli compose this layer
Mesangial cells provide structural support here

questions.question: What process occurs in the thymic cortex during T cell development?
questions.explanation: Positive selection in the thymic cortex ensures T cells can recognize self-MHC molecules. Thymocytes whose receptors bind cortical epithelial cell MHC with appropriate affinity survive; others die by neglect. This selects for MHC restriction.

questions.question: What structure in the ovarian follicle secretes estrogen before ovulation?
questions.explanation: Granulosa cells convert androgens (from theca cells) to estrogens via aromatase enzyme. Before ovulation, FSH stimulates their proliferation and differentiation. After ovulation, they luteinize to form corpus luteum producing progesterone.

Parietal (oxyntic) cells in gastric glands secrete HCl via H+/K+-ATPase pumps in extensive intracellular canaliculi. They also produce intrinsic factor necessary for vitamin B12 absorption. These large, eosinophilic cells are located in the upper gland portions.
questions.question: What cell type in gastric glands secretes hydrochloric acid?

questions.explanation: The iris contains sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic) and dilator pupillae (sympathetic) muscles that adjust pupil size. Constriction (miosis) occurs in bright light while dilation (mydriasis) occurs in dim light. Iris pigmentation determines eye color.
questions.question: Which structure regulates the amount of light entering the eye by controlling pupil diameter?

questions.explanation: Somatotrophs (most abundant acidophil) secrete growth hormone (GH), which promotes growth and regulates metabolism. GH secretion follows pulsatile patterns with nocturnal surges. GH acts directly and via IGF-1 produced in the liver.
questions.question: Which anterior pituitary cells secrete growth hormone?
Which lymphoid organ filters blood rather than lymph?
questions.explanation: The spleen filters blood, removing senescent erythrocytes and blood-borne antigens while mounting immune responses. Red pulp contains sinusoids where macrophages phagocytose damaged red cells. White pulp consists of lymphoid tissue surrounding arterioles.

Freeze-fracture splits frozen membranes along the hydrophobic interior, revealing integral membrane proteins as particles. Platinum-carbon shadowing creates replicas visualized by TEM. This technique maps protein distribution in membrane leaflets.
questions.question: What EM technique visualizes membrane protein distribution by fracturing frozen cells?

questions.explanation: PP cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide in response to meals, which inhibits pancreatic exocrine secretion and gallbladder contraction. These cells are more abundant in islets in the pancreatic head. PP secretion is cholinergically stimulated.
questions.question: What cells produce pancreatic polypeptide regulating pancreatic secretion?

options: Type I alveolar cells undergo mitosis after injury
Type II alveolar cells serve as progenitor cells
Alveolar macrophages divide locally in lung tissue
Capillary endothelial cells cannot divide in alveoli
Interstitial fibroblasts are post-mitotic in adult lungs
questions.question: Which cells are capable of dividing in the alveolar epithelium?
questions.explanation: Type II alveolar cells function as stem cells for alveolar epithelium, dividing to replace damaged type I and type II cells. This regenerative capacity is crucial for lung repair after injury. Type I cells, despite covering most alveolar surface, cannot divide and must be replaced by differentiation of type II cells.

questions.question: Which pancreatic cells produce bicarbonate-rich fluid to neutralize gastric acid?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic ductal epithelial cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid stimulated by secretin. The HCO3- neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum and creates optimal pH for pancreatic enzymes. CFTR channels in ductal cells are defective in cystic fibrosis.

ADH (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary increases collecting duct water permeability by inserting aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane. Without ADH, the epithelium is water-impermeable and dilute urine is produced. ADH deficiency or resistance causes diabetes insipidus with massive dilute urine output.
questions.question: What regulates collecting duct water permeability?
options: Aldosterone regulates collecting duct water permeability
Atrial natriuretic peptide modulates water permeability
Renin regulates collecting duct water transport
Erythropoietin controls water permeability in ducts

questions.explanation: PCR exponentially amplifies specific DNA sequences using thermostable DNA polymerase, primers, and thermal cycling. It enables detection and quantification of rare sequences, genetic mutations, and gene expression (RT-PCR). Real-time PCR provides quantitative data.
questions.question: What does PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) accomplish?

questions.explanation: CD8+ T cells recognize MHC class I-presented antigens on infected or transformed cells and induce apoptosis via perforin and granzymes. This cell-mediated cytotoxicity eliminates intracellular pathogens and tumor cells. They provide surveillance for abnormal cells.
questions.question: What is the primary function of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells?
What is the functional significance of hepatocyte binucleation?
