questions.question: A public health programme promotes HPV vaccination in early adolescence as a strategy to reduce future cervical cancer incidence. This represents which level of cancer prevention?

questions.explanation: Subacute haemorrhage (containing methemoglobin) appears bright on T1-weighted MRI because methemoglobin has paramagnetic properties that shorten T1 relaxation, causing the tissue to recover magnetisation rapidly and appear hyperintense. Other T1-bright substances include fat, protein-rich fluids, melanin, and gadolinium. Pure water-containing lesions (cysts, oedema) appear dark on T1.
questions.question: Which tissue appears BRIGHT (hyperintense) on T1-weighted MRI?

questions.explanation: The nine abdominal regions are created by two horizontal (subcostal and intertubercular) and two vertical (midclavicular) lines. The epigastric region is the central upper region, bounded superiorly by the subcostal line, inferiorly by the trans-umbilical (umbilical) plane, and laterally by the left and right midclavicular lines. It lies between the left and right hypochondriac regions. This regional anatomy aids in localising abdominal findings and clinical symptoms to specific organs.
questions.question: The abdomen is divided into nine regions using imaginary lines. The epigastric region is located in which position relative to these landmarks?
options: Central upper region, bounded laterally by the midclavicular lines
Central lower region above the pubis at all times
Complete absence of any radiation dose to the patient
Lower overall cost compared with plain radiography in all settings
Greater sensitivity for detecting small lytic lesions and better delineation of disease extent
Elimination of the need for any radiologist interpretation
Ability to assess bone mineral density with greater accuracy than DEXA
questions.explanation: Whole-body low-dose CT provides significantly greater sensitivity than conventional plain radiographic skeletal survey for detecting small lytic lesions and better delineates the true extent of skeletal involvement in multiple myeloma, while still delivering a substantially lower radiation dose than a standard diagnostic CT protocol through dose-optimised low-dose acquisition parameters. This has led to increasing adoption of whole-body CT or MRI as preferred staging modalities over plain radiography in many myeloma treatment guidelines. Radiation dose, while reduced compared with standard CT, is still generally higher than conventional plain film skeletal survey, representing a trade-off against improved diagnostic sensitivity.
questions.question: A whole-body low-dose CT scan is performed as part of a myeloma skeletal survey protocol instead of conventional plain radiography. What is a key advantage of this CT-based approach?

options: Oedema surrounding an MCA territory infarct
Haemorrhagic transformation of an ischaemic infarct
A hyperdense thrombus within the proximal middle cerebral artery
Calcification of the MCA wall in elderly patients
Contrast medium retained in the MCA after angiography
questions.explanation: The dense MCA sign is caused by a hyperdense (white) thrombus or embolus lodged within the proximal segment of the middle cerebral artery, visible on non-contrast CT as a tubular hyperdensity in the MCA distribution. It indicates acute large vessel occlusion and is an important early CT sign of ischaemic stroke. Fresh thrombus is denser than normal brain parenchyma due to its high haematocrit content in the acute phase.
questions.question: The 'dense MCA sign' on a non-contrast CT brain is caused by:
In ultrasound, what is the clinical significance of the 3 dB attenuation rule in soft tissue?
options: 3 dB corresponds to a doubling of signal intensity
3 dB corresponds to a reduction of the original signal intensity by half
3 dB attenuation occurs at every 1 cm of tissue for all frequencies
3 dB is the maximum attenuation allowable for diagnostic imaging
3 dB equals the acoustic impedance mismatch at all soft tissue interfaces
questions.explanation: In ultrasound physics, a reduction of 3 dB (decibels) corresponds to a halving of signal intensity (not amplitude, which would require -6 dB). Understanding this logarithmic relationship is important for interpreting time-gain compensation (TGC) settings and for understanding the progressive loss of signal with depth in tissue. Attenuation coefficient in soft tissue is approximately 0.5 dB/cm/MHz.

options: A solitary gallstone without surrounding changes
Thickened gallbladder wall with pericholecystic fluid
questions.explanation: Acute cholecystitis on ultrasound characteristically shows: (1) gallbladder wall thickening >3mm, (2) pericholecystic fluid (fluid surrounding the gallbladder indicating inflammation), (3) a positive sonographic Murphy's sign (maximal tenderness when the transducer is pressed directly over the gallbladder), and (4) gallstones or sludge. The combination of gallstones with these inflammatory features differentiates acute cholecystitis from biliary colic (which shows gallstones without wall inflammation or pericholecystic fluid).
questions.question: In the imaging of a patient with right upper quadrant pain, ultrasound is the first-line investigation. Which finding on ultrasound is most characteristic of acute cholecystitis?

questions.explanation: The first step in cancer assessment is always a thorough clinical history and physical examination. These guide the choice of subsequent investigations including imaging and histopathological biopsy. Initiating treatment without clinical assessment and confirmed diagnosis is inappropriate and potentially harmful.
questions.question: Which is the most appropriate first investigation when assessing a patient suspected of cancer?

questions.explanation: Osteoporotic compression fractures typically produce anterior wedging with preserved posterior vertebral body height and intact pedicles, distinguishing them from burst fractures where posterior wall retropulsion threatens the spinal canal. Pedicle destruction instead raises concern for an underlying malignant infiltrative process rather than simple osteoporotic collapse. MRI can help differentiate benign osteoporotic fractures from pathological fractures when the plain film appearance is ambiguous.
questions.question: A radiograph of the spine in an elderly patient shows anterior wedging of a vertebral body with loss of height greater than 20% but preservation of the posterior wall and pedicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastatic pathological fracture with pedicle destruction

questions.question: Which mediastinal compartment most commonly contains anterior mediastinal masses (the 4 Ts)?
questions.explanation: The anterior mediastinum contains the classic '4 T' masses: Thymoma, Teratoma/germ cell tumour, Terrible lymphoma, and Thyroid mass (substernal goitre). Accurate compartmental localisation on CXR and CT guides differential diagnosis. Posterior mediastinal masses are typically neurogenic tumours, while middle mediastinal masses include bronchogenic cysts and lymphadenopathy.

questions.question: A CT scan of the head in a patient with acute onset of hemiparesis shows loss of grey-white matter differentiation and effacement of sulci in the left middle cerebral artery territory within three hours of symptom onset. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Early ischaemic stroke on CT is subtle, manifesting as loss of grey-white differentiation and sulcal effacement due to early cytotoxic oedema, well before a clearly demarcated hypodense infarct becomes visible after 24 hours. These findings, along with a hyperdense MCA sign if present, are the earliest CT clues to large vessel occlusion. Recognising them within the therapeutic window is essential for timely thrombolysis or thrombectomy decisions.

Right ventricular enlargement causes lateral displacement of the left heart border with the apex displaced laterally but characteristically not inferiorly, distinguishing it from left ventricular enlargement. In contrast, left ventricular enlargement displaces the apex both laterally and inferiorly. This distinction helps identify the dominant chamber enlargement on CXR.
questions.question: In right ventricular enlargement on CXR, the cardiac apex is displaced in which direction?

questions.explanation: In a patient with acute renal failure, iodinated contrast agents (used in IVU and CT) are contraindicated due to the high risk of further contrast-induced nephropathy. Ultrasound is the first-line investigation because it is non-invasive, does not require contrast, is widely available, and can rapidly demonstrate hydronephrosis indicating obstruction, renal size, and cortical thickness. Retrograde pyelogram or MAG-3 may be considered subsequently if needed.
options: Ultrasound of the kidneys and urinary tract
questions.question: In a patient with acute renal failure and suspected urinary tract obstruction, which imaging modality should be performed FIRST?

questions.explanation: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (AVM) appears on CXR as a rounded opacity with visible feeding vessels leading into the mass. The feeding artery and draining vein provide the characteristic appearance. Pulmonary AVMs can cause right-to-left shunting, cyanosis, and paradoxical embolism. CT angiography is the definitive investigation.
options: Visible feeding vessels into the mass
questions.question: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) of the lung on CXR is suggested by which specific finding?

questions.explanation: MCU (micturating cystourethrogram) is the gold standard investigation for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) in children, typically performed after a urinary tract infection. Contrast is instilled into the bladder via catheter, and reflux of contrast up the ureters during filling and voiding is evaluated fluoroscopically. MCU also detects posterior urethral valves and bladder outlet abnormalities. VUR predisposes to recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scarring.
questions.question: Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) is MOST commonly performed to investigate which condition in paediatric patients?

questions.explanation: The craniocaudal (CC) view compresses the breast from above (cranial) to below (caudal), providing a superior-to-inferior image. Together with the mediolateral oblique (MLO) view, it forms the standard two-view mammography examination. The CC view is particularly useful for medial breast lesions.
questions.question: The standard view for mammography that provides a superior-to-inferior compression image is:

options: Local tumour removal, biopsy, and staging
questions.explanation: Surgical oncology encompasses local tumour resection, lymph node dissection, biopsy for diagnosis and staging, and reconstructive procedures. Surgery may be performed with curative intent in localised disease or palliative intent to relieve obstruction or control bleeding. It is the oldest and most effective treatment for many solid tumours when performed at an early stage.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the role of cancer treatment surgery as a modality?

questions.explanation: Air bronchograms represent air-filled bronchi visible within areas of alveolar consolidation (airspace disease). They appear because the normally invisible bronchi (air-density surrounded by air-density alveoli) become visible when the surrounding alveoli fill with fluid, pus, or blood (water-density). This is a hallmark of alveolar (airspace) disease. Interstitial disease (Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing) produces haziness without air bronchograms because the airspaces themselves remain air-filled.
questions.question: Which chest radiograph finding in respiratory failure indicates that fluid is filling the alveolar air spaces rather than the interstitium?

A CT scan shows a dilated appendix with a calcified appendicolith, wall thickening, and a large surrounding rim-enhancing fluid collection with gas locules in the right iliac fossa. What complication of appendicitis does this represent?
questions.explanation: A rim-enhancing fluid collection containing gas locules adjacent to an inflamed, obstructed appendix indicates that the inflammatory process has progressed to a contained abscess rather than remaining as uncomplicated appendicitis or a solid phlegmon. This distinction matters clinically because abscesses often require percutaneous drainage before or instead of immediate appendicectomy. Recognising gas within the collection also excludes a simple sterile fluid collection.

Automated segmentation tools can significantly reduce the time required to contour multiple organs at risk and improve consistency compared with fully manual contouring, but they still require careful review and correction by the treating radiation oncologist to ensure accuracy for the individual patient's specific anatomy, particularly in the presence of anatomical variation or pathology that may confuse the automated algorithm. These tools support and augment the human workflow rather than replacing clinical oversight and decision-making entirely. Understanding both the benefits and the continued need for expert verification is important as such automated tools become increasingly integrated into modern radiotherapy planning practice.
questions.question: A patient undergoing radiotherapy planning has their organs at risk auto-segmented by artificial intelligence software before manual review by the radiation oncologist. What is the primary clinical benefit of incorporating this automated segmentation tool into the workflow?
options: Improved consistency and reduced time required for contouring, while still requiring expert verification
Complete elimination of the need for any human review of contours
Automatic determination of the final prescribed radiation dose without further input
Automatic delivery of the treatment without any physician oversight
Elimination of the need for a planning CT scan altogether

questions.explanation: In a supine patient, free pleural air rises anteriorly and collects along the costophrenic angle, producing the 'deep sulcus sign' rather than the classic apical lucency seen erect. This sign is critical because supine trauma films can otherwise miss a pneumothorax. Prompt recognition avoids delayed tension pneumothorax.
questions.question: A supine trauma chest radiograph shows a deep lucent costophrenic sulcus extending along the lateral chest wall. This sign is most suggestive of which condition?

questions.explanation: Malignant neoplasms are characterised by their ability to invade adjacent tissues and metastasise to distant sites, unlike benign tumours which grow in an expansile but non-invasive manner. This distinction drives staging, treatment intent, and prognosis. Benign tumours can still cause significant morbidity through mass effect.
questions.question: What is the fundamental distinction between benign and malignant neoplasms in oncological terminology?
options: Benign tumours are always larger than malignant ones
Benign tumours always cause more symptoms
Malignant tumours invade and metastasise; benign do not

questions.explanation: Preoperative radiotherapy is delivered to tissue with intact blood supply and oxygenation, which can improve radiosensitivity compared with treating a postoperative tumour bed that may have compromised vascularity, and treating the tumour before surgical manipulation may also theoretically reduce the risk of tumour cell seeding during resection. This approach does not eliminate the need for surgery, which typically remains a necessary component of definitive local treatment for many sarcomas. Preoperative radiotherapy does, however, introduce specific considerations regarding surgical wound healing that must be carefully managed in the postoperative period, representing one of the trade-offs of this treatment sequencing approach.
questions.question: A patient with a large abdominal sarcoma is treated with preoperative (neoadjuvant) radiotherapy before planned surgical resection. What is a key potential advantage of delivering radiotherapy before surgery rather than after?
options: Ability to deliver a substantially higher total dose than would be used postoperatively
Avoidance of any radiation-related wound healing considerations
Reduction in the total number of required imaging studies before surgery
Improved tumour oxygenation and blood supply at the time of treatment, potentially improving radiosensitivity and reducing seeding risk during subsequent surgery
Complete elimination of the need for surgery altogether

questions.explanation: Intrathecal chemotherapy is injected directly into the cerebrospinal fluid via lumbar puncture or Ommaya reservoir. It is used for leptomeningeal metastases and CNS prophylaxis in haematological malignancies such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Systemic agents have limited blood-brain barrier penetration.
questions.question: Intrathecal chemotherapy is specifically used to treat cancer involving which site?
The Larmor frequency equation for MRI is ω = γ × B0. If a 3T MRI scanner is used instead of a 1.5T scanner, what happens to the Larmor frequency of hydrogen protons?
questions.explanation: The Larmor frequency is directly proportional to the magnetic field strength (B0). The gyromagnetic ratio of hydrogen (γ) is approximately 42.58 MHz/T. At 1.5 T, the Larmor frequency ≈ 63.87 MHz; at 3 T, it doubles to ≈ 127.7 MHz. Higher field strength increases signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which can be used to achieve higher resolution or faster imaging.

questions.question: A megavoltage photon beam used in radiotherapy demonstrates a 'skin-sparing effect,' with the maximum dose occurring below the skin surface rather than at the surface itself. What is the physical basis for this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: The skin-sparing effect occurs because megavoltage photon beams predominantly interact with tissue through Compton scattering, generating secondary electrons that travel forward and deposit their energy at increasing depth until electronic equilibrium is achieved at the depth of dose maximum, meaning the dose actually received at the very skin surface is lower than at this deeper point. This is clinically advantageous because it reduces the incidence of severe skin reactions compared with older orthovoltage units, which delivered their maximum dose directly at the skin surface. Beam energy directly influences the depth at which this maximum occurs, with higher energies producing deeper build-up regions.
options: Selective filtration of the beam by the treatment couch
Preferential scatter of photons away from the skin surface
Build-up of secondary electrons with increasing depth before electronic equilibrium is reached
Reduced photon fluence specifically at the skin surface only
Complete absorption of the beam by the outer skin layer

questions.question: During a fluoroscopically guided procedure, the operator increases the source-to-skin distance rather than keeping the tube close to the patient. What is the primary radiation protection benefit of this practice?
options: Reduced scatter radiation reaching the operator only
Improved spatial resolution of the fluoroscopic image
Reduced patient skin entrance dose due to the inverse square law
Increased contrast resolution of the image
questions.explanation: Increasing the source-to-skin distance allows the beam to diverge before reaching the patient, reducing the radiation intensity at the skin surface in accordance with the inverse square law, and is a key strategy for minimising the risk of skin injury during prolonged fluoroscopic procedures. This principle applies specifically to patient skin dose rather than directly to operator scatter dose, which is instead reduced through shielding, distance from the patient, and time minimisation. Awareness of cumulative skin dose is particularly important in complex interventional procedures with prolonged fluoroscopy times.

The Hampton line (also known as the Hampton's hump in the context of gastric ulcers) is a thin radiolucent line that represents non-ulcerated mucosa projecting over the neck of a benign ulcer crater. It indicates that the ulcer has not penetrated beyond the mucosa into malignant tissue. The ulcer mound is the surrounding oedematous submucosal tissue. Together these features help distinguish benign from malignant ulcers.
questions.question: On barium meal, the 'Hampton line' associated with a benign gastric ulcer represents:
options: Non-ulcerated mucosa around the ulcer crater (a thin radiolucent line)
The mucosal fold radiating toward the ulcer crater
The oedematous submucosa surrounding the crater
Malignant tissue undermining the ulcer margin
A duplicate mucosal fold caused by scarring

questions.explanation: ERCP combines endoscopic access to the biliary and pancreatic ducts with fluoroscopic contrast imaging, allowing not only diagnostic visualisation of ductal abnormalities such as stones or strictures but also simultaneous therapeutic intervention such as sphincterotomy, stone extraction, or stent placement, unlike purely diagnostic techniques such as magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography. This combined diagnostic and therapeutic capability makes ERCP the preferred approach when therapeutic intervention is anticipated, despite carrying a higher risk of complications such as pancreatitis compared with non-invasive imaging alone. MRCP remains valuable as a non-invasive first-line diagnostic tool when therapeutic intervention is not immediately required.
options: No requirement for sedation or contrast administration
Complete avoidance of any radiation exposure
Superior soft tissue contrast compared with MRI
Ability to assess the entire abdomen in a single pass
The ability to perform simultaneous therapeutic intervention, such as stone extraction or stenting
questions.question: A patient undergoes endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with fluoroscopic guidance for suspected choledocholithiasis. What is the primary advantage of this technique compared with purely diagnostic imaging such as MRCP?

questions.explanation: A boxer's fracture involves the neck of the fifth (and sometimes fourth) metacarpal, typically resulting from an axial force such as punching, producing volar angulation of the distal fragment. Bennett and Rolando fractures instead involve the base of the first metacarpal with intra-articular extension, carrying a different mechanism and management approach. Angulation degree on radiograph helps determine whether closed reduction is required.
questions.question: A radiograph of the hand after a punch injury shows a fracture at the neck of the fifth metacarpal with volar angulation of the distal fragment. What is this fracture commonly called?

options: Do not cause bone marrow suppression
questions.explanation: Nitrosoureas are lipid-soluble and can cross the blood-brain barrier, making them suitable for treating brain tumours such as glioblastoma. Most other chemotherapy agents are unable to penetrate the CNS effectively. Examples include carmustine (BCNU) and lomustine (CCNU).
questions.question: Nitrosoureas such as carmustine are unique among alkylating agents because they:
A 70-year-old woman with known carcinoma of the breast presents with back pain. Which nuclear medicine study is most appropriate to screen for skeletal metastases throughout the entire skeleton?
questions.explanation: Radionuclide bone scanning (whole-body isotope bone scan) with technetium-99m-labelled diphosphonate is the standard investigation for screening the entire skeleton for metastatic disease. It is highly sensitive for detecting osteoblastic activity and can identify lesions before they become visible on plain radiographs. A single scan surveys all bones simultaneously, making it far more practical than individual plain radiographs of all bones.

questions.question: A pregnant radiographer continues working in a diagnostic imaging department after declaring her pregnancy. What is the primary radiation protection consideration that applies specifically during this period?
options: Radiation exposure limits become less strict during pregnancy
No special precautions are required beyond standard practice
The radiographer must immediately cease all clinical duties for the remainder of the pregnancy
A lower dose limit applies to the fetus, requiring additional precautions such as monitoring and role modification if needed
Only ionising radiation from CT, and not general radiography, requires any consideration
questions.explanation: Once pregnancy is declared, a specific, lower dose limit applies to protect the fetus throughout the remaining gestation, and workplaces typically implement additional precautions such as personal dosimetry review, reassignment away from high-exposure procedures, or increased use of protective equipment to ensure this lower limit is not exceeded, rather than requiring complete cessation of all radiation-related duties in most circumstances. This reflects the increased radiosensitivity of the developing fetus, particularly during specific stages of organogenesis, compared with adult tissue. Appropriate risk assessment and role adjustment, guided by institutional radiation protection policy, allows many pregnant radiation workers to continue safely practising with modified duties.

questions.question: Which of the following cancer risk factors can be categorized as both lifestyle and environmental?
questions.explanation: A sedentary lifestyle reflects both a personal lifestyle choice and an environmental/behavioural context. It promotes obesity, insulin resistance, and inflammation, all of which increase cancer risk. Intervention through physical activity meaningfully reduces cancer incidence and mortality.

questions.question: A student notes that increasing the anode angle decreases the anode heel effect. This is because:
options: The focal spot size increases proportionally
Higher anode angles reduce bremsstrahlung production
Characteristic radiation output increases with a wider angle
Less of the emerging x-ray beam is attenuated by the anode material
questions.explanation: A larger (less steep) anode angle means the emergent x-rays travel a shorter path through the anode material before exiting, resulting in less self-attenuation and a more uniform beam intensity across the field. A steep angle forces x-rays emerging near the anode end to traverse more material, causing greater intensity reduction (heel effect) at the anode side.

questions.question: Hormonal therapy is classified under which category of cancer treatment modality?
questions.explanation: Hormonal therapy is a form of systemic therapy that targets hormone-sensitive cancers such as breast and prostate cancer. Agents include tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, and anti-androgens. Unlike surgery and radiotherapy which are local treatments, hormonal therapy acts throughout the body on hormone receptor-bearing cells.

options: Low-energy photons that would not reach the detector
questions.question: Beam hardening in x-ray imaging refers to the filtration of which component of the polychromatic x-ray beam?
questions.explanation: Beam hardening (filtration) removes low-energy photons from the polychromatic x-ray beam that would be absorbed by the patient without contributing to image formation. These undesirable low-energy photons increase patient dose without improving image quality. Added filtration (usually aluminium or copper) increases the mean beam energy, 'hardening' the beam.

options: A minor discrepancy with no meaningful clinical significance requiring no further action
A random statistical dose variation that cannot be prevented through any process improvement
An expected outcome of standard treatment planning that does not require investigation
A geographic miss or wrong-site error, prevented primarily through robust verification checks including site marking, imaging confirmation, and independent double-checking
An unavoidable consequence of normal biological variation between patients
questions.question: A radiotherapy quality and safety incident review identifies that a patient received treatment to the wrong side of the body due to a documentation error. What category of radiotherapy error does this represent, and what is the primary preventive strategy against such errors?
questions.explanation: A wrong-site treatment error represents a serious, generally preventable incident that should be identified and addressed through robust systematic verification processes, including clear documentation, site marking, image guidance confirmation, and independent checks by multiple team members at key points in the treatment pathway, rather than being attributed to unavoidable random variation. Such incidents warrant formal incident investigation and root cause analysis to identify systemic contributing factors and implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence. Robust quality assurance and verification culture throughout every stage of the radiotherapy pathway, from initial consultation through to daily treatment delivery, is essential to minimise the risk of such significant, potentially harmful errors.

Widening of the prevertebral soft tissues on the lateral cervical radiograph is an indirect sign of haematoma formation following fracture. In the presence of prevertebral soft tissue swelling, a fracture (including odontoid) is assumed to be present until excluded by CT or MRI. Normal prevertebral soft tissue width is less than 7mm at C2 level. This soft tissue sign may be the only clue when fracture lines are difficult to detect on plain film.
options: Widening of the prevertebral soft tissues
Subluxation of C3 on well-defined C4
questions.question: Fractures of the odontoid process (C2 dens) are considered unstable. What indirect radiographic clue on the lateral cervical film may suggest a dens fracture even before the fracture line is visible?

options: An intra-articular fracture communicating with the joint
questions.explanation: A lipohaemarthrosis, seen as a fat-fluid level on a horizontal beam lateral radiograph, indicates that marrow fat has entered the joint space through a fracture communicating with the articular surface, such as a tibial plateau fracture. Ligamentous injuries alone, without bony involvement, do not release marrow fat into the joint. This sign should prompt a careful search for a subtle fracture even when none is initially obvious.
questions.question: A knee radiograph shows a lipohaemarthrosis with a fat-fluid level on the horizontal beam lateral view following trauma. What does this finding most strongly suggest?
A mammogram shows a mass with spiculated, irregular margins and associated architectural distortion of the surrounding breast tissue. This appearance is MOST concerning for:
questions.explanation: Spiculated margins with architectural distortion are highly suspicious mammographic features for invasive breast carcinoma, reflecting the infiltrative growth pattern of malignant tissue into surrounding structures. Benign lesions such as fibroadenomas and lipomas typically show smooth, well-defined margins without this distortion. This appearance warrants urgent tissue biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

questions.question: Cyclophosphamide belongs to which subclass of alkylating chemotherapy agents?
questions.explanation: Cyclophosphamide, along with mechlorethamine, chlorambucil, melphalan, and ifosfamide, belongs to the mustard gas derivatives subclass of alkylating agents. These drugs were derived from mustard gas, a chemical warfare agent. Cyclophosphamide requires hepatic activation to its active metabolite phosphoramide mustard.

CT angiography provides rapid, non-invasive visualisation of the entire lower limb arterial tree from the aorta to the pedal vessels without requiring arterial puncture, making it an excellent initial diagnostic tool for triaging patients with suspected acute limb ischaemia before deciding on further management, which may include catheter-directed therapy if intervention is needed. Catheter angiography remains superior for extremely fine distal vessel detail and allows simultaneous therapeutic intervention such as thrombolysis or thrombectomy, which CT angiography alone cannot provide. The choice between these modalities depends on the balance between diagnostic speed, invasiveness, and the anticipated need for immediate intervention.
options: Complete elimination of any contrast-related risk
Ability to perform simultaneous therapeutic thrombectomy
Rapid, non-invasive assessment of the entire arterial tree without arterial puncture
Superior spatial resolution compared with catheter angiography in all cases
No requirement for any radiation exposure
questions.question: A patient with suspected acute limb ischaemia undergoes CT angiography of the lower limb runoff vessels. What specific advantage does CT angiography offer over conventional catheter angiography as an initial diagnostic test in this setting?

A lateral chest radiograph in a patient with suspected lobar collapse shows a wedge-shaped opacity running obliquely between the major and minor fissures. This appearance is MOST characteristic of collapse of which lobe?
questions.explanation: Middle lobe collapse produces a characteristic wedge-shaped opacity on the lateral view, bounded by the major and minor fissures, reflecting the anatomical position of this lobe between the two fissures. This differs from lower lobe collapse, which produces a more posteriorly and inferiorly located opacity. This lateral view sign is particularly useful because middle lobe collapse can be subtle on the frontal projection alone.

questions.question: A chest radiograph in an adult shows a globally enlarged, symmetrically rounded cardiac silhouette resembling a water bottle, without any specific chamber-selective enlargement pattern. This appearance is MOST suggestive of:
questions.explanation: A symmetrically enlarged, water-bottle-shaped cardiac silhouette without a specific chamber-selective contour is characteristic of pericardial effusion, since fluid accumulates around the entire heart rather than selectively enlarging one chamber. This differs from isolated chamber enlargement, which typically produces a more localised contour abnormality. Echocardiography is the appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis and assess haemodynamic significance.

questions.question: Which principle of chest radiograph interpretation requires knowledge of imaging modality physics, anatomy, and basic sciences?
questions.explanation: The principles of radiological interpretation encompass understanding the physics of different imaging modalities, thorough knowledge of anatomy, and application of basic science knowledge. These form the foundation for systematic and accurate radiograph reading. Additional components include appropriate search patterns, reading environment, and structured reporting.

questions.question: An MRI of the brain in a neonate with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy shows abnormal high signal in the posterior limb of the internal capsule and basal ganglia on T1-weighted imaging. What does this finding suggest about the injury pattern?
options: Mild partial prolonged hypoxic injury with watershed distribution
Severe acute profound hypoxic-ischaemic injury (basal ganglia-thalamus pattern)
questions.explanation: Involvement of the basal ganglia, thalami, and posterior limb of the internal capsule reflects a severe, acute, profound pattern of hypoxic-ischaemic injury, typically from an abrupt, near-total interruption of cerebral perfusion such as with a sentinel event during delivery. This differs from the watershed cortical and subcortical white matter pattern seen with partial, prolonged hypoperfusion. Basal ganglia-thalamus involvement carries a particularly poor prognosis for later motor and cognitive outcome.

options: Conclude no injury is present and discharge
Assume the fluid is physiological ascites
Repeat the scan in one week only
Attribute the fluid to old surgical adhesions without further review
Search carefully for an occult bowel or mesenteric injury
questions.question: A CT scan of the abdomen in a trauma patient shows free intraperitoneal fluid without a clearly identified solid organ injury. What is the most appropriate next consideration?
questions.explanation: Free intraperitoneal fluid without an identifiable solid organ source raises strong suspicion for an occult bowel or mesenteric injury, which can be difficult to visualise directly on CT, particularly in the absence of active contrast extravasation. Careful review of bowel wall thickening, mesenteric stranding, or discontinuity is warranted, and clinical reassessment with serial examination may be necessary. Missing a bowel injury can lead to delayed peritonitis and sepsis.

questions.question: A patient has two fracture lines in the mandible with a separate floating central fragment that may fall backward and obstruct the airway. This double fracture type through which location represents this dangerous pattern?
options: Angle and opposite condylar neck fracture
Horizontal ramus and ascending ramus fracture
Double fracture through the symphysis mentis
questions.explanation: A double fracture through the symphysis mentis (chin region) is unstable because it frees a central fragment of the mandibular body that may collapse posteriorly under the weight of the tongue musculature, obstructing the airway—a life-threatening emergency. The mandible behaves like a ring, so single fractures of the arch are stabilised, but bilateral symphyseal fractures release a mobile central segment. Immediate airway assessment and stabilisation are priorities.

questions.question: An abdominal CT in a patient with left iliac fossa pain shows thickened sigmoid colon wall with adjacent fat stranding and a small pocket of extraluminal gas near an outpouching of the bowel wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding and a small focus of extraluminal gas adjacent to a diverticulum indicates diverticulitis complicated by microperforation. Uncomplicated diverticulosis alone shows outpouchings without inflammatory change. CT staging of diverticulitis severity guides the choice between conservative management and surgical intervention.

questions.question: A febrile child's chest radiograph shows a round, well-defined homogeneous opacity mimicking a mass. Which diagnosis is most likely in this age group?
questions.explanation: In young children, incomplete collateral pathways (pores of Kohn, canals of Lambert) cause pneumonia to spread as a sphere rather than along lobar planes, mimicking a mass, a pattern called round pneumonia. Clinical fever and follow-up resolution after antibiotics confirm the diagnosis. This mimicry can cause unnecessary alarm if the paediatric context is not considered.

options: String of pearls sign, suggesting small bowel obstruction
Triple bubble sign, suggesting jejunal atresia
Double bubble sign, suggesting duodenal atresia
questions.question: A plain abdominal film in a neonate with bilious vomiting shows two distinct gas-filled bubbles in the upper abdomen with no distal gas. What is this appearance called and what does it suggest?
questions.explanation: The double bubble sign describes two discrete gas collections representing the distended stomach and proximal duodenum, separated by the pyloric constriction, with absence of distal bowel gas. It is classically associated with duodenal atresia, often linked to Down syndrome. Absence of gas beyond the two bubbles confirms complete obstruction rather than partial stenosis.

The line focus principle uses a slanted anode target so that the actual focal spot is large (for heat distribution) while the effective focal spot seen by the patient is small (for image sharpness). A steeper (smaller) target angle produces a smaller effective focal spot but also narrows the useful x-ray beam and field coverage, limiting the area that can be imaged.
options: A steeper target angle reduces the useful x-ray beam coverage
A larger anode angle creates a smaller effective focal spot
A larger anode angle reduces the anode heat rating
Line focus is achieved by using rotating anodes only
The principle applies only to mammography units
questions.question: The line focus principle is used in x-ray tube design to balance heat loading against image resolution. Which statement CORRECTLY describes this principle?

questions.explanation: Radioactive iodine-131 is selectively taken up by any residual normal or malignant thyroid tissue through the sodium-iodide symporter, allowing the emitted beta radiation to deliver a highly targeted therapeutic dose to these cells while sparing most other tissues that do not concentrate iodine, making it particularly effective for ablating thyroid remnant tissue and treating certain metastatic differentiated thyroid cancers. This selective uptake mechanism is fundamentally different from external beam radiotherapy, which irradiates a defined anatomical field regardless of cellular iodine avidity. Patients receiving this therapy require radiation safety precautions due to the systemic distribution and excretion of the radioisotope.
options: Selective uptake of the radioisotope by residual thyroid tissue, delivering targeted beta radiation to destroy remaining cells
Systemic chemotherapy effect throughout the body
Selective uptake by bone marrow to boost immune function
Direct external beam irradiation of the thyroid bed
Direct thermal ablation of the thyroid remnant
questions.question: An iodine-131 radioactive iodine therapy is administered to a patient following total thyroidectomy for differentiated thyroid carcinoma. What is the primary therapeutic mechanism of this treatment?

An abdominal ultrasound in a vomiting infant shows a hypoechoic muscular ring with an echogenic centre in the pyloric region, measuring increased muscle thickness and canal length. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis produces a thickened hypoechoic muscular ring around an echogenic mucosal centre, classically described as a 'target' or 'doughnut' sign on transverse ultrasound. Diagnostic criteria include muscle thickness greater than 3 mm and canal length greater than 15-17 mm. Ultrasound is the imaging investigation of choice given its accuracy and lack of radiation.

questions.question: In abdominal plain film interpretation, nephrocalcinosis refers to calcifications in which specific location within the kidney?
questions.explanation: Nephrocalcinosis refers to calcium deposits within the renal parenchyma itself (cortex or medulla), not within the pelvicalyceal collecting system. Medullary nephrocalcinosis (more common) is associated with renal tubular acidosis, hyperparathyroidism, and medullary sponge kidneys. Cortical nephrocalcinosis (less common) occurs in acute cortical necrosis and chronic glomerulonephritis. This distinguishes it from renal calculi (in the collecting system) and staghorn calculus (filling the pelvicalyceal system).

International radiation protection guidance, such as that from the International Commission on Radiological Protection, recommends an occupational effective dose limit of 20 millisieverts per year, typically averaged over defined five-year periods with no single year exceeding 50 mSv, reflecting an acceptable balance between the benefits of work involving radiation and the associated health risks. This differs from the public dose limit, which is set considerably lower at 1 mSv per year, reflecting the lower acceptable risk threshold for members of the public who receive no direct benefit from the radiation-related activity. Understanding these differing limits underpins appropriate radiation protection practice and monitoring in any facility using ionising radiation.
options: No annual limit is specified for occupational workers
20 mSv per year (averaged over defined periods)
questions.question: A radiation worker's annual occupational dose is monitored to ensure it remains below the internationally recommended effective dose limit. What is the currently recommended annual effective dose limit for occupationally exposed workers according to widely adopted international radiation protection guidance?

A chest radiograph shows blunting of both costophrenic angles with a meniscus-shaped opacity rising laterally. What volume of pleural fluid is generally required for this finding to become visible on an erect PA film?
questions.explanation: Blunting of the costophrenic angle on an erect PA chest radiograph typically requires around 200-300 mL of pleural fluid before it becomes radiographically apparent, though lateral views can detect smaller volumes. Smaller effusions may only be visible on ultrasound or CT. Recognising this threshold helps avoid false reassurance from a normal-appearing film.

The Rigler (double-wall) sign occurs when free intraperitoneal gas outlines both the luminal and serosal surfaces of the bowel wall, making it visible against both intraluminal and extraluminal gas. It is particularly useful on supine films where the diaphragm cannot be assessed. Its presence confirms significant pneumoperitoneum.
questions.question: A supine abdominal radiograph shows gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall, described as the Rigler sign. What does this indicate?

A patient receiving radiotherapy to the thorax for lung cancer has dose constraints applied to the lung tissue, expressed as V20 (the percentage of lung volume receiving 20 Gy or more). What is the clinical significance of exceeding an accepted V20 threshold?
questions.explanation: The V20 lung dose-volume parameter reflects the proportion of total lung volume receiving at least 20 Gy, and exceeding established threshold values is associated with a significantly increased risk of radiation pneumonitis, an inflammatory lung complication that can develop weeks to months after treatment completion. This specific dose-volume metric is one of several standard constraints used during thoracic radiotherapy planning to balance adequate tumour coverage against normal lung tissue toxicity. Careful respect of established organ-specific dose-volume constraints is a core principle of safe radiotherapy planning across all treatment sites.
options: Increased risk of skin desquamation only
Increased risk of spinal cord myelopathy
Increased risk of cardiac arrhythmia exclusively
Increased risk of oesophageal stricture only

questions.question: The largest sesamoid bone in the human body, which ossifies within a tendon, is:
questions.explanation: The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the human body. Sesamoid bones ossify within tendons and serve to modify the angle of muscle pull, reducing friction, and protecting tendons from excessive wear. The patella lies within the quadriceps femoris tendon and functions to increase the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps muscle. Other common sesamoid bones include those at the 1st MTP joint (big toe) and 1st MCP joint (thumb).

questions.question: MRI is preferred over CT in pregnant patients (particularly after the first trimester) primarily because:
questions.explanation: MRI does not use ionising radiation — it relies on radiofrequency pulses and magnetic fields, which carry no known ionising radiation risk to the foetus. This makes MRI the preferred cross-sectional imaging modality in pregnancy when detailed anatomical information beyond ultrasound capability is required. Gadolinium contrast in MRI is generally avoided in the first trimester due to theoretical risks.
options: MRI does not use ionising radiation
MRI images are faster to acquire
MRI contrast agents are always safe in pregnancy
MRI scanners are quieter than CT scanners

questions.question: In the AP view of the cervical spine, the pedicles appear as oval white structures ('eyes'). Absence of a pedicle on one side most likely indicates:
options: Previous fracture healing at all times
questions.explanation: The 'missing pedicle sign' on AP radiograph (or CT) of the spine indicates destruction of the pedicle, most commonly due to metastatic malignancy. The pedicle is a common early site of spinal metastatic involvement because its trabecular bone is rich in red marrow (a site of metastatic seeding). The pedicle appears as a round white 'eye' on AP radiograph; loss of this 'eye' is a classical sign of vertebral metastatic disease requiring urgent further investigation.

Gallbladder wall thickening greater than 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, a positive sonographic Murphy sign, and an impacted stone together confirm acute cholecystitis rather than simple biliary colic. Choledocholithiasis instead centres on common bile duct dilatation with a stone in the duct itself. Ultrasound remains the first-line investigation because of its high sensitivity for gallstones and wall changes.
questions.question: A right upper quadrant ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign in a patient with a shadowing gallstone at the neck. What is the diagnosis?
HPV vaccination is a form of which level of cancer prevention?
questions.explanation: HPV vaccination prevents infection by high-risk HPV strains (particularly 16 and 18) before exposure, placing it squarely in primary prevention. It is recommended for adolescents before sexual debut and has demonstrated significant reduction in cervical cancer incidence in vaccinated populations. It represents one of the most effective cancer prevention interventions available.

questions.question: Which congenital heart disease classically produces a 'boot-shaped' heart on CXR?
questions.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot produces a characteristic boot-shaped or 'coeur en sabot' appearance on CXR due to right ventricular hypertrophy and an upturned apex, combined with a concave main pulmonary artery segment and decreased pulmonary vascular markings. It is one of the most common cyanotic congenital heart diseases.

Pilocytic astrocytoma classically presents in children as a cystic cerebellar mass with a small, avidly enhancing mural nodule, generally carrying an excellent prognosis after resection. This appearance differs from medulloblastoma, which is more often solid and hyperdense on CT rather than predominantly cystic. Similar cystic-with-nodule morphology in an adult would instead raise suspicion for haemangioblastoma, particularly if associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease.
questions.question: An MRI of the brain in a child shows a cystic cerebellar lesion with a brightly enhancing mural nodule, causing mild hydrocephalus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: The internal auditory canal (IAC) is visualised on specially coned petrous bone views or Stenver's projection. An acoustic neuroma expanding in the internal auditory meatus causes erosion and widening of the IAC on plain films. However, in modern practice, MRI with gadolinium is the gold-standard investigation, demonstrating the tumour itself with far greater sensitivity and detail than plain radiographic assessment of bony canal dimensions.
questions.question: In a patient with suspected 8th cranial nerve tumour (acoustic neuroma/vestibular schwannoma), which plain skull view is appropriate to visualise the internal auditory canal?

A chest radiograph shows elevation of the right hemidiaphragm, a well-defined triangular opacity adjacent to the mediastinum, and shift of the trachea toward the right side. This pattern is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: Right upper lobe collapse characteristically produces elevation of the minor fissure, a triangular opacity adjacent to the mediastinum, and ipsilateral tracheal shift due to volume loss in the affected lobe. This differs from lower lobe collapse, which more typically causes diaphragmatic elevation without this specific triangular upper zone appearance. Recognising these specific radiographic clues allows accurate localisation of the collapsed lobe.

options: Convert AC to DC for the x-ray tube
Provide high voltage for x-ray production
Supply low voltage to the filament circuit
Permit fine adjustment of the output voltage by changing winding contacts
questions.question: An autotransformer in the x-ray generator circuit is used primarily to:
questions.explanation: An autotransformer uses movable contacts on a single coil to select different numbers of windings, thereby adjusting the output voltage fed to the step-up transformer. This allows the x-ray operator to select precise kV settings. It does not convert AC to DC (that is done by the rectifier circuit) nor supply high voltage directly.

options: Chemical shift artefact from fat-water interfaces
Aliasing from an undersized field of view
questions.explanation: Chemical shift artefact arises because fat and water protons precess at slightly different frequencies, causing a spatial misregistration that produces a dark or bright band at fat-water interfaces, most pronounced on opposed-phase sequences where the effect is used diagnostically to detect microscopic fat, such as in adrenal adenoma characterisation. This differs from susceptibility artefact, which is caused by magnetic field distortion from paramagnetic or ferromagnetic material rather than differing proton resonant frequencies. Recognising this artefact prevents its misinterpretation as a true structural abnormality.
questions.question: An MRI image of the abdomen shows a dark band (Indian ink artefact) at the interface between the kidney and adjacent perinephric fat on an in-phase gradient echo sequence. What causes this appearance?

options: Markedly hyperechoic (brighter than liver) at all times
Fairly homogeneous echogenicity with intact smooth capsule
questions.explanation: The normal prostate gland on transabdominal or transrectal ultrasound appears as a fairly homogeneous organ with uniform mid-level echogenicity and a smooth, intact echogenic capsule. Normal prostatic volume is 10-20 mL. Abnormal features include: heterogeneous echo texture (nodular hyperplasia or carcinoma), hypoechoic peripheral zone nodule (suspicious for carcinoma—requires TRUS-guided biopsy), disrupted capsule (local cancer extension), and increased volume (BPH). Seminal vesicles are visualised as paired structures posterior to the bladder.
questions.question: On ultrasound of the renal tract in a male, the normal prostate gland should have which echogenicity characteristic?

questions.explanation: T2 (transverse relaxation time) reflects spin-spin interactions between neighbouring protons with slightly different Larmor frequencies. These interactions cause the individual proton spins in the transverse (x-y) plane to lose phase coherence (dephase), resulting in decay of the Mxy magnetisation. T2 values are always shorter than T1 values for the same tissue and typically range from 25 to 250 ms in the body.
options: Proton interactions with the molecular lattice (spin-lattice)
Interaction of protons with the gradient magnetic field
Chemical shift between fat and water protons
Interaction of protons with gadolinium contrast
questions.question: Transverse relaxation time T2 in MRI is related to which type of interaction between protons?
On a plain abdominal radiograph, which finding specifically suggests mechanical small bowel obstruction rather than paralytic ileus?
questions.explanation: Mechanical small bowel obstruction (SBO) shows dilated small bowel loops (>3cm) with a characteristic 'stepladder' pattern of air-fluid levels on erect film, with a transition point beyond which the bowel (usually large bowel) is collapsed (no gas). This decompressed, gasless colon distal to the obstruction distinguishes mechanical SBO from paralytic ileus, in which gas is present throughout both small and large bowel without a transition point or collapsed segment.
options: Dilated loops of both small and large bowel
Gas present throughout the entire large and small bowel at all times
Dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and a collapsed large bowel
Air in the rectum on plain film
Irregular borders, rapid growth, lower zone
Multiple bilateral nodules with feeding vessels
questions.explanation: Tuberculomas are well-defined, rounded opacities measuring 0.5–1cm, typically located in the upper or mid zones, with frequent calcification and stable appearance on serial radiographs. Calcification within a pulmonary nodule strongly favours a benign aetiology. They represent a contained form of primary or post-primary tuberculosis.
questions.question: A tuberculoma on CXR is characterised by which features?

options: Positron (beta-plus) emission producing two annihilation photons
Isomeric transition emitting gamma rays directly
questions.question: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) differs from SPECT because PET uses radionuclides that decay by:
questions.explanation: PET uses radionuclides that decay by emitting positrons (ß+). Each emitted positron rapidly annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two 511 keV gamma rays travelling in exactly opposite directions (180° apart). PET scanners use coincidence detection — two opposing detectors simultaneously registering both photons — to localise the annihilation event. This provides superior sensitivity and spatial resolution compared to SPECT.

The Townes projection (half-axial or reverse-Townes) is taken with a 30-degree caudal tilt of the X-ray tube, projecting the occipital bone and petrous ridges free of overlying facial bones. It is essential for evaluating occipital bone fractures and the foramen magnum, which are poorly seen on standard PA or lateral views. The petrous bones and posterior cranial fossa structures are best assessed on this projection.
questions.question: The standard view for demonstrating the occipital bone clearly, particularly following head trauma, is:
A radiograph of the forearm in a child shows an isolated fracture of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head. What is this injury pattern called?
questions.explanation: A Monteggia fracture-dislocation combines an ulnar shaft fracture with dislocation of the radial head, and the radial head position must always be carefully assessed on any forearm radiograph because it can be easily overlooked. A Galeazzi injury is the reverse pattern, combining a distal radial shaft fracture with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint. Missing either injury pattern by failing to image the adjacent joint is a well-recognised pitfall.

options: Dissection flap extending into the descending aorta
Involvement of the coronary arteries and haemopericardium
Dissection flap reaching the renal arteries
Bilateral pleural effusions from aortic dissection
questions.question: In the management of a patient with aortic dissection (Type A—ascending aorta involved), which imaging finding would be most immediately life-threatening and require emergency surgery?
questions.explanation: Type A aortic dissection (involving the ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency. The most immediately life-threatening complication visible on CT angiography is extension of the dissection flap into the coronary arteries (causing acute myocardial infarction) and haemopericardium (cardiac tamponade). These complications carry extremely high early mortality without emergency surgical repair. Type A dissection requires immediate cardiothoracic surgery, while Type B (descending aorta only) may be managed medically or with TEVAR.

questions.question: Calcification of the pineal gland is seen on skull radiograph and considered a normal variant. It is clinically useful because:
questions.explanation: The pineal gland is a midline structure that frequently calcifies in adults (approximately 40-60% of adults), producing a visible calcification on lateral and AP skull radiographs. Because it is normally midline, displacement of pineal calcification from the midline (detected on an AP skull film) indicates mass effect causing midline shift—a finding suggestive of a space-occupying lesion such as tumour, haematoma, or cerebral oedema pushing the brain to one side.

questions.question: In testicular torsion, ultrasound with colour Doppler demonstrates which critical finding that differentiates it from epididymo-orchitis?
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion causes vascular compromise and ischaemia. Colour Doppler ultrasound demonstrates absent or markedly reduced blood flow in the affected testis (compared to normal flow in the contralateral testis), which is the critical differentiating feature from epididymo-orchitis (which shows increased vascularity/hyperaemia). Grey-scale appearances are similar in both conditions (enlarged, hypoechoic testis, hydrocele). Surgery must not be delayed for ultrasound if torsion is clinically suspected.
options: Increased vascularity (hyperaemia) in the affected well-defined testis
Absence of blood flow in the affected testis

questions.explanation: When IUCD threads are missing and ultrasound cannot confirm an intrauterine position, a plain radiograph taken with a uterine sound (metal probe) placed within the uterine cavity helps clarify whether the IUCD is within the uterus (the sound and IUCD will be superimposed or in close proximity on the film) or has perforated the uterus and migrated into the peritoneal cavity (the IUCD and sound will be separately visualised in different locations). This approach confirms intrauterine vs. extrauterine location.
questions.question: On a plain abdominal film, the IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) is occasionally visualised. If the IUCD threads are absent and ultrasound fails to show the device in the uterus, what is the next appropriate investigation?

options: MRI is faster than CT for all brain scanning
MRI is better for detecting acute subarachnoid haemorrhage than CT
MRI can detect skull fractures better than CT
MRI has lower cost and wider availability than CT
MRI provides superior soft tissue contrast, especially for grey-white matter differentiation and posterior fossa lesions
questions.explanation: MRI provides significantly superior soft tissue contrast compared to CT, making it the modality of choice for the brain, spinal cord, and posterior fossa. MRI excels at distinguishing grey from white matter, detecting demyelination, posterior fossa lesions (which suffer beam hardening artefact on CT), tumours, and subtle ischaemia. CT is faster and better for acute haemorrhage and bony injury. Non-contrast CT remains superior for acute subarachnoid haemorrhage.
questions.question: Which statement CORRECTLY describes the principal advantage of MRI over CT for neuroradiology applications?
Asparaginase is unique among chemotherapy agents because it targets which metabolic pathway?
questions.explanation: Asparaginase depletes the amino acid asparagine from the bloodstream, depriving lymphoblastic tumour cells that lack asparagine synthetase of an essential nutrient. Normal cells can synthesize asparagine, making them less susceptible. It is used primarily in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

questions.question: An abdominal ultrasound in an infant with intermittent colicky pain and red-currant jelly stool shows a target-like mass with alternating hyper- and hypoechoic rings in the right upper quadrant. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Intussusception produces a characteristic target or doughnut sign on transverse ultrasound, formed by the telescoped bowel loop within another, with alternating echogenic mesenteric fat and hypoechoic bowel wall layers. The classic triad of colicky pain, vomiting, and red-currant jelly stool supports the diagnosis clinically. Ultrasound is highly sensitive and often guides subsequent reduction by air or contrast enema.

questions.question: A patient with differentiated thyroid cancer undergoes radioactive iodine ablation after total thyroidectomy. What is the PRIMARY rationale for this treatment?
questions.explanation: Radioactive iodine ablation exploits the natural iodine-concentrating ability of differentiated thyroid tissue, including residual microscopic cancer cells, allowing targeted radiation delivery specifically to remaining thyroid tissue after surgery. This approach is not effective for undifferentiated or anaplastic thyroid cancers, which typically lose this iodine-concentrating capability. Understanding this selective mechanism explains why radioactive iodine therapy is reserved specifically for differentiated thyroid cancer subtypes.
options: All thyroid cancers are equally responsive to this treatment
Iodine-avid thyroid tissue, including microscopic residual cancer cells, selectively concentrates the radioactive isotope
This treatment works through a purely surgical mechanism
Radioactive iodine has no selectivity for thyroid tissue
This treatment is used only for anaplastic thyroid cancer

questions.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) causes a left-to-right shunt, increasing pulmonary blood flow. The CXR shows cardiomegaly (mainly left atrium and left ventricle) with prominent pulmonary vascular markings. In large PDA, the shunt volume can lead to pulmonary hypertension over time if untreated.
questions.question: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) on CXR of a neonate shows which combination of features?
options: Decreased pulmonary markings with boot-shaped heart
Right-sided cardiomegaly with clear lung fields
Right aortic arch with decreased flow

questions.question: Retrograde urethrography is the investigation of choice for which urological condition in males?
questions.explanation: Retrograde urethrography (ascending urethrogram) involves injection of contrast retrogradely through the external urethral meatus to opacify the urethra. It is specifically indicated for urethral stricture (demonstrating the site, extent, and degree of narrowing), urethral tears (from pelvic fracture or instrumentation), congenital abnormalities (hypospadias, posterior urethral valves in reverse direction), and urethral fistulae. Acute urinary tract infection and recent instrumentation are contraindications.

options: Blunting of the costophrenic angle only
Air bronchograms throughout the lower lobe
questions.question: On a chest radiograph, a pleural effusion of 300mL would most likely be detected by which radiographic feature?
questions.explanation: Small-to-moderate pleural effusions (approximately 200-300mL) first appear on erect PA chest radiography as blunting (filling in) of the sharp costophrenic angle. A minimum of approximately 200mL is required for detection on an erect PA film, whereas only 50mL is needed on a lateral view. Larger effusions produce a meniscus sign, progressive hemithorax opacification, and eventually mediastinal shift away from the effusion. Very large effusions (>1000mL) may produce a complete white-out.

options: Technical error with contrast injection only
Normal variation in renal excretion rate
Unilateral obstruction or renal artery disease
questions.question: On IVU, delayed or absent nephrogram on one side compared to the other is most likely caused by which pathology?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric, delayed, or absent nephrogram on one side in an IVU indicates impaired renal perfusion or function on that side. The commonest causes are ureteric obstruction (causing delayed, increasingly dense nephrogram that persists on later films—'obstructive nephrogram'), renal artery stenosis or thrombosis, or severely diseased/non-functioning kidney from chronic infection or tumour replacement. The delayed nephrogram becomes denser over time in obstruction—a helpful distinguishing feature.

questions.question: In modern LINAC-based stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for early stage NSCLC, the typical total dose and fractionation schedule is:
questions.explanation: SBRT for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) typically uses ablative doses of 45-60 Gy in 3-5 fractions (e.g., 54 Gy in 3 fractions for peripheral tumours, or 50-60 Gy in 5 fractions for central tumours). These high biologically effective doses (BED) are equivalent to or exceed radical conventionally fractionated radiotherapy and achieve local control rates comparable to surgery (approximately 90%) for stage I NSCLC in patients unfit for surgery.
options: 45 Gy in 3 fractions (15 Gy/fraction) or 54 Gy in 3 fractions (18 Gy/fraction)
74 Gy in 37 fractions for all lung tumours

questions.question: Which of the following plain radiographic findings of a long bone is considered an INDIRECT sign of an occult fracture, particularly around the elbow joint?
questions.explanation: The fat pad sign (sail sign) is an indirect radiographic indicator of joint effusion or haemarthrosis following trauma, particularly around the elbow. Normally, the anterior fat pad is flat and the posterior fat pad is invisible. When a joint effusion displaces these fat pads, the anterior pad elevates to resemble a sail, and the posterior pad becomes visible. This strongly suggests an occult fracture, even when no fracture line is directly visible.

questions.question: Posterior fossa (infratentorial) haemorrhage is best evaluated by which imaging modality in the emergency setting?
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT of the brain is the primary emergency investigation for acute intracranial haemorrhage including posterior fossa (cerebellar, brainstem) haemorrhage. CT is fast, widely available, and reliably identifies acute blood as hyperdense on non-contrast images. While MRI is more sensitive for brainstem lesions and subacute blood, it is less available in acute emergencies and takes longer to acquire. Non-contrast CT detects posterior fossa haemorrhage that requires urgent surgical evacuation (cerebellar haematoma with mass effect).

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a fluoroscopic x-ray examination performed by injecting iodinated contrast through the cervix into the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes. Its primary purpose in infertility investigation is to assess tubal patency (whether the tubes are open or blocked) and to evaluate the uterine cavity morphology (detecting fibroids, polyps, adhesions, or congenital anomalies that could impair implantation or tubal function).
questions.question: A hysterosalpingogram (HSG) is performed in a woman presenting with infertility. The MAIN purpose of this investigation is to:
options: Visualise the ovarian parenchyma for follicle development
Assess tubal patency and uterine cavity morphology
Detect ovarian cysts and fibroids by fluoroscopy
Evaluate the cervical os in cases of incompetent cervix

questions.question: A CXR shows haziness in the lower zones with loss of definition of the heart border. Which condition does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary venous hypertension leading to pulmonary oedema produces prominence of upper zone vessels, lower zone haziness, Kerley B lines, and slight loss of definition of the heart and mediastinal outlines. Perihilar 'bat-wing' opacity is seen in severe pulmonary oedema. Pleural effusions commonly accompany this picture.

questions.question: Which imaging modality is the investigation of FIRST CHOICE for acute head injury assessment?
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT of the brain is the investigation of first choice in acute head injury because it is fast, widely available 24/7, superior for detecting acute haemorrhage (hyperdense), skull fractures (bone windows), pneumocephalus, and midline shift. It guides immediate neurosurgical decisions. MRI, while superior for soft tissue detail and diffuse axonal injury, is slower and less appropriate acutely. Plain skull x-ray is now rarely used in the acute setting.

questions.question: A digital radiographic system is described as having a wide dynamic range compared with older film-screen systems. What practical advantage does this property provide?
options: Elimination of the need for exposure factor selection entirely
Removal of the need for any post-processing
Automatic correction of patient positioning errors
The ability to produce a diagnostic image across a wider range of exposure levels without repeat imaging
Complete elimination of all image noise regardless of exposure
questions.explanation: Wide dynamic range in digital detectors means that a broad range of incident radiation exposures can still be processed into a diagnostically useful image through post-processing algorithms, reducing the likelihood of image failure due to under- or overexposure compared with the narrower exposure latitude of traditional film-screen systems. This does not, however, eliminate the importance of selecting appropriate exposure factors, since excessive dose still unnecessarily increases patient radiation exposure even if the resulting image appears acceptable. Understanding this property helps explain why digital systems can sometimes mask technique errors that would have been immediately apparent on film.

options: External beam delivery from outside the body using multiple fields
A single very high dose delivered over a few minutes from a temporarily inserted source
A single fraction delivered using intensity-modulated external beams
Continuous low-dose-rate irradiation delivered over an extended period from permanently implanted sources
Systemic radiopharmaceutical administration distributed throughout the body
questions.question: A patient with localised prostate cancer is treated with permanent low-dose-rate brachytherapy using implanted radioactive seeds. What is the key dosimetric characteristic of this technique compared with a single high-dose-rate brachytherapy insertion?
questions.explanation: Low-dose-rate brachytherapy involves permanent implantation of small radioactive seeds (commonly iodine-125 or palladium-103) that continuously deliver a low dose rate to the surrounding prostate tissue over an extended period as the isotope decays, in contrast to high-dose-rate brachytherapy, which uses a single, much more radioactive source temporarily inserted through applicators for a brief treatment session before being withdrawn. Each approach has different radiobiological and logistical characteristics suited to different clinical scenarios and patient factors. Understanding this distinction is important for appropriate technique selection and patient counselling regarding treatment delivery.

Radioactive isotopes such as cobalt-60 are a recognised alternative source of therapeutic radiation used in some radiotherapy departments, in addition to linear accelerators that generate radiation electronically. Ultrasound and MRI use non-ionising energy and are not sources of therapeutic radiation for cancer treatment. Selecting the appropriate radiation source depends on available infrastructure and specific treatment requirements.
questions.question: A radiotherapy department uses a linear accelerator to generate high-energy X-rays for external beam treatment. Which of the following is an alternative recognised source of therapeutic radiation used in some clinical settings?

questions.explanation: Indirect radiation damage occurs when ionising radiation interacts with water molecules in cells, producing hydroxyl radicals (OH•) via: H2O → H2O⁺ + e⁻, then H2O⁺ → H⁺ + OH•. The hydroxyl radical is the most reactive and damaging species, causing strand breaks in DNA. Since cells are ~70% water, indirect damage accounts for approximately two-thirds of all radiation-induced DNA injury.
questions.question: Indirect radiation interaction with DNA is the MOST important mode of action in clinical radiotherapy. Which free radical is primarily responsible for this indirect DNA damage?

options: Intravenously and imaged during excretion through the urethra
Directly via the urethra in a retrograde direction to opacify the urethra and bladder
Via catheter into the bladder and images taken during voiding
Via a suprapubic catheter into the peritoneal cavity
Orally and imaged as it passes through the urinary tract
questions.question: In a retrograde cystourethrogram (RCUG), contrast medium is instilled:
questions.explanation: A retrograde cystourethrogram (RCUG) involves injecting iodinated contrast medium directly into the urethra in a retrograde direction (against normal urine flow) to opacify the urethra and fill the bladder. This is the procedure of choice for evaluating urethral strictures, fistulas, and trauma. It is performed without catheterising the bladder, unlike MCU, which fills the bladder via catheter and images during voiding.

options: Assessment of large pelvic masses above the pelvis
Early pregnancy complications and follicle monitoring in infertility
questions.question: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVU) is superior to transabdominal ultrasound for which clinical indication?
questions.explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound is superior to transabdominal scanning for early pregnancy assessment (detecting intrauterine pregnancy from approximately 4.5-5 weeks), early pregnancy complications (ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage), follicle monitoring in IVF, and endometrial assessment—because the high-frequency endovaginal probe is in direct proximity to the pelvic organs, providing higher resolution than the transabdominal probe. However, it has a limited field of view and cannot visualise large pelvic masses that extend above the pelvis.

Rigler's sign (double wall sign) on a supine plain abdominal film refers to the visualisation of both the inner (mucosal) and outer (serosal) surfaces of the bowel wall, which only occurs when free peritoneal air is present on both sides of the bowel wall. Normally, only the inner wall is visible (contrast of mucosa against intraluminal gas). This sign is an important indicator of pneumoperitoneum (visceral perforation) when an erect or lateral decubitus radiograph is not available.
questions.question: The Rigler's sign (double wall sign) on a plain abdominal radiograph is significant because it indicates:
options: Free peritoneal air on a supine film
Gas within the bowel wall well-defined (pneumatosis)
Invasion involves distant spread; metastasis is local
Invasion is local; metastasis involves distant spread
Invasion requires angiogenesis; metastasis does not
questions.explanation: Invasion refers to the local extension of tumour cells into surrounding tissues, while metastasis involves the dissemination of cancer cells to distant organs via lymphatics or blood vessels. Both processes require loss of cell adhesion and acquisition of migratory properties. Invasion precedes metastasis in the metastatic cascade.
questions.question: What distinguishes invasion from metastasis in cancer biology?
A tumour suppressor gene mutation leads to cancer primarily because:
questions.explanation: Tumour suppressor genes normally restrain cell proliferation by inhibiting the cell cycle, promoting apoptosis, or facilitating DNA repair. Mutations that inactivate these genes remove these inhibitory constraints, allowing uncontrolled cell growth. Classic examples include TP53, RB1, and APC mutations in common cancers.

options: Normal ageing changes of the disc spaces
questions.explanation: On cervical spine lateral radiograph, three alignment lines are assessed: the anterior vertebral line, the posterior vertebral line, and the spino-laminar (spinothalamic) line. Any interruption of these smooth lines—particularly the posterior vertebral body line—indicates loss of ligamentous or bony stability, suggesting an unstable cervical injury.
