When a patient cannot stand unaided or keep still, an AP semi-erect or supine film is obtained. This is preferable to a poor-quality or rotated PA radiograph. The AP view magnifies the cardiac silhouette more than the PA view, so this limitation must be considered during interpretation.
questions.question: When a patient cannot stand, a chest radiograph is taken in which position?

options: Direct visualisation of colonic mucosal detail
Real-time assessment of pelvic floor and organ movement during straining and evacuation
Static anatomical detail of the pelvic organs only, without movement assessment
questions.question: An MRI defecating proctogram (dynamic pelvic floor MRI) is performed in a patient with symptoms of pelvic organ prolapse and obstructed defecation. What specific functional information does this dynamic study provide beyond static pelvic MRI?
questions.explanation: Dynamic pelvic floor MRI captures real-time images during rest, squeeze, straining, and simulated evacuation, allowing functional assessment of pelvic organ descent, pelvic floor muscle coordination, and any obstructive defecation patterns that would not be apparent on static imaging alone. This dynamic functional information is particularly valuable for characterising complex pelvic floor dysfunction involving multiple compartments (bladder, vagina, and rectum) simultaneously. Static pelvic MRI alone provides useful anatomical detail but cannot capture the functional movement patterns central to diagnosing conditions such as rectocele, enterocele, or pelvic organ prolapse during physiological straining.

The cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) is measured on a standard PA erect chest radiograph as the transverse cardiac diameter (widest horizontal measurement of the cardiac silhouette) divided by the maximum transverse thoracic diameter (inner rib-to-rib width). A CTR greater than 50% (0.5) indicates cardiomegaly on a PA film. Note: AP films overestimate heart size due to anteroposterior magnification and should not be used to assess cardiothoracic ratio.
options: Left ventricular to right ventricular well-defined ratio
Transverse cardiac diameter to maximum chest width
questions.question: On a normal chest radiograph, which structure is used to assess the cardiac size, with a cardiothoracic ratio of more than 50% indicating cardiomegaly?
A standard PA chest X-ray is taken erect at which recommended distance?
questions.explanation: A standard PA chest radiograph is taken erect at 150 or 200cm (5 or 6 feet) from the X-ray tube to the film cassette. This distance minimises cardiac magnification. Erect positioning ensures physiological lung volumes, accurate detection of fluid levels, and air-fluid interfaces.

The Hounsfield scale assigns water a value of 0 HU as the reference point. Air is -1000 HU, fat ranges from -20 to -200 HU, soft tissue is +20 to +60 HU, and bone is approximately +1000 HU. These standardized values allow tissue characterization and comparison across different CT scanners worldwide.
questions.question: The Hounsfield Unit (HU) value of water in CT imaging is defined as:

questions.explanation: The right middle lobe lies adjacent to the right heart border, so consolidation there silhouettes the cardiac silhouette while sparing the diaphragm. Right lower lobe disease does the opposite, silhouetting the diaphragm instead. This distinction relies entirely on the silhouette sign.
questions.question: On a PA chest radiograph, consolidation obscures the right heart border but the right hemidiaphragm remains clearly visible. Where is the lesion located?
options: Posterior segment of right upper lobe

questions.question: A patient with suspected acute cholecystitis has an inconclusive ultrasound. A HIDA scan is performed and shows non-visualisation of the gallbladder despite normal liver uptake and excretion into the bowel. This finding is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: Non-visualisation of the gallbladder on a HIDA scan, despite normal hepatic uptake and excretion into the bowel, indicates obstruction of the cystic duct, which is the classic functional hallmark of acute cholecystitis. This differs from common bile duct obstruction, which would instead show impaired excretion into the bowel with a distended biliary tree. This functional imaging clarifies the diagnosis when ultrasound findings alone are equivocal.
options: Choledocholithiasis with common bile duct obstruction
Acute cholecystitis due to cystic duct obstruction

questions.question: In the Nuclear Medicine team structure, the 'Safety Umpire' role responsible for radiation protection and dosimetry is performed by which professional?
questions.explanation: The Medical Physicist in the Nuclear Medicine team serves as the 'Safety Umpire'—responsible for radiation protection (monitoring staff and patient radiation doses), calibration of gamma cameras and dose measurement equipment, quality assurance of nuclear medicine instruments, dosimetry calculations for therapeutic radioiodine doses, and ensuring compliance with radiation safety regulations. The Nuclear Medicine Physician leads the team clinically, the Radiopharmacist prepares radiopharmaceuticals, and the NM Technologist performs the imaging procedures.

questions.question: An erect abdominal radiograph in a patient with sudden severe abdominal pain shows crescentic lucency beneath both hemidiaphragms. What does this finding indicate?
questions.explanation: Free gas under the diaphragm on an erect film indicates pneumoperitoneum, most commonly from perforation of a hollow viscus such as a peptic ulcer. As little as 1 mL of free air can be detected with careful technique. This finding mandates urgent surgical assessment.
options: Free intraperitoneal gas from a perforated viscus

questions.explanation: Multiple vertebral bodies showing abnormal marrow replacement with low T1 and high STIR signal in a patient with a known primary malignancy such as breast cancer strongly suggests multifocal metastatic bone deposits rather than benign degenerative or age-related change, particularly given the correlating clinical symptom of new back pain. Simple haemangiomas typically show a characteristic bright T1 signal due to their fatty and vascular content, which is the opposite signal pattern to that described here. Whole-spine MRI is a sensitive tool for detecting marrow infiltrative disease and assessing for any associated cord compression requiring urgent intervention.
questions.question: A whole-spine MRI in a patient with known breast cancer and new back pain shows multiple vertebral bodies with abnormal low T1 signal and high STIR signal, without significant cord compression. What is the most appropriate description of these findings?

questions.explanation: Acoustic impedance Z = density (ρ) × velocity of sound (c), expressed in Rayls. The greater the difference in acoustic impedance between two adjacent tissues at an interface, the greater the fraction of the incident beam that is reflected. Air has very low Z (0.0004 × 10⁶ Rayls) while bone has high Z (7.8 × 10⁶ Rayls), explaining the near-total reflection at air-tissue and tissue-bone interfaces.
questions.question: Acoustic impedance (Z) of tissue is calculated as the product of which two properties?

options: Shielding the thyroid gland from radiation exposure
Increasing the total dose delivered to the target volume
Ensuring reproducible patient positioning across the planning scan and every treatment fraction
Filtering the therapeutic radiation beam before it reaches the patient
Providing therapeutic compression to reduce tumour size
questions.question: A patient undergoing head and neck radiotherapy is fitted with a rigid thermoplastic immobilisation mask before treatment planning imaging. What is the primary purpose of this immobilisation device?
questions.explanation: A thermoplastic immobilisation mask is moulded to the individual patient's head and neck contours and rigidly fixes their position relative to the treatment couch, ensuring that the anatomy imaged during planning is reproduced as accurately as possible at each subsequent treatment session, which is essential given the proximity of critical structures such as the spinal cord, brainstem, and salivary glands in this region. It has no direct therapeutic or beam-modifying function itself, serving purely as a positioning and immobilisation aid. Reliable immobilisation is particularly important for treatments with tight planning margins, such as those used in head and neck radiotherapy.

questions.question: A CT scan of the cervical spine in a trauma patient shows a fracture through the pars interarticularis of C2 bilaterally with anterior subluxation of C2 on C3. What is this injury commonly called?
questions.explanation: A hangman fracture involves bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis of C2, classically from hyperextension and distraction injury, with variable anterior subluxation of C2 on C3 depending on severity. A Jefferson fracture instead involves the ring of C1 from an axial loading mechanism. Careful classification of upper cervical spine fractures is essential because of differing stability profiles and management approaches.

questions.question: A pelvic radiograph in a young man with chronic lower back pain shows fusion of the sacroiliac joints and a 'bamboo spine' appearance of the lumbar spine. This combination is classically associated with:
questions.explanation: Sacroiliac joint fusion with a bamboo spine appearance, reflecting syndesmophyte formation bridging vertebral bodies, is classically associated with ankylosing spondylitis, a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. This differs from rheumatoid arthritis, which typically spares the sacroiliac joints and does not produce this bridging syndesmophyte pattern. Recognising this specific combination in a young patient with inflammatory back pain supports this diagnosis.

questions.question: A plain abdominal film shows a pelvic calcification with a central lucent ring, multiple in number. These are most likely:
questions.explanation: Phleboliths are calcified thrombi within pelvic veins, the most common pelvic calcifications seen on plain film. They are multiple, rounded opacities characteristically showing a central lucent ring (the lucent centre of the calcified ring represents the residual soft thrombus or a vessel lumen). They are clinically insignificant but must be differentiated from ureteric calculi (oval, irregular, positioned along the ureteric course) and from bladder stones (larger, within the bladder outline, often laminated).

questions.question: A fibroadenoma on mammography typically appears as which type of lesion?
questions.explanation: Fibroadenoma appears on mammography as a rounded or lobulated, well-defined soft tissue opacity. It is the most common benign breast tumour and typically affects young women. Its well-defined margins and lack of associated architectural distortion or microcalcification help differentiate it from malignancy.

options: Correlating internal fiducial position with external chest infrared markers and continuously adjusting beam delivery to follow tumour motion
Breath-holding technique enforced by a spirometer
Treating only during the end-expiration phase of breathing
Gating the beam on and off based only on a chest wall bellows signal
Compressing the abdomen to restrict diaphragmatic excursion
questions.question: In the CyberKnife system, the Synchrony respiratory tracking system manages lung tumour motion during treatment by:
questions.explanation: The Synchrony system in CyberKnife continuously monitors both internal fiducial markers (implanted near the tumour, tracked by X-ray imaging every few seconds) and external infrared diodes on a vest worn by the patient. A mathematical model correlates the internal and external motion, enabling the robotic arm to dynamically adjust the beam position to follow the moving tumour in real time throughout the patient's normal breathing cycle, without requiring breath-holding or treatment gating.

A cavernous malformation produces a characteristic popcorn-ball appearance from blood products of varying age within the lesion, surrounded by a complete low-signal haemosiderin rim that is particularly conspicuous on gradient echo or susceptibility-weighted sequences due to blooming artefact. Unlike arteriovenous malformations, cavernomas are low-flow lesions and typically lack visible flow voids or a dilated feeding artery. The blooming haemosiderin rim is the single most useful discriminating feature on MRI.
questions.question: An MRI of the brain shows a well-circumscribed lesion with a 'popcorn ball' appearance of mixed signal intensity and a complete low-signal rim on gradient echo/susceptibility-weighted imaging, without associated oedema or mass effect. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: A radiopharmaceutical is the combination of a carrier molecule (which determines biodistribution and organ targeting) with a radionuclide (which provides the detectable radiation signal). The carrier molecule may be an antibody, peptide, drug, or inorganic ion. The carrier molecule drives the radiopharmaceutical to the organ or target of interest, while the radionuclide provides gamma or positron emission detectable by imaging instruments.
questions.question: In nuclear medicine, the combination of a carrier molecule (drug or tracer) with a radionuclide forms a:

options: Dark shadow posterior to a well-defined calculus
Bright region posterior to a fluid-filled structure
questions.explanation: Acoustic enhancement (posterior enhancement) appears as a bright region posterior to fluid-filled structures (cysts, simple collections) because fluid transmits sound waves with minimal attenuation compared to surrounding tissue. The returning echoes from structures behind a cyst are therefore stronger than those from the same depth in adjacent tissue, producing the characteristic bright posterior enhancement seen in simple cysts.
questions.question: In ultrasound physics, the term 'acoustic enhancement' describes which of the following findings posterior to a lesion?

questions.explanation: Pulmonary stenosis in Tetralogy of Fallot obstructs right ventricular outflow, reducing pulmonary blood flow and causing decreased pulmonary vascular markings on CXR. The four components are VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Right-to-left shunting through the VSD causes cyanosis.
questions.question: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) produces decreased pulmonary markings on CXR due to which anatomical component?

options: Reducing the total number of treatment fractions required
Improving reproducibility of pelvic organ position and reducing bowel dose by displacing small bowel loops superiorly
Eliminating the need for daily positional imaging verification
Increasing the total radiation dose delivered to the bladder itself
Preventing any need for patient consent before each session
questions.explanation: A consistent bladder filling protocol, whether full or empty depending on the specific institutional technique, improves the reproducibility of pelvic organ position between the planning scan and each daily treatment session, and a full bladder in particular can help displace small bowel loops out of the pelvis and away from the high-dose treatment volume, reducing bowel toxicity. This positional consistency does not itself reduce the need for image guidance verification, which remains important to confirm actual daily anatomy matches the plan despite the standardised protocol. Patient compliance with bladder filling instructions is an important practical component of pelvic radiotherapy delivery.
questions.question: A radiotherapy patient undergoing treatment for a pelvic tumour has a full bladder protocol used during each daily treatment session. What is the primary purpose of maintaining a consistent bladder filling status?

questions.explanation: The normal cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) on a PA chest radiograph is less than 0.5 in adults, calculated as the ratio of the widest cardiac diameter to the widest internal thoracic diameter. A CTR of 0.51–0.55 is considered mildly enlarged and greater than 0.60 is massively enlarged.
questions.question: On a standard PA chest radiograph, the normal cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) in adults should be:

questions.explanation: Air visualised within the cardiac chambers after central line insertion indicates air embolism, a potentially fatal complication requiring immediate positioning of the patient in the left lateral decubitus (Durant) position with head down to trap air in the right ventricular apex, away from the pulmonary outflow tract, alongside high-flow oxygen and haemodynamic support. This differs fundamentally from pulmonary embolism, which involves thrombus rather than gas. Rapid recognition and positioning can be lifesaving in this rare but serious complication.
questions.question: A CT scan of the chest in a patient with sudden dyspnoea after a central line insertion shows air within the right atrium and right ventricle. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Air embolism, requiring left lateral decubitus positioning and supportive care
Normal post-procedural finding requiring no action

questions.explanation: The presence of an air bronchogram — visible air-filled bronchi within an opacified lung segment — confirms alveolar consolidation, as it requires air to remain within the airways while surrounding alveoli are filled with fluid or cells. In collapse, the bronchi are also atelectatic, so an air bronchogram is absent unless concurrent consolidation coexists.
questions.question: Which type of pulmonary opacity on CXR would be confirmed as consolidation rather than collapse by the demonstration of which sign?

questions.explanation: Ultrasound is valuable in the chest for evaluating diaphragmatic motion, detecting and characterising pleural effusions, and guiding thoracocentesis and chest drain placement. It is the preferred technique for real-time guidance of pleural procedures. While limited in evaluating aerated lung, ultrasound detects subphrenic collections and diaphragmatic eventration effectively.
questions.question: Diaphragmatic ultrasound in the context of lung disease is most valuable for:
options: Direct evaluation of pulmonary parenchyma and vessels
Detecting diaphragmatic pathology and guiding pleural drainage

questions.explanation: A calcified density at the vesicoureteric junction with upstream hydroureter and hydronephrosis indicates an obstructing stone at that common site of impaction. CT without contrast is the investigation of choice for suspected renal colic due to its high sensitivity for calculi regardless of composition. The location of obstruction correlates with the level of the patient's pain and guides management, such as likelihood of spontaneous passage.
questions.question: A CT urogram in a patient with acute flank pain shows a calcified focus at the vesicoureteric junction with proximal hydroureteronephrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A lateral soft tissue neck radiograph in a febrile child with neck stiffness and dysphagia shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissue space anterior to the cervical vertebrae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Widening of the prevertebral soft tissue space, generally exceeding the width of the adjacent vertebral body at that level, on a lateral neck radiograph suggests a retropharyngeal abscess, a deep neck space infection that can rapidly compromise the airway or spread to the mediastinum. CT with contrast is typically used to confirm the diagnosis and assess for drainable fluid collections. Prompt recognition is important because of the risk of airway compromise and descending mediastinitis.

Pruning describes the appearance of large, dilated central pulmonary arteries with abrupt tapering and markedly reduced peripheral vessel calibre, classically seen in advanced pulmonary arterial hypertension. This contrasts with pulmonary venous hypertension, which shows upper lobe redistribution rather than central-to-peripheral pruning. Recognising this specific pattern helps localise the underlying pathology to the pulmonary arterial circulation.
options: Pruning of the peripheral pulmonary vessels
questions.question: A chest radiograph in a patient with long-standing pulmonary arterial hypertension shows enlarged central pulmonary arteries that taper abruptly, with markedly attenuated peripheral vessels. This appearance is termed:

questions.explanation: UV radiation is classified as a physical environmental risk factor for cancer. It induces DNA damage through pyrimidine dimer formation, leading to mutations if repair fails. Excessive sun exposure is the primary risk factor for melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers.
questions.question: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is classified as which category of carcinogenic risk factor?

options: Superior long-term outcomes for all conditions
Quicker recovery and return to normal activity
questions.question: The advantages of IR procedures over traditional surgery include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: While IR procedures offer many advantages over open surgery — including reduced risk, shorter hospital stays, lower cost, greater comfort, and faster convalescence — they do NOT universally offer superior long-term outcomes for ALL conditions. For many vascular conditions, surgery may provide more durable long-term results. IR is often used first because of its lower immediate procedural risk, with surgery reserved for cases where endovascular treatment fails or is not feasible.

Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency requiring urgent empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, ideally within one hour of recognition, because delay significantly increases mortality risk in this immunocompromised population. Waiting for full culture results before starting treatment would dangerously delay life-saving therapy. Rapid recognition and immediate treatment are central to safe management of febrile neutropenia.
questions.question: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops a fever of 38.5°C with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10⁹/L. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Reassurance and outpatient follow-up in one week
Delayed antibiotic therapy pending full blood culture results
In the interstitial tissue between follicles
In the bloodstream bound to TBG at all times
In the colloid within follicular vesicles as thyroglobulin
questions.question: The thyroid gland is unique among endocrine glands because it stores its hormone in an extracellular location. Where is thyroid hormone stored?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland is unique among all endocrine glands because it stores its active principle (thyroid hormone precursor) extracellularly—within the colloid contained in the lumina of follicular vesicles as the glycoprotein thyroglobulin. This storage mechanism is unlike all other endocrine glands, which store hormones intracellularly within their secreting cells. The follicular vesicles can accumulate a several-week supply of thyroid hormone, providing a significant hormonal reserve.

questions.question: A tumour is found on PET imaging to have markedly increased glucose uptake compared with surrounding normal tissue, consistent with a shift toward glycolytic metabolism even in the presence of adequate oxygen. This metabolic alteration is termed:
questions.explanation: The Warburg effect describes the characteristic shift of cancer cells toward aerobic glycolysis for energy production, even when oxygen is available, which underlies the increased glucose uptake exploited diagnostically by FDG-PET imaging. This metabolic reprogramming is distinct from angiogenesis, which concerns blood vessel recruitment rather than the intracellular metabolic pathway used. Recognising this principle explains the rationale for PET-based tumour detection and monitoring.

options: Bladder outlet obstruction from prostatic enlargement
questions.question: An ultrasound of the kidneys shows bilateral dilatation of the pelvicalyceal systems with a distended bladder and bilateral hydroureter in an elderly man. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Bilateral hydronephrosis with hydroureter and a distended bladder in an elderly man most commonly results from bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostatic hyperplasia, causing back-pressure changes throughout the urinary tract. Bilateral simultaneous calculi are far less common as a cause of symmetric obstruction. Post-void residual bladder volume assessment supports this diagnosis further.

questions.question: A radiographer uses tight collimation to restrict the X-ray beam to only the anatomical area of clinical interest for a knee radiograph. Besides reducing patient dose, what additional image quality benefit does this provide?
options: Reduced spatial resolution of the image
Reduced scattered radiation reaching the detector, improving image contrast
Increased magnification of the anatomical structure
Elimination of the need for a grid in all cases
questions.explanation: Restricting the field size through collimation reduces the volume of tissue irradiated, which in turn reduces the amount of scattered radiation generated within the patient and reaching the image receptor, thereby improving image contrast in addition to reducing patient dose. This benefit is separate from grid use, which specifically absorbs scatter that has already been generated rather than reducing its production in the first place; both techniques can be used together for larger body parts. Appropriate collimation is considered good radiographic practice for both dose optimisation and image quality reasons.

questions.question: A patient with known breast cancer undergoes a bone scan showing multiple areas of increased tracer uptake in the axial skeleton. What is the PRIMARY reason bone scintigraphy is more sensitive than plain radiography for detecting these metastases?
options: It detects the osteoblastic reaction to metastatic disease before sufficient bone destruction is visible on plain film
It provides better assessment of soft tissue tumour extent
It avoids the use of any radioactive material
It provides higher resolution structural detail than CT
It is unaffected by any benign bone conditions
questions.explanation: Bone scintigraphy detects the osteoblastic reaction surrounding metastatic deposits, which occurs before enough bone destruction has accumulated to be visible on plain radiography, making it a more sensitive early screening tool for skeletal metastases. This functional sensitivity, however, comes with reduced specificity, since benign conditions such as fracture or arthritis can also increase tracer uptake. Correlating scan findings with plain radiography or CT helps clarify the significance of positive areas.

questions.question: A radiographer increases the tube current from 100 mA to 200 mA while keeping kVp and exposure time constant. What effect does this have on the resulting image?
options: Increased image density with unchanged contrast
No change in the resulting image
questions.explanation: Milliamperage controls the quantity of electrons produced and therefore the number of X-ray photons generated, which directly affects image density (blackening) without altering photon energy or beam penetration. Since kVp remains unchanged, the contrast, which depends on photon energy and differential attenuation, is unaffected. Doubling the mA approximately doubles the radiation output and image density, following a linear relationship.

questions.question: A STIR MRI sequence is used to image the spine. Which of the following would appear BRIGHTEST on STIR?
questions.explanation: STIR suppresses fat signal and is highly sensitive for fluid and oedema. Inflammatory or infective vertebral endplate oedema (associated with discitis or modic type 1 change) contains free water that appears very bright on STIR. Normal fatty marrow is suppressed (dark). Desiccated discs have little water and appear dark. STIR is the most sensitive sequence for detecting marrow oedema and soft tissue inflammation in spinal imaging.

questions.question: A cervical screening programme uses cytology to detect precancerous changes in asymptomatic women before invasive cancer develops. This represents which level of cancer prevention?
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention involves early detection of existing but asymptomatic disease, such as identifying precancerous cervical changes through screening cytology before progression to invasive cancer. This differs from primary prevention, which aims to prevent the underlying disease process from occurring at all, such as through vaccination. Recognising which prevention level a specific intervention represents helps evaluate its intended public health impact.

options: Repeat the same swallow without any change in approach
Switch to a higher concentration barium suspension
Stop the examination and assess for aspiration risk before proceeding further
Continue with standard barium as planned
Increase the volume of contrast administered
questions.question: A fluoroscopic barium swallow examination shows contrast tracking into the trachea during the study. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: Aspiration of contrast into the trachea during a barium swallow indicates a significant swallowing safety concern, and the examination should be stopped to reassess the patient's swallowing function, since continuing with standard barium risks further aspiration and potential respiratory complications. In some circumstances, a water-soluble low-osmolar contrast agent may be considered instead if further assessment is needed, since barium aspirated into the lungs can itself cause an inflammatory reaction. Recognising and responding appropriately to aspiration is a key patient safety consideration during fluoroscopic swallowing studies.

X-rays, gamma rays, and beta particles are classified as sparsely ionising (low-LET) radiations because they deposit energy in widely spaced ionisation events along their track. In contrast, alpha particles and negative pi mesons are densely ionising (high-LET), and heavy neutrons are intermediate. High-LET radiations cause more complex, irreparable DNA damage per unit dose than low-LET radiations.
questions.question: In radiation protection, which linear energy transfer (LET) category includes x-rays and gamma rays?
A clinician requests a barium swallow for a patient with dysphagia. In which organ system is this contrast study primarily used to evaluate pathology?
questions.explanation: A barium swallow is a fluoroscopic contrast examination that opacifies the oesophagus and demonstrates its anatomy and motility. It is part of upper GI contrast studies, which also include barium meal (stomach and duodenum) and barium meal with follow-through (small bowel). It is the appropriate first investigation for dysphagia evaluation in many clinical settings.

questions.question: Haematuria is one of the most common presentations prompting urinary tract imaging. In the initial evaluation of painless haematuria, which imaging modality should be requested FIRST?
options: MRI of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is the first-line investigation for haematuria as it is safe (no radiation), cheap, and widely available. It detects renal masses (including carcinoma), bladder tumours, and calculi. It is particularly valuable as a screening tool before deciding on further imaging. In the African context (and many low-resource settings), ultrasound should precede intravenous urography. CT urography is now the gold standard for haematuria evaluation in well-resourced settings, but ultrasound remains the practical first step.

questions.question: An axial CT of the shoulder after trauma shows the humeral head locked posterior to the glenoid with a wedge-shaped impaction defect on the anteromedial humeral head. What is this impaction defect called?
questions.explanation: A reverse Hill-Sachs lesion is an impaction fracture of the anteromedial humeral head that occurs when it is forced against the posterior glenoid rim during a posterior dislocation. This is the mirror image of the classic Hill-Sachs lesion seen with anterior dislocation, which affects the posterolateral humeral head. Recognising the correct lesion type helps confirm the direction of dislocation, which can be clinically subtle on plain films.

options: Normal finding in the supine position
Strongly suggests haemoperitoneum requiring further evaluation or surgery
Indicative of physiological ascites from dehydration at all times
questions.explanation: Free fluid in Morrison's pouch on FAST ultrasound after trauma indicates haemoperitoneum (blood in the peritoneal cavity), as healthy people do not have free intraperitoneal fluid in this location. A fluid stripe of 1 cm or more in Morrison's pouch corresponds to approximately 400-500 mL of free intraperitoneal blood. This finding triggers further assessment: a haemodynamically unstable patient proceeds directly to laparotomy, while a stable patient undergoes contrast-enhanced CT to identify the source and extent of injury.
questions.question: In abdominal emergency radiology, the FAST examination evaluates Morrison's pouch as a standard right upper quadrant view. What is the clinical significance of finding greater than 1 cm of free fluid in Morrison's pouch after trauma?
In the investigation of aortic dissection following severe chest trauma, which imaging modality provides the most detailed evaluation of the aortic wall and dissection flap?
options: Plain chest radiograph showing mediastinal widening
Plain chest radiograph with oblique views
questions.explanation: CT angiography (CTA) of the thorax is the investigation of choice for aortic dissection, demonstrating the intimal flap separating true and false lumens, the extent of dissection, involvement of branch vessels, and complications such as haemopericardium or mediastinal haematoma. CTA has largely replaced conventional aortography due to its non-invasive nature, speed, and multiplanar reconstruction capability. Plain chest radiograph may show a widened mediastinum but cannot characterise the dissection.

options: Pathological extrinsic compression by mediastinal lymph nodes
Normal anatomical extrinsic impressions on the oesophagus
Features of a pharyngeal pouch at the cricopharyngeus level
questions.question: A barium swallow demonstrates the mid-oesophageal impression caused by the aortic arch and left main bronchus. These impressions represent normal:
questions.explanation: On a normal barium swallow, the mid-oesophagus shows two characteristic extrinsic impressions: the aortic arch impression on the left side and the impression of the left main bronchus just below it. These are normal anatomical relationships and must be recognised to avoid misinterpreting them as pathological extrinsic compression from mediastinal masses or lymphadenopathy.

questions.question: Radionuclide bone scanning is described as 'sensitive but non-specific.' Which of the following best explains this property?
options: It detects only malignant bone lesions
It shows bone density changes after fracture only
It identifies areas of increased bone turnover
It measures cortical bone thickness precisely
questions.explanation: Radionuclide (isotope) bone scans detect areas of increased osteoblastic activity (bone turnover) using technetium-labelled diphosphonate compounds. This makes the scan highly sensitive for abnormal bone metabolism but non-specific since increased uptake occurs in fractures, infection, malignancy, and even normal healing. The scan is excellent for screening the entire skeleton for metastatic disease.

questions.question: Arthrography involves injection of contrast medium into a joint. The PRIMARY indication for this procedure is to:
questions.explanation: Arthrography involves injecting positive (iodinated) contrast medium, negative (air) contrast, or a combination (double contrast) into a joint under fluoroscopic or CT/MRI guidance. It outlines intra-articular structures (cartilage, ligaments, joint capsule, menisci) to detect tears, loose bodies, synovial abnormalities, and labral pathology. CT arthrography provides excellent cartilage detail; MR arthrography is particularly useful for shoulder and hip labral tears.
options: Reduce a dislocated joint under fluoroscopic guidance
Perform synovial biopsy under fluoroscopic guidance
Visualise internal joint structures and detect internal derangements

questions.question: On chest radiography, which of the following is characteristic of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) in sarcoidosis?
options: Bilateral lobulated hilar and paratracheal lymphadenopathy ('puffing bilaterally')
Bilateral pleural effusions with cardiomegaly at all times
questions.explanation: Stage I sarcoidosis classically presents with bilateral, symmetric, lobulated hilar lymphadenopathy (bilateral hilar enlargement) often accompanied by right paratracheal lymphadenopathy producing the characteristic 'hockey stick' or '1-2-3 sign' configuration on chest radiograph. The bilateral symmetry and lobulated margins distinguish it from primary lung cancer hilar involvement (unilateral) and infective lymphadenopathy. In 50% of patients, BHL resolves spontaneously without progressing to pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.question: In cancer staging, what does the symbol 'M1' indicate?
questions.explanation: In the TNM staging system, M1 denotes the confirmed presence of distant metastasis. M0 indicates no distant metastasis detected. The M classification, combined with T and N categories, determines the overall stage grouping, which guides prognosis and treatment intent from curative to palliative.

The principle of Justification states that no practice involving radiation exposure should be adopted unless it produces sufficient net benefit to individuals exposed or to society to outweigh the potential radiation harm. The benefit must exceed the cost, including the radiation detriment. This ensures that radiation is only used when there is a genuine indication for its use.
questions.question: The ICRP's three key principles of radiological protection are justification, optimisation, and dose limitation. Which principle requires that 'no practice should be adopted unless it produces sufficient benefit to offset the radiation detriment'?

questions.explanation: MRI Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) is the most sensitive technique for detecting acute ischaemic stroke within minutes of onset. DWI detects restricted diffusion of water molecules within ischaemic cells (cytotoxic oedema) as an area of high signal intensity, visible within minutes of ischaemia onset (much earlier than non-contrast CT which may appear normal for 6-24 hours). The Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) map shows a corresponding dark area confirming true restricted diffusion.
questions.question: The MOST sensitive imaging technique for detecting acute ischaemic stroke within the first 6 hours of symptom onset is:

questions.explanation: STIR (Short Tau Inversion Recovery) is an inversion recovery sequence in which the inversion time (TI) is set to null the fat signal. Since fat has a short T1, choosing an appropriate short TI makes the fat signal zero at the time of readout, effectively suppressing fat signal. This makes it highly sensitive for detecting bone marrow oedema and other pathological processes.
questions.question: Which MRI sequence is particularly useful for demonstrating fat suppression and detecting bone marrow oedema?

questions.explanation: Peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in toward the delayed phase is the classic enhancement pattern of a hepatic haemangioma. Hepatocellular carcinoma instead shows arterial hyperenhancement with washout on portal venous or delayed phases. This distinct temporal enhancement pattern is highly reliable for differentiating benign vascular lesions from malignancy.
questions.question: A contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen shows a well-defined hepatic lesion with peripheral nodular enhancement in the arterial phase and progressive centripetal fill-in on delayed images. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Heat from the x-ray tube anode is lost by conduction from the target to the copper anode base, by convection currents within the surrounding oil bath, and by radiation from the target to the tube housing and surrounding environment. Understanding heat dissipation is critical for preventing tube damage during high-exposure procedures.
questions.question: Heat dissipation from an x-ray tube anode target occurs via which THREE mechanisms?

questions.explanation: Left atrial enlargement causes posterior displacement of the oesophagus on a barium swallow study, seen on the lateral view as a smooth posterior indentation on the oesophageal column. This indirect sign is used when direct cardiac imaging is unavailable or equivocal. Anterior displacement of the oesophagus suggests a posterior mediastinal mass.
questions.question: Barium swallow in cardiovascular radiology demonstrates which indirect sign of left atrial enlargement?

questions.explanation: An appendiceal diameter greater than 6 mm, non-compressibility, periappendiceal fat stranding, and an appendicolith are classic CT findings of acute appendicitis. These features together carry high specificity for the diagnosis. CT is particularly valuable when clinical findings are equivocal or the patient's body habitus limits ultrasound assessment.
questions.question: An abdominal CT in a patient with right lower quadrant pain shows a dilated, non-compressible tubular structure measuring 9 mm with surrounding fat stranding and an appendicolith. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Rib notching in coarctation of the aorta is caused by hypertrophied intercostal arteries serving as collateral vessels bypassing the aortic obstruction. These dilated arteries erode the inferior surfaces of ribs 3–8 bilaterally. It appears after several years and is rarely seen under 5 years of age. The '3 sign' of the aortic knob is also characteristic.
questions.question: Which CXR sign is specifically associated with coarctation of the aorta in older children and adults?

questions.explanation: Aggressive (lamellated or onion-skin) and sunburst/spiculated periosteal reactions indicate a rapidly growing, aggressive process that repeatedly breaks through the periosteum as it is being laid down. These patterns are associated with aggressive malignant tumours (osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma) and aggressive infections. In contrast, a smooth, solid, well-defined periosteal reaction suggests a slower, more benign process such as osteoid osteoma or periosteal new bone formation from chronic trauma.
questions.question: On plain radiography, a periosteal reaction showing an 'onion-skin' (lamellated) pattern is associated with which type of bone pathology?
Extradural haematoma on non-contrast cranial CT appears as which shape, formed by blood accumulating between the dura mater and the inner table of the skull?
questions.explanation: An extradural (epidural) haematoma forms between the inner table of the skull and the periosteal dura, usually following middle meningeal artery laceration in temporal bone fracture. Because the dura is firmly attached to the inner skull table at suture lines, the blood cannot cross sutures, creating a biconvex (lenticular) hyperdense collection. In contrast, subdural haematomas cross sutures (crescent-shaped) because they lie beneath the mobile dural layer.

questions.question: Which MRI component is responsible for spatial localisation of the MRI signal across the body?
questions.explanation: Gradient coils create small, controlled variations in the main magnetic field (B0) along three orthogonal axes (x, y, z). Because the Larmor frequency depends on local field strength, these gradients cause protons at different locations to precess at slightly different frequencies, enabling spatial encoding (frequency encoding, phase encoding, and slice selection) and ultimately the reconstruction of anatomical images from the MRI signal.

questions.question: Smoking and alcohol consumption are classified under which cancer risk factor category?
questions.explanation: Smoking and alcohol are lifestyle risk factors for cancer. Tobacco smoke contains numerous carcinogens causally linked to lung, oral, laryngeal, and bladder cancers. Alcohol is associated with liver, colorectal, and breast cancers, particularly with heavy or chronic use.

questions.question: An undescended testis most commonly lies in which anatomical location?
questions.explanation: An undescended (cryptorchid) testis most commonly lies in the inguinal canal, being arrested along its normal path of descent from the retroperitoneum to the scrotum. In the remainder of cases, it may be found high in the scrotum, in the abdomen, or in the lower pelvis. If it cannot be palpated, ultrasound is performed first; if ultrasound fails to locate it, CT (or MRI) is used. Undescended testes carry an increased risk of malignancy and subfertility.

questions.question: A patient with suspected coronary artery bypass graft occlusion requires definitive assessment of graft patency before further intervention. Which imaging modality provides the MOST accurate assessment in this context?
questions.explanation: Coronary angiography, whether catheter-based or CT angiography, provides the most accurate direct assessment of bypass graft patency and is the definitive investigation when significant clinical concern exists. Plain radiography and fluoroscopy alone cannot adequately visualise graft lumen patency. This distinction guides appropriate escalation of imaging in patients with suspected graft failure.

SPECT acquires multiple planar scintigraphic images at different angles around the patient (using a rotating gamma camera) and reconstructs them into cross-sectional, three-dimensional tomographic images—analogous to CT but using gamma-emitting radioisotopes. This provides superior lesion localisation, improved contrast between lesion and background activity, better characterisation of lesion depth, and detection of smaller lesions compared to planar scintigraphy. SPECT/CT combines anatomical (CT) and functional (SPECT) information in a single study.
questions.question: The SPECT (Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography) nuclear medicine technique provides what imaging advantage over planar scintigraphy?
options: Uses X-rays instead of gamma well-defined rays
Three-dimensional tomographic images with improved lesion localisation

questions.explanation: A 21-day interval between chemotherapy administrations is commonly referred to as a standard 3-week cycle, allowing sufficient time for normal tissue, particularly bone marrow, to recover between doses. This scheduling balances maximising cumulative antitumour effect against permitting adequate recovery from toxicity. Cycle length varies by regimen but is a standard feature of chemotherapy protocol design.
questions.question: A patient receives a chemotherapy regimen administered on day 1 only, repeated every 21 days. This treatment interval is commonly referred to as:

options: Unilateral pneumothorax as the sole route
questions.explanation: Acute severe asthma produces bilateral hyperinflation (air trapping) on chest radiograph due to widespread bronchospasm causing incomplete expiration. Radiographic features include: increased anteroposterior (AP) diameter, barrel chest appearance, flattened/depressed diaphragms, increased retrosternal airspace on lateral view, and horizontal rib orientation. A chest radiograph in asthma is performed to exclude complications (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, consolidation) rather than to diagnose asthma itself.
questions.question: Bronchial asthma on plain chest radiograph during an acute attack typically shows which of the following findings?

questions.explanation: The International Retinoblastoma Staging System (IRSS) is specifically developed for staging retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood. It categorizes tumours from stage 0 to V based on tumour extent. Other paediatric tumours use their own specific staging systems.
questions.question: The International Retinoblastoma Staging System (IRSS) is specifically used for staging which tumour?

questions.explanation: CT angiography (CTA) is the current preferred first-line investigation for peripheral arterial injury due to its speed, wide availability, and accuracy in demonstrating the site and extent of vascular injury (occlusion, dissection, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula). Conventional digital subtraction angiography (DSA) remains the gold standard for both diagnosis and therapeutic intervention (endovascular repair, embolisation). Colour Doppler is used for screening but cannot provide the comprehensive vascular roadmap needed for surgical planning.
options: Plain radiograph of the affected limb at all times
CT angiography or conventional digital subtraction angiography (DSA)
questions.question: In the context of emergency radiology for vascular injuries, which investigation is the definitive 'gold standard' for characterising peripheral arterial injury following limb trauma?
A patient with abundant subcutaneous fat is difficult to image with ultrasound. The MAIN reason for poor penetration in obese patients is related to which ultrasound-tissue interaction?
questions.explanation: Fat causes considerable refraction (beam bending) described by Snell's Law when the ultrasound beam crosses fat-muscle or fat-organ interfaces, because the speed of sound differs on each side. This causes image distortion and contributes significantly to the difficulties in scanning obese patients. Additionally, fat has a moderately high attenuation coefficient (0.63 dB/cm at 1 MHz), reducing penetration.
options: Total internal reflection at the fat-muscle interface
Increased acoustic impedance of fat compared to muscle
Refraction causing beam displacement described by Snell's Law
Diffraction pattern alteration in fatty tissue
It increases the effective focal spot
It eliminates the anode heel effect
It greatly increases the heat capacity by spreading heat over a larger area
questions.question: A rotating anode offers a significant advantage over a stationary anode for the same x-ray production. What is the primary reason?
questions.explanation: A rotating anode continuously presents a fresh anode surface to the electron beam, effectively spreading the heat generated over a large annular area rather than a single small spot. This dramatically increases the heat capacity and load rating of the tube, permitting higher exposures without damaging the target material.

options: Direct competitive blockade of the oestrogen receptor
Blocking peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogen
questions.question: A postmenopausal woman with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is started on an aromatase inhibitor rather than tamoxifen. Which mechanism explains this drug's anticancer effect?
questions.explanation: Aromatase inhibitors reduce circulating oestrogen levels by blocking the peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogen, which is the primary source of oestrogen in postmenopausal women. Tamoxifen instead works by directly and competitively blocking the oestrogen receptor rather than reducing oestrogen production. Choosing between these mechanisms depends partly on menopausal status, since aromatase inhibitors are less effective when ovarian oestrogen production is still active.

options: Direct measurement of renal function without contrast
Improved spatial resolution compared with single-energy CT
Differentiation of uric acid stones from other stone compositions based on material-specific attenuation behaviour
Elimination of the need for any post-processing software
Complete elimination of all radiation dose to the patient
questions.question: A dual-energy CT scan is performed using two different tube voltages simultaneously to characterise a renal stone. What specific clinical advantage does dual-energy acquisition provide over single-energy CT in this context?
questions.explanation: Dual-energy CT exploits the fact that different materials, such as uric acid versus calcium-containing stones, attenuate X-rays differently at different photon energies, allowing material characterisation and differentiation of stone composition that is not reliably achievable with single-energy CT acquisition. This has practical clinical value because uric acid stones can potentially be dissolved with medical therapy, whereas calcium-based stones typically require other management approaches such as lithotripsy or surgery. Dual-energy techniques have additional applications including virtual non-contrast imaging and improved characterisation of other tissue types.

options: DNA intercalation and topoisomerase II inhibition
questions.explanation: Anthracyclines intercalate into the DNA double helix and inhibit topoisomerase II, causing DNA strand breaks and impairing replication. Doxorubicin is among the most active broad-spectrum anticancer agents. Cardiotoxicity is a significant cumulative dose-related adverse effect limiting long-term use.
questions.question: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin exert their primary cytotoxic effect through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Acute mucositis is an ACUTE (early) radiation reaction, not a late effect. Late effects of radiation develop months to years after treatment and include fibrosis, atrophic changes, hardening and loss of function, chronic vascular damage, and radiation-induced secondary malignancy. Early (acute) reactions include mucositis, diarrhoea, skin erythema, alopecia, and vomiting, occurring during or shortly after treatment.
questions.question: Radiation-induced late effects in normal tissue include all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Reduced scan time compared with fixed mA scanning
Reduced overall patient radiation dose while maintaining consistent image quality
Elimination of the need for iterative reconstruction
questions.explanation: Automatic tube current modulation adjusts the mA in real time according to the attenuation encountered in different body regions and projection angles, delivering just enough radiation to maintain diagnostic image quality while avoiding unnecessary excess dose in thinner body regions, such as the shoulders compared with the pelvis. This is a key dose-reduction strategy recommended as part of the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle. It does not directly affect scan speed or eliminate other artefacts such as beam hardening, which arise from different physical causes.
questions.question: A CT scanner's tube current is automatically modulated according to patient thickness in different projections and along the z-axis. What is the main clinical benefit of this automatic tube current modulation technique?

options: Removal of all clothing but no other preparation
Routine general anaesthesia for all radiotherapy treatments
Surgical tumour marking is required before all radiotherapy
Bowel preparation is required for every radiotherapy patient
CT simulation for treatment planning, patient positioning, and immobilisation device fabrication
questions.question: Preparing a patient for radiation therapy includes which of the following essential steps?
questions.explanation: Preparation for radiotherapy involves CT simulation (a dedicated CT scan in the treatment position), which provides 3D anatomical data for target volume delineation and treatment planning. Patient positioning and immobilisation devices (thermoplastic shells, vacuum bags, tattoo marks) are fabricated and documented during simulation to ensure reproducible setup for every fraction. IV contrast may be used during simulation for improved tumour delineation. Additional imaging (PET, MRI) may be fused with the planning CT.

options: Accepting a compromise plan with slightly reduced target coverage in the region adjacent to the critical structure
Ignoring the organ-at-risk constraint since target coverage is always the sole priority
Always prioritising complete target coverage regardless of organ-at-risk dose
Increasing the prescribed dose uniformly across the entire volume to compensate
Cancelling radiotherapy entirely whenever any compromise is required
questions.question: A radiotherapy treatment plan review identifies that the prescribed dose falls just short of covering the entire planning target volume due to proximity to the spinal cord. What planning approach is commonly used to manage this type of competing priority between target coverage and organ-at-risk protection?
questions.explanation: When a critical organ at risk, such as the spinal cord, lies very close to the planning target volume, treatment planners often must accept a carefully considered compromise, slightly under-dosing the portion of the target immediately adjacent to the critical structure, to avoid exceeding a dose that could cause serious, potentially irreversible normal tissue toxicity. This balancing of tumour control probability against normal tissue complication probability is a routine and fundamental aspect of radiotherapy planning, particularly for tumours situated near dose-limiting critical structures. Complete avoidance of any target under-coverage is not always achievable or appropriate when doing so would risk unacceptable harm to a critical adjacent structure.

Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant posterior fossa tumour in children, typically arising from the roof of the fourth ventricle as a midline, hyperdense mass on non-contrast CT due to its high cellularity, frequently causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Pilocytic astrocytoma instead more often arises within the cerebellar hemisphere with a cystic component and an enhancing mural nodule. The specific midline fourth ventricular location and hyperdense appearance favour medulloblastoma over other paediatric posterior fossa tumours.
questions.question: A CT scan of the head in a child shows a well-defined, hyperdense, midline posterior fossa mass arising from the fourth ventricle roof with associated obstructive hydrocephalus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Delivering a precisely measured dose to a defined tumour volume with minimal damage to surrounding healthy tissue
Complete surgical removal of the tumour with minimal margin
Administering the maximum tolerated dose regardless of side effects
Using radiation primarily for pain palliation only
Exposing the entire body to uniform radiation doses
questions.explanation: The aim of radiotherapy is to deliver a precisely measured dose of radiation to a defined tumour volume with the minimum possible damage to surrounding normal tissue, resulting in eradication of the tumour, high quality of life, and prolonged survival. Modern planning techniques (3DCRT, IMRT, IGRT) and conformal delivery systems are designed to achieve this balance between tumour control and normal tissue protection.
questions.question: The aim of radiotherapy as defined in radiation oncology is BEST described as:

questions.explanation: The ideal endotracheal tube tip position is 3–5 cm above the carina; positioning at the carina risks endobronchial intubation and single-lung ventilation. Slight withdrawal restores a safe margin above the carina. Left mainstem intubation and lung collapse can follow if this is not corrected promptly.
questions.question: A chest radiograph of an intubated ICU patient shows the endotracheal tube tip positioned at the level of the carina. What is the most appropriate next step?

questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT of the brain is the first emergency investigation in an unconscious trauma patient because it is fast (seconds), widely available, highly sensitive for acute intracranial haemorrhage (extradural, subdural, subarachnoid, intracerebral), skull fractures (on bone window), and cerebral oedema—all of which require immediate management decisions. CT is available in all major emergency departments and can be performed rapidly without patient cooperation. MRI provides more detail but is slower and less available acutely.
questions.question: In an unconscious patient following a motor vehicle accident, which emergency imaging of the brain should be performed FIRST?
options: Plain skull radiograph AP and lateral
Postoperative adjuvant treatment following total laryngectomy
Prophylactic treatment of asymptomatic distant metastatic disease
Purely palliative symptom control without curative intent
Preoperative downstaging before mandatory surgical resection
Organ preservation with curative intent while minimising dose to uninvolved surrounding structures
questions.explanation: Radical radiotherapy for early glottic cancer using small, precisely targeted fields aims to achieve cure while preserving laryngeal function and voice quality, avoiding the need for total laryngectomy that would otherwise be required for surgical management, representing a genuine organ-preservation curative strategy rather than a palliative approach. The relatively small, well-defined treatment volume required for early-stage disease allows this precise field design while still achieving high cure rates for appropriately selected early-stage tumours. This illustrates how treatment intent and field design are tailored specifically to tumour stage and the goal of functional organ preservation where oncologically appropriate.
questions.question: A patient with early glottic laryngeal cancer is treated with radical radiotherapy using small, precisely shaped parallel-opposed lateral fields. What is the primary treatment intent of this approach compared with more extensive head and neck fields?

A CT scan shows free fluid in the pelvis and perihepatic space with a linear tear through the liver parenchyma extending less than 3 cm in depth after blunt trauma. What grade of hepatic injury does this represent on the AAST scale?
questions.explanation: A laceration less than 3 cm in depth involving the hepatic parenchyma corresponds to a grade II injury on the AAST liver injury scale, generally managed conservatively in a haemodynamically stable patient. Higher grades involve deeper parenchymal disruption or major vascular injury requiring more aggressive intervention. Accurate grading guides the decision between observation and operative management.
options: Grade IV laceration involving 25-75% of a lobe

questions.explanation: Chemical mutagens react with DNA, causing base modifications, strand breaks, or crosslinks that alter the genetic code. If these changes are not repaired, permanent mutations arise that can activate oncogenes or inactivate tumour suppressor genes. Examples include alkylating agents and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
questions.question: A carcinogen classified as a chemical mutagen causes cancer primarily by:
Which condition produces bilateral ureteric 'lead pipe' calcification on plain radiograph?
questions.explanation: Urinary schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium) characteristically produces bilateral calcification of the ureteric walls (from deposition of ova) producing the 'lead pipe' or 'pipe-stem ureter' appearance on plain radiograph. Combined with bladder wall calcification (eggshell pattern), this is pathognomonic of chronic urinary schistosomiasis. Ureteric involvement causes strictures and hydronephrosis. The bladder changes predispose to squamous cell carcinoma—a well-recognised complication in endemic regions of Africa.

questions.question: Which principle of cancer control calls for leadership to create clarity, unity of purpose, and broad participation?
questions.explanation: The leadership principle of cancer control emphasizes creating clarity and unity of purpose, encouraging team building, and fostering broad participation and ownership of the cancer control process. Effective leadership ensures coordinated national cancer planning and program implementation.

Palliative care advocates for early, systematic assessment and treatment of pain using the WHO analgesic ladder: Step 1 (non-opioids: paracetamol, NSAIDs), Step 2 (mild opioids: codeine, tramadol), and Step 3 (strong opioids: morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl), with adjuvants at each step (anticonvulsants, antidepressants, corticosteroids for neuropathic or bone pain). Pain should be treated proactively, not reactively, with appropriate titration to adequate pain control.
options: Avoiding all analgesics due to addiction risk
Early, systematic assessment and treatment of pain using the WHO analgesic ladder with appropriate titration
Using opioids only in the last 48 hours of life
Relying exclusively on radiotherapy for pain control
Using pain management only when the patient requests it
questions.question: The role of palliative care in pain management for cancer patients is BEST described as:

questions.explanation: CT is superior to MRI for evaluating cortical bone details, subtle fractures, and bone fragment location due to its excellent spatial resolution for mineralised tissue. While MRI excels for soft tissue, cartilage, ligaments, and spinal cord, CT provides precise cortical bone assessment, fracture classification, and fragment localisation essential for surgical planning.
questions.question: Computed tomography is preferred over MRI for the assessment of which of the following musculoskeletal conditions?

questions.explanation: The International Retinoblastoma Staging System (IRSS) is specifically designed for retinoblastoma, incorporating features relevant to this particular paediatric tumour that are not captured by the general TNM framework. Using a disease-specific staging system where available improves the accuracy of prognosis and treatment planning. General staging systems such as TNM are not well suited to every tumour type.
questions.question: A retinoblastoma is being staged in a young child using a system specifically designed for this rare paediatric eye tumour. This staging system is termed:

questions.explanation: The normal aortic knob (knuckle) on CXR should measure less than 35mm. Enlargement beyond this value suggests increased aortic pressure, increased flow, or pathological change in the aortic wall such as aneurysm. The aortic knob is visible as a rounded opacity at the left superior mediastinal border.
questions.question: The normal aortic knob diameter on CXR should measure less than:

questions.explanation: Salter-Harris type III fractures cross the physis and extend through the epiphysis into the joint space, without metaphyseal involvement, and carry a risk of growth disturbance because the fracture violates the articular surface. Type IV fractures are similar but also involve the metaphysis, crossing all three zones. Precise classification guides prognosis regarding limb growth.
questions.question: A radiograph of the ankle in a child shows a fracture line extending through the epiphysis and physis but not involving the metaphysis, reaching the articular surface. Which Salter-Harris type is this?

questions.explanation: A T-score compares a patient's bone mineral density with that of a healthy young adult reference population, and a value of -2.5 or below is classified as osteoporosis according to World Health Organization criteria, while a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 is classified as osteopenia. A T-score of -2.7 therefore falls into the osteoporotic range, indicating significantly reduced bone mineral density and increased fracture risk. This classification directly guides decisions about pharmacological treatment for bone protection.
questions.question: A DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) scan report shows a T-score of -2.7 at the lumbar spine. According to World Health Organization criteria, how should this result be classified?

questions.explanation: Arterial vascular markings on skull radiography arise from the meningeal vessels and characteristically taper and branch as they run peripherally—becoming smaller in diameter toward the periphery. This branching pattern is in contrast to fracture lines, which are typically non-tapering, darker (radiolucent), irregular in outline, and may traverse vascular grooves. Fracture lines often have straighter margins and may cross sutures, whereas vascular grooves follow predictable anatomical positions.
questions.question: In the lateral skull radiograph, vascular markings of arteries are distinguished from fracture lines by which characteristic feature?
A patient with head and neck cancer receives radiotherapy and chemotherapy delivered together during the same treatment period, rather than one after the other. This treatment approach is termed:
questions.explanation: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy delivers both modalities together within the same treatment period, exploiting the radiosensitising effect of chemotherapy to improve local tumour control. Sequential treatment instead delivers one modality fully before starting the other. The concurrent approach generally achieves superior outcomes in locally advanced head and neck cancer compared with sequential treatment, though at the cost of greater toxicity.

options: Hyperdense filling defect at the proximal MCA on contrast images
Delayed but complete enhancement of the MCA territory
Absence of contrast opacification (filling defect) in the proximal MCA
Normal MCA with only parenchymal changes
questions.question: In CT angiography of the brain, arterial occlusion in the MCA at the proximal segment would appear as:
questions.explanation: On CT angiography (CTA), arterial occlusion appears as an absence of contrast opacification (a filling defect or 'cut-off') at the site of the occluded vessel. The occluded MCA segment will not fill with contrast medium, creating an abrupt termination of the opacified lumen. CTA is the primary imaging modality for assessing large vessel occlusion in acute ischaemic stroke and determines candidacy for mechanical thrombectomy.

options: Multinodular goitre with discrete focal uptake
questions.explanation: Diffusely increased tracer uptake throughout an enlarged thyroid gland is the classic scintigraphic pattern of Graves' disease, reflecting generalised hyperfunction of the entire gland rather than a discrete focal abnormality. This contrasts with a solitary toxic nodule, which instead shows focal increased uptake with suppression of the surrounding normal thyroid tissue. Recognising this distinct uptake pattern helps differentiate the underlying cause of thyrotoxicosis and guides appropriate management.
questions.question: A patient with Graves' disease undergoes a thyroid uptake scan showing diffusely increased tracer uptake throughout an enlarged gland. This pattern is MOST consistent with:

A hand radiograph in a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis shows periarticular osteopenia, symmetrical joint space narrowing, and marginal bony erosions. This combination of findings is MOST characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Periarticular osteopenia with symmetrical joint space narrowing and marginal erosions is a classic radiographic triad for rheumatoid arthritis, reflecting the inflammatory synovial process characteristic of this disease. Osteoarthritis instead typically shows asymmetric joint space narrowing with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis rather than marginal erosions. Recognising this specific combination helps distinguish rheumatoid arthritis from other arthropathies on imaging.

questions.question: A patient with hepatic encephalopathy and suspected large spontaneous portosystemic shunting is being assessed prior to a planned procedure. Which nuclear medicine technique is classically used to confirm and quantify shunting?
options: A technetium-labelled macroaggregated albumin lung perfusion shunt study
questions.explanation: A technetium-labelled macroaggregated albumin study can quantify portosystemic shunting by measuring the proportion of injected tracer that bypasses the liver and appears in the systemic circulation, detected as pulmonary uptake. This differs from a HIDA scan, which assesses hepatobiliary excretion rather than vascular shunting. Quantifying shunt fraction helps guide decisions about procedures that could further alter portal haemodynamics.

Palliative treatment intent focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life without an expectation of achieving cure, appropriate for patients with widespread incurable disease. This differs fundamentally from curative intent, which aims for eradication of all detectable disease and long-term survival. Clearly establishing treatment intent with the patient guides realistic goal-setting and informed decision-making.
questions.question: A patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer with widespread disease and poor performance status is being counselled about treatment goals. Which of the following BEST describes a palliative treatment intent?
options: Symptom control and quality of life without expectation of cure
Complete eradication of all detectable disease
Prevention of any future cancer development
Definitive cure with long-term disease-free survival
Immediate discharge with no further oncological input

questions.question: On retrograde urethrography, which projection is the standard view used to demonstrate the male urethra?
options: Erect lateral view at all times
questions.explanation: Retrograde urethrography (ascending urethrogram) in males is performed in oblique projections—specifically the 30-degree left anterior oblique (LAO) and the supine PA, plus the 30-degree right anterior oblique (RAO). The oblique projections open up the urethra to full visualisation without superimposition of the pubic symphysis. This allows assessment of the anterior urethra (penile and bulbar) and posterior urethra (membranous and prostatic) for strictures, tears, and fistulae.

Gradient echo sequences lack the 180-degree refocusing pulse used in spin echo sequences, making them highly sensitive to local magnetic field inhomogeneities caused by paramagnetic or ferromagnetic material such as haemosiderin or metal, resulting in an exaggerated area of signal loss known as blooming or susceptibility artefact. This property is exploited diagnostically to detect microhaemorrhages on susceptibility-weighted imaging. In contrast, chemical shift artefact arises from the differing resonant frequencies of fat and water protons rather than field inhomogeneity from tissue susceptibility differences.
questions.question: A gradient echo MRI sequence is particularly sensitive to magnetic field inhomogeneities caused by blood products or metallic material, producing pronounced signal loss around such areas. What is this phenomenon called?
A chest radiograph shows a solitary, well-defined pulmonary nodule with popcorn-like calcification. This appearance is MOST characteristic of which benign lesion?
questions.explanation: Popcorn calcification within a solitary pulmonary nodule is a classic and highly specific appearance of a pulmonary hamartoma, a benign lesion often containing cartilage and fat. This differs from a tuberculoma, which typically shows more diffuse or laminated calcification with associated upper lobe scarring. Recognising this characteristic calcification pattern can support a confident diagnosis without further invasive investigation in an appropriate clinical context.

options: I-131 gamma rays cause DNA double strand breaks in all body tissues
I-131 blocks TSH receptors preventing thyroid cancer growth
Thyroid follicular cells selectively take up iodine via the sodium-iodide symporter, so I-131 beta particles deliver lethal radiation doses to thyroid remnant and metastases
I-131 is preferentially absorbed by malignant compared to benign thyroid cells only
questions.explanation: I-131 (radioiodine) is selectively taken up by thyroid follicular cells via the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) that is expressed on both normal and differentiated thyroid cancer cells. After oral administration, I-131 concentrates in thyroid tissue and metastases. The beta particles (range ~2mm in tissue) deliver targeted radiation doses to thyroid remnant tissue and functioning metastases, causing cell death. I-131 gamma emission also allows post-therapy whole-body scintigraphy to detect residual or metastatic disease.
questions.question: Iodine-131 therapy for differentiated thyroid cancer works because:
In acute epidural haematoma, which blood vessel is most commonly responsible for the haemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Acute epidural haematoma in over 85% of cases results from laceration of the middle meningeal artery following temporal or temporoparietal bone fracture. The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the inner surface of the temporal bone; fracture through this groove tears the artery, causing rapid arterial haemorrhage into the extradural space. The classic clinical presentation is a 'lucid interval' (brief loss of consciousness, followed by recovery, then rapid deterioration from expanding haematoma compressing the brain).

options: Increased osteoblastic activity around metastatic deposits
Direct tumour uptake of the diphosphonate
Direct binding to tumour cell receptors
questions.explanation: Technetium-99m-labelled diphosphonate (MDP or HDP) accumulates in bone proportional to osteoblastic activity and regional blood flow. Skeletal metastases stimulate a host reactive osteoblastic response in the surrounding bone, resulting in focal increased radiotracer uptake ('hot spots') on the bone scan. This osteoblastic response can be detected weeks to months before the lesion becomes visible on plain radiographs (which require 30-50% bone loss before lytic lesions are visible). Purely lytic ('cold') lesions with no reactive bone may occasionally be false-negative.
questions.question: Nuclear medicine bone scanning using Tc-99m diphosphonate is most sensitive for detecting skeletal metastases. What is the mechanism by which the tracer localises to metastatic deposits?

questions.explanation: Linear calcification within the brain follows the course of blood vessels and is associated with vascular pathology. In Sturge-Weber syndrome (port wine stain, glaucoma, cortical atrophy), a characteristic 'tram-track' or gyriform linear calcification follows the cerebral cortex. Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) produce serpiginous linear calcifications along vessel walls. This pattern contrasts with the rounded calcifications of tuberculomas and the multiple small deposits of cysticercosis.
questions.question: Linear calcification in the brain visible on skull radiograph or CT, described as having an arteriovenous malformation or Sturge-Weber pattern, represents which type of intracranial calcification?
In cervical spine radiography, fractures most commonly occur at which vertebral levels?
questions.explanation: The lower cervical spine (C5-C7) is the most common site for cervical fractures and dislocations because this is the most mobile segment and the site of maximum stress concentration during flexion-extension injuries. Fractures at C5-C7 are of particular clinical concern due to proximity to the lower cervical cord and brachial plexus.
