Additionally, 20% of cervical fractures are not solitary and a second fracture level must be actively sought when one fracture is identified.

Virtual bronchoscopy uses CT volumetric data to generate three-dimensional endoluminal views of the tracheobronchial tree, simulating the appearance of conventional bronchoscopy. It is a non-invasive technique useful for planning endobronchial procedures, evaluating endobronchial lesions, and assessing airway stenosis. It represents one of the advanced radiological techniques in respiratory system imaging.
questions.question: Virtual bronchoscopy in respiratory radiology is performed using data from which imaging modality?

questions.explanation: Low unenhanced attenuation reflecting high intracellular lipid content is a characteristic and reassuring CT feature of a benign adrenal adenoma, differentiating it from lipid-poor lesions such as metastases or adrenocortical carcinoma, which typically show higher attenuation values. This attenuation-based characterisation allows many adrenal incidentalomas to be confidently classified as benign without further invasive investigation. Recognising this specific imaging clue avoids unnecessary biopsy of a likely benign lesion.
questions.question: A patient with suspected adrenal incidentaloma undergoes CT characterisation showing a lesion with low unenhanced attenuation values consistent with high lipid content. This finding MOST strongly supports:
The goal of radiotherapy when administered with curative intent is best described as:
questions.explanation: Curative radiotherapy aims to permanently eradicate all tumour cells within the treatment volume. It is used for radiosensitive tumours such as cervical cancer, head and neck cancer, and prostate cancer. Adequate dose, appropriate fractionation, and precise target delineation are critical for curative intent.

options: Mandatory use of general anaesthesia only
Routine use of high-flow oxygen throughout
Avoidance of high concentration inspired oxygen
questions.question: A patient receiving bleomycin for testicular cancer develops progressive shortness of breath and is found to have bibasal pulmonary fibrosis on imaging. This dose-limiting toxicity requires which specific precaution during any future anaesthesia?
questions.explanation: Bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis increases sensitivity to oxygen-induced lung injury, so high concentration inspired oxygen must be avoided during any subsequent anaesthesia in patients who have received this drug. This specific precaution is unique to bleomycin among chemotherapy agents. Anaesthetic teams must be informed of prior bleomycin exposure before any procedure requiring general anaesthesia.

Cobalt-60 teletherapy units generate their therapeutic beam from gamma rays emitted during the radioactive decay of a cobalt-60 source, providing a relatively fixed photon energy of approximately 1.25 MeV average energy, in contrast to linear accelerators, which produce a beam through bremsstrahlung interactions when accelerated electrons strike a target. Cobalt units require periodic source replacement as the radioactivity decays over time (with a physical half-life of approximately 5.3 years) and cannot be switched off, unlike a linear accelerator which produces radiation only when actively powered. While largely superseded by linear accelerators in many settings, cobalt units remain in use in some parts of the world due to their relative simplicity and lower maintenance requirements.
options: Neutron capture reactions within a reactor core
Bremsstrahlung X-rays produced by accelerated electrons striking a target
Characteristic X-rays produced by an X-ray tube filament
Positron annihilation photons from a radioactive source
Gamma rays emitted from the radioactive decay of a cobalt-60 source
questions.question: A cobalt-60 teletherapy unit was historically used for external beam radiotherapy before widespread adoption of linear accelerators. What is the source of therapeutic photons in this type of machine?

questions.explanation: A catheter tip coursing outside the expected vessel, combined with a new pneumothorax and mediastinal widening, raises concern for vascular perforation and associated haemomediastinum, a rare but serious complication of central line insertion. Immediate withdrawal of the catheter without further advancement and urgent surgical or interventional consultation are required. Recognising abnormal catheter tip position on chest radiograph is a critical safety check after every central venous access procedure.
questions.question: A chest radiograph in a patient with sudden collapse after a central venous catheter insertion shows the catheter tip coiled outside the expected vascular course, with a new pneumothorax and mediastinal widening. What complication should be suspected?
options: Catheter malposition with vascular injury and haemomediastinum
Normal catheter position with incidental pneumothorax

questions.question: On IVU, the standard adult dose of iodinated contrast medium is:
questions.explanation: The standard adult dose of iodinated contrast for IVU is 50 mL, administered as a bolus intravenous injection. This can be increased to 100 mL in obese patients or those with mildly elevated serum urea where a higher contrast load may improve visualisation. For paediatric patients, the dose is 1 mL per kg body weight up to age 15 years. Non-ionic (low osmolarity) contrast agents are preferred due to their superior safety profile compared to ionic (high osmolarity) agents.

Left lower lobe collapse classically produces a triangular retrocardiac opacity with loss of the medial diaphragmatic outline, sometimes described as a sail-like shadow behind the heart. This appearance can be subtle and easily overlooked if the retrocardiac region is not carefully scrutinised on the frontal view. Recognising this specific pattern is important given that this area is a frequently missed location on chest radiography.
questions.question: A chest radiograph shows a triangular opacity behind the heart on the frontal view, with loss of the normal outline of the left hemidiaphragm medially. This appearance is MOST consistent with:

questions.explanation: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence of a cell. Mutations can arise from copying errors during cell division, ionizing radiation, chemical mutagens, or viral infections. Persistent unrepaired mutations in critical genes drive cancer development.
questions.question: A mutation is defined as a change in which cellular component?
In musculoskeletal MRI interpretation, fat appears hyperintense on T1-weighted sequences. Which of the following pathologies would MOST likely mimic fat signal on T1W MRI?
questions.explanation: Subacute haematoma (approximately 1-2 weeks old) contains methaemoglobin, a paramagnetic compound that causes T1 shortening and appears strikingly bright (hyperintense) on T1W MRI, mimicking fat signal. This is a well-known pitfall in musculoskeletal and intracranial MRI interpretation. Simple cysts appear hypointense on T1W, while fibrous dysplasia and malignant tumours show intermediate to low T1 signal.

MAG-3 (Technetium-99m mercaptoacetyltriglycine) renal scintigraphy provides information about renal blood flow (from the initial perfusion phase), differential renal tubular function (secretion of MAG-3 by tubular cells), and urinary tract drainage to detect obstruction. Frusemide (Lasix) can be administered during the scan to differentiate true mechanical obstruction from functional delay. It is used in children for ureteropelvic junction obstruction and duplex kidneys.
questions.question: The MAG-3 nuclear medicine renal scan is performed to assess:
options: Renal blood flow, tubular function, and excretory drainage (urinary obstruction)
Bone marrow oedema or early infection
questions.question: A patient undergoes an MRI scan for knee pain. The radiologist notes that the medullary cavity of a bone appears abnormally dark on T1 but bright on T2 and STIR. The MOST likely diagnosis consistent with this signal pattern is:
questions.explanation: Bone marrow oedema (or early infection/infiltration) shows low signal on T1 (replacing the normally bright fatty marrow) and high signal on T2 and STIR. STIR is particularly sensitive for marrow oedema because fat suppression makes the oedema conspicuous. Fatty marrow would be bright on T1. Sclerotic metastases are dark on both sequences. Normal marrow in adults is bright on T1 due to fat.

The UICC TNM staging system classifies cancer by T (primary tumour size and extent), N (regional lymph node involvement), and M (presence of distant metastasis). It is the most widely used staging system internationally. Staging guides treatment intent, modality selection, and prognostication.
questions.question: The UICC TNM staging system assesses which three parameters?
Superficial x-ray therapy applicators (cones) are used to collimate the beam at the patient's skin surface. The focus-to-skin distance (FSD) for 15 cm FSD cones is clinically significant because:
questions.explanation: In superficial radiotherapy, the short focus-to-skin distance (FSD) of applicator cones (e.g., 15 cm) results in high output (dose rate) at the skin and a large influence of the inverse square law — small changes in FSD cause large changes in dose rate. This makes calibration challenging and requires precise distance measurement. Additionally, short FSD increases electron contamination scattered from the applicator edges. Both factors are unique issues in superficial therapy not seen with megavoltage equipment.
options: Shorter FSD means lower output and reduced inverse square law effect
15 cm FSD cones are used exclusively for prostate treatment
The FSD has no effect on output at the skin
Short FSD means high output and a large influence of inverse square law, requiring careful dose calculation
15 cm FSD reduces electron contamination in the beam
Presence of cortical bone irregularity at all times
Patient name, date, and correct side marker
questions.explanation: Before interpreting any radiograph, it is critical to confirm patient identification (name, age, sex), the date the radiograph was taken, and the correct side marker (right or left). Errors in patient identification or laterality can lead to serious clinical errors including wrong-site treatment. This systematic check is the first mandatory step in radiographic review.
questions.question: When interpreting a plain radiograph systematically, which of the following should be verified FIRST before clinical interpretation begins?

options: Fixed dose of 20 mL regardless of weight
questions.explanation: The paediatric dose for intravenous urography is 1 mL per kg body weight, up to age 15 years, with a maximum equivalent to the adult dose of 50 mL. Weight-based dosing ensures adequate contrast opacification proportional to the child's blood volume and glomerular filtration rate. Underdosing results in poor nephrogram and pyelogram quality, while overdosing increases the risk of contrast-induced adverse effects. Non-ionic (low osmolarity) contrast agents are particularly important in paediatric practice.
questions.question: During intravenous urography in a child, the dose of contrast is calculated differently from adults. The correct paediatric dose per weight is:
The pituitary gland sits in the pituitary fossa in which bone of the skull base?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland (hypophysis cerebri) is situated in the pituitary fossa (sella turcica), a saddle-shaped depression in the body of the sphenoid bone, located in the middle cranial fossa. It is approximately the size of a pea (about 1 cm in all dimensions). The pituitary is covered superiorly by the sellar diaphragm (a dural fold) and is connected to the hypothalamus via the pituitary stalk (infundibulum) through an opening in this diaphragm.

options: Absent testicular blood flow on Doppler
Normal epididymis with isolated testicular echogenicity change as the sole finding
Enlarged echo-poor epididymis with increased Doppler blood flow and associated hydrocele
questions.question: Epididymo-orchitis on scrotal ultrasound shows which finding that helps differentiate it from testicular torsion?
questions.explanation: Epididymo-orchitis shows an enlarged, echo-poor (hypoechoic) epididymis with significantly increased vascularity (hyperaemia) on colour Doppler—in contrast to torsion, which shows absent flow. A reactive hydrocele (small dark fluid surrounding the testis) is almost always present in epididymo-orchitis. Twenty percent of epididymo-orchitis cases also show testicular changes. The combination of enlarged epididymis, increased Doppler flow, and hydrocele in a febrile patient distinguishes it clinically from torsion.

questions.question: A patient with cystic fibrosis and recurrent pneumonia undergoes a chest radiograph looking for a specific chronic sign of long-standing airway disease. Which finding would MOST strongly support this diagnosis?
options: Bronchiectasis with thickened, dilated airway walls
A normal chest radiograph excluding chronic disease
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis, characterised by thickened and dilated airway walls sometimes described as tram-track or ring shadows, is a classic chronic radiological finding in cystic fibrosis due to recurrent infection and impaired mucus clearance. A normal chest radiograph would be inconsistent with the long-standing, recurrent infective history described. Recognising this chronic airway change helps confirm the suspected underlying diagnosis and disease chronicity.

questions.question: On a plain abdominal radiograph, the large bowel is distinguished from the small bowel by which characteristic feature?
options: Haustral folds that typically do not completely traverse the lumen
Valvulae conniventes (mucosal folds) that completely traverse the well-defined lumen
Central location within the peritoneal cavity
questions.explanation: The large bowel is characterised on plain abdominal film by haustral folds (haustra), which are thicker than small bowel valvulae conniventes and typically do not completely cross the bowel lumen—leaving a gap in the middle. The large bowel also characteristically frames the abdomen peripherally, while the small bowel occupies the central abdomen. These distinctions help in identifying dilated bowel loops in obstruction, though they can be unreliable in severely distended or air-filled bowel.

Mediastinal air tracking along the oesophagus after forceful vomiting, together with a pleural effusion, is classic for Boerhaave syndrome, a spontaneous oesophageal rupture that carries high mortality if diagnosis and surgical management are delayed. Contrast oesophagography or CT with oral contrast can help confirm the site of a leak. This differs from simple pneumomediastinum related to asthma or barotrauma, which lacks the associated oesophageal wall disruption and pleural effusion pattern.
questions.question: A CT scan of the neck and chest in a patient with sudden chest pain after vomiting shows air within the mediastinum tracking along the oesophagus with a small left pleural effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: A chromosomal translocation confined to tumour cells
questions.question: A young woman with a strong family history of early-onset breast and ovarian cancer tests positive for a BRCA1 mutation. This mutation is best classified as which type, given it can be passed to her children?
questions.explanation: A germline mutation is present in the reproductive cells and can therefore be inherited by offspring, as is the case with BRCA1 mutations causing hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. A somatic mutation instead arises only within body cells during a person's lifetime and is not heritable. This distinction underlies genetic counselling recommendations for family members of BRCA-positive patients.

questions.question: Left ventricular enlargement on CXR causes the cardiac apex to shift in which direction?
questions.explanation: Left ventricular enlargement increases the cardiopulmonary ratio and displaces the cardiac apex both laterally and inferiorly, producing a larger radius of curvature of the left heart border. This contrasts with right ventricular enlargement, which shifts the apex laterally without inferior displacement. The distinction aids in identifying the predominant chamber enlarged.

Pericardial fluid causing chamber flattening, particularly of the right ventricle, along with inferior vena cava distension from impaired venous return, indicates cardiac tamponade, a life-threatening emergency requiring urgent pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage. Simple effusions without these secondary signs of haemodynamic compromise can often be observed. Recognising the imaging correlates of tamponade physiology is critical for timely intervention in trauma patients.
options: Simple pericardial effusion without haemodynamic compromise
questions.question: A CT scan of the chest in a patient involved in a road traffic collision shows a collection of fluid within the pericardial sac with flattening of the cardiac chambers and distension of the inferior vena cava. What complication is this most consistent with?

questions.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism results from failure of the thyroid gland itself (most commonly Hashimoto's thyroiditis or post-thyroidectomy). With reduced T4 production, the negative feedback on the pituitary is diminished, causing the anterior pituitary to release increasing amounts of TSH in an attempt to stimulate the failing thyroid. This produces the characteristic biochemical pattern of elevated TSH with low free T4. TSH is the most sensitive early indicator of thyroid dysfunction—it rises before free T4 falls significantly (subclinical hypothyroidism: elevated TSH, normal free T4).
options: Low TSH with high free T4
Normal TSH with low free T4
Low TSH with low free T4
High TSH with high free T4
High TSH with low free T4
questions.question: In primary hypothyroidism, which biochemical finding is expected?

options: Air in the right iliac fossa
questions.explanation: The psoas muscle shadow (psoas line) is normally visible on plain abdominal radiograph as a faint soft tissue density outlining the lateral margin of the psoas major muscle bilaterally. Absence or obliteration of the psoas shadow indicates retroperitoneal pathology (retroperitoneal haemorrhage, abscess, tumour, or severe inflammatory disease) causing loss of the normal fat plane that delineates the muscle. This is an important indirect sign prompting further imaging of the retroperitoneum.
questions.question: In the abdominal evaluation, which radiographic sign on plain film is specifically associated with a significant retroperitoneal pathology?

questions.explanation: The Schatzki ring (B ring) on barium swallow lies at the gastro-oesophageal junction, specifically at the squamocolumnar mucosal junction (Z-line). The A ring (or mucosal ring) lies slightly above it in the lower oesophageal mucosa. The B ring is clinically significant as a cause of episodic solid food dysphagia. Both rings are at or near the distal oesophagus in the region of the diaphragmatic hiatus.
options: The gastro-oesophageal junction at the squamocolumnar junction
The level of the aortic arch
The level of the left main bronchus
questions.question: In normal barium swallow anatomy of the distal oesophagus, the 'B ring' (Schatzki ring) lies at:

questions.explanation: A lateral decubitus radiograph (lying with the affected side down) causes a free-flowing pleural effusion to layer along the dependent chest wall, confirming its fluid nature and mobility. If the opacity does not layer out and remains in the same position, it is likely a loculated (encapsulated) effusion or a solid mass rather than free fluid. This simple technique helps differentiate free from loculated effusions and can also reveal underlying consolidation or atelectasis previously hidden by the effusion.
options: Confirm that the opacity is a free-flowing effusion
Increase the effusion size for easier diagnosis
Show the underlying pulmonary infiltrate beneath the effusion
questions.question: A patient with known right-sided pleural effusion is placed in the left lateral decubitus position for a radiograph. The purpose of this position is to:

questions.explanation: Full-wave rectification, achieved with a minimum of four diodes in a bridge circuit, converts both positive and negative halves of the AC sine wave into positive DC pulses. This results in two pulses per cycle (at 60 Hz mains frequency, that is 120 pulses per second), compared to one pulse per cycle with half-wave rectification.
questions.question: In full-wave rectification using four diodes, how many current pulses per cycle are produced across the x-ray tube?
Which Nigerian regulatory authority is responsible for radiation protection standards and oversight?
questions.explanation: The Nigeria Nuclear Regulatory Authority (NNRA) is the Nigerian national body responsible for establishing and enforcing radiation protection standards, licensing of facilities, and regulatory oversight of all radiation sources in Nigeria. The NRPB is the UK body, USNRC is the US body, IAEA is an international agency, and UNSCEAR studies radiation effects globally.

Disease control is defined as reduction in incidence, prevalence, morbidity, or mortality to a locally acceptable level. This encompasses primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention strategies. Cancer control programs aim to reduce the overall cancer burden within a population.
questions.question: Cancer control is defined as a reduction in which disease parameters to a locally acceptable level?
In diagnostic radiology, which modality provides multiplanar imaging capability using X-rays processed through a computer to display cross-sectional anatomy?
questions.explanation: Computed tomography (CT) uses X-ray beams processed through detectors and computer algorithms to generate cross-sectional (axial) images of the body, which can be reformatted into coronal, sagittal, and 3D reconstructions (multiplanar imaging). This differentiates CT from plain radiography and fluoroscopy, which produce only projectional (2D summation) images. CT's cross-sectional display eliminates superimposition and improves spatial relationships between structures.

questions.question: The standard views for assessing facial bones following trauma include which projection as the primary film?
questions.explanation: The occipito-mental (OM or Water's view) projection is the standard radiographic view for facial bones and paranasal sinuses, taken with the neck extended so the petrous ridges project below the maxillary antra. This view allows assessment of the orbital margins, maxillary antra, zygomatic arches, and facial bone symmetry. A 30-degree OM may be added for better visualisation. The lateral view may supplement in cases of severe facial trauma.

Berry aneurysms are saccular outpouchings that typically arise at arterial branch points of the circle of Willis, with the anterior communicating artery being one of the most common locations, and are the leading cause of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Fusiform aneurysms instead involve circumferential dilatation of a vessel segment rather than a focal saccular outpouching. CT angiography is the primary tool for detecting, localising, and sizing these aneurysms to guide coiling or clipping decisions.
questions.question: A CT angiogram of the head shows a saccular outpouching arising at the junction of the anterior communicating artery, measuring 6 mm, in a patient who presented with sudden severe headache. What is this lesion called?

questions.explanation: Barium swallow indirectly demonstrates cardiac chamber enlargement and vascular rings through oesophageal displacement caused by adjacent cardiovascular structures. It is a contrast study using single or water-soluble contrast. While not commonly used today, it provides indirect signs of left atrial enlargement and mediastinal vascular anomalies.
questions.question: Barium swallow is used in cardiac imaging as an indirect method to demonstrate which finding?

questions.explanation: Higher detector speed class settings require fewer photons to produce an adequate image, reducing patient radiation dose, but this reduction in photon quantity increases statistical quantum mottle (noise) in the resulting image, potentially reducing the visibility of subtle low-contrast pathology. Selecting an appropriate speed class for the clinical indication involves balancing acceptable dose reduction against maintaining sufficient image quality for the diagnostic task at hand. This trade-off is a fundamental consideration in digital radiography exposure technique optimisation.
questions.question: A radiographer selects a higher detector speed class setting for a digital radiography system to reduce patient dose for a routine chest examination. What is the main trade-off associated with using a higher speed class?
options: Improved spatial resolution with no other change
Reduced image contrast with no change in dose
Increased quantum mottle (noise) in the resulting image
Elimination of the need for collimation

questions.question: X-ray quantity (intensity) is directly proportional to which combination of factors?
questions.explanation: X-ray quantity (the number of photons produced) is directly proportional to both the tube current (mA) and the exposure time (seconds). Their product, milliampere-seconds (mAs), determines radiation quantity. The kilovoltage (kV) primarily affects x-ray quality (photon energy), not simple linear quantity, though increasing kV also increases total output.

options: Bone fragment localisation in complex fractures
Intraosseous and periarticular soft tissue conditions
questions.question: When comparing CT and MRI for musculoskeletal assessment, MRI is specifically superior for evaluating which of the following?
questions.explanation: MRI is superior to CT for evaluating intraosseous conditions (bone marrow oedema, tumour invasion, avascular necrosis) and extraarticular soft tissue (muscles, tendons, ligaments, cartilage) due to its excellent soft tissue contrast resolution. CT outperforms MRI for cortical bone detail, calcification detection, and gas identification due to its superior spatial resolution for mineralised structures.

Non-MRI-conditional (non-compliant) cardiac pacemakers represent the most critical absolute contraindication to MRI because the strong magnetic field can inhibit pacemaker function, induce currents in pacing leads causing arrhythmias or cardiac arrest, and physically move the device. Modern MRI-conditional pacemakers exist but require careful protocols. Tattoos, dental fillings, and most titanium implants carry much lower risk levels.
questions.question: In MRI safety, which absolute contraindication poses the GREATEST immediate risk to a patient in the MRI scanner?

A CT scan of the head performed three weeks after a fall in an elderly patient shows a crescentic extra-axial collection that is now hypodense relative to brain parenchyma. What stage of subdural haematoma does this represent?
questions.explanation: Subdural haematomas evolve in attenuation over time: acute collections are hyperdense, subacute collections become isodense to brain over one to three weeks, and chronic collections become hypodense as clot breaks down and liquefies. A three-week-old hypodense collection is therefore classified as chronic. Recognising this temporal evolution helps estimate the likely timing of the inciting injury, which can be clinically important in elderly patients with unwitnessed falls.

questions.question: On a non-contrast CT brain scan, acute ischaemic infarction in the MCA territory would initially appear as:
options: Normal or subtly hypodense area with loss of grey-white differentiation
Diffuse hyperdensity throughout the subarachnoid space
Calcified lesion in the basal ganglia
questions.explanation: In the hyperacute phase (0-6 hours), ischaemic infarction may appear essentially normal on non-contrast CT or show only subtle hypodensity with loss of grey-white matter differentiation (early MCA infarction sign). The 'dense MCA sign' (hyperdense clot within the MCA) may be seen. By 24-48 hours, a clearly hypodense area with mass effect becomes apparent. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is far more sensitive than CT for hyperacute ischaemia.

questions.question: Thrombolysis in interventional radiology involves catheter-directed infusion of which type of agent?
options: Clot-dissolving (fibrinolytic) agents such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA)
questions.explanation: Catheter-directed thrombolysis involves placing a catheter directly into the thrombosed vessel and infusing fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) agents such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) or urokinase that activate plasminogen to dissolve the clot. This is used for DVT, acute peripheral arterial occlusion, and massive pulmonary embolism causing haemodynamic compromise. Direct intra-clot infusion achieves clot lysis at lower doses than systemic thrombolysis, reducing bleeding risk.

questions.question: The Law of Bergonie and Tribondeau states that mammalian cells are most sensitive to ionising radiation when they are:
options: Terminally differentiated with no mitotic activity
In the G1 phase of the cell cycle only
Exposed to high-LET radiation under hypoxic conditions
Rapidly dividing, undifferentiated and with a high mitotic index
questions.explanation: The Law of Bergonie and Tribondeau (1906) states that radiation sensitivity increases when cells are rapidly dividing, poorly differentiated (undifferentiated), and have a high mitotic index. This explains why rapidly proliferating tissues (bone marrow, gonads, intestinal epithelium) are more radiosensitive, while slowly dividing tissues (liver, kidney) and non-dividing cells (neurones, muscle) are more radioresistant.

options: Complete elimination of any procedural risk
Avoidance of the need for any sedation
Closer proximity to the pancreas allowing more accurate targeting with reduced risk of tumour seeding
Superior assessment of unrelated pulmonary pathology
Direct visualisation of distant liver metastases only
questions.explanation: Endoscopic ultrasound allows the probe to be positioned in close proximity to the pancreas via the stomach or duodenum, improving accuracy of fine needle aspiration while potentially reducing the risk of tumour seeding along a percutaneous needle tract. This anatomical advantage is specific to the pancreas given its deep retroperitoneal location. Selecting the appropriate biopsy approach based on anatomical location improves diagnostic yield while minimising procedural risk.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected pancreatic mass undergoes endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration rather than a percutaneous approach. What is the PRIMARY advantage of this endoscopic technique for this specific anatomical location?
A T1-weighted MRI sequence is characterised by which combination of repetition time (TR) and echo time (TE)?
questions.explanation: T1-weighted sequences use a short TR and short TE to maximise the differences in T1 relaxation times between tissues while minimising T2 contrast contribution, producing images where fat appears bright and fluid appears dark. In contrast, T2-weighted sequences use a long TR and long TE to emphasise T2 relaxation differences, making fluid appear bright. Correct selection of these timing parameters is fundamental to generating the desired tissue contrast for a given clinical question.

Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound is defined by the presence of =20 small follicles (each 2-9 mm) arranged peripherally (necklace pattern) around an increased central echogenic stroma in an enlarged ovary. However, this appearance is non-specific and occurs in up to 25% of normal women. PCOS diagnosis requires clinical (menstrual irregularity, hyperandrogenism) and biochemical criteria in addition to ultrasound, as ovaries may appear normal in 25% of confirmed PCOS patients.
questions.question: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) on ultrasound is described as showing bilateral enlarged ovaries with a specific follicle distribution. Which pattern is characteristic?
options: Multiple small peripheral follicles around increased central stroma
Bilateral ovarian cysts greater than 5 well-defined cm

questions.explanation: IVU is contraindicated in patients with very high serum urea (severe renal failure) because contrast-induced nephropathy can cause further acute-on-chronic kidney injury. Additionally, severely impaired kidneys cannot concentrate and excrete contrast, producing non-diagnostic or absent nephrogram/pyelogram. The general contraindications to IVU include: severe renal impairment, previous severe contrast reaction, dehydration, severe diabetes mellitus, and multiple myeloma (risk of contrast-induced precipitation in renal tubules).
questions.question: Intravenous urography (IVU/IVP) is contraindicated in patients with which of the following conditions?

A radiotherapy patient develops moist desquamation of the skin within the treatment field during the fourth week of a fractionated course to the chest wall. How should this acute skin reaction be classified in terms of radiotherapy toxicity timing?
options: A stochastic radiation effect unrelated to dose received
questions.explanation: Skin reactions such as erythema, dry desquamation, and moist desquamation typically develop during the course of fractionated radiotherapy or shortly after its completion, classifying them as acute radiation toxicities that arise from damage to the rapidly proliferating basal keratinocyte layer of the epidermis. This differs from late radiation toxicities, such as fibrosis or telangiectasia, which develop months to years after treatment through different underlying tissue mechanisms. Recognising and appropriately managing acute skin reactions, which are generally self-limiting deterministic effects related to the cumulative dose received, is an important aspect of on-treatment patient care during radiotherapy.

questions.question: Which lifestyle modification would most directly reduce the risk of developing hormone receptor-positive breast cancer?
questions.explanation: Obesity increases circulating oestrogen levels through peripheral aromatization of androgens in adipose tissue, elevating the risk of hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. Maintaining a healthy body weight reduces this excess oestrogen stimulation. Weight management is one of the most impactful modifiable breast cancer risk factors, particularly in postmenopausal women.

questions.question: Loss of homeostatic control is a key characteristic of malignant cells. What does this specifically mean?
questions.explanation: Loss of homeostatic control means malignant cells bypass normal regulatory mechanisms that govern cell growth and division. This results in uncontrolled proliferation and tumour mass formation. Normal tissue architecture depends on tightly regulated homeostasis, which is fundamentally disrupted in cancer.
options: Cells migrate to lymph nodes only

questions.question: A patient receiving 5-fluorouracil for colorectal cancer develops severe mucositis and diarrhoea. This toxicity reflects the drug's mechanism of action within which broader chemotherapy class?
questions.explanation: 5-Fluorouracil is an antimetabolite that interferes with pyrimidine synthesis, and its toxicity particularly affects rapidly dividing tissues such as gut mucosa, producing mucositis and diarrhoea. This differs from alkylating agents, which directly damage DNA through cross-linking rather than interfering with metabolic precursors. Recognising the drug class helps anticipate the characteristic toxicity pattern likely to occur.

Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) is identified on non-contrast CT as hyperdense (white) blood visible within the ventricular system — the frontal horns or body of the lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, or the fourth ventricle. Blood in ventricles layers dependently (haemorrhagic fluid level). IVH can be primary (rupture of arteriovenous malformation into a ventricle) or secondary (extension from intraparenchymal or subarachnoid haemorrhage into the ventricles).
options: The epidural space above the temporal lobe
The lateral ventricles, third ventricle, or fourth ventricle
The subdural space over the cerebral convexities
questions.question: Intraventricular haemorrhage in head CT is identified by the presence of hyperdense blood within:

questions.explanation: Acute haematoma (fresh blood) is spontaneously hyperdense on non-contrast CT due to the high protein concentration and high attenuation of haemoglobin in freshly clotted blood, typically measuring 50-70 HU. Hepatic steatosis appears hypodense (low density), simple cysts are near-water density (0-20 HU), abscesses and metastases are typically hypodense or isodense. Hyperdensity on non-contrast CT is a hallmark of acute bleeding.
questions.question: A 35-year-old patient undergoes contrast-enhanced CT. The radiologist reports a region appearing 'hyperdense' compared to the surrounding liver parenchyma on the non-contrast phase. Which of the following would most likely produce this finding?
The disease category requiring the GREATEST proportion of palliative care globally, according to palliative care needs proportions, is:
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular diseases account for the greatest proportion (38.5%) of patients in need of palliative care globally. Cancer is the second largest group (34%), followed by chronic respiratory diseases (10.3%), AIDS (5.7%), diabetes (4.6%), and other conditions including kidney and liver failure (6.9%). This highlights that palliative care is not exclusively for cancer patients but is needed across a wide range of life-threatening conditions.

options: Medial epicondyle avulsion visible on film
questions.question: A radiograph of the elbow in a child after a fall shows an abnormally elevated posterior fat pad with no visible fracture line. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The posterior fat pad is normally not visible on a true lateral elbow radiograph; its presence indicates a joint effusion, most commonly from an occult fracture such as a supracondylar fracture in children. An anterior sail sign may also be seen but is less specific since a small anterior fat pad can be a normal variant. Clinical correlation and immobilisation are warranted even without a visible fracture line.

questions.question: A lipoma on mammography appears as which type of density?
questions.explanation: A breast lipoma appears on mammography as a large, rounded, radiolucent (low-density) well-defined opacity with compression of adjacent parenchyma. Its radiolucency reflects the fat content. This distinguishes it from soft tissue tumours, which are denser than fat on mammography.

options: Regional myocardial blood flow and viability
questions.explanation: Nuclear myocardial perfusion imaging using tracers such as technetium-based agents assesses regional blood flow and tissue viability, identifying areas of ischaemia or infarction based on differential tracer uptake. This is functionally distinct from echocardiography, which primarily assesses structural and valvular parameters rather than perfusion. This functional information is particularly valuable in guiding decisions about revascularisation.
questions.question: A patient undergoes nuclear medicine myocardial perfusion imaging using a radiotracer that concentrates in viable, well-perfused myocardium. This investigation PRIMARILY assesses which cardiac parameter?

options: Any enhancement whatsoever, regardless of pattern
Absence of any prior surgical history
A completely normal signal intensity throughout
Progressive growth on serial imaging or restricted diffusion suggestive of high cellularity
questions.question: A patient with a suspected recurrent soft tissue sarcoma after prior surgery undergoes MRI showing an enhancing soft tissue mass at the surgical bed. What additional imaging feature would be MOST helpful in confidently distinguishing recurrence from post-surgical scar tissue?
questions.explanation: Distinguishing recurrent tumour from post-surgical scar tissue on MRI is aided by identifying progressive growth on serial imaging or features such as restricted diffusion suggesting high cellularity, since scar tissue typically remains stable in size and lacks these cellular features. Enhancement alone is non-specific, as scar tissue can also enhance, particularly in the early post-operative period. Correlating imaging findings with the clinical timeline and, where necessary, biopsy improves diagnostic confidence in this challenging scenario.

Barium swallow can indirectly demonstrate left atrial enlargement through posterior displacement or indentation of the adjacent oesophagus, though it does not directly visualise the heart or pericardium itself. This indirect sign was historically useful before widespread availability of echocardiography and CT. Modern practice now relies on direct cardiac imaging rather than this indirect radiological sign for most clinical purposes.
options: Direct visualisation of the pericardial fluid
Posterior displacement or indentation of the oesophagus
questions.question: A patient with a large pericardial effusion undergoes barium swallow as part of cardiac imaging assessment. What indirect finding would this investigation demonstrate in the presence of significant left atrial enlargement?

questions.explanation: Asymmetric joint space narrowing with subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and subchondral cysts together form the classic radiographic tetrad of osteoarthritis, reflecting degenerative rather than inflammatory joint change. Rheumatoid arthritis instead characteristically shows periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions rather than sclerosis and osteophytes. Correctly distinguishing these patterns guides appropriate management, since the underlying pathophysiology and treatment differ substantially.
questions.question: A knee radiograph in an elderly patient shows asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and subchondral cyst formation. This combination is MOST characteristic of:

questions.explanation: Chest ultrasound is particularly useful in infants and for evaluating soft tissue chest masses due to its non-ionising nature and portability. In adults, it is valuable for detecting pleural effusions and guiding drainage procedures. It is less useful for examining aerated lung parenchyma.
questions.question: Ultrasound of the chest is specifically indicated for which paediatric respiratory imaging purpose?
A radiologist describes a pulmonary lesion as 'an area of lucency.' This finding correctly refers to which appearance on the radiograph?
questions.explanation: Lucency on a radiograph refers to a darker (blacker) area resulting from reduced X-ray attenuation, as seen with gas or air-containing structures. Conversely, opacity refers to a brighter (whiter) area caused by increased attenuation. Correct use of these terms is essential for accurate radiological communication and clinical decision-making.

The lateral decubitus view demonstrates free-flowing pleural effusion as it redistributes along the dependent chest wall. Small effusions invisible on erect PA can be detected by this technique. It also helps distinguish free fluid from loculated collections and pleural thickening. Ultrasound is the preferred modality when available.
questions.question: Which CXR view is most useful for assessing the size of a pleural effusion when ultrasound is unavailable?
Normal endometrial thickness on ultrasound in a postmenopausal woman should not exceed which measurement?
questions.explanation: The endometrium atrophies after menopause and should measure no more than 5 mm in total (double layer) thickness on transvaginal ultrasound in a postmenopausal woman not on hormone replacement therapy. Endometrial thickness exceeding 5 mm in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding warrants further investigation (endometrial biopsy) to exclude endometrial carcinoma. Endometrial thickness varies with the menstrual cycle in premenopausal women (thinnest after menstruation, thickest in the secretory phase).

options: Absence of hepatic arterial branches in the tumour region
Normal hepatic arterial pattern with no abnormality
Tumour hypervascularity (neovascularity) with irregular arterial vessels and tumour staining
Venous pooling in the portal vein
questions.explanation: Malignant hepatic tumours typically demonstrate hypervascularity on hepatic arteriography, characterised by abnormal, irregular neovascularity (tumour vessels), arteriovenous shunting, tumour 'staining' (contrast pooling within the tumour in the venous phase), and displacement or encasement of normal hepatic arterial branches. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is classically hypervascular. This angiographic assessment helps plan the embolisation procedure and confirm the tumour's blood supply.
questions.question: A hepatic arteriogram performed before hepatic artery embolisation will demonstrate tumour vascularity as:
For tungsten (W, Z=74), characteristic x-rays from the K-shell are produced ONLY when the applied tube voltage exceeds a threshold. What is that threshold voltage?
questions.explanation: Characteristic radiation from the K-shell is produced only when incident electrons carry energy greater than the K-shell binding energy of the target material. For tungsten, the K-shell binding energy is 69.5 keV; therefore the applied voltage must exceed 69.5 kV. For molybdenum, this threshold is 20 kV.

questions.question: A rapidly growing tumour is found on imaging to have recruited a dense new network of blood vessels supplying its core. Which hallmark of cancer does this represent, and which molecular pathway is MOST relevant?
questions.explanation: Sustained angiogenesis allows tumours to recruit new blood vessels to support growth beyond the limits of simple diffusion, largely driven by vascular endothelial growth factor signalling. This is mechanistically distinct from immune evasion, which concerns escape from immune surveillance rather than vascular supply. Anti-angiogenic therapies specifically target this hallmark by inhibiting VEGF signalling.

questions.question: A CT scan of the head in a patient who sustained blunt orbital trauma shows herniation of orbital fat and the inferior rectus muscle through a defect in the orbital floor into the maxillary sinus, described as a 'teardrop' sign. What is the diagnosis?
options: Zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture without floor defect
Simple orbital rim fracture without floor involvement
questions.explanation: An orbital blowout fracture results from a sudden rise in intraorbital pressure that fractures the thin orbital floor, allowing herniation of orbital fat and sometimes the inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus, producing the teardrop sign on coronal imaging. Entrapment of the inferior rectus can cause restricted upward gaze and requires urgent surgical assessment in children in particular, due to the risk of muscle ischaemia. Distinguishing simple orbital rim fractures, which lack floor involvement, from true blowout fractures with herniation guides the urgency of surgical referral.

questions.question: On a plain radiograph, the four basic densities from darkest to lightest are arranged as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Radiographic densities are determined by the degree to which tissues attenuate X-rays. Gas (air) attenuates the least and appears darkest (most black), followed by fat (dark grey), then water/soft tissue (light grey), and finally mineral/bone, which attenuates X-rays the most and appears brightest (white). This sequence is fundamental to radiographic interpretation.

questions.question: Which cardiac imaging modality provides a calcium score for predicting future cardiac events?
questions.explanation: Coronary artery calcium scoring is exclusively performed with cardiac CT and quantifies the total calcium burden in the coronary arteries using the Agatston score. There is a direct correlation between calcium burden and the risk of future cardiac events. CT is the only non-invasive imaging technique capable of producing a calcium score.

questions.question: A CT scan of the abdomen shows a lesion with a Hounsfield unit value of +45. This value is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: A Hounsfield unit value of +45 falls within the soft tissue range of approximately +20 to +60 HU, consistent with solid organ parenchyma such as liver, spleen, or kidney, or with soft tissue masses. Muscle is also in this range. Air is -1000 HU, fat is -20 to -200 HU, calcification is +150 to +400 HU, cortical bone is approximately +1000 HU, and metal has very high positive values.
options: Soft tissue or solid organ parenchyma

questions.explanation: Cavitating pulmonary nodules are a recognised and important radiological feature of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, reflecting necrotising granulomatous inflammation within the lung parenchyma. A popcorn-calcified nodule instead suggests a benign hamartoma, an entirely different pathological process. Recognising this pattern in the appropriate clinical context, including renal involvement, supports pursuing this specific vasculitic diagnosis.
questions.question: A patient with suspected Wegener's granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) presents with haemoptysis. Which chest radiographic finding would be MOST consistent with this diagnosis?

An ultrasound transducer emits sound waves at a frequency of 10 MHz for imaging a superficial structure, compared with 3.5 MHz used for deeper abdominal imaging. What is the main trade-off of using this higher frequency?
options: No change in resolution or penetration
Improved penetration with no change in resolution
Improved spatial resolution but reduced depth of tissue penetration
Improved penetration but reduced spatial resolution
questions.explanation: Higher frequency ultrasound transducers provide improved spatial resolution because of their shorter wavelength, but this comes at the cost of reduced tissue penetration due to greater attenuation of higher frequency sound waves as they travel through tissue, making them suitable primarily for superficial structures. Lower frequency transducers instead sacrifice some resolution in exchange for the ability to image deeper structures such as abdominal organs. Selecting the appropriate transducer frequency for the clinical target depth and required resolution is a fundamental principle of ultrasound technique.

Low metabolic activity on FDG-PET/CT reduces the likelihood that a solitary pulmonary nodule represents an aggressive malignancy, since most cancers show increased glucose metabolism, supporting a more conservative follow-up approach in appropriate cases. However, this finding alone does not provide absolute certainty or replace tissue diagnosis where clinical suspicion remains significant. Combining PET findings with other clinical and radiological features improves overall diagnostic accuracy for indeterminate pulmonary nodules.
options: Supporting a lower likelihood of malignancy, favouring a benign process
Confirming definitive malignancy without any further assessment
Replacing the need for any follow-up imaging
Excluding all possible causes of the nodule with certainty
questions.question: A patient with a solitary pulmonary nodule undergoes FDG-PET/CT, which shows low metabolic activity within the lesion. This finding is MOST useful for which purpose?

questions.explanation: A blind-ending, non-compressible tubular structure exceeding 6 mm with a target sign on cross-section is the sonographic hallmark of an inflamed appendix. Ultrasound is preferred in young women partly because it can also evaluate pelvic organs to exclude gynaecological causes of pain. Graded compression technique improves diagnostic accuracy.
questions.question: An abdominal ultrasound in a young woman with right iliac fossa pain shows a blind-ending, non-compressible tubular structure over 6 mm in diameter with a target appearance in cross-section. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Haemorrhagic contusions beneath the fracture site
Normal brain parenchyma in all cases
questions.explanation: Depressed skull fractures (where a bone fragment is driven inward below the level of the surrounding skull) are frequently associated with haemorrhagic contusions (bruising and small haemorrhages) in the underlying brain cortex directly beneath the fracture site. This represents direct mechanical impact injury. CT bone windows demonstrate the fracture morphology, while soft tissue windows show the associated parenchymal haemorrhage, oedema, and any overlying extradural haematoma.
questions.question: In patients presenting with depressed skull fractures on CT, the underlying brain finding that most commonly accompanies this injury is:

questions.explanation: Intraparenchymal (intracerebral) haemorrhage occurs when a blood vessel ruptures WITHIN the brain parenchyma itself, causing a focal hyperdense haematoma on non-contrast CT, usually with surrounding oedema and potential mass effect. Common causes include hypertension (affecting deep perforators in the basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, and pons), amyloid angiopathy (lobar haemorrhages in elderly), arteriovenous malformations, and anticoagulant therapy.
questions.question: In neuroradiology, which type of haemorrhagic stroke is caused by rupture of a blood vessel WITHIN the brain parenchyma?
A patient presents with acute anuria after severe haemorrhage and hypotension. IVU shows bilateral non-functioning kidneys. This is most likely due to which emergency condition?
questions.explanation: Bilateral absent or markedly delayed nephrogram on IVU following severe haemorrhage and haemodynamic shock indicates bilateral acute tubular necrosis (ATN) from renal ischaemia. Profound hypotension causes renal cortical ischaemia, damaging the tubular epithelium. The kidneys cannot excrete contrast, producing an absent nephrogram. ATN is the commonest cause of acute kidney injury in hospitalised patients. Management is supportive with fluid resuscitation, dialysis if needed, and removal of nephrotoxic agents while awaiting tubular recovery.
options: Normal finding in a dehydrated patient
Markedly elevated due to pituitary stimulation
Variably elevated or normal depending on age
questions.explanation: In primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goitre), the thyroid autonomously produces excess T3 and T4. The resulting elevated plasma T4/T3 levels exert negative feedback on the pituitary, suppressing TSH secretion to very low or undetectable levels (below 0.1 mU/L; normal 0.3-5.0 mU/L). This low TSH in the setting of elevated free T4 is diagnostic of primary hyperthyroidism. Secondary hyperthyroidism (pituitary TSH-secreting adenoma) would show elevated TSH—a rare condition.
questions.question: In primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease), the anterior pituitary TSH level is expected to be:

questions.explanation: Geiger-Muller (GM) counters detect ionisation events caused by radiation passing through the detector tube. They are highly sensitive for detecting and locating radioactive contamination (beta and gamma emitters) in nuclear medicine departments, but are not designed to measure absorbed dose accurately. For personal dosimetry, TLD badges or optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dosimeters are used. GM counters provide count rate rather than energy-specific dose measurement.
questions.question: The Geiger-Muller counter, used as a radiation detection instrument in nuclear medicine, is BEST suited for:
options: Precise measurement of radiation dose in grays
Detecting and monitoring for contamination with beta and gamma emitters

questions.question: Arthrography as a musculoskeletal imaging technique is specifically used for evaluating which structures?
options: Intra-articular structures including cartilage and ligaments
questions.explanation: Arthrography involves injection of contrast into a joint space followed by imaging to evaluate intra-articular structures including joint cartilage, ligaments, capsule, and synovium. It is used in the shoulder, knee, hip, and wrist. MR arthrography, combining arthrography with MRI, provides superior soft tissue detail for diagnosing labral and cartilage tears.

For long bone trauma, two views at right angles to each other are mandatory because a fracture line may be completely invisible on one projection while clearly visible on the orthogonal view. Additionally, the degree of angulation and displacement cannot be accurately assessed from a single view. While two views are standard across skeletal sites, their necessity is most critical for long bones due to the projective nature of plain radiography and the clinical importance of accurate fracture characterisation.
questions.question: In the evaluation of skeletal trauma, two radiographic views are obtained at right angles. In which anatomical region is this standard protocol MOST critical for detecting all fractures?
The multidisciplinary team involved in palliative care includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Palliative care is delivered by a multidisciplinary team that includes physicians (from various specialities), nursing staff, support workers, paramedics, pharmacists, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, social workers, chaplains/spiritual care workers, and volunteers. No single profession delivers palliative care in isolation. Interventional radiologists may contribute (e.g., nerve blocks, tumour ablation for pain), but the team is broad — the notion that 'radiological interventionists exclusively' provide palliative care is incorrect.

questions.question: In Interventional Radiology, the term 'Seldinger technique' refers to:
options: The standard technique of vascular access using a needle, guidewire, and catheter in sequence
The method of deploying a covered stent graft for an aortic aneurysm
The method of positioning a biliary drainage catheter
The technique of placing an IVC filter via jugular approach
The approach used for percutaneous renal access
questions.explanation: The Seldinger technique (developed by Dr Sven-Ivar Seldinger in 1953) is the fundamental vascular access technique in interventional radiology: a hollow needle punctures the vessel, a flexible guidewire is passed through the needle, the needle is removed while the wire maintains access, and a catheter/sheath is threaded over the wire into the vessel. This technique revolutionised vascular imaging and intervention by avoiding the need for arterial cut-down.

questions.question: The three phases of biological damage following ionising radiation exposure in the correct chronological sequence are:
questions.explanation: Radiation-induced biological damage proceeds in three phases: the physical phase (10⁻¹⁸ s) involving energy deposition and ionisation, the chemical phase (10⁻³ s) involving free radical formation and chemical bond breakage, and the biological phase (seconds to years) during which the cell reacts to chemical damage, potentially leading to cell death or mutation.

questions.question: A chest radiograph in a patient with chronic constrictive pericarditis shows a normal or only mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette with visible pericardial calcification. Why might this presentation be easily overlooked despite significant haemodynamic compromise?
questions.explanation: In constrictive pericarditis, the cardiac silhouette may appear only mildly enlarged or even normal despite significant haemodynamic compromise, because constriction limits diastolic filling rather than producing chamber dilation. Pericardial calcification, when present, is a helpful supportive clue but may be subtle. This discrepancy between silhouette size and clinical severity means the diagnosis often requires a high index of suspicion supported by further imaging.
options: The cardiac silhouette size does not reliably reflect the degree of pericardial constriction
Constrictive pericarditis always produces massive cardiomegaly
Pericardial calcification is never visible on plain radiography
This condition never causes any haemodynamic compromise
Constrictive pericarditis is always accompanied by pulmonary plethora

questions.explanation: A tear is diagnosed on MRI when abnormal increased signal on a T2-weighted or proton-density sequence extends all the way to an articular surface of the meniscus, distinguishing it from degenerative intrasubstance signal that remains confined within the substance of the meniscus without reaching the surface. This distinction is critical because only surface-communicating signal reliably correlates with a true tear on arthroscopy. Meniscal tear morphology (horizontal, vertical, radial, or complex) further guides surgical planning.
questions.question: An MRI of the knee shows a horizontal high-signal line extending to the articular surface of the meniscus on a T2-weighted sequence. What does this finding indicate?
options: Degenerative intrasubstance signal not reaching the surface
A meniscal tear communicating with the joint surface

questions.question: A CT scan of the abdomen shows gas within the portal venous branches extending to within 2 cm of the liver capsule, together with pneumatosis intestinalis, in a critically unwell patient. What does this combination of findings suggest?
questions.explanation: Portal venous gas combined with pneumatosis intestinalis in a critically unwell patient is a highly concerning combination that most often indicates advanced bowel ischaemia or infarction, though portal gas alone can occasionally be a benign incidental finding after certain procedures. Peripheral extension of gas within 2 cm of the liver capsule is considered a particularly worrying feature. This combination should prompt urgent surgical assessment rather than reassurance.

options: Complete elimination of radiation exposure to the patient
Simultaneous acquisition of two orthogonal projections, reducing the need for repeated contrast injections and procedure time
Improved resolution compared with single-plane systems at equal dose
Automatic correction for patient motion during the procedure
Ability to perform the procedure without any contrast agent
questions.question: A cardiac catheterisation laboratory uses biplane fluoroscopy for a complex congenital heart procedure rather than single-plane fluoroscopy. What is the primary advantage of the biplane system in this context?
questions.explanation: Biplane fluoroscopy acquires two simultaneous orthogonal projections from different angles, allowing three-dimensional spatial understanding of complex catheter and anatomical relationships without needing to reposition the imaging system or repeat contrast injections for each view, which is particularly valuable in complex congenital cardiac catheterisation where precise anatomical delineation is critical. This can reduce total procedure time, contrast volume, and potentially overall radiation dose compared with sequentially acquiring single-plane views from multiple angles. The system does not eliminate radiation exposure, since two simultaneous X-ray beams are still in use during acquisition.

options: Both cortices fractured with complete displacement
Compression of the epiphyseal plate without fracture line
Only one cortex broken with bending of the other
Two fracture lines with a separate bone well-defined segment
Cortical irregularity without an actual fracture line
questions.question: A greenstick fracture in a child is correctly described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture unique to children (whose bones are softer and more pliable) in which only one cortex is disrupted while the opposite cortex bends without fracturing—analogous to bending a green twig. The intact cortex acts as a hinge. A torus (buckle) fracture shows cortical step without a true fracture line. A plastic (bowing) fracture shows bone bending without cortical disruption at all.

Mammography uses a low-energy X-ray beam (typically 25–35 kVp) to maximise contrast differences between soft tissues within the breast. Low-energy X-rays are more readily absorbed by dense glandular tissue than fat, enhancing contrast resolution. High-quality compression and screen-film or digital detectors further improve image quality.
questions.question: Mammography uses which type of X-ray beam to maximise differences in soft tissue density?

questions.explanation: CT density is measured in Hounsfield units (HU), where water is defined as 0 HU, air as -1000 HU, and compact bone at approximately +700 to +3000 HU. Fat is typically -50 to -100 HU, and soft tissues range from +20 to +80 HU. This standardised scale allows objective comparison of tissue densities across different patients and CT scanners.
questions.question: On CT, bony structures appear hyperdense while soft tissues show intermediate density. The CT density of a tissue is measured in which unit?

questions.explanation: Deep inspiration breath-hold increases lung volume and physically displaces the heart away from the chest wall and mediastinal treatment target, increasing the distance between the heart and the high-dose treatment region and thereby reducing cardiac radiation exposure, a technique particularly valuable for left-sided breast cancer and mediastinal lymphoma radiotherapy where cardiac proximity is a significant concern. This represents a specific, evidence-based motion management and positioning strategy rather than simply increasing dose or ignoring respiratory-related anatomical changes. Reducing long-term cardiac toxicity is particularly important in patients with otherwise favourable long-term survival prognosis, such as many lymphoma patients.
options: Increasing the total prescribed dose to compensate for cardiac exposure
Treating the patient in a fully supine position without any breathing instruction
Eliminating respiratory motion management entirely to simplify planning
Using only a single anterior beam without any additional planning technique
Deep inspiration breath-hold technique to increase the distance between the heart and the treatment target
questions.question: A radiotherapy patient with a large mediastinal lymphoma requires treatment while minimising cardiac radiation exposure. Which specific technique is commonly used to reduce heart dose during this type of thoracic treatment?

options: Observation with serial haemoglobin checks only
Urgent interventional radiology for pelvic angioembolisation
Immediate discharge once pain is controlled
questions.explanation: Active contrast extravasation on CT in the setting of a pelvic fracture indicates ongoing arterial haemorrhage, which is best controlled by urgent angioembolisation in a haemodynamically responsive patient, alongside pelvic binder application and resuscitation. Pelvic fractures with major vascular injury carry a high mortality risk if bleeding is not promptly controlled. CT is pivotal in identifying which patients need this time-critical intervention rather than conservative management.
questions.question: A CT scan of the pelvis in a trauma patient shows a large retroperitoneal haematoma with active contrast extravasation adjacent to a comminuted pelvic fracture. What is the most appropriate next step?
Radiotherapy achieves its anticancer effect primarily through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Ionizing radiation damages DNA through direct ionization of DNA molecules and indirect effects via free radical generation. Double-strand breaks are the most lethal form of DNA damage. Cancer cells with impaired DNA repair mechanisms are particularly vulnerable, forming the biological basis of therapeutic radiotherapy.

questions.question: Cancer of the breast affects men at what percentage of the overall breast cancer incidence?
questions.explanation: Male breast cancer accounts for approximately 1% of all breast cancer cases. While rare, it shares many characteristics with female breast cancer, including hormone receptor positivity in most cases. Male breast cancer is more commonly diagnosed at an advanced stage due to lower clinical awareness and absence of routine screening programmes.

questions.question: A chest radiograph in a patient with a tension pneumothorax shows a large area of pleural air. Which additional finding specifically confirms tension rather than a simple pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is distinguished from a simple pneumothorax by the presence of mediastinal shift away from the affected side, along with flattening or inversion of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, reflecting the build-up of positive intrapleural pressure. A simple pneumothorax shows pleural air without this mass effect on adjacent structures. Recognising mediastinal shift is critical because tension pneumothorax requires immediate decompression rather than routine management.
options: A visible lung edge without displacement
Mediastinal shift away from the affected side

questions.question: TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt) in interventional radiology is used to treat which condition?
questions.explanation: TIPS creates a channel between the hepatic vein and intrahepatic portal vein through the liver parenchyma via a jugular vein approach, effectively decompressing the portal circulation. It is used to treat portal hypertension complications: acute variceal haemorrhage refractory to endoscopic treatment, prevention of variceal rebleeding, and refractory ascites in cirrhosis. TIPS reduces portal pressure by shunting blood from the portal to the systemic venous circulation.
options: Hepatic artery stenosis after liver transplantation
Portal hypertension complications including variceal bleeding and refractory ascites
Budd-Chiari syndrome by caval stenting only

questions.question: A radiograph of a long bone lesion shows a purely lytic destructive area with a wide zone of transition, cortical destruction, and an aggressive sunburst periosteal reaction. This appearance is MOST concerning for:
questions.explanation: A wide zone of transition, cortical destruction, and aggressive periosteal reaction such as a sunburst pattern are classic radiological features suggesting an aggressive, malignant bone lesion such as osteosarcoma. Benign lesions like simple bone cysts typically show a narrow, well-defined zone of transition without cortical destruction. Recognising these aggressive features should prompt urgent further imaging and biopsy.
options: A primary malignant bone tumour such as osteosarcoma

questions.question: Which imaging modality is described as the 'gold standard' for assessing soft tissue contrast in the musculoskeletal system?
questions.explanation: MRI is the gold standard for musculoskeletal soft tissue assessment because it provides superior contrast resolution for distinguishing muscle, fat, fluid, tendons, ligaments, and cartilage. It enables direct multiplanar imaging without ionizing radiation. Its main limitation is the signal void produced by cortical bone.

A Colles fracture describes a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation and displacement of the distal fragment, classically resulting from a fall onto an outstretched hand. A Smith fracture instead involves volar displacement and typically results from a fall onto a flexed wrist. Correctly distinguishing the direction of displacement is important because management approaches can differ between these related fracture patterns.
questions.question: A radiograph of a displaced distal radius fracture in an elderly woman shows dorsal angulation and displacement of the distal fragment following a fall onto an outstretched hand. This specific fracture pattern is termed:

questions.explanation: The silhouette sign describes loss of visibility of a normally seen border (heart, diaphragm, aortic knob) when adjacent lung parenchyma is opacified by consolidation or collapse. The sign helps localise pulmonary pathology to specific lobes or segments. Its absence does not exclude disease in overlapping zones.
questions.question: In the silhouette sign on CXR, opacity adjacent to a normally visible cardiac or diaphragmatic border causes:

Linear accelerators (LINACs) for radiotherapy produce x-ray beams in the range of 4–25 MV and electron beams of 4–21 MeV. The key advantage of megavoltage radiotherapy over orthovoltage (250-300 kV) is:
questions.explanation: The skin-sparing effect is the cardinal advantage of megavoltage radiotherapy (from LINACs and cobalt units). Unlike orthovoltage x-rays which deposit maximum dose at the skin surface (causing severe skin reactions), megavoltage beams deposit maximum dose below the skin at a depth proportional to the beam energy (e.g., ~1.5 cm for 6 MV, ~3.5 cm for 15 MV). This allows delivery of high tumour doses while preserving skin integrity and reducing acute skin toxicity.
options: Lower cost and simpler shielding requirements
Complete elimination of scatter radiation within the patient
Skin-sparing effect with maximum dose deposited below the skin surface
Ability to treat only superficial lesions within 5mm depth
It uses higher radiation doses than CT
The patient becomes the radiation source by emitting gamma rays from administered radiopharmaceuticals
It uses magnetic fields rather than radiation
Nuclear medicine can only image bones
questions.explanation: Nuclear medicine is fundamentally different because the patient becomes the source of radiation after receiving a radiopharmaceutical. Gamma rays emitted continuously from within the patient as the radionuclide decays are detected externally by the gamma camera. This provides physiological and functional information about organ metabolism and blood flow. In contrast, CT, fluoroscopy, and plain x-ray use external radiation sources.
questions.question: Nuclear medicine fundamentally differs from other imaging modalities (CT, MRI, ultrasound) primarily because:

questions.explanation: Kerley B lines are short horizontal lines at the lung bases perpendicular to the pleural surface, representing fluid-distended interlobular lymphatics. They are characteristically seen in pulmonary venous hypertension (e.g., left-sided heart failure, mitral stenosis). They indicate lymphatic overload due to elevated pulmonary venous pressure.
options: Pulmonary venous hypertension and engorged lymphatics
Pulmonary arterial hypertension and pruned vessels
questions.question: Kerley B lines on CXR are seen in which condition and represent which pathological finding?

A radiograph of the femoral diaphysis in a child shows a permeative, moth-eaten lytic lesion with a laminated 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction and associated soft tissue mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ewing sarcoma classically arises in the diaphysis of long bones in children and produces a permeative, moth-eaten pattern of bone destruction with a laminated onion-skin periosteal reaction and a large associated soft tissue mass. This diaphyseal predilection contrasts with the metaphyseal location typical of osteosarcoma. Prompt recognition is important given the aggressive nature and need for combined chemotherapy and local control.

Plastic (bowing) fractures are unique to children and represent bone bending beyond its elastic limit without a visible cortical break or fracture line on plain radiographs. The bone undergoes plastic deformation and remains bent (does not spring back). This pattern is most common in the ulna and fibula. It differs from a greenstick fracture (one cortex broken) and a torus fracture (cortical buckling without frank fracture line).
questions.question: Which fracture pattern in children occurs exclusively due to the softer, more flexible nature of paediatric bone and involves bending without any cortical disruption?

options: Any size tumour without node involvement
questions.explanation: T0 in the TNM staging system indicates no evidence of primary tumour, used when the primary site cannot be identified or the tumour has completely responded to treatment. It differs from Tx (primary tumour cannot be assessed) and Tis (carcinoma in situ). T0 N+ staging suggests an occult primary with lymph node metastases.
questions.question: In the TNM staging system, what does 'T0' specifically signify?

A plain film of the pelvis in an 18-month-old shows the right femoral epiphysis in normal position within the acetabulum, but the left femoral epiphysis is smaller and displaced upwards and laterally. This is consistent with:
questions.explanation: Congenital dislocation of the hip (CDH/developmental dysplasia of the hip) classically presents on plain film with a smaller, displaced femoral epiphysis lying upwards and laterally outside the acetabulum. In this 18-month-old, the asymmetric epiphyseal size (abnormal side smaller due to altered stress forces) and lateral-superior displacement are characteristic. Early diagnosis is critical as untreated CDH leads to progressive degenerative hip disease.
options: Perthes disease of the left hip
Septic arthritis of the left hip
Congenital dislocation of the left hip
Replacing the need for a planning CT scan entirely
Reducing the total number of treatment fractions required to zero
Increasing the total prescribed dose to the prostate itself
Increasing the physical distance between the prostate and rectal wall, allowing reduced rectal radiation dose
Eliminating the need for any daily image-guided verification
questions.question: A radiotherapy planning target volume for a prostate cancer patient is expanded asymmetrically, with a larger posterior margin reduced compared with other directions, reflecting the use of a rectal spacer device. What is the primary purpose of inserting a rectal spacer before treatment planning?
questions.explanation: A rectal spacer, typically an injectable hydrogel placed between the prostate and rectum before planning imaging, increases the physical separation between these two structures, allowing the high-dose radiotherapy volume to more effectively spare the rectal wall and reduce the risk of rectal toxicity such as proctitis, while still delivering an adequate dose to the prostate target. This anatomical modification is reflected in the planning process through altered target and organ-at-risk geometry rather than simply adjusting dose or fractionation numbers. The spacer typically remains in place for the duration of treatment and gradually resorbs afterward.

5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is a pyrimidine analogue that inhibits thymidylate synthase, blocking DNA synthesis. It is widely used in colorectal, gastric, and head and neck cancers. Capecitabine is an oral prodrug of 5-FU providing similar activity with added convenience.
questions.question: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) belongs to which class of antimetabolites?

questions.explanation: Segmental bowel wall thickening with a target or double-halo appearance, reflecting submucosal oedema between enhancing mucosal and serosal layers, is a characteristic although non-specific finding of ischaemic colitis, often affecting watershed areas of the colon.
