questions.question: In radiotherapy, the term 'organ motion' refers to the movement of internal structures such as the lungs or bladder during treatment. Which imaging-based technique is commonly used to account for respiratory motion when treating lung tumours?
questions.explanation: Four-dimensional CT acquires imaging data correlated with the respiratory cycle, allowing visualisation of tumour and organ motion throughout breathing and enabling more accurate definition of an internal target volume that accounts for this movement, or techniques such as gating and breath-hold to reduce its impact. Standard single-phase CT captures only a snapshot at one point in the breathing cycle and can significantly underestimate or misrepresent true tumour motion. Managing respiratory motion is particularly important for thoracic and upper abdominal tumours where movement can be substantial.

options: The depth of penetration difference between the two beam types
The cost difference between proton and photon therapy
The ratio of biological effect produced by a given physical dose of one radiation type compared with a reference radiation type
The treatment time difference between the two modalities
The total physical dose delivered in Gray by each modality
questions.question: A radiotherapy physicist calculates the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) when comparing proton beam therapy with conventional photon therapy for the same physical dose. What does RBE quantify in this context?
questions.explanation: Relative biological effectiveness compares the biological effect produced by an equal physical dose of a test radiation, such as protons, against a reference radiation, typically conventional photon (X-ray) therapy, reflecting the fact that different radiation types with the same physical dose in Gray can produce different degrees of biological damage due to differences in their pattern of energy deposition, related to linear energy transfer. Proton therapy has an RBE modestly higher than photons (commonly assumed as approximately 1.1), meaning a slightly lower physical proton dose can achieve an equivalent biological effect. This concept is distinct from simple physical dose comparison and is essential when converting between different radiation modalities in treatment planning and prescription.

questions.question: A percutaneous vertebroplasty is performed for a painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture, involving injection of bone cement into the vertebral body under fluoroscopic guidance. What is the primary therapeutic goal of this procedure?
options: Stabilisation of the fractured vertebra and reduction of pain
Complete restoration of original vertebral body height in all cases
Decompression of the spinal cord directly
Treatment of the underlying osteoporosis itself
Fusion of adjacent vertebral levels together
questions.explanation: Vertebroplasty involves percutaneous injection of bone cement directly into a fractured vertebral body to provide mechanical stabilisation and pain relief, though it does not typically restore significant vertebral height, which distinguishes it from balloon kyphoplasty that attempts partial height restoration before cement injection. It addresses the mechanical consequences of the fracture rather than treating the underlying osteoporosis, which requires separate medical management. Real-time fluoroscopic guidance is essential throughout cement injection to monitor for cement leakage into the spinal canal or venous system, a recognised complication of the procedure.

questions.question: Which acquired phenotype allows cancer clones to evade the immune system and expand?
questions.explanation: Acquiring the ability to avoid immune destruction enables malignant clones to persist despite immune surveillance. Tumour cells downregulate immunogenic markers and recruit immunosuppressive cells into the tumour microenvironment. This is the rationale behind immunotherapy approaches such as PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade.

The anode heel effect describes the reduction of x-ray beam intensity toward the anode end, caused by attenuation of emerging x-rays within the anode material itself. The steeper the anode angle, the more pronounced this effect. Clinically, thicker body parts are placed under the cathode side where intensity is greater.
questions.question: A radiologist notices that the x-ray beam intensity is significantly lower on the anode side of the field compared to the cathode side. This observation BEST describes which physical phenomenon?

A CT-guided lung biopsy is performed for a suspicious pulmonary nodule. Following the procedure, the patient develops sudden breathlessness, and a repeat CT shows a new area of lucency around the lung with partial lung collapse. What complication has occurred?
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is the most common complication of percutaneous lung biopsy, resulting from inadvertent puncture of the visceral pleura during needle passage through aerated lung tissue, and presents with new lucency and lung collapse on post-procedure imaging correlating with breathlessness. Management ranges from observation for a small, stable pneumothorax to chest drain insertion for larger or symptomatic cases. Recognising this common and generally manageable complication promptly is an essential part of post-biopsy patient monitoring.
options: Air embolism into the systemic circulation

questions.question: Which feature of a breast lump is characteristically associated with malignancy rather than benign disease?
questions.explanation: A painless, hard, irregular breast lump with indistinct borders is the classic presentation of breast carcinoma. In contrast, fibroadenomas are smooth, mobile, and well-defined, while cysts are smooth and may be tender. The observation that most breast problems (9 out of 10) are benign should not diminish clinical vigilance for malignant features.
options: Smooth mobile lump in a young woman

questions.question: A CT scan of the head in a patient with reduced consciousness after cardiac arrest shows loss of grey-white differentiation with diffuse cerebral swelling and effacement of the basal cisterns. What does this finding indicate?
questions.explanation: Diffuse loss of grey-white matter differentiation with global cerebral swelling and effacement of the basal cisterns after cardiac arrest reflects widespread hypoxic-ischaemic injury from global cerebral hypoperfusion, a pattern with grave prognostic implications. This diffuse pattern differs from the focal, territorial distribution seen with a single vessel occlusion causing stroke. Recognising these features assists in prognostication discussions with families in the intensive care setting.

questions.question: A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis in a young woman with sudden severe pelvic pain shows an enlarged ovary with peripherally displaced follicles and absent or reduced blood flow on Doppler assessment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ovarian torsion classically produces an enlarged ovary with oedematous stroma displacing follicles to the periphery, and reduced or absent venous and later arterial flow on Doppler ultrasound as the vascular pedicle twists. Normal arterial flow does not entirely exclude torsion, particularly with a dual blood supply, but its absence strongly supports the diagnosis and mandates urgent surgical detorsion to preserve ovarian viability. Rapid recognition is critical because delayed treatment risks irreversible ovarian necrosis.

options: Greater depth penetration and lower resolution
Less depth penetration and higher resolution
Less depth penetration and lower resolution
Greater depth penetration and higher resolution
Identical depth penetration but higher resolution
questions.question: An ultrasound probe with a higher frequency (e.g., 12 MHz versus 3.5 MHz) has which combination of properties?
questions.explanation: Higher frequency ultrasound probes produce shorter wavelengths, which provide better spatial resolution (axial resolution is approximately equal to half the wavelength). However, higher frequency waves are more rapidly attenuated in tissue, resulting in shallower penetration depth. The 12 MHz probe is used for superficial structures (thyroid, testes, breast, vascular access), while 3.5 MHz probes are used for deep abdominal imaging.

questions.question: In the evaluation of infertility by HSG, a filling defect within the uterine cavity that is smooth and well-defined is most likely to represent:
questions.explanation: On HSG, a smooth, well-defined filling defect within the uterine cavity is most consistent with a submucosal fibroid (causing a rounded filling defect that distorts the uterine cavity) or an endometrial polyp (a smooth pedunculated lesion). Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) produce irregular, angular filling defects or multiple defects with irregular cavity borders. Uterine anomalies (bicornuate, septate) are detected by the characteristic shape of the cavity, not filling defects.

The double density sign on PA CXR represents two overlapping shadows at the right cardiac border, formed by the enlarged left atrium projecting behind the right atrium. This is pathognomonic for left atrial enlargement. It appears as two distinct right heart border densities at the right cardiophrenic angle. It is classically associated with mitral stenosis.
questions.question: On CXR, the 'double density' sign is pathognomonic for which chamber enlargement?

options: Proceed to urgent CT or laparotomy depending on stability
Repeat the FAST scan in 24 hours
questions.explanation: Free fluid in Morrison's pouch on FAST in a hypotensive trauma patient strongly suggests haemoperitoneum, most often from splenic or hepatic injury, and demands urgent action rather than delay. A haemodynamically unstable patient with a positive FAST should proceed directly to laparotomy, while a stable patient typically undergoes CT for further characterisation and grading. FAST is a rapid triage tool, not a definitive diagnostic study, so its result must always be interpreted alongside clinical stability.
questions.question: A FAST ultrasound scan in a hypotensive trauma patient shows anechoic fluid in Morrison's pouch. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options: Mediastinal shift away from the injury
questions.question: A patient presents with dyspnoea after a gunshot wound to the left chest. Chest radiograph shows a hydropneumothorax on the left. Which finding on this film confirms the presence of both air and fluid simultaneously?
questions.explanation: A hydropneumothorax (air and fluid in the pleural space) characteristically produces a straight horizontal fluid level on an erect chest radiograph—distinguishable from simple pleural effusion (which has a meniscus/curved upper border) because the presence of air above the fluid creates a flat air-fluid interface (gravity-dependent fluid with non-dependent air). The lucent (dark) area above the fluid level represents the pneumothorax component, and the opaque area below represents the haemothorax or effusion.

questions.question: Pulmonary angiography is primarily indicated for evaluating which condition when CT pulmonary angiography is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Invasive pulmonary angiography remains the historical gold standard for pulmonary embolism diagnosis, involving catheterization of the pulmonary arteries and injection of contrast under fluoroscopic guidance. It is now largely replaced by CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) but remains an option when CTPA is contraindicated (e.g., contrast allergy with severe renal impairment). It also enables therapeutic intervention.

questions.question: On a plain abdominal radiograph, the normal small bowel diameter should not exceed which measurement?
questions.explanation: The normal small bowel on plain abdominal radiograph should not exceed 3cm in diameter. Values greater than 3cm suggest abnormal small bowel dilatation. The 3-6-9 rule helps remember bowel diameter limits: small bowel =3cm, large bowel =6cm (cecum up to 9cm). These thresholds guide the distinction between normal and pathologically dilated bowel in suspected obstruction or ileus, though clinical context always informs interpretation of borderline values.

questions.question: Interventional Radiology (IR) is defined as minimally invasive, image-guided diagnosis and treatment. The colloquial term used for IR procedures because they start with passing a needle through the skin is:
questions.explanation: Interventional Radiology procedures are often described as 'pinhole surgery' because all IR procedures begin with passing a needle through a small puncture in the skin to reach the target organ or vessel. This distinguishes IR from open surgery and conventional laparoscopy, as the access site is as small as a needle puncture, minimising trauma, reducing hospital stay, and enabling faster recovery.

questions.question: Double contrast barium enema is preferred over single contrast for detecting which colonic pathology?
questions.explanation: Double contrast barium enema (DCBE), using barium plus air, provides superior mucosal detail compared to single contrast and is significantly more sensitive for detecting small polyps and early carcinomas. The thin barium coating outlines mucosal surface projections (polyps appear as filling defects or sessile densities), while air distension opens the lumen. Single contrast is more useful for demonstrating large obstructing lesions or intussusception.

questions.question: Which CT finding on a non-contrast scan is MOST consistent with an acute extradural haematoma?
questions.explanation: An acute extradural (epidural) haematoma appears as a hyperdense (bright white) biconvex (lens-shaped) collection between the inner surface of the cranium and the outer dural membrane on non-contrast CT. It is most commonly due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery from temporal bone fracture. The biconvex shape distinguishes it from the crescent-shaped subdural haematoma.
options: Hyperdense biconvex collection between the cranium and dura
Hypodense biconvex collection between the cranium and dura
Hypodense lenticular collection spanning the midline

questions.explanation: Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound requires a full urinary bladder as an acoustic window to displace gas-containing small bowel loops out of the pelvis and to visualise the uterus, ovaries, and adnexae clearly. Without a full bladder, bowel gas obscures the pelvic organs and renders the examination non-diagnostic. Transvaginal ultrasound, conversely, requires an empty bladder because proximity of the endovaginal probe to the pelvic organs provides superior resolution without needing the bladder window.
questions.question: On ultrasound assessment of the abdomen, which organ is specifically described as requiring a full bladder for adequate transabdominal visualisation?
Pulmonary tuberculosis most commonly affects which zone of the lung on CXR?
questions.explanation: Post-primary (reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis classically affects the upper zones and upper portions of the lower lobes, where higher oxygen tension favours Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth. Typical features include consolidation, cavitation, fibrosis, and calcification. Lower lobe TB is less common but does occur, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

questions.question: A patient undergoing MRI reports a warm, tingling sensation along a looped ECG lead resting against their skin during the scan. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Conductive loops formed by cables or leads in contact with the skin can act as antennae for the radiofrequency energy used during MRI, inducing electrical currents that generate localised heating and potential burns at the point of skin contact. Proper cable positioning, avoiding loops, and using appropriate padding are essential safety measures to prevent this complication. This differs from attraction-based projectile injuries, which relate to the static magnetic field acting on ferromagnetic objects rather than induced currents in conductors.
options: Induced electrical currents in the conductive loop causing localised heating
Static magnetic field attraction of the lead

questions.question: A chest radiograph of a patient with a chronic cough shows tram-track and signet-ring opacities in the lower lobes. This is most consistent with which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis produces dilated, thick-walled bronchi that appear as parallel tram-track lines when imaged longitudinally and as signet-ring shadows (dilated bronchus beside its smaller accompanying vessel) when imaged in cross-section. These findings reflect irreversible airway dilatation from chronic infection or inflammation. CT is far more sensitive than plain film for confirming the diagnosis.

An extradural haematoma classically appears biconvex (lentiform) because bleeding is confined between the skull and the tightly adherent dura at suture lines, most often from injury to the middle meningeal artery following a temporal bone fracture. Its inability to cross suture lines distinguishes it from a subdural haematoma, which is crescentic and can cross sutures freely. Rapid recognition is critical because of the risk of rapid neurological deterioration from arterial bleeding.
questions.question: A non-contrast CT of the head shows a biconvex, lens-shaped hyperdense collection that does not cross suture lines, associated with an overlying skull fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Certain chemotherapy agents, such as platinum-based drugs commonly used with cervical cancer radiotherapy, act as radiosensitisers, enhancing the cytotoxic effect of radiation on tumour cells when administered concurrently, which has been shown in clinical trials to improve tumour control and survival outcomes compared with radiotherapy alone in appropriately selected patients. This combined approach typically increases overall treatment toxicity compared with either modality used alone, reflecting the trade-off made in pursuit of improved oncological outcomes for locally advanced disease. The radiobiological synergy achieved through appropriately timed concurrent administration is central to the rationale for this now widely adopted standard treatment approach.
questions.question: A radiotherapy patient with locally advanced cervical cancer receives concurrent chemotherapy alongside external beam radiotherapy. What is the primary radiobiological rationale for combining these two treatment modalities simultaneously rather than sequentially?
options: Elimination of the need for image guidance during radiotherapy delivery
Radiosensitisation of tumour cells by the chemotherapy agent, enhancing the effectiveness of radiation-induced cell kill
Complete avoidance of any additional treatment toxicity compared with either modality alone
Reduction of the total number of radiotherapy fractions to just one
Reduction of the total radiotherapy dose required to achieve tumour control

questions.question: A lateral neck radiograph in a child with stridor and a barking cough shows subglottic narrowing on the frontal view described as the steeple sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The steeple sign describes symmetric subglottic narrowing on the frontal neck radiograph caused by mucosal oedema in viral croup, correlating with the classic barking cough and inspiratory stridor. This differs from the epiglottic thumbprint sign of epiglottitis, which is a more acute airway emergency. Croup is generally managed supportively with nebulised adrenaline and corticosteroids rather than urgent airway intervention.
options: Foreign body lodged in the trachea

questions.explanation: Tumour markers such as alpha-fetoprotein are primarily useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence over time, since a rising or falling trend correlates with disease activity. They are not generally used as a stand-alone diagnostic test replacing histological confirmation, nor are they validated for general population screening in most contexts. Serial measurement over time provides more clinically useful information than a single isolated value.
options: Providing a definitive stand-alone diagnosis without biopsy
Replacing the need for any imaging follow-up
Screening asymptomatic men in the general population
Determining the exact histological subtype alone
Monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence
questions.question: A man with a testicular mass is found to have markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein. This tumour marker is MOST useful clinically for which purpose in his subsequent management?

questions.explanation: Middle lobe collapse is best seen on the lateral view as a triangular opacity anteriorly, as the lobe collapses downward and medially. On the PA view, there is increased density lateral to the right heart border with blurring of its outline. The middle lobe is relatively small, making collapse subtle on PA.
questions.question: On CXR, the middle lobe collapse is best characterised by which appearance on the lateral view?

questions.explanation: A wedge-shaped, pleural-based opacity (Hampton's hump) associated with a filling defect on CT pulmonary angiography strongly suggests infarction distal to an embolic occlusion. Pneumonia does not typically show an associated vascular filling defect. The combination of parenchymal and vascular findings is key to this diagnosis.
questions.question: A chest CT in a patient with acute pleuritic chest pain shows a peripheral, wedge-shaped area of consolidation abutting the pleura, associated with a filling defect in a segmental pulmonary artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: The maximum minus minimum voltage per cycle, expressed as a percentage of maximum voltage
The variation in x-ray beam intensity across the field (heel effect)
The scatter-to-primary radiation ratio at the detector
The modulation transfer function of the imaging system
Variation in mA output during an exposure
questions.explanation: Waveform ripple is defined as (Vmax - Vmin)/Vmax × 100%, expressed as a percentage. A high ripple means the voltage across the x-ray tube varies greatly during each cycle, producing a wider spread of photon energies. A low ripple (approaching 0%) produces a near-constant voltage, creating a more uniform, higher-quality x-ray beam. High-frequency generators achieve near-zero ripple.
questions.question: X-ray beam waveform ripple is defined as:
In trauma to the spine causing cord injury, the clinical finding of 'spinal shock' with complete motor and sensory loss below the level of the injury is best evaluated by which modality?
questions.explanation: MRI of the spine is the definitive investigation for spinal cord injury because it directly visualises the cord parenchyma, detecting cord contusion (intramedullary signal change), oedema, haemorrhage within the cord (haematomyelia), epidural haematoma, disc prolapse, and ligamentous injury—none of which are visible on CT or plain radiography. The extent, level, and severity of cord signal changes on MRI predict neurological outcome and guide surgical decision-making. T2-weighted sequences are most sensitive for cord oedema.

questions.question: In the spinal column, which imaging modality is specifically indicated for evaluating spinal cord injury following vertebral fracture?
questions.explanation: MRI is the gold standard for evaluating spinal cord injury because it directly visualises the cord, its signal characteristics, contusion, oedema, haemorrhage, and epidural haematoma. CT is excellent for defining bony injury and fragment location but cannot visualise cord signal abnormalities. While myelography was historically used, it has been almost entirely replaced by MRI, which is non-invasive, provides superior cord detail, and guides surgical decision-making in cord injury.

questions.question: In the endocrine system, which imaging modality is specifically described as the primary investigation for evaluating adnexal masses and providing the most accurate preoperative assessment?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is the primary investigation for evaluating adnexal masses, providing initial characterisation (simple cyst vs. complex/solid), detection of ascites, and assessment of size and laterality. For complex masses with solid components, internal vascularity, or clinical suspicion of malignancy, CT provides staging information (peritoneal deposits, lymphadenopathy, distant metastases), while MRI offers superior tissue characterisation (fat content, haemorrhagic components, stromal detail) for specific tumour types. This sequential imaging approach optimises preoperative planning.

questions.question: A stepwise approach to cancer control planning means interventions should be based on which principle?
questions.explanation: The stepwise approach principle calls for planning and implementing cancer control interventions based on local considerations, needs, and available resources. It acknowledges that high-income country models may not be directly applicable to resource-limited settings. Incremental implementation aligned with local capacity ensures sustainable cancer control.

questions.question: Micturating cystourethrography (MCUG) is the investigation of choice for which specific urological condition in children?
questions.explanation: Micturating cystourethrography (MCUG) is the gold-standard investigation for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR), demonstrating the retrograde flow of contrast from the bladder up the ureter and into the pelvicalyceal system during micturition or bladder filling. VUR is graded I-V (severity). It is a common cause of recurrent urinary tract infections and pyelonephritis in children, and its early detection and management prevents renal scarring (reflux nephropathy) and long-term renal damage.

options: High spatial resolution of coronary arteries
Assessment of structure and function without radiation
questions.question: Echocardiography is reported as the second most common cardiac imaging examination. What is its primary advantage?
questions.explanation: Echocardiography (ECHO) is the second most common cardiac imaging examination after CXR and approaches ECG in clinical utility. It assesses both structural and functional cardiac abnormalities in real-time without ionizing radiation. It is highly operator-dependent and has multiple modalities including 2D, M-mode, and Doppler.

options: Reduced spatial resolution from increased geometric unsharpness
Increased scattered radiation reaching the detector
questions.explanation: A broad focal spot allows higher tube loading (greater heat capacity) because the electron beam is spread over a larger anode area, but this comes at the cost of increased geometric unsharpness (penumbra) at the edges of anatomical structures, reducing spatial resolution. A fine focal spot instead improves resolution but has lower heat tolerance, limiting achievable mA for a given exposure time. Selecting the appropriate focal spot size balances image sharpness against the practical thermal limitations of the tube.
questions.question: A radiographer notices that increasing the focal spot size from fine to broad allows for higher tube current without exceeding the heat rating of the anode. What is the trade-off of using the broad focal spot?

questions.explanation: Watershed (borderzone) infarction occurs at the junctions between the territories of the major cerebral arteries (ACA/MCA borderzone and MCA/PCA borderzone) due to global cerebral hypoperfusion. These 'border zones' are the most distal territories of each major artery and are most vulnerable when perfusion pressure falls (e.g., cardiac arrest, severe hypotension, carotid occlusion). They appear as linear or 'string of beads' infarction pattern on MRI, distinct from embolic or thrombotic MCA territory infarction.
questions.question: In neuroradiology, the 'watershed (borderzone) infarction' pattern on MRI occurs in which clinical scenario?
options: Embolic occlusion of the proximal MCA
Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage in the basal ganglia
Venous sinus thrombosis causing cortical venous infarction
Severe global cerebral hypoperfusion (hypotension, cardiac arrest) causing infarction at the junctions of major vascular territories
Amyloid angiopathy causing lobar haemorrhages in the elderly
Normal-sized heart with roughened pericardial outline
questions.explanation: Constrictive pericarditis shows a normal or non-massively enlarged heart with roughening of the cardiac outline due to pericardial calcification. This contrasts with pericardial effusion, which produces massive globular enlargement with clear lung fields. Calcification of the pericardium may be visible on lateral CXR.
questions.question: In constrictive pericarditis, the CXR typically shows which finding?

questions.explanation: Achondroplasia produces short-limbed dwarfism (rhizomelic pattern—proximal limbs shorter than distal) with short tubular bones, thickened muscular insertions, and a characteristic inverted-V or chevron-shaped (V-shaped) deformity of the epiphyseal-metaphyseal junctions. The skull shows large calvarium with small skull base, and the lumbar spine shows decreasing interpedicular distances (caudal narrowing), predisposing to spinal stenosis.
options: Ground glass appearance of medullary cavity
Expanded medullary cavity with thinned cortex
questions.question: Achondroplasia is a congenital skeletal dysplasia characterised on radiographs by which distinctive epiphyseal-metaphyseal finding?
The breast nipple normally overlies which intercostal space in the non-pendulous breast?
questions.explanation: The nipple normally overlies the 4th intercostal space in the non-pendulous breast. This is an important anatomical landmark for clinical breast examination, mammographic positioning, and surgical orientation. Knowledge of normal breast surface anatomy is essential for accurately localising breast lesions detected on imaging or clinical examination.

options: Plain radiographs of all body parts
questions.question: In emergency radiology, which imaging modality provides the most comprehensive assessment of a haemodynamically stable multiple trauma patient?
questions.explanation: Whole-body CT (trauma pan-scan—head, cervical spine, chest, abdomen, pelvis with intravenous contrast) is the most comprehensive initial assessment in haemodynamically stable major trauma patients. It rapidly detects all life-threatening injuries (intracranial haemorrhage, aortic injury, pneumothorax, haemoperitoneum, solid organ laceration, bony fractures) simultaneously in a single examination. CT-based trauma protocols have been shown to significantly reduce missed injuries and improve survival outcomes compared to selective imaging based solely on clinical findings.

Pulmonary hamartoma appears as a well-defined, lobulated opacity usually less than 4cm. Calcification, sometimes in a 'popcorn' pattern, may occur in larger lesions. It is an uncommon benign tumour composed of cartilage, fat, and epithelium. Serial imaging typically shows very slow or no growth.
questions.question: Which pulmonary opacity characteristically shows calcification, lobulation, and is usually less than 4cm?
A patient receiving vincristine for lymphoma develops progressive numbness and tingling in his fingers and toes after several cycles. This dose-limiting toxicity is:
questions.explanation: Vinca alkaloids such as vincristine characteristically cause a cumulative, dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy through disruption of microtubule function in neuronal axons. This differs from the cardiotoxicity seen with anthracyclines, reflecting the distinct mechanism and tissue vulnerability of each drug class. Dose adjustment or discontinuation may be required if neuropathy becomes severe.

questions.question: The focal spot of an x-ray tube exhibits 'blooming.' Which parameter change DIRECTLY causes this enlargement of the focal spot?
questions.explanation: Blooming refers to the enlargement of the focal spot that occurs as the milliampere (mA) setting increases. At higher mA, more electrons are produced, and the repulsion between adjacent electrons widens the electron beam striking the anode target. This increases the actual focal spot size and can reduce spatial resolution.

questions.question: A patient with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer taking tamoxifen asks how the drug controls her cancer. Which explanation is MOST accurate?
options: It reduces peripheral oestrogen production entirely
It directly damages tumour cell DNA
It stimulates programmed tumour cell differentiation
It competitively blocks oestrogen from binding to its receptor on tumour cells
It works only in postmenopausal women
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen acts as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, competitively blocking oestrogen from binding to its receptor on hormone-sensitive tumour cells, rather than reducing overall oestrogen production. This mechanism differs from aromatase inhibitors, which lower oestrogen synthesis rather than blocking the receptor directly. Tamoxifen is effective in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women, unlike aromatase inhibitors.

options: Air-fluid levels in dilated small bowel loops
Air under the diaphragm (free subdiaphragmatic air)
Gas within the bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis)
Air in the portal venous system
questions.question: In assessing a plain abdominal radiograph for free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum) on an erect film, which classic radiological sign is looked for?
questions.explanation: Free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum) in an erect patient rises to the highest point of the peritoneal cavity and collects under the diaphragm (subdiaphragmatic air), appearing as a crescent of radiolucency (gas density) between the liver/spleen and the diaphragm on an erect chest or abdominal radiograph. This is the most reliable sign of visceral perforation (peptic ulcer, perforated hollow viscus). Rigler's sign (gas on both sides of bowel wall) is seen on supine films.

options: Large bowel volvulus of the cecum
questions.question: A plain abdominal radiograph shows a large air-filled viscus in the pelvis, shaped like a 'coffee bean' or 'bent inner tube.' This is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Sigmoid volvulus produces a characteristic massive dilatation of the sigmoid colon with a 'coffee bean' or 'bent inner tube' appearance on plain abdominal radiograph due to twisting of the sigmoid at its mesenteric attachment. The two limbs of the distended sigmoid appear as a large inverted U-shaped opacity that may extend to the right upper quadrant. The 'coffee bean' appearance reflects the two parallel walls meeting at the point of torsion. It is the commonest cause of large bowel volvulus.

questions.question: A patient with lung cancer presents with facial swelling, distended neck veins, and headache that worsens on bending forward. This presentation is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: Facial and neck swelling with distended neck veins and postural headache are classic features of superior vena cava obstruction, typically caused by direct tumour compression or invasion of the superior vena cava, often from lung cancer or lymphoma. This differs from spinal cord compression, which presents with limb weakness and sphincter disturbance rather than facial swelling. Prompt recognition allows urgent imaging and treatment to relieve the obstruction.

Electron beam catheters are not used for tumour ablation in interventional radiology. IR tumour ablation techniques include radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MWA), cryoablation (freeze-thaw cycles), and chemical ablation with ethanol or acetic acid. Laser ablation and irreversible electroporation (IRE/NanoKnife) are also used. These techniques are applied percutaneously under CT or ultrasound guidance for liver, renal, lung, and bone metastases.
questions.question: Tumour ablation probes used in IR to destroy tumours include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: The markedly hyperechoic (bright) ultrasound appearance of adrenal myelolipoma is due to its abundant mature adipose (fat) tissue content. Fat reflects sound waves very effectively, producing strong echoes and appearing significantly brighter than the surrounding soft tissues and liver. This macroscopic fat content is also identifiable on CT as areas of negative HU (fat density, typically -80 to -120 HU) and on MRI using fat-suppressed sequences (fat signal disappears on fat-saturated T1W images).
questions.question: A myelolipoma of the adrenal gland on ultrasound appears markedly hyperechoic (bright) compared to the liver. What tissue within the tumour accounts for this appearance?

questions.explanation: Fluid loculated within an interlobar fissure (pseudotumour) can mimic a pulmonary mass on CXR due to its oval or lens-shaped opacity. It is commonly seen in cardiac failure and resolves with treatment, earning the name 'vanishing tumour.' Lateral CXR confirming the fissural location is diagnostic and prevents unnecessary invasive workup.
questions.question: Loculated pleural effusion in a fissure may mimic which radiological appearance?

questions.explanation: Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall) in an adult is an ominous sign most commonly associated with bowel ischaemia/infarction, where gas-producing bacteria enter the necrotic bowel wall. It may also occur in necrotising enterocolitis (neonates), bowel obstruction with strangulation, and occasionally as a benign incidental finding (pneumatosis coli—usually benign). In a symptomatic adult, it mandates urgent CT to assess for concurrent portal venous gas and mesenteric ischaemia.
questions.question: On the abdominal radiograph, the presence of air within the bowel wall itself (not within the lumen) is called pneumatosis intestinalis. In an adult, this finding is associated with which of the following conditions?

questions.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus produces ventricular enlargement disproportionate to the degree of cortical sulcal atrophy, classically associated with the clinical triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline, and often improves after cerebrospinal fluid diversion. This contrasts with Alzheimer disease, where ventricular enlargement is generally proportionate to diffuse cortical atrophy, particularly involving the medial temporal lobes. Recognising the disproportionate ventriculomegaly pattern is important because, unlike most dementias, this condition may be at least partially reversible with shunting.
options: Chronic small vessel ischaemic disease alone
questions.question: An MRI of the brain in a patient with progressive gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline shows ventricular enlargement out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, with a normal appearance of the aqueduct. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: MRI guidance is faster and less expensive
MRI needles are cheaper than CT-compatible needles
MRI can detect all types of metal implants safely
MRI provides superior tissue contrast without ionising radiation
MRI guidance requires no patient preparation
questions.question: The primary advantage of MRI guidance in interventional procedures compared to CT or fluoroscopy is:
questions.explanation: MRI-guided interventional procedures offer superior soft tissue contrast without any ionising radiation exposure, making them ideal for procedures near radiation-sensitive structures or in patients requiring repeated procedures. The trade-off is the requirement for expensive MRI-compatible instruments that do not interact with the magnetic field, longer procedure times, and limited availability of interventional MRI suites.

Radiotherapy employs external beam radiation and brachytherapy (internal radiation sources) as primary delivery methods. External beam radiation is delivered by linear accelerators, while brachytherapy places radioactive sources directly within or adjacent to tumours. Both exploit DNA damage as the primary mechanism of tumour cell killing.
questions.question: The sources of radiation used in radiotherapy include which of the following?
On ultrasound, a simple ovarian cyst demonstrates which of the following characteristic features?
questions.explanation: A simple ovarian cyst on ultrasound is characterised by: (1) anechoic (echo-free, dark) interior with no internal echoes, (2) a thin smooth wall without nodules or septations, and (3) acoustic enhancement (increased brightness posterior to the cyst). These features indicate a simple, benign, fluid-filled cyst. Functional follicular cysts are usually less than 6 cm and resolve on follow-up. Any cyst with solid elements, thick septations, or internal vascularity on Doppler should be considered potentially malignant.
options: Thick irregular wall with internal solid well-defined nodules
Anechoic interior with thin wall and acoustic enhancement

questions.explanation: Communicating hydrocephalus results from impaired cerebrospinal fluid resorption at the arachnoid granulations rather than an intraventricular obstruction, producing symmetric dilatation of all four ventricles including the fourth. Obstructive causes, such as aqueductal stenosis, instead dilate only the ventricles proximal to the block, sparing the fourth ventricle. Identifying which ventricles are involved helps localise the site of the underlying problem.
questions.question: A CT scan of the head in a neonate with an enlarging head circumference shows symmetric dilatation of all four ventricles without a clearly identifiable obstructing lesion. What type of hydrocephalus does this most likely represent?

questions.explanation: The zone of transition on plain radiography describes the interface between a bone lesion and normal bone. A narrow, well-defined sclerotic border indicates a slowly growing benign process (bone has time to create a sclerotic margin). A wide, ill-defined zone of transition, as seen in osteosarcoma and aggressive malignancies, indicates rapid growth where tumour advances faster than the bone can form a reactive margin—a key discriminator of aggressive behaviour.
questions.question: In the evaluation of a bone lesion on plain radiograph, a 'wide zone of transition' between the lesion and normal bone is most suggestive of which type of process?

questions.explanation: Pelvic radiotherapy for gynaecological cancers (cervix, endometrium, vulva) irradiates adjacent structures in the pelvis. Acute radiation side effects in the pelvis include radiation proctitis/diarrhoea (from rectal irradiation), radiation cystitis (from bladder irradiation), and skin erythema/desquamation in the perineal and groin areas. Alopecia occurs with cranial irradiation; pneumonitis with lung/thoracic irradiation; and hepatitis with upper abdominal radiotherapy.
questions.question: Which acute radiation side effect is expected in patients receiving pelvic radiotherapy for gynaecological cancer?
options: Acute radiation diarrhoea, cystitis, and skin erythema in the perineal area

questions.explanation: Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and cisplatin form covalent bonds with DNA, causing crosslinks and strand breaks that impair replication and transcription. This leads to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. They are among the oldest and most widely used chemotherapy drug classes.
questions.question: Alkylating agents in chemotherapy cause cell death primarily through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: The standard FAST examination consists of four views: cardiac (pericardial), right upper quadrant (hepatorenal—Morrison's pouch), left upper quadrant (splenorenal), and suprapubic (pelvic). These four views specifically evaluate for free fluid (blood) in the pericardium and peritoneum. The left lower quadrant is not a standard FAST view. Extended-FAST (eFAST) adds bilateral chest views for pneumothorax.
questions.question: The FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) examination evaluates four views. Which of the following is NOT one of the standard FAST views?

questions.explanation: Technetium-99m emits gamma photons at approximately 140 keV, an energy that is efficiently detected by standard gamma camera crystals while still penetrating tissue adequately to reach external detectors, combined with a convenient physical half-life of about six hours that limits patient radiation dose while allowing sufficient time for imaging. Its predominantly pure gamma emission, without significant particulate radiation, minimises unnecessary radiation dose to the patient compared with isotopes that also emit beta or alpha particles. These properties collectively make it the most widely used radioisotope in diagnostic nuclear medicine.
options: Emission of alpha particles for high linear energy transfer
Complete absence of any radioactive decay
A very long physical half-life exceeding several years
A gamma photon energy of approximately 140 keV, well matched to gamma camera detectors
Emission of high-energy beta particles for therapeutic effect
questions.question: A technetium-99m radiopharmaceutical is commonly used in nuclear medicine imaging. What physical property makes this isotope particularly favourable for diagnostic gamma camera imaging?

options: Radical and palliative radiotherapy use identical total doses
Palliative radiotherapy always uses IMRT; radical radiotherapy does not
Radical radiotherapy always uses higher total doses and longer treatment courses aiming for cure; palliative uses lower doses aiming for symptom control
Radical radiotherapy is given only in children; palliative in adults
questions.explanation: Radical (curative intent) radiotherapy aims for tumour eradication and typically uses higher total doses (e.g., 60-70 Gy in 30-35 fractions for lung cancer, 74-80 Gy in 37-40 fractions for prostate) with meticulous treatment planning. Palliative radiotherapy aims to control symptoms (pain, bleeding, obstruction) with fewer side effects, using lower total doses and fewer fractions (e.g., 8 Gy × 1 or 20 Gy × 5 for bone metastases, 30 Gy × 10 for brain metastases) to minimise treatment burden on patients with limited prognosis.
questions.question: The principal distinction between radical (curative) and palliative radiotherapy is:

options: Painful vertebral compression fractures by injecting bone cement
Vertebral haemangiomas by alcohol injection only
questions.question: Percutaneous vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty are interventional radiology procedures used to treat:
questions.explanation: Vertebroplasty involves percutaneous injection of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement into a collapsed, painful vertebral body under fluoroscopic or CT guidance. Kyphoplasty uses a balloon first to create a cavity and restore vertebral height before cement injection. Both procedures stabilise the fracture, relieve pain, and prevent further collapse. They are used for osteoporotic compression fractures and vertebral metastases. Major risks include cement leakage into the spinal canal or vascular system.

options: Hepatic artery catheterisation and selective injection
Direct intratumoral needle injection under CT guidance
questions.question: Selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT) using Yttrium-90 microspheres targets hepatic tumours via which vascular approach?
questions.explanation: SIRT (radioembolisation) with Y-90 microspheres is delivered via selective hepatic arterial catheterisation. Hepatic tumours (HCC and liver metastases) derive their blood supply predominantly from the hepatic artery (unlike normal liver parenchyma which is predominantly portal-vein supplied). This arterial supply difference allows selective delivery of microspheres into the tumour vasculature via catheter-directed hepatic artery injection, concentrating the radiation dose within the tumour while relatively sparing normal parenchyma.

questions.question: On CXR, which finding in the soft tissues should specifically alert the radiologist to a previous mastectomy?
questions.explanation: Following mastectomy, absence of the breast soft tissue shadow on the affected side makes that hemithorax appear more lucent (darker) compared to the opposite side. This is important to recognise to avoid misinterpreting the asymmetric translucency as a pathological finding such as a pneumothorax. Soft tissue assessment is a critical component of systematic CXR evaluation.

Rib crowding (approximation of adjacent ribs) is a CXR sign of long-standing pulmonary volume loss or chronic lobar collapse, commonly seen in children or in long-standing fibrotic processes. The narrowed intercostal spaces reflect the chronic reduction in lung volume on the affected side. Rib notching, by contrast, suggests coarctation of the aorta.
questions.question: Which of the following findings on CXR is considered a sign of long-standing pulmonary disease causing reduced lung volume over time?
On plain abdominal radiograph, which type of calcification is described as having a 'staghorn' pattern within the kidney?
questions.explanation: A staghorn calculus (or coral calculus) is a large renal calculus that grows to fill and conform to the shape of the entire pelvicalyceal collecting system—renal pelvis, major calyces, and minor calyces—producing the characteristic branching stag-antler appearance. They are most commonly composed of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and associated with urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella) causing alkaline urine. They rarely pass spontaneously and require percutaneous nephrolithotomy or surgery.
options: Large calculus filling the pelvicalyceal system
Bladder calculus with laminated well-defined rings

questions.question: Which radiation protection device is used by occupationally exposed personnel to monitor cumulative radiation dose received over time?
questions.explanation: Thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) badges contain crystals that store energy from absorbed radiation. When later heated, they release this stored energy as light proportional to the absorbed dose, allowing measurement of cumulative occupational exposure. TLD badges are worn by radiation workers and provide the regulatory record of personal dose for comparison with occupational dose limits.

options: Immediately after IV tracer injection (dynamic images at 2-3 seconds per frame)
2-4 hours after tracer injection to show bone uptake
24 hours after injection to show metabolic activity
After bladder voiding to reduce background activity
Following oral administration of the tracer
questions.question: In a three-phase bone scan, Phase 1 (blood flow phase) involves imaging:
questions.explanation: In the three-phase bone scan: Phase 1 (flow phase) involves dynamic imaging immediately after IV injection at 2-3 seconds per frame to assess regional blood flow. Phase 2 (blood pool or soft tissue phase) images at 5-10 minutes post-injection to assess soft tissue vascularity and inflammation. Phase 3 (delayed bone phase) images at 2-4 hours when Tc-99m MDP has distributed to bone. The three-phase scan is most useful for osteomyelitis and avascular necrosis.

options: Tracheal air column at all times
questions.question: On a standard chest radiograph, which structure normally appears as the most radiopaque (whitest) element visible within the thoracic cage?
questions.explanation: Bone (ribs and vertebrae) contains mineral (calcium), which has the highest radiographic density among normal thoracic structures, causing maximum X-ray attenuation and appearing white (radiopaque). The lung parenchyma is predominantly air-containing and appears dark (radiolucent), while mediastinal fat and soft tissue structures show intermediate grey densities between air and bone.

questions.question: On CT of the abdomen following blunt trauma, which finding is most specific for a splenic laceration?
questions.explanation: Splenic laceration on contrast-enhanced CT appears as a linear or irregular low-attenuation (hypodense) tear through the normal enhancing splenic parenchyma, often accompanied by perisplenic haematoma (high-attenuation blood clot) and/or free intraperitoneal blood in the left upper quadrant and Morrison's pouch. Active arterial extravasation ('contrast blush') indicates ongoing haemorrhage. The AAST spleen injury scale grades laceration severity (I-V) based on CT findings, guiding non-operative vs. interventional management.

questions.question: A radiograph of the cervical spine after trauma shows anterior displacement of one vertebral body on another with bilateral locked facet joints on the lateral view. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bilateral facet dislocation produces marked anterior translation, typically more than 50% of the vertebral body width, due to complete disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex and bilateral facet joint locking. Unilateral facet dislocation causes lesser anterior translation, generally less than 25%, with rotational malalignment on the anteroposterior view. The degree of translation is a key radiographic clue to distinguishing these patterns and assessing spinal stability.

questions.question: Establishing a histological diagnosis before cancer treatment is critical because it directly determines:
questions.explanation: Histological diagnosis is essential because treatment response and selection depend on tumour type, grade, and receptor status. For example, lymphoma subtypes respond differently to chemotherapy, and breast cancer receptor status determines endocrine or targeted therapy eligibility. Treatment without histological confirmation is inappropriate in most settings.

Cystosarcoma phylloides (phyllodes tumour) is characteristically a large breast lesion that may be benign but has malignant potential. It accounts for less than 1% of all breast tumours. Despite its name, most are benign, but recurrence and malignant transformation require wide local excision.
questions.question: A cystosarcoma phylloides of the breast is typically characterised by being:
Prostate cancer is managed using which hormonal treatment strategy?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer is hormone-sensitive, and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) — achieved through LHRH analogues, antiandrogens, or surgical castration — is the primary systemic treatment. ADT reduces testosterone levels, suppressing androgen-dependent prostate cancer cell growth. It is used in metastatic disease and as adjuvant therapy with radiotherapy in high-risk localized disease.

options: Reducing the total radiation dose delivered during the planning scan itself
Ensuring the planned dose distribution accurately corresponds to the patient's true anatomical position during treatment
Allowing the scan to be performed without any immobilisation device
Eliminating the need for any further imaging throughout the treatment course
Increasing the speed of the treatment planning computation only
questions.question: A radiotherapy planning CT scan is performed with the patient in the identical treatment position, using external skin markers and immobilisation devices matching those to be used during actual treatment delivery. What is the primary reason for this careful positional consistency during simulation?
questions.explanation: The radiotherapy planning (simulation) CT scan must accurately reflect the exact position and immobilisation the patient will be in for every subsequent treatment session, since the entire dose calculation and beam arrangement are based on this specific anatomical dataset, and any discrepancy between planning position and actual treatment position would undermine the accuracy of dose delivery to the intended target. This principle underlies the careful use of matching immobilisation devices, reference marks, and positioning protocols from the very first simulation session through to the final treatment fraction. Maintaining this consistency is fundamental to the entire concept of precision radiotherapy planning and delivery.

questions.question: An automatic exposure control (AEC) system is used for an abdominal radiograph but the central chamber is inadvertently positioned over a metallic surgical clip rather than soft tissue. What is the most likely consequence for the resulting image?
questions.explanation: Because a metallic clip attenuates the beam far more than soft tissue, the AEC chamber beneath it registers reduced transmitted radiation and terminates the exposure prematurely based on that chamber's reading, resulting in overexposure of the surrounding, less attenuating soft tissue. Correct chamber selection relative to the region of clinical interest is therefore essential when using AEC. This pitfall illustrates why radiographers must understand anatomical positioning relative to active AEC chambers.
options: Reduced patient radiation dose with normal image quality
Improved contrast resolution in the surrounding tissue
Overexposure of the surrounding soft tissue due to premature exposure termination
A single high-activity source (typically Ir-192) that dwells at pre-programmed positions within applicators for precise dwell times
Multiple permanent seed implants left in the patient indefinitely
External beam radiation focused on the brachytherapy volume
A low-activity source implanted permanently and decaying over months
questions.explanation: HDR brachytherapy uses a single high-activity radioactive source (commonly Iridium-192, activity ~10 Ci) that is remotely afterloaded from a shielded safe into the implanted applicators (intracavitary, interstitial, or intraluminal). The source pauses at pre-programmed 'dwell positions' for calculated dwell times, building up the prescribed dose distribution. Treatments take minutes. The high activity requires radiation protection measures; staff remain outside the shielded room during treatment.
questions.question: In brachytherapy planning, a High Dose Rate (HDR) brachytherapy system delivers treatment using:

options: Attenuation of scattered radiation to reduce occupational dose
Attenuation of the primary useful beam for diagnostic purposes
Complete elimination of all radiation exposure
Reduction of image noise on the fluoroscopic monitor
questions.explanation: A lead apron with a specified lead equivalence attenuates a substantial proportion, though not all, of the scattered radiation reaching the wearer during fluoroscopically guided procedures, significantly reducing but not completely eliminating occupational radiation exposure. It does not provide protection against the much higher intensity primary beam if a body part were placed directly within it. Lead aprons are one component of a broader radiation protection strategy that also includes distance, time minimisation, and additional shielding such as thyroid collars and lead glasses.
questions.question: A lead apron worn during a fluoroscopic procedure has a lead equivalence of 0.5 mm. What is the primary purpose of this protective garment?
In scurvy, which radiographic sign represents a metaphyseal corner fracture through a weakened lucent zone?
questions.explanation: Pelkan spurs are pathognomonic corner fractures of scurvy occurring through the metaphyseal lucent zone (zone of fragilitas). They occur because vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen synthesis, weakening the metaphysis. Other radiographic features of scurvy include osteoporosis, Wimberger's sign (pencil-thin epiphyseal cortex with loss of epiphyseal density), a dense zone of provisional calcification (due to excessive calcification of osteoid), and periosteal reaction from subperiosteal haematoma.

options: The workload, occupancy, and use factors of the room together with the primary and secondary barrier requirements
The colour of the paint used on the walls
The height of the ceiling alone
The brand of CT scanner installed
The number of staff car parking spaces available
questions.question: A radiology department is designing a new CT suite and must determine appropriate structural shielding for the walls. Which factor is most directly relevant to determining the required shielding thickness?
questions.explanation: Structural shielding calculations for a radiology room take into account the workload (amount of radiation produced), occupancy factor of adjacent areas, use factor (proportion of time the beam is directed toward a particular barrier), and distance to determine appropriate barrier thickness using established radiation protection formulas. Primary barriers, which intercept the direct useful beam, generally require greater shielding thickness than secondary barriers, which only need to attenuate scattered and leakage radiation. This systematic approach ensures that radiation levels in adjacent occupied areas remain within regulatory dose limits.

questions.question: An MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) sequence relies on heavily T2-weighted imaging to visualise the biliary and pancreatic ductal systems without the need for intravenous or intraductal contrast. What is the physical basis for this ductal visualisation?
questions.explanation: MRCP exploits the long T2 relaxation time of static or slowly flowing fluid within the biliary and pancreatic ducts, which appears markedly hyperintense on heavily T2-weighted sequences, while surrounding solid organ tissue with shorter T2 relaxation times appears comparatively dark, creating natural, contrast-free visualisation of the ductal anatomy. This non-invasive approach avoids the risks associated with the direct catheterisation and contrast injection required for conventional ERCP when only diagnostic ductal information is needed. MRCP has therefore become the preferred initial non-invasive investigation for suspected biliary or pancreatic ductal pathology, reserving ERCP for cases requiring simultaneous therapeutic intervention.
options: Rapid arterial blood flow within the ducts generates the image
Static or slowly moving fluid within the ducts produces high signal intensity on heavily T2-weighted sequences
Gadolinium contrast selectively accumulates within the ductal fluid
Fat within the ducts produces the bright signal seen
Iodinated contrast injected directly into the bile ducts produces the signal

questions.question: Which cellular target, when damaged by ionising radiation, is most responsible for cell death through mitotic-linked death?
questions.explanation: The DNA molecule is the critical target of radiation damage leading to cell death. Double-strand breaks in DNA are the most lethal lesions because they are difficult to repair correctly. Damage to DNA can be through direct interaction (high-LET radiation) or indirect interaction via radiation-induced hydroxyl free radicals. Cell death typically manifests at the next attempted mitotic division.

Ground-glass opacity is defined by a hazy increase in lung density that does not obscure the underlying vessels or bronchial walls, distinguishing it from consolidation where these structures are obscured. It reflects partial filling of airspaces or interstitial thickening. This distinction guides differential diagnosis in infective and inflammatory lung disease.
questions.question: A chest CT shows patchy hazy areas of increased lung attenuation through which underlying bronchovascular markings remain visible. What is this appearance called?
A chest radiograph of a cyanotic infant shows a small, boot-shaped cardiac silhouette with decreased pulmonary vascular markings. This appearance is classically associated with:
questions.explanation: The boot-shaped heart with decreased pulmonary vascularity is a classic radiographic description of Tetralogy of Fallot, reflecting right ventricular hypertrophy and reduced pulmonary blood flow from right ventricular outflow obstruction. This differs from a ventricular septal defect, which typically shows increased rather than decreased pulmonary vascular markings due to a left-to-right shunt. Recognising this pattern in a cyanotic infant strongly supports this specific congenital diagnosis.

The pencil-in-cup deformity, where one articular surface tapers while the opposing surface becomes cup-shaped from erosion, is a classic although late finding in psoriatic arthritis, often accompanied by distal interphalangeal joint predominance and associated nail pitting. This distal joint predilection differs from the more proximal, symmetric pattern of rheumatoid arthritis. Coexistent skin or nail psoriasis supports the diagnosis clinically.
questions.question: A hand radiograph shows 'pencil-in-cup' deformity at the distal interphalangeal joints along with adjacent soft tissue swelling and nail changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Bronchography involves instillation of contrast material into the bronchial tree under fluoroscopic guidance to demonstrate its anatomy. It was historically used for bronchiectasis diagnosis but has been largely replaced by CT, which provides superior non-invasive bronchial imaging. It remains listed as a contrast examination technique in respiratory imaging.
questions.question: Bronchography as a radiological technique is used to evaluate which structure?

questions.explanation: The Tc-99m MDP (methylene diphosphonate) whole-body bone scan is the most common nuclear medicine imaging procedure. It is used for detecting skeletal metastases (staging), metabolic bone disease, infection, fractures (including stress fractures), and avascular necrosis. Tc-99m MDP binds to bone via chemi-adsorption into hydroxyapatite crystals at sites of increased osteoblastic activity, making it highly sensitive for bone pathology.
questions.question: The most common nuclear medicine imaging procedure performed globally is:

questions.explanation: The hilum on chest radiography is composed of the pulmonary arteries (main contributors to hilar density), pulmonary veins, and bronchi (air-containing and less radiopaque). Lymph nodes are normally not radiographically visible at the hilum unless enlarged. Hilar enlargement may result from vascular causes (pulmonary hypertension), lymphadenopathy (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, lymphoma), or bronchial tumour.
questions.question: In the assessment of a chest radiograph, the normal hilum contains which of the following structures visible radiographically?
Stochastic effects of radiation are characterised by which of the following features?
questions.explanation: Stochastic effects of radiation (cancer and genetic mutations) are characterised by having no dose threshold — any dose, however small, carries a finite probability of causing the effect. The probability (but not the severity) increases with dose. Examples include radiation-induced cancer and heritable genetic effects. These contrast with deterministic effects, which have a threshold and increase in severity with dose.
options: Severity increases with increasing absorbed dose
They have a clearly defined threshold dose below which they cannot occur
They occur only in occupationally exposed workers
There is no dose threshold and severity does not depend on dose magnitude
They manifest only as deterministic skin reactions

questions.explanation: A filling defect within the superior mesenteric artery with bowel wall thinning and pneumatosis in a patient with a source of embolism, such as atrial fibrillation, strongly suggests acute mesenteric ischaemia from arterial embolic occlusion, a surgical emergency with high mortality if diagnosis is delayed. Bowel wall thinning rather than thickening reflects loss of normal enhancement and viability, differing from the thickened, hyperenhancing wall typical of inflammatory conditions. Prompt recognition on CT angiography guides urgent vascular or surgical intervention.
options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia from arterial embolism
questions.question: A CT scan of the abdomen in a patient with sudden severe abdominal pain and a background of atrial fibrillation shows a filling defect within the superior mesenteric artery with associated bowel wall thinning and pneumatosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A CT angiogram of the aorta shows an intimal flap involving the ascending aorta with extension into the arch. Which Stanford type of aortic dissection does this represent, and what is the management implication?
questions.explanation: Any dissection involving the ascending aorta is classified as Stanford type A regardless of how far it extends distally, and this classification mandates emergency surgical repair because of the high risk of aortic rupture, cardiac tamponade, and coronary or cerebral malperfusion. Stanford type B dissections, confined to the descending aorta, are instead typically managed medically unless complicated. This distinction is one of the most important classification-driven management decisions in emergency radiology.
options: Simple aortic ulcer, managed with antihypertensives alone
Stanford type A, requiring emergency surgery

questions.question: A foreign body lodged in the right main bronchus is likely to produce which radiological finding on chest radiograph?
questions.explanation: A foreign body in the right main bronchus (the more common site due to the more vertical orientation of the right main bronchus) can produce two opposite radiological effects depending on the type of obstruction: a ball-valve effect (air entry but not exit) causes ipsilateral hyperinflation (obstructive emphysema) with contralateral mediastinal shift, while complete obstruction causes ipsilateral lung collapse. The right lung and mediastinum shift aid in confirming the clinical location of the obstruction.
options: Right upper lobe consolidation at all times
Right lung hyperinflation (obstructive emphysema) or collapse

questions.explanation: A dose-volume histogram graphically summarises, for each contoured structure, what proportion (or absolute volume) of that structure receives at least a specified dose, allowing planners to quickly assess whether target coverage and organ-at-risk dose constraints are being met without needing to review every individual CT slice. It does not itself display spatial or anatomical shape information, which instead requires review of the dose distribution overlaid on the planning images. DVH analysis is a standard and essential tool for comparing and approving competing treatment plans.
questions.question: During treatment planning, a dose-volume histogram (DVH) is generated for both the target volume and nearby organs at risk. What information does this graphical tool primarily convey?
options: The cost-effectiveness of the treatment plan
The exact three-dimensional shape of the tumour only
The patient's total treatment time in minutes
The volume of each structure receiving a given dose or higher
The specific machine settings used for each beam

questions.explanation: A developmental venous anomaly consists of dilated medullary veins converging in a caput medusae pattern into a single larger collector vein, representing an anomalous but functional venous drainage pathway rather than a true vascular malformation with shunting. It is typically an incidental finding with a low risk of haemorrhage unless associated with a coexistent cavernoma. Recognising this benign entity prevents unnecessary intervention, in contrast to the higher-risk arteriovenous malformation.
questions.question: A CT scan of the head shows dilated cortical veins in a caput medusae pattern converging toward a normal draining vein, without a discrete nidus or arterial feeder. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically produces symmetric periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions beginning at the 'bare area' of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and later ulnar deviation deformities. Osteoarthritis instead shows asymmetric joint space narrowing with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis, without significant osteopenia. The combination of symmetry, erosive pattern, and osteopenia distinguishes rheumatoid disease from other arthropathies.
questions.question: A hand radiograph in a patient with chronic joint pain shows symmetric periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions at the metacarpophalangeal joints, and ulnar deviation of the fingers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Plain skull radiography is now largely replaced by CT and MRI. However, for which specific indication does a plain skull film remain the appropriate first investigation?
options: Evaluation of posterior fossa well-defined tumour
Suspected skull vault fracture or metastases
questions.explanation: Plain skull radiography retains limited indications in the CT era, including suspected skull vault fractures (in settings where CT is unavailable), assessment for sclerotic/lytic metastases (lateral view only—additional views unhelpful), suspected myeloma involvement, and evaluation of congenital bony anomalies. For suspected acute subarachnoid haemorrhage, intracerebral pathology, or stroke, CT or MRI are far superior and should be used whenever available.

questions.question: Resistance to apoptosis in cancer cells is most directly responsible for which clinical consequence?
questions.explanation: Resistance to apoptosis allows cancer cells to survive despite DNA damage or therapy. This is a major mechanism of treatment resistance, as chemotherapy and radiotherapy often work by inducing programmed cell death. Targeting anti-apoptotic pathways, such as BCL-2, is a therapeutic strategy in several malignancies.

questions.question: A patient with a suspected malignant pleural effusion undergoes thoracocentesis. Light's criteria are applied to the fluid analysis to determine whether it represents an exudate. What is the PRIMARY clinical value of correctly classifying the effusion as an exudate in this context?
options: It automatically confirms a transudative cause requiring no further work-up
It eliminates the need for any cytological examination of the fluid
It narrows the differential toward malignancy and other exudative causes requiring further specific investigation
It confirms the effusion is definitely benign
It replaces the need for any imaging of the chest
questions.explanation: Correctly classifying a pleural effusion as an exudate using Light's criteria narrows the differential diagnosis toward causes such as malignancy, infection, or inflammatory conditions, prompting further specific investigation including cytology. A transudate instead points toward systemic causes such as heart failure or hypoalbuminaemia, which would follow a different diagnostic pathway. This classification step is an essential early branch point in the diagnostic work-up of a pleural effusion of uncertain cause.

options: Ophthalmic (eye) biometry and axial length measurement
questions.question: The main clinical application of A-mode ultrasound today is in:
questions.explanation: A-mode (Amplitude mode) ultrasound displays echoes as amplitude spikes along a one-dimensional line and is now primarily used in ophthalmology for ocular biometry (measuring axial length of the eye for intraocular lens calculation before cataract surgery) and for detecting retinal detachment. For most other applications, B-mode (two-dimensional grey-scale) has replaced A-mode due to superior anatomical display.

Diffuse gland enlargement with surrounding fat stranding and fluid but preserved pancreatic enhancement and no necrosis corresponds to mild interstitial oedematous pancreatitis on CT severity grading. Necrotising pancreatitis instead shows areas of non-enhancing parenchyma reflecting devitalised tissue. CT severity index correlates with prognosis and helps guide the intensity of clinical monitoring.
questions.question: A CT scan of the abdomen shows diffuse pancreatic enlargement with peripancreatic fat stranding and fluid but no necrosis or pseudocyst formation. What severity grade of pancreatitis does this best represent on CT?
A blowout fracture of the orbit results in which characteristic radiographic finding on the OM view?
questions.explanation: A blowout fracture occurs when a direct blow to the eye (e.g., tennis ball) rapidly increases intraorbital pressure, fracturing the weakest point—the orbital floor (posterior to the orbital margin). Inferior rectus muscle and orbital fat prolapse through the defect into the maxillary antrum, producing a characteristic teardrop-shaped opacity in the superior maxillary antrum on the OM view. Enophthalmos and diplopia (from muscle entrapment) are clinical complications.
options: Air-fluid level in the frontal well-defined sinus
Teardrop opacity in the upper maxillary antrum

questions.question: In Marfan syndrome, the metacarpal index is sometimes used as a diagnostic tool. An increased metacarpal index indicates which bone characteristic?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome causes elongation (arachnodactyly) of tubular bones due to excessive ligament laxity and long bone overgrowth. The metacarpal index (ratio of length to width of metacarpals 2-5) is increased in Marfan syndrome, reflecting the characteristically long, slender metacarpals. Associated features include lens dislocation, mitral valve prolapse, and aortic root dilation with risk of dissecting aneurysm—a clinically critical association.

questions.question: A patient undergoes a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) lung scan. Which finding would be MOST suspicious for pulmonary embolism?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism (PE) typically produces an unmatched perfusion defect — a segment of lung with absent or reduced perfusion but normal ventilation (V/Q mismatch). A clot in a pulmonary artery prevents blood flow to a segment that remains ventilated. Matched V/Q defects (both ventilation and perfusion reduced in the same area) suggest intrinsic lung disease (pneumonia, COPD, atelectasis) rather than PE, and are classified as low probability for PE on V/Q interpretation.
options: Diffuse bilateral reduction in both ventilation and perfusion
Unmatched perfusion defect with normal ventilation (ventilation-perfusion mismatch)
Single ventilation defect with normal perfusion
Uniform bilateral perfusion with regional ventilation loss

questions.question: A patient with suspected gastrointestinal bleeding of obscure origin, not localised by endoscopy, undergoes a nuclear medicine study using labelled red blood cells. What is the PRIMARY advantage of this technique for this indication?
questions.explanation: Labelled red blood cell scintigraphy allows imaging over an extended period, improving sensitivity for detecting intermittent or low-rate gastrointestinal bleeding that might be missed by more time-limited investigations such as CT angiography. It does not provide the detailed mucosal visualisation offered by endoscopy but is valuable when bleeding source localisation remains elusive. This extended imaging window is the key advantage for this specific obscure bleeding scenario.
options: Immediate definitive surgical localisation without further imaging
High sensitivity for detecting intermittent, low-rate bleeding over an extended imaging period
Complete avoidance of any radiotracer injection
Superior assessment of unrelated pulmonary pathology
Direct visualisation of luminal mucosal detail
Isointense to fat on both sequences
