questions.explanation: Cortical bone, fibrous tissue (tendons, ligaments), and vessels containing fast-flowing blood all appear hypointense (dark) on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI sequences. Cortical bone has few mobile protons, fibrous tissue has dense collagen with restricted proton mobility, and fast-flowing blood undergoes signal void due to proton displacement out of the imaging slice before signal is collected.
questions.question: In MRI imaging of the musculoskeletal system, fibrous tissue, cortical bone, and rapidly flowing blood share a common signal characteristic. They appear:

questions.explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVU) is the primary imaging modality for diagnosing ectopic pregnancy due to its high sensitivity (>95%) for demonstrating an adnexal mass, the absence of intrauterine pregnancy, and free pelvic fluid (haemoperitoneum from tubal rupture). TVU in conjunction with serum beta-hCG measurement forms the diagnostic cornerstone for ectopic pregnancy. An intrauterine gestational sac is normally visible on TVU when beta-hCG exceeds 1000-1500 mIU/mL (the discriminatory zone); absence at this level suggests ectopic pregnancy.
questions.question: In the radiological investigation of gynaecological emergencies, ectopic pregnancy is best diagnosed by which imaging modality?

questions.explanation: Lymphocytes are among the most radiosensitive cells in the human body, despite being non-dividing in their circulating form. This apparent paradox (high sensitivity despite low mitotic rate) has been attributed to their unique propensity for radiation-induced apoptosis. Other highly radiosensitive cells include erythrocyte precursors, spermatogonia, and intestinal crypt cells. Nerve and muscle cells are the most radioresistant.
questions.question: Which cell population in the human body is most radiosensitive according to the principles of radiation sensitivity?
A chest radiograph in a patient with acute dyspnoea after a central line insertion shows tracking lucent streaks along the mediastinal borders extending into the neck. What does this represent?
questions.explanation: Air within the mediastinum outlines its borders as thin lucent streaks and often tracks superiorly into the soft tissues of the neck, producing the continuous diaphragm sign on some views. It can follow iatrogenic injury, barotrauma, or oesophageal rupture. Distinguishing it from pneumothorax is important because management differs.

questions.question: A young patient presents with localised nocturnal bone pain relieved by NSAIDs. A radiograph shows a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense sclerotic bone. This is classically associated with:
questions.explanation: Osteoid osteoma classically presents with nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs and a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by prominent reactive sclerosis on imaging. This benign lesion contrasts with the aggressive periosteal reactions and larger destructive changes seen in malignant bone tumours. The characteristic clinical pain pattern combined with the specific radiographic nidus appearance supports this diagnosis without requiring biopsy in typical cases.

options: Superior evaluation of extraluminal pathology compared with CT
Complete elimination of any risk of capsule retention
Ability to obtain tissue biopsies during the procedure
Direct visualisation of the small bowel mucosa throughout its length, which is difficult to access with other modalities
Ability to provide real-time therapeutic intervention
questions.question: A patient with a suspected small bowel pathology undergoes video capsule endoscopy after other imaging modalities failed to identify a source of obscure gastrointestinal bleeding. What is the primary advantage of this technique over conventional cross-sectional imaging for this indication?
questions.explanation: Video capsule endoscopy allows direct visualisation of the small bowel mucosal surface throughout its entire length, a region that is difficult to access with conventional upper and lower endoscopy and often poorly characterised by cross-sectional imaging, making it particularly valuable for identifying subtle mucosal sources of obscure gastrointestinal bleeding such as small angiodysplasias or tumours. It does not allow biopsy or therapeutic intervention, unlike conventional endoscopy, and its principal limitation is that it evaluates only the mucosal surface rather than extraluminal or transmural pathology, for which cross-sectional imaging remains superior. Capsule retention proximal to a stricture is a recognised, though uncommon, complication that must be considered before the procedure.

questions.question: A solitary pulmonary nodule on CT demonstrates dense, central 'popcorn' calcification. Which diagnosis does this pattern strongly favour?
questions.explanation: Popcorn calcification reflects chondroid tissue within a hamartoma and is a classic benign pattern that reliably excludes malignancy without biopsy. Malignant nodules more often show spiculation or eccentric, stippled calcification. Recognising this pattern prevents unnecessary invasive investigation.

questions.question: A patient's tumour cells show upregulated expression of PD-L1, allowing the tumour to suppress an attacking T-cell response. This hallmark of cancer is best described as:
questions.explanation: Immune evasion allows tumour cells to escape detection and destruction by the immune system, in this case through PD-L1 upregulation that inhibits cytotoxic T-cell activity. This mechanism underlies the rationale for checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy, which blocks this inhibitory interaction. It is mechanistically distinct from angiogenesis, which concerns vascular supply rather than immune interaction.

questions.question: A radiotherapy technique that shapes the radiation dose distribution to closely conform to the three-dimensional shape of the tumour while sparing surrounding normal tissue is best described by which term?
questions.explanation: Conformal radiotherapy uses multiple beam angles and customised field shaping, often with multileaf collimators, to sculpt the high-dose region so that it closely matches the three-dimensional shape of the target volume while minimising dose to adjacent normal tissue. This represents a significant advance over simple parallel-opposed field techniques, which deliver a more uniform, less tailored dose distribution across the entire beam path. Intensity-modulated radiotherapy extends this concept further by also varying the intensity across each beam for even more precise dose sculpting.

Clustered, irregular, branching microcalcifications without an associated mass are a classic mammographic feature suggestive of ductal carcinoma in situ, reflecting calcification within malignant ductal debris. Fibroadenomas and cysts more typically present as well-defined masses rather than a suspicious calcification pattern. Recognising this specific calcification morphology prompts biopsy for definitive histological diagnosis.
questions.question: A screening mammogram shows a cluster of tiny, irregular, branching calcifications within a small segment of breast tissue, without an associated soft tissue mass. This pattern is MOST concerning for:

options: Absorbed dose divided by quality factor
Absorbed dose multiplied by body surface area
Maximum organ dose minus minimum organ dose
Sum of dose equivalents to organs weighted by tissue weighting factors
Total body dose divided by the number of organs exposed
questions.explanation: Effective dose is the sum of dose equivalents to different organs, each weighted by a tissue weighting factor (wT) that reflects the organ's relative radiation sensitivity and contribution to overall radiation risk. This accounts for the non-uniform irradiation of the body during medical exposures and allows comparison of risk from different exposure patterns. It is expressed in Sieverts (Sv).
questions.question: In radiation protection, effective dose accounts for the fact that different organs have different radiation sensitivities. It is calculated as:

questions.explanation: FDG-PET/CT exploits the increased glycolytic metabolism of viable tumour tissue to help distinguish metabolically active recurrent cancer from inert post-treatment scar tissue, which can appear structurally similar on CT and MRI alone. This functional imaging capability addresses a specific diagnostic limitation of purely anatomical imaging in the post-treatment setting. Correlating PET findings with prior anatomical imaging improves overall diagnostic confidence in this challenging clinical scenario.
questions.question: A patient with suspected recurrent rectal cancer after prior surgery and radiotherapy has an inconclusive CT and MRI, showing an area of scar tissue that cannot be reliably distinguished from recurrent tumour. Which imaging modality is MOST useful to help resolve this uncertainty?

A patient with suspected temporomandibular joint dysfunction undergoes MRI with the mouth in both open and closed positions. What specific structure is primarily assessed by comparing these two positions?
questions.explanation: Comparing open- and closed-mouth MRI positions allows assessment of the dynamic relationship between the articular disc and the mandibular condyle throughout the range of jaw movement, identifying abnormalities such as anterior disc displacement with or without reduction, which are common causes of temporomandibular joint dysfunction and associated clicking or locking symptoms. Static imaging in a single position alone would not reliably demonstrate whether disc displacement corrects (reduces) with jaw opening, information that is important for guiding management decisions. MRI is the preferred modality for this soft tissue assessment given its superior contrast resolution of the articular disc compared with other imaging techniques.
options: Thickness of the masseter muscle only
Position and movement of the articular disc relative to the mandibular condyle
Bone mineral density of the mandible

questions.question: During an MRI acquisition, the specific absorption rate (SAR) refers to which physical quantity?
options: The rate of radiofrequency energy deposited per unit mass of tissue
The rate of gradient coil switching per second
The strength of the static magnetic field in tesla
The rate of image slice acquisition per sequence
The rate of contrast agent clearance from the body
questions.explanation: Specific absorption rate quantifies the amount of radiofrequency energy absorbed per unit mass of tissue, expressed in watts per kilogram, and is directly related to the risk of tissue heating during MRI scanning. Regulatory limits on SAR are built into scanner software to prevent excessive heating, particularly relevant in sequences with many closely spaced radiofrequency pulses. Understanding SAR is essential for balancing image quality against patient safety, especially in vulnerable groups such as pregnant patients and those with implants.

Paget's disease characteristically causes enlargement of the vertebral body with cortical thickening and coarsened trabeculation ('picture frame vertebra' or 'ivory vertebra'). The bone is enlarged but structurally disordered. Serum calcium is typically normal in uncomplicated Paget's, unlike in hyperparathyroidism or malignancy. Alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated. Sclerotic metastatic prostate cancer does not enlarge the vertebral body. Paget's is commonest over 55 years.
questions.question: An elderly patient with a lumbar spine radiograph showing increased bone density, cortical thickening, and vertebral body enlargement—yet with normal serum calcium—is most likely to have which condition?

questions.explanation: The lateral CXR is not routinely recommended because it adds radiation dose without providing consistently useful additional information in unselected patients. It should be reserved for further characterisation of an abnormality detected on the PA view. Judicious use of the lateral view follows ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) radiation principles.
options: It does not show the pleura
It significantly increases radiation dose without routine benefit
questions.question: The lateral CXR view is NOT recommended as a standard examination primarily because:

questions.explanation: Radiosensitisation describes the enhancement of radiotherapy's cytotoxic effect on tumour cells achieved through concurrent administration of certain chemotherapy agents, commonly platinum-based drugs. This differs from radioresistance, which describes tumour cells that are relatively unresponsive to radiation damage. This synergistic combination improves local tumour control compared with either modality used alone.
questions.question: A patient receiving concurrent chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer is told that the chemotherapy component enhances the effect of radiotherapy on tumour cells. This enhancing effect is termed:
Which characteristic CXR finding differentiates viral myocarditis from pericardial effusion?
questions.explanation: Viral myocarditis causes impaired ventricular function and pulmonary venous hypertension, producing cephalization and pulmonary oedema on CXR. Pericardial effusion produces a massive globular cardiac silhouette with characteristically clear lung fields due to external cardiac compression without impaired ventricular function. This distinction guides further investigation.
options: Globular cardiac silhouette in myocarditis only
Presence of pulmonary venous hypertension in myocarditis

questions.question: A patient with suspected bladder cancer undergoes CT urography as part of the diagnostic work-up. What is the PRIMARY advantage of this technique compared with a standard contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen?
questions.explanation: CT urography includes dedicated delayed imaging phases specifically timed to optimally opacify the collecting systems, ureters, and bladder, improving detection of urothelial lesions throughout the urinary tract. Standard abdominal CT protocols are not optimised for this specific purpose and may miss subtle urothelial abnormalities. This technique complements, rather than replaces, direct visualisation with cystoscopy in the full diagnostic pathway for suspected urothelial malignancy.
options: Dedicated delayed imaging optimally opacifies the urinary tract to detect urothelial lesions
It avoids the use of any contrast material
It provides better assessment of lung parenchyma
It eliminates the need for cystoscopy in all cases
It requires no delayed imaging phases whatsoever

questions.explanation: Concurrent treatment involves administering two or more modalities simultaneously, such as chemo-radiation therapy. This approach enhances tumour kill through radiosensitization and simultaneous systemic treatment. Concurrent chemo-radiotherapy is standard in cervical cancer, head and neck cancer, and locally advanced lung cancer.
questions.question: Concurrent treatment in oncology refers to which approach?

questions.explanation: DMSA accumulates within functioning proximal renal tubular cells, so a focal photopenic (reduced uptake) area on the scan indicates a region of reduced functioning renal parenchyma, which may represent acute pyelonephritic inflammatory change if imaged during an acute infection, or established chronic scarring if imaged after resolution of infection, typically several months later. This functional cortical assessment differs from ultrasound or fluoroscopic studies, which assess anatomical structure and reflux respectively rather than direct parenchymal function. DMSA scanning plays an important role in the follow-up of children with recurrent urinary tract infections to identify those at risk of long-term renal damage.
questions.question: A DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan is performed in a child following a urinary tract infection to assess for renal scarring. What does a focal area of reduced tracer uptake within the renal cortex indicate?
options: Vesicoureteric reflux directly, without cortical involvement
Cortical scarring or acute pyelonephritic change
Normal variant renal anatomy in all cases

questions.question: A standard 4-week chemotherapy cycle is also commonly known as which duration?
questions.explanation: A 4-week (28-day) chemotherapy cycle is one of the standard scheduling intervals used in oncology. Other common cycles are 3-weekly and weekly. The interval is designed to allow tumour cell kill while permitting normal tissue recovery before the next course.

Window width represents the total range of Hounsfield unit values selected for grey scale interpretation across the full display. A narrow window width spreads the contrast across fewer HU values, increasing visible contrast for a specific tissue range. Window level is the centre of that range. Clinicians adjust both to optimise visualisation of different tissues.
questions.question: CT window width determines which of the following?
options: The total number of HU values displayed on the monitor
The central HU value around which the grey scale is set
The radiation dose delivered during the scan
The pixel size of the reconstructed image
The number of detector rows in the scanner

questions.explanation: A pedunculated polyp appears as a rounded filling defect attached to the bowel wall by a stalk, best appreciated on double-contrast barium enema as the polyp head is outlined by barium while the thin stalk connects it to the mucosal surface, in contrast to sessile polyps which lack this stalk and lie flush against the wall. Diverticula instead appear as outpouchings of contrast beyond the expected bowel contour, essentially the opposite appearance of a filling defect. Recognising polyp morphology on barium studies has historically guided decisions about the need for colonoscopic removal, though colonoscopy itself now serves as both the primary diagnostic and therapeutic modality in most settings.
questions.question: A double-contrast barium enema shows multiple round filling defects with a stalk projecting into the lumen of the colon. What is the most likely nature of these lesions?
options: Extrinsic compression from an adjacent mass
All cancers are entirely genetically predetermined and unmodifiable
Tobacco use has no established link to cancer risk
Modifying a major modifiable risk factor reduces population cancer incidence
Primary prevention strategies are ineffective for cancer control
Lung cancer incidence is unrelated to any environmental exposure
questions.explanation: Tobacco control campaigns illustrate the broader principle that modifying major modifiable risk factors, such as smoking, can meaningfully reduce population-level cancer incidence over time. This contrasts with the false assumption that cancer risk is entirely fixed by genetics and unmodifiable by behaviour change. Recognising the substantial contribution of modifiable risk factors underlies much of modern cancer prevention public health strategy.
questions.question: A public health campaign specifically targets reduction of tobacco use in the general population as a strategy against lung cancer. Which broader principle does this intervention MOST directly illustrate?
Sedation is required for CT, MRI, and radionuclide imaging in paediatric patients below which age threshold according to standard radiological practice?
questions.explanation: Standard radiological guidelines recommend sedation for CT, MRI, and radionuclide imaging in children under 5 years of age. Younger children cannot remain still for the duration required by these investigations (particularly MRI which takes 20-60 minutes). Motion artefact significantly degrades image quality and may result in non-diagnostic examinations. Sedation protocols ensure patient safety and image quality while minimising unnecessary repeated exposures.

questions.question: MR angiography (MRA) of the cerebral vasculature has which major advantage over conventional catheter cerebral angiography?
options: MRA provides real-time imaging for endovascular treatment
MRA can be performed without any risks, including gadolinium
MRA is faster to perform than catheter angiography
MRA is non-invasive and does not require arterial catheterisation or ionising radiation
MRA detects 100% of cerebral aneurysms below 2mm
questions.explanation: MRA is non-invasive — it requires no arterial puncture, no catheter navigation through vessels, and no ionising radiation. This eliminates the risks of catheter cerebral angiography including arterial access complications, catheter-induced embolism, arterial dissection, and radiation exposure. MRA using time-of-flight (TOF) techniques or gadolinium-enhanced MRA can demonstrate the circle of Willis and detect large aneurysms. Conventional angiography remains the gold standard for small aneurysms and interventional treatment.

questions.question: Ultrasound waves are produced in transducer probes by materials that convert electrical energy to mechanical energy when an electric field is applied. This property is called:
questions.explanation: The converse piezoelectric effect (described by Gabriel Lippmann in 1881) refers to the conversion of electrical energy into mechanical (acoustic) energy when an electric field is applied to piezoelectric crystals. The direct piezoelectric effect is the reverse — mechanical deformation generates electrical voltage. Ultrasound transducers use both effects: transmitting sound (converse) and receiving echoes (direct).

questions.question: A young woman under 35 presents with a palpable breast lump, and her clinician selects ultrasound rather than mammography as the initial imaging investigation. What is the PRIMARY reason for this modality choice?
questions.explanation: Younger women typically have denser breast tissue, which reduces the sensitivity of mammography and favours ultrasound as the more useful initial imaging modality in this age group. This differs from the diagnostic pathway in older women, where mammography is generally the primary imaging investigation due to more favourable fatty breast composition. Selecting the appropriate initial modality based on age and breast density improves overall diagnostic yield.
options: Ultrasound provides higher radiation exposure and is safer overall
Mammography cannot be technically performed in any young patient
Denser breast tissue in younger women reduces mammographic sensitivity
Ultrasound always definitively excludes malignancy in this age group
Young age is an absolute contraindication to any imaging

questions.explanation: FDG is a glucose analogue that accumulates in cells with high glycolytic metabolic activity, and malignant cells typically demonstrate markedly increased glucose uptake compared with most benign tissues, reflected as a high standardised uptake value on PET imaging. However, some benign conditions such as active infection or inflammation can also show increased FDG uptake, so SUV values must always be interpreted alongside the CT morphology and clinical context rather than in isolation. This combined functional and anatomical assessment is the key strength of integrated PET-CT imaging in oncology.
questions.question: A PET-CT scan using fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) shows intense focal tracer uptake within a pulmonary nodule with a high standardised uptake value (SUV). What does this most likely indicate?
options: Complete absence of viable tissue within the nodule
Normal physiological uptake with no clinical significance
Increased glucose metabolism, raising suspicion for malignancy
Isolated increased blood flow without altered metabolism

questions.question: A mammography unit uses a molybdenum target and molybdenum filter for imaging a small, dense breast. What is the primary reason for selecting this low-energy, low-atomic-number combination?
options: To eliminate the need for compression
To produce a low-energy beam that maximises soft tissue contrast in dense breast tissue
To increase penetration for very large breasts
To reduce the need for a grid entirely
questions.explanation: Molybdenum target and filter combinations produce a relatively low-energy, quasi-monochromatic beam around 17-20 keV that maximises the subtle contrast differences between fibroglandular and fatty breast tissue, which is essential for detecting small masses and microcalcifications in dense breasts. Higher energy combinations, such as rhodium or tungsten targets, are instead preferred for thicker or denser breasts to maintain adequate penetration while managing patient dose. Selecting the appropriate target-filter combination is a key technical decision in optimising mammographic image quality.

A Colles fracture is a distal radial fracture with dorsal angulation and displacement of the distal fragment, producing the characteristic dinner fork deformity on clinical examination and typically resulting from a fall on an outstretched, dorsiflexed hand. A Smith fracture is the reverse pattern, with volar (palmar) angulation of the distal fragment. Correctly identifying displacement direction determines the appropriate reduction manoeuvre.
questions.question: A wrist radiograph after a fall shows dorsal angulation and displacement of the distal radial fragment with the classic 'dinner fork' deformity clinically. What is this fracture called?
The mnemonic CRITOE is used to remember the sequence of elbow ossification centres. The age of appearance of the trochlear (T) and olecranon (O) ossification centres, respectively, is:
questions.explanation: The CRITOE mnemonic represents the sequential appearance of elbow ossification centres: Capitellum (2yr), Radial head (5yr), Internal (medial) epicondyle (5yr), Trochlea (10yr), Olecranon (10yr), External (lateral) epicondyle (13yr). Trochlea and olecranon both appear at 10 years. Knowledge of this sequence is essential to avoid mistaking normal unossified epiphyses for fractures in paediatric elbow injuries.

Organs at Risk (OAR) in radiotherapy planning are the normal tissues or organs adjacent to or overlapping the tumour that must be protected from receiving doses exceeding their radiation tolerance. Examples include the spinal cord (myelitis risk), optic chiasm (blindness), rectum (proctitis in prostate cancer), heart (cardiac toxicity in breast cancer), and lungs (pneumonitis in lung cancer). Treatment planning must satisfy tumour dose objectives while respecting OAR dose constraints.
options: The tumour volume receiving the prescribed dose
Tissues that have already been irradiated in a previous course
Organs that enhance the tumour response to radiation
Normal tissues adjacent to or near the tumour that must be protected from excessive radiation dose
Any organ that must receive prophylactic radiation
questions.question: In radiation oncology, the term 'Organs at Risk' (OAR) refers to:

questions.explanation: A well-circumscribed, oval mass with smooth margins in a young woman is the classic mammographic and clinical appearance of a fibroadenoma, a common benign breast lesion. Invasive carcinoma more typically presents with irregular, spiculated margins rather than this smooth, well-defined appearance. Recognising these reassuring benign features helps guide appropriate conservative management with follow-up rather than immediate aggressive intervention.
questions.question: A mammogram in a 30-year-old woman shows a well-circumscribed, oval, mobile mass with smooth margins. This appearance is MOST consistent with:

questions.explanation: The gamma camera, first designed by Hals Anger in 1957, detects gamma rays emitted by radiopharmaceuticals administered to the patient. Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation that can penetrate tissues and be detected externally. Alpha and beta particles are stopped within tissues and cannot be detected externally, making gamma-emitting isotopes ideal for nuclear medicine imaging.
questions.question: In nuclear medicine, a gamma camera is used to detect radiation emitted by a radiopharmaceutical. What type of radiation does this camera detect?
Which MR sequence is most commonly used as the FIRST-LINE imaging sequence in the evaluation of suspected spinal cord pathology?
questions.explanation: T2-weighted sagittal MRI of the spine is the first-line sequence for evaluating spinal cord pathology because T2 imaging provides excellent contrast between the bright CSF, the intermediate-signal cord, and any intrinsic cord lesions (which appear as areas of high T2 signal). It detects cord oedema, contusion, demyelination, tumours, and syringomyelia. T1 post-gadolinium is then added to assess for enhancement (infection, tumour, active demyelination).
options: T2-weighted sagittal MRI of the spine

questions.explanation: Thermionic emission is the release of electrons from the surface of a heated conductor (the tungsten filament) when it is raised to a sufficiently high temperature (above 2200°C). The thermal energy given to electrons allows them to overcome the work function of the metal surface. These emitted electrons form the space charge around the filament.
options: Electrons are released from the heated filament wire
X-rays are emitted from the anode surface
Electrons are ejected from the anode by incident photons
The anode rotates due to electromagnetic induction
High-energy photons ionise anode material atoms
questions.question: Thermionic emission in an x-ray tube cathode is the process by which:

A patient undergoing head and neck radiotherapy is treated using a technique that shapes the radiation dose closely around the tumour while sparing the adjacent salivary glands. This modern technique is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: Intensity-modulated radiotherapy allows precise shaping of the radiation dose distribution around the tumour target while minimising dose to adjacent critical structures such as the salivary glands, reducing long-term toxicity such as xerostomia. Older conventional techniques deliver a more uniform dose across a larger field without this precise conformality. This dose-sparing capability is a major advance in modern head and neck cancer radiotherapy.

Concurrent chemo-radiotherapy is the standard of care for locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinomas. Platinum-based chemotherapy serves as a radiosensitizer, enhancing tumour cell kill. This approach achieves better locoregional control than radiotherapy alone while potentially preserving organ function compared to surgical resection.
questions.question: Head and neck cancers are commonly treated by which modality combination in radiotherapy practice?

questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid malignant tumour of childhood, most frequently arising in the adrenal medulla (50-75%). On ultrasound (and CT), it characteristically appears as a large, heterogeneous suprarenal mass with irregular echogenicity and coarse calcifications (present in up to 90% of cases). CT additionally demonstrates displacement of adjacent structures, lymphadenopathy, calcification, and vascular encasement. I-131 MIBG scintigraphy is highly specific for localising neuroblastoma and its metastases.
questions.question: In a patient with neuroblastoma (suprarenal mass), which imaging finding on ultrasound is characteristic of this tumour?
options: A suprarenal mass with heterogeneous echogenicity and calcifications
A small homogeneous hypochoic adrenal nodule
Adrenal mass with exclusively peripheral calcification at all times

questions.explanation: F-18 labelled fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is the most widely used PET tracer in oncology. FDG is a glucose analogue that is taken up by metabolically active cells proportional to their glucose utilisation. Malignant tumours typically have high glucose uptake (Warburg effect) and appear as areas of intense FDG accumulation. F-18 has a 110-minute half-life, appropriate for production at a cyclotron and transport to imaging facilities.
questions.question: Which radionuclide is most commonly used as the tracer for PET (Positron Emission Tomography) oncology scanning?

questions.explanation: Spinal stereotactic body radiotherapy uses highly conformal planning and image guidance to deliver an ablative, higher biological dose to a vertebral metastatic lesion while achieving a very steep dose fall-off that respects the strict spinal cord dose tolerance, potentially offering more durable pain relief and local tumour control compared with conventional lower-dose palliative fractionation schedules. This technique still requires very careful respect of spinal cord dose constraints, since exceeding cord tolerance remains a serious risk if planning margins or verification imaging are inadequate. The increased precision required makes daily image-guided verification essential rather than optional in this specific technique.
questions.question: A patient with metastatic disease to multiple vertebral levels is being considered for stereotactic body radiotherapy to the spine rather than conventional palliative radiotherapy. What is a key advantage of the stereotactic approach in appropriately selected patients?
options: Shorter overall treatment course with no need for any image guidance
Avoidance of any need for treatment planning imaging
Complete elimination of any risk to the spinal cord regardless of technique
Delivery of a higher, more ablative dose with improved durability of pain and tumour control while sparing the spinal cord
Ability to treat the entire spine in a single very large field

questions.question: A patient with multiple punched-out lytic lesions in the skull vault is most likely suffering from which condition?
questions.explanation: Multiple well-defined punched-out lytic lesions in the skull vault are the classic radiographic appearance of multiple myeloma, where plasma cell deposits destroy bone without reactive sclerosis. Multiple metastases (particularly from thyroid or renal carcinoma) can produce a similar appearance. Histiocytosis causes large irregular defects ('geographic skull'), hyperparathyroidism causes tiny ill-defined resorption pits ('pepper-pot skull'), and Paget's disease causes patchy sclerosis and thickening.

questions.question: A radiographer positions a lead apron and thyroid shield on a patient undergoing a lumbar spine radiograph to protect radiosensitive tissues outside the primary area of clinical interest. What is this practice an example of?
options: Grid use to reduce scatter reaching the detector
Filtration of the X-ray beam at the tube housing
Gonad and non-target organ shielding to reduce unnecessary radiation dose
questions.explanation: Shielding radiosensitive organs such as the gonads or thyroid, when they are not within the primary area of clinical interest, reduces unnecessary radiation dose to these tissues without compromising the diagnostic quality of the intended examination. This is distinct from collimation, which restricts the primary beam to the smallest area necessary for the clinical question, and from filtration, which modifies the beam's energy spectrum at the tube itself. Combining shielding, collimation, and appropriate exposure factor selection together forms a comprehensive approach to minimising unnecessary patient radiation dose.

questions.question: A patient with acute myeloid leukaemia and a very high circulating blast count develops headache, visual disturbance, and respiratory distress. This presentation is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: Leukostasis results from extremely high circulating blast counts causing hyperviscosity and impaired microcirculatory flow, presenting with neurological and respiratory symptoms as seen here. This differs from tumour lysis syndrome, which is a metabolic complication of cell breakdown rather than a hyperviscosity phenomenon. Recognising leukostasis as a haematological emergency prompts urgent cytoreductive treatment to reduce the blast count.

questions.question: The quality factor (Q) for alpha particles used in calculating dose equivalent is:
questions.explanation: The quality factor for alpha particles is Q = 20, reflecting their high linear energy transfer (LET) and greater biological effectiveness per unit of absorbed dose compared to x-rays, gamma rays, and electrons (Q = 1). Dose equivalent H = D × Q. Despite their short range, alpha emitters are extremely dangerous when inhaled or ingested due to their high Q value.

options: Contrast filling the pelvicalyceal system and ureters
Contrast visible only in the renal pelvis
Faint uniform density of renal parenchyma from contrast
Contrast in the renal cortex after 15 minutes
questions.explanation: The nephrogram phase of IVU occurs immediately after contrast injection and refers to the uniform mild increased density of the entire kidney as the contrast agent is filtered and concentrated within the renal tubules—before excretion into the calyces. This phase makes the renal outlines more clearly visible. It is followed by the pyelogram phase (contrast in the calyces, renal pelvis, and ureters), which is assessed at 5-15 minutes on standard IVU films.
questions.question: On intravenous urography (IVU), the 'nephrogram phase' refers to which radiographic appearance?

questions.explanation: Cardiac CT is particularly susceptible to artefact from metallic prosthetic material and dense calcification, which can obscure adjacent structures and limit diagnostic accuracy in these specific scenarios. This is a recognised disadvantage compared with modalities less affected by such artefact, such as echocardiography. Awareness of this limitation guides appropriate modality selection when metallic devices are present.
questions.question: A patient with a metallic prosthetic heart valve requires further imaging following an inconclusive cardiac CT due to significant artefact around the device. Which of the following is the MOST relevant limitation of cardiac CT contributing to this scenario?
options: Complete inability to use any contrast agent
Inability to assess any cardiac structure
Susceptibility to artefact from metallic and heavily calcified structures
Absolute contraindication in all cardiac patients

questions.explanation: Spiculated margins with radiating strands into surrounding lung (corona radiata) reflect malignant infiltration or desmoplastic reaction, making this appearance highly suspicious for cancer. Benign granulomas and hamartomas usually show smooth margins with popcorn or central calcification. Margin analysis is central to nodule risk stratification.
questions.question: A chest CT shows a solitary pulmonary nodule with spiculated margins and a corona radiata appearance. This morphology is most suggestive of which entity?

questions.explanation: Acute subarachnoid haemorrhage appears on non-contrast CT as hyperdense (bright white) material filling the basal cisterns (suprasellar, ambient, quadrigeminal cisterns), sulci of the cerebral cortex, and sylvian fissures. The commonest cause is rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm. CT within 12 hours detects SAH in approximately 98% of cases, but sensitivity decreases over subsequent days as blood becomes isodense with CSF. CSF xanthochromia on lumbar puncture is diagnostic when CT is negative.
options: Subdural space along the tentorium at all times
Basal cisterns and sulci of the brain
questions.question: On CT of the brain, an acute subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) appears as hyperdense material within which specific location?

A 22-year-old man presents with a pathological fracture. Radiograph of the femur shows medullary bone replaced by fibrous tissue and cystic areas with a 'ground glass' appearance. Which condition does this describe?
questions.explanation: Fibrous dysplasia is a congenital condition in which normal medullary bone is replaced by fibrous tissue and cystic areas, producing the characteristic 'ground glass' or 'smoky glass' appearance on plain radiography with mixed density. It commonly involves the facial bones, skull base, and proximal femur (shepherd's crook deformity). Lesions may cause pathological fractures, and the condition may be monostotic (single bone) or polyostotic (multiple bones).

M1 in the TNM system specifically denotes the presence of distant metastatic spread beyond the primary tumour site and regional lymph nodes. M0 instead indicates the absence of any detected distant metastasis. Correctly identifying M1 disease has major implications, generally shifting management from curative to palliative intent in most solid tumours.
questions.question: On staging investigations, a patient's cancer is found to have spread to a distant organ beyond the regional lymph nodes. In the TNM system, this finding is denoted as:
Three-phase six-pulse rectification produces a waveform ripple of approximately:
questions.explanation: Three-phase six-pulse systems produce approximately 14% waveform ripple — significantly less than single-phase systems (100% ripple) but more than 12-pulse systems (~4%) or high-frequency inverters (near 0%). Lower ripple means a more constant voltage, which produces a narrower x-ray spectrum with better average photon energy and more efficient x-ray production.

options: It cannot penetrate the chest wall
Higher dose is deposited in bone due to photoelectric absorption, risking bone necrosis
Orthovoltage cannot be used near metal implants
It produces excessive scatter requiring the patient to be sedated
questions.explanation: At orthovoltage energies, the photoelectric effect dominates interaction with matter, and photoelectric absorption is proportional to atomic number cubed (Z³). Bone has a much higher effective atomic number than soft tissue, resulting in substantially higher absorbed dose in bone compared to soft tissue for the same incident beam. This can cause bone necrosis and periostitis if the bone receives excessive dose. Megavoltage beams reduce this differential because Compton scatter (energy-independent) dominates.
questions.question: Orthovoltage radiotherapy (300 kVp) has which well-known disadvantage when treating lesions near bone?

A CT scan of the cervical spine shows a fracture through the base of the odontoid process at its junction with the vertebral body, without extension into the C2 body. Which type of odontoid fracture is this?
questions.explanation: Type II odontoid fractures occur at the base of the dens where it joins the body of C2 and are the most common type, carrying a higher risk of non-union due to relatively poor blood supply at this junction. Type I fractures involve only the tip of the odontoid, while type III fractures extend into the cancellous body of C2 itself, which generally heals more reliably because of greater surface area for union. Correct classification directly influences the choice between conservative and surgical management.

questions.question: An abdominal radiograph in an elderly patient shows a dilated, comma-shaped loop of bowel in the mid-abdomen with its apex directed toward the left upper quadrant, and a background of collapsed distal bowel. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Caecal volvulus produces a dilated, ectopic caecum that typically migrates toward the left upper quadrant, appearing comma- or kidney-shaped, distinct from the coffee bean shape of sigmoid volvulus arising from the pelvis. Distal colon is usually collapsed because the obstruction is proximal. Differentiating the two volvulus types by direction and shape informs management choice.

questions.question: A radiograph of the tibia in a young patient shows a small, round lucent nidus less than 1.5 cm surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis, with the patient reporting night pain relieved by aspirin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteoid osteoma presents as a small radiolucent nidus, typically under 1.5 cm, surrounded by dense reactive cortical sclerosis, with characteristic night pain dramatically relieved by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs due to prostaglandin-mediated pain generation within the nidus. Osteoblastoma is histologically similar but larger, generally exceeding 1.5-2 cm, and less reliably relieved by aspirin. CT is often used to precisely localise the nidus for treatment planning.

MRI is the gold standard for differentiating osteomyelitis from Charcot arthropathy in the diabetic foot. Osteomyelitis shows focal bone marrow oedema (T2 hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity in the marrow) beneath a skin ulcer or sinus tract, while Charcot arthropathy shows subchondral bone marrow changes and periarticular oedema without soft tissue sinus. White cell-labelled nuclear medicine scans are an alternative but MRI provides superior anatomical localisation and assessment of soft tissue infection extent.
questions.question: In the assessment of a patient with diabetic foot syndrome, which imaging modality best differentiates osteomyelitis from neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy?

questions.explanation: The ultrasound pattern of hydronephrosis (dilated calyces and renal pelvis) with a non-dilated ureter below the pelviureteric junction (PUJ) is the classic finding of PUJ obstruction—congenital or acquired. The ureter is not dilated because the obstruction is at the most proximal ureteric level. In contrast, obstruction further down the ureter (mid-ureter, VUJ) typically shows both dilated ureter and dilated pelvicalyceal system. PUJ obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis in the newborn.
questions.question: Ureteric obstruction at the pelviureteric junction (PUJ) on ultrasound shows hydronephrosis but normal ureter. What clinical feature helps distinguish this from complete ureteric obstruction?
options: Large bladder with multiple ureteric stones at all times
Dilated pelvicalyceal system with non-dilated ureter suggests PUJ obstruction

questions.question: Which CXR view is specifically used to detect whether a pleural opacity is free-flowing fluid or loculated?
questions.explanation: The lateral decubitus view (patient lying on the affected side) demonstrates free-flowing pleural effusion, which redistributes along the dependent chest wall. Loculated effusions do not shift with patient position. This view is used to confirm the presence of a pleural effusion and to estimate its size when sonography is unavailable.

The TNM system separately assesses tumour extent, nodal involvement, and metastasis, providing a standardised framework applicable across most solid tumour types including lung cancer. FIGO staging is instead reserved specifically for gynaecological malignancies. Correct application of TNM staging allows consistent communication of disease extent between different centres and specialists.
questions.question: A patient with non-small cell lung cancer undergoes staging that separately assesses tumour size and local extent, regional lymph node involvement, and presence of distant spread. This staging framework is:

questions.explanation: Intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) uses computer-controlled beam modulation to sculpt the dose distribution precisely around the tumour volume while minimising dose to adjacent critical structures (spinal cord, parotid glands, mandible, brainstem). This is particularly important in head and neck cancer where critical structures are in close proximity to tumour. IMRT has significantly reduced xerostomia and other toxicities.
questions.question: In head and neck cancer management, which radiation technique minimises dose to surrounding critical structures?
During emergency radiology of abdominal trauma, a CT finding of 'sentinel clot sign' is described. What does this sign indicate about the location of injury?
questions.explanation: The sentinel clot sign on abdominal CT refers to the observation that the highest-density blood clot (densest, most recently formed) is located in the region closest to the site of active bleeding. Blood clots in immediate proximity to a lacerated organ are denser than the surrounding free fluid/blood because they are freshly formed. This sign helps the radiologist identify the injured organ when multiple organs are potentially injured and guides surgical or interventional radiological management.

options: Contrast-induced nephropathy, requiring intravenous fluids alone
Delayed contrast reaction, requiring only outpatient follow-up
No treatment required as this is a normal expected response
Vasovagal reaction, requiring leg elevation only
Acute moderate contrast reaction, requiring prompt treatment with antihistamines and/or bronchodilators and close monitoring
questions.question: A patient undergoing an intravenous urogram develops sudden urticaria and mild bronchospasm shortly after contrast injection. What class of reaction does this represent, and what is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.explanation: Urticaria with bronchospasm shortly after intravenous iodinated contrast administration represents an acute moderate hypersensitivity-type reaction requiring prompt treatment, which may include antihistamines, bronchodilators, oxygen, and close monitoring for progression to a more severe reaction such as anaphylaxis. This differs from contrast-induced nephropathy, which presents later as a rise in serum creatinine rather than immediate allergic-type symptoms. Radiology departments must have clear protocols and emergency equipment readily available to manage the full spectrum of acute contrast reactions.

questions.question: A contrast-enhanced CT in a patient with severe abdominal pain shows non-enhancing areas of pancreatic parenchyma alongside surrounding fluid collections. What complication of pancreatitis does this represent?
questions.explanation: Failure of pancreatic parenchyma to enhance after intravenous contrast indicates devitalised, necrotic tissue, distinguishing necrotising pancreatitis from the milder interstitial oedematous form. This finding carries a higher risk of infection and systemic complications. Contrast-enhanced CT performed after 72-96 hours from symptom onset most reliably demonstrates the extent of necrosis.

questions.question: A child presents with respiratory distress. Chest radiograph shows air trapping on the right with contralateral mediastinal shift during expiration. This pattern suggests which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Air trapping in one lung with contralateral mediastinal shift during expiration (when the trapped air cannot escape) is the classic radiological pattern of a ball-valve foreign body obstruction in the main bronchus. During inspiration, the bronchus opens sufficiently to allow air entry; during expiration, the airway narrows and the foreign body acts as a one-way valve, trapping air in the obstructed lung. Comparison of inspiratory and expiratory films (or lateral decubitus films in children who cannot cooperate) demonstrates this dynamic air trapping.

options: The spleen (liver should be same echogenicity)
The aorta (liver should be hyperechoic to aorta)
The gallbladder (liver should be same echogenicity as bile)
questions.question: In abdominal ultrasound, the normal liver echogenicity is described in relation to which reference organ?
questions.explanation: Normal liver echogenicity on ultrasound is described in relation to the right renal cortex: the liver parenchyma is normally slightly more echogenic (brighter) than or equal to the cortex of the right kidney. If the liver is significantly more echogenic (brighter) than the kidney—especially when the renal cortex cannot be distinguished from the medulla due to liver brightness—hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) should be suspected. This comparison provides a reliable internal reference for assessing liver echogenicity.

Tertiary prevention focuses on minimising the impact of established disease and its treatment, including rehabilitation and psychosocial support to restore function and quality of life after cancer treatment. This differs from primary and secondary prevention, which act before or at early detection of disease respectively. Recognising the distinct goals of each prevention level helps structure comprehensive, whole-pathway cancer care.
questions.question: A cancer survivor undergoes structured rehabilitation and psychosocial support following completion of curative treatment, aiming to restore function and quality of life. This represents which level of cancer prevention or care?
A patient with a mammographically detected suspicious lesion undergoes an image-guided core biopsy rather than fine needle aspiration. What is the PRIMARY advantage of core biopsy in this context?
options: It provides tissue architecture allowing distinction between in situ and invasive disease
It requires no imaging guidance whatsoever
It eliminates the need for any further surgical planning
It always avoids the need for local anaesthesia
It cannot provide any information about tumour grade
questions.explanation: Core biopsy obtains a tissue sample that preserves architectural structure, allowing pathologists to distinguish between in situ and invasive carcinoma and to assess tumour grade, information not reliably obtainable from fine needle aspiration cytology alone. This detailed information is essential for accurate treatment planning. Image guidance ensures accurate targeting of the specific suspicious area identified on mammography.

On a full inspiration PA CXR, the right hemidiaphragm should lie at or below the level of the anterior end of the 6th right rib. This serves as a reference to confirm adequate inspiration. A diaphragm above this level on the right side suggests inadequate inspiration, expiratory film, or diaphragmatic elevation from an underlying cause.
questions.question: The normal right diaphragm on inspiration on a PA CXR should lie at the level of which rib anteriorly?

A renal scintigraphy study using technetium-99m MAG3 with diuretic administration is performed to assess for suspected pelviureteric junction obstruction. What does a rising renogram curve that fails to respond to diuretic administration suggest?
options: Renal artery stenosis without ureteric obstruction
True mechanical obstruction at the pelviureteric junction
questions.explanation: A renogram curve that continues to rise despite diuretic administration, which normally washes out tracer from a non-obstructed but dilated collecting system, suggests true mechanical obstruction at the level of the pelviureteric junction that prevents adequate drainage even under diuretic-induced increased urine flow. This diuretic renography technique helps distinguish functionally significant obstruction from simple dilatation without obstruction, which typically shows good tracer washout after diuretic administration. This functional information is important for guiding decisions about surgical intervention such as pyeloplasty.

Known severe iodine allergy (or prior anaphylactic reaction to iodinated contrast) and acute renal failure are major contraindications to iodinated CT contrast. Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) is a serious risk in patients with renal impairment. In hyper-acute renal failure, the creatinine may paradoxically appear normal before rising, so decreased urine output alone indicates renal failure and necessitates avoidance of contrast. Mild or controlled conditions carry lower risk.
options: Known iodine allergy and acute renal failure
Well-controlled type 2 diabetes without renal impairment
History of asthma without prior contrast reaction
questions.question: Which clinical condition is an absolute contraindication to the use of iodinated CT contrast medium?

questions.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome results from rapid breakdown of a large tumour burden following effective treatment, releasing intracellular contents that cause hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia, and secondary acute kidney injury. This differs from neutropenic sepsis, which presents with fever and infection risk related to bone marrow suppression rather than this specific metabolic derangement. Recognising high-risk patients before treatment allows prophylactic measures to reduce the risk of this potentially fatal complication.
questions.question: A patient undergoing induction chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma develops acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and hyperuricaemia within 48 hours of treatment. This presentation is MOST consistent with:

questions.explanation: HRCT of the chest is the gold standard for evaluating interstitial lung disease (ILD), providing detailed characterisation of ground-glass opacities, reticulation, honeycombing, and traction bronchiectasis. The specific HRCT pattern often correlates with histopathological diagnosis, guiding management and avoiding surgical biopsy in typical cases.
questions.question: High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest is the gold standard investigation for which category of lung disease?

questions.explanation: Features on ultrasound most suspicious for ovarian malignancy include: solid tissue elements within a cystic mass, thick irregular septations (>3 mm), mural nodules, papillary projections, ascites, and on colour Doppler, tumour neovascularisation with low-impedance flow (due to absence of muscular media in tumour vessels and arteriovenous shunts). Notably, the size of an ovarian cyst alone is NOT an indicator of malignancy—a large cyst may be benign while a small cyst may be malignant.
options: Simple unilocular cyst less than 3 cm at all times
Solid tissue components within a cystic mass with Doppler vascularity
questions.question: On ultrasound, malignant ovarian masses show specific features that distinguish them from benign cysts. Which of the following features is MOST suspicious for ovarian malignancy?

questions.explanation: The systematic approach principle requires a comprehensive programme with interrelated components sharing common goals, integrated with other health programs and the health system. This ensures coherence, efficiency, and equity across the cancer care continuum.
questions.question: A systematic approach in cancer control requires implementing comprehensive programs with what characteristic?
Which tissue or organ has the GREATEST radiation sensitivity based on the Law of Bergonie and Tribondeau?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow contains rapidly dividing, undifferentiated haematopoietic stem cells with high mitotic activity — all the features that confer high radiosensitivity according to the Law of Bergonie and Tribondeau. This makes bone marrow suppression a critical dose-limiting toxicity in whole-body irradiation. The brain, spinal cord, thyroid, and kidney are composed of more differentiated, less rapidly dividing cells.

options: Biliary gas from ERCP or bilioenteric fistula
Portal venous gas from bowel ischaemia
questions.question: On a plain abdominal radiograph, gas is seen in a branching pattern in the peripheral liver (not central). Combined with clinical sepsis, this most likely represents:
questions.explanation: Portal venous gas appears as branching gas in the peripheral liver (within portal vein branches) on plain film and CT, in contrast to biliary gas (which is more central/peribiliary). Portal venous gas combined with clinical sepsis is a highly ominous finding strongly suggesting bowel ischaemia/infarction with bacterial gas production. Prompt CT of the abdomen is required to assess for mesenteric ischaemia, which carries mortality exceeding 50% without urgent surgical intervention.

questions.question: Multiple well-defined nodules of varying sizes, more common in the lower lobes, most likely represent which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Multiple well-defined pulmonary nodules of varying sizes predominantly in the lower lobes are most commonly due to haematogenous pulmonary metastases. The lower lobe predominance reflects greater blood flow to this region. The varying sizes reflect different times of seeding. Metastases are the most common cause of multiple lung nodules.

questions.question: A chest radiograph in a patient with dyspnoea shows complete opacification of the right hemithorax with the trachea deviated AWAY from the opacified side. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this finding?
questions.explanation: A large volume of pleural fluid adds mass to the hemithorax, pushing the mediastinum and trachea toward the contralateral side. This is the opposite of the shift seen with collapse, where loss of volume pulls structures toward the affected side. Tracking shift direction is essential in differentiating these white-out causes.

questions.question: A young adult presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Chest radiograph shows a visible visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A thin white visceral pleural line with no lung markings lateral to it confirms free intrapleural air. A skin fold typically extends beyond the rib cage and shows markings on both sides, distinguishing it from a true pneumothorax. Correlation with sudden pleuritic pain supports the diagnosis clinically.

questions.question: A tumour biopsy from a patient with a long history of chronic sun exposure shows a characteristic mutation pattern linked to ultraviolet radiation damage. This risk factor is classified under which broad category?
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet radiation is classified as a physical carcinogen, causing direct DNA damage through energy transfer rather than through a chemical reaction or biological agent such as a virus. Chemical carcinogens instead act through direct interaction with DNA via reactive chemical species. Correctly categorising the carcinogen type informs public health prevention strategies specific to that exposure.

questions.question: A ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) lung scan shows a segmental perfusion defect with normal ventilation in the same region, described as a mismatched defect. What is this pattern most suggestive of?
questions.explanation: A mismatched defect, where perfusion is reduced or absent in a lung segment with preserved ventilation, is highly suggestive of pulmonary embolism, because the embolus obstructs blood flow to a region where the airways and alveoli remain normally ventilated. In contrast, matched defects, where both ventilation and perfusion are reduced in the same area, are more typical of parenchymal lung disease such as pneumonia or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Recognising the mismatch pattern is central to interpreting V/Q scans using standardised probability criteria for pulmonary embolism.
options: Normal lung with no significant pathology
Reduced need for accurate patient positioning
Increased patient radiation dose due to greater primary beam absorption
Reduced scatter clean-up compared with lower ratio grids
questions.question: A radiographic grid with a higher grid ratio is introduced to reduce scattered radiation reaching the image receptor. What is the main trade-off of using a higher ratio grid?
questions.explanation: A higher grid ratio, meaning taller lead strips relative to their spacing, more effectively absorbs scattered radiation and improves image contrast, but it also absorbs more of the useful primary beam, requiring an increase in exposure factors (and therefore patient dose) to compensate. Grids with higher ratios also demand more precise centring and alignment to avoid grid cut-off artefacts. This trade-off between scatter reduction and increased dose must be balanced against the clinical need for contrast improvement.

questions.question: Pulse Repetition Frequency (PRF) in ultrasound imaging is best defined as:
questions.explanation: Pulse Repetition Frequency (PRF) is the number of ultrasound pulses emitted by the transducer per unit time (per second), ranging from 1 to 10 kHz for medical imaging. The time between pulses must be sufficient for the sound to reach the deepest target and return before the next pulse is emitted. PRF determines the maximum unambiguous imaging depth and is different from the transducer's operating frequency.
options: The frequency of sound waves within each pulse
The maximum depth of penetration of the ultrasound beam
The number of cycles within a single pulse
The number of complete ultrasound pulses generated per unit time
The rate at which the transducer crystals vibrate

questions.question: A shoulder radiograph in an elderly patient after a fall shows the humeral head positioned inferior to the glenoid with the arm held in slight abduction and external rotation, resembling a light bulb hanging from a branch. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Luxatio erecta is a rare inferior shoulder dislocation in which the humeral head is displaced below the glenoid, with the arm typically fixed in marked abduction. It is frequently associated with neurovascular injury due to traction on the axillary vessels and brachial plexus. This differs from the far more common anterior dislocation, where the humeral head lies medial and inferior to the glenoid but the arm is adducted.

The Hounsfield Unit (HU) is the standardised measure of x-ray attenuation in CT, calculated relative to water (0 HU) and air (-1000 HU). Each voxel in the CT image is assigned an HU value representing the linear attenuation coefficient of that tissue relative to water. This standardisation allows tissue characterisation and comparison between different CT machines and institutions worldwide.
questions.question: CT scanning provides cross-sectional imaging using the principle of differential x-ray attenuation. The measure used to quantify attenuation at each voxel is the:

A CT scan of the abdomen in a patient with suspected hepatocellular carcinoma shows a lesion with arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout on the portal venous phase. This specific enhancement pattern is:
options: Typical of a simple hepatic cyst
questions.explanation: Arterial phase hyperenhancement with portal venous washout is a highly characteristic and diagnostically important enhancement pattern for hepatocellular carcinoma on multiphase CT or MRI. A simple hepatic cyst instead shows no enhancement at all, while a haemangioma typically shows peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in over time. Recognising this specific washout pattern can allow diagnosis without biopsy in an appropriately high-risk patient.

options: I-131 whole-body scan showing thyroid metastases
Thyroid scan showing diffuse homogeneous uptake
FDG-PET scan showing focal hot nodule
questions.question: In the evaluation of a patient with Graves' disease, which nuclear medicine study demonstrates diffusely increased uptake throughout an enlarged thyroid gland?
questions.explanation: Graves' disease (autoimmune diffuse toxic goitre) on thyroid scintigraphy (Tc-99m pertechnetate or I-123) shows diffusely increased, homogeneous radiotracer uptake throughout an enlarged thyroid gland—reflecting the generalised stimulation of all functioning follicular cells by TSH receptor antibodies. This contrasts with toxic multinodular goitre (heterogeneous uptake with multiple hot/cold nodules) and toxic adenoma (single hot nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland). Scintigraphy guides treatment (radioiodine dosimetry).

questions.question: Palliative radiotherapy for bone pain from skeletal metastases is most commonly given as:
options: A single fraction of 8 Gy or a short course (e.g., 20 Gy in 5 fractions)
Radical high-dose fractionated radiotherapy over 6 weeks
IMRT with 30 fractions to achieve complete pain relief
Intraoperative radiotherapy at the time of bone surgery
questions.explanation: Palliative radiotherapy for metastatic bone pain is typically given as a single fraction of 8 Gy or a short hypofractionated course (e.g., 20 Gy in 5 fractions or 30 Gy in 10 fractions). Multiple randomised trials show that a single 8 Gy fraction provides equivalent pain relief to multiple fractions in uncomplicated bone metastases, with the additional benefit of requiring only one visit. Longer courses may be preferred for weight-bearing bones with fracture risk or after surgical fixation.

courses.objectives:
Microbial Death Kinetics and Sterilization Methods: Q1–8
Sterility Testing and Aseptic Processing: Q9–14
Water Quality, Pyrogens and Endotoxins: Q15–19
Microbial Contamination, Enumeration and Antimicrobial Evaluation: Q20–27
Gram-Positive Pathogens and Spore-Formers: Q28–34

courses.title: Applied Pharmaceutical Microbiology II

questions.answerText:
(a)
E. coli is a typical coliform, a Gram-negative non-sporing rod; its cells cannot survive for a long time in water.
(b)
• Streptococcus faecalis is a Gram-positive non-sporing coccus, an intestinal organism frequently voided with faeces.
• Its cells cannot survive for a long time in water, just like E. coli.
(c)
• Clostridium perfringens is a Gram-positive, non-coliform sporing rod.
• It has enhanced viability in water for long periods and withstands temperature increase, pH change and dissolved substances.
(d)
• Bacteria of intestinal origin are significant in bacteriological examination of water; their detection is evidence of faecal contamination.
• They occur in water polluted by animal and human excreta (E. coli, S. faecalis, Proteus spp, C. perfringens); occasionally Salmonella typhi and Vibrio cholerae are found.
• Water used as an ingredient of pharmaceutical preparations should be free of microbial and other contaminants; E. coli O157:H7 in drinking water can be fatal (Walkerton: 2,000 sickened, seven died).
• Giardia and Cryptosporidium form cysts resistant to chlorine that can pass through many treatment filters.
(e)
• E. coli and S. faecalis detected together indicate recent faecal contamination.
• C. perfringens detected indicates long-standing (remote) faecal pollution.
• The difference rests on survival: E. coli and S. faecalis do not survive long, whereas the sporing C. perfringens persists.
questions.question:

(d) Explain the significance of detecting these organisms and other water-borne pathogens in water used in pharmacy and for drinking.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Salmonella typhi (with S. paratyphi A, B, C) is a Gram-negative, motile bacillus; endotoxin liberated causes the early fever, headache and discomfort.
(b)
• Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, motile, non-sporing, curved or comma-shaped rod.
• Its main pathogenic factor is the toxin choleragen, which attaches to the host cell membrane and activates cyclic AMP, causing oversecretion of fluid and electrolytes.
(c)
Shigella spp (e.g. S. flexneri, S. sonnei) are Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped bacteria causing shigellosis.
(d)
• Typhoid: chloramphenicol was the drug of choice; ciprofloxacin is now preferred because of resistance; the TAB vaccine is only about 60-70% effective.
• Cholera: fluid and electrolyte replacement (oral rehydration therapy) prevents mortality; antimicrobials are of slight value because they cannot handle the toxin; a vaccine dose lasts about 6 months.
• Shigellosis: tetracycline, ampicillin, chloramphenicol and co-trimoxazole; vaccines are not yet available.
• Salmonella also causes gastroenteritis and food poisoning; S. typhi and V. cholerae lose viability within 3 weeks to 1 month of storage of raw water.
(e)
• Typhoid: faecal-oral, bacteria spread through blood to organs over about 4 weeks; cholera: curved rod with sudden profuse watery diarrhoea and dehydration within hours.
• Bacillary dysentery: fever, pain, diarrhoea with blood and mucus.
• Note that Salmonella is reclassified by WHO as S. enterica, with different serovars.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• This is the Rideal-Walker phenol coefficient test (1903), the first quantitative evaluation of disinfectants; the organism is Salmonella typhi NCTC 786.
• The coefficient compares the dilution with growth at 2.5 and 5 minutes but not at 7.5 and 10 minutes: 1/95 divided by 1/300 = 300/95 = 3.16.
• It means the disinfectant is that many times as effective as phenol (in terms of minimal bactericidal concentrations) under the test conditions.
(b)
• Test culture: the right strain, preferably the organism dominant in the environment of use; established strains or freeze-dried fresh isolates.
• Culture medium: it affects the organism and is used twice (maintenance and recovery medium); nutrient broth pH 7.6 sterilised at 121 C for 15-20 minutes.
• Other limits: organic matter is ignored (except in Chick-Martin), only one organism is used, and contact times are arbitrarily fixed (7.5 minutes), disadvantaging slow-acting disinfectants.
(c)
• Chick-Martin (1908): 5% yeast suspension as organic matter and a 30-minute reaction time.
• AOAC (1960): recovery media with inactivators (cysteine and thioglycollate for mercurials/heavy metals; lecithin and Tween 80 for quaternary ammonium compounds) and two organisms, S. typhi and Staph. aureus.
• Kelsey-Sykes (1969, modified 1974): suitable for alcohols, aldehydes, biguanides, iodophors and phenolics; AOAC Available Chlorine Test for chlorine-releasing disinfectants.
(d)
• The coefficient of 3.16 is useful for phenolic products, routine examination and screening; phenol is inappropriate as the standard for non-phenolic agents.
• For non-phenolic disinfectants, Kelsey-Sykes is suitable; in-use tests under practical conditions are more complicated and time-consuming and so are not routine.
