Describe the evaluation of bactericidal and bacteriostatic activity by antimicrobial susceptibility testing: (a) purposes and the methods available, (b) broth dilution (macro- and micro-) and agar dilution, (c) interpretation of MIC and MBC.
(d) Give the principle and procedure including medium, inoculum and incubation.
(e) Explain how and why errors occur and how they are controlled.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Purposes include helping choose the most suitable antibiotic for a patient, guiding empiric use, recording epidemiological data on resistance, and monitoring and detecting resistance mechanisms.
• Methods: conventional phenotypic (dilution, disc diffusion, gradient, chromogenic agar), MALDI-TOF MS, automated systems, genotypic (PCR, microarrays, whole genome sequencing) and emerging methods.
(b)
Broth macrodilution uses twofold dilutions in tubes of 1 mL or more; broth microdilution uses microlitre volumes (100 microlitres or less) in 96-well trays; agar dilution mixes the agent with molten agar cooled to 60 C.
(c)
• MIC is the lowest concentration that inhibits viable growth; MBC is the lowest concentration killing 99.9% or more of the original inoculum; the MIC shows the degree of susceptibility or resistance.
• Bactericidal agents (beta-lactams, quinolones) leave bacteria non-viable on transfer to fresh medium; bacteriostatic agents (aminoglycosides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol) allow growth to resume.
(d)
• Medium: cation-supplemented Mueller-Hinton broth (reference medium), with 3-5% defibrinated blood for fastidious organisms; stock solutions at least 1000 micrograms/mL.
• Inoculum: 3-5 well-isolated colonies adjusted to 0.5 McFarland standard, giving a final inoculum of about 5 x 10^5 CFU/mL, inoculated within 15 minutes.
• Tubes and a positive control are incubated at 35-37 C for 24 h; the MIC is the tube with the lowest concentration showing no visible growth.
• MBC is found by subculturing wells or tubes onto non-selective agar and counting survivors after 24 h.
(e)
• Inoculum size greatly affects MIC endpoints, so standardisation is required.
• Macrodilution is limited by long turnaround time, space and labour; microdilution is limited by availability of commercial panels; agar dilution is labour-intensive.
• Quality control in AST is a component of the phenotypic methods.

questions.question:
Describe sterilization with ethylene oxide: (a) mechanism, (b) conditions and spectrum, (c) applications, advantages and limitations.
(d) State its suitable use for heat-sensitive materials, and describe the sterilizer design and operation.
(e) Explain the basis of failure and hazards of ethylene oxide sterilization.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ethylene oxide is an alkylating agent; it denatures proteins by replacing labile hydrogens (e.g. on sulphydryl groups) with a hydroxyethyl radical.
(b)
• It is effective against bacteria, their spores and viruses; items are treated in a sealed chamber in a humid atmosphere at 40-50 C for several hours.
• Sterilizer humidity of 30-70% is needed, often with preconditioning of the load at over 50% relative humidity; it is used in 10% mixture with carbon dioxide to reduce explosion risk.
(c)
• Applications: large medical equipment, plastics, dressings and mattresses (great penetration), bulk API, powders and container systems; in food it is an antifungal fumigant for dried fruit, nuts and spices.
• Advantage: good penetration into rubber, plastics, fabric and paper; limitation: highly explosive and highly toxic.
(d)
• Suitable for heat- and moisture-sensitive items such as plastics, which would be damaged by heat; plastic containers are sterilized by gas and residuals must be kept within regulatory limits.
• The sterilizer is a leak-proof, explosion-proof steel chamber (100-300 L), possibly with a hot-water jacket, with forced gas circulation.
• Operation: air removed by evacuation, load humidified with sub-atmospheric steam, then preheated vaporised gas is admitted from canisters or cartridges.
• Afterwards gas is evacuated, and filtered sterile air is admitted for air purging, which protects the operator.
(e)
• Organisms are more resistant in a dried state or when protected in crystalline or dried organic deposits; a minimum moisture level is required.
• Gas level falls through absorption, so excess gas and extra water are added to compensate; packaging must be air-, steam- and gas-permeable.
• Treated articles need desorption (many days for PVC on open shelves, 2-24 hours in forced-aeration cabinets) and flushing with sterile air to remove toxic residues.

questions.question:
Describe sterilization by radiation: (a) mechanism of ultraviolet (non-ionizing) and ionizing radiation, (b) spectrum and sources, (c) applications, advantages and limitations.
(d) State its suitable use for pharmaceutical dosage forms, packaging materials, air, surfaces and water.
(e) Explain the basis of resistance, failure or incompatibility of radiation sterilization.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• UV light (about 260 nm) is absorbed by purines, pyrimidines and aromatic amino acids; the energy ruptures chemical bonds and impairs cellular function.
• Ionizing radiation has shorter wavelength and higher energy; it produces reactive free radicals that disrupt macromolecules such as DNA and proteins.
(b)
• Gamma rays from cobalt 60 and accelerated electrons (electron beam) are the sources; ionizing radiation can penetrate packaging.
• Viruses are much more susceptible to UV than bacteria.
(c)
• Ionizing: surgical supplies (syringes, catheters, gloves), surgical instruments, sutures, prostheses, unit-dose ointments, plastic syringes and dry products; useful for heat-sensitive products.
• UV: sterilization of air, surface sterilization of aseptic work areas, and treatment of manufacturing-grade water; lamps are harmful to skin and eyes so are used only when people are absent.
(d)
• UV is unsuitable for pharmaceutical dosage forms because of low energy and poor penetration of glass, paper or fabric.
• Radiation sterilization is generally applied to articles in the dried state.
(e)
• Many bacteria can repair UV damage by enzyme-mediated photoreactivation.
• Aqueous preparations undergo undesirable changes because radiolysis of water contributes to damage.
• UV energy is much lower and causes less damage to microbial DNA than ionizing radiation.
• Certain glass or plastic packaging materials (e.g. polypropylene, PTFE) can be damaged by radiation.

questions.question:
A non-sterile peppermint oil-in-water emulsion containing chlorhexidine and cetrimide develops a bluish-green colour.
(a) Identify the likely contaminating organism and the changes by which microbial spoilage of such a product can be recognised.
(b) State the possible sources and routes by which microbial contaminants reach pharmaceutical products during manufacture.
(c) Describe the measures used to prevent contamination from the atmosphere, the working area and operating personnel.
(d) Describe how the contaminant would be detected and confirmed in the product, including the effect of the preservatives on the test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pseudomonas aeruginosa: such an emulsion is reported as contaminated by it, and it normally imparts a bluish-green colour to a formulation.
• Spoilage may show as unpleasant odour, discolouration, changes in consistency (cracking of emulsions, thinning of creams, fermentation of syrups), and turbidity or deposits.
(b)
• Sources: raw materials, atmosphere, equipment, operating personnel, final packaging containers, water, working surfaces and buildings.
• Routes: airborne dust, skin, clothing, moisture droplets and sputum from talking, coughing or sneezing; hands, hair, clothing and open wounds of operators; remnants in crevices of equipment; failure of container seal integrity.
(c)
• Atmosphere: allow only microbiologically clean air into the aseptic area; filtration is most common; chemical disinfection and UV (240-280 nm) also reduce counts.
• Working area: use a screen; vacuum floors (not brooms); mop daily with detergent; occasionally use phenols or quaternary ammonium compounds; disinfect benches, equipment and laminar flow unit before and after each session.
• Personnel: minimise air movement; wear non-shedding clothing, fresh head gear, over shoes, powder-free gloves and masks; wash hands and arms with soap and water; work in laminar flow cabinets.
(d)
• Culture 0.5 mL of the product on 0.03% cetrimide agar to detect P. aeruginosa, incubated at 30-35 C.
• Colonies are identified by Gram staining, oxidase test, pigmentation and fermentation of sugars (lactose, maltose, mannitol).
• Preservatives must be inactivated: cetrimide and chlorhexidine require lecithin and Tween 80, and all neutralising agents must be sterile.
• For topical preparations for damaged skin, P. aeruginosa must be totally excluded.

questions.question:
A child with insect bites on the skin develops superficial infected lesions, and an adult develops boils with pus formation.
(a) State the organisms involved and the risk factors.
(b) Describe the types of skin infection and their complications.
(c) State the antimicrobial and other treatment options and justify one, with its mechanism and the resistance issue.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Skin infections are easily caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.
• Risk factors: lesions or insect bites on the skin (impetigo in children), obstructed hair follicles or sebaceous glands (furuncles), and trauma or surgery (erysipelas).
• Bacteria normally struggle to infect skin because of the protein barrier of dermis and epidermis and the fatty acid secretions of skin glands.
(b)
• Impetigo: superficial, 81% due to S. aureus and about 6% to Streptococcus; furuncles: localised abscesses (boils) with inflammation and pus.
• Carbuncles: like multiple furuncles with several discharging sinuses; erysipelas: a severe pyoderma spreading laterally through lymphatics and leading to septicaemia.
(c)
• Options: surgical drainage of boils and abscesses; penicillins applied topically or systemically against septicaemia; ointments or powders of bacitracin, neomycin and polymyxin.
• Justification (penicillin): beta-lactams interrupt cell wall formation, making the bacteria osmotically fragile and prone to lysis.
• Resistance issue: destructive enzymes such as beta-lactamase in Staph. aureus are virulence factors.

questions.question:
A liquid pharmaceutical product with a high water content develops a pinkish-brown colour during storage.
(a) Identify the likely organism and name other organisms that commonly contaminate such products.
(b) State the source and route of the contamination, including the role of water and water activity.
(c) Describe control measures for the water and the formulation.
(d) State the quality-control tests that would confirm the contamination.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Serratia marcescens, which imparts a characteristic pinkish-brown colour to formulations.
• Products with a high percentage of water are susceptible to opportunistic pathogens such as Klebsiella aerogenes, Bacillus subtilis and Serratia marcescens, and free-living strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus.
(b)
• Water is an important constituent of many products; its microbial content depends on the source (lakes, rivers, wells), and mains or distilled water can be contaminated by prolonged storage or faults in the storage vessel or distribution system.
• Water activity (Aw = vapour pressure of solution / vapour pressure of water) measures available water; lower growth limits include Gram-negatives 0.95, staphylococci/micrococci/lactobacilli 0.91, yeast 0.88.
(c)
• Water: distillation, de-ionisation and reverse osmosis produce suitable water; distilled water for storage should be held at 80 C or more to control Gram-negative bacteria and blue-green algae.
• Formulation: lower the water activity by adding suitable levels of sugar, polyethylene glycols or sodium chloride, or by drying (as for foodstuffs).
• Good practice: keep the microbial burden low before sterilization and prevent contamination from air, equipment and personnel.
(d)
• Physicochemical evaluation by visual and sensory observation of colour, odour, taste and consistency.
• Microbial determination: total viable count by serial dilution and plating (cfu/mL or g).
• Detection of acute pathogens by culture on selective media with Gram staining and biochemical tests.

(a)
A cloudy or hazy solution indicates a contamination potential, since the 14-day period allows growth of any contaminating microorganism.
(b)
• Sources: drug product components (API, WFI, excipients), container system, cleanroom facilities, personnel, and equipment and process; also buildings, raw materials and the HVAC system.
• Personnel are a potential major source ('double-edged sword'); a poor HVAC system can disperse contaminants; aged equipment may leak lubricant or shear parts.
(c)
• Components are sterilized by heat, radiation, filtration (0.4 micrometre membrane then at least two 0.22 micrometre filters) or ethylene oxide; glass containers are washed and dry-heated; plastic containers use radiation or gas.
• Cleanrooms use HEPA/ULPA filtered unidirectional air, airlocks and gowning; automated filling, isolators or RABS and sterilize-in-place reduce personnel contact; staff are trained in aseptic technique and gowning.
(d)
• Sterility testing confirms the absence of viable microorganisms; media fills simulate the aseptic process; process and equipment validation are required.
• Environmental monitoring: particle counter, surface monitoring (touch plates, swabs, contact plates), active air monitoring (impaction, centrifugal, membrane samplers) and passive settling plates.
• Manual visual inspection with black and white backgrounds is only about 85% effective; double inspection and vision-system automation improve it.
questions.question:
Visual inspection, 14 days after an aseptic fill-finish operation, shows a cloudy or hazy solution in vials of a sterile parenteral product.
(a) State what the finding indicates and the cause of contamination.
(b) State the possible sources and routes of contamination in aseptic processing and sterile fill-finish.
(c) Describe the control measures.
(d) State the quality-control tests and monitoring used to confirm and prevent such contamination.

Describe the spore-forming bacteria (a) Bacillus species and (b) Clostridium species: oxygen requirement, examples, habitat and pathogenicity.
(c) Explain their significance in pharmacy and medicine (sterilization, contamination, infection).
(d) Distinguish between Bacillus and Clostridium.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bacillus subtilis is a spore-bearing aerobic opportunistic bacterium; Bacillus spp are commonly isolated from air, fresh water with organic matter and plant materials.
• Bacillus stearothermophilus is a thermophile (grows best above 60 C).
(b)
• Clostridium spp are spore-bearing, anaerobic (aerotolerant) bacteria found in air and in water polluted by soil.
• C. tetani is a Gram-positive spore-forming bacterium producing tetanospasmin, causing lock jaw; C. perfringens is a Gram-positive, non-coliform sporing rod.
• C. botulinum is an acute pathogen, and contamination of products in cans is due to anaerobic bacilli such as C. perfringens or C. botulinum.
(c)
• Endospores of Bacillus and Clostridium resist boiling sometimes for several hours, so heating beyond 100 C under pressure is needed; sterilization protocols should be based on endospore destruction.
• Spores of B. stearothermophilus are used to test autoclave performance; B. subtilis is a challenge organism for sterility test media.
• Talcum powder and surgical dressings have been contaminated by Clostridium spp; catgut is contaminated with spores of C. tetani and gas gangrene Clostridium spp, so its sterility test incubates 14 to 21 days.
• C. perfringens in water indicates long-standing faecal pollution; tetanus enters through open wounds.
(d)
• Tyndallisation exploits spore germination: heating at 90-100 C for 30 minutes on three successive days with 37 C incubation between kills germinated spores.
• Bacillus is an aerobe, whereas Clostridium is anaerobic and is cultured in media such as thioglycollate or Robertson's meat medium.

(a)
• S. aureus causes skin infections: impetigo (81% of cases), furuncles and carbuncles.
• A virulence factor is the destructive enzyme beta-lactamase; it is carried by healthy carriers and distributed in air.
(b)
• S. pyogenes causes sore throat (acute pharyngitis) in children and adolescents, with pain, redness and inflammation of the pharyngeal epithelium.
• It is also involved in skin infections: about 6% of impetigo and abscesses.
• Untreated sore throat may develop into rheumatic fever in about 3% of cases; the first line of treatment is penicillins or antimicrobial lozenges.
(c)
• Skin infections are treated by surgical drainage, penicillins, or bacitracin, neomycin and polymyxin ointments.
• Erysipelas leads to septicaemia.
• S. aureus and Streptococcus spp come from operators' skin, nose, throat and open wounds as contaminants, and S. aureus must be totally excluded from topical products for damaged skin.
• Mannitol salt agar detects S. aureus; oxidase and coagulase tests identify it.
(d)
• Differentiation uses culture characteristics, colony morphology, cell arrangement under the microscope and biochemical characteristics.
• Staphylococcal infections cause localised pus-forming lesions (boils); streptococcal infections include pharyngitis (sore throat) and abscesses.
questions.question:
Describe (a) Staphylococcus aureus and (b) Streptococcus pyogenes under the headings diseases caused, virulence factors, complications and treatment.
(c) Explain their significance in pharmacy and medicine, including their relevance as contaminants of pharmaceutical products.
(d) Distinguish between staphylococcal and streptococcal infections.

Describe sterilization by filtration: (a) principle, (b) filter types and pore sizes and the spectrum of organisms retained, (c) applications, advantages and limitations.
(d) State its suitable use for heat-labile liquids, air and gases.
(e) Explain the basis of filtration failure and the problem of endotoxins.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Rather than killing microorganisms, filtration isolates them by passing liquids or gases through filters of appropriate pore size.
• It is indirectly bactericidal: retained bacteria are alive for a time but eventually die when removed from their nutrient source.
(b)
• Membrane filters (nitrocellulose or polycarbonate) have largely replaced asbestos and sintered glass; they may be bought pre-sterilised and used with pressure or suction.
• A pore size of 0.22 micrometre removes bacteria and yeasts; mycoplasma and viruses can pass; a pore size ten times smaller lets only the smallest viruses pass.
(c)
• Used for solutions of antibiotics and culture medium components that are chemically altered by heat; HEPA filters create clean atmospheres in operating theatres and laminar-flow hoods.
• Limitations: filters clog easily, are relatively expensive and are not the preferred choice if alternatives exist.
(d)
• Heat-labile liquids and gases (air supplies) are filter-sterilised; in aseptic processing a 0.4 micrometre membrane is followed by at least two sterile 0.22 micrometre filters, tested before and after use.
• For water, filtration through membrane filters with small pore size is described as the best form of purification, with coarse filters installed first.
• Cellulose nitrate filters suit aqueous, oily and weakly alcoholic solutions; cellulose acetate suits strongly alcoholic solutions; specially adapted filters may be needed for antibiotics.
(e)
• Filters cannot be used when particle size of the component is too large.
• Membrane filters do not remove bacterial endotoxin, so endotoxin is controlled at the raw material stage; filtered water cannot be called sterile.
• Pyrogens are filterable and pass through bacteria-proof filters; the filtration process is particularly prone to breakdown, so all filtered drugs must be tested for sterility.

questions.question:
A patient develops fever, headache and general discomfort after drinking raw milk, and typhoid fever is suspected.
(a) Name the causative organisms and state the risk factors and route of transmission.
(b) Describe the progression of the disease and its complications.
(c) State the antimicrobial options and justify one, giving its mechanism.
(d) State the preventive measure and its limitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi (A, B or C), Gram-negative motile bacilli.
• Transmission is faecal-oral; typhoid is food- or water-borne; it can be contracted by drinking raw milk, and Salmonella is present in dairy products such as yoghurt, egg yolk and ice cream.
(b)
• Bacteria pass from the small intestine to lymphatics and mesenteric glands, multiply and enter the blood; average duration is 4 weeks.
• Week 1: bacteraemia with fever, headache and discomfort, largely due to endotoxin; week 2: spread to liver, gall bladder, spleen, kidney and bone marrow with severe fever and prostration.
• Week 3: intestinal haemorrhage and perforation, or pneumonia; week 4: critical stage and death may occur.
(c)
• Options: chloramphenicol (formerly the drug of choice), amoxicillin, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole; because of resistance, fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin are now the drug of choice.
• Justification: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV (Type II topoisomerases governing DNA replication), so cell division ceases and the organism becomes non-viable.
(d)
• Prophylaxis is the TAB trivalent vaccine (typhoid, paratyphoid A, paratyphoid B): 3 injections at one-week intervals and a booster at 3 months.
• Limitation: only about 60-70% success because of different strains of Salmonella.

(a)
Evaluation of microbial content by detection of acute pathogens and enumeration; the pathogens sought include E. coli (Enterobacteriaceae), Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and fungi.
(b)
• A volume of 0.5 mL of the product is cultured by streaking or spreading on MacConkey's agar (Enterobacteriaceae/E. coli), mannitol salt agar (S. aureus), 0.03% cetrimide agar (P. aeruginosa) and Sabouraud dextrose agar (fungi).
• The first three are incubated at 30-35 C; the Sabouraud plate at 25 C for 3-4 days for yeasts such as Candida albicans.
• Colonies are identified by Gram staining and biochemical tests: Enterobacteriaceae by indole, methyl red, Voges-Proskauer and citrate; staphylococci by oxidase and coagulase tests; pseudomonads by oxidase, pigmentation and sugar fermentation; fungi by filamentous cells, fruity odour and possibly germ tube test.
(c)
• A preservative or antibacterial sample must be inactivated by dilution (phenols, alcohols 1 in 50) or neutralised: mercurials with thioglycollate, sulphonamides with PABA, QACs and chlorhexidine with Tween 80 and lecithin, penicillins with penicillinase.
• All neutralising agents must be sterile; interference of any sort must be avoided.
(d)
• Topical preparations for damaged skin: not more than 10^2 opportunistic cells per g or mL and total exclusion of Enterobacteriaceae, P. aeruginosa and S. aureus.
• Mixtures, suspensions and emulsions: not more than 10^3 bacterial cells and 10^2 fungal cells per g or mL, with total absence of Enterobacteriaceae (especially E. coli), S. aureus and P. aeruginosa.
• Limitations: some methods lack sensitivity or fail to differentiate live and dead organisms, and sample types vary, needing specific sampling methods.
questions.question:
An oral mixture and a topical cream for damaged skin must be examined for acute pathogens and microbial limits as part of quality control.
(a) Name the test and the pathogens sought.
(b) Describe the principle and procedure including media and incubation.
(c) State the critical controls and precautions, especially for preserved products.
(d) Explain how the results are interpreted against limits and state the limitations.

Describe the chemical disinfection of water: (a) chlorine and chloramines (form and concentration), (b) spectrum and the removal of residual taste, (c) domestic methods of purifying water with their advantages and limitations.
(d) State the suitable use of these agents for raw water in a plant and in rural areas.
(e) Explain the basis of resistance, failure or incompatibility of water disinfection.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Disinfection is the chemical removal of microorganisms from raw water; chlorine is the most widely used disinfectant and is an effective bactericide at very low concentration (ppm).
• It may be used as gas or bleaching powder; chlorine gas is too toxic, so chloramines (chloramine T, dichloramine T, halazone) that release chlorine in water are preferred.
• Halazone is the most frequently used, at a concentration of 4 mg/litre per hour of disinfection.
(b)
The residual chlorine taste is removed by adding sodium thiosulphate.
(c)
• Boiling kills all vegetative forms except spores and removes temporary hardness; bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) is used at 0.4-0.5 ppm but imparts an unpleasant taste.
• Sodium hypochlorite solution (e.g. Milton) and potassium permanganate (water becomes pinkish) are also used.
(d)
• For raw water, disinfection is one of three ways of removing microorganisms, alongside storage and filtration; in rural areas boiling, bleaching powder, sodium hypochlorite or potassium permanganate are used.
• Storage of raw water reduces microorganisms through sunlight, predatory organisms and lack of nutrient; membrane filtration removes microorganisms.
(e)
• Giardia and Cryptosporidium cysts are resistant to chlorine and can pass through many filters; spores resist boiling.
• Disinfection or filtration does not remove bacterial endotoxin (pyrogens), so the water cannot be said to be sterile.
• Copper sulphate or cupric chloramine is added to stored raw water to prevent algal growth.

questions.question:
Before a sterility test, a batch of fluid thioglycollate medium is found to be pink in more than the upper 30% of its depth.
(a) Identify the indicator and what the colour shows.
(b) State the factors in the medium that affect this result.
(c) State the alternative media and corrective methods available.
(d) Give a reasoned conclusion on the most suitable approach.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Resazurin is the oxidation-reduction indicator; the medium turns pink when oxidised.
• The medium is not used to detect anaerobes if more than the upper 30% is pink.
(b)
• Oxidised conditions exist near the top and reduced conditions at the bottom, so the medium supports both aerobes and anaerobes.
• Sodium thioglycollate and dextrose are the reducing agents; agar increases viscosity; yeast extract, casein digest, dextrose and sodium chloride are nutrients.
• Thioglycollate broth without agar is oxidised more quickly and should be heated about 4 hours before use.
(c)
• Corrective method: heat the medium in a water bath to expel dissolved air and restore reduced conditions; this must not be done more than once.
• Alternatives: thioglycollate broth medium (no agar; good for semi-solids and turbid suspensions) and soya-bean casein digest medium (aerobic organisms and fungi).
(d)
• Conclusion: do not use the medium for anaerobes while more than 30% is pink; restore it once by heating; if it cannot be restored, an alternative medium must be chosen.
• For anaerobic testing the reduced condition is essential, and for oily products shaking is kept to a minimum to maintain anaerobic conditions.

(a)
Bordetella pertussis, a Gram-negative aerobic bacterium, causing whooping cough (pertussis), one of the commonest childhood problems that also affects adults.
(b)
• The bacteria attack the respiratory mucosa with an incubation period of 7-14 days and a protracted course of 4-8 weeks.
• Presence of the organism on the epithelial surface of the trachea and bronchi causes irritation, eliciting coughing, and toxin production.
• Thick mucilaginous fluids secreted on the walls of the trachea and bronchi cause paroxysmal coughing and bronchospasm.
• After about 2 weeks there are fits of rapid, violent, uncontrollable coughing leaving the patient exhausted, which may lead to anoxia, convulsion and lung collapse.
(c)
• Treatment uses appropriate antibiotics such as tetracycline, chloramphenicol and erythromycin; it is beneficial early, before respiratory lesions occur.
• Prophylaxis is DPT vaccine.
questions.question:
A child has spasmodic coughing ending in forced expiration, and a Gram-negative aerobic bacterium is identified.
(a) Identify the organism and disease.
(b) Describe its pathogenesis and the course of the disease.
(c) State treatment and prevention.

A patient presents with localised inflammation of the throat and nasopharynx with an exudate (membrane), and a Gram-positive bacillus is isolated.
(a) Identify the organism and disease.
(b) Describe its pathogenesis and the effects of its toxin.
(c) State treatment and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram-positive bacillus, causing diphtheria; the incubation period is about 2.5 days.
(b)
• Multiplication and attachment of the bacilli to the epithelial surface cause inflammation and leakage of serum protein and white blood cells, forming the characteristic diphtheritic membrane (exudate).
• The infection may extend into the trachea and obstruct air flow.
• The organism produces diphtheria toxin, which can cause systemic symptoms: myocarditis with congestive heart failure, and neurologic and muscular paralysis.
(c)
• Treatment is administration of diphtheria antitoxin supported with antibiotics such as penicillin or erythromycin.
• Prophylaxis is the trivalent DPT vaccine (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus).
• In developed nations diphtheria is almost eradicated by an effective vaccination programme.
• It is an upper respiratory tract infection, as is sore throat.

questions.question:
A batch of an oily injection and an ointment must be tested for sterility.
(a) Name the test and state why oils and ointments are troublesome to test.
(b) Describe the principle and the procedures that can be used (shaking/emulsification, filtration, direct inoculation).
(c) State the critical controls and precautions.
(d) Explain how results are interpreted and the limitations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sterility test: portions are placed in media supporting growth and examined for turbidity or pellicle.
• Oils and anhydrous semi-solids are difficult to disperse (oils form a surface layer, ointments float in lumps); dispersion makes the medium turbid and needs subcultures; contaminants are coated with an anhydrous film; a thick oil layer causes semi-anaerobic conditions and reduced recovery.
(b)
• Oils: vigorous shaking in screw-capped bottles of media (shaker in the incubator or once daily); thioglycollate medium with agar is used for anaerobes, the container almost full, with subculturing even if it seems unnecessary.
• Emulsification with a non-ionic surfactant (Tyloxapol) by magnetic stirring; incubate 7 days with 1 mL subcultures into 40 mL fluid thioglycollate on the second and fifth days.
• Filtration: low-viscosity oils through a dry membrane; viscous oils diluted with sterile isopropyl myristate; wash the membrane at least three times with about 100 mL peptone (1 g/L) containing polysorbate 80 (10 g/L).
• Ointments in a fatty base and water-in-oil emulsions may be diluted to 1% in isopropyl myristate (heated to not more than 40 C); for direct inoculation, creams and ointments are diluted about 1 in 10 by emulsifying.
(c)
• Include negative controls and positive/fertility controls; the product volume must not exceed 10% of the medium; neutralise any antimicrobial activity; work aseptically.
• Shake oily cultures gently each day, but keep shaking to a minimum in fluid thioglycollate to maintain anaerobic conditions.
(d)
• No growth: the product complies; growth: it does not comply unless the test is proven invalid; incubation is not less than 14 days.
• If turbidity prevents reading, subculture at 14 days and incubate for not less than 4 days.
• Limitations: the sample is destroyed so a representative sample is extrapolated, and the poor dispersion of oils hinders recovery.

(a)
• M. tuberculosis is a rod-shaped acid-fast bacterium causing tuberculosis, a chronic progressive pulmonary disease.
• It is transmitted in small airborne particles inhaled into the alveoli and phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages.
• The first stage begins when organisms enter the lymphatic system and may be asymptomatic; the second is chronic progressive pulmonary disease with rapid multiplication, fatigue, weight loss, coughing and fever.
(b)
• M. leprae is an acid-fast rod-shaped bacterium that causes leprosy, a central nervous system disease.
• It is morphologically similar to M. tuberculosis and causes a slow, progressive infection affecting the peripheral nerve endings of the skin.
(c)
• TB affects about 15 million people annually, with 3 million deaths.
• Treatment is difficult because of resistance to conventional antibiotics, so drug combinations (isoniazid, streptomycin, ethambutol, rifampicin, pyrazinamide) are used.
• The first 2 months use isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol, followed by 3-4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin.
• Prophylaxis is BCG vaccine, used to immunise children in the first 2 weeks and said to protect for life.
(d)
Both are acid-fast rods; M. tuberculosis affects the lungs while M. leprae affects peripheral nerve endings and skin.
questions.question:
Describe the following mycobacteria: (a) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (shape, staining property, transmission, stages), (b) Mycobacterium leprae (shape, staining property, disease).
(c) Explain the significance of these organisms in medicine, including treatment and prophylaxis.
(d) Distinguish between M. tuberculosis and M. leprae.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clostridium tetani, a Gram-positive spore-forming bacterium; the disease is contracted when the organism or its spores enter a human, especially through an open wound.
• Symptoms occur after spores germinate and the organism grows and multiplies.
(b)
• The major pathogenic factor is the toxin tetanospasmin, which affects peripheral nerves and those controlling the jaw muscle, causing abnormal contraction or spasm (lock jaw).
• As toxin increases, other muscles are affected, causing respiratory failure, exhaustion and death.
• About 300,000 persons contract tetanus annually and 50% die.
(c)
• Options: tetanus toxoid injection to stimulate antibody production in a previously immunised patient; antibiotics such as penicillin to eliminate the organism; muscle relaxants, sedatives and intensive artificial support.
• Justification for penicillin: beta-lactams interrupt bacterial cell wall formation.
• Limitation of antitoxin: it cannot neutralise toxin already bound to nerve tissue, only circulating toxin.
(d)
DPT vaccine in the first year of life protects for up to 10-20 years.
questions.question:
A patient with an open wound develops spasm of the jaw muscles (lock jaw).
(a) Name the organism and the risk factors.
(b) Describe the complications.
(c) State the treatment options and justify one, with its mechanism and limitation.
(d) State the prevention.

Surgical dressings (gauze, bandages) and talcum powder are found to be contaminated with Clostridium species.
(a) Identify the type of organism and the cause of the contamination.
(b) State the source and route of contamination.
(c) Describe the sterilization and control measures.
(d) State the quality-control test that confirms sterility of the product.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clostridium spp are anaerobic spore-forming bacteria; talcum powder and surgical dressings such as gauze and bandages are reported as contaminated by them.
• Contamination arises because endospores resist boiling, sometimes for several hours.
(b)
• Sources of contaminants include raw materials (which account for a high proportion), the atmosphere (Clostridium spp are commonly isolated from air), equipment, buildings, operating personnel and final packaging containers.
• Soiled dressings are themselves potentially hazardous and are destroyed by incineration.
(c)
• Dressings and fabrics are sterilized in autoclaves for surgical dressings, with careful choice of packaging, faultless packing and correct loading; mechanical air evacuation is essential for porous loads and 134 C is the minimum temperature.
• Ethylene oxide penetrates dressings well; radiation is applied to dry articles; dry heat is used for thermostable powders.
• Prevention of contamination also uses clean air, disinfected surfaces and gowned personnel.
(d)
• Sterility testing: samples are placed in media supporting aerobes, anaerobes and fungi, such as fluid thioglycollate medium for anaerobes.
• Controls: fertility, positive and negative controls; biological indicators using Bacillus stearothermophilus spores check the sterilizer.

questions.question:
One gram of an ointment is added to 9 mL of 0.1% peptone water, serially diluted, and 0.5 mL of the 10^6 dilution is plated by the pour plate method, giving 100 colonies.
(a) Identify the method and calculate the count.
(b) State the factors that affect the result.
(c) Name alternative methods of estimating microbial numbers.
(d) Give a reasoned conclusion on the suitability of the result and the most suitable approach.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Total viable count (an indirect count) by the pour plate method.
• TVC = 100 x 1/0.5 x 10^6 = 2 x 10^8 cfu/g (results are recorded as colony forming units).
(b)
• Growth conditions (medium composition, pH, temperature) decide which organisms grow, so viable count is selective and biased.
• Cells in pairs or groups give one colony, so the count is of colony forming units; preservatives or antibacterial activity in the sample must be inactivated or neutralised.
• Pour plate may miss very small colonies of strict aerobes, and colonies of different species look similar.
(c)
• Surface spread or drop plate; membrane filtration; most probable number; direct microscopic counts with counting chambers or acridine orange; impedance and manometric methods.
• Biomass methods: wet or dry weight, ATP, peptidoglycan, protein or nucleic acid, and turbidity.
(d)
• The count of 2 x 10^8 cfu/g is far above the limits given: 10^2 for topical preparations for damaged skin and 10^3 bacteria for other preparations.
• Sterile preparations should contain no microorganisms.
• The most suitable approach for a viscous ointment: membrane filtration is not suitable for viscous liquids, so pour or spread plate counts with inactivation of preservatives are appropriate, with direct counts reserved for total cell numbers.

(a)
Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a Gram-negative coccus, causing gonorrhoea, one of the most common STDs; it affects both sexes and sometimes children.
(b)
• In males the gonococci invade the urethral mucosa after an incubation period of 2-7 days, with pain, burning on urination and purulent discharge.
• Untreated, symptoms may subside after about 8 weeks but complications continue: chronic epididymitis and urethral stricture (blocking).
• In females the gonococci invade the cervical lining and less commonly the urethra, fallopian tubes and associated glands; the disease may be asymptomatic except for purulent discharge.
• About 20% of untreated cases progress to pelvic inflammatory disease affecting the fallopian tubes and ovaries.
• Infants may contract it at birth (neonatal gonorrhoea), a major cause of infant blindness (gonorrhoea ophthalmia).
(c)
Treatment: penicillin injection with probenecid (to prolong the action of penicillins); other drugs are spectinomycin, 3rd-generation cephalosporins (e.g. ceftriaxone) and ciprofloxacin.
questions.question:
A male patient has pain and a burning sensation on urination with a purulent urethral discharge, and a Gram-negative coccus is identified.
(a) Identify the organism and the disease.
(b) Describe its pathogenesis and complications in males, females and infants.
(c) State the treatment.

Bottled aqueous injections in their final containers are to be sterilized and the process verified.
(a) Name the method and its principle.
(b) Describe the procedure and stages.
(c) State the critical controls and precautions.
(d) Explain how the performance is tested, how results are interpreted, and the limitations of the tests.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Steam sterilization in an autoclave; steam under pressure at 121 C for 15 minutes (103 kPa) is the standard cycle for bottled fluids, acting by destroying enzymes and cell constituents.
(b)
• Stages: air removal and steam admission, heating-up and exposure (holding time, possibly including heating-up time established with thermocouples in dummy articles), then cooling.
• For bottled fluids air is removed by downward displacement; cooling uses jacket water or spray cooling with filtered compressed air (air ballasting) to limit container breakage.
(c)
• Air must be driven out so the atmosphere is pure steam; residual air lowers the temperature; superheating beyond 5 C must be avoided.
• Containers must not be removed until the temperature is below 80 C; spray-cooling water may itself be a source of contamination and must be monitored.
• Large loads or volumes need longer time; use of cleaned equipment and a low starting microbial load shortens the process.
(d)
• Instrumental method: a thermometer in the drain with a recorder, and thermocouples or thermistors in the load (dummy bottles); the drain thermometer cannot sense the load temperature.
• Cultural method: spore strips (Bacillus stearothermophilus) embedded in the load, cultured afterwards; growth appears only after 5 days, so no immediate result.
• Chemical indicators (e.g. colour-change tape, Brown's tubes, indicator tablets) are more convenient but less reliable than spore tests.
• Sterility testing is the direct method of verification.

questions.question:
A patient has chronic fatigue, weight loss, coughing and fever, and an acid-fast, rod-shaped bacterium is identified.
(a) Identify the organism and disease.
(b) Describe its transmission, pathogenesis and stages.
(c) State the treatment and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a rod-shaped acid-fast bacterium causing tuberculosis, a serious lower respiratory tract infection.
• About 15 million people are affected annually, of whom 3 million die.
(b)
• Tuberculosis is traditionally a chronic progressive pulmonary disease; the organism is transmitted in small airborne particles inhaled into the alveoli and phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages.
• The first stage starts when the organism enters the lymphatic system and may be asymptomatic; the second stage is chronic progressive pulmonary disease with rapid multiplication, fatigue, weight loss, coughing and fever.
(c)
• Treatment is difficult because of resistance to conventional antibiotics, so drug combinations are used from isoniazid, streptomycin, ethambutol, rifampicin and pyrazinamide.
• The first 2 months combine isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol, followed by a 3-4 month course of isoniazid and rifampicin.
• Prophylaxis is BCG vaccine, used in children in the first 2 weeks, said to protect from contracting tuberculosis for life.

questions.question:
Describe the kinetics of microbial death as the basis of sterilization processes: (a) definition and measurement of death, (b) death curve, D value and Z value, (c) sterility assurance.
(d) Explain the factors affecting microbial death (physical and nutritional).
(e) Explain why sterilization may fail and how this is controlled.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Death is the irreversible loss of ability to grow and reproduce; a cell is dead if it fails to form a colony on any growth medium.
• Death can be quantified only for populations; the probability of a cell dying is constant per unit time, so death is exponential: S = S0 e^-kt.
(b)
• The log of survivors plotted against time is a straight line whose slope is the rate of death K; the decimal reduction time (D value) is the time to reduce the population to one tenth (kill 90%).
• D falls at higher temperature (a mesophile falls from 50 min at 45 C to 5 min at 65 C); the Z value is the temperature increase needed to reduce D by a factor of ten.
(c)
Theoretically there are never zero survivors; sterility is generally assumed when the chance of a surviving cell falls to one in a million.
(d)
• Physical factors: pH (optimum 6-8), temperature (protein denaturation above optimum), oxygen (obligate aerobes, anaerobes, microaerophiles, facultative anaerobes), moisture, hydrostatic and osmotic pressure and radiation.
• Moisture: drying kills vegetative bacteria, but spores resist (anthrax spores survived 50 years dried on cloth); UV and sunlight kill, and ionizing radiation is lethal.
• Chemicals: bactericidal agents and metabolic poisons (H2S, CO, phenol) cause death; osmotic pressure causes crenation (shrinkage) or plasmolysis.
• Nutritional factors: carbon, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus, trace elements and vitamins; insufficient or excessive amounts may cause death.
(e)
• The larger the initial population, the longer the time needed; a less steep slope leaves more survivors.
• Protocols must be based on the death rate of the most resistant species (endospores); a regime effective for one organism may be wholly inappropriate for another.
• Control includes minimising the entry of bacteria and cleaning containers and equipment well; high organic matter can retard thermal destruction.

questions.question:
Describe the sexually transmitted infections: (a) gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and (b) syphilis (Treponema pallidum) under the headings Gram reaction, transmission, incubation, stages and complications.
(c) Explain their significance in medicine, including treatment.
(d) Distinguish between gonorrhoea and syphilis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• N. gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative coccus affecting both sexes and sometimes children; incubation in males is 2-7 days with burning urination and purulent discharge.
• Complications: chronic epididymitis and urethral stricture in males; in females invasion of the cervical lining, with about 20% of untreated cases progressing to pelvic inflammatory disease.
(b)
• T. pallidum is a Gram-negative anaerobic organism that affects only human beings.
• It is transmitted only during sexual intercourse by direct contact with a lesion containing the pathogen.
• After an incubation period of 2-4 weeks it progresses to primary, secondary and tertiary syphilis.
(c)
• Gonorrhoea can be passed to infants at birth, causing neonatal gonorrhoea, a major cause of infant blindness (gonorrhoea ophthalmia).
• Gonorrhoea is treated with penicillin injection plus probenecid, spectinomycin, ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin.
• Syphilis is treated with penicillin antibiotics.
(d)
• Gonococci are a coccus with a 2-7 day incubation and localised genitourinary signs; T. pallidum has a 2-4 week incubation and three stages.
• Gonorrhoea may be asymptomatic in females and can be acquired by infants at birth; syphilis is transmitted only by sexual contact.

(a)
• Vibrio cholerae, a curved or comma-shaped, Gram-negative, motile, non-sporing rod.
• It is transmitted by the oral route (food and water) into the small intestine, where it multiplies, penetrates and damages the intestinal mucosa.
(b)
• The disease has high mortality and morbidity, with profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting, muscular cramps, collapse of the extremities and acute dehydration.
• The main pathogenic factor is choleragen, which attaches to the host cell membrane and activates cyclic AMP, causing oversecretion of fluid and electrolytes lost through vomiting and diarrhoea (fluid and electrolyte imbalance).
(c)
• Options: fluid and electrolyte replacement (oral rehydration therapy); antimicrobial drugs are of slight value; a cholera vaccine is available for short-term use.
• Justification for ORT: it replaces the fluid and electrolytes lost through the toxin-driven oversecretion and is important to prevent immediate mortality.
• Limitation of antimicrobials: the drugs cannot handle the cholera toxin.
• A single vaccine dose lasts only about 6 months.
questions.question:
A patient has sudden-onset profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting and muscular cramps, and becomes acutely dehydrated, acidotic and shocked within a few hours.
(a) Name the likely organism and the risk factors or route of acquisition.
(b) Describe the consequences of the infection.
(c) State the treatment options and justify one, with its mechanism and the resistance or limitation issue.

Four powder products must be tested for sterility: a powder in a small ampoule, a powder in a large vial, a bulk powder (e.g. sodium chloride in a screw-capped jar) and an insoluble powder (e.g. talc).
(a) Name the test and its principle.
(b) Describe the procedure for each powder.
(c) State the critical controls and precautions.
(d) Explain how results are interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sterility test: portions of the material are placed in media able to support growth of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria and fungi and examined for turbidity or pellicle.
(b)
• Small ampoule: open it, dissolve the powder with liquid medium and transfer a volume corresponding to the recommended weight (100 mg if 200 mg or more; whole contents if under 50 mg), using a calibrated pipette.
• Large ampoule or vial: prepare the injection with the solvent (usually water for injection) by strict aseptic technique, then use the volume corresponding to the recommended weight; test the solvent separately for sterility.
• Bulk powder: 100 mg is aseptically transferred into a bottle of medium (e.g. 25 mL McCartney bottles); a much larger sample might make the medium excessively hypertonic.
• Insoluble powder: as for bulk powder, but aerobic containers are closed tightly and shaken vigorously at intervals during the first three days, then undisturbed for the last two or more days.
(c)
• Controls: fertility, positive (media, sample and about 100 cells of control organisms) and negative controls; the test is performed under aseptic conditions.
• Quantity of sample must not exceed 10% of the medium; antimicrobial activity of the sample must be neutralised.
(d)
• A clear supernatant after the powder settles indicates sterility, but subcultures are necessary if turbidity remains.
• No growth in any container after two consecutive tests means the batch passes; the same contaminant in repeat tests means failure.
• Limitations: only a sample can be tested and the tests are not infallible.

(a)
• LPS has three components: lipid A, core (R) polysaccharide and O polysaccharide; it forms about 80% of the Gram-negative cell wall.
• Lipid A is the hydrophobic, membrane-anchoring toxic region (phosphorylated N-acetylglucosamine dimer with 6 or 7 fatty acids).
• The core is a short sugar chain; the O polysaccharide is longer and a major antigenic determinant of the Gram-negative cell wall.
(b)
• Endotoxins are toxic microbial metabolites released after cell lysis or death and they persist in parenteral solutions after the organisms die.
• Properties: filterable, water-soluble, thermostable (withstand 120 C for over 3 hours), non-volatile (removed by distillation) and insensitive to pH changes.
• Effects are dose-dependent: low doses cause asymptomatic inflammation, moderate doses fever, and high doses shock, organ failure and death.
(c)
• Endotoxins are the pyrogens of major significance to the pharmaceutical industry and are difficult to remove from products.
• Sources in parenterals: water, packaging, chemicals, raw materials and equipment; detection is by the rabbit test and the LAL test.
• The colon contains Gram-negative bacteria in abundance but no pyrogenic effect occurs while the colonic wall is intact.
(d)
• A pyrogen may be internal (endogenous) or external (exogenous); LPS is a good example of an exogenous pyrogen.
• LPS is liberated by bacteria (particularly Gram-negative), blue-green algae and some fungi.
questions.question:
Describe Gram-negative bacterial endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide, LPS): (a) structure and the components, (b) properties and effects in the body.
(c) Explain its significance in pharmacy and medicine.
(d) Distinguish between endotoxins of Gram-negative bacteria and other pyrogens (exogenous versus endogenous).

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bactericidal agents kill bacteria, which remain non-viable after transfer to fresh medium; examples are beta-lactam antibiotics and quinolones.
• Bacteriostatic agents prevent growth and multiplication without killing; examples are aminoglycosides, clindamycin and chloramphenicol.
(b)
• Beta-lactams (e.g. penicillin) interrupt cell wall formation, making bacteria osmotically fragile and prone to lysis (spheroplasts).
• Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, stopping cell division.
• Aminoglycosides bind 16S rRNA in the 30S subunit (misreading, inhibited translocation); clindamycin binds 50S and inhibits translocation; chloramphenicol binds 50S and inhibits peptidyl transferase.
(c)
Bactericidal activity is concentration dependent and may be bacteriostatic at low levels; an agent may be cidal for one species and static for another.
(d)
• Because static agents do not directly destroy the pathogen, elimination depends on the host's own resistance mechanisms and the immune system.
• Refrigeration is bacteriostatic and allows long-term storage of bacteria; lyophilization and ultra-low freezing also preserve bacteria.
(e)
• Shutting off protein synthesis for a while does not impair the organism permanently; some synthesis continues at a low level sufficient to sustain life.
• When the agent is removed (eluted in vitro or metabolised in vivo), growth resumes.
questions.question:
Describe bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibacterial agents: (a) definitions and examples, (b) mechanisms of action, (c) spectrum and concentration effects.
(d) State the effect of each type on the host and in situations such as storage of bacteria.
(e) Explain why bacteriostatic action is reversible and why a cidal agent may fail.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• It investigates the sterile condition of products sterilized by any method, revealing viable aerobic or anaerobic bacteria, fungi or other microorganisms.
• Products include injections and infusions, solids for injection, water for injections, eye preparations, blood products, vaccines, implants and catgut; BP requires every batch of filtered injections to be tested.
(b)
• Random samples are taken: batch of 100 or fewer, 10% or 4 whichever is greater; over 100 but under 500, 10; 500 or more, 2% or 20 whichever is less.
• Quantity must not exceed 10% of the medium volume; liquids: under 1 mL whole contents, 1-4 mL half, 4-20 mL 2 mL, 20 mL or more 10%; solids: 50 mg or less whole, 50-200 mg half, 200 mg or more 100 mg.
(c)
Fluid thioglycollate medium (mainly anaerobes, also aerobes) is incubated at 30-35 C; soya-bean casein digest medium (fungi and aerobes) at 20-25 C; media must pass a growth promotion test with not more than 100 cfu.
(d)
• Principle: a portion is placed in media that support microbial growth and examined for turbidity or pellicle; membrane filters of pore size not greater than 0.45 micrometre are used for filtration, and incubation is not less than 14 days.
• Controls: fertility control, positive control (medium, sample and about 100 cells, set up in duplicate), negative control (medium without sample), and a method suitability/validation test for bacteriostasis and fungistasis.
• No growth means the product complies; growth means it does not comply unless the test was invalid (faulty monitoring data, faulty procedure, growth in negative controls, or growth ascribed to technique), in which case it is repeated.
(e)
• Only a representative sample can be tested because the sample is destroyed, so results are extrapolated and the tests are not infallible.
• Contamination during the test invalidates it, so it is done aseptically in a room with filtered air, UV-lamp screens, materials treated with ethylene oxide or UV, and experienced workers.
• Antimicrobial activity of preservatives can inhibit growth; it is removed by dilution, neutralisers (thioglycollate, PABA, lecithin and Tween 80, penicillinase) or membrane filtration.
• If the material makes the medium turbid, 1 mL portions are subcultured to fresh medium and incubated for not less than 4 days.
questions.question:
Describe sterility testing of pharmaceuticals: (a) purpose and products that must comply, (b) sampling and quantity tested, (c) culture media and incubation.
(d) Give the principle, procedure (direct inoculation or membrane filtration), controls and interpretation.
(e) Explain how and why sterility test failure or false results occur and how they are controlled.

Describe pyrogens and their detection: (a) nature and properties of pyrogens, (b) the in-vivo rabbit pyrogen test (principle, procedure), (c) interpretation of the rabbit test.
(d) Describe the in-vitro Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) test, its principle and limitations.
(e) Explain how pyrogen contamination occurs and how it is controlled or removed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A pyrogen is a substance that raises body temperature when it enters the bloodstream; the most important are endotoxins (lipopolysaccharide) of Gram-negative bacteria.
• Properties: filterable, water-soluble, thermostable (not destroyed below 200 C; withstand 120 C for over 3 hours), non-volatile, and insensitive to pH changes.
(b)
• The rabbit test measures febrile response in healthy adult rabbits of at least 1.5 kg, on an antibiotic-free diet, without weight loss in the preceding week and not previously used in a similar test.
• Rectal temperature is recorded (probe about 7 cm) from 90 minutes before to 3 hours after injection; the solution is warmed to 38.5 C and injected into the marginal ear vein within 4 minutes (0.5-10 mL/kg).
(c)
Animals varying by more than 0.6 C before injection are excluded; three rabbits pass if the summed response does not exceed 1.15 C and fail above 2.25 C; six rabbits pass at 2.8 C or less and fail above 4.3 C.
(d)
• LAL (from Limulus polyphemus amoebocytes) is more sensitive; the sample is incubated at 37 C and endotoxin reacts with a clottable protein to form a gel; no gel means non-pyrogenic; it detects only Gram-negative endotoxin.
• Limitations: preparations interfere, chemical inhibitors chelate divalent cations, siliconized glassware or plastic can inhibit clot formation, and false negatives may occur; the rabbit test is limited by endotoxin tolerance, low reactivity to Legionella and drugs that mask the effect.
(e)
• Sources: water in processing, packaging components, chemicals, raw materials and equipment, and incomplete removal of organisms from biologically produced drugs.
• Removal: distillation (most reliable for water), reverse osmosis, anion-exchange chromatography, and ultrafiltration.
• Destruction: acid-base hydrolysis, hydrogen peroxide, dry heat (250 C for 45 minutes for glassware), and sodium hydroxide for non-autoclavable equipment.
• Prevention: raw material screening, hygiene, regular tests; WFI is stored at 80 C or above or 2 C or below.
• The endotoxin limit is inversely related to the dose, and is 0.2 EU/kg for drugs reaching the CSF.

questions.question:
Water for injection is distilled in a still, and the electrical resistance of the distillate is found to be about half of the value of high-quality distilled water (500,000 ohm/cm).
(a) Identify the method used to check the distillate and what the value means.
(b) State the factors that can lead to contamination or poor quality of the distillate.
(c) State the alternative tests and quality standards for water for injection.
(d) Give a reasoned conclusion on the most suitable approach.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The purity of the distillate (apyrogenic water) is checked by measuring its electrical resistance, which is high when the water is pure.
• High-quality distilled water has a resistance of 500,000 ohm/cm or more; a distillate with about half this value should not be used.
(b)
• Distilled water is free from microorganisms as it leaves the still; contamination occurs from a fault in the cooling system (entrainment of droplets containing microorganisms), the storage vessel or the distribution system, and the flora is usually Gram-negative bacteria.
• Still design, build-up of scale from impure supply water, metal leaching (e.g. copper), dust in the air and uncleaned stills also affect quality.
(c)
• USP standards at point of use: conductivity below 1.3 microsiemens/cm at 25 C, total organic carbon below 0.5 mg/L, pyrogens below 0.25 EU/mL and total bacterial count below 10 cfu/100 mL; no suspended particles.
• Pyrogens are tested by the rabbit test (healthy rabbits, rectal temperature monitored) or the LAL test.
(d)
• The distillate must be rejected; the cooling system, storage vessel and distribution system should be examined.
• Distillation is the best method of removing pyrogens for water for injection; storage at 80-90 C and heat or ozone sanitization of tanks and pipes prevent bacterial build-up.

(a)
The lethal effect is largely due to oxidative processes, which are less effective than the hydrolytic damage caused by steam.
(b)
It uses higher temperatures of 160-180 C with exposure of up to 2 hours; bacterial spores are much more resistant than vegetative cells, and their resistance varies with dryness.
(c)
• Applications: glassware and metal surgical instruments (good penetrability, non-corrosive), non-aqueous thermostable liquids and thermostable powders.
• The range of materials treated is quite limited, mainly hospital items; it needs higher temperature and longer time than moist heat.
(d)
• The major industrial use is glass bottles to be filled aseptically; it may also destroy endotoxins (pyrogens), with about 250 C used for depyrogenation of glass.
• Apparatus made entirely of glass is better sterilized by dry heat; glass with rubber parts not made of silicone must be autoclaved instead.
• A hot-air oven has an insulated stainless steel chamber (up to 250 L), heaters placed to avoid cool spots, a rear fan and perforated shelves; thermocouples and a recorder monitor the cycle.
• Dry heat sterilizing tunnels use infrared or forced convection in filtered laminar airflow at 250-300+ C on a conveyer belt.
(e)
• Early studies did not control spore water content, producing conflicting data and varying pharmacopoeial times and temperatures.
• Heat is delivered by radiation and convection, so articles must be arranged to avoid obscuring centrally placed items; temperature variation must not exceed 5 C.
• Heating-up can take as long as 4 hours for poor conductors; it is shortened by preheating, narrow containers with dull non-reflecting surfaces.
• Wrappers (paper, cardboard tubes, aluminium) must be strong enough to protect against post-sterilization contamination; the chamber cools to about 40 C before unloading.
questions.question:
Describe dry heat sterilization: (a) mechanism, (b) temperatures, times and effect on spores, (c) applications, advantages and limitations.
(d) State its suitable use for glassware, containers with rubber parts, and depyrogenation, and describe the sterilizer and its operation.
(e) Explain the basis of failure or inconsistency of dry heat sterilization.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Heat acts by destroying enzymes and other essential cell constituents; the lethal events are fastest in the fully hydrated state (denaturation and hydrolysis), so less heat is needed under high humidity.
(b)
• Steam at 121-134 C is used; standard cycles are 121 C for 15 minutes (bottled fluids) and 134 C for 3 minutes (porous loads); 103 kPa (15 psi) gives 121 C.
• Boiling at 100 C for 10 minutes is usually enough unless endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium) are present, which can resist boiling sometimes for hours; heating beyond 100 C under pressure is required.
(c)
• Used for dressings, sheets, surgical and diagnostic equipment, containers and closures, aqueous injections, ophthalmic preparations and irrigation fluids.
• Advantages: more efficient than dry heat with shorter time and lower temperature; the only method for glass equipment with rubber or certain plastics.
• Limitations: unsuitable for anhydrous materials such as powders and oils, and for heat-sensitive injections and articles.
(d)
• Bottled fluids: air removed by downward displacement (avoids bottle breakage under evacuation); minimum 121 C; stages are air removal and steam admission, heating-up and exposure, then cooling.
• Cooling is by jacket water or spray cooling with air ballasting; containers are not removed until below 80 C.
• Porous loads: mechanical evacuation (e.g. pulsed) is essential before steam; minimum 134 C; the load is dried by steam exhaust and vacuum, then sterile filtered air restores pressure.
(e)
• Air left in the chamber lowers the temperature below that expected for the pressure and delays heat penetration; efficient air removal is a major aim.
• Superheated steam behaves like hot air and is inefficient (maximum 5 C superheat); 'wet' steam can soak a porous load and hinder penetration.
• Organic matter forms a protective coat; a larger initial population takes longer to kill; large loads need longer treatment.
questions.question:
Describe moist heat sterilization: (a) principle of action, (b) temperature-time cycles and effect on spores, (c) applications, advantages and limitations.
(d) State its suitable use and the stages of operation for bottled fluids and for porous loads such as dressings.
(e) Explain the basis of failure of steam sterilization (air, steam quality, load and organism factors).

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Viable plate count is an indirect count: serial dilutions are plated on suitable medium; each colony is assumed to arise from one cell, so colonies are counted allowing for dilution.
• Pour plate: 1 g or 1 mL is added to 9 mL of 0.1% peptone water; 1 mL of the last dilution goes into 20 mL molten agar (nutrient agar for bacteria, Sabouraud dextrose agar for fungi); incubate at 30-37 C for 7 days (bacteria) and 25 C for 3-4 days (fungi).
(b)
• Example: 0.5 mL of the 10^6 dilution giving 100 colonies gives 100 x 1/0.5 x 10^6 = 2 x 10^8 cfu/mL or g.
• Limits: injectables no microorganisms; topical preparations for damaged skin not more than 10^2 per g or mL with exclusion of Enterobacteriaceae, P. aeruginosa and S. aureus; other preparations not more than 10^3 bacteria and 10^2 fungi.
(c)
Pour plate: no pre-drying, suits lower concentrations, but small colonies of strict aerobes may be missed; spread plate: easier counting, but needs pre-drying and moulds may form confluent growth; membrane filtration: detects lower concentrations and removes antimicrobials, but not suitable for viscous liquids.
(d)
• MPN is a statistical method: samples serially diluted to extinction, multiple tubes (3, 5 or 10) inoculated, and the pattern of positive tubes read against probability tables.
• For coliforms, positive is lactose fermentation with acid (bromocresol purple turns purple to yellow) and gas (inverted Durham tubes).
• Direct counts use counting chambers (Petroff-Hauser); they are rapid but do not discriminate living from dead cells; acridine orange stains both living and dead cells.
(e)
• Viable count is selective and biased because no single set of conditions grows all organisms; clumps give colony forming units rather than cells.
• Serial dilutions range from 10^-1 to 10^-8 so that a countable dilution is obtained.
• Preservatives or antibacterial samples must be inactivated: phenols and alcohols by 1 in 50 dilution; mercurials with thioglycollate; sulphonamides with PABA; QACs and chlorhexidine with Tween 80 and lecithin; penicillins with penicillinase.
• All neutralising agents must be sterile to avoid interference.
questions.question:
Describe the enumeration of microorganisms in pharmaceutical products: (a) the total viable count (principle and pour plate procedure), (b) calculation and limits, (c) merits and demerits of pour plate, spread plate and membrane filtration.
(d) Describe the most probable number (MPN) and direct counting methods and their interpretation.
(e) Explain how and why errors or failure occur in these tests and how they are controlled.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• In terminal sterilization the product is filled and sealed in its final container and then sterilized by heat or irradiation.
• In aseptic manufacturing the drug product, container and closure are sterilized separately and then brought together in an extremely high-quality environment; it is used when terminal sterilization is not feasible.
(b)
• Cleanrooms control particulates; air is filtered, and recirculated in unidirectional flow through HEPA and/or ULPA filters; staff enter through airlocks in protective clothing.
• Cleanrooms are not sterile: only airborne particles are controlled, tested with a particle counter.
(c)
Surface monitoring (touch plates, swabs, contact plates), active air monitoring (impaction, centrifugal, membrane samplers) and passive air monitoring (settling plates).
(d)
• EM regularly collects, evaluates and interprets data on air and surfaces so trends and sources are recognised before product contamination; SOPs address frequency, timing, duration, sample size, equipment, alert and action levels and responses.
• Media fills use sterile growth media to simulate the aseptic process and validate its sterility; process validation tests the process under normal operating conditions.
(e)
• Personnel are the greatest microbial risk; control is by training, gowning, unidirectional airflow, automated filling and barrier systems (isolators with vaporised hydrogen peroxide, RABS).
• Equipment can cause contamination as it ages (damage, leaks, shearing); it must be designed, validated and maintained, with sterilize-in-place.
• Facility design should minimise occluded surfaces and be easy to clean; process validation problems include poor documentation and inadequate resources.
• Failure to comply with regulations can lead to FDA warnings, fines or product recalls.
questions.question:
Describe aseptic processing and its environmental control: (a) aseptic processing versus terminal sterilization, (b) cleanroom design and air quality, (c) environmental monitoring methods.
(d) Give the principle, procedure and interpretation of environmental monitoring and media fills.
(e) Explain how and why contamination or failure occurs in aseptic processing and how it is controlled.
