questions.question: The outer fibrocartilaginous rim of the intervertebral disc that attaches to the cartilaginous end plate is called what?
A physiotherapist uses the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) to interpret outcome measure change in a patient following lumbar stabilisation programme. The MCID is best defined as:
questions.explanation: The MCID represents the smallest change in an outcome measure score that the patient perceives as meaningful and beneficial, distinguishing it from changes that are statistically significant but clinically trivial. For example, a 2-point change on the Oswestry Disability Index may be statistically significant but if below the MCID of approximately 10 points, does not represent a meaningful clinical change from the patient's perspective. Physiotherapists use MCID to determine whether observed improvements justify continuation of a treatment approach and to set clinically meaningful treatment goals rather than purely numerical targets.
options: The smallest change that patients perceive as beneficial and meaningful to their condition
The smallest change that exceeds the measurement error of the assessment instrument
The statistically significant change in score demonstrated in randomised controlled trials
The largest change in score that can occur due to measurement error and chance alone
The average change score achieved by all patients completing a standardised rehabilitation programme

questions.explanation: The 'other' or non-mechanical syndrome category includes conditions such as spinal stenosis, hip disorders, sacroiliac disorders, and pregnancy-related low back pain. This subgroup accounts for less than three percent of cases and does not fit the three mechanical syndromes. Mechanical diagnosis and therapy techniques are not expected to resolve these conditions.
questions.question: Which condition falls under the McKenzie 'other', or non-mechanical, syndrome category?
Following Myofascial Release, which additional intervention is recommended to support new movement patterns?
questions.explanation: Strengthening should also occur following myofascial release to enhance neuromuscular reeducation. This promotes new, more efficient movement patterns once tissue extensibility has improved. Acute cases may resolve in a few treatments, while longer-standing conditions take more time.

questions.question: A physiotherapist applies a high-velocity low-amplitude thrust to a patient's lumbar spine. This technique is classified as:
options: Grade I mobilisation within early range of movement
Grade II oscillation not reaching tissue resistance
Manipulation beyond voluntary range within anatomical limit
Grade IV small amplitude movement at end of range
Grade III large-amplitude movement into resistance
questions.explanation: Manipulation involves a passive high-velocity low-amplitude thrust applied beyond the patient's voluntary range of motion but within the anatomical limit, distinguishing it from mobilisation techniques. Mobilisation uses oscillatory or sustained low-velocity movements within or up to the limit of range, while manipulation uses a sudden thrust that the patient cannot prevent. Physiotherapists must ensure informed consent, absence of contraindications, and clinical justification before applying manipulative techniques.

The Quick Test asks the standing patient to squat as far as possible, bounce two to three times, and return to standing. This action quickly screens the ankles, knees, hips, and sacrum for pathology. Caution must be exercised in patients with knee or ankle osteoarthritis and in pregnant women.
questions.question: During the lumbar 'Quick Test', the patient performs which functional movement?

questions.explanation: Among its indications, MET is used to correct postural imbalance by restoring more balanced muscle function around joints. It also improves musculoskeletal function and addresses joint dysfunction in regions such as the spine and pelvis. Restoring muscle balance supports more sustainable postural correction over time.
questions.question: MET is indicated for improving postural imbalance primarily by addressing what underlying issue?

questions.explanation: Mobilisation comprises a series of passive movements that stay within the normal range of motion. It is a slower, more controlled process intended to improve biomechanical elasticity. Unlike manipulation, the patient can typically stop a mobilisation technique.
questions.question: Mobilisation differs from manipulation primarily because mobilisation does not exceed what?
A patient with lateral epicondylitis is prescribed eccentric wrist extensor exercises. The rationale for eccentric loading in tendinopathy rehabilitation is that it:
questions.explanation: Eccentric exercises, particularly the Alfredson protocol for Achilles and Curwin-Stanish modifications for other tendons, promote beneficial tendon remodelling by stimulating tenocyte proliferation, increasing production of type I collagen, and improving the organisation of collagen fibres within the dysfunctional tendinopathic tissue. The mechanical tensile loading during eccentric contraction also appears to interrupt the neovascularisation and neuronal in-growth associated with tendinopathic pain, and may reduce expression of pain mediators including substance P and glutamate in the pathological tendon tissue.
options: Reduces tendon blood supply preventing further neovascularisation and pain production
Elongates the iliotibial band reducing compressive lateral epicondylar bursitis symptoms
Stretches the long head of biceps reducing tensile stress on the common extensor origin
Produces anaesthesia of the lateral epicondyle through repetitive mechanoceptor desensitisation
Promotes therapeutic tendon remodelling by stimulating collagen synthesis and organisation

questions.question: During examination, a physiotherapist finds that the shoulder reaches an abrupt hard end-feel at 60 degrees of elevation. This end-feel most suggests:
options: Normal capsular end-feel indicating full range has been achieved appropriately
Soft tissue approximation from large deltoid bulk limiting further motion
Muscle spasm end-feel associated with acute inflammatory joint condition
Springy block suggesting intra-articular loose body or disc derangement
Bony or capsular block requiring further mobilisation at progressive grades
questions.explanation: A hard or bony end-feel occurring prematurely well before expected range limits indicates pathological mechanical obstruction such as osteophyte impingement, loose body, or severely contracted capsule. Normal bony end-feel occurs only at end of normal range in structures such as elbow extension. An abrupt hard end-feel at only 60 degrees of shoulder elevation is clearly pathological and requires further investigation including neuroimaging or orthopaedic referral to exclude structural joint pathology before applying high-grade mobilisation techniques.

questions.question: Myofascial Release is best described as a specialised form of what intervention?
questions.explanation: Myofascial Release is a group of techniques used to relieve soft tissue from the abnormal grip of tight fascia, functioning as a specialised form of stretching. Fascia forms a continuous connective tissue network running throughout the body. Damage in one section can therefore impact fascia in sites away from the affected area.

The vertebral column contains 24 pre-sacral vertebrae comprising 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, and 5 lumbar segments. These mobile segments precede the fused sacrum and coccyx. Stability is further provided by ligaments, muscles, and bone shape.
questions.question: How many pre-sacral vertebrae allow movement and render the vertebral column flexible?

questions.explanation: Joint mobilisation stimulates mechanoreceptors (types I-III) in joint capsules and periarticular tissues, generating large-diameter afferent A-beta fibre signals that activate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn and close the pain gate according to Melzack and Wall's gate control theory. Additionally, supraspinal mechanisms involving the periaqueductal grey and descending noradrenergic and serotonergic inhibitory pathways contribute to immediate post-mobilisation hypoalgesia. Understanding this neurophysiological rationale helps physiotherapists explain pain relief mechanisms to patients and justify treatment choices.
options: Release of synovial fluid lubricating inflamed articular cartilage surfaces
Reduction of intra-articular adhesions improving range of motion mechanically
Structural realignment of zygapophyseal joints correcting mechanical dysfunction
Mechanoreceptor stimulation activating large-diameter afferent pain gate closure
Anterior capsular stretching releasing intra-articular disc fragments posteriorly
questions.question: A physiotherapist performs Grade III-IV lumbar mobilisation and the patient reports immediate pain reduction. This analgesia is primarily mediated by:
In Mulligan's treatment principles, the applied passive accessory glide must always be what?
questions.explanation: The passive accessory joint mobilisation applied within Mulligan's concept must itself be pain free, following Kaltenborn's principles. The therapist identifies a comparable sign, as described by Maitland, before applying this glide. The treatment plane and grade are then refined through trial of parallel or perpendicular glides.

questions.question: The Thomas test is used in physiotherapy examination to assess flexibility of the hip flexors. A positive Thomas test is observed when:
questions.explanation: The Thomas test is performed with the patient supine, bringing one knee to the chest to flatten the lumbar lordosis and eliminate pelvic tilt compensation. A positive result occurs when the contralateral thigh rises from the table surface during this manoeuvre, indicating that hip flexor tightness (iliopsoas, rectus femoris) is preventing the hip from achieving full extension range. If the knee of the tested side also bends, rectus femoris tightness is indicated. Accurately identifying hip flexor contracture versus lumbar lordosis compensation is essential for correctly directing the stretching and mobility component of rehabilitation programmes for patients with anterior hip impingement, lumbar spine dysfunction, and postural deviations.
options: Hip abduction occurs spontaneously during hip extension in the side-lying position
The patient reports anterior hip pain on full active hip flexion in the lying position
The tested hip elevates from the table with maximum contralateral hip flexion to chest
The lumbar spine remains flat while the tested thigh falls below the horizontal plane
The contralateral hip cannot be fully flexed to the chest indicating low back stiffness
Local cervical pain only on lateral flexion toward the tested side without radiation
Reproduction of ipsilateral upper limb radicular symptoms on compression and ipsilateral rotation
Bilateral shoulder elevation weakness reproduced by axial compression of the cervical spine
Relief of arm pain with distraction confirming the compressive aetiology of symptoms
Increased range of cervical rotation on the contralateral side indicating disc height loss
questions.question: During clinical examination of a patient with suspected right-sided cervical disc herniation, the Spurling test is performed. A positive result is indicated by:
questions.explanation: The Spurling test (cervical compression test) is performed by extending and laterally rotating the patient's cervical spine toward the symptomatic side, then applying downward axial compression. A positive result reproduces ipsilateral upper limb radicular pain or paraesthesia in the distribution of the suspected nerve root, indicating neural foraminal compression or cervical disc herniation. The test is highly specific (approximately 93%) for cervical radiculopathy, meaning a positive result strongly suggests the diagnosis, though its sensitivity is moderate (approximately 50%), so a negative result does not exclude radiculopathy.

The highest-quality evidence from Cochrane systematic reviews and international fall prevention guidelines demonstrates that the most effective falls prevention programmes for community-dwelling elderly individuals combine multiple evidence-based components: progressive strength training targeting lower extremity muscles, challenging balance exercises with progressive difficulty (eyes closed, unstable surfaces, dual-task), home hazard identification and modification, medication review to reduce high-risk drugs including benzodiazepines and antihypertensives, and vitamin D supplementation when deficiency is present. Single-component programmes are less effective than multicomponent approaches, reflecting the multifactorial nature of falls in the elderly population.
options: Strength and balance exercise combined with home hazard modification and medication review
Flexibility and relaxation exercises exclusively with balance training introduced only after 8 weeks
Education about falls only as knowledge is the most powerful modifiable risk factor for falls
Walking and cycling only as aerobic exercise is the primary evidence-based modality
Individual strength testing followed by prescribed rest periods to prevent overexertion injuries
questions.question: A physiotherapist implements a comprehensive falls prevention programme for community-dwelling elderly patients. The most evidence-supported multicomponent programme structure includes:

options: Progress immediately to Grade III stretching
Add a sustained Grade III distraction
Reduce the amplitude to Grade I oscillations
questions.explanation: If increased pain and sensitivity occur after initial treatment, the amplitude should be reduced to gentle Grade I oscillations. If the joint instead remains the same or improves, the same maneuver may be repeated or progressed toward sustained stretching. This stepwise reassessment guides safe progression of mobilisation dosage.
questions.question: Following an initial mobilisation, if the patient reports increased pain and sensitivity the next day, what adjustment is recommended?

questions.explanation: The patient holds the gentle isometric contraction against resistance for about five to ten seconds. After this hold, the patient relaxes and the practitioner stretches the muscle further. This process is repeated several times to achieve progressive relaxation and lengthening.
questions.question: During Post-Isometric Relaxation, the patient's gentle contraction is typically held for approximately how long?

Rheumatoid Arthritis and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Q1–7

Osteoarthritis and Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH): Q17–23

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clinical course: psoriasis of the skin or nails may precede or follow joint involvement, and the severity of joint and skin disease is often discordant; the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of fingers and toes are especially affected, with asymmetric involvement of large and small joints, including sacroiliac joints and the spine.
• Joint and skin symptoms may lessen or worsen together; arthritic remissions tend to be more frequent, rapid and complete than in rheumatoid arthritis, but progression to chronic arthritis and crippling deformity may occur.
• Deformities: inflammation of fingers or toes may lead to sausage-shaped (dactylitic) deformities not seen in rheumatoid arthritis; arthritis mutilans (destruction of multiple hand joints with telescoping of the digits) can occur in severe disease; enthesopathy (Achilles tendinitis, patellar tendinitis, elbow epicondyles, vertebral spinous processes) causes pain, and back pain is often accompanied by asymmetric syndesmophytes of the spine.

(b)
Extra-articular manifestations: psoriasis of the skin, most notably on the knees, elbows and scalp; pitting, ridging or dents in finger/toenails; recurrent redness and pain in one eye; inflammatory bowel disease; and associations with ischaemic heart disease and fatty liver.

(c)
• A combination of gentle manual therapy and soft tissue massage has been found effective, alongside joint flexibility exercises and muscle strength exercises.
• Hydrotherapy, including strengthening and aerobic exercises, is used, along with heat and cold therapies to ease joint pain and stiffness.
• Assistive devices can help the patient perform daily tasks, and life/activity modification helps conserve energy and protect joints.
• The overall goal is to reduce pain, restore or improve mobility, make it easier to perform everyday tasks, and prevent disability, with regular exercise helping to keep the joints functioning properly.

(d)
• Basis of deformity: sustained inflammation at tendon/ligament insertions (enthesitis) and within small joints (DIP, digits) leads to soft tissue swelling that produces the characteristic sausage digit, and, when severe and prolonged, to destructive changes (arthritis mutilans) with telescoping of digits.
• Asymmetric spinal and sacroiliac joint involvement with syndesmophyte formation contributes to back pain and reduced spinal mobility.
• Because joint and skin disease severity can be discordant, functional limitation is not always predictable from the visible skin disease alone, so joints must be assessed independently.
• The overall functional deficit therefore results from a combination of dactylitic joint swelling, enthesitis pain, potential destructive arthritis mutilans, and spinal involvement, all of which physiotherapy aims to manage through flexibility, strengthening, hydrotherapy and joint protection before permanent deformity develops.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the clinical course and deformities of psoriatic arthritis.
(b) Describe the extra-articular manifestations.
(c) State the principles of physiotherapy management for this condition.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Gonococcal arthritis (disseminated gonococcal infection).

(b)
Problem list: Impairments – joint pain, swelling, warmth and restricted movement (commonly wrists, ankles, hands, feet), tenosynovitis, skin lesions, fever/malaise. Activity limitations – difficulty weight-bearing or using the affected hand/wrist, reduced grip and mobility during the acute phase. Participation restrictions – inability to work/study or care for self during hospitalisation and acute treatment; risk of reinfection affecting sexual health and relationships.

(c)
Treatment plan: after antibiotic therapy with joint aspiration/drainage or arthroscopy, physiotherapy aims to strengthen the joint and surrounding muscles weakened by inactivity, increase ROM, decrease pain and stiffness, and increase cardiovascular levels; treatment includes cryotherapy, strengthening exercises, hydrotherapy, and cardiovascular activities; gentle mobilisation of the joint can begin about five days after medical treatment once the patient is responding well.

(d)
Precautions/contraindications: in the acute phase, the joint must be immobilised (temporary splinting) to manage pain and reduce further joint damage until proper antibiotic treatment has taken effect; avoid aggressive mobilisation before the patient is responding to antibiotics.

(e)
Patient education/joint protection/energy conservation: educate the patient on how to properly protect the affected joint; advise on the importance of completing antibiotic treatment and follow-up (including retesting for reinfection, and referral of sexual partners for evaluation); temporary splinting to prevent unwanted movement while the joint heals.
questions.question:
(a) A sexually active young adult presents with fever, painful/swollen wrist and ankle joints, and a pustular skin rash on the extremities, with a recent history of urethral discharge. What is the probable diagnosis?
(b) List the problem list – impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions.
(c) Outline the treatment plan including modalities and exercise.
(d) State the precautions and contraindications.
(e) Describe the patient education, joint protection and energy conservation advice.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) – an autoimmune, chronic inflammatory disease affecting joints, fitting the criteria of morning stiffness lasting over one hour, arthritis of three or more joint areas, hand joint involvement, and symmetric arthritis.

(b)
Pathological basis: RA is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovium; immune cells migrate into joints and produce cytokines/chemokines that activate more immune cells; B cells produce self-reactive anti-IgG antibodies; hyperplasia of the synovial membrane occurs (fibroblast-like synoviocytes proliferate), synovial fluid volume increases causing swelling and impaired mobility, and chronic progressive inflammation leads to joint damage, cartilage erosion and bone erosion.

(c)
• Physiotherapy assessment – Subjective: history of pain, swelling, warmth, redness, stiffness (especially morning or after inactivity), fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, fever; ask about joint distribution (polyarthritis, symmetry), sleep disturbance and impact on daily activities.
• Objective: observation for swelling/redness/deformity; palpation for warmth and tenderness; active/passive ROM testing; note limping, grip and dexterity loss; check for rheumatoid nodules; correlate with blood tests (RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP) and X-ray findings (erosions, loss of density) already carried out by the physician.
• Outcome measures: pain scales (numerical rating/visual analogue scale) and disease/region-specific functional outcome measures.

(d)
Management/goals: Short-term goals – reduce pain, increase range of motion, increase muscle strength, prevent deformity. Long-term goals – restore/maintain optimal physical functioning, correct deformity, reintegrate patient into community/work. Interventions: physical modalities (TENS, hydrotherapy, superficial/deep heat and cold, compression gloves), ROM exercises (active preferred, passive only if acutely inflamed), gentle strengthening (isometric during acute flares), cardiorespiratory exercise when not in the acute phase, patient education, joint protection and energy conservation.
questions.question:
(a) A 45-year-old woman presents with pain, swelling and stiffness affecting the wrists, MCP and PIP joints of both hands symmetrically, worse in the morning and lasting more than one hour before improving, present for several weeks. She also reports fatigue, poor appetite and low-grade fever. What is the most probable diagnosis?
(b) Explain the pathological basis of the joint changes seen in this condition.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy assessment you would carry out, including the subjective and objective findings and outcome measures you would use.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management and goals for this patient.

(a) Define rheumatoid arthritis and describe its aetiology.
(b) Describe the pathology of rheumatoid arthritis.
(c) Describe the clinical features of rheumatoid arthritis.
(d) State the diagnostic criteria for rheumatoid arthritis.
(e) Explain why rheumatoid arthritis is commoner in women than in men.
(f) Distinguish between rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition/aetiology: RA is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the synovial lining of joints; exact cause unknown but genetic and environmental factors (smoking, obesity, vitamin D deficiency, changes in microbiota, HLA type) are implicated, with viral infection (e.g. Epstein-Barr virus) and trauma as possible triggers.

(b)
Pathology: immune cells migrate into joints and produce cytokines/chemokines; B cells make self-reactive anti-IgG antibodies; synovial membrane hyperplasia occurs (proliferating fibroblast-like synoviocytes) with increased synovial fluid; granulation tissue (pannus) erodes cartilage, bone and ligaments, and tendon sheaths become inflamed and may fray.

(c)
Clinical features: symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints (hands, wrists, feet) with pain, swelling, warmth, redness and morning stiffness over one hour; fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever; rheumatoid nodules; extra-articular effects on eyes (Sjögren's), lungs (pleuritis), heart (pericarditis), spleen (Felty's syndrome) and blood vessels (vasculitis); flares alternate with remission.

(d)
• Diagnostic criteria: morning stiffness over one hour; arthritis of three or more joint areas; hand joint involvement; symmetric arthritis – criteria 1 to 4 must be present for at least six weeks.
• Diagnostic criteria (continued): rheumatoid nodules; positive rheumatoid factor; radiographic changes showing erosions or periarticular osteopenia in the hand/wrist.

(e)
Clinical basis for female predominance: RA occurs in 0.5-1% of people in the Western world, predominantly women aged 30-50, and is two to three times more common in women than men; genetics, hormonal and environmental factors and family history contribute to this higher female risk.

(f)
• Age of onset: RA begins from 15-50 years, whereas OA usually begins after age 40.
• Progression: RA may develop suddenly within weeks/months, whereas OA develops slowly over many years in response to mechanical stress.
• Manifestations: RA causes inflammatory synovitis with irreversible structural damage to cartilage and bone (pannus, erosion), whereas OA shows cartilage degradation, altered joint architecture and osteophyte formation without primary inflammation.
• Joint involvement: RA usually affects many joints bilaterally/symmetrically (MCP, PIP, wrists, elbows, shoulders, cervical spine, MTP, ankle), whereas OA affects fewer joints, usually asymmetrically (DIP, PIP, 1st CMC of hands, cervical/lumbar spine, hips, knees, 1st MTP).
• Joint signs/symptoms: RA shows redness, warmth, swelling and prolonged morning stiffness with pain increasing with activity, whereas OA shows morning stiffness usually under 30 minutes with pain increasing with weight-bearing/strenuous activity and loss of ROM.
• Systemic signs: RA is associated with general sickness, fatigue, weight loss, fever and possible rheumatoid nodules/ocular/respiratory/haematological/cardiac symptoms, whereas OA has none of these systemic features.

questions.question:
(a) An 82-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on immunosuppressive medication develops sudden severe pain, swelling, warmth and restricted movement of the knee with fever. What is the probable diagnosis, and what risk factors predisposed her?
(b) What complications can arise if this condition is not adequately treated?
(c) Describe physiotherapy management options appropriate to the different stages of the disease, and justify which you would prioritise for this patient now.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Septic (pyogenic) arthritis. Risk factors: advanced age (over 80 years), pre-existing joint disease (rheumatoid arthritis increases risk), and immunosuppressive medications taken for RA, which make infection more likely and can also make diagnosis difficult because signs/symptoms mimic an RA flare.

(b)
Complications: bone destruction and pathological joint dislocation, cartilage destruction leading to fibrosis or bony ankylosis, secondary osteoarthritis (in adults, from partial joint destruction), septicaemia, and (in children) growth disturbance presenting as localised deformity or bone shortening; if untreated, infection can spread to underlying bone or burst out of the joint to form abscesses and sinuses.

(c)
• Physiotherapy management by stage: acute stage – immobilisation to control pain since weight-bearing is often too painful, with the joint splinted or held in a functional position for passive ROM; heat modalities are avoided in the acute phase or before antibiotic treatment has begun. Once the patient responds well after about 5 days of treatment – mobilisation can begin, using electrotherapy (ice, hydrotherapy, heat, TENS, IFT, pulsed ultrasound) to manage pain and stiffness, followed by patient education on joint protection.
• Justification: since this patient is in the acute, actively inflamed stage, immobilisation/splinting and pain control take priority over mobilisation, which should only begin once she is shown to be responding well to antibiotic treatment.

questions.question:
(a) A 26-year-old man presents with several months of nocturnal low back pain and morning stiffness that eases with activity, kyphotic posture, and diminished chest expansion; he has a first-degree relative with a similar back condition. What is the probable "spot diagnosis"?
(b) What predisposing factors make a patient likely to develop this condition?
(c) Describe the pathophysiology and clinical features.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis.

(b)
Predisposing factors: male sex (3 times more frequent in men), onset typically between ages 20-40, presence of the HLA-B27 allele (present in about 90% of affected white patients, with about 20% risk in HLA-B27-positive first-degree relatives), and a first-degree relative with the disease (10-20 times more common among first-degree relatives).

(c)
• Pathophysiology: probably immune-mediated inflammation affecting the sacroiliac joints, spine and spinal entheses; inflammation gradually spreads to the joints between vertebrae (spondylitis), and over time new bone formation fuses vertebrae, producing ankylosis; other joints (shoulders, hips, occasionally knees) may be involved, and costovertebral involvement restricts chest movement.
• Clinical features: inflammatory back pain (often nocturnal), morning stiffness relieved by activity, paraspinal muscle spasm, flexed/bent-over posture (kyphosis) that eases pain, diminished chest expansion, low-grade fever, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, anaemia; systemic manifestations in about a third of patients include recurrent acute anterior uveitis, and rarely cardiovascular (aortitis, conduction defects), pulmonary or neurological complications; in late stages, accentuated kyphosis, loss of lumbar lordosis and fixed bent-forward posture with compromised pulmonary function may occur.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: exercise combining muscle strengthening, ROM, flexibility and cardiorespiratory work (land- or water-based, individual or supervised); Global Posture Re-education postures to stretch shortened muscle chains; patient education; manual therapy; modalities (short wave, TENS, infrared); balneotherapy/hydrotherapy for fatigue, pain, stiffness, function and wellbeing.

questions.question:
(a) A 70-year-old woman on long-term diuretics presents with chronic pain in several joints, with hard, whitish, non-tender lumps over the toes, elbow (olecranon) and ear helix that occasionally break down and discharge chalky material. What is the probable diagnosis?
(b) Explain the pathological basis of the joint and soft tissue changes.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy assessment for this patient.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management and goals.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Chronic tophaceous gout – the description of tophi (deposits of urate crystals) at the toes, olecranon and ear helix, developing in an older woman on diuretics (a recognised risk factor and cause of earlier tophus development), is classic.

(b)
Pathological basis: gout arises from deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints (causing an inflammatory response) and in soft tissues (where they do not, forming tophi); hyperuricaemia results mainly from renal underexcretion of uric acid (about 90% of cases) or overproduction of purines; tophi develop after about a decade in untreated chronic gouty arthritis and can grow within joints, damaging cartilage and bone and causing regular daily pain; urate is more likely to crystallise in the cooler, peripheral parts of the body.

(c)
• Physiotherapy assessment – Subjective: history of previous acute attacks (podagra), pattern of joint involvement, presence of visible lumps, functional limitation.
• Objective: inspection and palpation of joints and soft tissue for tophi, swelling, warmth, tenderness; active/passive ROM; correlate with investigations such as joint aspiration/synovial fluid analysis for urate crystals, serum uric acid, and imaging (ultrasound/CT for crystal deposits, X-ray for chronic bone/joint damage).

(d)
Management/goals: physiotherapists should be aware that patients with gout/hyperuricaemia should be referred for medical evaluation before treatment, particularly to exclude a septic joint. Goals are pain relief and preservation of function. During acute exacerbations – reinforcement of management, splinting/orthotics/assistive devices to protect affected joints. During intercritical phases – maintenance of ROM, strength and function, assistance creating a suitable exercise routine, and help with weight control, alongside general lifestyle advice (healthy diet, physical activity, joint protection via low-impact activities such as walking, cycling and swimming).

questions.question:
(a) Describe the history, examination and investigations used in assessing a patient with rheumatoid arthritis.
(b) What outcome measures/monitoring would be used?
(c) State the physiotherapy goals and modalities in managing rheumatoid arthritis.
(d) Explain why rheumatoid arthritis may involve organs other than the joints, and how this contributes to functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• History: ask about joint pain, swelling, warmth, redness, deformity and stiffness (especially in the morning or after prolonged sitting), pattern of joint involvement (polyarthritis, symmetry), fatigue, poor appetite/weight loss, fever, dry eyes, and chest pain.
• Physical examination/history taking follows a structured approach: history taking, observation, palpation, and specific/general examination.
• Investigations: blood tests (rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibody, antinuclear antibody, ESR, CRP), imaging (X-ray as baseline and to monitor progression, ultrasound, MRI), and arthrocentesis (joint aspiration) for synovial fluid analysis, which can also relieve pain and allow corticosteroid injection.

(b)
Outcome measures/monitoring: disease progression is monitored using American College of Rheumatology criteria based on changes in specific symptoms and laboratory findings; pain and function can be tracked with standard pain scales and functional outcome measures.

(c)
• Physiotherapy goals – short term: reduce pain, increase range of motion, increase muscle strength, and prevent deformity.
• Physiotherapy goals – long term: restore or maintain optimal physical functioning, correct any deformity, and restore/reintegrate the patient back into their community or work.
• Modalities: physical modalities such as diathermy, massage, TENS, hydrotherapy, counterirritants, topical ointments, compression gloves, superficial and deep heat and cold, and acupuncture.
• Therapeutic ultrasound and balneotherapy/spa therapy are also used; exercise (ROM, strengthening, cardiorespiratory) is prescribed according to disease activity.

(d)
• Basis of extra-articular involvement: RA is a systemic autoimmune disease, so besides synovial joints it can affect the eyes (Sjögren's syndrome causing dryness), lungs (pleuritis), heart (pericarditis), spleen (Felty's syndrome, causing reduced white cell count and infection risk), skin/subcutaneous tissue (rheumatoid nodules) and blood vessels (vasculitis).
• These extra-articular effects occur because the same autoimmune, inflammatory process that attacks synovial tissue can also target other tissues rich in connective tissue or subject to immune complex deposition.
• Functional deficit therefore results not only from joint pain, swelling, deformity and loss of range of motion, but also from systemic effects: fatigue, anaemia (from chronic inflammation suppressing red cell release), fever, and depression secondary to chronic illness.
• Because of this multisystem impact, physiotherapy management for RA must be planned alongside overall disease monitoring and medical management, addressing both joint-specific goals and awareness of systemic factors (fatigue, cardiopulmonary involvement) that affect exercise tolerance and rehabilitation planning.

(a)
Condition/stage: Gonococcal arthritis (disseminated gonococcal infection), presenting as the bacteraemic stage (arthritis-dermatitis syndrome) – positive blood culture picture with characteristic dermatitis and migratory arthralgia – which may progress to the septic joint stage (oligo-arthritis with positive joint culture) or remain an indeterminate variable presentation.

(b)
Structures affected: synovial membrane/joint (commonly knees, ankles, wrists and elbows), tendon sheaths (tenosynovitis), and skin (petechiae, macules, papules, pustules, vesicles, bullae); rarely, disease can progress to involve the liver (perihepatitis), meninges (meningitis) or heart valves (endocarditis).

(c)
Differential diagnoses: other causes of septic (pyogenic) arthritis (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus), reactive arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, viral arthritis, and gout/pseudogout, since joint pain, swelling, redness and systemic symptoms can occur in each.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: physiotherapy is not started until after antibiotic therapy with joint aspiration/drainage or arthroscopy, since the acute joint must first be treated medically and immobilised to control pain and limit further joint damage; once the patient is responding to treatment, gentle mobilisation can begin around 5 days later to preserve function and reduce ongoing disability, using cryotherapy, strengthening exercises, hydrotherapy, cardiovascular activity and temporary splinting, alongside education on joint protection.
questions.question:
(a) A sexually active 19-year-old woman presents with fever, a few days of migrating joint pain, tenosynovitis of the wrist, and a sparse pustular rash on the extremities. Joint aspiration and culture, arthrocentesis, and blood tests (raised WBC, ESR, CRP) are requested. What condition and stage of the condition do these findings suggest?
(b) What structures are affected in this condition?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses to consider?
(d) Explain your clinical reasoning for prescribing physiotherapy for this patient.

(a) A 30-year-old man presents three weeks after an episode of dysentery with asymmetric arthritis of the knee and ankle, painless ulcers in the mouth, and conjunctivitis. What is the probable "spot diagnosis"?
(b) What predisposing factors make a patient likely to develop this condition?
(c) Describe the pathophysiology and clinical features.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome).

(b)
Predisposing factors: male sex and age 20-40 years, recent genitourinary infection (Chlamydia trachomatis) or enteric infection (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter), and the HLA-B27 genotype (present in about 75% of patients with Reiter's arthritis); it is more common in white than black people, related to the higher frequency of HLA-B27, and patients with HIV have an increased risk.

(c)
• Pathophysiology: reactive arthritis is an RF-seronegative, HLA-B27-linked autoimmune condition that develops as a reaction to infection elsewhere in the body (cross-reactivity), marked by inflammatory synovitis and erosion at ligament/tendon insertion sites (enthesitis); organisms cannot usually be cultured from joint fluid despite evidence of microbial antigens in the synovium.
• Clinical features: the classic triad of arthritis (asymmetric, oligoarticular, lower-limb predominant, sometimes "sausage" digits), conjunctivitis/uveitis, and urethritis/cervicitis; enthesitis (plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinitis); mucocutaneous lesions (balanitis circinata, keratoderma blennorrhagicum); constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss); low back pain from sacroiliitis in severe disease.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: bed rest in the acute phase; NSAIDs for pain and inflammation; range-of-motion exercises and strengthening exercises to restore joint function; vigorous exercise is discouraged for the first few months after resolution of the syndrome.

(a)
• Definition/aetiology: septic arthritis is inflammation of a synovial membrane with purulent effusion into the joint capsule, most often due to bacterial infection (occasionally viral or fungal); it is a rheumatologic emergency because joint destruction occurs rapidly; infection may begin from an open wound, trauma, surgery or unsterile injection, or by organisms travelling through the bloodstream to the joint.
• Predisposing factors: extremes of age, existing joint disease (OA, gout, RA, lupus), immunosuppressive medication, fragile/broken skin (including psoriasis/eczema or infected wounds), haemophilia with haemarthroses, immunocompromise (sickle cell disease, HIV, chemotherapy), weak immune system (diabetes, kidney/liver disease), intravenous drug use, previous joint surgery/prosthesis, and sexual activity (for the gonococcal form).

(b)
Pathogenesis: spread is haematogenous (most common), by direct inoculation (trauma, injection, surgery), or by direct spread from adjacent bone (more common in children, from metaphyseal osteomyelitis); bacteria settle in the vascular synovium causing acute inflammation with seropurulent exudate, and articular cartilage is eroded by bacterial and host inflammatory-cell enzymes.

(c)
Clinical features: fever, a painful, swollen, inflamed joint with restricted active and passive movement (pseudoparesis/reluctance to move), local warmth, marked tenderness, and muscle spasm; in neonates, fever may be absent, but the baby is irritable, refuses feeds, and shows loss of spontaneous limb movement and loss of hip flexion/abduction/external rotation.

(d)
Investigations: blood tests (raised white cell count, ESR over 40 mm/hr, CRP over 20 mg/dL, possible positive blood culture), synovial fluid analysis, and imaging (ultrasound, X-ray) showing narrowing of joint space and, later, subchondral erosions, sclerosis or osteonecrosis.

(e)
• Clinical basis for extremes of age: infants and older adults are most likely to develop septic arthritis, with about 50% of cases occurring in children under 5 years, reflecting immature/impaired immunity and, in children, the vascular anatomy of the growing metaphysis/epiphysis that allows spread from osteomyelitis; elderly patients (especially over 80) often have pre-existing joint disease and weakened immunity that predispose to infection.
• The overall prevalence of diagnosed bacterial arthritis among adults with acutely painful joints is estimated at 8-27%, rising further (30-70 per 100,000) in patients with immunological disorders/deficiencies or joint replacements, again reflecting reduced host defence at both age extremes.

(f)
• Cause: septic (pyogenic) arthritis is usually caused by organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus reaching the joint by the routes above, whereas gonococcal arthritis specifically results from blood dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae from a primary sexually acquired mucosal infection.
• Joint destruction: unlike Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis, gonococcal arthritis is rarely associated with joint destruction, making its prognosis generally better if treated promptly.
• Population affected: gonococcal septic arthritis affects women about three times more often than men and is most common among sexually active young adults, whereas non-gonococcal septic arthritis is most common at the extremes of age and in patients with predisposing joint or immune conditions.
• Associated features: gonococcal arthritis often presents with the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome – migratory polyarthritis, tenosynovitis and a pustular/vesicular skin rash – features not typical of ordinary pyogenic septic arthritis.
• Culture findings: in gonococcal arthritis, culture is usually positive for gonococcus from the genital tract while joint cultures tend to be negative, whereas in typical pyogenic septic arthritis the causative organism can more often be recovered directly from the joint (synovial) fluid.
questions.question:
(a) Define septic (pyogenic) arthritis and describe its aetiology.
(b) Describe its pathogenesis.
(c) Describe its clinical features.
(d) State the investigations used to support the diagnosis.
(e) Explain why septic arthritis is more common at the extremes of age.
(f) Distinguish between septic (pyogenic) arthritis and gonococcal arthritis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clinical course: urate crystals build up in and around joints for years without symptoms; when enough crystals accumulate, some spill from the cartilage into the joint space and rub against the synovium, causing a painful attack (flare) with pain, tenderness, redness, heat and swelling that comes on quickly, often at night.
• An attack usually settles within about 5-7 days (occasionally longer); episodes of intermittent painful flares are followed by long periods of remission (intercritical phase, lasting weeks to years) with no symptoms.
• If gout is left untreated, attacks can become more frequent and spread to new joints; repeated bouts can progress to chronic tophaceous gout, a worsening, destructive form of arthritis.

(b)
Deformities: chronic elevated uric acid leads to tophi – hard, painless deposits of urate crystals – commonly over the toes, back of the heel, front of the knee, backs of the fingers/wrists, around the elbow and the ears; tophi can grow within joints, damaging cartilage and bone and causing more regular daily pain; they can also become inflamed, break down and leak gritty white material.

(c)
• During an acute flare: physiotherapy focuses on reinforcement of the medical management programme and use of splinting, orthotics or other assistive devices to protect the affected joint(s); the therapist should refer any patient with gout, hyperuricaemia or a possible septic joint for medical evaluation before treatment.
• During a flare, exercise on the affected joint is avoided, as it may worsen pain; rest, elevation and ice application for about 20 minutes at a time help reduce swelling, and a walking aid may relieve pressure on the joint.
• During intercritical (symptom-free) phases: physiotherapy assists with maintenance of range of motion, strength and function, and helps the patient develop a suitable exercise routine (ROM, stretching and strengthening exercises, and aerobic exercise such as pool-based activity) and manage weight.
• Proprioception exercises are also included between flares to help maintain maximal joint function, and general lifestyle advice (healthy diet, physical activity, low-impact joint protection through walking, cycling, swimming) is reinforced throughout.

(d)
• Basis of tophi: chronic hyperuricaemia (from underexcretion or overproduction of urate) leads to ongoing deposition of monosodium urate crystals in soft tissues, where they do not provoke the same acute inflammatory response as in the joint but slowly accumulate as visible white deposits under the skin.
• Basis of joint damage: within the joint, urate crystals continue to provoke inflammation with each flare, and crystal deposits (tophi) can also form within the joint itself, progressively damaging cartilage and bone with repeated or chronic exposure.
• Because urate is more likely to crystallise in cooler, peripheral parts of the body, tophi and joint damage are concentrated in peripheral joints and soft tissues (toes, fingers, elbows, ears) rather than central/axial structures.
• Over time, this combination of intra-articular crystal-driven cartilage/bone damage and extra-articular tophus formation converts episodic acute gout into chronic tophaceous gout with persistent pain, tophi and reduced joint function, underscoring the physiotherapy shift from flare management to long-term function preservation.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the stages/clinical course of gout, from acute attack to chronic disease.
(b) Describe the deformities that develop in chronic gout.
(c) State the principles of physiotherapy management at each stage of gout.
(d) Explain the basis of the tophi and joint damage that develop.

(a) Define osteoarthritis and describe its aetiology/classification.
(b) Describe its pathology.
(c) Describe its clinical features.
(d) State the diagnostic basis for osteoarthritis.
(e) Explain why knee osteoarthritis is commoner in obese females over 50 and hip osteoarthritis is commoner in males over 40.
(f) Distinguish between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: OA is a degenerative joint disease characterised by breakdown of articular cartilage and proliferative changes of surrounding bones, with synovial inflammation; it is a chronic musculoskeletal disease without systemic involvement. Classification: primary OA (etiology unknown, direct correlation with the ageing process, onset after 40 years) and secondary OA (etiology known – trauma, previous joint disorders such as congenital hip dislocation, infection, inflammatory disease such as RA, metabolic disease such as gout, haematologic disease such as haemophilia, or endocrine disease such as diabetes mellitus).

(b)
Pathology: cartilage properties and biomechanical problems underlie disease onset; chondrocyte function balances degradative enzymes (metalloproteases) against inhibitors, and this balance is disturbed by ageing, genetic and local biochemical factors, with IL-1, degradative enzymes and synovial inflammation together causing breakdown of cartilage.

(c)
Clinical features: pain related to use, worsening during the day, minimal morning stiffness (under 20 minutes) and gelling after inactivity, decreased range of motion, joint instability, bony enlargement, deformity restricting ADLs, crepitus, and variable swelling/instability.

(d)
Diagnostic basis: no pathognomonic laboratory findings exist for OA (laboratory analysis is used for differential diagnosis); diagnosis rests on clinical findings (joint pain) plus radiologic findings (osteophytes, joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, bone cysts), graded using the Kellgren-Lawrence classification (G1 normal to G4 severe).

(e)
• Clinical basis – knee OA: knee OA is more common in obese females over 50 years of age; excess body weight increases mechanical loading on the weight-bearing knee joint, and OA of the knee is found in 70% of the population over 60 years of age, consistent with age and mechanical loading as key drivers.
• Clinical basis – hip OA: hip OA is more common in males over 40 years of age, presenting with pain in the hip, gluteal and groin areas radiating to the knee, mechanical pain and limited walking function, again consistent with age-related, mechanically driven joint degeneration though with a different sex/joint predilection than knee OA.

(f)
• Age of onset: OA usually begins after age 40, whereas RA begins from ages 15-50.
• Progression: OA develops slowly over many years in response to mechanical stress, whereas RA may develop suddenly within weeks or months.
• Manifestations: OA shows cartilage degradation, altered joint architecture and osteophyte formation, whereas RA shows inflammatory synovitis and irreversible structural damage to cartilage and bone.
• Joint involvement: OA affects few joints, usually asymmetrically (DIP, PIP, 1st CMC of hands, cervical/lumbar spine, hips, knees, 1st MTP), whereas RA usually affects many joints, often bilaterally (MCP, PIP, wrists, elbows, shoulders, cervical spine, MTP, ankle).
• Joint signs/symptoms: OA morning stiffness is usually under 30 minutes with pain increasing with weight-bearing/activity and loss of ROM, whereas RA shows redness, warmth, swelling and prolonged morning stiffness with pain increasing with activity.
• Systemic signs: OA has none, whereas RA is associated with general sickness, fatigue, weight loss, fever, and possible rheumatoid nodules and ocular/respiratory/haematological/cardiac symptoms.

questions.question:
(a) A 65-year-old man presents with bilateral knee pain that is worse with activity and improves with rest, bony enlargement of the knees, crepitus, and reduced quadriceps strength affecting his ability to climb stairs. What is the probable diagnosis?
(b) List the problem list – impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions.
(c) Outline the treatment plan including modalities and exercise.
(d) State the precautions and contraindications.
(e) Describe the patient education, joint protection and energy conservation advice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osteoarthritis of the knees.

(b)
Problem list: Impairments – pain with mechanical stress/activity (and, in advanced stages, at rest), stiffness after activity, limited ROM (especially extension in later stages), muscle weakness (notably quadriceps), decreased proprioception and balance, bony enlargement/deformity. Activity limitations – difficulty with stair climbing, prolonged walking/standing. Participation restrictions – limitation in activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental ADLs, reduced participation in work/social activity.

(c)
Treatment plan: patient education and a home exercise programme; active ROM and joint-play mobilisation techniques to decrease stiffness; splinting/assistive equipment to minimise mechanical stress or correct faulty biomechanics, combined with strengthening of supporting muscles; stretching of restricted muscle/joint/soft tissue; low-intensity resistance exercise and muscle re-education to improve neuromuscular control, strength and endurance; balance training; non-impact/low-impact aerobic exercise (e.g. cycling, swimming) for physical conditioning; modalities such as heat/cold, electroanalgesia, ultrasound and core stabilisation exercises.

(d)
Precautions/contraindications: alternate activity with rest periods; avoid excessive mechanical stress and deforming forces on the joint; monitor for pain at rest in advanced disease, which indicates involvement of subchondral bone, synovium and joint capsule, and requires adjustment of activity level.

(e)
Patient education/joint protection/energy conservation: teach the patient about deforming forces and how to prevent them; reinforce the home exercise programme to minimise symptoms; advise on assistive devices and appropriate footwear; alternate activities and interspersing rest to conserve energy and protect the joint; weight loss where relevant to reduce joint loading.

(a)
• History: ask about age (mostly affects the fifth decade and older; earlier onset under 40 suggests a secondary cause), pattern of joint pain (single or multiple joints), speed of onset (insidious over several days for acute pseudogout), and any history of trauma, joint surgery, or conditions such as hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis or magnesium deficiency.
• Examination: inspect and palpate for joint swelling, warmth and tenderness, commonly at the knee, wrist, elbow and ankle; assess active and passive range of motion.
• Investigations: radiographs show chondrocalcinosis (calcium deposits) in the hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage of the knees, the fibrocartilage of the wrist's triangular ligament, the symphysis pubis and the acetabular labrum of the hips; joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis can identify calcium pyrophosphate crystals.

(b)
Outcome measures/monitoring: reassessment of pain, swelling and range of motion, and monitoring of response to analgesics/NSAIDs/corticosteroid injections and to physiotherapy modalities over the course of a flare.

(c)
• Goals: reduce pain and swelling during flares, and maintain/restore joint range of motion, strength and function between flares.
• Modalities: analgesics, NSAIDs and corticosteroid injections are used medically; physiotherapy modalities used in conjunction during joint flares include ice/cold compress, ultrasound, and low-intensity laser therapy.
• Precautions: no exercise during painful flare-ups since motion can be detrimental to the joint due to the crystals, which can destroy the joint surface during extreme joint motion; rest and elevation of the joint is recommended during a flare, with walking aids used to relieve joint pressure.
• After resolution of the flare-up, ROM, stretching and strengthening exercises, proprioception exercises (to maintain joint position sense), and aerobic exercise (especially in a pool) are introduced.

(d)
• Basis for varied presentations: CPPD results from an imbalance between crystal inhibitors and crystal promoters causing calcium pyrophosphate crystals to deposit widely in articular cartilage and fibrocartilage, so the clinical picture depends on which joints and tissues are affected.
• It may present as asymptomatic CPDD (radiographic deposits with no symptoms, most common, in knees, wrist, symphysis pubis, hips), acute pseudogout (a single painful swollen joint), pseudo-osteoarthritis (knees, PIP joints and spine, mimicking primary OA), pseudo-rheumatoid arthritis (symmetrical PIP/MCP inflammation with morning stiffness, in about 5% of patients), or as OA with superimposed CPDD.
• Because the underlying process (crystal deposition and joint inflammation) is the same but the joints and pattern involved vary between patients, CPPD can mimic several other arthropathies, which is why it must be considered in the differential diagnosis of gout, osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
• This variability means assessment must always include radiographic and synovial fluid confirmation rather than relying on the clinical pattern alone, since presentations of CPDD overlap closely with gout, osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osteoarthritis (OA) of the knee – the pattern of use-related pain, minimal morning stiffness (under 30 minutes), gelling after inactivity and crepitus, occurring in an obese female over 50, is typical.

(b)
Pathological basis: OA is a chronic degenerative joint disease with breakdown of articular cartilage and proliferative bony changes at joint margins, plus synovial inflammation; loss of chondrocyte balance between degradative enzymes (metalloproteases) and inhibitors, together with IL-1 and synovial inflammation, causes cartilage breakdown; cartilage splits and thins, losing its ability to withstand stress, leading to crepitus/loose bodies; capsular laxity from bone remodelling can cause joint hypermobility/instability.

(c)
• Physiotherapy assessment – Subjective: pain characteristics (mechanical, worse with weight-bearing/activity, relieved by rest), duration of stiffness, functional limitation in ADLs.
• Objective: posture, gait, joint inspection for deformity/bony enlargement, palpation for crepitus and tenderness, active/passive ROM (limitation especially in extension in later stages), muscle strength.
• Investigations: X-ray findings (joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, bone cysts), graded using the Kellgren-Lawrence classification (G1 normal to G4 severe); laboratory tests are typically normal and used only for differential diagnosis.
• Outcome measures: region-specific knee osteoarthritis outcome measures.

(d)
Management/goals: pain relief, preservation/restoration of joint function, and patient education. Non-pharmacologic management – patient education on deforming forces and prevention, weight loss, aerobic exercise programme, ROM and muscle-strengthening exercises, assistive devices/appropriate footwear, splinting/bracing, joint protection and energy conservation, occupational therapy. Physiotherapy modalities – cryoanalgesia, electroanalgesia, iontophoresis, ultrasonophoresis, soft tissue release, mobilisation techniques, muscle energy techniques and functional retraining, plus core stabilisation exercises.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pathogenesis: infection reaches the joint by haematogenous spread (most common), direct inoculation (trauma, injection, surgery), or direct spread from adjacent bone (more common in children, from metaphyseal osteomyelitis breaking through the periosteum); bacteria settle in the vascular synovium, provoking acute inflammation with seropurulent exudate.
• As pus forms in the joint, articular cartilage is eroded and destroyed partly by bacterial enzymes and partly by enzymes released from the synovium, inflammatory cells and pus.
• Outcomes/stages of joint healing: complete resolution of infection; partial loss of cartilage with fibrosis of the joint; loss of articular cartilage with bony ankylosis; or bone destruction with permanent joint deformity – if untreated, infection can spread to underlying bone or burst out of the joint to form abscesses and sinuses.

(b)
Deformities/complications: bone destruction and pathological joint dislocation, cartilage destruction leading to fibrosis or bony ankylosis, secondary osteoarthritis in adults from partial joint destruction, growth disturbance in infants/children (localised deformity or bone shortening), septicaemia, and coxa magna.

(c)
• Acute stage: immobilisation (splint or widely split plaster) to control pain, since weight-bearing is often too painful; in neonates/infants with hip infection the joint is held abducted and flexed about 30° on traction to prevent dislocation.
• During this stage physiotherapy aims to reduce pain intensity, positioning the joint in its functional position and allowing passive ROM activities; heat modalities are avoided in the acute phase or before antibiotic treatment begins.
• Once the patient is responding well, generally after about 5 days of treatment, mobilisation can begin, along with electrotherapy (ice, hydrotherapy, heat, TENS, IFT, pulsed ultrasound) to manage pain and joint stiffness.
• Throughout management the physiotherapist restores and maintains physiological joint function and educates the patient on properly protecting the affected joint; once the infection is well managed, physiotherapy allows maximum post-infection functioning.

(d)
• Basis of deformity: bacterial and host inflammatory enzymes progressively erode articular cartilage; in infants the still-cartilaginous epiphysis is destroyed, in children vascular occlusion causes epiphyseal bone necrosis, and in adults synovial proliferation causes extensive cartilage erosion.
• If infection is not controlled, joint healing occurs with fibrosis or bony ankylosis rather than a normal joint surface, restricting or abolishing movement at that joint.
• In children, destruction of the growth-related epiphyseal region can cause localised deformity or shortening of the bone as growth continues abnormally.
• The resulting functional limitation therefore comes from a combination of pain and muscle spasm limiting movement acutely, and structural joint damage (fibrosis, ankylosis, secondary osteoarthritis, or growth disturbance) limiting movement and function in the longer term, which is why early treatment and staged physiotherapy are important to preserve function.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathogenesis and stages/possible outcomes in the clinical course of septic (pyogenic) arthritis.
(b) Describe the deformities/complications that can result.
(c) State the principles of physiotherapy management at each stage of the disease.
(d) Explain the basis of the deformities/functional limitations that develop.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acute stage: symptoms develop suddenly, are of short duration, and typically do not recur; many cases of viral arthritis resolve within six weeks, with the classic triad of joint pain/stiffness (particularly in the morning), loss of range of motion, and symmetrical joint involvement.
• Chronic stage: some patients progress to a chronic stage where joint inflammation or pain can continue for weeks, months or sometimes even years, rather than resolving with the acute infection.
• The pattern and severity can also vary by virus (e.g. differing proportions of infected adults developing arthritis with hepatitis C, hepatitis B, rubella, Epstein-Barr virus, or alphaviruses), and rates may be higher in adults or children depending on the virus.

(b)
Extra-articular manifestations: joint symptoms are often preceded by or coincide with signs of viral infection such as fever, muscle ache and fatigue; a rash similar to that seen in rheumatic diseases may occur in some cases; pre-existing osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis may worsen due to the rapid onset of viral inflammation.

(c)
• Acute-stage management: physiotherapy targets symptom control, using cryotherapy to reduce acute swelling.
• Also in the acute stage: heat application is used to alleviate joint stiffness, alongside medical treatment (NSAIDs, analgesics), with treatments often started presumptively since they are commonly used for many inflammatory joint conditions.
• Surgical drainage is not indicated in the acute stage unless septic arthritis is considered likely, and corticosteroids are generally avoided as they can mask or worsen the underlying viral disease.
• Chronic-stage management: because a minority of patients progress to prolonged joint inflammation lasting weeks to years, ongoing symptom-focused physiotherapy (continued modality use and monitoring of function) and medical review are needed until resolution.

(d)
• Basis of joint symptoms: viruses can invade the synovium or surrounding tissue during infection; the viral particles are recognised as antigens, and the immune system deposits immune complexes into the joint space in addition to attacking freely circulating virus.
• These immune complexes help antibodies bind to antigens but also trigger acute inflammation, causing the joint pain and swelling characteristic of viral arthritis.
• Because the trigger (the virus and the resulting immune complexes) is systemic, joint involvement is typically polyarticular and symmetrical, similar in distribution to rheumatoid arthritis, and accompanied by systemic viral symptoms.
• Functional limitation arises from joint pain, stiffness and reduced range of motion across multiple joints during the acute phase, and, in the minority who progress to chronic disease, from persistent joint inflammation that can continue to limit activity for a prolonged period.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: SLE is an inflammatory multisystem disease with immunologic aberrations – excessive autoantibody production – in which tissue damage results from antibody and complement-fixing immune complex deposition; it is characterised by remissions and exacerbations and a wide spectrum of clinical presentation.

(b)
• Clinical features – constitutional: fatigue, fever, weight loss (non-specific but very common).
• Clinical features – skin: malar "butterfly" rash, generalised erythema, bullous lupus, subacute cutaneous lupus, discoid lesions, panniculitis, urticaria, vasculitis, livedo reticularis, oral lesions, non-scarring alopecia.
• Clinical features – musculoskeletal, cardiac and pulmonary: non-erosive, rarely deforming arthritis (occasionally Jaccoud's deformity), myopathy/myositis; pericarditis, myocarditis, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, coronary heart disease; pleuritis, pneumonitis, pulmonary haemorrhage, pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary embolism.

(c)
• Clinical basis for female predominance: SLE has a female-to-male ratio of about 9:1 (age 14-64), with peak incidence at age 15-40, though onset may occur at any age; in pre-pubertal and post-menopausal patients the female:male ratio is lower, about 3:1, suggesting a hormonal contribution to the female excess.
• Clinical basis for racial predisposition: SLE shows a racial predisposition, being about three times more common in black patients than in other groups, as stated in the epidemiology of the condition.

(d)
• Erosiveness and deformity: SLE arthritis is non-erosive and rarely deforming (occasionally Jaccoud's deformity, a reducible, soft-tissue-based deformity), whereas rheumatoid arthritis is characteristically an erosive arthritis with progressive structural damage to cartilage and bone, producing fixed structural deformity.
• Synovial findings: synovial fluid in SLE shows only mild inflammation, in contrast to the more pronounced inflammatory synovitis typically seen in active RA.
• Extra-articular pattern: while both are systemic autoimmune diseases with extra-articular involvement, SLE more prominently features skin (malar rash, discoid lesions) and serosal (pleuritis/pericarditis) disease as hallmark features.
• By contrast, RA more prominently features rheumatoid nodules, symmetric erosive small-joint disease and Felty's syndrome.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition/aetiology: gout is a common, very painful form of inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in and around joints, resulting from hyperuricaemia due to underexcretion of uric acid by the kidney (about 90% of cases) or overproduction of purines (less than 10%); risk factors include family history, obesity, alcohol (especially beer), diet high in purines/fructose, and certain medications (diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ACE inhibitors).

(b)
Epidemiology: prevalence is at least 1% and rising with an ageing population, increasing obesity and lifestyle change; gout is about three to four times more common in men, with peak onset 40-60 years in men and 60-80 years in women (after menopause); prevalence is relatively rare in black Africans (e.g. Nigerian men about 0.03%) but increasing with dietary change.

(c)
Clinical features: sudden, severe monoarthritis (classically podagra – the first metatarsophalangeal joint), reaching maximum intensity within hours, often waking the patient at night, with the joint red, hot, swollen, tender and shiny-skinned; without treatment attacks resolve within about 5-10 days; chronic disease produces tophi (urate deposits) around joints, hands, feet, elbows and ears.

(d)
• Diagnostic criteria (six or more needed): more than one attack of acute arthritis; maximum inflammation within one day; monoarthritis attack; redness over the joint; painful/swollen first MTP joint; unilateral first MTP attack.
• Diagnostic criteria (continued): unilateral tarsal joint attack; tophus (proved/suspected); hyperuricaemia; asymmetric swelling on radiograph; subcortical cysts without erosions on radiograph; joint fluid culture negative for organisms.

(e)
• Clinical basis for male predominance: gout is about three to four times more common in men because oestrogen has a uricosuric effect that helps women excrete urate before menopause; after menopause, oestrogen falls and urate levels rise, so women's risk increases (gout is rare before menopause).
• Clinical basis for joint distribution: urate is more likely to crystallise in cooler parts of the body, explaining why peripheral joints such as the great toe, foot, ankle, knee, wrist, finger and elbow are most commonly affected, while central joints (spine, shoulders, hips) are rarely involved.

(f)
• Cause: gout is caused by monosodium urate monohydrate crystals from hyperuricaemia, whereas pseudogout (acute CPP crystal arthritis) is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, often idiopathic in elderly people or linked to trauma, hyperparathyroidism or haemochromatosis.
• Onset: gout has sudden onset reaching maximum intensity within 8-12 hours, whereas pseudogout typically has a more insidious onset over several days.
• Joint distribution: gout classically affects the great toe (podagra), foot, ankle, knee, wrist, finger and elbow, whereas pseudogout commonly affects the knee, wrist, elbow and ankle.
• Deposits: gout produces tophi (urate deposits) at the ear, fingers, toes and olecranon, whereas pseudogout does not typically produce tophi but shows radiographic chondrocalcinosis of cartilage.
• Sex distribution and similarities: gout is male-predominant (about 3-4:1), whereas pseudogout affects males and females roughly equally (1:1); both present with acute joint pain, swelling, redness, warmth and tenderness, occur more after age 60, and are managed similarly with rest, ice, NSAIDs, corticosteroids and colchicine during flares.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clinical course: gonococcal arthritis results from blood dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae from a primary sexually acquired mucosal infection; three major subgroups/stages have been described – the bacteraemic stage (positive blood cultures, characteristic dermatitis, migratory arthralgias), the septic joint stage (oligo-arthritis with positive joint culture), and an indeterminate variable presentation.
• Some patients present within one of these stages, while others progress from the bacteraemic stage to the septic joint stage over several days.
• Gonococcal arthritis manifests either as a bacteraemic infection (arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, with the classic triad of dermatitis, tenosynovitis and migratory polyarthritis) or as a localised septic arthritis.

(b)
• Deformities/complications: unlike Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis, gonococcal arthritis is rarely associated with joint destruction; joints commonly affected with tenosynovitis or septic arthritis include the wrists, ankles, hands and feet.
• Extra-articular manifestations: skin lesions (painless or painful petechiae, macules, papules, pustules, vesicles, bullae) present in about 75% of patients with bacteraemia; rare disease progression may result in perihepatitis, meningitis or endocarditis.

(c)
• Bacteraemic/acute stage: intravenous antibiotic therapy is given first (switched to oral once improved); in the acute phase the joint is immobilised (temporary splinting) to manage pain and reduce the likelihood of further joint damage.
• If arthrocentesis alone is insufficient, joint drainage (daily aspiration) or surgical drainage/arthroscopy is used medically to remove accumulated pus from the joint.
• Once the patient is responding well to medical treatment, generally around five days, gentle mobilisation of the joint can begin.
• Physiotherapy at this stage aims to strengthen the joint and surrounding muscles weakened by inactivity, increase range of motion, decrease pain and stiffness, and increase cardiovascular levels, using cryotherapy, strengthening exercises, hydrotherapy, cardiovascular activities and continued protective splinting as needed, with patient education on joint protection throughout.

(d)
• Basis of deformity/limitation: the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome triad (dermatitis, tenosynovitis, migratory polyarthritis) reflects bacteraemic spread affecting skin, tendon sheaths and multiple joints simultaneously, producing functional limitation across several body regions rather than a single fixed deformity.
• Tenosynovitis specifically affects tendon gliding at the wrists/hands and ankles/feet, limiting fine motor and weight-bearing function during the acute stage even though permanent joint destruction is uncommon.
• Because permanent joint destruction is rare in gonococcal arthritis, functional limitation is usually reversible with prompt antibiotic treatment, joint drainage where needed, and staged physiotherapy (immobilisation followed by progressive mobilisation), in contrast to conditions where structural joint damage causes lasting deformity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• History: ask about pain related to use, pain worsening during the day, minimal morning stiffness (under 20-30 minutes) and stiffness/gelling after inactivity, and impact on activities of daily living.
• Physical examination: observe posture and gait; inspect and palpate for bony enlargement, deformity, crepitus and tenderness; assess active and passive range of motion (noting restriction, e.g. extension loss in later stages) and joint instability.
• Investigations: laboratory analysis has no pathognomonic findings for OA and is performed mainly for differential diagnosis (usually normal); radiographs show narrowing of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and bone cysts, graded using the Kellgren-Lawrence classification (G1 normal to G4 severe); diagnosis combines clinical findings (joint pain) with radiologic findings (osteophytes).

(b)
Outcome measures: region-specific hip/knee osteoarthritis outcome scores used to quantify functional capacity, alongside general pain scales.

(c)
• Goals: pain relief, preservation and restoration of joint function, and patient education.
• Non-pharmacologic modalities: patient education, weight loss where relevant, aerobic exercise programmes, ROM and muscle-strengthening exercises, assistive devices for ambulation, appropriate footwear/lateral-wedged insoles, bracing, occupational therapy, and joint protection/energy conservation.
• Physiotherapy-specific modalities: core stabilisation exercises, cryoanalgesia, electroanalgesia, iontophoresis, ultrasonophoresis, soft tissue release techniques, mobilisation techniques, muscle energy techniques, and functional retraining.
• Precautions: first confirm the pain is joint-related rather than an adjacent tendonitis/bursitis; avoid overstressing the joint with heavy resistance if there is significant instability; progress from initial treatment (strengthening, weight loss, acetaminophen, local heat/cold) to second-line (NSAIDs, intra-articular agents) and third-line (arthroscopy, osteotomy, total joint replacement) only as needed.

(d)
• Basis of functional deficit: breakdown of articular cartilage and proliferative bony changes cause pain with mechanical stress/use, joint stiffness after activity, and progressive loss of range of motion.
• Muscle weakness (particularly quadriceps around the knee) and decreased proprioception/balance develop secondary to joint disease and reduced activity, further limiting function.
• Bony enlargement, deformity and joint instability restrict normal joint mechanics, so tasks requiring full range of motion, load-bearing or fine positioning (e.g. stair climbing, kneeling, gripping) become difficult.
• Together, pain, stiffness, restricted ROM, muscle weakness and instability explain why OA is a major cause of disability in old age and the leading indication for joint replacement surgery, producing limitation in both activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living.
