questions.answerText:
(a)
Condition/stage: Rheumatoid arthritis, seropositive type (positive RF and anti-CCP), with radiographic erosive changes indicating disease that has progressed beyond the earliest stage, since erosions and periarticular osteopenia reflect established joint damage; progression is monitored using American College of Rheumatology criteria based on changes in symptoms and laboratory findings.

(b)
Structures affected: synovial membrane (hyperplasia, synovial fluid increase), articular cartilage and bone (erosion), joint capsule (stretched, leading to instability), tendons (tenosynovitis with possible rupture), and extra-articular structures/organs in some patients (eyes – Sjögren's, lungs – pleuritis, heart – pericarditis, spleen – Felty's syndrome, blood vessels – vasculitis, subcutaneous tissue – rheumatoid nodules).

(c)
Differential diagnoses: osteoarthritis (distinguished by asymmetric involvement, mechanical pain, shorter morning stiffness, and absence of systemic symptoms/rheumatoid factor), psoriatic arthritis (distal interphalangeal joint involvement, nail changes, absence of rheumatoid nodules), viral arthritis (self-limiting, resolves within six weeks), and connective tissue disease such as SLE (non-erosive arthritis).

(d)
Clinical reasoning: because the seropositive, erosive pattern with high inflammatory markers indicates active, potentially aggressive disease, physiotherapy is planned around short-term goals (reduce pain, increase ROM, increase muscle strength, prevent deformity) and long-term goals (restore/maintain optimal function, correct deformity, reintegrate the patient into work/community); active exercise is favoured over passive motion (reserved for acutely inflamed joints), with modalities (compression gloves, TENS, hydrotherapy, heat/cold) and patient education used alongside a multidisciplinary approach, since early referral and treatment reduce the risk of permanent work disability.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis – inflammatory back pain, morning stiffness relieved by activity, and diminished chest expansion from costovertebral involvement are characteristic, typically beginning in adolescence/early adulthood, more common in men.

(b)
Problem list: Impairments – back pain and stiffness, paraspinal muscle spasm, reduced spinal mobility, reduced chest expansion, flexed/bent-over posture, possible peripheral joint involvement, enthesitis (Achilles/patellar tendinitis). Activity limitations – difficulty with prolonged standing/walking, reduced ability to reach/bend, impaired breathing capacity affecting exertion. Participation restrictions – difficulty with occupational tasks, recreational activity, and social participation due to pain, fatigue and progressive deformity.

(c)
Treatment plan: combination of muscle strengthening, ROM, flexibility and cardiorespiratory exercise (land-based, water-based, home-based, individual or supervised); posture exercises with upper-back hyperextension avoiding lumbar hyperextension; breathing exercises for rib-cage excursion (abdominothoracic breathing); ROM exercises for hips and knees; modalities such as short wave, TENS, infrared; balneotherapy/hydrotherapy; manual therapy; the Global Posture Re-education method (postures held 15-20 minutes to stretch shortened muscle chains).

(d)
Precautions/contraindications: avoid lumbar hyperextension during posture exercises; avoid fatigue, include periodic rest periods; proceed cautiously with the standing trunk-flexion posture, using it only if the patient can cooperate and tolerate it (fatigue/pain permitting).

(e)
Patient education/joint protection/energy conservation: education programmes covering diagnosis, prognosis and therapeutic options for better self-management; proper sleeping posture on a solid flat bed without a pillow, frequent prone lying; bracing/corseting combined with exercise; pacing activity with periodic rest to avoid fatigue.
questions.question:
(a) A 24-year-old man presents with several months of low back pain and stiffness that is worse at night and in the morning but eases with activity, together with diminished chest expansion. What is the probable diagnosis?
(b) List the impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions this patient is likely to have.
(c) Outline a treatment plan including modalities and exercise.
(d) State the precautions and contraindications to observe.
(e) Describe the patient education, joint protection and energy conservation advice you would give.

(a) A 45-year-old man presents with hip, gluteal and groin pain radiating to the knee, mechanical in nature, with joint stiffness and limited walking function; examination shows an antalgic limp, limited and painful range of motion, and a leg length discrepancy; laboratory tests are normal and X-ray shows joint space narrowing with osteophytes. What condition and radiographic grade do these findings suggest?
(b) What structures are affected?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?
(d) Explain your clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy prescribed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Condition/stage: Osteoarthritis of the hip joint – more common in males over 40 years, with mechanical pain and limited walking function; the combination of clinical findings (joint pain) plus radiologic findings (osteophytes, joint space narrowing) confirms the diagnosis, and the degree of joint space narrowing/osteophyte formation/subchondral sclerosis can be graded using the Kellgren-Lawrence classification (G1 normal to G4 severe).

(b)
Structures affected: articular cartilage (breakdown), subchondral (para-articular) bone (sclerosis, cysts), and the joint margins (osteophyte/proliferative bony change); synovial inflammation and capsular changes may also occur.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: secondary osteoarthritis from previous joint disorders (e.g. congenital hip dislocation), infection (septic arthritis, tuberculosis, brucella), inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis), metabolic arthritis (gout), haematologic causes (haemophilia) and endocrine causes (diabetes mellitus), since these are recognised causes of secondary OA.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: because laboratory analysis is normal (as expected in OA) and the clinical/radiologic pattern is consistent with primary hip OA in this age/sex group, physiotherapy is prescribed for symptomatic and structure-oriented management – patient education on deforming forces, weight-loss advice if needed, aerobic exercise, ROM and muscle-strengthening exercises, assistive devices for ambulation and appropriate footwear, joint protection and energy conservation – reserving pharmacologic escalation and surgical options (osteotomy, total joint replacement) for cases where pain is severe and function significantly limited.

(a)
• History: ask about nocturnal back pain of varying intensity, morning stiffness relieved by activity, and (particularly in young men) diminished chest expansion, Achilles or patellar tendinitis, eye symptoms (unexplained anterior uveitis), and family history of ankylosing spondylitis in a first-degree relative.
• Examination: assess posture (flexed/bent-over posture, kyphosis), spinal and chest mobility (diminished chest expansion from costovertebral involvement), and peripheral joints (shoulders, hips, knees) for involvement.
• Investigations: lumbosacral spine and sacroiliac joint radiography; blood tests (ESR, C-reactive protein, HLA-B27, complete blood count); pelvic MRI in selected patients.

(b)
Diagnostic criteria: the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) criteria are most often applied, for patients with back pain for more than 3 months and onset before age 45; the imaging arm requires radiographic/MRI evidence of sacroiliitis plus at least one spondyloarthritis feature, and the clinical arm requires HLA-B27 plus at least two spondyloarthritis features (dactylitis, enthesitis of the heel, family history, inflammatory back pain history, arthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, HLA-B27, uveitis, elevated CRP, good NSAID response).

(c)
• Goals: alleviate pain, increase spinal mobility, improve functional capacity, reduce morning stiffness, correct postural deformities, increase mobility, and improve the psychosocial status of the patient.
• Modalities: a combination of muscle strengthening, ROM, flexibility and cardiorespiratory exercise (land- or water-based, individual or supervised); the Global Posture Re-education method; manual therapy; short wave, TENS and infrared; balneotherapy/hydrotherapy; patient education programmes on diagnosis, prognosis and therapeutic options.
• Precautions: avoid lumbar hyperextension during posture correction exercises; use periodic rest periods to avoid fatigue; advise proper sleeping posture on a solid, flat bed without a pillow and frequent prone lying to prevent deformity; combine bracing/corseting with exercise rather than relying on it alone.

(d)
• Basis of systemic involvement: AS is a systemic rheumatic disease with an association with HLA-B27, so besides the sacroiliac joints, spine and entheses, it can involve peripheral joints (predominantly lower extremities), the eyes (acute anterior uveitis in up to 40% of patients), enteric mucosa and skin.
• Systemic manifestations occur in about one third of patients and can include cardiovascular involvement (aortic insufficiency, aortitis, angina, pericarditis, conduction abnormalities), pulmonary involvement (dyspnoea, cough or haemoptysis from upper-lobe fibrosis/cavitation), and neurological complications (compression radiculitis, sciatica, vertebral fracture/subluxation, cauda equina syndrome).
• These systemic effects arise because AS is an immune-mediated inflammatory process not confined to the axial skeleton, so entheses and other tissues throughout the body can be affected by the same disease process.
• Functional deficit therefore results not only from spinal stiffness/fusion and reduced chest expansion (limiting exercise tolerance and breathing), but also from eye pain/photophobia limiting visual function during uveitis flares, and rarely from cardiac or neurological complications limiting activity.
• So physiotherapy assessment and management must consider more than spinal mobility alone, incorporating breathing exercises and awareness of extra-articular flares that may need medical referral.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the history, examination and investigations used in assessing a patient with ankylosing spondylitis.
(b) What diagnostic criteria/outcome information would you use?
(c) State the physiotherapy goals, modalities and precautions in managing ankylosing spondylitis.
(d) Explain why ankylosing spondylitis may involve organs/systems other than the spine, and how this causes functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Gout (podagra – acute monoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint). Risk factors present: male sex, obesity (more urate produced than kidneys can cope with), beer/alcohol intake (purine content of beer raises urate independent of alcohol), and possibly family history/genetics and a diet high in meat/fish.

(b)
Complications/deformities: repeated untreated attacks can become more frequent and spread to new joints; chronic tophaceous deposits (tophi) develop around joints (toes, heel, knee, fingers, wrist, elbow, ears), which can become inflamed, break down and leak crystals; tophi can grow within joints and damage cartilage and bone leading to more regular daily pain; long-standing hyperuricaemia can also cause urate nephropathy/kidney stones.

(c)
• Physiotherapy management by stage: During acute exacerbation – reinforcement of the management programme, splinting/orthotics/assistive devices to protect the joint, rest/avoidance of exercise on the joint, and referral for medical evaluation since gout, hyperuricaemia and septic joint must be distinguished; the joint should not be moved as this is when uric acid crystals can damage joint surfaces. During the intercritical (symptom-free) phase – assistance with maintenance of ROM, strength and function, and help creating a suitable exercise routine and weight control.
• Justification: for this patient, who is in an acute flare, the priority is rest/protection of the joint (splinting/assistive devices, avoidance of exercise, ice application) rather than exercise, since exercise during a flare can worsen pain and is contraindicated until swelling and pain subside.
questions.question:
(a) A 55-year-old obese man who drinks beer regularly wakes at night with sudden, severe pain, redness, swelling and warmth in the joint at the base of his big toe; the skin over the joint looks shiny and any light contact is unbearable. What is the probable diagnosis, and what risk factors in this man's history predisposed him to the condition?
(b) What complications or deformities can result if this condition is left untreated or occurs repeatedly?
(c) Describe the physiotherapy management options appropriate for the different stages of this disease, and justify which option you would prioritise for this patient during his current presentation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Viral arthritis – sudden onset, short duration, symmetrical small-joint involvement with morning stiffness, preceded/accompanied by signs of viral infection (fever, muscle ache, fatigue), and resolution within six weeks, is typical; possible causative agents include Parvovirus B19, hepatitis B/C, rubella, Epstein-Barr virus, alphaviruses or mumps virus.

(b)
Pathological basis: viruses can invade the joint during infection; viral particles in the synovium/surrounding tissue are recognised as antigens, so the immune system deposits immune complexes into the joint space in addition to attacking circulating virus; these immune complexes trigger acute inflammation, causing joint pain and swelling.

(c)
• Physiotherapy assessment – Subjective: history of a preceding or coincident viral illness (fever, malaise, rash), onset and duration of joint symptoms, pattern of joint involvement (symmetrical, polyarticular), morning stiffness and loss of ROM.
• Objective: inspection for rash and joint swelling, palpation for warmth/tenderness, active/passive ROM assessment; correlate with blood tests (antibody tests, PCR for viral DNA, IgM/IgG immunoglobulin tests) and tests to exclude RA (RF, anti-CCP) or OA (ESR, CRP) done by the physician.

(d)
Management/goals: since viral arthritis is usually self-limiting, treatment targets symptom control and restoration of joint function; physiotherapy includes cryotherapy to reduce acute swelling and heat application to relieve joint stiffness, alongside medical management (NSAIDs, analgesics); surgical drainage is not indicated unless septic arthritis is suspected.
questions.question:
(a) A young adult develops sudden-onset symmetrical pain and stiffness of the small joints of the hands and wrists, worse in the morning, about a week after a febrile illness with muscle aches; the joint symptoms resolve within six weeks. What is the probable diagnosis?
(b) Explain the pathological basis of the joint involvement.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy assessment (subjective and objective findings) for this patient.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management and goals.

(a) Define diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) and describe its aetiology.
(b) Describe its pathology.
(c) Describe its clinical features.
(d) State the diagnostic criteria for DISH.
(e) Explain why DISH is commoner in older men.
(f) Distinguish between DISH and ankylosing spondylitis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition/aetiology: DISH (Forestier's disease) is a type of arthritis affecting tendons and ligaments mainly around the spine, in which these tissues become hardened (calcified) and form bone spurs where they attach to bone; the exact cause of the calcium salt build-up is unknown, but it is associated with metabolic syndromes (obesity, diabetes, hyperinsulinaemia, dyslipidaemia, hyperuricaemia), long-term retinoid medication use, genetic factors (HLA-B27) and environmental exposures (fluoride, vitamin A toxicity).

(b)
Pathology: the anterior longitudinal ligament of the spine (most often thoracic) undergoes flowing ossification; enthesopathy can occur at sites such as the ischial tuberosities and greater trochanters, with paraspinal connective tissue fibrosis and degeneration of peripheral annulus fibrosus fibres; DISH most commonly occurs on the right side of the thoracic spine, attributed to a protective/mechanical-barrier effect of the pulsatile descending aorta on the left side.

(c)
Clinical features: may be asymptomatic; when symptomatic, mild-to-moderate stiffness (most noticeable in the morning) and pain in the back or other affected areas (shoulder, elbow, knee, heel), loss of range of motion (especially noticed on side-to-side stretching), and, if the neck is involved, difficulty swallowing or a hoarse voice.

(d)
Diagnostic criteria: flowing bridging ossification across at least four contiguous thoracic vertebrae; preservation of intervertebral disc space; absence of gross inflammatory or degenerative (spondylotic) change; absence of facet and sacroiliac joint fusion; ossification amount can be graded (no ossification, ossification without bridging, incomplete bridging, complete bridging) using the Mata scoring system, and the Utsinger criteria further classify possible, probable and definite DISH using bridging extent and peripheral enthesophytes.

(e)
• Clinical basis for occurrence in older men: DISH is rarely reported under age 50, with overall population incidence of 6-12%, occurring in about 25% of males and 15% of females, and prevalence increasing further in patients over 80 years.
• The disease course is thought to begin between the third and fifth decades of life but manifest clinically at a later age, and it is associated with metabolic syndromes (obesity, diabetes, hyperinsulinaemia) that are more prevalent with advancing age, which may explain the higher prevalence in older men.

(f)
• Age: DISH tends to present at a higher age than ankylosing spondylitis.
• Sacroiliac joints: DISH shows absence of sacroiliac joint erosions (though SI osteophytes may occur), whereas ankylosing spondylitis characteristically involves sacroiliitis with erosion.
• Facet joints: DISH shows absence of apophyseal (facet) joint obliteration, unlike ankylosing spondylitis where facet joint ankylosis occurs.
• Enthesopathy: DISH is typically absent of enthesopathies with erosions, whereas erosive enthesopathy is a feature of ankylosing spondylitis.
• Genetic association: DISH shows no association with HLA-B27, whereas ankylosing spondylitis is strongly HLA-B27 associated (present in about 90% of affected white patients).
• Severity: DISH tends to be a relatively mild or even painless disease often discovered incidentally in asymptomatic patients, whereas ankylosing spondylitis is typically a more clinically significant inflammatory disease with pain, systemic manifestations and progressive spinal fusion.

(a)
Condition/stage: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH/Forestier's disease), meeting the diagnostic criteria of flowing ossification across at least four contiguous vertebrae, preserved disc space, and absence of facet/sacroiliac joint fusion; using the Mata scoring system, the level of ossification (with or without bridging) indicates the stage.

(b)
Structures affected: the anterior longitudinal ligament of the spine (most commonly thoracic), with enthesopathy possible at extraspinal sites such as the ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, olecranon process, patellar ligament and calcaneus; paraspinal connective tissue fibrosis and degeneration of peripheral annulus fibrosus fibres can also occur.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: ankylosing spondylitis (differentiated by DISH's older age of onset, absence of sacroiliac joint erosion, absence of enthesopathy with erosions, and no HLA-B27 association), and other causes of spinal ossification/degenerative spondylosis.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: because DISH is often mild and may be asymptomatic, physiotherapy focuses on activity modification, mobility (stretching, strengthening and ROM exercises), pain relief (ultrasound, TENS, short wave diathermy, massage), weight reduction exercises, joint protection, and falls-prevention/balance training, reserving bracing/NSAIDs and surgery for more severe or complicated presentations (e.g. dysphagia, airway obstruction, fracture).
questions.question:
(a) A 58-year-old man has mild upper back pain and stiffness, most noticeable in the morning, with reduced side-to-side spinal movement. Imaging shows flowing ossification along the anterior aspect of at least four contiguous thoracic vertebrae, well-preserved disc spaces, and no sacroiliac joint inflammation or facet ankylosis. What condition and radiographic stage do these findings suggest?
(b) What structures are affected?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?

(a) Describe the history, examination and investigations used in the assessment of gonococcal arthritis.
(b) What outcome measures/monitoring would you use?
(c) State the physiotherapy goals, modalities and precautions in managing this condition.
(d) Explain why the disease may involve other organs/systems in addition to the joints, and how this causes functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• History: enquire about recent sexual activity/genitourinary symptoms (dysuria, discharge), joint pain for 1-4 days, fever and chills, malaise, pain/burning on urination, single or migrating joint pain, and skin lesions (raised pink-to-red sores that may contain pus).
• Examination: look for joint effusion, warmth, tenderness and restricted movement (commonly wrists, ankles, hands, feet), tenosynovitis, and skin lesions (petechiae, macules, papules, pustules, vesicles, bullae).
• Investigations: joint aspiration/arthrocentesis with synovial fluid examination and culture; blood tests – raised white blood cell count, raised ESR, raised C-reactive protein, and blood culture; radiographs may show joint effusion, juxta-articular osteoporosis, joint space narrowing and, in severe cases, ankylosis; a history of local gonococcal infection or positive genital/cervical smear and culture supports diagnosis.

(b)
Outcome measures/monitoring: repeat clinical assessment of pain, swelling, ROM and function, and monitoring of inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC) and response to antibiotic treatment.

(c)
• Physiotherapy goals: to strengthen the joint and surrounding muscles weakened by inactivity, to increase ROM, to decrease pain, to decrease stiffness, to increase cardiovascular levels, and to educate the patient on protecting the affected joint.
• Modalities/means: cryotherapy, strengthening exercises, hydrotherapy, cardiovascular activities, and temporary splinting of the joint to prevent unwanted movement.
• Precautions: physiotherapy follows antibiotic treatment (with joint aspiration, debridement or arthroscopy as needed); in the acute phase the joint should be immobilised to manage pain and reduce further damage; gentle mobilisation begins only about five days after medical treatment if the patient is responding well.

(d)
• Basis for systemic involvement: gonococcal arthritis results from blood dissemination (disseminated gonococcal infection) of Neisseria gonorrhoeae from a primary mucosal infection, so the organism/immune complexes can reach the skin (rash), tendon sheaths (tenosynovitis) and, rarely, other organs.
• Rare disease progression may result in perihepatitis, meningitis, or endocarditis, reflecting the bacteraemic spread of infection beyond the joint.
• Specific strains of N. gonorrhoeae have virulence factors (e.g. the porin 1A serotype) associated with dissemination, and the pathogenesis of disseminated infection may be partly immune-mediated, explaining involvement beyond a single joint.
• This systemic and multi-joint/tendon involvement produces functional deficit through combined joint pain/restricted movement, tenosynovitis affecting hand/wrist function, and systemic illness (fever, malaise) limiting overall activity and participation.
• Because gonococcal arthritis (unlike Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis) is rarely associated with joint destruction, functional deficit is usually reversible with prompt antibiotic treatment and progressive physiotherapy, though ongoing disability can occur if rehabilitation is neglected after the acute infection resolves.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the clinical course and extra-articular (multisystem) manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus.
(b) Describe the musculoskeletal deformity that may occur.
(c) State the principles of physiotherapy management during exacerbations and during remission.
(d) Explain the basis of the deformity and functional limitations that develop in SLE.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clinical course: SLE is an inflammatory multisystem disease characterised by remissions and exacerbations, driven by excessive autoantibody production and tissue damage from antibody/complement-fixing immune complex deposition, with a wide spectrum of clinical presentation.
• Constitutional manifestations: fatigue, fever and weight loss are common but non-specific.
• Skin manifestations: acute lesions (malar "butterfly" rash, generalised erythema, bullous lupus), subacute cutaneous lupus, and chronic lupus (localised/generalised discoid lesions, lupus profundus), plus non-specific lesions (panniculitis, urticaria, vasculitis, livedo reticularis, oral lesions, non-scarring alopecia).
• Cardiac manifestations: pericarditis, myocarditis, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and coronary heart disease.
• Pulmonary manifestations: pleuritis, acute or chronic pneumonitis, pulmonary haemorrhage (from vasculitis), pulmonary hypertension, and pulmonary embolism.

(b)
Musculoskeletal deformity: arthritis is the most common manifestation of SLE; it is non-erosive and rarely deforming, but a specific deformity called Jaccoud's deformity can occur; synovial fluid shows only mild inflammation, and tenosynovitis may be an early manifestation; myopathy can occur either as true myositis or secondary to drugs such as steroids or anti-malarials.

(c)
• During exacerbations (flares): apply ice or heat and elevate affected joints to reduce pain and swelling; increase rest, using support devices such as splints for stiff or painful joints, and keep hands/feet warm to protect circulation.
• During exacerbations, avoid overexertion and prioritise good sleep hygiene and stress management, since stress may slow healing.
• During remission: create a graded exercise plan to increase exercise tolerance, mobilise stiff joints and increase range of motion.
• Occupational therapy support for daily activities, patient education, smoking cessation advice, and a healthy diet (fruits, vegetables, lean meats, fish, low-fat dairy) support management throughout both exacerbation and remission.

(d)
• Basis of deformity: because SLE arthritis is non-erosive (unlike RA), joint damage is due to soft-tissue (capsule/ligament) laxity rather than cartilage/bone erosion, which is why deformity (Jaccoud's) is rare and, when present, is typically reducible rather than fixed.
• Functional limitation in SLE arises less from joint destruction and more from the combination of fatigue, multisystem involvement (cardiac, pulmonary, skin), myopathy (from myositis or drug side-effects), and the unpredictable pattern of flares and remissions, which physiotherapy must accommodate by adjusting activity level to disease stage.

(a)
Diagnosis: Acute pseudogout – calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPDD/CPPD) presenting as acute crystal synovitis with insidious onset over several days, resembling gout but with radiographic chondrocalcinosis.

(b)
Predisposing factors: ageing (occurs mostly in the fifth decade and older; earlier onset before 40 suggests a secondary cause), genetic abnormalities causing hyperproduction of pyrophosphate, metabolic conditions affecting calcium/pyrophosphate regulation (hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, hypomagnesaemia), kidney malfunction, hypercalcaemia, and joint injury/surgery. Pathological basis: an imbalance between crystal inhibitors and crystal promoters raises calcium pyrophosphate crystal levels in joint fluid, attracting white blood cells and producing a painful inflammatory attack; crystals deposit in articular cartilage and fibrocartilage.

(c)
Clinical features: several patterns are described – asymptomatic CPDD (radiographic deposits without symptoms, most common, affecting knees, wrist, symphysis pubis, hips); acute pseudogout (mild pain/swelling of a single joint); pseudo-osteoarthritis (knees, PIP joints and spine, as in primary OA); pseudo-rheumatoid arthritis (symmetrical PIP/MCP inflammation with morning stiffness, seen in 5% of CPDD patients); and OA with CPDD (crystals deposited in cartilage of already-osteoarthritic joints).

(d)
Physiotherapy management: used alongside medication (analgesics, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections) during joint flares; modalities such as ice, ultrasound or laser therapy (low intensity laser therapy to reduce pain and swelling and reduce medication need); ice/cold compress at home for flare-ups; no exercise during painful flares (rest and elevation); after resolution – ROM, stretching and strengthening exercises, proprioception exercises, and aerobic exercise (especially in a pool).
questions.question:
(a) A 68-year-old man develops sudden mild-to-moderate pain and swelling in a single knee joint over several days; X-ray shows calcification within the joint cartilage. What is the probable "spot diagnosis"?
(b) What factors predispose a patient to this condition, and what is its pathological basis?
(c) Describe the clinical features that may be seen with this condition.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• History: ask about a preceding or coincident viral illness (fever, muscle ache, fatigue, rash) and the onset, duration and pattern of joint symptoms (sudden onset, short duration, not usually recurring, resolving within about six weeks in most cases).
• Examination: inspect for rash and symmetrical joint swelling, palpate for tenderness and warmth, and assess active/passive range of motion for pain and stiffness (particularly in the morning).
• Because there is no single typical presentation, a careful, complete history and thorough physical examination are needed, since the classic signs (fever, rash, joint pain) can occur in many non-viral illnesses.

(b)
Investigations: antibody tests for disease-specific antibodies; polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests for disease-specific viral DNA; immunoglobulin (IgM/IgG) tests to track the stage and duration of infection; additional blood tests (rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP) may be used to rule out rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis.

(c)
• Goals: since viral arthritis is usually self-limiting, physiotherapy goals are symptom control and restoration of joint function.
• Modalities: cryotherapy to reduce acute swelling and heat application to alleviate joint stiffness, used alongside medical management (NSAIDs, simple analgesics such as paracetamol, or opioids if pain is severe; corticosteroids are generally avoided as they can mask or worsen the underlying viral disease).
• Precautions: surgical drainage is not indicated unless septic arthritis is suspected; because pre-existing osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis can worsen due to a viral flare, distinguish new viral symptoms from a flare of pre-existing joint disease.

(d)
• Basis for systemic, polyarticular involvement: viruses can invade the synovium or surrounding tissue during infection; the viral particles are recognised as antigens, and the immune system deposits immune complexes into the joint space (in addition to attacking circulating virus), triggering acute inflammation.
• Because the triggering viral infection is typically systemic (bloodborne or widespread), the resulting immune complex-mediated joint inflammation commonly affects multiple joints (polyarthritis) rather than a single joint, and is often symmetrical, similar in distribution to rheumatoid arthritis.
• Joint symptoms often accompany or coincide with systemic signs of the underlying viral infection (fever, muscle ache, fatigue, sometimes rash), reflecting the systemic nature of the trigger.
• Functional deficit therefore arises from joint pain, stiffness and loss of range of motion across several joints simultaneously, compounded by systemic symptoms (fatigue, fever) that limit overall activity during the acute illness.
• In most cases functional deficit resolves as the self-limiting arthritis subsides within weeks, but in a minority of patients symptoms can progress to a chronic stage lasting weeks, months or even years, prolonging functional limitation.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the history, examination and investigations used in assessing a patient with viral arthritis.
(b) What tests help confirm the diagnosis?
(c) State the physiotherapy goals, modalities and precautions in managing viral arthritis.
(d) Explain why viral arthritis tends to be systemic and polyarticular, and how it produces functional deficit.

(a) A 6-year-old child presents with fever, an irritable manner, and refusal to move the right hip; the hip is warm, tender and resistant to movement, with loss of hip flexion, abduction and external rotation. What is the most likely "spot diagnosis"?
(b) What predisposing factors make a patient likely to develop this condition?
(c) Describe the pathophysiology and clinical features of the condition.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Septic (pyogenic) arthritis of the hip.

(b)
Predisposing factors: extremes of age (elderly over 80 years and young children), pre-existing joint disease (OA, gout, RA, lupus), immunosuppressive medications, fragile/broken skin or infected wounds, haemophilia with haemarthroses, immunocompromise (sickle cell disease, HIV, chemotherapy), weak immune system (diabetes, kidney/liver disease), intravenous drug abuse, previous joint surgery/prosthesis, and sexual activity (for gonococcal arthritis).

(c)
• Pathophysiology: infection reaches the joint by haematogenous spread (most common), direct inoculation (trauma, injection, surgery), or direct spread from adjacent bone (more common in children, from metaphyseal osteomyelitis breaking through the periosteum). Bacteria settle in the vascular synovium, causing an acute inflammatory reaction with seropurulent exudate; articular cartilage is eroded by bacterial and synovial/inflammatory-cell enzymes; in infants this destroys the still-cartilaginous epiphysis, and in children vascular occlusion can cause epiphyseal bone necrosis; in adults synovial proliferation causes extensive cartilage erosion.
• Clinical features: fever, painful swollen inflamed joint, restricted active and passive movement, pseudoparesis (reluctance to move the joint), local warmth, tenderness, muscle spasm around the joint, and (in neonates) irritability and feeding refusal.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: aims are to reduce pain, restore/maintain joint function, and educate the patient/family. Immobilise/splint the joint initially since weight-bearing is too painful; begin mobilisation once the patient responds well after about 5 days of treatment, keeping the joint in a functional position and allowing passive ROM; electrotherapy (ice, hydrotherapy, heat, TENS, IFT, pulsed ultrasound) for pain and stiffness, noting heat should not be used in the acute phase or before antibiotics start; educate the patient on protecting the joint; once infection is controlled, physiotherapy allows maximum post-infection functioning.

(a)
Diagnosis: Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome) – the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis following a genitourinary infection, with enthesitis (heel pain) and mucocutaneous lesions (balanitis), fits the classic presentation. Risk factors: male sex, age 20-40 years, genital infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (or an enteric infection with Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia or Campylobacter), and the HLA-B27 genotype, which is a predisposing factor in over two-thirds of patients.

(b)
Complications: the arthritis may be self-limiting, recurring, chronic or progressive; most patients have symptoms lasting weeks to six months, but 15-50% have recurrent bouts, and chronic arthritis or sacroiliitis occurs in 15-30% of cases; repeated attacks over years can lead to chronic disabling arthritis, cardiac conduction abnormalities, aortitis with aortic regurgitation, ankylosing spondylitis and amyloid deposits.

(c)
• Physiotherapy management by stage: acute phase – bed rest, NSAIDs for pain and inflammation, gentle range-of-motion work; once the acute infection/inflammation is resolving – strengthening exercises and range-of-motion exercises to restore function, with vigorous exercise discouraged for the first few months after resolution of the syndrome.
• Justification: since this patient is still in the early, acutely inflamed stage (recent infection, active joint and eye involvement), rest and gentle NSAID-supported management take priority over vigorous exercise, which should be introduced gradually only as inflammation subsides.
questions.question:
(a) A 28-year-old man presents two weeks after an episode of urethral discharge with pain and swelling in the knee and sacroiliac joint, painless ulcers on the glans penis, conjunctivitis, and heel pain. What is the probable diagnosis, and what risk factors predisposed him?
(b) What complications can result from this condition?
(c) Describe physiotherapy management options for the different stages of the disease, and justify which you would prioritise for this patient now.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Psoriatic arthritis – psoriasis preceding joint disease, with dactylitis (sausage digit), spinal/back pain and nail pitting, is a classic presentation.

(b)
Problem list: Impairments – joint pain and stiffness (worse in the morning, loosening with activity then stiffening again after rest), sausage-shaped swelling of digits, enthesitis (e.g. Achilles tendon pain), possible spinal involvement with asymmetric syndesmophytes, skin lesions. Activity limitations – difficulty gripping/using hands and feet due to dactylitis, difficulty with prolonged activity due to the stiffness pattern. Participation restrictions – reduced work/social participation from chronic pain, visible skin lesions and fatigue.

(c)
Treatment plan: gentle manual therapy and soft tissue massage, joint flexibility exercises, muscle strengthening exercises, hydrotherapy (strengthening and aerobic exercise), heat and cold therapies for joint pain/stiffness, assistive devices for daily tasks.

(d)
Precautions/contraindications: joint and skin disease severity are often discordant, so assess both; avoid aggravating enthesitis sites; be aware drug therapy (e.g. methotrexate) may affect exercise tolerance; monitor for progression to arthritis mutilans (destructive joint disease).

(e)
Patient education/joint protection/energy conservation: educate on the disease process and the fluctuating (morning stiff, loosens with activity, stiffens again with rest) symptom pattern; advise on life/activity modification to conserve energy and protect joints; encourage regular physical activity, since it lowers inflammation, aids weight loss, reduces fatigue and depression, improves sleep and regulates bowel function; advise a healthy low-carbohydrate, Mediterranean-style diet rich in seafood to help reduce inflammation.
questions.question:
(a) A patient with a long history of scaly red skin patches on the elbows and scalp now presents with sausage-like swelling of a toe, pain in the spine, and pitting of the nails. What is the probable diagnosis?
(b) List the problem list – impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions.
(c) Outline a treatment plan including modalities and exercise.
(d) State precautions and contraindications.
(e) Describe the patient education, joint protection and energy conservation advice.

(a) Define reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome) and describe its aetiology.
(b) Describe its pathology.
(c) Describe its clinical features.
(d) State the diagnostic/investigative findings used to support the diagnosis.
(e) Explain why reactive arthritis is commoner in young men.
(f) Distinguish between reactive arthritis and psoriatic arthritis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition/aetiology: reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome) is an autoimmune, RF-seronegative, HLA-B27-linked arthritis that develops as a reaction to infection elsewhere in the body (cross-reactivity), most often precipitated by genitourinary infection (Chlamydia trachomatis) or enteric infection (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter).

(b)
Pathology: it is marked by inflammatory synovitis and erosion at the insertion sites of ligaments and tendons (enthesitis); although microbial antigens are found in the synovium, organisms cannot usually be cultured from joint fluid, suggesting infection or postinfectious inflammation rather than direct joint infection.

(c)
Clinical features: the classic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and urethritis/cervicitis; arthritis is typically asymmetric, oligoarticular, affecting large lower-limb joints and sacroiliac joints, sometimes with sausage-shaped digits; enthesitis (plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinitis); mucocutaneous lesions (circinate balanitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum); constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss).

(d)
Investigative findings: swabs/cultures of urethra, cervix or throat and stool for causative organisms; non-specific elevation of ESR and CRP; HLA-B27 positive in about 75% of patients; joint fluid shows inflammatory synovitis with a raised white cell count (predominantly neutrophils) but no crystals and a normal glucose level.

(e)
• Clinical basis for young male predominance: reactive arthritis most commonly strikes individuals aged 20-40 years and is more common in men, largely because the sexually transmitted form (linked to Chlamydia) occurs primarily in men in this age range, and HLA-B27 (a predisposing factor in over two-thirds of patients) is more frequent in white men.
• Patients with HIV also have an increased risk of developing reactive arthritis, and it can occur in epidemic form after outbreaks of enteric infection.

(f)
• Preceding illness: reactive arthritis follows a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection, whereas psoriatic arthritis is associated with the skin disease psoriasis, which may precede or follow the joint disease.
• Systemic triad: reactive arthritis characteristically includes conjunctivitis/urethritis in addition to arthritis, which is not a feature of psoriatic arthritis.
• Shared features: both conditions can show an asymmetric arthritis pattern, sausage-shaped digits, and distal interphalangeal joint involvement, and the skin lesions of reactive arthritis (keratoderma blennorrhagicum) can be histologically identical to psoriatic plaques.
• Constitutional symptoms: patients with reactive arthritis tend to have more constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss) than patients with psoriatic arthritis, who have fewer constitutional symptoms.
• Skin/nail findings: psoriatic arthritis is associated with psoriasis (skin plaques, nail pitting), whereas reactive arthritis is associated with mucocutaneous ulcers, balanitis and keratoderma blennorrhagicum rather than chronic psoriasis.
• Course: reactive arthritis may be self-limiting, recurrent, chronic or progressive after an infectious trigger, whereas psoriatic arthritis follows a more chronic autoimmune course linked to ongoing psoriasis, with remissions tending to be more frequent, rapid and complete than in rheumatoid arthritis but progression to arthritis mutilans possible.

questions.question:
(a) A young woman presents with fatigue, fever, weight loss, a butterfly-shaped facial rash, and pain and swelling of several joints that are not deformed on examination. What is the probable diagnosis, and what risk factors predispose to it?
(b) What complications can arise in this condition?
(c) Describe physiotherapy management options appropriate to the different stages (exacerbation/remission) of the disease, and justify which you would prioritise for this patient now.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) – an inflammatory multisystem disease with excessive autoantibody production, tissue damage from immune complex deposition, and a wide spectrum of clinical presentation including constitutional symptoms (fatigue, fever, weight loss), the malar "butterfly" rash, and non-erosive, rarely deforming arthritis. Risk factors: female sex (F:M ratio 9:1), age 15-40 years (peak incidence), and black racial background (three times more common).

(b)
Complications: cardiac manifestations (pericarditis, myocarditis, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, coronary heart disease); pulmonary manifestations (pleuritis, pneumonitis, pulmonary haemorrhage, pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary embolism); musculoskeletal complications include tenosynovitis and, though arthritis is non-erosive, occasional Jaccoud's deformity; myopathy either from true myositis or secondary to drugs (steroids, anti-malarials).

(c)
• Physiotherapy management by stage: the disease is characterised by remissions and exacerbations. Management includes rest as needed (good sleep hygiene, resting stiff/painful joints, support devices such as splints), an exercise plan to increase exercise tolerance, mobilise stiff joints and increase ROM, and occupational therapy support for daily activities; during flare-ups, ice or heat and elevation help reduce pain and swelling, and warm clothing/exercise of fingers and toes protects circulation.
• Justification: for this patient, who is presenting with an active flare (rash, fever, joint swelling), rest, joint protection and flare management (ice/heat, elevation) should be prioritised over vigorous exercise, with a graded exercise/mobility programme introduced as the flare settles.

(a)
• Clinical course: AS typically begins in adolescence/early adulthood (ages 17-45) with inflammatory low back pain and stiffness; inflammation gradually spreads from the sacroiliac joints to the joints between vertebrae (spondylitis), and over time new bone formation progressively fuses vertebral segments (ankylosis), causing the spine to become rigid.
• Classification by pattern: axial AS (predominantly axial involvement with radiographic sacroiliitis), non-radiographic axial AS (clinically similar but without radiographic sacroiliitis), and peripheral AS (predominantly peripheral joint involvement).
• The disease can also involve the shoulders, hips and occasionally knees, and, as it progresses, the joints between the spine and ribs, restricting chest movement; advanced disease increases the risk of vertebral fracture.

(b)
• Deformities: kyphosis and loss of lumbar lordosis develop because a flexed/bent-over posture eases back pain and muscle spasm; in late stages there is accentuated kyphosis and fixed bent-forward posturing with inability to lie flat; peripheral joint deformity can occur, sometimes with dactylitis of the digits.
• Extra-articular manifestations occur in about a third of patients: recurrent acute anterior uveitis (up to 40% of cases, causing eye pain and photophobia); cardiovascular involvement (aortic insufficiency, aortitis, angina, pericarditis, conduction abnormalities); pulmonary fibrosis/cavitation of upper lobes; neurologic complications from compression radiculitis, vertebral fracture/subluxation or cauda equina syndrome; rarely secondary amyloidosis.

(c)
• In all stages, exercise combining muscle strengthening, range of motion, flexibility and cardiorespiratory work (land-based, water-based, home or supervised) is used to improve aerobic capacity, muscle strength, flexibility and spinal mobility.
• Postural and breathing-focused management is emphasised throughout: posture exercises with upper-back hyperextension avoiding lumbar hyperextension, breathing exercises for rib-cage excursion, and ROM exercises for hips/knees to prevent flexion contractures.
• The Global Posture Re-education method (active postures held 15-20 minutes to stretch shortened muscle chains) is used, chosen according to pain level, load capacity and age, progressing as tolerated; the standing trunk-flexion posture is used only if the patient can cooperate given fatigue and pain.
• Manual therapy, physiotherapy modalities (short wave, TENS, infrared) and balneotherapy/hydrotherapy support pain, stiffness, function and wellbeing at each stage, alongside patient education on diagnosis, prognosis and self-management, and advice on sleeping posture/bracing to limit deformity.

(d)
• Basis of deformities: persistent inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, spine and entheses leads to new bone formation that bridges and fuses vertebral segments (ankylosis), fixing the spine in the position habitually adopted for pain relief – a flexed, bent-forward posture – producing kyphosis and loss of lordosis.
• Costovertebral joint involvement restricts rib-cage movement, reducing chest expansion and pulmonary function, which is why breathing exercises are a core part of management.
• Functional limitation therefore results from a combination of pain-driven muscle guarding/spasm, progressive structural fusion of the spine, and reduced chest expansion, all of which physiotherapy aims to counter through posture correction, mobility work and breathing exercise before fixed deformity sets in.

questions.question:
An older adult is assessed for nutritional status in a geriatric physiotherapy clinic.
(i) State the parameter being assessed and the instruments used.
(ii) Describe the standardised procedure for measuring weight, height, and waist and hip circumference.
(iii) State how body mass index and waist:hip ratio are derived from these measurements.
(iv) State the precautions/sources of error for this type of assessment.
questions.answerText:
(i) The parameter is nutritional status, assessed anthropometrically, using a portable scale, a tape/standometer, and a flexible steel tape.
(ii) Weight is measured with a portable scale, in light clothing (without shoes), to the nearest 0.1 kg.
Height is measured with a tape, standometer, or wall calibration, to the nearest 0.5 cm.
Circumferences are measured to the nearest centimetre using a flexible steel tape, with the subject standing; the abdominal (waist) circumference is measured at the end of expiration, wrapping the tape at the level of the umbilicus, and the hip circumference is measured at the maximum posterior protrusion of the buttocks.
(iii) Body mass index is calculated from the weight and height values (Wt/Ht²); the waist:hip ratio (WHR) is obtained by dividing the waist circumference by the hip circumference.
(iv) Anthropometry is noted as a convenient and reliable technique providing an indirect estimation of nutritional status, whereas direct methods such as bioelectrical impedance analysis and dual X-ray absorptiometry are used to measure fat-free mass and fat mass directly.

A(i) The Harpenden skinfold caliper measures skinfold thickness. The flexible steel tape measures body circumferences.
A(ii) Skinfold thickness is measured at 4 sites using the Harpenden skinfold caliper: triceps (posterior mid-point between the acromion and the olecranon), subscapular (just inferior to the inferior angle of the scapula), suprailiac (upper point of the iliac crest, at 45° toward the pubic symphysis), and thigh (medial point of the anterior surface of the thigh).
Circumferences are measured to the nearest centimetre using the flexible steel tape, with the subject standing; the waist is measured at the end of expiration at the level of the umbilicus, and the hip at the maximum posterior protrusion of the buttocks.
B. Skinfold thickness measurements (caliper) are used, together with arm circumference, to estimate muscle size, e.g. arm muscle circumference = arm circumference - (π × triceps skinfold), and arm muscle area = (muscle circumference)²/4π.
Circumference measurements (tape) are used to calculate the waist:hip ratio (WHR = waist circumference/hip circumference), an indicator of nutritional/adiposity status.
Both instruments are indirect anthropometric methods, as opposed to direct methods such as bioelectrical impedance analysis and dual X-ray absorptiometry, which measure fat-free mass and fat mass directly.
Anthropometric measurement generally is described as a convenient and reliable technique for evaluating changes in nutritional status.
C. The caliper measures a pinched skinfold at specific anatomical landmarks to estimate subcutaneous fat/muscle size, while the tape measures the circumference (girth) around a body part such as the waist, hip, or upper arm.
The caliper's four sites (triceps, subscapular, suprailiac, thigh) are point measurements, whereas the tape gives a single circumferential reading at each site (waist, hip, upper arm).
Both are indirect estimation techniques, most commonly used in clinical practice for assessing nutritional status.
The tape-derived circumferences are also used together to compute the waist:hip ratio, whereas the caliper-derived skinfolds are used together with arm circumference to estimate arm muscle circumference and area.
questions.question:
A. Describe the Harpenden skinfold caliper and the flexible steel tape as anthropometric instruments under the following headings:
A(i) what each measures
A(ii) sites/procedure of use
B. Explain the basis for choosing one instrument over the other for a given assessment (their respective uses).
C. Distinguish between the Harpenden skinfold caliper and the flexible steel tape.

A. Describe the physiological parameter of blood pressure, addressing:
A(i) definition
A(ii) unit of measurement
A(iii) normal values
A(iv) factors affecting it
B. Explain how blood pressure is interpreted in health and in dysfunction.
C. State the clinical significance of blood pressure to treatment planning and progress monitoring.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Blood pressure is the pressure exerted by the blood on the vessel walls.
A(ii) It is expressed in mmHg.
A(iii) Normal blood pressure is 110-130/70-80 mmHg; the systolic pressure is usually 120 mmHg and the diastolic pressure is usually 80 mmHg.
A(iv) These normal levels apply only in young and middle life; in older people, the pressure is likely to be higher and yet still normal, so age is a stated factor affecting it.
B. In health, blood pressure falls within the normal range stated (110-130/70-80 mmHg), noting that what is 'normal' is age-dependent.
In dysfunction, this is illustrated in a clinical vignette in which a 62-year-old woman's blood pressure was recorded as 160/100 mmHg, above the normal range.
Blood pressure is measured using a sphygmomanometer, an instrument whose method of operation is the deflection method, in which the value is directly indicated by deflection of a pointer on a calibrated scale.
C. Blood pressure is one of the vital signs, providing basic physiological information as objective evidence of disease.
In the clinical vignette, an elevated blood pressure (160/100 mmHg) is one of the recorded measurements used, together with other findings, in clinical reasoning to synthesise information and manage the patient's problem.
Health measurement of this kind facilitates the setting of treatment goals and priorities, and facilitates objective evaluation of the effectiveness of interventions.
It also facilitates the decision on discharge, and on referral to other healthcare providers or change of treatment modalities.

A(i) Respiratory rate is the inhalation and exhalation of air into and out of the lungs.
A(ii) Normal values: adults 14-18 per minute; children 20-40 per minute, the younger the faster.
A(iii) Abnormal patterns include stertorous (noisy, snoring-type) breathing, dyspnea (difficult or laboured breathing), apnea (cessation of breathing), Cheyne-Stokes breathing (deep and fast breathing followed by diminishing respiratory effort and rate, sometimes with a short apnea), tachypnea (an increased respiratory rate), and Kussmaul's breathing (gasping type, air-hunger).
A(iv) Method: count the breathing to obtain the rate.
B. In health, respiratory rate falls within the normal ranges stated for adults and children.
In dysfunction, the rate or pattern deviates from normal, for example as tachypnea (an increased respiratory rate observed by the clinician).
Other abnormal patterns such as apnea, Cheyne-Stokes, and Kussmaul's breathing represent specific deviations that are recognised clinically by their described character.
C. Respiratory rate is one of the vital signs, providing basic physiological information that constitutes objective evidence of disease or deformity.
It is grouped with pulse rate, temperature, and blood pressure as basic physical examination findings necessary in respiratory and cardiovascular assessment.
Diseases of the respiratory system are noted as one of the commonest causes of mortality and morbidity throughout the world.
Thorough examination of the respiratory system, including its rate, is therefore stated to be very important in properly diagnosing any respiratory problem.

questions.answerText:
(i) The condition is congenital hip dysplasia (instability of the hip); the tests used are the Ortolani test and the Barlow test (manual clinical tests, for screening).
(ii) Ortolani's test: the examiner's hands are placed over the child's knees, thumbs on the medial thigh, fingers placing a gentle upward stress on the lateral thigh and greater trochanter area, while the infant's hip is abducted.
Barlow's test: with the hands in the same position, hold the hip and knees at 90° of flexion, exert backward pressure, and slowly and gently adduct the hip.
(iii) In relation to paediatric physical diagnosis generally, one should never hunt for reflexes in children, and play therapy should be used when handling children.
(iv) Ortolani's test is positive when a clunk sound is felt/heard as the femoral head re-enters the acetabulum.
Barlow's test is positive when there is any feeling of the femoral head slipping out of the socket.
In later life, unilateral dysplasia presents as asymmetric shortening on the side of the dislocation, known as the Galeazzi sign, along with lateral rotation of the affected leg, tight hip adductors/decreased abduction, asymmetric thigh or gluteal folds, and a wider than normal space between the legs.
questions.question:
An infant is brought for physiotherapy screening for congenital hip dysplasia (CHD).
(i) State the parameter/condition being screened for and the tests/instrument used.
(ii) Describe the procedure and the anatomical landmarks for each test.
(iii) State any safety considerations when examining an infant.

questions.answerText:
(i) The technique is assessment of carotid pulse character, performed by observing carotid pulsations and compressing the carotid artery.
(ii) A pulse that weakens in inspiration is called pulsus paradoxus, and indicates tamponade or constrictive pericarditis.
(iii) A hypokinetic (small volume) pulse is found in low output states like heart failure, shock, and mitral stenosis; a collapsing (rapid up and rapid down/water-hammer) pulse indicates the wide pulse pressure of aortic regurgitation (also an AV fistula or hyperdynamic circulation).
(iv) Best checked on the carotid arteries: observe for carotid pulsations, place fingers behind the patient's neck and compress the carotid on one side, assess the amplitude of the pulse, the contour of the pulse wave, and variations in amplitude from beat to beat or with respiration, then repeat on the opposite side.
questions.question:
During carotid pulse assessment, a physiotherapist records that the patient's pulse weakens noticeably during inspiration.
(i) Identify the parameter/technique used to obtain this finding.
(ii) Interpret this specific finding.
(iii) State two other carotid pulse character findings and their clinical associations.
(iv) State the factors/technique needed to make this assessment properly.

questions.answerText:
(i) The parameter is the heart sounds and precordial activity; the instrument used is a stethoscope, together with palpation of the precordium.
(ii) Precordium examination: position the patient supine with the head of the table slightly elevated, and always examine from the patient's right side.
Inspect for precordial bulge, precordial movement, and the apical beat (the most laterally and downward positioned impulse).
Auscultation landmarks: the aortic position is between the 2nd and 3rd intercostal space at the right sternal border; the pulmonic position is the same level at the left sternal border.
Mitral sounds are heard best at the 5th left intercostal space, mid-clavicular line; tricuspid sounds are heard at the 4th left intercostal space, lateral to the sternum.
(iii) S1 signals the onset of systole and is caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves; it can be identified by palpating the carotid pulse while auscultating.
A loud S1 is found in mitral stenosis, tachycardia, and hyperdynamic circulation (e.g. anaemia).
A soft/muffled S1 is found in mitral regurgitation, bradycardia, and left ventricular failure (LVF).
