(i) State the parameter being assessed and the instrument used.
(ii) Describe the procedure and the anatomical landmarks used to auscultate each heart valve area.
(iii) Interpret and document findings of a loud first heart sound (S1) and of a soft/muffled S1.

A. Describe the technique for measuring height (stature) in a child aged two years and older who can stand, addressing:
A(i) equipment
A(ii) procedure/positioning
A(iii) recording
B. State the sources of error in this measurement and how they are minimised.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A standard measuring board with a moveable headboard (a stadiometer) attached to a flat wall is used.
A(ii) The child is measured wearing light clothing and without shoes and/or heavy socks.
The child is instructed to look forward and stand up straight, with buttocks, shoulder blades, and heels together, touching the wall or stadiometer.
The headboard is aligned perpendicular to the wall and lowered to the top of the child's head.
A(iii) The measurement is read to the nearest 0.1 cm or 1/8 inch.
B. The measurement is repeated twice, or until two measurements agree within 1 cm or ¼ inch.
The average of the two closest measurements is then recorded.
This repeat-until-agreement approach is the stated method of minimising error.
Height measured this way is also used, together with weight, to calculate the Body Mass Index (Wt/Ht²) for screening purposes.
Anthropometric measurements such as height help providers determine if a child is growing properly and select appropriate treatment options.

questions.question:
A. Describe the Mini-Cog and the Abbreviated Mental Test Score (AMTS) under the following headings:
A(i) purpose/type
A(ii) parts/items and procedure
A(iii) scoring/interpretation
B. Explain the clinical basis for choosing one of these tools (their advantages).
C. Distinguish between the Mini-Cog and the AMTS.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Both are tools for cognitive function screening in older adults, used to assess for the possibility of dementia.
A(ii) The Mini-Cog consists of two parts: 3-item recall plus a clock drawing test (CDT). The patient is asked to listen carefully as three unrelated objects are named and to repeat the object names.
The patient is then instructed to draw the face of a clock and, after adding the numbers, to draw the hands to show a specific time; this clock-drawing task serves as the recall distractor. The patient is then asked to repeat the three previously presented object names.
The AMTS is a 10-point test for rapidly assessing elderly patients for the possibility of dementia; it was first used in 1972.
A(iii) Mini-Cog scoring: 1 point is given for each recalled word after the CDT distractor (score 0-3); the CDT is normal if all numbers are present in the correct sequence/position and the hands readably display the requested time.
A score of 0 indicates dementia regardless of CDT result; a score of 1 or 2 with an abnormal CDT indicates dementia, while a score of 1 or 2 with a normal CDT indicates absence of dementia; a score of 3 indicates absence of dementia regardless of CDT result.
No specific scoring/interpretation for the AMTS is described, beyond it being a 10-point test.
B. The Mini-Cog is described as consisting of only two brief tasks (recall and clock-drawing), giving a quick score with clear interpretation rules as above.
The AMTS is described as being able to rapidly assess elderly patients for dementia, and is now also sometimes used to assess mental confusion (including delirium) and other cognitive impairments.
C. The Mini-Cog uses 3-item recall combined with a clock-drawing test, scored 0-3, with the CDT result used to qualify an ambiguous recall score of 1 or 2.
The AMTS is a 10-point test first used in 1972 and is also applied to assess delirium and other cognitive impairments, unlike the Mini-Cog, which is described only in relation to dementia screening.
Both tools are used for rapid screening of cognitive function in older adults.

questions.question:
A. Describe the technique for assessing oedema, addressing:
A(i) purpose
A(ii) procedure
A(iii) endpoint/finding
A(iv) recording/grading
questions.answerText:
A(i) Purpose: to assess the presence and degree of oedema in a particular area.
A(ii) Procedure: press two fingers into the particular area for 2 to 3 seconds.
A(iii) Endpoint/finding: if an impression is left once the fingers are removed, pitting (dependent) oedema is present; if otherwise, non-pitting oedema is present.
A(iv) Recording/grading: the degree of oedema is based on the length of time that the indentation lasts, graded from 1+ (the least) to 4+ (the worst).

questions.question:
A. Describe the measurement property of reliability, addressing:
A(i) definition and synonyms
A(ii) its components/types
A(iii) statistical methods used to determine it
B. Explain how reliability affects the clinical use and interpretation of a measuring instrument.
C. Distinguish between test-retest reliability and inter-rater reliability.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Reliability is the degree to which test scores are free from errors of measurement.
Synonyms include repeatability, reproducibility, consistency, accuracy, stability, agreement, and precision.
A(ii) The components are test-retest reliability, intra-rater reliability, inter-rater reliability, and internal consistency (homogeneity).
A(iii) Reliability is determined from the correlation, standard error of measurement, or agreement between two or more sets of scores obtained on different occasions or by different testers.
Statistical methods used include Pearson's correlation, Spearman's correlation, Standard Error of Measurement (SEM), and Intra-class correlation (ICC); Cronbach's α is used for internal consistency.
B. As reliability increases, the amount of error inherent in the measurement decreases, giving more dependable results for clinical decision-making.
Reliability is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for validity.
An unreliable measure is also an invalid measurement, because a measurement with a great deal of error has little meaning or utility.
However, a reliable measure is valid only if, in addition to being repeatable, it also provides meaningful information.
C. Test-retest reliability is the reliability of scores assessed on two or more administrations of a test, and is applicable to self-report instruments (questionnaires).
Inter-rater reliability is the consistency of performance among different raters or judges in assigning scores to the same objects or responses.
Intra-rater reliability, by contrast, is the consistency with which a single rater assigns scores to the same set of responses on two occasions.

questions.question:
A physiotherapist needs to assess pain in three paediatric patients: a newborn, a 5-year-old, and a 10-year-old.
(i) State why age-appropriate pain scales are needed in paediatrics.
(ii) Name the pain scale(s)/tool(s) appropriate for each age group.
(iii) State the property common to the scales used for pain assessment in children.
(iv) Justify the choice of tool for the 5-year-old specifically.
questions.answerText:
(i) Since babies are not able to communicate their pain verbally, other comprehensive scales are needed to assess pain in children.
(ii) Birth to 2 years: Premature Infant Pain Profile, and the Neonatal Infant Pain Scale.
3 to 7 years: the Wong-Baker Facies Pain Rating Scale, and the OUCHER Scale (also, the Faces Pain Scale, for children aged 3 years and above).
Above 7 years: the Verbal Rating Scale, the Visual Analog Scale, the Numerical Rating Pain Scale, and the Semantic Differential Scale.
(iii) These age-appropriate scales are described as comprehensive but validated and reliable.
(iv) The Faces Pain Scale is justified for the 5-year-old because it is designed for children aged 3 years and above, who match their level of pain to one of six faces ranging from no pain at all (smiling) to the worst pain imaginable (grimacing) - appropriate to a 5-year-old's stage of communication, unlike the infant scales (birth-2 years) or the verbal/numerical scales intended for children above 7 years.

questions.question:
A. Describe the measurement property of validity, addressing:
A(i) definition
A(ii) why it must be measured
A(iii) its types
B. Explain how each type of validity affects clinical use and interpretation.
C. Distinguish between face validity and content validity.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Validity is the appropriateness, meaningfulness, and usefulness of the specific inferences made from test scores; the older definition, 'the extent to which a tool measures what it is intended to measure', is no longer accepted as sufficient.
A(ii) Some health variables (e.g. health status, disability, functional ability, quality of life) are not directly observable, and validity is required when predicting human behaviours from certain observations, e.g. predicting a patient's performance in the community from a therapist's evaluation while still on admission.
A(iii) The types are face validity, content validity, construct validity, and criterion-related validity (with concurrent and predictive validity as types of criterion validity).
B. Face and content validity are determined by the judgment of experts and are a concern especially for self-report or observational tools.
Construct validity is empirically determined; because constructs are not directly observable, no absolute standard exists, so hypothesis testing is used to support the underlying construct.
Criterion-related validity is empirically determined by comparing scores from a new scale against a measurement standard or gold standard.
Concurrent validity applies when a new scale is compared with a measurement standard at the same time, while predictive validity relates to whether a test predicts future status.
Reliability is a necessary but not sufficient condition for validity: an unreliable measure is also invalid, but a reliable measure is valid only if it also provides meaningful information.
C. Face validity indicates whether, on the face of it, the instrument appears to be assessing the desired qualities; a panel of judges is asked whether the scale appears to assess what it is meant to assess.
Content validity consists of a judgement of whether the instrument samples all the relevant or important content or domains, i.e. the extent to which a measure is a complete representation of the concept of interest.
Content validity testing involves asking a panel of experts to review the items on a scale to ensure item relevance and wide coverage of the domains the developers intend to measure.
Both are technical descriptions of the judgement that a scale 'looks reasonable', but content validity requires a more systematic review of coverage than face validity.

questions.question:
A. Describe measuring instruments in general under the following headings:
A(i) classification according to function
A(ii) classification according to accuracy of measurement
A(iii) metrological characteristics used to specify them
B. Explain the basis on which an instrument would be chosen for a task (advantages/limitations of each accuracy group).
C. Distinguish between an optical interferometer and a dial indicator/vernier caliper.
questions.answerText:
A(i) According to function, measuring instruments are classified as: length measuring instruments; angle measuring instruments; instruments for checking deviations from geometrical forms; and instruments for determining the quality of surface.
A(ii) According to accuracy: the most accurate instruments are light-interference instruments, e.g. the optical interferometer.
The second group consists of less accurate instruments such as room microscopes, comparators, and optimeters.
The third group comprises still less accurate instruments, e.g. dial indicators, vernier calipers, and rules with vernier scales.
A(iii) Metrological characteristics: range of measurement (scale range and instrument range), scale spacing, sensitivity, and reading accuracy.
Sensitivity is the ratio of scale spacing to division value, i.e. the ability to detect the smallest change; reading accuracy is the accuracy attainable in using the instrument.
B. Instruments are grouped by their accuracy, from most accurate (light-interference instruments) to less accurate (room microscopes, comparators, optimeters) to still less accurate (dial indicators, vernier calipers, rules with vernier scales).
This implies that the choice of instrument should match the accuracy required for the measurement task, with the most accurate group being light-interference instruments such as the optical interferometer.
C. The optical interferometer belongs to the most accurate group of instruments (light-interference instruments).
The dial indicator and vernier caliper belong to the third, still less accurate, group of instruments, along with rules with vernier scales.
Both groups are nonetheless used for measurement, but differ in the accuracy of measurement they can provide.

questions.question:
A patient undergoes a full respiratory chest examination including percussion and auscultation.
(i) State the parameters/techniques being used and the instrument for auscultation.
(ii) Describe the procedure and the reference areas (landmarks) for percussion and for auscultation.
(iii) State how findings from percussion and auscultation should be documented (symmetry).
questions.answerText:
(i) The techniques are percussion and auscultation; auscultation uses a stethoscope.
(ii) Percussion is done with the middle finger of the right hand tapping on the middle finger of the left hand, which is placed firmly on the body; it is usually sufficient to percuss three or four areas anteriorly, three or four areas on the back, and two in the axillae.
Auscultation involves listening to the sounds generated by breathing, listening for any adventitious (added) sounds, and listening to the patient's spoken or whispered voice as transmitted through the chest wall.
(iii) The percussion note on two equivalent sides of the chest should be systematically compared, and the findings on both sides of the chest should be compared symmetrically; similarly, breath sound intensity/quality should be documented and compared between sides.

(i) The instrument is the vernier caliper.
(ii) It uses the coincidence method of measurement: the very small difference between the given quantity and the reference is determined by observation of the coincidence of scale marks.
(iii) Reading accuracy is the accuracy that may be attained in using a measuring instrument, and reading error is defined as the difference between the reading of the instrument and the actual value of the dimension being measured.
Sensitivity, the ratio of scale spacing to division value, is the instrument's ability to detect the smallest change; low sensitivity limits how precisely a reading reflects the true value.
The vernier caliper is classed among the 'still less accurate' group of instruments (with dial indicators and rules with vernier scales), compared with more accurate instruments such as optical interferometers.
questions.question:
During a practical class on measuring instruments, a student is given a small component and asked to measure its dimension precisely using a coincidence-type instrument.
(i) Identify the instrument.
(ii) Describe the principle of operation of this method of measurement.
(iii) The student obtains an inconsistent reading. Explain what factors could make this instrument's reading inaccurate.

A. Describe the outcomes criteria for a good outcome measure, addressing:
A(i) the six criteria and their defining questions
A(ii) which criteria concern accuracy of the score versus ability to detect change
B. Explain how each criterion affects clinical use of the outcome measure.
C. Distinguish between sensitivity and specificity.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Utility - is it useful? Reliability - is it dependable? Validity - does it do what it is supposed to?
Sensitivity - can it identify patients with a condition? Specificity - can it identify those that do not have the condition? Responsiveness - can it measure differences over time?
A(ii) Reliability and validity concern the dependability and appropriateness of the score itself; sensitivity and specificity concern identifying patients with or without a condition; responsiveness concerns the ability to measure change over time.
B. A useful (utility) and dependable (reliable) measure gives the clinician confidence that repeated use of the tool with a given patient will give a trustworthy score.
A valid measure (does what it is supposed to) ensures that the score genuinely reflects the attribute the clinician intends to track.
A measure with good sensitivity correctly flags patients who do have the condition, supporting diagnosis and case identification.
A measure with good specificity correctly identifies those without the condition, avoiding false identification of a condition that is not present.
A responsive measure can detect differences over time, which is essential for monitoring the effectiveness of an intervention and informing changes to the treatment plan.
C. Sensitivity is the ability of a measure to identify patients with a condition.
Specificity is the ability of a measure to identify those that do not have the condition.
A measure could therefore be good at correctly flagging those with a condition (sensitive) while being less good at correctly clearing those without it (specific), or vice versa.
Both are listed among the outcomes criteria alongside utility, reliability, validity, and responsiveness.

A(i) Internal validity refers specifically to whether an experimental treatment/condition makes a difference or not, and whether there is sufficient evidence to support the claim (e.g. did strengthening exercise actually increase muscle power, and not long-distance walking?).
External validity refers to the generalisability of the treatment/condition outcomes, i.e. whether it can be applied to the whole population and not just a sampled fraction.
A(ii) Threats to internal validity: history (specific events occurring between the first and second measurement, unrelated to the event being tested); maturation (processes within subjects as a function of the passage of time); testing (effects of taking an initial test on the outcomes of a second test).
Also: instrumentation (changes in the instrument, observers, or scorers producing changes in outcomes); selection of subjects (biases in selecting comparison groups); experimental mortality (loss of subjects).
A(iii) Threats to external validity: reactive/interaction effect of testing (a pretest might increase or decrease a subject's sensitivity/responsiveness to the experimental variable); interaction effects of selection biases and the experimental variable.
Also: reactive effects of experimental arrangements (difficult to generalise to non-experimental settings if the effect is attributable to the experimental arrangement); multiple treatment interference (as multiple treatments are given to the same subjects, it is difficult to control for the effects of prior treatments).
B. If internal validity is threatened (e.g. by maturation or testing effects), a clinician cannot be confident the observed change is really due to the intervention itself.
If external validity is threatened (e.g. by reactive testing effects or interaction with selection bias), findings from a study sample may not generalise to other patients or settings.
Both must be considered before applying a research finding, or a within-clinic measurement design, to broader clinical decision-making.
C. Internal validity concerns whether the treatment/condition itself is truly responsible for the observed difference, within the study/assessment as conducted.
External validity concerns whether the result can be generalised beyond the specific sample or circumstances in which it was obtained.
A study or measurement approach can therefore have strong internal validity but weak external validity, or vice versa, depending on which threats are present.
questions.question:
A. Describe internal validity and external validity, addressing:
A(i) definitions
A(ii) threats to internal validity
A(iii) threats to external validity
B. Explain how each type of validity affects the clinical/research use and interpretation of a study's findings.
C. Distinguish between internal validity and external validity.

An elderly patient with a progressive chronic illness is referred for assessment of functional independence in activities of daily living.
(i) Name two outcome measures/assessment tools that could be used.
(ii) State the measurement properties described for each tool.
(iii) State the limitations of each tool.
(iv) Justify which one you would choose for this patient, with reasons.
questions.answerText:
(i) The Katz ADL Index and the Lawton Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) scale.
(ii) The Katz ADL Index has established reliability and is easy to use; scoring ranges from categorical (yes/no) to point scaling (independent, some assistance, or dependent), and it creates a common language about a patient's function for caregivers.
The Lawton IADL is useful in rehabilitation settings to monitor improvements over time and differentiates task performance, including the amount of help and time needed for each task.
(iii) No further limitations of the Katz ADL Index are stated beyond its scope.
The independent activities of daily living (IADLs) are described as more sensitive for subtle functional deficiencies than the ADLs, implying the Katz ADL Index may be less sensitive to subtle change.
(iv) The Lawton IADL would be justified where continued independent community residence and subtle functional change must be tracked, since IADLs are more sensitive to subtle deficiencies than ADLs.
The Katz ADL Index would be justified where a simple, reliable measure of basic self-care independence and a common language for caregivers is needed.

questions.question:
A patient with knee osteoarthritis (OA) needs an appropriate combination of outcome measures selected for assessment.
(i) State the domains/outcomes identified for Knee OA.
(ii) State the measurement property/type considerations in choosing a generic versus a condition-specific tool.
(iii) State the limitation of using a generic tool alone.
(iv) Justify a combined approach for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) For Knee OA, the outcomes/domains identified are: pain, quadriceps and hamstrings strength, range of motion, disability, balance ability, and quality of life (QOL).
(ii) An integrated/generic self-report tool such as the SF-36 is not a tool specifically for functional assessment of physical and mental/emotional symptoms, whereas a condition-specific tool such as the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) targets a specific condition.
(iii) The limitation of the generic tool alone is that interpreting its results with respect to specific musculoskeletal impairments may prove challenging.
(iv) Combining a generic measure such as the SF-36 with a condition-specific outcome measure such as the ODI provides complementary information on the person's status, which would be the justified approach for this patient's Knee OA assessment alongside the disease-specific domains (pain, strength, ROM, disability, balance, QOL).

(i) A patient-reported outcome (PRO) questionnaire measuring health-related quality of life, and the Functional Independence Measure (FIM), a performance-based measure.
(ii) The criteria for choosing an outcome measure are: validity (is the measure valid or validated for use?), reliability (is it consistent over repeated measures when no change occurs?), responsiveness (can it detect important change when it occurs?), and feasibility (can it be used easily?).
(iii) Self-report/PRO measures rely on a patient's direct responses and perception, without interpretation by a clinician.
Performance-based measures like the FIM provide a relatively objective assessment of physical functioning, but results may vary among testers and even with the same tester on different days.
(iv) The FIM would be justified for this patient because it requires the patient to demonstrate self-care activities, transfers, locomotion, and bowel and bladder function, giving an objective, performance-based assessment of the functional independence relevant after stroke.
questions.question:
A patient recovering from stroke needs an outcome measure to track functional independence.
(i) Name a self-report and a performance-based outcome measure that could be considered.
(ii) State the measurement properties/criteria relevant to choosing between them.
(iii) State the limitations of each.
(iv) Justify your choice for this patient.

questions.answerText:
A(i) BMI is a calculation based on the relationship of height to weight (Wt/Ht²), used to screen for adiposity in individuals 2 years and older.
A(ii) Calculating and tracking BMI for children 2 years and older can help identify risks for overweight and obesity, or risks for underweight.
A(iii) The categories are: Underweight - less than the 5th percentile; Healthy Weight - 5th percentile to less than the 85th percentile; Overweight - 85th percentile to less than the 95th percentile; Obese - equal to or greater than the 95th percentile.
B. In health, a child's BMI falls within the healthy weight percentile range (5th to less than 85th percentile).
In dysfunction, a BMI below the 5th percentile classifies the child as underweight, while a BMI at or above the 95th percentile classifies the child as obese, and 85th-95th as overweight.
Due to the long-term, adverse health consequences associated with paediatric obesity, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians endorse universal screening of BMI.
They also endorse the use of BMI growth curves for plotting BMI percentiles to identify obese and overweight children.
C. BMI tracking over time allows identification of a child's risk for overweight/obesity or underweight, which is stated as important given the long-term, adverse health consequences associated with paediatric obesity.
It is calculated from height and weight, both of which are obtained using the anthropometric measurement techniques described for children (stature/recumbent length and weight).
questions.question:
A. Describe Body Mass Index (BMI) as used in paediatric assessment, addressing:
A(i) definition/calculation
A(ii) what it is used to screen for
A(iii) the percentile categories
B. Explain how BMI is interpreted in health and in dysfunction (over/underweight).
C. State the clinical significance of BMI to treatment planning and progress monitoring.

questions.answerText:
(i) The technique is chest percussion, used to determine whether the underlying tissues are air-filled, fluid-filled, or solid.
(ii) A dull percussion note indicates the presence of a solid mass under the surface; causes of dullness include tumours, lobar pneumonia, hydrothorax, haemothorax, empyema, fibrosis, atelectasis, and thick chest wall.
A hyper-resonant note indicates hollow, air-containing structures; bilateral causes of hyper-resonance include emphysema and bronchial asthma, while unilateral causes include pneumothorax and a large air-filled area in the lungs.
(iii) The percussion note on two equivalent sides of the chest should be compared systematically; it is usually sufficient to percuss three or four areas anteriorly, three or four areas on the back, and two in the axillae, with findings on both sides compared symmetrically.
questions.question:
During chest percussion, a physiotherapist notes a dull percussion note over one area of a patient's chest, and a hyper-resonant note over another patient's chest.
(i) Identify the parameter/technique used.
(ii) Interpret each finding, listing possible causes.
(iii) State the factors that may affect the accuracy of this technique.

questions.answerText:
(i) This is the fundamental (absolute) method of measurement, applied using a balance and known weights.
(ii) It is a method of measurement by direct comparison in which the value of the quantity to be measured is first balanced by an initial known value A of the same quantity; next, the value to be measured is put in the place of that known value and balanced again by a second known value B; when the balance indicating device gives the same indication in both cases, the value of the quantity being measured is derived from the two known balancing values A and B.
(iii) By balancing the unknown value against known reference weights and checking that the balance gives the same indication, this method inherently checks the instrument's reading against known standards, which functions as a check on the instrument's accuracy.
(iv) Reading error is the difference between the reading of the instrument and the actual value of the dimension being measured; reading accuracy is the accuracy attainable in using the instrument, and sensitivity (ratio of scale spacing to division value) governs the instrument's ability to detect the smallest change - a fault in any of these would make the balance's reading inaccurate.
questions.question:
A clinic technician needs to check the accuracy of a beam balance used for measuring body weight, using known reference weights.
(i) Identify the method of measurement being used and the type of instrument.
(ii) Describe the principle of operation of this method.
(iii) Explain how this method relates to calibration/checking of the instrument.
(iv) Explain what would make this instrument's reading inaccurate/faulty.

A. Describe self-report questionnaires and performance-based measures, used for assessing physical function, under the following headings:
A(i) purpose
A(ii) types/examples
A(iii) uses
B. Explain the basis for choosing one of these over the other, including their advantages and limitations.
C. Distinguish between self-report questionnaires and performance-based measures.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Self-report questionnaires: to have individuals assess their own pain and function.
Performance-based measures: to determine the physical work abilities of individuals who have sustained musculoskeletal injury and/or cardiovascular impairment.
A(ii) Self-report types: integrated, impairment specific, body part or region specific, and patient specific.
Performance-based examples: strength testing, balance/proprioceptive testing, 3-minute step test, hand grip, functional gait assessment.
A(iii) Both are used to assess work ability in individuals with musculoskeletal disorders and those with impaired cardiovascular/cardiopulmonary function, vision, and communication.
B. Integrated measures (e.g. SF-36) are hard to interpret for specific impairments; combining with a condition-specific measure (e.g. Oswestry Disability Index) gives complementary information.
Impairment-specific measures may not capture the additive/multiplicative effects of multiple impairments.
Body-part/region-specific measures address only that body part, and patient-specific measures may generalise poorly across patients.
Performance-based measures give a relatively objective assessment, but results may vary among testers and even with the same tester on different days.
C. Self-report questionnaires may be self-administered, provider-administered, or proxy-completed, and rely on the patient's own assessment of pain and function.
Performance-based measures instead require the patient to perform physical skills/tasks, looking at the functioning of the person as a whole rather than a part of the person.

questions.question:
A. Describe the physiological parameter of body temperature, addressing:
A(i) definition
A(ii) unit of measurement
A(iii) normal values/categories
B. Explain how body temperature is interpreted in health and in dysfunction.
C. State the clinical significance of body temperature to treatment planning and progress monitoring.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Body temperature is the degree of warmness or coldness of the body.
A(ii) Body temperature values are expressed in degrees Celsius.
A(iii) The categories stated are: below 35.0°C - hypothermia; below 36.6°C - sub-normal; 36.6°C-37.2°C - normal; above 37.2°C - febrile; above 41.6°C - hyperpyrexia.
B. In health, body temperature falls within the normal range of 36.6°C to 37.2°C.
Temperatures below 36.6°C are classed sub-normal, and below 35.0°C as hypothermia, representing dysfunction at the low end.
Temperatures above 37.2°C are classed febrile, and above 41.6°C as hyperpyrexia, representing dysfunction at the high end.
C. Body temperature is one of the vital signs, providing basic physiological information that is part of the objective evidence gathered in physical examination.
It is one of the basic physical examinations considered necessary in respiratory and cardiovascular assessment.

A(i) Responsiveness/sensitivity to change is the ability of an instrument to detect change in a clinical state over a period of time; these are relatively new terms in the psychometric lexicon.
A(ii) Two questions arise: do the two terms mean the same thing, and are they separate attributes from reliability and validity, or parts of them?
One school of thought holds that the terms mean the same thing; a second school of thought holds that they mean different things.
One school of thought holds that the terms are part and parcel of validity; a second school of thought holds that they are separate.
Many authors use the terms interchangeably.
A(iii) One author differentiated between them, as described in C below.
B. Because the terms are used interchangeably by many authors, a clinician must be aware that a stated 'responsiveness' value in a study may, in some usages, also encompass what another author calls 'sensitivity to change', or vice versa.
Where the author's specific distinction is used, an instrument reported as 'responsive' can be interpreted as capable of detecting clinically important change, which is directly useful for judging treatment effectiveness.
An instrument only 'sensitive to change' (in this author's sense) may register a change that is statistically present but not clinically meaningful, which affects how such a change should be interpreted before altering a treatment plan.
C. Responsiveness is the ability of an instrument to measure a meaningful or clinically important change in a clinical state.
Sensitivity to change is the ability of an instrument to measure a change in a clinical state regardless of whether that change is relevant or meaningful to the decision maker.
The key distinction, therefore, is the clinical importance/meaningfulness of the detected change, not merely whether a change is detected at all.
questions.question:
A. Describe responsiveness and sensitivity to change, addressing:
A(i) general definition
A(ii) the debate around the two terms
A(iii) one author's differentiation between them
B. Explain how this distinction affects the clinical use and interpretation of an outcome measure.
C. Distinguish between responsiveness and sensitivity to change, according to that author.

A 62-year-old woman was assessed by a physiotherapist and the following measurements were obtained: Weight = 76 kg; Height = 1.56 m; Pain intensity on ascending stairs = 5.2; Knee ROM on active flexion = 0-97°; Quadriceps muscle strength L = 3, R = 5; Quadriceps muscle bulk R = 70 cm, L = 58 cm; BP = 160/100 mmHg.
(i) Identify the parameter/technique used to obtain each recorded finding.
(ii) Interpret the findings.
(iii) State the clinical decision(s) and follow-up measurement this data would support.
questions.answerText:
(i) Weight and height are anthropometric measurements; pain intensity uses a pain rating scale; knee ROM on active flexion is a joint range-of-motion measurement.
Quadriceps muscle strength is obtained by manual muscle testing (graded); quadriceps muscle bulk is a girth/circumference measurement; blood pressure is obtained by sphygmomanometry.
(ii) There is a marked asymmetry between the left and right quadriceps in both strength (L=3, weaker, vs R=5) and bulk (L=58 cm vs R=70 cm), suggesting left-sided weakness/wasting.
Knee flexion is limited to 97°, and the blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg is elevated.
(iii) This kind of health measurement data facilitates the setting of treatment goals and priorities, and facilitates objective evaluation of the effectiveness of interventions.
It also facilitates the decision on discharge, and facilitates the decision on referral to other healthcare providers or a change of treatment modalities.
The same measures would be repeated as follow-up measurement to track these changes over the course of care.

A(i) Children under 2 years of age are weighed without clothes or a diaper, using a calibrated beam or digital infant scale, positioned in the centre of the scale tray.
A(ii) Children over 2 years of age are weighed on a calibrated beam balance floor scale or an electronic floor scale with increments less than or equal to 0.1 kg or ¼ pound; the child/adolescent is requested to stand in the centre of the platform and remain motionless until the measurement can be obtained.
A(iii) For children under 2, the reading is taken to the nearest 1 ounce or 0.1 kg (the AAP recommends the nearest 0.01 kg or ½ ounce).
For children over 2, the weight is measured to the nearest 0.1 kg or ¼ pound (the AAP recommends the nearest 0.01 kg or ½ ounce when using a digital scale).
B. Young children should be weighed without shoes and wearing underclothes only, unless privacy cannot be assured.
For older children and young children when privacy is a concern, the child is weighed wearing minimal indoor clothing and without shoes.
C. Using a calibrated scale (beam or digital) is the stated approach to obtaining an accurate weight.
Requiring the child to remain motionless in the centre of the platform/tray until the measurement is obtained helps avoid an inaccurate reading.
Reading to the finer AAP-recommended precision (0.01 kg/½ ounce) with a digital scale, rather than the coarser 0.1 kg increment, reduces measurement error.
questions.question:
A. Describe the technique for measuring weight in children, addressing:
A(i) equipment for children under 2 years
A(ii) equipment and procedure for children over 2 years
A(iii) recording
B. State the precautions to observe (clothing/privacy).
C. State the sources of error in this measurement and how they are minimised.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The pulse is the impulse transmitted to the arteries by contraction of the ventricle, customarily palpated in the radial artery at the wrist.
A(ii) It is measured as the number of beats/impulses per minute.
A(iii) Normal values stated are: 130 beats/min in the newborn infant; 110-120 in infants; 80-120 in children.
Also stated: 70-80 in the adult; 65-80 in women; 60-70 in men; 60-70 in old age.
A(iv) Method: palpation, customarily at the radial artery at the wrist, compressed with the index and middle fingers.
The pulse is counted for one full minute, and the rate and rhythm are recorded.
B. In adults, a normal pulse rate is 60-100 beats/minute.
Bradycardia is a rate of less than 60 beats/minute, and tachycardia is a rate greater than 100 beats/minute.
Rhythm is classed as regular, regularly irregular (e.g. ectopic beats, 2nd degree heart block), or irregularly irregular (e.g. atrial fibrillation).
C. Pulse rate provides basic physiological information as one of the vital signs, which are the chief or classical signs, or those signs peculiar to the disease itself.
Vital signs give objective evidence of disease or deformity that guides clinical assessment.
questions.question:
A. Describe the physiological parameter of pulse rate, addressing:
A(i) definition
A(ii) unit of measurement
A(iii) normal values across different age/sex groups
A(iv) method of measurement
B. Explain how pulse rate is interpreted in health and in dysfunction.
C. State the clinical significance of pulse rate to treatment planning and progress monitoring.

questions.answerText:
(i) The parameter is breath sounds (intensity and quality); the instrument used is a stethoscope.
(ii) Auscultation involves listening to the sounds generated by breathing, listening for any adventitious (added) sounds, and listening to the patient's spoken or whispered voice as they are transmitted through the chest wall.
(iii) Vesicular breath sounds are the normal breath sounds: soft and low pitched, heard throughout inspiration, continuing without pause into expiration, and fading away about one-third of the way through expiration (quiet, low-pitched, rustling sounds).
Rales are small clicking, bubbling, or rattling sounds believed to occur when air opens closed air spaces, and can be described as moist, dry, fine, and coarse; rhonchi are sounds that resemble snoring, occurring when air is blocked or becomes rough through the large airways.
Wheezes are high-pitched sounds produced by narrowed airways, heard on exhalation, and can sometimes be heard without a stethoscope; stridor is a wheeze-like sound heard on exhalation, usually due to blockage of airflow in the trachea or the back of the throat.
questions.question:
A patient with a respiratory complaint is examined by chest auscultation.
(i) State the parameter being assessed and the instrument used.
(ii) Describe the standardised procedure for auscultation.
(iii) Interpret normal (vesicular) breath sounds versus the abnormal breath sounds of rales/rhonchi and of wheezes/stridor.

questions.answerText:
(i) The instrument is the magnetometer.
(ii) It uses the null method of measurement: the quantity to be measured is compared with a known source, and the difference between these two is made zero.
(iii) Reading accuracy is the accuracy attainable in using a measuring instrument, and reading error is the difference between the instrument's reading and the actual value of the quantity being measured.
Sensitivity, the ratio of scale spacing to division value, governs the instrument's ability to detect the smallest change; low sensitivity would make it harder to bring the difference precisely to zero, producing an inaccurate reading.
questions.question:
In a measurement laboratory session, a student is asked to determine a quantity by comparing it against a known source until the difference between them is zero, using a named instrument.
(i) Identify the instrument.
(ii) Describe the principle of operation of this method of measurement.
(iii) Explain what would cause this instrument to give an inaccurate/faulty reading.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Purpose: to measure the largest circumference of the head; in infants and toddlers this may help identify neurological abnormalities, malnutrition, or other health-related concerns.
A(ii) Procedure: extend a non-stretchable measuring tape around the most prominent part of the occiput to the middle of the forehead, to obtain the largest circumference.
The tape is pulled snugly to compress the hair and underlying soft tissue.
A(iii) Recording: the measurement reading is taken to the nearest 0.1 cm or 1/8 inch.
B. The measurement is repeated twice, or until two measurements agree within 0.2 cm or ¼ inch.
The average of the two closest measurements is then recorded.
This repetition-until-agreement is the stated method of minimising error in this measurement.
At birth, the brain is 25% of adult size and head circumference averages 35 cm.
A newborn's head circumference is usually about half of the baby's body length in centimetres.
Head circumference increases an average of 1 cm/month during the first year, growth being more rapid in the first 8 months.
By 12 months the brain has completed half its postnatal growth and is 75% of adult size.
questions.question:
A. Describe the technique for measuring head circumference in a child from birth to age two, addressing:
A(i) purpose
A(ii) procedure and equipment
A(iii) recording
B. State the sources of error in this measurement and how they are minimised.

A patient with a suspected cardiovascular abnormality is assessed for the character of the arterial pulse.
(i) State the parameter being measured and the arteries used.
(ii) Describe the standardised procedure for assessing pulse rate/rhythm and for assessing pulse character.
(iii) Interpret pulse classifications based on rate and rhythm, and carotid pulse character findings of pulsus alternans and of a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse.
(iv) State the precautions/sources of error in this examination.
questions.answerText:
(i) The parameter is the arterial pulse (rate, rhythm, character, volume, and radio-femoral delay); major arteries used are the radial, brachial, carotid, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.
(ii) Rate and rhythm: the radial artery is preferred; compress it with the index and middle fingers, note whether the pulse is regular or irregular, count the pulse for one full minute, and record the rate and rhythm.
Character and volume: best checked on the carotid arteries; observe carotid pulsations, place fingers behind the patient's neck and compress the carotid on one side, assess amplitude and contour, and repeat on the opposite side.
(iii) By rate: normal is 60-100 beats/min, bradycardia is <60, tachycardia is >100; by rhythm: regular, regularly irregular, or irregularly irregular.
Pulsus alternans is alternating strong and weak pulses. A collapsing (rapid up and rapid down) pulse, or water-hammer pulse, indicates the wide pulse pressure of aortic regurgitation (also AV fistula or hyperdynamic circulation).
(iv) Compare findings on both sides.

questions.question:
A. Describe the technique for measuring recumbent length in a child under 24 months (or 24-36 months who cannot stand), addressing:
A(i) equipment
A(ii) procedure
A(iii) recording
B. State the precautions to observe when preparing the child for this measurement.
C. State the sources of error in this measurement and how they are minimised.
questions.answerText:
A(i) An infant measuring board with a fixed headboard and a movable footboard is used.
A(ii) Two people are required to obtain this measurement.
One person aligns the infant's head against the top of the headboard, and the other straightens the infant's body and legs, keeping the feet pointed upward and parallel to the footboard.
The footboard is then brought against the bottom of the feet.
A(iii) The measurement is read to the nearest 0.1 cm or 1/8 inch.
B. Remove any clothing that interferes with obtaining precise measurements, such as shoes and bulky clothes, before measuring the child.
C. The measurement is repeated twice, or until two measurements agree within 0.2 cm or ¼ inch.
The average of the two closest measurements is then recorded.
This repeat-until-agreement approach is the stated method of minimising error.
Anthropometric measurements such as length, weight and head circumference help providers determine if a child is growing properly.
They can indicate when a child's health and well-being are at risk, and assist providers in selecting appropriate treatment options for children and adolescents.
Identifying underweight or malnutrition is important, as malnutrition jeopardises a child's growth and impairs immunocompetence and cognitive/socio-affective development.

(i) The parameter is chest expansion, assessed by a manual method and by a tape measure method.
(ii) Manual method: place the finger tips of both hands on either side of the lower rib cage so that the tips of the thumbs meet in the midline in front of, but not touching, the chest.
A deep breath by the patient increases the distance between the thumbs and indicates the degree of expansion.
Tape measure method: place a tape measure around the chest at the level of the nipple.
(iii) In a fit adult the chest may expand 5-8 cm.
In patients with severe airway obstructive disease it may expand less than 1 cm.
(iv) If one thumb remains closer to the midline than the other, this is confirmation of diminished expansion on that side.
Causes of asymmetrical chest expansion include pleural effusion, pneumothorax, extensive consolidation, atelectasis and pulmonary fibrosis.
questions.question:
A physiotherapist needs to assess the movement of a patient's chest wall as part of a respiratory examination.
(i) State the parameter being assessed and name the two methods used to measure it.
(ii) Describe the standardised procedure for each method.
(iii) State the expected finding in a fit adult and in a patient with severe airway obstructive disease.
(iv) Interpret a finding of diminished movement on one side of the chest and list the conditions that could cause this.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The GMFM is a standardised assessment tool measuring changes in gross motor function over time or with intervention in children with cerebral palsy.
The Paediatric Balance Scale is a modified version of the Berg Balance Scale, used to assess functional balance skills in school-aged children.
A(ii) The GMFM-88 has 88 items spanning the spectrum of gross motor activities; the GMFM-66 is a subset that provides information on the level of difficulty of an item and can help with goal setting.
No separate versions of the Paediatric Balance Scale are described.
A(iii) The GMFM is for children 5 months to 16 years, in the context of cerebral palsy.
The Paediatric Balance Scale is used for school-aged children.
B. The GMFM's two versions allow either a comprehensive assessment across the spectrum of gross motor activities (GMFM-88) or a version that additionally indicates item difficulty for goal setting (GMFM-66).
The Paediatric Balance Scale, being an adaptation of the Berg Balance Scale, provides a balance-specific measure suited to school-aged children; no further limitations are stated for either tool.
C. The GMFM specifically measures changes in gross motor function over time/with intervention in children with cerebral palsy.
The Paediatric Balance Scale specifically assesses functional balance skills in school-aged children, and is a modified version of an existing adult scale (the Berg Balance Scale) rather than a purpose-built paediatric tool.
Both are described as standardised/adapted tools for specific domains of paediatric physical function.
questions.question:
A. Describe the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM) and the Paediatric Balance Scale under the following headings:
A(i) type/principle
A(ii) versions/items
A(iii) population for use
B. Explain the basis for choosing one of these tools (advantages/limitations).
C. Distinguish between the GMFM and the Paediatric Balance Scale.

An older adult's nutritional status is assessed using skinfold thickness measurement.
(i) State the parameter and the instrument used.
(ii) Describe the procedure and the anatomical landmarks for each of the four sites.
(iii) State how the skinfold results are used/documented to derive further indices.
questions.answerText:
(i) The parameter is skinfold thickness (as an indirect indicator of nutritional status); the instrument used is the Harpenden skinfold caliper.
(ii) Skinfold thickness measurements are taken at 4 sites: triceps and biceps, thigh, subscapula, and suprailiac.
The triceps skinfold is taken at the posterior mid-point between the acromion and the olecranon.
The subscapular skinfold is measured just inferior to the inferior angle of the scapula.
The suprailiac skinfold is taken at the upper point of the iliac crest, with the angle of inclination being 45° towards the pubic symphysis.
The thigh skinfold is measured at the medial point of the anterior surface of the thigh.
(iii) Estimates of muscle size are derived by computation: arm muscle circumference (cm) = arm circumference (cm) - (π × triceps skinfold [mm]); arm muscle area = (muscle circumference)²/4π.

(i) The technique is the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification of breathlessness.
(ii) This patient falls into Class II: symptoms with ordinary activity, e.g. walking up stairs, making beds, carrying large amounts of shopping.
(iii) Class I: no symptoms with ordinary activity, breathlessness only occurring with severe exertion, e.g. running up hills, fast bicycling, cross-country skiing.
Class III: symptoms with mild exertion, e.g. bathing, showering, dressing. Class IV: symptoms at rest.
(iv) Health measurement of this kind facilitates the setting of treatment goals and priorities, and facilitates objective evaluation of the effectiveness of interventions over time.
questions.question:
A patient reports breathlessness when walking up stairs, making the bed, and carrying shopping, but no symptoms at rest.
(i) Identify the parameter/technique used to classify this finding.
(ii) Interpret which class this patient falls into and state the defining description.

A patient's blood pressure needs to be recorded in the clinic using a deflection-type instrument.
(i) Identify the instrument.
(ii) Describe the principle of operation of this method of measurement.
(iii) State how calibration is addressed for such instruments.
(iv) Explain what could account for an inaccurate blood pressure reading with this instrument.
questions.answerText:
(i) The instrument is the sphygmomanometer.
(ii) It uses the deflection method of measurement: the value of the quantity is directly indicated by deflection of a pointer on a calibrated scale (the weighing scale is also given as an example of this method).
(iii) The pointer is read on a 'calibrated scale', but no specific calibration procedure is given.
(iv) Reading accuracy is the accuracy attainable in using a measuring instrument, and reading error is the difference between the instrument's reading and the actual value of the quantity being measured.
Sensitivity (the ratio of scale spacing to division value) determines the instrument's ability to detect the smallest change; an instrument with low sensitivity could therefore fail to reflect small but real changes in the reading.

courses.title: Exercise Therapy II

questions.answerText:
A. The general principles of exercise prescription are the mode of exercise, the intensity of exercise, the duration of exercise, the frequency of exercise, and the rate of progression of the patient's physical activity; these parameters must be considered whether prescribing exercise for a healthy individual or a patient with disease. Mode refers to activities using large muscle groups performed rhythmically and sustainable for 15-60 minutes, which should be aerobic in nature. Intensity for an apparently healthy individual is usually 40-85% of VO2max or 55-90% of maximal heart rate, determined using training/target heart rate formulas. Duration should be 15-60 minutes depending on physical work capacity. Frequency is usually three times per week, advanced over time to 5-7 times per week. Progression refers to increasing intensity, duration, frequency or amount of activity as the body adapts, achieved by modulating the load, repetitions, sets, rest period or frequency (overload).
B. For the cardiac patient, the ideal heart rate training zone is between 40% and 75% of the maximum symptom-limited heart rate determined from a graded exercise treadmill test, and intensity depends on resting and maximum heart rate and blood pressure and maximum METs attained; frequency is highly dependent on the patient's condition, for example a type I diabetic patient should exercise seven days per week to more effectively regulate blood glucose, since exercise training stimulates transport of glucose from the blood into the working muscle cells similarly to insulin; the more debilitated and untrained the patient, the shorter the exercise session should be.
C. If the dosage (frequency, duration and intensity together) is not correctly individualised to the patient's physical work capacity, the exercise session may be too demanding or ineffective; the rate of progression is one of the more artful aspects of exercise prescription, so the dosage is increased gradually (overload) as the individual progresses, by modulating the load or intensity, the repetitions per set, the number of sets, the rest period between sets, or the exercise frequency, to facilitate improvements in muscular strength and endurance without exceeding the patient's tolerance.
questions.question:
A. Describe the general principles/components of exercise prescription (mode, intensity, duration, frequency, progression).
B. State how these components relate to common clinical problems in different patient groups.
C. Explain how failure to individualise these components leads to functional loss or poor outcome, and how exercise therapy addresses this.

(i) On assessment, a patient shows weak shoulder flexion, adduction and external rotation in the upper limb, with reduced ability to bring the arm up and across the face. State the assessment findings relevant to this presentation.
(ii) Name the technique appropriate to address this weakness.
(iii) Describe the starting position, procedure and hand placement/grip used to apply the technique.
(iv) State the physiological effects and safety considerations of the technique.
(v) State how the technique may be progressed or modified.
questions.answerText:
(i) Assessment findings: weakness of the muscles producing shoulder flexion, adduction and external rotation, with reduced elbow flexion, forearm supination, and wrist and finger flexion, limiting the functional movement of bringing the arm up and across the face.
(ii) The technique appropriate is the Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation Upper Extremity Diagonal 1 (D1) Flexion pattern.
(iii) Starting position: the upper extremity is positioned in shoulder extension, abduction and internal rotation, elbow extension, forearm pronation, and wrist and finger extension, with the hand about 8 to 12 inches from the hip. Hand placement: the index and middle fingers of one hand are placed in the palm of the patient's hand, and the other hand is placed on the volar surface of the distal forearm or at the cubital fossa. Procedure: a quick stretch is applied to the wrist and finger flexors while the patient is told to squeeze the fingers, turn the palm up, and pull the arm up and across the face, against resistance, ending with the arm across the face in shoulder flexion, adduction and external rotation, partial elbow flexion, forearm supination, and wrist and finger flexion.
(iv) Manual contacts provide pressure to tactile and pressure receptors to facilitate contraction and guide the direction of movement; maximal resistance generates maximal effort and enhances kinesthetic awareness, strength, motor control and motor learning; positioning at optimal muscle length enhances weak contraction; normal timing runs from distal to proximal with rotation throughout the pattern for smooth, coordinated movement; the therapist must use a wide base of support and move with the patient to reduce therapist fatigue.
(v) Progression/modification: timing for emphasis can be used, resisting the stronger components isometrically while allowing motion in the weaker components to let overflow occur from strong to weak muscles; repeated contractions (repeated stretch) can be applied at the point of weakness to reinforce contraction until it weakens; strong, dynamic verbal action commands are used for maximal stimulation, while soft action commands are used when the goal is relaxation.

(i) Impairments and functional limitations: acute pain following the whiplash injury; reduced neck movement; a neuromuscular system that requires reactivation to improve strength and stability.
(ii) Indications: a technique that provides pain-free treatment for whiplash and reactivates the neuromuscular system through Neuromuscular Activation (Neurac). Contraindications/precautions relevant to manual therapy techniques at this stage include acute inflammation, and, for manipulation specifically, contraindications such as bleeding in a joint or a loose body in the joint; resistance exercise is contraindicated where there is severe joint or muscle pain during active-free movement.
(iii) Options include suspension therapy and manual resistance exercise. Suspension therapy is most appropriate here because it is a pain-free physical therapy option that can help provide treatment and relief while managing pain from the injury, and the Neuromuscular Activation used in suspension therapy can reactivate the neuromuscular system and help improve strength and stability after a whiplash injury; suspension therapy is also used for neck pain generally to help with tissue stretching as well as strengthening the neck muscles, usually in conjunction with other physical therapy methods.
questions.question:
(i) A patient recently experiencing a whiplash injury has acute neck pain that must be managed without provoking further pain. State the impairments and functional limitations for this patient.
(ii) State the indications, contraindications and precautions relevant to selecting an exercise approach for this patient.
(iii) State the exercise options available and justify which is most appropriate at this stage.

A(i) State the aim of diaphragmatic breathing exercise.
A(ii) State the starting position for diaphragmatic breathing.
A(iii) Describe the procedure for diaphragmatic breathing.
A(iv) State the effects and uses of diaphragmatic breathing.
B. State the dosage/application guidance for diaphragmatic breathing.
C. Explain the basis for using an alternative breathing technique when a patient has severe weakness of the inspiratory muscles.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Diaphragmatic breathing is designed to improve ventilation and oxygenation and the excursion (descent and ascent) of the diaphragm.
A(ii) The patient is prepared in a relaxed and comfortable position.
A(iii) The therapist evaluates the breathing pattern and the correct form of diaphragmatic breathing, places the hand(s) on the rectus abdominis just below the anterior costal margin, and asks the patient to breathe in slowly but deeply, keeping the shoulders relaxed and the upper chest quiet, allowing the abdomen to rise, then to slowly exhale.
A(iv) It can also be used to mobilise lung secretions during postural drainage and can be practised in a variety of positions; it forms part of dealing with shortness of breath, where the patient assumes a relaxed, forward-bent posture that stimulates diaphragmatic breathing.
B. All breathing patterns taught, including diaphragmatic breathing, should be deep, voluntary, controlled and relaxed; chest expansion is checked using the nipples as a reference point with a tape measure taken round the thoracic region, and lung sounds are checked by auscultation before and during teaching.
C. Glossopharyngeal breathing is used instead for a patient with severe weakness of the muscles of inspiration or who is ventilator-dependent because of absence or incomplete innervation of the diaphragm; the patient takes gulps of air into the lungs with the mouth closed, the tongue pushes the air back and traps it in the pharynx, and the air is then forced into the lungs when the glottis opens, increasing inspiratory capacity without relying on diaphragmatic muscle strength.

(i) Problem list: chronic back pain; weak stabiliser muscles and core muscles; pain limiting the ability to perform resisted or weight-bearing exercise in the normal way.
(ii) Goals: reduce chronic back pain; strengthen the stabiliser muscles and core; support the healing process of the back.
(iii) Technique: suspension therapy, in which the body part is suspended in the air by ropes and slings attached to fixed points above, working under the mechanical principles of friction (less friction in suspension gives smooth, easy movement), the pendulum (heavy material suspended by a weightless thread produces to-and-fro movement, used to maintain muscle properties, increase range of movement and strengthen muscles) and eliminating gravity (requiring at least muscle power grade 2); active participation is required so the patient learns to use the appropriate muscle for the desired movement, relaxation is promoted through secure support and smooth rhythmic motion, and little work is required of stabilising muscles because the part is supported.
(iv) Progression: the system can be modified to provide grades of exercise resistance, for example by moving the fixed point away from the muscle requiring resistance so that on effort the limb rises against gravity acting as resistance, with slow lowering controlled by eccentric lengthening; after instruction, the patient can often work independently of the therapist.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents with chronic low back pain and weak stabilising and core muscles, with the pain limiting active exercise. State the physiotherapy problem list for this presentation.
(ii) State the goals of treatment.
(iii) Describe the exercise therapy technique chosen, including its type, purpose and mechanism.
(iv) Describe how the programme would progress.

questions.answerText:
(i) Assessment findings: joint hypomobility of the shoulder resulting from capsular adhesion, with restricted abduction range of motion.
(ii) The technique appropriate is joint mobilisation, specifically distraction and caudal/inferior glide.
(iii) Starting position: the patient is positioned in the most comfortable position to aid relaxation and decrease muscle tension, since if the patient is not relaxed the therapist works against tension or tissue resistance. Procedure: the therapist observes correct posture and body mechanics, with the hands placed close to the joint space, especially during gliding, for fixation and mobilisation; in distraction, movement is applied at right angles to the treatment plane, distracting for 5 to 8 seconds and resting for four minutes, distracting for 10 trials with re-evaluation; a caudal/inferior glide is applied to the shoulder to improve abduction.
(iv) Distraction separates the articulating surfaces, providing more space for synovial fluid to fill the joint, reducing friction and allowing more fluid motion; treatment is contraindicated in acute inflammation, malignancy, bone disease such as osteoporosis, excessive pain, total joint replacement or metallic implant, and newly formed or weakened connective tissue.
(v) Treatment progression starts with distraction, because distraction increases range of motion in all directions, then proceeds to gliding; after 10 distraction trials, the joint is re-evaluated, and if there is no increase in range of motion, the approach is re-evaluated.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents with joint hypomobility of the shoulder resulting from capsular adhesion, with reduced abduction range. State the assessment findings relevant to planning treatment.
(ii) Name the technique appropriate to address this hypomobility.
(iii) Describe the starting position, procedure and hand placement/fixation used in applying the technique.
(iv) State the physiological effects and safety considerations of the technique.
(v) State how the technique would be progressed.

(i) A patient has recently undergone joint replacement surgery and needs to begin therapy as soon as possible with low impact on the healing joint. State the impairments and functional limitations relevant to this stage.
(ii) State the indications, contraindications and precautions for exercise therapy at this stage.
(iii) State the exercise options available and justify which is most appropriate at this stage.
questions.answerText:
(i) Impairments and functional limitations: restricted joint motion following surgery; the need to restore joint motion while minimising load on the joint; reduced neuromuscular control around the joint.
(ii) Indications: restoring joint motion after joint replacement surgery, when the surgeon wants physical therapy started as soon as possible after surgery. Contraindications/precautions relevant to manual and mechanical resistance and to mobilisation at this stage include total joint replacement or a metallic implant, newly formed or weakened connective tissue, and acute inflammation; resistance exercise should not be initiated at a maximal level, and pain should not occur during exercise.
(iii) Options include suspension therapy and manual resistance exercise. Suspension therapy is most appropriate at this stage because it restores joint motion, which is important after joint replacement surgery, and can often be started quickly because of its relatively low impact on joints compared with other types of physical therapy exercise; suspension also frees the body part from the friction of the surface it rests on and permits free movement without resistance, and active participation lets the patient learn to use the appropriate muscle for the desired movement while relaxation is promoted through secure support and smooth rhythmic motion.

(i) Problem list: painful joint with capsular adhesion; joint hypomobility; progressive limitation of movement from capsular adhesion or ligamentous contracture.
(ii) Goals: break down or reduce the adhesions; improve range of motion; lengthen muscles and tendons; reduce swelling and oedema; decrease pain; restore functionality.
(iii) Technique: joint mobilisation, a manual therapy technique comprising a continuum of skilled passive movements applied at varying speeds and amplitudes to the joint complex, which stays within the normal range of motion, unlike manipulation which goes beyond it; joint mobilisation restores the motion in the respective joint by removing restriction found in the joint, connective tissue or muscle, and by removing the restriction, the source of pain is reduced and the patient experiences symptomatic relief; distraction separates the articulating surfaces to provide more space for synovial fluid to fill the joint, reducing friction and allowing more fluid motion.
(iv) Progression: treatment begins with distraction, since distraction increases range of motion in all directions, then proceeds to gliding to increase range of motion in a specific direction, with 10 distraction trials followed by re-evaluation; if there is no increase in range of motion, the approach is re-evaluated.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents with a painful, hypomobile joint attributed to capsular adhesion and progressive limitation of movement. State the physiotherapy problem list.
(ii) State the goals of treatment.
(iii) Describe the exercise therapy technique chosen, including its type, purpose and mechanism.
(iv) Describe how the programme would progress.

questions.answerText:
(i) The presentation is uncoordinated movement, known as ataxia; deviation of gait while walking along a straight line, foot close to foot, indicates a cerebellar lesion, and swaying or loss of balance with the eyes open or closed on the Romberg test confirms impaired balance and coordination.
(ii) Coordinated movement requires a functioning cerebellum, spinal cord and peripheral nervous system, together with an interaction of the cerebellum, vestibular system, motor system, flexibility and range of motion, deep sensation and vision; diseases and injuries that damage or destroy these structures, such as traumatic brain injury, stroke, transient ischaemic attack, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, cerebral palsy or brain tumours, can lead to ataxia, so the effect on the body is loss of the ability to execute smooth, accurate, controlled motor responses with appropriate speed, distance, direction, timing and muscular tension.
(iii) Management follows the general principles of coordination exercises: constant repetition of a few motor activities; use of sensory cues (tactile, visual, proprioceptive) to enhance motor performance; increasing the speed of the activity over time; breaking activities down into components simple enough to be performed correctly; providing assistance whenever necessary; giving the patient a short rest after two or three repetitions to avoid fatigue; and giving high repetition of precise performance, since an engram requires thousands of repetitions to begin to form and millions to perfect, with various inputs such as auditory instruction, tactile sensory stimulation and visual stimulation used whenever a new movement is trained.
questions.question:
(i) A patient is asked to walk along a straight line, placing one foot directly in front of the other, and is observed to deviate from the line. On the Romberg test, the patient sways and loses balance when the eyes are closed while standing with the heels together. Identify the condition or deviation demonstrated.
(ii) State the contributing factors to this presentation and its effects on the body.
(iii) Describe the therapeutic exercise management appropriate for this patient.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Proprioceptive means any sensory receptors giving information about movement and position of the body; neuromuscular refers to nerves and muscles; facilitate means to stimulate; PNF is an approach to therapeutic exercise that combines functionally based diagonal patterns of movement with techniques of neuromuscular facilitation to evoke motor responses and improve neuromuscular control and function, also known as the Kabat and Knott approach.
A(ii) Afterdischarge: the effect of a stimulus continues after the stimulus stops. Temporal summation: a succession of weak (subliminal) stimuli summate to cause excitation. Spatial summation: weak stimuli applied simultaneously to different body areas summate to cause excitation. Irradiation: a spreading and increased strength of response when the number or strength of stimuli increases. Successive induction: increased excitation of the agonist follows contraction of its antagonist. Reciprocal innervation: contraction of a muscle is accompanied by simultaneous inhibition of its antagonist.
A(iii) Manual contacts, maximal resistance, positioning, position and movement of the therapist, normal timing, timing for emphasis, verbal commands, visual cues, stretch, approximation, traction, overflow (irradiation), and patterns of motion.
A(iv) Rhythmic initiation, reversal of the antagonists (dynamic reversals, stabilising reversals, rhythmic stabilisation), combination of isotonics (agonist reversals), repeated contraction (repeated stretch), contract-relax, and hold-relax.
B. PNF patterns are spiral and diagonal in character, combining motion in the sagittal, coronal/frontal and transverse planes, which closely resemble patterns used in normal functional activity and sport; manual contacts provide pressure to tactile and pressure receptors to facilitate contraction and guide direction, maximal resistance facilitates weak muscles to contract and enhances kinesthetic awareness and motor learning, and stretch of the elongated muscle facilitates contraction through the stretch reflex, so the combined sensory cues elicit the best possible neuromuscular response.
C. Contract-relax is a relaxation technique performed at a point of limited range in the agonist pattern, in which a strong, small-range isotonic contraction of the restricting antagonist muscles, with emphasis on the rotators, is followed by an isometric hold for 5 to 8 seconds, then voluntary relaxation and movement into the new range, with movement that can be passive but active contraction is preferred; hold-relax is usually performed in a position of comfort below a level that causes pain, using a strong isometric contraction of the restricting antagonist muscles that is resisted, followed by voluntary relaxation and passive movement into the newly gained range, and is indicated for limitations in passive range of motion with pain.
questions.question:
A(i) Define Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF).
A(ii) State the basic neurophysiological principles underlying PNF.
A(iii) List the basic procedures used in PNF.
A(iv) List the PNF techniques.
B. Explain the physiological or clinical basis of the effects of PNF.
C. Distinguish between Contract-Relax and Hold-Relax.

(i) A patient with chronic bronchitis and increased sputum production, on prolonged bed rest, is assessed as having reduced breath sounds and difficulty clearing secretions. State the assessment findings relevant to planning treatment.
(ii) Name the technique appropriate for airway clearance in this patient.
(iii) Describe the starting position, procedure and hand placement used in applying the technique.
(iv) State the physiological effects and safety considerations of the technique.
(v) State how treatment would progress or be discontinued.
questions.answerText:
(i) Assessment findings: increased production of mucus consistent with chronic bronchitis, prolonged bed rest, reduced breath sounds on auscultation, and difficulty clearing secretions, all indications for postural drainage.
(ii) The technique appropriate is postural drainage with percussion, vibration and shaking, combined with deep breathing and effective coughing.
(iii) Starting position: the patient is positioned according to the anatomy of the lung segment to be drained, using gravity to assist drainage, with tight or bulky clothing loosened, a sputum cup or tissue available, and sufficient pillows for positioning and comfort. Procedure: vital signs and breath sounds are checked, the patient is positioned correctly and observed for cyanosis, each position is monitored for 5-10 minutes; the patient breathes in deeply during drainage without hyperventilating, using pursed-lip breathing during expiration if needed; percussion is applied over the segment being drained with a cupped hand struck rhythmically, vibration is applied during expiration in the direction of chest movement, and shaking is applied as a vigorous bouncing manoeuvre during exhalation; the patient is encouraged to give a deep, sharp, double cough when necessary.
(iv) Percussion mechanically dislodges viscous or adherent mucus from the airways; vibration and shaking mobilise secretions toward the central airways during expiration; treatment duration should not exceed 45-60 minutes and the patient should sit up slowly afterward, watching for postural hypotension; treatment is contraindicated in severe haemoptysis, untreated acute conditions, severe pulmonary oedema, congestive heart failure, large pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, cardiovascular instability, cardiac arrhythmia, severe hypertension or hypotension, unstable angina and recent neurosurgery.
(v) Reassess breathing sound, type, colour, consistency and amount of secretion after each session; discontinue when the chest radiograph is clear, the patient is afebrile for 24-48 hours, normal or near-normal breath sounds are heard, or the patient is on a regular home programme; modify the position if the standard position cannot be tolerated.

A(i) Starting positions refer to body postures and alignments used to facilitate treatment and assess movement patterns; posture follows movement like a shadow, since every movement begins with posture and ends in posture; starting positions can be classified into fundamental positions (standing, kneeling, sitting, lying, hanging) and derived positions, each serving different therapeutic purposes.
A(ii) In standing, the heels are together on the same line with the toes slightly apart so the angle between the feet does not exceed 45 degrees, the knees are together and straight, the hips are extended and slightly laterally rotated, the pelvis is balanced on the femoral heads, the spine is stretched to its maximum length, the vertex is thrust upward, the ears are level and eyes look forward, the shoulders are down and back, and the arms hang loosely with palms facing inward.
