A(iii) In kneeling, the body is supported on the knees, which may be together or slightly apart, the lower leg rests on the floor with the feet plantarflexed, or in mid-position over the edge of a plinth, and the rest of the body is held as in standing.
A(iv) In sitting, a position is taken on a chair or stool of a height and width that allows the thighs to be fully supported, the hips and knees are flexed to a right angle, the knees are apart sufficiently to allow the femora to be parallel, and the feet rest on the floor with the heels vertically below the knees; the body is erect with the arms by the sides.
B. Standing is the most difficult fundamental position to maintain because the whole body must be balanced and stabilised in correct alignment on a small base by the coordinated action of many muscle groups; when segments are in good alignment and perfectly balanced, muscle work is reduced, but faulty alignment or external disturbing forces increase muscle work, with the antigravity muscles of the trunk and lower limbs working isometrically to hold the position. In kneeling, the lower leg is relaxed while the body is stabilised on the knees through interplay between knee flexors and extensors, with the hip extensors and lumbar flexors working more strongly than in standing to maintain pelvic tilt. In sitting, no muscle work is needed to hold the leg position because the thighs are fully supported.
C. Standing has a relatively small base and a high centre of gravity, so the state of body equilibrium is relatively less stable than in kneeling, and it is used as a starting position for exercise for those who can maintain it correctly; kneeling has a relatively lower centre of gravity than standing, so the position is only slightly more stable and is uncomfortable for most people, and it is used as a starting position for backward movement in the sagittal plane and to train control of the hip joints and lower trunk in preparation for standing.
questions.question:
A(i) Define and classify starting positions.
A(ii) State the description of the standing position.
A(iii) State the description of the kneeling position.
A(iv) State the description of the sitting position.
B. Explain the physiological/clinical basis of the muscle work required to maintain each fundamental position.
C. Distinguish between standing and kneeling as fundamental positions.

questions.answerText:
(i) The joint involved is the hip, and the muscle groups involved are the hip abductors (agonist for the movement being trained) and the hip adductors (antagonist).
(ii) On effort, the limb rises into abduction brought about by isotonic shortening (concentric contraction) of the abductors, with resistance offered by gravity; slow lowering into the resting position is controlled by isotonic lengthening (eccentric contraction) of the abductors.
(iii) The contributing problem is weakness of the hip abductor group, limiting the ability of the limb to rise into abduction against gravity.
(iv) In suspension therapy, if specific resistance to the abductor muscle work is required, the whole fixed point of suspension is moved away from the muscle requiring resistance, that is, towards the adductors; this means the abductors must work against the resistance offered by gravity as the limb rises into abduction, providing graded resistance without the need for the therapist's own strength, while the suspended limb is also relieved of the friction of resting on a surface, allowing free, smooth movement; slow, controlled eccentric lowering by the abductors is then trained as part of the same exercise.
questions.question:
(i) A patient shows weak hip abduction on examination, with the limb unable to rise effectively into abduction against gravity when tested actively. State the joint and muscle groups involved.
(ii) Describe the muscle work involved in resisted abduction, identifying the agonist and antagonist and the type of contraction on rising and on lowering.
(iii) State the contributing problem suggested by this pattern of weakness.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the suspension-based exercise approach chosen to address this weakness.

questions.answerText:
A. The overload principle states that a load exceeding the metabolic capacity of the muscle must be applied, challenging the muscle to perform at a level greater than that to which it is accustomed; if demands remain constant after the muscle has adapted, performance can be maintained but not increased, so overload is applied by progressively adjusting the intensity (how much resistance) or the volume (repetitions, sets or frequency). The SAID (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands) or specificity principle holds that the adaptive effects of training, such as improvement of strength, power and endurance, are highly specific to the training method employed, so exercises in a programme should mimic the anticipated function. The reversibility principle refers to the loss of adaptive changes once resistance exercise programmes are stopped, since increased strength or endurance is transient unless training-induced improvements are regularly used functionally or maintained through ongoing resistance exercise.
B. In a strength-training programme, the amount of resistance is incrementally and progressively increased, while in endurance training more emphasis is placed on increasing the time a contraction is sustained or the number of repetitions performed than on increasing resistance; the specificity principle helps the therapist select which parameters of exercise create specific training effects that best meet a patient's specific functional needs and goals, for example emphasising endurance-focused intensity and duration when the desired functional activity requires greater muscular endurance than strength.
C. Detraining refers to a reduction in muscle performance beginning a week or two after resistance exercise is stopped, which may continue until training effects are lost, so gains in strength and endurance can be lost if not incorporated into daily activities; exercise therapy addresses this by incorporating gains into functional activities as early as possible in a rehabilitation programme and by having patients participate in a maintenance programme of resistance exercise as an integral component of a lifelong fitness programme.
questions.question:
A. Describe the basic principles of muscle strengthening (overload, specificity and reversibility).
B. State how these principles relate to common clinical problems in rehabilitation.
C. Explain how failure to apply these principles causes loss of training effect, and how exercise therapy addresses this.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Postural drainage, also known as bronchial drainage, is an intervention for airway clearance and a means of mobilising secretions in one or more lung segments to the central airways by placing the patient in various positions so that gravity assists the draining process.
A(ii) Positions are based on the anatomy of the lungs and tracheobronchial tree, and postural drainage therapy also involves body positioning together with deep breathing and an effective cough to facilitate airway clearance.
A(iii) The manual techniques used with postural drainage therapy are percussion (performed with a cupped hand over the lung segment, struck in a rhythmic manner to dislodge viscous or adherent mucus), vibration (applied in conjunction with percussion during the expiratory phase, in the same direction as chest movement) and shaking (a vigorous form of vibration applied during exhalation using an intermittent bouncing manoeuvre with wide movement of the therapist's hands, compressing and shaking the chest wall).
A(iv) Indications: patients with pulmonary disease with increased mucus production such as chronic bronchitis and cystic fibrosis, patients on prolonged bed rest, after general anaesthesia, on the ventilator, with acute and chronic lung disease such as pneumonia or atelectasis, and with artificial airways. Contraindications: severe haemoptysis, untreated acute condition, severe pulmonary oedema, congestive heart failure, large pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, cardiovascular instability, cardiac arrhythmia, severe hypertension or hypotension, unstable angina, and recent neurosurgery. Discontinue when the chest radiograph is clear, the patient is afebrile for 24-48 hours, normal or near-normal breath sounds are heard, or the patient is on a regular home programme.
B. Never administer directly after a meal; coordinate treatment with aerosol therapy; treat early in the morning and early evening before sleep; monitor each position for 5-10 minutes to check tolerance; treatment duration should not exceed 45-60 minutes; have the patient sit up slowly and rest afterward, watching for postural hypotension.
C. A modified position is used for patients who cannot assume or tolerate the optimal positions, such as a patient with congestive heart failure showing orthopnoea, a ventilated patient following thoracic surgery, or a patient not allowed a head-down (Trendelenburg) position after neurosurgery, because a head-down position may increase intracranial pressure.
questions.question:
A(i) State the aim of postural drainage.
A(ii) State the positions used in postural drainage.
A(iii) Describe the procedure of postural drainage, including the manual techniques used.
A(iv) State the indications, contraindications and progression/discontinuation of postural drainage.
B. State the dosage guidance for postural drainage.
C. Explain the basis for modifying postural drainage in a patient who cannot tolerate the standard positions.

questions.answerText:
(i) Problem list: pain when the end of available range of motion is reached; soft tissue oedema; developing soft tissue, muscle and/or joint contractures; developing muscle weakness from reduced usage; decreasing functional use of the part and associated areas; possible joint effusion and muscle spasm.
(ii) Goals: educate the patient on anticipated recovery time and on protecting the part while maintaining appropriate functional activities; control pain, oedema and spasm; maintain soft tissue and joint integrity; maintain integrity and function of the part.
(iii) Techniques: cold, compression, elevation and massage within the first 48 hours, with the part immobilised by rest, splint, tape or cast and stressful positions avoided; gentle grade 1 joint oscillation within a pain-free position and passive movements within the limit of pain to maintain soft tissue and joint mobility and minimise contracture; intermittent muscle setting to maintain muscle integrity.
(iv) Progression: as repair and healing occur in the sub-acute stage and remodelling occurs in the chronic/rehabilitation stage, the programme progresses to active-assistive, free, resistive and/or modified aerobic exercise depending on proximity to associated areas and effect on the primary lesion, with adaptive or assistive devices used as needed to protect the part; the chronic stage uses dynamic and functional exercises.
questions.question:
(i) A patient presents within the first week following a soft tissue injury of a limb, with pain when the end of available range of motion is reached, soft tissue swelling, and reduced use of the injured part and the surrounding areas. State the physiotherapy problem list for this presentation.
(ii) State the goals of treatment for this patient at this stage.
(iii) Describe the exercise therapy techniques chosen for this stage, including the type of movement used, its purpose and its mechanism of action.
(iv) Describe how the exercise programme would progress as healing continues into the sub-acute and chronic stages.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Functional or muscle excursion is the distance a muscle is capable of shortening after it has been elongated to its maximum; the range of muscle work is the extent of muscular contraction that produces joint movement, estimated to be 50% of maximum extended muscle length.
A(ii) The types of muscle range are full range, outer range, inner range and middle range.
A(iii) Full range is used for maintaining joint mobility and increasing circulation, and ensures an emergency reserve of power; inner range is used to train extensor muscles and to move a joint in the direction of muscle pull; outer range is used extensively for muscle re-education; middle range, the functional range, is used to maintain normal muscle tone and muscle power because muscles work efficiently and are used most frequently in this range.
B. Full range is muscle work from the fully stretched (eccentric) position to the fully contracted (concentric) position, or the reverse when working eccentrically, and is rarely used by muscles; inner range work occurs either concentrically from a position of partial contraction to a fully contracted position or, in eccentric muscle work, the reverse; outer range work occurs concentrically from a fully stretched position to a partial contracted position; in middle range the muscle is neither fully stretched nor fully contracted, which is why it works most efficiently there.
C. Inner range muscle work is used to train extensor muscles and to move a joint in the direction of muscle pull, working from partial contraction toward full contraction (or the reverse eccentrically); outer range muscle work moves concentrically from a fully stretched position to a partial contracted position and is used extensively for muscle re-education.
questions.question:
A(i) Define the range of muscle work.
A(ii) Classify the types of muscle range.
A(iii) State the use of each type of muscle range.
B. Explain the physiological basis of muscle work in each range.
C. Distinguish between inner range and outer range muscle work.

(i) A patient is observed standing with faulty alignment, requiring visibly increased and sustained muscular effort to remain upright compared with a well-balanced posture. Identify the deviation demonstrated.
(ii) State the contributing factors to this presentation and its effects on the body.
(iii) Describe the corrective or therapeutic exercise management for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) The deviation is faulty standing posture with disturbed equilibrium; in standing, the whole body must be balanced and stabilised in correct alignment on a small base by the coordinated action of many muscle groups, and when there is faulty alignment or external forces disturbing equilibrium, muscle work is increased.
(ii) Contributing causes of bad posture include injury and muscle guarding, muscle tension and muscle weakness, daily habits, use of technology, sustained faulty posture, pregnancy, obesity, and weak abdominal muscles; the effect on the body is that the antigravity muscles of the trunk and lower limbs, which normally work isometrically to hold the position with minimal effort when balance is achieved, must work harder, increasing fatigue, since standing already has a relatively small base and a high centre of gravity, making equilibrium less stable than in other fundamental positions.
(iii) Management should re-establish the correct standing description: heels together on the same line with toes slightly apart so the angle between the feet does not exceed 45 degrees, knees together and straight, hips extended and slightly laterally rotated, pelvis balanced on the femoral heads, spine stretched to its maximum length, vertex thrust upward, ears level and eyes looking forward, shoulders down and back, and arms hanging loosely with palms facing inward; standing is then used as a starting position for exercise for those who can maintain it correctly, since a satisfactory standing pattern reduces fatigue and conditions the postural reflex.

A(i) Suspension is a special technique of exercise therapy in which a part, or all, of the body is suspended in the air by ropes and slings attached to fixed points above, to increase range of motion, increase muscle power and support body parts when the effect of gravity is eliminated; it frees the body from the friction of the surface it rests on and permits free movement without resistance.
A(ii) Axial suspension takes the joint axis as the point of suspension, with the limb supported by slings above the axis so the part moves parallel to the floor; vertical suspension takes the centre of gravity of the body part as the point of suspension, used to support the body part; pendular suspension shifts the point of suspension away from the joint axis so movement takes place against gravity, giving resistance to the muscle as it moves.
A(iii) Suspension works under the principles of friction (less friction gives smooth, easy movement), the pendulum (a heavy material suspended by a weightless thread produces to-and-fro movement when force is applied) and eliminating the effect of gravity (the patient should have at least muscle power grade 2).
A(iv) Indications include back pain (strengthening stabiliser and core muscles, healing a back injury), neck pain (tissue stretching and muscle strengthening), whiplash (pain-free treatment and neuromuscular reactivation), Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis (preserving range of motion and mobility), and joint replacement (restoring joint motion with low impact on the joint).
B. Active participation is required, so the patient learns to use the appropriate muscle for the desired movement; relaxation is promoted through secure support and smooth rhythmic motion; little work is required of stabilising muscles because the part is supported; and the system can be modified to provide grades of resistance, so after instruction the patient can often work independently of the therapist, although the equipment required is quite complex and extensive.
C. Axial suspension takes the joint axis as the point of suspension so the limb is supported by slings above the axis and moves parallel to the floor, used for relaxation, maintaining muscle properties, and increasing blood, venous and lymphatic circulation; pendular suspension shifts the point of suspension away from the joint axis so that movement takes place against gravity and the muscle receives resistance while moving, used to strengthen the muscle, increase muscle power and increase endurance.
questions.question:
A(i) Define suspension therapy.
A(ii) Classify the uses of suspension by type (axial, vertical, pendular).
A(iii) State the principles on which suspension therapy works.
A(iv) State the indications for suspension therapy.
B. Explain the physiological or clinical basis of the effects of suspension therapy.
C. Distinguish between axial suspension and pendular suspension.

(i) A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease suffers periodic attacks of shortness of breath and has difficulty clearing airway secretions. State the physiotherapy problem list for this patient.
(ii) State the goals of treatment.
(iii) Describe the exercise therapy techniques chosen, including their type, purpose and mechanism.
(iv) Describe how the programme would progress.
questions.answerText:
(i) Problem list: periodic attacks of dyspnoea (shortness of breath); airway obstruction secondary to bronchospasm or retained secretions; ineffective cough mechanism; inefficient or abnormal breathing pattern.
(ii) Goals: improve ventilation; increase the effectiveness of the cough mechanism; prevent atelectasis; improve the strength, endurance and coordination of respiratory muscles; maintain and improve chest and thoracic spine mobility; correct inefficient or abnormal breathing patterns; promote relaxation; teach the patient to deal with a shortness of breath attack.
(iii) Techniques: pursed-lip breathing, which decreases respiratory rate, increases tidal volume and improves exercise tolerance, performed by having the patient breathe in slowly and deeply and exhale through loosely pursed lips; for a shortness of breath attack, the patient assumes a relaxed, forward-bent posture to stimulate diaphragmatic breathing, uses the prescribed bronchodilator, regains control of breathing by reducing respiratory rate with pursed-lip breathing on expiration, and breathes in diaphragmatically after each pursed-lip breath, avoiding accessory muscle use; an effective, controlled double cough is taught, with deep inspiration, closure of the glottis, contraction of the abdominal muscles and elevation of the diaphragm to increase intrathoracic pressure, then explosive expiration.
(iv) Progression: postural drainage with percussion, vibration and shaking is added to mobilise and clear secretions when increased mucus production persists, with treatment discontinued when the chest radiograph is clear, the patient is afebrile for 24-48 hours, normal or near-normal breath sounds are heard, or the patient is established on a regular home programme.

(i) The abnormality demonstrated is dysmetria, in the form of hypermetria or hypometria, with an intention tremor, elicited on the finger-to-nose test in which the shoulder is abducted to 90 degrees with the elbow extended and the patient is asked to bring the tip of the index finger to the tip of the nose.
(ii) This is a sign of ataxia (uncoordinated movement or coordination impairment), which most commonly relates to damage or degeneration of the cerebellum, since coordinated movement requires a functioning cerebellum, spinal cord and peripheral nervous system; the effect on the body is loss of the ability to select the right muscle at the right time with proper intensity and loss of appropriate speed, distance, direction, timing and muscular tension in movement.
(iii) Management follows the general principles of coordination exercises: constant repetition of a few motor activities; use of sensory cues (tactile, visual, proprioceptive) to enhance motor performance; gradual increase of the speed of the activity over time; breaking activities into components simple enough to be performed correctly; providing assistance whenever necessary; a short rest after two or three repetitions to avoid fatigue; and high repetition of precise performance, since thousands of repetitions are required to begin to form an engram and millions to perfect it, with auditory, tactile and visual inputs given whenever a new movement is trained.
questions.question:
(i) On the finger-to-nose test, a patient's index finger overshoots and undershoots the target with visible intention tremor as it approaches the nose. Identify the movement abnormality demonstrated.
(ii) State the contributing factors to this presentation and its effects on the body.
(iii) Describe the therapeutic exercise management for this patient.

A(i) Define range of motion.
A(ii) Classify the types of range of motion exercise.
A(iii) State the indications and goals of passive range of motion.
A(iv) State the indications and goals of active range of motion.
B. Explain the physiological or clinical basis of the effects of range of motion exercise.
C. Distinguish between passive range of motion and active-assistive range of motion.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Range of motion is a basic technique used for examination of movement and for initiating movement into a programme of therapeutic intervention; it is the amount of movement at a joint, described in terms of joint range (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation) and muscle range (functional excursion of a muscle).
A(ii) Types are passive ROM (PROM), active ROM (AROM) and active-assistive ROM (AAROM); PROM is further classified into relaxed passive movements, passive manual mobilisation techniques (joint mobilisation and manipulation, controlled sustained stretching) and continuous passive movement (CPM).
A(iii) PROM indications: acute inflamed tissue, a paralysed or comatose patient, muscle re-education; PROM goals: maintain joint and connective tissue mobility, minimise contracture formation, maintain mechanical elasticity of muscle, assist circulation, decrease or inhibit pain, help maintain the patient's awareness of movement.
A(iv) AROM is used whenever a patient can actively contract muscles and move a segment; AAROM is used when a patient has weak musculature and cannot move a joint through the desired range, usually against gravity; AROM goals: maintain physiological elasticity and contractility of muscles, provide sensory feedback, stimulate bone and joint tissue integrity, increase circulation and prevent thrombus formation, develop coordination and motor skills.
B. PROM is produced entirely by an external force with little or no voluntary muscle contraction, so it will not prevent muscle atrophy, increase muscle strength and endurance, or assist circulation the way active exercise does; AROM depends on active muscle contraction crossing the joint, which is why it provides sensory feedback and a stimulus to bone, joint and circulatory tissue that passive movement cannot.
C. PROM is movement produced entirely by an external force such as gravity, a machine, another person or another part of the individual's own body, with little to no voluntary muscle contraction; AAROM is a type of active ROM in which assistance is provided manually or mechanically by an outside force because the prime mover muscles need assistance to complete the motion, so the patient still actively contracts the available muscles.

questions.question:
A(i) State the aim of joint mobilisation/distraction.
A(ii) State the positioning (patient and therapist) used for mobilisation.
A(iii) Describe the procedure and treatment direction for distraction.
A(iv) State the effects, uses and precautions of joint mobilisation.
B. State the recommended dosage for the distraction technique.
C. Explain the basis for progressing from distraction to gliding.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The purpose of mobilisation is to provide short-term pain relief and to restore functional movement by achieving full range at the joint, by restoring motion in the joint, connective tissue or muscle and thereby reducing the source of pain.
A(ii) The patient should be positioned in the most comfortable position to aid relaxation and decrease muscle tension, since if the patient is not relaxed, the therapist works against tension or tissue resistance; the therapist should observe correct biomechanics and posture, using the knee and lower back to prevent excessive load, with the hands close to the joint space, especially during gliding, for fixation.
A(iii) In distraction, movement should be done at right angles to the treatment plane; treatment progression starts with distraction because distraction increases range of motion in all directions, then proceeds to gliding, which is aimed at increasing range of motion in a specific direction.
A(iv) Distraction separates the articulating surfaces of the joint to provide more space for synovial fluid, reduce friction and allow more fluid motion, restoring range of motion and moderating pain intensity; it is used for painful joints, joint hypomobility, subluxation, progressive limitation and functional immobility; precautions/contraindications are acute inflammation, malignancy, bone disease such as osteoporosis, excessive pain, total joint replacement or metallic implant, and newly formed or weakened connective tissue.
B. Distract for 5 to 8 seconds and rest for four minutes; distraction can be given for 10 trials, after which the joint is re-evaluated before another 10 trials.
C. Distraction is started first because it increases range of motion in all directions, so once range has been gained through distraction the treatment proceeds to gliding, which increases range of motion in a specific direction; if 10 distraction trials produce no increase in range of motion, the approach is re-evaluated before continuing.

A(i) Both are relaxation techniques used to gain range of motion at a point of limited range in the agonist pattern by acting on the restricting antagonist muscles.
A(ii) Contract-Relax is usually performed at a point of limited range of motion in the agonist pattern; Hold-Relax is usually performed in a position of comfort and below a level that causes pain.
A(iii) Contract-Relax: a strong, small-range isotonic contraction of the restricting muscles (antagonists), with emphasis on the rotators, is followed by an isometric hold, then followed by voluntary relaxation and movement into the new range of the agonist pattern; movement into the new range can be passive but active contraction is preferred. Hold-Relax: a strong isometric contraction of the restricting muscles (antagonists) is resisted, followed by voluntary relaxation, and passive movement into the newly gained range of the agonist pattern.
A(iv) Contract-Relax is indicated for limitations in range of motion; Hold-Relax is indicated for limitations in passive range of motion with pain, since it is performed below a pain-provoking level.
B. The isometric contraction in Contract-Relax is held for 5 to 8 seconds before voluntary relaxation and movement into the newly gained range.
C. Contract-relax-active-contraction (CRAC) uses active contraction into the newly gained range instead of passive movement, and Hold-Relax-Active Contraction (HRAC) is similar to Hold-Relax except that movement into the newly gained range is active rather than passive; the active contraction in both variants serves to maintain the inhibitory effects on the restricting muscles through reciprocal inhibition, so they are used when the patient can actively move into the new range rather than needing it moved passively.
questions.question:
A(i) State the aim of Contract-Relax and Hold-Relax.
A(ii) State the starting position used for these techniques.
A(iii) Describe the procedure for Contract-Relax and for Hold-Relax.
A(iv) State the effects and indications of these techniques.
B. State the dosage guidance for the isometric hold in these techniques.
C. Explain the basis for using the active-contraction variant (CRAC/HRAC) when a patient has a limitation in range of motion.

(i) A patient is placed in kneeling with the body supported on the knees and the rest of the body held as in standing, as preparation for standing training. State the joints and movement pattern involved in maintaining this position.
(ii) Describe the muscle work occurring in kneeling, identifying the muscles maintaining stability and balance.
(iii) State the contributing problem this position is being used to address.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for choosing kneeling as the exercise approach for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) The joints involved are the knees, hips and lumbar spine; the lower leg is relaxed and rests on the floor with the feet plantarflexed, while the body must be stabilised on the knees.
(ii) There is interplay between the flexors and extensors of the knee to balance the femora vertically on the knees; the rest of the body works as in standing, except that the extensors of the hip and the flexors of the lumbar spine work more strongly to maintain the correct angle of pelvic tilt.
(iii) This position is used to address poor control of the hip joints and lower trunk, since although the centre of gravity is relatively lower than in standing, the position is only slightly more stable and is uncomfortable for most people.
(iv) Kneeling is used as a starting position for backward movement in the sagittal plane and to train control of the hip joints and lower trunk in preparation for standing, during which the feet will be pressed to the floor by the knee extensors and dorsiflexors, so it is a logical progression toward independent standing balance for a patient with poor hip and lower trunk control.

A(i) Resistance exercise is any form of active exercise in which dynamic or static muscle contraction is resisted by an outside force applied manually or mechanically, also referred to as resistance training; it is an essential element of rehabilitation programmes for persons with impaired function.
A(ii) There are basically two forms: manual resistance exercise, in which resistance is provided by a therapist, and mechanical resistance exercise, in which resistance is applied through equipment or a mechanical apparatus, also called weight training or strength training.
A(iii) Selection of a resistance training programme is contingent on the cause and extent of primary and secondary impairment, deficits in muscle performance, the stage of tissue healing, the condition of joints and their tolerance to compression and movement, the general abilities of the patient, the availability of equipment, the patient's goals and the intended functional outcomes.
A(iv) Contraindications: severe joint or muscle pain during active-free movement; acute inflammatory neuromuscular disease such as Guillain-Barre syndrome or inflammatory muscle disease such as polymyositis or dermatomyositis, since resistance exercise may cause irreversible deterioration of strength; acute inflammation of a joint, where only gentle static exercise against negligible resistance is appropriate; and severe cardiopulmonary disease or disorders with acute symptoms, with resistance training postponed for up to 12 weeks after myocardial infarction or coronary artery bypass graft surgery, or until cleared by the physician.
B. Resistance exercise enhances muscle performance (restoration, improvement or maintenance of muscle strength, power and endurance), increases the strength of connective tissues such as tendons and ligaments, gives greater bone mineral density, decreases stress on joints during activity, reduces the risk of soft tissue injury, improves capacity to repair and heal damaged soft tissue through positive impact on tissue remodelling, improves balance, and produces positive changes in body composition.
C. Manual resistance exercise is most effective in the early stages of rehabilitation when muscles are weak, allows finely graded resistance adjusted throughout the range of motion and direct manual stabilisation to prevent substitute motions, but the exercise load cannot be measured or documented quantitatively and is limited to the strength of the therapist; mechanical resistance exercise establishes a quantitative baseline measurement of muscle performance and is most appropriate in intermediate and advanced phases of rehabilitation when muscle strength is grade 4/5 or greater or exceeds the therapist's strength, but it is not appropriate when muscles are very weak and loads a muscle maximally at only one point in the range unless the equipment provides variable resistance.
questions.question:
A(i) Define resistance exercise.
A(ii) Classify the types of resistance exercise.
A(iii) State the indications for resistance exercise.
A(iv) State the contraindications for resistance exercise.
B. Explain the physiological or clinical basis of the effects of resistance exercise.
C. Distinguish between manual resistance exercise and mechanical resistance exercise.

questions.answerText:
A. Balance is the ability to stay upright or stay in control of body movement, and coordination is the ability to move two or more body parts under control, smoothly and efficiently; it is the ability to execute smooth, accurate, controlled motor responses through the optimal interaction of muscle function, to select the right muscle at the right time with proper intensity, and coordinated movement is characterised by appropriate speed, distance, direction, timing and muscular tension. It requires activation of motor units of multiple muscles with simultaneous inhibition of all other muscles to carry out a desired activity, and it involves fine motor skills, gross motor skills and hand-eye skills, requiring interaction of the cerebellum, vestibular system, motor system, flexibility and range of motion, deep sensation and vision.
B. Uncoordinated movement or coordination impairment is known as ataxia; its causes range from chronic conditions to sudden onset but most relate to damage or degeneration of the cerebellum, from conditions such as traumatic brain injury, alcoholism, infection, neuropathies, spinal cord injuries, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, stroke, transient ischaemic attack, genetic ataxias, cerebral palsy and brain tumours, or from toxins such as alcohol, seizure medications, chemotherapy drugs, lithium, cocaine and heroin, sedatives, and heavy metals.
C. Ataxia is examined through tests such as the finger-to-nose test and finger-to-finger test for intention tremor and dysmetria (hypermetria or hypometria), the finger-to-doctor's-finger test, adiadokokinesia/dysdiadokokinesia (inability to perform rapid alternating movements), the rebound phenomenon, buttoning and unbuttoning tests, walking heel to foot along a straight line, and the Romberg test for swaying or loss of balance; loss of coordinated control therefore spreads from fine motor tasks to gross motor tasks such as gait, causing functional loss. Exercise therapy addresses this through constant repetition of a few motor activities, use of sensory cues to enhance motor performance, gradually increasing the speed of the activity, breaking activities into simple components, providing assistance when necessary, allowing short rests to avoid fatigue, and giving the high repetition of precise performance needed to form and perfect an engram.
questions.question:
A. Describe the concept of balance and coordination.
B. State how the factors and causes of coordination impairment relate to common clinical problems.
C. Explain how coordination deficits arise and cause functional loss, and how exercise therapy addresses them.

(i) A patient recovering from an injury shows generalised muscle weakness in a limb with no active joint or muscle pain and no acute inflammation. State the impairments and functional limitations this presentation gives rise to.
(ii) State the indications, contraindications and precautions relevant to prescribing resistance exercise for this patient.
(iii) State the resistance exercise options available and justify which one is most appropriate at this stage.
questions.answerText:
(i) Impairments and functional limitations: enhanced muscle performance is required because strength, power and endurance are reduced; connective tissue (tendon, ligament) strength and bone mineral density may also be reduced; the patient is at increased risk of soft tissue injury and reduced balance and physical performance during daily, occupational and recreational activities.
(ii) Indications: deficits in muscle performance, an acceptable stage of tissue healing, and joints tolerant of compression and movement. Contraindications: severe joint or muscle pain during active-free movement, acute inflammatory neuromuscular or joint disease, and severe cardiopulmonary disease with acute symptoms. Precautions: keep the exercise setting comfortable and use clothing that allows heat dissipation, avoid pain during exercise, do not start at maximal resistance, avoid heavy resistance in children, older adults and patients with osteoporosis, avoid resistance across an unstable joint or an incompletely healed fracture site, avoid breath-holding, and discontinue if pain, dizziness or unusual shortness of breath occurs.
(iii) Options are manual resistance exercise (resistance provided by the therapist) and mechanical resistance exercise (resistance applied through equipment). Manual resistance is most appropriate here because it is most effective during the early stages of rehabilitation when muscles are weak, allows resistance to be finely graded and adjusted throughout the range as the therapist responds to the patient's effort or a painful arc, allows the range of joint movement to be carefully controlled to protect healing tissue, and allows direct manual stabilisation to prevent substitute motions.

A. Muscle tone is the tension in a muscle at rest, the muscle's response to an outside force such as a stretch or change in direction, occurring because a few motor units are always contracting in a resting muscle without producing enough tension for movement; it is maintained by a reflex arc from the muscle spindle to a lower motor neuron and is under central nervous system control. Postural tone is the steady contraction of muscles necessary to hold parts of the skeleton in proper relation to the changing attitudes and postures of the body, maintained by tonic muscle contractions acting against gravity to stabilise body segments; resting muscle tone is important for maintaining normal posture and stabilising joints.
B. Muscle tone may change according to stress, febrile state, pain, body position, medical status, medication, CNS arousal and degree of volitional movement. For simplicity, tone disorders are discussed as hypertonicity, hypotonicity or dystonia: hypertonicity includes spasticity (velocity-dependent increase in resistance to passive stretch) and rigidity (uniform resistance independent of velocity), secondary to a neurologic lesion of the CNS or upper motor neuron system, as in cerebrovascular accident, with no muscle wasting; hypotonicity includes flaccidity, from a lower motor neuron lesion such as spinal or peripheral nerve damage, resulting in muscle atrophy; dystonia is a hyperkinetic movement disorder with disordered tone and involuntary movement from a basal ganglia lesion, as in Parkinson's disease with excessive L-dopa therapy.
C. Because postural control depends on the visual, vestibular and somatosensory systems together with adequate muscle tone to stabilise the body's centre of mass, a change in tone disturbs the ability to maintain a controlled, upright posture and can appear as abnormal decorticate (flexion) or decerebrate (extension) posturing, causing loss of functional mobility and volitional movement. Muscle tone is evaluated passively as mild, moderate or severe resistance to movement, and actively as the ability to achieve full joint range and complete functional mobility. Exercise therapy addresses these deficits through relaxation techniques and coordination exercises that use sensory cues and repetition to restore controlled, efficient motor responses.
questions.question:
A. Describe the concept of muscle tone and postural tone.
B. State how the types and factors of muscle tone relate to common clinical problems.
C. Explain how deficits in muscle tone arise and cause functional loss, and how exercise therapy addresses them.

A. Describe the concept of group exercise/group therapy.
B. State how the factors considered in planning group exercise relate to common clinical problems.
C. Explain how failure to address these factors can cause the group approach to fail, and how proper planning addresses this.
questions.answerText:
A. Group exercise is a method of exercise in which a small number of patients (six at most) with similar types of disability are treated together; the therapist indicates the exercises to be performed, the patients practise individually, and the therapist goes from patient to patient giving individual coaching as required; it can take place in a gymnasium, a hydrotherapy pool, or as part of an educational programme during which patients also receive information about the nature of their condition.
B. Selection into a group must consider age, sex, psychological status, the stage in rehabilitation, past medical history and general fitness, and the equipment, facilities, space, layout and temperature of the room must be adequate; patients presenting with isolation, reduced performance, or a need for education about a condition benefit from group work, since it provides a good opportunity for the physiotherapist to educate and inform the group, and specialist groups such as ankylosing spondylitis or cardiac rehabilitation groups provide social support; group work can also involve difficulties such as pitching exercise at a level suitable for all members, monitoring everyone at once, and progressing all members appropriately.
C. Without proper selection, it is difficult to pitch exercise at a suitable level for all members, there is a temptation to place inappropriate individuals in the group to save time, and some people do not respond well in a group situation, so the competitive element may become counterproductive rather than helpful; proper planning addresses this by clearly stating the aim of the group work so selection criteria can be agreed, ensuring the session is safe and effective, and structuring the session with a warm-up (to improve circulation and body tissue temperature and limit metabolic build-up), a main exercise session based on the patients' ability, and a cool-down (to assist removal of lactic acid and waste products of metabolism), with examples including knee groups, shoulder groups, prenatal groups and hemiplegic groups.

questions.question:
A(i) State the aim of manual resistance exercise.
A(ii) State the starting position(s) used for manual resistance exercise.
A(iii) Describe the procedure by which resistance is applied and adjusted during manual resistance exercise.
A(iv) State the effects, uses and precautions of manual resistance exercise.
B. State the dosage/loading guidance for resistance training in conditioning programmes for healthy adults under 50-60 years old.
C. Explain the basis for modifying resistance exercise loading in a patient whose muscle is very weak.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Manual resistance exercise is used to enhance muscle performance, restoring, improving or maintaining muscle strength, power and endurance, and is most effective during the early stages of rehabilitation when muscles are weak.
A(ii) It can be performed in a variety of patient positions, with placement of resistance easily adjusted.
A(iii) Resistance is adjusted throughout the range of motion as the therapist responds to the patient's efforts or a painful arc, so the muscle works maximally at all portions of the range; the range of joint movement is carefully controlled by the therapist to protect healing tissue or to prevent movement into an unstable portion of the range, and direct manual stabilisation prevents substitute motions.
A(iv) It is an effective form of exercise for the transition from assisted to mechanically resisted movements and is useful for dynamic or static strengthening; it gives the therapist an opportunity for direct interaction with the patient to continually monitor performance; precautions include that the exercise load is subjective and cannot be measured quantitatively, the amount of resistance is limited to the strength of the therapist, and it is of little value for already strong muscle groups.
B. Perform dynamic exercises through the full, available, pain-free range of motion, targeting about 8 to 10 muscle groups of the upper and lower extremities and trunk, at moderate intensity (60% to 80% of 1-RM) allowing 8 to 12 repetitions per set, progressing to 2, then up to 4, sets of each exercise, with rest intervals of 2 to 3 minutes between sets, two to three times per week, increasing intensity gradually in increments of about 5% as strength and endurance improve.
C. If the muscle is weak, begin with minimal resistance, isometric and active-assistive range of motion, in open and closed chain and pain-free, and develop postural stability with stabilisation exercises, providing enough resisted exercise and repetition to challenge the muscle without allowing substitution by stronger muscles, before progressing to dynamic exercises that strengthen the weak motions and muscles first, so substitute action does not dominate.

questions.question:
A(i) State the aim of progressive relaxation technique.
A(ii) State the starting position used for progressive relaxation.
A(iii) Describe the procedure of progressive relaxation.
A(iv) State the effects and uses of progressive relaxation.
B. State the dosage guidance for progressive relaxation exactly as it is applied to each muscle group.
C. Explain the basis for modifying the technique when a patient cannot actively contract a muscle group.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The aim is to produce a reduction in muscle tension in the entire body or in the region that is painful or restricted, using systematic, distal to proximal, voluntary contraction and relaxation of muscles.
A(ii) The patient is placed in a quiet area free from distraction, in a comfortable position such as lying on the floor or reclining in a chair, with restrictive clothing loosened and glasses or contacts removed.
A(iii) The patient breathes in a deep, relaxed manner; the distal musculature of the hands or feet is voluntarily contracted for several seconds and then consciously relaxed; the patient is asked to feel heaviness in the hands or feet and warmth in the relaxed muscles; the sequence progresses to more proximal areas, contracting and relaxing each area in turn, until the whole limb and eventually the whole body feels relaxed and warm.
A(iv) Training is carried out in a quiet environment with low lighting and soothing music or an auditory cue to focus on, and the therapist uses a soft tone of voice; it is used with deep breathing or visualising a peaceful scene, and it is sometimes incorporated into childbirth education.
B. Contract the muscle group for 5 to 7 seconds and then consciously relax it for 20 to 30 seconds; in the extended sequence, tension is held for 15 seconds and then slowly released while counting for 30 seconds for each muscle area (forehead, jaw, neck and shoulders, arms and hands, buttocks, legs, feet).
C. Where a patient cannot actively contract a muscle group, biofeedback can be used instead, since it is a tool that helps a patient learn and practise the process of relaxation by allowing visual or auditory feedback so the patient can begin to sense or feel what muscle relaxation is and reduce muscle tension.

questions.question:
(i) A patient with a stiff, painful joint shows reduced motion at the end of the available range, with soft tissue, muscle and joint contracture developing from reduced use. State the impairments and functional limitations this presents.
(ii) State the indications, contraindications and precautions relevant to range of motion exercise for this patient.
(iii) State the range of motion exercise options and justify which is most appropriate at this stage.
questions.answerText:
(i) Impairments and functional limitations: pain at the end of available range of motion; developing soft tissue, muscle and/or joint contracture from reduced use; developing muscle weakness; decreasing functional use of the part.
(ii) Indications for passive ROM include acute inflamed tissue, a paralysed or comatose patient, and muscle re-education. Contraindications to ROM exercise are acute tears, fractures and recent surgery. Precautions: movement must be taken only through the complete pain-free range to the point of tissue resistance, not forced beyond the available range, as forcing motion turns it into a stretching technique; grip must be modified to support painful joints, and areas of poor structural integrity such as a hypermobile joint, recent fracture site or paralysed limb must be supported.
(iii) The options are passive ROM, active ROM and active-assistive ROM. Passive ROM is most appropriate at this early stage because the joint is painful with developing contracture; PROM performed accurately, rhythmically and smoothly within the limits of pain will maintain joint and connective tissue mobility, minimise contracture formation, maintain mechanical elasticity of muscle, assist circulation and help decrease pain, and it can be used to demonstrate the desired motion before the patient progresses to an active exercise programme.

questions.question:
(i) On examination of a patient's elbow, the biceps is found to be weak when tested from a fully lengthened position toward mid-range, while its strength improves toward the shortened, fully contracted position. State the joint and movement pattern involved.
(ii) Describe the muscle work occurring at the elbow, identifying the agonist, antagonist and any stabilising action.
(iii) State the contributing problem suggested by this pattern of weakness.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the exercise range chosen to address this weakness.
questions.answerText:
(i) The joint involved is the elbow, and the movement pattern is elbow flexion produced by the biceps working concentrically.
(ii) The biceps acts as the agonist contracting concentrically to produce flexion, working from the fully stretched (outer range) position toward the middle and inner ranges; the triceps acts as the antagonist, lengthening eccentrically to control the movement; when the muscle is neither fully stretched nor fully contracted (middle range), it works most efficiently and is used to maintain normal muscle tone and power.
(iii) The weakness noted when working from the fully stretched position toward mid-range suggests a deficit in outer range muscle work, the range used extensively for muscle re-education.
(iv) Because outer range work is the range used for muscle re-education, exercise should begin by training the biceps concentrically from the fully stretched position toward a partially contracted position to re-educate the muscle, with inner range work added subsequently to train the muscle in the direction of pull once outer range control has improved.

(i) Assessment findings: generalised muscle tension associated with stress, with no acute injury, indicating a need for relaxation training in the entire body.
(ii) The technique appropriate is progressive relaxation.
(iii) Starting position: the patient is placed in a quiet area in a comfortable position, such as lying on the floor or reclining in a chair, with restrictive clothing loosened. Procedure: the patient breathes in a deep, relaxed manner; the distal musculature of the hands or feet is voluntarily contracted for 5 to 7 seconds and then consciously relaxed for 20 to 30 seconds; the patient is asked to feel heaviness in the hands or feet and warmth in the relaxed muscles; the sequence progresses to more proximal areas, actively contracting and relaxing each area in turn, and eventually isometrically contracting and consciously relaxing the entire extremity, so that a sense of relaxation and warmth is felt throughout the limb and eventually the whole body.
(iv) The training occurs in a quiet environment with low lighting and soothing music or an auditory cue, the therapist using a soft tone of voice; the technique reduces muscle tension throughout the body or in the region that is painful or restricted, using conscious effort and thought.
(v) Progression: once the patient has learned how to tense and relax each muscle group through the full routine, they can practise tensing and relaxing a muscle area without going through the whole sequence.
questions.question:
(i) A patient shows generalised muscle tension associated with stress, without any acute injury. State the assessment findings relevant to planning treatment.
(ii) Name the technique appropriate to address this muscle tension.
(iii) Describe the starting position and procedure used in applying the technique.
(iv) State the physiological effects of the technique.
(v) State how the technique may be progressed.

A. Describe the concept of the stages of soft tissue healing (acute, sub-acute, chronic).
B. State how the impairments at each stage relate to common clinical problems.
C. Explain how untreated deficits at one stage spread to cause further functional loss, and how exercise therapy addresses each stage.
questions.answerText:
A. In the acute stage there is inflammation, vascular changes, exudation of cells and chemicals, clot formation, phagocytosis and early fibroblastic activity, with pain occurring before tissue resistance is reached. In the sub-acute stage, repair and healing occur, with removal of noxious stimuli, maturation of connective tissue, growth of capillary beds, collagen formation and granulation tissue formation that is very fragile and easily injured, decreased inflammation, and pain synchronous with tissue resistance. In the chronic stage, maturation and remodelling occur, with contracture of scar tissue, remodelling of the scar, collagen aligning to stress, absence of inflammation, and pain occurring only after resistance.
B. Acute-stage impairments are pain when the end of available range is reached, decreasing soft tissue oedema, developing soft tissue, muscle and/or joint contractures, developing muscle weakness from reduced usage, and decreasing functional use of the part and associated areas; inflammation, pain, oedema, muscle spasm and joint effusion (if a joint is injured or arthritic) are also present, together with decreased use of associated areas.
C. If pain, oedema and spasm are not controlled and soft tissue and joint integrity are not maintained in the acute stage, contracture and weakness from reduced use develop and spread to reduce functional use of the part and the areas associated with it; exercise therapy addresses the acute stage by educating the patient, controlling pain/oedema/spasm with cold, compression, elevation and massage, immobilising the part, and applying gentle passive movement and muscle setting within the limit of pain; in the sub-acute and chronic/rehabilitation stages, as remodelling occurs, the programme progresses to active-assistive, free, resistive and/or modified aerobic exercise and then to dynamic and functional exercises, restoring the part and associated areas to full function.

(i) The deviation demonstrated is bad/faulty posture, with sustained faulty postural alignment.
(ii) Contributing causes of bad posture include injury and muscle guarding, muscle tension and muscle weakness, daily habits, use of technology, sustained faulty posture, pregnancy, obesity, and weak abdominal muscles; the effect on the body is that proper postural control, which requires the ability to contract the appropriate muscles for a controlled midline posture and to make small adjustments in response to changes in position without compensatory motion, is disturbed, and postural tone (the steady contraction of muscles necessary to hold the skeleton in proper relation to its changing attitudes) is not being adequately maintained.
(iii) Management should address the causes identified, since muscle tension and muscle weakness and daily habits, including use of technology, are named contributing causes; correcting standing alignment (heels together, knees straight, hips extended and slightly laterally rotated, pelvis balanced on the femoral heads, spine stretched to maximum length, vertex thrust upward, shoulders down and back) and achieving a satisfactory standing pattern reduces fatigue and conditions the postural reflex, since when body segments are in good alignment and perfectly balanced, muscle work required to maintain the position is reduced.
questions.question:
(i) A patient who spends long periods using a hand-held device is observed with a sustained rounded, forward-leaning posture and weak abdominal muscles. Identify the deviation demonstrated.
(ii) State the contributing factors to this presentation and its effects on the body.
(iii) Describe the corrective or therapeutic exercise management appropriate for this patient.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Relaxed passive movements are performed to maintain joint and connective tissue mobility, minimise the effects of contracture formation, maintain mechanical elasticity of muscle, assist circulation and vascular dynamics, decrease or inhibit pain, and help maintain the patient's awareness of movement.
A(ii) A good starting position ensures comfort and support for both patient and therapist; fixation ensures the movement is localised to the moveable joint by fixing the proximal and distal joints; a full and comfortable support is given to the part being moved; the range of motion is done in the painless range to avoid muscle spasm.
A(iii) These are movements performed accurately, rhythmically and smoothly by the physiotherapist through the available range of motion and within the limits of pain, performed in the same range and direction as active movements; the sequence of movement must be from distal to proximal joints.
A(iv) Uses: to determine limitations of motion, to determine joint stability, to determine muscle and other soft tissue elasticity, to demonstrate the desired motion when teaching an active exercise programme, and it is often used preceding passive stretching techniques to prepare the patient for stretching. Limitations: passive ROM will not prevent muscle atrophy, increase muscle strength and endurance, or assist circulation the way active exercise does.
B. Speed must be slow and rhythmical with suitable repetitions of 8 to 10, given twice daily.
C. A patient may also provide the force and be taught to move the part with the normal extremity as self-assisted passive ROM, so that the motion can still be carried out within the free range of motion when a therapist is not present to perform it for the patient.
questions.question:
A(i) State the aim of relaxed passive movement.
A(ii) State the starting position/principles used for relaxed passive movement.
A(iii) Describe the procedure for relaxed passive movement.
A(iv) State the uses and limitations of relaxed passive movement.
B. State the recommended dosage for relaxed passive movement.
C. Explain the basis for using self-assisted passive movement when a therapist is not available.

A(i) Define manipulation and mobilisation.
A(ii) Classify manual therapy techniques.
A(iii) State the indications for mobilisation.
A(iv) State the contraindications to mobilisation and manipulation.
B. Explain the physiological or clinical basis of the effects of mobilisation.
C. Distinguish between manipulation and mobilisation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Manipulation is a passive, high velocity, low amplitude movement applied to a joint complex within its anatomical limit, a sudden low amplitude thrust that goes beyond the usual normal range of motion but within anatomical limits, intended to restore optimal motion, function and/or reduce pain. Mobilisation is a series of passive movements which does not go beyond the normal range of motion, a manual therapy technique comprising a continuum of skilled passive movements applied at varying speeds and amplitudes, a slower, more controlled process of articular and soft-tissue (myofascial) stretching intended to improve biomechanical elasticity.
A(ii) Manual therapy is classified into active techniques, involving movement by the patient, and passive techniques, in which the patient is inactive, further divided into dynamic techniques (joints mobile) and static techniques (joints not mobile); the three notable forms of manual therapy are manipulation, mobilisation and massage.
A(iii) Indications for mobilisation: breaking down or reducing adhesions, improving range of motion, lengthening muscles and tendons, reducing swelling and oedema, decreasing pain and restoring functionality; specifically for painful joints (e.g. from arthritis or capsular adhesions), joint hypomobility, subluxation, progressive limitation from capsular adhesion or ligamentous contracture, and functional immobility from prolonged immobilisation.
A(iv) Absolute contraindications: acute inflammation such as infection or joint effusion, malignancy such as osteosarcoma, bone disease such as osteoporosis, excessive pain, total joint replacement or metallic implant, and newly formed or weakened connective tissue; manipulation is additionally contraindicated with severe osteoporosis, tumour or malignancy in the area, vertebral artery dysfunction in the cervical region, bleeding in a joint, or a loose body in the joint.
B. Mobilisation consists of passive physiological or accessory movements that restore motion in the respective joint by removing restriction found in joints, connective tissue or muscles, thereby reducing the source of pain and giving the patient symptomatic relief; the accessory movements involved, such as distraction, compression, rolling, sliding and spinning of joint surfaces, provide the joint play that cannot be produced actively but is necessary for normal range of motion.
C. Manipulation is a sudden, high velocity, low amplitude thrust that takes the joint beyond its usual voluntary range but within anatomical limits and is often associated with an audible popping sound from joint cavitation; mobilisation is a slower, graded, continuum of passive movements at varying speeds and amplitudes that stays within the normal range of motion and is used to restore functional movement and give short-term pain relief.

(i) The joints involved are the scapular and glenohumeral joints, with the stabilising muscle groups around the scapula and shoulder being weak.
(ii) The weak stabilising muscles are unable to hold the scapula and glenohumeral joint steady during movement, so stronger muscles substitute to produce the movement instead of the intended weak muscle performing the work.
(iii) The contributing problem is substitution: allowing a stronger muscle to take over the action of a weak one means the weak muscle is never adequately challenged or retrained.
(iv) If the muscle is weak, exercise should begin with minimal resistance, isometric and active-assistive range of motion, in a pain-free open and closed chain, developing postural stability of the scapular and glenohumeral joint with stabilisation exercises, providing enough resisted exercise and repetition to challenge the muscle while not allowing substitution with stronger muscles; the programme then progresses to dynamic exercises, first strengthening the weak motions and weak muscles so substitute action does not dominate, developing muscle endurance and control, and progressing the pattern of motion and the trained muscle group to function in a coordinated sequence, using simple functional activities before progressing to more complex and challenging activities.
questions.question:
(i) On examination, a patient shows weak scapular and glenohumeral stabilising muscles, with stronger muscles substituting to complete shoulder movement during resisted exercise. State the joints and muscle groups involved.
(ii) Describe the muscle work occurring, identifying the roles of the stabilisers and the substituting muscles.
(iii) State the contributing problem suggested by this pattern.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for the exercise approach chosen to address this weakness.

questions.question: What accelerates creaming most effectively in practice?
questions.explanation: Flocculation accelerates creaming because aggregated droplets behave as single larger entities with increased effective size, greatly increasing sedimentation/creaming rate per Stokes' law. While individual droplets may be small, flocculated aggregates sediment much faster. This distinguishes flocculation's effect on creaming from coalescence, which directly increases actual droplet size.

options: High surface tension always improves wetting completely
Surface tension has no effect on wetting
Only solid surface chemistry determines wetting
Temperature exclusively controls wetting behavior always
Wetting depends on balance of interfacial tensions
questions.question: How does surface tension affect wetting of solid surfaces?
questions.explanation: Wetting depends on the balance between solid-gas (γSG), solid-liquid (γSL), and liquid-gas (γLG) interfacial tensions according to Young's equation: γSG - γSL = γLG cosθ, where θ is contact angle. Small contact angles (θ < 90°) indicate good wetting (hydrophilic surface), while large angles (θ > 90°) indicate poor wetting (hydrophobic surface).

questions.explanation: Rheological characterization during development identifies optimal formulations meeting performance requirements: stability (sedimentation/creaming prevention), manufacturability (pumping, filling), patient acceptability (pourability, spreadability, syringeability), and drug release. Comparing candidates' rheological profiles guides selection. Establishing rheological specifications for intermediate and finished products ensures batch-to-batch consistency and quality.

questions.explanation: Liquid viscosity generally decreases about 2% per 1°C temperature increase due to reduced intermolecular forces and increased molecular mobility at higher temperatures. This temperature dependence follows an exponential relationship: η = Ae^(Ev/RT), where Ev is activation energy for flow. Temperature control is critical in viscosity measurements and pharmaceutical processing.
questions.question: How does temperature typically affect liquid viscosity?
options: Viscosity remains completely independent of temperature
Viscosity decreases approximately 2 percent per degree
Viscosity fluctuates randomly with temperature changes
Temperature only affects solid material viscosity exclusively
Decreasing droplet radius significantly throughout system
Eliminating density differences between phases completely
Increasing droplet radius substantially in formulation
Reducing gravitational force during storage period
questions.explanation: Stokes' law (v = d²(ρs - ρl)g/18η) shows sedimentation rate is proportional to the square of droplet diameter, making particle size the most influential factor. Doubling diameter quadruples sedimentation rate. This explains why fine emulsions with small, uniform droplets exhibit superior physical stability compared to coarse emulsions.
questions.question: According to Stokes' law, which factor most increases sedimentation rate?

questions.explanation: Formulation viscosity affects atomization efficiency, droplet size distribution, spray pattern, and delivery consistency in aerosol products. Too-high viscosity prevents adequate atomization or clogs valves; too-low viscosity provides insufficient drug deposition. Pseudoplastic behavior may benefit certain applications. Propellant compatibility with rheological modifiers requires careful selection. Rheological testing guides formulation optimization.

Only propellant selection determines spray characteristics

Aerosol performance is independent of formulation viscosity

questions.question: What causes polymorphism problems with theobroma oil?
questions.explanation: Theobroma oil exists in four polymorphic forms (α, β', β, γ) with different melting points (18-35°C). The stable β form melts at 34-35°C. Heating above 35°C produces metastable forms that may melt at lower temperatures (18-28°C), causing suppositories to soften excessively at room temperature. Careful heating (not exceeding 36°C) and proper cooling maintain stable β form.

Proper viscosity and droplet size control minimize creaming.

To calculate the ratio: %A = (RHLB - HLB_low)/(HLB_high - HLB_low) x 100. This allows formulation of emulsifier blends matching the oil's RHLB precisely.

What molecular mechanism causes thixotropy in gels?
questions.explanation: Thixotropic gels contain asymmetric particles or macromolecules connected by numerous weak secondary bonds (van der Waals, hydrogen bonds) forming loose three-dimensional networks. Shear energy breaks these bonds, causing gel->sol transformation and molecular alignment with reduced viscosity. After shear removal, Brownian motion allows bond reformation and structure recovery over time.
options: Weak bonds breaking under shear rebuilding at rest
Permanent covalent bond formation between molecules
Complete molecular dissolution during shearing always
Crystallization followed by immediate melting cycles

questions.question: Which viscometer type is appropriate only for Newtonian fluids?
options: Rotational cone-and-plate viscometer with variable speeds
Brookfield viscometer with multiple spindles available
Couette cup-and-bob with adjustable shear rates
Any multi-point instrument with variable shear
questions.explanation: Capillary viscometers provide single-point measurements suitable only for Newtonian fluids where viscosity is constant regardless of shear rate. One measurement suffices because all shear rates yield the same viscosity. Non-Newtonian systems require multi-point instruments (rotational viscometers) measuring viscosity at multiple shear rates to characterize complete flow behavior.

Progressive increase in mean droplet size and broadening of size distribution indicate instability. Microscopic examination and particle counting devices (Coulter counter, laser diffraction) provide quantitative data revealing coalescence rates in different formulations.

questions.explanation: Depot injections (e.g., procaine penicillin G) require high yield values and rapid thixotropic recovery to form compact, cohesive deposits at injection sites that resist dispersion by tissue fluids. During injection through needle, shearing reduces viscosity (thixotropic breakdown) allowing flow. After injection, rapid recovery of yield value creates a depot that slowly releases drug, prolonging therapeutic action.
questions.question: What rheological property indicates controlled-release depot injection suitability?
options: Very low viscosity allowing rapid dispersion
Purely Newtonian flow at body temperature
Complete absence of any gel structure
High yield value with rapid thixotropic recovery
Nonionic surfactants generally have lower CMC values

questions.question: How do ionic and nonionic surfactants differ regarding CMC values?
questions.explanation: Nonionic surfactants typically have lower CMC values than ionic surfactants of comparable hydrophobic chain length, indicating more stable micelle formation. Electrostatic repulsion between charged head groups in ionic surfactants opposes micellization, requiring higher concentrations. Temperature affects nonionic surfactants' CMC more significantly than ionic surfactants.

questions.question: How does particle size affect powder adsorption capacity?
questions.explanation: Smaller particles have higher surface area per unit mass, providing more adsorption sites and greater capacity. For spherical particles, specific surface area = 6/(ρd), where ρ is density and d is diameter. Micronization dramatically increases surface area, explaining enhanced dissolution rates, oxidation susceptibility, and adsorptive capacity. Surface roughness and porosity further increase effective area.
options: Larger particles provide greater surface area
Smaller particles provide greater surface area
Particle size has no effect on adsorption
Only chemical composition determines adsorption capacity

questions.question: What advantage do rotational viscometers offer over capillary types?
questions.explanation: Rotational viscometers (cup-and-bob, cone-and-plate, Brookfield) allow viscosity measurement at various controllable shear rates, essential for characterizing non-Newtonian systems. They can generate complete rheograms showing how viscosity changes with shear rate, detect yield values, and measure time-dependent effects. This versatility makes them indispensable for pharmaceutical formulation development.
options: Require smaller sample volumes exclusively always
More accurate for Newtonian fluids only
Need no temperature control during operation
Measure viscosity at multiple controlled shear rates

questions.question: According to DLVO theory, colloidal stability results from:
questions.explanation: DLVO theory explains that colloidal stability arises from the balance between electrostatic repulsion (from the electrical double layer) and van der Waals attraction. When repulsive forces create an energy barrier exceeding thermal energy, particles remain dispersed despite attractive forces. If electrolyte concentration increases sufficiently to compress the double layer, attraction dominates and aggregation occurs.
options: Purely attractive van der Waals forces only
Complete absence of any attractive forces
Balance between electrostatic repulsion and attraction
Permanent covalent bonds between particles continuously
Mechanical barriers preventing all particle contact

questions.question: How does rheology affect topical pharmaceutical application?
questions.explanation: Rheological properties critically affect topical product performance: consistency in container, ease of removal, spreadability on skin, firmness during rubbing, skin feel after application, and drug release rate. Ointments should be firm but not brittle, spread easily with minimal shear, not feel greasy, and release drug effectively. Rheological testing guides formulation development for optimal patient acceptance.

Influences solely the product chemical stability
Determines spreadability firmness and skin feel
Adding large amounts of water continuously
Rapid cooling in ice bath immediately
Using synthetic hard fat bases instead
questions.question: What modification prevents theobroma oil polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Synthetic hard fats (hydrogenated vegetable oils like Witepsol, Suppocire) don't exhibit polymorphism. Their solidification points differ minimally from melting points (1.5-2°C), unlike theobroma oil's multiple polymorphic forms. Synthetic bases resist oxidation, set quickly, contract adequately without lubrication, and have higher melting points suitable for tropical climates. They have largely replaced theobroma oil in commercial suppositories.

questions.question: Which condition most likely causes emulsion cracking?
options: Slight temperature fluctuations within normal range
Addition of oppositely charged emulsifying agent
Gentle shaking during routine handling procedures
Storage in completely filled containers always
Maintaining constant temperature throughout shelf life
questions.explanation: Adding an emulsifier of opposite charge (cationic to anionic system or vice versa) causes neutralization of interfacial charges, destabilizing the protective film and leading to coalescence and phase separation. Other causes include emulsifier decomposition, addition of common solvents, microbial action, or excessive dispersed phase concentration. Temperature extremes can also precipitate or denature emulsifiers.

questions.explanation: Micelles are aggregates of surfactant amphipathic molecules that spontaneously form above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), creating colloidal-sized particles in solution. In aqueous systems, hydrophobic tails cluster in the core while hydrophilic heads face the aqueous exterior. This structure allows solubilization of lipophilic compounds in aqueous media.

questions.question: Why is thixotropy desirable in pharmaceutical suspensions?
questions.explanation: Thixotropic suspensions maintain high viscosity at rest (preventing sedimentation), become fluid when shaken (allowing pouring), and regain viscosity after dispensing (maintaining suspension). This ideal behavior ensures uniform dosing without requiring constant agitation. The gel structure at rest traps particles; shearing breaks structure for flow; structure rebuilds after shaking stops.

questions.question: What defines thixotropy in rheological terms?

questions.explanation: Thixotropy describes reversible, time-dependent viscosity decrease during constant shear, followed by gradual recovery when shear ceases. This isothermal sol-gel transformation occurs as shearing breaks down structure (gel->sol) faster than Brownian motion rebuilds it. After shear removal, structure gradually reforms (sol->gel) over time. Bentonite magma exemplifies thixotropic behavior.
